[THE COMPLETE WORKS OF ST THOMAS OF CANTERBURY.]

[Col. IX]

DEDICATORY LETTER

To the most distinguished man and reverend brother William Whewell, Master of Trinity College, Cambridge, and to his other friends who live as fellows in that same college, John A. Giles, their humble servant and fellow priest, greetings and the service due from a grateful heart.

To transmit to posterity the lives and deeds of great men belongs especially to those who, their contemporaries either in age or in close association, had the opportunity of learning with certainty everything which they might set down in writing. Among all the many and great men whom England has produced in highest renown, few can be compared with Thomas Becket, holy Archbishop of Canterbury and martyr. Since no fewer than fifteen, indeed perhaps more, have fully described his life and deeds, we may wonder that these writings have lain hidden in manuscript codices for so many centuries and have not yet been brought to light. In undertaking the labour of publishing the works of these writers and bringing them before the world as accurately as possible, I found within the walls of your college, excellent men, assistance which eased, expedited, and has now brought the undertaking to its conclusion. Gratefully mindful of that freely bestowed assistance, I lay my book at your feet, earnestly praying that, under your patronage, the renown of Thomas, long dormant for seven hundred years, may revive and flourish anew. Farewell, your brotherhood!

Given at London, on the Kalends of July, A.D. 1845.

[Col. IX]

SECOND DEDICATORY LETTER PREFIXED TO THE VOLUME OF LETTERS OF ST THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

To the venerable father and lord Ashurst Turner, Bishop of Chichester, John Allen Giles, his humble parishioner, greetings and the obedience canonically due.

It was the custom, Father, of our forefathers that anyone wishing to commend himself to the world by his writings should come before the public not relying on his own powers, but supported, according to an order observed for many centuries, by the authority of his diocesan. Desiring to observe that order, although I have lived in your diocese for only a rather short time, I lay my book at the feet of your fatherhood: a book indeed, if you consider its subject, more precious than at any price, since it contains the letters of St Thomas of Canterbury, now for the first time published in the Church for which he suffered martyrdom. Since his life and merits are sufficiently evident in another book recently published by me, I refrain from discussing them here; nor do I now wish to multiply words. It would have been enough for me to publish those letters, the first among Englishmen to do so, had not this further distinction been added: that I published them under the prelatical authority of your fatherhood.

J. A. GILES.

East Dene, near Eastbourne, in the county of Sussex. On the Ides of September, A.D. 1845.

[Col. IX]

PREFACE OF J. A. GILES

A SURVEY OF THE WRITINGS OF VARIOUS AUTHORS ON THE LIFE AND DEEDS OF ST THOMAS

The life of Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, is assembled from various testimonies of contemporaries, which may be enumerated in the following order:

First, the letters both of the Archbishop himself and of various persons of the same age, discussed below;

Second, all noteworthy matters collected from the chronicles of contemporaries—namely Matthew Paris, Brompton, and others;

[Col. XI] Third, the Lives themselves, likewise composed at that time, which are discussed more fully at the beginning of the first volume.

It will now suffice to recall briefly that very many Lives of Thomas were also written by contemporaries, of which:

I. LIFE OF ST THOMAS, BY EDWARD GRIM.—This Grim was a monk who met Thomas when he returned from exile to Canterbury; he was the companion of Thomas when he first spoke with those wicked men who were soon to kill him; he was also a witness of his death and certainly a faithful, though alas useless, helper. The work here given under his name has been found in three manuscripts of the British Museum [Ar. 27, Vesp. E. X, Vitell. c. XII]; a copy of one of these, transcribed by Gale, is now preserved at Trinity College, Cambridge. That this Life was written by Edward Grim is demonstrated by these words prefixed to the martyr’s history: “the arm of him who relates these things having been cut off by the same blow.” Surius abridged and published it in the *Acts of the Saints*; fragments of it also adorned several Passion narratives.

II. LIFE OF THE SAME, BY ROGER OF PONTIGNY.—It is taken from a manuscript of the Royal Library at Paris [no. 5615], a copy of which is also found among Gale’s manuscripts in the library of Trinity College, Cambridge. Who the author was is wholly unknown from the work itself; but the prologue reports that a certain monk ministered to the Archbishop while he lived at Pontigny; and, since from the preliminary remarks we see that there was a certain Roger, a monk indeed and Thomas’s attendant at Pontigny, who not long afterwards, after his lord had been taken away, was himself to write the history, we consider it highly reasonable to restore the work to its author. At the end of the Paris manuscript, moreover, one may see under the heading, “These following matters belong in another legend”: “Who can hear what follows without tears, etc.,” unless these words are to be referred to another Life by John of Salisbury. What follows is a prologue to visions, namely a brief compendium of Thomas’s miracles, narrated elsewhere also and much more fully. It ends with these words: “Here ends the Life and Passion, miracles and signs, of St Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, in the year of the Lord 1464, through me, Lodewin of Koblenz, brother of this house, on the morrow of Lucy, virgin and martyr.”

III. LIFE OF THE SAME, BY WILLIAM FITZSTEPHEN.—The most valuable of all, it was published by Sparke in the writers of English history, folio, London, 1723. Who the author was in name and rank, and how he acquired full knowledge of that wicked conflict in which Thomas was overcome, he himself wished to make known to us in the preface. In the first part, the description of the city of London under Henry II is praised, since it both instructs and greatly attracts the reader. The same work was printed far more splendidly in Leland’s *Itinerary*, but by no means more fully. We have compared each text with the other and prepared them most carefully for our purposes, adding besides many matters taken entirely from a manuscript given to the University of Oxford by Douce.

IV–V. LIFE OF THE SAME, BY ALAN OF TEWKESBURY AND JOHN OF SALISBURY.—Two Lives of the Archbishop survive in manuscripts in the Bodleian Library, so arranged and thence printed that it is clear Alan’s purpose was solely to supply everything lacking in John of Salisbury’s overly brief compendium. John’s work is included in part not only in a very ancient folio collection called the *Acts of the Saints*, but is also inserted in full in several manuscripts. We therefore wished to print it more accurately, after comparing Bodleian manuscript [no. 937], Douce [no. 287], and various passages taken from the *Quadrilogus*. Since a copious series of letters is attached to Bodleian manuscript no. 937, one must concede—if one accepts what is prefixed to the Letters at the beginning of Alan’s Life—that Alan, rather than John as is said, collected these letters, as having been written by Thomas and his contemporaries. Once admitted, this conclusion is supported and confirmed by the exceptional antiquity of Bodleian manuscript no. 937, such that it cannot be supposed to have originated later than Alan’s time.

VI. LIFE OF THE SAME, BY WILLIAM OF CANTERBURY.—Even a single copy of this Life is very much to be desired. Accordingly, the Editor made every effort to collect passages used here and there in the *Quadrilogus*, and to arrange what he had collected so that all should accord with the subject. In revising and correcting the text, he compared these fragments with Douai manuscript no. 810; rather hastily indeed, but attentively enough to find the writer or copyist unreliable in identifying authors and works. He therefore wishes to warn the reader that very many things have been cited under the name of this William of Canterbury which are demonstrably unrelated to him. There is almost no record of the author himself. Whether he is identical with that Prior of Canterbury who is said to have addressed certain letters to Gilbert Foliot [vol. II, p. 171] is also uncertain.

Perhaps one certain and uniquely valuable monument remains amid so many trifling words: namely, a specimen of a discourse composed in English, as the nature of the times and affairs required.

VII. LIFE OF THE SAME, BY E. OF EVESHAM.—Except for the prefatory matter and a chapter added concerning the translation of the martyr [A.D. 1220], the subject matter of this Life is identical with that of the second *Quadrilogus*. The work is contained in the sole, very ancient manuscript of the British Museum [Cott. Vesp. B XIV, fol. 33], written by E[lias] of Evesham and dedicated to Henry, Abbot of Crowland, apparently at the time when the translation of the martyr was a matter of the greatest concern. [Note: [Col. XI] This collector is indeed unknown, unless I learned it in some old book whose name I have forgotten: namely, that a certain Life of the Archbishop was written by Elias of Evesham.] Let the reader therefore pardon me if I seem to have omitted the whole body of the work, since I included everything that would be wanted—namely, the prefatory matter and all the other contents arranged in the added chapter.

VIII. LIFE OF THE SAME, BY HENRY, ABBOT OF CROWLAND, AND ROGER, MONK OF CROWLAND.—From a truly copious folio manuscript in the Royal Library at Paris, no. 5372. One preface is prefixed, followed by another: the first, by Henry, Abbot of Crowland, dedicates the work to Stephen Langton; the second is by a monk of Crowland named Roger. Although Roger says that Henry had ordered him to correct and enlarge the work for republication, he nevertheless declares that he himself added nothing new, except a few words intended solely to arrange in chronological order the Letters, a great part of which is also appended here. We took care to publish the work thus composed in no other form, for when we compared it with Lupus’s *Quadrilogus* and the Life by the author of Evesham, we found it so nearly word-for-word, and composed from the three to such an extent, that nothing whatever remains except the letters and the words of Roger the compiler. We therefore omitted the substance of the whole book, except its prefaces and, as it were, a specimen of its style wherever it differs most from Lupus’s published text. At the end of the prefaces, however, one may see that the work was first printed in the last years of King Richard, and again in A.D. 1213, the fourteenth year of King John.

IX. LIFE OF THE SAME, BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR WHO CALLS HIMSELF “THE TENTH.”—Or, as the compiler himself admits, extracted from various sources. Its prefaces appear no less important than those already mentioned for elucidating the histories and identifying their authors. The Life itself, however, is brief, written in twenty-two chapters. It occurs in two manuscripts of the Royal Library at Paris, nos. 5371 and 5373; but although it differs greatly in expression from the *Quadrilogus*, it was not found sufficiently worthy of inclusion in our collection.

X. LIFE OF THE SAME, BY BENEDICT, ABBOT OF PETERBOROUGH.—Formerly a monk of Canterbury and then Abbot of Peterborough, Benedict was himself an eyewitness of all that he arranged, and therefore of Thomas’s martyrdom. Since the full subject matter of his work has not survived separately, but had to be drawn from various passages scattered through the *Quadrilogus*, we compared the text of the *Quadrilogus* with a manuscript preserved in the library of Corpus Christi College, Oxford. Benedict appears to have written eloquently on the Life of King Henry II, and likewise on Thomas’s miracles. The latter work found its way into that exceedingly full collection of miracles which survives in the library of Lambeth, in Paris and Brussels, and in the Bodleian, though there much less fully. We readily omit these miracles, however, because they do not pertain to the authentic establishment of history; the more closely one investigates them, the farther they diverge from the purpose. [Note: [Col. XIII] Add “English.” For the conclusion is false because the premise is false. Miracles, even if supernatural, when nevertheless accomplished before the eyes of many, belong to authentic evidence, and therefore to the purpose.—ED. P.]

XI. PASSION OF THE SAME, BY THE ANONYMOUS AUTHOR OF LAMBETH.—In a folio manuscript of the Lambeth Library, written in the fourteenth century. It also contains the very extensive collection of Miracles just discussed. The author’s name is absent, as is the beginning of the work, as its abrupt opening shows. Since no date or year of completion is given, let each person determine it as he pleases. Whatever it may be, the work seems admirably suited to that age whose judgments and sentiments concerning the martyr’s life and character it so expressly embraces. The author himself, whoever he was, confirms this, since he declares himself an eyewitness of the martyr’s death.

XII. PASSION OF THE SAME, BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR.—A brief treatise, excerpted from Bodleian manuscript no. 509, fol. 15, which we collated with Paris manuscript no. 5278.

XIII. SECOND PASSION.—Another brief Passion, first published at the end of the works of St Gregory, Voss., quarto, Mainz, 1604, from a manuscript lectionary of the Basilica of St Peter in Rome. The text was taken from Paris manuscript no. 5308.

XIV. THIRD PASSION.—Not unlike the two preceding. Published from Paris manuscript [no. 3414].

XV. FOURTH PASSION.—Likewise from Paris manuscript [no. 5269].

XVI. FIFTH PASSION.—First published by Dom Martène in the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, p. 1737. If one accepts the rubric placed at its end, where appear the words of Edward Grim cited above—“the arm of him who relates these things having indeed been cut off by the same blow”—one must conclude that it was written by Edward Grim. But anyone who allows himself even slightly to become involved in examining these matters will admit quite the opposite: namely, that this Passion is not as ancient as it has been represented, and indeed is nothing more than a compilation, perhaps amplified without judgment or arrangement from whatever sources, like other works of equal value, for use in church lectionaries. We printed it after comparing Martène’s text with Valenciennes manuscript and Paris manuscript no. 5281. Other copies may also be found: namely at Brussels, no. 7959; at Mons; and in the British Museum in London.

Two further Passion narratives are added to these five: one, for example, preserved in the Burgundian Library at Brussels, beginning, “In England, etc.”; the other among Fulman’s transcripts in Corpus Christi College, Oxford. But since they are not of even the slightest importance, it is enough—and perhaps, you will say, more than enough—to have explained these few matters concerning such Passions.

XVII. LIFE OF THE SAME [*Quadrilogus* I].—That collection is far more valuable. It was published at Paris, quarto, 1495, under the title: *Life and Proceedings of St Thomas of Canterbury concerning ecclesiastical liberty*; but it is commonly called the *Quadrilogus*. The whole work consists of fragments from various writers; with one or two exceptions, it is the same as the second *Quadrilogus*. Therefore, after comparing the manuscripts, we published from the former only what is absent from the latter, unless those same passages were found elsewhere in the present book.

XVIII. *Life of St Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury and Martyr, compiled by an anonymous writer from the writings of others.*—Under this title is inserted the Life published by Lupus, or the second *Quadrilogus*. Nor is it surprising that one cannot restore to each author the fragments that are his, since the compiler says only in general that he took his material from Alan, Herbert, William of Canterbury, and John of Salisbury; to these one should add Roger, since he supplies very much of the substance of the third book. The work seems to us to have been printed before the *Quadrilogus*, though it is not the more recent. But, that the matter may become clearer, I shall state the order in which all these works were collected.

The first writer of the Archbishop’s Life seems to have been Guernes of Pont-Sainte-Maxence, who composed a poem on the subject in the fifth year after Thomas’s death. We shall shortly publish this work, preserved in the British Museum, in order to illustrate the old Norman language. But because very few poems are useful for the detailed investigation of historical matters, we decide to exclude it from our present purpose.

It is established that Herbert performed his work in the fifth year after Thomas’s death. But at what time John of Salisbury, Edward Grim, Roger of Pontigny, William of Canterbury, Benedict of Peterborough, and William FitzStephen wrote their respective Lives of Archbishop Thomas is obscure, if not wholly uncertain. This alone should be observed: because Edward Grim died before Herbert himself entered upon literary activity, the former was consequently earlier in narrating the Life of Archbishop Thomas.

Alan of Tewkesbury then published his brief compendium in such a way as to supply what John of Salisbury lacked; and he prefixed both works to Thomas’s Letters. If attention is paid to certain observations of Herbert of Bosham, all these were collected and written by Alan from John of Salisbury in A.D. 1185.

Next follows that writer of Lambeth, who was an eyewitness of the events and wrote whatever he wrote from himself. He is followed by two others: one, the author of Lansdowne manuscript [398], who, although he produced nothing important enough for us to restore in full, commends himself by an antiquity proving that he was a contemporary of Thomas; the other, the anonymous author of the Paris manuscript, whose preface we use, who asserts that he met Edward Grim already growing old when he himself was young. He should therefore be counted among Thomas’s contemporaries, had he not admitted that everything he wrote was collected by himself from the histories of various authors. We therefore judge that nothing of his work concerns us, except the preface.

These are the series of contemporary writers, followed by another series, that is, writers who were almost contemporaries. For, when Stephen Langton celebrated Thomas’s martyrdom at the time of the translation of Thomas [A.D. 1220], and many emulated him and wrote, Lives of Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, multiplied. There are indeed very many works of this kind, but they are so alike that, except for their prologues and certain passages differing only in manner of expression, one finds the same thing everywhere. Hence it is entirely unknown whether Elias of Evesham or Roger of Crowland came earlier, or the compiler of the first *Quadrilogus* or of the second. If one strives to settle this, it is no small undertaking but of the slightest importance. We therefore find it more satisfactory, as it appears more probable, that all had before them the same autograph or exemplar, which each tried in vain to make his own by labouring over prefaces, certain passages, or even errors. For although all alike lacked no intention of theft, none attained his aim. Finally, we wish to warn the reader that we have always followed the first *Quadrilogus* in collecting its words. In printing it, however, we separate it from all the passages claimed so often by the various authors named above. Therefore you will find here nothing in it that does not seem to belong to the compiler himself. Yet, if all parts were consistent and each author received what was his, it would doubtless remain a work of much less importance. Conversely, the second *Quadrilogus* contains nothing of its own, except perhaps the whole work called *Deeds after the Martyrdom*. But whose is this work: the compiler’s, who digressed to events after Thomas’s death, or Herbert of Bosham’s, who dealt with the same subject in the *Book of Melos* following the same chronological order? The dispute remains undecided. Finally, one may see that all excerpts which cannot be referred to a source because their author or manuscript is unknown are nevertheless marked with brackets, as though they had once occupied some place in manuscripts now lost or unknown.

XIX. Thus far concerning the Lives of Thomas; these are followed by a hymn excerpted from an Arras manuscript [no. 557], and so the whole series of biographers is completed.

HISTORICAL DOCUMENTS

XX. The case between the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of London.—Taken from Cave’s manuscript among the letters of Gilbert Foliot [Bodl. e Mus. 249], where it occurs as no. 176; neither the title nor the author’s name is given. It concerns the Bishop of London’s excommunication in A.D. 1169.

XXI. Chapters of the council of Alexander III held at Tours.—The acts and decrees of the Council of Tours, celebrated in A.D. 1163, are set out. They occur in the same Bodleian manuscript [e Mus. 249, fol. 231].

XXII. An explanation of the form of oath by which Girard la Pucelle bound himself in law when he was about to abandon the antipope’s party. It occurs in Lupus, *Letters*, book XV, no. 176, but belongs more suitably here among the Historical Documents.

XXIII. The following occurs in the Lambeth Library, in one of Warton’s transcripts, from a very ancient manuscript. Warton observed:

“Henry IV was the first among the kings of England to be anointed with that holy chrism which descended from heaven in a stone vial enclosed within a golden eagle [thus].” These rites are discussed sufficiently in Walsingham’s *History*, quarto, at its very beginning, and also in other histories cited by him. (See Selden, *Titles of Honour*, p. 153; manuscript in the Cotton Library. It appears to be the same as the text which may be read at the end of the third volume in the works of John of Tynemouth, in the Lambeth Library manuscript, folio no. 12, concerning which below.)

XXIV. This fragment is taken from vol. III of the latest manuscript of Thomas’s Letters, arranged in five folio volumes and now preserved in the library of Trinity College, Cambridge. This volume contains two transcripts of the same text, which agree in subject matter as far as the word *apostolicam* (“apostolic”), but diverge at the end from the subject and turn into the tenor of other letters. Hence one must conclude that the copyist erred and that the end of the fragment itself is lacking.

XXV. SUMMARY OF THE CASE, etc. Preserved from Douce manuscript [287] in the Bodleian Library. If one compares this document with the Life of Thomas by FitzStephen, one will see that those Lives themselves contain a certain excerpt quite at variance with the subject. Although the Editor noticed this error at the end of the volume, he could not restore the excerpt to its proper place. Further, the first part of the *Summary of the Case* occurs as no. 164* in the Letters of Gilbert Foliot from Cave’s manuscript [Mus. 249]; the second part, that is, “On the Compromise,” is found in Letter 12, book I, of Thomas’s Letters as edited by Lupus. Lupus, however, omitted the sixteen Constitutions of Clarendon because they had been published elsewhere. So do we. The third part, or “On the Exile,” etc., occurs as no. 158 in Cave’s manuscript.

XXVI. ON OATHS, etc. Found in the above-mentioned manuscript of Trinity College, Cambridge; likewise in British Museum manuscript, Titus D. XI, art. 8.

XXVII. From Cave’s manuscript no. 178; Douce no. 64*.

XXVIII. From Lambeth manuscript [136] no. 5, compared with Paris manuscript 5372, no. 47.

XXIX. From Claud. B II, book II, letter 130; Bodl. 947, no. 176, part III.

XXX. From Paris manuscript 5372.

XXXI. From Claud. B II. The letter follows those beginning with the words: “They are not ignorant.”

XXXII. A sermon of Stephen Langton, translated from Lupus’s edition.

XXXIII. Treatise on the promise of the blessed martyr Thomas, namely that such a successor would succeed him as would recompense the Church of Pontigny for the generosity bestowed upon him during his exile. From Martène’s *Thesaurus*, vol. III, p. 1873, after the histories of Blessed Edmund; of small value indeed, but it increases the number.

XXXIV. Excerpt from British Museum manuscript, Royal 13. E. VI.

XXXV. Thus far concerning the documents; the volume is completed by the fragment placed at the end, from a Life of the Archbishop written in the Lansdowne manuscript. Its author asserts that he lived in the time of the person whose life he subsequently discussed.

Thus far, then, concerning the various Lives and Historical Documents. We must speak below of Herbert of Bosham. Observe only that, when both were printed together, the matter belonging to each was arranged in such a fashion as cannot be understood unless the text is assembled and elucidated. Let us now proceed to Becket’s letters.

II. LETTERS OF ST THOMAS

[Col. XVII]

Of all testimonies to that great conflict in which Henry II and Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, contended for so long, the letters of those men who themselves took some part, however small, in so disastrous an affair are of the greatest importance. As may be gathered repeatedly from the letters themselves, several originals were committed by the Archbishop to the safekeeping of the Vatican Library, and perhaps to other places as well. Although very many copies of these letters are found, none is more valuable than that also surviving in the Vatican Library. Long ago many Letters had been printed in the *Four-Part History*, or *Quadrilogus*, published at Paris in 1495; but Lupus published the complete body—five or six hundred letters—which he had found in the Vatican, at Brussels in 1682, under the title *Life and Letters of St Thomas*. The editor prefixed to the saint’s letters a Life drawn from the writings of various authors and called the entire work, as it had formerly been called, the *Quadrilogus*. You will find all these again in Lupus’s folio edition. Moreover, about three hundred letters of Thomas and his contemporaries survive in the *Writers of French and Gallic Affairs*, first published by the most distinguished Monsieur Bouquet from two manuscripts of the Royal Library at Paris.

If one attends to the name of each subscriber, one finds first very many letters of Pope Alexander; then nearly ninety of John of Salisbury; five or six of Gilbert Foliot; many more of Arnulf of Lisieux; and very few of King Henry II. Since the letters of Arnulf and Gilbert Foliot were to be published separately with their other works, it did not seem advantageous to scholarship to repeat the same material twice. The same applies to the letters of John of Salisbury. Excepting these, however, you will find here all the rest that has hitherto been collected by all editors. You should only observe that the material was arranged by subject in such a way that one part of the letters was inserted in the Collection of Gilbert Foliot, another in that of Thomas. I have already noted this in the preface to Gilbert. But here their repetition is truly appropriate, lest you suppose that anything from earlier editions is lacking in ours.

At the end of the volume there is an index of the letters, arranged alphabetically, so that you may compare this latest edition with earlier editions and even with manuscripts—except that you should seek the letters of Arnulf and John of Salisbury, since they were published separately, in their own special place.

Thus was compiled our edition of the Letters, truly most full, since it brought so very many texts to light for the first time; with no exceptions, as we have said, except those belonging to the works of Arnulf and John of Salisbury, which are found in those books also published by us.

This entire series of Letters was first arranged by Alan of Tewkesbury, and afterward by Lupus, according to chronological sequence; yet you will find very many difficulties—if not errors—in that chronological order. Accordingly, as in the Letters of Gilbert Foliot, we have followed another course. Since one chiefly asks what was written and by whom it was written, we set forth the letters in order of dignity or rank, so that the matter may become clear to you. In both collections, therefore, read first the letters of Thomas or Gilbert Foliot, respectively—that is, of the person under discussion; then those of the Supreme Pontiffs, cardinals, archbishops, and so on down to the person placed last in the ecclesiastical hierarchy. If there are several writers of the same dignity or rank, they are to be collected alphabetically by the name of their see, abbey, priory, or even parish: Canterbury, for example, York, Mainz, and so forth. Finally, as is fitting, we place after these all lay writers—kings, queens, primates, knights, etc. Thus, at a glance, whoever you are, if you seek any letter, you will quickly find it. Perhaps, while attending rather superficially to details—small indeed—you may feel that the work has not been brought perfectly to completion as you would wish; but look more carefully, I beg you. You will see, for example, that the same name can be used in different places. But because the collection is so exceedingly abundant that it would plainly appear a crude and unarranged mass unless everything were recorded in the order in which it was written, a second index is appended, which clearly displays the chronological arrangement itself.

The work was compiled from many manuscript codices, of which fuller discussion is given in the notes. It will suffice here to recall what they are and whence they come:

Namely, 4 in the Bodleian Library, Oxford; 2 in the library of St John’s College, Oxford; 2 in the library of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge; 1 in the library of Trinity Hall at the same place; 1 in the Lomith Library, London; 6 in the British Museum; 3 in the Royal Library, Paris.

## CHRONOLOGICAL TABLE OF THE LIFE OF ST THOMAS

[Col. XIX]

**1116.**—Gilbert Becket is captured in the Holy Land and serves Amurath, whose daughter Mathilda falls in love with the Christian slave.

**1117.**—Gilbert escapes and returns to London, accompanied by Mathilda. Having married her, he then leaves her, again taking the cross.

**1118.**—Thomas Becket is born. On the same night Gilbert’s house is burned.

**1121.**—Gilbert returns.

**1130–35.**—About this time Thomas is entrusted, as a pupil, to the care of the prior of Merton.

**1139.**—Mathilda dies.

**1140.**—Thomas Becket devotes himself to study at Paris.

**1141–43.**—He serves as clerk to Osbern Octonumini [sic]. Not long afterward he enters the household of Archbishop Theobald, where, ordained first deacon and then archdeacon, he obtains the benefices of Otford and St Mary-at-the-Strand, the provostship of Beverley, and other privileges as well.

**1155 [or 1158].**—King Henry chooses and receives him as chancellor. Thomas reforms the peace of the realm.

**1159.**—War rages between the count of Toulouse and the king of the French.

**1160.**—Becket comes as an envoy to the king of the French.

**1161.**—April 16: Archbishop Theobald dies.

**1162.**—Thomas is chosen archbishop. His election having been confirmed at Westminster on Thursday in Easter week, he is ordained priest at Canterbury on Easter week, soon to be consecrated archbishop by Henry of Winchester. He dedicates Reading Abbey and presides over the translation of the body of St Edward, surnamed the Confessor, which, under his direction, is celebrated with the greatest magnificence. Privileges unlawfully imposed are revoked.

**1163.**—He attends the Council of Tours. Because he reforms the peace of the Church, he alienates the king from himself.

**1163.**—On the Kalends of October King Henry convenes a council at Westminster. John of Salisbury is absent in exile.

**1164.**—The Council of Clarendon is held. Thomas Becket attempts escape three times, unsuccessfully.

**1164.**—On the day before the Nones of October, or Tuesday, the Council of Northampton is convened. The archbishop flees on the third Ides—Tuesday—and, having passed through Flanders, approaches the pope at Sens; at the pope’s command he proceeds to Pontigny, where he is to reside.

**1165.**—He passes the year peacefully at Pontigny.

**1166.**—He excommunicates certain supporters of the king; at Vézelay he threatens the king himself with this excommunication.

**1167, 1168, 1169.**—During these three years, while men act deceitfully on every side and appeal to the Roman See under feigned good faith, Thomas binds the bishops of London and Salisbury with the bonds of excommunication. Then the king, in order to arrange peace among all parties, enters into consultation at Montmirail, Montmartre, and elsewhere with Frederick, the schismatic emperor.

**1170.**—At Fréteval it is at last granted that the archbishop may return to his see; yet for several months he cannot accomplish this, since the king constantly resists.

**1170.**—On the fourth day before the Nones of December, after the archbishop had returned again, after scarcely four weeks had elapsed, spent in London and Canterbury, he is slain by four knights in his own metropolitan church at Canterbury, at the fourth hour in the afternoon, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January; on the following day he is buried in the crypt of that same church.

**1221.**—Translation of Thomas: his relics, in the presence of King Henry III, the primates, and clergy of the whole realm, are deposited in a most splendid shrine.

[Col. 0001]

# THE FIRST LIFE OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY AND MARTYR, BY EDWARD GRIM

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0001A]

Those who profess the arts of this world each have their own endeavours by which they may ascend to greater things. Tirelessly considering what profit the perfection of the discipline they profess may bring, they soften the harshness of their exertions by the prospect of their goal; as though strengthened by a certain shortening of the road, they rise more vigorously toward what they have set before themselves. And indeed, in order to gain at some time a passing crown, what labours do they avoid? What contests do they evade? What injuries do they sometimes endure? Or what do they count impossible? Yet no one should attempt to maintain otherwise than that the industrious labour of those who serve the world will perish with the world.

Since our cause is different—since Christ is set before us as the way, and eternal life is promised as the end of our labours—how great, I ask, is the vigilance needed amid the varied and manifold changes of the world! Let not the enticements of an easier life weaken us in our purpose; let not the hardships of the road of labour call us back from the straight path, by which, through a blessed exchange, eternal things are prepared for fleeting things and heavenly things for earthly. And so that Christian devotion may strive toward these more eagerly, scorning the hostile rivalry of the perverse, let us walk in the path and rest upon the footsteps of those whose holy conduct establishes their faith, whose blessed end commends their life, and whose outstanding virtues proclaim their glory to us.

For it is not characteristic of the Christian profession to take a pattern for living from those whom either feeble conduct makes notorious or an imperfect will compels to fall back from their purpose. But if the authority of the ancients, however much it ordinarily kindles a weak soul toward paths of more reformed life, kindles you less because of temporal distance, the merciful providence of the Saviour everywhere provides and heals our lack of devotion. Thus, if we grow weary of the deeds of the ancients, may we at least be ashamed not to imitate one whom it has been possible to behold.

Therefore, while the love of many grows cold and wickedness abounds, the author of human salvation is believed to have given less care to temporal affairs. Yet, just as by the manifestation of humanity once assumed he visited and redeemed his people, so by the invisible working of his majesty through his own servants he continually invites those whom he redeemed toward better things. And lest this present age of ours seem deprived of so great a gift, let a new soldier of Christ come forward: blessed Thomas, an outstanding martyr, a spectacle of holiness, a standard of justice, an incitement to patience, an example of virtue, and an unconquered defender of truth.

“But,” you say, “what have I to do with martyrdom? What with miracles, whose effectiveness is not to be attributed to human powers but to God?” Fair enough: we do not set martyrdom or miracles before you for imitation. Rather, consider more fully the life of the martyr; contemplate his character; wonder at a man who, amid all the riches of the world and everything that human estimation holds precious, maintained such constancy of mind that neither prosperity softened him into love of the world nor any adversity could in any degree delay him from the love of his Creator, once knowledge of the truth had first entered his understanding. Thus founded himself upon the firm rock, he rightly cried out with the Apostle: “Who shall separate me from the love of Christ?”

For he suffered many grievous tribulations: exile from his rank, loss of all possessions, outlawry, and—what penetrated his heart more deeply and afflicted him most severely—the tears and desolation of those dear to him. Yet, transcending all these things with lofty mind, he became more devout day by day, wholly unlike the fool whom the psalm reproaches because “he will praise thee when thou hast done him good.”

Therefore, wishing piously to comply with the devotion of certain persons who are anxious to know more fully the deeds of the precious martyr, we shall endeavour briefly to record in writing, aided by the merits of him of whom we speak, those things which have come to our knowledge: namely, by the report of those who had been more closely attached to him during his life, or which we ourselves have observed. We warn the reader that whatever others have written, or shall write, contrary to this narrative of ours is in no way consonant with the truth.

Plainly, although no slight presumption commits us to this undertaking, unworthy as we are in relation to the dignity of the subject, and although poverty of understanding confounds us, nevertheless love raises the trembling writer again, devotion invites him, and the overflowing drops of graces from the abundance of God’s house encourage him mightily to speak—graces by which the Saviour does not cease, through this his servant, to water the face of the earth. For if we keep silence, the tongue of the mute, loosed in praise of the martyr, and his miracles will declare how acceptable both his life and his death were to the Creator.

[Col. 0003A]

May the Spirit of truth, through the glorious merits of our blessed Father, inspire our devotion never to overstep in writing the lines of rectitude, so that our pure and faith-filled discourse may pursue what we undertake with devout intention.

Thomas, holy in Christ and chosen before the foundation of the world, at his blessed birth adorned London, the head of the Britains. His father was Gilbert, surnamed Beket, and his mother Mathildis. Both were by no means inferior to their fellow citizens in nobility of birth and wealth; yet they far surpassed them in nobility of character and in the innocence of their devout manner of life. Persisting in works of justice, they lived, as tradition relates, without blame or complaint, so that England rejoiced in having received from them, as from Zacharias and Elizabeth, a new John.

Nor would I without reason call him, according to his measure, a John, whose likeness to John in penitence was shown by his labour and love of truth, for which, fighting even unto death, he did not tremble even under the sword, but bore witness to the truth. But let the following discourse speak of these matters. For the present, that we may take up the course of the story somewhat further back, we must briefly consider the visions by which, we believe, the future excellence of this holy offspring was foreshadowed.

## CONCERNING HIS MOTHER’S VISION

A short time after his mother conceived, she saw in a dream all the water of the river Thames flowing into her bosom. Overwhelmed by feminine fear and suspecting some strange travail, which popular interpretation commonly signifies by an overflow of waters, she heard instead an interpretation from a wise man, divinely inspired; by it she deserved to be greatly comforted. “He who will be born from you,” he said, “will rule many peoples.” Another, differing in no respect from the former’s opinion, added that he would receive streams of graces by which he would water his native soil like a river, recalling that Gospel saying: “He who believes in me, from his belly shall flow rivers of living water.”

A second time the woman seemed to herself to have come to Canterbury. There, as she began with the others present to enter Christ Church, her womb, because of the child she had conceived, swelled so greatly that no entrance through any of the doors was open to her. By this vision, as though she seemed unworthy to enter the church, the woman remained exceedingly sad and troubled until a third vision dispelled the sorrow of the preceding one.

For when the time of childbirth was at hand, the mother seemed to see twelve stars of unusual splendour fall from heaven into her lap. Greatly strengthened by this, she perceived that the vision signified something great concerning the child to be born. And we too, judging from the works which the Lord performed through his faithful servant the surpassing glory of his future rank, believe and confess that at the future judgment he will judge the world together with those twelve chosen luminaries of heaven.

Again, when the little child lay in his cradle, his mother saw him naked in a dream. Angered with the nurse, she said: “Why do you not cover the child?” The nurse replied: “Most certainly, my lady, he is covered with precious folded purple.” Immediately mother and maidservant rose and tried to unfold the covering in order to wrap the little child in it more carefully. But neither the narrowness of the bedroom nor a larger hall could contain its breadth, and even the street appeared far too narrow. Therefore both hurried, as it seemed, to Smithfield, a spacious place in the city, that there at least they might satisfy their wishes. While, confident in the roominess of the place, they applied themselves to their undertaking, a voice descending from heaven thundered to them: “You labour in vain. All England is smaller than this purple, nor can it encompass its breadth.”

[Col. 0004B]

At this voice the mother awoke, remembering indeed what she had seen but wholly unaware what it meant. We, however, to whom faith that sees with opened eyes reveals the meaning, interpret the precious purple as the blood of the martyr innocently slain: drenched and clothed in it he lay during his Passion; but now it has spread throughout so many realms and foreign peoples of the earth, as the preceding vision foreshadowed.

His relatives relate that, on the day when this little child of ours was born into the darkness of the world, a fire broke out from his father’s house and burned a great part of the city. And you too, if you consider carefully how great the devotion that burned from him has been, from the day when our martyr deserved to enter the eternal light—in building or restoring churches, clothing altars, giving liberally to the poor, promptly renouncing works of injustice, punishing sins by penance, and undertaking every work of mercy—you will confess that not only the city of London but indeed the entire city of God, wherever his name has been heard, has been kindled by the example of the martyr.

Now the lamp has been set upon the lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light. Now we see fulfilled in this man what the Saviour promises to the elect: “He who conquers, as I also conquered, I will make him a pillar of fire in my temple.” And now, giving thanks to providence from above, we hold fast to the pillar; let us look upon the lamp. Let us enter where it went, lest perhaps we strike our foot against a stone, because he who walks in darkness does not know where he goes. But now let us return to the order of the history.

When his tender age allowed it, the boy was handed over to be instructed in the rudiments of letters. Having completed these, he was sent to study the liberal arts, and is remembered to have grasped much in a short time. How teachable he was, and how great his diligence and quickness even in his tender years, was shown by his stronger age; indeed, once he became a man, he reaped abundant fruits of wisdom, in acquiring which he had laboured while still young.

But changing circumstances did not allow him to attend schools for long. His parents, as we have already indicated, formerly foremost among their countrymen in wealth and worldly distinction, were considerably reduced by frequent fires and other unfortunate losses; they are therefore known to have bestowed less care upon the education of their son. Yet we are in no way permitted to doubt that this reduction—or rather, a certain sober and honourable moderation—served their justification, since the divine word says: “Those whom I love I rebuke and chastise,” so that the furnace of poverty might burn away whatever worldly dust their former abundance had gathered.

The death of his mother doubled the son’s desolation. At that time she entered upon the universal way and left her son almost abandoned and exposed to his own counsels; for his father was already old, and the property that remained could not meet his son’s expenses. Nor is he said to have survived his wife much longer.

[Col. 0005B]

A nobleman, Richer de l’Aigle, exceedingly wealthy, used to stay as a guest in that man’s house whenever he came to the city. Thomas attached himself to him and for some time entrusted himself to his counsel and prudence. For, having now passed beyond boyhood, he had begun to excel in the best qualities: distinguished in intellect, pleasing in speech, agreeable in countenance with a gravity tempered by cheerfulness, handsome in appearance, and sufficiently elegant in form, he made himself welcome and lovable to all.

Having entered the common course of life, he gave his mind to those pursuits in which that age is accustomed to delight: he enjoyed the sport of the running of dogs, the speed of birds, and their flight and capture. Yet amid these and similar empty and varied pleasures of the world, the vessel of election was preserved whole and untouched by the temptations which especially beset tender youth. As a presage of his future constancy, love of truth is said to have adhered so firmly to the young man’s heart, although he still pursued worldly things, that scarcely, or never, in jest or in earnest did he utter anything contrary to truth. How perfectly he fulfilled this afterward, once he had become a man, will be made clear by what follows.

Thus, returning from school to the aforesaid rich man, and pursuing the varied interests of the world—now hunting, now bird-catching, which especially delighted his youthful mind—he stayed as he pleased, now at home with his father and now in the country with the rich man. And it happened that, thus released from his studies, he resolved to renounce scholarly pursuits.

One day, when Thomas went with the rich man to the riverbanks, a hawk pursued a duck flushed from the river. Following it as it turned in the water, the hawk sank with it beneath the stream. Seeing this, the young man pitied the hawk, which was now about to perish; he leapt from his horse and plunged himself into the deep water to rescue the bird. But before he could reach it, he himself was swept into the bed of the river; now submerged beneath the waters and now raised by the force of the waves, he began to be in danger. Those who watched thought that he had utterly perished, since no one could be present to extend a hand to the drowning man.

At last he was carried by the current to a mill that happened then to be grinding. When he first drew near the water outlets, the wheel stopped and did not move at all until the young man was pulled out alive indeed, but severely distressed. Yet the healing hand of the Saviour comforted him in his affliction: amid the waves it protected him, though despaired of, so that the lamp which was to be in Israel should not be extinguished—he by whose precious death we see such great benefits have resulted.

[Col. 0006A]

Again, Osbern, surnamed Octonumini, an eminent man in the city and a possessor of many estates, who was related to Thomas by blood, kept Thomas with him for almost three years, continually employing him in making abstracts of his expenses and revenues.

Thomas had now set foot upon the paths of the world. He began to aspire to honours, to pour out his mind upon external things, and to seek the empty grandeurs of the world. Both the wisdom of mind in which he excelled and the honourableness of his life offered him many opportunities for attaining these things. For there shone in the man, singularly and beyond his years, a certain mature old age, the grey hair of wisdom, a certain graciousness in counsel and conduct, and gravity, so that he rightly turned all men toward admiration and love of himself.

But he then learned what he later confessed: that a man’s way, no more than his life, is not in his own control, but that the steps of a man are directed by the Lord. He himself planned one thing; divine providence worked another thing, and in another manner, within him. For, to make advancement to honours easier for him, he was invited by a certain official of Archbishop Theobald’s household. Arriving there under the guidance of divine grace, he was received with the honour appropriate to such a man.

There, putting aside games and frivolity, he always formed his mind toward better things by the conversation of elders and wise men. Before long, when the man’s quick intelligence had been recognized through his words of wisdom, continually breaking forth as though in small sparks—as the Wise Man says, “the speech of a man declares him”—he was directed to take part in the archbishop’s counsels and business, in public and private causes.

[Col. 0006C]

For he was keenly alert in understanding, provident in counsel, prudent in reply, eloquent and restrained in speech; in coming and going at his lord’s command, in word and deed inferior to none. He appeared dear to his lord and agreeable to everyone, so that whoever did not love such gifts of grace in the man showed himself rather ill-disposed. At last he found such favour in the archbishop’s eyes, and bound the archbishop’s heart to himself by such assiduous service, that the archbishop openly declared that he had never before found anyone so upright in every matter and so faithful.

But the enemy of human advancement, seeing such industry of spirit, sharpness of intellect, and honourableness of conduct in the young man, and wasting away with envy, foresaw for him easy access to the highest honours if he continued, as he had begun, to run without stumbling. Therefore he raised up against him as a rival Roger, archdeacon of Canterbury, whom they called “of Pont l’Évêque.” So long as Thomas lived and breathed, Roger is known to have poured out against him, by every means available, the poison then conceived.

Meanwhile, in order to remove him from the court, Roger attacked him now with open abuse, now with mocking jests. In particular, he repeatedly called him, in witty insult, “the clerk with the axe” or “hatchet,” taking the nickname from the man who had invited him to the archbishop’s court. And indeed Thomas was to receive an axe in due time—or rather, Peter’s sword—by which he cut off Roger himself and his accomplices from the fellowship of the saints, so that, as they complained to the king, they did not even have the power to bless food. But of this elsewhere.

Meanwhile, the prudent man was not moved by these or similar things from remaining wakefully devoted to the archbishop’s service. He heard from the wise man that “the patient man is better than the strong man,” while conversely he heard that “he who utters insults is a fool”; nor can human malice weaken the divine plan.

During these events, William of York, of venerable memory, having entered the bounds of eternal blessedness, the aforesaid Roger was installed in his place through the aid and exertion of Archbishop Theobald, by whom, according to custom, he was anointed and consecrated. The archbishop gave the archdeaconry of Canterbury to Thomas, whom, as has already been said, he believed he would never have as an equal: a man good in all things and faithful in all his house. Without delay he also procured for his archdeacon the provostship of Beverley, and he heaped up churches and other revenues for him in many ways.

[Col. 0007B]

But Thomas, generous in spirit and judging according to the counsels of the wise that a good name is better than great treasures, strove to turn wealth to the increase of his reputation and the enlargement of his name, lest by sparing money he should obscure the splendour of his reputation by the stain of stinginess. Why weave delays into the account? As he advanced to higher things, he suffered none. He could not remain in a lowly position because of the flame of quickness, the nobility of spirit which filled that breast, and—what is more remarkable—in so great an elevation, the integrity of his life.

Greater possessions, more important than the former, were therefore brought to him, and his honours grew more abundantly. The archbishop, wishing to reward the man more highly, commended him to the royal majesty, recounting the excellence with which he was endowed: wisdom of mind, foresight in counsel, and, surpassing these, he declared him faithful and a lover of truth. The king was easily persuaded to retain in favour a man whom his own great merits sufficiently commended; and without delay he granted him his chancellorship.

Thus a new Joseph was raised over Egypt. He was set over all the affairs of the realm, second after the king. His honours, lands, possessions, wealth, worldly splendour, and glory multiplied. As was customary, innumerable bands of retainers followed him; companies of chosen knights attended him; and an entourage in no respect smaller than the king’s attached itself to the chancellor, so that the king sometimes reproved him for having emptied the royal household.

With a lavish and liberal hand Thomas expended both his own revenues and those of the kingdom upon soldiers’ wages and benefactions, expecting this to be beneficial; yet he remained faithful and upright to the king in intention and deed, and reserved all things for the king’s honour and glory. Conversely, the king is known to have bestowed upon him such honour, affection, and freedom as he had never bestowed upon any man; in later times the king himself often recalled this. Whatever Thomas established, altered, or decreed, throughout the reach of the king’s dominion, was held almost as law.

[Col. 0008A]

But—alas for the wicked world!—who could trust its great unhappiness and miserable condition? If you look more closely, you will see that almost the more powerful a person is in the world, the more prone to sin; the richer, the worse; the higher, the more inclined to fall. Again, the more firmly a person stands in earthly things, the more feebly he rises toward divine things; and the more prudent he is in human affairs, the farther he is from true wisdom, since the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God and prudence is death. For the more closely one embraces the world, the more tightly, blinded by the world’s smoke, one is bound in the night of sin and held fast.

The enemy of human nature approaches: a lover of evil, author of envy, herald of innocence, begrudging humanity the place of blessedness from which he fell irrecoverably through his own wickedness. Wishing, therefore, that innocence should perish, he besets the road by which men go to their homeland, sitting in ambush like a lion in his den in order to kill the innocent. He spreads snares, lays on fetters, conceals the hook with bait, so that whoever greedily seeks the bait may be slaughtered by the hook. He sometimes readily clears the road to honours and favours one ascending to high places, so that he may hold by right of possession in the heights one whom he could not approach in lower places.

The preceding discourse has explained how innocently and blamelessly St Thomas spent his earlier years in a lowly station before becoming chancellor. But now, placed on high, it is difficult to say how great were his boldness and presumption. Who could enumerate how many he put to death, or how many he subjected to forfeiture of all their possessions? For, accompanied by a strong force of soldiers, he attacked cities, destroyed cities and towns, and consumed villages and estates with devouring fire, without any regard for mercy. Wherever the enemies of his lord rose up, he made himself intolerable to them. In short, whom did he ever fear to offend, if only he might satisfy the king’s wishes and obey his commands?

[Col. 0008C]

Yet in all these matters—although some judged otherwise—he was chaste in body and humble in heart, though among the humble; for among the powerful he himself appeared more powerful and more exalted. None was considered more discerning than he, none more generous, none wiser. He supplied the poor with necessities without calculation; but all the gifts of grace were veiled beneath such outward magnificence that no one would have thought—even when he was archbishop—that he had acquired these gifts except for worldly pomp.

He also gained such favour with the king and the entire realm that public opinion counted blessed only those who could please in his eyes and in any way comply with the king’s counsellor and chancellor. Thus may a richer thanksgiving and voice of praise resound to the Redeemer, because he so mercifully rescued from the world one whom we know to have been bound with so many ties.

Let what has been said concerning the life he lived in the world suffice. Henceforth, with him himself as our guide, let our discourse be directed to how he trampled all worldly things underfoot in his mind.

Meanwhile Theobald, the archbishop, reached the end of his temporal life, and the see was vacant of a bishop. The king, believing that the chancellor would, as before, follow his wishes in all things and obey his commands, gave him the archbishopric. The affair was, however, delayed for some time, until he could extort the consent of the convent, which had from ancient times been accustomed to possess a free voice in the election of its bishop; for, while it objected, no king had been permitted to thrust in anyone by his own authority.

Therefore, that the convent might incline to his will, he sent three bishops to Canterbury, together with Richard de Luci, a nobleman and chief officer of the realm. He also sent the chancellor into England on various business, and especially that he might receive from all men fealty and submission for his son, who was then to be crowned king, and that they might swear allegiance to him as king.

The bishops, having crossed the sea, came to Canterbury and greeted the convent in the king’s name. In chapter, before all, Richard, a man of great eloquence, stated the purpose for which they had been sent.

“This,” he said, “the king commands you: that no slight danger threatens the flock if this Church is deprived of a bishop any longer. You are therefore to know that it is his will that, now as formerly, you should have free choice in the election of a shepherd; provided, however, that such a person be chosen as may suffice for so great a burden, be worthy of the dignity, and please the king.”

To him the prior replied: “May the Lord, the author of the whole world, who purchased his Church for himself by the shedding of his own blood, deign to provide a shepherd acceptable to himself, useful to us, and to his whole Church a pattern of virtue and an example of justice. And thanks be to the king, who has not deprived this Church of the dignity which it has possessed for so long a time.”

When all had answered, the messengers added: “Since it is the will of you all to obey the king’s commands, it is wiser that one be chosen who can freely defend the cause of our Church and who can avail for us in all matters with the royal majesty. For if a man is elected who does not please the king, you will be in schism and discord, and under such a shepherd you will have dispersion rather than refuge; whereas, on the other hand, you will experience no small increase of advancement if one is chosen in whom the king is pleased.”

Accordingly, after the wiser party of the council had been assembled apart, the election was discussed closely with the envoys. The Spirit of God was invoked, through whom rulers decree what is just; and the chancellor was elected shepherd and protector, amid the unanimous acclamation and vote, so that none might doubt that the choice had been divinely inspired. The king’s messengers approved the election, affirming that the king would readily assent and that no one in the kingdom was fitter or more honourable for this dignity.

Why say more? A solemn council was convened in London; the chancellor was elected by clergy and people, the election was confirmed, and it pleased all—except the bishop of London alone, who objected. But when the crowd cried out, “The voice of God, and not of man,” he fell silent and put his finger to his mouth. The election was presented to the king’s son, still awaiting coronation; he consented and received it gladly.

The bishop of Winchester, an aged and prudent man, addressed the assembly, and especially those to whom the king had entrusted his authority in this affair, so that whatever they did would be ratified:

“This man,” he said, “whom by common consent we elect as protector, as chancellor and chief officer of the realm had in his hands the king’s treasures and the revenues of the kingdom, and administered them as the various affairs required. But lest hereafter he be exposed to any exaction or accusation, as though he had squandered his lord’s goods through free inclination rather than for the kingdom’s benefit, we receive him as free and absolved from every claim and accusation. For it seems unfitting that holy Church should make for herself a father or protector who is proved to be a slave of money and liable to the necessity of human servitude.”

To this the king’s ministers replied: “From the king’s mouth we proclaim him free from every accusation and exaction, now and for all time.”

Thus iniquity for a time shut its mouth, and the accuser was silent, seeing with envy that he had fallen away from the hope which he had conceived. He was accordingly brought to Canterbury, received by the convent and city with the solemn devotion fitting to the occasion, enthroned, and canonically consecrated.

After the consecration had been celebrated and each had returned to his own place, the venerable archbishop likewise at once returned into himself and turned wholly to the Lord. And, marvellous to relate, he had scarcely been sacramentally anointed with the holy unction when his mind, made drunk by the reality and efficacy of the sacrament—that is, by the manifold grace of the Holy Spirit—was wholly changed: not indeed immediately in outward habit, but in mind. Or rather, this was not his doing, but “the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.”

In time, lest he should become proud through honour, he chose by various labours of penance to weaken the insolence of the flesh beneath the burden and yoke of God. He assumed both the rule and the habit of a regular canon, and preserved what he had assumed, together with the office of archbishop, so wonderfully that, though anyone may presume of himself, he will often fail in one or the other; whereas Thomas perfectly fulfilled both, and certain things more difficult still.

Meanwhile, being a man of higher understanding, he wished the eye of the world—which is always wicked—to remain unaware of what divine love had planted in his heart, until this new planting had struck its root more deeply and no longer feared the storms of the world. He therefore did not immediately change his dress. But when murmuring arose among the monks because, contrary to custom, he frequently attended choir in secular clothing, one of his household rebuked him and reported that a person of terrible countenance had stood before him and commanded in threatening words:

“Go, tell the chancellor”—the name of archbishop being withheld through excessive indignation—“to change his habit without delay. If he scorns this, I shall go against him all the days of his life.”

Hearing this, the venerable man wept most bitterly. He spoke only a few words to the man who had said this; but silently he considered within himself what he had done, what manner of man he had been, and what burden he had undertaken—regarding it plainly in every respect as a burden rather than an honour. Seeing that he was accountable for souls, he was divinely inspired to rise up against himself and entered upon this deliberation with himself:

“My soul, what are we doing? What account shall we render for the sheep committed to us, we who have lived negligently? Or what shall we say for others, we who are weighed down by our own transgressions? Until now we have lived for the world; we have served in warfare for earthly things. You now possess those vain heights which you desired, the glory of riches that will perish with the world; you have attained your heart’s desire. Do you strive to seek greater things than these, or to climb higher? Rather, this elevation will lead us down to the lowest depths of hell, if we do not act more wisely, redeeming the time and shortening our days while God’s patience invites us to repentance, lest that terrible day, coming like a thief in the night, carry us away unprepared and there be no one left to rescue us.

“It may be attributed to ignorance and youthful disposition that we passed the earlier times in contempt; but henceforth no shadow of excuse remains at all: the covering of ignorance is removed. For if our own condition has by no means compelled us to improve, let at least care for those entrusted to us make us anxious, lest, living wickedly, we ourselves perish and become for many the material of death, the cause of destruction.

“Therefore let us embrace the one refuge that remains. Let us listen with attentive ear to the saving voice of the Saviour, and imitate the merciful example of him who says: ‘Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.’ For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers loss to his soul and destroys himself? Therefore, that those whose care is entrusted to us may profit through us, let our light shine before men, that they may see our good works and glorify the Father. And that what we do may profit us, let us strive with unwearied effort to enter through the narrow gate into the breadth of the heavenly court, lest, if we seek entrance too late, we deserve to hear, when the door is already shut, ‘I do not know you.’”

With these and similar words, daily—indeed continually—the holy man armed his spirit for the contest of spiritual warfare and strengthened his resolve. Prevented by the inspiration of divine grace, and now seeing all earthly things beneath him and despising them, he ascended in spirit to heavenly things. Without delay, taking up the sword-point of spiritual zeal, he cut the knot of his former obligation by which he had until then seemed bound; and, as a tardy exactor, sacrificed himself to God as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God.

By reducing his food, he slew the appetite of gluttony. By constant sacred reading and prayer, he struck back the unlawful impulses rushing upon the mind; he restrained the insolence of natural ardour by shorter sleep; he exchanged softness of dress for a harsher hair-shirt. And, to omit much, crucifying his flesh with its vices and desires, he brought his whole self within the limits of necessity and became altogether different from the man he had been. Whatever was honourable, holy, or just, he both did and taught; and whatever was contrary to these things he utterly banished from himself.

From the beginning of his ordination, indeed, he received such love of God and holy devotion, and likewise such zeal against every injustice, that he spared no person, of whatever rank, who presumed anything contrary to the rule of justice entrusted to him by the Lord. Neither the king’s service nor his will, against the will of the King of all, could thereafter induce him to obey; neither threats nor affection overcame him.

What human being can worthily admire the immeasurable regard of divine mercy in so sudden and so perfect a change of a human mind? God is indeed wonderful in his saints. In a human being he displays the riches of his goodness: though the person is a sinner and an enemy of justice, God reconciles him to himself according to the multitude of his mercies. He does not persecute human beings but their vices; he calls back the one who departs, makes the one who has turned away return, and converts the despiser to himself. He inspires the desire for repentance, makes one hate whatever one had loved, and easily brings about what had appeared impossible.

Everywhere the examples of the saints stir us: on one side, those who fell and repented; on the other, the righteous who did not fall. That one who may have fallen should strive to rise, the falls of saints are set before us; and we read of the perseverance of the righteous, lest at any time we fall away from the profession we have undertaken. And lest we complain that examples are lacking, the venerable archbishop and martyr of Christ, Saint Thomas, is set before us as a perfect pattern of repentance.

After he had considered that he had sinned grievously in following worldly pomp, and had presumed to do many, indeed countless, things contrary to God’s will and command in order to keep faith with a mortal king, he turned, repented, and struck his thigh. Whatever fleshly or transitory thing he perceived in himself, he washed away with an abundant shower of tears and consumed with the fire of devout love in the bitterness of his heart. Declaring stern war upon himself, through penance he exacted from himself payment for whatever he remembered having committed through fault. Those things which he had formerly embraced with so great desire, he now, converted to the love of God, preached—seasonably and unseasonably—to be despised. Setting aside the will and service of the earthly king, he hastened to win for himself the supreme King by holy vigils, fasts, prayers, meditation upon sacred readings, and liberal distribution of alms.

For he daily supplied the necessities of life, both food and clothing, to so many poor people that, even if an infinite multitude of beggars flocked to him, he ceased giving because of their scarcity rather than any wish to withhold his hand. He remembered the prophetic saying: “He has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever and ever.”

Yet, so that frequent distribution and giving to the poor in this manner might not produce want, he laboured zealously to retain the possessions of the Church and recover those that had been scattered. He also endeavoured to take away church estates which his predecessors had granted less justly to persons connected by favour of secular power or some tie of kinship, and to restore the Church’s former right.

When he discovered negligence among the clerics who belonged to the king’s court, he asserted with such authority the churches and possessions that belonged to ecclesiastical jurisdiction, and continued thereafter to assert them, that sacrilegious invaders of Church property, joining certain bishops to themselves, inflamed the king and all his household against God’s saint. They protested that he had determined to nullify royal customs and grants and, according to the rules of the canons, to constrain and regulate alike the life of clergy and laity.

The king, moreover, perceived that the archbishop was showing him a lack of devotion unknown to him before; suspecting contempt from the man whom he had loved above all other men, he gradually grew bitter, and hatred entered in. He made him an outsider to the secret place of his heart and to his counsels.

Without delay there was present the accuser of the brethren, the inciter of hatred, the persecutor of concord, well aware of the king’s agitation; for he walks through the earth and goes round it seeking whom he may devour and bring into his possession. Thus he increased hatreds, prepared seeds of discord, supplied fuel for quarrels, and, having assembled his forces, attacked the holy archbishop: either to drive him shamefully from his purpose, if overcome by adversity he should assent to the law of injustice; or, if he remained firm in his judgment, to stain him with infamous murmuring and, though unable utterly to destroy his merit, at least to diminish it through impatience.

Again, he kindled the king’s mind to anger against his spiritual father and shepherd of his soul: partly through secret inward suggestion of his own, partly outwardly through the ministers of his wickedness. He armed it with malice and at last hardened it in deadly hatred. He next supplied material for hatred and arranged, as though rationally, adequate grounds for dissension. Finally, he infected bishops, princes of the realm, the king’s ministers, and members of his household with poisonous influences, so that, by making the party of the holy archbishop weaker, he might more easily overwhelm him while he fought alone in the arena; and so that, while they favoured the king’s presumptions against divine justice, he might draw the rest also to destruction.

These are Satan’s wiles, these the windings of the slippery serpent, who does not rejoice unless he has done evil and who obstructs the road by which one goes to the Lord. But Christ’s unconquered soldier, like a tower raised in Jerusalem facing Damascus, though alone in the contest, did not fear the attacks of Satan or of his followers. He sang confidently with the prophet: “The Lord is my strength, the Lord is my support, my refuge, and my deliverer; the Lord is my helper: I will not fear what man may do to me.”

Forewarned by the Saviour that those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake are blessed, he thought little of whatever the world or the devil could inflict for the defence of justice or truth, according to the saying of the apostle: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us.”

To return, therefore, to the order of the narrative: this, it is believed, was the beginning of the enmity between Saint Thomas the archbishop and the king.

## ON THE CUSTOMS WHICH THE KING WISHED TO ENROL IN THE TREASURY

While the king was staying on his estate at Woodstock, in the presence of the archbishop and the leading men of the realm, among other matters a question was raised concerning a certain custom observed in England. Two shillings were paid from each hide to the king’s officers who administered the counties in the place of sheriffs. The king wished to enrol these payments in the treasury and add them to his own revenues.

The archbishop openly resisted him, saying that they ought not to be levied as revenue.

“We shall not pay them as revenue, my lord king,” he said, “saving your good pleasure. But if the sheriffs, servants, or officials of the counties serve us worthily and protect our men, we shall by no means fail them in assistance.”

The king, angered by the archbishop’s answer, said: “By God’s eyes, they shall be paid as revenue and shall be entered in the king’s record; nor is it fitting that you should oppose this, when no one wishes to burden your men against your will.”

The archbishop, foreseeing and guarding against the introduction through his acquiescence of a custom by which posterity might be burdened, answered: “By reverence for the eyes by which you have sworn, my lord king, they shall not be paid from all my land; and, from the right of the Church, not even a single penny.”

The king was silent, checked by the bishop’s free objection. Yet the king’s anger did not rest. For, keeping silence for the time about secular matters which seemed less likely to work against the archbishop, his fury turned upon the clergy and his indignation spread against the ministers of the Church, whose injury would especially fall back upon the archbishop.

## ON A NEW METHOD OF HARMING THE ARCHBISHOP

A long-silenced accusation was revived as a newly devised method of harming the archbishop, against a cleric named Philip de Broi. He had been accused of the killing of a certain knight; but when the case had been heard before the bishop of Lincoln, he was cleared according to ecclesiastical law, and, the controversy having been settled, was declared free by the relatives.

But the king’s officer, to whose care that business belonged, wishing out of old hatred to destroy the cleric, brought the case forward again and renewed the charge of homicide. The cleric, being a freeborn man, was stung with grief and indignation and attacked the sheriff with insults. When the sheriff reported to the king the insult inflicted by the cleric, the king, as is believed, rejoiced at the opportunity to rage against him and poured out upon Philip the anger he had conceived.

When the case of the cleric was brought forward in the archbishop’s presence, the king declared that full justice would be done concerning both homicide and insult, and that the settlement already made should be of no effect whatever. The archbishop received the cleric within his own court and under the Church’s protection, that there he might speak in his own defence and answer his accuser.

The king therefore sent bishops and others of both orders to judge the cleric. He denied the homicide, maintaining that he ought not to be compelled to give an answer further on that charge; nor was a cause which solemn purgation had ended and peace made with the adversaries had buried to be brought forward again under the laws.

“But,” he said, “I confess that I dishonoured the king’s officer, overcome by bitterness of spirit; yet I promise full satisfaction for the abusive words, provided that the punishment does not exceed the bounds of reason.”
