“And we,” they replied, “decree that for two years your prebend and possessions, and all that you possess in revenues, shall remain in the king’s hand, to be spent at his pleasure upon the poor.”

The messengers further added that he should stand naked before the king’s officer, in the lay manner, offer him arms in recompense for the injury, and live in his subjection. The cleric obeyed the judgment, glad indeed to have escaped the sentence of death with which the king had threatened him.

The king, on the other hand, wishing the man to undergo judgment of death, complained that wrong was done to himself and prejudice caused to his court. He accused the bishops of having deferred to the man’s person because of the archbishop and of not having judged according to the demands of equity.

“By God’s eyes,” he said, “you shall now swear to me that you have rendered a just judgment and have not spared the man because he is a cleric.”

As they were prepared to swear, the king, not knowing what to do or where to turn in his rage, at last took counsel with the sons of Belial, who were inciting him against the holy archbishop. He constructed one device after another and, making manifest what he had conceived in his heart, summoned all the bishops who were present. With the archbishop and the princes of the realm present, he addressed them in these words:

“Lest, while we rule, the insolence of evil men spread as justice grows cold, it is my will and counsel—and reason itself supports it—that the customs and laws which I am about to deliver, and which my grandfather established, should be confirmed by you for the preservation of the people’s peace, without prejudice to the profession of your order.”

The bishops replied with one voice: “We obey your laws.”

To them he said: “I wish you to obey and confirm the laws of the kingdom which are known to have been instituted for the preservation of your order.”

Again the bishops gave the same answer as before. The king, turning to anger, swore terribly, in order to bend by threats those whom he could not bend by entreaty, that no escape would be open to them: the bishops must in every way confirm and observe the laws of the realm established for the preservation of peace.

He added that, in the time of his grandfather and earlier kings, the laws which he was now about to deliver had been observed by archbishops and bishops whom they knew numbered among the saints. Therefore, it ought neither to seem strange nor onerous to bishops now living if they followed the footsteps of their predecessors, and especially of saints.

But the venerable archbishop, suspecting the name of peace lest poison might perhaps lie hidden beneath honey, and knowing that it is not safe to set one’s foot on slippery ground or approach a danger surrounded by darkness, answered the king firmly that he wished to obey no laws shown to be contrary to divine laws. The others said the same; and that assembly broke up amid hostile contention on both sides.

The bishop of Lisieux, wishing to win again the favour of the king, who had for some time been hostile to him, arrived from overseas at this same time. The peace having been renewed, he showed by what spirit he was led: speaking what pleased the king rather than what was useful, he supplied material for deceiving his brother and conquering the archbishop, explaining the speediest way to accomplish it.

“My lord,” he said, “if the archbishop is easily to be turned from the purpose of his heart, first some bishops should be won back who will support your party and confirm your ordinances. Then, when his obstinacy has been weakened, he will not dare alone to raise his hand against the multitude. For while the steadfastness of his fellow bishops is strengthened and supported by assent, he remains unconquerable.”

It was done as he suggested.

At once three from the number of the bishops were captured unarmed, without bow or sword and without great or grave contest. Indeed, to speak more truly, they themselves, casting their weapons of war to the ground, gave their hands to the enemy. As the lord pope wrote reproachfully, like rams without horns, they departed without courage before the pursuer’s face.

Those who had crossed over to the king’s party were Hilary, bishop of Chichester; Roger, archbishop of York; and the bishop of London. From these the king’s error is believed to have received, if perhaps not its beginning, at least no slight support and increase. From them, therefore, tares were scattered; through their agency wicked seeds grew in the hearts of the rest. They promised to observe the royal customs, so that none of the others might fear to do what had been begun by those outstanding among them. The king promised that he would require nothing contrary to their order; and their security bent the others, as indeed happened without hesitation.

Armed, then, not with their counsels but with their snares and deceit, the king rose more fiercely against the archbishop. For they too sharpened their tongues like a sword against the Lord’s Christ, hurling poisoned arrows at him from the quiver of malice, now striking his strong heart with threats, now with flatteries, in order to kill the innocent man.

Accordingly, the above-named Hilary at first privately advised the saint to consent to the will of his lord the king and confirm the laws. He promised that he would restore him to the king’s friendship and make him once more a member of the royal household, as before.

But the holy archbishop replied: “You will never pervert me. It is not hidden from me that the lord of York and you, brother Hilary, have given your hands to the king’s ordinances, so that others may follow your example. But be certain that you labour in vain to stain me with participation in your guilt.”

Hilary then attacked the saint more harshly: “What do you understand in the words of our lord king, that we too may beware? The king promises that he will demand nothing unworthy of your order; and who would dare suspect otherwise? Yet, if he chooses, he will compel you, even unwilling, to observe the statutes of the kingdom, since by right of subjection you live under his power.”

The archbishop answered: “You must see whether it is expedient to fulfil what you have promised. I consent on no account.”

Meanwhile a man of great esteem among all arrived from overseas, then abbot of Eleemosyna (“the Almonry”). He declared that he had been sent by Lord Pope Alexander and carried the pope’s letters with him.

The tenor of the letters was that the archbishop should consent to the king’s will and thus be joined with him in peace. The abbot also warned him, on peril to his order, to do what the lord pope had commanded; he himself would bear the blame if the archbishop erred in any respect, provided only that he consented to peace.

The abbot also had letters from the cardinals, in which they stated that they had received assurance from the king that he would ask nothing else of the archbishop except that he assent verbally to the statutes he was about to deliver. Thus he would be publicly honoured before the magnates of the realm when they met together, and he would not be required to consent to any custom contrary to his order.

The abbot further added—being powerful in persuasion—that the king did not in any way wish to be defeated, nor was it fitting that he should be. “Let him yield to the king,” he said, “and there will be peace; the kingdom will be subject to him as before, all that belongs to the king will be his, and none of this disturbance will come to remembrance.

“Moreover, the king honoured your person above all men, and you served him with a fidelity greater than anyone’s. Therefore, lest the bond of affection be dissolved through the one from whom it ought to have received strengthening, and lest what you have gained by so many labours and such devotion perish through a brief disturbance.”

Why say more? The abbot did not cease until, by the persuasive words of human wisdom in which he excelled, he led the deceived archbishop with him to the king. For he was readily believed, being a man who appeared to possess such great authority.

As the abbot and the others assembled for the same purpose pressed him, the archbishop promised the king that he would keep the ancestral customs in good faith. He trusted that, as had been promised, he would hear no more concerning the matter; nor did he suspect deceit after the assurance had been given.

Hearing this, the king said: “In order that we may trust your pledge, it is fitting that you should acknowledge these things at a public hearing. For all know how greatly you have opposed me, contradicting the public laws of the realm. Let us now summon, for an appointed day, the magnates and leading men of the realm on my part, and the bishops and clergy on yours, so that when you consent before the multitude, none of the others may dare oppose our laws.”

Accordingly, at the royal castle of Clarendon a solemn council was assembled. The chapters of the customs to be observed were set forth, and the king called the archbishop to account concerning the promise he had made.

“I wish,” he said, “that according to the agreement you should publicly declare what you have promised.”

But the holy archbishop, led by repentance because he had conceded that he would observe a custom under which the liberty of the Church was certainly endangered, groaned deeply over his pledge. Considering that no slight injury to ecclesiastical peace would arise from this occasion, he chose to fall into the hands of men and incur the king’s anger rather than abandon the law of God. Having recovered from this lapse, he feared no threats of any human being that might lead him further from the straight path.

For the holy man perceived that this was the king’s design and endeavour: to reduce the liberty of the Church to royal right. And that it may be clear that this was the king’s intention and will, we have inserted in this work only six chapters of the constitution then made and published, the authority of which the saint himself condemned in his letter. They are these:

1. That no appeal may be made to the Apostolic See without the king’s permission.
2. That an archbishop or bishop may not leave the kingdom or come at the summons of the lord pope without the king’s permission.
3. That a bishop may not excommunicate anyone who holds directly of the king, without the king’s permission, or place under interdict his land or that of his officials.
4. That a bishop may not compel anyone concerning perjury or breach of faith.
5. That clerics be brought before secular courts.
6. That laymen—whether the king or others—may hear cases concerning tithes or churches.

Let those who still today accuse the holy archbishop of having resisted the king too obstinately consider whether it was just to show patience amid these and many things of this sort, rather than cry out with the prophet: “Zeal for your house has consumed me.” For he had certainly read that one who consents to sinners and defends another person in sin will be accursed before God and men, and will be rebuked with the most severe rebuke.

But when the king saw that the archbishop repented of his promises and withdrew from what he had agreed, unable any longer to contain himself through excessive indignation, he hurled disorderly threats: that he would bend their necks and, if power did not fail him, crush their pride. Yet neither threats nor admonitions could turn the saint from his judgment or humble him to the royal will. He was nevertheless harassed, in the hope that at some point, overcome by weariness, he might consent.

Two of those who still in some degree followed him—namely, the bishops of Salisbury and Norwich—besought the archbishop in much anxiety and sorrow to have compassion on their cause.

“Because of you,” they said, “the king’s indignation, renewed in its old hostility towards us, burns so greatly that all this malice will turn to danger for our lives unless today you make peace.”

The same exhortation was made by two counsellors who were of the king’s counsel: that he should provide for himself, have pity on the Church, and care for his own people. They added, threatening him, that unless he made peace with the king that day, he and they would fall into such great and unheard-of guilt that the king and the whole kingdom would be mocked by all around as a nation without counsel and without law.

But the holy archbishop, like an unconquered soldier hastening amid the enemy’s ranks toward the prize, whom prayers had not moved and who did not think it worthy to yield to threats, was still to be tested, so that after his lapse he might rise more strongly against the adversary; for all things work together for good to those who are chosen.

[Col. 0018D] Two Knights Templar, therefore—both men of great renown and, it is believed, no less distinguished in courage—saw that the king’s wrath would be implacable unless the archbishop complied with the royal will. They approached him with the same arguments as the former speakers, saying: “How long, lord, will you act thus, without having compassion on the holy Church whose governance you have undertaken? Give honour to the royal majesty; let the goads of anger be stilled, and you will be one again as at the beginning. Otherwise you have exposed the clergy and the whole Church to grievous and lamentable ruin.”

Moreover, they declared themselves assured and certain that the king required nothing unbecoming to the archbishop or contrary to proper order; and, should it prove otherwise if he consented, they boldly pledged themselves and their own integrity. Finally, lest he disbelieve their promises, they agreed [Col. 0019A] that they themselves should perish without remedy or end if there were any deception or fraud in the king’s conscience against the archbishop—except only that he should be honoured at a public hearing and should concede before all what he had opposed. They maintained that the king in no way wished to be defeated, lest he appear the lesser and others should more boldly disregard the king’s ordinances when they saw the archbishop resisting them.

The holy archbishop, deeply moved by the tears of these brethren, whom he knew to be emulators of truth and faith, and seeing opposite him the holy Church close to destruction unless his assent softened the king’s mind, said: “I yield to your counsels and assent to the king’s will.” Before all who heard, he promised in good faith that he would observe the laws and customs of the realm.

The king immediately, as if snatching this statement from the archbishop’s mouth, said: “You have heard what the archbishop has promised at my request. I wish him to impose upon the other bishops what he himself has conceded.” “I grant it,” he said. Without delay all assented in the assembly.

Then the king, having said to the archbishop, “You are always my adversary,” went on to address the magnates and counsellors: “Since we have the bishops’ promise concerning the observance of the laws of the realm, let us deal prudently and carefully with the matter, lest at some time we have need to discuss the laws again among ourselves. Therefore let the laws of my grandfather King Henry be recalled, written down, and publicly recited before all, with the utmost diligence, so that no one may presume to impose upon us anything new as though we had handed it down.”

When the business had been completed according to the king’s decree, he said: “I wish this writing to be sealed and confirmed with the archbishop’s seal.” Then the holy archbishop, at last perceiving the fraud he had suspected, and mindful of the faith he owed to God, replied: “This shall not be done while this soul breathes in this little vessel.”

For the king’s household officers, when they advised him to agree, had assured the archbishop that the laws would never be written down and that no recollection of them would ever be made, if only he honoured the king verbally in the hearing of the nobles; they also said that the king would wholly yield to the archbishop’s will and that all ill will on either side would cease. Now, seeing that he had been deceived by a feigned agreement, he was grieved to the depths of his soul and resolved to provide more cautiously for himself in future.

But the king and his counsellors, devising another scheme, divided the aforesaid written document as one divides an indenture and handed one half to the archbishop. He accepted it reluctantly, indeed, but with a view to his defence, and said to his own followers: “I know that what we have done will be condemned unless a sound intention excuses a discreditable act. Above all, from this we shall discover their deceit: their tricks will become clear and their snares exposed, so that henceforth they will spread their net in vain before the eyes of birds. Until now they have stretched cords into a trap in order to cast us down; but now all their fraud is uncovered, and we can readily be on our guard.”

When the council had at last been dissolved in this manner, the holy man went on his way, sorrowful and exceedingly angry with himself because he had consented to such monstrous wickedness. For he had obeyed the king, at least in part, yet had irreparably lost the king’s favour. Nor did he allow his error to pass unpunished: he suspended himself from the celebration of Mass and remained under this sentence until he was absolved by the lord pope.

Meanwhile the bishop of Évreux came from overseas to the king in order to reconcile the archbishop to him. But the king said threateningly: “These are my words: for all the days during which we both live, you may speak; yet there shall be no peace unless the archbishop obtains from the pope that he seal the laws of my realm with his own seal and ratify them by his authority.”

At the bishop’s urging, the holy archbishop wrote through him to the lord pope, asking him to deign to confirm the royal enactments by his authority and the impression of his seal. But the pope, immediately perceiving that the archbishop had made this request under the utmost compulsion, rejected and condemned the document with some indignation. When the king learned this, he took it badly that his plan had been frustrated; his wrath against the archbishop grew fiercer, and he attributed wholly to him the pope’s refusal to consent to his abuses.

From that day, therefore, the king summoned counsellors who spoke what pleased him rather than what was fitting. He multiplied contrivances and renewed his engines; nor did he care by what means it was done, provided that the archbishop’s constancy might be bent and his authority diminished. The royal household conceived that, if they could obtain from the pope for the archbishop of York a legation over the realm, they could easily shake the lord of Canterbury by this means.

Two clerics were sent to the pope, and much effort was made, with persistent urging, that the king’s will might be accomplished. Yet, after other answers, this was given to the envoys: that the Church of York had always been of lower dignity and authority than the Church of Canterbury; and he added, “It shall remain so as long as I live.” The messengers reported, protesting that, unless the requested legation satisfied the king, the archbishop would be punished by a sentence touching his life. Hearing this, the pope sighed from his heart.

But considering, as a very wise man, that one must sometimes consent to a lesser harm in order wholly to avoid a greater, he sent the legation to the king, yet strictly forbade it authority to burden anyone or to advance York against the lord of Canterbury. The envoys pressed him, affirming that it was not in the king’s mind to burden anyone on this pretext, but to humble the resistant archbishop by this permission and make him more devoted to the royal majesty. Above all, they said, this would prevent the audacity and actions of notorious persons under ecclesiastical orders from becoming insolent to the king’s injury, when they perceived that the king did not lack the power to burden the archbishop, under whose protection clerics did not fear to violate public laws.

Yet the envoys could by no means extort any legation other than that already described. Nevertheless, displaying it at public assemblies, the king caused it to be proclaimed that he had obtained authority from the lord pope by which he might restrain the archbishop’s presumptions—although, as has been said, apostolic authority had removed, even with the permitted legation, every power of inflicting harm or advancing anyone.

[Col. 0021A] Therefore, since he could neither by reason nor by this quasi-apostolic authority burden the archbishop in his own person, he persecuted his subjects instead. With a grim expression displaying the deadly hatred that he cherished in his heart, he did by threats what he could not accomplish by deed. In every possible way, and upon every pretext, he ceased not to oppress ecclesiastics and the Church of God in order to provoke the archbishop. We omit to recount how many disputes he had, how many injuries he endured from the king and royal ministers in defence of ecclesiastical liberty, and how many insults he suffered from invaders of Church property under cover of the king’s agitation.

But the disordered behaviour of persons in holy orders also increased the ill will between king and archbishop. At that time they appeared more abundantly than usual ensnared in public crimes; the king’s counsel and will decreed that they should be subjected to the public laws of the realm, but the archbishop protested in the freedom of his authority.

For it was the king’s will that those in orders caught in theft, homicide, or even treason should first be stripped of their orders and afterwards be delivered, according to the nature of the offence, to the loss of their limbs. Thus a deadly spectacle was created, mournful for every age. One might see men of the order of priests, deacons, and lower grades dragged before councils, there to be condemned by laymen against the sacred canons—either to death, or to mutilation and bodily disgrace, or to miserable imprisonment in the king’s gaol.

But the holy archbishop, grieving that his fellow servants, for whom Christ died, should be subjected to such indignities, and seeing in this the destruction of the Church’s liberty, took their miseries upon himself. He pleaded their cause and resisted on their behalf with all the strength he could. He promised the king that he would answer for the clerics in the court of the Church and would render them to justice for whatever accusation might be made.

The king, however, persisting in his determination, declared that none of those in custody should leave unless they were degraded, handed over to torturers, and had paid the penalties they deserved. On the other hand the archbishop answered that it would not be so: “I shall never degrade them; I shall never expose God’s ministers to lay justice. I shall correct offenders according to God’s laws and the decrees of the Fathers; and, so far as lies in me, I shall not allow the dignities of the Church, which the authority of the saints has transmitted down through so many ages to our own time, to perish.”

[Col. 0021D] Since, therefore, the king could not oppress those in orders as he had intended, because the archbishop resisted, he complained in these words to the magnates and set forth his case against the archbishop:

“I have sworn that I would preserve justice and peace in the kingdom entrusted to me by divine ordinance, and that I would condemn those who lived unjustly by just judgment according to their deserts. This I have done thus far, and would do to the extent of my power, if the archbishop did not disturb us and the realm by his obstinacy. By his authority he protects murderers, defends thieves and sacrilegious persons, and receives those who flee to him as enemies of justice, granting peace to those who confound the peace of the realm.

“And indeed we rightly pursue clerics, among whom, if one attends carefully, scarcely anyone will be found worse in every crime and disgraceful deed. Furthermore, to greater contempt, he draws accused persons out of public custody and prisons and absolves them; under an interdict of Christianity he withdraws them from my court, so that due justice may not be exercised upon them. Finally, what are we, what is the entire realm worth, if the laws of justice perish? They will surely perish if I spare them. But I shall not spare them if they have transgressed. Let clerics who have been apprehended be immediately delivered to the officers of justice; stripped of their orders, let them be subject to punishments according to the laws of justice.”

He added also how his grandfather, in his own time, had corrected those in orders according to the common laws of the realm, when there had been holy archbishops and bishops alike. “Therefore,” he said, “I declare that it shall be to his harm and confusion if the archbishop opposes these measures which, as we know, so many saints have patiently endured.”

Having said this, the holy archbishop, with great anger and indignation but withholding nothing of the truth, replied in due course to the king’s accusation: “If it pleased you, lord king, you would have spoken more correctly. For I am not accustomed to protect murderers or thieves, but to pursue them. Yet I have judged it wicked—and account it a crime—that persons consecrated to divine worship should, to the contempt of holy mother Church, be condemned under lay laws, confounded by deprivation of orders, and bodily destroyed.

“No law has taught this, nor does reason agree that a single transgression should undergo a double punishment. No argument shall move me from this position. When they have fallen and been apprehended in a capital crime, let them be deprived of their orders on the condition that thereafter they remain immune from bodily mutilation. If, after degradation, they return again to their vomit, then, if it pleases you, let them be swallowed alive, fastened to gibbets, and punished with unheard-of penalties.

“As for the assertion that your grandfather or anyone else raged to the death of clerics, we have learned that this was done once, through a sudden presumption; but it is exceedingly unsuitable to take examples of justice from those who affirmed as laws whatever they chose by their own arbitrary will.

“Finally, when holy David had designated Solomon as king, the priest Abiathar took part in crowning and consecrating Adonijah against the king’s purpose. For this schism and rash act, we read that he was indeed suspended from office and deprived of his former and paternal dignity; but he suffered no loss of limbs.

“Therefore it seems unworthy that a human judge should exact a double punishment for a single offence, when the Lord, Judge of all, judges no one, as it is written, ‘twice for the same thing.’ And what more severe disgrace can ever be imposed upon a man in orders than degradation? No greater reproach can be inflicted upon him. Therefore, since by divine dispensation I have been appointed to protect the Church of God and those in orders by my patronage and guardianship, nothing but death shall separate me from this resolve.”

When it was seen that the archbishop stood immovable in his judgment, neither yielding in any respect to the king’s presumptions nor allowing ecclesiastics to be treated dishonourably, [Col. 0023A] the king was wholly inflamed with rage. At last, breaking silence, he burst out in these words: “I shall humble the archbishop’s pride, and there I shall duly consume his obstinacy whence I raised him to so lofty a height.”

Much time passed in this dispute. The king strove to recall the archbishop from his judgment, in order to trample down ecclesiastical liberty; the archbishop, conversely, resisted by every means in defence of the clergy. Indeed, he now seemed to act alone, deprived of the fellowship of the bishops. Almost all had turned back and followed the king; fear of the king prevented even those thought to have remained from freely speaking against the evils being done. Thus they left him alone in the conflict and without human consolation. Yet he could not be alone, since justice fought with him.

The rest, loving human glory rather than God’s, turned their backs when they saw the array for battle. They increased the enemies’ strength and gave a horn to the sinner; for, fearing to draw the sword of God’s word, they trembled there with fear where no fear was. But God also shall scatter the bones of those who please men, because those who wish to please men are not servants of Christ.

Why they abandoned the archbishop, the lord pope explains, writing to the bishops that they rendered greater reverence to man than to God. Let them see for themselves what they will say and do at God’s judgment: they who, by speaking things pleasing to the king and favouring error, caused him himself to go astray—him whom above all they ought to have rebuked, lest others sin more boldly by his example. For how could he ever believe himself to be in error when, though one alone protested, the whole body of the others assented to the error? Thus, according to the prophet, “as the people, so the priest.” Indeed, the bishops’ consent alone would have sufficed for the dishonour of their order, had they not additionally armed the king’s mind against the man of God by wicked counsels.

## ON THE CONSPIRACY OF THE BISHOPS AGAINST THE ARCHBISHOP

The holy archbishop, therefore, seeing that nearly all the bishops had conspired unanimously against him; that the king’s indignation could by no reasoning be softened; and that in all this no sign of peace appeared, resolved for a time to withdraw his presence. He did so in the hope that, with the one thought to have supplied the cause of disturbance removed—because he did not favour the king’s usurpations—the king might at least have compassion on the desolated Church.

At the same time he determined to leave his native land for another reason: he intended to approach the lord pope and, by his authority and assistance, bring some relief in some measure to the oppressed king. Taking a few men with him, he embarked. At first the winds blew favourably; but when they were already being carried out to sea, the sailors spoke among themselves: “What are we doing, carrying the king’s enemy out of the kingdom? We act foolishly. We and all our descendants will be disinherited by perpetual proscription.”

They also told the archbishop that in such a wind no one could make land where he had ordered. Then he replied quite calmly: “If even the winds oppose our intention, let the Lord’s will be done; and you, make for whatever harbour the Lord assigns.” They immediately brought him back to England.

The holy man afterwards recognized and confessed to his companions that it had not yet been God’s will for him to cross the sea then. A grave conflict was still reserved for him, and trials through which he must pass so that he might appear more approved. And so it happened. But when the king heard that the archbishop had embarked, he remained sad and anxious until he learned of his return; for he greatly feared that, if the archbishop went to the lord pope, the realm would be placed under interdict.

## ON THE COUNCIL OF NORTHAMPTON

The king appointed a solemn council to be held at Northampton Castle and ordered all who held directly of him to attend; the archbishop also was summoned.

Before that council, one of the king’s household, a man powerful with the king, claimed before the archbishop’s court an estate which had belonged of old to the Church by right. When, justice objecting, the knight could not maintain his claim, he informed the king of the affair. He complained that the archbishop had taken away his right by an unjust judgment, asserted that the archbishop’s court had acted falsely, and alleged, upon oath, that this had redounded to the king’s injury.

The king, seeking occasions against the archbishop, ordered him to appear and answer the knight concerning the alleged violence. As he could not attend because severe illness detained him, he sent representatives to answer the king and excused his absence on the appointed day. But the king accepted no excuse at all, suspecting that he had evaded the public hearing. Thus, so far as the outward appearance of the case was concerned, the holy bishop was summoned to Northampton, as though he were to be judged on these matters before Caesar’s tribunal. In fact and intention, however—as the end of the proceeding shows—the object was that, publicly attacked and drawn away from his position, he might either consent to the king concerning the acceptance and observance of the laws of the realm, or, if he resisted more obstinately, receive a sentence of condemnation.

He came, therefore, as has been said, and immediately approached the king humbly, asking him, for the common benefit and safety of both parties, to deign to grant permission to go to the lord pope. At this request the king turned angry and replied that he would by no means depart as he hoped: “First,” he said, “you shall answer for having delayed to come when I summoned you.”

The archbishop replied: “Let not my lord speak thus. Illness detained and excused me.” But the king was softened neither by his humble excuse nor by illness; he ordered judgment to be made at once and the penalty for contempt determined. It was adjudged that he should give the king five hundred pounds in satisfaction for his delay.

When the judgment was read, the saint groaned, seeing iniquity in the place of judgment. As he tried to oppose the judgment, everyone cried out against him and urged him, laying anger aside, at least in this matter to make the king’s mind favourable to himself. At length he assented, hoping that the controversy thus raised might thereby be ended. He was required to give hostages who would answer for the stipulated money.

When these had been found, the knight’s case, from which the dispute had arisen, was again brought forward. Seeing that they were seeking an occasion on which to accuse him, the saint declared with complete freedom that he was obliged to answer no one in this matter outside the court of the Church. The knight had not been able to prove that anything contrary to justice had been adjudged against him in the archbishop’s court; moreover, the oath by which he had attempted to invalidate the judgment of the Church was neither customary nor lawful. Therefore the archbishop concluded that no reason compelled him to answer concerning this affair outside his own court.

And the knight who had not feared to burden the holy archbishop and lay his hand upon the Lord’s anointed, having in that same year lost two sons whom he had intended to make heirs of the Church’s patrimony, himself also lost both life and possession.

But when the king saw that these matters did not advance the archbishop’s accusation, he devised another charge. He ordered the archbishop to render an account of the monies he had received for safekeeping during his chancellorship, and without delay to state how and upon what he had expended them.

At first troubled by the novelty of this unexpected question, the archbishop finally answered that it was unfitting to reopen a case concerning matters long ago settled by a solemn discharge. The king swore by the eyes of Him who sees all things that he wished to hear an account of all these matters on the next day.

When the archbishop pleaded the shortness of the respite and said that it was neither lawful nor consonant with reason to answer concerning so great a matter with such haste, [Col. 0025C] the king swore again, as before, that no excuse would be accepted and no longer delay granted; he must answer on the morrow.

The saint had spent the day in disputes and, as evening had already come, was received into lodging. Soon seized by a violent pain in the spleen, he lay down in bed. Passing the night without food and sleepless, consumed by miserable pain, he scarcely lived to see the day. He was accustomed to suffer in this manner, but now he was more anxious than usual, his blood no doubt disturbed after the day’s anger and disputes.

The king’s officers came to press the saint to attend the council. He excused himself, pleaded illness, and showed the sweat that evidenced his distress. He promised that he would go to court when the violence of his sickness had passed. The king swore terribly: he must come; there would be no excuse. And the more anxiously the archbishop complained, the more messengers the king sent to bring him before the court.

At last, suspecting perhaps that the illness was feigned in order to evade the hearing, the king sent two of the noblest and foremost men of the realm, the earls of Leicester and Cornwall, to report to him lest the archbishop try to gain time by his pretence. The earls stood before the holy man and said that he must present himself before the court without delay or excuse. The saint explained the extremity of his distress. The earls pressed him; he begged them, adjuring them by the name of the Saviour that a delay might at least be granted for that day: “Tomorrow,” he said, “if life remains with me, I shall hear what pleases the lord king, or I shall attend carried in a chair.”

The earls returned after granting the delay, but subject to the condition laid down by the saint.

That same day he was told for certain that some of the king’s men had conspired to kill him, and that it had been discussed beforehand with the king that, if he went to court, he would either be beheaded or cast into prison. He was terrified by the grievous report and trembled in his whole body, as he afterwards confessed. He feared death less than chains, lest his freedom to speak for the Church’s cause should be taken away; and it is certain that he feared this not only then but always.

Having confessed his fear to a devout man who feared God, he was advised that, when he went forth to court in the morning, he should offer to the Saviour the saving sacrifice in honour of the blessed martyr Stephen, so that the enemies’ malice might not harm him that day. He obeyed; having celebrated the saving mysteries with much devotion and tears, he put the holy stole around his shoulders beneath his outer garments, fortified his right hand with the standard of the holy cross, and bore the cross in his own hands, lest the example of his Passion be far removed from him.

## ON THE ARCHBISHOP’S ENTRY

Thus the noble martyr, accompanied by God alone, entered the place where the bishops and certain nobles were seated. The king sat with his household in an inner chamber, for on that day king and archbishop did not see one another.

Entering, he sat at some distance, holding the cross. The bishop of London approached him and urged him to lay it down, lest he appear to have entered against the lord king as though carrying a drawn sword. “In this way,” he said, “anger is kindled, discord [Col. 0026C] is increased, and the king’s mind is exasperated.”

When he could not persuade him by words, he would have torn the cross from his hand by force, had not the man of God held it with both hands, resisting by equal force. The archbishop of York likewise repeated what had been urged by the former and exhorted him also to lay down the cross: “You enter armed against the lord king. But be assured that the royal sword cuts hard, and is already drawn against you, unless you act more prudently.”

Then the holy archbishop, speaking humbly so as to give no opportunity to those plotting against him, said: “I know that the king’s sword cuts—but it cuts flesh. The cross passes through the soul itself and pierces spiritual powers. Far be from me what you allege: that I should at any time bear a sword against the lord king. For the cross bears peace, not a sword, making peace between things in heaven and things on earth; and I desire peace, nor shall I relinquish the cross.”

The king had decided to revive the accusations formerly brought against the clerics in order to accuse the archbishop on that basis. But the magnates dissuaded him, lest, if a charge were raised against ecclesiastics, the bishops should each defend their own men together with the archbishop. “Another question,” they said, “must be proposed, one that seems to concern the archbishop in particular.”

Meanwhile those who had attended the king’s council informed the holy man that, unless he took counsel for himself, he would that day either be beheaded or cast into prison and chains, as he had heard the day before.

The venerable archbishop was fearless for himself, but troubled and anxious for the cause of the desolated Church and Christ’s poor, to whom he seemed to afford whatever shadow of protection he could. He considered carefully whether any refuge of escape lay open to him. After deliberating a little, when he saw absolutely no one who would speak a word to cool the king’s fury toward him, though bishops and magnates stood around him, he appealed to the Apostolic See, which seemed the sole remedy for the accused. “For,” he added, “this court inquires how the Church may be burdened.”

They were astonished at the sudden appeal and raged against him. The bishop of London, pricked, it is believed, by conscience, begged that the appeal be remitted in his case. The holy archbishop answered him: “I absolve neither you nor any of the rest; but by the force of obedience, under the authority of God and the lord pope, I command all of you together to exact full justice from any man, whoever he may be, who lays hands upon me.” Adding this, he commanded them under anathema and at peril of their order and souls not to spare such a person.

Then the bishop of Winchester, while all were agitated at the appeal that had been made, wished to secure peace and feared that something deadly might arise against the archbishop. He therefore exhorted him in these words: “Return the archbishopric, then, into the king’s hand and mercy. Perhaps in this way the king’s indignation against you and us alike, caused by you, may subside. Otherwise I foresee a deadly tumult, and no place remaining for peace or concord.”

The archbishop, on the contrary, protested with an unqualified oath that he would never surrender the archbishopric as long as he could retain it. “I did not receive it,” he said, “on condition that I should surrender it, but that I should spend myself for it.”

Thereafter, some of the bishops, perceiving that the king’s counsel was devising and hastening the archbishop’s death, conferred sadly and anxiously—especially because of the appeal that had been made—on how they might snatch him from the king’s hand and the present danger. For this reason they addressed the men whom they knew to have been, from the beginning, ministers of malice and instigators of discord: namely, the archbishops of York and London and the bishop of Chichester. (The two previously named had not yet associated the bishop of Salisbury with themselves.) They spoke as follows:

“Your whole body knows that from the beginning of his consecration you have persecuted the archbishop; indeed, there has never been sound love or fellowship between you. Therefore, if he is killed now while you are silent, it will redound especially to your disgrace and reproach. The king also will bear an everlasting stain, and all of us shall suffer irreparable suspension from our order and office.”

Finally, after conferring together, they all agreed that, if the king allowed them, they would appeal against the archbishop to the presence of the lord pope. By this stratagem they would rescue him from the present danger and, once removed from his see, condemn him to perpetual silence.

They approached the king and begged him to have compassion on himself, on them, and on the whole realm, lest by so great and such an act he and all his posterity be stained by everlasting disgrace. “Let this cause of the archbishop,” they said, “be entrusted to our care and concern. We shall humble him to your will and impose perpetual silence upon him henceforth.”

The king assented on this condition. Without delay, the bishops standing before the archbishop themselves appealed to the presence of the lord pope: they alleged that, at his command, they had accepted and confirmed as laws to be observed the royal enactments which, after making his promise, he was trying to assert were contrary to ecclesiastical institutions.

The holy archbishop gladly accepted the appeal, desiring nothing so much as that a hearing should be granted. But the king’s agitation still pressed on, and the limbs of the Devil—his wicked counsellors—so sharpened him that he ordered soldiers to demand that the archbishop immediately account for thirty thousand pounds which, during his chancellorship, [Col. 0028B] he had squandered without the knowledge of the king and of those responsible for the affairs of the realm.

The man of God replied freely that it was in no way fitting to raise a question concerning matters which, as the people bore witness, had been lawfully settled: “When I was chosen to this honour at the word of my lord the king, public authority declared me free from every future exaction. This ought not to have escaped your memory; nor is it hidden from my lord that I expended everything on the affairs of the realm and in his service, if he deigns to consider it. Therefore no reason compels me to enter a case on this account either.”

On hearing this answer, the king turned angry and, in his accustomed way, swore by God’s eyes: “He is my man and owes submission, yet will not render me an account? He holds broad estates from me and refuses to answer. Let it be determined at once to what sentence he is subject for contempt.”

“They say,” however, “that he is not to be judged for this alone. For his presumption is graver and his contempt more intolerable in that he seeks to accuse his lord’s court of falsehood while calling upon another court’s judgment.” And certain persons of episcopal rank, who need not be named here, are said to have taken part in this counsel.

They proceeded to judgment, where justice had no place: where the just man was oppressed, the innocent condemned, and the lover of equity sentenced, with none resisting or speaking against it. What greater wickedness could Pilate’s household, Herod’s soldiers, or Nero’s malice have devised? Here nothing was observed of law, nothing was left to equity. Finally, so that free licence to commit wrongdoing might be given without any protest, it was decreed that he should be reduced to chains and thrust into prison as a disturber and traitor to the common peace.

## ON THE TWO EARLS
Two consuls are at once sent—the same men who have already been mentioned three times above as having come to the man of God—to recite to the archbishop the sentence pronounced by the king and the princes. But when the holy archbishop was being assailed by many persons and on many charges, lest, by standing, he should dishonour the priestly office, he answered wonderfully, taking his seat, as was divinely inspired: namely, that a greater person ought not to be summoned to judgment by lesser persons, nor be bound by their sentence. “Order,” he said, “is thrown into confusion if the sheep strikes the shepherd, the disciple [Col. 0029A] the master, the son beats the parent; for gold is not more precious than lead to the degree that priestly dignity is above royal power.” He also told the envoys that he would by no means submit to a judgment after an appeal had been made. The messengers replied: “How,” they said, “will you evade a public decree, avoid the sentence? You hold great estates from the king, and will you not answer in the king’s court, will you not hear the judgment?” But as they urged all this, the saint looked upon them with some indignation and said: “What I hold is not an inheritance, nor is it from the king, but from God, to whom what I possess was given as alms. And I command you, by reverence for the divine name and for the sacraments of the Christian faith, that today you pronounce no sentence against me and hold no judgment.” Yet the laymen [Col. 0029B] from the king’s council who stood round about, and the suffragan bishops—indeed, rather, his opponents—condemned him nevertheless, while he said these things and appealed to the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, as the athlete of the Lord withdrew from the council of evildoers, they assailed him on every side with curses and insults, shouting, “Look, the traitor is going away.” Finally, when he had come into the hall, where the crowd was seated together with several of the royal ministers, he stumbled so severely that he could scarcely prevent himself from falling. What courage he had then, when he had lost every confidence of escape, he himself, who endured these things, could afterwards scarcely recount, fearing lest he should be torn to pieces. For immediately, as it is written, “Because the enemy does not hide himself in adversity,” Robert de Broc cried out: “The king’s traitor [Col. 0029C] is leaving, the king’s traitor is leaving,” while the others shouted along with him and, rushing forward, threw twisted straw and every light object at hand from every side. Then a disgraceful outcry arose, no less tumultuous than if fire or an enemy’s assault had overrun the four quarters of a city. But when it was suggested to the king that it would be a lasting reproach to him if he allowed the archbishop to be trampled upon and torn apart within his own court, it was cried out by the king’s command that he should be allowed to depart freely.

The man of God answered no one. Astonished and trembling lest perhaps he should be detained, and with day now declining toward evening, he withdrew to his lodging. There, when of his so numerous household he found no more than six attendants, [Col. 0029D] the rest having scattered through fear and threats from the royal party wherever each thought himself safe, he brought in crowds of poor people and took refreshment with them. Then he ordered the attendants who were present to carry his bed into the chapel of St Andrew—for he was lodging with monks—and to arrange it behind the high altar, as though he intended to rest there for refuge.

But when deep evening had now fallen, taking with him two brethren to whom he had previously disclosed the secret of his plan, and a faithful servant, only the four of them escaped through the northern gate. For a violent flood of rain and wintry storm ensured that absolutely no one would be concerned about their departure; all the other gates were more carefully barred. The man of God had certainly learned from informants that, if he awaited the next day, he would without delay [Col. 0030A] be thrust into prison. They travelled throughout the night; and when dawn at last broke, they entered Lincoln and lay hidden with a townsman named James, known to the brethren. The saint also assumed the dress of a lay brother and, changing his name, was called Brother Dermannus. From there, after a short crossing by boat, they rested for several days at Sempringham. Then, their strength having been restored, they were received at the granges of Chikestrande, where they found the concealment they desired.

And, that it may be clear how holy and pious was the intention with which the holy man undertook that flight, his faithful Saviour in later time honoured that very lodging with many miracles. Taking also a canon who was a priest, they travelled by night and hid themselves during the day in more suitable places, until at last they reached the harbour [Col. 0030B] of Sanwicum. There they were secretly carried over in a small boat and landed upon the sand at low tide, avoiding the public harbour. As they proceeded for some time over the sand in haste, the holy archbishop fell to the ground, impeded by the unusual bulkiness of his clothing and shoes. Rising, he raised his hands and, looking up, groaned heavily. Warned by experience as a teacher, he understood how little hope ought to be placed in uncertain riches, how deceitful and fleeting is all the glory of the present life. For the abundance which, only shortly before, had supplied him with powerful and costly horses according to his wish had now so diminished that scarcely the cheapest pack-animal could be found: a hired beast, haltered with hay and without a saddle, so that in Christ’s poverty, himself now made poor, he might begin to glory for Christ.

But what [Col. 0030C] alarm, what anxiety seized the fugitives, lest they should suddenly be captured and taken back—who could tell it? Finally, to increase their fear, when at St Omer they could no longer remain concealed, they encountered Richard de Lucy, who had been sent to the count on a certain mission.

When the knight recognized him, he approached the archbishop and urged him to return with him, promising to reconcile him to the king. The archbishop excused himself and refused to return; nor did he dare entrust himself to the knight, knowing that the king’s mind, once estranged, was implacable. Rather, he would go to the pope, and would thereafter return with the pope’s help and counsel. The knight swelled with anger and threats, forbidding him to place further confidence in the pope, but rather to avoid him as an enemy. To this the archbishop replied: [Col. 0030D] “I have deserved not threats or reproaches, but you owe me loyalty and obedience.” The man of God sent to the count, asking for a guide and free passage through Flanders. The count threatened him; but the archbishop turned to his Lord, who does not abandon those who hope in him nor withdraws mercy from the race of the righteous. With God himself as guide and the bishop of Thérouanne assisting, that very night he was delivered from the lion’s mouth and the beast’s hand; he avoided both king and count and passed safely through Flanders. The next day he sent word to his companions to hasten after him and come to Soissons.

When the archbishop’s flight became known and public, the king sent envoys to the king of France, asking that he not permit the archbishop to be received in his kingdom or to have [Col. 0031A] refuge there. They maintained that in their mutual reconciliation both had agreed that, if a fugitive from either of them were captured in the other’s kingdom, he should at once be detained and returned to his lord; “and now,” they said, “the most powerful man after the king has gone out by night and become a fugitive.” At first the king dissembled, as though ignorant of what or whom they meant. Then the messengers said that Archbishop Thomas, unable to render an account concerning the matters put to him, had, as proof of a guilty conscience, evaded his lord’s judgment and secretly left the kingdom.

The king replied: “I have seen Thomas as archbishop; I knew him well as chancellor. Nor is it hidden from me with what devotion he served the king—not merely outwardly nor in appearance, but in faithfulness. A worthy recompense is rendered for his service: the king neither makes peace with him nor permits him to find refuge here. Worthily indeed has he rewarded his service, pursuing in a foreign kingdom a man expelled from his own.” The envoys answered: “The archbishop whom you protect has proved an enemy and adversary to your kingdom. More than once he plotted your own death, and he subjected no small part of the kingdom of France to his lord’s power.” But the king swore an oath: “If,” he said, “he had served me according to my desire, I would by no means have proved ungrateful; and now, if I knew where he was, I would hasten to meet him as he came.”

The messengers begged him at least to do this for the king of England, out of reciprocal affection: to write against the archbishop to the pope, lest he also entrap the pope to the injury of the king and of the whole kingdom. The messengers departed; and the king immediately wrote through a trusted man to the lord pope, asking that he deign to extend to Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, the fatherly [Col. 0031C] affection which he had always shown the king himself, and to protect him, lest on any pretext he listen to anyone against one who pursues justice.

Meanwhile the holy archbishop prepared to set out for the pope in order to prosecute his appeal, but the king’s envoys forestalled him. For as soon as the king heard the French king’s answer, he sent to the pope the Archbishop of York, the bishops of Worcester, Exeter, and Chichester, together with other noble and distinguished persons. Standing before the lord pope, they pleaded the king’s cause with considerable ingenuity and eloquence, believing that they could deceive that breast full of wisdom with artfully composed speech. But the most holy pope, preserving in both parties [Col. 0031D] the traces of truth, rebuked and confounded one of these prelates, who was calumniating the holy archbishop immoderately and more harshly than justice allowed: “Brother,” he said, “restrain yourself. Do not speak evil of your neighbour, for I do not patiently listen to anyone who maligns the archbishop.”

The envoys continued, saying in the king’s name that, for the restoration of peace and concord between himself and the archbishop, and for the re-establishment of the divine laws, two cardinals should be sent from the Apostolic See to England. Full power to bind and loose should be granted to them; no one should dare oppose them; no appeal should be made against them; whatever they did should stand firm; and through them every transgression should be corrected. But the most holy pope, immediately perceiving that fraud lay hidden in their words, answered that this power ought to be granted to no cardinal [Col. 0032A] so that he might hold the pope’s place, nor, he added, would anything contrary to reason be granted to the cardinals through him. Bearing this answer, the king’s envoys returned to England without waiting for the archbishop, who arrived at Sens four days later.

Throwing himself at the feet of the lord pope, he set forth the cause of his arrival, though it was not unknown to him. In place of an offering, holding out with both hands the king’s written instrument, he presented it; and, rising upon his knees, said: “Lord Father, this is the cause, this is my entire fault, for which I have been driven from my Church and endure exile. These are the laws on whose account I feel the king’s implacable anger; these are the traditions which the king has proposed should be maintained in his realm and confirmed by oath so that they may be transmitted [Col. 0032B] to posterity. Therefore, detesting to give assent to these statutes, which are contrary to divine and apostolic laws, I have come to find the sole and customary refuge of your presence.”

And, as I have been reliably told, resigning the right of his archiepiscopal office into the lord pope’s hand, he requested that the pope appoint, as cardinal-bishop in their metropolis, some man of the English Church more learned and stronger than himself. But the holy pope raised his son, embraced and kissed him, mingling tears with tears and giving thanks to God because he had found a man so humble in spirit, a pastor so concerned for the salvation of the sheep, an advocate so steadfast in one cause—indeed, in many causes—of God. Therefore the lord pope decreed that the dignity which he had declined should be restored to him, since he knew that no one was stronger for this burden, even though Thomas resisted and was unwilling.

When the document which the archbishop had presented was read in the hearing of all, the holy man proved, by evident reasoning and elegant speech, word by word, its tendency, the end it would have, and how contrary it would be to divine laws and ecclesiastical institutions if it were maintained. But William of Pavia, cardinal, attempted to defend the king’s case with opposing objections, and other cardinals also spoke much for the king. When the alternating dispute had occupied the middle and full part of the day, and the opposing side had nothing further to object, the saint sat down beside the lord pope at his command, all [Col. 0032D] present marvelling at his prudence and the firmness of his replies. The pope ordered him to be calmer, promising due consolation after so great a labour. He also condemned by perpetual anathema both the document which had been read and its authority, and whoever should give assent to it.

After remaining for one month with the pope, the holy archbishop was sent by him to Pontigny and entrusted to the abbot and brethren, who were to care for him in all things required by human necessity. They carried this out with willing hearts.

But after the king learned that the archbishop had been placed in the secure harbour of a refuge, where neither his fury nor his threats could move him, royal rage raged against the fugitive’s relatives. Those of whom God declares himself father and judge—the fatherless, widows, wards, and innocent people wholly ignorant of any deeply rooted quarrel of the old man; women with little children hanging at their breasts; clerics and laypeople, of whatever age or sex, belonging to the archbishop’s kindred; and certain of his household—were, that he might be further distressed by it, stripped of all their resources by a pitiable proscription and ordered to leave the entire kingdom. His servants were cast into chains and held there. The archbishopric was taken back into the king’s hands and entrusted for guarding to Ranulf de Broc, the king’s official, because of the old enmities which he is known to have exercised against the man of God. This man, the inventor of all malice and the fuel of discord between king and archbishop, fiercer than any enemy, pursued and drove into exile the archbishop’s clerics and relatives wherever they could be found, without any [Col. 0033B] compassion.

What then were these unhappy people to do? Where could they turn to find a remedy for so great a calamity? Should they seek the archbishop, who, himself desolate and exiled, begged among foreign sheep? Yet they went to him, whom they thought the source of their miseries. But what, we may believe, was the courage of that most steadfast martyr when he saw his own people arrive, formerly prosperous and wealthy but now, because of him, naked and destitute? What torrents of tears, do we think, did he shed? What sighs did he draw when he saw little children at their mothers’ breasts condemned because of him to so dreadful and unheard-of an expulsion? He is believed to have endured a grave martyrdom in the sorrow of his own people, he who abounded in the bowels of compassion and mercy even for the affliction and misery of barbarians. His grief was increased because he had no means at all by which to relieve the poverty of his own.

Let no one call this merely our opinion: he would rather have chosen many deaths than behold so great a desolation among his people, of which he was believed from the beginning to have been the cause. But God, the comforter of the humble, did not abandon one humbled for his sake and for justice in this desolation. For the king of France, at God’s inspiration, and the princes of the kingdom generously supplied the holy man with means in abundance for himself and all his people. Nor was he a deaf hearer of the Lord exhorting his followers and saying, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake”; rather, he kindled his spirit for endurance. Finally, [Col. 0033D] wholly turned toward divine and heavenly consolation, he could readily persuade himself that one must enter the promised blessedness through many tribulations. Considering the footsteps of the saints, he patiently embraced the loss of temporal goods out of love for eternal things, recalling that Abraham was told: “Go out from your land and from your kindred.” As he had put aside his land, so he resolved altogether to put aside even his kindred for the honour of the Church.

Meanwhile, hearing that the lord pope had summoned the bishops of England, the king convened a council at Clarendon. There he exacted an oath from the bishops that none of them should leave the country on account of any appeal and that no one should receive a mandate from the lord pope. The bishops indeed promised this in such terms, while the laymen swore it. It was proclaimed by the king’s command [Col. 0034A] that if anyone appealed to the Apostolic See in any matter whatever, all his property should be entered for the king’s use and he himself should be delivered to prison. Shame upon it! Where then was the fear of God? Where reverence for the laws? Where the honour due to bishops? All appealed to the king’s judgment and presence. The people, ignorant of God’s law, dealt with the causes of the Church. Nowhere were the decrees of the Fathers found; nowhere was the Gospel heard. Divine law there fell silent, reason was silent, presumption alone held mastery. The poor were stripped of churches; the rich were clothed. The offering of the faithful called Peter’s Pence, because it was owed especially to Peter’s heirs, was withheld to be deposited along with the public revenue. Harbours and seacoasts were guarded more strictly, so that anyone who brought some mandate [Col. 0034B] would immediately perish by hanging or by some terrible death.

Nevertheless, at that time the lord pope sent several letters reproving the errors of the prelates and threatening suspension from office if they did not repent.

At the same time he also wrote this to the Archbishop of York:

“ALEXANDER, servant of the servants of God, to the Archbishop of York and all the bishops of England, greeting and apostolic blessing. ‘Of that dignity and—’” etc. (See the alphabetical index of letters.)

But the bishops, if one may say what they themselves did not fear to do, joined contempt to their breach of faith. For when the king wished his son to be crowned, the Archbishop of York performed the office of coronation, associating with himself Gilbert of London and Jocelin of Salisbury, [Col. 0034C] disregarding the authority and setting aside reverence for the lord of Canterbury, to whom, by the ancient right of kings, the anointing certainly belongs. On this occasion no mention was made, as customary, of preserving the liberty of the Church, nor was any guarantee given; rather, an oath was introduced that he ought to preserve inviolate the customs of the kingdom called ancestral, under which the Church’s dignity is endangered. These things are written in the lord pope’s letter, in which he suspended from pastoral office the bishops who irregularly took part in this coronation. More had indeed participated, but the matter depended upon the three named above and was carried out through them.

These ministers of this presumption, authors [Col. 0034D] of error, in order to satisfy the king’s will and obey acts of bad faith, showed neither honour to their own order nor obedience to apostolic commands, and patiently endured the proscription of divine law. Indeed, to confess what is truer, they strove to overthrow the Church’s liberty, stirring the king’s mind against the holy man by their counsels. They persuaded him that concord was useless to the kingdom and dishonourable to the king, fearing nothing more than peace, as the saint himself testified in writing to the pope.

Thus suspended from office and, deservedly for their contempt, in time to be bound by the bond of anathema, they nevertheless did not cease to provoke the saint in exile with darts of words, since they could not attack him by open action. For the three, joined in a like conspiracy, [Col. 0035A] collected for themselves whatever they could search out from the Scriptures and from examples of predecessors, by which they attempted to strengthen their own cause and that of the king against the holy archbishop, saying: “What your father at a distance—,” etc. (See the alphabetical index of letters.)

I have thought it fitting to insert these matters into this little work, so that the reader, gathering a few points from many, may understand that in his exile and desolation the holy archbishop found enemies in those from whom he ought to have hoped for consolation. But the man of God wrote back in the person of the Bishop of London as follows:

“A thing wonderful and greatly astonishing—,” etc. (See the alphabetical index of letters.)

The saint wrote more in this manner to the three named above [Col. 0035B]; and they assailed him with many frequent mandates. Thus it may be weighed on both sides how great was their zeal in justifying the king’s acts, and how great the saint’s constancy in asserting truth. Then they too, together with all the others who had participated in the coronation of the king’s son, were suspended by letters sent from the lord pope.

## ON THE HOLY MAN’S STAY AT PONTIGNY

The holy Thomas, while staying at Pontigny, to which the lord pope had commended him, as has been said above, imposed on his body many severe tribulations known to God alone. Mindful of the Lord’s admonition, “Let not your left hand know what your right hand does,” he concealed, as far as he could and with conscience as witness, whatever holy religious observance or devotion he found in himself. From that time, therefore, he was content with vegetables and coarser meals, and with food requiring less expense; he secretly withheld all delicacies from himself, without the knowledge of those who sat with him, and had them served to needy sick people.

He also secretly went down into the stream which runs through the monastic workshops; how many crosses he imposed upon his body by enduring that injury of cold beyond the strength of human frailty, in order to crush the impulses of desires which still seemed alive in him, was revealed by the sickness which followed. For not long afterwards one side of his face swelled and decayed as far as the inner throat, and the swelling developed into the disease called a fistula. After suffering for a long time [Col. 0035D] from this affliction, he was at last healed, though not without much discomfort and pain, when two bones were extracted from it.

One night, exhausted by the intensity of prayer and genuflection, when he gave himself to sleep, he saw as though in a dream that, after a grave dispute had arisen between himself and the king, he stood alone in the presence of the lord pope and the cardinals to set forth his case. The cardinals who supported the king’s cause, deeply enraged that the archbishop was acting so steadfastly against the king, rushed upon him and attempted to gouge out his eyes with their fingers and tear him apart. The pope cried out, but the shouting and tumult of the cardinals prevailed and made the protesting pope fall silent. Then, after they had gone out, he saw others entering, as though executioners sent against him while he was alone. Terrible in appearance [Col. 0036A] and filled with fury, they attacked the archbishop and, with drawn swords, shaved off the crown of his head over the whole breadth occupied by the tonsure, so that the shaved portion fell down upon his forehead.

Disturbed by the novelty of this dreadful vision, the man of God reflected deeply that it had not been shown without cause. More and more he gave himself to divine service and strengthened himself to endure every injury.

## HOW THE KING REMOVED HIM FROM PONTIGNY

When the king learned that the archbishop had been placed securely and lacked none of the things required for human needs, and that he could inflict no hardship either upon him or upon any of his people as long as he remained at Pontigny, he sought to remove him from there. But since he could not accomplish this through the king [Col. 0036B] of France, who, as a lover of truth and of all goodness, always revered the archbishop with the deepest affection and supported him with his own aid against his adversaries, he turned to other devices.

He wrote to the abbot of Cîteaux, to whom Pontigny, like the other houses of the same order, was subject by right of obedience. He declared that the abbot was harbouring his public enemy within the Order and throughout his entire kingdom, and that the abbot should be certain that, if the archbishop were permitted either to remain there or to seek refuge elsewhere in the order, he would send to him without opposition every monk of that order found in his kingdom. When the holy archbishop heard this, he replied calmly and kindly at the command of the abbot of Cîteaux: “Far be it from me,” he said, “to commit this transgression: that because of me I should allow so many men of virtue, so many innocent souls, to come into desolation, and so many places, so many monasteries acquired by such great labours, to be reduced to everlasting wilderness. For he will relieve [Col. 0036C] my poverty ‘who raises the needy from the earth and lifts up the poor from the dust’; and may the Father of mercies repay you and recompense the offices of charity which you have shown me.”

He therefore informed the king of France by what device the king of England had driven him from Pontigny, saying that he was ready to accept what had formerly been offered. For when he had first come as a fugitive from England to King Louis, the king had offered him, and urged him with many entreaties, to remain near him in whatever manner or place he preferred. At that time he had refused, lest anyone accuse him of binding himself to the king of France, as the more powerful ruler, to the injury of his lord, the king of England. By the pope’s counsel he chose Pontigny, delighting in a more sparing diet and a sober life.

The king received the archbishop’s message with every devotion and hastened to Pontigny. Entering the chapter-house of the monks, he thanked the abbot and brethren for having honoured France by receiving so great a guest. “And now,” he said, “lest any one of you incur the king’s displeasure and hatred for the assistance given him, let him come with me.” The monks turned to tears, lamenting the departure of the father of each of them and their singular consolation; remembering how gently and humbly he had lived among them, almost as one of themselves, they followed with mourning and sighs the man whom they had loved while present and who was now departing.

Leaving there with his companions, after he had spent two years in that place, he was conveyed to more remote parts of Gaul, namely to St Columba, a great monastery of monks situated near the city of Sens. There, received with the greatest attention by the king’s officials who had been sent ahead, he spent four years sustained by royal provision. During that time he could easily have stayed with bishops or archbishops, and many offered this; but the holy man, wishing more safely to cherish in silence the fire of heavenly love which the Saviour had sent into his bones and by which he now wholly burned, avoided public life. Removed from crowds and tumults, he occupied both times of day and night chiefly with sacred meditations, prayer, and compunction [Col. 0037B] of tears, in which he overflowed ever more abundantly. He did not cease from this practice except when concern for household affairs or unavoidable business compelled him.

## HOW THE KING TRIED TO DECEIVE THE HOLY MAN

But the adversary of peace, who through envy introduced death into the world, saw and envied this peace and purpose of the venerable archbishop. Once more he incited the king against him by the counsels of wicked men. The saint wrote—and we believe—that discord must be attributed more to them than to the king. They suggested that it would be disgraceful and a mark of cowardice if the king allowed to remain at peace a man who had raised such disturbances in the kingdom.

Therefore, since the king could do the man of God no harm unless the king of France consented, he attempted to entrap him as follows. He sent [Col. 0037C] his son, now crowned, into France to render homage and pledge fealty to the French king’s son, who was to succeed his father in the kingdom. Various kinds of gifts were sent, and precious things were given to the king’s household officers and counsellors. At last the kings met to speak about peace and concord for the future. When these matters had been discussed and agreements confirmed, they swore in the midst of them that, from that day, they would keep firm friendship and faith—especially in this: that neither would receive the other’s enemy, nor allow anyone received after this agreement to remain anywhere in his kingdom.

Once this agreement had been granted in this manner, the king of England without delay arranged another conference for the kings to meet. When the king [Col. 0037D] of France was prevented by his counsellors from attending, the king of England, seeing his efforts come to nothing, informed him that he was violating the agreement confirmed by their mutual oath by harbouring and protecting the public enemy both of himself and of his kingdom. The king of France sent back word that no mention of the archbishop had been made in the agreement, and that therefore he neither ought nor could be accused of violating it.

When the man of God learned that the king of England was trying to expel him even from France, he wrote to him, asking him to cease persecuting his servant and fruitlessly spending such great labour. He added that, through God’s providence, far more than the necessities of life required was available to himself and all his people; therefore he was now compelled to fear no one except the Lord of all, the promise of truth having been fulfilled in him which says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, [Col. 0038A] and all these things shall be added to you.” We have thought it proper to relate how diligently he sought the kingdom of God, and what consolation he received, and from whom, amid the labours of his exile, so that the reader may see that such a manner of life was deservedly consummated by martyrdom.

First, as we have learned, no day found him sleeping; he rarely rested in bed unless serious illness threatened. His first labour was to enter church, attend the divine praises, and celebrate the solemn offices of the sacred mysteries with the utmost devotion and reverence. After completing the canonical hours, he entered his oratory alone. With the door shut, praying within his chamber to the Father in a contrite and humble heart, through prayer and tears he daily offered himself to his Creator as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God. The saint’s household members, who with pious curiosity investigated his secret, inferred from his sighs and frequent groans what he did when shut in alone.

Then, at the hour of refreshment, he came out and ate with the poor and his household. He abstained from no food, avoiding every appearance of singularity; but in truth he took everything with the greatest sobriety, knowing that food is not culpable, but desire must be restrained. Rising from table, he nourished the hunger of his soul not with idleness, tales, or frivolity, but with holy reading. Whether he dealt with necessary matters or spoke instruction to his household, he encouraged them. This was the order of his day unless unavoidable business changed something.

At night, when the bed was arranged, as befitted an archbishop, [Col. 0038C] with clean and costly coverings, all supposed that he rested in it.
