But the saint, having solitude in his oratory, passed the silence of night in prayer. Then he awakened the chaplain, the only person whom he kept with him in the chamber in which he lay. Having devoted the entire day to holiness, so that he might be judged worthier of a crown than of a scourge, he removed the hair-shirt which he wore, offered the scourge, and humbly presented his back to be beaten. At first the chaplain trembled to do this; but compelled by the authority of obedience, he did not cease to strike the saint until blood came, and he himself who struck was sometimes overcome by pity and exhausted in body.

When the chaplain returned to bed, the archbishop did not rest from injury to his body, but tore and lacerated it with his nails. Amid sobs and sighs he burst forth in these words: “Wretched that I am, and most unhappy of all wretches—why was I born? Why have I come into this misery?” Afterwards, by the reckoning of him who was permitted to be present, he spent a full third part of the night in genuflection and prayer. When the excessive fatigue of his whole body compelled him at last to rest, he lay down on the ground, placing a stone beneath his neck; his rough garment and the multitude of worms caused such suffering that the slight sleep he got disturbed rather than refreshed him.

The witness and narrator of these matters was the venerable Robert of Merton, chaplain of the holy archbishop. He either learned all these things from him or saw them himself—things which Thomas wished no one except Robert to know. Robert had pledged that he would reveal none of them to anyone while the archbishop remained alive. The same man testified that from the day of his ordination the saint allowed no day to pass in which he was not severely scourged five, four, or at least three times. By these exercises of holy conduct, by this divine spur of love, the holy man mortified himself to the world, daily killed the affections of the flesh, put desires to death, and, thirsting to endure only the Saviour’s presence, sang with the Prophet: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?”

## HOW THE SAVIOUR APPEARED TO THE GOOD THOMAS

[Col. 0039B] Meanwhile, one day after the solemn celebration of Mass, while he lay prostrate before the altar and, through an excessive fervour of spirit, was rapt above himself and applied himself more watchfully than usual to prayer, the Saviour appeared to him in a clear vision and said: “Thomas, Thomas, in your blood you shall glorify my Church.” He replied: “Who are you, Lord, who have visited me?” “I,” he said, “am your brother and Saviour, who shall glorify my Church in your blood.” Then he said: “Would that it may indeed happen as the Lord has spoken!” Greatly strengthened by this oracle, he sighed more and more from day to day for love of the heavenly homeland, desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ.

## HOW THE KING OF FRANCE WISHED TO RESTORE PEACE BETWEEN THE KING AND THE ARCHBISHOP
[Col. 0039C] The king of the Franks pressed more earnestly to restore peace between the king and the archbishop, and there were frequent conferences between the kings on this matter. The commands of the lord pope were also read in the councils at which the kings had assembled. In them he rebuked the king—at first patiently and quite fatherly; afterwards, when patience did not soften him at all, he commanded him, with a threat of vengeance, to lay aside all malice, dismiss the complaints on both sides, and return to peace with his archbishop. The king dissembled for some time and, by changing the appointed day of peace, prolonged the matter. The saint therefore wrote this to the king at the council at Chinon.

## ON THE DESIRE TO SPEAK WITH THE KING OF ENGLAND

[Col. 0039D] “I have earnestly desired to see your face,” etc. (See the alphabetical index of letters.)

When the venerable pontiff’s letter had been read, the king, wishing neither to oppose it nor to assent to it, postponed his answer to a fixed day. At last the king and archbishop came together, and peace was restored between them, as was supposed, through the lord pope and the king of the Franks. Their complaints against one another were forgiven without anger, indignation, or any malice. The king promised to restore what had been taken away and whatever should be proved to belong to the archbishopric. He also granted leave for the archbishop and all his people to return, together with a lasting peace.

But the saint, mindful of the desolate flock which had strayed from the straight path during the absence of its shepherd, sent ahead one of his clerics, so that, in order to extend the kiss of peace to all without offence, he might absolve on the archbishop’s behalf any persons who perhaps had communicated in any respect with those under sentence. How he returned, and what was the reason that he did not return immediately after peace had been made, the saint himself explains in writing to the lord pope after his return.

### Letter of Blessed Thomas to the Lord Pope

“To the reverend father and most beloved lord in Christ, Alexander, supreme pontiff: Thomas, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, greeting and complete obedience with the highest devotion. Upon what just, upon what honourable conditions,” etc. (See the alphabetical index of letters.)

## ON THE RETURN OF THE BLESSED MAN TO CANTERBURY

Thus Saint Thomas, as the seventh winter of his exile was now passing, returned to Canterbury. So much the more fervently and devoutly did he hasten toward the life to come, the true life, because in this life he knew certainly that nothing remained for him except temptations and dangers. For although outward peace may perhaps have smiled upon him, he had long since imposed upon himself so severe a warfare that, even amid the world’s delights, the hardship—or rather the martyrdom—of a harsher wilderness was not lacking.

On the other hand, what pressed him more fiercely, though he desired to live piously, was that while living peacefully among those who hate peace and truth, he experienced in himself the Savior’s saying: a man’s enemies are those of his own household. For the very person upon whom reason dictated that he ought above all to rely—his own archdeacon—acted as an envoy against him, to persuade the king’s son [Col. 0040C] that the archbishop was plotting to diminish his crown, or even, if boldness were allowed free course, intended wholly to take it away.

Moreover, to disguise the malice of their own invention, the enemies of justice slandered the man of God, alleging that he had returned from exile, driven by impulses of leonine savagery, in order to overthrow the king’s purpose and institutions. Yet the outcome showed that he calmed hostile ranks by gentleness, when, like a lamb, neither resisting nor crying out, he offered his neck to the striker.

Meanwhile the magnanimous man strengthened his spirit for the contest soon to come by the exercises of holy devotion. He devoted himself to prayer, sacred reading, and preaching; and he was so intent upon these and so lavish in giving alms that those overseas to whom his holy manner of life had become known marvelled.

A short time before the Nativity of the Lord and Savior, wishing to visit the king’s son—upon whom the name of king was already being bestowed—in order to speak more privately with him during the holy festival days concerning the affairs of the Church, he set out for London. He had not yet entered the city when, behold, one of the royal household met him and announced to him, in the king’s name and by his command, that he was not to proceed any farther or enter royal cities, villages, or towns.

At first the holy man was alarmed and astonished, troubled by the unexpected announcement; and he replied to the king’s messenger: “What have I deserved, that I find even you my enemy? What sin have I committed, that you bring me such a message? Do you speak these things of yourself?”

“By no means,” said the messenger. [Col. 0041A] “I have not composed these words out of my own heart; rather, this is what the lord king commands you. He made peace with you, and you were the first to break the bonds of peace and violate the agreement, since you separated the king’s household and bishops from the Church, and you go armed through the royal cities with a band of soldiers. Therefore the king commands you to return to your see, apply yourself diligently to the duty entrusted to you, and go nowhere else.”

As the messenger continued further, adding threats, the saint said: “I thought that there was peace and suspected nothing else; but I see that there is no peace in which I can trust.” The messenger persisted, maintaining that the king had in every respect so commanded.

From the king’s words and command, then, the saint perceived most certainly the deed which afterwards occurred. He became all the more cheerful and all the readier for every will of God because, from what he had heard, he sensed that he was now drawing near to the palm of victory. How fervently he returned, inflamed by faith and by desire of heaven—how, as though consoled after hearing what could indeed have terrified him—we have as witness the grace of healings displayed from heaven during that journey, after the holy martyr had ascended to the heights. For wherever he stopped and laid hands upon little children suffering from various illnesses, health was restored to them.

Having returned, therefore, with the utmost devotion and purity of spirit, he celebrated the holy Nativity of the Savior, cheerfully reminding his people that a person’s way is not in his own power. On the day of the Lord’s Nativity, after he had finished preaching to the people, he condemned with a terrible sentence [Col. 0041C] one of the king’s household, who the day before, after beating the archbishop’s servants, had also shamefully docked their horses’ tails in insult to him. He punished with a like penalty Ranulf de Broch, this man’s kinsman in the flesh and no milder in spirit, the instigator of every evil, who had raged bestially against the archbishop’s men and relatives.

He also publicly informed the people that three bishops were subject to this sentence, so that no one might communicate with such persons—bishops who had not feared, contrary to the ordinances of their predecessors, to withdraw from Christ’s Church of Canterbury the anointing of kings. Finally he said: “May all who sow hatred or discord between me and my lord king be cursed by Jesus Christ, and may their memory be blotted out from the assembly of the saints.”

But those whom malice had once armed against Christ’s anointed did not fear the pronouncement of this terrible sentence. The aforesaid bishops, preferring to submit themselves to the king’s indignation rather than to the judgment of God and the Church, swiftly crossed the sea to approach the king. Throwing themselves at the king’s feet, they bewailed their suspension in a complaint and plea sufficiently capable of moving even a hard heart. They alleged how the lord of Canterbury had dealt with them: through his contrivance and ingenuity they had been wholly separated from their priestly office, to the disgrace of king and kingdom, so that they were not even able to bless bread. They added the accusation that he would yet dare something greater if the king bore this presumption patiently.

The king, ensnared by such words and as if maddened, beside himself with rage and not knowing what answer to make, is reported to have said repeatedly: [Col. 0042A] “I have nourished and raised up in my kingdom idle and wretched men, who bear no loyalty to their lord, whom they allow to be so shamefully mocked by some lowborn cleric.”

He withdrew from both the conference and the place to a private room, perhaps hoping solitude would give some relief to the wrath that had seized him, where the speech of his raging heart might more freely vomit forth its imbibed poison. Four knights, men indeed distinguished by birth and belonging to the king’s household, caught this utterance and interpreted it as ominous, and with an intention altogether different from that with which the king had spoken it. Without delay—doubtless stirred by him who was a murderer from the beginning—they unanimously conspired to kill the innocent man; and he who inspired the crime also gave them the means to carry it out.

They departed without the king’s knowledge, embarked on a ship, and, with favourable winds answering their wish, crossed into England. They made land at the harbour of Canum, and from then on ought themselves to have been called dogs—*canes*—and wretches, rather than soldiers. When the king learned that the knights had gone away, suspecting some evil, he sent after them that they might return quickly. But they had crossed with such speed that they could neither be recalled nor overtaken by messengers before the crime was committed.

That accursed presumption was contrary to the king’s purpose and will became sufficiently clear from what followed. For when the suffering of the venerable pontiff was reported to him, such confusion seized his mind, sorrow troubled it, and horror at the unheard-of crime alike swallowed it up and possessed it, that no speech can adequately explain these things. For, as later became known, he had decided either to restrain him in prison custody or in some other way, in order that he might revoke the sentence. But the providence of God, which sometimes makes good use of evils, thereby honoured His beloved one more highly where human malice believed it had humbled him. Human ingenuity and cunning are powerless against the counsel of divinity. It pleased the Savior to rescue by martyrdom from this misery one whom the fullness of faith had made worthy of martyrdom.

Therefore the men mentioned above, no longer soldiers but wretched and miserable men, upon their first arrival joined to themselves the king’s officials already condemned by the archbishop’s sentence of anathema. They gathered from the district a band of soldiers and retainers, lying in the king’s words and name against their lord. The crime was easily persuaded, because they asserted that they had come for this business by the king’s command. Now gathered into one body and ready for every impiety, on the fifth day after Christ’s Nativity—on the morrow of the Holy Innocents—they assembled against the innocent man.

The hour of refreshment having ended, the saint too had withdrawn with his household from the crowd into an inner room to discuss affairs. While the crowd waited outside in the courtyard, only the four men entered, with one retainer. They were received honourably as members of the king’s household and persons well known, and were invited to table while those serving the archbishop were still eating. They rejected food, thirsting instead for blood.

[Col. 0043A] At their command, the archbishop was informed that four men had come who wished to speak with him on the king’s behalf. At his signal they were admitted; and after sitting for some time in silence, they neither greeted nor addressed the holy archbishop. Nor did the man of great counsel greet them immediately upon their entry, so that, in accordance with the sense of Scripture, “By your words you shall be justified,” he might discern from their questioning the inward intention of their minds. After a delay, however, he turned to them, carefully observed the face of each, and greeted them peacefully.

But the unhappy men, who had made a covenant with death, immediately assailed his greeting with curses and hypocritically prayed that God might help him. At this expression of bitterness and malice, the man of God was flushed with incredible shame, already well aware that the men had come with the intention of harming him.

The man who seemed foremost among them and readiest for the crime, the son of Urse, breathing rage, burst out with these words: “We have something to say to you by the king’s command. If you wish it to be recited to you before the crowd, say so.”

But the archbishop, recognizing what and whence they meant to speak, said: “These things must be spoken not privately, not in a chamber, but publicly.”

The wretches burned so fiercely for the bishop’s death that, had not the doorkeeper called back the clerics—for he had ordered them all to leave—they would, as they later confessed, have pierced the archbishop with the shaft of the cross that stood nearby. When those who had left returned, the same man who above began the slander against the man of God with these words said: [Col. 0043C] “The king says: after peace had been restored between you, he sent you back freely, with every complaint laid to rest, to your own see, as you requested. But you, in return, adding contempt to your former injuries, have violated the treaty of peace and acted proudly against your lord, to your own ruin. For those through whose ministry the king’s son was crowned and raised to the honour of the kingdom, you have condemned, carried away by the swelling of a stubborn heart, to a sentence of suspension. You have also bound the king’s ministers, by whose counsels and prudence the affairs of the realm are conducted, with the bond of anathema. From this it is plain that you would take away the king’s son’s crown if opportunity were present; for your schemes and efforts to bring to effect what you have devised against your lord have now become known to all. Therefore declare whether you deign to come and answer for these matters in the king’s presence; for this is why we have been sent.”

The archbishop replied: “God is witness that it was never my will to take the crown from my lord, the king’s son, or to diminish his power. Rather, I would wish him three crowns and would help him, with reason and justice, to acquire the widest kingdoms of the earth. Nor is it just that the lord king should be angry, as you allege, because my people accompanied me and met me in his cities and towns, having been deprived by a seven-year banishment of the comfort of my presence. And now, wherever it may please my lord, I am ready to make satisfaction if perhaps I have committed an offence in anything. But he announced threateningly that I was not to enter his cities, towns, or villages. Furthermore, it was not I but the lord pope who suspended the bishops from office.”

“Through you,” the madmen said, [Col. 0044A] “they were suspended; and you must absolve them.”

“I do not deny,” he said, “that it was done through me. But it is above me, and wholly inconsistent with my dignity, to absolve those whom the lord pope has bound. Let them approach him whose injury it concerns that they have despised me and their mother, Christ’s Church of Canterbury.”

“Now therefore,” said the executioners, “this is the king’s command: that you leave the kingdom and the land subject to his authority with all your people; for from this day there shall be no peace for you or for any of yours, since you have broken the peace.”

To this he replied: “Let your threats cease and your quarrels be quiet. I trust in the King of heaven, who suffered on the cross for His own. For from this day no one shall see the sea between me and my Church. I did not come as a fugitive; whoever seeks me will find me here. Nor would it become the lord king to command such things. The insult already inflicted upon me and mine by the king’s servants is sufficient, even if he did not threaten the future.”

“These things,” they said, “our lord king commanded, and we shall prove it. You ought to have deferred to royal majesty and left vengeance to the king’s judgment; but, following the judgment of an enraged mind, you shamefully expelled the king’s ministers and household from the Church.”

In fervour of spirit Christ’s champion rose up against his slanderers and said: “Whoever presumes to violate the ordinances of the holy Roman See or the rights of Christ’s Church, and does not voluntarily come to make satisfaction—whoever he may be—I shall not spare, nor shall I delay to correct the offender by ecclesiastical censure.”

Struck by this speech, the knights sprang up, unable any longer to bear the firmness of his reply. Coming nearer, they said: [Col. 0044C] “We declare to you that you have spoken at the peril of your head.”

“Have you come,” he said, “to kill me? I have committed my cause to the Judge of all. Therefore I am not moved by threats; for your swords are no readier to strike than my spirit is for martyrdom. Seek someone who will flee from you; you will find me foot to foot in the battle of the Lord.”

As they went out amid tumult and insults, the man whom we have rightly surnamed Urse (“Bear”) shouted bestially: “On the king’s behalf we command you, clerics and monks alike, to seize and hold this man, lest he escape by flight, until the king has exacted full justice upon his body.”

As they departed, the man of God followed them to the door and himself cried out these words: “Here, here you will find me,” placing his hand upon his neck as though showing the place where they would strike.

When he returned to the place where he had previously sat, he comforted his people in the Lord and urged them not to fear. As it seemed to us who were present, he sat as unafraid as though they had come to invite him to a wedding, although he alone was being sought for death. Without delay the executioners returned in mail, with swords, axes, double-edged weapons, and other implements suited to carrying out the crime they had conceived in their hearts.

When they found the doors bolted and no one opened to their knocking, they turned by a more secret route through the orchard to a wooden barrier, which they cut, [Col. 0045A] broke down, and demolished. At that terrible, tumultuous crash, almost all the servants and clerics, trembling, scattered here and there like sheep before wolves.

Those who remained cried out for him to flee into the church. But mindful of his earlier promise—that he would not flee from those who killed the body for fear of death—he refused flight. In such a case one was not to flee from city to city, but rather to provide those subject to him with an example: that each should prefer to fall beneath swords rather than see contempt for divine law and the overthrow of the sacred canons. At the same time, having long burned with love of martyrdom, and believing that he had obtained the opportunity to fulfil it, he feared lest, if he fled to the church, he might postpone it or wholly deprive himself of it.

The monks insisted that it was not fitting for him to be absent from the evening praises already then being celebrated in the church. He remained motionless in a place of lesser reverence, resolved to await the hour of his consummation—blessed, longed for with many sighs, and sought with much devotion—lest, as has been said, reverence for the sacred building should deter the wicked from their purpose and deprive the saint of his heart’s desire.

For he was certain that after martyrdom he would depart from this misery. After he returned from exile, he is reported to have said in the hearing of many: “You have here Ælfheah, beloved of God and truly a holy martyr; divine mercy will not delay in providing you another.” O the sincere and secure conscience of the good shepherd, who in his flock’s cause and defence would not postpone his own death [Col. 0045C] when he was able, nor avoid the executioner, so that the rage of the wolves, satisfied with the shepherd’s blood, might spare the sheep!

But when neither argument nor prayers could persuade him to take refuge in the church, the monks seized him unwilling and resisting, dragged, carried, and forced him onward. Paying no attention to how vehemently he protested and commanded them to let him go, they brought him as far as the church. Yet the door leading into the monks’ cloister, which had been carefully bolted many days earlier, wholly removed every hope of escape when the torturers were already pressing from behind. Nevertheless, one man ran to it, and as soon as he touched the bolt, he drew it back with such ease—to the great amazement of all—as though it had been held fast with glue.

After the monks had withdrawn within the doors of the church, the aforesaid four knights pursued hard behind them at the swiftest pace. Among them was a certain subdeacon, armed with the same malice as the knights: Hugh “Bad-Clerk,” so surnamed on account of his wickedness, who showed reverence neither to God nor to the saints, as the following deed demonstrated.

When the holy archbishop entered the monastery, the monks abandoned the Vespers which they had begun to offer to God and met him, glorifying God because they saw their father alive and safe, though they had heard that he was dead. They hurried to bar the doors of the church in order to keep the enemies from killing their shepherd. But the wonderful champion turned to them and ordered the church doors to be opened: “It is not fitting,” he said, “to make the church of Christ, the house of prayer, into a fortress. Though it is not shut, it is sufficient for its own defence; and we shall triumph over the enemy by suffering rather than by fighting, for we have come to suffer, not to resist.”

Without delay, swords drawn, they entered the house of peace and reconciliation, striking no small terror into those who saw them by their very appearance and the clatter of arms. Those present were disturbed and in an uproar, for those who had been attending to the evening praises had now run to the deadly spectacle. In a spirit of fury the knights shouted: “Where is Thomas Becket, traitor to king and kingdom?”

When no one answered, they cried still more insistently: “Where is the archbishop?”

At this cry he came forth fearless and, as it is written, “The righteous shall be confident as a lion, without terror,” descending from the step to which the monks had brought him because of fear of the soldiers. [Col. 0046B] In a voice clearly audible he answered: “Here I am—not a traitor to the king, but a priest. Why do you seek me?” And he who had already said that he did not fear them added: “Behold, I am ready, in the name of Him who redeemed me by His blood, to suffer. Far be it from me to flee because of your swords or to depart from justice.”

Having said this, he moved to the right beneath a column, with the altar of the Blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary on one side, and that of Saint Benedict the confessor on the other. Crucified to the world and its desires by their example and intercession, with such constancy of mind as though he were not in the flesh, he endured and overcame whatever the executioner inflicted.

The executioners followed him. “Absolve,” they said, “and restore to communion those whom you have excommunicated; and restore office to the others who have been suspended.”

“No satisfaction has preceded this,” he replied, “and I shall not absolve them.”

“And you,” they said, “will now die, receiving what you have deserved.”

“I am ready,” he said, “to die for my Lord, so that through my blood the Church may obtain liberty and peace. But in the name of Almighty God I forbid my people, whether cleric or layperson, to harm anyone in any way.”

How piously he provided for his own people, and how wisely for himself, this excellent martyr: so that a neighbour might not be injured or an innocent person oppressed, and so that a sadder disaster befalling another might not overshadow the glory of one hastening to Christ. It was entirely fitting that the martyr, the soldier of his leader, should follow the Savior’s footsteps—He who, when sought by the wicked, said: “If you seek me, let these go their way.”

[Col. 0046D] Then, making an attack, they laid sacrilegious hands upon him, handling and dragging him harshly, intending either to slaughter him outside the boundaries of the church or carry him away bound, as they later confessed. But since he could not easily be moved from the column, he repelled one of them, who pressed him more violently and came nearer, calling him a pander, and saying: “Do not touch me, Reginald, for by right you owe me faithfulness and obedience. You act foolishly with your accomplices.”

Enraged all over by this repulse, the knight brandished his sword against the sacred head and said: “I owe you neither faithfulness nor obedience against the loyalty due to my lord the king.”

The invincible martyr, seeing that the hour was at hand which would put an end to wretched mortality and bring near the crown of immortality prepared and promised to him by the Lord, bent his neck as in prayer. With his hands joined and lifted upward, he commended his own cause and that of the Church to God, to Saint Mary, and to the blessed martyr Dionysius.

He had scarcely finished the words when the wicked knight, fearing that the people might snatch him away and that he might escape alive, suddenly leapt upon him. Striking away the summit of the crown that the anointing of holy chrism had consecrated to God, he wounded in the head the lamb to be offered to God, and by the same blow cut off the arm of the man who was saying these things.

For this man, though all the monks and clerics were fleeing, stood steadfastly by the holy archbishop and held him embraced in his arms until the arm he had interposed was cut off. Behold the dove’s simplicity; behold the serpent’s prudence in this martyr, who offered his body to the strikers so as to preserve unharmed in his own head—that is, his soul, or the Church. Nor did he devise precautions or stratagems against the killers of the flesh, however much he might thereby have escaped this necessity.

O worthy shepherd, who so confidently offered himself to the wolves’ bites lest the sheep be torn! And because he had rejected the world, the world, wishing to crush him, unwittingly exalted him. Then, receiving another blow upon the head, he still remained motionless. But after the third blow, the martyr bent his knees and elbows, offering himself as a living sacrifice, and said in a low voice: “For the name of Jesus and the protection of the Church, I am ready to embrace death.”

But the third knight inflicted a grievous wound upon him as he fell; with that blow he struck his sword against the stone and so severed from the head the crown, which was broad, [Col. 0047C] that the blood, made white by the brain, and the brain, made red by the blood, in the colours of lily and rose, dyed crimson the face of the confessor and martyr—the virgin and mother Church—by his life and death.

The fourth knight drove back those coming forward so that the others might perpetrate the murder more freely and unrestrainedly. The fifth man, however, was not a knight but the cleric who had entered with the knights. Lest the martyr, who had imitated Christ in other respects, should lack a fifth wound, he placed his foot upon the neck of the holy priest and precious martyr and, horrible to relate, scattered his brains and blood across the pavement, crying to the others: “Let us leave here, knights; this man will rise no more.”

Yet amid all these things the distinguished martyr displayed the virtue of incredible constancy. As is human weakness, he did not put up either hand or garment against the striker. When struck, he uttered no word, made no cry, no groan, no sound indicating any pain; but he held motionless beneath the drawn swords the head he had bowed, until, covered in blood and brain matter, his body lay upon the pavement as though bent in prayer, while his spirit was placed in Abraham’s bosom.

[Col. 0047D] Raised above himself through love of his Creator and wholly intent upon the sweetness above, he considered light whatever pain or bitterness the bloody executioner could inflict. How fearlessly this martyr would have fought when principally contending for his own salvation and faith, if for the protection of others—so that ecclesiastical matters might be administered according to ancestral traditions and the decrees of the Church—he offered himself to slaughter so manfully and devoutly!

For, to speak peacefully of the martyrs, each of them principally acted in his own cause when compelled to sacrifice to demons and worship idols; but this man came to purchase the salvation of others with his precious blood, judging that no love is greater than to lay down one’s life for one’s friends. Therefore, because of his wondrous constancy, we believe that this honour was divinely granted him: that he was permitted to triumph in a victorious death not over Jews, pagans, or any ignoble persons, but over the noblest and most powerful Christians.

Finally, his honour is increased because the clemency of his Savior so joined the martyrdom of His servant—or rather the martyr’s birthday—to His own, that, without impairing the prerogative of his fellow citizens, it could neither be more closely united nor prolonged any farther. Who can measure, moreover, the exalted dignity of the place appointed for martyrdom? The very house of Christ, the cradle of the King born the previous day, was painted with the fresh brain and blood of the martyr, so that by this deed both the brutality of the persecutors and the eminent dignity of the martyr might be shown.

Thus the priest of God, departing from the world, was born into heaven on the fourth day before the Kalends of January [29 December], in the year of the incarnation of our Lord and Savior 1171, on the day immediately following the feast of the Innocents; so that he who had long lived innocently and was innocently slain might receive his celebrated time immediately after the Innocents.

When the venerable pontiff had been consummated through martyrdom, those unhappy men—more brutal than all other murderers—exulted and rejoiced as though they had struck down the king’s adversary. Shouting the royal cry, they returned to the palace of the church and ran through the archbishop’s halls and workshops. Whatever was best in gold, silver, clothing, and precious vessels, together with books, the church’s charters and privileges, and other things too numerous to enumerate, they plundered with greed no less great than their cruelty.

Nor was their cruel impiety satisfied with this. Since it could no longer injure him who had been crowned by martyrdom, it did not cease to persecute him in his clerics, retainers, and relatives. Public authority seized whom it could, subjected them to various insults, and stripped them of their resources. With their shepherd struck down, they were scattered through unknown regions, wretched and destitute.

[Col. 0048D] Let the reader consider what was left for a Jew, what for the crucifiers of Christ. But when the sorrowful news of the pontiff’s death resounded, the city was shaken and people ran to the spectacle. Who could explain the astonishment of the beholders, their grief, the greatness of their lamentation? Yet no one dared openly declare that it was an evil deed, from fear of the king’s officers who ran about. Moreover, neither most of the monks nor anyone else had thought otherwise about his person than that which, had any one person fallen from the crowd, would have been thought; but the unprecedented crime enacted in the church brought horror upon all.

I speak of his person, for in our hearing a certain man of our habit and tonsure slandered him, saying that he should by no means be accounted a martyr, since he had been killed deservedly for his obstinacy. But the providence of the Savior did not delay in making known to the world, through the manifold glory of miracles, both the purity of His servant’s life and the justice of his cause—which alone, not the punishment, makes the martyr. During his life in the flesh he had so anxiously concealed knowledge of himself from the world.

Indeed, on the third day after the venerable martyr and bishop of Christ, now having passed beyond fear of mortality, entered the Holy of Holies, to live forever in heaven with Christ, a new light sent from on high restored the light of the world to one who invoked the martyr’s name.

## THE FIRST MIRACLE

The wife of a certain knight of Sussex, whom the severity of a long illness had made blind, heard that the lord of Canterbury had died in this manner. Immediately inspired by God, she burst forth in these words: [Col. 0049B] “Holy martyr of Christ Thomas, I devote myself to you. If you help me in this danger, I shall go with a devout offering to the place of your resting.”

She had scarcely completed her words when, in that same hour, she received the light for which she had long hoped; shortly afterwards she recovered perfectly from the remaining illness. Yet this miracle, like some others, was then kept silent, as though people did not believe it, until the abundance of miracles caused every impiety of opponents to yield and closed the mouth of those speaking wickedly.

That same night of his blessed consummation, the pontiff appeared to one of his household as though about to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass, clothed in pontifical vestments and ascending the step of the altar. When the same vision appeared on the second and third nights, the man who had seen it went further and questioned the saint, saying: “My lord, are you not dead?”

“I was dead,” the saint said, “but I have risen.”

Then he said: “If you have truly risen and are to be numbered among the martyrs, as we believe, why do you not reveal yourself to the world?”

Then the holy archbishop said: “I bear a light, but it cannot appear because of the intervening mist.”

A light indeed. For, leaving aside for the moment that ineffable light—the joy of his Lord, into which, as soon as he departed hence, he must be believed to have entered—those works of light in which the holy man had abounded still living were light; his martyrdom too was light, and especially this martyrdom, although it did not yet shine because the mist of persecution lay between.

But it is enough to have touched upon these matters as testimony, so that the reader may understand how precious in the Lord’s sight was the death of the holy archbishop, whom He commended with the glory of miracles in such swift abundance as we rarely read of in the case of any of the saints.

On the following day, while the sacred body was still kept in the church awaiting burial, one of the king’s attendants came early in the morning and publicly uttered these words with sacrilegious mouth: “This traitor has perished justly. It is indeed an excellent deed and worthy of praise that he has been removed from the midst, he who was trying to wrest the crown from the king’s son.” Then, turning to the monks, he said: “Take him and bury him in the earth as quickly as possible [Col. 0050A], lest he appear; rather, let his memory perish from the earth—he who has acted thus against his lord the king. Or I shall have him torn apart by horses and thrown into a stinking pit to be devoured by pigs and dogs.”

All were therefore disturbed and terrified, lest that impious man and his accomplices should do what he threatened. Their impious and envious minds could perhaps not be satisfied even by the saint’s death unless, after death, he too were treated with dishonour. They hastened to place him in the crypt. Yet first, as was customary, stripping the most pure body of the martyr in order to wash it, they discovered that beneath the clothing of a regular canon he had for so long worn the habit and belonged to the order of monks in such secrecy that even his own close associates had not known it. Finally, next to his flesh they found a hair-shirt so covered with little creatures [Col. 0050B] that anyone would judge the martyrdom of the previous day to have been lighter than this, and the greater enemies to have done him less harm than the lesser. Moreover—something we know no saint had undertaken—he had used hair-cloth drawers sewn so tightly to his legs that from above the knee there extended in length a channel beneath the seam of the hair-cloth, swarming with worms. When they saw these things, the monks, pierced with compunction by the miracle of this unforeseen religious austerity, immediately burst out: “See, see: this man is truly a monk, and we did not know it.”

What groans, what sighs, what abundant showers of tears interrupted the words of all who were present cannot be told. Yet no small consolation then came to them when the holiness of life and the unusual rigour of penance appeared—such as no one except a very few intimate associates could have believed possible in him [Col. 0050C]. From this point, no one could doubt that he had merited the crown of martyrdom, since his life had not lacked the worthiness of martyrdom.

Therefore, after the venerable body had been placed in the crypt with the honour and reverence due to it, they set outside the tomb the sacred blood, which they had gathered from the pavement together with the brains. By heavenly inspiration they took care that it should not be enclosed with the body; for such great benefits were bestowed in a short time through its most health-giving draught that, if they were written down individually, they would surpass the belief of the sick.

For this is the lover of the brethren and of the people of Israel; this is he who prays much for the people and for the holy city Jerusalem. Heaven rejoices in his triumph; the holy Church is confirmed in faith by his sufferings [Col. 0050D]; through his merits and intercession the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the dead rise, and the poor resound with glory to Christ—Christ who, at the first calling, gave faith to His chosen one; in suffering, steadfastness; and, finally, when he was perfected through martyrdom, the fullness of graces, and praise and glory to His name. He is God, blessed with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

**Here ends the Passion of Saint Thomas the Martyr.**

Thereafter Mother Church, bereft of her shepherd, mourned in sorrow and bitterness of heart for many days over the unjust death of her father. She rejoiced indeed for him who had passed to everlasting joy, but she was anxious for her own desolation, since she lacked the protection due from a pontiff [Col. 0051A]. For the course of a year, except only ten days, divine praise was silent within her and the solemnities of the Mass ceased, until the Dayspring from on high visited His people through the precious blood of His martyr. Thus he whose death was believed to have brought the beginning of grief became himself a cause of consolation.

Meanwhile the care of the archiepiscopate was committed to enemies of justice, to be trampled upon rather than guarded, to destroy souls rather than win them. Hence the poor were oppressed; the rights of the Church were violated; priests were compelled, against prohibition, to celebrate the dreadful mysteries; the canons were silent; the decrees of the Fathers were not even heard. There was no place for reason and none for equity. That alone was chosen which avarice suggested, and he who had greater power was judged the better man [Col. 0051B]. Finally, lest the king should be displeased by the malice of his officials, the royal revenues were increased from the offerings of the faithful and from relief intended for the poor; and things specially belonging to God were rendered to Caesar, contrary to the Saviour’s sentence. Yet whoever has presumed rashly to violate the integrity of the divine law shall by no means go unpunished.

One will come who shall judge the poor in righteousness and rebuke with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth, who now cry to the Lord in their tribulation. And see whether, even in this present vengeance, there does not appear a certain inestimable regard of divine mercy for humankind: namely, that while people are outwardly admonished by adversities, the inward mind may more readily be reminded of the sin it has committed, and so the transgressor may return to his heart, according to what the Psalm says [Col. 0051C]: “Fill their faces with shame, and they shall seek Thy name, O Lord.”

Therefore, when holy Mother Church cried to the Lord from the earth, saying, “Avenge, O Lord, the blood of Thy servant, which was innocently shed,” suddenly, contrary to everyone’s expectation, universal peace was thrown into confusion, seditions were stirred up, and civil war arose. Son rose against father and father against son, and a kingdom divided against itself threatened its own speedy desolation—and justly, where the death of the innocent man had gone before as a warning.

Normandy was delivered over to be struck by the enemy’s sword. So great a fury of war immediately invaded it that neither churches nor ecclesiastical ministers were spared, even amid the sacred solemnities of the Mass. For we learned that a priest standing at the altar in sacred vestments was slaughtered by impious men [Col. 0051D], and it was reported that at that time many other excessively horrible and unheard-of deeds were perpetrated. England accordingly trembled and was shaken at the prospect of the coming disaster, which it already saw hanging over its neck. Besieged by enemies encircling it on every side, while inwardly full of deadly seditions, so that trust was safe nowhere and no friend was trusted—one man arguing his father’s cause, another his son’s, as the more just—it awaited nothing but a general collapse.

But lest the blood shed should make the glory of His martyr more grievous, He who had brought wrath because of his death—of which no one doubted—again, through the merits of that martyr, restored peace and delivered His people from the hand of the enemy. For He does not will the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.

Who could ever have believed that the authors of so great a crime were preserved for repentance, unless Christ might thereby also magnify His saint? Hence one may now see even those same adversaries revering him dead with more devoted zeal than they had persecuted him alive [Col. 0052A].

Finally, the king himself, conscious of the innocent blood which had been shed—although neither by his command nor through his agency, yet because of the hostility he had borne toward Thomas—was shown in a vision that there was no other path to obtaining peace except by placating and being reconciled with the martyr. So great a confusion of affairs had already seized the entire kingdom in vengeance for him that no one hoped for peace without much bloodshed. Setting aside, therefore, his royal pride, with a contrite and humbled heart he came to the tomb of the precious martyr [Col. 0052B], intending to seek pardon for his presumption.

As he hastened there and was already near the city, he wished publicly to show how fervently devoted he was toward the saint of God and how deeply penitence afflicted him for what he had done against him. From the church of our blessed father Dunstan—the first church encountered by those entering the city—to the greater church where the body of the blessed martyr rests, he went barefoot and in ordinary clothing, weeping. Wherever the route through the city appeared rougher, he took it, considering neither the harshness of the journey, nor the tenderness of his feet, nor the spectacle he made to the crowd on every side, but the peril of his soul and the wound of his conscience.

It had indeed been customary for the community to go out joyfully to meet kings and solemnly render them certain services of reverence [Col. 0052C]. But he forbade all these honours to be offered to him, being nourished more by grief than joy, saying: “My harp is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of those who weep.”

Coming, therefore, to the doors of the church, he proceeded and prayed. Entering the place of martyrdom where the saint had fallen, he watered it with tears and kissed it. Having made his confession in the presence of the bishops standing there, he approached the tomb with great trembling and reverence. There, wholly prostrate in body and for no brief time intent upon prayer, what sobs he uttered, what sighs, with what copious shower of tears he drenched the very marble, cannot be estimated.

After prayer had continued for a long time, the bishop of London, making satisfaction on the king’s behalf to the monks and the multitude gathered there, began with these words [Col. 0052D]: “Since it is known that some hold an opinion other than the true integrity of events, as it stands before God, to whom all things are naked and open, and before Christ the Lord, whom he here venerates in faith and truth, and in the presence of your brotherhood, our lord the king acknowledges in a pure confession that evil men killed the venerable archbishop neither by his command nor even with his knowledge. But when he learned that he had been killed, he conceived such sorrow of heart—as we who were present then observed—as he had never suffered for any event whatsoever.

“Concerning the word which, carried away by anger, he uttered, from which profane rashness is believed to have taken occasion to kill him; and because he so stubbornly pursued him while he lived, he declares himself guilty [Col. 0053A] and asks pardon, ready in every respect to make satisfaction according to your judgment. Therefore he humbly asks for the support of you all, so that in the sight of our Lord and Saviour, who does not despise ‘a contrite and humbled heart,’ and that blessed Thomas the martyr may accept his humble repentance.

“Today he restores in full the dignities and rights of this church, whatever the Catholic Church is known to have possessed more freely in former times, whether in this kingdom or in other kingdoms throughout the world. Moreover, from his own resources he offers an income of thirty pounds as a gift to the martyr, so that, through your intercession, he may become gracious, forgetful of injuries. Furthermore, he forgives from his heart all ill will to all who seemed to have offended him in the cause of the venerable archbishop [Col. 0053B], and he receives today into his former favour and affection all who were of that archbishop’s household or cause—clerics, kinsmen, and servants—whom he had at any time distressed in any matter more than he ought.”

As the bishop delivered these words, when he had finished speaking the king graciously granted all these things and declared that they would remain valid in the future. After this, stripped of his outer garment, with shoulders and head bent into one of the windows of the tomb, in humility and devotion so complete that he moved everyone to mourning, he was struck first five times by the prelates, then by eighty monks and more, three strokes from each individual; and thus he was solemnly absolved.

When these things had been done, seated on the bare ground, with bare feet not even washed after the mud, and fasting as he had arrived [Col. 0053C]—for the pain of penitence did not permit him any indulgence of rest—he spent the entire night in prayer. With downcast face and the whole bearing of his body, he made sufficiently clear that this was the work and change of mind of Him “who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble.” Nor is it easy to find anywhere in the history of Christian times a prince humbler than this one in penance, or anyone more devout.

And lest anyone doubt that, through the merits of blessed Thomas the martyr, the severity of the divine sentence, which had been inspired, was changed and placated by the king’s satisfaction, an evident sign of this was shown even then. For on the very day when the king came to Canterbury to make satisfaction for his offences against the saint, the count of Flanders, who had besieged the coast with an immense army in order to make a sudden invasion of England, suddenly changed his plan and returned. On the following day, moreover—as was later discovered by calculating the dates—the king of the Scots, who had likewise set out to ravage and plunder the English of Northumbria, was captured in battle. All enemies were soon silenced, and those disturbing the kingdom’s peace were humbled [Col. 0053D].

And just as, in vengeance for the innocently shed blood, the wrath of God raged against both king and kingdom because of the king’s fault, so again, when the king was humbled and the venerable martyr intervened, the Godhead was propitiated, subdued the enemies, and restored a more abundant gift of peace. Therefore, illustrious martyr, we offer you the fruit of our lips and the labour of our hands, praying that, if our discourse has anywhere overstepped the bounds of truth [Col. 0054A], we may obtain pardon and life through your holy intercession and merits. Amen.

Through the accusation of certain persons whose business it is to sow discord among brothers, before he had assumed the priorate of Canterbury Lord Benedict incurred the king’s displeasure. The malice of perverse men so prevailed against the man with the king that, unless reverence for blessed Thomas—whose special protection he, as a monk, invoked—had checked the king’s fury, the king’s rage would have raged against him more fiercely than befitted royal majesty.

For it belongs to a criminal mind, when it does not itself pursue virtues, to persecute men of virtue, if not by deeds then by words. This invective, however, does not reproach the king’s mind as one that loves evil; rather, it bites at the malice of those at whose suggestion the king is believed to have conceived the heat of anger against Benedict [Col. 0054B].

Blessed Thomas, whose martyrdom and miracles this man of whom we speak transmitted to posterity in elegant style, thus reconciled him to the king in return for the service rendered: he had been cleared of the accusation which had brought him under suspicion, as though he were acting otherwise than the rule of his profession required.

For after he had obtained the priorate, when his brethren compelled him, on account of the Church’s affairs, to follow the king for a long time, he did not dare to approach him because of the king’s fearsome threats. A vision shown from heaven softened the king’s ferocity, which was swelling against the innocent man. For in a dream he saw himself walking across a very large and elevated bridge. When he reached the middle of a river flowing swiftly beneath, the decking on which the king’s foot rested suddenly gave way [Col. 0054C], and he immediately slipped through the opening and hung suspended by his arms in the middle, about to fall at once into the open abyss below; and the solitude of the place promised him no assistance at all.

After many attempts, when his strength was beginning to fail and all hope of human help had vanished, remembering that salvation belongs to the Lord, he repeatedly called upon the sweet name of the Lord and Saviour; he repeated also the name of Mary His mother, invoking every patron, while no one helped him in his peril: “Help me,” he said, “holy Thomas, martyr of Christ; come to my aid. Do not remember the injuries of recent times—you whom, in the beginning, I loved above all men.”

He had scarcely finished the words when, behold, Prior Benedict came running in haste [Col. 0054D]. Asked why or whence he came, Benedict answered the king: “The holy archbishop whom you invoked in faith has sent me to rescue you.” Extending his hand to him, he set him, rescued from the place of death and the pit of misery, upon the bridge; and the vision disappeared.

On waking, the king was disturbed by terror at the extraordinary vision and spent the rest of the night sleepless. A dreadful stupefaction of mind caused such distress throughout all his limbs that he scarcely rose from bed about midday because of extreme pain. Therefore, when the prior came, the vision was set forth, and the king rendered thanks to God and to precious Thomas the martyr no less earnestly than if his life had been restored from a real danger. For he testified that for no—even immeasurable—weight of money would he again undergo the terror of that vision [Col. 0055A].

And lest anyone maintain that these things happened by chance, and that a dream is not to be wondered at, we on the contrary venerate it as all the more sublime because it is more subtle; and we confess that it should be exalted with all the greater magnificence and praise because through it not a body, soon to die from some illness, but a soul destined to live for ever was raised from the abyss of deadly hatred.

For the king, who on the day before he saw these things had pursued this man both through officials performing public duties and personally through open verbal insult, was reproved by Him “who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble.” He received him into familiar favour [Col. 0056A] and generously granted with ready mind whatever he asked. Thus in this change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, He may be praised and adored, in whose hand are the hearts of kings. Since He is wonderful in His saints, He has shown, by a very subtle and manifold sign of miracles, for the praise and glory of His name, of what merit our outstanding martyr was. Others have told this differently, but this was the vision.

[Col. 0055]

# The Second Life of Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury and Martyr, by Roger of Pontigny

[Col. 0055B] ## Prologue

Since the venerable Passion of the most precious martyr Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, holds a singular place of reverence and devotion in the minds of all the faithful, many are nevertheless troubled that no complete history of his life and deeds is found anywhere. This is especially so since this lamp was not hidden under a bushel, but was placed conspicuously upon the Church’s lampstand, illuminating by its splendour not merely the narrow bounds of western regions but the breadth of the whole world.

For we have learned that, through ignorance of the truth, some have held not merely differing but even contradictory opinions concerning the blessed man. We judged that their ignorance should be remedied by a diligence necessary indeed, but perhaps rash and overly presumptuous [Col. 0055C], lest falsehood become for them a detriment to devotion and for posterity a seedbed of error.

Now the illustrious man John of Salisbury published something concerning the blessed man’s life and deeds and the triumph of his precious death, in language that was eloquent and faithful indeed, but exceedingly concise. Although this work greatly benefited the devotion of the faithful, it did not satisfy fully, because he used a summary manner of expression, as he himself asserts. He did not pursue more extensively and explicitly matters which at that time were very well known and widely circulated, lest he seem less necessary than superfluous.

Certainly, if John himself had chosen to do this, without doubt no one could have accomplished it more usefully or better than he: he possessed incomparable eloquence [Col. 0055D] and the most certain knowledge of the events. From his earliest age he had been closely attached to the blessed man and had been his inseparable companion in persecutions.

Concerning these matters, and concerning the ways in which the Lord glorified His saint after death and showed him to live, by merit of his precious death, not only in heaven but also on earth, the venerable Benedict, prior of the church of Canterbury, composed a full account. From it one plainly learns how precious before the Lord is his holy death; for the Lord does not cease constantly to commend him by such numerous signs of virtues and miracles [Col. 0056B].

Finally, we too, who ministered to the blessed man during his exile and received the priestly office through the sacred laying-on of his hands, have taken care to record those matters concerning him which have been less fully told, lest they wholly perish from memory through the passage of time. Our style is rough and unpolished, but wholly full of truth [Col. 0056C]. We insert absolutely nothing except what we ourselves saw and heard, or what we learned from the most certain and faithful report of those who were present. Yet if anyone should perhaps disdain the lowliness and plainness of the composition, let not truth, though clothed in a ragged garment, thereby be made cheap.

Thomas, then, was born in the city of London, of parents most eminent according to their civic station. His father’s name was Gilbert; his mother was called Matilda. Although she appeared distinguished by excellence of birth beyond her civic rank, manifold uprightness of character, devotion and religious observance, and constant almsgiving made her far more venerable and worthy of praise.

At one time, when she was pregnant with the child she had conceived [Col. 0056D] and had given herself to sleep at night, she seemed to see the River Thames, which flows past London, flow wholly into [Col. 0057A] her womb through her mouth. On waking, she marvelled greatly at the vision, nor did she consider it meaningless that something so unusual had happened to her. Seeking advice concerning the vision, she went to a certain religious and learned man. Although he had learned that dreams should not be heeded and did not attach much weight to women’s visions, nevertheless, out of respect for the matron who asked him, he replied that in Holy Scripture water signifies peoples. He wondered what it could mean that she had seen waters—that is, peoples—flowing into her womb, ignorant, of course, of what was to come, which today may openly be seen in the Church of Canterbury.

Thus corrected and instructed by that man not henceforth to believe in dreams, which have led many astray, she returned home.

Not long afterwards, as she slept, she again seemed to see herself come to Canterbury for prayer. As she approached the church, apparently just about to enter, her womb suddenly swelled, as it seemed to her, so greatly that she thought she could scarcely enter through the doors of the greater church. Yet after she entered with difficulty, her womb, as it seemed to her, swelled and grew to such vast and extended size that it occupied the whole space of the church [Col. 0057B]. Waking and remembering the dream, she was greatly astonished and afraid. Yet she did not dare return to the interpreter mentioned above, fearing that he would accuse her of curiosity. So she was silent, keeping these things in her heart.

When the time of childbirth was fulfilled, she bore a son. The boy was born on the feast day of blessed Thomas the Apostle, and on that same day, after Vespers, was baptized and received the name Thomas. Thereafter he was carefully brought up, having a nurse who spared his mother’s efforts in the care of the child, so that his mother herself might meanwhile devote herself more freely to prayer and her customary works of mercy.

One night, while the mother slept, anxious about her son, she seemed to see the boy lying naked and uncovered in his cradle. Therefore, as it seemed to her, she was deeply distressed and harshly rebuked the nurse for negligence and carelessness. But the nurse said that the boy was carefully wrapped and tightly swaddled; indeed, she declared that beneath him was laid a red cloth of pure silk, of marvellous brilliance and workmanship [Col. 0057C].

The mother seemed to herself to run quickly to ascertain whether the nurse spoke the truth about both the child and the cloth. Finding it as the nurse had said, she marvelled greatly at the beauty and brilliance of the cloth. Wishing to examine more certainly and fully the elegance of its marvellous workmanship, she began, with the nurse’s help, to unfold it partly; but the smallness of the room did not allow it to be unfolded at all. They went out into a larger house, but that too, owing to its own smallness, did not permit this. Then they went out into the street; but even when only a small part of the cloth had been unfolded, the whole street seemed occupied.

Therefore, with greater desire to see it, they finally went anxiously beyond the city into the field called Smedhefell, so that at least there, in the widest open expanse of the field, they might inspect to their satisfaction the beauty [Col. 0058A] and size of the cloth. Though they worked by every means to unfold it, the field itself now seemed to confine and constrain them by its smallness. They heard a voice saying that they were striving vainly and to no purpose, since not even all England would suffice to contain the size of that cloth.

We do not say these things as though we wished to establish the man’s greatness by women’s visions; but we do not wish to seem to suppress things known to have occurred, even if they are of this sort.

Nor does it seem unworthy of divine mercy for the future greatness and glory of a son to be revealed in this manner to a pious and religious mother, since Scripture contains many examples of such things.

When the boy reached teachable years, his mother entrusted him to the study of letters [Col. 0058B]. Even at that age, something of splendour and grace beyond that of his contemporaries appeared in his face and manners. But because “not first that which is spiritual, but that which is natural,” we shall set down briefly and in simple, faithful language how he spent the years of his earliest life, adding nothing in the manner of one praising or striving to commend someone.

As his body grew, the strength of his understanding grew with it. Such liveliness of mind and memory was in him that he easily grasped what he heard and could recall without difficulty, whenever and as often as he wished, what he had learned once. In explaining the most difficult propositions and unravelling perplexing questions, he seemed by the keenness of his happy intellect to surpass many serious and learned men [Col. 0058C].

He also possessed marvellous sharpness and subtlety of the bodily senses, as we ourselves frequently proved in his later life. Thus scarcely anything could be said in his presence, even at some distance and in a low voice, that he would not hear if he chose to listen. Likewise, no smell capable of affecting the sense of smell—however distant or foul—failed immediately either to offend his nostrils or delight his sense of smell. And whence came these things except from grace, which, although not yet spiritually, nonetheless worked in him bodily even then, to the wonder of many?

A knight named Richer of Aquila lodged in his father’s house, a man noble and honourable according to the world, but almost always occupied with the pursuit of dogs and birds. While Thomas was still a boy, during a half-year holiday from school, he gladly and frequently followed this man when he went out on such pursuits, taking great delight in these occupations. From this he is believed to have acquired the habit to which, later in life, whenever he had leisure, he also devoted attention [Col. 0058D].

It happened that the knight in question went out one day, according to his custom, on a similar expedition, and Thomas followed him on horseback. Their route crossed a very swift river, over which was a small and narrow bridge capable of carrying only pedestrians. Not far below was a mill, toward which this river rushed precipitously with great force, its banks built up on either side so that it would not overflow [Col. 0059A]. The knight, disregarding danger for the sake of a shortcut, crossed the bridge first. Thomas, secure and hooded, for he suspected no misfortune, followed directly in his footsteps.

And behold: when he had come to the middle of the bridge, the horse suddenly slipped, and the boy, with the horse itself, fell into the middle of the river. The waters received him, and he was separated from the horse by the violent force of the waves and carried downstream. Already he was approaching the mill, to be crushed by its wheel no less than drowned by the waters.

While this was happening, and Thomas seemed to stand at the boundary of death, the man who tended the mill, knowing absolutely nothing of what was occurring, suddenly cut off the water from the wheel. The knight and his companion followed the boy along the bank with loud and pitiful cries [Col. 0059B]. Hearing their voices now that the mill was quiet and its noise had stopped, the aforesaid man at last came out of the mill, wondering what was the matter. Seeing Thomas amid the waves, he quickly put forth his hand and drew him to land half alive and scarcely breathing.

No one should believe this occurred by chance, rather than that divine providence mercifully provided such sudden and unexpected assistance for the endangered boy and future bishop of His Church.

When his mother learned what had happened, she did not grieve so much over the danger as rejoice at his marvellous and unexpected rescue. Thereafter she gathered hope for the future, believing that divine mercy had not rescued him from death in such a manner without purpose [Col. 0059C].

Moreover, his venerable mother was accustomed at fixed times to weigh her son, placing alongside him bread, meat, clothing, coins, and other things necessary for the use of the poor, and to distribute all these things to needy people. By this she strove more earnestly to commend him to divine mercy and to the protection of blessed Mary ever-virgin.

For among the works of mercy which she performed diligently and without ceasing, she always had a special devotion to the remembrance of the Blessed Virgin. As Thomas himself used to relate, she carefully taught her son the fear of the Lord and urged him to embrace and venerate blessed Mary ever-virgin with special devotion [Col. 0059D], to invoke her constantly as the guide and patroness of his life and deeds, and, after Christ, to commit his hope to her.

When Thomas had completed his twenty-first year, his mother—who alone pressed him to receive an education—died, and thereafter Thomas began to apply himself less diligently to study.

Thus, disliking his father’s house as empty and desolate after his mother’s death, he joined a certain kinsman of his in London, a man of great name and honour not only among fellow citizens but also at court. Staying with him for nearly three years, Thomas gave many proofs of his good disposition to those who could then know him.

He so zealously and vehemently detested luxury, buffoonery, and avarice [Col. 0060A] that he would have made himself wholly hateful and unwelcome to those who delighted in such things, had not his outstanding gentleness and generosity made him worthy of affection even to those whom he displeased in this respect. For he cared for and reserved nothing of what he could possess, but distributed everything with generous liberality to serve the needs and wishes of his companions. By such beginnings grace was forming him for that contempt of worldly things and compassion toward the poor which afterwards shone out in him.

Sometimes, when conversation arose among his companions, he used ordinary and seemingly amorous expressions, lest he be considered entirely alien and inhuman even by that class of people. Yet he was admirable in the purity of his chastity [Col. 0060B]. He did this deliberately, with a skill he possessed in high degree, presenting an outward appearance not unlike others, in accordance with the counsel of the Wise Man, while inwardly all things were truly unlike.

At that time the most reverend Theobald, taken from the monastery of Bec, presided over the Church of Canterbury by both merit and rank: a man in every respect praiseworthy and distinguished, most experienced in both secular and ecclesiastical affairs. One of his officials, being obliged by the business entrusted to him frequently to visit London and having long been accustomed to lodge in Thomas’s father’s house for hospitality, had known Thomas fully from infancy. Seeing him now a handsome young man, cultivated in learning and adorned with prudence and good character, he began to urge him to travel with him to the court of his lord, the archbishop of Canterbury [Col. 0060C].

But Thomas judged that, if he put himself forward uninvited, he would be regarded not as dutiful but as presumptuous; and so he delayed again. At last, more fully persuaded by the advice of the aforementioned man, he presented himself, suitably and honourably equipped and accompanied by that man, before the reverend gaze of the pontiff.

The man of higher prudence observed him, perceived intelligence from the expression of his face, and received him graciously and honourably, commanding him to remain with him. Thereafter Thomas lived as a member of the court. In a short time he stood in such favour with the bishop that the latter had no one more intimate and, as he thought, no one dearer [Col. 0060D]. For the wise man, quickly recognizing the sincerity of Thomas’s gentleness and prudence, continually consulted him in his counsels and frequently entrusted his affairs to him. Finding him prudent in counsel and energetic and faithful in business, he strove to bind him to himself by a closer bond of affection and familiarity—yet not without envy.

There was a certain man, eminent both through his intimacy with the bishop and through ecclesiastical rank, named Roger of Pont, archdeacon of the bishop of Canterbury; and he did not bear Thomas’s great favor at court with equanimity. He not only wasted away inwardly with the plague of envy, but sometimes burst openly into insults and reproaches, so that he would often call Thomas the clerk of Baillehache [Col. 0061A], for that was the surname of the man with whom Thomas had come to court. Nor was this spiteful envy momentary and passing, as the subsequent outcome of events proved. Thomas, nevertheless, continued in his customary gentleness and grew in favor with God and men.

Meanwhile, insofar as he could, he applied himself to civil law and the sacred canons, so that he might be regarded as better prepared in pleading or deciding cases, and might acquire fuller knowledge of ecclesiastical affairs. An occasion arose for Theobald, bishop of Canterbury, to plan a visit to the Roman Church; and he set out, as befitted him, with an honorable and ample retinue, taking Thomas with him, in whose prudence and fidelity he placed especial confidence [Col. 0061B]. Nor without reason: during that journey and in his business he found Thomas necessary to him in many matters. On his prosperous return, more fully assured of Thomas’s excellence, and judging him worthy of greater things, he first bestowed upon him the church of Otford. Afterwards he sent him to Rome several times on ecclesiastical business, finding in every matter an industry deservedly worthy of praise. At that time William, archbishop of York, having happily completed the term of his life and his pontifical office, rested in a blessed end.

Thus, when the see of York was vacant, Theobald, bishop of Canterbury and primate of all England, strove by every means to place his archdeacon Roger, of whom we spoke a little before, over that see [Col. 0061C], so that in this way he might provide both for the dignity of the Church of Canterbury and for his own honor and that of his clerk, while opening for Thomas a road to greater things. Nor was he frustrated in his purpose. For when the aforesaid Roger, with the king’s connivance, had been installed and consecrated in the see of York, Theobald without delay assigned to Thomas the archdeaconry of the Church of Canterbury and the provostship of Beverley, which Roger had held, together with several other churches.

Thomas, then, having acquired these things, was no longer content with a private manner of life, but raised himself to greater, more conspicuous, and more evident proofs of virtue. He mercifully and abundantly distributed his revenues for the uses and needs of the poor, while spending all the rest as well [Col. 0061D]—for that too ought not at that time to be omitted—upon all persons with marvelous liberality and magnificence. The archbishop, seeing that his judgment concerning his Thomas had been in no way mistaken, indeed that results greater than his hopes had followed, took great pleasure in his splendor. Thomas himself, though deemed magnificent in all things and by all persons, conceived no arrogance from it; rather, with a humility and reverence greater than usual, he obeyed his bishop in everything.

At that time, namely in the year 1154 from the incarnation of the Lord, when Henry, son of Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and of the Empress Matilda, succeeded to his ancestral kingdom, various disturbances and ambitions for political change arose throughout England [Col. 0062A]. There was no small anxiety in the Church of that realm, both because of the king’s questionable age and because of the known ill-will of his close associates toward the rights of ecclesiastical liberty. Nor was this without cause, as the outcome showed.

The bishop of Canterbury, concerned for the present and fearful for the future, considered setting some remedy against the evils he feared were impending. It seemed to him that, if he could insert Thomas into the king’s counsels, very great tranquillity and peace might result for the English Church. For he knew Thomas to be high-minded and prudent, one who possessed zeal for God together with knowledge and who championed ecclesiastical liberty with his whole affection. Therefore the bishop of Canterbury summoned to himself Philip, bishop of Bayeux, and Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, upon whose counsels the king relied in his early years [Col. 0062B]. He began to speak of Thomas’s prudence, energy, and fidelity, and of the praiseworthy and admirable gentleness of his character. When the said bishops agreed in accordance with the archbishop’s wish and persuasion, Thomas entered the royal court and received the title and office of chancellor.

From that point it is not easy to explain how he bore a double character, namely ecclesiastical and courtly. Yet in his beginnings he endured such assaults by rivals and was provoked by such insolence from informers that, as he was accustomed to confess in familiar complaint to his bishop and other friends, he intended to withdraw from court if this could be done without reproach and the stain of dishonor. But [Col. 0062C], when the king had quickly recognized his fidelity and competence, he held him so dear with such affection that he is thought never to have loved anyone equally. Entrusting everything to him, the king devoted himself to youthful exercises, while Thomas energetically and authoritatively performed his duties and business: now, armored as commander of the army, he led the troops; now, free from campaigns, he administered justice to the people. Differing from the king in name alone, he ordered the whole realm as he pleased, with princes and magistrates subject to his nod, and all certainly knowing that the only thing pleasing to the king would be what Thomas judged expedient.

And although the king had already conceived in his mind what he later displayed in action, nevertheless during this period the state of the Church remained secure and tranquil under Thomas’s protection, because Thomas in every matter [Col. 0062D] cautiously, and as though from concealment so as not to give occasion for suspicion, frustrated the king’s perverse will and the secret machinations of his associates. For at that time it was not easy for anything to be done which Thomas’s judgment did not approve. To mark still further the greatness of his affection, the king entrusted to him his eldest son Henry, commanding him to procure for him the homages and oaths of fealty of the kingdom of England.
