He knew beyond doubt that so great a matter could be brought to completion by no one better than Thomas; and so it came to pass. For while the king was staying in Normandy, Thomas summoned the counts and all the leading men of the realm and carried the king’s command into effect without anyone contradicting or resisting. Very many marvelled, since it was thought that this could not easily be done without disturbance, nor even with the king himself present [Col. 0063A].

Although, therefore, he was most busily occupied in secular affairs, he neither forgot nor neglected the things of God. For he overflowed with such bowels of piety and mercy toward the poor that secular men regarded him in this respect as superstitious rather than religious. A great multitude of poor people was brought daily to his table, and such an abundance of food was set before them as might have sufficed even for the rich. Wherever he went, his hand was never empty of a gift, provided only that there was someone to ask; for he mercifully extended his hand to every person who met him and sought alms. The wretched and oppressed had immediate access to him, and the widow’s cause came before him; he diligently rendered judgment for the needy and redress for the poor.

Such a multitude of soldiers and persons of various ranks followed him that, compared with their number, the royal household sometimes remained almost as though empty, and the king himself appeared to live almost unattended [Col. 0063B]. Yet though he appeared excessively devoted to popular favor, piety of faith and zeal for ecclesiastical liberty burned within him. He also always preserved with watchful care the purity of chastity which he had embraced from early youth, knowing beyond doubt that, even if all things were lawful to him in view of the time and his power, not all things were beneficial. And although the world, and whatever allurements mortal life contains, seemed in every way to applaud him, it is certain that he never did anything [Col. 0063C] that injured or diminished his chastity in any respect.

We have certainly learned from those who attended him intimately in service for twenty years and more that they had never discovered anything of this sort in him. On the contrary, when physicians advised him to indulge his natural constitution in this matter, asserting that this suited both his age and his bodily temperament and would contribute greatly to preserving his health, he was accustomed to reply that such medicine was utterly contrary to him, since it would defile rather than help both body and soul.

At the same time, after Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, had died, the king resolved to give Thomas to him as successor, believing him most worthy of so great an honor and, in every matter [Col. 0063D], most ready to serve his own advantage and will. For Thomas deliberately showed himself almost exceedingly severe toward ecclesiastical persons and property, in order, by this opportunity, to cast off every mark of suspicion from himself and, beneath this disguise, to accord more fittingly with the king’s will, which he knew intimately. The king therefore believed that his purpose against the Church could above all be fulfilled through Thomas, whom he had found most faithful to himself in everything and inclined toward his wishes. He irrevocably resolved that Thomas should be appointed bishop over the Church of Canterbury.

Accordingly, he sent two bishops and with them a magnate especially faithful to him, namely Richard de Lucy, and commanded them to convene the community of Canterbury concerning the election of a bishop. Arriving at Canterbury [Col. 0064A] and entering the chapter-house, they first extolled in many words the king’s kindness and devotion; then they instructed Richard de Lucy to lay the king’s commands before them.

Then Richard said: “Since it so pleases our lords the bishops that we should make known to you the king’s will, know with certainty that our lord the king, as you have heard more fully from them, is exceedingly zealous in matters pertaining to God and bears the greatest and most particular devotion toward the holy Church; especially toward this present Church of Canterbury, which he humbly and faithfully acknowledges with filial love as his special mother in the Lord. Therefore, lest through the prolonged absence of a shepherd it should perhaps be disturbed or burdened in any respect, know that he has granted you freedom of election [Col. 0064B], provided, however, that you choose a person suitable for so great a burden and honor. For you are not unaware that in such a business our lord the king is accustomed to consider nothing except what he believes pleasing to God and beneficial to the holy Church. It therefore rests upon you henceforth, and is altogether expedient, that you elect such a man that under his protection you may rejoice according to God and according to men. For if king and archbishop cleave to one another in a welcome bond of affection and mutually cherish one another in friendship, there can be no doubt that the times will meanwhile be happy and that the Church’s condition will remain pleasant and tranquil. But if—God forbid!—the matter should turn out otherwise, I do not think your holiness can be unaware how many dangers, disturbances, labors, tumults, losses of property, and perils to souls would follow [Col. 0064C]!”

When Richard had ended his speech and the bishops themselves had approved it as worthy of praise, the prior of Canterbury first gave thanks to God and then, with due reverence, returned boundless thanks to the king for his goodwill and concern toward them. Then, at the bishops’ direction, he named and summoned several monks advanced in age and prudence and went outside. When they had sat down and begun to deliberate on what they had heard, it seemed to them that nothing could be said or decided without the counsel of the bishops and of Richard himself, who surely knew the king’s will best; and upon that will the entire substance of the election necessarily depended. They therefore summoned [Col. 0064D] the royal envoys—Bartholomew, bishop of Exeter, Hilary of Chichester, and Richard. When they had come and had at length conferred extensively with them on the proposed business, all unanimously, monks and bishops alike, with one voice and one judgment, elected the chancellor as shepherd and bishop of their souls.

The monks, however, had hesitated for some time over the election, not because they were ignorant that Thomas was a man of virtue, but because he did not display the habit of religion; for until those times the Church of Canterbury had almost always had as bishops men religious in life and habit. For Saint Augustine, monk of blessed and apostolic Pope Gregory, who preached the faith of Christ to the English people, had ordered and established the Church of Canterbury and many other churches in those regions under regular and monastic discipline [Col. 0065A], because the Church of Canterbury had hitherto observed customs, especially in the election of its bishop, more diligently than other churches. Nevertheless, balancing the one thing which they disliked in the character of their elect against consideration of the other virtues and graces that shone more brightly in him, they unanimously elected him with good heart and willing mind.

The bishops sent by the king for this purpose appointed a day in London for the prior and monks of Canterbury, on which the remaining rites of the election might be completed publicly before all the bishops and abbots of the whole realm, in the presence of the younger king. For his father had already arranged that he should have the kingdom and, as was said above [Col. 0065B], had caused the homages and oaths of fealty of the realm to be rendered to him through the hand of his chancellor. The king had also written to him concerning the election at the Church of Canterbury, signifying that whatever might be done in his presence he too would grant and confirm, and would hold valid for all time.

The said bishops, therefore, by the king’s command summoned to London on the appointed day all the bishops and abbots of the realm, as well as the priors of conventual churches, the counts and nobles, and all the king’s officers. When all had assembled together on the appointed day, the prior of Canterbury reverently declared before the presence and hearing [Col. 0065C] of all the bishops the form of the election celebrated at Canterbury by the king’s will and command, in the presence of the bishops whom the king had sent for that very purpose. He stated that, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, they had unanimously and canonically elected Thomas, chancellor of the realm, as archbishop. The bishops who had attended the election at Canterbury as envoys from the king repeatedly commended both the form of the election and the person elected; all gave their assent and blessed God in harmonious rejoicing, alike with their wishes and voices.

Only Gilbert Foliot, bishop of London, was found to object and mutter against it. Yet seeing the unanimous agreement of all and that his own solitary malice could achieve nothing, he too gave his assent. He was an aged and very learned man [Col. 0065D], and a monk by habit, who, according to common report, had long aspired to the archbishopric. Then all the bishops went together into the presence of the younger king, seeking his assent, favor, and goodwill for their election. He received them with great exultation, favored and approved it. The magistrates and officers of the realm also—for the king his father had written to them concerning the election—“received and praised the election with devotion and boundless joy.”

Henry, bishop of Winchester, no less eminent for birth than for prudence and religion, spoke thus to the boy king: “My lord, our elected chancellor has for a long time occupied the highest place in the household of your father the king and throughout the entire realm; and he has held the kingdom at his own disposal, nor has anything been done in the realm in his time except at his discretion. We therefore ask that he be handed over to the Church of God and to us, free and absolved from every bond and courtly service, from every accusation and suit, and from every occasion whatsoever; so that, emancipated and unencumbered from this hour onward, he may freely perform the things of God. For we have learned that your father the king delegated his authority in this matter to you and will hold welcome and valid whatever you determine concerning it.”

The king accepted this petition, and willingly surrendered Thomas, in accordance with the request of the bishop of Winchester, free and absolved from all secular service to the Church. Thomas himself, from the beginning when he learned that talk of his advancement had arisen, opposed it by every means in his power, lest the matter come to completion. For he knew beyond doubt that two masters whose wills differed so widely could not be served in harmony, and that whoever became bishop of Canterbury would soon have either God or the king as an enemy. Nevertheless [Col. 0066B], God disposing otherwise, Henry of Pisa, cardinal-priest and legate of the Apostolic See, a monk of the Cistercian Order, furthered the matter, urgently pressed it by every means, and encouraged and animated Thomas to undertake the governance. Thus his election had the outcome briefly related above.

The bishops, having agreed among themselves upon a day for the consecration, assembled at Canterbury. With them came an innumerable multitude of abbots, religious persons, clerics, and nobles of that land, desiring to be present at the consecration of so great a bishop and at the first fruits of the Masses and blessings [Col. 0066C]. Thomas himself also came for the day with a very great company of religious men and other venerable persons. The bishops, monks, clergy, and an innumerable multitude of people went out to meet him, with great joy and honor. So great was the devotion and rejoicing of those who came to meet him that it cannot be expressed in words.

Although the sound of joy and exultation rang out on every side, Thomas did not set his heart on these things. Instead, in great humility and contrition, with tears flowing abundantly, he approached on foot, thinking more of the burden laid upon him [Col. 0066D] than of the honor bestowed. He was accordingly ordained and consecrated bishop, the venerable Henry, bishop of Winchester, laying his hand upon him. This man was distinguished among his fellow bishops both for religious life and birth; for he was a monk and brother of Stephen of Blois, who had held the kingdom of England for nearly twenty years after King Henry the elder.

William the Bastard was succeeded by his son, surnamed Rufus, who expelled from his kingdom Saint Anselm, the holy and illustrious archbishop of Canterbury. William Rufus, while occupied in hunting, was killed by an arrow shot by a certain knight very dear to him—not so much by chance as, it is believed, by divine will. He was succeeded by his brother Henry, father of the Empress Matilda [Col. 0067A]. This magnificent and most powerful King Henry was succeeded by the aforesaid Stephen of Blois, brother of the bishop of Winchester and of the most illustrious Count Theobald the elder. While Stephen was still living and reigning, Henry, son of the Empress Matilda, arrived and took the kingdom. In the eighth year of that reign Thomas was consecrated bishop of Canterbury.

After his consecration, he took care to show more earnest zeal and diligence in making his life and conduct correspond to so great a rank. At once, divine grace cooperating, he was changed into another man: he put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new man in righteousness and holiness. Yet he again concealed his purpose from men by the decency of his accustomed clothing. Wearing haircloth next to his flesh, he continually devoted himself to reading and prayer [Col. 0067B], withdrawing and removing himself as far as possible from secular affairs so that he might attend more freely and effectively to spiritual pursuits.

Whenever necessity of office required him to take part in any causes, he displayed remarkable patience in hearing them, diligence in investigating or examining them, and justice in judging them. Setting aside entirely all regard for gifts or persons, he rebuked offenders with great freedom, always more severely the rich and powerful. He showed himself ready to punish every disobedience, proving it when expedient not only by word but also by deed. He also increased and multiplied the works of mercy and piety which he had diligently exercised while still chancellor, assigning to the uses of the poor all tithes that came to him anywhere for whatever reason [Col. 0067C].

He bestowed many benefits upon widows, orphans, the sick, and needy persons confined to bed, assigning permanently to very many of them daily allowances of food and clothing. His predecessor Theobald of pious memory had, out of zeal for mercy, doubled the alms of his predecessors; Thomas, in generous emulation, strove to double even double that provision. A great number of poor persons was brought daily to his table. Besides those who came to table, every day toward evening he caused another thirteen poor persons to be brought in more privately; after washing and kissing the feet of each, and after a plentiful meal, he gave each four silver coins [Col. 0067D]. If he happened to be prevented by some greater occupation from doing this with his own hands, he had it performed through his servants.

A varied abundance of dishes and drinks was brought daily to his table, so that he might both conform to the customs of his countrymen and abundantly comfort the needy from the leftovers. Various vessels of gold and silver both loaded and adorned his table, not indeed as a display of riches but according to the custom of the people and the practice of the country. Yet, so far as he himself was concerned, he regarded nothing of this sort as more than necessary use, using gold and silver vessels just as he used earthen ones. His outward clothing was still as before: splendid, costly [Col. 0068A], and honorable.

For this reason the monks of Canterbury, although in all other things they rejoiced and gloried in the Lord over the blessedness of his life and deeds, seemed to be scandalized and to murmur over this one matter. One of them, who was familiar with him, respectfully approached him privately on the matter and recounted a vision which the Lord had deigned to show concerning it to a certain religious monk and servant: “The Lord appeared,” he said, “to a religious and holy man, saying to him: ‘Go, tell the archbishop that he must change his garments without delay; for as long as he postpones doing so, he cannot have me propitious toward him.’”

On hearing this, the archbishop was moved to tears; nevertheless, he did not in the least reveal his purpose to the monk who told him this [Col. 0068B]. After a short interval, therefore, casting away entirely from himself costly and colored garments, together with various exotic furs, he wore, over the haircloth which he wore next to his flesh, lambskins covered only with clean fine linen. He strove continually to establish the merit of his religious life in his conscience before God, not in human estimation, while making his outward appearance suitable to ecclesiastical office. He also clothed himself in a dark—that is, black—cloak of little value, hanging to the ground, lined with lambskins.

Thus, made from his heart a pattern for the flock by his life, clothing, and example of religious devotion and holiness, he firmly resolved to devote his whole self to the ministry to which, at God’s call, he had been committed [Col. 0068C]. What the venerable bishop did and how he conducted himself could not escape the king, especially because his rivals—for they too were not lacking—more curiously scrutinized his life and reported everything to the king, though in a different light. They called him eccentric and superstitious rather than religious, and greatly agitated the king’s mind with deceitful and malicious accusations.

The king, however, cleverly dissembled, unwilling gratuitously to make an enemy of one whom he had not yet found opposed to him in any matter. Whenever an opportunity arose, he received Thomas with much reverence and honor and won him over with many services and flatteries. For he knew the man’s greatness of spirit and prudence and did not wish prematurely to oppose him because of the secret insinuations of informers [Col. 0068D].

It happened at that time, in a certain notable assembly, that Thomas delivered an address to clergy and people in the king’s presence. His discourse concerned the kingdom of Christ, which is the Church, and the temporal kingdom; the crowns of those two kingdoms, namely the priestly and royal crowns; and likewise the spiritual and material swords. Taking this occasion, he argued wonderfully at length concerning ecclesiastical and secular power, for he was exceedingly eloquent. The king noted his words point by point; and, understanding that Thomas placed ecclesiastical dignity immeasurably above every secular excellence, he did not take this calmly. For from Thomas’s words he perceived how far the archbishop stood from his own opinion [Col. 0069A], since the king was convinced that the Church possessed and could possess absolutely nothing except what he himself granted it.

Accordingly, it must now be related how the things hidden in the king’s heart came into the open, how the venerable bishop set himself as a wall for the house of the Lord, and with what constancy he exposed himself to royal fury in defending the right of ecclesiastical liberty. For the tyrants who had held the kingdom had utterly destroyed ecclesiastical rights. Following in their footsteps, this King Henry had usurped to himself the whole authority of ecclesiastical arrangement and administration: he granted bishoprics and abbeys to whom he wished; and by his command and ordinance, people, priests, and clerics alike were now indiscriminately dragged before secular courts [Col. 0069B].

The first occasion on which the archbishop’s purpose and constancy became known to the king was as follows. In those regions it was customary for the king, for the more ample security and protection of his realm, to appoint in each county one sheriff from among his faithful men. The counts and barons were accustomed to have their men give annually to that sheriff, the royal officer, two shillings from every measure of their land called in the native tongue *hides*, so that by such service and payment the sheriffs might restrain the counts and barons from burdens and vexatious claims made by their own men. But the king saw that those two shillings from each hide, if collected together [Col. 0069C], could amount to an immense sum—for there were many thousands of hides—and wished to apply them to his own uses and revenues.

Therefore, having summoned bishops and nobles of the realm to Woodstock, the king introduced for discussion the question of adding the aforesaid money to his revenues. When all fell silent at this proposal, the archbishop alone answered with great freedom, though quite moderately: “My lord,” he said, “it does not become your exalted station to divert another’s benefaction to your own uses, especially since those two shillings are granted to your ministers not from necessity or obligation, but rather from favor. For if your sheriffs conduct themselves peaceably and moderately toward our men, we shall gladly pay; but if they do not, we shall not pay, nor can we lawfully be compelled.”

At this the king angrily said: “By God’s eyes, they shall at once be enrolled!”—using this expression because royal revenues were entered in rolls—“but you yourself ought readily to assent to my will in this matter.” Then the archbishop said: “By the eyes by which you have sworn, they shall never be given from my land while I live.” The king, perceiving that the archbishop openly opposed him, took it exceedingly ill [Col. 0069D].

Not long afterwards a fierce dispute again arose between them concerning a certain canon named Philip de Broc, who had been accused by certain persons of killing a knight. After Philip had sufficiently answered before his bishop concerning the homicide charged against him, and his opponents had failed in the case, he had cleared himself by oath so as to establish his innocence more certainly. Yet a certain Simon, son of Peter, whom the king had appointed judge in the district of Bedfordshire, where Philip lived, tried to summon him again to trial. But Philip, since the case had already been concluded and determined by judicial procedure, refused to answer again, especially before a lay court. Indeed, when Simon pressed more persistently, Philip indignantly drove him away, assailing him with many insults and reproaches.

While the king was in London, the aforesaid Simon came to him and reported everything Philip had inflicted upon him. On hearing it, the king, in a fury, swore terribly in his customary manner by God’s eyes that he regarded the insults inflicted upon his knight as though Philip had inflicted them upon the king himself [Col. 0070A]. He therefore ordered Philip to be judged without delay. But the archbishop, being present and hearing this, said: “It shall by no means be so. Laymen cannot be judges of clerics. Whatever offence this man or any other member of the clergy has committed must be corrected in an ecclesiastical court. Therefore, whatever it may be of which the king, or his knight, complains that he has been injured, let him come or send to Canterbury; and from there he shall receive full justice by ecclesiastical authority.”

The king, greatly enraged and saying much, at last—though unwillingly—sent certain bishops and nobles to Canterbury for the day appointed for him by the archbishop. When they came, they pressed the old accusation of homicide strongly against Philip. When it had been judged that a case concluded by ecclesiastical judgment ought not to be reopened, they finally came to the insults inflicted upon the king’s knight [Col. 0070B]. Since Philip did not think fit to deny them—for he was a man of importance and high birth—his opponents stepped forward and said: “We demand judgment concerning an evident and undisputed injury.” Although Philip offered voluntary satisfaction, he nevertheless had to be judged.

It was therefore decided that Philip should surrender his prebend into the king’s hands for two years, and that the king should again do what he wished with its revenues; while Philip himself was to present himself before the knight, naked, to make satisfaction according to the custom of the country. When those who had been sent returned and reported what had been done [Col. 0070C], the king replied that his honor had been injured and justice denied him. The bishops said that they had judged justly, except that for the peace and honor of the king they had burdened Philip more than he deserved. The king, growing still more inflamed, said: “By God’s eyes, you yourselves shall swear to me that you have pronounced a true judgment.”

But it would be too long if we wished to recount in detail all that was improperly said or done by the king, or steadfastly said or done by the archbishop. Therefore, leaving these matters aside, let us proceed to the Church’s common cause [Col. 0070D].

There therefore arose discussion of the abuses of the ancient kings, which the king called the customs of the realm. The archbishop’s enemies—namely Roger, Archbishop of York [Col. 0071A], and certain other sons of Belial, whom the ancient enemy had stirred up for the disturbance of Holy Church—were promoting this discussion and urgently urging the king himself toward it. Having summoned all the bishops of the realm, the king began to require of them confirmation that the customs of King Henry, his grandfather, should be observed for ever.

But the venerable primate Thomas, who had long foreseen that this demand would one day be made, replied to the king as follows:

> “Holy Church, taught and established from the beginning of the Christian faith by the holy apostles and apostolic leaders, has most fully set forth the customs of Christian life and discipline in the canons and decrees of those same holy Fathers. Apart from these, my lord king, it is neither expedient for you—indeed, nor even lawful—to demand anything new, nor for us to grant it. For we, who, though unworthy, have succeeded our predecessors [Col. 0071B], are commanded not to believe in new ordinances, but humbly to obey and reverently to observe the old.”

“No,” said the king, “I do not demand that. I wish only that those things which are known to have been observed in the realm in the times of my predecessors, the kings, should also be granted to me and observed in my time. There were in those times archbishops better and holier than you, who saw these things and consented to them, and raised no difficulty or controversy about them with the kings of their day.”

To this the archbishop replied:

> “If former kings presumed upon anything contrary to the canon of ecclesiastical institution, and it was observed for some time by force through fear of kings, it must be called not a custom but an abuse. By the testimony of Scripture we are taught that a most depraved practice ought rather to be abolished than [Col. 0071C] propagated. As for your assertion that the holy bishops of those times kept silence and did not protest, let them see why they were silent; perhaps it was then a time for silence. Yet their example gives us no authority whatever to consent that anything be done against God, or against our order and office, in the Church committed to us by divine dispensation. Nevertheless, in all matters in which, without prejudice to our order, we can agree and consent to your will and good pleasure, you shall find us ready and obedient.”

The king, therefore, enraged and swearing in his usual fashion “by God’s eyes,” said:

> “No mention whatsoever shall be made of your order; but you shall grant and confirm to me my customs absolutely and expressly.”

The archbishop, however, steadfastly and freely maintained that he would grant nothing except with his order and ecclesiastical right preserved. The king, for the moment frustrated of his purpose, shortly afterward, while staying at Northampton, summoned the archbishop to him, wishing to test his mind and see whether perhaps he could bend and incline him to his own will.

When the archbishop approached the place and his arrival became known to the king, the king, by some unknown contrivance, sent certain men to meet him, saying:

> “The king is lodged in the town with many men, and you too have arrived with a very great company. There is not room enough to contain you both; therefore the king commands that you wait for him here. He will presently come to speak with you.”

When the bishop had withdrawn into a field [Col. 0072A], the king immediately arrived without delay. The bishop went to meet him and took care to anticipate him with the proper honour of greeting. But because of the neighing and kicking back of the restless horses on which they sat, they could not approach one another; at length, having changed horses, both stood apart together.

Then the king began thus to the bishop:

> “Did I not raise you from lowliness and poverty to the highest summit of honour and eminence? Nor did this seem enough to me unless I made you father of the realm and even set you above myself. How, then, could so many benefits and such evident tokens of my affection toward you, known to everyone, so suddenly slip from your mind that you prove yourself not only ungrateful but actually opposed to me in everything [Col. 0072B]?”

The bishop replied:

> “Far be it, my lord! I am not unmindful of your benefits, which not simply you yourself, but God, the giver of all things, has deigned to confer upon me through you. Therefore far be it that I should be ungrateful or opposed in any respect to your will—provided that you agree with the divine will. Your Highness knows how faithful I have been to you, from whom I expected only temporal recompense. How much more necessary is it for us to render faithful and sincere service to almighty God, from whom we have received temporal goods and hope for eternal ones. You indeed are my lord, but He is both your Lord and mine. It is expedient neither for you nor for me that I should pass over His will in order to comply with yours. For in His dreadful judgment we must both be judged as servants of one [Col. 0072C] Lord; there neither of us will be able to answer for the other, but each, with excuse set aside, shall receive according to his deeds. Temporal lords must indeed be obeyed, but not against God, as blessed Peter says: ‘We must obey God rather than men.’”

Then the king said:

> “I do not want you to preach to me now. Were you not the son of one of my peasants?”

The archbishop replied:

> “Indeed, I was not descended from royal ancestors, any more than was blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom the Lord deigned to give the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the primacy of the whole Church.”

“That is true,” said the king, “but he died for his Lord.”

The venerable primate answered:

> “I too shall die [Col. 0072D] for my Lord, when the time comes.”

Then the king said:

> “You cling and rely too greatly upon your props.”

The archbishop answered:

> “I trust and rely upon the Lord. For cursed is the man who puts his hope in man. Nevertheless, whatever you say to me and whatever I answer you, I am ready, as formerly so now, for your honour and good pleasure, with my order preserved. Yet concerning those matters which relate to your honour and to the salvation of your soul, you ought rather to have consulted me, whom you have so often found faithful and useful in counsel, than those who, under the pretext of your honour, zealously seek revenge upon me, who have not injured them, inflamed by the fire of unprovoked envy. Since, while I was still placed below holy orders, you will not deny, I think, that I was faithful to you, [Col. 0073A] you ought much more to judge me faithful to you in all things now that I have been raised to the office of priesthood.”

Although the archbishop had delivered many salutary words full of affection and loyalty, the king nevertheless pressed him vehemently to omit altogether that phrase, namely, “with our order preserved.” Since he could not obtain this, the archbishop remaining inflexible in his position, they departed from one another.

At the same time Arnulf, Bishop of Lisieux, crossed the sea and came to the king, whom he had offended, wishing, if possible, to make him favourable to himself. While he soothed him in every way and spoke words pleasing to him, he did not fear even to advise him against the archbishop. For he said to the king:

> “The controversy [Col. 0073B] between you and the archbishop is difficult and scarcely capable of being ended. It is impossible for the archbishop to submit to you as long as his suffragans are united and of one mind with him. Therefore, if you cannot tear all of them away from him, at least strive somehow to bring some of their number over to your side. Once this is done, the remaining party will not easily be able to stand. For if the bishops favour you, and the archbishop alone decides stubbornly to persist in his position, not only will he fail to prevail, but, through the bishops’ efforts, he may easily incur letters of suspension.”

Thus instructed by this counsel, the king summoned to Gloucester those bishops whom he believed more pliable, namely Roger of York and the Bishop of Lincoln. He dealt with [Col. 0073C] them so that they might be ready to confirm his customs, promising that he would require of them nothing contrary to their order. The two yielded, promising the king as he wished. Not long afterward the king joined Hilary, Bishop of Chichester, to his party.

After this Hilary came to the archbishop at Lentham and began to urge upon him what he could not persuade him to do: namely, to favour the king’s will, asserting that this was altogether greatly expedient. For he was remarkable in learning and possessed many polished and persuasive words. But the archbishop, who sought not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ, said:

> “Far be it that I should purchase the favour of an earthly king by such a bargain, exposing to him the Church which the heavenly King [Col. 0073D] purchased with His own blood. But you and the Bishop of Lincoln with the Archbishop of York—would that not with impunity!—have made ecclesiastical sanctions saleable, or rather, so far as lies in you, void, by promising the king that you will observe his customs, which are known in every respect to conflict with the canons of the holy Fathers. Yet whatever you do to us, or whatever others may perhaps do, you shall never have me as a partner in so dreadful a presumption.”

Hilary answered:

> “I ask you, what is this dreadful and enormous evil which you alone see and understand in this act, while no one else sees it with you? The king asked us to defer to him in this word and to honour him; and he himself promised us that, because of this concession, he would never require from us anything [Col. 0074A] contrary to our order. Is it, I ask, so great an evil and such an enormous presumption to honour one’s lord?”

The archbishop replied:

> “It is not evil, but rather good, to honour one’s lord, provided that God is not dishonoured, and that Holy Church is neither disturbed nor endangered. But know this with certainty: the king will demand from you whatever you have promised him; and you cannot compel him to keep his promises.”

At the same time Pope Alexander, then residing in France, sent a Cistercian abbot named Philip of Alms, a man of great reputation and authority, to restore peace between the king and the archbishop, if possible. That abbot therefore came to England, and, having associated with himself [Col. 0074B] Robert de Melidino, Bishop of Hereford, and John, Count of Eu, came to the archbishop at Herges. Philip handed him apostolic letters and writings of certain cardinals, containing words of exhortation that the archbishop should show himself moderate and yielding toward the king’s will.

Those letters also recalled that the state of the Church was troubled and clouded because of the schism, and that the utmost care must be taken lest the storm which had seized the head of the Church should spread also through its members, leaving no peace anywhere. Dispensation, meanwhile, was necessary; it was not expedient at present that ecclesiastical rulers should exercise due severity. Many things were to be overlooked, [Col. 0074C] and some were to be tolerated for a time.

The letters contained much to this effect. The bishop and abbot, together with their companion the count, added orally that the king had assured them on his word of truth that he would never require of the archbishop anything contrary to his order or will. The king, they said, had acted so obstinately with this intention because he thought it shameful to be defeated by the archbishop and unable to extort from him at least the honour of verbal compliance.

The men therefore begged and urged, and pressed in every way, that the archbishop should come with them to the king and favour his will merely by a simple word, omitting that phrase, “with our order preserved.” If this were done, both he and the whole English Church would obtain complete peace and favour with the king [Col. 0074D], and the mention that had been introduced concerning the customs of the realm would be abolished wholly and for ever.

Now the same Abbot Philip of Alms possessed such standing and reputation that he was readily believed. Accordingly, induced both by the counsel of the lord pope and cardinals and by the words of the abbot himself and those who had come with him, and credulous of their promises, the archbishop set out with them for the king.

The venerable pontiff found the king at Woodstock and addressed him with great gentleness. He set before him as examples the holy kings of that realm, whom faith and piety had made acceptable to God and whom, indeed, the crown of martyrdom had made glorious in the case of several. He exhorted and humbly entreated the king to cleave to their examples and footsteps, to abolish and condemn for ever the abuses of tyrants, and to strive to be joined to the merits and fellowship of holy kings.

> “And lest anything,” said the archbishop, “seem to be put forward by me as an obstacle to your good will, if the Lord has deigned to inspire it in you, know that I shall observe the customs of the realm in good faith, and henceforth shall obey you in every good thing, as is fitting and just [Col. 0075A].”

Then the king said to him:

> “It is known to all how stubbornly you have behaved over this phrase and how greatly, by your refusal, you have injured my honour. Therefore, if you have resolved to honour me as is fitting, what is known to have been taken from my honour in this matter must be repaired and acknowledged before everyone. Send, therefore, and summon the bishops, abbots, and all others eminent in ecclesiastical dignities; and I on my part shall summon all the leading men of the realm, so that in the presence and hearing of all this matter may be acknowledged in honour of me.”

When, therefore, all had assembled at Clarendon on the appointed day, the king began urgently to demand that the archbishop should repeat the aforesaid declaration concerning observance of the customs. But the archbishop perceived that the matter was far different from what he had heard from Abbot Philip of Alms, and that the king was in no respect softened from his evil purpose, but was rather applying his whole mind to establishing and confirming those accursed customs. He chose rather to give the king occasion for a charge against himself alone than [Col. 0075C] to put the cause of the Church wholly in jeopardy. Therefore he evaded and turned aside as far as he could from making any acknowledgment or concession there.

When this became known to the king, he became mad and furious and resolved to use no longer counsel but the sword, threatening that he would soon become another Saul to the priests of the Lord unless his will were fulfilled at once and without delay. Without delay the king’s anger became evident: all things were immediately thrown into confusion; all were in tumult; the king’s retainers ran about with faces more savage than usual, as though already preparing themselves for a crime. At once everything was full of horror and dread. Nor was this surprising, for the wrath of a king is like a lion’s roar.

Meanwhile the priests of the Lord stood like [Col. 0075D] a flock prepared for slaughter, exceedingly fearful and sorrowful. The archbishop alone, remaining cheerful and serene of countenance, comforted them, saying that such things befitted true priests of the Church. But those among the clergy assembled who were of more obscure reputation and standing fled here and there, withdrawing themselves from the danger which they feared was now imminent.

Among the bishops were two, Jocelin of Salisbury and Roger of Norwich, whom the king hated for different reasons. The Bishop of Norwich, related to the king by blood, although young in age, was nevertheless devout and a champion of ecclesiastical liberty; by more freely reproving the king for his offences, he had incurred his wrath. The Bishop of Salisbury had made the king hostile to him for other reasons. These two came to the archbishop and began in tearful voices to beg him to have pity on them, saying that unless he made full peace with the king that very day, even if he might spare others, he would by no means spare them from being killed [Col. 0076A].

The archbishop met their fear and faintheartedness with gentle consolation, remaining unmoved in his determination. At that very hour two of the greater and nobler earls of the realm came to him, namely William, Earl of Leicester, and Reginald, Earl of Cornwall, the king’s uncle. They earnestly advised and begged him to have pity on himself and those who had come with him, saying that the king was most violently angry and stirred up, already prepared, with sword drawn, to avenge his contempt.

> “While even we,” they said, “who are your friends and faithful men, beseech you to have mercy, know that unless you give the king full satisfaction today, we shall be compelled by inevitable necessity to carry out an unheard-of crime with our own hands.”

The archbishop replied:

> “It is neither great nor unheard-of if we should fall for ecclesiastical sanctions, since an innumerable multitude of saints has taught us this both in word and example. Only let the will of the Lord be done.”

When these had been repulsed and departed, two Templars approached him, themselves men of great name and standing in their order. One was called Richard de Hastings, master of the Templars throughout the realm; the other was called Hostes, likewise very prominent at court. The two stood before the archbishop [Col. 0076C] and addressed him thus amid sobs and tears:

> “Why, lord, are you so inexorable in the cause of Holy Church, which today will without doubt suffer a grave and hitherto unheard-of danger unless the king’s will is fulfilled? For we know with certainty that the king intends neither artifice nor deceit against you; but he finds it exceedingly grievous and intolerable to appear to have been overcome by you in this phrase. We therefore beg you in every way, and faithfully warn and advise you, to satisfy the king in words. You shall never again hear mention of those customs which you so greatly shun and detest; but as soon as you have honoured the king before a public assembly by a word alone, all [Col. 0076D] indignation and enmity will be wiped away, and complete peace and affection between you and him will be restored. We faithfully promise this to you on our word of truth, and concerning this matter we give ourselves as sureties and hostages. We solemnly invoke our souls, liable to eternal damnation, if the king hereafter asks of you anything against your will or your order.”

The archbishop, moved by their tears and by words delivered with such solemn protestation, and seeing also that the king and his followers were ready for the commission of crime and slaughter, first conferred with the bishops about what he had heard. Then he came with them to the king and said:

> “If the controversy between us concerned my own right, my lord king, know that I should at once, more swiftly than words, yield to your will without any contradiction. But since a grave and dangerous matter concerning ecclesiastical affairs committed to us, by God’s appointment, is being debated between us, Your Highness ought not to find it strange or unworthy if I have been somewhat scrupulous in God’s cause, knowing that I must render Him an account of my stewardship, for He spares not the delinquent. Now, however, having better hope in your prudence and gentleness, I willingly consent to your requests and declare that I shall observe the customs of the realm in good faith [Col. 0077A].”

Hardly had the word left the pontiff’s mouth when the king answered in a loud voice:

> “You have all heard what the archbishop has granted me for his own part. It remains that the bishops, at his command, should do the same.”

“I wish,” said the archbishop, “that, as I have done, they too should satisfy your honour.”

Then the bishops rose and assented. Jocelin, Bishop of Salisbury, alone did not assent together with the others; but while the others remained seated, he asked the archbishop whether he ought to do the same. When the archbishop said that he should, he assented. The king, shaking his head, reproached the Bishop of Salisbury, who had always been opposed to him.

The archbishop, although he thought the controversy ended according to what he had heard from the aforesaid Templars, was still anxious and, as it were, suspended in uncertainty, awaiting the outcome. The king then said:

> “I believe it has reached everyone’s hearing that the archbishop and bishops have granted me that the laws and customs of my realm shall henceforth be firmly [Col. 0077C] maintained and observed. Therefore, lest contention or contradiction between us recur hereafter, let the wiser and older nobles rise and, going out with my clerks, recall the laws and customs of my grandfather King Henry, write them down carefully, and bring them to me with all speed.”

This was done at once as he commanded. The king ordered the customs, having been written down and brought forward, to be read. When they had been read, the king said again:

> “Behold, these are the things granted to me. Therefore, lest any question arise concerning them hereafter, or perhaps new disputes emerge, we will that the archbishop append his seal to them.”

The archbishop replied:

> “By almighty God, while I live, my seal shall never be appended to these.”

Then the king’s clerks [Col. 0077D] and officials resorted to another device. At the king’s command they quickly drew up a chirograph; cutting it through the middle in the customary fashion, they handed one part to the archbishop. The archbishop said:

> “I receive it indeed, yet neither consenting nor approving, but for the protection and defence of the Church, so that by this evidence we may know against what we must act. For once the snares and traps stretched out against us are known, we shall, God consenting, be more cautious.”

Having said this, he rose angrily and departed. Although this had necessarily been done for the deliverance of the clergy assembled, the archbishop nevertheless accepted no consolation for his transgression, in which he had indeed sinned through deception. He imposed upon himself a most severe penance and suspended himself from the office of the altar [Col. 0078A], until, after sending messengers to Pope Alexander to inform him of the course and manner of what had occurred, he should deserve absolution from him. The lord pope, admiring his zeal and constancy, also sent him letters of consolation, full of honour and affection.

After this Rotrou, Bishop of Évreux, came to the king at Porchester, wishing to restore peace and concord between the king and the archbishop. The king replied that this could be possible in only one way: if he and the archbishop could obtain from the lord pope a bull strengthening and confirming his customs. Therefore the Bishop of Évreux approached the archbishop, urgently requesting and advising him to write to the lord pope about this affair.

But the archbishop, taking care not to give the king any just opportunity for malice, and knowing with certainty that his prayers would accomplish nothing for the king, wrote to the pope and asked him to confirm the customs in accordance with the wish of the king and bishop [Col. 0078B]. The lord pope, understanding that this petition proceeded not from free will but from necessity, immediately refused and dismissed the envoys sent for this purpose without hope of obtaining it.

When this became known to the king, he was inflamed with still more violent anger and repeatedly held counsel with his advisers as to what he should do. At length it seemed to him that, if he could obtain from the lord pope the legation for England for Roger, Archbishop of York, the holy man’s enemy, the archbishop could easily be subdued and his customs more firmly established.

He therefore sent two of his clerks, John of Oxford and Geoffrey, surnamed Ridel, to the lord pope to obtain the legation. The lord pope did not deem them worthy even of a hearing, saying:

> “From the time of the most blessed Pope Gregory, through whose agency the English people received the faith of Christ, nowhere is it read or remembered down to the present that the Church of Canterbury has been subject to York. Therefore we ought by no means to do what we know our predecessors have not hitherto done. It is established that the Church of Canterbury surpasses the other churches of that realm in dignity and primacy, and it is not just that she who is first should be made secondary.”

But John of Oxford, relying upon great cunning, [Col. 0078D] bent his knees before the pope and swore that unless the king rejoiced in their return on account of his petition, the archbishop would undoubtedly be endangered in his life. The lord pope, fearing and strongly suspecting the king’s malice, employed a dispensation necessary for the time and granted the legation to the king himself, on the condition, however, that he could neither assign it to the Archbishop of York nor burden anyone by the authority of the legation.

For he secretly sent other letters into England which were to strip the king of the legation at once should he attempt to exercise the power of legation or burden anyone. The king, receiving the letters that conferred the legation upon him, did not value such a legation highly. Yet he showed the letters to many people and made known that he was legate, in order to frighten the archbishop with his legation. At length, after keeping those letters uselessly for some time [Col. 0079A], he sent messengers and surrendered the legation to the lord pope in anger, returning the letters to him.

After this, while the king persecuted the Church and ecclesiastical persons more harshly than usual, and the archbishop nevertheless resisted steadfastly, the devil, instigator of evil, stirred up a grave complaint against the Church. For the king’s officials fought tirelessly and investigated diligently in every direction; they found certain clergy guilty of various crimes, seized them, and consigned them to bonds and prisons. Some of these were priests; others were deacons and clerics of various orders, who were known to be most criminal in thefts and homicides.

Yet the venerable primate did not judge even such men to be handed over to lay justice. On the contrary, he steadfastly demanded them from the king, forbidding under anathema anyone to presume to judge them outside the court of the Church [Col. 0079B]. He declared himself ready to bring them to justice and judge them according to the canons and decrees.

At length the king, compelled by the force of reason, consented that they should indeed be returned to the archbishop, but on condition that he himself, after depriving them of orders as their deserts required, should hand them over to his officers for condemnation. The archbishop, however, said that they should not be punished in this double manner, but that deprivation of orders was punishment enough for them. If afterward they were found guilty in crimes, then it did not belong to him to determine by what judgment they should be condemned.

This dispute was debated for a long time and in various ways, but for brevity’s sake we avoid relating more. At last, when the king and archbishop had assembled with a multitude [Col. 0079C] of bishops and nobles to take cognizance of this complaint, the king, understanding that the holy man could not be bent at all from ecclesiastical law, began angrily to threaten him, saying:

> “I will humble you and restore you to the place where I found you.”

While intolerable vexations and oppressions against the Church of God multiplied daily, and no hope of quiet or peace remained, the venerable pontiff judged it necessary to consult the lord pope, who was then residing in France, concerning these matters. His journey and vessel being prepared, with few aware of it, he embarked upon the sea at Romnallum. When he had already traversed a great expanse of sea, the sailors spoke privately among themselves, saying:

> “What [Col. 0079D] are we doing? We are taking from the hands of the king an enemy whom he hates and persecutes unto death, and do we suppose that this can remain unknown to the king? Certainly not. Therefore it is clear that we are acting against our own lives.”

They therefore approached the archbishop, saying that the voyage was exceedingly difficult and the wind contrary, and that they could not reach the land for which they were bound without danger to their lives. The archbishop, hearing that danger threatened and not understanding the deceit, ordered himself to be put back ashore whence he had departed.

Not long afterward, when word reached the king that the archbishop had put to sea and had almost crossed over, he was greatly distressed; for he feared that, if he should manage to reach the lord pope [Col. 0080A], he might place both the king himself under anathema and his kingdom under interdict. Therefore, lest he should thereafter be exposed to a similar contingency, he prohibited by public edict anyone from crossing overseas without documentary authorization from him. The king had also made a new ordinance which he thought would serve his own advantage; and all the magnates of the kingdom, greatly burdened by it, groaned in murmuring complaint. The ordinance was as follows:

“If anyone having a case in the court of any lord should see, after the first or second day of pleading, that his business was not prospering or proceeding as he wished, he might leave that court and hasten to the court of his lord’s superior; provided, however, that he had first sworn “with a third hand” that he had been unjustly delayed in his case.”

Now it happened that one of the magnates of the land [Col. 0080B], named John Marshal, having a case in the court of his lord the archbishop, invoked the authority of this novel ordinance and, after taking an oath, declined the judgment; and he withdrew from the court. Yet he had not taken the oath in the customary manner upon the text of the Gospels or the relics of saints, but upon a small book called a troper, which he had deliberately caused to be brought to him. This John, therefore, knowing that every occasion against the archbishop would be most welcome to the king, approached him, asserting that the archbishop had failed him in justice: “And this,” he said, “because I am your faithful man.” The king, seizing the occasion, ordered the archbishop to be summoned, directing him to appear and answer the charge that he had denied justice in his own court to one of his magnates.

But the archbishop [Col. 0080C], being at that time ill by chance and utterly unable to appear on the appointed day, took care to send the king a reasonable excuse for his inability. The king, who sought occasions for maligning him, replied that he would accept no excuse for his absence.

“Clinging, therefore, to this pretext, the king summoned by public edict bishops and abbots, also counts and magnates, all his officers, and indeed everyone of any authority or standing, to assemble on an appointed day at Northampton. He ordered also that the archbishop should be there without excuse. When the appointed day was at hand and the man of God drew near to the aforesaid place, his servants, who had gone ahead to it, met him, saying that the king’s servants had occupied all his lodgings [Col. 0080D]. For the king had ordered even this to be done in order to insult him. The venerable bishop therefore halted, and sent word to the king that he would proceed no farther until he had ordered his lodgings vacated. Without delay, at the king’s command, the archbishop’s servants came up and quickly drove the royal household out of his lodgings. The archbishop himself lodged in the monastery of St. Andrew, with the monks.

“When morning came, he went to court; and entering the chapel, where the king had come to hear Mass, he greeted him with due honor. Sitting beside the king, he humbly and respectfully requested that the king grant him permission to travel to the lord pope, because he had much concerning the counsel of his soul to communicate to him [Col. 0081A]. The king immediately refused, saying that it was impossible for either him or anyone else to obtain leave to cross overseas.

“Immediately after Mass, therefore, the king ordered the archbishop to answer the charge that, having been summoned by him for a certain day, he had not come. The archbishop replied that he had been detained by illness and had notified the king, at the proper time and according to custom, of his excuse. The king did not deny having heard the excuse, but replied that he had by no means accepted it; whereupon he ordered the archbishop to be judged at once for contempt. They went out immediately to judgment. The men whom the king himself named as judges decreed that the archbishop should pay the king five hundred pounds of silver on this account.

“When this was reported to the archbishop, he rejected the judgment and declared it void, saying that he could be judged neither by the king nor by any of them, since he had received from the Lord the power to judge them, not they to judge him [Col. 0081B]. When he wished to annul and quash, justly, that which had been unjustly judged, certain of his friends and household persuaded him by arguments and entreaties, saying: ‘The king should not be more seriously provoked over a matter of money; perhaps in this way, too, he may rest content once he has obtained what he wanted.’ The man of God therefore yielded to their advice and at once paid, after providing sureties, that which had been exacted by the iniquitous judgment. But this did nothing to soften the tyrant’s fury.

“For immediately another complaint was introduced concerning the aforesaid John Marshal, who was said to have been denied justice through the archbishop’s negligence [Col. 0081C]. The archbishop answered that he had not at all failed him in justice, but that John himself had wholly failed in his case and had been unable to prove his right; and that, having taken an oath contrary to custom, he had evaded judgment. When the king realized that he could obtain nothing in this case, he turned to other matters. The period during which the archbishop had administered the chancellorship was brought forward, and the king urgently demanded that he render an account of the revenues of the realm. The archbishop denied that he was bound to answer these charges, since at the time of his election he had withdrawn from court wholly free and discharged from all such obligations. Thus the day was drawn out into evening by various complaints and disputes, the king pressing quite wickedly and refusing to abandon his purpose.

“At length the king ordered him to be ready in the morning, all pretexts set aside, to answer the accusations [Col. 0081D]. But the man of God replied that it was contrary to law and custom that anyone should be compelled on the following day to plead a newly made complaint. The king, however, persisting in his purpose, shouted in terrible tones and with an oath that the business could no longer be postponed. At last the council was dissolved, and each returned home. The archbishop also retired to his lodgings.

“And behold, before midnight, after the man of God had yielded himself to rest following anxiety and labor, a violent pain seized his side and grievously afflicted him throughout that night and for no small part of the following day. He had often been accustomed to suffer in this way; but then, because of the distress that he had endured the previous day, the pain returned. When morning came, men were sent by the king to summon the archbishop to court [Col. 0082A]. They were told that he was ill and could not come. On hearing this, the king, thundering more terribly than usual, repeatedly swore by the eyes of God that no pretext or sickness should avail him as an excuse for failing to present himself before him.

“Again, therefore, the king sent two counts, Robert of Leicester and Reginald of Cornwall, to compel him to come to court, or at least to ascertain whether he was truly ill. For the king believed that he was feigning illness in order to gain a delay. When the said counts came to him, they conveyed the king’s command with great respect; but, finding that he was tormented by severe pain, they granted him a postponement until the next day. The archbishop said to them: ‘Let no one suppose that I deliberately seek pretexts or evasions [Col. 0082B]. Tomorrow, God willing, if life attends me, I shall be present—even if I must be carried on a bier.’

“That same day, however, the blessed man was informed by two magnates, who were his friends and faithful supporters but concealed this because of fear of the king, that if he committed himself to the court on the next day, he would without doubt be seized and either, after his eyes had been gouged out or his tongue cut out, consigned to prison, or else killed outright. Hearing this, the holy man trembled all over—as was no wonder—and, rising without delay, prostrated himself before the altar. There, lying for a very long time in great devotion and tears, he earnestly commended to almighty God the cause of His Church.

“Then he rose and sent for a certain religious man, with whom he spoke long concerning his situation [Col. 0082C], and received from him the following counsel: ‘Tomorrow morning, before you proceed to court, celebrate solemnly the Mass of the blessed Stephen, the first martyr. There, before the most holy mysteries of the body and blood of the Lord, commend the cause of His holy Church to Jesus Christ, and likewise to the blessed ever-Virgin Mary, to blessed Stephen himself, to our most blessed apostolic lord Gregory, to St. Elphege, and to the other patrons of the holy Church of Canterbury. When you have done this, go forward securely, trusting in God’s mercy and in the protection of the saints; and act confidently. For this is not your affair, but God’s, and He will be with you in all things. For we know how easily you could free yourself from every danger, if you wished, and could make the king not merely cease to be angry with you but even become reconciled and ready to fulfill all your wishes [Col. 0082D]. Therefore we firmly believe that divine favor will not fail you, since for its sake you have despised human favor.’

“The man of God accordingly did as that religious man had instructed him. Very early in the morning he devoutly celebrated the Mass of blessed Stephen, and, clothed as he was in his pontifical vestments, prepared to go to court. But at the persuasion of his attendants he put off the priestly ornaments. Dressed, therefore, in his usual manner, he merely fastened a stole around his neck and shoulders; then, mounting his horse and taking in his right hand the cross which customarily always went before him, he began to set out.

“Although he had many table-companions—for he had in his company almost forty clerics of the highest scholarly distinction [Col. 0083A], besides his chaplains and religious men—yet at this critical moment scarcely one was found who would follow him. As he went out from his lodging, carrying the cross in his right hand, an innumerable multitude of people met him. Most of them, shedding abundant tears, humbly and supplicantly bowed themselves for his blessing. It was a moving and pitiable sight: the devoted people, lamenting closely about him, followed the steps of their shepherd as he hurried, as though to a contest. For it had already become generally known that he was to be killed that day.

“When he drew near to the castle in which the king was, the gates were opened in great haste; and no less swiftly, after he had entered, they were closed again and carefully secured with bars. Immediately magnates and knights, and a crowd of people of various ranks, sprang up and converged from every direction [Col. 0083B]. They had assembled to look upon a man of incalculable steadfastness; even those hostile to him were astonished and marvelled at his high courage and confidence.

“Dismounting at the doors of the royal residence, accompanied by only one cleric and carrying the cross in his hand, he entered and passed through the hall, arriving at the inner chamber. The king, however, stood with his household in a more remote room. Certain bishops then came to the archbishop, among whom was Gilbert Foliot, bishop of London, and he spoke as follows:

“‘Lord Archbishop,’ he said, ‘you have taken bad counsel in daring to enter before the king with your sword thus drawn. Know without doubt that the king himself has drawn his sword against you and is brandishing it at you with great indignation. Therefore, so long as you stand thus opposed to one another, there can be no hope of peace. Take my advice, then, and lay down the cross from your hand.’

“And the archbishop said: ‘The cross is a strong protection and a sign of peace; therefore I will by no means lay it down.’

“Again the bishop of London said to him: ‘I am your dean and ought to minister to you; hand it to me.’

“‘By no means,’ said the archbishop, ‘will I give it up; for it is no burden to me.’

“Then the bishop of London laid hands on it and tried to wrench it forcibly from his hands; but, because the archbishop was stronger, he could not tear it away. Then the bishop of Worcester said to the bishop of London [Col. 0083D]: ‘Cease your irreverence, and leave our lord archbishop his cross. For he is no very good man who carries his lord’s cross.’

“And the bishop of London said to him: ‘You have spoken against yourself; for you will grievously pay for the word which you have just launched from your mouth.’

“The archbishop of York, who was present and stood by, said to the archbishop of Canterbury: ‘Lest the lord king become violently inflamed and enraged against you, take my advice and lay down from your hand your sword—that is, your cross. For the king’s sword is much sharper than yours.’

“The venerable bishop answered him: ‘The king’s sword indeed has a carnal sharpness, but mine a spiritual one; nor should the king be angered because I hold in my hands the cross of my Lord and his, but should rather be appeased.’

“When the king learned that the archbishop had arrived, he began with his companions to plan what accusation he should first bring against him. It seemed best to begin with the clerics whom, as we said above, had been caught in murders, thefts, and other crimes [Col. 0084A]. But he was advised that, if he began his attack there, all the bishops who now favored him would at once abandon him upon hearing this matter and stand with the archbishop, since the cause of the clerics was common to all bishops. He therefore decided to proceed from another direction.

“The king and the archbishop were stationed separately and not in the same place; the bishops acted as intermediaries between them and repeatedly ran back and forth. Thus the unjust king did not cease throughout the day to assail the venerable bishop with varied attacks of complaints and accusations. But he, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, evaded and refuted all the king’s accusations and quibbles with stronger answers of reason and argument [Col. 0084B].

“Meanwhile, the archbishop was informed by certain friends and faithful supporters who belonged to the king’s council that the king was now discussing his death. The bishops themselves, knowing what the king intended to do, came to the man of God with sorrowful and downcast faces and stood around him without saying anything at all, as though stunned and senseless. Then the venerable man, made more certain from the change in their faces of what had been reported to him, said to them: ‘I perceive that in this court, while you remain silent and raise no protest, I am being grievously oppressed by unheard-of means, and that the cause of the Church is turning to its injury; compelled by this great necessity, I appeal to the lord pope.’

“Then the bishop of London said: ‘I ask you to release me from this appeal.’

“The archbishop replied: ‘I release neither you nor anyone else. Rather, at the peril of your souls and of your order, I command all of you jointly that, if, as is said, I am killed or taken captive, you spare no one but do the justice that is due’ [Col. 0084C].

“But the bishop of Winchester, deeply anxious and afraid, said to the archbishop: ‘I beg you, lord, to comply with the words I am about to speak to you in good faith. Resign the archbishopric into the hand and disposal of the lord king; for present circumstances appear to demand this as an unavoidable necessity, until by his favor and indulgence you are restored to your honor.’

“The archbishop said to him: ‘You have vainly given me such counsel; for one and the same day and hour will end both my bishopric and my life.’

“To this Hilary, bishop of Chichester, added: ‘Would that you became and remained merely Thomas, without any other dignity!’

“Then the bishops of sounder mind summoned the archbishop of York, the bishop of London, and the bishop of Chichester, and said to them: ‘If the archbishop should be seized or killed in our presence, what remains for us except that, disgracefully stripped of our offices and honors, we should be subjected forever to anathema and to a reproach which no oblivion will erase? And if we fear this for ourselves, what will become of those through whose planning and instigation, as is said [Col. 0085A], so great a crime comes to be committed? We therefore urge that with common counsel we consider and decide how we may rescue him from the immediate danger.’

“After discussing among themselves for some time how this might be done, all of them at last went together to the king and said: ‘Foreseeing, lord, the danger to your honor which we fear in this affair, we ask that you grant us leave to proceed against the archbishop. For we have many charges that we may justly make against him, especially this: when, in your presence at Clarendon, he obeyed the command, he compelled us to observe your customs; but now, contrary to himself, he opposes our being required to observe them. Therefore, if it seems good and pleases you [Col. 0085B], we have resolved to appeal against him to the lord pope.’

“And the king said: ‘It pleases me.’

“They returned, therefore, to the archbishop and appealed against him to the lord pope. The archbishop said: ‘I hear it.’

“Although the king permitted the appeal to be made, he nevertheless did not abandon his purpose of having the archbishop killed. He sent his knights to him and ordered him to render an account of the affairs and revenues of the realm, especially of thirty thousand pounds of silver which certain persons alleged that he had spent less carefully from royal money during his time as chancellor.

“The archbishop replied that the king had often heard his accounting of all these matters; that he was no longer bound to answer concerning matters that did not concern him; and especially that, at the time of his election [Col. 0085C], by the king’s command and before the king’s son and the officers of the realm, he had been released from every accounting for his administration and from every possible occasion that might arise from it in any way: ‘as you yourselves saw and heard.’

“When this answer was reported to the king, full of rage and anger, he said to his attendants: ‘This man is my man, and he does not deign to render me an account!’

“Those who stood by him said: ‘Lord, there is another ground on which you can lawfully press him. For although, as you say, he is your man and is bound by the law of fealty to preserve your honor in every way and in all things, he has nevertheless, despising your honor and reverence and scorning the judgment of your court, presumed to appeal to another court. Therefore, if he deserves judgment, it is yours to decree’ [Col. 0085D].

“‘It is clear,’ said the king, ‘that he must be punished for all these things.’

“He immediately sent men in haste to judge him. The judgment reported was that the archbishop should be seized and consigned to prison until he had satisfied the king’s will in all things concerning the accusations already made or yet to be made. At the king’s command, therefore, Count Robert of Leicester and Count Reginald of Cornwall went to the archbishop to communicate to him, on the king’s behalf, the form of the judgment. Count Leicester accordingly addressed the archbishop:

“‘Hear the judgment rendered against you in the king’s court, which the king himself sends us to communicate to you.’

“The holy man looked sternly at him and said: ‘I will hear the judgment of no one, since I have already appealed to the lord pope.’

“The count replied: ‘And how [Col. 0086A] can it be avoided that you hear the king’s judgment? For you are the king’s man, and you hold from him in fee and barony towns, castles, and innumerable possessions. Therefore you must hear and submit to judgment in his court.’

“‘Far be it from me,’ said the archbishop. ‘I hold absolutely nothing from him in fee or barony. Rather, whatever the Church possesses, it possesses in perpetual liberty, not in fee or barony or under any subjection of earthly lordship.’ For whatever has been granted to God’s Church by kings, ancient or modern, is a perpetual alms, wholly free and exempt from every designation or subjection of temporal sovereignty, as the king himself declared and confirmed in his charters. ‘Therefore, by the authority and fatherhood with which divine ordinance, under the law of Christianity, has set and placed us above you [Col. 0086B], we forbid you to render judgment concerning me or to repeat a judgment already rendered.’

“Count Robert answered: ‘Far be it from me to transgress against my soul the command of so great an authority. Rather, imposing silence upon myself, from now on I shall be silent and, so far as concerns me, leave you free.’

“Turning to Count Reginald, he said: ‘You hear that silence has been imposed upon me by archiepiscopal—indeed divine—authority. From now on you must pursue what remains and announce what has been decided by the king.’

“And Reginald replied: ‘I shall not presume to do what has not been enjoined upon me. But if you wish to say anything, say it; for in this matter I wholly withdraw from you.’

“Count Robert then said again to the archbishop: ‘I beg you, lord, wait [Col. 0086C] until your answer has been reported.’

“The archbishop said to him: ‘Then am I under arrest?’

“‘Not at all, lord, by Saint Lazarus,’ said the count; for this was the oath which he customarily used.

“When the counts withdrew and returned to the king, the archbishop said: ‘I too am leaving, for the hour is passing’; and, lifting the cross which he held in his hand, he began to depart. When he had entered the hall, the crowd of knights and people of various kinds who had gathered there began, upon seeing him, to shout and insult him with reproachful and abusive cries, clamoring with noisy and injurious insolence. But when he had gone a little way as though with a deaf ear, and had stumbled slightly upon timbers lying in the middle, perhaps for preparing a fire, and had wavered a little [Col. 0086D], the voice of the mockers rose more violently, so that it might have been heard even by persons some distance away.

“A certain Ranulf de Broc met the man of God and said: ‘You depart as a traitor.’

“The reverend bishop judged him unworthy of a reply and passed on. Hamelin, the king’s illegitimate brother, also happened to meet him and said that he was departing as a traitor. The holy man said: ‘If I were permitted to be a knight, I would prove with my own hand that you lie.’

“At last he mounted his horse and came to the castle gate. Finding it carefully locked, he stopped, astonished and frightened. But one of his servants, named Peter de Mortorio, noticed a bunch of keys hanging some distance away, quickly took the keys, and—what seemed a miracle to some [Col. 0087A]—among so many keys, without delay or difficulty found the one he wanted and needed. He opened the gate quickly, with no one contradicting or resisting him.

“As the blessed man went out of the town, the people, who awaited the outcome of the affair, received him with joy and humbly sought his blessing. He continuously bestowed blessings with right hand and left; and although the crowds delayed him somewhat, he at last reached the monastery where he was lodging. Immediately he prostrated himself in prayer before the altar. After praying there weeping for some time, as soon as he rose from prayer he asked whether it was still the ninth hour. On hearing that the hour had passed, he chanted None and Vespers together, and at once ordered the table laid.

“Although scarcely ten of his very large household were present [Col. 0087B]—for all had fled in terror—he ordered the monks’ refectory to be filled again with poor people and an abundance of food set before them. Afterwards he himself sat down leisurely at table with his companions and showed himself cheerful and gracious toward them. Meanwhile, while he was still seated at table, he ordered his bed brought into the church and a place of rest prepared for him there. His bed was accordingly carried into the church before everyone’s eyes, and behind the high altar they prepared a place for him to sleep. At his direction, one of his household attendants was also stationed there to keep out anyone wishing to approach, saying that the archbishop, exhausted by the day’s labor, must not be disturbed.
