“But the man of God, rising from table, withdrew with a few companions to a more secluded place [Col. 0087C], carefully considering what might more advantageously be done in this pressing emergency for the cause of God’s Church. For it was certain that, if he waited for the next day, he would without doubt be seized and committed to prison, so that the king might appear to commit a less serious crime if, after some interval under prison guard, he were slaughtered on some pretext, as though without the king’s knowledge. And although the holy man was ready to die for ecclesiastical liberty, nevertheless, lest the cause of the Church should perish together with him in his fall, he resolved not to escape death but to defer it for the present.

“Day was again turning into night, for supper had been prolonged until twilight. The man of God summoned two religious lay brothers whom he had in his company, one called Robert de Cava and the other Scailmannus, and one of his own servants, named Roger de Brai, a most vigorous and faithful man. To these three alone he privately disclosed the plan he had formed for his protection, ordering them to be ready without delay [Col. 0087D]. For greater caution, lest even his own people should suspect his departure, he decided to take none of his own horses with him, but had four horses procured from elsewhere.

“Through the efforts of the aforesaid three, whom the man of God had selected for this business as the more faithful, four excellent and choice riding horses were immediately brought; and, outside the door of the house, as though they belonged to guests, they were kept under discreet guard until the proper hour [Col. 0088A]. Moreover, the very time and hour of the blessed man’s flight seemed as though divinely assisted and supported. For such a violent storm of rain broke out throughout the whole night that no one dared leave the door of his house. Such dreadful darkness prevailed, both from the density of clouds and rain and from the natural gloom of night, that one could not see even a person standing in the middle of the way.

“Although all the town gates were carefully guarded, inquiry was made as to through which gate the man of God could escape more conveniently and safely. It was found that guards had not yet been stationed at the northern gate. Therefore, while everyone believed that the archbishop was resting in the place prepared for him behind the altar in the church, he, with the three companions mentioned above, mounted their horses and made his way through the middle of the castle to the northern gate [Col. 0088B]. By God’s will, the darkness of night served him as a veil; the violent downpour of water concealed the sound of the horses; and thus, entirely unnoticed, he passed out through the northern gate.

Accordingly, hastening the business of his escape throughout that entire night, he finally reached Lincoln as day was drawing near. During that night he had endured such hardship from the abundance of rain that, unable to bear the weight of the water, he had his cloak cut short twice before daylight, to lighten it. On entering Lincoln he lodged with a certain citizen named Jacob [Col. 0088C], who was acquainted with the brothers accompanying him. When morning came, the bishop of Winchester, unaware of what had happened, arrived intending to speak with the archbishop. Osbern, the blessed man’s chamberlain, met him; he had guarded the archbishop’s bed in the church that night. When the bishop asked what the archbishop was doing, Osbern replied: “He is well. For he left us late last evening, and we do not know where he has gone.” When he whispered this in the bishop’s ear, the latter, drawing a deep sigh and filled with tears, said: “With God’s blessing!”

But when the king learned that the archbishop had departed, realizing that he had been deceived and struck by inward anxiety of heart, he was rendered speechless by excessive indignation and rage. After a little while, recovering himself, he said: “We have not yet finished with that man.” Then he immediately sent orders [Col. 0088D] that all the coasts everywhere be carefully watched. Thomas himself remained concealed that day at Lincoln in Jacob’s house. So that he might hide more effectively and safely, as the pressing necessity seemed to require, he put on the tunic of a lay brother (conversus), fitted rougher shoes to his feet, and ordered his companions henceforth to call him not Thomas but Christian. This was most elegantly done: there was a change in the name, while the assertion of truth remained in the designation.

At twilight he boarded a small boat, and, sailing all night along the river, reached a certain religious house called Sempringham. There he lay hidden for several days in the granges of that house; at last, secretly and in the hours of night, he hastened to the sea. On his journey [Col. 0089A], at Chicksand, he found a chaplain named Gilbert, a religious man, belonging, that is, to the same order as the brothers who were with him; he ordered him to come along with them. When he reached the sea and had hidden near the shore for a few days, he at last boarded by night a vessel made ready for him by a certain priest. Trusting in a favorable voyage granted by divine providence, while a great part of the night still remained, he landed in Flanders—not in any harbor, but upon the sand, for safety’s sake.

Necessity therefore required him to continue on foot. Bearing heavily this unfamiliar and intolerable exertion, he frequently staggered and fell on the slippery, sandy shore. His traveling companions, seeing so great a man exhausted by an unwonted labor—for by repeated falls he had already injured and wounded his hands [Col. 0089B]—could scarcely restrain their tears. At daybreak a boy appeared; meeting him, they begged him to seek out and bring them any mount at all, with his payment assured. He ran to the nearest village and remained there a long time, causing them great anxiety and fear that he might be a spy or informer. Yet at last he returned, leading a saddled beast, from whose neck there hung, in place of a bridle, only a rope made of hay.

But since necessity neither chooses nor does what it wishes, they threw the blessed man’s cloak over the beast and made him sit upon it. With this sort of mount he traveled for nearly two miles. Judging it more tolerable and more dignified [Col. 0089C] to go on foot, he again began to walk with his companions. As he entered a certain village, a woman saw them and was astonished. Looking more closely at the venerable man and perceiving, I know not what, something special and magnificent in his face, she pitied his hardship and, wishing to render him assistance, hurried into her house to find a staff which she could offer him for support. She seized a spit, foul with smoke and soot and also wet and greasy with the fat of fish that had hung from it, and offered it to him. He did not reject her kindness towards him, but gave thanks as though for a great gift, and accepted what was offered.

After they had gone on a little way, a certain knight stood in the doorway of his house holding a hawk in his hand [Col. 0089D]. Seeing four men passing by in religious dress and examining them more carefully, he said to those around him: “One of these is either the archbishop of Canterbury, or very much like him.” Brother Scailmannus replied: “Have you ever really seen the archbishop of Canterbury walking in this fashion?”

They came to a river, found a small boat, and sailed as far as Clairmarais. The abbot and brothers of that place, recognizing the venerable bishop, were filled with inexpressible joy and received him most attentively with every honor and reverence. He remained hidden with them for a few days. Meanwhile, some of his clerics, whom he had ordered, when fleeing Northampton, to follow him, came to him.

Meanwhile [Col. 0090A] Richard de Lucy, sent by the king of England, came to the count of Flanders. Hearing that the archbishop was staying at Clairmarais—for reports of him had by then spread everywhere—he approached him and urged him earnestly, though in vain, to return with him to the king in England. But, understanding from the blessed man’s answers that he was laboring to no purpose, he began to threaten him, saying that henceforth he would be his enemy. When the holy man said to him: “You are my man, and you ought not to speak such things to me,” he answered: “I return to you my homage.” The archbishop replied again: “You did not receive it from me as a loan.”

The venerable bishop therefore sent two abbots to the count of Flanders, asking him to grant safe-conduct until he had passed through [Col. 0090B] the count’s land. But the count, who was related to the king of England and supported his cause, replied that he would deliberate on this matter; adding also that he was powerful enough to keep one archbishop within his lordship and territory. On hearing this, the archbishop regarded such an answer with suspicion, fearing that the count might perhaps use violence against him in order thereby to gain greater favor with the king.

For this reason he reported these words to Milo, bishop of Thérouanne, who happened then to have come to him on a visitation. This Milo was English by birth, a very prudent and distinguished man, who honored the archbishop with the deepest devotion and affection. By the common counsel and contrivance of them both, deliberation between them was prolonged [Col. 0090C] until night. When night had come and darkness covered everything, the bishop rose and began to take his leave. The archbishop accompanied him as far as the gate, with candles going before them. Then the archbishop ordered lights to be brought, and, as though he wished to speak more privately with the bishop, withdrew a little from those standing around. Thus, mounting the white horse which the bishop had prepared for him, he reached Thérouanne with that same bishop during the night. On the following day he ordered his men to meet him at Soissons.

In this manner he escaped the threats of the count of Flanders and, under God’s protection, reached Soissons with his companions without hindrance. When the king of England learned [Col. 0090D] that the archbishop had entered France, he sent envoys to Louis, king of France: namely, Gilbert Foliot, bishop of London; Richard of Ilchester, the king’s clerk and one of the highest judges of the realm; and the illustrious William, earl of Arundel. Finding the king of France at Compiègne, they addressed him thus:

“Your Highness, lord king, may remember that when peace between you and our lord the king of England was last restored, it was agreed, among other provisions, that if any of your men, from either side, fled for any reason and came into the other’s kingdom, he should immediately, when claimed, be restored to his lord without objection. And now the archbishop of Canterbury [Col. 0091A], avoiding the judgment of his lord the king, secretly and furtively fled by night and entered your land. Therefore your faithful friend, our lord the king, earnestly asks that, to avoid insulting him and violating the agreement, you neither receive nor harbor the aforesaid archbishop in your kingdom.”

To this the most pious Louis, king of France, replied: “I do not remember the agreements of which you speak. But even if it were established that such an arrangement had been made, this would not prevent us from gladly seeing, graciously receiving, and honoring the archbishop. He is not to be counted among the men of your king; rather, he is the king’s lord and protector. Moreover—and indeed this surpasses all else—the clemency of our kingdom stands open as a refuge to all who are oppressed [Col. 0091B]. For the compassion of our heart requires us to make our kingdom express, through the testimony of deeds, the liberty proclaimed by its name.

“For it has reached our hearing how unjustly, and for what reasons, your king hates and persecutes this venerable man. We do not wonder, therefore, that a prudent man, taking thought both for his own life and for the cause of God’s Church, has avoided the king’s rage and fled beneath the wings of our protection. Therefore, if I knew where he could be found, I would long since have gone out to meet him with due honor.”

Then William, earl of Arundel, replied to the king: “Perhaps you do not know, O king, that the archbishop whom you have decided so eagerly to honor has always been hostile to you. He is the man by whose cunning and ingenuity your realm has many times been disturbed and thrown into turmoil [Col. 0091C]. For he laid waste your lands, captured your towns, and cut away no small part of your kingdom and dominion.”

The king answered: “You say nothing that would make him seem less dear or honorable to me. For, by your own statement, he did what he ought to have done: he fulfilled sincerely, in all things and entirely, the loyalty owed to his lord for the time being. He would have done the same for me had he been mine. But see with what reward your king has judged him worthy for such benefits as he conferred upon him, as you say, by inflicting losses upon me. Was it that he might repay evil for good, and drive from his own possessions the man who had subjected others’ possessions to him?”

Again the envoys spoke to the king, saying: “Your friend, the king of England, also asks [Col. 0091D] that you deign to instruct the lord pope not to grant the archbishop access to his favor and intimacy, and not to give credence to his lies.”

Angered by the shamelessness of their speech, the king said: “I shall indeed send instructions, but not as you request.” Calling Brother Francon, chamberlain of the lord pope, who happened at that time to be present at Compiègne, he said: “Say to my lord Pope Alexander on my behalf: if I have such standing with his Holiness that he wishes to grant me a favor or benefit, let him graciously receive the archbishop of Canterbury when he comes into his presence, and let him neither hear nor admit any unjust complaint against him.”

When the envoys returned and reported what had happened [Col. 0092A], the king of England immediately took care to dispatch other envoys in haste to the lord pope, that they might get ahead of the archbishop at the curia and turn the minds of the lord pope and the cardinals away from him. These are the names of those sent: Roger, archbishop of York; Gilbert Foliot, bishop of London; the bishop of Worcester; Bartholomew, bishop of Exeter; Hilary, bishop of Chichester; Richard of Ilchester and John of Oxford, clerks of the king; William, earl of Arundel; Guy Rufus; Hugh of Gundeville; Reginald of Saint-Valery; Henry, son of Gerald, a most intimate associate of the king; and others whose names we do not know.

All of these came to Sens and appeared before the lord pope [Col. 0092B]. They brought forward many charges against the blessed man, intending to undermine his cause. They could not prove them; and their pleading was so unjust and insulting that, when one of the bishops pressed his case too fiercely, the pope said: “Brother, restrain yourself. It is clear that you hate and persecute an innocent man without cause.”

The substance of their embassy was that the lord pope, at the king’s request, should send two cardinals to England with full authority, so that, appeal being set aside, they might judge between the king and the archbishop. They further asserted that the king was prepared, with great humility and devotion, to make satisfaction if he had in any respect committed an excess. Yet the king did this deceitfully, knowing that judgments of cardinals were not obtained without payment, and that he could easily secure through money whatever he wished [Col. 0092C] if he were allowed to proceed under the cardinals’ jurisdiction. This was not unknown to the lord pope. Therefore he was entirely unwilling to accede to such a request, although the cardinals strongly and persistently urged that the king’s petition should take effect.

For William of Pavia, one of the more important cardinals, favored the king in every respect and had induced the other cardinals to favor him as well—but not without payment. Thus disappointed of hope of obtaining their request, the royal envoys quickly returned. For the bishops carrying out this embassy did not consider it safe to await at the curia the archbishop, whom they had heard would arrive shortly.

On the fourth day the archbishop came to Sens. Having called together his clerics [Col. 0092D], he began to inquire which of them could most suitably explain his case in the lord pope’s presence. Although there were among them many experts in canon and civil law, exceedingly eloquent and practiced in pleading, no one was found who dared undertake the matter. They feared the king, knowing with certainty that it could not remain concealed which of them had argued for the archbishop in the curia.

On the following day, the holy man, placing his trust in the Lord, came to the curia holding in his hand that charter in which the king’s customs were contained—the document which, as we have said, he had received from the king’s hand at Clarendon in defense of ecclesiastical liberty. When he came into the lord pope’s presence and prostrated himself at his feet, he laid the document, unfolded and spread out, before them [Col. 0093A], saying:

“Behold, Holy Father, the customs of the king of England, contrary to the canons, decrees, and even to the laws of earthly rulers; for these we are compelled to endure exile. We have come in order to show them to your holy fatherhood and to take counsel about them. Therefore let your Holiness, if it please you, command that they be read and heard. Whoever hears them will surely have both ears ring, hearing Christians act against the law of Christianity and, with the venerable institutions of the holy Fathers condemned, introduce into God’s Church the presumptuous, unprecedented abuses of ancient tyrants.”

Having said this on bended knees, he rose at the pope’s command and stood in the midst of the crowd of his clerics surrounding him [Col. 0093B]. At the lord pope’s command those customs were read. When the reader had pronounced the first chapter, the venerable bishop began to argue wonderfully against the chapter proposed, more fully explaining and exposing the king’s intention in this matter. From the decrees and laws he demonstrated and proved in what respects and to what degree what had been proclaimed conflicted with the canons of the holy Fathers, and how great a danger threatened God’s Church if the king attained what he intended.

He did likewise with each chapter, while the lord pope willingly listened to him and carefully noted his arguments point by point. The cardinals, however, who had received money from the king and supported his party, caused the blessed man much trouble in his case—especially William of Pavia [Col. 0093C], who was more friendly and intimate with the king than the rest. Endeavoring by every means to hinder the blessed man, he rose up against each point, opposed him, proposed many objections, and asked many questions. The venerable man, however, untangled or refuted these without difficulty or hesitation, as though they were spiders’ webs.

For William thought that the archbishop was using a speech composed by another rather than his own; and that if he could divert him from the course of his discourse, he would at once become an object of ridicule and disgrace. But the archbishop, perceiving that William opposed him directly, on several occasions, by a counter-course of argument, so entangled and ensnared him with his own objections that it became clear to all that he was using not only his own resources and eloquence [Col. 0093D], but possessed an intellect and eloquence that could not be overcome.

When a great part of the day had been spent both in setting forth his case and in disputing with his opponents—for there were sixteen chapters of those customs, to which he had answered while standing—the lord pope, at last admiring his greatness and excellence, called him to himself. Ordering him to sit beside him, he said: “Welcome, dearest brother.” Repeatedly rejoicing that he had come, he began to thank him for having taken upon himself so great a burden and so arduous a task: namely, for daring to defend God’s Church in such dangerous times against the assaults of tyrants.

The venerable bishop likewise gave the lord pope abundant thanks, with due humility and reverence [Col. 0094A], because he had been deemed worthy of such honor. Then the lord pope condemned those customs in perpetuity and subjected their observers and enforcers to eternal anathema.

The man of God remained at the curia for some time and at length, with the lord pope’s permission and counsel, withdrew to Pontigny, where he stayed for nearly two years. The monks of Pontigny rejoiced beyond measure at the arrival of so great a guest, giving him thanks for turning aside to them, and especially thanking the lord pope, who had deemed them worthy to honor with so great a guest. Thereafter, with much fervor of charity and devotion, they most abundantly supplied the archbishop and his companions with everything necessary for food and clothing throughout the time he remained among them.

We shall refrain from recounting how holy and religiously this most reverend man conducted himself there [Col. 0094B], lest we repeat to our brothers what is already known and exceed the limits of brevity. Yet this must not be passed over in silence: among the other pursuits of holy emulation, he there desired and received the monastic habit. Sending a secret messenger to the lord pope, then staying at Sens, he asked and obtained that the religious habit be made, blessed, and sent to him. Among other things, the lord pope wrote back: “We have sent you, beloved brother, a habit—not such as we wished, but such as we had.”

When the king of England learned with what honor the venerable bishop had been received by the lord pope, and that he had chosen Pontigny as his place of residence, since he could no longer rage against him personally [Col. 0094C], he vented his fury upon the archbishop’s people with an unprecedented form of cruelty. He ordered that wherever any man or woman of the archbishop’s kin might be found, they should be disinherited, stripped of their property, and driven from the kingdom, after first being compelled to swear that they would go to Pontigny in order to grieve the archbishop. Then old and young alike belonging to his kindred were expelled; women also, with children and nursing infants, were compelled to go into exile.

The king also appropriated the archiepiscopal revenues and the entire archbishopric for his own use. Over the business of the bishopric he appointed a most wicked layman, named Ranulf de Broc, who had always, as far as he could, pursued hostility against the man of God. When all this became known to the archbishop [Col. 0094D], he received it with great steadfastness and magnanimity. He made little of earthly losses and of the exile of his people, provided only that God’s Church might someday obtain peace.

Thus the archbishop, applying himself more earnestly to reading, prayer, and the other pursuits of holy life, rested at Pontigny for two years. But the malice of the king of England did not allow him to remain undisturbed there longer. Devising craftily how he might drive him out even from that place, he sent certain Cistercian abbots to the general chapter of the order. He reproached them with the benefits which he had conferred upon their order, then accused them of ingratitude because, to insult him, they had received the archbishop and had for a long time supplied him with necessities.

When this became known [Col. 0095A], the archbishop, guarding against the possibility that the order might suffer any loss because of him, went to Louis, king of France, who had many times urged him by many earnest and pressing requests to come to him. At Sens, with Saint Columba, he spent the rest of his exile, while the king supplied all necessities.

The king of England then summoned a council of bishops and magnates at Clarendon and exacted from them an oath that none of them would provide any assistance to the archbishop, send him any message, or receive letters sent by him. To the oath he added that no one should receive letters or messengers from the lord pope, or appeal to him in any matter, but only to the king’s presence. He also decreed that no one should cross the sea without his permission [Col. 0095B] and letters. He stationed guards at every seaport, who were to allow no one to cross and to search carefully those arriving from overseas, lest anyone bring letters from the lord pope or the archbishop into his kingdom.

He further decreed that if anyone were caught with letters, he should be put aboard an old, broken-down little boat, taken out onto the open sea, and there, alone in that boat and without an oar, abandoned to the waves. When the bishops refused by every means available to take the oath, the king at last, after being greatly and long entreated, allowed them merely to promise by word; but the laymen swore. The king employed this stratagem because he had heard that the lord pope intended to summon all the bishops of the kingdom to himself.

Having thus shut up the kingdom, the king again ordered all to assemble in London [Col. 0095C]. When they had gathered, he began to act concerning the coronation of his son. While the bishops murmured, conferred with one another, and said that it was unlawful to presume upon such an act in the archbishop’s absence, since no one doubted that the anointing of a king belonged to that archbishop’s unique dignity, three bishops were found: Roger of York, Gilbert of London, and Jocelin of Salisbury. They said that the matter ought not be delayed on account of his absence and declared themselves ready to carry out the king’s will in this regard.

Therefore, since the king did not permit delay, his son was crowned, the three aforementioned bishops carrying out what belonged to the solemnity of the consecration [Col. 0095D], while the others could neither escape nor were willing to lay a hand to it. Thereafter the cause of the Church of Canterbury was handled in various ways. Yet peace could not be achieved, although Louis, king of France, in several conferences which he meanwhile held with the king of England, pressed strongly for peace and concord to be restored between the king and the archbishop.

The lord pope likewise, repeatedly sending his legates, urged the king by paternal affection, letters, and words toward peace with God’s Church; but nothing was accomplished. Understanding that the king could be dealt with only by a strong hand, he finally wrote to him, directing, exhorting, requesting, and commanding him to restore peace to the Church of Canterbury, which had long suffered from the absence of its shepherd [Col. 0096A], and to make concord with the archbishop.

He also sent other letters secretly and placed them in the hands of a certain bishop of France. They contained the expressly stated sentence of an interdict upon the kingdom of England: namely, that if the king despised the apostolic admonition, his kingdom should immediately be subjected to an interdict. This was not unknown to the king. The two kings therefore arranged a conference to discuss peace for the Church. Nearly all the bishops of France and Normandy came to the conference, especially those upon whom the lord pope had specially laid the burden of this affair.

At length, with difficulty and after much negotiation, peace was made between the king and the archbishop, the king wholly relinquishing all claims and ecclesiastical rights to canonical freedom. Yet [Col. 0096B] the king refused to offer the archbishop the kiss of peace. It was arranged that on the next day, during the celebration of Mass, the archbishop, receiving the peace from the priest, should offer it to the king. But the king craftily mocked this plan: as soon as he entered the church, he ordered a Mass for the dead to be celebrated, in which he knew the peace was not given.

This alone was clear evidence and proof that the king had not made peace with the archbishop in his true heart. The archbishop returned to Sens and began to arrange his return home. He sent before him to Canterbury Master John of Salisbury, later bishop of Chartres, so that he might solemnly celebrate a synod and, after imposing penance, absolve those who had communicated with the excommunicated.

Thus the man of God, on the first day of the seventh year of his exile, left the city of Sens to return to his own see, having received from the king of England, as a safe-conduct, one of the king’s clerks, named John of Oxford [Col. 0096C].

When he had come to the coast of Flanders, to the sea at a place called Witsand, he learned there that the three bishops who, as stated above, had wrongfully usurped for themselves the coronation of the younger king had met him at Dover and were awaiting his arrival there. He therefore quickly summoned a boy named Osbern, placed in his hand the lord pope’s letters, and commanded him, having crossed the sea swiftly, to deliver those letters to the aforesaid three bishops at Dover. When the bishops received them [Col. 0096D] and learned from their tenor that they had been excommunicated, they returned greatly dismayed in spirit. But the archbishop, having made ready ships, put out to sea and, sailing prosperously, when he approached England did not wish to land at Canterbury, lest perhaps those excommunicated men should still be there, whose encounter he avoided. Instead he turned aside to another harbour called Sandwich, which was his own proper place, and landed there.

The three nobles—namely Raynald de Warenne, Gervase de Cornhill, and Randulf de Broc—who had come to Dover with the aforesaid bishops, met the archbishop at Sandwich, intending, if possible, to oppose him in some matter. They complained, as though on the king’s behalf, that he had brought French clerics [Col. 0097A] into the kingdom, saying that he ought to give sureties or hostages for them, lest they perhaps devise some evil in the realm. Although he considered them unworthy of an answer, he nevertheless replied that he had brought them with the king’s consent and permission, and that he would do nothing which they required him to do. Having treated their words and quibbles with contempt, he proceeded to Canterbury.

The monks, with the clergy and all the people, came out to meet him in joy and exultation; rejoicing and praising God with loud voices, they conducted him into his own place. About twenty days before the Nativity of the Lord he entered Canterbury. During those days he applied himself more earnestly than usual to prayer and the giving of alms. He also administered justice to those who had been oppressed by an unjust judgment [Col. 0097B] and, entirely setting aside respect of persons, spared no one contrary to justice, but with great freedom of spirit justly pursued what was right, sparing no one who acted contrary to justice. He admonished the king’s clerics who had occupied churches by secular authority, and restored those churches to their former possessors.

Meanwhile those bishops whom, by apostolic authority, we mentioned a little earlier as excommunicated at Canterbury, quickly crossed the sea and approached the king. Throwing themselves at his feet, they gave him a sufficiently envious and malicious account of how the Archbishop of Canterbury had dealt with them, asserting that his entry into the kingdom had not been peaceful; they added also that he had acted not so much on their account [Col. 0097C] as in contempt of the king. On hearing this, the king in fury entered his private chambers; and, with knights and attendants standing around, he began fiercely to reproach them for their cowardice, because they had for so long patiently endured his being mocked by a most contemptible cleric.

Among those present were four knights, whose names were Raynald fitz Urse, William de Tracy, Hugh de Morville, and Richard Brito. Recognizing that the king’s words had been uttered in great indignation of spirit, and believing that whatever might be done to the archbishop would be pleasing to him, they began to devise punishment against the man of God. They conferred together, then, and with one accord withdrew from court without anyone knowing, and directed their journey with great haste [Col. 0097D] toward England.

Upon coming into the territory of Canterbury, they gathered a body of knights with them, declaring that it was the king’s will and command that the archbishop should either be captured or killed. The knights, ignorant of the truth and fearing the king, set out with them for Canterbury. They came there on the fifth day after the Nativity of the Lord, about the ninth hour, when the archbishop had already risen from table. The four knights who led the others left them outside and came before the archiepiscopal palace. Entering the hall, they found the servants who had waited at table still eating.

A certain William, son of Nigel, saw and recognized them. He went to meet them, greeted them, and spoke with them. When he heard from them that they wished to speak with the archbishop [Col. 0098A], he entered the chamber where the archbishop sat conversing with his monks and clerics, and informed him that four knights of the king’s household were standing outside and desired to speak with him. The archbishop said: “Make them come in.” William immediately brought them in. As they entered, the man of God was speaking attentively with a monk and did not look at them. They, speaking to no one, walked straight up to the feet of the man of God, and there sat down without saying anything even to the archbishop. A certain archer named Randulf had entered with them, and he too sat on the floor behind them.

When at last the man of God had finished his conversation, he turned toward them; seeing them silent, he looked at them very intently. At last, it is reported, he greeted them. [Col. 0098B] Yet they say that he greeted not all of them, but only William de Tracy, naming him expressly. They paid no heed to his greeting and gave no answer at all, but looked at one another. Raynald fitz Urse is said, however, to have said, as if contemptuously: “God help you.”

The man of God, seeing their altered faces and their persistence in silence, was astonished at their appearance. At last Raynald fitz Urse, with an angry countenance, burst into speech and said: “The king sends you words through us from beyond the sea. Say whether you wish to hear them more privately or in the hearing of all.”

The archbishop replied: “As you wish.”

“No,” said Raynald, “as you wish.”

Then, at his command, the clerics went out of the room into another chamber [Col. 0098C], and none of his people remained except the doorkeeper. Raynald therefore began to set forth certain matters as though they were the king’s commands. But at the very beginning of his speech, the man of God understood where he was heading and what he would say.

“These words,” he said, “must not be concealed.” He said to the doorkeeper: “Leave the door and call back those who have gone out; for I ought not to separate them from my counsel.”

While he was alone in the chamber with the knights, they considered killing him, taking advantage of his isolation. But because they had no sword or any other thing with which to accomplish it, they planned to strike him down with the staff of the cross which, by custom, was always before him. That this was so became known afterwards through their own confession.

When the clerics had returned [Col. 0098D] to the chamber, Raynald again began to deliver his message, saying: “The lord king commands that he made good and complete peace with you in a perfect heart, but that you have not kept it well. For he has heard that you passed through his cities and castles with a multitude of armed men; moreover, that you excommunicated the Archbishop of York along with the bishops who assisted him at the coronation of his son, and expelled many others of his most faithful men from churches. All this is not free from suspicion; indeed, it is plainly evident that you wish to take away the crown of his son and to oppose him in all things and in every respect. Therefore our lord king wishes to know whether you are willing to enter his court to answer for these matters.”

Then the archbishop said: “Have you anything further to say? If you have, say it.”

“First,” said Raynald [Col. 0099A], “we shall hear your answer.”

“No,” said the archbishop, “I do not wish to take the crown from the king’s son or in any respect diminish his honour; rather, I desire in every way to exalt his kingdom and glory. I entered his realm and our Church with his permission and safe-conduct. Nor ought the lord king to make an accusation against me because men of our Church, rendering us the honour due to us, accompanied us for a short part of the journey. As for the bishops of whom you have spoken, it was not I but the lord pope who excommunicated them: both because they usurped, at the coronation of the king’s son, what did not belong to them, and because, after committing that presumption, they scorned to come when summoned to make satisfaction. Yet [Col. 0099B] if I have exceeded in anything, I am prepared to perform what is right in the court of the lord king, or wherever it may please him.”

“Indeed,” said Raynald, “the bishops were excommunicated by you; and therefore the lord king wishes and commands that you quickly absolve them.”

“I do not deny,” said the holy man, “that this was done through me, but not by me. Therefore, unless they first approach the lord pope, who pronounced the sentence, with due humility and satisfaction, they cannot by any means be absolved through me.”

Then Raynald said furiously: “The king therefore commands that you swiftly and without delay depart from his land with your foreign clerics and all who belong to you. Not one of them may remain, because henceforth you will not even be able to protect yourself.”

To this the archbishop replied: “Never, from this hour [Col. 0099C] onward, shall the sea stand between my Church and me, unless I am dragged from here by my feet. For I did not come in order to flee; you will always be able to find me here. Nor ought you to have spoken such things to me on the king’s behalf. For I know his prudence and moderation: he would not have sent me such commands.”

They all answered with one voice, asserting that the king had so commanded. “Moreover,” said the holy man, “I could and ought justly to complain concerning the king’s men, who, since I entered my see, have inflicted many indignities and injuries upon me. Among other things, they struck my men; they dishonoured my packhorse by cutting off its tail; and they violently seized the casks of wine which the king himself had given me and caused to be brought here.”

To this Hugh [Col. 0099D] de Morville said: “If the king’s men have offended against you or yours in any respect, why was this not first reported to the king, instead of your taking vengeance upon them by your own authority and excommunicating them?”

The holy man replied: “Hugh, how high you carry your head! If anyone violates ecclesiastical rights in any matter and scorns to make satisfaction, I shall administer justice without waiting for anyone’s permission.”

To this Raynald said: “Those are exceedingly great threats.”

At these words the knights sprang up violently and stood before the man of God. Raynald said: “Thomas, on the king’s behalf I renounce allegiance to you.” The other knights shouted the same thing with one voice.

Then the man of God said to them: “I know that you have come to kill me [Col. 0100A], but I make God my shield.” And repeatedly striking his own neck with his hand, he said: “Here—here you will find me.”

Then the knights went out, threatening the archbishop fiercely and ordering, on the king’s behalf, that he be carefully watched lest he escape. They also frightfully threatened the servants whom they found in the hall in the king’s name, saying that anyone who remained with the archbishop would be held the king’s enemy and deserving of death.

Hearing their threats, the holy man rose and followed them to the chamber door. To a knight who threatened him, he said: “What are you saying? Say it—say it.” But they paid no attention to his words and passed on.

The man of God returned to his followers and sat on his bed. John of Salisbury said to him: [Col. 0100B] “This has always been and is your habit: whatever seems good to you alone, that you always both say and do.”

The holy man replied: “What do you wish, Lord John?”

John said: “You ought to have summoned your council, knowing most certainly that these knights seek nothing against you except an opportunity to hand you over to death.”

The holy man replied: “All of us must die, and we ought not to be turned away from justice by fear of death. I am more ready to receive death for God, for justice, and for the liberty of God’s Church than they are to inflict it.”

“We,” said John, “are sinners and are not yet prepared for death; and I see no one who wishes to die freely except you.”

And he said: “The Lord’s will be done.”

Meanwhile the departing knights armed themselves, intending to attack one who was unarmed [Col. 0100C]. The other knights, who had waited outside while the four spoke with the man of God, had come clad in mail beneath their tunics. When this was reported to him, the monks said: “Lord, come into the church, for these men are preparing either to seize or to kill you.”

He said: “I do not fear them. I shall wait here for whatever may please God.”

The knights, now ready, came with terror and clamour to the doors of the hall. Finding them barred, they could not break them down by any force, although they tried with all their might. There was with them a certain Robert de Broc who knew every entrance and passage of the house. He said to them: “Follow me, for I shall bring you in by another way.”

With him leading, they came through the orchard [Col. 0100D] and reached the chamber. But when they found no entrance there either, the aforesaid Robert climbed through a covered passage, which at that time was being renovated from its former condition, in order to open the doors. Those inside with the man of God, sensing that they were near, all fled except a few monks and one cleric named Master Edward. They seized the venerable man—for he was still sitting—and began, as he resisted, struggled, and protested, to carry him in their arms to the church.

Looking around, they saw the court full of armed men, and the orchard and the ways by which they were going to the church occupied beforehand by knights; and they were alarmed. Then they turned to another, more secret door, which had long been closed and barred and had afforded passage to no one. One of the monks ran ahead, wishing to test whether perhaps he could break the bolt by force. But as soon as he touched it, by divine prompting—to his own amazement and that of all present—it fell into his hands as though it had not adhered to the door at all [Col. 0101A].

Then the monk said: “Take hold of him and carry him.”

They took him and began to carry him, and did not release him until they had brought him into the church. Yet they stopped before reaching the church: twice in the cloister and once in the chapter house. For, angry with them, he resisted and slipped from their hands, unwilling to be carried by them.

When the man of God entered the church, the monks looked back and saw the knights already entering the cloister. They shut the church doors against them. But seeing the doors being shut, the man of God said: “By holy obedience I command that they be opened without delay. We ought not make a castle out of the house of God.”

Again the monks seized the man of God and began to lead him up the steps into the choir. He said to them: “Let me go, and withdraw. You have no business here. Permit God to dispose of my affair according to his will.”

Meanwhile the knights came into the church, shouting and crying out terribly: “Where is Thomas, the king’s traitor?” The man of God gave no answer to this. Therefore they cried out again and said: “Where is the archbishop?”

Then the holy man said: “I am both priest [Col. 0101B] and archbishop; and if you seek me, behold, you have found me.”

As he said this, he came down to meet them from the steps which he had ascended. Turning toward the northern side of the church, he stood there by the wall near the altar of blessed Benedict. The four aforementioned knights came up to him, together with a cleric whom they had brought with them, named Hugh the Evil Clerk, and said: “Quickly absolve the king’s bishops whom you excommunicated.”

He replied: “I shall do nothing other than what I have already said and done.”

Then they began to threaten him with death. He answered: “I do not fear your threats, for I am ready to die for God; nevertheless, release my men and do not touch them.”

They laid hands on him and began to drag him forcefully, striving to place him on William’s shoulders and cast him out of the church. But the holy man stood firmly [Col. 0101C] on his step and could not be moved from the place, for Master Edward—who alone of all his people had remained with him—held him against them with great strength.

When Raynald fitz Urse, who had first laid hands upon him, pressed him more violently, the man of God shook himself free and thrust him away, so that he almost fell upon the pavement. He said to him: “Get away from here; you are my man. You ought not touch me.”

Raynald replied: “I owe you neither fealty nor homage, against my loyalty to the king.”

Raynald saw that he could not move him from the place and feared that he might be rescued by the people who had assembled to hear Vespers. He drew his sword and approached, now intending to strike. The holy man, seeing that his martyrdom was imminent and that his assailant stood close at hand, joined his hands [Col. 0101D], covered his eyes, and, bowing his head, offered it to the striker.

“I commend myself to God, to blessed Dionysius, and to holy Ælfheah!” Having said this, Raynald approached and struck him powerfully and obliquely on the head, cutting off the top of his crown and knocking off his cap. The sword slid onto his left shoulder and cut through all his garments to the bare flesh. Master Edward, who stood beside the man of God, saw the blow coming and threw out his arm as if to protect him; it was almost completely severed.

Then William de Tracy came forward and struck him on the head with a great blow, though he did not yet fall. The same William struck again more forcefully, and at that blow the holy man fell face downward on the pavement. Richard Brito struck him as he lay prostrate [Col. 0102A] on the pavement and broke his sword in two against the stone beneath.

While these things were done, Hugh de Morville was occupied in driving away the people who were pressing near, and so it happened that he did not strike him with his hand. But Hugh the Evil Clerk, the most wicked of all men, came to the fallen man, put his foot upon his neck, drove his sword into his head, and scattered his brains over the pavement, shouting: “Let us go, for the traitor is dead.”

These deeds completed, the knights went out of the church by the way through which they had come, swords in hand and crying: “The king’s men! The king’s men!” Meanwhile they had left Robert de Broc and certain others in the archbishop’s chamber to guard the goods [Col. 0102B] that were there. Returning there again, they immediately broke open the chest and coffers, taking gold, silver, garments, and books, including privileges and everything found there. They also plundered all the horses and absolutely everything which they could find in the archiepiscopal houses fit for use.

The monks, having sent the multitude of people out of the church, shut the doors. Gathering the blood and brains of the new martyr that had been shed upon the pavement, they placed them in vessels. They also carried the most holy body and laid it before the high altar, where it remained through the night, while the monks sat around it in great sorrow and grief. They also placed vessels beneath it to receive the flowing blood, knowing that the blood of a martyr who had been shed for the love of God and the liberty of the Church [Col. 0102C] was most precious.

When morning came, a certain porter of the king—Robert de Broc, namely—was sent by Randulf de Broc. Having summoned the monks, he said: “The land has been cleared of the traitor, who deserved to be treated dishonourably both living and dead. Therefore take him out of the way and cast him into a place where he will not be known; otherwise know that he shall be dragged out most shamefully by his feet, torn to pieces, and thrown to pigs and dogs.”

The monks, therefore, in fear took the holy body and stripped it of its garments. When they had removed those garments which necessary use appeared to require, they found underneath the habit of a monk—that is, a cowl—and beneath the cowl, next to the flesh, a very rough hair-shirt; finally, beneath the linen breeches, likewise very rough hair-cloth drawers. [Col. 0102D] These garments too had been fitted by a certain art and with knots so that they could easily be put on and taken off for the purpose of discipline. For he was frequently scourged; indeed, on the very day on which he suffered, he is said to have been scourged three times.

He suffered in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1171, on the fifth day after the Nativity of the Lord, and on a Tuesday. It should also be said that this most blessed man was born and baptized on a Tuesday; that he fled from Northampton on a Tuesday; that he crossed the sea on a Tuesday; that likewise, on his return, he crossed the sea on a Tuesday; and that, as stated above, he fell crowned with martyrdom on a Tuesday.

The monks, seeing that the most blessed man possessed within his hidden garments every badge of holiness [Col. 0103A] and religious life, rejoiced beyond measure; and in amazement they said to one another: “Behold, truly a monk and truly a hermit; behold, truly a martyr, who suffered torments not only in death but also in life.”

Thus, unspeakably consoled in the grief which they had conceived at his death, rejoicing and exulting in the Lord, and secure in his protection, they buried him with the greatest honour and eager devotion in a most secluded crypt. There, through his merits, frequent and countless benefits of healings and miracles are bestowed upon the faithful. By the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever. Amen.

[Col. 0103]

## THE THIRD LIFE OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY AND MARTYR, BY WILLIAM FITZSTEPHEN

[Note: From the treatises of Grim and Roger of Pontigny, transcribed from Parisian and London manuscripts and now published for the first time, I shall add here neither notes nor variant readings. But I have collated the entire text of William Fitzstephen, formerly published by Sparke, with the manuscript preserved in the Bodleian Library [Douce no. 287]; and I have enclosed in brackets, as of suspect authority, most of what is contained in that manuscript but omitted in Sparke’s copy. The Douce manuscript [Col. 0104C] is imperfect at its beginning, namely at the point where this famous description of the city of London occurs; for that reason I have used the edition of this little treatise printed in Leland’s *Itinerary*. Besides the passages in which the Douce manuscript is unquestionably better, I have placed beneath the text a few readings, lest they should perish—or rather, lest readers be compelled to place excessive trust in my judgment.]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0103B] For the glory of almighty God, the perpetual remembrance of blessed Thomas, and the profit and edification of all who read or hear, I, William, son of Stephen, have undertaken to write the life and passion of Thomas, that good archbishop and martyr. I was a cleric, fellow citizen, and table-companion of the same my lord; invited by the speech of his own mouth to share in his burden of care, I was his secretary in the chancery; subdeacon in the chapel when he celebrated; reader of the letters and instruments presented when he sat in judgment of cases; and, when he sometimes commanded it, advocate in certain causes. I was present with him at the council held at Northampton [Col. 0104B], where events were of the greatest consequence; I witnessed his passion at Canterbury; I saw with my eyes and heard with my ears very many other things written here, and learned some from witnesses who knew them.

Plato fashioned a commonwealth in discourse; Sallust described the situation of Africa in his history, on the occasion of the Carthaginians’ rebellion against the Romans and of the Romans’ frequent expeditions sent to subdue them. And I shall describe the site and commonwealth of London on the occasion of blessed Thomas.

## DESCRIPTION OF THE MOST NOBLE CITY OF LONDON

[Col. 0103C] Among the noble cities of the world celebrated by fame, [Col. 0104C] the city of London, seat of the kingdom of the English, is one [Col. 0105A] which spreads its renown more widely, sends its wealth and merchandise farther abroad, and raises its head more highly. It is fortunate in the healthfulness of its air, in Christian religion, in the strength of its fortifications, in the nature of its site, in the distinction of its citizens, in matronly chastity, and also in the delightfulness of its games and its fruitfulness in noble men. It is pleasant to consider each of these separately.

There, indeed, the mildness of the climate softens men’s dispositions—not so that they become corruptly given to Venus, but lest they be savage and bestial; rather, they become kindly and generous.

There is there an episcopal see in the church of Saint Paul. It was once metropolitan, and is still believed destined to be so again, if the citizens should return to the island—unless perhaps the archiepiscopal title of blessed Thomas the martyr, together with his bodily presence, should preserve that dignity permanently to Canterbury [Col. 0105B], where it now is. Yet, since holy Thomas has adorned both cities—London by his birth, Canterbury by his death—each has, in respect for the saint and with justice added, something further to plead against the other. Moreover, as regards the observance of the Christian faith, both London and its suburb contain thirteen greater conventual churches, besides one hundred and twenty-six lesser parish churches.

On the east it has a royal fortress, very great and very strong, whose open space and walls rise from the deepest foundations, built with mortar mixed with the blood of animals. On the west are two most strongly fortified castles. The city wall is high and great, with double gates at intervals—seven-gated—and towers set along the northern side at intervening spaces. Likewise London was walled and towered on the south; but the great and fish-filled river Thames, flowing and ebbing with the sea and washing against it there, in the course of time washed away, weakened, and overthrew those walls. Further upstream to the west, a royal palace rises above the same river: an incomparable building, with an outer wall and defensive works, two miles from the city, connected to it by a populous suburb [Col. 0105C].

Everywhere outside the suburban houses are the citizens’ gardens, planted with trees, extensive, beautiful, and adjoining one another.

Likewise, to the north are fields, pasturelands, and a pleasant expanse of meadows, intersected by running waters, whose mill-wheels are driven with merry murmur. Nearby stretches a vast forest, wooded glades, and hiding places for wild beasts: stags, fallow deer, boars, and wild bulls. The city’s arable fields are not barren gravel, but the rich plains of Asia,

> Which yield joyous harvests and fill the granaries of their cultivators  
> With the heavy mass of cereal stalks.

Around London to the north are also notable suburban springs, with sweet, wholesome, transparent water, trembling through clear pebbles in its stream. Among them Holy Well, Clerkenwell, and Saint Clement’s Well are especially famous. They are visited with more frequent resort and greater crowds of scholars and city youth [Col. 0105D], who go out into the evening air in summer. The city is indeed good—if it has a good lord.

This city is honoured by men, adorned with arms, and populous with many inhabitants. Thus, in the time of the calamity of war, when King Stephen commanded that those fit for war should come forth from it for display, there were reckoned twenty thousand armed horsemen and sixty thousand foot soldiers. Wherever they may be, London citizens are considered conspicuous and known above all other citizens for elegance of manners, dress, and lavish table. The inhabitants of other cities are called citizens; those of this city, barons. For them, an oath is the end of every dispute.

The matrons of the city are themselves Sabine women.

In London three principal churches possess renowned schools by privilege and ancient dignity. Yet, often through the personal favour of some acquaintance, more schools are admitted there according to the discipline of philosophy. On feast days the masters hold assemblies at the festival churches. The scholars dispute: some demonstratively, others dialectically. Some turn enthymemes about; others make better use of complete syllogisms. Some exercise themselves in disputation for display, such as occurs between wrestlers; others pursue truth, in the manner proper to perfection. Sophists who feign knowledge are judged blessed for their troop and flood of words; others reason fallaciously. Certain orators sometimes speak fittingly in rhetorical speeches for persuasion, taking care to observe the rules of their art and to omit nothing belonging to the circumstances. Boys of different schools quarrel with one another in verse, or contend over the principles of grammatical art [Col. 0106A], or the rules governing preterites and supines. Others employ, in epigrams, rhythms, and metres, that old elementary wit: under cover of Fescennine licence, they attack their companions more freely while suppressing names; they hurl insults and jests; with Socratic witticisms they touch upon the faults of companions, or perhaps elders; or, with bolder dithyrambs, gnaw more sharply with the Theonian tooth. The audience,

> Ready to laugh heartily,  
> Repeats trembling peals of laughter, wrinkling the nose.

## ON THE ARRANGEMENT OF THE CITY

Those who practise each occupation, those who sell each kind of commodity, and those who hire out each kind of labour are all, every morning, separately assigned to their own places according to their trades [Col. 0106B]. Moreover, in London, upon the riverbank, among the wines offered for sale in ships and wine-cellars, there is a public cookshop. There, daily and according to the season, one finds provisions: dishes, roasted, baked, fried, and boiled foods; fish and little fish; coarser meats for the poor and more delicate ones for the rich; game, birds, and small fowl. If weary friends should suddenly arrive at the house of one of the citizens from a journey, and if they do not wish to wait hungry while fresh food is bought and cooked,

> The servants give water to their hands and bread from baskets.

Meanwhile one runs to the riverbank, where all desirable things are immediately available. However great a multitude of soldiers or pilgrims enters the city, at whatever hour of day or night, or is about to leave it, they may turn aside there, if they please, so that neither they go too long hungry [Col. 0106C] nor others depart without breakfast; and each refreshes himself according to his means. Those who wish to treat themselves luxuriously need not seek sturgeon, African fowl, or an Ionian attagen, when the delicacies found there are set before them. This is indeed a public cookshop, extremely useful to the city and belonging to civilized life. Hence one reads in Plato’s *Gorgias* that the cook’s art stands next to medicine as an imitation and flattery, a fourth part of civic life.

Outside one of the gates, immediately in the suburb, is a certain level field, level both in fact and in name. Every Friday, unless there is a greater feast of prescribed solemnity, a celebrated exhibition of noble horses for sale takes place there. Earls, barons, knights, and many citizens who are in the city come to look or buy. It is pleasing to see ambling horses walking gently with a smooth rocking motion, their feet on the same side rising together sideways, as it were, from subordinate and lowered positions. Then there are horses more suitable for squires, moving more roughly but nevertheless briskly, which, as though from opposite positions, lift and set down their feet together. Then there are noble young colts, not yet accustomed to the bridle:

> They step more proudly and set down their supple legs.

Then there are packhorses with strong and vigorous limbs; then costly riding-horses, elegant in form and of fine stature, with pricked ears, high necks, and ample haunches. In their gait purchasers first observe the gentler pace, then the swifter motion [Col. 0106D], in which, as though from opposite positions, the forefeet are lifted from and set upon the ground together, and the hind feet likewise.

When the race of such hoof-beating horses is about to begin, and perhaps that of others similarly strong for carrying burdens and vigorous for running within their kind, a shout goes up and the common horses are ordered aside. The riders of the swift horses—three boys together, sometimes two by agreement, competing two against two—make ready. Skilled in commanding horses, they restrain the mouths of unbroken animals with curb-bits; they take particular care that one does not cut off another’s course. The horses likewise, in their own fashion, rise to the contest of that race. Their limbs tremble; impatient of delay, they do not know how to stand still. When the signal is given, they stretch out their bodies, seize upon the course, and rush onward with stubborn agility. The riders compete for praise and in hope of victory [Col. 0107A], applying spurs to the horses let loose, pressing them no less with whips, and urging them on with shouts.

You would think that everything was in motion, according to Heraclitus, and that Zeno’s opinion was wholly false—the opinion which says that it is impossible to move or to traverse a stadium.

In another part stand separately the livestock of country people, implements of agriculture, long-flanked pigs, cows with swollen udders,

> The great bodies of cattle, and wool-bearing sheep.

There stand mares fit for ploughs, carts, and two-horse teams. Some have bellies swollen with offspring; others are attended by the young they have borne—more playful foals, an inseparable following. To [Col. 0107B] this city merchants from every nation under heaven delight to bring maritime commerce.

> Arabia sends gold; the Sabaean spices and incense;  
> Scythia weapons; Babylon, rich in its palm forest, oil;  
> The Nile precious stones;  
> The Seres purple garments; the Gauls their wines.

Norwegians; Russians; vair, grey fur, sables. This city is, according to the testimony of the chronicles, considerably older than the city of Rome. For it was founded earlier by Brutus, descended from the same Trojan fathers, than Rome was by Remus and Romulus; hence even now they use the same ancient laws and common institutions. This city too, like Rome, is divided into regions; it has sheriffs annually in place of consuls; it has senatorial rank and lesser magistrates; sewers and aqueducts in its streets; appropriate places and separate courts for deliberative, demonstrative, and judicial kinds of cases; it has its assemblies on appointed days [Note: [Col. 0107D] “Markets,” Douce manuscript].

I do not think there is a city in which the customs are more commendable: in visiting churches, honouring God’s ordained ministers, observing feast-days, giving alms, receiving guests, confirming betrothals, contracting marriages, celebrating weddings, furnishing banquets, cheering guests, and likewise attending to funerals and burying bodies. London’s only plagues are the excessive drinking of fools and frequent fires. Moreover, nearly all the bishops, abbots, and magnates of England are, as it were, citizens and burgesses of the city of London; having there splendid residences to which they repair, where they incur lavish expenses, when summoned into the city for councils and famous assemblies by their lord the king or their metropolitan, or drawn there by their own affairs.

## Concerning Games

Let us proceed also to the games of the city, since it is not fitting for a city to be merely useful and serious unless it is also pleasant and delightful. Thus, on the seals of the supreme pontiffs, down to the time of the last Pope Leo, on one side of the bull there was engraved, by an impressed image, Peter the fisherman, with a key above him, as though extended to him from heaven by the hand of God; and around him the verse:

> You left your boat for me; receive the key.

On the other side the city was impressed, with this inscription: “Golden Rome.” Likewise, in praise of Augustus Caesar and Rome, it was said:

> It rains throughout the night; the spectacles return in the morning:  
> Caesar, you share sovereignty with Jupiter.

[Col. 0108D] In place of theatrical spectacles and stage plays, London has holier games: representations of the miracles performed by holy confessors, or representations of the sufferings by which the steadfastness of martyrs was made illustrious.

Furthermore, every year, on the day called Carnival, to begin with the games of London’s boys—for we have all been boys—each schoolboy brings to his master his fighting cock; and the whole morning is given over to the boys’ sport of watching the cockfights in their schools. After dinner all the young people of the city go out onto the suburban plain for the famous game of ball. The scholars of each school have their own ball; and almost every group of craftsmen in the city has one of its own. The older men, fathers, and wealthy citizens come on horseback to watch the contests of the young; and in their own fashion they become young again with the young. The stirring of their natural warmth seems to be awakened by contemplating so much activity and sharing in the pleasures of freer youth.

On every Sunday in Lent, after dinner, “a fresh troop of young men” rides out into the fields on war-horses, horses foremost in competition, each of which is:

> A horse fit to run in circles and trained to do so.

The lay sons of citizens burst forth from the gates in troops, furnished with lances and military shields. The younger ones, with forked staves from which the iron has been removed, stir up images of war, play at battles in the fields, and practise military contest. Very many courtiers also arrive, with the king stationed nearby, and young men from the households of bishops, earls, and barons, not yet girded with the belt of knighthood, for the sake of competition. The hope of victory inflames every one of them. The wild horses neigh; their limbs tremble; they chew their bits; impatient of delay, they do not know how to stand still. When at last the hoof of the charger snatches up its course, the young riders, divided into companies, press upon those ahead of them without overtaking them; others catch up with their companions, unhorse them, and fly past.

During the Easter holidays they play at something like naval battles. For a young man stands high in the stern of a little boat, swift from many oars and the rushing current of the river, and is to strike with his lance a shield firmly fastened to a tree in midstream. If he strikes the shield with his lance, breaks the lance, and remains unmoved, he has achieved his purpose and obtained his desire. But if he strikes forcefully while his lance remains whole, he is thrown into the flowing river, while the boat, driven by its momentum, passes onward. On either side of the shield, however, stand two stationary boats, containing many young men, so that they may rescue the striker if he is swallowed by the river, when he first appears after rising to the surface, or when he again bubbles up upon the top of the water. Upon the bridge, and in the rooms above the river, are people watching such things, ready for much laughter.

Throughout the summer holidays the young men at play are exercised in archery, running, jumping, wrestling, throwing stones, hurling missiles fitted with throwing-straps beyond the mark, and the small shields of combatants. The lyre of maidens leads their dances until the moon is impending, and the earth is beaten by free feet.

In winter, on nearly every holiday before dinner, either foaming boars fight for their heads, and boars armed with lightning-like tusks, destined for the salted meat-store, or fat horn-butting bulls, or huge bears, fight with dogs set upon them. When that great marsh which washes the northern walls of the city is frozen, dense companies of young men go out to play upon the ice. Some, gaining a swifter motion by running and arranging the distance of their feet, glide a great distance with one side of the body stretched out. Others make seats for themselves from the ice, like great millstones; many runners, holding one another’s hands, draw a single seated rider. In the great speed of this slippery motion, they sometimes slip with their feet and all fall forward.

Others are more skilled at playing on the ice. Each fastens to his feet, and binds beneath his ankles, bones—that is, the shin-bones of animals—and holds in his hands poles tipped with sharp iron. When they strike these against the ice, they are carried along with as much swiftness as a flying bird or a bolt from a crossbow. Sometimes, too, two men come from opposite directions at a great distance, by agreement. They rush together, raise their poles, and strike one another; one or both fall, not without bodily injury. Even after falling, the force of their motion carries them far away from one another; and wherever the ice receives the head, it scrapes and strips it entirely. [Col. 0110B] Very often the shin-bone of the fallen man, or his arm if he falls upon it, is broken. But an age greedy for glory and a youth eager for victory train themselves in mock battles so that they may behave more bravely in real ones.

Very many citizens delight in sporting with the birds of heaven—sparrowhawks, hawks, and the like—and with hunting dogs in the woods. The citizens have their right of hunting in Middlesex, Hertfordshire, and all Chiltern, and in Kent as far as the River Cray.

The Londoners, then called the Trinovantes, repelled Gaius Julius Caesar, who delighted in having no routes save those opened by bloodshed. Hence Lucan:

> Terrified, he showed his back to the Britons he had sought.

[Col. 0110C] The city of London produced some men who subjected to themselves many kingdoms and the Roman Empire, and many others whom valour raised to the gods as lords of the world, as had been promised to Brutus in Apollo’s oracle:

> Brutus, beyond the setting of the sun, past the Gallic kingdoms,  
> There is an island in the ocean, enclosed on every side by sea.  
> Seek it; for it shall be your lasting dwelling-place.  
> There a second Troy shall arise for your descendants.  
> From your stock kings shall be born; beneath them  
> The whole circle of the earth shall be subject.

And in Christian times it produced that noble emperor Constantine, son of Queen Helena, who gave the city of Rome and all imperial insignia to God, through blessed Peter and Sylvester, pope of Rome; to whom he also performed the office of groom, and rejoiced to be called no longer emperor but defender of the holy Roman Church. And lest the peace of the lord pope be disturbed by worldly tumult on account of his presence, he withdrew altogether from the city which he had bestowed upon the lord pope, and built for himself the city of Byzantium.

London, even in modern times, produced illustrious and magnificent rulers: the Empress Matilda, King Henry III, and blessed Thomas, archbishop and glorious martyr of Christ,

> … than whom no fairer man  
> The earth bore, nor one more bound by every virtue  
> Of the whole Latin world.

# Life and Passion of Saint Thomas, Archbishop and Martyr, Written by Master William, Son of Stephen

[Col. 0111]

[Col. 0111A] Before blessed Thomas came forth from the womb, the Lord knew and predestined him, and by a revelation declared to his mother what kind of man, and how great a man, he would become. For while she was still pregnant, she saw in a dream that she had the entire archiepiscopal Church of Canterbury in her womb. And when he had been brought into the light, the midwife lifted him in her hands and said: “I have raised an archbishop from the earth.”

While he lay in his cradle as a tiny infant, one night his mother dreamed that she spoke to his nurse, complaining that the child had no coverlet. The nurse replied: “On the contrary, lady, he has an excellent one.” His mother said: “Show it to me.” The nurse brought it and showed it to her; wishing, but being unable, to unfold it completely, she said: “It is so large that I cannot spread it all out in this chamber.” The mother said: “Go into the hall and unfold it there.” As the nurse strove to do this, she said: “But I cannot unfold it all even here.” In amazement the mother said: “Go out of the house into the open square of the market-place; surely you will be able to do so there.” But the nurse could not do so even there, and said: “The coverlet is so great that I cannot find its end. It seems to cover all England, which is too narrow for its unfolding, and it extends beyond it.”

Thus Thomas was born in lawful marriage, of honourable parents: his father was Gilbert, who at one time was also sheriff of London [Note: [Col. 0111D] “of London” omitted by the Spark edition]; and his mother Matilda. They were middle-class citizens of London, neither moneylenders nor merchants engaged in business, but living honourably from their rents.

[Col. 0111C] We know from this that some sign concerning him was divinely revealed to his father. His father had entrusted the boy for a time to Prior Robert, in the religious house of canons at Merton, to be brought up. One day the father came to see his son. When the boy had been brought before the prior and his father, the father fell prostrate and adored his son. Angered by this, the prior said to him: “Old man, are you mad? What are you doing? Do you fall at your son’s feet? He ought to render you the honour that you show him.” The father said to him privately: “My lord, I know what I am doing: this boy will be great before the Lord.”

## Concerning His Boyhood

Having passed the years of infancy, childhood, and puberty simply at his father’s house and in the city’s schools, Thomas, once he had become a young man, studied in Paris. On his return, [Col. 0111D] he was received into a share of responsibility for the public affairs of London, [Col. 0112A] becoming clerk and accountant to the sheriffs. There, conducting himself commendably, he learned the prudence of this world, by which afterward he knew well how to administer excellently and generously the common concerns of the English Church and the public business of the whole kingdom. As the saying goes:

> After barking at a deerskin in the hall,  
> The puppy serves in the woods.

## How He Came to the Court of Archbishop Theobald

As his years and merits advanced, he attached himself to Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury of blessed memory. Through two brothers from Bologna, Baldwin the archdeacon and Master Eustace, who were often guests of his father and familiar friends of the archbishop, he was introduced to the archbishop’s notice. This was done the more readily because the aforesaid Gilbert spoke with the lord archbishop about kinship and lineage: for the latter was Norman by birth, of knightly rank, from near the village of Tierrici, and close to Gilbert in age. Through the introduction, I say, of these men and of his father, the archbishop enrolled Thomas among his flock; afterward he found him strong and good. Thomas first came to the archbishop’s court at the village of Herges [Note: [Col. 0112D] Harwe, Spark edition], with only one esquire, Ralph of London.

That following night his hostess dreamed that he sat upon the roof of the church and covered the whole church with his garments hanging down. On the following day she told the dream to her husband and interpreted it to mean that one of those young men—for she did not yet know which was Thomas—would become lord of the church in that village.

## On the Nobility of the Clergy of the Court

In that archiepiscopal court there were great and exceptionally learned clerics. The archbishop afterward promoted many of them to bishoprics in England, and Roger of Pont l’Évêque to the archbishopric of York. In comparison with them Thomas was less learned; but the rule of conduct is certainly far loftier than learning. He therefore applied himself to morality and prudence, so that, though still inferior to them in learning, he might appear more distinguished and more welcome in conduct. Later, indeed, he became most learned.

## On the Persecution by Roger, Later Archbishop

That Roger, envying Thomas’s growing success and the first fruits of his favour with the archbishop, twice obtained from the archbishop [Col. 0112D] an order that Thomas should leave the court. [Col. 0113A] But Thomas, inexperienced and modest, conscious of no offence on his own part, on both occasions found refuge with Walter, the archbishop’s brother, then archdeacon of Canterbury and afterward bishop of Rochester. Walter too resided at the same court, and through his intervention Thomas was restored to the archbishop’s favour and his former position.

As soon as his ability was understood, the archbishop sent him several times to Rome on the business of the English Church. There, by the Lord’s favour, conducting himself wisely, he was received into the abundant favour of the supreme pontiffs and of the holy Roman Church.

## On His Appearance and Character

He was of a gentle and handsome countenance; tall in stature; with a prominent, slightly curved nose; vigorous in bodily senses; elegant in speech; subtle in intellect; great in spirit. Advancing already upon the higher path of virtues, he made himself lovable to all. He sympathized with the oppressed and poor; resisted the proud; devoted himself to advancing his companions; reverenced all good men; was generous and witty; wary of deceiving or being deceived; at once a prudent son of this world and one destined to be a son of light.

## How He First Increased His Income

His first income came as a gift from John, bishop of Worcester: namely, the church of St Mary Littoreal. Later, by the archbishop’s gift, he received the church of Otford. Afterward he held a prebend [Col. 0113C] in London, in the church of St Paul, and another at Lincoln.
