Then, having obtained from his lord the archbishop permission to cross the sea, he studied law for a year at Bologna and afterward at Auxerre. As time and his merits progressed, the archbishop ordained him deacon and made him archdeacon of the Church of Canterbury. After bishops and abbots, this is the first and most distinguished office in the English Church; and it was worth one hundred pounds of silver to him.

## How He Became Chancellor

After Henry II had been consecrated king of the English by the hand of the same archbishop, Thomas, through the archbishop’s recommendation and influence, and the advice and active support [Col. 0113D] of the noble Henry, bishop of Winchester, was made the king’s chancellor, as though preferred before all others: a capable man, contemplating great enterprises and experienced in many great affairs. He discharged the obligations of this service and honour with such diligence, to the praise of God, the honour of the king, and the benefit of the whole kingdom, that it is uncertain whether any man was more noble, magnificent, and useful to the king in the affairs of peace and war.

The dignity of the chancellor of England is this: that he is held second to the king in the kingdom; that with one part of the royal seal, whose custody also belongs to him, he seals his own commands; that the king’s chapel is under his direction [Col. 0114A] and care; that he receives and preserves vacant archbishoprics, bishoprics, abbeys, and baronies which fall into the king’s hand; that he is present at all the king’s councils, and even approaches without being summoned [Note: [Col. 0113D] “Intrudes himself,” Douce manuscript]; that everything of the royal seal-bearer and royal clerks is signed by his hand, and everything arranged by the chancellor’s counsel. Likewise, if the merits of his life, by God’s grace, support him, he does not die except as an archbishop or bishop, should he wish it. Hence the chancellorship is not bought.

## On Peace Restored to England after the Expulsion of the Flemings

During the time of King Stephen, a storm of war, fought out in godless hatreds, had enveloped the kingdom of England; the devastation of war had raged everywhere; in nearly every third village caves of robbers—that is, hostile castles—had been established; the native nobles had been disinherited; and foreign Flemings and *marticolae* (“worshippers of Mars,” that is, warlike men) [Note: [Col. 0114D] *Maricolae* (“sea-dwellers”), Spark edition] had occupied Kent and a large part of the kingdom. Through the duration of a war of nearly twenty years, all things had become so disordered that it seemed impossible to expel the Flemings and restore the kingdom to its former condition, ancient dignity, and peace, especially under a new king still a youth.

Yet, by God’s mercy and through the counsel of the chancellor, the clergy, and the good men of the kingdom who desired the good of peace, within the first three months of the king’s coronation William of Ypres, the violent oppressor of Kent, departed in tears. All the Flemings, gathering their baggage [Col. 0114C] and weapons, made for the sea. Castles throughout England fell, except the ancient towers and towns maintained for preserving peace. The crown of England was restored in its completeness when its defections had been recalled; paternal rights were restored to the disinherited; robbers emerged from the hiding-places of forests into the villages, and, rejoicing in the common peace which held them fast, forged swords into ploughshares and lances into sickles. Frightened by the gallows, thieves likewise became cultivators of the soil or practitioners of other mechanical arts. Peace was everywhere; shields are brought in, sheepfolds carried out. Merchants go safely forth from cities and castles to fairs, and Jews to recover debts from their debtors.

Through the energy and counsel of this chancellor, aided by God’s ordained ministers, earls, and barons, that noble [Col. 0114D] kingdom of England was renewed like a new spring. The holy Church was honoured; a vacant bishopric or abbey was bestowed upon a worthy person without simony. The king, by the favour of the King of kings, prospered in all his affairs. The kingdom of England was enriched; a horn of plenty filled it to the full. The hills were cultivated; the valleys abounded in grain, the pastures in sheep, and the sheepfolds in bleating flocks.

Chancellor Thomas caused the seat of government, the palace of London, formerly almost a ruin, to be repaired. He completed so great a work with marvellous speed between a certain Easter and Pentecost, with so many carpenters and other workmen labouring with such energetic movement and noise that scarcely [Col. 0115A] could one man hear another speaking beside him.

The chancellor enjoyed the highest favour among the clergy, knighthood, and people of the kingdom. He could have obtained all vacant parish churches in villages and castles, for no patron would have dared to refuse him if he had asked. Yet he so overcame ambition through greatness of spirit that he disdained to forestall poor priests and clerics in seeking those churches. Being magnanimous, he sought rather great things: namely, the provostship of Beverley; the grant of the prebends of Hastings from the earl of Eu; the Tower of London with the service of its attached knights; the castellany of Eye with the honour of one hundred and forty knights; and Berkhamsted Castle.

[Col. 0115B] He often amused himself, though casually and without devoted application, with birds of heaven—hawks and falcons—and hunting dogs, and with the two-coloured pieces of the board-game:

> He played the battles of treacherous thieves.

## On the Honour and Table of the Chancellor’s Household

The chancellor’s house and table were open to all needy persons of whatever rank who came to the royal court, provided that they either were respectable or seemed to be so. He scarcely ate on any day without earls and barons whom he himself invited. He ordered that every day his hall should be strewn with fresh straw or hay in winter, and fresh rushes or green foliage in summer, so that the clean and cheerful floor might receive the multitude of knights whom the benches could not hold, [Col. 0115C] lest their costly clothes or fine shirts should take a stain from the dirt of the floor.

His house shone with gold and silver vessels and abounded in precious dishes and drinks, so that if some rare food or drink was recommended, no price ought to deter his purchasers from obtaining it. Yet he was extremely temperate in these matters, so that abundant alms might be gathered from a rich table. And, as I heard from Robert, a venerable canon of Merton and his confessor, no lust defiled him from the time he became chancellor. On this matter even the king himself laid daily and nightly snares for him. But, like a God-fearing man predestined to purity of the flesh, he kept his loins girded. Indeed, a wise man occupied with governing the kingdom and attending to so many public and private cares was less often tempted by such enticements. For:

> Take away leisure, and the bows of desire are destroyed.

The chancellor, a chaste man and hater of foulness and unchastity, cast out from his household and friendship a cleric of noble family, Richard of Ambli, because he had seduced and slept with the wife of one of his companions while the latter was far away overseas, having persuaded her that her husband had died. He had Richard imprisoned in the Tower of London and kept long afflicted in fetters.

## How He Brought Up the Sons of Nobles

[Col. 0116A]

The magnates of England and of neighbouring kingdoms sent their sons to serve the chancellor. He trained them in honourable upbringing and learning; once they had received the belt of knighthood, he sent them back with honour to their fathers and kinsmen, retaining some. The king himself, his lord, entrusted his own son, heir to the kingdom, to him to be brought up. The chancellor kept him with himself, as his rank required, together with many sons of nobles of his own age, all their appropriate attendants, teachers, and personal servants.

Yet amid all this splendour of worldly honours, he often received secret discipline, exposing his back to the lash: when near London, from Ralph, prior of Holy Trinity; and when near Canterbury, from Thomas, priest of St Martin. He was humble with the humble, fierce and forceful toward the proud; as though this were innate to him:

> To spare the subjected and to subdue the proud.

Countless nobles and knights performed homage to the chancellor, and he received them without prejudice to the fealty due to his lord the king; afterward he protected them further as men under his patronage.

When he was about to cross the sea, he sometimes had six or more ships sailing in his service, and allowed no one who wished to cross to be left behind. Upon landing, he rewarded his pilots and sailors according to their desire. Hardly a day passed without his giving some great gift: horses, birds, clothing, [Col. 0116C] gold or silver household goods, or money. For thus it is written: some give away what is their own and always abound; others seize what belongs to others,

> And there is always want in the diminished store.

The chancellor possessed so great a grace in giving that he was considered the love and delight of the whole Latin world. With witty discernment, he adopted each person according to his age.

By the prompting of almighty God and at the chancellor’s persuasion, the lord king did not retain vacant bishoprics and abbeys for long, so that the patrimonies of the Crucified might enrich his treasury—which afterward he did; may this be far from him—but without great delay bestowed them upon worthy persons, and according to God’s will.

Again, at the chancellor’s counsel, the lord king received into favour and familiarity the canonical church of Merton, where those dwelling there earn God’s reward. He completed at his own expense the church which he had taken over from the presbytery [Note: [Col. 0115D] “Confirmed,” Spark edition], and endowed it with perpetual revenues. There, on occasion, he observed with the religious community three-day vigils of penitence before Easter Day. After the night office called Tenebrae, though it is an office of light, on Good Friday until the ninth hour, he visited the churches of neighbouring villages for prayer, travelling on foot, concealed in a cloak, attended by one companion only, who guided him along the roads.

[Col. 0117A] Likewise, at Chancellor Thomas’s suggestion, the king recalled English poor men living in France whom public report praised as good men, whether monks in religious life or masters in study; and established such persons in his kingdom: for example, Master Robert of Melun in the episcopal church of Hereford, and William, monk of St Martin-in-the-Fields, in Ramsey Abbey.

Thus, because of the gifts of his virtues, his greatness of spirit, and the marks of merit which adhered to his character, the chancellor was most welcome to the king, clergy, knighthood, and people. When serious business had been dealt with, the king and he played together like boys of the same age, in hall, in church, in assembly, and on horseback.

One day they were riding together in a London street. An ugly winter shrieked. From afar the king saw an old poor man coming, dressed in worn and thin clothing, and said to the chancellor: “Do you see that man?” The chancellor said: “I see him.” The king said: “How poor, how weak, how naked he is! Would it not be a great alms-deed to give him a thick and warm cloak?” The chancellor replied: “Indeed it would be great; and, king, you ought to have the heart and eye for such a deed.”

Meanwhile the poor man came near. The king halted, and the chancellor with him. The king gently addressed the poor man and asked whether he would like a good cloak. Not knowing who they were, the poor man thought that they were joking, not acting seriously. The king said to the chancellor: “You shall indeed perform this great alms-deed.” Then, laying hands upon its hood, the king tried to take from the chancellor the new and excellent scarlet-and-grey-fur cloak which he wore, while the chancellor strove to retain it. A great commotion and uproar arose. The wealthy men and knights who followed them, astonished, hurried to discover the cause of so sudden a struggle between them. No one spoke, for each was intent on using his hands, so that they seemed at times almost ready to fall. After resisting for a while, the chancellor allowed the king to prevail, remove the cloak as he bent down, and give it to the poor man.

Then for the first time the king told his companions what had happened. There was great laughter from everyone; some offered the chancellor their own cloaks and mantles. The old poor man departed with the chancellor’s cloak, unexpectedly made rich, rejoicing and giving thanks to God.

Several times the king ate at the chancellor’s house, partly for amusement and partly to see for himself what was said about his household and table. The king sometimes came at full gallop into the chancellor’s residence while he sat at table; sometimes he came with an arrow in his hand, returning from the hunt or going to the wood; sometimes he drank and then departed after seeing the chancellor; sometimes, leaping over the table, he sat beside him and ate. Never were any two other men more united and friendly in Christian times.

The chancellor was once seized by a grave illness at Rouen, at Saint Gervais. Two kings came together to visit him: the king of the French and the king of the English, his lord. At last, being on the road to recovery and regaining strength, he one day sat down to play chess, dressed in a cloak with sleeves. Aschetin, prior of Leicester, came in to visit him, having arrived from the king’s court, which was then in Gascony. Speaking freely to him with the boldness of intimacy, he said: “What is this—that you wear a cloak with sleeves? Such clothing belongs rather to men who carry falcons. But you are an ecclesiastical person, singular in one respect but multiple in dignities: archdeacon of Canterbury, dean of Hastings, provost of Beverley, canon here and there, and also administrator of the archbishopric. And, as rumour is frequent at court, you will be archbishop.”

Among other things, the chancellor replied to this remark: “Indeed, I know three such poor priests in England, each of whose promotion to the archbishopric I would prefer to my own. For if perhaps I were promoted, knowing my lord the king as I do [Col. 0118B] inside and out, I should necessarily either lose his favour or—God forbid—put aside the service of the Lord God.” And so it afterward happened.

The king of England customarily has his own ship for crossing the sea. The chancellor caused not one ship alone but three excellent ships to be made for him at once, furnished with every necessity so that nothing was lacking; and he gave them to his lord the king as a gift.

Messengers of the king of Norway once came to England. When he heard of it, the chancellor sent men to meet them, to conduct them to the court of the lord king and provide them, in the chancellor’s name, with their necessary expenses.

Nicholas, archdeacon of London, once incurred the king’s displeasure. Therefore his house, after his household had been expelled, was sealed by royal command and put up for sale for the king. The good chancellor did not rest until he had reconciled the archdeacon to the king that same day and obtained his restoration to his property.

In the same way he once rendered a service to the bishop of Le Mans and to Gilo, archdeacon of Rouen. For during the schism of the Roman Church, Octavian and Emperor Frederick, who supported him, stood on one side; Pope Alexander, the catholic pope, on the other. At the counsel of his cardinals, both parties had sent their envoys to the king of France and the king of England, who was then overseas. When those kings had summoned many bishops and leading men of their kingdoms and were assembled at Neufmarché to hear those envoys and their arguments and deliberate upon the merits of the election and which obedience they should embrace, Alexander’s election finally pleased them, since it seemed to them, not without reason, more just and holier. Archbishop Hugh of Rouen had approved it, and through his nephew and archdeacon Gilo had directed his suffragans to receive it.

The king was violently disturbed and ordered the archdeacon’s houses to be pulled down, because he was afraid openly to rage against the archbishop himself, an elderly and magnanimous man. Then the chancellor humbly said to the lord king: “My lord king, that house which you order to be demolished belongs to Archdeacon Gilo, but it is my lodging.” By this and fitting words of persuasion, he at length soothed and persuaded the king, obtaining peace for the archdeacon [Col. 0119A] together with the preservation of his house.

On the following day the king heard that the bishop of Le Mans had received Pope Alexander in imitation of the lord of Rouen and had promised his envoys that he would maintain obedience to the pope. The king was angry that he had done this without his command, permission, and judgment. The king’s marshals, understanding his agitation or perhaps his command, went to the bishop’s lodgings, cut the harness-straps [*chamis*, reading uncertain], drove out the horses, carried the bishop’s baggage into the streets, and deprived him of his lodging. The bishop was compelled shamefully to withdraw from the court. The king had writs drawn up ordering the demolition of the bishop’s houses at Le Mans. Holding the sealed writs in his hand and displaying them publicly, the king said to those standing by: “The men of Le Mans will certainly hear a report concerning their bishop.”

All the clergy present at the court of the two kings grieved, and the chancellor above all. But, understanding that it was useless to address and petition the king in such anger, he ordered the king’s couriers, bearers of those letters, not to hurry. Though they could reach Le Mans in a journey of two days, they were not to arrive before the fourth day; and they obeyed.

On the following day the chancellor persuaded bishops to go to the lord king and intercede for the bishop of Le Mans. Some went and found the king inexorable; others went at the chancellor’s urging and suffered rebuff. At last the chancellor himself approached the king and pleaded for the bishop; and he did likewise the next day. Compelled by the chancellor’s persistence, the king finally consented, thinking that by then the bishop’s house would have been entirely or largely demolished.

The chancellor immediately sent the king’s letters granting peace to the bishop to the prefect of Le Mans through his own messenger, and charged him, as a matter of loyalty to their friendship, not to let his foot rest by day or night until he reached Le Mans. He reached Le Mans without interruption, with the bishop’s houses untouched, on the same day as the earlier envoys of the lord king, who had nevertheless arrived first and displayed the king’s letters ordering the demolition of the bishop’s houses. The king afterward rejoiced that he had been outwitted by this good deception of the chancellor, just as is read in Timaeus concerning that most salutary fraud of the married pair’s lot.

The chancellor had fifty-two clerics in his service. Many of them were in his retinue; they administered vacant bishoprics and abbeys, or his own ecclesiastical honours.

[Col. 0119D] The king of England once deliberated with the chancellor and certain other magnates of his kingdom about seeking from the king of France his daughter Margaret in marriage for his own son Henry. The counsel pleased them. For this is a great alliance of kings and great men:

> This matter both unites friends and preserves them once united.

Who was to be sent to make so great a request to so great a prince, if not the chancellor? He was chosen, and he agreed. Therefore the chancellor, considering the affair, the persons involved, and his office [Col. 0120A], and measuring himself against so great an undertaking, according to the poetic saying,

> Measure what you dare,

made his preparations as for a wedding.

He who is sent to arrange a future marriage. He prepares to display and lavishly expend the wealth of English magnificence, so that in every person and in every respect the person of the sender may be honoured in the envoy, and that of the envoy in himself. He had with him about two hundred mounted members of his household—knights, clerics, stewards, servants, squires, sons of noblemen in his service—all equipped with arms. [Note: [Col. 0119D] “Horses handsome in appearance and strong for carrying; shields and weapons were also borne and drawn by the right hands of his knights,” adds the Douce manuscript.] All these men, and their entire retinue, shone in new festive apparel, each according to his station. He also had twenty-four changes of clothing [Note: [Col. 0120D] “Wool repeatedly dyed with Tyrian purple, and several entirely silken garments,” added by the Douce manuscript], almost all intended as gifts and to be left overseas; and every refinement of vair, grey fur, and foreign pelts, as well as cloaks and tapestries, with which the chamber and bed of the bishop received as a guest were adorned.

He had with him dogs and birds of every kind used by kings and wealthy persons. In his company he had eight carriages; each was drawn by five horses, like war-horses in size and strength. Each horse had assigned to it a sturdy young man, girt in a new tunic, walking beside the carriage; and each carriage had its own post-horse and keeper. Two carriages carried beer alone, brewed in a decoction of water from the fatness of grain, in iron-bound casks, to be given to the French, who marvelled at this kind of liquid concoction: a drink indeed wholesome, clear, wine-coloured, and of a better flavour. The chancellor’s chapel had [Col. 0120C] its own carriage, its own chamber, its own tent, and its own kitchen. Other carriages carried some provisions of food and drink; others, hangings, tapestries, sacks containing night-clothes, baggage, and impedimenta.

He had twelve packhorses. Eight chests of the chancellor contained household plate—namely gold and silver articles: small vessels, bowls, basins, goblets, cups, little pitchers, wash-basins, salt-cellars, spoons, knives, and dishes. Other trunks and panniers of the chancellor contained money, a large quantity of coin sufficient for his daily expenses and gifts, as well as his clothes, several books, and such things. One packhorse, preceding the others, bore the sacred vessels and altar ornaments and books of the chapel. Each packhorse had its own groom, furnished as and in the manner appropriate. Every carriage [Col. 0120D] also had a dog tethered either above or below it—large, strong, and formidable, seeming capable of mastering a bear or lion. Moreover, upon every packhorse there was either a long-tailed monkey, or

a monkey, an imitator of the human face.

When they entered French towns and castles, first came on foot the pages,

born, as it seemed, to consume crops—about two hundred and fifty—walking in groups of six or ten, or more together, singing something in their own language [Col. 0121A] according to the custom of their country. At some interval followed coupled dogs, greyhounds in their leashes and loose slips—or whatever other names they deserve—with their runners and attendants. Soon afterward those iron-bound carriages rumbled over the stone streets, covered with large stitched animal hides. At a short distance followed the packhorses, their grooms riding with knees set upon the packhorses’ haunches. Some Frenchmen, coming out of their houses at such a noise, asked who was coming and whose household it was. They were told that the chancellor of the king of England was coming, sent to the lord king of France. The French said: “Wonderful indeed is the king of England, whose chancellor proceeds in such fashion and with such magnificence.”

After a further interval behind the packhorses followed squires [Col. 0121B] carrying the knights’ shields and leading their war-horses; then other squires; next young men; then those carrying birds; afterward stewards, masters, and servants of the chancellor’s household; then knights and clerics, all riding two by two; and finally the chancellor, with some of his household around him.

Upon arriving overseas, the chancellor immediately sent word beforehand to the lord king of France that he was coming to him. He came through the castle of Mantes. The king of France replied that he should meet him at Paris, and named the day. The king, wishing to provide for the chancellor—as it is both the nobility and custom of French kings to provide for every mortal who comes to the French court while he remains there—had issued an edict at Paris prohibiting anyone from selling anything to the chancellor [Col. 0121C] or to his buyers. When this became known beforehand, the chancellor sent his men ahead to the neighbouring markets—at Limas, Corbeil, Pontoise, and Saint-Denis—to purchase for him bread, meat, fish, wine, and provisions in abundance, with names and dress altered and concealed.

When he entered Paris, intending to lodge in the house of the Temple, his men met him and said that he would find the lodging furnished with every good thing for a stay of three days and for the daily maintenance of a thousand men. Certainly, in the account of King Solomon’s wealth one reads how much animal flesh sufficed for his daily expenses; and certainly, on one day a single dish of eels for the chancellor was bought for one hundred sterling shillings. This was so well known throughout the country [Col. 0121D] that for a long time it was on many lips as a proverb. Of his other dishes and expenditures I say nothing. From this one instance it may be understood that the chancellor’s table was lavish and ample.

How the lord king of France and those French nobles honoured him; how he in turn honoured them; and, besides, with what kindness he received the Parisian scholars and masters of the schools, and the citizens who were creditors of English scholars—I cannot adequately tell. It is recorded of Hannibal that, after Hasdrubal had been killed, he sent messengers to Rome, saying to them: “Go, and fill every mortal with money.” Perhaps the chancellor had read and attended to the same saying: he filled with gifts every noble French baron, [Col. 0122A] knight, servant of the king or queen of the king of France, masters of the schools, scholars, and the more distinguished citizens. He gave away all his gold and silver vessels and every change of clothing: to one a cloak, to another a grey cape, to another a fur garment, to another a palfrey, to another a war-horse. What more need be said? He won the favour of every man beyond all others.

He discharged his embassy successfully; he attained his purpose; what he asked was granted him. On his return he captured Guy de la Val, an assailant of the king of England and a plunderer of the country and public highway, and imprisoned him in chains at the castle of Neaufles. Such was Chancellor Thomas in his devotion to and time of peace. What shall I say of him when occupied in military affairs?

### How the chancellor served the king in his war of Toulouse

[Col. 0122B]

In the army and siege of Toulouse, when all England, Normandy, Aquitaine, Anjou, Brittany, and Scotland sent military forces and martial strength to support the king of England, the chancellor had from his own household a picked force of seven hundred knights. Indeed, had his counsel been obeyed, they would have attacked and captured the city of Toulouse and the king of France, who had involved himself in support of his sister, Countess Constance, and had done so rashly, without an army or strong force; so great was the army of the king of England. But the king, restrained by vain scruple and reverence and by the counsel of others, refused to fall upon a city in which was his lord, the king of France. The chancellor argued to the contrary [Col. 0122C] that the king of France had there laid aside the person of a lord, since beyond the agreements [Note: [Col. 0121D] *Pacta*, “agreements,” omitted in Spark’s edition.] made he had made himself his enemy.

Not long afterward the army of the king of France, summoned and assembled, entered the city; and the king of England, with the king of Scotland and his whole army, returned frustrated in desire and ineffective in purpose. Yet first he had captured the city of Cahors and many castles in the neighbourhood of Toulouse belonging to the count of Toulouse and his dependants, or which the count of Toulouse had previously taken from supporters of the king of England. To hold all these places, after the king of England’s return, when all the counts refused, the chancellor alone remained with his household and with Henry of Essex alone, the king’s constable and baron. Later, he himself, wearing breastplate and [Col. 0122D] helmet, captured with his men in strong force three most heavily fortified castles that seemed impregnable. He also crossed the Garonne with a military force against the enemy; and, after the whole province had been confirmed in the king’s obedience, he returned favoured and honoured.

### Likewise, how he conducted himself in the war with the French

Later, in the war between the king of France and his lord the king of England, in the March on the common frontier of their lands between Gisors, Trie, and Courcelles, the chancellor had, in addition to the seven hundred horsemen of his own household, another twelve hundred mercenary knights and four thousand servants for forty days. To each knight [Col. 0123A] there were given each day three shillings of that currency for the maintenance of horses and squires; and all the knights ate at the chancellor’s table.

Although he himself was a cleric, he engaged in combat with the valiant French knight Enguerrand de Trie. Charging from the opposite side, armed, with spur-driven horse, lowered lance, and horse at full speed, he threw him from his horse and gained his war-horse. Throughout the army of the king of England the chancellor’s knights were always the first; they always dared greater things and always performed brilliantly, with him teaching, leading, and encouraging them. At his command they sounded the advance and sounded the retreat on their curved trumpets, which, though his own within his army, were familiar to the whole army on both sides. Thus he himself, the enemy and conqueror of the king of France, and the ravager of that king’s land by fire and sword, [Col. 0123B] came into great favour with the king of France and the magnates of all France, aided by the merits of his outstanding loyalty and his very well-known nobility. In due time the king afterward showed him that favour. For courage is praised even in an enemy.

### On the election of the chancellor as archbishop

Meanwhile Archbishop Theobald closed his final day. The king of England therefore resolved to promote his chancellor to the archbishopric, in view of the merits of the man, trusting that, as chancellor, he had acted, so as archbishop he would obey the king’s pleasure and command. Thus, with the king’s wish preceding and known to all the clergy of England—which alone detracted from the merits of that election [Note: [Col. 0123D] The words “which alone … that election” are omitted in Spark’s edition]—the chancellor, archdeacon of Canterbury, was unanimously elected archbishop of that church [Col. 0123C].

Gilbert of Hereford alone, later transferred to London, a monk in habit who tasted neither wine nor meat, opposed it as far as he could. As was thought, he did not zealously oppose the election itself, but the person elected; for he was believed to be aspiring and working on his own behalf. Later he said that the king had done a remarkable thing in making an archbishop out of a secular man and a certain knight.

In the year of grace 1162, on the octave day of Pentecost, the feast-day of the church of Canterbury, namely the day of Holy Trinity, all the suffragan bishops having assembled in that metropolitan church, blessed Thomas, free, released, and at peace from every secular claim, was restored and presented to the Church of Canterbury by Henry, son and heir of King Henry II, and by Richard de Lucy and the other magnates of England who were present on behalf [Col. 0123D] of the king, then overseas. By the hand of Henry, venerable bishop of Winchester, he was ordained archbishop. Pope Alexander III sent him the pallium through his clerk John of Salisbury.

Devoutly, bowed down and barefoot, the archbishop went to receive that breast-and-shoulder band. For that insignia, peculiar to an archbishop, is a great mystery. The pallium was instituted in place of the golden plate on which, under the Law, the high priest bore on his forehead the inscribed four-letter Name of the Lord, the Tetragrammaton. The two hanging strips are the two laws, signifying Christ’s Passion; the little pins are the nails by which Christ’s body is fastened to the cross. At his ordination, flooded with the visible and invisible anointing of God’s mercy, he put off the secular man and put on Jesus Christ. He emptied himself of what had belonged to the secular chancellor, striving after what belongs to a good archbishop.

Accordingly, he watched over his soul with every vigilance. His words were serious, for the edification of his hearers; his works were those of mercy and piety; his judgments, of justice and equity. With a very rough hair-shirt reaching to his knees and alive with worms, he subdued his flesh by scant food and by his customary drink of water in which fennel had been boiled. Yet he tasted wine first [Col. 0124B] and gave it to those seated with him; and he ate something of the meats set before him, but sustained himself with bread. Yet all things are clean to the clean; and guilt lies not in food but in appetite. He frequently exposed his bare back to disciplinary scourging. Immediately above the hair-shirt he wore a monk’s habit, because he was abbot of the monks of Canterbury; on the outside, a canonical habit, to conform himself to the clerics. Yet he wore the stole, Christ’s sweet yoke, about his neck by day and night.

Outwardly his appearance resembled that of the multitude; inwardly everything was different. He imitated Saint Sebastian and Saint Cecilia: Sebastian bore beneath the concealment of Christ’s cloak the hidden identity of Christ’s soldier; Cecilia, subduing her flesh with haircloth, was outwardly covered with golden garments. In food and clothing he endeavoured to be more religious than he appeared. Intent upon prayer, he devoted himself to reconciling and in some manner uniting his created spirit with the Creator Spirit. As a kind of interpreter between God and men, he commended men to God by prayer and God to men by preaching. Devoted to sacred reading, he had his instructor in the divine page. Sometimes after dinner he conversed with his companions, listening to and questioning them. His table-companions were religious men and honourable, highly learned clerics. His household too was chosen, and devoted to receiving and reverencing good men. He was lavish in giving alms, sending to hospitals and poor colleges sometimes four or five marks, sometimes grain and meat.

For whereas Theobald, his predecessor [Col. 0124D] of pious memory, customarily doubled the fixed alms established by his predecessors, Thomas, in religious emulation, judged that even Theobald’s double ought itself to be doubled. To maintain this pious work, he consecrated tithes of everything he received under whatever title. In a more private chamber, daily, with bended knees, he washed the feet of thirteen poor men in memory of Christ; after fully feeding each of them, he gave each four silver coins. If on occasion—though rarely—he was prevented from doing this in person, he took the greatest care that it be done through a deputy. When alone, he was moved almost miraculously to tears; [Col. 0125A] and he performed the office at the altar as though he saw the Lord’s Passion being enacted bodily and present before him. He handled the divine sacraments with the utmost reverence, so that the very touching of them instructed the faith and conduct of those who watched.

Furthermore, he fed vagrants and needy persons in his house, and clothed many against the winter. At Canterbury he generally withdrew into the cloister and sat, like one of the monks sitting there, studying some useful book. Then he went to visit sick monks, that he might hear and fulfill their wishes. He was a comforter of the oppressed, a husband to widows, and a helper of orphans. He was also humble and approachable toward the gentle, stern toward those who exalted themselves. Against the injustice and insolence of the powerful he stood firm like a tower [Col. 0125B] built toward Damascus; neither the prayers nor letters of the king himself could benefit anyone with him unless justice were on that person’s side.

He was now especially filled with honourable shame, he who long before, even as chancellor, had not exceeded the bounds of chastity. He was in a sense another Moses, frequently entering and leaving the Lord’s tabernacle: entering at the fitting time for contemplation of God, leaving for pious action toward his neighbours. Like another Jacob, now he joined to himself fruitful Leah; now he clung to the embraces of fairer Rachel. He was like one of God’s angels, who upon the ladder whose summit touched heaven now descended to relieve human needs and now ascended to behold divine majesty and heavenly brightness. [Col. 0125C] Detached from earthly and transient things, he applied himself with all his might to heavenly ones.

He devoted himself to the virtues that bless both the present life and earn eternal life. First among them was queenly reason, which, as a mistress commands maidservants, so commands desires and the disordered movements of the soul. Thus, under reason’s guidance, he advanced in virtue, which, loving itself, rejects its opposites; arising from itself, it returns again to itself, and, embracing all that is its own, seeks nothing elsewhere. He possessed the four forms of virtue: prudence, which made him discerning in knowledge of things, assessment of persons, place, and time, avoidance of evils, and choice of things to be desired; justice, by which he strove to preserve for God and for every person what was each one’s own; courage, [Col. 0125D] which, defending him amid adversity, protected him from distress at present evils and fear of future ones; and temperance, which, allowing him to do nothing excessive in prosperity, recalled him from every sensual desire and from coveting temporal things, and did not allow him to exult with insolent joy. This is the chariot [Note: [Col. 0125D] Spark’s edition reads “charioteer.”] of Amminadab; this is the first tetrachord; this is the highest harmony in a human being. This is that sweet and pleasing concord in a human being which fills even God’s ears and leads one into the blessedness of life: the complete possession of goods, all hidden evils being excluded.

Endowed with this blessedness of life, and made blessed, [Col. 0126A] Archbishop Thomas took care to do everything steadfastly, splendidly, seriously, and honourably; to refer all things to the judgment of wisdom; to govern himself; to stand by the judgments of wisdom rather than those of the people; not to fear Fortune’s snares; to bear himself fenced, fortified, and unconquerable against adversity; to believe that he had been born not for himself but for all who needed his assistance, above all for his church, whose governance he had undertaken; to contemplate divine things on earth; to imitate Jesus Christ, born and sent for sufferings; truly to love him and keep his commandments; and to seek the salvation of his own soul and of the souls entrusted to him.

Hence it came about that he obtained favour with God and glory among men—solid indeed and openly expressed—in the unanimous praise of good men, whose uncorrupted voice judged him well. [Col. 0126B] Such praise answers virtue as an echo answers a voice, or an image its pattern. Since glory is the companion of right living, it is neither to be sought by good men nor rejected by them, but attributed to God. For the Apostle says: “For even if I should wish to boast, I should not be foolish; for I shall speak the truth.” Yet Thomas feared and despised this glory, lest pride perhaps creep in, mindful of the written warning that, however righteous a man may be, he is never secure.

There is another, false and empty glory, sought by proud and vain men, the rich and hypocrites: a shadowy image of glory, beneath which lies no substantial virtue worthy of praise, but which is a resemblance appearing in outward form and not existing in reality. And just as good men fear the glory of true praise, so evil men seek false glory; or even when they have done something rightly, by seeking from it praise or reward, they thereby lose both its name and its merit.

Glorious Archbishop Thomas, contrary to the expectation of the king and of all men, so abandoned the world, so suddenly was transformed by the transformation that is the right hand of the Most High, that all marvelled.

### On the devil’s temptation effected through evil and unjust men

The ancient enemy envied such a pillar raised in the Church of the Lord, such a lamp kindled upon God’s lampstand. “An enemy has sown tares.” First he took away the king’s goodwill toward him, as though the king ought to bear it indignantly that the man whom he had first made chancellor and then archbishop now withdrew himself from the king’s service and contradicted him in many matters. Courtiers seeking to please the king and to tickle his itching ears disparaged the archbishop and hated him without cause.

Moreover, certain courtiers, clerics of the king, feared rather that they would be deprived, under the archbishop’s jurisdiction, of some churches which they had wrongly acquired than that they would be instituted in others or advanced in his time to greater benefices. Both personally and through certain bishops, they tried to incite and stir up the king and his supporters against the archbishop. Nothing could now be said or done by him [Col. 0127A] which the malice of unhappy men did not distort. Indeed, they persuaded the king that, if the archbishop’s authority advanced, royal dignity would undoubtedly perish; and that unless he made provision for himself and his heirs, the man chosen by the clergy would ultimately become king and would reign as long as it pleased the archbishop.

Certainly, light is hostile to those suffering from ophthalmia or bleary eyes; and the just man was grievous for the unjust to behold, and opposed to their works. He sought to please God alone, and no one except in God; they rather laid snares for the ears of the earthly king. The friend of God is made an enemy of the world. The ill-tempered persecute the well-behaved [*moratum*; Spark’s edition: *morigeratum*].

This was the first cause of the archbishop’s persecution. [Col. 0127B] Very many bishops were added to the king and the royal party in this dissension, from fear of losing the land and earthly goods they possessed. The archbishop was deprived of their counsel and assistance. The king’s indignation, and that of the kingdom’s soldiery, was further aroused because he intended to recover from Roger, count of Clare, Tonbridge Castle and the whole honour, long alienated from the Church of Canterbury. For according to the decrees, predecessors and stewards of the Church were allowed to cultivate and increase its estates, not diminish or alienate them. Nearly all the nobles of England were connected by kinship to that count of Clare, who had as his wife the most beautiful sister in the whole kingdom, whom the king had once desired. Yet the archbishop had previously obtained from the king leave—first requested—to recover the estates of the Church of Canterbury which had been wrongly alienated by his predecessors or occupied by laymen.

Likewise, the archbishop had granted the church of Eynsford to a certain cleric, Laurence. For it belongs to him to grant vacant churches in the villages both of his barons and of the monks of Canterbury. William of Eynsford, lord of the village, protested and expelled Laurence’s men; the archbishop excommunicated him. The king immediately wrote to the archbishop that he should absolve him. The archbishop replied that it was no more the king’s right to order that anyone be absolved than that anyone be excommunicated. The king maintained that it belonged to his royal dignity that no one holding from him in chief should be excommunicated without consulting him. At last, in order to pacify the king, who was now becoming angry with him [Col. 0127D] and spoke with him only through messengers, the archbishop absolved William. And the king said of him at Windsor: “Now I do not thank him for it.”

Moreover, long before, namely in the time of Archbishop Theobald, the king had conceived certain measures generally against the clergy of England, provoked by the insolence of certain clerics.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] “From *Unde aliquando* (‘Hence at one time’) down to *sit* (‘may be’), col. 130, line 33, is omitted by the Douce manuscript; but it has the passage elsewhere, where it occurs under the title *summa causae* (‘summary of the case’). Another manuscript also has it [Col. 0128D]—Lambeth no. 138, fol. 205—which I have inspected only lightly. Yet these passages undoubtedly interrupt the sense and are badly placed in William’s book.”]

Accordingly, at one time in council the lord king began to propose some rather severe measures. First he complained of the violence of archdeacons: that they turned the offences of others into their own profit, that they exacted payments for sins.

[Col. 0128A] “And from these they carry their extravagance beyond measure, although they do not inflict the correction due upon sinners. I therefore wish that archdeacons should summon no one, however notorious, concerning any crime, without the knowledge of my official.” Then immediately turning his speech to another matter, he said: “I devise thoughts of peace and am greatly moved for the good of peace, which in my kingdom is disturbed by the wickedness of clerics, who commit robberies, thefts, and very often homicides. I therefore ask and require that, with the consent of you, lord of Canterbury, and of your fellow bishops, clerics caught, convicted, or confessing in crimes shall immediately be deposed from office and at once handed over to the officers of my court, so that, stripped of every defence of the Church, they may be corporally punished. I also ask and require that, at that deposition from office, you consent that one of my officials shall be present, so that he may immediately seize the deposed cleric, lest any opportunity be given him to escape corporal punishment.”

To this the lord of Canterbury, unable to obtain even until morning a postponement of his answer to this request, withdrew aside with his bishops. Arguments were immediately put forward on both sides. The bishops said that, according to secular laws, clerics deposed from office ought to be handed over to the court and, after spiritual punishment, punished bodily; because the more worthy they are in privilege, the worse they are judged in offence, and the worse in offence, the heavier the punishment they ought to receive. “Therefore,” they said, “it is not strange if deprivation of order is followed by punishment of the body.” They established this very point [Col. 0128C] not only by laws but also by authoritative examples, putting forward the Levites of the Old Testament, whom, when guilty perhaps of some shameful act forbidden by the Law, death of the body followed, or, according to the nature of the crime, mutilation of limbs.

But the lord of Canterbury, agreeing with the sacred canons, argued to the contrary, maintaining that it would be altogether unjust, contrary to the canons and contrary to God, for anyone to undergo two judgments for the punishment of a single offence. “For God does not judge twice for the same thing.” “For,” he said, “what the Church judges is either just or unjust; but you will not say it is unjust; therefore it is just. Since it does not contain acquittal, it contains condemnation. Therefore, if the accused person is condemned when he is deposed from office, no further judgment ought to be begun for condemnation of the same sin.” Further, he said, “we must take care lest, by our consent, the liberty of the Church be oppressed and perish—a liberty for which, after the example of our high priest, we are bound by office to contend even unto death. Yet you have not yet resisted unto death.”

To this the bishops said that the perishing liberty of the Church brought no danger to the Church. “Rather,” they said, “it is now expedient that it perish, lest we all perish. Let us therefore do what the king asks; otherwise escape will perish from us, and there will be no one to seek our souls [Col. 0129A]. But by consenting to the king, we shall possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance and sleep secure in the possessions of our churches. Much must also be conceded to the wickedness of this time.” This was said because of the schism then existing in the Roman Church; for there was a certain antipope in Germany. The bishops said these things as though the wickedness of the day were not enough for itself unless it were increased by the wickedness of bishops.

To this the lord of Canterbury, inflamed with zeal for God’s house, said: “I see that you console your wretchedness under the appearance of endurance, and that, under the pretext of your dispensation, the liberty of Christ’s bride is being suffocated. And who has bewitched you, O foolish bishops? Why do you cover your manifest iniquity with the prudent name of dispensation? Why do you call the loss of Christ’s whole Church a dispensation? Let names serve things; let names not be perverted together with things. As for your saying that much must be conceded to the wickedness of the time: I certainly agree, but not that sins must therefore be heaped upon sins. God is able to make the condition of his Church better, though you do not become worse. Is God unable to aid the holy Church except through the vices of the Church’s teachers? I suppose that you pity Christ’s weaknesses, as though he were unable to raise up his bride unless assisted by our opinions. In truth, God is testing you. For I ask: when ought bishops to expose themselves to danger? In tranquillity and [Col. 0129C] not in danger? You certainly blush to admit that it is in tranquillity. It remains, therefore, that when disturbance is in the Church, the Church’s shepherd must set himself against the danger. For it was no greater merit for bishops of old to found Christ’s Church in their own blood than it is in our time to shed blood for the liberty of the Church. And I myself, God being witness, affirm that it is not safe for us to depart from the model which we received from our holy fathers. Nor ought we to expose anyone to death, since we ourselves are not permitted even to take part in a judgment of blood.”

These words were immediately reported to the king. At once he saw that very many in the Church—not pillars, I do not say, but reeds—were being shaken and trembling in the wind, when they heard that they would not comply in all things with the king’s desire. And certainly [Col. 0129D] they would immediately have yielded before threats had they not perceived the steadfastness of the lord of Canterbury. But the king, seeing that he could not prevail in the matter in which he wished to prevail, quickly turned to other matters, asking them whether they would observe his royal customs in every respect. The lord of Canterbury, after taking counsel, said: “Yes, in all things—but with our order wholly and in every respect safeguarded.” When the king afterward asked the same thing of each man in turn, those words were indeed then in every mouth.

But when he pressed more insistently, repeating and rephrasing the question whether the lord of Canterbury would promise simply and absolutely to observe the king’s royal customs, without adding the reservation that his order be safeguarded, he could not obtain from Christ’s vicar what he wished. The king was therefore violently disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him. Suddenly, in that burst of violent passion, he sprang up and left London, all his business unfinished and his calculations unsettled. Then you could see murmuring among the people and agitation among the clergy. The bishops, troubled and trembling, followed the departing king, fearing that they would not find the king before hearing that they had lost all their goods. They immediately made a secret agreement with the king, setting aside every mention of God and of their order; and they gave assent to the king’s request so readily that they appeared to have agreed to exactly as much [Note: [Col. 0129D] Spark’s edition reads “before he.” The editor adds: “I do not know whether that is better.”] as he had asked. Thus those thought more learned among them became more eager to oppress the Church’s liberty.

But the primate of Canterbury alone remained seated, looking to the right and to the left, and there was no one who acknowledged him. He sought consolation among his brethren, but they had gone backward and no longer walked with him. Finally, seeing the peace of sinners and danger threatening him from every side, he said: “I have spoken one thing: that I would in no way observe the royal customs of an earthly king unless my order were safeguarded in all things. For this I incurred the king’s displeasure; for this my bishops abandoned me; for this I offended the eyes of the whole world. But what of it? Whether the world wills or refuses, in making covenant with a mortal man I shall never at any time, God willing, forget my God and my order. Far be it from me that through fear or favour of any [Col. 0130C] mortal I should be found to have despised God. If an angel from heaven should come and give me such counsel, let him be accursed.”

The king was on several occasions at York, where one of his burgesses of Scarborough came to him, complaining that a certain dean had taken twenty-two shillings from him, harassing his wife in many ecclesiastical chapters and accusing her, without any other accuser, of adultery. Against this custom the king had issued a prohibitory law. By the king’s order, that dean was summoned and charged before the king, in the presence of his archbishop, the bishops of Lincoln and Durham, and John, then treasurer of York and afterward bishop of Poitiers. He replied, as he had been instructed, that she had been accused by a certain deacon and another layman. [Col. 0130D] And when the woman’s canonical purgation had been adjudged to her upon her denial, he said that, so that she might be treated more leniently, her husband had given twenty shillings to his archdeacon and two to himself.

When the dean could not prove these assertions before the king by supporting testimony of those present, the king demanded judgment upon him, saying that the archdeacons and deans of his realm extorted more money annually from its inhabitants in this manner than he himself received. His barons went apart with that clergy to give judgment. At length John the treasurer said that, in his view, the money ought to be restored to the burgess and the dean subjected to the mercy of his archbishop concerning his office. To this Richard de Lucy said: “What, then, will you adjudge for the lord king, whose ordinance this man has violated?” John replied: “Nothing, because he is a cleric.” Richard said: “I shall not be party to this judgment.” Leaving them, he returned to the king with the other barons. The clergy afterward entered with this judgment, pronounced by the same John who had framed it. The king, turning away, appealed to Archbishop Theobald, appointing a day, and angrily declared the judgment altogether false. But before the day arrived, news was brought to him of the death of his brother Geoffrey; crossing the sea, he did not pursue the appeal.

Moreover, when the king’s itinerant justices were once at Dunstable, a dispute arose between Simon son of Peter and a certain canon of Bedford, Philip de Brois. Afterwards Simon complained to the king [Col. 0131B] that Philip had dishonoured him with abusive language while he was in the king’s service and before a large audience. Philip, rebuked by the king concerning this in the archbishop’s presence, could not deny it, but answered that, provoked by insults in the heat of anger, he had spoken—not by the judgment of his mind. The king demanded judgment. The clergy, seeking to appease the king, decreed that Philip should for a year be deprived both of the benefit of his prebend and of residence within the kingdom. This was done; yet the king was not satisfied.

The first estrangement between the king and Saint Thomas arose over a certain clerk who, in the territory of Worcester, was said to have lain with the daughter of a worthy man and, on her account, to have killed her father. The king wished this clerk to be investigated and judged by the judgment of a secular court. The archbishop [Col. 0131C] resisted, and had that clerk kept in the bishop’s custody, lest he be handed over to the king’s justice. Another case concerned a clerk who, in the church of the archbishop himself which is in London and is called St Mary’s Church in the market-place, stole a silver chalice. When he was seized, the king wished him to be judged by secular judgment. The archbishop had him deprived of clerical office by the judgment of the Church, and, beyond what was required, branded in order to appease the king.

### On the council held at Clarendon

Therefore the king, having long entertained certain grievances against the clergy generally, and now against Thomas the archbishop personally, while hostile resentments grew day by day through increasing provocation, resolved to deal with his royal prerogatives. A general council was summoned and assembled at Clarendon. The king set forth and wrote down certain prerogatives and customs which, he said, were ancestral and ought to exist in the kingdom of England. Robert, archdeacon of Oxford, who afterwards became bishop of Hereford, and Jordan, archdeacon of Chichester, household clerks of the archbishop’s establishment, along with certain others, having understood the lord king’s anger, which had been seriously conceived against him and was daily increasing, had taken leave and departed from him. The king also, from the very beginning, once he had conceived a deeper anger against him, contrived to remove far from him two worthy and honourable clerks, reared from youth upon the archbishop’s own resources, [Col. 0132A] one of whom was treasurer of York and the other a canon of Salisbury, both named John, lest the archbishop in his need avail himself of their counsel or aid. He caused one to be elected and ordained bishop of Poitiers, while he ordered the other into exile. He also obtained from the lord pope the transfer of Gilbert, bishop of Hereford, whom he had drawn closer to himself, to the bishopric of London, as was thought, so that he might use his counsel against the archbishop.

Many chapters of those customs concerned the trampling-down of ecclesiastical liberty and the total oppression of the clergy: for example, that a clerk accused of theft, robbery, or the like should first come before the king’s court; likewise, that for any crime whatsoever [Col. 0132B] no earl, baron, or royal official should be excommunicated without consulting the king; likewise, that appeals should not be made to the lord pope until the case had been heard in the ecclesiastical forum before the dean, archdeacon, bishop, archbishop, and finally in the king’s court; that bishops or other clerks summoned by him, appealed against, or appealing to him should not set out for the lord pope except by the king’s permission; that not every dispute concerning a breach of faith or oath should belong to the ecclesiastical forum, but only an oath imposed in connection with marriage, dowry, or similar matters, which ought not to be done except in the face of the Church. With respect to an oath otherwise given, such as regarding debts or the like, the king decreed that the case belonged in a secular court. Likewise, that bishops should be present at all the king’s secular judgments except a judgment of blood; and other provisions of this kind [Col. 0132C] which openly sounded in discord with the sacred constitutions of the canons.

Yet these customs had never previously been written down, nor indeed had they existed at all in the kingdom of England. And even if they had existed, the king, in establishing those spurious statutes, ought not to have relied upon antiquity and usage rather than law; for the Lord says: “Keep my laws.” Likewise: “Woe to those who enact unjust laws!” Nowhere, moreover, is the Lord found to have said, “I am custom”; rather, he said: “I am truth.” Nor does the usage or practice of long duration possess such authority as to overcome either reason, as the pagan emperor says, or law. Rather, once equity and truth have been revealed, usage must yield to reason, as the holy Fathers wrote in the decrees. Yet the Christian king enacted and wrote these measures against reason and ecclesiastical liberty.

But Archbishop Thomas, upright in life and free from crime, could not otherwise be assailed. Indeed, by most elaborate deceit and malicious artifice this was contrived for him: either, by confirming these traditions, he would fall into the hands of God, or, by rejecting them, into the hands of the king; he would be condemned as a disturber of royal majesty and an enemy of the crown, and killed. It was said that this scheme had been devised by Roger, archbishop of York, Gilbert of London, and John, bishop of Salisbury. For afterwards, most severely rebuked by the lord pope on this matter, they cleared themselves in the sight of men by taking oaths. But after Hilary had first died, the king sought the assent [Col. 0133A] of the clergy to confirm these statutes. At length the matter was put before the archbishop; and the king’s interpreters threatened him and the dissenting bishops with danger, as though he wished to take the crown of the kingdom from the king if he opposed confirming these decrees. Supported by the bishops, the archbishop resisted for a long time and objected for a long time. At last the king’s final messengers came and, drawing him aside, expressly informed him with tearful words what would happen if he did not yield. From fear of death, and to appease the king, he assented for the time being, by assent, by a stipulation “upon the word of truth,” and by the impress of their seals. The archbishop, the archbishop of York, and all the bishops confirmed those statutes, undertaking to observe them for the king lawfully, without evil deceit, and in good faith. Afterwards the king sent the same decrees to the lord pope for confirmation; having read and understood them, he rejected, recoiled from, and condemned them.

The archbishop, chosen of God, rose stronger after his fall, recovered his courage, repented, and began to afflict himself more severely with harsher food and clothing. He suspended himself from the office of the altar until, through confession and worthy fruits of penitence, absolved by the Roman pontiff, he deserved to be released. He truly repented, because, so far as lay within him, he was prepared to revoke and correct his errors; but his fellow bishops were unwilling to revoke what had been conceded, or did not dare to do so because of the king’s fear, which weighed upon them. The archbishop made his way to the king’s familiar residence, the walled park at Woodstock, where he had heard that the king was, intending to speak with him; but, repulsed from the door, he returned to Canterbury. At his coastal estate at Romney, the archbishop, intending to depart in order to avoid the king’s anger for a time, twice attempted to put to sea; but he had either no wind or a contrary one. When this was heard, it inflamed the king’s anger exceedingly.

### On the council held at Northampton

Consequently the king afterwards proclaimed another general council, appointing Northampton as the place. The appointed day of the council was Tuesday in the octave of St Michael; on that very day we came to Northampton. The archbishop did not see the king that day, because the king, amusing himself among streams and flowing waters with the birds of heaven as he travelled, [Col. 0133D] entered Northampton late. On the following morning, after Mass and the Hours had been said, the archbishop came to the court, to the king’s castle. Admitted into the first chamber, he sat awaiting the king, who was then hearing Mass. When the king came, the archbishop rose respectfully and showed a face steadfast and calm, ready modestly to offer the customary English courtesy of a kiss, and to receive it if the king anticipated him. He was not admitted to the kiss.

The archbishop first raised the matter of William de Courcy, who had occupied one of his lodgings, and asked the king to order it vacated for him. The king ordered it. His second speech was that he had come at the king’s summons concerning the claim brought against him by John Marshal. For John demanded from the archbishop a certain tract of land, a dependent portion of the archiepiscopal manor of Pagham. Several days had been assigned for that action, when the king’s writ arrived in the archbishop’s court. Since John made no progress there, being supported by no law—for that was then the law—he finally established the default of the archbishop’s court by producing a book of tropes from beneath his pallium. The justices of the archbishop’s court objected that he ought not to have brought either such a book for this purpose or any such book at all. Returning to the king, he obtained letters summoning the archbishop to answer him in the king’s court; the day fixed for the suit was the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. On that day the archbishop did not come, but sent the king four knights with his own letters and those of the sheriff of Kent, likewise attesting John’s wrong and the incompleteness [Col. 0134B] of his proof.

But what followed? The king indignantly resented that the archbishop, summoned by him, had not appeared in person to plead this defence if he wished. He treated the archbishop’s messengers badly, troubling them in anger and with threats, as persons who had brought to his court, in answer to the king’s summons, a false and inadequate excuse. At length, after sureties had been given, he scarcely released them. At the request of the aforesaid John, the king fixed another day for the same case and sent letters to the sheriff of Kent directing that the archbishop be summoned. Nor then, nor for a long time before, had he been willing to write to him, because he did not wish to greet him. Nor had the archbishop received any other formal and initial summons to the council through letters addressed to him, as ancient custom required.

The archbishop said, then, that he had come by the king’s command for John’s case. To this the king replied that John was in his service in London, but would soon come, and then he would investigate their case. For that John was with the treasurers and other royal receivers of revenue, coinage, money, and public funds in London, at the four-sided table called the “chequered boards,” commonly the Exchequer—though it is rather the king’s table with its white counters—where pleas of the king’s crown are also heard. Nothing further took place that day between the king and the archbishop; but the king told him to go to his lodging and return next day for his case. He returned.

On the second day, when all the bishops, earls, and barons of England were seated, and many from Normandy, except the bishop of Rochester [Col. 0134D] who had not yet arrived, and one other, the archbishop was charged with offending the majesty of the royal crown. That is, as was narrated above, though summoned by the king for John’s case, he had neither appeared nor properly excused himself. The archbishop’s defence found no place, although he alleged John’s aforesaid wrong, the jurisdiction of his own cause, and the unimpaired competence of his court. The king demanded judgment. None of the archbishop’s argument was accepted. It seemed to all, out of reverence for royal majesty, from the obligation of the liege homage which the archbishop had done to the lord king, and from the fealty and observance of his earthly honour which he had sworn to him, that he had been insufficiently defended or excused: summoned by the king, he had neither appeared nor alleged through messengers bodily infirmity or a necessary administration of ecclesiastical office [Col. 0135A] which could not be deferred. They said that he should be condemned to a monetary penalty, at the king’s mercy, of all his movable goods.

There was disagreement between bishops and barons over pronouncing the judgment, each side imposing the task upon the other and each excusing itself. The barons said: “You bishops ought to pronounce the sentence; this does not belong to us. We are laymen; you are ecclesiastical persons, as he is—his fellow priests and fellow bishops.” To this one of the bishops replied: “Indeed, this belongs rather to your office, not ours; for this is not an ecclesiastical judgment but a secular one. We do not sit here as bishops, but as barons. We are barons and you are barons; here we are equals. You rely in vain upon the grounds of our order, for if you consider ordination in us, you ought to consider it likewise in him. But precisely because we are bishops, we cannot judge the archbishop and our lord.” Yet when the king heard this dispute about pronouncement, he was moved, and they ceased to contend over it. The bishop of Winchester was charged to speak and at length, though unwillingly, pronounced the judgment.

The archbishop, however, because it is not permitted to contradict the sentence or record of the king’s court of England, accepted it on the bishops’ advice. A formal placing of his hand in the king’s hand was required of him to appease and honour the king, as though conceding the judgment, according to the custom there; and all the bishops gave sureties, except that Gilbert of London, who, when asked, refused to stand surety for him. This singularity made him conspicuous.

Afterwards, on the same day, the archbishop was charged concerning three hundred pounds received from the castellanies of Eye and Berkhampstead. The archbishop, first pleading a declinatory exception because he had not been summoned for this, said that he had sent this money—and much more—not in litigation, but for repairing the palace in London and the aforesaid castles, as could be seen. The king refused to be his authority that this had been done through him. He demanded judgment. The archbishop, consenting to return this money out of regard for the king, because he absolutely did not wish any sum of money, however great, to be a cause of anger between them, privately put forward as lay sureties Earl Gloucester, William de Eynsford, and a third man, [Col. 0135D] his own men. With this conclusion they departed that day.

On the third day, by a fixed condition [*cerci condictione*, “by a certain condition,” MS Douce], the archbishop was summoned through intermediaries concerning five hundred marks lent for the expedition to Toulouse, and another five hundred marks for the king’s suretyship on his behalf to a certain Jew there. He was likewise sued by an action of guardianship concerning everything received during the vacancy of the archbishopric, or of other bishoprics and abbeys vacant during his chancellorship; and he was ordered to render the king an account of all these matters. The archbishop answered that he had not come prepared or summoned for this purpose. If he ought to be proceeded against on this matter, he would do for his lord the king, at a proper place and time, what the law required. The king demanded from him surety by guarantors. The archbishop said that he needed the counsel of his suffragans and clerks on the matter. The king allowed this. The archbishop departed, and from that day onward the barons no longer came to his lodging to see him, as did the other knights, having understood the king’s disposition.

On the fourth day all those ecclesiastical persons came to the lodging of the lord archbishop. Separately with the bishops and separately with the abbots, he discussed such matters and sought advice. On the counsel of the noble Henry, bishop of Winchester, his ordainer, who promised him powerful assistance in this matter, they attempted to see whether they could soften the king with money; and he offered [Col. 0136B] him two thousand marks. The king refused.

There were some among the clergy who said to the archbishop that, by the duty of the office he had undertaken, he ought to protect the Church of God and have regard for his person and dignity; that he should honour the king in all things, preserving reverence for God and ecclesiastical honour; and that there was nothing adverse which he ought to fear, since no crime and no disgrace was charged against him. He had been restored to the Church of Canterbury, free from the chancellorship and from every secular claim of the king. For even any abbey during a vacancy will not accept as abbot a monk elected from another house unless he has been released to it free from every obligation of obedience to his own abbot.

Others, whose ear and mind were more secretly inclined toward the king, had a very different view, saying: “The lord king is angrily hostile to him. From certain signs we interpret the king’s mind to be this: that the lord archbishop ought in every matter, even in surrendering the archbishopric, to submit himself wholly to the king’s mercy.” Among them Hilary of Chichester, more inclined to the king’s side, said to him: “Would that you could cease to be archbishop and remain Thomas.” He had also said elsewhere of him: “Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up”—as though he meant that the king’s declared will had preceded his election. Concerning him the archbishop later said to someone in his exile: “And this man too obtained among the brethren the place of Judas the traitor.” Afterwards, before the archbishop’s restoration and reconciliation, he died, as though struck by God.

This bishop of Chichester continued, speaking for himself and certain of his accomplices: “From the society and familiarity of the chancellorship, you know the king better than we do. It is beyond doubt to us whether he is better overcome by resistance or yielding. In the chancellorship, both in peace and war, you performed service well and praiseworthily for him, not without envy [Note: [Col. 0135D] “And without envy,” ed. Spark.]; you found praise. Those who then envied you now inflame the king against you. Who could stand surety for you regarding so great an account, concerning money so uncertain? It is said that the king has declared that you will no longer both be in England: he as king, you as archbishop. It is safer to leave everything to his mercy, lest perhaps—God forbid!—he retain you, summoned as his chancellor and financial officer for his money, as a defendant charged with extortion and lacking sureties, or lay hands upon you; whereby the Church of England would incur sorrow and the face of the kingdom shame.”

Someone said: “Far be it that he should thus provide for himself and his bodily safety, and dishonour the Church of Canterbury which chose him! None of his predecessors did this, although they suffered persecutions in their days. Besides, perhaps he could for a time renounce into the lord king’s hand the archiepiscopal benefice—its estates and the like—without prejudice to the Church’s right; but never his office.” Thus their consultations were divided among varying opinions: some said one thing, others another.

The fifth day, which was Sunday, was wholly devoted to counsel [Col. 0137B]. There was scarcely an hour’s respite for refreshment. The archbishop did not leave his lodging.

On the sixth day, a sudden illness, as often happens, prevented him from going to court. His kidneys trembled with cold and pain, and pillows had to be warmed and applied in turn. On hearing this, the king sent all his earls and many barons to seek from him an answer upon the advice he had taken, asking whether he wished to provide surety for rendering an account of what he had received from vacant churches during his chancellorship, and to stand judgment on this matter in the king’s court. Through the bishops the archbishop answered that, notwithstanding his adverse bodily condition, he would come to court next day and do what he ought.

Next morning, at an altar of St Stephen the Protomartyr [Col. 0137C], he celebrated the Mass *Etenim sederunt principes* (“For princes sat”). The king’s informers, who were immediately lying in wait for him, reported the chant of that Mass, maliciously interpreting it as though the archbishop had celebrated it for himself, as another Stephen the Protomartyr, against the king and his followers who were unjustly persecuting him. Afterwards he went to court. As he passed, he said to Alexander, bearer of his cross: “I would have done better had I come in our vestments.” For he had proposed to enter before the king barefoot, vested, and carrying the cross, in order to supplicate him for the peace of the Church. But his clerks dissuaded him from this intention, and also from taking up the cross.

As he was about to enter the hall of the castle, after dismounting from his horse, he took into his hands the cross which Alexander of Wales had carried before him. At the door of the hall stood the aforesaid bishop Gilbert of London. Hugh de Nonant, a certain archdeacon of Lisieux, who had come with the archbishop and was of his household, said to him: “Lord bishop of London, why do you allow him himself to carry the cross?” The bishop replied: “Good man, he has always been a fool, and always will be.” For all gave way as the archbishop entered. He withdrew into the chamber and sat in his usual place, the bishops beside him and the bishop of London nearer at hand. All present were astonished, and everyone’s eyes were fixed upon him. The bishop of London urged him to hand the cross to one of his clerks. He said that the archbishop was prepared, as though he wished to throw the whole kingdom into disorder. “You hold the cross,” said the bishop of London, “in your hands; if now the king takes up his sword, behold a well-equipped king and a well-equipped archbishop.”

The archbishop replied: “If it could be done, it would be my wish always to carry it in my own hands. But now I know what I shall do.
