It is indeed for the preservation of God’s peace—for my own person and for the Church of the English. Say what you please; if you were here, you would think otherwise. But if, as you say, the lord king were now to take up his sword, that would certainly not be a sign of peace.” Perhaps the archbishop remembered how narrowly matters had stood at Clarendon, when the king’s messengers came to him in tears.

All the bishops were summoned to the king, and remained inside with him for a long time [Col. 0138B], together with that Roger, archbishop of York. He had come last to court, in order to make a more conspicuous entrance and not appear to belong to the king’s counsel. He also had his own cross carried before him in the opposite direction,

> like javelins threatening javelins.

He had also been forbidden by the lord pope, in letters sent to him, to carry his cross as a standard-bearer in the province of Canterbury; but, having received the prohibition, he claimed that it rested upon a false representation by the lord of Canterbury and entered an appeal, by which he considered himself protected.

Nor was it surprising that grief, groaning, and contrition of heart overwhelmed the archbishop. For he had heard that on that day he would either be seized by some sort of sentence, or, if he escaped this, he would be killed in an encounter, through a conspiracy of wicked men formed against him, as though without the king’s knowledge. Meanwhile Herbert, his master in Holy Scripture, said quietly to the archbishop: “Lord, if perhaps they lay impious hands upon you, have at hand a sentence of excommunication to pronounce against them, so that their spirit may nevertheless be saved on the day of the Lord.” William son of Stephen, who sat at the archbishop’s feet, said somewhat loudly, so that the archbishop could hear: “Far be this from him! The holy apostles and martyrs of God did not act thus when they were seized and carried away on high; rather, should this happen, let him pray for them and forgive them, and in his patience possess his soul. For if it should befall him to suffer for the cause of justice and ecclesiastical liberty, then, by the Lord’s granting, his soul will be at rest and his memory in blessing. [Col. 0138D] If he pronounced a sentence against them, everyone would think that, out of anger and impatience, he had done for his own revenge what was in his power. And beyond doubt he would act contrary to the decrees, as blessed Gregory writes to Januarius the archbishop: ‘You show that you think of nothing heavenly, but make clear that your manner of life is earthly, when, for revenge of a personal injury, you have brought in the curse of anathema, which the sacred rules forbid.’”

John Planeta [Note: [Col. 0137D] *Plenata*, ed. Spark.] heard this and struggled to restrain the tears breaking forth. Likewise Ralph de Diceto, archdeacon of London and later dean, wept greatly there that day. Hearing such words, the archbishop pondered them in [Col. 0139A] his heart. Shortly afterwards, the same William son of Stephen wished to speak to the archbishop, but was prevented by one of the king’s marshals standing there with his staff, who said that no one might speak to him. After an interval, William looked intently at the archbishop and, by lifting his eyes and moving his lips, signalled to him to look upon the image of his cross and of the Crucified which he held, and to remain in prayer. The archbishop understood the sign well and did so, strengthened in the Lord. Many years later, when the archbishop was an exile in Gaul at St Benedict’s above the Loire, he recalled this to the same William, who was going to the lord pope, among other memories of his troubles.

But, Christian king, what are you doing? On account of a barony [Col. 0139B] and a possession, you cause a son to judge his father, a subject his archbishop, a sheep his shepherd, in your secular court, when not even the humblest clerk is bound to answer in a secular court. You say: “Not so; the king judges a baron.” To this one replies: “Greater in you is the fact that you are a Christian, that you are a sheep of God, that you are God’s adopted son, than that you are king. And greater in him is the fact that he is archbishop and vicar of Jesus Christ than that he is a baron. Consider the ranks. His possession is less than his order, yet the greater takes precedence over the lesser, and the worthier over the less worthy. Therefore his order ought to be stronger and more effective in exempting him from your forum than his barony and possession in keeping him liable there. And if you examine his possession itself more deeply, it is not his but the Church’s. It was secular; once given to God [Col. 0139C], it became ecclesiastical. Its secularity has been absorbed into it under the title of divine law. Thus the archbishop is not liable to secular judgment even by reason of it. Therefore he is bound to be judged in no court either by reason of his person or by reason of the property he possessed.

“The archbishop must be reserved for the judgment of the pope alone, and the pope for that of God alone. If you had anything against him which could not be softened through the intervention of concord and charity, you ought to have referred it to the lord pope. Summoned away from your jurisdiction, he would answer there before our bishops and clerks serving as envoys; or you should have obtained that legates from the side of the lord pope be sent into your kingdom with the fullness of judicial authority.”

The bishop of Hereford, Master Robert of Melun, who had taught dialectic and Holy Scripture at Paris for more than forty years, once, at an assembly of several bishops and many clerks, posed a sorrowful question: “If it should happen—God forbid—that the lord archbishop be killed in this cause for the liberty of the Church, shall we regard him as a martyr? To die for the mother of faith is to be a martyr.” Someone replied: “Beyond doubt, if such a thing should happen—God forbid!—we should say that he had most gloriously gained the crown of martyrdom. Faith alone is not the cause of martyrdom: there are several causes—truth, the liberty of the Church, love of country or neighbour—and one cause is sufficient, provided God is in the cause.

“Blessed John the Baptist did not dispute with Herod [Col. 0140A] or Herodias concerning articles of faith, but died for truth because he said: ‘It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.’ Likewise this man says: ‘It is not lawful for you, O king, to oppress the Church with this servitude, so that men ordained of God for ecclesiastical office should be bound by your constitutions, which are contrary to the canons.’

“Likewise, the seven brothers, while their mother watched and urged them to stand firm like men, endured different kinds of martyrdom because they would not violate God’s command and the observances of the Fathers concerning eating pork. Blessed Lanfranc, archbishop, also consulted Saint Anselm, then abbot, about Saint Ælfheah, asking whether he ought to be numbered among God’s martyrs. He put forward that Ælfheah had been killed by foreign enemies who had entered England by ship because he had refused to give the gold which they had exacted from the sons and people [Col. 0140B] of the Church of Canterbury. Blessed Anselm replied: ‘He is especially to be regarded as a martyr, because, for the defence or prolongation of his own life, he would not allow his sons and neighbours to be harassed by payment of the money exacted by the enemy. He died for the liberty and safety of his neighbours. No one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends. And the title of innocence, where no conflict preceded, makes a martyr. Thus Abel too is called the first crowned in martyrdom.’

“Indeed, even among the pagans this was a sound judgment:

> … bitter fates drive on the Romans,  
> and the crime of fraternal slaughter,  
> after the sacred blood of innocent Remus  
> flowed upon the ground, accursed for his descendants.”

[Col. 0140C] Good God, how many clergy and knights who were present uttered true and eloquent sayings about contempt for the world, while the archbishop sat there alone holding the cross, and all his suffragan bishops, together with the earls and barons, had been summoned to the king and were separated from him! Someone said: “O deceitful age! Like a calm sea, though its surface may sometimes be serene, it nevertheless contains hidden storms within.” Another said: “All things undergo change. The Lord’s love is not a fief [Note: [Col. 0139D] *Feudum* omitted in ed. Spark.]. O honours of the world! Even what is hoped for in them must be feared.”

While the bishops were speaking privately with the king, they told him among other things that, when they had come to the archbishop that day, he rebuked them for their bad treatment of him. That is, he said that recently they had treated him too much as an enemy with the barons, judged him more harshly than was just, and acted in an unprecedented manner. Although they called it a single absence contrary to the king’s summons, it was not contumacy; therefore they ought not to have condemned him to the king’s mercy, in a monetary penalty of all his movable goods. In this way the Church of Canterbury could be destroyed if the king, without mercy, chose to harden himself. Such a judgment could also be a snare to bishops and barons themselves in a similar case.

But in each county a single sum of money had been fixed as the payment owed by those condemned to a monetary penalty at the king’s mercy. In London, for example, one hundred shillings had been fixed. In Kent, which lies closer to the sea, must keep pirates away from England’s shore, and claims the first blow in wars against foreign enemies; because its burden is greater, greater liberty has been granted to it. There forty shillings had been fixed for persons condemned in this way. Since the archbishop had his dwelling and seat in Kent, he ought at least to have been judged and assessed according to the law of Kent. The bishops also said that, that very day, within ten days of the sentence, he had appealed them to the lord pope, and had forbidden them, under the authority of the lord pope, henceforth to judge him for a secular claim brought against him concerning a time before he became archbishop.

The king, angered, sent his earls and many barons [Col. 0141B] to ask the archbishop whether he acknowledged himself as the author of this appeal and prohibition, especially since he was the king’s liege man and was bound to him by both a common oath and the special stipulation at Clarendon “upon the word of truth,” that he would preserve the royal prerogatives lawfully, in good faith, and without evil deceit. Among these prerogatives was this: that his bishops should be present at all his judgments except judgments of blood. They were also to ask him whether he would give surety, by providing pledges, for rendering the account of his chancellorship and stand judgment upon this in the king’s court.

The archbishop, looking upon the image of the Crucified, strengthening his mind and countenance, and remaining seated in order to preserve the dignity of his archiepiscopal office, delivered the following lucid and composed address, so evenly that he did not falter over a single word:

[Col. 0141C] “Men and brethren, earls and barons of the lord king: I am indeed bound to our lord the king by liege homage, fealty, and oath; but an oath, especially a priestly oath, includes justice and equity. I am bound by honour and fealty to the lord king to render him, for God’s sake, service in all things with submission as devoted as it is due, saving obedience to God, ecclesiastical dignity, and the episcopal honour of my person. I decline the suit, since I received no summons either to render an account or to any cause except John’s cause, nor am I liable here to answer another party in a cause or to hear judgment.

“I acknowledge and remember that I received many administrations and dignities from [Col. 0141D] the lord king; in them I served him faithfully on this side and beyond the sea. And, having expended all my own revenues in his service, I am glad that I bound myself indebted to creditors for a very great sum of money. But when, by divine permission and the lord king’s favour, I was elected archbishop and was to be consecrated, before consecration I was released by the king as exempt and restored to the Church of Canterbury, free, untroubled, and discharged from every secular claim of the king, although now in anger he denies this. Very many of you know this well, as do all the ecclesiastical persons of this kingdom. And I ask and implore you, who know this truth, to remind the lord king of it—against whom, even if it were lawful, it is not safe to name witnesses [Col. 0142A]; though there is no need now, because I am not litigating.

“After consecration, I resolved to cultivate by work and deed the honour and burden I had undertaken, and to benefit in some degree the Church of God, over which I appeared to preside. If I am not permitted to advance in this task, if, with adversity blowing against me, I cannot make progress, I attribute this not to the lord king or to anyone else, but principally to my own sins. The Lord is able to increase grace for whom and when he wills.”

> “I cannot provide sureties for rendering an account. I have already bound here all the bishops and my helpful friends; nor ought I to be compelled to do this, because it has not been adjudged against me. Nor am I involved in a case concerning an account, because I was not summoned to that case, nor was any summons issued to me concerning it, except [Col. 0142B] in the case with John Marshal. As for your pressing me concerning the prohibition issued today to the bishops, or concerning my appeal, I indeed acknowledge that I told my fellow bishops that, for a single absence—not, however, contumacy—they condemned me more severely than was just, and contrary to the custom and precedent of the distant past. Therefore I appealed against them, forbidding them, while this appeal is pending, again to judge me concerning a secular claim from the time before I assumed the archbishopric; and I still appeal, and place both my person and the Church of Canterbury under the protection of God and the lord pope.”

He had finished. Some of the magnates returned silently to the king, weighing and examining his words. Others said: “Behold, from his own mouth [Col. 0142C] we have heard the blasphemy of a prohibition.” Some of the barons and attendants of the royal household, walking with twisted necks and casting sidelong glances at him, spoke among themselves somewhat loudly, so that he might hear:

“King William, who subdued England, knew how to tame his clerics. He seized his own brother Odo, bishop of Bayeux, as a rebel against him. He condemned Stigand, archbishop of Canterbury, cast into a dark pit, to perpetual imprisonment. The father also of our lord king, Geoffrey, count of Anjou, who likewise subjected Normandy to himself by a strong hand, made Arnulf [Note: [Col. 0141D] Arnulf, ed. Spark.] the elect of Séez, and many of his clerics, renounce their claims; and he had the members of eunuchs brought before him in a basin, because Arnulf had assented, without Geoffrey’s approval, to his own election to the Church of Séez and conducted himself as [Col. 0142D] its elected bishop.”

Having received the archbishop’s reply, the king pressed the bishops, commanding and beseeching them, by the homage and fealty due and sworn to him, to pronounce with the barons a judgment concerning the archbishop. They began to excuse themselves on account of the archbishop’s intervening prohibition. The king did not yield, maintaining that this simple prohibition of his could not prevail against what had been enacted and sworn at Clarendon. The bishops, on the other hand, urged upon the king what the archbishop could impose upon them, and how he could lay his hand heavily upon them, if they did not obey the prohibition and appeal; and that, for the good of the king and kingdom, they wished and ought [Col. 0143A] to acquiesce in the prohibition that had been made.

At last the king was persuaded. The bishops, having taken counsel among themselves, went in to the archbishop. Robert of Lincoln wept, and some others could scarcely restrain their tears. Then the aforesaid Hilary, bishop of Chichester, began thus:

“My lord archbishop, with your leave, we have much of which to complain concerning you. You have greatly offended us, your bishops; you have enclosed us in a great narrow passage, as though you had placed us between hammer and anvil by this your prohibition. If we do not obey it, we are ensnared by the bonds of disobedience; if we obey it, by those of the constitution and of royal displeasure. For recently, gathered with you at Clarendon, we were summoned by the lord king concerning the observance of his royal dignities; and, lest perhaps we might hesitate, he showed us in writing those royal customs of his about which he spoke. At last we promised them our assent and pledged observance: you in the first place, and we, your suffragans, afterwards, by your command. When, moreover, the lord king required from us on this matter a sworn guarantee and the impression of our seals, we said that our priestly oath ought to suffice him: we told him, in a word of truth, that we would observe those royal dignities of his in good faith, without evil intent, and lawfully. The lord king, persuaded, acquiesced. Yet now you compel us to act against this, forbidding us to be present at the judgment which he requires of us. We appeal to the lord pope against this burden, and lest you add anything to our injury; and on this occasion [Col. 0143C] we render obedience to your prohibition.”

The archbishop said:

“I hear what you say, and, God willing, I shall attend to the prosecution of the appeal. But at Clarendon nothing was granted by me, or by you through me, except with the honour of the Church preserved. For, as you yourselves say, we retained there these three qualifications: ‘in good faith,’ ‘without evil intent,’ and ‘lawfully’; by these the dignities which our Churches possess by pontifical right are preserved. For what is contrary to the faith owed to the Church and to the laws of God cannot be observed in good faith and lawfully. Likewise, it is not a Christian king’s dignity where ecclesiastical liberty, which he swore to observe, perishes. Moreover, the lord king sent to the supreme pontiff for confirmation those same written royal dignities of which you speak; and they were returned by him as disapproved rather than approved. He gave us an example for our instruction, that we too should act thus: prepared with the Roman Church to receive what it receives and reject what it rejects. Furthermore, if we fell at Clarendon—for the flesh is weak—we must recover our spirit and, in the strength of the Holy Spirit, strive against the ancient enemy, who brings about both things: that one who stands may fall, and that one who has fallen may not rise again. If, under the stipulation ‘in a word of truth,’ we there conceded or swore unjust things, you know that those who swear unlawful things are bound by no law.”

The bishops returned to the king and, with his permission, were excused from judging [Col. 0144A] the archbishop; they withdrew from the barons and sat apart. Nevertheless, the king no less demanded from the earls and barons their judgment concerning the archbishop. Certain sheriffs and barons of secondary rank, men advanced in years, were summoned to join them and attend the judgment.

After some delay the magnates returned to the archbishop. Robert, earl of Leicester, who surpassed the others in maturity of age and character, instructing certain others to pronounce the decision, began, though they were reluctant, to recount point by point the business conducted at Clarendon, as he had done above. But Hilary, bishop of Chichester, was less [Note: [Col. 0143D] “As he had done above, and less,” MS Dom.] cheerful toward the archbishop, as though the injury to royal majesty and the breach of the promise then made “in a word of truth” were thereby manifest; and he told the archbishop [Col. 0144B] that he should hear their judgment.

But the archbishop did not allow him to say more. He said:

“What is it that you intend to do? Have you come to judge me? You ought not. Judgment is a sentence pronounced after a dispute. Today I have said nothing as a litigant. I was summoned here for no case except the case of John, who has not proceeded against me. In these matters you cannot judge me. I am, however unworthy, your father; but you are magnates of the court, lay powers, secular persons. I will not hear your judgment.”

The magnates withdrew. After an interval, the archbishop rose, carrying his cross, and made for the door, which, though most strictly watched throughout the day, seemed to open of its own accord for him. One abusive man following him said that he was leaving as the king’s perjurer; another that he was departing as a traitor [Col. 0144C] and carrying away the judgment of his lord king.

Oh, what a martyrdom he endured in spirit on that day! Yet he returned happier from the sight of the council, because he had been counted worthy to suffer with Christ for the name of Jesus. In the hall, crowded with men, he struck against a bundle of wood which he had not seen, but did not fall. He came to the door where his horses were. Mounting his own, he carried Master Herbert with him to his lodging, at the monastery of St Andrew, since Herbert could not obtain his own horse so quickly because of the excessive crush. Having prayed before the altar, he afterwards laid down the cross beside the altar of Blessed Mary. He sat, with his household about him. Then William son of Stephen said to him: [Col. 0144D] “This indeed—this was a bitter day.” He replied: “The last will be more bitter.” Shortly afterwards, having exhorted his people, he said:

“Let each of you keep himself in silence and peace. Let no bitter word come from your mouth. Answer none of the abusive with anything. Let them revile. It belongs to the superior person to endure this; to the inferior, to do it. As they are masters of their tongues, so let us be masters of our ears. It is not I who am cursed, but the one who recognizes in himself what evil is said.”

When the king heard of the archbishop’s departure and that his courtiers had followed him with abusive language, he was asked by Robert of Melun, bishop of Hereford—or perhaps instructed by someone else—and, while the archbishop had not yet gone far, sent orders that a herald’s proclamation be cried through the streets after him: that no one should hurt him by abusive speech or insult, and that no one at all should molest him or any of his people in any respect. The archbishop that evening ate among his household as usual. After supper all his knights who were present, having rendered him their homage and obtained leave, departed from him in tears.

Afterwards the archbishop sent three bishops to the king: Walter of Rochester, his chaplain, and two whom he had ordained, Robert of Hereford and Roger of Worcester, to seek from him leave and a safe-conduct for his intended departure on the following day. They found the king cheerful, but he deferred his answer until the next morning. On receiving [Col. 0145B] the messengers’ report, the archbishop feared that this delay in the king’s reply might bring some danger upon him.

It was night; the hour for Compline had been announced. The archbishop told his companions that he wished to keep vigil in the church. On one of the preceding nights he had spent the entire night in the church with his clerics, in vigils and prayers, practising bodily affliction and kneeling at the invocation of every male or female saint named in his litany. Some of his clerics said to him: “We too wish to keep vigil in the church with you.” He replied: “Certainly not; I do not wish you to be troubled.” In the silence of deepest night he departed secretly, accompanied by none of his clerics or knights.

When, on the following day, the king and the whole council learned this, they took counsel concerning what needed to be done. The king left all the possessions of the Church of Canterbury in peace to the archbishop, removing none of his officials, because appeals were pending on both sides. He immediately sent after the archbishop, close upon his heels, those who were to pursue these cases before the lord pope: the archbishop of York; four bishops, Gilbert of London, Hilary of Chichester, Bartholomew of Exeter, and Roger of Worcester; two earls and two barons; and three household clerics of his own. The rest of the day and of the council was spent discussing the infantry forces to be led against rebellious Wales and its treaty-breaking king Rhys; and each person, ecclesiastical as well as secular, entered in writing the number of foot-soldiers promised in answer to the king’s request for aid. [Col. 0145D] The council was dissolved.

On the following morning so many and such important messengers hastened rapidly toward Dover, the sea-port, thinking that they ought to overtake the archbishop. The archbishop, hiding among God-fearing men and his friends, and sometimes travelling by night, remained in England from the fifteenth day after St Michael’s Day until the second day of November, until a ship was made ready for him whose captain and sailors he could trust. On that same day—the commemoration, namely, of the faithful departed—both he and the envoys sent against him crossed the sea. They made for Grandport, though driven by so great a storm [Col. 0146A] that the bishop of London had to take off his cope and hood; the archbishop landed more secretly at Gravelines. From there he went on foot, poor and with only two fellow servants, as far as a barn belonging to the Cistercian monks of Clairmarais. Yet in greatness of spirit he despised Fortune now when she snarled, as formerly when she smiled.

On the way someone recognized him and said: “This is indeed he who was once chancellor of England and is now archbishop of Canterbury.” He replied: “Do archbishops of Canterbury usually travel in this fashion?” In a certain little village, when he could go no farther on foot, he hired a horse and mounted it without a saddle.

O good Jesus, many indeed are the tribulations of the righteous and the sufferings of this present time; yet are they not worthy to be compared with the rewards which you reserve for your own at the time [Col. 0146B] of recompense? Behold, this your servant the archbishop has left all things; poor, destitute, and needy, he has followed you. With respect to all the saints, I will say this: if each person offers to God as much as he leaves behind for God’s love, it will not easily be found that anyone surpasses Thomas. For Christ and the liberty of the Church, he despised his possessions and his own people; he despised the proscription of his clerics, officials, and kinsmen. What more? He despised the world; he despised himself also. But the man of God bore all these things with much patience, preferring to undergo the loss not only of his goods but even of his salvation, rather than that the justice of God and the liberty of the Church should be endangered without assistance, or at least without protest.

[Col. 0146C] They reached that barn. From there he was conveyed by boat to Clairmarais, and thence to Saint-Omer. There he was received by the abbot of Saint-Bertin and the convent, with pious tears bursting forth and still fuller joy. At the request of Philip, son of Thierry, the illustrious count of Flanders, he obtained, having been received with fitting compassion and reverence [Note: [Col. 0145D] “Convent,” ed. Spark.], a safe-conduct and security for going to the lord king of France. Remaining for some time with the abbot of Saint-Bertin, he awaited some of his fellow priests, clerics, and members of his scattered company. There horses, chapel furnishings, clothing, and every necessity for himself and those of his followers who came to him were supplied in full through the count’s generosity and the liberality of the abbot and neighbouring persons.

There Richard de Luci, the English king’s envoy, returning from the king of France, first made many attempts to persuade him to return home, and then rendered him his homage. As he continued his journey to the lord king of France, he already had forty horses for his use. When his arrival was announced to his clerics, of whom he had many in France, they hurried and joined him. From every direction venerable persons of the Church in France met him at a place called Strata (ad Stratam). Henry, archbishop of Rheims and brother of the king of France, bishops, abbots, archdeacons, and provosts of churches congratulated so great an exile with due reverence, freely placed themselves and their possessions at his disposal, and pressed him, with insistence born of devout charity, to accept [Col. 0147A] necessities.

His arrival became known to Louis, king of France, son of King Louis; and he piously sympathized in the Lord with one suffering insult, and rejoiced with one who had escaped. At length this report was spread to Pope Alexander III, who was at Sens. For there was a schism in the holy Roman Church—alas!—and Frederick, a vigorous emperor, had he loved God, together with the whole following of all his lands, supported one, another, and a third schismatic. But the arrival of the English king’s envoys also became known to the lord pope. Compassionating the exiled archbishop with due pity and rejoicing that he was contending for the liberty of the Church, he wrote to him that he should withdraw apart to rest [Col. 0147B] and recover his breath until summoned to him.

Moved by pity, all France sympathized with the archbishop, and everyone’s feeling was stirred against the envoys of the king of England, especially against the bishops. Understanding this, the archbishop of York, the four bishops, and the others made William of Albini, earl of Arundel, their leader. When casually asked whose such a great household and retinue might be, they said it was the earl of Arundel’s, suppressing the bishops’ names—shameful!—and at last came to the lord pope.

From every side all who could come to the lord pope’s court flocked there, from the kingdom of France and Burgundy, to see and hear so many and such notable envoys of the king of England: what kind of case they had, and what they would say or do. In a celebrated consistory the archbishop of York and all the bishops except Roger of Worcester, together with the earl of Arundel and Reginald of Saint-Valery, all spoke before the lord pope. Nearly all expressed one opinion: praise of the illustrious king of England as a Catholic prince, a devoted son and benefactor of the lord pope, a patron in his own sphere of the holy Roman Church, an honourable man, lover of peace, magnificent prince, reverer of ecclesiastical persons, and giver to the churches of his realm according to God and without simony. If now there were a disagreement between him and his archbishop, it was not the king’s fault. The God of peace and love, through the efforts of [Col. 0147D] the lord pope and the Roman Church, would, when it pleased Him, settle it well and clear their cloud. One of them, among other things, carefully recounted the power and wealth of the king of England. No one at all said anything against the archbishop’s person, or anything touching him, the king’s case, or the king himself.

To each the lord pope replied in the same manner: “It pleases us that the king of England should be such a man, so good. Would that God may increase in him the growth of virtues.” Three or four of the archbishop’s clerics were seated together at the feet of the lord pope. When they were capable of speaking for their lord, the lord pope restrained them, saying that there was no need, since nothing was being said against the archbishop.

The earl of Arundel spoke more effectively and more rhetorically than the others, [Col. 0148A] amid universal favour, and carried every point. In private they whispered in the lord pope’s ears about deposing the archbishop, trying to influence the pope with very great promises. Finally they added that the king would establish and confirm in perpetuity that the annual penny of St Peter—which in England was then paid only by villeins bound to the soil, and not even by all of them—should be paid by every inhabitant of the land, from every house from which smoke issued, in cities, castles, boroughs, and villages. The annual revenue of the Roman Church in England would thereby increase, beyond its present amount, to one thousand pounds of silver.

But when they found the lord pope unmoved and a strict guardian of what was honourable, and since they had been ordered not to remain at the curia longer than three days or to wait for the archbishop in order to pursue the cases, they received leave and blessing and returned.

But then, one day, on the other bank of a certain river, they saw more than three hundred mounted men of the archbishop’s company going to the lord pope. By common counsel they sent back one of the king’s clerics, Guy, dean of Waltham, to see and hear how the arrival of the archbishop of Canterbury was likely to be received in the Roman court. As the archbishop of Canterbury approached Sens, a great part of the cardinals rode out to meet him and receive him joyfully.

The lord pope rose at his entrance and received him with a kiss, tears, and embraces, with fatherly compassion; he consoled him with abundant reverence and encouragement. On the vigil of the following Christmas, [Col. 0148C] the king of England received his envoys at Marlborough, along with one of the lord pope’s own envoys. But the king, relentless in his purpose, ordered that, on the next day, Christmas Day itself, the archbishop should immediately be stripped of all possessions; that the Church of Canterbury, with all its lands and appurtenances, and all churches and revenues of all the archbishop’s clerics, should be taken into his hand; and that all the archbishop’s kinsmen and clerics or lay members of his household should be outlawed and expelled from his realm.

On the second day of Christmas, the king’s officers came to London, among them a certain Ranulf de Broc,

more savage than all others in wickedness. [Col. 0148D] To this most cruel layman and most bitter enemy of the archbishop, the king entrusted that holy Church of Canterbury, the chief see of the English, to be guarded—or rather, to be destroyed. This man, with several others, executed the royal command: they did what was ordered, and worse than what was ordered. Summoned outside the city, at Lambeth, in the archbishop’s own house, all his kinsmen found in London were sworn into exile: at the first wind coming from land, they were to leave the sea-port and their native soil and go by a direct route to the archbishop himself—so that they too, his flesh, might mortify his flesh, add sorrows to his sorrows, and that as many of his people as appeared before him, expelled for his sake, so many swords of their expulsion might pierce through his soul.

No accumulation of possessions can be as pleasant as departure is grievous. His kinsfolk of both sexes emigrated, and infants—some in cradles, others hanging at their mothers’ breasts. All his clerics and servants who were found did likewise; so too did those who had received him, wandering and fleeing from the king’s face in England, into lodging for a single night. But what then? Noble France, taking pity, received them all: the king of France himself took some; archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, earls, barons, provosts, and castellans each took some. Nuns received the women and the cradles. Noble men divided among themselves these poor exiles of Jesus Christ: the scattered company of the good archbishop, his desolate household. And none among those noble Frenchmen lacked what he needed, for they had not forgotten beneficence and fellowship. By what offerings God is won!

[Col. 0149B] The good exile, Thomas, archbishop and servant of Jesus Christ, privately confessed to the lord pope that he had sinned in having been elected with the prior approval of the king of England; likewise, that at Clarendon he had consented to the king’s enactments, contrary to divine decrees. It is said that he renounced the archbishopric into the lord pope’s hand, regarding himself as unworthy of it on these grounds, and that the lord pope kept it thus for three days and afterwards restored it to him. Having understood in confession the archbishop’s life and his inward and more severe penitence, the pope admitted him to a deeper and purer affection, knowing him to be a just and holy man, striving toward the summit of perfection by God’s grace and the aid of his inward virtues.

After remaining for some time with the lord pope, the archbishop, by his counsel and will, went down to Pontigny [Col. 0149C] to reside there: namely, to the abbey of Cistercian monks, who were hospitable and generous in providing necessities for him, his many clerics, and his household. During almost the whole seven-year period of his exile, the archbishop devoted himself to cultivating penitence, cleansing conscience, and sanctifying life. After the celebration of masses and contemplation of divine things, he also gave himself to the study of letters, especially Holy Scripture, to writing books, and to seeking privileges from the lord pope.

In all the libraries of whatever churches in France, he heard of no book of antiquity or approved authority which he did not have copied, and no privilege which he did not seek for his Church. Thus at no earlier time had the Church of Canterbury been so enriched and ennobled with excellent volumes and privileges as he eventually filled it. The archbishop sought to bear with equanimity the neediness of his own exile and that of his people. Stripped of all his goods and awaiting the hand of another’s mercy, he preferred the freedom of exile to servitude at home, and bore it patiently. He cast his care upon the Lord, and He nourished him. The Lord gave him favour in the sight of all flesh.

The exiled archbishop held the same view as Teucer: “A homeland is wherever a man fares well”; and that of Naso:

> Every soil is a homeland to the brave.

O England, how highly you must be valued, from which good and [Col. 0150A] religious men are driven out, when due liberty is denied to good prelates and a cruel necessity of emigration is imposed! Albucius, exiled from Athens, pursued philosophy with a most even mind. This would not have happened to him had he remained quietly in the state and obeyed Epicurus’ laws.

When news was brought to the exiled archbishop of the death of any of his nephews or relatives, he was not disturbed; when it concerned one of his clerics, messengers to the lord pope, he concealed his grief poorly. In one case he found consolation in the common necessity of bearing the human condition: that life must be harvested from all like crops and earth returned to earth. In the other, he praised the virtue proper to each person and lamented fate.

[His clerics: some were exiles with him beyond their native land. Their fathers, mothers, brothers, and wealthier kinsmen were compelled after them to swear exile and to present themselves to the archbishop. Others remained behind and did not follow him. William of Salisbury, a priest among them, was seized and held for half a year in Croft Castle. Three wealthier men fixed the price of their ransom: Stephen of Elratoria, one hundred pounds; later, on another occasion, Alfred of Walthamstow, one hundred pounds; Thurstan of Cromdon, one hundred marks—and he also spent one whole day in a filthy thieves’ prison in London. Others wandered and lived as fugitives in England; for a long time their relatives and friends were afraid to see them, it was dangerous to speak with them, and unlawful to help them with lodging or food. For the younger exiles, or those undeservedly proscribed into the hands of hunger, many Frenchmen petitioned the king in pious [Col. 0150C] compassion. The king of France took in some; the empress, mother of the king of England, some; the count of Flanders some; and other bishops and earls of France others.

William son of Stephen obtained peace through a prayer which he composed and gave to the king in the chapel at Bruhulla. This, moreover, is that prayer, belonging to the lord king of England himself.

King of all ages, king of the heavenly height,  
Ruler of heaven, ruler of earth, most high King of kings:  
You who rule the sea also, disturb it and stir it up,  
And when you please, it lies still; you calm its motion.  

You created, you formed, heaven, earth, and seas;  
All things which you made and established, you govern.  

[Col. 0150D] Every good thing is your gift, Almighty One;  
Every pleasing thing your gift, Lord of lords.  

### On the blessedness of the good

You crown and endow with manifold glory  
Those who live in the world a simple life with a pure heart.  
They are made blessed and crowned in the realms above the moon,  
Whose minds burn with the fire of the Holy Spirit.  

### On the evil and the punishments of the evil

The sinner who does not set the Lord as his helper,  
Exalted and lifted above the cedars of Lebanon,  
You plunge into the infernal, Gehenna-like furnace.  
In the dark prison of Avernus, of hell,  
You hold confined the guilty who dared to despise you, God.  
There the guilty, by God’s command, as the form of their sentence,  
[Col. 0151A] mourn, shiver, burn, screech, and are tortured on every side.  
There is fear, there weeping, there gnashing of teeth.  
There every punishment is full of the voices of groaning men.  
Here are pains more grievous than other pains;  
Here torturers more wicked than other torturers.  

### Acknowledgement and adoration of God

My God, I, guilty, humble myself before you.  
True God, have mercy on your adopted son.  
Your suppliant, your servant, most merciful God,  
I adore you and implore the gift of your grace.  

King of heaven, receive me, called king of the English.  
Rule the king, who cannot rule himself by his own law.  
To reign is to minister to you with all one’s heart,  
[Col. 0151B] to obey and serve beneath your rule.  
May I, your knight, avoid the base acts of sins;  
May I extinguish the ever-renewed incitements of lusts.  
May I reject the false, pleasant, habitual things of the rich and exalted.  

### Self-accusation

I do not earnestly seek, with a pure heart, to love you as God.  
I value little, scarcely attend to, how I conduct myself.  
I glory too much in the fleeting things of this present light;  
Lingering overmuch in sins, I die in them.  
I have wandered and sinned, I confess, my Lord.  
I have rashly violated the just laws of chastity.  
The scars of my crimes have stunk and festered,  
Of one reckoned and feigned among those going down into the pit.  
I have all too securely broken the law of honour and chastity;  
My life has slept too long amid evils.  

[Col. 0151C] Do not rebuke me, unclean as I am, according to my sins—  
You who humble the proud, the wounded—these and those.  
But, corrected and regarded by your grace, O God,  
Grant me to praise and love heavenly things.  
Cleanse and amend all that I have committed.  
Give me the hope of salvation, the substance of virtue, an innocent life;  
Grant me the gifts of chastity and purity.  

### Prayer against anger

Whenever I boil over in fierce anger of mind,  
Dear God, restrain in me what I cannot restrain.  

### Against covetousness

Let it not be my concern to take away anyone’s rights  
Or to tear up the boundaries of my neighbours.  
Although they may overcome me in wealth, arms, or intelligence,  
[Col. 0151D] in the splendours of a [Bragnani?] king, or of a pagan king,  
We possess what we have when we do not covet other things;  
Unless I first seize those cities, castles, and villages,  
May I not feel them absent from me or lacking to me.  
The towers of kings and the possessions of the poor fall in like destruction;  
The man full of wealth and the needy man fall by an equal death.  

### Prayer for his heirs

Grant that my heirs may ascend the throne of the realm after me,  
And, with your protection, govern the kingdom in a peaceful state.  

### For his clergy

Grant that my clergy may choose what is right and lawful with sincerity,  
And love you, God, with a wholly devout mind.  
May they live so good a life that they please you;  
May they furnish to us a rule and pattern of life.  

### For his people

[Col. 0152A]

May every member of the people entrusted to my rule  
Be directed and subjected to your governance.  
Attend to them, defend them, make yourself their shield—  
You whose sceptre and kingdom rule the nations.  
Take away wars and the scourges of your wrath;  
Spare us, repel our enemies, grant us peace.  
Human strength is vain: you know what is in man.  
For we are not saved, Lord, by our little arms.  
Strength, often tried and confidently relying on free aid,  
Retreats, falls back upon itself, and is powerless without counsel;  
But from your throne heavenly strength comes as a gift,  
Through which victory over the enemy is given and achieved.  

### For the fruits of the earth

May our sowings, made tenfold, gladden us with their crop;  
[Col. 0152B] may our cultivated fields multiply abundance through a plentiful harvest.  
May we use and enjoy temporal goods in such a way  
That we may rejoice and delight with you in heavenly things.  

### For his dead

Have pity on the souls of my relatives;  
Absolve and free them from the stains of their sins.  

### For the living and the dead

To all faithful persons, living and dead, Lord,  
Grant a peaceful and blessed life in heaven. Amen!

Around the first completed year of his exile, when the king’s anger ought by then to have cooled, the good archbishop wrote to him that exhortatory letter, “With desire I have desired,” etc. See the alphabetical index of letters.

[Col. 0152C] Certain religious men of France petitioned the king of England, when he had returned to Normandy and those regions, on the archbishop’s behalf; but they found him inexorable. The archbishop wrote very many letters to his fellow bishops, sometimes to all jointly, sometimes separately to individuals, urging them to recover the Spirit of God and, casting aside earthly fear, to set themselves as a wall before the house of God.

Gilbert of London repeatedly wrote back to him. He also frequently sought to persuade the lord pope in that cause, hoping, after royal blood had conquered, to conquer it in turn: that the pope might incline more readily to the king’s side, and that, on the archbishop’s account, he might say nothing harsh against the king; lest perhaps, in that general schism, the king with all his lands might join the opposing party [Col. 0152D] supporting the apostate emperor, and then, to use his own phrase, the lord pope might “go wholly into lamentations.” There would be enough men to receive the churches and pastoral staffs of the English king’s bishops from the hand and obedience of the idol.

This same bishop had received from the king’s hand the revenues and churches of the archbishop’s proscribed clerics to keep. Although he could without penalty have given very great comfort to many of them—either openly, distributing and giving his goods to poor and destitute clerics, or at least secretly, beneath the concealment of his cloak, strengthening their souls—he was neither a Lawrence nor a Sebastian. Robert Uscarl, his clerk and officer in collecting the revenues of those churches, a thrifty man, leased the churches for a smaller [Col. 0153A] rent so that, through the grants of leases, he might receive a greater sum for himself and greater gifts might come to him from them, which were not paid into the king’s treasury.

But the archbishop had excommunicated all who, either by their own presumption or by the king’s authority, occupied the goods or churches of the Church of Canterbury, or the personal goods of his clerics. Alas, they did not behave as excommunicated persons. Afterwards many of them died in the flower of youth, including Robert and Nigel of Saltcote, the king’s seal-bearers. Some persons excommunicated by the archbishop were wounded in their flesh by a grievous ulcer and died as though struck by God, such as Robert, vice-archdeacon of Canterbury, and the priest of Chierlewda.

The bishop of London, severely rebuked by the lord pope, resigned to the king, near the end of the year, his charge of those churches. The archbishop, I say, most earnestly urged his suffragans in letters he sent out to remain united with him and with his mother Church of Canterbury, lest through their connivance or dissimulation the king rage so fiercely against the Church of Canterbury and oppress the clergy of England with such unjust laws.

[There at Pontigny, when one day the same blessed Thomas had celebrated Mass, and after Mass had remained for some while prostrate before the altar in prayers, tears, and groans, as was his custom, he heard a voice: “O Thomas, Thomas!” And he said: “O Lord, who are you?” And the Lord said to him: “I [Col. 0153C] am Jesus Christ, your Lord and your brother: my Church shall be glorified in your blood, and you shall be glorified in me.” Shortly afterward, rising and about to depart, he who thought that he alone had heard this saw the abbot of the place, who was his confidant, standing nearby and awaiting him beneath a column of that church. When he realized that the abbot had heard it, he made him promise to tell no one while he himself lived. After the archbishop’s martyrdom, that man revealed these things.]

He also condemned in writing those Constitutions of Clarendon, and released from their observance all who had assented to them. Stirred by these and similar actions, the king caused the archbishop to be removed from Pontigny; for the monks feared that, if they continued to retain the archbishop as though an enemy of the king, the king of England would expel from his lands all the countless members of their order whom he held in his territories [Col. 0153D].

In the king’s chapel, during that festive chant, *Christus vincit* (“Christ conquers”), when they came to the verse concerning the archbishop, they did not say: “the archbishop, peace, salvation, and life.” Likewise, at the solemn prayers after his sermons or in his synods, the bishop of London, addressing either the clergy or, on feast days, the people, did not name the archbishop so that the Church might pray to God for him when there was no prospect of peace between the king and the archbishop; but when there was a report of their reconciliation, he then made mention of the archbishop—a practice noted by many hearers. Similarly, afterward, when the kings of England, father and son, were at peace, they said in the prayer at Mass: “Grant to our kings [Col. 0154A] …”; but when they were at variance, they said: “Grant to our king,” namely, to the elder king, possessor of the kingdom, “to cultivate knowingly the triumph of your power,” etc. Nor were there lacking those who often noticed such things.

Then the most pious and God-worthy Louis, king of the French, did what he had wished and had offered to do for Saint Thomas from the beginning: he received him into his protection, and from his revenues in the Sens district granted him money, provisions, and wine for his support—whatever his servants wished to receive. He also frequently honored him with gifts and presents, and by his personal presence when visiting; and sometimes, when Thomas or his clerks gave him thanks, he would say: “Do not thank me. Never have I given my bread to any person or persons in a way that has been so pleasing to me.”

That archbishop of Sens, William [Col. 0154B]—son of Count Theobald, nephew of King Henry the Elder of England, brother of the queen and of three counts of France—though young in years, surpassed them by the gravity of his conduct. By the favor of his merits he had deserved to hold two noble churches, Sens in title and Chartres in commendam. He cherished the archbishop with true love; so too did all the clergy and knighthood of France. Thomas resided outside the city of Sens, at Saint Columba’s.

By now the lord pope had begun to write more urgently to the king of England on Thomas’s behalf, since so much time had elapsed that the hatred and indignation ought already to have expired, had they been mortal. After many most gentle written exhortations, he sent certain envoys. Thus, alternating between these means, he tried to recall the king from the heat of his mind. But when the door was not opened to him as he knocked, he sometimes, though moderately, added threats, carefully impressing upon him that he had borne with him long enough; that patience had summoned him to amendment; and that he could no longer endure him in this manner without jeopardizing his own soul’s salvation. At times he also gave the archbishop counsel and permission to take action against his rebellious sons. He further honored and exalted the archbishop by granting him the legation and primacy of England, so that whatever Thomas lacked through the loss of his possessions [Col. 0154C] might be made up by an increase of dignities, and what he had less of in revenues he might recover in honors.

He sent to the bishop of London the lord pope’s letters concerning Thomas’s legation and his own letters as legate, both sets [Col. 0154D] containing commands: the bishop was to announce to the bishops of England that Thomas was the pope’s legate, as his dean, and was to forward the letters which he wrote to each individual bishop. The bishop refused this obedience. On another occasion Thomas had previously summoned this same bishop by letters addressed to him, admonishing, ordering, and commanding him to come and, as his suffragan and one pledged to the Church of Canterbury, to assist him with counsel and aid in the cause of the Church. The bishop would not do so.

This same bishop had once absolved Alan of Neuville, who had been excommunicated by the archbishop and was intending to go to Jerusalem, without the knowledge either of the lord pope or of the archbishop himself, although Alan had sworn that he would visit the lord pope on the way and receive from him the remedies of whatever penance was to be imposed.

[Col. 0155A] Roger, bishop of Worcester, having been summoned and having undertaken to follow the archbishop and to stand with his father and lord in counsel and aid in the cause of the Church, obtained leave once to cross the sea. Under the pretext of studies, being younger in age, he stayed overseas, sometimes at the king’s court, to which he was most closely connected by kinship. This is his celebrated praise and splendid memorial: alone among the bishops of England, he dared and wished to share exile with his exiled father, to endure poverty with the poor man, to stand for the liberty of the Church, and in the day of cloud and darkness to resist the king in his errors. Whoever resists a friend in error becomes a more welcome friend when that friend comes to his senses.

The archbishop had at last excommunicated his archdeacon, Geoffrey Ridel, after repeatedly reproving and summoning him for disobedience. [Col. 0155B] They reported this to the king, who nevertheless concealed the matter and paid no heed to it. The bishop of Worcester too, who came to court much later, was kindly received by the king. Indeed, the king gladly heard him, though he did not follow his counsel.

One day they entered the chapel; the king was about to hear Mass and stood in his place. The bishop was farther inside in his own place. Not long afterward the archdeacon of Canterbury entered. At the sight of him the bishop departed. The king was astonished, but understood the reason, and was swept by the prompting heat of anger. Yet he immediately sent a messenger to tell the bishop to return and explain why he had left. When the bishop had plainly stated the reason, the king again sent after him someone to say that he should leave the king’s land at once.

The bishop sent for his companions and attendants to follow him [Col. 0155C], and departed immediately, sending word to the king that he already had one foot in the stirrup—or whatever other name he might deign to give it—ready to leave his land; and he went. His people, having gathered their baggage and equipment, were now following him. After a considerable interval, as the angry king burst out into insulting and threatening words, someone said to him:

“Lord, what have you done? You have driven from your lands a bishop most closely joined to you in loyalty and blood. If it may be said, you have not acted well. Moreover, you have rendered to the archbishop a service most welcome and most desired by him. The lord pope previously had no cause too just and evident for taking action against you; now he will make use of an occasion not sought but offered. You give sorrow to your friends [Col. 0155D] and joy to your enemies, in proscribing an innocent man and expelling a bishop.”

Persuaded by these and similar words, the king relented and sent someone spurring his horse to recall the bishop. The bishop refused to return. The king again sent others on very swift horses, and a third set of messengers, among whom was a count, either to coax the bishop back or to bring him back against his will and under compulsion. He returned, and spoke more freely to the king. While he remained at court, that archdeacon never entered the chapel or thrust himself into the king’s presence when the bishop was present.

The bishop of Hereford likewise, summoned by letters from the lord archbishop, came to the sea in order to cross; but, prevented from crossing, he grieved deeply. When he had returned home, amid the violence of that grief he was also struck by illness, choked, and breathed his last.

On one Palm Sunday, after the procession and sermon, the lord archbishop excommunicated at Clairvaux the bishop of London—summoned three times but irrevocably disobedient—in the presence of many religious and faithful servants of God, and likewise certain others residing in England or at the king’s court, for reasons set out in his surviving letters. [Col. 0156A] For whenever the archbishop excommunicated anyone, in the letters which he issued he stated their crimes, the reasons for their excommunication, and the laws or decrees appended thereto, so that it might be clear that he exercised no severity from the heat of anger, rashness, or personal enmity, but was moved over their transgressions rather by the dutiful affection of fatherhood.

The report immediately reached England: “Rumor

> Gains strength through mobility, and acquires power as it goes.”

As soon as he heard it, the bishop of London came into the city to the cathedral church. He summoned the canons and clergy of the city of London, as well as abbots, priors, and incumbents of neighboring churches; he publicly announced such a report concerning himself, declaring that he had been excommunicated, yet did not conduct himself as excommunicated, to the astonishment of prudent men. Not long afterward he summoned a general synod and proclaimed the same things, with no opponent replying to him—as though he himself had been absent, defended, and had not been summoned.

But a person to carry the archbishop’s letters of threefold citation, or any other summons, could hardly be found: so great a chasm had been fixed between them, not merely of sea and land but of the king’s anger and threats [Col. 0156B]. Nor could this formal process of citation be carried out by messenger where a messenger did not dare to declare either his own name or the archbishop’s. Moreover, the bishop maintained that he was not answerable or subject to the archbishop or Church of Canterbury. He said that he had formerly been bishop of Hereford and, in the name of that bishopric, had made profession to the Church of Canterbury; but that he was now released from that obedience, because he had been transferred to the Church of London, and the bishop of London had made no profession to Canterbury.

Further, he asserted that by the reckoning of the chronicles he himself ought to be archbishop. For in the time of the Britons, before the island had been conquered by the English, London had indeed been the metropolitan see. Thus he declaimed; but the case was presented with no opponent. Having heard him and left him to himself, each returned home.

He himself did not behave as excommunicated. Yet there was one who said to him privately that reports ought both to be believed and not believed. He had not yet heard or seen the letters of the sentence passed against him, and solely because of reports he was carried so far beyond himself and exposed his soul to such great peril, through his disobedience and his exertions in pursuing such a cause against the archbishop. He should wait until he heard the letters of the sentence pronounced; if he could not avoid hearing them. Meanwhile, by conducting himself as a Catholic, he should then take counsel.

The bishops and justiciars of England knew that people were being sought to carry such letters into England, and they had the seaports guarded with the utmost strictness. The prior of the Church of Canterbury withdrew from the Church [Col. 0157A]; the bishop of Rochester did likewise; likewise the bishop of London and his dean, lest, wavering between king and archbishop and faithful to neither side, they should receive such letters when they came to them . . . and fall into that whirlpool; if they did not receive them, Charybdis would swallow them.

The archbishop found a young man, unlearned but a layman, who, exposing himself to great danger yet not fearing to die for God, carried the letters of this sentence into England. On the renowned feast day of the Lord’s Ascension, a certain vicar named Vitalis, a God-fearing man and honorable priest, was celebrating at the high altar of the episcopal church of Saint Paul in London. While the offertory was being sung and the priest had offered the oblation of bread and wine and prepared the chalice, Berengar arrived and, kneeling [Col. 0157B], handed the priest the letters as though they were his offering. The priest, astonished, first stretched out his hand toward the offering and received them.

Berengar said: “Neither the bishop of this see nor the dean is here. I see that you are here as a minister of Jesus Christ. On behalf of God and of the lord pope, I deliver to you here the letters of the archbishop of Canterbury concerning the sentence passed upon the bishop of this Church, and also his letters to the dean, requiring that he and the clergy of this Church observe this sentence. And by God’s authority I tell you that, after this Mass, you are not to celebrate further until you show the bishop his letters and the dean his.”

He said this and went away amid the thick crowds of people, as was customary after the Gospel on a feast day, when they were returning home; for he had heard his Mass that morning at the parish churches [Col. 0157C]. There was some murmuring from those gathered nearer to the altar, who asked the priest whether the celebration of the divine offices had been interdicted in the city. When the priest answered, “No,” the people fell silent and did not question him further.

While the priest continued the celebration of Mass, Berengar was quietly and anxiously sought by the king’s officers both within and outside the city, at the crossings of the roads, but was not found at all. Later this same Berengar came to York with letters from the lord pope containing bitter charges, yet escaped unharmed.

A few days later the bishop of London and the dean came into the city. The clergy of the city and the senior citizens were summoned to the church. There, publicly before all, that priest Vitalis recounted the proceedings to the bishop [Col. 0157D] and offered him his letters, whose tenor was as follows: “[Excessus v.].” He likewise offered the dean his letters, which contained the following: “[Vest. n. d. la. pr. q. f.].” Both letters were read publicly.

From then on, by common counsel, the bishop conducted himself as excommunicated and reported what had happened to the king. The king replied to him in this manner: “[Audivi gr.].” The bishop crossed the sea and, through the intervention of the lord king and by the agency of his own envoys, obtained absolution from R., archbishop of Rouen, and R., bishop of Exeter, to whom the lord pope had delegated authority to absolve him by extraordinary power. He returned, together with certain bishops and envoys of the lord king and of himself who had come from the lord pope; and it was publicly proclaimed in the cathedral church that he had been absolved.

[Col. 0158A] Jocelin, bishop of Salisbury, had incurred the displeasure of the king of England. Seeking to win the king’s favor, he had granted the deanery of Salisbury to a clerk of the king, John of Oxford. Yet he had previously been forbidden by letters of the lord pope to grant that dignity to anyone without the knowledge and consent of his canons, some of whom, as leading men of the Church, were fellow-exiles with the archbishop. Therefore, by authority of the lord pope, the archbishop excommunicated him.

[And he did this fortified also by the example of the fourth predecessor of blessed Anselm, who, while in exile at Cluny, excommunicated the count of Meulan, whose counsel William II, king of England, employed against the liberty of the election of bishops and abbots, arrogating to himself the grant of pastoral staffs.]

He involved the bishop of London in the same sentence for the threefold disobedience noted in the letters, although the bishop had not been summoned and was absent and undefended. Hence the bishop of London himself afterward dared publicly and in synod to contend that the sentence did not bind him. But no one could be found to carry into England the archbishop’s letters of threefold citation or any other message sounding a harsh note. The archbishop also excommunicated certain barons and household clerks of the king for particular transgressions of their own, and ordered that they be publicly declared excommunicated. Thus indeed, before the lion, the cubs are sometimes beaten. A bearer for this sentence was scarcely found to take it into England.

A request was sent by the king of England to the lord pope for their absolution; he was now promising hope of peace. The pope wrote back that they should be absolved, and by someone other than the archbishop—an extraordinary measure indeed, but intended to soften the king. [Col. 0158C]

[On several occasions the king of England, by sending envoys to the lord pope, obtained absolution for certain of his barons whom the lord archbishop had excommunicated, indicating, as though from fear of death, that he was going to lead them in an army against Welsh enemies. On this occasion very many were at one time absolved at the church of Holy Trinity in London.]

For a time the pope also took from the archbishop his instrument—that is, his power to bind the king or his men—so that even in this way he might make the king victorious and incline him to the counsel of God and himself. Long held in suspense by this hope and finally disappointed, the lord pope, when his oil did not heal their infirmities, again opened the archbishop’s mouth and again attempted to pour in wine.

The angry king ordered that the annual penny of Saint Peter in England be withheld for himself. Again, taking more subtle precaution in the end, he ordered that no one crossing the sea into England should be admitted unless he possessed the king’s letters, lest someone perhaps carry into England a sentence of interdict which he knew the archbishop possessed.

For their part, the bishop of London and the other bishops of England, to prevent the archbishop from imposing any interdict upon their persons or upon the realm, lodged appeals and wrote to the archbishop for almost an entire year without fifteen days, but did not pursue them. Once the year had elapsed, they renewed the appeals and notified the archbishop, thwarting his authority by such evasions. They refused to understand that appeal is a human invention, belonging to civil law [Col. 0159A], introduced to repel unjust burdens threatening our possessions or bodies. Thus Saint Paul also, fearing for his body when he was being arrested, said: “I appeal to Caesar.”

“*I appeal*” has its place in such matters; nor does it seem to wise Catholics that it ought to be extended to abolish obedience, nullify the greater ecclesiastical authority, or crush excommunication, which derives not from human law but from the mouth of Jesus Christ, who gave this power to his apostles when he said: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose shall be loosed.” Far be it that human law should prejudice divine law, or that what is a human invention should nullify that which is divinely instituted!

[Col. 0159B] Meanwhile, very many of the bishops of England passed away, so that besides the archbishopric of Canterbury the king held six vacant bishoprics in his hand in England. Some, worn out by age, were at the point of death; others had died.

For his part, the lord king of France and the magnates of France, often at the exhortation of the lord pope and often moved by their own spirit, observing the distress of the king and kingdom of England, repeatedly approached the king for the sake of peace. At length the king of England agreed that the archbishop of Canterbury should be summoned to a conference with them. Many conferences were held between them, but it will suffice to say something briefly about a few of them.

At the conference at La Planche, Cardinals William of Pavia and Otto, and the archbishop of Rouen [Col. 0159C], strongly pressed the archbishop. “The complaint about providence is old,” they said, “and the written royal customs have always been a source of contention between kings and archbishops of England. This is the chief point of dispute, the origin of all evils. Since you say that you love the peace of your Church above all things and execrate these customs, it will now be evident; you will now give certain proof. The peace of the Church lies in your hands. Will you renounce the archbishopric if the king renounces the customs?”

He replied: “These things are not weighed in an equal balance. I cannot renounce the archbishopric while preserving the honor of my Church and my own person; for this is unheard of among my predecessors. The king’s honor and the salvation of his soul are better preserved by renouncing than by retaining the customs. This is clear from the fact that the lord pope has condemned them, and you along with the Roman Church.”

When they could not catch him in this argument so as to make him renounce, they asked whether he would litigate before them against the king over the disputes that had arisen. They pretended to possess, though they did not possess, plenary authority in the case. He answered: “Yes, provided that restoration is first made in full.” They said: “That is impossible.” He replied: “It cannot otherwise be advantageous either to him or to the Church of God.” Then the bishops of England, with a year less fifteen days included, made an appeal, which the cardinals wrote to the lord pope.

At the conference at Montmirail, the king of England made such favorable promises to him through the mediators of peace that he was nearly induced [Col. 0160A] to submit himself altogether to the king’s will, so that the king would seem thus to have conquered. Supporting this position were the archbishops of Rheims, Sens, and Rouen; the king of France; bishops; and the abbot of Mont-Dieu, of the Carthusian order. They urged that he should not speak of the written customs of Clarendon. “For,” they said, “what need is there to speak of these? By your own writing, with the authority of the lord pope, you have condemned them and released all who had assented to them from their observance.”

At the conference on the following day he always retained the phrase: “saving the honor of God and the liberty of the Church.” All the persons named above were astonished. The king of England said: “All these qualifications must be absent. There shall be no sophistry here.” When the mediators mentioned above urged him to abandon these words and he did not comply, they departed as though in despair [Col. 0160B], leaving him as one who had deserted their counsel.

Returning to his companions, he said among other things: “God did him the highest honor that day, for which they especially ought to have given thanks to God: they had preserved in all things the honor of God, which all the others set aside.” But many of his companions, longing to return to their native land, were troubled because peace did not proceed and because, although the king offered him return and restoration, he adhered to these qualifications.

While returning from that conference, in the very retinue of the king of France, a certain clerk of his, Henry of Houghton, happened to be riding just before the archbishop. His horse stumbled and fell headlong. Henry then said clearly, so that the archbishop might hear, ironically to his horse: “Go on, [Col. 0160C] saving the honor of God and Holy Church and of my order.” The archbishop bore this painfully but remained silent.

After an interval, having drawn aside with his clerks so that their horses might breathe and sweat, he said to them: “Beloved companions, who have suffered everything with me, why do you think and speak so against me? Our return and restoration are indeed the least matter; the liberty of the Church, of which the king says nothing, is of far greater worth. I shall eventually receive peace, such that I shall be unable to receive a better; but never have you seen a market bargain so short.”

Nevertheless, later all the aforesaid men agreed with the judgment of the good Archbishop Thomas; they condemned their error, acknowledged him as a holy man and a strong athlete of God, and were henceforth more firmly bound and confirmed in love for him.

[Col. 0160D] At the conference at Montmartre, when the king of England had come to Saint-Denis for the sake of prayer and had placed upon the altar an excellent pallium and eighty gold coins as an offering, and had there been honorably received by the king of France and by all the clergy and knighthood who had come to meet him: afterward, when peace between him and the archbishop was discussed, and the archbishop was pressed and questioned upon the usual articles, he was always found unchanged. He sent the king his petition written on a schedule: that the rights of his Church of Canterbury and the possessions taken from himself, his clerks, and his men should be restored; that fraternal peace and liberty should be restored to the clergy of England; and that he himself would be faithful and devoted to the king as lord and king in all things, saving the honor of God, Holy Church [Col. 0161A], and his order.

The king did not agree to these terms. To satisfy those present, he offered to stand, in deciding their case, by the judgment of the clergy of France or of the scholars of Paris; but he said nothing about first making restitution. He then withdrew to Paris to see the queen and Philip, the king’s son, as though he had thus scorned the archbishop and broken off the conference. The archbishop took this ill, saying among other things that perhaps he would be summoned three times before he came again for further discussion. As they parted from one another in this discordant fashion, days passed. At length it was reported to the lord pope that reconciliation was not proceeding.

A conference had been appointed to take place at Pont de l’Isère. On the appointed day the archbishop of Sens and the bishop of Bethlehem were present; [Col. 0161B] the king of England refused to come there, but sent them word through a messenger from their party that, if they would come to Gisors, he would speak with them. Thus their journey and the archbishop’s expectation were frustrated.

The king, counts, and magnates of France at one time approached the king of England on behalf of the archbishop’s principal clerks who had remained with him, asking at least that he restore their revenues. If they served the archbishop for the sake of his advancement, this was not surprising. The dispute between himself and the archbishop did not concern them: while the two of them were at odds with each other, those clerks were suffering punishment without deserving it. The king of England consented that those clerks should come to him, with safe conduct, secure standing, and safe return guaranteed. They came to Angers at Easter, on Low Sunday; for the king had there celebrated the Easter feast. One day he sat down to hear those clerks among his household.

The first summoned to enter was John of Salisbury. After greeting the king, he first asked for peace and for the restoration of his ecclesiastical benefices, since, though aware of the king’s displeasure, he had deserved it in no respect, and was prepared to be devoted, subject, and faithful to the king as to his earthly lord, saving his order. On the king’s behalf it was said to him that he had been born in the king’s land, had there his own dependants and close kin, and had grown from the goods of the king’s land into a rich harvest of many virtues and possessions; therefore, as a native of the king’s realm, he ought to be faithful to the king against the archbishop and all men. The following form of oath was proposed to him: if he would swear that he would be faithful to the king in respect of his life, limbs, and temporal honour against all men; and, specifically, that he would lawfully maintain the king’s written customs and royal dignities, whatever the lord pope, his archbishop, or his bishop might do.

He granted everything else, but hesitated over the archbishop’s customs. He said that from youth he had been supported from the possessions of the Church of Canterbury, and had sworn obedience to the lord pope and to his own archbishop. He could neither fail the Church of Canterbury nor his lord the archbishop, nor undertake observance of any customs against the lord pope and the Church of Canterbury. But although he declared himself ready, together with the lord pope and the archbishop, [Col. 0162A] to accept what they accepted and reject what they rejected, the king would not agree. He was ordered to withdraw.

Master Herbert of Bosham was summoned and entered. The king said to his men of him: “Now you will see a proud man enter.” He was indeed tall in stature and handsome in appearance, and also rather splendidly dressed: he wore a tunic and cloak of a certain green Auxerre cloth, the cloak hanging from his shoulders in German fashion down to his ankles, suitably adorned with the things proper to it. Having given the aforesaid greeting to the king, he sat down. He was addressed in the same manner as John, and began to answer much as John had; but he held firm concerning the archbishop, fidelity, and those written customs.
