He highly commended the archbishop’s upright life and his fidelity to the king, saying that he alone was faithful to the king who does not permit the king to err where he can call him back. For one who says what pleases a king, conceals his error—if it is an error—and whom his silence convicts, is not faithful to the king: he abandons fidelity and lies against his oath. Therefore, he said, he could not swear that true fidelity to the king unless he were willing to remain the king’s inseparable companion and rebuke him wherever he ought justly to be rebuked; and he knew the king to be of such disposition and temper that he would neither listen to nor tolerate this.

Concerning the customs he said what John had said, adding that he found it remarkable that the king had caused them to be written down. “For,” he said, “there are also in other kingdoms certain evil customs against the Church of God, but they are not written down; and because they are not written, there is greater hope that, God inspiring their kings, [Col. 0162C] they may be abolished.”

Wishing to catch him in his words, the king said: “And what evil customs are there in the realm of our lord the king of the French?”

Herbert replied: “The customs of toll and passage-dues, which are exacted even from clerics and pilgrims. Again, when a bishop dies, the goods of his household, his vessels, all movable property, even windows and doors, are carried off and become the king’s. Again, perhaps there are similar or other evil customs in the realm of the king of the Germans, but they are not written down.”

The king said: “Why do you detract from him in the matter of title, calling him not emperor of the Germans?”

Herbert replied: “He is king of the Germans; but when he writes, he always styles himself ‘Augustus, emperor of the Romans.’”

The king said: “Shameful indeed! Great is the indignation. What is this priest’s son doing, disturbing my kingdom and troubling my peace?”

Herbert replied: “I am doing nothing of the kind. Nor am I a priest’s son, because I was not begotten while my father was a priest, although he afterwards became a priest; nor is anyone a king’s son except one whom a king has begotten.”

Then one of the barons sitting by, Jordan Tarsun, said: “Whatever man’s son he may be, I wish I had given half my land for him to be my son.” The king received this remark favourably and was silent. Shortly afterwards he ordered Herbert to depart, and he withdrew.

Philip de Calva, a Londoner by birth, who two years before the archbishop’s exile had studied at Tours, hearing lectures on the divine page and teaching law, a man of the first rank in learning and most eloquent, but ill; and therefore neither accompanying the archbishop in person, nor being sent to Rome, [Col. 0163A] nor involving himself in the quarrel between the king and him—was summoned and entered. The king had been informed there of what was said about him, and he had good intercessors who told the king that, when he heard that on account of the archbishop he had been deprived of his possessions in England, he had said: “Good God, what does this good king seek from me?” The king was thus persuaded; and, lest he should grant no favour at all, he remitted the proposed oath for this man, gave him his peace, granted restoration of his possessions, and, rising, turned to other business.

At length it was reported to the lord pope that reconciliation was making no progress. The archbishop had likewise received from the lord pope authority to pronounce sentence against the king’s person; but he intended rather, by patience and pressure, to recall him to repentance and satisfaction.

[Col. 0163B] When he heard this, the king sent to the lord pope a messenger, Reginald Lombard, to negotiate with him either concerning transfer of the archbishop to the title of another archiepiscopal church—since the lord pope, though repeatedly and vainly urged to depose him, had always been found immovable and contemptuous of money—or concerning revocation of the power entrusted to the archbishop to take action against the king, or concerning a postponement of the sentence to be pronounced, on the hope of the archbishop’s peace and reconciliation, which the king permitted the lord pope to entertain. Reginald did indeed obtain this last concession from the lord pope.

Again and again, by gentle addresses and exhortations, the lord pope pressed the king. “Since he makes no progress by this course, he threatens to lay the axe [Col. 0163C] to the root of the tree.” Understanding this without doubt, the king made all England swear, from every layman twelve or fifteen years old and upwards, against the lord pope and the archbishop, that they would not receive their letters nor obey their commands; and that, if anyone were found carrying their letters, he should be delivered to the authorities as a capital enemy of the king’s crown.

Yet a certain noble lady, daughter of Baldwin de Reivers, [Note: [Col. 0163D] “Byervers,” Spark’s edition.] acted manfully and, zealous for obedience to God, neither swore that oath of apostasy nor permitted any of her men to swear it. The archbishop of York did the same freely. The other bishops who had remained in England—alas!—allowed that oath to be sworn in their dioceses. Hearing this, the archbishop, deeply grieved by such error and apostasy, secretly sent letters to certain God-fearing men and declared absolved from the oath all who had sworn unwillingly. The king caused the sea-ports to be watched with the utmost strictness.

Meanwhile he returned to England and, by the laying-on of the hand of the archbishop of York, the aforesaid Roger, caused his son Henry to be crowned at London, suddenly and contrary to the expectation and opinion of nearly the whole kingdom. The archbishop of Canterbury had turned his eyes to Providence in this event, and had obtained letters from the lord pope, delivered on the Saturday of that coronation to the archbishop of York and the bishop of London, forbidding them or any other bishops of England, unless he had been summoned back for the purpose, [Col. 0164A] to lay hands upon the young king in crowning him; for this coronation belonged to the Church of Canterbury. Nevertheless, on the eve of the feast of Saints Vitus and Modestus he was crowned.

The king immediately crossed back overseas. But before this, when the king of England had resolved to crown his son, he informed the bishop of Worcester, then overseas, ordering him to return home from overseas and be present, with the bishops who very few indeed remained in England, at the coronation of his kinsman. Yet he did not tell him that he wished the young man crowned by the laying-on of hands of the archbishop of York. Hoping for better things, the bishop consented and came to the sea-port of Dieppe. The king had arrived in England. The queen, who had remained in Normandy, and Richard de Humet, justiciar of the Normans, sent letters to the bishop of Worcester at the said port forbidding him [Col. 0164B] to cross the sea; they also sent letters to the provost and to the ship-owners and ferrymen, ordering that they should neither carry that bishop into England nor permit him to cross.

They understood clearly that the bishop would not allow the king to be crowned, while the archbishop of Canterbury lived, in the province of Canterbury by the hand of the archbishop of York; for the consecration of a new king belonged to Canterbury’s dignity. Thus forbidden to cross, the bishop remained in Normandy.

After that coronation, the king, as has been said, immediately crossed back into Normandy. Beyond Falaise, the bishop of Worcester [Note: [Col. 0164D] “Wig.” omitted in Spark’s edition.] came to him three miles outside Falaise. The king showed him an angry face and at once burst into insulting language:

“Now it is plain that you are a traitor. I myself ordered you to attend the coronation of my son, and told you the day; you refused to attend. In this you have plainly shown that you love neither me nor the advancement of my son. It is clear indeed that you favour my enemy more and hate me and mine. But the revenues of your bishopric shall no longer remain to you. I shall tear them from your hands, because you have proved yourself unworthy both of the bishopric and of every benefice. You were never truly the son of my good uncle Count Robert, who brought up both you and me in that castle, and ensured that we there were taught the first elements of conduct and letters.”

Secure in his innocence, the bishop simply and modestly recounted the facts to the king: how he had come as far as the port and how he had received letters prohibiting him from [Col. 0164D] crossing the sea. The king, not believing him and inflamed with the greatest anger, said: “The queen is in that castle of Falaise, and perhaps Richard de Humet is there or will shortly be near. Do you name them as the authors of this?”

The bishop replied: “By no means the queen, lest perhaps she conceal the truth out of reverence or fear of you and you rage more fiercely against me. But if she confesses the truth, you will rage irreverently against that noble lady. It is not worth so much to me that she should hear one bitter word from your mouth on this account. I would rather that this had happened than that I had attended that coronation, which was unjust and against God—not because of the person crowned, but because of the presumption of the one who crowned him. Had I been present, I would not have allowed him to crown him there.

“You say that I was not the son of Count Roger. I do not know; but I was the son of my mother, with whom my father acquired the right and inheritance of the whole earldom and honour. Yet by your conduct you do not show a fitting return: my father, that Count Roger, was your uncle; he brought you up with due honour; for your sake he fought King Stephen for sixteen years, endured him as enemy and assailant, and was at last captured in battle for your sake. Had you recalled to mind these and similar services of my father, you would not have reduced my brothers so greatly to ruin and destruction.

“You have reduced my brother the count’s tenure and honour of a thousand knights—which your grandfather, the illustrious King Henry, gave whole to my father—to a fief of two hundred and forty knights. You have allowed my other, younger brother, the valiant knight R., as he is called, to become so poor and needy that, because of poverty, abandoning secular knighthood and life, he gave himself to serve the Hospital of Jerusalem forever and took its habit and rule. Thus you know how to enrich your household kinsmen and friends; thus you are accustomed to reward those who have served you well.

“Why do you threaten me with evils, because you wish to strip me of the benefices of my bishopric? Am I disturbed as you please? I am not disturbed. Let them be yours, if what you unjustly receive from the archbishopric, six vacant bishoprics, and many abbeys does not suffice you—alms of your fathers, good kings, and patrimonies of Jesus Christ—which you divert [Col. 0165C] to your secular uses, certainly at peril to your soul.”

These and similar words were spoken in the hearing of all who rode alongside the king as attendants on either side. A certain knight of Aquitaine, who did not know the bishop, said to his companions: “And who is this who speaks in such a manner?” He was told that he was a bishop. He replied: “Indeed it has gone fortunately for the king that he is a priest. If he were a knight, he would not leave the king two acres of land.”

Another man, seeking to please the king, reproached the bishop more bitterly. Hearing this and taking it ill, the king turned upon him and disgraced him with the grossest abuse, saying among other things: “Do you suppose, wretch, that because I may say whatever I wish to my kinsman and bishop, you or any other person may therefore dishonour him in words [Col. 0165D] or assail him with threats? I can scarcely keep my hands from your eyes. Let it be unlawful for you and all others to utter a word against the bishop.”

They came to their lodgings. After dinner the king and bishop spoke privately and peacefully, including about peace with the archbishop.

At one time a great disturbance had been raised in England by the king’s justiciars, who laid a sort of charge against certain abbots and ecclesiastical persons in England: that they had sent counted money to the exiled archbishop, the king’s enemy, as they called him. They did not dare make this charge against the bishop of Winchester, who, by frequent visits and timely transmissions of gold and silver, had out of a pious feeling of compassion relieved the poverty of his lord the archbishop, whom he had ordained.

Of those against whom the charge had been brought, some who had indeed done this denied it under pressure of fear, so as to have peace; they bought that peace with their own money. One man dared openly say: “Why do you accuse us of performing a work of mercy for a needy exile and our father, and of giving him money of our own? He is neither religious nor sufficiently Christian who neglects one in calamity, does not sympathise with the afflicted, and does not pity the poor. You say that he is the king’s enemy; we do not know this, nor do we believe it. Yet even if he were our enemy, we are commanded for God’s sake to love an enemy, to feed the hungry, and to give drink to the thirsty.”

It was reported that someone had said or written to the king of England concerning the [Col. 0166B] archbishop: “Why is he kept excluded? He will be kept better enclosed than excluded.” The saying was sufficiently clear to one who understood it. Therefore the king hurried to a conference concerning peace, and there granted everything previously denied that had been requested of him.

Yet first he had caused his son to be crowned so suddenly because of some eventuality that might occur; and if anything evil happened, the realm ought not to be punished on his account, since he himself would not be king. This was an inexpressible secret fold of the king of England’s heart; God knows it, “who searches the reins and hearts,” not I. But those who believed from his deeds before the event, in the event, and after the event understood this of him.

Likewise the king of France and the lord pope’s envoys suddenly pressed the king of England about reconciliation and peace with the archbishop, [Col. 0166C] because the lord pope could neither endure nor wish any longer to overlook the king’s great excesses, the great misery of the archbishop and his fellow-exiles, and the sufferings of the afflicted English Church.

The king consented to be entreated that same summer. [Note: [Col. 0165D] “Soon after,” Spark’s edition.] Therefore, before the sixth year of Archbishop Thomas’s exile was completed, on the eve of Blessed Mary Magdalene, the archbishops of Rheims, Sens, Rouen, and Tyre assembled at Fontevraud; [Note: [Col. 0166D] “Freitevile,” Spark’s edition.] so did the lord king of the French, the bishop of Nevers, the abbot of Grandmont in the place of the lord pope, the bishop of Poitiers, and nearly all the bishops of Normandy; and nearly all the counts and magnates of Gaul, to restore peace between the king of England and the archbishop of Canterbury. None of the bishops of England was there [Col. 0166D] except Roger of Worcester.

That very day, when the king of England came to the lodging of the king of the French, after they had spoken privately, the king of England shortly afterwards said jokingly: “And tomorrow your robber will have his peace; indeed, he will have a good one.”

The king of France replied: “What robber, I ask, among the saints of France?”

The king of England said: “That archbishop of Canterbury of ours.”

The king of France replied: “Would that he were ours as he is yours. It will be an honour to you before God and men if you make a good peace with him, and we shall be grateful to you.”

These things were said publicly; privately they spoke as they wished. On the following day all went out to that conference. The king [Col. 0167A] of France did not mount his horse, perhaps because it had been agreed between them at the request of the king of England, who promised that he would do without him everything he had asked. For he had previously wearied the king of England with many entreaties for the archbishop.

And since the king of England had now come to this conference in the king of France’s territory, the king of France consented to be present at this conference and reconciliation more in spirit and authority, but absent in body, and to loosen the reins of the king of England’s own freedom and generosity. Thus the king of England might seem more fully his own master; since the king of France burdened him neither with prayer nor presence, the mercy, peace, and favour he restored to his archbishop would appear more conspicuous, because he was left there to his own will and subject to no necessity. For the prayers of wise lords are commands.

[Col. 0167B] After many persons had said many things on both sides for the good of peace and the restoration of their favour, and the king had consented to every article of peace, the Church’s liberty, restored favour, and restoration due to the Church of Canterbury and the archbishop’s person; and to restoring lands and churches to the clerks and all persons despoiled on behalf of the archbishop; and to leaving to the archbishop the benefices of churches belonging to the archbishopric that had fallen vacant in the meantime—for the king had given them to his own clerks—the good archbishop, unwilling to conceal from the king anything that might later cause offence or scandal between them, for it is the part of a wise man to wish neither to deceive nor to be deceived, delivered this address:

“My lord king, I often recall all the benefits of my first and second advancement and of your great reverence toward me; I receive them as welcome and acceptable, giving thanks in all things. As king and earthly lord, I am indebted and bound to you, saving the honour of God and holy Church; and now especially, because you restore and receive me into your peace and favour. But among all the articles of wrong which I have endured in your anger and indignation—my proscription, despoiling, and expulsion, that of my people, and every oppression of the Church of Canterbury—there is one which moves me more than the rest and which I can neither ought nor can leave untouched and uncorrected. That is: you caused your son to be crowned by the archbishop of York in the parish of Canterbury, and [Col. 0167D] by this act deprived the Church of Canterbury of the dignity of consecrating a king—a Church which anointed you king with the anointing of God’s mercy, and which among all its dignities possessed this as peculiarly, properly, and specially its own from ancient time, since Blessed Augustine first established Canterbury as a metropolitan see.”

The king replied: “I have received and learned that among the other royal dignities of my realm this is one: if the king of England wishes during his lifetime to advance his son to be king, he may do so wherever he wishes and through the archbishop or bishop of whatever city he wishes. And my great-grandfather King William, who subdued England, received consecration and the crown at London from the archbishop of York. And my grandfather King Henry received them by the hand of the bishop [Col. 0168A] of Hereford.”

The archbishop replied: “It is indeed true that those men crowned those kings, but the dignity of the Church of Canterbury was not diminished in their coronations. For when that archbishop of York anointed King William, the see of Canterbury was, as it were, vacant. Stigand, who then appeared to preside over the Church of Canterbury, was not an archbishop; he had never received the pallium from the holy Roman Church. Therefore, while the Church of Canterbury was vacant, the archbishop of York was pre-eminent and more immediately responsible among the English clergy.

“When King Henry was to be crowned, Saint Anselm was archbishop of Canterbury, but he was far away in exile at Cluny. Since delay in recalling him could be exceedingly dangerous to the realm, lest meanwhile war arise over the face of the land, one of his suffragans, the bishop of Hereford, took the place and performed the office of the absent archbishop, preserving the dignity of his father.”

The king replied: “That may well be true. What I said, I did not say as a case against the Church of Canterbury. It consecrated me; everywhere I wish its dignity to remain secure. If I have committed any offence against it, I am ready to correct it according to the judgment of the lord pope and the Roman Church. And you may demand redress from the archbishop of York and the bishops of England for injuries done to the Church of Canterbury and to you.”

The archbishop was satisfied; and, intending to thank the king for this reply and concession, he dismounted and was about to bow at the king’s feet. Understanding this, the king quickly leaped from his horse, [Col. 0168C] embraced the archbishop, lifted him up, received him with cheerful countenance and joyful brow, and pledged peace and restored favour to him. As the archbishop was mounting, the king performed the service of holding the stirrup upon which his right foot was placed. Pious tears burst forth from all persons of good will who were present.

Then the king was asked to give him the kiss of peace. For long before, when reconciliation, return, restoration, and all such articles had been discussed between them and granted by the king, peace had long stalled solely because the kiss was refused: the king said that in anger he had once sworn never to kiss him. When consulted, the lord pope absolved the king from such an oath, if he had made it, and enjoined upon him, for the salvation of his soul, that he should kiss the archbishop in good peace.

The king said: “In my own land I shall kiss his mouth, hands, and feet a hundred times; a hundred times I shall hear his Mass. But let this be deferred for the present. I am not speaking evasively. It is an honour to me that he should appear to yield to me in something; and if I give the kiss in my own land, it will seem a greater act of favour and kindness than if it were done here, where it might appear compulsory.”

With everyone’s assent, the archbishop agreed. All rejoiced—clergy, knighthood, people, every age, every rank—who saw and heard these things. Afterwards the lord king and the archbishop alone held long private consultation apart. The assembly was dissolved.

It was agreed between the king and the archbishop that the archbishop should return into France to thank his benefactors and the lord pope by messenger and letter. Having received leave and arranged matters for returning home, he was then to return to the king, who, if possible, would bring him into England in person; or would send with him the archbishop of Rouen, so that he might be received upon his return with much honour. Meanwhile, by the king’s command, possessions taken away were to be restored to him and to every person deprived of them.

The king wrote concerning the archbishop’s peace in these words: [lacuna].

[Note: [Col. 0169D] The letters mentioned here and there will be found in their proper places among the letters of St Thomas and Gilbert Foliot. They would have been wholly absent from manuscript A [Col. 0170D] had they not been copied on thin slips of parchment inserted between the pages of the book.]

Restoration was celebrated for the archbishop’s clerks, though not fully; nor was it complete for the archbishop himself. As stated above, during the dispute the king had granted to others certain churches of the archbishop which had fallen vacant. According to the terms of peace, he revoked those grants and left the churches to the archbishop. The officials of the clerks to whom [Col. 0169B] the archbishop had granted them entered into possession. But not long afterwards they were expelled by the king’s officials, and those to whom the king had given them re-entered. Moreover, the revenues and rents of the manors of the archbishopric, due at the next term of St Michael, were collected not by the archbishop’s officials but by the king’s. Many wise men silently observed these matters and drew their own conclusions.

But the archbishop had immediately sent his messenger to give thanks for the peace to the lord pope and the holy Roman Church, and had written to him the terms of peace and the king’s concession concerning redress for the injury of the coronation; perhaps he was awaiting that messenger. Meanwhile he was occupied in visiting separately through France his religious communities and helpful friends, thanking them and taking leave of them.

The noble Frenchmen supplied him and his people most abundantly with horses, clothes, and every necessity, so that those whom they had supported as exiles might be sent home with honour. When taking a most sweet and affectionate leave of the king of France, with every expression of gratitude, he said among other things: “We are going to England to play for our heads.”

The king of France said: “So it seems to me. Indeed, my lord archbishop, since he has not given you the kiss of peace, if you trusted me, you would not trust your king. Stay: while King Louis lives, you shall lack neither wine nor food nor the abundance of Gaul.”

He replied: “God’s will be done.” With tears they said their final farewells to one another.

Likewise, when the bishop of Paris embraced him, he said among other things: [Col. 0169D] “I am going to England to die.”

In England, a certain servant of the king’s court, confessing his sins to a religious and honourable priest, Richard of Halliwell, said among other things that with his own hands he had sealed letters sent into England ordering the archbishop’s death; that Nigel de Sackville had written them weeping; and that he had also confessed this to a bishop of England and asked him to impose penance. That bishop said to him: “What of it? You did your lord’s command,” and imposed nothing upon him, as though he had done no evil.

[Col. 0170A] One day Reginald de Warenne entered the chapter-house of the canons of Southwark, to whom he was bound by familiar affection, participation in their brotherhood, and the bestowal of many benefits. Speaking among other things of this unclean world, of the wickedness of criminals, and of the vices which the present more corrupt age, degenerating from the nobility of our fathers, dares to devise and practise, he said to them: “I beg you, pray God more earnestly for me. Before long you may perhaps hear that things are done in England which have neither been done nor heard of since the beginning of time; and as for me, they will be done against me and against my will, but I am not my own master.”

The canons who heard these words were horrified, not knowing what he meant or of whom he spoke, until, with Reginald preserved innocent of this righteous man’s blood, [Col. 0170B] the deed was at last done by others.

Meanwhile the king of England wrote letters recalling the archbishop, through Hugh the clerk, saying that his delay in France was suspicious to him; the archbishop should therefore hasten back to England. When all was ready, the archbishop returned to the king as agreed. He first came to him at Tours. There neither did the king give him the kiss, though asked, nor did the archbishop ask for it, lest he seem excessively hasty and precipitous.

Again he came to the court at Amboise. The king was still to hear Mass that day. Nigel de Sackville, the king’s clerk and keeper of the seal, to whom the king had given one of the valuable churches of the archbishop and who now feared losing it, told the king that the archbishop [Col. 0170C] was in the chapel and had perhaps come so early, before Mass, in order that he might offer the king the kiss of peace at Mass; but that, if the lord king wished, the archbishop could be cheated of the kiss.

The king said: “How?”

He replied: “Let the priest say a Mass for the faithful departed.”

The king consented, and it was done. After that Mass, there was said, as is customary in honour of our Lady, the perpetual Virgin Mary, *Salve, sancta parens*—“Hail, holy Mother.” When this had been said, the priest kissed the text of the Gospel and handed it, for presentation to the king, to the archbishop, who came forward and kissed it. After the king had kissed it, the archbishop said to him: “Lord, I have now come to you in your land; give me also, for the time, place, and agreement, the kiss of peace.”

The king replied: “Another time you shall have enough.” The archbishop and all others silently took note of [Col. 0170D] this rebuff.

That day the king and archbishop spoke for a long time alone. In the final terms of the reconciliation, however, the king had agreed to come to Rouen, pay all the archbishop’s debts to his creditors, make satisfaction from the rest of the archbishop’s money which had been received, receive him there with a kiss, and accompany him into England; or send the archbishop of Rouen with him to his son the king, who would make good anything lacking in the full restoration of the archbishop or his people. There, when he had requested leave of the king of England for the last time, he departed.

[Col. 0171A] The king said to him: “Go in peace. I shall follow you; I shall see you at Rouen, or in England, as soon as I can.”

The archbishop replied: “Lord, my heart tells me that I depart from you as one whom you will not see again in this life.”

The king said: “Do you take me for a traitor?”

The archbishop replied: “Far be that from you, lord.”

Departing thence at the king’s wish, the archbishop came to Rouen. There, however, he received only the dean of Salisbury, sent by the king as guide for his journey. The king’s excuse for not coming to England with him was that the king of France was preparing to attack his men of Auvergne. When the dean of Salisbury heard why he had come, the archbishop said to him: “O what a change of circumstances!”

The archbishop of Canterbury said: “He ought to provide you with a safe escort into England, and somewhat more securely than you provide one for him.”

To the archbishop of Rouen, through whom the aforementioned terms between them had been agreed, he said: “Where are these things agreed between the king and me? Why is the king not present in person? What of the kiss of our peace? What of the money? I have brought my creditors. The king does not keep his word.”

When the archbishop of Canterbury also asked the archbishop of Rouen whether he had received the king’s command to accompany him into England, he replied: “By no means.” Nevertheless, he would attend him out of affection if he wished, though it was not necessary. He said that everything was secure: his peace and safety had been arranged and confirmed under such authority and in the presence of so many persons.

There the archbishop of Rouen gave him three hundred pounds of his own coinage as a gift. The archbishop went to the Flemish coast, accompanied only by the aforesaid John, dean of Salisbury, as guide. He pondered all these things in his heart, above all that he was still denied the kiss of peace promised in the reconciliation. Yet, secure in the Holy Spirit, he pursued the journey he had undertaken, unafraid to die for God and the Church.

He had now received a messenger and letters of exhortation from the lord pope, bidding him return fearlessly to his Church and fulfil his ministry; as well as letters of most severe justice concerning the presumptuous coronation of the new king of England: suspension of the archbishop of York and all bishops who had been present at the coronation, except Bartholomew of Exeter alone; and letters for the renewed excommunication of the bishops of London and Salisbury, since [Col. 0171D] they had previously been excommunicated on another occasion. Before these letters of justice went a messenger, who found the archbishop of York and the bishop of London at Canterbury just as they were preparing to cross the sea. When they had read the lord pope’s letters thundering forth sentence, among whose words was this: “We shall fill your faces with disgrace,” their faces fell to the ground.

At the port of Wissant the archbishop had already arrived. The sky and sea were calm; the archbishop’s ship was ready, and several other vessels were crossing. The archbishop waited. Some of his fellow-exiled clerics, longing for their native land, said to him: “Lord, now we see England: the sails of very many crossing vessels are swelling. Why do you not board the ship? Are we going out like Moses, who indeed saw the land of promise but did not enter it?” He replied among other things: “Why are you in such haste? Before forty days have passed from your entering the land, you will prefer to be anywhere in the world rather than in England.”

Everything was now ready; and perhaps he had received some message from England that, if he landed at Dover, he would find brigands waiting to meet him who would quickly carry out their purpose; and that the archbishop of York and bishop of London had gone down to the coast, the more firmly to encourage the perpetrators of so wicked an undertaking, so that the nearby presence and security of those men might make them bolder. The good priest of God, Thomas, boarded the vessel and urged the helmsman to make for the port of Sandwich, since that was his own port and his people would rejoice at his arrival. Thus, on the third day of the week, the Kalends of December, he landed at Sandwich. When the king’s officials heard this, Gervase of Cornhill, sheriff of Kent, and Reginald de Warenne, with very many of their knights armed beneath cloaks and tunics with mail shirts, rushed to meet him as he disembarked. But when they saw and heard John, who was his guide in the king’s stead, the men said to be armed withdrew. Yet, lest nothing be done, the sheriff and Reginald, among other remarks, asked whether any foreigner had come with him, so that in accordance with a law proclaimed by the king they might demand from him the king’s letters authorizing his entry into England, or at least an oath of loyalty to the king. Perhaps they spoke thus in order to provoke him or stir up a disturbance; but in vain.

There the archbishop answered peaceably that his entry was peaceful, and that no one had come with him except men of peace: his clerics and his household. To be sure, a certain archdeacon of Sens had come with him, a man who had bestowed many benefits upon him and his companions during his exile; the archbishop said that this cleric had attached himself to him. Such demands—for letters or for an oath—ought customarily to be made, he said, of persons plausibly suspected of coming to spy out the kingdom’s weaknesses. It was unheard of for such demands to be made of the clerics of the archbishop of Canterbury, or for the matter to begin with him. Thus the affair came to rest, except that afterward the sheriff told him that he had entered the land with fire and sword; that he meant to uncrown the king; that he had excommunicated the archbishop of York and all the bishops on account of their service to the king; and that unless he soon adopted mature counsel in this matter, something would happen which he might better have left undone.

To this the archbishop replied that he was not challenging the king’s coronation; indeed, if he could do so according to God’s will, he would gladly seek for him four such kingdoms. Rather, he acted against those who, contrary to God and to the dignity of the Church of Canterbury, had unjustly usurped this consecration. Nor was it to bring fire and sword into the land to exercise the justice due for the bishops’ sins. Let no one threaten him with death: he had come prepared to stretch out his neck for justice and truth. He immediately wrote to the lord pope concerning his entry into England.

It was announced to the Church and city of Canterbury that the lord archbishop had landed. All, from greatest to least, were exceedingly glad. The appearance of the church was adorned; they clothed themselves in silks and costly garments; they prepared a manifold feast and the most capacious couches. The archbishop was received with a celebrated procession. The church rang with chants and organs, the courts with trumpets, the city everywhere with overflowing joy.

He delivered a most eloquent address in chapter, beginning with this verse: “For here we have no abiding city, but we seek the one to come.” Two archdeacons—Geoffrey Ridel of Canterbury and Richard of Poitiers—members of the king’s household and council, though men whom the archbishop had advanced to the positions in which they stood, and who were also his own men, had already come into Kent in order to cross from there to the king. But when they heard that the archbishop had landed at Canterbury, they immediately turned their reins and headed toward ports on the western sea. Many regarded this journey as an evil sign.

The archbishop of York, and the bishops of London and Salisbury, sent clerical messengers to address the archbishop. They said that he had not come in peace but in fire and flame, trampling down all his fellow bishops and making them his footstool: men neither summoned, heard, nor judged. Yet they said that his suffragans had gone to meet him at the sea in order to receive him in procession with the Church of Canterbury; but, beyond expectation and desert, they wore certain black and discordant tunics, which they would have to remove before coming to him, if it pleased him.

Among other things, he said: “I see that the peace of sinners is not peace. Until now, during the days of my absence, some of our bishops have endured such things as seemed to them to make for peace; but the lord pope has sent a good war, that an evil peace may be broken. Let a rule be applied to sins which inflicts fitting penalties. Again, there is no true peace except for people of good will. Jerusalem, abounding in luxuries and indulging itself too greatly, thought that it had peace; but the Lord, in pity, wept over it, because the severity of divine vengeance threatened it, though hidden from its eyes.”

Again, the bishops say that they were neither called nor heard according to law. Certainly, not every case requires an inquiry. Where crimes are manifest, they need no investigation but rather the correction due to them. To this he answered: “This sentence of suspension or excommunication is not mine but the lord pope’s; nor is it ours to dispute his judgment. I understand well that the proposals put forward by the bishops through you, their messengers, are probing and deceptive: so that, if I confess that I did not come with power to absolve them, they may make little of me, as a legate weak in this respect; but if I have that power, they may extort their absolution from me through lay force. I lay no snares for them. They thirst for my blood. Would that they might drink it; and they shall drink it.

“And when at last sound counsel had been given them to repent and make satisfaction, they did not acquiesce but appealed. The bishop of London wished afterward, as was said, to choose the better part for himself, so that, penitent and humbled before his legate and archbishop, and having sworn to submit to judgment, he might be absolved. But perhaps lest he be left alone in the struggle, the archbishop of York—trusting in his wealth of money—would not allow it. He used sometimes to say that, through his services, he possessed both pope and king. He advised that they should go together to the king across the sea and report everything to him.”

After the good Archbishop Thomas had remained eight days in his see, he sent a messenger ahead to the young lord king, announcing that he was coming to see him as his king and lord. He had brought with him three precious riding horses, of remarkable swiftness, elegant stature, and handsome form. They stepped high, set down their legs lightly, flicked their ears, quivered in every limb, and could not bear to stand still. They were covered in horse-cloths patterned with flowers and colours, which he intended to offer as a new gift to his new lord. For he loved him greatly as his lord and king: as a boy, the archbishop himself, then chancellor to the boy’s father the king, had formerly brought him up in his own household and court.

The bishop and Church of Rochester went out to meet him and received him on one day with due reverence. In London he had a third procession, to the church of the regular canons of Blessed Mary in Southwark. An innumerable multitude of clerics, men, and women, had come out of the city to meet him as he returned from exile, with great rejoicing, praising and blessing God for his longed-for return to his homeland. Poor scholars, gathered on their own initiative, and clerics of the London churches, about three thousand in number, had gone out of the city to meet him. When they saw the archbishop approaching them, they began to sing very loudly and serenely: “We praise thee, O God” (*Te Deum laudamus*). They themselves wept for joy, and almost all their hearers were moved to tears of compassion. Rejoicing with their devotion and exultation in the Lord, he bowed his head in thanks; then, putting his hand into his alms-purse, he had money drawn out and distributed to them with full compassion and generosity.

When at last he came and dismounted at the church of the canons in Southwark, where he was to be lodged in the houses of Henry, the aforementioned bishop of Winchester, the religious canons came out in procession to meet him at the church door with every joy. As they and many others burst into devout tears, they began to sing the responsory: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel” (*Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel*). There an innumerable multitude—clergy and people, every age and rank—continued the hymn of thanksgiving and common joy with abundant rejoicing and resonant voice.

There, amid all the other noise, a certain foolish, shameless, and sharp-tongued woman, who thrust herself into public courts and assemblies, Matilda, cried out and repeated several times: “Archbishop, beware the knife!” Thus all wondered what portentous thing she herself had heard, which she signified to him as a warning under this cloak of words. Staying one day in the lodging of the aforesaid Bishop Henry of Winchester, on the next day he received a messenger from the young king, Jocelin of Arundel, the queen’s brother. He said that the king did not wish him to come to him, nor to travel through the cities and castles of the kingdom, but rather to return to Canterbury and remain in his see, not leaving it. The archbishop was astonished and understood that such instructions did not arise from the disposition of that young king. He asked Jocelin whether the king was announcing to him that he had been excluded from the king’s communion and confidence of peace. Jocelin replied: “He instructed you what I have said.” As he left, looking angry, he saw a certain London citizen whom he knew, a wealthy man, coming toward him; and he said: “Have you also come to the king’s enemy? Go back quickly; I advise you.” The other answered: “We do not know him as the king’s enemy. We heard and saw the overseas king’s letters concerning this man’s peace and restoration. If anything else is concealed, it is concealed from us.” These were, before the event, foretastes and signs of coming evils.

The next day, as he was returning to Canterbury, someone came to tell him that Ranulf de Broc had seized his cargo-ship, which had landed with his wine; had cut the ropes, taken the anchors, beaten some sailors, and imprisoned others at Pevensey Castle. He immediately sent the abbot of St Albans and the prior of Dover to the young king, informing him of what was being done to him; by the king’s command the ship was restored. Some of the archbishop’s knights accompanied Thomas as he returned to Canterbury, lest, as ill signs converged and multiplied, certain young men should rush upon him from ambushes beside the road. In his company were only five knights’ shields, riding horses, and lances. It was immediately reported to the overseas king that he was traversing the kingdom with a great army armed in mail and helmets, intending to storm cities and drive his son from the kingdom.

On the first evening of his return toward Canterbury, at Wrotham, a certain priest named William came to him, poor and religious in appearance, who had then celebrated at Chiddingstone. Admitted to the archbishop’s private conversation, which he had requested, he said: “Lord, behold, I bring you relics of Saint Lawrence, Saint Vincent, and Saint Cecilia, by command of Saint Lawrence, who appeared to me in a nocturnal vision and said that these relics which I had with me belonged to those saints.”

The archbishop said: “Brother, how do you know that these are relics of those saints?”

William replied: “Lord, I too asked blessed Lawrence in my vision for some sign, saying that otherwise you would not believe me. Blessed Lawrence told me as a token that you recently put your hand into your bosom and found torn the hair-shirt which you wear next to your flesh; and, while considering whether you should have it repaired or put on another new one, shortly afterward you put in your hand and found it whole.”

To this the archbishop said among other things: “By the power of the Holy Spirit, by the force of obedience, I command you to tell no one while I live.”

The priest said, “So be it,” and added: “I am poor; I serve in another man’s church. Think of me.”

The archbishop said: “Come to me within four days of the Lord’s Nativity, and I shall provide for you.” The man departed.

Ranulf de Broc and Gervase of Cornhill, royal officials, concealing evil evil-mindedly, as though issuing orders from the king’s own mouth, caused the priors of churches and citizens of note in the city of London to be summoned and cited. They had secretly had the names written down of all who went out to meet the archbishop, so that they might come before the king’s court and give sureties to stand the judgment of that court, since, as they said, they had gone out to meet the archbishop, the king’s enemy. Yet the priors and ecclesiastical persons did not come. Very many citizens who did come replied on the appointed day that they saw no letters of the king ordering that they be cited or required to give such security, nor any letters of the justiciars. They were the king’s citizens and faithful subjects, not answerable to these men; at the king’s command they would do what they ought. Thus the matter remained. For in this they had committed no sin; rather, they had rendered to God the service of justice, and to their archbishop and legate the honour due him both by obligation and by devotion.

The good Thomas came to Canterbury. The five knights went back to their own homes, and he remained there with only priests, clerics, and his household. The notorious household of Ranulf de Broc, his neighbours at Saltwood Castle, laid nightly ambushes for him along every road leading about Canterbury. To provoke him to impatience and his men to quarrelling, they hunted without permission in his enclosed hunting-ground and took deer. More than this, they seized and kept the archbishop’s own hunting dogs in his woods. More still: one day before Christmas, a certain Robert de Broc, once a cleric and afterward a monk in white garments, but later an apostate and deserter to the world, met on the king’s highway the archbishop’s packhorse, travelling from one of the Church’s manors to Canterbury with the archbishop’s provisions. Through the hand of his nephew John de Broc, he had one horse’s entire tail cut short, in dishonour of the archbishop.

But Thomas, the lover of God, chariot and charioteer of the English Church, patient alike in prosperity and adversity, the dwelling-place of outstanding virtue, reflected upon all these preceding signs of his impending martyrdom. Strengthening his spirit for his exodus from Egypt, day by day he prepared himself: more lavish in almsgiving, more devout in prayer, more solicitous in every care for his soul. He also said several times while speaking with his clerics that this cause could not be brought to an end without the shedding of blood, and that he would stand in the Church’s cause unto death. His followers did not understand this, thinking these mere words; but afterward those who saw the deeds recalled such words. The archbishop also wrote to the lord pope that nothing but death and the sword threatened him, beseeching him to pray more earnestly to the Lord God for him.

As the archbishop of York, and the bishops of London and Salisbury, came from this side toward the court of the overseas king, and from the other side the archdeacon of Poitiers—for the archdeacon of Canterbury had suffered at sea and had not yet arrived—they encountered the king of Tyre, perhaps while he was on his way to see the archbishop. They related the acts concerning the excommunication or suspension of the bishops, as the king had already heard them reported; they imputed everything to the archbishop of Canterbury, accused him of treason, and charged him in his absence and without defence. Yet they were fearful that he might someday be summoned and heard. In this they were more cruel than the Jewish high priests who plotted the death of Jesus Christ: for Jesus was permitted to answer for himself in public, but this was by no means permitted to Thomas, his disciple.

They laid their cause, which was ecclesiastical, before the eyes of a secular prince; by their complaints they incited the king, far too ready to believe them, against the man with whom he had recently made peace, against the holy archbishop of God. Evils were doubled by falsehood. The king was told that the archbishop was traversing the kingdom with a strong force of armed knights. The king sought counsel from the archbishop of York and the bishops of London and Salisbury. The archbishop of York said: “Seek counsel from your barons and knights; it is not ours to say what must be done.” At last one said: “Indeed, lord, while Thomas lives you will have neither good days, nor a peaceful kingdom, nor quiet times.”

The king therefore conceived such indignation, bitterness, and agitation against the same archbishop, and displayed it so clearly in face and gesture, that four of his household barons—Reginald FitzUrse, William de Tracy, Hugh de Morville, and Richard Brito—understanding his anger and seeking to please him, as was said, swore to kill the archbishop. They departed from the court and made for various ports of the sea. A marvellous thing: under the leadership of the devil, the ancient enemy of every good, they assembled about the same hour of one day at the household of the Brocs near Saltwood Castle, on the day after they had departed the king’s court intending to kill the archbishop.

The king had addressed his barons in his chamber, complaining of the archbishop: that he had entered his land like a tyrant; that on account of their service to him he had suspended all the bishops and the archbishop of York, and excommunicated some; that he had disturbed the whole kingdom; that he intended to deprive the king’s son, and the king himself, of crown and diadem of the kingdom; that he had procured a legation superior to the king; that he had obtained from the supreme pontiff a certain privilege for himself and the bishops concerning grants of churches, eliminating the patronage of counts, barons, and even the king himself.

The earl of Leicester answered first: “Indeed, lord, the archbishop and my lord father the earl were most intimate friends. But know for certain that since the archbishop departed from your land and affection, he has seen no messenger of mine, nor I any messenger of his.”

Engelger de Bohun, a man long hardened in evil days, uncle of the bishop of Salisbury, who, being excommunicated, bore the mark of the beast upon his forehead, said: “I do not know how you can take vengeance on such a man unless he is hanged on a gallows, with stout rods twisted into a rope, and stretched out upon a cross.”

William, surnamed the Evil Neighbour, nephew of Count Eudo of Brittany, was the third to speak. “Once,” he said, “when I returned from Jerusalem and passed through Rome, I questioned my host there about the Roman pontiffs and, among other conversation, heard that some pope had been killed there because of intolerable insolence and arrogance.”

When these speeches were finished, the king immediately sent William, count of Mandeville, Saher de Quincy, and Richard de Humet after those four men into England. The report was that they were to seize the archbishop. Count William and Saher came as far as the seaport but did not cross. Richard, proceeding to another port, crossed over. The king’s son was at Winchester. Richard sent to his tutors, Hugh de Gundeville and William fitzJohn, asking them to go secretly, without the king’s knowledge, to Canterbury with the knights of the royal household. He himself lay in wait near the coast, so that if the archbishop should attempt to seek refuge in flight at some seaport, he might be captured. Count William and Saher were doing the same across the sea, so that if he crossed over, he might be captured there.

A marvellous and astonishing thing happened. For the four barons named above—Reginald FitzUrse and his companions—who had made for various seaports, under the leadership of the devil, the ancient enemy of all good, assembled at about the same hour of one day in England, at Saltwood Castle, with the household of the Brocs. Yet before they arrived, the blessed archbishop had been informed with complete certainty of the coming arrival of his killers. He was all the more strengthened in the Lord, acting manfully and putting on the armour of God, so that he might stand firm on the day of the Lord. But he kept the matter secret, lest disturbance arise during so great a feast, so far as lay within his power.

On the night of the Lord’s Nativity he read the Gospel lesson, “The book of the generation,” and celebrated the night Mass. Before the great Mass on that day, which he himself also celebrated, he delivered an eloquent sermon from the pulpit to the people, taking as his principal theme the words, “On earth peace to people of good will.” Speaking of the holy fathers of the Church of Canterbury, confessors who are there, he said that they had one martyr, the holy archbishop Ælfheah; it was possible that before long they might have another. After the very shameful injury done in cutting short the horse-tail of his poor tenant in service to the Church of Canterbury, he bound Robert de Broc with a sentence of excommunication, as he had previously announced to him through messengers, inviting him to make satisfaction. Robert had defiantly replied through a certain knight, David de Ruminel, that if the archbishop excommunicated him, he should do as an excommunicated man does. He also involved in the same sentence two other violent occupiers of the churches of Herges and Thierlewda, who had refused admittance to his officials when they came.

On the feast-day of Saint Stephen he also celebrated the great Mass; and likewise on the feast of Blessed John, apostle and evangelist. On that day he secretly sent three of his clerics to France: Master Herbert, Alexander the Welshman, bearer of his cross, and Gilbert de Glanville, who was to go on to the lord pope. He sent two others, Richard the chaplain and John Planeta, to the bishop of Norwich, to absolve temporarily the priests from the lands of Count Hugh who had knowingly celebrated the divine offices while excommunicated. First, however, they were to receive security from those priests that within a year they would go to the lord pope, or would send two of their number on behalf of all, to receive from the pope satisfaction for their penance.

The archbishop, now remembering his priest William, who had come to him at Wrotham, had him sought through William Beivin, an acquaintance of his, if he might be found at court or in the city. When he was not found, the archbishop had a charter drawn up by which he granted and confirmed to him the chapel of Penshurst, with an excommunication subscribed against anyone who should presume to take it from him. He handed the charter to William Beivin, to give to the priest when he saw him. Who can say that he was not foreknowing of his martyrdom? By means of that charter, the priest afterward held his church in peace from the young king, who said, when he heard of the charter and miracle, that he did not wish to incur the excommunication of the holy archbishop.

[Indeed, men assigned to guard the castles around Canterbury—Dover, Rochester, Saltwood, and Blechingley—had already been summoned. Perhaps this was so that the archbishop and his men, shutting themselves within Canterbury Church, might be kept enclosed there. Any approaching force of those knights stationed nearby might besiege and overwhelm them; if the good archbishop wished to flee, wherever he went he would fall among enemies. Perhaps, if the citizens of Canterbury or neighbouring peoples should wish in zeal for God to rise against those wicked attackers in revenge for his mutilation, the unrighteous men would have a refuge in one of those castles. Or, in order to defend themselves, they might immediately request that military support be sent to them from those castles.]

Therefore, on the fifth day of Christmas, the aforesaid four barons of the king, with all their own men and with the household of the Brocs, came from Saltwood Castle to Canterbury. Very many knights were added to them, whom they had summoned by proclamation from the castles and neighbourhood of Canterbury as though for the king’s service. About twelve of them, with the four barons, made their way smoothly and directly to the archbishop’s court. Meanwhile they instructed the officials and chief men of the city throughout the town and ordered them on the king’s behalf that all citizens, armed, should come with them to the archbishop’s house for the king’s service. When the city, astonished at their fury, resisted, they immediately ordered the citizens to keep the peace and remain still, whatever they heard or saw. This was their design: either that the inhabitants of the city should be added to them in their crime, or at least that they should not hinder them or fight for their archbishop.

Those barons and knights who had gone ahead were ushered into the inner chamber before the archbishop. It was about the tenth hour of the day. The archbishop had eaten, but the household of servants was still eating. On entering, he greeted them first; their response was either none or indistinct. They sat down before him among the clerics and monks. Reginald FitzUrse began thus:

“The lord king overseas sends us to you, that you may absolve the bishops excommunicated at your entry into England, restore to their offices those suspended, and afterward go to Winchester to his son the king, whom you intend to uncrown, to make satisfaction for so great an offence and submit to the judgment of his court.”

The archbishop replied: “I did not excommunicate these excommunicated persons, nor did I suspend those suspended. Rather, the lord pope, in his letters, rebuked his sons in this manner and punished those who had deserved ill: the archbishop of York, because in my absence, without my being summoned, aware, or consenting, and to the prejudice of my Church, he usurped in my diocese the coronation of the new king, which is due to the Church of Canterbury and to me, though forbidden even by letters of the lord pope; the bishops, because, though they are suffragans and professed subjects of the Church of Canterbury, they tolerated this and made no protest for the right of their mother Church. It is not for me to reconsider the lord pope’s sentence: an inferior power cannot absolve those whom he has bound.

“Nevertheless, though I have no power to absolve or bind in the case of the archbishop, I granted, when asked by my suffragans of London and Salisbury, that I would absolve them from anathema and restore all the others who were suspended, provided only that they would either humbly invoke mercy or give security to submit to ecclesiastical judgment. But those who approached me refused. I am still ready to do this. Let the coronation of the new lord king remain firm, stable, and unshaken; and, with the dignity of the crowned king preserved, the lord pope punishes the wrong of the consecrator: because one who ought not, and where he ought not, anticipated the dignity of our office. And our bishops are punished for their silence and acquiescence.

“All this occurred by the permission of the lord king and by the leave granted me on the day of our reconciliation. Nor do I seek thereby to disinherit the new king; rather, saving the rights of their possessors if it could be done, I would wish many kingdoms of the world for him. I had recently set out to go to him, not to make satisfaction to him—for I have offended him in nothing—but to congratulate, with the honour due, the advancement of my lord. But in London I received his messenger and command to return, which grieves me.”

Then they at once burst forth into threats without restraint. He said: “I marvel indeed that you so clamour and threaten evils. You know that the lord king received me into his peace and favour on the feast of Mary Magdalene; I saw some of you present there; and, as I understood, it pleased you. I entered the land with the king’s letters and safe-conduct.”

Then Master John of Salisbury said to him: “Lord, speak more privately about this matter.”

“It is not expedient,” said the archbishop. “They put forward and demand things which I can neither do nor ought to do.”

Reginald FitzUrse said: “From whom, then, do you hold the archbishopric?”

He replied: “Spiritual things from God and the lord pope; temporal things and possessions from the lord king.”

Reginald said: “Do you not acknowledge that you hold your whole self from the king?”

“By no means,” he replied; “but we must render to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”

Reginald and the others, as if he had said something astonishing, grew still more enraged and inflamed, and gnashed their teeth at him.

But the righteous Thomas was fearless, confident as a lion, ready to contend unto death for justice, for the liberty of his Church, and for his soul. He said: “You threaten me in vain. If all the swords of England hung over my head, your terrors could not turn me aside from observing God’s justice and obeying the lord pope. You will find me foot to foot in the Lord’s battle. Once I withdrew as a fearful priest; I have returned by the counsel and obedience of the lord pope. Never again, for all eternity, shall I abandon it. If I may exercise my priesthood in peace, it is good for me; if not, God’s will be done concerning me. Besides, you know what lies between me and you; therefore I marvel the more that you dare to threaten an archbishop in his own house.”

He said this in remembrance that Reginald, William de Tracy, and Hugh de Morville, while he was still chancellor, had each made themselves his men by personal submission, saving their allegiance to the king; each of the three had accepted his right and authority, being his inferior in rank. These men, who ought thereby to have become gentler, were now raging and beside themselves with anger. They said: “There is nothing between us except what concerns the king.”

Reginald said: “We dare well threaten an archbishop, and do more. Let us withdraw.”

A great part of the archbishop’s household stood there with clerics, many others, and several knights who had gathered when they heard the men speaking more loudly. Looking at them, Reginald said: “We tell you, on the king’s behalf, whose men and faithful subjects you are, to withdraw from this man.” Perhaps, just as their companions in the city feared that the citizens might fight for the archbishop, so these men within feared that his household might fight for their lord or rise against them. When all remained unmoved, Reginald immediately gave the contrary command: “We order you to guard this man, so that he does not leave.”

The archbishop said: “I am easy to guard; I shall not leave.”

Among others, those attackers noticed a certain knight, the archbishop’s steward, William fitzNigel, who had hurried from his chamber over some account. They seized him and led him away, saying: “You will come with us.”

The knight said to the archbishop: “Lord, you see what they are doing to me?”

The archbishop said: “I see. This indeed is their violence and the power of darkness.”

The archbishop then rose and followed them a few steps while they were still within the chamber, asking them quite mildly to release his knight to him. Obstinate, they withdrew; meeting another of the archbishop’s knights, Ralph Morin, they likewise seized him and took him away. Passing through the middle of hall and court with their following, they searched everything with terrifying looks and threats, crying: “Arms, arms, men!”

[Meanwhile, in a large house belonging to a certain Gilbert, which stood opposite the archbishop’s gate, the whole hostile band was gathering. At last, upon receiving the signal, they burst out in a single rush, entered the archbishop’s gate—which had been opened to them and was immediately shut—and cried out terribly: “The king’s knights! The king’s men! The king’s men!”]

For some of their companions, having sent more familiar men ahead quietly lest the gate be shut at the noise, were inside the archbishop’s gate. They had removed the archbishop’s gatekeeper and put in their own, so that no one from the city might enter to help the archbishop, and no one might leave carrying away any of the archbishop’s goods. Before the shut gate, with only the rear entrance open, within the courtyard of the hall there were on horseback William fitzNigel—at dinner the archbishop’s man and knight, but now assigned to this service against him—and Simon de Crioil, a neighbouring knight of the abbot of Saint Augustine. Reginald armed himself apart in the very outer court, and compelled Robert Tibia, the archbishop’s shield-bearer, to give him assistance and service. Reginald took an axe from a carpenter who was repairing some steps there.

Meanwhile, we remained with the lord archbishop in the same chamber, comparing what they had said and threatened with the archbishop’s replies. We felt differently: some thought there was no cause for fear—they had come drunk; sober and unfed, they would not speak such things. It was the Nativity of the Lord; peace with the king had been agreed for us. Others said that we should fear lest they carry out their threats in deed. Many signs of cruelty had been foreseen.

Meanwhile, from the direction of the church we heard the lamentable outcry of people of both sexes and almost every age, grieving for [Col. 0182C] us as for sheep being slaughtered; they had seen the armed men in the city hurrying toward the archbishop under orders. We heard our own people hastening down the steps into the church through the middle of the hall, fleeing before the armed men who, the gate having been opened to them, were entering the courtyard.

[Osbert, Algar, and certain other servants of the archbishop, seeing the armed men rush in, shut the door of the hall and made fast its bolts. When Robert de Broch saw this, he began to break down a wall with an axe; entering by that way through the inner parts of the house, he opened the hall door to those parricides, and cruelly beat and wounded those who had secured it.]

We clergy, within with the archbishop, also heard those blows of Robert de Broch as he demolished the wall [Col. 0182D]. What could come over us monks, clerks, and companions of the archbishop but fear and trembling? Behold, what the holy man of God had said above was fulfilled: “In a short while they would rather be anywhere on earth than in England.”

But that good Thomas was a despiser of death, since death is for holy men a harbor, an entrance into eternity, and an everlasting refuge in which they feel no evil. Moreover, the holy man bore himself confidently, as though rejoicing that he had found an honorable cause for dying—for justice, liberty, and the cause of his Church—and as though desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ. So great was his love for ecclesiastical liberty that he measured it not by his own downfall but by its resurrection and preservation.

Then the many monks who were present said to him [Col. 0183A]: “Lord, enter the church.” He answered: “God forbid; do not be afraid. Most monks are more fearful and faint-hearted than is right.” They would not yield. Some raised him by laying hands upon him and compelled him; others persuaded him that he ought to go, because the monks were to say Vespers and he was to hear None and Vespers.

He therefore ordered the cross of the Lord to be brought forth. One of his clerks, Henry of Auxerre, carried it. When we had come into the monks’ cloister, they wished to shut the door behind him. He endured this unwillingly, and walked slowly last of all, driving everyone ahead of himself like a good shepherd his sheep. Indeed, the fear which the love of God had cast out could not be detected either in his bearing or in his step; it was as far from all his outward conduct as from the inner citadel of his mind [Col. 0183B]. Once he turned his eyes over his right shoulder—perhaps to see whether those royal men were close upon his track; perhaps lest someone left behind should put the bolt across the door.

They entered the church itself.

[The monks of the church, as fearful as they were stunned by so great an uproar, abandoning Vespers before they had completed the chanting, came out from the choir to meet the lord archbishop as he entered the church. They rejoiced and gave thanks to God that they saw and received him alive, though they had already heard that he had been cut to pieces. While some wept through joy or fear, and others urged one course, others another—as Peter said to the Lord, “Be gracious to yourself”—he, not afraid to die for the liberty and cause of God’s Church, ordered them to go away and withdraw from him, surely lest they impede his passion [Col. 0183C], which he had foretold would come and saw to be imminent.]

He was going to the upper altar, where he was accustomed to hear his private Masses and the Hours, and had already gone up four steps, when behold, at the cloister door stood Reginald fitz Urse, who had arrived first, armored, with drawn sword, crying out: “Now here to me, men of the king!” Not long afterward his three aforementioned companions joined him, likewise clad in mail covering their bodies and heads except for their eyes alone, and with naked swords. There were also very many others without mail but armed, from their retinue and companions; and some men of the city of Canterbury, whom they had forced to come with them. On that day and for the four days afterward, as was said above, soldiers were posted on guard at the neighboring castles of Dover, Hastings, and elsewhere.

[Col. 0183D] The king’s household men were at the overseas ports: Count William at Wissant, Saier de Quincy elsewhere, so that if the archbishop attempted the sea passage, he might be captured upon landing here or there. Seeing these armed men, I say, the monks wished to secure the church door; but the good man, trusting in the Lord and not terrified by the sudden dread of the rushing powers of the wicked, came back down from the steps, forbidding the door of the Church to be shut, and saying: “[God forbid that we should make a castle of God’s church.] Let all who wish to enter the church of God be allowed to enter. Let God’s will be done.”

As the archbishop descended from the steps toward the door to prevent its being closed, then John of Salisbury and all his other clerks—except Robert the canon, William son of Stephen, and Edward Grim, who had only recently come to him—seeking protection and looking to place themselves in safety, abandoned him: some went to the altars, others to hiding places [Col. 0184A].

And indeed, if the archbishop had wished to avoid them and save himself through the protection of flight, he could have done so very easily, the opportunity of time and place being offered rather than sought. It was evening. The very long night was approaching. A crypt was near, with many passages, most of them dark. There was also another nearby door by which he could have ascended by a spiral stair to the chambers and vaults of the upper church: perhaps he would not have been found, or meanwhile something might have occurred. But he wished none of these things. He did not turn aside, did not beg the murderers, did not utter a murmur, made no complaint throughout his entire agony; but, patiently awaiting the last hour [Col. 0184B] which threatened him for Christ and the cause of the Church, he displayed a strength and constancy of mind, body, and speech greater than we have ever heard attributed to any martyr, until all was completed.

Now behold, those spearmen, driven by fury and seeing contrary to expectation that the door was open, rapidly entered the church.

> “Where, where are you rushing, wicked men?  
> What madness, unhappy men! What license of the sword is this?”

One of them said to the monks who stood with him: “Do not move.” At first, as though confused and stunned by reverence for his countenance, those assailants stepped back upon seeing the archbishop. Then someone cried: “Where is that traitor?” The archbishop, possessing his soul in patience, made no reply to that word. Another said: “Where is the archbishop?” [Col. 0184C] He answered: “Here I am—not a traitor, but a priest of God; and I marvel that you have entered God’s church in such attire. What do you wish?”

One assailant said: “That you die; it is impossible for you to live any longer.”

But he replied: “And I receive death in the name of the Lord, and I commend my soul and the cause of the Church to God, to blessed Mary, and to the patron saints of this church. God forbid that I should flee because of your swords; but by God’s authority I forbid you to touch any of my people.”

One of them carried both a two-edged axe and a sword, so that, should the church door be secured against them, they might knock it down with axe and two-edged implement; but, keeping hold of his sword, he set down the two-edged axe, which is still there.

One struck him between the shoulders with the flat of his sword [Col. 0184D], saying: “Run away; you are dead.” He stood unmoved, offering his neck and commending himself to the Lord; and on his lips were the holy martyred archbishops, blessed Dionysius and Saint Ælfheah of Canterbury. Some said: “You are taken; you shall come with us,” and, laying hands upon him, tried to drag him from the church, unless they feared that the people would snatch him from their hands. He replied: “I shall go nowhere. Here you shall do what you wish to do, and what you have been commanded.”

He resisted as best he could, and the monks held him back. With them was Master Edward Grim, who received on his arm the first blow of a sword which William de Tracy swung at the archbishop’s head. By that same blow the archbishop, whose head was bent, was wounded in the head, and Grim himself was severely wounded in the arm [Col. 0185A].

> “Oh! As Saint Basil says, the fierceness of beasts is tamed by the power of God; human madness is not softened even by the example of beasts!”

Wiping from his head with his arm the blood flowing down and seeing it, the archbishop gave thanks to God, saying: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.” A second blow was dealt to his head; he fell face down, first dropping to his knees, with hands joined and stretched out toward God, beside the altar of Saint Benedict which was there. He took care—or was granted the grace—to fall decently, covered by his cloak down to his ankles, as though about to adore and pray.

[He fell on his right side, to go to the right hand of God.]

As he lay prostrate, Richard Brito struck him with such force that the sword broke both on his head and on the pavement of the church [Col. 0185B], and said: “Take this for the love of my lord William, the king’s brother.” This William had sought marriage with the Countess of Warenne; but the archbishop had opposed it, because this William, through his mother the Empress Matilda, and William, Count of Warenne, through his father King Stephen, were sons of first cousins. Therefore William, King Henry’s brother, grieved inconsolably, and all his followers became enemies of the archbishop.

The holy archbishop received four blows in all, all to the head; the entire crown of his head was cut away. Then one could see how his limbs served his spirit. For just as he did not struggle in mind, so neither by the opposition nor collapse of his limbs did he seem to contend against death; for he received death as voluntary through his desire for God [Col. 0185C], rather than violent through the swords of soldiers.

One Hugh de Horsea, surnamed “Evil Clerk,” pressing the neck of the prostrate holy martyr with his foot, drew out blood and brain with the point of his sword from the hollow left by the severed crown. O sad spectacle! O unheard-of cruelty in those who ought to have been Christians! Yet worse are those who, under the Christian name, perform pagan deeds than those who openly, through the error of ancestral traditions, are unbelievers.

O truly happy and steadfast holy martyr of God, Thomas! He could be killed, but he could not be bent. And indeed, just as once, while Christ suffered in his own body, so now, while he suffered in his soldier Thomas, the sun turned away its eyes [Col. 0185D], hid its rays, and darkened the day lest it see this crime; a dreadful storm drew in the sky; sudden rains poured down; thunder sounded from heaven. Afterwards a great redness flashed through the air—a sign of the blood that had been shed, an horror at the crime, and a token of the severe vengeance to come upon those who had made themselves so monstrously savage and defiled themselves with this expiatory crime, and upon those who were the cause of this death—persons hateful and stripped of every gentleness proper to human nature.

[How swift their feet were to shed blood; how impious their hearts; how grim their eyes; how cruel their right hands; how bloody their swords. This crime overwhelms all who hear and consider it by the rarity of its example, strikes them back with horror, stuns them by its singularity, and leaves them helpless by its monstrosity. The sons killed the father in the womb of their mother: indeed, the flowers of the Church lack neither lilies nor roses; and in the passion of blessed Thomas, as the savage blade is drawn forth, there come forth both white brain and red blood. Surely these are true and most certain signs that the archbishop and champion was Christ’s shepherd, laying down his life for the sheep; confessor and martyr, destined to receive from the Lord a double robe: white for the archbishopric faithfully administered and purple for martyrdom happily accomplished.
