In life he had the dove’s simplicity through innocence of deeds, and the serpent’s cunning through holy prudence. He retained both also in death. As a dove, he did not resist death and provided no obstacle to his killers; as a serpent, he exposed his body to the strikers [Col. 0186B], preserving not his head but his soul—or the Church. His death was also revealed to many through visions and portents. Master Ralph, canon and priest of the church of London, a man of great integrity and a preeminent doctor of Holy Scripture, saw in a dream, as he fixed his gaze upon the sun, a bishop clothed in episcopal vestments within the body of the sun. Likewise, an honorable woman saw the moon fall from heaven and be wholly cut to pieces by the swords of certain gladiators.]

Sated with the pious blood for which those impious parricides had thirsted, they went out; and because a certain French boy belonging to the archdeacon of Sens was weeping for the archbishop, they bloodied him by inflicting a grave wound. Meanwhile others occupied themselves with plundering. They went through the whole house of the archbishop [Col. 0186C], searched the rooms, broke open chests and coffers, and took golden and silver vessels, money and gold coins, papal bulls, rings, books, precious cloths from which copes, tunics, and dalmatics ought to have been made for the adornment of the church. They entered the chambers of the clerks and carried away their clothes, books, silver, baggage, and all their household goods. Others led horses from the stables, so that absolutely nothing belonging to the archbishop, the clerks, or his household might remain that could fall into the hands of the robbers. I estimate that the goods carried off and seized there were worth more than two thousand marks. Those villains divided all these things among themselves, just as the crucifiers of Jesus Christ divided his garments.

But they sent the privileges and bulls of the lord pope that they found to the king overseas, thereby seeking the king’s favor; in all other respects they were faithless to him, disloyal to him, and perjured against him. For, if not the Church’s, then at least the king’s ought to have been all the possessions of an archbishop who died intestate.

O unheard-of death! O execrable crime! These murderers are more detestable than all other killers of holy martyrs. For the crucifiers of our Lord Jesus Christ, simply believing him to be a man and saying that he broke Sabbaths, invalidated their ancestral traditions, and made himself the Son of God—though he was Mary’s son and was thought by them to be the son of a craftsman—hanged him upon the wood out of zeal for the Mosaic Law, not understanding whom they so treated. “For had they known, they would never have crucified the Son of God.” Therefore the Lord himself [Col. 0187A] prayed for them, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.”

The murderers of the other holy apostles and martyrs likewise did not act against their own consciences: unbelievers, idolaters, and pagans drove Christ’s faithful into the path of extermination, thinking that they pleased God in this, as he foretold to his disciples: “The hour comes when everyone who kills you will think that he is rendering service to God.” But these assailants were fellow Christians of blessed Thomas, his sons and his men. Fellow Christians, I say, in sacraments, but not in the reality of the sacraments; his sons, but sons of perdition; his men, but stripped of all humanity. Moreover, among pagans and Jews there was great reverence for sacred things, places, and times.

[Col. 0187B]

> “[lacuna] let no one make an olive grove.”
>
> “[lacuna] the place is sacred for boys: outside  
> Urinate,” it is written among the pagans, when a mournful *bidental*—a place struck by lightning—must be revered and held sacred.

The pagan also kept holy days as festivals and marked his birthday with a better pebble. Likewise the Jew observed his Sabbaths and other feasts, and would not permit human blood to be shed within the city; hence the Lord suffered outside the gate.

But these swordsmen pierced the holy archbishop with their swords at the holiest time, on the fifth day of the Lord’s Nativity, in the holiest place in all England: in the principal metropolitan see, the church of the Holy Trinity, which is exalted both by the patronage of the many saints resting there [Col. 0187C] and by the dwelling there of religious monks serving God. Such a man was killed by such men, at such a time, in such a place: the spiritual father of the entire kingdom, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury itself, primate of all England, legate of the Apostolic See, servant of Christ Jesus, imitator and follower of the holy Fathers, a religious man,

> A guardian of true virtue and its stern attendant,  
> Caring to be better rather than to seem so,

a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, an abode of holy virtues.

He suffered for this cause: indeed, for justice, truth, and the liberty of the Church. For defending ecclesiastical laws and invalidating those of the king which were contrary to them, giving way for a time to the wrath of his earthly king [Col. 0187D] and commending the cause of his Church to God, he drank the cup of many sufferings during long exile and the savage proscription of himself and his followers; he endured many hardships amid the waves of innumerable troubles. He begged off no kind of punishment or adversity. Finally, recalled in the seventh year, with peace promised to him but ill observed, he was, as it were, imprisoned by being ordered not to leave his see. After a few days, sought by soldiers, he offered himself, and, as has been said, struck down by swords, drank the cup of his martyrdom—not heard in a court of law, not judged, because no cause of death could have been found in judging him. Those who procured this knew that well: his malicious rivals, his wicked sons, brothers of the most cruel Herodias, who likewise once caused blessed John the Baptist first [Col. 0188A] to be imprisoned for truth’s sake, and afterward procured his beheading without a hearing or judgment. O happily done: the accused man whom we see thus acquitted.

[For a long time he lay there almost alone, abandoned by clerks, monks, and everyone else. Before daylight was gone, Osbert, his chamberlain, tore from his own shirt with a little knife enough cloth to cover what remained of his half-shorn head.]

When it became known that the murderers had departed, his clerks and monks, servants, and countless people from the city gathered around the holy archbishop. Silence was broken, and all burst forth more freely into groans and lamentations, which they had previously restrained under the pressing fear of the assassins. They prolonged their weeping and wailing far into the night.

At length it was decided to carry the body of the lord archbishop, placed upon a bier, through the middle of the choir before the altar [Col. 0188B], the empty skull being covered with clean linen, secured above by a small cap. Even then his face retained sweetness and steadfastness of spirit. There too there was much weeping.

Brother Robert, priest and canon of the religious house of Merton, an honorable man who had clung to him as chaplain and inseparable companion from the first day of his ordination, after commending the archbishop’s true religious devotion and integrity—which he knew as the hearer of his confession—showed the monks, among other things, what all of us had previously not known: that the archbishop wore haircloth. He put his hand into the archbishop’s bosom and showed [Col. 0188C] the hairshirt next to his flesh, and above the hairshirt the monastic habit. For, though he had been elected while a clerk, because he was abbot of the monks of that church of Canterbury, beneath the concealment of his canonical cloak he bore hidden within himself a monk of Christ and of blessed Benedict.

Then the monks, greatly rejoicing in spiritual joy, lifted hearts and hands to heaven in praise of God; they turned grief into spiritual joy and lamentations into cries of gladness. Instructed by sight concerning both his martyrdoms—his voluntary martyrdom while living and his violent one in dying—they fell to the ground, kissed his feet and hands, invoked him as Saint Thomas, and all proclaimed him the glorious holy martyr of God. Everyone ran to see in haircloth the man whom they had seen as chancellor in purple and fine linen [Col. 0188D].

Shortly afterward a monk of the church, Arnald the goldsmith, and some others returned to the place of his martyrdom. They collected most carefully into a basin his blood and brain, spilled across the floor of the church; and lest that place be trodden under the feet of passers-by, they placed movable benches across it. The vigil of that night was pious, holy, and sober. The monks said only the commendation of the soul in silence.

The next morning a rumor spread through the church that the household of de Broch and their accomplices had prepared to drag him from the church, grieving that they had slaughtered him in the church. Fearing this, the monks hastened quickly to bury that holy body [Col. 0189A] and place it in the tomb. The abbot of Boxley and the prior of Dover attended the rite, having previously been summoned by the archbishop, because, by their counsel, he wished to make one of the monks prior, since there was no prior in the Church of Canterbury.

They resolved that he was not to be washed otherwise than as he had been washed in his own blood. Once his ordinary outer garments had been removed and distributed, he was buried in the hairshirt in which he had been found; with the customary undergarments of haircloth and outer garments of linen; in the same hose; and in the monastic habit which he wore. Over these were placed the very vestments in which he had been ordained: an alb, called in Greek a *poderis* (“foot-length garment”), a simple amice, chrismal vestment, mitre, stole, and maniple. He had ordered that all these be kept, perhaps for the day of his burial. Above these [Col. 0189B] he had, in archiepiscopal order, a tunic, dalmatic, chasuble, pallium with pins, chalice, gloves, ring, sandals, and pastoral staff—according to the customary rite and with the honor due.

When the king’s son heard of the death of Saint Thomas, he was exceedingly grieved and struck to the heart; he stretched his hands to heaven and lifted the eyes of heart and body to God, saying: “Alas, yet, God, I give you thanks that this was done without my knowledge and that none of mine was there.” For the four unhappy assailants had completed the deed before the aforesaid Hugh de Gundeville and William son of John reached Canterbury.

When all things belonging to the burial had been completed and arranged, the sacred body of the lamented archbishop was laid in a new marble sarcophagus, in the crypt before two altars, without Mass, because [Col. 0189C] the church had been violated by the entry of armed men.

Immediately after the burial rite, that very night and in that very week, the operation of divine power appeared, a fitting manifestation of so great a martyrdom:

[One of the citizens of Canterbury, who had been present among the spectators of his martyrdom, dipped part of his shirt in the martyr’s blood. At home he had a wife long afflicted with paralysis. When her husband returned home, she learned in order about the passion and constancy of the holy martyr—what he had heard amid the tumult, the tears of the weeping, and the disordered voices of those recounting it. Seeing the holy blood upon her husband’s garment [Col. 0189D], devout in faith toward the Lord, raised in hope of healing, and supplicating the martyr in her vow, she asked to be washed and to receive the blood in water, so that she might drink healing. It was done, and she was cured at once. This was the first of the signs God performed for his martyr on that very night.

From this, I believe, under divine inspiration, arose the practice of putting some of Saint Thomas’s blood into water and distributing that mixture of blood and water to Saint Thomas’s pilgrims in tin flasks, to be carried back for the healing of their sick. I myself saw inscribed upon many vessels this one-line verse:

> Water mixed with Thomas’s blood is carried in flasks.

And indeed, God working according to the petition of the faithful, with the holy martyr interceding and faith meriting—for nothing [Col. 0190A] is impossible to faith—that water mixed with blood not only benefited countless sick people by healing them, but also some who were dying, so that they did not die. I say more, though it may be difficult to believe: it benefited some dead people, so that they rose again alive.

On the fourth night after his passion, with which Saturday dawned, it was revealed to a cleric of London that a certain London priest, William de Capella, who had become mute, should go to the tomb of Saint Thomas and be healed there. And it happened so. A certain religious man saw in a night vision Jesus Christ crucified in that part of the crypt where the earthly man, blessed Thomas, was laid. Truly so, because Christ suffers in each of his martyrs: he who met blessed Peter on his way to Rome for martyrdom and, when Peter asked the Lord, “Where are you going?”, answered [Col. 0190B]: “I am coming to Rome to be crucified again.”

There was a certain woman, a lay anchoress, who had not learned letters and knew no Latin speech except some psalms, the Lord’s Prayer, and the Creed. In those days and nights, during the newness of that martyrdom, grieving, anxious, and sometimes placed in ecstasy, she sent the monks of Canterbury one day these written words, said to her by a certain most beautiful Lady who appeared to her in a night vision: “Do not weep for the archbishop: his head rests in the lap of my Son.” These were the beginnings of miracles, by which God revealed Thomas the martyr to be holy; for that saint’s life is made manifest by virtues and his death by miracles.

[Col. 0190C] But concerning his miracles, established in England by the testimony of priests and worthy men and publicly recited in the chapter of the Church of Canterbury, there exists a great written codex, apart from the other things which Saint Thomas worked far and wide in France, Ireland, and throughout the world, for the recording of which no writer was available.]

But while the de Brochs were threatening in those days and stood by night against the walls of the lodgings at Canterbury, so as to seize anyone who spoke openly in praise of the archbishop and drag him before their tribunal, the faithful at first dared speak of God’s great works only in silence. Then, through God in the power of the Holy Spirit, the grace of healings and the concourse of peoples there spread so widely that love cast out fear. The plotters themselves, who formerly even registered the bridges and crossings of roads to identify those visiting him alive or perfected by martyrdom, said [Col. 0190D]: “What we are doing is nothing. There is no counsel against the Lord. Behold, all England is going to him.”

There indeed God, for the glory of his name, the consolation of his Church, and the strengthening of our faith, showed that the innocent blood which had been shed cried to him from the pavement of the church, glorifying his martyr by the grace of miracles and vindicating his cause. The blind received sight; the contracted had the contours of their limbs stretched and straightened; hearing was restored to the deaf; paralyzed limbs were joined together; the possessed were freed; prisoners escaped. Many other infirmities were cured: cancers, dropsy, fistulas, swellings, epilepsy [*epiltasiae*, probably *epilepsiae*], and strangury. Seven lepers were cleansed there within the first year.

Moreover, several dead persons throughout England were restored to life when water mixed with the blood of blessed Thomas was poured into their mouths. Christ’s faithful carry this water away from there in tin vessels hanging at their breasts, as a sign of their pilgrimage and a remedy for their sick, and suspend it in their churches as holy relics—by a certain divine ordinance, so that the glory of blessed Thomas the martyr might be proclaimed among all nations and, in every Church, his blood might seem to cry to God for the liberty of the Church. By the just judgment of God it came about that where iniquity abounded beyond anything heard concerning any suffering apostle or martyr, there, above the glory of any saint, the grace of miracles [Col. 0191B] might abound—the Lord working, and Christian faith, to which all things are possible, assisting.

[All these things are worthy and devout to believe concerning the Lord’s saint. The authority of Jesus Christ confirms them, saying of his holy one: “The works that I do, he too shall do, and he shall do greater works than these.”]

Even in the street where his feet stood while he confirmed infants brought to him, the grace that works miracles is not lacking to Christ’s faithful, where the devotion of neighboring believers builds chapels,

> And constructs altars to be sworn by in his name.

Those placed in utmost danger at sea, having been delivered through his patronage, returned to give thanks at his tomb and left a token of so great a miracle and of their rescue.

[Col. 0191C] That soul of Saint Thomas the martyr adhered so affectionately and graciously to the desires and love of many—indeed, of all pious souls and all persons of good will—that from boys who, playing together in the streets, recount his passion, sing his glory, and complete his praise, to feeble old men rejoicing that they had survived to see these great works of God, every age and every rank venerates him, seeks his protection, bears his love in its heart and his name on its lips, and keeps his memory in glory and his glory in memory.

[Note: [Col. 0191] “Sweet” (*Dulcis*) in the Douce manuscript. In the margin Douce noted that “many” (*multis*) is read in the Cotton manuscript, Julius A. XI, British Museum.]

He stirred every inhabitant of England—counts and barons, as well as neighboring kingdoms on every side—to devotion to God, which had long grown lukewarm in English hearts, and to pious desires of improving life, undertaking holy pilgrimage, and giving alms. Before approaching his tomb, his pilgrims [Col. 0192A] confess their sins and remove their shoes; and from so great a gathering of both sexes and such devout eagerness in visiting him, this is one of the greatest among God’s mighty works.

A man full of holiness and grace, God’s martyr, most renowned by land and sea, a ready helper in times of need—as it is devout to believe—is honored by God with a more abundant multitude of signs in proportion as greater wickedness raged in the cutting down of his head. For, in the cause and for the liberty of the Church, he, Christ’s minister, was cruelly pierced in the crown [Col. 0192B] of his head: an archbishop by Christians in name only; by his sons; a lord by his own men; in the peace promised him; in the holy metropolitan church of God; and on the holy Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Saint Thomas the martyr, innocent in mind and harmless in life, is companion and fellow of the Holy Innocents; himself killed beneath God’s altar, he is one of those brethren to whom the Innocents received the answer that they should wait a little while until their number was fulfilled. Accordingly, translated to the glory of the Holy Innocents, he fittingly joins his memorial to the remembrance of their glory.

A certain cleric also understood and said, not implausibly, concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, blessed Thomas the Apostle, and this blessed Thomas the martyr: blessed Thomas the Apostle, suffering in India, illuminated the East with faith; this blessed Thomas the martyr, suffering in England, illuminated all the West; Jesus Christ suffered at Jerusalem and, as the common light, the true light enlightening every person coming into this world, joined the extremes as if from a middle point. What is true of the places is likewise a contemplation of their feasts: the Nativity of the Lord in the middle, with the apostle’s feast preceding it on the fifth day and the martyr’s following.

Concerning the time of the passion of Saint Thomas the martyr, someone composed this couplet:

> The year one thousand, one hundred, seventy,  
> And one—the year in which Thomas the primate falls by the sword.]

May he intercede with God for the peace, liberty, and unity of the Church, and for the salvation of all living faithful and the rest of the dead—he who is victorious in his martyrs and glorious in all his saints, through endless ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0193]

# The Fourth and Fifth Lives of Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury and Martyr, by John, Dean of Salisbury, and Alan, Abbot of Tewkesbury

[Note: [Col. 0193B]

The reader will not doubt that I have rightly joined the work of Alan, now for the first time extant in its entirety [Col. 0193C], with the brief inserted treatise of John of Salisbury. Moreover, on rereading the work, I remain in no doubt that it was Alan, not John of Salisbury, who first collected Saint Thomas’s letters into a single body. Alan’s little work exists separately in a manuscript preserved at the Hôtel Soubise in Paris, but it is of a more recent age and contains several additions. In Lupus’s *Quadrilogue* there are only two fragments which do not yet appear in Alan’s work. Whether they rightly have Alan as their author is highly uncertain. The second of these, indeed, takes for itself the place of Letter 87 in Book V among the letters edited by Lupus, and has one variant which I shall give here at col. 000: Letter 87, vol. 10, has *Dominicam*, namely the Sunday immediately before the Ascension of the Lord.

Besides the *Life of Saint Thomas*, two sermons of Alan, of no value, survive in a Bodleian manuscript; likewise, in a Cambridge manuscript, certain letters, all, I think, concerning Saint Thomas. I shall take care to transcribe and publish them.]

.

# Alan’s Prologue
[Col. 0193A] The honour and glory of the blessed martyr Thomas shine forth sufficiently of themselves throughout all lands; his splendour illumines the world and stirs the four quarters of the earth to devotion towards him. People flock from every side to his memorial. Every sex, age, and condition devotes itself to his service. His fame, flying abroad, draws even barbarous nations to the same end. For those who thirst to know the man’s life and manner of living, and moreover the cause and occasion of his martyrdom, sufficient answers may be found in what was written on this subject by the venerable man of life and outstanding virtue, John of Salisbury: clerk of the martyr himself, companion in his exile, and participant throughout in his tribulation, later bishop of Chartres. He sketched briefly and concisely Christ’s champion and his contest.

But because that work [Col. 0193B] reaches the matter itself without fully setting out its form in every respect, it seemed fitting and necessary that letters should follow that writing, letters in which the sequence and order of the whole are contained, so that whoever desires and is able to do so may have the entire account—if anyone seeks the man’s life, the manner of his exile, the progress of the case, or its outcome. The letters, collected from various scattered sheets, are brought together into one body, as far as this could be done, each retaining its own place and order. If, however, some general letters, which express the affair itself less directly, appear to have been placed differently, this does not greatly affect the sequence of events. Certainly, if anyone, with a more diligent hand, can improve these letters through fuller and more careful examination, there will be no one [Col. 0194A] to begrudge it.

They are divided into parts according to the course of the affair. The first part contains the material from the beginning of the exile until the arrival of the cardinals William and Otto. What was done, when, where, and through whom, will become more fully known from the letters themselves. The second part runs from those cardinals to Gratian and Vivian. From them the third part continues to Simon, prior of Val-Dieu, and Bernard of Corilo. From them likewise the fourth part continues to Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen, and Bernard, bishop of Nevers; and finally to William of Sens, now archbishop of Rheims. The fifth contains the settlement, passion, and canonisation of the martyr himself, and the reconciliation of Christ’s Church.

[Col. 0194B] In these materials the diligent and devout reader will find the image of the man of God depicted more fully. Moreover, should he wish to examine the traces of Thomas’s works, there he will find an abundance of weapons fashioned by the finger of God. There priestly dignity and episcopal authority may recognise themselves in the mirror of their warfare, so as to render Caesar his due service and God honour. Nor will anyone need to wander farther afield in search of how the liberty of the Church ought to be defended. Let him trace the path through the martyr’s letters, and he will immediately encounter what had to be done and in what manner. Let John’s work, therefore, be read first; through it the way will be opened to what follows.

## Prologue of John of Salisbury

[Col. 0195]

[Col. 0195A] The ancient enemy attacks the most holy Church without ceasing; but the Son of God, who redeemed her by his own blood, vindicates and advances her into true liberty by the blood of his members. Foremost among these are the glorious choir of apostles and the purple-clad army of holy martyrs. By their teaching the living stones in the structure of Christ’s body are joined together; by their example they are strengthened; by their blood, as if by cement and a kind of glue, they are made firm, so that the Church, advancing, may be enlarged and grow both in the number of believers and in virtue into a holy temple in the Lord.

But although all martyrs possess the prerogative of everlasting glory, the title of those who exercise the office of teachers, worthy of a double honour, is more illustrious than the rest, and their crown shines more brightly: those who have become from the heart an example to the flock, [Col. 0195B] and in time of necessity lay down their lives for their sheep. For as star differs from star in brightness, so, in the resurrection [Col. 0196A] of the saints, each righteous person in his own order shall shine like the stars; and those who instruct many unto life shall be as the brightness of the firmament for everlasting eternities. Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, must rightly and deservedly be joined with them: since he was Christ’s companion in tribulation and patience, he may be their fellow-heir in Christ himself of consolation and glory.

That his merits may shine forth more clearly, let a concise and very brief account run through the outline of his manner of life. For anyone who wishes to know the sequence of his deeds must borrow it from the large volumes written by him and about him. His letters [Col. 0196B] and the writings of others, full and worthy of record, indicate—so that the grace of God, which “blows where it wills,” may be praised—how, in so brief an interval, he filled many hours with varied occupations. If carefully considered, they can encourage both those now living and posterity toward virtue.

## Here begins the Life of Saint Thomas, by John of Salisbury

[Col. 0195]

[Col. 0195C] The aforesaid most blessed Thomas, then, a native of the city of London and the distinguished offspring of parents of moderate station, was endowed from the first years of youth with manifold grace. He was tall in stature, handsome in appearance, keen in intellect, gentle and pleasing in speech, and lovable, for his age, in the charm of his manners. His power of reasoning was so vigorous that he prudently resolved unheard-of and difficult questions; and he enjoyed so happy a memory that what he had once learned, whether in ideas or in words, he could repeat almost whenever he wished without difficulty. Many more learned men, unable to attain this mental quickness—especially in one devoted to varied occupations—attributed it to miracles. Thus grace, his nurse, attended the future bishop, supplying him, as the saying goes, with whatever he needed at hand in discussions [Col. 0195D] or in the course of speech.

From his earliest age, as he used to relate, he learned from his mother the fear of the Lord, and to invoke more sweetly the blessed Mary, Mother of God, as the guide of his paths and patroness of his life; and after [Col. 0196C] Christ to cast all his confidence upon her. He publicly felt deep compassion for beggars and aided them in deed, so that he could say with blessed Job: “From the beginning compassion grew with me, and pity came forth with me from my mother’s womb.”

After leaving the schools of the liberal arts, he turned to the occupations of public business. In their serious matters and their trifles, as his spirit led, he soon excelled, and thus easily surpassed his fellow-knights and contemporaries. Although he was occupied with youthful pursuits, as the impulses of his age pressed him, zeal for the faith and greatness of spirit nevertheless flourished in him. Yet he was excessively eager for popular applause; and I should not hesitate to affirm of him what is read of Saint Brice of Tours: that although he was proud [Col. 0196D] and vain, and sometimes foolishly put on the appearance and uttered the words of men in love, he was nevertheless admirable and worthy of imitation in bodily chastity.

When, however, he saw many things done in the courts of nobles contrary to the honour of the clergy, and saw that their way of life was in more destructive opposition to the purpose to which he was devoted, [Col. 0197A] he attached himself—rather by the prompting and guidance of grace than through the advice or intervention of friends—to Archbishop Theobald of Canterbury, of pious memory. Through the merit of his industry, he was soon found worthy to be numbered, among a very few, as one of Theobald’s most intimate associates. How many and how great labours he underwent there for the Church of God; how often he visited the thresholds of the apostles in order to settle ecclesiastical necessities; and with what fortunate result he accomplished the tasks laid upon him—this is by no means easy to tell, especially in an abbreviated account that does not set forth every particular, but seeks to gather the substance of events and explain the cause of his martyrdom.

So that readiness might be prepared for the bishop predestined by God in pleading and deciding cases and in instructing peoples, [Col. 0197B] he devoted himself to civil law. And so that through experience of affairs he might more easily acquire practical knowledge of ecclesiastical administration, he was appointed archdeacon by the aforesaid archbishop of the holy Church of Canterbury, at whose breasts he had been nourished, [so that, by God’s ordering, in his own time, rank, and place, the archdeacon might be advanced to become archbishop].

After a short interval, when Henry, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, son of Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and of the Empress Matilda, succeeded King Stephen to the kingdom of England, the aforementioned archbishop worked to have his archdeacon made chancellor of the realm. For he distrusted the king’s youth and feared the folly and malice of the young and wicked [Col. 0197C] men by whose counsels the king seemed to be guided. Lest, at their prompting, he act too insolently by a victor’s right—he thought that he had subdued the people, though matters stood otherwise—the archbishop arranged for a chancellor to be appointed in the court. By this man’s aid and work, he might restrain the new king’s violence against the Church, moderate the malice of his counsel, and curb the audacity of officials, who, under the pretence of public authority and the pretext of law, had conspired to plunder the resources both of the Church and of the provincials.

At the very outset of his chancellorship he bore so many and such great difficulties arising from diverse needs, was worn down by so many labours, crushed under so many afflictions, assaulted by so many ambushes, and exposed to so many snares in the court through the malice of its inhabitants, that, as [Col. 0197D] he was accustomed to tell his archbishop and friends with tears as witness, he often grew weary of his life every day; and, after his desire for eternal life, desired above all that he might be freed from the bonds of court life without the stain of disgrace. For although the world seemed to flatter and applaud him with all its enticements, he was not unmindful either of his station or of his burden. Each day he was compelled, on the one hand, to contend for the safety and honour of his lord the king, and, on the other, for the needs of the Church and the provincials, both against the king himself and against his enemies; and by diverse arts to evade diverse deceits. But what especially pressed upon him was the unceasing necessity of fighting the beasts of the court, of conducting business, as the saying goes, with Proteus, and of being trained as though in a wrestling-school. For at almost every [Col. 0198A] breath, unless grace and diligence preserved him, ruin and downfall threatened.

While serving as chancellor in the king’s palace, he found such favour in the king’s eyes that, after the death of the aforesaid archbishop of Canterbury, the king procured his appointment to the foremost see of the Britains, so that he might more easily govern the whole English Church.

For he had tested Thomas’s greatness of spirit and loyalty in many matters, believed him fully adequate to so lofty a station, readily bendable to his own interests, and prepared to carry out everything at his command in ecclesiastical and secular affairs. If premature death should cut short the king’s own days, he was also providing his heirs with a most faithful guardian. For he was a man of great experience, accustomed to measure future events with more than ordinary facility; [Col. 0198B] and he weighed very shrewdly the danger of so weighty a responsibility, since long use had taught him how much burden and how much honour that see carried. He knew also the king’s habits, the wickedness and obstinacy of his officials, and the effectiveness of informers’ malice in that court. From these facts he most truly concluded that, if Thomas accepted the office offered, he would lose either the grace of God or that of the king. For he could not cling to God while complying with royal practices, nor avoid having the king as his enemy if he preferred the laws of the saints to the king.

Therefore, for some time he resisted the king and the others who wished to promote him. But the divine election prevailed so greatly that, at the persuasion, inducement, and insistent urging of the venerable Henry of Pisa, cardinal-priest and legate of the Apostolic See, he yielded to the king’s desire [Col. 0198C] and to the counsels of his friends. He preferred to expose himself to danger with the king rather than permit the desolation of the Church, which lay under many perils, to be prolonged further. He resolved firmly in his mind either to free her from the misery of such slavery or, in imitation of Christ, to lay down his life for his sheep. For public authority, removing the Church’s privilege, indiscriminately summoned ecclesiastical cases, no less than secular ones, to its own tribunal; and priest as well as people was trampled underfoot.

Thus he whom God had chosen beforehand to be bishop and martyr, although some jealous men at first attempted to obstruct his promotion contrary to the counsel of divine providence, was unanimously elected by all.

[Col. 0198D] Immediately upon being consecrated, he put off the old man and put on haircloth and the monk, “crucifying the flesh with its vices and lusts.” Remembering also the office of teacher and shepherd that he had undertaken, he discharged the duty of preaching, devoting almost all the time he could withdraw from pressing affairs to prayer and reading. When alone, he was soaked with tears almost miraculously; and he performed the service of the altar as though he saw Christ’s Passion being enacted bodily before him. He handled the divine sacraments with the greatest reverence, so that the very act of touching them instructed the faith and conduct of those who watched. He shook his hands free from every gift and utterly banished the filth of avarice from his household.

[Col. 0199A] He was also prudent in counsel; a diligent and restrained hearer in the examination of cases; penetrating in questions; ready in answers; just in judgments; and, having altogether put aside respect of persons, a most upright executor of law in every respect. Beneath the propriety of his clothing, he took particular care to conceal Christ’s soldier, lest vain glory diminish his merits; so that, in accordance with the sage’s injunction, his outward appearance might conform to the people, though almost everything within was different. Nor did he enter his hall for the meal until poor people had first been brought in. He wished the table to be made more splendid and abundantly supplied for this very purpose: that he might console the needy more fully and generously from its remains. No door-to-door beggar went away empty from his doors. Through his servants he diligently sought out the homes of the sick and infirm and visited them with benefits, supporting very many daily with food and clothing.

[Col. 0199B] Since his predecessor Theobald, of pious memory, had customarily doubled the fixed alms of his predecessors, Thomas, in devout emulation, judged that even this double amount should be doubled. To maintain this pious work, he consecrated tithes of all he received under whatever title. In a more private chamber he daily washed the feet of thirteen poor persons on bended knee, in memory of Christ, giving each of them, after a full meal, four silver coins. If he was ever prevented, though rarely, from performing this in person, he took great care that it should be carried out by a deputy.

He received religious men with such reverence [Col. 0199C] that one might have believed he was venerating in them the divine presence or angels. In practising hospitality and other works of generosity, he was so eminent that everything in his possession might have been thought the common patrimony of all good people. Although his household, according to the custom of the nation, was furnished with precious utensils and varied equipment for its affairs, he nevertheless despised riches, wealth, and all worldly furnishings for Christ’s sake as dung, using transient things rather to meet necessities than enjoying them to satisfy the pleasures of desire. In food and drink he held to the mean of temperance, lest total abstinence expose him to an accusation of superstition, or excessive consumption burden him with drunken excess. Avoiding almost equally the reproach of criminal and hypocrite, he judged the best kind of fasting to be the maintenance of moderation in sobriety.

[Col. 0199D] Indeed, poor in spirit while wearing costly clothing, contrite in heart while cheerful in countenance, choosing want at a lavish table, sometimes with his stomach more empty than refreshed, more often restored than filled, always remaining sober, he conformed himself to those who lived with him. He followed the apostle who, by a most salutary dispensation, became all things to all people in order to gain all. He delivered the poor from the powerful, for he had truly been given by the Lord as a father of the poor and comforter of the sorrowing. He freely rebuked the vices of authorities of every kind, knowing that where the Spirit of the Lord is, there also is liberty. Yet, being a discerning man, he weighed the character of those whom he rebuked or admonished, lest he give what is holy to dogs [Col. 0200A] or scatter pearls before swine.

Because the heavenly anointing taught him, he conversed both with learned and unlearned people. He appeared wonderfully learned and eloquent; and his preaching was pleasing and effective, both in the weight of its ideas and in the purity of its language. After meals and after such sleep as necessity required, he again, beyond the prescribed offices, applied himself to business, writings, or honourable conversations, carefully fleeing idleness, lest his enemies see him and mock at his Sabbaths. Whatever he could take from nightly sleep without serious injury to his body he gave to tears, prayers, and holy meditations. He pursued chastity in body, preserved purity in heart, modesty in speech, and justice in deed, so that those whom he was [Col. 0200B] to instruct by word might be moved more powerfully by the example of his holiness.

He fought tirelessly against heretics and schismatics, and could never be induced to communicate with the excommunicated. Whoever opposed sound doctrine, he did not doubt would be his enemy in Christ. Burning also with zeal for justice, he strove to preserve for each person what was his own, altogether putting aside favouritism and the acceptance of gifts.

But when the ancient enemy saw that so great a man would be of very great benefit to the Church of God, he became envious. To prevent the land from enjoying for longer the peace for which it hoped, he chose many great instigators of discord. Through them he scattered seeds of hatred in the heart of the king and his courtiers. For when, at their contrivance, a dispute arose over the customs of the realm and ecclesiastical law, he stirred up the sons of perdition [Col. 0200C] for the destruction of the holy man—men who sought to overthrow the liberty of the Church.

Though all were oppressed, the Church of Canterbury afflicted him most, since its authority, honour, and advantage were gravely impaired. First Roger, archbishop of York, rose against him; then many nobles; and those who were bound in obligation by the Church’s loyalty and benefactions. The king himself repeatedly and obstinately forbade him to exercise canonical justice upon subjects whose faults demanded it. For lay power, disregarding ecclesiastical law, usurped control over the property and persons of all at its pleasure, while the bishops were silent or murmured rather than resisted. The king therefore tried by promises and flatteries to bend the archbishop to [Col. 0200D] his agreement. But the man of God, founded and established upon the rock, could neither be softened by flatteries so as to stray from the worship of justice, nor frightened by threats.

The wicked therefore attempted, by malicious interpretation, to obscure this change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. They attributed his stricter life to superstition; they falsely called his zeal for justice cruelty; they ascribed to avarice his care for the Church’s interests; they said that his contempt for worldly favour was a pursuit of glory; his courtly magnificence was represented as pride; and because in many things he followed a will taught by God, they branded him with arrogance. Because he often appeared to exceed the boundaries set by his predecessors in defending the law, they judged it a sign of rashness. Nothing could now be said or done by him that the malice [Col. 0201A] of unhappy men did not distort. Indeed, they persuaded the king that, if the archbishop’s power went forward, royal dignity would without doubt perish; and that unless the king provided for himself and his heirs, the one whom the clergy chose would henceforth be king, and would reign only as long as the archbishop pleased.

When bishops and nobles assembled by the king’s command to settle the needs of the realm, a dispute perhaps arose between king and Church. Prolonged for a long time, it was daily increased more and more at the devil’s instigation. Since all the bishops together with their archbishop were unanimous in their purpose to obey the king most devotedly in matters that belonged to God, and neither to make any promise nor enter into any obligation with him except so far as they could do so without prejudice to their order, [Col. 0201B] every effort was made to break the unity established in the Church. This was done through certain bishops who appeared to be pillars of faith and religion, so that either the archbishop might be corrupted with them, or, if he stood alone, might easily be crushed.

Very many laboured to trip up the man of God; but his familiar enemies pressed him most destructively. The man of invincible constancy remembered that one whom God assists is not alone. Secure through God’s inspiration, he ascended against them, setting himself as a most solid wall for the house of Israel. He could be neither broken by threats nor softened by flatteries. For he preferred, poor himself, to follow poor Christ rather than forsake Christ’s law; and Christ the comforter assisted him through the small number of poor people who sympathised with him.

When, after countless vexations and injuries, bishops and nobles had finally assembled at Clarendon by the king’s will, [Col. 0201C] the king demanded more insistently that the customs of the realm, which his grandfather seemed to have observed according to the flattering assertions of the nobles, should be publicly recited and confirmed by the express and unqualified assent of all the bishops, with no condition whatsoever added. Recognising this, the archbishop and bishops tried, as far as they could, to prevent or at least postpone it, measuring the danger inevitably threatening from both sides. If they consented to abuses rooted in long-established corruption, peril to faith and salvation would undoubtedly follow. But if they resisted, the peace of the Church and the safety of their lives would be exposed to certain dangers. Nor was there any lack of just cause for fear, since, according to Solomon: [Col. 0201D] “As the roaring of a lion, so is the wrath of a king.”

But the burden of the conflict was directed against the archbishop. Without his counsel, as without that of their head, the bishops dared undertake nothing; yet they feared to advise him to yield. He, however, was more anxious over the dangers of certain bishops—upon whom, because of the king’s long-standing hatred, the loss of limb and life seemed to threaten—than over his own, though very many and very grave dangers hung over him. Deceived both by the urgent necessity and by the persuasive words of great men professing religious devotion, he agreed that the king’s demand should be made in words only. Thus both he and those bishops for whom fear was entertained escaped bodily danger, though at the cost of the cause. But the bishop, fearing in this deliverance of bodies the ruin of souls, began to afflict himself more severely with harsher [Col. 0202A] food and clothing, and suspended himself from service at the altar until, through confession and worthy fruits of repentance, he deserved to be released by absolution from the Roman pontiff.

Yet even then the king’s indignation did not rest, but through threats and terrors he promised greater cruelty unless the customs which he sought to introduce against the Church were confirmed in writing by the authority of archbishops and bishops. Because Christ’s confessor and future martyr dared oppose these attempts, he was meanwhile attacked with many losses, assailed with insults, and afflicted with injuries. At last he was brought to Northampton under unjust legal process. Though he patiently endured being condemned by an unjust judgment in a certain financial case, he gave fully adequate security for payment to the king of what had been adjudged.

Then, under the pretext of rendering an account for matters entrusted to him during his administration of the chancellorship—though he had certainly not been summoned for this purpose—they levelled further accusations against him. So violently was he harassed contrary to law and right that, in order to prevent the bishops from condemning him by an unjust judgment and thereby currying favour with the king, he had to appeal to the Apostolic See; and he likewise appealed from them to the hearing of the lord pope.

[Col. 0202B] Nevertheless the nobles, although an appeal had been lodged against them and they had been forbidden under anathema to pronounce sentence upon their father and judge, still presumed against him. He had neither confessed nor been convicted, but had merely asserted and invoked the Church’s privilege and the protection of public law. To complete their own condemnation, they presumed not so much to pronounce [Col. 0202C] a sentence against him as to vomit forth the madness of their conceived fury. When they wished to publish it publicly, the holy man raised high the cross of Christ which he held in his hand and bore continually in his heart and on his body. He departed from that deadly court, while the wicked shouted that he should be seized as a traitor, deservedly hanged, and, so that the faithful servant might acknowledge the title of his Lord, he heard cries on every side: “Crucify him, crucify him.” But he, passing through their midst, went on his way.

When he had withdrawn to his lodging, two great and most faithful nobles came to him in the very dead of night, wretched and tearful in countenance, beating their breasts and confessing and declaring, by the dreadful judgment of God, that they knew beyond doubt that great men, notorious for evil deeds and stained with many crimes, had conspired to kill him and had bound themselves mutually by oaths to murder him. Therefore, lest the cause of the Church, which was not yet fully known, should suffer eclipse in his death, that same night he set out in flight; with only one brother affording him comfort, he lay concealed by day and travelled by night, and on the sixteenth day reached the port of Sandwich. Since no better means of transport was at hand, he crossed to Flanders in a frail little boat, carried over by two priests, with a few others rather hindering the vessel than bringing any aid or comfort.

Thus, driven into exile, the confessor of Christ was honourably received at Sens by Pope Alexander and was commended by him to the monastery of Pontigny. But the king of the English sent his bishops and nobles to the Roman Church, promising much if legates might be dispatched who, all appeal set aside, would determine the cause of the Archbishop of Canterbury—which he most urgently demanded should be remitted. For it seemed that the cardinals could be swayed and that an abundance of witnesses could very easily be procured for every point of the case. But when, from the messengers on their return, he learned that he had been rebuffed in this request, he ordered the church and all the goods of the archbishop and of his people to be confiscated; and, as is recorded in no sequence of any history, he sentenced to banishment the whole of his kindred and all who were connected with him by familiarity or by any title, without distinction of rank, order, condition, fortune, age, or sex. For women lying in childbirth and infants crying in their cradles were driven into exile.

The monstrous rage and cruelty, horrible to devout ears, went further still. Although the Catholic Church prays even for heretics, schismatics, and faithless Jews, it was forbidden for anyone to assist him even by the support of prayers. The officers of public authority also compelled every adult to swear that he would go to Pontigny in order to grieve the archbishop. There the holy man long mortified himself with fasts and prayers, continually praying for the Church, for the king, and for the kingdom of England, until the king contrived to drive him thence through the Cistercian abbots who had assembled from his land for the general chapter.

But before he departed, he was strengthened by divine revelation: a sign shown him from heaven declared that he would return to his church in glory and would thence pass to the Lord after gaining the palm of martyrdom. And as the Blessed Virgin—whose soul the sword of sorrow pierced through in the Passion of her Son—is said to have been more than a martyr, so Christ’s confessor, having endured in himself and his people many, great, unheard-of, and prolonged sufferings, made the merit and crown of martyrdom shine more gloriously. Fearing that, because of his assertion of right, loss might threaten holy persons, he departed voluntarily and betook himself to Louis, the most Christian king of the Franks. Receiving him reverently, Louis most humanely supplied his necessities until peace should be restored. He also urged the supreme pontiff, by the force of love and under a declaration of devoted service, not to prolong fruitless delays further, if he loved the kingdom of France and the honour of the Apostolic See.

Moreover, William, the venerable bishop of Sens, moved by pity for the desolation of the English Church, sought the Apostolic See and obtained from the Roman Church that the king of the English should, all appeal having ceased, be subjected to anathema and the kingdom to an interdict unless peace were restored to the Church of Canterbury. Meanwhile, through the contrivance of those who hated the Church’s peace, Roger, Archbishop of York, after the pope’s prohibition, presumed in the province of Canterbury, contrary to the dignity of the Church of Canterbury and ancient custom, to crown Henry, the king’s son, with his suffragans assisting him and raising no protest for the right of the Church of Canterbury.

Accordingly, as injuries multiplied and wicked men continually abused Christ’s patience, manifold, certain, and swift threats advanced more and more against the king and his adherents. The peremptory day pressed on, so that sentence could no longer be deferred. Constrained therefore by canonical severity, the king at last consented that peace should be restored to the English Church. The kingdoms rejoiced, all believing that the business was being genuinely transacted rather than deceptively devised; but the outcome showed what certain persons were doing. For Christ’s pontiff, measuring others by his own good faith, hoped better things from those who were negotiating with him. And although many urged him not to presume to return unless peace were more securely established, yet, fearing danger to souls, he returned in the seventh year of exile to his church, the king providing him an escort, and was received by clergy and people as an angel of the Lord.

When the lord pope, upon Saint Thomas’s complaint, heard of the aforesaid presumption of the said Archbishop of York and of the bishops who had supported him, he suspended both the Archbishop of York and the bishops favouring him from episcopal office, and subjected Gilbert of London and Jocelin of Salisbury to the sentence of anathema. This severity, publicly announced at Saint Thomas’s entry, further embittered the king and made the poisonous tongues of detractors more effective for harm. Thus again the athlete of Christ was afflicted with losses, again with injuries more atrocious beyond measure and number, and by public edict was forbidden to leave the precincts of his church. Whoever showed a cheerful face to him or to any of his household was regarded as a public enemy.

Yet the man of God bore all these things in great patience, preferring to suffer loss not only of possessions but even of life, rather than allow the justice of God and the liberty of the Church to be endangered without assistance, or at least without protest. With the permission of all saints, I would say: if each person offers to God as much as he leaves behind for His love, one will not easily find anyone who surpasses Thomas. For Christ’s sake he despised his own possessions and his own people; he despised the world; he despised himself also.

And because my pen hastens to the passion of the confessor, the authors and cause of which are evident from many great indications, I judged that I should not linger longer upon it—especially since its subject is now known and published almost throughout the Latin world from the accounts of very many persons. Yet I did not believe the following should be left unspoken amid so great a gift of divine providence: to the glory of God and of His martyr, all marvel that every circumstance concurred in the bishop’s contest so as forever to illustrate the title of the sufferer, reveal the impiety of the persecutors, and stain their name with everlasting reproach.

For if one wishes to look at and assess the persons on either side, there appears on this side a religious archbishop, primate of the Britains, legate of the Apostolic See, a most incorruptible judge—one who accepted neither persons nor gifts—defender of ecclesiastical liberty, and, like a tower raised in Jerusalem facing Damascus, a hammer of the ungodly but a comforter of the poor and sorrowful. Let whoever wishes consider who advances on the opposite side.

And if the cause makes the martyr—as no rightly minded person doubts—what cause was more just, what more holy than his? Despising for Christ’s love riches and all worldly glory, the affection of friends and of his whole kindred, he underwent exile and exposed himself and all his people to danger and poverty. For the defence of the law of his God and the abolition of the abuses of ancient tyrants, he fought unto death. Nor, after he had once fallen into the trap of those lying in wait, could their deceit induce him to promise anything that was demanded of him; rather, in all things he added that God’s honour and the Church’s dignity must remain secure.

Nor did he endure adversity merely for a little while, as it were for an hour, believing only briefly and withdrawing at the point of temptation; rather, he prolonged exile and bitter proscription into the seventh year. With such strength of constancy he walked the royal road, following the footsteps of Christ and the apostles, that his unconquered spirit could neither be broken by the onset of raging fortune nor softened by flatteries.

But consider also where he was sacrificed. Surely in the Church which is the head of the kingdom and the mother of all others in Christ: before the altar, among fellow priests and in the hands of religious persons, whom the tumult of armed executioners had caused to assemble for a spectacle astonishing and pitiable. He who for a long time had presented himself as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God; who had crucified his flesh, with its reproaches and desires, by prayers, vigils, fasts, and the harsher use of haircloth; whose back—known only to his closest household—he had been accustomed, like a little servant of Christ, to expose to scourges; who had been accustomed to offer Christ’s body and blood upon the altar—prostrate before the altar, he offered his own blood, poured out by the hands of the ungodly.

*[To whom was the title of martyrdom ever more glorious?]*

Nor was it permitted to the ministers of Satan, in the sacrifice of the disciple and servant, what had been permitted to their predecessors in the crucifixion of the Master and Lord. For Christ, lest the city be defiled and the Sabbath polluted, though already condemned by an unjust judgment, received whatever opportunity of pleading for himself was granted him; and, led out of the city beyond the gate, he was crucified by the agency of Gentiles who did not know God and by the authority of public power. He was handed over as guilty by those whose law he was thought to have attacked, while the disciple, the son of perdition, procured the treachery of betrayal.

But this man was slain not merely in the city, but inside the church; not on a profane day, but on the day consecrated by the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity. And it was altogether fitting that the feast-day of one who had lived innocently and most holily should follow the feast of the Holy Innocents. Indeed, as is believed, traitorous disciples procured his death and the leaders of priests devised it, surpassing Annas and Caiaphas, Pilate and Herod by as much in wickedness as they took greater care that he should not be brought to judgment, not be confronted by accusers, not appear before the governor, and not escape their sacrilegious hands through the privilege of sacred place, sacred time, dignity, rank, restored peace, or security pledged—not the hands of Gentiles or enemies, but of men professing God’s law and friendship’s faith.

Certainly, by the wonderful dispensation of God, who orders all things wisely and beneficially, it came about that He who permitted these things to be done so wickedly and so imprudently did not permit them to be hidden, so that even here in time might be fulfilled what Truth declared: “For there is nothing hidden that shall not be revealed.” For what has been widely published concerning the notorious speech of Judas, the standard-bearer of traitors, ought by equal right to be applied to his accomplices, since the judgment is manifestly the same concerning similar deeds, so that all Christians may know by faith that the heavens will reveal their iniquity and the earth rise up against them. And what believer would dare doubt that God would either convert or crush the authors and perpetrators of so great a sacrilege?

Now, as has been said, Christ’s martyr was to suffer in the church before the altar. Before he was struck, when he heard the soldiers who had come for this purpose crying out amid a crowd of clerics and monks, “Where is the archbishop?”, he met them upon the steps, which he had climbed in large part, with an undaunted face, saying: “Here I am. What do you want?” One of the accursed soldiers, in a spirit of fury, answered him: “That you may die at once; for it is impossible that you should live any longer.”

The archbishop replied with no less constancy of word than of spirit—for, speaking confidently according to the judgment of my heart, with due respect to all martyrs, no one seems to have been more steadfast than he: “I too am ready to die for my God and for the defence of justice and the liberty of the Church. But if you seek my head, I forbid you, on behalf of Almighty God and under anathema, to harm in any respect any other person, whether monk, cleric, or layman, greater or lesser. Let them be free from punishment, just as they were free from the cause; for if any of them undertook the cause of the suffering Church, it is not to them but to me that it must be imputed. I willingly embrace death, provided that through the shedding of my blood the Church may obtain peace and liberty.”

Who was more steadfast than he? Who seems more fervent in charity? While offering himself to persecutors for the law of his God, his sole concern was that the flock entrusted to him should suffer no harm in any respect. Do not his words seem to express Christ saying in His Passion: “If you seek me, let these go their way”?

Having said this, seeing the executioners with drawn swords, he bowed his head in the manner of one praying, uttering these final words: “To God, and to blessed Mary, and to the patron saints of this church, and to blessed Denis the martyr, I commend myself and the cause of the Church.”

Who can recount the rest without sighs, sobs, and tears? Piety does not permit one to relate in detail each deed committed by those most savage executioners, contemptuous of the fear of God and forgetful alike of faith and of all humanity. For it did not suffice them to profane the church with a priest’s blood and to violate the most holy day with murder, unless, after the crown of his head—consecrated to God by the anointing of sacred chrism—had been cut away, they also, horrible even to say, cast out the brains of one already dead with their accursed swords and most cruelly scattered them across the pavement with blood and bones. In this they were more savage than Christ’s crucifiers, who did not judge that His legs should be broken after they had seen that He had died, as they did those still living.

Yet amid all these torments, the martyr, of unconquered spirit and admirable constancy, uttered neither word nor cry, gave no groan, and raised neither arm nor garment against the striker; but he held motionless the head which he had bowed and exposed to the swords until all was completed. Finally, falling to the ground with his body straight, he did not move foot or hand while the murderers assailed him, having betrayed the peace of their country in the slaughter of the traitor.

The executioners, no less greedy than cruel, then returned, to the injury alike of royal authority and divine majesty, to the palace of the church. They plundered with insatiable greed and astonishing audacity all its furnishings and whatever could be found in the chests or packs of the archbishop and his household—gold, silver, clothing, various ornaments, books, privileges, every kind of document, and horses—and divided it among themselves as they pleased. Thus they became imitators of those who divided Christ’s garments among themselves, although in some manner they surpassed them in crime. And so that human favour might be taken away from the bishop now crowned through martyrdom, all writings stolen by the sacrilegious robber were sent to the king in Normandy.

But by divine ordinance it came about that, the more human rashness strove to obscure the glory of this most valiant athlete, the more abundantly the Lord made it illustrious by clear proofs in the display of powers and miracles. When the impious men who hated him insatiably saw this, they prohibited, in the name of public authority, anyone from daring publicly to publish the miracles being performed. Yet who desires in vain to cloud what God purposes to glorify? For miracles spread all the more widely precisely as they appeared to the wicked to require more diligent concealment.

Man sees the outward appearance; God alone searches kidneys and hearts. For when the body of the blessed martyr was to be committed to burial and clothed according to pontifical custom, it was discovered, as very few of his intimates knew, wrapped in haircloth filled with lice and worms; and his inner breeches, made of haircloth down to the knees—a thing previously unheard of among our people—were likewise found.

Who can recount the groans and the great floods of tears shed by the company of holy persons present at the disclosure of such veiled religious devotion? And who can recount or hear without tears what followed? The church that had been violated—or rather consecrated—by sacred blood did not dare, without much hesitation and deliberation because of fear of the wicked, to suspend divine worship in protest against the injury done to God. Yet such terror from the manifest signs seized the people of the province that no one at all, or scarcely anyone, dared cease from divine worship in order either to display justice or solemnly render, as a duty of humanity, the service owed in Christ to the dead.

In all this, the rage of the persecutors did not cease. They said that the body of a traitor ought not to be buried among holy bishops but should be cast into a most vile marsh or hung upon a gallows. Therefore the holy men present, fearing violence against themselves, buried him in the crypt, before the attendants of Satan who had been summoned to commit sacrileges could assemble, before the altar of Saint John the Baptist and Saint Augustine, apostle of the English, in a marble sarcophagus.

There, to the glory of almighty God, many great miracles occur through him, as crowds of people flock together to see in others and feel in themselves the power and mercy of Him who is always wondrous and glorious in His saints. For both at the place of his Passion, and where he lay overnight before the high altar before burial, and where he was finally buried: paralytics are healed; the blind see; the deaf hear; the dumb speak; the lame walk; lepers are cleansed; those with fevers escape; the possessed are freed from demons; the sick are cured of diverse diseases; blasphemers possessed by demons are put to shame. And, what has not been heard since the days of our fathers, the dead rise again—He working these and more things, too many to recount, who alone is God blessed above all things for ever. Amen.

[Col. 0207] Thus ends the treatise of John of Salisbury on the Life of Saint Thomas.

## THE LIFE OF THE SAME SAINT BY ALAN, PRIOR OF CANTERBURY, LATER ABBOT OF TEWKESBURY, BEGINS

[Col. 0207D] The glorious martyr of God, Thomas—what manner of man he was, what his life and conduct were, and how great were the hardships he suffered for the liberty of the Church—has been elegantly described by the martyr’s own cleric and familiar associate, Master John of Salisbury, afterwards bishop of Chartres. But because certain matters were deliberately omitted there in keeping with the brevity of a history, matters which, if added, may stir the devotion of reader and hearer, especially since they concern the explanation of the letters which follow, we have thought it proper to add in summary those events which are said, according to the truth of history, to have occurred from the council of Clarendon until the departure of Pope Alexander from France and the consummation of the martyrdom itself. The letters themselves pursue the remaining matters more fully in their proper places.

Therefore, while blessed Thomas was at Clarendon, at the urging of his brethren he reluctantly promised, certainly by his priestly word, that he would observe with the others, at the king’s pleasure, the customs called “ancestral.” But after he had departed from the king’s court, he diligently recalled how great a loss to ecclesiastical liberty could arise from them. As he withdrew from the royal court, murmuring arose incidentally among his household: some, as commonly happens, urged that this had to be done because of the urgency of the times; others were indignant that the authority of ecclesiastical liberty should perish at the whim of one man.

Among them one pressed the point more sharply, saying: “Public power throws everything into confusion; wickedness raves even against Christ Himself; the synagogue of Satan profanes God’s sanctuary; rulers have sat down and gathered together as one against Christ. No one who loves justice is safe. With the world as judge, today the only wise and honoured persons are those who comply with the prince’s wish. This storm has shaken even the pillars of the Church; and while the shepherd loses his senses, the scattered sheep lurk beneath the wolf. Henceforth, what place will remain for innocence? Who will stand against this? Or who will triumph in battle, once the prince has been overcome?”

These were the complaints of the man who carried the cross before the archbishop; the others were silenced by distress. Taking up the parable more boldly, he added: “Why, son,” said the archbishop, “do you say these things?” “What strength,” he replied, “has he retained who has betrayed both conscience and reputation? It concerns you yourself: today you have wholly betrayed conscience and reputation, leaving to posterity an example hateful to God and contrary to honour, when you stretched out hands consecrated to God to observe accursed customs and joined with the wicked ministers of Satan in confounding ecclesiastical liberty.”

Then the archbishop groaned and said with a sigh: “I repent; and, greatly horrified at my offence, I judge myself henceforth unworthy to approach in priestly office Him whose Church I have entered into so vile a bargain concerning. I shall therefore sit silent in mourning until the Dayspring from on high visits me, so that through God Himself and the lord pope I may deserve absolution.”

He immediately sent a messenger to the Apostolic See. Meanwhile the king learned that the archbishop wished to withdraw from that aforesaid undertaking, especially because he openly resisted affixing his seal, as had been agreed, to the written text of those customs. From then on the enraged king began to harass the archbishop with heavier and more elaborate exactions, so that those who understood could plainly see that his blood and life were being sought.

Fearing this, he resolved upon flight. Coming to his manor called Aldington, while the others slept, he secretly slipped away, accompanied by only two persons; and, finding a ship, committed himself to the sea. Long battered by an adverse wind, he scarcely returned alive to land at daybreak. When his departure became known, it scattered his household and servants one by one. Yet one of them, bolder than the rest, came to Canterbury and withdrew the following night into the archbishop’s own chamber. After supper he began anxiously to grieve over the misfortune and distress of his lord.

When much of the night had passed and he wished to rest, he said to a boy: “Go and shut the hall-door more securely, so that we may sleep more safely.” The boy went there with a lighted lamp; opening the door, he saw the archbishop sitting alone in a corner. At this sight he fled in terror, thinking he had seen a phantom. When this was reported, that cleric was altogether unwilling to believe it until he had proved the truth in person. He came and found it exactly as had been said. The archbishop therefore summoned certain brethren of the Church of Canterbury and explained to them what had happened to him, and that it was not yet God’s will that he should depart.

Refreshed by a modest supper, he rested. But in the morning the king’s officers rushed in to confiscate everything, since they believed that the archbishop had fled; yet when they heard and saw that he was present, they were confounded and kept silent.

Thereupon the king pressed his hand more heavily upon the archbishop, causing him to be peremptorily summoned to answer the king on an appointed day concerning the accusations laid against him.

When the day arrived, they came; and, after a proclamation had been made, our lord was summoned to Northampton and brought into court. Thus, while the lord of Canterbury sat apart in an inner chamber with his fellow bishops, the doors were locked by the king’s command so that there might be no exit. The royal party brought forward against the lord of Canterbury this charge: that, although he had held vacant bishoprics, abbeys, and many revenues of the lord king in his own hands for many years, he had rendered no account to the king concerning them, which the king now required to be produced.

“On these matters,” said the Archbishop of Canterbury, “we wish to consult wiser persons and answer after consultation.” While they maintained a silence among themselves, at the lord of Canterbury’s request, Gilbert, Bishop of London—dean of the Church of Canterbury and therefore first in counsel after the Archbishop of Canterbury—said: “Father, if you remember whence the lord king raised you and what he has bestowed upon you, consider, given the evil character of the times, what ruin you will prepare for the Catholic Church and for us all if you wish to resist the king in these matters. You ought to yield not only the archbishopric of Canterbury but ten times as much, if it were worth so much. And perhaps, if the king sees this humility in you, he will restore you in full.”

“That is enough,” said the Archbishop of Canterbury. “It has become clear what answer you have given after deliberation.”

Then Henry, Bishop of Winchester, added: “This form of counsel is utterly ruinous for the Catholic Church; it binds and confounds us all. If our archbishop and primate of all England leaves us this example, that every bishop ought, at a prince’s pleasure and threat, to abandon the authority and care of souls entrusted to him, what future condition will there be for the Church except that nothing will be done according to right, but everything will be thrown into confusion according to whim, and so priest and people alike will be the same?”

Then Hilary, Bishop of Chichester—who was also distinguished in speech—added: “Unless the urgency of the times and the disturbance of the Catholic Church required otherwise, we ought indeed to stand by the words of this judgment. But when the authority of the canons wavers, much must be remitted from strictness, so that dispensation may accomplish in this case what severe correction might destroy. I therefore judge that the royal will should be yielded to for the present, lest we rush too hastily to decide something that will require a harsher retraction afterward.”

Then Robert, Bishop of Lincoln, a simple man indeed and of less discernment, said, not without embarrassment: “It is evident that this man’s life and blood are being sought, and that one of two things must necessarily be surrendered—either the archbishopric or life. What benefit then will come from the archbishopric if life must consequently be surrendered? I do not see it.”

But Bartholomew, Bishop of Exeter, said: “It is plain that the days are evil; and if, beneath the cover of dissimulation, we can pass through the onset of this storm unhurt, that must especially be sought. Yet we cannot easily achieve even this unless much is remitted from strictness. The urgency of the times demands it, particularly since this persecution is not general but personal. It is better therefore that one head be endangered in part than that the whole English Church be exposed to unavoidable danger.”

Roger, Bishop of Worcester, being asked what he himself thought, framed his answer so that by declining to speak he openly showed what was in his mind. “I shall give no counsel in this matter,” he said, “because, if I say that the care of souls received from God ought to be abandoned at the royal will and threat, my mouth will speak against my conscience and to the condemnation of my own head. If I judge that the king must be resisted, behold, his men are listening, through whom this becomes known to the king; immediately I shall be cast out of the synagogue, and thereafter my lot will be with public enemies and condemned men. Therefore I neither say this nor advise that.”

When these things had taken place, they sat silent for a while, and no one remained to add anything further. When they had contrived a way to obtain an exit—for they were shut in—the lord of Canterbury said: “I wish to speak with two earls who are with the king.” He named them. When summoned, they entered quickly through opened doors, believing that they would hear something that would satisfy the royal will.

With them present, the archbishop said: “We have consulted concerning those matters for which the lord king has summoned us. And because at present we do not have those to whom the matter itself is better known, we ask for a postponement until tomorrow, when we shall answer as God inspires us.” The Bishops of London and Rochester were sent to convey this to the king. But the Bishop of London, hiding beneath the fox’s skin, distorted the business entrusted to him. He told the king that the archbishop was asking him for time to prepare documents, as though he would render an account on the appointed day concerning the charges, thereby binding the archbishop more tightly to perform the king’s will.
