Accordingly, two earls were sent to the archbishop carrying the postponement requested from the king, provided that he approved what had been represented to the king on his behalf through the bishops. Hearing this, the archbishop said that he had given no such instructions and did not approve what had been represented to the king; rather, on the following day, God being his author, he would come and answer as might be granted him from above.

The Bishop of London blushed when he saw that he had fallen into the trap he had cast to deceive his father. The council was therefore dissolved that day, and they departed from one another. But the multitude of knights and others who had assembled there with the lord of Canterbury, terrified by fear of the king, withdrew apart and no longer stood with him. Learning this, he ordered the hedges and lanes to be searched and the poor, lame, and weak to be summoned to him, saying that through such a soldiery a swifter victory might be gained than through those who had withdrawn most shamefully in the time of temptation.

[Col. 0212C] Thus his house was filled with those reclining at table, and that day was spent in joy in the Lord, with no public mention made of the former disturbance.

On the following day, very early at dawn, our lord was struck by an intestinal complaint—for he was often afflicted by it—to such an extent that he could not raise himself from bed. Accordingly, after a longer delay, his envious opponents believed that he did not wish to go down to the king’s court, and men were sent to summon him more sternly to answer. “When this pain has subsided,” said the lord of Canterbury, “tomorrow, God being my helper, I shall appear.”

When that day had passed, and he had at length performed the night watches with utmost devotion, he rose in the morning for the solemn celebration of Mass. Clothed, as customary, in sacred vestments and invoking divine aid for himself through the merits of blessed Stephen the martyr, he ordered the Introit of the Mass to be begun: “For rulers indeed have sat down,” etc. He completed with greater devotion the whole office and all that belonged to it, while the king’s officers present silently observed, thinking that the matter portended something special. For that year and that day, according to the course of years, marked the hundredth anniversary of the Normans’ entry into England.

When the service had been completed, he removed the pallium and mitre from his shoulders; clothed in the remaining sacred vestments, with a clerical cope laid over them, he proceeded to the king’s court. As he was about to enter the king’s chamber—for the king was waiting there at the very door—he carried the cross in his own hand, the bishops following and interpreting this otherwise than was fitting.

Robert of Hereford met him and said: “Father, wait, that I may carry the cross before Your Presence in the chaplain’s place; for this is proper.” The archbishop said: “It is more just that I myself carry that cross under whose protection I remain safe; and when I behold its banner, I need not doubt under what leader I serve as a soldier.”

The Bishop of London replied: “If the king sees you entering armed, he will draw a stronger sword against your head; and then you will see what good your arms do you.” The archbishop said: “We commit these matters to God.” And the Bishop of London: “Until now you have been foolish, and, as I see, henceforth you will not withdraw from this folly.” And they proceeded.

But when the king heard that the archbishop was coming armed, forgetting—or laying aside—the sword of which the Bishop of London had spoken, he quickly withdrew into a more inner room. There the archbishop sat apart, alone with his men, while a few bishops sat opposite, united in place and purpose.

Finally, the bishops were summoned to the king’s council, while the Archbishop of Canterbury was left under the yoke. Time was drawn out while the condemnation of an innocent man was sought. But Canterbury, with resolute countenance, put on steadfastness. As he was leaving, Roger, Archbishop of York, said to the clerks whom he found there—for Master Robert, surnamed Grandis, and Osbert of Arundel were there: “Let us withdraw from here; it is not fitting for us to see what is soon to be done here against Canterbury.” Master Robert replied: “No; I will not leave here until I see what God’s will has decided in these matters. If he fights for God and His justice unto blood, he cannot end his life more nobly or better.” [Col. 0213C]

Accordingly, when the Archbishop of York had withdrawn from the king’s chamber, Bartholomew, Bishop of Exeter, came and fell at the feet of the lord of Canterbury, saying: “My father, have mercy on yourself; have mercy also on us, for today we all perish through hatred directed at your head.” For an edict had gone forth from the king that whoever should continue to stand with Canterbury was to be judged a public enemy and punished capitally. It was also said that Jocelin, Bishop of Salisbury, and William, Bishop of Norwich, who still held out, were immediately to be dragged away for punishment and mutilated in their limbs; they too begged Canterbury for their own safety.

Then Canterbury, looking upon the Bishop of Exeter, said: “Flee from here, for you do not savour the things that are of God.” [Col. 0213D] At length all the bishops came out together from the king’s council in tumult toward Canterbury. One of them, the eloquent Hilary, Bishop of Chichester, broke out in speech:

“Once you were our archbishop, and we were bound to obey you. But because you swore fealty to the lord king—that is, that through you his life, limbs, and earthly dignity should remain secure, and that the customs which he demands be preserved—and because you strive to destroy those customs, especially since they concern his earthly dignity and honour, we therefore declare you guilty of perjury; and henceforth we are not bound to obey a perjured archbishop. We therefore place ourselves and what is ours under the protection of the lord pope, and summon you to appear before him to answer concerning these matters.”

[Col. 0214A] And he fixed a day. The archbishop said: “I hear.”

They withdrew and sat apart opposite him for a long time in profound silence. At last earls, barons, and a great crowd came from the king to the archbishop. The first of them, Robert, Earl of Leicester, said: “The king commands you to come and render account concerning the charges brought against you, as you promised yesterday that you would do. Otherwise, hear the judgment.”

The archbishop said: “Judgment?” And he rose, saying: “Rather, my son Earl, you first hear. It is not unknown to you, my son, how intimate with the lord king and how faithful, according to the condition of this world, I have been. For this reason he was pleased that I should be advanced to the archbishopric of the Church of Canterbury—God knows, though I did not wish it. For my weakness was known to me. And I acquiesced more for his love than for God’s. This is sufficiently plain today, when God withdraws both Himself and the king from me.

“Nevertheless, at my promotion, when the election was held in the presence of Henry, the king’s son and heir, to whom this very matter had been entrusted, the question was asked: in what condition should they give me to the Church of Canterbury? And the answer was: free and untroubled by every bond of the court. Thus, being free and absolved concerning those matters from which I have been released, I neither am bound nor wish henceforth to answer concerning them.”

The earl said: “This is otherwise than the Bishop of London had represented to the king.”

The archbishop continued: [Col. 0214B] “Yet attend to this, my son Earl. As much as the soul is worthier than the body, so much more are you bound to obey God and me than an earthly king. Neither law nor reason permits sons to judge or condemn their father. Therefore I decline the judgment of the king, of you, and of the others, being to be judged under God by the lord pope alone; and in the presence of you all I appeal to him, placing the Church of Canterbury, my order and dignity, together with their appurtenances, under God’s and his protection. Moreover, you, my brothers and fellow bishops, because you obey man more than God, I summon to the hearing and judgment of the lord pope. And thus, fortified by the authority of the Catholic Church and the Apostolic See, I withdraw from here.”

As he departed, courtiers and envious persons followed him, shouting insults and injuries, calling him traitor and perjurer. When he came to the outer gate, the door was shut and he could not leave, no keeper being found there. [Col. 0214D] While the matter stood in fear and uncertainty, by God’s prompting it happened that many keys were hanging in a bunch on the wall. One of the archbishop’s attendants seized them and tried them one after another, until he opened the door.

As they went out, a crowd of poor and sick people suffering from the king’s evil met them, crying aloud and saying: “Blessed be God, who has delivered and saved His servant from the face of his enemies.” For he was already thought to have been put to death. Therefore, with a crowd of poor people before and behind him, he was conducted with clergy and people in joy and gladness to his lodging—namely, the conventual monastery of the religious monks at the church of St Andrew. Seeing the people’s exultation as they followed him, he said: [Col. 0215A] “What a glorious procession conducts us away from the face of our persecutor. Let all Christ’s poor, sharers in our tribulation, enter with us, that we may feast together in the Lord.” And the house and the surrounding courts were filled with diners.

During the meal the Bishops of London and Chichester came to the table, saying that they had found a way of peace. When the archbishop asked on what terms, they said: “A monetary dispute is at issue between you and the king. If, therefore, you assign to the king for a time, as a pledge, your two manors of Otford and Muncheaham, we believe that he will thereby be appeased, will restore the manors, remit the money, and quickly restore his favour to you.”

The archbishop replied: “The manor of Hecham was formerly, as I have learned, the property of the Church of Canterbury, [Col. 0215B] though the king now holds it in his own domain. Although an action for recovery rightly belongs to the Church of Canterbury for its restoration, I have no hope whatever that this can be done in these times. Nevertheless, before I should renounce the ancient right which the Church of Canterbury is said to have in that manor, whether to quell any disturbance or to recover royal favour, I would expose this head to every danger and peril.” And he touched his head.

The bishops therefore went back in indignation and reported this to the king; and the king’s anger was kindled against them.

Two bishops were also sent to ask the king for a safe-conduct for the lord of Canterbury on his return to his church. The king said that on the next day he would consult his household [Col. 0215C] concerning this and would then give a considered reply. Canterbury, understanding that delay was dangerous for him and that ambushes might be prepared for him through it, began to consider flight. He ordered a bed to be prepared for him that very night in the church of St Andrew, between two altars. Going there with a litany, and pronouncing the names of the saints one by one, he made a genuflection for each. When this was completed, exhausted, he threw himself upon the bed, pretending that he meant to take rest.

Then, secretly withdrawing and leaving by the back way, accompanied by one attendant and faithful companion, he disappeared. When morning came, a sudden and ominous rumour of the archbishop’s clandestine flight fell upon those who had adhered to him, [Col. 0215D] compelling them all to seek safety by hiding. Yet a public edict announced that no one was to lay hands upon Canterbury.

While this turmoil ran everywhere, the archbishop, as we have said, fleeing secretly by night with a brother of the order of Sempringham as guide, made toward the north, toward that noble city of Lincoln. Knowing and prudently choosing not the direct route, he travelled more cautiously, so that, should pursuers be sent after him, he might escape their snares and avoid them. At night he came to a village called Grabam, about twenty-five miles from Northampton. There, after allowing himself a little sleep, he set out the next day and came to Lincoln, about twenty-five miles away, lodging in the city [Col. 0216A] in the house of a certain felon.

There is there a body of water flowing through the city which reaches, by water, a certain secluded place situated amid the waters, called the Hermitage, belonging to the house of Sempringham, about forty miles away. There, because of the solitude of the place and the difficulty of access, since it lies amid the waters, he remained safely hidden for three days, restoring his strength for the journey that remained. One day, when the brother who ministered to him saw him sitting alone at table and eating pottage, he was pierced with grief and could not restrain his tears. He immediately went out, lest his tears, shed during the meal, disturb the man of God.

From the hermitage he came ten miles to St Botolph’s; and from there he came to a place called Haverolot, belonging to Sempringham. [Col. 0216B] Thereafter he travelled only by night, fearing detection. For he was now making toward the east, toward Kent, where he was better known by the people of the country from sight. Thus he travelled at night and hid by day, completing by night the journey of eight days, until he reached Kent, at a village situated above the sea called Estere, where he intended to cross the water.

There he remained the more cautiously, and so the more safely, because that village was part of the endowment of the sacred community of his metropolitan see and only eight miles distant. The future light of the world lay hidden in that village until All Souls’ Day. Making a hole in a wall—for he was near the church—he heard the solemnities of the Mass while the people were unaware; the priest too was receiving the sacrament. [Col. 0216C] A certain clerk who knew of the matter brought the kiss of peace to the archbishop; and when the people departed after the service, unaware of his presence, the bishop bestowed his blessing more devoutly.

At last, after arranging a passage, and being repeatedly driven here and there with difficulty, he scarcely reached Flanders at great cost. Therefore, because circumstances required it, he proceeded on foot, dressed in a white garment with a monk’s cape thrown over his shoulders, through storm, rain, and mud—travel wholly unlike his former custom. As he passed along, it happened that some young men were standing by, and one of them held a hawk in his hand. Seeing the bird, Canterbury fixed his attention upon it, remembering his former condition and forgetting his exile. One of them, seeing this, said: “Unless I am mistaken, here is the Archbishop of Canterbury.” [Col. 0216D] Another said: “You are a fool. What need would the Archbishop of Canterbury have to go about like this?” Canterbury was alarmed, fearing discovery; perhaps that fear at that moment was able to wash away the fault of that vain distraction.

When he reached the town of Celerum Mariscum, exhausted, he rested.

[But because he had been wearied by the frequent and deep tossing of the sea, having crossed in a small boat, he was unable to walk for long. After proceeding a little way, he lay down upon the ground, unable to go on, and said to the brothers with him: “I will not leave here unless you carry me, or find me a mount.” They obtained a beast for one silver coin; it had not a bridle, but only a rope [Col. 0217A] around its neck. They placed garments upon its back and made him sit on top of it.]

Then, after travelling a short distance, he lodged at a cell of St Bertin near the abbey itself. There certain attendants who had already left England came to meet him. Taking him thence by boat—for their route lay by water—they hastened toward St Bertin’s. On the journey one of them said: “Lord, you are tired from the road, and today we shall come to men of outstanding hospitality, who will greatly rejoice in the Lord that you have escaped unharmed. Therefore show them charity, so that on your arrival today they may eat rich food.”

“The fourth day of the week,” said the lord of Canterbury, “is Wednesday, and we must today abstain from such things.” Another added: [Col. 0217B] “Lord, perhaps they do not have an abundance of fish, and we shall have to accommodate ourselves to them.”

“The Lord’s task,” said Canterbury, “is to provide it.”

While they were speaking, by God’s prompting a great fish leapt out of the water and hurled itself violently into the lap of the man of God. This fish, I say, is called a *Brenham* [identification uncertain], and that journey became joyful for them in praise of God.

When he was brought to St Bertin’s and received there courteously, he remained there awaiting his followers. Meanwhile, a dreadful disturbance agitated the state of affairs, each person looking to his own interest and seeking occasions to fulfil the king’s will by destroying the Lord’s anointed. Therefore the Archbishop of York, the Bishops of London, Chichester, Exeter, Worcester, and Lisieux, [Col. 0217C] together with a large company of earls and barons, were sent from the king’s side to the lord pope, with great display, gifts, and presents, in order to pervert judgment according to their ability and blind the eyes of the wise. For they believed that in this way the Roman court, at some point wavering in this matter, could be bent toward what they sought. Certain bishops had, indeed, given this counsel against Canterbury.

At their arrival, fear on one side of the public disturbance that might arise from the king’s anger, and hope of profit on the other, compelled many cardinals to waver. Disagreement arose among them: some called Canterbury a defender of ecclesiastical liberty and therefore maintained that he supported a just cause; others called him a disturber of peace and unity, [Col. 0217D] and therefore held that the force of his presumption ought rather to be restrained than supported. The enemies’ insinuation prevailed so far that the lord of Canterbury’s envoys—men previously sent ahead, of exceptional courage and judgment—did not even deserve to be received by the cardinals with a kiss. Seeing their lord’s cause drawing near to danger, they too were distressed.

[Yet that same evening, having obtained access to the lord pope, they greeted him in the archbishop’s name, as father and lord, with the devotion and humility that were fitting, saying that they were only two men who had escaped from the heat of the house of Rechab and had come to the feet of His Holiness to announce that Joseph’s son still lived; but he did not rule in the land of Egypt—rather, he had almost been crushed and destroyed by the Egyptians. [Col. 0218A]

They then willingly recounted, to one who listened and sympathized with fatherly feeling, the grievous straits and sufferings of his son the archbishop: the dangers in that struggle at Northampton before the beasts; dangers among false brethren; dangers in flight; dangers on the road; dangers at sea; dangers even in the very harbour; toil, want, misery, and, to avoid ambushes, the change of his dress and name. Hearing this, the father of all fathers was moved in the depths of paternal compassion for his son; unable to conceal his fatherly affection, he wept. Deeply affected, he said to them: “Your lord is still alive in the flesh, as you say? Yet even while living in the flesh, he already claims for himself the glory of martyrdom.”

And because it was now very late, he promptly sent the envoys, weary from travel, to their lodging, after giving them his blessing and apostolic consolation.] 

The next day, however, the lord pope sat in judgment, the cardinals having assembled and the gathering having been convened. Canterbury’s envoys were also present, in order at least to see the outcome. Then the king’s envoys rose on the opposite side. The first, and standard-bearer of the others, the Bishop of London, began as follows:

“Father, the care and solicitude of the Catholic Church belong to you, so that those who are wise may be fostered by your prudence as examples of conduct, while those who are foolish may be rebuked and corrected by apostolic authority, that they may become wise. But he is not believed to be wise in your judgment who, trusting in his own wisdom, strives to disturb both the concord of brethren and the peace of the Church [Col. 0218C] and the king’s devotion.

“Recently in England a dissension has arisen between kingship and priesthood from a slight and less-than-useful occasion, which could more easily have been extinguished had moderate treatment been applied to it. But because the lord of Canterbury, following his own singular counsel in this matter rather than ours, pressed his case more fiercely than was right, without considering the evil of the times or what loss, and of what kind, might arise from such violence, he wove snares for himself and his brethren. Had our agreement favoured him in his purpose, the matter itself would already have come to a worse reckoning. But because he could not have our connivance, as indeed he ought not, for the aim toward which he tended, he seemed to turn the guilt of his rashness against the lord [Col. 0218D] king, against us, indeed against the entire kingdom. Therefore, to disguise the disgrace of our mutual brotherhood, with no force used against him or threats directed at him, he took flight, as it is written: ‘The wicked flee when no one pursues.’”

The lord pope replied: “Spare, brother.”

The Bishop of London said: “Lord, should I spare him?”

The lord pope replied: “I do not say, brother, that you should spare him, but yourself.”

At that apostolic voice and trumpet, the Bishop of London’s understanding was made foolish by the Lord, so that he could say nothing further. The eloquent Hilary, Bishop of Chichester, then took up the speech, trusting more in his own eloquence than in justice and truth, as became known from what followed.

“Lord Father,” he said, [Col. 0219A] “it concerns your Blessedness to restore promptly to the proper state of peace and concord what has been wrongly done to the ruin of all, lest the unmeasured presumption of one man produce the destruction of many and a schism in the Catholic Church. The lord of Canterbury paid little attention to this when, abandoning more mature counsel, he consulted himself alone and so brought heavier labours and distresses upon himself and his own people, the king and kingdom, people and clergy. Certainly this neither befitted nor ought to have befitted, nor ever ought to have befitted, a man of such authority. [Hilary of Chichester thus displayed his grammar by saying, ‘It ought-to-have-befitted’ (*oportuebat*).] Moreover, his own people, had they been wise, ought not to have given him their assent in such matters.”

When they heard how that eloquent man of grammar leapt from harbour to harbour, everyone burst into laughter. Among them [Col. 0219B] one cried out: “At last you have come badly into harbour.” By that remark the Lord so confounded that bishop that thereafter he became mute and tongueless.

The Archbishop of York, observing the downfall of those before him, tried to restrain the impetuosity of his spirit.

“Father,” he said, “no one has known Canterbury’s habits and pursuits better than I. From the beginning I have known this purpose of his mind: that what once he has taken up on principle cannot easily be torn away from him. Therefore it is more readily to be believed that, in accordance with his usual disposition, he has fallen into this obstinacy through his own fickleness. Nor do I see another way to correct him unless your discernment applies a heavier hand to achieve it. I think enough has been said for one who understands.” [Col. 0219C]

The Bishop of Exeter added: “Father, there is no need to linger long over these matters. This case cannot be settled in Canterbury’s absence. We therefore ask for legates who can hear this cause between the lord king and Canterbury and, when they have heard it, determine it.” He fell silent; nor did any of the bishops add anything after him.

Seeing this, the Earl of Arundel—for he stood in his place among a company of knights—asked leave to speak. When silence had been made, he said:

“Lord, what the bishops have said we unlettered men wholly do not know. Therefore we must state, as we can, that for which we have been sent: certainly not to contend or to offer insult to anyone, especially in the presence of so great a man, to whose will and authority the whole world by right submits itself, but doubtless to present before you and the whole Roman Church the devotion and love which our lord king has customarily borne, and still bears, toward you. Through whom, I ask? Through the greatest and noblest men he could have in all lands subject to him: namely, archbishops, bishops, earls, and barons. [Col. 0219D] He found none greater within his power; had he found them, he would surely have sent them, out of reverence for you and the holy Roman Church.

“To these we add the lord king’s faithfulness and devotion, which Your Paternity sufficiently experienced at the beginning of your promotion, when he completely subjected himself, his people, and all that was his to your will. Certainly, under the unity of the Catholic faith which you govern in Christ, as we believe, there is none more faithful than he, none more devoted to God, nor more measured in preserving that peace to which he has been called.

“Likewise, the lord Archbishop of Canterbury, in his own rank and order, is equally well equipped: provident and discerning in matters which concern him, though, as some have thought, too acute. If the present dissension between the lord king and the lord archbishop did not exist, kingship and priesthood would rejoice together in peace and concord under a good prince and an excellent shepherd. Therefore this is our petition: that Your Grace may devote more earnest attention to removing this dissension and restoring peace and love.” [Col. 0220A]

The earl thus spoke elegantly, but in his own language, and his restrained discernment was widely praised by all.

The lord pope, attending carefully to this, replied: “We know, son Earl, and remember well the devotion with which the king of England has conferred upon us very many and very generous benefits. Given the opportunity, we desire with all our power to respond according to his merits. But because you have requested legates, you shall have legates.”

After kissing the lord pope’s foot, they withdrew, believing that they had prevailed in the case, because the cardinals gave them hope that they could be corrupted. Therefore, by prior arrangement, [Col. 0220C] the Bishop of London returned and asked the lord pope with what authority the cardinals would come.

“With the authority proper to them,” said the lord pope.

“But, lord,” said the Bishop of London, “we ask that they may decide the cause with appeal removed.”

“This,” said the lord pope, “is my glory, which I will not give to another. And certainly, when he is to be judged, he shall be judged by us; for no reason permits that we send him back to England to be judged before adversaries and among enemies.”

Hearing this, the opposing party, disappointed in the hope it had conceived, withdrew angrily, intending to report to the lord king what answer it had received.

These things having occurred at Sens—for the lord pope was there—and after the others had departed, the lord of Canterbury came with [Col. 0220D] his companions to the court. He was received coolly by the cardinals, whose nostrils the scent of gain had befouled for the sake of profit; nevertheless he was admitted into the lord pope’s presence. [The pope received him as he came with fatherly kindness, sympathizing as a father with his many vexations and with so perilous and harsh a journey.]

While these and other matters were being discussed orally, he was at last directed to set out the causes of his exile before the brethren on the following day. The next day he was summoned to present himself before the lord pope. When it was asked among his companions who should explain this cause, each excusing himself, the weight of speaking fell upon the archbishop. Thus taught by God and unprepared in advance, while he sat first before the lord pope and wished to rise out of reverence, he was ordered to remain seated and explain his cause. He began:

“Though not very wise, we are not so foolish as to abandon the king of England, his people, and what belongs to him as nothing. For if we wished in every respect to please his will, there would be no one in his power or kingdom who would not obey us at our pleasure. While we served him on this condition, what was there that did not succeed for us according to our desire? But once we entered upon another path and became mindful of the profession and obedience which we had undertaken for God, his former affection for us indeed grew cold. [Col. 0221A]

“Even now, if we wished to depart from this resolve, we would need no one’s intervention to recover his favour. But because the Church of Canterbury is accustomed to be the sun of the West, and in our times its brightness has been darkened, we would more willingly receive in the Lord every torture, even a thousand kinds of death, if so many occurred, than endure by concealment the evils it suffers in these days. But lest I seem to have begun this out of curiosity or an appearance of vain glory, it is proper that the disposition of our heart be shown by visible proof.”

Then, producing a written document in which the customs under dispute were contained, he said with tears: “Behold what the king of England has established against the liberty of the Catholic Church. If these things may be passed over without danger to the soul, you must judge.”

When these had been read, all were moved to tears. Even those who had previously opposed him as far as they could could not restrain themselves; with one voice they praised God that He had preserved for Himself even one man who, in that storm, had dared to rise in opposition for the Church of God. Those who had previously seemed to dispute variously on this cause now came to one judgment: that, in the person of the Archbishop of Canterbury, aid must be given to the universal Church. [Col. 0221C]

[But when the lord pope had read and reread, heard, and carefully and attentively understood each of the customs, he was sharply stirred and immediately grew angry with the archbishop. He reproved and sternly rebuked him because he himself, as he confessed there, and the other bishops, by assenting to those practices—not customs, but tyrannical usurpations—had renounced their priesthood and enslaved the Church of God. He declared that it would have been far better to endure every danger than to assent to such great overthrowings of God’s law.

“He added: ‘Among these abominations which have here been read and heard, none indeed are good; but some are tolerable, which the Church can in some way endure. Yet the greater part of them has been rejected and condemned by ancient and authoritative councils, as directly contrary to sacred enactments.’

“The lord pope repudiated these matters in the hearing of all and declared that they ought thereafter to be condemned by the Church. Turning to the archbishop, he said: ‘With you, brother, although your transgression and that of your fellow bishops has been great and monstrous, we must proceed more gently. Though, as you yourself confess, you fell, you endeavoured to rise immediately after your fall; and because of that fall you have already endured many grave and harsh things. Immediately after you had fallen, while you were still in England, you sought from us and obtained by our mercy the benefit of absolution. It is therefore fitting that we pardon you, or that in your adversities you should experience the consolation and favour of our mercy more fully and affectionately than other ecclesiastical persons, inasmuch as you have abandoned greater things and endured more grievous ones for the liberty of the Church and for your faith and devotion.’]

Thus the apostolic man first rebuked the archbishop with fatherly severity, restored to him the sweetness of maternal consolation, and then dismissed him. [Col. 0222A]

On the following day, in a more private chamber, with the cardinals seated with the lord pope, the lord of Canterbury was present and said:

“My fathers and lords, no one is permitted to lie anywhere, still less before God and in your presence. Therefore, willingly but also grieving, I confess that my wretched fault has stirred up these troubles of the English Church. I entered Christ’s sheepfold, but not through the door itself: not a canonical election called me, but the terror of public power intruded me. And although I took up this burden unwillingly, human, not divine, will brought me to it. What wonder, then, if it turned against me?

“Yet if, at the king’s threat, as my fellow bishops urgently urged, I had renounced the privilege granted me by episcopal authority, a ruinous precedent for the Catholic Church would have been left to the will and desire of princes. I therefore delayed until your presence. But now, recognizing that my entry was less than canonical and accordingly fearing that a worse end may befall me, and seeing my strength unequal to the burden, lest I be found to preside to the ruin of the flock to which I have in whatever manner been given as shepherd, I resign the archbishopric of Canterbury into your hand, father.” [Col. 0222B]

And he wept with sobbing, moving the lord pope and all who were present to weep as well.

Indeed, who could hear this and refrain from tears? Therefore, while the archbishop sat apart with his companions, who were scandalized by these words—for they had already begun to despair—the lord pope began to deliberate with the cardinals. Various and conflicting opinions arose on either side. Some thought that, the opportunity having been offered, the king’s anger could more easily be appeased if the Church of Canterbury were reconciled in another person, while better provision might elsewhere be made for blessed Thomas. [Col. 0222D] These were, indeed, among the Pharisees.

But those whose eyes were open took the contrary view. They asked whether one who, for the defence of the Church’s liberty, had exposed to utmost danger and peril not only wealth and glory, dignity and authority, but even his life, ought at the king’s pleasure to be deprived of his right; and whether, if his justice were preserved intact, this would become a model for others in a similar cause of resisting kings. If he fell, all bishops would fall with him, so that in future times no one would dare to oppose a prince’s will. Thus the state of the Catholic Church would totter and the authority of the Roman pontiff would perish.

“It is therefore fitting,” they said, “that he be restored even against his will, and that every possible aid be given to him who fights for us.”

This judgment pleased all except the Pharisees.

[Col. 0223A] Blessed Thomas and his companions were therefore summoned, and the lord pope spoke this judgment:

“Now at last, brother, it is clear to us what zeal you have had and have for the house of the Lord, since with a sincere conscience you have set yourself as a wall in opposition. Since you have made a pure confession concerning your entrance, and by your resignation have washed away, as it could and ought to be washed away, the guilt of your offence, you may now securely receive anew from my hand the charge of the pontifical office, since we restore you to your full position. Rightly so: we know you to be a man tested by many kinds of temptation, prudent and discerning, dear to God and men, and wholly faithful to us and the holy Roman Church.

“And as you have become a participant and inseparable companion in our persecution, so, with God as author, we shall be unable to fail you in anything as long as vital breath endures in this body. But until now you have abounded in delights. Therefore, that you may henceforth learn to be what you ought to be, a comforter of the poor—and since you could not be taught this except by poverty itself, the mother who teaches religious life—we commend you to the poor of Christ, to be brought up by this Abbot of Pontigny” (for he was present by arrangement), [Col. 0223B] “and by his brethren.

“I do not say brought up splendidly, but simply, as befits an exile and an athlete of Christ. Among them, with a few necessary attendants, your remaining companions having been distributed among friends, you must live for a time, until the day of consolation breathes upon us and the time of peace descends from above. Meanwhile be of good courage, and resist manfully those who disturb the peace.”

[Col. 0223C] Having therefore received the blessing, blessed Thomas entered Pontigny with a few household attendants, the rest having been sent elsewhere, as was said. He judged that he had not worthily received pastoral charge from the apostolic hand unless he also took up the religious habit: for he was to have monks as his firstborn sons to govern in the episcopal see, and had learned that, from the first foundation of the Church of Canterbury, almost all its pastors and bishops had been monks; nor, according to ancient histories, had any division or transfer of the kingdom occurred except when someone of another profession had presided over the Church of Canterbury. Messengers were accordingly sent, and the lord pope sent him the monastic habit, which he himself had blessed: namely, of coarse, unbleached woollen cloth. He also charged the messengers, saying: [Col. 0223D] “Tell the lord of Canterbury that we have sent him the habit that we had, not the one that we should have wished.”

Now while the abbot of Pontigny was clothing blessed Thomas privately and in secret in that habit, one of his attendants stood by—the very man who had proposed that puzzle at Clarendon on the preceding day, namely, “What virtue has he retained who has betrayed his conscience and reputation?” When he saw that the hood on that habit was too small to fit the whole garment, he said: “That was indeed done deliberately; whether according to rule, I do not know. Yet it is clear that the lord pope has attached the hood of the cowl rather awkwardly.” Blessed Thomas smiled and said: “Take care lest you can mock me again, as you did the day before.” He replied: “Where and when, my lord?” And the archbishop said: “The day before yesterday, [Col. 0224A] when I was being vested in the sacred garments for the solemnities of Mass, and, girded with a belt, seemed padded out, you asked what had made my posterior parts swollen. If therefore the hood, hanging from the shoulders, were larger and displayed there the appearance of swelling, you could still mock me as hunchbacked. For that reason I have provided more cautiously against insults of that sort.”

The archbishop in fact wore a hair-shirt, from his bare neck down to his knees, hidden even from his own attendants. When he was tightly girded, the stiffness of the hair-shirt extended outward, and he appeared stouter though he was thin, yet cheerful in countenance.

Meanwhile messengers were running to and fro for the restoration of peace. At length it pleased both sides that the lord pope and the king should meet one another at a fixed day and place, so that the way of peace might more easily be found through their mutual conference. The king said that he would come, but in the archbishop’s absence; for he declared that, if the latter were present, he would not so much as look upon the lord pope’s face. The archbishop informed the lord pope that he would on no account make use of a conference with the king without his own presence, since that man’s character was known to him. “Indeed,” he said, “the Apostolic See may the more readily be deceived by the king’s diversity of speech if no diligent interpreter is present to draw out the purpose of the royal mind from the recesses of his heart. And if the king learns beforehand the lord pope’s weaker points, he will block the exits of his ways with stumbling-blocks.”

When this had been received, the lord pope sent back to the king, in a measured reply, that it was unheard of through the ages for the Roman Church, at the beck of any prince, to reject anyone from its protection—especially one exiled for justice’s sake; and that it was a privilege and authority granted to the Apostolic See to aid exiles and the oppressed, even against the anger of princes and the violent assaults of the wicked. The indignant messengers therefore departed to report this to the king.

The lord pope, intending to return to Rome, set out on his journey; the archbishop accompanied him as far as Bourges. There, having received leave and a blessing, he returned to Pontigny, never again to see the lord pope’s face in this flesh.

We have thus pursued the narrative historically from the Council of Clarendon to the lord pope’s departure from France, in order to elucidate the events that occurred in the interval, because the letters written in the meantime do not state the course of events so expressly. The subsequent letters, however, are individually so clear in their proper places, down to the conclusion of the whole affair, that they seem to require less historical support—except for what occurred at the conference of the kings, when the prosecution of the lord of Canterbury’s cause was entrusted by the lord pope to Simon, prior of Mont-Dieu, and Bernard of Corilo. At other times the restoration of peace was disturbed because the man of Canterbury would not pass over in silence the phrase “saving my order”; at another time because the king would not give the kiss to the man of Canterbury under the covenant of peace: as becomes more fully known from the letters arranged in their places. But there the following occurred.

It was suggested to the king of England that the lord of Canterbury was altogether willing to submit himself to his judgment; therefore he received his presence there more graciously. [Col. 0225A] Accordingly, when many people of both kingdoms had assembled for this purpose, the lord of Canterbury fell at the feet of the king of England, saying: “I submit to your judgment the entire cause from which dissension has arisen between us, saving God’s honour.”

On hearing this phrase, the king immediately grew angry and said to the king of France: “My lord king, pray observe. Whatever displeases this man of Canterbury, he will say is contrary to God’s honour, and thus he will claim all that is his and mine for himself. But lest I seem to wish in any respect to oppose either God’s honour or him, I offer this. There were many kings in England before me, of greater or lesser authority than I possess. Before him there were many archbishops of Canterbury, great and holy men. Therefore, let him do to me what the greatest and holiest of his predecessors did to the least of mine, and I shall be satisfied.”

From every side came the cry: “The king humbles himself enough.” When the archbishop had been silent for a little while, the king of France added: “My lord archbishop, do you wish to be greater than holy men, or better than Peter? Why do you hesitate? Behold, peace is at the doors.”

To this the archbishop said to the king of France: “It is true that our predecessors were far better and greater than I. Yet each in his own time, although they did not cut away everything that raised itself against God, cut away some things. And if they had then uprooted everything from the roots, who would now stir up against us the fire of such temptation? So that, tested with them by this trial, we too may be found worthy with them of praise and glory. By God’s providence it has been much better ordered for us that, as we have laboured in their lot and number, so we may share their labour and reward. Nor, if one of them perhaps grew lukewarm or went astray in some matter, are we bound to follow the example of his lukewarmness or error in this.

“For we rebuke Peter when he denied Christ, but we commend Peter in every way when he reproved Nero’s assault even to the peril of his own head. Certainly, because Peter would not consent to him in that which he could not conceal without peril to his soul, he fell in the flesh, victorious over his enemies. Under such pressures the Catholic Church arose and grew. Our fathers suffered because they would not suppress the name of Christ; and ought I, that a man’s favour may be restored to me, to suppress the honour of Christ? Far be it!” he said.

The magnates of both kingdoms then rose up, charging the archbishop’s arrogance with obstructing peace. One count among them openly protested that, because the archbishop resisted the counsel and will of both kingdoms, he would henceforth deserve the assistance of neither; France should not receive one expelled from England.

When the conference had broken up amid considerable murmuring, they returned to their respective places, while the fellow-exiles of Canterbury were reduced to utter despair. The king of France had been accustomed, after each conference of this sort, to go down to the lodging of the man of Canterbury, under the pretext of consolation and out of respect. But on this occasion he did not even acknowledge him, either in person or through his servants. Thus he passed three days’ journeys in the king of France’s company, without the king or anyone on his side approaching him. Although in such affairs the lord of Canterbury had been accustomed to receive provision from royal generosity, after that conference, and throughout the period just mentioned, nothing whatever was supplied to him. At times, while passing through Sens, the archbishop, or at other times the bishop of Poitiers, or some other person distressed by his misery, supplied him as though he were a beggar. This greatly terrified his companions, as though they were now deprived of every human aid.

But on the third day of that journey, while they sat in their lodging discussing these things among themselves and wondering whither they might turn, the lord of Canterbury, with a cheerful countenance, as though he had suffered no adversity and were unconquerable against every stroke of fortune, gently jested with those who grieved for him: “I alone am attacked; and if I yield, there will be no one to persecute you more fiercely, nor, once you have obtained your friends’ benefits, to deprive you further. Therefore take courage, and do not be afraid.”

They said to him: “We pity you more, because we do not know where you can turn—a man of such authority, abandoned by friends both highest and lowest.”

The archbishop said: “We entrust our care to God. Since entry into both kingdoms is closed to us, and it does not suit us to turn to the Roman robbers for consolation—for they plunder the spoils of the wretched indiscriminately—another road must be taken. We have heard that around the river Saône in Burgundy, as far as the parts of Provence, the people are more generous. One companion and I will go to them on foot; perhaps, when they see our distress, they will pity us and supply provisions for a time, until God visits us. God is able to assist his own even at the very last throw of misery; and he who despairs of God’s mercy is worse than an unbeliever.”

And immediately God’s mercy was at the door. For a servant of the king of France hurried up and said: “The lord king summons you to court.” One of them said: “So that we may be driven out of the kingdom.” The archbishop said: “You are neither a prophet nor a prophet’s son; do not prophesy evil.”

When they came, they found the lord king seated with a sad expression, and not rising in the customary way for the archbishop. What happened at the beginning was a sad omen. When they had sat down and had still been addressed coldly, after a lengthy silence the king, with bowed head, seemed sorrowfully and reluctantly to be considering expelling them from the kingdom; and while they themselves feared precisely this, he burst into tears, sprang up with sobs, and threw himself at the archbishop’s feet, to the astonishment of those present. As the archbishop bent down to raise the king, the king at last, scarcely recovering himself from his distress, said: “Truly, my lord father, you alone saw.” And, sighing with grief, he repeated: “Truly, my father, you alone saw. We were all blind, we who, against God, gave you counsel that in your own cause—indeed, in God’s—you should, at a man’s bidding, relinquish God’s honour. I repent, father, and I repent deeply. Forgive me, therefore, and absolve me, wretch that I am, from this guilt. Moreover, I commit myself and my kingdom to God and to you; and from this hour I promise that I shall not fail you or yours as long as, with God’s help, [Col. 0227A] I live.”

The king having therefore been absolved and given the blessing, the archbishop entered Sens with his companions in joy, where the king of France provided for him royally until his return to England.]

On hearing this, the king of England sent word to the king of France that he wondered greatly how, or on what legal ground, he could support the archbishop against him, since in the king’s own presence the latter had so humbled himself, prepared for every form of justice; nor had the archbishop’s failure to obtain peace been due to the king, but rather the archbishop had arrogantly and insultingly rejected it. Therefore, he said, the king of France ought henceforth not to give support in his kingdom to such a man, to the disgrace and shame of his own faithful subject.

To this the king of France said to the messengers: “Go and report to your king that if the king of England does not permit the ancestral customs, as he calls them—though they are said to accord rather poorly with divine law—to be abolished, because they pertain to royal dignity, then still less may I overthrow the right of that generosity which belongs to me by hereditary right together with the crown of my kingdom. For from ancient times France has been accustomed to receive all wretched and afflicted persons, especially those exiled for justice’s sake, and, so long as they have no peace, to cherish and protect them. By God’s favour, while I live, at no one’s instigation shall this honour and distinction be diminished in the exile of the man of Canterbury.”

We have set these matters out here in order that the sequence of letters should not be interrupted when we come to the place [Col. 0228A] where the letters touch upon the same matters, though more obscurely. This is in the fourth part, where the prior of Mont-Dieu and Bernard of Corilo were designated executors of the lord pope’s mandate. All the remaining letters, in their order and place, explain the events more clearly, so that they sufficiently serve the reader’s understanding by themselves.

Yet certain letters are prefixed, on the occasion of which, while the contention was being pursued between the king, blessed Thomas, and the archbishop of York, the archbishop of York, having learned and clearly perceived that the prosperity of the man of Canterbury could not easily be overcome, strove to inflame the king’s mind against him. He therefore more readily yielded to preserving those ancestral customs, in order thereby to win royal favour for himself through Canterbury’s humiliation. He also took as his associate Gilbert, bishop of London, who had likewise long aspired to the archbishopric of Canterbury. Accordingly, when by carefully contrived deceits and snares he had vainly attempted to cast down the man of Canterbury, he exerted himself more earnestly, though craftily, to see whether in some way he could transfer the pallium from the Church of Canterbury to London. These two, therefore, the standard-bearers of the rest and instigators of the whole disturbance, induced the king, for the reasons stated, to establish and promulgate in the kingdom of England the following customs against ecclesiastical liberty.

[Col. 0227] Here ends the work of Alan on the Life of Saint Thomas, as it is found separately in the manuscript codices. There are, however, two other fragments found in Lupus’s *Quadrilogus*, to which I could not suitably assign a place in the preceding work: the first concerns the legation over England granted by the lord pope; the second, King Henry’s penance.

## Fragments

[Col. 0227C] **FRAGMENT I. On the apostolic legation.** For he had obtained from the apostolic man the legation of the Apostolic See over England, and this as a precaution: namely, so that every ecclesiastical sentence would be regarded as firmer and more authoritative if it were henceforth issued by him either against the kingdom or against persons in the kingdom. First he summoned, with the utmost precision, certain clerics of the royal court who were bound to him by reason of their order or ecclesiastical benefice and were obliged to render obedience, that they should not delay in coming to him. He also commanded certain things of some of them by the force of obedience, under peril to their order and benefice; but they neither came nor obeyed him. Therefore, paying no heed to an appeal, he publicly anathematized them and caused them to be declared anathematized.

This concerned not only court clerics but also lay courtiers, and for various causes: some because they were invaders, others as violent possessors of ecclesiastical goods; and not merely people of either class, but also some of his own men, because of manifest disobedience and especially because they had proved to be instigators of the entire dissension between the king and himself, which they did not cease daily to foster.

Among those anathematized, the bishops of London and Salisbury were first. He also anathematized John of Oxford and Richard of Ilchester, who had fallen into condemned heresy by taking an oath of schism; likewise Richard de Lucy and Joscelin de Balliol, who had been authors and contrivers of those perversities; and Ranulf de Broc, who had seized the goods and people of the Church of Canterbury, both clerical and lay, and held them captive. He also anathematized Hugh of St Clair and Thomas son of Bernard, who, without his permission, had occupied and retained the goods and possessions of that church; and all who thereafter should lay violent hands upon the possessions and goods of the Church against his will and consent.

Those anathematized from among the court were among the king’s more intimate associates and counsellors. Consequently, almost everyone at court was either expressly excommunicated or, by associating with excommunicates whom they could neither avoid nor were permitted to avoid, implicated in their excommunication; so much so that scarcely anyone was in the king’s chapel who could offer the king that sacramental kiss of peace at Mass without being excommunicated either by name or by participation.

**FRAGMENT II. On the king’s penance.** The king and the legates first met at Gorham, on the Tuesday before Rogation Days, where they received one another with the kiss of peace. On the next day they came to Savigny, where the archbishop of Rouen and many bishops and magnates gathered. When they had there treated of the Lord’s peace, which the king refused outright to swear according to their instructions, the king departed from them indignantly, saying: “I return to Ireland, where many matters press upon me. But go in peace through my land wherever you please, and carry out the legation as you have been charged.”

Thus they separated. Then the cardinals, having held a more private consultation, summoned back the bishop of Lisieux, the archdeacon of Poitiers, and the archdeacon of Salisbury; and through them it was arranged that on the following Friday the king and the cardinals met at Avranches. There they came to a complete agreement, in that the king graciously accepted and granted whatever was proposed to him on behalf of the cardinals. But because the king wished his son to be present, so that he too might confirm what his father permitted, the term was postponed until the following nearest Sunday, namely the feast of the Ascension of the Lord.

Then, at a public hearing, the king swore with his own hand touching the most holy Gospels that he had neither commanded nor wished the archbishop of Canterbury to be killed; and that, when he heard of his death, he grieved more over it than he rejoiced. He added of his own accord that he had never grieved so greatly even over the death of his father or mother. He also swore that he would fully perform whatever penance the cardinals imposed on him as satisfaction. For before all he said that he understood himself to have been the cause of the archbishop’s death, and that whatever was done had been done on his account—not because he had commanded it, but because his friends and household, seeing the disturbance of his face and eyes, perceiving also the sorrow of his heart, and often hearing his complaints about the archbishop, had prepared to avenge his injury without his knowledge. Therefore, with all humility and devotion, he declared himself subject to whatever the legates should command.

The legates then imposed upon him that he should provide, at his own expense, two hundred knights for a full year—namely, three hundred gold pieces for each knight in the land of Jerusalem against the pagans, according to the direction of the Templars.

Second, that he should wholly abandon the wicked statutes of Clarendon and all evil customs introduced into the churches of God in his days. But any that had been evil before his time he should moderate according to the lord pope’s command and the counsel of religious men.

Third, that he should restore to the Church of Canterbury all its full integrity in lands and other things, as it had been in the year before the archbishop incurred the king’s anger; and that he should restore peace and favour, together with the fullness of their possessions, to all whom he had offended on account of the archbishop.

Fourth, that, if necessary and if the lord pope commanded him, he should go to Spain to free that land from the pagans.

They also imposed upon him privately fasts, almsgiving, and certain other matters that did not reach the public hearing.

To all this the king most graciously gave his consent, saying before everyone: “Behold, my lords legates, my body is in your hand. Know for certain that whatever you command—whether setting out for Jerusalem, Rome, Saint James’s, or whatever it may be—I am ready to obey.” Hence nearly all who were present, seeing his humility and devotion, could scarcely hold back their tears. When this was completed, lest anything be wanting for the consummation of the good work, the legates, by the king’s own wish, led him outside the church door; there, with bent knees—yet without removing his clothes or applying scourges—he was admitted into the church. And so that some men of the kingdom of France might know that these things had thus occurred, they ordered that the archbishop of Tours and his suffragans should appear before the king and legates at Caen on the first Tuesday after the Ascension of the Lord.

What the king swore, his son confirmed with his own hand in the hand of Lord Albert the cardinal: that he would observe it on his own part; and that if his father the king, prevented by death or another manifest cause, could not complete the penance mentioned above, he himself would fulfil it.

## Two Additions

To the booklets of Alan of Tewkesbury and John of Salisbury, of which the former occurs in a manuscript codex of the library of the British Museum, Additional no. 11506, folio 66; the latter in another codex of the same library, Additional 10050.

[Col. 0229]

**ADDITION I.** To establish the credibility of this history by a certain argument, it has seemed proper to insert here an old fragment concerning the controversy of Saint Thomas for the liberty of the Church.

[Col. 0229D]

On the fifth day of the Nativity of the Lord, about the evening hour, while the archbishop was sitting in his chamber with his clerics, William de Tracy, Reginald fitz Urse, Hugh de Morville, and Richard Brito, coming from Normandy and driven as if by fury, suddenly burst into the chamber. They announced on behalf of the king, who was staying in Normandy, that he should restore to office the bishops of England suspended from their duties and absolve those excommunicated. He answered them that it was not for an inferior judge to dissolve a superior’s sentence, and that no man might invalidate what the Apostolic See had decreed. Nevertheless, if the bishops of London and Salisbury would confirm by oath that they would obey his command, he would absolve them for the peace of the Church and out of reverence for the lord king.

Enraged, they departed violently, hastening to bring the impious crime conceived in their minds to effect. The archbishop, however, warned by his clerics and pressed by the advancing evening hour, entered the principal church to sing Vespers. The four wicked satellites named above meanwhile put on their military arms and immediately followed the archbishop. When they came to the church, they found its doors open, as the archbishop had commanded. “For,” he said, “we shall not, in disordered fashion, turn God’s church, which ought universally to be a refuge for all, into a fortress.”

As crowds flocked together from every direction, the four men entered the church irreverently and began to shout: “Where is the king’s traitor? Where is the king’s traitor? Where is the archbishop?” When the archbishop heard the title “archbishop,” he came back to meet them from the third or fourth step of the presbytery, which he had already climbed, and said: “If you seek the archbishop, behold, you have me ready before you.” When they made their bitterest threats, he said: “I am prepared to die, preferring the defence of justice and the liberty of the Church to life; yet I ask that my people not be liable to punishment, since neither were they inciters of this cause.”

When the wicked attendants rushed upon him with drawn swords, he said: “I commend myself and the cause of the Church to God, to blessed Mary, to the patron saints of this church, and to blessed Dionysius.” Thus sacrificed before the altar, he received his deadly wound in that part of his body which the pouring of holy oil had more especially consecrated to the Lord; and he who had so often exposed his head for the liberty of the clergy, and raised his eyes to heaven, fell struck down with bowed head.

Robert de Broc and his accomplices plundered the archbishop’s furnishings, the clothing of the clerics and servants, and even the utensils of the workshops. All horses that they found in the stable, given over to plunder, they swiftly carried away. The archbishop’s body, which had lain on the pavement to the right of Saint Benedict before the high altar, was carried away in the twilight of that day. There, what had been known only to the chamberlain was revealed to those standing by. For although the archbishop had concealed the monastic habit, which he had secretly assumed long before, under canonical dress, he took care to subdue his flesh, worn down by a hair-shirt, with hair-cloth drawers.

And, to summarize briefly certain things that had converged by divine ordering: for the defence of the Church’s liberty the archbishop had resolved to endure labours, exile, the proscription of his kin, and even death. Thus, that such a cause might run its course in its own way, he left the king’s court in Normandy on a Tuesday, as stated above. On a Tuesday he crossed the sea, to undergo exile in France. Returning to England at the lord pope’s counsel, he landed on a Tuesday. On a Tuesday he fell, pierced by the hands of wicked men.

Early on the following Wednesday, the wicked report spread that the vile executioners had agreed to drag the archbishop’s body away from the holy place and throw it beyond the walls for dogs to tear apart or birds to devour. The abbot of Boxley, the prior, and the convent of the Church of Canterbury, on prudent counsel, resolved to commit swiftly to burial that body which seemed not to require washing with any waters, especially since it had been made radiant by long fasting, cleansed by the hair-shirt, and purified in its own blood.

After the king of England had landed in Normandy, he immediately hurried to Lords Albert and Theodwin, cardinals and legates of the Apostolic See sent into those regions by the lord pope. Yet after long and extensive negotiations, first held at Savigny, at Avranches, in the presence of the legates, the lord king swore that the death of the most glorious martyr Thomas had been committed neither by his will nor with his knowledge, nor procured by his contrivance. But because evildoers had taken from words that he had uttered less cautiously while inflamed by the heat of anger an occasion to kill the holy man, he humbly requested and obtained absolution from them.

Thus solemnly absolved in the sight of the Church, in accordance with the cardinals’ will and command, he promised that from the coming feast of Pentecost for one year he would give enough money that, at the discretion of the brothers of the Temple, two hundred knights might be procured for a year to defend the land of Jerusalem. He also promised that appeals should be permitted freely; that customs introduced in his own time against the liberty of the Church should be revoked and rendered void; that the possessions of the Church of Canterbury which had been taken from it after the departure of the archbishop of holy memory should be fully restored; and that clerics and laypersons of both sexes who had left the kingdom for Archbishop Thomas should be permitted freely to return with the king’s peace and receive their goods. The lord pope enjoined the king to promise and do all this for the remission of all his sins.

The king’s son swore and promised the same things his father had sworn and promised. And so much concerning this matter.

**ADDITION II.**

A certain knight of noble family and wealth, named Walter de Enicurt, having been struck by leprosy, came to Canterbury. Having received permission from the prior, he visited the tomb of Saint Thomas for three nights. In a dream the saint appeared to him, embraced his head with both hands, and vanished. When the knight awoke, he felt himself wholly changed from the man he had been; he gave thanks to God and to his holy martyr, and in the morning entered the monks’ chapter-house. Before all who heard, he declared in a clear voice that his whole body had been healed; having received the brothers’ fellowship, he returned home rejoicing and exulting.

A certain woman, whose eyes had been darkened by long-standing blindness, anointed her eyes with the saint’s blood and received sight.

Another woman, oppressed by severe illness for two years, had kept to her bed. She mixed a little of Saint Thomas’s blood with water; on drinking it, she immediately vomited up all the matter of her illness.

[Col. 0233A] One born blind and mute, using the same remedy, received along with sharpness of sight a complete and perfect power of speech.

[Col. 0234A] A certain blind man, well known in the city of Canterbury, whom I myself saw, rubbed his eyes with a little cloth dipped in the martyr’s blood, and in that same hour received sight.

[Col. 0233]

# The Sixth Life of Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury and Martyr, by William of Canterbury

(We possess only fragments of this treatise, namely those extant in the *Quadrilogus*.)

[Col. 0233B] **FRAGMENT 1.** Thomas, a native of the city of London, the illustrious offspring of parents of middling rank, grew up like a cedar from brambles and spread branches greater than his root. Divine goodness enriched him in both the inward and outward man with the manifold grace of natural gifts, so that he seemed a vessel fashioned for great service, and from nature’s endowments was predicted to be a future prelate. For his speech was pleasant and modest: boys found him winning, young men affable, old men agreeable. Tall in an elegant manner, well-behaved as an example, wise in prudence, his face displayed youthful beauty and manly gravity. Once committed to literary studies, he advanced in the liberal arts insofar as the high spirits of youth and the brevity of time allowed.

[Col. 0233C] **FRAGMENT 2.** After his mother died, being left with his father, whose resources were diminished by frequent fires, he spent his twenty-second year in leisure. At length he attached himself to one of the citizens as a clerk. Then, leaving the schools of liberal learning and transferring himself to the business of the court, he began to mature into the flower of worldly prudence and to promise the fruit of discretion.

**FRAGMENT 3.** Seeing him act prudently in resolving difficulties and show foresight in counsel, they entered into an alliance with him, agreeing to combine their support in seeking ecclesiastical benefices for themselves. There were three: Roger of Neustria, John of Canterbury, and Thomas of London. Thus the primate did few things in which all, or one, of these men had no part.

[Col. 0233D] **FRAGMENT 4. How he was made chancellor.** Not long afterward Henry, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, succeeded Stephen, king of the English, to the kingdom. The aforesaid archbishop, suspicious of the young new king, whom the counsels of evil men were attempting to corrupt, worked to have his archdeacon made the king’s close associate and chancellor. by whose aid and exertions the new king’s impulse to rage against the Church might be restrained, the malice of his counsel moderated, and the boldness of officials repressed who, under the pretence of public authority and the pretext of law, had conspired to plunder the resources both of the Church and of the people of the province.

For the bishop saw that young man, whose character and ability he had already tested in various events: vigorous in action, trustworthy in counsel, steady in uncertainty, high-minded in adversity, magnificent in display, generous in giving, ready at command, diligent in service, and in every undertaking prudent and circumspect. He accordingly judged that such a man would be worthy of the court and welcome to it, and not without reason, hoping that under his direction the favour of peace and bond of unity between kingdom and priesthood would thereafter be more firmly preserved. Thus, through the bishop’s action and direction, Thomas entered the court and, the king granting it, received the office of chancellor.

### FRAG. 5. What he was like as chancellor

The archdeacon, therefore, having entered the court and, as we have said, been bound there to the office of chancellor, for the time laid aside the deacon and put on the chancellor. For, adapting himself to the king’s habits, he strove alike to attend to trifles and serious matters, alike to hunt, and to observe the same hours for eating and sleeping. Moreover, he embraced the witty amusements of courtiers, rejoiced in a numerous retinue, sought glory, and delighted in the breezes of popular favour. For, not to speak of his household furnishings, using silver bridles with foaming bits, he brought treasure into the mouth; he surpassed the tables and expenditures of the earls, so that in one respect he seemed little mindful of the archdeacon, and in another was thought to employ the devices of an evildoer. [Col. 0234D]

Nevertheless, though the world seemed to flatter and applaud him in all its allurements, yet—what happens more rarely—in the abundance of his possessions he was admirable and worthy of imitation for bodily chastity, so that in his vanity and chastity he seemed to reproduce Bricius, the mocker of blessed Martin. And because the occasion calls for it, I should like briefly to relate what comes to mind.

There was in a town of Staffordshire a beautiful woman, worthy even of royal delights, with whom the king was said to have had an intimacy. Since she frequently sent many gifts to the chancellor when he came to that place, the townsman who had received him as a guest supposed that the woman was inviting him to an embrace and procuring for herself a new lover, she who, being nearly despised, enjoyed less love than usual. Wishing to ascertain the matter, in the silence of the untimely night he took a lamp and secretly entered his guest’s chamber. Seeing him absent, he supposed that he had gone to her. But raising the light, he saw before the bed a man lying prostrate, with feet and shins uncovered, who, after kneeling and praying, had fallen asleep. Thus he was found to be devout whom he had thought licentious—perhaps the Lord thereby displaying our rashness, we who readily judge a person while not knowing what is in that person. [Col. 0235A]

### FRAG. 6. By what services he acquired the king’s favour

Amid all the allurements of a flattering world and the applause of smiling prosperity, Thomas nonetheless remembered his condition and the burden laid upon him. Daily he fought, on the one hand, for the safety and honour of his lord the king, and, on the other, for the needs of the Church and the provincials against the beasts of the court. So far as royal severity and reverence allowed, he contended against the king, as though by some foreknowledge of future events he were fighting in battle-line during a time of peace. [Col. 0235B]

### FRAG. 7

The king, seeing that he discharged his office wisely and was utterly faithful to him, conceived the plan of setting him over the foremost see of the English. He believed him quite equal to the summit of so great an honour, having so often experienced his magnanimity in grave perils. He hoped that Thomas would benefit his heirs in obtaining the kingdom, should a fatal day prematurely remove the king from human affairs; and that through him he himself would manage ecclesiastical affairs as he did secular ones according to his will, should he enjoy a longer life. [Col. 0235C]

### FRAG. 8

Yet the bishop of London alone spoke against it. But he who was supported by no party and seemed to have sought his own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ deserved to have his opinion refuted by the very ease with which he had presumed to oppose the majority.

### FRAG. 9

Thus, when blessed Thomas had been consecrated, so that with the sacrament he might attain the reality of the sacrament, he resolved to renew the old man. Accordingly, as though already transformed into another man, he became more abstinent, more watchful, more frequent in prayer, and more diligent in preaching. Believing that the right course of renewal ought to begin with himself, he judged that he could rightly rule others only if he had first learned to rule himself. Subjecting his body to servitude, he taught it to serve and his spirit to rule; and, having assumed a monastic habit with haircloth, he filled with merits the spiritual man whom, beneath the respectability of his clothing, he concealed from human eyes. [Col. 0235D]

Known to few, he served beneath the breastplate of faith, rejoicing that in a threefold garment he bore a threefold person: by his outer garment he appeared a cleric; by the inner he concealed a monk; by the innermost he endured the hardships of a hermit. He rejoiced that by the outer garment he deceived the world, by the inner he conformed himself to his brethren, and by the innermost he restrained unlawful impulses.

For he had received this counsel from a cenobite of the Church of Canterbury, of most holy conduct, to whom the Lord had spoken in a vision: if Thomas put on the monk’s habit, he would deserve to find the Lord gracious and helpful in his affairs. He rejoiced also that by assuming this habit he avoided the ruin of two of his predecessors, namely Stigand and Elfin. Stigand, while in clerical dress, was deprived of his dignity by apostolic censure and ended his life in prison. The other, frozen by Alpine cold and wrapping his feet in the dung of a split pack-animal, was not permitted, though no monk, to sit in the sacred seat of the monastic fathers. [Col. 0236A]

### FRAG. 10

From this arose the seed of conflict. For when the primate was burdened with pastoral care, he sent to ask the king to provide him with a chancellor, since he could scarcely suffice for one office, much less two. The second cause of anger was this: the ministers of public authority throughout England customarily collected money from every hide, to use the words of the provincials, as the wage for the labour which they expended upon the defence of the country. When the king strove to bring this money into the treasury as revenue, the primate opposed him, saying that what was given at his own and others’ discretion ought not to be counted as revenue. There was also a third matter which kindled the king’s anger. [Col. 0236B]

### FRAG. 11

Shortly afterward, it happened that the bishop of Lisieux crossed from overseas to the king in order to be reconciled with him, for he had fallen out of the king’s friendship. Perhaps, to recover the favour he had lost, he advised him—would that it had not harmed his own reputation—to draw part of the clergy over to his side, lest they prevail against him while they stood together as though in a close-joined battle-line and supported one another by common counsel and aid.

Accordingly, efforts were made to break the Church’s established unity and turn the bishops to the king’s side, so that the archbishop too might be turned, or, if he stood alone, might easily be crushed. Once the bishops had been turned—those to whom, because of the king’s long-standing hostility, danger of loss of limb and life seemed imminent—others too were turned, who had placed their house upon sand and could not withstand the assault of the rushing river. [Col. 0236C]

### FRAG. 12

One day Robert, bishop of Hereford, the count of Vendôme, and the abbot of l’Aumône had a lengthy discussion with the primate concerning the aforesaid customs. The abbot declared that he had been sent by the Roman pontiff to persuade him to comply with the king’s wishes. He said that the lord king had assured the lord cardinals by oath that he sought nothing prejudicial to the Church, but desired only to be honoured before his nobles; and that, for restoring peace, even a shadowy and merely nominal assent of whatever kind to his requests would suffice. If anything should thereby be presumed, the lord pope preferred that it be imputed to himself rather than that peace should not be restored.

We should not doubt that good men desired the good of ecclesiastical peace; yet, insufficiently cautious, they paid too little attention to the fact that the king would exceed moderation in his demands, and that the shoots of promise would degenerate into presumption. [Col. 0237A]

### FRAG. 13. On the summoning of the archbishop at Clarendon
