The king, then, zealous, as it seemed, for peace between kingdom and priesthood, but taking too little thought for himself and his archbishop, summoned the whole realm at Clarendon. When the prelates and magnates had assembled, the king pressed urgently for the fulfilment of what had been promised him.

But the archbishop, although he had promised assent to the king, nevertheless suspected the king’s promise; and because princes frequently stretch out their hands toward what is unlawful, not knowing moderation, he chose to risk himself before the king rather than before the law of God, and to crush the bronze serpent before perversity should take root among God’s people. Thus, although he feared exile or imprisonment, he valued God more highly and rose up in opposition. The one threatens; the other resists. The one raves; the other sighs in silent prayer.

Meanwhile the bishops of Salisbury and Norwich, upon whom punishment for an old hostility was waiting, fearing for themselves because of the occasion offered by the troubled time, tearfully entreated the archbishop to have mercy on his clergy and relax the obstinacy of his mind, lest he incur prison, the clergy exile, and they themselves condemnation to death. Two counts also, the most powerful in the kingdom, approached him and said that unless he yielded to the king’s will, by the king’s command they would be compelled to employ violence, which would bring perpetual disgrace both to the king and to themselves. [Col. 0237B]

The man of unconquered constancy, founded upon the rock of Christ, neither softened by flatteries nor shaken by terrors, was at last torn away from the bosom of truth and from the embrace of his mother, to whose liberty he clung. And lest, victorious in the struggle, he should swell in mind with pride, declining from the point at which he ought to have advanced, he was left to himself for a time: that he might fall and rise again after falling; that, falling, he might recognize human frailty, and, rising, understand the divine mercy shown toward him.

Thus, lest anyone put confidence in his own virtue, Peter, prince of the apostles, and holy David fell. We do not, however, propose their example for falling, but for rising again if one has fallen. Peter fell, indeed; but when the Lord looked upon him, he wept most bitterly and rose stronger. David fell; but when the prophet rebuked him, he completely wiped away the guilt of his fall by repentance and escaped punishment. So blessed Thomas was left to temptation for a time, that later, mindful of his own frailty, he might rise stronger for battle. [Col. 0237C]

Therefore, when for the third time he was warned through Richard, a man of great name who then presided over the Temple of Jerusalem, to take heed for himself and have mercy on the clergy, he did not yield to their entreaties or their kneeling. For they seemed to lament as though swords were brandished over his head, and to mourn the impending deed as though it were a funeral already present. Therefore, moved by pity for the clergy rather than for himself, he consented, on their advice, to comply with the royal will.

Accordingly, before all the others, the archbishop first bound himself in the aforesaid form: namely, that he would observe the royal customs in good faith, omitting the phrase, “saving his own order.” And as though adding the guarantee of an oath, he promised on the word of truth that he would do this—adding sin to sin. [Col. 0238A]

All the bishops individually swore the same thing in the same form. Immediately after the obligation had been made in this form, certain magnates of the realm, who ought to have known them, set forth an acknowledgment of the royal customs, and they were enumerated both publicly and expressly. But when many had already been stated, and, as it seemed, many more still remained to be stated, the archbishop intervened, saying that he was neither among the older men of the kingdom, who would know the ancient constitutions of the realm, nor had he been long in the archiepiscopate; therefore he said that he did not know these matters. Further, since the day was already declining, so great a business ought to be postponed until the next day.

The proposal pleased them, and they withdrew to their lodgings, returning on the following day to the same matter. The royal customs omitted the day before were then acknowledged and stated, committed to writing in the form of a chirograph, and designated “royal customs.” Yet many of them, as was reported, were by no means royal customs, but a poison of rivalry and envy, vomited forth against the archbishop in order to enslave the Church—even the king himself not knowing that men intended by this device to sow the tares of dissension between him and his archbishop. For the king, still young, knew the ancient customs of the realm only from others’ reports, just as the archbishop, newly appointed, did. Whoever wishes to know more fully what these royal customs were will find them written at the end of this history. [Col. 0238B–C]

### FRAG. 14. How the archbishop, returning to himself, repented of what he had done

When the customs had been written down and reduced to the form of a chirograph, the king asked the archbishop and his fellow bishops, for greater security and confirmation, to append their seals. But the archbishop, though deeply grieved, concealed it, unwilling at that moment to grieve the king. Prudently, he did not refuse outright, but said that it should still be delayed. Although they were prepared to act, he said that the importance of the matter deserved at least a short postponement, since, according to the Wise Man, nothing grave should be done without counsel; after some deliberation, he and the bishops should be asked again concerning it more fittingly.

Nevertheless, he received the written document containing the said customs, deliberately and prudently, so that he might have the record of his cause with him. Another portion of the document was received by the archbishop of York; the king himself took the third, to be deposited in the archives of the realm. Then the archbishop departed the court and set out for Winchester. [Col. 0238D]

### FRAG. 15

Led by repentance because he had rashly consented to unlawful things, although he excused his fault by the persuasion of great men and justified his cause on account of the clergy, he nevertheless exacted punishment from himself, as though he had committed the deed for his own sake. He afflicted himself with fasting and rough clothing, and meanwhile suspended himself from the office of the altar. [Col. 0239A]

### FRAG. 16. On the archbishop’s zeal for the dignity of the Church

Meanwhile the bishop of Évreux worked to reconcile the king and the archbishop. Yet the king could not be brought to reconciliation without confirmation of his laws, not heeding the lawgiver who says: “Woe to those who make unjust laws, and to writers who have written injustice, in order to oppress the poor in judgment and do violence to the humble of God’s people!”

Therefore, while the bishop pressed for peace and the archbishop desired the Church’s welfare, which could not arise without peace, he sent to the Roman pontiff as if asking for those customs to be confirmed. What such sudden change in the man was this? What such inconstancy in one so steadfast, that he now requested confirmation of enormities to whose acceptance he had previously been unable to incline? Clearly, he left to the judgment of a greater authority what he had not dared to do himself, in order to shift blame from himself and satisfy his lord. But the piety of the blessed pope could not be deceived: he learned in due order of the contest between king and archbishop. [Col. 0239B]

Supported, then, by apostolic authority and exhortation, the archbishop, fervent in spirit as he was, immediately shook himself free, and with the prophet’s hoe uprooted, destroyed, scattered, and eradicated whatever he found badly planted in the Lord’s garden. His hand did not rest; his eye did not spare. Whatever was perverse, rough, or crooked, he cast down now not with the prophet’s hoe but with the Gospel axe. He preserved the good royal and ecclesiastical customs, but cut away, as bastard shoots, those introduced to the Church’s injury or the clergy’s disgrace, lest they strike deep roots.

And, as from a woodland too wild and thorny, he strove with all his strength to erase and root out entirely from his people whatever was harsh, disordered, unbecoming, or obstructive, so as to make crooked things straight and rough places into level ways. [Col. 0239C]

### FRAG. 17

When the king saw that he made no progress in the things he attempted, he turned, on the advice of ill-wishers, to transferring the apostolic legation to the rival of the lord of Canterbury. When he requested this through envoys and did not obtain it, because from ancient times the Church of Canterbury was known to enjoy the privilege of the legation, the Roman pontiff understood and inferred—both from the envoys’ representations and from the well-known cruelty of courtiers—that vengeance would be taken against the archbishop unless the king were permitted to confer the legation upon whichever of his own men he wished.

Accordingly, he decided that letters should be sent to the king which seemed to grant the legation and its office, while forbidding the infliction of any burden upon the archbishop. Thus those who had been sent, being unable to bend the holy man to another course, returned with a shadowy and empty legation. Receiving it, the king, it is reported, gloried in the shadow of the title, as though he had received power over the archbishop. [Col. 0239D]

Nor did the quarrel and anger subside within these limits, but advanced without measure from one side against the other. For the king brought clerics who were murderers, thieves, robbers, assassins, or given to other crimes before secular judgment, so that, if they confessed or were convicted of the crime, they should be deprived of their office and, once deprived, handed over to the court.

But the archbishop, considering what was permitted to each judge in such cases, found that secular power has nothing to do in an ecclesiastical criminal case, since it cannot decide matters pertaining to God, according to that constitution: “If the crime is ecclesiastical, then the investigation and punishment of the case shall proceed from that person’s bishop according to the canons, other judges having no participation in cases of this kind.”

Considering this and similar matters, the archbishop permitted notorious clerics to be summoned only before ecclesiastical judges. There, if convicted, they were stripped of the office of their proper rank, but were not mutilated; for God does not judge twice for the same thing, and lest, perhaps, punished by a double penalty, they should seem inferior in condition to notorious laymen. But if, after degradation, they fell again into a like crime, they were to be punished under public laws by the secular judge. For, as he said, it was not fitting that even disordered persons should be judged disorderly. [Col. 0240A–B]

These and such matters kindled the king’s anger. His headlong wrath was now carried onward, and, growing stronger through the length of time, turned into hatred. Therefore the bishops, forgetting that they had been set over nations and kingdoms to uproot the plants of vices, not only failed to take up the shield of faith and stand for the house of the Lord on the day of battle, but even laid their body upon the ground so that it might become a roadway for the passer-by.

Nevertheless, the man of God, mindful of the authority he had received, left to God and himself, remained immovable. The fir-tree had sent its roots deep down; and though its leaves and branches were stripped away, it could not be cast down by the storm of winds. [Col. 0240C]

### FRAG. 18

“Under so great a discord between the two sides,” he says, “peace is banished forever. Not even hope of favour can be reckoned upon.”

### FRAG. 19

But he went rejoicing from the council’s presence because he had been judged worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus. Yet he refuted as liars Count Hamelin and a certain Ranulf, who above the others accused him of the stain of treachery; in turn he reproached them with matters they could not refute—one as a varlet and bastard, not worthy even of a man’s rebuke; and the other because his kinsman—something which had by no means happened within Thomas’s own family—had been hanged by a noose for a crime. [Col. 0240D]

### FRAG. 20

“Behold the fugitive hedgehog,” concerning whom a certain deacon saw a vision. For while the king of the English was gathered with all his archbishops, bishops, counts, magnates, abbots, and priors in the wood called Waberghe, a hedgehog leapt out from their midst, as though roused by the commotion of hunters. Seeing it, they all began to chase it, pursuing it with shouts and taunts.

But it, outrunning the crowd, hastened toward the sea, not straight ahead but by winding paths, carrying on its back a book entitled *Acts of the Apostles*. None of those who followed was without some bodily defect: one appeared blind, another one-eyed, another lame, or mutilated in lips or nose. At last the hedgehog came to the sea, threw itself into it, and did not emerge again. Those who had pursued it, seeing this, returned.

Then behold: a dense, dark mist arose and covered the face of the earth, followed by a rain of blood. The king turned aside into a royal hall built in the aforesaid place and sat there clothed in a white, linen, broad garment, his head encircled as with a wreath by foxes’ tails. Blood did not cease to drip upon him, because the house, being deserted in a desolate place, had no repaired roof; through it, running down the hanging fox-tails, the blood flowed into his lap. When it had filled his lap and the folds of his voluminous garment, it began to overflow and, in abundance, filled even his mouth. [Col. 0241A–B]

### FRAG. 21

Proceeding a little further, he met certain armed men, according to the custom of that people. When they asked whether he was the archbishop of Canterbury, he answered: “Does the archbishop of Canterbury go thus adorned with trappings?” And he was not recognized by them, although he bore testimony concerning himself. [Col. 0241B]

### FRAG. 22

At the same time it happened that Richard de Lucy, a familiar of the king, returning from abroad, came to the same place. Hearing of the archbishop’s departure from Britain, he came to him, promising that he would restore the king’s favour to him if he returned. But the prelate did not trust him, fearing the snares he had escaped. Richard, unable to bring him back, left him estranged and did not show the due reverence to his lord and father. [Col. 0241C]

### FRAG. 23. On the proscription of the archbishop’s entire kindred

When the king learned from the returning envoys that he had been refused in his petitions, he ordered all the possessions of the archbishop and his people to be confiscated. He consigned to proscription and exile all his kin, and all who had any connection with him through familiarity or any other title. Neither a crying infant, nor a feeble old man, nor a woman lying in childbed was spared. The empty fury went further, becoming a cruelty horrible to pious ears. Adults were compelled to swear that, to grieve the archbishop, they would seek him out wherever he might be found. It was forbidden that the Church should pray for him, as it is accustomed to do for heretics and schismatics. [Col. 0241C–D]

Thus every day a new multitude of exiles flowed to him—except that many, released from the aforesaid oath by apostolic authority, remained in Flanders, especially those who, because of weakness of age or sex and the great severity of the weather then prevailing, could not make their way to the archbishop as they had sworn without serious injury to themselves. The others came to him daily in crowds, weeping and lamenting that they had been expelled from their native soil, deprived of their goods, and separated from friends and relatives.

Thus every day they moved the man of God. With what anxiety, then, do you suppose he was burdened, when he continually had before his eyes those whose misery he had caused, and to whom, beyond compassion, he could offer little or nothing? Surely he was placed between anvil and hammer and received so many persecutions in himself. Before martyrdom he was made a martyr; before the blows of the stonecutters he was squared into a cornerstone; before the furnace he was transformed from bronze into silver; before the millstone, from straw into grain; and without the breaking of the alabaster jar, he gave forth the sweet fragrance of nard. [Col. 0242A]

The apostolic man, powerful among his brethren, and nations and kingdoms, hearing these things, immediately stood amazed; condemning the deed as utterly profane, they sympathized, with all the fullness of compassion, with the archbishop and that great multitude of exiles. Since the archbishop could not carry so great a crowd with him, he sent them with his supplicatory letters among various nations and provinces, to various persons. All were kindly received by those to whom they had been sent, both from hatred of so great a wickedness and from favour toward the sender. And so, with the Lord favouring all, provision was soon made for them such that there was no needy person among them; indeed, many lived more happily in exile than they had in their homeland. [Col. 0242B]

### FRAG. 24. How the archbishop began to live more austerely

But although, through God’s mercy, provision had thus been made for the proscribed, the archbishop nevertheless saw that his exile and punishment were made heavier by so great a multitude of exiles. He therefore resolved to increase the strictness of his penance, so that, in addition to the hairshirt which he wore daily and the frequent secret disciplines which he received while being scourged, he himself might live more strictly than usual.

Accordingly, one day he privately instructed a brother who customarily served him at table that, among the richer foods which he usually ate, the brother should cautiously set before him each day the common food of the community—so that no one would notice—for he had resolved to use only these. For greater caution and secrecy, a table was set daily for him alone, apart from his attendants. Thus for several days he ate only dry and tasteless dishes, in accordance with the regular observance of the Cistercian Order.

But after mortifying himself in this manner and living contrary to his accustomed way for some time, he was struck by serious illness and took to his bed. Having been brought up in luxury from his earliest years, he could not use coarser food without injury to his health. Yet at the admonition of a certain familiar, to whom, though not without importunate urging, he decided to disclose privately this cause of his illness, he took food suitable to him, with sobriety as companion. With God’s favour, he was soon restored to health. [Col. 0242C–D]

### FRAG. 25. How the king removed the archbishop from Pontigny

Therefore he who oversows tares in the Lord’s field envied such progress. Because the man of God had advanced through tribulation while he himself had fallen by his own scheming, he was moved by greater bitterness and strove to drive the guest from his lodging, as though he had grown in stature from the place itself.

At his prompting, as may rightly be believed, the king of the English sent letters to the general chapter of the Cistercians, threatening their Order severely if they retained his adversary among them any longer. When this was reported to the archbishop, he took counsel with his companions and promptly replied that he did not wish, on any account, for the Order to suffer any injury on his account or for his hosts to incur even the slightest loss, since, despite its own strict observance, it had shown such humanity to him and his companions.

He added that wherever he went, wherever he laid down his head, he would leave them at once: “Provided,” he said, “that the Lord supplies me and my fellow exiles, he who feeds the birds of heaven and clothes the lilies.” He therefore sent a messenger to the glorious king of the Franks, Louis, to announce his departure from Pontigny and its cause. [Col. 0243A]

When the king heard this, he was greatly astonished and immediately related everything he had heard to those present. Repeating it before all who heard, he said: “O religion, O religion, where are you? Behold: those whom we thought dead to the world fear the world’s threats. For transient things, which they profess to have despised for God’s sake, they turn back from the work of God which they had begun, driving from themselves God’s cause and the one exiled for God’s cause.”

Then, turning to the messenger, he said: “Greet your lord the archbishop, and confidently announce to him in my name that, even if the world and even those who seem dead to the world abandon him, I will not abandon him. However much the king of the English—though he is my liegeman—may plot and act against him, I will receive one exiled for God’s sake and suffering adversity for righteousness’ sake. Let him therefore tell us to what place within our dominion he would prefer to go, and he will find it ready.” [Col. 0243B–C]

Soon the messenger returned and reported these words to the archbishop in the king’s name. To complete the remaining time of his pilgrimage with his companions, the archbishop chose the splendid royal city of Sens, twelve miles from Pontigny, both because of the place’s great advantages and because of the citizens’ praiseworthy character, their devotion and especially their generosity toward strangers, their gracious affability, and their agreeable sociability. Thus, when he had already completed two years of his pilgrimage at Pontigny, he departed from Pontigny. [Col. 0243C]

### FRAG. 26. On his departure from Pontigny and the revelation of his martyrdom

As he was setting out toward the territory of Sens and was about to bid farewell to those escorting him, he burst into tears. Rebuking him, the venerable abbot of the place said: “What are you doing? I am astonished that a man of unconquered constancy should degenerate into womanly softness. Does the need of your household require greater expenses? Or do a thinner retinue and fewer servants draw forth these tears? If your need demands anything which our resources can supply, let it be shown and it shall be done.”

The archbishop replied: “None of these things, but my affairs are drawing to their end. In a vision of the past night, the Lord has deigned to show beforehand to your servant both the end of his life and the manner of that end. I shall not escape the sword of the executioner.”

Smiling, the abbot said: “Then you will perish by martyrdom? What have a lover of good food, a drunkard, and a martyr to do with one another? The cup of wine which you drink and the cup of martyrdom do not fit together well, nor do they remain in one seat.”

The archbishop said: “I confess that I indulge bodily pleasures; nevertheless the good Lord, who justifies the ungodly, has deigned to reveal the mystery to one unworthy.” [Col. 0243D–0244A]

### FRAG. 27

While blessed Thomas was thus residing at Sens, the king of the English, bearing most indignantly that he was refused in his requests by the one from whom his adversary was protected, seized the goods of priests dying within the diocese of Canterbury and occupied vacant churches, appointing persons according to his own will. He also alienated himself from Pope Alexander, whom the Lord, having taken pity on the Roman Church, had now restored to his see.

Therefore, seeking to vent his anger in a matter of faith, he sent two clerics, namely John of Oxford and Richard of Ilchester, to Frederick, emperor of Germany, who had convened a council to deliberate concerning peace for the Roman Church. He instructed them that, if Frederick renounced the name and obedience of Pope Alexander, the king would share the schism with his bishops and archbishops.

Frederick, having supporters of the schism, consented on the advice of the archbishop of Cologne, who, after Octavian’s death, had already raised up a successor. Thus, while the magnates swore with the emperor, and certain bishops willingly did so, while others objected and resisted even to tears, the king’s envoys likewise swore in a similar form on his behalf. [Col. 0244B–C]

And, as though he had not yet sinned sufficiently, the king ordered the ports to be guarded with the greatest care, establishing deadly edicts against those who brought the pope’s commands or letters into England, or received them when brought. He also publicly ordered and compelled, throughout villages, castles, and cities, everyone from an old man to a boy of twelve years to renounce Alexander, the successor of blessed Peter.

Thus, as all renounced their head, the thoughts of many hearts were revealed. Then one might see misery: very many Dathans and Abirams arising everywhere throughout England, and Lucifer sitting upon the sides of the north. [Col. 0244C]

### FRAG. 28. On the appeal of the bishops against the archbishop

Shortly afterward, certain bishops and abbots assembled in the city of London by the king’s command, and it seemed right to appeal against the archbishop. For it was feared that he might extend the hand of correction against the enormities being presumed throughout the kingdom.

The bishop of London and the bishop of Salisbury, sources of provocation and prevarication, appealed first. The bishop of Exeter could not be compelled to appeal. The bishop of Rochester excused his absence by a feigned illness, as was said. The bishop of Winchester likewise excused his own absence by letter, saying: “Summoned by the supreme pontiff, I neither appeal nor wish to appeal.” Because of the ambiguity of the title, it was supposed that he had been summoned to the hearing of the supreme pontiff, that is, the lord pope. But he understood by “supreme pontiff” the supreme judge, before whose tribunal he was about to be brought for examination, since he had reached an advanced age and was approaching the limits of life. [Col. 0244D–0245A]

But the archbishop repeatedly admonished the king with paternal charity, both in writing and through men who, by reason of their standing, deserved to be heard, to desist from oppressing ecclesiastical liberty. The Roman pontiff also earnestly pressed him on the same matter through the Archbishop of Rouen, through the former Empress of the Romans, his mother, and through the Bishops of Hereford and London. While each applied his diligence to these commands, and the Bishop of Hereford followed him with letters as he was leading an army to the borders of Wales, they obtained nothing except that the archbishop should return home voluntarily [Col. 0245B], as he had voluntarily departed.

The Bishop of London, however, was believed to have carried out the commands less faithfully, because, when he had written back to the lord pope concerning the execution of his mandate and the king’s reply, he was not ashamed to urge him away from the exercise of ecclesiastical severity which he intended against the violators, so that the Church of Canterbury might mourn the perpetual exile of its shepherd and the English Church its shipwreck. But the successor of the apostles and pillar of the Church was not moved. For he knew who it was that spoke. Therefore he did not listen to him at that time, but provided for the unimpaired rights and dignity of both the archbishop and the church over which he presided, as he had promised him before the exile, saying:

> “We wish you to believe [Col. 0245C] without any doubt and to hold firmly that, God willing, it shall never enter our mind that we should wish you or your church to be subject in ecclesiastical matters to any person, nor to obey anyone except the Roman pontiff alone.”

For, having heard that the Archbishop of York had raised his cross upon a staff of exaltation and carried it through the province of Canterbury contrary to custom, he forbade him to presume to do this thereafter. Thus the Archbishop of York, restrained from this rash attempt and distressed over his cross, joined to himself the Bishops of London and Salisbury and, together with the assembled bishops of England, as has been said, appealed against the Archbishop of Canterbury, notifying him in writing of the appeal and its appointed term. But he, replying in all patience and gentleness [Col. 0245D], reproving and rebuking their restless minds, strove in vain to restore them to the unity of ecclesiastical peace. For Christ God had to suffer, and the iniquities of the Amorites had to be fulfilled.

## FRAG. 29. Concerning the legates sent by the lord pope

Meanwhile, at the king’s request, two legates were sent by the Roman pontiff. One was William, cardinal priest, a close friend of the king, who, as the archbishop himself says of him, chose rather to be a hammerer of clerics by serving princes than to obtain divine grace by incurring the displeasure of kings. The other was a cardinal deacon named Otto. Both were more devoted to greed than justice, and, unless they had been delegated by the lord pope, were more worthy of banishment than of a legation.

[Col. 0246A] They received full authority to decide the questions at issue between the king and the archbishop, and to impose upon them their due conclusion, appeals being excluded as an obstacle. But the archbishop, knowing that one was the king’s close friend and had been urgently sought by him, and having the other under suspicion for other reasons, rejected both. He said that he ought by no means to submit in this case to William’s jurisdiction, since he was being sent at the king’s urging rather than coming because he himself had been compelled and sent; and because it was not consistent with justice to undergo the judgment of one who sought to trade with him in his own blood and to obtain a name and glory at its price.

Indeed, he rejected him so firmly that he preferred to be subjected to excommunication rather than to undergo his judgment in any matter outside the Roman curia. For [Col. 0246B] William had exerted every sort of ingenuity in seeking to obtain judicial authority over him. Yet the lord pope, considering the malice of the times and wishing to moderate the power of those who could trouble the Church, judged it necessary to grant them judicial authority for a time.

Accordingly, when they came into France, William boasted that he had come to bring about the harm and humiliation of the lord of Canterbury by carrying out the king’s will. Hence the French Church was afraid; and those who had expected the good of peace were cast down on hearing of Canterbury’s overthrow. But he who intended humiliation was himself confounded and rendered useless, becoming less formidable to his adversary as he brandished his threat with an uncut brow. For before the case was heard, they were stripped of the authority they had assumed by virtue of their office, the king of France writing to the lord pope [Col. 0246C] that the greatest scandal would be inflicted upon the Church if its innocent defender were deposed, and that loss of dignity would arise from that from which the reward of advancement ought to be deserved.

Therefore the lord pope, though placed between Charybdis and Scylla—for on one side the king of England pressed him with gifts, promises, and threats, while on the other the king of France opposed him with prayers and admonitions; on one side there would be disturbance in the Church if arrogance were restrained, and on the other a mark of infamy if an innocent man were condemned—recalled his decision. He wrote to the legates that they should not preside judicially between the king and the archbishop, but should devote themselves by every means to establishing full peace between them, provided that the ancient rights of the archbishop and his Church remained whole and inviolate [Col. 0246D]; and that they should do nothing important in the king’s land, nor enter his realm, should he wish them to do so, unless the archbishop had first been fully reconciled with the king. For in these matters much was being detracted from both himself and them, and he himself was being torn apart by the hostile slander universally voiced against him.

When they had received these instructions, they nevertheless continued the remnants of their legation. Their arrival gave the king proportionately less pleasure as they possessed less authority; for he already knew, and bore it with great indignation, that their power had partly expired. Yet, lest nothing be done, they summoned the archbishop to a conference, and a time and place were fixed.

Accordingly they met: on one side the exile with his fellow exiles [Col. 0247A], and on the other the legates, accompanied by a great many archbishops, bishops, and abbots. On the night immediately before the conference, the primate saw a dream, as he himself related in the morning to those going with him to the meeting: namely, that poison was being offered him in a golden cup. And so it happened. For one of the cardinals, the aforesaid William, eloquent in speech and possessing persuasive words, offered him sweet and flattering language of peace. On the surface the words seemed good and peaceful; yet, if anyone looked within, they seriously undermined ecclesiastical peace and liberty.

Thus nearly every proposal for peace put forward by the cardinals was suspect to the archbishop and his companions, who feared being caught in words that were soft and honeyed [Col. 0247B] and yet nevertheless weapons. The conference was therefore prolonged for a long time and in vain. At last peace having failed—or rather, all hope of peace being thereafter made through them having vanished—the archbishop and legates departed from one another, the legates returning at once to the king.

At Le Mans, in the city of Le Mans itself, certain persons of the realm had already assembled. Seeing that peace could in no way be made through the cardinals, they renewed their appeals in the legates’ hearing, appealing again to the Apostolic See on behalf of the king, the realm, their own persons, and their churches. After some time the cardinals, greatly honoured by the king and burdened with ambitious gifts, returned to the Roman Church, peace between the archbishop and the Church [Col. 0247C] having failed.

## FRAG. 30

The archbishop, hearing new reports and knowing that abuses, together with the old ones, had grown into most evil fruits and were daily springing up throughout his diocese, knew the prophet’s curse upon one who withholds the sword from blood and one who performs God’s work negligently. Therefore, lest the Lord’s vineyard should be corrupted because its rotten branches had not been cut off, he girded himself and exercised the sickle of ecclesiastical severity against many.

## FRAG. 31

For on one side, fearing ingratitude, he considered the king, who had heaped benefits upon him when he rejected the Roman schism; on the other, he considered the Church, endangered if he left transgression unpunished. Wishing to test whether he might still heal the wounds without incision [Col. 0247D] and soften the king’s hardness without the rigour of severity, he sent two learned and discreet men—one his subdeacon and notary, the other an advocate of the Roman curia—and earnestly requested that the king restore to the archbishop his archbishopric with his favour.

## FRAG. 32

During this storm the king of England went to France for prayer. There, at the request of the king of France and the magnates of the realm, at Montmartre, in reverence for the divine majesty and the memorials of the saints whom he had come to venerate, he agreed, laying aside all hostility, to restore his favour to his archbishop. Although he first complained that the archbishop had not come to meet him, he granted that he should return home in peace and safety, recover his possessions and archbishopric, and hold them [Col. 0248A] with the right and liberty with which his predecessors had customarily held them.

## FRAG. 33

Soon after the aforesaid conference, the king of England crossed over into England. As the feast of blessed John the Baptist approached, under the pretext of arranging the kingdom and having summoned the magnates of the realm, he entrusted the reins of his kingdom to his eldest son. Some said that the king had thereby made provision for the heir who was to succeed him; others maintained that he did it out of hatred for the primate and to injure the dignity of the Church of Canterbury.

The Archbishop of York laid hands upon him in the diocese of Canterbury, namely in the church of St Peter at Westminster, contrary to the dignity of the Church of Canterbury and ancient custom. Assisting [Col. 0248B] him and supporting him were the Bishops of London, Salisbury, and Rochester, who made no protest concerning the right of the Church of Canterbury, to whose dignity and right the coronation of the kings of England has from ancient times been recognized as belonging. After the coronation, when the feast had been held, the king condescended to serve the king—father serving son—and declared that he was not king.

In the course of time he repented of both word and deed; and by the proof of events he learned that he had not so much injured the Church of Canterbury as raised up against himself, in vengeance for those whom he had persecuted, an adversary from his own loins.

On hearing these things, the primate could scarcely believe them at first. For, being a prudent man and one to whom everything concerning his adversaries was suspect, he had obtained letters from the Roman pontiff addressed before the coronation to the Archbishop of York [Col. 0248C] and the other bishops of England. By apostolic authority and in virtue of holy obedience, they were forbidden to place a crown upon the king’s son to the prejudice of the Archbishop of Canterbury, who was in exile for justice’s sake. Certain bishops received these letters addressed to them before the coronation; others, forewarned of their contents, refused to receive them. They therefore attended the coronation in defiance of the apostolic prohibition.

But let us briefly consider how profane, how hateful, how hostile this anointing and consecration was—if indeed it should be called consecration rather than execration—being deprived of apostolic blessing, indeed performed in transgression against the apostolic man; and proceeding from sheer [Col. 0248D] hatred, anger, and indignation: hatred for the spiritual father devised by the carnal father. This is proved by the mournful events resulting from this consecration, detestable to all ages yet to come: the suspension and anathematization of priests; the murder of the primate; rebellion between father and son once and again; and, finally, the detestable prevention by premature death, in adolescence, of that distinguished consecrated boy, for all future ages.

Therefore one must lament and cry:

> “O your death, Henry—O death, how dreadful! How hard and bitter is your memory, you who cut down such and so great a glory of the world while it was still beginning! How thoughtless, how inhuman you were, who with one brief and violent blast of your breath extinguished such a certain hope of the world, as it was thought, while its fruit was still in so splendid a flower! May He who is the death of death be your death, so that he who was hoped to live not for himself but for the world may pass through you into life.”

I would here have inserted more concerning the deeds of this Henry—though young in years, yet vigorous—and concerning the manner of his departure from life, had not the law of the history which we have undertaken to write stood in the way. Let us therefore return to the order begun.

## FRAG. 34. Concerning the suspension of the bishops

Once holy Thomas had learned for certain, through his messengers, that the coronation had been performed, [Col. 0249A] he reported fully to the Roman pontiff both orally and in writing how far peace had progressed, where it had stopped, and concerning the coronation. He humbly and tearfully begged that the son of one shaken might now shake himself, and rise especially against the false [Col. 0249B] brethren, who, by so great an injury to their father—who endured exile and proscription on their account—and to their mother, the Church of Canterbury, were manifest transgressors even of the apostolic command.

When the apostolic man heard all that had been done, and how it had been done, he was vehemently moved against both the king and the bishops, and felt still more paternal compassion for the primate. The king of France also urged him, in the strength of love and with a protest of devoted service, not to prolong further fruitless delays, if he loved the kingdom of France and the honour of the Apostolic See. William, Archbishop of Sens, likewise pitying the desolation of the English Church, petitioned the Apostolic See and obtained from the Roman pontiff that [Col. 0249C] the king of England, all appeal being set aside, should be subjected to anathema and the kingdom to interdict unless peace were restored to the Church of Canterbury.

## FRAG. 35

And the king said to the archbishop: “You wish, as you say, to return to France; but I think it expedient that you remain with me for a few days, so that what is not yet believed may be seen openly. Everyone knows our enmities; few know that peace has been made.”

The archbishop said: “I shall rightly be regarded as ungrateful if I do not at least bid farewell to my benefactors. I will go and return.”

## FRAG. 36

One day, as the archbishop was walking with his companions along the shore, considering the conditions of the elements, as is customary for those about to cross the sea, [Col. 0249D] he saw a certain Milo, dean of Boulogne, approaching. Smiling, he got ahead of him, as though Milo were hurrying to collect passage money. Milo said:

> “We are hurrying not to collect passage money, but to convey a command. My lord, the Count of Boulogne, commands you this: take care for yourself. Men are ready who seek your life; they are watching the ports beyond the sea, so that, when you leave the ship, they may seize and kill you, or cast you into chains.”

The archbishop replied:

> “Believe me, son: not even if I were to be torn limb from limb would I desist from the journey I have begun. Neither fear, nor force, nor tortures shall henceforth turn me back. Let it suffice that the Lord’s flock has mourned the seven-year absence of its shepherd. I ask from all my prayers that this final request may be obtained from my own people. For nothing is more owed to human beings [Col. 0250A] than that their last will, once they can will nothing else, should be fulfilled: namely, that they should not think it burdensome to carry me, dead at least, to the Church from which I am barred while living.”

## FRAG. 37

For Reginald de Warenne, Sheriff Gervase, and Ranulf de Broc, whom he had previously anathematized, had conspired against the archbishop, either at another’s will or from their own malice, together with the aforesaid bishops; and with an armed force they were watching the shore.

## FRAG. 38

Entering the monastery, he lay prostrate with his whole body, displaying the form of humility. Then he received all the brethren, from the least to the greatest, with tears in the kiss of peace. For, while abroad, he had heard that some of them had communicated with excommunicated persons; therefore, through Master John of Salisbury, his fellow exile, whom he had sent on ahead a month before himself, he had instructed Brother Thomas, a venerable man, to exercise the power of absolution, so that [Col. 0250B] whatever contagion from the scab of the schismatics had infected the flock of brethren might be erased by the antidote of reconciliation.

## FRAG. 39

For the Archbishop of York is said to have declared:

> “Thanks be to God, our treasury still holds eight thousand pounds in ready money. If necessity should require such expenditures, it shall be wholly demolished to restrain Thomas’s stubbornness and scatter an arrogance greater than his strength. I beg you, brothers, do not let him outwit your religious profession. Let us rather go to the lord king, who to this day has supported with faithful patronage the cause that has long been at issue between us and [Col. 0250C] him, and will bring it to completion hereafter unless the matter is hindered by us.
>
> “If you fall away by attaching yourselves to him, whom the king has as an enemy—for after such great and inexorable enmities favour will never be restored—you will be judged by us according to reason as deserters. And if he deals strictly with you, he will expel you from your possessions according to the equity of law. What then will you do? Tell me: in what lands will you, poor in household goods, beg? But if, on the contrary, you stand with him with whom you have stood, what more will the man who has condemned you do? He has done what he could against you: by a wicked suggestion he extorted the sentence.”

## FRAG. 40

And the Archbishop of York said:

> “Lord king, I alone am permitted [Col. 0250D] to utter a word. No one can speak with these two companions of mine, to whom water and fire have been forbidden, unless the speaker himself becomes involved in the same sentence of condemnation by which they are struck—a sentence which that ungrateful man, forgetful of the return allowed him, has poured out upon them and upon all who consented to the coronation of your son.
>
> “Now, having obtained his native country and taking care not to be proscribed again in future, he proceeds surrounded by a great retinue of horsemen and foot-soldiers going before and following, ranging about and seeking to be received into strongholds. Lord king, it is not constant vexations that stir us so greatly, nor labours that break us, nor enormous losses that trouble us—these we regard as of little account, provided we please you, our lord king, by preserving faithfulness—but repeated exactions, the maimed dignity of our office [Col. 0251A], and the diminishment of our endangered reputation. As though we had committed some shameful crime, we have become a spectacle and are judged guilty, though we have no doubt about the purity of our conscience.”

The king replied: “If all who consented to the coronation of my son are subject to excommunication, then I too, by the eyes of God, am not excluded.”

But the Archbishop of York added:

> “One must bear calmly a storm that one cannot avoid, so that, when provoked and suffering injuries, one may deserve to appear possessed of a tranquil mind and moderation in endurance. This can easily be done if for the present you can conceal the injuries inflicted and let the wrongdoer go for a time as though he were safe.”

## FRAG. 41

For the present, we shall set forth the effectiveness of the sentence against him. When the aforesaid Robert had held a feast in his house at Canterbury, which he had built from the woods of the archbishop, cut down everywhere at his pleasure, for certain persons communicating with him, the dogs refused bread which his hands had touched, although they eagerly took anything offered from other hands. When everyone put out food to them and mixed his leftovers with the fragments of others, the dogs seemed to abstain from both alike as though contaminated by their touch [Col. 0251B].

## FRAG. 42

And he added:

> “One man who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me. One man, insulting my benefits, dishonours the whole royal race and tramples the entire kingdom underfoot without an avenger. One man, who, riding a pack-horse and lame, first broke into the court, has driven out the royal stock and, while you look on, companions of Fortune, exults triumphantly upon the throne.” [Col. 0251C]

## FRAG. 43

These are their names. The first was Reginald, fearing no crime, as they asserted, and deriving beastly savagery from his father Urso (“Bear”). The second was Hugh de Moreville—namely, “the estate of death” or “the estate of deaths.” However it may be said, the name denotes a man of death.

His wife, it is reported, passionately loved a young man named Lithulf. When he refused sexual violation, she devised a woman’s cunning stratagem. She asked him, with drawn sword, to play before her the part of one at sport and to let his horse enter. When he did so, she herself cried out to her husband, who was passing by:

> “Huwe of Morevile, war, war, war, Lithulf haveth his swerd ydrawen . . .”

That is, in Latin:

> “Hugh [Col. 0251D] de Moreville, beware, beware, beware: Lithulf has drawn his sword.”

For this reason the innocent young man, as though he had stretched out his hand to shed his lord’s blood, was condemned to death; boiled in hot water, he completed his martyrdom. What can we expect from a brood of vipers? Do we gather grapes from thorns, or figs from a thornbush? If a bad tree cannot produce good fruit, as Truth testifies, it follows that from an evil and poisonous root an innocent shoot cannot arise.

The third was William de Tracy. Though he had often performed bravely in military engagement, his way of life was such that, as his sins required, he deserved to fall into parricide or some other crime. The fourth was Richard Brito, who through the depravity of his life had become a brute from being a Breton; and while he fought in the church, in place of the name of a warrior he incurred the mark of betrayal.

## FRAG. 44

Therefore Satan’s henchmen, thinking that heaven and earth smiled upon their crime, became readier and bolder, flattering themselves amid the elements’ favourable calm. Ranulf de Broc had gone out to meet them; and, having stirred up the whole coastal region, he came attended by many soldiers.

## FRAG. 45

Already, in the midst of the brethren singing Vespers, two boys had run ahead, announcing the hostile invasion more by terror than by voice.

## FRAG. 46

[Col. 0252B] Accordingly, the doors having been opened, behold: after searching the palace of the Church, the executioners rush in a mass through the cloisters. Of them, three carried axes in their left hands; one carried a double-edged axe; all brandished sharp swords in their right hands.

## FRAG. 47

Struck back by these words, the assassin recoiled two or three paces, becoming like those who, at the Lord’s Passion, when the Lord said, “I am he,” went backward and fell on their faces.

## FRAG. 48

Therefore Urso’s son, hastening to win a trophy from the first blow and gain profit from his hasty treachery, attempted with all his force to inflict a wound upon the exposed head; but he dealt a severe sword-wound to the arm of a certain cleric.

## FRAG. 49

[Col. 0252C] The man who had struck cried out, triumphing as though over a defeated enemy: “Strike, strike!” Immediately some who were still standing in prayer scattered, according to that Gospel saying: “I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered.” For the Lord did not instil a slight fear in all, but a great one, capable of overcoming even the most steadfast person.

That cleric, fearing wound upon wound and graver injuries after grave ones, withdrew to the nearby altar, where several brethren had fled in fear for their lives, not knowing who had struck him. But we infer the author of the wound from the fact that William de Tracy, when his accomplices at Saltwood Castle recounted how fiercely each had behaved toward the martyr and boasted of their crime, [Col. 0252D] said that he had also cut off the arm of John of Salisbury. One of the brethren too, moving about the father out of compassionate concern, received a blow. Yet the prayer of the good shepherd obtained that, the flock not being diminished, he alone should fall. Thus, struck with the flat of a sword, he bore away a stunned head.

## FRAG. 50

For, with the beauty of his countenance preserved, even in death he displayed in outward appearance a certain joy and holiness which he bore in his mind, so that he seemed not to have expired, but rather, his eyes and mouth closed and his living colour retained, to have fallen asleep.

[Col. 0253]

# The Seventh Life of Saint Thomas, Archbishop and Martyr of Canterbury, by E. of Evesham

[Col. 0253A]

To the venerable lord and father Henry, by God’s grace Abbot of Crowland, E., humbly styled monk of Evesham, greetings in the Author of salvation.

The authority of our forebears has sufficiently and wisely established that the lives and deaths of illustrious men, and especially of saints, should be committed to writing. For thereby God, glorious in his saints, is praised; and posterity is edified when stirred by the praiseworthy example of those who went before. Among these, like a certain Lucifer at the end of these evil days—like the end of some dark and wearisome night—shone blessed Thomas, the new martyr. How praiseworthy his life was and how precious his death, the volumes of authoritative men who have written on these matters testify.

Since these writers were many, and it could not be otherwise than that one might lack something [Col. 0253B] which another perhaps possessed, your fatherhood commanded that, from the written books of each, I should excerpt only those things which would suffice to continue the history of the martyr, and arrange the excerpts in sequence. We read that something of this sort was done from the Gospels themselves by the man who made one for us from four. For here too there were four authors: John, Bishop of Chartres; Alan, Abbot of Tewkesbury; William, subprior of Canterbury; and Master Herbert of Bosham. Benedict, Abbot of Peterborough, wrote only of the end and of the things which occurred after the end.

I confess that I hesitated at your command; and although such a work was commendable, measuring so great a task against my abilities, I held my hand back. But your condescension, undertaking the work together with me, urged on my hesitation.

Therefore, commanded and relying equally upon your assistance, I obeyed as I could. You judge whether I have satisfied you; let others judge as they wish. If anyone can arrange it better, I shall not begrudge it. I have at least supplied an example and, as it were, shown a road. This little work is divided into three parts: the first contains the beginnings of the holy man and the rest down to [Col. 0254B] the exile; the second, the deeds done in exile; the third, the martyrdom and the things done after the martyrdom. So that it may be known what has been taken from each author, wherever the style changes, the author’s name is prefixed to that chapter. May your fatherhood prosper in the Lord.

[Col. 0253]

*(Thus ends the prologue; but the work itself is the same as the Quadrilogue published by Lupus. Therefore, since we shall speak below concerning this Quadrilogue, let us hasten now to the translation of blessed Thomas, which the same E. of Evesham—whoever he was—who compiled this Life, added to the end of his work.)*

# The Translation of Blessed Thomas the Martyr Begins

[Col. 0253C]

In the fiftieth year after the Passion of the most glorious martyr Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, the venerable father Stephen, his successor—the fourth, that is, after him—and the convent of the Church of Canterbury, intending to translate the body of the aforesaid precious martyr, made most diligent provision for everything which they believed necessary for so great a solemnity.

After the appropriate fasts and prayers had first been held, the aforesaid archbishop, Richard Bishop of Salisbury, and the convent of the Church of Canterbury assembled, as arranged, at the beginning of the night on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the crypt where the body of the blessed martyr lay. After they had devoted themselves to prayer for some time, they caused the marble stone covering the martyr’s tomb to be removed. As all present looked on, that former instrument of the Holy Spirit was found clothed in priestly vestments—though partly consumed by age—and in the other insignia fitting the burial of a high priest [Col. 0254C].

All wept for joy and prayed. The monks appointed for the purpose lifted the precious body in their hands and handed it to the archbishop to be placed in a shrine. While the others continued the prayers begun, the archbishop received the body from the aforesaid brethren and placed it all in the reliquary with his own hands, except for a few small bones which he kept outside the shrine to distribute, in honour of the martyr, to great men and churches. Once the body had been suitably arranged by the archbishop’s hands, the shrine was most securely fastened with iron nails; and, borne by the monks’ hands to a fitting place and bier, it was kept there in secrecy until the day appointed for the solemn celebration of the translation [Col. 0255A].

## MIRACLE

As the day for celebrating the translation approached, an innumerable people flowed into Canterbury, both to pay the martyr the honour due to him and to obtain his aid in their necessities. Present at this solemnity were the venerable father Pandulf, legate of the Apostolic See; Stephen of Canterbury; William, Archbishop of Reims; Henry, King of England, with all his household and magnates [Col. 0255B]; also bishops, abbots, priors, and other ecclesiastical men from various regions, whom we omit to enumerate individually lest their multitude weary the ears of hearers. So great a people had assembled for this festival that the city of Canterbury, the neighbouring villages, and the surrounding district could scarcely contain the crowd.

## MIRACLE

The third hour on the Nones of July was approaching, when the king, archbishops, bishops, abbots, princes, and magnates who had assembled carried the aforesaid treasure from the crypt where it had been kept to the altar of the holy martyr. They placed it before the people in the place prepared for this purpose and there sealed it most securely; they then spent the remainder of the day in praises of the martyr [Col. 0255C] and in gladness of heart in the Lord. Thus the devotion of the faithful faithfully rendered to the martyr what it owed him.

Nor did the martyr withhold the consolations of his grace from his faithful people. For when the archbishop, the convent, the other faithful, and especially the Londoners were pouring out their resources and labour so that nothing which their exertions could accomplish should be lacking from the martyr’s honour, the martyr himself, as though repaying the devotion of the devout, adorned the entire solemnity of his translation with signs and miracles going before, accompanying, and following it.

## MIRACLE

A short time remained before the translation of blessed Thomas was to occur. A certain woman at Kembella had only one surviving little daughter out of four children whom she had borne to her husband [Col. 0255D]. The girl began to be severely ill and died in her mother’s lap. The woman’s tears and groans in mourning her daughter seemed to exceed all measure.

A noble matron, a widow and the lady of that village, ran up. Moved by the mourner’s tears and taught by the girl’s death to invoke divine help, she took the little girl and, invoking aid from the mother of the deceased, measured her; and the girl rose. The mother made a candle and intended to send it to St Thomas, but the girl fell ill again and, as her mother testified, died a second time. Recalling that she had shown herself insufficiently grateful and devoted to the martyr, the mother vowed that she would bring the girl to St Thomas if he recalled her from the dead a second time. Thus the glorious martyr, tempering the rigour of justice [Col. 0256A] by the gentleness of his grace, again restored the dead girl alive to her mother.

## MIRACLE

A certain man from Devizes, wishing with many others to visit the threshold of blessed Thomas in prayer at the time of his translation, came to Brentford Bridge near London. In the middle of the bridge, meeting a cart, he was thrown into the water. But he did not forget himself: he continually invoked St Thomas, asking that he would not allow his pilgrim to perish. He was immersed five times to the bottom of the water and as often returned to its surface, and was cast out upon dry ground. With great amazement he testified that he had felt no discomfort at all from water in his mouth, nostrils, or ears.

Another man travelling with him lost his cloak in the same place [Col. 0256B] where the first man fell into the water; and no one could ever find the cloth that had sunk in the river.

A knight from the county of Northampton married a widow. Her three-year-old son, whom she had borne by her former husband, stood one day at the table while the aforesaid knight was dining and received in his mouth from the knight’s hand a morsel of meat. The boy, attempting to swallow the morsel, choked and died. At first the mother suspected the knight of causing her son’s death and, crying and weeping, repeatedly called him a murderer.

Though he had a clear conscience, the knight was nevertheless deeply overcome and made a vehement declaration; then he rose and laid a silver coin upon the boy, vowing that he would take the child to St Thomas [Col. 0256C] if he restored him to life. A little after the vow, as they waited to see what the Lord would do, the morsel of meat that had closed the way of life sprang from the boy’s throat into his mouth. The boy gradually revived and, through the merits of the martyr, was fully restored to life and to his friends.

**MIRACLE.** A certain knight of Countess Elugi, named Robert, set out with his twelve-year-old son, also named Robert, for Canterbury, to visit the thresholds of blessed Thomas in prayer. Having entered the sea at Wythsand, he sailed safely almost to mid-sea. But his aforesaid son, overcome by sleep, went to the prow of the ship either to urinate or to do something else; and, while standing carelessly, fell into the sea. When the father saw this, [Col. 0256D] he cried out, saying: “Saint Thomas, have mercy on me, and preserve my son for me.” The boy, having sunk a little into the sea and immediately been borne back to the surface of the water, said: “Saint Thomas, if you will, you can help me.”

Meanwhile, driven by the wind, the ship was carried away from the place where the boy had fallen as far as one might shoot an arrow two or three times. Then, at the knight’s cry, the sailors lowered the sail and, although with difficulty, turned the ship back to seek the boy. Thus, after an interval of one hour—or, as the knight himself testified, as long as he might have covered two or three French leagues riding at a moderate pace—they reached the boy, finding him sitting upon the waters and unharmed, except that [Col. 0257A] in his fall he had swallowed a little salt water. But when the boy saw the ship withdrawing from him, overwhelmed by excessive grief and despair of life, he plunged his head into the [Col. 0258A] sea so that, by ending the pain of his heart through bodily death, he might perish more quickly. Taken aboard the ship, the boy reported these things when his father questioned him; and he added that, when he wished to drown himself, a certain bishop supported him so that he could not sink.

[Col. 0257]

# THE EIGHTH LIFE OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY AND MARTYR

By Henry, Abbot, and Roger, Monk of Crowland.

## LETTER OF ABBOT HENRY TO STEPHEN LANGTON, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0257B]

To the most reverend father and lord, most beloved in Christ, holy Stephen, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury, Primate of all England, and Cardinal of the holy Roman Church: his devoted son H. . . , by divine permission Abbot of Crowland, greeting, and reverence in all things as devoted as it is due.

If, as the will is present to me, so the ability were also at hand, I would embrace your holy fatherhood, which I cherish in Christ with the affection of sincere love. . . . For both the sublimity of your rank and the holiness of your life require that every honour and reverence be rendered to you by all, with a great heart and a willing spirit. For you, like a new Bezalel, notably build and adorn the mystical tabernacle of the Lord, [Col. 0257C] that is, the holy Church. Therefore we render abundant and devoted thanks to divine grace, which in your person has provided us with a worthy archbishop and primate, ever possessing beside him pomegranates of fruitful action together with the bells of sacred preaching.

Moreover, the teaching in which you excel pre-eminently effectively instructs you to live well, soberly, and justly, with godly aid. Your deeds indeed, most reverend Father, bear witness concerning you that you have been and are conformed to your predecessor, the most blessed martyr Thomas, not only through an evident likeness of character, but also through a brave and even-minded endurance of exile and other hardships. Hence it is to be believed that, as [Col. 0257D] you have been companions in tribulations, so you shall be in consolations; and as you have suffered with him, so, by the Lord’s favour, you shall also reign with him.

As proof of this, fastening the anchor of our faith in firm hope, and wishing in some measure to add on earth to the glory of the glorious martyr which he enjoys in heaven, you have determined to set the lamp of his body upon a lampstand, so that, translated from beneath the bushel of earth, it may shine more openly for those who yearn for the same glory. Thus it is that you have deigned to invite [Col. 0258B] even my insignificance, among others, by letter to that glorious translation. I therefore return most devout thanks to your graciousness and lordship; and because I do not doubt that, at this distinguished solemnity, many will make many offerings, as is fitting, in honour of the most sacred martyr and out of reverence for you, I too, wishing to offer something according to my measure, have judged it fitting to send to your excellency a book compiled in your presence concerning the holiness and magnificence of that martyr.

The appended prologue clearly sets forth both the method of this compilation and the arrangement of the whole volume: namely, how this compilation has been drawn from the writings of five historians, and contains the origin and life, [Col. 0258C] pursuits and deeds, exile and struggle, passion and canonization of the glorious martyr; and also how, through letters of the said martyr—that is, letters which he wrote to others, or others to him, or on his behalf, or against him, or written by others—fittingly inserted in appropriate places, the aforesaid compilation possesses no small strength of authority. Although the life and passion of the precious martyr have been elegantly committed by us to the memory of letters, nevertheless, when you have leisure to inspect this volume more fully, you will, I think, find it acceptable.

Therefore I humbly and devoutly beseech your holiness graciously to receive, in place of a small gift, this book diligently and, as I believe, fruitfully composed for the praise and glory of the most blessed martyr and for the edification of the faithful. I earnestly ask that its first and inaugural use [Col. 0258D] be reserved to your fatherhood, and that, if it please you, you apply to it the file of your correction, so that thereafter it may be more acceptable and more pleasing for others to read. For, just as it has deserved commendation from your wisdom, so from your excellency it will deserve no small approval among posterity, to the martyr’s honour and the benefit of many. May your holy fatherhood fare well in the Lord.

[Col. 0259A] [Between the letter of Abbot Henry and that of the monk Roger, who enlarged the work in a second edition, the Paris manuscript contains the following note.

Here begins the prologue to the Life of Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury and Martyr, excerpted from various little works; written in the year of the Lord 1411, and completed on the eve of Saint Lucy the Virgin, by me, John Waning of Germany.

Pious servant of God, remember me!]

## LETTER OF ROGER, OR PROLOGUE TO THE LIFE OF SAINT THOMAS

To his most beloved lord and father, Henry, by God’s grace Abbot of Crowland, his Roger, humble monk of the same place: that which is due to a lord and father.

The holy Church venerates the glorious [Col. 0259B] triumph of the glorious martyr of Christ, Thomas, all the more specially because she recalls that through his blood she herself won a more noble triumph. For, saving the peace of all the saints, from the time of the apostles no greater or more useful victory has been granted to Christ’s Church through the death of one man. Although he appeared to be defending only the English Church, it is proved by the outcome that he acted for the cause of the universal Church.

For, once she enlarged the place of her tent and the city of God, of which glorious things were spoken, was established in the pride of the ages, envy followed glory; and secular power, like another Ishmael, began now openly, now secretly, to oppress her members. Hence arose that old and inveterate [Col. 0259C] dispute between kingship and priesthood concerning investiture; hence the other controversies, too lengthy to enumerate, all or almost all of which were either quelled or settled in the martyrdom of this new Zechariah.

Therefore, although this saint’s cause, truly worthy of God, shines sufficiently by itself, like a lamp set upon a lampstand for all who are in the house, many nevertheless endeavoured, as though adding oil to its flame, to make it brighter through their writings. The talents of many great men laboured in this work, so that they might faithfully commit to the memory of posterity what they had seen and heard, leaving volumes full of faith and worthy of record concerning the man’s life, character, exile, and martyrdom.

Your prudent and vigilant discernment, observing this, and wishing to prevent anything discordant being found or criticized in various authors writing on the same subject—or anything wearisome through prolixity or repetition—long ago, out of a special devotion to the martyr, caused a concise selection to be made from various volumes by different authors, and a certain sweet and agreeable blend to be composed. [Col. 0259D] In it all that is most elegant in them all has been gathered into one body, so that nothing is subtracted from historical truth, while due provision is nevertheless made for brevity.

But because there remained letters written by the man of God himself, or to him, or concerning him, by authoritative persons, your wisdom perceived that, if these were inserted in suitable places within the aforementioned compendium, this would henceforth provide much authority for the history and no small benefit to its readers. It pleased you to lay this task upon my insignificance. Receiving it reverently out of reverence for him who imposed it, I have completed it as best I could; and, having completed it, I submit it to the examination of your discernment, so that, if anything in this part has been done praiseworthily, it may be yours, since you commanded it; but if otherwise—as I fear—it may be attributed to my imperfection.

In this matter I would warn, and let the kindly reader be warned, that should he encounter letters that are not complete but cut short or perhaps interrupted, he should know that this has been done deliberately. For when the text of a letter included several matters, the rest was omitted and only those sections were selected which seemed to bear upon the matter then at hand. Yet because the insertion of so many letters could not fail to produce prolixity, the work itself is divided, for the reader’s refreshment, so that he may have somewhere to catch his breath at intervals, into seven books according to the course of the affair. [Col. 0260B]

The first contains the character and deeds of the blessed man up to his exile. The seventh, which is also the last, relates his return and what was done after his exile. The intervening books contain whatever occurred during the period that he spent in exile, namely six years and one month. Since in your compendium you touched upon this entire period briefly for the sake of brevity, necessity has compelled me here to add some matters omitted there, and to alter certain things otherwise arranged there, so that the sequence of events may be explained. Thus the first, second, and last books explain the events more fully by historical narrative. In the others history is less laborious, because letters frequently intervene.

And since your compendium bears the author’s name written above in the margin beside each item of events, it pleased me to preserve the same practice in the present work, so that, should any question arise, trust may rest with the authors. There were five: Master John of Salisbury, later Bishop of Chartres; Alan of Tewkesbury; William, subprior of Canterbury; Benedict, Abbot of Burgh; and Master Herbert of Bosham, who, after all the others, adding what others had omitted, testified in truthful style to what he saw and heard. [Col. 0260C]

Therefore let trust be given to these men; let them speak with the letters inserted. Nothing of my own will intervene, except perhaps where necessity compels the addition of some brief material for continuity or for the insertion of letters. That first compilation was made at Crowland through your urging prayers and cooperative assistance in the final year of King Richard; and this addition to the same compilation was likewise made at Crowland in the fourteenth year of the reign of King John, which was, according to Dionysius, the year 1213 from the Incarnation of the Lord. [Col. 0260D]

[Two or three leaves are missing here in the Paris manuscript. Everything that remains appears to agree sufficiently with Lupus’s Quadrilogue; therefore I have excerpted from this book only four chapters, together with the conclusion of the work, which do not agree with the aforementioned Quadrilogue.]

In place of Chapter XI, the following material is found.

Thus the archbishop came to the lord pope at Sens. Although he was received coolly by the cardinals, he was admitted into [Col. 0261A] the presence of the lord pope, who received him as he approached with fatherly kindness, compassionating him in a fatherly way over his many troubles and his journey, so perilous and difficult. After some days, however, it pleased the archbishop, on his own counsel and that of his companions, to set before the lord pope and the cardinals the cause of the entire dispute between the king and himself in England, and the reason for his departure from the land.

Yet the lord pope had not at that point asked this of him, perhaps waiting for the archbishop, as a prudent man, to do so without being asked. The archbishop therefore chose this course. For although the origin and cause of the whole evil had previously been made known through his own messengers, and reported piecemeal by others travelling here and there, it nevertheless seemed more advisable that he himself should lay out the merits of his case, recount the truth of the events, [Col. 0261B] and personally efface the accusations which the aforesaid messengers of the king of England had tried to impress upon him.

Accordingly, some days after his arrival at the curia, with the lord pope and venerable cardinal-lords present—not publicly in consistory, but more privately in a chamber—he narrated the matter with a pleasing and concise brevity: pleasing, I say, because his eloquence was modest and elegant and his speech ever faultless. And while he sat first before the lord pope and wished to rise out of reverence, he was ordered to remain seated and speak. He then delivered his speech and produced a written document, etc.

Between Chapters XI and XII the following is inserted.

## HOW HE SATISFIED THE WISE MEN OF THE CURIA WHEN THEY REPROACHED HIM FOR HIS ACTIONS

[Col. 0261C]

But on the next day the archbishop was reproached, with a certain kindly and friendly severity, by some of the cardinals and by very many other great and learned men of the curia, powerful in the Scriptures—for the curia was accustomed to abound and flourish in such persons—as though by his friends and supporters. They reproached him because, in those evil days, namely at the time of schism and amid the Church’s ruins, he had risen against his prince, against so great a power. They said that he ought rather to yield to the times and endure, since it was then the hour and the power of darkness, when Peter was commanded not to draw his sword but to put it back.

And, as they added, the tares sown by the enemy among the grain were not then to be gathered by the Gospel servants, lest perhaps, in uprooting them, they uproot the wheat as well. Therefore, according to the householder’s command, both are allowed to grow together until the time of [harvest]. [Col. 0261D] This is also the counsel of the Teacher himself, who urges that time be redeemed because of the evil of the days: “Redeeming the time,” he says, “because the days are evil.” Likewise the prophet: “Therefore,” he says, “the prudent shall keep silence at that time, because it is an evil time.”

Having heard these and similar arguments, the archbishop, who as a prudent man had expected that such objections would be raised against him at the curia by its great and wise men—and had therefore discussed this with his companions and already prepared his words for judgment—immediately answered the objections prudently according to the wisdom and grace given him, and sufficiently satisfied those who objected.

[Col. 0262A] What follows concerns the conversation which Saint Thomas subsequently had with the pope, and his residence among the monks of Pontigny.

When the archbishop had decided to withdraw to some monastery of the Cistercian order, he chose Pontigny in Burgundy among the others, because it was near the aforesaid city of Sens, where the lord pope was then residing because of the schism, only twelve leagues away; and also because the resources of the monastery were ample and abundant and its generosity in giving was great. Therefore, at his request, the lord pope summoned the abbot of that place and the leading brethren and commended to them the man of God, Thomas, to be cared for. They gave thanks to God, both from the lord pope’s report and from the fame of the man’s renowned virtue, because, by God’s inspiration, his champion had chosen such a place as a kind of training-ground for his contest. [Col. 0262B]

After he had spent about three weeks at the curia, he set out for Pontigny with apostolic leave and blessing. He was received by the entire community with such eagerness and delight as they could scarcely have lavished upon a heavenly victim sent from above. They showed every kindness to him and his companions and, apart from the rule of their order, willingly and readily allowed them meat and certain other things. Indeed, the kindness and humanity of the order toward them appeared greater than can now be told.
