Therefore, on the third or fourth day after his arrival, he entered the chapter-house and commended to God and to their prayers the cause of the Church which he was pursuing.

The fourth excerpt concerns the king’s anger.

## HOW THE KING BECAME ENRAGED BOTH AGAINST THE POPE HIMSELF AND AGAINST SAINT THOMAS

[Col. 0262C]

But while the archbishop and his companions were being instructed and exercised at Pontigny in great peace and leisure, behold, after some days there came from England an ominous rumour, bearer of harsh news. For when the king of England learned from those returning that all his petitions against the archbishop had been rejected, and discovered that his adversary, as he called him, was not only supported but received by the Apostolic See, he first became violently enraged against the lord pope, then against the archbishop; and against each, so far as he could, he gave vent to his wrath and exercised vengeance. By royal command he ordered that Saint Peter’s penny [Col. 0262D] throughout England be paid into the treasury; that all the possessions of the archbishop and his followers be confiscated; and that all his kindred, together with all who were connected with him by household association or by any title whatsoever, be sentenced to exile, as his letters testify. [See the letters written on this matter.]

Thus these and those persons were expelled and proscribed: kindred and acquaintances alike, rich and poor together, wise and foolish, men and women, young men and maidens, old people with the younger, little children in cradles and infants hanging at their mothers’ breasts. The hostile fury proceeded yet further, to a cruelty horrible to pious ears. For since prayer was offered daily in church for their exiled archbishop, a public edict prohibited any further prayer for him—prayer which the Church was accustomed to offer even for heretics, schismatics, [Col. 0263A] and faithless Jews.

A certain courtly retainer was appointed to carry out all these measures and this penal enforcement, solely because of his bitter hatred for the archbishop—a man who had long hated the archbishop with inveterate hatred. Such a man was selected to execute this malicious undertaking so that the archbishop might be still more deeply afflicted, and because there was every confidence that he would pass over none of these punitive commands. This was Ranulf, surnamed de Broc, who is also believed to have added something of his own beyond the command, adding pain upon pain.

## CONCLUSION OF THE WORK

But, to return to the martyr: following the example of princes, young men and maidens, old people with the young, flocked to the tomb of this our new martyr, [Col. 0263B] including, among others and before others, those who for whatever reason had disagreed with him while he was still alive. Every day you might see fulfilled that prophetic saying: “Those who spoke against you shall come to you and worship the footsteps of your feet.” Whoever could obtain either some of his blood [Col. 0264A] or a memorial object from his garments considered himself fortunate.

At first the monks distributed to those who came blood mixed with water; but when this could not suffice for the multitude, water sanctified by contact with his relics was carried through the whole world in pewter flasks. It became, as it were, the distinguishing mark of pilgrims of blessed Thomas that each should carry away his own flask. Chapels were established; altars were raised; so that you could scarcely find even beyond the sea a city or town that did not preserve a memorial of blessed Thomas. For in England there were almost as many altars erected in his honour as there were churches.

The working of miracles seemed to follow the martyr’s memorial, so that the sick were now cleansed not only at the place of his passion, whether from demons or various [Col. 0264B] illnesses, but everywhere that his relics were kept or his feet had stood—since he who is wonderful in his saints was plainly working wonders for the glory of his saint. To him be honour and glory, praise and dominion, through all ages of ages. Amen.

Pious servant of God, remember me.

[Col. 0263]

# THE NINTH LIFE OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY AND MARTYR

By an anonymous author who calls himself the tenth.

[Col. 0263C] Jesus Christ, the same yesterday and today, abiding for ever, has in our days revealed to mortals things unknown since the first beginning in profound darkness: things hidden even beneath the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy-seat—indeed, even to the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge. For “God,” he says, “has revealed them to us through the Holy Spirit,” while the hidden manna, the wild honey, the abundance of his sweetness, namely the kindness and humanity of our Saviour, gradually and, as it were, step by step become known to the world. These things are shown to have existed from the beginning through the oracles of the prophets, and in the end through the constancy and miracles of martyrs—not sophistical or phantasmal miracles, as many unbelievers have thought.

Falsehood was once found in heaven; after this, truth sprang up for us from [Col. 0263D] the earth—the truth which is Christ. Finally, when Christ suffered in the flesh, the veil of the temple was torn, the mysteries were revealed; and when blessed Thomas was perfected by martyrdom, the alabaster vessel was broken and the house of God—that is, the Catholic Church—was filled with the fragrance of the ointment. O ointment upon the head, descending [Col. 0264C] from Christ to Thomas, upon the beard, the beard of Aaron! Behold a great priest from a barbarous people. Behold a true Israelite, the honour and glory of his age and people, from the regions of the North, so that the West may enlighten the whole East.

For this reason I have thought it worthwhile to unite into one history the various, though not conflicting, volumes written about him, restrained with such moderation that it may contain neither wasteful abundance nor harmful over-refinement, so that at least its very variety may relieve the readers’ weariness until one previously wearied becomes diligent. For in this way, we read in Cicero, a sculptor fashioned a statue of singular beauty, devised from the different forms of several maidens. Saint Hilary, too, produced a little book on synods, interweaving from varied talents whatever was best: not, as he himself says, the author of the work, but its arranger. So also that compiler of the Tripartite History: “We gather,” he says, “the choicest flowers from each of the authors.”

May the Spirit of truth inspire us for the commendation of God’s grace—he without whom the mind conceives nothing lofty—so that the discourse which we undertake with pious intention according to our powers may proceed in purity and full faith. It is most certain that constancy in truth belongs to those whom we have imitated, among whom the right hand excels which was cut off while its arm was sacrificed before the martyr, and which left us these things to transcribe. As a boy, I saw the man as an old man. Therefore this little book does no injury to those who wish and are able to read the works of the earlier writers, according as each arranged his own treatise.

Their concern was to arrange, and thereby embellish, the narrative, omitting some suitable material. But I have thought it worthwhile simply to weave together the truth of the history and thus to repeat things omitted by others, since in Luke’s account of the Acts there are certain sections concerning the deeds and words of the Lord untouched by the rest, which are most powerful bulwarks of our faith. But since it is difficult to follow another’s lines without at some point exceeding them, if it happens here also that I stray slightly from the sequence of narration, ignorance of fault will grant pardon. Yet because, as Pliny says, it is full of honourable modesty to confess through whom one has accomplished one’s work, I think that the chief authors of this work should be briefly enumerated in the preface. [Col. 0265B]

First in rank, because he was a bishop, is John of Chartres; second is Herbert of Bosham, likewise a distinguished teacher. Next is Edward, surnamed Grim, whose arm, as we have said, was mutilated at the martyr’s sacrifice. And fourth, likewise, is another Edward of the same name. Also eminent for life and learning are Benedict and Alan, both abbots, [Col. 0265C] and their abridger, the Abbot of Clairvaux. The monks are William and Roger: the former of Canterbury, the latter of Pontigny, minister at Pontigny to the holy man exiled for Christ. Not to trust these men is to be unbelieving.

After these, I, the tenth gleaner, have gathered clusters and fallen grains, so that something like a sluggish ointment may be made from myrrh and aloe, and that Ruth the Moabitess may have, in the vinegar of Christ’s sufferings, where to dip her morsel—from the letters of the blessed martyr himself, extracting, like a bee from little flowers, honey sweeter in its sweetness than Attic honey. We have thought those letters should be inserted in suitable places throughout the history, so that he who performed what he commanded may be crowned also by his writings, and so that every order, rank, and condition may borrow from him: from one place what to imitate, from another what to admire, since he is wonderful in each matter, singular in his wonders. [Col. 0266A]

Those for whom the world was not worthy must be restored to the world through the remedy of writing; and the contests of blessed martyrs must be heard more attentively, so that we, who drink Christ’s cup, may, when the opportunity happily arises, be prepared to shed our blood for Christ.

[After much similar material, which we have omitted, the prologue ends with the following words.]

To this is added that I was asked to write by the distinguished man, namely Abbot Giles of Alna in the territory of Liège. He proposed this plan of composition to me: requesting that, by noting the author’s name in the margin, I should indicate who narrates this thing and who that, and that a marginal annotation opposite should name the author wherever each writer claims from the common work something distinctive to himself, [Col. 0266B] especially where more excellent matters are treated.

Therefore, what I have received as not to be concealed, after investigating with the greatest diligence the libraries of the French, Flemings, English, Britons, Scots, and Irish dwelling beneath the setting sun, I communicate to all: to the glory of the holy martyr, to the reader’s favour, and to my own pardon. We believe that there is nothing here which does not profit or delight. Accordingly, so that it may adhere more easily to memory, we have divided the entire work, marked with definite numbers beforehand, into eighteen chapters, recording nearly all those distinguished men only who before us applied their pen to this subject, and whose works it has been granted to us to examine.

Finally, we have refrained from inserting our own person more expressly in these pages for posterity to know, since shortly, as Ecclesiastes says, it will be erased among the anonymous by oblivion. We feared Jeremiah’s saying: “Those who depart from you shall be written in the earth,” because they are less concerned to be numbered in the book of life, provided they attain what they desire—that is, to be called Rabbi—when the will alone is guilty, God saying: “Do not be lifted up on high.” [Col. 0266C] But let these remarks, though extended yet not superfluous, suffice by way of preface. Virtue consecrated by public religion has no need of private commendation: its light and praise are evident, its fame unsetting, although it is beneath the West.

[After this begins the treatise on the Life of Saint Thomas, which, since it appears to have been compiled from other writers, we have omitted.]

[Col. 0267]

# THE TENTH LIFE OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY AND MARTYR

By Benedict, Abbot of Peterborough.

(Only fragments of this treatise survive, published by Lupus in the second *Quadrilogue*.)

[Col. 0267A]

**Fragment 1. How the knights approached the archbishop and confronted him.** On the fifth day after the Nativity of the Lord, while the archbishop was sitting in his chamber about the eleventh hour of the day, with some clerics and monks seated on either side and discussing business and matters of benefit with him, behold, the four previously named attendants, having gone out from the face of the Lord with their father Satan, entered the archbishop’s chamber. Some of those seated at the entrance greeted them, as is customary; they returned the greeting, but in subdued voices, and proceeded to the archbishop.

Sitting upon the ground before his feet, they greeted him neither in their own name nor in the king’s, as men from whom salvation was far away and death and destruction near at hand. For a short while they restrained in silence the venom of asps which they bore beneath their lips, so that it might afterward burst forth more violently, while the most innocent Christ of the Lord likewise kept silence. [Col. 0267B]

When they had passed a short interval in this silence, not without the amazement of those sitting by, Reginald fitz Urse—bearish rather in mind than by lineage—addressed the saint thus: “Sent to you by our lord king from the regions beyond the sea, we bring you the king’s commands. We wish, therefore, to know whether you prefer them to be spoken privately or publicly.”

But the man of God, neither hoping for worldly prosperity nor fearing adversity, answered in a plain and submissive voice: “I leave this to your judgment and your will.”

Reginald said: “Then let them be spoken more privately, while those now present withdraw.”

The saint, trusting neither in the number of his followers nor fearing solitude, commanded all his people to depart. When they had left and only the four attendants remained in the chamber with the archbishop, the doorkeeper hurried up and left the door open, so that those who had now seated themselves outside might turn their eyes toward their lord, the anointed of the Lord, and behold both him and those enemies of God.

When the aforesaid Reginald had set forth certain royal commands, and the most prudent man of God had perceived more clearly than light that they offered no appearance either of peace [Col. 0268A] or of any good, recalling also, as an omen of the future, that Gospel saying, “Jesus did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all men,” he summoned the doorkeeper and ordered both his clerics and whatever monks might be present to attend, excluding all laypeople. When they entered, the saint said to the attendants: “Behold, lords, in the presence of these men you may say whatever pleases your will.”

Reginald answered: “Since you have chosen that these matters should rather come into public view than be kept secret, we likewise, satisfying your wish in this regard, shall make them public in the presence of these men. We bring you a command from the lord king, who is dwelling in the regions beyond the sea: that you go to his son, the new king on this side of the sea, and render him what you ought to render to a lord and king.”

The saint said: “And what is it that I ought to render him?”

Reginald replied: “That ought to have come to your knowledge rather than ours.”

He said: “If I knew it, I certainly would by no means say that I did not know it. But I believe that I have altogether done whatever I owe him.”

Reginald answered: “Not at all. Many things still remain to be done, many things to be corrected.”

When the archbishop maintained that he did not know what he ought to amend with respect to the royal majesty, unless their goodwill—which indeed was nonexistent—would tell him, Reginald said: “Since you confess yourself wholly ignorant in this matter, we shall explain to you what you ought to do. Our lord king commands you to go as quickly as possible to his son the king, who is residing in the lands on this side of the sea, to swear fealty to him under oath [Col. 0268C] and to make amends for what you have committed against the royal majesty.”

The man of God answered and said: “On what grounds do I owe him a confirmation of fealty by touching the sacred things? Or in what respect have I become guilty of an offence against the royal majesty?”

The attendant, omitting the latter part of the question, which he could not answer at all, thus resolved the first: “Fealty confirmed by oath is demanded of you for the barony which you hold from my lord king. And an oath of security is likewise demanded concerning the clerics whom you brought into his land, if they wish to remain in his land.”

The archbishop replied: “With regard to the barony, I am prepared to do for my lord king whatever law or reason may prescribe. But, all ambiguity removed, let him know for certain that no oath can be extorted either from me or from any of my clerics. Too many things have been extorted beyond measure, and now, as perjurers and excommunicates, they plainly seem to be going too far. But already, thanks be to God, I have absolved very many, bound both by the crime of perjury and by the bond of anathema; and, when the Lord grants it, I shall deliver the rest from the same dangers.” [Col. 0269A]

Reginald said: “We understand that you will do none of the things which we have proposed to you. Moreover, the lord king commands that you absolve his bishops, whom you have excommunicated or suspended without his permission, both from the sentence of condemnation and from that of silence; and that, both concerning these matters and concerning others which he may wish to allege against you, you submit to judgment.” [Col. 0269B]

And the archbishop said: “I neither suspended nor anathematized the bishops; rather, our lord the pope did so, to whom authority is known to have been granted by the Lord. If you wish to reopen the case on these matters, let the case be conducted between yourselves and him. It is no concern of mine to answer you about them.”

Reginald said: “Even if you did not do it in your own person, it was nevertheless done through you and at your instigation.”

And the Saint said: “If the lord pope, taking notice of the excessive wrong unjustly inflicted upon my church, has exacted vengeance, I confess that it does not displease me.”

But the son of impiety, who up to this point had exerted all his strength, speaking craftily in the hope of trapping the most prudent Lamb of God in speech, or of turning him from the straight path of righteousness in matters concerning the honour of God and of the Church—of which he was an invincible defender—, when he saw that he had cast his net in vain before the eyes of the winged creature, assailed him with abusive accusations, saying: “By clear evidence you show that it pleases you that, to the dishonour and contempt of royal majesty, his bishops should be driven from their episcopal sees and shut out from the thresholds of holy mother Church, because they dared to crown our lord the new king—whose inheritance belongs to him by right, being the son of a king and queen and bearing also the sign of empire upon his shoulder. And since you have dared to rise against the king upon this exaltation of his, it is quite credible and exceedingly probable that you wish to steal away his crown and, having seized the kingdom, to be called and be king of the land. But, God permitting, you shall by no means advance as far as the title of royal dignity.”

The Saint, however, mindful of the saying: “An angry man stirs up quarrels, but a wise man calms those that have been stirred,” applied the medicine of a gentle answer to the bitter mind of the knight, saying: “By no means, Reginald, by no means do I aspire to the name or dignity of king, nor do I desire to tear his crown away from him. Rather, if my resources answered to my wish, I would gladly place three or four such crowns upon him. Nor do I think that anyone exists in the world, except his father alone, my lord the king, who loves him more tenderly than I do or wishes him more good. And this, if life remains and the Lord permits, I shall prove to him by my deeds. Moreover, concerning the bishops whom you maintain were suspended or excommunicated by me or through me, let your discernment know for certain that whatever was done was done by royal consent and counsel. For when, on the feast of blessed Mary Magdalene, peace between us had been restored and I had been received again into former favour, and when I laid before him my complaint concerning the injuries and violence inflicted upon me and mine—especially concerning the bishops, who, in contempt of their mother the Church of Canterbury, did not fear to usurp what belonged to my office—he graciously permitted me to seek from the lord pope whatever redress of right and equity I could obtain; so much so that he deigned not only to incline to consent, but even to promise me assistance.”

Reginald cried out, as devoid of courtly wit as he was full of rage: “Do you hear what you are saying? It is unparalleled and unheard-of treason that the lord king should have granted you leave to excommunicate or suspend his bishops, who attended, at his command, the coronation of his son. Such a thing never entered his mind. Know yourself to be the author of immense evil, since you accuse our lord the king of such treason.”

The archbishop said: “Reginald, Reginald, I do not accuse the king of treason. Yet the reconciliation between us and the agreements held between us were by no means made so secretly that archbishops, bishops, many eminent men, many exceedingly religious men, and even five hundred knights or more were not present at them and did not hear them. You yourself also, Lord Reginald, were present.”

The enemy of truth replied and said: “Truly, I was neither present there, nor did I see or hear these things.”

But the Saint, most restrained both in word and voice, affirming gently and plainly, said: “Indeed, God knows; for I am certain that I saw you there.”

But he again denied, under oath, that he had been there, and perjuring himself said: “It is strange and unheard of that you should fasten the charge of such treason upon our lord the king. He cannot endure this from you in any way, nor shall we, who are his faithful men, endure it any longer.”

Then the other knights also shouted, bursting into the same threats and swearing again and again by the wounds of God that they had endured him beyond measure. Thus the foolish were troubled in heart and spoke iniquity on high [Col. 0270D]; they heaped insult upon insult and threat upon threat.

But the man of God, who had come not merely to suffer threats and insults but gladly to expose even his head to swords for the defence of the Church’s liberty, in accordance with the saying of the moral poet,

> While fury is in full course, yield to the rushing fury,

answered more gently: “Since I came into these lands under God’s and the king’s full peace, by the king’s own safe-conduct, I have endured very many threats, reproaches, and losses. For example: my men have been captured and their goods violently taken away; Robert de Broc mutilated the tails of my horses; Ranulf de Broc violently detained my wines, which the lord king caused to be conveyed through the midst of his lands beyond the sea into England. I have also suffered many other injuries and insults, although our lord the king commanded and ordered his son the king, both by writs and by the spoken messages of envoys, that firm peace should be kept for me and mine. And in addition to all this you have come to threaten me. Know that I bear such things with great distress.”

Reginald said to this: “If anyone perhaps presumed to do something that seemed to redound to your injury, why did you not set it forth and obtain whatever right or reason prescribed?”

The archbishop said: “Before whom was I to lay my complaint?”

And the knight said: “Before the king on this side of the sea.”

The archbishop said: “Friend, I have complained enough; I have sufficiently set out the injuries inflicted upon me; I have laboured enough, and in vain, to obtain satisfaction. Moreover, injuries are daily heaped upon me in such number; I am afflicted by so many and such grievous evils; the complaints of my poor men ring in my ears by night as well as day in such number that I cannot find a messenger for every individual need. And even though I state my injuries, the benefit of right and reason will be denied me. For the king on this side of the sea and his justices, depending upon the counsel of the lord king residing in the lands beyond the sea, do nothing in his absence and without his advice. The benefit of justice and equity is denied to me, and my people are denied the opportunity of crossing the sea and approaching the king. Thus I am treated exceedingly badly. But since I find no right or justice either here or there, I shall exercise such authority as an archbishop can and ought to exercise; I shall not abandon it for any mortal man.”

At this declaration one of them cried out: “Threats, threats! Will you even subject the whole land to an interdict and excommunicate us all?”

And another said: “So may God be merciful to me, he shall not accomplish it. He has cast far too many into the bonds of anathema.”

As they leapt about, gave rein to anger and insults, twisted their gloves, flung their arms about furiously, and showed plain signs of madness both by bodily gestures and by the violence of their shouting, the archbishop too rose. Indeed, amid the excess of tumult and confusion, no one could readily distinguish what poisonous words each of them was pouring out against the Anointed of the Lord.

At length the sons of Belial turned to the monks who happened to be present and, though in vain, tried to arm them against their own father and the father of the whole country in these words: “On the king’s behalf, we command you diligently to guard this man, lest he go anywhere, so that you may present him again to the king when it pleases him.”

When they repeated this demand again and again, the pious father answered on behalf of his sons: “What is this? Do you think that I wish to slip away in flight? I shall not flee for the king or for any living person. I did not come in order to flee, but to await the frenzy of those who rage and the malice of the impious.”

“Truly,” said the knights, “truly, God willing, you shall not escape.”

This utterance was not prompted in the most holy man by pride swollen in contempt of the king, but by constancy founded upon Christ and perfected as an example of virtue. Accordingly, while they departed amid great uproar and insults, making many threats, the archbishop followed them as far as the chamber door, calling out to Hugh de Morville—who ought to have surpassed the rest both in nobility of birth and in soundness of judgment—to return and speak with him. But he and the others, being now unable to contain themselves in their rage, went away in pride and indignation. The man of God returned, sat down, and complained before his own people of such commands of the king and insulting words of the knights.

One of his clerks, namely Master John of Salisbury, a man of extensive learning, great eloquence, and profound judgment, and, greater than these, grounded in the fear and love of God [Col. 0272B], gave this answer to his complaint: “My lord, it is a most astonishing thing that you admit no one’s counsel. What necessity was there for a man of such high rank to rise, further inflaming those wicked men, and to go after them as far as the door? Would it not have been better, after consulting those who are present, to give a milder answer to men who devise every evil they can against you and seek to provoke you to anger, so that they may at least catch you in speech?”

But the Saint, who longed for the straits of death on behalf of justice and the liberty of the Church as for the delights of rest, said: “All counsel has already been taken. I know well enough what I must do.”

And Master John said: “Would that, God permitting, it may be good!”

The profane knights therefore went out, hurried to their companions and accomplices in the court, armed themselves more quickly, and returned in mail shirts, with swords and axes, bows and arrows, double-edged axes, and other instruments, either to demolish locks and doors or to carry their planned crime into effect. Some ran ahead and shouted to the archbishop: “Lord, lord, they are arming themselves.”

But he said: “What concern is that? Let them arm.”

Among that detestable fellowship of destruction was that son of perdition, Robert de Broc, whom, as we have said, the holy man had cut off from the communion of the faithful, having anathematized him at Christmas because of the enormity of his crimes. He knew every entrance and exit of the court, since, while the archbishop was in exile, he had held the custody of the whole archbishopric under his lord Ranulf de Broc. Thus, when they hastened to seize the door of the hall, the servants, taking precautions, shut them out. When entrance had been altogether denied them by the closed door and bars placed against it, under the guidance of the aforesaid Robert they quickly turned aside to more secret steps, by which there was a descent from the outer chamber into the garden; after demolishing a nearby window, they also unfastened the door.

When servants running ahead shouted from every side to the most steadfast athlete of God that he should flee, he to whom nothing was more contemptible than fearing death for Christ was moved neither in place nor in spirit. Though clerks and monks alike pressed him and urgently urged him to flee, he nevertheless sat fearless, not knowing how, with those who believe only for a time, to withdraw in time of temptation. But the few monks who happened to be present broke the fastening of the door leading through the cloister to the church and strove to lead out their father, although he was unwilling, offering him a more honourable reason for leaving: namely, that it was the hour when he ought to perform evening praises in the church.

Then the Saint, not forgetting even in the literal sense the Lord’s command, “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me,” ordered a cross to be carried before him. When he went out and those passing by urged him to hurry, he stopped his pace, as though ashamed of flight. Yet the monks continued to press him urgently to proceed; either because he was acting with less reverence than usual, or in order to strengthen and console his own people, he repeatedly said to them: “What is this, lords? What are you afraid of?”

When they had approached the cloister door and could neither break it open nor find the key at hand, behold, two cellarers of the Church of Canterbury, Richard and William, who, hearing the tumult and clash of arms, were hurrying there along the cloister passage, tore off the bar and opened that door for the approaching archbishop.

**FRAGMENT 2. On the archbishop’s entry into the church.**

On hearing of the armed men’s approach, some of the brethren still remained in prayer, while others, in fear, sought hiding places. As some were coming to help, one of the brethren went out, saying: “Enter, father, enter; remain with us, so that, if necessary, we may suffer and be glorified together. May your presence comfort us, who are disheartened by your absence.”

He replied: “Go and fulfil the appointed duty of divine service.”

Then, pausing at the door, he said: “So long as you hold the entrance, I shall not enter.”

When they gave way, he entered the monastery and stood upon the threshold. Driving back the laypeople crowded about him as though for a spectacle, he said: “What does this people fear?”

The answer was given: “Armed men are in the cloister.”

“I am going out to them,” he said.

But when the brethren prevented him from going out, he began to be watched at the threshold; and though he was urged to proceed and retire into the Holy of Holies, so that reverence for the place might protect him, he would not consent.

Meanwhile, as the clerks were in tumult and some brethren were drawing a great iron bar across, he said: “Go away, faint-hearted men; let the wretched and blind rave. We command you by virtue of obedience not to shut the door; for it is not fitting that a church should be turned into a castle.”

Leaving Vespers unfinished, some monks ran up and, though their shepherd resisted, led him in, hastening to shut the church doors and exclude the enemies. But the holy father immediately returned and sharply rebuked them, saying: “Let my people enter.”

He ran to open the door; moving both his people and the others away from the doors, he drew into the church with his most holy hands those of his own who had been left outside to the teeth of wolves, saying: “Enter, enter quickly,” so that he might say with the Lord: “Of those whom you gave me, I lost none of them.”

At length, forcibly drawn away from there by the entreaties of his sons, and with the enemies now close at hand, he left the doors open, lest their path being blocked, his martyrdom should be impeded—a martyrdom by which he knew, and had foretold, that he would be blessed. For while he was still in the lands beyond the sea, he had plainly foretold to two abbots, those of Pontigny and of Vauclair, as we stated above, that he would suffer martyrdom and be killed in a church. He had also foretold to each that he would go to England, not so much because of the lord pope’s command as because of the revelation of his martyrdom.

**FRAGMENT 3.**

And although the man of God could readily have avoided that hour of death, had he wished, when the aforesaid knights and others entered the monastery, some shouting, “Where is that traitor?” and others, “Where is the archbishop?”, the Saint, knowing in the Spirit all that was to come upon him, went to meet them from the steps, some of which they had already mounted. With fearless countenance he said: “Here I am—not a traitor, but archbishop,” imitating, that is, the Lord, who went out to meet the Jews seeking him and said: “I am he.”

The first of them to approach said to the Saint: “Flee; you are a dead man!”

The Saint said: “I shall not flee.”

Then the sacrilegious knight laid his hand upon him, knocked off his cap with the point of his sword, and said: “Come here; you are taken.”

But the Saint said: “Here you shall do to me what you wish to do,” and shook the fold of his cloak from the man’s hand.

**FRAGMENT 4.**

Turning to another man in mail whom he saw approaching with drawn sword, he said: “What is this, Reginald? I have conferred many benefits upon you, and you come armed against me in church?”

Did he not seem by these words, as an imitator of Christ, to portray Christ saying to the Jews: “Have you come out with swords and clubs to seize me as though I were a robber?”

The knight, full of the spirit of fury, said to him: “You shall soon know; you are dead.”

**FRAGMENT 5.**

And, bowing his head, he awaited the coming of the second wound. When the second blow was inflicted upon his head, he fell to the ground with body upright, as though prostrating himself in prayer. The third, cutting off a very large portion of his skull, horribly enlarged the preceding wound. The fourth, rebuked by one of the others for being slow to strike, swung his sword into the same wound; and when the sword broke upon the marble pavement, he left in the church both its point and the hilt of his sword.

It might reasonably seem that this event signified something. For what does the breaking of the adversaries’ sword appear to signify except the true overthrow of hostile power and the victory of the Church, destined to triumph through the blood of the martyr? Nor did it seem enough to that son of Satan to have committed so great a crime against the priest of God, unless he also—horrible to tell—thrust his sword into the most holy head when he was already dead, drove out the brain, and most cruelly scattered it over the pavement, crying to his accomplices in the same crime: “He is dead; let us go quickly from here.”

It may be inferred that they feared lest some of the holy martyr’s knights or his lord’s servants should arrive and avenge his blood. As they left the monastery, they cried, as commonly happens in battle, in token of an illustrious victory: “The king’s men! The king’s men!” Others mocked, saying: “He wanted to be king; he wanted to be more than king. Let him now be king; let him now be king.”

In this they resembled those who mocked the Lord hanging upon the cross, passing by and shaking their heads, and saying among other things: “For he said, ‘I am the Son of God.’”

**FRAGMENT 6.**

What martyrdom ever possessed a more glorious title? For although individual martyrs, each pleading an individual cause, entered a singular contest for their own salvation, this man, undertaking the cause of the universal Church, contending against princes and tyrants and against the hirelings rather than shepherds of the holy Church, permitted the knights to win a triumph over his body in order that he might prevail. Men of another sect killed those martyrs; this man was killed by worshippers of Christ and his own children.

**FRAGMENT 7. On the spoils and garments which the knights divided among themselves.**

The workers of iniquity, no less tormented by thirst for greed than drunk with the shedding of innocent blood, hurried back with their accomplices to the archbishop’s palace. Some violently dragged horses from the stable; others beat his servants; others turned over all the household furnishings and packs, broke open chests, and divided among themselves as they pleased whatever gold or silver, garments, or various ornaments they found.

For it pleased divine mercy, which powerfully and wisely orders all things, that, becoming imitators of those who divided Christ’s garments, they should make the passion of the servant more fully resemble the passion of the Lord; so that by a manifest likeness of events all the faithful might understand that the Church was to be delivered from the world’s slavery by the blood of the martyr, just as it was redeemed from the devil’s power by Christ’s death.

Moreover, all the writings and privileges found by those malicious men were handed over to Ranulf de Broc, that son of perdition, for conveyance to the king in Normandy, so that whatever appeared contrary to the customs of his kingdom, or to support either the liberty of the universal Church or the dignities defended by the Church of Canterbury, he might at his pleasure either destroy or shut away, never again to be seen. Such were the deeds of the knights.

**FRAGMENT 8.**

When the holy body was lifted from the ground, there were found beneath it a small iron hammer and a double-edged axe left by those parricides, which he had fallen upon as though, in token, he was to become a hammer against evildoers and they could not escape the sentence of his vengeance wherever they turned, except to repentance.

Although blood lay pooled around his head like a diadem, perhaps as a sign of sanctity, his face appeared entirely free of blood, except for a narrow streak descending diagonally from the right side of the forehead across the bridge of the nose toward the left side of the face. [Col. 0276A] With this same mark he later appeared in visions to many people wholly ignorant of it; and they described it in their accounts no differently than if they had seen it with bodily eyes.

While he still lay on the pavement in blood, some anointed their eyes with it; others brought vessels and took away as much as they could; others competed in dipping pieces of cut cloth into it. No one thereafter thought himself sufficiently blessed unless he had carried away at least some small share of that precious treasure. In the universal disturbance and confusion, everyone was free to take what he pleased. But the portion of blood left to the church was most cleanly gathered into a very clean vessel and stored in the church for preservation.

His cloak and outer fur garment, as they were stained with blood, were bestowed upon the poor in a less than discerning act of piety for his soul. They would indeed have been very fortunate, had they not immediately and rashly preferred a small price to them by selling them.

**FRAGMENT 9.**

That night passed lamentably, in grief, groaning, and sighs; and, neither for a moment conscious of joy nor ignorant of sorrow, it brought the day, made more dreadful by greater malice.

**FRAGMENT 10. How the holy martyr’s body was brought for burial.**

On the next day, when once more a great force of armed men had assembled outside the city walls, a report spread everywhere that they had gathered with the purpose of a greater outrage: namely, to tear the holy martyr’s body from the bosom of holy mother Church by violence and either drag it through the entire city with horses, hang it from a gallows, or tear it into pieces or fragments and cast it into a marsh or some other still more contemptible place, unfit even to be named, in greater contempt of God and the Church. They said that the body of a traitor was not to be buried among the holy bishops.

The monks, fearing both for themselves and for the Saint—lest he should be treated still more disgracefully or they themselves lose the precious treasure—strove to bury him with the utmost haste. Thus they were not permitted either to wash his most sacred body or to anoint it with balm, as is the custom of the holy Church of Canterbury. This is believed to have happened not so much through human malice as through divine mercy. For what need had one for whom the Lord had provided the anointing of his own blood of the fragrance of a baser ointment?

When they removed his outer garments and clothed him in pontifical vestments, they found his body wrapped in a hair-shirt, made troublesome not less by its own roughness than by anything else. They also found—what we have neither read nor heard to have been exemplified in any saint—his inner hair-cloth breeches reaching to the knees, and, beneath the garment he wore, the monastic habit, namely a flamma [the garment-name is textually uncertain] and cowl. Looking at one another and amazed beyond belief at the sight of such hidden religious devotion, their material for pious grief was multiplied and they renewed their tears manifoldly.

What greed is to be imagined in this man, what treason? Did he aspire to an earthly kingdom when he is known to have preferred a hair-shirt so secretly to the pleasures of the world? Was he a traitor to royal majesty, rather than betrayed himself, who did not wish—even when he could—to kill or resist his own betrayers, those sons of treason?

For he could, had he wished, either prudently have avoided or by greater force repelled the hostile fraud and frenzy: as a powerful man, as one who knew beforehand, and as one forewarned. He was powerful because, even if his enemies had come tenfold in number, he could, had he wished, have repelled them with a force a hundredfold greater. He knew beforehand because, when on Christmas Day he had ministered the bread of God’s word to the people, he said among other things: “I returned from exile for no other reason than either to free them from the yoke of the servitude inflicted upon them, or to suffer the punishment of death among them and for them.” He had also, as stated above, mentioned his coming passion to abbots beyond the sea.

Moreover, as he was instructed concerning these things by divine mercy, so he was forewarned and prepared by human diligence. In this respect, although he is said to have gained merit by the goodwill of many, two cases are certainly established. A knight familiar with Richard, cellarer of the Church of Canterbury, assured him under pledge of faith that the same saint of God would not see the evening of the third day. Yet, contrary to the pledge by which he had been bound to those murderers in the killing of their father, he preferred to incur whatever danger there was in violating his pledge to them rather than conceal the guilt of so detestable a murder.

When the aforesaid Richard reported this to that most blessed servant of God, he smiled and replied: “They are threats.”

But, having been more certainly informed by a citizen of Canterbury named Reginald that those who had conspired to kill him had already landed in England, he wept bitterly, whether for the destruction of their wickedness or for the Church’s peace not yet attained, and said: “They will find me prepared for death. Let them do what they wish. I know, my son, and am certain that I shall die by weapons. Nevertheless, they shall not kill me outside my church.”

Do not these words prove that he knew beforehand not only his passion but also its manner and place? But because his kingdom was not of this world—for if it were, his servants would surely have fought so that he might not be delivered to them—he chose willingly and joyfully to drink the Lord’s cup rather than stain the strength of his former constancy by cowardly flight or summon to arms those who would fight in his defence. In this he imitated him who would not call upon the twelve legions of angels which he could have requested from his Father for his own defence. Nor do we readily believe that the passion of any martyr can be found which appears to correspond to the Lord’s Passion with such close resemblance.

**FRAGMENT 11.**

The outstanding athlete of God, Thomas, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, primate of all England, and legate of the Apostolic See, suffered martyrdom in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1170, in the fifty-third year of his life, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January [29 December], on Tuesday, at about the eleventh hour; so that the fifth day after the Lord’s Nativity became for him a birthday into glory through misery. By the grace of the same Lord Jesus Christ, to whom with the Father and the Holy Spirit belong honour, power, and dominion through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

The foregoing, excerpted from Lupus’s *Quadrilogue*, bears the name of Benedict as author. Whether the materials which the compiler of this *Quadrilogue* appends under the title *On Events after the Martyrdom* have Benedict or another author, I do not know. I have published all of them below in this *Quadrilogue*, unless, as I strongly suspect, they are found in the work of Herbert of Bosham, a complete copy of which I hope will soon come into my hands.

[Col. 0277]

# PASSION OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY AND MARTYR, BY THE ANONYMOUS AUTHOR OF LAMBETH

Since many people shrink from prolixity and obscurity of discourse, an account of the martyrdom of the most holy Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, shall therefore be given in concise and simple language. It is known, God bearing witness, to have occurred in the presence of myself, who relate these things, and of very many others. And because to recount this suddenly, with no preface, would be like coming to table without washed hands, the preceding events of his life shall first be sampled.

Blessed is he who hears the words of this reading and keeps them as an incentive to martyrdom, that, should circumstances perhaps require it, he may be more ready to give his life, or at least suffer insult for the name of Jesus.

## I. HOW HE WAS BORN

[Col. 0278D]

Among the towns, villages, and cities of England, London is held to be the best and greatest. After it came under Norman rule, very many natives of Rouen and Caen, the more distinguished places of Normandy, moved there, choosing to become inhabitants of the city because it was better suited to and more abundantly supplied with the commerce they were accustomed to pursue.

Among them was a certain Gilbert, surnamed Becchet, a native of Rouen, well regarded among others for family, energy, and material means. He was indeed of honourable, though bourgeois, origin; industrious in commercial pursuits, he conducted his own household in a manner sufficiently distinguished for his station in life, living among his fellow citizens not merely without reproach but known also by the reputation of a good man.

He had a wife named Rose, a native of Caen, likewise of bourgeois birth no less respectable; she was comely in figure but more comely in character, a good head of her household, and faithfully obedient to her husband in the fear of God.

## II. THE OMEN OF HIS BIRTH

When she had conceived him, she found herself in a dream before the doors of the Church of Canterbury; as she seemed to advance to enter, she could scarcely get in because of the swelling bulk of her womb. This was indeed an omen of things to come. For she then bore within her a son whose future greatness was plainly foreshadowed by the enlargement of her womb.

Already great, though not yet born, he was being carried into the Church of Canterbury, because, illustrious in the royal court yet still to be brought forth for Christ’s service, he was to be raised to the pontifical chair of that church. He could scarcely be brought in because of his size, because, though many envious persons in the world longed intensely for his high advancement, he was at first scarcely to be promoted, afterward scarcely to be restored from exile, and finally to be added to the number of the Church’s saints through the narrow entrance of suffering. These matters become fuller and clearer from the sequence that follows.

## III. HIS EARLY UPBRINGING

[Col. 0279C]

Accordingly, in due time after the dream, this son of handsome appearance was born. By divine prompting his godfathers called him Thomas, so that he might not lack the name of the apostle whose apostolic life and end he was to have. Immediately after he was born, his parents dedicated him to the service of the Church’s militia; and when his infancy had passed, they entrusted him for instruction in the rudiments of letters.

Keen in intellect and retentive in memory, as he grew in years he advanced in learning. He could soon have equalled the better scholars had he pursued, with the speed with which he began learning, the course of things to be known. But once he had escaped his master’s discipline and become his own master, he gave himself, as the frivolity of youth commonly leads, to slippery pursuits. Neglecting serious studies, he clung to the frivolities of worldly occupations, devoted himself to the activities of fowlers and hunters, and embraced the vanities and trifles of courtiers.

Yet he was found to have done nothing shamefully notable in these pursuits. Avoiding the reproach of rusticity and seeking the renown of urbanity, he always strove to be held first even among the most polished men.

## IV. HOW HE BECAME ARCHDEACON OF CANTERBURY

The man whom divine grace had foreseen must be raised as a loftier pillar of the Church it at length turned toward bearing the yoke of ecclesiastical service. Since it was unfitting that the greater light destined for England should lie hidden beneath a bushel, grace brought him to serve in the more celebrated court of England.

For it caused him to be summoned into the household of Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury and primate of England, so that, as it were, by the practical experience of his life with him, he might learn to become the imitator of one whose successor he was to be. From that time, putting away many things that belonged to childhood, he strove to redeem the lapses of youth by mature manhood. Applying himself to the serious business of a court that dealt with great affairs, he soon employed his inborn diligence, proving in the conduct of his lord’s affairs both a prudent adviser and a vigorous executor.

Thus, increasingly gaining his lord’s intimacy, he obtained a place among the foremost of his assessors. As an indication of his great worth, he was gradually advanced through many ecclesiastical benefices and was eventually made archdeacon of Canterbury. Divine grace was again providing him a ladder and opportunity for ascent to the episcopate. For the higher and greater he became in his church, the nearer he came to assuming its governance.

## V. HOW HE BECAME THE KING’S CHANCELLOR
And since, for the accomplishment of this matter, the king’s assent could contribute most especially, it was providentially arranged, to make the path of advancement easier, that he should become one of the king’s confidential advisers. For not long afterwards, when King Stephen had died and Henry II, grandson of King Henry I, was raised to the kingship of England by hereditary right of succession, the aforesaid archdeacon obtained, above the other ecclesiastical persons of the realm, appointment as chancellor of the new king. [Col. 0280C] So great a prince was very fittingly served by such an envoy. For he was handsome in face and comely in appearance, discerning and ready in counsel, polished and fluent in speech, and reverend through a certain natural excellence of bearing. Indeed, he surpassed the other magnates of the court in the splendour of his magnificence as much as he excelled them in the singularity of his office. By these qualities he earned with the king the privilege of affection and, among his counsellors, primacy; daily advancing and growing until he became exceedingly great. For he directed all that belonged to the king, and the whole body of subjects attended to the command of his mouth.

## VI. HOW HE BECAME ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0280D]

Meanwhile Archbishop Theobald having been removed from human affairs, the king rejoiced that he had gained an opportunity to confer the vacant place of honour upon his beloved friend. Having tested his greatness of spirit and fidelity in many matters, he believed him fully equal to so lofty a station; but he also thought him one who would always be readily inclined to his own interests and, should untimely death cut short his days, would be a faithful guardian to his heirs. Therefore, exerting all his strength, he did not desist until he secured from the clergy of England that he be installed as archbishop.

## VII. CENSURE OF THE APPOINTMENT

Yet some thought that there was something less than canonical in his advancement, [Col. 0281A] because the king’s insistence had done more to bring it about than the wishes of clergy or people. It was also called an act of presumption or indiscretion that one who scarcely seemed fit to hold an oar assumed the foremost place at the helm—especially in a church served by a community clothed in the habit of religion, whose bishop also customarily professes the religious life.

But he himself, scarcely professing even the clerical state by dress or manner, rather displaying himself more delicately in the changes of soft garments among the pampered courtiers of the palace, and being more worldly minded, is thought not to have recoiled from so holy a height of such great dignity and declined it, but to have ascended it of his own accord. In this he differed indeed from either Moses, the friend of God, or Jeremiah, sanctified from the womb. For when the latter was sent by the Lord to prophesy to Jerusalem, [Col. 0281B] he modestly answered: “Ah, ah, Lord God: I do not know how to speak, because I am a child.” Moses also, though chosen by the Lord to lead his people, was frightened by the burden and said: “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?” And again: “I beseech thee, Lord, I am not eloquent; send whom thou wilt send.”

It is also frequently read of the saints of the New Testament that they were advanced to the episcopal office more under compulsion than voluntarily. Blessed Gregory was even brought back from flight and, unwillingly, placed in the Roman see. Blessed Ambrose likewise, resisting strongly and confessing accusations against himself in order to be rejected, at length received the episcopate at the command of the Emperor Valentinian. Blessed Martin too, [Col. 0281C] surrounded and seized by the pious stratagem of the citizens, was consecrated only under compulsion and with sorrow. Therefore, many judged that, following their example, the chancellor would better have excused himself as unworthy and unequal to the task; they sharply accused him of having acted otherwise.

## VIII. HIS DEFENCE

Yet, lest truth be denied, as one experienced in many matters and accustomed to measure well what lay ahead, he clearly foresaw and weighed the peril of so great a charge. For undoubtedly he knew both the honour and the burden of that height. He knew that, as he would become head of the whole church of the kingdom, every ecclesiastical offence would also fall back upon his own head. He knew [Col. 0281D] that he would have to renounce his customary pleasures and wholly put off the old man if he wished to walk the due path of his office. He knew likewise that he would become the reproach of men and the outcast of the people if the vigour of ecclesiastical correction cooled in him; or, if he proceeded in this matter as was fitting, that the resentment of many would increase. Finally, he would lose either the beloved king, his lord, or God. For he would not deserve to reign with God if he obeyed the king’s impulses, nor could he rejoice with the king if he set the laws of God’s saints before them.

Undoubtedly foreseeing these things and repeatedly turning and returning them in his mind, constrained and frightened by them, he greatly recoiled from the arduous ascent and fled from it in spirit. He also tried earnestly, by excusing himself against the king’s insistence, to decline it, not concealing from the king [Col. 0282A] that, once elevated, he would be deprived of the favour of either God or the king. But the more he resisted, the more fiercely the king burned for his purpose, so highly did he think of the singularity of his virtue, and so fully did he trust his loyalty and devotion toward himself. He undoubtedly had to comply, or expose himself to the certain danger of proscription and hatred.

In those same days Henry of Pisa, cardinal-priest of the Roman Church, was exercising the office of legate in Normandy. His counsel and persuasion also contributed the more earnestly to this end: that he should not reject, for Christ’s Church, an office so urgently offered, nor despise so honourable an opportunity, by which, freed from human service, he might henceforth devote himself to the service of God.

Finally, when the clergy of England gathered to appoint a metropolitan over themselves, the petitions of both the mother church and the suffragan bishops were found to agree unanimously and urgently upon him. And although, as commonly happens in such cases, certain rivals sighed not a little, nothing was publicly advanced that could either hinder or delay the matter. [Col. 0282B] Unable, therefore, to withstand such influences, he cast his thought upon the Lord; judging rightly that what such human effort pressed upon him was God’s decree, he chose rather to fall into God’s hands, entrusting and submitting his whole self to His mercy.

As his later life and constancy in suffering finally showed, he did not refuse that burden especially because he intended to devote his zeal and labour to the liberation of the Church, then dangerously imperilled in England. For against the Church’s laws, in ordering ecclesiastical affairs as though they were secular, the royal hand did more than canonical discipline; and ecclesiastical persons, repeatedly burdened with many wrongful exactions and extortions, were worn down. [Col. 0282C] Since the king’s counsel seemed to depend upon him, his rivals even called him the instigator and approver of this enormity.

More truly, however, the king’s own high-handedness itself appropriated these powers. Exalted by the glory of extensive authority and led by the impetuosity of youthful will, he did not know how to regard himself as king unless those entrusted to him for government were also subject to his personal will, and unless he extended the authority of his tribunal over clerics no less than over laypeople. This high-handedness was further strengthened by the favour and prompting of his intimates, who, applauding his exaltation, wished to please him and sought their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ. [Col. 0282D] For they thought that, insofar as the king’s power increased, their own lofty status too should be enlarged together with profit.

To oppose all these things was not safe for the chancellor alone; nor did he bear the role of a censor fit to correct them, since he remained under the necessity of obedience, not the authority of rebuke. Therefore, since it was a time and a power of darkness, he had sailed more prudently through the middle course: concealing usurpations rather than urging them, enduring them rather than approving them. Yet he sometimes groaned with zeal for God’s house; at times he even ventured to dissuade such conduct, though with the restraint required lest he incur the king’s displeasure.

But when the grace of advancement was offered, he saw that, if the Church’s prayers were fulfilled, he would thereafter be bound chiefly to help it, and ought more justly and could more freely urge the king on its behalf. [Col. 0283A] Accordingly, submitting himself to danger for the Church itself, he did not reject that favour; but, at the clergy’s request and the king’s insistence, he accepted it, though unwillingly. It was as though one of the seraphim had flown to him and touched his lips with a live coal taken from the altar with tongs; and when the Lord afterwards asked whom He should send, he answered: “Here am I; send me.”

For he resolved that henceforth, among a people of unclean lips, he would neither be silent nor rest; and that, if he could not secure the Church’s liberation from the king through the privilege of affection lending aid, he would labour to obtain it at least by the force of reason.

## IX. HOW HE LIVED AS ARCHBISHOP

[Col. 0283B]

Therefore, in order to obtain this end more effectively and powerfully, even before he was elevated he did not yield to flesh and blood, nor seek the pleasures, pomp, or gains of the world. Rather, putting on the new man, he entered firmly and resolutely upon the path of religion. First of all, resolutely turning away from evil, he strove daily to redeem the offences of earlier days by manifold remedies: whenever he stayed overnight, he spent the early morning in abundant prayers and copious tears; then, after confessing to a priest, he offered his back to the lash. Afterwards he devoutly either heard Mass or, more frequently, celebrated it; and, having completed the canonical hours before noon, he attended either to hearing cases or to his own affairs—[Col. 0283C] prudent in arranging his own concerns, prompt and just in deciding cases, turning neither toward avarice nor toward gifts, a compassionate consoler of the oppressed and swift avenger of those who inflicted wrong. If he were free from business, he devoted himself entirely to reading or to necessary conferences with his own household.

Every day too, whenever he could do so more privately, he customarily bent his knees in a more secluded chamber to wash the feet of thirteen poor persons, after the example of the most famous female sinner; in Christ’s memory, he watered them with tears, wiped them with his hair, and humbly kissed them. He also gave each four silver coins. If occasion to perform it himself was lacking, he took care that this work of mercy be carried out through a deputy. [Col. 0283D] Finally, surrounded by a great and noble gathering of the court, he approached the table after twenty-six poor persons had first been brought in.

As befitted an archiepiscopal house, it too abounded in ample and splendid provision of necessities. Yet amid the luxuries of food and drink he always observed this middle course of temperance: he did not abstain from them altogether, lest he be branded superstitious; nor did he take them immoderately, lest gluttony weigh him down. For outwardly he conformed himself to the others, in food as in dress, and was cheerful and pleasant among them; inwardly, however, he took care to differ, according to the saying of the wise man: “Let our outward countenance conform to the people, but inwardly let all things be different.”

Thus, poor in spirit while wearing costly clothing; contrite in heart while cheerful in face; choosing privation at a lavish table, [Col. 0284A] sometimes more empty than refreshed in stomach, and more often merely sustained than filled, he always remained sober. Avoiding unusual and ostentatious fasting, so as to escape the name of hypocrite, he judged the best kind of fasting to be maintaining the measure of sobriety. He also endeavoured to have a richer and more plentiful table so that he might more fully assist the poor from its remnants.

For he had great care for the poor. Apart from the fact that none of those begging door to door ever went empty away from his doors, he himself diligently investigated, through his agents, the dwellings of sick and weak poor persons and visited them with alms, sustaining very many even by daily food and clothing. And whereas his predecessor had customarily doubled the alms established by his predecessors, he, following him in the religious liberality of adding more, judged that this doubled amount itself should be doubled; he continued this observance of the pious work and devoted to it also the tithes of all he possessed. [Col. 0284B]

After meals and such sleep as necessity demanded, he again, beyond the prescribed Hours, occupied himself with business, writings, or honourable conversation, zealously fleeing idleness lest his enemies see him and mock his sabbaths. At the time of night’s sleep, though lying in bed, he gave himself rather to vigils—then especially, with God alone as witness, lamenting the losses of his earlier life, bewailing them with abundant tears, pressing more earnestly upon prayer, and sometimes applying himself to holy meditations. Such was the daily course of his life after becoming archbishop: by such strict disciplines he cleansed the worldly pleasures he had previously enjoyed. This was in him a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.

For striving to become a model for the flock he had undertaken to govern, he accustomed himself to the Lord’s sweet yoke and light burden: pursuing chastity, maintaining humility, observing moderation in speech and justice in action, so that those whom he was to teach by word he might more powerfully admonish by the example of his holiness. Whether he spoke to laypersons or to learned people, he appeared remarkably learned and eloquent; and his preaching, pleasing through the weight of its thoughts and the purity of its words, was effective. [Col. 0284C] In this it is plain that the anointing taught him; for he had neither received nor learned it from a human being, since he had devoted little time and labour to literary studies.

He also burned with zeal for justice toward his subjects, striving, without respect of persons or temporal reward, to preserve for each what was his own. Above all, he was troubled by concern for the church entrusted to him: in many ways its advantage was thwarted, its honour diminished, and its authority curtailed. Certain powerful men denied it a portion of its rights; the Church of York, beyond what was due, treated itself as its equal; and, to a great extent, what ought to have been permitted to it with respect to its subjects was forbidden by royal prohibition. It also plainly redounded to its injury that secular power usurped authority over its churches’ property or persons.

The more, therefore, he was distressed by these matters, the more earnestly he devoted himself to opposing them and seeking the reform of the rest. [Col. 0285A] For these reasons too he pursued more strictly the path of holier life, so that divine grace might more effectively direct these endeavours and he might have greater authority to achieve them.

## X. HOW THE DEVIL FIRST TRIED TO OVERTHROW HIM BY FLATTERY

Observing this change in him, the Evil One was greatly astonished: he had seen him formerly pursuing more eagerly than others the pleasures and glories of the world, and now marvelled that he should turn all these things into contempt and accustom himself to the humility of abasement, whom he had expected to raise higher into the swelling pride of eminence. Yet, supposing that this proceeded instead from disgust—as though he despised what he possessed because he could not use the power he had received as he pleased—[Col. 0285B] he thereafter endeavoured to entice him with the prospect of a far higher title.

He had already more sharply instilled into the hearts of those ill-disposed toward him that they should more boldly and shamelessly criticize his actions and character; and that the very things for which they truly attacked him—the narrow way that leads to heaven—they should turn into grounds for envy. For they construed as superstition his keeping a stricter path; as cruelty, his zeal for justice; as greed, his seeking the advantage of his church; as austerity, his setting aside human favour; as a hunt for glory, his maintaining the magnificence of a noble court; as pride, his often following his own judgment in action; and as presumption, his striving in ecclesiastical matters to exceed the bounds set by the ancients. [Col. 0285C]

In short, they scarcely saw him do anything good without twisting it to the sinister interpretation; and, being many, they prevailed in persuasion through their numbers rather than through truth. Thus he incurred the hatred of many and, consequently, frequent accusations in the king’s hearing. At length it was reported to the king that, in his effort to expand his own power, he proposed even to prefer the canons to royal dignities; and that evidence of this would be that he would bind to himself by oath all the better men of the realm, and was preparing to establish his pre-eminence over great and small alike in the kingdom, so that he might seem openly to have said: “I will exalt my throne and be higher than the king.”

Hence arose in the king the beginning of evil suspicion; hence the seedbed of anger; [Col. 0285D] hence intolerable resentment. For he could no longer fail to fear that the man whom he had reckoned as father and protector of himself and his own was, in truth, an adversary in many matters.

While the king was then overseas, he said: “I will cross the sea and see whether the outcry that has reached me is fulfilled in deeds as has been alleged.” Not long afterwards, when he arrived and encountered him, he did not at once show an angry face or reveal his mind, but judged that he should first entice him with flattery. For he had held him more closely and affectionately dear, and had said of him: “I have found a man after my own heart.” Above all others, he had often found him faithful and indispensable in his affairs. He had also placed his chief hope in him for preserving the established condition of his realm. [Col. 0286A]

He could neither immediately nor appropriately decide wholly to break this hope, reject his counsel, or cast off his affection. Rather, he began with blandishments. Having permitted the most dutiful manner of greeting and kiss, he thereafter took care to show him great reverence and to pay much honour to his honour. For the Evil One devised that he might be more easily broken by the humility of so great a prince and more readily captivated by the greatness of his promises.

When an opportunity for fuller conversation had been obtained, the king, not harshly but kindly, not in the hauteur of one threatening but in the spirit of a friend, recalled the reports made to him about the archbishop. He urged him humbly and gently to correct what he had begun against him, to abstain from harmful endeavours, to pursue peace and joy with him, and not to oppose his will. [Col. 0286B] For he wished and worked to restore the condition of church affairs in his kingdom to the pattern of ancestral times. In those times, however, the authority of the Roman See had customarily had little or no place in them; rather, all things, even ecclesiastical matters, were conducted more according to the king’s will, though the archbishops of that time presided and retained their own measure according to the custom of the realm.

He therefore believed that he was justly claiming for himself what his predecessors had possessed. For, as he was persuaded, the rights of his dignity did nothing contrary to the law of the Gospel, the apostles, the prophets, or the saints; and therefore he believed that their observance ought lawfully to be defended, not abolished because of contrary constitutions of emperors or bishops. Earlier kings, too, had held their subjects under the same system, and several of those kings are honoured with an unquestioned memory of sanctity. [Col. 0286C]

He also declared that he wished, hoped, and believed that the archbishop’s salvation and honour could remain unimpaired; he even swore that it would be greatly to his satisfaction if the archbishop presided over these matters more exaltedly and happily, promising to support this with all his power, counsel, and help. For he said that his chief glory would be this: that the man whom he had appointed should obtain no less favour with God and men, and that the divine judgment should be shown to agree with his choice.

Above all, detesting and wishing to avoid the haughtiness and ambition of the Roman court, he strove to make his own subjects answerable to the archbishop’s judgment alone; consequently, he supposed that they would also be subject to himself, and that certain troublesome or unfaithful clerics could be restrained at his discretion. [Col. 0286D] For who in the kingdom could impede an undertaking in which king and archbishop acted together? See what a height of authority in ecclesiastical affairs he was procuring for him.

He still more urgently and persistently begged him to assume the government and care also of the secular affairs of his kingdom, so that he himself might devote himself more effectively and securely to overseas concerns; and that he might also undertake the guardianship and instruction of the king’s son, the future king, so that nothing necessary to his lordship might be lacking. For he saw that the archbishop could not suffer loss in royal dignities without the reproach of a defrauder, since he had undertaken their guardianship. He saw also that, while authority over both swords passed to the archbishop, neither sword would pass away from himself. See with how many enticements he solicited him, with how many he vexed him, with how many he almost overcame him—enticements under which a base and faint-hearted man would give way, and which none but the most perfect could resist. [Col. 0287A]

But he, being of higher counsel, neither immediately assented to the royal will nor openly opposed it; nevertheless, he held firmly in his heart that he would follow neither course. For he judged that it was neither possible nor safe to govern the care of the Church well together with the affairs of the realm, because “no one can serve two masters.” He also saw that tolerating the ecclesiastical order of ancestral times plainly involved danger to both his office and his soul, because ecclesiastical vigour had added certain requirements, and because he had sworn fidelity to the Roman Church—which he would by no means keep if he despised the authority of its statutes.

He accordingly framed his reply so as to offer, so far as his strength allowed, the service of his aid and counsel for governing the realm, [Col. 0287B] provided that, being still very inexperienced in the new burden already so great, he should not take upon himself in particular that second burden of government. As for royal dignities and rights, he promised firmly to preserve what was Caesar’s for Caesar, provided that he also rendered what was God’s to God. Often summoned and importunately pressed in this kind of reply, he remained unmoved.

## XI. HOW THE DEVIL AFTERWARDS ASSAILED HIM WITH INJURIES

When the Evil One saw his purpose firm and rooted in good, he envied him; and, since he could not overthrow him by the pomp of the world, he thereafter devised to overthrow him by injuries. He had thought that the archbishop would be brought under his sway by consenting to the usurpations committed against the Church. [Col. 0287C] He had thought that he would yield more to royal flattery than to the fear of God. He had thought that he would seek peace and worldly glory more than heaven. But now he saw that the greatness of the archbishop’s power was becoming a cause of virtue: through the occasion of honour, he was proved to go “from strength to strength.”

Therefore he turned the contrivances of his fraud henceforth to this end: either to cast him down or to bring him into submission through fear of being cast down. He judged that he could achieve neither result more readily than by making his persecutor the man who had been the author of his elevation. Once the king had become an enemy, he reckoned that the archbishop’s adversaries would rise in proportion to the number of subjects who had envied him through fear of the king. Indeed, he thought that scarcely anyone would thereafter stand by him in obedience when they saw the king opposed to him. [Col. 0287D] And from the weight of royal power he calculated a swift and easy downfall for him. Therefore, when the king did not find him compliant with his will as he had hoped, he began daily to be more deeply stirred by the evil of suspicion and to discern nothing but guile in the archbishop’s words.

## XII. THE RISE OF THE CONTENTION BETWEEN HIM AND THE KING

Not long afterward, a gathering of bishops, abbots, and magnates was assembled in London concerning royal business and the strengthening of the kingdom’s peace. Among the other complaints there presented, archdeacons were accused of exercising tyranny rather than the moderation of prelacy over their subjects, wearying laypeople with vexatious lawsuits and clerics with unjust exactions. [Col. 0288A] Certain members of the clergy were also brought forward, accused of various disgraceful crimes. Such men, it was said in particular, disturbed the peace of the kingdom and ran riot in new enormities of crime, secure in their escape through the privilege of their order.

The king urgently demanded their correction from the bishops. More than this, he pressed that, by the bishops’ own counsel, he should be permitted in the case of clerics charged with public crimes to do what he recalled had been done in his ancestral days: such persons, once apprehended and convicted or confessed, were then immediately degraded and subjected to public penalties, as laypeople were. When the king more insistently demanded that the bishops decree that this too should be lawful for him, they long held back, taking care not to admit what seemed contrary to the divine law. For the prophet Nahum says: “God will not judge the same thing twice.” Thus they could seem to have resolved that persons be judged twice against God if, after degradation, they consented that the convicted should suffer the penalty of death or mutilation. [Col. 0288B]
