Solomon, the most prudent and upright king of judges, guarded against this. For when Abiathar the priest appeared deserving of death, like Joab, because they had turned against Solomon after his brother Adonijah so that he might become king, Solomon nevertheless did not punish Abiathar with death as he did Joab, but removed him only from the priesthood, saying: “Go to Anathoth, to thy estate. Thou art indeed a man of death, but today I will not kill thee, because thou didst bear the ark of the Lord before my father David.”

Moved by such considerations together with the archbishop, the bishops hesitated to make law at the king’s discretion, especially lest it could be drawn into prejudice and accusation against innocent persons, so that they might be compelled either to undergo purgation or be subjected to the lot of the guilty. [Col. 0288C] Here, then, was the beginning of the contention. For the king, thinking that the archbishop and bishops sat in ambush against him and intended to oppose the dignities of royal customs, first grew exceedingly angry, and then rushed to extort a promise that they would observe those customs.

But after a long private deliberation, wishing to calm the king’s anger, they thought that they had arranged a cautious reply when, while preserving their order, they consented that the request be granted. The royal party, however, interpreted the qualification they had supplied as a safeguard as a trap, and there was a long struggle to have it removed; but because the bishops stood unanimously firm, this was not then obtained. Hence, when the assembly was dissolved, the king departed violently enraged and threatening, and thereafter ordered his officials to press more harshly upon the seizure and harassment of episcopal property. [Col. 0288D]

Fearing this distress, some bishops afterwards turned back and, abandoning their holy unanimity in resistance, followed the king’s will. Thereupon the constancy of the others, who feared the same affliction, also began to waver, so that what Truth says happened in them: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste.” Even the archbishop’s strength was somewhat shaken, especially when he saw the Church more dangerously imperilled to his own injury, the aid of his fellow bishops failing him, and the whole cause and burden of the contention being turned upon himself.

By then he had lost the privilege of royal familiarity; the king’s customary serenity of countenance toward him had changed into cloudiness; and, love having been cast out, hatred had begun gradually to increase. Many too who had previously been accustomed to follow him no longer walked openly with him, avoiding the king’s displeasure. [Col. 0289A] His efforts then began to be turned into mockery, his authority into contempt, his honour into nothing; and in proportion to his glory, his disgrace was multiplied. See by how many stumbling blocks the Evil One assailed him because he had been unable to subject him by flattery.

Caught in the tangled sinews of Leviathan’s testicles, he did not know what to do, what to choose, or where to turn. It was not clear which of the impending evils it would be more useful to avoid. If he yielded to the king, danger to his office and soul was plainly present. If he resisted persistently, he could fear enormous harm to the Church. If amid these difficulties he sought counsel from his subjects, there was no one able to give a sound answer in every respect. If he sought to exercise punishment against sinners, there was no one whom he could trust to stand with him for justice.

For ecclesiastical discipline then had little strength, owing to the pretext of the German schism, which had greatly oppressed and humbled the Roman Church. [Col. 0289B] For, against blessed Pope Alexander, another man had been raised up by the emperor’s power as an idol in the apostolic see; under his apostasy all Italy groaned, its orthodox clergy partly subdued by fear, partly driven from their sees, and elsewhere replaced by the plague of greed. Since the same danger was feared in other provinces too, the vigour of the Church’s prelates was accordingly more relaxed and the presumption of secular princes more ready.

In view of that schism, Gilbert, then bishop of London, had at first advised that the king should be yielded to for a time, so that he might be permitted to act more severely against apostate and criminal clerics; but the judgment of the others prevailed in opposition. This bishop had formerly held the see of Hereford, and there had been much murmuring among the people because, owing to the distinction of his name and the king’s will, he was to be installed as archbishop. [Col. 0289C] For among the ecclesiastical persons of England he possessed a more celebrated reputation, since he seemed, in habit and life, to profess religion, and was also judged superior in eloquence and learning. The king gladly listened to him and, having heard him, did many things.

But when it pleased the king more that his chancellor should receive the archbishopric, he wished that some honour should nevertheless be conferred upon Gilbert. By authority of the Apostolic See he obtained his transfer to the chair of the Church of London. For after the archiepiscopal see, this was the seat of greater dignity in the kingdom; and summoned from there, he could more readily take part in deliberations concerning both Church and kingdom. This transfer, however, was especially undertaken and secured on the counsel of the archbishop himself, [Col. 0289D] who greatly trusted in Gilbert’s religious character and prudence and hoped well of him, believing that he would be a faithful colleague and vigorous helper in upholding the Church. But he experienced otherwise later.

## XIII. HOW THE CONTENTION OUGHT TO HAVE BEEN SETTLED

Therefore, after the evil of contention had arisen, he often employed that man as mediator in restoring peace; and, while others also interceded with the king, he at last obtained permission to be received for a conference. Consequently they called a new assembly at Clarendon to settle the dispute and entered into closer consultation.

The king, however, demanding his former promise unchangeably and obstinately, the archbishop and his fellow bishops finally agreed, for the good of peace, that—with the entanglement of any qualifying addition removed—they would promise, “in the word of the Lord,” to observe all the royal customs as requested. [Col. 0290A] They had reasoned beforehand that this could be done without sin or danger, considering that by the name “customs” only good customs were to be understood, since bad ones are not properly called customs but rather abuses. Nor are customs good unless they do not conflict with the laws of the Church. They therefore believed that in this sense they lawfully promised to keep all customs—and with better reason because they promised all customs generally, not certain ones expressly; for things expressly stated harm, but things not expressly stated do not harm. [Col. 0290B] Thus they completely satisfied the king and his assessors, who followed the usage of words rather than their precise meaning.

## XIV. INVECTIVE AGAINST THE BISHOPS
Did they not, then, offend against the plain sense of Holy Scripture, which teaches that, by whatever verbal artifice a man swears, God understands it as the person to whom the oath is sworn understands it? Did they not also take too little care for their own reputation, when the laity began on that account to believe and say that the pastors of the Church had assented to royal abuses? [Col. 0290C] Better then would it have been to remember the memorable courage of Eleazar, who, when he was pressed by Antiochus’ officers to violate the Law, and was persuaded by friends to eat lawful meats, pretend that he had eaten pork, and so escape, said: “It is not worthy of my age to dissemble, lest many of the young, supposing Eleazar, one hundred and ten years old, to have gone over to the life of foreigners, should themselves be deceived through my pretence, and through this I should acquire for my old age a stain and an abomination.” Having said this, he was dragged to execution; and he chose rather bravely to die than, through dissimulation, shamefully to expose himself to danger with the ruin of others.

Had the bishops felt the same as he did, they would even then have taken more honourable care to resist in simplicity of heart [Col. 0290D] than more irreligiously to escape by words. For what violence was there, or what compulsion, such as made surrender necessary? Certainly, nothing had yet been done by cruelties, but only by threats. Nothing was being proposed deserving death or imprisonment. Nor did danger threaten from the treachery of heretics or the savagery of pagans. Faithful sons of God and of the Church had brought against their fathers rather a lawsuit than a persecution. They did not thirst for blood, but claimed royal right. They ought to have resisted them boldly and steadfastly—those who might better have been overcome by firmness in opposition.

Then the bishops should firmly and together have said: “We ought to fear God rather than men. We ought to honour God’s bride, the Church, rather than earthly power. We ought to look more to her liberty than to conform to the custom of men.” For the integrity of honour is not preserved for an emperor when anything is taken away from Augustus’ right. Then they should also have reflected courageously in their hearts that it was a vapour soon to appear for a little while, or a little cloud quickly to pass away. But if, following the threats, the enormity of violent assaults had come, then they ought rather to have gone up in opposition and made themselves a wall for the house of the Lord, that they might stand in battle. Then, with the free voices of priests, they should have resisted power, fighting against evils by argument, admonitions, and threats. Then they should have struck with the goads of stern restraint, as judiciously as strictly, so that they neither grew torpid under the name of patience nor raged under the pretext of zeal.

Nor could the kingdom long have endured the united and steadfast censure of all in vindication of justice, nor could violence have obstructed it, [Col. 0291B] because it would not have been safe to oppose the whole college of the fathers and pastors of the realm. It should most justly have been believed that nothing harsher was to be ventured against them all; nor, if they had determined upon a particular injury, should it have been reckoned a common one against all. For the king would not have wished, above other kings of the earth, to be perpetually branded with the title of such tyranny: that he was said to have cast off Christ’s flock and law, and that, by yielding even to the schismatics’ party, his name should be darkened in every age by the notorious disgrace of apostasy.

Even if this might rightly have been feared, it would nevertheless have been better then to overlook the evils and temper the discipline of severity than to incur the prejudice of a perilous promise. For where the destruction of many lies before one, it is no sin to relax something of severity, [Col. 0291C] provided that the ruler neither approves by silence nor provokes by insolent rebuke. For God imputes to one who endures in this way neither his own sins, because he did not commit them; nor others’ sins, because he did not approve them; nor negligence, because he was not silent; nor pride, because he remained in unity. But because they either did not foresee or despised these considerations, the bishops seem altogether to have strayed from the way, becoming like dumb dogs unable to bark—like hirelings rather than shepherds—when they were silent and yielded even though they saw only the shadow of a wolf, not the wolf himself.

## XV. THE REVIVAL OF THE CONTROVERSY

The Evil One took greater care to entangle them, because they sought rather to free themselves, together with their head, the archbishop whom he strove to hinder. For immediately, as though in recompense for their dissimulation, a graver crisis of the whole dispute arose. Through the great men of the court the king at once caused the customs, newly examined, to be put in writing, and demanded that they be confirmed by the seals of the bishops and the archbishop, in order to remove all ensuing doubt and contention concerning them. Among the provisions expressly stated were some plainly contrary to ecclesiastical ordinances. Lest what has passed be unknown, these are some of them:

That no appeal may be made to the Apostolic See in any cause without the king’s permission.

That neither an archbishop nor any bishop or abbot may leave the kingdom, nor even come at the summons of the lord pope, without the king’s knowledge.

[Col. 0292A] That no one who holds directly of the king may be excommunicated unless he has first been consulted.

That clerks must appear at the king’s summons and before his justice for every cause.

That no layman may be summoned before an ecclesiastical judge concerning breach of faith or perjury in a money matter.

It was therefore plain that by these provisions the liberty and power of the Church were greatly diminished. If the bishops confirmed them, they would openly attack the Church; if they did not confirm them, they could not escape the king’s anger. Thus pressed into a narrow place, they finally turned to seeking a delay; and the last things became worse than the first. For the king’s party interpreted it as manifest deception when they declined to confirm in writing what they were thought to have promised on oath. [Col. 0292B] The king therefore, exceedingly enraged and thunderously uttering terrible threats, seemed plainly about to blaze out in cruel zeal against some of them, while several of his own men sharply incited him to this. Nor was there lacking a just reason for fear, since, according to Solomon, “As the roaring of a lion, so is the wrath of a king,” and again, “As the growling of a lion, so is the terror of a king.”

## XVI. THE ARCHBISHOP’S FALL

But the burden of the conflict was directed especially against the archbishop, without whose counsel, as their head, the bishops attempted nothing; and they feared to advise him to yield. He, however, could not but be moved as a man. Yet he was more anxiously troubled over the safety of certain bishops and of his own people than over his own safety, [Col. 0292C] since it was more justly feared that the king would rage against those who were suspect to him; and this the more certainly because no firm expectation could be placed in the steadfastness of the others for vengeance. Therefore, when signs of graver evils appeared—here the Evil One prevailing, here reason yielding to the flesh—he finally gave way and consented that the king’s demand should be made in words only.

He was inclined to this especially by the prompting and deceptive assurances of certain persons familiar both to himself and to the king. They persuaded him that the king would proceed no further if he merely appeared to have won; and so he reckoned that, having prevailed over the head, the king had thereby secured the rest. Indeed, he regarded the consent of all the others as a small matter, trusting that, on the pretext of those unsettled times, confirmation of the same customs could easily be obtained also from the Roman See—[Col. 0292D] confirmation which he later sought but by no means obtained.

## XVII. HIS PENANCE

Once he had escaped, sharper grief seized the archbishop. Struck by his fall as by God’s scourge and summoned to better things, he thereafter devoted far greater labour to advancing the holiness he had begun: more watchful in avoiding evils and more frequent in works of virtue. To punish his former faults more severely and unlearn his accustomed luxuries, he bound a dreadful hair-shirt tightly beneath his clothing against his flesh. Having laid aside the former adornment of his changes of dress, he began to wear outwardly garments neither ostentatious nor mean, but clean and clerical, and even in them often to rest when he slept; he also often lay down at night upon the ground [Col. 0293A] rather than upon a bed, chastising his flesh also by many fasts.

Above all, sick and impatient with grief for his own fall, he took care thenceforth to be stronger and bolder against royal usurpations. For examples and authorities taught him that what he had wrongly promised need not be kept. The holy king David swore by the Lord that he would kill the foolish man Nabal; but his greater piety lay in not fulfilling that oath. The wicked Herod likewise swore that he would not refuse the daughter of Herodias whatever she asked; but, in giving her John’s head when she asked for it, he displayed greater impiety. For divine law decrees that an oath by which evil is rashly promised is not to be kept.

To annul more effectively what he had promised in fear, he repeatedly attempted to cross to the Roman court in order to seek absolution; [Col. 0293B] but a contrary wind continually drove him back from the sea and did not allow him to cross. For the Evil One opposed his good endeavours and, seeing him better disposed after his fall, judged that he ought to be driven into worse adversities.

## XVIII. THE CAUSE OF HIS FLIGHT

Finally, wishing to entangle him more tightly, he laid a new snare for him. Summoned to a third assembly at Northampton, the archbishop was overwhelmed by royal litigation, so that he might satisfy an accounting for the revenues administered while he was chancellor. Yet when he was elected, he had been handed over to the Church free and discharged, in the presence of the king’s son and the magnates, to whom the king had entrusted from overseas the whole care of his elevation. This was also notified to the lord pope in royal letters when the pallium was afterwards sought for him from the Roman See.

Nevertheless, the king, no less angry on these same matters, then demanded either an accounting or judgment by his court, or at least by the bishops. The archbishop therefore rightly thought fit to refuse to render an account, because of the manifest calumny. Nor did he consider it safe to enter upon the case in the king’s court, lest, by a judgment against the head, further derogation should be made from the privilege of clerks. For laws and canons establish that clerks, when summoned, ought to answer only before the Church. It is also specially written concerning bishops that none but the Church ought ever to judge them. Nor was he bound to submit himself to the decision of his bishops, since the sacred canons direct [Col. 0293D] that one must always go where authority is greater, and that in every controversy one must be guided to the judgments of the higher see.

He thought rather that they should be avoided as suspect. They had already withdrawn their support from him, so that, by favouring the king more, they might provide better for their own peace. They advised him also to yield altogether to the king’s will, as though by allowing himself to be conquered he would conquer better. But he himself knew the prince’s disposition and purpose more intimately, and rightly feared injury to his Church and prejudice to himself.

## XIX. HIS FLIGHT AND ITS DEFENCE

Meanwhile, deprived of all assistance and heavily pressed by the burden of the court, fearing something dreadful for himself, he began to carry about the cross as his refuge. Then, when, as was said, a harsher sentence was imminent, he chose an apostolic hearing by appeal and withdrew amid insults and threats. [Col. 0294A] For the king, concerned for his reputation and unwilling that the peace of the royal court should be violated, had ordered that he and his people be spared, even against the fury of certain men.

But the following night, having learned from the king’s more faithful servants that imprisonment or the sword threatened him, he departed secretly, changed his dress, and with a few companions turned aside into more remote regions of the kingdom, that he might more cautiously elude his pursuers. He wisely judged that envy must be yielded to and room given to madness—just as Jacob did with his brother Esau; as David did with Saul, the most obstinate of his enemies; and as Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, fled throughout the world under the persecutor Constantius, so that he might be preserved against the Arians for the Catholic faith. The Apostle Paul did likewise when he was let down through a window in a basket, that he might escape the hands of the governor of Damascus and survive for the enlargement of the Church. Finally, Christ himself did likewise: both when he was carried away by his parents from Herod’s plots and lay hidden in Egypt, and when the Jews wished to stone him and he hid himself and went out of the Temple.

Strengthened by such great examples, he also followed the instruction with which Christ himself taught his disciples: “When they persecute you in one city, flee into another.” Nor did he deserve the reproach of the hireling who sees the wolf coming and flees, because he has no care for the sheep. For he did not abandon the flock entrusted to him to danger, since no rage was directed against it; rather, he wisely withdrew himself from the peril specially prepared [Col. 0294C] for himself alone as its head. Not long afterwards, secretly returning to a suitable place on the coast, he boarded a ship and sailed safely to Flanders. From there he made his way to Lord Pope Alexander, who was then residing at Sens. He sought him in order to have him as judge, to ask pardon also for his perilous promise, and above all to reform the state of the Church.

For after the promise, patience toward things already being outrageously done in ecclesiastical affairs could only be blameworthy; before it, such patience might, through the necessity of the time, have been pardonable. For a promise plainly demonstrates consent, whereas necessity has an excuse. But the mercy of the Almighty directed his steps; and the more steadfastly he clung to God amid such great temptations, [Col. 0294D] the less power the Evil One’s designs now had against him.

## XX. HOW THE DEVIL AFTER THIS SOUGHT TO CAST HIM DOWN

Yet he did not cease to persecute him, now openly bringing his full strength to bear for his complete overthrow. For thereafter his ill-wishers, more fiercely inflamed by him and having obtained a better opportunity for detraction and calumny, stirred the king more powerfully to hatred of him. They prevailed so far that the king, utterly despairing henceforth of one so turned away from conversion, and inwardly touched by anguish of heart, at last said: “It repents me that I have made man”; and again: “I will destroy man whom I have created.” No longer restraining himself, he sent after him a great company of archbishops and bishops, counts and barons, [Col. 0295A] so that he might be unable to stand against the accusations of so many great men.

The Lord therefore willed that he should thereafter have raised up against him, as it were, another Hadad the Edomite: one who might strike him with blows lest he be exalted, and might, like a certain thorn in the flesh, admonish him not to think too highly because of the greatness of his virtues, nor to suppose himself set on high and lifted up by the faults of others. The archbishops of York and London in particular were said to have conspired with the king for his overthrow: the archbishop of York as his rival in a dispute concerning equality of rank; that of London because he resented the archbishop’s precedence over him and, as was said, aspired again to the same office.

Entering the Roman court, they unanimously and resolutely accused the absent archbishop of imprudence and presumption, laying many calumnies against him and requesting that he be sent back into the kingdom, as being better examined and openly convicted there. [Col. 0295B] They also requested the appointment of legates to hear and settle the case there, without the obstacle of an appeal. But they departed unheard, because the religious prudence of the lord pope judged it neither safe nor fitting to reserve the decision of so great a matter for anyone but himself. Nor did it seem canonical that the archbishop should be returned to the province from which he had fled in justified fear, and where scarcely anyone would stand by him—indeed, where all would rather oppose him at the king’s nod.

## XXI. HIS AFFLICTION THROUGH THE KING

[Col. 0295C]

the king, therefore, deeply troubled and angered by this, withdrew from the lord pope his goodwill and the pope’s visitations of the kingdom. He also seized into his own hand and power all the possessions of the archbishop and of his clerks, which had been taken away from their use. Besides this, every one of his household, together with their families, was stripped of property and compelled to leave the kingdom: orphans and widows, wards and innocent persons, altogether ignorant of the whole dispute, were pitilessly driven into the misery of exile. Since the Evil One could not overthrow him, he then strove at least to crush him through the losses and affliction of his people.

## XXII. HIS CONSOLATION THROUGH GOD

[Col. 0295D]

But God is good, and makes all things work together for good to those who are good. What had been contrived as the disgrace of his abandonment was openly turned into consolation for him; and from what seemed calculated to break him, he was made stronger—stronger through the expulsion of his people with him, and more welcome among foreigners because of his proscription. These great losses moved him little or not at all, whether in flesh or blood; nor could concern for them bend him in the least from the straight path. Thus, the less he cared for these things, the more the grace of God procured grace for him, so that the king himself and the magnates of France eagerly supplied the necessities of him and his people.

## XXIII. THE LORD POPE’S INDULGENCE TOWARD HIM

[Col. 0296A]

By divine inspiration he also easily drew the lord pope to his side, once he had instructed him in the truth of his just cause. Afterwards, taught by unquestionable proofs of his prudence and holiness, the pope graciously and readily granted him remission both of whatever fault he had incurred in his elevation and of his subsequent fall. He decreed also, by the authority of his own see, that he should henceforth govern the episcopate entrusted to him, and added the office of legate for England.

Yet this eminent title did not change or puff him up in the least. Steadfastly pursuing the path of virtue on which he had entered, he turned every occasion of favour to the honour of the Church and the service of God, thereafter more vigorously zealous for correction of what was wrongly done in England. Nevertheless, for a whole year he restrained the exercise of his authority, mercifully trying and waiting to see whether patience might perhaps lead the offenders to repentance. Meanwhile he laboured to obtain, with all the strength he could, support for his cause. For he knew the king’s character more intimately and inferred much from it: that the king would not abandon what he had begun unless constrained by a strong hand.

## XXIV. HIS DEFENCE AGAINST CERTAIN MEN’S REPROACHES

Many nevertheless objected that, if he strove for the truth of religion, he ought not then to have settled among the chief enemies of his lord or thence to have procured the troubles of retaliation. Yet David provides a contrary example: fleeing Saul, his lord, he handed himself over to foreigners, preferring to be subject even to enemies rather than to the envious. [Col. 0296C] But this man did not pass into partnership with enemies. Rather, he first lay concealed at Pontigny, in the religious house of the Cistercian monks, in order there to punish his sins more severely and obtain God’s mercy more effectually.

When, because of the king’s hostility, the Cistercians did not dare support him any longer, the holy generosity of Louis, pious king of the French, came to his aid, abundantly and magnificently furnishing him and his people with every necessity in the metropolitan city of Sens. Yet he did not remain there from a desire or purpose of hostility. Rather, because, owing to his lord’s wide-reaching power, he could find nowhere else to lay his head, he was mercifully received by Louis. Nor would he have been justly blamed even if he had sought the assistance of earthly power in support of ecclesiastical censure. For, as the saints judge, defenders are rightly requested from and appointed by emperors against the power of the rich, by whose oppression the Church is harassed.

Nevertheless, the affection of charity firmly rooted toward his lord prevailed so that he did not do this against him; he could not fail to show deference even to one persecuting him, or to spare him even at risk to himself. [Col. 0296D]

## XXV. HIS ZEAL

Yet zeal for the Church consumed him no little in the meantime; and the imminent burden of the dignity he had undertaken burned him intensely. He thought and repeatedly reflected upon Augustine’s saying: that in this life nothing is more difficult, laborious, or perilous than the office of bishop, but nothing is more blessed before God if it is performed in the manner commanded by our Emperor. [Col. 0297A] He knew that he had been stationed at the prow and held the helm in a ship shaken, as he well knew, by a savage storm.

For he had no doubt that laymen, sons of perdition and readier for every crime, were preying upon the possessions of his Church and persevering in plunder and oppression; that they kept its servants cast into chains; that ecclesiastical persons were harassed by calumnies and straits and, contrary to the canons, dragged before secular judgment; that holy things were openly trampled upon; and that the revenues of himself and his people—resources unquestionably intended for the use of the poor—were being wickedly assigned to soldiers’ pay. Therefore it was not safe for the master of the ship to sleep long amid so many and such great storms. Rather, he had to labour with all his strength to escape the danger. [Col. 0297B]

## XXVI. HIS FIRST CENSURE

Accordingly, he often strove to bend the king by great entreaties, remonstrances, and threats; but, being unable to prevail, after waiting a year he published and condemned the royal written decree concerning the aforesaid customs at the public assembly of the people at Vézelay. He pronounced an anathema generally upon those who exacted, observed, or consented to these customs, and particularly upon certain of the king’s household, the counsellors or executors of the abuses. Since he had achieved nothing for so long by yielding patiently to the storm, he judged, like a vigorous oarsman, that a remedy must then be sought by resistance and by breaking the waves of the tempests. [Col. 0297C]

He did not fear before the king either the risk of greater offence or the disturbance of a heavier oppression, judging that courage is nowhere more necessary than in a storm and constancy nowhere more useful than in persecution. For under persecutors the Church has often diminished through the fearful, and has continually grown through brave champions. This was also foreshadowed by Noah’s ark: the more it was lifted by the flood, the higher it too was borne. He first stretched out his hand against counsellors plotting against the king’s reputation and salvation. As though intending to lay the axe to the root, he solemnly summoned the king himself also, as one upon whom he would pronounce an anathema by name on an appointed day, unless he corrected and abandoned what he had begun. [Col. 0297D]

## XXVII. THE RESTRAINT OF THE CENSURE AND THE REASON FOR IT

This undertaking was hindered by an appeal made to the lord pope on the king’s behalf. The pope then restrained the archbishop’s power for a little while. He had been told that patience would conquer better. It also seemed prudent that he should still act more gently on account of the schism. For he recalled what was written: whenever one of the brethren is found in such a sin as to deserve anathema, this is to be done where there is no danger of schism. [Col. 0298A] Public rumour had it that, through schismatics’ many great promises, the king was being strongly solicited, under colour of the dispute, to enlarge the schism and would soon be won over.

The pope therefore judged that it was better still to bear with him in kindness than to cut him off in severity. For this reason he also arranged for the king’s excommunicated adherents to be absolved. The archbishop bore this prudent moderation the more easily because, through the restraint of superior authority, he no longer appeared to be neglecting his office.

## XXVIII. THE GROUND OF THE CENSURE

His rivals, indeed, twisted his steadfast severity into an accusation of rashness. Yet he believed that he ought to act in this way once there was no hope of conquering by patience. For he had read: “Crimes of whatever kind, wherever they become known, if they have not been healed by the medicine of gentle patience, must be burned and treated as by a fire of pious rebuke.” But if the remedy of one who bears patiently and rebukes mercifully does not succeed, those who, long endured and healthfully reproved, refuse correction should be cut off, like rotten members of the body, by the sword of excommunication. [Col. 0298B]

He also confidently trusted that the king, whom he knew more intimately and had often tested in many matters, would not endure harsher censure for long either against himself or his people. He was sure that a man impatient of correction would not bring the glory of his high estate to the detestable point of apostasy. Perhaps the lord pope judged otherwise, as one less acquainted with the man’s character, farther away, and influenced by reports; he therefore moderated severity for a while. [Col. 0298C]

## XXIX. HOW PEACE WAS OFTEN SOUGHT TO BE RESTORED

Yet, lest he leave his son, an exile for his sake, utterly abandoned, not long afterwards the pope sent from his side men of great renown, cardinals of his Church, that through these mediators the king might be more powerfully urged toward reconciliation. After negotiations for peace had been begun and prolonged, they finally withdrew with the affair unresolved; and again the king’s party ran to the expedient of an appeal. The necessity of pursuing that appeal was afterwards remitted by the lord pope, and a further delay was granted, until other religious men had been sent from France and peace was again discussed—but nothing was achieved. [Col. 0298D]

After this a conference was held with the king of France. There, surrounded by a circle of many bishops, counts, and magnates, the king, when peace was requested by the archbishop, granted it, provided that he retained what the holiest of the former archbishops had retained for the weakest of the kings his predecessors. This concession seemed most just and unexpected to the whole assembly standing by. But the archbishop wished the words added: “Saving the honour of God and of the king himself.” The king rejected this as superfluous or deceptive, and won the favour of all when the archbishop, contrary to their counsel, refused what was offered.

See how the Evil One strove to bring about his complete abandonment, when he sought to take away from him that sole consolation which still remained—the support of the Church of France. Yet not even this fear could bend him to yield to the many entreaties of great men. For he saw, when others did not, the trap in the words: perhaps the holiest of archbishops had retained for kings both evil things and good, whereas obedience to all such things in general was demanded but could not be granted—especially since the king had added, “as was promised to me,” recalling the promise concerning the disputed customs, not the customs of other archbishops. [Col. 0299A]

Thus, from the very source from which he seemed about to be abandoned, he became more joyful; and he thereafter won greater favour among his hosts, in proportion as he was found wiser against the trap and more invincible against the persuasion of so many. For it was openly apparent that he was guided more by God’s Spirit than by the favour of men.

## XXX. HOW, AND WITH WHAT CONFIDENCE, CENSURE WAS RENEWED

By now the strength of the schism had lost no small part of its force, and its fury had greatly subsided. Its leader, the emperor, had been expelled from Italy and was much reduced; the strength of the Roman Church had in large measure revived. It was also plainly evident that in the overseas lands the king could not undertake to increase the schism among his people and clergy without very great risk; and for this reason it was thought that his abuses in England could more easily and justly be restrained. [Col. 0299B]

Taking and fostering confidence from this, when negotiations for peace did not proceed as he desired, and he had already grown greatly weary of delay after a long waiting, while the danger increased, the archbishop judged that the due severity of punishment should be delayed no longer. Yet he thought that deference must still be shown to the royal person, yielding to reverence for the king’s exalted rank and following the command of the Apostolic restraint. At least he stretched out his hand against the greater and more intimate men of the kingdom, by whose counsels the king acted and through whose services he employed coercion, although they had on this occasion also already protected themselves by appeal. But the appeal so often interposed seemed vexatious and dilatory. Moreover, the lord pope had forbidden the remedy of appeal.

## XXXI. THAT THE CENSURE WAS CANONICAL AND JUST

[Col. 0299D]

Although absent and cited, he nevertheless judged them worthy of punishment as manifest and unquestionable supporters and patrons of the notorious king’s offence. In manifest cases judicial procedure is not required; the accused, as though confessed guilty of evil by the evident fact of the deed, is rightly struck at once. On this ground he also bound certain bishops—namely those of London and Salisbury—with anathema, though they were unaware and had not been summoned.

For he had found them, along with others, neglectful of their office and nourishing the pestilence by failing to apply the necessary discipline. To neglect, when one is able, to restrain the perverse is nothing other than to encourage them; [Col. 0300A] nor is he free from the stain of secret consent who ceases to oppose a manifest crime. He had also found that they had failed him in their support, contrary to the decrees of the saints. For it is written: “For this God has appointed beforehand all who exercise the highest priesthood: that they may remove injustices, cut off presumptions, and especially aid those labouring in the priesthood. Whoever withdraws himself from their assistance is shown to be more a schismatic than a priest.”

Among the rest, he had plainly learned that the bishops of London and Salisbury had not merely failed in assistance but had been adversaries in the cause of God. The bishop of London had not hesitated to take upon himself the whole burden of the dispute, opposing the archbishop’s commands issued for justice. Under the pretext of avoiding schism, he evaded those commands, and always set up the impediment of appeal against the good of obedience and the more powerful remedy for all evils. [Col. 0300B] He also drew the Church of England into partnership in this, though it did not dare truly to protest. The bishop of Salisbury, moreover, was manifestly his associate and helper in every contrivance and evasion of appeals, devising with him manifold expedients of legates and delays to elude justice in the king’s notoriously unjust cause.

## XXXII. THAT THE CENSURE COULD LEGALLY HAVE BEEN MORE SEVERE

For this reason, argument and examples showed that they deserved not only anathema but deposition. For we read that similar action was taken against certain protectors of the notorious crime of Emperor Lothair. Pope Nicholas says: [Col. 0300C] “The crime which King Lothair committed with the two women Theutberga and Waldrada is known to all. Moreover, almost the whole world, gathering at the Apostolic See, reported that the bishops Theutgaud and Gunther had long been his protectors and supporters in such a deed. Therefore, the holy synod decreeing with us, they undoubtedly stand deposed from the priestly office, excommunicated, and removed from the government of the episcopate.”

The same pope says to Lothair: “Thus you consented to the impulses of your body and cast yourself into the pit of misery, so that you, who had been set over the governance of peoples, became the ruin of many. The lawful case of Theutgaud and Gunther, formerly bishops, proves this. Because they did not suitably instruct you, but rather strove to cover your transgression with their arguments and, under a certain appearance of justice, to bury equity beneath specious inventions, they have by our authority been deposed and regularly excluded from every government of priesthood and episcopacy.” [Col. 0300D]

Since, therefore, the same penalty ought legally to have been inflicted upon the aforementioned bishops, the archbishop nevertheless spared them greatly by stopping at the sentence of anathema alone. He did not wish them wholly cast down, but rather frightened and brought to their senses, so that they might in turn cause the frightened king to come to his senses. The lord pope’s moderation had until then also spared them their labours and expenses, remitting the necessity of pursuing their appeals, so that in return for this kindness [Col. 0301A] peace might more easily and promptly follow through their aid. Yet neither this remission moved them, nor did diminishing confidence in the schism stir them, nor did grief at the scandal increasing among them animate them, after so long an interval, to recover priestly firmness and protest against such great abuses.

Indeed, abuse of patience had made them not merely more secure but even more eager to evade. Therefore, because tasteless salt is good for nothing except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by men, they were at last rightly cast out by the Church through anathema together with the other counsellors of the king. Thus, when the cubs had been chastised before the lion, the lion’s anger might subside; and he who had wandered might, overcome by the terror of passion and age in his counsel, return to the way of health and salvation. Thereafter his anger followed with greater implacability in proportion to the greater cause of sorrow. For he could not but reckon the humiliation of his own men—inflicted especially on his account—as his own.

## XXXIII. HOW THE ARCHBISHOP IS TO BE DEFENDED AGAINST CERTAIN MEN’S DETRACTIONS
Nor were there lacking those who openly accused the archbishop as an enemy and disturber of the realm, and inflamed the king’s hatred against him as against one who hated him. Yet he had done nothing in fury or hatred, but wished to correct the king as a most beloved son; and, loving him as his sole lord, he sought his good in every respect with the utmost ardour. For not everyone who strikes is an enemy, just as not everyone who spares is a friend. The wounds of a friend are better [Col. 0301C] than the kisses of an enemy. It is better also to love with severity than to deceive with gentleness. Those indeed deceived him who encouraged his wrongdoing, who increased the danger by neglecting correction. But he truly loved who grieved at the danger, who took care to oppose it, who laboured to save him even against his will. For it was charity that had now cast out that old fear, that had expelled dread of giving offence, that weighed the salvation of one in peril more profitably than it avoided his wrath. If earlier, as many reproached him, he had fled as a man, now, taking on the spirit of a priest, he was ready to protest freely and to resist bravely. He walked more steadfastly upon the royal road of censure, and behaved as one who, not pursuing earthly gain or showing favour to persons but an unbending champion of rectitude, was unwilling henceforth to spare his opponents in anything.

### XXXIV. OF HIS PROGRESS DURING THE DAYS OF EXILE

Moreover, that long period of exile had contributed not a little to his person. Applying all his strength meanwhile to reading the divine law and the decrees, he compensated by the intensity of study for the losses of earlier days and the occupations of the court, so that he became far more learned for exercising the dignity he had undertaken. No less, by a most rigorous repentance—not public but secret—he strove to cleanse the falls of the former time; so that, with the seven-year period of penance, during which pardon is sought even for the gravest crimes, almost complete, he was found to be the purer, the more secure, and the more ardent in exacting [Col. 0302A] repentance even from offenders.

### XXXV. OF THE AFFLICTION INCREASED BY THE KING

But in response to this zeal of his, the swelling pride of the unruly bulls in England became still more swollen. Immediately the storm was increased: the ports were watched, and the possibility of sailing was restricted; there followed also throughout England an abjuration of receiving and observing commands from the archbishop or from the lord pope on his behalf. Thus the malice of ill-wishers had persuaded the king, so that either the force of schism might prevail, or at least fear of it might secure a remedy at the discretion of the king and the royal party.

### XXXVI. OF THE RESTORATION OF PEACE AT LAST THROUGH THE LORD POPE

As though the growth of schism had begun to threaten at the doors [Col. 0302B] and the evil seemed likely to proceed to something worse, the moderation of the Apostolic See was at last moved by the king’s repeated supplications to provide a remedy. A little earlier, indeed, the lord pope had laboured through prayers, admonitions, threats, letters concerning reconciliation, and new mediators sent from his own side, urgently addressing the king as was fitting. The impediment to peace, however, was this: the king granted the archbishop his return and the authority due to him, “saving the dignity of his realm.” The mediators wished also to add, “saving the liberty of the Church.” Since these words did not seem capable of agreement, they could not agree upon peace. But the lord pope, no longer able to endure the scandal, judged that that added formula of words should be removed on both sides. Entrusting care of the affair to new negotiators, [Col. 0302C] he prescribed the terms and form of peace, urging it upon the king with much gracious prayer and admonition, and even setting remission of sins as its reward. That the king’s mind might be softened more quickly, he granted beforehand to his bishops the favour of absolution. Overcome by these things, the king at last restored his peace and favour to the archbishop; and, as the mediators requested, granted that he and his people should return and recover their possessions intact, as they had held them three months before their departure, and that he should exercise the authority which the authority of Holy Scripture confers. Then, through these same mediators, the other faithful men of the king who had been placed under anathema also received absolution.

### XXXVII. OF A CERTAIN PARTIAL INJURY TO THE ARCHBISHOP

[Col. 0302D]

Not long before this, however, very great derogation had been made from the chief prerogative of the Church of Canterbury. For whereas by what was said to be ancient right the crowning of a new king belonged solely to the Archbishop of Canterbury, advantage having been taken of his absence, the prelate of York, making himself out to be his equal, obtained permission to consecrate the king’s son, whom the father’s will had elevated as king. This took place not in his own province but in that of Canterbury—namely, at London, which was known to be a city of that province. The suffragan bishops of the metropolitan see of Canterbury were also present and performed the service at the coronation; through them, above all, that honour belonging to their own archbishop—the chief token of his authority in the making of a king—seemed [Col. 0303A] now abolished, and henceforth no less liable to be transferred to anyone else at the prince’s discretion.

Therefore the archbishop, inwardly pierced with grief of heart at this enormous injury to his Church, wrote to the lord pope that a further wound had been added to his own grief, declaring himself altogether without hope of peace. From this he had received, before the peace, a rescript by which the prelate of York, as one who had presumed upon another’s right, was suspended from episcopal rank—especially because he had usurped authority beyond his boundaries in another’s province, above all against one exiled for the cause of justice; an act which could belong to him neither by reason nor by the constitutions of the holy Fathers. He had also obtained another rescript by which the pope, after sharply rebuking his suffragans because, after such long waiting, they had neglected to protest in priestly fashion against the perversion of established custom—indeed, because, though forbidden, they had provided the assistance of their ministry for the coronation of the king’s son to the prejudice of the metropolitan Church—likewise suspended them from episcopal rank. Moreover, he recalled some of them, namely the bishops of London and Salisbury, to the sentence of anathema, as so much the more guilty because they had previously received the greater favour of absolution and remission. From this it is clear that a proper zeal for justice had first existed in the archbishop, which the vicar of Peter afterward extended against certain bishops, making his hand heavier and renewing it against the former offenders, although he had earlier relaxed that same sentence by dispensation. But although peace had meanwhile, as stated, been made, the archbishop did not seek the removal [Col. 0303C] of the aforesaid penalties, because he was not secure concerning the stability of the peace. For the promises were not fulfilled; rather, many things were again done contrary to the terms of peace. Restitution was not made to him and his people of what was theirs; indeed, through the king’s officials, their possessions suffered grievous diminution and dispersal, as though malice thus sought to dissuade him from returning, in order to impede his purpose of martyrdom.

### XXXVIII. OF HIS RETURN AND THE NECESSITY OF RETURNING

Nevertheless, when the king later pressed him and promised to amend everything, he hastened back to England. This had also been the counsel of the lord pope and the cardinals. Above all, however, he was moved to return by the many scandals through which the Church was being afflicted, so that, like a vigorous and valiant athlete, he might lay down his life for his sheep. For he now believed that his time had come. It was now sufficiently evident who he was; the truth of his cause was sufficiently manifest to the world. He might indeed earlier have provided for his own person’s martyrdom by flight, but the injury to the Church would not thereby have been fittingly relieved, because his death would have done little toward a remedy unless he had secured the support of authority for his life and cause. For this reason also he had more willingly remained in the Church of France, the watchtower of the Churches, so that, better instructed by counsel and better fortified by aid, when need arose he might enter battle with the greater weight of a great name and be more powerful for victory. Therefore, having now greatly satisfied his purpose, he judged it neither worthy nor safe to indulge any longer, outside the realm, in the comforts of peace and security while his subjects laboured in such danger. Especially since the whole upheaval raged because of him, and the Church’s condition perilously wavered, he was pierced by David’s example and now said: “What has this flock done? Let your hand, O Lord, be upon me.” He now considered Isaiah’s consolation to Ahaz: “Do not fear, he says, and let not your heart be dismayed at the tails of smoking firebrands.” He had now taken up the boldness of Mattathias, saying: “Do not fear the words of the sinful man, for his glory is dung and a worm: today he is exalted, and tomorrow he will not be found.” He now emulated the rebuke of Christ’s Baptist, so as not to fear to say to the king: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife; it is not lawful to defile the Bride [Col. 0304B] of Christ.”

If, therefore, he had earlier fled according to the example of Christ, Paul, and certain other followers of Christ, seeking a more suitable time and a greater advantage for the Church, now certainly, when the time counselled it—after a course of holier life, after the justice of his cause had been made public, and amid more grievous and pressing scandals to the Church, while his fellow bishops were neglecting their due ministry even at great peril—he resolved to return. Following Christ’s example, when men sent by the prince came out to meet him, he would say: “Whom do you seek? If you seek me, let mine go.” For he was now ready to go to death or imprisonment, ready not to spare his own head or body if the Church’s welfare could not otherwise be secure. Indeed, as though foreknowing that he would give his head, he foretold to several persons that this would happen. The recollection of many great and trustworthy persons bore witness to this after his struggle. [Col. 0304C] His letters also later came to light, written to the lord pope during his return: humbly and devoutly giving him thanks because he had supported his cause so powerfully and steadfastly, and earnestly begging him to continue the aid of paternal defence for his Church, for which, as he added, he was certain that he was going to die.

### XXXIX. OF THE TIME OF HIS RETURN AND THE CAUSE OF THE NEW DISTURBANCE

Thus he came in the seventh year of his exile, after enduring for so long an almost unbearable penance, after greatly increasing his learning in ecclesiastical matters, and after acquiring everywhere a reputation for holiness and wisdom. By grant of the Roman See he now held, besides the dignity of legate, the rank of primate in England which was due to him. Before he boarded ship, he sent on the aforesaid letters of the lord pope. The first to receive them were the prelates of York, London, and Salisbury, who were then on the opposite shore awaiting a favourable wind, in order to cross to the king at his command. The king was staying across the sea so that, by their counsel, new bishops might be appointed to the vacant English sees; the persons of the vacant Churches had also been summoned there, as though to make elections.

### XL. HOW HE WAS ACCUSED OF RASHNESS

Some thought that he had used, without due consideration, the punitive force of the letters after the peace, although they had been issued only in despair of peace. The lord pope had even stated the reason for sending them: namely, that in seeking redress for the archbishop he had so far obtained nothing beyond an empty parade of words. Since, therefore, the occasion no longer existed, it was judged that it would have been more prudent to suppress the letters as well, or to have provided a dispensation concerning the bishops’ absolution in order to strengthen the peace; otherwise he might seem unworthy of peace, as one who did not pursue it at all. They thought he ought better to have deferred the restoration of his rights until more secure times.

### XLI. OF THE NEW DISTURBANCE

But the cunning of the wicked was now devising something more evil against him. Since it knew that it could neither seduce him by prosperity [Col. 0305B] nor crush him by adversity, but saw that he advanced through every temptation, it strove to bring victory upon him in death—acting, as it were, so that the Church might not breathe beneath his wings, and so that in the crime of his persecutors it might compensate itself for its failure to prevail against him. Thus, at its instigation, the action taken against the bishops crossing over to him was represented as an injury to the king, and at once a great movement of new disturbance arose. There followed fierce indignation among the king’s adherents, scarcely restrained fury among his officials, and an evident omen of future calamity. At his very landing there was a rush of knights and retainers to the shore; and the impatience of the enraged would have hastened vengeance, had not the safe-conduct granted to him by the king restrained their madness. [Col. 0305C] Yet, by the providence of divine recompense, a nobler end and a greater glory of suffering awaited him.

### XLII. OF HIS RECEPTION AND THE ESTIMATION OF HIM

Meanwhile, steadfast and undaunted, he entered his see with a magnificent *hypapante*—a ceremonial procession of welcome—and was received with immense rejoicing and glory; the solemnity of his return was splendid indeed. Thereafter much murmuring arose in the kingdom. Some said, “He is just and great-hearted”; others, “No: he deceives himself and acts rashly.” For what could he have undertaken more dangerous than so formidable a punishment concerning a crown allegedly bestowed unlawfully? Or in what way could the kingdom’s honour be more disfigured than by withdrawing from him all the deference due to pontifical honour?

### XLIII. HIS DEFENCE

[Col. 0305D]

Yet, as the truth stands, he could not overlook the injury that threatened. For after the prerogative of creating a new king had been taken from him, it was further arranged, to his still greater humiliation, that the consecration of suffragans to be appointed should occur without his ministry. Consultations concerning the appointment of these men had been planned without his counsel. For this reason, while he was returning to the kingdom, assemblies of the vacant sees were summoned even outside the kingdom; he was to have no part in their deliberation, while, to his greater prejudice, everything was done on the advice of his rival, the prelate of York. Since the bishops of London and Salisbury chose to associate themselves with him, they plainly seemed [Col. 0306A] to have conspired toward their own destruction as well.

It was likewise being prepared contrary to the canons, because under the custom of the realm the Churches retained no freedom to elect, but only the necessity of obeying in appointments: there was no election except a disguised one, and only the command of the royal will was awaited. Thus an evident danger threatened him, and a manifest indication that the peace would not be observed. Therefore he judged that letters of coercion ought properly to be sent ahead, so that, with his adversaries bound, they might have less power to do harm; and, since they would have to attend to themselves, they could not occupy themselves with injuring him. Moreover, before returning, he had complained to the king about those who presumed against his rank, and had obtained the king’s consent to pursue his right lawfully. And lest he be marked as a disturber of peace, although it was dangerous for him to absolve those whom the lord pope had bound, he nevertheless offered them absolution, provided they took the customary and due oath: that concerning the cause of their excommunication they would obey either his judgment or that of the Apostolic See. But demanding to be dismissed altogether free, especially on account of the peace that had now followed and the honour of the king to whom they were making their way, they departed unheard because they were disobedient.

### XLIV. OF HIS STEADFASTNESS

Meanwhile, as the force of the disturbance increased daily, he did not arrange his household with any less diligence or courage, and attended, with the eminence fitting to ecclesiastical persons, to ecclesiastical matters—an undaunted and constant defender of ecclesiastical liberty, like a tower raised in Jerusalem against the face of Damascus. To visit the new king at Winchester, he travelled as far as London. There he was honourably received and visited by clergy and laity alike, thereby stirring much envy against himself among ill-wishers and no slight danger of hatred for those who visited him. At the instigation of certain ill-wishers, he there received the new king’s command that he should beware of travelling through royal cities and towns and remain within his own possessions. He therefore returned and chose to remain in the houses of his see at Canterbury. Yet in all these things his severity was not turned away, but his hand was still stretched out. For, holding immovably to his judgment that the Church’s right must be defended, and walking the path of severity as a strict guardian of what is honourable, he turned neither to the right nor to the left.

### XLV. HOW HIS STEADFASTNESS WAS CENSURED, AND HOW IT IS DEFENDED

[Col. 0306D]

Although very many judged that even then he ought more wisely to have turned for a while toward the path of gentleness and moderation, and through the restraint of patience to have deviated somewhat—enduring lesser evils and avoiding worse—so that the peace of the Church, which had scarcely yet entered the door, might not depart by his entrance. Yet, secure in the purity of his life and strongly kindled by zeal for the Church’s honour, and guarding against prejudice to his former promise, he showed himself ready to perform what befitted the exalted rank of Christ’s Bride and prepared to suffer undauntedly whatever threatened. For those things that had been wrongly usurped in ecclesiastical affairs through the laxity of leniency could no longer be reformed except through the force of strictness. Therefore it was all the more necessary that the medicine should exceed its measure, so that the immoderateness of abuses might yield more powerfully. Thus contraries are cured by contraries. So too, when crooked pieces of wood are straightened, one does not fear bending them in the opposite direction.

Moreover, as he bore the name and dignity of legate of the Apostolic See, contrary to the custom of the realm and without the king’s consent, he weighed everything in the balance of great authority. Hence the spur of rage and hatred among his ill-wishers was sharper; hence their violence against his property greater; hence the blows of injuries more frequent. Yet in all these things his severity was not turned away, but his hand was still stretched out: he wielded the spiritual sword against all who deserved it. For there were those who repeatedly presumed to inflict upon him and his Church, against right and justice, the distress of injury and dishonour. When ecclesiastical censure punished them for this, the wrath of ill-wishers swelled still more against him, until the audacity of the more powerful accomplished what the madness of these others had failed to accomplish—as indeed happened.

### XLVI. OF THE CAUSE AND MANNER OF HIS PASSION

Meanwhile, the fury of his persecutors, inflamed by memory of old grievances and unable to bear the vexation of new burdens, took counsel to repress his efforts by seizing and throwing him into prison. They thought that in this way their lord the king’s anger would be appeased. Accordingly, certain nobles and intimates of the king, hastening from overseas [Col. 0307C] from the court, as though the wicked one directed them toward the deed, came to Canterbury on the fifth day after Christ’s Nativity, without delay or obstacle, having secretly obtained assistance from inhabitants of the place and enemies of the archbishop.

That same day, after dinner, when the household was customarily absent, they came alone as though to visit him; but their real purpose was to discover whether they could seize him unawares. Being well-known and distinguished young men of the royal court, they were quickly and easily admitted even to the inner chamber, where the prelate was holding afternoon conversation with his clerics and monks for the love of God. Received by him graciously and with the honour due to them, they answered his inquiries concerning the success of their journey and the welfare of the lord king. Then they proceeded bitterly to accuse him of sentences unjustly and rashly pronounced against the king’s well-wishers. When he sought to defend himself against them with just arguments, they, as if wearied by his manner, shouted insults and threats and hurried out, violently taking with them some of the archbishop’s household by invoking the royal name, so that their conceived undertaking might have easier success. Yet in all these things his severity was not turned away: from that time his mind was more intent upon the things of Jesus Christ, and he was not moved in the least. He behaved as though he considered all this to be mere intimidation, while nonetheless resolving to endure whatever might be inflicted.

Meanwhile there was a rush of retainers into his courtyard [Col. 0308A] and no small clash of armed men, so that the guards of the archiepiscopal household, struck by justified fear, shut and barred the doors against the assault of those rushing together, in order either to delay or to repel the evil that threatened. Moved and terrified by the tumult and noise, the group of clerics and monks gathered around the archbishop could scarcely persuade him—indeed, could scarcely compel him—to go into the church. Yet he was frightened in no respect, but seemed entirely secure; rather, he behaved as though he regarded any delay of martyrdom as a diminishing of his reward. After they had bolted the doors behind him, he immediately had them opened, saying: “Far be it from us to make the church of God a castle!” He certainly could have turned aside, had he wished, and escaped the hands of the wicked; but he judged it utterly unseemly and plainly dangerous to yield any further, especially since it had already been publicly proclaimed that he had come to give his head for the Church.

That same day, after hearing Mass in the morning, he had remained until dinner in the chapter-house of the monks. There, it is said, he confessed his sins with the greatest contrition to two of the more devout monks of the church, and made himself obedient for satisfaction according to their judgment. For he had long practised this safeguard of humility: wherever he had access to any religious person, he submitted himself to that person’s counsel. He was therefore proceeding in order to stand before the high altar, to complete the struggle, if necessary, in his own see, and to shed his blood for Christ where he had been accustomed to offer Christ for the salvation of himself and the world. [Col. 0308C] But when their company had assembled, the evildoers, unable to seize him in his own house as they had wished—indeed, unable even to enter the house—burst through a certain window and entered through the monks’ cloister, despite their prohibitions and resistance. Their guide was one Robert de Broc, a son of Belial, who had always raged more wickedly and fiercely against him, his property, and his adherents, and who for this reason was under anathema.

When they shouted, “Where is the archbishop?”—for toward evening the place was darker, so that they could not immediately distinguish him—he came down to meet them from the steps, which he had partly ascended, saying: “Here I am. What do you want?” And when one of the knights cried, “That you may die; for it is impossible that you should live any longer,” he answered steadfastly: “And I am ready to die for God and my Church.” They had come in mail and helmets, with drawn swords. The clerics and monks, suddenly terrified by them, scattered here and there, as though here again what is written was fulfilled: “I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.” At first they intended to seize and carry him off. Despairing of being able to do this, because he refused to follow them and resisted them with words alone, and fearing that arriving assistance might rescue him and enable him again to leave the kingdom, they were at once inflamed with the frenzy of murder against him, as though the devil hurried them to the crime.

Therefore, when he was about to be struck, one of the clerics, named Edward and surnamed Grim, sprang forward. Emulating, as it were, the confidence of blessed Peter to defend his master, he boldly interposed an arm wrapped in his cloak against the raised swords, crying out that they should spare his archbishop. Although this act was pious, the bishop of Christ forbade it as nonetheless misguided; mindful, as it were, of that rebuke by which the Lord said to Peter, after he had cut off the ear of the high priest’s servant: “Put your sword into its sheath. Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?—Stop, brother; the Lord does not desire this kind of defence.” [Col. 0309A] Yet the deadly knight did not spare the cleric. First raging against him, he cut almost through the middle the arm which he had interposed with his sword, and by the force of the blow cast him, stunned and as if lifeless, to the ground. O how praiseworthy, that he alone was found ready to suffer with his father! O how happy too, had it been granted him also to die with him! For he too would have deserved the name and reward of martyr if, in laying down his life for his master, he had especially undertaken to defend his master’s cause. Yet it is rightly believed that he was preserved by divine providence, lest the holy man, whose struggle was principally at issue, be deprived of the glory due to his praise, and lest the perversity of ill-wishers attribute the miracles that followed solely to the disciple’s merits.

Then the strong athlete said to the executioners: “If you seek my head, on God’s behalf I forbid you by anathema to touch any of my people, for they are not to be charged with anything that I have done”—thus following, if not the very words, at least the sense of the Lord’s reply: “If you seek me, let these go.” Then, fortifying himself with the sign of the cross, joining his hands to God in the manner of one praying, and bowing his head unmoved before the swords that threatened him, [Col. 0309C] he spoke these last words: “To God, and holy Mary, and the saints of this Church, and blessed Dionysius, I commend myself and my Church.” But the assault of the enraged, impelled by the devil, at once attacked him with swords—more wickedly because he was less armed and unprepared, and without having been tried or examined, though constant and apparently disturbed in nothing. For his severity was not yet turned away: stretching out his neck, he bravely received mighty blows upon his blessed crown, consecrated with holy chrism.

What need of more? Alas for sorrow! On the fifth day after Christ’s Nativity, the savage cruelty of cruel men cut down and felled the Lord’s Christ, God’s anointed, before the altar of Saint Benedict, his head being struck off at the crown with his brain. Thus, by God’s wondrous providence, he met death before the burial places of his dead fellow archbishops; neither resisting, nor complaining, nor murmuring, nor groaning, but after several blows stretching himself upon the pavement as though for prayer. Thus here also his severity was not turned away; from that time his soul, wholly intent upon heaven, rightly left behind the fear of a more terrible vengeance. For it is rightly believed that, when he departed, he pursued vengeance for the injuries done to the Church all the more vigorously in proportion as he had been more deeply afflicted by the experience of his suffering; while he bore his own injuries more joyfully, in proportion as he had the surer hope of recompense. For he had finished the course and kept the faith, and worthily trusted that the crown of justice was henceforth laid up for him.

Then one of the knights, himself also [Col. 0310A] a son of Belial, more detestable in crime than all other criminals throughout all ages, searched out with the point of his sword the remaining portion of brain in the remnant of the now lifeless skull, cast it out, and scattered it on the ground—not so much lest doubt remain concerning death in one already dead, as that his frenzied cruelty might satisfy itself.

### XLVII. INVECTIVE AGAINST THE EXECUTIONERS

O how hard a cruelty! O how dreadful a madness! O how astounding a wickedness, which presumed so irreverently, so atrociously, and so abominably to probe those sacred parts of that consecrated head! The ear recoils from the enormity of the crime; the mind cannot comprehend it, and speech is insufficient to describe it. A singular and singularly wicked event will not allow its memory to be extinguished; its commemoration will always renew in those who recall it the fresh astonishment of horror. Yet the assassins were not content to have completed the abominable slaughter. Acting further in the manner of robbers, they showed themselves by their subsequent ignoble deed to be as base in greed as they were detestable in crime. For after the crime had been accomplished, they burst into the church’s palace, searched every corner of the buildings, and by the violence of insatiable avarice seized for themselves all the furniture and whatever could be found in chests, bags, or packs, whether belonging to the archbishop himself or to his household: gold and silver, cloth and clothing, books, horses, and all baggage. They left nothing to the richer or poorer members of the archiepiscopal household except their daily clothing.

### XLVIII. DETESTATION OF THE DEED

[Col. 0310C]

The deed itself, therefore, was as ruinous as it was detestable. For if they did this in the green wood, what was there not thereafter to fear in the dry? Every church of God had been accustomed to be an asylum for anyone, however wicked and criminal. But if the mother Church of the realm; if a church bearing the title and name not of some one saint but of all the saints of the Lord; if a church protected by great privileges and revered for many holy relics—if this could not be a safeguard for its father and pastor, where thereafter could anyone hope for refuge? And what place for pardon remained for the perpetrators of the crime? If the blood of Abel, shed in the field, and the blood of Zechariah, poured out between temple and altar, cry to the Lord from the earth, [Col. 0310D] how much more terribly does that blood cry out by which the Holy of Holies itself was so grievously and profanely defiled before the altar! Truly they there surpassed Doeg and the agents of King Saul: executioners so much more abominable as the pontiff of our time was more sacred than Abimelech and his whole house.

Nor does it excuse them that they persuaded themselves they were killing him as a criminal and traitor to their lord. First, no treason had been established; moreover, everything belonging to the earlier period had been erased through the intervention of peace and pardon. Further, to rage in this manner even against a criminal who was the Lord’s anointed could not be anything but sacrilege—indeed, sacrilegious parricide—and all the more so because the place was more sacred, the day more solemn, and the person more exalted. Saul was wicked and rejected; nevertheless, holy David, whom Saul also persecuted, was deeply stricken in heart because he had cut off the hem of Saul’s cloak, and said: “May the Lord be merciful to me, that I should not lay my hand upon him, because he is the Lord’s anointed.” And again, to the Amalekite who confessed that he had killed Saul: “Your blood,” he said, “be upon your head; for your own mouth has spoken against you, saying: ‘I killed the Lord’s anointed.’” How much more, then, are they worthy of death—indeed, not even to be expiated by death—who rage against one who is not only the Lord’s anointed, but also makes the Lord’s anointed: namely, one who establishes the king himself and the priest, who performs every sacrament, and who does not fear to consecrate on the altar Christ, King of all kings.

### XLIX. EXAGGERATION OF THE CRIME

[Col. 0311B]

And certainly the holiness of the sufferer greatly magnifies the enormity of the crime. His holiness was plainly proved, first by signs of great self-denial, and then by frequent miracles wrought through him after death. For when he was stripped of his garments in order to prepare him for burial, he was found clad from shoulders to loins in a horrible hair-shirt, wholly sewn around him; above it he wore the habit of a monk, as father of monks, while outwardly bearing the dress of a canon. Thus he lacked no kind of religious garment. What was more wondrous and previously unheard of, he wore also hair-cloth drawers beneath his linen clothing, next to the flesh. Moreover, so great a multitude of lice was seen crawling in the hair-shirts that the spaces appeared more covered than empty. Very many of them were seen, their way already penetrated through the skin, clinging more deeply to the flesh. In this press he had spent a full seven years, as the few who knew of it themselves testified: buried so many days before his death, and food for worms.

Truly wondrous was the strength of that blessed man, who condemned to the burial-cloth of the dead a body accustomed to luxuries, making it so subject to humiliations after purple and fine linen. Truly great was his contempt for earthly things, when a man of such power and honour made himself of such low estate. O what sighs and lamentation from all, and especially what mourning of the monks, when this sight was disclosed to them! Who could restrain tears? Who could refrain from praising the Creator? Who would not sympathize with the afflicted man? Who would not rejoice that he had been delivered from such great evils? Who would not give thanks to God, who had granted so great a grace of perseverance? Who could rightly disbelieve that recompense followed? For he had truly borne the cross in his body, having for so long been crucified with vices and desires. He had truly also completed the cross in his head, at last so cruelly struck in him. It could not justly be supposed otherwise than that, having faithfully followed Christ, he had been happily rewarded by Christ.

### L. WHY HE OUGHT AT ONCE TO HAVE BEEN JUDGED A MARTYR

For he ought to have been believed and reckoned among the martyrs by reason of the title of his precious death, and so much the greater a martyr because the cause of his death was more singular. Almost no one, unless ill-believing, refuses to die for faith in Christ; but hardly anyone except one more perfect in charity desires to die for the statutes of the Church. Therefore that which is rarer and more difficult should rightly be considered more glorious as well. For one faithful in a little thing is faithful also in greater things. The glory of this man’s suffering was also made illustrious by the example of him than whom no greater arose among those born of women. Because he zealously upheld the law, saying to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife,” John became one of the greatest martyrs when his head was cut off. The Church likewise considers and praises the Maccabees as illustrious martyrs because they fought bravely unto death for their ancestral laws.
