Thus this man too was necessarily to be numbered among the chief martyrs, so that, having gained an equal glory through a similar cause—the defence of ecclesiastical liberty—he might be proclaimed as their equal.

### LI. OF THE CONTRARY JUDGMENT OF ILL-WISHERS
[Col. 0312B] There were, however, those who dared to say that he had laboured more from a desire for vain glory, more from zeal for personal vengeance, and that he had contended not without a mark of pride, although beneath the shadow of justice. Yet it is written that the cause makes the martyr, not the punishment, because Truth says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.” But just as punishment alone does not suffice, so neither does the cause alone. First, zeal for justice not according to knowledge is foolish. For the Apostle commanded all not to think more highly than they ought, but to think soberly. Secondly, what exceeds measure is not right. For Solomon says: “Do not be excessively righteous; for there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness.” Nor does the suffering of martyrdom profit apart from charity. For, as the Apostle says: “If I distribute all my possessions to feed the poor, [Col. 0312C] and if I deliver my body so that I may be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.” For love of God cannot dwell together with hatred of one’s neighbour. “For he who does not love the neighbour whom he sees, how can he love God, whom he does not see?” Without love of God, moreover, the dwelling-place of heaven is not obtained, and thus the penal horror of hell is not escaped. There is no middle state; for He who cannot lie says: “He who is not with me is against me.” One must either be a retainer of Babylon or a fellow-citizen of Jerusalem.

Nor, in this world, is there true virtue—even in the best conduct—without the root of charity. Very many indeed possess the appearance of virtue, but not its reality. For often, as blessed Gregory testifies, [Col. 0312D] vices pretend to be virtues: thus avarice wishes to appear thrift, extravagance generosity, cruelty zeal for justice, and laxity compassion. Hence many obstinately argued that neither the reality of virtue nor the reward of martyrdom could have existed in the archbishop, since he appeared in many respects pompous, arrogant, covetous, cruel, and terrifying—and especially since this was not untried by those who belonged to him. For where so great a host of vices is present, virtue cannot be its companion. Virtue and vice cannot exist together. For, as Augustine testifies, covetousness is the root of all evils and charity the root of all goods; the two cannot exist together. Unless one has been uprooted at its root, the other cannot be planted. Where pride reigns, humility has no [Col. 0313A] place. Where cruelty exists, the uprightness of justice does not exist. Where vanity of glory is found, hope of reward does not remain. Therefore, as they maintained, the edifice of martyrdom could not rise upon such foundations. And the greater the popular favour that accompanied him, they answered, the more it was to be feared that it might be said to him: “Amen, I say to you: you have received your reward.”

## LII. WHAT SHOULD MORE TRULY BE JUDGED

Rather, as truth requires, after the days of the repentance he had undertaken, no deed of cruelty or covetousness could be alleged against him except falsely; and it was proper to believe that the faults of the earlier time, if there had been any, had been effaced by repentance. Nor did he suffer from the fault of ostentation, pride, or terror; rather, holding humility within and guarding against contempt from without, he weighed the honour of the office he bore and enhanced the authority of his dignity by his own ability. Especially, in order to avoid the *doxa*—reputation or popular glory—which he had been accustomed to pursue, he sought to provide for himself more by conscience than by human favour. Thus he often displayed something stern in his outward bearing, but in his works always followed the things that are of Jesus Christ; and he concealed the good things in which he excelled so completely that no one took greater care lest his own shameful acts be made public than he did lest his own virtues be disclosed.

Although these virtues may not have been publicly established, yet in doubtful matters the more favourable judgment ought to have been preferred, so that deeds whose motive was uncertain ought to have been interpreted in the better sense. For what is written, “You shall know them by their fruits,” was said of manifest [Col. 0313C] acts that cannot be done with a good intention, such as fornications, thefts, and blasphemies. But there are intermediate acts, good in themselves, such as deeds of virtue, because they may be done with either a good or an evil intention—for example, feeding the poor or clothing the naked. It is rash to judge such things, especially to condemn them. And many such things appeared in connection with the archbishop’s life and death; the more numerous and wonderful they were, the more they ought to have persuaded men to judge him favourably.

For, although before his elevation he had shone in the world as one of its eminent men, afterward he strove no less to stand out among the foremost orthodox Christians while serving Christ. Whatever rank of life he received, he knew only how to be among the greatest. Therefore, immediately [Col. 0313D] after his elevation, he entered upon the narrow way of life, ever proceeding along it more narrowly as it was more tightly constrained by temptations. He burned more conspicuously with concern for his Church and became a more abundant champion of the canonical traditions. If he had set these aside, if he had chosen rather to please men, if he had made more of their ordinances, he could have remained the more powerful master and ruler of the king and of all that belonged to the king, precisely because he was the more exalted. But, as though recalling that saying of the tempter, “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me,” he embraced rather Christ’s saying: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.” He also guarded against the saying of Pope Anacletus: “Nothing is more miserable than that shepherd who glories in the praises of wolves,” and chose “to be lowly in the house [Col. 0314A] of God rather than to rule in the tents of sinners.”

Who could deny these things when they were beyond doubt, or who, even without the subsequent testimony of miracles, ought not to have interpreted them in the better sense? Therefore he boldly defended the ordinances of the Church which curtailed royal power. From this hatred began and grew; from this persecution raged; and from this at last came that wretched event of abominable slaughter. It is known, however, to have been perpetrated not by common, lowly, or even moderately placed men, but by distinguished courtiers and nobles of the realm; so that, though fulfilled tragically, it may nevertheless be seen as honourable. In that same deed, the circumstances that concurred greatly increased both the ignominy of the act and the glory of the passion: the nobility of the assailants, the holiness of the place, and the solemnity of the time.

And in this too there is the more remarkable wonder: between the passion of this Thomas and the feast-day of the apostle Thomas lay the Nativity of Christ. Thus the fifth day is found to have followed, as it were, the fifth feast, just as the fifth day had preceded it; as though the feast-days of men not differing in name and not unlike in passion were not unequally distant from Christ’s feast, and they themselves were not differently distant from Christ. But who would dare compare him with an apostle? Yet Saint Augustine says: “I think that, without any insult, Bishop Cyprian is compared with the apostle Peter insofar as the crown of martyrdom is concerned.” Still, I ought rather to fear lest I seem insulting to Peter. For who does not know that the summit of apostleship is to be preferred to any episcopate? But [Col. 0314C] although the grace of their seats differs, the glory of martyrs is one.

Therefore, since no evils were evident in him, ought not the good things that were seen to have been more justly interpreted in the better sense? His cause was indeed highly commendable, his life highly praiseworthy, and his end highly wonderful. And if there was any fault at the beginning of his honour, the singular glory of his end plainly excused it and ought to be believed to have expiated it. It was therefore plainly right to judge that he had been granted by grace in heaven that which he had always laboured to attain on earth: namely, to obtain a distinguished place among those who abide there.

## LIII. HOW HE APPEARED A TRUE MARTYR

Pressed down and blinded by the cloud of old hatred, the sight of the ill-disposed did not consider the matter with its circumstances as it should have done; and what the fear of the greater men prevented, the faith of the lesser at first feared to proclaim. Yet the people’s murmurs whispered, as far as they dared, the praises of God, until the testimony of truth burst forth from the darkness; and at last, even among the unbelieving greater men, that which the murmur of the lesser had sounded out shone brightly through miracles. O how far human judgments differ from heavenly ones! We had considered his life madness: not content with the boundary set by his predecessors; defending, contrary to custom and against the counsel of his own supporters, the rights of the Church; neither bent by favour nor fear; neither dreading losses nor death; he resisted face to face a king to whom, besides England, the greater part of the French kingdom was subject, at whose very name kings and nations round about [Col. 0315A] trembled, and to whom almost everything he sought came under submission.

But the greater this adversary was, the stronger was his opponent; and, from what followed, he appeared the more righteous athlete, truly numbered among the sons of God. This appeared from the greatness of the miracles that followed at his tomb, at the place where he was slain, and at the place where his bier first stood; and afterward in many parts, first of the kingdom and then of the world, where his aid was invoked. Since signs are for unbelievers, not believers, it must be believed that divine mercy acted thus so that the justice of his cause might appear more certainly to unbelievers and so that, by this fear, the Church might breathe more freely against its penitent adversaries.

His glory thereafter was indeed multiplied far beyond the injury inflicted upon him. Within a short time, the report of the event penetrated not only the innermost and remotest corners of England, but also spread among many peoples of foreign nations. Indeed, it stirred cities, towns, villages, and even rural hamlets throughout England to such a degree that, from the least to the greatest, few remained who did not come to see and honour the tomb of the illustrious martyr. Clergy and laity, poor and rich, commoners and nobles, fathers and mothers with their children, masters with their servants—the same spirit of devotion drew them there. The roads leading to Canterbury were so crowded by the throngs of those travelling and conducting business in booths and stalls that almost everywhere there appeared a density like that of a fair. Neither nights much less than days, nor winters much less than summers, delayed [Col. 0315C] the journey of travellers; and the harsher the season, the more sweetly they regarded fulfilling the vow of visitation, because where access was more arduous, hope of recompense was greater.

So great likewise was the concourse of pilgrims there from remote and overseas regions that they differed very little from the natives in number or frequency. And, as great and trustworthy men testified who had visited holy places throughout the world, neither at the see of blessed Peter, nor at that of the greater James, nor at the shrine of any saint—indeed, not even at that glorious tomb of Christ—had there been seen so continuous a gathering, a greater concourse of persons, or a more conspicuous veneration in offerings. Certainly, clearer and more certain than other miracles, however certain and clear, shone this miracle: that so many persons of so many nations had assembled in one zeal of such great devotion. Who could be believed to have inspired that wondrous unanimity in so many hearts, especially for the exaltation of Christ and his Bride, except He who is wonderful in his saints and makes those of one mind dwell in a house? Who could be judged to have wrought that magnificence of veneration except He who crowns his servants with glory and honour, and restores a hundredfold to those who leave behind for his sake what is their own?

Truly our glorious athlete ascended with his Lord above the west, because through the passion in which he died for righteousness he rose, without comparison, greater in the opinion of men. For God exalted him and gave him a name above every name of the saints, so that, other names being for the time set aside, oaths were sworn in this man’s [Col. 0316A] name, supplications were made in this man’s name, and the needy begged alms and the wealthy gave them for love of him. Greater still: although the metropolitan church in which he suffered was dedicated to the Holy Trinity, as though he had won it for himself by the price of his blood—with God in this respect yielding to his martyr—it began to be designated rather by his name. So much so that anyone travelling to Canterbury or returning from it considered himself guilty of no small offence if he did not expressly acknowledge that he was going to Saint Thomas or returning from Saint Thomas.

The first and only customary signs of pilgrimage had been these: those returning either from Christ’s tomb or from Saint James used to bring back, the former shells and the latter palm branches. Those returning from Saint Thomas adopted a third sign, but one far more precious: as though it were the martyr’s easy yoke and light burden, namely a pewter flask hanging from the neck upon the breast, filled with holy water mingled with a drop of the sacred blood. How great its power and efficacy were among innumerable sick persons in countless places throughout the world cannot be fully described by man.

What glory, then, ought he to be believed to have in heaven, to whom God’s gracious condescension took care to grant so much honour on earth? And indeed, in the very manifestation of his martyrdom one may perceive what our Lord Jesus Christ, his master and head, had already prefigured with respect to faith in his divinity. For, as is read in ecclesiastical history, when everywhere the report spoke of Christ, Pilate reported his deeds to Emperor Tiberius and how he was already believed by very many to be God. Tiberius [Col. 0316C] reported these things to the senate; the senate is said to have rejected them because the people’s judgment had anticipated its authority. What, then, should be believed to have been done in this except that the Christian religion might be seen to be more the work of God than of men? For divine reason willed that faith in Christ should rest more upon his inspiration than upon Roman authority, lest otherwise the envious should complain that force had been brought upon them to believe.

The ill-disposed toward our martyr made the same complaint when, at first, it was sought from the Apostolic See that he should be placed in the catalogue of saints, but this was not obtained. It was obtained, however, through divine power that, by public celebration, the martyr should receive pre-eminent honour; and the excellence of that honour most fittingly compensated even for the previous injuries to the holy place. Indeed, far more rejoicing arose from the glory of subsequent deeds than there had been confusion over the wicked murder. There also came to the churches and ecclesiastical persons the desired time when, the audacity of vexations being restrained, a deeper peace and a fuller honour in honour of the martyr were restored to them.

There was also good hope that what the man full of God had often foretold while still alive would be fulfilled: namely, that the Church of God was to be freed by the shedding of blood alone. He had earnestly desired that this should happen by his own blood, and had not ceased to pray for it; and there was already much indication that he would be heard because of his reverence. For at last fear and amazement compelled even his more powerful rivals, among the other nobles and counts of the realm, to throw themselves down in tears and groans before the sacred mausoleum, devoutly to beseech mercy, and [Col. 0317A] to ask forgiveness for their deeds.

It would surely be the height of madness not to heed so many and such manifest mighty works of God, and, since the voice of the people is the voice of God, to dissent from the harmonious testimony of so great and so many persons. Moreover, He in whose hand are the hearts of kings touched more powerfully the heart of the illustrious and devout king himself. In order to obey the legates of the Roman Church, he crossed with remarkable speed from Ireland, which he was subjugating, through England into Normandy; and there, before them and his overseas clergy, he first cleared himself by oath of complicity in the abominable murder, wishing to preserve his reputation. Then, acknowledging himself guilty at least in this—that his excessive anger had furnished an occasion for the crime—he subjected that summit of imperial power to the humblest penitence, undertook a great and grave burden of satisfaction at the legates’ discretion, and promised to correct what had been wrongly presumed in England. [Col. 0317B] [Col. 0318A]

He conquered—plainly, the distinguished defender of Christ’s Bride, though slain, conquered and wrested from them what he could not obtain while living by warnings, threats, or the terrors of ecclesiastical censure. The sequence and variety of the miracles attributed to his merits will be more fully evident from the writings of those to whom it was granted to see or verify them. For our own concern has rather been to hand down to knowledge and memory the martyr’s holiness, the justice of his cause, the reality of his martyrdom, and its manifestation, so that posterity might have grounds for being warned not again to raise such a question. Whoever does not beware will surely have much cause to fear Him whom zeal for his house consumed: Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honour and dominion through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0317]

# THE PASSION OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY AND MARTYR, BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR

## [FIRST PASSION]

[Col. 0317C] Worthily, brothers, is the splendid feast of this day, thronged by the devotion of the faithful, solemnly and famously observed and celebrated. On it, the death of Thomas, our father and protector of our country, an unconquered athlete, is made precious in the sight of God, and his victory is known to be glorious before angels and men.

For today, made a spectacle to God, angels, and men, he fought manfully for the law of his God even unto death; remaining steadfast in the sacred faith, distinguished by a triumphant death and crowned with his own blood, he surrendered his body to the earth and brought his blessed soul into heaven with ineffable joy. Such a death is therefore fittingly called a birth, because it gives birth to life. For the present life is wretched and mortal, while that death is blessed and life-giving. Thus our glorious [Col. 0317D] martyr passed from this mortal life, through this life-giving death, to life eternal. Today, adorned with the manifold glory of his merits, he exchanged the exile of his earthly prison for his heavenly homeland; he passed from labour to rest, from the world to the Father.

Today honour and reverence are offered on earth to blessed Thomas by the faithful; in heaven, blessedness and glory have been conferred upon him with the angels—joy because of newness, security because of eternity. Hence, mighty on land and sea and reigning with Christ, he gladdens mortals with wondrous signs and does not cease to shine on earth through marvellous miracles. Yet since it is altogether fitting that worthy sons should strive to imitate a loving father, it is expedient briefly and in plain speech to unfold what outstanding merits went before in the life of so great a bishop, by whose prerogative he enjoys so great a glory of blessedness [Col. 0318C] and excels in such great power of miracles.

Therefore, when Archbishop Theobald of happy memory had fallen asleep with his fathers in a good old age, Thomas, archdeacon of the Church of Canterbury, was solemnly chosen in the name of the Holy Trinity as archbishop and primate of all England, and shortly afterward was consecrated. Devout minds held a firm hope and confidence in the Lord that, once consecrated, he would preside with his outward attire changed and his character improved. For it was most firmly held that that see was the see of saints: it either received a saint or made one, or else swiftly and easily rejected an unworthy man. This too was mercifully fulfilled in blessed Thomas.

Therefore, when the chosen bishop of God had been elevated and anointed with the sanctification of sacred unction, he immediately received the reality of the sacrament and was filled with manifold grace of the Holy Spirit. Walking in newness of life, as a new man he was changed into another man, and all things in him were turned to the better. He consecrated the beginning of his episcopate with such great grace that, clothed—though secretly—in monastic garb, he fulfilled the work and merit of a monk. And he who, after the example of the Baptist, had perfectly conceived in his heart with steadfastness a zeal for justice, strove also to be made equal to him in the garment of penitence. Casting aside the fine linen which he had hitherto been accustomed to wear while the luxuries of kings flattered him, he clothed himself in the harshest hair-shirt over his bare flesh. He also added hair-cloth drawers, in order more strictly to mortify the flesh and give life to the spirit.

These things, [Col. 0319A] like the other exercises of the spiritual life, he concealed beneath other garments, with very few persons aware of them, from the eyes and knowledge of men, because he sought glory not from man but from God. Then that illustrious man, entering upon the ordinances of God, began to be more abundant in fasting, more frequent in vigils, more prolonged in prayer, and more earnest in preaching. He performed with every diligence the pastoral office entrusted to him by God, so that he would by no means allow the rights of clergy or Church to be impaired.

He was accustomed to have such a grace of compunction in the secrecy of prayer and in the solemnities of Mass that, his eyes trained to weeping, he wholly poured himself out in tears and, in this grace, recalled Arsenius. Knowing also that mercy mitigates judgment and that godliness has the promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come, he bore such bowels of compassion toward the afflicted and the poor that he was accustomed to anticipate the needy with blessings of almsgiving. He counted among his acquaintances and intimates the humblest persons whom a reputation for religious devotion distinguished, and, in order to learn from them to hunger and thirst for righteousness, he more frequently enjoyed their more private conversation. Toward such servants and soldiers of Christ the merciful man chose to be generous and liberal in clothing and food, though in both he had resolved to be moderate and sparing toward himself.

For what would he deny Christ, when he was to shed his own blood for Christ? Since he owed a cloak or tunic to one who asked, he strove to give beyond measure even his own flesh. For he knew that no one would ever be lavish with his own flesh if he were known to be covetous of any temporal thing. This is the fragrance of the garments of our Jacob, like the scent of a field blessed by the Lord. These are the changes of raiment of our great priest. This, I say, is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. Until then the merciful Lord, who makes poor and makes rich, humbles and exalts, had willed to heap riches upon his servant and enlarge him with honours; thereafter he determined to test him by adversities. By testing him He more certainly proved whether he loved Him, but granted grace more abundantly. For He made with the temptation a way of escape, so that he might endure it.

Therefore, when the envious enemy saw the new bishop, the new man, flourishing with such manifold grace of virtues, he devised to send the scorching heat of temptation, so that he might suffocate the newly arisen shoot of merits. [Col. 0319D] Without delay, he who separates a man from his Lord and a friend from his neighbour sowed irreconcilable discords between the king and the archbishop.

[Meanwhile, at the instigation of the man of God’s opponents—indeed, of God’s opponents—a dispute arose concerning the customs of the kingdom and ecclesiastical law. When contention over these matters had been prolonged for some time, the king summoned a council and, in accordance with the assent of the nobles, proposed the ancestral customs of the realm. With obstinate insistence he demanded that they be confirmed by the authority and in writing of the archbishop and the suffragan bishops. In this he prevailed to such a degree that, as the bishops and archbishops swore under fear of imminent danger, he himself, having given an oath, consented only verbally and unwillingly that the king’s demand should be granted. But soon recovering his courage, and stronger after his fall, he steadfastly refused to confirm those customs, unlawfully conceded against the liberty of the Church.

> **Note:** In place of the material enclosed here in brackets, the Paris manuscript has the following: “And when the king’s anger, kindled and inflamed by the torches of those who disparaged him, grew hotter day by day, many nobles of the realm who had seemed friends in calm times became Satans to the archbishop. Finally, summoned to the court at Northampton [Col. 0320D], ostensibly to give security for observing certain customs of the realm which he testified were contrary to truth and reason, he refused; and, setting his authority against the dangers—or rather exposing it—he threatened a sentence in defence of ecclesiastical liberty.”]

The poison of anger and discord advanced so greatly by such developments that, when he was summoned to that council, almost everyone rose against the bishop with calumnies and accusations and assailed him with shameful insults. Since scarcely anyone could be found who would speak with him or do him good, while everything turned against him and delay was drawing on a certain danger, he appealed, yielded to injustice, withdrew secretly with a few companions, reached the sea, [Col. 0320B] and crossed over. But he went on his way rejoicing and exulting, because he had been deemed worthy to suffer insult from the council for righteousness.

Having approached the most blessed Pope Alexander, who at that time had come into France, he carefully laid before him certain difficult matters, as he had also done before, both concerning the salvation of his own soul and concerning the oppressions of the Church which he had undertaken to govern. When the universal father and shepherd had fully learned the cause of his fellow-bishop’s arrival, he gave thanks for so great and such a pillar raised up in the house of God. He rejoiced yet more that so wonderfully burning and shining a lamp had been found to illuminate the western darknesses of the world.

At that time Louis, the most Christian king of the French, received the venerable archbishop into great favour and, at the pope’s request, generously supplied him and his companions with all necessities. For the revenues of the lord of Canterbury had already been ordered confiscated. Thus, in exile, the most blessed Thomas in the utmost humility expiated the pride into which he had entered amid his former glory, and brought every movement of his soul back to uprightness and contempt for the world. Angered by these and other fragrances of virtue, the wicked extortioner, the devil, whetted his fury against the relatives, kinsmen, and household of the holy bishop and stirred up against them proscription with monstrous cruelty. Then one could see the pitiable spectacle of persons of both sexes, of different ages and conditions: men and women, husbands with their families, even nursing infants with pregnant women, sent into exile and, to increase his grief and humiliation, presented before their loving father desolate and mourning.

When the holy bishop beheld the removal of old men and little children, whose sustenance still hung upon their mothers’ breasts, the sword of compassion pierced his soul more deeply, so that the force of grief wholly took possession of him. Thus he became a martyr before his death, afterward to receive a double crown for his future martyrdom. Yet he was not thereby drawn away or enticed. For, perfect in charity, he did not know how to be led astray by flatteries, deceived by falsehoods, or [Col. 0321A] broken by adversities. The branch of the heavenly vine could be shaken, but not torn away.

Thus he persevered, more ready for temptations, awaiting in patience the regard of divine mercy; and by the merit of his conduct he won the favour of all. He was most welcome to the king of France in counsel, very familiar to the princes of the kingdom and the fathers of the churches, and held in reverence by all as was fitting. For Thomas’s counsel was desirable like that of Hushai, his companionship delightful like Jonathan’s, and his work zealous for justice like Phinehas’s. The fame of his goodness grew daily among foreigners, among whom he lived innocently, so much that the natives of the kingdom called him not simply “the archbishop,” but “the holy archbishop.”

[Col. 0321B] Thus the most blessed father, in exile with his companions, completed almost six years. During these years he had grown into a perfect man, while throughout that entire time peace between him and the king of England could by no means be restored, but seemed rather to have become more distorted. At last it pleased God, disposer of all things, to recompense the merits of his Thomas and to complete his long labours with the victorious palm of martyrdom. Therefore He changed the king’s mind for the better; and through the fatherly exhortation of the lord pope, the counsel of the king of France and many bishops, and the suppliant intervention of princes, the king received the archbishop into favour and permitted him to return to his Church.

At the beginning of the seventh year, when the man beloved by God had now been sanctified by spiritual exercises and made more perfect by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, he hastened to return as quickly as possible to his see. For the loving father did not wish to leave the Church of Canterbury desolate any longer; nor did he wish to delay what, as is believed, he had seen in the spirit—the glory of his struggle—or by dying elsewhere to deprive his own see of the honour of his martyrdom. Having crossed the sea, the archbishop and future martyr was received in great glory and honour, especially by the monks, with a solemn procession as though he were an angel of the Lord. In his church all wept for joy and cried with thanksgiving: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Having received all with the kiss of peace, he dwelt familiarly among them and edified everyone by his conduct and by the word of exhortation.

Soon afterward, having received orders not to travel through England in carrying out his office, the bishop remained in his own church, fearlessly awaiting the hour at which he would receive from God the crown of martyrdom. For, forewarned by many persons, he knew that his life would be short and death was at the doors. There, as though he had only then begun to live, he strove to redeem the time already spent in life through spiritual exercises. Knowing that the present life is a way and warfare, he freed himself from vices so that he might be holy in body and spirit; armed with virtues, he girded himself for the course and for the conflict of battle. Thus, completing the race, he ran, not as one uncertain; fighting well, not as one beating the air. Then [Col. 0322A] his thought and speech were almost always about the end of this way and the misery of this life.

The father had remained scarcely a month in his church when, behold, on the fifth day of the Lord’s Nativity, four knights came to Canterbury—rather, sworn satellites of Satan. They were men conspicuous for the eminence of their birth, but soon by the audacity of monstrous crime to condemn the glory of knighthood and the title of their lineage to perpetual infamy. Entering to the archbishop, since no greeting prompted by goodwill was at hand for them, they omitted any formula of salutation and addressed him with haughtiness and pride. They gave and received threats, adding a reply to threats. At last, leaving behind reproaches and insults, they went out; then immediately returned and burst into the monks’ cloister with a large retinue of armed men, themselves armed.

The bishop had already gone ahead of them, with modesty and dignity, into the oratory. The monks had advised him—indeed compelled him, because of the solemn day—to perform the evening synaxis, when he saw the armed men behind him in the middle of the cloister. Their own malice ought to have kept them out of the church; but reverence for the solemnity did not dissuade them from the crime, nor did the patriarch’s innocence restrain them from bloodshed. So completely had the desire to commit a shameful and grievous crime possessed and blinded them that they considered neither the loss of their knightly honour nor the danger of any consequence. Therefore, headlong and senseless, pursuing the archbishop with drawn swords, they entered the church, furiously crying: “Where is that traitor?” When no one answered, [Col. 0322C] they repeated: “Where is the archbishop?”

Knowing that, as Christ’s confessor and soon-to-be martyr, he was falsely attacked under the former title but that the latter belonged to him by office, he came down from the steps to meet them. “Here,” he said, “I am.” He displayed such steadfastness that neither his spirit seemed shaken by fear nor his body by terror. The knights immediately laid hands on him and held him in order to drag him outside the church to carry out their purpose. But fearing the crowd of both sexes running together from every side, lest he might somehow be rescued and their intent frustrated, they hastened the crime.

When one of them stretched out and swung his sword at the archbishop’s head, he nearly cut off the arm of a cleric standing nearby and at the same time wounded the Lord’s anointed himself in the head. For that cleric had stretched his arm over the father’s head in order to receive—or rather to dash against it—the blow of the assailant. The just man stood, suffering for justice, like an innocent lamb, without murmur or complaint; offering himself as a whole burnt offering to the Lord, he invoked the patronage of the saints. And lest any of the deadly satellites should be charged with wickedness for having left the bishop untouched, the second and third struck their swords cruelly upon the crown of the steadfast athlete, shattered it, and threw the victim of the Holy Spirit to the ground. The fourth, raging with more than deadly—indeed, fiendish—cruelty, when he was already fallen and already expiring, cut away the tonsured crown, shattered the skull, and, thrusting his sword-point into the crown of the head, spilled his brains with blood [Col. 0323A] upon the stone pavement.

The differing substance of the two, distinctly separated in their mingling, seemed to teach one who devoutly regarded it the martyr’s merits. For in the brain shone the fine linen of innocence; in the blood reddened the purple of martyrdom. Adorned fittingly with both as with a wedding garment, the martyr Thomas was made worthy to be a guest at the heavenly table. Thus our most blessed and unconquered martyr Thomas, adamantine in the virtue of steadfastness, a precious stone of the heavenly building, squared by the blows of swords, was joined in heaven to Christ, the corner-stone.

[Col. 0324A] Thus our Abel, perfected in the glory of martyrdom, fulfilled many years in a short time. Countless miracles proclaim his innocent life and the disposition of his mind, precious before God through the merit of his cause; they are wonderfully displayed not only at the place of his resting, but also in diverse nations and kingdoms. Therefore, brothers, longing after him, follow the paths of truth and justice, so that with him we may attain the kingdom of light and glory, in which God reigns through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

# ANOTHER, SECOND PASSION

[Col. 0323]

[Col. 0323B] Dearest brethren, as we celebrate the birthday into heaven of the glorious martyr Thomas, since we cannot adequately recount the distinguished features of his whole life and conduct, let a brief discourse run through the manner and cause of his passion.

Blessed Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, therefore, just as he had been incomparably vigorous in the conduct of affairs in his former offices of chancellor and archdeacon, so after assuming the office of shepherd he became devoted to God beyond all human expectation. For once consecrated, he was suddenly changed into another man. He secretly put on haircloth; he also wore haircloth drawers reaching to the knees; and, concealing a monastic habit beneath the respectable dress of a cleric, he wholly compelled the flesh to serve the spirit. Applying himself to God, [Col. 0323C] he strove without interruption to please Him through the exercise of every virtue; and, knowing himself to have been appointed a watchman in the house of the Lord, he diligently fulfilled the ministry entrusted to him. He endeavoured to restore and bring back to their proper condition the rights and dignities of the Church which secular power had usurped for itself. Hence, when a grave dispute concerning ecclesiastical right and the customs of the realm arose between himself and Henry, king of the English, a council was convened, and those customs were put forward which the king himself stubbornly demanded should be confirmed in writing both by the archbishop and by his suffragans. The archbishop steadfastly refused, maintaining that they plainly overthrew ecclesiastical liberty. He was therefore subjected to boundless insults, crushed by harsher losses, and assailed by innumerable injuries. [Col. 0323D] At length, when death was threatened against him, since the cause of the Church had not yet been fully made known and the persecution appeared personal, he judged that malice must be yielded to. Thus driven into exile, he was honourably received at Sens by Pope Alexander III, and was diligently commended to the monastery of Pontigny.

[LESSON 2.] Meanwhile, in England the revenues of its archbishop are confiscated, his estates devastated, and his possessions plundered; and, a new form of punishment having been devised, [Col. 0324B] Thomas’s entire kindred is proscribed at once. All his friends and household, and whoever was connected with him under any title whatever, are likewise banished indiscriminately, without regard to condition or fortune, rank or order, age or sex. For old and decrepit persons, infants crying in their cradles, and women lying in childbed were driven into exile. All who had reached the age of discretion were compelled, upon touching the most holy things, to swear that, once they had crossed the sea, they would immediately present themselves to the Archbishop of Canterbury, so that, pierced by the sword of compassion, he might bend the firmness of his purpose to the king’s will. But the man of God, setting his hand to mighty deeds, patiently endured exile, losses, insults and reproaches, and the proscription of parents and friends for Christ’s name, [Col. 0324C] utterly unbroken or changed by any injury. Indeed, so great was the constancy of Christ’s confessor that he seemed to teach all his fellow exiles:

> Every land is a homeland to the brave.

[LESSON 3.] But when the king heard of his immovable constancy, he sent threatening messages through certain abbots of the Cistercian Order to the general chapter and procured his expulsion from Pontigny. Blessed Thomas, fearing that holy men might suffer loss on his account, departed voluntarily. But before he left that place, he was strengthened by a divine revelation, a heavenly sign being shown to him that he would return to the Church in glory and depart to the Lord through the palm of martyrdom. Expelled from Pontigny, [Col. 0324D] he was received by Louis, the Most Christian King of the Franks, who treated him with the greatest humanity until peace should be restored. Yet Louis too was repeatedly, though unsuccessfully, urged not to bestow any benefit of kindness upon the traitor of the King of the English. The final fury proceeded to monstrous lengths and to a cruelty dreadful to pious ears. Although the Catholic Church prays even for heretics, schismatics, and faithless Jews, it was forbidden that anyone should assist him with the support of prayers. Thus, exiled for six continuous years, afflicted by various and countless injuries, and like a living stone being squared for the construction of the heavenly building by manifold cuttings and pressures, [Col. 0325A] the more he was pressed to fall, the more firmly and immovably he was proved to stand. For gold so anxiously tested could not be consumed, nor could a house founded upon firm rock be overthrown.

[LESSON 4.] Finally, through the intervention both of the supreme pontiff and of the King of France, many days were appointed for restoring peace. Because the servant of God would accept it only with the honour of the Church and his own integrity preserved, they departed from one another unreconciled. At length the supreme pontiff, taking pity on the desolation of the English Church, by issuing threats scarcely [Col. 0325B] at last extorted the restoration of peace to the Church.

The kingdoms rejoiced, therefore, that the king had received the archbishop into favour: some believing the business genuinely conducted, others conjecturing otherwise. Thus, in the seventh year of his exile, the shepherd returned to England, either to free Christ’s sheep from the bites of wolves or to spend himself for the flock entrusted to him. He was received by clergy and people with inexpressible joy, all weeping and saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” But after a few days he was again subjected to losses and injuries beyond measure and number; and by public edict he was forbidden to leave the bounds of his church. Whoever showed a cheerful face to him or to any of his household was deemed a public enemy. Amid all this [Col. 0325C] his courage was not broken, but his hand still stretched out for the liberation of the Church. On the fifth day after the Lord’s Nativity, four courtiers came to Canterbury, men distinguished indeed by birth but notorious for evil deeds. Entering, they assailed the pontiff with insulting words, provoked him with abuse, and at last gravely threatened him.

[LESSON 5.] The man of God modestly answered each point as reason required, adding that many injuries had been inflicted upon himself and the Church of God, and that there was no one to correct the wrongs; henceforth he could neither be silent nor wished to be silent, but would exercise the office of pastoral care.

The foolish in heart were disturbed by these words, and, speaking iniquity on high, immediately went out. [Col. 0325D] After they had gone, the pontiff proceeded into the church to render Christ the evening praises.

Satan’s mailed attendants followed behind him with drawn swords, a great armed force following. As the monks barred them from entering the church, the priest of God, hastening forward—and soon to become Christ’s sacrifice—opened the door to his enemies: “The church,” he said, “is not to be shut up like a fortress.” As they burst in, some furiously demanding, “Where is the traitor?” and others, “Where is the archbishop?”, Christ’s confessor went forth fearlessly to meet them. When they threatened him with death, he said: “I too shall gladly accept death for God’s Church; but on God’s behalf I command you not to harm any of mine.” Thus he imitated Christ, who in His passion said: “If you seek me, [Col. 0326A] let these go their way.” Therefore the ravening wolves rushed upon the shepherd; degenerate sons upon their own father; most cruel executioners upon Christ’s sacrifice. With deadly swords they severed the consecrated crown of his head; casting the Anointed of the Lord to the ground, they most cruelly scattered his brains and blood over the pavement—a thing horrible even to tell. Thus the grain of wheat was cut down amid chaff, the keeper of the vineyard in the vineyard, the leader in the camp, the shepherd in the sheepfold, the cultivator on the threshing-floor; thus the righteous man, killed by the unrighteous, exchanged his house of clay for the heavenly palace.

The martyr’s final words, scarcely distinguishable amid the confused shouting, were, according to the testimony of those standing nearest, these: “To God and blessed Mary, to Saint Dionysius, and to the patron saints of this church [Col. 0326B] I commend myself and the cause of the Church.” In all the torments endured by this most unconquered athlete of God, he uttered no cry, gave no groan, and opposed neither arm nor garment to the striker; but holding motionless, until all was accomplished, the head which he had bent to meet the swords, as though prostrate in prayer, he fell asleep in the Lord.

[LESSON 6.] The wicked men then returned to the holy pontiff’s palace and divided among themselves whatever valuables they could find. Great grief at the death of the innocent man and the plundering of his goods seized all, together with unbounded anguish of heart. Yet, so that his passion might more closely resemble the Lord’s Passion, divine mercy suddenly made a way of escape with the trial; and through certain visions, as though foreshadowing future [Col. 0326C] miracles, it indicated that the martyr would shortly be glorified by signs, that joy would return after his death, and that a multitude of sick persons would obtain the favour of benefits. Truly this saint was to be glorified: fighting for the Church, he suffered in the church, in a holy place, at the season of the Lord’s Nativity, among fellow priests and the hands of religious men, so that in the contest of the pontiff all circumstances might concur both to reveal the impiety of the persecutors and to stain their name with everlasting reproach. After the martyr’s death, divine vengeance raged so fiercely against his persecutors that they were swiftly removed from the midst and appeared no more. Some were suddenly carried off without confession or the viaticum; others tore off their own fingers or tongues piecemeal with their teeth; [Col. 0326D] others, running with putrefaction, wasted through their whole body, and tortured with unheard-of agonies before death; others struck down by paralysis; others made mad; others expiring in frenzy—all left clear indications that they were paying the penalties of their unjust persecution and their devised parricide. Therefore let the virgin mother Church rejoice that she has gained a new martyr’s triumph; let her rejoice that a new Zechariah has been slain in the temple for her liberation. Let her rejoice that the blood of a new Abel cries to the Lord for her against men of blood. For the voice of the shed blood, the voice of the brains scattered by the swords of deadly attendants, filled both earth and heaven with renowned clamour. At the cry of this blood the earth was shaken and trembled; the powers of heaven also were shaken, [Col. 0327A] so that nation seemed to rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom in vengeance for innocent blood—indeed, so that a kingdom became divided against itself, and terrors from heaven and great signs occurred. But that it might openly appear to the world that the Lord had magnified His saint, the martyr began, from the first time of his martyrdom, to shine forth in many miracles: restoring sight to the blind, walking to the lame, hearing to the deaf, and speech to the dumb. Then cleansing lepers, strengthening paralytics, curing dropsy and every kind of incurable disease, raising the dead, and wonderfully commanding even demons and all the elements, he extended his hand also to unprecedented and unheard-of signs of his power. For those deprived of eyes or genitals deserved through his merits to receive new [Col. 0328A] members. Certain persons, moreover, who presumed to disparage the saint’s miracles were suddenly struck and compelled, even unwillingly, to proclaim them. Finally, the martyr prevailed so greatly over all his rivals that all who disparaged him came and venerated and worshipped at his tomb.

The outstanding athlete of God, Thomas, suffered in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation, according to Dionysius, 1174, on the Kalends of January, on Tuesday, at about the eleventh hour, so that the Lord’s Nativity might be for his labour a birth into rest. May the same God and our Lord Jesus Christ deign to bring us to that rest—He who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## THIRD PASSION

[Col. 0327]

[Col. 0327B] While negotiations concerning the restoration of peace between the King of England and the Lord of Canterbury continued for a long time, the king, having sent envoys to the lord pope, promised to observe whatever form of peace the lord pope might prescribe. The lord pope therefore decreed that the king should fully receive the archbishop into his favour and restore to him, for free possession under his authority, everything taken from him, while hostages were given—namely the King of France, the Count of Flanders, and certain others—as security for the future keeping of peace. Yet while these matters were being transacted, the King of England had already caused his son to be crowned, relying on the authority of certain letters which he had obtained from the lord pope when he first entered the regions of Gaul. Their content was this: that it pleased the lord pope that the son of the King of England should be crowned. [Col. 0327C] Nor was this directed against the Lord of Canterbury, whose right it was to crown the King of England. The Archbishop of York also had laid his hand upon the king’s son, relying on the authority of certain letters which the king had obtained from the lord pope; their content was this: that York had permission to crown the king if the see of Canterbury were vacant. When all these things had been completed in this manner, the Archbishop of Canterbury went to receive the king into his favour. The king received him quite amicably, though not with a kiss, and promised to restore all his possessions; but he did not fulfil this, for he refused to restore some of the immovable property. When Canterbury had again informed the Roman curia of this, the lord pope, writing to the king more sternly than before, commanded that all the archbishop’s possessions be restored. The archbishop also obtained [Col. 0327D] secret letters with this content: if within forty days his possessions were not restored to the archbishop, the king should be subject to excommunication and his land be placed under suspension. He received besides other letters: namely, letters of excommunication against two bishops of England and of suspension [Col. 0328B] against the Archbishop of York and many others. When the king received the papal letters, he promised to restore everything to the archbishop. But on the appointed day when the archbishop was to be restored, the king did not come in person to conduct the archbishop through the duchy, as he had promised, but sent a single cleric to escort him. Thus, as the archbishop prepared to cross the sea, he heard that the bishops of England were gathering to meet him; and, fearing to be vexed by appeals from them, he sent ahead letters of excommunication against some and of suspension against others, which, as we have said, he had obtained from the pope. Then, entering the gateway of England, he found the aforesaid bishops assembled. When they requested absolution and restoration from him, the archbishop addressed them very gently in this manner: [Col. 0328C] “If you present yourselves to your mother in fitting humility, we shall show you mercy as far as we can—indeed, beyond what lies within our right.” They did not accept this, but instead crossed the sea to approach the king. The archbishop, however, proceeding on his begun journey, was honourably received in his city; there, celebrating the solemnities of Mass, he excommunicated certain persons who had sinned against him, freely exercising his authority. Then, having gathered a company, he prepared to visit the king’s son. Hearing this, the latter commanded him to return to his own territory and be content with its bounds. Yet the archbishop went to London; and there, after celebrating the solemnities of Mass, he excommunicated certain persons. Returning thence to Canterbury, he held ordinations there and celebrated the feast of the Nativity solemnly, surrounded by a great [Col. 0328D] crowd of people. Meanwhile the aforesaid bishops, approaching the king, complained that some of them had been excommunicated and others suspended. The king was therefore violently moved and complained that no one wished to avenge his injuries. Four noble knights and intimates of the king, whether stirred only by these words [Col. 0329A] or receiving some other command, set out that same day and crossed the sea toward England. On the second day after the feast of the Innocents, having gathered on the way a force sufficient to carry out the crime, they came to Canterbury. At about the ninth hour of the same day, the archbishop, refreshed by a meal, sat with his clergy. Hastening in to him, they commanded on the king’s behalf that he absolve the bishops of England, adding threats of death if he did not do so. But he said, “Do you bring letters for this embassy?” and added, “If they present themselves to Holy Church in due humility, they shall receive absolution.” But they departed, declaring that the archbishop had lost the king’s favour; not withdrawing far from the door of the house, indeed arming themselves in the episcopal court itself, [Col. 0329B] they prepared to return. Those about the bishop, seeing this, begged him to seek safer places in the monastery. But he said: “My brothers, it is not fitting that the church should be polluted with the blood of sinners; rather, we must wait here, and whatever threatens must be borne patiently.” But they seized him by force and brought him into the monastery. He went by certain steps to the altar of Blessed Benedict, which stood at the entrance of the church. Meanwhile the knights, bursting through the cloister doors behind him, reached the bishop with drawn swords. The archbishop met them on several steps, begging for the lives of his men and praying for his own killers. “Gladly,” he said, “so far as my frailty permits, I shall accept death.” [Col. 0329C] Then, bowing his head, full of confession, he received the first blow of death and rendered his soul to God; his lifeless body fell to the ground. The first of the torturers cut off the top of his head; while two others struck him upon the head, the fourth drove his sword more deeply into it and scattered his gouged-out brains over the pavement. The monks of that church then gathered the brains and blood that had been spilled; after scraping the pavement, they placed the brains upon the head and bound it about with cloths. Also, as I learned from the truthful report of men, the body, long dead, raised itself up, [Col. 0330A] signed both itself and those standing by with the life-giving sign of the cross, and again fell to the ground. Then the monks removed his garments and found beneath them the roughest haircloth, his flesh horribly torn and full of worms. Seeing this, even some of the evildoers struck their breasts. There were found beneath him letters which he had received on the night before the Lord’s Day from certain intimates of the king, concerning his imminent death. Meanwhile, as we have again truly learned, a certain blind man who had belonged to his household ran up, touched his own eyes with the blood of the slain man, and received sight. We have also heard that while the archbishop was still alive, a London priest who had for a long time lost the use of his tongue saw in a vision that, if his tongue were touched with the archbishop’s [Col. 0330B] blood, it would immediately be loosened. The same vision concerning the aforesaid mute man was repeatedly revealed to a member of his household. Therefore both arose and went to Canterbury; and, as they were drawing near the city, they heard that the archbishop had been killed. Made more confident by this, they entered the city and requested that some of the slain man’s blood be given them. Thereupon the tongue of the mute man was touched and loosened. Very many who afterwards heard his Mass reported to our acquaintances what had happened. A monk of that same church, spending the night in prayer in the crypt in which the aforesaid archbishop was buried among certain other martyrs, saw first one of the martyrs buried there celebrating Mass, and then, after incense had been kindled, walking round the company of the archbishop. When he had seen this frequently [Col. 0330C] and at last reported it publicly, five members of the convent were sent to open the tomb. Opening it, they found a fragrance of marvellous sweetness and the joints of his hands pliable as if he still lived; the whole convent then ran up and recognized this. Very many other miracles are also said to occur there. I have taken care to commit to writing what I could know more certainly. A certain man was present when I had written the foregoing, asserting that one of the archbishop’s killers, driven mad, had killed his own son.

## FOURTH PASSION

[Col. 0329]

[Col. 0329D] The most blessed Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, after a peace apparently restored with the venerable Henry, King of the English, through Pope Alexander, King Louis of France, archbishops, and many others, returned by God’s will to his Church. There he devoted himself so earnestly to prayers and preaching, almsgiving, vigils, and fasts that even those to whom his religious devotion had been known in the regions of Gaul marvelled. But he had not yet remained a month in his Church when, behold, four attendants came from beyond the sea, whose [Col. 0330D] names we think should be recorded as a mark of their wretched soldiery: Richard Brito, Reginald son of Urso, Hugh de Morville, and William de Tracy. They addressed him in this manner: “We bring a command from our king and lord that you go to his son, now reigning, to do what you owe him to do, to submit to the law if you have offended him in any respect, to restore to communion the excommunicated bishops—namely Gilbert Foliot of London and Jocelin of Salisbury—and to restore office to the rest who are suspended.” But the archbishop, possessing the simplicity of the dove [Col. 0331A] and the prudence of the serpent, replied: “I have received a new command from the king that I should not travel through his cities and towns or come to him. Moreover, it is known that the aforementioned bishops were not excommunicated or suspended by me, but by the lord pope, because within my diocese, without my consent, they presumed to consecrate and crown this new king—may the Lord grant him saving grace. Therefore their satisfaction must precede their absolution.” But at these words, the aforesaid men—brutish in their sense of crime and without understanding—at once broke out in threats. As they went out amid tumult and insults, the holy prelate replied: “Seek someone who fears your threats; for your swords are not readier than my spirit for martyrdom. Seek someone who will flee from you; for you will find me foot to foot in the battle of the Lord.” [Col. 0331B] Without delay they returned in mail, with swords, axes, double-edged weapons, and other implements suitable for accomplishing the crime conceived in their minds. But the servants, taking precautions and locking the door without the archbishop’s knowledge, shut them out. The sons of Satan, led by their father, turned to the wooden obstruction and cut it, split it, and tore it down. At the immense and terrible crash the clerics, as was their wont, were almost beside themselves; but the archbishop, who alone was sought to be killed, comforted in the Lord the others who had been terrified by vain fear. To us he appeared to sit as undaunted as though they had come to invite him to a wedding. When his followers urged him [Col. 0331C] to flee to the monastery, he who had earlier promised not to flee from the killers of the flesh more courageously fulfilled his promise. But when he was told that the hour and the feast required him to celebrate the evening office in the church, at last and reluctantly rising, he ordered his cross to be carried before him. The order was therefore reversed: the prelate who ought to have gone before followed the hastening clerics with measured pace, like a shepherd driving his sheep into the fold.

As he entered the monastery, the monks met him, having abandoned the Vespers which they had begun to offer to God. They gave thanks to God that they saw their father, whom they had heard was already dead, alive and unharmed. Saying this, they hastened to bar the church doors and keep the enemies from [Col. 0331D] killing their shepherd. But the holy father turned back and removed both these and those from the doors, lest, if the enemies’ path were impeded, his martyrdom might be impeded—the martyrdom which he knew and had foretold was immediately impending. When they entered and shouted behind him, “Where is the traitor to king and kingdom, the false prelate?”, he who had foretold that he did not fear them turned back, saying: “Here I am—not the king’s traitor, but God’s priest. Why do you seek me? Here I stand ready, in the name of Him who redeemed us by His blood, to suffer. Far be it from me to flee because of your swords or to depart from justice!” As he said this, they swiftly laid sacrilegious hands upon him, dragging him outside the church so that they might accomplish their begun sacrilege. But, held by one of his clerics, he could not easily [Col. 0332A] be moved from there. One of the aforesaid sons of Leviathan therefore raised the sword he held and almost cut off the arm of the aforementioned cleric; with the same blow he struck the lamb to be sacrificed to God, killing his own father in his mother’s womb and extinguishing the day about the eleventh hour. Behold the serpent’s prudence in this martyr: he offered his body to the strikers, that he might keep his head—that is, the Church or his soul—unharmed. Behold the dove’s simplicity: he devised no ambush or any kind of enclosure, even against enemies and fleshly killers. O shepherd worthy indeed, who so confidently offered himself to wolves’ bites lest the sheep be torn to pieces! And because he had rejected the world, the world, seeking to crush him, unknowingly exalted him. Then, receiving another blow upon the head, [Col. 0332B] the martyr bent knee and elbow, offering himself to God as a living sacrifice. As he thus fell, the third inflicted a grievous wound; the fourth separated from his head the crown, which was of broad extent, so that whitened blood from the brain and brains reddened by blood, in the colours of lily and rose, adorned the face of the virgin and mother Church in the death of her confessor and martyr. Thus God’s priest, departing from the world, was born into heaven on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1170. On the following day the monks, as is customary, stripped the body of the most pure man for washing, and discovered that he had long lived under the habit and rule of monks so privately that even his close companions had not known it. Closest of all to his flesh they found haircloth so covered with lice that [Col. 0332C] anyone might judge the martyrdom of the preceding day lighter than this, and that greater enemies had harmed him less than lesser ones. And, as we know has hitherto been done by no saint, he had worn haircloth drawers so tightly sewn with crosses that, from the knee upward, a trough extending lengthwise beneath the seam of the haircloth teemed with little worms like bubbling water. On the following Saturday it was revealed in a vision to a certain cleric in London that a priest of that city would recover lost speech at the tomb of the apostle of the English, the confessor and martyr, through the aid of his merits. And so it happened. I also know that a certain holy man, in the same part of the crypt in which the archbishop was buried, saw, as he believed, Christ crucified, shown by an angel. A certain most holy recluse, who knew neither Latin speech nor French, sent word to the monks of Canterbury shortly after the archbishop’s death that she had received from a most beautiful woman, though she did not understand, this Latin saying: [Col. 0332D] “Do not weep for your archbishop, for his head rests in the bosom of my Son.”

A crippled boy, begging the martyr for the grace of walking and, with his head resting above the sarcophagus, happening to fall asleep, was confronted by the holy father, who said: “Why do you lie upon me? You shall not have healing; I shall do nothing for you. Depart.” He awoke at these words and told both us and his mother, not without much contrition of heart, what he had heard. Certain of the irrevocability of the sentence, he had himself moved to another place. Yet, when we urged him to persist in prayer, he assented, but spent time without gaining the benefit of healing. Another person too appeared to someone sleeping upon the tomb and said: “Why do you lie here? The archbishop has commanded you that you shall by no means obtain healing. A sin committed before you were born deprives you of health. Nor do we therefore believe that the son bore the iniquity of the parents; rather, that the Lord wished to scourge the parents in their son, so that the bodily harm of the son might become a punishment of sorrow to the parents.” A few days later the boy departed from this life. Salerna, the daughter of Thomas of Yffelo, led astray by the counsel of servants of her father’s household, stole cheese from her mother and gave it to them. Her mother happened to notice that the cheese had been taken and accused [Col. 0333B] the girl of the deed. When she denied it, the mother threatened her. Failing to prevail by threats, she added blows, declaring that she would scourge her until she gave up the spirit unless on the following day she confessed the offence. That day was Saturday. Then the girl, more troubled by the future evil than grieved by the past one, spent almost the whole ensuing night sleepless, weeping and wailing, and saying: “Saint Thomas, take care of me; Saint Thomas, help me. Help me, Saint Thomas; take care of me, Saint Thomas.” In the morning, when she knew that her mother had gone to church, she went out and proceeded to a well, intending to cast herself into it, so that, if she could not avoid death, she might at least change the manner of death. As she approached the well, she saw beside her what seemed to be a little woman walking along; this woman, seeking her life, used force against her, driving her toward the precipice and saying: [Col. 0333C] “Go, go; you shall enter, you shall enter.” At last she sat on the well, hanging by her hands over its mouth; at the prompting of him who is from below, she cast herself down, crying in a loud voice: “May Almighty God and Saint Thomas take care of me.” She fell into the abyss and was not dashed to pieces, because the Lord put His hand beneath her. For He heard her and her voice, descended with her into the pit, and drew her out of many waters, lest the depth of the abyss swallow her or the well of hell press its mouth upon her. Thus, after being immersed three or four times and emerging as often, when she cried out for breath, “Saint Thomas, help me,” by a certain divine impulse the girl’s whole body was thrust out of the water as far as her feet; and God—or the martyr, indeed God and the martyr—placed her feet upon one stick, [Col. 0333D] and put another stick into her trembling hands. Standing upon the first on the water’s surface, she leaned upon the other, which extended against the wall of the well, wholly unaware [Col. 0334A] how she had come upon the stick or who had placed the second stick in her hands. But we hold it constant and most certain that a few days before, a young man had cleaned that very well and had left in it neither rod nor stick nor even a straw. While she stood thus, the girl also heard a voice comforting her and repeatedly uttering the same words of comfort: “Do not fear, daughter; you will come safely up. Daughter, do not fear.” She also testifies that she saw the person speaking standing near her, clothed in the whitest linen. Such, then, were the events in the well. Someone from the household, standing in a neighbouring field, heard the voice of the falling girl; he saw the girl sitting above the well and, astonished, rebuked her. Running, he called by name the young man sleeping in the house, repeatedly declaring that Salerna had fallen into the well. But the young man, waking as if from sleep, heard the shout but could not shake off his dream. For he saw before him what seemed a deformed man, tall in stature and terrible in face, holding a great club in his hands and unceasingly saying: [Col. 0334B] “If you rise, you are dead; if you move, I shall kill you.” At length, aroused by the insistent shouting, he ran with the boy to the well. He went down into it but, seized by fear at so great a precipice, came out. Thus both stood anxiously over the calamity, not knowing what ought to be done. Then one said to the other: “Hurry; mount a horse, hasten to the church, and report to our lady the pitiable misfortune that has occurred.” Mounting the horse, he hurried away and, after a long delay, brought back with him not only the lady but the entire parish which, as was customary on that day, had gathered at church. The young man was lowered by rope into the abyss of the well, and meanwhile the girl, remaining upon the stick, was drawn out, crying and saying: “Measure me for Saint Thomas”—that is, desiring that a candle equal to the length of her body should be made and offered to the martyr in gratitude for her rescue. When she had been drawn out, she was found unharmed, though almost afflicted to death by cold. She said: [Col. 0334D] “Behold, he was just now with me in the well; now he has gone.” “Who,” they asked, “was with you?” And she replied: “The most blessed martyr Thomas, in white clothing; and he spoke to me in the well thus and thus.” And all who stood there blessed the martyr of the Lord, who does whatever He wills in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the deeps. The depth of the well from the surface of the ground to the water is 150 feet. The depth of the water is 60 feet.

## FIFTH PASSION

[Col. 0335]

[Col. 0335A] For the praise of the most blessed martyr Thomas and the edification of the faithful, I undertake a work unequal to my learning; nevertheless, in conscience I recount what, God being witness, is known to have occurred in my presence. But since to recount at once his martyrdom would be like approaching the table with unwashed hands, the preceding events of his life shall first be tasted beforehand. Blessed is he who hears the words of this reading and keeps them as an incentive to martyrdom, so that, should the king perhaps demand it, he may be more ready [Col. 0336A] to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus.

(2.) Let us therefore proceed with the person of the martyr, the cause of his martyrdom, the tyranny of his persecutors, and the constancy of the sufferer; with the place and time of his passion, so that from all these circumstances and from the frequent testimony of miracles it may become clear to our false brethren with what blessedness and praise Christ predestined His soldier and martyr to be crowned in heaven and glorified on earth.

[Col. 0335] Here ends the Prologue.

THE PASSION OF THE SAME BEGINS.

[Col. 0335B] Thus, when Henry II first ruled over the monarchy of the English and also over many intervening regions beyond the sea, this blessed martyr, born of no mean citizens of London, held the archdeaconry of Canterbury under Archbishop Theobald. Since he had united the eloquence bestowed on him by nature to the highest prudence, he seemed handsome and gracious in countenance, gentle in appearance, just in deed, elegant in bearing, tall in body, and altogether fitted for affairs. Before long he was admitted by the aforesaid king into such intimacy that throughout various regions those who could obey him as counsellor and chancellor to their lord considered themselves blessed. (3.) And although none in the royal palace was considered more powerful, more generous, or more discerning than he, nevertheless he so moderated these things by the gift of grace that he was recognized as eminent among the powerful and humble in spirit among the lowly.

Meanwhile Archbishop Theobald entered upon the way of all flesh and left the Church of Canterbury bereft of its shepherd. The clergy therefore gathered for an election; with royal consent, the aforesaid Thomas was elected and consecrated archbishop. Yet, marvellous to say, no sooner had he been anointed with the sacred unction than his mind, through the reality of the sacrament, was filled with the manifold grace of the Holy Spirit.

For immediately after his initiation, lest he should become proud through honour, he chose to restrain his flesh under the burden and yoke of God. He assumed the order and habit of a regular canon [Col. 0335D] and preserved it, once assumed, so wonderfully together with the office of archbishop that, though anyone presumptuous of himself often fails in one or the other, he fulfilled both, and indeed certain things more difficult than these. (4.) Carried away into contemplation, he weakened his body by continual vigils, fasts, prayers, and readings [Col. 0336B] so that, though young in years, he appeared through his manner of life and order of priesthood greatly changed from the chancellor he had been. Having devoted the whole day to holiness, so that he might be deemed worthy rather of a crown than of a scourge, at last—what we can scarcely say without sorrow—when he had put back on the hairshirt which he wore, he offered his back, like a little child of Christ, to be scourged by some holy member of his household.

And because it befitted shepherds to descend from contemplation to the consolation of our weakness—whence Jacob saw angels not only ascending but also descending by the ladder, and likewise had taken as wives not only Rachel, fair of face, but also Leah, who was bleary-eyed and through whom the active life is signified—therefore, when this angel and shepherd had to condescend [Col. 0336C] to worldly people and to his sheep, he would now cheer their bodies with bodily food, now strengthen their souls by the word of preaching. Thus the mark of true love for God could be discerned in him, according to that Gospel saying: “If you love me, feed my sheep.” (5.) And truly in this shepherd a light arose for us: rising regularly from prayer before the dawn, he girded himself with a towel and, carrying a basin of water in his consecrated hands, gathered thirteen poor persons in a more private place. With bended knees he kissed, washed, and dried their feet, giving each four silver coins, so that he might consecrate to God—the One whom he imitated most expressly—the first fruits of the day’s work. Daily, too, he provided as many poor people with the necessities of life, both food and clothing [Col. 0336D]; and while providing for them he preached. Although an innumerable multitude of beggars flocked to him, he ceased to give from the smallness of his resources rather than from any wish to restrain his giving hand.

Remembering the prophetic saying, “He scattered abroad; he gave to the poor,” he gave not all to one, but portions to many [Col. 0337A], so that he might reap in joy what he sowed here. The more he judged movable possessions to be things to scatter and give to the poor, the more diligently he endeavoured to retain immovable possessions, from which those things were received, and to reclaim what had been dispersed. Hence he strove to take back estates of his church which his predecessors had granted less than justly to persons endowed with excessive power or connected to them by kinship, and to restore the Church’s former right; for it is lawful for a church steward to cultivate and increase ecclesiastical estates, not to neglect or diminish them.

(6.) When he detected the negligence of clerks who belonged to the royal court, he also claimed for himself and thereafter judged them and all other things belonging to ecclesiastical jurisdiction. Thus sacrilegious invaders of ecclesiastical property, together with certain bishops and clerics of like garb, inflamed the king and all his household against the holy lord [Col. 0337B], declaring that he had purposed to annul the royal customs and, according to the rules of the canons, to restrain and regulate the life of clergy and people.

But now let our discourse turn to the bishops—or rather, to speak more truly, to Epicureans. Why, wretches, have you armed yourselves against Peter and his Church—indeed, against yourselves? The Church will not fail amid the various storms of the world until her Bridegroom comes; rather, your present thrones will be overturned by Him who drove sellers and buyers out of the Temple, so that you may be reckoned not as bishops but rather as shameless dogs by Him and by His members. And would that no greater confusion might hereafter follow this your disgrace! Look back, therefore, wretches, and grieve that you have been deposed: you who, though set in honour, have appointed for yourselves a human being rather than God as your helper. (7.) Imitate Lot, who first followed the angel into Zoar and then ascended the mountain; and let that woman who looked back and was changed into salt be salt and seasoning for your spiritual food.

The members of Zebul so sharpened the king against him that the holy bishop was summoned to Northampton, as though to be judged before Caesar’s tribunal.
