On the appointed day, when he had been reliably informed that certain men had conspired to kill him, because he had long since clothed the inward person with the priestly garment, according to the saying, “I will clothe the priests with salvation,” he now more secretly protected the outward person beneath his cloak with the outer vestment of a priest. Carrying the cross in his own hands, he would not allow the example of his passion to be removed from him. Thus the noble martyr, accompanied by God alone, while accusations were brought against him on many and grave matters, replied—sitting, lest by standing he dishonour the priestly office—that it had been wonderfully revealed to him by God that a greater person ought not to be summoned to judgment by lesser persons, nor bound by their sentence. For order is overturned if a sheep strikes its shepherd, a disciple his teacher, or a son beats his father; nor is gold more precious than lead to the degree that priestly dignity surpasses royal power. Yet the laity and his suffragan bishops—or rather, opposing bishops—nonetheless condemned him as he said these things and appealed to the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0338A] Therefore, as the athlete of the Lord withdrew from the council of evildoers, a reproachful cry and tumult arose, no less violent than if fire or the assault of enemies had seized the four quarters of the city. And though he could rightly have declared that saying from Jeremiah’s Lamentations, “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow,” he who was struck with the fist so that he might benefit those persecuting him nevertheless carried the cross, gave thanks to the Crucified One, and went rejoicing from the council, because he was counted worthy to suffer this insult for the name of Jesus.

Accordingly, the holy man secretly, accompanied as best he could by a few, pursued his appeal and found the most holy Pope Alexander III at Sens. Throwing himself at his feet, he explained the cause of his coming to one who was not ignorant of it; and, as has been reliably reported, he resigned into the lord pope’s hand the pallium of his archiepiscopate and requested that he appoint as cardinal and bishop in their metropolitan see some man from the English Church more learned and stronger than himself. But the holy pope raised his son, embraced and kissed him, mingling tears with tears and giving thanks to God that he had found a man so humble in spirit, a shepherd so solicitous for the salvation of his sheep, and an advocate so steadfast in the cause—indeed, in many causes—of God. Therefore, because he knew no one stronger for this burden, the lord pope decreed that the dignity Thomas had rejected should be restored to him, even though he resisted and was unwilling.

The controversy between him and the king thus continued. The king wished to uphold ancestral customs [Col. 0338C], according to which the clergy’s free election in the creation of a pontiff was not to be awaited, nor the request or consent of the people to whom the bishop was given, as the canons prescribe; rather, all this was to be done at the king’s nod and will, he himself giving the episcopal ring and staff. Thus men of whatever kind—even those who did not understand the language of the people placed under them—occupied the chair of Moses with every reverence for the canons trampled underfoot, and ordained as priests unlearned and disorderly men like themselves. Consequently, the people, having no one from whom to seek the law and commandments of the Lord, were more readily drawn into vices; for, taught neither by word nor example, they descended in crowds to the depths, following their leaders who bore the standards before them.

Let those murderers of souls, enthroned contrary to the law, take heed [Col. 0338D]—those who have violently acquired not the dignity but merely the name of bishops, to the wounding of the head of Mother Church—that Matthias was admitted into the place of Judas the traitor not by the judgment of an emperor or king, but by the apostles’ free election by lot. Let them also remember Gregory’s truthful judgment: unless they first renounce powers acquired in this manner and humble themselves in most severe repentance, they will without doubt be handed over eternally to the powers of demons, together with the laymen who confer such powers upon them. But the archbishop steadfastly preached that this and many other customs, which it would take too long to enumerate, conflicted with the truth made manifest through God’s elect, and that custom must yield to manifest truth. For Christ is found at one time to have said, “I am the truth,” but He never said, “I am custom.”

And so the dispute under this warfare was conducted between these persons for seven years, while the most pious King Louis, son of King Louis, reigned over the French nation and supported the aforesaid archbishop. The archbishop was wholly proscribed from the affairs of the Church, together with the clerks who were with him, until they should return to the favour of the often-mentioned king and promise not to oppose the customs over which the dispute had arisen. But since the holy priest was not bent in any respect by the banishment of himself or his clerks, both adults and children of his kindred, of either sex, and also certain of his household—so that he might be more distressed through them—were commanded to go into exile. When the holy martyr of God learned of the deportation of infants whose nourishment still depended on their mothers’ breasts, he was grieved as though a sword had pierced his soul. But remembering that Abraham had been told, “Go out from your land and from your kindred,” he firmly resolved to set aside both land and kindred for the honour of the Church.

Nor should this be passed over: I received it from the trustworthy account of one of the companions and leaders of his exile. He testified to us repeatedly, by God and by the relics of the martyr in the Church which the martyr made sorrowful by his passion and which honours him in burial, that he had apprehended with eyewitness certainty that it happened as he reported. When the holy martyr had devoted himself with special attention to meditation upon the divine Scriptures at the monastery in the land of France called Pontigny [Col. 0339C], while the man whom we praised as the author of this account sat beside him, behold, one of the brothers—who had already been confined to bed for three years—was afflicted with some disorder that had swollen him so greatly that his stretched skin could scarcely contain his bloodless and emaciated body. Shaking the door-ring, he was admitted to the saint of the Lord.

The sick man immediately threw himself at the lord’s feet and said: “Lord, it has been made known to me by a vision that I ought to confess to you, so that, when the inward person has been cleansed from sins, the outward person may be healed and cured from this painful swelling by the touch of your consecrated hand.” The holy priest willingly complied with the first request, excusing himself from the second; at last, overcome by the weeping petitioner’s groaning [Col. 0339D], he granted both. Without delay, when what he had requested had been done, the sick man rolled at the saint’s feet, foaming as though afflicted with epilepsy, suddenly thrown to the ground, then twisting himself like a rope or serpent. With immense frenzy he vomited up eleven little frogs and was immediately restored to perfect health.

A marvellous thing: the more it was concealed, the more brightly did the martyr’s power shine forth like a clearer star. Sick persons flocked to him along with the poor, that they might be freed from hunger and illness by fragments of bread and vegetables upon which the holy man fed. Among others, a certain knight came, bringing his daughter, whom a continual illness had wasted for a year and a half. As soon as she had tasted the remnants of fragments fallen from the archbishop’s hand [Col. 0340A], she gave thanks to God and to the holy exile, and returned safely home with her father.

Among all the martyrdoms which this martyr endured before he was killed, I have thought it right to relate this. Once, when a treaty of peace repeatedly broken seemed to have been renewed between the king of France and the king of England, the two kings agreed that the archbishop’s exile should finally be ended by the remedy of peace on this condition: that he should commit the conclusion of his dispute to the judgment of the clergy of France and Normandy, undertaking to observe whatever they should decide. But the holy man, fearing that God’s cause might fall into manifest danger—for he considered that the customs of both kingdoms frequently contradicted decrees both through obstinacy and through ignorance of the law—added that he would submit to the judgment [Col. 0340B] of those named, provided that the dignity of the Church and of his own order were preserved. Since this word of holiness could not be torn from his mouth by kings, bishops, or his own household, the French and his household were more violently disturbed against him. Thus this saying was continually carried to and fro in the saint’s ears, now uttered by persons who outwardly professed the religious habit: “Now his pride and insolence appear; now the treachery comes to light which the archbishop has long devised for the overthrow of his lord and his kingdom.”

O how great the pain! O how lamentable were the sighs that tortured the athlete of the Lord! O how deeply the tears flowed when he saw that enemies were made for him from every quarter among those necessary to him! Yet holding fast [Col. 0340C] to the prophetic saying, “The Lord is my helper; I shall not fear what man may do to me,” he alone set himself as a wall for the house of the Lord against all, steadfastly maintaining that neither death nor life would separate him from that declaration: namely, that peace, if it were to come, must be established with the dignity of the Church and of his order preserved.

At last peace was restored, as he believed, through the lord pope, the king of France, and the archbishops; and, by God’s will, the venerable pontiff returned to his church. He then devoted himself so earnestly to prayer, preaching, alms, vigils, fasts, and other good works that even those to whom his most holy religious life had previously been known were astonished. Yet he had not remained in his church for a month when, behold, four satellites of the devil came swiftly from beyond the sea. We have thought it fitting to record their names as a sign of their wretched soldiery: Richard le Breton, Hugh de Morville, Reginald FitzUrse, and William de Tracy. They addressed him thus: “We declare to you the command of the king and our lord: go to his son, the new king, to do what you ought to do for the king and to submit to law in his judgment if you have offended against him in any matter. Restore to communion also the excommunicated bishops—Gilbert Foliot of London and Jocelin of Salisbury—and restore their office to the others who have been suspended.”

But the archbishop replied: “I have received a command from the new king not to travel through his towns and cities, but to withdraw entirely from speech with him and from his sight, as unworthy. Furthermore, it is known that the above-named bishops were not excommunicated or suspended by me, but by the lord pope, because in my diocese, without consulting me, they presumed to consecrate and crown this new king—may the Lord grant him saving grace. Their satisfaction must therefore precede their absolution.” At these words, however, the aforesaid knights—not knights, but accomplices in the same crime—like brutish men devoid of understanding, broke into threats. As they departed amid uproar and insults, the holy bishop replied: “Seek someone who fears your threats. Your swords are not more ready than my spirit is for martyrdom. Seek someone who will flee you; for you will find me foot to foot in the battle of the Lord.”

And behold, the man whom we have rightly surnamed Bear cried out bestially: “On behalf of the lord king we command you, clergy and monks alike, to seize and hold this man until the king has obtained full justice concerning his body.” [Col. 0341B] O how astonishing, foolish, and pitiful a command: that the clergy should keep their father for punishment, for whose protection the heavenly King had already prepared for him an unfading crown! From the border of this command arose another lamentable thing. For the dreadful voice of a herald grew loud through the streets: “Arm yourselves, men, arm yourselves! Attack the archbishop’s house. It is unfit that he should live among us in common life who has shamefully deprived the chief men of our kingdom of communion.”

Without delay the four courtly dogs already named returned in armour with swords drawn, together with retainers bearing double-edged axes and other implements suited to committing the crime conceived in their minds. But the servants, taking precautions and without the bishop’s knowledge, locked the door and shut them out. The sons of Satan, led by their father, turned to the wooden barriers; they struck, tore apart, and broke them down. At the immense crash and terrifying din the clerics, in their accustomed manner, nearly lost their senses from fear. But the archbishop, who alone was sought for destruction, comforted in the Lord the others who had been terrified by empty fear. To us he sat as undaunted as though they had come to invite him to a wedding. Though his followers cried out on every side that he should flee into the monastery [Col. 0341D], he who had previously promised not to flee from the killers of the flesh fulfilled his promise more courageously. For in such a case he ought not to flee from city to city; rather, he ought to give his subjects an example, that each might prefer to die in battle rather than see the evils of his people and the overthrow of the holy canons.

But when he was told that, since the hour and feast-day required it, he ought to celebrate the evening office in the church, he finally rose and hastened toward the cross, commanding that the cross be carried before him. Thus the order was reversed: the priest and bishop, who ought to precede, like a shepherd driving his sheep into the fold, followed at a measured pace the clerics hurrying before him. As he entered the monastery, the monks came to meet him, having abandoned the Vespers they had begun to offer to God. They gave thanks to God because they saw their father alive and unharmed whom they had heard was dead; and, saying this, they hastened to bar the church doors to keep enemies from killing their shepherd. But the holy father returned and removed both groups from the doors, lest, if the enemies’ path were impeded, his martyrdom should be impeded.

When the executioners entered and cried, “Where is that traitor to the king and kingdom, that false bishop?” he who had foretold that he did not fear them turned back and said: “Behold, I am here—not a traitor to the king, but a priest. Why do you seek me? Behold, I stand ready to suffer in the name of Him who redeemed us by His blood. Far be it from me to flee because of your swords or to depart from justice!” Then one of them, more wicked than the others, hastened forward and laid a double-edged axe upon his consecrated breast [Col. 0342B]—alas!—threatening to tear out his most holy heart. But refraining from a blow, he and the others laid violent hands on him, dragging him out so that they might accomplish outside the Church the sacrilege and inexpiable crime they had begun.

But since he could not easily be moved from there, one of the aforesaid sons of Leviathan raised the sword he held and struck upon the head the lamb to be sacrificed to God, cutting off with the same blow the arm of the man relating these things, killing his own father in his mother’s womb, and extinguishing the day at about the eleventh hour. Behold the serpent’s prudence in this martyr: he offered his body to those striking him, that he might keep his head—that is, the Church—or his soul unharmed. Behold the dove’s simplicity: he set neither snares nor any barrier even against the killers of the flesh, but forbade the monastery to be shut, since the ordinances of the holy fathers have decreed that by right of religion it ought to stand open to all Catholics. O shepherd worthy indeed, who exposed himself so confidently to the bites of wolves lest his sheep be torn apart! For he knew that one whom fear compels to flee in such a crisis of death is unworthy of a crown.

What would he not do? To what storms would not that vessel of virtues, so solid in steadfastness, so purified by tribulations and afflictions, so worn down by vigils and fasts, and so rubbed smooth by continual disciplines, expose itself—he who deserved to be borne to the throne of glory, there to be offered among the delights of the highest King? For he had left the world for Christ, and had so despised it with its flower [Col. 0342D] that he counted all its things as refuse. Seeing this, the world grieved greatly, declared deadly war against him in its obstinacy, and summoned its prince as helper: “Come,” it said, “let us oppress this just man, because he is opposed to our works.” Yet it came about marvellously that he who strove to extinguish a spark of light shining in the western regions of the earth and in one corner alone, while wishing to crush it, exalted a great luminary that kindles flashes from west to east.

Then, receiving another blow upon the head, the martyr bent his knees and elbows, offering himself to God as a living sacrifice, and said: “For the name of Jesus and for the protection of the Church, I am ready with a willing mind to embrace death.” He then added: “To God, and to the Blessed Virgin Mary, and to Saint Dionysius, and to all martyrs, I entrust the cause of the Church.” When he had said this, the third of the deadly knights struck a grievous wound into his neck as he lay prostrate. The fourth—horrible to tell—so separated from his head the crown, which was of broad extent, that the blood whitened by the brain and the brain reddened by blood dyed with the colours of lily and rose the face of the virgin and mother Church in the death of her confessor and martyr. O most wicked of men, whom neither the pitiable compassion of their bloodied mother nor the admirable goodness of their father could soften from hunting out and spilling the brain within his sacred head!

When these things had been done and the other executioners had withdrawn, Reginald, son of Urse, surpassing all the rest in cruelty, dug out what remained of his brain [Col. 0343B] and threw it upon the pavement, lest a fifth wound be lacking to one who had imitated Christ in the others. For, speaking without offence to the martyrs, they chiefly acted in their own cause when they were told, “Sacrifice to Jupiter; reject the Crucified One.” But this man came to purchase the salvation of others with his precious blood, so that those marked with Christ’s sacred character might be governed according to the ordinances of the Church, judging that no love is greater than to lay down one’s life for one’s friends. How fearlessly would this martyr have fought when his own salvation and faith were at stake, when, for the protection of others, neither dragged nor led, he offered himself for slaughter! Therefore, because of his marvellous constancy, we believe that divine honour was bestowed on him: that he conquered in victorious death not Jews or pagans, but eloquent and fierce Christians.

But who could measure the exalted dignity of the place assigned to martyrdom? The very house of Christ, the place where the provision for our salvation was customarily sacrificed, was painted with the fresh martyr’s brain, like the cradle of a king born the day before, so that by this deed the persecutors’ cruelty and the martyr’s eminent dignity might be signified.

Thus the priest of God, departing from the world, was born into heaven on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1171, on the day immediately following the feast of the Innocents. Thus he who had long lived innocently received his celebrated time after the Innocents, through the great mercy of the newborn King, who so joined the martyrdom—indeed, the birthday—of His soldier and martyr to His own that no fellow citizen could be more closely joined to Him without prejudice to the prerogative of His own saints, nor could it be delayed further.

On the following day, the monks, as was customary, stripped the most pure body of the martyr in order to wash it. Beneath the habit and order of monks they discovered that he had for so long secretly lived in this manner that even his own household had not known it. Finally, next to his flesh they found a hairshirt so covered with little creatures that anyone might judge the martyrdom of the preceding day lighter than this, and the greater enemies to have harmed him less than the lesser ones. And, as we have learned was done by no saint, he had long used haircloth drawers sewn so tightly around his legs that a channel extended lengthwise above the knee beneath the seam of the haircloth, swarming with worms.

[Col. 0344A] Let our God be magnified, who did not allow the lamp of the Church to remain longer hidden under a bushel, but set it upon a lampstand for the confusion of unbelievers and schismatics, so that those entering might see the light and openly recognize that what this martyr rejected was not the Church but the disgrace of schism, and that unbelief consists in thinking otherwise about God than he preached.

For at the approaching feast of the proto-martyr Stephen, before this most noble martyr had been enrolled among the fellowship of martyr-soldiers, a priest named Ralph, serving as parish priest in a certain church of Blessed Mary in London, had been invited to a rich man’s feast in his parish. When he wished to speak during the meal, he was deprived of the instruments of speech and became mute. Thus, after physicians found the powers of theriac ineffective [Col. 0344B], the man who had become mute rose sadly from table and returned home. Afterwards, when the dead martyr’s funeral rites and divine offices had been performed, a venerable-looking man appeared to a cleric named Ralph, brother of that priest, in whose house the priest had been deprived of speech. The cleric was chanting the Matins of the Blessed Virgin and Mother of Christ and lingered over the Canticle of the Three Children. The man appeared with such brightness in his face that, although it was about midnight, the house seemed to shine with his splendour. He said: “Ralph, on God’s behalf tell the priest Ralph that, if he cannot confess by mouth, he should at least confess his sins first in writing with true repentance and approach the new martyr, the apostle and confessor of the English, so that through his merits he may recover the loss of speech.”

Thereafter, when the priest obeyed this command, he was not deprived of the benefit. I report this miracle with greater confidence because, when after my lord’s martyrdom I was confined to a sickbed at Canterbury and afterwards came to London, I learned from citizens that it had happened thus. I also spoke twice with the priest to whom this had occurred, who was speaking quite clearly, and with the trustworthy Ralph to whom the aforesaid vision had appeared while he was awake.

I also know that when a physician had despaired for nearly a year of the healing of my arm, the venerable martyr stood beside me one night, took hold of my arm, and wrapped it in a moistened piece of linen cloth, saying: “Go; you are well.” Afterwards I wrapped my arm with a cloth dipped in holy water and his blood [Col. 0344D], until by the joint healing grace of God and the martyr the bones adhered to the bones. The right hand of that same arm, which wrote these things for you to read, bears witness to its healing. The Lord has also performed many other works as signs of His love for our blessed martyr: cleansing lepers, as we have seen; driving out demons; healing dropsical persons, paralytics, the deaf, mute, blind, and lame, and those suffering from other ailments. For these works we await the trustworthy testimony of the Church of Canterbury, under whose sight and knowledge they are known to have increased.

Here ends the Martyrdom of the blessed Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, issued by Master Euvrard.

[Col. 0345]

LIFE AND PASSION OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY AND MARTYR, BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR.

(This little book was published at Paris in the year of the Lord 1495.)

THE PROLOGUE TO THE LIFE, PASSION, AND CAUSE OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY AND MARTYR, CONCERNING ECCLESIASTICAL LIBERTY, BEGINS.

[Col. 0345A]

“Professors of the arts,” etc. (See the Life of St Thomas by Edward Grim, column 1, as far as “Therefore, desiring dutifully,” etc., column 2.)

Therefore, desiring dutifully to comply with the devotion of certain persons who are anxious to know more fully the deeds of the precious martyr, we have taken pains to weave into a single historical narrative the works and studies of four historians—namely, the great Herbert of Bosham, John of Chartres, William of Canterbury, and Alan, abbot of Tewkesbury. They had portrayed all things concerning the precious martyr in an eloquent style, since throughout the whole time both of his commanding nobility and of his holy, abject humility they had been more intimately attached to him. We took the greatest care that nothing concerning the substance of the matter or the truth of the whole event might be lost through silence, from the beginnings of his perfect manly undertaking until the day when, for his God and the liberty of the Church, he completed his life’s course through martyrdom.

Certainly, in the judgment of most persons, Herbert—who was able to tell each detail from knowledge, since he testifies to what he saw and heard—exceeded the limits of brevity through a love for his master that was just but rather excessive. John, however, writing amid the storm of public power, set forth a concise truth with an inadequate pen. The other two likewise, because they did not fully satisfy those thirsting to know the substance of the event, gave occasion for weariness in study and nevertheless generated distaste in serious readers.

Undertaking this work, therefore, by the Lord’s gift—difficult though it is, yet, as we believe, acceptable to posterity—we have endeavoured through fitting brevity to assist the weary and through full truth to satisfy diligent students [Col. 0345C]. Yet we have not curtailed prolixity so greatly for the sake of pleasing readers that we omit anything among the necessary occurrences; not because we wish to defraud those desirous of a complete history, even in a small matter of truth. For it is altogether absurd that anyone should say that the praises of a person should be omitted when he proposes that person’s character and deeds for imitation. It is, I say, altogether absurd to pull down part of a building whose perfect finished end he intends magnificently to display.

Therefore, with the merits and intercession of the glorious martyr assisting us, we have devoted ourselves for a time to this present work, to his praise and to the glory of Him who grants strength to His saints on the way and bestows rewards in their homeland [Col. 0346A], so that a concise fullness may remove distaste from the wearied and may provoke greater desire in studious readers. May the Spirit of truth, never departing from the line of rectitude, through the glorious merits of our blessed father inspire our devotion, so that a prayer of pure faith may fully pursue what we undertake with pious intention.

Here ends the prologue to the Life and Passion of Saint Thomas the martyr; and the fourfold narrative of the Life, Passion, and Cause of the same martyr begins.

CHAPTER ONE. ON THE LIFE AND CHARACTER OF THE PARENTS OF SAINT THOMAS.

“Thus chosen before the world,” etc., as far as “to the truth” [the same material as is found above in Edward Grim, [Col. 0346B], column 3].

CHAPTER II. ON THE MARVELLOUS BIRTH OF BLESSED THOMAS.

But now, in order to take up the course of the history from a somewhat earlier point, we have considered it not irrelevant to insert at the beginning the quite remarkable truth concerning the marriage of his father and mother, for those reflecting upon the event. From this it may readily be perceived with what care and mercy the wonderful predestination of the Saviour gathered into one, from sunrise and sunset, persons so different in race and condition, from whose offspring He purposed that His bride, the Church, should be triumphantly exalted and adorned throughout the whole world.

Accordingly, the aforesaid Gilbert, while still a young man, took up the Lord’s cross [Col. 0346C] in fulfilment of a penitential vow, intending to go to Jerusalem. He took with him a certain member of his household, named Richard, being content with this one man alone as his servant. When at last they had arrived there safely, amid the hostilities between Christians and pagans, he entered the holy places with others for the sake of prayer. But when permission was given to return, all the visitors were seized together, chained, and held in the prison of a certain Amiral, a distinguished prince among the pagans, so that by daily tasks imposed upon them they might somehow procure for themselves whatever food they could.

Gilbert, living as a slave in the captivity of the Slavs for a full year and a half, was considered more honourable and more distinguished than the rest; and he found such favour and goodwill in Amiral’s eyes above all others that he frequently came before him [Col. 0347A], though still in chains, at table, visited those reclining there, and they duly conversed with one another about knowledge of lands and the customs of different peoples. Moreover, through Gilbert’s favour, many benefits were bestowed on his fellow captives, while the only daughter of the same Amiral—a very courtly and beautiful maiden—also privately assisted in the matter as far as she could. She loved Gilbert, indeed, with a remarkable affection, as will appear below.

One day, having found an opportunity to speak more freely with him, the maiden asked from what land and city he came; concerning the faith, religion, and way of life of Christians; and what was the hope of believers and the reward of the world to come. When he answered that he was an Englishman and a citizen of London, and had explained the Christian faith as well as he knew how, she then asked him:

“Would you willingly and fearlessly undergo death for the preservation of your God and the faith of Christ which you profess?”

“Most willingly,” he said; “I would die for our God.”

On hearing this, the maiden at once, as though wholly transformed by the power of his words, declared that she would become a Christian for his sake, provided that he promised to take her as his wife within his faith. He was silent, deliberating within himself; and, fearing deception, he would not immediately consent to her pressing requests by making a promise. Rather, by evasion, he put it off from day to day, unwilling quickly to give his consent.

As the maiden was grievously distressed and grew, day by day, more anxious because of the delay—as is women’s wont—Gilbert meanwhile began to plan flight with his fellow captives. [Col. 0347C] After a year and a half, one night they broke their chains and the prison, escaped, and spent all that remained of the night racing onward until they reached Christian territory. At daybreak, when the overseer of the works came according to custom to send them to their usual labours and found the prison broken open, he pursued them with a strong force. But, being prevented by the Christian borders, they returned at last, robbed of all hope and not a little enraged.

When the maiden heard of this, from that very hour she too began to think of setting out and following after them. As she pondered the matter wonderfully day and night, and burned in meditation upon the more prudent means of escape, one night, while all were overcome by sleep, she alone—unbeknown to anyone—took with her only a little necessary provision for the journey and, in order to undertake the difficult road more readily, committed herself to the manifold perils of flight. She cared nothing for all that belonged to her by hereditary right, reckoning the fulfilment of her desire according to her wish to be wealth enough.

[Col. 0347D] O greatly admirable both the boldness and the love of this woman, who dared such difficult and arduous things! Though the glory of her father’s immense wealth might have ennobled her, she did not hesitate to forgo it irrecoverably. Delicate and frail as she was, she did not tremble to undergo punitive poverty; nor did she hesitate to travel alone through so many regions and through innumerable kinds of peril on the shipwrecking sea, seeking the love of one man so remote and unknown, even though she had no assurance that he was alive or that she would find him—indeed, not even assurance of marriage if she did find the man she sought.

Setting out, she successfully passed through pagan territory and sailed toward England with certain pilgrims and homeward-bound merchants who knew her language. Having passed all the hazards encountered on the way and arrived in England, now separated from her companions, she knew no question to ask for the road except this alone: “London, London.” At last reaching it, she wandered like a stray beast through the city streets, looking about at everyone she met in the manner of one searching; and she was mocked by all, especially by boys staring at her and following her through the lanes, marvelling alike at her unfamiliar dress and language.

[Col. 0348B] It happened that, as she thus moved through streets and lanes, she came by chance before the house in which the aforesaid Gilbert lived, in the city’s more solemn and crowded market-place—where there is now a hospice built in honour of St Thomas. There it became widely known that a certain young woman, seemingly simple-minded, was wandering about while boys and others followed and mocked her. Richard, Gilbert’s servant mentioned above, heard of it and ran with the rest, as if to a spectacle. Drawing nearer and recognizing her, he immediately hurried back to his master and secretly told him that this was Amiral’s daughter, at whom a crowd of people had gathered to gaze in astonishment.

On hearing this, Gilbert was beyond measure amazed and unable to believe it, since such an occurrence seemed altogether impossible. He could not trust Richard’s account until Richard continued for some time upon oath, by which he was made somewhat less incredulous. At length, considering the reason for her arrival, he judged it more prudent to provide for her elsewhere than to keep her with himself in his own house. He ordered Richard to bring her to a neighbouring widowed matron, who was to treat her in every respect as her own daughter.

When the maiden saw Gilbert and recognized him, she immediately fell down as if dead, lying upon her back in an ecstasy. When she awoke from that alienation of mind and came back to herself, Richard brought her to the said matron as his master had commanded. [Col. 0348D]

Gilbert, however, considering the maiden’s arrival, began to fluctuate in mind among various thoughts and to conceive conflicting reflections. It came into his mind to go and consult the bishop of London at St Paul’s, where on a certain day six bishops were present to discuss difficult affairs of the kingdom or of the Church. Standing before them, he set out in order the truth of the event described above. Immediately the bishop of Chichester, breaking forth before the others into a prophetic utterance, confidently declared that this calling was not human but rather divine, and that she would necessarily bear offspring for a magnificent work, by whose holiness and labour the universal Church would be exalted to Christ’s glory.

The other bishops present agreeing in this judgement, and approving that Gilbert should take the maiden as his wife provided she wished to be baptized, she was brought on the following appointed day to the church of St Paul in the presence of the said bishops. A font had been suitably prepared there in which she was to be baptized. When, placed in their midst, she was asked through the aforesaid Richard, their common interpreter, according to the Church’s custom, whether she wished to be baptized, she answered:

“For this purpose I have come here from very distant parts, provided Gilbert wishes to be joined to me in marriage.”

The maiden was therefore baptized, the six bishops celebrating the great sacrament of baptism with solemnity, because she was a woman of distinguished blood—indeed, more distinguished still through a divine calling. [Col. 0349B] The bishops at once gave her to Gilbert in marriage with celebration, after she had briefly been instructed in the Catholic faith appropriate to marriage. When he brought her home, on the first night of their mutual union and harmony they conceived St Thomas, the future archbishop and martyr of Canterbury.

The next day, Gilbert was so seized by longing to return to the Holy Land that, agitated by sighs, he wore an unaccustomed expression of sadness more continually than not. Yet he considered his young wife’s tender and fragile sex, her susceptible age, and her ignorance of the language of the country; and he thought that, on account of such not inconsiderable dangers, harm could easily befall her during his absence.

When his wife observed his countenance changed in various ways from what it had been yesterday and the day before, she was greatly afraid and wondered whether she herself might perhaps be the cause. She pressed him with prayers day and night, seeking the truth of such deep sadness, and did not desist until what was hidden had been fully revealed. [Col. 0349C] Wearied by the urgency of her entreaties, Gilbert disclosed his desire to his wife. But she, being a woman of great hope and strengthened in the faith of Christ, not only assented to her husband’s vow, but begged and urged him to carry out, as promptly as devoutly, whatever he had conceived in his mind as likely to please his Creator, without any consideration for herself. She added:

“I firmly hope and have such confidence in my God, who called me to knowledge of his name, that even in your absence he will not forsake me, but, just as before I knew him, will preserve me untouched by every danger. I ask only this for my comfort: leave Richard with me, since, being better instructed in my language, he will know better than the others how to attend to my needs.”

Hearing this, Gilbert became exceedingly glad and prepared his necessities. Having arranged as quickly as possible what concerned his wife and household, he departed for Jerusalem, where he remained for three and a half years before returning home. He found his son Thomas very handsome in appearance and pleasing in the eyes of all who beheld him.

## Chapter III. On His Mother’s Visions, by Which We Believe the Future Excellence of Her Holy Offspring Was Foreshadowed

[Col. 0350A]

After a short interval, etc., as far as “foreshadowed” [the same material, including this passage, is found in Edward Grim, above, cols. 3–4].

## Chapter IV. How He Conducted Himself in Youth

When his boyish years had passed, he began to excel in the finest character: distinguished in intelligence, agreeable in speech, cheerful yet grave in countenance, handsome in appearance, and of sufficiently elegant form. He showed himself pleasing and lovable to everyone. Divine goodness enriched him, moreover, in respect of both the inner and outer person, [Col. 0350B] with the manifold grace of natural gifts, so that he seemed a vessel fashioned for a great mystery; and from nature’s gifts he was foretold to be a future bishop, as a heavenly vision more fully made known while he was still a boy.

For when he was for some time seized by a fever, and as it grew stronger a burning sweat gradually burst from within through his whole little body, a certain lady of tall stature, serene face, and beautiful aspect was seen standing by his bed as he lay there. Having comforted the boy by promising recovery, she gave him two golden keys into his hand, saying:

“Thomas, these are the keys of paradise, whose keeping you are yet to have.”

Having said this, she disappeared.

[Col. 0350C] At the time when his father had entrusted him for a while to Prior Robert in the religious house of Merton, to be brought up, his father came one day to see his son. When the boy had been brought before the prior, the father fell prostrate and worshipped him. Indignant, the prior said:

“What are you doing? You fall at your son’s feet? He ought to do to you what you are doing to him.”

The father said to him privately:

“Lord, do not wonder. I know what I am doing to him: this boy will indeed be great before the Lord.”

The father, naturally, was awestruck by such marvellous things divinely revealed to him concerning his son; but, because of his amazement, he judged that they should be concealed under the seal of silence. After Thomas had been committed to literary studies and had attained the liberal arts as far as the frivolity of his age and the limits of time allowed, he made progress in them.

[Col. 0350D] From his earliest age, as he was accustomed to relate, he learned from his mother the fear of the Lord and to invoke more sweetly the blessed Mother of God as guide of his ways and patroness of his life; and, after Christ, to place his entire confidence in her.

After his mother died, he was left with his father and spent his twenty-second year in leisure. Having studied at Paris for some time, he returned and was received into a share of the administration of the city of London. Conducting himself commendably there, he learned the prudence of this world, by which afterward he knew well how openly to manage the common concerns of the English Church and the public affairs of the whole kingdom. He attached himself closely to a certain man in the city, distinguished by birth and especially eminent for many possessions; following the various pursuits of the world—now hunting, now the capture of birds, by which the youthful mind was especially nourished. [Col. 0351A] At his pleasure he lived now at home with his father, now in the country with the wealthy man. Thus, having been left to himself in this manner, he prematurely abandoned his scholarly studies.

One day it happened that, while Thomas was going to the riverbank with the wealthy man, a hawk pursued a duck stirred from the river and, following it as it turned in the water, plunged beneath the surface with it. Seeing this, the young man pitied the hawk, now about to perish; he leapt from his horse and threw himself into the whirlpool to rescue the bird. But before he could touch it, he himself was swept into the river channel; now submerged beneath the water, now raised by the force of the waves, he began to be in danger [Col. 0351B] and was thought by the spectators to have utterly perished, since no one could be present to extend a hand to the drowning man.

At last he was carried by the current to a mill which happened then to be grinding. As soon as he approached the first outlets of the water, the wheel stopped and did not move at all until the young man was drawn out alive, though severely injured. But the healing hand of the Saviour cared for the afflicted man whom it had protected, though despaired of amid the waves, lest the lamp destined for Israel should be extinguished—he from whose precious death we see such great benefits have arisen.

He then turned to courtly occupations and began to attain the flower of worldly prudence [Col. 0352A] and to abound in the fruit of discernment. His keenness of reason was so vigorous that he prudently solved unheard-of and difficult questions. His memory was so fortunate that whatever he had once learned in sense or words, he could almost whenever he wished bring forth without difficulty. Since many men of greater learning could not attain this, they ascribed such penetration of mind—especially in a man devoted to varied occupations—to a miracle. Divine providence, indeed, was thus training and exercising in lesser matters the man whom it called to greater things, as though in certain preparatory exercises for the future, so that in conferences or sermons, as the saying goes, he might have ready to hand what was necessary.

As a presage, too, of his future steadfastness, they report that love of truth clung so persistently to the young man’s mind—even though he pursued worldly things—that scarcely, or never, either in jest or earnest did he utter anything contrary to truth. How perfectly he fulfilled this thereafter, once he had become a man, the following account will show.

(After this, the present first *Quadrilogue* agrees almost word for word with the second *Quadrilogue*, of which we shall speak later. Yet instead of three it comprises five books: the fourth is *On Events after the Martyrdom*; the fifth contains some seventy letters. This is enough to say of this compilation. The book itself containing these materials has now become rare and is valued and sold at a fairly high price. In the library of Saint-Omer there is a manuscript book on the Life of St Thomas which is almost the same as the published first *Quadrilogue*, and which, besides this, contains a few passages on the siege of Toulouse excerpted from the work of William fitz Stephen.)

[Col. 0351]

# Life of St Thomas, Archbishop and Martyr of Canterbury, Compiled by an Anonymous Writer from the Writings of Others

[Published at Brussels, 1682.]

## Here Begins the Life of Blessed Thomas, Martyr and Archbishop of Canterbury, Collected from the Narratives of Many; More Extensive than That Below, Which Lord Peter Roger, Pope Gregory XI, Caused to Be Written

[Col. 0351C]

After the illustrious champions endowed with the highest gift of favour—who, beginning auspiciously to contend for Thomas from the cradle in which he cried until the sword by which he fell, have portrayed everything—I may seem, if I stretch my pygmy hand to the pen for a similar work, to be moved by love’s imperious power for the martyr to beg indulgence from the kindly for my presumption.

John of Salisbury, Master Herbert of Bosham, William of Canterbury, and Alan, abbot of Tewkesbury—four couriers in the four-horse chariot of the flaxen tongue—have driven the contest of our athlete through the four quarters of the world. Gilding the majesty of a subject in itself worthy of recommendation with the flowering purple of their outstanding eloquence, they hasten the history onward with greater power to please. Yet I seem to picture a furrowed brow confronting me:

“What work, then, do you undertake when the work is complete? Why spend labour, and, when the weary soldier has left the field stripped bare, why do you, a late fighter, keep vain watches? Why, when the giant is asleep after winning the prize, does a dwarf gird himself in vain for the course? Why, after that swan has been sung with drawn-out trumpets, do you prepare to make music on a brittle reed, when nothing has been omitted from what must be told, nor is there anything in what has been told that need fear polishing?”

Let my critic, I beg, endure me briefly, if perhaps the profession of truth can wash away the stain of rashness. Whoever rereads the earlier historians will encounter here the extended prolixity, mother of tedium, and there the compressed brevity, stepmother of the truth that must be expressed. Herbert, since he could speak about every detail from knowledge and bears witness to what he saw and heard, was carried beyond the bounds of concision by love for his master; leaving nothing untouched, he lengthened his narrative immeasurably. [Col. 0353A] John was shaken out before his style had reached completion by the storm raised by the turbulence of public power. The other two neither satisfied the thirst for the substance of the events nor escaped the disdainful brow of the fastidious reader.

Hence I have undertaken the costly task of abridging the work: to accommodate brevity to the delicate, without defrauding the studious of truth. Especially for this reason, I have traversed the shadowy breadth of the more expansive forest with the more abundant writers, namely Herbert and William; and entered the enclosed garden of the more polished writers, namely John and Alan. From all of them I have gathered the brighter flowers and, performing the office of an excerptor, sprinkled my book with the fragrance of another’s writings. I claim nothing from the whole structure of the edifice for myself except a rough sheet, asserting the place of a foundation.

[Col. 0353B] Moreover, lest the book be stained in any respect by the accusation of theft, it bears in the margin of its foreign page the names of its native authors, so that the name of the craftsman placed opposite may declare what each claims for himself from the common work. Indeed, since seams cannot be joined into a garment without a chain of thread, nor stones be raised into a wall without the bond of mortar, I have only fastened loops to the curtains and inserted clamps into the boards, so that the parts belonging under the roof of this united structure may hold together more firmly.

But just as a horse released to race across the breadth of an open field, if you draw back the reins for a while, after its feet have rested a little burns with renewed ardour for the course, so we too have divided the work into three parts, so that the reader, breathing now and then after what has been begun, may finally recover a more cheerful eagerness for reading.

[Col. 0353C] The first, extending from childhood to exile, sows in the garden of the mind faith like a tiny mustard seed. At first, because of its smallness, it escaped the gaze amid the display of worldly pomp; but afterward, growing into a taller tree, it gave rest and shade to the birds of heaven.

The second, under exile, unfolds the bitterness of the threshing-floor, where the wheat, in hope of the repose prepared for it in the granary, refrained from leaping away from the threshing-floor.

The third, taking up the Apostle’s more excellent way in the Passion, shows him becoming prodigal of his own life in order to gain Christ and testing, by the outpouring of his blood, that neither sword nor death could separate him from the love of Christ. There, by raising the wavering liberty of the Church to a firmer state, he repelled with the offering of his blood the ruin already threatening. And what we weaker people, trembling even at the name of a wolf, had judged impossible in event, he, meeting a lion, showed by the ease of his deed and the example of his own conduct: namely, that “the good shepherd gives his life for his sheep.”

[Col. 0353D] But if devouring envy has whetted the teeth of the spiteful to tear apart this little work, I have borrowed one reply to set against it:

> Envy everyone, envious man: no one envies you.

(Thus far the prologue. What follows from this point—namely, the nine chapters of the first book—consists solely of excerpts from the little works of John, Alan, Herbert, and William of Canterbury. There follows Chapter X, in which are found many things that seem to me to fill the gap in Herbert of Bosham, at Chapter 7 of Book III of the *Life of St Thomas*, below.)

[Col. 0354A] Or perhaps for this reason: lest some occupation, as often happened, should draw him elsewhere. Whenever that occurred, the same service was performed through one of the brothers responsible for the poor. Or certainly it was done at night, because in daylight there could not have been such devout leisure. And truly at that time the leisure was devout—most devout. His devotion found leisure in the night.

For you might see the bishop, in the silence of deep night, like a light in darkness, throwing himself at the feet of each person, asking prayer from each and weeping for each. His tears streamed from his eyes like the outflowing of waters, so that the feet of each seemed to be washed more by tears than by water.

The second banquet took place, not now in the concealment of night, but at dawn. For behold: when those thirteen, to whom the bishop had ministered while girded for service, went forth from the heavenly banquet, twelve others entered. As they reclined, the brother who carried the purses for the needs of the poor ministered in the bishop’s place, humbly and devoutly washing the feet of each: without silver vessels, indeed, but with abundant food. A third banquet was held in the advancing daylight at about the third hour of the day, when one hundred poor persons of those called prebendaries were brought in. Two brothers responsible for the poor ministered to them.

[Col. 0354C] Thus the bishop’s table was threefold, setting these three tables daily, as though he celebrated three Masses each day: the first at night, the second at dawn, the third in full daylight. Truly, instructed mystically by the teaching of anointing, he did this so that through these three tables, as through three Masses, pleasing sacrifices offered to God, the new birth of the Saviour might strengthen its own newness in him as a birth: so that the new birth of Christ might free the person whom old servitude had held under the yoke of sin, and thus the new person might put on Christ, the new man.

Therefore, after the synaxis (the assembly-service) had been chanted and that Gospel banquet, at which, as we have said, he himself had ministered, was over, he first took a brief sleep to restore his senses. While the others were still sleeping, he alone rose early to the sacred books. Summoning only one of his own household, who had been exercised in such matters for some time, to unfold with him the mysteries of Holy Scripture, he gathered, as though heaven’s floodgates had been opened, the manna of heavenly refreshment at the very beginning of the morning as food for the spirit. [Col. 0354D] This was the disciple who bears witness concerning these things, who saw and wrote them: Master Herbert of Bosham.

For, as Herbert himself confessed, if he proceeded without a guide through so many depths and obscurities of the Scriptures, he always feared error. Therefore, in plain matters Thomas sought him as a witness to his understanding, and in obscure matters always as the guide of his inquiry. But when the conference was finished, the person who had been summoned was immediately dismissed, and the bishop remained alone, shut up in his chamber, as though brought into the bridegroom’s wine-cellar. No one had access to him for any reason, even until the third hour of the day.

Behold Thomas: although he had already put his hand to mighty things and had ascended a watchtower, both through pre-eminence and through a certain lofty height of virtuous deeds, yet he walked along the way of the Scriptures so humbly and simply that in this he neither ran ahead of his teacher nor presumed upon himself. [Col. 0355A] Thus he, who had long contracted an ingrained roughness amid the brambles and thorns of the world, was so quickly instructed and so refreshed by that heavenly manna which he gathered each morning that he now poured forth for others what he had tasted, sowing the seed of God’s word upon every water, now among clergy, now among the people.

He was carried by such love of the Scriptures that, very often while travelling, he would turn his horse aside, summon the disciple mentioned above, and devote himself on the road to sacred instruction. He frequently repeated:

“Oh, if it were granted me, with worldly cares and business put aside, to devote myself in leisure and peace to such things! With the Lord’s favour, what fruitful labour I would spend upon them! How diligently I would repair the loss of wasted time!”

He used to fold in his loose sleeves little written sheets containing some not-to-be-despised edifying matter, so that by reading he might always have at hand more readily something to say. Nor should this be passed over in silence, but rather exalted in praise: he always kept with him many great men, endowed with every honour of conduct and life and distinguished by learning; most ready in the plain passages of Scripture, practiced in its mysteries, and fruitful in sacred discussion. [Col. 0355C] Among them any wise person would become wiser daily. This greatly advanced the bishop’s purpose and desire. For whenever he had leisure, he progressed from them no little day by day in wisdom and knowledge. With the Lord’s favour, near the very end of this whole history we shall arrange in sequence a catalogue of these learned men, setting down each of their names in order.

## Chapter XI. What He Was Like in the Office of the Altar

At about the third hour of the day the bishop came out of his chamber to consecrate the heavenly sacred things in priestly ministry. I now pass over those days on which he merely attended. For he did not celebrate every day; as he himself confessed, this was due not to negligence but to reverence. Even among good and holy priests practice varies in this matter. Some celebrate every day, others on fixed days. In those who celebrate I seem to see a great proof of holy conduct; in the others, a sign of reverence and humility.

[Col. 0355D] The canonical writings neither command nor forbid, neither discourage nor encourage, a priest’s daily offering; rather, they testify that it is enough to offer once on one day, just as Christ also was offered once. They declare very blessed the person who celebrates worthily on a single day. For the present I pass over as unworthy even of mention those priests not of Christ but of Mammon, who, for gain from offerings, do not merely once each day but rather repeatedly—more willingly—not so much consecrate as tear apart the one victim of Christ, offered once, making the Son of God a means of profit and display.

Putting these aside, let us return to our great priest, to be counted among those reverent priests of the Most High who fear and reverence to offer every day. Therefore, as soon as blessed Thomas prepared himself to offer, and the ministers brought the mystical and priestly vestments, immediately at the first sight of them, while not yet clothed in them, he shook and poured out his whole self. He poured out, I say, his heart and shook himself so greatly that a kind of fountain of tears flowed from his head.

When, clothed in the priestly vestments, he stood at the altar, first to pray for his own sins and those of the people and afterward to offer, his heart was so humbled and contrite that, in the sacred prayers, sobs rather than words were uttered with tears. In order to restrain empty and wandering thoughts of the heart while celebrating, he used always to hold some ethical writer in his hand while the ministers, during that Mass called the Mass of the catechumens, attended to the spiritual chants. [Col. 0356B] More often at that hour he held in his hands a certain little book of prayers, which one of his predecessors—an instrument of Catholic faith, staff against heretics, hammer of tyrants, treasury of the Scriptures, trumpet of the Gospel, and pillar of justice, blessed Anselm—had drawn forth in a style at once salutarily piercing, or piercingly salutary and elegant, from the inmost marrow of his holy devotion. This, I say, he had there, moving from prayer to reading.

Thereafter he was always accustomed to complete swiftly this special kind of prayer called the Mass. At the entrance of the Mass he said one collect, usually; three on occasion, but more rarely, or scarcely ever, or never. The original institution was indeed that only one collect should be said, so that, as there is one epistle and one Gospel, there should also be one collect. Later, in the passage of time, several were added; but, according to the form of the canons, they do not exceed the number seven.

In this special form of prayer, moreover, he observed this brevity and this haste in the sacramental eating of the flesh of the spotless Lamb out of reverence for that passage of the Lord, instructed by the Lord as such a priest should be, according to what is written in the Law: “You shall eat in haste,” for it is the *pascha*, that is, the passing of the Lord. [Col. 0356D] Thus he ate quickly because of incursions by evil angels—that is, the harmful onset of vain thoughts—in receiving the sacramental body of the Lord: neither slow nor lingering, and adding nothing new beyond what is appointed in the canon. At that particular hour, however, he poured out most profound tears and sobs, as though Christ’s wounds, once touched, shook all the inward parts of his heart and poured them out.

All who frequently stood by while he offered in public can bear witness to such great devotion. This man also kept his hands free from every gift and utterly banished the filth of avarice from his household.

(The second gap, which you will find in Herbert’s little book at Chapter 9 of Book III of the *Life of St Thomas*, below, seems to me capable of being supplied from what follows.)

[Col. 0357A] And immediately he went out publicly to recline at table with that distinguished company of his learned men. Reclining in the middle, he placed his learned men at his right, and monks and religious at his left. Knights and all other powerful persons always reclined separately and by themselves, so that the reading which sounded daily at the bishop’s table from the beginning to the end of the meal might not trouble those unable to understand it.

(Let us now hasten to the second book, which begins with these words:)

## Chapter I. What Happened at Court When the Archbishop’s Flight Became Known

Having dealt above with the matters from which arose the cause of discord between king and archbishop, and with the great and various injuries by which blessed Thomas was attacked, provoked by insults, shaken by rage, and compelled to seek in flight the protection of exile, let us proceed to set forth the history of his exile and the order of events that occurred in exile . . . etc. . . .

**The second book ends.**

# The Third Book Begins

After the courses of faith and hope have now been manfully traversed, in which blessed Thomas displayed to later ages both an argument and an example, unparalleled, of supreme steadfastness and exceptional patience, let us gird ourselves to contemplate more attentively the exertion of the more excellent way—the broader charity—through which, when he had arrived at the goal, he received from the supreme Judge the prize of eternal reward before his fellows.

For God had so directed his steps and perfected his feet in the broad paths of charity that, neither frightened by the threats of persecutors, did he depart in any degree from love of his God; nor, softened by the promises of flatterers, did he cease to strive for the just advancement of his shipwrecked mother, the Church, or of his brethren and neighbours. Rather, burning with the ardour of charity, he fought for the law of his God even unto death, and at last laid down his life for the sheep entrusted to him.

But leaving these matters for the diligent reader to investigate more subtly, let us continue the course of the history we have begun. Yet, in order that the truth of the holy man’s Passion and triumph may receive more certain credence, in this section we add a fifth witness to the four mentioned above: Benedict, of pious memory, later, in reward for his great merit, abbot of St Peter’s at Borough. On the very day when the victorious martyr fell, he stood among Thomas’s household in especially close attendance upon him; and, as a faithful witness, he arranged in truthful style and in order every particular that he saw and heard. [Col. 0357D] . . . etc.

# Events after the Martyrdom

[The third book is followed by a treatise bearing the title *Events after the Martyrdom*, a great part of which is excerpted from Herbert of Bosham’s *Book of Apples*. I do not know from what source the passages given here derive.]

## Chapter I. How the king grieved over the deed and tried to clear himself

When the king of England heard that blessed Thomas had fallen by the swords of his own men, after a few days he sent his clerks with letters. On arriving at Canterbury, they assembled the brethren and said:

[Col. 0358A] “The misfortune which has occurred among you has distressed the lord king to such an extent that he has abstained from entering a church for three days; and from the day on which he heard of it until the third [day] he has taken no food except almond milk. He has admitted no comfort and has not appeared in public, knowing that the cruelty of his followers’ action redounds to his disgrace, and that it cannot readily be persuaded that he did not seek the life of one whom he had so often grieved to find opposing his decrees, whom he had felt to be the sole obstacle in his kingdom to arranging ecclesiastical affairs as he wished.

“A deed indeed detestable has been accomplished, an unprecedented crime; and he must be believed the less likely to have been privy to such a thing, since there is [Col. 0358B] no doubt that until the present day he had preserved him in safety. One matter, however, bites his conscience. For when he learned that all who had been present at his son’s coronation were excommunicated, he could not conceal his grief, since he believed that, under the peace which had been concluded, every fuel of anger and enmity had now been lulled to rest. Calling his close associates, he gave voice to his complaint concerning the injury thus revived. They sympathized with his grief, and were moved all the more violently because he was being opposed by the man whom he had promoted.

“Therefore, without his knowledge, wishing to avenge his wrongs and thus believing that they would please him, those four men who committed the crime secretly withdrew from court. When he heard this, knowing them to be most fierce and the wickedest of all who lived within the bounds of his kingdom, he feared lest something should be done which would bring [Col. 0358C] disgrace upon the royal house. Immediately he sent the swiftest men, that by occupying the ports they might prevent the madness of the sons of Belial. But they, as though assisted by favorable winds, had crossed over to their own ruin, accomplishing, without his knowledge, that which will never be consigned to oblivion. For on the very day on which the deed was done he believed that they were present with him.

“Brothers, we have been sent to make this known to you, lest you suspect anything sinister concerning the serenity of so great a prince. But if he has incurred any guilt because he seems to have said something which invited the assailants to undertake the crime, it is fitting that this be expiated by your prayers. And now he orders that the body be honorably committed to burial, to be laid with his fathers. For he does not persecute him when dead, [Col. 0358D] although he had regarded him as hostile while alive; rather, whatever he has done amiss against himself, he forgives to his soul. He pays no heed to former reversals; he does not recall the injuries inflicted upon him as king.”

By this some might think the king’s innocence cleared, had not the taunts of the king’s royal attendants rendered the king’s protestations suspect. For when William de Mandeville came to Canterbury from overseas, he said: “Had I found the primate, I would have dealt distinctly with him concerning matters pertaining to the royal dignity; and if he had submitted according to what was demanded, peace would have been made. But if he had presumed, in obstinate contumacy, to resist, he would without doubt have had to be compelled to yield.”

Others likewise threatened that, if the monks had dared rashly to conceal [Col. 0359A] the king’s traitor, all their hiding places would have been burned down to a single stump, so that, defeated, they might surrender for capital punishment the man whom they had protected, to their own destruction, as guilty of treason against the royal majesty. Some even forbade them to mourn that seditious man who had thrown the whole kingdom into confusion, lest they too should be drawn with him into mourning. These and similar remarks made the king’s conscience suspect.

### On the king’s penance

Accordingly, when that deadly deed had been published everywhere and the news reached the king of England, he was afflicted, as we have said above, with great distress. In the very celebrated town of Normandy called Argentan, he sat mourning for forty days. [Col. 0359B] Throughout that whole penitential period he made a lament far more bitter than mourning for the dead: he ate the food of mourners, mounted no horse, admitted to himself no cause of litigants, no consultation concerning affairs to be conducted, no complaint of petitioners; no concern for the governing of so many lands was put before him, as though in his grief he set all things aside.

He sat alone, continually groaning and grieving over what had happened, often and again repeating: “Alas, alas, that this has happened to me!” Yet this was the provident course toward salvation taken by the penitent king. At the very first hearing of the sacrilege he sent distinguished and capable men to Pope Alexander at Rome, seeking counsel from him, as the supreme protector of the Church and father of all, as to what ought to be done; and, as is credible, humbly confessing wherein he had sinned. [Col. 0359C] But since confession is not customarily made, nor ought it to be made, either by writing or through intermediaries, and since the living voice of the confessor, in proportion as it increases devotion, possesses greater efficacy, the apostolic man sent from his side two cardinals: Master Theodwin, bishop of Porto, of pious memory, and Albert, chancellor of the holy Roman Church—men certainly endowed with every sanctity and learning of religion. They were to absolve canonically those of the realm who, for the aforesaid reasons, had been anathematized or suspended, and to provide for the salvation of the king who sought it. Thus they were sent for the consolation of the king and of the whole Church. At their arrival, they obtained from the clemency of the lord pope and of those who had been sent the absolution which they had not deserved. [Col. 0359D]

## Chapter VIII. On the death of King Henry the Younger, supernaturally shown to the archbishop in a vision

We cannot here be silent concerning the death of the boy Henry, the younger king, which was spiritually foreshown to the archbishop. While the archbishop was still in exile at the French city of Sens, one night, after the nocturnal office had been sung, he withdrew to his bed for rest. But, as he himself confessed, the cares and thoughts which then pressed upon him, as they commonly do, did not allow him to give himself to sleep.

Among other thoughts, there came to him a reflection concerning the lord king of England: his greatness, his prosperity in sons, riches, and broad dominions. As he pondered these matters for a long time—especially [Col. 0360A] his sons, and above all among them his firstborn, Henry, whom he loved beyond the others—and one other son. The next day, however, as he related, he did not know for certain which of the others he had then been considering: whether Richard, then count of Poitou, or Geoffrey, count of Brittany.

As he thus thought of the king, the father, and his sons, he desired to know what would become of them and what dispositions the Most High had made concerning them. While he continued for some time in such desiring thought, he began, amid his meditation, as it were to doze. And behold, a voice came to him, expressing itself in a hexameter verse. The verse was:

> One death has taken two; another has taken, but grievously, their father.

Let no one suppose that this verse was composed by chance by one half asleep—something which he could not have composed even when wholly awake and alert—for he had never pursued the art of versification, even to a slight extent, under any scholarly instruction. [Col. 0360B] The next day he reported the verse which he had heard to his companions, and added mournfully: “Alas, our Henry will die before his father or his brothers!”

And indeed, in Henry’s death—alas, the grief, and cause for grief!—the archbishop was proved a most true prophet by the outcome of his prophecy. The archbishop’s prophecy was likewise fulfilled in Geoffrey’s death. Five or six years after Henry’s death, Geoffrey too died before his father. And this enhances the miracle and commends the prophecy still more: “One death has taken two.” Truly it was one death, because both brothers were killed by the same kind of death, dysentery. [Col. 0360C] As those who were present testified, they were taken away from the midst well and holily.

We refrain from speaking of the father’s death, which the verse just quoted also appears to have foretold, because it is too well known to nearly the whole world; and it must be lamented by those who read of it, and especially by those who know it, that so great and such a prince departed from the world in such a manner and so suddenly. All who devoutly believe should pray for him, that, as he was peaceful and a lover of peace, he may obtain from Him who is the author and lover of peace everlasting peace and rest.

## Catalogue of the Learned Writings of Blessed Thomas

(This treatise has been taken verbatim from Herbert’s work.)

[Col. 0360D]

# THE CAUSE OF THE EXILE AND MARTYRDOM OF BLESSED THOMAS THE MARTYR

We have also endeavored to insert in this little book that fatal and famous written decree: namely, those royal customs promulgated at Clarendon. We include them here so that future ages may read them and thereby recognize how just and manifest was the cause, first of the exile and afterward of the martyrdom, of the glorious new martyr Thomas.

### Chapter I. On advowson, etc.

[See the same material in Herbert.]

[Col. 0361A]

### Other constitutions

These are the constitutions which King Henry established in Normandy, after blessed Thomas had been banished. He commanded that they be sworn and observed against Pope Alexander and Archbishop Thomas by his justices, Richard de Lucy and two archdeacons—Geoffrey Ridel, archdeacon of Canterbury, and Richard, archdeacon of Poitou—and by all the nobles and peoples of England. Their bearers were Winier, priest and chaplain, and Walter of Grimsby, sheriff.

### Chapter I

If anyone is found carrying letters or a command of the lord pope, or of the archbishop of Canterbury, containing an interdict of Christian observance into England, let him be seized, and justice be done upon him without delay as upon a traitor to king and kingdom.

[The Bodleian manuscripts [Col. 0361B] read: “let him be seized and held until the king or the justiciar shall have ordered his will concerning him.”]

### Chapter II

Let no clerk, canon, monk, lay brother, or person of any religious order be permitted to cross the sea or to return to England, unless he possesses letters of the justiciar for his crossing, or letters of the lord king for his return. If anyone is found acting otherwise, let him be seized and held.

### Chapter III

Let no one carry any command to the lord pope or to the archbishop of Canterbury; and if anyone is found who has carried one, let him be seized and held. Let no one appeal to the lord pope or to the archbishop of Canterbury. Let no plea be held by their command, nor let any command of theirs be received in England by any person. [Col. 0361C] And if anyone has held, received, or negotiated such a command, let him be seized and held.

### Chapter IV

Likewise, it is generally forbidden that anyone, clerk or layman, carry any command to the lord pope or to the archbishop. If such a person is found, let him be seized and imprisoned.

### Chapter V

If bishops, clerks, abbots, or laymen observe the sentence of interdict, let them be expelled from the land without delay, together with all their kin; and let them take none of their chattels with them, but let everything be seized into the king’s hand.

[Col. 0362A]

### Chapter VI

Let the chattels of all who favor the lord pope or the archbishop, and all their possessions, and those of all persons belonging to them—of whatever rank, order, sex, or condition—be seized and confiscated into the demesne of the lord king.

### Chapter VII

Let all clerks who possess revenues in England be summoned through every county to come into England within three months to their revenues, if they value them and wish thereafter to return to England. If they do not come by the prescribed term, let their revenues be seized into the king’s hand.

### Chapter VIII

Let Saint Peter’s Pence no longer be paid to the Apostolic See, but be diligently collected, kept in the king’s treasury, and spent at his command.

[Col. 0362B]

### Chapter IX

Let the bishops of London and Norwich be at the king’s mercy, and let them be summoned by sheriffs and beadles to appear before the king’s justices, to render right to the king and his justices concerning their interdicting, contrary to the statutes of Clarendon and at the pope’s command, the land of Count Hugh; and concerning their publishing through their dioceses, without permission of the king’s justices, the excommunication which the lord pope had pronounced against him.

Next come four letters whose openings are: “Know that this is …,” “It is a cause for rejoicing …,” “It gives off the fragrance …,” … “Because in the place of blessed …,” … Then follow Alan’s prologue, beginning “Honor …,” and John’s prologue, beginning “The most holy ….” [Col. 0362C] To all of these is appended the following note.

The compiler of these acts and letters, after these prologues, appends the Life of Saint Thomas written by John of Salisbury, and certain collected materials concerning the contest of the glorious martyr, drawn from the other writers of his life praised above, which assist in understanding the letters. Their body appears in the preceding pages, and therefore need not be repeated here.

The compiler concludes.

[Col. 0361]

# PROLOGUE AND BEGINNING OF THE LIFE OF SAINT THOMAS

Preserved in the British Museum among the Lansdowne manuscripts, no. 398.

## THE PROLOGUE BEGINS

[Col. 0361D] I am about to relate notable matters, confirmed by common testimony; and matters which, in the conscience and the spiritual advancement of the faithful to whom our letter is addressed—or rather, who are Christ’s letter through faith, written [Col. 0362D] not in ink but in the Spirit—make an argument more certain and evident than in our little writing.

Would that Apicius might so season our truth that what I am about to say may profit all for edification, and that the examples of charity, humility, and patience set forth in imitation of the blessed bishop and martyr Thomas may please each individual. For we do not intend to embellish a panegyric, but to unfold a plain history; not to paint an itinerary, but simply to explain what was done.
