We do not intend to color what is lowly or cloak what is despised, but to attend more to the truth of things than to elegance of language.

Whatever I can say will fall short of praise of the martyr, much less of God glorified in the martyr. Therefore, to begin from the very egg, lest I begin where there is no beginning, and lest, artificially following the poet:

> Now I shall say what now ought to be said,  
> so that the things to be said may cohere with what has been said;

[Col. 0363B]

> lest the beginning differ from the middle, or the middle from the end—

let truth, lending credibility to the account, always accompany the narrative. For as it is unjust to blaspheme or detract from the saints, so it is unacceptable to add anything contrary to truth.

I was unwilling that the memory of Thomas, that eminent [Col. 0364A] martyr, should perish in silence; rather, by the service of letters, the labor of my pen, the hands of writings, the tongue of teaching, and the eyes of knowledge, I commend it to posterity. And although I do not doubt that the life of this saint has been most diligently treated by more learned men, compelled by love for him I too offer what I can.

Since I intend in no way to depart from truth, let no one censure his own person if he sees it represented here otherwise than he himself would wish. For one who was formerly bad may perhaps have been corrected; and one who is not yet corrected may perhaps become what this man is. Thus, if in discussing the holy martyr I insert, for the sake of historical truth, what was done, let no one be angry or inflamed because matters which are true are also introduced concerning him. For, as is said in ecclesiastical [Col. 0364B] history, it becomes a writer to place all things after truth.

But if any have treated the life of this holy martyr better, we do them no prejudice in this small work; rather, we yield to the more learned. Let those who read forgive our lack of skill, and pardon the effort of one who offers all that he could, though he could not fulfill his intention.

## THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 0363]

[Col. 0363C] Blessed Thomas, archbishop and martyr, born of citizens of London of modest means, rose step by step in worldly rank: from a poor scholar he advanced to become archdeacon; then, having become the king’s chancellor, he was raised to the dignity of archbishop. Thus it was shown by this advancement through ranks in the flesh that there would be a great advancement of virtues in his mind.

For this reason he was raised so high by the Lord from poverty: that he might love the more, in proportion as he had been made great out of nothing. Or it was because, according to Paul’s saying, God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, the weak things to confound the strong, the ignoble and contemptible things, and things which are not, to bring to nothing those which are. What is wiser than this fool for Christ? What is stronger than this weak man? For that which is foolish [Col. 0363D] in God is wiser than men, and that which is weak in God is stronger than men.

But why was this fool and weak man of Christ stronger and wiser than men? While still subject to childhood, he neither greatly benefited nor injured many, because he was still incapable. He was not yet remarkable for any grace, though already anticipated by magnificent grace. How the light lay hidden in him beneath a bushel, I shall disclose—with the saint’s permission.

For as rest after labor is welcome, refreshment after hunger pleasing, and day radiant after darkness, so the examples of good men shine more clearly through the preface and comparison of preceding evils. Who was more violent than Paul? Who more dissolute than Magdalene? Yet the one became the Lord’s vessel of election and teacher of the Gentiles; the other was an example of true—indeed, wonderful—[Col. 0364C] repentance. He was the least among the apostles in rank, greatest in grace; she, the apostle of the apostles. Who therefore should despair? Yet let no one presume. Let the evil person look to Paul and Mary; let the good person fear the sentence of the Judge.

I do not say this because blessed Thomas was ever evil or perverse, but because he at some time began the good which he performed. For Jesus had not yet said to Thomas, who was to become Peter through faith: “Follow me”; nor to him who was to become Paul through hope: “My grace is sufficient for you”; nor to him who was to become John through charity: “Thus I will that you remain until I come.” He still let the wild ass go free in the desert, and the Lord sat upon the colt of an ass which had never borne a yoke. But that day will come on which it will be said to you, Thomas: “When you were younger, you girded yourself [Col. 0364D] and walked where you wished; but soon another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.” But now let us continue the history.

His father and mother were both righteous before God: steadfast in faith, persevering in hope, fervent in charity, abundant in almsgiving, foremost in hospitality, fearing the Lord and honoring all people for Christ’s sake; very sparing toward themselves, yet according to their means lavishly generous to others; prudent in speech. For when has anyone, rich or poor, entered the kingdom of heaven without difficulty? No one is crowned unless he has contended lawfully. The kingdom of God indeed suffers violence, and the violent seize it. And if the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and sinner appear? Therefore, that blessed Thomas’s renunciation of household wealth might be abundant, his property increased.

When the archdeacon of Canterbury had been promoted elsewhere, and all the clergy requested it, the people acclaimed it, and Archbishop Theobald consented—indeed, preferred it—blessed Thomas was happily appointed to the archdeaconry, as one who excelled in good character. [Col. 0365A] In that office he made every effort, as in his earlier manner of life, that his secret might be hidden from all, yet laid open before the eyes of the highest God. He said that God alone must be served, saying with Moses, loving and continually affirming the testimony of his own conscience and not that of another; never trusting anyone more than himself concerning himself, and saying with Isaiah: “My secret is mine; my secret is mine.”

Truly, what is yours is yours; what belongs to all belongs to each person for himself. For each lives for himself or dies for himself, according to the saying: “I will not give my glory to another.” Nor can I give my punishment. Therefore blessed Thomas, taking counsel for himself and consulting himself, endeavored in his archdeaconry to be known only to God and to himself. Yet he endeavored to displease himself that he might please God, recalling the Apostle’s words: “If I were still pleasing men, I would not be the servant of Christ.”

He lived without offense in himself, without complaint toward his neighbors. For the first degree of perfection is guarding oneself; the second, mercy toward one’s neighbor; the third, love of God. The first is innocence, the second beneficence, the third devoted love. But because man sees the face while God looks upon the heart—He alone knows human hearts, understands thoughts from afar, according to the Psalmist, and, according to another saying, “searches hearts and kidneys”—[Col. 0365B] blessed Thomas arranged, so far as he could, to remain hidden from the world. He was one person within and appeared another without: not a whitewashed wall, not corrupted by the leaven of the Pharisees, not like a tomb of the dead, not a wolf in a lamb, not crafty beneath the fox’s guise. Rather, concealing himself and what was his, he preferred to be good rather than to seem so, making little of being called evil; for even the Lord is called a Samaritan and said to have a demon.

But the Lord, seeing the constancy of His servant, tested him still more surely, while bestowing grace more abundantly. He now set him before the whole world: surrounded him with riches, tested him with pleasures, enlarged him with honors. And what did he do? He was not burned in the fire, nor drowned in the stream. He who tested him through such things, also making with the temptation a way out that he might endure it, preserved him unshaken by all.

For now, when the graciousness, industry, liberality, and courtliness of blessed Thomas had become known and proven—since he was cheerful in expression, gentle in address, humble in service, prudent in counsel, discerning in judgment, faithful in what was entrusted to him—he was enrolled at the court of King Henry II, at the king’s own request, though the archbishop presented him unwillingly. [Col. 0365C] There again, to commend his future glory, I say: he was able more than usual to serve the world, but he preferred Christ.

Having become chancellor and bearer of the seal-tablet, he was joined to the king in such friendship that he bore the king’s will in his own mind, spoke with the king’s mouth, and himself directed the affairs of the realm. He promoted whom he wished and deposed whom he wished; whatever he ordered was done, whatever he forbade was left undone. Like a maiden naturally fitted for the task, he bound the rhinoceros with his cord and led it wherever he wished. Thus he aroused great envy among the magnates against himself.

Yet, though placed in so great power and endowed with such glory and dignity, his former humility remained; his natural independence clung to him, and his native generosity. Chastity was ever his companion, charity his partner. Each virtue was an inseparable companion to him: the sixty mighty men from among Israel’s mightiest, surrounding the bed of our peaceable one, each with his sword upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night. Truth was always in his mouth; falsehood was always absent. And if he was perhaps at any time tempted by carnal pleasures, he was neither drawn away nor enticed.

Like a second Samson, he broke the bonds of all sins by the scent of fire—that is, of the Holy Spirit—and, rushing upon his most wicked enemies, namely vices, pursued Amalek to extermination. The sword of Ehud spared none; he who used either hand as his right. Although blessed Thomas possessed such great power, God held him aloof from the tumult of every deadly action. [Col. 0365D]

But because no one is without sin, not even an infant whose life upon earth is one day: if there was anything in him needing purification, there was nevertheless nothing needing burning. “If anyone’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss.” If there was anything in him to be examined, there was nothing to be condemned. If perhaps he did anything in which there was vanity and presumption of spirit, there was nevertheless nothing in which there was blasphemy against the Holy Spirit—that is, malice.

And though he lived in the flesh, he did not wage war according to the flesh. He abstained, like a vessel of election, not only from crimes and great offenses but also from lesser ones. His counsel was like Hushai’s, better than Ahithophel’s; his companionship like Jonathan’s; his action like Abishai’s. As for the deeds he performed—how judiciously he conducted himself in peace, how powerfully in war, how much he devised against the king’s enemies, how much he ordered in the realm, how much he acquired outside the country—are not these written in everyone’s knowledge? Let us therefore pass over these, for we hasten to other matters.

And because what is to be treated exceeds me, the sails of greater effort must be spread, the capacity of the mind enlarged, and the majesty of the Trinity invoked. When Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, had fallen asleep with his fathers, the metropolitan Church was deprived of its shepherd. No golden plate shone on anyone’s forehead; no breastpiece was seen upon anyone’s breast; no ephod was borne on shoulders; the bells were silent and the other pontifical ornaments were wrapped up. [Col. 0366D]

But since there could not long be lacking one to whom the primacy of the English and the legation of the holy and apostolic see should pass, and upon whom the rights of all Christian England should depend; and since the sons of the Bridegroom could not fast long lest they perish: all the clergy and the entire assembly, according to ecclesiastical decrees, canonical enactments, and the privileges of the Church of Canterbury, asked the king to provide them with a worthy shepherd.

The king rejoiced because he had found the man whom he loved to raise to this high place. He put forward, recommended, urged, and commanded that the archdeacon of Canterbury and his own chancellor be received as shepherd. And because he seemed a person insufficiently religious, having until then remained in secular dress and never worn the habit of religion, and therefore seemed less suitable for so great a rank, they would gladly have rejected him if they had dared. But because it was not safe to oppose openly the will of king and lord, they too assented to the solemn election of the bishops.

Having been enthroned, however, he afterward voluntarily and canonically resigned into the hands of the supreme pontiff Alexander the irregularly obtained honor which he had acquired less than canonically; as what follows will make clear, he received it again, restored and confirmed, only with reluctance and under compulsion of apostolic authority. [Col. 0367A]

[Col. 0367B] [Here the first reading begins.] Thus promoted, initiated, anointed with the sanctification and consecration of holy unction, he advanced so greatly that he declared his previous life to have been as nothing, as though he had always been dying until then and had only now begun to live. So eagerly did he strive to redeem the time of life that had been lost.

Accordingly, he suddenly seized the summit of all perfection, as though he would die on the next day. Where sin had previously abounded, grace afterward superabounded, so that one might say that the Holy Spirit had descended upon him in the form of a dove and remained with him. Remembering that Platonic—indeed Christian—maxim, that true philosophy is meditation upon death, and Jerome’s saying, “He easily despises all these things who always thinks that he is going to die,” he did not think proudly but feared.

Although, having been educated from earliest childhood in the liberal arts, he might have gloried in secular wisdom and worldly philosophy, he nevertheless learned to know nothing among mortals except Jesus Christ, and Him crucified. Fastened to the Crucified One upon the cross, he mortified his former members with their vices and desires, saying with the Apostle: “The world is crucified to me, and I to the world”; and again: “I live, yet no longer I; rather Christ lives in me.”

Casting off the old garment and the old man with his deeds, he put on the new man, who was created according to God in the spirit and holiness of truth. Walking in newness of life, he became a new man, changed into another man—truly another, because transformed—whose every quality was turned toward what was better. [Col. 0367C]

For pride, if any had been present, was expelled and humility adopted; excess was banished and frugality introduced; prodigality was eliminated and thrift brought in; luxury, if any had been present, was replaced by abstinence; lust, if any, by continence; effeminacy, if any, by severity; vanity, if any, by maturity; curiosity, if any, by repose; inconstancy by stability; immoderation by temperance; every unlawful movement of the mind by virtue; and every useless desire of the world by contempt for it. [Col. 0367D]

[Second reading.] He was now more gracious in conversation, more cheerful in giving, more serene in countenance, sparer in dress, more moderate in expense, more diligent in prayer, more prolonged in contemplation, more earnest in preaching; patient in tribulation, compassionate in suffering, ready in acts of mercy, abundant in almsgiving, slow to anger, first to forgive, prompt in modesty, wholly gentle, devout in assistance, firm in faith, certain in hope, perfect in charity.

This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High; these are the changes of clothing with which Jesus the great priest, son of Jozadak, is clothed at the Lord’s command. This is the change of Tamar’s clothing as she sat at the crossroads. This is the change of David’s appearance when he feigned madness and fell at the gates of the city before Achish. This is the fragrance of Esau’s very good garments, with which not Esau but Jacob is clothed, likened to the smell of a field full and blessed by the Lord. They were owed to Esau, but Jacob received them, and therefore was blessed by his father. Esau lost his birthright, which Jacob obtained. This is what the Apostle says: “We are a pleasing fragrance to God.” [Col. 0368A]

Therefore our archbishop and martyr, possessing an anointing from the Holy One, received the oil of joy in place of mourning, the garment of praise in place of a sorrowful spirit. Proceeding by the forked road of Pythagoras’s letter, he despised the branch cast down and bending low, and took the upright path that stretches to heaven. He says with the Apostle: “We have no abiding city here, but seek the one to come”; and again: “Our citizenship is in heaven.”

Although he could have pursued many private concerns from his revenues, he devoted all to the common fellowship of the brethren, in accordance with that saying in the Acts of the Apostles: distribution was made to each according as need required.

> Calling nothing his own which the swiftly changing hour  
> may now by prayer, now by price, now by force, now by final death,  
> transfer to new masters and yield to another’s rights.

[Col. 0368B]

In mind and deed he diligently recalled the Apostle’s injunction: “A bishop must be blameless, chaste, sober, prudent, adorned in character, modest, hospitable, not given to wine,” and so forth; and he showed himself to be such a man.

[Third reading.] Set amid such great concern for his subjects, he labored with utmost watchfulness and great effort—rebuking, reproving, exhorting—that no one should perish and that, when the ravening wolf came, it should not scatter the sheep. Rather, mounting up against it, he set himself as a wall for the house of Israel against every enemy; in the contest he fought manfully. He sustained churches, confirmed ecclesiastical rights by his authority, reclaimed what had been lost, recalled what had been taken away, restored what had been diminished, and restrained the impious and rebellious by a sentence of anathema.

But the devil envied his great happiness and advancement. He stirred up his members, kindled and driven by the torches of envy, to malign the man of God. They disparaged him in corners, slandered him in chambers, and laid snares by every means they could—as dragons in secret and lions openly. They sat in ambush in hidden places with the rich, to kill the innocent. [Col. 0368C]

But what did our champion do? Zeal for the house of God consumed him: it kindled him, devoured him, and therefore the reproaches of those who reproached fell upon him. O how ardent and holy was the holy man’s jealousy, through which he might unite that one perfect beloved, that one dove, with her one Bridegroom, while he himself, as the one minister, was joined to them; and, admitted to the bridal chamber and privy both to their love and embrace, might sing the marriage song and say: “Behold, you are beautiful and fair; therefore the King has brought you into His chamber.” And again concerning the Bridegroom: “Your beloved is white and ruddy.”

Moved by this zeal for God’s people, he desired with the Apostle to be accursed from Christ for his brethren, and with Moses to be blotted from God’s book, so that the people’s offense might be forgiven. O what great confidence in God’s mercy! He desired, for Christ’s sake, to be separated from Christ; for Christ’s sake to refuse to possess Christ; to be blotted from the book of life, that he might be written more firmly in the book of life!

Reflecting upon the Apostle’s saying, “He who desires the episcopate desires a good work,” whereas at first he thirsted for honor rather than labor, he now desired, on the contrary, work rather than wealth; a burden rather than exaltation. Presenting himself as an example, he turned upon himself the Apostle’s words: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.” Thus he taught nothing that he had not done, as the proper order of teaching demands; but, contrary to the order which does not demand it, he was ashamed to teach many things which he was not ashamed to do. He served God in secret, but not so as to remain concealed; rather, he served as a spectacle shared by human beings and angels. For what he did secretly in his chamber, and what he hid even in the inner sanctuary of his mind, was now preached upon the housetops. [Col. 0369A–0370A]

[Fourth reading.] Meanwhile, under the reign of the most glorious Henry II, king of England, the land rested from robbers; there was peace and security from thieves; justice awoke; the buildings of the saints were restored. Song and rejoicing were heard among the clergy, etc.

(What has been transcribed from this Passion is sufficient for the present; whoever wishes to read the rest should seek it in the manuscript itself [Col. 0370B].)

[Col. 0369]

# HYMN OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0369B]

> Canterbury, crowned with a new Thomas,  
> as Rome with her own Peter,  
> rejoice.  
> Nay, let the whole Church militant  
> be devout, fulfilling  
> its pious vows of praise.
>
> [Col. 0369C] This Thomas, while he defends  
> the law of God, earns  
> the wrath of England’s king.
>
> Therefore, driven from the city, he departs,  
> and, crossing the sea, entrusts  
> himself to the king of France,
>
> who visits him gladly and worthily,  
> so devoutly, so kindly,  
> as though he were his father.
>
> There, like a new recruit,  
> Thomas, with marvelous fervor,  
> serves the King of kings.
>
> At last, peace
reformed,
Peace veiled by guile,

Returning to his own affairs,

He serves God while preserving the law;

Then the enemy rages and behaves insolently

[Col. 0369D] with varied artifice.

Now, like a crafty fox,

Now, like a violent tiger,

He tries every avenue.

Now he threatens, now he flatters;

But the other is softened by nothing,

Remaining wholly the same.

When the king finds that

The man, a champion of truth, cannot be moved,

Nor his resolve broken,

He arms the sheep against their shepherd,

Having incited his retinue

To bloodshed.

[Col. 0370B] Therefore, that those parricides,

Most foully and faithlessly,

May remove the patron of liberty

And usurp the throne,

They rush into the church.

[Col. 0370C] The bishop, praying in secret,

Comes forth openly, scorning the enemy;

Nor is the peace of his mind disturbed

By fear of the raging crowd,

But he advances to meet them.

The desired head of the holy priest,

Sought by a thousand prayers,

In the bosom of the holy mother

Drinks the sword; blood flows;

And there, amid the very tumult,

He heals a blind man.

What need is there to speak of what follows?

The miracles everywhere

Speak sufficiently for themselves:

The demon yields, death obeys,

Health returns to the desperate,

The stain of leprosy flees.

King of the English,

[Col. 0370D] do you not know that the King of angels

Weighs the merits

Of all, each one individually?

Each will reap what he sows;

Nothing will go unpunished;

Not even a hair is lost,

Much less the heads themselves.

O Thomas, bright jewel of the clergy,

By the efficacy of your prayers

Subdue the stirrings of our flesh,

So that, rooted in Christ, the true vine,

We may receive the rewards of true life. Amen.

[Col. 0371]

# HISTORICAL DOCUMENTS CONCERNING SAINT THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

## I. THE CASE BETWEEN THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY AND THE BISHOP OF LONDON

[Col. 0371A] The archbishop states that he publicly excommunicated the bishop of London for just and notorious causes: namely, as an instigator of schism, a manifest disturber of ecclesiastical peace, and a person guilty of continual disobedience. For he asserts that, on the pretext of schism, the bishop had manifestly supported certain rebels against the Church and oppressors of ecclesiastical liberties, and had hitherto openly contemned both the canons and his own commands concerning their restraint and punishment. Since these matters were manifest and notorious, as he says, he did not think judicial procedure had to be observed in the bishop’s excommunication; but, although the bishop was absent, unaware, undefended, unheard, neither cited nor warned, he nevertheless condemned him justly and canonically, as he alleges, as one convicted of his crime by the evident character of his acts.

For Ambrose writes: “Manifest matters require no accusation.” Likewise Pope Stephen says: “In a manifest cause, known to many, witnesses need not be sought.” As Ambrose expounded concerning the Corinthian fornicator: “In other cases a judge ought not condemn without an accuser, since the Lord did not reject Judas, although he was a thief, because he had not been accused. But when the aforesaid deed of the fornicator became known, the Apostle judged that he should be expelled from the fellowship of the brethren. For everyone knew the crime: publicly he had his stepmother in the place of a wife. In that case there was no need, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasive device. Concerning him the Apostle says: ‘Though absent in body, yet present by the authority of the Spirit, which is nowhere absent, I have already judged, as though present, [Col. 0371C] that the man who committed this deed be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.’” Likewise Pope Nicholas says: “What King Lothair did requires no accusation. The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness,” etc. For he had dismissed his lawful wife and publicly kept another woman brought in to replace her; thus, although neither accused nor cited, he was nevertheless canonically excommunicated.

[Col. 0372A] Similarly, therefore, the archbishop asserts that he rightly condemned the bishop of London, although outside judicial procedure: as one who, through zeal for schism, was a manifest disturber of ecclesiastical peace and a publicly inexcusable transgressor, by his acts of contempt, of the canons themselves and of the archbishop’s commands.

He argues that the bishop manifestly disturbed ecclesiastical peace on this ground: when the lord king, contrary to sacred laws and canons and to the liberties of the Church, publicly set forth in his council many observances which he claimed were to be kept by custom of the realm, and demanded them of the bishops, this bishop, he alleges, became there like a dumb dog unable to bark. He did not rise up in opposition nor set himself as a wall for the house of the Lord [Col. 0372B] to stand in battle. Rather—and this was much worse—under the pretext of the schism of the Roman Church, he openly endeavoured to persuade them that concessions ought to be made to the king. He above all weakened the spirits of his fellow bishops, whom, as foremost among them in power and pre-eminent in authority, he both ought and could above all have encouraged to resist.

The archbishop maintains that he did this for no other reason than to avoid losing the king’s favour, which at that time he enjoyed above the others. Yet Anacletus says to the contrary: “Nothing is more wretched than the shepherd who glories in the praises of wolves. If he seeks to please them and chooses to be loved by them, great destruction will thereby come upon the sheep.” Accordingly, the archbishop continues, through the bishop’s connivance the king became bolder and more eager than was fitting to exact his demands. Although the others held out for a time, he then began to be angry with them, harsh, terrible, and hostile toward them in many matters; whereas he admitted this bishop into a notably closer intimacy. Thus, he concludes, it is plainly beyond doubt that the bishop disturbed the Church’s peace. For, as Pope John says, “He undoubtedly shares the guilt of the doer who neglects to correct what he is able to correct.” For it is written: “Not only those who do such things, but [Col. 0373A] also those who consent to those who do them, are judged participants. For to neglect, when one can cast down the wicked, is nothing other than to encourage them; nor is he free from the taint of hidden consent who ceases to oppose an evident crime.” Likewise Innocent: “An error which is not resisted is approved, and truth, when it is not defended, is oppressed.” Likewise Gregory: “He consents to one in error who does not come forward to cut away what ought to be corrected.”

Then, the archbishop continues, after the lord king had gained his demands through fearsome intimidation and many oppressions, that same archbishop not long afterwards, coming to himself again under the pressure of fear and inwardly pierced by grief of heart, without regard for dangers or losses to himself or his associates, went into exile. [Col. 0373B] There he performed the most severe penance for the promises made against the lord and the Church; and, after the proscription of himself and his companions and after a year’s waiting, he pronounced a general and public sentence of anathema upon those who exacted and observed those promises and those consenting to them.

In order that this sentence might be proclaimed throughout England, he immediately wrote to and commanded the bishop of London, dean of the suffragan bishops, under obedience. He likewise commanded him, under obedience, to carry out certain other measures which were according to God. The bishop, he says, fulfilled none of these commands, but openly evaded them by certain pretexts; and thus, by the clear evidence of his conduct, manifestly confessed his crime and openly incurred the sentence of excommunication. Pope Adrian, indeed, placed under anathema violators of the canons and those consenting to them, saying: “By a general decree we establish that an execrable anathema shall fall upon, and that he shall always stand guilty before God as a transgressor of the Catholic faith, whoever among kings, bishops, or magnates hereafter believes or promises that the decrees of the Roman pontiffs may in any respect be violated.” Likewise Pope Damasus: “Violators of the canons are gravely judged by the holy Fathers and condemned by the Holy Spirit, at whose inspiration they were composed; for those who either do or say anything contrary to those holy canons, or consent to those wishing to do so, rightly appear to blaspheme the Holy Spirit.” Likewise Gregory: “It is lawful for no one either to wish or to be able to transgress the commands of the Apostolic See. Let anyone who wishes to oppose apostolic decrees lie prostrate in grief at his own ruin; let him thereafter have no place among priests, but be banished from the sacred ministry. Let no one thereafter concern himself with his judgment. No one can doubt that he is condemned by his disobedience and presumption against his holy and apostolic Church, who was bound not only to obey the commands of the aforesaid holy Church but also to impress them upon others lest they be disregarded. Let him be excluded from divine and pontifical offices who refuses to obey apostolic commands.”

The archbishop adds that the bishop visibly increased this guilt when he so obstinately [Col. 0374A] and evasively declined and manifestly avoided the archbishop’s commands to pursue what was according to God. Therefore, as one notoriously guilty, he was rightly named and excommunicated immediately, without observance of judicial procedure.

The bishop, in reply, denies that the sentence of excommunication pronounced against him, though issued in fact, is valid in law, since it was plainly given against law and the order of laws and canons. For many times, though it may be imposed in fact, it binds neither before God nor before men; for example, if someone is excommunicated in order to compel him to become or remain a schismatic or heretic. Pope Gelasius says of such persons: “Let him upon whom a sentence has been imposed abandon error, and it is void; if it is unjust, he should take the less notice of it because no unjust sentence can burden anyone before God and his Church. Therefore, he ought not seek absolution from a sentence by which he sees himself in no way bound.”

Likewise, if anyone excommunicates either his superior, his equal, or a parishioner of another, it is evident that none of them is in any way bound by the excommunication. Pope Calixtus writes: “Let no one usurp another’s boundaries or presume to excommunicate another’s parishioner.” Therefore such an excommunication will be neither ratified nor have any force, since no one is bound by the sentence of any judge other than his own. Thus it was established by a council at Compiègne for the common good: “When one bishop has excommunicated another bishop’s parishioner on account of a cause of plunder; likewise, one who appeals from his prelate in any cause to a higher hearing [Col. 0374C] is no longer subject to that prelate’s jurisdiction with respect to that cause.” Accordingly, he can and ought thereafter neither to be judged nor excommunicated by that person on account of it.

For, as Pope Sixtus decreed: “Whenever bishops think themselves aggrieved by their fellow provincials or by their metropolitan, or hold them suspect, they shall immediately appeal to the Roman See, and meanwhile no one shall presume to excommunicate them. If anyone presumes otherwise, it shall be nothing and shall lack force.” It was also at times customary that an appeal, even one made immediately afterwards, should suspend a sentence of excommunication, as it did other sentences. For it is written in the Digest: “The former state must remain whole when an appeal has been interposed.” Therefore, even if someone is ordered to abstain by due process and appeals, he may meanwhile take part, since it is established by law that nothing is to be altered while an appeal is pending. This still obtains: if any cleric is suspended from office and appeals, he is not meanwhile regarded as suspended; nor is one who has been degraded regarded as degraded, nor one deprived of a benefice as deprived.

The case is perhaps now otherwise in excommunication, because it carries its own execution with it: for it immediately excludes a person from the Church and removes the right of speech. No appeal can be made against the execution of the sentence and therefore none against the excommunication. Yet, although a subsequent appeal does not suspend an excommunication, a preceding appeal undoubtedly prevents it from being imposed. Even if it has followed in fact, [Col. 0375A] the appeal invalidates and nullifies it in law, because it preserves the appellant’s former status entirely intact.

Likewise, it must be clear that an excommunication imposed contrary to the sanction and order of the canons has no force. Procedure must indeed be observed. Pope Adrian thus established: “No one is to be suspended from communion unless, having been summoned to answer a charge, he has failed to appear.” Likewise, at the Council of Paris: “No one is to be judged prematurely or out of order—that is, neither warned nor convicted.” Likewise Augustine: “It was established in a council of bishops that no cleric not yet convicted ought to be suspended from communion unless he fails to present himself for examination of his case.” Likewise: “We cannot forbid anyone communion unless he has either confessed voluntarily [Col. 0375B] or been convicted.”

Thus, when one who has neither been convicted nor confessed—indeed, who has not even been heard, cited, or warned—is excommunicated, such an excommunication should rightly be held to have no force, as made contrary to the canons and ecclesiastical procedure. Likewise, as is read in the Code, “a sentence pronounced contrary to the customary order of judicial proceedings is certainly not endowed with the authority of a matter adjudged.” Likewise: “Measures decreed against absentees who have not been summoned in the customary manner by notices—where absence is not due to contumacy—do not obtain the firmness of a matter adjudged.”

This must surely be maintained still more strongly concerning excommunication: the more terribly and violently it casts a person down [Col. 0375C] into the power of the devil and even into the death of the soul, the less it ought to be imposed contrary to procedure—especially upon a bishop, who ought neither to be excommunicated nor even heard except in a synod. Pope Julius testifies: “No bishop, unless charged in a lawful synod, is to be heard, judged, or condemned.” Likewise Pope Zephyrinus: “No bishop is to be heard, judged, or excommunicated before he has been duly summoned to an assembly of his own bishops and his case reasonably determined by them.” Likewise Pope Hyginus: “No metropolitan shall undertake anything in causes concerning bishops without the participation of all his fellow provincials, because proceedings conducted otherwise than after being examined in the presence of all shall be void.” [Col. 0375D] Likewise Pope Calixtus: “If a metropolitan attempts to act, without a council of all his fellow-provincial bishops, in any matter other than that which belongs solely to his own parish, it shall be void and empty.”

The bishop does not deny the archbishop’s assertion that, in a notorious crime, a sentence of excommunication may rightly be given even without observance of the procedure. But he wholly denies that there was in him a notorious crime—namely, disturbance of the Church or disobedience. He asserts that he made no effort whatever to disturb the Church’s peace but worked, with every counsel and aid he could provide, to foster and increase it. Nor, on the pretext of schism, did he act maliciously against the Church in any respect. Rather, lest the evil of schism should also seize England [Col. 0376A] as it had often done, out of fidelity to the lord pope and the Roman Church, he judged and acted that affairs should not be conducted arrogantly, contentiously, or with excessive severity. In some matters he considered forbearance and temporary patience more tolerable than increasing the destruction of division. In this he followed the example of the holy Roman Church itself, which in those days had overlooked and endured many things, and the teaching of the saints.

Pope Urban says: “Where the slaughter of many lies before one, something must be deducted from severity.” Likewise Augustine: “Where, through grave rifts of dissension, there is danger not to this or that individual but slaughter among peoples, something must be deducted from severity, so that sincere charity may bring aid to the healing of greater evils.” The same writer says: “When any of the brethren and Christians established in the fellowship of the Church is found in such a sin as to deserve anathema, let this be done where there is no danger of schism.” Likewise: “Correction cannot be salutary unless the person corrected has no multitude as his associate.” And below: “Counsels of separation are empty, destructive, and sacrilegious, because they are impious and proud, and disturb weak good people more than forceful evil ones.”

The bishop says that, following these principles, if he knew that anything was being exacted or done against the Church, he did not immediately incur the guilt of consent or deserve punishment if he did not resist, defend, or punish it, since this was another’s office. For he omitted nothing through timidity or malice, but, usefully and advisedly overlooking some things and enduring others, he often approached the lord king fearlessly but kindly. He also often tried to frighten him with many considerations, but did not move him: setting, as Augustine instructs, God’s judgment before his eyes, alarming his blood-stained conscience, and urging straightforward repentance. By the modesty of supplication, he often secured that many things either would not be done or would be corrected—things which he would by no means have obtained had he followed the misguided course of contention and severity.

It ought not to be counted as a fault against him, or distorted into grounds for hatred, that he sought or retained the lord king’s favour, especially since he harmed no one through it and often benefited many. This might have happened much more easily and fully to the archbishop, as one more specially beloved, had he chosen the path of modesty [Col. 0376D] and humility. Therefore, the bishop concludes, he was not a neglecter of his office, a contemner of the canons, or a violator of them; because, if he did anything then through necessity, he did not do it willingly. Pope Damasus defines violators of the canons as “those who act against them not under compulsion of necessity but voluntarily, or consent to those acting against them.”

Moreover, he says, he neither did evil nor consented to evils, but opposed them as far as he was able and thought useful, fulfilling the prophet’s saying: “Depart, go out, and touch no unclean thing.” Augustine says: “What is it to touch what is unclean, except to consent to sins? And what is it to go out from there, except to do what pertains to the correction of evils, as far as can be done, according to each person’s rank and position, without breach of peace? Did the sin committed by anyone displease you? You have not touched what is unclean. Did you rebuke, warn, correct, and, if the matter required it, employ fitting discipline that violates no one? You have gone out from it. This is not to touch what is unclean: not to consent in will and not to spare with the mouth.” Likewise: “Do not consent to evils by approving them; do not be negligent by failing to rebuke them; and do not be proud by rebuking them insultingly.” Likewise: “Whoever either corrects by rebuke what he can correct, or, when he cannot correct it, cannot exclude it without preserving the bond of peace, disapproves it in justice and endures it with firmness—such a person is wholly free, entirely secure, altogether uninvolved.” Likewise: “A person associates with evil people if he commits some evil with them or favours those committing it; but if he does neither, he is in no way associated with them. Further, if he adds a third thing—if the righteous person rebukes mercifully, or, if he holds that office and the preservation of peace allows it, rebukes even before all; removes them either from some rank of honour or from the communion of the sacraments—then he has most fully fulfilled his office. But where the other measures are prevented, the first two, when always retained, keep him untainted: namely, that he neither does evil nor approves what has been done.”

From these authorities, therefore, the bishop maintains that he is not only excused from the charge of consenting to evil, but also gives in himself manifest evidence of moderation and prudence, in that he endured evils better than if he had exposed them openly, and thereby prevented the impending danger of schism.

He further says that he did not immediately yield to the lord king’s exactions or advise yielding to them. Rather, he stood with his fellow bishops, at no lesser peril and with no less concern, until, some time later, they jointly thought it right, in order to calm the king’s anger and avoid no small disturbance of the Church, that they should all promise in general to observe the royal customs, without specifying any particular ones—for what is expressly specified harms, whereas what is not specified does not harm—understanding, nonetheless, only good customs by the word “customs.”

But when the lord king afterwards specified the customs as he wished them to be and put them in writing, urgently demanding and severely pressing that this be confirmed by the seals of the archbishops and bishops, after much hesitation prolonged with the bishops through an entire day, the archbishop at last yielded and consented alone, without the others. Let him consider whether he worthily preferred some fear to the honour of God and his own order; whether he also kept faith with the lord pope and the Roman Church, to whom he was more strictly bound by a special oath. Let him also consider whether, after the Scyllaean gulf, he did not fall into Charybdis as well, when he afterwards broke every promise to the king. The bishop denies that he was a participant in or guilty of any of these things, and denies, as truly as plausibly, that he was an instigator of schism or a disturber of the Church’s peace.

He no less excuses himself from the charge of disobedience.

For whatever commands of the archbishop he saw did not harm the state of the Church, he diligently carried out, as he asserts, more from his office than from any debt of obedience—an obedience, indeed, to which he constantly maintains that he was not bound. In other matters, whose execution might increase the evil of schism, he held back: both because it was necessary and because he did not believe himself obliged to execute them. Yet, for added security, as it were, he always appealed, before receiving the commands, to the lord pope against all the injuries of the Church, the kingdom, and himself, choosing the pope’s hearing.

When afterwards, across the sea, he was ready before the legates of the Apostolic See to prosecute the appeal, but there was no one either to oppose it or willing to judge it, he immediately renewed the appeal in the presence of his fellow bishops. The lord pope afterwards communicated this appeal to them through their own letters and those of the legates; he completely absolved them from the archbishop’s prosecution [Col. 0378B] and by his letters granted them peace and a truce against the archbishop until he should return to the king’s favour.

But when in the meantime a report was heard of certain new threats and designs by the archbishop, lest the bishop, as previously, might somehow be bound as though forestalled, he at once again appealed publicly. Entirely refusing and rejecting the archbishop as one lawfully suspect to him on manifest grounds, he chose instead the hearing of the lord pope. Thus, he concludes, even if he were bound to obey the archbishop, he could not in any way be found disobedient, particularly because his appeal, made not evasively but always in advance as necessity required, provided both a remedy and an excuse against the charge of disobedience; especially since he has never evaded, nor even now wishes to evade, prosecution of that same appeal.

But he considers and asserts that he owes no obedience whatsoever. From the profession which he made at the city of Hereford to Archbishop Theobald of good memory, he says that he was bound only while he was bishop of Hereford. When he ceased to be so, he likewise ceased to be bound by that profession, having been wholly freed and absolved from it through the lord pope; for it had been made tacitly, though not expressly, for a time only—namely, while he remained bishop there. A very strong argument for this, he says, is that he would surely not be bound if he became bishop of another province.

Certain conditions are often tacitly understood to be present in promises even though not expressed; as, for example, when a dowry is absolutely promised to someone in expectation of a particular marriage. A tacit condition is no less involved: that the promise binds only if the marriage follows. Likewise, as stated in the Digest, when a landlord and a tenant agree that the tenant shall not be expelled from the land during the term of the lease, although nothing is said about payment of rent, it is nevertheless probable that they agreed to non-expulsion on the condition that the tenant pays the rent and cultivates the land properly.

But, the bishop adds, when transferred to the see of London he did not make a profession to the archbishop at all; therefore he says that he owes him nothing, even in the name of the Church of London. Once freed, he did not fall again under that authority, just as a son in paternal power does not, as a matter of forum-law, fall under it again when he becomes the adoptive son of an outsider, though he draws his adoptive father into his own power.

Indeed, he ought rather to be said to have been freed through that very see, especially because by right the Church of London is not the daughter but the mother of the Church of Canterbury. Such, it is reported and read in authentic writings, she had been from the first establishment of the Church in England, in the fifty-second apostolic year; and blessed Gregory, when renewing Christianity there, judged and ordained that she should henceforth be so, as his own writings testify. Yet the contrary came to prevail because paganism, which could not immediately be extirpated from London. For this reason the archiepiscopal see began, contrary to regular order, to be at Canterbury, where Christianity was first renewed [Col. 0379B] and from which it gradually spread through England, though the bishops of London continually protested.

Thus the bishop, declaring himself free in good faith and upon just grounds—as one once manumitted and exempted by apostolic authority, never afterwards subjected to the servitude of a new subjection—shows himself guilty of no disobedience, because he owed no obedience.

If the archbishop replies that he was at least bound to obey him as legate of the Apostolic See, the bishop objects the bar of his appeal and recusation; thereby he plainly establishes that thereafter he was subject to the lord pope alone. He also adds that the archbishop does not yet have jurisdiction in England by right of his legation. For the legate of the Roman See is as a legate of Caesar: namely, governor, corrector of a province, or proconsul. Thus the Digest says: “Contentious jurisdiction does not belong to a proconsul before he comes into the province.” Likewise: “A governor has authority only over persons of his province, and this only while he is in the province.” Therefore, the bishop concludes, the archbishop cannot exercise authority in England as legate in any way, since he is not there and has not come there since the time of his legation.

Thus the bishop concludes that the sentence of excommunication imposed upon him is in no way binding: first, because it was pronounced outside due procedure when no notorious crime was present in him; secondly, because he had previously appealed; and thirdly, because he was not subject to the archbishop’s jurisdiction.

[Col. 0379D] To this the archbishop replies: Although the aforesaid matters are not notorious in the bishop, nevertheless, because they are publicly alleged and believed concerning him, he was justly condemned on their account, even without observance of judicial procedure—especially because the liberty and dignity of the Church were endangered in many respects by his, as the bishop himself calls it, forbearance and patience. It was just and useful that he should therefore be punished outside ordinary procedure, so that other rebels and disturbers of the Church might be more greatly terrified and return to their senses when they could not doubt that what they had seen inflicted upon a man of such name and power would be inflicted upon themselves.

For the variety of necessities often advises and compels many actions contrary to the strict tenor of reason and the customary order of an institution. As Pope Innocent says: “One thing is legitimate order; another is the usurpation which the times compel to be done.” Pope Silvester is likewise said to have taken action against certain enemies of his, as he himself writes: “Usiliarius the Patrician ordered me to come peaceably to him; and, concerning certain ecclesiastical disputes, he detained in the prince’s palace, at the first and second veil, all the clergy and people who had come with me, except myself alone and my deacon Vigilius. But I was seized by force and sent into exile, where I am sustained on the bread of tribulation and the water of affliction. Yet I did not and do not therefore abandon my office; but with such bishops as I could gather, I anathematized those who did these things against me.” The same writer says to Vigilius: “Receive, together with those who consent to you, the sentence of full condemnation; and recognize that, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by apostolic authority exercised by us, the name of priestly ministry has been taken from you: you are condemned.”

By this example, therefore, the archbishop thinks he may suitably argue that he quite rightly condemned the bishop, although outside ordinary procedure, for a crime not notorious indeed but nevertheless manifest and certain to himself; as though he could and did lawfully do so, especially since he acts in the lord pope’s stead and is his legate.

The bishop replies: Judgments, he says, must be made not by examples but by laws; consideration must be given not to what was done at Rome but to what ought to have been done. It has always been lawful, and is lawful, for the lord pope often to act contrary to strict law, especially when necessity demands it. [Col. 0380C] For, though he lives under laws, he is nevertheless released from the laws. And as Christ fulfilled our sacraments in himself, not from any necessity of his own but out of the will to summon us to imitation, so the lord pope often obeys the canons, not because he must, but so that his authority and example may urge others to obey. He also often does not abide by them.

For it is in his power both to make new canons and to moderate old ones, either by relaxing or tightening them, sometimes even by wholly omitting their sanction or acting contrary to it. He alone received this power and continually retains it for himself. Although he often entrusts his functions to others, he calls them into a share of responsibility, not into the fullness of power. Even when he grants them a wider licence at times, not so far as to permit them anything beyond the limits of antiquity, especially those limits which they are bound to observe by the authority of the Old and New Testaments. Indeed, not even the lord pope may transgress these, as Pope Zosimus testifies: “The authority of this see cannot grant or alter anything contrary to the statutes of the Fathers.” Among us antiquity lives with unshaken roots, to which the sayings of the Fathers have established reverence.

Now antiquity has always been observed, even from the first sin of man: that a person guilty of a crime is condemned only after he has confessed, been convicted, or been cited. For Adam was not condemned before he was cited and warned, when it was said to him: “Adam, where are you?” nor before he confessed, when he said: “The woman gave me, and I ate.” Likewise, as Pope Evaristus writes, the Lord did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom merely upon hearing of them, before he knew them manifestly, although all things are naked and open before his eyes. Thus he says: “I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled the outcry by their deeds.” By this example we are warned never to be hasty in pronouncing sentence or to judge in any manner after a rash and careless examination, since the voice of Truth says: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged.” Nor is it plainly recorded that Pope Silvester did anything contrary to these principles against Usiliarius and Vigilius.

Therefore, against the procedure which God himself observed so carefully and taught by his own example to be observed, [Col. 0381B] and which the authority of the saints has handed down as requiring such unalterable observance, ought what the archbishop did to stand good even if he was a legate? Or ought it not rather to be void—especially since he could not be both accuser and judge at once?

Pope Nicholas says concerning a suspect person: “Both reason itself dictates, and many examples prove, that suspect persons and enemies ought not to be judges. For what could anyone give an enemy more pleasing than the opportunity to attack someone whom he might wish to harm?” And below: “Thus the pious Emperor Justinian is known to have promulgated in his laws: let one who considers a judge suspect be permitted, before the suit begins, to challenge him, so that recourse may be had to another. In this way it is, as it were, natural to avoid the snares of suspect judges and to wish to flee the judgment of enemies.”

Likewise: “Anastasius, bishop of the Pyrenees, had been summoned three times and, because he did not appear, had been condemned by his patriarch. But solely because, when summoned to the synod, he cried out that the man judging him was his enemy, he was reserved by the holy Council of Chalcedon for examination of the sentence imposed, the prior condemnation being treated as though it were nothing.” Augustine also testifies that the same person ought not to be accuser and judge at once: “Who dares arrogate both roles to himself, so as to be both accuser and judge of any person?” Likewise Pope Fabian: “Let no one ever presume to be at once accuser and judge, or witness; for in every judgment four persons must always be present: namely, the judges must not be the same persons, but there must separately be accusers, separately judges, and separately accused persons.”

Therefore, the bishop concludes, what can be thought of one who acted contrary to all the foregoing so manifestly, so indiscriminately, and so precipitately, except that his act is an empty utterance and a casting of words into the wind, undeserving even of the name of a sentence?

The archbishop further adds that, after a prolonged wait, he had often tried by many entreaties and threats to bend the lord king, but had not prevailed; and that at last, when he was on the point of laying the axe to the root, since he could neither spare him further nor ought to do so, the bishop set himself up as the first opponent in the king’s cause—an altogether indubitably and notoriously unjust cause—and as its vehement defender to such an extent [Col. 0382A] that he even appealed against the pursuit of justice. Thus he openly and inexcusably displayed notorious consent in a notorious crime; and consequently he can by no means deny that he is justly and firmly bound by the excommunication, even though it was imposed out of the usual order.

The bishop, on the contrary, replies that by interposing that appeal he had consulted not merely for himself but for the whole Church of England, and had acted in concert with it; not by consenting to evils or intending to defend evil deeds, but out of fidelity to the Roman Church and for his own peace—namely, by checking the archbishop’s excessive and exceedingly dangerous severity, lest the danger of schism should be increased. There could be no doubt that this would have followed with enormous damage to the Church if the archbishop’s efforts [Col. 0382B] had succeeded; especially since it is evident that he could have conquered more effectively through humble patience, and had already exasperated the king rather dangerously enough by multiplying harsh measures. If the archbishop replies that consent to evil is no less, but rather more, notorious because it is found in a multitude of associates, the bishop, on the contrary, plausibly acknowledges the prevention of schism and utterly disavows consent to evil. Moreover, this ought to be done only after a second and indeed finally a third correction, as the Lord commands in the Gospel, saying: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him; if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two others; and if he does not listen to them, tell the Church; and if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican.” Therefore, as the bishop concludes, a sentence is not wrongly deemed to have no force when it is found to have observed no order whatsoever [Col. 0382C].

To this the archbishop determines that order is not to be omitted when it can be observed; but when it cannot be observed, it must nevertheless be regarded, by interpretation, as having been observed. For elsewhere too, what was done in God’s sight because it could not be done is nevertheless accepted as done; as in the case of one who desires the sacrament of baptism or penance but cannot receive it.

“For such a person,” as Cassiodorus says, “the vow is reckoned in place of the deed, namely because of impossibility. And among men too the rule of law is that in all cases a thing is accepted as done when someone frightens another so that it cannot be done; as the Code says concerning one who does not appeal because of force or fear: nevertheless the case shall be handled by the law of appeal. Likewise, therefore,” the archbishop argues, “he says that he proceeded lawfully in the case against the bishop, although not in his own synod and although without a prior warning or citation. For he had another’s synod, since he could not have his own. And he maintains that the bishop should be regarded as cited and forewarned, since he ought rather to have presented himself, a man whose reputation was so severely at stake; and he could not diligently summon or warn him for many reasons. First, because a vast gulf of lands lay between them; then, because he had long been a wanderer and exile among foreign peoples, sustained by their alms [Col. 0383A], and could have no official to make citations or warnings unless someone perhaps offered himself freely and solely for God’s sake; thirdly, because some men sent on occasion had been seized by the king’s officials, beaten, abused, imprisoned, and exposed to danger of mutilation or death, while the rest, prevented by justified fear, thereafter did not dare undertake so dreadful an embassy.” Thus, he concludes, the sentence was lawfully and canonically issued against the bishop as against one cited and warned, and remains firmly valid.

The bishop, on the contrary, replies that not everything which ought to be done is to be considered done when it cannot be done because of force or fear. For elsewhere too, as is written in the *Digest*, the law lays down that a thief is made manifest by being caught in the act. But if, while I was stealing from you, you hid yourself so that I would not kill you, then—even if you saw the theft happen—it is nevertheless not manifest theft. Likewise, when through fear you do not make a will, do not join issue in a suit, do not recover property, or do not accuse an offender, there is nevertheless neither a will made, nor issue joined, nor property recovered, nor anyone accused. The same applies in many similar cases [Col. 0383B]. Finally, the statement that something omitted through fear or force is considered done does not apply to things the law commands to be done, but to remedies which it grants, such as appeals and the interpretations of prescriptions. For if these are omitted because of force or fear, they are nevertheless considered done, especially if one publicly protests that he did not dare make them.

Therefore the archbishop is plainly shown to have been able to observe the order even of warnings and citations, because he ought much more not to have feared to send the preliminary measures for imposing excommunication: for he did not hesitate to circulate throughout England publicly the notification already issued, eagerly presenting through his messengers his letters concerning the avoidance of excommunicated persons in bishops’ synods, public assemblies of churches, and even gatherings of nobles [Col. 0383C]. Since, therefore, as the bishop argues, the order was neither observed nor to be treated as observed, it is clear that an excommunication imposed out of order is unworthy of the name of excommunication.

The archbishop presses the point in yet another way. “No appeal,” he says, “can be made against a notorious crime. For the Code says: ‘Those who have been openly and manifestly convicted are denied the benefit of appeal.’ Again: ‘It must be observed that no one who has committed manifest violence is to be heard when appealing.’ Again, in the *Digest*: ‘Constitutions concerning the admission of appeals have no place in the cases of persons whom it is publicly expedient to condemn.’” Now, he assumes that the king’s most dangerous and manifest transgression against God and His Church, and likewise his manifest violence in plundering himself and his own people and outlawing innocents, cannot be denied even by the king himself. The clear evidence of his deeds publicly proves these things, and he is convicted of them also by the unanimous detestation of the entire world. Hence, the archbishop argues, as one openly and manifestly convicted [Col. 0384A], the king ought not to be heard in appealing in these matters, especially since it is publicly expedient that he be punished for them, both so that he himself may be compelled to repent and be saved, and so that the condition of the Church may be reformed.

Thus, he adds, appeal is entirely excluded in the king’s case: neither the bishop nor anyone on his behalf may appeal or be heard when appealing, particularly because the *Digest* says, “No one may appeal in another’s case.” “Unless perhaps,” as the same passage makes an exception, “they have a mandate or transact another’s business, which the defendant immediately ratifies.” But here, he assumes, neither a mandate nor ratification can occur—and it ought not to occur. Likewise, those who have an interest are customarily, and properly, heard when appealing: “But these,” as the same passage says, “are truly defending their own cause [Col. 0384B].” It is plain that a person’s own cause is one whose benefit or loss pertains to that person in his own name: for example, where the seller is defeated and his agent acts, or conversely; or where the debtor is defeated and his creditor acts, or conversely. But the king’s cause, the archbishop assumes, concerns neither the bishop nor anyone else, so that they may intervene; rather, the entire Church of the faithful ought jointly to employ its advocacy to correct him. For it is a matter of public concern that so great an evil be restrained rather than fostered under the pretext of some necessity. Therefore, he concludes, in a matter so detestable, no appeal may be made by the king himself, the bishop, or anyone else, nor may an appeal once made be received.

The bishop replies, on the contrary, that the king, the bishop himself, or anyone whatever could rightly appeal in the king’s name, especially because the lord king had never withdrawn himself from justice but had always offered to submit to it. Indeed, he continued urgently and very anxiously to request that judges be delegated to hear the matter against the archbishop, before whom he promised beforehand to make satisfaction, provided he could be secure that satisfaction would afterwards be made to him. Meanwhile the archbishop was attempting, contrary to laws and canons, to be both prosecutor and judge in the king’s case. Against so manifest an injury, both the king and anyone in his name could most justly appeal [Col. 0384C].

Further, even if the king disdained to appeal for himself, this ought nonetheless to have been permitted to others, as it is permitted in the case of persons condemned to death. For the *Digest* says: “Not only is the person who is led away to punishment allowed to appeal, but others also in his name; not merely if he has given them a mandate, but whoever else wishes to appeal.” Nor is any distinction made as to whether the appellant is a relative or not; for humanity requires that every appellant be heard. Therefore this applies even if the condemned person himself acquiesces in the sentence, and no inquiry is made as to whose interest is involved. “What then,” the bishop asks, “if the condemned person remains and hastens to perish? Should I still think that the execution ought to be delayed?” If this, therefore, is allowed in a case involving danger to the body and temporal punishment, how much more ought it to be allowed where the soul is endangered even unto eternal death—namely, in a case of anathema. Inasmuch as the soul is more worthy than the body, so much more powerfully [Col. 0385A] ought aid be given to it.

Likewise, that the bishop and others could appropriately and rightly appeal is plain, he says, because it concerned him greatly—indeed, it concerned the whole Church—that schism not be extended; nor, he says, can it be denied that he himself appealed against injuries affecting his own just cause.

The archbishop further adds that he had been granted a legation and entrusted with authority to inflict punishment on rebels and disturbers of the Church, with the obstacle of appeal removed; and therefore that a subsequent or prior appeal did not impede the already imposed punishment of anathema or weaken it in any way.

The bishop replies: although execution was entrusted to him without the obstacle of appeal, it was not entrusted to him contrary to laws and canons [Col. 0385B]. For although he had received by mandate even free and general jurisdiction, he did not thereby acquire the power to transgress the customary and lawful order of jurisdiction. This is demonstrated by the following passage in the Code: “Whenever an imperial grant is issued by which free power to make a will is conferred, the emperor is understood to grant nothing other than the ability to employ the lawful and customary mode of making a will; for it cannot be believed that the Roman emperor, who upholds the laws, intended by such a phrase to overthrow the entire observance of substitutions, devised and discovered through many watchful efforts.”

Likewise, the bishop argues, even if the lord pope gave the archbishop a general and free legation—if indeed he gave it—he did not permit him to do anything contrary to the lawful and customary order of law. If he acted contrary to it, as he has certainly been shown above to have done, then the act is nevertheless void and invalid by the law itself, no less because he is a legate or because appeal was forbidden. Again, the bishop adds, even if appeal against the archbishop’s punitive action was forbidden by the lord pope, he was nonetheless permitted to appeal. For elsewhere, as the *Digest* says: “Although there is neither power nor right to appeal from the emperor, sometimes an appeal suspends even his judgment. For when a governor of a province has no right to deport someone to an island or punish a decurion, he must nevertheless make a notation [Col. 0385C]—that is, inventory the man’s goods—when he considers him fit for deportation or punishment; then he must write to the emperor, sending his full opinion as to why he thinks the man ought to be deported or punished, so that the emperor may judge whether his opinion should be followed and finally assign the punishment by deporting him to an island or punishing the decurion.”

Thus, the same passage says that they could appeal not only when the governor wrote to the emperor, but also when the emperor replied concerning the island or the punishment. For what if the governor loaded with lies before the emperor the man whom he was seeking to have deported or punished? It is rightly said, therefore, at humanity’s prompting, that at both stages they make an appeal not in vain, because they appeal not against the emperor but against the judge’s cunning. The status of those concerned is also ordered to remain unchanged once an appeal has been entered [Col. 0386A]. Therefore, even if a decurion has been ordered by the emperor to abstain from his rank and has appealed, he may meanwhile retain participation, since it is established and lawful that nothing be altered while an appeal is pending.

Therefore, the bishop argues, just as no appeal may be made from the emperor, ought not likewise a bishop—whom the archbishop is forbidden by canonical censure to punish on his own authority—to be permitted to oppose by appeal, and retain his unimpaired status, even if the lord pope had degraded him at the archbishop’s suggestion? All the more, then, if not the lord pope but the archbishop, through the lord pope, had similarly proceeded against him, even with the obstacle of appeal removed, the subsequent remedy of appeal ought nevertheless to assist him [Col. 0386B]; and a prior appeal ought much more to prevent anything from being done. The bishop concludes that this ought likewise to hold good in a sentence of excommunication, no less if power to punish persons generally, than if power specifically to excommunicate had been granted to the archbishop despite appeal.

Again, he adds, even if an appeal, as forbidden, could not weaken the sentence, the repeatedly prior request for a hearing before the lord pope against the archbishop weakens it. For Pope Sixtus decrees both points: “When bishops have appealed to the Roman Church or have sought to be heard by it, let no one presume to excommunicate them in the meantime. If anyone presumes otherwise, it shall be nothing and shall lack force [Col. 0386C].” In accordance with this, the deposition of Anastasius, bishop of the Pyrenees, was also mentioned above as having had no force.

After this the archbishop turns to certain specific charges. He says that he had long ago rebuked the bishop because he promoted sons of priests to holy orders contrary to the canons, including one whom he advanced to the rank of priest in a certain church where he knew that the man had succeeded his father. He also charges that the bishop not only failed to correct the incontinence of clerics in his diocese, but even tolerated it upon payment. For this reason, he recalls, he immediately added a mandate: unless the bishop made satisfaction before the judgment of his fellow bishops for such serious offences. Since, he says, the bishop neglected to do this [Col. 0386D], the punishment of anathema was lawfully imposed upon him as one warned beforehand and openly contumacious; and it ought not to be deemed invalid on the occasion of an appeal. For, as has been said: “One condemned for contumacy is not heard if he appeals.”

The bishop, on the contrary, endeavors to excuse himself from contumacy, because he is bound to obey neither the archbishop, since he is not subject to him, nor the legate, since he is suspected and has been challenged, but only the lord pope—especially after he has appealed to him and chosen his hearing. The contumacious, moreover, as the *Digest* says, are not judged to be those who do not obey unless they were bound to obey—that is, unless they belong to the jurisdiction of the person whom they refuse to obey.

The bishop also plainly denies that he permitted clerical incontinence through the intervention of payment [Col. 0387A], or neglected its correction. Rather, as he replies, it is well known that he repeatedly and diligently admonished all alike in synods and separately in chapters; he often publicly threatened all as was fitting, and at last duly rebuked and corrected some. But if the vice has not been completely uprooted, he says it should be imputed not to him but rather to the multitude of offenders and to a custom scarcely, if ever, capable of being abolished. For what is sinned by many is a great evil, particularly an evil to which the human race has been subjected so invincibly from the first condemnation of sin.

As for the charge that he ordained sons of priests, he does not admit that this was permitted without qualification. He knew well that all such persons were forbidden to minister, but he could not reject all of them; and therefore he did what was fitting and possible. Namely, he carefully put his archdeacons under oath—men who have fuller knowledge of the clergy and whose office it is to present them—and strictly commanded them not to admit or present anyone contrary to canonical censure. If anything therefore happened less canonically, he says, the responsibility ought rather to fall upon the archdeacons [Col. 0387B].

He also says regarding the priest’s son whom he found already established in a church by his predecessor and ordained deacon, and whom he himself afterwards found bound by some arrangement to pay annually to a cleric of the archbishop a rather heavy rent from the church: because the man could not support a chaplain from the remainder, he admits that he promoted him to the priesthood [Col. 0387C], especially because he knew him to be otherwise not unworthy, but of sufficiently good reputation. Therefore, even if he was insufficiently diligent in this or another matter, even if he were bound to obey the archbishop, he is not thereby proved contumacious or contemptuous of the archbishop’s mandate because he did not make satisfaction before the judgment of his fellow bishops as directed. He did not evade that judgment, nor was he bound to correct before them, without an accuser present, an offence which he denied. But if he committed any fault, he has in no respect avoided the censure of the lord pope, who is both the author of the canons and the avenger of their transgression.

Finally the archbishop says that a sentence, though unlawful or illegitimate, nevertheless binds, citing the Council of Paris, where the following is read: “Concerning unlawful excommunication, the law of Emperor Justinian, which it approves and observes, decreed that no priest may excommunicate anyone before the cause has been proved for which the canons command this to be done. But if anyone excommunicates another contrary to this, the person excommunicated shall be restored to the grace of holy communion by the authority of a higher priest. But the person who unlawfully excommunicated him shall abstain from holy communion for such time as the higher priest considers appropriate [Col. 0387D].” “Behold,” he says, “an excommunication, though unlawful or illegitimate, nevertheless binds, so much so that the one thus excommunicated must return to communion—that is, be absolved—through a higher priest.” He therefore concludes that the same must consistently be held concerning the bishop.

Again, he adds: if the sentence does not bind at first, it binds once it is despised. For Gregory says: “The sentence of a pastor, whether just or unjust, must be feared or observed, lest one subject to him, perhaps unjustly bound, should by another fault deserve the very sentence of binding. Therefore, one judged under the hand of his pastor should fear to reproach him, lest, even if he is unjustly bound, through the swollen pride of that reproach a fault which did not exist should come into being.” Thus the archbishop maintains that the bishop is truly bound, at least by the subsequent fault of contempt, and therefore must in every way be avoided even if the sentence is unjust.

As is stated in the Council of Sardica: “If perhaps a bishop, which ought not to occur, is angered and quickly and harshly stirred against a priest or deacon, and wishes to expel him from the Church, provision must be made lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion. Therefore the person cast out has authority to appeal to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard and carefully examined. The bishop who cast him out, whether justly or unjustly, should patiently permit the matter to be considered, and his sentence either be confirmed by several bishops or corrected.
