Nevertheless, before all matters have been carefully and faithfully examined, no one should presume to admit to communion, before the hearing, the person who has been deprived of communion [Col. 0388A; 0388B]. If he presumes to communicate or exercise his office, he is shown to deserve a more severe punishment under the decrees.”

For the Council of Antioch [Col. 0388C] says: “If a bishop condemned by a synod, or a priest or deacon condemned by his bishop, should dare to perform any part of the sacred ministry, they may in no way have either hope of restoration in another synod or opportunity to make satisfaction.” Again, in the Council of Pope Martin: “If a bishop has been excommunicated in a council, or a priest or deacon by his bishop, and after excommunication that bishop, priest, or deacon presumes to make an offering or perform the morning or evening sacrifice in his office as before, he may not have hope of reconciliation even in another council, nor be reconciled thereafter.” Again, in the African Council: “It pleased the whole council [Col. 0388D] that if one who has been excommunicated through his own neglect, whether bishop or any cleric, presumes to communicate during the time of his excommunication before being heard, he is to be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon himself.” From all these authorities, therefore, the archbishop concludes that the bishop is shown not only to be truly excommunicated, but also to be altogether deposed because of his contempt.

The bishop replies, on the contrary, that an unlawful or illegitimate sentence is defined as an unjust one, either in respect of its ground—where there is no fault for which it is imposed—or in respect of intention, where it is perhaps imposed through anger or ignorance for a lesser fault than is fitting. This accords with the Council of Agde: “If bishops, setting aside priestly moderation, presume to excommunicate innocent persons or persons guilty only of very slight causes, they are to be admonished by neighboring bishops [Col. 0389A].” Such sentences, the bishop continues, when issued in due order and not impeded by appeal, certainly bind even though unjust: that is, before the Church, though not always before God. Conversely, they often bind before God when they have not been imposed by the Church. For Origen says: “He departs from the city, from faith, from charity; through these things he departs from the camp of the Church, even if he is not cast out by the bishop’s voice. Conversely, if someone is sent outside by an unsound judgment, provided he has not acted and does not deserve it, he suffers no harm. For sometimes one who is sent outside is inside, and one who is outside appears to be retained inside.”

The bishop nevertheless admits, following Gregory, that even an unjust sentence must be feared and observed, not despised, lest, if it is despised, through the swollen pride of reproach—as Gregory adds—a fault that did not exist come into being. That is, the man who was previously bound before the Church only by the pastor’s judgment may thereafter be bound before God as well through contempt [Col. 0389B; 0390A]. This, the bishop distinguishes, is where the sentence has some legal existence as well as factual existence, even if unjust. But where, though it exists in fact, it has no legal existence—such as a sentence issued contrary to legal order, contrary to an appeal, or contrary to the reason of subjection—there it is truly unjust, as the bishop rightly judges, or can be called unjust; nor does it gain force through contempt if it is not observed. For sentences which are invalid from the beginning cannot become valid by the passage of time. Nor is the person who communicates contrary to such a sentence, or continues to perform his office, guilty in any respect, nor is he at all subject to the punishments of the canons set out above. Thus the bishop lawfully defends his unimpaired status [Col. 0390B], proving that he is neither truly excommunicated nor in need of absolution—indeed, that he is not guilty at all, either from any prior or subsequent act.

## II. Chapters of the Council of Alexander III Held at Tours

[Col. 0389]

[Col. 0389B] **Chapter I.** Since an outrageous custom, contrary to the decrees of the holy Fathers, has become established in certain places whereby priests are appointed to the government of churches for an annual payment [Col. 0389C], we prohibit this by every means. For when the priesthood is arranged for sale under such a wage, no regard is had for the reward of eternal recompense.

**Chapter II.** Avarice is not rebuked with sufficient vigor among the people unless every precaution against it is taken by those established in the clergy, and especially by those who, having despised the world, profess the name and rule of the religious life. We therefore forbid money to be demanded from those wishing to enter religion; and we forbid priories or any chaplaincies of monks or clerics to be sold through annual alienation, or any price to be exacted from the person to whom their governance is entrusted for that entrustment. The authority of the holy Fathers plainly declares this to be simony [Col. 0389D]. Therefore, whoever hereafter presumes to do this, whether giver or receiver, should have no doubt that he shares in simony. Likewise, no charge is to be made to anyone for burial or for receiving chrism and oil; nor may anyone defend his guilt under the pretext of any custom, since length of time does not diminish sins but increases them.

**Chapter III.** Since in certain bishoprics deans or archpriests are appointed, for an annual payment, to act in the place of bishops or archdeacons and to decide ecclesiastical cases—and this undoubtedly tends to the disparagement of the priesthood and the overthrow of justice—we strictly prohibit this from being done further. Whoever does it is to be removed from the Lord [Col. 0390B]. A bishop, moreover, who tolerates this in his diocese and allows ecclesiastical judgments to be overturned through his own connivance is to be punished with canonical severity.

[Col. 0390C] **Chapter IV.** The envy of the ancient enemy does not exert itself chiefly to cast down the weak members of the Church; rather, it lays its hand upon her precious things and strives to trip up every one of the elect, as Scripture says: “You are among his chosen ones.” For he thinks that he has brought about the fall of many when, by his cunning, he has dragged down some more precious member. Hence, transforming himself as usual into an angel of light, under the pretext of caring for the bodies of infirm brethren and more faithfully conducting church business, he draws certain religious from their cloisters to read civil law and weigh out medical preparations. Therefore, lest spiritual men be entangled in worldly business under the pretext of learning, and fail in inward things precisely because they think they are providing for others in outward things [Col. 0390D], with the assent of the present council we decree that after a vow of religion and profession made in any religious order, no one whatsoever may be allowed to leave in order to study medicine or secular laws. If anyone does leave and does not return to his cloister within two months, let him be avoided by all as excommunicated; and if he attempts to offer legal advocacy in any cause, let him not be heard. On returning, let him always be last among the brethren in choir, chapter, at table, and in all other matters; and, unless perhaps by mercy of the Apostolic See, let him lose all hope of promotion.

**Chapter V.** Although it is judged exceedingly grave and worthy of the punitive judgment of God that laymen usurp in ecclesiastical affairs certain things belonging to priests [Col. 0391A], still greater fear and grief arise from the assertion that they sometimes find fuel for their error in God Himself, while some of our brethren and fellow bishops and other prelates of churches grant them tithes and the administration of churches, and compel onto the paths of death those whom their preaching ought to call back to the way of life. Of such persons the Lord says through the prophet: “They consume the sins of my people, and provoke their souls to iniquity.” We therefore decree that whoever grants a church or tithe to any layman remaining in the world shall be cut down from his office, like a tree that occupies the ground uselessly, and shall lie prostrate in grief over his downfall until he amends.

**Chapter VI.** While the greater benefices of the Church remain intact, it seems altogether unseemly for the lesser prebends of clerics to suffer division. Therefore, so that the Church may retain firm unity in her lesser as in her greater members, we forbid divisions of prebends or exchanges of dignities [Col. 0391B].

**Chapter VII.** Many clerics—and, shamefully, even persons who have abandoned the present world by profession, word, and habit—while shunning ordinary usury as more plainly condemned, lend money to the needy and take their possessions as pledge, receiving the resulting fruits beyond the principal. Therefore the authority of a general council decrees that no person henceforth in clerical orders may presume to practice this or any other kind of usury. And if anyone has hitherto accepted another’s property as a pledge under this arrangement in return for money advanced, then, after deducting expenses, if he has received his principal from the proceeds, he shall restore the property to the debtor unconditionally [Col. 0391C]. But if something remains owing to him, once it has been received, possession shall freely return to the owner. If, after this decree, anyone in clerical orders is found to persist in the detestable gain of usury, let him incur the loss of ecclesiastical office—unless perhaps it concerns a benefice of the Church which must apparently be redeemed from a layman’s hand in this way [Col. 0392A].

**Chapter VIII.** In the regions of Toulouse a damnable heresy arose long ago, which, like a cancer, has gradually spread into neighboring places and has already infected very many people through Gascony and other provinces. Since it conceals itself like a serpent within its own coils, the more secretly it creeps, the more grievously it devastates the Lord’s vineyard among the simple. We therefore command bishops and all priests of the Lord dwelling in those regions to be vigilant against it, and under threat of anathema to forbid anyone, wherever adherents of that heresy are recognized, to presume to grant them shelter or protection in his territory [Col. 0392B]. Nor is there to be any association with them in buying or selling, so that, deprived even of the solace of ordinary human interaction, they may be compelled to come to their senses and abandon the error of their way. Whoever attempts to act contrary to these provisions shall be struck with anathema as a participant in their wickedness. If the heretics are apprehended, they are to be placed in custody by Catholic rulers and fined by forfeiture of all their goods. And since they frequently gather from different parts in one hiding-place and dwell in one residence for no reason of cohabitation other than agreement in error, such assemblies are to be investigated more carefully; and if found, they are to be forbidden with canonical severity [Col. 0392C].

## III. Oath of Master Girard Pucelle and Others Returning from Schism

[Col. 0391]

[Col. 0391D] I, Girard, reject and anathematize every heresy that exalts itself against the holy Catholic Church, and especially the schism and heresy of Octavian and Guy of Crema. I also pronounce their ordinations void; and henceforth, as before, I shall be obedient and faithful to Lord Pope Alexander and his Catholic successors. So help me God and these holy Gospels of God.

## IV. Account of Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, concerning the Vial of Holy Oil with Which the Kings of England Are to Be Anointed at Their Coronation, Divinely Shown to Him

[Col. 0391]

[Col. 0391D] When I, Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, was fleeing England in exile for France, I came to Pope Alexander, who was then at Sens, in order to show him the evil customs and abuses which [Col. 0392D] the king of England was introducing into the Church. One night, while I was praying in the church of Saint Columba, I asked the Queen of Virgins to give the king of England and his heirs the purpose and will [Col. 0393A] to amend their conduct toward the Church, and to make Christ, in His mercy, cause him to love the Church with a fuller love.

Immediately the Blessed Virgin appeared to me, bearing upon her breast this golden eagle and holding in her hand a small stone flask. Taking the eagle from her breast, she enclosed the flask within it and placed the eagle with the flask in my hand; and she spoke these words to me in order:

“This is the anointing with which the kings of England ought to be anointed—not those who now reign or will reign, for they are and will be evil, and because of their sins they have lost much and will lose more. But there will be future kings of England who will be anointed with this anointing; they will be gracious and champions of the Church. For they will peacefully recover the land lost by their forefathers, so long as they possess the eagle with the flask.

“There will be [Col. 0393B] a future king of England who shall afterwards be anointed with this anointing and who will recover for his own the land lost by his forefathers, namely Normandy and Aquitaine. This king shall be greatest among kings. He will build many churches in the Holy Land, drive all pagans out of Babylon, and build more churches there. And whenever the king bears the eagle on his breast, he will gain victory over his enemies, and his kingdom will always increase. But you shall be a martyr.”

Then I asked the Blessed Virgin to show me where I should keep so precious a sanctuary. She said to me:

“There is in this city a man, William, a monk of Saint Cyprian of Poitiers, unjustly expelled from his abbey by his abbot. He asks the pope to compel his abbot [Col. 0393C] to restore him to the abbey. I entrust the eagle and flask to you, so that he may carry it to the city of Poitiers and conceal it in the church of Saint Gregory, which stands beside the church of Hilary, at the head of the church toward the west, beneath a large stone. There it shall be found at the proper time, and it shall be the anointing of the kings of England. [Col. 0394A] The “capi …” of the pagans [source fragment incomplete] shall be the cause of the discovery of this eagle.”

And I delivered all these things to him, enclosed in a certain leaden vessel.

## AN ANCIENT PROPHECY CONCERNING THE SAID FLASK AND THE KINGS OF ENGLAND, ETC.

(This prophecy was transcribed in the year of the Lord 1407, on the feast of Saint Matthias, from a very ancient slip of parchment, *qd Fyshborne*.)

In the year 6,587 from the creation of the world, the lily reigning in a noble part of the world shall move against the seed of the lion, and shall come into the lion’s land and stand in a field among the thorns of that region. Then the Son of Man shall come, bearing three beasts upon his arm, whose kingdom is in the land of the moon. With a great army he shall cross the waters and enter the land [Col. 0394B] of the lion, which lacks assistance, because the beasts of its own region have torn its skin.

In that year the eagle shall come from the eastern side, its wings spread beneath the sun, with a multitude of its young, to help the Son of Man. In that year many strongholds shall be destroyed; there shall be great terror in the world; and in one part of the lion’s realm there shall be war among several kings. On that day there shall be a flood of blood, and the lily shall lose the crown with which the Son of Man shall afterwards be crowned.

For the following four years many battles shall take place in the world among those who hold the faith, and the greater part of the world shall be destroyed. The head of the world shall be bowed to the ground. But the Son of Man, together with the eagle, shall prevail. Then there shall be peace throughout the whole world and an abundance of crops. Then the Son of Man, taking up a wonderful sign, shall pass into the land [Col. 0394C] of promise, because the things promised to the First Cause [primo causae; reading uncertain] shall then remain fulfilled.

The eagle is the emperor; the Son of Man is our king; the lily is the king of France; the lion is the duke of Burgundy; and our said king possesses the said eagle with the flask.

## V. CONFERENCE BETWEEN THE CARDINALS AND THE ARCHBISHOP

[Col. 0393]

[Col. 0393D] This is the proceeding held between the lord of Canterbury and the king of England, between Gisors and Trie, in the presence of the cardinals William of Pavia, cardinal-priest of Saint Peter in Chains, and Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

In the octave of blessed Martin, the lord of Canterbury came from Burgundy into the region of the Vexin, to the town of Trie, for a conference with the cardinals, who were to meet the archbishop at Gisors on behalf of the king of England, coming from Caen. Those two cardinals sat together between Gisors and Trie with the archbishop of Rouen and many others on the king’s side; likewise the archbishop of Canterbury, then papal legate appointed by the Apostolic See, and with him his exiles: John of Salisbury with Herbert of Bosham, Lombard of Piacenza, Alexander of Wales, Geoffrey, prior of [Col. 0394D] Pantenia, and Garin, canon; Robert and Gilbert, canons and chaplains of Canterbury; John of Canterbury, Alan, Richard, Henry, and many others.

The cardinals began to set forth at length the pope’s affection and the great concern with which they were daily troubled, in seeking peace and security for the pope, the archbishop of Canterbury, and his people. Then they spoke of their arrival from the city of Rome, and of the labours and dangers of their journey, having left the city in the middle of March and reached Normandy in November; then of the greatness of the king of England and the needs of the Roman Church, which had been accustomed to receive many benefits from the king and his kingdom, of which it was then deprived because of this discord. They then spoke of the evil condition of the times, and of the affection and benefits with which the king of England had provided for [Col. 0395A] the archbishop of Canterbury, and of the honour he had always shown him.

To these matters they added the grievances and injuries by which the king complained that he had been wronged by the archbishop of Canterbury, alleging among other things that he had stirred up against him the war of the king of France. Finally, they sought advice on how they might placate the indignation of so great a prince, since, they said, without much humility, moderation, and the rendering of great honour, no remedy could be applied to such dangers.

They said this deliberately, in order either to break his spirit through fear or provoke him to anger, so that he might answer either less wisely or less humbly. But the lord of Canterbury, in all humility and gentleness of spirit, with serene countenance, radiant eyes, and a rosy face, first gave thanks in most eloquent and polished Latin [Col. 0395B] to the lord pope for the affection and concern he had shown toward himself and his fellow-exiles. All the multitude present marvelled at his wisdom and reply.

For he answered each point they had proposed, one by one and in the same order, with true and persuasive reasons, refuting the king’s complaints and openly setting forth the Church’s injuries and intolerable losses. Because they required humility and the rendering of honour from him, he replied that he would most willingly show every humility, honour, and reverence to his lord king, to the utmost of his power, provided that the honour of God, the liberty of the Church, the dignity of his own person, and the possessions of the churches were preserved. If they thought anything ought to be added, he asked the cardinals to give counsel, [Col. 0396A] saying that he intended to comply, provided the liberty of his condition, profession, and order remained intact.

They answered that they had not come to be advised by him, but to advise him and attempt a path of reconciliation. The cardinals then asked the archbishop whether, in his province, he would promise observance of the customs of Clarendon, that is, “Cleri-Damni” (“the Clergy’s Harm”); customs which, according to the king’s persuasion of them, the kings of England had been heard to employ in the times of his archiepiscopal predecessors, after great gifts had been given and greater ones promised. Thus, with all complaints suppressed, he might return into favour and regain his see, administration, and peace for himself and his followers.

The archbishop answered that none of his predecessors had ever been compelled by any king to make such a profession; nor would he, with God’s help, ever promise to observe customs that manifestly contradict God’s laws, overthrow the privilege of the Apostolic See, destroy the Church’s liberty, and had been condemned by the lord pope at Sens in the presence of those men and many others. “And I,” he said, “following the authority of the lord pope, have anathematized certain of those same customs together with those who observe them, as the Catholic Church is known to have done already in many councils. Therefore I have declared null and shattered that written document of royal constitutions which he is known to have established at Clarendon, together with the abuses it contains—especially because no appeal is allowed to the Apostolic See.” (See what we have said in the preface.)

## VI. SUMMARY OF THE CASE BETWEEN THE KING AND THOMAS

[Col. 0395]

[Col. 0395C] Concerning the first cause of the manifest discord between the lord of Canterbury and the lord king.

Henry, illustrious king of England, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou, came to London on the Kalends of October in the year of the Incarnate Word 1163, together with Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, Roger, archbishop of York, and all the bishops of England. The sole and principal purpose of the council was solemnly to demonstrate that the metropolitan of Canterbury was primate of all England; only the archbishop of York opposed him in this. But, beyond everyone’s expectation, the king of England began to propose certain rather harsh measures.

First, he complained of the violence of archdeacons: that they converted the offences of others into their own profit, exacted the price of sins, and spent their gains [Col. 0395D] upon excessive luxury, though they did not inflict due correction upon the offenders. He said that he wished archdeacons not to summon anyone, however notorious, on any criminal charge without the knowledge of his official.

Then immediately turning his speech to another matter, he said: “I devise thoughts of peace, and am much concerned for the good of peace, which is disturbed in [Col. 0396C] my kingdom by the wickedness of clerks, who commit robberies and thefts, and very often homicides. Therefore I request and will that, with the consent of you, lord of Canterbury, and your fellow bishops, clerks caught, convicted, or confessing in evil deeds shall immediately be deprived of office, and then handed over to the officers of my court, so that, stripped of every protection of the Church, they may be physically punished. I also will and request that, at that deprivation, you consent to the presence of one of my officials, so that he may immediately seize the deprived clerk, lest he be given any opportunity to escape bodily punishment.”

To this the lord of Canterbury, being unable to obtain even until morning a postponement for answering this request, withdrew apart with [Col. 0396D] his bishops. Immediately arguments were made on both sides. The bishops said that, according to secular laws, deprived clerks ought to be handed over to the court and, after spiritual punishment, physically punished; for the more worthy they are through privilege, the worse they are judged to be in their offence; and the worse they are in offence, the graver the penalty which should be inflicted upon them. “It is therefore no wonder,” they said, “that [Col. 0397A] deprivation of order should be followed by punishment of the body.”

They supported the same point not only by laws but also by authoritative examples, adducing the Levites of the Old Testament, whom, if convicted of some grave crime forbidden by law, death of the body followed, or, according to the likeness of the crime, mutilation of their limbs.

But the lord of Canterbury, agreeing with the sacred canons, argued the contrary, asserting that it would be altogether unjust, contrary to the canons and contrary to God, for someone to undergo two judgments for the punishment of one offence. “For God does not judge twice for the same thing.” For, he said, what the Church judges is either just or unjust. But you will not say that it is unjust; therefore it is just. And since it does not contain absolution, [Col. 0397B] it contains condemnation. Therefore, if the accused is condemned when he is deprived of office, another judgment ought not to be begun for the condemnation of the same sin.

“We must also take care,” he said, “that the liberty of the Church not be oppressed and perish through our consent; for it is our duty, following the example of our High Priest, to contend for it even unto death. Yet you have not resisted unto death.”

The bishops replied that the perishing liberty of the Church brought no danger upon the Church. “Rather,” they said, “it is expedient now that it should perish, lest we all perish. Let us therefore do what the king requests; otherwise escape will perish from us, and there will be no one to seek our souls. If we consent to the king, we shall possess God’s sanctuary as an inheritance, and in the possessions of [Col. 0397C] our churches we shall sleep securely. Much also must be yielded to the evil of this time.” [This was said because of the schism then existing in the Roman Church; for there was a certain antipope in Germany.] The bishops said these things as though the evil of the day were not sufficient of itself, unless it were increased by the wickedness of bishops.

At this the lord of Canterbury, inflamed with zeal for God’s house, said: “I see that you console your cowardice under the appearance of endurance, and that under the pretext of your dispensation the liberty of Christ’s bride is being choked. And who has bewitched you, O foolish bishops? Why do you cover your manifest iniquity with the prudent-sounding name of dispensation? Why do you call the loss [Col. 0397D] of Christ’s whole Church a dispensation? Let names serve realities; let names not be perverted along with realities.

“As for what you say, that much must be yielded to the evil of the time: I certainly agree, but not that sins should for that reason be accumulated upon sins. God has power to make the condition of His Church better, even if you do not become worse. Is God unable to help the holy Church except through the vices of the Church’s teachers? I think you pity the weaknesses of Christ, as though He were unable to raise up His bride unless aided by our counsels. In truth, God is testing you. I ask: when ought bishops to expose themselves to danger? In tranquillity, and not in danger? You would certainly be ashamed to confess that it is in tranquillity. It remains, therefore, [Col. 0398A] that when there is disturbance in the Church, the Church’s shepherd should place himself in peril.

“For the bishops of old had no greater merit in founding Christ’s Church in their own blood than we have in our times in shedding blood for the Church’s liberty. And I, indeed, God being witness, affirm that it is not safe for us to depart from that pattern which we received from our holy fathers. Nor ought we to expose anyone to death, since we ourselves are not permitted even to take part in a judgment of blood.”

These words were immediately reported to the king. He saw at once that very many who were not, I will not say pillars, but reeds shaken by the wind, were trembling in fear because they had heard that they would not comply in every respect with the king’s wish. They would indeed have yielded immediately, before any threats, had they not perceived the constancy of the lord of Canterbury. But when the king saw that he could not prevail in the matter in which he had wished to prevail, he turned more quickly to other matters and asked whether they would in all things observe his royal customs.

The lord of Canterbury, having spoken with counsel, said: “Yes, in all things, but with our order preserved in all things and entirely.” When afterward the king asked each one of them in turn the same question, this indeed was then the voice in every mouth. But when he pressed more persistently, repeatedly demanding whether the lord of Canterbury would simply and absolutely promise to observe his royal customs without the added reservation for his order, he could not obtain from Christ’s vicar what he wished. The king [Col. 0398C] was therefore violently disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him. Suddenly, in that violent agitation of spirit, he sprang up and departed from London, all his business unfinished and his accounts unsettled.

Then you might have seen murmuring among the people and commotion in the clergy. The disturbed and trembling bishops followed the departing king, fearing that they would not find the king before hearing that they had lost all their possessions. Immediately they made a secret agreement with the king, setting aside every mention of God and their order. They gave assent to the king’s request so readily that they seemed to have consented before he had asked; indeed, those thought wiser among them became the readier to oppress the Church’s liberty.

But the archbishop of Canterbury alone remained seated, looking to the right and [Col. 0398D] to the left, and there was no one who recognized him. He sought comfort among his brethren; but they went backward and no longer walked with him. Finally, seeing the peace of sinners and danger threatening him from every side, he said: “I have spoken one thing: that I would by no means observe the royal customs of an earthly king unless my order were preserved in all things. For this I incurred the king’s displeasure; for this my bishops abandoned me; for this I offended the eyes of the whole world.

“But what of it? Whether the world wills it or not, in making an agreement with a mortal man I shall never at any time, God willing, be unmindful of my God and of my order. Far be it from me to be found to have despised God through fear of, or favour toward, any mortal! If an angel came from heaven and gave me such counsel, let him be anathema.”

[Col. 0399A] Concerning the undertaking and agreement of the archbishops and all bishops respecting the customs of the realm.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1164, the sixth year of Alexander’s papacy, and the eleventh year of Henry II, most illustrious king of England, this record or recognition was made in the presence of that same king of a certain part of the customs, liberties, and dignities of his predecessors—namely King Henry, his grandfather, and others—which ought to be observed and maintained in the kingdom. Because disputes and discord had arisen between the clergy and the justices of the lord king, and the barons of the realm, concerning the customs and dignities of the realm, this record or recognition was made before the archbishops, bishops, clergy, earls, [Col. 0399B] barons, and magnates of the kingdom.

The same customs, recognized by the archbishops and bishops, earls and barons, and by the nobler and more ancient men of the realm, Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury of holy memory; Roger, archbishop of York; Gilbert, bishop of London; Henry, bishop of Winchester; Nigel, bishop of Ely; William, bishop of Norwich; Robert, bishop of Lincoln; Hilary, bishop of Chichester; Joscelin, bishop of Salisbury; Richard, bishop of Chester; Bartholomew, bishop of Exeter; Robert, bishop of Hereford; David, bishop of St Davids; and Roger, bishop-elect of Worcester, granted and firmly promised by their word of truth, orally, to maintain and observe for the lord king and his heirs, in good faith and without fraud, in the presence of these men: Robert, earl of Leicester; Reginald, earl of Cornwall; Conan, earl of Brittany; John, count of Eu; Robert, earl of Clarendon; Count Geoffrey of Mandeville; Hugh, earl of Chester; William, earl of Arundel; Count Patrick; William, earl of Ferrers; Richard de Lucy; Reginald of Saint-Valery; Roger Bigod; Reginald de Warenne; Richer de l’Aigle; William de Braose; Richard de Camville; Nigel de Mowbray; Simon de Beauchamp; Humphrey de Bohun; Matthew of Hereford; Walter de Meduana; Manasses Biset, steward; William Malet; William de [Col. 0399D] Courcy; Robert de Dunstanville; Joscelin de Balliol; William Lanvalei; William de Caisneto; Geoffrey de Ver; William de Hastings; Hugh de Morville; Alan de Neville; Simon son of Peter; William Malduit, chamberlain; John Malduit; John Marshal; Peter de Mara; and many other magnates and nobles of the kingdom, both clerical and lay.

A certain part of the customs and dignities thus recognized is contained in the present document. The chapters of that part are these:

**CHAPTER I. Concerning advowson, etc.** (See these sixteen constitutions in Herbert of Bosham, below.)

The aforesaid royal customs and dignities were recorded by the aforesaid archbishops, bishops, earls, barons, and the nobler and more ancient men of the kingdom at Clarendon, on the fourth day before the Purification of Saint Mary Ever-Virgin, with Lord Henry, the king’s son, present there with his father the lord king.

Concerning the exile and proscription of the lord of Canterbury and his kinsfolk.

Thomas, therefore, the archbishop of Canterbury, worthy of God, according to the ordinances of the holy Fathers, strove to preserve what he knew rightly belonged to his church and to recover what had been dispersed. He endeavoured to reclaim estates of the Church which his predecessors had, for various reasons, granted away or relinquished less than justly to men endowed with excessive power or connected with the king by kinship, and to restore the Church’s former right; for an administrator of the Church may cultivate and increase [Col. 0400B] ecclesiastical estates, but may not neglect or diminish them.

He also asserted his authority over clerks belonging to the king’s court when he discovered their negligence, and over all other matters belonging to ecclesiastical jurisdiction. Thus sacrilegious invaders of ecclesiastical property, together with certain bishops and clerks wearing the same garb, embittered and so inflamed the king and his whole household against the Lord’s holy one that, after the undertaking made at Clarendon, around the next feast of Saint Michael, the said chief bishop was summoned to Northampton as though to be judged before Caesar’s tribunal.

On the appointed day, when he had been reliably informed that some of the king’s party had conspired to kill him, because he had long since clothed the inner man in the priestly garment, according to the saying, “I will clothe her priests with salvation,” he now more secretly fortified his outer man beneath a cloak with the outward vesture of a priest, carrying the cross in his own hands lest the example of his Passion be removed from him.

Therefore the noble archbishop, attended by God alone, when he was accused by everyone and on many charges, responded wonderfully, while seated so as not, by standing, to burden the person of a priest, with what had been divinely inspired in him: namely, that a superior ought not to be summoned to judgment by his inferiors, nor bound by their sentence. For order is confounded if a sheep strikes the shepherd, a disciple his master, or a son his father. Gold is not more precious than lead to the extent that the dignity of priesthood [Col. 0400D] is higher than royal power.

Yet his lay suffragans—indeed, now rather his opponents—condemned him nonetheless while he was speaking these things and appealing to the Apostolic See. But the holy man, secretly and with such few companions as he could, pursuing his appeal, found the most holy Pope Alexander III at Sens. Throwing himself at his feet, he explained to one who was not ignorant of it the cause of his arrival.

Afterwards, as has been reliably learned, the chief bishop resigned into the lord pope’s hand the right of his archiepiscopate, asking him to establish as cardinal in their metropolitan church some man from the English Church more learned and stronger than himself. But the holy pope raised and embraced his son, kissed him, mingling tears with tears, and gave thanks to God because he had found a man so humble in spirit, [Col. 0401A] a shepherd so zealous for the salvation of his sheep, and an advocate so constant in the cause—indeed, in many causes—of God.

Therefore the lord pope decreed that the dignity which he had declined should be restored to him, though he resisted and was unwilling, because he knew that no one was stronger for this burden. Thus contention was carried on between him and the king: the king wishing, as he alleged, to confirm the customs of his kingdom; the archbishop—or rather the Roman Church—protesting that those customs in many cases contradicted the truth revealed to God’s elect, and that customs must plainly yield to truth. For Christ is found at one time to have said, “I am the truth,” but He never said, “I am custom.”

And so this dispute was conducted under that warfare between these persons, while the most fortunate King Louis, son of King Louis, reigned over the French nation and supported the aforesaid archbishop—since he had been entirely proscribed from the resources of his church—as well as the clerks dwelling with him, who had likewise been deprived of their possessions, until they should return to the favour of the aforesaid king and promise that they would not oppose the customs over which the dispute had arisen and which was still suspended by appeal.

For the king had issued such edicts against them, commanding each sheriff of England as follows:

“I command you that, if any layman in your bailiwick appeals to the Roman court, you shall seize him and keep him securely until I give further command concerning my will. And you shall seize into my hand all revenues and possessions of the archbishop’s clerks, as Ranulf de Broc and [Col. 0402A] my other officers shall tell you; and you shall place under safe pledges the fathers and mothers, brothers and sisters, nephews and nieces, and chattels of all clerks who are with the archbishop, until I give further command concerning my will. And you shall bring this writ with you when summoned.”

He wrote to each bishop as follows:

“You know how wickedly Archbishop Thomas has acted against me and my kingdom, and how wickedly he has departed. Therefore I command you that his clerks who were with him after his flight, and other clerks who have disparaged my honour and the honour of my kingdom, shall receive nothing from the revenues which they held in your bishopric except through me, nor shall they have any aid [Col. 0402B] or counsel from you. Witness Richard de Lucy at Marlborough.”

But since the holy priest was not bent in any respect either by the proscription of himself or of his clerks, persons both great and small, of both sexes, from among his kindred, as well as certain of his household, were ordered into exile so that he might be more deeply grieved by this. When the aforesaid archbishop learned of the removal of little children whose nourishment still depended upon their mothers’ breasts, he was grieved as though a sword had passed through his own soul.

But remembering that it was said to Abraham, “Go forth from your land and from your kindred,” he resolved to set aside not only his land but even his kindred entirely for the honour of the Church, because nothing is owed by any person against the Lord.

## VII. CONCERNING OATHS PUBLICLY SWORN THROUGHOUT ENGLAND AGAINST THE ROMAN AND CANTERBURY CHURCHES

[Col. 0401]

[Col. 0401C] In the year 1069 from the Lord’s Incarnation, King Henry caused all England, every lay person above twelve or fifteen years of age, to swear against Lord Pope Alexander and blessed Thomas, archbishop, that they would neither receive their letters nor obey their commands; and that if anyone were found carrying their letters, he should be handed over to the authorities as a capital enemy of the king’s crown. When the archbishop heard this, deeply grieving over so great an error and apostasy, he sent the following letters (see St Thomas’s epistle, col. 550) to certain God-fearing men, that they might absolve the rest.

The chapters of the constitutions which King Henry established in Normandy in that same year and commanded to be sworn and observed against the lord pope and the archbishop by his justices [Col. 0402C] Richard de Lucy and the two archdeacons Geoffrey Ridel of Canterbury and Richard of Poitiers, and by all the princes and peoples of England, are contained in the first part of the letters, together with the chapters of the royal dignities and ancestral customs which were recalled and confirmed at Clarendon, in the presence of the lord king, by the archbishops, bishops, barons, and the nobler and more ancient men of the kingdom.

(For these constitutions promulgated in Normandy in 1169, see the Second *Quadrilogus*.)

## VIII. A FRAGMENT CONCERNING THE EXCHEQUER

[Col. 0401]

[Col. 0401D] You shall declare, upon your oath, what the sheriff or their bailiffs have taken in any manner from each [Col. 0402D] hundred, each vill, and each person, since the king crossed the sea. You shall declare what lands, and how many, the sheriff or their bailiffs have bought or taken in pledge. You shall declare what and how much the sheriff or their bailiffs have given to itinerant justices. You shall declare what has been done with the chattels of fugitives who fled because of the Assize of Clarendon. You shall declare whether anyone was accused and afterwards released for a bribe and returned. You shall declare what was given for marrying the king’s daughter, and to whom it was delivered. You shall declare whether the sheriff, their bailiffs, or the lords of vills have made or are making any settlement with aggrieved persons so that no complaint might come before the king or the justices. You shall declare, concerning those amerced, whether anyone has been released and by whom. You shall declare whether anyone has failed to perform homage to the lord king [Col. 0404A] or to his son. You shall declare concerning the lord king’s demesnes whether they are as the king commanded before he crossed the sea. You shall declare concerning those who hold any bailiwick of the king in custody—whether archdeaconries, bishoprics, abbeys, or any escheat—what they or their bailiffs have taken, or what they have acquired in that bailiwick. You shall declare what foresters or their bailiffs have taken from the lord king’s forests, and whether they have released anyone accused concerning the forest. You shall declare what the lords of vills or their stewards have taken beyond rightful custom. You shall declare what and how much archdeacons or deans have taken unjustly and without judgment.

## IX. CONCERNING THE RENEWAL OF THE SCHISM

[Col. 0403]

This is the oath sworn at Cologne by John Sil. and Henry of Oxford; because of that oath the schism, now almost dead, revived in Germany. He himself, together with his companion Richard of Ilchester, became involved in the condemned heresy; and in England too, through participation with that great and notorious schismatic Reginald of Cologne, they incurred a sentence of excommunication.

[Col. 0403B] When the emperor had assembled a very large number of clergy and his princes at his council during this solemnity of Pentecost, on Saturday and Monday there was discussion of restoring peace and concord between us and himself. Then the elect of Cologne came forward and declared publicly before them all:

“Lord Emperor, the councils which you have hitherto convened against Pope Alexander in order to depose him have been of no benefit to you and have done him no harm. For very many even of our own party obey and adhere to him, such as the lord of Mainz and others. But if you will accept me and my counsel, both Alexander’s overthrow and the exaltation of our Pope Paschal will be readily achieved. Behold, I have won over to our party fifty bishops with their archbishops, and still more in number from the dominion of the king of England, who will adhere to Pope [Col. 0403C] Paschal and to us, if you renounce obedience to Alexander and, when he dies, to anyone elected from his party. And, as proof of this matter, behold: two envoys of the king of the English are present, prepared to swear in the person of their lord that he will ratify and swear whatever you here swear and enact concerning this.”

The emperor approved the proposed plan and promised that he would renounce for ever the name and obedience of Alexander. When the clergy were asked for their judgment and assent and were more urgently pressed to agree, the archbishop of Magdeburg and many others said that, since future events are uncertain and God often rejects the man whom princes elect, while He disapproves the man whom the people approve, such an oath was rash; and that they would sooner surrender their regalian rights than swear in this way. The emperor said that he must both retain the regalian rights and swear thus with him.

As the emperor’s anger was now growing hot, the archbishop of Magdeburg, in order to mitigate or postpone the matter, said: “If the lord of Cologne, [Col. 0404B] who urges such counsel and such an oath, first of all renounces Alexander and swears that he will receive his appointment and consecration from Paschal, he will make us more certain of his inward intention; he will remove every scruple of wicked suspicion from our minds; and thus he will more easily induce us to accept such a resolution and oath.”

The emperor agreed. When the man of Cologne, ordered to swear first in this manner, refused and resisted even to tears, the emperor, violently enraged, said:

“Behold, it is clear that you have acted against me and my life as a traitor. Behold, it is clear that the late man of Mainz gave me sound counsel when he said, on Octavian’s death, that, since the Lord had already delivered me from the greatest danger by his death, I should take care not to involve myself again [Col. 0404C] in a similar peril. Therefore I wrote to you with commands sent that you should undertake nothing concerning the election of a pontiff to replace him without consulting me; but you, without my knowledge, chose this man on your own authority and caused the *Te Deum laudamus* to be sung. You prepared a pit for us; now you shall be the first to fall into it.”

Thus the man of Cologne first, and without qualification, swore according to the form stated above. Afterwards the emperor renounced obedience to you and to anyone elected from your party, while retaining and determining this proviso: if it should happen that both you and Paschal die, and both parties agree together upon the election of one person, he should be free to assent to and receive that person.

Then the man of Cologne added, “provided that the election has been celebrated with your consent”; [Col. 0404D] and he added that he would make his princes swear, both those present and those absent, in their respective regions and provinces, in a similar form; and that, if the emperor should die, they would not invest another with the imperial insignia until his successor had taken the same oath [Col. 0405A] of renunciation.

Then the duke of the Saxons, Margrave Albert, a certain count palatine, the emperor’s brother, and a certain nephew—his sister’s son—swore. At last the archbishop of Magdeburg also renounced, and did so with tears, adding the condition that this held only so long as he retained the regalian rights, and provided all those absent should swear the same. Afterwards the bishop of Brünn [Col. 0406A] and two other suffragans of his swore, as did the envoys of the king of England in his person. Two bishops, excused because their archbishop was absent, did not swear; the oath of these and of the others who were absent was postponed until the octave of Peter and Paul.

## X. DEGREES OF KINSHIP BETWEEN THE KING AND QUEEN

[Col. 0405]

The cardinals of Poitiers presented this calculation when Saint Thomas was in exile, but they were not heard.

[Col. 0405B] The degrees of kinship between the king of the English and the queen were calculated as follows. William, king of the English, and Robert, count of Mortain, were brothers by the same mother. Henry was born of William; of Henry, the Empress Matilda; [Col. 0406B] of Matilda, King Henry. Likewise, Beatrice, countess of Poitiers, was born of Count Robert; of Beatrice, Count William; of Count William, Queen Eleanor.

## XI. REVOCATION OF THE ARTICLES WHICH KING HENRY II WISHED THE ENGLISH CHURCH TO OBSERVE

[Col. 0405]

[Col. 0405C] In the name of God, Amen. In the year of the Lord 1173, in the presence of the venerable fathers and lords in Christ, Lord Albert, by divine favour priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and Theodwin, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Vitalis, legates of the Apostolic See; with the prior and convent of the Church of Canterbury and very many other persons of the kingdom of England assembled in the conventual church of the Holy Trinity at Canterbury: We, Henry, by the grace of God king of England and duke of the Normans, desiring humbly and devoutly to perform the penance imposed upon us by you, lords legates, by apostolic authority for the remission of our sins, hereby publicly and openly, in these written letters, revoke, reject, renounce, and surrender all those evil customs wickedly introduced by us against the ancient [Col. 0405D] liberties of the English Church. We wholly relinquish them, individually and collectively, for ourselves and our heirs for ever—those customs for which blessed Thomas, lately archbishop of Canterbury, contended even unto death.

Furthermore, for the honour of almighty God, of the blessed Virgin Mary, and of all the saints, and for the remission of our sins, we grant for ourselves and our heirs that the Church of Canterbury and all other English churches shall be free and shall possess [Col. 0406C] all their liberties unimpaired, as they were accustomed to possess them before our coronation; and that all churches henceforth to be founded in our kingdom of England by us or by our heirs shall enjoy each and every one of the aforesaid liberties.

Thus, on the occasion of the vacancy of those same churches, or of any one of them, their temporal possessions, which are to be granted by us or by our heirs, shall by no means be taken or seized into our hands or those of our heirs; and if, on any of the aforesaid grounds, they are taken or seized, we will and grant by these presents that they shall without delay be restored and released in full, without any payment or demand of any fixed exaction being in any way required or ordered by us or our heirs from those churches or from any one of them on that account.

We further declare [Col. 0406D] and promise in good faith, for ourselves and our heirs, that we shall assist, correct, amend, and enlarge the aforesaid revocation, rejection, renunciation, and surrender in a better form, for the honour of God and of the Church, whenever this shall be submitted to us or to our heirs for that purpose by the archbishop of Canterbury or by any prelate of our realm who shall then be in office and shall have duly requested it. These things were done in the aforesaid year of the Lord.

## XII. THESE ARE THE ARTICLES OF THE PURGATION

[Col. 0407]

Which the archbishop of York made by the fourth hand of oath-helpers, one of whom was Master Vacarius.

[Col. 0407A] That he had confirmed neither in writing nor by oath the ancestral customs concerning which the dispute between the king and the lord of Canterbury had arisen.

That neither by deed nor word, neither personally nor through an intermediary, had he knowingly contrived anything that might bring the lord of Canterbury to his death.

[Col. 0408A] That he had neither received nor seen the lord pope’s letters sent into England forbidding the coronation of the king’s son, nor caused anything to be done which prevented his seeing or receiving them.

That at the coronation of the king’s son he received the due oath in its entirety, and omitted nothing which is customarily performed at the coronation of the king of England.

## XIII. TREATISE OF STEPHEN LANGTON, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, ON THE TRANSLATION OF BLESSED THOMAS

[Col. 0407]

[Col. 0407B] 1. As we recall with the devotion of annual observance the memory of the translation of blessed Thomas, let us set before the eyes of our mind what is said through the prophet to the opponents of the primitive Church, so that we may discharge more faithfully the debt of our service and equip ourselves more vigorously to fulfil our ministry. For Zechariah says:

> “Those who drink shall be drunk as with wine; they shall be filled like bowls, and like the horns of the altar; and the Lord their God shall save them on that day, as the flock of his people, because holy stones shall be raised above the earth.”

Let no one think it unfitting or unworthy that we set warriors before those wishing to keep a feast-day as an example. For it is necessary that those celebrating solemnities be prepared for spiritual warfare, lest, while they venerate the merits of the saints, they be wounded by the enemies’ [Col. 0407C] arrows. This is well signified by that distinguished warrior, Judas Maccabaeus, who, intending to cleanse the holy places and renew the Temple of the Lord by the office of dedication, appointed men to fight meanwhile against those who were in the citadel.

2. Following his example more solemnly, let us fight manfully against the evil spirits dwelling in the citadel of pride. By mixing the poison of sin with the wine of the feast, they kill the wretched—those who, under the pretext of solemnities, make a business of their bellies and corrupt spiritual joy by carnal revelry. Therefore, dearest brethren, let us imitate Mattathias and his sons, who, together with the faithful resisting Antiochus, prudently decreed that they should fight with one accord against the nations which attacked them on Sabbath days.

Let us therefore prudently [Col. 0408B] and courageously resist the enemies who disturb our Sabbaths and wickedly contrive that spiritual joy, established for the remedy of souls, should become their ruin. For if, loosening the reins of joy under the pretext of joy, we embrace wantonness, and if, having cast off the belt of discipline, ecclesiastical men become dissolute, enemies looking upon the Church will mock her Sabbaths. Since, therefore, we read in the Psalm that in the tents of the righteous there resounds a voice of exultation and salvation, if we wish to be righteous, let us carefully ensure that, if there is among us a voice of exultation, it is likewise a voice of salvation. Let not exultation exclude salvation, nor temporal joy introduce everlasting grief.

3. With the whole intention of our mind, let us avoid, in accordance with the testimony of Thaddaeus, turning into licentiousness the grace of our God established in the glory of the saints. For those who presume to attempt the boldness of this rashness have been marked out for judgment and are already branded with the title of condemnation. The end of a dishonourable life, according to the prophetic word, will turn into lamentation and mourning the feast-days which joy attends in this life.

Who should wonder if those are compelled to serve the Lord in punishments who compelled Him to serve in their sins, as He complains through the prophet concerning those who turned His glory and that of the saints toward pleasure and guilt? Scripture prescribes the manner and form in which solemnities are to be celebrated. Describing the joys of a most celebrated feast, it asserts that everything was delightful according to the countenance [Col. 0409A] of the saints. But what this solemnity is like, the Apostle teaches when he says:

> “Fornication and every impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as befits saints; nor shamefulness, foolish talk, or buffoonery, which is inappropriate, but rather thanksgiving.”

For although a holy man may dwell in Jericho, he does not lose the countenance of one going to Jerusalem: although bodily life keeps him in the world, he retains the countenance of one longing for heavenly things.

4. Let us therefore, as we have said, imitate the first warriors, whose excellence invites us to attack enemies bravely on feast-days. The prophetic speech says in praise:

> “Those who drink shall be drunk as with wine; they shall be filled like bowls, and like the horns [Col. 0409B] of the altar,”

and so forth. These words do not merely point to the first combatants; they also instruct those who celebrate the saints’ solemnities. For three things are marked in these words, on account of which it was beneficially ordained that the Church should solemnly celebrate the saints’ feasts.

The first cause is joy: that we may rejoice in the Lord, rejoicing in the blessedness of those whom He lovingly loved, gloriously adorned, clothed in the robe of glory, and magnificently crowned. The first clause of the prophetic saying just quoted denotes this joy.

The second cause is example: that we who recount the merits of the saints may follow their footsteps with the understanding of good works and imitate with the steps of our minds those in whose patronage we glory. The second clause set above signifies this cause. For those who, according to the measure [Col. 0409C] of their strength, conform themselves to the works of the saints are suitably compared to sacred vessels and the horns of the altar, as what follows will make clear.

The third cause is aid: that those who rejoice in the merits of the saints may glory in their patronage; that the saints may not fail them in assistance, but may repay, in grateful return, the service rendered to them. The third clause of the saying denotes this third cause.

These three refresh the traveller tending toward heavenly things and, through the annual festival, yearning for the unending one. For he is guided by example, sustained by aid, and revived by joy. Example performs the office of a guide; aid, that of a helper; and, lest he lack consolation, joy stands alongside these two.

[Col. 0409D] 5. What could be more advantageous to a traveller than that his journey should be certain, safe, and joyful? These three suffice for all this: “For example provides certainty, aid safety, and joy gladness.” See how great is the sweetness flowing from the observance of festivals, indicated by the joy of which we have spoken. See what fruits are gathered from solemnities if they are kept with devout devotion: aid and example, mentioned above, signify these fruits.

Thus, when the prophet had said that holy stones were to be raised above the earth—thereby indicating that the bodies of the saints were to be gloriously translated from their tombs—he immediately added, wishing to declare how fruitful the glory of translation is for believers:

> “For what is his goodness, and what [Col. 0410A] is his beauty, except the grain of the elect and wine making virgins flourish?”

Aid and example, which arise from solemnities, as has been shown above, signify the grain of the elect. For just as grain is threshed on the threshing-floor in order to separate it from chaff, so in the Church the deeds of the saints have been sifted, so that, once the chaff of vanity has been shaken off, their memory may be as holy as it is solemn; and, preserving grains without chaff, we may be helped by their aid and instructed by their examples. Grain is also stored in a clean granary to be preserved; nor can votive solemnities be observed as they ought without purity of heart.

6. Holy joy attached to festivals is signified by wine making virgins flourish. For the wine of spiritual joy produces virginal purity, because it nourishes and preserves chastity. But the wine of worldly joy produces, or makes flourish, harlots, because it arouses and inflames lust. Let this wine be absent from ecclesiastical festivals, at which another wine is to be served.

Thus the Lord declares through the prophet that His eunuchs keep His Sabbaths: those eunuchs, namely, “who,” as He Himself says in the Gospel, “have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdoms of heaven.” These are they who, for desire of the heavenly kingdom, cut away and sever from their flesh the shamefulness of harmful pleasure.

It should be noted that the usefulness of solemnities is excellently commended when goodness and beauty are joined in exalting it highly. Thus the Psalmist commended the concord of brethren when he said:

> “Behold [Col. 0410C] how good and how delightful it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!”

Likewise, the wise man praises the service of Christian devotion, consisting in the fear of God and the keeping of His commandments, saying:

> “Nothing is better than to fear God, and nothing is better than to look to His commandments.”

7. The Lord indicated through the prophet the three things mentioned above—joy, aid, and example—which, as we have said, are connected with festivals:

> “The sons of the stranger who cleave to the Lord to serve him, everyone keeping the Sabbath so as not to profane it, and holding fast my covenant—I will bring them to my holy mountain, and I will make them joyful in my house of prayer. Their whole burnt-offerings and [Col. 0410D] their sacrifices shall please me upon my altar.”

Holy Scripture calls the Gentile people a “stranger.” Hence it was said to the Jewish people:

> “The stranger living with you in the land shall rise above you and be higher, but you shall descend and be lower.”

This has plainly been fulfilled in the Jewish and Gentile peoples. Therefore all of us who are born of the nations are sons of strangers.

The prophetic speech also plainly expressed the manner and form of divine worship when it said of those who worship God: “who cleave to the Lord, to serve Him.” For it is written: “He who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit.”

8. It teaches that worshippers of God who venerate Him at festivals must be spirit and not flesh, because the worship of God requires [Col. 0411A] spiritual, not carnal, joy. Conversely, of the horses of Egypt, by which the powerful of this world are signified, the prophet says: “Their horses are flesh, not spirit.” For the powerful of the world are often sluggish and slow toward spiritual things, but swift and ready for carnal things; and the prophetic saying is fulfilled in them:

> “I paid attention and listened: no one speaks what is good; no one does penance for his sins, saying, ‘What have I done?’ All have turned to their own course, like a horse rushing headlong into battle.”

The following words are rightly added: “everyone keeping the Sabbath so as not to profane it, and holding fast my covenant.” For whoever violates by any transgression a festival assigned to divine worship does not keep the covenant made with the Lord.

In ancient times, moreover, a covenant was ratified by the shedding of blood. Let us therefore, on the feasts of those who shed their blood for Christ, strengthen with all the desire of our minds the covenant which we have entered into with our Lord. We read that when the people of Israel made a covenant with the Lord through Joshua, he set up a very great stone in the sanctuary and made it a witness to this event. In Holy Scripture holy martyrs are often signified by stones, as what follows will show. Therefore a very great stone is raised in the sanctuary of the Lord when the relics of some great martyr are exalted on high in the Church.

9. Since, therefore, today we recall how a great stone has been raised in the sanctuary—that is, the glorious martyr Thomas has been raised from the tomb—let us direct the understanding [Col. 0411C] of our heart to this stone and strive to fix upon it the affection of our mind, so that it may be willing and able to be a witness to our devotion.

Of those who worship God with sincere minds it is subsequently said:

> “I will bring them to my holy mountain and make them joyful in my house of prayer; their whole burnt-offerings and their sacrifices shall please me, as my altar.”

In these words example is first indicated, joy second, and intercession third—those same three things stated above. For the example of the saints brings us to the mountain of the Lord, that is, to the height of eternal blessedness. Example, as we have said, shows the straight way to those tending toward heaven, acting as a guide. Hence the Psalmist says:

> [Col. 0411D] “Send forth your light and your truth; they have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles.”

What is more rightly denoted by the name of light, which figures God’s grace, without which nothing is bright, nothing serene, but all things dark?

10. Truth is the holy conduct of the righteous. The life of the wicked is vanity and falsehood; the life of the good is truth. Hence the prophet says: “Love peace and truth.” The righteous man loves peace with his neighbour and truth in himself.

Light and truth lead the righteous man, bringing him to the mountain and the tabernacles: through the preceding grace of God, by the examples of the saints, we shall reign in our homeland and make progress on the way. The mountain on which the city is built refers to the homeland; the tabernacles [Col. 0412A] of travellers refer to the way.

The spiritual joy joined to annual festivals is plainly expressed when it is added: “I will make them joyful in my house of prayer.” In the whole burnt-offerings and sacrifices mentioned next are signified the saints’ intercessions. For we offer sacrifices and whole burnt-offerings for you when we present to the Lord on our own behalf the merits of those who through faith conquered kingdoms and offered themselves to Him as an odour of sweetness, so that by their prayers we may be able to appease His displeasure.

11. Let us now examine the prophetic saying proposed at the outset: “Those who drink shall be drunk as with wine,” and so forth. Holy Scripture frequently signifies spiritual joy by eating and drinking. Thus Ecclesiastes says:

> “Every man who eats and drinks and sees good from his labour—this is the gift of God.”

He sees good from his labours who exercises himself in holy works and sets eternal reward as the fruit of his labour. Of this it is written: “The fruit of good works is glorious.” Spiritual joy is the seasoning of a praiseworthy life. Those who toil at fruitful and honourable labours fittingly rejoice. Thus the Apostle Peter says: “Rejoice as sharers in Christ’s sufferings.” It does not become one who shrinks from the imitation of suffering to exult, “because he will not be a companion of the Redeemer in glory who has not been His companion in punishment.” For, as the Apostle testifies, one who does not suffer with Him will not reign with Him.

Partnership [Col. 0412C] in suffering, because it is bitter to those who taste it, must be sweetened by spiritual joy. Hence it is said to the Lord through the prophet: “You met him who rejoices and does righteousness.” For the Lord, like a ready helper, meets the person who joyfully crucifies his flesh with its vices and desires.

12. Therefore, when a man eats and drinks and receives good from his labour, this is the gift of God, according to Solomon’s testimony. For the Lord alone cheers the afflicted mind and gladdens the spirit of the sufferer amid torments. The preceding sentence clearly reveals and shows how one who diligently attends to good works eats and drinks. For this is first stated:

> “I knew that there was nothing better [Col. 0412D] than to rejoice and do good in one’s life, to eat and drink and rejoice.”

To see good from one’s labours is the same as to do good in this life.

The Bridegroom, indicating spiritual joy in the Song of Songs, says:

> “Eat, drink, and be drunk, my beloved.”

As spiritual joy is signified by food and drink, so its abundance is signified by drunkenness. Therefore let it be openly said: let all who are united to the Lord by friendship rejoice and exult. Yet let those rejoice more fully who draw nearer to Him more intimately through the higher friendship of charity.

But let us carefully consider what precedes this exhortation. For after He had said, “I gathered my myrrh with my spices; I ate my honeycomb with my honey; I drank my wine with my milk,” He then [Col. 0413A] invites His friends to eat and His dearest ones to become drunk.

13. The Lord gathers myrrh with spices in His garden when, in the Church, He receives bodily discipline seasoned with the admixture of good works. Contemplation is figured by the name of honey; and this figure suits the thing, since the sight of heavenly things is honey-sweet. He compared contemplation to honey who said: “As one who eats much honey finds it not good, so the investigator of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory.”

The honeycomb is the inward sweetness of the mind joined to contemplation of heavenly things. Therefore the Lord eats His honeycomb with His honey, because the service of contemplation, offered with love of heart, is pleasing to Him.

Wine bites and heals bodily wounds. Thus compunction is signified by wine; although it pierces within, it is the medicine of spiritual wounds. By milk, by which the simple and little ones are nourished, is understood simplicity of heart. Therefore the Lord gladly drinks wine with milk, because He accepts that sorrow which simplicity of heart commends to Him.

14. After this preface, the words which follow are fitting: “Eat, friends,” and so forth. Those who please God by such services fittingly exult. And because drunkenness, as we have said, signifies an abundance of spiritual joy, those who venerate the Lord in the memorial of the saints are rightly said to be made drunk, so that it may be plainly marked that they ought to abound in holy joy.

It should be noted, however, that drunkenness estranges from temporal things the mind which it exhilarates. Hence it is written: [Col. 0413C] “He who makes others drunk shall himself also be made drunk.” For the person who by exhortation to salvation separates the minds of others from earthly things will have his own mind torn away from them, through the working of the mercy of Him who brings prisoners forth in might. Thus the Lord says through the prophet:

> “If, in converting, you convert to me, you shall stand before my face; and if you separate the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth.”

Through the same prophet it is also said:

> “I have become like a drunken man, and like a man soaked with wine, because of the Lord and because of the words of his holy ones.”

The face of the Creator makes the beholder drunk, because it snatches the contemplative mind from transient things and leads it to everlasting goods. Hearing the divine word also makes its listeners drunk, because holy words consume the love of earthly things [Col. 0413D] and kindle desire for eternal things. Hence they are compared to living coals, which consume foodstuffs and straw. Spiritual joy, like drunkenness, implants the mind in heavenly things and turns it away from earthly things. In this manner those who venerate our mother are made drunk, so that, attending to heavenly things, they may despise fleeting goods and desire abiding ones.

15. Again, drunkenness removes the sense of pain, to such a degree that even when a drunken person endures what should hurt, he is cheerful. Hence the wise man gives the drunkard this speech:

> “They beat me, and I did not hurt; they dragged me, but I did not feel it.”

Jeremiah likewise, speaking in the person of the carnal man, says: “He made me drunk with wormwood.” Explaining the meaning of this phrase, blessed Gregory says: “A drunkard does not know what he suffers.” He is drunk with wormwood who endures the bitterness of the world and yet does not know what he suffers.

Thus the warriors of the primitive Church were like drunkards: with inward joy they conquered bodily torments and, according to the Apostle’s word, “received with joy the plundering of their possessions.” Spiritual delight, likewise, removes the sense of sorrow and pours holy cheerfulness into minds assailed by persecution.

16. The Psalmist declared what kind of exultation ought to accompany the saints’ festivals when he said:

> “The exultations of God are in their throats, and two-edged swords in their hands.”

The enemy of the human race confidently lays snares for those whom he finds entangled in worldly joys. For a grieving mind examines its weaknesses more deeply than one rejoicing. Unless the crafty tempter had known that the time of joy was suited to temptation, he would never, while Job’s sons and daughters were feasting in the house of their first-born brother, have overthrown the corners of the house and destroyed the whole offspring of that blessed man.

Since, therefore, as we have said, the entrance of exultation often leads the mind into the snares of temptation, it is most necessary that, while exultation occupies the throat, the hand should grasp a sword: that sword, namely, which the Apostle calls the Word of God. The sword must be borne in the hand, because it is too little for the Word of God to be turned over in the heart unless one strives to fulfil it in works. Therefore let the hand grasp the sword, so that what is understood in the heart may be confirmed by the testimony of good works. Thus blessed Job says: “My bow shall be renewed in my hand.” [Col. 0414C] The bow is renewed in the hand when the instrument of heavenly battle, from which arrows are shot at enemies, is strengthened by the assistance of good conduct.

17. Therefore let the present festival so receive the sweetness of joy that it does not exclude the severity of the sword. The Psalmist also plainly shows what kind of joy should be attached to the saints’ festivals:

> “Serve the Lord in fear, and exult before him with trembling.”

The Lord must be served with fear, because exultation ought to be sharpened by fear just as fear is seasoned by exultation. For if an occasion of spiritual service introduces worldly joy, it is fitting that the instruction of fear restrain it, so that in the refreshment of sacred sweetness there may at once be a seasoning [Col. 0414D] of sweetness and sharpness.

The Psalmist also plainly showed this elsewhere, saying:

> “Lead me, Lord, in your way; I shall walk in your truth. Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name.”

He walks in the way of the Lord who wisely serves Him. One serving enters into the Lord’s truth when his service is directed toward heavenly things. The manner of service is revealed in the words: “Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name.”

18. He elegantly expressed how one ought to rejoice in the Lord’s service: he asked to rejoice so that he might fear. Joy ought to be such as in no way diminishes the fear of the Lord; and the safeguard of fear ought to be such as does not exclude spiritual joy. Thus, after the Psalmist had first said, “Serve the Lord in [Col. 0415A] fear,” he rightly adds, “and exult before him with trembling.”

Since, as the Apostle says, children of the Church must work out their salvation with fear and trembling, it is necessary that, when exultation is present outwardly, fear should moderate its entrance inwardly, lest it enter wholly into the heart and weakness be suffocated by its immoderate entry. Let fear and trembling exclude this danger: namely, let the mind anxiously fear the evils that may happen, and let the body reverently devote itself to obeying the mind.

19. It follows: “They shall be filled like bowls, and like the horns of the altar.” By bowls and the altar’s horns a twofold form of righteousness is intimated to us, to be observed under differing considerations. Holy conduct, so to speak, sometimes passes from narrowness into breadth, expressing the form of a bowl, which has a narrow base but a wide and spacious mouth; and as it rises upward, it gradually spreads out in breadth. So righteousness, as it advances, gradually receives increase and expands in good works.

At other times holiness progresses into a point, just as the altar’s horns begin broadly but are then narrowed and terminate in a sharp point.

20. Completed righteousness is compared to these horns: once it has attained perfection, it constrains itself through the moderation of humility, although it was previously expanded in excellence of merits. For it attends to the saying of the wise man: “How great is the power of God alone, and He is honoured by the humble.” Through this consideration, the more the righteous man raises himself toward perfection, the more he humbles and lowers himself, lest he think proudly of himself and fall headlong through presumption, or vanish away through vain glory.

21. Solomon teaches how advancing righteousness expands, saying:

> “The path of the righteous is like a shining light; it goes forward and increases unto the perfect day.”

For when righteousness begins, it first shines with a faint light; but when it reaches perfection, it scatters the rays of its brightness on every side. Hence the Psalmist says: “I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart.” And again: “I walked in a broad place, because I sought your commandments.”

Likewise, in Proverbs the father says to the son:

> “I will show you the way [Col. 0415D] of righteousness; I will lead you through the paths of equity. When you have entered them, your steps will not be hemmed in, and when you run you will have no stumbling-block.”

For righteousness hurrying toward its reward is neither constrained by narrowness nor hindered by an obstacle, because the Lord removes what is contrary to it and levels its impediments. Thus, when Holy Scripture described David’s progress, it said: “David was advancing and always becoming stronger in himself, but the house of Saul was daily declining.” For the righteous man shall ascend through increases of merit, but the unrighteous shall decline through the diminution of evil works.

22. But the person who devotes himself to progress in the virtues, by progressing as it were surpasses himself. For he abandons the corruption of the flesh and vigorously girds himself for the spiritual height. Had not he grown beyond himself who said: “I live—yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me”? Did he not seem to rise above himself when he said: “Forgetting what lies behind, I stretch myself toward what lies before”? What we said above about the increase of virtue—namely, that justice is enlarged as it advances—was plainly prefigured in the construction of the Temple.
