For the upper storey of the Temple had a greater width, while the lower had a lesser. The lowest storey was five cubits wide, the middle six, and the upper seven.

23. The storeys with which the Temple walls are adorned are the faithful of the Church, who clothe and adorn her, as it is said to her through the prophet: “As I live, says the Lord, you shall be clothed with all these as with an ornament, and you shall surround yourself with them as a bride.” The storeys aptly signify Catholic men, whose hearts charity has enlarged, heavenly discipline has fashioned, and simplicity has levelled smooth. It well accords with this meaning that the upper storeys were broader, because the minds of the faithful constrain themselves with respect to temporal things and expand themselves toward heavenly things. Likewise, the Temple shown to Ezekiel is said to have been broader above. He who teaches whom the name of the Temple signifies says: “Do you not know that you are the Temple of God?” And if this saying seems sweet, what follows will sting sharply: “If anyone violates the Temple of God, God will destroy him.”

24. Concerning the Temple mentioned above, the prophet is also recorded to have heard: “But you, son of man, show the Temple to the house of Israel, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities.” For sinners are beneficially ashamed when the lives of the righteous are proposed to them as an example. In this mirror they recognize their own stains; they wash them away by tears and wipe them clean by the lamentations of penitence. This Temple is elegantly said to have been broader above because, as we have said, the hearts of the righteous are narrowed in lower things and enlarged in higher things. For the hearts of the good are very like a censer, which, though closed below, is open above. In accordance with this likeness, devout minds close themselves to earthly things and open themselves to heavenly things. For this reason the Angel is read in the Apocalypse to have held a censer [Col. 0416D] full of the prayers of the saints. Angels are guardians of those hearts from which the smoke of prayers rises—prayers by whose fragrance the Lord is delighted and by whose sweetness He is appeased.

25. Let us now show from the testimonies of Scripture how perfect justice, when it has been brought to completion, constrains itself; and how that which is enlarged below is narrowed above. Noah’s ark expressly prefigured this: that is, it was finished above in one cubit. What is more fittingly figured by Noah’s ark than the Church, which, with the bosom of its mind expanded, receives the breath of the Holy Spirit? Moved by this breath, it cuts through the waves of the world and hastens with all the intention of its heart toward the harbour of life. It is enlarged below and narrowed above because, though it had breadth and length below, after it has spread itself out in the exercise of virtue, when it considers heavenly recompense, it despises its works and judges them as small; it compresses itself beneath the guard of humility and restrains with the foot of virtue the harmful swelling. The Saviour shows that these things must be carefully done, when He says to His disciples: “When you have done all things well, always say: We are unprofitable servants.” He who does all things well enlarges himself in good works. But he who afterwards counts himself an unprofitable servant narrows himself through the moderation of humility. Hence again the Bridegroom says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Your belly is like a heap of wheat, surrounded by lilies.”

26. The mind is often signified by the name “belly,” because thoughts are digested in the mind as food is digested in the belly. Thus it is said through the prophet: “My belly aches; my belly aches.” What pain he was lamenting he immediately made clear when he added: “The feelings of my heart are troubled.” Therefore the mental distress of the lamenting prophet was the pain of his belly. Hence also it is written of the ungodly: “His womb prepares deceits.” But it is clear that the bodily womb cannot prepare deceits; rather, the womb that prepares deceits is the mind that devises schemes of fraud. Thus the belly of the bride is significantly compared with a heap of wheat, which, though broad below, is narrow above. For the faithful soul first spreads itself out in the exercise of good works, then, after contemplation of heavenly things, returns into itself and, through humility, as we have said, constrains itself.

27. It is rightly compared with a heap of wheat because, once the chaff of vanity has been shaken out, it gathers and keeps the treasure of sacred meditation like grains of wheat in the granary of conscience. This heap is said to be surrounded by lilies because the faithful soul is encircled on every side by the purity of chastity. It is said to be surrounded not merely by a lily but by lilies because true chastity has a twofold effect: it embraces both heart and body. Hence it is figured in the Law by twisted fine linen and two turtledoves. What has been said agrees with Wisdom’s statement concerning herself: “I am like a cypress on Mount Zion.” This saying is understood both of the head and of the members, so that the voice of head and members is one. The cypress has a most beautiful crown of foliage, whose summit rises into this crown. Therefore the righteous man is like a cypress, because his beautiful crown is a fair manner of life. He is said to be like a cypress on Mount Zion because, established upon the summit of contemplation, he restrains himself by consideration of heavenly things; and, gathering himself into the inward bosom of his mind, he constrains himself beneath the guard of humility.

28. Ordinary experience offers a clear illustration of this. A domestic bird accustomed to catching other birds crouches down when it sees the prey which it eagerly desires and toward which it knows itself to be directing its course. Who, then, should wonder if the mind compresses itself in humility when it considers the prey of blessedness toward which it longs eagerly to aspire? Therefore, by bowls and the horns of the altar, as we have said, spiritual men are signified: warriors in the divine contest, equipped with the ornaments of virtues as with heavenly armour. Bowls (*phialae*) are said to derive from Greek *phialui*, meaning “glass,” because glass vessels are properly called *phialae*. Hence the prophet says of those who drink luxuriously: “Drinking wine in bowls.” For luxury is not content that the flavour of wine pleases the taste unless its colour also delights the sight. Therefore Solomon, wishing to restrain this luxury, says in Proverbs: “Do not look upon wine when it grows yellow, and when its colour shines in the glass.” He then shows the danger attached to it: “It enters smoothly, and in the end it will bite like a serpent and spread poisons like a basilisk.” The basilisk infects flying birds, whereas the serpent seeks out and inhabits hiding places. Wine is therefore aptly compared both with the serpent and with the basilisk: with the serpent, because it arouses lust, whose shame seeks concealment; with the basilisk, because wine taken immoderately sometimes enfeebles great men, who could fly toward heavenly things upon the two wings of abundance and power, if they directed their course rightly.

29. Although *phialae* are called glass vessels, the bowls which the Lord commanded to be prepared in the Tabernacle were golden. This fittingly applies to righteous men: they should be like glass, yet in truth golden; that is, apparently weak, yet truly strong. He wished the righteous to be such when, as was said above, He told His disciples: “When you have done all things well, always say: We are unprofitable servants.” Certainly, he is strong who does all things well; but he judges himself weak who calls himself an unprofitable servant. Was not he a golden vessel who laboured more than all others, yet presented himself as a glass vessel because he did not judge himself worthy even of the name of apostle? In this respect righteous men should resemble glass: they should admit the ray of the sun and the light of brightness, but exclude the blast of the wind; that is, receive grace but resist harmful temptation. Bowls are also regarded as vessels for libation-offerings. Thus spiritual men are filled as bowls if they overflow abundantly with the offerings of sacred thoughts and devout intentions together with zeal for good works. Yet it should be known that liquid offerings were called libations. The offerings of the righteous ought likewise to be liquid. This indeed happens if the soul is melted by the ardour of devotion. Hence the Psalmist says: “I pour out my prayer in Your sight.” Prayer can be poured out if it is tearful, but it is by no means poured out if it has been frozen by hardness of heart. They were also called libations because the ministers tested them by tasting, to see whether they were fit for offering. Thus those who minister to the Lord should examine their thoughts and intentions as if by tasting them, lest anything occur in them that ought to displease the Lord.

30. Holy men are also filled as the horns of the altar. The blood of the victim was placed upon the horns of the altar, and hence they are said to be filled by it. Those who celebrate these solemn rites are filled, as it were, by the sprinkling of blood upon the altar’s horns, because, in venerating the martyr, they are imbued with the memory of his passion. The memory of the martyr imbues the minds of those whose manner of life displays within itself the form of his fortitude. For they imitate the martyr who, although they have not been granted to suffer for Christ, nevertheless despise all perishing things for love of Him, afflict the flesh, and vigorously gird themselves to obtain heavenly rewards.

31. Therefore it especially befits us, who rejoice in the special protection of the martyr, to afflict ourselves particularly in his service, Scripture saying: “He who moves stones will be afflicted by them.” The following matters will show that martyrs are signified by the name “stones.” Thus those move stones who devote the services of their devotion to the translation of martyrs: namely, those who raise their relics from lowly places in order to place them more highly and more solemnly with due veneration. We have therefore moved a precious stone, when we took care to render such service as we could for the translation of the martyr. Therefore, in order that the scriptural saying set above may be fulfilled in us, let us, in veneration of him who offered himself as a sacrifice for the Lord, offer our flesh to the Lord as a living sacrifice, cutting away from ourselves harmful desires and wicked longings. Thus, by the Lord’s generosity, let us fulfil the mystery of our service, so that the members may answer to the Head according to their measure and strive, insofar as they can, to imitate the Father of the Son.

32. Concerning righteous men, the prophetic word which we have undertaken to expound adds: “He saved them as the flock of His people.” The Lord chooses that people for salvation which, though strong in reason, nevertheless conforms itself to a flock by a certain likeness. For it is fitting that the faithful who serve the Lord should be a people through wisdom and discernment, and a flock through gentleness and simplicity. Hence the Psalmist says: “We are Your people and the sheep of Your pasture.” They are both people and sheep who are prudent as human beings and simple as sheep. Again the Psalmist says: “You who lead Joseph like a sheep.” The righteous man is led by straight paths to heavenly things as he advances in good works like Joseph; for Joseph means “increase.” Yet, like a sheep, he abandons neither simplicity nor gentleness. Holy men dedicated to their Creator are led in this manner to their homeland, because they diligently pursue progress and simply and humbly submit to their shepherd. Thus the tower of the flock, of which Scripture speaks, aptly signifies the excellence of religious life. By the flock humility is signified; by the tower, height. What, then, is the tower of the flock but lofty humility or humble height? The religious state observes both, for there is loftiness in labouring activity and humility in one’s estimate of that labour. Hence Balaam, seeing the camps of the children of Israel, said: “How beautiful are your tabernacles, Jacob, and your tents, Israel, like wooded valleys!” The ranks of religious life are signified by the camps of the children of Israel, and are excellently compared with wooded valleys, because a valley is low and a grove is high. What, then, is a wooded valley but lowly loftiness or exalted humility? Religious persons preserve this pattern of life well, because they are humble in their hearts and outstanding in their works.

33. The prophetic saying continues: “The Lord their God saved them, because holy stones shall be lifted up over His land.” Thus the lifting up of holy stones over the land brings about the salvation of the faithful. That holy martyrs are designated by the name “stones”—because they were firm in constancy, strong in justice, and hard against torments—is attested by him who says: “Whom the rains of the mountains water, and, having no covering, embrace stones.” The rains of the mountains water those whom men exalted both in knowledge and life instruct by words and examples alike. Those lack a covering who do not possess the adornments of good works. For works of virtue are like garments by which the soul is fittingly adorned and the foulness of shameful actions is covered, lest it be seen by the proud Judge. Hence it is written: “Blessed is he who keeps his garments, lest he walk naked”; and the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says: “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a house not made with hands in heaven.” And a little later he adds: “Provided that we are found clothed and not naked.” For the clothed person is led to the kingdom, but the naked is cast out to torments. Again it is written: “Are not garments warm when the earth has been breathed upon by the south wind?” The earth is breathed upon by the south wind when it is filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “Rise, north wind; come, south wind; breathe upon my garden, and its spices shall flow.” The quiet of the cloister may most properly be called the Lord’s garden: there heavenly doctrine is planted, holy conduct is propagated, and the shrubs of vices are cut down. The Lord must therefore be asked to exclude the breath of the north wind from His garden, so that the breath of the south wind may freely come to it. For cloistered persons must pray that the Lord may repel the enemy’s snares from them and cause the Holy Spirit to rest upon them. The breath of the south wind causes spices to flow; that is, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, the fragrant works of cloistered persons are carried out to those outside as the reward of praiseworthy reputation, so that the examples of the righteous may shame the wicked and convert them. Therefore the Holy Spirit is the south wind, and His inspiration is the breath of the south wind. Good works, as we have said, are signified by garments. The breath of the south wind therefore makes garments warm, because heavenly inspiration, illuminating and inflaming the heart, makes works of virtue fervent with devotion; for light and warmth come from the south. Thus those whom the rains of the mountains water, and who, having no covering, embrace stones, are sinners weighed down by the burden of their sins: having been instructed by saving doctrines or compelled by their own calamity, they venerate martyrs’ relics so that their nakedness may be covered through the intercession of the saints.

34. Again it is written concerning these stones: “The eagle dwells on precipitous rocks.” By the eagle is understood the contemplative man, who fixes the sight of his mind upon the sun of justice and, penetrating lofty things in flight, directs his attention to the consideration of heavenly things. “A precipice,” as blessed Gregory says, “is that of which one part has fallen and one part remains.” Martyrs are therefore rightly compared with precipitous rocks: their bodies have fallen through martyrdom, but their spirits rest in heaven; and, as is sung of holy men, “they gave their bodies back to earth and bore blessed souls to heaven.” Thus the eagle dwells on precipitous rocks because contemplatives appointed to the service of martyrs rest in their remembrance and devote themselves wholly to their veneration and imitation. Otherwise the eagle does not dwell upon rocks unless those who serve the martyrs strive to render the duty of their service both in mind and body. He does not dwell upon a rock who chants psalms or sings before a martyr while his mind wanders outward amid the vanities of the world.

35. Therefore, as we have shown, the holy stones are the martyrs of Jesus Christ. Holy stones are lifted up over the land when martyrs’ relics are translated from their tombs. It should be noted, however, that holy stones are not merely said to be lifted up over His land because the relics of the saints are raised not only upward, but their elevation is reverently performed in the Church, which is called the Lord’s land. The prophetic discourse which we have pursued shows that God’s people receive salvation from this. Let us therefore also hope that the translation of our martyr, which we celebrate solemnly, will obtain for us in the present forgiveness of sins and, after the course of this life, everlasting salvation to be received from the Lord. Certain signs which God’s mercy showed you when the translation took place greatly strengthened this hope. For those who translated the martyr had provided that he should be translated on Tuesday, because he suffered on Tuesday, so that a day such as had rendered service to his passion might serve his glory. But we testify in Christ that, beyond human planning, God’s grace so arranged it that, in the fiftieth year after his passion, his venerable body received the glory of translation. What, then, is intimated to us by this event? The force of the number fifty points us to remission, as every reader of Holy Scripture knows. Therefore, by willing to be translated in the fiftieth year, he gave us sure hope that, unless the fault lies with us, he will obtain for us the grace of remission.

36. Another thing happened which human deliberation had not in any way arranged. The year of the translation was a leap year, in which the number of days is full and complete; from this event we may hope that the intercession of the martyr will bring our present days to a good completion and lead us to the fullness of days in the life to come.

37. There also occurred that memorable event which, it is believed, took place through the Lord’s providence for the martyr’s glory. The martyr was translated from the earth on the day on which King Henry, in whose time he suffered, was buried in the earth, so that what is read in Scripture might thus be fulfilled: “A falling mountain crumbles away, and a rock is moved from its place.” Mountains are those which rise above the earth in the fullness of their height and lift their summits on high. Mountains, then, are kings and princes who possess dominion over lands and rise above others in the eminence of their power. Thus a great mountain fell when the earth’s bosom received the dead king. As the mountain crumbled away, a rock was moved from its place: when the king’s body was laid in the earth, the martyr’s body was honourably raised. The martyr also wrought various miracles at the time of the translation, through which he showed that his favour was present with those carrying out and venerating the translation.

38. To declare, through the merits of the translation, the glory of the body of most blessed Thomas, let us recall the Gospel parable: “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, nor under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light.” Heaven and earth testify that the blessed martyr whose solemnities we celebrate was a lamp burning and shining: burning, I say, in the example of holiness; shining in saving teaching. The Lord lit this lamp when He raised His elect to the summit of exceptional prelacy. He also trimmed this lamp when He permitted His martyr to be afflicted by long exile, insults, losses, and countless injuries. For that immense mass of tribulations was like the snuffer of this lamp, because the flame of this furnace consumed whatever the blessed man had to be purified. The Lord extinguished this lamp when He perfected His servant through martyrdom. But while He extinguished it bodily, He lit it more brightly spiritually, because after his death He illustrated the title of his holiness by frequent testimonies of miracles. Therefore the Lord did not hide His lamp, because He manifested His martyr’s glory by proof of miracles. For some time, however, this lamp lay hidden under a bushel; but the Lord revealed it at a fitting time. Since a measure is called a *modius* (“bushel”), a tomb can rightly be signified by the bushel, for it measures itself to the dead person and conforms itself to the body being buried. And as grain for distribution to the needy is measured by a bushel, so divine bounty often proceeds from the martyr’s tomb for the sick. Thus the lamp lay hidden beneath the bushel as long as the martyr rested in the tomb. But now the Lord has drawn it out from its hiding-place and exalted it above the lampstand, because He has reverently taken the martyr’s relics from the tomb and placed them on high in a precious shrine set apart for the martyr’s use. For what could I more properly call the martyr’s chest than a lampstand of light, since it presents to those who behold it that outstanding light which illuminates those who come to it both in heart and body? Therefore, dearest brethren, let us approach this lamp with all our minds and present to it the stains of our lives, because, as the Apostle says: “All things that are reproved are made manifest by the light.” If, then, we approach the brightness of this light, by its benefit we shall recognize the evil in ourselves which we were previously unable to see. Let us recall what is written in the Gospel: “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved.” Yet let us flee this example and imitate what follows: “But he who does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, because they have been done in God.”

39. Again, to indicate more fully the fruit and glory of the translation, let us consider that testimony of Scripture: “A holy man remains in wisdom like the sun; a fool changes like the moon.” Solomon, describing the fool in Proverbs, says: “The fool transgresses and is confident.” For he is a fool who breaks the commandments and yet flatters himself with impunity. But, according to Gospel truth, he is especially a fool who builds his house on sand. Sand is temporal abundance, because it is barren and heavy. It is barren, as Solomon says: “He who loves riches shall not receive fruit from them.” It is heavy, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Those who wish to become rich fall into many useless and harmful desires, which plunge a man into ruin and destruction.” Hence Solomon also says: “I saw all things that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit.” Vanity indicates barrenness, affliction of spirit heaviness. Thus the fool builds his house upon sand because the lover of earthly things fixes his mind in temporal desires. But he changes like the moon. Since worldly mutability is signified by the moon, the fool is aptly said to change like the moon: prosperity exalts him and adversity breaks him. The truly holy man remains in wisdom like the sun. It is fitting that all who serve the Lord should be holy. Thus Moses was told: “Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel, and say to them: Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy.” Yet those especially are holy who are devoted to the contemplation of heavenly things. “For holy,” as Bede says, “is called in Greek ἅγιος (*hagios*), which means ‘outside the earth.’” Therefore saints are those who, separated from temporal things, dwell in heavenly ones. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Israel is holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of His harvest.” As the interpretation of the name indicates, Israel is one who beholds higher things and contemplates heavenly things. Those who are intent upon heavenly things are the firstfruits of the harvest in the Lord’s field, because they desire higher things more fervently the more often they feed themselves by contemplating them. The holy man is like the sun: warm and fervent in spirit, shining in example. The holy man remains in wisdom; the foolish man soon abandons it, if he ever takes it up. Hence it is written: “Wisdom is exceedingly harsh to unlearned men, and the senseless man will not remain in her.” Conversely, it is said to such a man: “Approach her with all your soul, and with all your strength keep her ways. Seek her, and she will be revealed to you; and, having taken hold of her, do not forsake her.” The Lord Himself plainly showed that the blessed martyr was a holy man. Having weaned him from the sweetness of temporal things through the bitterness of afflictions, the Lord invited him to the delights of His table and disclosed to him the blessedness toward which he ought to aspire. He remained in wisdom because, while he lived, he faithfully served God and at the last gave his life for Him. He was like the sun, because through the rays of his blood he illumined the holy Church.

40. Therefore we solemnly venerate the elevation of this sun when we celebrate with sincere minds the translation of this martyr. Let the congregation of his servants carefully heed what is written: “The sun was raised up, and the moon stood in its order.” This congregation is the moon, drawing its light from the sun and receiving from the martyr’s example the pattern of life. Let the moon therefore stand in its order because the sun has been raised up; that is, let those who serve the martyr not decline from the rule of their order. Rather, let them behold their patron set on high before their eyes and confidently await his aid in good works. How the height of the sun contributes to the observance of order may be gathered from what follows. For the sun raised on high supplies an abundance of light and warmth. Let us therefore hope that our sun, lifted from the tomb, will grant his servants light, which will drive from them the darkness of harmful ignorance, and will also confer warmth, which will kindle their minds in the love of divine worship. The abundance of light will also ensure that decency is preserved, since it would reveal disgrace if it occurred; therefore it allows nothing dishonourable. The abundance of warmth, however, causes all things to be done according to order. In these two things consists the sum of religious life: that among those who submit their necks to religion, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, all things may be done honourably and according to order. Again, the sun raised on high draws up the drops of the sea. Hence the Sun of Justice says of Himself: “If I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself.” He speaks of Himself as a sun illuminating the world: “When I have been lifted up over the earth, I shall draw to myself innumerable drops of the sea.” Thus the glory of the translation benefits righteous men, because the elevation of the sun keeps the moon in its order. It also benefits the sinners of this world, because when the sun has been raised it will draw the drops of salt water, to which sinners are most aptly compared, both because of the brevity and saltness of mortal life and because of the bitterness of sins.

## XIV. TREATISE ON THE PROMISE OF BLESSED THOMAS THE MARTYR, NAMELY

[Col. 0425]

That there would succeed him one who would recompense the Church of Pontigny for the liberality bestowed upon him during his exile.

[Col. 0425A] 1. Those who ascribe government of this kind to God judge rightly, because not even a leaf carried away by the wind exceeds His power; nor has the wind itself, which is brought forth from His treasuries, power to blow contrary to His command. Although human beings, being animal in nature, wonder at certain works in this world as though they were corruptibly flowing and rushing on without the guiding mastery of a governor and contrary to the order of rectitude, so that they may cry out with the prophet: “Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why is it well with those who act perversely?” nevertheless, it must by no means be stubbornly asserted that anything happens in this world except under God’s governance or, at times, His permission. For since He Himself is the first and principal cause, influencing all caused things in a most orderly and serene flow, it is certain that those things which receive their cause from Him are most rightly ordered toward a good end.

2. But evils are without cause and have neither a right order nor an end. To the extent that they fall away from the good, they tend toward nothingness; and there is in them nothing but the privation of good, which places nothing in a thing—just as lameness in a human being or horse adds nothing except the privation of walking properly. Although a reason cannot be given for everything as to why this or that occurs, there nevertheless remains with God a certain accounting for the cause of all things: hidden indeed from us, but manifest to Him who dwells in inaccessible light. Hence sacred interpreters and teachers have endeavoured, through mystical expositions and allegorical meanings, to provide plausible explanations of remarkable things. Their examples are innumerable; and, if necessary, many may be understood from one example that has been given. Let us therefore set forth one example of that greatest teacher, blessed Gregory, and let it be the foundation of the whole matter that follows. For in his exposition of the Gospel of blessed John, where the Lord’s resurrection is discussed, he says as follows: “When the disciples, struck with consternation, were told that the Lord had been taken from the tomb, then,” he says, “two were running together, and the other disciple ran ahead faster than Peter.” “What,” says blessed Gregory, “what, brothers, does this running signify?” By his question he wished to draw forth a great argument for some signification.

To this question I wish to add something that must not be neglected in our own time. Although human carelessness allows many things to pass by through neglect, things to which it ought to have given the increase of desired success, we have nevertheless taken pains faithfully to record, insofar as we have learned them, matters worthy of report, lest they be erased from memory. It is indeed fitting to recall to honoured memory that blessed Thomas, Archbishop and Primate of Canterbury, choosing exile, preferred to live in exile rather than to enslave the Church of Canterbury over which he presided. Having departed from England, he came to Pontigny; and there, having endured, as is said, the conditions of exile for six years, he was admonished in a vision while prostrate in contemplation before the altar of blessed Stephen to return to England, so that he might receive, as the reward of his labour, the crown of eternal blessedness. Made more joyful by this vision, the holy bishop—soon afterwards to become a martyr—hastened more swiftly toward the crown of victory promised him. The brothers of that monastery followed him in sorrowful, indeed almost funereal, countenances and tearfully begged him not to abandon them, not to deprive them of the consolation of so great a hope, not to leave them as orphans; but either to remain among them altogether or, if this must be, to return as swiftly as possible. To this the devout Father gave them a brief answer: “It must be so, and one must not resist the divine commands.” But, he said, they should know that some one of his successors would sufficiently repay the grave expenses and generous outlays which the monastery had supplied during his need. The brothers of that monastery, in their great simplicity, were then scarcely able to understand this; but the event that followed proved it, as is said of the disciples of Jesus Christ: “His disciples did not at first understand these things; but after He had risen from the dead, then they understood, and these things were done to Him.” Thus the brothers of the monastery of Pontigny most truly did not understand what blessed Thomas meant by these words; but afterwards they understood that he had spoken of these matters, as will appear in what follows. For after he had suffered, been crowned with martyrdom, and been shown by resplendent miracles to have pursued a just cause, while one successor after another had been installed, that saying uttered by the martyr had already passed from memory, though it had been reserved for its fitting time.

3. For after several successors of the said martyr, that great and celebrated doctor of the Church, namely Lord Stephen of Langton, cardinal of the Roman Church, was at last installed in the Church of Canterbury through the providence of the Apostolic See. [Col. 0426D] Having received the pallium and letters necessary for his purpose, and having first sent messengers into England, he hastened to follow. But when he came into the regions of France, he received from the messengers who returned to him the answer that [Col. 0427A] the king of England refused to admit him because he had resolved to appoint another. Although the king had often been admonished on this matter by letters and legates of the Apostolic See, he nevertheless persisted, hardened in his purpose. Thus the aforesaid Archbishop Stephen came to the monastery of Pontigny and, like the blessed martyr Thomas, awaited in exile for six years the outcome of his cause.

For the king’s anger became so powerful that all England was placed under ecclesiastical interdict on that account. Indeed, as the storm of opposition grew stronger, several English bishops were obliged, out of devotion and obedience, to withdraw from the kingdom and join their archbishop. As evidence of this, one of them—the bishop of Worcester—was subsequently buried at Pontigny. [Col. 0427B] The archbishop feared that the monastery would be burdened by the presence of so many persons; but the brethren rejoiced that they had been found worthy to receive so many and such great men for so noble a cause.

After the stormy tempest had subsided following the clouds, the aforesaid prelate was summoned back to England with due honour. This brought joy to him and to his people, but for himself alone it became an occasion of great anxiety and distress. The prudent man considered how to repay the lavish expenses incurred for himself and his company; but at that time he neither possessed the means of repayment nor easily found any way of obtaining them. How sorrowfully, then, he departed on this account! Yet afterward he redeemed that sorrow by a noble recompense. For after attaining the fullness of his honour, [Col. 0427C] he assigned to the monastery of Pontigny, in perpetuity, an annual revenue of fifty marks.

Then it was believed that the prophecy of blessed Thomas, explained above, had been fulfilled: that some successor after him would be appointed who would make satisfaction for them both. But although this opinion endured for some time, and many thought that the prior promise had then been wholly discharged, so that no one would assert the contrary, nevertheless we see that it was fulfilled otherwise.

4. For after that archbishop had died and been buried in peace at Canterbury, blessed Edmund, after some time, received the archiepiscopal chair—not willingly, but reluctantly. He chose to undertake the chair of Canterbury [Col. 0427D] not through human ambition, but, as we believe, through divine dispensation. Once he had undertaken it, what lay hidden in his breast came forth afterward more clearly in the harvest. For he was like a lamp placed beneath a bushel; but after it was set upon a lampstand, it was then certainly revealed to those who walk confidently in the house of God.

For in his days he pleased God and was found righteous; and, through zeal for justice, he neither feared the king nor the great men of the kingdom, nor did he heed even those of his own household whom the king had enticed with unrestrained persuasions, seeking to gain time. But girded with mighty strength, he set himself as a wall for the house of the Lord, preferring, like his predecessors, to suffer exile for the people of God rather than to enjoy the pleasure of temporal sin in his own country. [Col. 0428A] He therefore withdrew from England and entered the monastery of Pontigny as though enclosed by an impregnable wall; and, hidden from the turmoil of men in the shelter of the Lord’s countenance, he rested as it were in the tabernacle of the Lord. But from this repose the Lord chose to summon His servant into the inward sweetness of the unending state of eternal rest.

5. Thus he died at a good age, with a secure mind, certain hope, a blessed consummation, choosing the place of his burial where he and his predecessors had formerly at times dwelt. Yet, because he had never pursued gold nor placed hope in treasures of money, he had nothing with which to repay the monastery of Pontigny for all that it had bestowed upon him. Still, lest he seem ungrateful, he did what he could, and [Col. 0428B] added an annual income of ten marks to the earlier pension assigned by Lord Stephen.

Thus it was again believed that what we recalled above as promised by blessed Thomas had been fulfilled. But surely the goodness of God knows how to provide more generously than human weakness dares to hope. For not without reason did the Lord say: “Whoever leaves house or brothers for my sake shall receive a hundredfold in the present, and eternal life in the future.” So kind and generous is our householder that He not only rewards those who love Him in the future, but also grants rewards in the present to those who use His gifts well. Therefore, what was lacking to His beloved during life, He Himself—most beloved and loving—supplied at the death of His lover.

For, as miracles shine forth, the sick come to his vigil and are healed; [Col. 0428C] offerings are brought; and things which had been intended for worldly display in gold and precious stones are dedicated at the tomb of the holy bishop. There you might see royal brooches gleaming, golden head-ornaments flashing, necklaces set with most precious gems somehow sparkling, rings adorned with various precious stones radiating light, and representations of various figures as though worshipping the saint of the Lord. You might also see offerings of people of both sexes and of the common crowd, like small coins—perhaps very great in God’s sight—being brought together into the Lord’s treasury.

And thus, certainly and without any doubt, we see today, as it were eye to eye, fulfilled what was once foreshadowed in the prophetic utterance of blessed Thomas the martyr. For we believe that [Col. 0428D] what was lavishly expended upon the holy bishops has been restored twofold or fourfold. This may be one reason, and no small one, why it was by divine providence that blessed Father Edmund gave himself, as it were, as a hostage for himself and for his predecessors; and, by paying the debt of charity or hospitality—though legally not owed—generously freed both himself and them. It should be thought that the brethren of his house receive this debt, converting everything owed by donors, as though into a gift, to adorn the shrine of the blessed Father himself.

6. Turn now somewhat aside, reader, if you are willing to be content with a simple discourse, and say with blessed Gregory, applying his words to your own understanding: “What, brothers, does this course signify? Do you believe that it happened by chance [Col. 0429A] that that chosen man of the Lord, blessed Thomas, the greatest defender of ecclesiastical law, fled from England to lodge himself in the monastery of Pontigny, and there, spending six years and sojourning elsewhere, served as a soldier of the Lord; and at last, returning, completed his course by a blessed martyrdom? Is it a matter of no significance that his successor, that great Cardinal Stephen, made archbishop, before entering England, having almost similarly taken up her cause for liberty, followed in the footsteps of his predecessor, lived there for so many years, and at last, recalled to his own country, was buried in peace at Canterbury?

“Do we believe it devoid of the mystery of charity that the successor of such great men—though not their inferior—the blessed Father Edmund, who conducted himself praiseworthily in his own country, was raised, absent and unaware, to the summit of the metropolitan see, and at last, clothed in the breastplate of righteousness, exiled for righteousness’ sake, dwelt for some time in the aforesaid monastery in the accustomed works of holy life, was buried there, and afterward transferred to a place fitting for his honour? [Col. 0429B] Or should all this, concerning three such eminent men—namely patriarchs or primates, the same in substance but different in name—be ascribed to chance or fortune rather than to enduring divine disposition?

“Did He who said concerning two sparrows bought for a farthing that not one of them falls to the ground without our Father, whose care extends to all things, will that these events occur for nothing? Does He take greater care of two sparrows than of three bishops? Of these, the first, leaving his own borders, returned after exile and was consummated in martyrdom. The second endured exile before entering his country, and finally, established in his own see, died and was buried there as well. The third, enthroned in peace but exiled amid an age without peace, sought in exile the peace of the heart and found it, and passed from it to the peace of eternity.

“There is, therefore, much conformity in all three, and also a distinct diversity among them. It is permissible to consider, with some rational support, what this signifies, and to set down the probable result of that reflection with a pen, however humble. Let whoever wishes to criticize what has been said have leave either to strike it out or to reshape the matter itself into a better form and dress.”

[Col. 0429D] 7. The holy Apostle, doctor of the Gentiles, setting the Fathers of the Old Testament in a catalogue under a certain summary, naming some individually and designating others by their works of righteousness, finally concludes and says that such men conquered kingdoms through faith. For faith received testimony from works—more from the working work than from the work accomplished. Thus he concludes at the end: “And all these were approved by testimony.”

The Fathers of the New Testament likewise were proved by the testimony of faith, because they became witnesses unto death. Hence in praise of the Innocents it is said that, though not speaking, they bore testimony to the Lord Jesus Christ; and therefore, from the Greek word meaning “witness,” they were called *martyr* or *martyrs*. It may therefore reasonably be asked how blessed Thomas can properly be called a martyr, [Col. 0430A] since, seemingly, he did not receive martyrdom for the faith.

For it is established that the king of England under whom he suffered, and likewise those by whom he suffered, were Christians and believers—at least with unformed faith. Nor was the said bishop being compelled to defend any article of faith or to put incense upon the altars of idols. Rather, there was a dispute between king and bishop concerning certain rights, which the one judged an injustice and the other justice. Such a dispute could both arise and be settled without injury to either man’s faith.

But to this a sufficient answer is that there is faith in the articles, faith in the sacraments, and faith in Catholic dignity and ecclesiastical liberty. For faith in the articles expressed in the creeds, saints stood in the contest against pagan rulers. For faith in the sacraments and the power of the keys, doctors of the Church stood against heretics and schismatics who had strayed from the faith. For faith in ecclesiastical liberty, strong prelates of churches have fought, and still fight today, against rulers and tyrants who are Christian in name only. [Col. 0430B]

In this last battle blessed Thomas, Lord Stephen, and Saint Edmund were made strong in war; and by their testimony they proved that one who defends ecclesiastical liberty is no less a witness than one who champions the Christianity of articulated faith. Otherwise the Lord would not reproach the wicked rulers of churches through Ezekiel: “You did not set yourselves as a wall for the house of the Lord, that you might stand in battle against those coming up from the opposite side.”

For the Lord fortified His vicar, namely blessed Peter, with great power: when He gave him the power of the keys, that is, of binding and loosing, He immediately added the promise that the gates of hell would by no means prevail against this power of authority. By “the gates of hell” He intended heresies and tyrannical powers.

8. Therefore, according to the precept of the divine law which says, “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand,” it is evident that through these three eminent witnesses the cause and defense of ecclesiastical liberty were most fully proved. As a demonstrative sign of that proof, reason required that at least two of the three should remain in the Church of Canterbury, whose cause was at issue, as a monument of victory: two witnesses of lawful proof, [Col. 0430D] not only living witnesses, but their dead bodies as well. They were to be like a triumphal inscription, urging their suffragans to like deeds and to hope for victory in the struggle.

It was not necessary that the third be added, since by divine dispensation he was usefully reserved elsewhere to enlarge the renown of ecclesiastical honour. It does not prejudice the Church of Canterbury that the body of blessed Father Edmund does not rest there with the others; for it loses nothing thereby, nor is his honour diminished. Rather, to one who considers the matter well, it is certain that both the person and the place gain very great honour from it.

His memorial remains, never to be forsaken through the ages: that such a man was Archbishop of Canterbury, that he was patron and defender of that see on earth, and that, beyond doubt, [Col. 0431A] he is in heaven a devout intercessor for those who have believed what must be believed. But suppose that his body had been buried in England: what honour and favour would Gaul then possess, for so many benefits received from such great fathers and successive exiles? England would indeed then be joyful; but the land of the French, in which such splendid miracles have shone, would erase so celebrated a memory after a short span of time.

But now, by divine dispensation, as we believe, better provision has been made: one kingdom rejoices that it gave birth to so devout a servant of God and possessed so great a patron; the other kingdom likewise rejoices that such a heavenly gift has been bestowed upon it—namely, that it retains the treasure, the vessel, I mean, of his body, more precious than every precious stone.

9. There is another memorable and noteworthy point in this matter. His predecessors, blessed Thomas and Lord Stephen, were solemnly recalled to their church. Whether this was done sincerely or deceitfully, we who do not know the facts cannot say; the outcome of the matter showed it better. Saint Edmund, confessor of Christ the Lord, was not recalled with any due solemnity. How, then, could he have come back unwillingly—or rather shamelessly—when he was conspicuous in the judgment of men and in Christian reality for chastity both of mind and body? [Col. 0431B]

He therefore did what he ought, and did not thrust himself forward of his own accord, lest he give occasion for shamelessness; rather, he withdrew himself from the place and country of those who, in order willingly to draw him back for a time, ought to have gone into exile with him outside their country, and after his death should endure the exile which, against their will, they had wished to endure with him during his life.

God therefore provided better [Col. 0431C] that he should be brought to his end outside his country, where his enemies were not granted broad licence to slander or insult him. Such licence would easily have smothered the life and miracles of that Father, had his body been present in his fatherland. Thus provision was made that matter for their detraction should be withdrawn from them, and that by this means the Lord should advance His saint to greater things. For his miraculous miracles are extant both in England, over which he presided, and in France, which he visited.

10. Another reason, and one that seems more abundant, now occurs as to why God’s dispensation thus arranged the separation of the said fathers. It is certain that in England the precious miracles of blessed Edmund, king and martyr, shine forth, by which that land is wonderfully adorned and God is proclaimed wonderful in His saint. [Col. 0431D] But if it be assumed and granted that the blessed confessor of Christ, Edmund, had obtained the place of his burial in that region, then, because of the identity of their names, the attribution of miracles would have been obscured, at least among the unlearned, and consequently perhaps diminished.

And although among saints there is no ground at all for dissension, but rather joy and exultation at another’s preeminence as at one’s own good, nevertheless the ignorant crowd would readily take up material for contention, and dispute about the miracles and merits of the saints beyond what reason required. The pretext for controversy was therefore removed, and miracles become more conspicuous when referred from one Edmund to the other.

And perhaps this is seen, as it were, in the Spirit: that Edmund, confessor of God, yielded the kingdom to King Edmund [Col. 0432A] with a certain reverence fitting for saints—the kingdom in which the latter had previously ruled piously and had anticipated him in time and place through the glory of martyrdom—so that, because the king was first in place and time, precedence might be yielded him in the honour of charity. It is likely that, had so devout a king lived in the time of blessed Bishop Edmund, the bishop would never have departed from that country.

Indeed, the bishop seems by the very deed to have honoured the martyr, since, as said above, he yielded the place to him. For he received from the martyr the name identical with his own, not by chance but according to the event of divine predestination. For, as is narrated more fully in his Life, when the mother of the holy bishop was carrying him in her womb and came to the tomb of the blessed martyr, she first felt the movements of life in the little child whom she bore. [Col. 0432B] The infant Edmund, not yet called Edmund, seems by his movement to have greeted the martyr and thereby obtained the grace of their shared name. Already living, he greeted the dead; and, dying, he gave place to the martyr living in heaven.

What else should be considered in this matter except that it should be believed to have been done by the Lord—through whom whatever occurs among the living or the dead is ordered, whether in a most hidden or in a manifest way, by the most just ordinance of divine providence?

11. Finally, we believe this should be added: the reason set out above required that blessed Thomas the martyr be buried in the Church of Canterbury. For his glory it was arranged that so great a doctor, cardinal, and primate should eventually succeed him, who would worthily and fittingly translate his holy body from the place of burial and leave written memorials concerning the translation itself. As is found today in the Church of Canterbury, [Col. 0432C] the aforesaid Lord Stephen, archbishop, transferred with his own hands the body of blessed Thomas the martyr from the crypt in which it had been placed immediately after his death to the upper place of the high altar. In the presence of the king of the English, almost all bishops and princes, and other great men of the realm, he placed it upon a golden, gem-studded, star-like throne. He described the manner and order of the translation in eloquent language, and afterward fell asleep in the Lord with him whom he had prudently described.

Blessed Bishop Edmund, however, deserved to have a similar burial—not in place, but wholly in manner—and also a similar translation, glorious with like signs. For he was buried in the church of Pontigny with glory and honour, as narrated above. But after it pleased the Lord to exalt His saint still more, so that a more distinguished place might receive him and the memory of his renown might be doubled, then, I say, it was provided by apostolic authority that, to commend the glory of this translation, the Cardinal Bishop of Albano, formerly Archbishop of Rouen, and not he alone but also the Bishop of Tusculum, likewise a cardinal, together with many archbishops and bishops, should come and most devoutly celebrate the rite of translation before the illustrious king of the French and, as it were, before the whole household of nobles of the kingdom of France. [Col. 0433A]

The similarity in these events is therefore exceedingly great: each translation was performed at the command of the supreme pontiff; in each case cardinals, archbishops, and bishops were present; kings and nobles of both kingdoms attended; and a multitude of faithful people participated with every reverence with which the act ought, needed, and could be performed. Thus it could be shown, as it were, by a finger through the event itself that God, not man, willed these distinguished acts to be undertaken for the honour of His saints and the awakening of the faithful’s devotion. He wills to be proclaimed glorious, wonderful, most praiseworthy, and most exalted in His saints—in all things, from all things, and above all things. To Him be honour and glory, dominion and power, through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

Here ends the treatise on the promise of blessed Thomas the martyr made to the men of Pontigny.

XV.

EXTRACT FROM BRITISH MUSEUM ROYAL MANUSCRIPT 13 E. VI.

[Col. 0433]

[Col. 0433B] Omitting everything which Thomas, of whom we have undertaken to write, did in his youth, in his archdeaconry, in his provostship, or in the office of chancellor, let us bring to a praiseworthy conclusion the long-protracted conflict between Henry, king of the English, son of the Empress Matilda, and the same Thomas, after his promotion to the archbishopric of Canterbury, briefly under certain headings marked with the sign *o-c*.

Thomas, made archbishop, resigned the king’s seal.

At the king’s request, the archbishop delayed transferring the archdeaconry of Canterbury.

Clarembald sought to receive consecration without profession, having the king as his supporter.

Roger, earl of Clare, refused to perform homage to the archbishop, with the king’s consent.

[Col. 0433C] William de Ros acknowledged the king, not the archbishop, as lord.

William, lord of Eynsford, expelled Laurence from the church; the archbishop excommunicated him without informing the king.

The king’s envoys did not obtain from the lord pope confirmation of the customs which they call ancestral.

The customs of the kingdom were confirmed by archbishops and bishops.

Philip de Broc, canon of Bedford, was expelled from the kingdom because of wrongdoing.

John Marshal was equipped with a case against the archbishop in the king’s court concerning a certain manor.

[Col. 0433D] The archbishop appealed against the bishops, and they appealed against him.

The archbishop, brought into a case before the legates William of Pavia and John of Naples, sought restitution of what had been taken away, but did not obtain it.

The king utterly refused and forswore giving the archbishop the kiss of peace.

After peace had been made, the archbishop, returning to England, found many armed men coming to meet him.

What happened concerning the person of the archbishop on Tuesday will be found below.

William, archbishop of Sens, addressed letters to the lord pope.

[Col. 0434B] The Church of Canterbury was reconciled by the bishops who gathered together.

Archbishop Thomas was canonized by Pope Alexander.

Whenever, in reading about the archbishops of Canterbury, you encounter Thomas, the first martyr in Norman England, do not pass over in silence his praiseworthy life, outstanding deeds, exile, passion, constancy in death, and, after his departure from this light to the heavenly homeland, the frequent marvels of miracles.

In 1172, when the clergy of the entire province of Canterbury had been generally summoned to London, in the presence of Henry, the king’s son, and the justiciars of the realm, Thomas, archdeacon of Canterbury and the king’s chancellor, was solemnly elected archbishop, no one objecting. [Col. 0434C] Henry, bishop of Winchester, recited the election, which had taken place without any opposition, at Westminster in the monks’ refectory, on the Wednesday before Pentecost. On the Saturday of Pentecost, the elect was ordained priest in the church of Canterbury by Walter, bishop of Rochester, vicar of the Church of Canterbury for ordinations and dedications. On the following Sunday he was consecrated by Henry, bishop of Winchester, acting in place of the bishop of London, because the see of London was then vacant, its bishop Richard II having departed this life. Walter, bishop of Rochester, maintained that this belonged to his own right, but did not prevail.

Envoys having been sent to the lord pope—whom William of Montpellier had honourably received as his liege lord when he was travelling into Gaul—it was quickly reported [Col. 0434D] that the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury had elected a pastor for themselves, who, with the unanimous concurrence of all votes, had already been consecrated by his own synod. This report was well received by the lord pope. Therefore, after the letters of the bishops, the letters of the prior and convent of Holy Trinity, and also the king’s letters had been read aloud, a petition having been made before the cardinals in consistory, ready and joyful assent was given according to the request of all.

Thus the pallium was entrusted to the envoys with the solemn gravity, delay, and ceremony customary in such matters. [Col. 0435A] Thomas the archbishop received it at the high altar in the see of Canterbury, wrapped in the customary conditions and bound by oath. But after he put on the garments bestowed, by the Lord’s ordering, upon the highest priests, he so changed his outward habit that he changed his mind as well. Since he did not approve of taking part in the cares of the court, he sought release from the court; devoting himself to prayer and attending to the affairs of his Church, he sent a messenger to the king in Normandy, resigning the chancellorship and surrendering the seal.

This struck deeply into the king’s heart, for he attributed to himself alone the cause of so sudden a resignation. For he had heard that the archbishop of Mainz under the king in Germany, and the archbishop of Cologne under the emperor in Italy, claimed for themselves the title of archchancellor. They do not think the offices of public affairs disturbed by mixed duties if they carry the pastoral staff in their right hand and devote themselves more earnestly to managing the necessities of kingdom or empire and to securing the peace of the Church, provided that the chancellor of the court carries at his left side the seal now of the king, now of the emperor—the official called the protonotary. [Col. 0435B]

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, coming to meet the king as he returned to England, was received with a kiss, but not with fullness of favour, as the face immediately turned away from all who had assembled plainly showed.

Thomas, raised from archdeacon of Canterbury to the archbishopric, at the king’s most insistent request delayed for a long time the transfer of the archdeaconry. At last he transferred it as the king requested; but he afterward perceived that the king’s favour, which had seemed temporarily withdrawn and then restored, had not been restored in full.

Clarembald, abbot-elect of Saint Augustine’s, sought to receive consecration from Archbishop Thomas, but in his own church, without a profession, and with every prospect of future subjection wholly removed. Since the king did not oppose such terms, but urged that the boundaries of ancient practice be maintained and promoted them by every means by which this could be done, he seemed more inclined to one side.

[Col. 0436B] Seek the following chapters below in this codex under the year 1173, etc., etc., etc.

[Col. 0435]

LETTERS OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.

[LETTERS OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.]

LETTER I. TO POPE ALEXANDER.

[Col. 0435C]

The letters of consolation which your Fatherhood has deigned to send us might indeed bring great relief to a moderately anxious mind; or, if at least our distress were fixed upon one matter alone, we might conceive some hope of drawing breath from them. But since evil grows stronger day by day and injuries multiply—not ours, but Christ’s, and indeed, because they are Christ’s, all the more ours—while storms follow one another like waves, we see shipwreck alone threatening us. Nor does any other counsel remain, except that, rousing Him as though asleep in the ship with all our strength, we say: “Lord, [Col. 0435D] save us; we are perishing.”

Indeed, wickedness has found a more favourable opportunity for malignity because it sees the condition of the holy Roman Church weakened. Thus it is plainly apparent that whatever flows down upon the head—whether good or evil, sweet or bitter—descends by the beard and leaves not even the hem of the garment untouched. [Col. 0436C] What Jesus Christ purchased with His blood is being taken from Him. Secular power stretches out its hand against His own allotted portion. So far has this gone that neither the decrees of the holy Fathers nor the statutes of the canons—whose very name among us is now hated—can even protect clerics, who until now had been exempted from this jurisdiction by a special privilege.

Because it would be long and tedious to recount or set down in writing what we suffer, we send to your Fatherhood Master Henry, your faithful and familiar servant and ours. We have placed in his mouth every detail, in due order, to be explained to you as he has seen and heard it. If it please you, believe him as if you heard us speaking in person. Know this, however: if it were possible, we would much rather visit you in our own person [Col. 0436D] than through another. We speak to you as to our Father and lord, and we ask that what we say be concealed with the utmost secrecy. Nothing is safe for us, since nearly everything said to us in private or in our ear is reported to the king.

Woe to us, who have been preserved for these times, in whose days these evils have come! We who in the former state possessed so great a liberty, with what harsh and miserable servitude do we now repay it? At least we would flee, lest we see the patrimony of the Crucified given over to plunder; but where should we flee, unless to Him who is our refuge and strength? We do not know. Concerning the Welsh and Owen, who calls himself prince, my lord, make provision, because the lord king is especially agitated and angered about this. Dearest Father and lord, farewell.

LETTER II. TO THE SAME.

Thomas’s case before the lord pope.

To your hearing, most holy Father, I flee, that you who redeemed the liberty of the Church at so great a risk to yourself may consider that it is the sole—or at least the chief—cause of my persecution: namely, that I followed your example. [Col. 0437B] For I grieved to see the condition of the Church somewhat shaken and its rights scattered to the greed of princes, and I believed that the advancing disease must be resisted. The more I knew myself bound to that lord of mine, to whom, after God, I owe all else, the more safely I judged that his unjust instigations should be resisted—until they prevailed and clouded his favour toward me.

Then, as is customary among princes, they brought forward accusations and slanders as grounds for my persecution, and I preferred expulsion to subscribing. These evils were compounded when I was summoned before the king like a layman to make answer; and I was abandoned by those from whom I had hoped for support. For I perceived that our lords and brother bishops stood ready, at the court party’s pleasure, to take action against me. Thus, almost crushed as all assailed me, I found breath in recourse to the hearing of your mercy, which does not neglect even those in extremity.

Before it I stand ready to show that I ought neither to have been judged there nor by them. For what else would this be, my fathers, except to take your rights away from yourselves? What else but to subject spiritual things to temporal? Once born, this precedent would extend to many cases. [Col. 0437C] Therefore I believed that resistance must be all the firmer, because a more ready inclination to do harm would arise if they first recognized weakness.

“But,” they will say, “what was Caesar’s ought to have been rendered to Caesar.” Yet though in many things the king must be obeyed, he must not be obeyed in those things by which he ceases to be king. Those would not be Caesar’s things but the tyrant’s, matters in which—even if not for my sake—they ought to resist him for their own. For if final judgment is reserved to Him who has power to judge body and soul, shall the ultimate and supreme power among men belong to one who judges according to the spirit?

If they supported a just cause, why did they attack me? Why do they accuse me for appealing to Him before whom it is either unlawful or useless to lie? Either they proceeded against me unjustly, or they distrusted your justice. For I would have been put to shame in two ways if I were convicted before your Holiness. I do not wonder that laymen devise such an imposition upon the clergy, but I do wonder that my lords and brothers were not only aware of this faction but even acted as its spokesmen. For why should I fear persecution from those for whom I had exposed myself to so many attacks? [Col. 0437D] I would have prevailed, had they wished it. But the head fares badly if it is abandoned by the members—indeed, if the eyes and tongue rise against the head.

Had they foreseen rightly, they were plotting their own ruin; and princes used their aid to enslave them. What cause of such great hatred was this, that in seeking to destroy me they destroyed themselves? Thus, while they neglect spiritual things for temporal, they fail in both. What is more, they dared condemn their father to his prejudice even while I protested and appealed to your hearing. What if they made the same conspiracy against the whole Church together with a prince offended against us? That suspicion could likewise touch you, most holy Father.

“But,” they will say, “they were bound to the king by the obligation of homage.” Yet they were bound to him corporally, but to me spiritually. To whom could they be bound more properly than to themselves? Should not the loss of temporal things have been neglected rather than that of spiritual things? Again they say that at this time the ruler ought not to have been provoked. [Col. 0438B] How subtly they argue for their own slavery! Rather, they provoke him who, by their excesses, furnish him with means and support. For he would have remained quiet if they had not acquiesced.

And at what time is constancy more required than among persecutors? Are not dependants proved in persecutions? If they always yield, how will they prevail? At some point they must resist. Therefore, most holy Father, stoop to my flight and persecution; remember that in your time I was once great, and that I was assailed with injuries for your sake. Use your severity; restrain those at whose prompting the name of this persecution has arisen. Yet let none of this be imputed to the lord king, who is the instrument of this scheme rather than its inventor.

LETTER III. TO THE SAME.

Venerable Father and lord, we believe that your prudence is by no means unaware how greatly the Church of Canterbury deserved to be exalted through the excellence of life and distinction of character of blessed Augustine, who founded it both by morals and by stones, and of his successors. Indeed, under their sound governance and provident administration it obtained adornment with primatial dignity and the honor of the primacy, attested by many privileges. For among all the Western Churches it shone as much in dignity as it excelled in faith and devotion toward the most holy Roman Church. Certainly it could never be torn from the bosom of its mother, the holy Roman Church, even in the time of schism, when immense tribulations were overwhelming that Church itself. But in our times, upon which the ends of the ages have come, shaken by repeated blows of adversity, it is beginning to be subjected to servitude. For behold: he who is known, almost from earliest age, to have sucked at her breasts as a son does those of his mother, now strikes her sides on every hand—though it is established that by her support he was raised to the honor which he now enjoys. We speak of the lord Archbishop of York, who, though he ought to render every reverence to the oft-mentioned Church, is attempting to deprive her of her ancient dignity. [Col. 0438D]

For although throughout our whole province we possessed ancient liberty, in our time—something which, as he himself well knows, had never before been usurped upon any pretext—he raised cross against cross, set cross against cross, signifying that Christ was divided, and stirred up the scandal of the cross. When, admonished by us in brotherly charity, he would not desist, we delivered to him letters from Your Holiness forbidding him to do this. Yet, despising your command, he nevertheless carried the cross. After four or more days, however, on a false allegation he appealed against us to your hearing, appointing the feast of Saint Luke for the appeal. At that time, God so disposing, we shall meet him, fully prepared to answer him in every respect. But if some most urgent cause prevents us from coming into your presence, we have appointed Odo, subprior of our church, as our representative in the present cause and in every question which may arise, firmly promising that we shall ratify whatever he does. May Your Holiness, dearest Father, ever prosper and flourish.

## LETTER IV. TO THE SAME

The king of England abuses the patience of the Church and continually rages with such savagery against Christ’s bride that Peter, to whose faith and zeal she has been entrusted, is compelled to draw the sword and, in the power of the Holy Spirit, restrain the malice of Christ’s persecutors. For Christ is again seized [Col. 0439C] and dragged to the cross; the disciples are scattered—though at the onset of the tempest they have not altogether cast away faith—while others again devise how they may betray the Son of God with a kiss of peace, and, under a pretext of law and reverence for law, subject justice and lawfully assail God.

Because, mindful of our duty and fearing the judgment of God, in which no sin will be spared, we have dared to raise our voice for justice, we have been made an object of reproach to many, exposed for Christ to every danger like a target for the arrow. At last we have been condemned to exile with all our people—clerics and laypersons, women and little children, the small and the great—so that neither reverence for rank, nor consideration for sex, nor pity for age might diminish anything of their wrath or fury. Many of them have already died in exile; [Col. 0439D] since they suffered innocently for justice, we trust that they have hastened to rest and have received, with the elect, the reward of their labors. Very many others still await God’s mercy amid hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness. Others are held in chains; among them is our chaplain, a devout priest, who had remained in England with the knowledge and consent of the king, and who, by the king’s command after that which they call the appeal, is kept afflicted in prison.

We endured all these things, trying whether by the patience of our meekness we might in some way soften his cruelty. But the more we suffer, the more his savagery grows harsh, so that he openly declares that he can by no means be appeased unless the Church is delivered up at his pleasure and his customs—indeed, his perversions—are accepted by all with our consent: customs not merely contrary to canons and laws, but utterly hostile to the Gospel of Christ. Since, therefore, we do not submit, and preach that God must be obeyed rather than man, he seeks our life in order that, with it, he may take away the liberty of the Church and everywhere overthrow in his kingdom the privileges of the Apostolic See. [Col. 0440A]

With this purpose, lately at the general chapter of Cîteaux, he declared hostility against the whole Order, and said that he would expel all their houses from his land unless the Cistercians cast me—an exile and outlaw for the Lord, for fidelity to the Roman Church, and for the liberty of the clergy—out of the monastery of Pontigny, against the will of the abbot of that place and the brothers. Out of reverence for your prayers, and through the intervention of the most Christian king of France and the magnates [Col. 0440B] of Gaul, they have most kindly and generously shown great humanity to me and mine—may the Most High repay them for it—and are still prepared to show it, if permitted.

And although we alone, with our little ones who preferred faith to riches and pleasures, are afflicted and crushed for the liberty of the whole Church, nevertheless he strives, by the counsel of certain bishops on this side and beyond the sea, for the overthrow of justice and liberty. Above all others, they are wise in doing evil and eloquent in unteaching the law. They are his mouth; they are his pen. Relying on their help, his supporters boast that they will pierce us with our own weapons and crush us with spoliation. They are confident that Jordan will flow into their mouths. Yet justice will answer them [Col. 0440C] according to its own measure; and Peter, with whom and for whom we fight, will, by God’s mercy, deliver us through the strength of your arm.

We have often declared to the wicked man his wickedness, lest his blood be required at our hands. You too have uttered threats, so that at least in this way he might escape the snare of condemnation. But he, deafening himself to every voice of the Lord, has thrown himself into the snare by laying violent hands upon a priest. He attacks the laws; indeed, so far as lies in him, he overthrows even the ordinances of the Gospel. He assigns himself a share in schism together with the schismatics, with whom he communicates and contracts various wicked obligations; knowingly and deliberately he incurs the sentence of anathema. For he himself knows that whoever lays violent hands upon clerics is excommunicated by the deed itself. Does not he who orders—indeed compels—such acts bear the guilt of the doer? David is said to have killed Uriah, but with the sword of the sons of Ammon. Ahab is accused and punished for shedding Naboth’s blood, though this was done in his name by the agency of wicked men; his approval proves that it pleased him. [Col. 0440D]

May it therefore please Your Grace to remedy diseases so grave and to provide for our affliction—indeed, for that of God’s Church—so that he who, by his rashness, contempt for law, and power turned against his own head, has drawn upon himself the condemnation of anathema through the perversity of his deeds, may be compelled by the severity of justice to seek absolution.

The Bishop of London has usurped precedence in England contrary to ancient custom and perpetual equity, so as to boast that nothing can be commanded or established in our province [Col. 0441A] except through him. The others do not bear this Pharisaic arrogance of his with equanimity. At first we passed it over; afterwards we rebuked this swelling. But since it hardens toward destruction, we cannot long endure it without correction. May the Lord restrain the tongue of the man of London from evil, and the lips of the man of Lisieux (*Lexoviensis*) from speaking deceit, to the destruction of him whose counsels they serve—and also to their own destruction.

John of Oxford presumes to appear before Your Holiness; and, as though he had done a worthy deed—having sworn an oath with schismatics for the perpetration of schism, which thereby gained strength—he again assails the Apostolic See with deceit, in order to deceive by an impure purgation and elaborate frauds that See which he could not overthrow by perjury. Unless he bears the mark of the beast upon his forehead, we fear that whatever honor he may obtain for himself [Col. 0441B] will turn into confusion for the Apostolic See, disgrace for the whole Church, and encouragement for the schismatics.

We have entrusted the rest to our messengers, to whom, if it please you, may Your Majesty’s Grace give credence; and may it provide that our innocence is not endangered at the arrival of Lord William of Pavia, through whom our persecutors openly boast that they will procure our deposition. Yet we do not know whether he will come with this authority; but we hold it certain that, unless compelled by Your Majesty, we shall submit to the judgment of no one but Your Holiness. You may remember, if you please, with what faith and charity certain persons have dealt with us, and with what sincerity they have promoted the pleas of the king of England, justifying the cause of the man [Col. 0441C] persecuting the Church—a man against whom the earth cries out because of his clamorous crimes, and the heavens will reveal them, since his iniquities are neither veiled nor concealed.

Far be it from God’s Church that those things should be fulfilled which a priest, the cleric of our aforesaid friend and lord, lately promised to the king of England: namely, that a legate should determine, according to the king’s will, the cause pending between us. The brother of the priest who is held in chains will explain the rest. Have mercy, if you please, on us and on them—indeed, on the whole Church of God.

## LETTER V. TO THE SAME

To the most loving Father and lord, ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, THOMAS, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, due and devoted obedience. [Col. 0441D]
