Most loving Father, I have endured more than enough while awaiting the correction of the king of England, and I have obtained no fruit at all from my patience; rather, through incautious endurance, I have increased the injury and destruction of the authority and liberty of God’s Church. I approached him many times through devout and suitable messengers, and repeatedly invited him to make due satisfaction. In letters, copies of which I sent you, I also threatened him with divine severity and vengeance unless he repented. But he advances ever further toward worse things, trampling down and oppressing God’s Church, and persecuting both my person and those who are exiles with me so greatly that he even tries, by threats and terrors, to take away the benefactions of God’s servants [Col. 0442A] who provide us with provisions for God’s sake and yours.

For he wrote to the Abbot of Cîteaux that, insofar as he loves the abbeys of the Order which are within his power, he should make us strangers to the Order’s assistance and fellowship. Why say more? Under our patience, the impiety both of the king himself and of his officials has advanced so far that, even if a multitude of men, however religious, were to affirm to you under oath that the matter is as we state it, I wonder whether even then Your Holiness would place any trust in their assertion.

Considering these matters, therefore, with anxiety of heart, and weighing the peril to both the king and myself, I have publicly condemned those pernicious practices—not so much customs as perversities—by which the English Church is disturbed and thrown into confusion. I have subjected to general excommunication both their observers and enforcers, and also their supporters, counsellors, and helpers, whoever they may be, clerics or laypersons. [Col. 0442B] I have also annulled the document and the authority of the document by which those perversities had been confirmed, and released our bishops from the oath by which they had been violently bound to observe them. These are the matters which I specifically condemned in that document:

That no appeal may be made to the Apostolic See in any cause without the king’s consent.

That a bishop may not excommunicate anyone who holds anything of the king without the king’s permission.

That the king’s land, or that of his officials, may not be placed under interdict without his or his officials’ permission. [Col. 0442C]

That a bishop may not excommunicate anyone for perjury or breach of faith.

That clerics or religious men may be brought before secular courts.

That laypersons—whether the king or others—may try cases concerning churches or tithes.

That an archbishop or bishop may not come when summoned by the lord pope without the king’s permission.

And other matters of this kind. I also excommunicated by name John of Oxford, who communicated with that schismatic and excommunicated man, Reginald of Cologne; who, contrary to the command of the Lord and of Your Holiness, usurped for himself the deanery of the Church of Salisbury; [Col. 0442D] and who, at the imperial court, swore the oath of which you yourselves have heard.

Likewise, we declared Richard of Ilchester excommunicated, because he had fallen into the same condemned heresy by communicating solemnly with that most notorious schismatic of Cologne, and by publicly plotting and contriving every evil with the schismatics and those Germans for the destruction of God’s Church, especially the Roman Church; and because he swore an oath concerning the contracting of a marriage with the duke of Saxony. Together with him, we also excommunicated Richard de Lucy and Jocelin de Balliol, who proved to be supporters of royal tyranny and contrivers of those heretical perversities.

We likewise excommunicated Ranulf de Broc, Hugh of Saint-Clair, and Thomas, son of Bernard, who usurped the possessions [Col. 0443A] and goods of the Church of Canterbury without our permission and consent.

All these, I say, we bound with the bond of anathema. Yet we have not as yet pronounced sentence against the king’s person; perhaps, by God’s mercy, we shall do so soon unless he repents and learns discipline from what we have done. Therefore, most blessed Father, in order that the authority of the Apostolic See and the liberty of God’s Church—which has almost wholly perished in our regions—may in some measure be restored, it is necessary and in every way expedient that you ratify unconditionally what has been done by us.

## LETTER VI. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0443B]

To the most loving lord and most holy Father ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, THOMAS, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, a wretched and pitiable exile: greetings, and unfailing constancy of spirit against the savagery of princes.

Concerned for your welfare and prosperity, we had long wished to hear certain news of your safety and that of our fellow brothers: also, what God’s magnificence has done for you and for his Church. For a report has sounded in our ears, and throughout all Gaul, of a thing newly said to have been done by the Lord: namely, that the schismatic Frederick has been shamefully humbled and made an object without honor before people and nation. Yet since it is both right to believe rumors and right not to believe them, we earnestly entreat Your Fatherhood [Col. 0443C] that by return letters and messenger we may hear from you as speedily as possible, and rejoice with you, if God has done for you what he customarily does for those who hope in him, who do not make flesh their arm and have no trust in princes, in whom there is no salvation.

If he has acted toward you as he acted toward Hezekiah against Sennacherib, turning the punishment back upon the one who was seeking to destroy Hezekiah himself together with all his people; if the outcome stands as rumor has proclaimed it, blessed be God, who knows how to show mercy to his servants. Behold how great is God’s power, how great his compassion. Unless he himself guards the city, the guard who watches it watches in vain. No more manifest display of God’s power has been heard of from age to age, if one rightly weighs what has happened; nor a more just exercise of his justice, by which he crushed the very contrivers of this evil, the authors of so great a persecution, and consumed them also by a death of utmost notoriety. [Col. 0443D]

Would that he had now also made that living prince an object of reproach to every people and of derision to every passer-by, so that all may point at him with the finger, and he may become like a common proverb on the lips of the populace, saying: “Behold the man who did not make God his helper.” If, trusting in his own power, he failed in that very vanity of his, it would have been better and more glorious before men for him to fall in death while attacking his adversaries than to live and become an object of contempt and mockery to all. This is God’s power and the strength of his arm.

Who, then, henceforth, holding Christ’s place on earth, would dare to comply with the will of princes, to the disgrace of the Church, by failing to punish offenders? Let whoever wishes dare it; I will not, lest the punishment of the offender be transferred to me, lest I be judged guilty through neglect of vengeance, lest I pass into guilt though I did not commit the offense. I think enough has been said to my lord on this point. Whoever wisely investigates the works of God and diligently considers his mighty deeds will prudently understand what must henceforth be done. [Col. 0444A]

Moreover, Your Holiness will learn that what we feared has happened to us—what we foretold openly concerning the presumption and insolence of Lord William of Pavia—as you may perceive from the letters sent us immediately upon his arrival. From him, in accordance with the tenor of your mandate sent to the lord king of France and to us, we had hoped rather for the comfort of peaceable consolation than for the confusion arising from the settlement of disputes between the king of England and us. For he is not one to whose jurisdiction we ought to submit in this cause, especially since the urgency of the king compelled you more to send him than he himself was constrained and sent by you.

We believe, indeed, that it is not consonant with justice for us to undergo the judgment or examination of one who seeks to make merchandise from our blood; from its price—would that it were not the price of iniquity—he seeks a name and glory for himself. Therefore we earnestly beseech Your Fatherhood, if you have concern for us, that his power—if indeed he has any—concerning us and our affairs may be annulled. [Col. 0444B] Let this hammer be removed from us: he chose rather to be a hammerer of clerics by obeying princes than to incur the displeasure of kings by pursuing divine favor.

In these matters, and in the others which the bearer of this letter will explain to you, we humbly beg Your Holiness, for the sake of mercy and our exile, to grant our petition. May your serenity have compassion on our long-enduring misery, whose end all await. Let the authority of the teacher recover its strength; let it wield the sword of blessed Peter; let it avenge the injury done to Christ and to his own. Let those who despised Peter’s hands while he was for a time forbearing feel them heavy, so that in this way the liberty of the Church, which has long languished in oppression, may breathe again; and that the world may rejoice, glorifying God, who has shown you his mercy, so that through you Peter’s little boat, which almost everyone believed sunk, may rise again, [Col. 0444C] and the presumption of tyrants, which seemed to have prevailed, may expire.

I have much to write to Your Holiness on this subject; but, lest I become troublesome to you through a long discourse, I conclude, wishing to hear and see concerning you what my soul desires. Yet I add one thing only, which must by no means be passed over in silence. Perhaps Lord William believed that, together with his king, he had in the course of time deceived your authority through fortuitous events. But, as the Lord turns adverse events toward good, he himself, who hoped that you had been deceived, will be deceived; by God’s mercy he will fall into the snare into which he hoped, by his wishes, that you and we had fallen. May Your Holiness prosper and, for our welfare, flourish for long ages.

## LETTER VII. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0445A]

The accumulation of our miseries and the bitterness of our griefs had struck our hearts and those of our fellow exiles; and compassion for the Church—which, upon the arrival of John of Oxford, seemed to have been handed over into the hands of those seeking its life in order to take it away—had most grievously scandalized the most Christian king and the magnates of the kingdom of the Franks, so that their wounded minds complained that faith and truth had been banished from the earth. But may the Father of mercies repay your compassion, most holy judge, most loving Father, and most faithful guardian of the Church of God; for, according to the multitude of sorrows in our hearts, your consolations [Col. 0445B] have gladdened our souls. For now we have been saved in hope; and the most Christian king of France and his kingdom, offering numberless thanks to your apostolic office—may God make it excellent and extend it through long ages—have directed all their indignation against those who boasted that, by their oaths, they had triumphed over your majesty.

For the king himself, after receiving your gracious letters of explanation, proclaims and extols the renown of your prudence, justice, holiness, and blessedness; and he gladly exposes, to those who speak against them, the malice and deceits of those who had scandalized the Gallican Church by false reports, sometimes forcing the matter into the ears of the opposing party even when unwilling, if I happen to be present. Yet he rejoiced still more after the conference with your envoys. Receiving them reverently, he learned from them, as he himself admits, that they had not come to prejudice the liberty of the Church or us, but to arrange a settlement between the king of England and ourselves and, if possible, to make peace between him and the Church. May they prosper by God’s help in this path, in which they will find us most ready helpers for the honour of God and the liberty of the Church.

When summoned by them to a conference on the tenth day at the borders of the lands, we then had, to speak from conscience, only three horses in our household. We obtained an additional seven days, in which we might summon our fellow exiles, miserably scattered as they were—being necessary both for the support of the journey and for counsel in conducting the discussion. Though they could scarcely assemble within so short [Col. 0445D] a period and amid such scarcity of resources, on the octave of St Martin we met your lordships’ envoys between Gisors and Trie. The most Christian king, through servants appointed for this purpose—may God richly repay him in mercy—provided generously and most kindly for us and for our fellow exiles, Christ’s outcasts, streaming in from every quarter.

And, as some have informed you, our persecutors diligently contrive that we may be harassed by journeys and expenses, and made burdensome and unwelcome by the weight of our costs to the king of the Franks, who dispenses his alms to us among Christ’s other poor. They would seem to have gained a great advantage for their malice if they could drive us from the dwelling prepared for us by heaven and deprive us of the consolation of the prince’s alms, just as [Col. 0446A] they have shaken off the assistance of the Cistercian Order. The Archbishop of Rouen came alone with our lords; the bishops and abbots of our province whom the king had wished to summon were kept at Rouen.

They therefore set before us from the outset the king’s hardness, the malice of the times, and the necessities and calamities of the Church, which is attacked almost everywhere in the world, France excepted, and battered by scarcely tolerable storms. They added much concerning the greatness and power of the prince; the affection and honour he had shown the Roman Church; the familiarity, favour, and benefits he had bestowed upon us. They further exaggerated the complaints and injuries by which he declares himself to have been harmed by us and ours, saying that we had procured for him war with the king of France and the count of Flanders. They urged [Col. 0446B] us, by great humility and a complete display of devotion and moderation, to strive to appease his anger, if by any means such fierceness might be softened and such unmeasured harshness mitigated. They also sought counsel from us, who had been accustomed to know him more fully, on how they might soften his hardness. For he had shown himself harsher even toward them after learning that, contrary to John of Oxford’s promises, they were not permitted to pronounce against us, at his will, a sentence of condemnation contrary to God and every right.

What he said in the hearing of his bishops will, God willing, be more suitably communicated to your ears orally by the messenger than in writing. We, however, giving thanks to your graciousness—which, by God, is moved to seek the peace of the Church and ourselves, a peace which is God’s glory and yours—refuted with true and probable reasons the suspicions by which the king seeks to stigmatize us. And on the following day the king of France, so far as concerned him, cleared our innocence under oath in the presence of the cardinals—an innocence which, as the Searcher of hearts and Judge knows, is free from this accusation.

For we are not so dull, nor so slow to believe the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel, as to think, at such a moment of necessity, that carnal weapons ought to be taken up—especially by priests—after spiritual arms and the defences of apostolic discipline have been abandoned. We know that trust must not be placed in princes, and that cursed is the man who makes flesh his arm. And so that no such thing could plausibly [Col. 0446D] be invented about us, we long kept ourselves apart from the king’s conference, until at length, summoned by him, we went to present him with our letters of excuse and to obtain safe passage and conduct from Lord Otto the legate, who had sent us his clerk Papia for this purpose.

The king viewed the outcome of this legation with suspicion, both because the king of England had obtained it, and because, as he says, he recalled having been harmed by them on another occasion, when he had recently received you as father and lord; and also because he heard with the greatest displeasure the boasts of John of Oxford and his like. But when our explanation had been gratefully received and passage obtained, we returned to our little dwelling of poverty, awaiting in patience the Lord’s salvation.

Because your lordship’s envoys demanded from us the humility and demonstration of moderation by which so great a prince might be appeased, we replied that we would most willingly and devotedly show him, as our lord and king, every humility, service, and devotion according to their counsel, saving the honour of God and of the Apostolic See, the liberty of the Church, the dignity of our person, and the possessions of the churches. And if they thought anything should be added, removed, or altered in these terms, we asked them to tell us, because we were willing to obey them insofar as the necessity of our condition and profession allowed.

But they said that they had no settled advice on this point, nor had come then to advise us, but also to consult us. Testing us, they asked—using Lord William’s words, “because we are no better than our fathers”—whether we would be willing, in their presence, to promise the king that we would observe all the customs employed by his predecessors in the time of our predecessors; and thus, once all complaints on both sides had been laid to rest, if they could obtain this—which they did not think easy—we should recover our see and return to his favour.

We replied that none of our predecessors had been compelled by any kings to make this profession; nor, God helping us, will we ever profess observance of those customs that destroy the liberty of God’s Church, overthrow the privilege of the Apostolic See, and openly oppose God’s law—customs from which at Sens, in their presence and that of many others, [Col. 0447C] you absolved us through your mercy. We added that, God mercifully granting it, the saying worthy of an apostolic mouth would never pass from our memory: that we ought first to expose our necks to the archer’s arrows rather than consent to such perversities, and through shameful bargaining for temporal things or greed for life thus abandon pastoral care.

In their presence those reprobate customs were read out, some of which we had condemned; indeed, even before us the Catholic Church, from the beginning and with those who observed them, had condemned them under anathema in many councils. We therefore asked whether a priest might not merely observe them but even connive at them without peril to his order and salvation. We added that we had sworn fealty to the king, with our ecclesiastical order reserved, and would willingly keep it, provided that we did not thereby nullify the faith owed to God.

Then one man—whom, as you know, we had from the beginning both had and ought to have suspected—suggested that it would be better for us to yield altogether than for the Church to be so harassed. Many persuasive arguments on this point were multiplied; the living voice will relate them more suitably. We replied to the speaker that for this very reason we would not yield: it would be a ruinous precedent; it would promote the destruction of ecclesiastical liberty; and perhaps it would result in harm to the Christian faith. For who thereafter would dare speak? When pastors thus yield, who will rise up against the enemy and stand as a wall for the house of Israel? We added that neither you nor any apostolic men had instructed God’s Church by such examples. Did not all Egypt, as the credible testimony of histories records, return to idolatry when its pastors fled—Egypt, where religion had flourished most vigorously from the beginning?

Proceeding from this point, they asked whether we wished to abide by their judgment concerning the matters disputed between ourselves and the king. If we were to refuse judgment, we would seem to justify the king’s cause, and perhaps our reputation would suffer with many. Yet we ought not, if it please you, to have as judge the man who has proved our adversary; nor can we be safe anywhere in this matter except in your presence. For by banishing us and ours, harassing others, and inflicting losses, that king has so terrified, and continues to terrify, everyone that no one, with his knowledge, dares mention us favourably.

Having considered all this, we moderated our answer so that we neither said [Col. 0448B] that we declined judgment nor plunged ourselves into so perilous a lawsuit. For we said that, when we and ours had been restored to our see, administration, and all our goods, we would willingly submit, where and when we ought, to your judgment or to that of whomever, or of whichever persons, ought by your mandate to judge. We neither wish nor have wished to evade justice. Meanwhile, we cannot be compelled by any reason to litigate; our poverty is unequal to such expenses and lawsuits; nor can the generosity of the most serene king be extended without burden to support us and Christ’s poor fellow exiles for a long time in other people’s houses with the money he presently needs. For where victuals abound, our expenses are more easily borne.

They proceeded to a third question, asking whether we would accept before them as judges the suit of the bishops who had appealed against us. But we answered that we had received no mandate from you on this matter and that our poverty was not equal to such costs and litigation. Yet our adversaries, as we learned from persons who could not have been ignorant of the affair, were pursuing this: that under any pretext they might discredit our person before the envoys and thus inflict any injury they pleased. For they conjecture that none of the provincials would dare assist us against the king, and so they would seem to have brought about our downfall.

The king summoned only those known from the beginning of this storm to have opposed us and incited such great malice: namely, the Archbishop of York [Col. 0448D], the bishops of London and Chichester, and, along with them, the bishop of Worcester, so that the malice of the others might be veiled by his presence. Yet, as your discernment may remember, these men who now above all applaud the king’s will and, as is publicly known, thirst for our blood, raised both the form of our election and our person in their letters requesting our pallium with many proclamations of praise. Now, contradicting truth and themselves, they have rendered themselves contemptible by the audacity of lying and flattery, since at the prince’s nod, like comic servants, they now say yes and now no.

These, Father, are the men who give horns to the sinner; and, if he is not sufficiently mad, incite him further, placing a cushion beneath his elbow and lulling his head, sick with vices, to sleep in the softness of a pillow. Since therefore even those who ought to be and seemed to be pillars of the Church encourage and arm, by counsel, assistance, authority, services, and expenditure, the persecutors of divine law and of our lowliness against the Church and ourselves, it is neither safe nor possible for us to submit to judgment except in the presence of your holiness and under your own examination.

For although the Church ought to hope for the integrity of one of the legates, and we trust him, especially in matters of God, nevertheless there is no man apart from you to whom we dare commit this cause of the Lord. May God make the other legate such as is expedient for his salvation and such as becomes a priest-cardinal of the Roman Church. We fear, however, that what, if you please to remember, we foresaw will happen may indeed occur: namely, if Lord William’s prudence, eloquence, and authority should coincide with the power and hard will of the king of England. We fear that, when their plan has been formed, petitions may be offered to us whose hearing will be grievous to us, whose fulfilment impossible or displeasing to God, and odious to the world.

Since the care of all churches rests upon you, turn your eyes, if you please, toward the West; observe and see how the Church is treated there. Let Lord Otto, whom we believe to be moved by the Spirit of God, tell you what he has seen and learned concerning the Church and province of Tours, what he has heard concerning England, and what he has experienced in Normandy. We believe you will say with tears: “There is no sorrow like this sorrow.” For, to say nothing of the Churches of Canterbury and Tours, which he treats as you have heard—and would that you knew more fully—he has long kept seven vacant bishoprics in our province and that of Rouen in his own hand, and permits no pastors to be ordained there. The clergy of the kingdom have been handed over to his retainers for trampling and plunder.

If we pass over these matters, best Father, what shall we answer Christ on the day of judgment? Who will resist Antichrist when he comes, if we already accommodate such patience to the preliminary signs of his vices and crimes? For by such connivance powers grow insolent, and kings of the nations become tyrants, so that they judge no right and no privilege of the Church to remain except at their own discretion [Col. 0449D]. But blessed is he who takes and dashes the little ones against the rock. For if Judah does not, by the command of the law, destroy the Canaanite, he grows perpetually into an enemy and a thorn to him.

Take courage, Father, and be strong: more are with us than with them. The Lord has shattered Frederick, the hammer of the wicked, and will soon strike others too unless they repent and make peace with the Church of God. Finally, we await only the judgment of your mouth, or of Him who is accustomed to take away the spirit of princes and to deliver the poor from the mighty. The messengers’ voice will supply more that we did not think fit to entrust to writing. Let your serenity hold this certain: if from the beginning we had been willing to acquiesce in wicked customs, the intervention of any cardinal—indeed, of any person—would not have been necessary.

Likewise, by the Lord’s agency, the examples of the Sicilians or Hungarians are proposed to us in vain; they would not at all excuse us on the day of judgment if we preferred the barbarity of tyrants to apostolic institutions and believed the insolence of secular powers to be a rule of life rather than the eternal testament confirmed by the blood and death of the Son of God. Therefore, to conclude all that has been said with a lamentable end, let your holiness consider whether this ought to be the fruit of our labour, work, and exile: that we should be judged naked, wretched, stripped of every possession, and subjected to the straits of lawsuits because we dared to oppose the fiercest oppressor of the Church in defence of its liberty—while we had expected, day by day, consolation for our desolation [Col. 0450B], joy after misery had been fully endured, and from God and from you a fitting vengeance upon the oppressors of the Church for Christ’s injury.

Could it not suffice those who seek our lives that they have put some of ours to death, and that we live our lives only with difficulty amid poverty and calamity, sustained by others’ alms? Must we, by the authority of this legation—which ought never to have existed—be dragged and drawn out through years upon years, from grief to grief and misery to disgrace, so that our right and justice also turn to the ruin of ourselves and our wretched companions? Good God, what will be the end of this grief? Arise, O God; judge your cause; avenge the blood of your servants wickedly slain, and of the others who, intolerably afflicted, are failing, since [Col. 0450C] there is no one besides the lord pope and the very few with him who is willing to rescue us from the hand of our enemies. May your holiness live and flourish for long ages, that we and our poor companions may live and recover.

## LETTER VIII. TO THE SAME

To his most loving lord and most holy Father, ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, THOMAS, humble minister of the wretched Church of Canterbury, wretched and pitiable exile, offers the service of due submission, and victory in every respect over the chief enemies of the Church.

[Col. 0450D] It is a familiar proverb: “What can be redeemed, whether by an extension of time or otherwise, is not feared.” There is another, still more familiar: “It is easier to avoid a quarrelsome man than to escape a deceitful one.” Therefore we inform your highness how our lord the king of England, by his deceptions and false promises, when we seemed to stand at the gates of peace—as all his own people likewise hoped and believed—has newly deceived us on the occasion of certain messengers of his returning from your majesty. They boasted and pretended that they had obtained from you, at the king’s request and insistence, a mandate and authority for the irreparable humiliation of the Church of Canterbury and for our ruin, God forbid, and that of our fellow exiles.

Indeed, on this occasion, as often before, he deceived not only us but also religious men who brought us words of peace on his behalf, which we have entrusted to the bearer of this letter to communicate to your holiness; likewise the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Sées, who sent us letters declaring his knowledge, will, and command, a copy of which we transmit to you. Yet whatever he may do to us, may he not, even this time, have deceived your serenity by smooth and empty promises, as he often boasts he has done, so that through delay there may unexpectedly occur what his eyes shall never see nor his ears hear.

And because we have often, in season and out of season, appealed to your prudence, often knocked at the ears of your serenity, that by the authority of blessed Peter you would impose the fitting end, through the censure of severity, upon so great an evil and persecution; and because, our sins requiring it, we have not yet been heard, for the salvation of the English Church and the disclosure of the oppression of ourselves and ours—which grows daily harsher and more bitter against us through your patience and waiting, which may it not be further deceived by delusive promises—we can now scarcely breathe. Nor is there anyone among us who henceforth wishes to expose himself to this danger or submit himself to so great a risk, especially since bitter death has overtaken many of them in pursuing this cause.

We send your holiness the bearer of this letter, who, moved by compassion and solely through his own generosity, has kindly undertaken to carry our case to you—would that he may do so effectively. We ask, if you please, that your kindness receive him kindly, and hear him still more kindly concerning what we ask of your serenity through him—just as, in your final necessity, you desire to be heard by Him who gives salvation to kings and takes away the spirit of princes—if you have care for our life and salvation. We have become outcasts and miserable, not in order that we may live more securely and quietly by avoiding the importunity of so great a persecutor, but in order that the Church of God may flourish and may breathe more effectively in liberty in times to come. For hard and heavy things are happily endured for a time, that happier things may follow.

And indeed, if we had long ago believed this of our king, the Church, as we firmly believe, would long since through God’s mercy have obtained victory over him through you, and you glory and honour among other princes by his example. For this is the lot of tyrants: he who terrifies others is himself more afraid.

## LETTER IX. TO THE SAME

To his most loving lord and most holy Father ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, THOMAS, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, wretched and pitiable exile, offers greeting and, amid every peril, firm and true obedience.

We send to your holiness the bearer of this letter, very familiar to us by reason of his condition, and, we believe, trustworthy by reason of his great capacity. May your clemency, if you please, graciously hear him on our behalf and concerning us, as suits and benefits our misery. That misery has become wearisome to our friends through despair—would that it has not become hateful; to you, which grieves us more, through manifest inaction, contemptible, as many judge—would that it is not; and even to our enemies, pitiable through compassion.

Arise, O Lord, and delay no longer. Let your face shine upon us; deal with us according to your mercy; and save us with our poor companions, who are failing under excessive pressure, for we perish. Let us not be put to shame among men; let not our adversaries—rather, the adversaries of Christ and the Church—insult us; let not our fortune become an object of mockery to nation and people, for we have called your name upon us. Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, make a great name for yourself; restore your glory; reveal the renown of your name. That renown has been greatly diminished in the regions of France by the return of that excommunicate, perjured schismatic—John of Oxford I mean—and by his false preaching.

God knows that I do not lie; and if I am not believed, let inquiry be made of those in France who cherish your honour more and desire the Church’s advancement more earnestly. I mean that renown which hitherto stood blameless among men, was preserved unharmed amid every peril, remained alone undefiled when the rest was lost, and was everywhere held sound and celebrated. Therefore let the master’s authority recover its strength; let it restore the noble action, formerly commendable but afterward wickedly blackened, so that that talkative man may realize that he spread falsehoods and preached lies. Let him experience severity who had earned leniency; let him endure punishment who abused kindness, so that the world may know that he has found Christ’s vicar founded upon a firm rock—not easily moved, not a reed-staff, as the malicious whisper, but an observer of equity and justice, no respecter of persons, sparing no one in judgment, and faithfully and impartially administering the fairness of the law to king and private person alike. May your holiness prosper, that we and our poor companions may prosper.

## LETTER X. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0452D]

To his most loving lord and most holy Father ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, THOMAS, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, wretched and pitiable exile, with his fellow exiles, offers greeting and every good.

We send to your holiness our faithful bearers of this letter, namely two of our poor companions and fellow exiles whom we can presently send, and in the way we can send them, so that through them you may hear and understand, by a more certain and mournful report, what has recently been done concerning us in these days, and the immense hardships of our own miseries and those of our companions.

[Col. 0453A] May we swiftly receive from your holiness, if you please, the due and long-delayed deliverance from the oppression of the Church and ourselves, and relief from our sorrows through the hand of your mercy, lest, crushed enormously and repeatedly, we fail in this tribulation, more severe than any since the days of sorrows. For we have long been drawn out, and, as your excellence knows, are drawn and dragged—no less cruelly than unjustly—through time and times in misery and grief, so that perhaps, within the limits of a long time, our soul may fail under affliction; that, worn down, we may be extinguished; utterly exhausted by the narrow straits of miseries; while meanwhile your authority expires—God forbid—which, through God’s mercy, is destined to relieve our misery and that of others, before it ends, contrary to the desire of the wicked and the deceit of the malicious.

Therefore incline your ear, Lord, and hear; open your eyes and see whether there has been injustice like this. Consider more diligently whether there is grief like the grief of us and ours, who have been given over to plunder, unless God’s mercy swiftly comes to our aid through your hand. We have been made an object of scorn and mockery to those around us by the authority of your legates, who—would that they had not acted more outrageously than presumptuously in matters concerning us and the Church. For if these things have been done to us by them in the green wood, what shall be done in the dry, if this legation, which ought never to have existed, is to endure?

So far as lies in their power, they have suspended us from all authority that we had in the churches and persons of England—something which neither God’s grace nor yours has ever done at the request of any prince or other person, nor, through God’s mercy, will do, as your sublimity granted us by a definite promise. Why, Lord, did you grant a legation to a man at whose entry my lord ought, if I may say so without offence to him, to have considered what the fruit of this legation would be, and also to have weighed its outcome? For his whole soul from the beginning has been poured out, and remains poured out, toward the ruin of ecclesiastical dignity and of yours, in order thereby to win the prince’s favour.

Lord, Lord, our eyes are upon you, lest we perish. Help us, Lord, and deal with us according to your promises, which may they not have gladdened our souls in vain. For we waited at the command of your highness. We waited, I say, for peace, and it did not come. We expected good through the work of your legates’ hands, and behold, greater affliction for us, fiercer turmoil. Therefore have mercy upon us, Lord; have mercy upon us, since after God there is no one to fight for us except you alone with your faithful ones. Have mercy, I say, upon us, that God may have mercy upon you at the strict judgment, when you must render an account of your stewardship.

For after God we have no refuge except you, since even those who ought, from regard for compassion and justice and out of reverence for the most holy Roman Church, to stand with us and fight for us, oppose us out of human favour. With our resources exhausted and our harassments innumerable, we certainly have no means henceforth to pursue even the smallest of these vexations. Therefore let your highness swiftly aid us and our Church, if you please, and put an end to this malice, lest it be further prolonged, for it is time. We can scarcely breathe amid such excessive straits. Hasten, therefore, that we may feel the benefit of your grace before we die. May your holy kindness—beloved by us and, after the love of God, necessary to us above all things—prosper and live through long ages, that through your generosity we too may begin to live again, who have already begun to die.

Moreover, let your discernment know that three days before these evils came upon us, our messengers had departed with our letters, by which we informed your holiness how we had parted from your legates. For the most Christian king of France and the queen wrote to you, as did certain princes and bishops of his kingdom and some of your lesser friends, rejoicing and glorifying God and giving thanks to God and you, because it had become clear from the arrival of your legates—as they themselves had represented it face to face to the lord king—that the claims made by that spokesman John of Oxford and other messengers of the king, concerning the burden and overthrow that would be inflicted on us through the legates, were false, indeed utterly false. Hence an unspeakable scandal had arisen throughout the kingdom of France and among all to whom that report had come, except the enemies of the Church and of ourselves. But this harp has been turned into mourning, this joy into sorrow, and this error has become worse than the former one.

We therefore ask that it please your holiness to apply a swift remedy to this newly arisen disease, so that it may become manifest to all, as the truth of the matter stands, that these acts were presumptuously undertaken contrary to your knowledge and mandate. May your holiness prosper again and for ever.

## LETTER XI. TO THE SAME

To his most loving Father and lord ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, THOMAS, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, wretched exile and more pitiable than usual, offers greeting and due obedience in all things, even adverse things.

[Col. 0454D] We send back to your holiness the bearer of this letter. He will explain to you more faithfully and diligently the misery of his business and how, because of your letters, he and his brothers were treated in the kingdom of England. Unless divine clemency soon comes to their relief through your hand, the condition of that order is utterly overthrown. Therefore may he and his brothers, if you please, perceive that our prayers have benefited them; for their unjust harassment fittingly makes them more worthy to be heard by your holiness.

And would that my lord might consider more deeply and lay more firmly to heart into how great and how irrevocable a disgrace the English Church has recently fallen, in every order dwelling in that kingdom, through that unheard-of and lamentable indulgence, which our king—would that he were not the Church’s persecutor—boasts that he extorted by his own exertions through the intervention of certain friends of his at the curia, who would that they were friends of God and the Church more than of themselves, and desired more to enjoy divine grace than the favour of princes. Although it is believed that you can easily revoke this indulgence as void, the precedent of the deed thus obtained nevertheless remains; so that, even if for the present he may enjoy what he has obtained, the source of the benefit secured remains with him and his successors. Having gained the opportunity of obtaining it perpetually for himself and his successors, he conceived the boldness to think that, by some craft of his own or of his friends, he could evade the sentence due for his offences against him and his accomplices—a sentence which he had not dared hope to escape.

Yet there is one thing that consoles us miserably, if I may say it without offence to you: the Roman Church knows how to bless its friends and faithful servants in this way. May God console it better than it has provided for itself, and for the English Church, ourselves, and our poor companions, in this matter. I know—and this grieves me more—that no crime is ever buried by the passing of ages; no wicked deed is ever driven away by forgetfulness; rather, deeds that have ceased to be crimes become precedents. May your holiness prosper and flourish, and may it soon please you to deign to relieve our misery, that we may at least be able to live, though we perish even while somehow living. God knows this is undeserved.

## LETTER XII. TO THE SAME

To his most holy lord and dearest Father, ALEXANDER [Col. 0455C], by God’s grace supreme pontiff, THOMAS, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, offers greeting and every obedience with devotion.

They flee to the feet of your Majesty—our poor people, believed to have been preserved by God’s will so that they may lament the slaughter of their brethren cruelly put to death and set before your ears the miseries of the Church now almost perishing. For now there is scarcely anyone who, even with great difficulty, dares amid so many dangers and deaths to pursue our necessities, since we hear almost daily that some are imprisoned, others captured, others scourged, others dead. And the king of the English, known to be the cause of so great evils, not only remains unpunished, but rejoices [Col. 0455D] in the Church’s confusion and laughs at others’ dangers; although long ago, if he were led by the Spirit of God, your gentleness, enduring in much patience, ought to have summoned him to repentance. But he, while he heaps sins upon sins and lesser offences upon greater ones, seems to himself to be storing up wrath and, by reckless provocation, hastening vengeance.

For the whole five-year period he has raged against the Church; and I, though I do not say this without fear, see Christ almost daily crucified in his members, holy things profaned, and the Church—of which I was appointed guardian by the Lord—torn apart and trampled underfoot. Yet I have not, with Peter, drawn the sword of God’s word, to cut off the ear of raging Malchus. Whenever I read of the zeal of Phinehas, Elijah, Mattathias, and his sons; whenever apostolic fervour comes to my mind; whenever [Col. 0456A] I review the deeds of the holy Fathers who set themselves as a wall before princes and powers for the house of the Lord, I groan at my danger, and fear for my wretched soul—I mean my own soul—a just condemnation for dissimulation and unjust, unwarranted patience.

For since those who commit an offence and those who consent to it are alike in guilt, and since one who, by a power received from God, does not correct what he does not doubt should be corrected falls into the fault of one consenting, I see a dreadful judgment hanging over me, who have so long endured by remission, as I fear, the enormous offences of my subjects. For blessed is he who destroys the newborn little ones of such people, or dashes them against the rock once they are born, as soon as they are seized. I fear, Father, that the Lord will require at my hand [Col. 0456B] the blood of that man and of those allied with him in evil. I fear that the stern Judge will exact from me many deaths of those whom he has proscribed and who labour for the Church’s cause even unto death, since it is written: “Cursed is he who withholds the sword from bloodshed.”

For, as Solomon says: “He who delicately nurtures his servant will afterward find him rebellious.” And the Church indeed perceives this through frequent and most certain experience. If anyone had checked his first assaults, if anyone had struck down the recklessness of those inciting him to evil and fostering his fury, the pestilential trees would never have put forth so many and such great plagues. For the faults of the young are more quickly removed; but when they gain strength through long continuance, they in a manner pass into nature. Certainly such great presumption ought to have been restrained: both because of its own enormity, which required rebuke, and [Col. 0456C] because it corrupts the whole Latin world by its destructive example.

May your clemency, I beseech you, hear through your subdeacon Master Gratian, whose name we believe corresponds to the fact, because, like a son of grace, he has earnestly sought to advance the Church’s cause faithfully and prudently, with all modesty and sincerity. May it hear, I say, how in our western region, unless you speedily bring aid by God’s favour, the Church is dying; and at last may it take pity and impose a due end upon such great miseries. For if you wait until the king’s envoys and the supporters of malice have no lies to put forward, life will fail us, you, and them. And at the strict judgment each of us will be compelled, without respect of persons, to render an account of his own work.

[Col. 0456D] Behold, he now says that he does not demand from me an account of the administration of his chancellorship, nor the money which I then received or promised; rather, he asks only for what, he says, I received from his property during my archiepiscopate. But, God favouring us, it is known to all among us that, an account having already been rendered to him on this matter, I am not bound. Likewise, he says that he has not disputed concerning his customs, though, merely changing the word, he asks that they be observed under the name of “dignities.” For my part, I will gladly preserve the dignities of the realm, as I have often offered to do, provided my order and fidelity to the Roman Church are preserved.

But I can be induced by no necessity to introduce into the Church of God a new form of oath, God being my author and your piety watching over me. For whatever he now obtains from me, he will undoubtedly demand from all bishops and from the whole Church. Some are compelled to swear that they will observe the canons, but not even that they will fulfil the commands of the Gospel; certainly this would not be safe. And shall bishops be constrained, by the unprecedented necessity of an oath, to observe customs or dignities? The form of fealty in the French and English Church requires the prelates of churches to swear to princes that they will keep faith with them, preserving life, limb, and earthly honour, provided their order is preserved. This form is also included among his reprobate customs. I swore in this form; I shall publicly profess that I so swore; and he ought to be content with it. Nor shall I rashly transgress in this respect the bounds established by the Fathers.

He also insists that he need not restore, or make satisfaction for, what has been taken from me and mine—indeed, from the Church—saying that his ancestors, whose measure he is filling or exceeding in persecuting the Church, drove many of my predecessors into flight and never restored anything to them. But, lest this be drawn into a precedent, provision must be made promptly for destroying the destructive example. For one who leaves to posterity an example of error is rightly convicted of having driven them into guilt. Thus Jeroboam son of Nebat is said to have caused Israel to sin by imitation of his crime. But who will remit sin if what has been taken is not restored or satisfaction made? Every care must surely be taken that, just as he derives the authority for his wrongdoing from his predecessors, he may leave to his successors an example of correction.

Otherwise it is to be feared that he will become a Jeroboam to his successors, and that I, if henceforth I fail in [Col. 0457C] the correction I owe, will hurl my own people into the ruin of condemnation like another Eli—or rather, like a priest of the high places. Let no one falsely say that I reject concord, provided it is made in the Lord and without injury to the Church. For I am not so senseless as to despise with such ease things which are supremely important in temporal affairs and most welcome to men, unless it is because I do not wish to purchase them at the loss of eternal things. While accusing me of contempt, let no one defend his own error in seeking empty tranquillity or worldly possessions. For God, who cannot be mocked, will shortly reveal, when we all stand before his judgment-seat, with what intention each person has lived. Him, the examiner and witness of consciences, I have; him I await as judge, [Col. 0457D] whom no cunning deceives against justice, nor any power bends.

Remember, Father, with how great mercy He has regarded you; how He has crushed your enemies—indeed, the enemies of the Church—for the glory of his name. Rise with him to aid him who in his members is unjustly proscribed, tortured, spat upon, and crucified. If it please you, hear our poor people; and hear more mercifully the prayers which the Church of Canterbury has offered, and still offers, to you through them, so that after such great miseries she may rejoice that she has received from her father the consolation due to her. Crush her persecutors; and cause those whom we have delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh—whose names will be stated to you if they come or send to you—to be treated as excommunicated until they make satisfaction to the Church of God and to us. The envoys will supply you with what remains to be said, although they will not be able to set forth, as necessity requires, the full weight of the English Church’s miseries. May your Holiness ever flourish and be strong.

## LETTER XIII. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

To the most holy lord and most dear Father, ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, THOMAS, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, greeting and every obedience with the utmost devotion.

We have taken care briefly to inform your Holiness what Master Vivian did concerning the business of God’s Church and ours after Lord Gratian’s departure, and how diligently he acted. That he himself remained [Col. 0458B] for some time in France after his companion’s departure is believed to have occurred to the confusion of those oppressing the Church, so that the Church’s justice—whose obscuring many were striving to effect by wicked deeds—might be declared before the eyes of all nations.

This aforesaid son of yours indeed endeavoured to accommodate the man, so that, summoned by his letters, as he asserts, and by much entreaty, he might incline him to peace. From his many and great promises he had received an unquestioning hope; and he followed those promises to the point at which, in the presence of the Most Christian king and the nobles of France, he demonstrated the man’s malice and hardness. How greatly he laboured to arrange a conference between the kings; how much work and diligence he there applied to restoring peace; how urgently he solicited every person, individually and collectively, whom he believed fit for this task—we cannot sufficiently express in words. Had we not been present, we could scarcely have given credence to those reporting it.

Therefore, because during his delay the justice of the Church was, through the mercy of God—who does not abandon those who hope in him—more fully manifested, as it seems to us and to all who were present, we beg your Majesty on bended knees to receive him with fatherly kindness into the bosom of your clemency as he returns.

## LETTER XIV. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

We are often compelled to implore the help of the Apostolic See, [Col. 0458D] since, to the contempt of God and injury to you, Father, we are tortured by many great and continual afflictions, dishonoured by insults, and provoked by wrongs. Injuries which hurt a person are less readily recalled to mind; but it is a form of impiety to conceal, under the empty pretext of patience, so great and manifest an injury to Christ.

I shall therefore once more speak to my lord before God on behalf of his Church, committed to my smallness, uttering a word lest her blood, whose cry has now ascended to the height, and the condemnation of those who torture and destroy her, may be charged to my silence. And indeed, if from the beginning your compassion had heard her cry, which in her distress she sent forth through my mouth, dashing Babylon’s little ones against the rock [Col. 0459A] and crushing the shoots of malice in travail, the recklessness of our persecutor would never have grown to such impiety.

But your divine gentleness, which by its own merit and by the prayers of the universal Church possesses a fuller grace of the Holy Spirit, setting aside the counsel of my lowliness, judged that vessels of wrath should be borne with in much and long patience, so that fatherly kindness might summon erring sons to repentance. Although this has at present seriously harmed the whole Church of God, it is nonetheless credible that this was arranged by the Holy Spirit, who governs your counsels and directs your acts: namely, that the iniquity which strove to hide itself by many subtle devices, continually abusing your patience, might emerge into public with unveiled face, and that the reproaches of Egypt might be exposed before all who saw them.

For John of Oxford and all the other ministers of such great impiety, returning from the Apostolic See in triumph and as though victorious in justice, gave horns to the sinner; and the authors and inciters of this error, as though they were not already sufficiently mad on their own, began to urge him more fiercely with the spurs of their impunity and glory. Yet poisoned minds—or rather, poisonous men—ought not further to have been drugged with poison; neither Ahithophel nor the Judas of our time ought to have been stirred up or encouraged to crime.

Moreover, those whom your compassion, while discharging such an embassy, adopted as sons and raised to honours have become, for the English Church, a crooked bow. Thus the wretched Church of Canterbury, mother nevertheless of all the others on the island, since she gave them birth [Col. 0459C] and reared them in Christ, may rightly say: “The sons of my mother have fought against me; my own children, whom I bore and exalted, have trampled and wounded me, and still seek my life in order to take it away.”

Not that she grieves at your generosity, which was pious, or at their promotion, which was hoped to be useful; but she grieves that they are faithless to you, most destructive, and most manifest persecutors of the Church. For they are the very people who incite and inflame the lord king’s savagery, and labour by every means not merely that all reverence toward me be removed—for this they accomplished long ago—but that my name and that of my fellow-exiles, now few because most have passed from the persecutor’s presence into death, may be erased from the earth.

You had commanded others, and above all the bishop of London, to devote diligent effort to restoring the Church’s peace, which, it was believed, he could readily do. But once he heard that your favour had restored to me and conferred upon me the due power of punishing the Church’s evildoers, he immediately, in person and through his accomplices, stirred up and troubled the land, fearing that the wounds which he had caused might be healed. Nor did he do this secretly, but everywhere—and, that his iniquity might be more manifest, in London, at a very public place where the officials of the whole realm had gathered to conduct public accounts.

It ought to have sufficed him that your clemency had endured him so long, and that he had hitherto escaped punishment despite having incurred a sentence of anathema because of disobedience and other manifest crimes. Yet from impunity he conceived the audacity for every kind of presumption, confident that the Jordan would flow into his mouth. For the bishop of Salisbury, hitherto disobedient and rebellious, depends upon his counsel, as does Ranulf de Broc, who preys upon the Church of Canterbury, and our other despoilers.

Accordingly, as the requirement of law demands and the spur of conscience presses us—conscience which vehemently accuses us of such silence amid so grave a danger to the Church—we have publicly excommunicated, on just and manifest grounds, the bishops of London and Salisbury, and the aforesaid Ranulf together with others whose names are written above, while also citing other persons known to have shared in their faction and sedition. Unless they repent, we shall, by the Lord’s authority, bind them with the bond of anathema and compel them to appear before the tribunal of the Apostolic Majesty, marked with the character of the beast.

Therefore may your Holiness provide for the Church’s liberty and peace. If on this occasion you believe us, all things will be arranged according to your wish; and we shall see eye to eye that the arrogance of Moab, who is proud and terrifies little ones, is greater than his strength. Approve, if it please you, what we do; and yourselves lay your hand to what necessity requires. Crush the audacity and malice of the ungodly, lest, God forbid, if they prevail as they have seemed to do hitherto, the Church’s salvation be crushed and perish. Furthermore, we entreat that you command our petitions—both those formerly presented and those now presented—to be fulfilled with speedy effect, since in our judgment all of them concern your honour and advance the Church’s benefit.

## LETTER XV. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

Those most hinder the Church’s peace, which your piety seeks with unceasing care, who ought, both by the obligation of their office and by reverence for your command, to labour more diligently for its restoration. Therefore the Church mourns that she is discoloured and blackened by her sons, and that her spoils are plundered by those appointed as her guardians.

For if Geoffrey, our arch-devil, and Reginald of Salisbury, [Col. 0460D] and John of Oxford—once dean in name and profit of a Church eminent in Christ, but in service and devotion a retainer of the royal court—together with their accomplices, had not perverted the king’s mind, the Church’s peace would, it is believed, already have been restored at the arrival of your envoys. For nearly all those who supply arms to iniquity among us are clerics. Some of them boast of familiarity with you and of the privilege of the Apostolic See, declaring that, whatever they do, they will answer to none but the Roman pontiff.

If this boast is true, it will stain the Roman Church’s reputation, and, God forbid, the honour of the whole Church will soon be overthrown, while all persons are encouraged to every act by the examples of those who enjoy privileges. With funds supplied from plunder, it is easy for them to make frequent journeys [Col. 0461A] and, though previously unknown and poor, to gain themselves name and profit by persistently soliciting courts, working, insofar as they can, to ensure that the Church never has peace.

For this reason Reginald of Salisbury and Richard Barre are now said to be hastening to you. What faith and moderation they possess, you will shortly hear, God willing, from your envoys’ reports. Meanwhile, let your fatherhood know for certain that they knowingly communicated with persons excommunicated by name. Indeed, the aforesaid Richard went to our archdeacon Geoffrey, whom he knew to be excommunicated, in order to support his error; and he freely associates with him and with other excommunicated persons.

We therefore beg your Holiness that, when they come to you, you treat them as sharers in the anathema, and do not admit their petitions before your envoys return. For if on this occasion you deal rather severely with these deceivers, by God’s favour you will achieve the peace desired.

## LETTER XVI. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

Up to now the king of England has despised the riches of your long-suffering—indeed, the abundance of divine goodness—ignorant or pretending not to know that your patience sought to call him back to repentance. He has turned a deaf ear to prayers and admonitions, boasting, to the dishonour of the Apostolic See and in insult to your blessed name, that you granted him a privilege by which he will remain safe, as long as he wishes, against us and the Church of Canterbury, [Col. 0461C] although he persecutes her and us more fiercely. And in order more easily to persuade everyone of a false and incredible matter, he has copies of the letters which you granted him against us—and would that they were not also against you—circulated throughout Germany, France, England, and various adjoining provinces.

Thus he repays your goodwill; thus he renders thanks for your gentleness: his later acts are always more atrocious than the former. Yet, God being our author, what we wish you had believed from the beginning has now been declared before all: our justice, the cause of our exile and proscription, and the direction of his whole intent.

For recently, at the second conference, in the hearing of the Most Christian king and all persons present on either side, he admitted that, after he had repeatedly rejected your threatening letters, he had at last scarcely received them; and that he asks nothing else of us but observance of his customs, which, as you have seen and may still observe, plainly conflict utterly with divine law and the sacred canons. At the insistence of the Most Christian king and the religious men whom you sent, with many intercessors employed, he agreed to say nothing of “customs”; but he changed the word, not his intention. For he required us to profess, simply and absolutely, on our word of truth, that we would do what our predecessors did. This alone, he said, was the way in which we could have our Church and peace in the realm—though not yet his favour.

He adds this because he thinks, by authority of your rescript, that we have been deprived of the power belonging to our office until he chooses to restore us to his favour. When the religious men, Simon, prior of Mont-Dieu, and Brother Bernard, presented this demand to us, we replied that we did not fully know in our conscience what our predecessors had done. Yet we knew from authentic writings that some of them had been exiled in a similar cause and had finally obtained this: that, just as kings claimed for themselves the rights they believed belonged to them, so the things of God should be rendered to God.

We declared ourselves ready for every service to him, even beyond what our predecessors had performed, provided our order was preserved. But to undertake new obligations, outside the Church’s form and never made by any of our predecessors, would be unlawful for us: both because the example would be destructive and because you yourself, when in the city of Sens you absolved us from the observance and obligation of those customs hateful to God and the Church, extorted by force and fear, had specifically forbidden us—with a grave rebuke first given, which, God being our author, will never fade from our mind—ever again to bind ourselves in a similar matter except with God’s honour and our order preserved.

You also added, if you please to remember, that not even for his own head ought a bishop bind himself except with God’s honour and his order preserved. We therefore promised the religious men that, if the king fulfilled your command by restoring to us his favour and peace, and restoring the Church with what he had taken from us and ours, we would devote all our strength to serving him and his children, provided God’s honour and our order were preserved. But we said that without your authority it was unlawful for us to alter the ecclesiastical form [Col. 0462C] which the whole Western Church observes and which is expressly set out even in those reprobate customs that are the cause of our exile.

For it states that those elected must, before consecration, swear to the king that they will be faithful to him concerning life, limbs, and earthly honour, with their order preserved. Why, then, are we alone compelled, in the deceptive obligation demanded from us, to omit the honour of God and the preservation of our order? What Christian has ever required this of a Christian?

He deceived the insistence of the religious men by varying answers; now affirming, now denying, he sent them away complaining that their labour and expense had been wasted. He nevertheless pretended that he would summon the bishops of England to consult them. But in truth he awaits the arrival of the envoys whom he has sent to you. For, as we have truly learned from persons who ought to be believed, they have boasted that, as on another occasion, by promises or threats they will obtain from you against us what the king desires.

Yet it is unbelievable that the Apostolic See should compel anyone to omit the honour of God or forbid mention of preserving his order. And certainly, if you send his envoys back confounded, as is just, you will free the Church of God and the reputation of the Apostolic See. Therefore act bravely, if it please you. For if you choose to terrify the ungodly man, we firmly believe that you will restore peace to the Church and a soul now perishing to God. You have experienced what gentleness has achieved with him. [Col. 0463A] Now take another course, and without doubt you will most swiftly triumph in the rigour of justice.

Demand what has been taken from us, down to the last farthing, lest the impunity of such great plunder, made known among contemporaries and posterity, grant boldness both to him and to his successors to offend similarly. For if we learn that he repents and wishes to enter upon the way of satisfaction, we may, under the guidance of your counsel, temper the rigour of law as we see expedient for God’s Church, ourselves, and future times. Otherwise, if he persists in crime and causes such scandal in the Church, by what right will he be absolved? For he is bound by God with the bonds of impenitence, more grievously and strictly fettered than Lazarus. If stolen property can be restored and is not restored, repentance is not performed but feigned.

There is one thing that he especially desires, and in which, God favouring us, iniquity lies to itself: if he saw mourning—may God avert it—in the Catholic Church, he would without hesitation subject the English Church, and indeed every church within his power, to his laws. But be certain of this: we cannot observe what he demands of us and also maintain faith and due obedience to the Apostolic See, for these are mutually opposed.

We also earnestly ask that, should our evildoers and excommunicated persons come or send to you, you do not cause them to be absolved to our prejudice; for if this had not been done on the other occasion, the Church would already enjoy its proper peace. Indeed, if he compels us—though, God favouring us, he will not do so even for temporal life—to enter this obligation, we have not forgotten what we swore to you and to the Roman Church when receiving the pallium. Emboldened by so great an example, he will bind not only bishops but the whole clergy in the same way. And it is easy for other princes to imitate his unpunished audacity. What he demands from us is not demanded in our land even from soldiers or peasants.

## LETTER XVII. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

If the malice of our adversaries had not blackened before you, holy Father, the cause of our exile, we firmly believe that the king of England would not have abused your patience for so long and with such impunity. But behold, God favouring us, the truth has been declared by the testimony of our persecutor himself.

For recently, when we, with knees bent, in all humility implored him before the Most Christian king, archbishops, bishops, counts, nobles, and all who were present, he declared that he sought nothing else from me than that I should promise, as priest and bishop, absolutely and precisely, upon my word of truth, to preserve the customs of his realm which our predecessors had observed toward their princes—as our envoys will faithfully explain to you.

May it therefore please your Holiness mercifully to hear the bearers of this letter, our faithful men and companions in our proscription, who were present at everything; and to provide swift medicine to the English Church, now at the point of death unless the right hand of God and yours [Col. 0464A] comes to its aid. For we have placed our words in their mouths.

The king of England moreover boasts that you have conferred on him a privilege such that, even if we return to our see, all our authority is void until he chooses to restore it to us. It has been unheard of among us from ancient times that any bishop should be compelled to bind himself to a secular prince beyond observance of what is contained in the form of fealty. We therefore fear that, if—God forbid, and by God’s aid may it always be far from us—a further obligation begins with us, the destructive precedent may infect other princes and involve not only our contemporaries but our successors.

It is clear, moreover, that if the customs demanded prevail, the authority of the Apostolic See in England will altogether vanish, or be reduced to the least degree. As is publicly known from the writings of our ancestors and the reports of elders, this would long ago have occurred had not the Church of Canterbury sought to oppose itself to princes for the faith of the Apostolic See and the Church’s liberty. For scarcely anyone has presided over that Church who has not either faced the sword for justice, endured the hardships of exile, or suffered the wrong of proscription. It is therefore astonishing, and worthy of every amazement, that the persecutor of the Apostolic Majesty rather than of our own name boasts that he has found and has more supporters among you in such a cause.

Nor need you henceforth fear that he will pass over to the schismatics; for Christ has so subdued him into the hand of his servant, the king of France, that he can no longer withdraw from that king’s allegiance.

## LETTER XVIII. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

[Col. 0464C]

The persecutor of the Church and of ourselves abuses your patience, not knowing or pretending not to know that your kindness bears with him in much gentleness in order that he may have time to repent; and that, if—God forbid—he persists in fury, the justice by which you will condemn him may be manifest before all nations. For whenever his envoys return from your Holiness, he becomes more insolent, rages more cruelly against God’s Church, and from the impunity in which he has long been exalted conceives greater audacity to offend, as though his works provoking inexorable judgment upon his own head were not manifest.

For John of Oxford, as though the man were not already mad enough, urged him still further upon his return; and he withdrew from us the obedience and reverence of our province, causing excommunicated persons to be absolved without oath or satisfaction. By what justice, let God see and judge. John Cumin followed him, boasting that he had obtained greater things. To withdraw the Most Christian king and the nobles of the kingdom of France from aiding us and our fellow-exiles, he travelled throughout France and burst into Burgundy, spreading in churches and noblemen’s houses that he was certain of our speedy deposition. Yet he said that he concealed the time and manner because he did not dare reveal the secret of the Apostolic See.

Those who returned most recently boast that the king has been granted a delay [Col. 0465A] and that you have suspended our authority, so that we cannot extend the hand of justice against either him or any person of his land on any grounds. The abbot of St Augustine’s also boasted that he had received from you the gift of a blessing, if it were safe for him to be tonsured. Would that he were made worthy by blessing of what is not yet believed in his own neighbourhood. They do not conceal that, unless their petitions were advanced, they declared hostilities against the Catholic Church and left the curia in indignation, but were recalled to the curia through the zeal and diligence of your brethren, who are regarded as pillars of the Church. They proclaim these things at crossroads, so that their greatness of spirit may be known—and perhaps so that the rulers of nations may be incited to similar conduct.

And indeed, holy Father, the power of our office can easily be suspended. But the right hand of God, which already brings down the heads of tyrants, cannot be restrained. Your faithful people fear that, while you await more favourable times for administering justice, the best opportunities may slip away. For they are in a narrow place; and he who terrifies others is himself more afraid. The Lord says: “Be strong and be stouthearted; do not fear their faces, for I am with you.”

The boasts of the king’s envoys would not be believed, were it not that a cardinal holds the same opinion and has informed us by word and letter. We have therefore sent your most beloved son, most faithful to you and proved to us in every respect, our companion in tribulation, Master Lombard. He knows fully our miseries and the malice of the opposing party, and will most faithfully report what is said in the French Church about the things done against us. If it please you, hear him as you would hear us, for no one more faithful to you and the Church, or more useful to us, could be found.

Hear then, if it please you, this witness of our conscience, observer of the Church’s miseries, defender of truth, lover of justice, and most proven son of the Apostolic See in affection and devotion. We send him so that at least through him consolation may be given to the English Church, so weakened and afflicted that henceforth she cannot set forth her needs by the journeys of envoys, but is compelled to lay them before God alone and entrust her cause to him.

The persecutors of the Church await and desire that divine mercy be withdrawn from them: they wish to see, at your passing, the grief of the faithful who mourn, so that after your days they may subject the Church to slavery with no one opposing them. For this is the purpose of the delays they seek against God and justice. But your divine discernment, most holy Father, will take more diligent care to punish such great enormities before the end of life, lest on the day of judgment you be compelled to render an account for overlooking injury done to God.

## LETTER XIX. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT
My soul, Father, is in bitterness, since, together with my fellow-exiles in misery, from the time when by your letters—which, as you saw fit, suspended us—I became “the reproach of men and the outcast of the people.” And what burns my soul more bitterly still, the Church of God has been exposed to the will of the wicked. The persecutor of the Church and of ourselves had given certain hope of peace to great men—the Count of Flanders and other magnates of the realm; but when his envoys returned, relying on your authority, he closed against us every path to reconciliation. What then were those men and our other friends to do, struck down and repulsed by your action as though by the club of Hercules? Would that your ear might hear what bishops, nobles, and the peoples of both kingdoms say upon this matter, and your eye behold the scandal with which the Gallican Church is filled. What will that man not henceforth hope for, who has thus outwitted, through men distinguished only by crimes or other stains, those who possess the key of knowledge; who has overthrown the stewards of justice; who terrifies with empty threats [Col. 0466A] and drives the majesty of the Apostolic See before him? For there is no doubt that John of Oxford has deceived you—yet with impunity. Certainly, to be deceived at the outset, especially in so grave a matter, is a misfortune. Even if it is passed over, the English Church will feel it painfully throughout our lifetime. But that venerable abbot of St Augustine—formerly a runaway monk and excommunicated for his own deserts—who now wastes and defiles the church over which he presides, together with the other envoys of the king, has now deceived your Holiness far more grievously.

Behold: that king, who desires nothing but either your death or ours, has attained his desire, hoping—may God avert it—that, during the course of this delay, one of these two things will happen. Yet you urge us meanwhile to have patience. Father, you do not consider how costly this “meanwhile” is to the Church and how greatly it diminishes your honour. Meanwhile, he converts vacant bishoprics and abbeys to his own abuses and does not permit pastors to be appointed in them. Meanwhile, he rages with irrevocable fury against every parish, church, venerable place, and the whole clergy. Meanwhile, both he and the other persecutors of the Church make what is lawful equal to their own pleasure.
