Who meanwhile will care for Christ’s sheep and snatch them from the jaws of wolves, who no longer merely roam about, but have entered the very folds, biting, tearing, and killing, while no one protests? From which shepherd have you not taken away his voice? Which bishop is not suspended in our suspension? For it was imposed without precedent and without merit; and it will give both him and other princes, in your time and after your days, boldness to trample upon the Church, proscribe the innocent, and declare hostility against the Roman Church unless it connives at or overlooks their acts and lends authority to their iniquities. [Col. 0466B]

For behold, they have before their eyes the example of your dispensation; and there is no doubt that, unless your hand acts more swiftly, he and his descendants will draw it into a consequence and almost turn it into a privilege: namely, that for any crime no sentence of excommunication or interdict may be pronounced against the king, persons of the realm, or the land without authorization from the Apostolic See. In truth, in the course of time wickedness may gain such strength from this precedent that not even the Roman pontiff will find in the whole kingdom anyone willing or daring to obey him against the king or princes. This is what they are pursuing; this is what gave occasion to our exile. For it is not—as I hear certain of our lords, your brothers, whisper—that the deprivation from you of the visitations of England, which had customarily been made in the time of your predecessors, should be imputed to me. Rather it should have been imputed to me and to Christ’s poor, my fellow-exiles, that anything at all was reserved to you in that land.

Let the little book of condemned customs be read, if you please—the customs which he asserts against the Church and which are the cause of our exile—and you will clearly see how, before we made proclamation, he shut the mouths of those appealing to you; how he forbade ecclesiastical persons to cross the sea without sworn security; how he strangled the rights of elections; how he drew every judgment, ecclesiastical as well as secular, to the examination of his own court; and how, in those same customs, he cut the throat of every ecclesiastical liberty. Who, in your time or that of your predecessors, could obtain justice against him by petition, payment, or right when appealing to the Roman Church? The Bishop of Exeter still pays the price of his predecessor’s appeal, grieving that the church of Bosham was taken from his church contrary to all justice. The Bishop of Salisbury, whom the king now pretends to favour because of the crime of disobedience, loses the castle of Devizes and many other possessions of his church because, bound by the sacred obligation of an oath to make restitution, he dared to summon him by letters of your predecessors Anastasius and Adrian. [Col. 0466C]

A day would not suffice if I wished to recount similar acts undertaken against every individual church of the kingdom: in this way possessions have been taken from some, and liberty has been destroyed for all alike, so that no hope of deliverance has been left to anyone. Let that book, reprobate before God, be read, I say; and let our lords who favour the king see what privilege, what prerogative, is reserved to them in his land. But perhaps they say that the book was composed from hatred of my name. Yet from the beginning of his assumption of power he has persecuted the liberty of the Church as though by hereditary right. Was I archbishop when his father forbade the envoys of blessed Eugenius to enter his land? Was I archbishop when Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Angelo, foreseeing this man’s tyranny, persuaded Lord Eugenius not to permit the coronation of Eustace, son of King Stephen, saying that it is easier to hold a ram by its horns than a lion by its tail? This history is known to you. And consider what letters he then obtained who is now Archbishop of York and who, together with that king, persecutes my name—or rather strives to extinguish ecclesiastical liberty. Was I archbishop when the king, because of the affront of an appeal, transferred the church of Bosham to the Bishop of Lisieux, so that he might defend it against the justice of the Church of Exeter by his grammatical learning and skill in pleading?

And what did the Bishop of Chichester accomplish against the abbot of Battle, who, relying upon apostolic privileges, had cited him in court and declared the abbot excommunicated? He was immediately compelled, before all, to communicate with that same man without any absolution and to receive him with the kiss of peace. For so it pleased the king and the court, which dared contradict him in nothing. And this, most holy Father, occurred in the time of your predecessor and ours. Let those who say that all these evils happened because of hatred for me state, if they know, who in his kingdom, during his reign, has obtained justice from him or concerning those whom he wished to protect by authority of the Apostolic See. Certainly, so far as I remember, they will not produce even one; and they will be able to name many who suffered peril under him because of hatred for the Roman name. [Col. 0466D]

Why was Achard, abbot of St Victor, elected bishop of Séez, not permitted to be ordained? Because Pope Adrian had confirmed his election. Why did the king allow that same man later to become Bishop of Avranches? Plainly because no election had preceded the king’s will. Likewise Frogerius was not elected to the Church of Séez but intruded into it; and I had not yet been promoted. Nor do I doubt that the dispute between us concerning the liberty of the Church would already have been extinguished, had he not found in the Roman Church patrons of his will—indeed, lest I call it perversity. May God repay them as is expedient for His Church and for them, and may the most powerful and most just Judge decide between us. Certainly I should have had no need of their patronage had I wished to expose the Church of God and acquiesce in his will. For I could have flourished, abounded in the riches and delights of the realm, been feared, honoured, and revered by all, and provided at my pleasure for my own in worldly delight and glory.

But because the Lord called me—unworthy and most wretched sinner though I am, yet flourishing in the world above all my fellow-countrymen—to the governance of His Church, I chose, His grace going before and cooperating, to be lowly in His house and to end my life in exile, proscription, and utmost misery rather than cause loss to ecclesiastical liberty or prefer human traditions, especially unjust ones, to the law of God. Let those do this who promise themselves long days and look forward, on the testimony of their merits, to better times. For I am certain that my days are short; and if I keep silence concerning the wicked man’s iniquity, his blood will be required from my hand by Him before whom, without the assistance of human patronage, I must render account for things committed and omitted. [Col. 0467A]

There gold and silver will not profit, nor gifts which blind even the eyes of the wise. Soon we shall stand before Christ’s tribunal. By His majesty and dreadful judgment I entreat you, as father, lord, and supreme judge on earth, to render justice to His Church and to me against those who seek her life in order to take it away. Do not permit her any longer to be so shamefully trampled beneath the feet of the ungodly. I have been so reduced and afflicted that, supported by another’s table and by the sustenance of the Most Christian King, I can no longer press you through envoys, for I have absolutely nothing with which to provide for them.

May it therefore please your Majesty to end the misery of the Church of Canterbury and remove the scandals which have lately arisen, are sprouting, and give wicked men boldness to sin in both kingdoms: by absolving the child of your Holiness, and by writing to the Most Christian King and to the Gallican Church that, unless the King of England obeys your admonitions and restores peace to us, together with what he has taken away and the liberty of the Church, from that point you permit us to exercise against him and his land the power of our office; and you wish the sentence which, with the Lord as author, we shall pronounce to be inviolably observed by all bishops. [Col. 0467B]

## LETTER XX. TO THE SAME PERSON

How many and how grievous distresses and tribulations we have now, for almost seven years, miserably endured while striving in prolonged exile, together with a numerous and innumerable multitude of Christ’s poor, to defend the liberty of God’s holy Church, your prudent discernment, most holy Father, ought to know more fully; nor can we easily believe that what we have endured can escape your mind. Rather, dearest Father, it ought to remain rooted in your memory with whom also, my dearest lord—that is, with the King of the English—we contended in struggle almost unto death. Your experience knows this more fully, for you too, like us, have learned his craftiness and deceits through experience of events.

With respect to our own affairs or those of others who may henceforth be willing to cross over to you for the business of our Church and ourselves, we have been so exhausted by long exile that we can scarcely find anyone—indeed, in truth, no one at all. Therefore, dearest lord and Father, falling at the knees of your Holiness, we beseech you for the English Church, for ourselves, and for our temporal life: graciously and fully to grant the petitions which we have submitted to your Holiness through Master Lombard and our envoys whom we sent to him and to your fatherhood; and to deign henceforth to send us aid as speedily as possible for the support of God’s Church and of our life, lest we, and the Western Church, fall disgracefully, overthrown by the tyrant. [Col. 0467C]

We have sent to your Holiness the bearer of this letter, an honourable and religious man, earnestly asking and beseeching you to receive him kindly in our place; and that what we inform the Lord Bishop of Ostia and Master Lombard should be communicated to your fatherhood through him, you may, since you desire provision alike for God’s Western Church—and especially for Canterbury—and for our life, fully and entirely grant as we request, and deign to send it back promptly, fulfilled, through our envoy. If Master Lombard is present, let this letter remain with him; but if not, with our lord and father, the Lord Bishop of Ostia, or with Gratian, son of grace. May your Holiness, most holy Father, prosper for longer times. [Col. 0467D]

## LETTER XXI. [TO THE SAME PERSON]

The Count of Troyes is attempting to exempt the Church of St Stephen from the jurisdiction of the bishop and from subjection to the mother church. We do not believe that his will can be fulfilled unless something which belongs to the greater Church by common right is taken away from it; unless the privilege which your kindness rightly granted it is, not without suspicion of wrong, revoked and made void; and unless, at peril to souls, freedom to sin is extended into still further license. For you know, we think, what manners prevail in that city and what men especially flourish there. If the small degree of fear and shame which now hangs near them from episcopal authority is withdrawn, it is to be feared that crimes, through impunity, will be emboldened to the dishonour of the Roman Church and—what is more to be feared—to the peril of the salvation of those who seek or bring about this emancipation; and consequently that all decency and religion will be overthrown. [Col. 0470A]

Moreover, not merely one church will be taken from him: episcopal authority will be so mutilated that he will scarcely be able to correct any enormity throughout the city. For all will immediately take refuge in the sanctuary of that church, where they will be protected by the favour of secular power and defended by the safeguard of the Apostolic See. To speak our mind plainly, it would have been more just to provide that bishop with neighbouring helpers so that this threshing-floor might be cleansed of filth, than to weaken him so that he cannot exercise the care of souls required by his office. Indeed, in these days one bishop, however religious, can scarcely suffice for this task.

Certainly, among us no precedent for such emancipation is either heard of or read; and would that it may always remain foreign to the holiness of your time! It had been hoped that you would console and strengthen in some other way the devotion of the bishop, who has always been dutiful and faithful to you, and whom you know to dwell among ostriches and scorpions, so that he might stretch more powerfully the sword of the dove to crush the necks of Christ’s enemies, recall unbelievers to the wisdom of the just, and—whatever others may say—we still trust that you will rather give strength to the bishop, that he may be strengthened in the things of God, than take from his Church, to such ruin of souls, what it is known to have possessed throughout the tenure of this bishop. [Col. 0470B]

We therefore beseech your Majesty with all the affection we can that you preserve intact for the oft-mentioned bishop his right in the aforesaid matter, and order his petitions, insofar as you see they serve his need and the Church’s advantage, to be carried into effect. God knows that we have written these things more from regard for your reputation and the honour of the Church than from favour for the aforesaid bishop or hatred of the count. God and conscience witness that we love him as a noble man and a friend with sincere charity in Christ; and in other matters, where the Church is not harmed and your reputation is not endangered, we desire and ask you to grant his requests in the Lord.

We are bound to you, Father, by the bond of fidelity and, more than that, of true charity; nor can we keep silence with a safe conscience when we see and believe that anything is being attempted to the detriment of your honour. Whatever you do in great matters is consecrated to posterity through the ages which succeed one another; for as soon as such acts come to the knowledge of the churches, they are entered into annals and mark the sequence of notable chronicles. If these considerations should not move your Holiness—which is not credible—let at least fear of the divine judgment come before your reason. It follows by every right from the fact that, in almost all churches thus emancipated, regular discipline languishes, religion grows cold, vices multiply, and enormity prevails, because the authority of correction has been taken from neighbouring bishops; and the Roman pontiff is far away, unable to see or hear the frequent excesses arising in his churches. If at length he should perhaps hear of them, he generally has no clear knowledge of the cause, and he entrusts investigation and correction to others—sometimes negligent, sometimes corrupt—as they please; and, frequently occupied with greater or personal affairs, he cannot attend to lesser and foreign matters. Meanwhile souls perish, for whom he must render account at the strict judgment. [Col. 0470C]

## LETTER XXII. TO THE SAME PERSON

Your dignity has often offered prayers to the illustrious Count of Flanders and his most distinguished chancellor Robert, provost of St Omer, for the relief of the need of ourselves and our people; and they have always taken care to receive them devoutly and fulfil them generously. For, to say nothing at present of ourselves, to whom their kindness has never failed in so many extremities of distress and throughout so long a bitterness of proscription and exile, all our people who have fled to their clemency have been received by them with such humanity and refreshed by such indulgent generosity that they seem to receive not poor, exiled, and proscribed persons, but to venerate the Lord of Majesty in their own household.

Yet although the aforesaid count surpasses the other princes of the realm after the Most Christian King in nobility of birth; and, what is more, in strength of character, cultivation of peace and justice, glory in military exercise, extent of principality, and abundance of wealth: nevertheless the devotion he bears to the Apostolic See, the reverence he shows to churches and ecclesiastical men, the liberality he practices toward the holy, and the compassion he extends to Christ’s desolate members must be attributed above all to the provost. He gives wholesome and honourable counsel to his lord, and by his judgment not only the count’s household but so great a principality is most excellently governed. For the administration of all things depends upon his decision; and if anything has been undertaken against the Church, it is openly and prudently restored to the rule of law. [Col. 0470D]

Therefore the Lord is to be praised, who chose such a counsellor beforehand; and he too is to be praised, who directs the way of the Lord along straight paths. Both are faithful and devoted to you; indeed, throughout the whole kingdom—this we say from heartfelt conviction—there can nowhere be found men like them who desire with such devotion and effectiveness to serve your commands in all things. Presenting a small petition to your Holiness, they believe themselves able to be aided by our intercessions, as we too presume upon your mercy; and if they had asked a great thing from your Majesty, they would be worthy to be heard.

They ask, and we join them in petition with all the earnestness we can, that you grant the provost a prebend in the Church of St Martin of Tours. We do not doubt that this will be pleasing to your son, the Most Christian King, and we believe it will benefit that church. For he will powerfully address its many needs and, relying on the strength of friends, will often, with God’s help, snatch prey from the very jaws of the mighty. He knocks at your door so that, avoiding the secret backdoor of Simon by the safeguard of due procedure, he may be admitted through the apostolic hand—a way by which many are not ashamed or afraid to steal in. For that road lies open and has been worn smooth for many by use and age; but a just and God-fearing man does not walk upon it. [Col. 0471A]

Father, in granting this prebend you will give it not to one person but to many, among whom are we ourselves; for what is found among the goods of the aforesaid provost is the common patrimony of Christ’s proscribed people. While he lives, no one throughout the count’s land will dare devise anything that harms the Church or ought to offend your Holiness. Therefore, by one small benefit you will bind to yourselves so great a count and all that he can do, and will make the provost, from your faithful servant, one purchased for yourselves. [Col. 0471B]

## LETTER XXIII. TO THE SAME PERSON

The venerable lord of Sens—a man who, we hope, with God’s help will illuminate the Gallican Church by the rays of his virtues—desired, as we have learned, to come to the Apostolic See in order to receive from your Holiness the grace of consecration in accordance with his intention. But your most devoted son, the Most Christian King of the Franks, fearing on the one hand the dangers of the journey and openly setting forth on the other the necessities of the kingdom, advised, in the presence of the bishops of the province of Sens and the magnates of the realm, that the elect postpone his journey and that his consecration be performed rather than delayed, as we have learned from those who were present.

Thus drawn and in some manner compelled by a certain force of charity and the prompting of public necessity, he was consecrated by his own synod, in the presence of the king, queen, and leading men of the realm. They said that safety was being withdrawn from Church and kingdom if they were deprived, even for an hour, of so great a man’s counsel and aid—especially amid such a clash of kingdoms and the machinations of the Germans, who, under the pretext of a feigned advantage, by deceitful promises are attempting to renew the fires of the schism which is now almost extinguished. [Col. 0471C]

Would that your eyes, Father, had seen how prudently and effectively the lord of Sens lately frustrated their designs. For very many magnates, and even certain men of great name whom we presently leave unnamed, advised that the wishes of the Germans be granted and alliances made with them. And because the machinations of the schismatics do not cease to solicit the Most Christian King by frequent embassies and great promises, and because they strive to overthrow the faith of many bishops as well as magnates, neither he nor others of sound judgment have thought it safe to allow a man of such fidelity and prudence to depart from them, particularly during this storm. May it therefore please your Holiness to take favourably what has been done concerning the aforesaid Archbishop of Sens, beneficially, as is publicly hoped; and to honour a man most faithful to you and most useful to the Church of God, both by the grant of the pallium due to him and by the conferment of privileges. The more authority this person receives from your Majesty, the more effectively he will be able to serve the honour and interests of the Apostolic See. For the greater he is, the more the Roman Church will flourish through him in the kingdom of the Franks. [Col. 0471D]

## LETTER XXIV. TO THE SAME PERSON

A most eloquent writer testifies that the success of an orator is promoted above all when he has foreknowledge of the character of the judge and hearers and regulates the work of his speech according to their quality. I think that this principle may reasonably be extended to many other matters, especially since no one ought to be ignorant of the condition of the person with whom he enters into an agreement. Above all, if events turn out contrary to expectation or opinion, he ought to blame himself who preferred to entrust a common business, according to his own judgment, to the hands of fortune rather than, after considering other circumstances and especially the character of his partner, measure its resources and outcome.

Father, if your discernment had attended to this from the beginning in the matter of the Church and the King of the English, the English Church would never have fallen into such calamities, nor would the Gallican Church—of which we cannot speak without grief—be attacked or oppressed by so ruinous an example. Yet many of our faithful friends warned you that the King of the English can indeed be overcome more easily by severity, but cannot be softened by any gentleness, services, or benefits. He flatters those whom he fears; he honours with services those whom he desires to deprive of possessions, character, or the title of a more honourable reputation. But then you were unwilling to believe those who warned you. If the public testimony of all did not move you, let at least experience itself now persuade and compel you to change your judgment: answer the persecutor of the Church according to his deserts; and let him who despises divine and apostolic authority feel that there is a prophet in Israel and that Peter’s zeal has not yet gone into exile from the Apostolic See. [Col. 0472A]

For if he is an enemy of the Church and a fomentor of schism, he must be punished and crushed. If he is a friend, he ought to be chastised and corrected because of his services. But there is a proverb: “The Greeks bearing gifts are to be feared.” Certainly, the envoys of the King of the English are in some fashion Greeks; and, though not joined to them by descent, they resemble Sinon in craft and imitation. They promised you satisfaction in order to prolong the calamity of God’s Church and our exile. They obtained that the king should still be summoned through the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Nevers, as though he had not already been summoned enough and his wickedness had not provoked judgment. For heaven and earth cry out against him, and only the cardinals who sit at your side do not hear. Yet whoever is deaf here will hear at the judgment the harsh word: “Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire.”

The aforesaid archbishop and bishop, exceeding the terms of your mandate, grant delays, comply with the king’s will, and, whether by error or deceit—as you can perceive from the letters which we send you—make perpetual the Church’s calamity. [Col. 0472B]

The Bishop of London, whom you ordered to be absolved in accordance with your will and who was absolved as much contrary to justice as contrary to the form which you set down, obstructs both the peace of the Church and ours. Led by the Archbishop of York and assisted by the king’s clerks, whom you have customarily received more graciously and heard more effectively, he schemes against his profession so that, once the king’s son has been crowned against God by the hand of the aforesaid Archbishop of York, the Church of Canterbury may never have peace. You had indeed forbidden this to be done; but they, on the contrary, boast that they have obtained from you permission for it to be done, whether by the hand of the Archbishop of York or through the ministry of whatever bishop the king may choose. Because the bishops of our province refuse this, the Bishop of Séez, standard-bearer of those who do not fear God, boasts that he will do it, should the others fail, by your familiar command. He has already crossed the sea for this purpose. Since there is no help from elsewhere, may the Lord hedge in his ways with thorns.

We have placed the rest in the mouth of the bearer of this letter. We beseech you with all the affection we can that you put faith in him regarding our affairs, and, since the need of the Church and our own need demand it, order the petitions which we send to your Holiness through him to be carried into effect more swiftly. Whatever they may do, know that neither death nor life, nor things present nor things to come, will, by God’s grace, separate us from your charity, obedience, and service; for we know without doubt that your spirit does not rest in those who, through respect of persons and gifts, give their favouring patronage to wrongs and take their portion with the ungodly, seeing a sacrilegious man and running with him. [Col. 0472C]

May your name be blessed for ever, and may He more swiftly and effectively console the Church, for which you must render account. [Col. 0472D]

## LETTER XXV. TO THE SAME PERSON

To the most serene lord and dearest father, ALEXANDER, by God’s grace Supreme Pontiff: THOMAS, humble minister of the holy Church of Canterbury, greeting and every obedience with utmost devotion.

God looked with the eye of compassion upon His Church, and at last changed her sorrow into joy. Nor is there any doubt, Father, that if we who spoke the truth had been believed from the beginning, the horns of those who were tossing, battering, and wounding the Church with various blows [Col. 0475A] would have been blunted, so that, once her liberty had been utterly exterminated and the authority of the divine law annulled, the customs—or rather, the abuses—of ancient tyrants might prevail; the Roman pontiff might be unknown in England; and the privileges of Christ’s bride might be erased without hope of restoration. For behold: upon receiving your latest letters, in which you informed the lord king of England that you would spare him no further, just as you had not spared Frederick, called emperor, when he learned that his land, all evasions removed, was to be subjected to an interdict, and that any bishops who perhaps did not obey were to be suspended and excommunicated, he immediately made peace with us, to the honour of God and, as we hope, the great benefit of the Church.

For concerning the customs which he had been accustomed to maintain with such obstinacy [Col. 0475B], he did not venture even to utter a word. He demanded no oath from us or from any of ours. He granted us the possessions of our Church which he had taken on the occasion of this dispute, as we had set them out in a schedule; he promised peace, security, return for all our people, and the kiss of peace—if only we were willing to press him so far that he should appear not merely defeated on every point, but should be called perjured by those who had heard him swear that on that day he would not receive us with the kiss.

But after taking the counsel of many wise men, and especially of the lord of Sens, who was pursuing our peace more anxiously and effectively than the rest, we went with him to the king’s conference. By God’s doing—God having removed all those who were accustomed to circumvent Your Holiness by various deceits—we found the king so changed [Col. 0475C] that, to the amazement of those standing round, his mind seemed in no respect hostile to peaceful counsels. For as soon as he saw us approaching at a distance, he sprang from the crowd around him and hurried to meet us. With his head uncovered, he forestalled us, who were eager to burst into words of greeting, by greeting us first. After a few words had passed, with only ourselves and the lord of Sens present, he drew us aside—he turning away, while all were astonished—and spoke with us for a long time with such familiarity that it might have seemed that no discord had ever existed between us.

Almost all present were amazed with the greatest joy; tears streamed down the cheeks of many [Col. 0475D]; they glorified God and blessed holy Mary Magdalene, on whose feast the king turned from his former ways, in order to restore joy to his whole land and return peace to the Church. We rebuked him with the moderation proper to the occasion, plainly setting forth the course he had pursued and the dangers threatening him on every side. We begged and warned him to return to his senses; by producing worthy fruits of repentance and making satisfaction to the Church, which he had injured no little, through a manifest recompense of good, he should cleanse his conscience and redeem his reputation. For he was suffering grave loss in both respects, rather through the counsels of wicked advisers than from an impulse of his own will.

When he heard all this not merely patiently but kindly, and promised amendment [Col. 0476A], we added that his salvation, the safety of his children, and the preservation and indemnity of the authority divinely granted to him required him to make fuller satisfaction in this matter to his mother, the holy Church of Canterbury, in which he had lately injured her most grievously. For he had caused his son to be crowned in outrageous violation of the most ancient right of our Church, through the usurpation of the archbishop of York, who, contrary to the most ancient custom, after your prohibition, and even in another province, had in excessively blind and reckless ambition presumed to perform this consecration.

He resisted a little, though protesting that he did not then, nor would thereafter, intend to contend. “Who,” he said, “crowned King William, who subjected England to himself, and the kings who succeeded him? Was it not the archbishop of York, or another bishop, as pleased the man who was to be crowned king?” To this we replied, as is clear from the well-known history of our people, that at the time when England was conquered by the Normans, the Church of Canterbury had no bishop of its own, but was held, as if captive, by one Stigand. He had occupied it, as also the churches of Winchester, London, Worcester, and Ely, by the force of public authority and of his friends, contrary to the prohibition of the Roman pontiff, being deprived of communion and favour with the Apostolic See. By the command of that see, he was captured by the aforesaid king and died in prison. Owing to that necessity, on that occasion—something neither read nor heard of either before or after—the archbishop of York, who was held in better repute, placed the crown upon that king.

But Lanfranc consecrated his son, King William, surnamed Rufus from his colour, as king, in the presence of Thomas, archbishop of York, who claimed no share in that office. After his death, when Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, was in exile for the same cause as we are, one of the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury, namely Gerard of Hereford, acting in the place of his then absent archbishop, consecrated King Henry without objection from the archbishop of York. But when blessed Anselm returned from exile, King Henry came to him, handing him the diadem and asking him to crown him, and not to impute it to him that, constrained by the needs of the realm [Col. 0476D], he had not waited for him. For before all he acknowledged that it was the dignity of the Church of Canterbury to anoint and consecrate the kings of England. Appeased by this satisfaction, the holy archbishop approved what his suffragan had done and placed the crown upon the king.

Why, then, was the archbishop of York silent on that occasion and endured a suffragan of the Church of Canterbury being preferred before him? Would Thomas the elder, who governed the Church of York and, swelling with the abundance of letters and friends against Lanfranc of Canterbury, had devised many troubles and greatly enlarged his church—would he have kept silent, yielding to a poor bishop, unless he had been certain of the primacy and dignity of the archbishop of Canterbury?

Further, it is absolutely certain that, thirty-six years later, King Stephen, your predecessor, was consecrated by our predecessor William, in the presence of Thurstan, archbishop of York [Col. 0477A], who neither involved himself in the business nor objected. After Stephen had died nineteen years later, Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, of good memory—who, for your advancement, endured with all his people innumerable labours, irreparable losses, and many perils dreadful to remember or recount, and restored to the children of your grandfather the kingdom that had already passed into another family—anointed and crowned you king. Roger of York, who is now archbishop, was present, as you know; he neither assisted nor objected, nor did anything except what the least of bishops might do: clothed in sacred vestments, he stood by and witnessed the solemnity.

Why, then, through such easiness of spirit—or rather through the perversity of your advisers—have you despoiled your mother, the Church of Canterbury, without investigation of the case, of an ancient right which she is known to have possessed without challenge for more than eighty years? Did you wish to perpetuate enmities between the Church and your children? Or, if the archbishop of York was to be allowed such presumption as to confer the rite of consecration upon a new king, why, passing beyond his own province, did he invade ours? Why did you drive both him and our suffragans into the crime of disobedience? For they had received the pope’s prohibition that they should in no way presume to do this in our absence.

Finally, if you were hurrying to complete the appointment of your son and his consecration [Col. 0477C], why did you not take care to exclude from the solemnity of so great a sacrament those whom you knew had been individually excommunicated by the mouth of the supreme pontiff and by us? Did the consecration not seem fit to be performed without a share in execration?

After carefully and modestly laying before him these matters and many others relevant to this point, which the brevity of a letter does not permit, we earnestly asked him to repair this loss inflicted upon us, for the love of God, for his own salvation, and for the safety of his children; and to correct the excess of so great a presumption. But he answered that he was secure against this petition of ours by virtue of your mandate, which he had obtained long before; and he produced letters on the matter establishing that the bishops who were to perform this rite had been granted permission for him to have his son crowned by whichever bishop he wished.

In reply, we begged him to recall when and why he had obtained the letters by which he sought to defend his own excess and that of the bishops. For it was established that they had been obtained while the Church of Canterbury was vacant, for the purpose of preventing the archbishop of York, should the said Church of Canterbury remain vacant for a longer time, from daring to aspire, before the other bishops of our province, to crown the new king. And, my lord king, that you may recall this more faithfully and intimately: did you not then openly assert that you would rather have your son beheaded than have the often-mentioned archbishop of York lay heretical hands upon his head [Col. 0478A]?

It is certainly true that a later mandate derogates from an earlier one. Grant, then, that you obtained such letters at that time: ours, being later, ought to have overridden them. From this you and other wise men know how much weight should be attached to that which has been usurped contrary to right—especially since a king’s consecration, like the other sacraments, has its cause and derives its whole substance from law. Nor should these words appear to mean that we wish your son to be degraded or diminished in any respect. We desire his success and an increase in his glory, and shall labour for it by every means in the Lord; but we seek that you may avert from us and from them alike the indignation of almighty God and of the saints who rest in the Church of Canterbury and have been grievously wronged.

We do not believe this can be accomplished except through fitting satisfaction; for it has been unheard of for ages that anyone should injure the Church of Canterbury and not be corrected or crushed by Christ the Lord. The king then added, with cheerful countenance and pleasant voice: “If you love my son, you do what you ought by a double right. For I too gave him to you as a son, and, as you may remember, you received him from my hand. And he loves you with such affection that he cannot look upon any of your enemies with a favourable eye. He would already have restrained them, had reverence and fear of my name not hindered him. But I know that, as soon as he has time and opportunity, he will avenge you upon them more severely even than is proper. Nor do I doubt that the Church of Canterbury is the noblest of all churches in the West, and I do not wish it to be deprived of its right [Col. 0478C]. Rather, according to your counsel, I shall endeavour that it be relieved in this matter as well and recover its former dignity in every respect. And, God favouring me, I shall answer those who have hitherto betrayed both me and you as the deserts of traitors require.”

When I dismounted from my horse and humbled myself at his feet, he seized the stirrup and compelled me to mount; and, seeming to weep, he said: “Why say more? My lord archbishop, let us restore our former affections to one another, and let each render the other whatever good he can; let us be altogether forgetful of the preceding hatred. But I ask you: show me honour before those who are looking on from a distance.” Then, going over to them—for he saw there a few whom the bearer of this letter will identify, lovers of discord and instigators of hatred—he said, in order to close the mouths both of them and of all others against speaking evil: “If, when I find the archbishop ready for every good thing, I do not in turn treat him well, then I shall be worse than other men and shall prove true the evil things said of me. Nor could I judge any other counsel more honourable or more useful than to strive to anticipate him in kindness and surpass him in charity as well as benefits.”

Almost all who were present received the king’s speech with the greatest rejoicing. He therefore sent his bishops to us to urge us to make our petition before everyone. Had we trusted the counsel of some of them, we should have committed both ourselves and the entire cause of the Church wholly to his arbitration. For from the beginning until now iniquity has gone forth from his scribes and Pharisees [Col. 0479A], and has prevailed through the authority of the elders, who ought to have governed the people. But blessed be God, who did not permit our soul to enter into their counsel or allow us to expose the Church’s liberty or God’s justice to the will of any human being.

Having dismissed them, and deliberated with the lord of Sens and Christ’s poor companions in our pilgrimage and exile, we firmly resolved neither to commit to his arbitration the question of the customs, nor the losses he had inflicted on our Church, nor the complaint concerning the usurped consecration, nor any injury to ecclesiastical liberty or our honour. So, approaching the king and his party, we humbly begged through the mouth of the lord of Sens, who was the bearer of our words [Col. 0479B], that he restore to us his favour, peace, and security, both to ourselves and our people; restore the Church of Canterbury and its possessions, except those which he had read out in the schedule; and mercifully repair what had been presumptuously done against us and our Church at his son’s coronation. We promised him love and honour, and whatever service an archbishop can render, in the Lord, to a king and prince.

He received the proposal favourably, consented, and received us and our people who were present into his favour. Since you had not commanded him to restore the things taken from us and ours, and since it could not be obtained from us—and, with God as author, cannot be obtained—that we should relinquish them, their recovery has, according to your mandate, been deferred, not abandoned. For if you had commanded their restoration with the force expressed in your latest letters [Col. 0479C], without doubt he would have made satisfaction and would have given posterity an example of perpetual benefit to the whole Church of God, and especially to the Apostolic See.

At last, after conferring with us much and long, and after the two of us had spoken almost alone until evening, according to the custom of former intimacy, we agreed that, when he departed, we should return to the most Christian king [of France] and our other benefactors to give thanks, and should return to the king himself when matters had been settled, remaining with him for some time before returning to England, so that all might know into what great familiarity and favour he had received us.

We shall remain in France until our messengers return, whom we sent to recover our possessions; for it is not our intention [Col. 0479D] to return to him while he has withheld even a footstep of the Church’s land. For in the restoration of our possessions we shall easily perceive with what sincerity he acts toward us. Yet we do not fear that he will fail to fulfil his promise, unless he is hindered by advisers whom the sting of a corrupt conscience does not permit to rest. To prevent themselves from being caught in the works of their own hands, they seek to secure pardon for their errors through impunity, under the authority and protection of royal majesty.

They strive to force us into the lot of Balaam’s followers, so that, by making alive souls that do not live, we may absolve without repentance and confession of error criminals caught in their wickedness. God neither granted that power to others nor reserved it for Himself. Unless we consent, they contrive to break the peace and concord made with the lord king. But, God being our author, not even thus will they lead us to set ourselves in opposition to the Most High and vainly boast that we make alive those whom He puts to death, or put to death those whom He makes alive. For it is certain that no pastor’s sentence is valid by the truest right if it is rejected by divine judgment.

Nevertheless, at the very time of our departure, whether envying the peace or wishing to provide for his friends and dependants, the bishop of Lisieux, at the urging, as is said, of Geoffrey, archdeacon of Canterbury, pressed this point rather cleverly and insistently in the presence of the king, bishops, and nobles. He said that, just as the lord king had received our faithful followers into favour, so we ought to receive into favour all who had stood with him [Col. 0480B]. We replied that, if it pleased him, a distinction must necessarily be admitted here. Among those whose cause he had undertaken were persons of differing condition: some more guilty, some less so; some in the communion of the Church; some excommunicated by contact with and participation in an anathema or sentence; some who had incurred the constitution of the supreme pontiff and cannot be absolved without his authority; and others who, for various reasons, had been justly condemned to anathema by us or by their other pastors. Therefore, in persons and causes so dissimilar, the principle of law and equity forbids the judgment to be the same.

For our part, extending peace and charity to all insofar as lies in us, after hearing the lord king’s counsel, we shall, God favouring us, regulate the matter for the honour of God’s Church, his honour and ours, and also the salvation of those whose reconciliation is sought, so that if any of them—God forbid—should lack peace and remain unreconciled [Col. 0480C], he must impute this to himself, not to us.

When the said Archdeacon Geoffrey, still excommunicated, as an instigator of discord and a despiser of a just sentence, replied more arrogantly, the lord king, lest words arising on either side should renew causes of hatred and fuel the enmity that had been put to sleep, drew us away from the crowd and asked us not to heed what was said by such persons, but with calm and peaceful mind, after giving him leave and blessing, to return under God’s grace and his own to our lodging.

Afterwards we learned that the venerable men, the lord archbishop of Rouen and the bishop of Nevers [Col. 0480D], whom you had ordered to be mediators between us and the lord king and who had been concerned for our peace, instructed the bishop of Sées, as he was crossing to England, to absolve our excommunicated persons. But it is uncertain whether they prescribed to him the form which you had given them; or, if it was prescribed, whether that bishop would follow it. Yet they could not lawfully command him except insofar as they received authority from you, nor did he accomplish anything if he exceeded the limits you prescribed.

Therefore, if it please you, it is necessary that, should they have been absolved otherwise, you order them to be bound by the sentence under which they were held until, according to the form of the Church, they swear—as you previously commanded—that they will obey your mandate. And impose upon those who have deserved to be absolved in this manner, under the force of obedience, that they inviolably observe the command which we shall issue to them on your behalf, or come before you within a period you set, to hear your order; subject to the penalty that, if they do not obey, they be restored to their former sentence, the impediment of appeal being removed [Col. 0481A].

God is witness that we say this not in pursuit of vengeance, since we know it is written: “You shall not seek revenge, nor remember the injury done by your fellow citizens”; but so that through the example of correction the Church may, by God’s grace, be strengthened in the future, and the punishment of a few may edify many. For, as the Holy Spirit declares, “When the pestilent man is scourged, the wise man is instructed.” Nor can the authority of the Apostolic See prevail unless those too are struck down who, abusing the protection of laymen, though excommunicated or forbidden, have presumed to celebrate the divine offices.

For what can a bishop alone, however devoted to the Roman Church, accomplish if priests and his clergy withdraw from obedience to him at the nod of powerful men? Nothing weakens the Church more than the Apostolic See’s readily passing over such offences unpunished when they arise. In saying this, we know that great labours, though with God’s favour conquerable, threaten us if you decide that these measures are to be carried out. Yet we choose rather to follow the narrow and strait way that leads to life than the broad and spacious way which, through the enticements of the world, draws men down to hell.

By your mandate, the demand for our damages is for the present silent [Col. 0481C]. May it please Your Serenity to hear from the bearer of this letter how you ought to proceed here, and to correct the injury inflicted upon us and our Church in the coronation of the king’s son, when another, contrary to ancient custom and your mandate, invaded our right and our province. Necessity compelled us to exceed the proper measure of a letter; fear and reverence compelled us to suppress much that might have been said. But may apostolic graciousness and the clemency of paternal mildness, if it please you, forgive the excess, hear with customary compassion from the bearer of this letter what needed to be said, and order the petitions we submit through him to be carried out more swiftly.

## LETTER XXVI. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

[Col. 0481D]

Since, Father, the trumpet of the apostolic threat sounded in the ears of the king of England, and he believed that the severity of the Church threatened both him and his land, he made peace with us, firmly promising that from the whole content of your mandate he would not pass over one iota or one stroke without fulfilling it completely. But when he had thus escaped the storm of the impending sentence, he withdrew from the agreement in certain points, still withholding from us some possessions of the Church which our predecessor possessed undisturbed throughout all the days of his life, and which we possessed thereafter until the tempest of this present storm arose in the English Church.

Yet when we approach him concerning their restoration, he sometimes promises that, if we wait while showing him our former devotion, he will make such satisfaction that no occasion for just complaint will remain [Col. 0482A]. But his known character and his failure to perform give the lie to his promises, since we have so far been able to obtain nothing from him except words. To make this clearer to you, we have taken care to send to the presence of Your Holiness the bearer of this letter and the letters received from the agents who ought to have conducted our affairs in England.

Meanwhile, insofar as lies in us, we take every precaution not to break the agreement of peace that has been made, though our conscience reproaches us because we do not seek by priestly authority recompense for the injuries done to the Church of God, to Christ’s poor, and to those exiled and banished for God’s justice. We greatly fear the ruinous example this will provide to our contemporaries, unless divine mercy remedies it, and the harm it will cause to posterity. But because the prudence of Your Majesty and of our lords around you judged that we ought to act thus, for the good of peace we have been silent and remain silent—neither remitting nor intending to remit to the impenitent any divine right which, with the Searcher of hearts as witness, we proclaim in the ears of you and of the Church.

We know that at the final judgment the strict Judge will not pass by things left unclaimed. The shaken and torn Church daily cries to Him in tears: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me.” Together with her and for her, we too cry, according to your counsel and mandate, meanwhile embracing the opportunity of a shadowy peace [Col. 0482C], until the day breathes and the fleeing shadows incline. We shall seek the favour of the man, as far as we can without compromising the liberty and honour of the Church; and, with the testimony of our conscience, we shall test whether he can even thus be recalled to gentleness.

Your Clemency sent us letters, certainly conceived and dictated by the Holy Spirit for the rebuke and correction both of the archbishop of York and of our fellow bishops, letters which reprove the king’s offences with the authority befitting the successor of Peter and vicar of Christ. But because we fear that a biting word may inflame the sensitive ears of a very powerful man and obstruct the peace newly made, we lie before Your Holiness with all devotion and beg that, removing mention of the king’s offences, the enormity of the oath given, the perverse customs, and the security not exacted at the new king’s coronation, you impose the same sentence upon the aforesaid archbishop and bishops, because, while we were exiled for the justice and liberty of the Church, he presumed to perform this coronation in our province. For all know that our Church held the possession of crowning the king for many years, and that she ought not to have been despoiled of it without judgment [Col. 0482D].

Thus, we hope, so great a presumption may easily and fittingly be punished, to the glory of God and the honour of the Apostolic See, while no impediment is brought upon the Church’s peace. We also say that it is necessary for you to write affectionately to the lord king that the Lord has appointed the Apostolic See to the watchtower over the whole Church so that it may examine the causes of all the faithful and render to all according to their deserts, in punishment or reward. Therefore no one ought to be disturbed if, at its command, each gathers his cause into his bosom, lest, because of indiscipline, he be cast before angels and men into eternal fire.

You have shown great deference to the king; but although you have spared him, you do not dare to overlook the offences and crimes of priests. Furthermore, because we fear that the recent peace may be hindered or disturbed by various causes, may you, if it please you, entrust to discretion the suspension or excommunication of our bishops [Col. 0483A]—we shall report everything to the best of our ability in conscience, as we say it by God’s word, for His honour and yours—excepting, if you think fit and reserving to your own judgment, the archbishop of York, who is the instigator and head of all evils.

And although the bishop of London has been the standard-bearer of this whole sedition—lest we call it schism—we beg that we may be allowed to show mercy both to him and to the bishop of Salisbury if they cannot be punished according to your mandate without renewing the schism. And because you ordered us in this matter to proceed according to the counsel of the most Christian king of France, withholding or producing your letters, we have acted upon his counsel. He advises that we obtain from you special letters concerning the suspension of York without injury to the king; other letters concerning the excommunication of the two bishops; and a third set concerning the suspension of all bishops [Col. 0483C]. Obtain this also: that we may use each letter individually as the time and necessity of the cause require.

For, although she appears to have come into harbour, the English Church is still tossed by the waves. Unless the king fulfils the conditions of the peace he promised her, she must be fortified with the arms and protection of your consoling aid against the snares of evil men and attacks of persecutors. This will be done if by your letters you command our venerable brother, the lord bishop of Meaux, and B . . . . ., abbot of Saint-Crépin of Soissons, a man of proven religious life, to meet with the king and require him to restore the Church’s possessions and make good the losses inflicted upon our people and ourselves; he is to know that ecclesiastical severity will be exercised against him and his land unless he obeys your commands.

And if he does not think fit to comply even then, grant us, if you please, the authority that you conferred on the lord archbishop of Rouen and the bishop of Nevers, or even broader authority. For the more powerful and fierce he is, the tighter bonds and harsher staff are needed to conquer and restrain him [Col. 0483D]. Moreover, because the seedbed and fuel of disturbances of this sort has been the withdrawal of obedience by the Church of York from its mother, the holy Church of Canterbury, restore, if you please, the unity of the English Church by commanding that, all appeal and pretext removed, the archbishop of York and his church obey ours by right of primacy. If you wish to follow in the footsteps of your predecessors, it is clear, upon careful inspection of their registers, that this must be done.

God knows that we do not seek this for our own glory; would that we had never undertaken the pastoral office—an office doubtless full either of eternal death or of the greatest distresses! Rather, we seek that, in our days and yours, the occasion of the schisms that so frequently arise may be cut off, and that enduring peace be restored to the English Church through your favour. We say this to you before Him who is judge of us both and to whom we must render account for all things. May He inspire and teach you what you ought chiefly to do.

You have heard of our struggle; but, as our country’s proverb says, only the man whose neighbour is fire feels the heat. We believe that we shall set out for England, though whether for peace or punishment we do not know; it is divinely ordained what fate awaits us [Col. 0484B]. Therefore we commend our souls to your fatherhood, giving thanks to you and the Apostolic See for all the consolations it has supplied to us and ours in so great a crisis of necessity. Moreover, know without doubt that our venerable brother Bartholomew, bishop of Exeter, is free from blame for the presumptuous coronation, and during this storm has suffered much from the enemies of the Church on account of justice.

## LETTER XXVII. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

To the venerable father and dearest lord in Christ, ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, THOMAS, humble servant of the Church of Canterbury: greeting and every form of obedience with the utmost devotion.

[Col. 0484C]

With what just and honourable terms we made peace with our lord the king of the English has, we believe, come to your knowledge both from our own report and from that of many intermediaries; and likewise how that same lord of ours has withdrawn from his agreements and promises. Yet we believe this should be imputed not so much to him as to the priests of Baal and the sons of false prophets, who from the beginning have been the instigators of all discord. But the chief among all these are that man of York and the bishop of London, who formerly, when you were at Sens, returning from you before the lord king had either been approached or heard, did not fear to despoil us, standing at the feet of your clemency in the court, of our possessions [Col. 0484D], although they knew beyond doubt that we were prosecuting before you the cases of two appeals: for we had been appealed by the archbishop of York, and had appealed both him and our fellow bishops, having in turn been appealed by them.

Accordingly, when these standard-bearers of Balaam heard that we had made peace with the lord king, they associated with themselves the bishop of Salisbury and their other accomplices, and traversed sea and land in order to break the unity of peace that had been established. Both personally and through others they persuaded the lord king and his advisers that reconciliation was useless and dishonourable for the realm unless the grants of our churches which the king had made remained secure, and unless we were compelled firmly to observe the customs of the realm over which contention had arisen between us. They advanced so far [Col. 0485A] in their perversity that, at their prompting, the lord king took away, after the peace made on the feast of blessed Mary Magdalene, all our revenues and those of our people until the feast of Saint Martin; only then did he restore to us empty houses and demolished granaries. His clerks, however—namely Geoffrey Ridel, our archdeacon, and Nigel of Sackville—still hold occupied two of our churches which they received from lay hands. And he himself refuses to restore to us and to our Church several possessions of our Church which he had promised to restore in the settlement of the peace.

Although he behaved otherwise than befitted him, contrary to his agreements, as is known to many, nevertheless, seeing the Church’s enormous and irreparable losses and guarding against worse, we resolved, guided by our own counsel and that of the lord cardinals [Col. 0485B], to return to our Church, torn apart and trampled down; so that, if we could not raise and restore her, we might at least perish with her, and, present in her cause, render up our spirit more confidently for her. When our messengers learned this more certainly, it is uncertain what they feared; but they took counsel with the king’s officials and with that most wicked son of perdition, Ranulf de Broc, who for seven years now, abusing the resources of public authority, has raged with exceptional licence against the Church of God.

They therefore determined that the sea-ports at which they suspected we would arrive should be watched by an armed force, with the guard and vigilance of soldiers and retainers, lest we could enter the land without their minutely searching all our baggage and taking from us all letters which [Col. 0485C] we had obtained from your Majesty. But by divine direction it happened that their designs became known to us through friends—designs which their own insolence, born of excessive presumption, did not allow to remain concealed. For the retainers mentioned above went armed along the shores, directing their steps as the aforementioned bishops of York, London, and Salisbury prescribed to them. They had selected to execute this wickedness those whom they knew to be especially hostile to us: namely Ranulf de Broc, Reginald de Warenne, and Gervase, sheriff of Kent; and these openly threatened that, should we dare to land, they would cut off our head.

The bishops repeatedly mentioned came to Canterbury in order to spur them on further, should the retainers of public authority not rage sufficiently [Col. 0485D]. Thus, after their counsels had been more carefully investigated, your letters were sent ahead one day before we embarked; and those letters also by which the bishop of York was suspended, and the bishops of London and Salisbury were recalled into the sentence of anathema, were delivered to them. On the following day we boarded ship and, after a favourable voyage, reached England. At the king’s command we brought with us John, dean of Salisbury, who saw the armed men mentioned above hastening, not without grief and shame, toward our ship in order to use violence upon those arriving.

The aforesaid dean, therefore, fearing that any harm inflicted upon us or ours would rebound to the lord king’s disgrace, went out to meet the armed men [Col. 0486A], declaring to them on the king’s behalf that they were not to injure us or ours; for to do so would brand the king himself, with whom we had made peace, with the mark of treachery. He persuaded them to approach us unarmed. Yet because we had brought with us Simon, archdeacon of Sens, who had decided to visit the friends he had in England, they demanded from him an oath of fealty binding him to our kings against all men, with no exception for you or anyone else. But we did not permit such an undertaking to be made, fearing that the clergy of the realm might be compelled to a similar oath by the force of precedent if members of our household had made obligations of this sort. This is assuredly what the frequently mentioned bishops of York, London, and Salisbury and their accomplices are contriving to the detriment of the apostolic see: namely, that its authority should be nullified or diminished within the realm.

The officials who demanded the oath were too few to compel us against our will to do anything in that place, because the people, rejoicing at our return, would have been stronger if forces had been assembled. Thence, coming to our Church, we were received with great devotion by clergy and people, although intruders still violently press upon our churches. Foremost in every plague and harassment of the Church are Geoffrey Ridel, our archdeacon, and Nigel of Sackville, his clerk. The one, Geoffrey, occupies the church of Otford; the other, Nigel of Sackville, the church of Herges—churches which, together with the revenues received, they ought to have restored, by your command, to us and to our clerics to whom they belong [Col. 0486B–C]. For you commanded the lord archbishop of Rouen and the bishop of Nevers to absolve them upon receiving the oath according to the Church’s custom, and by your authority to order the churches, together with their revenues, surrendered to us.

But after we came to our Church, the king’s officials immediately approached us, declaring on his behalf—as the bishop of York and the bishops of London and Salisbury had instructed them—that we should absolve the suspended bishops and the excommunicated, because what had been done against them redounded to the king’s injury and to the overthrow of the customs of the realm. They promised that, after absolution, the bishops of our province would come to us and willingly obey, saving their legal rights and the honour [Col. 0486D] of the realm.

We replied that it is not for an inferior judge to dissolve the sentence of a superior, and that no person may invalidate what the apostolic see has decreed. Yet because they pressed us more insistently and threatened that, unless we complied, the lord king would do astonishing and dreadful things, we told them that, if the bishops of London and Salisbury would swear before us in the Church’s form that they would obey your command, then for the peace of the Church and reverence for the lord king, with the counsel of the king himself, the bishop of Winchester, and our other brethren, we would expose ourselves to risk and do whatever was compatible with reverence for you; and we would love them as most dear brothers in Christ and treat them with all gentleness and humility.

When this was reported to the bishops [Col. 0487A] by the intermediaries, the bishop of York, seeking partners for sedition and instigators of schism, replied that such oaths ought not to be made without the king’s will, especially by bishops, because this was contrary to the prince’s dignity and the customs of the realm. It was answered on our behalf that these same bishops had previously been excommunicated by us and had deserved absolution only after taking an oath, although they had importuned us with many entreaties. And if our sentence ought not to be dissolved without an oath from the bishops, much less ought yours to be dissolved—being far stronger and supported by authority incomparably greater than ours and than that of all mortals.

In response, as those present reported to us, the bishops were so moved that they resolved to come to us and receive absolution according to the Church’s custom, judging it unsafe to oppose themselves to the Church and attack apostolic sanctions for the preservation of the realm’s customs. But the enemy of peace and disturber of the Church, the bishop of York, dissuaded them, advising them rather to approach the lord king, who had always supported them, and to send messengers to the new king, to persuade him that we wished to depose him—whereas, God being witness, if he would benefit the Church, we would prefer that he possess not merely one kingdom but very many and most extensive kingdoms of the earth.

The standard-bearer of this embassy is our archdeacon. For the bishop of York and the two aforesaid bishops crossed the sea with haste so that, God avert it, they might deceive the lord king and inflame his anger against the Church [Col. 0487B–C]. They caused six persons of vacant churches to be summoned, so that by their counsel, contrary to the canons, before the king in a foreign realm and in the absence of their brethren, they might hold an election of bishops for our province. If we refuse to consecrate those so elected, they imagine that they will have grounds for sowing discord between us and the lord king. For there is nothing they fear more than the peace of the Church, lest their deeds should become visible and their transgressions be corrected. The messenger will add many further matters, which we judged should not be inserted in this letter lest it produce weariness. If it please you, kindly hear our prayers. May your Holiness, dearest Father, flourish for ever.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO THE SAME, ON BEHALF OF THE BRETHREN OF NEUBOURG

[Col. 0487D]

We believe that your discernment has heard both from many persons and from the bearers of this letter what evils the archbishop of York has done, and continually does, to holy men. What increases the man’s audacity is that until now he has done everything as he pleased, believing with impunity that everything which he sees unpunished is lawful. Nor does he believe that there is a judge in Israel, since amid so many, so great, and so manifest offences he has never seemed to come to judgment or to render an account of his remarkable deeds. He trusts in the abundance of riches which he has amassed beyond measure, increasing:

> “If he can, rightly; if not, wealth by whatever means.”

Against these poor people, who, driven by necessity, as we have learned from men full of faith, have fled to the apostolic see, he has now at last fastened teeth and claws. He will not cease to despoil, slaughter, and destroy unless the clemency of the lord pope and ours comes to their aid. Since it is both your virtue and your customary practice to deliver the poor from the powerful and the needy from those who despoil them, we most earnestly commend the cause of these persons to your mercy. We ask that you cast down and expel that imitator of the apostate angel, lest he pollute further the Holy of Holies.

No greater calamity can befall the Church of God than that those should rise against her who, by the obligation of their office, ought to protect her and lay down their lives for her in the hour of need. For many years the English Church has felt this, [Col. 0488A–B] in which scarcely any iniquity can be found that has not proceeded from the elders who seemed to govern the people, and from those nourished, advanced, and enriched by the Church’s benefices. Indeed, error has now become so utterly shameless that bishops blush at the Gospel and glory in exercising butchery—not sacrificing cattle, however, but their brothers, for whom Christ, the Son of God, was sacrificed. Nor do they fear that these things will be required of them, trusting in their abundance of riches and presuming on the friendship of secular powers.

For if any man wishes to imitate the footsteps of the Fathers and tries to express in his deeds the character of a bishop, he is immediately exposed not only to contempt and mockery but also to many dangers; yet more grievous than all other evils are those inflicted by false brethren. Who is their standard-bearer, who has been the author of discord between kingdom and priesthood, who has been the instigator of rancour and all perversity, is clear from his deeds. But because that matter concerns us, we reserve the wrongs and losses inflicted upon the Church of God, upon us, and upon our people, for the judgment of Him who says, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,” and for yours, whom He has appointed lord of His household and ruler over all His possession.

Meanwhile we more earnestly commend to your fatherly care the cause of the brethren of Neubourg and of the clerics who flee with them to the feet of your Majesty. We ask that the graciousness of your compassion may comfort them, unjustly oppressed as they are, according to what we have learned from men of proven faith [Col. 0488C]. Unless your mercy comes to their aid, ruin threatens the religious houses, as they will explain to you more fully in person, and they cannot long stand before the face of their oppressor. For Lucifer has once more raised himself against the Most High, setting his seat in the north, intending there to mutilate Christ; since he cannot occupy the whole dominion unless Peter’s vicar comes forth in the Spirit and power of Elijah, crushing the hammer of the whole earth [Col. 0488D].

## LETTER XXIX. TO ALL THE CARDINALS

To his venerable lords and Fathers, all the bishops, priests, and deacons, cardinals by God’s grace of the holy Roman Church: THOMAS, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, wretched and pitiable exile, greeting and due service in all things [Col. 0489A].

It is not easy for a wretched man to make acceptable speech; for one who is pitiable, it is indeed difficult to keep moderation in speaking. Let indulgence, then, we ask, be granted to the wretched man, pardon to the pitiable. We believe, most holy Fathers, that by divine inspiration you have been placed in this highest station in order that you may remove injustices, cut off presumptions, kindly assist those labouring in the priesthood, allow no place to the reproaches and calamities inflicted upon them, bring aid to the oppressed and burdened, more sternly restrain calumniators, and most severely punish oppressors. For not to trouble the perverse and not to resist those persecuting the Church is nothing other than to encourage them. He seems secretly to consent who does not oppose an open crime [Col. 0489B].

We understand from this that you have no alternative but henceforth to devote all your efforts most diligently to this cause of ours, which is at issue between our king and ourselves—indeed, primarily between you and him—and in which the safety of the universal Church is imperilled. You had entered into conflict with him; victory was already at your threshold, had not a crafty cunning, false hope of peace—believed by the knowledgeable, proclaimed by travellers, and affirmed by those more intimately acquainted with the king’s counsels—outwitted the authority of your religious office. Such peace is extracted from tyrants by preparation for conflict rather than secured by negotiation. For peace is won through preparation for war.

It is surely fitting that the bowels of your compassion should be closed against one who seeks to extinguish the Church’s liberty. You ought therefore to be free from every offence and wholly independent of outside favour if you rightly manage others’ affairs, if you speak truth among the people, if you love justice when you execute judgment in the nation. For the Lord says: “Love righteousness, you who judge the earth.” It is indeed to be loved and observed everywhere. It alone makes and preserves peace. Thus Isaiah says: “The work of righteousness shall be peace”; and David in the Psalm: “Righteousness and peace have kissed.” These two love one another so deeply that whoever does righteousness finds peace, and not otherwise. Therefore act thus and observe justice thus, you to whom judicial power has been entrusted, so that when the just Judge comes, rendering to each according to his merits, He may reward you [Col. 0489C–D] with a worthy recompense for justice well observed.

Why say more? I recall this briefly to your memory: once there was a small spark in Alexandria, but because justice, by its dissimulation, did not immediately suppress it, its flame ravaged almost the whole world. And, to come to the point, tell me, most holy Fathers: with what conscience do you overlook the injury inflicted on Christ in me—indeed, certainly in yourselves, who ought to represent Christ’s person on earth? Is not my cause like yours—indeed, wholly yours? Or do you pretend not to know that the king of the English has occupied, and daily occupies, ecclesiastical possessions; overturns the Church’s liberty; stretches out his hands against the Lord’s anointed, indiscriminately and everywhere against clerics [Col. 0490A], imprisoning some, mutilating others, gouging out others’ eyes, compelling some to judicial combat and others to the ordeal of fire or water; compelling even bishops not to observe obedience to their metropolitan, lesser clerics not to obey their prelates, and persons lawfully excommunicated not to regard themselves as excommunicated? Indeed, what is worse, he wholly removes the Church’s liberty, after the likeness of that great schismatic, your oppressor, who seeks utterly to disembowel the Church.

If our king does these things with impunity, what will his heirs do? What will be endured from your successors? Consider that evils, occasions, and the inventions of evil men increase daily. Good God, will He allow these things with impunity? Christ did not proceed by this path, nor did the apostles, whose imitators you ought to be—and we together with you. Why do you depart from the ways of the Lord, in whom lies your confidence? It is to be feared—God forbid—that ruin and unhappiness may befall your paths, that you may not have known the way of salvation, and that the fear of God may not be before your eyes [Col. 0490B].

Who will snatch you from the hand of the oppressor? Who will deliver you from the jaws of the beast, which is already at the gates to swallow you all, unless God Himself? Certainly not silver, gold, human favour, or the favour of princes. Therefore do not, do not put your trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation; for cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm. Do, my lords, do to others what you desire Christ to do to you, so that you may escape the danger which is close at hand. For the same measure with which you have measured will be measured back to you.

Do you not know that your silver will be cast outside, your gold will become dung, and that silver and gold will not be able to deliver you on the day of the Lord’s wrath? Therefore do not, do not store up wrath for yourselves on the day of wrath, but store up treasures in heaven for yourselves by resisting oppressors and aiding the oppressed. Otherwise let God Himself, with whom there is no respect of persons, judge between you and me, my fellow exiles, orphans, widows, infants in their cradles, and all other clerics and laypeople. May He require the blood of my dead from your hands, and avenge this dissimulation—He who sits on high as the just Judge, observing your evasions and injustices [Col. 0490C–D], and who will render to each of you according as he has dealt with me, whether good or evil.

For you have set us, though undeserving, as a target for arrows, so that, hemmed in on every side, we can neither ward off the missiles hurled at us nor escape save in the mighty hand of God. You have made us a reproach to every passer-by, a mockery to our neighbours, a derision to those around us—would that you yourselves were not among them! Good God, what strength will remain in the members if the vigour of the head itself withers? It is now cried in the streets and proclaimed through cities and villages that justice is not done at Rome against the powerful.

Why do you hedge our paths with thorns? Why do you place before us a stone of stumbling? Why do you take away all our authority, so that we may not avenge [Col. 0491A] Christ’s injury, repair the losses of our days, for which no one gives help, or compensate, as we are now able, the Church’s loss at least by ecclesiastical censure?
