This should prevent unshaken impunity from growing strong through silence, and should bring into the light the authority of so great a disturbance and the deserved punishment of such deliberate presumption, so that in time to come it may be seen that things so monstrous and detestable were by no means undertaken with impunity, but without right.

Be assured: this delay contains very great danger and no safety. The disease must be treated otherwise, unless through your dissimulation you wish all the kings of the earth to be infected by it. For the bitter servitude of the Church is sweet to every tyrant, and it is not easily removed unless its very sweetness is swiftly made bitter to him by the severity of justice. Matters have come to such a point that our king follows even the Sicilians—indeed, surpasses them. Clerics throughout England run to his court; they become court chaplains and, under that pretext, are bound by the necessity of an oath, so that in his land he may henceforth more freely maintain what at present he establishes as law by his own will. The course is swift toward irreparable loss to the Church, since there is no one who does not yield to the runner, who effectively rebukes the wrongdoer, or usefully punishes his transgression [Col. 0491B].

What will remain for us and you in that land if this immense danger is not more swiftly met, if the dangerous presumption of so monstrous an innovation is not more sharply checked? Judge for yourselves. I had certainly resolved to save my own soul in this matter and manfully meet the danger, unless, as we believe, you had deemed me unworthy, and undeservedly so, of this act. May God forgive those who have done it. For I would have had easier access to peace with him if, God forbid, I had sought to overlook the Church’s perils without you. Yet whatever you have done with me, whatever you may do, by God’s mercy nothing is done by me without you, nothing to the prejudice of the Church, if life remains with me. I have chosen this way; with Christ as guide I will not change my resolve. For this is the way of salvation for me.

I write this to you not in any indignation—God knows, who searches hearts—but as a warning, lest the day of the Lord come upon you like a thief: the day of vengeance that spares no one. Therefore believe me, your faithful servant in all things, most beloved lords [Col. 0491C–D]. Gather your strength, gird yourselves with the most powerful sword of the word of God, draw the sword of blessed Peter, avenge the injury done to Christ and to His people; let your eye spare no one. Do judgment and justice without delay for everyone suffering injury. This is the royal way; this is the way that leads to life. You must walk in it, that you may follow the footsteps of Christ and of the apostles, whose vicars you are. The Church is not to be governed by evasion or contrivance, but by justice and truth, which delivers its observer from every danger. Do this and you will assuredly have God as your helper; nor henceforth fear what man may do to you. Fare well, that it may be well with us and with the whole Church.

## LETTER XXX. TO ALBERT THE PRIEST

[Col. 0492A]

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to ALBERT, cardinal priest: greeting and due reverence.

Nothing could be given us in this present crisis more pleasing than the opportunity of your presence, so that we might confer together concerning our condition and receive the counsel of your discernment, which we have found in all things lively and effective. Such a conference, I say, would be pleasant to us because it is exceedingly necessary. For among us we find few or none who walk without limping from the path of pure truth, as though they sought and cared for their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ [Col. 0492B], striving rather to please an earthly king than fearing to displease the heavenly one.

We speak to you as to a special patron and most faithful friend, not fearing to lay open our heart to you from its depths, while humbly entreating you in faith and love that what we say may pass to no other hearing. In so many and such great ways is the liberty of the holy Church attacked among us that we can scarcely bear even to see or hear it. New things arise daily, and things unheard of in earlier ages are exacted. The laws are silenced; the rule of the canons is wholly excluded from the Lord’s lot; clerics are subjected to new laws and dealt with according to the will of lay power.

We know that you love and steadfastly support the lord king, and therefore [Col. 0492C] we speak more openly with you, so that you may grieve more keenly. It is difficult and lengthy to include everything in writing; therefore we send to you Master Henry, your faithful familiar and ours, who will explain more fully the sequence of events according to what he saw and heard. If it please you, believe him as you would us. Yet if it could be done, we would rather visit you in our own person and hear living words from you and give them in return than do otherwise. Unless God provides it, no counsel is at hand for us, since it would be better for us to serve among barbarians than to see these evils in the holy Church in our own days. Farewell, dearest lord.

## LETTER XXXI. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0492D]

Would that, my beloved friend, your ears were turned toward the voices of our people and heard what is sung at the crossroads of Ashkelon to the disgrace of the Roman Church! The latest messengers of ours seemed to have brought some consolation in the letters of the lord pope from the apostolic see, but their authority has been nullified by letters sent *a latere*, so that Satan might be loosed to the destruction of the Church. For the bishops of London and Salisbury have been released by apostolic command. One of them is recognized to have been, from the beginning, an instigator of schism and artificer of all wickedness; he has driven both the bishop of Salisbury and all whom he could into the crime of disobedience.

I do not know how it is that the Lord’s party [Col. 0493A] is always slaughtered in the court, so that Barabbas escapes and Christ is killed. By the court’s authority our proscription and the Church’s calamity have now been prolonged into a sixth year. At your court the wretched, exiled, and innocent are condemned, and, to speak from conscience, for no other reason than that they are poor followers of Christ, weak, and unwilling to depart from God’s justice. On the other hand, absolution is given to sacrilegious men, murderers, robbers, and unrepentant persons. Though the whole world protests, I pronounce freely, with Christ as my authority, that not even Peter himself, were he presiding, could absolve them before God.

For He says in the Gospel according to Luke: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. And if he sins against you seven times in a day and seven times turns to you, saying, ‘I repent,’ forgive him.” Are Christ’s words idle when He says, “If he repents,” “if, having turned, he confesses, saying, ‘I repent’”? By no means. He will render account on the Day of Judgment not for idle speech, but rather will condemn those who presume, contrary to the form He gave, to justify wicked men by empty absolutions without confession and repentance, and to give life to souls that do not live [Col. 0493B].

Certainly, if something taken away can be restored and is not restored, repentance is not performed but feigned. Truly, as is written, the Holy Spirit will flee what is feigned, because He is truth and not pretence. Let him who dares bind himself by such a judgment, and let him not fear the sentence of the Judge to come. Let him absolve unrepentant robbers, sacrilegious men, murderers, perjurers, men of blood, and schismatics; I will never remit to an unrepentant person what has been taken from the Church of God. Are not the gifts and promises which the king’s messengers lavish upon cardinals and courtiers our spoils—or rather, the Church’s? What open iniquity is there, if that which is practised against the Church of God among us is hidden?

We cannot defend the Church’s liberty because the apostolic see has prolonged our proscription now into its sixth year. Let God see and judge. But we are ready to die for it. Let whatever cardinals wish rise against us; let them arm not merely the king of the English but, if they can, the whole world for our destruction. With God’s favour I will depart neither in life nor in death from fidelity to the Church. Henceforth I commit His cause to God, for whose sake I wander in exile and am proscribed; may He heal it as He knows best [Col. 0493C]. I no longer intend to trouble the court. Let those approach it who prevail in their wickedness and, justice defeated and innocence captive, return in glory to the Church’s shame. Would that the Roman road had not destroyed so many wretched innocents for nothing! Who will henceforth dare resist that king whom the Roman Church has encouraged by so many triumphs and armed with an example whose ruinous force flows down to posterity? May your Holiness ever prosper, remembering us before God.

## LETTER XXXII. TO THE SAME

“Of those slain for the cause of the Lord,” etc. See the similar letter addressed to Cardinal Hyacinth.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO THE SAME AND THEODWIN

[Col. 0494A]

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to the cardinals ALBERT and THEODWIN.

We do not doubt that the Church’s troubles, the afflictions of the innocent, and the miseries of those who have zeal for God are more bitter to you in proportion as we certainly know that you adhere more intimately and sweetly to apostolic institutions. Indeed, the Church of God cannot stand if those whose duty it is to provide for her safety are inclined to her ruin. For if shepherds abandon their place through love or hatred, greed or neglect, hope or fear of temporal things, or yield to vices, it remains that their lampstand be removed and that they become a snare and ruin to the people.

Therefore, that we may speak before God [Col. 0494B], whom we await as judge and invoke to judge His own cause: although we have greatly loved our lord the king of the English and, before the priesthood was laid upon us, served at his will with all our strength, yet without consciousness of crime, unwilling to consent with him in injury to God and trampling of the Church, we have opposed him for God’s sake. We preferred, by offending him, to call him back to pardon rather than, by flattery, to precipitate him into Gehenna. The cause which he presses against us is between himself and God, since we seek from him nothing other than what God, made immortal in the flesh He assumed, left to His Church for her by an eternal testament.

Therefore, in the faith and charity of Christ, Christ Himself being witness, we entreat you to rise with us to aid the shipwrecked Church. With the authority and prudence bestowed upon you [Col. 0494C], confront this man, for whom no abundance of successes suffices if the Church of God enjoys liberty. If you do not believe us or our people, ask concerning the character of the man the Gallican and the Church of Tours, the Aquitanians and Normans, and the pilgrims to Rome who flock from the realm of the English. You will certainly find nothing by which you can doubt the sincerity of our cause unless you deliberately darken your eyes so that they cannot behold what is true.

We place fuller confidence in you, especially in God’s cause, and are ready to serve you. What we cannot do, God will supply, repaying according to the measure with which you have measured us. But concerning ourselves, hold this for certain: we judge it preferable to incur temporal death than to deserve eternal death, and to undergo the utmost miseries for Christ rather than perpetuate the straits of wretched servitude. For the outcome of this controversy will extend into future ages: either the Church will mourn in perpetual afflictions—God forbid—or she will rejoice in enduring liberty [Col. 0494D].

Neither cardinals nor any human intervention would have been necessary for us or ours if, from the beginning, we had been willing to agree with the king in those things which, to the clergy’s harm, he established—not customs, but perversions—and simply and absolutely to subscribe without attaching any reservation of our order. Therefore, if he prevails in establishing such great iniquities with the Roman Church consenting or passing them over, who will dare thereafter to utter a word against him? Who will shake from the hand of his heirs what their father obtained by not so much courage as obstinacy? Who will prevent other princes, equally noble and powerful, from claiming similar things? For evil examples are seized upon more quickly, and posterity, retaining the vices of their ancestors, very rarely rises to the practice of virtue.

If the fruit of your labour and ours is that princes may subject the Church to servitude and crush us because we have dared to be zealous for God’s law, to profess justice, and to stand in opposition for the house of Israel, then henceforth there will be very few or none who do not wholly follow the will of princes; who keep faith with the Roman Church; who reverence the decrees of the apostolic see; who obey the commands of the supreme pontiff; or who do not despise the law of God itself as a fable, as words without truth or fruit [Col. 0495A].

We therefore commit the Church’s cause especially to you, whom we trust to be steadfast pillars of the Church. For in time of need help must be sought from those who have received from the Lord both the authority of justice and the will to carry out mercy. Nor do we think you ignorant that the just Judge will pour into your bosoms a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, of the things you have done against God or according to God. Amen [Col. 0495B].

## LETTER XXXIV. TO BERNARD, BISHOP OF PORTO

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to BERNARD, bishop of Porto: greeting and due reverence.

[Col. 0495C] The well-known constancy of your holiness encourages us and gives us confidence to speak, so that we may make known to your discernment what holy Church is suffering in us and in her other members within the kingdom of the English, hoping to receive from you sound counsel and a remedy necessary for so great a grief. But, considering the course of this calamity of ours, since it is neither easy nor safe to commit it to writing, we send to you Master Henry, a faithful and intimate friend of both you and us, that he may set all matters before you in a trustworthy account, as he saw and heard them. We ask that credit be given to his words as to our own. But you, lord, according to the wisdom granted you by God, once you have learned of our condition, do not delay to impart the consolation of your counsel [Col. 0495D] to us—indeed, to the entire Church of the English. For we are in dire straits and expect help from none but God and the holy Roman Church. May your holiness prosper and come to our aid.

## LETTER XXXV. TO THE SAME PERSON

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Bernard, Bishop of Porto.

We received the words of your consolation with a joyful heart; but immediately afterward, upon receiving letters sent by the other side—which the king of England is having published at the crossroads and in public gatherings of both kingdoms, to our injury and the confusion of the Apostolic See—our harp was turned into mourning [Col. 0496A] and our joy passed into sorrow. For we have become burdensome and wearisome to our benefactors, since they have been driven to despair of our peace on hearing that the persecutor of the Church and of ourselves, who attacks us with our own spoils against the justice of God, has prevailed through his threats, emptiness, and manifold malice.

May God see and judge between me and him, and the others whose support he has employed, so that he may make what is lawful equal to his pleasure and rage with impunity against the Church of God, with no one protesting. If it is God’s will that we should die in exile for the liberty of the Church, may He find the sacrifice acceptable; for we have resolved to die rather than put the liberty of the Church up for sale at any price in the world. Far be it from us to sell to an impious king the inheritance [Col. 0496B] of our fathers, which Holy Scripture teaches in the Spirit to be the law of God!

Yet, because you have for many days extended your patronage to the holy Church of Canterbury, now almost destroyed, we beseech your holiness to bring it swift assistance, as though it were at its last breath: that the lord pope may remove the suspension inflicted on us, or shorten its term; also, that he may write open letters to the king of the French and the Gallican Church, declaring that unless the king of England, in accordance with his warning and threat, restores to us peace and what has been taken away, together with the Church’s liberty, he thereafter permits us to exercise against him and his land the authority of our office; that he decrees the sentence which we shall issue against the Church’s evildoers and our own to be held valid; and that he commands [Col. 0496C] all the bishops of his land to observe it inviolably until they are compelled to make satisfaction.

Moreover, we earnestly pray that, for consolation in her misery, you obtain for the Church of Canterbury a full restoration of her primacy; and that the archbishop and Church of York be commanded to render us obedience as their primate. For since through you we have obtained confirmation of that same primacy, it will be honor and glory to you if the confirmation obtained through you receives full force. That your charity may have some consolation amid our tribulation, know that the Most Christian King counts our lot as his own. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Col. 0496D]

Many envoys have been sent to the king of England, and the labor of them all has been fruitless. How the efforts and expense of these latest men, Lord Gratian and Vivian, came to nothing, you may hear, if you please, from their own report. The king and his party, as always, obstructed peace, although I and my fellow exiles obeyed the envoys in every respect, as the lord of Sens and the bishops present heard. And even now, so far as I can do so without prejudice to my rank and fidelity to the Roman Church, I am prepared to preserve and increase the dignities of the king and kingdom.

But, with God as author, a new and ruinous form of fidelity shall never be introduced into the Church of God on my example. I ask, however, that he restore or make satisfaction to me and mine for what has been taken away, which he retains freely and without cause. For he has openly confessed both to the envoys and to many others that, for the whole period of my chancellorship, he demands no account either of money or of administration. The losses of property trouble me less than the ruinous example, which will readily drive contemporaries and posterity into error and into daring to attempt similar things, if this plague remains unpunished and uncalled to account.

The rest, lest by prolonging the writing I cause you weariness, has been entrusted to the mouths of Christ’s poor who are being sent to you. If you please, hear them and grant their request for Christ’s sake, whose cause they pursue; and apply effort and diligence that the Church may attain her due liberty. But should the bishop of London and Geoffrey Ridel, forerunners of Antichrist, [Col. 0497B] happen to come to the curia, treat them as members of Antichrist ought to be treated by the anointed of the Lord.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO BOSO

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Boso, cardinal.

We firmly believe—and it is true—that there is no one in the curia who knows more fully than you what faith, obedience, and devotion the Church of Canterbury has customarily shown to the Apostolic See. For, to say nothing of our other predecessors, by whose teaching, virtues, and examples the Church is illumined, and who now shine through miracles, God answering their merits, our most recent predecessor—your friend indeed and a most devoted son of the Roman Church—was twice expelled from his own see for faith and obedience. King Stephen persecuted him because, against the king’s prohibition, he had come when summoned by Pope Eugenius to the Council of Rheims, while the other bishops remained at home in disobedience, except for three who came by the king’s order to excuse the absence of the rest.

As you know, another cause of his persecution was that, against the prohibition of the Roman pontiffs, he refused to crown Eustace, the king’s son. What other bishops in our whole island have you seen or read of setting themselves against rulers, apart from the archbishops of Canterbury, to defend the liberty of the Church, preserve [Col. 0497D] the institutions of the Fathers, and uphold the reverence and obedience due to the Apostolic See? In our own age, indeed, not one has done so; and if ancient histories are reviewed, none will be found. But some men of Canterbury have shed their blood for God’s law; others offered it to their persecutors to be shed.

If the customs—or rather abominations—which are demanded of us had prevailed in our predecessor’s time, then, when the king forbade him, he would not have exposed himself to shipwreck for obedience’s sake; nor would the supreme pontiff have publicly returned thanks to him in full council for the devotion he had shown. For, in his own words, he had come to the council “rather by swimming than by sailing.” If these perversities had prevailed, he would certainly, after the Apostolic prohibition, have crowned the king’s son, since that royal court had decreed that it ought to be done. That king, too, had among the instigators of this tinder some of those who now persecute us.

Do you not recall how the man who is now archbishop of York went to Rome, conducting the cause of that king and his nobles? Since they could not bend the archbishop of Canterbury, they sought at least to obtain from Pope Eugenius release from the Apostolic prohibition. But why review matters well known, especially in your hearing—you who hold in memory the events of that time, and who have learned the faith and devotion of the Church of Canterbury most fully not only by reading books but by sight and hearing? She has always been devoted to you; and, with God as author, [Col. 0498B] her devotion to you will not grow cold in our time.

Indeed, it is right that it should rather increase, since from the time of Guido of Pisa we have personally contracted a close relationship, and through us you formed friendship with our predecessor. It is our purpose that, as age advances, charity should grow stronger and, if opportunity permits, our services should be multiplied. Therefore we earnestly beseech your affection to bring these matters to the knowledge of the lord pope, so that, with our other lords and friends—or above all of them—you may obtain from him that he not hand over to beasts a Church which has always served God and the Apostolic See, and that with outstretched arm he may rescue us with her from the hands of those who seek our life to take it away, and who, through our abasement, would destroy the liberty of the whole Church.

[Col. 0498C] For King Stephen did not cease from persecuting our predecessor until the lord Eugenius of pious memory, every obstacle of appeal having ceased, ordered all bishops by Apostolic authority to pronounce upon his head the sentence of anathema and upon his land the sentence of interdict. A wolf is not easily driven from the sheepfold unless frightened by the barking of dogs and the staff.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO GRATIAN, PROTONOTARY

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Gratian.

The schemes of the impious cannot ultimately harm the children of grace, because God does not permit them to be tested beyond their strength, directing all things to the benefit of the elect and wonderfully drawing glorious advantage from every event. The Lord indeed has regarded your faith: He turned Master Vivian’s delay, and everything that he did in France after your departure, into glory for your name, making you “a god to Pharaoh.”

For when the lord king of England learned that you were returning to the curia with the lord of Sens—whose zeal he fears beyond what can be said—and saw that you were ready to exercise justice, he at once strove, personally and through his agents, to persuade the aforesaid Vivian to return. He promised that, through him, he would make peace for the honor of God and the benefit of the Church if Vivian procured an interview between him and us. For he said [Col. 0499A] that he wished to show Vivian this favor because he had found him compliant with himself; although it was rather your absence than Vivian’s presence that cooperated with God’s grace and pressed him toward peace.

In hope of peace, as will become more fully known from the letters summoning us, we came to the conference. What was done there your discernment may readily judge from what we have written below to the lord of Sens and our companions. We fear that, if we recount everything, the length of the account may cause weariness, especially since we know for certain that your diligence is occupied with many concerns. But just as an Ethiopian cannot change his skin or a leopard its spots, so those who from the beginning of life until mature age have taught their tongues to speak falsehood and have labored to act wickedly do not know how to put off deceit and fraud.

Thus, to use Master Vivian’s own words, this was the sum of all those promises which he found: that this king lives and speaks more sophistically than all mortals and therefore ought to be hateful to God and men. At length the said Master accepted your judgment; and, as we have learned from persons whose testimony should be trusted, he openly exposed the king’s deceit at Saint-Denis. As we have heard, he refused to accept the money sent to him as he was departing, detesting the king’s duplicity and malice. He also wrote back letters of rebuke, exhortation, and threat, as has been reported to us; we have ordered a copy of them to be presented to you.

All who saw the outcome of the intimacy formed, or heard Vivian speak, publicly declared that Gratian alone, among all who had been sent to the king of England, had acted wisely. If Vivian agrees with these things in the curia, then through Vivian’s agency, willingly or unwillingly, the renown of your name will shine more clearly there. If he should dare to support the side which he denounced among us, he deserves to undergo, with Christ’s betrayer, the shameful punishment of hanging. Yet we hope better things from him, nearer to salvation and honor; for, so far as we and those with us could observe, and as we have certainly learned from many, he conducted himself commendably at the end. You will learn the full course of the affair in due order. Please advance with diligence [Col. 0499D] our necessities and the honor of the Church. For if the lord pope and the Roman Church stretch out their hand in requital, we shall very quickly have peace, and the authority of the Roman Church will flourish both in England and in the lands on this side of the sea subject to the king of England.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO THE SAME PERSON

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Gratian, cardinal.

> [Note: [Col. 0499D] The reader will observe that Gratian is classed among the cardinals. This happened because in certain manuscripts the title “cardinal” is attached to “Lord Gratian.” But Gratian, I think, was never a cardinal. [Col. 0500D]]

We give manifold thanks to your kindness for the matters which, issuing from the pure fountain of affection, you have taken care to communicate to us through the bearer of this letter. Know for certain that, if you had come to us as we desired, we should surely have shown you every honor in our power with the utmost diligence—both in consideration of your person, whom we embrace with the greatest affection, and in consideration of the devotion which we have toward the most holy Roman Church. You would also have had a shorter and safer passage through our regions had you come to us, although our rivals and enemies, as though to our disadvantage and lest we should enjoy one another’s conversation together, persuaded you otherwise. We grieve greatly at having been most wickedly deprived of this.

Yet we earnestly beg you, with all the supplication we can make, that henceforth, if you please, you hold our person—and also the Church of Canterbury—in a certain special place of affection and familiar regard; and that you carefully extend to us your patronage at suitable times and places, taking pity at least on our tribulations and distresses, of which you already know some part, however small. Know without any doubt that neither death nor life nor any present circumstance can separate us from fidelity to the lord pope and the Roman Church—even if she herself, God forbid, should first utterly fail us. Farewell; and, if you please, trust the bearer of this letter regarding what he will convey more fully to you orally on our behalf.

## LETTER XL. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Col. 0500C]

No one sent by the Roman Church to the king of England in the Church’s cause, except you, has failed to injure her and give horns to the sinner. But you had raised her up, so that peace would necessarily have followed shortly, unless, after the curia had recovered strength, iniquity had regained its vigor. Recently we seemed to have received some consolation in the lord pope’s letters; but their authority vanished before they were delivered, for letters were sent in the opposite direction by which Satan was released to rage more freely against God’s Church.

For when, by the lord pope’s command, the bishops of London and Salisbury were absolved, everyone was emboldened to follow the king’s will. Thus he frees his supporters, however criminal; thus he triumphs over the Apostolic See; thus his envoys always return glorious, in defiance of God and His justice. In contrast, the hearts of the good are dismayed when they see such manifest and great iniquity continually prospering in its ways.

See how the injury done to you and the lord pope’s envoys has been punished; see how our fidelity has been rewarded and the calamity of God’s Church restrained. See how it has been avenged that he recently sought, by extorted oaths, to separate England from obedience to the lord pope. It is God’s mercy, indeed, that [Col. 0501A] he could not do so, since his malice omitted nothing within its power. For six years the curia has prolonged our exile and proscription. Innocent, wretched men have perished on the road without cause for the liberty of the Church; while the Church’s persecutors promise and bestow our spoils upon cardinals and courtiers. Thus Barabbas is released and Christ is crucified.

Our creditors have been exhausted; and those who were moved by pity for our exile, seeing what is done by the lord pope, are driven to despair. But the Lord will provide even here on the mountain, and that terrible Majesty who takes away the spirit of princes will judge the ends of the earth. By His grace, whether living or dead, we are and shall be ready to endure for the liberty of the Church exile, proscription, and every hardship of the world, for as long as it shall seem good to Him. Would that we may be found worthy to suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake!

Certainly, for this cause, we expose ourselves to be tortured, as it may please the Lord, not only by cardinals who attack the Church with the Church’s authority; but even if the whole world—God forbid—should rise up, we shall not, through God’s mercy, depart from the fidelity to the Church which we have professed. Let whoever henceforth has concern take pity on us and protect the liberty of the Church which the Apostolic See exposes. We shall not deliberately trouble the curia, but shall yield the cause to those whose iniquity is accepted there, who proclaim and sing of its venality in the streets. Yet in sparing them we keep silent about what has been granted to whom, and what has been promised, on account of this trafficking. There is no doubt that some [Col. 0501C] of those who returned as victors would have preferred not to have triumphed.

But you, who have undertaken the Church’s patronage in such danger, persevere in your good purpose—not out of regard for us, who are permitted to do nothing, but for Him who will undoubtedly reward your service most abundantly in return, and who will grant us the ability to render to your affection a fitting return of service, as we wish and ought. Meanwhile we shall remember you before God; and you, if you please, remember us with like affection.

## LETTER XLI. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Col. 0501D] Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Lord Gratian.

That experience is the mother and nurse of affairs is a celebrated and true maxim of ancient philosophy, confirmed even by Apollo’s testimony. Nor is this without reason: every experienced person can judge more faithfully concerning matters in which he has been engaged, while the imagination of the inexperienced concerning unknown matters is generally empty and deceptive. I have said this beforehand so that it may now at least be observed with what danger to the Church and to myself—or rather to the Apostolic See, whose privileges I undertook to defend not without great danger to myself—the lord pope refused to believe me, though experienced, about how he and the Church of God should deal with the lord king of England.

For behold, as soon as the voice of the latest Apostolic threat reached his ears—namely, that he was to be reduced to the condition of Frederick, styled emperor, that his land was to be subjected to interdict, and that bishops violating the mandate were to be suspended and excommunicated—he immediately made peace for the honor of God and the benefit of the Church, as must be understood from the conditions included in the agreement. Its form is clear from the letters sent to the lord pope. There is no doubt that he would have made it within the first two years of our exile if the lord pope had attacked him by this means from the beginning, or if those first sent to him had possessed our spirit. For what could the king have done against them, since it is eternally true: “Hope for nothing and fear nothing: you will have disarmed the anger of the powerless”?

[Col. 0502B] Or what did he attempt against you, whom he could not turn from the straight path by prayer, price, flattery, threats, or any entreaties whatsoever? Yet because the Roman Church—to speak this in your hearing with all due peace—has made fear its foundation, seeks things or shows favoritism to persons, and does not confront those doing wrong with the authority in which she is preeminent, therefore God’s heavy scourges, scarcely bearable by the whole world, come upon her; so that, made unstable, she flees from the face of the persecutor and scarcely endures amid tribulations.

But with whom could I more rightly lament these things than with one who, through God’s grace, is free from the aforesaid vices; who alone has compassion on the wretched and brought consolation; and who confronted that great king and all his accomplices to their face because he was blameworthy and attacked the Church freely and excessively? Since your courage has protected the Church of Canterbury amid adversity, it is right and wholly consonant with justice that she should submit herself to your patronage and will in prosperity.

It will be yours to prescribe whatever you please by request or command, for it is our purpose—mine, I mean, and that of my companions—to obey your instructions. Therefore, out of sincerity of conscience, we seek the service of you; we send to you the bearer of this letter, earnestly commending both him and the petitions which we present through him to the lord pope to your affection. Let this be most certainly known, and through you be made known to our lord: if he had exercised the same rigor in every article of our cause—or rather, his own—he could easily have compelled the king to make satisfaction in all matters. Matters deliberately and intentionally passed over here will, God willing, be supplied orally by the messenger. Let your discernment also see that the more urgent and effective letters which our lord sent to the king of England on the Church’s behalf are entered in the register; for whenever examples of the ancestors encourage posterity, they are a great incitement to virtue. We send back to you the letters concerning our affair which we received, so that, if copies of the issued documents are lacking, you may borrow them from the transcripts.

## LETTER XLII. TO HENRY OF PISA, PRIEST

[Col. 0503A]

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Henry, cardinal-priest.

If I should speak to you otherwise than according to my soul, I should seem equally unjust toward myself and you, and sufficiently faithful to neither. For I have often experienced that my safety and the welfare of the English Church depend, after God, upon your counsel. Although my affection toward you is great and my confidence in you abundant, it is not fitting to multiply words, since few suffice for the wise—especially since charity customarily brings aid unasked to the necessities of friends.

From the letters which we send to the lord pope and from the report of the messenger, who is brother to the imprisoned religious priest, you will readily understand in what balance our cause—or indeed certainly yours and that of the whole Church of God—now hangs. Henceforth it will be for your prudence to oppose such great evils, to forestall by counsel and assistance such wicked and destructive men, and to render their efforts ineffective. We have delayed pronouncing against the king the sentence of anathema which he has deserved and continually provokes by repeated injuries; but he himself, while laying violent hands upon Christ’s priests and despoiling churches of possessions and liberty, has twisted the anathema back upon his own head.

For canon law excepts neither power nor primacy, but strikes sinners alike with an equal punishment of condemnation. Unless perhaps you also judge ecclesiastical laws to be comparable to civil laws, which, as Anacharsis complains, are like spiders’ webs: they impede and hold flies, but, when torn, let larger winged creatures pass through. This is what the Lord reproaches ecclesiastical judges for, so that they almost say with the pagans:

> “Can the divine powers be so greatly angry with the wretched?”

But the law of the Lord is not so: it begins vengeance from His sanctuary; it exercises the harshest judgment upon those who preside; and it declares that the powerful are to be punished powerfully. Israel is recorded to have committed fornication with the Midianites, and the leaders were struck by punishment for the crime. For the Lord says: “Take all the leaders of the people, and hang them before the sun upon gibbets.” And when justice decrees that the soul which sins shall die, so that neither father bears the son’s iniquity nor son the father’s, by what transposition [Col. 0503D] of divine law does it come about that rulers eat the sour grape and private persons’ teeth are set on edge; that the powerful man is released in his crime and the innocent poor man is assigned to punishment?

I beg you to give credit to the messengers and to exert effort and diligence, lest the priest, a clerk of William of Pavia, have recently made a true promise to the king of England, assuring him that his master, once he had received the legation, would settle the cause of the Church which we support according to the king’s will. But let it be certain that we shall entrust neither our own person nor the Church’s cause except to the judgment of the lord pope, by whom the English Church shall stand or fall. Yet she shall stand through the mercy of Him in whom she is founded and by whose blood she has been redeemed. Your discernment remembers with what sincerity certain men have dealt with us, so that for a just cause we may decline their judgment.

(See also the letter beginning “Enough and more than enough,” addressed to Conrad, Archbishop of Mainz, together with Cardinals Sabinus, Henry, and Hyacinth.)

## LETTER XLIII. TO HUGH, CARDINAL OF BOLOGNA

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Hugh, Cardinal of Bologna.

We thank your affection for the love which you have always shown to us and ours, desiring, with the Lord as author, to respond to your devotion according to its merits. Since the preceding display of benefits has given us full confidence in your favor, we earnestly ask you to rise to our aid against the persecutors of ecclesiastical liberty and enemies of the Apostolic See. By God’s help they are now almost spent among us. For the faithful hope that the Church’s salvation is at the door if the lord pope strikes with the sword of Apostolic severity the bishop of London, instigator of the whole wickedness, and his accomplices, whom we have excommunicated as their faults required.

There will be no need thereafter to exercise a harsher vengeance, if he permits us to cure the sickness of the members and cut away the rotten parts that will not accept treatment. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIV. TO HUMBALD, BISHOP OF OSTIA

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Humbald, Bishop of Ostia: greetings and ready service offered with reverence.

We have thought it fitting to disclose to your holiness, whom we venerate as an immovable pillar in God’s temple, how many and how great are the oppressions under which God’s Church labors in our regions, and how perilous a misery she endures both in us and in her other members. To report this more fully to you, we send Master Henry, a faithful son of the holy Roman Church and our intimate associate, asking you to give credit to his words as though they proceeded from our own mouth.

We need a prompt response containing your counsel; and, since from day to day the insolence of unlawful exactions—indeed, exactions utterly contrary to the sacred canons and to our order—grows stronger against us, we flee to you after God, having no other refuge. May your holiness prosper and remember us.

## LETTER XLV. TO THE SAME PERSON AND HYACINTH

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Humbald, Bishop of Ostia, and Hyacinth, cardinals.

Others console us with words, but your kindness does so through deeds and works. You have grieved for our condition and the Church’s calamity, and you have regarded the distresses of Christ’s poor, exiled with us, as your own. On that day the just Judge will repay you the rewards of brotherly charity and the fruit of true compassion—He who promises abundant mercy in grace to the merciful.

You did not go after the gold by which certain persons were recently captured, to our injury and the confusion of the Apostolic See. By their patronage, once the Apostolic letters were received—letters which the king of England has them repeatedly read at the crossroads of both kingdoms—he has boasted that he has triumphed over the Roman Church. Nor without reason: he has achieved his desire, and now he rages at will in God’s Church, no one opposing him, hoping—may God avert it!—that either the lord pope or I shall in the meantime die as he wishes. For there is nothing he desires more than the death of one or the other of us.

You invite us to patience; but for four years now we have practiced it, exposed with our fellow exiles to the greatest sufferings—in hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, amid every assault of raging fortune. For which of those exiled with us is weak and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble and I do not burn? But what torments me more severely is that I can neither see nor speak of the Church reduced to miserable servitude without grief. Therefore I suffer, but unwillingly, because I suffer with her. Would that our lords the cardinals might suffer with her, all of whom preach patience—some from awareness of virtue, others to conceal their own fault.

The Lord surely knows who are His, and the Church already perceives in part who are not His. For the king of England proclaims who are his; nor is it hidden what gold has been distributed and to whom. Yet his gifts are our spoils, the spoils of the Crucified One’s poor—indeed Christ’s own spoils, indeed but the smallest portion of the spoils. What, then, will He answer on that day to those who despoil Christ through the hands of tyrants, when He judges the living and the dead and conscience gives testimony to each and all?

Let these words not be understood as though some end of patience exists other than the crown, or as though we, Christ’s exiles and outcasts in His cause, do not intend to die before being conquered. Rather, in such great straits, we need the support of the counsel of our lord and other lords and friends. For the man who placed the suspension of our authority at the king of England’s discretion—namely, until we return to his favor—has closed every path to peace for us. The king had invited us through the count of Flanders to a conference; but when his envoys presented him with this Apostolic rescript, he became so elated that he despised God and men with equal fury, but the Romans above all.

May it therefore please your affection, which God has disposed to patronize the necessity of the Church of Canterbury, to obtain from the lord pope through yourselves and other friends of God that he either remove this suspension or shorten its term, writing to the king of the French, etc.

## LETTER XLVI. TO THE SAME PERSON

Thomas of Canterbury to Humbald, Bishop of Ostia.

The illustrious orator’s famous dictum is that to be deceived once is a misfortune, twice utter folly, and a third time disgraceful. Yet would that the envoys of the king of England, armed with deceits and threats, had not mocked the religion of the Apostolic See three or four times—if indeed those can complain of being deceived who, knowingly and deliberately, by concealing the crime, publicly gave sinners boldness to sin.

For how could the Roman Church, which directs the eyes of its providence over the whole world and to which the affairs of provinces are referred, fail to know what is known to the bleary-eyed and barbers, proclaimed in the streets, and sung at the crossroads of Ascalon? For five years I have endured the proscription of myself and my companions; I have lamented before you injuries both to the Church and to myself. You have seen some funerals of those exiled with me, who have fallen asleep in Christ for whom they suffered, and you have heard of more. Yet you still do not restrain the fury of the king of England, whose hand is stretched out to abase the Church and trample the saints.

Where, I ask you, Father, is the zeal of your priesthood by which patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and apostolic men opposed principalities and powers for the house of the Lord, standing in battle on the day of peril and conquering kingdoms through faith? Were these things written in order that they should be tales told by storytellers, rather than examples of conduct and a pattern of life? For preachers turn them over in their mouths; but—what I cannot say without shame and sorrow—their life proves that they do not hold them in their hearts. Or rather, if they retain them in their conscience, they are most justly inscribed there as evidence of condemnation against those who teach good things and do not do them.

And indeed, more than others, I fear lest the blood of the Church—so long, so atrociously, and openly afflicted, [Col. 0506C] and still unavenged—soon be required of me; since before long we shall all stand before Christ’s tribunal, without respect of persons, to render account for our deeds and our evasions. But you repeatedly chose that the king should be admonished, as reason required, so that his malice might be exposed; and he has been admonished by letters and foreign messengers, by subdeacons, by your cardinals, by bishops, by abbots, and now at last, at the end of the fifth year, almost by a peremptory decree through Lord Gratian and Master Vivian. Yet his latest actions have always been worse than the former. Lord Gratian will report this; he has conducted himself in this affair with such integrity and prudence that he ought to have earned great favour with God and men. [Col. 0506D] Peace was not restored through no fault of his, nor of ours.

But because the king now affirms, now denies, and surpasses Proteus in changeableness, Geoffrey the archdeacon also prevented the peace that was nearly concluded, persuading the king to make no settlement unless he extorted an undertaking to observe the customs—which, so that he may obtain them more easily, he now calls by the more favourable name of “dignities.” I, indeed, grant and gladly accept that, without prejudice to my rank, all the dignities of the king and kingdom may stand and flourish. But I do not consent to swear observance of them. For I do not presume to swear that I shall fulfil either the canons or the precepts of the Gospel; nor do I see that the people of the land are bound by such an oath.

He still labours to avoid being compelled either to restore what was taken away or to make satisfaction for it, which is manifestly [Col. 0507A] unjust—especially since he himself has openly confessed that I owe him nothing in respect of my administration of the chancery. The messengers will supply further details. If it please you, deign graciously to hear them and, as is your custom, to advance our petitions. May my lord and Father prosper.

## LETTER XLVII. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Humbald, Bishop of Ostia, afterwards pope.

We are often compelled to lament in the ears of your holiness the afflictions of our misery, because they have multiplied beyond number and measure. Apart from you, there is no one—or scarcely anyone—who consoles us in so great a tribulation [Col. 0507B] or promises hope of relief.

Let there for the present be silence about the deaths of kinsmen which we have endured, the slaughter and imprisonment of Christ’s priests, and the cruelty of the murderous edict, by which Herodian savagery, without regard for condition, rank, age, or sex, exterminated and proscribed all who had incurred suspicion, on whatever grounds, of being affectionate toward us or of keeping faith with God and His Church. And so that, by the length of the torment, its inhumanity might surpass Herod’s envy of blood, it banished the cradles of crying infants; it tore nursing children from their mothers’ or nurses’ breasts.

For the more pain is prolonged, the more bitter its force becomes; and any punishment, however great, becomes milder when compressed into a moment. It ought to have been enough [Col. 0507C] for our persecutor that he had hitherto tortured the Church with impunity, that he had so afflicted us and ours with five years’ exile and proscription, while we waited for our patience to bring him to repentance. Let ancient histories, if you please, be unrolled; let the deeds of old tyrants be reviewed; let the annals of the Church’s birth be traversed. Among all her persecutors one will not easily find one who persecuted a single man as he has done, seeking by so many refined methods to accomplish so great a slaughter of innocents.

Since, therefore, his purpose is so evident from the testimony of those very events—he who, though, as has been said, he thirsts for our blood with such eagerness, thirsts yet more eagerly to destroy the liberty of the Church and to banish the authority of the Apostolic See from his territories—it is marvellous in [Col. 0507D] the eyes of all wise persons who fear the Lord on what grounds the Roman Church has tolerated him so long, with what patience she has heard him demand so many unjust and monstrous things, when she was divinely established to uproot and scatter every power and height that exalts itself in injury and insult to Christ.

“To spare the conquered and crush the proud” was the distinction of the pagan Romans; and certainly Christ’s teaching humbles the proud and exalts the humble. “Behold,” He says, “I have set thee over nations and kingdoms, that thou mayest pluck up and destroy, scatter and overthrow, build and plant.” Should there be respect of persons among Peter’s successors, Christ’s vicars? [Col. 0508A] Certainly this is not with God, who answers each person, prince and commoner alike, according to merit. What glory is there before God or men in decreeing rights for poorer people, while powerful persons are not restrained by any authority of law from the greatest and many crimes? True justice indeed punishes the powerful powerfully, and exercises the most severe judgment upon those who rule.

Who, while the Roman pontiff knew and saw it, has abused the goods of churches with such licence as the King of England now abuses them? For five years now he has possessed our bishopric and all the property of all our people; likewise he has converted the bishoprics of Lincoln, Bath, Hereford, and Ely to his own uses. He has distributed almost all the possessions of the Church of Llandaff among [Col. 0508B] his soldiers. He does not permit Bangor, which has now lacked a bishop for almost ten years, to receive one by ordination. What shall be said of the abbeys which he holds? Their number is uncertain.

He even glories that he does this lawfully, by right of the customs which, with peace to you all be it said, the Roman Church ought publicly from the beginning to have condemned, together with their authors and observers, as hostile to God and contrary to the eternal law. If we, Father, had wished to yield to them, no loss at all would have come to us or ours. Even now, if we wished to give way, the most direct road would lie open to every intimacy and favour of the king, and to dominion over the whole kingdom. But far be it from us to betray the Church’s public liberty for the bargain of private advantage, to wrest from the Church the privilege of the Apostolic See, and for temporal profit to incur eternal loss.

[Col. 0508C] Because we refuse to cast down the Church, the king seeks our overthrow from you. Because we refuse to transfer the law of God so that the iniquity of tyrants may replace it, he seeks to have us transferred, without necessity, without benefit, and against authority, to another Church. Because we refuse to follow one who summons us into partnership in iniquity, he asks you to summon us away, so that on the journey he may conduct some kind of business in our blood with the companions of his iniquity.

For what else does it mean that he incites the Milanese, Cremonese, and Parmesans, corrupted by payment, to destroy us? [Col. 0508D] What injury have we ever done to the Pavians or other cities of Italy, that they should procure our exile? In what have we harmed the learned men of Bologna, who, though solicited by entreaties and promises, refused to consent to our ruin after hearing the case? Certainly, we had not proscribed Robert of Basseville; nevertheless, he was induced by solicitations to secure the perpetuation of our proscription before you. But afterwards, when he learned of the deceit, moved by repentance, he asked that his unjust petition should not be heard.

Richard, bishop-elect of Syracuse, corrupted by the hope of receiving the bishopric of Lincoln, aided our persecutors with resources, armed them with counsel, and strengthened them with force. They even promised the King of Sicily himself, within whose territories you now reside, a daughter of the King of England in marriage, so that they might win him over to the destruction of the Church and [Col. 0509A] of us. Did they not bring in, as though hired camps, bread-breakers, the household of the lion, a nation of robbers, and other most powerful Romans, in order not so much to bend as to break the Roman Church? They also promise the peace of the emperor and of the Saxons; and they promise that by money they will induce all Romans to render allegiance to the lord pope—provided that, in our overthrow, he satisfies the will of the King of England.

It is plain what a safe passage, what a pleasant journey, this man’s careful concern was preparing for us. Certainly he did not much concern himself with how our creditors might be satisfied, how our companions—if any could be found—might be supplied with necessities for setting out, how the costs of travel might be met, [Col. 0509B] or how the exiled multitude, needy and afflicted after five years of exile, might receive relief before being abandoned amid such calamities. The same careful planners of these things—since we do not believe that the king’s name ought to be brought under this suspicion—could poison the household utensils of guests; and it is difficult for a person to preserve life unharmed when one who has authority over the whole household lies in wait for him.

And, lest this letter and its words be drawn out on this point: while life remains our companion, we shall never expose ourselves to such great and numerous perils for any summons whatever. For one who, for any reason, does not shrink from death can more easily end life by sword or noose.

Recently the same king sent his envoys—the Bishop of Séez and Geoffrey, Archdeacon of Canterbury—[Col. 0509C] to the Most Christian King, urging him by prayers and promises to drive us from his land. But that man, full of God, replied that he had inherited this as a hereditary right from his predecessors, and that it had always been the custom of the kingdom of the Franks kindly to receive all persons exiled for justice and to afford them the consolations of due humanity. He said that he would never abandon, for any cause whatever, so praiseworthy and God-pleasing an inheritance.

He added that he had received us from the hand of the lord pope, whom alone he has as lord on earth; and therefore that neither for emperor nor king nor any worldly power would he cease to protect us and our cause as long as necessary, since God is with us and we endure so many wrongs and losses for the defence of His law. [Col. 0509D] With this answer he dismissed them in confusion; and toward us—may God reward him for it—he is more kindly and generous than usual, though he has always been kind and generous.

He says that in our cause he will test the integrity and strength of the Roman Church, and the sincerity of the lord pope. He especially praises the pope’s loyalty and steadfastness in rejoicing that the King of England has been rejected in his unjust requests. This is so, however, if what he has heard from rumour-mongers is true, and if the lord pope perseveres in what he promised us.

There are persons on the opposing side who advise us not to seek restitution of what has been taken, and, if peace must perhaps be negotiated, to pass over everything perfunctorily. They do not consider how dangerous it would be as an example, [Col. 0510A] since avarice, once inflamed by profit, may thereby be encouraged to exile and proscribe bishops at will, and then return to the Church’s favour if, at whatever loss to it, it makes some sort of peace. Such connivance inflames greedy powers and gives wicked men boldness to offend.

It would be better for us never to have been born than to have introduced into the Church the plague of so pernicious an example—especially since he could easily compensate, in great measure, for losses of property by immunities, privileges, uncultivated estates, and other benefits, on our prior advice.

Nor, if the lord pope supports us, is it difficult to extort this. Though he puts forth threats, he is wholly shaken with fear now that he has seen contumacious bishops, [Col. 0510B] other accomplices in his wickedness, and minions of iniquity handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. If these men are crushed, he will be subdued sooner and more easily, and his lightning-bolts will turn into rain. Believe those who have experience, who know the man’s character, who have borne the burden and heat of the day, and who still do not fear the conflict for the Lord and the Church’s liberty. Believe, I say, that he is a man of such a disposition that he cannot be corrected except by punishments.

And because the Bishop of London, the instigator of all his wickedness, lately rushed into such shamelessness as to say that he owed no obedience, since his translation, to the Church of Canterbury, to which he had made a profession; he even boasts that he will cause the archiepiscopal see to be transferred to the Church of London. It is necessary that the head of so great [Col. 0510C] an iniquity be crushed, so that the English Church may recover strength.

Our brethren and fellow bishops lately opposed him when he was plotting a schism in the Church. To overthrow them, he summoned the king’s officials from the cis-marine regions, so that those who would not consent with him to receive the mark of the beast might be afflicted through them. May it therefore please your graciousness, whom the Lord has raised up as patron of the Church of Canterbury, to recall these matters to the lord pope’s mind; according to your custom, strengthen your brethren in support of the Church, and obtain that, through our patient endurance of suffering, the Apostolic See may gain the liberty of the English Church.

For we choose rather to die in the bitterness of exile for the Lord than to see the Church profaned by the accursed betrayals [Col. 0510D] of tyrants and the force of the divine law made void. Forgive me for prolonging my words: necessity compels them to be prolonged; and it is no small part of consolation to pour out one’s own calamities in the ear of a sweetest Father and most compassionate lord. For indeed:

> It is sweet for the miserable to speak and recall their former complaints.

And, that you may more often call these things to mind, prostrate at your feet we implore you most earnestly. May your holiness always prosper, mindful of us before God.

These are the names of the excommunicated, who, having been found incorrigible and contumacious, were denounced in the second denunciation: Geoffrey, Archdeacon of Canterbury; Robert, his vicar; Richard of [Col. 0511A] Ilchester; Richard de Lucy; William Giffard; Adam of Charing.

## LETTER XLVIII. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to the Bishop of Ostia.

As rivers return to the place from which they issue, so that they may flow again, so we ought to approach on the bended knees of the mind to render thanks to your compassion; that through you we may be strengthened in the service of the Church, since after God we received strength from your mercy lest we fall into the enemy’s hand. Our friends and neighbours stood against us, sharpening the swords of persecutors; and, in order to confound and crush us, they themselves became a crooked bow. But your faith, ever tested [Col. 0511B] in the furnace of our tribulation and the affliction of the Church, shines brightly; and your charity, seeking not its own interests but those of Jesus Christ, has obtained from the Father of mercies a peace which the world could neither give nor hope for.

For we, approaching our lord the King of England with due humility, have made peace with him—a peace whose entire substance nevertheless rests in hope, but which, with God as its author, will not disappoint. For He who began it will Himself bring it to completion. Some persons, even some who seemed to be pillars of the Church, urged that we should submit ourselves and the whole cause of God to his arbitration. But, God being favourable, it neither has been nor will be obtained from us that we should submit to the judgment of a man the question of losses inflicted on God’s Church and ourselves; the complaint concerning customs—or rather abuses; or the observance of the divine law, which, whether rulers will or not, must be kept by the faithful. [Col. 0511C]

For however great a power is divinely ordained, it is less than Him who established it; and it is a clear and perpetual principle of law that sins cannot be forgiven to the unrepentant. If property taken away is not restored by one able to make repayment, it is plain that true repentance is not shown, but rather a fiction of malice veiled by falsehood is practised—or, more truly said, doubly defiled. The former error indeed remains, and is heaped up more heavily by fresh fraud.

The messenger will supply the rest. We desire that both he and the petitions which we present through him to the lord pope be more carefully commended to your fatherhood and promoted.

## LETTER XLIX. TO HYACINTH, DEACON

[Col. 0511D]

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Hyacinth, Cardinal Deacon: greeting and reverence with the utmost devotion.

Evils have overflowed upon our heads; we are afflicted beyond measure by insults and injuries; we are filled with reproaches. Those who rise against us might perhaps have swallowed us alive, had we not fled to the angel of supreme counsel and the holy Roman Church. After God, the sum of our hope rests in her; if, God forbid, we fall away from her, deprived of all counsel, we utterly do not know what we ought to do.

Therefore, that you may know more fully the course of what we suffer, [Col. 0512A] we send to you Master Henry, our faithful and familiar friend and yours. From his report you will be able to assess the misery of our condition. If it please you, believe him in what he tells you on our behalf as though you heard it from our own mouth. I beg that your discretion not delay to disclose to us your counsel; for we are in straits, and we await comfort from you, in whom we have the greatest trust, as our chief friend and patron. May your holiness prosper and have compassion upon us.

## LETTER L. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Hyacinth, [Col. 0512B] Cardinal Deacon.

We have placed the Church of England and ourselves in your hands, so that our advancement may most rightly be referred to your glory, upon whose help we rely; and so that our desolation may count as your loss, since with most ready affection we have devoted ourselves and our affairs to your will. The persecutors of the Church have advanced so far in malice that they cannot proceed further; whether willing or unwilling, they will fail in themselves unless the Roman Church gives them strength for their own destruction.

Their thunderbolts will become thunder, and the whirlwind of this windiness will easily be dissolved by rain. With God as author, it will shortly come to pass that you have conquered, provided you can await a swift and certain victory. Remember your Pompey, whom your Caesar likewise said to be invincible, if only he knew as well how to conquer as he knew how to fight.

At first the King of England acted to prevent any appeal to the Apostolic See. Through the ministry—indeed, the perjury—of John of Oxford, who now dares to appear before your eyes, he cast in his lot with schismatics in schism. But now he has been brought to such a point that he has been compelled to flee to Peter’s See and invoke the name of the lord pope, whose invocation he formerly forbade. [Col. 0512C]

And he would rightly flee to the Roman Church if he avoided injury rather than inflicting it; if he offered devotion to the Church rather than seeking its overthrow; if, by promising feigned friendship and false service, he did not do more harm than he did as an openly declared enemy. Behold, sweetest Father and Lord, now it will appear what sort of men you are.

Recall that:

> The pipe sings sweetly while the bird-catcher deceives the bird.

Let not intentions concealed beneath the fox deceive you. If, for the sake of any advantage to yourselves, you ever do harm to the Church at his prayers or gifts, he himself will, in his customary fashion, proclaim this to your shame and the reproach of the Apostolic See. What he now frequently says to many—that everything at Rome is for sale—he will then have publicly proclaimed from the rooftops.

Would that you alone had heard what he has said about those legates whom he received, and also about the one whom he pretends to love and whom he is said again to have requested as legate! You alone, I say, so that the ears of fools and the credulous might not have been infected by the insults of an unbridled tongue. Kindly, if you please, receive our messengers, through whom you will hear the rest. [Col. 0513A]

Have compassion upon the priest whom, after that so-called appeal, he caused to be violently seized and thrown into prison. For thereafter, if we have appealed—indeed, we who appealed in his presence and have for two years awaited and demanded a judgment—he ought not to have introduced any innovation against us or ours. Observe how he has stripped churches of possessions and liberty, and with what cruelty he persecutes us and those of ours who endure, for the Church’s liberty and the faithfulness of the Apostolic See, and who are still ready to suffer to the extent of the strength God has granted us.

The priest-clerk of William of Pavia recently promised the King of England that his master would decide this case according to the king’s will, if he received the legation. But let it be certain that we shall entrust neither our person nor the Church’s cause to one whose disposition toward us and the king we have long sufficiently experienced. This judgment will issue from the countenance of the lord pope; by it the Church stands or falls. Yet through God’s mercy, and your help and counsel, she will stand. [Col. 0513B]

## LETTER LI. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Hyacinth, Cardinal.

[Col. 0513C] The more confidently we rely on the affection of your integrity, the more confidently, in the difficulties arising for us and for the Church entrusted to us, do we have recourse to you as our sole and final aid. Therefore, holding unquestioned confidence in you as a specially beloved friend, we recall to the remembrance of your loving integrity that you graciously received us and our Church—indeed, rather your own Church—under your protection. It is now necessary, and highly expedient for both us and you, to demonstrate by the performance of deeds that you preserve untouched her dignities and rights. For the performance of a deed is proof of love.

Accordingly, we earnestly entreat your affection by every means in our power to take diligent care, through your zeal and wisdom, that the dignities, liberties, and rights of our Church be preserved untouched and unimpaired. But enough of this.

Behold, my lord, the letter of the lord of Pavia, which, at the beginning of his arrival, he sent us—not wholly lacking [Col. 0513D] the glory of pomposity. You may inspect it; and, we think, you will find that it is by no means entirely free from a certain boastfulness. We hoped that his coming would bring us consolation and peace; instead, it brought us an increase of desolation rather than help toward consolation.

For he boasts that the lord pope chiefly sent him into the land of the King of England to settle the disputes between us and the king, according as he should judge best for the advantage of God’s Church. We neither believed nor obtained from the Roman curia that we should be subjected to the judgment of his arbitration, since the whole court, no less than we, knows well that he is our enemy and that of our Church, and indeed a more than manifest foe. But, as we tell you truly, we shall avoid his judgment for ever. [Col. 0514A]

Henceforth, after God, we cast all our hope and trust entirely upon you, earnestly asking that, since we can by no means hope for peace or reconciliation through him, you so effectively employ the care of your prudence against him with the lord pope that he may firmly command, by his letters, persons both on this side of the sea and beyond it, and enjoin them by virtue of obedience, firmly to maintain and observe the sentence which we shall reasonably pronounce against the king and his land.

Moreover, use your efforts more diligently so that through you we may obtain confirmation of our primacy, which the lord pope granted us at Sens upon our first arrival. Farewell, and be mindful of us, as we are of you. Make arrangements to dispatch and send back to us the bearer of this letter as soon as you can, informing us of the condition of the Church, the lord pope, and yourselves. Farewell again.

## LETTER LII. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Hyacinth, Cardinal.

The blood of those slain for the Lord’s cause and the liberty of the Church cries out to the Lord; and all the wretched survivors flee, amid these miseries, to the feet of your holiness. Only those who have experienced it know how many and how great things the English Church has suffered throughout this entire five-year period; among them I am foremost, together with my wretched fellow-exiles, Christ Jesus’ proscribed ones. [Col. 0514C]

May He whose inheritance is attacked, whose law is trampled underfoot, and whose holy things are profaned swiftly be gracious to His cause, as He stands the most faithful witness of my conscience; and may He bring against the persecutors and oppressors of the innocent the judgment which He has promised. The King of England has been admonished by letters, by messengers, by abbots, by bishops, by the subdeacons of the Roman curia, by cardinals, and now at last almost by a peremptory edict through Lord Gratian and Master Vivian. You may hear, from Lord Gratian’s report—he who has conducted himself faithfully, modestly, and with every integrity in this affair and now hastens to you—what progress they made.

For peace was not prevented through us, but through him who trusts in his own power, in the riches of the Church whose spoils he plunders with impunity, in the craftiness of his adherents, and in the favour of certain of your people, whom until now he has had as defenders in protecting his perverse acts. [Col. 0514D] For, as the world perceives, grieves, and groans, no one brings a cause so unjust to the Roman Church that, when hope of profit is conceived there—not to say the scent of filth—he does not find a helper and patron.

But the Lord also sees this upon the mountain, before whose tribunal we shall all soon stand to answer for our deeds and consciences. Hear, if you please, the terms upon which our cause now rests. The king consents that I and my people return to our own homes—that is, to empty houses—to preserve God’s honour, provided his dignities be safeguarded; [Col. 0515A] by that name he means those corrupt customs which you have heard of and which, as is established, are condemned by divine law and the authority of the Roman Church.

We, however, accept that the dignities of the kingdom may stand and flourish without prejudice to God’s honour and to faithfulness to the Roman Church; they must be restrained within the bounds of the divine honour. God’s honour is not to be constrained by their standard. But he does not consent unless we absolutely profess, under religious obligation of an oath, to observe the dignities—something which not even the least person among the people of the land has yet done. Nor has the clergy anywhere been compelled to swear that they will observe either the sacred canons or the Gospel’s precepts. Certainly it would not be safe, because we all offend in many things.

He refuses to restore what was taken or make satisfaction, although he has publicly professed both to the aforesaid messengers of the lord pope and to others that I owe him nothing from the time of the chancery. [Col. 0515B] Yet he gives as a reason for this unjust retention that his predecessors, when our predecessors—whom they had often expelled—returned, are not found to have restored anything to them. But histories and the testimony of living persons prove this false.

Is not, then, the man to be restrained who appropriates the violences and impieties of his ancestors as law? Certainly, if—God forbid—he prevails in this, he will leave to all nations and ages the worst example of wicked advantage. Let him then exile and proscribe as many and as great persons, and for as long as he wishes; when they return, he will exclude their petitions by this example—indeed, now by this law. For I call God to witness upon my soul that the destructive force of this example moves me more than the temporal loss of possessions.

Therefore, since he demands new and undue obligations and asserts such perverse customs under the name of dignities, let no one persuade you that I create an obstacle to peace; rather, it is he who overturns God’s law and throws the whole Church into disorder. [Col. 0515C] Whatever I can do without prejudice to my rank and without the destructive force of an example, I shall gladly do to recover his favour and my peace. But far be it from me knowingly to act against God for a momentary quiet and for goods not merely perishable but already perishing!

I have written these matters to your fatherhood more fully. Yet, lest written words cause weariness, many further necessary points have been placed in the mouths of the messengers. If it please you, receive them with your customary kindness, and support the Church’s cause as your own, because it is God’s cause. I and my little ones are, and always shall be, yours.

Likewise to Lord Albert, Cardinal Priest.

Likewise to Lord Theodwin, Cardinal Priest.

## LETTER LIII. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Hyacinth, Cardinal.

If the labouring farmer ought first, after rendering the first-fruits to God, to eat, it is most just that your charity—which, in raising up the holy Church of Canterbury, now almost perishing, has laboured longer and more than nearly anyone, and, what is more, more faithfully and effectively—should receive from it the fruits of its labour in every thanksgiving and performance of service. [Col. 0516A]

For when the faith of almost all other friends had failed, you raised their spirits from faint-heartedness into hope, strengthened feeble hands, made weak knees firm, and, as a diligent hearer of the word, a true disciple of Christ, a sharer with the Apostle, and Peter’s heir, confirmed by example and word your brethren, who had been appointed to the worship of justice and the patronage of the Church.

For Satan had demanded the Roman Church in your tribulation, as in ours, in order to sift it like wheat, to test her own people and prove the faithless. But Christ brought forth from that very temptation an outcome joyful and useful to all the faithful, [Col. 0516B] and especially glorious to you, who surpassed others in faith. By God’s grace and yours, we have made peace with the lord King of England, to the honour of God and, we hope, the advantage of the Church. The bearer of this letter will explain its terms to you. We desire that he be carefully commended to you and that the petitions he carries be promoted with your customary diligence.

(See also the letter beginning, “More than enough,” etc., addressed to Conrad and others.)

## LETTER LIV. TO JOHN, CARDINAL OF STS. JOHN AND PAUL

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to John, Cardinal of Sts. John and Paul.
