[Col. 0516C] Your discretion is not unaware with what integrity of faith, devotion of obedience, and performance of services the Church of Canterbury, beyond all the others of our whole island, has always adhered to the Apostolic See; nor could she ever be torn from fidelity to it, whether by the allurements of prosperity or the storms of adversity.

She was accustomed to rejoice in your patronage, to await from you in the time of our predecessor consolation in tribulation, and in her needs to be instructed by your counsel and strengthened by your assistance. She was devoted to you and counted it among her successes if she were given an opportunity to serve you, if by her merits she seemed in any way diligent in your service. We ourselves also, who, though unworthy, by divine favour administer her, have often—as we remember clearly—devoted care and diligence to serving your will and your interests. Would that it had not slipped from your memory!

But because in this matter you seem more forgetful than is expedient for us, we ask that you at least believe our brother, whom we do not think forgetful of your service, concerning our devotion toward you. If, after receiving the episcopal rank, we have not served you in our own person, our will certainly was not lacking, but our means. We hoped especially in you, not withdrawing our service though delaying it. We had resolved that, when opportunity came, we would repay with multiplied devotion and service what had been deferred, to a friend and lord who kindly awaited it.

We therefore marvel exceedingly who has turned you away [Col. 0517A] from love of the Church of Canterbury and our protection, especially in God’s cause. If it were endangered—God forbid—the liberty of the whole English Church would be lost, the authority of the Roman See excluded from England, and all things would proceed at the king’s nod. If from the beginning we had wished to agree to the customs he demands, we should not need your intervention or anyone else’s with him.

You must consider whether, at the words of a notorious oath-breaker, whose frauds have been exposed by God’s favour, one ought so quickly to withdraw from a friend and so easily to despise the service of the Church of Canterbury. Yet even thus rejected and injured, she will not withdraw from you; nor, if it please you, shall we cease from your service, but whenever opportunity is given shall strive with still greater devotion to serve your honour and that of yours. [Col. 0517B]

Trusting, therefore, in this purpose and the security of our conscience, we earnestly ask that you not reject the Church of Canterbury as she offers herself to you, nor abandon God’s cause, which is unquestionably in your hands, lest God abandon you—He who will judge you by the judgment with which you judge. Let the Church of Canterbury now experience the faithfulness of an old friend; for one who abandons a friend in need is not that person’s friend, but fortune’s.

Therefore, as to a faithful friend and lord, we inform you that cultivating the friendship of that oath-breaker and his like will not benefit you as much as it will harm you if you cast away the service of the Church of Canterbury. For it is a servile disposition that is corrected only by punishments.

## LETTER LV. TO THE SAME RECIPIENT

[Col. 0517C]

To the venerable brother—and would that he were a friend—Lord John of Naples, by God’s grace Cardinal Priest of the holy Roman Church: Thomas, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, wretched and pitiable exile, greeting; and may you so pass through temporal goods that you do not forfeit the eternal.

The evangelical word is: “He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters.” And now, what wrong has there ever been on our part against your eminence, what want of devotion on the part of our insignificance, that, in the time of our tribulation, your gracious prudence should not be kind to us, that your goodwill should not act [Col. 0517D] with us—indeed, what is harsher, that your hand should not cease to add to the importunities and troubles of an exile and outlaw, that your works and efforts should not cease, whenever opportunity offered, to increase the misery of a wretched man? Surely, such testimony of conscience ought not to have become your glory. Therefore, henceforth spare us, if you please; spare us, I beg you—and now is the time to spare. Let your indignation cease to aggravate an unfortunate man’s misfortune and to tear at his innocence. For even if I was once fortunate, according to the condition of the time I have learned now to be unfortunate; nor is anything more fortunate for the unfortunate than to know his own lot. Moreover, how could it ever have slipped from your memory that, at the request of the lord king of France, in his grove near Orléans, [Col. 0518A] in the presence of Count Theobald, your discretion received us from the king’s own hand, to protect us and thereafter to cherish us against every person except the lord pope? Why has that undertaking vanished? We certainly do not believe that from that time onward any fault of the king himself has lapsed; and we know for certain that on our part no offence against you has intervened, by which we should have forfeited your favour and earned your displeasure. Thus far on this matter.

But, to come to the point: the bishop of London is hastening to the curia with great speed, as is said, at your urging, so that, finding none of our envoys there and few friends, he may there secure favour [Col. 0518B]—now by flattering blandishments, now by countless promises, now by his own threats and those of the king; that he may extort absolution where he more deserved punishment, and obtain acquittal where he more deserved condemnation. Nor should any of you allege that this is the seat of mercy, which more often, out of regard for compassion, is accustomed to pity sinners than to correct offenders. But we answer you with what Scripture says: justice and peace love one another only insofar as he who does justice finds peace, and not otherwise. For justice and peace have kissed one another. Yet there is one thing which above all we ask never to be absent from your mind: greed, the tracker-down of hidden gains, is always stretched out, a gulf most eager for manifest prey, unhappy in the fruit of possessing and most miserable in the desire of seeking. See then, if you please, lest the crafty malice of a deceitful man [Col. 0518C] deceive you—his religion worn as a cloak, his unlawful inquisitiveness, his empty promise, his gifts (far be it!), which blind the eyes and bend the force of authority. Their end is destruction; their fruit, dust and ashes, easily scattered and vanishing into the wind. Do not, tempted by the prospect of dishonest gain, cover by your authority the crime which ought to be punished in that man.

What more need be said? May the Holy Spirit so act with you that, through your ministry and that of your fellow brethren, the son of perdition may be revealed, and iniquity itself be turned upon its own head. May God scatter Ahithophel’s counsel and set him against his own face, so that in this curia he may receive what he has wickedly done and carry away what is fitting, [Col. 0518D] where the sword of blessed Peter is customarily and ought to be drawn for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. So may there be glory thereby in heaven before God and His angels, and peace on earth to people of good will.

May your beloved person prosper now and always, so that it may go better for us and our wretched fellow-exiles, especially in the present business.

## LETTER LVI. TO THE SAME PERSON

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to John of Naples, cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul.

The holy Church of Canterbury has long enjoyed both your friendship and your protection; and it still rejoices in the hope of your compassion and consolation. Therefore [Col. 0519A] it sends its poor men with greater confidence to the bosom of your love: they have been left alive, survivors of the slaughter of their brethren killed for faith and the liberty of the Church. The blood of the slain cries to the Lord against the persecutors and oppressors of the Church—and would that it did not cry against me and against those who ought to have stood with us for the laws of the fathers and the house of the Lord. Please hear and understand from the envoys recently sent how clearly the obstinacy of the king of England has been convicted of duplicity and wickedness, and at what point the Church’s cause has come to rest. For now, as always, it was the king who prevented peace from being restored. For my part, so far as I can, without prejudice to my rank and to my loyalty to the Roman Church, I willingly agree that his dignities should be maintained and increased; but I do not [Col. 0519B] consent that a new and ruinous form of allegiance should be introduced into the Church by my example. I demand, by every right, restitution of what has been taken from me and mine, or satisfaction; lest the destructive force of precedent, if such manifest robbery remains unchallenged, turn into law and give both our contemporaries and our successors boldness to offend in the same way. Therefore, if you please, rise to the assistance of the Church, now almost failing, and persuade the lord pope and your brethren not longer to overlook so manifest an injury to Christ, to whom, together with us and without respect of persons, you will shortly render an account of all your works. For opportunity often slips away while it is awaited. And he is a partner in guilt who neglects to amend what he can correct. The envoys [Col. 0519C] will supply the rest; please hear them for Christ’s sake, in Christ’s cause. And if perhaps the bishop of London and Geoffrey Ridel come to the Roman Church, treat them as members of Antichrist, in whom he is already working the mystery of his iniquity. May your holiness prosper.

## LETTER LVII. TO THE SAME PERSON

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to John, priest-cardinal of Naples.

I appeal to your brotherhood in Christ to stand by the English Church for Christ’s sake. For I remember without doubt and with gratitude that you firmly promised me counsel, aid, and protection [Col. 0519D] wherever and against whomever justice should support me. Now you may hear from the lord pope’s envoys, Lord Gratian and Master Vivian, and from the venerable Peter, archdeacon of Chartres, upon what issue my cause—or rather the cause of the English Church—stands; and, if you please, you will clearly learn that it was not I, but the king and his men, who, as usual, brought the obstacle to peace. For I am ready to preserve and increase his dignities insofar as this may be permitted without prejudice to my rank and loyalty to the Roman Church; but, God being favourable, I shall never introduce into the Church a new and ruinous form of allegiance. I ask that what has been taken from me and mine be restored, or that satisfaction be made to the Church, because it is now evident, by God’s ordering, that those things remain with him on no just—or even unjust—ground. [Col. 0520A] For he has publicly confessed to the lord pope’s envoys and to many others that, for the whole period of my chancellorship, I owe him no account either of money or of administration. Therefore act, if you please, so that the destructive force of precedent may be removed—a precedent which will ensnare contemporaries and posterity if, God forbid, such manifest robbery and injury to Christ remain unpunished. For his obstinacy has now been exposed, and there is no reason why it should longer be endured, unless one who cherishes or overlooks error calls upon himself the punishment due to another’s crime. I and my fellow-exiles—or rather, the English Church, for whose liberty we suffer persecution and as outlaws are tormented by various wrongs—henceforth entrust our cause to God; or rather, His cause, so that He Himself, in whose sight we shall shortly stand without respect of persons and without [Col. 0520B] advocacy, to render an account of our acts and intentions, may judge between us and the persecutors and oppressors of the Church, and for the glory of His name may speedily fulfil the truth of the promise by which He consoled His little ones while present in the body. Meanwhile, trusting in your promise and charity, I most earnestly beseech you kindly to hear our poor bearers of this letter and to advance Christ’s cause for Christ’s sake. But if the bishop of London and Geoffrey Ridel come to the Roman Church, treat them as those ought to be treated who sow discord among brethren. The Church of Canterbury offers you its service, which with most ready devotion it will render to you and yours [Col. 0520C] when, through the protection which we hope for from you, it has been rescued from the tribulation and sorrow inflicted by the wicked.

## LETTER LVIII. TO THE SAME PERSON

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to John, cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul.

The Church of France has heard that, in the cause of the English Church, you have changed your position: that, abandoning your protection of the persecutors whom, through ignorance, you were supporting because you believed those who made falsehood their hope, your discretion has, before all others, passed into the company of those who have been patrons of truth. It has heard this, I say, and rejoiced greatly, because this is a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, for the liberty of the Church of God; and it will contribute to the eternal glory of your name. [Col. 0520D] The report is welcome in everyone’s ears, but most welcome to us and to the Church of Canterbury, which has always been accustomed to rejoice in your protection and is glad to have returned to your favour. It is just, therefore, that it should return to your service and devotion. And we shall apply more willing effort and diligence, that it may obey your commands with the greatest devotion. For we were yours, and we desire to be yours: ready indeed for service, if the king of England allows the dutiful goodwill which we bear in our hearts to find expression. Nor is there any doubt that you will cease to protect our persecutors, in proportion as they have proved more harmful to you; for they are unjust, greedy, and makers of lies, deceiving their friends and those credulous enough to trust them in every undertaking. And when they have deceived or [Col. 0521A] harmed them, they break into laughter, glorying in their own cleverness as though triumphing over enemies. May your brotherhood, ever dear to us in the Lord, prosper always. Farewell.

## LETTER LIX. TO MAINFRED

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to Mainfred, cardinal, who had been captured at Ancona.

We give thanks to God, who has rescued you for the consolation of His Church from the mouth of the Lion, delivered you from the hand of the Beast, and from every hope of the heresiarch of Crema, Frederick, and the whole rabble of schismatics. We have felt, to speak our heart’s mind, the losses caused by your absence; for at the request of the king of England, without any fault on our part preceding, [Col. 0521B] we were suspended, with the day of our restoration, as he boasts, placed at his discretion. My lord, had you been here, the vigour of the Church, as we hope, would not have been so dead or languid, nor would authority have been granted to that king and his accomplices, Satan’s henchmen, to rage meanwhile against the Church. But now it is certain that you will strive with all your might to oppose these perversities, because you fear the Lord and love the beauty of His house. May it therefore please your love to obtain from the lord pope that he remove the suspension, or shorten its term, writing open letters to the king of France and the Church of France that, unless the king of England, according to the pope’s admonition and threat, make peace with us and restore what has been taken, together with the Church’s liberty, he grant us henceforth leave to exercise the authority of our office against him and his land, declare that the sentence which we pronounce against the evildoers of the Church and against our own persecutors is to be held valid, and order all bishops throughout his land to observe it inviolably [Col. 0521C] until they are compelled to make satisfaction. Further, we earnestly beg you to obtain for the Church of Canterbury, as consolation in its misery, the full restoration of its primacy: namely, that the archbishop and Church of York be ordered to render us obedience as their primate. For since through you we have obtained confirmation of that same primacy, it will be an honour and glory to you if the confirmation obtained through you receives full force. And, so that your charity may have some consolation amid our tribulation, know that the Most Christian King regards our fortune as his own.

## LETTER LX. TO OTTO, DEACON OF THE TITLE OF SAINT NICHOLAS IN THE TULLIAN PRISON

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to Otto, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

For the affection of your sincerity and the integrity of your faith, we return you manifold thanks, as to one in whom we have unhesitating confidence and whom we regard as most dear and eminent among our friends. We remember that in your gracious letters you returned us many thanks because we had so diligently approached the king of France on your behalf and had applied whatever effort we could towards bringing your business [Col. 0522A] to a successful conclusion. Know assuredly that, with the king and our other friends, not only in this matter but in all matters in which we can help, so far as divine grace allows us, we shall effectively render counsel and assistance for your honour. For we bear in mind, and shall always bear in mind, that from the time you came to know us, neither for love of kings nor favour of princes did you ever wish to desert us or, from desire for any advantage, estrange us from your affection. But, as we informed you through the master of Pavia, there was a time when, for any great sum of money, we would not have approached the king so that he might receive your letters, both because of the shame we felt and because of the evasions which we perceived in the king himself. As for [Col. 0522B] his forbidding you, on account of the legation—or in your capacity as legate—to enter his land, he did what he wished; nor ought you therefore to be angry, because, as your discretion knows better, it should not seem strange if one who is quick to speak is quick to change. We cannot but wonder at the making of our peace, which through delay of time seems to be deferred and, in some people’s opinion, in a manner weakened. We more earnestly entreat your love to strive to apply such diligent and effective labour to restoring it between us and the king that you may receive a worthy reward from the almighty Lord, and that henceforth we may remain bound at all times as debtors to your effectiveness. May your holiness prosper [Col. 0522C] for a long time.

## LETTER LXI. TO THE SAME PERSON

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to Otto, cardinal.

Upon hearing of your eminence’s arrival, the company of Christ’s outlaws who are fellow-exiles with us was gladdened; and, as though an angel had been sent from heaven for the consolation of the Church and the liberation of the clergy, all the Church of the saints exulted and gave thanks. And although your colleague is suspect to many, who say that he is a respecter of persons and gifts, an intimate partisan of the lord [Col. 0522D] king, wishing in all things to patronize him and to pierce and slaughter us—or rather the Church of God—with our own spoils: nevertheless, the reputation of your name, or rather of your virtues, shines brightly. Thus you have, with Moses, the angel of the Lord—that is, the Holy Spirit—as a guide preceding you in the law, to keep you always and not permit you to hold God as a recent acquaintance, by preferring to the word of God either gift, person, or cause. “God,” says the prophet, “is not before his eyes; his ways are defiled at all times.” Therefore the English Church does not doubt that you will go by clean and level paths, because it confidently hopes that you will have your way by straight paths. Nor does it fear that, in the prostitution of justice, you will accept our goods, since you know that money so obtained [Col. 0523A] may not be put into the treasury, because it is the price of blood. Certainly,

> Base booty does not have good outcomes.

Very many insult us, especially our own people—or rather, the adversaries of the Church—saying that the cardinal of Saint Peter in Chains was rightly sent against us so that Peter might once again be bound through his ministry. Yet I meanwhile believe that the intimacy which he has formed with the lord king in our humiliation will contribute to the Church’s liberation, the king’s salvation, and God’s glory. Yet one thing I greatly fear: that one of the brethren of whom the Apostle complains, departing from the face of the Lord, may mix the wild gourds formerly gathered into the prophets’ pot, [Col. 0523B] so as to undermine the divine meaning with the crude food of swine—that is, persons living voluptuously—and so that the imagination of life may attempt to overthrow the mind of the law. But when the man of God hears from one of the sons of the prophets that there is death in the pot, he will cast into it flour from the grain that died in the earth for us, in order to bear much fruit, so that the shoot of innate malice may no longer be able to harm the good. I judge you to be a man of God sent to us by the Lord, who may gladden the desolate Shunammite woman in England, heal the powerful Syrian of leprosy, and strike down the Gehazi adherents with the condemnation due to their crime. If, after these have been removed, you recall our glorious king, immediately, as we hope, he will repent, confess his fault, and, humbly making satisfaction to the Church, restore liberty and peace, and restore to us all that has been taken with integrity, security, and favour. Nor will he further contend for retaining the customs which—without mentioning the condemnation inflicted upon them by the perpetual laws—the lord pope at Sens condemned with the unanimous counsel of the brethren, as I think, in your hearing; nor will he demand oaths which cannot be observed without compromising faith and religion. But these matters will become more fully known to you when you see the Balaamite bishops—not all, I say, but very many—who see vanity and folly and do not reveal the means by which men ought to be called to repentance. They sit in the gate and speak against us—or rather, against the Church; and even he who does not drink wine sings against us. Since, therefore, all eyes are directed toward you, apply yourself, if you please, to God’s honour and the peace of the Church, and prescribe what we ought to do [Col. 0523D] so that the Church of God may enjoy its due liberty. For there is nothing which can be done with a safe conscience and honour that we would not most willingly do to recover the lord king’s favour. A chasm has been fixed between us, so that no one of us can cross over to you, even if he wishes and has the means. May my lord always prosper and have compassion on the outlaws.

## LETTER LXII. TO THE SAME PERSON

The lord of Canterbury, to Otto, cardinal.

We offer your love thanks—not those which we owe, but as great as we can for the present—because for us, indeed for the Church of God, you have endured much and have consoled us to the extent of your strength in all our tribulation. The king of England recently confessed [Col. 0524A] before the Most Christian King, archbishops, bishops, nobles, and all who were present that he seeks and has sought from us nothing except observance of the customs, many of which overthrow the majesty of the Apostolic See and prejudice the liberty of the Church. The bearers of this letter will more fully report how the matter proceeded. And because we refused simply and absolutely to swear to the wording of his customs, he departed indignant, unable to endure any mention of God’s honour, our rank, or divine law. We therefore entreat your goodness, in which we trust as in ourselves, to stand by us in the Lord’s cause and to endeavour, with the lord pope, to settle our necessity—or rather, that of the Church of God—of which you will hear from the envoys, as is the hope [Col. 0524B] of us and of all.

## TO THE BISHOP OF SABINA

(See the letter addressed to Conrad of Mainz and others, which begins: “More than enough,” etc.)

## LETTER LXIII. TO THEODWIN

“Of those slain for the Lord’s cause,” etc. (It resembles the letter sent to Hyacinth, cardinal.)

(See also another letter, beginning “Of the Church troubled,” etc., sent to Albert and Theodwin.)

## LETTER LXIV. TO WILLIAM OF PAVIA

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to William of Pavia: greeting, and strength against the insolence of princes.

[Col. 0524C] We recently received the letter of your eminence: in its beginning it offered the appearance of honey, poison in the middle, and oil at the end. It states that at this time you have come down into these regions to settle the disputes between the lord king of England and ourselves, as you shall see fit. We do not believe that you have come for these purposes, nor indeed do we receive you for this purpose, for many reasons which we shall make known at the appropriate place and time. Nevertheless, if through your hand anything good and peaceful should happen to us, thanks be to God and to you. May your eminence prosper, so that it may go better for us thereby.

## LETTER LXV. TO THE SAME PERSON

To the venerable lord and friend deservedly to be loved, [Col. 0524D] William, by God’s grace priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Peter in Chains and legate of the Apostolic See: Thomas, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, greeting, and strength against the insolence of princes.

We thank your love because at last you have deigned to visit our insignificance by letters from your eminence. Many estimate that insignificance from the condition of the present time rather than from the past; yet God can, from His mercy, when He wills and judges it fitting, raise it in the future to a better state. As to your saying—as many appear to think—that you have been divided among various purposes concerning our interests, and that this was done for our advantage lest you be suspected by the king and thereby become less devoted [Col. 0525A] to the Roman Church or less favourably disposed to make peace with us: God, the searcher of hearts, knows; and the outcome itself will make the matter plain. But if you have now come down into his land, as your letters state, to decide the disputes between us and him as you judge most advantageous to the Church, this indeed is possible. Nevertheless, we believe that we know with certainty why you have come and for what purpose we ought to receive you. Therefore we desire that your discretion be most earnestly exhorted in the Lord to conduct yourself in this affair so that it may bring honour to God, relief to the Church, and glory to you among peoples and nations. But if through your effort and diligence [Col. 0525B] anything good and peaceful should happen to us and the English Church, thanks be to God and to your solicitude. Would that you would consider with compassionate devotion how great are the burdens which we and the English Church have endured and still endure, and how greatly the universal Church is harmed by our affliction. The eyes of all are fixed upon this business and await its outcome, in which either the insolence of princes will take up horns for itself, or, more worthily, it will suffer defeat. And would that it suffer defeat rather than recover its strength through your arrival. Farewell; and may it go better for us and for the Church through you; farewell always.

## LETTER LXVI. TO THE SAME PERSON

To the venerable lord and brother in Christ most dear, [Col. 0525C] William, by God’s grace priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Peter in Chains and legate of the Apostolic See: Thomas, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, greeting, and courage against the insolence of princes.

From the tenor of your letters we perceive that you have obtained the unalloyed favour of our most illustrious lord, the king of France, and rejoice in having obtained it. We regard this as welcome and acceptable, all the more because in this matter neither your efforts nor those of our other friends have been disappointed, and what we asked has succeeded according to our wish. Therefore, as his welcome favour remains gratefully in our mind, we ask, for his love and reverence—whose concern for us and our cause is, as you say, not slight—that the Most High, the rewarder of the good, repay him who is able to do so. May your assistance be the more welcome to us; although we have earnestly desired it for a long time, we now more certainly entreat it with greater effectiveness through the intervention of the lord of Chartres and Master P[...], of Pavia, [Col. 0525D] so that we may rejoice in its having been obtained, and that the Church, which is grievously vexed together with us, and we with it, may experience an advance in your goodwill, and through that advance receive what is just. We know indeed and firmly hold that, just as equal offences are abolished by mutual compensation, so reciprocal acts of favour are joined together by mutual devotion. We believe enough has been said [Col. 0526A] to the wise man.

Moreover, concerning the future peace, for which a better hope is promised to you, [verb omitted in the supplied text] to almighty God, provided it be made to the advantage of the Church and of ourselves. Would that you would consider this more deeply and impress it more carefully upon your minds, taking care lest you be deceived by vain hope and your solicitude be frustrated by false promises. Truly it is true that the wise man dissimulates for a time. But it is proverbially said: “While the time is awaited, it flees, slips from one’s hands, and does not return as desired.” And the physician says: “While it hurts, take it.” But I tell you: may what I desire not easily pass beyond our ears or slip lightly from your mind. Hold fast with both hands the present fortune that lies bare before your eyes; make use of it in season, for it is slippery and cannot be retained against its will. Thus far. [Col. 0526B] But please inform us three days beforehand of your arrival at Paris, so that, if perhaps we can find mounts—for at this time they are scarce with us because of the war—we may meet your discretion at a suitable place and enjoy the desired conversation with you. But if, God forbid, this cannot be done, let us send you one of our household, who may report to us your condition and where you intend to lodge. Farewell; do not forget us, so that it may go better for us and our poor people.

## LETTER LXVII. TO THE SAME PERSON

To the venerable lord and brother William, by God’s grace priest-cardinal of the holy Roman Church, [Col. 0526C] Thomas, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury and wretched exile, greeting, and so to act that you may live in the Lord.

I did not think that I was to be offered for sale to buyers, so that out of my blood you might obtain profit from the price of iniquity, making a name and glory for yourself. You ought to seek your revenue elsewhere, if, not too forgetful of your very perilous position, you weighed the mockeries of fortune differently. But perhaps, in order to do this more effectively, you took my present fortune into your counsel; while looking upon its sorrows, you ought sometimes to have hoped for happier things. For the vicissitudes of affairs alternate; as the fall from prosperous success is easy, so is the reverse. Nor do I believe it unknown to your prudence, [Col. 0526D] even if you have not learned it by experience, that nothing is so secure that danger is not near to it—and conversely. I write this to you so that henceforth you may examine the sudden turns of fortune more carefully, observe them once examined, and yield to them once observed. Peter’s little ship ought not to have been exposed to such chances: although it is often shaken, it does not know how to be torn apart; although repeatedly tossed by waves, it rises without being submerged. Therefore, if you wish to be a true disciple of that true fisher and best helmsman, a good sailor, then, just as the calm breeze has often bestowed upon you the favour of fair weather, so against the violent storm and strengthening tempest you ought to have opposed all the powers of your ability—even yourself, with courageous spirit, under every danger. For if you gratefully received peaceful things from His hand [Col. 0527A], why will you not patiently endure adversities, perhaps soon to expire? Thus Peter too, that master and prince of the apostles, by resisting princes—not yielding, but shattering the peace of iniquity with his blood—earned a name on earth and glory in heaven. Thus the Church’s strength grew when it was thought to be extinguished. This also, in sum, is my wish for you: act happily, so that you may live in the Lord. Farewell, that I too may fare better thereby.

## LETTER LXVIII. TO THE SAME PERSON

Thomas of Canterbury to William of Pavia.

Lord Gratian, who together with Master Vivian was sent to the king of England [Col. 0527B] for this purpose, is hastening to return: as we have certainly learned, they were sent in order that the king’s obstinacy, if he did not restore peace to us, might be more clearly convicted. How the business proceeded you will hear more fully, by God’s ordering, from the envoys who report it; and, if you please, question Master Peter, archdeacon of Chartres, a man distinguished both in learning and integrity, since he too has experienced the gentleness and moderation of the aforesaid king, and with what devotion he reveres the Roman Church. But you yourselves also heard and saw in person how he oppresses the Church, and through experience of events you have learned the man’s character more intimately. What witnesses, then, do you further require to convict his obstinacy on behalf of the Church? For you yourselves, as we believe, heard blasphemy from the man’s own mouth and, as we hope of you, [Col. 0527C] unwillingly saw it proclaimed in his deeds. Therefore the wretched English Church appeals with greater confidence to the protection of your serenity, begging you to bring it aid lest it fail in this tribulation. Recall, if you please, how you received me and the Church’s cause from the hand of the Most Christian King of France, who directed our wretched survivors to flee safely to the feet of your clemency. For a great part of Christ’s outlaws, striving for faith and the Church’s liberty, has been taken from the world and begs before the Father of mercies for vengeance upon the shedding of its blood, which was unjustly poured out. That company, as we trust, stands before God’s face; we who remain, awaiting the Lord’s coming or call, [Col. 0527D] meanwhile cry to you with every supplication we can, that through your efforts the Church may obtain its justice and peace. By what consequence of law can the Church’s goods which the king seized remain with him unpunished and without satisfaction, when, as he has publicly confessed to the lord pope’s envoys and many others, he now exacts nothing for the entire time of my chancellorship—although he once pretended that accounts were owed—but alleges this: that his own men restored nothing to my predecessors, whom they had often driven away, when they returned? Yet, let it be said with his leave, it is clear from many considerations that this is not true. But every means must be used to prevent the destructive force of precedent from becoming law. Under the name of dignities he strives to restore condemned customs. But, to remove from myself every occasion [Col. 0528A] for wrongful suspicion, I shall willingly observe his dignities as far as I can, without prejudice to my rank and my loyalty to the Roman Church; and in the Lord I shall endeavour to multiply and increase them. But far be it that, by my example, a new form of making allegiance should be introduced into the Church, especially a ruinous one. Nor can it be unknown to you with what savagery the bishop of London, instigator of all this discord, has persecuted me. If you please, stand against him as disobedient and excommunicated, for the house of the Lord; because in the downfall of him and Geoffrey Ridel, as the hope of the faithful is, the storm will cease. The remaining matters have been placed in the mouths of the envoys; please receive them kindly and advance, for Christ’s sake, the cause of Christ which they bear. May your holiness prosper. [Col. 0528B]

## LETTER LXIX. TO THE SAME PERSON

To the venerable lord and most dear father William, by God’s grace priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church: Thomas, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, greeting and the service of sincere devotion.

It is not expedient for us to multiply words in your holiness’s ear, since your sincerity is inclined to protect truth; since the malice of the opposing party cannot be concealed from the eyes of a wise man; and since charity considers it shameful not to refresh with due consolation a friend long afflicted for the liberty of the Church. Such is the confidence of the Most Christian King in you; such is ours, who through him have returned to your favour. Such is the hope of the faithful who proclaim the glory of your name. Strengthened and encouraged by this, we earnestly beseech you to rise manfully, as you promised the lord king of France, to the aid of the Church and of us, and with the wisdom divinely bestowed to crush the enemies of ecclesiastical liberty and of the Apostolic See. For if the Roman Church now resolves to accept the victory already prepared, it is easy for its enemies to flee and perish before its face. For, terrified, they seek hiding places and do not know where to turn.

## LETTER LXX. TO THE SAME PERSON

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to William, [Col. 0528D] cardinal of Pavia.

Truth may indeed be overshadowed, but it cannot be extinguished; and light is more gratefully received after the troubles of darkness. Would that it had been established for you from the beginning what is now known to all from the testimony of our very persecutor! For recently, before the Most Christian king, archbishops, bishops, counts, nobles, and all who were present, he publicly declared that this alone was the cause of our exile and proscription: that we refused to observe for him the customs which our predecessors had been accustomed to observe for his predecessors. He further asserted emphatically that he sought nothing else from us whatever, except that we should promise him this simply and absolutely, upon our word of truth—namely, without adding, “saving our order,” or [Col. 0529A] “the honour of God,” or anything else that might preserve the integrity of honour and conscience. Since we refuse absolutely to promise observance of customs, some of which nullify the authority of the apostolic see and destroy the liberty of the Church, the king departed without peace being concluded. We therefore beseech your affection tirelessly to undertake the patronage of the Church of Canterbury—indeed, of justice itself. And, as your kindness promised us at your departure, do not shrink, as befits your honour, from standing for the liberty of the Church and for our person, ever ready for service; but set yourself also against those who are known hitherto to have opposed truth and justice, and place unquestioning trust in our messengers concerning those matters which they shall lay before you on our behalf.

## LETTER LXXI. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Col. 0529B]

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to WILLIAM of Pavia.

It is right that the Church of Canterbury, which, after God, through the exertion and labour of you and a few friends, has come safely to harbour, should acknowledge itself bound to you and yours in every devotion and rendering of service. For we have enrolled you among our chief and foremost friends and lords, because, with God’s help leading the way, she has been rescued from the tribulation and distress of evil men. You crossed seas for her, penetrated and crossed the Alps, fought with beasts in our regions, and in the very curia, where we were more fiercely and vigorously assailed, [Col. 0529C] you often and long bore the burden of the day and the heat; and at last, because your labour was in the Lord, you triumphed wisely and courageously. We felt this recently in the agreement which we made with the lord king of England. If it please you, learn its terms from the bearer of this letter; further the petitions which we present through him to the lord pope with your customary kindness; and keep this man earnestly commended to you.

## LETTER LXXII. TO ALL THE CHILDREN OF THE CHURCH. CHARTER OF PROTECTION AND LIBERTY GRANTED TO THE CHURCH OF CHRIST AT CANTERBURY

THOMAS, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the apostolic see, to all to whom [Col. 0529D] this present writing shall come, greeting and blessing.

The events of times past are therefore committed to the record of letters, so that by means of evils already undergone, present and future evils may more cautiously be avoided. We wish therefore it to come to the knowledge of all that the holy Church of Canterbury, at whose breasts we were nourished, which by God’s authorship has advanced us, though unworthy, to what we are, has, because of hatred directed against our head, been burdened with many calamities and various anxieties for as much as seven years—a fact known to almost all Christendom—and is still daily harassed by innumerable threats and losses. Since she is wont to be the sun of the West, and in our times her charity has been darkened, we would more willingly [Col. 0530A] receive in the Lord any torment, even a thousand kinds of death, if so many should occur, than dissemble the evils which she suffers in these days.

Therefore, although we are ready to expose head and body to persecutors for her peace and safety, and, lest she perish or suffer even a slight loss, to perish ourselves, whatever may happen to us, yet, desiring to provide for her future security, we place that Church, with all her persons, lands and tenements, appurtenances and revenues, and also her liberties and dignities, under the protection of God, of the Roman curia, and of ourselves. We forbid, on God’s behalf and under perpetual anathema, anyone to presume, under any pretext or cause, to alienate the rights of the Church of Canterbury without the consent of the whole chapter of the monks of Canterbury. For it has been unheard of through the ages [Col. 0530B] that anyone has injured the Church of Canterbury and not been crushed or corrected by Christ the Lord.

We therefore condemn under perpetual anathema, until fitting satisfaction has been made, robbers and alienators of possessions, dignities, and property, as well as those who detain them, their supporters and accomplices, and anyone who maliciously reveals the secrets of the chapter to any person. Nor do we wish to permit anyone of another profession or order to involve himself in the chapter’s secrets. We also especially confirm to our beloved sons, the monks of the same Church, in perpetuity, those things belonging to them—namely, villages, estates, the churches of those villages and estates, and gifts, with their appurtenances and revenues—as is contained in their charters. [Col. 0530C] We likewise grant and confirm to them in perpetuity the free liberty of appointing or removing their officials and servants, and of disposing of everything pertaining to them, both within and without, as shall seem best and most useful to them by the common counsel of their chapter. Thus, as we hold these liberties in our own possessions according to the charters of kings, they may have a like power over their portions, saving regular discipline for ourselves and our successors.

In addition, by the authority which we exercise, we grant and permit them to pronounce sentences of suspension, excommunication, and anathema against wrongdoers of the Church if, after being warned once and twice, they refuse to amend. And they may at all times appeal to the apostolic see against every [Col. 0530D] grievance. Moreover, because our adversaries threaten that they wish to transfer elsewhere the metropolitan or primatial see of England, which has been established at Canterbury from the time of blessed Gregory through Saint Augustine, we prohibit under perpetual anathema anyone whatsoever from ever presuming, under any pretext or cause, to attempt this. We further forbid that the suffragan bishops of the Church of Canterbury, or abbots, be consecrated anywhere other than in the Church of Canterbury, to which they are bound by profession and due subjection, except by the common consent of the entire chapter of the monks of Canterbury; nor may chrism or oil to be distributed through the province of Canterbury ever be received from any source other than the Church of Canterbury.

We also will and beseech [Col. 0531A] in the Lord that the monks of the Church of Canterbury show every reverence and honour to the suffragans of that Church—that is, its bishops and abbots. Let those bishops likewise love the monks of the Church of Canterbury in true charity, which is God. For it is fitting and consonant with reason that those bound to the same Church of Canterbury by profession and subjection alike should preserve true mutual love, while due reverence and authority are reserved to ourselves and our successors. We also confirm to clerics and laymen who have become fellow-exiles with us and partners in our labour all their rights, revenues, and churches; and we beseech in the Lord that no one inflict injury or annoyance upon them.

But if anyone should wish to violate this page of our confirmation, [Col. 0531B] or harass or diminish the Church of Canterbury in any respect, or inflict any injury upon our beloved sons, the monks, let him have the eternal curse of God and ours, unless before death he shall have made fitting satisfaction by restoring what has been taken away. But upon all who love and support her we invoke the grace of Almighty God, the fellowship of all the saints who rest in the Church of Canterbury, and we bestow our blessing. Amen.

## LETTER LXXIII. TO THE SUFFRAGANS OF THE PROVINCE OF CANTERBURY

THOMAS, by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to his venerable brethren, the Bishop of London and [Col. 0531C] the other bishops of the whole province of Canterbury: may they so pass through temporal goods as not to lose eternal ones.

My most beloved brethren, why do you not rise up with me against evildoers? Why do you not stand with me against those who work iniquity? Do you not know that the Lord will scatter the bones of those who please men? They shall be put to shame, because the Lord has despised them. Your discernment knows well enough that an error not resisted is approved, and truth, when it is not defended at all, is oppressed. And, as Gregory testifies, he seems to consent to error who does not intervene to cut away what ought to be corrected.

For this reason we have endured the lord king of England more than sufficiently, [Col. 0531D] and the Church of God has gained no benefit whatever from our endurance of him. Henceforth it has seemed dangerous and intolerable to us to leave unpunished, as heretofore, such great offences of his and his officials against the Church of God and ecclesiastical persons—especially since we have very often sought, by messengers, letters, and other suitable means, to recall him from his perverse purpose. Since we have scarcely been heard by him, and in no way heeded, we have publicly condemned and annulled that writing in which are contained those not customs but rather corrupt practices by which the English Church is at present disturbed and thrown into confusion, together with the authority of the said document, having invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit. We have also excommunicated every observer, enforcer, counsellor, [Col. 0532A] and defender of them. And by God’s authority and our own we absolve all of you bishops from the promise by which, contrary to ecclesiastical institution, you were bound to their observance.

For who doubts that the priests of Christ are to be regarded as fathers and masters of kings, princes, and all the faithful? Is it not known to be pitiable madness if a son should try to subjugate his father, or a disciple his master, and by unjust obligations subject to his own power one from whom he believes that he himself can be bound and loosed not only on earth but also in heaven? Therefore, lest we incur the penalty of this sentence, we have declared void and annulled the authority of that document and the document itself, together with the abuses contained in it—especially these:

That no appeal may be made [Col. 0532B] to the apostolic see in any case without the king’s permission.

That an archbishop or bishop may not leave the kingdom and come at the summons of the lord pope without the lord king’s permission.

That a bishop may not excommunicate anyone who holds directly of the king without the king’s permission, nor place under interdict the king’s land or that of his officials.

That a bishop may not compel anyone concerning perjury or violated faith.

That clerics be brought before secular courts.

That laymen—whether the king or others—handle cases concerning churches or tithes.

And other matters of this kind.

We also declare excommunicated, and excommunicate by name, John of Oxford, who has fallen into condemned heresy by swearing an oath to schismatics, through which a schism now almost extinct in Germany has revived; by communicating with that most notorious schismatic, Reginald of Cologne; and because, contrary to the mandate of the lord pope and ourselves, he has usurped for himself the deanery of the Church of Salisbury. This act, as contrary to law as it is pernicious to the Church of God by its example, we have wholly annulled and declared void, commanding the Bishop of Salisbury and the chapter, by virtue of obedience and on peril of their order, that henceforth, upon seeing our letters, they should not regard him as dean by reason of that act.

Likewise we declare excommunicated, and have excommunicated, Richard de Ivelc., because he has fallen into the same condemned heresy by communicating [Col. 0532D] with the same schismatic Reginald of Cologne; and because, in accordance with agreements concluded between the lord king and those persons, he has plotted and contrived every evil with the schismatics and those Germans for the destruction of God and the Church, and especially of the Roman Church.

We also excommunicate Richard de Luci and Jocelin de Baill., who have been the authors and fabricators of those corrupt practices.

Likewise Ralph de Broc, who has seized and retains the goods of the Church of Canterbury—which are by right the sustenance of the poor—and has captured and keeps in captivity our men, both clerics and laymen.

Also Hugh of Saint-Clair and Thomas, son of Bernard, who have, without our connivance, seized and retain the goods and possessions of the same Church of Canterbury. [Col. 0533A]

We likewise bind with the same sentence of excommunication all who hereafter lay violent hands upon the possessions and goods of the Church of Canterbury contrary to our will and consent, in accordance with that decree of Pope Lucius: “We anathematize all robbers of the Church and alienators of her resources, condemn them, and judge them sacrilegious, excluding them from the thresholds of the same mother Church.” And not only them but also those consenting to them, because not only those who commit such acts are judged guilty, but also those who consent to those committing them. For an equal punishment embraces both the actors and those who consent. And elsewhere Scripture says: “He who consents to sinners and defends another who sins shall be cursed before God and men, and shall be reproved with a most severe rebuke.” And again: “If anyone defends a sinner, let him be restrained more severely than the one who sinned.”

We have, however, delayed hitherto in pronouncing sentence upon the person of the lord king, awaiting the possibility that, inspired by divine grace, he may come to his senses; but we shall pronounce it shortly unless he repents sooner. Therefore we command your brotherhood, and enjoin you by virtue of obedience, that you too regard and cause to be proclaimed as excommunicated, as is fitting, the aforementioned men whom we have excommunicated, in accordance with the decree of Pope Honorius: “Let it be the concern of all bishops to notify the names of all excommunicated persons alike to neighbouring bishops and to their own parishioners, and, having posted them in a prominent place before the doors of the church, to impress them upon all who come; so that by this double diligence ecclesiastical access may everywhere be denied to the excommunicated, and every ground of excuse may be removed.” [Col. 0533C] But upon you, brother Bishop of London, we lay this charge by virtue of obedience: make known and show the present letters to all our other venerable brethren and fellow bishops of our province. Farewell in Christ, and pray earnestly for us.

## LETTER LXXIV. TO THE SAME PERSONS

THOMAS, by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury and legate of the apostolic see, to his venerable brother GILBERT, Bishop of London, and to all the bishops of the province of Canterbury, [Col. 0533D] greeting.

If we are concerned to be what we are called, and wish to know the meaning of our name, by which we are called bishops and pontiffs, we must with constant solicitude consider and imitate the footsteps of him who, appointed by God high priest for ever, offered himself for us to the Father upon the altar of the cross and, from the lofty watchtower of heaven, continually observes all actions and the intentions of actions, at last to render to each according to his works. For we have undertaken to exercise his office on earth; we have received the glory of the name and the honour of the dignity, and temporarily possess the fruits of spiritual labours, succeeding the apostles and apostolic men in the highest places of the churches, so that through our ministry the dominion of sin and death may be destroyed, and the building of Christ, growing in faith [Col. 0534A] and in the advancement of virtues, may increase into a holy temple in the Lord.

Indeed, the number of bishops is great. At our consecration we promised a more diligent care and devoted attention to teaching and feeding the flock, and we profess this daily in words; but would that the fidelity of the promise might be strengthened by the testimony of deeds! The harvest is indeed abundant, and one person, or a few, would not suffice to gather and bring it into the Lord’s barn. From the time when the people of God, then confined solely to the Hebrew nation, began to be governed under the divine law, judges had to be multiplied and there had to be many reprovers of vices and reformers of morals, because the lawgiver alone could not bear the burdens of so great a multitude. Thus, at the Lord’s command, seventy elders were chosen and brought [Col. 0534B] to the door of the tabernacle, which prefigured the Church. They received from God a share of the spirit of Moses, by whom the law is understood, so that they might prophesy and examine and decide the causes of the people; greater matters, however, being reserved and referred for examination to him to whom the administration of the whole law had been entrusted.

And if we search the Scriptures more attentively, we shall find that these rulers of the Hebrews were those whom we read were beaten by Pharaoh’s taskmasters in Egypt, so that, worn down by weariness and various punishments, they complained that their names stank before the Egyptians. Yet because they endured patiently and, obeying Moses, accepted the word of God, they merited, through grace preceding them, by faith and constant experience of toil, to be set with Moses over the people whose salvation they had procured; [Col. 0534C] and those who had listened diligently were made teachers out of disciples.

Likewise, at the beginning of the rising Church, as the blessed Apostle teaches: “Christ, ascending into heaven in order to fill all things, gave some indeed as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers, for the instruction of the saints in the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ.” For not every office was to be entrusted to one person, but each member was to be endowed with its own function—yet so that the head, in which, as in a citadel and a kind of capitol of virtues, all the senses are gathered, should provide for all and for each, and that all things should in turn serve it according to the character of their condition. The Teacher of the Gentiles, [Col. 0534D] who boasts that he learned the Gospel not from man nor through man but was taught by Christ, went up to Jerusalem after fourteen years and conferred concerning the faith with the prince of the Churches, lest perhaps he should be running, or had run, in vain. And, as is evident from very many examples, all the streams of the Gospel return to the sea from which they arose, that they may flow forth again. For the fountain of paradise is one, but it is divided into many rivers so that it may irrigate the earth on every side.

Who doubts that the Roman Church is the head of all Churches and the fountain of Catholic doctrine? Who does not know that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted to Peter? Does not the whole structure of the Church rise upon the faith and teaching of Peter, until we all meet Christ as a perfect man, in the unity of faith and knowledge of the Son [Col. 0535A] of God? There must indeed be many who plant and many who water, because the progress of the word and the expansion of peoples require it. Even the ancient people, for whom one altar sufficed, had of necessity several teachers—much more so now amid the gathering and influx of nations, for whom Lebanon does not suffice for fuel, and the animals not only of Lebanon but not even of all Judaea would suffice for a burnt offering. But whoever plants or waters, God gives increase to no one except to him who has planted in Peter’s faith and rests in his teaching.

Certainly, the greatest judgments of the people are referred to the Roman pontiff for examination, and the officers of Mother Church established under him, called to share his solicitude, exercise the authority entrusted to them. Thus the priest refers to the bishop what he cannot beneficially decide among the people committed to him; the bishop brings matters above his own competence to the archbishop or primate; and from them everything of the greatest importance is reserved to the Roman pontiff. [Col. 0535B] Peter taught this order; the Catholic Church has preserved it until now; and, with the Lord as author, whatever iniquity may devise, it shall never be overthrown.

But in the kingdom of the English—something which we cannot recall without great sorrow or speak of without tears—much presumption is exercised against Peter. So far as perverse authorities can do so, the authority of the apostolic see is attacked and endangered, while those whom necessity compels to undertake the journey to the lord pope for the shortening of penance, the remedy of a case, or a duty of visitation are hindered in their journey, despoiled, treated very cruelly, and forbidden to cross the sea; or else, being forced by persons seeking occasions to do evil, they take unlawful oaths to hinder clerics and penitents. Therefore, by laying violent hands upon clerics, those persons incur by their act the condemnation of anathema.

Accordingly, using the authority of the holy Roman Church, we command your brotherhood by apostolic authority, enjoining you by virtue of obedience and at the peril of your order, henceforth to prevent this from being done; publicly to declare excommunicated those who lay violent hands upon clerics; to cause this declaration to be made throughout your bishopric; and, by the authority of the lord pope and ourselves, to command your neighbouring fellow bishops to do likewise in their own bishoprics. [Col. 0535D]

Further, in the same manner and under the same threat, we command you to declare that those who impede appellants or penitents travelling to the lord pope or to us, or returning from the lord pope or from us, incur the sentence of anathema—both those who do this in person and the king’s officials who compel others to commit this crime. But those who, under compulsion, have taken unlawful oaths to hinder travellers, we absolve from that oath, so that they may thereafter desist from so great an iniquity and, repenting of what they have done, learn henceforth to obey God rather than man. If anyone [Col. 0536A] promoting the justice of his Church and keeping faith with the apostolic see fears losses, let him remember that the Church stores up virtues far more safely and profitably than fleeting riches. Christ, who presides over the Roman Church, restrains all hostile powers. He who will punish the mighty mightily has decreed that every disobedience shall be punished. Yet he does not bring the humble into judgment, but humbles the great ones of the earth through the ministry of the Church, against which even the gates of hell shall not prevail.

Beloved brethren, be ashamed to administer unjust judgments. For, as the nobles of the realm taunt us, if a poor man offends in the slightest matter, he is immediately excluded from the Church by us and our officials; but if a rich man commits crimes, he is not even confronted with a word. Thus, in making such decrees, that pagan saying may be turned against you:

> Can the gods be so greatly angered against the wretched?

Provide for yourselves and your churches, lest, if you further conceal this injury to the Roman Church, you deservedly appear to have conspired with the ungodly against her and to have blocked the paths of appellants. Do not seek your own advantage from her loss. Remember rather how our fathers were saved, how and through what tribulations the Church grew and was enlarged; what storms Peter’s ship escaped, having Christ as its helmsman; and how those whose faith shines more brightly through tribulation attained the crown. Thus Moses merited leadership of the people; thus the seventy judges attained the grace of prophecy; [Col. 0536C] thus David was raised to be king; thus the apostles were appointed judges of the world. Thus the whole company of saints advanced, so that it is perpetually true that no one is crowned unless he has striven lawfully, and that there is no passage at all from the delights of worldly exile to the delights of the kingdom.

But to you, brother Bishop of London, we give this charge and command, by apostolic authority, by virtue of obedience and at the peril of your order, to show these present letters with speed and diligence to our other brothers and fellow bishops of the same province, and to ensure that what they contain is strictly observed. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXV. TO THE SAME PERSONS

[Col. 0536D] THOMAS, by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to his venerable brethren, all the bishops by God’s grace of the province of Canterbury—if indeed all have written—greeting, and that they may do what they have not yet done.

We recently received unexpectedly the letter of your brotherhood, though we cannot readily believe that it proceeded from the common counsel of your prudence. Its tenor seems to contain more bitterness than comfort; and would that it had been issued more from zeal for compassion and the affection of charity than from obedience to will. For charity seeks not its own things, but those of Jesus Christ. It was surely required by the right of your office—if the Gospel has truth, as indeed it has—if you rightly perform his office and faithfully conduct his business whose image you represent, that you should [Col. 0537A] fear him more who can cast both soul and body into Gehenna than him who can kill the body; that you should obey God rather than men, the Father rather than the lord, following the example of him who became obedient to the Father unto death. He therefore died for us, leaving us an example that we should follow his footsteps. Let us therefore die with him; let us lay down our lives to free the Church from the yoke of servitude and the oppression of her afflicter—the Church which he founded, whose liberty he purchased with his own blood—lest, if we act otherwise, that Gospel saying deservedly lay hold of us: “He who loves his life more than me is not worthy of me.”

You ought to have known very well that, if what the emperor commands is just, you ought to carry out his will; but if it is contrary, you should reply: “We must obey God rather than men.” One thing I say to you, speaking with due regard for your peace: for a long time I kept silent, waiting in case the Lord might perhaps inspire you to recover your strength—you who turned back on the day of battle. Perhaps at least one among you all might climb up against the enemy and set himself as a wall for the house of Israel; might at least make a show of entering the contest against those who do not cease daily to reproach the army of the Lord. I waited: there is none who climbs up. I endured: there is none who sets himself in opposition. I was silent: there is none who speaks. I concealed my response: there is none who even makes a pretence of fighting. What remains to me is an action of complaint, so that I have good cause to cry: “Arise, O God; judge my cause. Avenge the blood [Col. 0537C] of the Church, which has been disembowelled, which has been left lifeless by oppression.” For the pride of those who hate her liberty continually rises, and henceforth there is none who does good—not even one.

Would that, most beloved brethren, we had as much zeal for defending the liberty of the Church as is displayed and offered to us in its disgrace by your letters, as we believe, of deficiently lawful appeal! Yet she is founded upon the firm Rock, and no one can uproot her, though one may shake her. Why then do you seek to put me to shame? Rather, you bring shame upon yourselves in me—and me along with you: I, the man who took upon myself every danger, endured so many reproaches, suffered so many injuries, and experienced proscription on behalf of you all. It was fitting that one man should suffer affliction for this Church, that she might at least in this way be shaken free from servitude.

Examine this cause with an unprejudiced mind; investigate the matter; consider diligently what its end ought to be. Lay aside the majesty of dominion and wholly put aside respect of persons, of which God is not a respecter; let God himself make you understand what you have done and what you intend to do. May God himself remove the veil from your hearts, that you may know what you ought to do! Let any one among you who knows say whether, after my promotion, I ever took the ox or ass of any one of you, the money of any one of you, or judged the cause of any one of you unjustly; whether I gained advantage for myself at the loss of any of you. I will restore fourfold. But if there is no offence I have committed, why [Col. 0538A] do you leave me alone in God’s cause? Why do you take care to set yourselves against yourselves in this cause, than which no cause more particularly belongs to the Church?

Do not, brethren, do not, so far as lies in you, bring yourselves and the Church of God into confusion; but turn to me, and you shall be saved. For the Lord says: “I do not will the death of the sinner, so much as that he turn and live.” Stand with me courageously in battle; take up arms and shield, and rise to my aid. Gird yourselves with the sword of God’s most powerful word, that together, all of us, we may be more able, strong and mighty, to resist those who do evil, those who work iniquity, those who seek to take away the soul of the Church, which is liberty—without which the Church neither flourishes nor can prevail against those who seek to possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.

Let us all therefore hasten together to act, lest the wrath of God descend upon us as negligent and idle shepherds; lest we be considered mute dogs, unable to bark; lest passers-by reproach us: “From the elders of Babylon iniquity went forth.” Truly, if you heed me, know that the Lord will be with you and with all of you in all your ways, to establish peace and defend the Church’s liberty. Otherwise, may God judge between me and you, and demand from your hands an account of the Church’s disgrace. For, whether the world wills it or not, she must stand firm in the word of the Lord in which she is founded, until her hour comes to pass from this world to the Father. God will judge you because you have left [Col. 0538C] me alone in the contest, and among all my dear ones there is no one willing to go up with me to battle. So alone that each one of you may think or say: “Woe to him who is alone, because, if he falls, he has no one to lift him up!” But this hope of mine has been placed in my bosom: that he with whom the Lord is is not alone; when he falls, he shall not be dashed down, for the Lord himself upholds him with his hand.

To come then to the matter, tell me, my brethren: has it slipped from your memory what was being done to me and to the Church of God while I was still in England? What was done at my departure, what after my departure, and what is being done even in these days? Above all, what occurred at Northampton, when Christ was again judged in my person [Col. 0538D] before the tribunal of the governor; when the Archbishop of Canterbury, because of injuries everywhere inflicted upon himself and the Church of God, was compelled, without qualification, to appeal to the Roman tribunal and to place his goods—wrongly called his, since they are the goods of the poor and the patrimony of the Crucified, entrusted rather than given to him—under the protection of God and of the Roman Church? Who ever saw or heard the Church of Canterbury judged, condemned, and compelled to provide surety in the king’s court, especially by its own suffragans—even though divine mercy has at some time declared her unjustly proscribed? Where has this authority—indeed perversity—against law or canons been found? Why does this enormity not produce shame in you, shame not bring confusion, confusion not elicit repentance, repentance not bring forth satisfaction before God and men?

Because of so many and such great injuries inflicted upon God and his Church in my person, and upon me for God’s sake—injuries which I could not endure with my conscience intact, could not remedy without danger to my life, and could not pass over without peril to my soul—I chose rather to withdraw for a time, that I might dwell more safely in the house of the Lord than in the tents of sinners, until iniquity should be completed, the hearts of the wicked revealed, and the thoughts of hearts made manifest. [Col. 0539A] Thus the infliction of so many injuries was the cause of my appeal. This was the occasion of my departure, which you call unexpected, though, according to what was alleged against me and done to me, it ought—if you who know are speaking truth—to have been all the more unexpected, lest it should be prevented by being known beforehand. But as the Lord turned adverse events to the better, provision was made for the honour of our lord king and his people, lest anything be done to me to the dishonour of himself and his lineage. Better provision was also made for those who longed for my death, thirsted for my blood, and, as is commonly said and believed, aspired to the height of the Church of Canterbury for our destruction—would that less ambitiously than greedily!

We appealed and were appealed against; and, while the goods of the Church of Canterbury, and our own and those of our followers, remained secure as justice requires, we pursued our appeal.

If matters were disturbed when we departed, and during our departure, as you say, let him who gave the cause, who procured this, impute it to himself. Without doubt this fault belongs to the doer [Col. 0539C], not to the one withdrawing; to the persecutor, not to the one avoiding injuries. For he seems to have inflicted the loss who gave cause for the loss. Why say more? We presented ourselves at court; we set forth the injuries done to ourselves and to the Church; we stated the cause of our coming and of our appeal. No one was present to answer us in any respect. We waited, and no one came to allege anything against us. No judgment was rendered against us before the matter was brought before the king. While we were still, according to custom, waiting at court in case anything should be objected against us, our officials were approached and forbidden to obey us in any respect concerning temporal matters, or to provide anything either to us or ours against the king’s command [Col. 0539D] and conscience—by you, brother of London, together with Richard of Ilchester and the Archbishop of York, as is said, pronouncing the sentence. From there haste was made to the lord king; let him see to it—upon his own head be it turned—who gave this counsel. Without judgment, without reason, after the appeal, while we were still remaining at court, the Church was despoiled; we and ours were despoiled; clerics along with laypeople were outlawed, men with women, women with infants in their cradles. The goods of the Church—the patrimony of the Crucified One—were assigned to the treasury: part of the money was turned to royal uses, part, brother of London, to yours, if what we have heard is true, and to the uses of your church. If this is so, we require of you, commanding you by virtue of obedience, that within forty days after receiving these letters [Col. 0540A], you restore to us in full, without any pretext or delay, within the aforesaid period, whatever you have taken from it or whatever has been converted to the uses of your church. For it is unjust and very contrary to law for one church to be enriched by another church’s loss. If you commend the author of these acts, you should know that, regarding goods taken from a church, one who violently commits an injury cannot lawfully confer authority.

By what perverse law, then, by what inversion of the order of the canons, can sacrilegious robbers and invaders of ecclesiastical property defend themselves without restoring what has been taken from the Church? Will they put forward the obstacle of an appeal? Far be it! What new things—indeed, what things contrary to law—are you introducing into these churches? Consider what you are doing [Col. 0540B]. Certainly this bean will be ground for you; and for your churches, unless you take better counsel for yourselves. For the Church of God would be dangerously situated if a sacrilegious robber, an invader of others’ goods—and especially of the Church’s goods—were secure against it by the aid of an appeal. In vain does he invoke the aid of law who does not obey the law—indeed, who is opposed to law. Are these the injuries which we add to injuries, the labours which we add to labours: that we have not endured these and other monstrous acts that were and are being done in this Church; that, oppressed, we appealed; that we withdrew from court; that we dared to complain of injuries to the Church and to ourselves; and that we do not keep silence about all these things, because we are preparing to correct them? Behold, he is dangerously afflicted to whom even the consolation of making complaint is denied. You, my friends [Col. 0540C], who think yourselves wiser than others, who present yourselves as more prudent than others—since the children of this world are accustomed to be more prudent than the children of light—why do you deceive your brethren and subjects? Why do you lead them into this error? What authority, what Scripture, has bestowed on princes this prerogative in ecclesiastical affairs which you wish to confer upon them? Do not, brethren, do not confuse the laws of the kingdom and of the Church. These powers are distinct; one derives force and authority from the other. Read the Scriptures, and you will find how many kings, and which kings, perished because they appeared to themselves to usurp the priestly office. Let your discernment therefore take care lest divine pressure crush you for this injury. If it comes, you will not easily escape it [Col. 0540D].

Give counsel also to our lord the king, whose favour you purchase at the expense of the Church, lest—God forbid!—he himself and his entire house perish, as those perished who were found in a similar offence. But if he does not desist from this undertaking, with what conscience shall we fail to punish these acts? With what purity of conscience shall we conceal them? Let him dissemble who has authority to dissemble; not I, lest this concealment come upon my soul! In your letters you imply—indeed, you plainly say—that I was promoted while the kingdom protested and the Church itself sighed and groaned. Do you know what Truth says? “A mouth knowingly speaking a lie kills the soul.” The words of a priest, moreover, ought always to have truth as their companion. [Col. 0541A] Good God! Would not even someone from this common people blush to say such a thing? Consult your consciences; consider the manner of the election, the agreement of all those to whom the election belonged, the prince’s assent through his son and through those sent for this purpose, and that of his sons together with all the chief men of the kingdom. If any one of them objected, if he protested in any respect, let one who knows speak; let one who is aware declare it. But if someone was disturbed by it, he should not say that an injury was thereby done to the whole kingdom and the Church on account of his own displeasure. Consider also more carefully the letters of the lord king and of all of you, urgently requesting the pallium for us, and obtaining it. Such is the truth of the matter. But if envy tormented anyone, if ambition afflicted anyone, if an election so peaceful, so lawful [Col. 0541B], so free of contradiction, impressed pain and bitterness upon anyone’s mind to such an extent that on this account he plots and wishes everything to be disturbed, may the Lord and we pardon him, provided that he does not at all conceal his fault and is not ashamed publicly to confess before all his resentment of mind.

You say that I have been raised by him from exile to glory. I am not, indeed, [lacuna] descended from ancestral kings.

Yet I would rather be a man in whom nobility of spirit makes a lineage for itself than one in whom nobility of lineage degenerates. Was I perhaps born in a poor hut?
