Yet, through the assistance of divine mercy, which knows how to show mercy to its servants and chooses what is lowly in order to confound [Col. 0541C] the strong, in my modest circumstances, before I entered his service, I lived sufficiently amply, sufficiently abundantly, sufficiently honourably—as you yourselves know—in a manner more abundant than that of my neighbours and acquaintances, whatever their rank might have been. David too, taken from following the ewes with young, was appointed to rule the people of God; strength and glory were increased to him because he walked in the ways of the Lord. Peter, however, chosen from the trade of fishing, became prince of the Church; by his blood he deserved to have a crown in heaven for Christ’s name, and on earth a name and glory. Would that we too might act likewise! For we are successors of Peter, not of Augustus. The Lord knows with what intention He Himself desired that we should be exalted. Let his own intention answer for him, and we shall answer him [Col. 0541D], as the duty of our office requires, more faithfully, by God’s mercy, in severity than those who flatter him with lies. For the blows of a friend are better than the deceitful kisses of an enemy.

You charge us with the stigma of ingratitude by a certain insinuation. We believe that no criminal sin brings infamy unless it proceeds from intention. Thus, if someone commits homicide unwillingly, although he is called and is a killer, he nevertheless does not incur the guilt of homicide. So we say: although by the law of the Lord we owe service to our lord the king; although by royal law we are bound to render reverence; although we have supported the lord and approached the son with paternal affection; if, in an assembly, unheard and grieved, compelled by the necessity of our office, we exercise the censure of severity [Col. 0542A], we believe that we act more for him and with him than against him, and that we earn from him more favour than the stigma or penalty of ingratitude. Certainly, a benefit is very often conferred upon one unwilling. Hence the welfare of one is more advantageously protected when, even if not otherwise, necessity compels him to be recalled from committing an offence. Moreover, our Father and patron, Christ Himself, defends us against the charge of ingratitude. By paternal right we are bound to obedience to Him; if we do not observe it, we shall be punished by the just penalty of disinheritance. For a father may disinherit a son for just cause. He Himself says: “If you do not announce to the wicked man his iniquity, and he dies in his sin, I will require his blood at your hand.” Therefore, if we do not approach the offender, if we do not rebuke one who will not hear, if we do not restrain one who is obstinate [Col. 0542B], we transgress the command and, as guilty of disobedience, are lawfully disinherited.

By right of patronage, because we are His freed people—for when we were slaves of sin, through His grace we became free for righteousness—we are bound to Him in reverence and service. Therefore, since we are subject to no one except with preservation of faithfulness to Him, if anyone stubbornly acts against Him to the detriment of the Church, then rightly, if we do not punish the offence in that part of the charge to which we have been called, He alone will withdraw from us, on account of ingratitude, the benefit bestowed; and thereby we shall truly appear ungrateful.

You set before us the danger to the Roman Church and the loss of temporal goods: certainly our danger and that of ours; no mention is made of danger to souls. [Col. 0542C] You also utter a threat that the lord king may withdraw—God forbid!—from fidelity and devotion to the Roman Church. Far be it, I say, that the devotion and fidelity of our lord the king should ever depart from the fidelity and devotion owed to the Church for temporal advantage or disadvantage! This would be criminal and damnable in a private person, much more in a prince, who draws many after him. Far be it also that any of his faithful should ever think such things, much less that some careless person should say them, much less a bishop! Let your discernment therefore take care lest the words of your mouth infect someone, or several persons, to the loss and damnation of their souls, like the golden cup called Babylon’s, smeared with poison within and without: when someone drinks from it, he does not fear the poison because he sees the gold; and thus the effect of your work may come [Col. 0542D] into public view. For He who is not deceived brings hidden work into the light and lays bare wicked schemes.

In tribulation and the shedding of blood the Church is accustomed to grow and multiply. For it is characteristic of the Church that it conquers when it is wounded, understands when it is rebuked, and prevails when it is abandoned. Do not therefore, brethren, weep over her, but over yourselves: you who make a name for yourselves, though not a great one by this deed and saying in the mouths of men; you who provoke God’s hatred and that of all people against yourselves; who prepare a snare for the innocent; who devise new and ingenious arguments for overthrowing the Church’s liberty. Brethren, by God’s mercy you labour in vain. For the Church herself shall stand, though often shaken, in that strength and firmness in which she is firmly founded [Col. 0543A], until the general falling-away comes, until that son of perdition arises, whom we do not believe will rise from the western regions unless the order of things and sequence of the Scriptures are perversely altered. But if temporal matters are in question, we ought to fear danger to the soul more than temporal dangers. Scripture says: “What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and suffer loss of his soul?” Therefore we utterly reject danger to ourselves and ours. For we should not fear him who destroys the body, but Him who destroys body and soul.

You reproach us concerning the suspension of our venerable brother, the Bishop of Salisbury, and the excommunication of that schismatic John, formerly dean; as you say, these penalties were inflicted before lawful proceedings based on cognizance of the matter, and were issued contrary to the canonical order of judicial process [Col. 0543B]. We answer that a just sentence of punishment marked each of these men: suspension in the one case, excommunication in the other. If you fully grasp the sequence of the affair and rightly consider the order of the proceedings, this will not, we believe, be your judgment. The authority that ought not to escape you says that such inquiry is not required in manifest and notorious cases. Consider more carefully what the Bishop of Salisbury did concerning the deanery after the prohibition of the lord pope and our own prohibition, made under excommunication, and then you will understand more rightly whether suspension properly follows manifest disobedience. Hence blessed Clement says: “If all persons of whatever order, and all princes both of lower and higher rank, together with the remaining people, do not obey their prelates, they shall be not only infamous but also excluded from the kingdom of God, from the fellowship of the faithful, and from the thresholds of God’s holy Church [Col. 0543C].”

Concerning John of Oxford, we say that different persons are excommunicated in different ways: some by a law declaring them excommunicated; others are marked by sentence; others by communion and participation with excommunicated persons. But since he fell into condemned heresy by communicating with schismatics and with persons excommunicated by the lord pope, and contracted upon himself the guilt and stain of excommunication—which, like leprosy, infects and taints, and confounds by a like penalty those who act and consent alike—and since, excommunicated, he usurped the deanery of Salisbury contrary to the express command of the lord pope and our own command under anathema, we declared and excommunicated him, and we firmly hold him excommunicated. What he did in and concerning the deanery we have annulled and hold annulled, as the lord pope himself has already annulled it by the authority of the Eighth Synod, whose judgment is this: “If anyone openly or secretly speaks with an excommunicated person or joins him in communion, he immediately incurs upon himself the penalty of excommunication.” And the Council of Carthage says: “Whoever communicates with an excommunicated person, if he is a cleric, shall be deposed.” Let your discernment therefore take care that none of you communicates with him. For Pope Callixtus says: “Let no one receive persons excommunicated by priests [Col. 0544A] before a just examination of both parties; nor communicate with them in prayer, food, drink, or a kiss, nor say ‘Ave’ to them. For whoever knowingly communicates with excommunicated persons in these or other forbidden ways shall, according to the institution of the apostles, himself be subject to like excommunication.” This is the canonical order: not, as we believe, unknown to the canons, but supported by their authority.

And lest you wonder if someone is at times condemned in his absence, read Paul, who expelled from the fellowship of the faithful and judged to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh a man publicly committing fornication with his stepmother—though absent, neither convicted by witnesses nor confessing, whose crime all knew and did not rebuke—as we have done with this man, whom royal power does not defend by right [Col. 0544B]. Moreover, since at this time many enormities of this kind, and sufficiently grave ones, are being committed in those regions during our absence, which henceforth, though absent in body, yet present in authority, we neither ought nor can, with a clear conscience, leave uncorrected: to you, brother of London, who ought to have known that decree of Gregory VII: “If any bishop in his diocese, through payment, prayers, or the intervention of favour, consents to the fornication of priests or deacons, or to the crime of incest, or does not oppose an offence committed by the authority of his office, let him be suspended from his office”; and that of Leo: “If any bishops consecrate as a priest a man who ought not to be such, even if they in some way escape loss [Col. 0544C] of their own rank, they shall thereafter have no right of ordination and shall never participate in any sacrament which they improperly conferred.” Since, as we have learned for certain, you have sinned in two ways according to the judgment of these canons, we command you, and by commanding impose upon you by virtue of obedience, that, if this is so, within three months after receiving these letters, you take care, by the counsel of your venerable brother bishops, to submit yourself to correction and satisfaction for so great an offence, lest others fall into a like offence by your example and we be obliged to lay a more severe command upon you because of your negligence.

Against fear of burdens you set before us, not a remedy through appeal [Col. 0544D], but an impediment preventing us, as we understand it, from exercising the censure of ecclesiastical discipline against wrongdoers and invaders of ecclesiastical goods: so that we may not enact anything against our lord the king or his land, or against your persons and churches, in the manner in which, as you say, we proceeded against the Bishop of Salisbury and his dean. Far be it from us ever to have enacted or to enact anything disorderly against him or his land, or against you and your churches! But what if you offend in the same or a similar manner in which the Bishop of Salisbury has already offended? Can you by this appeal suspend our authority, so that we may not exercise the discipline of severity against you or your churches if the enormity of the offence requires this [Col. 0545A]? Consider more carefully whether this is a lawful appeal, and what kind of form of appeal this is.

We know that every appellant appeals either in his own name or in another’s. If in his own name, he appeals either from a burden inflicted upon him or from one he fears will be inflicted upon him. We firmly maintain, thanks be to God, that no burden has been imposed on you by us from which you ought to seek the remedy of appeal. Nor do we believe that you currently have any cause against us that is specifically yours. If you appeal from fear of burdens, lest hereafter I enact anything against you or your churches, consider whether this is a fear that should arise in men of the greatest constancy, and whether this is an appeal that ought to suspend all our authority and power over you and your churches. [Col. 0545B] Wise men believe it—and we believe it—that such an appeal has no force whatever, both because it does not appear to have the form of an appeal and because it is not consonant with reason; indeed, it is wholly without the support of any law.

If you have appealed in another’s name, it is either in the lord king’s name or another’s. If not another’s, then the lord king’s. If the lord king’s, certainly your discernment ought to have known that appeals were introduced to repel injury, not to inflict it; to relieve the oppressed, not to oppress them further. Thus, if someone appeals not in confidence of a just cause but to cause delay, so that sentence may not be pronounced against him, such an appeal is not to be received. [Col. 0545C] What condition will the Church be in if, once its liberty is overthrown, its goods occupied and retained, its bishops expelled from their own sees or not allowed to return peaceably with complete security and restitution of all that was taken, robbers, occupiers, and invaders may freely appeal and defend themselves by appeal in order not to be restrained? What destruction of the Church will this be? Consider what you are doing and saying. Are you not Christ’s vicars? Do you not exercise His office on earth? Is it not yours to approach, rebuke, and restrain wrongdoers, so that they may at least cease persecuting God’s Church? Is it not excessive enough that they rage against the Church, unless you also oppose us, on their behalf, to the destruction of yourselves and the Church? Who has ever heard such marvels? It will be heard and proclaimed among [Col. 0545D] every people and nation that the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury—who ought to live and die with their metropolitan, and endure every loss, in defence of the Church and its liberty—wish, at the king’s command and insofar as lies within them, to suspend his power and authority so that he may not exercise the discipline of severity against those offending against the Church.

One thing I certainly know: you cannot rightly play two roles at once, those of appellants and persons appealed against. You are the persons who have appealed; you are those against whom appeal is made. Is not the Church one, and are you not of its body? Behold a contest sufficiently lawful, sufficiently canonical: that those who are members of the Church should enter into contest with their head, which is Christ. I fear, brethren, lest—God forbid!—it may be said of [Col. 0546A] you: “These are the priests who said, ‘Where is the Lord?’ And those who held the law did not know it.” Furthermore, we do not believe that your discernment is unaware that appellants are not ordinarily heard unless they have an interest, or have been given a mandate, or conduct another’s affair. Is it your interest that those who offend against the Church should not be restrained? Far be it! Certainly the contrary is true. But if one who overthrows the Church’s liberty, invades and occupies its goods, and turns them to his own uses, is not heard appealing in his own defence on this matter, then much less are those who appeal on his behalf. Therefore the appeal issued by you for the lord king neither assists him nor appears to benefit you on his behalf. Hence, if in this case he cannot appeal or give a mandate, neither can you receive from him a mandate concerning it [Col. 0546B]. We add also that in this matter you can in no way conduct his affair. No bishop can conduct another’s cause against himself, especially in the oppression of the Church, of which he himself is the defender, and particularly when the Church’s condition is injured generally. Therefore, if it is not your interest to appeal, if you cannot receive a mandate concerning this matter, and if you cannot conduct another’s business, then your appeal is neither heard nor legally binding.

Is this, then, your devotion and consolation—the affection of fraternal charity—which your brotherhood has shown to your metropolitan, rejoicing on behalf of you all? May God forgive you this harshness. Or do you not know, brethren, that a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, in fraud of law and canons, [Col. 0546C] so that none of yours can cross to us without danger of death, imprisonment, or mutilation of limbs, though some of ours could cross more freely to you if they wished? We therefore wonder what order you demand where no order is observed concerning us, the churches, or ecclesiastical persons, but only horror—which may it not be everlasting!—and injuries, since we and ours have been despoiled. Some of these, clerics as well as laypeople, were captured and ransomed after our appeal made at Northampton and after your appeal against us. Moreover, after this appeal of which you speak, a general edict has, as is said, been issued, that no one of ours found in England should escape capture [Col. 0546D], and that no one of you or of our other friends should dare receive our letters or messengers. You yourselves may judge what reverence due to an appeal has been shown and observed—during the period of which, if the appeal is just, nothing ought to be altered. By what law, then, by what procedure do you ask that we receive and hear your letters and messengers kindly? We do not say this because, whatever is done to us and ours, we have ever done, or by God’s mercy shall ever do, anything disorderly concerning the person of the lord king or his land, or concerning your persons and churches.

We believed, indeed, if you understand rightly and desire to assist the Church profitably, that you would blame us more for excessively ordered and prolonged patience than commend us for delay in severity [Col. 0547A]. For delay draws danger to itself, because excessively ordered patience has more of laxity than of commendation, more vice than virtue. Therefore we tell you briefly and affirm firmly that our lord the king will in no way be burdened unjustly if the censure of severity proceeds against him: he has been lawfully approached repeatedly and by letters and messengers, by the lord pope and by ourselves, and, though able to make satisfaction, is unwilling to do so. For one whom law lawfully punishes is not burdened unjustly. To conclude everything in the briefest terms, hold it certain that robbers, invaders, and occupiers of the Church’s goods, and overthrowers of its liberty, are neither protected by the authority of law nor defended by appeal. Moreover, brethren, if you wish to help him as is right—and we too wish this, God who searches hearts knows it [Col. 0547B]—take care to help him in such a manner that you do not offend against God, against the Church, or against your order, and so that he may more readily and beneficially escape the danger to his soul, which is already at the door. We have said these things so that, if divine mercy inspires him, he may make satisfaction to the Church on your counsel. The Church will rejoice at the return of her son and has been, and always is, prepared to receive him with thanksgiving and manifold devotion; and we too shall rejoice.

But your judgment, in which you say that he is willing to make satisfaction and even ready to give satisfaction if any dispute has arisen between him and us concerning some liberty of the Church—as you say—greatly astonishes us, if this is doubtful to any of you, when it is known to nearly [Col. 0547C] the whole world. For it is not consonant with reason—indeed, it is wholly contrary to law—that, if we do not receive [it]—indeed, because we do not receive [it]—we are at fault. Is this a sufficient cause, a decisive cause, why one who has been repeatedly and canonically summoned, who does not make satisfaction and adds injuries to injuries, should not be restrained by divine severity? Far be it! For we know that for no reason can you exercise the office of judge between him and us in this cause: first, because you are and ought to be his adversaries in it, for the defence of the Church’s liberty, the care and responsibility for defending which have been entrusted to you by necessity of your office; if you neglect or dangerously conceal this, you yourselves must consider the consequences. Secondly, because we do not read that superiors, especially metropolitans, can be judged by inferiors, above all by their own suffragans. Thirdly, because some of you are suspect to us and to the Church [Col. 0547D]—would that not all were so—for various reasons which we presently leave unspoken.

Let my lord therefore hear the petition of his faithful servant, the counsel of a bishop, the exhortation of a father: may God bless him and increase his days and the years of his sons into long ages! Let him allow his Church to enjoy peace and liberty under him, as under a most Christian king; let the Roman Church enjoy the right and liberty in his land which it ought to have and has in other kingdoms. Let him restore to the Church of Canterbury and to us its rights and liberties, and all things taken away, together with our peace and security, so that we may freely and peacefully serve God under him, and that he may enjoy [Col. 0548A] our service as he pleases, with the honour of God and of the Roman Church, and the order proper to us, preserved. These are royal dignities; these are the best laws, which a most Christian king ought to seek and observe, and in which he ought to rejoice, and under which the Church ought to flourish. These are laws obedient to, not derogating from, the divine law; whoever does not observe them makes himself an enemy of God. For “the law of the Lord is undefiled, converting souls.” The Lord says of His laws: “Keep my laws.” And the prophet says: “Woe to those who make unjust laws, and to writers who write injustices, in order to oppress the poor in judgment and do violence to the cause of the lowly among God’s people.” Let my lord therefore not be ashamed to return to his heart, humble himself before the Lord in contrition of heart and the gentleness of humility, and make satisfaction to Him and to His Church [Col. 0548B] for the injuries inflicted. For God does not despise but most sincerely embraces a contrite and humbled heart. So too holy David, when he had sinned, humbled himself before the Lord, sought mercy, and obtained pardon. Likewise the king of Nineveh and the whole city, when the severity of destruction had been threatened: because it humbled itself before the Lord in ashes and sackcloth, the sentence being changed, it deserved by contrition of heart and compunction of tears to redeem itself from the censure of vengeance.

Brethren, we write these things not to put your faces to shame, but so that, after reading and understanding our letters, you may be able and willing to exercise the obligations of your office more firmly and vigorously. I desire that henceforth you may always act better, so that peace may come to you more swiftly and the liberty of the Church may be greater [Col. 0548C]. Pray for us, that our faith may not fail in tribulation, but that we may confidently say with the Apostle: “Neither death nor life, nor angels, nor any creature will be able to separate us from the love of God,” which has subjected us to tribulation until He who is to come comes, who will show us His mercy and lead us into the land of promise, a land flowing with milk and honey, which He will give only to those who love Him. Farewell always in the Lord, all of you; and we ask that the whole English Church pray more earnestly for us.

## LETTER LXXVI. TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF ENGLAND

[Col. 0548D] THOMAS, by the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brethren and dearest friends in Christ, all bishops established throughout England and Wales: greeting, and perseverance in a blessed purpose in those things which are God’s.

A hidden word, fit to remain hidden through all ages, has again been brought to us: namely, that peace between us and our lord the king is being negotiated, and that, to the injury of the holy Church of Canterbury and ourselves, he is being urged to have his son crowned by the hand of our venerable brother the Archbishop of York. We, for our part, have always offered ourselves in the Lord for the restoration of peace, ready even now to render in every respect due honour and reverence in Christ to the lord king and his son. And, if it should please the lord king, we are ready, by the duty of our office, to anoint and crown his son king, just as our predecessor is known to have consecrated our lord himself—whose safety may God preserve in all prosperity for long ages, to His own honour and to the benefit of clergy and people [Col. 0549A]. Hence a greater and more manifest injury would be inflicted upon our mother, the Church of Canterbury, and upon us, if anyone else, at the instigation of whomever it may be, should presume to usurp this act. The supreme pontiff, by an authority surpassing all others, forbids it; as you may observe from his letters which we send you. He declares openly that danger to rank, office, and benefice threatens anyone who may presume to attempt it, if indeed anyone does so presume.

Relying upon his authority, we likewise command and enjoin your whole body, by a command under anathema and by virtue of obedience, under peril to rank and benefice, that none of you attempt this or assist anyone attempting it; rather, by apostolic authority, each of you, when a suitable opportunity is diligently sought, must forbid the presumptuous person to usurp it and refrain from communion with him [Col. 0549B]. Farewell always, most beloved brethren in Christ.

## LETTER LXXVII. TO THE CHILDREN OF THE CHURCH ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT KENT. CHARTER CONCERNING THE LIBERTIES OF THE CHURCH

THOMAS, by the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury, Primate of the English, and legate of the Apostolic See, to all faithful children of holy mother Church established throughout the district of our diocese of Kent: greeting.

Although we ought diligently to preserve the rights of the churches subject to our jurisdiction and punish, by swift and fitting correction, those who presume to diminish them, it is nevertheless fitting that with greater vigilance we preserve whole and inviolate the liberties and dignities of the Church of Canterbury, over which divine mercy has placed us, liberties and dignities belonging to it by ancient right. We therefore forbid, by the authority we exercise, your whole community, and clerics in particular, to let no one presume to hinder any of his parishioners, or any other person, who has requested burial in the cemetery of the Church of Canterbury, or whose friends request it on his behalf [Col. 0549C]. The cleric in whose parish the deceased has died shall accompany the body as far as the Church. If he is unwilling, the monks shall freely carry the body of the deceased to the Church, after the appropriate rites have been performed, and bury it.

Moreover, by the same authority we decree that it is forbidden for any person to presume to intervene—whether archdeacon, dean, provost, or any ecclesiastical or secular jurisdiction—if anyone in the aforesaid church or within the circuit of its walls, the church and court of ours and of the monks, commits homicide or theft, sheds blood, injures any person by word or deed, or commits any unlawful act against anyone. We decree that correction and satisfaction for offences occurring in the places mentioned are reserved solely to the person of the archbishop and to the monks of our church. If anyone presumes to infringe this our ordinance or attempt to contravene this privilege, let him know that he will without doubt incur the indignation of Almighty God [Col. 0550A] and our own.

## LETTER LXXVIII. TO ALL WHO HAVE SWORN AGAINST THE LORD POPE

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to all persons established in England who have sworn against Pope Alexander.

Know, dearest friends, that we have written out of great tribulation and anguish of heart, not indeed to make you sorrowful, but that you may understand how abundant is the love we have for you. For God is my witness how I long for you all in the bowels of Christ Jesus. Therefore, having learned what has recently been done in times unheard of, to the peril both of your bodies and of your souls, and indeed to the injury of God himself, we are greatly saddened and ashamed on your account. For common report makes plain how you have abjured the lord pope, who bears the image of Christ himself, and likewise me, who, although unworthy, have nevertheless been appointed the father and bishop of your souls. This, above all the other things which we have endured for several years as an example of God’s just judgment, has added an unbelievable increase to our affliction. For how much scandal that utterly detestable and disgraceful oath now produces in the world, offence to God, guilt to you, and distress to us! To abjure those set over you by God is an injury to him who appointed those rulers; and the authority dishonoured and the obedience nullified are not ours who preside, but rather his who set us over you.

[Col. 0550C] This fault, indeed, I say plainly to you, but tearfully for your sake, is equal and akin to idolatry, as the prophet says: “To resist is as the sin of divination, and to refuse compliance is as the crime of idolatry.” Accordingly, by the ordinance of the old law, such persons received the sentence of bodily death as true idolaters. But you seem to have done what is worse: not only do you resist, but you also confirm by oath that you will resist. What, finally, is it for sheep to reject their shepherds? Surely those who abandon their shepherds have already been invaded by the wolf. And unless the shepherd whom they have abjured now protects them, he will devour them utterly. Many testimonies of Scripture and examples of saints might be adduced in condemnation of your offence.

[Col. 0550D] Yet the enormity of so great an excess is clear even to men of the dullest understanding. If, however, you entered into it not voluntarily but unwillingly, the sin is excused in part, but not wholly excused. For it would have been better to lose the body itself than to commit so execrable an oath. Hence all of you are children of death, who, as the prophet says of his people, “You too have been struck by the blow of an enemy, with cruel chastisement.” But, in order to show our concern for you before God, we have taken care to apply to so savage a wound the sole remedy now remaining; and we absolve, in the place of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and Roman pontiff, and in our own place, those who repent of such an unlawful oath—especially those who swore not willingly but under compulsion. To our venerable diocesan brother bishops, and also to the lesser priests where episcopal sees happen to be vacant, we commit our offices for imposing upon the aforesaid penitents outward satisfaction. Let all of you know this: you are in no way bound by such an oath, nor obliged to obey it, lest, after the manner of Herod, under a pretext of piety you become impious and excuse by an oath a crime worse than the oath itself. As one writer says: “An oath by which evil is rashly promised is not to be observed.” And again: “Break faith in evil promises. Change your resolution in a shameful vow. Do not do what you rashly vowed.” There are many further statements consonant with these, which I now pass over.

At last I beseech you—I who am bound in the Lord; I beseech you as sons whom I must always embrace in [Col. 0551B] Christ—that you walk worthily of the calling by which you have been called: first holding the faith of Christ himself, and afterwards obeying those set over you by him, submitting to them. For they keep watch over you as those who must render an account for your souls. But I wish you to know, brethren, that unlawful oaths and the many other enormous acts committed against us, through wicked counsels, in the oppression of justice and truth, will, with truth herself assisting, rather turn to her own advancement. For truth may be hindered and bound, but cannot be conquered; she is content with the small number of her own people and is not frightened by a multitude of enemies. May the Spirit of counsel and wisdom grant you to think the same thing toward one another, so that, being of one mind and with one mouth, you may honour the shepherds and bishops of your souls, whom that [Col. 0551C] great shepherd of the sheep, Jesus Christ, established in the blood of the eternal covenant; and, through the love of the Holy Spirit, may you extend the hands of your prayers to your father now shipwrecked, that I may be delivered from unbelievers, who even forbid prayer to be made in church for me while I am imprisoned—though such prayer is the common aid alike of believers and unbelievers.

May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all, because you have come to your senses concerning an ill-given oath and have repented worthily and humbly. As for the rest, may God either quickly convert them or afflict them temporally, until they come to their senses and perform worthy repentance.

## LETTER LXXIX. TO HIS SUFFRAGANS

[Col. 0551D]

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to his suffragans.

I give thanks to my God, whom I now serve in my bonds, because your obedience has already been proclaimed throughout the world of God’s churches. This is now my glory: that we now dwell together as one, that most unhappy Judas having been cast aside, like a most rotten limb amputated—he through whom such scandal came into our body, who, like an unruly beast of burden, did not draw in the yoke but disturbed the sweetness of our unity. Therefore, giving glory to him who by his power has strengthened the pillars of his Catholic Church, we beseech you, most beloved brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together unto him, that you be not quickly moved from [Col. 0552A] our judgment, nor troubled, whether by a spirit, by speech, or by a letter purportedly sent from the Church. I say this because many will come, and I certainly know and do not doubt that some have already come, who, like a pestilential wind, corrupt the land, borne along by the verdigris of lies. For these are prophets of Baal, sent to deceive the people, so that religious lies may more readily induce belief in their statements. “From the prophets of Jerusalem this pollution goes out over the land.”

For behold, there are men of our own profession who, in persecuting us, set their feet in motion and do not rest: they send letters full of lies throughout the world, pollute the ears of hearers, and pursue us throughout the whole world with their tongues. Having become servants of wealth, at the nod of the masters from whom they hope to receive, they are like comic slaves: now they affirm everything, now they deny it. Yet our sorrow is tempered by the fact that our mother has long endured this inward suffering of her bowels. Hence the Lord himself threatens such prophets—who were not few even under the old law—through the prophet: “Behold, I will feed them with wormwood and give them gall to drink. For from the prophets of Jerusalem pollution has gone out over the earth.” Nor will she be wholly healed from this sickness until he comes who heals all infirmities and renews his youth like that of an eagle. But you, brethren, do not listen to these prophets. Ralph of Landaff, whatever sort of archdeacon he may be, and Richard Barre are said to be the leaders of this prophecy. Do not, I say, believe them. For a prophet will be shown by the outcome of his prophecy.

[Col. 0552C] And you will know without doubt that, shortly—certainly not after many days—by the Lord’s action, vain speeches will perish in the time of visitation. For when the particular falling-away has come and the man of sin, the son of perdition, has been revealed, there is no question concerning the imminence of the Lord’s day. But stand firm and be strengthened in the Lord, lest that day overtake you like a thief. For behold, today God has made you a fortified city, an iron pillar, and a bronze wall against the whole land—against the king of the land, its princes, and the people of the land. If they wage war against you, they shall not prevail, because the Lord will be with you.

Therefore, being not a little confident in your obedience, we firmly enjoin you and, by the authority of our command, forbid you under the obligation of obedience [Col. 0552D] to enter into new obligations of oath or even of promise demanded from you. Otherwise—God avert it—the Lord will number you, fallen into the guilt of disobedience, with those who work iniquity. Finally, brethren, pray that, the rumours of false speakers and the devices of manifold fraud being suppressed, the truth of God may run and be glorified through us, and that we may be delivered from troublesome and evil men, who have long held the truth of God captive in falsehood. And may the God of patience and consolation grant you to think the same thing toward one another according to Jesus Christ, that, bearing one another’s burdens, being of one mind and with one mouth, we may honour the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ and his bride, our mother, the holy and apostolic Church.

## LETTER LXXX. TO THE CLERGY AND LAITY OF KENT

[Col. 0553A]

THOMAS of Canterbury, to the clergy and laity established throughout Kent.

Let all of you, most beloved brethren, know that for just and manifest causes we have publicly excommunicated Gilbert, bishop of London; Ranulf de Broc; and the others whose names are written above. Therefore we declare to you, as our dearest sons and brethren, that you must entirely abstain from their communion until they repent and make worthy satisfaction. Furthermore, know that we absolve you from subjection and obedience to Geoffrey the archdeacon and Robert his vicar; and we forbid you to render them obedience or reverence [Col. 0553B] until they make worthy satisfaction to us and to the Church of God for the crime of disobedience, by which they are known to have greatly injured her. Nor are you to endure their exactions any longer. Let not your heart be troubled in these matters, nor be afraid, because, God being favourable, we are protected by the safeguard of the apostolic see against the evasions of the malicious and the subterfuges of appeals.

## LETTER LXXXI. TO THE CLERGY OF KENT

THOMAS, by the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the apostolic see, to all clergy established throughout Kent and living in Christian communion: greeting, and obedience to God rather than to men.

[Col. 0553C] Your discretion knows in part how many and how great injuries the lord king of the English has inflicted upon the Church of God, upon you, and upon us; and how long we have endured him and his followers with great patience, waiting for our gentleness to lead him to repentance. But now, because he has always abused the patience of the lord pope and our own, and because it will endanger our soul if we conceal any longer so many injuries done to Christ, we command and direct all of you, by apostolic authority and our own, under obedience, anathema, and peril of rank and benefice, that unless the aforesaid lord our king makes the satisfaction due to the Church of God and to us by the Purification of blessed Mary, from then on you entirely cease from [Col. 0553D] the celebration of divine offices, except baptism of infants, penance, and the viaticum which must be prepared in cases of necessity: the doors of the church being closed, lay persons excluded, and without ringing of bells or solemnities such as the Church is accustomed to observe in times of peace and joy.

Furthermore, under the same threat, we command you to declare that Geoffrey Ridel and Robert his vicar, Richard of Ilchester, William Giffard, Richard de Lucy, Nigel de Saccaville, and Adam de Chering are excommunicated and must be avoided. And, by the authority of the lord pope and our own, we forbid any of your parishioners henceforth to obey Robert the vicar, whom we have deprived of ecclesiastical benefice, or further to comply with the exactions which he has been accustomed to impose.

[Col. 0554A] Moreover, unless John, dean of Salisbury; Guy, dean of Waltham; John Cumin; Ralph, archdeacon of Landaff; and Wimar, the dependant of Count Hugh, make satisfaction by Christmas to the Church of God which they have injured and to us, publicly declare that from then on they are to be avoided as excommunicated persons. We command that all persons who receive churches or ecclesiastical benefices from the hand of laymen; who compel clergy and ecclesiastical persons to disobedience; who hinder the envoys of the lord pope and our own from pursuing the needs of the Church; who, in order to escape lawful correction and oppress ecclesiastical justice, have recourse to secular powers; who teach or compel others to prefer human traditions and the usurpations or abuses of the powerful to the divine law; and priests of another ordination who, after our departure, have presumed to celebrate divine offices in our bishopric without our authority—whether they have received a concession from those usurping our offices or not—unless, after this declaration has become known to them, they desist from so great a presumption; and likewise those who hereafter admit them into their churches: all these persons, I say, we command to be publicly declared excommunicated.

[Col. 0554B] Do not fear, most beloved sons, their multitude or their appearance, because there are more with us than with them; and consolation will soon be given you from heaven, while all the saints plead with God that he may swiftly convert or crush the adversaries of the Church for the glory of his name. May divine grace grant you perseverance in faith and obedience, without which, as you know, no one obtains the crown of righteousness.

## LETTER LXXXII. TO THE DEANS OF KENT

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to the deans of Kent.

Your belovedness knows how the lord king, always abusing the patience of the apostolic see and our own, has continually added worse evils to former ones for the destruction of the Church. Therefore we command and direct you, under obedience and peril of rank, office, and benefice, that within fifteen days of receiving this letter you forbid the celebration of all divine offices in the churches within your jurisdiction, except the baptism of infants and penance for the dying; and, so far as lies in you, cause the sentence of this interdict to be inviolably observed by all. Moreover, under the same threat, we command you to arrange for our letters to be presented to the community of the Church of Canterbury.

## LETTER LXXXIII. TO WILLIAM THE SUBPRIOR AND THE COMMUNITY OF CANTERBURY

THOMAS, by the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all England and legate of the apostolic see, to his beloved sons in Christ, WILLIAM the subprior, ODON, and the other brethren who serve the Lord in the holy Church of Canterbury [Col. 0555A]: greeting and that peace which, as the world does not know it, so Christ alone acknowledges.

How much and how great suffering our smallness has hitherto endured for the honour of God, the liberty of the Church, reverence for the apostolic see, and preservation of its privileges, your brotherhood cannot fail to know and ought not conceal. Although it has not yet, as it ought, shared in the necessities of us and of Christ’s poor who are exiled with us in him, nevertheless it has heard from the testimony of many, and has partly seen with the faith of its own eyes, the bitterness of exile, the injuries of proscription, the insults of detractors, the cruelties of persecutors, the schemes of those lying in wait, and the powers of tyrants poured out freely, fiercely, and persistently against our person and household.

[Col. 0555B] Yet among all these things the gravest dangers for us have been those which we endured from false brethren, who put forward offices of peace and services of piety while secretly setting traps. They spread snares, sharpened their tongues like a sword, and raised the engines of others, so that, after we and ours had been altogether erased from the company of the living, they might abolish the title of the holy Church of Canterbury and take from it the glory of that honour and pre-eminence which is known to have been acquired by the blood of the saints resting there and by many great labours. May the Lord repay them according to their works and according to the wickedness of their devices.

From the beginning, the instigator and standard-bearer of these men was that bishop of London, who first divided the unity of the English Church to the destruction of ecclesiastical liberty and of us. He armed the hearts and hands of the king and his officials; then, supporting and cleaving to our brother and friend, the archbishop of York, he cunningly deceived some of our brethren, so that, against their mother, to whom by their profession they were bound to faith and obedience, they should write to the lord pope on behalf of the aforesaid archbishop, that he might be permitted to carry through our province his cross, rival to the saving cross, since it is set upon the wood of pride, so that he might seem in some measure to attain equality with the Church of Canterbury. Ever since that archbishop was promoted from the Church of Canterbury to the archbishopric, he has always laid as many snares against her as he knew how and was able.

[Col. 0555D] May God spare those who were deceived; and may he either convert to his honour or crush those who deceived or compelled simple and weak brethren. Let us for the moment pass over what would take too long to recount: how, by how many and what efforts and machinations, together with the aforesaid archbishop, Richard de Lucy, and Richard, then archdeacon of Poitiers, in the presence of the lord pope’s envoy, he devised and caused our exile and proscription to be prolonged now into its fifth year; and how, through the agency of tyrants, he compels Christ’s innocent poor to live miserably in banishment—lest we seem to pursue a private injury.

This was done by that son of the Church of Canterbury—would that he were a true son! This was the proof of faith by a priest and bishop who professed faith and reverence. These were the works of a brother, friend, familiar associate, attached to our side and order, who, when the needs of the Church arose, was first with us in the council of priests. Long, dearest friends, have we been silent and so far have we overlooked such manifest dangers and crimes that our patience seemed to holy men possessed of God’s Spirit and to discerning persons worthy rather of the name of cowardice and laxity than of virtue.

[Col. 0556A] But what has he done? We speak unwillingly of his error—lest we call it madness—by which he disclosed the malice of his mind; and you will not hear it patiently when you recognize another Absalom plainly arming himself for the overthrow of the holy city, in order to transfer your inheritance and the glory of the saints through whom your church is illustrious to the North. He is like him who wished to be made equal to the Most High by usurpation of glory, not conformity of goodness. For he boasts that he will establish an episcopal see at London, and that he owes no obedience to the Church of Canterbury because, since he was translated, he has not renewed his profession.

Why are you troubled at this, and why do thoughts rise in your hearts so that injured devotion cannot restrain its tears? For we know that there is none among you—or very rarely one—and comparable to that parricide, who does not groan at this report, whose mind is not ulcerated and pierced by the force of grief, and who would not rather die first, with heart and innards torn out, than see what that presumptuous man threatens. But by divine will it has happened that his iniquity should betray itself: he who has resolved to cast down the innocent hastens toward the ruin he deserves and, with his author, will suffer an irreparable fall for usurping glory.

[Col. 0556C] For who has ever risen so savagely against the Church of Canterbury, the seat of saints from ages past, and has not been cast down from on high? How many and how great persecutors of yours has the Lord cast down before you? Therefore be comforted, brethren, having learned that the arrogance of Moab is greater than his strength; and the time is near when, after stirring up long tumults, he shall be laid waste and fall silent in a night. But will you, against whom such a great injury is being prepared almost beyond all others, continue to be indifferent and, together with those who inhabit the land of Meroz, hold back your hands from vengeance—when God is the avenger of his own injury and of the injury done to us? You remember what is written: “Curse the land of Meroz,” said the angel of the Lord.

And indeed the curse has already seized him, because, his sins demanding it, he has been delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, marked with the character of the beast, and avoided by brethren and fellow bishops who hold right views, lest the stain of condemnation infect them through sharing in his leprosy. Therefore gird yourselves, mighty sons, and be ready for battle against the overthrow of your church. Whoever belongs to the Lord, let him join us; and whoever inwardly favours that man’s enterprises, let him openly cleave to him. Henceforth you cannot serve two masters or obey two bishops, because the Lord has sent the fan of his judgment into the land, that the grain may be separated from [Col. 0557A] the chaff. Those, however, who adhere to him shall, God willing, be like him in destruction of the flesh, made for burning and fuel for the fire. For henceforth we shall spare no one, but the measure of vengeance shall be applied according to the measure of guilt.

Therefore, because—as God knows—we love all of you with sincere charity, and because we have resolved, should the matter require it, to lay down our lives for the right of our mother, the holy Church of Canterbury, as the present day shows, we counsel, warn, and command you under the obligation of obedience to prepare two of your brethren, whom, after consultation with you, we have judged necessary for this purpose. Sufficiently instructed, they may, together with our envoys, confront this most malicious man and, from copies of our privileges, sufficiently fortify the lord pope and the Roman curia, assail him in his court, and overthrow the enemy of public welfare. For now it will appear with what faith, devotion, and zeal each person has hitherto lived and served his church.

We have overlooked the faults of those who communicated with our excommunicated persons, although for the greater part we have their names recorded; but unless they behave more cautiously hereafter, there will be no place for forbearance. Those whose names are subscribed below are excommunicated, and it has been granted us, both by the justice and clemency of the apostolic see, that we should not delay exercising ecclesiastical severity against them on the pretext of any appeal. For the lord pope, knowing the manifest malice of our opponents and the justice of our cause, which is clear to all, proceeds in our case without doubt as he judges that one ought to proceed in the necessity of a uterine brother.

[Col. 0557C] We were about to say more for your consolation, but after mature deliberation we have paused, meanwhile waiting and praying that the heart and soul of all of us may become one in the Lord; that no one may seek what is his own, but what belongs to Jesus Christ, and what will serve the public good, the liberty of the Church, and its future dignity. Take courage, faint-hearted ones, for the time is near when you will see the glory of God and the confusion and disgrace of those who persecute the Church of God. Let no one trust in worldly equipment or the companionship of retainers, because:

> Filthy plunder has no good outcomes.

[Col. 0557D] And there is no faith among the faithless. And lest a stricter account be required of us if we further overlook the great and manifest offences of those who persecute the Church—whom we have endured in much patience for almost the whole five-year period so that they might repent—we announce to your brotherhood that we have publicly excommunicated Geoffrey, archdeacon of Canterbury, and Robert his vicar; Richard of Ilchester; William Giffard; Richard de Lucy; Adam de Chering; and likewise those who have received ecclesiastical offices or benefices from lay hands contrary to the ordinance of the sacred canons, or have usurped them by their own presumption. Likewise also those who hinder the envoys of the lord pope or our own from pursuing the needs of the Church.

[Col. 0558A] Therefore, by the authority of the lord pope and our own, we command you to regard and cause them to be regarded in our archbishopric as the discipline of the sacred canons prescribes that persons solemnly excommunicated are to be regarded.

## LETTER LXXXIV. TO THE SAME PERSONS

THOMAS, by the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the apostolic see, to his beloved sons in Christ, WILLIAM the subprior and the entire community of the Church of Canterbury: greeting, and steadfast perseverance in the strength of faith and obedience.

For five years we have lamented with the prophet, astonished with grief and wonder at how she who was lady of nations, chief of provinces, once numerous in the offspring of her children and glorious in the abundance of her peoples—and, more glorious and illustrious still, mother, nurse, and propagator in Christ of the Britains—has for so long been reduced to solitude and wretched servitude, so that she dares neither remember liberty nor declare to the nations the law of Christ for which she was founded, nor publish ecclesiastical decrees.

[Col. 0558B] It would be superfluous to recount, especially to you who saw and heard them in person, the atrocious injuries and the things rashly undertaken against God and the Church without pity and with every reverence for law cast aside. It was hoped that our patience might lead the lord king to repentance; but, what we cannot announce without tears, his cruelty has always increased through impunity, and through our forbearance he has become more inhuman.

[Col. 0558C] We fear, therefore, lest his blood and that of the Church, now almost perishing, be justly required from our hands, if so great an offence remains any longer unpunished and unchallenged by us. For Eli too is described as having perished because, although he saw and rebuked the offences of his sons, he chose to act with the affection and gentleness of a father rather than the severity and authority of a bishop.

Therefore, lest justice count us guilty before God and assign us to condemnation for consenting through concealment of crime, we command and direct you, under obedience, anathema, and peril of office, rank, and benefice, by apostolic authority and our own, that unless he makes satisfaction to the Church by the Purification of the blessed Virgin Mary [Col. 0558D] and renders the peace due both to her and to those who are exiled or proscribed on her account, you cease from divine offices, except what canonical custom permits religious men to perform, with lay persons excluded, without the solemn ringing of bells and signs of ecclesiastical rejoicing, and in a low voice.

Do not fear those whom the Lord sometimes allows physically to afflict the saints, for the greater crown of the elect, but who can do nothing against souls; because in this furnace the Lord will plainly judge whom he ought to crown in the future. We have publicly excommunicated those who receive churches and ecclesiastical benefices from lay hands contrary to canonical ordinances; who compel clergy by punishments or threats to disobedience; who impede the envoys of the lord pope and our own from pursuing the needs of the Church; who teach that human traditions are to be preferred to divine law; who compel the usurpations or abuses of the powerful to be set above the institutions of Christian religion; and, by name, Geoffrey, archdeacon of Canterbury; Robert his vicar; Richard of Ilchester; William Giffard; Nigel de Saccaville; Richard de Lucy; Thomas son of Bernard; and Adam de Chering.

[Col. 0559A] If the king of England does not correct his excess even through the punishments imposed upon his subjects, then, though we say it unwillingly, we shall not spare his person, at the peril of our salvation, as we have hitherto done with the Lord’s authority. For such mercy is shown to be impiety, since it is written that he who spares the rod hates his son. Moreover, by the same authority and under the same threat, we command you, from Christmas Day onward, to avoid as excommunicated John, dean of Salisbury; Guy, dean of Waltham; John Cumin; Ralph, archdeacon of Landaff; and Wimar, priest and dependant of Count Hugh, unless they take care to render due satisfaction to the Church of God which they have injured and to us. May the word of God shine in your hearts and works, so that, preferring the fear of God to human fear, you may gain the crown of glory and happily transmit to your contemporaries and descendants an example of obedience and courage.

Likewise to Richard, prior, and the chapter of Dover, and to the monasteries of Kent.

## LETTER LXXXV. TO THE SAME PERSONS

[Col. 0559C]

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to WILLIAM the subprior and the community of Canterbury.

How many and how great persecutions the English Church has endured without cause now for six years, you know all the more certainly because you have in great part felt them all the more bitterly through experience itself. Therefore, since the lord king, while being urged to repentance by the great patience of the holy Roman Church and our own, is not merely uncorrected but continually adds worse evils to the former ones, lest his blood and that of the Church, which is almost wholly perishing, be required from us, we command all of you under the obligation of obedience and peril of rank and order that in the Church of Canterbury, within fifteen days of receiving this letter, you cease from [Col. 0559D] all divine offices, except penance for the dying and the viaticum, which religious favour requires to be prepared with doors closed, lay persons excluded, without ringing of bells, and without every solemn sign of joy.

We command you, using our authority concerning the tenor of this special mandate, to notify all deans established throughout the archbishopric, under obedience and peril of rank, office, and benefice, that in all the churches within their jurisdiction they cause the sentence of this interdict, so far as lies in them, to be inviolably observed. May the grace of God preserve you, who obey God rather than men.

Likewise to the abbot of Faversham and the other abbots and priors established throughout the archbishopric, except that they are not bound to command anything to the deans.

## LETTER LXXXVI. TO GEOFFREY RIDEL, ARCHDEACON OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0560A]

THOMAS, by the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury, to GEOFFREY Ridel, archdeacon of Kent.

For a long time we have awaited your fidelity, devotion, and obedience. But because your fidelity has hitherto brought us little advantage, your devotion has shown still less favour, and your obedience has earned you no merit, we command you and, under obedience and peril of your rank and possessions, direct that within forty days after receiving our letters you present yourself before us, preserving fidelity toward your lord, devotion toward your father, and obedience toward your archbishop, so that you may at least thus learn to discharge the obligations of your office—whose benefits, would that you had deservedly enjoyed them.

## LETTER LXXXVII. TO THE SAME MAN

THOMAS, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury and legate of the apostolic see, to GEOFFREY, disobedient archdeacon of Canterbury: that he should provide more wisely for himself because of his disobedience.

We sent you long ago mandatory letters, under threat of punishment and with a delay of forty days, ordering you to come to us within that period and make satisfaction to us for the duty of your office. We now send corrective letters—and deservedly punitive ones—if you do not come to answer us concerning your disobedience, make satisfaction for communion with our excommunicated persons, and receive for both matters what you have deserved.

[Col. 0560C] For carrying this out we appoint for you a peremptory day: namely, the fortieth from the presentation to you of our letters, whether through your fraud they were insufficiently received by you, or through presumption rejected. Come, that you may escape the punishment for not coming. Hurry, that the Church may rejoice in your conversion. Do not be ashamed, that you may experience the benefit of shame; that you may be converted, let what you have deserved come upon you.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. TO THE SAME MAN

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to GEOFFREY, archdeacon of Canterbury.

It is just that obedience be withdrawn from one who persists openly [Col. 0560D] in the crime of disobedience; and whoever knowingly communicates with persons whom he does not doubt to be excommunicated plunges himself into condemnation through their accursed fellowship. We are exceedingly astonished at the recklessness with which you presume to exercise authority over the clergy and parishioners of the Church of Canterbury, and to perform our episcopal office—by making appointments to churches and conferring the cure of souls, a function which the decrees of the holy Fathers withhold from archdeacons—and to burden parish churches with various exactions, especially since we have publicly excommunicated you, as we have the Bishop of London himself, Ranulf de Broc, and the others whose names are written above. We wholly release our clergy and parishioners [Col. 0561A] from obedience and reverence toward you, until, mindful of the faith and oath which you rendered to us, you return to our obedience with fitting satisfaction.

Moreover, by the authority of the lord pope and our own, under obedience and at the peril of your salvation and orders, we forbid you henceforth to concern yourself with our archdeaconry, until you deserve to be absolved by us. Let this also be known to you and to all: by the authority of the lord pope and our own, we revoke as void all appointments to churches made during our absence; and we forbid you to contaminate the parishioners of the Church of Canterbury by your communion. And indeed, by God’s favor, we are protected by the safeguard of the Apostolic See against the evasions of malicious persons and the subterfuges of appeals [Col. 0561B]; and we subject to anathema also those who, at the king’s command or by their own rashness, have seized our goods or those of our people, or who, through councils, accusations, or deceits, have stirred up the king’s mind toward the proscription of innocent persons or the plundering of the poor of Christ’s Church; likewise those who hinder the pope’s messengers and ours from pursuing the needs of the Church. We command them to abstain from the fellowship of the faithful until they repent and make fitting satisfaction.

## LETTER LXXXIX. TO GUNTHER

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to his beloved GUNTHER [Col. 0561C].

Gilbert the canon, whom we had sent to the curia, returned to us and informed us that Master Hervey has so far achieved nothing in our affairs, but is being held by promising assurances of hope. Yet here is a time and opportunity in which, with God’s favor, the aforesaid affairs may readily be brought to completion. For our lord and friend, the Archbishop-elect of Mainz, is now great—as he ought to be—in the eyes of the lord pope, and can now very easily obtain from him whatever he asks. We have therefore written to him, asking that he act for us before the lord pope and urgently request that our affairs be brought more swiftly to their proper conclusion. For we do not know what the coming day may bring.

Therefore let your watchfulness press the matter and, with every care, ensure that while our aforesaid friend, the lord Archbishop-elect of Mainz, is present, our affairs may be carried into effect as we instructed Master Hervey [Col. 0561D]. Take particular care, however, that these matters do not come to the knowledge of William of Pavia or John of Naples. And lest the nature of the business escape your memory: our petition is that the lord pope restore in full to us and to our Church the ancient dignity of the primacy, and firmly command and decree that the Archbishop of York, without appeal, having laid aside the privilege of carrying the cross before him, be subject to us and to our Church by right of primacy, and that he no longer dare under any circumstances to claim for himself that privilege of the cross within our province.

Likewise, he should command and decree [Col. 0562A] that, similarly without appeal, the abbot of St Augustine’s make profession to us and receive pastoral blessing from our hand in our church, if possible, or elsewhere. We both wish and ask that you strive with all your strength to urge the aforesaid lord and friend of ours, the lord of Mainz, to obtain these things for us. For if—God forbid—we allow the opportunity of the present time to pass unused, perhaps we shall never be able to find another like it.

## LETTER XC. TO JOHN, HIS CLERK OF CANTERBURY

THOMAS, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to JOHN of Canterbury, greeting.

[Col. 0562B] From the matters set down below you will be able to judge in some measure how we have newly become a reproach to our neighbors, an object of mockery and derision not only to those around us, but to almost all peoples of both realms—French and English—and perhaps of the Empire; and what a report, not to say infamy and scandal, flies through the ears and mouths of all against the lord pope, a matter over which, God knows, we grieve more than over our own person, while they fiercely attack the whole curia, mock it, and heap upon it irreparable reproaches. You should communicate these matters privately to the lord pope and to our friends, if indeed any remain.

Behold, John of Oxford and the other envoys of the king have returned from the curia, exalting themselves above all that is called or worshipped as God [Col. 0562C], declaring that they have obtained at the curia whatever they desired: namely, that the king is exempt, with respect to being bound by excommunication, from the jurisdiction of all bishops except the lord pope; and that he will have the legate whom he requested, William of Pavia—our more than manifest enemy—with plenary power throughout the king’s whole land, to build and plant, but especially to uproot and pull down, with every remedy of appeal removed, and above all to decide the principal case between the king and ourselves, together with all consequential matters—matters which, it is said, will henceforth bring prejudice against every exception. With this pomp, with this arrogance, John of Oxford returned to England.

[Col. 0562D] When he landed at a certain port, he found nearby our brother, the Bishop of Hereford, secretly awaiting a favorable wind for crossing the sea; for he could not do so openly, having been forbidden by the king’s officials, on the king’s behalf and by his letters. Having found him, John first forbade him to cross in the king’s name, and then in the pope’s name. When the bishop asked—as his messenger, who later came to us to excuse his lord, reported to us—whether he had letters from the lord pope concerning this, John said that he did: letters by which the lord pope forbade both him and the other bishops of England to come at our summons or to obey us in anything, until there should arrive a legate from the side of the lord pope, obtained by the king, who should determine with plenary power, all obstacle of appeal removed, both the case concerning the appeal [Col. 0563A] which they had made and the principal case between the king and ourselves, as well as all other consequential matters.

When the bishop pressed to inspect the letters, John said that he did not have them at hand, because he had sent them, together with his prohibition, as far as Winchester, which is twelve miles from the port of Southampton. The bishop therefore, after taking counsel with his own men, sent his clerk Master Edward, a worthy and, as we believe, faithful man, with John to Winchester. Edward saw the letters together with the Bishop of London, who likewise wished to cross the sea. When the latter had seen the letters, he broke out joyfully, saying: “Henceforth my Thomas will not be archbishop.” John also added [Col. 0563B] that the king was a privileged person, so that henceforth he could not be excommunicated by us, nor even summoned except in the presence of the lord pope; that he had free power to grant the deanery of Salisbury Church to whomever he wished; and that our dignity and jurisdiction were in all respects diminished and suspended until the coming of the expected legate.

The bishop conveyed all this to us through his chaplain, a regular canon and religious man, whom he had sent to excuse his failure to come at our summons. For we had summoned him once, twice, and finally a third time, by a peremptory edict, to appear before us by the Purification, as a man of great influence and intimate with the king [Col. 0563C], in order to negotiate peace, if possible, between the king and ourselves.

The canon was prepared to swear that he had received these things from the bishop’s own mouth, to communicate them to us on his behalf. If they are true, then beyond doubt the lord pope has strangled and suffocated not only our own person, but himself and all ecclesiastical persons in both kingdoms—indeed, both Churches, French as well as English. What will other princes of the earth not dare, after so dreadful an example, against ecclesiastical persons? To whom will they have recourse? How will they be able to trust the Roman Church, which has so abandoned and forsaken us, who stand for her and contend even to bloodshed? What will happen if, while these unheard-of [Col. 0563D] and detestable privileges and emancipations of the king’s person and of others remain in force, it should happen—God forbid—that the lord pope dies, or that all things in the city are thrown into confusion?

Certainly these grants will pass to their heirs and cannot be torn from their hands. Worse still, other princes will, by this example, extort similar privileges and emancipations from the Church, whether she wills it or not. Thus all liberty of the Church, and the jurisdiction and power of bishops, will perish, since there will be no one able to restrain or repress the crimes of tyrants, whose entire purpose is now to rage against the Church of God and her ministers; nor will they cease until they have reduced them, like others, to slavery. Yet what the end will be, we do not yet know. But this we know: we are oppressed beyond measure [Col. 0564A], whether the allegations made are true or false. For neither bishops nor abbots nor any other members of the English clergy obey or regard us in any respect as they formerly did, already being almost certain of our deposition.

But let the lord pope be assured that we shall under no circumstances enter the king’s land to litigate, nor stand before the judgment of our enemies, especially of the Pavia man, who thirsts for nothing but our blood, so that he may obtain our see—which, indeed, as we have learned, has been promised to him, provided it can be freed from us. There is another matter in which we are distressed. Noble men, both magnates and bishops and other prelates of the French realm, now almost despairing of us, have sent back to us our fellow-exiles whom they had mercifully maintained. Henceforth these men will perish from cold and hunger, as some already have perished [Col. 0564B]. Carefully represent all this to the lord pope, that he may provide us with some remedy against these evils, as we ask—if any zeal for God remains in him, as we still hope; and may that hope not be put to shame. Farewell; and send this messenger back to us as quickly as you can, so that through him we may be more fully informed of these matters and others, being in such straits, if the allegations are true.

## LETTER XCI. TO ALEXANDER AND JOHN, HIS FAITHFUL MEN

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to ALEXANDER and JOHN, his faithful men, greeting.

Before your departure you learned that we had sent a regular canon of St John’s [Col. 0564C] to the lord cardinals with a copy of the lord pope’s letters concerning the absolution, upon oath, of our excommunicated persons, in this form: that they should restore everything taken from us and ours, or otherwise be replaced under the same sentence in which they had previously stood. Afterwards we sent the lord pope’s letters themselves to the cardinals through Lord Osbert, subdeacon of the curia. Through the aforesaid canon they replied that the excommunicated persons whose names we had specified to them in a schedule had, by the king’s command and with his authority, received our revenues and those of our people; therefore they could not exercise justice against them while they remained in his land. They further added that our name was so hateful to the king [Col. 0564D] that neither they nor anyone else dared speak to him concerning us or approach him in any way about matters which concern us.

Lord Otto also told the messenger privately—though it must remain secret among yourselves and be disclosed to no one except the lord pope and our most faithful friends—that it would be futile for the lord pope to command the cardinals to do anything of this kind against the king; for while they stayed in his land, they would not offend him in any manner, whether for the pope himself or for anyone else. Therefore it is altogether expedient—indeed, more than necessary—that you employ every effort in your power and exert yourselves before the lord pope so that the oft-mentioned cardinals may be recalled and compelled, under threat of penalty, to leave the king’s entire land. But remember also the Bishop of London [Col. 0565A] and the Bishop of Salisbury, and strive to accomplish what we charged you. Through the bearer of this letter we send you the king’s letters concerning us, the letters of the cardinals which they sent us through the aforesaid canon, and Lord Otto’s private letters, which we likewise wish to remain private among yourselves and be shown only to the lord pope.

Furthermore, someone has informed us that, as William of Pavia suggested to the king, and perhaps to others, unless the king had perceived that it was the lord pope’s will for us to be transferred, he would never have adopted or persisted in his present course. But let the lord pope and our other friends know—and state it to them constantly and firmly—that we would rather allow ourselves to be killed, God knows, who searches hearts, than suffer ourselves while living to be torn away from our mother, the Church of Canterbury, which nourished and raised us to what we are [Col. 0565B]. They should therefore make no effort toward that end, for we would sooner undergo any danger whatsoever.

Add also that, even if there were no other consideration than that that man is taking the possessions of our church and of other churches in that land, we would rather—God knows—die by any death than live dishonorably while he goes unpunished and does not bear the penalty due from us, unless perhaps he makes satisfaction.

## LETTER XCII. TO THE SAME PERSONS

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to JOHN and ALEXANDER, his clerks [Col. 0565C].

You will learn more fully from the copy of the letter which we sent to the Archbishop of Sens what occurred at the conference of kings held at Saint-Denis on the octave of St Martin. But, fearing that it might weary him, we have taken care to set down in this letter certain points absent there, to be communicated to that lord and friend of ours through you. For he will understand the matter more readily when you can report orally many things which we judged should by no means be inserted in that letter.

The Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Sées, who ought to have been mediators for restoring peace, required us to state the names of the landed possessions which we sought to have restored with us to the Church of Canterbury. We replied that we, who had been absent so long and entirely deprived of intercourse with our people and land, could not know which lands the lord king or his officials had alienated or disposed of; but that we wished restored to us all the lands which our predecessor of blessed memory, Archbishop Theobald, held while he lived, and which we ourselves held when we assumed the government of the Church of Canterbury, and afterwards when we went to the Council of Tours [Col. 0565D], and always before the king persecuted us and the Church.

Besides these, we sought and seek the land which Henry of Essex held from us, because, once he had been disinherited for such a cause, it ought to have returned to the lordship and ownership of the Church, just as the lands which he held from the king returned to him [Col. 0566A]. The king also took from us William de Ros’s fief, contrary to the oath which he swore to King Stephen when Stephen adopted him as his son and, having received his homage, appointed him heir to the kingdom. For then he publicly and solemnly swore that he would preserve forever to the churches the lands which King Stephen, his lord and father by adoption, had granted them. He also took from us the land of Mundeham, which he granted, against God, his own salvation, and every equity, to John Marshal. By divine judgment, as you know, blessed Anselm vindicated his own wrong; and John, together with his children, whom he supposed would succeed to the prey, died a few days later.

We expressly sought [Col. 0566B] and still seek these three possessions: Henry’s, William’s, and the land granted to John. We prefer perpetual exile to making peace ruinous to the Church by abandoning them. The mediators tried to give us hope by words that the lands would be restored, but they spoke more coolly concerning the movable property which the king had taken, although the Bishop of Sées and Master Vivian asserted that, if peace went forward, a thousand marks would be restored to us. They said they had received this from his own mouth.
