We required half of what had been taken for necessary uses, declaring that we would comply with the counsel of the lord pope or of religious persons concerning the remainder.

Above all, we fear the destructive force of precedent, and fear alike for our salvation and his: for ours, if we foster so great a sacrilege by concealment; for his, if, when payment is due, he neither restores nor makes satisfaction for what was taken. For in such a case it is wholly certain that sin is not forgiven if what has been taken is not restored [Col. 0566C]. There are various forms of compensation, which he can perform without great loss to himself and which we are prepared to accept. But that we should remit to him—especially while unrepentant—what he has taken from God’s Church, divine mercy protecting us, he shall never obtain by any devices whatsoever. If, however, he repents and makes satisfaction in part, we shall bear with him in all patience concerning the remainder, in view of the devotion which he shows to the Church and the charity which he has toward us. For it is expedient for both the Roman and the English Church that something remain in our hands which may rightly be set against him when he devises tumults and seditions. Otherwise, whoever wholly releases him [Col. 0566D] will arm his savagery for slaughtering the Church.

But he is now so placed in the balance, and so fears the sentence hanging over him and his land, since he learned that the lord of Sens and that Gratian—whose memory is held in glory and blessing in both kingdoms—were going to the curia, that he does not dare deny the lord pope anything, whatever he may pretend or threaten, if the pope has resolved to press his hand heavily upon the king’s lands on this side of the sea and send back his envoys disgraced. Nor will it be necessary for the sentence to take effect, because the threat alone will very easily obtain whatever has been sought.

Recently he sent Geoffrey Ridel into England to torment ecclesiastical persons and bind them by wicked oaths to the crime of disobedience. Together with Richard, Archdeacon of Poitiers [Col. 0567A], and other royal officials, he ordered in the king’s name that all the bishops should meet in London and give security that they would observe the king’s edict: that no one should receive the lord pope’s messenger or letters, nor ours, without consulting the king; that no one should obey an interdict if one were promulgated; and that no one should dare pronounce a sentence of anathema against any of the king’s faithful men. But no bishop or abbot, except that emissary of St Augustine’s, wished to appear at that little council of officials, because they preferred to incur the anger of public power, if they could not avoid it, rather than abandon God’s law.

First, therefore, the Bishop of Winchester publicly protested and solemnly declares that he will obey with all devotion, in every respect and so long as he lives, the apostolic commands and the Church of Canterbury, to which by his profession he owes faith and obedience; and he orders his clergy to do the same [Col. 0567B]. The Bishop of Exeter imitates him, ready for every obedience, and has withdrawn into a community of religious men until iniquity passes away. The Bishop of Norwich, when forbidden on the king’s behalf in the presence of the officials, excommunicated Count Hugh and others as he had been commanded. Descending from the pulpit, he placed his *cambuca*—that is, his pastoral staff—upon the altar, declaring that he would see who would stretch out hands against the lands or goods of his church. Then he entered the cloister and lives with the brethren.

Likewise, the Bishop of Chester is prepared to carry out the commands; and, to remain safe from the officials, he has withdrawn into that part [Col. 0567C] of his bishopric which the Welsh inhabit. From this it is clear that the lord pope is triumphing in England to the glory of God and the perpetual honor of the Apostolic See, so that his authority may flourish and bear fruit there, if he perseveres in vigor and does not reject the crown divinely prepared for him. For impiety does not know where to turn, and, as its adherents attest, it always has before its eyes the lord of Sens and Gratian, the son of grace.

Vivian’s delay, too, greatly advances Gratian’s reputation. Vivian has at last experienced the deceiver’s tricks, and he has not ceased to proclaim publicly among us the deceiver’s wickedness and various frauds. When he has done this at the Roman Church—if there is faith in the man—the lord Gratian will be further vindicated by Vivian’s testimony in his actions [Col. 0567D]. You yourselves, and through Lord Hyacinth, should labor to ensure that he refutes the envoys of his deceiver in accordance with his promise. If he does this and walks faithfully with you, deliver to the lord pope the letters which we are writing for him. For, as we have learned with certainty, he is now privately and steadfastly accusing the king of perfidy, and has in large measure restored the reputation which he previously damaged. But if he wishes to walk by two paths—which we do not believe, since he is said to have refused money—then retain the letters and take care that he cannot do harm.

Certain persons, by the king’s knowledge and command, have urged us to go to him in Normandy. We do not refuse to do this, if at the border of the lands, as promised, men meet us who can provide sufficient security for us and ours [Col. 0568A]. But press the lord pope to forbid us to give any new security contrary to the custom of the French and English Church; to ensure that he does not depart from the form which we sent in writing to the king; to command that a fitting part of what has been taken be restored to us; to frighten the king by the threat of an interdict in his lands on this side of the sea; to write more earnestly to the king of England that he receive us with the kiss of peace; and in other letters to order him to restore to the Church of Canterbury the lands which we named above, without which peace cannot exist. Likewise, let him forbid us to presume to absolve anyone from the bond of anathema unless that person has first sworn according to the custom and form of the Church. For among the rights of the customs which the king claims against God, if those who have experienced them are to be believed, this will clearly be found to be almost the most destructive. If he falls from this presumption, then, we hope, he will not persist in the others so greatly, lest he be put to shame more often.

Furthermore, let the lord pope write to the most Christian king, thanking him for our consolation and sending a letter of exhortation and encouragement [Col. 0568B], stating how great a crime of sacrilege it is to plunder the Church’s goods and, without just cause, by contrived pretexts to deprive ecclesiastical persons of their property; and that sin is not forgiven without repentance and satisfaction, especially when there is time and an abundance of resources. For if a thing taken is not restored when it can be restored, repentance is imaginary, not true repentance that avails for salvation, but one which accumulates condemnation.

We send you the petition which we presented to the king; do not depart from it in any way unless you can improve the case. We also send the letters which we sent to Master Vivian, and those which, as we have learned, he sent to the king of England, so that, being more fully informed, you may more effectively advance the Church’s cause. If any chatterer presumes to criticize us because we refuse to enter his land unless he receives us with the kiss of peace, let him recall Robert of Silliac, whom neither the kiss of peace publicly given nor the oath of fealty bodily sworn to the king of France made secure; and, unless he is devoid of reason—as we believe he is not—he will immediately excuse our precaution. May the Lord direct us and you, that in all things [Col. 0568D] we may do his will and, whether through prosperity or adversity, restore to his Church the liberty due to it.

You will convey these matters on our behalf to our Father, the lord of Ostia, together with the other things which we wrote to the Archbishop of Sens; then, with his counsel, to our remaining friends who await and will seek the redemption of Israel.

The Bishop of Lisieux, as you know, persecutes us while clothed in the name of friend. Imitating the pattern of his Sinon—whom, while living under episcopal profession, he has always represented—he gives arms to the Danaans against the Amazons and supplies weapons to the Amazons against the Danaans, in order to provide for his own peace: now he furnishes ecclesiastical men with arms against secular men, now secular men against ecclesiastical. Look at the letter which he has just written for the Bishop of London [Col. 0569A], whose merits you know; recall the counsel which he habitually gave us, and you will plainly see another Sinon running back and forth between Danaans and Dardanians. For he too, if you consider the force of his name, is “if not” (*si non*)—one who cherishes, but not in his bosom. With his tongue he devises deceits; and out of the abundance of his heart, almost always in the causes of his friends and in matters of faith, he has willed, dwelt on, and repeated, “Yes and no.” The priest-clerk of the lord of Pavia has remained the same in our cause as he was from the beginning. What that means is not hidden, we believe, from Lord Gratian. For he stood by Gratian while the latter was present, and afterwards always adhered to the king.

## LETTER XCIII. TO THE SAME PERSONS

[Col. 0569B] THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to ALEXANDER and JOHN, his envoys.

Be diligent concerning our affair, and maintain prudence and continual watchfulness against our adversaries, especially against that bastard, fornicator, and enemy of ecclesiastical peace, the priest’s son Reginald of Salisbury. So far as he can, he everywhere defames and dishonors our person, saying that we are a traitor and that we gave him our pledge that we would not harm his father in anything. We would no more have done that for him than for a dog. He also says that, if the lord pope should die, he would have us erased from the book of life, boasting that the Roman curia is so venal that by gifts he can obtain whatever he wishes.

He has also urged the king of England to make petitions of this kind to the lord pope: that he should commit to some bishop in England the authority to crown the king’s son and consecrate bishops, so that he might thus deceive the lord pope. When the king replied that he believed he could not obtain those petitions from the lord pope, Reginald answered: “The lord pope will act as a fool and an idiot unless he grants your petitions.” We therefore ask your affection, in which we confidently trust, that with our Roman friend Hugotio, who has gone from France to Rome, and with all our and your other friends, you stand firmly for us, but also for the justice and liberty of the Church, and labor watchfully with your whole purpose [Col. 0569D] to ensure that that contriver of fraud, deviser of deceit, and fabricator of falsehood, disappointed in the expectation of his wickedness, may be everywhere put to shame; and that through you his iniquity may be exposed and recoil upon him, so that he may regret having come to the curia and may recognize that he is deservedly tormented by the witness of his own wickedness, which he constantly bears in his breast.

For, as you well know, if the lord pope should in any way accede to the king’s petitions in this matter—God avert it—let him know without doubt that the authority of the Roman Church in England will perish forever, so that no one there will dare mention apostolic authority. But if the lord pope, as is expedient for him, dismisses the king’s envoys refuted and frustrated in their purpose, let him know that we shall soon have peace, through God’s mercy. For the king of England is pressing these two points: the coronation of his son [Col. 0570A] and the consecrations of bishops; and he will be greatly constrained to make peace with us if he sees the lord pope’s steadfastness.

Above all, take care not to have any discussion with the aforesaid Hugotio in the presence of cardinals or others concerning our affair. When you have an opportunity, discuss privately with him the execution of the matter, in such a way that no one can discover that you have any intimacy with him.

## LETTER XCIV. TO ROGER, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK

THOMAS, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother ROGER, Archbishop of York and legate of the Apostolic See [Col. 0570B], greeting and success in the life of both worlds.

Your discernment knows more fully that God is the avenger upon those who, unmindful of grace received, return evil for good and, seizing an opportunity to inflict injury, do not fear to harm those whom they ought, according to their merits, to honor and revere. It is unnecessary to repeat in the hearing of your reverence how many and how great benefits you have received from the holy Church of Canterbury, and how she advanced you to the highest rank of priesthood; both because this is known to almost everyone and because it is incredible that such things could escape the memory of your piety.

Indeed, your mother remains ready, as long as it shall please your holiness, to continue the devotion of love and reverence which she began toward you [Col. 0570C], hoping and praying that your eminence will repay her with a return of affection. It will not be through us that we are not diligent to preserve with you the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Although we are exiles and outlaws for the Lord’s sake, we hope that, through the favor of him for whom we suffer, we may in the Lord repay you with a return of service.

But we catch whispers that certain persons are endeavoring to incite and arm your sincerity against the holy Church of Canterbury, so that you may place the crown upon the head of the king’s son—may God direct his ways in what pleases him—and unlawfully advance him as king. Since it is perfectly clear that this would be against the dignity of the Church of Canterbury, should it be attempted—God forbid—the lord pope, as is evident from his letters which we send you, forbids this to you and to all the bishops of England. And we prohibit it by apostolic authority, lest anyone attempt it, appealing in this matter against every person who may devise it, and fixing the day of the Purification of St Mary [Col. 0570D]. And, lest anyone subject to our jurisdiction by metropolitan or legatine right should assist this presumption, we absolutely forbid it under obedience and anathema.

Likewise to all the bishops of England.

## LETTER XCV. TO THE SAME PERSON

THOMAS, by the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother and friend ROGER, by the grace of God Archbishop of York and legate of the Apostolic See [Col. 0571A], greeting, and the happy fulfillment of pastoral watchfulness.

How long our mother, the holy Church of Canterbury—from whose breasts we were nourished, and which by God’s authorship advanced each of us to what he is—has been afflicted by such great calamities cannot be unknown to your brotherhood, especially since almost the entire Latin world has learned that her devastations have hitherto prevailed contrary to law and equity and beyond all measure. We had awaited the king’s correction. The clemency of the supreme pontiff, our own patience, and the fear of divine judgment—which a faithful soul especially reveres—ought to have moved him to repentance. But he, continually abusing God’s mercy and human patience in this affair [Col. 0571B], has endlessly added loss to loss and piled most atrocious injuries upon still graver injuries.

Therefore, lest the Lord require his blood from our hands because of excessive patience and unjust dissimulation while the Church is perishing, we send apostolic letters to your brotherhood, asking and beseeching you in the Lord Jesus Christ, by the unity of charity and the bond of ecclesiastical peace, and, by the authority of the lord pope, declaring through the fidelity which you owe to the Apostolic See: within fifteen days of receiving this letter, throughout your whole province which lies in the power of the aforesaid king, forbid the celebration of every divine office except the baptism of infants and penances for the dying, and cause the sentence of interdict, insofar as lies in your power, to be inviolably observed by all your subjects [Col. 0571C]. Otherwise—God forbid—you may be involved in the penalty of condemnation with those who are to perish in their crime. Provide for the bearer of this letter, as you wish provision made for yourself and your order. May the Most High lead your brotherhood by straight paths and make you a participant with those to whom the kingdom of heaven is promised in the Gospel.

## LETTER XCVI. TO CONRAD, ARCHBISHOP-ELECT OF MAINZ

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to CONRAD, Archbishop-elect of Mainz: himself and all that is his.

Our messenger, whom we had sent to the curia, has returned. [Col. 0571D] Our affairs are still pending and are being held in suspense by promises of good hope. But since delay is sometimes dangerously admitted in matters of this kind, we turn to our special friend, earnestly imploring him to act and labour for us and on our behalf. If perhaps—God forbid—you doubt whom we mean, it is you yourself to whom we speak: you, I say, our special and unique, our inmost and intimate friend in the Lord, to whom we entrust our affairs with complete confidence. We pray—if prayers are needed with such a friend—that you may deign by every means to press for their advancement and for their being brought, in your presence, to their proper conclusion. For behold, this is the time and place in which our petitions must by no means suffer refusal. Therefore, as you love our life and [Col. 0572A] soul, we ask you to take care to be solicitous for us and for our church, urgently requesting the lord pope, in recompense for all the labours which we both endure for the faith and unity of the holy Roman Church, to restore to us and to our Church the former dignity of the primacy. In accordance with what we have written to you, our clerks Hervey and Gunther will also write to you. We further ask you to make haste to inform us, through your messenger—if you yourself are delayed—of your position with the lord pope and the lord cardinals, and of theirs toward you. Know, moreover, that we have heard nothing from our own people. Farewell.

## LETTER XCVII. TO THE SAME MAN, AND TO SABINUS, HYACINTH, AND HENRY, CARDINALS

[Col. 0572B]

The lord archbishop to Conrad, archbishop of Mainz, and Sabinus, bishop, and to Hyacinth and Henry, cardinals of the holy Roman Church: greeting and a will ready for service.

I have endured more than enough, my lords and fathers, while awaiting the correction of the king of England, and I have found absolutely no fruit of my patience. In dealing with him I have carried out by messengers, letters, and other means everything that I ought; but he, continually abusing my patience and solicitude, proceeds from bad to worse, trampling down and oppressing the Church of God and meanwhile pursuing my person with implacable hatred. Thus he has already written to the Cistercian abbot, asking that, as he loves the abbeys [Col. 0572C] of his order which are in the king’s power, he should exclude us and our fellow-exiles from the order’s assistance and fellowship.

Since the king’s excesses and impiety, and those of his ministers, can indeed scarcely be described, but even more scarcely believed, and since I consider both my own danger and his, I have publicly condemned those pernicious usages—or rather abuses—by which the English Church is disturbed and thrown into confusion, together with the document and the authority of the document by which they had been confirmed. I have generally excommunicated both their observers and enforcers, their paternal supporters, and all their advisers or helpers, whether clerics or laymen; and I have absolved our bishops from the oath by which they had been violently bound to their observance. [Col. 0572D]

These are the provisions which I specifically condemned in that document:

- That no appeal may be made to the Apostolic See for any cause whatsoever without the king’s consent.
- That a bishop may not excommunicate anyone who holds anything directly from the king, nor place under interdict his land or that of the king’s officials, without the king’s permission.
- That a bishop may not coerce anyone for perjury or breach of pledged faith.
- That clerics or religious men may be dragged before secular courts.
- That laymen—the king or others—may deal with cases concerning churches or tithes.
- That an archbishop or bishop may not come when summoned by the lord pope without the king’s permission.
- And other matters of this sort.

I have also excommunicated by name John of [Col. 0573A] Oxford, who communicated with that schismatic and excommunicate man Reginald of Cologne; who, contrary to the command of the lord pope and of ourselves, usurped for himself the deanery of the Church of Salisbury; and who, at the emperor’s court, took an oath for the renewal of the schism. Likewise, we have declared excommunicate and excommunicated Richard of Ilchester, because he fell into the same condemned heresy by communicating with that most notorious schismatic, and by contriving and fabricating every evil with the schismatics and those Germans, to the ruin of the Church of God, and especially of the Roman Church, under the agreements made between the king of England and them. We have also excommunicated Richard de Lucy and Jocelin de Baill., who proved supporters of royal tyranny and fabricators of those heretical abuses; [Col. 0573B] Ranulf de Broc, Hugh of Saint-Clair, and Thomas son of Bernard, who appropriated to themselves the possessions and goods of the Church of Canterbury without our permission and consent. We have also excommunicated all who hereafter lay hands upon the possessions or goods of the Church of Canterbury against our will and consent.

We have not yet personally excommunicated the king himself, still awaiting his correction; yet we do not deny that we shall excommunicate him unless he speedily comes to his senses.

Accordingly, I most earnestly entreat and admonish your charity to stand firm in this matter, diligently reminding the lord pope to ratify what has been done by us. Otherwise, apostolic authority [Col. 0573C] will be diminished beyond measure in those regions, and the liberty of the Church—which has already for the most part perished—will undoubtedly perish altogether. For behold, the king’s heirs are growing up; they will be imitators of their father’s cruelty unless these pernicious offspring are cut away at the root with the immense force of ecclesiastical severity.

For my own part, I would far rather resist not only unto blood but unto death itself than leave such shameful crimes unpunished any longer in the Church of God. Know also that the archbishop of Rouen and certain others have told the king to his face that none of them will communicate against the lord pope’s command; rather, if sentence is pronounced against him and his land, [Col. 0573D] they will firmly observe it at the lord pope’s command. We also know and hold for certain that the king’s obstinacy would be broken very quickly if a strict sentence were imposed upon his transmarine land.

## LETTER XCVIII. TO THE SAME MAN

The lord of Canterbury to C., archbishop of Mainz.

We regard all that is ours as yours, because we ourselves are wholly yours. This ought to suffice for persuasion. We therefore ask you to provide for our necessity, which you will readily perceive from the copy of the letter that we send to the lord pope. We send that copy to you, no less confident in you than [Col. 0574A] in ourselves, because we are as concerned for your affairs as for our own.

Behold that schismatic John of Oxford, who by his perjury procured our exile so far as he could, is seeking the Apostolic See, in order to circumvent it and overthrow justice. We ask that his own iniquity may answer him, and that he may feel Peter to be at home—the Peter whom he dared repeatedly to cast down, by attacking him before kings and princes. Let him learn that there is a prophet in Israel who judges justly at the fitting time.

The clerical priest of the lord of Pavia recently promised the king of the English that his master, once he had received a legation, would settle according to the king’s will the dispute between us and him. Our enemies, the persecutors of the Church—and indeed of Christ—already openly boast [Col. 0574B] of our deposition. Unless unavoidable necessity compels us, however, we shall submit to the judgment of no one except the lord pope, fearing the overthrow of the English Church and the disgrace of the Roman Church more than our own ruin. Therefore keep watch with the lord pope and the cardinals, that they may provide for their salvation before God and their honour before men. For whatever they do in either direction will be remembered for ever and ever.

## LETTER XCIX. TO THE SAME MAN

To the half of his soul: the greeting which he wishes for himself, and greater still, since for himself it is least.

Placed between an excellent conscience and the harshest fortune, I do not know how to spare either my spirit or [Col. 0574C] the time. The bitterness of my soul pains me: at the peril of my own life, I must say what I think. The urgency of the time presses me: at the peril of the Church, I must not keep silent about what I ought not. Good God, where shall I turn? Danger lies on both sides. I am unequal even to speaking without danger; in speaking, I fail amid the Church’s peril; in silence, I perish together with her.

Yet lest I perish through the Church’s peril, I say—with grief—a thing all too grievous. The illustrious city which had almost brought the whole world under its sway has been taken captive, overthrown by human greed for favour. She, who could not perish by the sword, succumbs infected by western poison. Alas! By her downfall, the liberty of the Church suffers loss everywhere, to the advantage of temporal things. Men make their way toward her ruin through the winding paths [Col. 0574D] of riches. She has been prostituted like a harlot exposed in the street to the lust of many; all the powerful commit fornication with her, so that, subdued, she may yield to ambition, conceive iniquity, and bear oppression upon the undeserving.

Woe to us! What shall we do? The city’s authority collapses: how will our neck not be bent? Her sons are shut out and stepsons admitted, so that strangers may enjoy the maternal goods that should have supported the lawful heirs. She who would graciously receive the oppressed into her bosom, and in the bowels of charity heal the sick, raises up their oppressors and crushes the downtrodden beneath the mass of burdens.

Where henceforth will refuge remain for us, if, without making satisfaction, men deserve absolution from that for which they ought rather to have been condemned more severely; if those who deserved vengeance wipe away, as though a good deed had been done, their offence by remission; if those who, conscious of their deserts, expected punishment, carry back [Col. 0575A] glory from indulgence? Would that this lot had not found me alive, so that I might not see the evils of our people and of the saints—were it not that, as Scripture says, the righteous must for the love of justice suffer many temporal evils.

Yet there would be some consolation if the sweetness of the fruits compensated for the bitterness of the root. Harsh beginnings commonly conclude with a better end. But lest anything be lacking to the crown, this present tempest turns all things against us: having endured hard beginnings, and with all hope of good emptied out, we must, by the contrary course, expect things still harsher.

We have been excluded from a mother’s bosom; a father’s heart has been closed to us. The undeserving has stripped the deserving of his spoils; the guilty has taken the thing belonging to the innocent; the sluggish has seized the prize of the one who ran well; the man who ought to be punished has snatched the crown of the one lawfully contending. [Col. 0575B] But wretched I—wherein have I sinned? What evil have I deserved? If I showed a devotion beyond men’s expectation; if I kept faith against my friends’ wishes; if, leaving all things through the impulse of devotion and stripped bare in the contemplation of faith, I followed my father and lord amid my miseries, exposing myself to every danger—shall this be the recompense for our disgrace, the restoration of the lost, the compensation of the bitter root by sweet fruits? Will these things not henceforth be in the mouth of the common people as a proclamation of unjust reward?

May God see, examine, and judge the equity of this law. A matter too astonishing, a thing marvelous beyond wonder: law is coined for a name—or rather, to speak more truly, something contrary to law, destroying the authority of justice and equity. The rashness of the persecutor who has been persecuted passes into law, so that one who should receive punishment is granted victory; one without merit carries off glory; one who should be conquered prevails. [Col. 0575C]

This legation would never have been the agent of such great evils, fashioned for the destruction of so many wretched exiles and destined to bring about the ruin of the whole Church. Certainly, though they burst themselves, they will not, Christ helping me, tear me away from the path of justice, from the liberation of the Church from bondage, from that share of solicitude to which I have been called, or from the love of God, which has subjected us to tribulation until the just Judge comes. He will dispense with an equal balance to each alike—to young and old, king and private person, to all equally according to each one’s deserts.

This is the Judge whom I seek; this avenger of our wrongs I seek, upheld by an excellent conscience, secure in sincere devotion, strengthened in true faith, certain that those who endure injury for love of justice ought by no means to be confounded, and that those who break the horns of the persecutors of the Church in zeal for vengeance can by no means be deprived of the hope of eternal reward. [Col. 0575D]

I write these things to the half of my soul, that he may feel the straits of a grieving friend, drive away the pains of one suffering, and lift the pressures of one perishing. For there is no sorrow like my sorrow. For I am said to be delivered into the hands of enemies, betrayed to the will of the envious, to be torn by the teeth of the malicious, and to be destroyed by the judgment of one of my persecutors. A matter altogether abominable: horrible in its own cruelty, hateful in its own malice, contemptible in its very ease, and eternally damnable in its own injustice.

It ought to have sufficed for the Pavians to overthrow Italy, [Col. 0576A] unless in their concern they should also destroy the world together with the Church’s liberty. I would write more to you if, worn down by injuries and afflicted with insults, I did not fear that the account of my pains might disturb the peace of your mind, increase your anxieties, and assail the tranquillity which it is necessary for me that you preserve, lest I perish. Let, therefore, the sound part of me be well, so that the sick part may recover. Let it hasten to help me, lest the whole perish, so that it may receive thereby glory on earth and a crown in heaven. May it be well again and always; and, if you please, have faith in this messenger and in the others who, by God’s mercy, will shortly come.

## LETTER C. TO THE SAME MAN

[Col. 0576B] Thomas, pitiable exile of the Church of Canterbury, to more than the half of his soul: greeting, and his whole self, misery excepted—a thing from which I always desire my friends to be free.

May the Lord console you in all your distresses, you who grieved over the lot of myself and my fellow-exiles as though it were your own, and who, as I have learned by experience, have striven with all your strength to ward from the Church of God and from our poor household the goads of proscription and manifold misery. The king of England trumpets abroad our suspension at the cross-roads of both kingdoms as though by a herald’s proclamation; and, to make me more burdensome and hateful to men as a proof of my disgrace, he produces apostolic letters. He boasts also of the period granted to him, until he chooses to receive me into favour—a thing which, if he is permitted, he will do at the Greek Kalends, that is, never. [Col. 0576C]

You advise me meanwhile to bear it patiently; you extol the virtue of patience in high praises; and you do not consider that someone is not lacking to introduce from the comic poet that saying: “All, when we are well, give sound advice to the sick. But if you were here, you would think otherwise.” For who is being slaughtered without feeling pain, unless he is stupid and senseless? Yet this too, since it must be so, I shall command my spirit to endure bravely for as long as the Lord sees fit—not I, however, but the grace of God with me.

You commend to me the sincerity, friendships, and diligence of the lord cardinals. Of some of them, indeed, I do not despair, especially in the cause of God and of the Roman Church [Col. 0576D] rather than in mine or my companions’. May God reward them for the good things which they do and will do for the proscribed exiles of Christ. But may He recall the others, that they may think the same thing in the Lord and may not seek gifts to the subversion of justice, the dishonour of the Apostolic See, and their own condemnation, making gain from false accusation and pursuing rewards.

They too write that they sympathize with me and my companions. But the moralist, smiling in reply, says: “All sympathize; no one helps.” And rightly so. For the works which they do bear witness concerning them. You advise me to labour by every means to restore peace to myself with the tyrant, persecutor, and torturer of the Church. But the Roman Church and certain cardinals, by whose counsels he acts, as he boasts, have barred to me the way of peace.

For recently, when hope of peace had been given, he had already for the second time summoned me by the count of Flanders to a conference. Then his own messengers and those of his cardinals returned from the lord pope, presented him with letters of my suspension, [Col. 0577A] and gave him horns with which, as long as he wishes, he may both reject peace and meanwhile harass the Church of God as though by authority of the Apostolic See.

You write that fortune is working, to the detriment of the Roman Church, to break the unity of Italy’s most powerful cities. Why, my soul, do you think this has happened, unless because you render inadequate thanks to God, your deliverer, but seek the things that are your own, as though your own exalted hand, and not the Lord, had wrought the great deeds of the past year? I do not say this of ourselves or of others who walk in the right way, but of those who expose the Church of God to persecutors and seek profit.

And because the Church of Canterbury is almost destroyed, and I and my fellow-exiles are weakened and afflicted beyond measure, I pray you more attentively that, with your friends’ assistance, you obtain from the lord pope, as comfort in our misery, the restoration of the primacy of the Church of Canterbury, etc.

## LETTER CI. TO THE SAME MAN

To the half of his soul: the greeting which he wishes for himself.

With great longing we awaited day by day a message of salvation from the lord pope, from you, and from your brethren. We waited, but no one came bringing good or certain news. And because to a longing spirit nothing comes quickly enough, [Col. 0577C] we send to you the bearer of this letter, so that by a return letter, or through this same man, we may learn most speedily whether, as report widely spread in many places among us proclaims, the Lord has magnified His mercy toward His Church and toward you, dispersing and crushing the persecutors of His Church and yours.

We think this is to be believed the more certainly because He is accustomed to be terrible toward the princes of the earth and terrible in counsels over the sons of men, who fight against Him and assail the Church. And now, that you may believe the words of the Psalmist who says, “Do not put your trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation,” it is time, setting aside the favour of princes [Col. 0577D] and abandoning the confidence which you had in men, that henceforth you cling firmly to Him alone, who does not forsake those hoping in Him; that you place hope in Him alone, who knows how to scatter the counsels of princes; and that you act valiantly in Him. For if you keep faith with Him, He will bring all enemies of the Church and of yourselves to nothing.

Therefore henceforth do judgment and justice for everyone who asks and everyone who suffers wrong, so that, just as the Lord delivered you according to your desires from the pressing danger that was already at the doors, from the oppression of the afflicter, you too may assist those who suffer injury, steadfastly restraining the savagery of tyrants and punishing offenders. Thus the Church of God will be exalted, and its strength, long languishing in depression, will rise again. Do this, that there may be joy for you before [Col. 0578A] God and the angels, honour and glory among people and nation, and relief for the Church.

So much for this. But that you may know that what we feared has now happened to us, and that what we foretold concerning the presumption and insolence of Lord William of Pavia is now, as it were, manifest, see the letters which he sent us immediately upon his arrival. In them he boasts—as you yourselves can observe—that he has now come into the land of the king of England in order, with Lord Odo, to decide the questions pending between the king and ourselves, as may seem most expedient to the Church. Further, he sent word to the lord king and his people that he had come to our injury and disgrace in order to do his will. If he does these things in the green wood, what will he do in the dry?

This authority, from which scandal arises for the people, loss for the Church, and disgrace for us—who rather needed consolation, having now for three years endured the hardships of exile among so many kinds of people and lived shamefully on others’ alms—would never have existed. We did not believe that he had come to decide disputes between the king and ourselves; nor had we understood this from the lord pope and from you. Rather, we understood that he had come to make our peace, if God should in any way permit it to be made through his work and diligence. Yet we believe this least of all, since he is wholly the king’s man, prepared by every means to obtain his favour and, “by whatever means, the thing.” [Col. 0578C]

We have many times declared to the lord pope and to you, and still firmly declare, that by God’s mercy we shall never submit in any matter to the judgment or examination of one who seeks to make merchandise from our blood, and who seeks for himself a name and glory from the price—would that it were not the price—of iniquity. We ask, then, that grief not be added to our grief and danger to our danger; and that, if your charity has any concern for us, through you and your friends his power over us and our affairs may be annulled, if indeed he has any such power—which we do not readily believe. For God knows that we would sooner allow ourselves to be excommunicated and remain in excommunication until the day of our death than submit outside the Roman curia to his judgment or examination in any matter.

For it is plainly contrary to the canons to be subjected to the jurisdiction of one who was and is our enemy for the king’s favour—as is plain even to “the bleary-eyed and the barbers”—and who laboured with manifold ingenuity to obtain this authority over us. We have always rejected him as judge before the lord pope through our messengers; we still reject him, and shall reject him at all times. Therefore may your solicitude kindly and steadfastly accomplish what we ask. Farewell always, that we too may fare well; and may we experience, if you please, in this petition and in the others which we have sent you, your goodwill and the fruit of our desire.

## LETTER CII. TO FULCO, DEAN, AND THE CHAPTER OF RHEIMS

The lord of Canterbury to Fulco, dean of Rheims, and to the whole chapter.

Since we are established in the body and of the body of Christ, [Col. 0579A] we are members one of another; we ought therefore to serve one another by mutual offices and, under the holy necessity binding us together, to bear one another’s burdens. This we ought to do with all the more affection because, besides the bond of catholic communion, we are bound all the more firmly to the same end by the special bond of clerical profession. Especially when the dispensation of heavenly mercy has decreed to instruct us through adversity, the consolations of brotherly charity ought cheerfully to meet the emergencies that befall us—consolations to be offered all the more readily and gladly because they are understood to be more due in pressing need and more opportune in burning tribulation.

Accordingly, now deprived of our possessions by the will of our prince and lord, we send to the charity of your graciousness the bearer of this letter, our clerk Master Philip of Calcia, commendable in conduct and learning. Because, amid the storms that have broken upon us, he adhered to us as he ought, he has been stripped of his own goods. We ask and beseech you earnestly to provide for his necessities, as befits him, for as long as the need of this present exile presses upon him, for the sake of God, of love for us, and in consideration of his services. [Col. 0579B] Whatever good you do him, we shall regard as done to ourselves; and as opportunity of place and time permits, with willing and prompt affection, both in intention and in deed, we shall answer with due devotion by reciprocal bestowal of blessings. May the charity of your brotherhood flourish and be strong.

## LETTER CIII. TO THE SAME FULCO

[Col. 0579C]

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to Fulco, dean of Rheims.

We were greatly gladdened on hearing of your promotion, not doubting that it has been done by the Lord, whose work it is to unite the wills of the faithful so that they may be of one heart and one soul. The Church of Rheims did this in your case all the more commendably because it did so with greater unanimity. May He, therefore, who directed so many minds’ desires in electing you, grant you grace in your ministry, so that, as you proclaimed grace the fountain and fuel of all good things, you may experience that same grace as going before and helping you [Col. 0579D] in all your works, to God’s glory.

This we wish for you and pray on your behalf, although we are unworthy to be heard for another when we are not sufficient to blot out our own offences. Nevertheless, we presume upon the mercy of Him who died for the ungodly, that He will heed the prayers of confessing sinners [sic]; He who, in order to recall those who deny to pardon and draw those fleeing to salvation, urged persecutors and enemies toward grace with a certain compulsion of charity—yet with freedom of choice remaining—gave His back to the scourges, received the disgrace and penalty of the cross, and, from what He suffered, established a school of right faith and true virtue. He persuaded men that the world’s perils should gladly be embraced for truth, and that the elect have no commerce with worldly pleasure.

From this we have greater confidence that He will mercifully admit the prayers [Col. 0580A] of our lowliness, for whose law we suffer persecution, being given over to reproach and mockery by those who do not know God and becoming a burden even to those whom we have not yet burdened.

We have been scattered with our fellow-exiles to every wind. Only those share in our misery who have learned from the Apostle to share the necessities of Christ’s poor. Though we cannot repay them as their merit and our desire demand, it is most certain that they will receive the best reward, with an increase of grace and joy, in abundant mercy. For they make their bargain with a debtor who is accustomed to repay a hundredfold with eternal glory and disdains to leave even a cup of cold water unrewarded.

But since the blows of our chastising Father still press upon us and the savagery of our persecutor has not yet softened, we earnestly ask you to ensure that our exile is remembered in your prayers and in those of the holy persons known to you: that He for whose law we contend in the contest may preserve us from sin, lest our faith fail; may convert our persecutors, if they are predestined; and may deliver His Church. We make this same request through you to the Church of Rheims, which we love with sincere charity, thanking it for the honour and love which it has shown to us in our fellow-exiles, Master Philip, Ralph, and others whose necessities it is known to have shared. [Col. 0580C]

Our necessity especially compels us to ask this of you: receive into your household the youth bearing this letter, the son of our sister, and compel him to apply himself to letters in the schools of grammar, so that the Father of the poor and Judge of orphans may provide for your necessities and those of your poor.

## LETTER CIV. TO ROTROU, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen.

As your prudence knows, we have long awaited the correction of the lord king, and have yet found in him no fruit of our diligence or endurance. Hence, though with inward pain of heart, we are rightly compelled to say: “We waited for peace, [Col. 0580D] and did not find it; we sought good things, and behold, trouble.”

Therefore, considering danger both to ourselves and to the king, should we have wished to leave such great excesses unpunished as hitherto, we have lately condemned and annulled that document in which those heretical abuses are contained. In particular, we have declared void the following: “That a bishop may not,” etc.—as is set out above in the letter directed to the archbishop of Mainz and in many others, down to the words, “unless he comes to his senses.” All these persons, I say, we have bound with the bond of anathema. We also desire and ask that you declare them excommunicate. We have likewise excommunicated all who hereafter lay hands upon the possessions and goods of the Church of Canterbury without our will and consent.

## LETTER CV. TO THE SAME MAN

[Col. 0581A]

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to the archbishop of Rouen.

Your discernment remembers how, at the command of the messengers of the lord pope and after an oath had first been taken, you absolved our excommunicates—namely Geoffrey, archdeacon of Canterbury; Nigel de Sackville; and Thomas son of Bernard—because hope had been conceived for peace in the Church, which it was believed would more quickly result from this dispensation. Meanwhile we bore this patiently and waited in all meekness for the fulfilment of the promise until the deadline which the lord pope had set for the messengers to return.

Since peace did not follow, when the deadline had passed we publicly excommunicated the aforesaid Geoffrey, Nigel, and Thomas. In accordance with the institutions of the sacred canons, we notify you that throughout your province you are to ensure, as ecclesiastical discipline prescribes, that they are avoided by all the faithful as excommunicates. [Col. 0581B]

We have also decreed in canonical fashion that John, dean of Salisbury; Guy, dean of Waltham; John Cumin; Ralph, archdeacon of Llandaff; and the priest Wimar must make satisfaction to the Church of God, which they have injured, and to us within the octave of Saint Martin. For, God being the author, we shall then excommunicate them unless they make satisfaction in the meantime. We have also excommunicated those who hinder the messengers of the lord pope or our own messengers from pursuing the Church’s necessities.

## LETTER CVI. TO THE SAME MAN

[Col. 0581C]

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen, and his suffragans.

By the authority of the sacred canons it is commanded that every bishop shall announce the names of his excommunicates to neighbouring bishops, who are to make them known to their parishioners, so that ecclesiastical access may everywhere be barred to those excommunicates and every ground of excuse be removed. For those who knowingly communicate in prayer, food or drink, a kiss, or even by saying “Ave” [“Hail”], or carry on intercourse of speech, with persons who complain that they have been unjustly bound, before a just examination of both sides—except those whose association ought to concern their conversion—shall likewise be subject to excommunication, according to the sacred institution of the canons. To oppose this knowingly and obstinately is impious in purpose and heretical.

We speak to one who knows and observes the Church’s constitutions, who, having zeal for the law, teaches others to fear Him who can cast both body and soul into Gehenna. Nor do we doubt that you place the decrees of the Apostolic See—whose observance the profession of a bishop expressly undertakes at his consecration—before the edicts of secular powers. It cannot be believed that a human day of advantage can move the prudence of your holiness, through consideration of any threatened loss or gain, to enter into a criminal partnership of iniquity with anyone. [Col. 0582A]

We have heard, and hold it almost certain, that our excommunicates, whom we have excommunicated for just and manifest causes under the compulsion of our office and at the prompting of legal reason, frequently come into your province. Therefore, guarding against danger to ourselves and to you, we have taken care to identify them by their proper names according to the rule of the Church, lest the Church entrusted to you incur the stain of condemnation through association with them.

These are their names: Gilbert, bishop of London, etc. We therefore notify you, on behalf of the lord pope and ourselves, that you are diligently to avoid them as the censure of the canons prescribes, and through public proclamation throughout your province to ensure that they are avoided by all the faithful. There are also others whom we have cited by formal summons and whom, God being the author, we shall excommunicate on the day of the Lord’s Ascension unless in the meantime they take care to make worthy satisfaction to the Church of God, which they have injured, and to us: Geoffrey Ridel, archdeacon of Canterbury; his vicar Robert; Richard of Ilchester; Richard de Lucy; Adam de Cirringis; and William Giffard. [Col. 0582B]

By like sentence we have condemned and excommunicated those who have occupied the goods of the Church of Canterbury and of our clerics, whether at the lord king’s command or by their own rashness; those who, through malicious counsels, accusations, and intrigues, have incited the mind of the same our lord king to the proscription of the innocent or the despoiling of Christ’s poor; and those who hinder the messengers of the lord pope or our own messengers from pursuing the Church’s necessities—until they repent and make worthy satisfaction.

Let no one seek to excuse himself by fraudulent wording, by the pretext of an improperly procured absolution, or by a claim of innocence. For no apostle, angel, or any power whatsoever can absolve before God those who remain unrepentant, persist in crime, or persist in the will to sin: God condemns them by the severity of His judgment, even as the Church delivers them to Satan. We long—and would that not too long—overlooked such injuries and insults to Christ, waiting for our patience to work the fruit of repentance in them. But because their pride and impiety have continually risen, henceforth, God favouring us, we shall employ the power divinely conferred upon us, fortified by the authority of the Apostolic See against the evasions of appeals [Col. 0582D] and the subterfuges of malicious men.

## LETTER CVII. TO THE SAME MAN

Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to the archbishop of Rouen.

We give thanks to your affection, which takes care for us; but would that your concern, in the absolution of the bishop of London which you mention, had not exceeded the mandate of the lord pope! For you know what, in the common business, you were permitted to do without your colleague: especially since he had not yet been summoned, nor was it established that, if summoned, he could not be present, [Col. 0583A] whereas only then would either of you have been permitted to do anything in this case, if the other could not be present. For the lord pope inserts this condition, which plainly did not obtain; and from this perhaps the wise may determine whether anything was done when the condition was lacking. But why prolong these matters? You know what you have done, and we, with God as our author, are not ignorant of what is due to you. But what you command to be secret—how can it remain secret? Let those who can take care of that—if indeed any can. For before we received your mandate, it was being sung in the streets among you; and through the Londoner’s own diligence it was published among you, he who solemnly celebrated the divine offices in our city and church.

## LETTER CVIII. TO THE CHAPTER OF ROUEN

[Col. 0583B]

To the venerable brethren G. . . . . . . . dean, the archdeacons, and the whole clergy and people of Rouen: THOMAS, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, greeting, and prosperity in both lives.

We believe that it has come to your knowledge how Lord Gratian and Master Vivian, envoys of the lord pope, caused our excommunicated persons—namely Geoffrey, Ridel, Nigel of Saccavilla, and Thomas son of Bernard—to be absolved, in the hope of peace having first exacted from them an oath that they would abide by their command. Since, after their absolution, peace did not follow as it ought, but was, it is said, impeded by one of those who had been absolved, [Col. 0583C] the aforesaid envoys of the lord pope, returning with the affair unresolved, gave commands to the venerable Fathers, the archbishops of Rouen and Bordeaux. By the authority of the lord pope and their own, and in virtue of obedience, they ordered them to declare to the aforesaid Geoffrey, Nigel, and Thomas, by force of the oath which they had sworn, that they were not to enjoy the benefit of the absolution granted them unless peace were restored to the Church by the then approaching feast of Saint Michael; but that they should regard themselves as excommunicated, once they knew that we had pronounced upon them a sentence of anathema.

Therefore, since within that time the Church did not obtain peace, but its injuries have been increased and multiplied, we have bound the often-mentioned Geoffrey, Nigel, and Thomas with the bond of anathema, declaring this to you [Col. 0583D] and to other churches according to the ordinances of the canons, so that you may beware of communion with them until they deserve absolution. For it is not unknown to you that anyone who knowingly presumes to communicate with excommunicated persons binds himself with the snare of a like condemnation.

Following the canonical practice, we have also notified John, dean of Salisbury; Guy, dean of Waltham; John Cumin; Ralph, archdeacon of Llandaff; and Wimar the priest, that they must make satisfaction to the Church of God, which they have injured, and to us, within the octave of Saint Martin; unless they make satisfaction in the meantime, we shall thereafter, with the Lord as our author, excommunicate them. We have likewise excommunicated all who impede the envoys of the lord pope and ours from pursuing the necessities of the Church.

For a full five years now [Col. 0584A] we have endured with great gentleness the hardships of exile, the injuries of proscription, and the many goads of those persecuting us and ours and provoking our patience. Yet we dare no longer endure the injury done to Christ and such ravaging of the Church, lest it should deservedly be imputed to our sloth or negligence—God forbid!—since before God he is proved guilty through dissimulation who, by reason of his office, does not restrain or rebuke the faults of his subjects.

But if the lord king, and all who have injured us, render to God His due honour in restoring ecclesiastical peace, and strive to fulfil the offices of charity, then by God’s grace we shall be joined to each and every one in sincere affection of charity, and shall take care to preserve unimpaired for each person his rights in the Lord; but for the king more diligently and effectively, [Col. 0584B] as for a most beloved lord, pre-eminent above all others in every worldly right. We judge that God alone, and the things that are God’s, must be preferred to him and his followers, if he permits it; and we obey his will in all things in such a way that there remains to us unimpaired and inviolate only that order bestowed by the Lord which cannot, without loss of salvation, admit violations of the divine law and Christian institution.

May God give you a heart to worship Him, faithfully fulfilling His will and remembering us in your prayers, almsgiving, and works pleasing to God. Recall to mind that ethical saying: “Death with impartial foot knocks at the towers of kings and the huts of the poor.”

Likewise written to all the bishops of Normandy, [Col. 0584C] as to the archbishop; and to the chapters, as to that of Rouen.

## LETTER CIX. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

To the reverend Father and dearest friend WILLIAM, by the grace of God archbishop of Sens: THOMAS, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, whatever devotion an exile and outlaw can offer.

It is impossible for the mind of the wicked man to be at rest: the sting of conscience continually agitates him and instils an unceasing fear lest at every moment he receive what he deserves. Thus continual anxiety weighs upon him as he seethes; and while he rends all men, even those who have deserved well of him and are his closest friends, with suspicions, from his own guilty faithlessness he supposes that others lack the fidelity which his conscience [Col. 0584D] does not possess.

Thus the king of England, having heard of your departure, conscious of his own wickedness and fearing the zeal for the law and the steadfastness of virtue which you possess and exercise in the Lord, fears beyond measure lest a legation to his lands on this side of the sea be entrusted to your holiness, because throughout the whole Gallican Church no other person confronts him through whom his malice may be restrained or crushed. Nor, as his own people testify, does he fear anyone in the Roman Church as he fears Lord Gratian. For, if his boast is true, all others who have approached him for any cause have proved pliable at his nod, and sometimes not without the stigma of an unfavourable reputation.

Therefore, when he learned that Lord Gratian was returning in your company, he was so disturbed that he could not conceal [Col. 0585A] his agitation, saying that through you he would be compelled to make peace or else undergo perpetual disgrace with great loss to himself and his people.

Accordingly, through letters of his own, of the lord of Rouen, and of Geoffrey Ridel, he summoned Master Vivian. And, as Vivian himself confessed publicly before many hearers, the king gave him his word in person that, in restoring peace to the Church, he would follow the command of the lord pope and Vivian’s own counsel. He also had letters sealed with his seal, which he showed to whomever he wished. In them he promised that, for love of the lord pope, he would restore to us the Church of Canterbury, the possessions taken from us and ours, and peace and security, so as more strongly to urge the aforesaid Vivian to negotiate the terms of peace—the peace which, from fear of you and Lord Gratian, whatever another may boast, [Col. 0585B] he seemed to seek.

But he made no mention of the things taken away, except that he intimated that, if we followed his judgment in restoring peace, he would place us at the head of the kingdom and would on no account allow us to be in want. Then, when Master Vivian had been recalled and trusted his words, the king went with feigned devotion to Saint-Denis; but in truth he went in order to do what he nearly did—namely, to deceive the Most Christian King. For they agreed in conference at Saint-Denis that he would entrust his son Richard to the king for support and instruction, and that he would summon to Tours the count of Saint-Gilles, to answer Richard concerning the county of Toulouse. Indeed, that place [Col. 0585C] seemed prudently most convenient: there the supporters of the parties could meet in greatest safety, the claims of the litigants could be freely asserted, and those who were to pronounce judgment could, as reason required, condemn one party in favour of the other without fear or hesitation.

The lord king of France, Master Vivian, and other wise men compelled us to attend that conference, so that, while we were staying at Paris and he was at Saint-Denis, our peace might be negotiated more conveniently at close quarters. There, when the oft-mentioned Vivian met with him more urgently and diligently, that he might fulfil the pledge of his promise, he reverted to his usual manner and showed himself such a man to Vivian that, returning to us, Vivian openly said before many persons present that he could not remember ever having seen or heard of anyone so mendacious. Yet even in the king’s own presence, as we afterwards learned from those present, Vivian did not keep silent about what had to be said. Rather, openly exposing his duplicity, he recovered in large measure the reputation he had earlier injured, complaining that he had been so thoroughly caught in the king’s snares.

[Col. 0585D] We inform you of this so that, if on returning to the Roman Church he should presume to support the cause of the deceiver or conceal his frauds, your affection may more faithfully make known the truth of the matter to the lord pope and the cardinals. For, just as by a divine dispensation Lord Gratian returned after acting vigorously, and you—whom God has placed, as we frequently say, as a most steadfast pillar in His Church, and who know this man’s character more fully—set out for the Apostolic See: so by that same dispensation, it is believed, Vivian, whatever was in his mind, remained in France [Col. 0586A] in order to make the justice of the Church conspicuous and to extend Gratian’s glory; so that the king of England, through his supporter, might become more fully known to the people whom he is accustomed to deceive, and so that the deceitfulness of his words might henceforth less readily entrap the lord pope and the curia, hitherto excessively credulous towards him.

When the aforesaid king of England was leaving Saint-Denis and passing near Montmartre, we met him there. Through venerable men—the lord of Rouen, the bishop of Séez, and certain others who had offered their services by word—we asked him, for the love of God and of the lord pope, to restore to us and ours his favour, peace, security, possessions, and the things taken away; offering ourselves [Col. 0586B] ready to render him whatever an archbishop owes his prince. He answered that, for his part, he willingly and wholeheartedly forgave any offences and complaints which he had held against us; and that concerning the matters which we might wish to allege against him, he was prepared to stand judgment before the court of his lord, the king of France, or before the judgment of the Gallican Church, or of the scholars of Paris.

When we heard this, we answered that we did not refuse the judgment of the lord king’s court, if it pleased him, or of the Gallican Church; yet we preferred, if it were agreeable to him, to reach an amicable settlement with him rather than litigate. And if he wished to restore the church and possessions to us and ours, and to grant us favour, peace, and security by the kiss of peace, we were ready to receive these things. We asked that he restore to the Church half the movable goods which had been taken away, [Col. 0586C] for payment of our debts and those of our people, for repairing ruined buildings, equipping estates, and repairing the Church’s various necessities, which the plundering and fraud of his officials had brought to the utmost extremity of calamity.

And, lest our requests appear to exceed proper bounds, and so that the agreements, put into writing to guard against the man’s inconstancy, might be observed more faithfully, we caused a petition—written out and sent to you, revised and moderated at the judgment of his envoys—to be presented to him, so that all might know that we rejected no condition of peace tolerable to the Church of God. But when he heard the document, approved by all for its extreme moderation, he replied in his mother tongue, [Col. 0586D] twisting the turns of his words, as is his habit, so that to the simpler hearers he appeared to grant everything, while to the more cautious he mingled in perverse and intolerable conditions.

Yet all agree on this one point: he did not consent to receive us with the kiss of peace. Therefore the Most Christian prince added that, not for an amount of gold as great as himself would he advise us to enter the king’s land before first publicly receiving the kiss of peace. Count Theobald added that it would be the most foolish presumption, many of those standing by saying to one another and recalling what had happened to Robert of Silliac, because even the kiss itself did not seem a sufficiently firm guarantee of preserving peace and security.

Yet he took no care to convey this answer to us through the aforesaid bishops, expected mediators of peace, [Col. 0587A] or through anyone else. Rather, while we awaited an answer, he turned aside towards Meudon. On the road Lord Philip, the blessed son of the Most Christian King, was brought to him. Those who brought him say that he saw the child somewhat sadly, addressed him briefly, and hurriedly sent him away. Yet God inspired the soul of His chosen boy, formed and guided his tongue, so that—to the astonishment of those present—he admonished and begged the king, who was hastening to depart, to love the king and kingdom of France, and himself, because by this he would obtain the favour of God and men.

The lord king of France accompanied him as far as Meudon, and thence nearly to Pacy, waiting for him, according to their agreement, to hand over his son Richard. But [Col. 0587B] he promised to do this at the conference at Tours, where the lord king and his people clearly discovered that he was dealing deceitfully with them. And, as subsequent signs showed, they parted from one another with less affection than they had had when they first met. Nor is that conference which he seeks believed likely to take place, for this scheme is exposed to many impediments.

We returned without his answer to the places of consolation divinely provided for us, casting our hope upon Him who does not forsake those who hope in Him, and awaiting the comfort of your affection. The king of England afterwards sent a messenger and twenty marks, it is said, to Master Vivian, asking him to undertake once more the restoration of peace. [Col. 0587C] But Vivian, as we have learned for certain, both refused the money and answered him by a letter, a copy of which we send to your affection. Nothing presses him towards peace so much as the fear which he conceived from your and Lord Gratian’s departure. Nor does he seek Vivian for any other reason than that he may not fall into your hands and Gratian’s.

We have also been told that he has sent Giles, archdeacon of Rouen; John of Oxford; and John of Séez to the curia to prevent a legation being granted to you into his land, or anything else being done that might be troublesome to him or to the count of Flanders. You know in part the identities of these envoys, but perhaps our people, who are with you for our sake, know them more fully. Since, then, such fear of you has seized this man because of the tried fidelity of your sincerity and of Lord Gratian, [Col. 0587D] it is clearer than daylight that, if the lord pope had frightened him from the beginning by the authority of the supreme pontiff rather than borne with him in the pious gentleness of a father, the Church of God would long ago have been made tranquil and the fury of the man would have subsided—the man who pursues without pity those who flee and are unarmed, yet yields to those who resist manfully.

We have lamented in your hearing part of the condition of our misery, since it would be wearisome to recount every detail. It will be for your condescension and charity to obtain from the lord pope a peace suitable both to the Church of God and to us and our afflictions, and worthy of himself; for the eyes of all are fixed upon him, awaiting what he will do in this affair. If the robber does not restore what he has taken away or [Col. 0588A] make satisfaction, if he extorts from us a new obligation contrary to the Church’s custom, especially under the authority of the supreme pontiff, the ruinous precedent will never be erased, but will pass from us to other nations.

What less could have been demanded than what the appended petition contains, framed and moderated at the judgment of his own people? Certainly, if the lord pope should even now at last send back his envoys disgraced and resolve to lay a heavier hand upon his lands on this side of the sea, he will wish to command nothing that he cannot obtain only with difficulty and delay. For the magnates of the Church favour him; and clerics alone water with their exhortations the obstinacy of the rage which they have sown by poisonous counsels, fostering and advancing it with their incitements. Some of them rage in England amid the Church’s torments; [Col. 0588B] others, through frequent journeys, now solicit the Apostolic See, now the public powers of the Latin world, against the Church. And, what we cannot say without pain and astonishment, the powers of the world cannot be induced into partnership in so great an outrage; but in the Roman Church they always find some who, the wicked boast, are partners in their criminal purpose.

## LETTER CX. TO WALTER, BISHOP OF ALBANO

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to WALTER, bishop of Albano.

It is superfluous to set forth words in the hearing of one accustomed to infer much from little, and who, charity being his teacher, does not fail friends making just requests. Having often experienced this in many great matters, we send to the bosom of your clemency the bearer of this letter with complete confidence, earnestly commending both him and the petitions which we present to the lord pope through him to your holiness, and more earnestly asking that your affection may endeavour to advance them with its accustomed kindness.

[Col. 0588C] If it please you, you will hear from him how we have made peace with the lord king of England, to the honour of God and, as we hope, the benefit of the Church and the enlargement among the English of the authority of the Apostolic See. The messenger will supply the remaining matters, which are here deliberately and intentionally withheld.

## LETTER CXI. TO GEOFFREY, BISHOP OF AUXERRE

[Col. 0588D] THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to GEOFFREY, bishop of Auxerre.

Following your assurance rather than my own judgment, not without trouble to myself and my people, whom I had summoned from various places, I came as far as Pontoise, humbly accepting the opportunity for the hoped-for restoration of peace. There, having received your letters by which it became known to me that I and my people had been deceived, I have been persuaded henceforth not to believe every spirit, and not so readily to afflict further my fellow exiles—the poor and outlawed of Christ—with fruitless journeys and great expenses.

And if you had believed me when I spoke the truth, better provision would have been made for each of us. But now I have become a fool: you know more fully who compelled me and who induced me. Nor do I say this because I am not grateful to you for the care you have bestowed in God’s cause, but so that each of us may conduct business more cautiously in future and remember that words are only words. If, therefore, you hear anything else, do not be surprised. And because I followed your assurance, offering myself to every condition of peace in the Lord, I ask that through you the lord of Cîteaux, who with you has been appointed agent of this reconciliation—or, lest I say deception—may learn how I have been treated and am being treated. It concerns your honour and his that the truth should be known more widely. Farewell.

## LETTER CXII. TO DAVID, ARCHDEACON OF BANGOR

THOMAS, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to DAVID, called archdeacon of the Church of Bangor: greeting, and a salutary opening of the eyes of the heart.

[Col. 0589B] Your mother, the Church of Bangor, has for many years mourned, bereft of her own pastor; and those who ought to have consoled her have become her bitterest enemies amid her distress. You are said to be their forerunner and standard-bearer by those who both groan over the miseries of mother Church and complain that her goods have been turned to the abuses of her sons and daughters; and, what is more intolerable, who assert that the ordering of the Church is lamentably obstructed by your schemes.

Therefore, since we can neither can nor ought any longer to overlook the excesses of such presumption, we command and order you, in virtue of obedience, to come to us—every excuse set aside—within four months after receiving these letters, in accordance with the apostolic mandate, there to obey our admonitions and commands in the Lord. Otherwise, if you neglect this, you are thereafter to be irreparably deprived of ecclesiastical office and benefice; and, if even then you do not repent, to be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. For we must fulfil the apostolic mandate and provide more speedily for the dangers of a Church in shipwreck. May the grace of God preserve you in His good pleasure as one obedient to these admonitions.

## LETTER CXIII. TO THE SAME MAN

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to the archdeacon of Bangor.

[Col. 0589D] We have received the letter of your affection gratefully, and thank you for it. But this may be the chief occasion on which we shall have greater and more abundant thanks to render you, if we hear that you are solicitous concerning the peace of the Church of God and the discipline of the clergy.

Concerning the election of a bishop, we command you and your brethren that no election or nomination of anyone be made until, after seeing our letters and our messenger, you have heard our counsel on this business. For we shall, as the Lord grants, take care by every means to devote effort to the peace of the Church of God and to yours. We have heard that your clergy migrate to foreign provinces for the purpose of ordination. Wishing to know whether this is true, we command you, by the fealty in which you are bound to us, to make us certain about this.

Concerning the bearer of this letter, who has come to you through many dangers, [Col. 0590A] we command and direct you to cause him peacefully to possess his church and his full tithes; to make him immune from the injuries and violence inflicted upon him by Arthur of Chargis on account of the tithes; and to compel Arthur henceforth to cease troubling him. If Arthur should refuse to do so, let him present himself before us, by the Purification of Blessed Mary, to make satisfaction.

## LETTER CXIV. TO THE SAME MAN AND THE CANONS OF BANGOR

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to the archdeacon and canons of Bangor: the greeting they have deserved.

[Col. 0590B] It has been reported to us that you have sinned most grievously and without cause against God, against us, and against the Church of Canterbury, your mother. For, as we have been assured, you unanimously gave your counsel and consent to the schemes of Arthur and his associates, to the injury of the Church of Canterbury, which is your mother. Nor, as we believe, could so detestable a deed, so abominable a crime, have been committed at all unless you had given your counsel and consent in it.

But we address you, David: it ought by no means to have escaped your memory that you are sworn to us, and likewise to the Church of Canterbury. Neither you nor the canons of the Church of Bangor ought to have consented that the bishop of your church—if indeed there was one there—should go to Ireland and there [Col. 0590C] receive consecration, as though from a newly established metropolitan set over him.

Accordingly, commanding you, we direct and enjoin you, under peril of your benefices and order, to present yourself before us in mid-Lent, together with your son and three or four of the greater and more important persons of the Church, to answer and make satisfaction concerning these things and others which will be laid to your charge. Likewise, by this letter we command and direct your entire body, and enjoin you under peril of your benefices and order, to present yourselves before us within the prescribed time. For we shall confer with you concerning the election of your bishop. We also forbid you, by apostolic authority and our own, to do anything in the meantime concerning the election of a bishop or to elect anyone.

## LETTER CXV. TO THE SAME CANONS

Because it is fitting that the Church of God be free, and because, especially in the holding of elections, the unanimity of the brethren—not the violence of power—must prevail, the lord pope has mercifully absolved you from the oath which Owen, prince of the Welsh, is said to have extorted contrary to good morals and the discipline of the sacred canons: namely, that you should elect no one as bishop except at his discretion. The pope commands that you receive as bishop whomever we appoint for you, setting aside every appeal and objection.

Therefore, commanding you [Col. 0591A] in virtue of obedience, we direct your whole community diligently to carry out the apostolic mandate in accordance with what our envoys shall make known to you. Know that, if you neglect it, we shall pronounce, with the Lord as our author, a sentence of anathema against your persons, and a sentence of interdict against the church and places which you inhabit. Farewell.

## LETTER CXVI. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF BATH

To you, most beloved brethren, etc. (See below the similar letter addressed to the clergy and people of Chichester.)

## LETTER CXVII. TO HILARY, BISHOP OF CHICHESTER

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to the bishop of Chichester.
