Because we have endured the lord king of England more than enough, and have derived no fruit whatsoever from our forbearance toward him, it has appeared to us altogether dangerous and intolerable henceforth to leave unpunished, as hitherto, such great excesses of his and his officials—especially since we have striven by envoys, letters, and other means, yet have been unable to recall him from his perverse purpose.

Accordingly, we have publicly condemned and annulled that document in which are contained not customs but rather corrupt practices, by which the English Church is disturbed and thrown into confusion; and we have annulled the authority of the document itself. We have also excommunicated all who observe or exact those practices, and their advisers, helpers, and defenders; and [Col. 0591C] have absolved our bishops from the promise by which they were bound to observe them. We have declared void the authority of the document, the document itself, and the matters contained in it. Especially this: “That it is not permitted to a bishop,” etc. As above (in the letter addressed to the archbishop of Mainz and in others), as far as: “Unless he repents.”

Therefore we command you and direct you in virtue of obedience that you likewise regard and cause to be declared excommunicated, as is fitting, those whom we have excommunicated, in accordance with that decree of Pope Honorius: “Let all bishops take care to communicate the names of excommunicated persons both to neighbouring bishops and to their own parishioners alike, and, having posted them in a public place before the doors of the church, to impress them upon all who come, [Col. 0591D] so that, by both measures of diligence, ecclesiastical entry may everywhere be denied to excommunicated persons and every pretext for excuse may be removed.”

## LETTER CXVIII. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF CHICHESTER

THOMAS, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to the prior and ROBERT, archdeacon, and to the whole clergy and people of the Church of Chichester who hold Christian communion: greeting, and obedience to God rather than men.

It cannot be unknown to you, most beloved brethren, that the atrocity of the crime and its prolonged duration have now filled almost the whole Latin world. Let the proscriptions of the innocent which you have seen and mourned be for the present passed over in silence; let the unheard-of confiscation of the Church’s goods be passed over; let mind and tongue refrain from recounting the atrocity of punishments and the oppression of the poor, matters which cannot be related. Let us rather jointly lament the loss of public liberty and our salvation, we who have kept silence far too long regarding Christ’s manifest injuries and have not, as we ought, publicly destroyed the ruinous precedent.

[Col. 0592A] For grief must be common where Christ, Lord, redeemer, and judge of all, is dishonoured; where the Church’s freedom is destroyed; where public salvation is in danger. Churches bereft of pastors mourn; infants die without the fullness of the sacraments; the consecration of churches and virgins ceases; among many peoples there is no one to receive criminal persons making confession for their consolation; no one publicly absolves penitents for forgiveness; no one rebukes the offences of the erring with due correction; no one can examine and determine major causes; no one promotes those whom the Church requires to be promoted for her needs—unless perhaps some foreign bishop, hired or compelled, contrary to the prohibition of the Lord’s law, puts his sickle into another’s harvest.

Where, however, the greater churches have their bishops and the necessary help of priests has been provided in lesser places, these men are suspended from their offices by edict and violence of the civil power. For [Col. 0592B] persons of greater rank, or anyone holding even the smallest benefice or office from the lord king, are not permitted to exercise pastoral care unless leave has first been obtained.

It is superfluous to demonstrate in words how greatly these things oppose divine institutions and detract from the salvation of all, since the facts themselves are plain even to the slowest, much more to you, whose faculties are trained in the law of the Lord. Deliberately, lest we be burdensome, we pass over many matters. Whoever among the faithful does not notice them is blind; whoever does not grieve lacks the feeling by which one advances toward salvation.

While our lord king was admonished by letters, envoys, bishops, abbots, subdeacons of the curia, and most illustrious cardinals to correct his evil presumptions, a full five years have elapsed in great bitterness for the grieving and languishing Church; and among all those dear to him no one has been found who might obtain relief for her cause before him. What is more to be lamented and wondered at, what we cannot recall or say without heavy grief, is that certain of the more eminent [Col. 0592D] bishops have proved faithless and have furnished the persecutors with weapons of iniquity through their aid, help, and counsel.

If you recall, most beloved, what has been done under this tempest in injury to Christ, in the oppression of the Church, and in the crushing of us and ours, you will rightly, we believe, wonder that we were able to endure all this with so patient a spirit—especially since, as many know, we have long had full power to restrain and coerce our persecutors. Yet their savagery has been such that the men of old acted more mildly toward Christ’s confessors. If you review their ancient histories, you will find that they did not injure relatives and friends unless these were held to be accomplices and marked by public confession.

Therefore, since neither the length [Col. 0593A] of our patience nor the many displays of humility have cooled the anger of the aforesaid our lord, but he has become more obstinate and cruel through impunity, we dare no longer leave his great offences unpunished. For the concealment of guilt is equivalent to consent; and the divine law condemns those who act and those who consent to equal punishment.

Therefore, beloved sons—dean, archdeacons, and those who act in the archdeacons’ stead—we command and direct you, in virtue of obedience, under anathema and under peril of rank and order, by apostolic authority and our own: unless the oft-mentioned lord king, by the Purification of Blessed Mary, corrects the aforementioned enormities through due satisfaction and restores to the Church the peace due to her with freedom and dignity, you are thereafter wholly to cease from the divine offices and, by the same authority and under the same sanction, to forbid their celebration throughout [Col. 0593B] your entire diocese in every church.

The sole exceptions are the baptism of infants, penance, and viaticum, which may be administered behind closed doors, with lay persons excluded, without the ringing of bells and without the solemnity of chant and rejoicing which the Church customarily observes on joyful days. Do not fear those who are sometimes permitted by the Lord physically to afflict the saints for the greater crown of the elect, but who can do nothing against souls; for in this furnace God will plainly judge whom He ought to crown in the world to come.

Those, moreover, who receive churches and ecclesiastical offices or benefices from the hand of laymen contrary to canonical institutions; who compel clerics by penalties or terrors to disobedience; who hinder the envoys of the lord pope and our envoys from pursuing the needs of the Church; who teach that human traditions are to be preferred to the divine law; and who compel the usurpations or abuses of the powerful to be set before the institutions of the Christian religion—we publicly excommunicate; namely, Geoffrey, archdeacon of Canterbury, and his vicar Robert, Richard of Ivelcestre, William Giffard, Nigel of Sacca-Villa, Richard de Lucy, Thomas son of Bernard, and Adam of Cheringis. And if the king of England does not correct his excesses even by the punishment of his subjects, then, reluctantly as we say it, we shall henceforth not spare his person, to the peril of our own salvation, as hitherto, God being our author. For such pity is proved to be impiety, since it is written: “He who spares the rod hates his son.”

By the same authority and under the same penalty, we command that from the day of the Nativity of the Lord you avoid John, dean of Salisbury; Guy, dean of Waltham; John Cumin; Ralph, archdeacon of Llandaff; and Wimar the priest, foster-child of Count Hugh, as excommunicated persons, unless within that time they take care to render due satisfaction to the Church of God, which they have injured, and to us. May the word of God shine in your hearts and deeds, so that, preferring the fear of God to human fear, you may acquire for yourselves the crown of glory and happily transmit to posterity an example of obedience and steadfastness.

In the same form, to the clergy and people of Lincoln.

[Col. 0594A] And to the clergy and people of Bath.

## LETTER CXIX. TO RICHARD, BISHOP OF COVENTRY

THOMAS, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the apostolic see, to his venerable brother RICHARD, bishop of Coventry: greeting.

We had written to you and to our other brethren that you should suspend the publication of the excommunication of those whom we had excommunicated, until it should become known from the envoys of the lord pope, who had come for the restoration of peace to the Church, whether they could obtain it from the lord king according to the form prescribed by the lord pope. But because the lord king does not comply with apostolic commands, and the envoys return with the peace unaccomplished, we command you, under the force of obedience, [Col. 0594B] that you announce the aforesaid persons excommunicated by us—namely Geoffrey, archdeacon of Canterbury, his vicar Robert, Richard of Ivelcestre, William Giffard, John Cumin, Nigel of Saccavilla, Richard de Lucy, Adam of Cheringis, Thomas son of Bernard—as excommunicated, and command that throughout your parish they be avoided by all the faithful, as the censure of the canons prescribes.

Likewise announce as excommunicated those who receive churches, ecclesiastical offices, or benefices from the hand of laymen contrary to the institution of the sacred canons; who hinder the envoys of the lord pope or our envoys from pursuing the needs of the Church; and who compel ecclesiastical persons to celebrate divine offices contrary to obedience owed to their prelates. For the Catholic and Apostolic Church condemns all such persons by a just anathema. Farewell.

## LETTER CXX. TO HUGH, BISHOP OF DURHAM

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to H., bishop of Durham.

Let your brotherhood know that, for just and manifest causes, compelled by the necessity of our office and persuaded by the reason of law, we have publicly excommunicated Gilbert, bishop of London, Jocelin of Salisbury, and the others whose names are written above. We therefore notify you, by the authority of the lord pope and our own, that you are to cause them publicly to be declared throughout your bishopric as persons to be avoided by all the faithful, according to the censure [Col. 0594D] prescribed by the canons. Let not your heart be troubled in these matters, nor be afraid, because, God favouring us, we are protected by the safeguard of the Apostolic See against the evasions of malicious men and the subterfuges of appeals. These are the names of the excommunicated: Ranulf de Broc, etc.

## LETTER CXXI. TO GILES, ELECT OF ÉVREUX

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to GILES, elect of Évreux.

We received the letter of your exhortation with that devotion with which we perceived it to have been written, observing that it proceeded from the richness of charity, was shaped by a spirit of discernment, [Col. 0595A] and in every letter displayed the fear of God. Yet, as you write, the mouths of those who speak wickedly are opened among you with a freedom greater than usual. This was indeed an old complaint among us; but the more numerous host of detractors, and the contrived fictions of slander which we have long endured without cause, have worn our brow more deeply through the constancy of patience. For we recall to mind that all Israel sharpened its tongues against the sons of the prophets, and that every house is a source of bitterness everywhere.

But will priests therefore cast Deuteronomy out of the tabernacle of the Lord, bringing in the altar of Damascus with the profane rites of the nations? Certainly this will not happen without extreme peril to the prophets: that, the Holy Spirit departing from them, they should be compelled to seek the divine will from women. The prelates of the Churches indeed retain their hard task: they cannot please both God and men. And the Apostle, as he testifies of himself, says that if he had pleased men, he would not have become a servant of Christ. Therefore, if under so great a burden you fear and groan, we do not wonder; but the consolation of the Scriptures lightens fear. For it is certain that Bezalel, scarcely ten years old, built at God’s command that tabernacle of more laborious workmanship and more splendid expense, which prefigures the Church surrounded by such diversity; and David was chosen from behind the ewes with young by Him who, laying the foundations of the Church at its birth, chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and raised up the lowly, that they might sit in judgment with the princes and senators of the earth.

Yet we do not doubt that you are noble in blood, [Col. 0595C] so far as worldly glory is concerned; and we trust that your life is illuminated far more brightly by the distinctions of virtue than even by those of letters and eloquence. Would that we could stretch out our hands to your mouth—that is, fulfil in deeds what you exhort us to do. For this we ask to be aided by the support of your prayers, hoping that such good as may be in us may benefit you before God and men, as it benefits us.

We sincerely love the lord king, and shall in all things serve him and his children in the Lord, rendering more faithful service than those who place a cushion beneath every elbow and a pillow beneath every head, fattening it with the oil of the sinner. And the approaching day of the Lord will indeed reveal that this is so. Meanwhile, love us, your devoted friends, as you have been accustomed to do; for, God being our author, our affection for you has neither grown cold nor will grow cold. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXII. TO NIGEL, BISHOP OF ELY, AND RICHARD HIS ARCHDEACON

THOMAS, by the grace of God, etc., to his venerable brother NIGEL, by the same grace bishop of Ely, and to RICHARD his archdeacon: greeting, and prudent direction of foresight toward the future.

The discipline of the sacred canons prescribes that bishops notify their fellow-provincials of the names of those whom they have excommunicated, lest one diseased sheep infect the flock of the faithful. But by the special command of the lord pope, we have bound Count Hugh with the bond of anathema; and we command you to cause the sentence, which proceeded from the decision of the supreme pontiff, to be published in all the churches of your bishopric, as is decreed by canonical ordinances.

Following also the authority of the Apostolic See, which we have before us, we have excommunicated Gilbert of London and Jocelin, bishops of Salisbury, Ranulf de Broc, and the others as above. Therefore, under the force of obedience and at risk to your rank and order, we command you to cause both the aforesaid count and the bishops just named, together with all the others previously named, to be publicly proclaimed excommunicated throughout your entire diocese, and to be avoided by all the faithful as the rigour of ecclesiastical teaching requires. If one of you, through any hindering necessity, cannot carry this out, the other must in every way carry it out, as he loves his honour and office.

But you, son Archdeacon, should take more diligent care in this matter, lest stricter account be demanded of you if, under the pretext of the bishop’s illness, the command of the lord pope and ours is carried out inadequately, or if the Church—which now, as report has it, depends upon your discretion—through your fault incurs ruin or suffers grievous loss. Farewell in the Lord.

## LETTER CXXIII. TO ROBERT, BISHOP OF HEREFORD

THOMAS, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to his venerable brother ROBERT, by the same grace bishop of Hereford: greeting, and the grace to do good in all things.

[Col. 0596C] If our letter has stirred your brotherhood to concern, would that I had not written again to one sluggish in affection, nor found you less watchful with respect to carrying out the office you have undertaken. I chose to be cast off, an anathema for all of you, the reproach of men and the rejection of the people, lest I should see the evils done to the saints and overlook the injury done to our people. I waited to see whether perhaps any among you, zealous for God’s law and at least desiring the Church’s liberty, would come forth after me and follow, so that we might not give horns to sinners.

And behold, you, whom I believed the Lord had given me to build, uproot, and plant with me, offer me a goad toward ruin, comfort toward desolation, preaching humiliation—indeed, degradation—and proclaiming good news when there is disturbance everywhere, to the destruction of the Church and clergy. Whereas you ought to have strengthened the resolve of a wavering mind, joined me in the struggle to defend the patrimony of the Crucified One, to restrain and overcome the Church’s enemies, and instilled into my ears and inspired my mind to entreat more urgently, rebuke more sternly, and reprove more harshly. And if they did not hear me, you certainly ought to have cried out against me: “Arise, why do you sleep? Draw the sword of blessed Peter; avenge the blood of Christ’s servants that has been shed, and the wrongs done all day long to the Church in us and ours.”

Has it slipped from your memory how many injuries I have suffered, by what insults I was afflicted, when Christ was again judged in my person before the prince’s tribunal, against every authority and every form [Col. 0597A] of law? Certainly, I do not call back to mind an injury to my own person, except insofar as it is an injury to the Church. Consider more carefully; lay up more deeply in your heart what was done before my departure, at my departure, afterwards, and what is still done every day in that land against God’s Church and its ministers. With what constancy of mind can you conceal these things—you from whom it was hoped that you would redeem Israel and free the Church from servitude?

And now, because you have been silent so long, I grieve over you, brother, my firstborn son. I fear that another may succeed you who will take away your firstborn rights and remove the blessing of the firstborn—may this be far from you! Nevertheless, although you have been excessively silent until now, take strength again, dearest son. Cry aloud; do not cease. Raise your voice against them; instil fear into them; bring down contrition; exact satisfaction, lest God’s wrath descend upon them and the whole nation perish—or, God forbid, its great men. For divine vengeance is already at the doors.

I write these things to you not to shame you but as a warning, so that, supported by God’s authority and ours, you may henceforth be able and willing to discharge the demands of your office more bravely and effectively. This one thing I wish you to know in sum: by God’s mercy, the humiliation of the Church shall not be extorted from me. Moreover, I thank you because even now you have visited me and strengthened me by your consolation.

What more? There is one thing which I cannot bear without great bitterness of spirit. I weep indeed for our most beloved lord king. Fear and trembling have come upon me, and darkness has covered me, because I see tribulation and anguish threatening my lord the king. Nor is this surprising. For he has shaken the Church of God and troubled it, showing harsh things to his clergy and giving them the wine of error to drink. Therefore the Lord says to him: “Where now are your wise counsellors, who gave you foolish counsel? They said: You are the son of wise men, the son of ancient kings, whose customs must be observed in England. Whoever does not observe them is not Caesar’s friend; he is an enemy of the crown, liable to judgment.” Yet certainly—and this is greater—he is a friend of Christ’s cross.

For woe to those who enact unjust laws and have written oppressions, in order to crush the poor in judgment and do violence to the cause of the humble among God’s people; that the Church and widows [Col. 0597D] may become their prey, and that they may plunder the goods of clerics and others. What will they do on the day of visitation and of calamity coming from afar? To whose aid will they flee, and where will they leave their glory, lest they bow beneath the bond and fall among the slain? Where now are his wise men? Let them come forward, announce to him, and make known what the Lord of hosts has planned against England. His wise men have become foolish, his princes have withered; they have deceived England, the corner of the nations. The Lord has mingled in her midst a spirit of dizziness. They have made England err in its work, as a drunken man errs, vomiting and trembling. And England shall have no work that head or tail can perform, because they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his place. And they said, “Let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance,” reproaching its priests and princes.

[Col. 0598A] “Where will you flee from our hands, or in what do you place your trust? Why have you withdrawn and opposed our commands?” O how empty are these thoughts, how evil these deeds in the sight of the Lord! He sees indeed that they are vain. For he himself will mock one who thinks and acts thus, seeing that his day is near and already at the doors. And it shall be said: “Behold the men who did not make God their helper, but hoped in the multitude of their riches and prevailed in their vanities.” But they act in vain. The Lord will not leave his Church or his clergy without a defender, without most severe vengeance. For it is founded upon the firm rock; and the rock is Christ himself, who founded it with his own blood.

Certainly, unless they amend these things, they shall not bear them unpunished, because they have trampled upon the Holy of Holies—the house of God—afflicting its priests with injuries and insulting words. These are those to whom the Lord himself says: “You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High”; and elsewhere: “He who hates you hates me; he who despises you despises me; he who touches you touches the pupil of my eye.” Let them therefore return to their heart, cast these evils from themselves, and do penance with the utmost humility. Otherwise it is to be feared—may it not be so!—that our Lord may soon come, bringing upon them and their land the sword of recompense and most grievous vengeance. Behold, our Lord will come and will not delay, and he will save us. Indeed, he never forsakes those who hope in him.

For the prophet says: “Hope in the Lord and do good, and you shall be fed upon his riches.” And elsewhere: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully; let your heart be strengthened, and endure the Lord; and you shall soon be delivered from the snares of hunters and from harsh words.” And, to conclude all the rest with its proper end: since the Lord has shown us what and how great things we must suffer for his name and for the defence of the Church, it is necessary that you and the whole Church committed to you pray earnestly for us, so that what we cannot endure by our own merits, we may be enabled to endure through your intercession and that of the holy men under your jurisdiction, and may thereby deserve to attain eternal grace. Farewell, and be strong. May the whole English Church fare well and be strengthened in the Lord, that we too may fare well.

## LETTER CXXIV. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0598D]

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to ROBERT, bishop of Hereford, and ROGER, bishop of Worcester.

Both the reason of law, the sincerity of your faith and honour, and your continual exercise in sacred literature readily persuade us that the assault of no storm can separate your charity from the faith and obedience of the holy Roman Church. Since every soul is bound to that Church by the institution of the Son of God, who founded the Church upon himself as the most solid rock, the order of bishops is bound by a still closer bond. At their consecration bishops make special profession, in word and writing, of observing the divine law and sacred canons, and of obeying the commands of the Apostolic See [Col. 0599A] and those from whom they receive the gift of consecration.

And we do not doubt that we too are bound to the Roman Church on behalf of our fellow provincials, since it gave rise to the election of each of you and, through our ministry, to your consecration. Therefore you ought especially to be subject to our person, not merely to the Apostolic See, from which only an unbeliever, heretic, or schismatic withholds faith and obedience. Accordingly, having the fullest confidence in your faith and obedience, we send apostolic letters to your brotherhood, so that it may become known to you and through you to your other brethren that the lord pope has entrusted his authority to us in the kingdom of England.

We speak to those who know and teach the law, and whom we do not believe belong among those who, holding the law, did not know the Lord; who seek their own salvation, not an evasion of Scripture, which cannot be broken, so that, by assailing faith, they may appear faithful and be accounted learned in law, though, destroying themselves and others, they have destroyed the laws, and may be thought sons of obedience when, under whatever pretext, they can colour their disobedience. But this is in vain. For there is no wisdom and no counsel against the Lord, who has now begun, by the testimony of manifest works, to reveal the counsels of hearts. He continually consoles his little ones and does not permit them to be tempted beyond what they can bear. The earth cries out against the wicked, and the heavens shall reveal their iniquity.

Therefore be comforted, be comforted, beloved ones, says the Lord, because, by his own agency, your deliverance is near. And unless your faith fails, salvation is at our doors and already knocks at the doors of your churches [Col. 0599C] to be admitted. Meanwhile, under the force of obedience and by apostolic authority, we command you to take swift and diligent care that our brethren and your neighbouring fellow-bishops—namely those of Winchester, Bath, Salisbury, Chester, Exeter, and St Davids—may learn through your diligence that the office of legation has been entrusted to us, as is apparent from the letters of the lord pope. But before these letters are shown to them, we command by the same authority that they be shown by you, with our letters, to our brother the bishop of London, so that he may show them both to his fellow provincials and to the bishop of Durham. For danger threatens you—indeed, all the others as well—unless this affair of the lord pope and of the whole Church is conducted more faithfully and diligently.

## LETTER CXXV. TO THE SAME

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to ROBERT, bishop of Hereford.

A complaint has reached our ears that the canons of Bromfield were made monks in the monastery of Gloucester by a certain deception and fraud, and that the possessions and goods of the Church were on this occasion transferred to the aforesaid monastery. Furthermore, a canon of that Church, who had undertaken a journey to come to us and complain to us concerning so outrageous a deed, was, as we have learned, seized and imprisoned. Concerning this matter we command your brotherhood carefully to inquire and investigate the truth of the case together with the bishop of Worcester, and not delay informing us of it by your letters.

We also command you, and under the force of obedience prescribe, that within two months from receipt of this letter, setting aside every excuse and pretext, you undertake the journey to come to us. For we have to deliberate with you concerning great and difficult affairs of the Church, for the dispatch of which we greatly need your presence. Further, let your brotherhood know that we have condemned and annulled that writing in which those heretical perversities are contained, and have declared void what is written in it—especially this: that a bishop may not excommunicate, etc.

## LETTER CXXVI. TO GODFREY, BISHOP OF LLANDAFF

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to GODFREY, bishop of Llandaff.

Apostolic ordinances must be obeyed without contradiction or delay, and the sicknesses and dangers of souls must be remedied with all speed and diligence. Therefore, carrying out the apostolic command, we direct your brotherhood, in accordance with the lord pope’s order, either to return to the Church over which the Lord has set you, or, by resigning it, to yield its care to another who, God being the author, may be able to preside and benefit. [Col. 0600C] Otherwise we shall no longer allow that Church to be deprived of its proper shepherd, but shall proceed with its appointment in accordance with the instructions we have received. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVII. TO THE SAME

Your brotherhood ought not to be ignorant that he deserves to lose a privilege who abuses the power granted him. Yet, as we have learned, in the bishoprics of others, when their churches are vacant, you presume to loose and bind other people’s sheep; and at the petition of laymen or others to whom the dispensation of sacraments does not belong, you dedicate churches and perform other acts for which you have received no authority from the Apostolic See or from your mother Church of Canterbury.

This seems all the more credible because it is certain that formerly, without a special mandate from the Roman pontiff, you absolved, so far as lay in your power, persons excommunicated by us—something wholly impermissible—without observing the tenor of the lord pope’s letters. Whether you did this rightly, your discretion will consider, since you will have to render account concerning it. For those who persist in crime and in the will to sin, who plunder the goods of churches and violently seize them, not even Peter himself could absolve before God.

Therefore, lest henceforth you presume anything similar at anyone’s instigation, we forbid you, under the force of obedience and at risk to your rank and order, further to exercise pastoral care and episcopal office outside your own bishopric; rather, be content with the power [Col. 0601A] which the Church conferred upon you in your ordination. We do not, however, prohibit you, at the request of those of your fellow bishops with whom you may lawfully communicate, from carrying out their functions in lawful matters when necessity demands. But we command you to abstain from the office of vacant churches and of bishops who are excommunicated, and to exercise pastoral care, so far as opportunity permits, within your own bishopric.

## LETTER CXXVIII. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF LINCOLN

To you [lacuna].  
(See the similar letter addressed to the people of Chichester.)

## LETTER CXXVIII*. TO GILBERT OF HEREFORD, LATER OF LONDON

[Col. 0601B] THOMAS, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to his venerable brother G., by the same grace bishop of Hereford: greeting.

How noble and renowned the city of London is above the other cities of this kingdom is unknown to none of us. There, indeed, because of the public business of the realm, the lord king and the magnates of the kingdom customarily hold more frequent assemblies. Therefore, since the Church of London has long been bereft of its shepherd, it desires that such a bishop be appointed for it as may match the city’s eminence by the merit of an honourable life, learning, and prudence in secular affairs.

After great deliberation, the unanimous request of the clergy, the will of the lord king and our own, and also the apostolic ordinance, have agreed upon this: that, for the common benefit of the realm and the need of the Church, you ought to be transferred to the governance of the Church of London and exercise pastoral care and solicitude there. Therefore, having received the lord pope’s command in this matter, we enjoin upon you by his authority that you do not delay giving your assent to the request of the Church of London, which concerning your translation to it was made in the presence of the lord king and ourselves with the unanimous assent of the whole clergy; and that you approach its governance with all the more devotion and promptness because it is known to need the counsel and governance of so great a person.

We urge your brotherhood most earnestly to let the reflection of your own affection invite you even more warmly to that to which the necessity of obedience draws you, so that he whom the affection of sincere love joins to us may, through nearness of place, be able more conveniently to offer himself for our needs and those of God’s Church. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXIX. TO GILBERT OF LONDON

T., by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to his venerable brother GILBERT, formerly by the grace of God bishop of Hereford and now by the same grace bishop of London: greeting.

Do not take it grievously, beloved brother in the Lord, that we have imposed a greater burden upon you and called you to the care of a greater church, trusting that this has been beneficially provided by divine mercy. Your character, your well-known religious devotion, your wisdom given from above, and the good work which you performed in the Church of Hereford have merited this, so that it may be said to you: “Friend, go up higher; you have been faithful over a few things, and deservedly shall be set over many.”

We have not entrusted Peter’s ship to a man untrained and inexperienced in navigation, as you write from humility; but to one who, long practised upon a river, must henceforth steer that same vessel on the deep. The lit lamp, which seemed hidden under a bushel, has now been placed upon a lampstand, that it may shine far and wide in the Lord’s house. The Church of London, to which we have transferred you by God’s agency, adheres more closely than the others to the Church of Canterbury, which is in the kingdom of England as the head is in the body; so that, being near your mother Church of Canterbury, to which [Col. 0602B] you owe all that you can do, you may be able with us to bear burdens.

Moreover, since the lord pope has entrusted to you in particular the care of the soul of our lord king, where is it more fitting that you should sit than in the royal city? There, coming frequently on public business, he may often be instructed by your conversations and strengthened by your counsel. Therefore do not fear to come where your merit calls you, where the Lord commands you, and where you will receive consolation from our aid and help, as is due to a friend and fellow-worker. For we believe that this is a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, flowing from the fountain of divine providence—not only so that the Church of Canterbury may lean more strongly on so great assistance in its affairs, but also that what is incomplete in us, as we see in many respects, may be supplied by your blessedness.

Would that, if it had been possible, you had come to London on the preceding Sunday, so that we might have received your arrival with fitting honour, since we were present there at that time. But now, because our affairs have drawn us away from that place, we have entrusted our functions to our archdeacon, joining to him also the lord bishop of Rochester, if he can be present. May your brotherhood fare well in Christ, most beloved brother.

## LETTER CXXIX*. TO THE SAME

THOMAS, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to his venerable brother GILBERT, by the same grace bishop of London: to glory more in Christ than in the world, and to hope more in the Lord than [Col. 0602D] in worldly embraces.

Although we have long owed you many and lengthy letters, because there is much matter, for the present we choose brevity of expression, that amid these beginnings we may set forth to you in few words what we think. Perhaps we take care to enjoin nothing, or little, upon you on our own behalf; but at this juncture something concerning yourself and for your own sake. We call to your remembrance with what conscience you endured, with what patience of mind you overlooked, the injury done to God in us, to us for God’s sake, and also to you in us, when the Lord Jesus was again being drawn before the prince’s tribunal and being prepared to be crucified again in us.

Did you do so in order to preserve yourself and yours unharmed from the burden of confiscation and the hardship of exile? Certainly Christ did not choose to save himself thus, when he also laid down his life for those whose brother and flesh he is, leaving us an example that we too should do likewise. Nor did the apostles act thus: they did not fear to profess Christ’s faith and name before princes and powers of the age, even at risk to their life and flesh.

We say these things to you from the root of charity, not from any resentment, so that you may at least recall them to mind and, regarding the stain upon your conscience and the fault of your patience—if indeed there can be fault in patience, though, with your leave, we more certainly believe it should be called, in ordinary speech, remission or negligence—you may be more fittingly ashamed before yourself of endurance not a little harmful in example, and may more effectively restore your reputation before God and men by repenting more affectionately of the wrongful act committed through this patience.

For this reason we wish to exhort you: do not regard the world’s glory as though it stood firm; do not love your own possessions too much for yourself, for your own sake, or for your people—possessions which truly ought to be, and indeed are, not yours but Christ’s poor people’s, if the truth is faced—and thus lose both yourself and what is yours, those things called yours in the sense just stated. Do not let flattering present prosperity hide its end from you, only for adversity without end to follow. For the turns of events alternate, and the descent from prosperous success into its opposite is easy. Let not temporal joy cover the eternal grief which it produces, and produce the grief which it covers. Let death not be thought far from you, only to seize you unprepared; and let not life, while it is awaited, abandon one conscious of evil. As it is written: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come, as upon a woman with child, [Col. 0603C] and they shall not escape.”

Believe that we have written these things to you for greater caution, so that, taking account with yourself of past, present, and future things, you may correct your errors in such a way that you rejoice in their correction; and that, rejoicing with you in brotherly charity over your joy, we too may obtain the fruit of joy by feeling it and may feel it by obtaining it. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXX. TO THE SAME

THOMAS, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to GILBERT, by the same grace bishop of London: that, as stated once already, he should so pass through temporal goods as not to lose eternal ones.

It is astonishing and deeply shocking that a prudent man, trained in sacred letters, especially one who displays religious devotion in his bearing, should so manifestly—not to say irreverently—and with the fear of God set aside, turn away from truth, resist justice, and seek, in order to confound all right and wrong, to overthrow the condition of the holy Church which the Most High himself founded. It is Truth who says: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” Therefore he cannot be thought sound-minded who threatens it with ruin: he is like a man attempting to throw down a great mountain by tying a rope around it.

But have I grown hot with anger or hatred, so that, embittered, I am compelled to hurl words of this kind against my brother, colleague, and fellow bishop? Far from it. Rather, I have gathered such conclusions from your letters, which I received as sent to me through your archdeacon. For I could not gather grapes from thorns or figs from thistles. [Col. 0604A] To make clear whether this is so, let us set them forth and bring their contents to light. The end, compared with the beginning, assumes the likeness of a scorpion: the beginning approaches us with flattery, while the end stings us sharply and contrives to impose silence upon us.

For what else is it first to acknowledge the subjection owed to us and promise the obedience joined to that subjection, then, lest you should have to obey, to run to an appeal? Is “yes and no” found with me, as the Apostle says? Nor should it be found with a disciple of the Apostle. The disciples necessarily received from the Lord the power to tread upon serpents and scorpions. For Ezekiel dwells even today among scorpions. Consider also in what sense you said: “We have recourse to the remedy of appeal.”

You call yourself a follower of Christ; in this assertion you are found to be otherwise. For Christ commended to us obedience as an effective—indeed, the most effective—remedy for all our evils, not only in word but by the clearest example, becoming obedient to his Father unto death. And with what face do you call an impediment to obedience its remedy? It should more rightly be called not a remedy but a detriment. And with what confidence do you presume this? Do you hope to have as a defender of disobedience one who has received both office and command to exact vengeance upon every disobedience? It is wrong to hope this of him, and gravely to offend against him.

The first and second rebuff which you have already suffered might have restrained you from such presumption. For first your spoken words and then your letters, composed to persuade, have learned by experience how firmly he stands, how truly he is Peter’s vicar—a man whom you could not move by prayers, gifts, threats, or promises. Yet he must be assailed a third time, that, after his Lord’s example, he may carry off triumph upon the third assault.

[Col. 0604D]

Moreover, that nothing might be lacking to our oppression, you fixed for your appeal a term of almost a year. You had no pity either for our exile or for the labour of the holy Church, the bride of Christ, which he acquired for himself by his own blood. And, to omit these things—though they ought not to be omitted—you ought to have taken thought for him whom you say you favour, our lord the king: so long as he acts thus against us or against Christ’s Church, he will be unable either to undertake wars or to live in peace without danger to his soul. Let us pass to the rest.

You recall that certain things were disturbed at, and as a result of, our departure. Let the authors and counsellors of this disturbance fear lest they themselves also be disturbed. You exalt me with great praises, as though because of the good beginning of my exile. It is indeed the part of a wise man not to neglect his reputation, and of a discerning man to believe no one about himself more than himself. I am accused of injuries, as though inflicted upon our lord the king. But since you name none of them specifically, neither do I know to which I ought to reply. Therefore, since I am accused only superficially, I excuse myself in this matter only superficially. Yet receive meanwhile this answer: I am conscious of no such offence; yet I am not thereby justified. You threaten us concerning the threatening which we have committed against him. [Col. 0605A] What father sees his son going astray and remains silent? Who does not strike with a rod, lest he encounter the sword? A father despairs of the son whom he does not correct by threat or scourge. Far be it from us, however, to think with you that our lord the king is impatient of correction and will fall into apostasy unto destruction. For the planting of the heavenly Father shall not be rooted up.

A most savage storm shakes the ship. I hold the helm, and you summon me to sleep. You heap up and set before our eyes the benefits bestowed upon us by our lord the king, and remind me that from low estate I was advanced to high rank. But, to reply for a while to these things—albeit in my folly—from what low estate do you suppose me to have come? If you look to the time when he appointed me in his service, the archdeaconry of Canterbury, the provostship of Beverley, [Col. 0605B] very many churches, several prebends, and no few other possessions bearing my name at that time, contradict your assertion that I was so insignificant, as you say, in matters of this world. If you look to the stock and forebears of my family, they were citizens of London, living without reproach among their fellow citizens, and by no means of the lowest rank. But if at last, with the darkness of the world removed, we are to be judged by the light of truth, what is more glorious: to be born of people of middling or even low condition, or of the great and honoured men of the world, when the Apostle says: “We surround the less honourable members of our body with more abundant honour”?

“What do pedigrees accomplish?” says the pagan poet. What ought a Christian, [Col. 0605C] a bishop, a learned and religious man, to say? But perhaps, by recalling my humble estate, you wished to cast upon me a mark of disgrace. Yet how great a guilt it is to shame one’s father, you may see yourself from the commandment which you received concerning honouring one’s father.

As for the king’s favour, which you recommend to us by recalling his benefits, there was no great need to labour over such a reminder. For I call God as witness that I place nothing under the sun before his favour and welfare—provided only that what belongs to God and to the holy Church remains safe. For otherwise he cannot reign happily or securely. Let it be so: his benefits toward me are far more numerous and even greater than your discourse can recount. Ought I, for all of them—even if they were increased a hundredfold—[Col. 0605D] to expose the liberty of God’s Church? Much less ought I to do so for the preservation of my reputation, which has more than once departed from the truth. If I have done too little in other matters, in this I spare neither you nor anyone else, nor even an angel if he should descend from heaven; but as soon as I hear one giving such counsel, he shall hear from me: “Get behind me, Satan; you do not savour the things that are God’s.” Far from me be such madness. May God avert from me this madness: that by any evasions I should be persuaded to enter into a bargain over Christ’s body, by which I should be likened to Judas the seller and my Lord to the Jews, the purchasers of Christ.

Concerning my promotion, which you write was effected while the mother of our lord the king discouraged it, the realm protested, and the Church, so far as it could, groaned, I reply to you this: [Col. 0606A] we heard not the realm’s protest, but rather its acclamation. As for the opposition of our lord’s mother, if there was any, it never came into public view. It may have happened that some ecclesiastical persons, as is customary, aspiring to the same promotion, groaned when they found themselves disappointed of the hope they had conceived; perhaps even today, in revenge for their disappointment, they are the authors and counsellors of the present dissension. But woe to him through whom scandal comes. Yet over the aforesaid obstacles—and any others that there may have been—divine providence prevailed, as may be seen today. I am therefore required by justice itself, which is God, to put no one whatever before him who, in his mercy, set me in this rank.

[Col. 0606B]

Nor did I judge it right to pass lightly over, or without examination, that which you seem to have advanced in justification of the lord king. Would that he did not depart from justice, and that our complaint against him appeared less just! You say that he has always been ready to make satisfaction. You say this confidently; you assert that you preach it. Endure then a little, and answer what is asked. In what sense do you understand the phrase which you use, “ready to make satisfaction”? You see those of whom God calls himself Father and Judge—orphaned children, wards, widows, innocents, and indeed persons wholly unaware of the dispute that moves us—proscribed, and you are silent; clerics driven out, and you do not protest; others despoiled of their goods and subjected to insults, and you do not object; my servants cast into chains and held there, and you are mute; the goods of your mother, the Church of Canterbury, [Col. 0606C] plundered, and you do not resist; me, your father, scarcely escaping swords now hanging over my neck, and you do not grieve. But what is worse, you are not ashamed to stand openly with my persecutors against me, against God, and against his Church. Is this to make satisfaction: not to redress evils committed, and day by day to add worse evils to evil? But perhaps you understand it in the contrary sense: that making satisfaction means serving the will of the ungodly, according to the saying, “I will make my arrows drunk with blood.”

But you say to me: “My father, I clear myself briefly of the charges you bring against me. I fear for my coat.” It is true, my son, and all too true, what you answer. And therefore you do not have the sword. For what you write—that he is prepared to stand judgment before his own realm—as though this were adequate satisfaction: [Col. 0606D] who on earth, or even in heaven, would presume to judge a divine ordinance? Human matters are judged; divine matters are left altogether unassailed. How much better, my brother, and more salutary for him, safer for you, if you impressed upon him and strove by every means to persuade him of God’s will: that the peace of his Church be preserved; that he not seek things not granted to his administration; that God’s priests be honoured—without considering who they are, but whose servants they are.

You accuse me of abusing my authority to the prejudice of the bishop of Salisbury and John of Oxford—not a dean, as you say, but an invader of a deanery. But you should have remembered that certain plain facts precede judgment. And you say that you are moved. Why should you not be?

“Lucca trembles when the neighbouring wall burns.” [Col. 0607A] And would that you were rightly moved by that in which you have not acted rightly! Let then our lord know and understand, at your prompting, that he who rules in the kingdom of men and also of angels has established beneath himself two powers: princes and priests. One is earthly, the other spiritual; one serves, the other presides; to one he granted power, to the other he willed reverence to be shown. Whoever subtracts from the right of either these or those resists God’s ordinance. Let not our lord therefore disdain to defer to those to whom the highest Lord of all does not disdain to defer, calling them gods repeatedly in the sacred Scriptures. Thus he says: “I said: You are gods,” etc.; and: “I have made you a god to Pharaoh”; and: “You shall not speak evil of the gods,” that is, of priests. And, speaking through Moses of the man who was to swear an oath, he says: [Col. 0607B] “Bring him before the gods,” that is, before the priests. Nor should our lord presume to wish to judge his judges. For the keys of the kingdom of heaven have not been entrusted to earthly powers, but to the priesthood. Hence it is written: “The lips of the priest shall preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.” Paul also says: “Do we not judge angels? How much more, men?”

Let this too, at your suggestion, be recalled to our lord: it is worthy of remembrance and imitation, what is read in Ecclesiastical History concerning Emperor Constantine. When written charges against bishops had been presented to him, he accepted the bills of accusation; then, summoning the accusers, he burned those same bills in their presence, saying: “You are gods established by the true God. Go and settle your causes among yourselves. For it is not fitting that we men should judge gods.” [Col. 0607C] O great emperor! O ruler who governed discerningly on earth! Not usurping what belonged to others, and meriting an eternal kingdom in heaven. Let the lord king therefore strive to imitate so great, so discerning, so fortunate a prince, whose praiseworthy memory is celebrated on earth and whose life is everlasting and glorious in heaven. Otherwise let him fear what the Lord threatened in Deuteronomy: “Any man who acts presumptuously, refusing to hear the priest or the judge, shall die.” For he was called to this, and for this purpose the peace and magnificence of the temporal kingdom—of which you remind us—are supplied to him from heaven. Otherwise the king is not saved [Col. 0607D] by his great strength, even though kingdoms be subjected to him and nations bow down.

But enough of this. Whoever the writers of the aforesaid letter may have been, let them know that what has been answered to you has been answered to them. For the future, brethren, I admonish, entreat, and beseech you: do not let schisms divide you or quarrels cloud you; rather, let there be among you one heart and one soul in the Lord. And let us hear him who says: “Strive for justice for your soul, and contend unto death for justice; and God will fight your enemies for you.” Let us not forget that strict Judge, before whose tribunal, when we stand, truth alone will judge us, every fear of and confidence in earthly power being removed. May your holiness prosper in the Lord.

## LETTER CXXXI. TO THE SAME GILBERT AND THE OTHER BISHOPS OF ENGLAND

[Col. 0608A]

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to GILBERT of London and all the bishops of England.

We send you the letters of the lord pope, in which, under threat of anathema, he commands that everything taken from our clerics be restored to them in full, whatever persons may hold it by the king’s order. Therefore, under the same threat, by apostolic authority we command you, directing you, that within two months after receiving these letters you cause whatever you have received from this source to be restored to us, lest what the lord pope threatens [Col. 0608B] come upon you. We also command that you similarly compel your parishioners who have taken or received their revenues or goods to make restitution.

## LETTER CXXXII. TO THE SAME

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to GILBERT, Bishop of London.

We remember that, in accordance with the constitution of the holy Fathers, we notified you of those whom we excommunicated because of injuries inflicted upon the holy Roman Church, the Church of Canterbury, and other churches in the kingdom of England; and that, by virtue of obedience, we commanded you to cause them to be avoided throughout your bishopric as [Col. 0608C] excommunicated persons, and to notify your brethren and fellow bishops of this. If you have faithfully fulfilled this duty of obedience, as you ought, for the honour of God and the Roman Church, for the benefit of the Churches, and for your own salvation, we rejoice with your charity in the Lord. But if not, we grieve—not so much for injury to ourselves as for the injury to the lord pope, the apostolic see, and yourselves. May God, to his honour and to our good, avert this harm. For although the hand and indignation of the supreme pontiff may seem relaxed and slow to many, it is nevertheless effectual and severe, and when merits demand it is accustomed sometimes to inflict a wound that cannot be healed. For there is none under the sun who can snatch anything from his hand. [Col. 0608D] Only the unbeliever, or the heretic surpassing him in error, or the schismatic, maligns obedience to apostolic commands. We speak of the law to one who knows it, and who publicly teaches that obedience is to be preferred above all sacrifices, so that a wise man—and especially one raised in religion and worn by religious exercises—need not be instructed what affections of the virtues, or what virtues of the affections, accompany obedience. One may contrive fraud against his own soul, but the word of God cannot be defrauded of the truth which it possesses substantially, when it says: “Woe to those who justify the ungodly, call evil good, and make darkness light.” And now indeed it says “Woe” to them; but shortly it will bring upon them a most bitter woe, punishing the powerful mightily and exercising the harshest judgment upon those [Col. 0609A] who rule without profit and refuse to announce his ungodliness to the ungodly. But God will then happily crown in triumph those who have faithfully obeyed, and meanwhile consoles them in many ways as they contend against injustice.

We therefore ask and beseech you in the Lord Jesus: since evils against the Church are multiplied upon the earth and, our sins demanding it, have grown exceedingly strong, rise to the aid of God’s Church and draw the sword of the word entrusted to you, in the power of the Holy Spirit, for vengeance upon evildoers and comfort for the good, lest you also bear it without cause. Those whom you see more sluggish or lukewarm in doing justice, raise up and encourage; and understand that Christ spoke to you at the moment of his Passion, since he is again crucified by the ungodly: “And [Col. 0609B] you, once converted, strengthen your brethren.” You shall have us as helpers and leaders in the liberation of the Church; and in matters which we know pertain to God’s honour we shall fail you in nothing, insofar as divine mercy supplies us strength. The lord pope too will gladly provide the assistance due; and he has already entrusted to us his authority in the kingdom of England, that we may oppose iniquity more effectively, as you can perceive from his letters which we send you. Therefore we command your brotherhood, both by virtue of obedience and at peril of your order, by apostolic authority, to show them promptly and diligently to your brother and fellow-provincial bishops and to the bishop of Durham, and afterward [Col. 0609C] cause those letters to be returned to us. By the same authority and under the same threat we order you to show due honour to the bearers of these letters, who are known to transact the lord pope’s business, and to provide for their safety as you wish provision to be made for your own honour.

## LETTER CXXXIII. TO THE SAME

THOMAS, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to GILBERT, Bishop of London—would that he were indeed a brother—may you turn away from evil and do good.

We endured your excesses while it was possible; and [Col. 0609D] would that the gentleness of our patience, which has proved harmful to us beyond measure, may not result in the ruin of the whole Church! But because you have always abused our patience, and have been unwilling to hear either the lord pope or us in the word of your salvation, while your hardness has continually grown worse, necessity of office pressing us and the reasoning of law persuading us, we have for just and manifest causes struck you with the sentence of anathema, excommunicated you, and cut you off from Christ’s body, which is the Church, until you make fitting satisfaction. Therefore, by virtue of obedience and at peril of salvation, dignity, and order, we command that, as the rule of the Church prescribes, you abstain from all communion of the faithful, lest your participation contaminate to destruction [Col. 0610A] the Lord’s flock which ought to have been instructed to life by your teaching and shaped by your example.

## LETTER CXXXIV. TO THE SAME

THOMAS, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to GILBERT, Bishop of London—would that he were indeed a brother—may you turn away from evil and do good.

Your prudence ought to have remembered with what affection your mother, the Church of Canterbury, always loved you; with what diligence she strove to win for you the favour of the Apostolic See; how she always watched over your honour and advantage as if they were her own salvation. But, once you received the means of doing harm, you raised your heel against both; and you injured them, like [Col. 0610B] a nail in the eye and an arrow in the side, all the more ruinously because the impiety hidden under a covering of religion was less guarded against, and perfidy attacked the profession of faith more deceptively and fraudulently. We often warned you; and would that your heart had not swelled up or hardened against the words of more salutary counsel and exhortation. The supreme pontiff wrote to you to devote diligence to restoring peace between the Church and the king; but, as is publicly known, through you a fiercer disturbance has been stirred up against the Church. Indeed, many great things had preceded which called for your condemnation, had not the Apostolic See borne with your brotherhood in great gentleness. Although we were most grievously injured, we concealed your plots against the Church and against us as long as we could, so that all who think rightly and possess zeal for the law may judge that our patience has exceeded its measure. But because your latest acts have always been found worse than the earlier, and we could no longer conceal them, we have, for just and manifest causes, struck you with the sentence of anathema and cut you off from Christ’s body, which is the Church, as a limb of putrefaction, until you make fitting satisfaction. Therefore, by virtue of obedience, at peril of salvation, dignity, and order, we command that, as the rule of the Church prescribes, you abstain from all communion of the faithful, lest your participation contaminate to destruction the Lord’s flock, which was to be instructed to life by your teaching and shaped by your example. [Col. 0610D]

## LETTER CXXXV. TO THE SAME

THOMAS, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to GILBERT, Bishop of London—would that he were indeed a brother—repent of evil and obey God rather than men.

Although your efforts, by which you have deliberately sought with all your power until now the ruin of the Church and of ourselves, have deserved exclusion from the communion of the faithful and even from the exchange of greeting, nevertheless we set before you, with the anxious charity required by our office, those things which we unquestionably believe concern your salvation—a salvation which, God being witness, we desire. We recall to your mind [Col. 0611A] that those who inhabit the land of the south are instructed to meet even a fugitive with bread; and that Christ, who is shepherd and model of shepherds, came not for the righteous but to restore sinners through repentance. As he never rejects true repentance, so he always abhors and condemns feigned repentance, examining both by contrition of heart and convicting them by their works. For a tree is known by its fruit, and each person’s works bear witness concerning him. Therefore, as we could neither pass over nor ought to have passed over your disobedience and contumacy unpunished any longer—passing over other matters for the present—so we shall receive with the readiest charity your conversion and fruits of obedience worthy of it, remembering no longer anything that you have committed against us, [Col. 0611B] if your sincere repentance and fitting satisfaction are established. Calling you back to this with fatherly affection, we warn and exhort you in the Lord to set your heart upon your ways and henceforth do works worthy of a bishop, lest we be compelled, in carrying out punishment for your contumacy, to proceed further.

Moreover, by virtue of obedience and at peril of your rank and order, we command you to send us without delay the lord pope’s letters concerning our legation, which we sent you to communicate through yourself to our brethren and fellow bishops. If you communicated them as you ought, you did well. But if not, know without doubt that we shall demand an even stricter account of their suppression. May divine mercy grant you a repentant heart. If [Col. 0611C] you come to your senses and hasten to make satisfaction, may God spare you and turn you swiftly.

## LETTER CXXXVI. TO THE SAME

THOMAS, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to the venerable man GILBERT, Bishop of London: may you walk faithfully before his face.

You knew the calamities of your mother, the holy Church of Canterbury, all the more fully because from the beginning you viewed them more closely and plainly, present in body—would that you had not been absent in spirit. We have now waited through almost the whole course of six years for the lord king’s repentance; but he has, as we say with grief, so continually abused the mercy [Col. 0611D] of God and the patience of the holy Roman Church that his latest acts have daily become worse than the earlier ones. Therefore, lest through excessive dissimulation the blood both of him and of the perishing Church be required of us at the strict judgment, we command you, the authority of the lord pope leading the way, by virtue of obedience and at peril of order, honour, and benefice, that within fifteen days of receiving this letter you forbid throughout your entire bishopric the celebration of all divine offices, except baptism of infants and penances of the dying; and that you cause the sentence of interdict, as far as lies in your power, to be observed inviolably by all your subjects. And you are to communicate the lord pope’s letters which we send you to your brethren and fellow bishops and to the chapters of vacant churches, [Col. 0612A] and not delay in returning them to us once they have inspected them, providing also for the bearer of this letter as you wish provision to be made for yourselves and your order. Unless you faithfully fulfil these directions, know that a sentence of eternal damnation hangs irrevocably over you.

In the same manner to the Bishop of Salisbury.

## LETTER CXXXVII. TO THE CLERGY OF LONDON

THOMAS, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to the dean, archdeacon, and clergy of London: greetings, and faithfully abstain from communion with the excommunicated.

Your prudence ought not to be unaware that nearly [Col. 0612B] the whole Latin world has learned how unjustly Gilbert, Bishop of London—our brother, would that he were a true one—took advantage of the opportunity supplied by the general schism in dealing with the cause of the Church and endeavoured to disturb its peace. For we have borne with him until now in great patience, which he has always abused; by continual transgressions he has heaped up, beyond correction, the ever-growing crime of disobedience. We therefore, since we could not dissemble, publicly excommunicated him, necessity of office pressing and the reasoning of law persuading us; and we command you, by virtue of obedience and at peril of order and salvation, to abstain entirely from his communion, as is fitting for Christ’s faithful. Under the same threat we likewise command that those whose names are written below be avoided. By a similar [Col. 0612C] sentence, with God’s help, we shall condemn on the day of the Lord’s Ascension those solemnly cited by us, unless in the meantime they make satisfaction: namely Geoffrey, Archdeacon of Canterbury, and Robert his vicar; Richard of Ilchester; Richard de Lucy; William Giffard; Adam de Chere; those who, by aid or counsel of the lord king, by his command, or by their own rashness, have occupied the goods of ourselves or of our clerics; those known to have incited the king, by aid or counsel, against the liberty of the Church, the proscription of innocents, and devastation; and those who hinder the lord pope’s envoys and ours from pursuing the Church’s necessities. Let not your heart be troubled or afraid in these matters, because by God’s favour we are protected by the defence of the Apostolic See against both the evasions [Col. 0612D] of the malicious and the subterfuges of appeals. These are the names of the excommunicated: Jocelin, Bishop of Salisbury; Count Hugh; Ralph de Broc; Thomas son of Bernard; Robert de Broc, clerk; Hugh of St Clair; Letard, clerk of Norfolk; Nigel de Sacca-Villa; Richard, brother of William de Hastinga, who also occupied our church at Manech. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXVIII. TO STEPHEN, BISHOP OF MEAUX

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to the Bishop of Meaux.

With the prophet I might rightly say: “Woe is me, because [Col. 0613A] I have been silent!” For I did not disclose the distress of my wound and pain to him who, more than others, has been accustomed to provide medicine and the remedies of necessary consolation to me and my fellow exiles, Christ’s proscribed people, in the kingdom of France. But a reasonable mistake excuses the fault of such silence: your return was expected and hoped for daily by your friends. Yet I believe it happened by divine direction that both the necessity of the cause and the will of the holy Roman Church compelled you to remain so long, so that, through long association and the familiarity thereby contracted, your virtue might shine more clearly and might thereafter help more effectively with the Apostolic Majesty those in need, of whom I am the first. Already the wretched English Church has experienced the aid of your compassion in many necessities; and, [Col. 0613B] for which it thanks you, all who return report that you show in our affairs a solicitude such as you would exercise in your own—or perhaps even greater. Therefore Christ’s little ones flee to you more confidently with all the devotion they can, and the holy Church of Canterbury casts itself at your feet, asking that by the assistance of your intercessions you rescue it and all its neighbouring churches from the snare of death which our persecutor lays under the cover of an honourable peace.

For, at Lord Gratian’s urging, he has come so far as to admit now, for love of and at the request of the lord pope, what he rejected last year: namely, that God’s honour shall be preserved. But immediately he added: “Subject to the preservation of his dignities.” Under the name of these dignities [Col. 0613C] he intends to maintain customs long ago condemned and destined to be condemned for ever. For this is the prince’s view, as I understand it: that God’s honour flourishes only if it does not resist the dignities which he claims; otherwise those dignities are to prevail. Gratian, however, proposed that he should enjoy the liberties of the kingdom with the Church’s liberty preserved; but at the term “the Church’s liberty,” unheard by him before among the stated conditions, the pious king of France became greatly enraged and could scarcely endure the phrase. His people maintain that no restitution of what has been taken should be made to the Church, because their predecessors, as they falsely claim, never restored anything to archbishops and bishops, whom they very often expelled for the same cause. Yet restitution must be sought, and will be sought, from us all the more steadfastly because evil examples [Col. 0613D] gain strength more quickly; and, with God’s help, insofar as we can, we shall avoid transmitting to posterity and perpetuating the destruction of so great an enormity and crime.

The same king strives to overthrow the form of fealty which clerics customarily make to princes, refusing to admit in the final clause binding himself that the order shall be preserved, but only God’s honour. For, as they say, he has been persuaded by his grammarians, whom he has enlisted to injure the Church, that God’s honour will not be diminished if clerics are not permitted everywhere to appeal and pursue appeals; if bishops or others summoned do not attend each summons of the lord pope or his legates—although they are bound to do so by the necessity of their office. We therefore beseech your holiness to persuade the lord pope not to admit any peace to the detriment [Col. 0614A] of ecclesiastical liberty; not to compel us to desist from demanding restitution of our losses; and not to allow the well-established form of fealty to be altered by our example. For what he obtains once, especially by authority of the Roman Church, he will wish to be perpetual for himself and his children.

Moreover, if it please you, support and receive the bearers of this letter, Master Godfrey and Master Walter, envoys of our venerable brother the Archbishop of Trondheim, with the same kindness with which your charity has been accustomed to receive us and ours. May your holiness always prosper, and deign to communicate these anxieties of mind to the lord Bishop of Ostia and the lord Hyacinth.

## LETTER CXXXIX. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0614B]

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to STEPHEN, Bishop of Meaux: greetings, and the little that the devotion of an exile and proscribed man can offer.

For the consolation which you have always shown to us and ours, we are unable to render to your love the thanks which are due. But Christ will render them—he for whose honour we suffer persecution. And we, if ever we are able to do anything, stand ready, as is most just, for service to you and yours. By God’s favour, who always makes the justice of his Church manifest, we shall be able to do so; and now, as you may hear from the venerable Father the Archbishop of Sens and from Master Peter, Archdeacon of Chartres, he has most plainly [Col. 0614C] exposed the malice and hardness of the king of England. May God reward Gratian, the son of grace, according to his faith and according to the sincerity with which he handled the Church’s cause. For neither respect of persons nor gifts had any power with him; rather, he acted everywhere faithfully and wisely for the honour of God and the Roman Church. If it please you, give him thanks and carefully hear from him the merits of the parties.

We send our envoys to the mercy of your serenity. If it please you, hear them in Christ’s cause as you would hear ourselves, and work so that the lord pope may more swiftly console our misery to God’s glory and his own honour. We pray earnestly, with all the devotion that a wretched sinner can offer, that God may make your journey prosperous [Col. 0614D] and grant you happy success in the things you desire.

## LETTER CXL. TO THE BISHOP OF NEVERS

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to the Bishop of Nevers, under another’s name because of snares.

May the Lord direct your steps, so that in the cause of the Church, the execution of which has been entrusted to you in part, you turn neither to the right nor to the left, but walk upon the royal road; so that neither entreaties, nor threats, nor elaborate deceits may prevail against your prudence and integrity; no one who has had dealings with him has ever escaped his snares. And, unless I am mistaken, you will have to fight with beasts, since he will bring forward bishops, abbots, and discerning men, in order through them to assault your constancy, if he perceives that he cannot ensnare you with promises and flattering speech. Since it is not easy to detect the many disguises of that monster, whatever he says, whatever guise he assumes, let both he himself and all that belongs to him be suspect to you, and be considered full of deceit, except where the proof of an evident act establishes their good faith.

But if he perceives that he can corrupt you by promises or frighten you by threats, so as to gain something contrary to your honour and the unimpaired state of the cause, your authority will immediately vanish altogether in his eyes, and you will become an object of contempt, mockery, and derision both to him and to his followers. But if he sees that he cannot bend you from your purpose, at first he will feign rage, swear and forswear, imitate Proteus, and at last return to himself; and, unless he is prevented by you, thenceforth you will always be a Pharaoh to God. Among the other qualities for which he is known to friends and neighbours, he especially prides himself on being an examiner of character, a plotter against good men, a deceiver and mocker; so that, if perhaps some rather incautious word slips from anyone, he immediately produces witnesses and, as though under the pretext of an injury done to himself or of another’s error, prepares an escape, so that he may seem to withdraw with justification.

When you meet with him, therefore, moderation must be employed in everything, and much speaking must be avoided. Let the articles of the case be gathered briefly, and insist more carefully that he answer the matters proposed, since by habit he is troublesome and perverse. Above all, delays must be avoided—delays which he has always been accustomed to introduce and which, because of the urgency of the apostolic mandate, you cannot admit. Nor is it expedient that our counsel become known to anyone, for they are scorpions who wear the face of friends.

The most suitable opening seems to be from the letters which the lord pope sent them. In these he states that it had been represented to him by the king’s letters and messengers that the king had granted the Archbishop of Canterbury leave to return to his church in complete security, and that all his people might return to their own homes, having all their possessions as fully as they had held them when they were in the king’s favour.

The second article is that he should receive the same archbishop with the kiss of peace. This is the solemn form among every people and every religion, and without it peace between persons previously at variance is nowhere confirmed. Nor would the archbishop appear to have received peace from the king by the kiss of the king’s son’s deputy, so much as to have returned into the favour of the king’s son. If that expression were once heard among the crowd, it is evident how easy an opportunity would be given for maligning the peace which had been made. And if anything untoward—God forbid—happened to the archbishop, the king would, under the pretext that the kiss had been refused, be thought exempt from disgrace.

Let Robert of Silliac and the others come to mind, who made peace with him through the hand of the Most Christian King. If neither a kiss publicly given nor the respect due to so great a mediator conferred upon them a true peace, you will not wonder why the aforesaid archbishop demands the solemn guarantee of a public religious act.

If the king refuses to acquiesce in any of the aforesaid articles, then, if you wish the cause to succeed for you, take leave immediately; and unless, in obedience to the lord pope’s mandate, he recalls you, do not delay to return promptly.
