But if he acquiesces, specify the names of the possessions, as they are set out for you in the written schedule; and do not admit his deceits and fictions by which he will try to despoil the Church of its goods. For while he takes away a foot’s breadth, he cannot make peace with the archbishop. For he would rather remain an outlaw forever than, with his consent, see the Church outlawed even in the smallest matter. But if he should refuse this also and you accept the offered opportunity of returning, [lacuna]

The third article of the same letters is that he should immediately restore the thousand marks promised to the archbishop through Vivian, so that he may have the means to provide what is necessary for himself and his household. If he denies that he promised them, remind him that the Bishop of Séez likewise promised them at Montmartre, and that he would in no way exceed the limits of his commission. If he stubbornly refuses to repay this money, let him find your brow harder than his own, worn though it is exceedingly hard. And before you abandon this article, press for your return with such urgency that everyone may unquestionably believe that you will cross the sea.

If, however, it finally becomes clear that he cannot by any means be overcome, then, as though yielding to the king, defer this request—but by no means remit the money—and accept the form of peace which was set out in the preceding articles. For you know from the letters which the lord pope sent you that you have no authority to remit the money. Even after peace has been made, you are bound to summon him concerning the complete restoration of what has been taken away and the abolition of evil customs. For, as is expressed in the letters sent to the king, the lord pope sent you to carry out the peace, so that through you the condition of the Church may be improved and neither the archbishop nor his people may suffer any injury. You have no authority in this matter.

The fourth article concerns the absolution of the excommunicated, in which a twofold precaution is necessary for you. First, you must on no account do this unless you have received a certain hope of peace and reconciliation. Second, you must absolve no one except after a solemn and public oath has been made, in accordance with the apostolic mandate. For you cannot otherwise absolve them.

But how will you conceive a certain hope from a slippery man whose words and oaths have the same force and must be weighed in the same balance? It would indeed be difficult; yet, if he could be induced to make several of the magnates of the realm, or at least one of them, swear at his command that the king would faithfully carry out the form of peace without evil design, and if they became sureties, then some image of certainty might for the time being be believed. Nevertheless, if he cannot be persuaded to have these assurances given, require that, in open letters authenticated by his seal, he write this to the archbishop and likewise to the others; in the same manner to the lord pope; and to you also, as a third recipient, lest you seem to have omitted anything arising from the circumstances and to have been too readily certain of the promise of a man whom one can scarcely ever trust without danger. Moreover, let him deliver to you the possessions of the Church, his retainers having been removed and the archbishop’s officials installed through you.

For although these are not sufficiently certain signs of secure peace—since he is accustomed readily to act contrary to his own written instruments and might eject the archbishop’s officials with the same violence as usual—nevertheless, because they involve the hope of a firmer obligation, they appear in some fashion to promise a certain hope. And, if they are obtained, they will excuse your diligence from the fault of rashness, whatever may thereafter occur.

But if the king refuses to make these arrangements, namely written attestation and surrender of the possessions, it follows that you ought not to conceive a certain hope or proceed to the absolution of the excommunicated. For even if they had been absolved, you are bound by the apostolic mandate to restore them to their former sentence if peace—God forbid—does not follow.

And if we know the man rightly, he will begin with the absolution of these persons and will say that he will hear no one and do nothing good until his household retainers are absolved. Once he obtains this, perhaps he will feign moderation, promise great things, and, as if under the guise of religion, in order to be thought more innocent, confess sins and disclose certain stains of conscience which he can immediately wash away with borrowed or fictitious virtues. But once he has gained his object, he will put on his inveterate hardness; and he who prayed humbly will thereafter be incapable of being moved by any human appeal.

Let Gratian and Vivian persuade you that these things are so. He bound himself to them by a bodily oath that he would follow their counsel concerning the making of peace with the archbishop if they absolved the excommunicated. Once they had absolved them, he recoiled from everything he had promised as though he had not exchanged a word with them. Therefore those who had been absolved were restored to their former excommunication, and this with all the greater justice because they had striven by every means wickedly to hinder the peace in hope of which they had been absolved.

Take care, therefore, not to rush into absolution unless you are certain that peace will follow. And when you make it—if indeed you are to make it—receive from those to be absolved the oath prescribed to you, declaring to them that, unless they fulfil by subsequent acts the assurance they have given, they will be restored to the former sentence of excommunication, all excuse and appeal set aside. Meanwhile avoid their communion most carefully, lest you give scandal to the weak, cause your ministry to be reproached, encourage the wicked to despise ecclesiastical discipline, and bring no small loss upon God’s cause.

If the king should demand that the archbishop return to his land in order to receive in person his possessions and the kiss of peace, arrange that what can be done in his absence be done: that the ministers of the Church receive his houses and possessions, so that they may prepare necessities for his return. And arrange that some of the magnates of the land—something I do not doubt certain bishops would willingly do—come to the archbishop by the king’s command, to provide him with safe-conduct and security, so that reconciliation between them, according to the form previously established by you, may be completed without hindrance.

Otherwise, unless the cause has been examined and security received, the archbishop will enter into no conference with him. And if, contrary to what should be believed of your prudence and constancy, the king deceives or compels you to exceed the apostolic mandate to the injury of the Church or of Christ’s exiles, let it be most certainly known to you that the archbishop will ratify none of the things you may thus have done, nor will he assent against his conscience to the counsel of any mortal.

You may on no account absolve Count Hugh, because he has nothing to do with this cause. Furthermore, beware lest he prolong you by delays beyond the lord pope’s mandate, for you have no business here. When you are to cross the sea, do not take with you the original letters which you received, but copies; for he has laid ambushes and most serious spies upon the shore, who are accustomed to seize letters of this kind. For you received the originals, and the lord pope informed the king that he was going to send you. You are neither bound, nor is it expedient, to let the king learn so soon everything entrusted to you.

And because it is uncertain whether, through fear of the impending sentence, he will soon devise some obstacle to prevent your return, it is necessary—if you please, and if you wish, as you ought, to provide for the cause—that you write to the bishops on this side of the sea, following the tenor of the lord pope’s letters, commanding them to forbid divine services throughout their dioceses once the term granted to the king has expired. Entrust the same letters of yours to the lord of Sens, who, when circumstances require, will arrange for your command to be published in the churches. This too may carry great weight with the king, if he is persuaded that the bishops on this side of the sea are bound, whatever happens to you, to carry out the apostolic mandate.

Certainly, whenever you must deal with the aforesaid king on any matter, let the brethren of the Temple and of the Hospital of Jerusalem, the cardinals and the lord pope’s messengers, the Carthusians and Grandmontines, the Cistercians and the bishops of his land come back to your mind. In their various dealings with all these persons, while accomplishing in whatever way his own malicious will, he caused them to be marked with infamy, though they had often not deserved it.

If he asks whether he will possess lasting peace concerning the goods taken away and the injuries inflicted, should he recall the archbishop as has been said, tell him that neither you nor anyone else can absolve him without repentance, or enable him to merit forgiveness. For in the Gospel according to Luke the Lord says: “Take heed to yourselves. If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. And if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turns again to you, saying, ‘I repent,’ forgive him.” Let him therefore repent if he desires fruitful peace with you or with another; for, as the Apostle says, no one is permitted anything against the truth. Nor is sin forgiven at all unless, where the means exist, what has been taken away is restored. Either Christ’s words are superfluous, or conversion, repentance, and true confession are necessary for obtaining forgiveness.

## LETTER CXLI. TO WILLIAM, BISHOP OF NORWICH

Thomas, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother W. . . ., by the same grace Bishop of Norwich: greeting; and may you faithfully wield, and prosperously wield, in the Holy Spirit the sword of Peter against the persecutors of Christ.

Whoever, by neglecting punishment, gives wicked men boldness to do wrong through the authority divinely bestowed upon him is known to make himself liable to the penalty of their crime. For the blood of the wicked is required from the hand of the negligent or conniving priest. As Scripture teaches, thorns and thistles grow in the hand of the drunkard.

Therefore, lest by overlooking manifest crimes guilt enfold us and we be convicted of having kept too much silence to the ruin of the Church, we have bound Count Hugh with the bond of anathema, following nevertheless the mandate of the supreme pontiff. We command you publicly to cause him to be declared excommunicated throughout your bishopric, and to have the fellowship of the faithful withdrawn from him, as ecclesiastical discipline prescribes.

Moreover, your brotherhood may remember that for a long time we overlooked the faults of the Bishop of London, who—to say nothing of his other offences—would that he had not been so shameless an instigator of schism, nor encouraged public power and armed its servants for the overthrow of ecclesiastical liberty and right. Accordingly, relying upon the authority of the Apostolic See, we have publicly excommunicated him; likewise the Bishop of Salisbury for disobedience and contempt; and others whose names are written below, for various just causes.

The excommunicated are therefore Thomas son of Bernard, Ralph de Broc, Robert de Broc the clerk, Hugh of St Clair, Letard the clerk of Norfolk, Nigel of Sacca-Villa, and the clerk, brother of William of Hastings, who occupied our church of Monechete. By apostolic and our own authority, in virtue of obedience and under peril to your salvation and order, we command you to have them publicly declared excommunicated throughout your whole diocese, and to order all the faithful diligently to avoid their communion. Farewell in the Lor—

## LETTER CXLII. TO THE SAME

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to William, Bishop of Norwich.

We have rejoiced greatly to learn from your dear brotherhood that, in the absolution of the nobleman Count Hugh, all things had been solemnly and duly completed according to our command. For we rejoiced with great joy over the lost sheep, because it has been brought back upon the shoulders of the merciful shepherd through the pathless wilderness to the flock.

And when you added that you lift your hands to almighty God, who in these last days has deigned to look upon the earth, my soul likewise magnifies the Lord, who has dealt magnificently with us, making our storm into a breeze and calming the motion of the waves. From him we now earnestly pray that we may be worthy to see you before you depart and fly away from this region of mortals to that of the eternal ones, where your fellow citizens and members of God’s household are.

For we hope that from your presence no small spiritual grace will be imparted to our faint-heartedness to strengthen us, since blessed be God, who in these days has made you an immovable pillar of his house. As to those interdicted clerics on whose behalf the illustrious Count Hugh wrote to us, we have decided for the present to alter nothing, but wish them to remain as they are until, by the Lord’s favour, we ourselves come, intending to avail ourselves of your counsel upon these and the other affairs of the Church.

Nevertheless, for reverence toward the sender of this letter, and also in compassion for this bearer’s own labour, we permit him the exercise of preaching, and likewise of baptizing and administering viaticum, if the last necessity of life should compel it. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLIII. TO THE SAME

We give thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ, who never abandons those hoping in him, but in the grace of his customary mercy mercifully deigns to visit them and can rescue them from the calamities of miseries. Accordingly, we wish it to come to your knowledge that, on the feast-day of blessed Mary Magdalene, we made an honourable and good peace with our lord Henry, the illustrious King of the English, to the honour of God and his Church, and equally to the honour of the king and ourselves.

We have communicated this to you so that you may take no small consolation from the peace made for us and may now rejoice in our return. May you long and always prosper, you whom may our eyes see before we die.

## LETTER CXLIV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS

To his venerable brother and dearest friend in Christ, John, by God’s grace Bishop of Poitiers, Thomas, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury: greeting, and himself wholly.

Dearest brother, why have you done this to us? Why have you strangled both us and yourselves? Behold, you have given that man an occasion for disparagement and for malicious speaking against both us and yourselves. Behold, that creature greedy for glory and excessively inclined to the destruction of the Church will cause it to be spread abroad and cried through the streets and in the face of the Church that we have absolutely and unconditionally submitted ourselves to his counsel, every condition having been kept silent, with no mention made either of God’s honour or of our order. Yet these are matters which undoubtedly ought in no way to be concealed at a time when the chief intention and entire purpose is that they should be concealed to the Church’s shame and confusion; and this is a most manifest kind of apostasy.

But this was not the manner or form in which you left us at Étampes, if you remember rightly. You know, if you please, that at our mutual departure we told you to press only this article: that this man, in accordance with the lord pope’s command, should restore to us his favour and peace and should leave our church to us under our free direction.

And when he asked us whether we would accept a day for a conference with him if he wished to speak with us, we answered that we would accept no day for speaking with him before he had answered the lord pope’s command and also satisfied it; but that afterward we would gladly come on the appointed day and do whatever we could, preserving God’s honour and our order. This, dearest brother, was the manner in which we parted from one another.

You ought, if it pleased you, to have stood within these limits, since you know perfectly well—better than anyone—that we dare not proceed further for any reason and can neither do nor ought to do anything further according to God. Therefore we wish you, the half of our soul, to know that we have no intention, nor indeed does it seem safe, either to accept a day or to come to his conference until he has accepted the lord pope’s mandate and, if he sees fit, has put it into effect; lest, God forbid, by giving him an opportunity for futile delay, it may deservedly also be imputed to us that the pope’s command is not carried into execution—a result which plainly cannot be to our advantage. Fare well always.

## LETTER CXLV. TO FROGER, BISHOP OF SÉEZ

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Froger, Bishop of Séez.

We return such thanks as the occasion permits to your affection, which bears concern for us and renders dutiful charity to the Church of Canterbury, at whose breasts we were nourished. Would that, by God’s favour, that Church might someday advance your lampstand, and we through it repay due return for the compassion which, with a few chosen persons, you show for the Lord’s sake to us and our afflicted companions.

Indeed, we do not despair of God’s grace, which has always protected the Church of Canterbury and has been accustomed to bless or punish, according to their deserts, both its servants and its persecutors. For although Christ is gracious and patient to his Church, he is nevertheless mighty, just, and certainly a requiter.

And although we are indebted to you in many respects, you have especially earned our gratitude in this: that, as you wrote, through your intervention the lord king has from his heart remitted his indignation against us. Confiding also in his prudence and in that of the wise men about him, we confidently hope that he will do nothing against his mother, the Church of Canterbury, which advanced him and his predecessors, nothing against the salvation of his soul or to the ruin of his son, whom may the Lord protect from every adversity.

You recently wrote that we should meet you and the lord of Tyre at Paris on your return from the King of France. Although you did not, as you should have done, fix a day, we were nevertheless ready to set out when we heard that you had returned to Normandy. We therefore remained in astonishment that you had taken no care to notify us either of your return or of our journey.

Now you write likewise that we should meet you on your return, yet again you specify no day, as though we could divine your return, or had sufficient means to stay and wait for you in other people’s houses without burdening friends, who are often necessary both to us and to our people. Thus we cannot meet you in uncertainty, though we are ready, once the benefit of our journey is apparent, to approach the lord king and comply with his will in whatever we can according to God and the honour of the Church. May your dear brotherhood, beloved to us, always fare well and prosper in the Lord.

## LETTER CXLVI. TO JOCELIN, BISHOP OF SALISBURY

Thomas, by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to his venerable brother Jocelin, by the same grace Bishop of Salisbury: upon seeing our letters, immediately repent of evil, and henceforth do good more steadfastly.

There is a well-known proverb: “It is easier to avoid a quarrelsome man than to turn aside from a deceiver.” Thus, although, because of the cunning of deceivers, the weakness of your spirit, and the danger to your body and your people which you have proposed to yourself, you may seem in some degree excusable, we nevertheless hold it no less certain that you have gravely offended in contempt of the lord pope; that you have deservedly incurred the sentence of our interdict; and that you have done such a thing that the whole world has cause to cry out after you.

This is especially so because, contrary to the express command of the lord pope—that no dean should be appointed in the Church of Salisbury, either by you or by your clerks, without the consent and knowledge of its canons, who are exiles for us and with us—and also contrary to our prohibition made under anathema, you have confirmed the intrusion of a dean newly and improperly created in your church. Through the occasion of his oath, as is commonly known, the schism which had almost died out has now revived in Germany. We believe that by law itself he is involved in condemned heresy: he who, through participation in that great and notorious schismatic—I mean the man of Cologne—has brought upon himself a sentence of excommunication by authority of Leo’s decree: “If anyone has defiled himself by the contagion of heretical communion, let him count it a great benefit if, all hope of advancement having been taken away, he remains in the order in which he is found.”

Therefore, since we know that no fraud can be done to one who knows, and that it is unjust and contrary to all canonical law for so detestable a thing—detestable both because of the act and because of the person, so disadvantageous to your Church and so pernicious as an example to others—to remain valid and firm, since it has no force by law itself, we, by apostolic authority and by the authority we exercise, revoke and declare void that election—or rather intrusion—of John of Oxford to the deanery, together with your confirmation and assent concerning it; and we utterly annul the whole proceeding.

And because, contrary to the common order of the Church and to the lord pope’s command, as we have said, that man, having fallen into condemned heresy, an excommunicate by participation in an excommunicate, dared to accept the deanery, lest the rashness of invaders increase with impunity, we command you and your canons, in virtue of obedience and under peril to your orders, that, upon seeing our letters, you shall no longer have him as dean because of this act. For we now declare him excommunicated to you and firmly command you to declare him such.

Furthermore, lest you escape unpunished for this offence, by which you have provoked a more severe sentence against yourself, we suspend you by God’s authority and our own from episcopal and priestly office. We command you, within two months from receiving our letters, to set out to come to us, to make satisfaction to God and to us for so great a transgression and so manifest an injury. When you have repented and amended the offence, farewell to you.

## LETTER CXLVII. TO THE SAME

Thomas to his venerable brother Jocelin, Bishop of Salisbury: greeting.

God knows with what sincere affection and charity we have embraced your person, and how much we have desired and promoted your honour and advancement in Christ. But you, on the contrary, as we have certainly learned—though we write it not without sorrow—act openly in contempt of the lord pope and of us, and perhaps to your own loss and the peril of your order; nor do you observe in any degree the sentence of suspension which we imposed upon you for disobedience. Your prudence, we believe, is by no means unaware how detestable and pernicious as an example this is.

We therefore wish you to know that unless you correct your errors and more promptly make satisfaction for your now twofold disobedience, we shall be unable any longer to overlook matters so grave without punishing them more severely. We also greatly wonder that you know our chaplain William to be held imprisoned in chains in your diocese, yet have so far exercised no justice in the matter.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, in virtue of obedience and under threat of anathema, we command your brotherhood that you yourselves cease from the celebration of divine offices and cause your whole diocese to cease for as long as the same William is held in chains or captivity. Nor are you to lift the interdict before you know that the often-mentioned William has been released from captivity and full satisfaction has been rendered to the Apostolic See, to us, and to him for so enormous a crime. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLVIII. TO THE SAME

The calamities of Mother Church, etc. (See the similar letter addressed to Gilbert, Bishop of London.)

## LETTER CXLIX. TO THE CHAPTER OF SALISBURY

Thomas, by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to the entire chapter of the Church of Salisbury: the spirit of knowledge and counsel.

We cannot sufficiently wonder at your prudence: with what audacity—or rather what rashness—you have elected as dean of your Church a man excommunicated by law itself, because he has fallen into condemned heresy; the very man who, by an oath committed in Germany, as everyone knows, renewed the schism there. We mean John of Oxford. You did this without consulting those who are in exile with us for justice and the liberty of the Church, especially when a special prohibition from the Roman pontiff had reached you that this should not be done without them. Our prohibition also was issued, though I do not know whether it reached you.

Therefore we utterly annul and declare void what was less than prudently done concerning the deanery—indeed, what was done contrary to every order of law. We inform you that we regard the aforesaid John as excommunicated and declare him excommunicated to you; and by apostolic authority and our own we forbid you to regard the said John as dean or render him the obedience or respect due to a dean.

We also command you, under peril to your orders and benefices, to present yourselves before us within two months of receiving these letters, to make satisfaction concerning the injury and contempt shown to the lord pope and to us. Farewell.

## LETTER CL. TO RICHARD, ELECT OF SYRACUSE

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Richard, Elect of Syracuse.

Your kindness invites us to hear you, and the bestowal upon us of your benefits has made us and ours indebted to you and yours in many ways. Having therefore entered into this exchange of services, especially under the pressure of necessity, we do not fear to contract a debt with a kind creditor, hoping in the Lord that he will mercifully discharge our debts both to you and to others, who, when it is expedient, frees those who fear him from every strait of necessity.

You received our fellow-exiles and kinsmen; but beyond doubt you received in them him who faithfully promises to repay whatever is bestowed upon one of his poor. In this you have gained the gratitude of your fellow countrymen, earned glory among posterity, and made us your purchased servants.

And because divine providence presently deprives us of a personal meeting, we ask you to trust the bearer of this letter as you would trust us. To his fidelity we have entrusted what we judged should not be committed to writing. He is a man conspicuous for learning, endowed with grace of character, distinguished by the holiness of monastic religion, and among the approved Cluniacs an example of perfection to be desired. He manages the needs of the Church of Cluny and the commands both of the Most Christian King and of ourselves. When you receive him with due reverence, you will receive in him the most holy prince whose servant he is, and also ourselves.

There is one matter, however, which we desire to have confidentially discussed with you, requested of you, and obtained: that you diligently secure from the king and queen the recall of the nobleman Stephen, Elect of Palermo, both for reasons which we intentionally keep silent at present and in order that you may acquire forever the favour of the aforesaid king and of the whole kingdom of France. Farewell.

## LETTER CLI. TO THE SAME

Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Richard, Elect of Syracuse.

Your affectionate letter brought us much consolation. It bore signs of your health, which we greatly desire; elegance of expression, sincerity of faith, and the grace of prudence. And, greater than all these, every stroke of its pen, by its fervour, could inflame to the love of God and the pursuit of righteousness not merely a lukewarm soul but even one grown cold.

From it it became plainly known that neither the rashness of fortune, nor distance of places, nor length of time had been able to empty—or even weaken—the charity which not even many waters can prevail to quench. For you offered earnest and affectionate prayers for us to Lord William of Pavia, your friend; and would that they were not in vain. But if he could make what is permitted equal to what he desires, he would be to us a nail in the eye and an arrow in the side, killing souls that do not die and giving life to those who have rejected and cast away life.

May God spare him and his companions, lest at the last judgment our blood and that of our fellow-exiles—indeed that of the Church—be required from their hands, because they have given horns to sinners and, so far as in them lies, exposed the law to be profaned by the Gentiles and trampled underfoot.

But why do we recount these things except that you may have compassion upon the Church and give us, before God and the Roman Church, the aid of your prayers, should an opportunity arise? A witness greater than John bears witness against them, because the works which they do bear witness concerning them. The Church indeed will be delivered, and we, as long as it pleases God, shall willingly suffer the shipwreck of exile, scattered to every wind with our afflicted people. One of these is the bearer of this letter, G. . . ., son of our sister. Whenever he needs your aid, we commend him to you all the more confidently because we trust more fully in your affection, giving thanks to God that he has made so much of us that all our blood and that of our people is demanded for punishment on his behalf.

## LETTER CLII. TO ROGER, BISHOP OF WORCESTER

Thomas, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable and dearest friend Roger, by the same grace Bishop of Worcester: greeting and the affection of deepest love.

We do not believe that it has slipped your memory that last year, by letter and messenger, we instructed you to come to us and firmly commanded you, by virtue of obedience; yet you have not obeyed our commands, since you have not yet come to us. Let your affection therefore know that, for many intervening reasons, we have deferred to you and, with a father’s affection, spared a son: both because we know you to be exceedingly devoted and faithful to your mother, the Church of Canterbury; because of the nobility of your birth; because alike of the religious character and uprightness of your person; and also because we sincerely love you with all the affections of our heart. Therefore, by a repeated command, and under peril to your order, we command and firmly enjoin you by virtue of obedience that, since you have come into the regions on this side of the sea, you are not to depart from them before coming to us and speaking with us. For we have much [Col. 0626B] to say to you. Furthermore, in commanding you we nevertheless direct that, concerning the matter at issue between you and the archbishop of York, and likewise concerning all those excommunicated in St Oswald’s and throughout his whole parish, you do nothing—whether through entreaty, payment, anyone’s threats, or even the intervention of the king himself, a cardinal, or any other person—without our counsel and knowledge, nor absolve those excommunicated persons, or any one of them.

## LETTER CLIII. TO THE SAME MAN.

To the venerable brother ROGER, bishop of Worcester: greeting, and that he may fear above all him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna.

[Col. 0626C] We have carefully examined the letter of your affection. The counsel which, out of faithful purpose, your discernment supplied to our need, we have weighed with deliberation, balancing the reasons on either side; and we judge that it proceeds from the sweetness of brotherly charity. We infer that your faith can no longer be restrained from freely pursuing the word of God before princes, as befits the nobility of a high-born man and the zeal of a devout bishop.

We therefore give thanks for your devotion, congratulate your prudence, and heartily approve your purpose of resolving to approach the lord king on our behalf—indeed, on behalf of God’s cause—with more than customary vigilance and urgency. We ask that you promptly undertake what you promise in this respect, do so more frequently, [Col. 0626D] and, omitting nothing that may occur, carry it out with greater diligence. For there is hope that the Lord will add abundant power to the word faithfully proclaimed; for he is faithful in all his words, he who has promised this to the shepherds of the Church.

Indeed, it is credible—and nothing else can persuade us—that if you and our other brethren had approached him from the beginning, as was right, the counsels of the wicked would never have been allowed such scope for the ruin of the Church. But because there was none, or scarcely one—something we say only with shame and grief—who would set himself against him face to face and call him back from the counsel of the ungodly, matters have fallen into such danger and misfortune that he believes himself not liable to rebuke for any cause, recalling that in such great presumptions and manifest impieties he has [Col. 0627A] been rebuked by no one.

We ourselves also kept silence for a long time; and would that my soul, which so greatly dissimulated Christ’s injuries, did not have to say in conscience: “Woe to me, because I have kept silent!” We were patient with the Roman Church, which bore with him as with a delicate and tender son in great gentleness, so that her patience might, as was fitting, provoke his noble spirit to repentance. Would that he had not always abused her patience and ours.

And lest it be said that we omitted anything which seemed incumbent upon us, before the Most Christian king and the chief men of the whole kingdom of France we humbled ourselves, prostrate at his feet, referring the entire case between us to his judgment, saving God’s honour. But when he heard mention of the divine honour, he grew vehemently angry against our innocence; and, asserting what he wished—certainly what he ought not, since, with his leave be it said, the matter stood otherwise—he strove, by his own inventions, to burden our reputation, may God forgive him, in insult to a suppliant imploring mercy and offering service with every devotion, so that he might trouble us even in the place of exile.

We heard everything patiently, hoping that his anger would be softened if he fully poured out, without contradiction, the bitterness he had conceived in his mind; particularly since the majesty of the lord pope intervened, the presence of the aforesaid king and the chief men of France was earnestly interceding, and the most holy men, the Carthusians and Grandmontines—whom it would have been right to hear even for their reverence alone—[Col. 0627C] were most urgently imploring mercy. They informed him, more familiarly and expressly, of what they had learned by eyewitness trust: that the lord pope had restored and conferred upon us full authority to take action against him, his land, and the evildoers of the Church.

Yet in all this his rancour has not been turned away; his hand remains stretched out to this day, and he grows still more cruel in laying waste the Church. Nor is he himself unaware that authority has been restored to us, since he knows this with complete certainty from the apostolic letters which he received at the second conference. Furthermore, besides what those letters contain, other powers have been granted to us, which, with God as author, we shall use against [Col. 0627D] him and the other persecutors of the Church unless he restores peace. These may soon become known, as you desire, if it is God’s will that we speak together; or if one of your people comes to us, it will be necessary that they be communicated to him.

For we await the amendment of one whom we believe to rage so fiercely against the Church rather through another’s prompting than from his own spirit. Therefore, for their part, we have delivered them to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, for just and manifest causes, compelled by the necessity of our office and persuaded by the rule of law: so that by the punishment of the members the head may be healed and drawn out of the snares of hell, with which, while persecuting the Church, he continually binds himself.

The rest, as has been announced to you, we shall, God so disposing, condemn by a like anathema [Col. 0628A] unless in the meantime they avert the impending sentence by fitting satisfaction. Thus far we have deferred to the king himself, and in hope of peace we still intend to delay; nor shall we subject him to anathema or his kingdom to interdict, so long as this may be passed over without harm to salvation and without impairing the ordinance of the Apostolic See.

But as to what you asked—that you may be permitted to associate with the excommunicated, as though through this offence against God the path to the king’s favour and the restoration of the Church’s peace might be easier, as though that peace were to be restored not by God but by human craft—it is astonishing how such a thought could enter the mind of a wise man, especially a bishop, who ought to have zeal for the law and who has heard the Apostle dissuading us: “Let us not do evil that [Col. 0628B] good may come.” What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? What accord has the temple of God with idols? What sharing has faith with iniquity?

“But you fear the king.” Certainly God ought to have been feared more. Poverty is dreadful, as is the injury of outlawry. Yet Christ recognizes as his confessors those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, declaring them blessed—not those clothed in saffron, who occupy the first places at table, receive distinguished greetings, feast splendidly every day, and whom the flattering world fawns upon, crying at each of their words or deeds, “Well done, well done!” “If I were pleasing men,” says the chosen vessel, “I should not be Christ’s servant.” For those who desire to please men will be put to shame.

Perhaps you recall the edicts by which he is reckoned a public enemy who, against the king’s will, presumes for any reason to condemn anyone by a sentence of anathema. But has it slipped from memory that the Holy Spirit declares to the priest: “Unless you announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood from your hand”? Is not one who refuses to hear the Church’s rebuke to be regarded as a heathen and a publican? But you will object that the times are evil, as though God had not ordered even them, and as though they were not blessed who do judgment and justice at every time. Do not fear where there is no cause for fear, beloved brother: for more are with us than with them. And he who gives their food to the beasts and to the young ravens will not abandon his servants in need.

[Col. 0628D] To state our counsel briefly: consult the Law and the Prophets; consult the Gospel and the words of the Apostle; review the ordinances of the holy Fathers. By the authority of all these it will be plain that, without loss of salvation and of office, you cannot associate with the excommunicated. Christ declares that no one can serve two masters, God and Mammon.

And assuredly, if we set our hearts upon our ways and examine our consciences more closely, most of us priests fear offending the powerful lest riches be taken from us, or deceitful, momentary, shadowy favour. Let this not be said as though we suspected your nobility of serving Mammon—your nobility, which is known always to have despised riches for the sake of honour—but in order that, if it can be stimulated by words, we may by this exhortation make the ready obedience of your faith still readier to burn in charity.

Therefore, having full confidence in your sincerity, we command, by virtue of obedience and under peril to your salvation and office, that you avoid the previously announced excommunicated persons, and throughout your bishopric, as the censure of the canons prescribes, publicly cause them to be avoided by all the faithful. You know that obedience is better than sacrifices, and the will not to obey is compared with idolatry.

We are fortified and secure against the evasions of our opponents. Nor is there any doubt that shortly, by God’s grace, the truth will set us and you free. For five years now the persecutor has devastated the Church, outlawed the innocent, [Col. 0629B] reduced the clergy to bondage, and closed the mouths of priests—indeed, of bishops—lest they speak God’s law. He restrains and extinguishes the rights of ecclesiastical authority lest crimes be punished; and are we required to keep silence amid so great an insult to Christ? Hirelings are silent and indeed will remain silent; but whoever is a shepherd of the Church will without doubt join us.

If we were to dissemble further, we should have to fear lest the sword of the avenger of God’s injuries should deservedly turn upon our heads. Nor be moved because we do not grant at your request a dispensation which cannot be granted; for not even the Roman pontiff possesses this authority. Although he may lawfully absolve excommunicated persons, he nevertheless knows that participation with them is perpetually forbidden him by law. But the Apostle does not lawfully absolve—nor does an angel—those who are unrepentant and persist in crime and in the will to sin. Farewell.

## LETTER CLIV. TO THE SAME MAN.

THOMAS, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother ROGER, bishop of Worcester: greeting, and a devout regard for the future.

Having examined the letters which we have recently received from England, you may observe how maliciously the bishop of London—who from the beginning of our tenure of the see lay in wait for our life, to take it away—now raises his heel against his mother and ours, the holy [Col. 0629D] Church of Canterbury, and endeavours to rob her of the inheritance, glory, and name of primacy.

Our brethren recently resisted him commendably before the king’s officers, whom he was stirring up to persecute the Church. Suspending themselves from his communion, they commanded by public edict throughout their dioceses that he be avoided by all the faithful. This was first done by our venerable brother, the bishop of Norwich, in the synod recently held; then by the bishop of Chester in his bishopric; and by the lord bishop of Winchester and the bishop of Chichester on the very next day after they had received our letters.

Since, therefore, your nobility and religious character require you above all to adorn the Church, honour your ministry, and stand firmly—even unto blood—for the safety of the mother who brought you forth into the company of bishops, [Col. 0630A] we ask, admonish, and exhort in the Lord your brotherhood, which is more closely bound to us by the consecration received from us, and in which we have greater confidence because of the consciousness of virtue and the nobility of your blood: faithfully assist your mother, whose safety is attacked by so shameless a crime, in this great necessity; set yourselves against the impiety of another Absalom.

May the discernment of your sincerity and your charity, greatly to be embraced in Christ, also take care that, according to the tenor of the preceding commands, you avoid both the aforesaid bishop and the others announced to you as excommunicated; and, as our brethren and fellow bishops have done, cause them to be avoided by the faithful throughout your bishopric by ecclesiastical edict, as the authority of the canons ordains.

[Col. 0630B] And because the atrocity of this parricidal crime must be referred to the Apostolic See, write to the lord pope as a son ought to write for the safety of his mother against an Ishmaelite and bloodthirsty brother: for although he does not shed blood with his own hands, yet he thirsts for our blood and that of Christ’s poor. He indeed sheds it by his counsels, abusing the agency of tyrants.

The remaining matters have been entrusted orally to the bearer of this letter. Hear him in what he will say to you on our behalf as you would hear us. The French bishops write on behalf of the Church of Canterbury, as you may learn from the letters of the lord bishop of Paris; but you will write more expressly, since you are bound more closely and love more ardently.

Let this also be stated in the letter which you send to the lord pope: that the aforesaid bishop of London, after receiving the apostolic letters concerning our reconciliation, which your brotherhood transmitted to him, [Col. 0630C] became hostile. Not only did he make no word to the king on behalf of the Church’s peace; he did the contrary. By himself and through the king’s officers, he pressed for bishops, abbots, and all prelates of churches, in their own name and that of their subjects, to appeal against the apostolic command—even though it has been granted to us not to defer to appeals of this sort.

But by God’s better providence his malice was thwarted: religious men did not consent to him, either from fear of the officials or because of the command of the public power, whose authority he claimed in exerting force. In this necessity of hers the Church will test your faith; and you will leave to God and men, present and future alike, an example most welcome of outstanding virtue. Let neither the flatteries nor threats of deceivers frighten or move you, since it is certain that the hope of the wicked will perish and bring forth confusion; he who fears frost, snow will fall upon him; while those who fear God lack nothing advantageous.

## LETTER CLV. TO THE SAME MAN.

THOMAS, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother and dearest friend ROBERT, bishop of Worcester: greeting, and enduring progress in zeal for faith and the fervour of sincere charity.

Your father, the illustrious Robert, earl of Gloucester, is said, though he had several sons, to have loved you with greater affection than the rest, because he begot you in old age and, as your natural disposition promised, by God’s cooperating grace poured the entire seedbed of his prudence and virtues into the offspring whom, as most precious, he consecrated to the Lord from earliest youth.

Consider how prudent, faithful, magnanimous, and steadfast he was: he attacked and overcame the forces of a flourishing, warlike, gracious, high-born, and wealthy king, who was also duke of the Normans and count of Boulogne. He not only deprived him of the kingdom but cast him captive into chains. So greatly did he despise fortune’s hostility, having regard to faith and virtue, that for the sacred obligation of restoring the oath he shrank from no dangers; and at length, when captured, [Col. 0631B] he preferred imprisonment to allowing his sister, and the lady entitled to his allegiance, to suffer loss.

Though he was captured through fortune’s envy, he was nevertheless held in such esteem while in chains by the judgment of wise men that they considered his release should be exchanged for, and compensated by, king and kingdom. Let contemplation of this most illustrious man add courage to you; represent him to contemporaries and posterity in character and virtue, him who made you illustrious by the title of noble blood.

To this is added the nobler title of virtue to be cultivated: the summit of episcopal office. Just as it makes those faithfully fulfilling the episcopal office shine conspicuous with greater glory and honour, so it renders the timid and cowardly inglorious by more abject baseness. Salt that has lost its savour is useful for nothing; it becomes so contemptible by its degradation that it is not even fit for dung, by which the barrenness of fields is remedied.

For, as the martyr Cyprian says: “If a bishop is timid, it is all over with him.” “All over,” he says, because when worldly fear has infected him, it follows that he is rendered useless for doing all things conducive to salvation. Therefore let charity cast out this fear, that it may free the leader of the people; for the exhortation of a leader weakened by fear can in no way strengthen soldiers’ minds for brave deeds.

Indeed, we believe it has occurred by divine direction that in these days you have crossed the sea to repel the injury done to your mother, the holy Church of Canterbury, so that you may personally resist those who have long afflicted her without cause and still seek her life, to take it away—as you promised us. [Col. 0631D] In order that, with God’s grace leading the way, you may do this more effectively, we have decided that you should be fortified beforehand by the lord pope’s letters as by weapons of war, so that you may more effectively strengthen our brethren’s hearts in the Lord.

We ask and beseech you in the Lord Jesus Christ, and command you by virtue of obedience and under peril to office, honour, and benefice, to show the apostolic letters we send you to our venerable brother Roger, archbishop of York, and to our other brethren and fellow bishops. By the authority of the lord pope forbid the aforesaid archbishop of York to presume to confer consecration upon the lord king’s son, or, should this be requested of him, to place the crown upon him.

Under the same threat we command that you similarly forbid the bishops of London and Salisbury, [Col. 0632A] and the rest, should any one dare attempt this. Before God as witness and judge, we issue this command not from any intention of injuring the lord king, his son, any Church, or any person, but from the necessity by which we are compelled, to the best of our ability, to preserve the rights of the Church of Canterbury. For if it please the lord king, we are prepared, as our office requires, to crown his son and certainly to render him the honour and reverence due.

Let not your faith waver in carrying this out, dearest brother, for God is faithful and will not suffer you to be tempted beyond your strength. Trust therefore in him who conquered the world, and remember: “He who fears frost, snow will fall upon him”; and “He who avoids iron weapons often falls upon a bronze bow.” “Fear will betray degenerate spirits,” [Col. 0632B] but grace will aid those who dare bravely, and glory will crown them.

Whatever others may do, we are convinced that no onset of storm will break your constancy; that what has proceeded from your mouth, and is contained in writing both by you and by the bishop of Lisieux, sealed and declared under each of your signs, will not prove void. Far be it that noble blood should be the dwelling-place of a degenerate soul; that through you the titles of your fathers should be effaced; that any trembling of mind or cowardice in action should prove your father—who preferred you to all his children—to have erred in judgment and should exclude the affection of ancient love.

For, as the faithful devoutly believe, he lives more happily in God than in his children; and by diligent or reprobate deeds you can either earn or forfeit his favour.

## LETTER CLVI. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER.

THOMAS, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to his venerable brother HENRY, by the grace of God bishop of Winchester: the spirit of knowledge and counsel.

He who searches hearts knows best how affectionately we sympathize with you. We know indeed how many and great are the things which disturb and move you, and how none or few there are to strengthen your spirit and establish you in this storm. But act manfully; let your heart be strengthened, lest our enemies prevail and entangle you in their tricks and snares. Rather catch the foxes that destroy the vineyard. For among serpents and those walking a crooked path, serpentine shrewdness is necessary. We say this to you as to a brother and beloved in Christ.

But we have something against you, concerning which we have been not a little grieved by your transgression. For we have received certain information that you have alienated your golden cross from your Church—a deed we judge to have been done very imprudently and against every censure of the canons. Alienations of this kind are altogether forbidden by the canons. Therefore we command you, and in commanding firmly order you by virtue of obedience, that within forty days after receipt of our letter you endeavour by every means to restore the aforesaid [Col. 0633A] cross to the right and ownership of the Church over which, with God as author, you preside. If you do not accomplish this, do not delay, from that fortieth day, to come before us within two months to make satisfaction regarding the alienation carried out. May your brotherhood fare well.

## LETTER CLVII. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER.

THOMAS, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother and dearest friend HENRY, by the grace of God bishop of Winchester: greeting, and enduring zeal in the defence of Mother Church.

Your discernment cannot be ignorant of the acts of presumption known to have been committed against the Church in the kingdom of the English before [Col. 0633B] your eyes—indeed, before the sight of surrounding and distant nations. And, as we say without fear of divine judgment, it is to be feared that our dissimulation has increased the faults of the presumptuous and that impunity has nourished their boldness in wrongdoing.

For five years now we have endured exile and outlawry. Innocent people, without pity for age or sex and without respect for condition or rank, have been deprived of their goods, condemned to exile, and subjected to various and cruel injuries. Sacred things are profaned; the Church’s possessions are plundered; priests are forbidden to fulfil the Lord’s law and to exercise the canonical sanctions they have professed. Under pretext of royal dignity, abuses prevail which the holy Fathers of old in their days, and the Apostolic See in ours, have condemned.

The lord king has often been admonished to correct these matters—by bishops, abbots, subdeacons of the curia, and cardinals; and now at last, as by a peremptory edict, through lord Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Apostolic See, and Master Vivian, archdeacon of Civita Vecchia: either to correct these presumptions through them, or to feel in himself and his land the exercise of justice which he had deserved. Yet they were not merely unheard by him, but received grave injuries in the person of the venerable Master Peter, archdeacon of Chartres, and in the other messengers whom they had sent to him with words of peace.

[Col. 0633D] For amid all the gentleness of the lord pope, the long endurance of our patience, and the display of humility, his savagery neither ceased nor was softened; rather, made fiercer by impunity, it has always grown worse. Therefore, lest further dissimulation on our part prove that we have consented to wickedness, and make us liable to condemnation before the eyes of the strict Judge, with whom there is no respect of persons, we can neither pass over nor dare henceforth to pass over such great offences without investigation.

Accordingly, by virtue of obedience, under anathema, and at peril to dignity and order, by apostolic authority and our own we command your brotherhood: unless by the Purification of Blessed Mary the lord king strives to restore what has been taken from God’s Church and from us, to recall the outlawed innocent by due restoration of right, to allow the Church’s sacred sanctions to remain in force, and to permit clergy and [Col. 0634A] people, as is right, to obey the holy Roman Church, then from that time throughout your entire bishopric you shall forbid all divine offices to be celebrated in every church, except baptism of infants, penance, and viaticum. Priests are permitted, for the necessity of salvation, to administer these behind closed doors, without ringing bells and without any solemnity of ecclesiastical rejoicing.

And if not even thus, under this chastisement of the people, the aforesaid lord our king corrects the stated offences by due satisfaction, know and declare to him without contradiction that we shall spare neither his person—though we say it unwillingly—nor the dangers to our own salvation, as hitherto we have done, any longer, God so authorizing.

Under the same threat we command that you publicly cause the following to be declared excommunicated: those who receive churches, ecclesiastical offices, and benefices from the hand of laymen contrary to the ordinance of the sacred canons; those who compel clerics, contrary to the prohibition of their prelates, to celebrate divine offices; those who hinder the messengers of the lord pope and ours from pursuing the Church’s needs; those who do not permit churches to be canonically ordered for God’s honour; and those who preach or forcibly compel that human traditions or customs be preferred to the ordinances of the divine law.

But by name, publish by canonical edict that all the faithful must avoid Geoffrey, archdeacon of Canterbury; Robert, his vicar; Richard of Ilchester; William Giffard; Nigel of Sackville; Richard of Lucy; Thomas son of Bernard; and Adam of Charing, whom we have previously excommunicated. [Col. 0634C] Moreover, if John, dean of Salisbury; Guy, dean of Waltham; John Cumin; Ralph, archdeacon of Llandaff; and Wimar, priest and fosterling of Count Hugh, do not make satisfaction to the Church of God, which they have injured, and to us by the day of the Nativity of the Lord, then publicly declare them excommunicated from that time.

Be strengthened in the Lord and in the might of his power, for he is faithful and will not suffer you to be tempted beyond your strength. But when, together with Joshua, you have sounded the priestly trumpets according to the law, he will overthrow and scatter all the enemy’s strongholds before you. Then it will be proved who are Christ’s priests and who Belial’s servants. May God direct your works according to his good pleasure, [Col. 0634D] and deign, by his power and grace and through your ministry, to restore peace to his Church.

To Walter, bishop of Rochester, the same, where it reads “throughout your bishopric,” is to be read “throughout all Kent.” As to Henry of Winchester, so also to the bishops of Norwich, Chichester, Exeter, Worcester, and Durham. But to David of St Davids, Nicholas of Llandaff, and Godfrey of St Asaph: “Throughout his whole land which is within your bishopric, in all churches.”

## LETTER CLVIII. TO THE SAME MAN.

To the venerable lord and father HENRY, by the grace of God bishop of Winchester—most dear both for maturity of age and holiness of character, and for the gift of consecration—THOMAS, by the same mercy archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See: greeting, and the happy completion of the course of blessed combat.

[Col. 0635A] Beloved father, we offer your sincerity such thanks as the times permit for the honourable counsel, full of wisdom, maturity, and divine fear, which your charity, in a spirit of fortitude, recently gave us through the bearer of this letter; and for the consolation which your compassion has often supplied to our necessities.

Thus, Father, it becomes a man noble in blood and illustrious through royal ancestors, but most illustrious in the cultivation of virtue and the practice of religion, to adorn the nobility of his lineage. Thus ought a priest and bishop of Christ to complete his life: that while living he may honour his ministry, build up Christ’s Church after death, and, leaving posterity an example of integrity, make them imitate his footsteps, whether equal to him or more perfect.

The memory of such persons will flourish with perpetual blessing through generations of ages, and their splendour will shine unto eternity like the brightness of the firmament. Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit has bestowed on you, before your fellow countrymen and contemporaries, the talent of counsel and fortitude among countless gifts of grace, we earnestly entreat your fatherhood to remember to strengthen your brethren and to endeavour to encourage and fortify them by exhortations as well as examples.

For according to Solomon: “A brother aided by a brother is like a strong and impregnable city.” Certainly your works henceforth ought to be armour for the strong. It is right that what others do praiseworthily should be credited to your titles, Father. For what can they accomplish except what they see one more advanced in wisdom, age, and grace accomplishing? And indeed, that some of them are already raised up and, as we hear and hope, intend to stand with us against Satan’s members, they attribute to your merits, having heard what was recently done.

Nor ought you to fear in these days, since nobility, prudence, abundance of resources and friends, and the reverence due to your age defend your position against the injury which can threaten persons of unlike station. For perhaps some who might have thought that you were not to be spared will undoubtedly spare you, because they fear to offend your kinsmen in this crisis; and the wicked man will suspend the scourge from your house, lest through your relatives’ agency there come upon him what he has deserved.

The remaining matters, not to be written in a letter, have been entrusted to the bearer of this letter’s fidelity, to be communicated only to your ears. If it please you, receive and hear him as a brother of proven truth. May your holiness fare well, beloved Father; and may it remember to commend to God in its prayers its own creation—by which we mean our lowliness.

## LETTER CLIX. TO THE SAME MAN.

For the glory of the saints and the condemnation of the reprobate, it is necessary that scandals arise, so that the elect may be tested by tribulations; tested through patience, they gain for themselves the crown of glory and benefit others by their example. But woe to him through whom scandal comes! Therefore, since the Bishop of London does not refrain from causing scandals and, among the other works of his manifest malice, after being delivered over to Satan, has even raised his heel against his own and your mother, the holy Church of Canterbury, with such shameless boldness and parricidal impiety that he has dared to say that, since his translation, he owes her no submission or obedience whatever; and since, to crown his condemnation, he has added that he will bring about the transfer of the archiepiscopal see to London—we beseech your brotherhood, in whom we place full confidence, with all the earnestness we can, [Col. 0636B] to oppose for your mother the shield of defence against this son of Belial. Alone among all the Philistines, like another Goliath of Gath, he has not blushed, with the Lord permitting it, to come forth from the camp of the uncircumcised, nor has he feared to challenge the whole body of the sons of the Church of Canterbury to combat, while he thirsts for their mother’s blood and abandons the unity of Catholic peace.

He had written to the lord pope on behalf of our brother, the Archbishop of York, urging him—even with false and deceitful testimony—to allow him to carry the cross through our province, suspecting, I know not what advantage might accrue to himself if, out of hatred for our person, he could in any manner injure the Church to which, by his profession, he owes faith and obedience. But Christ, who from its first foundation has guided and cherished the Church of Canterbury [Col. 0636C] amid diverse storms and many great tempests, mercifully brought it about that, in full consistory, his falsehood and injustice were exposed through witnesses beyond all exception.

We give thanks first to God, and then to you and our other brethren, because, as was fitting, once it was established that he stood condemned by anathema, you withdrew yourselves from participation with him, and by public edict commanded that both he and our other excommunicates be avoided throughout your bishopric. Here your faith shone forth; the steadfastness of your virtue gleamed, judging the threats of public power and its officials no less than their flatteries to be set below the commands of God. You have set free your consciences and cleansed your reputation, [Col. 0636D] teaching both by the word of truth and by the example of courage that one must obey God rather than men.

Let your sincerity therefore hold it certain that, since so great a charity of God, poured into your hearts through the Holy Spirit, has come publicly to light in the testimony of this noble work—servile fear having been driven out and shaken off—God will soon crush Satan under your feet and bring forth from the struggle a glorious outcome. Indeed, it will be so much the sooner and more gloriously as you persevere more fervently and steadfastly in the truth you have undertaken. We therefore ask and entreat you in the love of God, and adjure you by the faith, obedience, and sincere devotion which you owe to your mother, the Church of Canterbury, that you rise to assist us in defending the dignity [Col. 0637A] and rights of the Church of Canterbury, to which you have rendered profession, against the aforesaid bishop; and that you write to the lord pope and to the curia a testimony of truth such as sons ought to give for their mother’s cause.

For anyone who withheld this at a crisis of such danger would beyond doubt be deemed faithless, and worse than a faithless person; against him all the faithful would be entitled to rush, even to destruction. Yet this matter can involve no danger, since the truth is plain and, as the saying goes, evident to the bleary-eyed and the barbers. But because “cursed is he who holds back his sword from blood,” and a pestilent person must be scourged so that the wise may be taught unto salvation, whoever does not meet the parricide with stone and [Col. 0637B] sword subjects himself to the curse of the law. For one appears to give consent who, though able, does not rebuke or prevent a person committing such deeds.

And lest a stricter account be demanded of us if we should thereafter overlook the great and manifest offences of those who persecute the Church, and whom, in order that they might do penance, we have endured with much patience for nearly a full five years, we notify your brotherhood that we have publicly excommunicated Geoffrey, Archdeacon of Canterbury, and Robert his vicar, Richard of Ivelcestre, William Giffard, Richard of Luci, Adam of Cheringis; and likewise those who have received ecclesiastical offices or benefices from a lay hand contrary to the institution of the sacred canons, or who have usurped them by their own rashness. Likewise [Col. 0637C] we have excommunicated those who obstruct the messengers of the lord pope or our own, so that they may not pursue the necessities of the Church.

Therefore, by the authority of the lord pope and our own, we command you to regard them and to cause them to be regarded in your bishopric as the discipline of the sacred canons prescribes that persons solemnly excommunicated ought to be regarded. May your brotherhood ever flourish in the Lord, and remember to commend us and the cause of God, which is in our hands, to the prayers of the saints. Farewell.

## LETTER CLX. TO THE SAME PERSON

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to HENRY, Bishop of Winchester.

To speak somewhat like the Apostle, we give thanks [Col. 0637D] to God, who through you makes manifest in every place the fragrance of the knowledge of himself. For, as we have learned from widespread report, your faith has shone out at this moment of storm, and charity has gleamed more abundantly, shown in a pillar of courage and in the exercise of pontifical authority. For when the sons of distrust, men of Belial, in whom Satan more openly works the mystery of iniquity, recently wished to divide the Church and, by extorted oaths, attempted to extinguish the force of obedience and faith, you rose up against them, set a wall before the house of Israel, repressed their boldness in the spirit and power of Elijah, and courageously raised, as was fitting, the hearts of those in the clergy who were afraid, so that they might fear God before men and follow the footsteps of the fathers in Christ.

He stood by you as your helper in these matters, [Col. 0638A] and he will crown your perseverance in heaven; here too he will shortly console you, placing beneath your feet those who boast deceitfully against the Lord because they have been granted a momentary indulgence of power. Stand therefore in what you have begun, and do not by interruption cast away the crown of faith which you have already merited—you whose anchor, through God’s grace, is firmly fixed in the harbour of consolation and peace.

Take care meanwhile that the enemy does not deceive you, lest, with your consent, anything be attempted against the Apostolic See or against your mother, the holy Church of Canterbury, which may later cause labour to them and loss and repentance to you. For we have received word that certain malicious men are trying to persuade the lord king, to the injury of your mother, the Church of Canterbury, [Col. 0638B] and to our harm, to have his son—whom may God deliver both from this misfortune and from every evil—crowned king by the hand of our venerable brother, the Archbishop of York. Since this is recognized to be contrary to the dignity of the Church of Canterbury, the lord pope, by his letters which we send to you and our other brethren, forbids it both to the aforesaid archbishop and to all the bishops of England.

And if, God forbid, that same archbishop or another should presume to attempt otherwise, by apostolic and our own authority, in virtue of obedience and under anathema, we absolutely forbid you, any of our brethren, and those who are subject to us either by reason of our office of legate or by metropolitan right, to dare to assist them; appealing against [Col. 0638C] every person who ventures to involve himself in so great a presumption, and appointing the feast of the Purification of Saint Mary as the day.

## LETTER CLXI. TO THE SAME PERSON

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to HENRY, Bishop of Winchester: greeting, and may you in the way of God’s commandments gain the prize of the heavenly calling.

The calamities which have for six years now afflicted the English Church, but especially your mother, the Church of Canterbury, cannot be unknown to your brotherhood. As you ought, from charity, to suffer with her miseries, so, from the necessity of your office and the profession you have rendered, you must obey her commands. We awaited the repentance of the lord king; but he—something we cannot say without sorrow—has so continually abused the mercy of God, of the holy Roman Church, and our patience that his latest actions against the Church of God have day by day become worse than his earlier ones.

Therefore, lest his blood and that of the Church that is perishing be required of us, we command your brotherhood, prescribing it in virtue of obedience and at peril of your order, honour, and benefice, that within fifteen days of receiving these letters you forbid throughout your whole diocese the celebration of every divine office, except baptism of infants and penance for the dying, and cause the sentence of interdict to be inviolably observed by all your subjects, so far as lies in your power; [Col. 0639A] taking heed for the bearer, as you wish heed to be taken for yourselves and your order. Otherwise, know that you yourselves will thereby be suspended from episcopal and priestly office.

May the Shepherd of shepherds and Prince of princes crown your reverence, obedient to God rather than men, with the unfading crown of eternal glory.

In the same manner to all bishops of England and Wales.

## LETTER CLXII. TO ROBERT, PROVOST OF ARQUES

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to ROBERT, Provost of Arques.

If what you have heard is true, it cannot be unknown to the lord pope; and through our messengers, whom we daily await, we trust that we shall shortly be informed concerning it. Truly, we desire the honour of our lord and friend as greatly as our own soul’s salvation. For he is most worthy of the highest honour from Christ: he has nobility to govern an empire, prudence supports his lineage; by the rigour of justice he restrains offenders; by the moderation of gentleness he governs subjects obedient to law; he reveres and protects the Church; in his ministers he receives Christ; and by kindness he wins the favour of all and binds their affections by services and benefits. He does not rage against his subjects, nor under the pretext of justice seek occasions [Col. 0639C] by which to torment the poor, drain the wealthy, and despoil them.

This was once the noble character of the Augustan emperors, which this man practises contrary to the custom of his neighbours and contemporaries; he knows and has learned, most beneficially and honourably,

> To spare the subject and to subdue the proud.

Therefore, with ready and willing mind, if God gives an opportunity, we shall exert effort and diligence that it may be done for him, in the Lord’s good pleasure, according to your desire. But we should wish the matter to proceed duly in its proper order, so that the rank of honour owed to one ascending may not be absent—the rank lying between what he possesses and what he desires. We believe that enough has been said to a wise man. Meanwhile, we earnestly ask you to hear carefully and heed what has been communicated to you through Master Robert, our clerk; and we ask you still more earnestly that, returning from us, you may be able to attend the hoped-for conference of the king and the count. [Col. 0639D]

## LETTER CLXIII. TO CLAREMBALD-ELECT AND THE BRETHREN OF SAINT AUGUSTINE’S

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to CLAREMBALD-elect and the brethren of Saint Augustine’s.

The greater the intimacy you have contracted with the Holy Roman Church, the more manfully you ought to rise up to repress and avenge her injuries, and demonstrate by the testimony of deeds how faithfully you adhere to her. Nor is there any doubt that it redounds to her injury that, though she has forbidden them, so many and such great acts have for so long been presumed against the English Church, against us, and against our people; although the lord king has often been warned through bishops, abbots, [Col. 0640A] subdeacons of the curia, and cardinals, whom he ought to have heard out of respect for their office, and although his later acts have always proved more atrocious than the earlier ones.

Therefore, because it is to be feared that further dissimulation may bind us guilty to condemnation before God, with whom there is no respect of persons and who punishes the powerful powerfully, we command you by the authority of the lord pope, whose office we exercise, and by our own authority, prescribing it in virtue of obedience, under anathema, and at peril of rank and order, that unless before the Purification of the Blessed Mary our aforesaid lord king has rendered fitting satisfaction to the Church of God and to us, you shall from that time cease from the celebration of divine offices, except penance, viaticum, and those things which the dispensation of the sacred canons permits, in favour of religion, at venerable places: [Col. 0640B] with doors closed, lay persons excluded, without ringing of bells or the solemnities which the Church customarily observes in times of peace and joy.

Further, we command that Geoffrey, Archdeacon of Canterbury, Robert his vicar, Richard of Ivelcestre, Nigel of Saccaville, William Giffard, Richard of Luci, and Adam of Cheringis, since they have been publicly excommunicated, be avoided by all the faithful; for whoever knowingly communicates with an excommunicated person condemns himself by equal anathema through unclean participation.

Likewise, to the convent of Malmesbury, and to Laurence, Abbot of Westminster, the Abbot of Saint Albans, and the Abbot of Saint Edmund’s, thus: from that time you shall wholly cease from the celebration of divine offices, and in all churches subject to your jurisdiction [Col. 0640C] forbid the celebration of every divine office, except the baptism of infants, penance, and viaticum.

## LETTER CLXIV. TO THE SAME PERSONS

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to CLAREMBALD, vice-abbot of Saint Augustine’s, and the brethren of the same place.

The more abundant the favour with which the most holy Roman Church has endowed your monastery, the more diligently you ought to obey her commands. Therefore, having firm confidence in your obedience, by the authority of the lord pope and our own, in virtue of obedience and at peril of honour, office, and rank, we command you that within fifteen days of receiving [Col. 0640D] these letters you abstain from all divine offices, except penance for the dying and viaticum, which necessity requires and the favour of religion permits to be administered privately, with doors closed and lay persons excluded.

Under the same threat we also command that, in every place under your ecclesiastical jurisdiction, you cause the sentence of this interdict, as far as lies in your power, to be inviolably observed.

Likewise to the abbots of Westminster, Saint Albans, Saint Edmund’s, and Malmesbury.

## LETTER CLXV. TO ARTHUR OF BURGHS AND HIS ACCOMPLICES

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to ARTHUR of Burghs and his accomplices.

[Col. 0641A] It has been reported to us, Arthur, that you have gravely and without cause offended both against us and against the Church of Canterbury, your mother. For, as has been represented to us, you and your accomplices presumed to go to Ireland, and there by false preaching, both yours and theirs, contrived that clerics and bishops of Wales should receive orders and sacraments as though from a new metropolitan established for them in Ireland. Know truly that by contriving such things and acting to the injury of the Church of Canterbury, your mother, you have sinned beyond measure.

Accordingly, we command and strictly enjoin upon you, at peril of your order and benefices, that you present yourself before us, together with Laurence, James, and Hucteridius, on the Purification of the Blessed Mary, to make satisfaction [Col. 0641B] to God, to us, and to the Church of Canterbury, your mother, concerning these things and others that shall be alleged against you.

## LETTER CLXVI. TO RICHARD, PRIOR, AND THE CHAPTER OF DOVER

“We have lamented,” etc. See the similar letter addressed to the convent of Canterbury.

## LETTER CLXVII. TO SIMON, PRIOR OF MOUNT OF GOD, AND BERNARD OF CORILO

THOMAS, Archbishop, to SIMON, Prior of Mount of God, and BERNARD of Corilo.
