Your belovedness received the command of the lord pope that you should meet the king, so that he might restore to us our church and his favour. We, however, were prepared, as you saw when present, [Col. 0641C] wholly to place ourselves, for the honour of God and of the king, at the mercy of God and of the king. This arrangement did not please him unless we bound ourselves to observe the customs which our predecessors had observed toward his predecessors. We therefore promised that we would willingly observe them so far as we could without prejudice to our order; and that we would most devotedly do whatever we could according to God in order to recover his favour. He would not consent unless we promised without qualification that we would observe those customs. This, however, was wholly unlawful, because some of them have been condemned by the Apostolic See.

Yet we are ready, if it pleases him, in accordance with the apostolic command, to receive back our church and our see together with his favour. [Col. 0641D] Remember that the lord pope, who imposed upon you in virtue of obedience the execution of his command, did not command that we should bind ourselves by any promises. We therefore beseech your holiness not to be reluctant to execute the obedience owed to the lord pope, but to strive to fulfil it as befits holy men.

## LETTER CLXVIII. TO BROTHER NICHOLAS OF MONT-ROUEN

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Brother NICHOLAS of Mont-Rouen.

Your brotherhood knows how patiently we have borne the losses, injuries, and insults inflicted on us and ours by our most beloved lord, the illustrious King of the English. But abusing our patience, he has broken forth into injuries against his most holy mother—the bride of the Crucified, we mean—and he has not feared to enslave her, for whose liberation the Son of God, God himself, willed to be condemned to a most shameful death. [Col. 0642A]

We warned him with a father’s affection; we repeatedly entreated him with the loyalty owed to a lord; we rebuked him with a pastor’s authority. But in our person he likewise despised his faithful father and pastor; and, lest anything henceforth be withheld from the truth, he despised Christ, whose office we bear—an act more perilous to the Church and more ruinous to himself. Let these things be counted vain and let him despise them, as he customarily does, if the Son of God does not say to the pastors of the Church: “Whoever despises you despises me”; and, “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye.”

Our concern proceeded further: for the peace of the Church, the supreme pontiff addressed earnest prayers to him, but was not heard. He employed exhortations and [Col. 0642B] found a deaf hearer. He added rebukes; they were despised. At last the apostolic trumpet sounded threats, but not even so could faith and reason be awakened. Lest we omit anything possible, the King of France, who is his friend and lord, applied every effort and diligence; yet even he, despite the respect due to him, deserved not to be heard.

We came to meet with him, but were not admitted even to his presence; nor did he permit mention to be made of our name or of God’s cause. Afterwards we sent him honourable men as messengers and open letters, as he had requested, which set forth both the justice of the Church and the substance of our petition; but, so far as he was concerned, our labour and theirs came to nothing. We had relied upon the good faith of the Empress, as you know, and she herself ought not to be unaware of it; but he utterly deceived us.

Therefore, since this patience of ours is harmful to the Church of God, yet more harmful to him whose latest acts are daily becoming worse than his earlier ones, and most harmful to us, who will have to render account before the judgment-seat of the Bridegroom not only for our own acts but also for his blood and the affliction of the Bride, [Col. 0642C] you may know for certain—and inform the Empress—that against his person and land we shall shortly, indeed very shortly, if life remains and God is the author, draw the sword of the Holy Spirit, which penetrates more sharply than any two-edged sword, so that it may bring ruin to hardened flesh and salvation to the sleeping—indeed, extinguished—spirit.

Persuade our lady, therefore, to hold us henceforth excused in that we can no longer dissemble; and let her know certainly that, if her son revives and, hearing God’s voice, accepts his mother’s counsel, she will find us ready for God’s honour and her will. Meanwhile, let us together mourn her dying son with the same affection, we who, God being witness, alike desire and pray with a like longing for his salvation and honour. We say these things with grief, tears, sobs, and sighs, as though our inward parts, torn by bitterness from the enclosure of our breast, were being seared with a burning brand. God knows it: in injury to him we must no longer exercise impious pity, preferring on earth mother, father, sister, or lord to him. There is no sorrow like this sorrow; but the charity of God, and the welfare and honour of him for whom care is taken, compel us to endure it with a strong spirit. Farewell.

[Col. 0643A] Greet and urge our brethren to obtain for us a spirit of counsel and courage, praying for the lord king that the spirit of repentance and godliness may be present with him, so that his peace with the Church of God and with us may be restored in the Lord.

## LETTER CLXIX. TO SILVESTER, TREASURER OF LISIEUX

His own to his own: greeting, and steadfastness of spirit.

If he who knows how to produce marvels by the traffic of oath-taking speaks great things and spreads grand claims, we think it no wonder, nor should we yield to amazement at the matter. For it is better that we perish through another’s crime than through our own fear. But hold this certain: whatever falsehood the notorious craftiness of the oath-taker may utter, whatever threats the crafty severity of the torturer may make, [Col. 0643B] through God’s mercy neither death nor life nor angels nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the charity of God which has subjected us to tribulation.

But not even that man of Pavia, until iniquity is brought to completion, until the pressure of our condition vanishes. Let at least the traces of liberty begin to appear for the encounter with him; and, with the same zeal by which liberty itself was being prepared for utter destruction and was believed to be extinguished from its roots, let its traces show themselves more conspicuously and liberty itself rise again stronger. Do you not know that great trees grow for a long time and are uprooted in one hour? He is foolish who expects their fruits and does not consider their fall.

Let it therefore console you that the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they have been honoured and exalted, will vanish away as smoke vanishes. Wait a little, [Col. 0643C] to see what the whisper of the gentle breeze—in which is the Lord—will hiss at them: “Yet a little while, and the sinner shall not be; you shall seek his place, and shall not find it.” Thus far.

Moreover, if our excommunicates are to be absolved, or have already been absolved, it is established that they are or were excommunicated. It follows, therefore, that those who knowingly communicated with them have incurred upon themselves the stain of excommunication. What follows from this hereafter, let them see to it themselves. Know one thing: John did not receive those benefices for nothing. He has some recompense, for we have certainly heard from men returning from the curia that, through him, the king has renounced the royal customs which the king demanded that we should grant and confirm to him. We desire this to reach the ears of the king and [Col. 0643D] your fellow provincials through your agency, while my authorship remains concealed. Yet do not allow yourself to be praised as its author, so that, at least in this way, that talkative man may be put to shame for his presumption and stripped of renown for the vanity of his glory.

But be strengthened and be stout-hearted, for through God’s mercy our salvation—or the vigour of ecclesiastical censure—is nearer than false cruelty pretends or deceitful flattery assures itself. Farewell.

May our Nicholas also prosper with you. Await the end with joy, for it is customarily the most important part of every matter, whereby each person receives certain proof of what he has awaited. Farewell again, and always.

## LETTER CLXX. TO THE CANONS OF PANTANEIA

[Col. 0644A]

Greeting, and may you confidently await the Lord’s consolation in the strength of patience.

Let not your heart be troubled, beloved ones, nor be afraid; for, by God’s favour, the salvation of the Church and your peace are at the doors, and you will shortly receive your prior, who passed safely and gladly through us, having attained his desire. Meanwhile, let your faith not fail, for you know well and retain in memory that perpetual woe is announced to those who have lost endurance, while for those who persevere in faith a crown of glory is laid up in the bosom of the Father of mercies, who humbles the proud and exalts the humble.

Nor must his help be distrusted if it is often not bestowed upon the patient according to their desire. For, as the Apostle teaches, patience is tested through the straits of tribulation and shines forth more brightly; advancing virtue is ennobled by the fruitful offspring of merits, through which it is crowned with more august glory as its reward. [Col. 0644B] Without doubt, however, a Christian is worse than an unbeliever if he thinks God forgetful of his justice, mercy, and truth to such an extent that he suspects the tormentors of the Church and of Christ’s poor can escape God’s judgment, and that tears may continue forever in the eyes of the saints contrary to truth’s promise.

The wicked do sometimes receive from the Lord a momentary power over the children of grace, so that through their agency they may be cleansed, tested, or guarded. But blessed Job, the model of patience and virtue, was given as an example and proof to believers that the Lord will not long leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the just. Therefore, if the spirit of the followers of Satan, swollen by power received, has risen against you; if it seeks to drive you from the place where you promised God conversion of life and stability, let your steadfastness in the Lord by no means abandon the post entrusted to it. Rather, let it await the Lord’s saving help, and, as befits saints, confidently oppose the shield of patience to terrors and threats.

By the authority of the lord pope and our own, in virtue of obedience and at peril to your salvation and order, we forbid you to leave your church and houses for any reason, unless harsher force and inexorable necessity drag you away unwilling and compelled. We have, moreover, by a special [Col. 0644D] command of the lord pope solemnly excommunicated Count Hugh; and we command you, in virtue of obedience and at peril to your salvation and order, to deliver our letters of notification to our venerable brethren William, Bishop of Norwich, and Nigel, Bishop of Ely, so that the sentence which proceeds from the judgment of the Apostolic See may obtain its due force. Take every precaution not, in the absence of your prior, to make a settlement or do anything else that may redound to the Church’s harm.

## LETTER CLXXI. TO GILBERT OF SEMPRINGHAM

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to GILBERT of Sempringham: greeting, and may you gather scattered Israel in the spirit of gentleness.

[Col. 0645A] We remember having written to you on another occasion, directing you to recall our brethren who have been scattered on account of an oath to maintain their profession—an oath which, as we have heard, no institution of any religious order has customarily required. You were to remit the oath that caused so great a scandal, and thereafter treat them with such moderation as might suffice to restrain and correct faults and as befits a father and shepherd of souls. The lord pope also commands this very thing; not to obey his commands is tantamount to the greatest crime and is compared with the sin of idolatry.

But, as the frequently repeated complaint of your brethren indicates, you have either despised or ignored our command and have not yet taken care to remove so great a scandal from the Church. Yet you know that the Lord, whose essence is truth and whose words are life, [Col. 0645B] declares that woe hangs over him through whom scandal comes. Accordingly, we direct your brotherhood by repeated command, ordering you in virtue of obedience, to strive to recall and gather your brethren and restore the unity of peace in the house of the Lord, lest we be compelled by apostolic command to enact something harsher against you.

We also ask, warn, advise, and command you, in Christ’s stead and by the authority with which we are invested, to temper the severity of the zeal you have in the Lord, so that the fruit of our labour may endure and the work and expenditure of so great a labour may not perish after your days. For, as you know, “he who squeezes too hard draws blood,” and excess is the stepmother of salvation. We also ask [Col. 0645C] that, if the bearers of these letters have committed any fault, you show them mercy, and commend our pilgrimage to the prayers of the saints who are with you.

## LETTER CLXXII. TO THE SAME PERSON

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to GILBERT, the canons, brethren, sisters, and all members of the order of Sempringham.

How greatly, Brother Gilbert, we have hitherto loved, and still love, you personally and all members of the order of Sempringham, God knows; you also know it, Gilbert; and the whole order knows it. For, as our conscience bears witness, we have always loved, cherished, and supported that order and the whole body of the order more spiritually than all other orders. Therefore, the more we love you, the more disturbed and grieved we are when we hear that such things have arisen from you and your order as offend not only human eyes but God himself.

For we did not believe, since we have loved you so specially above others, that you ought to have undertaken anything important in your order without our counsel and knowledge. Yet there have reached the ears of the lord pope, and once also ours, most serious scandals arising from the order and houses of your order, scandals which have been disgracefully spread abroad through the greater part of the world. Therefore, to correct these scandals and wholly, through God’s mercy, [Col. 0646A] to root them out from the entire order, let all of you know that the lord pope has appointed us and commanded us to correct them and to regulate for the better the order and the houses of the order.

Accordingly, Brother Gilbert, we command and enjoin you firmly, in virtue of obedience, at peril of your possessions and under sentence of anathema, that you receive the letters of the lord pope and ours with due reverence and cause them to be read before the whole body of your order. Moreover, under anathema we command you, within the period fixed for you by the lord pope in his letters, to labour most diligently, setting aside every pretext and excuse, to carry out whatever he has commanded you. If you do not, we shall, in accordance with the command received from the lord pope, with the Lord willing, [Col. 0646B] put our hand to the work and, as he instructed us by his letters, diligently strive, with God’s aid, to accomplish and complete all things.

Nevertheless, we command you by way of counsel to present yourself before us on the Purification of the Blessed Mary, to answer and make satisfaction to the lord pope and to us concerning disobedience and other matters which may reasonably be alleged against you, unless you have carried into effect everything according to the tenor of the lord pope’s letters and within the period he has fixed for you.

## LETTER CLXXIII. TO MASTER VIVIAN

THOMAS, by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to Master VIVIAN, his faithful servant and advocate of the Holy Roman Church: [Col. 0646C] greeting, and may you in all things think and understand rightly.

Taking account of the legation entrusted to you and of the business committed to you, would that, through your approach to the lord king of England, nothing had been lost from the substance of the business, no derogation made from the authority of him who sent you, and nothing attempted, said, or done to the detriment of that authority and of ourselves. For, since you have once discharged the office entrusted to you, whether well or badly, the fixed period assigned for completing the legation ought to have made you—knowing the laws and professing legal learning—sufficiently cautious in every respect. See therefore that you are wise in prudence and proceed prudently, lest you become a byword and an object of derision to the magnates [Col. 0646D].

But if by your own authority you have obtained a new and recent office of legate, let the person concerned obey, and let him bear the burden to whom the advantage will belong; for such jurisdiction binds me in no respect. And indeed, when you say that you have as a fellow labourer the chamberlain of the supreme and great cardinal—I mean the priest who represents his lord—I am no less astonished at the presumption of this associate than at the concern of the principal person in this matter. And if this has been done at anyone’s risk, let him look to himself, that he may more cautiously avoid the danger of such presumption. Enough, I think, has been said for a wise man.

We nevertheless thank you for the concern which you bear for peace between us and our people—would that it were no less prudent than solicitous. But I fear lest, amid the subtleties and windings of words by which you conduct the affair, your work and industry may perish—God forbid!—and thus the concern of one who labours may be harmed. Moreover, as to your urging us to come down to the conference of the kings which they are to hold next Sunday at Saint-Denis: with what assurance, with what hope of peace, and on what grounds you have done this with such urgency we cannot understand from your mandate; and thus we greatly wonder that you have been so ready to summon us. Yet, out of reverence for the Holy Roman Church and affection for you, though, as we fear, into uncertainty, we shall, at your insistence and by God’s mercy, meet you on Friday at the castle of Corbeil, so that we may hear more promptly from your own mouth what fruit we are to obtain from your labour and undertaking, and what honour and glory you are to receive. [Col. 0647A]

[Col. 0647B]

Farewell; and may God provide that you are not caught in the king’s mousetrap, from which scarcely anyone who has entered into dealings with him has been able to escape.

## LETTER CLXXIV. TO R., ABBOT, AND WILLIAM, PRIOR OF THE VALLEY

To the venerable brethren R., abbot, and WILLIAM, prior of the Valley, THOMAS, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, greeting.

Your affection may remember that, just as we had been troubled at the departure of Master Gerard, clerk and our friend, so, on hearing of his return, we were greatly gladdened through you. Therefore, through you, beloved brother prior, and through our clerk Master John, Gerard’s intimate acquaintance, we gave him counsel which, God being witness, we believed at the time to be more conducive to his honour and advantage [Col. 0647C]. But he, preferring to follow the impulse of his own mind, turned to the service of the lord king of the English, binding himself, as we have certainly learned, by the bond of fealty and oath. Would that he may conduct himself there in such a way as neither to offend God nor injure his reputation!

He knows—he before whom we shall render account in the strict judgment of our deeds, words, and the movements of his own soul—how often, by letters and messengers, and with what earnestness, we pressed the supreme pontiff to grant us leave to recall him, excusing his departure under the pretext of a permission which the said Gerard claimed to have obtained from the Apostolic See. But the lord pope steadfastly denied that he had given this permission. At last our messengers returned [Col. 0647D] from the Apostolic See, bringing us leave to recall him and the prescribed form of oath; once this has been sworn, he is directed to be absolved and restored to his former condition. The lord pope also requests the most Christian king of the French to restore his favour to him on this account and to permit him to remain in his land according to custom.

We send you both the form of oath and the rescripts of the apostolic letters, earnestly asking that you make these known to him and advise him to provide for his salvation and honour, and to set the witness of conscience and the dreadful judgment of God before worldly splendours and temporal goods. If he is willing to fulfil the lord pope’s command, we shall receive him as a most dear son and treat him with brotherly love. But if he refuses this, [Col. 0648A] we ask that your diligence make this known to us as well.

## LETTER CLXXV. TO MASTER LOMBARD

THOMAS of Canterbury, to Master LOMBARD.

We send to you the bearer of this letter, a poor clerk, who comes from a certain poor house of nuns serving God in England. He will explain to you more fully in person their miseries and troubles; and we wish you to set these before the lord pope, together with our own troubles and losses and those of the Church of Canterbury, as earnestly as you can.

Your discretion knows well how the king of England, while you were with us, despoiled the English Church, and especially that of Canterbury, of its goods and possessions, and attempted utterly to destroy it [Col. 0648B]. Now again, to our disgrace and to increase our humiliation, he is extorting a very large levy throughout our see and through all vacant bishoprics; he has also ordered this to be done throughout every church in his kingdom, both great and very small. That is, through the intervention of bishops, he has permitted bishops, abbots, and lesser clergy in each church to make this levy themselves, so that, once it has been made, they are to assign wholly to that same king and his agents whatever they receive from it.

Moreover, he utterly destroys, alienates, and lays waste the woods, towns, and all possessions of the Church of Canterbury. In addition, he has publicly circulated throughout his whole kingdom, and especially in every church, both very small and great, to our humiliation, the letters of our suspension which the lord pope, as it pleased him—although we had not deserved it—sent to that king [Col. 0648C]. We tell you this truthfully, so that you may communicate it with all possible diligence to the lord pope and to our friends. Further the business of the bearer of this letter, as far as justice permits, for the love of God and of us.

## LETTER CLXXVI. TO A CERTAIN FRIEND

THOMAS, by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury, to his beloved N. . . . , greeting and the affection of sincere love.

Let your affection know that, by the favouring grace of God, we are safe and well, and that all things will be prosperous. Since we possess most complete hope and confidence in the sincerity of your affection, we command you to seek out carefully what you know to be expedient for your mother, the holy Church of Canterbury, and for us, and to make it known without delay, more promptly, through the bearer of this letter or another [Col. 0648D].

## LETTER CLXXVII. TO HENRY II, KING OF ENGLAND

To HENRY, king of England, THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury.

A consideration of twofold reason urges us to lay before your royal majesty, with ready and faithful mind, those things which we know to be expedient for you. Since we are joined to your highness in most sincere affection, and contemplate the recompense of the last judgment with the inward eye [Col. 0649A], we see plainly how incumbent it is upon us both to urge upon you, with ready exhortation, those things which pertain to the glory of earthly honour, and to recall you, with most dutiful concern, from that which opposes your salvation. Especially because, if one whose office gives him the duty of speaking does not bring forth saving warnings when another’s salvation is in danger, he makes himself guilty of his brothers’ blood, since by deadly silence he leaves in the perversity of his way the person to whom he refuses necessary counsel.

Lest perhaps you attribute this to our own inventions, we set down for you the words of the prophet, in which it is said: “If, when I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ you do not announce it to him, so that he may turn from his evil way, he indeed shall die in his iniquity; but I shall require his blood from your hand.” We therefore, terrified by this prophetic—indeed divine—threat, and joined to your royal highness by the bond of faithful affection, have always endeavoured to advise you through fearless admonition concerning what we thought altogether expedient for your salvation, for your glory, and indeed for earthly honour itself [Col. 0649B].

In particular, at our last conference, when we took leave from you to return, we remember that we represented to you with pious concern that, whatever your sovereign authority might allow concerning other articles, this seemed wholly unworthy, alien from all reason, condemnable not merely by human judgment but also subject to divine judgment: namely, that because of the archbishop of Canterbury you compelled so many other persons—men and women, clerics and laypeople, young and old, entirely innocent of every royal offence—to go into exile from their own homes [Col. 0649C], especially when, as they say, some of them have no blood relationship whatever with that same archbishop.

Since you graciously heard these things, deigned to acknowledge that we spoke truth, and promised me a favourable reply shortly thereafter, we wonder that we have received nothing further from you on this matter; although we attribute this to your great occupations. We ask that, in accordance with the assurance you gave us by your word, you relax your edict concerning them, and do not conceal from the ears of a faithful friend what you decide to do in this matter.

## LETTER CLXXVIII. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0649D]

To his most reverend lord HENRY, by God’s grace illustrious king of the English, duke of the Normans, count of Anjou, and duke of Aquitaine, THOMAS, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, greeting, and the grace to act rightly in all things.

To speak about God requires a mind very calm and free. Therefore I shall speak to my lord—and would that he were peaceable toward all. I beseech you, my lord, to endure with patience some admonition which, through the grace of God that is never idle, contributes to the salvation of your soul and to my deliverance. Distress surrounds me on every side. For tribulation and anguish have found me, set between two most grave and fearful things, and fearful between two grave alternatives [Col. 0650A]: silence, I mean, and admonition.

If I keep silent, death awaits me, nor shall I escape the hand of the Lord, who says: “If you do not announce to the sinner his sin, and he dies in his sin, I shall require his blood from your hand.” If I admonish you, I fear—God forbid—that I shall not escape my lord’s displeasure. Let there not happen to me what that wise man says: “When one who is unwelcome comes or is sent to intercede, one must fear lest the mind of the angry person be provoked to worse things.” What then shall I do? Shall I speak or be silent? Certainly there is danger either way. Yet, because it is safer to fall into a man’s displeasure than into the hands of the living God, trusting in the mercy of the Most High—in whose hand are the hearts of kings, and who will incline them wherever he wills, and would that it be to the better part [Col. 0650B]—I shall speak to my lord, since I have begun once already. For good things are often conferred upon unwilling people, especially when their benefit rather than their wish is considered.

In your land the daughter of Zion, the bride of the great King, is held captive, oppressed by many and afflicted by those who have long hated her—those by whom she ought rather to be honoured than afflicted. This is especially so in your case, when one considers the individual benefits which God bestowed upon you at the beginning of your reign, in its middle years, and almost until now. Release her and permit her to reign with her Bridegroom, so that God may do you good, your kingdom may immediately begin to recover strength, reproach may be removed from your line, and the fullest peace may arise in your days.

Believe me, most beloved lord, most serene prince [Col. 0650C]. The Lord is a patient rewarder and a long-suffering observer, but a most severe avenger. Hear me and do good. Otherwise, it is to be feared—God forbid!—that the Most Mighty may gird his sword upon his thigh and come with a strong hand and a great host to free his bride from the oppression and bondage of her oppressor, not without a great blow. But if you listen to me, since in this present moment the Lord must test your service as that of his valiant soldier, God will do you good and add glory to your glory in the generations of your sons and daughters through long ages. Otherwise I fear—may God avert it—that the sword will not depart from your house until the Most High comes openly to avenge the injury done to himself and his people [Col. 0650D], just as it did not depart from the house of Solomon. Although the Lord chose Solomon and bestowed on him such wisdom and peace that people said, “This is the son of wisdom and peace,” nevertheless, because he departed from God’s way and walked in iniquity upon iniquity, God divided his kingdom and gave it to his servant—especially because, after his sin, he did not at once seek to appease the Lord, as did David his father, who immediately after his offence humbled himself before the Lord, amended his fault, sought mercy, and obtained pardon.

Would that you too, by God’s grace, might do likewise. These things I write to you now; the rest we have entrusted to the mouth of the bearer of this letter, a religious man of great repute and, as we believe, faithful also to you. I beg that, if it please you, you trust him faithfully. Yet we desire rather to enjoy gracious and kindly conversation with you. May my lord fare well, once and always. [Col. 0651A]

## LETTER CLXXIX. TO THE SAME

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to HENRY, king of England.

“I have earnestly desired to see your face and to speak with you.” This is much on my own account, but especially on yours. On my own account, that when you saw my face you might recall the services which, while I acted in your service, I rendered to you devotedly and faithfully according to my conscience. So may God help me at the last judgment, when we shall all stand before his tribunal to receive according to what we have done in the body, whether good or evil [Col. 0651B]. And that you might be moved with compassion for me, who must live by begging among strangers—although, by God’s grace, we have provisions in abundance sufficient for our needs. We also have great consolation in what the Apostle says: “All who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution.” And the Prophet says: “I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread.”

There are three reasons why I speak especially on your account: because you are my lord, because you are my king, and because you are my spiritual son. Since you are my lord, I owe and offer you my counsel and whatever service a bishop owes his lord, in accordance with the honour of God and holy Church. Since you are my king, I am bound to show you reverence [Col. 0651C] and admonition. Since you are my son, by the nature of my office I am bound to rebuke and correct you. For a father corrects his son, now gently and now harshly, so that in this way or that he may recall him to doing good.

You ought to know that by God’s grace you are king. First, because you must form yourself as king, and your life, by the best morals, so that others may be stirred by your example to better things, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “The world is fashioned after the example of its king.” Secondly, you must guide others: soothing some and punishing others by the authority of power which you have received from the Church, both through the sacrament of anointing and through the office of the sword which you bear to restrain evildoers against the Church. For kings are anointed in three places: on the head, breast, and arms. This signifies glory, knowledge, and strength [Col. 0651D].

Those who in ancient times did not observe God’s ordinances but transgressed his commands had glory, knowledge, and strength taken away from them and from their line: as happened to Pharaoh, Saul, Nebuchadnezzar, Solomon, and many others. But to those who, after sinning, humbled themselves before the Lord in contrition of heart, the grace of God came with all the aforesaid gifts more abundantly and perfectly, as to David, Hezekiah, and very many others.

Christ founded the Church and purchased its liberty with his own blood, enduring scourges, spitting, nails, and the anguish of death, leaving us an example that we should follow in his footsteps. Therefore the Apostle says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him. If we die with him, we shall also rise with him.” The Church of God consists of two orders [Col. 0652A]: clergy and people. Among the clergy are the apostles, apostolic men, bishops, and the other teachers of the Church, to whom the care and governance of that Church have been entrusted. They are to conduct ecclesiastical affairs so that everything may be directed to the salvation of souls. Thus it was said to Peter, and in Peter to the other rulers of God’s Church—not to kings or princes: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.”

Among the people are kings, princes, dukes, counts, and other powers, who are to conduct secular affairs so that they may bring everything to the peace and unity of the Church. Since it is certain that kings receive their power from the Church, not the Church from them but from Christ, then, with respect to your peace, you have no right [Col. 0652B] to command bishops; to absolve or excommunicate anyone; to drag clerics before secular tribunals; to judge concerning churches or tithes; to forbid bishops to hear cases concerning the violation of faith or an oath; or to do many other things of this sort which are written among your customs, which you call ancestral. For the Lord says: “Keep my laws.” And again, through the prophet: “Woe to those who enact unjust laws, and to scribes who write injustice, that they may oppress the poor in judgment and use violence against the cause of the lowly among God’s people.”

Let my lord therefore, if it please him, hear the counsel of his faithful servant, the admonition of his bishop, and the correction of his father. Henceforth let him have no familiarity or communion with schismatics, nor make any agreement with them in any way [Col. 0652C]. For nearly the whole world knows how devotedly and honourably you received the lord pope; how greatly you cherished and honoured the Roman Church; and how greatly the lord pope and the Roman Church loved and honoured your person, and heard you in all matters in which, according to God, they were able to do so.

Therefore, lord, if you desire the salvation of your soul, do not, on any pretext, take away from that Church what belongs to it, nor oppose it in anything contrary to justice. Rather, permit it to have in your kingdom the same liberty which it is known to have in other kingdoms. Remember the profession which you made and set down in writing upon the altar at Westminster, concerning the preservation of the liberty of God’s Church [Col. 0652D], when you were consecrated and anointed king by our predecessor. Restore also the Church of Canterbury, from which you received promotion and consecration, to the condition and dignity in which it stood in the times of your predecessors and ours. Restore to us in full the possessions belonging to that Church and to us—the towns, castles, and estates which you have distributed at your pleasure—and all things taken away, whether belonging to us, our clerics, or laypersons. Permit us also, if it please you, freely, peacefully, and in complete security to return to our see and freely exercise our office, as we ought and as reason requires.

And we are ready faithfully and devotedly, according to our power, to serve you as our most dear lord and king in whatever we can, saving the honour of God and the Roman Church and preserving our order [Col. 0653A]. Otherwise know for certain that you will experience divine severity and vengeance.

## LETTER CLXXX. TO THE SAME

To his lord and friend HENRY, by God’s grace illustrious king of the English, duke of Normandy, count of Anjou, and duke of Aquitaine, THOMAS, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury—formerly his in temporal matters, but now much more in the Lord—greeting, and true repentance accompanied by amendment.

“I waited and waited” for the Lord to attend to you, that you might turn and do penance, departing from the perverse way, and cut off from yourselves your crooked counsellors, at whose prompting and counsel you have, as is believed, almost fallen into the abyss. But I fear—God forbid!—that it may be into that abyss of which it is said: “When the sinner comes into the depths, he despises” [Col. 0653B].

Although until now we have waited in vain, silently considering and most earnestly expecting whether a messenger might come who would say: “Your son the king, your lord, long deceived by guile and led into the Church’s ruin, is, through the inspiration of divine mercy and in the abundance of great humility, hastening toward the liberation of the Church, toward every satisfaction and amendment”; yet we do not cease every day to entreat the Almighty in suppliant devotion, that what we have long celebrated in prayer concerning you and for you we may obtain in a swift and fruitful result [Col. 0653C].

And this is why the care of the Church of Canterbury—over which God has at present appointed our priesthood, though unworthy, while you govern the temporal affairs of this kingdom—constrains us, especially because we are still held under the hardship of exile, to send your majesty letters of admonition, exhortation, and rebuke. We must not become an excessive dissembler concerning your offences, if any there are—though indeed there are, and we grieve over them not a little—especially those which are everywhere committed by you against the Church of God and ecclesiastical persons, without regard for the dignity either of office or person; nor must I seem so negligent as to endanger my soul. For one who neglects to amend what he ought to correct unquestionably shares the fault of the person acting [Col. 0653D].

For it is written: “Not only those who do evil, but also those who consent to it, are judged participants.” Those consent who, when they can and ought, do not resist, or at least rebuke. For an error which is not resisted is approved; and truth, when it is not defended, is oppressed. Nor is he free from the guilt of hidden complicity who ceases to oppose a manifest crime.

Just as, most serene prince, a small city does not diminish the prerogative of a present kingdom, so your royal power ought not in the least to unsettle or alter the measure of religious administration. By right, judgments concerning priests have always proceeded from priestly counsel. For bishops of whatever sort, even if human error has entered in, provided that they do not in any way transgress against the religion of faith, are in no wise seen as capable of, or subject to, punishment by secular power [Col. 0654A].

The duty of a good and religious prince is to restore shattered and torn churches, build new ones, honour God’s priests, and protect them with the highest reverence, following the example of Constantine, the pious prince of most blessed memory. When a question concerning clerics was referred to him, he said: “You cannot be judged by anyone”—that is, by secular judges—“for you are reserved for the judgment of God alone.” We read also that the holy apostles and their successors, established under divine attestation, commanded that persecutions and disturbances should not be inflicted upon them; that one should not begrudge those labouring in the Lord’s field; and that the stewards of the eternal King should not be expelled from their own sees.

For who can doubt that Christ’s priests are to be regarded as fathers and teachers of kings, princes, and all the faithful? [Col. 0654B] Is it not recognized as pitiable madness if a son attempts to subjugate his father, or a disciple his teacher, and to subject by unjust bonds to his own power the person from whom he ought to believe that he himself can be bound and loosed not only on earth but also in heaven? If you are, and wish to be, a good and Catholic king—as we believe and still more earnestly desire—then, with respect to your peace, you are a son of the Church, not its prelate. You ought to learn from priests, not teach them; in ecclesiastical matters you ought to follow priests, not go before them.

You possess the privileges of your authority, received from God for administering public laws, so that, not ungrateful for his benefits, you may usurp nothing against the disposition of the heavenly order [Col. 0654C]. But, that you may possess sounder judgment, relinquish with all humility and manifold satisfaction, and do so most swiftly, those things which perhaps more through malicious intelligence and counsel than through your own will you have improperly usurped against the Church. Otherwise, the hand of the Most High, stretched out against you, may shoot arrows at you as at a target. For the Most High has bent his bow to shoot in the open at you, who are unwilling to repent.

Do not be ashamed, whatever evil men may suggest to you or traitors murmur—traitors not only to you but to God—to humble yourself under the mighty hand of God. He is the one who exalts the humble and casts down the proud; who takes away the spirit of princes in vengeance for himself and his own. For he is dreadful, and who shall resist him? [Col. 0654D] You ought not to have forgotten in what state God found you, how greatly he advanced, honoured, and exalted you; how he blessed you with the begetting of children, established the throne of your kingdom, and enriched you with abundant possessions to the envy of all your enemies, so that almost everyone up to now has cried out in admiration: “This is the one whom the Lord has chosen.”

And what will you render, or what can you render, to him for all that he has done for you? At the prompting and insistence of those around you who persecute the Church and ecclesiastical men, and have always persecuted them as far as they could, will you repay good with evil—oppressions, tribulations, injuries, and afflictions inflicted upon churches and ecclesiastical persons? Are these not they of whom the Lord says: “Whoever hates you hates me. Whoever despises you despises me. Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye”? Certainly, even if, leaving all that you possess, you take up your cross and follow our Lord Jesus Christ, you will scarcely—or not at all—appear as a faithful and grateful requiter of the benefits received from him [Col. 0655A].

Search the Scriptures with those who know them, and you will find that Saul, although chosen by the Lord, perished with his whole house because he departed from God’s ways. King Uzziah of Judah also, whose name was widely and far spread because of the many victories granted him by the Lord, became so lifted up in heart to his own destruction—because the Lord helped and strengthened him everywhere—that, scorning reverence for the Lord, he wished to appropriate for himself what belonged not to his office but to that of priests: namely, to burn incense upon the Lord’s altar. For this he was struck with leprosy by the Lord and expelled from the Lord’s temple by the hands of priests; and so he remained until the day of his death, full of the leprosy for which he had been expelled from the Lord’s temple [Col. 0655B].

Many other kings, holy men of immense riches, because they exalted themselves in the marvels of the world and presumed to rebel against God, perished in their mysteries, and in the end found none of their riches in their hands. King Ahaz also, because he too usurped the priestly office, was likewise struck with leprosy by the Lord. Uzzah likewise, though he was not a king, because he touched the ark of the Lord and held it when it tottered toward falling, the oxen kicking against it—since this did not pertain to him but to the ministers of the temple—was struck by divine wrath and fell dead beside the ark of God.

It is a proverb of the king: “When the neighbouring wall is on fire, your own concern is at stake.” A man corrected by another’s misfortune provides better for himself. Most beloved king, God willed that the ordering of matters belonging to his Church should pertain to its priests, not to secular powers [Col. 0655C]. He willed those powers, if faithful, to be subject to the priests of his Church. Therefore do not claim for yourselves another’s right and ministry, which has been assigned to someone else. Do not contend against him by whom all things are established, nor appear to fight against the benefits of him from whom you have received your authority.

Almighty God willed that clerics of the Christian religion be ordained and judged not by public laws or secular powers, but by pontiffs and priests [Col. 0655D]. Christian kings ought to submit their acts of execution to ecclesiastical prelates, not place them above such prelates. For it is written that no one but the Church ought ever to judge priests, and that it does not belong to human laws to pronounce judgment in such cases. Princes ought to obey the Christian statutes of the Church, not set their own power above them; princes should bow their heads to bishops, not judge bishops.

For there are two powers by which the world is chiefly governed: the sacred authority of the pontiff and royal power. The burden of priests is the heavier inasmuch as they must render account, even for kings themselves, at the divine judgment. You surely ought to have known that you must depend on their judgment [Col. 0656A], not that they can be reduced to your will.

Very many bishops have excommunicated some kings and others emperors. If you inquire into a particular instance involving imperial persons, blessed Innocent excommunicated the emperor Arcadius because he consented to the expulsion of Saint John Chrysostom from his see. Saint Ambrose also excommunicated the great emperor Theodosius, for an offence which did not seem so grave to other priests, and expelled him from the church. At last, by suitable satisfaction, he deserved to be absolved. There are many other examples of this kind.

When David had committed adultery and homicide, the prophet Nathan was sent to him by God to rebuke and correct him. He was rebuked, and swiftly amended his conduct. For the king [Col. 0656B], laying aside the diadem of his head and casting off imperial majesty, did not blush to humble himself before the prophet’s face, confess his sin, and ask pardon for what he had done. What more need be said? Moved to penitence, he sought mercy and obtained forgiveness.

And you, most beloved son, most serene king, most reverend lord, following the example of the most excellent David, the most devout king, of whom the Lord says, “I have found a man according to my heart,” turn to the Lord your God with a contrite and humble heart, and perform exact penance for your offences. For you have fallen and erred in many things, which I still pass over in silence, waiting to see whether perhaps the Lord will inspire you to say with the prophet: “Have mercy on me, O God [Col. 0656C], according to your great mercy, for I have sinned greatly against you and done evil in your sight.” For the Lord is near to those who are upright in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit.

These things, my lord, I write to you for the present, passing over the rest in silence, waiting until I see whether my word takes hold in you; whether it brings me from you worthy fruits of repentance; and whether I hear from those who report it, and rejoice with those who say: “Your son the king was dead, but has come to life; he was lost, and has been found.” But if you do not hear me—who formerly, before the majesty of Christ’s body, used to pray for you amid abundant tears and no small groanings—then there indeed I shall cry out against you and say: “Arise, O God, judge your cause. Remember your reproaches and the injuries which are done to you and yours all day long [Col. 0656D] by the king of the English and his people. Do not forget the humiliations of your Church, which you founded by your blood. Avenge, Lord, the blood of your servants which has been shed. Avenge, Lord, the afflictions of your servants, whose number is infinite. The pride of those who hate and persecute you and yours has risen so high that we can endure them no longer.”

King, whatever your people do, all these things will be required from your hands. For he who gives the cause of damage is held to have caused the damage. The Son of the Most High himself, unless you come to your senses, unless you cease from harassing churches and clerics, and unless you restrain your hands from troubling men, will come, at the groans of those in chains and at the voices of those crying to him, with the rod of his wrath; for it is now time for him to execute judgments against you in the equity and severity of his spirit [Col. 0657A]. For he knows how to take away the spirit of princes, and he is dreadful among the kings of the earth.

We do not say these things to you in order to put you to shame, or to provoke you to greater indignation and anger, as perhaps the malicious persons about you—who lie in wait for your soul day and night and strive, by their wicked and unjust whisperings, to turn your mind away from us—mutter and insinuate. May God give them according to their works, and according to the wickedness of their devices. Rather, we say them in order to make you more cautious in providing for and caring for your soul, and in avoiding the danger now at the door. And because it especially concerns us to provide for your soul [Col. 0657B], since its care and charge have been entrusted to us, and since we must render an account of it at the strict judgment, hear these things kindly and act upon them. Make use of our service as may please you, provided that we do not offend God or, by action or connivance, work to the detriment of your soul and ours. For what will it profit you to gain the whole world at the peril of your soul? Consider where the emperors are, where the kings and other princes are, where the archbishops and bishops are who have gone before us. They indeed laboured, and others entered into their labours. What more is there to say? Thus the world and its glory pass away. Therefore remember your last things, and you shall never sin; and if you do sin, you shall repent during your life. [Col. 0657C] May your dear favour avail me, if you are converted to the Lord your God in true humility and prompt repentance. Fare well thus, again and always.

## LETTER CLXXXI. TO THE SAME PERSON

To his most beloved lord HENRY, by the grace of God king of the English, duke of the Normans and Aquitanians, and count of Anjou, THOMAS, by the same grace humble minister of the holy Church of Canterbury: greeting, and perseverance at all times in good; and manful resistance to malicious and corrupting suggestions, which easily corrupt good men.

We write briefly to you, lest through a multitude of words we become more wearisome; though would that we were [Col. 0657D] more acceptable to you, as to our most beloved lord. He who searches hearts knows this, whatever our enemies may otherwise and falsely mutter and whisper—and indeed, to speak more truly, they are more your enemies than ours. Therefore we still exhort you on behalf of almighty God, we adjure you by the power of the Holy Spirit, and for the remission of your sins we require of you: the restoration to us and ours, without evil intent, of your favour, true peace, and secure safety; likewise, to the Church of Canterbury, restoration in that fullness and liberty in which our predecessors held it better and more fully, and in which we ourselves held it after becoming archbishop; and restoration of the possessions, churches, and prebends pertaining to that same church which have fallen vacant [Col. 0658A] since this dissension arose between you and us. Likewise, restore these things to our people, so that under your lordship we may enjoy and use them as freely as our predecessors used them, and as we ourselves did after our promotion. Thus the Church may rejoice at our return—having, as we believe, been deprived for so long a time of our presence, to the peril of your soul and ours for many reasons—and may cease to grieve at the hardship of our absence. Do this, my gracious lord, with a joyful and glad heart, so that God may grant and restore to you and your heirs that peace which your heart desires for the salvation of your soul and of the people entrusted to you by the Lord. And we certainly are, and shall be, ready to render every service to you more earnestly and devotedly than [Col. 0658B] we have ever done before, provided that we do not offend against God or against our order.

Concerning the movable goods taken from the Church of Canterbury, from us, and from ours, we solemnly assure you before God and the whole world—even were the whole world present—that sin is by no means, on no grounds, forgiven unless what has been taken is restored, if the person who took it or caused it to be taken has means from which to restore it. Hence blessed Augustine says: “If a thing taken away is not restored when it can be restored, repentance is not performed but feigned.” And elsewhere: “I say with the greatest confidence that the man who intervenes on another’s behalf so that he need not restore what he has taken, and the man who does not compel, insofar as he honourably can, one who has fled to him for refuge to make restitution, are partners in fraud and crime.” For [Col. 0658C] we more mercifully withhold our aid from such men than we grant it. Hold this as certain; do not doubt on any account that it is most true. And if anyone should preach the contrary to you—even an angel from heaven—he is accursed, and let him be, and shall be, so long as he persists in that judgment. Take heed, therefore, my dearest lord, how cautiously you proceed in this matter, lest retention of an ill-gotten thing, which is nothing but ash and worm, drive you—God forbid—into impenitence and expose you to a peril from which you cannot be cleansed, either by prayer or by fasting.

Furthermore, your discernment ought to know that, although not all bishops are holy, they nevertheless occupy the places of saints. Even if they do not shine by merit of life, they ought nevertheless to be imitators of those whose places they hold, insofar as [Col. 0658D] divine mercy has granted this to them. Therefore, since holy men fought for the law of their God even unto death and were not afraid of the words and threats of their persecutors—for He is to be feared more, who can cast both soul and body into Gehenna—we too must, as God inspires us, keep, cherish, and defend His laws. This must not be imputed to us as pride or malice, but as the necessity of our office. For the Lord says: “Keep my laws.” And again in the Gospel: “Whoever shall break one of these least commandments of mine and shall so teach men shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven.” We believe that enough has been said to the wise; and therefore, as from a most dear lord, we ask in the name of our Lord Jesus [Col. 0659A] Christ to be heard and favourably heeded by you, so that God may hear and heed you at the strict judgment and receive you among His elect, when neither strength nor power, nor dominion nor riches, nor secular laws or customs, will be able to help anyone—nor anything else except divine mercy and the fruit of preceding works. Would that this may rest most firmly in your mind every day and never depart from your thoughts. May my lord gladly admit, hear, and always heed counsellors in this matter, so that God may do him good and increase life and peace for him and his heirs for long ages. Nor may those escape temporal punishment who, by their wiles and elaborate frauds, have striven to overturn and disturb my lord’s good purpose—his purpose, conceived, as we believe, with much devotion of heart during the first seven years of his reign, of showing honour to churches and ecclesiastical persons. [Col. 0659B] May my lord flourish for ever; and, for the greater good of God’s Church and of us, may he live for long ages.

## LETTER CLXXXII. TO THE SAME HENRY II

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to HENRY, king of England.

Your royal nobility may remember that, in the presence of the lord king of France and very many others who were there, I offered you that, for the honour of God and your own honour, I was ready to put myself wholly at the mercy of God and of you, and thus obtain your peace and favour. This form of words, lord, did not please you [Col. 0659C] unless I promised observance of the customs which our predecessors had observed toward yours. I therefore granted that I would observe them insofar as I could without prejudice to my order; and if I knew how to promise anything further or more explicit in the Lord, I was ready, and still am ready, to do so in order to recover your favour. I have never served you more willingly than I am prepared to do now. And because it has not yet pleased you to accept these things, I beseech your majesty to remember my services and the benefits which you conferred upon me. For I remember that by oath I owe you the protection of your life and limbs, all earthly honour, and whatever I can do for you according to God; as for my dearest lord, I am ready to do this. And God knows that I have never served you more willingly than I shall do, if it pleases you. May my lord ever flourish.

## LETTER CLXXXIII. TO THE SAME HENRY II

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to the king of England.

Christ, the searcher of hearts, judge of souls, and avenger of sins, knows with what purity of mind and sincerity of affection we made peace with you, believing that you were dealing with us simply and in good faith. For what else, most serene lord, ought we to have understood from your words, by which the humanity of your kindness toward us [Col. 0660A] shared itself with us, whether in reproving or soothing us? What else but complete goodwill, peace, and security did your letters, sent to our lord the king, your son, commanding that everything which we and ours had possessed before we departed England should be restored to us and ours, signify? Yet behold: as God knows, we regard the manner in which things are being carried out as more serious for the risk to your honour than for the injury to your interests; it does not display simplicity or good faith. For the restitution which you commanded to be made to us and ours has been deferred until the tenth day, on the pretext of Ranulf, whom the counsellors of our lord, your son, judged should meanwhile be consulted so that your command might be fulfilled. Who these men are, how matters were conducted, and with what good faith, [Col. 0660B] you may investigate when it pleases you. But we are persuaded that this is being done to the detriment of the Church and of your salvation and honour, unless you correct it more carefully. For in the meantime this aforesaid Ranulf is ravaging the goods of the Church and openly even now storing our provisions in Saltwood Castle. As we have learned from persons prepared, if it please you, to prove this before you, he has boasted in the hearing of many that we shall not long enjoy your peace, because we shall not eat whole bread in England before he, as he threatens, takes our life from us. You know, most serene lord, that a person who can correct a fault yet neglects to amend it shares in the guilt. And what could the aforesaid Ranulf do unless he were supported and armed by your will and authority? [Col. 0660C] Your discernment shall hear and judge as it sees fit what he answered the letters of the lord king, your son, writing to him on this affair. And because, as now appears from clear indications, the holy Church of Canterbury, mother in Christ of the Britons, is perishing through hatred of our head: lest it perish, but may escape, we shall, God propitious, expose our head for it against the oft-mentioned Ranulf and his accomplices, persecutors of the Church, ready for Christ not merely to die, but to endure a thousand deaths and every torment, if by His grace He deigns to grant us strength for endurance. I had intended to return to you, lord; but necessity draws me, unhappy man, to an unhappy Church. With your permission and favour I shall return to it, and perhaps [Col. 0660D] perish lest it should perish, unless your mercy deigns to afford us another consolation more swiftly. But whether we live or die, we are yours and shall always be yours in the Lord; and whatever happens to us and ours, may God do good to you and your children.

## LETTER CLXXXIV. TO THE SAME PERSON

This we request from our lord the king, according to the command and counsel of the lord pope: that, for the love of God and the lord pope, and for the honour of holy Church and the salvation of himself and his heirs, he receive us into his favour; grant his peace and full security, without evil intent, from himself and his people to us and to all who left the realm with us and on our behalf; restore to us the Church of Canterbury in that fullness and [Col. 0661A] liberty in which we held it best after becoming archbishop; and restore all its possessions, to be held and possessed as freely, peacefully, and honourably as the Church and we held and possessed them more freely and honourably after our promotion to the archbishopric. Likewise, let our people have these things; and let us have all churches and prebends belonging to the archbishopric which have fallen vacant since we left the land, so that we may dispose of them as of our own, according to our pleasure. And we shall do for him whatever an archbishop owes his king and prince, saving God’s honour and our order.

## LETTER CLXXXV. TO LOUIS, KING OF FRANCE

[Col. 0661B] To his beloved lord LOUIS, by the grace of God most illustrious king of the French, THOMAS, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury: greeting and the blessedness of both lives.

Having received and read the letters of your highness, we have perceived clear tokens of your generosity and affection toward us. Although, to confess the truth, no merits of ours have preceded so as to obtain what you offer freely, we know and are certain that you have greatly loved us from the prompting of your own noble nature. May He who is the rewarder of all good things reward you. For our part, according to our ability, we are ready, before God and before men, to answer your kindness with every service we can render. Yet though we have always experienced your generosity toward us, we have now found it fuller and more welcome, when in our desolation you deigned to visit us by your letters [Col. 0661C] and offered us, should it be necessary, the refuge of your consolation. By this word you acquired for yourself whatever remained of our heart, rendered it all beholden to you, and strengthened our hope. For, apart from my lord the king of England, there is no mortal man in whom we put greater confidence for goodwill, honour, and aid, should we need it, although we have never deserved it. Nevertheless, words concerning peace have passed between my lord the king and us, and we hope that God will incline his mind and turn his course away from hostility to us. But if it please you, should it happen that you speak with him, rebuke him because he has ever believed anything adverse concerning a man who served him so greatly and faithfully, who always loved him with true affection, and upon whom he himself conferred so much honour. And you, dearest lord, command us if ever we can do anything for your honour and pleasure; for there is no man in the world who would do it more gladly than we.

## LETTER CLXXXVI. TO THE SAME PERSON

To his lord LOUIS, illustrious king of the French, THOMAS, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury: greeting, and loving devotion in service.

We believe that it has come to the knowledge of your serenity [Col. 0662A] that a dispute had arisen before the lord king between the clergy and barons of England on the occasion of certain customs of the king and kingdom. When, on this account, great indignation against us and our fellow bishops was increasing, at length, God being propitious, we reached such an agreement that peace was restored on both sides and the favour of the lord king—who had been somewhat angered against us on this account—was restored to us in full. Moreover, by the exigency of our sins, a certain report stirred up a greater indignation against us in the lord king: it declared that we had defamed him before the lord pope and before you, and had wickedly represented him as a persecutor and oppressor of holy Church. My lord, your highness knows well enough whether we sent you this report concerning our lord [Col. 0662B] king; and, as you know, we ask that you carefully excuse our innocence and that of our people before the lord king. For neither did we say these things about our lord, nor, if perhaps others have said them, do we give authority to their words. For it is neither true that he is such a man, nor does it seem that such a thing could have been said. We also wish you to know that, however much the lord king may have been angered, he has nonetheless shown honour and reverence to ecclesiastical persons; nor has he, on the occasion of this indignation, laid hands upon their persons or ecclesiastical possessions. If anything else has been reported to you, lord, know it to be contrary to the truth. And, as said above, between the lord king and his clergy no discord remains, thanks be to God; every controversy having been put to sleep, peace has been wholly restored. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXVII. TO THE SAME PERSON

To his most beloved lord LOUIS, by the grace of God illustrious king of the French, THOMAS, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Canterbury: greeting from Him who gives salvation to kings.

When we consider the events of your time and the fortunate condition of you and your kingdom, more and more every day God, the rewarder of all good things, seems to prosper your ways and actions, granting you also, through His great mercy, continual triumph and victory over your enemies. Nor is this surprising, for all things work together for good to those who love God. And behold, dearest lord in Christ, your faithful abbot of Pontigny has been promoted, by the common assent of clergy and people, to be archbishop of the Church of Lyons, and was consecrated by the lord pope at Montpellier on the Sunday before the approaching feast of blessed Lawrence. [Col. 0662D] Concerning him, indeed, we confidently trust by God’s grace, as concerning our dearest friend, that both for love of you and for ours he will always, as long as he lives, be faithful to you, and will subject and bring into subjection to you and your kingdom, as is right and to the extent of his power, his city and those regions. Fare well in Christ, dearest lord.

## LETTER CLXXXVIII. TO THE EMPRESS MATILDA

[Col. 0663A]

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to the Empress MATILDA.

We give thanks to God, who has made your nobility more illustrious by the distinguished marks of virtue than by those of birth; and who, having raised you high in the Roman world through most famous blood, does not cease to glorify you in the world through good works. For from East to West your name is great in the Lord, and the churches of the saints recount your alms. Although the aid which you dispense to God in His members is highly pleasing to Him, we believe that your concern for ecclesiastical peace and liberty is no less pleasing to Him—a concern which, as report has it, you pursue with such great zeal that you can say with the Apostle: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” Therefore we, who remember that by the ties of humanity and your benefaction we are deservedly beholden to you, speak more confidently in your hearing concerning the peace of the Church, for your salvation and the temporal and eternal glory of your son. We earnestly ask and beseech you in the Lord to approach him more diligently, so that with the same devotion [Col. 0663B] he may procure peace for the Church as he desires, through the merits of the saints, that God’s peace may be procured for himself, his heirs, and his lands. For, to our profound grief, it has been proclaimed from East to West that he oppresses the churches of his kingdom intolerably and exacts from them certain unheard-of and unprecedented demands. Even if they sought these things, [Col. 0663C] former kings nevertheless ought not to have sought them. It may indeed be that in his time—upon whom God has bestowed much wisdom—so great an oppression can somehow be endured. But perhaps after his days there will reign men who desire to devour the Church with their whole mouth and who, hardened like Pharaoh, will say: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go.” At your prayers and exhortations, we ask him to remember how God raised him above the titles of his noble fathers, beyond the boundaries of his ancestors, and extended his borders beyond their expectation. What profit will it be to him before the Lord if he transmits his sins to his heirs and, as it were, appoints opponents of God and the Church in his testament? What good does it now do his predecessors if he, taking occasion [Col. 0663D] from their offences, has offended God as though by hereditary right? Others, most serene lady, had to appease God by acts of service; other gifts ought to have been offered for the salvation of their ancestors and the redemption of sins. Sacrifices from plunder do not please God—unless perhaps it can please the Father that the Son be sacrificed to Him. If he repents, the Father of mercies is still ready to forgive; but without doubt He will judge without mercy those who do not show mercy. He is mighty, and punishes the mighty mightily. He is terrible, and takes away the spirit of princes, so that stronger torment may press upon the stronger. He has bent His bow and prepared it, and has placed in it instruments of death, soon to shoot them, unless they permit His bride—out of love for whom He deigned to die—to be free, and allow her to be honoured with the privileges [Col. 0664A] and dignities which He purchased for her on the cross with His blood. You should, if it please you, employ both a mother’s diligence and a lady’s authority in calling him back: you who acquired a kingdom and duchy for him by many labours and transmitted hereditary rights to him, on the occasion of which the Church is now oppressed and trampled down, innocent persons outlawed, and the poor intolerably afflicted. What we can do for your salvation and his, we do gladly, continually imploring God’s mercy by such prayers as we can make. We shall pray confidently if, peace having been restored to the churches, he returns with ready devotion to God, his author and benefactor. Nor should he be ashamed to humble himself before God by repentance, since among the ancient kings [Col. 0664B] whose memory is blessed, nothing is more ascribed to glory than the renown of repentance, a king’s zeal for God, reverence for the priesthood, and humility, the most faithful guardian of virtues. By such sacrifices King Hezekiah, Josiah, and Constantine pleased the Lord and attained glory among men from generation to generation.

## LETTER CLXXXIX. TO OWAIN, KING OF WALES

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to OWAIN, king of Wales.

We render you abundant thanks because, amid the hazards of war and the hostile harassment of enemies, you do not neglect, as we have learned from your letters, [Col. 0664C] to bestow care and attention upon God’s Church. Yet there has lodged in our mind, not without concern, a statement which we read in your letters: namely, where it was said that the Church of Bangor ought not by right to be subject to us, although we overlook this because of the affection which binds us to you. But as to your request that, with our consent and permission, a bishop be consecrated in that church by someone other than ourselves, we do not agree at all and never shall agree. We shall send you our messenger, or certainly something else which for the present we do not wish to entrust to a letter, as we inform you through the bearer of this letter. Meanwhile we command you to ensure, by your diligence, that the aforesaid church and the Church’s honours remain at peace, and that no election or alteration of the Church’s [Col. 0664D] temporalities takes place. If it does, we shall declare it void.

## LETTER CXC. TO THE SAME PERSON

THOMAS, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury, to OWAIN, prince of the Welsh: greeting, and the rendering of devoted service to Him whom to serve is to reign.

To whom more has been entrusted by the Lord, from him an account is due for more. As He glorifies those who serve faithfully with a happy reward, so He strikes the undevout with a terribly severe vengeance, so that though comfort may be brought to one who fails, he is nevertheless not sustained amid miseries. But among all services rendered to Him, He accepts none more graciously than when the honour owed by the faithful is given to the bride for whom He shed His blood; and nothing does He punish more severely than when she is afflicted before His eyes with shameful injuries. [Col. 0665A] You yourself, beloved son, can recognize this, knowing with how great bitterness husbands avenge insults if they are inflicted upon their wives before their eyes. But since you are faithful to Christ your Lord, His bride is the Church of Bangor, which, as you know, now for almost ten years, deprived of its own pastor through the contrivances of those who ought to have sympathized with and provided for it, has groaned tearfully over its desolation before the eyes of the bridegroom. Therefore, because we love you with sincere charity and desire your honour to be advanced in the Lord, we urge your affection by entreaty, counsel, and an injunction for the remission of sins, to permit this aforesaid church, according to the command of the lord pope, kindly to be relieved of such great miseries by the due provision of a pastor. [Col. 0665B] Do not admit anyone’s counsel against this, where so great a danger to souls is at stake. But if you have bound yourself, by the counsel of any cleric or layperson, man or woman, to something which hinders the church from being ordered according to the canons, we absolve you from that promise or obligation by apostolic and our own authority. We forbid you, on peril of your soul, to comply hereafter with whoever that person may be, against your salvation. Furthermore, we command you to restore to the Church to which they are addressed, and to us, the letters of the lord pope which you caused to be suppressed; and to permit the cleric who carried them—whom we absolve from the obligation by which you bound him not to return—to come to us as he ought, without any impediment. Until now we have shown you deference, and we shall continue to show it as to a beloved son wherever we can do so according to God. But unless you obey the apostolic commands and ours, especially in matters known to concern your salvation, we shall no longer be able to show you deference to or spare you, but shall diligently carry out what God commands and the Apostolic See urgently enjoins. [Col. 0665C]

## LETTER CXCI. TO THE SAME PERSON

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to OWAIN, prince of the Welsh.

The searcher of hearts and judge of souls knows that we love your honour and salvation with sincere charity in the Lord, as those of a most beloved son in Christ, whose care has been so greatly entrusted to us; that we desire and pray [Col. 0665D] for the highest good to come to you as to ourselves; and that the greater our love for you, the more earnestly we make known to you what concerns your salvation and honour. Remember therefore, son, what great blessings the Lord has done for you; and, for the honour and successes which He has granted you, give Him worthy thanks, with His mercy going before you. Thus may He who comforted your youth and manhood in adversity, raised you up, and directed you toward prosperity, bring your maturity to a blessed end and a glorious departure, reward your labours with rest and eternal glory. For God glorifies those who glorify Him and makes His despisers ignoble. We know you to be a discerning man, able to weigh by the balance of reason the rewards of good and evil, right and wrong, and mindful through frequent meditation [Col. 0666A] that you must die. As experience teaches, young men die soon and easily; but it is impossible for those who are old to live long. But suppose that, contrary to the usual course, an old man’s life is extended longer: certainly they fail as they live, and death, imperceptible, gradually steals through all the limbs of the body, while the senses grow duller. For:

> The passing years plunder each thing from us  
> and take away the pleasures in which we once rejoiced.

But although the end of all, both righteous and sinful, is one and common destruction, there is nevertheless a grave difference between the deaths of the former and the latter. The death of God’s saints is precious in His sight, for it conveys them out of misery into eternal glory; but the death of sinners is most evil, for it carries unrepentant transgressors of the law into Gehenna, where moths shall be spread beneath them and worms shall cover them—worms, indeed, which do not die, just as the fire shall not be quenched for ever. [Col. 0666B] What profit, then, son, is it if someone gains the whole world, which he can scarcely retain for a moment, and thereby acquires for his soul both these torments and the rewards of its labours?
