Since the merciful Lord has exalted and honoured you above all your contemporaries among your people, waiting for you with much patience and summoning you to repentance through many benefits and dangers alike, we ask, admonish, and exhort your nobility in the Lord; and for the remission of sins we enjoin upon you that you more favourably receive and more diligently carry out the apostolic command concerning the leaving of your kinswoman and the ordering of the Church of Bangor. [Col. 0666C] Thus may God heap up and multiply for you and your offspring the fruit of obedience which you rightly desire, both in this life and in the eternal recompense of the righteous. Otherwise we cannot refrain from carrying out the command laid upon us. If you love your kinswoman, you possess abundant resources with which you can provide for her usefully and honourably. Love her as a kinswoman, not as a wife; for it ought to be enough that God and His Church have hitherto endured your sin in so manifest a fault, with great scandal and pernicious example. Henceforth so great a scandal cannot be endured, and it is necessary that the Church, so long deprived of its pastor, receive its own bishop, who, [Col. 0666D] with the Lord’s help, may procure the salvation of souls. Farewell.

## LETTER CXCII. TO MATILDA, QUEEN OF SICILY

To the most serene lady and most beloved in Christ MATILDA, illustrious queen of the Sicilians, THOMAS, by divine dispensation humble minister of the Church of Canterbury: greeting, and may you so reign in Sicily in this temporal life that you may rejoice eternally with the angels in glory.

Although we do not know your face, we cannot be ignorant of your glory, which the splendour of noble blood enhances, the distinction of many and great virtues adorns, and the renown of fame renders illustrious with countless praises. Yet among the other virtues which we gladly embrace with those who have heard of them, [Col. 0667A] we owe especial thanks to your generosity, and return the fullest thanks with such devotion as we can now offer: for it has comforted our fellow exiles, Christ’s outlaws, and our kinsmen, fleeing to your lands from the face of the persecutor in their tribulation. This indeed is a great part of true religion most pleasing to God: that mercy bring consolation to those suffering for righteousness; wealth assist the poor; and the unfettered amplitude of power share in the needs of the saints. For God is won by such sacrifices, temporal glory is made glad and enlarged, and the gracious favour of all good things is gained. By these merits you have earned, especially among others, our own devotion; all that we are and can do we devote to your service. The first-fruits of this devotion, [Col. 0667B] insofar as time allowed, we recently offered to your excellence by advancing your requests before the most Christian king, as you may perceive from his petitions presented to our beloved, the illustrious king of Sicily, and from the words of the venerable prior of Crispin. His literary learning, purity of life, and unblemished reputation make him beloved and commendable to all good people. He is a man of most approved conduct, sound doctrine, and, insofar as human judgment can determine, sanctity perfect for his time. We desire and ask your highness to hear him with as much reverence as you would hear the whole Western Church if it stood at your feet. This is both out of reverence for his person and because of the merit and authority of the Church of Cluny, [Col. 0667C] whose needs he administers. From the days of our fathers, that church has been recognized throughout the Latin world as possessing, almost as its own, the glory of perfection in monastic religion. In other matters which he may tell you on our behalf, believe him, if you please, as you would us. Farewell.

## LETTER CXCIII. TO STEPHEN, CHANCELLOR OF THE KING OF SICILY

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, to STEPHEN, chancellor of the king of Sicily.

It is indeed likely that, for the salvation and consolation of many, the Lord has raised you to a position suited to your nobility and merits, so that your material resources may correspond to your virtue, and that the will born—or rather [Col. 0667D] bestowed—by the Lord to aid the needy may obtain its welcome effect. Many therefore resort to you, yet we have heard of none returning without consolation. A new day-star shines forth from the East upon the western world; it sends out the rays of its brightness as a pledge of public happiness and, strengthening all the broken-hearted, persuades them that better times are at hand. But shall the Church of God alone be deprived of the fruit of public joy? Shall she be disappointed in her hope—she who nurtured you, and for whom your father, noble by the blood of his ancestors and by his own virtue, so often exposed himself to swords, and in the confession of Christ, as is the hope of the faithful, attained in peace the palm of martyrdom?

Yet among all churches holy Canterbury is more afflicted, and there is no sorrow like hers. All her friends have forsaken [Col. 0668A] her; indeed, they persecute her in her distress. Whoever defends the law is counted an enemy of the king. We are scattered; we have been proscribed. Our crime is the assertion of ecclesiastical liberty. For under our persecutor, to profess it is an indictment for injured majesty. For he alone is thought faithful who approves contempt for religion, who persecutes the divine law, to whom insult against priests is welcome, and who reveres the slaughterhouses of the ancient tyrants as though they were a sanctuary of justice. Because we have dared to speak for the house of the Lord, we live in exile with all our kinsmen and friends, one of whom is our sister’s son. We ask that, wherever necessity requires, he may be aided by the generosity of your highness, all the more earnestly because it is right that we, and the others who suffer for the Lord, should conceive firmer hope from your nobility [Col. 0668B]. We also ask that you believe him concerning what he will tell you on our behalf, and that, if occasion should arise, you promote the cause of God and our own before the Roman Church.

## LETTER CXCIV. TO ROBERT, COUNT OF LEICESTER.

THOMAS, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to his beloved son and friend in Christ, the noble man ROBERT, Count of Leicester: greeting with blessing.

I expected a letter of consolation from you, as from a most dear friend; words of satisfaction, as from a most devoted son of the Church and one truly penitent. But since neither does your letter announce consolation nor your words suggest satisfaction, with fatherly affection I recall your offence to your mind [Col. 0668C], so that the penance inflicted upon you by God may at least thus elicit from you satisfaction conducive to your soul’s salvation—a salvation which, as my conscience bears witness before God, I desire for you no less than for myself.

Your mother, the Church of Canterbury, has a mother’s cause to complain of you and your princes; and I also, your father in Christ and, such as I am, her spouse. First, because of the injury inflicted upon us; secondly, because it has not been revoked; thirdly, because of your delayed repentance. Perhaps you disregard the injury, fail to revoke what has been inflicted, and—what is more dangerous, and gives me greater grief—approach repentance more slowly than you ought, though without it no guilty person is absolved. Setting aside filial affection, sons have entered into their mother’s very bowels, with no regard for humanity [Col. 0668D], despising also the reverence and devotion owed by children to their fathers: against every form of law, against all ecclesiastical authority, and even against the customs of this very realm, which they call ancestral. By the destructive pretext of those customs all things have been thrown into turmoil; by their harmful consequences the liberty of the Church has been harshly shaken and for a time oppressed—a liberty which, by God’s grace, can be overthrown by no human ingenuity. Through the straits imposed by them, injury is done to Christ through damage to the Church, and the path leads to ruin.

The father’s spoils have been taken away; the father has been judged and condemned by his sons, and counted among the wicked. Has what has been done in these times and in this land ever been heard of since the beginning of the world? That the Archbishop of Canterbury should be judged, condemned, and compelled to give surety—he whom the divine judgment once declared to have been unjustly proscribed [Col. 0669A]? Truly the land has been delivered into the hands of the ungodly, whose wickedness is not yet complete. For the rod of Assyria, the rod of the Lord’s wrath, has been entrusted to them for the correction and restraint of clerics. When its task is fulfilled—as now, through God’s mercy, it is almost upon the threshold—there is reason to fear that, God forbid, the Lord’s wrath may turn the other way, and, more fiercely inflamed, may crush and destroy from His city every worker of iniquity, young and old alike, in vengeance for the injury done to Himself and His own.

Nor is this surprising. For at this time there is no one who does good, not even one. Who ever afflicted father and mother with insults, treated them with injuries, condemned them to punishments, and did not fall under the curse that proceeded from the mouth [Col. 0669B] of the Most High? “Whoever curses father or mother, let him himself be accursed.” And if this is the punishment for cursing, will not the punishment for evil doing be more severe? It surely will. Therefore turn back, most beloved sons; perform speedy penance, lest—God forbid—the divine vengeance now at the doors fall upon you and upon your children. Has it slipped from your memory what Scripture says: “They who seek by inheritance to possess the sanctuary of God shall go into extermination unto the third and fourth generation”? For Christ founded the Church and purchased her liberty with His own blood. Who then is he who seeks to reduce into slavery the price of this purchase, to judge another’s servant? He must stand or fall to his own Lord.

But if you desire to remedy this disease, lest danger come upon the nation, meet the peril to your souls [Col. 0669C], and provide also for the salvation of your most serene prince and lord. Should you perhaps ask how aid may be given, I answer that ample and prudent provision will be made for the prince’s salvation and your own if, with humble repentance and suppliant satisfaction, he withdraws from injury to Christ and the Church. These things are fitting for a prince; they win divine favour and preserve honour for himself and his descendants. These words also are full of humility and, as I judge, of the affection which a priest owes his king: fearing for his own danger and that of his prince, and desiring for him the salvation he desires for himself, both by reason of benefaction and by the necessity of his office. Farewell.

Moreover, if it please you, receive our messengers kindly [Col. 0669D], hear them more kindly still, and with them promote the cause of God and of His Church effectively, as occasion may most suitably present itself, for the remission of your sins. Farewell again, and always.

## LETTER CXCV. TO COUNT HUGH.

THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, to HUGH, Count.

Having read the expressions of your charity and examined the canons’ letters, in which they testified that they daily experienced the benefits of your generosity, my spirit was so gladdened that all my inward being brought forth praise, pursuing with manifold thanksgiving Him from whose gift comes your conversion, so fruitful, salutary, and illustrious [Col. 0670A]. For this gains glory for you in heaven, joy for us in spirit, and for the whole kingdom the sweetest fragrance of an example. Thus the other enemies of Christ’s cross may learn from you, if they wish, to shake off the devil’s yoke and run after us in the fragrance of your ointments.

For this reason also, with the Lord’s favour, we shall henceforth devote ourselves more diligently at all times to the honour and advancement of you and yours. At the beginning of our peace, even before we had entered the land, you fulfilled our command and counsel no less magnificently than kindly, presenting yourself as an example to others to do likewise. Nevertheless, your persistent urgency of entreaty on behalf of those disobedient priests places us under no small constraint [Col. 0670B]. For your discretion knows, dearest son, that as humble poverty deserves reward, so pride deserves punishment. Consider, if you please, how contumaciously and proudly disobedient and resistant those poor clerics have been, as you write; and I do not doubt that you will refuse their prayers a hearing if you weigh the enormity of their offence. These are the men who, persisting in manifest disobedience, fought against God Himself and brought scandal and mourning upon the world. Moreover, polluting the whole body of Christ by the ruinous contagion of their detestable example, they presumed—while persisting, as we have said, in manifest disobedience—to consecrate Christ’s body and celebrate other divine offices. To that ministry men would undoubtedly still be unworthy, even if they put on angelic purity [Col. 0670C].

But we do not now proceed to assail their crimes, lest we be compelled to aggravate their punishments. And certainly, had not reverence for your intercession, which is exceedingly welcome to me, stood in the way, these fruitless trees would altogether be cut down by the axe laid to their roots. Yet those whom their own wickedness condemns eternally shall, by favour of your petition, obtain no small mercy. We nevertheless wish them to remain as they are until, as we hope, we soon come and see you, intending to fulfil, as far as we can according to God, your wishes concerning the absolution of those under interdict. Meanwhile, out of reverence and affection for you—an affection we hold altogether dear [Col. 0670D] and welcome—we have granted this bearer permission to preach the Gospel, to baptize, and to administer viaticum, provided only that the last necessity of mortals compels it.

## LETTER CXCVI. TO HIS BELOVED DAUGHTER IDONEA.

THOMAS, by the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved daughter IDONEA: greeting, and enduring strength in the virtue of obedience and zeal for justice.

God chose the weak things of the world to overthrow the strong; and when men failed, leaders lost courage, and priests almost abandoned the law, the virtue of a woman extinguished Holofernes’ audacity, swollen against God. Esther was chosen to secure the salvation of the exiled and condemned Church. When the apostles faltered [Col. 0671A], fled, and—what is worse—fell into unbelief, holy women followed the Lord when He was given over to His Passion; and, an even clearer sign of greater faith, they faithfully attended Him even when He was dead. Thus they deserved to be strengthened by the sight and speech of angels, to receive the first fruits of the Lord’s resurrection, and to announce the Redeemer’s glory and the Gospel’s grace to the disciples as they lay hidden and almost overwhelmed by despair.

We hope, however, that by God’s agency you will enter the fellowship of those women, whose example you embrace, inflamed by zeal for Christ. For the spirit of charity, which has cast fear out from your heart, will by its grace make those things which the necessity of the Church demands be done more steadfastly and urgently seem to you—not only possible, though arduous, but even easy to one who believes. Therefore, in the hope conceived from the fervour [Col. 0671B] you have in the Lord, we command you and enjoin it upon you for the remission of sins: deliver the letters of the lord pope which we send you to our venerable brother Roger, Archbishop of York, if possible in the presence of our brethren and fellow bishops; or, if you cannot have them present, do this in the presence of whoever may happen to be there.

And lest the original document be suppressed by some evasion, hand its copy to those standing around to be read aloud, and explain to them the purport of the letters as the messenger will instruct you more fully. A great reward is set before your labour, daughter: remission of sins, imperishable fruit, and the crown of glory which the blessed sinful women, Magdalene and the Egyptian woman, after the stains of all their former life had been wiped away, at last received from Christ [Col. 0671C] the Lord. May the Mother of Mercy be present with you, to entreat her Son—whom she bore for the world’s salvation, God and man—that He may be guide, companion, and protector [Col. 0672A] of your journey. And may He who shattered hell’s bars and broke the demons’ power restrain their licence, lest they harm you, and hold back the hands of the wicked. Farewell, bride of Christ; and always think Him present.

## LETTER CXCVII. TO THE COUNTESS OF WARENNE.

T., by the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury, Primate of the English, and legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved daughter M., Countess of Warenne: greeting.

A remarkable complaint has reached our ears from the religious brethren, the monks of the Church of Lewes. They state that, by an ancient gift of the Counts of Warenne—namely, the grandfather and father of William your husband, and William himself, before you had received your dower [Col. 0672B]—they had always peaceably possessed, as the endowment of their church, a tithe of the money revenues from all the count’s demesnes. Yet after receiving investiture of your dower, you withdrew from those brethren the same tithe of money belonging to your dower. If this is so, we are greatly astonished, since you neither ought nor can claim for your dower anything known to have been bestowed in alms upon God and His Church. For it is cruel and close to sacrilege to reclaim what has once been devoutly offered upon the divine altar and transfer it to secular uses. We therefore offer you sound counsel and admonish you in the Lord: as you wish your own right to be freely preserved for you by God, so leave their right intact to the monks, and by no means retain for your dower the tithe of money granted to them [Col. 0672C]. Otherwise, we shall be unable to fail them in justice, whose debtors we are to all.

## VARIOUS LETTERS ADDRESSED TO ST THOMAS AND TO OTHERS.

[Col. 0671]

## LETTERS CXCVIII–CCCXIX.

Of POPE ALEXANDER III: to St Thomas; to the people of Canterbury; to Roger of York; to Henry of Rheims; to Rotrou of Rouen; to William of Sens; to the Bishop of Tours; to the bishops and clerics of England; to John, Dean of Orléans; to the Bishop of Aversa; to the clergy and people of Bangor; to Hugh of Durham; to Robert of Hereford; to Gilbert of London; to Stephen of Meaux; to Bernard of Nevers; to Jocelin of Salisbury; to the Bishop of Troyes; to Roger of Worcester; to Clerembald, elected abbot and monk of St Augustine’s; to the abbot and brethren of Pontigny; to the Cistercians; to the abbot of Clairmarais; to Simon, Prior of Mont-Dieu, and Bernard of Corilo; to Henry, King of England; to Louis, King of France; to the King of Scotland; to Count Henry; to Philip, Count of Flanders; to R., son of Henry; and to John Cumin.

(See under ALEXANDER III for the year 1181.)

## LETTER CCCXX. FROM ROTROU, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN, TO HENRY, PRIEST-CARDINAL.

[Col. 0671D]

ROTROU, Archbishop of Rouen, to HENRY, priest-cardinal.

On behalf of the lord King of England we give every assurance [Col. 0672D] that he has made neither oath nor promise, either personally or through messengers, to the emperor that he wishes to adhere to the schismatic and abandon the Church. Indeed, we are certain that, in whatever marriage negotiations were held, although the Germans laboured over this matter for three days, he was never willing to concede anything except with fidelity to the lord pope, the Church, and the King of France preceding everything else. By your letters, the empress and we ourselves have instructed him to clear himself of this imputation as swiftly as possible.

When we were at Rouen, and the emperor’s envoys were there, we heard of them but did not see them. When they earnestly sought to see the empress, she replied that she dared not because of the bishops. Nor did they see her. Let there be no doubt among you that she has wavered in any way concerning this matter. Indeed, girded with courage, she is greatly astonished at such reports. We sent to her the messenger whom you directed to us; he will tell you what he heard. Once the lord king’s messengers have returned from the emperor, we shall not delay informing you of the whole truth of the matter after careful inquiry [Col. 0673B]. You can judge from the tenor of the statements how false they are, since the king does not possess fifty bishops to produce. So far as lies in our power, we could neither endure nor look upon damage to the Church. You will report to the lord pope concerning these matters whatever seems proper to you.

## LETTER CCCXXI. FROM THE SAME TO THE KING OF ENGLAND.

ROTROU, Archbishop of Rouen, to the King of England.

We could not obtain from the legates the wording which you left with us, because many and ambiguous conditions were being advanced on both sides, by you and by them [Col. 0673C]. Yet it seemed that their abruptly departing without hope of peace would be consistent neither with your honour nor with your advantage. Therefore, while very much was being discussed between us, a proposal arose which in no way detracts from your dignity or honour, nor supplies Canterbury with any matter for future litigation. The proposal is this: that, for the love of God and the lord pope, you grant that the archbishop return to England, cause him to hold his archbishopric as fully as he held it before he departed, and likewise restore their own possessions to those who departed with him or because of him. We were pleased by the brevity and simplicity of this proposal, since it seemed entangled in no contrivances or suspicions. We therefore counsel and urge you not to hesitate to give it [Col. 0673D] your assent.

## LETTER CCCXXII. FROM THE SAME TO POPE ALEXANDER.

To POPE ALEXANDER, ROTROU, Archbishop of Rouen.

“Summoned by our lord king,” etc. See under Alexander III.

## LETTER CCCXXIII. FROM THE SAME TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY.

To THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, ROTROU, Archbishop of Rouen.

We know that your prudence is aware that obedience is better than sacrifices, and that it is the sin of idolatry to refuse submission, especially to him to whom all obedience is owed in the present Church [Col. 0674A]. And the lord pope, who has the power to compel, prescribed to us and to our venerable brother the Bishop of Nevers a definite form by which we should absolve our venerable brother, the Bishop of London. The mandate further provided that, if both of us could not be present, the other should nevertheless absolve him when requested. Accordingly, when he requested it of us on Easter Day, we absolved him according to the prescribed form, by the authority of the lord pope; and we enjoin you that this be kept secret by you, as will appear more clearly to your discretion from the papal rescript which we send you. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCXXIV. FROM WILLIAM OF SENS TO THE KING OF ENGLAND.

[Col. 0674B]

WILLIAM, Archbishop of Sens, to the King of England.

Your serenity informed us that, with our advice, the papal envoys might absolve the excommunicated without sworn security. But we have no authority from the lord pope concerning this, nor dare we advise them to transgress the lord pope’s mandate or to proceed in any affair contrary to the custom of the Roman Church. Saving his favour, they ought not to have shifted blame onto us, since they knew the lord pope’s mind more fully. For we judge that we benefit ourselves if we can in any way advance your honour or promote your advantage [Col. 0674C].

## LETTER CCCXXV. FROM THE SAME TO GRATIAN AND VIVIAN.

WILLIAM, Archbishop of Sens, to GRATIAN and VIVIAN, legates.

We are not a little astonished that you wished to transfer to us the burden of the question concerning the absolution of the excommunicated, so that, as we gather from the tenor of the letter of the lord King of England, under the cover of our counsel you represented to that king that you could be excused from the charge of transgression. You should not have shifted blame onto us in a matter in which no one can stain our integrity. But because we are bound to the lord pope and the Roman Church in such intimate devotion and by so indissoluble a bond that we ought neither to think nor advise anything by which the Church’s honour might seem diminished or the integrity of its reputation violated, we dare give your discretion no other answer than this: do not transgress the limits of the lord pope’s mandate, and do not in the present matter wish to establish anything that appears contrary to ecclesiastical ordinance and to the Roman Church—indeed, to the general custom of the whole Church—or that may in the future lead to the consequence of a pernicious precedent, unless perhaps you have received something different from the will of the lord of Canterbury [Col. 0674D]. May the Angel of counsel and strength be with you.

## LETTER CCCXXVI. FROM THE SAME TO POPE ALEXANDER.

[Col. 0675A]

To POPE ALEXANDER, WILLIAM, Archbishop of Sens.

“Still, Father, to your mercy,” etc. See under Alexander.

## LETTER CCCXXVII. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME.

To POPE ALEXANDER, WILLIAM, Archbishop of Sens.

“Impunity, mother of crimes,” etc. See there.

## LETTER CCCXXVIII. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME.

To the lord pope, the Archbishop of Sens: greeting [Col. 0675B], and every obedience with the deepest devotion.

“How, at the second conference of the kings,” etc. See there.

## LETTER CCCXXXIII. FROM PETER OF CELLES, LATER ABBOT OF ST REMIGIUS, TO THOMAS THE CHANCELLOR.

[Col. 0675D]

To his lord and dearest friend THOMAS, Chancellor of the King of England, Brother PETER, Abbot of Celles: himself and his possessions.

A man whom his own good fortune does not exalt is more admirable for his humility than for his high station. Glory contends with prosperity on your behalf—as I have learned from those who have seen and known you—more eagerly than competitively; and when defeated it is never confounded, nor does it ever grow insolent in victory. Glory trusts in prosperity, but in prosperity that is both glorious and prosperous. Whichever prevails, it does not cut away your humility or moderation [Col. 0676A]. Glory comes, but not pride; prosperity comes, but not extravagance. This is why, from the cloud of so great an eminence, you sent to the hiding-place of our poverty because you could not come yourself.

You asked for familiarity and friendship. If what you asked were granted, it would undoubtedly be regarded with amazement because of the respective stations of the petitioner and the person petitioned. For what proportionate relation is there between the Abbot of Celles and the Chancellor of the King of England? There is almost no comparison where there is no corresponding estimation. Who does not know you as second after the king in four kingdoms? Who does not count me first among the miseries of our brethren? I shall speak briefly: as much as I recognize in you what is more excellent, so much do I feel and know what is more lowly in myself. I therefore do not at all stretch out my hand to enter into friendship. But if I may belong even to the flock of incidental friends, I shall judge that your condescension has done well by me. I do not send those first fruits, because I hasten to confer a greater favour. I did not have those discourses of Master G., but I am seeking them; and at once, with all urgency, I appoint a copyist to this work for your use [Col. 0676B]. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCXXXIV. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME.

To his lord and dearest father THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, Brother PETER of Celles, a minister of whatever worth: himself.

We have become as men comforted by the consolation of your holiness, so affectionate, so pious, so full [Col. 0676C] of sweetness and charity. May the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, return to you the consolation by which you were pleased mercifully to regard our desolation. For the receipt of your letters raised our hearts, if not dead, yet already languishing. We showed this condescension and consolation of yours to our lords and friends; and, in divine hope and with their counsel, we sent your martyr to you as a wanderer. Receive him; and because he scarcely has where to lay his head in his own land, let him meanwhile serve beneath your protection and bring us back fitting wages. We indeed trust in God’s goodness and in your generosity of spirit, of which we have already had a foretaste, that although he crosses your sea with his staff, he will return in companies bearing many blessings [Col. 0676D]. We commit our brethren and messengers to the discretion of your holiness, that you may make provision for them. We also count you, our lord and fellow-brother, among all our people in every prayer and good work. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCXXXV. TO THE SAME.

To his lord and dearest father THOMAS, venerable Archbishop of Canterbury, Brother PETER, Abbot of St Remigius: most devoted greeting from his whole heart.

As I anxiously turn over in my mind what subject I should take up when I wish to write to you, scarcely anything presents itself—not because there is no lack of what may be said, but because reverence restrains the hand from speaking to one such as you. For I can say nothing worthy of the fortitude of your spirit; add nothing to your most steadfast endurance; and, in short, teach nothing to a mind that sees all things from afar and most fully measures the ends of events and future causes. Why should I set a heap of hay and straw before a manger to which you cling, abundantly fattened and satiated with richness and fatness [Col. 0677A]?

Yet I find this one service not unworthily reserved for me, to expend in your obedience: if I could drive away the flies that seek to sting your holiness with envious barking, or at least strive to blacken the sincerity of your faith by perverse interpretation. With the Lord’s help, these dead flies—the swarms abundant in Egypt, which surround Pharaoh king of Egypt as the “man of flies”—will not spoil the sweetness [Col. 0677B] of the ointment. For it will be kept for the day of Jesus’ burial, and in generation after generation it will be proclaimed that the Archbishop of Canterbury, setting himself as a wall for the house of Israel, imitates the footsteps of the ancient saints, while he follows Christ hanging naked on the cross, himself naked.

How then, like Abraham, shall I drive away these same flies that wish to defile the Lord’s unblemished sacrifice, unless I make a fan from the authoritative Scriptures, by which they may either be struck or at least driven away? For they say that the archbishop ought not so insistently to demand back his own from the King of England as to abandon the peace of reconciliation for lost money. They are mistaken by the appearance of truth or the flattery of falsehood. Those deceived by the appearance of truth must be instructed; those moved by flattery of falsehood must be repelled. Simplicity must be recalled [Col. 0677C]; malice wholly rejected.

Certainly, in every agreement and action one must weigh what should be done or left undone for the sake of what; and one must also weigh the times and their differing conditions, according to which the merits of causes change. In the primitive Church, patience alone had its place: the man who took one’s tunic was to be allowed the cloak as well. For one person, and elsewhere—that is, outside the Church—was persecuting; another person, and elsewhere—that is, within the Church—was suffering. But now that the Church has come to maturity, what was once permitted to the enemies of the Church is not permitted to her children. It is fitting for a mother to correct her son, as it was fitting for an orphan to endure an adversary.

For the bridegroom’s belly is read as adorned with sapphires; so that, just as before His Passion Jesus had said, “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple,” and similar things, so in His Passion He says to the apostles: “Let him who has no sword sell his tunic and buy one.” A just cause might rightly demand words that are good and consoling in God’s eyes, though doubtful and weak in the eyes of fools—unless the virtue of patience transcended every consolation, and you rejoiced more in consolation than a striking hammer gains from the blow. Iron sharpens iron, and through the wickedness of the King of England your invincible virtue is more brightly displayed. The more forcefully the press squeezes the olive, the more abundantly it produces oil. Bezalel does not make the hammered lampstand of purest gold in the Lord’s tabernacle except by drawing out sheets through the crushing [Col. 0678A] of file and hammer.

The hammer of the whole earth has not yet been broken; it is still necessary, that it may supply what is lacking of Christ’s sufferings in your body. But whom am I advising? Whom am I exhorting? To whom am I applying spurs? Surely, to one who needs no bridle; who is ready to walk farther than the road extends; who quickly passes even the finishing-mark, delayed by no dangers. For from afar he scents battle. He counts exile as homeland, because every soil is a homeland to the brave. Without labour he labours; without hunger he hungers; without pain he suffers; without bitterness he feeds on gall and wormwood. He is one man among thousands. While the giants groan beneath the waters, he laughs and mocks fortune as its wheel turns upside down. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCXL. FROM THE SAME TO CARDINAL ALBERT.

[Col. 0678D]

To CARDINAL ALBERT, SIMON, Prior of Mont-Dieu.

I and my brethren have earnestly desired to hear something of you, but for a long time this consolation has by divine providence been withheld from us. It will be like the greatest of gifts if you are pleased to assure our concern regarding your condition. For we have greatly desired to hear of the successful outcome of your legation. Our own condition is such as you have been accustomed to hear. For we are sinners, and would that, through God’s grace rather than our own merits, we might be able to offer God fruits worthy of repentance.

Furthermore, we earnestly entreat your charity to give aid and counsel to the lord of Canterbury, whom it is certain is in exile for justice’s sake. For, as the King of England confessed in the presence of the lord King of France and all who attended the conference [Col. 0679A], the sole cause of his exile and proscription is that he refused unconditionally to promise observance of customs which are admittedly contrary to God’s justice and the liberty of the Church. Moreover, the same king boasts that he has a privilege from the lord pope by which the power of the lord of Canterbury is suspended for as long as the king wishes to withhold his favour from him. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCXLIV. FROM NICHOLAS OF MONT-ROUEN TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY.

To THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, Brother NICHOLAS of Mont-Rouen.

Concerning your affair, let not the greatness of your fatherhood suppose, if you please, that we have been less than diligent because you have not yet received letters from our insignificance. For until now we judged that nothing should be written worthy for your holiness to hear. We believe that it is sufficiently well known even to you that the boy who delivered the letters to the king was put under severe restraint, with fingers applied to gouge out his eyes [Col. 0679D] until blood was shed, and hot water poured into his mouth, until he confessed that he had received the letters from Master Herbert. Yet he has not been released from his chains, although the king received an order from his mother that he should be allowed to go. In the octave of St Martin, as we have learned, the king and Count Theobald held a conference at Tours. On the feast of St Andrew he is to come to us, to confer together with the Flemings. We have also learned from England that the bishop of Lincoln and Count Geoffrey have paid the debt of the flesh—that is, have died. It is also said that Richard de Lucy has now taken upon himself the sign of the cross, in order to go to Jerusalem.

Furthermore, know for certain that no one appears willing to utter even a single word before the king concerning you [Col. 0680A]. He took his seal from Master Walter because he did not detain the boy who had brought the letters; yet afterwards he restored it to the archdeacon. Before the lord of Rouen and several others, the archdeacon, saying that he would send a messenger to you, made an appeal on the Feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary. As to the pope’s command that the king be summoned, the lord of Rouen did nothing openly with his suffragans—perhaps he spoke with the king more privately. Nor should this escape your holiness: the master of the infirmary at Canterbury, coming into our region, reported to us that the bishop of London had restored to the king’s exchequer everything he had received from the revenues of your clerks. He also told us that the prior of Canterbury had put a certain monk in custody [Col. 0680B], because he had left the procession, crying out and declaring that they favoured you and not the king. And Scaiman, the serjeant, having been captured, escaped; after hiding for several days in the monastery of Holy Trinity, he was finally set free, and we do not know where he went. We have also heard concerning the king’s soldiers, who wished to rebuild and fortify Basinwerth, that, when the Welsh suddenly attacked, very many were killed and most wounded. May your holiness prosper.

## LETTER CCCXLV. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME

The same to the same archbishop.

We grieve deeply, and mourn beyond what we can say [Col. 0680C], that until now we have been unable to come to you. But the cause is manifold and serious. We are so deeply burdened with debt, especially on account of the house which we bought last year, that almost every day we must enter the city to beg for a postponement of the payment term, since we do not have enough money to pay the amount due. We are also hard pressed from another side, because the king and his people are staying at Rouen. Thus, if we were absent in the meantime, we should fear that this might become known to him. For it is a harsh and detestable word in his ears that any mention at all should be made of you. Nor does anyone appear who speaks well of us, or who dares even to mention us in his presence. You know far better than we [Col. 0680D] how hard pressed he is, and that he does not know which way to turn. For the kingdom of France opposes him on one side; on another he fears the Poitevins; on another he dreads the Welsh; he regards the Bretons with suspicion; he fears his own people and is safe nowhere. Nor is it surprising that one whom the Church does not protect should fall among many enemies.

But if occasion and opportunity present themselves, as quickly as can be done one of us—either I or Master Herbert—will come into your presence and bring you a full report of all that can meanwhile be learned. Yet let this be known to you in the meantime: whatever peace we can obtain from the king of France, we shall not delay in accepting. May your holiness prosper for ever.

## LETTER CCCXLVI. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME

[Col. 0681A]

To THOMAS, by the grace of God Archbishop of the Church of Canterbury: Brother NICHOLAS of Mont-Rouen sends greeting with the fullness of his devotion.

With what bowels of compassion our smallness of mind receives and considers within itself the adversities of God’s Church which your magnanimity has resolved to endure, neither writing could sufficiently express nor a tongue too inarticulate could fully utter in spoken words. Yet concerning our affection, such as it is, which is yours, because we know it to be lowly and of little worth in the sight of God, we thought it better to be silent than to speak at length. But [Col. 0681B] this, although it is not unknown to your excellency, ought not to be passed over in silence: it will be most pleasing to your sublimity even in its mere recollection, and it is a great token of security for a mind assailed by waves of disturbance, that the efficacy of its own strength renders the delicate shoulders which you have placed beneath the burdens of men more fit for such loads. The Church of Christ’s poor, whom the gentleness of your humility has adopted as sons, whom the greatness of your faith has wished to have as advocates before God, whom your generosity has made indebted to itself in the reckoning of giving and receiving—this Church, hanging with the whole intensity of its spirit upon the matter, hastens night and day to obtain from the Lord that in your days he may grant his Church tranquil [Col. 0681C] freedom. It asks in faith, not wavering.

Therefore, with all your strength and eager zeal, complete the work you have begun, and do not falter in anything. For God has granted you such honour and such blessedness that Jesus Christ is witness in heaven to your work, and conscience is witness in your heart. Moreover, what happens rarely and to few has been added for your fuller encouragement and gladness: the devotion of the whole multitude offers you help in God. And the speech of all the people burns with good testimony concerning what you are doing. But enough of this.

John of Oxford, who, on the advice of your bishops, returned to the court and, coming from the court, passed through the empress’s presence in order to inflame her against you—as previously both he [Col. 0681D] and others had done—pressed upon her as much malice as he could. Since he could not plausibly censure your action, he attacked your intention, asserting that everything you do has been undertaken from pride of heart and zeal for domination. He and the other royal messengers also maintain that you direct ecclesiastical liberty, which you defend, not to the gain of souls but to increasing the bishops’ revenues. And although they admit that you have not yet done this because your prelateship is new, they nevertheless insist that you aspire to it. For in England the offences of delinquents accused before bishops are not punished by the imposition of penance but by payment of money. They say likewise that she ought to recognize from this that God is not the cause of your undertaking [Col. 0682A]: from the beginning of your archbishopric, you gathered about yourself not religious men but noble scholars. They call them by a disgraceful name, which I think it better to leave unspoken. They likewise assert that you have conferred ecclesiastical benefices not from consideration of God, but on account of service to yourself, even upon men whose shameful conduct is publicly known. They also assert that you departed not because of the royal customs, but over a financial matter. It was proper that you should not be unaware of these malicious fabrications against you, both for your precaution and because they furnish the empress an occasion for exasperation.

On the third day after their departure, we came to the empress. For a while she delayed receiving your letters, and spoke quite harshly to us [Col. 0682B] because we had gone on to you once it had become known to us that you were at court. For she did not believe that you would go so quickly to the court. Nevertheless, we did not desist, but on that occasion and again on another occasion we urged upon her, as though she were unwilling, whatever good things we could. On the third occasion, after a few words, she received your letters kindly but secretly. She wished her clerks not to know of it, and commanded us to read them aloud. After hearing them, she first excused herself for having said harsh things about you either privately or publicly, to me or to others, or for having sent such words to the lord king. For she asserted that her son had concealed from her everything that he intended to do concerning ecclesiastical affairs, because he had learned that she favoured ecclesiastical liberty more than the royal will. But now [Col. 0682C] she had sent letters to her son through one of her clerks, ordering him to tell her by letter everything that he had in mind concerning the state of the churches or your person. “And then,” she said, “when I have learned his will, if I perceive that my effort can be fruitful, I shall endeavour, to the extent of my power, for both ecclesiastical peace and his own.”

After these words, leaving her, we brought your letters to the lord of Lisieux at his manor of Nonant, near Bayeux. Receiving us kindly, he received your letters privately; and he willingly embraced both what you had charged us to communicate and whatever good measures we ourselves could devise. He affirmed on his word of truth that, from the time when he was first sent to the court, although in bodily presence [Col. 0682D] he had stood against you, yet in mind and counsel he had stood for you. He had also promised us this during that journey, when we spoke with him concerning your affair—not on your behalf, for you had given no such command. In private he commended, as far as he could, both your cause and your person to the lord pope. He praised the king’s envoys for asking only those things which he knew could not be hindered. Therefore know for certain that, if the lord king shares his counsel with him, he will work to the extent of his power for the liberty of the Church and your peace. He sympathizes with your hardship with no less affection than if this whole adversity had fallen upon you because of his own Church or person. You would have him as an ally within a short time, if he were not burdened by debt.

[Col. 0683A] Therefore his counsel now is that you make such careful provision in your expenses that you do not pour out much money in a short time—if indeed you have much, as the king’s household officers claim. If you do not have it, take care that this is not known to very many. For your adversaries had resolved to advise the king on this side of the sea not to seize your revenues for the present, but to forbid your officials to provide you with anything from them. If, therefore, they see that you are willing and able to endure longer without revenues, peace will be restored to the Church more easily and swiftly. During these feast days he will send you a letter by his own messenger. He would have sent one now, had he possessed at the manor a writer to whom he wished to entrust this secret. He is also sending to England his most intimate associate, Ranulf of Ardern, through whom, after investigating everything [Col. 0683B] done or deliberated at court, he will tell you by letter whatever he learns.

Having returned to the empress, we again related in order everything which you had instructed us to report. We described the king’s customs orally, because Master Herbert had lost the written memorandum. We added that some of those customs were against faith in Jesus Christ, and nearly all were against the liberty of the Church. Therefore there was reason for her and her son to fear eternal danger and also temporal danger. She then ordered us to send to you for those customs. By God’s will, the memorandum was found that very day; and on the next day, after everyone had been dismissed from her chamber and her presence, she ordered us to read them in Latin and explain them in French. The woman is of a race of tyrants, and she approved some of them [Col. 0683C], such as the provision that the king’s justices and officials were not to be excommunicated without his permission. Yet I refused to explain the others until I had first disputed this point, showing the evangelical command in which Peter is told, “Tell it to the Church,” and not, “Tell it to the king,” together with many other arguments. She disapproved very many of the articles. Above all, it displeased her in every respect that they had been reduced to writing, or that the bishops had been compelled to make some promise to observe them. This had not been done by their predecessors.

After many words, when I asked her insistently what might be the first occasion for peace, we suggested this to her, and she assented: if it could perhaps be brought about that the lord king should submit himself to the counsel [Col. 0683D] of his mother and of other reasonable persons, who might so moderate the matter that, once the promise and written document were removed, the ancient customs of the realm might be observed, with such moderation added that neither should the Church’s liberty be taken away through secular judges nor should bishops so abuse ecclesiastical liberty. Know that the lady empress is shrewd in defending her son: in excusing him through zeal for justice, through the bishops’ wrongdoing, and through identifying the origin of the Church’s disturbance, she is reasonable and discerning. For she says certain things in which we both praised and assisted her judgment. Bishops indiscriminately ordain clerks who are assigned no church title. Hence the multitude of those ordained, through poverty and idleness, falls into shameful deeds. A man assigned to no church does not fear losing a church. He does not fear punishment, because the Church will protect him. He does not fear the bishop’s prison, since the bishop prefers that a penitent go free unpunished rather than take on the trouble of feeding or guarding him. The Council of Chalcedon—one of the four which Gregory embraces with all devotion as the four books of the Gospel—testifies that the ordination of one who is assigned to no church is invalid, to the dishonour of the man who performed it [Col. 0684A]. Many other canons say the same.

Likewise, four, seven, or more churches or prebends are bestowed on a single cleric, although the sacred canons everywhere openly forbid a clerk to be counted in two churches. Consider, again, how many disputes arise concerning gifts and presentations to churches from the occasion of this corrupt custom. The lady empress spoke on this subject because of Richard of Ilchester. Yet let bishops who do to their relatives what laymen do to persons serving them keep silent. Likewise, that bishops receive large sums of money concerning sins excused before them is hardly consistent with the canons. For although the penalty for sacrilege is monetary, this is not always so; rather, it is justly paid to whatever persons are concerned in a complaint of sacrilege. Since ecclesiastical disturbance arises from these and like matters, it is very strange why the axe of episcopal judgment is applied not to the root of the tree, but to its little branches [Col. 0684B]. Indeed, by divine dispensation it has come to pass that the fruit of bitterness has publicly sprung from such a root.

Therefore, you love the liberty of the Church for God’s sake: show by words and deeds that the aforesaid matters displease you. And if you send letters to the lady empress, indicate this same point in some measure. On our word of truth, we tell you that we have written the foregoing out of love for righteousness and the salvation of our soul. If anything has been spoken foolishly, forgive us. Let what we have said remain secret. We could not send to you more quickly. For at the very time when we read the customs before the lady empress, we prepared these letters with all speed to be sent to you. We now earnestly ask that you direct letters to us, containing your situation and intention. Whatever you command, we shall faithfully carry out. Again we ask pardon [Col. 0684D], both for our prolixity and for our boldness.

## LETTER CCCXLVII. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME

To THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury: NICHOLAS of Mont-Rouen.

We rejoiced greatly when your letters informed us that you had condemned by public anathema the evil enactments to whose observance our prince, the king of England, wished to bind the bishops. Since you know well that few are now found either to resist evil deeds or publicly to shun those whom you have excommunicated, we know that you have placed your confidence for carrying out the sentence not in human aid, but in him who gave such power to men [Col. 0685A]. Looking to him, Moses subdued the man who oppressed him not by bodily strength or the armour of power, but by a word. For you have begun more nobly and more sincerely than if you had pronounced sentence against the king’s own person. By condemning the aforesaid evils, you have barred for yourselves every avenue of return short of the liberation of God’s Church.

Accordingly, Brother G . . . . . , who ought to have carried your letters, did not come; for this reason we read and delivered them to the lord of Rouen in the presence of the boy who bears this letter. The boy knows in part with what mind and expression he received them. He neither said nor denied that he would withdraw himself from communion with those whom you have excommunicated. He asserted that he would not publicly denounce them, saying that you had commanded this because [Col. 0685B] you wished to have more companions in exile. We also learned from his own mouth that, in order to invalidate either a sentence already pronounced or one which you might pronounce, the archbishops of Rouen and Lisieux and the bishop of Sées are prepared to prove that they had gone to you in order to offer you every satisfaction, according to the judgment of those who ought equitably to judge between you and the king.

Therefore it seems to our smallness, if it appears fitting to your discretion and to those who are with you, that you should send letters to the lord of Rouen and the aforementioned bishops, informing them that you were, are, and will be prepared [Col. 0685C] to return to your see and undergo whatever judgment an Archbishop of Canterbury ought to undergo according to the censure of the canons, provided that they can first obtain from the king security for your return, the lady empress and the lord of Rouen using their influence, as the lord pope has decreed. Likewise, provided that the Church is restored in full—both to the liberty in which it once stood before the dispute arose between you and the king, namely when the bishops were not bound to observe evil enactments, and to the things afterwards taken from you and yours. You should also ask them that, if they cannot obtain from the king what canonical authority dictates should be done, he may not have them as helpers in injury to the Church, since he refuses to comply with them in matters pertaining to the judgment of charity. We believe that these things should be communicated to them before sentence is pronounced against the king—not because they will do any of them, but lest they may in any way oppose what has been or will be done by you. If you send them letters, send us a copy of them.

Furthermore, the lord of Rouen complained to the empress that we had delivered letters of this kind to him. He attributes everything you do either to arrogance or to anger. Know for certain concerning us that we shall not communicate even in a word of greeting with those excommunicated by you. Therefore we earnestly ask you to write back to us whether, if you pronounce sentence against the king, we ought to abstain from communion with him in certain matters, such as prayer and greeting [Col. 0686A], or in these and in every other matter, so that it is not lawful either to receive anything from him or to name him in the celebration of Mass. For we believe that every earthly advantage or danger should be set aside, so that, as far as lies in us, all that accords with the strictness of ecclesiastical censure may be fulfilled.

We are keeping the letters which you were sending to the bishop of Chichester, waiting to learn for certain where he is staying, or whether he may perhaps have approached our region, so that we may deliver them to him. Furthermore, many at the king’s court as well as among us assert that you ought to hold the chancellorship of the king of France. Others also conjecture that on the feast of St Mary Magdalene you will pronounce sentence against the king’s person. When the lady empress heard against whom you had pronounced sentence, she took it almost as a jest and replied that they had long since been excommunicated. Afterwards, when she was greeted on Richard of Ilchester’s behalf, she made no reply.

We know little of the rumours at court, except that the barons of the bishopric of Le Mans have made peace with the king. As for the Bretons, no one has yet reported anything; but on the vigil of the Apostles the king, with his army, was four leagues from Fougères. When the abbot of Derby returns, we shall send you fuller information. Ralph of the Hospital, coming from England, told us that the bishops, meeting about the feast of St John, had appealed against you to “the Man of Galilee,” because you suspended the bishop of Salisbury without their counsel [Col. 0686C], and because you threatened to pronounce sentence against their lord the king. Your archdeacon is striving, as far as he can, to obtain permission to cross the sea. He has not yet received your letters. Through Brother Adam, a regular canon, who loves you for zeal for justice, you may write whatever pleases your fatherhood, since he will return to us without delay. May your holiness prosper.

Know this for certain: your bishops, including even the bishop of Hereford, speak harshly against you, saying that you disturb the English and Roman Churches. The bishops and all abbots are to hold a council at Northampton in the octave of the Apostles.

## LETTER CCCXLVIII. FROM HENRY, ABBOT OF STRATFORD, TO POPE ALEXANDER

[Col. 0686D]

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff ALEXANDER: Brother HENRY, called abbot of the monastery of Stratford, and the humble convent of the same place, offer due obedience to their father and unceasing earnestness of devotion and prayer before the Lord for your welfare.

“Since the Apostle teaches us, lord, we have learned,” etc. See under Alexander.

## LETTER CCCXLIX. FROM THE CHURCH OF HOLY TRINITY, LONDON, TO POPE ALEXANDER

To the venerable Father ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: S . . . . , humble servant of the Church of Holy Trinity, London [Col. 0687A], sends greeting and the obedience of due subjection.

“When before the supreme Judge,” etc. See in the same place.

## LETTER CCCL. FROM WILLIAM, PRIOR OF THE CHURCH OF HOLY TRINITY, LONDON, TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff ALEXANDER: Brother WILLIAM, cloister prior of the Church of Holy Trinity, London, and the humble convent of the same place, offer due filial love to their father and humble obedience in all things.

“Apostolic teaching,” etc. See under Alexander.

## LETTER CCCLI. FROM ERNISIUS, ABBOT, AND R., PRIOR OF ST VICTOR, PARIS, TO ROBERT OF HEREFORD

[Col. 0687B]

To ROBERT, Bishop of Hereford: ERNISIUS, abbot, and R., prior of St Victor, Paris.

Our church conceived great joy at your promotion, and your hearers were made glad with no slight hope; indeed all scholars were encouraged by the example of your labour and success toward love of letters and the cultivation of virtues. We rejoiced for this reason: because we loved you above others, and we trusted that the English Church—which, beyond the charity we bear toward all churches, we love with a certain special affection at nature’s prompting—would advance through your learning, be stirred by your religious devotion to the worship of the divine law, be strengthened against adversity by the office of your preaching and the example of your virtue. Now [Col. 0687C], however, we grieve exceedingly because neither have our hopes concerning you been fulfilled nor has the Lord heard our prayers for you. Would that your ears were turned to the mouths of scholars and you heard the sighs of religious men, so that your spirit, said to be oppressed by the weight of riches and weakened by the love of episcopal office and the abundance of luxuries, might be raised up. For, as they say, the riches—which in school and in the frequent commerce of conversation you used to call *canigenae* (“dog-born,” i.e. dog-like things)—have confirmed you.

You once depicted in words the ideal bishop, whom now, in fulfilment of our hope, you ought to portray in learning and life. Were you then performing the office of the whetstone,

> . . . . which can render iron sharp, though itself incapable of cutting?

[Col. 0687D] It is strange if your ears do not ring from the talk of scholars, the detraction of rivals, and the complaints of friends. You recently appealed against your father and consecrator—himself an exile for justice and the liberty of the Church—together with others who seek the overthrow of justice and their own ruin; and, by setting your portion with the wicked, you have, to our intense grief, greatly blackened your reputation. Did you not see the letters of appeal which the bishops sent to their archbishop? Certainly, if you did not see them, then, with your leave, charity speaks truth: it was foolish to affix your testimony, without examination, to so grave a matter, one which must be carried to the Roman Church. But if you saw them [Col. 0688A], with what conscience, with what face, did you dare to assert and, as you write, to proclaim with all confidence what not only the whole neighbourhood but almost the entire Latin world knows to be false?

For you proclaim—and, in order that he may make especial use of your authority, you sign the document with the bishop of London—the following concerning the king: although he may sometimes have sinned as a man, he is ready to correct all his offences, to obey justice in all things, and, if he is not believed, even to offer security; and you add: “For he loves those who correct him, and willingly listens to rebukes.” But whoever thinks this true, what will he believe false? The man’s character is well known; you who preach such things would need to seek a foreigner, and one outside the Latin world. But you who uphold his justice, what innocence do you allege in the expulsion of women and the proscription of innocent little children? Yet the Lord will judge these things and things like them, and will strike with equal punishment both the perpetrator and those who consent [Col. 0688B]. Meanwhile consider what sentence those bishops will then receive who now lend support to such enormous wrongs.

Dearest Father, we have written this to you in sincere charity, so that you may remember your learning, your office, our hope, and the divine judgment; so that you may redeem your reputation and strive to raise up the Church which is collapsing in your hands. We were yours, we are yours, and, God willing, shall always be yours—ready for your honour and service.

## LETTER CCCLII. FROM THE PRIOR OF ST VICTOR, PARIS, AND R., ABBOT OF ST AUGUSTINE, TO POPE ALEXANDER

[Col. 0688C]

To Pope ALEXANDER: the prior of St Victor and R. . . . . , formerly abbot of St Augustine.

“To holy men,” etc. See under Alexander.

## LETTER CCCLIII. FROM WILLIAM, ABBOT OF READING, TO POPE ALEXANDER

To the most blessed Father and lord A., by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the Catholic Church: Brother WILLIAM, unworthily called abbot of Reading, least of your sons, wishes the ship of Peter entrusted to you to be guided unharmed to the harbour of tranquillity.

“Since to your holiness,” etc. See in the same place.

## LETTER CCCLIV. FROM WILLIAM TO HUGH OF DURHAM

[Col. 0688D]

To the venerable Father and lord H., by God’s grace illustrious bishop of Durham: his William sends greeting and happy success in accordance with your prayers.

Troubled by the pitiable novelty of reports, and far more bitterly afflicted whenever I learn that the serenity of your mind is darkened by a cloud of grief, I anxiously investigate the course of events, so that, if I discover anything to be brought to your ears, I may communicate it to you in writing. Know, then, that the archbishop of Rouen; the bishops of Worcester, York, and Lisieux; and the clerks Reginald Lombard, Richard Barre, Master Henry of Northampton, and many others, came to Sens on the very day of the Conversion of St Paul [Col. 0689A], either to soften by prayers the mind of the archbishop of Sens—who there on that same day had gathered all his suffragans to carry out the lord pope’s command, that he might not pronounce the sentence of interdict upon the king’s land—or to suspend the sentence itself by appeal. But he yielded neither to their prayers nor to their appeal. Having publicly produced the letters containing the sentence and excluding recourse by appeal, he imposed it upon the whole of the king’s land in the regions beyond the sea.

The archbishop of Rouen did not accept the sentence. He said that authority and power to pronounce the sentence had been conferred not upon the archbishop of Sens alone, but upon both of them, since the letters had been addressed to each of the two. He also added that the case had changed. For the lord pope had commanded that the aforesaid sentence should be executed if the Archbishop of Canterbury were held captive. To these two objections the archbishop of Sens answered as follows. To the first: although the letters were addressed to both, they nevertheless contained the provision that if either one ceased from pronouncing and executing the sentence, the other should carry into effect the command laid upon both. To the second [Col. 0689B]: if the pope had decreed that injury to the lord of Canterbury should be punished in this way in a lesser case, then much more strongly did he wish the same to be done in a greater and so detestable case. After lodging an appeal, all the aforesaid departed for Rome, except the bishop of Lisieux.

Concerning the lord king of France, I considered it necessary to report this: on the Thursday immediately following the Conversion of St Paul, he left for the conference, at the emperor’s request, to be held between himself and the emperor on the Sunday when *Invocavit* will be sung, at the frontier of the kingdom and empire near Meschisi [reading uncertain]. There it is hoped that the restoration of ecclesiastical unity and peace will be discussed and that friendship will be confirmed between them by marriages and other bonds of peace. Among the innumerable things which I have learned from report—indeed, from truth as teacher—I have decided to convey to your hearing only those stated above, since I suppose the rest either trivial or known to you. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCLV. FROM LOMBARD TO POPE ALEXANDER

To the reverend Father and lord ALEXANDER, by God’s grace [Col. 0689D] supreme pontiff: Lombard, his faithful clerk, offers the service of obedience.

“When the boy of your holiness,” etc. See in the same place.

## LETTER CCCLVI. FROM THEOBALD OF BLOIS TO THE SAME

To his most reverend lord and Father ALEXANDER, supreme pontiff: THEOBALD, Count of Blois and regent of the kingdom of France, sends greeting and due reverence with filial subjection.

“It pleased your majesty,” etc. See in the same place.

## LETTER CCCLVII. FROM W., A MONK, TO GILBERT

To the most reverend Father and lord, honoured in the bowels of Christ, the venerable G., Bishop of London: Brother W., son of Adelelm, his son and monk, wishes him to be enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit and strengthened in all things by its power.

What joy and delight your condition of safety and prosperity brings me, and, conversely, what pain and sorrow any adversity that may arise inflicts upon my soul, he alone knows who searches hearts. But I hope and trust in the Father of mercies that he will turn the storm into a gentle breeze and crush beneath your feet all who oppose and malign you. My Father, let it neither offend your ears nor vex your mind that what follows comes from your son’s inmost heart. I call Jesus and his angels to witness that I say this not in the manner of flatterers but as testimony [Col. 0690B]. While spirit governs these limbs, while we enjoy the provision of this life, I pledge, promise, and undertake that my tongue will always speak of you, my labours will be devoted to you, and my talent will toil for you.

Moreover, I received your holiness’s writings with as much delight as I had previously desired them eagerly. I read them; as I turned the words of their sentences in my mouth, I felt sparks in my heart, by which my heart also grew warm within me—though in my meditation the fire has not yet blazed forth. Oh, how great is the fire that burns in your meditations, from which sparks of this kind fly out! Blessed are you by the Lord, who has deigned to anticipate me with blessings of such sweetness that, as you wrote first, I was given confidence to write in return—though I had long desired to write to you, yet had not dared [Col. 0690C].

I fear to say it, but I shall nevertheless say it: whenever I reread your writings, a certain image of your presence appears before my eyes, seeming to proclaim to my thirsting soul the sum of all perfection. Hence I love your utterances so ardently, because they seem most richly to refresh my soul. Send, sweetest Father, what you have not yet sent, for you will have more abundantly if I have it. Let the father remember the son, as the son can never forget the father. A word to the wise is enough. May my lord—my glory and the lifter up of my head—live and prosper.

## LETTER CCCLVIII. FROM MASTER VIVIAN TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0690D]

To THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury: Master VIVIAN sends greeting and victory in the urgent undertaking for the honour of God and the Church.

…so that, with the lord of Tours or his envoys, we might return to the curia with all possible speed, God being our author, we turned aside to Tours; and on the fourth day before the Kalends of November [29 October] we received letters of the king of England, the archbishop of Rouen, and the archdeacon of Canterbury, through the prior of the abbey of Bec and another nobleman. We send a transcript of them to Your Blessedness, beseeching you not to yield to the suggestion of any cleric, even though he should shine with the illustrious dignity of a primacy, unless you receive in the king’s open letters what is expedient for your honour, as has very often been proposed. [Col. 0691A] And we ask you to send to us with the greatest haste a courier or some cleric, through whom you may disclose your will to us, if it please you; nor should you show such deference to Master Gratian that you utterly trample, in our person, the honour of your dearest friend and foremost defender in the Roman Church.

## LETTER CCCLIX. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME.

To his reverend Father and dearest lord, THOMAS, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See: VIVIAN, called Master despite himself, advocate of the Holy Roman Church and most faithful spokesman for its honour and yours, wishes a return in joy and glory, without delay, to his own country.

[Col. 0691B] Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is prepared, contrary to the expectation of many, to unite walls that have been divided by the counsel of wicked men in the now indissoluble bond of charity. Having been summoned back, we approached the king’s presence; and, by grace cooperating from above, found terms in which the honour of God and of the Church suffers no violation. If therefore you have already received the envoy of the most Christian king of the French and of the lord of Rouen, as we confidently believe, we rejoice; for thus it was settled. And if Master John of Salisbury, your clerk and our dearest companion, has returned to you, as we hope, since he received the message, we are glad.

Whatever may be the case, reverend Father, we ask—and, in asking, advise on behalf of the lord pope and the Roman Church—that, setting aside every excuse, [Col. 0691C] you most eagerly attend the conference between the two kings which will be held at Saint-Denis on the first Sunday after the feast of Saint Martin. For there, God granting it, you will receive the angelic hymn: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to the lord of Canterbury.”

The master and priest who is chamberlain of the supreme and most eminent Cardinal William, your most faithful servant, greets you as his own lord. He is with us as a companion in our labour; he represents his lord, and carries certain secrets of the king which in every way concern your advancement. There is besides something which, when we are present, we shall explain: he advises you by all means to come promptly to the conference, because you will have the king and his sons according to your own judgment.

We hasten to the most serene king of the French and use a safe-conduct in order to see you, so that you may immediately proceed with us to the appointed conference. We most sincerely greet all those placed with you in exile. We hope that our dearest companion, Master Longus, may, in the manner of his nation, show prudent wisdom in this affair.

## LETTER CCCLX. FROM THE SAME TO POPE ALEXANDER.

To the most blessed Father and lord ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the universal Church, VIVIAN, his holiness’s most devoted servant, offers the service of due submission.

“Because [you have considered] our condition,” etc. See under Alexander.

## LETTER CCCLXI. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME.

[Col. 0692A]

To Pope ALEXANDER, Master VIVIAN.

“He employed every effort,” etc. See in the same place.

## LETTER CCCLXII. FROM THE SAME TO KING HENRY.

To the most serene lord HENRY, by God’s grace king of the English, Master VIVIAN, advocate of the Holy Roman Church, greeting, and willingness to accept salutary counsel.

God knows—and your prudence ought not to be ignorant—how greatly I have laboured for your honour, and what diligence I have applied so that, to the glory of God and of yourself, you might make peace with the Church. For I pressed your cause so earnestly that I lost the favour of many great men [Col. 0692B] and became the subject of slanderers’ tales. I therefore wonder that you wished to render me, whom you would not hear when I spoke for your advantage and honour, infamous as though corrupted by money.

But because I began to honour you with service, and am not accustomed easily to withdraw from friends, I pray and advise you in every manner to return to your right mind and confirm by your charter the petition which the lord of Canterbury has sent you in writing. Add that you will receive him with the kiss of peace; send [word] to him and recall him, before your land is subjected to an interdict and those are struck with anathema whose names are entered in the record of their condemnation. For they are many, necessary to you, and the time is short.

Why certain persons have been unwilling to urge you to this, your discernment will readily perceive, if it weighs true friends and the faithfulness of men. Moreover, concerning the movable goods which you have taken away, answer the archbishop with such moderation that both your liberality may shine more brightly before men, and your conscience may wash away before God the guilt of so great a crime; and so that the archbishop himself and his people, as long as they live, may be bound to remain more faithful and devoted to you and your heirs. [Col. 0692C] But if you are unwilling to hear me even this once, repentance will come too late. Nor say hereafter that what threatens you was not foretold.

## LETTER CCCLXIII. FROM LAURENCE, ABBOT OF WESTMINSTER, TO POPE ALEXANDER.

To Pope ALEXANDER, LAURENCE, abbot of Westminster.

[Col. 0692D] “The assertion of truth,” etc. See under Alexander.

## LETTER CCCLXIV. FROM MASTER WILLIAM TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY.

To THOMAS, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, Master WILLIAM, son of Richard Bonhart: nothing beneath his power, but [only what is] above it.

“Though strength be lacking, the will nevertheless deserves praise.”

“I likewise suppose that the gods are content with this.”

Since your ears are occupied with greater matters, I make my report brief, having judged it worthy to bring to your knowledge how Berengar delivered your letters in the church of Saint Paul on Ascension Day. When the Gospel had been read, that messenger came to the altar and thrust your letters, in my presence and sight, into the hand [Col. 0693A] of the priest named Vitalis, who thought that he was about to receive an offering from him. He held the hand firmly together with the letters, commanding him, on behalf of the lord pope and of yourself, to deliver one letter to the bishop and another to the dean, and not to celebrate Mass before the letters had been read.

He called William of Norhallis as witness, the man who read the Gospel on Ascension Day, likewise charging him on your behalf not to remain at Mass until the letters had been read; he charged also the subdeacon, named W. Hog. After this Berengar, turning to the people, cried out in a loud voice: “Know that Gilbert, bishop of London, has been excommunicated by Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See.” On hearing this, many who were prepared to seize him heaped insults upon him. But I caused him to leave, lest a tumult arise among the people; and as people were streaming out in crowds, I covered him with my cloak and escorted him from the church to the lodging from which he had come.

I have as witnesses to this deed Berengar himself, Richard, nephew of William de Cap[lacuna], and the son of William Wannoc. The priest did not wish to celebrate Mass contrary to the prohibition issued on your behalf, nor would William of Norhallis remain. William reported these things to Nicholas the archdeacon, who replied: “Would the priest refrain from eating if a messenger told him, on behalf of the archbishop, not to eat?” And Mass was celebrated without the letters being read, except secretly, as I heard.

When this was reported to the bishop of London, [Col. 0693C] who was at Stepney, on the Saturday next after the Ascension of the Lord he caused the clergy of the Church of London to be summoned. After much consultation had taken place among the bishop, dean, archdeacon, and canons, they at length took their seats. At the bishop’s command the priest Vitalis appeared with your letters, related in order what had been done, delivered the letters sent to the bishop to him, and the others to the dean.

The bishop, embittered with rancorous malice, his brows knit and words scarcely issuing forth, read the letters and attacked before all the sentence which you had pronounced against him with the following arguments. His first point he took from the Old Testament: Adam sinned in Paradise; God did not immediately condemn him, but walked about so as to give him opportunity to present himself. Afterwards he called him, saying, “Adam.” Thirdly he rebuked him, saying, “Where are you?”
