Likewise, his second point was from the New Testament. In the Gospel it is said to Peter: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him privately; afterwards before two or three; thirdly, tell the Church. Only then, if he remains uncorrected, regard him as a heathen and a publican.”

He also said: “Let not the archbishop say, ‘I could not cite the bishop of London.’ It is clear that he could have done so. For he who could do the greater thing—namely, excommunicate—could do the lesser, namely, cite.”

He also said: “It is the privilege of the pope alone that no appeal may be made from him; from all others appeal may be made. And, protected by my appeal through invocation of the most holy name of the Holy Trinity, I dash down his act upon the firm Rock [Col. 0694A] on which the Church is founded.”

He also said: “In every criminal case there must be four parties: accuser, accused, witnesses, and judge. Out of hatred for me, he confounds all these, since he alone accuses, testifies, and judges. It is therefore clear that, if he could, he would cut off my head with the material sword.”

He also said: “He puts his sickle into another’s harvest. For he has no power either over my person or over my church: not over my person, because I have never made either profession or obedience to him; nor has the Church of Canterbury, in the name of this church—that is, the Church of London. Not over the church, because the Church of London claims what was long ago taken away by the irruption of pagans: namely, that the archbishopric ought to be in London, which we shall prove. And we renew the appeal previously made.”

He also said: “Even if what he says is true, that he possesses this power from the lord pope by right of legation, he still cannot extend that hand over me, because he has not yet entered those territories in which he ought to be legate.”

The dean, archdeacon, all the canons, and all the priests of London made an appeal. But the canons of Saint Bartholomew, Saint Martin, and Saint Trinity refused to make any appeal. Finally the dean caused the letters sent to him to be read a second time.

What I now write took place at Westminster before the Ascension. The bishop of London summoned the bishop of Exeter, Richard of Ilchester, the abbot of Westminster, Guy Rufus bishop of Salisbury, and the barons of the Exchequer. The bishop of London sent word beforehand to the bishop of Exeter not to offer him the kiss of peace; [Col. 0694C] yet the latter did not refuse, for the bishop of Exeter kissed him.

When they were all seated, the bishop of London addressed them, striving by many arguments to induce the bishop of Exeter to stand with him in the appeal. But he stood like an impregnable wall against the assailants of the Church’s liberty. When the bishop of London mentioned the sentence imposed upon them by you, the bishop of Salisbury replied: “If Archbishop Buinard, or my foolish archbishop, commands me to do something I ought not to do, shall I do it?”

God forbid that this be committed to memory in such a way that punishment may be exacted for it. For crimes always grow when they are not cut off, and men rush into greater offences when they sin in the security of impunity.

Farewell; and consult the Angel of Great Counsel, so that by his prompting you may do what is honourable and useful in all your affairs.

## LETTER CCCLXV. FROM HERVEUS THE CLERK TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY.

To his most moderate lord THOMAS, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury, his own HERVEUS: greeting, and the attainment of sincere charity.

Your spirit, hitherto shaken by the enormity of events, has grounds on which it can and should breathe again. For the holy and inviolable Bride of Christ, the Church, mother also of religion—languishing for some time and shamelessly torn—recovers and is restored. She regenerated you from her own bosom, abundantly nourished you with her own provisions, and at last, through the favour and grace of her Bridegroom, placed you as bishop in the lofty watchtower of her care. Since there she found you watchful, faithful, and a companion sharing in her sickness and injury, she rightly does not leave you excluded from the restoration which she receives through Christ’s mercy. [Col. 0695A]

For this is contained in the right and privilege of maternal affection: that she turns her children’s weeping into laughter, embracing more tenderly those whose tears she recognizes as more favourable to her. What favour the oppression you endured has brought you is known to the religion of catholic holiness, spread far and wide through the various regions of the world. Every tongue and nation, I think, knows in how many places joyful favour cherishes the memory of you, where a doubled authority would have brought no recognition. The disturbance which arose has benefited you more than the continuance of tranquillity would have done.

Formerly, arrogant and misled, you were thought fortunate in the abundance of friends, until a cloudy fortune stripped them away and showed you by manifest proofs that you had been mistaken. Those whom long periods of smiling fortune had promised to remain unmoved, the moment of altered fortune scattered in a light whirlwind and taught that they belonged to themselves, not to you. Yet confidence in such men is perhaps pride and arrogance.

Unfruitful adversity removed these things and others like them, exchanging arrogance for humility and error for discernment, and making you more instructed on every side by its goads. Although it revealed few friends of sincere fidelity, it nevertheless distinguished them from deceitful and chance companions, and added great stores of caution and experience to the treasures of your prudence. [Col. 0695B] It made you better known to yourself than you had customarily been, and taught you by experience how far you should trust in the inward strength of your own heart.

Indeed, the constancy which a mind, gently deceived and arrogantly flattering itself, had promised itself without yet being tested by the examinations of raging fortune—how great it was and of what sort you found it, when the shameful violence of fate and the loss of life’s breath threatened—you who know better should set down faithfully in your own memory. Do not make light of the knowledge of yourself and your friends which testing adversity has afforded you.

Moreover, the greater part of the people of our way of life, having tested you in many ways, reverently approves and honours you. Above all does he whose authority is pre-eminent, who, with the arms of full devotion and charity, embraces you by a special prerogative among the most approved sons of holy mother Church, and commends you to every honour. Let hope therefore arise in you; let the mind oppressed by troubles lift itself up; let the heart buried in sorrows breathe again: peace stands at the gates.

God has cut down the tree that bore bitter fruit. Though a new shoot may have sprung up from its root, it receives no help from the dew of heaven; it neither strikes roots nor spreads branches nor receives increase, but withers. The leaf it now puts forth, already fading, is a burden to it, not an honour. The ground will scarcely remain to it on which it may stand, for it is publicly proclaimed that it has occupied it to no purpose. [Col. 0695D] He indeed through whose assistance this decaying plant sprouted and stands is hostile to its inhabitants and labours greatly in his own defence against the native people.

The supreme householder, the Dayspring from on high, stands ready to cut down the insipid tree; when he brings in his own husbandmen, he will root out this kind of planting and will not allow its author to go unpunished. The Lord of Hosts will do these things. When his wrath has burned for a short while, blessed are all who trust in him.

Therefore let your soul rejoice confidently, and let no trace of confusion remain within you. The Lord is our God, and he does not abandon those who hope in him. The terror of the storm which arose long ago might seem to have subsided during an interval of gentler air. But if, under its returning darkness, the clouds have not yet ceased, you have conquered lightning and thunderbolts in vain if you are overwhelmed by the lighter remaining motion of the storms.

You sail in an unbroken vessel; rise vigorously to the oars. The harbour is near. You will enter it when, content with the lot divinely appointed for you, you reckon every condition of events that may arise as beneficial to you in the love of Christ. For we know that all things work together for good to those who love God.

Do not grieve over pleasures lost in the past, nor fear the future troubles of the world. You will easily pass through present changes:

> Believe me: it is not the part of a wise man to say, “I shall live.”
>
> Tomorrow’s life comes too late: live today.
>
> Believe every day that dawns upon you to be your last;
>
> Then welcome will come the hour that is not hoped for.

If God, who kills and makes alive, had immutably assigned you forty days and no more as, so to speak, the canonical extension of your life, you would assuredly not attempt any flight into barbarous lands. Rather, you would more profitably flee to the bosom of the Church entrusted to you and to the prayers of your holy predecessors, keeping watch there in compunctions and prayers. [Col. 0696C] You would have little dread of popular clamour or the anger of powerful men. Nor would you strive to punish every man’s rashness; you would reserve something for the supreme Judge to judge. Ordering your affairs and household wisely, and not greatly anxious about the morrow of your last day, you would treat with contempt the tumults of evil men.

Scripture instructs us, saying: “As dying, and behold, we live.” Therefore, admonished by the rule of this teaching, banish from your heart the wandering and disturbing anxieties of impatience. Strive by continual conduct and the due performance of your office, as if at the point of death, to honour the most splendid and exalted seat of your dignity. Supported there by the patronage of holy places, fearlessly render full justice to those who ask it, so far as blameless moderation permits.

Whenever royal majesty summons you, obey and approach reverently. Never lacking a word of gentleness and patience, endeavour wisely to moderate everything. Wherever the impunity of rampant wickedness has met resistance, take your seat cautiously and have recourse to the aforesaid protection of the saints.

Finally, if you aspire to settled happiness, you must bear with an even mind whatever happens within fortune’s threshing-floor. This page may profit if it is not despised—its counsels are known to proceed from sincere faith, though they are insufficiently mature. Although dogs may have barked at them, they would not offend the regard of a prudent man. [Col. 0697A] In these matters I ask pardon for expressing, through a plurality of titles, a reverence not properly due—one created not by the rule of Latin, but by a flattering tongue.

Most serene lord, I have arranged to offer you these counsels in view of present wickedness; if peaceful times suppressed it, this counsel might perhaps be changed in some respects. Meanwhile, with your prudence thus awakened, let it rise energetically and always proceed from good to better. May your health and holiness, dearest lord, flourish and be extended long into life. Farewell likewise for ever.

## LETTER CCCLXVI. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME.

To THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, HERVEUS the clerk.

[Col. 0697B] In accordance with the tenor of your letters, I showed the document concerning the profession, written more secretly, to the lord pope, reading it distinctly, with no cardinal present except Lord Mainfred. In their lodgings I likewise explained the same document to the lord of Ostia, Lord Hyacinth, Otto, and also the lord of Porto, to whom your affairs have been communicated by the counsel and command of the lord pope.

As to your desire that a messenger be sent to you now concerning your affairs, which you perhaps believed already completed, this could not yet be done, because I have not yet been able to obtain those things. This is not because the lord pope or your friendly cardinals have withdrawn in any respect from carrying out their good promise, or have shown themselves less diligent. They burn with love for you, and the lord pope has added that he will execute still better what he promised well.

But because I spent fifteen days in cautiously circumventing and drawing over the lord of Porto—using all necessary diligence and excluding every improper importunity—I brought it about that he, first among your friends at Clermont, should approach the lord pope regarding our petitions. The lord pope, however, with paternal design, in order especially to provoke the lord of Porto and the others to earnest urging, presents himself at first sight as severe, hard, and almost not sufficiently open to entreaty. This is the reason for delay, which by God’s mercy will be of advantage to us hereafter. The lord of Ostia greatly approves the lord pope’s use of such policy. [Col. 0697D]

When God permits your desires to be brought to fulfilment, I shall employ whatever prudence God grants me, so that they may be conveyed to you. Moreover, it is the lord pope’s advice that, if the king of France honourably offers you provisions, you should receive not only bread and wine but meat also. He thinks that, as a precaution, nothing should be accepted openly from the three counts. From the count of Flanders, however, he considers it best to receive the things offered, provided that he summons and invites you by his letters, lest anything be disguised. Yet the lord pope cannot fear this because of the noble birth and good character of that man, whose intervention he hopes will be advantageous to you. May my lord prosper for ever.

## LETTER CCCLXVII. FROM HUGH TO THE SAME.

[Col. 0698A]

To his lord THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, his own HUGH: greeting.

I rightly called you lord, since I have willingly chosen and vowed to serve you. Yet would that my lord attended more diligently to, and loved more sincerely, those who love him in truth. Many assume the appearance of disciples and anticipate the blessing due to sons, although they ought to be called hirelings, since they do not deserve the grace of a father’s blessing. These are those who love quickly but despise more quickly. Of them it is said: “They believe at once, but in time of temptation they fall away.”

These are those who laugh openly and mock inwardly; who speak publicly and slander secretly; who hiss in private and obey in public. Of them it is said: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.” They make covenants with prosperity; they pursue prey, not the man; they are friends not of the person but of fortune, not of the person but of the moment.

For if the horror of adversity descends, they immediately tremble and despair violently, sighing deeply for the former state of glory. But if even a slight breath of prosperity shines forth, loosened by some sudden itching desire, they are tossed more swiftly than any wind, seeking what is their own, not what is Jesus Christ’s. Such people long for the pots of meat in Egypt and do not fear to abandon the people of the Lord in the camp.

Perhaps such men hasten with David [Col. 0698C] to Bathsheba’s embraces; for us, with Uriah, it does not yet seem lawful to enter our house until the Lord’s people enjoy their due victory. For I judge it more glorious to be taken from the millstone than from the bed, and to be clothed with John in camel’s hair in the desert than to be adorned with soft garments in a royal house. It is indeed more blessed to die for Christ than to serve an earthly prince.

Whatever others may do, wherever their precipitate will may carry them, I, the least of those whom the king hates without cause, will always be with you; and if it is necessary for me to die with you, I shall not deny you. Yet it is fitting that you pray that my faith may not fail. For if you do not fail me in will alone, I shall be present for you with all my strength.

Furthermore, I thank my lord because he has deemed it worthy to ask the counsel of his little servant in so great a matter. For the present, therefore, I defer counsel, because I am a child. But would that my lord might first receive a more certain message from the king of the English before he turns his reins toward a foreign prince. For shortly you will see the glory of the Lord, and his brightness will cast its shadow over you. For the Lord has made the heart of our king—our king, I say, now most gracious—yielding and has made his face gentler.

Whatever pleases you, always command me. For I am ready on your behalf to go both to prison and to death. Certainly nothing commanded by you will seem burdensome to me. Therefore be of steadfast spirit and take courage, because the Lord will come and will not delay; nor will our Lord God leave you without help in the time of the proud. May he always preserve your person unharmed. [Col. 0699A]

## LETTER CCCLXVIII. FROM HIS MESSENGER TO THE SAME.

To his venerable lord, his own servant, may he always prosper in those things which are of God.

At the end of the letter which I sent you the day before yesterday—if indeed you received it—it is stated that the king, since certain sparks of anger had been kindled between himself and the lord pope, came to the curia at your prompting, indeed at God’s prompting. When they had spoken privately together, whatever resentment had arisen was extinguished by the grace of God.

Likewise the discord that had sprung up among Henry of Pisa, John of Naples, and William of Pavia—for each of them was troubled by the same spirit—was outwardly soothed through the king’s mediation. Some others also, previously at variance, were reconciled by him, so that when he departed many said: “This man came to bring peace, not a sword.”

On the third day after his departure, Brother Franco and I, having received a most secret instruction, were sent to him. When I came to Paris, I found Master Roger, envoy of York, who had already filled the city with rumours: namely, that the king of England had fallen from his horse at Worcester and had been severely injured in his right arm; that there had also been a harsh answer which the king had made there through his own messengers before the Welsh; and many other things which none of us, who have become like exiles, would in any way dare [Col. 0699C] to report.

Coming to Senlis, I found with the king a servant who had presented him with two dogs in your name. Being a discerning man and concerned for his friend, the king feared that it might have been done through the malice of one of your enemies, so that letters obtained from him or some tokens might provide an occasion for malicious action. He therefore kept the man with him as a spy until I should come to him—for he knew that I would come shortly.

Although I did not know the man completely, yet because I heard many things from him about the manner of your tokens, which were sufficiently known to me, and because I feared that if he were subjected to any harm contemplated in the king’s mind, word might reach hostile ears, I allowed him to depart after the king had given him twenty shillings. The king sent you letters full of great affection and consolation. Because of certain matters contained in them, I did not dare entrust them to the bearer of this letter, but retained them with myself.

Having completed the lord pope’s business for which I had been sent, I returned to the curia as quickly as I could. Without any difficulty I obtained from the lord pope that no messenger, at the prompting of that enemy of yours, should obtain from him anything that could in any way harm you; and that he himself would, to the best of his ability, provide in all things for your honour and advantage. On your behalf I kissed his foot for this.

His petitions, secretly made, were as follows. First: that the lord pope should compel the bishop-elect of Saint Andrews in Scotland to come to York for his consecration; and that, if he did not come, the archbishop might suspend him. But this could not be obtained.

Another: that he should unconditionally annul whatever his predecessors William and Henry, and all others, had sold off or alienated from the lands of the Church of York. This was obtained in this form: that he might lawfully revoke whatever had been unjustly disposed of by his predecessors without the consent or privilege of the Roman pontiff. [Col. 0700A]

Third: that he should not be compelled to ordain or confer an ecclesiastical benefice upon any persons begotten or born of persons constituted in holy orders. This was obtained.

Fourth: that he might be permitted to redeem from laymen the advowsons of churches. This has not yet been obtained.

There were other requests which I have not mentioned, for they were of no consequence. But we feared that something more might lie concealed: for “a serpent lies hidden in the grass.” He was pretending to his envoys that he would leave shortly, whereas I discovered from his hosts that this was not so.

I could write you nothing certain concerning his payment for service. Although he had already remained fifteen days at the curia, the lord pope had yet received nothing, nor had any cardinal, except perhaps the Neapolitan, whom he had almost alone as a favourable friend. The latter appeared grieved unto death because matters did not succeed at his command. Whether he himself brought payment was uncertain.

Yet when I returned from the king by way of Paris, I inquired of his host concerning his condition and learned that, though he had three horses, he travelled laden. Whether this was so or not, however, matters little to us. For by God’s grace we are near the harbour, and the Lord has delivered us from the lion’s jaws.

At the same time William of Pavia, once drawing me aside in the palace, asked whether I had heard anything concerning you. When I replied, “No,” he said, with much of his customary solemnity: “Do not wear a troubled countenance any longer, but keep the joy due to your birthday. For the lord archbishop has made an alliance with the king and obtained his peace.” From whom he had learned this I could not discover from him.

Afterwards, on the second day, the subdean of Bayeux and one of his canons privately reported to me that, while lodging at Lisieux with the bishop of Lisieux, that bishop had instructed them by letter and orally to tell William of Pavia and John of Naples that they should know for certain that peace had been made between you and the lord king. [Col. 0700D] What precisely this was intended to signify—since this instruction was given to them in that manner and by one who had been under the same condemnation as they—was uncertain.

When this became known through me to the lord pope, Hyacinth, and our other friends, it seemed remarkable to all. Yet all rejoiced at your peace as at their own. Some said that that messenger wished to seek greater things than these; but because no proof of this appeared, and the lord pope had commanded us to be wholly secure, I refrained from writing it to you.

Moreover, if anything else emerges, your Highness shall know it as soon as we can inform you.

That report about the son of Osbert the archdeacon has now filled everyone’s ears, and all recoil from it. We, however, give thanks to God and to you because all who come from you speak in agreement. What they proclaim upon the housetops concerning your honour is what they had told us in the ear.

The emperor’s chancellor, coming to Vienne, summoned a considerable number of archbishops. First he demanded soldiers from them for the emperor’s service; afterwards he urgently approached each one concerning the reception of Guy of Crema, whom the emperor had received. There he was disappointed of his hope and desire. Some of them were ready to excommunicate Guy himself in his presence.

But when he could not succeed as he wished, he declared that he wanted to hold a conference with Count Henry. At the time I wrote this to you, the count had passed through Paris in order to consult the king about it; but we did not yet know what he would do. [Col. 0701B]

I would have written more about the state of the Church, the Lombards’ rising again against the emperor, and the oath generally sworn by the Romans to Pope Alexander and others, had not the length of the page prevented me. I also feared to burden ears occupied with so many and such great affairs. May God preserve you unharmed for us and for your friends.

The lack of mounts which I suffer may be harmful to you. Unless the archdeacon of Salisbury, who is solicitous to the best of his ability in all matters concerning you, had helped me, necessity would have compelled me to abandon some matters which I have pursued quite profitably. Please remember my household and my possessions. The peasants’ harshness is such that, unless your authority intervenes, they will spare me in nothing. It is therefore expedient for me that you send your letters concerning this to them and to your officials.

## LETTER CCCLXIX. FROM HIS MESSENGER TO THE SAME.

To his most loving lord, his own servant: greeting, and the wish that he may always be well.

By the mercy of God, which does not abandon those who hope in Him, it happened that on the very day on which my lord pope was informed [Col. 0701D] of Octavian’s death, the envoys of the lord king R. and H. arrived at the curia. By putting forward, on the king’s behalf, such an appearance of humility, and with one voice and letters consonant with their words, they seemed to move my lord pope and certain cardinals so deeply that, as I learned from the report of some who favour us, they could scarcely restrain their tears. After many assertions concerning the manner and disposition with which the king had received him, the great reverence he had always shown him and would show as long as he lived, and matters of this kind, they returned to my lord pope many letters concerning the legation which your archdeacon had obtained, somewhat improperly, while I was with you in England. Yet the condition under which he obtained them the lord [Col. 0702A] king wholly denied, through these envoys, to have been made or sought by himself. My lord pope received them with such feeling and eagerness—as though something he had long desired were being offered him—that some sitting beside him were greatly astonished.

In this matter, I could not safely inform you how I conducted myself, or what my lord pope entrusted to me concerning it, until the envoys had departed from the curia. Afterwards, when those envoys pretended that they wished to return in great haste, the three cardinals who pursue you in every way—the Neapolitan, the Bishop of Porto, and the Pavesan—strove insistently to obtain from my lord pope general letters concerning the legation, or at least the same letters which had been returned, unconditionally, in order to mitigate [Col. 0702B] the king’s anger. Since they could obtain neither (for my lord pope had assured me concerning this that they should never again return into his hands, and had privately entrusted this to me), they turned to the affair of the abbot of St Augustine’s. You will learn from the letters of our companions how matters proceeded in that case. It is therefore for you to act manfully on your own behalf and not to fail the grace of God, which freely offers itself to you. May your fatherhood prosper.

The king’s envoys declared before my lord pope that I was his particular enemy, and that it would not be expedient for me for all Arabia’s gold if he had power over me. Yet even so my faith cannot be frightened, so that I may say with Peter: “I am ready [Col. 0702C] to go with you both to death and to prison.”

## LETTER CCCLXX. FROM HIS ENVOY TO THE SAME

To the venerable lord and dearest Father THOMAS, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury and Primate of the English: greetings from the least of his faithful servants, with happy success according to his wishes.

Let your fatherhood know that Octavian, the schismatic whom they had raised up as their head and the Belial, or leader, of schism, died in the city of Lucca on the Wednesday after the octave of Easter, and was buried in a monastery outside the city. For when the canons of the greater church and the regular canons of St Fridian [Col. 0702D] refused him burial—preferring to depart from their own dwellings rather than admit the body of a schismatic whom they believe buried in hell—the corpse was brought by the emperor’s retainers and by his own household to the wretched monks. His chapel, moreover, and whatever else he possessed, together with his horses—for he possessed nothing else, having long lived in pressing poverty except by plunder—were taken to the emperor. When the emperor learned this, he summoned to himself the Bishop of Pavia, who was living in exile at the monastery of St Michael near the Clusa; but what he intends to do is still uncertain. Some say that he wishes to appoint another in Octavian’s place; others, that he will return to Catholic unity. Moreover, the cities of Italy are less ready than usual to obey him; so much so that the Pavians [Col. 0703A] and Cremonese, through whom he subdued and crushed Italy, resist him openly and have declared that they will wholly withdraw from him unless he abandons tyranny and assumes civil manners, so that they may be free, as in the days of other emperors.

Fifteen days before his death, Octavian became continually delirious and fell into such madness that he remembered neither God nor himself. My lord pope had indeed heard of Octavian’s death from faithful and truthful informants; and, like another David, he lamented his persecutor when dead, and sternly rebuked the cardinals who rejoiced at his death. This was right, because the loss of a soul is irreparable where guilt is not removed by repentance. Nor do we remember from any age that a heresiarch [Col. 0703B] or author of a schism has done penance except under compulsion and against his will. If you review histories, I believe this will prove true; but God rejects every sacrifice unless it is voluntary.

While this report was much discussed at the curia, behold, the lord king’s envoys arrived, returning letters obtained from the Apostolic See. They had scarcely returned them when other letters arrived immediately from Italy and were presented almost at the same time, setting out carefully both Octavian’s death and the events occurring in Italy. It is also said, not only to my lord pope by Italians but to the King of the French by Gauls returning from Apulia, that the emperor was suffering from a quartan fever and that the empress miscarried in childbirth. Hence all Gaul has turned more devotedly to obedience to my lord pope, [Col. 0703C] and the Roman Church ought to be less troubled by men’s threats. And, as we have learned for certain, the Archbishop of York’s legation has wholly expired, every hope of its recovery having been removed.

The aforesaid lord was thus legate of the English in such a fashion that he was neither annual, nor monthly, nor even daily, since in his legation he had neither a year, nor a month, nor a day. Yet, by some means I do not know, the envoys departing from the Apostolic See—although they are inferior to those who preceded them—boast that they have obtained for the Augustinians what was denied to their superiors, and that they have inflamed the curia against your envoys. They further say that the schemes which Geoffrey Ridel and John of Oxford pursued against the lord king have become known to them, so that they deserve exile and confiscation of all their goods if they presumed such things without royal consent and authority. They say also that certain cardinals have notified the lord king in letters, to excuse themselves, how maliciously Geoffrey and John attacked him, and how presumptuously your envoys everywhere and always speak ill of the king. [Col. 0703D] My companions remaining at the curia have told me nothing of these matters; I learned them from outsiders.

Nevertheless, whatever the perversity of malicious men may contrive against your innocence, I beg and advise that, insofar as you can do so according to God, you acquire and preserve the lord king’s favour; for this is beneficial to God’s Church. Nor do I see how you can preside usefully so long as, matters remaining as they are, the king opposes you in everything. Especially since the Roman Church receives from you nothing but words and attributes to you and to itself the loss it suffers elsewhere, because it does not allow you to be crushed at the king’s pleasure. Now, from this opportunity, it will easily retain for itself the monastery of St Augustine altogether unless you take precautions, since it is credible that all would prefer it to belong to itself rather than another. Nor do I see how you can avoid this except through the king, to whom it may perhaps plausibly be represented that it is far better and more honourable for him, and more tolerable for you, to crush your person at his pleasure than thus to mutilate and ruin the church.

But what has the Church of Canterbury done to deserve his anger? Is it worthy to be afflicted and crushed because it elected you and set you over itself? Yet he, if he examines the case correctly, will impute this to himself, not to the church. Certainly it would be better for you to save your soul in any cell whatever than for your own and all other churches to be crushed through hatred of you, and for the clergy to remain in the servitude to which it has been subjected in our days. Perhaps, too, by such a humiliation as the Lord will inspire in you, you will move the king, if you speak these things at the right place and time, with the modesty, contempt for possessions, and constancy which the cause requires. If you have him truly reconciled, all these matters, with the Lord’s help, will very easily be settled. And if this cannot otherwise be achieved, I beg and advise by every means that you visit him more frequently. Do not think that you abandon the office of a shepherd in him if you retain even this one soul in the worship of God, upon whose decision—God so ordaining—countless souls depend. For, as the moral philosopher says: “The world is shaped after the example of its king.” And Solomon says that as the ruler of a city is, so will its inhabitants be. Why multiply words? The sum of my prayers and counsel is that, as far as you can, provided it is according to God, you obtain the king’s goodwill.

Yet your companions—whom you have had, have, and will have as familiar associates so long as God permits—lie when they say that I advise you otherwise, asserting that I urged you to withdraw from the lord king’s service and to honour no knight. God knows, and you know, that I have always advised you to render the king the service due to him and to preserve your honour before [Col. 0704D] God and men.

## LETTER CCCLXXI. FROM HIS FRIEND TO THE SAME

To the reverend lord and Father THOMAS, by God’s grace venerable Archbishop of Canterbury: from his own devoted servant; may he not abandon patience in tribulation.

We read that in the days of the emperor Constantius certain bishops, insufficiently spiritual, neglecting their own churches, frequently attended court, disgraced Caesar by shameful flattery, obeyed royal rather than evangelical decrees, and placed their confidence more in the aid of princes than of the Lord. By contrast Martin, Bishop of Tours, of incomparable merit, avoiding as far as he could the tents of sinners, dwelt more devoutly in the house of his God entrusted to him, though despised by the world. Yet whenever he happened to be summoned by the aforesaid prince, he showed him words and a countenance of severity; he reproved the unworthy flatteries of his fellow bishops; he restrained the excesses of an undiscerning prince; preferring in spirit to lack human favour through checking the faults of the mighty rather than to fall from heavenly favour by fostering the errors of offenders. And behold, we now see the times of Constantius renewed. For today very many shepherds of our Church run from the ends of the earth to hear and do the will of Solomon. They plainly deem it inadequate and insignificant to be fulfilled with the abundant gift of God’s grace unless they also gain admission to royal counsels.

That old civil and domestic plague of the Maccabees likewise now disturbs our Church by a similar event. When Antiochus lately rushed in fury against the Lord’s priests, intending to trample holy things in Jerusalem, recall the Hebrews from their ancestral laws, and humiliate the dignities of the temple’s officers, behold, some men went out from Israel—truly pestilent men—who, fearing the approach of imminent calamity, or perhaps envying the primacy of the high priest, anticipated the king’s anger with sufficiently abject submission. They eagerly sought what might serve for peace, earned a shameful compact with him, and secretly disparaged the loyalty of their prelate. But may He who has established His place in peace scatter those who desire wars. May He who rejects the counsels of princes render foolish the counsels of Ahithophel [Col. 0705C] and his companions against innocent David. And whoever, with Korah, Dathan, or Abiram, has presumed in the camp of this militant Church to provoke the Lord’s holy Aaron, may he be struck by the sentence of Dathan and Abiram: deprived of heaven, let him be swallowed by the earth. Thus, in proportion as they have removed their minds farther from seeking the will of heaven by persecuting the just and innocent man, may they be buried more deeply under earthly passions through committing unseemly acts.

I have said this in an anguished spirit, because, when our Stephen, full of grace, tirelessly ministered the word of life to his brethren and fellow sufferers, having committed no deed worthy of death and nothing marked by crime, the wicked laid an assault upon him. Behold, the enemies of the Son of Man, girded with swords and prepared to harm, are sent across the sea and through lands by secular power, so that they may speedily uproot that same fruitful tree which He planted, humiliate without cause him whom He exalted with cause, and thoughtlessly diminish the dignity of His faithful servant which He had prudently bestowed. What then shall the gentle and innocent athlete of God do, unaware and ignorant of the sword stretched out against him? Whither shall he flee, besieged by the counsel of the wicked? It remains for him, encouraged to endurance, like a ram chosen from the flock and fattened with the richness of charity, to offer himself to the Lord for sacrifice. It remains for him, made an imitator of his Head, to endure without murmuring and without the impediment of resistance the various injuries of the wicked; and, while suffering, not to threaten, but indeed to pray even for the crime of those who injure him.

Therefore let Moses stand in the breach before the gaze of the divine majesty, diligently interceding for brethren who lately worshipped, without his knowledge, a molten calf—a calf, indeed, full of gold. Yet, once the moment of tribulation has passed and the acceptable time of recompense has come, may he punish those same men more strictly in vengeance for their crime, whom he first piously mourned in brotherly compassion, so that, according as they sowed in cursing, they may reap from cursing the fruit of their deed. Thus may it come to pass that Joseph, proved by the trial of adversity, at last gaining Pharaoh’s favour, may rule in glory over the princes of Egypt and his own brothers, whose envy had grieved him. Then, when they too are overwhelmed by tribulations, may they rightly recall that they suffer such things because they sinned against their brother without any fault demanding it.

For, in a remarkable and subtle fashion, Job’s fellow citizens strove to overthrow their friend when certain of our priests lately went to meet the chief priest, more fearfully than sincerely, seeking by every art to persuade the incorrupt one, themselves corrupt; the unleavened one, themselves leavened; to consent to be leavened likewise—he who knows nothing of the bitterness of leaven. Priests therefore came from Jerusalem to John, investigating who he was and of what integrity; but, not finding him a reed shaken by the wind, they departed useless and without honour. [Col. 0706C] Indeed, those sent in this manner were Pharisees. Would that they might also find a prophet in Israel who, casting out the leprosy of his prince lest he himself share the leprosy, rejects the abundance of gold or garments offered him—indeed, even of an entire kingdom. Thus King Balak, together with his supporters, sought to corrupt Balaam by gift or promises, so that he might expose the people enclosed by God to the enemies’ curse, both in deed and word, though that people is governed by God’s blessing.

But behold one greater than Balaam—indeed, not Balaam at all—who could not be compelled by prayer, price, or added threats to hand over the souls of the poor to beasts, since he once understood long ago the saying concerning these matters: “Feed my sheep.” In Daniel, therefore, the young man who did not worship the statue of the king of Babylon, I admire the faith which I find not at all in the elders and his fellow sufferers. Oh, if our sons of Aaron did not mingle with the nations, if they were not contaminated by the wealth of the nations, if they maintained undivided the dignity of their order: how freely and peacefully would they govern and carry about the tabernacle of the covenant with its ministers, unshaken in the midst of the Amorites! But because the lax and undisciplined sons of Eli fell in battle through their own negligence, behold, the ark of God was captured by the Philistines and carried about according to the will and direction of the enemy; and when the sons were turned backward into alienation, their ruin was multiplied.

But whatever elders of Israel may be defiled by transgressing the commandments, let our Phinehas stand alone, not swerving from the commandments of his God; and let him not cease, with frequent tears, to appease heaven’s wrath until the shaking that threatens the Church ceases. And may this be reckoned to him as righteousness from generation to generation for ever. Amen.

## LETTER CCCLXXII. FROM HIS FRIEND TO THE SAME

To THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury: from a certain friend of his.

Know that this is the tenor of the commands which King Henry has sent into England: namely, that every port is to be guarded with the utmost care, so that letters of interdict may by no means be brought there. If any religious brings them, he is to have his feet cut off; if a cleric, he is to lose his eyes [Col. 0707B] and genitals; if a layman, he is to be hanged; if a leper, he is to be burned. If any bishop, fearing his interdict, wishes to depart, he is to take nothing with him except a staff. He also wills that all scholars be compelled to return home or be deprived of their benefices; and those who remain shall remain without hope of returning. Priests who refuse to sing are to lose their genitals; and all rebels against him are to be deprived of every benefice. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCLXXIII

It is difficult to act prudently where reason is rejected, justice trampled underfoot, the supreme pontiff despised, and reverence shown more to the foulest men than to God. I ought, indeed, to have acted in this way and that. This was very easy to say but exceedingly difficult [Col. 0707C] to do, both because every person lends mutual support to the others, and because etc. I therefore judged it safer and less dangerous to try the whirlpool of boiling anger with the staff of humility than, in a rash venture of boldness or attack, to cast one’s whole body into the whirlpool of the deep. I had also another consideration in this matter: I did not wish to uncover my reverend father’s nakedness with an irreverent brow. It seems to me, then, that one acts more wisely by sitting beneath the shelter of a shrub while the storm mutters, because, God willing, after this disturbance of the air the grace of calm will follow. Observe, therefore, that the purpose of our cause is largely rendered void because an alteration of accents was suddenly made.

## LETTER CCCLXXIV. LETTER OF BROTHER R. TO BROTHERS G. R.

[Col. 0707D]

To the lords G. … G. R., beloved brethren in Christ: Brother R. wishes them abundance of the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

Blessed be God, who, although late in doing so because your merits demanded it, has nevertheless looked upon you in order to visit those sitting in darkness, disperse the sackcloth of your misery, turn mourning into joy, and, after the draught of tears, cheer the sadness of long grief with the wine of unexpected gladness. I heard, indeed, and rejoiced in the things said to me, and my soul exulted to magnify the Lord—yet much more abundantly on your account, whom He loved, but in the Lord. For from Him and through Him our ground of affection was formed in Him. Hence, when I perceive the matters in which you watch more devoutly for God’s sake, I embrace them with a more joyful mind and a more abundant affection of goodwill. How much I grieved over your oppression and desolation has been made known by the repeated complaint of my groans. I regarded the distress of your calamity as my own. Though I endured it less in bodily presence, I was nevertheless never absent in spirit. Yet, through the grace of divine mercy, I who formerly feared have now begun to hope.

For who should fear an unjust cause, especially one sustained by so many and such great protections? Or who should distrust when the lord pope commands by the authority of the Apostolic See, royal power also protects, and the diligence of so many judges provides piously, justly, and kindly for everything? Who, moreover, could despair of a joyous and prosperous outcome in so discerning a beginning of so necessary a reform? The matter therefore needs only painstaking diligence, so that perseverance may bring to completion the work of holy equity reasonably undertaken. Gird yourselves, then, and be of good courage; for you shall see the Lord’s help upon you, so that, once the destroyer is expelled, the condition of your church’s possessions may be restored for the better.

For already I seem to see the seed of Jacob, from the tribe of Ephraim and the house of Manasseh: that is, a man undertaking the care of your church, who, after supplanting his adversaries, may make its living possessions fruitful and labour to restore religious beauty; who, forgetting what lies behind, may stretch himself toward what lies ahead, earnestly seeking heavenly things while not failing to administer temporal things discreetly. That most beloved day will come, I say, will come by the Lord’s gift, when we shall see God’s mercy and rejoice in the perfect fruit of the good we desire. Take care, therefore, in the cause of blessed Peter, so diligently entrusted to you by the vicar of blessed Peter, that you neither relax anything through negligence nor intensify anything too vehemently: lest negligence be dangerous or vehemence suspect, and the oppression of your house not be revealed because, in prosecuting your injuries, you seem to pursue your own advantage or burn with a desire for vengeance.

Stand therefore, acting manfully, swerving neither through fear nor flattery from the state of uprightness, but holding the zeal of God according to knowledge, walking simply and rightly, neither broken by faint-heartedness nor softened by weakness. [Col. 0708D] For I know and do not doubt that both the head of this evil and its members strive in many ways to deceive your simplicity. But, since it is useless to be deceived and shameful to deceive, the Lord not without reason wished the children of holy mother Church to resemble both the serpent and the dove. Attend, therefore, to these matters, and provide for yourselves in the future and for your church; for you will be cast down all the more grievously because there would be no further place for rising again, if, after the lord pope’s command and the contempt of so great fathers, they should bend the inconstancy of your minds toward the inclination of their perversity.

This, then, is the purport and settled judgment of my counsel: believe no spirit in any direction other than that which you have undertaken to do, lest, if it should again be necessary to restore the cause, you be unable to stand in it or for it, and you become alike subject to danger of life and loss of reputation. But if you are compelled to appeal, or if he, seeking an evasion, appeals, caution is needed in this respect also. For it is especially dangerous to travel with those whose relatives and blood-kindred may lie in wait for our blood. Rather, requesting from the delegated judges appointed for you, out of your church’s resources, the expenses necessary for so long a journey in prosecuting the church’s cause, and furnished with their letters—called apostolic letters—do not delay to set out as swiftly as you can for my lord pope. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCLXXV. FROM HIS ENVOY TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0709B] To THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury: from his envoy.

I did not find the Count of Flanders; and, while looking for him, I believed it dangerous for me to make diversions and not advantageous to you. The King of France received me at Soissons with great joy, together with what had been sent to him through me; and immediately he dispatched to my lord pope, with his letters, the prior of St Medard at Soissons, a discerning man of great authority. He also gave him certain oral instructions concerning our affair which it was unsafe to commit to writing. When I was leaving him, holding my hand in his, he promised on his royal word that, if you should happen to cross into his territories, he would receive you not as a bishop or archbishop but would make himself your partner in his kingdom. In the same way the Count of Soissons, with many oaths interposed, declared that he would devote the county of Soissons and all its revenues to your use; and that, if my return journey passed through him, he would convey this to you in his own letters.

Having arranged these matters as best I could, I hastened to the curia with the aforesaid prior through the land of Count Henry, both because the road was shorter and because his company afforded security. The prior, however, presented the king’s letters and discussed the oral matters entrusted to him two days before I appeared before my lord pope. Then, when I too came, my lord pope received me with a sigh and not without tears. For before I arrived, he and the whole curia had heard everything that was done in the council—concerning the persecution of the Church, your steadfastness, which bishops stood with you, how he who was not of us went out from you, the judgment passed upon the cleric, and almost everything entrusted in secret—and these matters were proclaimed in the streets. When we had withdrawn apart, I carefully explained to him each point as our memorandum contained it. He continually magnified God, who had granted such a shepherd to His Church. The whole curia also commends the courage it finds in you, though it finds itself wholly lacking in it. For all suffer such weakness of spirit that they seem to fear men more than God.

Because Radicoforum in Tuscany, together with the brother and nephews of my lord pope, and certain other castles together with the relatives of cardinals, have been captured by the Germans; because John Cumin has remained so long with the emperor; because Count Henry has refused to come to my lord pope; because they have received no envoy from the King of England for a long time; and because many other circumstances concur, they are so terrified that at this time they dare not offend any prince in any matter—especially the King of England—nor, even if they could, attempt to assist the Church of God, which is in danger throughout the world. But enough of this.

You will learn clearly from the earlier letters of the lord of Poitiers—who, by God’s grace, arrived one day before me and laboured carefully and faithfully in your affairs as a friend—what was done concerning your petitions and how they were handled. For the pope, avoiding royal anger in every way, sends letters to you and to the Archbishop of York, not commanding letters but exhorting both of you to establish and maintain peace between yourselves. He sends to you a certain brother of the Temple to meet each of you and orally command each, on my lord pope’s behalf, that no dispute henceforth be held between you concerning carrying the cross or concerning anything else, until the Roman Church, by God’s mercy, obtains the tranquillity of peace. Thus the Roman Church may be able to decide these matters and any others which may arise between you in the meantime. To the Archbishop of York, however, the pope writes that he is not to presume meanwhile to carry it in [Col. 0710C] your diocese. We could obtain this only with great difficulty. A similar letter is written to the Bishop of London; but from what source does an exalted spirit more readily swell into pride than awaken to virtue? For this reason my lord pope wished a copy of these letters to be sent to you, so that, having inspected it, if you judge that they do not benefit you and the Church, the letters themselves might remain with you.

Much was debated with my lord pope and the lord of Poitiers concerning the profession to be made. At last, however, we obtained this: if, when asked about it, he should deny it to you, then only would the pope compel him and cause it to be rendered. You will learn this more fully from the later letters of the lord of Poitiers. [Col. 0710D] Which are the earlier and which the later will appear from their subscriptions. Concerning the affair of St Augustine’s we could obtain absolutely nothing. For he asserts that he has seen the privileges granted to the monastery by Roman pontiffs, and that to oppose them, as he says, is not to show due authority to the decrees of the Fathers and ecclesiastical institutions. Finally, when we made him the request that he should command you to come to him and send you letters on this matter, he seemed to answer with grief and much anguish of mind: “Far be it. May our days end before we see him depart in this manner and leave his church so desolate.”

May God preserve you in all your ways. At Clairvaux, Cîteaux, and Pontigny, through my lord pope’s intercession, prayer is continually made for you and for the church entrusted to you by God. Let my lord inform me of his condition as soon as he can, so that my soul may at least be consoled by news of his welfare.

## LETTER CCCLXXVI. FROM THOMAS’S ENEMIES TO THE POPE AND CARDINALS

To Pope ALEXANDER and all the cardinals: from the enemies of THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

“It is a time for remedy rather than complaint,” etc. See under Pope Alexander III, for the year 1181.

## LETTER CCCLXXVII. FROM A CERTAIN FRIEND TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

To his lord and Father: from his own servant, though degenerate and deservedly abandoned because of his own cowardice. May he so suffer with Christ [Col. 0711B] as also to reign with Him.

Concerning the matters which, after inspecting your holiness’s letters, we learned should be investigated, we approached very many persons with all the diligence we could, as we believed proper; and among them—and before all others—we approached all the more urgently because we trusted him more, the man whom we believed to be another you. We found him indeed the same man and in the same state. Having heard the contents of the letters, his eyes filled with tears; after sobs and many complaints concerning the conduct and manner of life of our Censorinus, he said that he had often found his mind, thoroughly tested in this matter, vehemently hostile and difficult to recall, since those whisperers continually and insistently breathe the poison of their malice into his ears. They watch without ceasing lest he hear anything that might soften his mind from the obstinacy of the malignity he has undertaken. With all their efforts they labour to inflame his hatred of you so greatly that by the intervention of no plea or person may you be brought into the favour of any kind of reconciliation. Nor do they think they can live happily until they know for certain that they have accomplished this.

Among them that hateful Richard de Luci, enemy even of his own surname, weaves these snares more than the rest—to such an extent that he often offends even the man whom he strives to please, while he attempts too vehemently and irreverently to blacken your person, acts, and counsels. Thus, at one time Censorinus himself, weary of the trifles he heard from him, said, upon turning aside to the person from whom we learned this, that he wondered how that man was not ashamed to weave so many fabulous stories, which he had neither seen himself nor learned from a certain authority. Afterwards, however, when he spoke with that same friend of yours concerning the state of affairs, he entered upon this discussion and seemed to waver somewhat in mind, so far as that friend could infer, as though he were ashamed to have begun more bitterly what he could not easily end as he wished.

He also appeared to fear an encounter with the Welsh, lest perhaps, while occupied with them, men from across the sea—namely the Flemings and French—should endeavour to disturb him. Therefore, if he had even a slight but honourable occasion to cross the sea, he wished to visit the lands overseas, so that, after establishing peace with those people there, he might attack these more safely. Yet he said that he remained undecided and had formed no settled plan concerning this. That friend of yours therefore thought that, if my lord pope summoned him by letters, or through a special legate, on account of the Church’s imminent dangers, the calamity of the city of Antioch lately reported to him, and other matters of that kind, intending to confer with him before returning to Rome, he would readily go to those regions. Then it would be not unseemly but honourable for him to comply with the admonitions of so great a father concerning that matter about which he now does not deign even to hear anyone. This would be the one and only remaining way to restore peace between you.

But the utmost care must be taken that nothing seems to be done by him on account of your cause, especially before, by the Lord’s gift, it happens that they meet. May He for whom you suffer preserve you unharmed for His Church. If the small services of our insignificance can be of use according to your holiness’s desire, let us be instructed by a reply; we shall comply with devoted affection. May your fatherhood ever prosper in the Lord.

## LETTER CCCLXXVIII. FROM A CERTAIN FRIEND TO THE SAME

To THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury: from a certain friend of his.

Your messenger, who had come to Lord Nicholas, I did not see; but I received Nicholas’s boy, so that through him I might report to you some news worthy of being conveyed and useful to be known. Therefore, after your boy’s departure from me—he has long since returned to you—I first learned this: on a certain day, when the king was at Caen and was anxiously discussing his affair with the king of Scotland, he burst out into insulting words against [Col. 0712C] Richard de Humez, who seemed to be speaking to some extent for the king of Scotland, and openly called him a traitor. The king, therefore, inflamed with his customary rage, threw his cap from his head, unfastened his belt, flung far away the cloak and garments he was wearing, removed with his own hand the silken covering that lay upon the bed, and, sitting as though on a dung-heap, began to chew stalks of straw. The following day, while he was in a meadow near the chapel and Richard of Ilchester wished to approach him, the Templars hurried to meet him; after removing their caps, they immediately offered him the kiss, had not the king, with many looking on, driven them away, saying that he did not wish them to give the kiss to an excommunicated man.

[Col. 0712D] After this, when the king came to Touques, the bishop of Lisieux came to him, requesting and entreating, under the pretext of poverty, permission to leave the land: so that he, being burdened by debt, might at least be able to recover his breath for a year, and, having returned free of debts, might more readily withdraw to a religious house. The king, looking at him, said: “Truly, your face has changed more than you realize, and, as it seems to me, you cannot bear toil much longer. Yet you shall never leave my land because of want. For I shall speak with your creditors, shall help you in some ways, and shall make you exempt and free from harassments and burdens.” He promised nothing from his own resources, therefore, but promised to assist him through others.

After this the king went to his conference with the count of [Col. 0713A] Flanders, where those things occurred which you know. There the king promised that he would give Count Matthew of Boulogne one thousand pounds yearly. There the messenger of the lord pope was seized, and is still held in chains and prison. There the Lord rescued Master Herbert from the hands of those seeking him. Certainly he ought not to have undergone such danger for so trifling a matter. For it is foolish to be bold where the accomplishment of the undertaking brings neither the praise of great glory nor the benefit of much profit.

When the king had returned to Rouen, he summoned the archbishop and the bishop of Lisieux, and those two began to discuss the seizure of the bearer of the lord pope’s letters, and the indignation which he had conceived against the clerk of Geoffrey Ridel because he had received your letters and had not detained the messenger; and they reproved the king to some extent on these matters. [Col. 0713B] Then too the archbishop began more openly to explain to the king the meaning of the letters which he had formerly received from the lord pope on your behalf, and gently rebuked him in his usual way, until the king said that he knew in full whatever the letters contained, and feared such threats very little.

While this was happening, Master Reginald, clerk of the dean of Tours, approached the king, anxiously seeking many opportunities by which he might more honourably rebuke him for this deed and fully learn his will. But the king, mocking the prosperity of the lord pope and the tranquillity of the court’s condition, scarcely allowed him to speak of such matters. After this the king returned to Caen; and the bishop of Lisieux, coming to [Col. 0713C] him in order to obtain more fully permission to leave, was carefully questioned by the king as to how much he owed and how much he required. When the bishop repeatedly stated that, if he remained, he needed two hundred marks, the king declared that he did not possess so much silver, but nevertheless sent him sixty marks that same night. Would that he had not accepted the prince’s diminished money: for henceforth the king will believe that he has bought with it the man whom he saw to be in need, and will use him as an instrument to complete the evil of his iniquity. For perhaps the king will trust him more; and he, I fear, will be more faithful to the king in unfaithfulness.

In these same days Alfred, clerk of the bishop of Hereford, came to the king, declaring that his bishop [Col. 0713D] and Lord Roger would, in accordance with the tenor of your command, depart from the land and shortly come to you, unless they remained through the king’s help and counsel. The king therefore complained greatly concerning Lord Roger, and used a prohibition as counsel, saying that those whom the remedy of appeal could help to remain could not be compelled to depart. He added also that they could leave, but could not return. These things have indeed occurred among us.

For the rest, know that on the octave of Saint Martin the king is to confer at Tours with Count Theobald; there he will presently pay the five hundred pounds which he had promised him annually, and will lie concerning the future. On the following Sunday there will be a conference at Chinon with Poitou and the neighbouring lands. After this, on the feast of Saint Andrew, he will be [Col. 0714A] at Rouen, so that on the octave he may meet the count of Flanders. There he will promise Count Boulogne that he will give him one thousand pounds annually for peace and concord between them; and he has firmly declared and sworn that he will do nothing else for him.

In all these matters the king wavers and is uncertain; hoping in the chances of the future, he has placed the sole foundation of his strength in the possibility that the lord pope may enter upon the way of all flesh, or that something human may happen to you—which God forbid.

Therefore, while you have time, stretch out the hand of requital, and know that it is written: “The Lord will abundantly repay those who act proudly.” Let the sentence of your severity therefore punish those who exalt themselves against God. And cut off with the rod of uprightness the twisting head of the serpent, [Col. 0714B] so that Satan may swiftly be trampled beneath your feet. For unless by a strong hand and an uplifted arm, the Church of God will not have peace. Nor can this lion, wholly sunk asleep in the treachery of his unbelief, be roused except by the father’s roar. Come then: bend the bow, send forth the arrows, until they are weakened. For it is wicked to be merciful where God’s mercy is annulled and faith is imperilled. He is badly faithful who does not preserve the rights of faith; and him whom we see acting against faith we rightly call unfaithful. Act, therefore, and be silent no longer, for silence nourishes assent, and the offence of subjects is often turned back upon the shepherd through the lethargy of silence. Call, then, those whom you can, and compel them to depart from the midst of Babylon. For it is better to die [Col. 0714C] with you in battle than to behold together the evils of one’s people and of the saints. Call, I say, and let those who have scorned to hear the shepherd’s summons immediately feel the judge. May your holiness and health flourish for many days. Believe that I am always yours, and prepared for everything that may please you. Farewell again, and always.

## LETTER 379. FROM HIS FRIEND TO THE POPE.

To ALEXANDER, pope, from a certain friend of his.

“The emperor, when he had summoned his princes to court,” etc. See under Alexander III.

## LETTER 380. FROM A CERTAIN FRIEND TO THOMAS.

[Col. 0714D]

To his lord and father, from his own man.

To accompany a friend in exile both in body and spirit is a pledge of ardent and unquestioning love. Indeed, we know many who, while at home, share in their friends’ exile in mind. Yet we have heard of no few who, leaving mind and heart at home, merely share their friends’ exile in body. Your true friend, the lord bishop of Worcester, chose for himself the more commendable manner of sharing suffering: following the path of your exile, compassionately abiding with you, he turned neither the eyes of his body back toward his see nor the constancy of his heart toward the blandishments or threats of earthly power. He alone, indeed, was found to bear at once in body and spirit the troubles of his father, and to prefer reverence for his prelate [Col. 0715A] to pleasures and riches.

Therefore, the stronger the proof of his fidelity appears, the safer and more useful it would be for you to set this same man as a stronger bulwark against the dangers of the world, where, when the occasion was suitable and the prince perhaps softened gave opportunity, he might keep you in remembrance and speak of you. It would therefore seem to me more prudent and more advantageous for you that this aforesaid friend of yours should return to his homeland at his prince’s summons and there exercise that vigor of charity with which he embraces you. There he would find abundant material for exercising it. Here, as matters presently occur to me, he will not be able to assist you equally, nor display the goodwill which he bears toward you. May my lord prosper.

## LETTER 381. FROM A CERTAIN MEMBER OF HIS HOUSEHOLD TO THE SAME.

[Col. 0715B]

To his lord, from his own man: salvation in all things, as for himself.

On the Thursday next after the octave of Saint Martin, the cardinals came to the monastery of Le Bec; on the following day to Lisieux; on the third day to Saint-Pierre-sur-Dives; on the fourth—that is, Sunday preceding the Advent of the Lord—they came to Argentan. That same day the king met them two leagues away, showed them a cheerful face, and accompanied both cardinals as far as their lodging. The following day, that is Monday, quite early after Mass, they were summoned and came to the king; they entered the chamber for consultation with the archbishops, bishops, and abbots who [Col. 0715C] had been admitted. When they had remained inside for about two hours, the cardinals came out, and the king went with them as far as the outer door of the chapel. As they went, the lord king publicly said this word, even with the cardinals themselves hearing: “Would that my eye might never again see any cardinal!”

He dismissed them with such haste that, although their lodging was quite near, they did not wait for their own horses to be brought, but horses found by chance nearest before the chapel were given to them for departure. The cardinals left with no more than four companions. The archbishops, bishops, and abbots remained with the king and entered the chamber for consultation. [Col. 0715D] After they had stayed there until approximately the evening hour, they came to the cardinals, and all their faces appeared troubled. After remaining with the cardinals for some time, they returned to their lodgings.

The next day, after remaining with the king until the sixth hour, they came to the cardinals, then returned to the king, then again to the cardinals, carrying secret responses back and forth. The following day, the vigil of Saint Andrew, the king rose at first light and went out to sport with dogs and birds of the air, as was believed and supposed—deliberately making himself absent. That same day they assembled quite early at the king’s chapel and immediately went to the chamber. After holding a deliberation there in the king’s absence, they went out to the church beside which the cardinals had their [Col. 0716A] lodgings.

When the cardinals had taken their seats, those called to hear what was to be proposed by them were present: on either side sat the archbishops of Rouen and York; the bishops of Worcester, Salisbury, Bayeux, London, Chichester, and Angoulême; very many abbots; and a great multitude of clerics and laymen. The bishop of London rose; and his insipid and rather graceless speech showed that his mind was troubled. He began thus:

“You have heard that the letters of the lord pope have been brought to us, and we have them in hand. In them the lord pope informed us that, whenever we were summoned by you, we should meet you, and that the causes at issue between the lord king and the lord of Canterbury, and between us bishops of England and that same lord of Canterbury, had been entrusted to you with the fullness of authority. Therefore, on hearing of your arrival in these regions, we have come to meet you, fully ready and prepared to abide by your judgment, and to bring an action or make an answer. The lord king also offers that whatever judgment you pronounce between him and the lord of Canterbury, he will hold ratified.

“Since, therefore, neither the lord king, nor you, nor even we stand in the way of the fulfilment of the lord pope’s command, let responsibility be assigned as it ought to be assigned. But because the archbishop, as he does everything precipitately, strikes suddenly and even suspends and excommunicates before he threatens or admonishes, [Col. 0716C] we have forestalled his sudden and hasty sentence by an appeal. We formerly made the appeal, now renew it, and by this appeal all England is enclosed.”

He then set forth your case and that of the lord king: namely, that the king demands from you forty-four thousand marks of silver, an account of revenues entrusted to you when you were chancellor; and that you reply that you were not involved in the accounts when you were raised to the dignity of the archbishopric, and that, even if you had been involved, by the very fact that you were promoted you were absolved. There the bishop of London mocked you, saying that you believed that, just as sins are remitted in baptism, so debts are released upon promotion.

He also related the dangers for which he and the other bishops of England had appealed: namely, their own oppression and that of their churches, and even separation from the Roman Church. For the king might perhaps withdraw from the Roman Church if they obeyed your interdict. He also related how you defamed him because of his decrees. There he publicly declared that the king had relaxed this interdict because of the appeal, and had instituted it for the sake of poor clerics, but now would annul it because they were ungrateful. [Col. 0716D] Likewise, if the cause were civil, they would contend before a civil judge; but if ecclesiastical, they would plead their forum and contend before their own judge.

Finally, he said that you exacted undue servitude from him: that is, that he must carry your writs throughout England, and that not even forty runners were sufficient for this service. He also advanced another burden by which, he said, you oppressed him: that you had exempted nearly forty churches from his jurisdiction. For they had formerly paid a due to the monastery of Holy Trinity or Saint Augustine, and you immediately emancipated them from his jurisdiction. You also had your dean in the city of London, who laid snares for him and before whom the causes of the aforesaid churches must be decided. He said that he was more oppressed by these burdens than any other bishop.

The bishop of Salisbury also included himself, and the bishop of Winchester, in this appeal. Salisbury, however, said that he had heard you had excommunicated him, but that he had appealed immediately upon hearing it, and was then likewise appealing. A cleric, the archdeacon of Canterbury, also appealed there against you, [Col. 0717B] as did a monk of the church of Canterbury. When the appeal had been made, they sought letters certifying their appeal from the cardinals; and letters of appeal were given them, as is believed.

The cardinals departed from the king on the Tuesday after *Ad te levavi*. At their departure, however, the king humbly begged the cardinals to intercede for him with the lord pope, that he might free him from you entirely; and immediately, in the presence of the cardinals and others, he wept. Lord William the cardinal appeared also to weep. Lord Otto could scarcely restrain himself from a burst of laughter.

The sum of the matter is this: Lord William of Pavia is sending a certain clerk of his, believed to be a kinsman of Master Lombard, with haste to the lord [Col. 0717C] pope; and the king is sending two messengers—one of the bishop of London’s men, called Master Henry Pinchin, and with him Reginald, son of the bishop of Salisbury. Furthermore, on the Saturday before the second Sunday of Advent, Master Jocelin of Chichester and the precentor of Salisbury departed from the cardinals, who were at Évreux, intending to come to you in order to notify you that an appeal against you had been made by the persons of England.

They also bear letters. In this form the cardinals greet you, call you legate of the Apostolic See, and at the end of their letter command you by the authority of the lord pope not henceforth to lay any interdict upon the kingdom of England or its persons. Lord Otto secretly informs the lord pope that he will neither promote nor consent to your deposition, although the king seems to ask for nothing else but your head upon a dish. Farewell.

## LETTER 382. FROM FRIEND TO FRIEND.

From a friend to a friend: the words of the lord of Canterbury with the legates between Gisors and Trie.

Because I do not doubt that you are concerned about the state of the Church and the outcome of the legation which has been obtained, I have judged that the following should be briefly set down for your consolation and that of others who fear God. Know, then, that the lord of Canterbury, with several of his fellow exiles, came on the octave of Saint Martin to a conference with the legates between Gisors and Trie. When [Col. 0718A] they had said much concerning the charity of the lord pope and his concern for our affairs—the attentive concern he bears for their labours and the dangers of the journey—concerning the greatness of the prince and the need of the Church, the evil of the times, the love and benefits by which the lord king had anticipated Canterbury, and the honour which he had always shown him, they added also the complaints and injuries by which the king says that he has been harmed by Canterbury. Among other charges, they alleged that he had stirred up against the king the war of the king of France. They sought counsel as to how they might calm so great an indignation, since they knew that no remedy could be applied to such dangers without much humility, moderation, and an exhibition of honour.

But Canterbury, in all humility and gentleness of spirit, after due thanksgiving to the lord pope and to them, answered each point, refuting the king’s complaints with true and probable arguments and openly setting forth the injuries of the Church and its intolerable losses. Because they required humility and an acknowledgement of honour from him, he answered that he would show every humility, honour, and reverence as fully as he could: provided that the honour of God, the liberty of the Church, the dignity of his person, and the possessions of the Church were preserved. If anything seemed to them to require addition, removal, or alteration, he begged them to give him counsel, declaring himself resolved to comply, provided the condition of his profession and order was preserved.

When they said that they had not come in order to take counsel from him, but to counsel him and attempt a path to reconciliation, [Col. 0718C] the archbishop was again asked whether, in the legates’ presence, he would promise observance of the customs which kings had employed in the time of his predecessors; and thus, with all complaints laid to rest, return to the king’s favour and receive his see, administration, and peace for himself and his followers.
