To this the archbishop replied: “None of my predecessors was compelled by any king to make this profession; nor shall I, God being my author, ever promise to observe customs which openly oppose the law of God, overthrow the privilege of the Apostolic See, and destroy the liberty of the Church—customs which the lord pope condemned at Sens, in the presence of these men and many others, and which I afterward, following the authority of the lord pope, subjected, together with their observers, to anathema, as the Catholic Church is known to have done in many councils.”

He was also asked whether, if not confirmation, he would at least promise dissimulation and toleration; or, without either side making any mention of the customs, receive his see and peace. The archbishop answered that there is a proverb of our people: “A silent man wears the spirit of one confessing.” Since the king appears to himself to possess the customs, and unjustly and violently compels the Church to observe them, if, once silence had been obtained, the conflict ceased—especially with the legates’ authority intervening—he would immediately appear to himself and to others to have prevailed in this cause. [Col. 0719A] He added that he would rather be exiled and proscribed forever, and, if God so ordained, die in defence of justice, than enter into this peace to the detriment of his salvation and the prejudice of ecclesiastical liberty. For God is he who forbids priests to be silent in such a cause, and has prepared hell for those who dissemble, where there will be no dissimulation of punishment.

The written schedule of those abominations was read, and the cardinals were asked whether it was lawful for Christians to observe such things, much less for shepherds to dissemble about them.

They proceeded to another question, asking whether he would submit to their judgment in the matters at issue between himself and the king. He replied that he trusted in the integrity of his cause and that, when he and his people, who for a long time had been deprived, had been fully restored in all things, with due account being taken of causes, resources, and time, he would willingly obey the law. He could neither and would not decline to undergo, where, when, and how he ought, the judgment of him or of those to whose judgment the lord pope should decree that he must submit. Meanwhile, neither he nor his people could be compelled to litigate, nor was their poverty sufficient for it, since they lacked even provisions unless they lived at the expense of the most Christian king of France.

He did not wish at the outset to decline judgment, even though he could with the greatest right regard some of them as suspect, lest he seem to justify the king’s cause. Nor did he wish to plunge into litigation before he had been restored in all things, so that he might sufficiently prepare his case and, relying on God’s grace, not fear any wealthy adversary.

Proceeding further, they asked whether he would answer before them as judges the bishops who had appealed against him, since they were present. [Col. 0719C] The archbishop, mindful of the letters by which that whatsoever-sort-of appeal—or rather no appeal at all—had been presented to him, framed, as is there stated, in the name of all the suffragan bishops, abbots, and persons of the realm dwelling in the province of Canterbury; and certain that these men had not assembled at Rouen, that very many of them had been unaware of this appeal, and that it displeased many who knew of it, being, so far as lay in its authors, an evasion of justice rather than an appeal, replied likewise that he had received no command of the lord pope concerning this; and that when he received one, he would answer after deliberation and do what reason dictated.

Moreover, he said that his own poverty and that of his followers were not adequate for the expenses of journeys and lawsuits; and that the clemency of the most Christian [Col. 0719D] king could not suffer trouble for this end, namely that his generosity, which had resolved most humanely to comfort exiled bishops, should be compelled to maintain him and his fellow exiles often and long in other men’s houses. For where there is an abundance of provisions, expenses are more easily supplied.

On the following day, the most Christian king admitted the legates to a conference and, under the sanctity of an oath, cleared the lord of Canterbury of blame. He bore witness that Canterbury had always counselled him to preserve peace, with the honour of both kings safeguarded and both peoples enjoying their due tranquillity. The archbishop asked the legates to give some counsel to the Church and, if he erred anywhere, to show him a more right path. They approved the zeal which he had in the Lord and sympathized with him, but said that nothing in his purpose ought to be changed. Thus, after giving one another the blessing, they departed from one another. It has been resolved, and by God’s aid it shall be maintained in these regions, until the Church recovers strength and her persecutors either are converted or perish.

She prayed this for you, and does not cease to pray it: that your faith may not fail; and that you, whenever opportunity arises, having turned to them, may strengthen your brethren. You will show these things to those to whom you have been sent: raise up the fallen, strengthen those who stand, that they may be steadfast. For the Church has more patrons and defenders than assailants. He who laid down his life for her liberation will not abandon her in tribulation. They will not abandon the cause of the holy, for which they did not fear to give their blood. The host of all heavenly powers guards her; and the Majesty which [Col. 0720B] crushes Satan beneath its feet will, over his members—the ministers of wickedness—quickly, easily, and happily triumph, as is the hope of the faithful and the promise of the Fathers.

## LETTER 383. FROM A CERTAIN FRIEND TO THOMAS.

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, from a certain friend.

On the day of the Assumption of the Blessed Mary, letters of the lord pope were delivered at Argentan by the messengers; and when they had been read, the king was greatly disturbed. The next day he sent John, dean of Salisbury, and Reginald the archdeacon to meet the messengers. On the vigil of Saint Bartholomew the messengers came to Domfront. When Geoffrey Ridel and Nigel de Saccaville heard of their arrival, they departed from Domfront with sudden haste. Why they left is quite well known to you.

That same day, when it was already late, the king came from the wood and turned aside to the messengers’ lodging before going to his own. He received and greeted them with much honour, reverence, and humility. While he was still standing and speaking with them, behold, Lord Henry, the king’s son, came to the door of the same lodging with many boys, each sounding a hunting horn, as is customary, over the capture of a stag, which he gave them all. They did this so that the guest might hear it. Behold the trappings displayed to the people.

The next day, about the first hour, the king came to the messengers’ lodging. The bishops of Séez and Rennes entered the chamber with him. After some delay John, dean of Salisbury, and Reginald the archdeacon were admitted; shortly afterward, the archdeacon of Llandaff also. Standing until the ninth hour, they spoke sometimes peacefully, but sometimes in quarrel and tumult. [Col. 0720D] The lord king’s purpose was that the excommunicated clerks should not swear. A little before sunset the king came out very angry, complaining bitterly about the lord pope because he had never listened to him in anything. In a spirit of defiance the king said: “By God’s eyes, I shall do otherwise.” Gratian graciously replied: “Lord, do not threaten. We fear no threats, for we are from such a court as is accustomed to command emperors and kings.”

Then all the barons and the White Monks who were present, and almost all from the chapel, were summoned; and the lord king asked them to testify for him at the appropriate time how great and what kinds of things he had offered—namely, restoration of the archbishopric and peace. At the end he seemed to depart from them somewhat pacified and assigned an eighth day for a definite answer. By that date the archbishops had assembled: those of Rouen and Bordeaux, the bishop of Le Mans by chance, and all the bishops of Normandy. The bishop of Worcester had not come on the day when these matters were transacted and are to be reported, but he was expected the next day, and came. The bishop of Poitiers pleaded as an excuse for not coming the synod he was holding, but sent word that he would come immediately after the synod.

On the day before the Kalends of September [Col. 0721B] at Bayeux, the messengers presented to the lord king the lord pope’s letters, requesting your restoration and peace. But the lord king, after setting forth the whole narrative of the matters which he was accustomed to allege against you, said: “If I do anything for this man at the lord pope’s request, he ought to owe me many thanks.”

The next day all the bishops met with the messengers at a place called Le Bur. As soon as the messengers arrived, the lord king entered the park, and all the bishops with him, along with only those who had been summoned by name. The lord king immediately held counsel with the messengers alone, asking them to absolve his clerks without an oath. When the messengers firmly refused to do this, the lord king ran to his horse, mounted, and, in the hearing of all, swore that never in his life would he listen either to the lord pope or to anyone else concerning your peace and restoration. On hearing this, all the archbishops and bishops present came to the messengers and begged them to do this for the love of God. They yielded, though with the greatest difficulty.

After this, the lord king dismounted and again held counsel with them. Soon afterward, summoning everyone in the park, he began his narrative and said that he wished them to know that you had not departed England because of him; that he had repeatedly recalled you to come and make satisfaction concerning the matters he had against you; and that you had refused. “But now the matter stands thus: at the lord pope’s request and command, I fully restore to you your archbishopric and peace, both to you and to all who left my land because of you.” [Col. 0721D] The lord king made this grant of peace about the ninth hour; afterward he remained very cheerful and caused certain other matters to be handled in his presence.

When these were dealt with, he again came to the messengers, asking them to go to England in order to absolve the excommunicated persons there. When they firmly refused, the king grew angry and again requested that at least one of them go while the other remained, or that they send one of their clerks, to whom he would restore revenues before he returned. When Gratian—who, as we hope, is a son of grace—again refused, the lord king withdrew from them in extreme anger and said in their hearing: “Do what you wish. I value neither you nor your excommunications at one egg, nor do I fear them.” After these words he mounted his horse to depart. But all the archbishops and bishops there followed him and told him that he had spoken badly. Afterwards he dismounted and spoke with them.

The sum of that consultation was that they should all write to the lord pope that, in their hearing, he had offered you peace and was prepared to fulfil every command of the lord pope, and that it was owing to the messengers that this did not happen. Then, after they had spent some time composing the letters, and after he had repeatedly departed from them as if highly enraged, the bishops came to him, saying that these messengers had already received and shown a mandate [Col. 0722B] from the lord pope that everyone should do whatever the messengers commanded. The king replied: “I know, I know: they will lay an interdict on my land. But shall I, who can take a very strong castle every day, not be able to take one clerk if he lays an interdict upon my land?”

But when they promised that they would do some things according to his will, the storm entirely ceased; he regained his composure and said: “Unless you make peace tonight, you will never again come to this point.” After they had worked for some time upon this proposal, he summoned everyone and said: “I must do much at the request of the lord pope, who is my lord and father; and therefore I restore to him his archbishopric and my peace, and to all who are outside the land because of him.” Then the messengers and all the others gave thanks. The king then added: “If I have done too little now, tomorrow I shall supply it by our counsel.”

The next day, that is, on the Kalends of September, they assembled at the same place about midday. After lengthy discussion of absolving the excommunicated persons without their swearing, it came to this: Geoffrey Ridel, Nigel de Saccaville, and Thomas son of Bernard, extending their hands over the Gospels placed before them, said upon their word of truth that they would carry out the messengers’ command. Then the messengers requested that all the possessions of your churches which the lord king had meanwhile granted should remain with those to whom the king had given them. But, as we have heard, it came to this: that they should return freely to your disposal.

Afterward it was arranged that the bishops should write the form of peace which [Col. 0722D] the king had granted. The lord king was earnestly pressing that one of the messengers should cross to England to absolve the excommunicated persons. When they had parted, after almost the third hour of the night had elapsed, the king said that this should be written in the form of peace: “Saving the dignity of his kingdom.” But Gratian, as we have heard, firmly refused to allow this on any grounds. The matter still stands upon this point; they are to return on the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Caen, in order to confirm this fully. The bishop of Lisieux laboured to flatter the king; the archbishop of Rouen, to please God and the lord pope. Farewell.

## LETTER 384. FROM A CERTAIN FRIEND TO THE SAME.

[Col. 0723A]

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, from a certain friend.

This is the arrangement on which I met with the king: I tried to see how I might persuade the archbishop, concerning those words which had broken the peace between you, to submit himself to the counsel of the lord of Rouen, of Le Mans, of Séez, and of myself, and of the other bishops who had been present at the conference; or, if any one of them were suspect to him, that he should remove that one, and that you should accept in his place whichever other bishop you wished, provided he were from your realm; and that, according to their counsel, you should wholly remove or alter those words into a definite form which would exclude every doubt whatsoever. [Col. 0723B]

The archbishop replied to me that neither the counsel of the lord of Rouen, nor mine, nor that of any mortal, had ever proved so fruitful or honourable to him as yours; nor had he obtained so great an honour by the counsel of any mortal. Therefore, if it pleased you to admit him into your counsel, he would submit himself to your counsel, provided that you first had regard to the honour of your realm and to your own honour, and thereafter to his, so that he should not offend against the lord pope, to whom he is bound, nor injure the Church, which he ought to benefit.

It would, moreover, be fitting that this counsel should be so settled and made certain before you met that no question should remain when you came together, lest perhaps you should then part from one another less honourably, as you recently did. The king himself received this proposal more kindly than I had expected, and added that, in the counsel which he gave, he would first preserve the honour of God, then his own and that of his realm; and would so provide for you that, so far as he reasonably could, he would not injure your person. But he said that a definitive settlement of the words could not be made between you while he and you were in places so far apart. You must come to some place near him, from which messengers dealing with these matters could pass more closely and easily between you. It would please him if he were at Tours and you at the greater monastery. Or, if you do not wish this, he at Tours and you at Choisy, where, namely, the lord pope had held a conference with the kings, a little beyond Blois. A day has also been fixed for the feast of St Peter’s Chair, provided that eight days beforehand I inform him in Normandy whether you are willing to observe that day. [Col. 0723C–D]

## LETTER CCCLXXXV. FROM A FRIEND TO A FRIEND

A friend to a friend. Concerning the absolution of the bishops.

The lord of Canterbury granted, in our presence and that of the lord of Troyes and certain others, to the envoys of the lord pope, Lord Gratian and Master Vivian, for the sake of peace, that on this occasion they should absolve his excommunicated persons temporarily, after receiving from them an oath that they would abide by the command of the said Canterbury, if they could accomplish this in any way; otherwise, by his own command. [Col. 0724A]

And they in turn promised the lord archbishop in good faith that, if peace had not followed between the king and himself before their departure—which would not be delayed beyond the feast of St Martin—they would, from that feast, restore them to the same sentence in which they had been; nor would they release them because of any appeal made or to be made by those persons, or by anyone else on their behalf, unless within twenty days from the aforesaid feast—provided they remained so long—they had made satisfaction to the lord of Canterbury for the matters on account of which he had excommunicated them. And if they departed before the said feast, they would likewise restore them to the same sentence from the day of their departure, unless, as has been said, they made satisfaction to the same Canterbury.

For they fear to provoke to intolerable injury one who has already endured exile for so long a period for the liberty of the Church; one who, according to the judgment of the lord pope, having been vexed in a few things, has advanced in many, as is believed by those who know the intimate counsels of the same Canterbury. [Col. 0724B]

## LETTER CCCLXXXVI. FROM A FRIEND TO A FRIEND

A friend to a friend. Concerning the names of the excommunicated.

Gilbert, bishop of London, and Jocelin, bishop of Salisbury; Geoffrey Ridel, archdeacon of Canterbury; Richard of Ilchester, archdeacon of Poitiers; Nigel of Sackville; Richard of Hastings, nephew of Richard of Hastings; Letard, nephew of Archbishop Theobald; Robert de Broc; Robert, brother of William of Eynsford; Robert, vicar of Geoffrey, archdeacon of Canterbury; the man who holds the church of Chere; the man who holds the church of Hele; Richard de Luci; Hugh of St Clair; Thomas son of Bernard; Ranulf de Broc; William of Edesford; Robert, butler of Archbishop Theobald; Alan of Reclingis; William de Becco; the man who holds the land of Mundeham, from the manor of Pagaham, which the king took from the Church of Canterbury on account of John Marshal—if there is another holder of it besides the king; the man who holds the land of Lese, from the manor of Otford, which John, brother of William of Eynsford, held—if there is another who holds it besides the king; John Cumin; [Col. 0724C] and Guy Rufus, who is bound, like all the others named above, to restore to the said Canterbury whatever he received from the revenues of the treasurer of Lisieux.

These are those who hold ecclesiastical and lay possessions of the Church of Canterbury and of the lord of Canterbury, which he desires and demands to be restored in their entirety to himself and his people. From the bishop of London, moreover, he demands that whatever he received from the revenues of his clerics be restored to him. If there are any others who have received, from the king’s hand or by his grant, ecclesiastical or lay possessions belonging to the Church of Canterbury, they are excommunicated until they restore those same possessions, and all proceeds received from them, to the Church of Canterbury and to the lord archbishop of Canterbury.

Moreover, Wimar, who was clerk to Count Hugh, Adam of Charing, and William Giffard have been excommunicated by the same archbishop. [Col. 0724D–0725A]

## LETTER CCCLXXXVII. FROM LOUIS TO CARDINALS HUMBALD AND HYACINTH

LOUIS, king of France, to HUMBALD, bishop of Ostia, and HYACINTH, cardinals.

We offer your affection abundant thanks on behalf of the archbishop of Canterbury, whose cause you have supported so piously and perseveringly, out of love for God and for us. Even if your ministry and patronage have not obtained the due completion through your service, the favour shown to your anxious diligence has nevertheless earned no less praise and no less gratitude.

In our kingdom a report producing scandal has been spread; a murmur has arisen which cannot easily be quieted. Everywhere men recall with astonishment that the lord pope, in a desire for vain glory, recently granted public letters to the king of England against the lord of Canterbury, in which the mouth and hand of Canterbury are suspended, and in which all power is forbidden him, both within the kingdom of England and over persons of the realm, until he has fully obtained the king’s favour. [Col. 0725B]

We have no right to accuse the lord pope or openly rebuke him, because he is our lord; but we cannot altogether keep silent concerning those things which tarnish his reputation. And unless your prudence or that of the lord pope instructs us on this matter, we cannot discover what adequate answer we may give to the emperor or to other schismatics who reproach us.

## LETTER CCCLXXXVIII. FROM A CERTAIN FRIEND TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, from a certain friend. [Col. 0725C]

Although I have not more frequently visited the fatherhood of your discretion with the comfort of letters, you ought by no means to wonder at this, since scarcely anyone, or almost no one, sets out for you from the curia to whom confidential written communications may be entrusted; and since I have sent you several letters which, as I have learned for certain, never reached your presence.

Know, therefore, that I have been anxious and watchful in your affairs to the extent of my ability, and have diligently applied myself to their advancement, especially through Master Walter, who above all others laboured effectively with the lord pope for promoting those same affairs, and, by drafting the documents, brought them, God willing, to the desired conclusion. For, as you can see more clearly in the letters and transcripts sealed under a closed bull which are sent to you from the lord pope, your petitions have obtained their due effect. [Col. 0725D]

Furthermore, the bishop of London has been firmly commanded by the lord pope to observe firmly and unshakenly the sentence which you pronounced against him; nor is he in any way to be absolved, without the lord pope’s command, by the archbishops of Rouen and Lisieux, to whom the lord pope writes again on this matter, unless perhaps, after receiving the pope’s earlier letters which they received on this matter, he has given them the oath prescribed by the Church’s form. [Col. 0726A]

Take courage, therefore, and act steadfastly. Like one founded upon firm rock, do not be moved, frightened, or troubled in any way by the blasts of whatever winds. Nor, as is your custom, appoint every passer-by to be an interpreter of your secrets, so that you may seem to trust more in justice than in a multitude; for where there is a multitude, especially in such matters, very frequent confusions usually arise and very many impediments result. Let what I write concerning the bishop of London remain secret with you, since nothing has been written to you about him. I say this because of malicious persons, lest I be said to reveal secrets.

But when God restores you to your former estate—which I hope will happen shortly—remember Master Walter and me, if you please, lest, amid the multitude who look to you, we slip from your memory; for perhaps we shall not then be present. [Col. 0726B]

## LETTER CCCLXXXIX. FROM A CERTAIN FRIEND TO THE SAME

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, from a certain friend.

The king is to be in London next Sunday, and has summoned for that day the archbishop of York, all the bishops of England, and the barons from every part of the land. On that day the archbishop of York will certainly crown the king’s son, while his wife—the daughter, that is, of the king of France—has been left at Caen and, as it were, repudiated, to the insult and contempt of her father. [Col. 0726C]

That boy whom we mentioned will assuredly be crowned, and at the time we said, unless the Lord closes the sea to one wishing to sail, or withers the hand of the archbishop of York, or unless the king of France prevents it by some means of prohibition. For the boy is hastening to the sea, and is awaited by his father on the opposite shore. By the king’s command, the bishops of Bayeux and Séez go with the boy. Richard de Humet will not go. The queen will remain at Caen until she receives certainty of this rejoicing.

The letters of the lord pope forbidding this consecration crossed the sea long ago, but were made wholly useless: they perished in the hand of the person to whom they were entrusted, neither shown to anyone nor made public in any way. What good, then, are letters which are thus concealed, by which neither the imminent placing of the crown nor the anointing of the person will cease? [Col. 0726D]

Know most certainly that this will happen without delay; and, if the archbishop of York did not dare, the executioner of Séez would nevertheless lay on his bloody hands. This is done against you, so that you may no longer even be allowed to hope for peace: not only is peace delayed for you, but the entire hope of peace and reconciliation is taken away.

For Richard of Ilchester told us—he who came the other day as far as Caen to hasten the boy’s crossing, and immediately returned with him—that he would delay your peace by every means; and that if he could not otherwise do so, the king would remain disobedient not only to the lord pope but even to God himself, until death, rather than have peace with you.

Do not, therefore, hope in wickedness, nor trust those Templars, who do not walk in simplicity but, wishing to carry out the king’s will rather than yours, bring you nothing but lies from the king and from the father of lies, in order to deceive you. Whatever the king does in dealing with you is deceit and malice. But, with your leave, I say that he deceives a fool with empty words, in order meanwhile to provide better for himself and, through the passage of time, to prepare greater ambushes and stronger snares against you. [Col. 0727A]

What then will you do, most miserable of men, if within a short time that for which you have sighed through so many years is taken away from you? If a king is made through another, who ought to have reigned only through you? Indeed, what will you do if your enemy consecrates a king hostile to you, so that, in aid of your country against you, a hand may rise up which is stronger the younger it is?

But what will the king of France himself do, whose daughter is thus despised, from whom a kingdom is taken, whose hoped-for descendants are condemned? For why should his son, who may perhaps yet be born to him, obtain the glory of the kingdom, if she is now judged unworthy of the crown? Perhaps that exceedingly just king will not be greatly moved, nor avenge the contempt shown to himself and his daughter. Yet he will perish all the more in his justice. I speak moderately concerning the Lord’s anointed; nevertheless, he will abandon the crown of France for nothing, he who so readily takes away the crown of England.

Therefore the one and singular remedy for him and for you is that he should without any delay send messengers to the queen and to Richard de Humet, who on his behalf may forbid this act; and, if it has been done, may separate themselves from both parties in defiance. For, frightened in this way, Richard and the queen will send to the king, and the king’s will shall be impeded. No messenger of the king of France or of yours could gain access to our king. If he brought letters of the lord pope, he would be sent to prison; if he delivered yours, he would be handed over to death; if he carried letters of the king of France, he would be held honourably, but would not proceed until the affair reached the king’s ears. [Col. 0727B–C]

Run, then, at once to the king and summon the archbishop of Sens, so that some obstacle may be opposed to this undertaking, which is known to be pursued in contempt of the king’s person and to the prejudice of your cause.

Furthermore, know that Thomas, the new archdeacon of Bath, recently came from the king to the archbishop of Rouen and obtained from the bishop of Nevers a truce for crossing until the following Sunday. For that Thomas publicly proclaimed, and many others proclaim daily, that the king will come soon; this is altogether false. The bishop of Nevers therefore proceeds at an ant’s pace through bishoprics, abbeys, and royal residences as far as Mont-Saint-Michel; and, though he would be content with fifteen mounts in his own land, he brings thirty-six mounts among us. It is said, therefore, that he thirsts more for the king’s money than for the kingdom’s peace, and more for his own profit than for your advantage. And the matter is shown by sufficiently plain indications. [Col. 0727D]

For on the Friday after the octave of Pentecost he came to Caen, from which the king’s son had then departed, and with him the bishop of Nevers could very well have crossed, if he wished. But he is told that the king will soon come, or that a royal ship will come for him. Thus this man, wholly ignorant of the customs of our people, is caught by deceits, and the word of the Lord does not prosper in his hand.

But if he understood these stratagems, and hurried to the sea at a rapid pace, the archbishop would have to cross before him, leaving this man to await the king’s reply. And even if he wished altogether to cross, he would indeed find a ship and its equipment, but no helmsman would appear. For each man would flee, or say that he knew nothing, or swear that the wind was completely adverse. Foolish, then, was the man who wished to come to you, when he planned to go through Flanders.

Send immediately, therefore, the king’s letters, the letters of the archbishop of Sens, and your messenger to the bishop of Nevers, so that he may meet the queen staying at Caen with all speed, in order that she may arrange his crossing. [Col. 0728A] If she refuses because of manifest impossibility, let the same bishop return to you, to do sooner what he is going to do.

Do not spare yourselves hereafter, but pour out your whole spirit and draw your whole sword; for the king’s eye will never again look upon you. But may the eye of divine mercy look upon you and upon the sheep of His pasture, and may He deign to grant to His Church glory of victory over princes rather than the peace of princes, which is not true. Farewell. And if adversity increases, do not fear, because the Lord puts His hand beneath you. [Col. 0728B]

## LETTER CCCXC. FROM THE FELLOW-EXILES OF BLESSED THOMAS TO CARDINAL ALBERT

To the most holy lord and dearest father ALBERT, by God’s grace cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church: the wretched men of Canterbury, exiles and outlaws, offer all that little which remains to them—the affection of sincere faith and true love. [Col. 0728C]

Those who have lost the integrity of conscience do not know how great a good an innocent conscience is. Nor does one fear to harass another person with deadly counsels who, once shame has been abandoned, seeks to have eminent men as partners in error, to defend his own shamefulness. Would that the holiness of the lord pope had not learned these things from our dangers, to the confusion of the Church and the dishonour of the curia; and that from the beginning he had rejected with the strength of wisdom and authority, in which he surpasses all others, counsels hostile alike to their welfare and their honour—counsels offered by those who dared urge him to prolong the proscription of innocent people for six years by derisive delays. [Col. 0728D]

Certainly, whoever and however great that counsellor may have been, he should immediately have heard: “Get behind me, Satan, for you do not understand the things that are of God.” Nor will the world be persuaded that these advisers understood God; rather, they scented money, which they thirst after with the immoderate heat of avarice. Accordingly, clinging to robbers and sacrilegious men in agreement, furnishing them with counsels and arming them with patronage, they rose against Christ’s poor, accepting gifts and pursuing rewards.

Their names cannot remain hidden: both the evident nature of their actions reveals them, and the report of messengers from the opposing party, and the testimony of letters in which they boast before the king of England that they stood stoutly for him and persuaded the lord pope—when without their words he was inclined to believe it—to endure with such patience the savagery of the aforesaid king. In this there is cause for fear lest the deceived holy man has erred so greatly that, even when he wishes, he may be unable to repair what he has done wrong against the Church of God. [Col. 0729A]

God commonly punishes such offences in this way: whoever does not use an opportunity divinely offered for action has it taken from him forever. We speak to one who examines the law and knows it, one who has clear examples of what we say from things familiar to himself. Yet, so that the curia may seem to clear the fault which it thereby increases, it throws back upon our messengers the fact that justice has not been rendered to the Church of God for injuries and losses so manifest.

Thus, as though the matter had been well handled, they advise us to send wiser men—as though the injury were not evident in itself, the losses few or slight, the robber had not often been warned, our messengers had not suffered more atrocious wrongs, or correction had not been awaited long—indeed, far too long, beyond every measure and against equity. [Col. 0729B]

We do not possess, Father, those wise men whom they seek, nor the powerful or wealthy men whom we always see prevail in the curia against the Church of God and against us, so that they continually return in triumph. We are scarcely supported by others’ charity; and, unless grace preserves us, we who alone in the western world contend for the Roman Church are nearly worn down by it and compelled to abandon Christ’s cause and disdain the liberty of the Church.

At the beginning, the blame for our proscription and for the plundering of the Church could have been laid upon the king of England alone. Through himself and his retainers, without mercy for age or sex and without respect for rank or order, he sentenced about four hundred innocent persons to exile; he confiscated the Church of Canterbury with all its possessions and goods; he seized the goods of vacant sees; and he did not permit bishops and abbots to be regularly ordained in them. [Col. 0729C]

It cannot be said how many souls have died without the sacrament of confirmation; how many criminals have died without penitence and absolution; how many sacred virgins have been deprived of their desired consecration; how many causes have lapsed, to the loss of churches and of those unjustly oppressed; how much injustice has possessed all England; or how wide a gate of the destruction of souls has been opened to Satan, while Christ’s shepherds were either driven into exile, compelled to become mute and keep silence from good things, or enticed, under the pretext of religion and dispensation, to furnish weapons of iniquity to sin and to poison with destructive counsels the serpents themselves and the members of the ancient serpent. [Col. 0729D]

We have often—indeed continually—pursued in your tribunals for six years injuries to Christ so great and so manifest, ready, in the very newness of these evils, while you were still at Sens and the king’s messengers were present, to prosecute the appeals instituted either by us or against us. It did not please you that we should be heard then, when we still had some resources, however small, and our friends and helpers had some hope. It would be long, and, we fear, tedious to you, to recount how often we offered ourselves to proceed and were not heard; while our adversaries, the oppressors of the Church, were granted—as you know—the indulgence of not having to prosecute an appeal. [Col. 0730A]

Meanwhile, if our father the lord of Canterbury had wished to remit what had been taken away and to furnish contemporaries and posterity with the destructive example of entering into a settlement, he could have made peace with the king without your intervention and returned to the favour of their former intimacy. But may this plague be far from our minds: that for any temporal profit we should murder our souls, wound our consciences with an incurable wound, sell the liberty of the Church in the accursed commerce of pleasure or avarice, and corrupt posterity by a wicked example.

Let others do this if they wish—or rather, let no one do it—for we were not so instructed by the holy fathers who governed the Church of Canterbury amid many labours and at length received from the Lord the reward of their labours. God Himself, author of this resolve and witness of our conscience, knows that the lord of Canterbury chose rather to die in exile than to enter into an agreement destructive or shameful to the Church. And if—God forbid—he attempted this, there is scarcely anyone among us, if indeed any, who could thereafter endure his lordship or fellowship. [Col. 0730B]

Peace for the Church was being negotiated with us through friends when John of Oxford, departing for Rome and, openly justified by many, returned a triumphant perjurer. From the apostolic see he brought horns to the sinner who raged, as though he were not already sufficiently mad by himself. From that day our proscription, which formerly could have been charged upon the king alone and his followers, found in the Roman Church, through dissimulation or consent, an author as well; since delay was granted to the persecutor who persisted in malice, and in some manner permission given him to brood over the churches and torture the innocent.

And whenever any consolation seemed to be offered to us, it was immediately impeded by legates or letters sent from the pope’s side, lest it receive the desired or due effect. Even if we kept silent, the events themselves prove that this is so. For behold: when our peace, as many know, was at the doors, and the Church had received, as we thought, effective consolation from the most holy father, the Roman pontiff, the king’s messengers arrived and removed the peace; and, by absolving our excommunicated opponents, seemed even to have shut off hope of reconciliation. [Col. 0730C–D]

For they announced to them and to the other adversaries of the Church that, if they wished, they might prosecute at the feast of St Luke the appeals of six years which we have so often pursued and sometimes obtained. They knew that they would suffer no loss of honour, office, benefice, or reputation because they had been excommunicated for so long. Yet, among our people especially, ecclesiastical justice has force precisely in this: those who endure excommunication for a year are customarily marked with infamy. But behold: by the precedent of this innovation, and by what is almost an apostolic privilege contained in the letters, ecclesiastical rigour has been dissolved. What remains, then, except that a sentence shall be of no consequence among provincials when they see it can so easily be dissolved without any penalty? [Col. 0731A]

They have, it is said, sworn that they will abide by the lord pope’s command; but it is ordered that this be concealed. Good God! What does it mean that acts against the Church are freely proclaimed in the public square, so that they may be drawn into precedent, while, if anything is done for the Church which could furnish a praiseworthy example and be useful in the future, the apostolic see orders it concealed?

Since Christ’s cause is thus handled among you, where the supporters of the king—or rather of malice, or lovers of money—prevail, why are we required to send wise messengers, as though you yourselves ought not to have defended so just and manifest a cause even had everyone been silent? For this is why you are set at the hinge of the world: that you may free the poor from the mighty, and determine and do justice among the children of men. [Col. 0731B]

We believed them to be honourable and learned men, whom the Roman road has swallowed up. Yet what benefit is their blood to us? Shall we send more, that they too may die, so that the number of the innocent may be reduced or annihilated and the tyrant, once they are extinguished, may rule the Church freely with no one contradicting him? If the appeals must be pursued, why were they not examined when they were arising or had not yet lapsed? It would have been better for us if they had then been settled, or at least if we had been told, so that we might undertake some other business by which we could somehow sustain our lives, and commit His cause to God to be resolved.

We are despoiled and naked. We believe it wiser, now that we have been sufficiently wearied by such deceptions, to end our life in prayers rather than in lawsuits, taught by examples from our own household; lest hereafter not only our labour and expense be endangered, but our soul as well. May Christ, to whom we entrust it, henceforth be the patron of His Church and of His cause. [Col. 0731C]

But perhaps someone will say that both what we have set forth and the delay so often granted were done for the good of peace, and that a method of dispensation was admitted. Certainly, if peace is expected from God, it ought not to be procured through sins and things done against the law. If it is not to come from God, it is neither necessary for the Church nor useful to anyone. God does not need our good things, but certainly He needs our sins still less in carrying out His justice and mercy. Perhaps peace has been delayed so long because it was pursued not by the way of the Lord but by human cunning.

We have exceeded measure, but necessity presses us—a necessity confined neither by measure nor rule. And the Holy Spirit who is in you will persuade you to pardon and pity those who exceed measure out of necessity. Falling at the knees of your total compassion, we earnestly beg you to make all these matters known to the lord pope and persuade him hereafter not to trust deceivers, who, attracted by love of filthy gain, strive to induce him to lose his soul and Christ’s cause by injuring us. [Col. 0731D]

## LETTER CCCXCI. FROM THE SAME TO GRATIAN

To GRATIAN, subdeacon of the Roman Church, from the fellow-exiles of blessed THOMAS the martyr.

The harms of a wound are most wisely disclosed to one who sympathizes or heals; and in necessity no one ought rather to be approached than one accustomed faithfully to relieve it. The necessity of the English Church is indeed most grievous, and its wound, now almost incurable after many days. Very many promised a remedy for it, but now that almost the full course of six years has elapsed, besides you there has been no one descending from the Roman Church to help. Perhaps the others sought their own interests and put behind them Christ’s glory and the Church’s honour. [Col. 0732A]

But from that man, who is accustomed to corrupt those whom he gathers round him with corruptible gold and silver and the various enticements of worldly goods, you have received nothing but the integrity of conscience. Do not regret having rendered this service to God’s Church without payment; nor suppose that you have already received only a small reward, for a twofold fruit of virtue has been repaid to you—one in conscience and the other in glory. Perseverance will multiply both; and while the English Church breathes in Christ, it will deservedly remember that it is indebted to you. [Col. 0732B]

You know how miserably she has thus far been torn and trampled down; by what varied deceits and how often her justice has been hindered; how often the due consolations which seemed granted her have been withdrawn through letters or messengers sent from the apostolic see in the opposite direction, and through delays granted to the adverse party; and how, indeed, wounds have been added to the wounds of the afflicted by the lord cardinals and friends of the curia, so that there is now no sorrow like her sorrow.

At the beginning, these things could have been attributed to the king of England and his accomplices; the king is the cause and contriver of all of them to God’s injury. If, before the curia had justified the man who had been a promoter of schism, we had wished to remit what had been taken from us and to give a destructive example of settlement to the Church’s injury, we would have obtained peace through friends, with the apostolic see ceasing its activity. [Col. 0732C]

But far be it from us that a cause begun for God should thus end against God; that for any profit we should sell off Christ’s title and the liberty of the Church. The Searcher of hearts bears witness that our lord and father would prefer to die, and that we would prefer to be buried with him, provided only that we die in the Lord.

But since the days of John of Oxford, we suffer violence not merely from the aforesaid king but from the Roman Church as well, which, by granting delays, prolonged our exile to the end of the sixth year, and sends back with triumph and glory the persecutors of the Church—men corrupted by our spoils and corrupting others. Returning, they incite the king, as though he were not sufficiently mad by himself; and by threats, terrors, and elaborate frauds they make those who had resolved to adhere to the Church pass over to the opposing side. [Col. 0732D]

We have experienced this frequently, and especially now when the latest envoys returned; for they recalled the king, who was inclined toward agreement, from the very entrance into peace. They advised him to permit his men to prosecute at the feast of St Luke their appeals, introduced by various evasions even after the lord pope’s prohibition, because, if he persists, he will not be compelled to do anything against his will. Meanwhile those who deserved excommunication—the instigators of this schism and our despoilers—have been absolved, and granted the privilege that they should incur no loss of honour, office, benefice, or reputation because they had been bound so long by the chain of anathema. Whether this was rightly and beneficially done for the Church, let God see and judge. [Col. 0733A]

Yet they are said to have sworn that they will abide by the lord pope’s command, and it is ordered that this be concealed, lest something done for the Church, which concerns its honour, should become known; while, on the contrary, anything rashly attempted or granted to its ruin is publicly proclaimed in the public square.

Since our party from the beginning has pursued every appeal and has offered each year, while the adverse party fled, and since that party has advanced further in its malice than we in our innocence and justice, who in his right mind would dare advise us to follow these delusions any further? What benefit is there in so many labours, expenses, and in the blood of the innocent who laid down their lives for God’s covenant? Surely it is not worth so much to us to be harassed in the curia without result by new deceptions that we who remain should wish, without cause, to share the death of those who have died. Rather, we commit His cause to God to direct. [Col. 0733B]

For if any one of us is summoned to set out for the curia, he will answer as the cautious fox once answered the sick lion:

> For all the tracks frighten me  
> that face toward you; none turn back.

And he will detest this journey until hope of success shines from another quarter. [Col. 0733C]

Therefore, falling at your feet, we earnestly beg that through you all these things may become known to the most holy father and shepherd of the Church, the lord pope; and that you persuade him not to allow himself henceforth to be so easily deceived. And if eye, foot, or hand should hereafter cause him scandal, whoever it may be, let him not hesitate to cut it off from the body of his counsel. For it is better, when the author of scandal has been cut off, that he attain eternal life without him than that he permit himself to be dragged by him—God forbid!—into Gehenna.

## LETTER CCCXCII. LETTER OF A CERTAIN FAITHFUL MAN TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, from his faithful servant.

Last Sunday the king, at London, girded his son with the belt of knighthood. [Col. 0733D] The Archbishop of York immediately afterwards anointed him king. There the king divided his lands among his sons, to the wonder of all, who ask what he intends to do hereafter. He has his arrival in Normandy proclaimed daily, in order that he may be more feared. But he will not come while he enjoys peace with the king of the French. He also instructed Richard de Humes to equip, suitably for crossing the sea, with clothing, mounts, and attendants, the daughter of the king of the French, who is staying with the queen at Caen, whenever he himself should give the order. This was done so that the king of the French might hear of it and for a while be calmed from the indignation he conceived at the slighting of his daughter. For no order has been given that she should go immediately; she is merely commanded to prepare herself, so that, when the king sends for her, she may not delay in going. Perhaps, therefore, they are trying to steal the consecration [Col. 0734A] of the girl, just as they did that of the boy. But even if it were done openly, see that the anointing of the daughter of the king of the French is not in any way prevented through you. Nor should you be overly disturbed about the anointing of the boy; rather, blame yourselves, since you did not send letters that could have prevented the consecration. Therefore pronounce no sentence against either the king or your bishops while your peace is being negotiated; instead, endure patiently until the day of joy and peace comes, or the day of wrath and indignation.

I nevertheless believe that your peace will not be made through the Bishop of Nevers, because the Archbishop of Sens seeks peace with the king of the English more eagerly than he seeks yours. For he very much desires to speak with the king, and he told me plainly that, if the king were willing to grant you the kiss, he would be quite content to spare the king sufficiently in all other matters. [Col. 0734B] He even rebuked me for speaking thus about you and against the king; and, as I have certainly learned, your peace cannot prosper in his hands. For this reason the Archdeacon of Bourges, your most faithful supporter, withdrew from him; and that bishop is staying at Mantes, where he will await the arrival of the king of the English for fifteen days. Afterwards, if the king has not come, he will return by Normandy to the sea, so that he may receive the royal maintenance which he has hitherto accepted and prolong his stay. Yet he himself requested the queen and Richard de Humez to set sail and open to him the sea-route which they had caused to be forbidden not only to him but to all persons on his account. But they refused. Therefore the bishop ought to have begun counting the days from this manifest contempt and failure, but he would not do so. [Col. 0734C] On the contrary, he had a familiar conversation with the queen and granted such a truce as she wished, being, as is said, more eager for the king’s favour and for the Archbishop of Sens’s peace with the king than for yours.

See therefore that no one deceives you, lest those who are mutually hostile find the favour of reconciliation in your death. See also to whom you entrusted your cause; and, if you judge well of him, you certainly judge differently from everyone else who sees him. Moreover, make haste and speak with that Bishop of Nevers, with the Archbishop of Sens present, so that he may immediately carry out the charge entrusted to him, or abandon it altogether; and arrange his journey not through Normandy but rather through Flanders. Meanwhile proceed to no sentence, unless perhaps you could impose one upon [Col. 0734D] the Archbishop of York. The Bishop of Worcester, a most faithful son of the Church of Canterbury, has not yet crossed the sea, but is wholly devoted to the Church’s honour and liberty. May my lord prosper, and write at greater length to me, his servant, concerning his wishes and circumstances. May he prosper for ever and beyond.

## LETTER CCCXCIII. FROM A CERTAIN FRIEND TO JOHN OF SALISBURY

To John of Salisbury, from a certain friend.

> Things received through the ear move the mind more slowly  
> than those set before the faithful eyes.

If, therefore, I give a less vivid account of matters which I have learned by hearsay alone, I ask pardon. For the certainty of the truth and a clearer exposition of the matters you have sought [Col. 0735A] belong to those who witnessed the event. Your affection knows that the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Nevers were sent by the lord pope as envoys to the king of the English, to arrange a settlement between that king and the Archbishop of Canterbury. Accordingly, the Bishop of Nevers, undertaking the journey in obedience to the pope’s command and carrying with him the form of settlement dictated by the pope, together with threatening letters addressed to the same king, arrived in Normandy. Having met the Archbishop of Rouen, he was ready to undertake the effort of crossing the sea. For the king of England was then in England, as your affection also knows.

When the king heard this, he sent to meet the Bishop of Nevers, directing and advising him not to expose himself to the hazards of the sea, but patiently to await the king’s arrival in Normandy. [Col. 0735B] For he was about to return at once to those regions. Therefore the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Nevers, having carefully arranged a meeting upon his return, presented to him the pope’s letters of admonition containing the proposed terms of peace. Their discussion finally came to this conclusion. The king promised the aforesaid legates that, at the pope’s pleasure and will and without feigned hostility, he would restore to the Archbishop of Canterbury his peace, his church, all the possessions of his church intact, and also his own favour—although he was not compelled by the apostolic command to restore his favour. He worked hard to except from the pope’s demands one thing only: namely, the kiss, since he had publicly forsworn it at Montmartre in the presence of the French.

The Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Nevers then returned to the Archbishop of Canterbury at Sens, on Thursday, as I recall, in the week preceding the feast of St Mary Magdalene, reporting what they had obtained from the king and proposing that they jointly appoint there a day for effecting reconciliation. [Col. 0735C] Meanwhile the king of France and the king of England had set a day for a conference: Monday before the feast of St Mary Magdalene, at their frontier between La Ferté, a town in the district of Chartres, and Fréteval, a castle in the territory of Tours. The Archbishop of Sens had meanwhile advised the Archbishop of Canterbury to attend the kings’ conference together with himself, the Archbishop of Rouen, and the Bishop of Nevers. He added that, while so great a distance of places separated him from his king, no settlement could possibly be made.

The Archbishop of Canterbury, though at first unwilling to attend the conference without being summoned, eventually accepted the Archbishop of Sens’s counsel. Together the Archbishop of Canterbury, the Archbishop of Sens, the Archbishop of Rouen, and the Bishop of Nevers set out for the conference. The kings accordingly met at the appointed time. Having dealt with their own affairs on Tuesday and Wednesday before the feast of St Mary Magdalene, they made no mention of the Archbishop of Canterbury—so much so that, on the second day, his clerks returned from the conference to their lord and told him that the kings, their business concluded, were departing. Those who had come to the conference without invitation were greatly alarmed lest they return in confusion.

Nevertheless, meanwhile, with their customary diligence, [Col. 0736A] the Archbishop of Sens, the Archbishop of Rouen, and the Bishop of Nevers interceded with the king of England for the Archbishop of Canterbury. At last the king granted them that on the feast of St Mary Magdalene he would speak with the Archbishop of Canterbury and would restore everything to him in accordance with the pope’s command, except only the kiss. Not even the king of France’s entreaties could induce him to grant that kiss at Montmartre. He further added, and confirmed by oath, that in refusing it he would lay no snares for the Archbishop of Canterbury; repeatedly calling God to witness, he offered the Archbishop of Sens as surety upon the peril of his order. It is also said that, as they were departing, he privately hinted that, although unwillingly, he would give the kiss before he and the Archbishop of Canterbury should depart unreconciled, with the peace left unmade.

The Archbishop of Sens therefore returned to the Archbishop of Canterbury and described to him the sweetness and graciousness he had found in both the king’s expression and words. He begged and urged him not, by exacting the kiss, to lose his lord’s ready affection. After much further discussion, he added that the king himself had previously publicly promised the same thing: that, when he came into his own possessions, the king would receive him with the kiss of peace and with the greatest expressions of gratitude. [Col. 0736B] By the Archbishop of Sens’s advice, the Archbishop of Canterbury—ready, as it were, to lay down even his life for his sheep—yielded; and, when evening came, his response was announced to the king.

On the morning of the feast of St Mary Magdalene, at earliest dawn, the king proceeded with an innumerable multitude of his people to the frontier previously appointed for the conference between himself and the king of France, which he had also assigned to the Archbishop of Canterbury as their meeting-place. The Archbishop of Canterbury, setting out later and accompanied by the Archbishop of Sens and Count Theobald, arrived at the appointed frontier; crowds of Frenchmen who had come with their king to the conference also gathered there. [Col. 0736C] As soon as the king recognized the Archbishop of Canterbury approaching, he broke away from the surrounding multitude, went to meet him, and greeted him first. When they had exchanged greetings, clasped hands, and embraced, the king, the Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Archbishop of Sens withdrew apart.

The Archbishop of Canterbury complained to his king of the wrongs inflicted upon himself and his Church. He spoke in terms greatly calculated to move the king, and, as the returning Archbishop of Sens testified, in a manner entirely suited to such a subject. Then the two alone—the king and the Archbishop of Canterbury—retired apart and discussed their private matters for a great part of the day, so that very many of the bystanders grew weary of the long delay caused by their conversation. [Col. 0736D] There the Archbishop of Canterbury complained of the injury done to his Church’s dignity, especially in the coronation of the new king. He recounted how much and what that Church had bestowed upon the king, particularly when the dispute over the crown of the realm was being conducted between him and King Stephen.

Assigning the reason for the said coronation, as well as for the condition of the kingdom and the anger he had exercised against the Archbishop of Canterbury, the king promised to correct everything in accordance with the archbishop’s wishes. He added that the daughter of the king of France, not yet crowned, would be crowned by him; and that his own son would again receive the crown from him, with acknowledgement of the dignity belonging to the Church of Canterbury. In thanks for these promises, the Archbishop of Canterbury dismounted and humbled himself at the king’s feet. The king promptly dismounted too and held the stirrup—commonly called a *strivarium*—as the Archbishop of Canterbury remounted. [Col. 0737A]

Thus the king returned to his own people and the Archbishop of Canterbury to the French. Without taking further counsel, the king publicly announced that he had made peace with the Archbishop of Canterbury, to God’s honour and his own. Summoning those standing by on both sides, he restored to the Archbishop of Canterbury his peace, his favour, his church, and all the possessions of his church intact. The Archbishop of Canterbury’s fellow-exiles who were present then came forward and humbled themselves at the king’s feet. Restoring to each his own possessions, the king graciously granted them his peace and favour.

After these events, the king wished the Archbishop of Canterbury to come immediately with him into Normandy, both for recreation and so that the length of their former disagreement should not conceal their reconciliation. He also promised sufficient provision of necessities to the archbishop and his companions. But because the Archbishop of Canterbury could not leave without permission from the king and Church of France without injury to his reputation, he requested a delay before returning to him. The king accordingly ordered the Archbishop of Canterbury meanwhile to send one of his clerks to England to receive the possessions belonging to himself and his followers; but the envoy was first to come to the king and, having received his letters to his son and to the other guardians of the realm, to cross safely. [Col. 0737B] When these matters had been arranged, the king took leave, having requested the Archbishop of Canterbury’s blessing.

Since this embassy has been entrusted to our friend—indeed our dearest friend, and in every respect devoted to your wishes—Master Herebert, I ask that, aided by your prayerful intercession with God, he may proceed more safely. Farewell, and remember me.

## LETTER CCCXCIV. FROM HIS ENVOYS TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

To their dearest lord, from his servants: greeting and faithful service.

We have fulfilled your command as far as we could. We delivered your letters to William de Eynsford and William son of Nigel, and by every pressure brought them to London together with Thurstan [Col. 0737D] and Osbert. When we were prepared to show the younger king of England the letters of the lord king which we had in your presence, none of those to whom you had entrusted this matter dared to appear before the king. They had received advice from certain people who had wholly withdrawn from supporting them in the affair.

We, however, upon whom the business rested, taking with us only Robert, sacristan of Canterbury, approached the king boldly and with all diligence, after consulting William son of Aldel and Ralph son of Stephen. We came to him in his chamber at Westminster on the Monday immediately after the feast of St Michael. Present with the king were Count Reginald, the Archdeacon of Canterbury, the Archdeacon of Poitiers, William de St John, and many others. [Col. 0738A] When Count Reginald heard of the peace, he, like many others—but not all—devoutly gave thanks to God for it in the king’s presence. When the letters had been read, the king answered that, after we had withdrawn, he would take counsel upon the matter.

Then Walter de l’Isle was summoned and counsel was held with him. We were recalled, and, in our presence, your Archdeacon of Canterbury replied in these words: “The lord king has received his lord father’s instruction and command and has taken counsel concerning it. He therefore gives this answer: Ranulf de Broc and Ranulf’s officials, together with other officers, hold, by the command of the king his father, the lands and possessions of the archbishopric, and the goods, churches, and revenues of the archbishop’s clerks in various places. Since the condition of the archbishop’s estate and manor cannot truly be known and investigated unless those officials are present, the lord king appoints and assigns you Thursday next, the feast of Pope St Callixtus, as the day for more fully carrying out the present command.”

Some who heard this postponement, entirely despairing of a firm peace, confidently declare it to be an evil sign for the peace. Others prefer to regard it as fixing a return date; this is the more credible interpretation. [Col. 0738B] All your supporters whom we found in England are so despairing of peace that they neither will nor can believe the lord king’s letters, which we displayed with their seals hanging externally, nor us, who were present at the making of the peace and affirm it by a living voice under oath.

When the lord king was travelling from London towards Windsor, some of us approached him on the road and greeted him on your behalf with every humility and diligence. He answered us graciously and showed us a much more cheerful countenance on the road than he had previously shown before his justices. Yet many of our friends privately advise you through us to remain near the lord king, if that can in any way be done, until you may more fully obtain his favour and good will. Almost everyone with whom we spoke loves your person and longs with eager desire for your arrival and presence—more than you would scarcely believe—but fear forces them to dissemble, as though they did not love you.

My lord, we have heard—and have learned certainly from a former member of your household; indeed, we know it is true—that the lord king of England, through Walter de l’Isle and through writs dispatched by him into those regions, has summoned Roger, the so-called Archbishop of York; Gilbert, the Bishop of London; Jocelin, Bishop of Salisbury; and four or six clerics from among all the churches vacant in England, [Col. 0738D] so that they may elect bishops in accordance with his will and with the counsel of the aforesaid bishops, and send those elected according to his will and their counsel to the supreme pontiff for consecration—to the detriment of the Church of Canterbury and to your humiliation, may God avert it.

This is why he so greatly desires your arrival in England, and why he so frequently and shamefully persists in seeking the humiliation of your person. We see exceedingly clear and credible indications of this devilish scheme, apparent to everyone inhabiting that region. For that so-called Bishop of London—but no true bishop—has for a long time lingered in the district of Beverley. Pretending to make a pilgrimage there in order to venerate St John, he has feigned a false pilgrimage, so that from there, like his lord, he may disparage the deeds of his pastor and plot to cut his throat with bloody hands. [Col. 0739A]

Venerable lord, take diligent care for yourself in all these matters; and, according to the counsel bestowed upon you from above by God, strive with sleepless care and discerning judgment, by the help of God—who does not abandon those who hope in him—to shake off forcefully the attacks of those who lie in wait for you. Furthermore, my lord, as soon as the lord king’s letters were seen and heard, we heard it said that the king and the archdeacons immediately sent a certain messenger to the king in Normandy; but what they directed him to say, we do not know at all. We therefore send the bearer of this letter to you with the greatest haste, so that we may report to you what we have heard and learned.

Do not delay in sending him, or another messenger, back to us without delay, and report to us more fully your will and decision in these matters. As this man can tell you orally, we are alone, without a head or help. [Col. 0740A] None of those whom you designated has dared to obey either your instruction or command, except Robert the sacristan, who has given assistance in the business as far as he knew and was able. If it should happen that, on the day appointed for us, they make restitution of your property, we shall immediately report to you whatever we hear and discover. May our lord prosper.

This bearer will privately recount certain things to you orally which are abominable if they are believed true—and yet they are true. There is no need, my lord, for these disclosures to become more widely known; if you please, let the words remain buried once you alone have heard them. This we impress upon your memory often and repeatedly, my lord: do not hasten to come into England unless you can obtain a more unreserved favour from the lord king. For there is not a man in England, not even one among all those in whom you trusted, who does not wholly despair of peace. All alike avoid and flee our conversation and association with those very persons who ought to advise you and in whom we chiefly trusted. [Col. 0740B] Farewell.

# LETTERS OF GILBERT FOLIOT, FORMERLY ABBOT OF GLOUCESTER, THEN BISHOP OF HEREFORD AND AFTERWARDS OF LONDON; AND OF VARIOUS PERSONS TO HIM AND OTHERS

Now first edited from manuscript codices by J. A. Giles, LL.D., priest of the Church of England and formerly fellow of Corpus Christi College, Oxford.

(Oxford and London, 1845, octavo, 2 vols.)

[Col. 0739]

## DEDICATORY LETTER

To the Right Honourable Sir James Graham, one of Her Majesty’s Principal Secretaries of State, through whose ready kindness the editor was enabled so early to place before the public this first complete collection of the letters of Gilbert Foliot, Bishop of Hereford and London, and rival of Thomas Becket, these volumes are most respectfully dedicated.

Corpus Christi College, Oxford, January 1845.

[Col. 0739]

## PREFACE

Of the letters written in connection with the dispute between Henry II and St Thomas Becket, very many acknowledge Gilbert Foliot as their author—a man distinguished no less by learning and piety than by his expertise in matters relating to the government of the kingdom.

[Col. 0741] That eminent man might, in a more favourable age, have attained the highest dignity in both Church and state, and surpassed his contemporaries by far in renown and glory. But it fell to him to be overcome by the loftier genius of Thomas Becket, who, raised above him to the metropolitan see of Canterbury, thereby became exposed to no slight degree of hatred and envy, as often happens.

The Foliot family came to England with Duke William the Conqueror. Gilbert himself was educated in the celebrated Cluniac monastery, where from his earliest years he distinguished himself in learning and austerity of life. In 1139, through the care and support of Milo, sheriff of the city of Gloucester, and Robert of Bath, Bishop of Hereford, he was elected and advanced to be abbot of St Peter’s, Gloucester. He governed that wealthy and very powerful monastery for nine years; and in 1147 or 1148, after the death of Robert of Bath, he was raised to the vacant episcopal see of Hereford. There, through learning, piety, and ascetic discipline—in which he is said to have surpassed all his contemporaries—he gained an even greater reputation.

> “He held great authority not only among his own order, but also among secular men of exceptional distinction. At his prompting, as seems more probable, the Earl and Countess of Leicester embraced the monastic life. When Reginald of St Valery oppressed the monks of Osney, the Bishop of Hereford, although the matter did not belong to his office, took care to have the oppressor rebuked.”

After some years, namely in 1161 or 1163, he was translated to the see of London; but, as will presently appear, his promotion is entangled in considerable chronological difficulties. From very many passages in his letters, now for the first time published, it will clearly appear that Gilbert Foliot, notwithstanding his opposition to Becket, held no low opinion of the Church in general and, in particular, of the privileges of the see of Canterbury. If we wish to examine this historical fact fairly and without partisan feeling, the arguments that can be produced on either side of the question must be weighed with great care. But before these volumes appeared, such a method could by no means have been applied to an investigation than which none in English history is more difficult and hazardous.

For the Reformation that occurred in the Church three hundred years ago unquestionably strove by every means to turn all minds against Thomas Becket and the cause which he defended. Consequently, all who had taken the king’s side against him acquired undeserved favour; prominent among these were Roger, Archbishop of York, and Gilbert Foliot, Bishop of London. Yet the hatred that had fallen upon Becket’s name, and the favour bestowed upon his opponents, were, if not wholly undeserved, at least equally excessive because the arguments that could be adduced on both sides had not been equally weighed. These volumes now published will be found to throw the clearest light upon the controversy that arose between the rival bishops. It is of great importance for the reader to remember that these letters contain arguments of great authority that might have been advanced by those who embraced the cause of King Henry against the Archbishop of Canterbury. Yet, since it is not useful to separate Gilbert’s person and letters from the celebrated cause in which he played so large a part, these few observations will provide a sufficient introduction to the present collection; we shall defer a fuller inquiry until the entire body of evidence has been completed by publication of Becket’s letters and those of his supporters.

It remains now to inform the reader upon what authority these letters are here published as genuine writings of Gilbert Foliot.

In the Bodleian Library there is a manuscript codex, written about the year 1200 (Mus. 249), containing more than four hundred letters; the present edition rests upon this foundation. About forty of these letters are found in another manuscript preserved in the British Museum (Reg. 8 A XXI). Another exists in the cathedral library at Hereford; but no opportunity has yet been available to inspect it, because the library has recently undergone restoration and, though the dean searched for it with the greatest care among the disordered volumes, the codex containing the letters at issue has not yet been found. It is nevertheless supposed to contain only very few letters, and none that does not occur in Cave’s manuscript.

This volume of great importance, donated by Cave to the University of Oxford, has not escaped the notice of many scholars and antiquaries. Yet the immense labour of transcribing so extensive a collection has until now deterred everyone from submitting it to the press. At last, however, owing to opportunities peculiar to the editor, the whole codex, with all its contents, will be published, with as few errors as works published from a single original manuscript commonly contain. Nevertheless, since the Letters lie in it without any attempt at arrangement, it was necessary to put them into an order better suited to the object of this edition. Some had already been printed; many occur twice, even three times, in Cave’s manuscript. It is therefore exceedingly difficult to state how many distinct letters that codex contains—an observation equally applicable to Becket’s letters. Accordingly, if the reader wishes to ascertain in what part of the volume any particular letter is found, he should consult the index placed at the end of the volume.

In arranging the letters, we first placed those written by Gilbert Foliot while he was Abbot of Gloucester, from 1139 to 1148; then follow those written after 1148 while he was Bishop of Hereford; and thirdly, finally, those written after his promotion to the see of London. There seems long to have been a difference of opinion concerning the date when he was invested with this last dignity. Some have maintained that it did not happen until the king, hostile to Becket, summoned Gilbert to London out of hatred for the Archbishop of Canterbury. But this assertion is doubtless ill considered: Foliot must have become bishop, at the latest, in April 1163, before the king and Becket came into conflict. Yet the question is so complicated that the editor does not dare at present to discuss it. It is enough to say that, if he became Bishop of London in April 1161, letters 145 and 412 in this collection must have been written by Theobald; but if in 1163, the transition from friendship to enmity among him, Becket, and the king must have occurred in an almost incredible interval of time.

In the first and second divisions of the Letters in this collection no order has been observed in publishing them except the general classification described above. In the third division, the letters are arranged according to the rank and degree of their addressees: first, to the pope; second, to cardinals; third, to the sons of the Church generally; fourth, to archbishops, bishops, deans, abbots, and persons of various dioceses, in alphabetical order; fifth, finally, to kings, laymen, and others. Under each of these heads no effort at arrangement has been made, because, although all the letters in this collection are in themselves of the greatest importance, they are chiefly recommended by their connection with Becket’s letters. Both are therefore joined in a chronological index at the end of the volume.

Yet Cave’s manuscript contains many letters written by other contemporaries of Gilbert Foliot. Some of these occur, intermingled with Foliot’s letters, in the first and second divisions of this collection; but in the third [Col. 0743] division all letters of this kind have been moved to the end, where they are arranged according to the same order employed for Gilbert’s letters.

Furthermore, five or six letters written by the Bishop of London are found in manuscripts of Becket’s letters, and only one in Wilkins’s *Councils*. All these have been transferred into the present collection, together with other letters perhaps not found in Cave’s manuscript. In a word, so that nothing may be omitted, this rule has been followed, by which the reader may learn what he should seek, both in these volumes and in the accompanying series containing Becket’s letters.

This collection contains all Gilbert Foliot’s letters; the other collection all Becket’s letters.
