But letters written by Pope Alexander, King Henry, or others have been divided between the two collections: several will be found at the end of the present collection, and the rest at the end of the collection containing Becket’s letters.

The author of these letters is thought to have composed two other works: a Commentary on the Song of Songs and a collection of Homilies. Manuscript codices of both works occur in the British Museum and elsewhere; the former has been printed. But neither was considered worthy, whether on grounds of merit or from any other source, of admission into this collection, although their dedicatory letters or prefaces have been excerpted and will be arranged in their proper and appropriate places in these volumes. [Note: [Col. 0743] The Preface to the Song of Songs is Letter 212; the Preface to the Homilies, Letter 329. We shall publish both elsewhere with Gilbert’s exegetical works. EDITOR OF THE FATHERS.]

The catalogue of popes and kings, together with English bishops contemporary with Gilbert Foliot, which we have drawn up here, will spare the reader the laborious task of consulting other works. Yet, since the headings of many letters in Cave’s manuscript give only the initial letter of the name of the person to whom they are written, if the reader has good reason to think that a particular letter should be attributed to another person rather than to the person named in its attached title, the editor will not hesitate to acknowledge himself at fault in a matter so plainly liable to error.

[Col. 0743]

## CATALOGUE OF KINGS AND POPES CONTEMPORARY WITH GILBERT

### 1. Kings of England

Stephen reigned from 1135 to 1154. Henry II, king of England, reigned from 1154 to 1188.

### 2. Supreme Pontiffs

Celestine II, 1143–1144. Lucius II, 1144–1145. Eugenius III, 1145–1153. Anastasius IV, 1153–1154. Adrian IV, 1154–1159. Alexander III, 1159–1181. Lucius III, 1181–1185.

### 3. Prelates of the English Church

Archbishops of Canterbury: Theobald, 1138–1161; Thomas, 1162–1170; Richard, 1174–1183.

Bishops of St Asaph: Geoffrey of Monmouth, 1151–1175; Adam, 1175–1180.

Bishops of Bangor: Maurice, 1139–1162; William, 1162–1171; Guy, 1177–1188.

Bishops of Bath: Robert, 1136–1174; Reginald, 1174–1191.

Bishops of Chichester: Seffrid, 1125–1132; Hilary, 1148–1172; John, 1174–1180; Seffrid II, 1180–1204.

Bishops of Lichfield and Coventry: Walter, 1149–1161; Richard, 1162–1182; Gerard Puella, 1182–1184; Hugh Nonant, 1186–1199.

Bishops of Hereford: Robert, 1131–1148; Gilbert, 1148–1161; Robert of Melun, 1164–1167; Robert Foliot, 1174–1186.

Bishops of Llandaff: Uchtred, 1139–1148; Geoffrey, 1153–1154; Nicholas, 1154–1183; William, 1185–1188.

# LETTERS OF GILBERT FOLIOT

## LETTER I. TO B., ABBOT OF CERNE

[Col. 0745A]

To his dearest brother B., by God’s grace Abbot of Cerne, Brother G., styled Abbot of Gloucester: may you always be renewed by the spirit of consolation and counsel.

You lament your misfortune and bewail the hardships which we too should mourn with equal sorrow, unless the Spirit of the Lord himself taught us that all things work together unto good for the good. But because it is certain to us that this is so for those who are called according to his purpose to life, we therefore rejoice and give thanks in all things received from the hand of the Lord: discerning his goodness in prosperity, his discipline in adversity, and knowledge in both; for the Lord chastens every son whom he receives (Heb. 12). And a good father, though he does not visit iniquities with the rod in anger, will nevertheless not withhold mercies.

Therefore, if until now you have groaned between anvil and hammer, this groaning shall become song for you, when, like a clean vessel fashioned wholly according to the will of the supreme craftsman, you shall shine forth purer than gold tested by fire after the Lord’s repeated blows, and shall receive from him whom you have obeyed the rewards of strength, steadfastness, labour, and endurance. But since your inheritance has been turned over to strangers, and alien sons have lied to you—grown old in evil days, ever limping away from good paths, retreating after Satan, choosing rather to persecute Christ in us than to follow him through you—I do not think it useful to sow seed any longer in barren soil or to scatter pearls before swine (Matt. 7), or to smell at close hand the stench of traitors.

Therefore, when you depart from Egypt, at the coming council you shall seek and, God granting it, obtain absolution from the lord pope: your life remaining unstained, your reputation unharmed in every respect, and your spirit most ready to serve the Lord, who has brought forth your righteousness as light and will lead forth your judgment as the noonday—the Lord to whom you have made known your ways, in whom you have hoped, and who himself will act (Ps. 36). God granting it, I myself shall be present and shall be your helper. Yet I beg one thing: do not depart from us either in heart or in body; let there be for us one sharing in good things, one charity, an indivisible fellowship of life. Where you have passed the first training of a good life, there lay up the adornments of perfection; and, having now experienced almost every fortune, despise the world and what belongs to it, and from on high—now yourself higher than it—mock it. Farewell. More fully informed about the journey, yet truly intending to go, I shall send you fuller news.

## LETTER II. TO . . . . . . . .

I could have restrained myself in silence, had grief not driven my mind; but the burden of the injury now being inflicted compels me to lament. The day after you left us, we received worse news. A brother returning from Hereford reported that our dear friend—whom I may rightly call a worthy man, the dean of the Church of Hereford—had been assailed by the outrages of wicked citizens and had left the city amid tears, pursued by persecution.

Though vexed in his own person, he bore the loss of his possessions readily. For impiety is easily drawn on to crime. Houses were broken open, storehouses burst apart, vessels carried off, money dispersed, furnishings scattered everywhere. But what are these things? Has that burning thirst for possession thereby been extinguished? We have not recognized such as the nature of this passion. Rather, greed knows how to be inflamed more fiercely by remedy. They proceed to further injuries; they pass into the villages; they come to the barns; provisions are shaken out, straw carried away, the church is made poor, castles are fortified. Alas, how greatly the enemy has raged in the holy place! (Ps. 73).

Let the Church’s tears burst forth; let lamentation break out; let dirges be brought into the open; let her harp be turned to mourning and her organ into the voice of those who weep. Hagar rules Sarah (Gen. 16); she who was free has become a slave, and the daughter of a prince has been made tributary. Baldness is given her in place of curling hair; her robe of glory is changed into sackcloth, and her breast-band is exchanged. The Chaldean has entered the sanctuary; he has freely wrought evil; the glory of the Lord is reckoned as nothing. Tears stand upon the cheeks of the sons: who will wipe them away? The face of the daughters of Zion is desolate: who will comfort them? With pride thus mounting, what end will there be to misery, what future satiation of injuries? Who will stand against crime? Under whose presidency shall wrongdoing be checked?

Surely it is the head’s concern to provide for the body. The trouble of each part belongs to it. It is set on high, not that its sight may be deceived, but that it may survey all the lower parts with freer vision. Its more rounded form, elevated position, implanted senses, and the ministry of ecclesiastical dignity depict this by a certain reasoning. These things concern you, Father; these laments demand relief from you. If you hold the staff with which to support, you have not surrendered the rod with which to correct. According to the prophet, “The sword is sharpened; it is polished that it may shine” (Ezek. 21). Let it stand in the hand of one who strikes and avenges the reproaches of the hosts of the God of Israel. Have you heard the godless man reproaching the Lord and not fitted your hands for battle and your fingers for war? Will you, without necessity, prove feeble in the hazard of war? Far be this from your glory, lest your praise incur such loss—that, though you can and ought to avenge, you consent not to do so.

And indeed you ought, because you are a shepherd; you can, because you bear the sword. You do bear the sword, and the whole armour of the strong protects you. If you seek a belt, you have stood with loins girded in the Lord’s threshing-floor; if a breastplate, you have put on righteousness like a giant; if a helmet, you await the common hope; if a sword, the word of God is living and effective (Heb. 4), and it shall itself devour flesh from your mouth; if a shield, orthodox faith will foil those attacking you; if footwear, we abound in the examples of the Fathers. Let the soldier go forth into the camp, to fight the Lord’s battles; let him go forth and act with confidence. The enemy may be cast down by a stone from the torrent and the whirl of a sling.

But perhaps you fear losses in worldly goods, lest by multiplied troubles the enemy heap injuries upon you. Such fear is pious, but great steadfastness is needed. For if you lose a little for righteousness’ sake, what you have done is a sacrifice. If the plunderer takes everything, it is a whole burnt offering that you have offered. In short, no valuation can be placed on virtue: it is so much more precious as it has cost you a greater loss of temporal goods. The hidden treasure and heavenly pearl rightly fell to the good merchant, because, having sold all things, he bought it for himself. Virtue likewise shall be allotted to you if it costs you dearly.

Virtue is a mustard seed: the more it is crushed, the more strongly it burns (Mark 4). It is aromatic powder: the more it is pounded in the mortar, the more effective it is for healing. If we attend to the prophet, incense is not rightly kindled beneath the shade of oak, poplar, and terebinth. The shade of the terebinth is everything in which we delight below. Beneath the eyelid of dawn, when the sun shines and the great day has breathed upon us, this shade will incline, because it is vanity. Blessed is the man for whom that very vanity becomes an occasion of virtue. Therefore the righteous shall flourish like the palm (Ps. 91), because his desire for lower things is restrained and thus is enlarged toward things above. Therefore the righteous one of the Lord is kindled like a lamp, because, refusing consolation in lower things, he opens his mouth and, drawing breath from above, shines wholly toward things above.

Act then, distinguished shepherd: when your cloak is shaken from you, cast off your tunic also. If we remove your brambles, you will pasture the flock among the lilies, where the whole company will also applaud the virtue that has followed you.

## LETTER III. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER, LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE

To his father and lord Henry, by God’s grace Bishop of Winchester and legate of the holy apostolic see, Brother G., called abbot of the Church of Blessed Peter at Gloucester: the service of all obedience and charity.

Because the care of the Churches of God has been entrusted to your discretion, beloved Father in Christ, with praiseworthy circumspection, we set before your diligence certain matters affecting us, concerning events between the lord Bishop of Hereford and the lord Miles, earl of that city. As many causes of disagreement arose between them, matters were at last brought to such a point that the lord Bishop of Hereford prohibited the divine sacraments to the earl himself and his men, and indeed to the whole city of Hereford.

Accordingly the earl, compelled no less by piety than by necessity, presented himself to the church, before us and many others standing by. First, by a pledge given into the hands of the canons, and afterwards with the Gospel-book placed upon the altar, he promised under the Church’s witness that on an appointed day he would be present before the bishop and the church itself, and would carry out whatever should be decreed by ecclesiastical jurisdiction. On the appointed day, with both parties present, the affair was brought forward; at the request of some persons, and with the lord bishop’s consent, it was postponed to another day. Yet this was subject to the condition that, should any necessity of imperial service compel a further postponement, either party should announce it before the day fixed for the contested proceeding.

Hindered by such necessity, the earl sought a postponement of the action. But the lord bishop judged that this had not been done according to the agreement; relaxing none of his severity, he pronounced sentence. And when, by letters received from your authority, he urgently required the lord Bishop of Worcester to impose the same sentence upon the churches of Gloucester, the earl, both by the formal tenor of letters sent by him and through honourable and suitable persons, offered himself for full satisfaction. In accordance with the lord Bishop of Worcester’s pleasure, he asked that a place and time be assigned to him for executing and fulfilling justice. And, lest he be suspected of evasion or any duplicity, he put forward the lord Abbot of Tewkesbury, the Prior of Llanthony, and me as sureties that he would fulfil that undertaking.

Yet his humility and the surety of all of us were held of little account, and sentence was nevertheless pronounced against us. Thus, while monasteries are forbidden among us to the living, burial to the dead, and the divine offices too are interrupted, we are bound in punishment in many ways, though we are not bound in guilt. It will therefore belong to your diligence, if the matter has been aggravated too severely, to moderate it in the spirit of gentleness. For according to Pope Stephen, a dispute of this sort ought by no means to proceed beyond the bounds of the province, but should be heard within the province and decided by fellow-provincials, unless an appeal has been made to the apostolic see—which has certainly not occurred here.

Nor can it escape your prudence that severity is then greatly to be diminished when the overthrow of churches and the slaughter of peoples threaten; whereas it must be vigorously applied when those corrected thereby become better in simplicity, not when evil men, exasperated, become worse. May your eminence prosper and be preserved for ever unblemished.

## LETTER IV. TO SIMON, BISHOP OF WORCESTER

To his father and lord Simon, by God’s grace Bishop of Worcester, Brother Gilbert, called abbot of the Church of Blessed Peter at Gloucester: with piety, to produce the fruits of righteousness.

Charity compels me, and the obedience due to you urges me, to communicate to you in person when opportunity permits, and to remind you in writing when absent, of anything which I learn may preserve or in some measure enlarge your honour. Dangerous times press close, and evil days have come upon us (2 Tim. 3), in which tares sown by the hand of an enemy may almost be able to choke or suppress the good harvest (Matt. 13).

Yet the condition in which we are is not paganism, but an inhuman cruelty worse than every paganism: a cruelty for which whatever it pleases is permitted, whatever is honourable has become worthless, and which desires nothing that is not plainly opposed to Christian simplicity and sacred laws. Indeed, to pass over reports we have merely heard, in the preceding week we saw the church of the holy Mother of God at Slohtres wonderfully broken open, its roof torn away by sacrilegious hands, and troops most ready to serve impiety introduced into fortifications never built in its walls. We saw it, I say, and grieved: the place of sanctuary dishonoured, the Church of God foully defiled, and by rash daring changed into a dwelling-place of Satan.

On the occasion of this wickedness some men also began to assault those persons. While some cast stones, missiles, and torches into that church and others resisted, two miserable days were spent there, not without the shedding of blood and the injury of many men. We know that wolves are still lurking within the walls of that church, in the very sheepfold of the Lord, tearing the Lord’s simple and innocent flock. They cannot be driven away otherwise than if the good shepherd comes, terrifies them by the blast of the trumpet and the barking of dogs, scatters them, and destroys them.

Therefore I urge your fatherhood, offering you the charity I owe in counsel, to perform a shepherd’s office toward the erring sheep: hasten with your more honourable and learned clergy to the scene of this outrage, and cause the Church entrusted to you first to be purified and then restored. Or, if the sacrilegious hand should dare to disregard your admonition, strike the perpetrators and helpers of the crime with the sword of the Lord, they themselves knowing and seeing it. Then, when offences of this sort are considered at the coming council, it may be an honour to you before those seated together that you stood as a wall for the house of Israel and manfully repelled or avenged the insults inflicted upon it. Farewell.

## LETTER V. TO POPE CELESTINE

To his father and lord, Celestine, supreme pontiff by God’s grace, Brother G., called abbot of the Church of Blessed Peter at Gloucester: all that humble and ready devotion can offer in obedience and service.

The Lord is faithful in all his words (Ps. 144), and does not cease unremittingly to perform what he has promised to the Church. To establish faith and strengthen hope, he promised that he would not fail the Church until the end of the age; and, abiding with us for ever according to his word (Matt. 28), he is recognized by unshaken faith as holy in deed and true in promise.

Recently a cloudy darkness had troubled the minds of us all. At the death of our lord and father Innocent, of venerable memory, our beloved had fled from us over the mountains of Bethel and had withdrawn for a while to the fragrant hills above. But when we receive you in his place upon the summit of the apostolic office, we embrace again in you the presence of that beloved one, and reverence you with every thanksgiving and with all the gladness of our hearts. Gold had been darkened for us and its finest colour changed (Lam. 4); but behold, the festal adornment of the Church shines more brightly, turning all things for us into joy, gladness, and splendid solemnity.

The sun, turned away into darkness, had made night for the world; but, having resumed its brightness, it illuminates all that was darkness with the ray of most welcome light. Tears clung to our cheeks and pain seethed enclosed within our breasts, while at the very summit of affairs we feared with devout dread that the schism of so great a dissension might occur. But sudden good fortune followed sudden misfortune; and, as there is one God, one faith, one baptism (Eph. 4), so one shepherd on earth governs the whole Church, binding all her parts together in charity and causing them all to rejoice with one piety.

We therefore entrust ourselves and what is ours to your care and prudence. And, so far as dutiful devotion may presume, we beseech your serenity on behalf of our lord and friend Nigel, Bishop of Ely: receive him with that charity with which you do not cease to embrace your sons, and, by piously helping him in his needs, bind your other sons to yourself by a closer bond of charity. May your eminence be preserved unharmed for ever, beloved Father in Christ.

## LETTER VI. TO THEOBALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

To his father and lord Theobald, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury, Brother G., called abbot of the Church of Blessed Peter at Gloucester: all that belongs to peace, grace, and salvation.

I give thanks to your benevolence, beloved Father in Christ, which has deigned both to call me son and to regard me as friend, and which has wished even to provide for my expenses, so that I might become your companion on the journey you have undertaken. I rejoice indeed if the time has come and opportunity has been granted by the Lord whereby your Church may be snatched from the hand that is choking it and, by whatever means and whatever labour, restored to the liberty of its former dignity.

God, the searcher of hearts, knows how ready I should be to carry out this business, were I not afraid for the Church to which I am bound, surrounded on every side by rising danger. Yet may your holiness know that until this day no storm has broken upon us more violently. Today we are pressing a case, with much toil, against the earl of Hereford, whose thirst has flamed out against everything we possess. The very man whom, had we been absent, we hoped would be the protector of our Church, we find, now that we are present, to be its most hostile enemy.

We are already sharpening episcopal weapons against him and stand, as if drawn up for battle, against him and all his men. There is no number to the others attacking us: against them we fight, some bearing iron, others stones, and we scarcely make progress. Therefore your paternal kindness will excuse your son on this occasion: necessity, not will, withdraws me from you for the present. My tears shall be upon my cheeks every day until I hear of your return and success, and gladly meet the returning Father. Meanwhile I shall accompany my lord in prayer; and though absent in body, I shall stand present in spirit and in the affection of my mind in every undertaking. Farewell.

## LETTER VII. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord Theobald, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury, Brother G., called abbot of the Church of Blessed Peter at Gloucester: by piously completing the six, happily to attain the Sabbaths of Sabbaths.

Beloved Father, I received from your eminence a letter of instruction that I should present myself before you before Christmas Day, ready for the journey and labour undertaken by you. My disposition toward you and the charity binding me to you are such that for your sake I count as light every difficulty that may threaten: the hardship of travel, bodily discomfort, or the pressing authority of adverse power.

But beyond these, my daily concerns are innumerable. They hold me not merely bound by chains, but even render me, as it were, immovable. Since I cannot possibly deal with them all, it is difficult for me at present to presume to undertake greater matters. Farewell.

## LETTER VIII. TO UCHTRED, BISHOP OF LLANDAFF

To his father and lord U., by God’s grace Bishop of Llandaff, Brother G., called abbot of the Church of Blessed Peter at Gloucester: to administer what has been entrusted to him with the fitting moderation of reason.

At your request I send letters to your affection which I should have sent without being asked. Your prudence cannot fail to know that the peace of God’s household is the ordered harmony of those dwelling together in commanding and obeying. Nor can it fail to know that it is rightly administered when the humble and ready devotion of sons obeys the pious and prudent counsel of their elders.

But if the audacity of subjects despises obedience to the just commands of prelates, there can be no doubt that what has been disgracefully overthrown in contempt of one redounds to the injury of all prelates. We therefore beg your benevolence, also offering the charity we owe in counsel, to exercise a shepherd’s office toward the erring sheep. Recall to peace and obedience that brother who walks disorderly, who presumed to occupy the church of Stringnen against the will of his abbot and of his whole Church; and, lest he utterly perish, carry him back upon your pastoral shoulder to the sheepfolds of the flock, as a sheep rescued from the lion’s mouth.

For it is dangerous to admit anyone to the Church’s benefits, much less to her sacraments, who is found stubborn or rebellious against those whom he ought to obey. Humility will accept gentle admonitions of salvation; but if he proves obstinate, let charity diligently apply the rod, so that disobedience may be checked and all may be informed, through your zeal, how rebellion ought to be requited. Farewell.

## LETTER IX. TO ROBERT, BISHOP OF HEREFORD

To his father and lord R., by God’s grace Bishop of Hereford, Brother G., called abbot of the Church of Blessed Peter at Gloucester: to draw the net cast into the sea, full of good fish, all the way to shore.

Your generosity, beloved Father, tested by me so often, has made me a debtor to its favour even in this respect: recently, by gifts sent, it deigned both to feed and to teach me. I count that a perfect gift which refreshes the body and no less enriches the soul. Unhappy are feasts where the whole body is consumed and the spirit receives no refreshment. But consideration of your gift persuades me that I feast very differently.

You sent me fish—two of them: one larger, the other smaller; both good and of the same kind. All this fills my inner person with so many dishes because it instructs me with so many lessons. First of all, because you sent fish, you recalled to my mind that great fisherman: the fisherman whom, called by the Lord from the boat, the Lord wished not only to fish for human beings, but also, because of his ready confession of faith, advanced to the prerogative of the apostolic summit.

You suggest that my soul should unceasingly set before its eyes that he drew me out, after I had long been tossed by waves, with the hook of his fishing, and assigned me to the fellowship of his monks in a great city. Yet I do not say this as though I were now secure concerning my conversion or manner of life; for a person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred (Ecclus. 9), and all things are reserved for each person in the future. For it is not praiseworthy merely to have been in a holy place, but rather to have remained in holiness. We run in vain if we do not attain the prize; and only completion rewards well-begun beginnings.

Thus the children of Israel, after leaving Egypt and crossing the sea, because they did not stand firm in heart, were tested and perished (John 6). Whom would this matter not move? This parable concerns us. To leave Egypt is to come from the darkness of blindness and ignorance to the light of faith. To cross the sea is, through the power of baptism, to breathe again from the oldness of sin into the newness of grace. To perish in the desert is, after receiving knowledge of truth and grace, to yield to the slavery of sins and end one’s life in them.

For one who departs does not immediately receive the promised delights. That famous Jordan, struck by the Lord’s rod, divided within itself: the waters on the left were carried by their current into the sea, while those on the right, gathered into one, rose upward (Ps. 113). The Lord’s rod is everything by which we are struck. Some are wearied in body, others in spirit; but for the children of the right hand all things work together for good. Whether they receive adversity from the Lord’s hand or prosperity, they do not cease to give thanks, but lift up their heart and raise the governing part of their mind toward heaven.

Those who are on the left believe for a time but fall away in time of temptation. Those unable to bear the light stroke of the rod quickly slide away and flow off; mingled with the whirlpool’s salt water, they are miserably submerged and perish. Therefore I am not permitted to glory in the bodily fellowship of saints unless diligent charity considers and imitates in me the pursuits of saints.

This you yourself suggest to me in pious counsel when you send fish drawn from the deep, yet dead: you very wisely teach me to beware lest, drawn from the depth of the world, I incur the work of death. For our fisherman carries out the work of his fishing very differently: he knows how to fish those dead in sin into life. Therefore, one who dies after being drawn out is not held within the compass of his net.

That you sent two fish, one large and the other small, is pleasant to me in its meaning and more pleasant still in the intention of the sender. You represent to me the mystical labours of the prince of the apostles. From the Gospel reading we know that he applied himself twice to fishing. In the first, because of the abundant multitude, the net was broken (Luke 5); in the second it was drawn to shore full of large fish (John 21). The first catch is the calling of all; the second is the bringing of the elect into life. Hence in the first the net is rightly broken, because very many fall away from the grace in which they were called and, as their faults deserve, are eternally rejected. In the second the net is not broken, because the Lord will draw all his elect to life, and there is none to snatch any of them from his hand (Ps. 49).

By effective admonition you instruct and shape me, lest, like a fish escaped from a broken net, I wander and perish; rather, conformed in the quality of my life to those one hundred and fifty-three great fish, I should fashion my life and conduct after the pattern of the elect. If I understood more deeply the hidden meaning of your thought, perhaps I might conjecture that, by the gift of fish, you recall to my mind the Gospel fish and that, by this occasion, your prudence strongly urges my sluggishness to embrace more earnestly the study of reading.

Those loaves from which the people are fed and the baskets filled are the five books of the Law; the two fish are prophecy and the Psalms (Matt. 14). Fish live while they inhabit the deep. If they are drawn into the light, they perish, extinguished by the light. Thus before the Saviour’s coming, doctrine in the prophets was dark, amid the clouds of the air. In that depth prophecy lived in its own manner while, foretelling what was to come, it promised it. But once the promise was fulfilled and Christ more fully illuminated the world, prophecy was drawn into the light and in a sense was itself drawn out, since truth fulfilled in the promises no longer needs promise. Hence the Lord says: “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke 16).

Thus you weave riddling coverings around me and desire that I be spiritually exercised in every way: on the one hand, you draw me by prophetic obscurity toward reading; on the other, you compel me toward prayer and praise by the very sweetness of the Psalms, as by the delight of the other fish. It remains for me to understand why you determined that the fish you sent should be of the same kind.

You commend unity and peace to me. For the number two belongs to good, but it is also found in evil. The good of two is love of God and neighbour; another good of it is that the disciples were sent out two by two to preach (Mark 6). Since charity exists at least between two, two likewise has its misfortunes. Unclean animals were sent into the ark two by two (Gen. 6). For because two is the first number to fall away from unity, everything by which peace is split or concord dispersed is rightly assigned to it.

You therefore persuade me to follow him who is holy, who “makes those of one manner to dwell in a house,” lest I be divided by anger or inflamed by hatred; but, preserving peace with all and charity, I should endeavour to avoid divisions and schisms, and gather into the Lord’s house fish of one kind—that is, brothers of one observance, charity, and faith.

Under the same meaning, the Lord said to Moses: “You shall make me an altar of unhewn stones, which iron has not touched” (Exod. 20). Hewn stones are those who, though polished by knowledge, are separated from the fellowship of brothers by schism or discord. No altar is built for the Lord from them, because nothing from their life is offered acceptable to the Lord. But an altar is built for the Lord from unhewn stones, because from those made firm in unity through faith, Christ’s body is completed.

That I called both fish good has this meaning. Clean fish are those which have scales and fins. Their scales are joined together and cover the body on every side. They therefore signify virtues, which, all joined together in the root of charity, clothe, defend, and adorn the inner person with a kind of many-coloured, full-length garment. The fins signify the heights of contemplation. By them fish are lifted from the deep and make, as it were, certain leaps above the waters, though by their natural weight they fall back again to the same waters.

What do these fins signify except the efforts of the soul, by which it is sometimes raised toward that highest good and invisible light, and strives to taste something of that inward sweetness, although it is hindered by the bodily burden to which it is bound? “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9). These thoughts on the meaning of your gift occur to me for the moment; when we enjoy the desired sight of one another and conversation, you yourself will teach them more fully. Meanwhile, if it please you, consider what remains.

Through the messenger who bore your gift you commanded me not to be tortured by envy, not to waste away in pining, and not to increase my own dry barrenness because of the happiness granted to you and your abundance of such and so great fish. In words you warn me not to envy; in deed you draw me to envy. What wonder if I wither with envy, when the small undertaking of making a pond is forbidden me by the broadly powerful, long-established pond of a neighbour? You command me to put away envy; you yourself will be able to root it out by granting permission to make a pond. It will be no small proof of friendship. Do not allow one to be tortured for long when you know that the cure of his sickness depends upon your help. Farewell.

## LETTER X. TO R., PRIOR, AND THE BRETHREN OF MALVERN

To the lord R., prior, and the brethren with him at Malvern, G., called abbot of the Church of Blessed Peter at Gloucester: not utterly to forget those who love him.

Trusting in the goodwill toward me which I had not deserved but hoped for from you, I sent to you a certain kinsman and member of my household, humbly presenting requests that you would graciously grant him to hold from you what you possessed in the church of Estlethe. Yet he was to give assurance upon the sacraments that he would not defraud you of the benefit—not merely what you presently had, but what you had had from that Church in a time of tranquil peace.

But you, considering the matter more deeply and not wishing an ungrateful friend to receive a benefit which had long remained in the giver’s hand, did not hear one who, even had he requested great things, ought to have been heard on account of the claim of charity. Indeed, I say that you did not hear him; after delaying your decision, you sent back to us empty those whom I had sent to you.

I take it ill, not that what I asked has not been accomplished, but that I am compelled to hope less than usual from friends. I asked with confidence for what I would not refuse to a request from those who love me. I asked for something for which I certainly ought to have been asked. I asked lest the benefit of your Church be displeasing to that people if it should happen to be administered in some measure through us.

And because it is a great rebuff when something small is denied to a friend, I set the matter before your eyes, so that you may judge from it how much I asked and how little you denied. When I have fully paid the portion of that Church which concerns us, fulfilled for the minister of the altar the reward of his ministry, and answered to episcopal authority for what belongs to it, the profit remaining after all these things scarcely amounts to enough for a friend to have deserved such a refusal from those who love him.

Therefore, if you should wish to change your decision for the better, you would make me greatly indebted for a small matter; and I should either satisfy according to his wish that clerk to whom you have hitherto granted the matter, or render you wholly excusable against him in every hearing. I ask you to send back, by the bearer of this letter, letters indicating your decision. Farewell.

## LETTER XI. TO POPE LUCIUS

To his father and lord Lucius, supreme pontiff by God’s grace, Brother G., called abbot of Blessed Peter at Gloucester: increases of peace and salvation.

I judge that it cannot escape your serenity, beloved Father, by how many storms of misery the Church of Salisbury is shaken. It belongs to your care not only to sympathize with the losses of all Churches, but also to provide for their advantages. Long deprived of its own ruler, it was wavering in uncertainty, both through the assault of wicked men and because its own members were not of one mind concerning the election of their father. It would have reached utter desolation, had the Lord not granted it, as we hope, a bishop chosen as his worthy servant: Jocelin, a son worthy of your holiness, commendable in life and grace, whom he has made its father and shepherd.

So far as the devotion of a most humble person may presume—not, I say, of a son, but of a servant—we earnestly wish to commend him to your eminence, since we have found him worthy of commendation. Before his calling, he constantly devoted himself to the pursuit of virtue; and now, not taking this honour for himself but, as we hope, called by the Lord, he does not cease through the merit of a praiseworthy life to honour the episcopal see. He courageously endures or repels assaults rushing upon his Church; and where he perhaps is insufficient for himself, our humility, presuming upon your benevolence, desires and requests that you extend to him a hand of help and counsel.

We therefore commend to your holiness his canon, Master R. de Meisi, a man commendable in life and conduct. Since we know that he has undertaken the present business against Lord Azon, Dean of Salisbury, we beseech your blessedness concerning this very matter: support him in the cause of justice and truth, and provide by paternal favour for the honour and benefit of the Church of Salisbury. May your eminence prosper, beloved Father in Christ!

## LETTER XII. TO HAMON OF BORDESLEY

To his rare friend Hamon, abbot of Bordesley.

Mindful of your affection and kind request, by which you asked me to write or dictate something for you, I at last comply; and, if any leisure is granted me, I gladly devote it to the service of your kindness. For, when you had heard that, by reason of the office of stewardship entrusted to me, I had on several occasions addressed words of exhortation to the brethren, you too, being present, began to urge me that, if the Lord had revealed to me in the Scriptures anything from the bounty of His Spirit, I should not ungratefully set it down in writing, and should myself gratefully publish, for the edification of some, what I had received freely. For you maintain that the manifold grace of the simple word of God is to be imparted to devout minds not in one manner only, but must be handled in diverse forms of instruction. Yet, just as nature has made the bodily senses themselves—by which a path to understanding lies open to us—distinct and various among themselves, so the word of God must be handled in varied forms of teaching, and conveyed to devout hearts now by proclamation, now by the aid of writing, until Christ be formed in us and we all be taught by God (John 6).

You add besides that those things which are delivered in church, as it were in the manner of an oration, seem to perish from memory along with the sound unless they are held fast by writing as by a kind of tether; and that memories are restored through the intervention of sight when such things are presented to the minds of readers. How insistently you repeat that saying of the Wise Man: “Gold scattered abroad shines more brightly than gold stamped”; gems differ in no respect from common stones unless they are made public. A thought too, when distributed, gains increase; and, scorning an avaricious possessor, it slips away unless it is published. Finally, lest excuse should find any avenue, you strongly terrify our idleness by that saying of the Lord: “Wicked servant” (Matt. 18), why did you not put my money on the table? Thus you gather many arguments to shake off torpor, repel sloth, and draw me—who until now have scarcely dared to come forth in public—from the hiding-place of silence into the light of eloquence. You press me with imperious affection. You use such force upon me that I have no answer except either that I cannot do what you demand, or that I do not wish to render to a friend what I can do. Whichever I say, you are so minded as either to accuse me of deceit or of injury. I fear both; and, while you hold me bound in the golden fetter of charity, I do what captives commonly do today when they are questioned about ransom and are afraid: I promise wholly what the exacter wills. Thus I too, lest I suffer loss in charity and be loved less in Christ, dare refuse you nothing. But matters which until now I entrusted only to safe ears I now commit to your examination and scrutiny. I know with what great favour you will receive whatever it is that I offer, and that you will value highly the two small coins which a friend gives, because he gives not from abundance but from scanty means.

## LETTER XIII. TO JOCELIN, BISHOP OF SALISBURY

To his father and lord JOCELIN, by God’s grace bishop, G., called abbot of the church of St Peter at Gloucester, wishes daily prosperity in grace.

Having often been asked to write to your highness concerning the affair of the brethren of Cerne, we have until now delayed, judging that the matter had not advanced so far as to make it expedient for us to write about it. For he who was presiding over that church, though assailed by many accusations, nevertheless remained for some time in a state of expectation, and had not yet renounced the pastoral charge which he had undertaken with the solemnity that was required. But now, as we have heard, you have celebrated his obsequies; and, the axe having now been laid to the root of the fruitless tree, you have cut down with praiseworthy severity, as report has it, that tree which stood uselessly. Since, therefore, you have now made ready a fruitful place for trees, we ask—indeed, we ask and desire—that what is counted worthy of justice in us may be brought by a praiseworthy completion to glory.

The brethren of Cerne came to us, bringing also letters under the seal of their church, and asked that one of our brethren, by the common election, as they say, of all the brethren, might be given and released to them as their father and shepherd. We hope that the man whom they choose is worthy both of honour and favour, since he is a man in whom knowledge abounds for teaching and character for upright conduct, fit to govern souls and safeguard possessions. Had we not believed him praiseworthy, we certainly should not have commended him to you. Yet determining nothing in this matter except according to the decision of your will, we ask, if it please you, that your counsel be made known to us, whether you are willing to grant assent to this petition. Our will shall serve your command. And if your authority were to confirm the honour of our church, in some measure already anticipated by this very election, you would find us bound by an immeasurable debt of gratitude and in every respect more ready to serve your will. We pray that the Spirit of counsel may be with you, to direct you and order your work with moderation pleasing to Him. Farewell.

## LETTER XIV. TO JOCELIN, BISHOP OF SALISBURY

To his father and lord J., by God’s grace bishop of Salisbury, G., called abbot of the church of St Peter at Gloucester, wishes that he may reap fruits of righteousness with joy and exultation.

Beloved Father, with shared lamentation we lay our troubles before the ears of your holiness, humbly begging that your admonition may recall our wrongdoers or your discipline restrain them. John of Merleberga and Walter of Pincheum do not cease to harass us, your humble friends, and to seize by violent hand the resources of our pilgrimage, and they do not blush to spend them in the service of wickedness. Hitherto we have patiently borne the burden and heat of the day (Matt. 20), hoping that at last the fury of malicious men might either be exhausted or that they might be turned back to lawful paths by some salutary persuasion. But since, according to the Wise Man, “Whom God has rejected, man cannot correct” (Ecclus. 7), we ask with the confidence which we rightly place in you that those whom holy admonition cannot recall may be humbled by the pastoral rod in your hand.

Moreover, let your holiness know that those two named above have taken from us more than two hundred marks, in coin and in the value of coin, and have nearly reduced our possessions situated around them to nothing. We therefore desire to be strengthened by the Spirit of Him who said, “Take courage; I have overcome the world” (John 16), who shall make all His enemies the footstool of His feet (Ps. 109), through whom we shall laugh and mock at the destruction of the wicked (Prov. 1), when what they deserve has befallen them. You do not bear His sword in vain, but that you may strike the Philistines not only, like Shamgar, with the handle of the plough, but also, like Ehud, with the edge of the sword (Judg. 3). Let not grow dull in your hand the sword of Him who, according to the prophet, “is sharpened that it may glitter; it is polished” (Ezek. 21). Opportunity for valour meets you on every side. Charity grows cold; scandals will grow cold. The Church cries to you from every quarter as avengers of crimes. Let that word of God therefore be drawn forth, we beseech you, living and effectual, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow (Heb. 4), so that at that great feast you may have glory before those seated together at table, because you set yourself as a wall for the house of Israel and either courageously repelled or avenged its injuries. Farewell.

## LETTER XV. TO B., ABBOT OF CERNE

To his beloved brother and dearest son B., by God’s grace abbot of Cerne, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, wishes him “to act manfully and be strengthened in the Lord” (1 Cor. 16).

It belongs to a good man neither to be lifted up by prosperity nor broken by adversity. You yourself know this; you yourself have put on this pattern. Therefore do not quickly be frightened by anyone’s threats, or shaken from your judgment by pressing and urgent poverty. If any storm should rise against you, when the Holy Spirit blows it will swiftly settle into a breeze and its waves will be still (Ps. 106). If poverty oppresses you, always obey the Lord in godly fear, and He will not forsake those who hope in Him (Ps. 16). Remember how simply you have walked; remember that you have committed your sails not to covetousness but to obedience and truth alone. Keep before your eyes that He for whom you serve accepts obedience above every sacrifice. Walk simply, and you shall walk confidently. We shall all cry to the Lord, and He will open His hand and fill you with blessing (Ps. 144).

You find no counsel either within your house or outside in your possessions. Your house is in your own hands; within it you possess the anointing of the Spirit, which will teach you concerning all things (John 14). You have also your dearest son Jocelin, whom, because he fears the Lord, we believe to abound in sound counsel. We have sent Lord Hugh to you; he will obey you diligently and assist you with devoted service. If you desire one or more of our men in addition, send to us, with whichever of your own horses you please, whether young or old, and you shall obtain from ours whom you wish. We shall count your affairs as our own. You can endure adversities, but you cannot bear them alone. We are one, and always one in the Lord (Gal. 3), and we shall serve Him shoulder to shoulder.

If all other comforts fail, one at least cannot fail. Your house may advance day by day through whatever labour or counsel is available, but it cannot grow worse. Evil is, as it were, at its highest point and finds nowhere further to go; your good may make daily progress. If your blessing is delayed, it is not taken away. You know that a bishop’s blessing does not make an abbot, but the common election of the brethren. We shall lay this burden upon the shoulders of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; our face cannot be put to shame. The minister and messenger of the apostles himself appointed you. We shall report to him what we hear concerning you; and concerning him we hope in every respect to obtain that he will not permit the first planting which I planted in this realm to be shamefully uprooted by the labour or contrivance of any man. Farewell; and if riches increase, do not set your heart upon them (Ps. 61). If poverty burns fiercely, obey and be patient. You know that saying of the Wise Man: “Holy poverty has its own riches.” Poverty too is an honourable and joyful thing; indeed, it is not poverty if it is joyful.

## LETTER XVI. TO J., LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE

To his father and lord J., by God’s grace legate of the holy apostolic see, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, offers the charity and obedience due to a father.

Compelled, Father, by pressing necessity, we seek the aid of your bounty, in which we place great confidence. A dispute has recently arisen between the lord bishop of Llandaff and our brother J., prior of the church of St Michael, situated in the same diocese of Llandaff, concerning the body of a certain lady M., namely of London. Being at the point of death, with her husband and her relatives standing by, and with the priest whose parishioner she was both consenting and requesting it, she granted by her last will that she should be buried in our place, into the hand of the aforesaid prior acting in our stead. For, at the dedication of our church in the time of that bishop’s predecessor, namely Lord Bishop Urban, her father and mother, she herself, and all their offspring gave themselves to our said place, in the bishop’s presence and with no one objecting. She was received, died not long afterwards, and was brought to our church—indeed, to her own church.

Thereupon the lord of Llandaff became more angry with us than was just, and ordered the body to be removed from our church and carried by our people into his own. The prior opposed this command with apostolic authority, which, by the force of privilege, grants to our churches the bodies for burial of brothers and sisters. Consequently, as though the prior himself had named something profane, he was immediately suspended from communion and our churches were put under interdict. Feeling himself aggrieved by this, the prior appealed to your hearing for the day ‘Adae in tua misericordia’ [phrase uncertain]. We therefore beg your kindness that you grant divine offices to our churches, because on the appointed day, life permitting, we shall appear before you, ready in spirit to obey whatever judgment your jurisdiction decrees. May my most beloved lord prosper.

## LETTER XVII. TO POPE EUGENIUS

To his father and lord E., supreme pontiff by God’s grace, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, offers obedience and the charity due to a father.

Beloved Father, we cannot refuse this small thing to the charity of our friends; and common compassion requires that, bearing one another’s burdens (Gal. 6), we likewise render you reciprocal assistance of counsel and aid. Therefore, although no merits commend us to your majesty, nor have services rendered or expenses incurred secured for us any favour with you, yet out of charity we dare, though we are not worthy to be heard even for ourselves, to make a pious and bold entry before paternal mercy on behalf of another.

A clerk of your beloved son, the lord archbishop of Canterbury, Master R. de Ponte, bishop, comes to seek your protection under urgent necessity, that he may implore from your serenity protection in preserving what he lawfully possesses. Prostrate in heart at the knees of your holiness, we ask that compassion may proceed from the fountain of justice; and that you receive into favour him whom we believe worthy to be commended before the apostolic majesty alike for his life and learning, and send him back graciously heard in his just petitions. May the Most High Majesty preserve your highness long in safety for itself and its own.

## LETTER XVIII. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord E., supreme pontiff, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, wishes that he may happily attain the glory of eternal life.

Beloved Father in Christ, we cannot resist necessity without obeying the charity which powerfully commands us from the hearts of brethren. It is this which brings us, though we desire rather to remain hidden, into public view, so that we may send words of truth to your hearing, before which we cannot at present stand. Thus we could not refuse to testify to your highness concerning what we have seen and heard about an eminent and honourable man, Master Godfrey, most excellently learned in both divine and secular writings.

William Cumin having, for many compelling reasons, been bound by the bonds of anathema, and having now remained under that bond for more than a full year, and the jurisdiction of a general council having stripped him of every ecclesiastical benefice, the lord bishop of Worcester, by the counsel of religious men, invested the said Godfrey with his archdeaconry and appointed him archdeacon of his church with religious devotion. We know that he has conducted himself religiously in that office and has prudently and discreetly administered what belonged to his charge. We know also that he is necessary to that church as bishop, if it please you, and that in him not merely this benefice but much more besides would be secure. May your judgment decree in this matter so that your glory may always increase and those who have recourse to you may conceive good hope of obtaining both counsel and aid in the matters for which they resort to you. May almighty God protect you unto length of days, Father in Christ.

## LETTER XIX. TO JOHN, PRIOR OF ST MICHAEL

G., by God’s grace abbot of Gloucester, to his beloved son JOHN, prior of St Michael, greetings.

You shall carry the letters directed to you to the lord of Llandaff. If he hears you, give him thanks; but if he persists in his purpose, you shall resist him by apostolic authority. For we have at hand an apostolic privilege enabling us freely to receive all free persons who have given themselves to our houses for burial. If he persists in this matter and keeps you under interdict, you shall appeal, with witnesses brought forward, to the hearing of the lord legate, and name for him, for this action, the day ‘Adae in tua misericordia’ [phrase uncertain]. Farewell.

## LETTER XX. TO B., ABBOT OF CERNE

To his beloved brother and dearest son B., by God’s grace abbot of Cerne, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, wishes greeting and steadfastness of mind.

For the present, we omit answering individually the matters which you entrusted to us in your letter, because we know that the end of our affair, as the Lord has disposed it, is soon at hand. Nevertheless, we always expect better things from the Lord Himself, the giver of good things: as He has granted us good gifts, may He multiply them and never cease to crown with further grace that grace by which He has anticipated us. He Himself turns our “woe” into joy, if there is anything of it in the present; and if He has struck us in any matter with an envious eye, He will bring its outcome to joyful completion.

Moreover, know that, life and health permitting, I shall come this next Sunday to Winchester to the lord legate. We order you—and in ordering, likewise enjoin you—not to omit meeting us there for any reason whatsoever. Farewell.

## LETTER XXI. TO UCTRED, BISHOP OF LLANDAFF

To his father and lord, the bishop of Llandaff by God’s grace, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, greetings and due reverence.

We give thanks for the care and labour which you have expended so that your affairs might prosper under you. By this very fact we acknowledge ourselves obliged to you and debtors to your favour. We neither desire nor approve that any injury should be done to you by ourselves or by our brethren. Yet we do not presume, by diminishing apostolic authority, to order the body which you demand to be expelled from the church into which it was brought and to which it had assigned itself by last will. We therefore ask that, if it please you, this pardon may be granted us, and that favour may be added as a gift of your customary bounty: do not deny us the bodies of the dead which belong to us by right, and receive from us and all our people such honour and dutiful service as we can render. Farewell.

## LETTER XXII. TO THEOBALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

To his father and lord THEOBALD, by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all England, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, offers humble obedience springing from unfeigned charity.

Beloved Father in Christ, we ask your kindness to accept the excuse which necessity presently puts forward for us, and, if we do anything short of your command, to forgive it us with paternal charity. Far be it from me to fabricate anything in your presence, since I judge it my greatest consolation to spend the days of this earthly sojourn together with you in the undivided union of life. But those around us know more than sufficiently how recently the Welsh fell upon us, and how they drove off almost everything that we possessed beyond the river Severn, even into the depths of Wales itself. It is therefore necessary for me, on this very Sunday when you will meet in London, to attend a conference of Welsh kings in Glamorgan, or to suffer an irrecoverable loss of more than three hundred marks. Since charity wholly rules in every region of your heart, grant this pardon to your pleading son: by paternal leave, may I now serve the pressing and most urgent necessity of our church. May my beloved lord and father prosper.

## LETTER XXIII. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord T., by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all England, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, offers humble obedience and wholehearted affection.

To carry out what you commanded, we and many of our friends have met once, twice, and a third time, in order to hear fully and decide the case of the lord abbot of Reading and his brethren against Lord Roderic and the other monks of St Denis. The case brought before us was carried as far as this conclusion. The men of Reading complained that their church of Stanton had been unjustly deprived of the parish of Camora, a tract belonging to St Denis. They asserted that their said church of Stanton had continuously and peacefully held parochial rights in that land of Mora, in both spiritual and temporal matters, for thirty years and more. To prove this possession they produced many witnesses: monks, priests, many clerks, and not a few respectable laymen, all entirely ready to give proof if it were adjudged to them. The men of Reading therefore asked that their proof be admitted and that they be put into possession.

But Lord Roderic and those standing with him argued the contrary. They said that the proof offered by the men of Reading should not be admitted, nor ought they in any way to be invested with the said possession. They declared that the parish in its entirety belonged by right to St Denis and pertained to their church of Teintona, not through some recent usurpation but through an ancient prescription of long duration. They firmly asserted that their church of Teintona, from its first foundation, had continuously and peacefully possessed the said property for more than sixty years, and that they themselves still stood invested with that possession on the very day of the action, as with their own. In support of their assertion they produced the lord abbot of Evesham and a substantial part of his convent, together with other priests, clerks, and many laymen, all ready to testify.

Since in cases of this kind the condition of one who affirms and possesses is better than that of one who merely claims, Lord Roderic asked that proof of his possession be admitted and that thereafter, if it were just, he be left undisturbed. When we were deciding each point with the lord of Hereford, the dean of London, the archdeacon of Oxford, and the other men who had assembled, before any judgment was given the prior of Reading, complaining that he was wronged by the archdeacon of Oxford and the abbot of Evesham, though we do not know in what respect, appealed to the hearing of the lord pope and thereby put an end to the task enjoined upon us. Therefore, lest these proceedings before us should escape your prudent notice, we have copied them out for you, whom we desire to be wholly defended and always safe. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIV. TO SIMON, BISHOP OF WORCESTER

To his father and lord S., by God’s grace bishop of Worcester, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, greetings.

Our multiplied affairs compel us often to write to you and frequently to appeal to your goodwill. Where we hope and expect relief from our troubles, there we often lament and disclose our hardships. As we have heard from many, one of your officers, Algodus the dean, carries out the office committed to him most wretchedly and does not cease, under the stewardship entrusted to him, to persecute and oppress our clerks from hatred. The more notable and sacred the festivals he sees approaching, the more, as though he had obtained an opportunity for doing harm, does he place our churches under interdict and forbid our clerks to minister in their orders.

We therefore ask your gentleness, with our ever-confident appeal to your mercy, to permit our clerk B. of Colna to minister in his order on these days; and, on a day appointed for him, if you cannot attend to the matter yourself, to order that everything which the aforesaid Algodus may bring against him be determined before your archdeacon. We regard as suspect the judgment of one whose hatred we know to be manifest; and if it pleased your discretion that our clerks should be judged by such a man, it ought to be by one whose upright life commended him: one who, from the citadel of prudence, judged the incestuous, not one who, from a bed of softness, offended the Lord’s priests. Farewell.

## LETTER XXV. TO POPE EUGENIUS

To his father and lord E., supreme pontiff by God’s grace, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, wishes that he may happily obtain that one thing which they ask from the Lord.

Beloved Father, charity persuades us on one side, humility terrifies us on the other, to presume to address your majesty by letter. Yet we choose rather to be reproved by a father for boldness than condemned by our dearest lords and brethren for neglected charity. We therefore offer humble prayers to your highness with the affection of suppliants, that you may receive with the favour befitting your goodness the lord bishop of Lincoln who comes to you, and hear him in his just requests. Since knowledge abounds in him for teaching and character for upright conduct, it is fitting that he should experience from a father everything that belongs to favour and compassion. We pray that the Lord’s saying may prevail concerning him: “Him that comes to me I will not cast out” (John 6); that he who runs after grace may lay hold of grace, and he who hastens to a father may rejoice to have found a father. The virtues of very many will be kindled by love when they see uprightness worthily rewarded by you, and see that virtue has its reward neither diminished nor withheld. May He who does not sleep, the guardian of Israel (Ps. 120), preserve you for long ages.

## LETTER XXVI. [TO SIMON, BISHOP OF WORCESTER]

To his father and lord S., by God’s grace bishop of Worcester, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, offers due obedience and such charity as he can.

By letters we presented prayers to your highness, asking you, by grace alone, to defer until our return the case being brought against our clerk Wimund. Yet by a higher providence this was otherwise arranged, and he has been adjudged a purgation of the accusation by the hand of seven. We therefore presume upon your goodwill in affection and ask that you temper this sentence with such mercy as you can, and mitigate it by such reasoning as you ought.

You know how carefully even in secular causes it is customary to guard against a judge making himself an accuser, unless, perhaps, public notoriety compels him to do this when there is no accuser. If this should sometimes happen to a judge, he then appears not as an accuser but as spokesman for public report; nor does he thereby lose his office as judge, in lending his support to the voice of pursuing report. But in this case the matter is otherwise. We know what the neighbours cry out and what the people attest with the mouth of many. That woman of whom Wimund is accused was delivered and sent as a hostage for her husband, not at his urging or persuasion, but through the pressing insistence of her brother, Eilwin the priest. When she was sent with him, Wimund did not withhold the assistance due to her, but kindly gave what aid his means allowed. Afterwards he pursued his own brother—namely, her husband—even to enmity, in order to work effectively for her redemption.

What then if that woman was overtaken by death? Shall he pay who did not deserve it? But who has ever perished innocent? Or when have those who are upright been destroyed by the judgment of the Church? If a clerk of St Peter assisted the said woman with his own resources when she was sent as a hostage, if he reminded her husband concerning her ransom, if he urged her brother Eilwin likewise, what other judgment can be made than that he has in large measure cleared himself? We therefore beseech your blessedness that, in the present affair, your eyes may see equity (Ps. 16), and that you receive with the favour which you customarily show him who is accused by no one and pursued by no ill repute, and send him back cheered by the splendour of your presence.

## LETTER XXVII. TO THEOBALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

To his father and lord T., by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, wishes that he may, by devoutly fulfilling the number six, happily attain the Sabbaths of Sabbaths.

Beloved Father, from our whole heart we cannot render sufficient thanks because your bounty long ago opened to us the bosom of kindly charity and, as we know from the very outcome of events, assigned us more fully to the number of your own. And indeed this is so, not because we deserve it, but because it so pleased you: by the very fact that you admitted us to the favour of friendship, you should always possess us wholly as your own by a fuller title of merit. You have a debtor for manifold favour, whom benefits bestowed sufficiently bind, while no merits commend him with you.

But because the performance of past kindnesses is certain to us and the expectation of future ones remains, we take great courage and, with ever-pious charity, presume to offer earnest prayers to your highness also for our kinsman and dearest friend R. de Beaumis: that you may admit him to the benefices of the church which the bishop of Chichester has granted him in full donation, and which he asks may be confirmed by your authority through ratification of that gift. Indeed, your recommendation would greatly commend this R. to us, had not public fame long since shown him to be received amid universal congratulations: a man in whom knowledge abounds for teaching and character for upright conduct, a man worthy to be occupied in God’s service and at the same time enriched with benefices, so that by the excellence of one work you may bestow favour upon us and glory upon your own virtue.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord T., by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all England, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, wishes that he may enjoy, in the region of light, the desired object of his longing according to his prayer.

Beloved Father in the Lord, it pleased your highness to summon our lord and father, the lord bishop of Worcester, to your hearing, to answer certain charges laid against him. Nor does he less gladly obey your command and will in all things with devotion. Therefore he comes before the judge in all fear of the Lord and humility of heart; yet with good hope and the full abundance of charity he hastens to the Father. For there is nothing which a son need fear in the judgment of a father, when within the Father there is an affection which knocks and entreats for him.

Yet lest your eye be clouded in examining the present case, we make known to your discretion what is known to us. You yourselves decreed concerning the condition of the Church of Worcester that, in order to restore the dignity both of the bishop and of his church, the former prior should himself be restored for a time, and that within a prescribed day the need of that church should be provided for by substituting another. When the lord bishop was returning from you to his church, intending to obey your will, some of the brethren of his church, unaware of your arrangement and bearing the restoration of their prior more bitterly than they ought, immediately began, as report has it, to disperse the church’s goods and, as the people cry out, departed after filling their purses dishonestly. You yourselves will sufficiently judge what this is like. To disperse by infamous sale the goods of the church entrusted to them was evil; to take sudden flight from the presence of a father who was pursuing them in no respect, but was bringing back from you useful counsel, was much worse; and not even to deign to hear what had been decreed by you was worst of all.

As for their complaint that they were seized and improperly detained on the road while hastening to you for the benefit of their church, nearly everyone testifies among us that the lord bishop was ignorant of this while it was happening and, when he learned of it, dealt with it in paternal charity. I judge it better to believe one bishop and the truth than an angry and rebellious crowd of monks. Even if he had recalled or detained them from their disorderly journey, there would have been in that either no fault or a very slight one. Nevertheless, hear those who have been summoned concerning this. In addition, we know that the lord bishop has removed his prior from the priorship, but has not yet appointed anyone in his place because of the unrest of the rebellious brethren. I judge that this has been divinely arranged so that you may put the final hand to a good work and, by providing a suitable shepherd for your daughter, consult both your own will and her welfare. The Church of Worcester will comply with your admonitions, and we do not doubt that the lord bishop will obey according to your pleasure. May He who does not slumber, the guardian of Israel (Ps. 120), preserve your safety for long ages.

## LETTER XXIX. TO OSBERN

Brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, to his beloved son Osbern, wishes him “not to be afraid where there is no fear” (Ps. 52).

I urge you, dearest son, to build and plant, and to work and diligently cultivate your land with the plough which you know. It has produced enough thorns and thistles hitherto (Gen. 3); but, as you have begun well, if you apply yourself diligently to good labour and activity, I know, I know that the Lord will not deprive you of good fruit. I wish you to keep all the vessels of your house safe and clean, and to fortify and adorn your house with whatever clean and honourable furnishings you can. I also commend your strengthening the bars of your gates and surrounding your house with a good rampart and an impregnable wall, lest that people which, as you say, looks upon you with bristling brow and grim eyes, break into it and seize in one assault all your labours and sweat.

I do not wish you to have baggage for migration, nor to display in any respect the appearance of migration, but rather a purpose of stability in your land, which the Lord God has given you, and of long continuance there. You shall tell our Welsh friends that you will do absolutely nothing concerning what they have heard without consulting them. Yet we see that your people make light of the fear of the Lord and reverence for the sanctuary, while we hear that the Welsh diligently honour God, holy places, and persons consecrated to the Lord. For all these reasons it is hard for us that you should be joined more closely to those who scarcely care for you and torn away from those who honour you. Farewell; and know that we would rather you were stationary or advancing than retreating.

### Letter XXX. To Jocelin, Bishop of Salisbury

To his father and lord J., by the grace of God bishop of Salisbury, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: that he may administer, by the fitting moderation of reason, what has been entrusted to him.

Let your holiness know, beloved Father in Christ, that we have been unable to persuade our brother Bernard to receive his blessing either from you or elsewhere under any condition requiring the payment of money. Although this perhaps is not wrong, it nevertheless creates a scruple in a simple mind, lest the manner of his entry appear to him somewhat less than pure. Therefore we beseech your benevolence to bend for a little while the severity of your mind toward us; omit these conditions for recovering money, and, a little after granting the blessing simply, exact whatever you judge ought to be exacted. For my part, I bind myself fully to your holiness by the obligation of a surety, that after that blessing he will obediently, humbly, and devoutly perform whatever the Church adjudges concerning all these matters. If, after this blessing, he himself delays, nothing remains except that, in the house committed to him, he wait diligently for the will of the lord pope. Farewell.

### Letter XXXI. To Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury

To his father and lord T., by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: all that humble and ready devotion can offer.

Charity does not reject humility. Therefore, because we have seen William Cumin humbled, we have begun to dare to intercede for him with your highness. If, at the instigation of him who tempts, he departed from the unity of the Church, he now returns to it, recalled by the Holy Spirit, who gives life. Therefore we knock, with a pious boldness, at the throne of your mercy, that, if you know from the testimony of great and religious persons that he has made sufficient satisfaction for the fault into which he fell, you may not allow him to be kept suspended from communion.

The bishop of Worcester will not receive into communion, except through you, one whom he deprived of communion by your authority. We therefore ask the moderation of your mind that, since you rejoice that he has sighed from Ur of the Chaldeans toward Jerusalem (Gen. XV), you will not allow her gates to be shut against one wishing to enter—lest you send shamefully naked to the husks one to whom heavenly mercy has also granted sandals, a robe, and a ring.

### Letter XXXII. To R., Prior, and the Brothers of Cerne

To the beloved brothers in Christ, R., prior, and the rest at Cerne, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: wisely to attain, through service, the gift of grace.

The charity which you have shown and bestowed upon us for some time now toward us, and for long toward your house, moves us not to delay visiting you further by letters at least, since we have not yet been able to do so in bodily presence. Therefore, giving thanks in every respect to your holiness, we declare ourselves bound to you in every spiritual favour: for you have long begun to hope well of us, and, what is highest and most excellent among gifts, you have wished us to share in your progress and spiritual growth in the Lord.

For how abundantly in charity you extend your goodwill toward us may be understood from this: although throughout the whole world the Church of God shines far and wide with the bright praise of her merits and glorious titles, your concern nevertheless has been pleased to unite us to your Church by a certain closer bond of love, and to choose from it for yourselves a father and shepherd. We write this not as though glorying, either in ourselves or in our people, in the mitre or chair of your place, but as gratefully accepting in every way the unity of spirit established between us through a firm and indissoluble bond of charity and peace.

For when you had recourse to us concerning the matter pressing upon you, we indeed assisted you with unfeigned charity. From our own body we did not cast out and throw toward you something as though it were an injured or decaying limb; rather, although to our own loss, we granted you, with full affection, a part of our body that is sounder and more useful. For if you have desired, with as much love as we hope, that which is holy, honourable, sound in doctrine, and of good reputation, then in the adoption of a Father you have, beyond doubt, grounds both to give thanks to the Lord and to be bound to us by immeasurable gratitude. For you have a man in whom knowledge abounds for teaching and character for uprightness; you have one in whose life and conduct virtue will shine fully upon you; you have one whom, by humbly obeying, you will gloriously bring to completion the path of virtues which you have undertaken, by attaining the reward of virtue.

But perhaps there are among you some whom virtue has not yet fully drawn into desire for itself; indeed, as I hear with sorrow, there are some who despise the work of virtue the more hatefully in proportion as it is more laborious. There are also those who have shamelessly turned away from him whom we chose and whom you received as Father; they have now gone backward, no longer hearing his voice but following some stranger, I know not whom. Not only do they themselves refuse obedience, but, as report says, they endeavour by wicked attempts to uproot and cast him out.

Was our kindness to be repaid in this way? Did our ready willingness to serve you deserve this? Hear, dearest brothers, and heed with an ear of charity what we say out of charity. I fear, I fear, lest a judgment coming from on high should perhaps press upon you. You know that according to the merits of subjects both the life of rulers is ordered; and just as the Lord is holy with the holy, so also with the perverse he is deservedly found perverse (Ps. XVII). He orders things mercifully for the good; and to those who sigh for life he gives a Father and shepherd by whom they may be led and drawn to life.

Long ago the Israelites served Pharaoh and built cities for him with brick and clay; but when Egyptian servitude began to displease them, they cried out to the Lord and, with Moses leading, set out on a journey of three days (Exod.
