VIII). Those wishing to enter into life are deservedly granted a ruler through whom the entrance into life may be opened. I confidently declare: if the works of Pharaoh had still pleased the children of Israel and they had not cried out to the Lord, they would not yet have had a saviour. It is the rule of justice: “Let the righteous still be justified, and let the one who is filthy become still more filthy” (Rev. XXII). Thus those who are blind enough to demand to be led by a blind man receive heaven’s judgment, that they may fall together into the pit (Matt. XV).

We say this not because we distrust the greater and better part of you, but because we marvel and are indignant that you permit those who trouble you to rule and hold sway among you. I hear that Adelard—whom I do not call carnal, but flesh itself—has gone to Canterbury, perhaps intending from there to proceed to Rome. But what if he comes to Rome? The axle will feel the weight, and perhaps the curia will bend beneath so great a burden. This is an old complaint, and the conflict between flesh and spirit has raged violently from the very cradle of the Church. Long has the flesh desired against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. V). But we shall walk against the flesh and cut off the works of the flesh.

Let Master Adelard hear, take heed to the works of the flesh, and understand his own face. For the works of the flesh are fornication, uncleanness, shamelessness, lust, and such things (ibid.). Whoever follows such things shall have no communion with your fellow-soldier. Yet we say this not as though persecuting your brother in any respect, or even suspecting such things of him at last; we pursue vices, not persons. We speak harshly while ourselves wishing for better things. Perhaps he is deceived by an empty impression. He judges Rome to be like a reed that can be shaken by every wind. We know that truth can be obscured at Rome, but never, once recognized, rejected. That throne is justice; that seat judges equity. Nor is this a cause ashamed to come into the light. We have said nothing in the ear which we would not wish proclaimed from the housetops.

“We have entered in innocence, and, hoping in the Lord, we shall not be weakened” (Ps. XXV). We therefore ask you, beloved brothers, to strive for unanimity and peace; and, honouring your Father in all things as befits sons, to render him the reverence due to him and us the charity for which we hoped—not with lips only, but rather with the heart. You have one man: if you receive and honour him in your hearts, you will possess all of us entire in that one. But if you turn your face away from him, toward whatever quarter you may be driven by the spirit’s impulse, you will leave no one in doubt. We cannot fail our son and dearest brother; with all our effort we shall attempt to withstand your attacks together with him. He may indeed endure adversities, but he cannot bear them alone.

But may the Lord avert this: may the pleasant beginnings of your fellowship not have so bitter an end; and may he who is the beginning and the end bring your beginnings to a pleasant conclusion. And if you deem us worthy of your friendship, consider us also your friends and wholly well disposed toward you.

### Letter XXXIII. To Robert, Chancellor of the Holy Apostolic See

To his dearest master and lord, worthy of honour for his merits, Robert, chancellor of the holy apostolic see, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: due reverence and wholehearted affection.

My heart has rejoiced in the Lord, beloved Father in the Lord, and I have been filled with spiritual gladness, because the Lord has looked down from heaven, remembered your humility, granted grace for grace, and rewarded the moral integrity and refinement which you have hitherto worthily preserved with the fitting glory of his generosity. Invited to the wedding feast, you had chosen to occupy the lowest place; but it pleased the Father well in you that he himself should presently proclaim the Gospel saying, “Friend, go up higher” (Luke XIV), and should bestow upon you glory and honour before the other guests.

I indeed wondered and silently considered for whom the Lord had reserved his new things together with his old, since he had amassed in one person such accumulated marks of every excellence. And although the beauty of your life and sweetness of your teaching shone out to countless people and kindled in many a wonderful desire to imitate you, I nevertheless imagined something greater in my mind. I conceived, with a kind of certain hope, that such great light, although not hidden under a bushel (Luke XI), would bestow the benefits of its radiance upon the Church from some more eminent position.

I hold what I wished; I see what I hoped: so that I may now proclaim the great works of the Lord, “sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. CX). Of one from whom I could hope for great things, I have now deserved to see great things; and, since I do not doubt that you have loved justice and hated iniquity (Ps. XLIV), I applaud with all my heart that, in the council of the righteous and congregation of the saints, you lay down the laws of all equity beside the blessed and supreme pontiff.

For this reason we cannot sufficiently give thanks: you have gladdened our father of Canterbury and restored his Church to its former dignity, so that she who walked with a mutilated face now shines in full light—on this side with the glory of the archbishopric, on that with the honour of her customary primacy. And it was divinely arranged that mercy toward us should proceed from the fountain of justice through your promotion itself.

We ask for your benevolent and kindly favour always toward us; and, for reverence toward the Lord Jesus, we humbly entreat you to extend a hand of mercy to our Arnold and, strengthened by the help of your compassion, send him back joyfully to his own place. You know how unseemly and troublesome it is for a good cleric, long received amid public congratulations, now to labour by begging for assistance, and in the latest days of his life to be weighed down, unusually and contrary to custom, by hunger. I trust in my lord and dearest master that he will always open his heart to mercy and, in the necessity now pressing and the storm urgently threatening, assist both this man and the other clerics of the Church of Salisbury. May almighty God preserve my master and lord for long years, to benefit his Church.

### Letter XXXIV. To Simon, Bishop of Worcester

To his father and lord S., by the grace of God bishop of Worcester, brother G., called abbot: to fight the Lord’s battles with confidence.

What is public and widely known needs no proof by witnesses or arguments. Therefore, if we have had a ready will to serve you, I do not prove by arguments what I do not doubt that no one, or scarcely anyone, doubts. Indeed, if we have been unable to serve you in great matters, we have nevertheless made diligent efforts at least to stand beside you in lesser matters with supporting action. Therefore our humility, if you please, and the charity toward you which has continued until now deserved that your prudence should have pursued somewhat more carefully the case which we entrusted to your highness against H. and R. de Calder.

You know, and the testimony of many establishes, that the lord archbishop openly forbade you to absolve either of them unless ecclesiastical satisfaction were rendered to you. Yet you have not induced them, by any warning, to make satisfaction to us; nevertheless, you have absolved them. What follows from these facts is public and clearer than light. I shall say it—saving your peace and favour—I shall say that by this act you have rendered neither obedience to the lord archbishop, nor the friendship we hoped for to us, nor honour or reverence to your order and office.

These soft, lax, and excessively easy mercies bring your authority into contempt and reduce the justice entrusted to you to nothing. For an entire year we watched in the hope that, in an assembly of bishops, we might hold our wrongdoers bound by the bond of anathema. But how easily our labour vanished! Lord H. puffed out his cheeks and the trumpets sounded. At the single sound of that inflated spirit—what shall I say? The bishop was frightened: shame upon it, to fear his threats whose sword itself ought to have been despised! Since we have been injured so often, to whom shall we run for justice to be done us? Is it easy for us to travel around provinces, trouble the lord archbishop, summon a council, and seek from many what the favour of one man can again remit through some empty indulgence?

Indeed, since taking up this burden under which I labour, nothing has happened to me more distressing or bitter. I am likewise ashamed and repent that I ran uncertainly; I fought, but as one beating the air (1 Cor. IX). And after losses and labours alike, my enemies insult me; now utterly unrestrained, having obtained secure licence to sin, they imperiously provoke us to fresh injuries. We have therefore considered these things fit to be communicated to your knowledge, so that, however the matter has been conducted until now, you may, if possible, reform it by your counsel, that honour may be increased for you and some provision, if not complete provision, may be made for your cause.

### Letter XXXV. To G., Prior, and the Convent of Hereford

Brother G. to his beloved lovers, Guar., prior, and the brothers with him at Hereford: to bring a good beginning to a good completion.

I would more gladly have visited you in person than sent letters or messengers to you; but since multiplied affairs prevent what I would wish, receive our letter in the meantime in place of conversation, that from it you may judge what you ought to think of our charity toward you. Not every spirit is to be believed; for some spirits are not from God (1 John IV). Therefore, if an impious man, sowing tares over the field, tries to cloud the sincerity of our charity, discernment of spirits is necessary for us, so that we may not be carried about by every wind of doctrine or easily acquiesce in error (Eph. IV). Rather, always proving the better things, let us strengthen charity in Christ, in whom the anchor of our hope has been cast.

For we believe and hope in vain unless we love one another. Let us attend to the Apostle’s saying: “Charity never fails” (1 Cor. XIII): a brief phrase, but a fruitful judgment. Here it is plainly established either that we did not love in Christ, or that we did not lightly fall away from charity. One does not truly love in Christ who is easily moved to hatred.

### Letter XXXVI. To Pope Eugenius III

To his father and lord Eugenius, by the grace of God pontiff, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: to minister delights to kings in the beauty of virtues.

Since, beloved Father, the diligence of your charity exerts itself for the benefit of each individual, perhaps that which is diffused to countless persons in the immensity of its benefits is less held in admiration, and is restrained within the bounds of its own judgment by the narrow rule of humility. Yet how greatly the flood of divine grace has drenched your mind may be understood from this: the fragrant reputation of your virtue and holy name has already drawn not a few, from the uttermost ends of the earth, into a strong desire for you.

We know that many hasten to you with great eagerness of heart, so that each may now say and all may cry out: “Draw us after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song I). The lord A. [lacuna], bishop of Lincoln, ought to be received by your majesty with as much reverence as we know he is drawn toward you in charity. His household—men of proven religious character and grace—bear good testimony to his life; the more intimately they associate with him, the more they glory in the Lord over his uprightness.

We know also that the Lord has for some time touched him to some degree with the scourge of tribulation, so that whatever dross there was in him has now been fully refined; and that whatever, through a moderate excess, the wandering licence of the kingdom of England allowed for some time has now been removed from him, and he is proved perfect. We report what we believe to be true to a special friend of truth, that you may not be reluctant to receive your son into favour, to whom it is fitting to show honour and favour. May your highness prosper, beloved Father in Christ.

### Letter XXXVII. To J., the Legate

To his father and lord J., by the grace of God legate of the holy apostolic see, brother G.: greeting and wholehearted affection.

We sent the letters of your graciousness, beloved Father, to the bishop of Salisbury, that he might confirm with episcopal blessing the man whom you appointed abbot of Cerne. But he, postponing this until now—we do not know in what spirit or through what effort—multiplies vexations and devices against him, as we have heard from many, after your departure. Would that this may be far from your glory: that your praise should suffer so great a loss, that your planting should thus be uprooted and the work of your hands be destroyed to your dishonour.

Therefore we entreat your honour and glory that, by letters containing your command, you admonish the bishop of Salisbury not to delay his blessing beyond the day which you appoint for him. And, if he is a lover of true religion, let him not further delay, after being admonished a second time by your authority, to perform with grateful heart and most ready will that which he should already have done. We ask that your face may not be put to shame in your work, but that your glory may always increase, so that all may know: “This hand is yours, and you, Lord, have made it” (Ps. CVIII). May my lord and dearest Father prosper. As you commanded, I would already have come to you, had not repeated persecutions against us at this time kept me not merely hindered but most grievously fettered.

### Letter XXXVIII. To Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury

To his father and lord, the archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all England by the grace of God, T., brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: the joy of salvation and the service of obedience.

Even now that incubus of Cerne boldly occupies what is not his by right; and he who has been expelled from there begs at strangers’ thresholds because justice has failed him. The bishop of Salisbury perhaps pities the extreme poverty of the expelled abbot and the desolation of that Church itself, but no compassion of his assists either the needy abbot or the Church now collapsing. He devoutly receives the letters of your command, yet, for some lofty consideration I know not what, omits to obey your command.

We therefore seek from your fatherhood the justice which elsewhere we have not found: if it please you, excommunicate that Scot, disobedient toward you and manifestly contumacious and wicked, and place the Church itself under interdict so long as he remains in possession. If thereafter you command the earl of Gloucester to expel your excommunicate, we know that he will not delay obedience to us; indeed, by obeying without delay, he will prescribe a pattern of obedience to the lord of Salisbury. Farewell.

### Letter XXXIX. To the Same

To his father and lord, the archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all England by the grace of God, T., brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: fullness of salvation and joy.

Because love is strong as death (Song VIII), just as we cannot prejudice one person, so we cannot resist another. Therefore, beloved lord, what you wish I too must necessarily wish. But because those returning from you speak to me, some in one way and some in another, I ask that through this brother of ours you send me letters indicating your will, and that you enjoin, with the authority in which you preside and have power, whatever decision concerning me rests in your judgment.

For I am so disposed toward you, so bound to you by charity, that in whatever I learn I can obey and please your holiness, I count as light everything that the difficulty of the journey or the pressing authority of an opposing power can threaten me with. Moreover, Brother B., abbot of Cerne, has appealed to the apostolic see. Therefore, although all that belongs to him ought to be under the protection of the lord pope, it is nevertheless plundered by his persecutors no less now than before.

He therefore asks through me—and I ask that your fatherhood may be entreated concerning this also—that you take his Church under the protection of the lord pope and of yourselves, and entrust its care to Lord A., the archdeacon; so that he may provide this man with what is necessary for going to the lord pope, as circumstances require, and may diligently care for anyone whom he finds serving the Lord in that place. If it please you, inform us of the day of our journey. If you preferred it to be deferred until the feast of Saint Michael, perhaps you would have those who are to travel with us more prepared. Farewell.

### Letter XL. To Robert, Bishop of Lincoln

To the venerable lord and dearest brother Robert, by the grace of God bishop of Lincoln, G., minister of Hereford: the joys of peace and salvation.

This matter is of vital concern to me, and my eyes are turned toward you, that in this necessity you may fulfil my desire. The king’s anger against the abbot of Gloucester and the Church has been violently inflamed by the counsel of ill-wishers; and unless the abbot himself complies with his will within a short time, the king threatens to take for himself all the lands of that Church which are in his power and alienate them from the Church.

Therefore, with the confidence we place in you, we offer prayers to your benevolence, that you may “stand as a wall for the house of Israel” (Ezek. XIII), and, by mitigating the king’s anger, endeavour to reconcile the abbot and that Church to the lord king and settle this affair according to the Church’s means. You have been placed in this position by the Lord, that through you he may provide well for those below, and that what Gloucester cannot obtain through itself or through Hereford, it may obtain through Lincoln.

To explain your goodwill fully would require great prolixity of writing. But two things restrain my pen: the wise are taught with few words, and a friend is readily persuaded. May the Lord be at your right hand, so that in this matter and in all things you may strive to obtain favour.

A knight served for some time not God but Satan. For a whole month he served persons whom you had excommunicated, after he knew them to be excommunicated. Since we do not wish to absolve your excommunicate except through you, we ask that whatever justice decrees against him may be tempered mercifully by your intercession.

### Letter XLI. To Pope Eugenius

To his father and lord Eugenius, supreme pontiff by the grace of God, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: humble obedience and the service due from his office.

Although the greatly desolated face of the Churches of all England sighs toward you, beloved Father, there is one Church, that of Malmesbury, for which, unless assistance comes quickly, no consolation now remains except what is worst in adversity: that it was once prosperous. For, like a little sheep caught in the jaws of a wolf and finding no escape, it is hemmed in by the walls of a castle situated on its estate and in its very precincts, oppressed by its inhabitants; it has lost almost all its worldly resources, and groans that the religion and order which it cherished have altogether disappeared.

Hardly anything can now be added to its calamity: its place has been given over to utter desolation and its children to dispersal. Where the praise of God resounded from the time of the holy Father Aldhelm, there today an armed crowd of retainers and a troop of soldiers, most ready for every impiety into which it is hired, rages. Thus our beloved brother, Lord Peter, abbot of that Church, has only this choice: by the compassion of your counsel, either to have his Church rescued from the aforesaid assaults, or never to return to it at all.

If, according to the prophet’s voice, “the sword of the Lord has been sharpened; it has been polished, that it may shine” (Ezek. XXI), may it stand, we pray, in the hand that strikes and avenges the reproaches against the host of the God of Israel. Nothing could your charity show us more mercifully than to send someone into our parts who knows how to handle with fitting zeal the matters of God and of yourselves. May he who does not sleep, the guardian of Israel (Ps. CXX), preserve your welfare for long years, beloved Father in Christ.

### Letter XLII. To John de Cant.

To the diligent defender of apostolic majesty, Lord John de Cant., brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: if it please him, to keep his witticisms within the bounds of modesty in a praiseworthy manner.

I gladly hear that, in imitation of the Apostle, you are a more abundant and more perfect zealot for the traditions of the fathers than your fellow-countrymen; and I desire with ample charity that your good zeal may always receive increase. Nevertheless, if anything has been done or said by us which in any way concerns the lord pope, I do not wish you, brother, to be disturbed on that account; I do not wish the delicate peace of your Sabbath to be troubled thereby in any degree.

For we have appealed to the lord pope, and at his name the whole dispute has come to rest for us. We have publicly put forward the name of peace, and all things are peaceful for us in its warmth. Yet lest we seem to have assumed the name of thanks merely for our own advantage and to his injury, our messengers are already engaged in this very business: by our letters they will inform the lord pope what has been done by us and to what extent appeal has been made to him.

The bond of appeal which we have tied to him we have taken care not, as you suppose, to dissolve presumptuously ourselves, but to present to the lord pope, so that he may receive from your hand the means by which he may draw us away if he does not wish otherwise, or, if it rests in his judgment, send us back. For it will be glorious for us to appear before him if he commands, and safe to refrain from action if he permits. Therefore, “Not to us, not to us, but to his name he will give glory” (Ps. CXIII); and we shall obey his *disperio* (so printed) in whatever he wills.

Although I plainly approve your zeal, you nevertheless do not conform in this matter to the most discerning man of our age: you treat vague rumour as authority and regard knowledge based on opinion alone as certain. If we are weak in any respect, dearest brother, I did not expect you to investigate the weakness of our land. But perhaps this is his sword who came not to bring peace, but a sword (Matt. X).

Moreover, as to your added assertion, circulated at court, that I twice denied my Seneca to Master W., I advise you kindly to take care and act prudently in matters in which you bring accusations boldly. For with what face do you maintain that I denied twice what, written with prolonged labour, I am at this very moment delivering or sending to a lord and friend who requested it? You see, then, John, what vain exertions you have made and how without cause you have provoked a friend. If you drag him through an unjust court case, how will you not be condemned to reimburse me for my efforts and expenses, since you expose an innocent man to losses?

Therefore, lest you appear to have strained out a gnat and swallowed a camel (Matt. XXIII), forget for a little while, I ask, any negligence which may perhaps be mine, and turn yourself to great matters. For charity grows cold, scandals abound, and throughout the region of the Jordan shoots arise which it would bring glory to a judge to cut down with the apostolic sickle, and a crown to one who presses the action. Exercise yourself in these matters, I ask; occupy your talent in them; and grant the benefits of light to those for whom light is hateful. For in such matters favour may be bestowed upon you, and perhaps one will not be lacking in whose name you may be baptized.

Act, then, so as to be one whom we know to lack neither Jupiter’s brain nor Maingena’s *petasus* [winged cap]. We shall shortly hear the lord pope’s will, God granting it; and, should he command, we shall appear, or, should he release us, we shall give thanks. We wish you well—to yourself and to your friends—while things go well with you; or at least, that you may spare them.

### Letter XLIII. To Jocelin, Bishop of Salisbury

To his father and lord Jocelin, by the grace of God bishop of Salisbury, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: himself.

This, beloved Father, is what I intended in my frequent letters: that, in the matter between us, neither might my burden be increased nor your due honour and reverence diminished in any respect. But since what I feared has happened and the authority of an appeal now intervenes, I ask that you, if it please you, settle the affair concerning those things which pertain to you; and we shall do what we can with the lord archbishop toward withdrawal of the appeal.

Lord Bernard demands restoration of everything which he lost after he had announced to you his journey to the lord pope. He asks that the church of Simon Desberga be restored to him; that those monks through whom this dispute arose against him be sent to regular cloisters according to the lord archbishop’s command; and that at the church of Cerne, with your counsel and assistance, monastic religion worthy of the monks be restored according to the lord pope’s command.

Write back to us your wish concerning these matters. In those things which you kindly grant us, you will have us humble, obedient, and helpful. May your holiness prosper.

Know that the lord archbishop’s letters which are now sent to you were issued before the appeal was made.

### Letter XLIV. To Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury

To his father and lord, the archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all England by the grace of God, T., brother G., called abbot of Gloucester.

We waited, my lord, for peace, and it did not come; we sought good things, and behold, disturbance (Jer. 14). Brother John, a monk of Cernelia, was carrying your letters to the earl of Gloucester, as you yourselves [Col. 0777D] know, containing nothing except what concerned the peace and benefit of that same Church. When, therefore, having left Cernelia, he hastened to the earl carrying those letters, one of the sons of William the Scot, formerly abbot of Cernelia, meeting him with certain others in an ambush prepared for him, threw him from his horse and inflicted most severe blows upon him; leaving him half-dead, he withdrew to the thieves’ den at Cernelia. Nor is anyone in those parts allowed to doubt that Father Scot was the instigator, occasion, and instrument of this deed for his son Scot. Hence these matters too are manifest, already leading toward judgment. Moreover, the aforesaid William, openly rebellious against your authority and utterly rejecting ecclesiastical discipline, still hangs over the monastery of Cernelia [Col. 0778A] and usurps there for himself the plenitude of all power. And while throughout the whole island of Britain and the broad-spreading western isles the Church of God glories in obeying your authority, there is but one church at Cernelia which, lifting its heel against you, presumptuously cries: “What portion have we with David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” (3 Kings 12). These are alien sons, grown utterly old, always limping away from the good paths (Ps. 17). These sons of Belial establish as abbot whom they wish; when they wish, they expel one already established; when they wish, they recall one expelled; and they obey only whom they wish. And although, like utterly wretched beasts, they have long rotted in their own dung (Joel 1), and have for a long time [Col. 0778B] emitted abundantly from themselves the stench not only of incontinence but of every disgrace, there has been no righteous man to look upon them, nor any who sought, by recalling them to the way, to bring back their souls as gain.

Therefore may we see in your hand the prophetic rod, that is, the watchful rod; and may we rejoice that that place of filth and crimes—which we know has become obsolete not merely through being left uncorrected but through being wholly neglected—be purified, to the honour of God and of yourselves, to the adornment of God’s house and the reverence of the entire monastic order; that it be rescued from Ur of the Chaldeans (Gen. 15) and restored and repaired in a form worthy of religion. The form of restoration, if it please you, is this: if you pass a fitting sentence upon the perpetrators and accomplices of the aforesaid crime and announce it to the lord bishop of Salisbury; if you enjoin the earl of Gloucester, under obedience, [Col. 0778C] to remove the aforesaid Scot and, if it please you, commit him to our care and custody; if you command Robert of Arundel, his son Roger, and Robert of Nicole, under anathema, no longer to support the folly of that same Scot or, by occupying the lands of Cernelia, obstruct your Bernard; if you admonish William, the earl’s son, concerning this matter itself; if by a public document you grant your blessing to the helpers of Abbot Bernard and terrify his wrongdoers by a sentence of malediction; if you also stir up the zeal of the lord of Salisbury, that he may burn against such persons and, in restraining the obstinate, may not grow lukewarm in aiding Lord Bernard. For the holy anointing teaches you concerning all things.

## LETTER XLV. TO UCTRED, BISHOP OF LLANDAFF

[Col. 0778D]

To his father and lord Uctred, by God’s grace bishop of Llandaff, Brother G., called abbot of the church of Saint Peter at Gloucester, greeting and the filial affection due to a father.

We ask your goodwill and that moderation of spirit which we have so often experienced in you, that you may pursue this case, which you have now raised against our brothers concerning the body of the sister of Lord Maurice, in such a way as neither to lessen your charity toward us nor to attempt to contravene the privilege of the lord pope. For we hold a privilege, which at a suitable time we shall also present to you, by which apostolic authority grants us that we may receive for burial, without prejudice to anyone, the bodies of any free persons [Col. 0779A] who in their final will have granted themselves to burial in our places. We therefore ask your affection not to seek an occasion against us by which we might be prevented from serving you and grow cold in the charity which we have hitherto borne toward you. For we are ready to serve you as our lord at every place and time, provided only that we see the throne of your justice obey apostolic authority. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVI. TO THEOBALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

To his father and lord T., by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all England, Brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: may you devoutly will the things of God and [Col. 0779B] always fulfil them in deed.

My lord, we are compelled to entreat your highness on behalf of friends, though we are scarcely found worthy to be heard even for ourselves. Yet we choose rather to be reproved by a father for compassion than condemned by brothers for disregarded charity. Summoned to appear before your tribunal, the lord of Llandaff excuses himself on many grounds: on one side, the difficulty of the journey; on the other, suspected plots by his opponents; and, above all, he pleads bodily infirmity. But our brothers who have recently returned, whose faithfulness and truthfulness we do not doubt, testify concerning his illness. Therefore, from his bed of sickness, he also petitions through us that the hearing of the present cause be deferred until [Col. 0779C] your return, provided that the matter itself in controversy remain meanwhile in the undisturbed possession of the brothers of Goldclive. If in this matter you see that neither your majesty is diminished nor your brothers’ justice impeded, by granting this petition you would make us, as in all other matters, so also in this matter, wholly indebted to your favour. May God be glorified in you, and may the crown of your merit continually increase, beloved Father in the Lord Jesus Christ.

## LETTER XLVII. TO UCTRED, BISHOP OF LLANDAFF

To his father and venerable lord, Uctred, by God’s grace bishop of Llandaff, Brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, greeting and affection.

Although the clear evidence of your kindness toward us leaves no doubt, and although we do not equal the favour of your mind, yet in whatever we can we stand ready to serve you. We therefore send you the lord archbishop’s letters, that from them you may consider what must be done by you, and prudently carry out whatever you perceive ought to be done. For, as you wrote, it is necessary that you leave undisturbed to the monks of Goldclive, until the lord archbishop’s return, the possession concerning which you contend, and that in the meantime you keep peace with them in all other respects. By so doing, you will be able to have the judge favourable, and, when it becomes necessary to undertake the case, the business can be settled more advantageously. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVIII. TO THE PRIOR AND BROTHERS OF GOLDCLIVE

Brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, to his beloved brothers in Christ, the lord prior of Goldclive and the other brothers, greeting and affection.

The lord archbishop, carefully providing for your peace and quiet, notifies you through me that on this occasion you are not to pursue the case which you have against the lord of Llandaff. For it has pleased his serenity that the proceeding itself be deferred until the octave of Epiphany, or until his return thereafter, provided that the possession in controversy remains meanwhile in your undisturbed possession. For the lord of Llandaff, as he testifies in his own writing, likewise agrees to this and undertakes to keep peace with you in all respects in the meantime (Isa. 26). Farewell; and, giving thanks for his fatherly affection toward you, comply in every respect with his counsels.

## LETTER XLIX. TO SIMON, BISHOP OF WORCESTER

[Col. 0780B]

To his father and lord S., by God’s grace bishop of Worcester, Brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, greeting, and such service as charity may make possible.

Ralph of Worcester asks us to intercede for him with your highness. But in this matter we dare ask nothing except what we judge useful to your honour and to his salvation. For we know that “sin is not forgiven unless what has been taken away is restored.” But this is true of those who possess the means by which they can restore what they have taken. If perhaps those means are lacking, although what has been taken is not returned because it is impossible, pardon is nevertheless not denied to a contrite and humbled heart (Ps. 50). Therefore, if your discernment [Col. 0780C] recognizes this man as penitent, prudent dispensation ought indeed to be allowed for absolving him, so that what is lacking in restitution of what was taken may be made up by the severity of his penance. We therefore entreat your goodwill, so far as we may, remembering that you should not break the bruised reed or quench the smoking flax (Isa. 42); but, having received assurance that he will not return to his vomit, and having imposed penance, recall him in a spirit of gentleness, and, if possible, carry the wandering sheep back on your merciful shoulder to the Lord’s folds (Luke 15). Farewell.

## LETTER L. TO ROBERT, BISHOP OF HEREFORD

To his father and lord Robert, by God’s grace bishop of Hereford, Brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, the joy of salvation [Col. 0780D] and the service of obedience.

Urgent necessity compels us, concerning the business now in your hands, to seek letters of support from our lords and friends to the lord pope. We therefore ask your goodwill, in the charity which we trust in you, that you grant us letters to the lord pope giving testimony for our brother Bernard, abbot of Cerneleia, such as perhaps you have heard concerning him yourself or have been able to hear from religious brothers. For him whom we have known worthy of commendation both in learning and in life, we confidently request to be commended by the friends of truth in the very presence of the Bridegroom. And because he has a case against certain brothers of Cernelia, we ask that you add what is common report concerning his election and expulsion [Col. 0781A] and concerning the dissolution of the church of Cernelia, and whatever you know to be true and useful to our cause. We ask great things from a lord and friend whom we do not refuse to obey and serve even in great and difficult matters. Finally, beloved Father in Christ, we pray that you may fare well in God.

## LETTER LI. TO JOCELIN, BISHOP OF SALISBURY

To his father and lord J., bishop of Salisbury, Brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: not to be more angry with the wretched than is enough.

The style is humble and the subject lowly: to plead for one already dead, that, after he has acted sufficiently and the Father has at last shown mercy, he may somehow be called back to life. [Col. 0781B] With the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. 6), you have long since cut Alard off from life. Would that he had not deserved it—or, if he deserved it, would that he had found with you the means of making fitting satisfaction! Since this has not yet been done, we knock at the door not only of a friend but of a father and lord, that it may at last somehow be opened to us, and that our cry may be heard in the inner chamber, where, upon the bed of a good conscience, that same friend and lord delights and rests richly with his children, who are now purified souls. For we hope that, when we come back to you in our need, you will give neither a stone for bread, which is the harshest refusal; nor a serpent for a fish, which is a laborious and deceitful delay; nor lastly a scorpion for an egg (Luke 11). Far different gifts ought to shine [Col. 0781C] from a pontiff’s hand. There are some whose glory is—but not before God—to rejoice more at the downfall of the wretched than to glory in their restoration. He who runs to meet the returning man with an embrace counsels far otherwise.

We therefore ask you, most beloved in the Lord, that, forgetting injuries for a little while, that blood of yours—never in any respect degenerate—may return to itself, and that you may then deem yourself conquered when the conquered now entreat you. “Whom do you pursue, king of Israel? Whom do you pursue? A dead dog and a living flea” (1 Kings 24). If you intend in your heart to order matters belonging to the liberty of the Church; if you propose to surpass all others in redeeming our brothers and fellow bishops in their churches from the hands of laymen, so that laymen may not even be allowed to present persons to them: all this indeed is praiseworthy [Col. 0781D], so that religion may always be placed at the summit. But, I ask, do not exact so harshly from the least what has not yet been attempted among the greatest. You surely know how dangerous despair is. What if Abner should meet Asahel, pursuing without restraint, with a spear? (2 Kings 2:23). Take care lest the blood of both be required at your hand (Ezek. 3). The authority of custom and long usage is not trifling; and where there is no sin against God, it is tolerable that antiquity remain undisturbed in its roots. If you grant us what it is well known that all your fellow bishops grant to all their own people, who, I ask, will ever blame you?

I know to whom I speak: to a father and lord, whose inborn goodness of spirit persuades him to all that is praiseworthy. Whatever bitterness you may inflict upon Alard [Col. 0782A], let him at least be permitted to present a person who, in the church of Finchehamestude, will obey and comply in every respect with your commands. Farewell.

## LETTER LII. TO THE EMPRESS MATILDA

To the venerable and illustrious lady M., empress, daughter of King Henry, Brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: may you please the supreme King in the splendour of virtues.

Please hear with equanimity, if it please you, my answer concerning the matters on which your excellence has instructed me. Concerning the religious character of Lord Nivard, brother of our most beloved father, the lord abbot of Clairvaux, I am so certain that, if he had known more fully the things done between us and the men of Cernelia, he would not only have raised no [Col. 0782B] complaint against me, but would have wished the things done at equity’s prompting and by the lord pope’s decree to remain firm, and would have urged you to uphold them. For the monks of Cernelia, approaching the lord pope, asked that judges be appointed for them in England for the case which they were bringing against their abbot, and obtained four bishops for this purpose. Bringing the lord pope’s letters to these bishops, they were solemnly heard on the appointed day according to the tenor of those letters, and, failing in every respect, were condemned by public judgment. Furthermore, not only were they deprived of the priesthood, but they were also judged infamous for ever and committed, both by the lord pope’s writing and command, to the custody of regular cloisters. Therefore, since by the lord pope’s authority we have received some of them, we can neither, nor ought to, [Col. 0782C] release them except by the same authority. Let not your serenity, then, be troubled if we obey the apostolic command, from whose will we judge withdrawal to be a kind of sacrilege. But in matters in which we can and ought to comply, we are ready to comply with your commands. Yet where the authority of the Church is offended, we have a full excuse if we are required to do what we ought not. May your highness flourish for ever.

## LETTER LIII. TO JOCELIN, BISHOP OF SALISBURY

To his father and lord J., by God’s grace bishop of the Church of Salisbury, Brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, greeting and service.

The importunate persistence of lamenting Alard presses me [Col. 0782D] so that what perhaps ought to be denied to rashness cannot be denied to persistence. I therefore offer my prayers with customary confidence to your highness, asking that you soften, with the moderation proper to one consoling his children, the sentence which you have directed or have already pronounced against Adelard, so that you neither break the bruised reed nor quench the smoking flax (Matt. 12). Concerning the priest’s goods, which you rightly demand, if anything has not been restored, he will make full restoration under the assessment of an oath. If anything has in any way been presumed against your dignity, he will make fitting satisfaction to your mercy. Yet we humbly ask one thing: that you grant him, in the church of Finchamstude, what you have hitherto been accustomed to deny to none of your parishioners—namely, that he may present to you a suitable person whom you permit to minister in the aforesaid church.

It would indeed be just that, as the donation of churches, so also the presentation of persons should not belong to laymen. But what has not yet been introduced into custom in this kingdom ought not to be begun with the least, nor ought that to be exacted from lesser persons which cannot be forced from greater ones. If, therefore, you wish in any degree to tear antiquity up by its roots, the beginning must be made at the head, so that the Lord’s ointment, descending thence upon the beard, may also reach the hem of the garment (Ps. 132), and thus bathe the whole body of the Church all the better, the more widely it is diffused, in the sweetness of its fragrant perfume. I ask that my petition be granted on no other confidence than this: because you have always heard me when undeserving, hear me still, and hear one who is not ungrateful. Farewell.

## LETTER LIV. TO WILLIAM DE CHEISNEIA

[Col. 0783B]

G., by God’s grace abbot of Gloucester, to William de Cheisneia, greeting.

I thank you for all the good you have done me, hoping well of you, that you may always proceed from good things to better. For if you have answered me harshly at present, I can blame the necessity that presses you, but I cannot blame you. I know that friend would gladly spare friend, and uncle nephew, if pressing necessity permitted it. Indeed, this would be good for me, but much better for you. For if you assist us in temporal things, we do not withhold our spiritual goods from you. Every day among us all, remembrance of you is made there [Col. 0783C] where the Son is sacrificed to the Father. But perhaps you do not know what this is; or, if you know it well, you do not care. And pressing necessity does not allow you greatly to distinguish between friends and others.

Therefore we send you fifteen marks of silver, asking that, as we send them with good will, so you receive them with good will, lest, if you press too hard for payment, you lessen toward yourself the affection of those who are for you before the Lord. Remember that your life is a little smoke, and all your glory dust and worm. Today you are, and tomorrow you will not be; or, if you are tomorrow, you do not know whether you will be afterward. And when you depart from the body, you will carry away none of your glory with you. Your castles will remain here, and one who will give you no thanks will have them; perhaps [Col. 0783D] a stranger will glory in your labour. Only your sins will follow you, and it does not yet seem to you that you are sinner enough; but then you will wish that here you had sinned less. On that day, when you look upon misery and see against yourself the howling of widows, the groaning of the poor, the lament of orphans, and the complaints of churches, what will be your state of mind? To whom will you look? Which of all the saints have you not offended? Which of God’s poor around you have you not injured? Unless you provide for yourself while you can, your deeds will accuse you before God so vehemently that his justice will neither be able to endure you long in this life nor show you any mercy in the life to come. The Lord has warned you from nearby: he has taken your loved ones from your midst; his rod is already stretched out against you. May he himself open your heart and pour his grace into it, that before [Col. 0784A] your last day a good work may spring from you, through which the Lord may save you. Farewell.

## LETTER LV. TO F., ABBOT OF READING

To his most beloved father F., by God’s grace abbot of Reading, and to all the sons of the church of Reading, Brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, and those whose charge has been entrusted to his ministry, greeting and affection.

Most beloved, word has reached us that Master Serlo of Arundel repeatedly urges you, with entreaties, to make some agreement with him concerning the church of Berkeley and, by conceding to him certain things that have been mentioned between you, to hold that church henceforth. We also hear that he asserts he possesses certain things which he does not possess and, by displaying certain charters which he produces, leads you to believe the things which he affirms. We therefore forewarn your affection to assent to his statements in such a way that you do not incur, by some unconsidered exchange, damage which cannot easily be remedied. For be certain that we have been invested by apostolic authority with the church of Camme, the church of Herlingeham, [Col. 0784B] and all that belongs to it; and that neither by any exchange nor by any gift of Lord Serlo nor by anyone’s assent can you claim anything in them without doing us the gravest injury.

Moreover, know this also: our clerk Reginald has one prebend in the church of Berkeley and is subject to Serlo in no respect. Therefore, if [Col. 0784C] you make an exchange concerning a church in which he has a parsonage equal to Serlo’s, while he not only does not consent but actively objects, you will be doing what pleases you rather than anything consistent with law. For things of public right are counted among no one’s private property, and one person’s agreement cannot transfer ownership in a common matter. We do not wish you to be unaware that the aforesaid Reginald, last year, when Serlo pressed him concerning the things that he now claims from us, appealed to the lord pope, appeared in person on the appointed day, and, because Lord Serlo did not appear, returned home invested with them by the lord pope’s favour. Finally, not to pass over what is most important, I have no doubt that you are certain that holding a church by an unlawful agreement [Col. 0784D] is unlawful. We therefore earnestly offer prayers to your discernment that in this matter you regulate everything so that you neither bring reproach upon your religious profession nor easily diminish, for the sake of gain, the charity hitherto maintained between us. Farewell.

## LETTER LVI. TO UCTRED, BISHOP OF LLANDAFF

To his father and lord U., by God’s grace bishop of Llandaff, Brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: “because the days are evil, to bring strength to perfection in weakness” (2 Cor. 12).

Beloved Father, truth is my witness, as is the conscience that does not lie to me concerning myself, how with a pure heart and unfeigned charity (1 Tim. 1) I have loved you from the first time I knew you; and how, wherever I have been able, I have always been a helper and fellow-worker, with careful attention, for both your honour [Col. 0785A] and your advantage. Though this may perhaps not have reached you, it was not unknown to these men: namely, the lord of Canterbury, the lord pope, and those of his household. When I was present before them, if anything unfavourable concerning you was ever discussed, it was not only suppressed and laid to rest by my protest and vigorous resistance, but vanished altogether like a cloud of falsehood.

To confess the truth: even if we have not served you greatly, we have reconciled to you the hearts of powerful persons; and, not keeping silent about the good things we hope of you but declaring them openly, we have brought you into their favour—a favour neither small nor to be despised. For charity [Col. 0785B] never fails (1 Cor. 13), and indeed we do not fully know it even when it is perfect. Yet this is what readily persuades us to hope well of you in every respect and, in matters where your jurisdiction is necessary to us, to request equity and justice with some confidence. We therefore offer prayers to your highness that our hope in you may not be disappointed and that, as the letters attest, you may settle with such diligence the matter of the tithes which we justly demand from Lord Leofric that no burden be inflicted on us, to the detriment of our Church, by some shameful diminution; and that thanksgiving and the rendering of due honour may be returned to you as father and lord, not only by me but by our whole community. We do not reject the judgment [Col. 0785C] of an even balance; nevertheless, lest friends be offended, we would prefer the matter to be concluded by an honourable settlement. Farewell, beloved Father always in Christ the Lord.

## LETTER LVII. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord U., by God’s grace bishop of Llandaff, G., called abbot of Gloucester: may you please God by the right of your merits.

Beloved Father, I esteem it a welcome gift that by the reminder of your letter you summon me to virtue. For there is nothing which a father can either advise his son more usefully or commend to him more honourably. For virtue alone renders service worthy of the Lord of virtues, and, hating everything transitory, dares to desire eternal things. [Col. 0785D] Virtue raises minds aloft; fleeing all by which we are troubled in lower things, it seeks and finds its place in higher things. Its beauty is lovable and its form desirable (Ps. 45); “and,” as the Wise Man says, “if it were granted to be beheld fully by bodily eyes, it would awaken in all no small desires for itself.” Therefore I give thanks for your fatherly diligence, which has stirred my mind not a little toward the virtue which I commend.

For by carefully teaching and urging me to manage what has been entrusted to my care, you bring me to the bounds of prudence and form me in the fullness of that discernment which is most necessary in every office. Accordingly, if the brother whom I sent into those parts rendered too little reverence to your beloved goodwill, he certainly doubled the offence [Col. 0786A] against me, because he offended not only a bishop but a lord—indeed, a father most friendly to me in very many proven ways. I therefore ask you to receive him corrected and admonished, and, by forgiving us this injury, to increase your benefits toward us and not cease to crown grace added upon grace. As for the portion which you justly claim, I have commanded and command that it be restored to you in full; and I omit for the present certain matters to be communicated to you more secretly until the arrival of our clerk Ralph. Farewell.

## LETTER LVIII. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER

To his father and lord H., by God’s grace bishop of Winchester, Brother G., called abbot of the church of Saint Peter at Gloucester: by devout compassion to merit mercy.

[Col. 0786B]

Charity compels me humbly to implore your serenity, beloved Father in Christ, that you command a certain knight named Roger Foliot, whom your men hold imprisoned at Merendune, to be sent out for ransom by your favour and at our request. In this matter, trusting in your highness, I devoutly ask that you admit neither the evasions nor the superfluous words of William de Cheisnei, nor permit Roger to be burdened according to William’s will, nor give credence concerning him to the words of those who hate him. For let your holiness know that Roger’s father never possessed more than half a hide of land, while he himself had absolutely nothing except what he acquired through the practice of knighthood. He has until now served Lord Brientius for a gift; and now, by losing his horses and arms, he has lost everything he had at once and altogether. We therefore ask that your eyes look upon the poor man (Ps. 10), and that, by bringing the bound man out of prison (Ps. 67), you may obtain favour from him who frees the fettered (Ps. 146), and may count me as indebted to your favour in whatever I can do. Farewell.

## LETTER LIX. TO GEOFFREY, PRIOR OF WINCHESTER

G., by God’s grace abbot of Gloucester, to his venerable lord and dearest friend Geoffrey, prior of Winchester, greeting and affection.

I have many thanks to render to your goodwill, because you have kindly assisted my kinsman Roger Foliot [Col. 0786D] and generously provided for him in his needs. But since, among friends, the performance of past good deeds is a sure expectation of future ones, we ask that your charity may not grow cold, so that our humility may serve you in this matter. We therefore ask you to intercede for him with the lord of Winchester, that he may cause him to be brought out of prison and command him to be sent for ransom. For he is held in prison disgracefully and is now distressed by extreme poverty. I therefore earnestly ask that you attend to the present affair, so that you may count us indebted to your favour in whatever we can do. Farewell.

## LETTER LX. TO ……………… BISHOP

“I rejoiced in the things that were said to me” (Ps. [Col. 0787A] 121); recently, through widespread report, I have learned of you. I hear that a bishop has conceived thoughts worthy of a bishop and has resisted with a spirit of holiness unlawful presumption. A judgment had at some point gone forth that Christ’s Bride should be reduced under tribute. But in you pastoral concern has awakened, so that what has been presumptuously conceived may by no means be carried into effect. You rebuke, entreat, reprove (2 Tim. 4), and defend; and those whom you cannot heal by soothing treatment, you do not fear to cure by the iron of excision. A breast indeed worthy of commendation, which offers favour to the meek and discipline to the obstinate. When divine authority places manna with the rod in the sanctuary, it thus instructs the fullness of a pastor: that from the breast he may supply all sweetness from the good things of grace, and restrain obstinacy by discipline.

I indeed rejoice that you have clearly observed the pastoral [Col. 0787B] rule and that you have carried out, as became a bishop, with no less courage than prudence what you knew ought to be done. Indeed, in the very work of virtue the whole of virtue shines out to me. For prudence is to know what is fitting; justice, to render to each what is due; courage, not to fear man because he is flesh, and in the strength of the Spirit to dare all that is holy. It belongs to temperance that nothing has been done from anger or from the impulse of a stirred-up will, but that, solely from the love of virtue, you have blazed with the fire of the Spirit to avenge the injuries of the supreme King. Therefore act with confidence. Farewell.

## LETTER LXI. TO UCTRED, BISHOP OF LLANDAFF

To his father and lord U., by God’s grace [Col. 0787C] bishop of Llandaff, Brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, greeting.

I have become importunate, but you compelled me; I asked, but did not receive; I knocked, but you have not yet opened to me. Yet I hope that a father, at last opening affectionately to his knocking friend (Luke 11), will offer not a stone to one asking bread, nor a serpent to one asking fish or an egg, nor a scorpion (ibid.). We ask peace from a son of peace, a father and lord, and a friend proven by many experiences. It will not be a happy day for me when, even under necessity’s compulsion, I must stand in judgment against you. Let the bishop, therefore, do what is worthy of a bishop, and, if any dispute or controversy has arisen among his children, bring all things back to a state of peace. [Col. 0787D] We demand from Lord Leofric the tithes with which our church was endowed and of which it has been despoiled without judgment. It is a more grievous loss to forfeit what manifest justice demands back. In other matters we shall defer to your good pleasure, according to what Lord Jocelin has told you. Let this concern keep watch over the affection of a father and shepherd, so that from his children it may receive both favour and service in fitting measure. Farewell.

## LETTER LXII. TO JOCELIN, BISHOP OF SALISBURY

To his father and lord J., by God’s grace bishop of Salisbury, Brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, and the humble convent of the church of Saint Peter: such small thing as they are, and such services of devotion as they can offer.

Our complaint, beloved lord, was long ago brought to you [Col. 0788A]. Though compassion has not yet aided it, our humility nevertheless does not despair of your goodwill. Therefore, heavily oppressed and afflicted, we have recourse to you again, asking help for our troubles and aid for our losses. For because we have complained to you, we are afflicted more than usual; and because they think we have gained little or nothing by our complaint, armed by their very impunity, they regard us as abandoned and boast that all things are permitted to them against us, as though some licence had been granted them by you. We therefore humbly ask—I, though I am little, and all our brothers, who indeed are much—that you do not, if it please you, make light of our injuries, but honour your ministry as is fitting by rendering us justice, and count us indebted to your favour in whatever we can [Col. 0788B] do. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIII. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord J., by God’s grace bishop of Salisbury, Brother G., called abbot of the church of Saint Peter: not to deny pardon to the penitent.

“The just man is the first accuser of himself in the opening of his speech.” Therefore, because I desire to conform myself to justice, I first accuse myself. For so far as lay in me, I diminished in some measure both your majesty and my own honour when I did not meet your humility and gentleness, as you came to meet me, with a most welcome embrace and a most humble heart. Yet why I delayed, if it were granted me to enjoy speech with you, I would communicate better by speaking than by writing. If, therefore, there remain in any respect any remnants of your former charity toward us [Col. 0788C], if according to the Lord’s command the episcopal breast is not closed to the penitent (Ezek. 33), I ask that, when my journey is soon directed to the lord archbishop, I may not be denied an opportunity to speak with you.

Since I recently went beyond bounds by setting for you the place and day of the meeting, I, presumptuously at fault, do so no longer but commit the whole matter to your will. Kindly write back to me, if it please you, mindful sparingly of anger, what your judgment determines concerning this. Three days before you must come to the appointed place, you shall again have my messenger. If you appoint Abingdon or Reading as the place, you will spare me very much labour. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIV. TO ROBERT, BISHOP OF HEREFORD

[Col. 0788D]

To his father and lord R., by God’s grace bishop of Hereford, Brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: may you prosper ever more happily, day by day, in grace.

To the synod which, dear Father, you are holding, I had myself set out; but the letter of the lord bishop of Worcester compelled us, by the command of obedience and charity, to await him at Gloucester on this very Monday. Therefore, since we cannot do so at present, we petition your holiness, dear to us, in writing, that you render us justice against the Welshmen—those of Herchenefeld, Idel, and Chenedin—and their accomplices. For they avenge their wrongs upon us, though undeserving; and although I have harmed them in no respect, they have inflicted upon us damage exceeding sixty marks, and in a single attack and raid have carried off everything which we had long laboured over at Brantonia. [Col. 0789A] We hope that you will weigh our losses and injuries, and that you will not deny to your sons’ just petition the assistance which you withhold from none who justly asks it. We further make known to your holiness that your clerk Gunni of Stantuna, being at the point of death, seeks from you, as father and shepherd of his soul, the aid of your holy prayers, so that, fortified by your intercession, he may await the Lord’s mercy with greater assurance as he is now about to depart.

The disposition of his goods is this, to which he himself subscribed in the presence of the undersigned witnesses. Whatever grain there is in his house, he grants to his servants and to those to whom he is bound by any debt. Of all the rest he bequeathed one third to you, [Col. 0789B] and assigned the remaining two thirds to our church, in which he received the monastic habit. The witnesses to this his last will are Nicholas the sacrist, Grimpater, and Walter. And because nothing is more due to humanity than that the wording of a last will should be free, and that a choice from which there is no return should be lawful, he humbly asks that you confirm by your authority what he has done out of a regard for piety; or, should it seem otherwise to you, that his will shall not prejudice yours. Farewell.

## LETTER LXV. FROM SIMON, BISHOP OF WORCESTER, TO ALL THE CHILDREN OF HOLY MOTHER CHURCH

Simon, by God’s grace bishop of Worcester, to all his beloved brethren in Christ, children of holy mother Church, perpetual salvation in the Lord.

For the more secure establishment of the Church’s peace in this matter, we make known to your diligence that we have at last settled, with the assent of both parties, the dispute recently arisen in our presence between our sons, namely the monks of Gloucester and the canons of Llanthony, concerning the body of the lord Miles, earl of Hereford. The dispute, conducted over two days, was settled on the following terms. The canons relinquished freely and without disturbance the body itself—which the monks asserted, with many witnesses, ought to be buried in their church—making no claim whatsoever of right, both by parochial right and by the free gift which the earl himself had made of his person to their church before he gave himself to the church of Llanthony. [Col. 0789C–D] The monks, at the request of our venerable brother Robert, bishop of Hereford, of ourselves, of Lord Roger the earl’s son, and of many barons and knights, granted that the body should be committed to burial in the church of Llanthony, to which it had been brought.

Yet this was on the condition that they granted to the church of St Peter, freely, peaceably, and without any claim, Lord Robert the earl’s son and his wife, all their heirs for ever, and the lord of Gloucester Castle, whoever he might at any time be. To confirm this act, I, Simon bishop of Worcester, receiving Lord Robert the earl’s son by the hand through the hand of our son Gilbert, abbot of Gloucester, attached him and his successors to the church of St Peter; and by episcopal authority ordained that, wherever in the world they should die, they were to be buried and interred in that church. [Col. 0790A] Farewell.

## LETTER LXVI. TO SIMON, BISHOP OF WORCESTER

To his father and lord S., by God’s grace bishop of Worcester, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester, and the humble convent of the church of St Peter: greeting and obedience.

What things, lord, we have long endured from Lord William de Beauchamp, you will learn more fully from the account of our brethren. For, passing over what is past, it is not long since we lost through him forty-three loads of thoroughly cleaned wheat which were being brought for the use of our brethren; and, deceived by hope of the promised peace, we have hitherto delayed recovering them. Moreover, for a long time we have been compelled to pay three shillings each month for the maintenance of his servants, and at each of the two sowings to plough and sow sixty acres of his land, and to reap it for him. [Col. 0790B] Besides this, there are innumerable daily services of labour, by which he does not cease to oppress, pursue, and afflict our men unto utter misery; and the greater the patience we show toward him, the less he fears to do against us and all our property whatever he pleases as though by right.

Behold, his latest wrongdoing burns fresh: this week, as his fasts were beginning well, he broke into our houses, threshed out and carried away the grain, and promises worse hereafter. Therefore we lay petitions before your highness, [Col. 0790C] that you restrain this audacity of his and delay no longer in rendering us justice. For, so far as our will is concerned, justice against him shall be delayed no longer unless he restores, not by promise but in deed, what has been taken from us, and henceforth renounces these unjust exactions throughout all the land of St Peter. Having been summoned three times in our church on this coming Sunday, he shall, with your permission, be excommunicated. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVII. TO JOCELIN, BISHOP OF SALISBURY

To his father and lord J., by God’s grace bishop of Salisbury, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: may he please the Lord in the meditation of his heart and the utterance of his mouth.

[Col. 0790D] Since you have written well, we ask that you also act well, completing in deed the assistance which you promise us in word. That incubus of Cerne occupies with audacity what belongs to another’s right; having been violently expelled from there, he begs at others’ thresholds solely because justice has failed. Therefore, prostrate at the knees of your holiness, we humbly entreat that your charity may pity and relieve both our troubles and the Church’s extreme desolation, and that zeal for your justice—whose integrity we do not suspect—may be kindled against one who is obstinate, disobedient, and rebellious.

You have no excuse against our petitions. For you can do what we ask, and ought to do it. Therefore pronounce against him and his accomplices, who manifestly deserve it, the sentence of anathema, and do not keep our souls [Col. 0791A] in suspense any longer. We send you the letters of the lord archbishop; unless you obey him fully, only one person remains for us to approach concerning this failure of justice. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVIII. TO BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX

To Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, the Lord’s most faithful helper, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: may I, if only it may be so, be made a participant in your prayers.

It is fitting among the children of light that, if anything of night should intervene, it should, when the brightness shines forth more fully, not merely disappear but rather vanish altogether. Therefore we make known to your serenity what is almost beyond doubt among us, lest in matters we know the truth should be allowed to be obscured in your presence.

[Col. 0791B] We know that William, formerly abbot of Tintern, received from William de Berkeley, advocate of the place, the site of Kingswood, which no monk had yet inhabited, with the assent of the governing powers—namely the Empress and Miles of Gloucester—and without anyone’s objection; that he built there, established at that place a community from the house of Tintern itself, and, once the community had been established, appointed as abbot there Thomas, formerly prior of Tintern, from that same house of his. Then, in the course of time, the said William, abbot of Tintern, having associated with himself our most dear brother Hamo, abbot of Bordesley, presented the said Thomas to the lord bishop of Worcester and obtained his blessing as abbot; and thereafter he provided for and assisted him in many matters as a son, and for Kingswood as though it were an only daughter. [Col. 0791C]

Since it is free for anyone to renounce his own right, let the church of Tintern see whether it has renounced its right, cast away what it held, and alienated from itself what it had received. It is of age; let it speak for itself. We have taken care to disclose to you what is well known among us and, so to speak, on everyone’s lips. May almighty God preserve you, beloved father in Christ, in health for many years, for the benefit of his own.

## LETTER LXIX. TO THEOBALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

To his father and lord, the archbishop of Canterbury by God’s grace and primate of all England, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: may he serve delicacies to kings with the richest bread.

I consider it, lord, an act of duty to communicate to you everything that brings you to my mind or suggests you to my soul. Therefore we have sent this bearer to you, so that by a letter sent through him you may inform us both of your condition and of your wishes. Our circumstances are as follows. Very many people harass us and disturb not only our church but all the churches around us with multiplied oppressive demands. If we strike them with the sword, they find that Malchus’s ear, when the Lord stretches out his hand, is quickly healed [Matthew 26], and, unafraid of this, continue to sin. [Col. 0791D–0792A] Therefore letters from you to the lord bishop of Worcester and the lord bishop of Hereford are necessary to us, that they may watch over the protection of our church and, whenever we happen to be absent, may more readily extend to it the hand of counsel and aid.

We are equipped for the journey and, God consenting, shall be ready to attend at your command. Very many things oppose us, but love knows no obstacles whatever. May your highness flourish for many years, beloved father in Christ.

## LETTER LXX. FROM SIMON, BISHOP OF WORCESTER, TO HIS PARISHIONERS

Simon, by God’s grace bishop of Worcester, to all his beloved sons and parishioners in the Lord: greeting, blessing, and grace.

Since we are frequently occupied by many and great affairs and cannot attend, as we should wish, to each person’s needs, we have granted, in the benevolent charity of our authority, to our beloved brother G., abbot of Gloucester, [Col. 0792B] that if any person in our bishopric should grant to him and his church any church or ecclesiastical benefice—provided, however, that no violence or injury is inflicted on another person or church—then, even though we are absent, he shall not fail to accept what is granted to him by a pious gift. Yet he is to approach our archdeacon, or, if he should be absent, our dean who presides in those parts, and receive investiture through his hand. Since we wish this to be known to you and binding upon him, we have taken care to notify you and to confirm it to him by this present writing. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXI. TO UCHTRED, BISHOP OF LLANDAFF

[Col. 0792C] To his father and lord U., by God’s grace bishop of Llandaff, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: greeting.

Since obedience is compared to a command, we make known to your excellence, dear to us, by this present writing that, just as we have not hitherto ordered our clerk Ralph to bring any unjust claim against Tewkesbury, so now, if he is found obstinate in his injustice, we in so far as concerns us ratify that course to some extent. For since the precepts of law are these—to live honourably, to harm no one else, and to render to each his own—just as we wish what belongs to our right to remain unharmed to us, so we desire that what belongs to others should suffer no injury or loss through our action.

I do not wish your fatherhood to be unaware [Col. 0792D] that the lord abbot of Tewkesbury, wishing to satisfy me, remitted to me for one year, for three shillings, the tithe from the land of R. Foliot—the tithe, I say, which the aforesaid R. claimed belonged by right to the church of Llancarfan. I therefore wish it plainly known to your prudence that in this manner investiture in that tithe has devolved upon him. Wherefore I earnestly and urgently entreat your charity not, on account of me or of the aforesaid R., to burden the said abbot in any respect concerning this matter, nor to permit him to be burdened. I do not wish to seek after or possess what belongs to another, contrary to justice and the decrees of the Fathers, because I ought not. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXII. TO R., BISHOP OF EXETER

To his father and lord R., by God’s grace bishop of Exeter, [Col. 0793A] brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: the joy of salvation and the service of obedience.

Your discretion well knows, lord, how great reverence is owed to apostolic majesty and what obedience to its commands; for your knowledge abounds no less in instruction than your character in honourableness and every grace. We therefore address prayers to your serenity, that the persuasion of the men of Cerne may not turn you aside from obeying the lord pope.

The day appointed for hearing the cause of Lord Bernard, abbot, and the monks of Cerne is at hand: namely, the Sunday after the Ascension of the Lord. On that day all the others will be present at Bath, to whom, together with you, cognizance of this same cause has been delegated by the lord pope. Therefore, if you should be absent, [Col. 0793B] the said monks will be given an opportunity to evade judgment if they see any of the appointed judges absent. For us, this would be not merely a continuation but a repetition of labour, and an accumulated multiplication of burdens. Let your discretion therefore take care, if it please you, that your absence may not be a detriment to our cause and add to our exertions. For by a single appearance you will obey the lord pope and make us, your humble friends, debtors to you for a greater favour. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIII. TO POPE EUGENIUS

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff, brother G., called abbot: would that his days be good and his blessed times long.

[Col. 0793C] Beloved father, we make known to your highness a matter which, with the Lord’s help and your favouring grace in this affair, we trust will benefit the Church’s need. For while we were staying during the days of exile with your son, our lord and most dear father, the lord of Canterbury—having, as it were, no fixed seat or proper place, but moving from place to place through the necessity of affairs—we arrived at Arras in July. There, with extraordinary desire and with the concordant wishes of almost the entire clergy and people, we found the election of our beloved brother Hugh, archdeacon of that same church of Arras.

We have known him from his earliest age through almost all our life: first as a disciple of upright conduct; afterwards as a master, sufficiently well known through his authority; then received amid public rejoicing; and finally as archdeacon of the church of Arras. We know that he has continually maintained an unblemished reputation for good character, and we confidently testify this in the present letter; nor do we doubt that the testimonies of many religious persons concur. [Col. 0793D] Therefore, insofar as our smallness dares presume before your majesty, dear to us and ever to be honoured, we ask that you look with that kindness—by which it has been granted to you to surpass all others—upon him whom the Lord has regarded in his humility; and that, through the authority given you by the Lord, you may reward virtue in him, so that through the example of one man you may direct very many toward love of religion and the cultivation of virtue. May the Lord surround you with his impregnable wall and ever protect you with the arms of his power, beloved father in him. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIV. TO ROBERT, BISHOP OF HEREFORD

[Col. 0794A]

To his father and lord R., by God’s grace bishop of Hereford, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: greeting and obedience.

We would gladly report to you the greeting of the lord pope, the congratulations of the whole curia, and also certain private remarks of some of his own people, setting complaint aside; but at present the severity of these wrongs compels us to complain, so that, after enduring much, we may at least lay a tardy complaint before your justice. The excessively harsh power of Lord Badoron and his wife rages against us; and although we have harmed them in no respect, through breakings, beatings, imprisonment of our men, [Col. 0794B] and seizure of goods, we are compelled by manifold servitude to pay for what we did not take. Since these matters are manifest and are now proceeding to judgment, we ask, if it please you, that you render us justice concerning them, and by rendering it protect them from sin and us from injury. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXV. TO HIENARD, JOHN, AND THE CHAPTER OF ST DAVID’S

Brother G., by God’s grace called abbot of Gloucester, to his friends Hienard, sacrist of the church of St David, Master John, and the whole chapter: greeting and affection.

We hope your prudence does not fail to know that a mandate ends, by the nature of a mandate, with the death of the mandator. Therefore, if any mandate was imposed by your lord and father, Bishop Bernard of good memory, concerning the case which is being litigated between us and the monks of Cerne concerning the church of St Ishmael, it is evident that, while the matter still remained intact, it expired with the death of that bishop.
