[Col. 0794C] Therefore, although no necessity compels us to come to you about this matter, yet our will urges it and friendship counsels it: do not decline to judge this same cause, if it has been entrusted to you alone or belongs to your office.

But because we are wearied by a journey recently completed and are occupied with the lord pope’s business—matters not merely great but many—we ask that, out of reverence for him, you permit us and our affairs to remain in peace for the present and defer the present action until a bishop is appointed in your church. Farewell, and do not fail to hear a friend making a just request. [Col. 0794D]

## LETTER LXXVI. TO ROBERT, ARCHDEACON OF LINCOLN

To his most dear Robert, archdeacon of Lincoln, his own G.: true prosperity, strong and enduring through time.

The hearing of our cause has been postponed until the lord of York arrives in England, by the counsel of the lord of Clairvaux and at the wish of the lord pope. Therefore, with everything remaining intact, we have returned together, safe and cheerful, the Lord helping us well in all things. We shall answer before the lord of York, in the presence and court of the lord king, on the fortieth day after his arrival, if it please him.

The bishops of Durham, Worcester, Bath, Exeter, [Col. 0795A] and especially Winchester, have been suspended from every episcopal office; perhaps they will obtain favour later through good messengers. The lord of Canterbury, many other bishops, and all of us petitioned for the lord of Winchester, but were heard in no respect whatever. Yet Earl Theobald hopes to obtain, by the urgency of the bishop’s messengers, what we could do less effectively.

Concerning matters pertaining to your church, the lord pope, wholly refusing to yield in any respect to the lord of Winchester, granted the fullness of authority for advising your church to the lord of Canterbury, so that in all matters pertaining to this, you are to obey the lord of Canterbury as the lord pope. Robert Foliot, having already obtained the lord pope’s letters on these matters before our departure, will bring them to you. Act, therefore, with confidence. For whatever would please the lord of Winchester more in this matter will in every way displease the lord pope. The lord pope has driven out the man of Fécamp, the man of Hulme, and the man of Westminster; he has now rejected them with great indignation and severity. [Col. 0795B; note: Col. 0795D: “The passage is obscure.”] Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVII. TO ROBERT, BISHOP OF BATH

To the venerable lord and most dear brother Robert, by God’s grace bishop of Bath, brother G., called abbot of Gloucester: greeting.

Since your favour precedes us in many matters, our services rightly offer and present themselves to you. For whatever we are, know, or can do, we desire that we may be, know, and be able for your honour. Therefore, with a ready and willing mind, we inform you of what we hope will benefit your advantage and honour. [Col. 0795C] The lord pope has entrusted and committed to the lord of Canterbury the power, in accordance with the arrangement made between them, to release not only abbots but also bishops of this land from the apostolic sentence by which they are bound.

In this we trust that provision has been made for you by the Lord, so that you need not undergo the hazards of sea, mountains, and foreign lands: an appropriate remedy hastens to you in the very arrival of the lord archbishop, the Lord thus ordaining. Charity has prompted us to judge this worthy of being reported to your affection, so that you may make provision accordingly and, if it please you, report it to the lord bishop of Exeter, our lord and most dear friend. [Col. 0795D] Farewell; and I ask that you count and regard me among your friends.

## LETTER LXXVIII. TO THE CANONS OF THE CHURCH OF HEREFORD

G., by God’s grace abbot and, by the command of the lord pope, vicar of the church of Hereford, to his beloved brethren, all the canons of the church of Hereford: greeting and affection.

Since, dearest brethren, we cannot recall the earl of Hereford—warned once, twice, and a third time—from the error of his most wicked way, this alone remains to us: that we restrain his audacity by ecclesiastical justice. Therefore, by the authority of the lord pope and the lord of Canterbury, we command you that, immediately upon receiving our letter, you cease from divine offices, except baptism, confession, and viaticum; and, because daughters ought not rejoice while their mother mourns, we command you to proclaim the same sentence throughout your whole parish and ensure that it is firmly observed. [Col. 0796A] Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIX. TO BRIENT, SON OF THE EARL

To his lord and most dear friend Brient, son of the earl, brother G., called abbot of St Peter’s, Gloucester: may he not be deprived of the fruit of justice as he runs well.

Some are drawn into amazement because, although you have not learned letters, you have nevertheless published a book. But know that this was no miracle to me, since I have learned that the force of love has in some measure dictated within you what skill in the art denied you. For love accepts neither consolation from impossibility nor remedy from difficulty. If it is genuine, it always performs great things; or, if it refuses to act, it is not love. Hence, though you have not learned letters, you have nevertheless charged no feebly into the field of letters. [Col. 0796B]

May the memory, worthy of honour, of the holy King Henry remain fixed in your mind—Henry whose good days and once golden age the nation of his bereft country mourns, and whose memory the rust of the present age commemorates frequently but sorrowfully. You have not forgotten that he advanced you from boyhood, reared you as a young man, and, having given you the knightly belt, enlarged you with gifts and honours. Yet this is why he made you mindful of himself and why he lives in recent memory with you: because the greatly desolated face of all England recognizes that, with the repeated flood of miseries, he has died to her.

From him your filial love extends to the royal line—to his only daughter and heir of his kingdom. Her cause you uphold and defend not only by arms but, as we have heard and now seen, by the grace and truth alike of your eloquence. [Col. 0796C] For you embrace in a brief argument all that may draw those hitherto ignorant of the truth to favour her party and may either confirm those long aware of the truth, if they are friends, or blunt them so as to free them again, if they are enemies.

Yet do not commend the woman of whom you speak to anyone’s injury. You maintain that what belonged to King Henry is owed by right to his only daughter, born in lawful marriage. Every rule of law seems suited to support what you maintain. For there is divine law, natural law, and human law.

By divine law we have heard the Lord in the Gospel, when his mother said to him, “Son, why have you thus dealt with us?” answer: “Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be occupied in my Father’s affairs?” [Luke 2]. Great is the Lord in compassion toward his handmaid, and great is the heavenly inheritance compared with a temporal and passing one. Yet the Lord speaks as though no one ought to doubt that what belongs to the father is owed by natural right to his son. But the man who misses no opportunity, when one is offered, to carp at your words will contend that the person of whom we speak is not a son but a daughter, and that royal sceptres, which belong more properly to a son, ought not be assigned to a daughter. [Col. 0796D–0797A]

Let us hear what divine law answers to this. In the last chapter of the Book of Numbers you will find something concerning it. Zelophehad was a Jewish man of the tribe of Manasseh; he had daughters only and no son. Some thought that, because of the weakness of their sex, they ought not be admitted to their father’s goods. When consulted on this point, the Lord promulgated a law that everything held by their father should pass whole and undivided to the daughters of Zelophehad [Numbers 36]. Let those who wish go on and set their mouths against heaven, and, if they please, devise snares against the stars. For us, what has been established by eternal law shall remain fixed.

But if you examine natural law, you will find no small support and strength for this cause. Natural law is that which nature has taught all animals, not merely human beings: accordingly, each according to its kind forms a certain affection for itself, propagates offspring, and loves and preserves those propagated. If you ask yourself, from the tenor of this law, what is nearer to nature in such matters, you will rightly answer that what is nearer to nature for each is that toward which natural affection draws it more strongly. [Col. 0797B]

But I want you to state it more plainly: each person’s affection is drawn more strongly toward that which is begotten from the same, as it were, participation in flesh and blood. Consider, therefore, whether you will separate human beings from nature, or concede that the same must hold in them by natural right. From father and mother, the first descent is to son or daughter. Place a grandson—or any other degree in the line of blood. Already love weakens and affection grows cool, while blood itself, as it were, has lost heat through its longer course. Therefore toward son and daughter alike love is more ardent, affection more prompt, and nature more compelling.

But you will say that all we have said about natural law concerns the quality of an inward disposition, not succession to possessions. It is not so. For whom you judge nearest by nature, it remains that you should consider less alien from that person what is possessed. See what nature teaches you thoroughly. Fish inhabit the stretches of sea and bays of shores into which natural birth poured them. Wild beasts do not leave the glades in which they were reared. [Col. 0797C] Birds fill with their own music the woods in which they were born; and in each case nature not only instils a deeply rooted affection of disposition, but grants, by whatever right it can, to its successive offspring the outward possessions which it holds. See that you do not drive nature out from yourself; wisely acquiesce in its judgment. Pronounce, on unshakable grounds, the worthy offspring of King Henry—his only daughter, brought forth and reared under the laws—to be heir of that king.

This is urged by divine law; this by natural law; this is affirmed by the sanction of human law. For human law is called partly civil law and partly the law of nations. Civil law is what each city has established for itself to be observed. The law of nations is what not one city but every nation has judged should be observed. Both civil law and the law of nations have carefully decreed that no head of household may disinherit or repudiate a son or daughter born in lawful marriage, except where certain causes intervene. [Col. 0797D–0798A] Such causes are these: if someone has laid hands upon his father; or, by manifest indications, wished for his death; or has proved ungrateful for benefits; and other such cases, when these faults intervene, the law permits even children to be disinherited.

But you will find none of these in the present case. For when was she, whose cause you press with such anxious concern, rebellious to her father? When ungrateful for his benefits? We have heard that, by her father’s counsel, she ventured upon seas, crossed the Alps, entered unknown lands, and there married at her father’s command; and that she remained honourably and piously for a long time at the very summit of affairs and height of empire, until, after her husband’s death, she returned to her father—not because necessity pressed, nor lightly driven by an impulse of feminine will, but because the father who had sent her recalled her.

And though, as has been said, she had remained at that summit of affairs, so that she was both called and was empress of the Roman world, she was in no way lifted up with pride. Instead, she was subject to her father’s will at every nod; and, again by his counsel, she contracted a second marriage, marrying a man strong and valiant, as we have heard—the lord of the Angevins, the people of Le Mans, and the Tourangeaux, and then, as we have heard, the most illustrious conqueror of the Normans. [Col. 0798B] In all these matters which have been mentioned, you will find no reason why she ought to have been disinherited or repudiated by her father.

Indeed, she was not repudiated; rather, by a pious and prudent counsel, she was established in dominion over all England and Normandy, confirmed by the oath of all the bishops and nobles of this kingdom. For among those who, as it is said, were accustomed to be summoned by name to her father’s appointed council, absolutely no one remained who did not promise her under the sacred obligation of an oath his counsel for obtaining and preserving, after the king’s death, the kingdom of England and the duchy of Normandy.

O times worthy of silence! I am ashamed to recall the name of our common disgrace—what should I call disgrace? Each man swore what he ought, yet quickly and lightly departed from what had been sworn solemnly. Who has made England foolish? Whoever he is, I call him a wretched head, upon whom so many perjuries, murders, burnings, crimes, desolations, and scandals flow back. When shall he be safe, who has defiled the kingdom, polluted the priesthood, and inflicted a grievous disgrace not only upon the present age but upon future posterity? [Col. 0798C–D] Truly, an inheritance which is hastened after in the beginning will lack blessing in the end.

Who now could recount England’s calamities? Ancient history records that, after Alexander’s death, his boys placed diadems upon themselves and began to reign, each in his own place, and evils were multiplied in the lands. So—yes, so—they are multiplied today as well. I lament to the ears of a friend what I feel. We endure as many kings as we are oppressed by marriages. We serve in mud and brick, and have only the shadow of liberty; now doing nothing freely, but serving those who have risen today as though we obeyed voluntarily. For:

[lacuna] endurance becomes lighter.

Whatever may not lawfully be corrected [Col. 0799A]. And what will be the end of misery? I shall say what I think. So long as the abomination stands, desolation cannot be lacking. God has been grievously offended, and the whole world fights on His behalf against the senseless. Let the order of things be recalled to justice; good beginnings will be followed by a praiseworthy end. Among the other things which you said, this too was commendably stated. He does not go wholly to ruin who turns back midway from an evil path. You have indeed turned back—not merely turned back, but been converted. You heard that the multitude had sinned, and for a time you followed the rush of the multitude. You sinned more with your mouth than with your heart. Whatever you promised with your mouth, you kept faith with your heart. The children of Israel at one time were mingled among the nations; they learned their works and served their graven images (Ps. 105). You likewise, when the multitude was rushing headlong [Col. 0799B], did not withstand its first assaults. Nor did you uselessly and vainly cast your arms against the torrent. Having found an opportunity, you showed by deed what you cherished in your heart; but he who pursues you with envious malice may perhaps bring against you the accusation of a double perjury. To have sworn falsely once is evil; to have repeated perjury is far worse. Thus you departed from justice more by being twice perjured than once. What if you had stood with the king? You would indeed have committed perjury once, but would not have repeated it, and therefore would have acted better. Do not let this empty husk frighten you. You promised fidelity to one man, and fidelity to another: first to him to whom you owed it, afterward to him to whom you did not owe it. You would not have sworn falsely the first time, had you not gone astray the second. You withdrew from this error, and thus healed everything. You escaped these snares, though perhaps you will fall into others. The king’s election is alleged against you, so that the Church may lawfully reject you, because you despise its institutions and scorn its sacraments. But will sacraments lead you to justice? Let sacred things accomplish their own effects. Let them sanctify us rather than turn us from a purpose of holiness; let them justify those cleansed from sin, rather than plunge into hell those entangled in crime, bound hand and foot. The sacrament is wrongly relied upon if through it guilt is not released but liability increased. In our judgment, there is nothing here by which the Church may justly press you, provided that an impartial judge examines this cause. Unless perhaps she blushes because you, as though a guide, showed her the path by which she ought to go [Col. 0799C].

Yet I want you to consider what I heard hurled forth more vehemently on this side [Col. 0799D]. Not long ago you heard that Pope Innocent convened the Church and held a notable assembly at Rome. I too was present at that great gathering with our lord and father, the lord Abbot of Cluny—the least of the Cluniacs. There this case was brought forward and debated for some time. The Bishop of Angers stood for the Empress; and when he had set forth her case in a careful speech, a public proclamation was cried out against it, as it were in the voice of a herald. Since the Bishop of Angers advanced especially two grounds—the hereditary right and the oath sworn to the Empress—the response to these two points was in these words:

“In all cases which rest upon a plurality of rights, one must consider especially [Col. 0800A] what is the principal right in the case, upon which the case itself chiefly rests, and what is secondary and dependent upon that principal right. For when the principal right is removed, the secondary is necessarily removed. In this case, then, the principal point is that which the Bishop of Angers advances concerning inheritance, and upon this depends all that is added concerning the oath. For he declares that the oath was sworn to the Empress as heiress. Therefore all that is advanced concerning the oath must necessarily be emptied of force if the hereditary right itself is not established. This right, however, is refuted as follows. We declare that the Empress of whom he speaks was not born of lawful marriage. King Henry departed from the lawful path and married a woman whom he was not permitted to marry; from that union her birth sprang [Col. 0800B]. Therefore sacred law declares that she ought not to succeed her father as heir.”

This was shouted out in the public hearing of many, and absolutely nothing was answered from the other side. I ask you to answer me on this point. Meanwhile, I shall state what I think. I have often consulted elders, religious and holy persons, about this matter. I hear that the marriage union in question was solemnized with Saint Anselm, Archbishop, officiating. I dare call him nothing other than a saint. For when a certain brother doubted whether he ought to be called a saint, this revelation was divinely granted to him. While he was praying and was carried away from prayer into an ecstasy of mind, a book was put into his hands; turning its first pages, he found nothing written except “Saint Anselm” [Col. 0800C]. And when he ran through every other page, he found nothing except “Saint Anselm.” Hence it is certain that the Godhead is not pleased for him to be called otherwise than saint. It is certain that he lacked no part of that perfect charity which casts out fear (1 John 4). For we have heard a remarkable testimony concerning him from holy persons: he would have allowed his hands to be cut off rather than stretch them out to an unlawful deed. Far, then, be it from the understanding of good people—let it be erased from every heart—that anything but what was lawful and holy should be believed to have been done by so wise a king and so holy a bishop. Nor let such a mockery ever again strike Roman ears, since by the testimony of all good people it is known to be false.

But concerning the mother of the Empress herself [Col. 0800D], we have learned from the report of certain holy persons that from her very cradle she was marked out for royal dignity by a divinely displayed oracle. For when Queen Matilda, wife of King William, lifted her from the sacred font, the little girl put out her hand, seized the veil lying over the queen’s head, and wrapped her own head in it. Some persons still living, reflecting more deeply upon this and interpreting the sign that had been shown beforehand, plainly foretold the royal dignity to which she was afterward raised.

The letter has run to length because we have touched upon a great subject, though we have not fully explained it. You stirred me by the words which you sent to me through your knight; and when I had begun to run, the very memory of you increased my spurs, so that I could scarcely tear myself away from the little work [Col. 0801A] which brought your memory before me, but have almost extended myself to the reader’s weariness. Therefore, hold fast at the end that you may remember the end, and exercise the charity of a kindly mind toward the Church of God and her poor. Remember your mother, who is plundered and trampled by all, and who finds most hostile enemies in those whom in the days of her distress she ought to have found most beloved sons. Let not your zeal be kindled against her because in the present case she did not use the freedom of speech she ought to have used, since the authority of the presiding officer not only hindered her but, as though binding her in chains, made her in this very matter immovable. But now, God being propitious and Pope Celestine favoring this side, the bonds will be loosed; those who were mute will speak. Farewell. And pray for me for at least two days [Col. 0801B], because for two days my prayer has been interrupted while I dictated this letter to you.

## LETTER LXXX. TO NIGEL, BISHOP OF ELY

To the venerable lord and dearest brother N., by God’s grace Bishop of Ely, Brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford: “So run that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9).

The rarer virtue and learning are, the more precious they are; and since we see very few indeed devoting themselves to learning and virtue, we ought to judge those zealous for them worthy of fuller reverence. For this reason we most earnestly commend Master Robert of Clare to your goodwill, since both his uprightness of life and the brilliance of his learning have long been known to us [Col. 0801C]. We ask, so far as we can avail with you, that you preserve by your protection unharmed and undisturbed the church which he holds under your guardianship. For, if it please you, you will easily crush everything alleged by those who have long since made a settlement with him concerning that possession. For it is most certain that one must abide both by a matter adjudged and by a settlement. Before a judge I do not presume to perform the office of instructor; rather, from the outset I make the appeal of a petitioner. I ask for a friend; but if I ask before a friend, I shall confess it if I deserve to obtain my request.

## LETTER LXXXI. TO RALPH, DEAN OF HEREFORD

The Venerable Father Gilbert, Bishop of Hereford [Col. 0801D], sent this letter to Lord Ralph, Dean of Hereford.

Though far from you, we experience not from afar the insults offered to you, with the very sword of transfixing grief by which we know you have been wounded. The hand of the persecutor has been directed against you, but it inflicts one wound upon all whom the care of unfeigned charity had bound to you. You are driven as an exile and fugitive from your church and city; and, as though you had violated every sacred thing, a knight forsworn sharpens swords against you, though he has nothing to allege except that you resisted his audacity in holiness and justice. You did resist, and we rejoice; you have been expelled, and we grieve. We grieve, I say, more over the shame of those rushing upon you than over the honor and glory of your praise. For we know that against that venal mob, most ready for every impiety for which a price is agreed [Col. 0802A], wrath is revealed from heaven; but glory is reserved forever for your humility and patience.

Rejoice, my beloved; rejoice and consider. Consider, I say, with what pious devotion the whole company of good people follows you, while you bear in your body the marks of Christ Jesus, while you carry His cross, while you contend in the struggle for justice and the freedom of the Church. You did not enter the Lord’s battles as a delicate soldier. Bare feet, a woolen garment, and the banner of the cross in the hands of the highest King set forth your armor. What we have hitherto sung, we now see in you: that saying of the supreme confessor, “Protected by the sign of the cross, not by shield or helmet, I shall safely penetrate the ranks of enemies.” This is Christ’s sword and His pilgrim’s staff, by which He crushed brazen gates [Col. 0802B] and broke iron bars (Ps. 107). You too, by wise counsel, have scattered your enemies with the horn of the cross and, with the nobility of a great heart, have despised those rising against you (Ps. 44). Everything I hear about you resounds with joyful victory: though unarmed, you have nevertheless escaped the snares of plotters, swift and spirited. You have indeed been expelled from your church, but how joyfully the holy Church, your mother, comes out to meet you! From the hem of her garment, to which you fittingly clung, she raises you up; she opens her bosom to you; gathers you within, holds you, caresses you, and nourishes you (Eph. 5). You are torn for a time from the embraces of your bride, but are cherished in your mother’s lap.

Yet the worst men mock you because you have left both house and city. You have indeed gone out [Col. 0802C]; but consider the days of old. Did not David, fleeing from his son, bear with moderation the man who mocked him and said: “Go out, man of blood; go out” (2 Sam. 16)? Though your persons differ, I judge you alike in the cause. Let us use examples close to home. You know that the Lord went out from Pilate into mockery, crowned with thorns and clothed in purple (Matt. 27). At last, too, as though He were refuse by which the city might be polluted, He suffered outside the gate (Heb. 13), enduring the final outrage so that the world might suffer outrage no longer. We ought to arm ourselves with this thought: following Him outside the camp, we must always bear His reproach upon our heads (ibid.). Blessed is your departure, by which you are named among the company of saints. But they reproach you because you fled. Yet you did not flee; you reserved yourself to fight more fiercely for justice.

Paul nevertheless escaped from Damascus by being let down in a basket, and in writing this he does not blush but rather glories in that very thing (2 Cor. 11) [Col. 0802D]. For if he had not fled, he would not have confounded the raging beast of the world or planted the Lord’s banner upon the very summit of empire. The good Master teaches us: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 10). Flee therefore, my beloved, in obedience to this command; flee from Ur of the Chaldeans into Jerusalem (Gen. 15), so that the Church may have someone for whom to fight, someone to reserve for herself for the time of the enemy and of war. You will yet stand as a son for your mother, perhaps when Leviathan rises more fiercely against her. Already you have filled us with a sweet odor, and by the strength of your constancy the Church gives forth a good fragrance, because you disdained to abase yourself before a prince [Col. 0803A] and bend the knee before Baal. The confessor is offered a choice: either renounce what he had done holily, or yield what he possessed. Temporal reward becomes worthless in your eyes, and suddenly made poor, with what serenity of mind you sing: “But I am needy and poor; the Lord has helped me” (Ps. 70). We too sing Davidic hymns, but what we sing you read fulfilled in yourself; and your more fully elaborated and sacred book of conscience presents to you the praiseworthy deeds of the saints which we extol.

Run through the psalms; let those instruments, filled with the sweetness of the Holy Spirit, resound from your mouth. Whatever praiseworthy thing is sung in them concerning piety, justice, or courage, you possess wholly in yourself. Truly you are the blessed philosopher who has laid up his goods where not even the hand of a greedy robber can snatch them away. Long ago, when we were in the schools, we heard various discussions about poverty of spirit. Now let it answer you at close hand, as one which has gone out with you from the threshold of your house and accompanied you on the road, that it may be more richly consulted concerning the promise of the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0803B].

For how slight is that which they allege against you? They oppose the apostolic saying: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers; and he who resists authority resists the ordinance of God” (Rom. 13). This is true indeed. But secular power has a law by which it is bound; it has fixed limits within which obedience is owed to it—namely, if it keeps the law, observes the commandments, and does not rashly presume anything against God. But if it shamelessly exceeds those limits to the injury of the highest King, it cannot use the privilege of Him whose laws it despises. As for what remains, they labor at the tasks of prudence and discernment. Prudent men, they say, are not inflamed with their whole zeal over slight faults; but if sin is committed deeply, all fervor should blaze forth. Thus they say that a slight offense by a prince—some portion of a wall having been torn down—ought to be punished more mildly. These points are neatly arranged. But according to Wisdom, “He who despises small things shall gradually fall.” I pass over the extent of the hard-hearted audacity which not only treats holy places lightly, but lays them waste. I hasten to those considerations which will not merely fail to accuse you, a lover of virtue, but will powerfully excuse you. I consider it a great proof of virtue to choke the budding shoots of vices at their birth. Once the serpent has put in its head, its whole body easily slips in. Considering this, you resisted the first assaults [Col. 0803D]. Why should you not? Had you not resisted, perhaps the madness once begun would by now have climbed to the summit of the temple. But you rose up in opposition and set yourself as a wall for the wall of the house of Israel.

From the smallest things one may infer great ones. What if it had fallen to your lot to contend for the faith and for the sacraments of the Church—would you stand firm at the cross as Peter’s companion, and at the sword as Paul’s? Let an attendant go forth; let him meet you with drawn dagger, bent on your death. If he strikes the sacred body, you will be received victorious into heaven; if he spares you, your glory is no less. Therefore you shall continually be honored among us with the praise of good people. For you have adorned our times with the merits of virtues; you have reformed us for the better by your example; you have recalled manly strength and the constancy of martyrs into an age grown lukewarm. A striker was lacking to you, not virtue. Therefore you shall live illustrious in the glory [Col. 0804A] which you have deserved. You shall live, I say—but blessed are you who resolved to die for justice.

## LETTER LXXXII. TO HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK

To his father and lord H., by God’s grace Archbishop of York, Brother G., called Bishop of Hereford: the affection of one who loves sincerely, and the office of one who obeys gratefully.

Charity is sometimes presumptuous: what it would readily grant if asked by another, it does not despair of obtaining from a lord and friend. Trusting greatly, therefore, in that charity which rules within your heart, we offer petitions to your highness, that you show yourself gracious and merciful to our common friend and your canon Gilbert, precentor of your church; and that, if anything has been committed against you by any of his people without his knowledge or wish, you do not lay the guilt of that deed upon your clerk and, so far as possible, your friend [Col. 0804B]. For he loves both you and those who love you; and if any of his household opposes you or exalts himself against you, whoever he may be, Gilbert is ready to disown and remove him. If, therefore, you restored to him what had been taken away through another’s fault rather than his own, you would not depart from the bounds of justice; and you would make both the Earl of Hereford and us, who together supplicate your excellency for him, debtors to you for greater favor. Nevertheless, in accordance with his own custom, we both ask pardon, that he may not feel in this matter the pricks of your severity, in which not merely difficulty of will but impossibility itself prevents him. With the Lord’s help, and with provision for the safety of his journey, he will soon come to you, most gladly ready in all things to obey you as father and lord. Farewell; do not turn your face away from the petition of your friends; and, lest it be necessary to ask often for a friend, appoint Christmas Day for the date of his arrival.

## LETTER LXXXIII. TO THEOBALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

To his father and lord, the Archbishop of Canterbury by God’s grace and primate of all England, T., his own G., minister of the Church of Hereford: not to fail in tribulation.

I have waited and waited long for my lord [Col. 0804D], hoping that some messenger would be sent from your highness to report to me good or adverse news—whether to make me sad by adverse tidings or glad by joyful ones. For if charity is so complete that one ought to be weak with any brother who is weak, or burn when anyone is caused to stumble, then when we see our father and lord—indeed, our head in Christ—shaken, wearied, and troubled, what remains except not merely to be weak or burn, but to be consumed to the very marrow within by the inmost flame of zeal? If, then, the Lord has not yet risen to command the winds and sea, if your storm has not yet been calmed into a settled breeze, it seems to me most necessary that every armor of the strong should fortify your sacred breast, and that the more fiercely the enemy rises, the more fiery and fervent in the Holy Spirit he may find you [Col. 0805A].

For it is neither new nor unusual that Egyptians harass Israel and Chaldeans Jerusalem. Christ says through the Apostle: “All who desire to live godly lives in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3). But through that same Apostle He says: “What is light and momentary in our tribulation works in us beyond measure an eternal weight of glory” (2 Cor. 4). To one who suffers persecution for justice, not something slight but the kingdom of heaven is promised. Elijah wraps himself in his cloak while avoiding the rage of persecutors, and, standing in the cave of the enemy, beholds the glory of the Lord (3 Kings 19). To you also is promised the crown of glory which the righteous Judge will render to you on that day (2 Tim. 4). I have grown impatient with myself, desiring to see and speak with you, or to hear something from you by which I might be made more certain concerning the things that surround you [Col. 0805B]. Our princes are ready; our churches too are at hand, if need be, not only to receive you but gladly to come forth to meet you in their embrace and to provide from their own resources whatever they can. I would not wish this; but, if it is necessary, you will find them kindly disposed and prepared for everything. I beseech you, dear Father, do not deny me your letters, and disclose in some measure your will, condition, and counsel. We pray that you may flourish in the Lord and please Him in all things.

## LETTER LXXXIV. TO POPE EUGENIUS

[Col. 0805C]

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff Eugenius by God’s grace, G., minister of the Church of Hereford: humble and due obedience, and a son’s love toward his father.

Since, dear Father, a portion of God’s Church has been entrusted to our smallness, by the Lord’s working, the stewardship entrusted to us by the Lord itself compels us to provide for and watch over its welfare. But because the acts established by us are less firm unless supported by apostolic authority, we humbly and devoutly offer petitions to your highness, asking that your authority ratify and your privilege confirm what we have done, for God’s honor and the increase of His worship, concerning the church of Saint Guthlac at Hereford. At length, and with much labor, we rescued that church from lay control; and because the Lord was served there less fittingly, we granted it to our beloved son Hamelin, Abbot of Gloucester, and to the church of Saint Peter, over which he is known to preside, with the assent of the clergy of the same church and with the consent and desire of our chapter [Col. 0805D]. We have also taken care to unite it, together with the church of Saint Peter at Hereford, long previously held by the aforesaid monks, into one body; and we have now restored there a convent of monks devoutly ministering to the Lord. Because we believe this pleases the Lord, we dare to beseech your serenity that what we have done with right intention and solely in view of piety, you may establish and confirm forever to the church of Saint Peter at Gloucester. May God be glorified in you [Col. 0806A], and may the crown of your merit ever increase in the Lord, Father beloved in Christ.

## LETTER LXXXV. TO JOHN OF DINAN

Gilbert, by God’s grace Bishop of Hereford, to his friend J. of Dinan: greeting and affection.

Listen, dearest friend, to what I command you, and do not disdain to comply with my admonitions if they are from God. You have good testimony from many that you have hitherto held God and His Church in great reverence, and have diligently honored clerics and men of every religious order. You have not oppressed the poor who are subject to your service, but have rather cherished them with a fatherly affection and kept them unharmed. God has looked upon this justice and goodness of heart of yours [Col. 0806B], and, having now shown you some mercy, will show you greater mercy in the future. I hear from many that certain persons have conspired against you and, while you were unaware and absent, have prepared certain very evil things to your detriment. But the Lord, it is said, scattered and exposed their counsel; and He likewise kept you unharmed, since you had kept Him unharmed in His members. Do not, dearest friend, attribute this to yourself; rather give thanks to Him.

If, therefore, you have wickedly laid hands upon His Church and its ecclesiastical goods at Stantune, I admonish you, by His authority and by the office enjoined upon us by Him, to restore before the synod everything belonging to that Church, leaving it unimpaired in every respect, lest you fall from the grace I have spoken of through a grave separation. For know certainly, and hold this final point firmly [Col. 0806C]: ecclesiastical property cannot be pledged to any mortal by anyone’s suretyship unless the bishop is present and consenting. The pledge which you took, without my knowledge, in the ecclesiastical goods stolen from R. is not binding upon you, but is decreed free from every legal force. May almighty God keep you obedient to our admonitions.

## LETTER LXXXVI. TO RO. OF BURNHAM

Gilbert, by God’s grace Bishop of Hereford, to his friend Ro. of Burnham: greeting and affection.

The greater the charity with which we are disposed toward you, the more we are admonished by that same charity to make provision, insofar as concerns us, both for you and for your reputation [Col. 0806D]. From your own words and from the report of many, we have learned that you wish to withdraw from the settlement made between us concerning the church of Wiredesberia, and to defraud the church of Gloucester of the annual payment publicly promised to it by you. In this matter I warn you to consider the outcome of actions, lest, if you act otherwise, repentance may follow wrongdoing. For although this case does not principally concern us, it does concern us secondarily. In lawsuits the plaintiff holds the first place, the witness the second. If, therefore, I am produced as a witness in this cause, I cannot fail the church to which I am bound by the whole fullness of charity in bearing witness to the truth. Very many religious men also stood with us in the same settlement [Col. 0807A]; if you begin to deny anything, they will bring the acts to light. Reconsider, therefore, if you please, your plan; faithfully observe what, faith having intervened, you agreed in the presence of many. Otherwise, if you should begin to stray, convicted by the testimony of many, you will incur danger not only to your ecclesiastical benefice but also to your order. Bearing in mind the saying of the Wise Man, “The rebuke of a friend is better than the kisses of a flattering enemy” (Prov. 27), I have set harsh words before a friend whom I have sought to recall from what is harmful and dishonorable to him. Farewell, and in every temporal advantage put honor first.

## LETTER LXXXVII. TO POPE EUGENIUS

[Col. 0807B]

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff Eugenius, G., minister of the Church of Hereford: with Satan trampled beneath your holy feet, may you always triumph in the Lord.

As it pleased my lord, so it was done: at your command the hand of consecration was laid upon me, and the care of the Church of Hereford was entrusted to me. Hence our eyes look more intently toward you, hoping and awaiting from your highness that assistance through which we received an increase of honor and rank. Our Church cries out and complains that our predecessor, Lord Robert, bishop of good memory, transferred four of its prebends to the church of Lantony, and, through the excessive love by which he was bound toward Lantony, in order to enlarge them, despoiled his own clerics of those four prebends [Col. 0807C]. We therefore humbly beseech your serenity: if the aforesaid men of Lantony approach your majesty, do not confirm by your authority what our clerics complain was unjustly taken from them. That same predecessor also granted two castles of our Church to the most noble men, the Count of Meulan and Hugh of Mortemer, to the grave inconvenience and loss of that Church. Since they were improperly alienated and, so far as concerns us, have been alienated almost beyond recovery, we ask that they be recalled by your authority.

As for what concerns the Church of Lincoln, we speak and testify confidently, as those who have heard and seen. For the clergy and people of that Church, together with a considerable number of religious persons of the same diocese, unanimously elected Lord Robert, Archdeacon of the same Church, as their bishop, no one at all dissenting [Col. 0807D]. Presenting the election to the Archbishop of Canterbury, they obtained it for many necessary reasons. We ask that this be reinforced by your judgment, so that, by extending to him the hand of favor, you may have him steadfast in the office in which he has been placed, a faithful son henceforth and most ready for every will of his father. May your majesty be preserved whole and unharmed for ages, Father beloved in Christ.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff Eugenius [Col. 0808A], G., minister of the Church of Hereford: the devoted and due service of all obedience.

Because it is highly fitting, dear Father, to obey charity, we cannot refuse the request of the Church of Lincoln, but must make known to your highness what we ourselves, being present, saw and heard concerning its affair. For when we were in London with our father, the lord Archbishop of Canterbury, and very many of our brethren and fellow bishops, we saw the dean, cantor, and archdeacon—all the canons likewise of that Church of Lincoln—with no small multitude of religious persons from the same diocese, all urgently persisting in seeking leave, by the counsel of the Archbishop of Canterbury, to elect Robert, Archdeacon of Leicester, as their father and bishop [Col. 0808B]. And when the Archbishop of Canterbury saw the votes of all converge upon him, unwilling that the aforesaid Church should be further disturbed or more severely worn down, he followed the counsel of the bishops, assented to their petition, and consecrated the aforesaid archdeacon as bishop, amid the great gratitude and favor of those petitioning. His teaching and life, both within and without, have good testimony, and in the office which he has hitherto discharged he has shown conspicuous grace. Therefore, reverend Father, we pray your kindness that what is due to him with justice alone pleading for him, he may obtain more readily and graciously through the prayers of our lowliness. May your holiness flourish, Father beloved in Christ.

## LETTER LXXXIX. TO ALL THE CHILDREN OF HOLY MOTHER CHURCH

[Col. 0808C]

To his beloved brethren in Christ, all the children of holy mother Church, Brother G., called Bishop of the Church of Hereford: greeting and affection in the Lord.

By this present writing we make known to your charity that, on the reliable testimony of religious persons, we have learned that the bearer of these presents, Benedict, before the court of our predecessor, Bishop R[obert] of blessed memory, swore with the oath of seven priests that his brother, whose death had made him suspect, had never incurred death through Benedict’s plot, consent, or will. And, in order to show fully his innocence in this matter, he swore in our presence, with many sitting with us, also in this manner: “My relatives, who have hitherto been regarded as suspects in the death of my brother, did not inflict death upon him. Nor did anyone, on my account, contrive his death: so may God help me and these holy things.” Immediately twelve priests confirmed the oath in this form: “We are certain that this Benedict has sworn truly concerning this matter; so may God and these holy things help us.” Since this was done in our presence, we testify to what we saw, and by this writing and the impression of our seal declare the act performed, lest he should henceforth be burdened by the customary infamy of public notoriety [Col. 0808D]. Farewell.

## LETTER XC. TO ROBERT, BISHOP OF LINCOLN

[Col. 0809A]

To his lord and dearest brother R., by God’s grace Bishop of Lincoln, G., minister of the Church of Hereford: to taste and know those things which God in His sweetness has prepared for the poor.

If you are well, it is as we wish; our joy thereby is brought to perfection and filled to every measure of gladness. You order the Digest to be corrected and glossed, and behold, your Ambrose does not cease to labor at the mill. The other things which you commanded will not be delayed, God granting it. The fortunes of our cause together with our powers are still uncertain; as soon as the matters now in suspense begin to be settled, you will immediately learn by a swiftly dispatched letter. They have been granted to us by Lord Henry until Palm Sunday [Col. 0809B], but we are requesting their further extension through a messenger who has been sent and has not yet returned. In these matters we shall discover what end the Lord grants, hoping good things from Him, who rejects the thoughts of peoples and scatters the counsels of princes. We wish that you may flourish in the Lord and be renewed and advance in Him from day to day, most beloved in the Lord.

## LETTER XCI. TO THEOBALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

To his father and lord T., by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury, G., minister of the Church of Hereford: after wrath, to remember mercy.

If your serenity has been somewhat moved against the Bishop of Llandaff, we must supplicate your highness all the more humbly because we know that it has been stirred against the said bishop for a more just cause [Col. 0809C]. For an appeal was sufficient to support his case against his opponent, if he had observed toward you in every respect the reverence due. If this was not done, it must undoubtedly be imputed to the misconduct of the clerics of Llandaff, not to the bishop’s own malice or ingratitude. For he is the work of your hands and your planting; if perhaps you crush him for a just cause, you will crush the work of your hands and uproot him whom your right hand planted. Far be this from your glory; nor let your praise suffer such loss, that one whom you once enrolled among friends you should so readily proscribe, barred from access to your favor.

He has indeed come to you in humility and gentleness, entertaining no lofty thought against you, but, whatever may have been done by you, wholly expecting and awaiting from you all that befits a good lord and a loving father [Col. 0809D]. Far be it that the day of your mind should be so turned into darkness that anger should either injure grace in you or make nature void; rather, within your fatherly breast may there be one who pleads and entreats for a son, and may that affection be heard. If therefore our supplication can avail with you, if the sad things we say have not wholly fallen from your heart on account of an empty cause, receive your bishop into favor and provide for his peace and honor, lest he be compelled to seek a father elsewhere, but may glory that he has found with you all that is loving and moderate [Col. 0810A]. In this prayer we prostrate our hearts at your feet, which in supplication we ourselves would more willingly embrace with our hands. Let your discernment therefore take care, if it please you, not by denying our requests to shut up our prayers henceforth in mute silence. We pray that you may long flourish, Father beloved in Christ.

## LETTER XCII. TO POPE EUGENIUS
To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff Eugenius, G., minister of the Church of Hereford, the joy of salvation and the service of due obedience.

Because, beloved Father, we desire to be friends of truth, we confidently attest in your presence what we ourselves saw and heard concerning the case of Lord Bernard, abbot of Cerne. For we saw the prior of Cerne himself, together with very many persons of that same church, lying prostrate at the feet of Lord Hiemar, bishop of Tusculum, then legate among us, humbly petitioning that he would grant them the aforesaid Bernard—then prior of the Church of Gloucester—as abbot, and that, by granting him, he would satisfy both their request and that of their whole convent. We also know that Lord Hiemar, at their request, imposed upon the aforesaid brother Bernard, though he refused and was unwilling, by the authority which he possessed, the duty of governing the Church of Cerne, and of providing for it in every respect as befitted an abbot. We nevertheless know that the convent of Cerne received him freely in solemn procession, and that afterwards, at their own request, the lord bishop of Salisbury confirmed him as abbot by episcopal blessing.

Since we have found him worthy of much commendation both in life and teaching, we offer prayers to Your Exaltedness on his behalf: that you may hear him in his just petitions, and by apostolic authority restrain the monks of Cerne, who are unjustly and shamefully obstinate against him. For that house of Cerne is one to which, as public report has it, upright conduct alone has long been displeasing; nothing except what was contrary to religion and to order could please it. Because the aforesaid brother Bernard resisted, with such strength as he could, their disorder—which ought rather to be corrected than mentioned in your presence—he has been driven out by their violence as though he were a profane person, and separated from their communion.

Therefore, not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory (Psalm 113), so that, by checking the audacity of wicked men, you may restrain similar fault in others; and by worthily rewarding the good, may increase in very many the pursuit of virtue. May the almighty Lord preserve you safe for a long time, beloved Father in Christ.

## LETTER XCIII. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, the most holy Pope E., brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford, the affection of one who devoutly greets him and the office of one who humbly obeys.

To Your Exaltedness, beloved Father, we pray all the more confidently on behalf of the Church of Lewes, because we do not doubt that everything dutiful and honourable is pleasing to your serenity. For this church shines among the churches of England so greatly through its firm observance of order and the riches of perfect charity that it dispels the darkness of our West by the light, as it were, of honourable conduct and the worship of pure religion. This mother of the poor and consolation of the sorrowful displays herself to all with such conspicuous grace of merits that, long since received into public rejoicing, she shines like a mirror at the farthest limits of the earth and as a singular example of holiness.

Therefore we earnestly offer prayers to Your Excellence, that you may hear its just petitions with fatherly gentleness and not permit it to be diminished in those things by which, in the time of your predecessors, it was happily founded and enlarged. Your prudence will do this all the more securely because whatever you grant to one church, you will bestow not only upon a great and commendable community of monks, but also upon an immeasurable multitude of poor people, travellers, shipwrecked persons, and the infirm. Thus, if in this action anything should be derogated from the law of the decrees, the charity of Christ, ministering most abundantly to his members, may powerfully excuse it before the supreme Judge. May my lord and dearest Father in Christ prosper.

## LETTER XCIV. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff Eugenius, brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford, the service of humble obedience.

We know, dearest Father in Christ, we know that not to obey an apostolic command is apostasy, and that to oppose your will is a kind of true sacrilege. Far be this from a faithful man; far be it from a Catholic; above all, far be it from a son bound and indebted in many ways by the benefits shown to us through your generosity.

Certainly the bishop of London is so much the work and creation of your hands that this may rightly be said to him openly: “What have you that you did not receive from the lord pope?” For no one among us is ignorant, scarcely anyone unaware, of how apostolic power raised him up against the wishes and combinations of princes. Therefore that saying seems rightly applicable before your serenity on his behalf: “You will stretch out your right hand to the work of your hands.” For what can a vessel, however excellently formed, do if its maker decides to dash it to pieces with an iron rod?

Far be this from your glory; nor may your praise suffer such loss, that one whom you once received within the bounds of grace you should undeservedly remove from access to it, or exclude though innocent. We believe your prudence does not know that the archdeaconry which you commanded to be given, with praiseworthy generosity, to Lord John of Canterbury had already been granted to another. As testimony to this fact, we confidently declare that the lord of Lincoln does not deviate from truth even in the least. We know indeed, and firmly maintain, that the bishop of London does not wish to redeem by perjury the permanent loss even of his whole bishopric.

The bishop of Lincoln himself testifies, and is prepared to swear, that before the bishop of London learned your will either in writing or through any messenger, he granted the said archdeaconry to Master Ralph of Die, a man in whom learning abounds for teaching and good character for honourable conduct. It is indeed to be embraced with every expression of thanks that you have decided to reward integrity and learning in John. Yet this is an easy thing for the apostolic see to do, in such a way that you do not offend the bishop whom you have distinguished by singular grace.

In this matter we offer prayers; in this matter we entreat your fatherly charity: that, privately with the Father, someone may plead for the son and bishop, and may obtain so much by affection that one perhaps more loving may not be received less favourably, nor one far readier to obey be heard less graciously. May my lord and dearest Father in Christ prosper.

## LETTER XCV. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff E., brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford, the devoted and due service of obedience.

Since divine generosity, Father, has made you a debtor to all, those demand this common debt more urgently who submit themselves in every respect to your protection with more eager and ampler devotion. It therefore greatly concerns your honour and glory that you extend a helping hand to the Church of London, shaken by its present storm, and that, sustaining with the kindness of counsel the cause for which it labours with much sweat, you do not allow it to be dashed upon rocks or overwhelmed by waves.

Though it shines in the Church of England with much splendour of merits and dignities, at present it has been ennobled by this very title of outstanding praise: after the death of its father and pastor, amid the threats of princes and the drawn swords of raging men, it looked to God, not man; it stood firm and undaunted; boldly exposing itself to dangers and refusing to allow the honour of God and liberty of the Church to be diminished in any respect, it elected for itself, by unanimous consent, a suitable father and pastor, no less devoutly than wisely. Since the courage of those electing and the constancy of their minds make this worthy of praise, the person elected fills it out with grace and honour, so that both what was courageously done for the honour and liberty of the Church and what was provided with commendable foresight in such a person are altogether most worthy of favour.

For we write confidently of matters known to us, and speak with assurance of what we know. R. de Bealmeis, archdeacon of London, is, as far as human eyes can judge, honourable in life, praiseworthy in learning, lovable in generosity, and illustrious through the noble stock of his very birth. Since the Church diligently calls and awaits him for its governance, if—God forbid—he is rejected, injured virtue will blush at this wrong, and the complaint of those who say, “In vain have I justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent” (Psalm 72), will gain no small increase.

Therefore let apostolic exaltedness act; let the Father act, so that the Church of the English may rejoice and applaud him. Let a good conclusion complete the good beginning. Let him honour one most worthy of honour, so that praise may be his in the present and reward be laid up for him in the future; and that they may know, “Your hand has done this, and you, Lord, have made it” (Psalm 108). May your safety be preserved long, beloved Father in Christ.

## LETTER XCVI. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff E., brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford, the affection of one who devoutly greets him and the office of one who humbly obeys.

From the tribulation of evils and pain, the Church of Reading flees to your serenity, Father. There it hopes and awaits a remedy, where all who are afflicted glory that consolation is not lacking. Situated on the very border between the various regions of our kingdom, it has long endured the assaults of each side upon the other; from the beginning of the wars, passage and return from each side to the other have taken place through its lands. Thus weakened by fires and the slaughter of its people, diminished by the plundering of both movable and immovable goods, and having already spent much upon physicians who do nothing, it hastens and runs to the hem of your garment, hoping for remedies from the source from which proceeds the power that heals others.

Therefore, with humble devotion, we offer prayers to Your Exaltedness: that, raising up what has fallen and strengthening what has been broken, you may aid your devoted daughter; and that, with compassion prompting and justice always working effectively within you, you may cause what has been lost to be restored, so that what became dead to her when her founder died may happily revive for her while the Father acts prosperously in her affairs. May my lord and dearest Father in Christ prosper.

## LETTER XCVII. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff E., brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford, obedience and the affection owed to a Father.

We cannot deny, beloved Father, to the love of our friends that little which we are, so that, bearing one another’s burdens (Galatians 6), we may render each other the reciprocal help of counsel and assistance. Therefore, although no merits of ours commend us before your majesty, nor have services or expenditures acquired for us any favour with you, nevertheless out of charity we dare—though we are unworthy to be heard even for ourselves—to burst into an appeal to fatherly mercy on behalf of another.

For Master Roger of Ponte, a clerk of your beloved son the lord archbishop of Canterbury, urgently needs and implores from your serenity your protection and remedy, in order to defend what he canonically possesses. Therefore, prostrate in heart at the knees of your holiness, we pray that mercy may proceed from the fountain of justice; that you may receive into grace one whom we believe worthy of recommendation before the apostolic majesty both by life and learning; and that you may graciously send him away having been heard in his just petitions. May the Most High Majesty preserve Your Exaltedness safe for a long time for yourself and yours. Amen.

## LETTER XCVIII. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0814A]

To his lord and father, the supreme pontiff E., brother, minister of the Church of Hereford, may he happily attain the glory of eternal life.

We cannot resist necessity, beloved Father in the Lord, without obeying that charity which powerfully commands us from the hearts of our brethren. It is this charity that brings us, though we desire rather to remain hidden, into public view, so that we may send at least words of truth to your hearing, since at present we cannot stand before you. Thus we could not fail the distinguished and honourable man, Master Godfrey, exceptionally learned in both sacred and secular writings, but had to testify to Your Exaltedness what we have seen and heard concerning his case.

When William Cumin, for many compelling reasons, had been bound by the chains of anathema, and had remained under that bond for more than a full year, and when the jurisdiction of the general council had stripped him of every ecclesiastical benefice, the lord bishop of Worcester, on the counsel of religious men, invested the aforesaid Godfrey with his archdeaconry and in devout concern appointed him archdeacon of his church. We know that he persevered devoutly in that office and administered prudently and discreetly those matters which belonged to his care. We also know that he will be necessary to that church, and that its benefice is preserved in him not merely, but much more abundantly.

Let [therefore] consideration be given in this matter, so that your glory may always increase, and that those who have recourse to you may conceive a good hope of obtaining both counsel and aid in the matters for which they resort to you. May the almighty Lord protect you unto length of days, beloved Father. Amen.

*(Letters 97 and 98 are the same as 17 and 18; but because of the difference in their superscriptions, we print them again.)*

## LETTER XCIX. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff E., G., minister of the Church of Hereford, the due service of affection and obedience.

Beloved Father, we have sent to Your Exaltedness this clerk, bearer of the present letter, with a written account of his case, so that he, who had almost been pierced through by the darts of Satan, may be restored to life by the consolation of your grace. This man, a certain dean of ours—a priest honourable in conduct and altogether vigorous in undertaking and enduring the affairs of the Church, received into public congratulation for the merit of his learning and life—was publicly excommunicated, though he had no other offence than that, by the gift of our predecessor of good memory, Lord Bishop Robert, he had received and ministered in a certain church which had belonged to his father.

After long affliction and fasting, he deserved absolution, having taken an oath in this form: that, so long as life remains and no necessary accident prevents him, he will approach Your Exaltedness under the law of penance prescribed for him, prepared to obey whatever your command may be in order to obtain pardon for his fault. In this matter, according to the wisdom and grace given you by the Lord, you will provide for the sinner, both that the fault may be suitably punished and that the ancient enemy, fallen from his triumph, may by no means glory. May Your Exaltedness be preserved uninjured and safe for a long time.

## LETTER C. TO ELIAS DE SAI

Gilbert, by the grace of God bishop of Hereford, to his friend Elias de Sai: greetings.

Dearest friend, you know how steadfastly you promised love to me and honour and peace to the Church which is in your territory. Would that you had kept that promise so that no complaint concerning you would have been brought to us, and we would have needed to write nothing to you except what was peaceful and friendly. I should greatly wonder at many things; but I wonder much more at this concerning you: that you drag our priest and dean before the judgment of your court and claim for yourself against the Church a power which kings and emperors, despite much sweat and labour, have been unable to obtain against it to this day.

Therefore, dearest friend, we command you to allow our clerks to be judged by us; and in particular not to presume to judge this man or any others, but to permit them, according to the order granted to them, to serve the Lord in peace. If you do not heed us, we shall not delay—even though we are unwilling—to pronounce upon you and your possessions whatever sentence we can. But if you have any complaint against Lord Walter, we offer you full justice concerning him. We wish you health and that, by doing good, you may please the Lord.

## LETTER CI. TO . . . .

Walter, our clerk, complains that he has suffered a double loss. A man named Hugh of Cluny paid to Gilbert Anglicus money which he thought Hugh owed him; and, since Hugh asserts that he owed nothing to the aforesaid Gilbert, he then made a settlement with Hugh upon payment of money. Therefore I ask you by this command: when these three have been summoned for a fixed day, hear fully Walter, who seeks recovery of the money paid, though he maintains that it was owed to Gilbert; and on our behalf admonish Hugh of Cluny to testify to the truth in this matter.

If it is established that the aforesaid knight received from Walter any sum on account of the debt, he is to be compelled to restore to Walter as much as he received. But if the knight proves that Hugh owed him this money, you will reserve for us the case between Hugh and Walter.

## LETTER CII. TO PHILIP DE SARNEFELD

To his friend and parishioner Philip de Sarnefeld: greetings.

I hear that in the court of the lord abbot of Reading a legal proof has been adjudged against you: namely, that you must swear with twelve hands that neither you nor your predecessors ever paid to the church of Lumin five shillings from the land of Sarnefeld, which it claims from you. Yet by the certain recollection of Holy Church I recognize that this cause was both argued in the presence of Lord Bishop Robert, of blessed memory, and settled by his counsel.

Therefore, because in making this legal proof I understand there to be certain things contrary to the welfare of you and yours, we command you and, upon your Christian faith, order you neither to take this oath yourself nor permit any of yours to take it, until you have spoken with us and received fuller counsel concerning this matter. For by my letters I entreat the lord abbot that you incur no detriment to your case because of this delay. Farewell.

## LETTER CIII. TO G., ARCHDEACON OF WORCESTER

Gilbert, by the grace of God bishop of Hereford, to his dear master G., archdeacon of Worcester: greetings.

You know, dearest friend, you know that peacemakers have been adopted into the prerogative of the children of God. Therefore the peace of our neighbours must be attended to all the more diligently because greater is the reward that we hope and expect from the Lord for this work. We therefore ask that, in this hope, your goodwill may show itself ready and open to our entreaty: recall the lord of Worcester from persecuting our brethren, namely the monks of Evesham, and devote your efforts to restoring peace between them.

Even if our prayers did not move you to this, reverence for the lord pope ought long ago to have drawn and compelled you. For since an appeal has been made to him, it would be right that every peace and security should be preserved for the appellants. Yet we have heard from many persons that, after the aforesaid brethren appealed to the lord pope, the lord of Worcester not only suspended them from their orders, but also works to expel them from their monastery and to confine them under prison guard so that they cannot approach the lord pope. If he does this, he cannot be excused from grave offence against the lord pope.

Therefore let reverence for the lord pope, the charity also due to the lord of Worcester, and our prayers move you either to labour for peace to be restored from this point, or not to deny your counsel and assistance to those in your archdeaconry who flee to the name of the lord pope. Do not allow them to be dragged away and afflicted by any lay hand, nor allow their possessions to be seized. We write this to you out of charity, lest equal guilt involve one who consents with the one who acts. For consent is not to resist when one can or ought to do so. In this matter, a manifest conclusion imposes upon you either complicity or the defence of the monks. Farewell.

## LETTER CIV. TO ROBERT, BISHOP OF EXETER

To his beloved lord and dearest brother R., by the grace of God bishop of Exeter, brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford: greetings and affection.

Where confidence is great, presumption too is often great. Hence we offer our prayers with much assurance to your kindness, always dear and worthy of love to us, asking that in certain matters which concern you, you may aid us in the necessity that has now arisen. Hugh de Cotes, a canon, has long filled everyone’s ears with complaints, asserting that he was violently expelled by us from the church of Stanley and unjustly despoiled of his goods. To our complete disparagement he has also brought the same complaint before the lord pope and obtained letters from the lord legate for investigation of this matter.

But since your prudence is not unaware of how the aforesaid Hugh lived for some time in your parts, and to what religious observance he was attached, we ask you to grant us letters reporting this matter, thereby making us debtors to you for still greater favour in all things. If it is established that he confined himself to a stricter observance, it is likewise established that he renounced what he had previously possessed. Since we have heard this of him, we await testimony from a friend of truth. And because, for the correction of many, things discreditable are often brought forward most honourably to lovers of religion, if anything is publicly known that may shame the face of our adversary, we ask that this too be made clear in those letters. Farewell.

## LETTER CV. FROM ROBERT, BISHOP OF EXETER, TO POPE EUGENIUS III. ON AN INCONTINENT CLERK

“At the request of the venerable …,” etc. See among the various letters to Eugenius, *Patrologia*, vol. 180.

## LETTER CVI. [TO HENRY, DUKE OF THE NORMANS]

To H., son of the count of Anjou, duke of the Normans, and lord in large part of the kingdom of the English, of royal nobility and, as we have heard, outstanding character: G., by the grace of God bishop of Hereford, greetings and service.

You were pleased to admonish me by letter to come quickly to you, in order to do what I had promised in the hand of the lord abbot of Bord'. Ready to fulfil my promises as speedily as I could, I hastened to you; but because you had gone farther on, I waited two days at Hereford for your return. Yet obedience not merely called and advised me, but pressed and drew me elsewhere; therefore I could not wait longer.

I ask you, if it please you, to hold me excused on this occasion and, by bearing my absence equably this time, make me your debtor for favour. If there are any rivals or ill-wishers of mine who, from hatred of me, seek by malicious suggestion to draw you into injury to God and detriment to the Church, it is good for you to set the fear of God against the counsels of malicious men and to retain in memory that saying of the wise man: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly” (Psalm 1). For every judgment proceeds from God; if you offend him by beginnings that are not good, your outcomes cannot be honourable. May the Lord give you understanding and moderation, so that churches may pray for you and subject peoples may long for your rule. Farewell.

## LETTER CVII. [TO THEOBALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY]

To his father and lord T., archbishop of Canterbury, brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford: greetings and obedience.

Since we received your letters, this has been the fruit of our labour: we have brought over to our side Roger the subprior, a good man, Lord David, G. R., and their accomplices. The Nicolaitans, however, as from the beginning, still oppose you, and strive by every means to acquire and prepare here whatever is necessary for their journey.

Therefore, unless another course seems good to you, I judge it advisable that Lord Richard, the prior, and Lord Samson should set out as soon as possible to the lord pope. For it is unworthy that they should present themselves before the court as though they had a good conscience, while our people, who walk in the way of the Lord in truth, should remain in hiding as though conscious of wrongdoing. It is therefore necessary that you send common letters to the prelates of churches and convents in our regions, asking them to testify to the lord pope according to their conscience, by their letters, how much farther the party of the convent of Evesham which supports the election of Lord William is to be regarded as greater in number and sounder by the very purity of its merits.

Lord Reginald will explain to you the remaining matters necessary to the business; with all desire he hastens to your presence and to see the face of his elect. Farewell.

## LETTER CVIII. [TO THE SAME]

To his father and lord T., by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury, G., bishop of Hereford, the service of affection and obedience.

We have learned from the report of certain persons, Lord, that W., prior of Saint Bar[tholomew’s], has in some manner intervened on his own behalf in the case concerning Stanley and claims for himself a right in the church of Saint Leonard against the church of Gloucester. You may, if you please, observe from the following how lawfully he does this.

When the aforesaid church, at the request of the lord of Salisbury and of those whom he had there with him—namely Walter, Roger, and Henry—had been received by us from the hand of the lord of Worcester, the lord prior immediately lodged a complaint against us before the lord bishop of Worcester and caused us to be summoned to answer in court concerning the aforesaid church. When, on the appointed day, the case had been debated between us for some time in the presence of the said bishop, and that bishop asserted that he had never granted anything in the frequently mentioned church to the prior, the lord prior appealed against us to your hearing on a fixed day.

When we pursued the appeal and appeared before you, after hearing all that the prior had alleged against us concerning the church of Saint Leonard, we offered ourselves for judgment, refusing no answer. But he forestalled us: before we had made any response, in your hearing he renounced the suit entirely, and publicly declared, before many witnesses, that he would claim nothing further in the aforesaid church. Therefore let your equity decide, since he voluntarily renounced the suit which he had brought concerning that church, whether he has sufficient desire to renew that suit. For we testify to what we know to be true and are prepared to prove it at a suitable place and time. Farewell.

## LETTER CIX. [TO ROGER, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK]

To his father and lord R., by the grace of God archbishop of York, brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford: greetings and service.

If the secret place of your former affection still admitted us, we would seal our private matters with a sign and would not entrust letters addressed to the Father to the gaze of many eyes. But because we know ourselves excluded, we now send letters that scarcely remain outside rather than letters placed within, that they may ask pardon and, if possible, reconcile their lord to his grace by restoring favour with you. Yet we do not easily hope that this trembling little sheet can accomplish it, for we think that neither your hand can be extended to it nor your eyes easily turned towards it.

Therefore, if just displeasure has rejected us, we at least wish others not to be unaware of what we seek: since we can no longer bear your anger, we ask forgiveness for our offence. For if we have said anything against you, we retract it in this very palinode, written out in our own hand against ourselves; and if we have moved your mind even a little, we confess the fault with our own mouth, because, rashly breaking forth, and without any merit of yours demanding it, we offended our lord and friend.

We stood indeed with charity in the cause of the Church which we support; and if, through our thoughtless handling, the iron slipped from its handle, what counsel remains except that we flee with repentance and lamentation to that great Elisha? There is great hope that the preacher of repentance will not reject one who repents, and that he who proclaims groanings will not cast away one who groans deeply.

We could indeed have discharged the obligation owed to charity prudently and honourably, and resisted by ecclesiastical disputation according to the form of law, without God being displeased at this. But what had we to do with pointing a finger at you, twisting our arms against you, and—though we were persons of no importance—with wretched lips uttering not only foaming words but swelling boasts?
