Where on that day had our shame, honour, ecclesiastical discipline, and the sobriety to be desired in a sound mind gone? How badly everything slipped from us at once in a moment, so that, stripped of goods, we immediately became most worthy to fall from grace.

But when one falls, shall he not add that he may rise again? (Amos 1.) Or does iniquity press us so hard on every side that there is no access for us to grace? Or if moderation has failed us, has mercy likewise failed you? And if girded with a rope we are led away into the law of sin, has that golden belt been torn from your breasts? Far be it that one who daily asks that his own debt be forgiven should not forgive the debt owed by his suppliant fellow-servant; and that, when the mist of anger has been wiped away, your mind should not return to its accustomed serenity and open to us the approach to pardon.

For how little is our offence—except that any offence against so exalted a dignity must indeed be regarded as great? We joined word to word and, as is customary in debate, matched like with like. For when you said that you had spared us up to that point, we replied that we too had many matters in which we had spared Your Exaltedness. Because of the unhappy ending of those words, did we perhaps, with cynic savagery, attack the disordered conduct of our lives or, God forbid, faults of mind? Far be it that such an opinion should creep into your mind and that you should confound an innocent man by a suspicion of this sort.

I call to witness that inaccessible light which penetrates and illumines the hidden places of good minds, and also that common hope which the devotion of the saints embraces: by those words we understood nothing other than that, out of reverence for you, we had kept silent and suppressed many matters relating to the substance of the case. For when corrupt letters were under discussion, many harsher charges could have been made on this point and, as you well know, amplified by rhetorical *auxesis*. And although those same letters implied both a claim of right and dispossession, we did not set our mouth in heaven so as to presume even slightly to accuse the falsity of the petitions—whereas the legal formula provides that, even if a petitioner in such a case produces a sacred oracle, he wholly loses the benefit sought.

These are the trivial matters, and others like them, in which we spared you, and which we had in view when we spoke too proudly. For if, compelled by charity, we became foolish for a time on behalf of the brethren, we were not mad enough to utter insults against you, whom above others we have loved hitherto, and whom we have often exalted with titles of praise, to the envy of many.

Father, you will rightly place confidence in no one concerning your secrets more than in us; for “who knows the hidden things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him?” (1 Corinthians 2). Behold, before God, I do not lie. We had no bitterness within us against you except that which, with an interpreter present, we confessed in writing. Accordingly, we accused ourselves more bitterly than the matter itself required, because we endure even the slightest indignation of yours against us with the greatest distress.

Someone may suppose that we do not say this sincerely, but in order, by soothing your mind, to avoid in some degree the burden of the appeal made against us. This is not our outlook: if we belong to Christ, we shall stand confidently before his vicar. Let fates run their course; let all things receive the outcomes provided for them. We lament the losses of a friendship that has slipped away rather than fear dangers that threaten.

Farewell; and would that that spirit of compassion might move you, so that you may run to embrace a returning friend even while he is still far away.

## LETTER CX. [LETTER OF ROGER, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK, TO GILBERT]

To his venerable brother—and would that he were a friend—G., by the grace of God bishop of Hereford, R., by the grace of God archbishop of York: greetings.

Having received from the hand of our beloved son H. what you call your recantation, I examined it carefully before any copy of it was made available to anyone, fearing above all lest the written characters of the letter should express the heat of your living voice—if I may say so without offence to you. It would certainly have remained with us and that secret would have perished in our hands; it would have been denied the freedom to wander out into public, lest a double injury should shut off every path to reconciliation. I confess that I was somewhat moved by those things which the heat of your spirit supplied; yet not so moved that a breach of brotherly charity was made in me, or that the sun of justice was darkened over the emotion of my anger. For from long habit I keep both heart and lips especially circumcised toward a friend; Christ, the unique example of patience, bound this by a stricter law when he willed, through his grace, to gird the slippery motions of my mind with the priestly girdle. For there cannot fall from my heart what was commanded by the priestly law: namely, that when a turtledove or similar bird is sacrificed, its head is to be bent back toward its wings; and that, in the description of the tables of the Temple, their lips are said to be bent inward all around. For the sower of the divine word, watchful on every side, ought to recall his speech to his heart, hear what he says, and do what he preaches, lest, after drawing the bow and striking his hearers’ vices with the arrows of Holy Scripture, he should turn back in the day of battle and the aid of his sword be withdrawn from him, nor should it help him in battle (Ps. 88:44).

I greatly wonder, and cannot wonder enough, whence Your Holiness believed me so simple as to suppose that I was offended because you returned my own words to me. In those words, as God and my conscience bear witness, I thought then that I had received no injury, nor do I think so now—especially since words of this kind are customarily offered to temper anger and restore the favour of friends. But if beneath their ambiguity I had thought my reputation in any respect burdened, I should have been guilty of a heinous offence, I who had first provoked so great a friend to this insult. Something more serious was said outside the cause at issue; and the person to whom its bitterness appears directed is so deeply involved in it, and was so involved, that—unlike other injuries—it could by no means be effaced through dissimulation. But enough of this. However concise speech may be on this point, it is as distasteful to us as it is dangerous. Let us therefore return to the earlier matters.

There occurs that passage of your letter in which you say that lighter matters were alleged to win our favour, while graver matters were withheld. These you called trifles, both truly and elegantly. But the appearance of the affair will readily show otherwise. Was not an accusation of forgery brought forward? Would it have seemed to you that more severe treatment had been employed had the falsity of the prayers been charged? Would that you had set forth everything: judges could readily have been given proof of violent spoliation, not merely by witnesses but by the arguments and instruments in which we abound. To allege these and similar matters, which you suppressed for the sake of our cause, belongs to the duty of an advocate, whose task is to pursue what the cause requires, while nevertheless abstaining from injury. And indeed you might have said even harsher things without injury to the adverse party, had not laws and canons alike excluded you from advocacy in this cause. For you know how carefully I disclosed the secrets of this affair, not only before I set out to the lord pope, but also after my return, at Worcester. You were given copies of the letters which I had obtained from the Apostolic See concerning this business. Nothing at all concerning what I had set down about the settlement was concealed from you. Therefore I do not dare stretch out my hand against your rights, lest perhaps I injure my friend more grievously than I myself have been injured. It is better for me to pass over some matters to the detriment of the cause than to speak them to the detriment of modesty.

As for the *auxesis* which you call rhetorical—though it belongs more properly to orators—it is certain that it had no place in this case, since it properly chooses its position only at the very end, once the issue has been established and proved. Thus, had it been introduced, the injury would have redounded not so much upon us as upon the law. But why say more? Can your letter, fortified with so many safeguards of Holy Scripture, burdened with so many weighty maxims, adorned with so great a splendour of rhetorical embellishment, have laboured in vain and return empty to its lord? Far be it! Yet pardon will be given to one who asks pardon, provided that, if God grants him access to you, your disposition does not differ from your prayer. Behold: your old friend now hastens to meet you. Already in my Father’s house are heard music and dancing; the servants rejoice, the fatted calf is slain, and a robe and ring are being prepared for you (Luke 15). It is fitting, then, that each of us alike sacrifice the calf for sin at the entrance of the tabernacle, so that, with feet washed in the water of the sanctuary and clothed again in fitting garments, we may feast and rejoice together; lest those brethren who sow discord and rejoice in the worst things should glory over us (Prov. 2), but rather be confounded and perish with those who hasten to destroy all things. Farewell.

## LETTER CXI. [TO ROGER, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK.]

To his father and lord R., by God’s grace Archbishop of York, brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford, greeting and service.

A garden of spices breathes sweetly, and the united sweetness of many fragrances gives forth a pleasant scent. Such, Father, is something that your letter has brought me. As I return again and again to it, having already read it often, I seem plainly to be in a certain garden of delights. On one side, that gracious beauty of expression breathes upon me; on the other, the lofty depth of its thoughts. Thus, while it delights and at once edifies, the letter of which I speak carries wholly into itself its reader, bound by a double bond.

I had sent words to my Father, and, sorrowful and anxious, had lamented that I had in however small a measure disturbed the peaceful tranquillity of your mind. But behold, you have turned my mourning into joy (Ps. 29), and I confess that I have happily offended: in exchange for my fault I receive not the punishment I might have expected, but the gift for which I had despaired. For I count it a great gift to contemplate, even from afar, the face of Moses descending from the mountain (Exod. 19), and to behold in some measure the brightness of his countenance—which a weak eye can scarcely bear—through, as it were, certain thinning folds of the veil set before it.

For, passing through cloud and darkness, upon the very summit of the mind—which is truly a sacred mountain—you discoursed holy things in the light itself inhabited by holy minds. There, drawing from the fount of light, you poured into your letter many things that might correct us by teaching us and illumine the darkness of our western region with the gracious abundance of your light. Hence you show me the disposition of a mind well ordered toward me, so that, by placing before me the mirror of virtue, you may provoke my mind to desire virtue. In this way holy persons often disclose their good qualities, not to exalt themselves with praise, but to show others in themselves what they may beneficially imitate.

Hence that holy circumcision of heart and lips is set before me in your conduct, so that henceforth I may distribute within myself, with a suitable moderation of reason, what ought to be said, to whom, and when; and that inward heat of the mind may so break forth openly that my voice may burn outwardly with that fire which the Lord came to cast upon the earth (Luke 12), not with that which the enemy is ever intent upon kindling from Gehenna. The prophet’s lips were cleansed by the touch of the coal brought from above; and the superfluities of my own mouth can be cleansed through the example of a father and lord who lovingly admonishes me.

Why should I speak of the patience which you so holily set before me, so that, by presenting it to me, you may henceforth make me the possessor of my own soul? For while the soul is rebellious against reason, resists the spirit, murmurs when injured, and goads and inflames itself for vengeance, it is not yet possessed. But when turned toward Christ and changed for the better according to his example, it forgives its injuries, now bears adversity gladly, and, bound at last by the reins of patience, is restrained from every impulse of disordered will. Subjected to the rule of reason, it is then possessed under full mastery, as Truth testifies when it says: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21).

The mystical turtledove also persuades me: it has not its head cut off in sacrifices, but twisted back toward its wings. It cries and preaches this to me: if I sacrifice to the Lord anything of those things which the dove itself figuratively expresses, I must not, by seeking empty glory or favour, sever myself from the true body of Christ, which is the Church, through some colouring of pretence. Rather, I must turn back the governing faculty of the mind—which is truly the head of the inward person—toward the true wings of virtues, and toward those two wings of charity by which one flies to heaven, in sincere truth.

No less does that heavenly table delight me which, as you write so holily, turns its lips inward upon itself and instructs the teacher of divine law always to return with diligent reflection to himself in what he teaches and says, lest life disagree with word, and lest he overthrow by example those whom he builds up by word. Thus it is written in praise of the good: “Jonathan’s arrow never went backward, and Saul’s sword never returned empty” (2 Sam. 1). For the word of God is both sword and arrow: a sword because it strikes, and an arrow because it pierces. This sword returns empty when the speech uttered neither cuts away vices nor raises the hearer toward the fruit of virtue. But Jonathan, whose name means “giving dove” or “gift of the dove,” does not strike with an arrow turned back, because every spiritual teacher who receives gifts of grace from Christ and does not fail faithfully to minister them turns the lip prudently inward upon himself when he lives wisely and holily.

These are the things I have gathered from the bosom of your letter, while I range through it—as through certain pastures of life—with whatever exercise of mind I can manage. And if perhaps anything harsh adheres to these delights, I receive it gladly, as though by its mixture the whole were seasoned for me with a kind of salt. To repel me from advocacy in this cause, you add that its secrets were disclosed to me by you at Worcester. But, if I may say so without offence to you, if you ever shared secrets with me in confidence, you only showed what pleased you concerning the settlement and what letters you had received from the lord pope. Those letters themselves, not long afterward entrusted to the hands of bishops, I saw and understood to be made known indiscriminately to everyone.

For what was spread abroad at Bruges almost as at the crossroads, except that the bishops of Lincoln and Ely had received instructions to hear your cause and decide it after removing the appeal? But upon what foundations the claim of your cause rests; by what supports it is sustained; whether your witnesses’ reputation is established or discreditable; whether their number is sufficient or not; whether proof of your possession is straightforward or involved; and, in sum, whatever could in any respect harm or benefit the cause—none of this was disclosed to me in the least. Since the merits of causes are made known by the assertions of the parties, what can rightly be objected to me concerning the secret character of this cause, when none of these matters was ever opened to me?

Further, just as we call the speech delivered by an orator “rhetorical,” and speak also of rhetorical topics and figures—whence the saying, “He is no rhetorician whom anger makes pale”—so too I rightly maintain that the *auxesis* which you disparage is nevertheless rhetorical, though it belongs to orators; for the rhetorician teaches it, while the orator enlarges as occasion demands. Since it has its place once an issue is established, it could appropriately have been inserted in this controversy after there had begun to be no doubt, on the evidence of sight, concerning the corruption openly committed in the production of the letters. But what are these matters? Am I turning myself to Cicero’s doctrines and looking back, with some notable frivolity of mind, to studies long since bidden farewell and now as though ancient to me? Far be this from me. I sigh for the favour of my father and lord. To be reconciled with you, I have added sheet to sheet, although I have answered inadequately one advancing in full dignity, offering a cup to one who proffered a goblet.

## LETTER CXII. [TO WILLIAM DE HINET'.]

Gilbert, by God’s grace Bishop of Hereford, to his beloved brother William de Hinet': may you bring the novice-service consecrated to the Lord to its blessed and persevering end.

When I heard what has happened concerning you, I rejoiced wholly in the Lord, giving thanks to him who forestalls every merit and graciously distributes to his own the gifts of grace. Yet, hearing of so sudden a change, I was for a little while astonished, until, returning to myself, I set before my eyes that the word of the Lord runs swiftly where it wills (Ps. 147), and that his right hand mightily changes whom it wills. This word was spoken to you; this hand took hold of you. This word gave you counsel; this hand supplied you help. This word formed good will in you; this hand brought that very will to the effect of action. This word, touching and illuminating your heart from heaven, powerfully strengthened in the spirit of fortitude what you had conceived in the spirit of counsel. It showed you, while hidden in darkness, the way by which you advance; and this hand has likewise now led you where it might show you the salvation of God.

I seem to behold the pen of the heavenly scribe engraving the tablets of your heart and deeply impressing upon them the invitation by which bridegroom and bride say, “Come” (Song 4). As I hear, brother, you did not receive this invitation lukewarmly or sluggishly. Hearing and understanding prudently the voice of your beloved knocking at the door, so that you might immediately open to him the bolt of your door (Matt. 7), you at once arose, saying, “The voice of my beloved knocking” (Song 5). You have followed counsel truly worthy of praise: you have prepared a dwelling for the Author of life, not only in yourself but your very self for him.

You experience yourself what was revealed to the Apostle from above: “It is hard for thee to kick against the goads” (Acts 26). For there is a goad of life and a goad of death. The goad of death is sin (1 Cor. 15). As cattle are driven by a goad to rush and strike where the one who goads them wills, so sin—when it pierces a person—drives and hurls him without doubt into death. “For the wages of sin is death” (Rom. 6). But the goad of love moves the mind in a wholly different way. It is the goad of life, and it powerfully drives the lover toward life. To kick against it is as hard as it is difficult to resist charity. For “love is strong as death” (Song 8). Death separates from flesh and divides from the world; so too holy love, though far more nobly, nevertheless separates from the world and the flesh. It draws from where it itself is: it is not from the world, nor from flesh, nor from blood, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but is born of God (John 1). May it draw you to him, for he is love’s end. Of this David says: “I have seen an end of all perfection” (Ps. 118). Love tends toward this end; and holy love is not wandering. It has before it the one whom it loves, saying this in its heart and singing it with its mouth: “My eyes are ever toward the Lord” (Ps. 24).

You have fixed your gaze upon this object; in him you have found delight, and we hope that he too has found delight in you. You have followed him by the narrow and steep way; drawn by the cord of love, you have turned neither right nor left. You have not looked back toward prosperity, nor deigned to fear adversities. By bearing his cross, you follow the Crucified One; you express the cross in your dress and contemplate the cross in your mind. Raising its head on high, it now rules the heavens and presses down the lower regions. Embracing from side to side the whole breadth of the world with the hands of him affixed to it, you have been seized by those hands; now you bear the reproach of the Lord Jesus, that you may one day share also in his crown. For a short time you will bear his marks, and in your flesh you will fix his nails. Rough clothing, less-prepared food, hard bedding, manual labour, severity of discipline, continual silence: these stamp within you the very nails of the Saviour, which pierce you. You also have, in the likeness of the lance fastened in his side, the very sting of charity, which continually inflicts a wound upon your breast. He who forms charity in us—the one and highest Spirit—wounds in this way. She languished with this wound who said: “Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Song 2). O good wound and sweetest languor, accompanied by that death of which it is written: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115).

Now lift up not only the eyes of your mind but also those of your body. The vineyard of the Lord now occupies every woodland, has filled the wilderness, and the saints’ struggle is with thorns. They make crooked things straight and rough places into level ways (Luke 3); and what they undertake within by the spirit, they show outwardly by bodily exercise. For within they uproot the thorns of vices; the aged trunks of sin are consumed by the fire of charity. They cast down the heights of pride, and render the desert ground, dry and trackless, abundant in the supplies of virtues. Dead alike to sin and to the world, they sanctify themselves to Christ, despising everything besides him. This is the death of saints which the prophet declares precious in the sight of the Lord. For what is dearer to Christ, what is more precious to him in us, than that by imitating him we overcome death by death? And what death of the soul is so great as the foul heap of vices? Yet by that death whereby we die to the world, this death itself is conquered and slain, according to the Prophet: “I shall pursue my enemies and press on against them; I shall not turn back until they fail. I shall break them, and they shall not be able to stand; they shall fall beneath my feet” (Ps. 17).

To the first parents it was said: “You shall die by death” (Gen. 3). For the death of sin is truly the servant of eternal death. But to the children of obedience the Apostle says: “You are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ” (Col. 3). Truly blessed is the death which is at once cause and servant of that life which is with Christ. The wound of love inflicts this death upon you, so that you may now rightly claim for yourself what was said: “Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Song 2). For what is understood by flowers but the recent conversion of saints, and by apples but the consummation of those same persons now made firm in virtue? A flower has a good fragrance and the promise of coming fruit. The conversion of saints gives forth this fragrance in the Church; in those who have now been formed into a perfect man, the fruit of life is produced and ripened.

Therefore the soul, now languishing, asks to be strengthened and longs to be surrounded by these, that, with the examples of saints set before it, it may burn fervently in the beginning of its blessed conversion, make progress in its advance, and be intensely inflamed at its end. Whence shall I obtain flowers, whence apples, with which to strengthen you, dearest brother, and satisfy your soul now languishing in the Lord Jesus? But why demand of me what is in your own possession and what you now behold openly with unimpeded sight? The Cistercian Church has flowered widely throughout the world. Gathering from every quarter the loveliest flowers of the world, it has transplanted them into itself and transformed them, by a heavenly change, into certain flowers of paradise. Behold them in your mind as young olive trees springing up around its table. You will best run after their fragrance, for they, like maidens without number, do not cease to run after the fragrance of the Bridegroom. And if after flowers you seek fruits, it too sings with a certain prerogative to its heavenly Bridegroom: “All fruits, new and old, my beloved, I have kept for you” (Song 13).

Within it is the flock of shorn sheep, who, having put off the fleece of sin, have newly come up from the washing of repentance. Within it is the flock of ewes with young, who, having dwelt longer in the pastures of Bethel, are most fittingly clothed in the wool of virtues. Within it also are sheep that have earned their rest, who, after producing a numerous offspring and now ceasing to give birth, long to be carried upon the shoulder of the good shepherd to those folds of the citizens above.

O who am I, that I should worthily mention that holy shepherd and most fruitful sheep, the most illustrious Abbot of Clairvaux? What pen or what eloquence could enable me to reach even slightly the summit of his virtue? A man renowned for knowledge, most famous for holiness, supremely holy without pretence; a distinguished writer, an outstanding preacher, mirror of his order, enlargement of the Church, sun of his age, disperser of clouds; humble in his own eyes, exceedingly dear to the world and to Christ; a great priest, who in his days pleased God and was found just, and who, at the time of wrath, with the Lord Jesus working wondrously in him, became the reconciliation of those in discord. A man terrible in his austerities: when his flesh was consumed, skin clung to his bones on every side; his stomach knew no gluttony and his mouth no delights save spiritual ones. When a bodily eye looked on him, he was accounted contemptible by the world. When a spiritual eye regarded this man of our time, he far surpassed others in the merits of virtues.

Who can worthily recount his labours? He never rejected Tamar joined to him, but, drawing out her bitterness throughout the whole course of life, he carried inwardly the delights of virtues and outwardly thorns. A learned husbandman planted vigorously everywhere, watered abundantly, and the Lord gave plentiful increase to his innumerable plantations. Therefore, brother, I do not set before you Pauls, Antonys, Hilarions, Arseniuses, or the old fruits of the ancient trees of paradise for the refreshment of your spirit. Behold, here is one present: his authority is recent; you yourself deserved, I think, to behold him with your eyes and hear him teaching. He has indeed been taken from us to the things above, and his reward is with the Lord. But his name shall live for ever, and his memory shall not depart from the Church (Ecclus. 39). This tree of paradise was wisely planted by the Lord in these days before the eyes of the Church, so that whoever wishes to undertake the steps of virtues may find in him every exemplary virtue to imitate.

You too, who ask to be surrounded with apples, pluck from this source as many as you wish. Yet in writing this I do not urge you immediately to attempt the highest things. No one becomes excellent all at once. Money is best saved when it is put away gradually by the hand that collects it. Every virtue is brought to perfection by its own increases and steps. The very choir of virtues in a well-ordered mind is distinguished according to a definite method. If you would wisely raise a spiritual building, let humility first be laid for you, and add to it gentleness of mind. Let obedience adhere to these, strengthened by the vigour of patience. Let holy perseverance refresh them all with the food of discipline. Thus ordered into a perfect man, you will enter the broad realms of charity. When you enter there joyfully, immediately changed into another man, you yourself, made new, will marvel at all things as new in yourself. Thereafter you will account nothing hard or harsh in the way of the Lord; all that your flesh shrinks from will become sweet to your spirit in virtue. There you will feed upon virtues among the lilies, until the day of eternity breathes forth, when you happily attain the Lord Jesus whom you have followed in mind. Farewell in him; remember me, dearest brother.

## LETTER CXIII. TO POPE A.

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff A., brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford, the service owed by charity and obedience.

No one, Father, looks more deeply than you into the bond by which pious love connects the hearts of brethren. With you charity—the mistress of virtues—holds noble pre-eminence; and, as the Lord worthily rewards virtue, he has made you the chariot and driver of all Israel. Under charity’s strong command, we pity our beloved brother Nicholas, the bearer of this letter, and, weeping with the mourner, we humbly entreat Your Highness on his behalf. Though we have no hope from merit, we trust in the grace of apostolic kindness. Though absent, innocent, and unaware, he was stripped of an archdeaconry which he both possessed justly and administered soberly, without any observance of law or order.

Therefore, since he has already repeatedly approached his bishop, even through the intervention of many persons, and has found no comfort or remedy whatever, he has fled to the special help of the oppressed: there the Lord gives judgment to the poor and admits the cause of the afflicted widow within the inner chamber of his tribunal. When, as justice requires and mercy prompts, you graciously hear him, you will kindle in many a longing and prayer to the Lord, that you may happily order and judge Israel for a long time—you who discern its causes not by acceptance of persons but by supreme equity. May my lord and father, most dear in Christ, flourish.

## LETTER CXIV. TO THE SAME.

To his father and lord, the pontiff A., brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford, the service owed by humility and obedience.

Although it belongs to a judge to give careful attention to individual causes, those which are brought against the innocence of sons under an accusation of crime deserve more particular attention. Deadly and clamorous voices must be checked in those who pursue the lives and reputations of innocent persons and, though they cannot prove their guilt, strive through envious malice to draw them to punishment.

The beginning, course, and conclusion of the case between Osbert, Archdeacon of York, and the clerk S. were suspended by his appeal, as Your Highness may learn in full light of truth from the letters of your legate, the lord Archbishop of Canterbury. We have indeed examined these carefully and plainly testify that every article of the cause proceeded exactly as the same letters describe. For S., accusing the aforesaid archdeacon of having poisoned Archbishop William to death, as he alleged, and of certain other crimes, refused to enter into a formal accusation against him and pursue the matter before an ecclesiastical judge. Since he alone stood against so great a multitude of relatives and friends of the deceased archbishop, and uttered charges supported by no witnesses, he all the more confidently proposed against the aforesaid archdeacon the ordeal of a heated iron plate, because he expected that the Church of God would not admit a proof of this kind. He appealed all the more confidently to the king’s hearing because he maintained that this judgment could not lawfully be held before a secular judge.

Since a judge’s mind ought not to be moved against anyone by what cannot be demonstrated, we offer prayers to Your Highness for the said archdeacon, that he may not incur wrath before you, whom both much generosity . . .

*Some material is missing.*

## LETTER CXV. [TO KING HENRY.]

To the most serene lord and most excellent prince, the illustrious king of the English, H., brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford: may Satan be trampled under your holy feet, and may you triumph happily in Christ.

Beloved lord, divine goodness has set you over the rule of many peoples so that through you it may assist many and may bestow upon those over whom you preside the manifold gift of its grace. We know that this has been fulfilled in our nation, over which you so act as lord that you also show yourself a father. You restrain the proud in such a way that you never cease gently to order, govern, and raise up the meek and humble. The Church experiences you as its protector, the orphan as its father, the widow as its comforter, and all who suffer wrong as their gracious judge, by the very evidence of events.

And while all enjoy profound peace, it seems that, under your secure rule, only the fields—formerly painted with grasses and flowers—may complain that they are now being cultivated into every abundance of crops and wounded night and day by hoes and ploughs. From the Lord into you, the head of the kingdom, and from you into all its regions, the oil of grace overflows in abundance. Therefore I humbly entreat at the knees of your Highness that the bearer of this letter, recently orphaned—the first-born son of Ralph of Worcester, formerly your faithful servant—may obtain from you the gift of compassionate favour. May the divine majesty preserve you safe and powerful for a long time, lord most dear in Christ.

## LETTER CXVI. [TO B., ARCHDEACON OF LEICESTER.]

G., by God’s grace Bishop of Hereford, to his venerable brother and dearest friend B., Archdeacon of Leicester: may you always prosper well in the Lord.

Dearest brother, we do not doubt that your prudence knows fully what obedience claims for itself in us. We have learned, from the fragrance of the good report which reaches us concerning you, that you act praiseworthily in the camp of obedience and serve God in devout offices. Therefore we affectionately address prayers to your brotherhood, beloved to us in the Lord, that you remit to your clerks—whom we summoned by apostolic authority to act and testify—the fact that they did not attend the synod which you held; and that, in consideration also of apostolic authority, you grant this pardon to a friend who asks it.

For since one who gives occasion for loss is considered also to give the loss itself, if your zeal should be inflamed against them because of this fault, if you should exact a fine for their absence, it might be imputed to us. For, although authority had been delegated to us, perhaps we did not use it fully enough and ought to have watched more carefully to ensure their immunity. We wish you well in the Lord.

## LETTER CXVII. [TO MATTHEW, ARCHDEACON OF GLOUCESTER.]

G., by God’s grace Bishop of Hereford, to his friend Matthew, Archdeacon of Gloucester, greeting.

Some time ago the bearer of this letter, U. de Pedeure, came to us complaining that you had suspended him without any just cause intervening and had, by your authority, promulgated the sentence which your dean had pronounced against him. Now, however, returning to us again, he confesses that he had believed otherwise than the facts were, and declares that whatever his dean may have done rashly against him, the dean did so without your knowledge. Therefore, to the degree that he then filled your ears, as one ignorant of the facts, with complaints, he now likewise extols your fairness with praises. Since an error of fact ought to harm no one, we entreat your kindness to receive him kindly as one well-disposed; and, with his former favour restored, to forgive at our request the slight offence which intervened. Farewell.

## LETTER CXVIII. [TO A., COUNTESS OF LEICESTER.]

G., by God’s grace Bishop of Hereford, to his beloved A., venerable Countess of Leicester, whom he must always love in the Lord: greeting, both the peace which now is and that which we hope for in the Lord.

Dearest lady, when I heard the event concerning you which report laments everywhere, I was at once shaken in heart; and whatever joy or gladness had settled in my mind, anxious grief suddenly extinguished at the news of so terrible a misfortune. For we heard that you had lain grievously in a bed of pain and, having almost entered the path of the flesh, had nearly undergone in your whole person everything which death of the flesh can threaten to a human being. But he whom the tears of King Hezekiah, when death was near, moved to pity so as to add fifteen years to him, has himself, moved by the tears and sighs of many saints, graciously restored you, as I gladly hear, who desired him in mind and spirit and who tended with all affection toward the blessed homeland; and, when you stood as it were at the point of departure, he has most mercifully recalled you to us.

You had, I think, already begun to smell the flowers of the heavenly country and perhaps lament that joys already tasted were being deferred from you. Bear the Lord patiently, I beg you, dearest lady: what he postpones he does not take away; what he suspends for a time he afterward restores in glory, increased. There is no one in paradise who can need examples of good persons for his own advancement. Where perfection is absent, an example is plainly needed. We know that many have advanced through your example; and, now that you have been taken away from their midst, lest they run uncertainly, they have cause to give thanks because they retain you as an example of virtue. Keeping it before their eyes, they should strive to conform themselves to virtue.

Act therefore, dearest lady, and take care that we do not lose through your negligence you whom we have received back by so great a gift of God. You have around you experienced fathers, faithfully assisting you and embracing you with the same charity as themselves. I beg you: obey their admonitions and assent to their counsels. Your flesh has been deprived of strength by extreme weakness; having struggled with death, it would not have escaped unless the Lord had brought help. Yet I do not doubt that you always zealously pursue virtue; therefore I fear even the fasts which now press upon you. I beg you not to recoil from what I write; for the present, accept wholesome advice. I beg you, support your exhausted flesh with fleshly food, and generously repay to the Lord’s poor the small amount by which you restore yourself.

I think that the brethren around you agree with me in this: that, until [uncertain: the text is corrupt at this point], you should allow your weak limbs and your life, as it were placed upon your very lips at the last extremity, to be sustained by food of flesh; and that, while providing for yourself against exhaustion, you should distribute food and clothing meanwhile to thirteen brethren and graciously assist their need with charity.

> **[Note: Col. 0831D]** Something appears to be missing here.

Farewell, dearest lady, and cheer the mind of your supplicating friend by a kindly hearing.

## LETTER CXIX. TO KING HENRY.

To his lord, dearer to him than all others, the illustrious king of the English H., brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford: the service of a devoted mind offered every day to the Lord.

[Col. 0831D] I beg my lord not to be angered if his humble friend makes a brief supplication to his clemency. The lord chancellor urges me to undertake the charge of the bishopric of London and, from the revenues of the bishopric, to maintain the bishop himself and his household, while reserving the remainder to be expended for my lord king as the Spirit of God may suggest to him. Since this is perilous for me and gravely detrimental to my soul, I cast myself in heart at the feet of Your Highness and beseech that Your Highness free me from this burden and entrust this office to be administered by another whom you please. I trust in the Lord’s mercy that, at my petition, He will incline the heart of my lord king and gladden me by your gracious hearing, [Col. 0832A] so that I may give myself more devoutly to the service owed to God and, with all the powers of my soul, pray to Him for your welfare all the more purely because more freely. May the Lord surround you with His impregnable wall and always protect you with the weapons of His power, my lord most beloved in Christ.

## LETTER CXX. TO THEOBALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

To his father and lord T., by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury, brother G., minister of Hereford, the faithful offering of obedience from the affection of deepest love.

The reason why we write at present to Your Highness, beloved by us and always to be loved in the Lord, is that we may, as far as we can, exempt the venerable man Hugh, dean of London, from an impending loss, lest, by furnishing an occasion for loss, we ourselves may seem thereby to have inflicted that loss upon him. Our beloved Richard, of good memory, formerly bishop of London, when suffering his final illness, found that all those whom he had promoted or bound to himself by benefits feared, on various pretexts, to undertake the administration of his affairs. Therefore the lord of Lincoln and I, when we had come to visit him, advised him not to permit his household any longer to fluctuate in an uncertain condition, but to commit the administration and care of his affairs to the aforesaid dean and to Nicholas the archdeacon, compelling them to this by the force of obedience. They, indeed, having considered the burden of the business, would have declined this command with much entreaty, [Col. 0832C] unless at last they had yielded to the prayers and counsels of the lord of Lincoln and ourselves in this matter.

Accordingly, because the agreement of every contract enlarges or restricts its nature, and the circumstances give their form to every act, we earnestly present our prayers to Your Highness: defer the action which the creditors of the aforesaid bishop have brought against the aforesaid dean on account of this administration, until we can be present with you, so that by our report and testimony together you may learn in what manner and on what terms he undertook this administration. Know that he by no means undertook the bishop’s burden of debts, nor assumed this administration otherwise than in order to manage his affairs and faithfully maintain him [Col. 0832D] and his household. And if anything remained from his revenues and annual proceeds, he was to pay it where the necessity of debt pressed most urgently—not as a creditor might wish, but as the circumstances required.

We took care to make this known to Your Holiness lest you compel your clerk to pay what he did not take, nor, by allowing him in any way to be burdened with unjust payments for this work of charity, deter your other sons henceforth—God forbid!—from rendering service to their father. We wish you health, dearest Father in Christ.

## LETTER CXXI. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord T., by God’s grace [Col. 0833A] Archbishop of Canterbury, brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford: may you so fight, if only that you may conquer.

This bearer of the present letter, my lord—our intimate associate, a canon of our church, commendable for his merits—we most earnestly commend to Your Highness, beloved by us in the Lord. We affectionately beseech you, for God’s love and at our petition, to support his cause insofar as justice requires, and not permit his right to be oppressed through the craftiness of his adversaries or to perish in your presence. Although those opposing him envelop the matter in a great cloud of falsehood, we hope from the fairness of your judgment that falsehood will soon vanish before you, and that the darkness of iniquity will easily be scattered by the light of your examination.

May that spirit therefore be strong in you [Col. 0833B] which long ago preserved innocent blood in the prophet, so that, when in the spirit of discernment you have rescued our clerk from the charges maliciously fabricated against him, you may have us as debtors to your favour and him as ever bound to your service. We wish you health, dearest Father in Christ.

## LETTER CXXII. TO ALL THE SONS OF HOLY MOTHER CHURCH

To all the sons of holy mother Church beloved by him in the Lord, brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford: love in Christ and everlasting salvation.

Agreements entered into by the consent of contracting parties acquire stable force only when they are received in the documents, and confirmed by the seals, of those whose authority can ratify them. Therefore we have taken care to commit to writing the agreement made between Herebert, our canon, and William, chaplain of Lord T., Archbishop of Canterbury, concerning the church of Hinteberga, so that, in the matter pledged between them upon their given faith, each may be held bound to the other by a written account faithfully setting forth the transaction.

Herebert granted to the aforesaid William, to hold and possess in perpetual vicarage and alms for an annual rent of thirty shillings, a certain part of his prebend: namely, the church of Hinteberga with the chapel of St Lawrence and all else belonging to that church. In the presence of us and our chapter, [Col. 0833D] he invested him with it. But since by law a canon may not dispose of his prebend beyond the day of his death, I and the whole body of our chapter extend this agreement through the whole life of the aforesaid William. By unanimous consent we grant and establish that, if William survives Herebert, he shall be bound to pay to the person substituted for Herebert in that prebend the same sum, and no greater, if that successor should wish it; but, upon payment of the aforesaid rent, he shall enjoy the fullest security through our authority and that of our chapter.

After William’s death, however, our canon—whoever he shall then be—shall have free power to dispose of the same church: either to hold it himself or to grant it to whomever he wishes at a larger rent. Since we deem this firm and unshakeable, [Col. 0834A] I and our chapter confirm it by this present writing and by the attachment of our seals. Witnesses . . . (The remainder is absent.)

## LETTER CXXIII. ROBERT, BISHOP OF HEREFORD, TO THE SAME

To all the brethren, sons beloved in Christ, of holy mother Church: R., by God’s grace bishop of Hereford, [wishes them] diligently to await the Lord and joyfully to embrace Him when He comes.

Since, by the Lord’s permission, we have undertaken to govern the Church of God and administer some part of it, we ought, by the stewardship entrusted to us, to consult and provide for its welfare as far as we can. We judge that this may rightly be done if, by strengthening what has been broken and restoring to one body what has been dispersed, we strive to serve both its preservation and the increase of divine worship.

Therefore, since it is evident to all who devoutly believe that neither a marketplace is suited to religion nor a castle—a place of tumult and bloodshed—to the peace fitting for those who serve the Lord, we have united into one ecclesiastical body the church of Blessed Peter, situated in the marketplace of Hereford, and the church of St Guthlac, inconveniently placed within the enclosure of that castle, with all their possessions, parishes, and dignities. We have established by episcopal authority, for the perpetual service of the Lord, the church of the Apostles Peter and Paul and of St Guthlac, which we have caused to be built outside that city in a place most suitable to religious life.

And lest we seem, [Col. 0834C] by our authority, to burden anyone or prejudice anyone’s right, we make known by this present document to those now living and to the sons who shall be born and arise after us that Roger de Port, who had long unjustly held the church of St Guthlac as a layman and unworthily dispersed its possessions, acknowledged this great sin. In my presence, and that of brother Ralph our dean, and of our canons Hugh de Clifford and many others, clerical and lay, he entirely surrendered the church into our hand, so that it might be more fully assigned to divine offices.

Therefore, at the devout request of Roger himself, and with the gracious assent of our venerable brother the abbot of Gloucester and his convent, we joined the aforesaid churches into one, and designated this church, endowed and provided with all their possessions, dignities, and appurtenances, for the perpetual veneration of the Apostles Peter and Paul and St Guthlac. And because, God so disposing, we are to receive there, through the hand of the aforesaid abbot of Gloucester, a convent of brethren serving God and living there according to the Rule, we have committed this same church of the Apostles and St Guthlac to the obedience of the aforesaid abbot and all his successors, and to the guardianship and subjection of the church of Blessed Peter at Gloucester, with the unanimous assent of the chapter of our church in all these matters.

Whoever shall devoutly consider this work of piety and extend a helping hand, with faithful devotion, to confirm it, may receive the perpetual fellowship of the prayers offered there, an episcopal blessing from me, however unworthy a minister of the Church, and eternal recompense from Christ, the supreme pontiff. Amen.

## LETTER CXXIV. TO A. (POPE ADRIAN)

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff A., brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford: due reverence and affection to apostolic highness.

The reason, my lord, why we write to Your Blessedness concerning the case of an honest and poor clerk, Simon, canon of Lichfield, the bearer of this letter, is that we endure with distress an injury done to him which indeed redounds upon the dignity of the stewardship entrusted to you. When he had appealed to your jurisdiction against the prior of Coventry and his brethren, who were attempting to expel him from a part of his prebend, namely the church of Hunitune, and when afterwards the lord bishop of Chester and I had met at Worcester on Church business, he renewed his appeal in our presence. For the protection and defence of himself and his goods, he cited the prior himself, then present, to appear before Your Highness on Laetare Jerusalem Sunday.

Although, in view of the eminence of your authority, all things ought then to have been secure, a sacrilegious hand nevertheless broke forth with such audacity as to seize within the bounds of the cemetery his tithes and the fruits of the current year, gathered by him with great labour, and to carry them away. Whether this was done with or without the prior’s knowledge, we do not doubt that it was perpetrated by his men. Thus we cannot restrain our indignation from beseeching Your Holiness to correct this presumption: may your apostolic hand justly punish this injury in order to correct others, and mercifully assist the needy man in his distress.

For we have inspected the charters of Lord Roger, formerly bishop of Chester, and of our beloved father Lord Theobald of Canterbury, and have thereby learned with certainty that this church had been conferred upon him as a prebend before the settlement made, through the hand of Pope Eugenius of holy memory, between the churches of Chester and Coventry. May Your Holiness flourish in the Lord, my lord Father.

## LETTER CXXV. TO THE PARISHIONERS OF THE CHURCH OF HEREFORD

[Col. 0835D]

GILBERT, by God’s grace bishop of Hereford, to all the parishioners and sons of the same Church beloved by him in the Lord: salvation, grace, and blessing.

What our predecessor of good memory, Lord Bishop Robert, wholesomely did and established for the honour of God and for the beauty and benefit alike of holy Church, we, following in his footsteps, grant and confirm by the authority bestowed upon us by God. Since the aforesaid our predecessor decreed to unite into one body the church of Blessed Peter situated in the marketplace of Hereford and the church of St Guthlac founded within the circuit of Hereford Castle; to establish one church of the blessed Apostles [Col. 0836A] Peter and Paul and St Guthlac from the possessions of the aforesaid churches; to build it outside the city in a place most suitable to religious life; and to establish there a convent of monks: we ratify and approve this same measure. We grant to the aforesaid church of the blessed Peter and Paul and St Guthlac all the possessions, dignities, and liberties which the aforesaid two churches possessed in former times and which were confirmed to it by the aforesaid our predecessor; and by this present writing and the attestation of our seal, [we grant] that they may remain secure to it for ever. We have thought fit, however, to state these matters in the following precise terms. (The remainder is lacking.)

## LETTER CXXVI. TO THE BRETHREN OF TEWKESBURY

[Col. 0836B]

G., by God’s grace minister of the Church of Hereford, to the brethren beloved by him in the Lord, who render service to the Lord at Tewkesbury: greetings.

A wise man is taught readily, and those who abound in learning need only a brief reminder. If you voluntarily renounce the liberty concerning the election of your Father which apostolic authority grants and confirms to you, to the great—God forbid!—prejudice of your church, it is surely just that thereafter you should lack that liberty and long bear the yoke which you have accepted by your own choice. Since this is a deceitful, indeed an exceedingly dangerous, course for you, we command you and counsel you in brotherly love unanimously to devote yourselves to preserving your liberty, [Col. 0836C] lest, if you should perhaps do otherwise to oblige anyone, you later mourn with a late and fruitless repentance over damage to your church when you can no longer repair it. May your charity flourish, dearest brothers.

## LETTER CXXVII. TO R., COUNT OF LEICESTER

To the venerable lord and dearest friend in Christ, Count R. of Leicester, brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford: salvation and grace, and everlasting blessing from the hand of the Father on high.

In matters which my diligence can accomplish, dearest one, you ought to employ not request but command. For you have, and always shall have, full authority to command me; and for my part a ready will to obey you neither fails nor ever shall fail. Indeed, reason so orders your requests and commands, honourableness adorns them, and modesty, their constant companion, moderates them, that for those who desire what is honourable it is most difficult to refuse them.

In the business regarding which I lately received the command of Your Highness—the business, namely, of the brethren of Tewkesbury—I would certainly have helped them more readily and much more effectively with counsel and aid had they at least communicated with me, even by word, on the day when the urgent command of the lord of Canterbury and the force of obedience imposed upon me obliged me to go there and inquire into the election that had been made. Since I was not admitted by them, I could not bestow a benefit upon them against their will; now, for the love of God and in reverence for your command, I shall not refuse it even to the ungrateful.

For I approve and commend the worthiness of the person elected. And if, when the matter itself is handled, it should happen that I am present, then, prompted by your request, I shall do all that I can, without prejudice to the peace of the prelates, toward his promotion for the honour and advantage of the brethren and the monastery of Tewkesbury. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVIII. TO ROBERT, BISHOP OF LINCOLN

To the venerable lord and dearest brother R., by God’s grace bishop of Lincoln, brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford: may you wisely and soberly walk while bearing Christ within yourself.

Upon receiving the letter with which your diligence deigned to gladden us, a day at once more welcome than usual and brighter than customary dawned upon us. For, having heard of the events of affairs [lacuna], and, through a certain subtle complexity of circumstances, that peace had been removed from our midst, we had hoped neither that it could quickly be restored once broken nor that the greatly estranged minds of kings could easily be reconciled to one another. But He who commands the winds and makes the storm at sea quickly become a calm, and who, by the sovereign power which He possesses, at once turns troubled things toward the good of peace, whenever He wills, by removing the cloud of discord—He does so.

Thus, since our peace depends upon the peace of our lord the king, that very hope of peace which we have conceived from the now favourable report brings, with the Lord’s help, a kind of anticipatory joy of rejoicing to the Church and kingdom of England. What is especially relevant to ourselves is this: with deepest affection we rejoice at your safety, which the letter sent by you declares, giving thanks to Him who kindly walks with His own and, with an angel as companion, accompanies their journey and their actions. We now await your return with longing; for to a desiring heart, one never hastens enough. We bear the delay with distress and, that we may meet you in longed-for embraces, day by day hope for and await news of your coming. May my lord and dearest brother in Christ flourish.

## LETTER CXXIX. TO ALL THE SONS OF HOLY MOTHER CHURCH

To all the sons of holy mother Church beloved by him in the Lord, brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford: the salvation which now is and which we hope for from the Lord.

[Col. 0837D] Matters once troubled by the disturbance of litigation are restored to peace when its fuel has been extinguished. Once peace has been restored between certain persons, however, it must be strengthened by lawful agreements lest it readily disappear upon the emergence of some new cause; so it must also be recorded in writing and, for its lasting firmness, attested and strengthened by the memorial of documents.

Let your discretion therefore know that the suit long disputed between John, clerk, and Reginald de Pagabam concerning the church of Credintune, which our father Lord Pope Alexander delegated to us, that we might carefully hear it and, having diligently heard and considered the arguments of each party, decide it by means of justice after removing the impediment of appeal, was at last settled in the following manner. For when John, having produced a multitude of witnesses, sought restitution to himself of the said church in its entirety, Reginald, knowing the facts of the case to be uncertain, forestalled judgment by conceding to John in every respect one full half of the said church, and thus, by settling with him, put an end to the suit. John preferred to accept in peace the portion of the church offered to him rather than burden his witnesses with proofs and oaths.

The Gospels having therefore been touched, each party swore that neither should henceforth defraud the other of his own portion, but that each should preserve the other’s right whole and unimpaired. Should either die while the other survives, his right shall revert to the survivor in respect of the other’s part, this provision remaining fully intact. Since this was done before us, desiring that all things should be brought to the end of peace, we approved it and gave our assent to the settlement thus concluded. We confirm it, that it may remain valid for ever, by this present writing and the attestation of our seal.

## LETTER CXXX. TO RICHARD, BISHOP OF LONDON

To the venerable lord and dearest brother R., by God’s grace bishop of London, brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford: greetings and affection.

You know, dearest one, what is written: whatever may happen to the righteous, it should not disturb him at all. For he contemplates with the eyes of his heart the Apostle’s saying that all things work together for good to those who are good (Rom. 8). Accordingly, if prosperous events abound, he joins the prophet in singing: “I will sing to the Lord who has bestowed good things upon me” (Ps. 12); if adversities meet him, he sings with the lips of his heart: “You have overshadowed my head in the day of battle” (Ps. 139).

While I reflect upon these matters, dearest one, I fear no assault of fortune for you. If fortune comes happily, it is received gently; if it rushes upon you adversely, it is not feared. The firmness of your mind and the perfection of your ways, long known to me, readily persuade me of this concerning you. If, as we firmly hope, these things plant their root in the soil of your mind, then the blast of temptation will find you not a reed shaken by the wind in the mire of many waters, but a cedar of Lebanon, firmly rooted in the virtues.

Nor do I say this as though the tenor of your letter had reported to me some adversity befalling you. It does indeed report an appeal lodged against you and the solemn completion of your already effected grant suspended by appeal to the lord pope. But what is discerned in this except that the slackness or torpor of your mind is stirred or shaken off? For, having found a man after your own heart, and having advanced him by grace to something better, you ought to have advanced him—not merely, I say, to something better, but to become in you another self.

Thrift at the bottom of the purse is now nearly too late; except that it is both expedient and necessary for you to redeem your torpor by some bodily exertion, and to accomplish, through the energy of the mind rousing and vigorously exerting itself, what was previously done too little. In this I see no cause for sadness. For, removed for a time from the storm of this realm, you shall, by the Lord’s gift, take a quiet and peaceful journey; strengthened by the aids of the virtues, you shall fearlessly see the face [Col. 0839A] of the supreme pontiff and assuredly stand with favour before the senators of the curia.

Nor should the welcome reception given for some time to your adversary in public celebrations trouble you. For from this I conceive hope, where perhaps another predicts despair. If a well-behaved and educated young man has deserved to be heard and to please among the gods, what favour will be withheld from a bishop no less adorned in morals or fortified in learning—who is nonetheless far higher in rank and more powerful in fortune—so that he too should be unable to win favour among good men? You contend as a defendant deserving goodwill, not to gain profit but to avert loss. You desire that what, before receipt of the lord pope’s letters, you conferred through a proxy upon a person suitable by every testimony should remain valid.

I know that temple of justice—the apostolic breast—from which equity flows out to all, to dispense all things with moderation. He who was able not to deny another what belongs to your right will not, once the reverence due to him has been paid, consider it a great matter to restore to you what is yours. The Lord will provide honourable and beneficial outcomes for you, and the Godhead, appeased by prayer, will turn into the glory of the good what your adversary’s wickedness contrives to your dishonour.

For my part, the present arrival of the duke of the Normans has so hindered me that I lack the means for this journey, though my will wholly urges it. You will therefore go without me, half of my soul, and the sails which you bring back will affect my mind, held in suspense, according to the tidings they bear. Since after my episcopacy I have in nothing served the lord pope or the curia, I have been afraid to send them words. For I do not know what or how to write, and I know that my letter would add little to your presence. Yet for your journey, both in what you have directed and still more in what inward affection urges, I shall most gladly make provision. Meanwhile, if an honourable settlement offers itself, I beg and advise that it be accepted. May my beloved flourish.

## LETTER CXXXI. TO THEOBALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

To his father and lord T., by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury, primate of England and legate of the apostolic see, brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford: greetings and obedience.

Desiring to know what concerns you and to obey you in all things according to our ability, we send to you the bearer of this letter, that from your reply we may learn something certain about your crossing of the sea and your delay either on this side or beyond the sea. For, with the Lord’s help, we shall not run uncertainly when we have certain knowledge concerning you.

Further, if it please you, we ask you briefly to consider the case pending between the count of Hereford and G. de Laci. G. de Laci complained to us that the count of Hereford had seized one of his knights, namely Richard Brito, in a certain cemetery. The knight, sending messengers to us from the prison in which he was held, offered proof of this matter and besought our office to grant him temporary freedom of his person, so that he might appear in court on his own behalf [Col. 0840A] and present whatever he had to allege for his release. Judging this consonant with equity, we enjoined the count, by judicial decision, to grant the aforesaid knight access to himself on an appointed day, so that he might, as stated, appear in court and act on his own behalf—on condition, however, that unless the Church released him, he should return himself to the count.

But the count, asserting that he was aggrieved, set the day immediately after the feast of St Lawrence and appealed to your jurisdiction. Since it seems inhumane that the aforesaid knight should be prolonged into a distant appeal while nevertheless being held in prison and chains, we present our prayers to Your Highness that you order the count to produce the aforesaid knight before you on an appointed day, with every security given that, unless your judgment releases him, he will return to his chains. We judge this equitable and good, most worthy of the authority to which appeal has been made, and likely to provide greatly not only for your honour in this matter but also for our peace.

One further point remains which we earnestly ask your most prudent wisdom to consider. The count of Hereford communicates in all things with William de Bellocampo, whom you have excommunicated. It is most necessary that by a strict command you urge both him and us to ensure that he either abstains from communion and association with William or is himself involved in an equal sentence of anathema. For the authority of anathema is cheapened unless fitting severity also corrects those who communicate with excommunicated persons. Therefore, should it please you to exercise your zeal in this matter, unless he ceases from the aforesaid conduct, he ought to be publicly declared excommunicate. May my dearest lord flourish.

## LETTER CXXXII. TO . . . . .

The affection of one who offers pious greetings, and the duty of one who loves sincerely.

We warmly rejoice, beloved brother in the Lord, at your welfare, which we have learned from the report of certain persons. With inward delight we rejoice that you visited the thresholds of the Apostles, stood with favour before the supreme pontiff and the holy curia, successfully concluded your affairs, and happily returned home. Since at the request of certain persons an occasion arose to write to you, we thought it right to signify to you the affection of our heart, [Col. 0840D] so that, should anything concerning us please your charity, you might employ neither entreaty nor request, but, extending yourself powerfully in the role of a friend, employ rather your authority than in any way seek favour by the office of a petition.

We also conceive hope of obtaining our desire if we set before your kindness the wish of ourselves or of our friend. There is with you a certain associate of ours, namely Peter, clerk of Roger de Mand’ [uncertain expansion]. Our devotion commends him to your protection and patronage, beseeching that you establish by your authority, insofar as reason permits, the benefaction which his lord has resolved to confer upon him in certain churches. Thus you will have him ever bound to your service [Col. 0841A] and us as debtors to your favour. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXIII. TO RICHARD, BISHOP OF LONDON

To the venerable lord and dearest brother R., by God’s grace bishop of London, brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford: greetings and affection.

At present no other advice occurs to me concerning your business except that, if an honourable settlement offers itself, it should be accepted. But you, undertake your intended journey, and, with the Lord’s help, brandish the horn of justice against those opposing you on the Field of Mars. We hear Scyllas of envious barking breaking forth on every side; with every breeze of the Holy Spirit blowing, you shall sail prosperously. If necessity demands it, it is better to serve the lord pope even to the point of astonishment and miracle than to succumb in the contest you have begun. We speak harshly, although we hope for far better things. For the lord pope has written harshly, but we certainly believe that all this will be moderated by apostolic gentleness when we are present and press our suit. Farewell; stand firm in the faith; act manfully (1 Cor. 16); and may the God of peace swiftly crush every Satan beneath your feet. Amen. We are sending our monk to you, that we may receive certain news of your condition.

## LETTER CXXXIV. TO ROBERT, COUNT OF GLOUCESTER

G., by God’s grace bishop of Hereford, to ROBERT, illustrious count of [Col. 0841C] Gloucester: the companionship of peace and justice.

Among the praiseworthy titles of your merit, beloved count, this shines with a special lamp of pure light: that in places under your power you kindly foster and protect the Church of God, and preserve the peace of those who serve God not for the vile price of a payment in rusty bronze, but by the generosity of a most pure mind. Since every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights (James 1), this benefit has undoubtedly been bestowed upon you not from the earth below but from heaven above: alone among the powerful and noble of this realm, you shine in wisdom, character, and honour, and, as we hear, ever advancing toward what is better, you abundantly yield to the Author of your life fruits worthy of Him.

Since this is a gift of heavenly treasure, it must be preserved and sealed all the more diligently. I rejoice and rejoice with you that the Lord Jesus has found a dwelling with you beneath fine linen and purple, and that, though young in years, you have nevertheless gone forward mature in judgment among the badly corrupt rulers of this realm without the taint of vice, commendably devoting earnest labour to peace and wisdom rather than youthful frivolities. This, beloved count, is what wins you favour before God; what obtains for you the prayers of religious minds; what grants you fellowship not only in the prayers but also in the holy private devotions of God’s servants.

We therefore wish that, having begun to run well, you may finish the course excellently, and that on that day you may receive from the Watcher of hearts and Giver of graces rewards worthy of the reverence so often shown to Him and to His Church. Further, through us the poor church of Winchcombe petitions you that through you it may find favour with your churchwarden, Peter de Saltemareis, and that your piety may provide for its peace with him. If you grant this request, you will make them bound to your service and us debtors to your favour. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXV. TO R. OF WORCESTER

G., by God’s grace bishop of Hereford, to his dearest friend R. of Worcester: greetings.

That you sympathize with the affliction of my reputation in a friendly spirit, I repay with manifold thanks, reckoning as a consolation in misfortune the sincerity of friendship that I experience in you. Yet I would have you be one who grieves over what ought to be grieved over, and bears with equanimity what ought not to be grieved over. For very many are carried away by one error: unless whatever their own will may be is obeyed, they think that no justice whatsoever is done to them. If such men disparage me, if with envious barking they bite and tear apart my reputation, whatever it may be, I bear it calmly; and while reason supports me, while the form of law agrees with me, I despise all these men, as it were from some higher ground of reason and understanding. For I consider not how many dislike me, but what sort of men they are.

I would have you also keep a reluctant ear for accusations. “He who judges hastens quickly to repentance.” If I have acted less than I ought, if I have exceeded due measure, judge yourselves; decide yourselves, I beg you. When word reached me that the Count of Hereford had seized your knights in Evesham church, I hoped that I, as vicar of the Church of Worcester, and our judgment on these matters ought to be sought and awaited. Hence I appointed a day for the parties, and I too took my seat in their midst, hoping to hear and judge the case. There judicial authority was taken from my hands, and the Archdeacon of Worcester declared that the fullness of this authority belonged so completely to himself that he admitted no intermediary at all between himself and the lord of Canterbury; and by adjuring and calling upon them as witnesses he entirely turned away from me all the persons who had assembled. He asserted, on the testimony of many, that the lord of Worcester had so determined on his departure and had so decreed by full authority.

What was I to do amid these circumstances? Episcopal dignity would not allow me to submit myself, in judging the Church’s causes, as inferior to one who was inferior in rank. Yet the authority and dignity entrusted to me did not permit me to stand alongside an equal or superior. You, R., notice the injury to yourselves and your knights; but if the aforesaid archdeacon spits in my face, you entirely disregard that. Judge now, then; decide now what remained for me to do. Was I to judge in that very Church, which neither recognized me as judge nor entrusted cases to me for judgment? For it is a fault to involve oneself in business that does not concern one.

But perhaps you will object: whatever that archdeacon proclaimed, you were nevertheless vicar of the Church of Worcester, and, if he himself had pronounced anything irregularly, you ought to have corrected and punished it in him. R., you are stirring up wars for me. I answer you plainly: the game is not worth the candle to me. I count it a burden, not an honour, to be entangled in other men’s affairs. He rendered me a service who withdrew me from this care. Let those to whom great matters are entrusted carry out their great affairs; my own small concerns suffice for me. Let their own proclamations of praise follow those happy men; let it always remain fixed in my mind to delight either in no praises or in true ones.

Act, then, and rescue me now, if you please, from the teeth of those who tear me to pieces; and do not allow me, who have deserved no evil, to be choked by the words of detractors. Your men have one whom they may follow, from whom they may demand redress for their wrongs: one who may punish offences by the vigour of justice, repair what has fallen, restore what has been lost, and whom they may extol with their praises if he has acted well; but if he has acted badly, he too will find this.

Yet I wish you to understand what was done. A day was appointed for the Count of Hereford by the lord archdeacon; after the allegations of the parties had been heard, judgment was pronounced. The count obeyed the judgment and departed absolved by the judge. What that judgment obtained for you, you know well enough. I know one thing: after the legate’s letters which you sent had been read in the count’s presence, the count immediately appealed to the legate himself, asserting that he was grievously oppressed because a case concerning which he had complied in every respect with the judgment of the Archdeacon and Church of Worcester was being instituted against him anew and revived.

He has before him what is written: “Rescripts that have been obtained ought not to be admitted if cases once decided by a judicial sentence—which no appeal has suspended—are involved; rather, those who have procured such writings are to be excluded even from the threshold of the courts.” But now again you will be inflamed, and, unless after an appeal has been made I pronounce a sentence of interdict or anathema against the count whom your judge has absolved, you will regard me—[lacuna]—as a contemner of ecclesiastical justice and as the cause of your losses, not indeed in your own judgment, but in that of your men. If you do so, I consider patience necessary for myself and trouble necessary for you. Yet, I beg you, keep yourself commendably within the bounds of this trouble.

If I thought myself wholly competent in military business, since I do not doubt that you are sufficiently experienced in such matters, I would embrace your counsel in this with every pleasure. You likewise, since you have advanced no little way into the field of letters and ecclesiastical causes, do not, I beg, despise the counsel of a friend. For since I have, so to speak, spent my lifetime in matters of this kind, I seem to myself at least to claim a certain right to this teaching.

Know, dearest friend, what is written: “What you request is not new: although the authority of my rescript has intervened, nevertheless the right of appeal is not to be denied.” Hence it is indeed clear that, after receipt of the lord legate’s letters, I could not prevent the count from appealing. Again, know what is written in the passage immediately following: “Once an appeal has been entered, even though rejected by the judge, it has very often been determined that nothing is to be done to the prejudice of the deliberation, and that everything is to remain in the state in which it was at the time of the pronouncement.” Hence it is plainly understood that, after the appeal had been made, I was not permitted to alter anything concerning the appellant’s position, whether by interdict or anathema.

But perhaps you will say that this was not granted to the appellant with respect to the sentence, but only with respect to execution of the sentence. Know, however, what is written: the execution of a judgment is customarily suspended if the person against whom judgment has been rendered promises to show that the judicial authority was deceived by false allegations.
