Since the count asserts that he will do this on the day after the feast of Saint Lawrence, we for the present leave him, as having escaped our jurisdiction, undisturbed; and we commit him, together with our letters containing the course of events, to the lord legate, in accordance with the authority of laws and canons. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXVI. TO A., BISHOP OF LINCOLN

[Col. 0844B]

Brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford, to the venerable lord and dearest brother A., by the grace of God Bishop of Lincoln: greeting.

Hastening to enjoy the hoped-for sight and conversation with you, we had now arrived at Prestbury. A fateful misfortune interrupted our desire; while another necessity drew you away, the momentum of our journey was dashed and, against our wish and will, restrained. Yet we write to you as a proof of affection—indeed, as a claim upon every bond of friendship—that you may support our kinsman and friend G. Foliot in the case which his Church is bringing against him, and may have him supported by your own counsel and that of your people; so that your presence may make up to him for our absence, and that, through kindness and favour bestowed upon him, he may recognize what influence we have with you.

At your feet—which we would more gladly embrace with our hands, though for the present we cannot—we lay these petitions in supplication, expecting great honour from being heard, or no small embarrassment from a refusal. Moreover, if it should please you to communicate privately to our counsel some matter from your writings not to be shared with others, do not be weary of remembering our former studies, of returning for a moment to the schoolroom, and of writing with your own hand what the slenderness of our understanding may answer when the matter is not communicated to another. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXVII. TO RICHARD, BISHOP OF LONDON

[Col. 0844D]

Brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford, to the venerable lord and dearest brother R., by the grace of God Bishop of London: greeting.

I congratulate you on the peace which has been restored with John. I hope, however, that the matters which have lately arisen may be pacified through the intervention of some discerning prudence. I am grieved and wholly dismayed in spirit that you allowed such things to break out against you—things which even moderate, provided prudent, foresight could have suppressed altogether. For although what is said is false, it is nevertheless being spread abroad, casting the evil tale of this accusation through the ears of many.

I judge the diligence of the lord of Lincoln necessary, so that by whatever means he can he may summon Henry to himself and apply himself to the affair, with the result that Henry, returning to his senses, may abandon both what anger has prompted and his intended course and appeal. This will certainly not be difficult for a wise man to achieve, if he knows how to leave no stone unturned. For it is easy to make an accusation, but to convict a bishop or an honourable cleric in such a matter is surely beyond his powers. He should certainly fear lest the punishment which he threatens against another overwhelm and entangle himself.

Whatever he does, however, you must go to the lord pope; though you would act much more honourably if, upon the confession of the penitent, the charges made against you were erased. Moreover, I am prepared to meet you for conversation at Oxford on the Wednesday next after the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin. But for the journey which you require, I am altogether unprepared. For although what I possess is at peace, I nevertheless understand that my own presence is wholly necessary for preserving it. Even if, in my absence, it should happen not to be disturbed, yet the bruchus would consume among us so thoroughly what the locust has left that after the bruchus the caterpillar would find nothing left to eat. Farewell; and, if he is available for our meeting, summon the lord of Lincoln.

## LETTER CXXXVIII. TO GILBERT DE LACY

G., by the grace of God Bishop of Hereford, to Lord Gilbert de Lacy: may you obtain the benefits of salvation by acting well.

My lord king has commanded me to render you canonical justice against the Count of Hereford, who, it is said, is compelling your knights, captured in a church and cemetery, to pay ransom. In this matter, know that, insofar as I can do so without prejudice to my office, I shall gladly obey the royal command. But under the statutes of the laws and the authority of the sacred canons, I am permitted to do nothing further in this matter than what is known to have been done by me before I received the letters. For I appointed a day for this case, heard the parties’ dispute, and gave judgment on what I heard. Since I neither can nor could prevent anyone from appealing, I heard the count’s appeal against the adjudicated matter.

Once the appeal was made, it is just and canonical that I should undertake nothing further concerning this case, except to transmit, through both parties, letters containing almost the entire sequence of events to the judge to whom appeal has been made. Immediately after the appeal, I offered these letters, which are also called apostoli, both to the count and to your knights. Since you did not accept them, perhaps you will obtain less on the very day of appeal. Beyond this, I have no more authority in this matter than the humblest cleric of my bishopric.

I call Truth itself, which is God, to witness that, had the count not prevented me by entering an appeal, no judgment against him would have been delayed through love, hatred, or any favour whatsoever. But if you do not believe that I can do nothing contrary to an appeal, hear the canon itself: “If anyone, disregarding the authority of the judge to whom appeal has been made, nevertheless carries out by execution a matter adjudged even lawfully by himself, he strips himself of the judicial authority with which he shone.” Again, it is written elsewhere: “Once an appeal has been entered, even though rejected by the judge, it has very often been determined that nothing is to be done to the prejudice of the deliberation, and that everything is to remain in the state in which it was at the time of the pronouncement. Hence it is plainly understood after an appeal has been made,” etc.

For if we lose sheep, oxen, or other things of that kind, by the Lord’s gift we can recover them. But if through ignorance, folly, or stubborn disobedience we are once deposed from bishopric and office, we shall not easily find someone to give us another. Therefore, in matters of this kind it is better for us to suffer whatever loss than to endanger our office.

If it pleased you to hear my advice, you would not seek an occasion against me; for I, thank God, am prepared for every fortune, both favourable and adverse. The less I possess, the less, certainly, I shall fear; and, with the Lord’s help, the more I shall be able to do. If you would receive from me the letters mentioned above, await the appointed day, and send to the archbishop the squires of R. Brito and the captured knights, then, with the Lord’s help, you can clear him there by proof; and those who will be present on my side will certainly not harm that purpose.

Concerning the king’s command that I recall what was done in his presence regarding the two oxen: I remember it well. The case which I had against you I did not remit, even at his request; but when the archbishop later involved himself, I placed it in a favourable postponement. To this command of the archbishop I shall answer that, had he known of the appeal made to himself, he certainly would have commanded nothing in this matter. To obey him, therefore, is to ensure that nothing be altered in the sequence of the matter itself, and to disclose to him in every respect whatever you may say against us. We nevertheless wish you well.

## LETTER CXXXIX. TO DAVID, BISHOP OF ST DAVIDS

G., by the grace of God Bishop of Hereford, to his venerable brother and friend David, Bishop of St Davids: greeting and affection.

How pleasant and useful the good of peace and concord is may readily be perceived if we consider more carefully how great are the losses arising from contention and discord. For if we consider the various disturbances and the wars that press upon us on every side, it is plainly evident how dangerous it is for the Church to take burden upon burden and, beyond the external troubles which oppress her, to stir up internal wars for herself.

Therefore, if it pleases you to acquiesce in our counsel, let us diligently labour to find some means of peace between you and the lord Bishop of Llandaff. Since this cannot easily be done unless the three of us meet together in one place, we ask you to designate a place where, when we meet, discussion may be held among us concerning your peace. If you choose Hereford for this, we shall be present on whatever day you appoint for it, nor will our entreaties to the lord of Llandaff cease until we bring him too to be present. Let your affection know that we have written to the lord of Llandaff in the same terms and await the agreement and reply of you both. Farewell.

## LETTER CXL. TO WILLIAM, ARCHDEACON OF LONDON

G., by the grace of God Bishop of Hereford, to his beloved William, Archdeacon of London, and Master Henry: greeting.

According to Solomon’s saying, “Many stand before the face of princes, but every judgment proceeds from God.” The hearts of kings are in His hand, and He bends them, when He wills, to everything that He ordains (Proverbs 21). Therefore, if the lord king has not yet given his assent to the undertaking which you have courageously assumed, you must not despair or withdraw from your purpose [lacuna], since it is most easy for God to incline his heart and mind to what shall please Him.

You have already fulfilled what is the chief thing in this affair; I beg you not to fail in the least point of care. Let not an election canonically celebrated fail through your failure—an election which will soon possess full strength if you yourselves do not fail at all. For the greater the favour with God and the glory with men that you have gained by courageously undertaking God’s cause, putting all else aside, the more abundant will be the disgrace that follows if—God forbid!—you abandon, deprived of the spirit of fortitude, that cause which reconciles to you the hearts of the lord pope and almost all men.

Let your heart therefore be strengthened in the Lord (Psalm 30), dearest friends; and, according to the paths which the Lord opens to you, complete what you have begun. Trust in us, so far as we can act, as friends in this affair. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLI. TO THEOBALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

Brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford, to his father and lord T., by the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury, Primate of the English, and legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and obedience.

You commanded us, on the complaint of the abbot and monks of Combermere, to summon Herebert of Halgod Castle and admonish him to restore to the aforesaid monks the place called Prena and to return everything taken from them in that place. When this command reached us, we persuaded the monks, who brought the mandate, not to begin this suit in the absence of their abbot, but, after awaiting his return from overseas parts, to bring the action in his presence. Since they accepted this advice, we postponed the matter with their consent.

Recently, however, when we were sitting at Leintwardine on certain business, the abbot of Combermere—whose return we had not previously known of—was present. There he complained against the prior of Wenlock that the prior had driven his monks from the place called Prena [lacuna], and had taken not only their cattle but also their chalices, books, vestments, and the whole equipment of their house. The prior raised a dilatory exception, replying that this suit had not at all been set forth to him and that he had not been summoned to answer concerning it.

When, with the agreement of all opinions, it was decided that it was equitable and consonant with law to appoint a day for both parties and to settle by judgment a case sufficiently heard, the complaining abbot, because what he sought was not immediately restored to him, rushed to appeal. If you know that anything in the judgment thus given ought to be corrected, you will correct it according to the wisdom granted you and impose whatever you please upon those who will obey your command. May my lord and dearest father in Christ prosper.

## LETTER CXLII. TO THE SAME

Brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford, to his father and lord T., by the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury, Primate of the English, and legate of the Holy Apostolic See: greeting and obedience.

Father, I inform your highness of a case heard before us and suspended by an appeal made to you. Four knights of Robert de Lacy brought before us a complaint against the Count of Hereford: the count, they said, had violently seized them in a cemetery to which they had fled for fear of him and had compelled them to pay ransom. They petitioned your office that what had been taken from them be restored, and that they, as men torn from the threshold of the church, be freed from the count’s hand.

The count replied that he had seized them outside the cemetery and had therefore lawfully compelled them to pay ransom, since they had lain in ambush for him. They were also liable to the excommunication imposed upon violators of the peace of holy days: during the very week of holy Pentecost, in the sacred Ember fast, at night, without preserving the Church’s peace, they had come to seize one of his houses and, caught in the act, had then fallen into his hands. Moreover, that we might more certainly credit his statements, the count added that he would prove what he said by the testimony of suitable witnesses. He voluntarily offered, repeatedly, this proof that he had captured them outside the cemetery, namely while they were engaged in the wrongdoing which they were plotting against him.

Knowing that manifest and hidden matters must be judged differently, we adjured both clerics and laypeople of that place, yet could discover no trace by which the truth might shine forth to us. For the time suited the mystery: the deed had been committed under the silence of night. Further, considering that proof rests upon the plaintiff, and that the person bringing the action ought to furnish proofs by which to establish what he alleges, we asked the knights what proof they offered for their accusation against the count. We found nothing except that three of them, wishing to use one another’s testimony, each produced as witnesses in support of his claim two companions in the same suit, adding nothing except that they had seen him being led, not in the cemetery, but through the cemetery.

After this testimony had been debated for some time, we finally judged it less suitable, both because of the suspicious exchange of mutual benefit and because in this case every one of them presented himself alike as plaintiff against the count and as witness. And malice would often go unpunished by law if [lacuna] men who had been caught in wrongdoing, while inventing respectable accounts of themselves, were permitted to use many testimonies in this fashion.

Since they thus failed with respect to proof, and we could discover nothing certain from their proof, we awarded the count the proof which he had offered in law, so that we might thus put an end to the controversy. This is the judgment which we gave; before it was pronounced, the count offered himself for its execution. After it was pronounced, he appealed to your hearing eight days later. In accordance with the wisdom given you, therefore, either correct it, if you please, or, if it can in any manner stand by law, confirm it.

For our eye may have been dim, but we passed no judgment corrupted by filth or favour. Rather, we do not doubt that the Fathers have often judged in the same manner: when the plaintiff faltered in proof, they tendered an oath to the defendant either for purgation or concerning some harmful allegation, and so put an end to disputes. Yet we know what is written: “If the plaintiff does not prove his case, the defendant shall prevail even if he has provided nothing.” We further infer that, if a defendant who provides nothing prevails, much more shall one prevail who provides many proofs. The judge too, moved by reason, frequently tenders an oath to the defendant.

This reasoning also moved us: the sacrilege perpetrated by the count in Evesham church was still aflame; scandal was increasing at the monastery of Leominster because of a similar offence by the count; and by the secret confession of certain persons who had been present with the count when the knights were seized, we learned that the knights’ complaint rested on truth. Moved by all these considerations, we burdened the count with the proof already mentioned—though we would more gladly have accepted the knights’ proof against him, if the form of law had admitted it. May my lord and dearest father in Christ prosper.

## LETTER CXLIII. TO R., BISHOP OF LINCOLN

G., minister of the Church of Hereford, to the venerable lord and dearest brother R., Bishop of Lincoln: the joys of peace and salvation.

Fasting and abstinent, we have now for an interval of five months lacked, dearest Father, the sight of your face and conversation with you. Therefore we ask that word be sent us whether you are well or otherwise, so that we may share in joy at your prosperity, or, if matters are otherwise, may each in turn put a shoulder beneath adversity as far as we can. For a day dawns bright and more serene for us than for others when we learn that things have gone well for you. But adverse news covers us with darkness and enfolds us in bitterness.

Let consolation, then, be granted to a longing heart, and let a little letter concerning your condition and health be sent back to us—would that it might bring good news. Of ourselves, however, we cannot report anything except what is the case. We suffer continually from weakness of the head, having from the Lord a warning to recognize that what is being shaken by the inward hand of Him who strikes cannot last forever.

Moreover, we are being urged strongly and repeatedly to attend upon the Duke of Normandy and comply with his wishes. Though we have deferred until now, if our condition remains sound, after the Sunday on which he has summoned me we can delay no longer. We shall therefore attend the one commanding us and shall not delay to inform you of what we learn by experience of events.

Moreover, since I have once begun, I shall speak to my lord; and do not, I beg, be indignant if I speak. Gilbert Foliot has the utmost devotion of spirit to bind himself entirely to your service and to spend in your household service what he now wastes in idleness. Therefore, with the prayers of many joined to his own, he petitions that prayers be offered on his behalf: that you may receive him and employ him in your service at his own expense, so that, if you find him suitable and according to your heart, you may count him wholly among your own. Although this would be an honour to him, we would not have it be a burden to you. For where there are many riches, there are also many who consume them. Thus we would have him serve near you at his own cost, so that he may receive this advantage from his labour: acquaintance with your lordship; and, if we learn that he has pleased you, we may have confidence in seeking greater things from you. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLIV. TO W., BISHOP OF CHESTER

Brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford, to the venerable lord and dearest brother W., by the grace of God Bishop of Chester: greeting and affection.

You ask whether there is room for an appeal when you have received the lord legate’s command to answer the monk Ingenulf, appeal set aside. Perhaps Ingenulf did not explain sufficiently carefully to the lord pope the case pending between you, so as to show that what has been done by you against him was done by apostolic authority. Therefore, if, by moving the judge to pity through feigned humility and simulated innocence, he obtained a rescript which, through an allegation of falsehoods, not only burdens but punishes your obedience, you will, if you please, defeat his claim.

For your prudence is not unaware what is contained concerning this in the first book of the Code, in these terms: “When a plea of falsehood is raised, if falsehood is discovered either in the statement of law, in that of fact, or in fraudulent concealment, the judge must take cognizance and pronounce sentence in accordance with the tenor of truth, not with the assertion of the petitioner.” Hence it is added in consequence: “We command that all judges who forbid the falsity of the petition to be challenged be punished”; and immediately: “Even if not investigation but execution is commanded, the truth of the petitions must be inquired into, so that, if fraud has intervened, the whole matter may be investigated.” In the fourth passage likewise it is added: “Even if a lying petitioner has obtained something consonant with the laws, he shall be entirely deprived of what he has obtained and be subject to the severity of the judge.”

It is good, therefore, for the lord pope’s letters to be heard repeatedly and carefully examined, so that, if you perceive in them anything by which you can challenge the falsity of the petitions, you may press that challenge and compel the judge, by the laws now set forth, to pronounce in your favour. But if utmost necessity should determine that you must resort to appeal, nothing else occurs to us on this point except what we find in the seventh book of the Code: that in all causes, great and small, those whom the law does not except have the right of appeal. Hence Alexander Augustus says in the same Code: “What you request is not new: although the authority of my rescript has intervened, nevertheless the right of appeal is not to be denied.”

Yet, neither setting our mouth against heaven nor presuming to judge the writing of the lord pope, we have explained not what ought presently to be done as a matter of law, but what we would do in a case of this kind. Laws have certainly been promulgated specifying persons and cases in which appeals ought not to be received. Since no such law affected or designated this case, we would certainly appeal to him whom we do not doubt is obliged to receive every appeal which the law does not except. May my lord and dearest father in Christ prosper, and in the spirit of counsel see what must be done.

## LETTER CXLV. THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, TO GILBERT

Thomas, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to his venerable brother G., by the same grace Bishop of Hereford: greeting.

No one among us is unaware how noble and renowned, above the other cities of this realm, is the city of London. There, indeed, because of the public affairs of the realm, the lord king’s residence and the gathering of the realm’s magnates are customarily more frequent. Therefore, since the Church of London has long been deprived of its pastor, it desires that such a bishop be appointed to it as may equal the city’s own distinction by the merit of an honourable life, learning, and prudence in secular affairs.

Accordingly, after great deliberation on this matter, the unanimous request of the clergy, the will of the lord king and our own, and the apostolic ordinance have agreed upon this: that, for the common benefit of the realm and the need of the Church, you ought to be transferred to the governance of the Church of London and exercise there pastoral care and solicitude. Having therefore received the lord pope’s command in this matter, we enjoin upon you by his authority that you do not delay to give your assent to the request of the Church of London—made concerning your translation to it in the presence of the lord king and ourselves, with the unanimous agreement of the whole clergy—and that you approach its governance all the more devotedly and promptly because it is known to need the counsel and direction of so great a person.

We urge your brotherhood especially to this end: that the duty of obedience which draws you to this may also be more warmly invited by consideration of our affection, so that he whom the affection of sincere love unites to us may, through closeness of place as well, be more conveniently available for our needs and those of God’s Church. Farewell.

## LETTER CXLVI. POPE ALEXANDER TO GILBERT

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G., Bishop of Hereford: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0852A] From the letters of our dearest son in Christ, Henry, illustrious King of the English, and of our venerable brother T[homas], Archbishop of Canterbury, etc. See under Alexander III, years 1159–81.

## LETTER CXLVII. KING HENRY TO GILBERT

H., King of England and Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, to G., by God’s grace Bishop of Hereford: greeting.

The soundness of your mind, trained in such great virtues, together with the unimpaired integrity of your honourable person, has commended—and continues to render commendable—your excellence to me. And not to me alone, but to all whom the fame of your name has reached; yet proof has been made to me above others, since I have often received salutary counsel for my soul, proceeding from the judgment of your heart. Concerning the dignity of my own person, the state of the realm, and the affairs to be conducted in the realm, you have again and again offered sound and effective counsel.

Therefore, desiring, if possibility allows, your continual proximity in body and mind, and considering that it would serve the preservation and increase of honour and advantage for myself, my heirs, and my realm, I earnestly beg you not to delay carrying into effect, in accordance with the lord pope’s command, the petition of the Church of London made concerning your person. In doing this you will render me a very great service and will gain the increase of my favour and affection, if it can be increased towards you, as well as that of all my barons.

For there, since continual presence is denied, your visits, repeated as often as possible, may cherish both my mind and body. There, whenever some great matter must be undertaken in my realm, councils must be held and advice taken. There barons gather to strengthen their affairs by counsel. Therefore, so that the greatness of your goodness and boundless virtue may be more widely spread and made known, the lord pope has rightly taken care to command you to accept the pastoral solicitude and care of the Church of London—thus providing for that Church’s need of such a shepherd, and making no small provision for me, my heirs, and my realm.

Let no business, therefore, delay your haste, nor any occasion impede it; let every delay be put far away, so that the lord pope’s command and the will of us all may be accomplished more swiftly, with increase to your honour and advantage. Witnessed by Archbishop Theobald. At Windsor.

## LETTER CXLVIII. TO POPE ALEXANDER

Brother G., minister of the Church of Hereford, to his father and lord, A., supreme pontiff: devoted and due service of charity and obedience.

Who, though lately we mourned more deeply, our Mother being shaken by the grievous error of schism and covered with a cloud of sorrow, nevertheless, when the light of truth dawned upon good hearts, rejoiced with all fullness of joy, Father beloved in Christ, because by God’s gift the storm was stilled for us into a gentle breeze, and after the night a day shone upon us [Col. 0853A] as welcome as it was clear.

Many were indeed influenced by that much-discussed council at Pavia, as they called it. One who was a stranger to the Church both in name and in reality wrote an account of its proceedings, composed, to win the favor of its hearers, with a great deal of embellishment and ornament, as it were with verbal trappings. When this had been brought to us and read publicly in the presence of the Church, what had been dictated with a perverse mind naturally pleased the eyes of some whose lot was on the left. Others, however, despised with a lofty and nobly Christian spirit the beast vomiting forth what it had wickedly conceived from an evil spirit. They had before them the sacred letters issued in your name, which your holy authority dictated and sent to the universal Church; firmly relying upon these as upon a column shining in a dark place [Col. 0853B] and containing within itself a full testimony to the truth, they judged that sacrilegious assembly to be truly a synagogue of Satan. Turning away from it with the utmost readiness of mind, as though from Pilate’s judgment hall, in which the miserable cry was uttered, “Not this man, but Barabbas” (John 18); “Away, away, crucify him; his blood be upon us and upon our children” (John 19), they determined, by the judgment of sound reason, that everything profanely decreed by those men must in every respect be rejected.

Light was added, as it were, to light when your sacred pragmatic letter concerning bishops, priests, deacons, and cardinals followed; and when your prudent epistle, full of truth, cried aloud and proclaimed to the world that all those to whom an apostolic election pertains had, by common vote, unanimous assent, and the unfeigned integrity of charity, wholly consented to your apostolate [Col. 0853C] and had rendered the service of their devotion in this matter with pious fidelity to Christ. For if one departed from the number of pontiffs, one ought to remember him who departed from the number of the Apostles, concerning whom Truth testified in this fashion: “Now is the Son of Man glorified, and now shall he be glorified” (John 13).

And if two brethren took the other side, ought the whole body of the Church therefore to have inclined to them, when authority itself declares that the absence, whether necessary or accidental, of a few persons does not invalidate what has been salutarily determined by the greater part of an order? Likewise: “Two parts of an order established in a city represent the whole order.” And elsewhere: “What the assent of the greater part has approved, let solemn authority confirm.” If anything could surpass the brilliant rays of such great lights, the letter of your faithful servant, the bishop of Lisieux, full of the grace of sweetness and prudence, supplied this to overflowing. In it, while the purity of his faith and the strength of his obedience shone openly before all assembled together, he most perfectly strengthened the wavering minds of many in doubtful matters, lest thereafter they should be moved like a reed shaken by the wind (Luke 7), as though a mirror of virtue had been set before them and as though the Spirit of the Lord, through him, were exhorting them more fully.

Finally, the sacred attestation of your legates, completing all things, brought the whole matter to a blessed conclusion, so that the holy Church may now confidently proclaim from the rooftops what [Col. 0854A] it had first heard in the ear; our most pious king may receive your apostolate with humble devotion; and the English Church, together with the Gallican Church, may now obey you openly throughout all its borders rather than speaking in secret. Therefore, Father most dearly beloved in Christ, we receive you as the father and shepherd of our souls. We have heard and recognize your voice; we do not follow a stranger. But those who have miserably torn Christ’s tunic—which was not torn even during the Passion—we deliver, in the power of the Holy Spirit, to Satan for the destruction of the flesh (1 Cor. 5).

Therefore, in view of the honor divinely conferred upon you, Father, that the English Church may rejoice more fully in unity, it most devoutly petitions in these blessed beginnings of your pontificate that your most faithful son Laurence, abbot of Westminster, may be permitted, as his holiness desires, to honor the body of blessed King Edward: to raise it from the earth, place it in a fitting shrine, and exalt it in the church, amid the public rejoicing of all the people. Edward established that church from its foundations, endowed it most generously, ennobled it with everything that pertains to the beauty of God’s house in honor of God and blessed Peter, and brought it to a most blessed completion.

This body, as we have frequently heard from persons whom we believe deserve credence, has been found, whenever visited, whole and incorrupt from a hundred years ago until now. Although he lived in marriage, he nevertheless remained, as is proclaimed, a virgin throughout the entire course of his life, with the highest virtue of soul; after death he was also granted the blessed incorruption of his body. They firmly affirm that he possessed the spirit of prophecy and, while living in the flesh, foretold future events revealed by the Lord. They recall that he was gentle, merciful, and meek beyond all others, and so devoted to blessed Peter that he lamented as wholly lost any day on which he had bestowed nothing upon Peter’s church. His laws still regulate judgments among us, and his prudent care preserves unharmed in many respects, even to this day, the poor of his kingdom. Since we do not doubt that the honor shown to saints is pleasing to the Lord, we jointly beseech your serenity to honor the kingdom of England, ever most devoted to the apostolic majesty, and to permit its faithful people to render the honor and reverence due to saints to their king, whom, for many reasons that the narrow compass of a letter cannot contain, they truly judge holy. May divine power preserve you unharmed for long ages, Father beloved in Christ.

## LETTER CXLIX. TO THE SAME.

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff A., brother G., minister of the Church of London: the due service of apostolic reverence, charity, and obedience.

As a door is governed by its hinge, so, by the sacred governance of the holy apostolic see, all churches are ruled—God thus ordaining and providing in every way mercifully for his holy Church. Since that see extends to all the equity of judicial censure, it preserves sacredly and inviolate each person’s right [Col. 0855A]. Thus it mitigates anger, restrains the fuel of quarrels, strengthens charity, and restores peace throughout every part of the Church whenever, perhaps because an enemy has sown tares among the wheat (Matthew 13), peace has been disturbed in any respect, doing so with holy and supremely praiseworthy prudence.

Accordingly, with all our mind and with the entire affection of the inward person, we offer supplicating prayers to your holiness, beloved by us and always to be loved in the Lord: look with a serene heart and kindly disposition upon that special and most devoted daughter of the holy Roman Church, namely the Church of Canterbury. You defend the right of each person; therefore, for the merits of blessed Gregory and of Augustine, its holy founder, do not permit it, God forbid, during the time of your apostolate either to be oppressed or [Col. 0855B] to be obscured by unjust oppressions from the ancient brightness of its dignities.

For if paternal traditions are to be believed, just as Canterbury was enlightened in faith by the holy Roman Church, so York was undoubtedly converted to the faith through Canterbury. Indeed, it is very well known from the histories that Laurence, successor of blessed Augustine, sent Paulinus for this purpose; and that through his ministry he rescued the city of York from the darkness of unbelief, and thereby deservedly obtained the dignity and glory of the primacy for Canterbury. The Church of Canterbury possessed this honor of primacy in the times of many of your predecessors and exercised it over the Church of York in many ways and by acts worthy of remembrance.

Therefore the entire body of the Church of Canterbury beseeches your sublimity: do not allow the daughter to raise her heel against her mother and effectively aspire to equality with her; and, by apostolic authority, take prudent care that the man of York does not continue to carry the insignia of the cross—whose use antiquity testifies was granted to Canterbury alone—through another province, to the scandal, God forbid, of the English Church and the astonishment of the kingdom. For if it is fitting to increase benefits for those who have deserved well, then the Church of Canterbury ought beyond doubt not merely to retain its ancient privileges, but also to be continually distinguished by new dignities, since it has always most devoutly acknowledged itself, in all matters within its power, subject to the apostolic see.

## LETTER CL. TO THE SAME.

[Col. 0855D]

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff A., brother G., minister of the Church of London: the devoted and due service of charity and obedience.

We are expediting with all possible diligence the task laid upon us of collecting the census of blessed Peter. Although we have not yet collected it in full, we are anxiously considering among ourselves by what route we may transport the sum once collected and with what security we may send it safely. Because our own counsels do not fully suffice us in this matter, we have thought it necessary to consult your sublimity. It is not safe for us to carry this money through unknown peoples and unfamiliar kingdoms, except insofar as [Col. 0856A] the reverence and protection arising from the peace of our lord the king of England is known to extend. With conscience as our witness, we are not speaking of our own labors or complaining of expense; rather, we fear the dangers inherent in the situation itself.

Therefore we beseech your holiness that, if it please you, about the Kalends of October your messengers may meet our messengers at Rouen, and either undertake to convey to you, with such security as you shall provide, the money carried there by us, or entrust this task for execution to one of your faithful servants, as your authority shall determine.

## LETTER CLI. TO THE SAME.

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff, A., brother G., minister of the Church of London: the due service of affection [Col. 0856B] and obedience.

When, in accordance with the form of your command, lord, we had appointed a day for Master Matthew, chancellor of the illustrious king of England, against R., prior of Monmouth, concerning the church of Llangarren, he appeared on that day before us against the aforesaid prior and complained that the said church, together with the parish adjoining it, was unjustly withheld from him by the prior. He asserted that the same church with its whole parish belonged by right to his church of Llangarren; that the church of Llangarren in question had possessed it for a long time; and that it had lost it not by any judgment but solely through the violence of the Church of Monmouth.

When he was prepared to prove this before the witnesses present, the prior immediately raised a peremptory exception and replied that, when Master Matthew was proceeding against him concerning that same church before us some time ago, he had appealed to an apostolic hearing, and had come prepared to the apostolic see. There, he said, he had long awaited Master Matthew’s arrival; but as neither Matthew nor anyone appearing on his behalf came, he had sufficiently shown, by documents, witnesses, and oaths, that the church of Llangarren belonged by right to the Church of Monmouth. By the judgment of the Apostolic See he had, as he asserted, obtained victory in this litigation through a sentence of Pope Adrian of good memory. As testimony to that proof and the sentence issued in his favor, he produced a privilege of the same Pope Adrian [Col. 0856D], attesting the same proof and confirming the church of Llanrwst to the Church of Monmouth.

Master Matthew, hearing that sentence had been passed against him while absent and undefended, asserted that the prior had obtained it by false suggestion. To prove this in your presence, he appealed to your hearing for the feast of All Saints. May my lord and father most dearly beloved in Christ prosper.

## LETTER CLII. TO THE SAME.

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff A., brother G., minister of the Church of London: the devoted service of charity and obedience.

When Geoffrey de Lucy, archdeacon of Derby, pressed us to secure justice, in accordance with the form of your command, against Thomas the clerk concerning certain tithes belonging, as he asserted, to [Col. 0857A] his prebend, Thomas immediately sought to decline our jurisdiction. He showed that, after your letters had been sent to us, another command had issued from your sublimity to the bishop of Winchester: the cause previously delegated to us was to be heard and determined by him after summoning the parties. Since Thomas had these letters in hand and produced them, we have taken care to keep the matter suspended until it becomes more fully clear to us from you which of us ought to bring the suit to an end. May my lord and father most dearly beloved in Christ prosper.

## LETTER CLIII. TO THE SAME.

[Col. 0857B] To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff A., brother G., minister of the Church of London: the due service of affection and obedience.

Even had my lord commanded some great thing of me, I ought in every respect to obey; how much more so when he has ordered me to send him a humble covering to be placed beneath his feet. I therefore send the thing about which he wrote—though not such as your sublimity described—hoping that the affection of the sender may enlarge this small gift, and that, if it lacks roundness of design, the scarcity among us of an artisan who knows how to make such a thing may excuse it. For carpets are not made among us, but are brought from lands beyond the sea. Having inspected these with diligent inquiry throughout our whole city, I have taken care, with great gladness of heart, to send to your holiness, beloved by me in the Lord, the best that I could find [Col. 0857C]. May the Lord surround you with his impregnable wall and always protect you with the arms of his power, Father beloved in Christ.

## LETTER CLIV. TO THE SAME.

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff ALEXANDER, brother G., minister of the Church of London: all the humble devotion and ready obedience that is in his power.

Father dear to me and ever to be loved in the Lord, with all the strength of my soul I give thanks to your holiness, because you have mercifully opened to me the inward compassion of the Apostolic See, and, piously sympathizing with my distress in the extremity of my need [Col. 0857D], have turned upon me the eyes of mercy. Though the harshness of a hostile authority had unjustly entwined me in the snares of death, in anger—if there was anger—yet mindful of mercy, while preserving everything required by justice and discipline, you have at last, by fatherly charity, willed that I should breathe again into life.

This benefit is assuredly all the more welcome and is judged far more acceptable to me because it was shown not at royal entreaties, not through the intercessions offered for this purpose by many persons, not through weights of wealth given or promised, but from the clearest fountain of charity—that is, from the apostolic heart. It proceeded in mercy toward a son, was granted not because of my merits but by grace alone, which goes before every merit. Therefore, Father, I acknowledge myself bound in all things to the munificence you have shown toward me, in whatever service and honor I can render; so that not only the authority of the see over which you preside, but also the magnitude of the great benefit bestowed—and indeed the resolve I had long before formed concerning this matter—alike compel and persuade me to will whatever you will and to undertake wholly whatever you command [Col. 0858A].

Your holiness, therefore, shall exercise over me such commands as are pleasing to itself. In all matters corresponding to my ability, a son shall obey his father and a servant his lord. I shall deem nothing harsh or grievous which I know to be pleasing to the apostolic gentleness shown toward me. For let my lord know and hold it certain that, from the beginning of this storm by which we have long been shaken, I have always had this wish and purpose: to attend upon you on whatever occasion and, standing before you, to set forth the anxiety of my heart; so that, having mercifully obtained from your sublimity release from the office to which I am bound, I might at least escape naked from the waves overwhelming me and, if I could not provide for the safety of many, might at least provide somewhat for my own safety.

For all who travel from the bounds of England as far as you, seeking to please certain persons, proclaim me maliciously as a seedbed of discord, a destroyer of the Church, an incitement to evils, and fuel for every quarrel and hatred. They do not cease to instill into your holy ears, against me, by their promises and prayers, things that are neither true nor ever, with the Lord’s help, capable of proof. And behold, Father, I die, though I have done none of these things and am conscious of none of them. Sentences are pronounced against me though I have neither confessed nor been convicted, nor even summoned. A notorious case is fabricated and forged; and, that nothing may be lacking to raging envy, they boldly assert that what is known to no one is most notorious. The blood which I did not shed is demanded from my hand (Ezekiel 3), and I am most unjustly compelled to pay what I did not seize (Psalm 68).

Fearing that all these things would fall upon me, I had already appealed, forestalling every sentence, to the apostolic presence, wishing to appear before him who is certainly not mistaken in law. If I did not pursue that appeal, the reason was that you entrusted to the legates sent by your side to our lord the king both the cognizance and the determination of all matters disputed between the lord of Canterbury and ourselves. You sent letters [Col. 0858D] to us commanding that we present ourselves before them and firmly observe whatever, after hearing the parties, they should determine concerning us. Since they pursued the matter not at all, and since I had again appealed, together with our brethren, in their presence because of imminent danger, the prosecution of that appeal too was remitted to us by your grace through the intervention of our lord the king. The letters in our possession, authenticated with the apostolic seal, bear witness to this.

Although a judge ought not to take offense if, when suspected of causing injury, he is challenged before a superior, nevertheless the lord of Canterbury, offended because I appealed to your hearing, resolved to attack my head and, disregarding due order, to crush me by excommunication. Foreknowing this, I forestalled the sentence and again appealed to your clemency [Col. 0859A], seeking the examination of him who, rightly weighing the merits of causes, preserves to each person his own right by impartial reason.

What is written—that in one and the same cause no appeal should be made a third time—does not mean that, whenever a bishop believes himself aggrieved by his metropolitan, he may not freely appeal. Rather, it means that one defeated by a judgment approved after appeal by three judges in successive degrees ought not to appeal. We say this not to assist the sun with torches, but to offer at least a brief answer to those who reproach us for repeated appeal. Thus I appealed to the apostolic throne, hoping that this would protect me, so that before the day fixed for the appeal my status could not in any way be overthrown by him against whom the appeal had been made.

For the firmness of the Apostolic See is that of which it was said to the sea: “Thus far shall you come, and here shall you break your swelling waves” (Job 38). A judge’s sentence, once issued, is suspended when it has dashed itself against that see by appeal, if an appeal has been made beforehand; if pronounced afterwards, it wholly lacks force, so that it must be regarded as completely nonexistent both in fact and in name—more properly void than requiring annulment by some external solemnity. Yet because ordinary people do not understand the niceties of law and the hidden matters of the canons, I conduct and present myself in every respect as if I were bound by the sentence pronounced against me after the appeal. I preferred to be blamed by learned men for humility rather than, in asserting what is divine [reading uncertain], to be rebuked by the multitude for a seemingly sacrilegious audacity. I therefore conduct and present myself in every respect as if I were bound by the sentence pronounced against me after the appeal. Yet from the very beginning of its pronouncement the apostolic sublimity to which the prior appeal had been made annulled that sentence; the appeal most powerfully prevented the sentence from having any force whatsoever [Col. 0859C].

Although this point can be extensively argued on this side with the support of the authority of the Fathers, nevertheless, having considered the letters by which your charity deigned to instruct and console me, I rejected contention. In accordance with the form of your counsel, having received absolution, I bound myself before the Gospel to undertake what your holiness might command me; according to my ability, I shall obey your command in every respect and shall not depart from my promise. Let paternal charity, I beseech you, moderate its command until it finds me guilty in law upon the accusation of someone and the testimony of a suitable witness.

If I delayed returning thanks for your favor as it deserved, summer heat, the difficulty of travel, fear of plunder, and fear of imprisonment caused the delay. If I began the journey toward you yet did not proceed, I was hindered by the snares of spies and summoned back under grave threats by the messengers of our lord the king returning from your sublimity. I beseech you, through the mercy of Jesus Christ our Lord, that a father may put away anger against his son from his heart, receive under his protection one who henceforth belongs wholly, to the full extent of my power, to his every will. May the Lord preserve you in health, Father beloved in Christ.

## LETTER CLV. TO THE SAME, AFTER THE PASSION OF THE LORD OF CANTERBURY.

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff A., brother G., minister of the Church of London: the service of complete submission and obedience due.

[Col. 0860A] At your displeasure, Father, my strength has long since been exhausted by tears and the misery of my body; the vastness of my innate inward grief has almost made everything subject to my senses neglect its proper functions. For at your estrangement I immediately became the outcast of the people, a reproach to those who knew me, and an occasion of utter confusion to my friends (Psalm 21). Unless the pious care of the merciful physician had drawn even a little soft tissue over the wound of the languishing man, a longer delay would have hardened the ulcers of the sufferer into the scar of a despairing recovery.

But now, Father, since from what fatherly mercy has granted the son I may hope for some measure of healing, my spirit revives, my soul rejoices, and for the more gracious gentleness shown me my entire mind rises to give thanks. Prostrate at the feet of your holiness [Col. 0860B], it longs to pray with all its strength and to entreat with all its desires that, after the biting wine of severity, the oil of pious gentleness may be poured into my wounds, and that the harshness of paternal correction may at last be received for me in the breasts of maternal compassion. Let there now be within the Father the affection that may plead and entreat for the son: receive into favor one punished sufficiently already, and hold as firmly devoted to your service one severely corrected. May fatherly mercy advance one recalled within the camp, and may the apostolic hand at last, by just compassion, bring the favor already tasted by me to perfection, lest I be compelled to spend my days in grief and misery and to end the remaining small number of my days in bitterness. May the Lord preserve you in health, Father beloved in Christ, for the benefit of his Church through many times to come [Col. 0860C].

## LETTER CLVI. TO THE SAME.

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff A., brother G., minister of the Church of London: greeting and the due service of honor and obedience.

Father, prostrate in heart and body, I give the humblest thanks for the kindness you have now repeatedly shown me. By prevailing grace you have at last removed from me the burden that anxiously oppressed me, and through the affection of compassion pleading within the Father for the son, you have mercifully led me from the darkness of sorrow into a certain serenity of desired hope. Therefore, released from the bond by which I was held [Col. 0860D], there is nothing further, Father, that I could wish or desire more ardently than to stand before your holiness, lay myself wholly open in your presence, and dedicate to the Lord, under the governance of your counsel, all this small remainder of my days, withdrawn from tumults and storms.

For this reason, whatever prevents me from accomplishing what I desire and from bringing my long labors and protracted weariness at last to their wished-for conclusion adds grievously to my misfortunes.

Hence sorrow sits heavily upon me, and anxiety enfolds my spirit on every side, while many things arise from many causes to call me away from my purpose and, not by a single occasion but by manifold necessity, draw me back from what I began. Foremost and chief among these causes is this: it has long since reached everyone’s ears that a sentence has been pronounced against me by your highness, while the favor granted me in part is scarcely yet known to a few [Col. 0861A]. Hence the fury of all who lie in wait along the roads and swarm like ants in every direction along the direct paths to you has been inflamed. Fearing neither God nor human beings, they judge that everything may lawfully be done to me without penalty; they believe themselves to be rendering service to the Lord if, laying hands upon me, they afflict me with both losses and insults, consign me to prison custody as a man condemned and rejected by the supreme pontiff, and compel me, by exquisitely devised inflictions of punishment, to redeem myself down to the very last penny.

Rumor has now filled every roadway against me: “He will pass this way—the man whom the apostolic hand has exposed to all. To despoil him as Egypt was despoiled, to suffocate him, and to afflict him in every manner is a pleasing odor of sacrifice to God and perfect praise in the Church. Ready your hands; keep watch, lest he escape in disguise or through some contrivance. Behold, riches lie for you at London’s gates. Only negligence will henceforth make you poor.”

This, Father, is the wall raised against me; this is the obstacle cast in my way on every side. Even if, with the Lord’s help, I should somehow succeed in crossing it, old age, which has overtaken me for many years now, prevents me from either undertaking this journey or being able or daring in any degree to attempt this labor with strength equal to it. These matters have now brought upon me so many hardships that it would take too long to enumerate them; shame compels me rather to suppress them than disclose them in writing [Col. 0861C].

## LETTER CLVII. TO THE SAME.

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff A., brother G., minister of the Church of London: the humble and due service of charity and obedience.

The conspicuous merits of our venerable and most dear brother, the lord bishop of Norwich, from his earliest age even to a good old age, fully require that those who delight in honorable conduct and have religion at heart should fittingly commend him and, with most ready affection, make supplication for him before your holiness. It is sufficiently well known that, almost from the cradle, he has conducted himself honorably in the Church through every stage of life and has now reached what may be called a fruitful old age [Col. 0861D]. In the Church over which he presides and the bishopric that he administers, he has been received with such public rejoicing that whatever honor and favor you bestow upon him will be received by the whole body of his Church with the highest thanksgiving.

Since it is a father’s part to delight in good sons, we beseech apostolic clemency that, in his present necessity, concerning which he has recourse to you through messengers sent directly, you may look upon him with eyes of mercy. By restraining with apostolic severity those who unjustly oppose him, permit him to close his day in peace and to depart in peace from you to the Father of all. Otherwise virtue, injured, will be ashamed; iniquity, having overstepped justice, will prevail to the ruin of many; and things now lulled in deep peace will, made more bold by this example, undoubtedly cause disturbance. Fare well.

## LETTER CLVIII. TO THE SAME.

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff A., brother G., minister of the Church of London: the affection of true love and the service of humble obedience.

Light, lord, shines more pleasantly after darkness; and when joy is restored after the cloud of grief, the mind which sorrow afflicted grows more happily cheerful. Thus, Father, the English Church, deprived of its shepherds, had for a long stretch of time continued in mourning and tears. But when, through your concern, which you always diligently devote to the welfare of your children, it obtained through the venerable men Albert and Theodwin, legates of the Apostolic See sent from your side, the glorious liberty of choosing its shepherds and prelates, the more severely grief had afflicted it, the more abundantly did it rejoice inwardly in the spirit, flooded with richer joy [Col. 0862B].

According to the prophet, it had been given a rope instead of a girdle, baldness instead of curled hair, and continual sackcloth instead of a breast-band. But all these things have now been cast far away from it, the Lord powerfully working his strength through you. Having been granted liberty of elections, it now stands before its bridegroom and king, clothed as it were in garments of glory, as gloriously as confidently, using the liberty which it has attained through you by the Lord’s grace.

That holy Church of Canterbury, the spiritual and most devoted daughter of the holy Roman Church, called together its suffragan bishops and the other persons of its province. In choosing for itself a father and archbishop, it diligently observed the statutes of the sacred canons. Finding among its own members one fit for its governance, it did not wish to summon a stranger. Having before its eyes what is written: “Let each man have the fruit of his own service in the Church in which he has spent the whole of his life; let no other intrude into another’s pay, nor let one dare to claim for himself another’s wage which is due to him, according to the saying of the Prophet: ‘In place of your fathers sons are born to you’” (Psalm 44), it chose as its father and archbishop a son whom it had nurtured, whom it had long instructed in the sacred institutions of regular observance: Richard, prior and monk of that same church, commendable for his merits of virtue, acceptable, as we believe, to God and human beings, abounding alike in learning for instruction and good character for upright conduct. The whole convent, bishops, and other persons concurred in their votes. Having solemnly celebrated the election and raised him to that high office, it gladly rendered praise and glory to God with much thanksgiving and the applause of the whole people [Col. 0862D].

When the suffragan bishops had assembled for his consecration on the Sunday following the octave of Pentecost, and those necessarily absent had sent their messengers and letters of ratification, letters unexpectedly drawn up in the name of the younger king were produced and presented in the midst of the assembly. They contained an appeal against elections not held in his kingdom with his assent. Since, while his father survives, nothing is owed to anyone in the kingdom except with reservation of fidelity to his father, and although the letters presented appeared suspicious to us for many reasons too lengthy to enumerate, nevertheless, showing due reverence to your majesty and wishing fully to preserve your honor, we abstained from the consecration and jointly determined that the matter should be referred to your judgment.

Therefore we all jointly offer heartfelt prayers to your holiness: do not turn our harp into mourning and our organ into the voice of those who weep; rather, graciously extend your right hand to the work of your hands. “Let all know, O Lord, that this is your hand, and that you, O Lord, have made it” (Psalm 108), and bind the whole body of the Church of Canterbury to you in fuller gratitude [Col. 0863B].

## LETTER CLIX. TO THE SAME.

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff A., brother G., minister of the Church of London: the due service of charity and obedience.

With what confidence or countenance shall I stand before my lord and dearest father to plead for another, when I myself, more than anyone, need an advocate to reconcile me to your favor, as widespread report declares? For one known to be displeasing in a person’s eyes is not a fitting mediator—the very person who, by setting himself in the middle, ought to have shown that person appeased. Yet, Father most beloved in Christ, when I consider myself and examine my whole self without sparing myself, though I am no longer young, nothing at all comes to my mind for which it would be just that I should be cast away from your presence and excluded from the most sacred approach to your kindness [Col. 0863C].

For I have always shown myself ready for your service, nor can any changing fortune ever draw me away from fidelity. “Those who hate you, Father, I have hated”; and, to dare something in the freedom of the spirit, I have at times steadfastly repelled and confounded those resisting your honor.

## LETTER CLX. TO THE SAME.

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff A., brother G. [Col. 0863D], minister of the Church of London: the affection of sincere and true love, and the service of humble obedience.

In rendering thanks to Your Holiness, Father, our humility plainly fails us, because the Church of God among us, oppressed through many past times by the yoke of servitude and bereft of every hope of recovering liberty, has at last, through your concern—which you watchfully devote to the benefit of the flock committed to you—been restored to her birthright. The Lord having changed her condition for the better, she has now unexpectedly been granted the liberty she so greatly desired. For the prudent care of the legates whom your laudably circumspect authority sent into our regions to seek remedies for the Church has at length wisely and powerfully secured this: that churches in the kingdom of England, long [Col. 0864A] bereft of their pastors, may in every case freely choose persons suitable to govern them. Hence many churches among us rejoice in their elect, trusting in your mercy that those whom they have chosen unanimously may, through the gift of your favor, be advanced and also obtain the office of consecration. Among these, the Church of Bath has directed its desires toward our venerable brother Reginald, archdeacon of Salisbury, unanimously requesting him and, with none objecting or raising any contradiction, solemnly electing him, and committing to him with its whole heart the care and governance of itself.

We believe it unnecessary to commend him to Your Holiness by titles of praise, because, as we believe, you yourselves have recognized from the evidence of events his learning, character, [Col. 0864B] industry, and effectiveness in conducting the Church’s affairs; and because you have raised him—bestowed upon us by your favor and made illustrious among us through your recognition—to such a height of favor that the Church which elected him may hope, on this very account, to find no small favor with Your Holiness. Since, with the Lord’s help, we believe that he will be a good fellow-worker in the house of the Lord, moved by fraternal charity and emboldened thereby, we ask that you graciously extend your right hand to the work of your hands and, by hastening his consecration, bind both him and, through him, many others more closely to your favor.

## LETTER CLXI. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0864C]

To his father and lord, A., supreme pontiff, brother G., minister of the Church of London, the service due in charity and obedience.

Richard, the bearer of this letter, has complained before us, lord, that he is being unjustly deprived of the church of Bardintuna, and that it is unjustly withheld from him by Walter, a clerk. He asserted that, in order to recover the said church, he had long ago approached Pope Adrian of blessed memory and brought from him a mandate to our venerable brother, the lord bishop of Chichester, directing him to investigate the matter and bring it to its proper conclusion. The said bishop, therefore, intervening in the matter on his behalf, according to Richard’s assertion, Adam, clerk and then holder of the said church, [Col. 0864D] made this agreement with him: that he should pay Richard twenty shillings yearly in the name of the church, and, so long as he made this payment, should retain the church for his lifetime. Subsequently, when Adam ceased making this payment, Richard asserted that he again approached the pope, that the said church was adjudged to him by the pope, and that he referred execution of this judgment to the lord of Chichester. He further asserted that he again made the following agreement with the said Adam: that Adam should render fifty shillings yearly to him and, upon this payment, retain the church.

Relying therefore on the apostolic authority by which the said church had been adjudged to him, and because neither twenty nor fifty shillings, nor indeed anything at all, was now being paid to him in its name, he asked that the church be [Col. 0865A] restored to him and that due reverence be shown to the apostolic judgment.

Walter, however, asserting that matters transacted and judged between others ought neither to harm nor benefit others, replied that he had canonically acquired the said church and had been instituted as its parson by our predecessor Robert, bishop of blessed memory, before the time of the litigation mentioned. When he later remained in France for study, he said that, if litigation had been conducted and a settlement made concerning his church between Richard and Adam, his agent in the matter, while he himself was absent and unaware of it, this could not prejudice him, absent and ignorant as he was—a principle, he maintained, of very well-known law. On returning from his studies and coming home, he possessed by his own right the church which he had lawfully acquired; nor did he regard as valid, or intend to regard as valid, Adam’s agreements concerning [Col. 0865B] his property, made without his knowledge.

Wishing to understand Richard’s right, if he had any, more fully, we diligently inquired who had instituted him as parson in the said church. He replied that our predecessor, the elder Lord Richard, had granted this church to him; but he could neither then establish the credibility of this assertion by writings, witnesses, or any other proofs, nor promise that he would do so later. Asked whether he could prove that Adam had possessed the church in his own name at the time when he made his settlement with Richard, or that Walter had subsequently ratified what had been done between them, he answered that he was wholly without proof of these matters also. Therefore, since it was not evident that his case rested on [Col. 0865C] truth, yet showing due reverence to the letters of the lord pope, we did not absolve W. from its determination, but judged that the matter should be postponed to another day, so that Richard might more fully provide for his case. Richard, however, refusing to pursue the matter again before us, referred it to Your Holiness and appealed to the feast of Saint Giles. We wish you health in the Lord, dearest Father in Christ.

## LETTER CLXII. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, A., supreme pontiff, brother G., minister of the Church of London, devoted service in charity and obedience.

When your mandate concerning Count [Col. 0865D] Hugh and William de Vaus had been conveyed to us, Father, and received with due reverence, Count Hugh immediately sent messengers to us and anxiously complained that the brethren of Panteneia had deceived Your Excellency to his injury and had obtained, by false representation, the judgment now issued against him. He maintains that the case between the canons and himself proceeded in the following manner.

Almost no one among us is unaware that the vill of Panteneia is held from Count Hugh. He swears and affirms in every way that he never gave it to the canons of Panteneia and never confirmed it in writing. He admits that, two years ago, he summoned before a solemnly convened court William de Vaus, who claimed the said vill as his patrimony and said that it belonged to him by hereditary right; [Col. 0866A] the canons praise this William and his father as the authors of the possession which they hold in that vill. Before all, the count solemnly recovered the vill from William, maintaining that it had never been given to William’s father and never granted to him by hereditary right. After this recovery, by judgment of his court, he took possession of the vill and held it as his own, or as he hoped would become his own, for some time.

The said brethren, resorting to you in this emergency, brought us a mandate directing that we strictly summon the said count and, unless, after admonition by us under your authority, he restored the said vill and everything taken from them in full, we should place all his land under interdict and, unless he gave satisfaction even then, should not delay to pronounce [Col. 0866B] sentence of excommunication against him. Accordingly, after we had carried out your mandate with much labor, and our lord king had effectively lent his hand, the vill itself was restored to the canons, and everything taken from them was restored to them most completely by us, according to their oath and proof. If anything different has been represented to Your Excellency, you can clearly learn from the testimony of our venerable brother, the lord bishop of Norwich, and of other persons of the same diocese, that the matter proceeded in this way.

Later, when we had met our lord king at Oxford, since litigation concerning this vill, claimed by Count Hugh, had long continued and the disputes had been prolonged, it was [Col. 0866C] proposed in the king’s presence that the canons should surrender the disputed property to the count and receive another from his gift, where they might live in peace and serve the Lord in peace. Although the prior of that house assented to this proposal, with the king thus advising, it was nevertheless provided that nothing further should be done and that the matter should not be concluded until the will of the entire convent of Panteneia was known and common agreement obtained. Since the convent did not approve but disapproved, the matter proceeded no further; nor, as they assert, was anything exchanged, brought to them, or in any way diminished for them by our lord king, the count, or any of their men. Rather, as regards their possessions, everything remains in the state in which it stood in the time of your predecessors, when, under their authority, the long-protracted litigation and controversy between them and William de Vaus was [Col. 0866D] settled and ended.

The count, first through messengers and then in person, alleging the falsity of the petitions, appealed to your hearing. He says that he will show that he neither seized their possessions by the rash violence which they allege, nor acquired, through the proposed exchange that did not proceed, his place, the vill, or anything belonging to them; and that he did not deserve the judgment rendered against him, which he bears with great humility and patience. He fixed the Ascension of the Lord as the term for his appeal; and because, whether the investigation of his case or the execution thereof be ordered, the falsity of the petitions must always be [Col. 0867A] alleged, he obtained from us these letters as testimony of his appeal. In this matter, so that the opposing party might not be disadvantaged through ignorance of the facts, we took care repeatedly to notify the said brethren of Panteneia, by letters and trustworthy messengers, of both the form and the ground of the appeal made. We wish you health in the Lord, dearest Father in Christ.

## LETTER CLXIII. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, A., supreme pontiff, brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting and the devotion of humble obedience.

It is fitting that matters which an appeal made to you before us has suspended should be referred to you, Father. [Col. 0867B] Certain tithes were claimed before us by the monks of Saint Ulmar from a certain knight, our parishioner, connected by marriage with Baldwin, archdeacon of Norwich. The same knight eventually named the said archdeacon as the author of his title to those tithes. When the abbot of Saint Ulmar and the archdeacon himself appeared before us on an appointed day to litigate against each other concerning these tithes, the archdeacon appealed to our father, the lord of Canterbury. When they were before him, the abbot suspended the matter by appealing from the lord of Canterbury to your hearing.

Pursuing their appeal, the monks brought letters from Your Sublimity to the lord of Chichester, directing him to hear the cause and decide it by hearing it. [Col. 0867C] After he had summoned the parties, as we have learned from his letters, the case reached the following conclusion. The said tithes were adjudged to the monks, and the aforesaid knight renounced them on oath. Letters were sent to us by the lord of Chichester attesting this and enjoining us, under your authority, to put the said monks in corporal possession of the same tithes. Thus the monks obtained possession.

When a year had passed and the harvests were being gathered, the archdeacon sent his servants to collect the said tithes, prepare them in his name, and place them in safe keeping. The other party immediately resisted and did not allow the tithes adjudged to them under your authority to be carried away. [Col. 0867D] Rather, they repelled those who wished to use force and retained what was theirs. The lord archdeacon referred a complaint about this to us. When, on an appointed day, he demanded that the said tithes be restored to him as one who had suffered violence, the authority of the adjudicated matter was set against him. He replied that a matter judged between others ought not to prejudice others, that he had not attended the judgment of the lord of Chichester, and therefore that the judgment ought not to prejudice him. When the others relied on possession adjudged to them under our authority and asserted that it ought not be disturbed, the archdeacon complained that he was being burdened, appealed to your hearing, and obtained these letters as testimony of his appeal. We wish you health in the Lord, beloved Father in Christ.

## LETTER CLXIV. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0868A]

To his father and lord, A., supreme pontiff, brother G., minister of the Church of London, the service due in charity and obedience.

It is right, Father, that matters which, an appeal having been made to you, have been suspended and seek the judgment of Your Sublimity for their decision should be reported to your knowledge. We therefore notify Your Excellency that, because of the pressing complaint of the relatives of Count Alberic, we set a day and summoned both the count himself and his wife, the countess, into our presence, in order to hear the matters at issue between them and, having more fully ascertained the truth, decide them through justice.

When the parties were before us, the count’s relatives alleged [Col. 0868B] that the union of the count and countess was by no means lawful, because, before the count took her as wife, the count’s brother, namely Geoffrey de Ver, had entered into an agreement, confirmed by a pledge of faith, with the countess’s father to take her as wife. They further alleged that the matter had proceeded so far that the countess’s father, when she was already three years old, gave her to the said Geoffrey as his future wife; Geoffrey entrusted her to his brother, Count Alberic, to be kept for him; and, when she had completed six years, Geoffrey received her from the count’s hand, brought her to his own house, and showed her every honor, both personally and through his servants, as his future wife, excepting marital intercourse, until her twelfth year was almost completed. [Col. 0868C]

Since these arrangements between the countess’s father and Geoffrey, the count’s brother, had been confirmed by a pledge of faith, they maintained that Geoffrey’s and the countess’s betrothal had been made binding, and that she who had been the betrothed of one brother could not afterward lawfully marry the other. They added that this contract was confirmed by the countess’s own consent when she reached the age mentioned, and that throughout this entire span of years she never, even for a moment, objected to what was being done.

The countess replied that she had been wholly unaware of what was done by her father when she was only three years old, since her age did not yet permit consent. If her father made a contract with Geoffrey, as stated, she firmly maintained that she neither knew it then nor subsequently approved it, nor ever gave assent to what had been done [Col. 0868D] between them. Since in contracting betrothals the consent of those whose future marriage is at issue must be sought, she said that she had never been Geoffrey’s betrothed, since no one had ever asked her about entering a marital union with him, nor had she ever consented to it in her own will. Therefore, if she was given by her father to Geoffrey, received from Geoffrey by the count, later restored by the count to Geoffrey, and brought by him to his own house, and if she resided there for some years, she obeyed necessity in all these matters; yet she never consented to a marital bond with Geoffrey, either by act or by will.

To declare this by clear evidence, she added that, when she had grown somewhat older, she sent letters to her father and made it plainly known that she would never give consent to a marriage with Geoffrey. [Col. 0869A] The count’s relatives, invoking paternal authority over offspring, objected that a father could choose a husband for his daughter and that, unless he chose one who was either base-born or unworthy, she could not dissent from his will.
