As the parties thus litigated against one another, when we had already sat for the third time, the countess complained that her advocates, through fear of the count and his men, were giving her cause’s defense less safely and less diligently than they ought. Claiming to be prejudiced in this respect, she appealed to your hearing for *Laetare Jerusalem*, and obtained from us these letters containing the matter as it was transacted. We wish you health in the Lord, dearest Father in Christ.

## LETTER CLXV. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0869B]

To his father and lord, A., supreme pontiff, brother G., minister of the Church of London, humble service of obedience at every command of his father.

We receive the commands of Your Sublimity with due reverence, lord, and reverently apply whatever effort and diligence we can to carrying them out. If at times we do not immediately fulfill them according to the wishes of the complainants, this is not because we pursue the matters entrusted to us negligently or lukewarmly, since some necessity of law or fact undoubtedly prevents us from deciding matters quickly. Thus, if we prolonged for a short time the case of the clerk Herlewin against the venerable man, the abbot of Ibreio, the reason was that, under the delay granted, truth entangled in words and evasions might be extracted, and that the litigation, long protracted, might finally be quieted by a lawful conclusion. [Col. 0869C]

The inquiry proceeded to such a point that, after several days had been set and the parties had litigated against one another, the lord of Winchester and we, by documents and witnesses, clearly established that the tithes which Herlewin seeks by every means to extort belong by the fullest right to the church of Docchinges, which your authority had long since adjudged to the said abbot, and that no right whatsoever to them belongs to Herlewin.

The transaction upon which Herlewin relies is this. In time of war, when in the kingdom of the English nearly everyone was permitted to do almost whatever he could, a certain man named William [Col. 0869D] acquired the said church. Herlewin, greatly harassing him because a certain uncle of Herlewin’s—a priest—had previously possessed that church, at length induced William to grant him, on William’s sole authority, the tithes of the church to hold for an annual payment, so that Herlewin might thereby desist from harassing him. Not long afterward, this William turned toward a better way of life and surrendered the church, with everything belonging to it, into the hand of the lord of Norwich, that he might dispose of it and provide a parson for the now-vacant church.

When the church was thus vacant, William of Ibreio, lord of the land, presented the abbot of Ibreio to the lord of Norwich and obtained by petition that, when he instituted a parson in that church, he should grant it, with all its appurtenances, [Col. 0870A] to his monastery by a pious and perpetual donation. Herlewin, however, holding that, by the agreement made with William—never confirmed by episcopal authority—the abbot was bound to render him the said tithes, did not cease to claim them, although he showed no ground of law by which they belonged to him. Since he showed no right whatever in these matters and, although he said that the tithes had at some time been granted to him by episcopal authority, wholly failed even to prove this, we absolved the abbot from his claim and, under apostolic authority, enjoined the lord of Norwich to restore the said tithes to the abbot and provide henceforth for his peace.

Seeking to nullify all this, Herlewin falsely represented to Your [Col. 0870B] Excellency that, although we had undertaken to determine the case within two months, we set a day only after eleven weeks and had thus departed from the form of your mandate. We explain what was done in this matter, so that, if we have erred in law, instructed by you in such obscurities, we may walk more cautiously in the future. We did indeed undertake to determine the case within two months, and, in setting a day for the case within that same period, the lord of Winchester and I met in London on the very day. But because the lord of Winchester was drawn on that very day into the king’s court by a most urgent matter, and because he perceived that the day of the jurisdiction committed to him was expiring and that, through lack of time, he could not attend to the case, he wished to be excused to Herlewin.

Herlewin nevertheless insisted strongly, [Col. 0870C] and the abbot consented; therefore we set a day beyond the term prescribed for us and concluded the case as stated. There was, however, long dispute about this. Some maintained that it was not permissible, proving their position by the following law: “When a judge appointed by a provincial governor has not pronounced on the day which the governor ordered, but, after days have elapsed, has rendered judgment at a later time, the governor shall hear the matter anew in its entirety.” Others, maintaining that a judge ought to proceed from like cases to like and administer law accordingly, cited the following concerning a judge appointed up to a fixed sum: “A judge who appears to have authority to judge up to a fixed sum may also judge a greater matter, if this has been agreed between the litigants.” Drawing an argument from the analogous case, they held that a judge appointed for a fixed time [Col. 0870D] might likewise hear the case at a later time if the parties consented. They confirmed this by the law concerning an arbitrator: although no provision is made concerning an extension of the day, he may extend the day of the submission if the parties consent that he pronounce the award.

Interpreting your mandate in this fashion, therefore, and judging that what has been granted for someone’s benefit ought not be turned to that person’s detriment, we proceeded in the matter as just described, in accordance with the Church’s custom among us in mandates of this kind. We followed especially what we find expressed thus in the book of the *Digest*: “If a judge is appointed for a period and all litigants consent, then, unless an extension has been specially prohibited by the principal order, the time [Col. 0871A] within which he appeared to be to settle the case may be extended.” We wish you health . . . .

## LETTER CLXVI. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, A., supreme pontiff, brother G., minister of the Church of London, all the humble and ready devotion that obedience and service can offer.

It is right, Father, that matters which, an appeal having been made to you, have been suspended and seek the judgment of Your Sublimity for their determination should be brought to your knowledge. Since the merits of cases are made known through the assertions of the parties, we set forth in these letters to Your Sublimity the case litigated before us between our beloved son and canon Henry and William of Pontefract [Col. 0871B], and suspended by an appeal made to you.

Henry complained that, while he was absent and occupied in scholarly studies, the said William had erected a chapel within the bounds of Henry’s parish of Stubeheia and had caused divine services to be celebrated there to the injury and detriment of the mother church. On account of that chapel, William had for a long time unjustly withheld tithes and other ecclesiastical revenues from the mother church. Henry demanded, supporting his claim with abundant arguments and authorities, that the chapel secretly built in his parish be demolished, the matter restored to its former state, and what had unjustly been withheld from him be restored through our office.

William, however, denying that it was a new work, replied that the chapel had existed from ancient times on his land [Col. 0871C] and that he had now renewed it by his right; and that he had celebrated divine worship there to the injury or detriment of no one. He added that he had paid the tithes from his land to the mother church according to agreements entered into and confirmed between his predecessors and Henry’s; that he had paid four shillings yearly for them, as the agreement provided; and that, when an appeal had once been made to the lord of Canterbury to annul this agreement, he had been judicially absolved from the claim advanced against the agreement. Although William alleged these things, he supported none of them by documents or witnesses. [Col. 0871D]

Henry, however, asserted that before the lord archbishop the judgment of absolution concerned only the tithes of the year in which that case was then heard. He added that he too had suspended that judgment by an appeal to your hearing, and that Your Sublimity had delegated cognizance of the entire case to the lord of Winchester, but that he himself, hindered by other business, had not pursued the case. When Henry pressed his claim and established by a large number of witnesses the right of his church in the said tithes, showing through their oral testimony that he had also received them, and demanding restoration of what he had possessed, William declined the examination of our jurisdiction, appealed to the hearing of Your Sublimity, and fixed the feast of All Saints as the date for his appeal. We wish you health in the Lord, dearest Father in Christ.

## LETTER CLXVII. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0872A]

To his father and lord, A., supreme pontiff, brother G., minister of the Church of London, may you triumph happily in Christ, with Satan trampled beneath your holy feet.

Since, Father in Christ most beloved, by the Lord’s ordering, the care of all churches belongs to Your Sublimity, it is nevertheless fitting that you should more graciously turn the eyes of mercy toward those whom greater charity commends, and toward all those to whom a more ready kindness in charity is inclined through devoted service. Since experience itself teaches that this has long prevailed in the Church of Fécamp, that church now has recourse with confidence to Your Holiness in the necessity under which it presently labors. [Col. 0872B] It hopes that aid will come to it from the source from which, as they report, compassionately extended mercy has laudably brought it the desired remedy.

For, through a recent accidental fire—while the enemy of humankind ever envies the good fortunes of the faithful—it has been burned to such a condition of misery that it, once the dwelling-place of a most noble convent and a refuge for the poor, pilgrims, and all who need hospitable charity, now has nowhere to lay its head (Matt. 8), nowhere to celebrate divine worship, nowhere to maintain its rule, nowhere to relieve the need of those who arrive. Therefore we make supplication and affectionately offer entreaties to Your Sublimity, asking that the mercy graciously granted through your letters may assist it, so that what [Col. 0872C] the evil one’s contrivance has most grievously burned may be restored by your authority, to his disgrace and to Christ’s everlasting glory; so that, through your aid, its shattered order may recover strength, ancient charity may flourish again, and, having established an enduring memorial of you, that convent of brethren may always keep you before its eyes and unceasingly render thanks to Your Holiness. May the Lord preserve your safety, beloved Father in Christ.

## LETTER CLXVIII. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, A., supreme pontiff, brother G., minister of the Church of London, all the humble devotion and readiness to obey that he can offer of himself.

[Col. 0872D] The Church of Winchester sighs to you, Father, and because the care of all churches belongs to you, anxiously laments before you its misfortunes. Bereft of a father, it has long sought aid elsewhere and summoned bishops from distant regions to administer to the people entrusted to them the sacraments established from heaven. Even while its father lived, it had long lacked a father, because the weakness of his body had for a long time prevented him from administering those things by which the Church of God is founded, raised up, and brought to perfection.

It rejoiced that an end had now come to its sighing and breathed again with great gladness of heart [Col. 0873A] in its elect, whom it had desired with all its wishes and had solemnly chosen, with no one at all objecting or protesting, as father and pastor for itself. But hearing that its wishes are deferred and that the consecration of its elect is being long postponed, it is now covered by a cloud of sorrow; and because hope deferred afflicts the soul, it urgently appeals to all its friends and neighbors that they may lay its desires before you and, in supplication, offer prayers to Your Holiness. It asks that, if it please you, you may be willing to condescend and show compassion to its distress and, in this matter, because of the Church’s manifold need, if any dispensation may be allowed in this matter because of the Church’s manifold need, grant that its elect—whose honorable character and integrity of conduct are worthily commendable—be consecrated without delay. “Desire that comes is a tree of life.”

Therefore, if you receive the prayers of those petitioning Your Sublimity in this cause, you will render no small assistance to the Church of Winchester and will bind all of us to you, Father, in all the gratitude we can [Col. 0873B] offer. May the Lord preserve you for many years, beloved Father in Christ.

## LETTER CLXIX. TO THE SAME, ON BEHALF OF THE ELECT OF HEREFORD

To the lord pope, the lord of London, on behalf of the elect of Hereford.

We hope, Father, that the Church of Hereford has rendered service pleasing to the Lord. Having been granted freedom to choose a father for itself, it has, as common opinion holds, chosen for its governance a suitable man as pastor, one approved by common judgment and acceptable to God and humankind. For how great are the distinguishing marks of virtue in which the elect of Hereford shines is proclaimed by report, confirmed by public opinion, and attested by the unanimous assertion of all who [Col. 0873C] declare that Robert, archdeacon of Oxford, passed through every stage of his life so innocently and honorably that his reputation has never suffered even a slight detraction, nor has hostile rumor been able in any way to darken his manner of life or malign speech to stain it with wickedness.

We commend him, dearest Father in Christ, to Your Holiness’s favor, affectionately offering our prayers that you may receive the petition of the Church of Hereford, which has recourse to you and which we truly believe just; and that you may, if it please you, provide with paternal favor for the consecration of its elect. Otherwise, if he meets rejection, virtue, having suffered injury, may blush and in future less readily kindle others to seek and cultivate it.

## LETTER CLXX. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0873D]

To the lord pope, the lord of London.

Father, charity, which commands us imperiously, compels us to write to Your Holiness and, as necessity requires, affectionately offer the prayers of our brethren. For by its law we are bound to love them as ourselves and, considering their affairs our own, certainly not to deny them what we would wish to be shown to us in a like need.

We testify that our venerable brother Geoffrey, archdeacon of the Church of Canterbury, is a prudent and energetic man, provident in counsel, discerning and eloquent, most well suited for conducting the Church’s affairs and for relieving and sustaining its needs. Since knowledge, we believe, abounds in him for teaching and character [Col. 0874A] for honorable life, the Church of Ely, through our hand, received letters from your legates, by which it was admonished under apostolic authority to choose a bishop for itself. It then sought Geoffrey as its father and pastor and, by the unanimous vote of all—with none objecting or raising any contradiction—and with the prince giving his consent, solemnly elected him to the governance of the bishopric of Ely.

Since we believe that, by the Lord’s aid, he will greatly benefit the Church to which he is called and will show every devotion he can to you and the holy Roman Church, we knock with the Church that knocks and, with the petitioner, affectionately offer prayers before Your Holiness: that you may confirm by the authority [Col. 0874B] which you hold and can exercise what has been done; that, setting your final hand to this matter and hastening his consecration with paternal compassion, you may bind both him and the Church committed to him more closely to you in every gratitude and fullness of charity; so that the liberty recently granted through you to churches in the kingdom of England may grow strong in its beginnings and, as the Lord increases grace, may vigorously strengthen in the course of time itself.

## LETTER CLXXI. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, A., supreme pontiff, brother G., minister of the Church of London, the affection of one who offers pious greeting and the service of devoted submission.

The English Church, Father, acknowledges itself bound to Your Holiness in every thanksgiving, because, Father, you graciously received the elections of our brethren presented to your eminence, and by your pious and fatherly favour permitted them to be confirmed through the office of our father, the lord Archbishop of Canterbury, and the elect themselves to be consecrated by his hand. In this matter the hand of apostolic compassion has wiped away the continual tears which long-standing sorrow had for many years drawn forth from many; and it has exalted the Church of the realm to the rank of its former dignity and most powerfully restored it. For through your grace, the Lord ministering, the holy see of Canterbury, long vacant and long left empty, now recognizes its own bishop within itself; and the clergy and people of Winchester, with their elect’s consecration granted them, rejoice and exult in the Lord as having most fully attained their desire. The Churches of Bath, Hereford, Chichester, and Ely, now by your gift of grace possessed of those whom they had chosen according to their desires, celebrate a distinguished day of solemn thanksgiving.

The Church of Lincoln alone, lord, remains; while praises resound everywhere in the other Churches and drums of glory are beaten on every side, it has groaning instead of song and, breathing a spirit of sorrow, is wholly given over to lamentation. In the Father’s house symphony and chorus are heard everywhere; but this Church stands outside and does not enter, and, having once suffered rejection, is afraid to go in to the Father. Yet, considering the abundance of charity which flows without ceasing from the fountain of the apostolic breast and makes glad on every side the city of God, and recalling the evangelical saying: “Everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matt. 7), it conceives hope that the brightness of your serenity may dispel the cloud of its sorrow, and that the merciful Father may hear the prayers of a most devoted daughter pleading alike for the reception and advancement of her elect.

It knows, however, that certain persons among us have “built many things upon his back” and “surrounded his innocence with words of hatred” (Ps. 128), and have prevailed so far that the face of your clemency has, as it is said, been turned somewhat away from him, and that many have now formed an unfavourable opinion of him. But, if it please you to consider, credit concerning his conduct and life should chiefly be given to those to whom he has been known from his earliest years, under whose eyes, as they most certainly testify, he grew up innocently; and, having now reached, as they assert, his thirtieth year, he has completed the first watch of his life honourably and innocently under the testimony of many. The Church of Lincoln, your devoted daughter, having conceived good hope of him and having observed and approved his prudence in the archdeaconry which he administered, hopes that his advancement will be of very great benefit to it for many reasons too numerous to recount. It therefore unanimously chose him as its father and urgently asks that, by your favour, this its desire may be fulfilled.

Having hope therefore in the Lord that both his honourableness and prudence will increase daily to the honour of God and the Church, and that he will prove a vigorous fellow-worker in relieving the Church’s necessities, we join the pleading Church in offering prayers to Your Holiness that you may extend to him the hand of grace; and, by granting it what it asks, may supply to the Church of the English the joy which it still lacks and make us all debtors to the favour of your eminence in this respect. May the Lord preserve you in health, beloved Father in Christ.

## LETTER 172. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff Alexander, Brother Gilbert, minister of the Church of London, offers the devoted and due service of complete obedience.

In collecting St Peter’s penny, we have taken care to employ all the concern and diligence we could. Our beloved brethren and fellow bishops, whose bishoprics are known to be subject to this obligation, having been admonished by us under your authority according to the tenor and contents of writings diligently sought out and found in the archives of the Church of Canterbury, all fully acknowledged and paid the amount due—except our venerable brother and fellow bishop, the lord Bishop of Exeter. He did not recognize the sum assessed upon his diocese; and because he offered less than the written calculation required, he carried back unpaid all that he had offered. Thus, although often and repeatedly admonished, he has hitherto wholly refrained from payment.

We have arranged for the entire remaining sum—namely two hundred pounds, except for the nine pounds and five shillings which the aforesaid brother was to pay to the abbot of Saint-Bertin—to be sent through a certain faithful agent of ours, in accordance with your command conveyed to us by a brother sent from the abbot himself. As for what should be done concerning that remaining portion which still has to be paid, Your Holiness will provide when it sees fit. Keeping our office within the limits of your command, we neither accept one who offers less, nor impose any coercion upon one who refuses to pay. May Your Holiness prosper.

## LETTER 173. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff A., Brother G., minister of the Church of London, offers himself and, insofar as he can, the service of obedience and humility.

Long ago, Father, I appealed to your hearing because the commands of our father, the lord Archbishop of Canterbury, imposed no slight burden upon me. On hearing of the arrival of your legates in Normandy, I hastened to meet them, ready to show before them the grounds of my appeal to you and humbly to obey their judgment in all things. Since they did not intervene in this case, I was compelled by the many necessities occasioned by the dangers threatening me to appeal anew to Your Holiness.

Since the very necessity of my undertaking this journey required me to return to England and provide what was necessary for travel to you, I set the term of my appeal for the day of St Martin’s passing—not in order to seek delay, but for the sake of legitimate preparation. Therefore, if divine goodness turns its eyes of mercy toward me and graciously grants me a passable journey to you, I shall, on the appointed day, if life remains and the Lord accompanies and assists me, appear before Your Holiness, hear the charges brought against me, and most devotedly submit in every respect to your judgment or counsel.

For God, the inspector of all things, is my witness that in all that has been done among us I have served neither flattery, nor arrogance, nor ambition, even in the smallest degree; rather, according to my modest ability and understanding, I have faithfully sought the interests of Your Holiness and the holy Roman Church, and of the whole English Church. For having in one place a father and in another a lord, set between two swords, fearing on one side to fall upon the material sword and on the other dreading the spiritual, I can scarcely hold on, protected only by the authority of your name; and, long since wearied by these disasters, I await the end which the Lord will give them.

I therefore most devotedly entreat that compassion with which apostolic mercy is accustomed both to sympathize with and to accommodate itself to its children: do not, I pray, regard as void the appeal made to you on an honourable and most just ground; do not wholly expose to him my head, which my father and lord of Canterbury relentlessly pursues with unjust hatred. Rather, hear yourself the case which we have briefly set out, as equity requires; or, if the difficulty of the journey does not permit this, entrust it for examination and determination to your legates who are with you. I entrusted to my messenger certain matters to be communicated more privately to Your Holiness; if you mercifully assent to them, at your command . . . will fittingly reward this service. I pray that you may prosper in the Lord, dearest Father in Christ.

## LETTER 174. TO THE SAME

To his father and lord, the supreme pontiff A., Brother G., minister of the Church of London, offers the due service of sincere charity and humble obedience.

Receiving your command, dearest Father in Christ, with due reverence, we immediately went to your son and our dearest lord, the illustrious king of the English, although he was then campaigning on the very borders of Wales. Joining to ourselves our venerable brother Robert, Bishop of Hereford, we addressed him carefully and earnestly in accordance with the form of your command. Setting before his eyes every matter expressed to us in your letters, we begged him and—so far as befitted royal majesty—rebuked him; firmly and insistently we urged him to make satisfaction for what had been laid to his charge. If he had departed from the path of reason, he was not to delay returning to the way of truth and justice at your summons conveyed through us; admonished piously by his father, he was wholly to desist from wrongful acts, love the Lord with a pure heart, regard his mother, the holy Roman Church, with customary reverence, not hinder those who wished to visit her, not obstruct appeals made to her, and, kindly recalling and restoring our father the lord Archbishop of Canterbury, remain steadfast and immovable in reverence for St Peter and for you. Attending to works of mercy, he was neither to burden Churches and ecclesiastical persons in his kingdom or land himself, nor permit them to be burdened by another; but was to preserve them through his royal protection, so that He through whom kings reign might preserve for him his temporal kingdom on earth and bestow the eternal kingdom in heaven. Otherwise, unless he yielded to these salutary warnings, Your Holiness, which had endured patiently until then, could not endure further in patience. We added that he ought to fear lest, if he did not correct his errors, he should soon incur the wrath of almighty God, who would permit neither his kingdom to stand long nor his people to prosper, but, having exalted the humble man, would now cast down one already exalted from the very summit of royal power, dashing him down more harshly.

He, however, received your rebuke with much thanksgiving and answered every point with great self-command and modesty. First, he asserted that his mind had in no way turned away from you, nor had he ever conceived any such intention in his heart. Indeed, provided that you show him fatherly favour, he will love you as a father, venerate and cherish the holy Roman Church as a mother, and humbly comply with and obey your sacred commands, without prejudice to his own dignity and that of his kingdom. If for some time he has not regarded you with his customary reverence, he alleges this as the cause: although he stood by you in your need with all his heart, mind, and strength, when afterward he had recourse to you in his own need through messengers, Your Holiness did not answer him in a manner worthy of his merits. He complains and is ashamed that in nearly every request he has suffered rejection. Yet, trusting in fatherly favour—which, when it wills, will hear the son—and hoping and waiting for a more gracious countenance, he persists with unshaken constancy in loyalty to St Peter and to you, as stated. Accordingly, he will not in any way impede anyone who wishes to visit Your Holiness, nor, as he asserts, has he hitherto impeded anyone.

Regarding appeals, he claims as a matter of honour and obligation under an ancient constitution of his kingdom that no cleric of his realm having a civil case against one of his earls or barons may leave the bounds of the realm unless he has first learned by experience whether, through the king’s authority and command, he can obtain his right. If he cannot obtain it even thus, anyone may appeal to Your Eminence when he wishes, the king raising no objection whatever. If in this any prejudice is caused to your right or honour, he promises, with God’s help, shortly to correct it by the counsel of the whole Church of his kingdom.

Although he knows that emperor to be schismatic, he says that to this day he has not learned that he has been excommunicated by you. If he learns this by your declaration, and if he has made an unlawful treaty with him or with anyone else, he promises to correct this as well by the judgment and counsel of the Church of his kingdom.

He declares that he has not at all expelled our father, the lord Archbishop of Canterbury, from his kingdom. Therefore, just as he departed voluntarily, so he may return in full peace to his Church whenever he sees fit—provided that, in making satisfaction to the king concerning the matters of which he complains, he is willing to preserve intact the royal dignities and those to which the king himself has sworn.

If any Church or ecclesiastical person shows that it has been burdened by him or his agents, he will be ready to make full satisfaction according to the judgment of the whole Church.

These are the answers we received from our lord the king; would that we had received something more ample in conformity with all your wishes. We judged it right to make these matters known to Your Eminence, so that your discretion might determine from his answers by what conclusion to bring this affair to an end. The lord king appears greatly to justify his position, since in all the matters mentioned he promises to obey the counsel and judgment of the Church of his kingdom and not in any way to obstruct the return of our father, the lord Archbishop of Canterbury, as has been stated.

We therefore considered that we should entreat Your Excellency to keep before your eyes the words: “A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoking flax he will not quench” (Isa. 42). If it please you, restrain for a time within the bounds of moderation that holy zeal which has been laudably kindled by the fire of the divine Spirit to avenge every injury inflicted upon the Church of God, lest, by pronouncing either a sentence of interdict or that final decree of severance, you should sorrowfully see all the Churches overthrown and turn away irrevocably from your obedience—God forbid!—both the king himself and countless peoples with him. It is better for a limb to adhere to the head while wounded than to be separated from the body once it has been cut off. Wounds return to health, but limbs once severed scarcely grow together again with the body. Severance produces despair; the work of the physician often restores health. For what if your word has not yet fully taken hold or been received? Is divine grace to be despaired of, since it can quickly, when it wills, both take hold and be received? Has the Lord’s hand been shortened, that it cannot save, or his ear made heavy, that it cannot hear? (Isa. 59). That word of the Lord “runs swiftly” (Ps. 147): as soon as it wills, it changes all things and grants unexpected things through the prayers of the saints. Royal blood allows itself to be conquered only when it has conquered; nor is it ashamed to yield when it has prevailed. He must be endured with gentleness and overcome through warnings and patience.

What if patience shown for a time brings some loss of temporal things? There can be no doubt that severity must give way when the slaughter of peoples threatens; and when a storm comes on, much must be thrown into the sea so that the ship may be brought safely to harbour. We speak foolishly, yet with unfeigned charity: if the end of the matter should be such that the lord of Canterbury, deprived of his possessions, suffers perpetual exile, and England thereafter does not obey your commands—God forbid!—would it not have been better to endure patiently for a time than to have served severity with such zeal? What then? Even if persecution cannot separate more of us from your obedience, there will nevertheless be someone who bends the knee before Baal and accepts the pallium of Canterbury from the hand of an idol, with no regard for religion or justice. There will be no lack of those who, occupying our sees and sitting in our chairs, obey him with complete devotion of mind. Many already chew over such designs, hoping that scandals may come and straight paths be made crooked. Therefore, Father, we do not lament or bewail our own disadvantages; rather, unless you meet these evils, we tremble as we see the disgraceful overthrow of God’s Church impending, lest we soon, through weariness of life, wish that the day had perished on which we were born to behold such spectacles.

Furthermore, no one in the kingdom would have answered us concerning St Peter’s tribute, even in the smallest amount, unless the lord king had issued a general command on the matter. By his command, it will be collected at the time fixed of old and, with the Lord’s help, transmitted to Your Holiness through our hand.

## LETTER 175. TO THE SAME

To Pope Alexander, Gilbert, Bishop of London, offers humble obedience in all things, so far as my insignificance can do so.

Having rightly become suspicious, from certain things heard and learned, of the severity of our father, the lord Archbishop of Canterbury, and fearing that he might bind and entangle me in the snares of an undeserved penalty, I appealed to your clemency about the beginning of Lent. I fixed the day for the appeal as the octave of the Purification of Blessed Mary, so that I might avert by your protection the anger with which he unjustly persecutes me, and might in some measure avoid, by invoking your name, the bonds in which he was preparing to involve one undeserving of them, until the day set for the hearing of the case in your presence.

Therefore, my beloved Father in the Lord, prostrate with my whole spirit, I beseech Your Holiness: do not, I pray, take away from me the common remedy granted to all who are oppressed. Do not cast me off as a reprobate from the protection of your defence. But, accepting the appeal made to you, if any sentence beyond due measure has been pronounced against me, either declare it void, as is just, or keep it suspended, so that on the day when, with the Lord’s help, I am ready to appear before Your Eminence, you may determine concerning me according to my deserts—either reject me if convicted, or absolve me as innocent, if that seems right.

For my fault, if I have one, is simply this: feeling myself burdened by the weight of commands which I necessarily had either to evade or to accept with failure and every misery, I dared to appeal to the apostolic hearing, that I might commit myself entirely to your counsel and, after consulting you, either depart from the kingdom or remain in the Church entrusted to me with the burden of commands lightened. For, to state briefly what is true, while matters stand in this way between the lord king and the lord of Canterbury, it is impossible for me or any other bishop of that kingdom to accept the command of one and avoid the unbearable anger of the other.

Let fatherly mercy therefore act, if it please you, so that if, after an appeal was made to your eminence, any sentence has been hastily or improperly pronounced against me—though I have neither confessed nor been convicted, neither summoned nor cited, nor in any manner proceeded against—you may, as is just, deprive it of force. And if you remit anything from your own holiness, at least call to mind the injury done to St Peter and to his holy see; you will find me altogether most ready for every service you command. May the Lord preserve you safe for a long time, most beloved Father in Christ.

## LETTER 176. TO WILLIAM OF PAVIA, CARDINAL

To the venerable lord and dearest friend W., Cardinal of Pavia of the holy Roman Church, Brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting and the due service of obedience.

A few words readily persuade when the friendly kindness of the person to whom one writes is inclined to hear. Since we trust this to be so of your sincerity, we briefly set forth the affair in which we ask assistance from your goodwill. We have received the lord pope’s command to summon Hugh, Earl of Norfolk, strictly; and, unless upon admonition he restored to the canons of Pentney the vill of Pentney and the other things which they complain were taken from them, to subject both him and all his land to interdict; and, unless even thus he came to his senses within forty days, not to delay binding him by a sentence of excommunication.

But royal authority strongly opposes us in this matter. The king asserts that the highest dignity of his kingdom requires that, whenever he is ready to render full justice to anyone who has a complaint against one of his earls or barons concerning lands or fiefs, neither an archbishop nor any bishop of his realm shall press that earl or baron with interdict or subject him to excommunication. He affirms that his predecessors have possessed this right up to the present with the assent of the Roman pontiffs, and recalls that all of us, the bishops of his kingdom, have affirmed it to him by oath. He demands that we stand by established custom, do not diminish the privileges of his kingdom, and do not depart from what we have promised him under the sacred obligation of an oath.

Thus what is commanded by authority is forbidden us under grave threat. We are in such a strait that, unless apostolic gentleness moderates its command, we must incur either the danger of disobedience—God forbid!—on this side, or the reproach of perjury and breached fealty before the lord king on the other. I would rather not have been a bishop than incur either of these alternatives. Both swords are grievous: one kills the soul, the other the body. That one is indeed the more grievous, yet this one bears more heavily. And what profit will there be to my dearest lord, the lord pope, in my blood (Ps. 29), if, by going down into this condemnation, I am held either perjured or disobedient—may that always be far from me? If I do not obey my lord, death awaits me; if I obey him, there remains only that I should depart from a kingdom whose laws I do not accept and withdraw from fealty to whose king.

If the cause were of such a kind that it was worthy to undergo the punishment of death or exile, I would indeed rejoice in my banishment or death to render a service pleasing to my lord. But is the cause of six brethren at Pentney, living most miserably and without any observance of either rule or order, so great that, for the restoration to them of a few acres of land, a dispute must be raised between the supreme pontiff and our lord the king of England—formerly his friend and, God granting, still to be his closest friend—concerning the eminence of their respective dignities? Especially when in this case it is easy to render each person his right and peacefully restore what has been disturbed to peace and the due conclusion of justice?

If the lord king is permitted, he will immediately settle this case by the counsel of bishops and other prudent men. If the lord pope delegates the case to judges, Earl Hugh will not refuse to abide by their judgment. For we have strictly summoned him, announcing to him the sentence set out in the lord pope’s letters. When he heard them, he immediately challenged the falsity of the petition, asserting that he had never granted Pentney to the canons in question, nor delivered to them the document which they produce and display under his name on the matter, nor given assent that he should acknowledge it. Since, therefore, he alleges that the instrument on which they rely is false, let Your Prudence consider whether the matter is so straightforward that it requires no proof and ought not to be brought to judgment. For even if not the determination of the case but the execution of a sentence is commanded, the truth of the petition must nevertheless be investigated.

## LETTER 177. TO THE SAME

To the venerable lord and dearest friend William of Pavia, cardinal priest of the most holy Roman Church, Brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting which now is, and that which we hope for from the Lord.

You know, lord—and the world knows it well enough—what punishment I have long endured and what penalty besides, I who received the enormities of a most severe punishment before the measure of my fault had become known to me. At the word, as I hear, of a single Welshman, although he is not distinguished by the honour of eminent rank, I received the adverse verdict of condemnation without having been cited, warned, or made liable even to the reproach of a notorious crime; and though my leprosy was neither examined nor recognized by the priest, I was nevertheless cast outside the camp of the Church.

But because it is not lawful to set one’s mouth against heaven, and because to scrutinize the acts of one’s superiors is acknowledged to be akin to sacrilege, it is safer to flee to the help of a healer than rashly to break forth in complaint. It is, however, customary that one whose condition harms him should have recourse rather to the person whose favour he judges will be readier toward him in his affliction. Trusting therefore in the excellence of your affection—whose sincerity and fidelity the more certain teaching of experience has demonstrated—and pressed by urgent necessity, I ask your aid: may the favour previously shown to me through you be brought, through your effort, to its intended result; and may what you know to be lacking for the discharge of my office be restored to me through your care, with the Lord’s help.

What gives confidence to my petition is that you have already extended to me the hand of grace and, through the urgency of your pious plea, removed the burden under which I was anxiously oppressed. Freed from the disgrace of dishonour, you prudently obtained that I should be placed within the camp of the Church. I am therefore all the more devotedly bound to you in thanksgiving because, moved by the impulse of your own will, you most advantageously managed the affairs of an absent friend. Inborn goodness moved you to this compassion, a grace not preceded by any merits of mine. Yet I desire to deserve what I did not deserve, and I regret not having deserved it; I regret too that I have wished so late for what I ought to have pursued from my earliest efforts. Let grace therefore, if it please you, do and complete what belongs to it; let it render wholly indebted to itself the man whom it has begun to make deserving; and, having restored me to myself, let it henceforth possess me, in full right, wholly for itself and for its own. We pray that you may prosper in the Lord.

## LETTER 178. TO THE SAME, ON BEHALF OF THE ELECT OF WINCHESTER

To Lord William of Pavia, on behalf of the elect of Winchester, [I offer] myself and, insofar as I can, the service of a devoted mind.

A few words readily persuade when the friendly kindness of the person to whom one writes is inclined to hear. Therefore, because we fully trust in your goodwill toward us—not through our merits, indeed, but solely through your grace graciously granted and powerfully shown to us—we earnestly offer prayers to your eminence, asking that you support and promote the cause of our friend and dearest kinsman, the lord elect of Winchester. Since we do not doubt that you are great in counsel and powerful in intervention, use the wisdom and diligence given you by God to procure the prompt completion of his consecration.

Administration is usually entrusted to a wise person. The multiplied necessity of the Church asks at last to be relieved. If sacraments are beneficial, if any salvation of souls consists in them, it is nonetheless no slight loss and danger that they are withheld from so many peoples, and, because of the shortage of bishops, are administered late, or not at all, to so many who require them. The Church of Winchester has now passed through almost three lustra under a mourning garment and in the condition of widowhood. Long deprived of episcopal blessing, absolution, the laying on of hands, the promotion of clerics to orders, the renewal of chrism within itself, the consecration of churches, and the other things necessary to spiritual life, it has almost forgotten them. The word of God is silent; a profound silence holds all things; and in many ways too long to enumerate, the gains of souls are lost.

We ask that, by your help, relief be given to these dangers, so that when the elect of Winchester has been consecrated through you, we may rejoice in the Lord together with his Church and may always retain in future memory the honour and benefit shown us. We pray that you may prosper in the Lord.

## LETTER 179. TO JOHN, CARDINAL OF NAPLES

To the venerable lord and dearest brother John of Naples, cardinal priest of the most holy Roman Church, Brother G., minister of the Church of London, [wishes] that he may enjoy the successes he desires, together with health.

We receive with greater gratitude services performed not because necessity has compelled them, but because the affection of purer goodwill alone has procured them. It is an approved custom that we should be more closely bound to those who, exercising sheer liberality, confer voluntary benefits upon us, than to those whom the performance of previous merit has moved to do the same. Thus your service binds us more strongly because you preceded us with blessings, and we experienced through certain events the fruit of your affection before there was known to you any evidence of a reciprocal affection.

What you have bestowed is gratuitous; what we repay in love has unequal merit. Simple liberality increases the favour of the former; in the latter, a will prompted by preceding merits and benefits makes the grace less free. All this invites us to fuller acts of thanksgiving, which we offer in desire—would that we might fulfill them in deed. We offer you our person and resources, intending, when God gives opportunity, to prove our words by their effect.

For the care you have given our affairs and the honour bestowed upon our clerics, we devote ourselves and them to you in thanksgiving, earnestly entreating that what has been successfully accomplished in part may be brought to completion through the diligence of your discretion. In accordance with the plan of your counsel, we would have attempted to undertake the journey to you, had a fuller hope of peace between the lord pope and the king not now appeared and more certain proofs of his devotion become clear. Moreover, we thought it necessary to fear that our departure might be judged by our legates to have been made somewhat in contempt and injury of them, and that they might interpret our flight as despair of our cause. We therefore judged that it was not expedient for us, without consulting them, to turn aside anywhere, since, as is said, the lord pope has sent them from his side on our account.

The difficulty of the journey also frightens us, and the dangers threatening travellers compel us to waver greatly in this matter. Yet the desire conceived would banish every concern of fear if the weakness and infirmity of my body could in any way suffice to endure this labour. For there is nothing I could wish more, nothing I could desire more eagerly, than to stand personally before the lord pope and refute, by the power of Him who is truth, those who in his presence and before the holy court speak against me and make false allegations. Hoping often to bring this about, we have nevertheless always been delayed by the obstacle of some necessity; now, however, infirmity joined to old age compels us, though we desire the judge, to despair through manifold necessity of being able to stand before him.

We therefore more urgently implore your care, that through your aid and efforts the lord pope may grant us full favour and, by apostolic gentleness and compassion together, finally bring the benefit already mentioned to completion for us. We have entrusted certain matters to be communicated to you by our messenger; I pray that you hear him attentively and give credence to what he sets before you. We pray, dearest one, that you may prosper in the Lord.

## LETTER 180. TO J., CARDINAL DEACON

To the venerable lord and dearest friend J., cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, Brother G., minister of the Church of London, offers pious affection and whatever service dutiful charity can render.

The hearts of those who love one another speak to each other, and the minds of friends, though separated by local distance, are nevertheless firmly joined to one another through an inwardly working power, by a kind of indissoluble affection. Love makes present to itself the person whom it loves, and charity henceforth does not allow its beloved to be absent from it. Thus, notwithstanding distance, friends help one another while absent in necessity and, fulfilling Christ’s law, do not fail mutually to bear one another’s burdens.

Prompted by this charity, dearest friend, and strongly encouraged by your goodwill toward us, we offer to Your Eminence our prayers, dear to us in the Lord, asking that you carefully consider the cause of the bearer of this letter and his brethren, the monks of Warden, and provide for them, for the love of God and at our request, as you judge their necessity requires. You will learn from the letter of our beloved brother, the lord Bishop of Exeter, how great are the injustices under which they are oppressed. By coming piously to the aid of the oppressed, according to the wisdom given you by God, you will have, as we hope, the Lord as your rewarder, and us as debtors in gratitude and service. Farewell.

## LETTER 181. TO ALL CHILDREN OF HOLY MOTHER CHURCH

To all beloved children in the Lord of holy mother Church to whom these letters shall come, Brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting in Christ.

By apostolic letters we received a mandate to summon before us the abbot of Grestene and John, bearer of these letters, and to restore to John in full, setting aside every pretext and excuse and removing every remedy of appeal, whatever we should find had been taken or withheld from him after his appeal to the Apostolic See, whether by the abbot himself or by his agents; and to procure for him suitable satisfaction for the losses and [Col. 0885B] injuries inflicted upon him. Once restoration had been made and satisfaction rendered, we were to decide, notwithstanding the cessation of the appeal, the case pending between them concerning the chapel of Cherlechestone.

Following this form, since we had full and certain knowledge of John’s appeal, publicly made before us, and, after careful and strict inquiry into the truth through the lawful testimony of suitable witnesses, of the violence subsequently inflicted upon him by the monks of Grestene, of his expulsion from his house, and of the losses caused by the invasion, we pronounced—by counsel of our brethren and by our own resolve, relying on apostolic authority in [Col. 0885C] this matter—that the church of Ferles itself, with all its integrity and all its appurtenances, ought to be restored to the said John. For the losses inflicted upon him, assessed and proved under oath according to our valuation, we condemned the abbot to pay him eighteen marks of silver.

Further, in the case which the often-mentioned John had long pursued concerning the chapel of Cherlechestone against Henry the priest and the aforesaid abbot of Grestene—whom Henry had named as his warrantor in that case—we proceeded in accordance with the tenor of the rescript as follows. John sought restoration to himself of that chapel in the name of his mother church of Ferles, since, as he asserted, it had been founded within the parochial boundaries of that church and had from its foundation been subject to it in filial dependence.

[Col. 0885D] He further alleged that, when he formerly received the parsonage and investiture of the mother church of Ferles from the hand of the bishop of Chichester, upon presentation by the abbot of Grestene—as the bishop himself informed us both orally and in writing—he also received the chapel together with the greater church, and possessed it fully and peacefully for so long, until a dispute was raised against him by Henry. Then a certain monk of Grestene, acting at that time in England in the abbot’s stead, made an agreement with Henry and presumed to surrender the chapel to him and alienate it, although John objected and the lord pope had prohibited this by his authority. The abbot whom Henry had summoned publicly and judicially acknowledged both that the chapel belonged to the mother church of Ferles and [Col. 0886A] that John had possessed it for a long time.

Yet, by way of exception and to the prejudice of John’s claim, he alleged that John had been present at the agreement made with Henry and had approved it by his consent. But when the controversy over this point had been vigorously contested, and the abbot at last wholly failed to prove the alleged consent, we carefully examined the witnesses to the objection whom John produced, found them consistent, and admitted them as trustworthy. Accordingly, on the basis of their testimony and the opposing party’s admission, we adjudged full restoration of the aforesaid chapel to the often-mentioned John. Having assessed and proved the losses for the intervening period under our valuation, we condemned Henry by judgment to pay him twelve marks of silver [Col. 0886B]. Since these acts were performed in discharge of our office under the commission of the lord pope, we have taken care to notify your whole body and to confirm them by the authority we exercise, lest they may hereafter be called into doubt or annulled. Witnesses: H., dean of St Paul’s; Nicholas, archdeacon of London; Master W.

## LETTER CLXXXII. TO THE SAME PERSONS.

G., by the grace of God bishop of London, to all beloved sons in the Lord of holy mother Church to whom these letters shall come: greeting in Christ.

Let your charity know that H., bearer of these letters, has been advanced to the rank of priesthood by divine blessing and the laying on of our hands [Col. 0886C]. Since we do not wish this to be open to doubt, we have taken care to make it known by this present writing to you all, asking and exhorting your charity in the Lord that, for the love of God and reverence for his order, you kindly receive him in the exercise of his office and render him the honour due to him for God’s sake. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXIII. TO THE SAME PERSONS.

Brother G., minister of the Church of London, to all beloved sons in the Lord of holy mother Church: greeting, grace, and blessing.

[Col. 0886D] Things given to the Lord, dearest friends, do not perish for the giver, but are surely kept forever for the one from whom they were given. Therefore we admonish your charity in the Lord that you grant from your resources, as the Lord shall inspire you, some assistance to R., bearer of these letters, who, for the love of God and the salvation of his soul, is working to repair the bridge of London, so that on that day you may receive from God a hundredfold for what you have bestowed upon him. To all who provide him any benefit for accomplishing the aforesaid work, we grant a share in the prayers and benefits of our church; and further, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, we remit twenty days of their penance to those who have confessed. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXIV. TO THE SAME PERSONS.

[Col. 0887A]

G., by the grace of God bishop of London, to all beloved sons in the Lord of holy mother Church to whom these letters shall come: greeting in Christ.

When our venerable brother Robert, abbot of [Ibreio], and Herlewin, clerk of Dochinge, were both present before the lord bishop of Winchester and ourselves, to whom cognizance of the case between them concerning the tithes of Dochinge had been delegated by mandate of the lord pope, we clearly recognized from the allegations and arguments of the said abbot that [the aforesaid tithes] belonged by right to his church of Dochinge. Accordingly, by our own resolve and the common counsel of our brethren, we adjudged those tithes to the abbot and, through him, to his church in perpetuity [Col. 0887B]; and by judgment we absolved him and his church from Herlewin’s claim, since Herlewin, who claimed the same tithes as his own, wholly failed in proof. Since we do not wish this hereafter to be called into doubt or annulled, we have taken care to notify you all of it by this present writing and to confirm it by the authority we exercise.

## LETTER CLXXXV. TO THE SAME PERSONS.

GILBERT, by the grace of God bishop of London, to all sons of holy mother Church: greeting.

[Col. 0887C] We wish it to be known to you all that Geoffrey son of Baldwin and his mother Beatrice de Bollers, as we have ascertained from their charters and verified from their own oral testimony, granted and gave to God and the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem the advowson of the church of Herefelde, with all its appurtenances, as perpetual alms; and they presented to us Brother Richard the Turk, prior in England, that we might invest the said Hospital through him with the parsonage of the aforesaid church, insofar as episcopal right pertains to us.

Since ready and cheerful consent should be given in matters assigned to the necessary uses of the poor, and since we had special regard for the religious character and need of that Hospital, we gratefully received and readily approved the said grant. When R., priest and then parson of that church, freely and voluntarily resigned it into our hands, we immediately delivered it to Prior Richard and, through him, granted to his Hospital the parsonage of that church. Since we wish this henceforth to remain ratified and unquestioned: **[Some portions are missing.]**

## LETTER CLXXXVI. TO THE SAME PERSONS.

G., by the grace of God bishop of London, to all beloved sons in the Lord of holy mother Church of London: greeting, grace, and blessing.

We must take care that controversies decided before us are not revived in litigation. Let your charity therefore know that the case long contested between Master Godfrey and his uncle Ernald concerning the church of Castello was finally settled as follows [Col. 0888A]. Ernald, acknowledging his nephew’s right in the aforesaid church, surrendered it into our hand by the text [of the Gospels]; and we, restoring it in like manner by the text to Godfrey, instituted him as parson thereof. Thereafter, at Godfrey’s request, we received Ernald as vicar in the same church, upon the following agreement: Ernald shall hold the aforesaid church for as long as he lives, under an annual pension of half a mark, to be paid yearly by him to Godfrey in the name of that church; one half of the stipulated pension being paid in mid-Lent, and the other at the feast of St Michael [Col. 0888B].

Since this was done in our presence with the full consent of both parties and confirmed by the religious obligation of an oath on each side, we have taken care, lest it may hereafter be called into doubt or annulled, to make known to you all by this present writing the course of events and to confirm for each party, by the authority of our seal, what belongs to him. Witnesses: Ralph the dean; Peter, archdeacon; Walter, archdeacon; Master Ranulf; Henry, brother of the earl; Ivo, treasurer; Ralph de Ledeberia; Master Geoffrey de Cliforde; Master Walter de Ardep’; Roger de Burkell’; Roger son of Maurice; Ralph the scribe.

## LETTER CLXXXVII. TO THE SAME PERSONS.

[Col. 0888C] G., by the grace of God bishop of London, to all beloved brethren, sons of holy mother Church: greeting, grace, and blessing.

Disputes settled by an amicable conclusion are known to be fully extinguished only when the agreements made for peace between the parties and mutually granted are recorded in the letters and fortified by the affixed seals of those whose authority lawfully confirms them. Therefore we have taken care to commit to common knowledge by this present writing, and wholly to remove between them every future occasion for renewed litigation, the agreement made before us and mutually granted between our venerable brother R. Pic’, archdeacon, and A., clerk, concerning the church of Mideltona.

Alexander, who was pursuing a possessory action under the authority of the lord pope’s letters to recover possession of the church of Mideltona, abandoned this claim before us. He agreed that he would thereafter receive and hold that church in the name of the aforesaid archdeacon—for it unquestionably belongs to the prebend which our venerable brother, the said archdeacon, is known to hold in the church of Lincoln—paying the archdeacon an annual pension of fifteen marks for as long as he remained canon of the aforesaid prebend. In our presence, touching the Gospels, he swore that he would never thereafter bring any suit, harassment, or disturbance whatsoever against the archdeacon concerning the church of Mideltona while he was canon of that prebend; and that he would lawfully and faithfully observe the agreement concerning the aforesaid pension [Col. 0889A], subject nevertheless to any right which, should the archdeacon cease to possess the said prebend while he himself survived, he might have to seek or recover it. Since this was done in the presence of ourselves and our chapter, we—to whom cognizance of this case had been delegated by the lord pope—have held it ratified and taken care to strengthen it by the writing of this present document and the attestation of our seal.

## LETTER CLXXXVIII. TO THE SAME PERSONS.

Brother G., minister of the Church of London, to all beloved sons in the Lord of holy mother Church: greeting, grace, and blessing.

Things given to the Lord, dearest friends, are by no means lost gifts, but are surely reserved forever for the one by whom they were given [Col. 0889B]. Therefore we admonish your charity in the Lord that you grant from your resources, as the Lord shall inspire you, some assistance to R., bearer of these letters, who, for the love of God and the salvation of his soul, is working to repair the bridge and causeway of Stretforde, so that on that day you may receive from God a hundredfold for what you have bestowed upon him. To all who provide him any benefit for accomplishing the aforesaid work, we grant a share in the prayers and benefits of our church; and further, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, we remit twenty days of their penance to those who have confessed. Farewell in Christ.

## LETTER CLXXXIX. TO THE SAME PERSONS.

[Col. 0889C]

G., by the grace of God bishop of London, to all beloved sons in the Lord of holy mother Church: greeting in the Lord.

We make known to your charity that R., bearer of these letters, was advanced to the rank of priesthood by our predecessor of good memory, R., formerly bishop of London; that he ministered for a long time in this bishopric; and that he conducted himself worthily, as befits the priestly office. Since a necessity which has now arisen draws him into foreign parts, we have granted him these letters testimonial of his ordination and good character, and also testimonial of the leave we have given him to depart. We earnestly offer prayers to your benevolence, beloved in the Lord [Col. 0889D], that, out of reverence for the divine order, wherever he may come among you, you receive him in charity and mercifully render him the honour which it is just to bestow upon the ministers of the Lord. We wish you health in the Lord.

## LETTER CXC. TO THE SAME PERSONS.

G., by the grace of God bishop of London, to all sons of the Church: greeting, grace, and blessing.

It is fitting to take especial care that matters once properly concluded are not revived in disputes, above all those confirmed by the sacred obligation of faith, lest they be overthrown by unlawful usurpation. Therefore we make known to you all that T., clerk, in the chapter of London, while we were sitting to hear the case concerning the same matter, renounced before many persons the complaint which he had intended to bring for a second time before us against our venerable brother, the bishop of Norwich, concerning violence, and confirmed by a pledged faith that he would observe this forever [Col. 0890A]. That this may be clear hereafter, we fortify it with the protection of this present writing and the affixing of our seal. Farewell.

## LETTER CXCI. TO THE SAME PERSONS.

Brother G., minister of the Church of London, to all beloved sons in the Lord of holy mother Church: greeting, grace, and blessing.

Controversies settled by an amicable agreement are known to receive the strength of lasting stability only when they are both committed to writing and secured by affixed seals through the authority of those who can confirm them [Col. 0890B]. Therefore we have taken care to bring into public view, by this present writing, the agreement between our venerable brother [Walter], bishop of Norwich, together with the monks of that place, and Herbert, clerk of Marisco, concerning the question of a wall and other complaints between them, so that every unjust occasion of renewed litigation may thereafter be wholly removed.

Accordingly, while we were sitting by mandate of the lord pope to hear the same dispute, Herbert produced in court the authentic instrument of the lord bishop of Norwich and, touching the most holy Gospels, swore that he would observe faithfully and inviolably everything contained in that instrument; and he declared orally that he renounced all complaints hitherto existing between himself and the aforesaid persons [Col. 0890C]. Therefore, as the order of law required, we wholly absolved both the lord bishop and the monks from the claim of the said H. Witnesses: **[lacuna]**

## LETTER CXCII. TO THE SAME PERSONS.

Brother G., minister of the Church of London, to all beloved sons in the Lord of holy mother Church: greeting, grace, and blessing.

It is fitting for us, lovers of peace, to take more attentive care that matters concluded by judicial decision or settled by amicable agreement are not again revived in disputes. Therefore we judged it worthy to commit to writing the final settlement, reached by the mutual concurrence of both parties, of the controversy long contested between R. de Warewic and W., clerk, concerning the church of Hattona [Col. 0890D], cognizance of which had been delegated to us by apostolic authority.

Accordingly, R. shall hold the church of Hattona, which he formerly claimed, for as long as he lives, paying the aforesaid W. one mark of silver yearly within the octave of St Michael; the right to the aforesaid church remaining entire and reserved to whichever of them survives the other. Each party promised, under the sacred obligation of an oath, to observe this agreement in good faith. Since this was done with such solemnity, we confirm it by the testimony of this present writing and secure it by the affixing of our seal, so that it may have force hereafter. Witnesses: **[lacuna]**

## LETTER CXCIII. TO THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.

[Col. 0891A]

To his father and lord T., by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury, Brother G., minister of the Church of London: may he always dispense what has been entrusted to him with the fitting moderation of reason.

The good Master teaches us to ask; he teaches us also to seek; and, that it may be opened to us, he teaches us to knock at the door of the heart of him to whom prayer is made—not merely at a fitting time, but insistently (Rev. III). At his prompting we ask and knock, that, if it please you, an entrance to favour may be opened for us with your Excellency and access to what is just may not be denied.

Hubert, clerk of St Paul’s, appeals to us, asserting that he has a lawful exception against Baldric, clerk, so that he ought not legally be compelled to pay the twenty which Baldric demands of him [Col. 0891B]. He therefore asks to be heard, so that by the sacred authority of laws and canons he may repel Baldric from this claim. Because we believe this consonant with justice, we add prayers to prayers and beseech you to decree what is equitable in this matter, and in judging the clerk of St Paul’s now to exercise not power in binding, but equity.

For, when he offers himself for litigation in order vigorously to defeat the claimant’s demand—or, if he should fail in this, to undergo condemnation not only in respect of what is claimed but also, if just, in costs—who can be unaware that a day ought to be set for him and that he ought to be heard in these matters? For the objection that acts once performed should not be relitigated, and that it is the mark of a fickle and inconsistent person to contravene his own agreements—matters which have also been concluded either by judgment or by amicable settlement and ought not be recalled to litigation—what force this has is fully known to your authority [Col. 0891C]. For what has been done is not being relitigated: Baldric, newly demanding the twenty under the agreement, is repelled by an exception; and its proof initiates a new suit against him.

What if Hubert has already paid this debt, or Baldric perhaps remitted it, or covenanted not to demand it? Or what if, since this agreement is outside the nature of a contract of strict law, he promised, if action were brought to establish it, to furnish authority? If any of these things be proved, Hubert plainly is not bound. Since, therefore, the exception clearly defeats this remaining claim, as Hubert is confident, we beseech your Highness with earnest affection that you relax the sentence by which you order our clerk to be bound, for love of justice and at our request, and allow the case newly instituted between the clerks to take its own course between them.

And if our supplication does not prevail, still the appeal made to the lord pope before sentence, under a specified number of witnesses, ought to have prevailed [Col. 0891D]. For this is not the case which apostolic authority ordered to be determined with appeal removed. For where one thing is claimed, another answered, and an entirely different judgment sought, it is recognized beyond doubt to be a different case. Therefore, if it please your moderation, act so that by this relaxation you graciously hear your humble friend, render the honour due and, as I think, firmly promised to the lord pope [Col. 0892A], and in no respect diminish Baldric’s right, if he has any, even though it be rightly deferred for a time; and thus, departing from the lawful path in no respect, even a small one, to anyone’s injury, bring all matters to a happy conclusion. Farewell.

## LETTER CXCIV. TO THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.

To the venerable lord and Father in Christ THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, GILBERT, minister of the Church of London: greeting.

By your deeply considered and copious reply, Father, you set before us an extensive and manifold subject; and although we are concerned with pursuing our appeal to the lord pope, your Highness nevertheless compels us, through a grave necessity pressing heavily upon us, to reply to you [Col. 0892B]. For, having scattered praises broadly abroad, you single us alone out from the whole body of our brethren for reproaches, so as to heap upon us personally, though undeservedly, shameful insults and abuse.

It is astonishing that a man of sober judgment, a personage of venerable gravity, a master reverently subject by reason of his pre-eminence and learning to the truth of doctrine, should have flared up so violently at words of truth and, as though summoned to anger, should not only have refused to accept the innocence of a son advising his father dutifully, but should also, without merit requiring it, have stained his opinion with some mark of malice of which he is wholly unconscious. Since public writings denounce us as wishing to overthrow God’s Church, confuse right and wrong, cast down that mountain which is the Church and pillar of the living God with an unsound head, to have coveted your possessions, and—because we were repulsed from obtaining them—to have rashly disturbed your peace and that of God’s Church, and to have turned our backs in the Lord’s battle, it is difficult for us to remain silent or, by silence implying confession, to allow this opinion against us either to be accepted by those now present or to pass undefended to future posterity [Col. 0892C].

Since greed is the root and origin of evils, necessity itself commands us to begin here, lest those easily persuaded toward wickedness should hold us suspected of it. The Apostle says: “Who knows the hidden things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him?” (1 Cor. II.) The hidden things of men are indeed concealed from men, but the Lord looks upon the abyss of hearts from heaven. Nothing unknown escapes him; hidden things do not deceive him. For the word of God is living and efficacious, more penetrating than any two-edged sword; and no creature is invisible in his sight (Heb. IV).

We speak to him and before him; under his judgment we answer confidently and freely, not with vain or feigned assertions but with those supported by the truth of conscience. We declare that we never, even for a moment, felt the impulses of ambition toward the things that are yours. We never envied anyone this honour. We never served anyone, by gift or service, favour or patronage, to obtain this grace, so as by any means or assistance to contrive for ourselves a sacrilegious approach to the heights of this eminence. Who, Father, can judge this better or more clearly than you? At that time you were archdeacon of the very Church and the chosen man of our lord king; it is well known that among thousands you were not merely counsellor but heart and counsel, without whom it was not merely difficult, but altogether impossible, for anyone to advance in such matters [Col. 0893A].

What favour did we lodge with you? Did we ever, through ourselves or another, seek your favour by gifts or services, that through your assistance we might be raised to that which could not be attained except through you? From this, Father, it is just to measure our prudence: how we behaved toward others, who neither sought base gain through supplication even from your Highness, upon whom the whole weight of affairs rested, nor ever took pains, even in the slightest degree, to flatter for the sake of favour.

We conclude the matter in this way and confidently [Col. 0893B] lay this burden upon ourselves: may it be laid up for us on that day, if our heart reproaches us in any respect as conscious of this fault (1 John III). Therefore, Father, it was not our own rejection that we lamented at your promotion. On that day we desired with all the affection of our hearts not our own interests but those of our Lord Jesus Christ; that glory in all things should be rendered not to us but to his name (Ps. CXIII). We grieved that the matter was done otherwise. Seeing the right of the Church overthrown, right and wrong confused, the summit of that great mountain of which you speak bent downward, and the bride of Christ shamefully deprived of the former liberty that had always until then been reverently preserved and afforded to her, we groaned with deep sighs in the Lord. Many in God’s Church foresaw, through a certain prompting of the divine Spirit, sure foreshadowings and omens of the sufferings which we now continually experience [Col. 0893C].

At that time it was surely necessary to remember what is written: “It is difficult for things begun from evil principles to be brought to a good conclusion.” If we return to the beginnings themselves, who in our whole world does not know—who is so heedless as not to know—that you obtained that dignity of the chancellorship by a fixed bidding of many thousands of marks, and, carried by the impulse of this wind into the harbour of the Church of Canterbury, at length acceded to its government? How piously, how holily, how canonically, and through what merit of life requiring it, this was done, is well known to many; and it has been written in the hearts of good men [Col. 0893D] in a script of inward sorrow.

That good man and our father of blessed memory, Theobald, formerly archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, had ended his days; and you, who had by no means closed the eyes of your heart in watchfulness against this event, swiftly returned to England from Normandy. From the side of our lord king there was sent after an interval a great and wise governor of the realm, Richard de Luci—whom today you have suitably and deservedly honoured as one bound in the snares of anathema. He held the king’s authority over all men, so that the monks of Canterbury and the suffragan bishops of that Church should demand you, elect you, and receive you as father and shepherd without prolonging the matter by any delay of deliberation; otherwise they would not escape the royal anger, but would recognize, by the facts themselves beyond all doubt, that they were enemies of the king [Col. 0894A] and of his adherents.

What we say, we know by experience. For, observing God’s Church being grievously stifled, and consequently speaking out in some measure for its liberty, we immediately heard the word of proscription and were cruelly condemned to exile—not only our own person, but also my father’s household, those related to us by marriage, and our whole kindred. This cup was offered to others also, and more besides.

Yet it is written: “The lion will roar: who will not fear?” (Amos III); and, “As the roaring of a lion, so is the terror of a king” (Prov. XX). Who could deny what the king ordered with such force of will, what he urgently pressed to be brought about by so great a messenger, what they knew you all had fixed the eyes of your hearts upon, and what all your party vigorously pressed by threats and terrors, promises and inducements [Col. 0894B]? Who could resist this torrent of royal will and command? The sword of the realm stood in your hand, flashing, as though with a certain fire of fierce and unbearable wrath, against whomever you looked upon grimly.

That sword your hand had shortly before plunged into the vitals of holy mother Church, when, in order to convey an army into Toulouse, you burdened her with so many thousands of marks.
