Lest it should again be sharpened by you for wounds, the Church obeyed the commands; and, avoiding what it feared, it pretended to will what it did not will. Oh, how far the hearts of all good people were from this act itself, how opposed their desires! Yet, by pressure and compulsion, that was done which had been commanded under the most terrible threat [Col. 0894C].

Thus you entered the sheepfold, not indeed by the door, but climbing in by another way (John X); and by this entrance, Father, you took away the Church’s liberty, preserved for her through the course of so many ages. If, as you write, that liberty is her life, you surely rendered her lifeless. Good God, what horror seized everyone that day, when that customary portent was seen and set before the eyes of those standing around! I mean that portent which, as though the Evangelist Matthew were prophesying, was produced as a sign of the future disaster: the Lord said to the fig tree which bore no fruit, “May fruit never grow from you forever,” and immediately it withered (Matt. XXI).

That day they ought therefore to have answered the prince who gave an unrighteous [Col. 0894D] command: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V). Would that on that day the fear of him who can destroy the soul in Gehenna, and not merely kill the body, had wholly possessed our hearts! (Matt. X.) Because matters were otherwise conducted, this enormity produces shame in us, shame confusion, and confusion repentance, which, the Lord permitting, will bring the fitting remedy of satisfaction. Thus continual tears remain upon our cheeks until the Lord restores the captivity of Zion (Ps. CXXV), comforts those mourning in Jerusalem, and turns the eyes of his mercy toward desolate Jerusalem.

Meanwhile, to continue in due order the account of what was done, let us hear what fruit has resulted from your elevation. From the time when our pious king undertook the governance of the realm until that day, holy Church had flourished in the highest peace—except that, as we have said, in raising an army for Toulouse she had already found your hands excessively heavy upon her. Otherwise, under a good prince all things rejoiced, all things were most gladly glad. The kingdom, devoted to the priesthood, rendered holy obedience; and the king’s authority was most firmly supported by the priesthood for every good purpose. Within the Church the two swords were exercised, serving the Lord Jesus in devoted obedience. They did not stand opposed to one another, nor, aiming at contrary ends, did they resist each other. “There was one people and,” as it is written, “of one speech,” striving to pursue sins, rejoicing to see vices [Col. 0895B] vigorously uprooted. Such was the peace of kingdom and Church: they cherished one another with reciprocal favour and were joined by one will.

At your promotion we hoped and expected an increase of blessings; but behold, because our sins demanded it, all things were immediately thrown into disorder. It is virtue to meet sin when it arises, and at once to dash against the rock—which is Christ—the evil offspring of the mind as soon as they are born. Your prudence, therefore, ought to have foreseen that disagreements, slightly arising between the kingdom and yourself, should not grow to an immeasurable size; that so great a fire should not arise from a slight spark to the ruin of many. The opposite was done. For reasons too numerous to recount, the disagreements increased; anger was inflamed [Col. 0895C] and hatred strongly hardened.

This was the cause; hence arose the occasion why our lord the king turned his mind and counsel toward demanding and jointly setting forth the royal dignities. When their observance was required of you and of the suffragan bishops of your Church, we refused to give assent, except to those which could be observed without prejudice to the honour of God and our ecclesiastical order, because in certain of them the liberty of God’s Church seemed to be oppressed. Our lord the king urgently demanded that we promise him, without qualification, to observe them; but what conflicted with the Church’s liberty and with fidelity to the lord pope could by no means be obtained from us. On this account assemblies were held and councils convened.

What need is there to recall what was done in London, and again at Oxford? Let us call to mind what was transacted at Clarendon. There, for three continuous days, this alone was sought: that we should make an unconditional promise to observe the customs and dignities of the kingdom. There we stood with you—whom we believed to stand firmly in the Spirit of the Lord. We stood unmoved; we stood undaunted. We stood ready to lose our fortunes, suffer bodily torment, undergo exile, and—even, should the Lord permit it—undergo the sword. What father ever had sons more united in his confession? Who were ever more unanimous? All of us were shut in one chamber. On the third day, when the princes of the realm and indeed all the nobles [Col. 0896A] had burst into the greatest rage, they entered the room where we sat amid shouting and tumult, their cloaks thrown back and their arms bared, and addressed us thus:

> “Take heed, you who despise the statutes of the kingdom, you who do not accept the king’s commands. These hands which you see are not ours; these arms are not ours; these bodies, finally, are not ours, but belong to our lord King Henry. They stand ready, at every nod, to avenge every injury done to him and to execute whatever his will may be. Whatever command he gives will be wholly just to us by reason of his will alone. Reconsider your counsel; bend your minds to the command, so that, while it is still lawful, you may avert the danger which shortly can no longer be avoided.”

What then? Who fled? Who turned his back? Whose spirit broke? Your letter reproaches us that “in the day of battle we turned back” (Ps. 77 [78]), that we did not go up against the enemy, that we did not set ourselves as a wall for the house of the Lord. Let the Lord judge between us; let Him judge for whose sake we stood, for whose sake we could not bend before the threats of princes. Let Him judge who fled, who proved a deserter in the battle. Without doubt there stood the noble man, Henry of Winchester, most steadfast in spirit in the Lord; there stood Nigel of Ely; Robert of Lincoln; Hilary of Chichester; Jocelin of Salisbury; Bartholomew of Exeter; Richard of Chester; Roger of Worcester; Robert of Hereford; and Gilbert [Col. 0896C] of London. All these lacked an assailant, not courage; moreover, reckoning temporal things as dung, they exposed themselves and their possessions for Christ and the Church.

Let, therefore, what is true be said; let what happened under the sun, in our presence and before our eyes, be related. The commander himself gave way; the leader of the field fled. The lord of Canterbury withdrew from the fellowship and counsel of his brethren. After holding a separate discussion, he returned to us after an interval and burst out in these words:

> “It is my lord’s will that I commit perjury; and for the present I submit to and incur perjury, intending, as I can, to do penance for it hereafter.”

Hearing this, we were astonished; gazing at one another, we sighed and groaned over this fall of a man whom we considered at the height of virtue and constancy. With the Lord there is not “yes and no”; nor did we expect His disciple could be so moved. When the head languishes, the other members soon languish, and its weakness immediately spreads to the remaining limbs. He assented to what was demanded; and, promising unconditionally upon his word of truth that henceforth he would faithfully observe for our lord the king the royal dignities and ancient customs of the kingdom, set forth jointly from the memory of the ancients and committed to writing, he bound us also, by force of obedience, to a like pledge. Thus the dispute was brought to an end; thus the peace of the priesthood was reconciled with the kingdom.

Israel went down into Egypt, whence it is later read that it ascended with much glory. So too great hope remained with us: that what our lord the king, moved by anger, had for the time required might, when his mind had calmed, [Col. 0897A] be reformed anew for God’s glory and his own honour. But that ancient disturber of tender peace begrudged peace. And we, who after weathering storms hoped now to reach harbour, are behold compelled by the blasts of the north wind into the deep.

Fresh was the promise made to the king upon your word of truth: that you would not depart from the realm unless leave had been obtained from him. It is written: “Let the words of a priest always have truth as their companion” (Mal. 2); likewise, a man owes truth to what he says and faithfulness to what he promises. Yet, after a few days had passed, you committed your sails to the winds and arranged your departure from the realm while the king was entirely unaware of it. When he heard this, no one was more astonished than the king, none grieved more. He was astonished that what the pontiff had promised, as though by oath, had not been fulfilled. He grieved, knowing that a grave scandal was being raised against him and that his reputation—hitherto unblemished—would be most seriously attacked among peoples and kingdoms because of this flight.

For what else could those ignorant of the truth suspect from these events, except that the king, forgetful of royal piety, had blazed into a tyrant’s fury and, from hatred of Christ, had expelled His minister from his kingdom and the bounds of his dominion? He would rather have received at your hand a most grievous wound in his own flesh than suffer this injury to his reputation throughout the Christian world through you and yours. What more need be said? With the north wind filling the sails, the voyage would already have been completed, had not a more favourable south wind opposed its course; under that wind the ship was prosperously brought back to the shore from which it had begun to sail.

When events had thus brought you into the king’s hands, did he follow anger or exercise power against you? Did he exceed proper action, or speak anything harshly? Far from it. Rather, receiving you kindly and honouring you with the reverence due to you, he sent you back to your own place. Humbly and graciously he urged you to remain in the realm, govern the Church committed to you, and show him in deeds the affection and gentleness of your heart. Hardly had the south wind ceased to thunder when the north-west wind was already flashing lightning. Hardly had the emotions on either side subsided, when once again there arose a matter from which they might boil up more fiercely.

A royal command was conveyed to you: that you should render to a certain nobleman of the realm what was just concerning an estate which he claimed from your Church. He, after the appointed days, returned to the king and asserted [Col. 0897D] that he had been unable to obtain justice from you; and that, in accordance with the statutes of the kingdom, he had proved this before you by an oath of himself and suitable witnesses. When he continued to pursue the king and daily petitioned that justice be rendered to him, a summons from our lord the king was sent to you: that, on an appointed day, your eminence should appear before him, so that, under his cognizance and with the case decided by judgment, you might complete what you had not done at his command.

You did not accept this summons. Rather, the reply sent from you to him declared that you would by no means obey him in this matter. Thinking that by this his right and authority were seriously impaired, the lord king ordered the Church of the realm to be summoned to a council at Northampton. The people assembled as one man; and, sitting with those whose rank and order entitled them to do so, he set forth, with fitting restraint and dignity, his complaint against you concerning the contempt of his command. Moreover, your immediate confession confirmed his accusation without awaiting or seeking the counsel of your brethren. You added that you had not obeyed the command because that John, who had brought you the king’s order, had sworn in your presence not upon the Gospel but upon a certain troparion-book.

It was therefore publicly said that this was not a reason for disregarding the royal command; and that, according to the custom of the realm, in offences of this sort the king’s mercy is appeased by a monetary fine assessed for the matter. Your eminence fully obeyed the judgment, giving security for payment of what had been adjudged. Yet your prudence was not unaware of that apostolic decree expressed thus:

> “No bishop, whether for a civil or a criminal cause, shall be brought or presented before any judge, whether civil or military.”

And this:

> “If a cleric is summoned before a secular judge, he shall neither answer nor make a claim.”

And that of Pope Gelasius to Bishop Helpidius:

> “With what boldness, with what rashness, do you write that you are preparing to go to Ravenna, when the canons plainly command that no bishop at all should hasten to the royal court unless we have first been seen or consulted?”

But perhaps you discern these matters with loftier knowledge and clearer spirit. Because divine anointing sanctifies the king, his hand is anointed for holiness of deeds; the joining of his arms for chastity of embraces; his breast for purity of heart; [Col. 0898C] his shoulders for endurance of labour for Christ. Chrism is poured upon his head, so that, following Christ—from whom *chrism* takes its name—and consecrated in His name, he may always endeavour with fitting moderation to administer what has been entrusted to him. You distinguish him from other men and regard him as not merely a secular judge, but an ecclesiastical judge also. To reinforce this, perhaps you cite what Pope Leo IV wished to amend through imperial judgment, writing thus to Emperor Louis:

> “If we have done anything improperly, and have not preserved in our subjects the path of just law, we desire all things to be corrected by your judgment or that of your envoys, so that all may be settled by their lawful examination, lest anything indiscriminate be able to remain in future.”

If this is your view, a great many agree with your discernment: because of reverence for the sacrament, they judge that the king ought to investigate and determine by examination of royal jurisdiction—not all causes, but those Church causes and persons of the Church which they distinguish. For the Church possesses certain things by divine law alone, and other things, as they attest, by human law.

By divine law alone she possesses ecclesiastical ranks, sacred orders, and the dignities and powers connected with them. Thus, if she baptizes or consecrates, absolves or binds, preaches and instructs, these are solely spiritual matters, bestowed from above from one human being to another; they are propagated not by human gift but by the divine Spirit working inwardly. “No one takes this honour for himself, but only one called by God, as Aaron was” [Col. 0899A] (Heb. 5). Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, not called by the Lord, sought these things and perished by an unheard-of death (Num. 16). Jeroboam and Uzziah, intruding themselves into sacrifices, were struck—the one with a withered hand, the other with leprosy (Zech. 11).

In all these matters every priest, as father and pastor, is held superior to every king; the king, as son and disciple, is held far inferior. Therefore, if the king sins against God, let him, in imitation of Theodosius, seek reconciliation through the works of priests. If priests accuse one another, let the king not usurp judgment of this matter; rather, let him walk backward, lest he behold the shame of the Fathers, and cover such a case with the cloak of praise.

There are also certain corporeal possessions which the Church holds by divine law alone: among these are tithes, offerings, and firstfruits, which the Lord set apart and sanctified for Himself, establishing by eternal law that they should serve the use of those who minister to Him. Since He commands these by divine law alone, royal power does not extend to taking cognizance of them. By human law, however, the Church possesses many things granted to her solely through human donations—not because the Lord commanded this or established a law about it—so that she is no longer limited merely to the Levitical portion, but enlarged by exceptional gifts and possessions. Kings transferred their ample patrimonies to her; chosen princes transferred theirs; so that even bodily there may now be fulfilled what the prophet long ago foretold concerning the children of the Church: “You shall eat the strength of the nations, and shall glory in their glory” (Isa. 61); and, “That he may give them the inheritance of the nations” [Col. 0899C] (Ps. 110 [111]); likewise Isaiah: “Enlarge your tent, make your cords long; you shall spread out to the right and to the left” (Isa. 54).

Ancient history records that, for the work of the ancient tabernacle, that people offered gifts with such devotion that the craftsmen were compelled to tell Moses: “The people bring more than is needed” (Exod. 36). Yet whatever their devotion, it does not equal that of the children of grace, for whom it is often not enough to give individual things unless they give over and above their whole possessions. Everyone is free, when transferring what is his own by gift, to attach to the gift whatever condition he wishes, provided it is not contrary to laws or good morals. They therefore judge that this condition is attached to royal gifts, and affirm that it has prevailed by the custom of so many ages: that Churches render kings military service and certain other services connected with estates, and acknowledge that these possessions are held from kings by homage and fealty promised by the person of their principal before the Gospel.

Thus the Church has a twofold power: in one respect she serves the heavenly King; in another, she renders to the earthly prince what pertains to him. This power makes her ministers, in one respect bishops through authority bestowed by God, in another earls or barons through authority received from the king. By this power the Church holds great pre-eminence in the royal court, since in all judgments of the realm—except where a danger to life or bloodshed is concerned—she herself holds the foremost place. This, they say, binds us to the king, so that, when summoned by him, we must attend and jointly investigate and judge the causes of individuals.

For although in matters pertaining to God we are distinguished by rank, so that some are considered and are superiors, others inferiors, in this respect they consider us equals: if a dispute has arisen among us or against us concerning lands devolved upon the Church by royal grant, the king’s judgment is to determine what pertains to each of all of us. Nor is it surprising if a judgment pronounced by a son binds a father, when manifest reason proves that the son himself is lord of his father, and when fealty has been reverently rendered by homage.

Since, therefore, there is from God a twofold power, priestly on the one hand and royal on the other, they confirm by the authority of the Fathers that each in a certain respect presides over the other, and in a certain respect may be judged by the other. Thus there is this reciprocity of kings and bishops: they judge one another and are judged by one another—perhaps a certain bond of charity, a debt of reverence, and indeed a necessity for preserving peace between them. Considering this and higher matters, you honoured the king “as supreme” [Col. 0900B] (1 Pet. 2), as the Apostle exhorts, and rightly acknowledged him as judge by obeying his judgment. While preserving for him what was his, you wisely and prudently admonished him to obey your eminence in matters concerning God.

Holy humility submits itself to every human creature for God’s sake; and the lower it humbles itself, the more it deserves, according to the Lord’s word, to be exalted more highly and gloriously. Would that the whole affair had rested within these bounds of humility. When our lord the king demanded certain debts from you—when, concerning a sum of money which he said had accrued from certain escheats while in your hands, he sought only that what justice dictated should be rendered to him—would that your zeal had not then raised itself in order to avoid the judgment of the royal court.

For what danger could a judgment given upon that claim have caused? He wished you to be transferred from the court to the governance of the Church, and thereby, as many believe, released you from its obligations. But if such release does not apply to debts—if advancement to an office does not release one from debt—the matter might very largely have been settled by a procedural objection. If something could not be included in the accounting, adequate satisfaction for the remainder could have been made to one reclaiming what was his more in anger than avarice. This civil cause could have been honourably settled in peace without this tumult of affairs.

But you say it is unheard of that an archbishop of Canterbury should ever be compelled to answer such matters in the king’s court. Yet you have said something equally unheard of: that an official of the court should ever, by such sudden transition, have been raised to that Church as hitherto to administer the court today and the Church tomorrow; that one who had lately attended to birds, dogs, and the other agreeable occupations of the court should so soon stand at the altars and administer spiritual things to the bishops and priests of the whole realm. Therefore, while custom pointed in different directions because circumstances differed, you entered the royal house bearing a cross in your hands and immediately made the king suspected by all of a certain execrable wickedness. Yet his patience showed that his innocence deserved the highest praise. Though he took the bringing of the cross against him ill, he nevertheless did not exceed the bounds of royal restraint. [Col. 0901A] Moved by no anger, he did not blaze up; neither in speech nor deed did he act maliciously. He endeavoured to bring the claim he had raised in recovering what was his to the end required by justice.

But, avoiding judgment, you appealed to the lord pope; and, as at your entry, so at your departure, you recognized the king’s great gentleness and forbearance through proofs of the peace maintained toward you. For as a father’s affection cried out when the army marched against Absalom, “Spare me the young man Absalom” (2 Sam. 18), so by his command it was immediately proclaimed to all that, if anyone should molest you or any of your people, he would perish by the avenging sword.

You added to this, as though he were plotting against your life or blood: beginning a flight by night, changing your dress after hiding for a while, you secretly crossed from the realm; and, though none pursued you and none expelled you from the lands of his dominion, you chose for yourself another seat outside the kingdom for a time. From there you propose to steer the ship which you abandoned in waves and tempest after withdrawing the helmsman; and from there your authority commands and exhorts us to turn to you and be saved, to follow in your footsteps, undergo death for Christ, and not fear to lay down our lives for the liberation of His Church.

Certainly, if we consider how great are the things promised us in heaven, whatever is possessed on earth ought to become cheap in our estimation. For neither tongue can express nor understanding comprehend how great are the joys of that heavenly city: to share in the choirs of angels, stand with the most blessed spirits before the glory of the Creator, behold God’s present face, feel no fear of death, and glory forever in the gift of one’s incorruption. “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in the saints.” And what is now the light and momentary burden of tribulation “works in the elect a weight of eternal glory beyond all measure” [Col. 0901C] (2 Cor. 4). These things have long been fixed in our minds; these promises have long drawn our aspirations after them.

Would that the executioner’s sword had struck off the head resting upon my shoulders, provided only that I had fought in a lawful contest pleasing to God! Yet punishment does not make a martyr, but the cause does. To suffer hardship in a holy cause is glory; to suffer it wickedly and obstinately is disgrace. To undergo the sword for Christ is consummate praise and victory; rashly to provoke it against oneself is manifest madness. And if we weigh, Father, not merely your words but your deeds, we shall not rush into death rashly or lightly. For in bending the knee at Clarendon, undertaking flight at Northampton, concealing yourself for a time in changed clothing, and secretly emigrating from the boundaries of the realm—what was done? What did you procure by doing these things, except that you so anxiously avoided the death which no one deigned to inflict?

With what face, then, Father, did you invite us to a death which by such manifest signs you showed, more clearly than light to the whole world, that you both feared and fled? What charity persuades you to impose upon us a burden which you cast aside? A sword hangs over us, though you fled it; you chose to cast a sling-stone at it rather than fight it hand-to-hand. Perhaps you invited us to a similar flight. But the sea is closed to us; after your departure, every ship and harbour has been forbidden us. Islands are the strongest prisons of kings, from which one can scarcely escape or extricate oneself. If we must fight, we shall contend at close quarters. If battle is joined with the king, where we strike with the sword, there we shall find the sword striking back; where we inflict a wound, we shall be unable to avoid wounds.

Are your yearly revenues worth so much to you that you wish to acquire them at the blood of your brethren? Yet when Judas brought back this money, the Jews rejected it, recognizing it as the price of blood. But perhaps you advance another reason to us. Let us therefore digress a little, so that we may consider more fully the reason by which death is being urged upon us.

Thanks be to the Lord: among us there is no dispute concerning faith, none concerning the sacraments, none concerning morals. Right faith flourishes in the prince, in the prelates, and in the subjects. The Church of this kingdom soundly embraces every article of faith. No one is separated from obedience to the supreme pontiff by the madness of the present schism. All venerate and cultivate the Church’s sacraments, receive them themselves, and communicate them devoutly and holily to others.

As regards morals, indeed, “in many things we all offend” [Col. 0902B] (Jas. 3). Yet no one preaches or defends his own error; rather, he hopes that what he commits may be washed away by the remedy of repentance. The whole dispute with and concerning the king, therefore, concerns certain customs which, he asserts, were observed and rendered to his predecessors, and which he wishes and demands to be observed for himself. Though admonished about this by your eminence, he does not abandon his purpose or renounce what antiquity and the long custom of the kingdom have established.

This is the reason why you run to arms and strive to brandish a sword against a holy and noble head. It matters greatly that he did not establish these customs himself, but found them instituted, as all the antiquity of the realm testifies. For what has deeper roots is more difficult to uproot; the plant which has long driven its roots down deeply clings more tenaciously. If anyone wishes to transplant it, it must not be uprooted by force, lest it immediately wither. It must first be dug around and the soil removed, the root laid bare on every side, so that prudent care may accomplish properly what force, inaptly applied, could not accomplish conveniently.

Examples must be drawn from good men; and when matters of this kind are handled, their deeds must be considered with special care. Your predecessor, Father Augustine, uprooted many enormous abuses from this kingdom. Illuminating the king himself with faith, he eliminated from him many evil customs—not by curses, indeed, but rather by blessing and preaching, by salutary exhortation, and by strongly inclining the minds of the powerful toward good. That John of Crema, sent into these regions in our days by the holy Roman Church, altered customs of the kingdom in which they had already grown old. He obtained this not by curses or threats, but by sound teaching and holy exhortations. He sowed in blessing and reaped a harvest of blessings. Had these men run to arms, they would have achieved little or nothing.

When the pious king of the Franks was recently granted by divine power the long-desired offspring, many burdens were remitted in that kingdom, burdens which antiquity had hitherto established as unshaken. These were removed, as we have heard, at the Church’s urging and admonition, not by her launching threats against the chosen prince. Finally, who can explain how great and numerous were the dignities, liberties, immunities, and possessions given to God’s Church by pious kings throughout the world through piety alone, not through the compulsion of a curse? Time would fail anyone wishing to recount them; for this is the praiseworthy nobility of kings. From them a suppliant obtains what one who stands erect in threats could never obtain by any exertions. What each would violently seek to snatch by force is accounted so cheap by them as a thing of little value, and he would soon discover, to his disappointment, great defenders of their own property in a small matter.

These things, therefore, ought to have been considered not with novel fervour but with mature counsel. The counsel of your brethren and of many others should have been sought in these matters; the actions of prudent Fathers should have been considered; the Church’s advantages weighed against her disadvantages. Only then, perhaps, should such a sentence have been given—when no hope of a remedy remained. And when it is given, according to the rule of the sacred canons, it must be considered against whom it is given, why it is given, how it is given, whether what is given benefits the Church, and whether it harms her if it is not given.

The man whom you attack—let us remind you of what is known to you—is he not the very man whom the sweetest pledges of children, a most noble and honourable wife, very many kingdoms subject to him, gatherings of friends, hosts of peoples obedient to his nod, and every precious thing in the world scarcely hold back, scarcely persuade by flattery, from going forth naked after the Lord Jesus carrying His cross, despising all things? Contemplating the poverty which Christ endured, he strives in deed to fulfil what Christ Himself taught, saying: “Whoever does not carry his cross and come after me is not worthy of me” [Col. 0903C] (Luke 14). Is this the stubbornness of mind; this the cruelty to be overwhelmed with curses; this the wickedness to be proclaimed throughout God’s Church and the whole world? If you heap curses upon him, the Church will rightly grieve that the noblest part of herself is wounded by her own weapons. When he is wounded, not a small number of her children, but a great multitude of peoples, will groan that she herself is wounded.

In such cases sacred authority teaches thus: where, through grave cleavages of dissension, “the danger is not that of this or that man, but the slaughter of peoples lies prostrate,” something must be taken from severity so that sincere charity may come to the aid of greater evils needing cure. And again: “Correction by many cannot be salutary unless the person corrected has no multitude as his companion.” To what physician’s skill would one ascribe the cure of one wound when he inflicts another far greater and far more dangerous? To what discernment would one attribute abandoning the Church in this way, rising against the prince, and, with the peace of the whole kingdom’s Church shaken, taking no care for the dangers to the souls and bodies of subjects, in order to obtain certain things which could be gained more lightly and more readily? Ambrose yielded estates; he did not approve abandoning the Church.

For what could your prudence, Father, fail to hope from a good prince whom it knew to be pierced by the divine Spirit and to be longing for Christ? What do those customs—which bring him absolutely no temporal advantage—matter to him, when the world’s glory itself, however great it may offer itself, has now become almost wholly worthless to him, and is so far from his heart’s desire that, speaking often to the Lord, he says what is written: “I hate the adornment of my head, O Lord; you know.” Should he not have been cherished, and the holy dove nesting within him left undisturbed, until Christ fully formed in him should draw his hidden things into the light and bring them forth, and he himself, as though with his own hand, distribute not only the liberties now at issue but far more generous ones? [Col. 0904B]

In these matters we speak what we know; what we have learned, we confidently affirm. Our lord the king would long ago have rejected the customs at which you are most inflamed, having been corrected, had not two considerations gravely impeded this purpose. One is that he fears it would be dishonourable for anything to be taken away or diminished in his days from a kingdom handed down to him by his Fathers. The other is that, if he relaxes anything for the Lord’s sake, he is ashamed that it should be thought to have been extorted from him by force.

Yet he had already trampled down the first consideration with the foot of holiness. Fear of God, innate goodness, the holy admonition of the lord pope, and the continued petitions of many had led him to wish voluntarily, out of reverence for Him through whom he has been magnified far above all his Fathers, to convene the Church of God and to alter and correct, in great devotion of spirit, the customs of the kingdom which he knew brought her a burden. Had humility persisted on your side, joy, widely diffused, would already have gladdened God’s Church in the realm.

For petition had already gained the end at which you aim, when a recent disturbance arising from you disastrously impeded the whole matter. For while Brittany had not yet been added to his titles, and while that people, hitherto untamed, was raising its heel against him, when he was leading an army against disturbers of the peace, you sent him terrible letters, wholly without the fragrance of a father’s devotion or a bishop’s moderation. What the admonition of the supreme pontiff and the suppliant, earnest devotion of many had laboured to obtain, you at once swept away by breathing threats; and you drove both king and kingdom into a scandal almost more grievous than all that had gone before.

May God avert the end which, while the affair proceeds thus, we fear—lest it break forth in our times. For the honour of God and reverence for holy Church; for your own advantage, if you please; for the common good of peace; to lessen scandals and, with the Lord’s help, restore to peace what has been disturbed, we have appealed to the lord pope, in order that we may restrain, at least for a time, the headlong rush of your course carrying you against the king and kingdom. In this matter it is right that your zeal should choose to restrain itself within the bounds of moderation, lest, as it seeks to overthrow the rights of kings, so also, by refusing to accept appeals interposed to the lord pope, it should strive excessively and from on high to empty out the reverence owed to him. [Col. 0905A]

If it pleased you to notice that the Lord did not turn aside to Zacchaeus until he had already come down from the sycomore tree (Luke 19), perhaps you too would come down and strive, by peaceful words, to soften the man whom you have embittered by threats—not merely by demanding, but also by offering humble satisfaction, even though perhaps you have suffered an injury. The Lord set a child before the apostles as an example: one who, when injured, is not angry, does not quickly remember a wrong, and plots nothing maliciously; while seeking no greatness for himself, he repays all this by the remedy of an innocent life and by life’s most abundant delight (Luke 9). He is the singular example of virtue who absolved those crucifying Him, who commands that persecutors and enemies be loved with expansive charity, and who orders that, if a brother sins against us, forgiveness be granted not merely seven times but seventy times seven [Col. 0905B] (Matt. 18).

What could such humility not accomplish with our lord the king? What could such perfection of conduct not obtain? This is the straight path that rightly leads to peace. When you, Father, have entered it, you will immediately attain peace; dispersing the clouds of sorrow, you will fill all things with peace and all things with joy. And from the most pious king and our dearest lord, with the Spirit of the Lord kindling his heart and ever enlarging it in love for you, you will happily obtain not only what you presently seek, but things far greater.

## LETTER 195. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Col. 0905C] To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, Gilbert, Bishop of London: may he administer what has been entrusted to him with the fitting moderation of reason.

Your severity, Father, being not without reason suspected by the bishop of Salisbury, by myself, and by our other brethren on account of past and acknowledged matters, we greatly feared that you might decide to pronounce a sentence of curse or interdict against our lord the king of England, or against his kingdom, or against us bishops, suffragans of the Church of Canterbury, or against the churches entrusted to us; and that you might entangle us—defenceless, though always ready to abide by the law—in the bonds of the aforesaid penalty. Lest this should be entirely within your power, we appealed to the clemency of the lord pope about the beginning of Lent; and, appointing as the day for the appeal the octave of the Purification of Blessed Mary, we have taken care to notify you of this by the present writing, so that, if you have anything against us which you wish to pursue by judicial process, we may then, with the Lord’s help, answer in his presence and humbly and most devoutly obey his decision in all things. May the Lord turn away His wrath, lest you bring what you propose to the desired conclusion.

## LETTER 196. TO THE SUFFRAGANS OF THE CHURCH OF CANTERBURY

G., by the grace of God bishop of London, to all the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury: greeting and the due service of brotherly love.

It has come to the attention of our Father, the lord archbishop of Canterbury, that, in this realm, persons whom necessity compels to undertake a journey to the lord pope—whether for the shortening of penance, the remedy of a case, or the obligation of visitation—are hindered in their journey, despoiled, harshly treated, and prevented from crossing the sea, either by those who seek occasions to do evil, or by persons who have been compelled to swear unlawful oaths to hinder clerics or penitents. Therefore, by apostolic authority, in virtue of obedience and at peril to our office, he enjoins upon us all that we forbid this henceforth; that we publicly declare excommunicated those who lay violent hands upon clerics, or who impede appellants or penitents travelling to the lord pope or to himself, or returning from him; and that we cause this declaration to be made throughout our bishoprics, against both those who do this and those who compel others to do it. Since this is strictly enjoined upon us, we have taken care to command and notify you, so that we may obey, as is right, the command of him who commands. We wish you well in the Lord.

> [Note: Col. 0905D. Earlier, Letter 330.]

## LETTER 196 bis. TO THE SUFFRAGANS OF THE CHURCH OF CANTERBURY CONCERNING THE ELECTION OF POPE URBAN

To the venerable brethren and dearest friends in Christ, the suffragans of the holy Church of Canterbury: G., by the grace of God minister of the Church of London, greeting in the Lord.

We have sent to your brotherhood, as required by our office, a copy of the letters of our lord and pope, Pope Urban, which we recently received through the lord of Canterbury, so that, having examined their contents more carefully, you may henceforth not be unaware what shepherd divine providence has newly appointed over the Roman Church, and how greatly the favour of that same shepherd has increased the dignity of our venerable Father, the archbishop of Canterbury. (The letter of Urban referred to here is placed below in its proper sequence under no. 381.)

## LETTER 197. TO G., ARCHDEACON OF CANTERBURY

GILBERT, by the grace of God bishop of London, to his venerable brother and dearest friend G., by the same grace archdeacon of Canterbury: greeting and the affection of sincere love.

A talent has been entrusted to you, dearest friend, which your prudence must increase and expend for the benefit of many, so that, when by it you have relieved the needs of many, you may receive from the Lord on that day a reward a hundredfold (Matt. 19). This talent is the familiarity with our lord the king which has been granted you by the Lord: if anyone compares it with gold, it is more precious than gold, and is rightly judged far dearer than any amount of money. To dispense this talent faithfully, you must frequently and earnestly remind him to relieve the misery of the oppressed; and in this matter you must persist with insistence not only when it is timely but when it is untimely, if compassion demands it. Thus merit may be laid up for him with the Lord, and no small favour may be accumulated for you before God and men from pursuits of this sort.

We have said this by way of preface because Roger of Derneford, the bearer of this letter, is connected to us by such a relationship that we cannot fail him, but must, since necessity requires it, petition on his behalf those in whose favour and charity we trust. The lord abbot of Westminster has laid hands upon this man so heavily that he intends most harshly to dispossess him of an inheritance confirmed to him by the charter of his predecessor and of the whole chapter, and further strengthened by the charter of the Empress, mother of our lord the king. We therefore make petition to your goodwill with all the earnestness we can, asking you to undertake this man’s service and secure from our lord the king confirmation of his mother’s grant, subject to such assessment of service as you yourself approve; so that you may have him always bound to service, and me, at your pleasure, a debtor both in service and favour. We wish you well in the Lord, dearest friend.

The manuscript reads: “If anyone should call the emperor faithless, cruel, unjust, or utter anything similar, if it proceeds from frivolity, it is to be despised—for a slip of the tongue ought not readily to be drawn into punishment; if from madness, from frenzy, or drunken rage, it is worthy of compassion; if from injury, it is to be referred to us.” Therefore, from the persons of those involved we should judge whether such a statement ought to be punished or left unpunished.

## LETTER 198. TO MAURICE, ARCHBISHOP OF PARIS

[Col. 0907C]

To the venerable lord and dearest brother in Christ M., by the grace of God bishop of Paris: brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting and the affection of sincere love.

Let it be known to your charity that, following the tenor of your command and likewise the authority of your authentic document, which remains in our possession adorned with your seal, we have, with all the diligence that we could and ought, provided for the indemnity of the citizens of Paris on whose behalf you wrote to us, namely the creditors of William of Beaumont. Moreover, in the presence of your envoys, suitable and sufficient sureties gave security on William’s behalf that, at the approaching feast of Saint Lawrence, eight marks of silver would be paid to the aforesaid creditors; and, within fifteen days after the following feast of Saint Michael, another eight marks. Thereafter, within fifteen days after the next Easter, the remainder, up to the sum of sixty-four Parisian pounds and ten shillings, will be paid. Since this could not be settled more promptly because of the creditor’s poverty—  
(This letter is incomplete.)

## LETTER 199. TO R., ARCHBISHOP OF POITIERS

G., by the grace of God bishop of London, to his kinsman and dearest friend R., archbishop of Poitiers, and to the other justices of the lord king: may they reap the reward of the righteous by performing justice.

[Col. 0908A] You bear for a time, beloved friends, the royal sword, which is consecrated for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. I desire that the wicked may so experience it from your hand that—God forbid—the good are not punished by it also; that corrupt parts may be cut away in such a manner that limbs which are healthy and free from disease are not assailed by blows and torments. You have heard of the accursed crime: namely, that an honourable cleric was not merely wounded by the ambushes of wicked men, but, after being beaten, was miserably left half-dead (Luke 10). In the synod recently held, we delivered the perpetrators of this crime to Satan for the destruction of their flesh, so that those who accepted him as instigator may, with the Lord impelling them, feel and experience him as the avenger of their committed crime.

As I hear, you have apprehended some of them, and, binding them in the snares of law as the severity of judicial authority requires, you have in no respect departed from lawful paths. I commend you, and wholeheartedly applaud your praiseworthy exercise of the responsibility entrusted to you. But lest your administration be blemished even slightly, I humbly ask that, for reverence toward the Lord Jesus—whose mark they bear, whose likeness their tonsures signify—you restore to me, to be restrained by ecclesiastical jurisdiction if their accuser has anything against them, that deacon and acolyte whom you caused to be confined because of this affair. Otherwise, if you keep the Lord Jesus imprisoned in His members with a bold assurance—God forbid!—you may compel Him, when divine justice demands it, to close to you on that day the gate of life. We wish you well in the Lord, dearest friends.

## LETTER 200. TO ROTROU, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

[Col. 0908C]

To the venerable lord and dearest Father R., by the grace of God archbishop of Rouen: brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting and the affection of sincere love.

With all the gladness of our heart we give thanks to the Lord because He has brought into public view the goods of virtue amassed in you, and has been pleased to make you, set upon a higher lampstand for the edification of the whole Church, shine forth more eminently than usual. Desiring to preserve our old friendship with you—a friendship by no means grown old—we trust in your goodwill, that we who rejoice in the favour bestowed on us may also obtain a place in your more abundant favour.

Accordingly, we earnestly beseech your goodness, dear to us in the Lord, that you grant our beloved master Ranulf, son of Erchem, secure possession of the benefice of the church of Saint Amand, which your predecessor restored to him, in the presence of ourselves and many witnesses, as the parson of that church; and that you either remove his deputy and defrauder Roger from that vicariate, if this is just, or compel him, under a pledge of faith, to abide by the agreements made. The granting of this petition will ensure that you have Master Ranulf bound to service, and ourselves debtors for a fuller favour. We wish you well in the Lord, dearest Father in Christ.

## LETTER 201. TO ROGER, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK

[Col. 0909A]

To the venerable lord and dearest friend R., by the grace of God archbishop of York: brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting.

We have received the letters of your affection. They refreshed us with all the truer joy because they gave us more certain information concerning your welfare, your prosperous return, your arrival in our region, and fulfilled the desires we had formed according to our wish. Therefore, lest we delay our wishes any longer, God willing, we shall meet you, having arrived and been established on the Sunday immediately after the Purification of the glorious Blessed Mary, [Virgin], so that on the following day, if it please you—  
(The remainder is missing.)

## LETTER 202. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0909B]

To the venerable lord and dearest Father R., by the grace of God archbishop of York: brother G., minister of the Church of London, all things fitting for salvation, and whatever honour and service we can render him.

A few words readily persuade when the friendly kindness of the person addressed is ready to listen. Since we have long conceived great confidence in your goodwill toward us from its actual demonstration, inferring the future from the past and hoping well in every respect from your moderation toward all, we earnestly offer to your eminence such petitions as we know and are able to make: look more mercifully upon your cleric and our kinsman W. Foliot, whom you have for some time regarded with a less favourable eye, and, if it please you, receive him again into your accustomed favour. It is enough, if it please you, that you have long afflicted one who did not deserve it and humbled him while he patiently bore all things. Perhaps you have severely reproved no fault of his, or at least a slight one, and in all this have wisely instructed your son. Therefore, now that you have abundantly poured wine into the wound, we beseech you henceforth to apply oil, by fully restoring to your cleric what was taken from him; and thus have both him and ourselves—and, if it please you, all that is ours—at your disposal. Farewell.

## LETTER 203. TO J., DEAN OF AUGY

GILBERT, by the grace of God bishop of London, to J., dean of Augy: greeting.

We have heard and certainly learned that certain priests or deacons of your deanery, wholly despising and rejecting our admonition, do not at all avoid the forbidden society of women, but still foster and frequent, as shamelessly as irreverently, their customary cohabitation with concubines. Therefore, lest our patience, which they have abused for so long, be construed as consent, we command you by the present letters, under the force of obedience, to suspend from priestly and Levitical office, by God’s authority and ours, all persons of the aforesaid order established in your deanery who are known to be entangled, and still ensnared, in so infamous, intimate, and unlawful a connection; and to keep them suspended until, by fitting satisfaction, they obtain from us the grace of restoration. Farewell.

## LETTER 204. TO THE BISHOP OF CHESTER

The bishop of London to the bishop of Chester: the joy of salvation and, with every gladness, the service of ready devotion.

Those whom nature has made kin to us, the rule of charity does not permit to be separated from us. Hence it is fitting that we should attend to their affairs as far as we can with God and justice, and labour by every means to bring them, through our diligence, to their desired result. Since, therefore, we have often learned by experience of your favour what we can accomplish with your goodwill in affairs concerning ourselves and our people, the past gives us, so to speak, a sure hope that the liberality innate in you will not grow cold in the future.

Therefore, dearest brother and lord, receive, if it please you, our most devoted letters and petition with the affection that you have customarily shown; and, in the case of our kinsman R., who, as we have heard, has been presented to your holiness for the church of Idelesham, grant that church to him and fulfil without delay the act of institution which we request. You know how many opportunities for obstruction are commonly found in such matters through delay, opportunities which often deprive a bishop of the authority to institute and, by the wicked cunning of certain people, prevent the person to be instituted from enjoying the benefice which could justly have been conferred on him.

May divine mercy therefore move the bowels of your compassion. May the love and devotion which we bear toward you grow into an abundance of charity, so that you may deign to advance the aforesaid R. in the matter described, and, by the favour granted to him, bind both us and his other friends more closely to your service. We wish you well in the Lord, dearest friend.

## LETTER 205. TO HILARY, BISHOP OF CHICHESTER

To the venerable lord and dearest brother HILARY, by the grace of God bishop of Chichester: brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting and the affection of sincere love.

That we acted on behalf of John the cognitor was obedience. That we pronounced judgment for him against the abbot of Geresten was observance of law and right. That, without your knowledge, I caused the judgment to be executed through your official, namely the dean of Beddig’, was undoubtedly the result of necessity of time. For we, as you also were, had been commanded by the lord king to set out on pilgrimage; we were to meet by agreement at Duur’ on the Wednesday next after the judgment was pronounced, and from there proceed to the lord pope as quickly as possible.

Therefore, lest matters prolonged by reason of your departure should further be delayed to the detriment of a poor cleric, we entrusted execution of this matter, by authority of the Apostolic See, to your dean, who happened to arrive at that most timely moment, with great confidence indeed in your goodwill toward us. If your gentleness has been in any degree angered against him because of this, we most devoutly ask, for reverence toward the lord pope, that he be granted pardon by us and restored to his former rank and favour. Otherwise, abandoned to our confusion—God forbid!—he may compel us to hope less than we are accustomed to hope in your goodwill—God forbid! We would petition still more urgently and heap petitions upon petitions more insistently, were this not something like the judgment of a distrustful mind, presuming too little upon brotherly charity. Farewell.

## LETTER 206. TO HUGH, BISHOP OF DURHAM

To the venerable lord and dearest brother H., by the grace of God bishop of Durham: brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting and the affection of sincere charity.

It is a very common practice that whenever a worthy occasion requires it, we offer earnest petitions, with confidence of obtaining what we seek, to those from whose affection we have fuller hope. Since we neither ought nor can fail our friends, especially those whom a bond of nature unites to us, in their affairs, trusting more in your energy than in our own merit, we earnestly beseech your kindness to bring to a happier conclusion what you have commendably begun in advancing your men, W. and H. Thus they may feel that our petitions have profited them with you; and you may have us as debtors of gratitude and them as debtors of service. Farewell.

## LETTER 207. TO BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF EXETER

[Col. 0911C]

To the venerable lord and dearest brother B., by the grace of God bishop of Exeter: brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting and the due service of brotherly love.

We cannot refuse our friends and well-wishers the support of petitioning, when their need or that of their people demands it, those in whose charity toward us we trust. Therefore, since the bearer of this letter is a familiar associate and friend of our friends, we kindly offer petitions to your goodwill, dear to us in the Lord, that you advance his business, which lies before you, as far as equity permits, and that, by providing for his indemnity, you make him bound to you in service and us debtors to you in gratitude. We wish you well in the Lord, dearest Father in Christ.

## LETTER 208. TO ROBERT, ARCHDEACON OF OXFORD, LATER BISHOP OF HEREFORD

G., by the grace of God bishop of London, to R., archdeacon of Oxford: the joy of salvation and that affection which the grace of nature adds.

At the urging of many, I offer petitions to your goodwill that you do not withdraw, through anyone’s persuasion or intervention, in any degree from the agreements confirmed between you and Master Adam of Longueville; but that you keep in your own hand the church which, as he asserts, you hold in his name for an annual pension. Otherwise, should another intrude into it through you, then after your promotion, God granting it, or your transfer—by the Lord’s inspiration—to pursuits of a humbler life, or perhaps after that final day which no one escapes, a difficulty, entangled as such things commonly are, may prevent him from recovering his property anew for his own use.

Since I do not doubt that you are willing to observe what is equitable, I offer my petitions with confidence that they will be granted, asking you to perform more cheerfully at my request what you would have done even without my petition. We wish you well in the Lord.

## LETTER 209. TO THE SAME

GILBERT, by the grace of God bishop of London, to R., archdeacon of Oxford: manifold thanks for the consolation received.

Oppressed by many burdens of care, I have no ready answer to write to a friend except that prophetic saying alone, which, though I have often sung it, I am now compelled in my bitterness to experience and say: “All day long my shame is before me, and the confusion of my face has covered me” (Ps. 43 [Vulgate]). “I have become a spectacle to the world and to men” (1 Cor. 4), because “the enemy has sorely afflicted me” (Ps. 41 [Vulgate]); “the hand of the Lord has touched me” (Job 19), which, raising me very high, has at last violently dashed me down.

To the accumulation of miseries is added the fact that no remedy can readily be sought or hoped for. The sea is closed to me and every harbour around is forbidden. To remain among friends and acquaintances is death to me; to be wholly separated from them is impossible. Therefore I sent a messenger to the lord king with all the haste I could, in order that, having obtained permission to cross the sea, I might approach the lord pope and with him either defend my cause, if that is possible, or, if it is otherwise, seek from him remedies for the wound inflicted.

I greatly desire a conference with you, and beseech you that I may have your presence in London on the Saturday of Pentecost, so that, instructed by your counsel and that of my brethren, I may understand what is expedient for me in that assembly. I wish you well, dearest friend!

## LETTER 210. TO ROBERT, ELECT OF HEREFORD

GILBERT, by the grace of God bishop of London, to his beloved in the Lord Robert, by the same grace elect of Hereford, and to the whole chapter of the same church: greeting.

Whatever we recognize as tending to establish or more securely safeguard the peace of the Church, we ought, charity undoubtedly urging us, to assent to more diligently and to strengthen by writings and other instruments so that it may remain permanently valid. Therefore, by this present document, we notify your brotherhood that the case long disputed between our venerable brother Roger, prior of Malvern, and Roger, priest of Lenhale, concerning the church of Lenhale—and greatly prolonged by various turns of events—has at last been settled in your presence and received an end consonant with peace. We had received an apostolic mandate either to impose an end upon it by amicable settlement or, having heard both parties, to decide it by a canonical conclusion.

The aforesaid Roger of Lenhale, acknowledging the right of the church of Malvern in the aforesaid church of Lenhale, resigned that church into our hand and permitted the prior of the church of Malvern, through our hand and by apostolic authority, to be invested with it. When this had been done with due solemnity, the prior, with the assent of his whole chapter, granted that same church to Roger through our hand, apostolic authority intervening, to be held by him during his lifetime for an annual pension of half a mark payable at Easter.

He further agreed, with the assent of his entire chapter, as an increase of charity, that when the aforesaid Roger either dies or turns himself to the fruit of a better life, Walter, priest of Daubo—who had for some time ministered in that church in Roger’s name—shall minister there in the name of the prior and the church of Malvern, and shall remain its perpetual vicar, paying annually at Easter a pension of one mark, until he either dies or renounces secular life. But upon the death of the said Walter, or upon his taking the religious habit, the church of Lenhale, with all its entirety, shall accrue to the possessions of the church of Malvern, and thereafter the church of Malvern shall possess it fully.

Because we decree that this shall remain ratified and unshaken, saving the right of the church of Hereford, we confirm it by the attestation of the present writing and the affixing of our seal.

Witnesses: Robert de Broi; Maurice de Sabricteswrde; Roger of Hereford; Richard of Salisbury; Louis; Walter the almoner; Master William de Bernes; Hugh, chaplain of Hedam; Samson, cleric of the prior; Reginald the chamberlain; Walter Foliot; Richard Brudle; Jocelin; Alan.

## LETTER 211. TO THE SAME

GILBERT, by the grace of God bishop of London, to his venerable brother and dearest lord R., by the same grace elect of the Church of Hereford: greeting and success in the Lord, ever answering your desires.

A few words readily persuade when the friendly kindness of the person addressed is inclined to listen. Accordingly, we earnestly offer petitions to your goodwill, dear to us in the Lord, that, for love of God and in regard for our request, you preserve the church of Lideberi, in both its head church and the chapels belonging to it, in the integrity in which it is known to have been established in our time and in that of our predecessors, on account of the episcopal see which it has long possessed and the reverence due to the holy bishops whose bodies rest there. Thus, when you have heard our petitions in this matter, you will have God made favourable to you thereby and us as debtors to you for a fuller favour.

## LETTER 212. TO THE SAME. PREFACE TO THE COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS

To his lord and dearest friend ROBERT, by the grace of God bishop of Hereford: brother GILBERT, minister of the Church of London, [wishes him] humbly to be occupied with the things of God and to be consummated in them with a most blessed end.

Lest the authority of your command, my lord, should seem empty or slight to me, I immediately sent you the book which you requested: namely, the book which, with the Lord’s help, I recently composed on the Song of Songs, etc. See Gilbert’s *Exegetical Works*, among the volumes of the *Patrologia* shortly to be published. EDITORS OF THE PATROLOGY.

## LETTER 213. TO THE SAME

To the venerable brother R., by the grace of God bishop of Hereford: brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting.

If we asked for words, satisfaction has been given; if for the thing itself, not so much. Yet for the highly honourable and elegant refusal with which you rejected our requests, we owe how great thanks to you and your notaries; these thanks, the Lord permitting, we shall render when there is occasion for thanksgiving.

But we cannot sufficiently wonder that you write that our petitions, which we offered to your brotherhood for the restoration of those cast down from their possession, ought by your interpretation not to be granted, lest you commit a grave offence—God forbid!—against the Church of God and the sacred canons. For these are the first principles both of divine and human law: that no one is permitted to pronounce law for himself; that persons violently dispossessed must be restored for every action; that even robbers and violent possessors are to be aided by an interdict against the true owners; and many things of this kind which the laws affirm, the decretals confirm, and the excellent interpreter of both, custom, commends. Though perhaps these principles are disregarded in an injury done to us, we know that your prudence does not ignore them.

But now, since, as your statement concludes, you do not wish to deny us anything which you could grant a friend—and which ought not to be denied even to an enemy—we ask that a day, a place, and a hearing be provided for our dispossessed persons.

## LETTER 214. TO THE SAME

The bishop of London to the bishop of Hereford: greeting and the due affection of true love.

I fear to approach a friend as an importunate petitioner and to demand from him anything that might trouble him even slightly. Yet, when I consider that praiseworthy moderation of your mind, I conceive the hope that you will kindly endure a friend, even one making great requests, who by the boldness of his petition invites you to offer him such requests and, when the Lord affords an opportunity, cheerfully to grant them.

I have learned from the report of certain persons that Ralph of Lideberi, your cleric, has the intention and purpose of wishing to resign into your hand the prebend which he holds in the church of Hereford, provided he has hope that your goodwill may be pleased to confer it upon my nephew Henry. This, therefore, is what I ask; this is what I desire to be shown us as a proof of affection and an increase of charity. If I understand that it is troublesome to you in any respect, I withdraw wholly from the request itself. May my lord and dearest friend in Christ fare well.

Whatever in this world is known to be more fortunate, and in the world to come more excellent, ought to be brought to fulfilment by the effect accompanying a sincere request of the will, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the thing requested may undoubtedly acquire strength. Therefore, to your excellency, thanks and acts of thanksgiving.

How greatly the affection of my heart delights in your love neither voice nor the pen of one writing can express. Yet, to comprise much in few words, know that, so far as I am able, I am always bound to your will. Your affection will surely prove this when it wishes something to be done by me.

## LETTER 215. TO THE BISHOPS OF HEREFORD AND WORCESTER

To his beloved elect, the lord of Hereford and the lord of Worcester: brother G., minister of the Church of London, the joy of salvation and such service as active charity can render in the Lord.

Your prudence, we know, is not unaware that ignorance of fact often gives rise to ignorance of law, and that in controversies, when it is less clear what has been done, an uninstructed judge understands less fully what must be decided. Therefore, by the present writing we notify you, concerning the case now pending between Robert and Henry, what we saw, what we heard—indeed, what we ourselves, following the forms of laws and canons, with many sitting beside us, judged, and took care to commit to lawful execution.

After the death of Richard, who had ministered for a long time in the church of Witeberne, we believed that he had held the parsonage of that church until the day of his death and had ministered there in his own name. Deceived by Robert’s fraudulent concealment of what he knew, and at length moved by the urgency of his many petitions, we granted the aforesaid church to him and, although he had knowledge that it belonged by right to another, invested him with it, being unaware of this.

When this became known, Walter de Broward, canon of the church of Hereford, came into our presence and asserted that the aforesaid church belonged to him by right and had been canonically granted to him by our predecessor, Robert, bishop of good memory. He requested that a day be appointed to prove this and that Robert be summoned to answer on the matter. Therefore, on the appointed day, when two chapters had been convoked at Lidebury, Walter, in Robert’s presence, asserted that the church of Witeburne belonged to him by right, as already stated; and he proved fully, by a sufficient number of suitable witnesses who gave bodily oaths on the matter, that Richeward had resigned it into the hand of Lord Robert the bishop and that the same bishop had canonically conferred it upon Walter.

Accordingly, we adjudged that church away from Robert and restored it by judgment to the aforesaid Walter. After Walter’s death, we granted it to another of your clerics, Roger; and after he later resigned it, we bestowed it—vacant of every incumbent and possessor—upon Henry, the bearer of this letter. Once the judgment has been reconsidered, it is easy for one deciding the matter to determine which of these is to be held stronger in law: the one who relies upon acts lawfully performed, or the one who relies upon a gift. We wish you well in the Lord, dearest brethren in Christ.

## LETTER 216. TO G., DEAN, AND THE CHAPTER OF HEREFORD

G., by the grace of God bishop of London, to his beloved in the Lord G., dean of Hereford, and to the whole chapter: greeting and the affection of sincere love.

It is a common practice that we offer petitions more abundantly to those from whom we do not fear refusal and in whose charity we have more assured confidence, with unhesitating trust that we shall obtain what we desire. Since the evidence of the past makes us more secure in making requests, we earnestly ask each of you together with all the rest that, in the established affairs of R. Colec’ [lacuna], you act mercifully, in good faith and in consideration of your canon, divine compassion, and our petition, so that while he remains at the schools he may not suffer loss of the portion which belongs to him. For it is merciful to assist those whom love of learning makes exiles.

Nor certainly ought anything done exceptionally in wicked causes to be made a precedent. As you know, a request is more pleasingly received when it is offered than when it is squeezed out of an unwilling person by the calculations of a judicial decision; and would that willingness to act preceded necessity, and pure liberality forestalled compulsion! For you know what has been given us in command, which we have refrained from executing, wishing to spare your labours and expenses. We wait in the firmest hope that the desire and necessity of the aforesaid Richard will be satisfied rather by your will than by a sentence. We still hope that this will happen, joining petition to petition, so that the event itself may declare that our prayers have benefited him with you, and that you may have him as a debtor in service and us as debtors in gratitude.

## LETTER 217. TO THE SAME

To G., dean, and the whole chapter of the church of Hereford: greeting in the Lord.

We have always claimed your goodwill and favour with great confidence; and therefore, when the need of ourselves or our friends calls for it, we confidently come before you, with every hope of obtaining whatever the charity of friends can and ought to grant a friend. For our nephew R., also your canon, by his own purpose and our counsel, is lately about to cross the sea, by God’s grace, for the sake of study.

Accordingly, we earnestly beseech your community, dear to us and always to be cherished in the Lord, that, in view of so favourable a purpose and at the intervention of our request, if it please you, you grant us this one permission: that his absence meanwhile be treated as excused, if it please you, without any diminution of the benefices of his prebend and without detriment to himself. Thus you will make him more devoted to your services and us debtors to you for a fuller favour on his behalf. May each fare well; may all fare well.

## LETTER 218. TO UHTRED, BISHOP OF LLANDAFF

To the venerable lord and dearest brother in Christ UHTRED, by the grace of God bishop of Llandaff: brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting in the Lord.

A certain parishioner of ours, named Matilda, came to us and repeatedly showed us, with tearful complaint, that a certain James, son of Lebrand, of your nation and now a parishioner by residence, had, as she asserts, received and taken her as his wife in solemn marriage and with priestly blessing; but afterwards, without judgment or the Church’s knowledge, had left her deserted for the whole of the last seven years, and, in violation of the faith of the marriage-bed and the law of Christ, had wickedly and irreverently brought in another woman, leaving her entirely deprived of a husband’s support. [Col. 0917B] Concerning this matter, so that we might write to you what was true and report it confidently as certain, we made a strict and diligent inquiry into the truth of the matter through the archdeacon, through the priest who had officiated at and arranged the marriage, and through several laymen, grave and honourable men. We plainly discovered to be true what the aforesaid Matilda had repeatedly persuaded us concerning her marriage contracted with James, more by tears than words.

Therefore, since the aforesaid J. resides within your jurisdiction and, as is said, in your territory at Grenning, [Col. 0917C] we earnestly address petitions to your brotherhood, begging and beseeching you in the Lord that, out of reverence for God, you rebuke him with canonical severity and compel him by the coercion of ecclesiastical justice both to provide for his wife what is due and to furnish her support. Thus he may know that you and we have one and the same zeal for Christ’s law, and may feel that avengers against its transgressors are not lacking on either side. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXIX. TO NICHOLAS, BISHOP OF LLANDAFF

To the venerable lord and dearest brother Nicholas, bishop of Llandaff, Brother G., minister of the Church of London: greeting and the service owed by fraternal charity. [Col. 0917D]

Know that I am safe and well, and that I earnestly desire conversation with you, so that from a friend’s presence I may receive the consolation for which the soul so greatly longs. Since this is hindered by various events, let that charity, I pray, supply what our bodily absence from one another takes away: charity which knows no absence, and always knows that the person whom it loves is present to it in spirit.

Moreover, at the request of William, son of R., I am compelled to offer you the petitions of his goodwill: that you may be pleased to promote B., his clerk, long since advanced to the order of deacon, to the priesthood. By granting this for God’s love and in consideration of my petition, you will make him indebted to you in prayer, and indebted to God and to me in gratitude, as in [Col. 0918A] all things. Farewell in Christ, dearest friend.

## LETTER CCXX. TO ROBERT, BISHOP OF LINCOLN

To the venerable lord and dearest brother R., bishop of Lincoln, Brother G., minister of the Church of London: may you serve Christ devoutly in a fruitful old age.

You may perhaps have learned, from public report, what resources belong to the place called Haliwelle. It is indeed a narrow and small site, entirely bounded within the space of three acres of land. Twenty veiled sisters, consecrated to the Lord, dwell there, continually engaged in divine praises and regularly serving the Lord. Their temporal food and clothing are supplied by the church of Dunt’, piously bestowed upon them by Master Roger, the bearer of this letter, [Col. 0918B] and mercifully confirmed by your grace. If that provision is taken away, the place inhabited by the said sisters will suffice them for burial, but in no way for sustenance.

I pray, therefore, that your mind be moved by the calamity into which these sisters will undoubtedly fall if, God forbid, they are deprived by judicial severity of the aforesaid church. Let that pastoral mercy, then, intervene—the mercy which until this day, through the benefit conferred, has fed and clothed the Lord’s handmaids—lest, by adjudging away from them everything they possess beneath heaven, it leave them desolate and utterly deprived of all help and counsel. Let them, if you please, be granted canonical respite; let lawful delays not be denied them; let an advocate’s aid be supplied, so that they may find in you [Col. 0918C] a heart compassionate toward their poverty insofar as equity permits, and friendly to religion. If the strict necessity of the case requires it, let a settlement rather be made than that the fleece of the Lord’s fold be stripped to the skin by judicial sentence.

We earnestly commend to your brotherhood Master R. of Duntone, the bearer of this letter, whom the aforesaid sisters appoint as their representative in the present case under our testimony, because, poverty preventing them, they cannot find a conveyance in which to travel to you. We pray that you may prosper in the Lord, dearest brother in Christ.

## LETTER CCXXI. TO THE SAME

To the venerable lord and dearest brother R., by God’s grace bishop of Lincoln, Brother G., minister of the Church of London: greeting such as to himself.

Our friend and kinsman R. Brito has shown himself so capable and energetic in matters within his power that, in those needs which exceed his means, he seems not undeserving of assistance from his friends. By the Lord’s bounty, in whose hand are the hearts of kings (Prov. 21), he obtained such favour in the king’s sight that our lord the king granted to his eldest son, as a marriage portion with the daughter and heiress of William Gulafre, the barony of that same William, which had reverted to the king’s hand. The king also saw to it that his own daughter was honourably married, ennobled by a noble husband and a great marriage portion through royal generosity. In this matter both the king’s munificence is deservedly praised [Col. 0919A] and the father’s diligence is equally approved. For he who earns well and he who rewards well are both to be praised.

There remains another son, whom he has resolved to educate in letters, dedicate to God, and commit to ecclesiastical order. Since his father’s services cannot, and ought not, to assist in his advancement, he rests, after God, upon the single hope placed especially in the two of us: that we ought to take charge of him and provide for him for God’s sake. He therefore acts as my envoy to you in this matter, so that he may obtain more readily through my intercession the favour which he does not despair of obtaining on his own account.

The father therefore petitions for his son, I for my nephew, and we both for our great-nephew, that you may, if you please, enrol under the titles of your [Col. 0919B] Church that which paternal devotion has devoted to divine service, and admit him into the holy inheritance and ecclesiastical household by granting, or promising for the present or future, a benefice—so that the father’s anxiety, wholly fixed upon his son, may breathe again, cheered either by its realization or at least by hope.
