If in this matter my petition seems to you importunate and burdensome, know that you should rather attribute it to yourselves and to your brother, Lord William de Caineto. For I did not know Brittany; I had not known the Bretons; neither acquaintance with nor even the name of R. the Breton had reached me, until you two commended him to my favour and with much diligence brought him into friendship and kinship with our people. You bound me to him by such an obligation that it should no longer be judged importunity, but rather a necessity of duty, for me to petition your affection on his behalf. [Col. 0919C]

Besides and beyond all this, Lord R. de Almari gives me much encouragement to ask, and confidence that my request will be granted. In this very business, as is said, he boldly lends his support to you and, in the manner of courtiers, imperiously arranges everything. For I cannot despair with you in a cause which, on the one hand, the majesty of the court and, on the other, the humility of myself and other friends strive to commend to your goodwill in so honourable a desire. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXII. TO THE SAME

To the venerable lord and dearest brother R., by God’s grace bishop of Lincoln, Brother G., minister of the Church of London: greeting. [Col. 0919D]

We speak to you as to ourselves, and others do not wish secrets entrusted to them. Regarding the matter which you took care to communicate to us, this first occurs to us at present: you have promulgated a definite sentence concerning an uncertain matter. Although the fact was not established, you nevertheless took care to pronounce as though it had been established. For since possession itself creates an adversary to our action, it was necessary to establish not only before judgment but at the very beginning of the suit who possessed the property, from whom the claimant might reclaim what he alleged was his by right.

But now, with Richard de Ambli in possession and asserting through the manager of the litigation that the thing is his by right, judgment was made not between the claimant and the person in possession, but rather between other persons who were outside possession; it was not examined, but judged. [Col. 0920A] For neither the monks’ admission concerning themselves nor that of your archdeacon or dean, when no proof had been produced regarding the other party, could establish a legal inquiry for you. It is therefore clear what harm the sentence thus pronounced does to Richard de Ambli, since a matter adjudged between others does not prejudice other persons.

Let your prudence therefore consider what you have written to the lord pope. For, as the tenor of his letter states, you wrote that the case had been argued between Roger and Richard and concluded by judgment. If the matter was conducted in that way, we disapprove both the act itself and the written account of it. If, however, it was not so, but—as the human eye often sees unclearly—the lord pope understood the affair otherwise than it was transacted or written, then in our view the objection of those who allege the falsity of the petition submitted and of the representation made must be admitted. [Col. 0920B] For this is not just any falsehood, but one that destroys the entire substance of the case: it deprives of possession one who was never summoned, against whom no action was brought at law and no judgment ever pronounced. He who confirms a sentence said to have been rendered between that man and Roger, when no such sentence exists, appears to confirm nothing.

If you defer the lord pope’s mandate, you do not omit it; nor should such delay be regarded as futile when it rests at once upon truth and reason. It will therefore be proper, if you please, to write back to the lord pope and explain on what grounds and for what weighty reason you have deferred his mandate. Since it depends upon allegations submitted, no one is unaware that it should be deferred once their credibility has been impugned. But we do not judge it equitable to assist a poor man extraordinarily and to another’s injury, since the divine law says concerning this: “You shall not show favour to a poor man in judgment”; and Justinian himself decrees that a judge ought not to weep for the afflicted. [Col. 0920C] Farewell, and do not fail to prefer the sounder judgment.

## LETTER CCXXIII. TO B., ARCHDEACON OF LINCOLN

G., by God’s grace bishop of London, to R., archdeacon of Lincoln: greeting.

By apostolic authority we appointed for you a day for the case pending between you and R., the priest. On that day, for the purpose of clearing yourself of the injury, as is alleged, done by you to the lord pope and the holy Roman Church, you neither appeared nor arranged to send an advocate. [Col. 0920D] We therefore appoint another day, and this a peremptory one, ordering and enjoining you by apostolic authority that, unless you have received the aforesaid R., the priest, as entirely absolved from the sentence of interdict, and have caused to be fully restored to him the revenues of his church which you withheld while he pursued his appeal to the lord pope, you shall appear before us at Windleshores on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September [22 August], so that you may obey the lord pope’s mandate concerning the aforesaid case, as justice shall prescribe.

He who raises an objection is bound to prove what he objects. If you intend to maintain that the pronouncement which the lord of Canterbury issued against me, contrary to the statutes of the canons and to the injury of the lord pope and the holy Roman Church, binds me and prevents and obstructs me from executing the apostolic mandate, then, when you have proved this objection in law, you will rightly avoid our judgment. [Col. 0921A] Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXIV. TO THE PARISHIONERS OF THE CHURCH OF LONDON

G., by God’s grace minister of the Church of London, to all the parishioners and children of the same Church, beloved in the Lord: greeting, grace, and blessing.

At the castle of Stortford there is a place of venerable beauty, once assigned to the sanctuary of God and to divine service. Even now, after its ruins, the faithful people venerate and revere it with great devotion because signs of holiness are said frequently to have appeared there. We therefore, for the love of God and reverence for the holy place, intending to restore the matter to its former state [Col. 0921B] and rebuild a basilica there for God, announce to your charity our purpose in this pious undertaking, wishing that we may make you our fellow-workers in the pious work and at the same time partakers of its due fruit and worthy reward.

We therefore pray and exhort your love in the Lord that, in consideration of piety, you devote help and effort to this holy work; and, so that what has been begun may come to completion, that you contribute something from your goods toward repairing the house of the Lord who has bestowed all things. Let those who comply with our exhortations in this matter know that we specially make them participants in the prayers and benefactions of the holy Church of London. To penitents who have confessed their sins and charitably bestow something upon this work in honour of God, we mercifully remit twenty days from the satisfaction imposed upon them. [Col. 0921C]

## LETTER CCXXV. TO THE SAME

Gilbert, by God’s grace bishop of London, to all parishioners and children of the holy Church of London, beloved in the Lord: greeting, grace, and blessing.

Whoever shows himself a helper of good works becomes a participant in the reward; nor does that which has been expended for pious purposes on behalf of the poor remain unrewarded. For the Lord says: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25). Therefore we earnestly admonish [Col. 0921D] and ask you, and enjoin you for the remission of your sins, that for the building of the hospital newly begun in London at Southwark, in honour of God and of blessed Thomas the martyr, for receiving and sustaining alike the poor and sick, you mercifully extend a helping hand out of love for God and in consideration of piety. By contributing from the means granted you by the Lord for the refreshment and support alike of the poor, may you have God as the rewarder, and giver to you of eternal life, for the grace bestowed upon him in his members; and may you make yourselves participants in the prayers and benefits that shall be performed in the aforesaid hospital.

To all, moreover, who extend a helping hand to the aforesaid work of piety and assist the poor of that place, even in a small degree, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, we remit twenty days [Col. 0922A] from the penance imposed upon them, and grant that they shall participate in the prayers and benefits performed in our Church.

## LETTER CCXXVI. TO THE SAME

Gilbert, by God’s grace bishop of London, to the archdeacons, deans, and all prelates of churches established in the bishopric of London, beloved in the Lord: greeting, grace, and blessing.

The authority of our office admonishes and exhorts us to take care that benefits which the devotion of the faithful has bestowed, or shall bestow, in charity upon Christ’s poor within our diocese are confirmed to those poor and strengthened with perpetual stability for the future. Therefore, with the episcopal authority granted us by the Lord, we grant to the aforesaid brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem and confirm to them forever under the testimony of this writing the church of Standuna with its appurtenances; likewise the church of Chingesboria with its appurtenances; and the church of Chauria with all that belongs to it. As we have learned from their authentic charters, the founders and patrons of those churches assigned these to God, to Saint John, and to the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem, as perpetual alms for the salvation of themselves and their people. [Col. 0922B]

Witnesses: Hugh, dean of Saint Paul’s; Richard, archdeacon of Oxford; Richard, archdeacon of Colchester; Master Nicholas; Master Walter; William de Norhala, canons of Saint Paul’s; William de Piro; Henry the Painter; Robert Huscharle; Robert de Fuleham; Alfred Bechet; William de Ver; and others. [Col. 0922C] Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXVII. TO THE SAME

Gilbert, by God’s grace bishop of London, to all parishioners and children of the same Church, beloved in the Lord: greeting, grace, and blessing.

Those who serve the Lord more devotedly are rightly heard by his faithful in their just petitions. Therefore we make known to all of you by this present writing that we have granted to our beloved brethren—the monks of Cluny, namely, and specifically the prior of Rumuli and the convent of that place—all churches and ecclesiastical benefices which were given and granted to them by Count Eustace, confirmed by his charter which we have inspected, and peacefully and undisturbedly possessed by them for many years already.

Among these, we have thought it proper to specify in their own names the church of Stanford; the church of Angra; the church of Lahaphara and Little Lagaphara; the church of Cogeshala; the church of Orteia; the church of Langahou; and everything belonging to them in chapels, lands, and tithes—namely, tithes of pigs, lambs, wool, cheeses, calves, foals, pannage, hay, and flax. [Col. 0922D] We grant the aforesaid churches with all their appurtenances to the aforesaid brethren, confirm them by episcopal authority, and strengthen this our gift by the attestation of our seal. Witnesses: Richard, archdeacon . . . . [Col. 0923A]

## LETTER CCXXVIII. TO THE SAME

Gilbert, by God’s grace bishop of London, to all parishioners and children of the holy Church of London, beloved in the Lord: greeting, grace, and blessing.

The affection of charity compels us to petition you all on behalf of the need of the brethren of Priten’. They are plainly unable to complete the building of their church, which they have begun, from their own expenditures, unless the devotion of the faithful mercifully comes to the aid of their desires. [Col. 0923B] Therefore we commend to your favour, under the testimony of our letters, the bearers of this letter, the messengers and agents of their poverty. We pray and exhort you in the Lord, and enjoin you for the remission of your sins, that you may graciously receive them, who labour piously for the common need of the brethren, and mercifully devote your alms and benefactions, from the means bestowed on you by the Lord, to the construction of the aforesaid fabric of the church. Thus, by building the Lord’s house on earth, you may prepare for yourselves buildings that shall endure in heaven.

We especially beseech the clergy, priests, and incumbents of churches established throughout our diocese to devote diligent attention to receiving, assisting, and honouring them, and to commend them with devout prayer to the peoples entrusted to them. [Col. 0923C] Let all who honour them with lodging or any benefaction know that we make them participants in the prayers and benefits of the holy Church of London. To penitents who have confessed their sins and are subject to our priestly jurisdiction, because they need a greater remedy we add greater mercy: if they are under a penance of seven years or more, we remit twenty days from the satisfaction imposed upon them; if under less, ten days.

## LETTER CCXXIX. TO THE SAME

G., by God’s grace bishop of London, to all parishioners and children of the same Church, beloved in the Lord: greeting, grace, and blessing. [Col. 0923D]

The more brightly, beloved, the generosity of almsgiving shines among works of charity, the more earnestly we exhort you in the Lord to persist in distributing alms. For if you sow works of mercy during this pilgrimage of the present age, you shall reap eternal life in heaven with multiplied fruit. Therefore we earnestly ask and admonish you to have compassion on the poverty of the brethren of Cuwella, who cannot, for lack of resources, build a church suitable to their religious life. Moved by pious compassion, provide them with the assistance they desire in view of eternal things, so that, aided by your support and having built an oratory for themselves, they may be able most fervently to adhere to the law of God’s commandments.

Trusting in God’s mercy, we remit ten days from the penance of those who give anything from their means to that place, [Col. 0924A] and, with the Lord’s help, make them participants in all the good works performed in our Church. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXX. TO THE SAME

G., by God’s grace bishop of London, to the bishops, archdeacons, clergy, established throughout the bishopric of London and beloved in the Lord: greeting, grace, and blessing.

Things mercifully expended for the use of the poor are not lost to their donors; indeed, they are kept for the glory of eternal recompense, and the pious bestowal of temporal goods works eternal life. Therefore, solicitous for the advancement of your salvation, we earnestly exhort your charity in the Lord to devote yourselves to pious works, so that, from the goods granted to you by the Lord’s permission, while you have time, while it is permitted, you may merit the fruit of eternity. [Col. 0924B]

We therefore, sympathizing with the poverty of Christ’s handmaids, who continually serve God and the most blessed Mary of Northampton, ask, admonish, and exhort you in the Lord that, when they come to you setting forth their poverty, you receive them kindly and relieve their want from the abundance of your resources, so that you may participate in the good works performed, by God’s authorship, both in our Church and in theirs. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXXI. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0924C]

G., by God’s grace bishop of London, to the archdeacons, deans, and all prelates of churches established in the bishopric of London, beloved in the Lord: greeting, grace, and blessing.

Let your love know that R., clerk of Ardel’, voluntarily and unconditionally resigned into our hands the church of Ardel’, and bound himself under the sanctity of an oath that he would claim no further right in it. At the request and presentation of the patron, we granted it in its complete integrity to our beloved G. de Sur’ to hold in perpetuity and possess canonically, and with due solemnity installed him as its incumbent. Since we do not wish this to be capable in future of being called into doubt [Col. 0924D] or rendered void, we have taken care to notify all of you of it by this present writing and to confirm it by episcopal authority. Witnesses . . . .

## LETTER CCXXXII. TO THE SAME

G., by God’s grace bishop of London, to all ministers of holy mother Church and also to all persons of Christian profession dwelling in his diocese to whom these letters shall come: may you abound in bowels of compassion.

Dearest brethren, let the frequent and daily admonition of evangelical teaching take hold in us: by it we are instructed and formed eagerly to extend the hand of mercy to those in need of help and to assist the necessities of the oppressed by providing a remedy from heaven. [Col. 0925A] For it is written: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so we shall fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. 6). And again: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9). Elsewhere: “Give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke 6). And again: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4). Elsewhere: “Charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13).

Let us therefore, each according to the measure of his means, gladly assist the church of the Holy Virgin N. and the brethren dwelling there in Christ’s service, mercifully bearing the burden of their pressing poverty; and let us give something with cheerful heart from the blessings God has bestowed upon us toward rebuilding the church destroyed by a fire. To all, however, who extend a helping hand to the aforesaid work of mercy with the devotion appropriate to it, trusting in the Lord’s grace and the merits of so great a Virgin, we remit twelve days from their penance and, with the Lord’s help, make them participants in all the good works performed in our Church. [Col. 0925B]

## LETTER CCXXXIII. TO THE SAME

G., by God’s grace bishop of London, to the archdeacons, deans, and all persons of churches established throughout the bishopric of London, beloved in the Lord: greeting, grace, and blessing.

What has been bestowed upon religious places in view of divine contemplation ought rightly to be secured by episcopal authority, lest it can hereafter be overthrown by the easy instability of human affairs. Therefore, following the authentic instrument of the nobleman Walter, son of Robert—by which he confirms to the church of Saint Neot and the monks serving God there the right of divine service and of advowson which he had in the church of Wimbis and in the church of Saint Andrew within the walls of London—we likewise grant this same right to them; and, so that it may remain firm and unshaken for them hereafter, we strengthen it by episcopal authority and the attestation of our seal. [Col. 0925C] Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXXIV. TO THE SAME

G., by God’s grace bishop of London, to all parishioners and children of the same Church, beloved in the Lord: greeting, grace, and blessing.

[Col. 0925D] I trust, dearest friends, that you are not unaware how useful and necessary for the benefit of many is that hospital house built near the church of Blessed Bartholomew in London. There works of mercy are carried out, and the need of Christ’s poor is continually relieved with much care and diligence. Although in former times it has vigilantly devoted itself to works of this kind, now, through the Lord’s ministering grace, it shines more brightly than usual. Through the zeal of the good brethren Adam, G., and G., who recently committed and submitted themselves to the services of that house for Christ’s sake, it displays works of piety more abundantly than usual to all who resort there and now diffuses ever more widely around itself the fragrance of a good odour.

Although glory had already smiled greatly upon them and an abundance of temporal goods sufficiently met their desires, [Col. 0926A] these men left for Christ everything which had come to them either by hereditary right from their parents or which they had acquired through anxious labours by land and sea. They bestowed it upon the needs of Christ’s poor; and, in order to offer the Lord a more complete acceptable holocaust, they most humbly devoted themselves personally to serving them. They diligently provide food for the hungry, drink for the thirsty, coverings for the naked, rest beneath a roof and in a bed for the weary, and abundant mercy for the sick. They hope and await from the Lord the reward for their labour and service—that reward, certainly, which he himself has promised to those who love him.

Since we do not doubt that their life and works are pleasing to the Lord, we earnestly petition you all to love more affectionately the house in which they continually serve the Lord, and confidently entrust to them—or to those whom they appoint—your alms, to be faithfully disbursed through their hands for the common good of Christ’s poor. [Col. 0926B] To all who, by the Lord’s inspiration, give anything from their resources to that house in support of works of mercy, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, we remit twenty days from the penance imposed upon them, and, with the Lord supplying our confidence, make them participants in the prayers and good works performed both in our Church and in theirs. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXXV. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0926C]

G., by God’s grace bishop of London, to the archdeacons, deans, priests, and all parishioners and children of the same Church, beloved in the Lord: greeting and the fullness of every grace.

Since all holy places in which the relics of the saints have been deposited by the holy devotion of the faithful await their blessed octave and ought to be venerated, exalted, and reverently enlarged by pious gifts of good things, no one can doubt that this place above all ought to be celebratedly adorned with the services of the highest devotion: the place in the middle of the Valley of Jehoshaphat, between Mount Zion and the Mount of Olives, granted as the burial-place of the blessed Mother of the Lord and provided from eternity for the service of her humanity. [Col. 0926D] In memory of her, who, as we believe, was also carried bodily from there into heaven by the hands of angels, it ought by every means to be honoured.

Act therefore, dearest friends; comply with these saving admonitions. Receive with joyful minds the messengers of the blessed Mother of the Lord, as though sent from her side; rejoice at their coming; and, as cheerful givers ought, confidently place in their hands something from what the Lord has bestowed upon you. Thus, through them, you may suitably send it to the blessed Mother of the Lord, to adorn her burial-place and to defend with your gifts from the rage of unbelievers the place which her Son, her Lord Jesus, foresaw for himself, so that he might ascend thence to himself.

For those who, complying with our admonitions, contribute something of their own to this cause, trusting in the patronage of the blessed Mother of the Lord, we remit twenty days if they are under penance of seven years or more; if they are bound by a lesser number, we remit ten days. [Col. 0927A] Farewell in Christ.

## LETTER CCXXXVI. TO THE SAME

G., by God’s grace bishop of London, to all parishioners and children of the same Church, beloved in the Lord: greeting, grace, and blessing.

The bearers of this letter are messengers of the sick persons of Berceram’. Setting before you their need through these messengers, they devoutly beg that, out of reverence for God, you assist them and share from the resources bestowed upon you by divine mercy some benefaction, as the Lord inspires you, for the relief of their want. [Col. 0927B] We join our own petitions to theirs, asking and exhorting you in the Lord to open your hearts to Christ’s poor and, while you are able and life remains to you, to honour the Lord in his members. Recall that he will say to his own at the end: “What you did to one of the least of mine who believe in me, you did to me” (Matt. 25). Keep this before your eyes and fulfil it in deed, so that what you give here to Christ’s poor out of reverence for him may be received back a hundredfold in the life to come (Matt. 19).

To those who comply with our admonitions and assist them in some way, for Christ’s sake, in sustaining life, trusting in his mercy, we remit ten days from the penance imposed upon them. [Col. 0927C]

## LETTER CCXXXVII. TO THE SAME

G., by God’s grace bishop of London, to the archdeacons, deans, and all prelates of churches established in the London diocese, beloved in the Lord: greeting, grace, and blessing.

A lamp is not needed in daylight, and when something is clear by its own nature, it is unnecessary to establish it by witnesses or testimony. How great are the endeavours of charity, the aids of piety, and indeed the services of every kind of humanity which the holy Jerusalem hospital—that is, the holy house of the Hospital—bestows upon poor pilgrims of Christ and all suffering need, has long ago become known to the world from the evidence of events themselves. [Col. 0927D] Hence faith is now owed in this matter not to our testimony, but rather to the truth universally known. This venerable place, distinguished by the excellence of its merits, has deserved to be adorned with numerous privileges from both royal and priestly authority.

Following with due veneration in the footsteps of our fathers and prelates, we send to you, under the testimony of our letters, the bearers of this letter, the messengers and agents of that religious house. With all the devotion we can command, we commend them to your favour, asking and exhorting you in the Lord and enjoining you for the remission of your sins that, whenever they come among you to collect the alms of the faithful, you kindly receive them as pious ministers of the work, mercifully assist and promote them in help and deed, and, according to the lord pope’s exhortation and the privileges granted to them, show them in all things the reverence due.

You should also diligently admonish those subject to you to enter this fraternity and, once entered, faithfully keep it to the end, knowing that those who make themselves helpers of good works cannot fail to share in their fruit. [Col. 0928A] We establish that all who, for love of God and Christ’s poor, join themselves to this fraternity and complete its annual observance, as is customary, shall participate in the prayers and all benefits of the Church entrusted to us by God. To our parishioners, however, toward whom we are especially indebted—namely, penitents who have confessed their sins and keep this association with due devotion—we mercifully remit forty days from the satisfaction imposed upon them if they are under penance of seven years or more; if less, twenty days. [Col. 0928B]

## LETTER CCXXXVIII. TO THE PARISHIONERS OF ST PAUL’S

G., by God’s grace bishop of London, to all parishioners and children, clerics and laypeople, of the church of the Blessed Apostle Paul, beloved in the Lord: greeting, grace, and blessing.

Writing to your charity, most beloved, we at once recall to your memory the blessed Apostle Paul, with this purpose: that, for reverence and favour toward our Lord Jesus Christ and His Apostle, you may look to his Church and, with kindly devotion, assist its need—which has become sufficiently known to all—as the Lord inspires you. Though it was founded long ago and has already been built in great part by your alms, it requires and consumes such expenditures that, because we cannot supply them ourselves, unless your kindness brings aid, we shall henceforth despair and refuse to make provision for it. But since what unity strives for in vain is often effectively accomplished by a multitude, if we have you as helpers we conceive a good hope that in your days you may see a work long prolonged completed, the Lord mercifully setting His hand to it through you.

Act, therefore, and render devoted service to your patron and excellent advocate, blessed Paul, so that, by building him a house on earth, you may through his intercession obtain a blessed dwelling in heaven. Keep this, I ask, before your eyes: your patron and apostle Paul laboured more than all the apostles. In order to cleanse the world from the error of unbelief, he was once stoned for Christ, scourged five times, beaten with rods three times, and, after innumerable dangers endured on land and sea, at last suffered a glorious passion for Christ at Rome, being put to death by the sword (II Cor. XI). You ought to rejoice in such a patron and exult in so great an advocate. Although he planted churches throughout the world and illuminated the world by faith, nowhere on earth, as we have heard, was an episcopal see established for him except here among you, where a Church was founded in his honour and perpetual remembrance and raised to episcopal dignity, the Lord mercifully and especially providing this for you. [Col. 0929A]

You therefore have the blessed Apostle Paul as bishop of your souls. He received this office especially from the hand of the Lord: that while you live in the flesh he may protect and defend you by his holy prayer, and, when you have put off the flesh, may lead you to the throne of the Father. I shall use his own words to you. For he says: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a man sows, that shall he also reap” (Gal. VI). Hear your master; hear and accept sound counsel:

> “You can now sow what you may receive in eternal life. It is now winter; now is the time for casting seed. If the final hour closes your eyes, it will no longer be time for sowing. When the bridegroom has shut the door behind him, the cry of the foolish virgins will then be vain.”

Let us therefore hear our bishop thus exhorting us: “Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all” (ibid.). The present time of mercy presses upon the time of injustice. Whoever does not show mercy now should then expect justice from the Lord. Therefore, beloved, as you turn to yourselves, attend to your beginning, consider your course, and look ahead to your end. First the narrowness of the maternal womb enclosed you; afterward this life received you naked and bringing nothing into this world except sin; next the narrow dwelling of the grave will confine you; and at the last there will undoubtedly receive you either the breadth of hell—God forbid!—or the height of heaven. [Col. 0929B] Beyond expression for a human being in this life are both the misery below in hell and the blessed glory above in heaven. What has been prepared on either side for the elect and the reprobate surpasses speech.”

Let your discernment therefore act, beloved, so that, as your bishop and Apostle Paul admonishes, you may avoid the way of hell and, by living justly and holily, attain the joys of heaven. Your bishop admonishes you through us to keep the vessels of your bodies clean and honourable, lest by living shamefully you drive away from yourselves the Holy Spirit, who claims these as His temple. Devote yourselves to works of mercy, lest, if these are omitted—God forbid!—you experience on that day from the Lord judgment without mercy, in words all too severe (James II). [Col. 0929C]

Turn the eyes of compassion toward the Church of blessed Paul, your father and bishop; and, each of you conferring upon it benefits both yearly and finally at the end of your life, bind him most closely to yourselves by the benefits you render, so that he may watch over your protection and salvation and obtain for you from the supreme Giver, the Lord Jesus, a hundredfold restoration in eternity of the little which you now give in time. To all, moreover, who contribute anything of their own yearly and at their death toward the building and maintenance of the Church of the blessed Apostle Paul, if they are burdened with a penance of seven years or more, we, trusting in the mercy of Jesus Christ the Saviour and of that blessed Apostle himself, remit forty days each year; and we permit them to attend divine services within the walls of the church, except that in each seven-year period they shall remain outside for one Lent and thus complete their fasts. [Col. 0929D]

Since in the celebration of masses lies our highest holy salvation, with the consent of our entire synod and by firm and certain promise we decree that for all who have undertaken and observed this fraternity, each priest throughout the whole diocese of blessed Paul shall sing thirty masses: fifteen for those still in the flesh, and fifteen for those who have died. In the Church of blessed Paul itself, likewise, with the consent of our whole chapter, we decree that two masses shall be celebrated every week: one for the living and the other for brethren already deceased. We further decree that, if any brother of the Church of blessed Paul, as often happens because of sins demanding it, is overtaken by death and falls into a case for which burial in sacred places is customarily denied to the dead, he shall nevertheless be received as a brother and helper of the Church of blessed Paul and buried in a sacred place. [Col. 0930A]

And lest you suppose that your generosity and this free gift may ever be turned into an obligation for you, by this present writing we absolve all from every necessity and customary practice of giving anything, so that nothing of this kind may be demanded from you as though owed; but what has been freely given may be repaid to you a hundredfold by the Lord on that day. Amen.

## LETTER CCXXXIX. TO THE SAME PERSONS

G., by the grace of God Bishop of London, to all the parishioners and children of the Church of the blessed Paul, beloved to him in the Lord, greeting, grace, and blessing.

[Col. 0930C] That holy city Jerusalem cries out to you, beloved, in which our Lord Jesus Christ by His death delivered you from everlasting death. The Lord’s tomb cries out to you, that most holy place from which the Lord Jesus, rising on the third day after conquering death, confirmed us in faith and hope of resurrection and eternal salvation. All those holy places cry out to you, which the Lord long ago frequented in His bodily presence and marvellously illuminated with signs and miracles in order to call us back from the error of unbelief. These places, splendidly liberated and rescued from pagan power by the labour of Christ’s faithful, tremble at falling once again into the hands and power of those same pagans.

The holy places mourn the lamentable downfall of their princes: some have been slain by the sword and others carried into captivity; and that holy land, now without a defender, lies exposed as prey to unbelievers and enemies of Christ’s cross unless the Lord soon sets His hand to it. [Col. 0930D] Our beloved brethren, the Knights Templar, bear this burden. For the defence of the holy places and of the faithful Christians dwelling there, they are prepared to expose themselves to every danger and even to undergo death itself for Christ and for the salvation of their brethren. Your discernment does not fail to know how great the resources needed to repel that innumerable multitude must be.

Therefore the entire Eastern Church implores your compassion: since you cannot aid it by your bodily presence, assist it by making a gift of your resources through the hand of its defenders, namely the Knights Templar, and remove from it its imminent dangers by the help of fraternal love. [Col. 0931A] The lord pope exhorts your charity in this matter; we also exhort you, beloved in Christ. To all who undertake their fraternity and, yearly and at their death, contribute to them—as the Lord inspires them—at our prayer and admonition, we grant the suffrages of our Church’s prayers; and, by the authority granted us by the Lord, we remit forty days each year from their imposed penance while they remain in that fraternity. We wish you well, beloved in the Lord.

## LETTER CCXL. TO ROBERT, ARCHDEACON OF ESSEX

GILBERT, by the grace of God Bishop of London, to his beloved ROBERT, Archdeacon of Essex, greeting, grace, and blessing.

Consider, I pray, most beloved, how far away you have gone, how much labour and weariness you have undertaken out of love for learning alone; and take care diligently that, with grace cooperating, you may at some time bring us fruits worthy of so great labour. Let not your days flow away while you can and while your suitable age permits it. Learn now what you may afterward teach, and gather into the storehouse of your mind what, when necessity demands, you may in due time distribute to many.

Nothing can suitably excuse a lack of diligence on your part: by the Lord’s gift your body is healthy and sound; you have the age for study, resources at hand, a place rich in the goods that you desire, an abundance of teachers, and the welcome company of companions. [Col. 0931C] Let love of study and the willing application of your mind be present, and you will be able to progress day by day; becoming far better than yourself, you will delight in your most pleasant labours.

Consider what it is to have spent time at Bologna and shamefully to be ignorant of those things for which that famous city has become distinguished. This second *Kiriath-sepher*, that is, “city of letters,” has deservedly been so called: by the subtlety of its supreme intellect it has sharpened a world made dull over so many ages, opened the treasures of the laws, and at last, through the vigorous force of study, brought the hidden things of wisdom powerfully into the light. I beg you, beloved, be ashamed to return from there ignorant of letters—God forbid!—and destitute of understanding, lest what has brought glory to almost all should bring disgrace and shame upon you. [Col. 0931D]

I am recalling Archdeacon Richard. If he remains longer, I fear that he may be taken away from our midst; you must bear his burdens, which, as soon as he comes, we shall lighten with the Lord’s help. We desire that you fare well and make progress in every way, most beloved.

## LETTER CCXLI. TO P., BISHOP OF NEVERS

To P., by the grace of God Bishop of Nevers, Brother G., minister of the Church of London: an affection of pious greeting, if not expressed in this little letter, yet conceived in the heart.

The Bishop of Évreux, our beloved brother, had informed both the Bishop of Salisbury and me that the Abbot of Pontigny had returned to France. Wishing, therefore, that the business of our absolution, entrusted by the lord pope to you and the aforesaid abbot, might be completed in our case, we hastily undertook the toil of travelling to you. As we were approaching Le Mans in all haste, we were recalled by an urgent return-order from the lord pope, who sent a rescript stating that the charge of our absolution had been imposed upon you and the Bishop of Beauvais. [Col. 0932A]

Since, therefore, the change in the person joined with you required a change in your plan, we immediately sent our messengers to the aforesaid bishop, bringing him the lord pope’s rescript and informing him of the day and place appointed for us by you. But since unforeseen accidents often thwart even the most diligent, and we are uncertain where or in what circumstances that bishop may be found, we earnestly offer prayers to your goodwill, to which we are indebted in many matters: wait at Sens for our messengers for two or three days beyond the time you had proposed, if delay in their arrival makes this necessary. They will bring you the aforesaid bishop’s answer. [Col. 0932B] For we shall make every effort to prevent this delay and, with the Lord’s help, meet you at the day and place appointed for us.

## LETTER CCXLII. TO WALTER OF NORWICH

You know, most beloved, that missiles foreseen do less harm, and that it is better to meet a danger long beforehand than, once the cause has been wounded, to deliberate far too late about seeking a remedy. Therefore, considering that our Father of Canterbury is most ready to pronounce a curse and is prepared to exercise against our lord the king and his realm, against us and the Churches entrusted to us, contrary to the form of the sacred canons, the power which he ought to have received for the building up and not the destruction of the Church, we have long since appealed to the apostolic hearing; and, by pursuing this appeal before the judges assigned to us, the Lord granting grace, the storm by which we feared to be shaken, up to [lacuna].

## LETTER CCXLIII. TO JOCELIN, BISHOP OF SALISBURY

While the Lord of Canterbury devises these evils against the commonwealth of this realm as far as he can, he particularly, as is said, sets us two apart as targets, upon whom he may first pour out his attacks and exercise a power for evil such as I do not remember ever having experienced through any benefit of my own. For he, it is said, has newly issued summonses calling the two of us by name into France, publicly threatening and declaring that he will issue against us a sentence of excommunication unless we appear before him in France as soon as possible.

Since I perceive that I am aggrieved in this, I have already publicly appealed against it to the Apostolic See. I have arranged to notify the Lord of Canterbury of this both by letter and through a messenger—namely one of my clerks—who, God willing, will set out next Friday. I have also taken care to inform your affection, so that, if you think fit to follow the same counsels, one of your clerks may be sent from your side to undertake the journey with him, so that they may comfort one another by shared counsel and mutual companionship. [Col. 0933A] If you have received anything more certain concerning this matter, please inform us at London, where I intend to remain from Friday of this present week until Wednesday of the following week. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXLIV. TO THE SAME PERSON

[G.], by the grace of God Bishop of London, to his venerable brother J., by the same grace Bishop of Salisbury, greeting which is now ours and which we hope for from the Lord.

Because vices are springing up in the Church of this realm and branches are growing in the Lord’s vineyard which must be cut down by the pruning-hook of more prudent judgment, it has seemed good to our Father Richard, by the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury, Primate of all England and legate of the Apostolic See, according to the ancient custom of the Fathers, to summon his brethren and fellow bishops and the other prelates of the Churches to a council. There, matters needing correction may, by the censure of shared counsel, either be wholly condemned or reformed for the better, the Lord supplying grace. [Col. 0933B]

Since it is recognized that summoning our brethren and fellow bishops to the council belongs to our charge, we have received his command to do so. Therefore, by his authority we command your brotherhood, and impose it upon you under obedience, that on the Sunday on which is sung “Sing unto the Lord a new song” (Ps. XCV), you shall be present in London to sit with him for the aforesaid purpose. In the meantime, with every care and diligence investigate the offences from which your diocese suffers, so that, once brought forward, they may be subject to correction and censure. By his authority we likewise enjoin you to make this matter known to the abbots, archdeacons, priors, and deans of conventual places in your diocese, and by his authority to summon them to appear before the lord legate in council at the appointed place and time. [Col. 0933C] Farewell.

## LETTER CCXLV. TO THE SAME PERSON

To the venerable lord and most beloved brother J., by the grace of God Bishop of Salisbury, Brother GILBERT, Bishop of London, greeting.

The woman in the Gospel rejoices when she finds the drachma which she had lost (Luke XV). We too should rejoice, because those whom we sent far away and in a manner lost, having at last sailed past the Scyllas of envious barking, we have received safe, sound, prosperous, and bringing good news, the Lord piously ordering all things. It seems to me, therefore, that it would be wise for us to hasten without any delay to the place appointed by the lord king, namely Argenton, so that there either we may await the king’s arrival or, if he orders us to come to him, we may have a more ready route from there further onward.

Communicate this to the Bishop of Chichester. If he thinks otherwise, please let him signify it to me by the returning messenger, lest he eat bread in idleness. [Col. 0934A] I wish you well in the Lord, most beloved.

## LETTER CCXLVI. TO THE SAME PERSON

To the venerable lord and most beloved brother J., by the grace of God Bishop of Salisbury, Brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting and the affection of love owed to a lord.

Few words readily persuade when the friendly kindness of the person addressed is inclined to listen; and because we fully place our hope in your favour, we earnestly offer prayers to your goodwill, beloved to us in the Lord. Please allow the benefice of twenty shillings which you granted my nephew in the church of Chilton to remain wholly his, lest, by taking anything from so small a matter, you render the matter itself diminished and in a sense unworthy of its donor. [Col. 0934B]

We do not wish your highness to be unaware that my nephew and his clerk W. have entered into an agreement, confirmed by the arrangement itself: W. is to pay him twenty annually and, by taking upon himself, is to bear all the burdens of that church which your moderation or that of your archdeacon shall impose. Therefore we again pray that, if according to custom you have taken fleece from the sheep, you may spare the lamb … still in its first year, until, by merciful grace, it is more abundantly clothed with wool. We wish you well in the Lord, most beloved brother in Christ.

## LETTER CCXLVII. TO THE SAME PERSON

To the venerable lord and most beloved brother J., by the grace of God Bishop of Salisbury, Brother G., minister of the Church of London: the gift which he considers greatest in his possession, himself.

As I hear, you have fulfilled the Gospel’s example: the fatted calf has been killed, the fattened fowls slain, and, with the son returned, you have celebrated the proper rejoicings. It remains for you to provide him with the first robe, shoes, and a ring, lest he feel that anything from the Gospel is lacking to his completeness. Moreover, since you intend to celebrate revels at Le Mans when the royal command has sounded to you, please summon me from Sées, from the festival of Ceres. We wish you well in the Lord, most beloved [fem.].

## LETTER CCXLVIII. TO ROGER, BISHOP OF WORCESTER, ON BEHALF OF THE PRIOR OF MALVERN

[Col. 0934D]

The Bishop of London to the Bishop of Worcester: may you, in the fullness of virtues and graces, please the Lord.

Trusting in the natural privilege of your goodness, whenever need arises and the matter requires it, I confidently have recourse to your goodwill and, never knowing rebuff, immediately receive the gift of grace answering my wish. Since I have very often experienced this already through the evidence of events themselves, I confidently break in upon the threshold of the favour to which I am accustomed, asking that you may hold Brother W.—whose learning is abundant for teaching and whose character is abundant for uprightness, whom, as I hear, you have now admitted into favour and whom by election of the brethren of Malvern you have made prior—dearer than what is already dear, for love of God and in consideration of my request. By protecting and honouring him as accords with your honour and benefits his humility, make both him and me, along with many others beside us, debtors to you for greater favour and service from this. [Col. 0935A] May your kindness long remain safe and sound, and persevere in the Lord, most beloved.

## LETTER CCXLIX. TO THE SAME PERSON

To his venerable brother and most beloved friend R., by the grace of God Bishop of Worcester, Brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting with the deepest affection of love.

To your inquiry, most beloved brother, I answer in charity what the charity that asked me concerning this matter answers: regarding the weavers whom you have apprehended and detained in your parish, who, as you state, hold erroneous opinions concerning certain articles of our faith, and whom not merely a bare avowal of blasphemy but also persistent assertion and obstinacy of purpose demonstrate to be heretics, I advise that they be held under strict and watchful guard until in some place a well-attended assembly of priests and other faithful persons is held for a need of the Church or business of the realm. There, after the grace of the Holy Spirit has been invoked, a common judgment may be issued concerning the common matter, able safely and sincerely to determine what ought to be done in this case. [Col. 0935B]

Meanwhile, keep them separately, lest they strengthen one another in evil by mutual conversations. Suitable men of seriousness, men of proven faith and skilled in the divine law and letters, should be assigned to their care and custody. They should visit them with the word of holy preaching, soften them by admonitions, terrify them with threats and fear of punishments, at times restrain them with lashes and scourges exercised with moderate severity, and in every way endeavour, as charity suggests, to recall them to the unity of the Church.

For these and similar remedies of ecclesiastical correction, which the examples of the saints set before us, are appropriate for us to try in charity when the salvation of subjects is at issue—we who hold among the people the name of father and the office of shepherd—lest we ever determine anything rashly to the destruction or peril of a brother’s salvation. For often those whom words do not move are advanced by blows, and what fear of punishment does not achieve, experience of punishments itself sometimes compels. Good is the necessity which either prohibits evils or compels better things. [Col. 0935C] By God’s grace, we must hope for both results through this course, if neither time for repentance is taken from them nor any opportunity for malice is left. May He who has endowed some more deeply and pours the Spirit in more abundant grace come to the aid of your desires with holier counsel. Farewell.

## LETTER CCL. TO THE SAME PERSON

To the venerable lord and most beloved brother R., by the grace of God Bishop of Worcester, Brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting and the deepest affection of love.

It is customary for prudent persons to seek counsel even in matters not doubtful. Your discernment wisely observing this custom, wished to ask us what we thought concerning those weavers who recently entered your diocese and attempted to cover and entangle it with the spider-webs which they had miserably woven; and, unless the Holy Spirit through you had opposed them, to render it foolish by wickedly oversowing tares. They preach to the populace the heresies conceived in their hearts and, when arraigned and admonished in law, do not fear to defend the same with brazen face.

Lest their speech creep into the depths like a cancer and entangle very many in a like error, we advise that they themselves be restrained under strict custody; and, lest compassion be lacking to duty, that they be visited frequently by your more honourable and prudent clergy and carefully admonished to turn their minds to repentance and the unity of the Church, and to change their hearts. The word of God is living and effective: through a suitable minister it swiftly changes dominion and immediately raises the sinner. [Col. 0936B]

But because evil conversations corrupt good morals, keep each one separately, lest, if they exchange words among themselves, they be encouraged in obstinacy and reject sound counsels. If neither holy affliction nor piously administered admonition gives understanding to their hearing, we advise that the final question of punishment—whether they should be punished, by what punishment they should be punished, and by what judge or person delivering them for punishment they should be punished—be reserved for a common assembly of our brethren and fellow bishops.

For this is a grave question, and one debated extensively by the holy Fathers and doctors of the Church. Some proclaim the Church’s gentleness and clemency, according to the saying, “The law of clemency is on her tongue” (Prov. XXXI), and the Lord’s words, “Neither do I condemn you” (John VIII). Others, lest many should perish, are undoubtedly inflamed by the piety of holy zeal for the punishment of such persons. [Col. 0936C] These recall that a frenzied son should be bound with tight bonds and kept thus. Others, declaring that what is committed against divine religion is carried as an injury against all, invoke for this public crime the Julian law of treason. Others, judging by precedents of this kind, decide that they should be burned. Others temper this severity with the judgment of blessed Augustine, who seeks that Donatists be corrected not by being killed but by lashes and punishments.

Therefore, because it is written that “he who judges hastens quickly to repentance,” we advise that this question be reserved for the common assembly of our brethren, so that, as there is, by God’s gift, one Church in this realm, so there may also be one and undivided judgment and action of all in such cases. We do not prejudge the sounder opinion, for we always desire you to pursue the better course. [Col. 0936D] We wish you well in the Lord, most beloved brother in Christ.

## LETTER CCLI. TO THE SAME PERSON

To his venerable brother and friend ROGER, by the grace of God Bishop of Worcester, Brother GILBERT, minister of the Church of London, greeting and the deepest affection of love.

Our beloved son, William of Northall, bearer of this letter, declares that he rests upon a considerable hope in you, which he long ago conceived from the promise of your generosity and favour. For he ought not to regard as void or ineffectual the word which he knows has been secured to him by your promise. Therefore, with him and on his behalf, we entreat your goodwill: when an opportunity given by the Lord arises, please fulfil the beneficence which you have proposed and promised, more readily in consideration both of him and, if you please, of our request, with such kindness toward him that you may satisfy both his desire and your own truthfulness. For what we say we owe to truth; what we promise, to faith. [Col. 0937A] Farewell.

## LETTER CCLII. TO THE SAME PERSON

To his venerable brother and friend R., by the grace of God Bishop of Worcester, Brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting and love.

[Col. 0937B] We are pleased that Master Frome has found with you the favour of which we learned from your writing, though more certainly from his own account. For, as he states in that same writing, you wish to be informed by us concerning the benefice which the prior and canons of Stodley are said to have conferred upon him—namely, what precisely and how much was assigned to him in our presence. We too desire that his justice in all things may abound in evidences for men, so that it can never be overthrown by any falsehood.

But such a tumult of business surrounds us that we can scarcely attend to our own affairs, much less gather together with the precision you request those of another person, which are so remote in both place and time. But if witnesses are not lacking—persons whose evidence ought to be trusted more than [mere] testimonies—if the prior and canons, from whose act the land-benefice arose, do not revoke it, and if the other things necessary for the case are available and support it at home, why is our attestation required? Why labour over superfluities? [Col. 0937C]

We ask therefore that your conscience may not be scrupulous against him because he does not bring our testimony. Even if we happen to remember the transaction, we do not recall the particular circumstances of the act which the form of a written instrument would require. Moreover, we commend our word to your affection: hold favourably, at our request, the man whom you have admitted to acquaintance and favour because of his own merits; and preserve his rights whole through your justice, so that you may make both him devoted to your services in consequence and us debtors to you for greater favour on his behalf. [Col. 0937D] Farewell.

## LETTER CCLIII. TO THE SAME PERSON

To his venerable brother R., by the grace of God Bishop of Worcester, Brother G., minister of the Church of London, greeting.

Your letter, which I most recently received concerning the chapel of Saint Michael through the hands of a most untrustworthy bearer, has brought me unexpected thanks full of ingratitude. What have I done to deserve your brotherhood’s anger against me, that your appeal should break forth against my person, that I should be called to lawsuits and labours? Do you render me these thanks because you remember that I have kindly maintained your interests? Could the statement of our mediator—or rather, your liar—have persuaded you concerning me that I either usurp what is yours by right or, God forbid, would in any way consent to one who usurps it? It is not right to form so quickly a mistaken judgment about the character of a friend.

That messenger and agent of yours appealed against me and against my Church in the case which you call yours. But you, as you write and assert in writing, propose to pursue the same appeal. By your own authority you revoke the postponement granted us by the very first appellant until Quasimodo Sunday, and restrict the term for the appeal to Invocavit Sunday. [Col. 0938A] Since this results in a burden and prejudice to our side, we ask you, if you please, to desist. But if you persist, so that that restriction of the appeal may not stand, as I earlier appealed orally, so now I have appealed in writing, appointing Ascension Day as the term of our appeal.

You also demand *apostoli* from me. What confusion of affairs is this? You acknowledge as judge the one from whom you seek *apostoli* [letters certifying an appeal], but choose as adversary the person against whom you issue written pleadings of appeal. Your prudence ought to have known that no one ought to write himself as party in a testament, in *apostoli*, or in public instruments; for no one can be judge, witness, or public official in his own case. You also ask that I reform the condition of the aforesaid chapel as a duty of my office. First I must be instructed whether I ought to exercise a judge’s office in a matter entirely removed from my jurisdiction by appeal, especially when you summon me in this matter as an adversary while nevertheless calling upon me as judge. [Col. 0938C]

Finally, the Church of London entreats you, and we likewise entreat you, that the wickedness of a liar may not have such influence with you that fraternal charity suffers a rupture between us. Hold this certain: we cannot and will not derogate in any respect from your right. If you do not trust our testimony in this matter, trust the truth, which, when more certainly investigated, will bear witness to you. But if it is necessary to pull the contentious rope, we say what Hannibal is recorded long ago to have said: “I accept,” Hannibal says; “I seek peace. If from this you grow insolent, on both sides there will be iron; on both sides human bodies.” We wish you well in the Lord, [Col. 0938D] most beloved brother.

## LETTER CCLIV. TO THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF LA CHARITÉ

G., by the grace of God Bishop of London, to his venerable brother and friend, the Prior of La Charité, and to the whole convent: greeting and the affection of sincere love.

How fully, brethren most beloved in Christ, we embrace you and your house in charity neither words can explain nor proofs of action demonstrate. Yet whatever belongs to you among us we do not consider alien to our care; we welcome your joys joyfully. If anything should happen otherwise—God forbid!—it does not fall upon you alone; we too bear it together with no alien affliction of mind. Whenever an opportunity arises for your advancement, or for the advancement of those whom you are certainly to promote, the devotion of charity by which we are bound to you undoubtedly does not permit us either to neglect it or idly to pass it by.

Accordingly, when the election of an abbot of Evesham was being discussed at Canterbury with an assembly of our brethren and fellow bishops, as well as other religious men who had come together to conduct ecclesiastical business, it was finally the unanimous inclination, following your counsel, although many others were tending elsewhere, that those to whom the election belonged should elect the Prior of Bermondsey, a special son of your Church, and that the others whose consent was expected in this matter should give their unanimous assent. [Col. 0939A]

Although his merits of character and honourable conduct among us were reported as holy and praiseworthy, we rejoiced not a little that our recommendation had been received so favourably: we judged that a man coming forth from the discipline of your school was worthy of the pastoral office of a dignity so great. Now our wishes concur. What we approve, our lord the King of England approves; the Lord of Canterbury confirms the same by his authority. Now the attention of all of us is directed toward you, that you may set the final hand to the work; for its completion depends upon your decision.

Therefore, for the Church of Evesham, long bereft and now seeking and awaiting its chosen man, we earnestly offer prayers to your brotherhood beloved to us: give your assent to his election, grant it the pastor whom it has chosen for itself, and bring with kindly favour to effect what we have begun in pious devotion for the honour of God and the benefit of Holy Church. [Col. 0939C] Farewell.

## LETTER CCLV. TO A., ABBOT, AND THE CHAPTER OF CIRENCESTER

G., by the grace of God Bishop of London, to his venerable brother and most beloved friend in Christ, A., by the same grace Abbot of Cirencester, and to the whole convent of that place: greeting and sincere love in the Lord.

The bearer of this letter, Brother A., left you some time ago, perhaps at the prompting of a spirit not good. But now he returns, as we hope, recalled by the Holy Spirit; he knocks at the door of your mercy, and, in support of the wretched and anxious cause which he pleads, he employs our advocacy with you, so that by our intervention he may more readily obtain the favour of which he distrusts his own ability to obtain.

Having long experienced, he has recoiled from the severity of your Order, and has recognized himself unequal to so great a burden and to observances so strict. Therefore he knocks and asks; he invites us also to pray for him with tears, and urges us strongly to this end: that, with your permission, he may henceforth serve, free and released, under obedience to the brethren of the Hospital. The brethren of the Hospital themselves seek and earnestly desire this all the more, since they have long found the said brother—though unequal to your profession—useful for their own purposes. In this matter we too, if there is still room for it, beseech you: having compassion upon the brother’s weakness, although what we ask is not lofty, nevertheless hear our pious desire for him; and, having given letters of dismissal, assign him free and released to those for whom he is suitable, lest, God forbid, by rejecting the simplicity of us all you confound him to the evil of despair. Farewell.

## LETTER 256. TO THE SAME PERSONS

G., by the grace of God Bishop of London, to his venerable brother and dearest friend A., by the same grace Abbot of Cirencester, and to the whole chapter of that church: greeting, grace, and blessing.

By the office laid upon us in the Church of God—which, by His permission, we have undertaken to govern in some portion belonging to Him—we are compelled to provide with due solicitude for the honour of the Church, to which it is espoused. Therefore, because the reputation of your manner of life, by the very holiness of its merit, has spread far and wide among all, it has entered into the counsel of the Church of the Holy Trinity in London—as we believe, the Lord inspiring this, and the Church over which we preside consenting—that they should unanimously elect as their prior the prior of your church, namely Master Osbern, in whom learning abounds for teaching and character for uprightness; and all have unanimously desired that he be granted to them as father and pastor.

Since honourable counsels must always be assisted and promoted, we earnestly offer prayers to your goodwill, dear to us in the Lord, that you may answer the desires of the aforesaid brethren in deed; and that, releasing him canonically from your obedience for the honour of God and of your Church, and appointing him henceforth to obey the Church of London, you may promptly and freely grant him to the said brethren, without delay—which often brings danger to undertakings—to undertake and carry out the care of their house. Thus you will have the whole body of the Church of London henceforth bound to your service. We wish you health in the Lord, dearest friends.

## LETTER 257. TO STEPHEN, ABBOT OF CLUNY

To the venerable lord and dearest father Stephen, by the grace of God Abbot of Cluny, Brother G., minister of the Church of London: the joy of salvation, and whatever dutiful service charity can render him.

I rejoiced wholly in the Lord, dearest friend, and was filled with spiritual gladness when I heard that our mother, the Church of Cluny, has at last found relief in you, and has chosen you for herself as father and lord with such foresight and, as I hope, so salutarily and happily. For, with you as guardian of the flock entrusted to you, the pastures of life cannot fail it: from boyhood you have, so to speak, consecrated your breast to the Lord as a storehouse of Holy Scripture and a fragrant chamber of virtues.

Your land will not lament after you with a cry, since it will be abundantly watered by the streams of teaching; and, that it may yield a full harvest of virtues, it will be incessantly urged by the examples of virtues set forth in you toward things holy and highest. Blessed is the community whose merits of virtue made it due that it should, through the consolation of so great a father, find relief from the tribulation of evils and grief, and that the storm which it had long endured should be changed for it into a breeze by the watchful care of a good householder.

I confess, dearest in Christ, I confess that the sight granted me from heaven of your person, and your conversation, proved no small incentive to virtue for me. Hence I deem blessed those who are always with you, who constantly accompany you, to whom it is granted to possess this mirror of virtue, by which they may always advance to better things. A man’s face, gait, and dress, as Scripture records, proclaim what he is; and those who attend to these things in you may readily be transformed into a perfect man.

Though these things were seen only for a moment, they have nevertheless sunk deeply into my mind, so that at times, passing by contemplation of you into a certain new man, I seem in some way to have passed beyond myself. Therefore I embrace you absent with the whole arms of charity—I who most deeply desire to see you present and to venerate you with devoted and due services.

But since charity sometimes makes one presumptuous, the end of this letter will contain this request: that you may mercifully hear our brother, Lord Thomas, Prior of Lantone, concerning his release, for which he presses strongly; and, after our brother Robert of Broi has been substituted in his place, make him a debtor to your holiness in service, and me, if possible, in fuller favour. May my lord and dearest father in Christ prosper.

## LETTER 258. TO R., ARCHDEACON OF COLCHESTER

[Col. 0941C]

Gilbert, by the grace of God Bishop of London, to his beloved R., Archdeacon of Colchester: greeting, grace, and blessing.

I received the letter sent to me by you with great eagerness of joy; but, having looked it over a little, I read through it with a mind undoubtedly distressed. I had hoped that glad news would be announced to me, and behold, what is reported brings me grave sorrow. I grieve for the most noble young man who prematurely fulfilled the lot of death. I fear a similar event in your case, since, as I hear, illness has already attacked you in several ways.

Therefore I direct you, and in directing command you, to put aside every pretext: if you find the situation at Bologna suspicious, or in even a small degree adverse to your health, leave and flee at once, to save your soul, and do not fail to hasten your return to us. But answer for whatever obligations you know yourself to be encumbered with, and, coming quickly to us, hasten to settle them and discharge what is owed. Know that I am still remaining in Normandy, and that I alike await and desire your return to me. Farewell, dearest friend.

## LETTER 259. TO H., ABBOT OF ST EDMUND’S

G., by the grace of God Bishop of London, to his venerable brother and friend H., Abbot of St Edmund’s, and to the convent: greeting.

We wish matters carried out in our presence to be strengthened with such firmness that arrangements made with prudence cannot be overthrown by any perversity of malicious persons. Therefore we make known to your whole community that, in the presence of many persons, we produced before Reginald, clerk of Coton, the authentic instrument in which the agreement between you concerning the church of Coton is inserted.

Asking R. himself before all whether he gave his assent to all that had been written, we received from his answer that everything pleased him according to the tenor of the instrument. And, for abundant precaution, at the request of the same H., we received his oath, upon the sacred Gospels having been touched, that he would observe inviolably and in good faith what had been agreed and entered in writing. Therefore, lest what has been done so solemnly should later be called into doubt, we confirm it by the attestation of the present writing and the affixing of our seal. Witnesses: [lacuna].

## LETTER 260. TO H., ABBOT OF GLOUCESTER

[Col. 0942B]

Gilbert, by the grace of God Bishop of London, to his venerable brother and dearest friend H., by the same grace Abbot of Gloucester: greeting and the due service of brotherly charity.

We cannot recall without tears the death of our dear Master Walter. In his passing we have cause for common grief, since the Lord’s hand weighed upon us and we lost, in the very flower of his most welcome youth, a clerk and most faithful friend shared by us all. What good things have been taken from us with him, and how many holy consolations withdrawn, we can indeed experience but cannot express in few words.

May your holy prayer and that of our brethren assist him, we beg, so that the Lord may be pleased to admit him, who has been taken from us, to the fellowship of His own. When he was at the point of death, he begged us to commend to your goodwill his only surviving brother, Wigod, the bearer of this letter. Therefore we earnestly offer prayers to your kindness, dear to us in the Lord, that out of love for God, in consideration of our request, and in view of the petition of a friend in his final wish, you may receive him into your protection and permit no worsening whatever of his condition. Rather, let the increase of your mercy and charity make good for him the loss which he presently suffers. We wish you health in the Lord, dearest friend.

## LETTER 261. TO MATTHEW, ARCHDEACON OF GLOUCESTER

[Col. 0942D]

To Matthew, Archdeacon of Gloucester: greeting.

This is the question which you set forth and require to be answered: whether you ought to admit the woman in question to the oath adjudged to her, or whether you ought by law to allow her to undergo the ordeal of red-hot iron, as she promised under compulsion from her husband, who threatened her with death.

Various cases frequently arise. A woman is sometimes caught in the act; at other times, though not caught, she is nevertheless accused as a suspected offender. The Law of Moses stoned the woman caught in the act (Leviticus 20); the law of jealousy tested the suspected woman (Numbers 5). The suspected woman drank the most bitter waters into which the priest had put curses; these waters did not harm the innocent woman but immediately burst open the guilty adulteress. The law of rulers punished the adulterer and adulteress, and punishment in many forms threatened unhappy mortals, whose condition is precarious.

Thanks be to the Lord Jesus, who, renewing all things, changed them for the better. By mixing the wood of the Cross with the waters of Marah, He tempered the harsh and bitter things of the Law. Here He freed the woman brought to Him, caught in the act and guilty of sin, and transformed those hard stones of the Law, of which it is said: “For thy servants have taken pleasure in her stones” (Psalm 101). For our stones are rebuke, correction, and the urging of the sinner to tears, groans, confession, and manifold satisfaction. With these the adulteress is well stoned when she dies to sin and is inwardly made alive by Him who says: “Neither do I condemn thee; go, and sin no more” (John 8). From the death of the soul which she had incurred, she is raised to newness of life.

Accordingly, when a good husband sees his wife being stoned, he himself ought to die with her who is dying, to weep with her who is mourning, and to give of his own means so that the penitent woman may have at hand what may redeem the sin and relieve her in suffering necessity. Thus they may be found to be two not merely in one flesh but also in one spirit.

But if she is only suspected, then, in order that suspicion may be removed and peace restored to the husband, the prescribed oath will suffice, since Paul declares an oath to be the end of every controversy (Hebrews 6). For if under compulsion she promised anything, far be it from an ecclesiastical judge to admit what judges of the secular courts know must be rejected. For that which is done or said by reason of force or fear he does not hold valid; and according to Pope Alexander, if anything has been extorted from anyone by force, fear, or fraud, it is valid to no one’s prejudice or harm. Farewell.

## LETTER 262. TO WILLIAM, ABBOT OF READING

G., by the grace of God Bishop of London, to his venerable brother and friend W., by the same grace Abbot of Reading: greeting and affection.

I give thanks to your goodwill, which not only does not cease to provide for me and to watch over my interests, but has also taken care, with brotherly charity, to warn and fortify me concerning those things which are maliciously contrived against me. The one remedy which all the sacred canons prescribe against every extraordinary oppression—the aid of appeal—I have now publicly invoked against the summonses already issued, as they say, and against the plots proposed by the Lord of Canterbury.

And lest any prejudice be done concerning my person or possessions, my rank or honour, I have taken care to protect myself by invoking the authority of the Apostolic See, placing complete confidence in divine grace and in the clemency of the holy Roman Church. If anything outrageous is done against us in these matters, it will, I trust, redound rather to their confusion than to our punishment. Farewell.

## LETTER 263. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0944A]

G., by the grace of God Bishop of London, to his venerable brother and friend William, by the same grace Abbot of Reading: greeting and the affection of sincere love.

We received the letter of your affection, which filled us with joy all the more truly because it answered our concern more certainly regarding your condition and safety. For the prodigal rumour of reports which had flown ahead of your messenger announced many various and inconsistent things to us about your departure, your stay upon the shore, the storm, and the dangers. Therefore fear, the worst prophet in doubtful matters, distracted us anxiously: we knew well, from frequent experience, that navigation is often dangerous and always uncertain.

But now, having received news of your health and safety, we give thanks to divine grace on your behalf, since it did not permit you to be endangered amid such dangers. We greatly desire conversation with you; but necessity drawing us elsewhere prevents us from meeting you before the day of your arrival. We intend, however, then to be in London; and if it should be suitable and pleasing for you to proceed as far as Fulham, we ask that this be reported to us as quickly as possible by a returning messenger. We wish you health in the Lord, dearest friend.

## LETTER 264. TO THE ABBOT OF RIEVAULX

The Bishop of London to the Abbot of Rievaulx.

[Col. 0944C] The more cheerfully your reputation and that of your house are proclaimed, the more you must take care that what is held by common opinion is not darkened by the counsel or deed of any of your brethren. The sons of Bricthmer of Taunton, formerly your brother and benefactor, complain greatly that you refuse to pay them a large sum of money owed to their father, although they have already repeatedly demanded it; nor do you answer their father’s deserts with deeds, as your religious profession would require.

They would long ago have sought letters from the lord king concerning this, had not our concern delayed them out of reverence for you and your house. We therefore earnestly beseech your goodwill that, for the love of justice and in consideration of our request, you either pay them what they justly demand, or, if they demand what is not due, do not take it ill to establish this by legal process.

## LETTER 265. TO F., ABBOT OF SAUMUR

G., by the grace of God Bishop of London, to his venerable lord and dearest brother F., by the same grace Abbot of Saumur: greeting and the affection of sincere charity.

Dearest brother, we greet the beginning of your office with much goodwill of heart, wishing that this praiseworthy beginning of your advancement may always be guided in a happy course and, with the Lord mercifully lending His hand, may at last be completed in a blessed end. We rejoice indeed and are filled with full gladness of mind as we observe the hand of the Lord leading you in much glory and continually drawing you from good things to better.

For it is this hand which tore you away from the enticements of this world; which, leading you through the steps of virtues, and using the words with which it is accustomed to address the humble so that they may ascend higher, raised you—soberly—from the lowly place you had chosen, through the agreement of many good men and, as we hear, the unanimous election of your brethren, to the summit of pastoral office. In this we give thanks for prevenient grace; for grace that follows, we offer prayers: that, placed on high in the house of the Lord, you may shine forth as a mirror of virtue, and by honourable conduct show the way of virtue to lovers of virtue, as a leader truly going before them toward life.
