This is done by Him who, the higher He raises His own in dignity, the more firmly and securely establishes them in humility; and who brings to perfection those things which are brought forth in all through the charity diffused by His Spirit. It would be easy to suggest more to your brotherhood in this manner; but, confident in the anointing which fully teaches you inwardly, we entrust your sails to Him whom we know with certain truth to bring His own to harbour after the storm of this world has been sailed through, while the sweet breeze of the Holy Spirit happily fills the folds of their minds.

We turn our pen to that matter for which we have undertaken the present necessity of writing to you. We set forward three requests, in which we ask with the whole affection of our mind and with the earnest entreaty of a pleading soul to be heard by your serenity: at present we act as it were on an embassy for three persons. They are our beloved son Baderun of Munemne, [lacuna], a benefactor of your church; and our dearest friend in Christ, Robert [of the New Castle] of Casteillunarco, your humble and devoted friend.

For Baderun grieves that the former benefits of his parents, and those later bestowed by himself upon the Church, have been reduced to such nothing that he has fallen away from your heart not merely as though dead, but has also, by no merits of his own as he hopes, incurred your anger, to his complete distress. If he wishes anything, he complains that you do not wish it; if he asks anything, he is ashamed that you turn away your face. He would rather never have entered into friendship with your house than have lost in this fashion a friendship acquired by many services.

Therefore, if there is anything which clouds your serenity against him, we ask that this pardon be granted to us, that this cloud may be wholly dispelled by the breath of the Holy Spirit, and that so great a friend of your house be received into full favour and supported by gentle and honourable replies; we ask, command, and enjoin this. For it is expedient for your church that [lacuna] should be alienated from the favour of one whose generosity has conferred ample benefits upon it.

Return our prior—already for too long detained in your house, distinguished by merits of virtue—to us without delay, no obstacle on your part intervening, asking also for us, as a friend, concerning whom [the text is incomplete] in every respect well.

From this point the course of our discourse flows on to our dearest brother Robert of the New Castle. When we remember him, our mind is drawn in different directions. For if he is a friend, why do we so greatly desire that his presence be removed far from us? Yet one ought rather to wish that a friend live absent than die present. In the subarctic region, under the narrow northern zone, beneath the northern axis, all things are hostile to him: cold air, perpetual ice, water useless and drinkable only when boiled, supply complete cause and material for the fever by which he is continually afflicted.

Therefore we offer prayers to your kindness, dear to us, that you may receive him with favour as though returned from exile; and, lest, weighed down by the yoke of obedience, he should fail while groaning more sadly, permit him, while dwelling with you, to enjoy the air whence he drew more healthily his origin and birth. We have confidently entered the camp of friendship and, though we ask much, we believe that we ask nothing offensive to you. By hearing us in these matters, your favour will securely claim our services for itself, not only through old friendship but also through a recent benefit. May the Lord preserve your safety and success.

## LETTER 266. TO LAURENCE, ABBOT OF WESTMINSTER

[Col. 0946B] G., by the grace of God Bishop of London, to his venerable brother and friend L., by the same grace Abbot of Westminster, and to the convent of that church, beloved by him in the Lord: may you always be wise, understand, and provide for the last things.

Brothers, I have learned by the report of certain persons something which I have judged as useful as it is humble to bring to your notice through myself before it is communicated to a wider hearing. Between the church of St Paul and ourselves a small spark of new litigation has, it is said, been kindled. If it is not soon extinguished and breaks forth into flames, it will undoubtedly spread to the detriment of both parties.

For causes of even slight disagreement are accustomed to furnish fuel for most serious disputes. Unless they are checked at their very beginnings, through the zeal of the parties and the passage of time they often grow so strong that, after very great expense and immense labour, it is exceedingly difficult to bring parties long distrustful of each other back in any degree to the serenity of their former peace.

Therefore, since prudent examination is accustomed to measure the outcome of affairs, I address an earnest request to your brotherhood, dear to me in the Lord, and also offer paternal advice: do not seek an occasion of discord against your mother and brothers; do not strive to tear a daughter away from her mother’s embraces. Rather, by showing her the customary and due reverence, be willing to pass this short span of days with us in peace and unity of charity, disdaining with a certain holy nobility of mind to recoil, through an inconsiderate presumption, from the good of peace which has hitherto endured between the churches entrusted to us, on account of a slight and ignoble gain.

Indeed, the unanimous testimony of the whole surrounding neighbourhood proclaims that the church of St Margaret, concerning which this recent dispute has arisen, has from its earliest foundations until these days been subject to the Bishops of London and their archdeacons without contradiction or objection. No one in those parts is ignorant that in my own time it paid to R., Archdeacon, the customary and due cathedraticum. If, therefore, you withdraw twelve annual [units—apparently payments] from your mother, you will inflict grave dishonour upon her in a small matter and confer a certainly very slight benefit upon the common table from a trifling sum.

Therefore, yielding to useful advice, accept, if it please you, my counsel on this occasion: let the appeals on both sides be withdrawn; let any sentences issued against anyone be relaxed; permit the aforesaid money to be paid to the archdeacon; and allow everything to remain in the condition in which it stood at my departure. Do not, by withdrawing from your mother’s favour for a slight advantage, judge sweet and savoury that which has been retained for itself by your usurpation to her injury.

Thus you will be able to conciliate favour between us; thus you will have me ready and prepared for your service; thus the clear evidence of your own conduct will show more brightly than light that, in my humiliation, you have not rushed forward to the humiliation of the Church entrusted to me. “Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof” (Matthew 6). I am sufficiently burdened by the injury which oppresses me. If you add pain to pain and injury to injury, you will leave no one in doubt that you have little compassion for my misfortune.

Insofar as we can, we cannot [the text is corrupt] injury to ourselves; and if you persist in what you have begun, you will strongly spur us and all our people to repel the injury according to our strength. We desire you to prosper and to spare us in our tribulation, dearest friends.

## LETTER 267. TO KING HENRY

To his dearest lord, H., illustrious King of the English, Brother G., minister of the Church of London: the salvation which now is, and that which we hope for from the Lord.

While your presence, lord, protects us, every injury against us has wholly subsided. But in your absence we shall immediately experience the harm done to our peace. Your Excellency knows that, when we were still serving the Church of Hereford, you alone granted to us, with royal munificence and liberality, certain clearings of Malvern belonging to your crown.

We bestowed these upon four of our servants, who had for some time laboured faithfully with us in the business of that church, as a modest reward for their service; and from your grace we obtained your assent and confirmation in this matter. But our venerable brother, the Lord Bishop of Hereford, immediately after your departure expelled them from these same small possessions; and when he was asked about it, moved neither by reverence for your charter nor in any respect by our request, he showed himself wholly inexorable toward us.

Therefore, having recourse to the well-known protections of your clemency, we humbly beseech you that you may, if it please you, crown the many good things bestowed upon us with this further favour: command that William Folet, upon whom we have conferred a modest grant, and also the aforesaid servants, be reseised until your return of those possessions of which, after your departure, they were despoiled without hearing or judgment.

When divine grace has brought you back into your kingdom, hear in our presence the matters done by us, and correct with royal equity, as you please, whatever you find requiring correction. The total which we seek to have restored is not fully ten marks; although the condition of that church was improved, through your gift and our labour during the time in which we served it, to an income of fully one hundred marks. May God preserve your health for long years, beloved lord in Christ.

## LETTER 268. TO THE SAME

To his dearest lord, H., illustrious King of the English, Brother G., minister of the Church of London: greeting and the due service of devoted fidelity.

We believe, lord, that your Excellency is not unaware how the Lord of Canterbury has laid his hand heavily upon me and certain other of your faithful men and, as far as he could, has turned the spiritual sword against us in violation of public law by the right hand of iniquity. For this is a most familiar canon: that no one be judged precipitately or irregularly—that is, without being warned and convicted—and that a bishop should never excommunicate anyone until the cause for which the accused person is charged has been proved.

Since, therefore, he has departed from the law, we trust in the Lord that, in brandishing the sword against us, he has struck the air rather than inflicted upon us a spiritual wound either in body or soul. For we forestalled his blow by appealing to the lord pope, and the appeal made at the beginning of Lent wholly invalidated the sentence pronounced on Palm Sunday. For Pope Sixtus thus decreed:

> “Whenever a bishop considers himself oppressed by his metropolitan, or holds him suspect, he shall immediately appeal to the Roman See. While he requests to be heard by it, no one shall excommunicate him before the case has been concluded by the authority of the supreme pontiff. If anything is presumed otherwise, it shall be void and wholly without force.”

## LETTER 269. TO THE SAME

The Bishop of London to the king: greeting and the intimate affection of love from the very depths of his heart.

I delayed, lord, in writing to your Highness because I learned that the things done concerning the churches of your kingdom had been made known to you by messengers before I could write. But now, though late, I write and, for God’s mercy, humbly beg you not to give credence to those who disparage me, nor to put any faith in the monks of Canterbury in the malicious things which they say against me.

For they say that I aspire to the archbishopric of Canterbury and that, for this reason, I hinder in every way the elections which they make concerning others. He who is Truth itself knows that none of this is true. At my first promotion, at Cluny I was made prior in the Order; afterwards I was prior of the abbey of Ville. Then I was Abbot of Gloucester, afterwards Bishop of Hereford. From there I was translated to London. I confidently assert that I sought none of these offices, though, with God’s permission, I obtained each in succession.

Therefore in the secrets of my heart I say to the Lord my God that His grace is sufficient for me; and I say to you, my dearest lord, that your grace has most kindly granted me sufficient favour in these things. May the Lord turn this ambition away from me. May the Almighty turn you away altogether from any willingness to give assent to it.

But if I have in any degree hindered their elections, you may discern the reason from the following. First there was discussion of the Lord of Bayeux. Although this appeared burdensome to the bishops of your kingdom, I nevertheless induced them all, with the Lord’s help, to assent to him and to be ready to receive him. The monks alone rejected the man whom they knew you especially wished.

Afterwards there was discussion of the man of Bec. Although this appeared most burdensome to all the bishops of the kingdom, I nevertheless obtained, by much effort and exertion, that in assenting to him they should set aside their own preference. Finally recourse was had to the Abbot of Cerisy. Although this seemed not merely burdensome but most unworthy to the bishops, to all the abbots of your land, and to all persons of your kingdom, I nevertheless obtained at last—though amid the great anger and indignation of all—that, if the monks of Canterbury were willing to show the bishops of your kingdom even slight respect in the proclamation of the election, they should consent to him and allow the matter to be settled on these terms, lest your mind should be disturbed against them.

But they, arrogating everything to themselves and more harshly excluding all bishops both from counsel and from the election and from the proclamation of the election, compelled its further delay by employing excessive obstinacy, though they could then have obtained their aim by acting with some modesty.

In this matter, if it please you, provide for your honour, carefully considering what is more expedient for you: to ascribe everything to the monks, who are bound to you neither by homage nor by fidelity, or, in choosing the chief person of your kingdom, to attribute some respect to the bishops, who, bound to you either by homage or fidelity, are obliged by a double necessity to preserve your honour in God.

It would therefore be good, if it please you, that you moderate with the restraint and wisdom which you possess the harshness of the monks, who conceive so many designs from your humility; and that you recall their counsel to some person of your kingdom. Saving the right of both parties, concerning the first voice to be held in the election in the future when it shall be appropriate to address that question, arrange that the election itself be proclaimed jointly by the prior and one of the bishops, or in whatever other manner God reveals to you and your counsel. Thus, through your wisdom, when the condition of the Church has been pacified, you may wholly disperse, by the Lord’s granting grace, the cloud which still hangs over your kingdom from this disagreement.

## LETTER 270. TO THE SAME KING HENRY

The Bishop of London to the king: greeting and the devoted service of due fidelity.

We hope, lord, that those persons are worthy of your favour whom the Church of God, learning, and manner of life commend. Therefore we commend to your Excellency, with all the greater confidence, our clerk Ralph de Diceto, Archdeacon of the Church of St Paul, because we have long known by certain experience that he possesses an abundance both of learning for teaching and character for uprightness.

To these is added an undivided love and the complete devotion of his affection toward you: embracing you in his heart with the arms of charity, rejoicing in your honour and glory, he always desires happy success for you in the Lord, and, whenever opportunity offers, never ceases to urge those entrusted to him to obtain this for you from the supreme King.

As he has recourse to you in a necessity which has arisen for him, seeking nothing except what is due in law and equity, we entreat from our heart’s inmost affection that, out of reverence for God, in consideration of our request, his uprightness, and the fidelity shown and always to be shown to you, you may graciously hear him and, according to the wisdom given to you by God, ensure both justly and mercifully that the portion of his prebend which both apostolic authority and your royal authority grant and confirm for him may be restored to him in full.

## LETTER 271. TO THE SAME

To his dearest lord, Henry, illustrious King of the English, Brother Gilbert, minister of the Church of London: with Satan trampled beneath your holy feet, may you triumph happily in Christ.

We recently received, lord, a mandate of the lord pope ordering us to receive from our brethren and fellow bishops the payment of St Peter’s Pence and quickly transmit it to him through the messengers whom he sent to us. Since this depends wholly upon your favour and cannot be carried out except through you, we notify your Excellency of it, that you may, if it please you, write to your justices on this matter and order to be done whatever accords with your will.

We desire that holy divinity may possess your heart and so order and direct all your actions that you neither offend against God nor furnish the lord pope—whom we know you have greatly loved—with a just ground and matter for complaint against you or your kingdom.

Moreover, the day is approaching which we set for the appeal made to the lord pope. To pursue it, we must henceforth know more certainly your will and counsel. For, since weapons foreseen do less harm, we must fear that, if everything is deferred until the critical moment, each matter, being less foreknown and less carefully considered, will be settled less suitably than necessity requires. May the finger of God write upon your heart what ought to be done, and may His hand everywhere protect and guard us, lord most beloved in Christ.

## LETTER 272. TO THE SAME, CONCERNING ST PETER’S PENCE
Census due to Saint Peter, my lord, we have received, except for forty-two pounds from the bishopric of Lincoln and one hundred shillings from the bishopric of Ely, which we have not yet received. We have also long detained with us the lord pope’s agents—namely, eight merchants of Flanders—who lent him three hundred marks of silver at Rome, hoping to receive that same sum from the hand of your mercy. We had hoped to hear some word from your Highness through the dean of Waltham which might cheer both the lord [Col. 0951A] pope and his agents. Since this has not yet happened, we can detain them no longer. Yet we greatly fear that their return empty-handed may seriously prejudice your cause. In this matter your discretion will usefully determine what is expedient, what befits your honour, and what advances the salvation of your soul. Your faithful men who are with you, who desire in every respect the prosperity of your affairs, would wish your counsel in this matter to change, so that, by rendering to the lord pope what is his, you might have him not as an adversary in your concerns, but as wholly well-disposed and obliged to you. May the Lord make his face shine upon you, and always bring your affairs to a good conclusion, most beloved lord in Christ.

## LETTER CCLXXIII. TO THE SAME.

[Col. 0951B]

GILBERT, bishop of London, to HENRY, king of England: the affection of a devout greeting and the service of faithful obedience.

We have thought fit, my lord, earnestly to commend to your Highness our venerable brother, the bishop of Salisbury. We know him assuredly to be faithful to you, and we have recognized beyond doubt that with unfeigned charity he desires your success in all things. Therefore it will undoubtedly redound to the honour and glory of the royal majesty if you look graciously upon him and direct the eyes of royal kindness more attentively toward him. For he will send you a faithful clerk of yours, so that from his words and from the writings which he has in hand you may learn how solicitous the lord of Canterbury is concerning [Col. 0951C] him. At present he bears the burden of suspension; and, having already been summoned, he will shortly incur a sentence of excommunication—whether justly or unjustly, as we gather from the documents and plainly infer from preceding events—unless through you he escapes it. If such a sentence is pronounced against him, it will certainly bring disgrace upon him and, equally, alarm and disturbance to all persons in your kingdom. If your kindness summoned him to yourself, he would hasten to you; and, relying on your aid, he would, with the Lord’s help, most effectively avert this imminent danger.

Therefore, we ask with him who asks, and plead with him who pleads, that you may, if it please you, presently grant this yearning faithful servant of yours access to you; and that you permit him to frustrate, until the arrival of your legates, the efforts of the man who opposes you [Col. 0951D] in every way, by appeals and by other means which the Lord will reveal. We believe this will bring honour to you and security to us all, since we may safely entrust our affairs, under your protection, to our most faithful brother, so that his abundant caution may avert whatever an indiscreet power—God forbid—may wish to devise wickedly against your kingdom. We pray that you may prosper in the Lord and reign happily for a long time, most beloved in Christ.

## LETTER CCLXXIV. TO THE SAME.

GILBERT, bishop of London, to HENRY, king of England: the salvation which is not now present, and which we hope for from the Lord.

[Col. 0952A] It pleased your Excellency that the churches of the archbishop’s clerks situated in the diocese of London or in Kent should be placed in our custody. Since we understood this to have been inspired in you by an impulse of piety—namely, lest ecclesiastical goods, the offerings of the faithful, alms for the poor, and tithes of the people, should be administered by lay hands or treated otherwise than is lawful—we willingly undertook that burden with much and pure charity, as God knows: both to keep you clean and free from sin in this respect, and, should the clerks at any time recover your favour with due humility, to preserve them likewise unharmed.

But the archbishop, who, as though sitting in ambush, seeks occasions especially against my person, strives to injure me through that by which I had laboured to benefit others. In letters recently sent to me, he commanded me, by virtue of obedience and by the power of the Holy Spirit, not to fail to restore to him and to his clerks, within forty days after receiving the letters, whatever I had received from those churches. But I, having invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit and raised the remedy of appeal, suspended until a hearing before the lord pope the command by which he sought unjustly to burden my innocence; and for the time being I set aside what had been suspended. I am indeed certain that he and those assisting him are fashioning these things and graver burdens upon my back. Therefore I entreat your Highness, with that confidence in which you have always been accustomed to hear me, that you entrust the custody [Col. 0952C] of the aforesaid churches to another person whom you can honourably provide for, and, if it please you, relieve me of this burden, so that I may more strongly bear and more promptly discharge in the Lord the other burdens being prepared for me.

I also ask, if it please you, that I may, with your favour and permission, place in safe keeping with any ecclesiastical person the money which I received and held in deposit from this source, amounting to one hundred and eight pounds, fourteen shillings, and six pence; and that, although those for whose benefit this is done are ungrateful, I may keep it deposited and secure for them until the Lord determines to what end this matter should come.

There remains another matter in which the whole Church of the English, together with us, entreats you—especially those who most love and cherish [Col. 0952D] your welfare and your honour. For more harshly than befits your magnificence are those treated among you whom the Lord has appointed his own household servants, whom he has admitted to his private household, whom he has appointed stewards of his table: namely, the priests, who in the kingdom of England enjoy neither lay liberty nor are dealt with by ecclesiastical courts. Though all are silent in this matter, I shall not be silent; though all despair, I shall not despair. Therefore, absent in body but present in spirit, I beg and implore you by your welfare and for the sake of your welfare, to order that William, formerly the archbishop’s chaplain, and very many clerks throughout England—whom your ministers presume to punish before they are either confessed or convicted, rather than first judging them—be restored to the Church of God, to whose service they are assigned. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLXXV. TO THE SAME.

So great a weight of command now oppresses us, my lord, and such authority confronts us, that the utmost necessity compels us to seek both counsel and aid from you. For what apostolic authority commands, an appeal does not suspend. Nor can there be any remedy against its command: what is commanded must be fulfilled, or one incurs the guilt of disobedience. On the feast of Saint Paul, while we were standing at the altar in London, we received from the hand of a man wholly unknown to us letters of the lord pope, by which the legateship throughout [Col. 0953B] all England, except the diocese of York, is granted to the lord of Canterbury and confirmed by apostolic authority. By that same authority all of us bishops of that kingdom are also commanded humbly to obey him as legate of the Apostolic See; to assemble at his summons without objection; to answer him fully regarding those matters which pertain to our office; and firmly to accept and observe whatever he determines.

It is further added that we are to compel, by sentence of anathema and with every appeal excluded, all those who, by your command, received the benefices of the archbishop’s clerks during their absence to make full restitution to them within two months. We are also commanded to exact Saint Peter’s penny from our brothers and fellow bishops [Col. 0953C] and deliver it whole to the agents sent to us. We are further commanded either to send or present to the bishops to whom he dispatches them the letters concerning the aforementioned legateship and the archbishop’s letters, if we wish henceforth to remain unimpaired in our standing and order.

Therefore, prostrate in heart at the feet of your Highness, we beseech you not to cease, amid the great concerns supplied by royal care, to look upon us; but, lest we be utterly reduced to nothing in the extremity of our disgrace, to provide for us with royal compassion. You will indeed do this well if you permit us, with your peace, to obey the apostolic commands; if Saint Peter’s penny is rendered; if, within your mercy, the clerks are restored to what is theirs; and if you command all bishops that, should they perceive in the archbishop’s letters any burden contrary to the customs of the kingdom, they may immediately and confidently appeal to the lord pope or to the legates being sent to you. Thus you will perform a work of mercy, preserve us from the guilt of disobedience, and provide, by the common appeal of all, that your cause suffer no loss in any respect. May the Lord teach you to do his will, and urge you to relieve the distress which we now experience. May my most beloved lord in Christ prosper.

## LETTER CCLXXVI. TO THE SAME.

GILBERT, bishop of London, to HENRY, king of England: the service of devoted fidelity.

[Col. 0954A] We believe, my lord, that it has not escaped your Excellency how the lord of Canterbury has laid a heavy hand upon me and certain other of your faithful servants and, so far as he could, has hurled against us with the right hand of iniquity a spiritual sword, to the injury of public law. For this is a most important canon: that no one is to be judged prematurely or out of due order—that is, without first being warned and convicted; nor is a bishop ever to excommunicate anyone until the cause upon which the accused person is charged has been proved. Therefore, since he has departed from the law, we trust in the Lord that, in brandishing the sword against us, he has struck the air rather than inflicted a spiritual wound upon us in body or soul. For by appealing to the lord pope, we forestalled his blow; and the appeal made at the beginning of Lent entirely deprived of force the sentence pronounced on Palm Sunday.

For Pope Sixtus decreed thus: “Whenever a bishop considers himself oppressed by his metropolitan, or regards him as suspect, let him immediately appeal to the Roman See. While he requests to be heard by it, let no one excommunicate him before the case is concluded by the authority of the supreme pontiff. If anything is presumed otherwise, it shall be null and utterly without force.”

## LETTER CCLXXVII. TO THE SAME.

We send to you, my lord, our familiar clerk Master H. . . . . , certainly your faithful servant, earnestly beseeching, with all the affection we can, that you may graciously hear him, if it please you, concerning our petitions, and aid us by royal clemency in our extreme necessity. You will do well if you write somewhat warmly to the lord pope on our behalf, that he may admit the appeal which we have made to him, as the equity prescribed by law requires, and suspend, by the justice which he can and ought to exercise, the sentence pronounced against us after the appeal, until he hears our case and renders to each person what his merits deserve. We also request, if it please you, letters to your cardinal friends, so that they may incline the lord pope to this and, through your prayer, obtain for us from him the benefit granted to all the oppressed: the admission of our appeal.

For Pope Sixtus decreed thus: “Whenever a bishop feels himself oppressed by his metropolitan, or regards him as suspect, let him immediately appeal to the Roman See, [Col. 0954D] and, while he requests to be heard by it, let no one excommunicate him before the case is concluded by the authority of the supreme pontiff. If anything is presumed otherwise, it shall be null and utterly without force.”

Furthermore, because we have the greatest need frequently to enjoy your audience and counsel, we most devotedly beseech your Excellency to grant us leave to cross the sea and permit us to await in lands beyond the sea the agents whom we send to the lord pope. May almighty God preserve your welfare for many years.

## LETTER CCLXXVIII. TO M., KING OF SCOTS.

To his dearest lord, the illustrious king of Scots, M., brother G., minister of the Church of London: may he through whom kings reign grant you a long and happy reign.

[Col. 0955A] Most dear lord, we write to your Highness with this confidence: that we love you with sincere affection of heart, and would regard it as welcome in every respect if we could render you any service pleasing to you. We also hope that the root of equity and just judgment has been planted in your heart by the very hand of the Holy Spirit, and that in cases concerning your subjects your mind can readily be inclined by the prayers of good men toward what is just. For it is written: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times” (Psalm CV). And Wisdom says: “Remove the rust from silver, and a most pure vessel will emerge. Remove injustice from the heart of a king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness” [Col. 0955B] (Psalm XXV).

Accordingly, we earnestly offer prayers to your royal nobility for the bearer of this letter, Elias, our close kinsman: that, for the love of God and at our request, you receive his service and grant him a hearing concerning his inheritance, thereby making us, and many with us, debtors to you in gratitude and service. If he finds favour in your eyes, he will find many helpers for your service, each of whom will gladly assist him from his own resources. We would by no means presume to ask this if we knew that his father had acted faithlessly or maliciously against you and your fathers. But we have heard that he was disinherited because of his fidelity to your father; and we hope in your mercy that you will never send down with sorrow to the underworld the grey hairs of one whom you know to have served your father faithfully according to his ability. May my dearest lord prosper, and may the Spirit of God fill and possess his heart.

## LETTER CCLXXIX. TO ROBERT, COUNT OF LEICESTER.

To his venerable lord and dearest friend ROBERT, count of Leicester, brother G., minister of the Church of London: may you bring the consecrated beginnings of blessed perseverance to their completion in the Lord.

Since the companionship of vices and riches is exceedingly congenial, I congratulate you and wholly rejoice within myself, dearest friend, that by a singular grace riches in you serve virtue. You have heard of that rich man clothed in purple and fine linen, feasting splendidly every day, who was miserably led down to hell, where, tortured by flames, he could not obtain even a drop of water to cool his tongue. [Col. 0955D] You have also heard in the Gospel of the rich man whose field produced abundant crops, saying to himself: “I will tear down my barns and build larger ones; there I will gather all the goods which have grown for me, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, and make merry” (Luke XII). To him it was said by God: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you. And the things which you have prepared—whose will they be?” (ibid.).

And if, with the light supplied by God’s Spirit, we turn the eyes of the mind everywhere over the fullness of the world, we recognize that the world abounds in rich people whose riches are a fuel for vices rather than an increase of virtues, since they are possessed by their riches rather than possessing them through the noble character of a holy mind. The Lord says that such rich people will not easily attain the kingdom of God, and that it is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle than for them to enter the kingdom of heaven. A fearful saying, to be dreaded by such rich people. I congratulate you and wholly rejoice within myself, dearest friend, that you abhor their paths and have long turned aside from their tracks. I rejoice that you reflect upon your latter end and contemplate with the eyes of your mind that saying of the Psalmist: “They slept their sleep, and all men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Psalm LXXV). Had they faithfully dispensed what had been entrusted to them, on awaking that day from the sleep of death they would have found those things in their hands.

[Col. 0956B] The divine voice has said: “You shall not appear empty before the presence of the Lord your God” (Deut. XVI). Everything that you now distribute to the Church of God and to the poor, you will find prepared on that day; and what you now dispense in generous compassion, you will present to the Lord with confidence on that day. Many are blessed and wise; yet I judge only those blessed and only those wise who, through frequent meditation, consider the goods that endure forever, occupy their minds with them, keep watch over them, and direct their whole mind toward grasping them if they can.

I believe, dearest friend, that you have pleased the Father. I hope that the holy dove which appeared above the Lord at the Jordan has now made its nest in you. Run after the Spirit who draws you, who will adorn you inwardly with his goods and enrich you with the perfect love of Christ. If that true love touches you, seizes you, and absorbs you, it will lift you up above yourself according to the prophet, because it will exalt you above the height. Having found an occasion to write to you, I can scarcely restrain myself, dearest friend.

## LETTER CCLXXX. TO THE SAME.

To his venerable lord and dearest friend R., count of Leicester, brother G., minister of the Church of London: the salvation which is now present, and which we hope for from the Lord.

Few words readily persuade when the friendly kindness of the person addressed is prompt to grant a hearing. Therefore, hoping the very best of you in all respects, we are so encouraged by charity that we trust we shall not be repulsed in the matter for which we have recourse to you. Your letters of summons have been sent to a certain canon and friend of ours, Baldwin by name, requiring him to appear before you in person at Oxford at the next assembly and answer one of your men, a virtual peasant, concerning the alleged non-observance of a certain agreement between them, confirmed by charter.

[Col. 0956D] The matter is trifling, the case very small: it concerns half a virgate of land, with an annual rent of twelve pence. Therefore, if any suit has arisen between a clerk of Saint Paul and that man of yours concerning land belonging to his church, it is for us, if it please you, to hear what has occurred and to render justice in every respect to the complainant. Since he despises our jurisdiction and leaps without intermediary to your Highness, we ask that this respect be shown to Saint Paul and to us: that, with your mind and intention inclined toward us for the preservation of the dignity of God’s Church, he may understand that he will also give you a full account of whatever is just. We return to you your letters of summons, because in them we do not recognize the style of your notaries. We pray that you may prosper in the Lord and render to Caesar what is Caesar’s in such a way that you also render to God what is God’s.

## LETTER CCLXXXI. TO A., COUNTESS OF LEICESTER.

G., by the grace of God minister of the Church of London, to A., venerable countess of Leicester: may you receive what you seek and, when the pious course has at last been completed, attain that toward which you strive.

[Col. 0957B] Most beloved lady, at your request I send you a letter which I ought to have sent without being asked. If I have omitted to do so for some time, the reason was that day after day I thought I would myself go ahead of and anticipate my messenger to you. Because hope always draws us with an uncertain face toward tomorrow and says, “What I have not done, I shall accomplish tomorrow,” I hoped to conclude my affairs and, with causes quieted for a time and cares set aside, quickly cross over to you and be refreshed by the delightful solace of your wished-for conversation. But the more I seek an opportunity, the less I find it; and when I have cut off certain heads and suppose that I have slain the beast of the world, I am immediately struck with dread at its heads multiplying and growing again.

[Col. 0957C] There is indeed no end to cares, and day by day the world gives birth to new means to afflict wretched souls and turn them from the purpose of devout intention. Ah, why should I recall the holy soliloquies which my soul once mingled with her bridegroom, lifted up in spirit while the silences of the cloister sheltered and held her? When, ignorant of worldly things, she climbed in a sense with Moses onto the mountain, she left cloud and mist below her; having put the world behind her, she pressed wholly toward that fire in which God dwells, desiring nothing but him. When her weakness called her back, she did not withdraw far away or go outside, but remained in mind more attentively at the Lord’s very feet and, recalling her past years in bitterness, washed her former transgressions in the streams of her own tears.

[Col. 0957D] Now concern for household affairs distracts me on one side, and the weight of secular cases entangles me on the other. Now fear oppresses me, now hope prolongs matters; now prosperity lifts me, now adversity casts me down, so that I almost learn from the evidence of circumstances themselves beneath how great a heap of miseries unhappy humanity is subjected. What, then, can my spirit now dictate to you, most beloved lady—you who dwell in purity of mind and desire and long for nothing to refresh your delicate spirit except spiritual delights? That dove which hovered over Christ at the Jordan, and which always indwells him with every fullness of grace, has made its nest in you. And from this fullness you have received as much as he has granted; and the more abundantly you taste his gifts, the more abundantly, with a mind hungry for spiritual things, you desire that they be bestowed upon you.

[Col. 0958A] I seem to behold that soul of yours, in the fervour of its spirit, proclaiming and singing: “Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Song of Songs II). Where may I find flowers, dearest lady, to supply your spirit, so that, burning, it may be more kindled and, striving upward, may be carried more eagerly there? These are the flowers of paradise which the saints share with you: those who, ignorant of and rejecting worldly things, inhabit, as it were, the paradise of a consecrated mind. I ask that by your prayer you reconcile them to me, so that, as I groan under the weight of cares, you may raise and sustain me before the Lord by their intercession. For the little that I possess, from the beginning of our friendship I have neither ceased nor failed to share with you in the Lord. I pray that you may prosper in Christ, dearest lady.

## LETTER CCLXXXII. TO COUNT ALBERIC.

[Col. 0958B]

GILBERT, by the grace of God bishop of London, to the venerable man Count ALBERIC: greeting, grace, and blessing.

It has come to our hearing that, on account of the dispute which has long been conducted between you and the countess, and was at last suspended by appeal to the Apostolic See, you keep her confined with excessive severity, so that she can neither prepare her case nor procure any defender for her side. Nor is she permitted to attend church or, as the saying goes, to appear in public, so that she seems no longer merely placed in custody but rather condemned to prison. It is also said that you have long denied her all access to your bed, your person, and your conversation, so that your will seems in some measure to have separated those whom the authority of the Church joined.

[Col. 0958C] If these reports are true, as we have received them, we declare that you must correct them as swiftly as possible. Otherwise you have much to fear, lest you provoke against yourself the wrath and indignation of God, which, the more slowly it comes, the more severely it afflicts. Recall how worthy of reverence is the sacrament of marriage: the Lord first instituted it at the beginning of the world and confirmed it by his blessing; he himself sanctified it by his bodily presence at Cana of Galilee; and among every people, faithful and unbelieving alike, it is commanded to be observed with the highest veneration.

For it is certain and very well known alike from histories and examples that violators of this sacrament are not only reserved for final vengeance, to be banished from the land of the living, which is the paradise of God, but are also frequently disinherited in this land of the dying, either in themselves or in their descendants, so that their inheritance passes to strangers and others enter into their labours. Accordingly, by episcopal authority we command you—praying, exhorting in the Lord, counselling in charity, and enjoining this upon you for the remission of sins—that for God’s sake and out of reverence for the Christian law you treat your wife, who is part of your body, more moderately and gently; that, removing the excess of the aforesaid severity, you graciously restore her to her due liberty, and yourselves to companionship and consolation, as befits bridegroom [Col. 0959A] and bride. Thus she may not, without judgment of the Church, be deprived of the marital companionship which, with the Church as witness, you promised her under the solemn pledge of betrothal.

If you do not believe us in this, believe the Apostle, who says: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church” (Eph. V). And again: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release” (1 Cor. VII). Charity and the necessity of our office compel us to place these and similar things before your affection. Since we have hope concerning you in the Lord that, as you ought, you are also willing to acquiesce in our counsels in matters concerning God, we counsel you in charity to strive to observe sincerely and without pretence the law and condition of married people to which you have lawfully subjected yourselves, lest you fall into the hands of the judge who is not mocked, whose judgment you cannot evade as one guilty of violating his law. May almighty God avert this. Amen.

## LETTER CCLXXXIII. TO MASTER DAVID.

GILBERT, by the grace of God bishop of London, to his beloved Master DAVID: greeting and success in accordance with your desires.

Having examined the letters sent to me by your diligence, it is plainly evident that, because someone has sown discord between us, you have conceived material for both agitation and anger. Whoever he may be, listen to him less henceforth, and, I beg you, place no further faith in his inventions. For the tongue of a third party often confounds the minds of friends; I beg that such a tongue, worthy to be confounded, since it bears incentives to anger [Col. 0959C] and hatred, not be admitted among us. For I entertain no hostile thought concerning you and cherish nothing in my heart against you; but once you have been admitted into my favour, I ask you to preserve the mutual exchange of favour and goodwill. Furthermore, since Italy has long abundantly tasted your wit, it is good that England too should now experience it whenever it may please you. Farewell, dearest friend.

## LETTER CCLXXXIV. TO WILLIAM DE MALA PALUDE.

G., by the grace of God minister of the Church of London, to his dearest friend WILLIAM de Mala Palude: greeting and sincere affection.

Though your gracious exhibition of services has long obliged me to you in many respects, this especially makes me indebted to you in consummate friendship: that you helped my brother and nephew in their need and gave them counsel and assistance as the situation required. I pray that, if necessity should again compel them to have recourse to you, you may supply from your own resources whatever is needed, not to them but to me—and to them for my sake—so that you may have me as debtor for service and favour. As soon as they have returned to us, you shall have our messenger; and whatever you may wish in relation to us, you will communicate to us through them and obtain. May my dearest friend prosper.

## LETTER CCLXXXV. TO H., COUNT OF NORFOLK.

G., by the grace of God bishop of London, to his venerable lord and dearest friend H., count of Norfolk: greeting and affection.

[Col. 0960A] We have received the answer of the canons of Panteney, brought by the messenger returning to us together with letters bearing their chapter’s seal. They ask that you be informed that they will accept neither money, nor land, nor anything else from you in exchange for granting you Panteney and withdrawing the claim which they are pursuing against you. They say that they choose rather to undergo exile and suffer every adversity than consent to surrender to anyone, and alienate from the Church, a place consecrated to the Lord and so often confirmed for divine uses by apostolic authority.

Accordingly, they urgently demand of us that we carry the lord pope’s command into effect and defer no longer the justice which we have been enjoined to render concerning them. For this reason we have taken care to send to you your familiar and friend, Lord Stephen, canon of Saint Osyth, so that through him we may disclose to you what we do not wish to commit to writing. You know that this necessity lies upon us: either to pronounce sentence against you, or to report to the lord pope the cause by which we are impeded. Once that is done, it will shortly follow that what we have presently omitted will undoubtedly be carried out by him; and the sentence which perhaps we defer for now will be pronounced against you with so much the greater danger because it will come from a judge far holier and far more exalted.

[Col. 0960C] Therefore, because a prudent person measures the outcome of events, we beseech your discretion—more for your advantage than to avoid danger to ourselves—to take counsel in this matter not merely with those who savour earthly things, but with wise men who fear God; and to keep before your eyes him through whom you live, through whom you draw breath, through whom you possess many good things, who preserved you amid adversities, protected you against enemies, who will take away your spirit when he wills, and who will bring all your works into judgment. Today you are, and tomorrow perhaps you will not be; and the misery of hell, like the glory of heaven, will endure without end. On that day, when sins will accuse from one side, terrifying justice from another, the burning world rage without, conscience burn within, the dreadful chasm of hell yawn below, and the angry Judge stand above, whatever is rendered to the Lord during this life will doubtless seem little to anyone.

[Col. 0960D] May the Spirit of God therefore touch your heart, so that in the present affair you may follow good counsel and not, God forbid, by experiencing an apostolic sentence against you, feel a confusion far graver than you now suppose. We pray, dearest friend, that you may have wisdom and understanding and provide for your latter end.

## LETTER CCLXXXVI. TO R. DE SAINT-VALERY.

G., by the grace of God bishop of London, to his dearest friend R. de Saint-Valery: may you happily attain, through the power of merit, the glory promised to the good.

Your generosity, dearest friend—your liberality—has by now become so well known to me that some people hope that, in matters they have with you, they may be assisted by my prayers when these are offered to you on their behalf. Therefore I confidently commend to your charity those whom I love in Christ and concerning whose good conduct in the Lord I have no doubt, earnestly beseeching that, for the sake of that blessed hope by which we press toward God, by which in hoping well we run after Christ, you may at last open the bosom of mercy to the humble brethren of Osney; and that, by sympathizing with their sufferings, you may by your kindness put an end to their hardships.

[Col. 0961B] Remember, dearest friend, how great a merit it is to construct holy places, to build a dwelling for the Lord in which he may without end be praised, honoured, and adored until his coming; consider how great it is not merely not to hinder spiritual good things, but also to supply from your own resources occasion and means for them to abound to God’s glory. Remember, dearest friend, that you have waged the Lord’s wars valiantly, that at your own expense you have fought for him, that by exposing yourself and offering yourself as a kind of whole burnt offering you have repelled the faithless and unbelieving. You who put to shame those rebellious against the Lord in Asia, I beseech you, do not put to shame his humble servants in England.

But, in order that you may bring everything to a good conclusion, offer to the Lord, the head, the tail also of the victim; so that, having made a good beginning to your satisfaction, you may add a praiseworthy end also, and on that day receive a hundredfold from the great hand of the Lord all that you have expended for his sake upon his servants. I pray that you may prosper and, in compassionate mercy, remember before the Lord those for whom I plead. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLXXXVII. TO . . . . .

The Son of the King of the heavenly Jerusalem went forth to behold the lower kingdoms of his Father. Having surveyed them all, he returned to his Father and said: “Father, I have traversed all the kingdoms of the earth and carefully observed what was done in each of them. I have also found true the cry of the Sodomites which had risen to you, and I have punished them with due vengeance. But now it is time for me to make provision for my future: to take a wife, beget children, and henceforth govern my household myself. I saw in the house of the Babylonian king the bride whom I have chosen to possess; that king holds her captive, and, lest she be recognized by anyone, he clothes her in cheap and filthy garments.” [Col. 0961D]

To this the Father said to the Son: “Far be it from you to do this thing, my only Son, coeternal and consubstantial with me. That Ethiopian woman of whom you speak is not worthy of your lineage or of your immensity.” The Son replied: “I have resolved both to take a wife and to join no one to myself except her.” “If this is so,” said the Father, “you, coeternal, consubstantial, and co-omnipotent with me, have it in your power both to free her from Babylonian captivity and to take her as your bride as you will.”

Immediately there appeared an innumerable multitude of angels and heavenly hosts, preparing to minister to the Son of the highest King at these nuptials. From among them he chose one—namely Gabriel—to be his paranymph, or bridegroom’s attendant. Gabriel, chosen by the Son of the highest King, said: “Behold, I am your strength; if you command, I can and am ready to snatch by force from the midst of Babylon the woman whom you seek.” [Col. 0962A]

“It must not be done thus,” said the Son of the eternal King. “No violence is to be inflicted on the Babylonian king. She whom I am to join to myself must be rescued from Babylonian captivity by hidden counsels and wisdom. O Gabriel, the mystery of my purpose must secretly be conveyed to Mary, a virgin of David’s line; with her, in her bridal chamber, the banquet of my marriage must be begun and celebrated.” Gabriel descended to Mary and faithfully performed what had been commanded him. But he who had sent him had already come to the virgin before the announcement was made. There that most holy nuptial banquet was begun; there it was celebrated.

But will so great and such a bridegroom come to his bride empty-handed? By no means. He brought gifts and distributed those he had brought. Since he came in wintertime, he first gave his bride winter garments: namely, a lambskin coat and a cape, both made from a lamb. Yet one, the wool from which the cape is made, is taken without pain to the lamb; the other, namely the skin from which the coat is made, cannot be taken from the lamb without grievous pain.

This bridegroom is the Lamb, as Scripture bears witness: “Like a sheep led to slaughter” (John LIII), and so forth. And elsewhere: “Behold the Lamb of God” (John I), and so forth. This Lamb made a cape for his bride from his wool when he taught humility in words, saying: “Learn from me, for I am meek,” etc. (Matthew XI). [Col. 0962B] He gave her the lambskin coat when, by fasts, prayers, vigils, and other afflictions of his flesh—finally by the passion of the cross—he showed his bride mortification of the flesh.

The cape in which he is clothed is concealed. It signifies humility, because whoever is Christ’s bride remains hidden and refuses to be known by the world; while the coat, made from dead animals, indicates mortification of the flesh. These gifts belong to wintertime.

At Eastertime, however, he gave her an ermine garment around the neck and hands, prepared with red throats. This garment is the holy preachers: white because of the resurrection accomplished in Christ which they proclaim, and which they preach as future for the bride. When they proclaim Christ’s passion, they bear a red throat around the neck. But because some preach Christ’s preaching without feeling it in their hearts—of whom the apostle Paul says, “Some proclaim Christ not sincerely, supposing that they raise affliction for my bonds” (Philippians I)—they ought to feel in their hearts what they say with their mouths. [Col. 0962C] For she would be less becomingly adorned if her garment had attractive red throats only around the neck and not extending to the breast.

Preachers also have red throats around their hands when, in their works, they share in Christ’s sufferings. Therefore the bride’s ermine garment is made when it is spiritually white as a sign of joy, because of the hope of resurrection, and is adorned with red throats around the neck and down to the breast, and around the hands: because she feels in her heart the passion of Christ which she preaches with her mouth, and attests it by her deeds. [Col. 0962D]

At Eastertime Christ also gave his bride his cordovan shoes, which signify the two Testaments, by which the bride’s affections are protected from touching the earth; or continence and charity, which shoe the two inclinations the bride formerly had—one toward her flesh, the other toward vices. The inclination toward the flesh is guarded by continence, or by disciplined restraint; that toward vices is extinguished by charity. But unless these cordovan shoes are fastened by profession and obedience, they slip from the feet. For we have seen many who possessed continence of the flesh from charity, or had resolved to live according to the two Testaments; but because they did not bind themselves under obedience and profession, they fell grievously. Thus the cordovan shoes are either the two Testaments [Col. 0963A] or continence and charity; their fastenings are profession and obedience.

Christ also gave his bride two gloves. The bride’s hands are action and contemplation. Although elsewhere the active life is understood by the left hand and the contemplative life by the right, as in the words, “His left hand is under my head” (Song II), and so forth, here contemplation is signified by the left hand and action by the right, on this analogy: we more often keep the left hand hidden beneath our clothing, but more frequently expose the right for work.

Therefore the right hand, that is, action, has a glove divided into five compartments to receive five fingers, because a good work must be right, voluntary, pure, discerning, and steadfast: right in intention; voluntary, so that it is done neither from fear nor under any compulsion; pure, so that vanity does not render it empty while it is being done through some breath of self-display; discerning, so that it does not extend beyond measure; and steadfast, so that it perseveres. [Col. 0963B]

The left hand likewise has a glove divided into five. For contemplation has five elements: consideration of sins and hell; contempt for present things and for future things [the reading is uncertain]; the kingdom; the state of the body after the resurrection; the glorification of the human spirit; and eternity, with which it is to be united. For one who contemplates rightly considers his sins—what and how great are the offenses he has committed. It would profit little to consider them unless he feared being punished for them in hell; and therefore consideration of hell is rightly joined to consideration of sins.

Likewise, if the torments of hell, what and how great they are, were considered while no memory of sins were retained, perhaps the mind would contemplate hell unconcernedly, since no recollection of sins would distress it. For this reason, both sins and hell are joined in the contemplative mind, so that fear may be produced by each. But in the mind thus terrified there immediately arises contempt for present things, joined with hope of future things. [Col. 0963C]

Yet lest hope make the mind lax, it is restrained by judgment, because it considers that it must pass through that dreadful and strict judgment to attain the things for which it hopes. The kingdom, however, consoles the fear arising from judgment; therefore the kingdom is joined to judgment. In that kingdom it is considered what we shall be: first, the condition of the body, which will be immortal and incapable of suffering; then its glorification, because it will be of ineffable beauty and splendid brightness, as it is written: “The righteous shall shine like the sun” (Matthew XIII). [Col. 0964A]

After these things is considered the blessedness of the soul: namely, the soul itself and God, for whom it is to live. This is the last consideration and the consummation of all things.

These five things which we have contemplated in consideration are seen through five windows. Christ, however, is, in respect of his humanity, as it were a wall, with divinity shining through the humanity. Thus Christ is a window—indeed, five windows are considered in him: his incarnation, manner of life, teaching, resurrection, and ascension. Through these, the five things spoken of concerning contemplation are perceived. For through Christ’s incarnation sins and hell, formerly unattended to, became manifest to many. His manner of life openly taught contempt for present things and directed hope toward future things. His teaching sufficiently treats of judgment and the kingdom. In his resurrection the state and glorification of the body were shown, because such as he is, such also shall his people be according to their measure. [Col. 0964B] In his ascension, moreover, there was revealed, however little, how our spirit is to live with God. For how could that man have been raised and carried upward without any vehicle and without the aid of any created thing, except through the divinity united to him?

Therefore the bride’s gloves are, on the right hand—that is, in action—that it be right, voluntary, pure, discerning, and steadfast; and on the left hand—that is, in contemplation—that sins and hell first be considered, then contempt for present things and hope of future things should follow; after judgment and the kingdom should follow the state of the body and glorification; and finally our union with God.

Ascending, Christ fulfilled all these things in his bride and committed her to the apostles to be guarded; he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem until they were clothed with power from on high. After ten days, on that very day, namely Pentecost, he sent from heaven a great and mighty army—that is, the Holy Spirit—who bestowed on them peace, joy, and the other fruits of the Spirit enumerated by the Apostle. [Col. 0964C] Made steadfast and strong by these gifts, they attacked the enemy’s battle-lines; and Peter converted five thousand Jews to Christ in one day, and three thousand on another.

When these things had been done, the apostles said: “Far be it that our lady, Christ’s bride, should walk any farther on foot! Let us seek for her an animal which, carrying her, may convey her more swiftly and honorably wherever she needs to go. Yet it shall not be a horse, the animal of pride and discord; nor an ass, because it is foolish and unclean; but a mule, because it walks firmly and steadily.”

Thus a mule is given to the bride because a people made up of Jews and Gentiles has finally been converted. For just as a mule is born from different animals, so the primitive Church was gathered from different peoples: from Jews and Gentiles, from the presumptuous and the despairing. [Col. 0964D] Christ wonderfully healed those suffering from different and contrary weaknesses by one remedy, namely his cross. There were—and still are—those who are excessively self-confident and those who despair. The former say, “I was conceived in my own substance,” and “I have never forcibly taken anything from anyone,” and the like; and, “What reason is there for me to despair of life and fear hell?” But if they attend to the fact that Christ, “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found,” and so forth, nevertheless ended his life by the most shameful death, namely the cross, they abandon their pride; broken by fear, they are converted to humility and to sharing Christ’s sufferings.

Then again there are those defiled by so many and such great crimes that they distrust the possibility of forgiveness. But if these consider that Christ suffered not for himself but for sinners, they take heart and are healed of despair. Thus Christ heals the presumptuous by his cross, because the innocent one suffered; and the despairing, because he endured for sinners. The Church, gathered from these different kinds of sinners, is the mule which the apostles prepare for the bride. [Col. 0965A] To the bride, resting upon it and advancing through them toward diverse places, they give one spur, namely love for the bridegroom, by which she compels her own people to advance. They also give her a whip with which to strike backward, because they are distressed over their committed iniquities.

When the holy Church had multiplied and expanded, the apostles, having completed the struggle of their contest, departed this life and entrusted her government to the martyrs. Fighting bravely for her and shedding their blood in her defense, they said: “Since the apostles gave our lady one mule, it is fitting that we too contribute something toward her adornment and beauty. And since the season has now grown warm, she ought not to be burdened with heavier garments. Let us make for her something new, elegant, and light: namely, a variegated mantle covered with red purple.”

This variegated mantle is the holy martyrs: partly virgins, signified by the white of its variety; partly widows or married persons, signified by its middle color; red is laid beneath, because, slaughtered for Christ, they are sprinkled with blood. [Col. 0965B] In their times they governed the Church manfully, advanced it, and multiplied it.

When they had departed, holy teachers and illustrious confessors succeeded them: Ambrose, Hilary, Augustine, and the like. The devil, seeing that he had gained nothing by the open warfare he had waged against the Church in the time of the apostles and martyrs, but that she had rather increased and prospered through tribulations, turned to fraudulent and hidden persecutions. He sought to seduce some of her members, through whom he might conduct the work of his malice all the more effectively because more secretly. Therefore he armed Arius, Pelagius, Photinus, and men like them with his arts; pretending to be Christ’s ministers, they led his bride far astray. [Col. 0965C]

When the holy teachers perceived this, they came forward, fought in disputations, refuted the heretics, and brought their lady back to the way of truth. Since, while she was walking through the deserts of Arius and the byways of Pelagius, her garments had been somewhat worn, they made her a cloak of *famis* [reading uncertain]: that is, they adorned her with their chaste life and honorable morals.

Behold, the enemy has now been defeated both in open persecutions and in the hidden seductions of heretics. The bride proceeds with a great retinue, none opposing her. Yet the twisting serpent still attempts to despoil her; and, since he cannot do so on the road, he sets his snares beside the road. There he erects his tents: in one place he makes his money-changers sit with much gold and silver displayed; elsewhere he clothes them in abundant and varied arrays of different ornaments; in another place he stations sellers of every kind of food; elsewhere he arranges taverns for sellers of wines and every kind of drink; elsewhere he erects triumphal arches for those glorying in worldly pomp, and displays dances of girls and every inducement to lust. [Col. 0965D]

Whoever is wise travels with the bride and clings to the bride as she proceeds by the straight road. The foolish and senseless leave the road, delight in the devil’s tents, and no longer return to the bride. And indeed many today leave the road and delight to remain in the devil’s taverns. Whoever loves silver is captivated by the appearance of gold and prefers this to Christ: he dwells in the devil’s tent. Likewise, whoever delights in costly clothing, more luxurious foods, honeyed wine and other kinds of expensive drink, women, games, and secular songs, and prefers these to Christ, is in the devil’s tents. [Col. 0966A]

What, moreover, shall I say about those who ought to govern the Church of God, but leave the road, gaze about in admiration at the things in the devil’s tents, and desire them? Lacking the means to buy what they covet, they plunder the bride’s ornaments and shamefully expend them in satisfying their evil desires. Thus, torn on every side around the shoulders, she scarcely retains a little of her covering—that is, a few monks in whom religion is not perfect, and a few regular canons; among nearly all other classes of men, scarcely any at all. This the bride suffers.

## LETTER CCLXXXVIII. TO . . . . .

Remember mercy after anger.

H., the bearer of this letter, coming to us, showed us with tearful lamentation that by a grave offense he had disturbed the tranquillity of your mind, and that, moved by the heat of anger, he had not merely opposed you in word but had irreverently raised his heel against you. Stricken therefore with inward sorrow of heart, he is prepared to undergo the regular discipline which you may decree, to make satisfaction to you in humble devotion, and henceforth to obey you in all things as his dearest father.

But since the Lord never rejects one offering worthy fruits of repentance, and since there is joy among the angels of God over a sinner doing penance, and since he gives a singular example of virtue by running to meet in an embrace and kiss the penitent son returning to him, we ask that, for his sake and in consideration of our petition, you receive him back converted whom you rejected when turned away. And because the world would have perished unless mercy had put an end to anger, remit your anger toward him, and signify this by your letters to Abbot H.; for, as we have learned by the testimony of some, if he knows that H. has been reconciled to you, he will admit him to the community of brothers. [Col. 0966D]

## LETTER CCLXXXIX. TO . . . . .

Joy and exultation overflow within me whenever, through the service of report, I learn that you are well and flourishing. For it is customary for me to honor you as my lord, to embrace you, and to count your advancement and welfare among my own successes. Thus the prosperity that attends you contributes to the fullness of my joy, while your safety adds its crowning measure. May I be charged with falsehood if you ask anything from me in vain that can and ought to be bestowed upon a friend. Meanwhile, I ask that a letter from you be sent to me, by which I may learn the mystery of your purpose and welfare. [Col. 0967A]

## LETTER CCXC. TO . . . . .

To offer the Lord hospitality worthily in oneself.

We warmly return thanks to your goodwill, dearest brother, because you were nevertheless pleased graciously to grant our petition, by whatever course it proceeded. Yet, searching our conscience on every side, we find, God bearing witness, absolutely no hatred, bitterness, pretense, or crafty duplicity in ourselves against you. Rather, walking in simplicity, we took care to request, solely in brotherly charity and with no exaltation of mind, no pride of preeminence, and no exaction, what we hoped would be honorable and useful for you and for your house. [Col. 0967B]

Indeed, we loved your brother R., and in the business which he diligently conducted with us on your behalf, we bore with him, observing that the Lord graciously directed his efforts. We rejoiced in this. But if perhaps, by a higher counsel, you have turned your face away from our request, we, because charity cannot be bound, shall at least continue to love him wherever obedience may draw him.

## LETTER CCXCI. TO . . . . .

[Col. 0967C]

While we act in the place of the Church of Worcester, while we bear its burden, though reluctantly, we surely offend the Lord unless, when reason requires it, we admonish its parishioners and children concerning the things that pertain to their salvation. Therefore we earnestly beseech and admonish your highness in the Lord that you allow your church of Tewkesbury, which daily raises its hands to the Lord for the salvation of you and yours, freely to choose for itself a father and pastor; and that you in no way impede the liberty which apostolic authority confirms to it, and which the gracious piety of both your grandfather and your father has hitherto preserved for it. [Col. 0967D]

For this is dangerous to you and contrary to your salvation. For from their privileges we have learned that apostolic authority most severely binds all who obstruct this liberty by force, fear, or any contrivance whatsoever, and renders them wholly estranged from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, as persons delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, unless they repent worthily. We ask, admonish, and indeed counsel you in true charity that this may never come upon you: by setting aside your anger at an offense, render to God the things that are God’s, and permit divine matters to be administered in a divine manner. Thus, when you have shown due reverence to God in this and other matters, may he preserve you during the course of this temporal life, [Col. 0968A] and after it has passed reward you with his own, in the due recompense of obedience and piety.

## LETTER CCXII. TO . . . . .

A talent has been entrusted to you, dearest friend, which your discretion must increase and expend for the benefit of many, so that, when you have increased it by relieving the needs of many, you may receive from the Lord on that day a hundredfold reward. This talent is the familiarity with our lord the king which has been granted you by God; if anyone compares it with gold, it is more precious, and it is rightly valued far above any amount of money. You must faithfully disburse this talent: frequently and earnestly remind the king himself to relieve the misery of the oppressed, [Col. 0968B] and persist in this with insistence not only when the moment is convenient but also when it is inconvenient, if compassion requires it. Thus merit may be laid up for him before the Lord, and no small favor with men may be accumulated for you from such exertions.

## LETTER CCXCIII. TO . . . . .

Know that I am healthy and safe, and that I earnestly desire conversation with you, so that from the presence of my friend I may receive what my soul most greatly longs for. May that charity which knows no absence, and which always knows the person it loves to be present to itself in spirit, I pray, supply the consolation which the mutual bodily absence of us both takes away amid the varying events of affairs.

Furthermore, compelled by the request of William, son of R., I am obliged to offer a petition to your goodwill concerning B.: that you may be willing, after B.’s promotion to the order of deacon, in due course to promote him to the priesthood. By fulfilling this for the love of God and at my request, you will make him bound to you in prayer and me indebted to your favor in all things. [Col. 0968C]

## LETTER CCXCIV. TO . . . . .

It is customary for those in love never to tire of hearing mention of the object they love; rather, by the very frequency of conversation, human affection toward the thing it loves is kindled more intensely.

Things bestowed by the devotion of the faithful, for the honor of God and the benefit of the holy Church, for the use of the poor, must by no rashness be taken away from them by anyone; rather, they must be preserved for those uses and increased. [Col. 0968D]

From the time we came to know your person, we have clung to you with more devoted charity and, whenever opportunity presented itself, have given careful attention to promoting your honor. Therefore we confidently commend to your discretion those matters which appear likely to add honor to your learning and integrity. We therefore entreat you in every way and earnestly urge you to love D. and devote all your strength to his advancement. For your reputation will win very great commendation and favor if you hold dear and endeavor to exalt a man of such integrity and such profound learning, whom the Church of London esteems highly and strongly commends, adorned as he is by the beauty of eloquence. [Col. 0969A] Provide for him, then, as befits both giver and recipient, lest perhaps, if his highly praiseworthy merits remain unrewarded, your reputation might deservedly suffer in consequence.

## LETTER CCXCV. TO . . . . .

Since hitherto we have readily obtained the fulfillment of our wishes from your clemency, we clearly infer from the past what we ought to hope for in the future. Therefore, trusting alike in your kindness and affection, we most devoutly beseech your generosity, that for the love of God and, if it please you, in consideration of our request, you will be willing to fulfill in deed what you promised in word.

For our spirit exults in God our Savior, because the Dayspring from on high has looked upon and visited you. I give thanks to him because his clemency has deigned to inspire you with zeal for repentance. You had been driven by the devil’s contrivance to fall, but the right hand of the Lord received you through the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0969B]

## LETTER CCXCVI. TO . . . . .

Let it be known to present and future alike that I, Gilbert, Bishop of London, gave to William Cook, my servant, for his service, all that land of the ancient manor at Fulham which lies about the church, as it is divided by the ditch: on one side from the bishop’s grove, and on the other from the public road [Col. 0969C] which descends to the Thames. I gave it to him to hold freely and hereditarily from me and my successors for one pound of pepper yearly, payable therefrom at the feast of Saint Michael. And because I wish this to remain firm and unshaken, I confirm it by the present writing and attestation of my seal. Witnesses: . . .

## LETTER CCXCVII. TO . . . . .

G., by the grace of God Bishop of London.  
(The following line is erased.)

I hear, brother, that you have scented Sicilian riches and that, newly breathed upon by the breeze of yellow metal, you are making for foreign lands not merely in mind but also in body. [Col. 0969D] In this matter you plainly show both what you are and how shamefully you are ambitious: broken in spirit or wearied by poverty, you plan miserably to acquire riches at the cost of yourself or even of your soul. You have read of the fortune of Crassus, who, drinking what he thirsted for, fatally sated, died an ignominious death. You likewise, desiring not to become rich but to be rich at once, prefer to rush richly into death rather than not to be at this moment what you desire.

Therefore, lest you depart to death without farewell, I send you, though you now refuse salvation, this word of salvation, in case somehow at last you may recover your senses: in case, remembering affections, your homeland, your parents, companionship, and favor, you may finally wipe away with the hand of discretion the ophthalmic secretion from your blinded eye; and, emerging as prudently as bravely from the pit of despair into which you have fallen while sloth dragged you down, may hasten back to us without hesitation, with great certainty of hope in the goodness of Jesus, who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach them. [Col. 0970A]

## LETTER CCXCVIII. TO . . . . .
