The care of the priestly office and the obligation of charity admonish us to intercede earnestly for learned and honorable men and diligently to attend to their interests. Therefore, with every earnestness, we ask your affection, in which we place great confidence, that you grant to Archdeacon R., long our clerk and friend, the church of Saint John, which we have learned was ceded to him by Lambert. Thus, through the intervention of our prayers, take care to make him your devoted and faithful clerk in that matter, [Col. 0970B] so that from the effect of your affection we may henceforth be able to trust with greater confidence and may be bound to commend it according to its merits. For whatever kindness and favor—especially at the prompting of our request—we learn that you have bestowed upon him, we shall regard as gratefully and acceptably bestowed upon ourselves. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXCIX. TO . . . . .

Amid the changes of this world, direct the gaze of the mind to that place where there is no danger of change.

It is just to bear witness before your serenity to the honorable conduct of those whom uprightness of life commends to favor and religion, long made manifest by pious merits; and, with prayers devoutly offered, to entreat that they may be graciously heard by your favor in their just petitions. The Church of the Holy Trinity, founded in London long ago by Matilda, Queen of England of blessed memory, and nobly established with an honorable community of regular canons, has shone widely from its foundation until now both through the fullness of its charity and through observance of the order it has undertaken. [Col. 0970C] Emitting from itself the sweetness of a good fragrance, it has shone among the churches of its order as a kind of mirror and an example of purified religious life.

Since at present, in the necessity which has arisen for it, it has had recourse to you by an appeal, we ask with it that asks, and petition with it that petitions, that you graciously receive its messenger sent to your holiness; and, lest it suffer loss of the property by which it relieves the needs of many, provide for it, so far as justice permits, with paternal favor, if it please you. [Col. 0970D]

## LETTER CCC. TO . . . . .

Greeting and dutiful service with every devotion.

The affection and demonstration of honor which your excellency has not ceased to bestow upon me for many years past have earned from me such affection toward you that I ought deservedly, with every zeal and effort, to advance as though they were my own affairs whatever I believe conducive to the interests or honor of you or yours. [Col. 0971A] Therefore, if the lord abbot finds your concern in this matter to be earnest, he will neither wish, as I believe, nor dare to oppose your will. You ought to pursue this business all the more earnestly because others, encouraged by this man’s example, will more willingly entrust themselves to your counsels when they see him promoted to his right by your aid. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCI. TO . . . . .

In proportion as our merits are almost nothing before your highness, dearest friend, so much the more gratefully will the benefit be valued which your generosity grants, moved by prayers alone. The bearer of this letter, our kinsman and familiar friend, wishes through us to be commended to your protection. He hopes for the best outcome if you are willing to enroll him among the number of those obedient to you. [Col. 0971B] His great generosity of spirit and abundance of learning commend him to favor, so that he is himself worthy, on his own account, to be admitted to that which he desires to obtain at another’s request. When you assist him at our request and offer him help in need, you will make both him bound to you in service and us debtors to you for greater favor.

## LETTER CCCII. TO . . . . .

If we trust in your goodwill toward us, our merits toward you do not demand it; rather, your generosity and favor alone produce it. Yet we wish you to know this for certain: we are ready for your service with a most willing spirit. Hoping likewise for your favor, we earnestly ask you to hear diligently the business of our friend R., the bearer of this letter, and, by advancing it through his service with King D., to hold us as debtors to you both in service and in favor. Farewell. [Col. 0971C]

## LETTER CCCIII. TO . . . . .

Because one generation passes and another comes, and what is done by those who pass away is not held valid by their successors unless it is made clear by definite proofs, we have thought it useful to confirm the sequence of transactions by the testimony of writing and the impression of a seal. Let all therefore know:

To yield compassionately to the misfortune of poor friends;

To adhere firmly to a sacred purpose;

To possess perfect love together with due submission;

To hope more in the Lord than in man.

To be adopted by God as a son.

We must take care and provide diligently that disputes settled in our presence may not, on any occasion, be revived anew in controversy. [Col. 0971D]

## LETTER CCCIV. TO . . . . .

A., the bearer of this letter, having conducted himself honorably among us, was received by us into the clergy and canonically promoted to the rank of deacon. Having pursued studies in letters as far as your province, he declares that the customs of your people and holy friendship have so bound him to them that he desires to compensate for his native soil by so great a sweetness, and, dwelling there with our permission, to complete the course of his life. [Col. 0972A]

Finally acceding to his wishes and requests, we send him to your highness with the testimony of this document, asking that, for the love of God and reverence for the order he has received, you graciously receive him, permit him to minister among you in his order, and, if uprightness of life merits it, be willing to promote him further. We allow him, now free and released from further subjection to us, to serve your obedience, if it please you. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCV. TO THE CLERGY AND LAITY OF LONDON

[Col. 0972B]

G., by the grace of God Bishop of London, to his beloved in the Lord, the clergy and laity established throughout the diocese of London: greeting, grace, and blessing.

It is right, dearest brothers, to hasten in the course of charitable purpose through works of mercy, so that at the time of the eternal harvest we may obtain the prize of the salvation we desire; to sow while life remains, so that, when fruit has been multiplied, we may receive the robe of awaited joy. Therefore we earnestly exhort you in the Lord that, in confidence of the promised recompense, you devote more earnest care to pious deeds, among which shines the giving of alms, which wipes away the offense of sins and pours into us the light of love for God and neighbor.

Since the lepers of Saint Leonard of Northampton are tortured not only by intolerable bodily suffering but are also known to be afflicted by extreme hunger, the affection of compassion moves us to petition all of you on their behalf. [Col. 0972C] Through this bearer of the present letter, their messenger, send them some portion of your resources, relieve their misery, and let them rejoice that, aided by your expenditure, they have through you what is sufficient for their wretched sustenance—what they cannot provide from their own means.

Trusting in God’s mercy, we grant twenty days’ remission to those who give even a little to the brothers just mentioned, and make them participants in all the good works performed in our Church. [Col. 0972D] Farewell in Christ.

## LETTER CCCVI. TO . . . .

The authority of our pastoral office warns us to take special care that the perversity of litigants does not revive into quarrels disputes which have been put to rest before us by a settlement, and that what has been usefully arranged is not called into question again. Therefore, in order that the agreement entered into by mutual consent between M. and A. may have full force, we have decreed to commit it to writing; it was at last brought to rest in our presence with this conclusion. Accordingly, we approve this agreement not only by the authority entrusted to us, but also confirm it by the affixing of our seal, earnestly requesting your brotherhood [Col. 0973A] to give in these matters your assent and authority.

(Much is lacking in this letter.)

### LETTER CCCVII. TO . . . . .

Those who desire to attain the heavenly homeland must diligently devote themselves to works of mercy and, from the resources bestowed on them by God, distribute alms to the poor, and especially to pious places devastated by fire. Therefore, being concerned, as is right, for the advancement of your salvation, we ask, admonish, and exhort all of you in the Lord to contribute some assistance toward the work of the church of Saint N., so that through this and through the other [Col. 0973B] good works which you do in this life, you may happily attain eternal joys. Farewell.

### LETTER CCCVIII. TO . . . . .

R., the bearer of this letter, a man of honourable learning and unstained reputation, asks to be assisted by our prayers with your goodwill. Since we can neither fail nor ought to fail him in a reasonable petition, we desire to find your generosity favourably disposed; asking on his behalf and with him that, out of regard for piety and at the intervention of our prayers, you hear him in his petition and charitably advance his business which lies with you, so that you may make him bound to you in service and us debtors to your favour.

### LETTER CCCIX. TO . . . . .

[Col. 0973C]

Greeting, and joy always in the Lord.

Although we are bound to do good to all whom the Christian religion commends to us, piety nevertheless urges us to give more ready attention to those who, rejecting the perfidy of the Jews and reborn through the sacred water of baptism, choose rather to profess nakedly the faith of Jesus Christ than, while possessing transitory wealth, to wish to follow the killing letter of the Law. And lest the pressing demands of daily necessity disturb their zeal for righteousness in the resolve of good will, provision must be made with greater care, because it is more justly feared that in neophytes the plant of new instruction may wither before it is firmly rooted in the enduring root of charity.

Therefore, beloved in Christ, we exhort your [Col. 0973D] charity to turn more graciously the eyes of mercy and the bowels of compassion toward the bearer of this letter, newly converted to Christ’s faith in London; so that the devotion of brotherly charity shown to him, still such a novice, may strengthen him more fully toward the perfection of the grace he has received and may invite others to the same. Moreover, trusting in God’s mercy and in the intercession of the apostles Peter and Paul, we remit twenty days of the penance imposed upon those who, with a view to eternal reward, give this Nicholas some portion of their resources to relieve his poverty; and we make them participants in the prayers and benefactions performed in our Church. Farewell in Christ.

### LETTER CCCX. TO . . . . .

[Col. 0974A]

. . . . . And in order that this agreement between them may be preserved unharmed, we confirm it by this present writing and by the affixing of our seal.

### LETTER CCCXI. TO . . . . .

Most beloved Father, I regard it as a welcome gift whenever, from letters sent by your holiness, I learn that your affairs remain in sound condition. For my spirit exults, and that inner man of mine keeps a festival day, when letters or a messenger bringing glad news about you make known to me that my most dear friend and lord is healthy and safe and prospering in all things. [Col. 0974B] This is the work of that charity which holds primacy among virtues: binding the minds of friends to itself by an indissoluble law, it unites in spirit those separated by local distance, joins them in affection, and, by its power continually and mightily at work within, makes those absent present to one another. This cannot be erased from the page of my memory; no vicissitude of affairs will disturb it, so as to prevent me from remaining devoted to your service and ready to obey your commands. Farewell.

### LETTER CCCXII. TO . . . . .

Things done for the honour of God and the benefit of holy Church ought rightly to stand firm and remain unshaken upon their roots. Therefore, because we judge the agreement concerning the church of Simin, concluded between A., abbot of Saint Osyth’s, and the convent of that church, and G., treasurer of the Church of London, to be pleasing to God and advantageous to holy Church, we approve it as it is set forth in the written agreement made between them and confirmed on both sides by their seals. Strengthened by the authority granted us by God, we confirm it by the attestation of our seal, that it may remain unshaken in future generations.

### LETTER CCCXIII. TO . . . . .

Greeting, and the reverence due to your rank.

It is right to grant assent to the just desires of petitioners whenever their requests do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, considering the devout concern of the brothers of [Col. 0974D] Dunstable regarding the person of our beloved son and your canon, Lord T., whose conduct breathes integrity and whose prudence savours of virtue, we have graciously assented to their request. We release him from the obedience by which he was bound to us and grant him freedom for the ministry to which he has been called by the Lord through the unanimous election of the brethren: henceforth he is to obey the Church of Lincoln and comply, as is right, with its commands and admonitions.

Therefore, lest you depart from your head—which God forbid!—and also offend against the common law of brotherly charity, we command and advise you, and, by the episcopal authority entrusted to us by the Lord, enjoin you to hold valid what has been done by us and, at the pious request of those concerned, release him from the obedience by which he is bound to you, so that you may receive from the Lord grace and the due rewards of charity. [Col. 0975A]

### LETTER CCCXIV. TO . . . . .

What is given to the Lord, most dear friends, does not perish for the giver; rather, according to the Lord’s saying, it is preserved for most ample recompense to the one from whom it was given, and “[will] give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing.” Therefore, concerned for the advancement of your salvation, we admonish your charity in the Lord to contribute some assistance from your resources for the repair of the church of Saint Ives and for restoring the bridge and causeway of the same town, where the passage of travellers is very greatly disrupted [Col. 0975B] from [your] resources; and, by honouring [God in] his saints, obtain for yourselves [grace] from God and forgiveness of sins. To all, moreover, [who for the aforesaid] work, urged by God, shall have contributed anything . . . . , trusting in the Lord’s mercy, we remit ten days of the [penance] imposed upon them, and make them participants in all the good works [and prayers] performed in our Church. Farewell.

### LETTER CCCXV. TO . . . . .

Let your affection know, most dear friend, that I shall gladly comply in all things with your service; and, if anything should perhaps arise, devoted performance of the deed [Col. 0975C] will answer the promise.

### LETTER CCCXVI. TO . . . . .

From your kindness and affection we offer humble and devoted prayers to your fatherhood on behalf of N., the bearer of this letter, earnestly asking that, for the love of God and out of reverence for blessed . . . ., you may, if it please you, graciously receive and mercifully hear him in consideration of our prayer. Whatever favour and kindness he finds in your eyes, regard it as granted to us.

### LETTER CCCXVII. TO . . . . .

This bearer of the present letter, having, as he confesses, at one time a zeal without knowledge, followed his former father Simon and departed from your community with insufficient consideration—something which he now mournfully regrets. Now, pierced with remorse and returned to himself, taught by experience how grievous it is to be separated from the unity of brethren, he knocks and sighs at your door, imploring and desiring with all the strength of his soul that you open to him the gates of mercy and admit him into your number, since henceforth he will obey more prudently and perfectly.

Therefore, because the Church never closes her bosom to one who returns, rejoicing more over one sinner converted to repentance than over many who do not need repentance, we knock with him who knocks and pour out prayers with him who supplicates, that, for love of God and out of regard for brotherly charity, you forgive him from your heart any anger conceived against him [Col. 0976A] and mercifully hear both his petition and ours, if this can be done without injury to your order and without scandal. Farewell.

### LETTER CCCXVIII. TO . . . . .

Greeting, and the ready service of devoted fidelity.

It is an old and ancient saying: “He who loves confidently speaks confidently”; nor can anyone doubt the affection of one whose sincere love removes every dreg of suspicion. Therefore we cannot refuse your requests, especially where your persistence prevails and great authority and affection intervene.

### LETTER CCCXIX. TO . . . . .

[Col. 0976B] Trusting, my lord, in your generosity, I earnestly entreat your fatherhood that, so that I may be ever more devoted to you in all things from devotion, your excellence may deign to call me to some benefice in your church which it would be honourable for you to give and for me to receive from your generosity.

### LETTER CCCXX. TO . . . . .

That I presume to ask something of your goodness is caused not by confidence in previous merits, but by regard for your kindness.

### LETTER CCCXXI. TO . . . . .

I hear that you sin grievously, since you do not fear to lay your hands upon [Col. 0976C] the tithes of the church, which belong to divine right alone. Therefore I command you, and enjoin it upon your Christianity, that you cause the tithes belonging to the church of Fulham to be restored to it without delay; lest, if you unjustly retain them, you incur thereby God’s wrath and receive the sentence you deserve.

### LETTER CCCXXII. TO . . . . .

Although each of the virtues, most dear friends, is acceptable in God’s sight, none is read to please God more than almsgiving. For it is written: “Give alms,” says the Lord, “and all things are clean for you” (Luke 11). Whoever therefore desires to please God should distribute to the poor from the benefits divinely bestowed upon him and strive to assist [Col. 0976D] the necessities of others, so that on that day he may be able to receive a hundredfold from the Lord on account of what he has bestowed upon them. Therefore, because by the office entrusted to us we have care of you, we more earnestly admonish your brotherhood that you take heed that your almsgiving may stand forth to many as an example of good work.

### LETTER CCCXXIII. TO . . . . .

We believe that some have learned how greatly poor people journeying to the hospital beside Saint Bartholomew’s in London are comforted, and how greatly that house is in need, which is necessary to so many thousands and supplies relief to all every day. Therefore, out of regard for this most religious house, we earnestly exhort all of you, asking and beseeching you in the Lord, and enjoining this upon you for the remission of sins: kindly receive among you the bearers of this letter, the messengers and procurators of that venerable place, to sow God’s word; and through yourselves and the people entrusted to you mercifully assist the brothers there, devoted to divine service, with benefactions and the distribution of alms. [Col. 0977A] We likewise, trusting in divine mercy, grant participation in all the prayers and benefactions of the Church of London to all who, for the [love] of God, confer any benefaction on that house. Farewell.

### LETTER CCCXXIV. TO . . . . .

[Col. 0977B] May you be crowned with glory and honour for ever.

We earnestly commend to your charity the bearer of this letter, our son B., who, so far as is known to us, has conducted himself honourably among us. We offer devoted prayers in this matter, that you may receive him with favour as a devoted son and, in consideration of our request, hold him dearer than dear, so that you may have us indebted to you both for affection and for greater favour.

### LETTER CCCXXV. TO . . . . .

By this present writing I notify all of you that I have granted in alms to H., clerk, the church of Wicham with its chapel, namely the church of Langford, and all other things belonging to it; and by the authority granted us by God, I have instituted him as parson in those churches. In order that this may not be recalled into doubt, I have taken care to attest and confirm it alike by the writing of this present document and by the affixing of my seal. [Col. 0977C]

### LETTER CCCXXVI. TO . . . . .

Because we ought readily to grant assent to pious wishes, we notify all of you by this present writing that, by the grant of the noblewoman Cecilia Talbot, we have, by the authority which we exercise with the Lord’s permission, granted in perpetual alms the church of Feenges, situated in her patrimony, to the church of Saint James above the hill at Rouen and to the brothers and sick persons dwelling there and continually rendering service to the Lord. [Col. 0977D] We have also, with due solemnity, instituted our venerable brother Herbert, prior of that church of Saint James, as parson there in the name of the church of Saint James itself.

Lest this may henceforth be recalled into doubt or overthrown by any contrivance, we confirm it by this present writing and strengthen it by the affixing of our seal. And because a threefold cord is not easily broken, we trust, with the Lord’s help, that this donation, confirmed first by the charter of the aforesaid church, then by ours, and afterwards by the charter of Saint Thomas, formerly archbishop of Canterbury, shall remain valid for ever. These being witnesses.

### LETTER CCCXXVII. TO . . . . .

Compassionating the need of sick persons at Colchester who suffer from prolonged illness, we ask and earnestly exhort in the Lord your kindness, which is dear to us in the Lord, that for the love of God and out of regard for piety, when their messengers and procurators come to you, you receive them graciously for the remedy of your souls and relieve their poverty from the bounty of your alms as God inspires you. To all, moreover, who have confessed their sins and extended to them a hand of mercy in some measure, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, we remit twenty days of the penance imposed upon them and grant them participation in the prayers and benefactions of our church. [Col. 0978B]

### LETTER CCCXXVIII. TO . . . . .

[Col. 0978C] Brothers, we consider it safe and useful to preserve in written records those matters which it is certainly expedient to establish peace between ecclesiastical persons, or to preserve it more firmly in the future, lest things brought to peace by the forbearance of judges and the assent of parties through settlement or amicable agreement should fade from memory through the passage of time, or should again happen to arise into renewed litigation. Hence, because the controversy . . . . The remainder is lacking.

### LETTER CCCXXIX. TO . . . . .

Preface to the Book of Homilies.

Brother, you have what you desired, what charity could no longer deny to one who had been asking for it so long. For, being placed within [Col. 0978D] . . . etc. See Gilbert’s *Exegetical Works*, among the volumes of the *Patrology* shortly to be published. EDITOR OF THE FATHERS.

### [LETTER CCCXXX.]

[Col. 0977]

Gilbert’s Letter CCCXXX, to the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury, concerning the election of Pope Urban III, which had been omitted from its proper place in the De Gilles edition, has been placed above under no. 196 bis. EDITOR.

### LETTERS CCCXXXI–CCCLXXX.

Three letters of Pope Alexander III to Cardinals William and Otto; [letters] to Cardinals Albert and Theodwin concerning the reconciliation of the Church of Canterbury; to the same men; to the archbishop of Bourges and the bishop of Nevers; to Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, concerning the canonization of Anselm; to the same; to all the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury; five letters to the archbishop of Canterbury and his suffragans; to the archbishop of Canterbury and Gilbert; to the monks and canons of Canterbury; to W., prior, and the chapter of Canterbury; to Richard, archbishop of Canterbury; to Roger, archbishop of York; to the same; to . . . . concerning the dignity of the Church of York; to Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen; to the bishops of England; to the bishop of Orléans; to Bartholomew, bishop of Exeter; to the same and Abbot Simon; to the archdeacon of Lincoln; to Gilbert, bishop of London; to the same; to the same and R., archdeacon; four letters to the same; to William, bishop of Norwich; to the same; to Roger, bishop of Worcester; [Col. 0979] three letters to the same; to Simon, abbot of Saint Albans; to the abbot and monks of Saint Andrew’s; to the abbots and brothers of the Cistercian Order established in England; to Roger, abbot of the monastery of Ibreio; to the monks of Saint Mary of Laurentium; to the abbot and brothers of Neubothe; to King Henry, concerning Thomas Becket (spurious); to the same; to Louis, king of France.

(See under ALEXANDER III, years 1159–1181.)

### LETTER CCCLXXXI. OF POPE URBAN III TO B., ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, AND ALL BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN ENGLAND. Concerning his election.

[Col. 0979A]

URBAN, bishop, etc.

“The heavenly height of counsel,” etc. See under Pope Urban III, years 1185–1187.

### LETTER CCCLXXXII. LETTER OF POPE HONORIUS III TO ALL CHRISTIANS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT ENGLAND, CONCERNING THE TRANSLATION OF BLESSED THOMAS.

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all Christ’s faithful, nobles and others established throughout England, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The heavenly King, Lord of angels, has in our times honoured the kingdom of England above other kingdoms and distinguished the English people by a certain special prerogative. For, while the world lay in wickedness and human malice was growing, he chose from it for himself a man without blemish, who was not merely made a priest in the time of wrath for reconciliation, but, invited also to the heavenly banquet, deserved to taste the cup of suffering which the Lord had drunk. And because he was found worthy before God, God crowned him with glory and honour, setting on his head a crown of precious stone, so that one of the English, established among the angels over the works of the Lord’s hands, might become an intercessor for the sins of all peoples.

Therefore let the happy Church of Canterbury sing a new song to the Lord, [Col. 0979C] whose altar the martyr Thomas crimsoned with his precious blood. Indeed, the whole city itself can and ought deservedly to rejoice with a voice of exultation, since, made red with the rose-coloured blood of its martyr, it has become beautiful and appeared fair. Hence, as a multitude of various peoples from almost every nation under heaven most earnestly venerates his celebration, the city seems once to have received its own name from the event, as though by a happy omen—as if Canterbury (*Cantuaria*) were expressly called “sing-song” (*cantusare*).

You, I say, if you carefully consider this honour, ought to render continual thanksgivings to the giver of all good things, to whom, by reason of the lavish blessing bestowed, you may know yourselves indebted for your land; thus you may avoid the vice of ingratitude and may be called devoted sons. And although at every time you ought to bless and honour the Lord with a pure heart, nevertheless on this occasion especially you must put on wedding garments and rise joyfully in praise of your Creator, since the solemnity of the coming feast requires it.

Indeed, we have recently received word from our venerable brother Stephen, archbishop of Canterbury and cardinal of the holy Roman Church, that, wishing to show in action the fervour of devotion with which he venerates the memory of the aforesaid martyr, he proposes to raise his most sacred body from the earth and, once translated, place it more honourably. It seems worthy and fitting to him to exalt on earth, so far as lies in his power, the one whom the Lord has exalted in heaven. Therefore, accepting the pious and praiseworthy purpose of the aforesaid archbishop, we have thought fit to admonish and exhort all of you, commanding by these apostolic letters that, preserving mutual peace and concord in the bond of charity, you cleanse your consciences of every perversity and apply yourselves to good works. Thus, when the day of this solemnity arrives, you may venerate your most holy martyr and patron at his translation with due honour in such a manner that by your example you teach others how glorious should be the memory of the aforesaid martyr, celebrated throughout the various regions of the world. [Col. 0980B]

Given at the Lateran, 8 Kalends of February, in the third year of our pontificate.

### LETTER CCCLXXXIII. OF THE SAME TO W., PRIOR, AND THE CONVENT OF CANTERBURY.

HONORIUS, pope, etc., to his most beloved sons, the prior and convent of Christ Church, Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

To your church, which the venerable martyr Thomas rendered adorned by the blood of his body, it is fitting that we grant such favour that, just as it is greater than others in name and renown, so it may restore to us, the Roman Church wearied by age, the prerogative [Col. 0980C] of special favour. Since, therefore, as we have learned from your report, the archbishops and bishops who have gathered from various places for the translation of the body of that martyr have decided to grant various remissions to those coming within fifteen days for the solemnity of his translation, we ourselves remit forty days from the penances imposed upon the same persons. Inclined by your prayers, we decree that what has been done in this matter by you and by them shall remain valid in perpetuity as a remission of one year and of the aforesaid forty days.

Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our grant or rashly oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter [Col. 0980D] and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, 15 Kalends of January, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

### LETTER CCCLXXXIV. OF CARDINAL ALBERT TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY.

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, ALBERT, cardinal.

The lord pope rejoiced, and the brethren rejoiced with him, when they heard that peace had been restored to you and to the Church of Canterbury. I too, one of those awaiting and rejoicing, except that a certain hesitation arising from the evasions of your adversaries held my joy in suspense. But when your letters arrived and we understood that more had been granted to you in incidental matters than in essentials, we began to hesitate still more; and we understood that an Ethiopian does not readily change his skin, nor a leopard its spots. Now, however, just as a man is not to be praised during his life, so neither is he to be judged before the time. Thus, as we are not without joy over what we have heard, so we cannot rejoice fully because of what we fear. Wavering, therefore, between hope and fear, we have sighed to him who is able to do exceedingly more than we ask or hope, that he himself may fulfil our joy [Col. 0981B] and that no one may take this joy from us.

### LETTER CCCLXXXV. OF THE SAME MEN AND THEODWIN TO KING HENRY.

To HENRY, by God’s grace king of England, A., by divine favour cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and T., cardinal-priest of Saint Vitalis and legates of the Apostolic See: greeting in him who gives salvation to kings.

Lest matters which are done should come into doubt, both custom and a common consideration of usefulness require that they be recorded in writing. Accordingly, we have thought fit to commit to writing the injunction which we impose upon you because you fear that those evildoers who killed Thomas, of holy memory, formerly archbishop of Canterbury, proceeded to that crime because of the agitation and disturbance which they saw in you.

Yet concerning this deed, you have voluntarily made a purgation in our presence: namely, that you neither commanded nor wished him to be killed, and that, when the report came to you, you were greatly distressed. Since, however, you feared that what was done had been done on your account, you shall, from the present feast of Pentecost until one year has elapsed, give enough money that, at the discretion of the brothers of the Temple, two hundred knights may be maintained for one year in defence of the land of Jerusalem. From the following Nativity of the Lord until the term appointed, you shall take the cross, intending, with the Lord’s guidance, to depart thither in person in the following summer, unless this is deferred by the lord pope or his Catholic successor.

If, however, because of urgent necessity you go against the Saracens in Spain, you may prolong the aforesaid period for the Jerusalem expedition by as much time as you have spent from the time you began that journey. You shall neither impede appeals nor permit them to be impeded, but shall allow appeals in ecclesiastical causes to be made freely to the Roman Church—in good faith and without fraud or evil device—so that causes may be heard by the Roman pontiff and attain their effect. Provided, however, that if any persons are suspect to you, they shall give security that they will not seek harm to you or your kingdom.

You shall wholly abandon the customs introduced in your time against the churches of your land and shall no longer exact them from bishops. You shall fully restore any possessions of the Church of Canterbury which were taken away, as it held them one [Col. 0982A] year before the archbishop departed England. Furthermore, you shall restore your peace and favour and their possessions to clergy and lay persons of both sexes who were dispossessed because of the aforesaid archbishop. This we impose and command you, by the authority of the lord pope, for the remission of all your sins, to observe in good faith and without fraud or evil device.

The king swore this, and his son also swore to abandon the new customs. Both swore that they would not depart from you and your successors so long as you treated them as Christian and Catholic kings.

### LETTER CCCLXXXVI. OF THE SAME MEN TO THE CONVENT OF CANTERBURY.

[Col. 0982B]

ALBERT and THEODWIN, cardinals, to the convent of Canterbury.

We rejoice, and the whole assembly of the righteous which hears this rejoices, that God has shown in his sight the death of Thomas, of holy memory, formerly your archbishop, to be so precious, and has illumined his venerable memory with so many miracles, that the fragrance of his ointments now spreads through almost the whole body of the Church and his power is commonly proclaimed in East and West. Thus those who envied his blessed deeds while he lived now, after he has been removed from human vicissitudes and, as we believe, transferred into the fellowship of heavenly things through faith and priestly zeal, [Col. 0982C] venerate his power and render thanksgiving to him who alone does great wonders.

Since, therefore, it seems fitting that the throng of peoples should sing aloud the mighty works done among you, and that thanksgiving and a voice of praise should resound together, your church, which divine grace has enriched with so great a gift, ought no longer, under the pretext of the atrocity, to refrain from praise of its Creator. Returning to us an exchange of greetings and concurring with your request in devout assent, we command your brotherhood to summon those bishops and abbots of your province whom you judge suitable for this purpose, and with fitting solemnity, applying such moderation as seemed good to your elders, consecrate your church anew. If anything be lacking in solemnity, it may be supplied by the splendour of divine miracles. Indeed, if there is anything we can do for your benefit and that of your church, we shall do it willingly, as far as we can with God’s help. “We praise thee, O God.”

### LETTER CCCLXXXVII. OF THE SAME MEN TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS.

To our venerable brother and friend always to be embraced in the bowels of Christ, W., by God’s grace bishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See: ALBERT, by divine favour cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and THEODWIN, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Vitalis, legates of the Apostolic See—what God has promised those who love him.

Because we believe that you are waiting to hear something concerning our condition [Col. 0983A] and the advancement of the business entrusted to us, we have thought fit to inform your brotherhood by this present writing how God has dealt with us and through the ministry of our lowliness in these days.

Know, then, that after the illustrious king of the English learned truly that we had come into his kingdom, removing every obstacle of delay, he came from Ireland into England, leaving aside the business pressing upon him; and from England he went into Normandy. At once he sent several honourable messengers to us, asking in what place we preferred to meet and speak with him. At length it pleased us to assemble at Savigny Abbey for a conference, where we might be assisted by the prayers of religious men. We gathered there, and many persons of both orders from his kingdom also gathered; and we discussed as diligently as we could what concerned his salvation and the obedience laid upon us.

But, since we could not agree in all things, he left us as though intending to go to England; and we expected to depart for the city of Avranches on the following day. On the next day, however, the bishop of Lisieux and two archdeacons came to us; and, after what we asked had been granted, we proceeded to the aforesaid city. There, on the Sunday on which is sung “The Voice of Joy,” we assembled with many persons, and he assembled with us. With such humility did he fulfil what had been agreed that it may be believed without doubt to have been the work of him “who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble, who touches the mountains and they smoke.” [Col. 0983C]

It is unnecessary to recount in this brief letter how he took care to show himself God-fearing and obedient to the Church. His deeds sufficiently manifest it, and will manifest it still more fully, as hope has also been given to us for the future.

First, concerning the death of Thomas, of holy memory, formerly archbishop of Canterbury, he cleared his conscience, not at our demand but of his own will, touching the most holy Gospels and swearing that he neither commanded nor wished it, and that, when he heard of it, he grieved intensely. But because he feared that what was done had been done on his account, he gave the following oath concerning the satisfaction to be rendered.

First, he swore that he would not depart from our lord Pope Alexander and his Catholic successors so long as they regarded him as a Catholic and Christian king; and he caused his eldest son to swear the same. He also swore that for one year he would give the Templars enough money to maintain two hundred knights in defence of the land of Jerusalem. From the coming Nativity of the Lord until three years have elapsed, he will take the cross and depart for Jerusalem in the following summer, unless the lord pope or his Catholic successors decide otherwise. If, meanwhile, necessity requires him to go against the Saracens in Spain, he may prolong the aforesaid term by as much time as he spends on that journey.

He also abjured all customs which appear to have been introduced during his time against [Col. 0984A] the churches of his kingdom. He will allow appeals in ecclesiastical cases to be made freely to the lord pope, and cases to be heard by him and concluded by their proper end. If anyone should nevertheless be suspect to him, that person shall give him security that he does not seek injury to him or his kingdom. He will restore any possessions of the Church of Canterbury which have been taken away, as it held them in the first year when the archbishop was leaving the land. He will do the same concerning persons who appear to have gone into exile because of him. To these also he restored his favour and goodwill, and did this under oath.

He further promised freely to do other things which need not be set down in the sequence of this document. We have written these things so that you may know him to be obedient to the Church and much more earnestly disposed toward divine service than he has been hitherto. Know also that his son swore with him to abandon the aforesaid customs. Moreover, in order that no room for doubt might remain, he publicly undertook to perform again at Caen, in a larger gathering of persons, what was done there. Furthermore, he released the bishops from the promise which they had made to him concerning the customs and promised that he would not exact it in the future. [Col. 0984B]

### LETTER CCCLXXXVIII. OF THE SAME MEN TO GILBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA.

To the venerable and beloved brother in Christ, GILBERT, by God’s favour archbishop of Ravenna, ALBERT, by divine favour cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and THEODWIN, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Vitalis, legates of the Apostolic See—what God has promised those who love him. [Col. 0984C]

Since we believe that you desire to know our condition, etc. (The same as in the preceding letter down to:) And he caused his eldest son to swear this very thing in the charter of absolution for the death of blessed Thomas. He also swore other things, very necessary for clergy and people; all of which we carefully recorded, in order and exactly as he had sworn them, in his charter of absolution. He also promised, of his own free will, to do other things which need not be set down in the sequence of this document. We have written these things so that you may know him to be obedient [Col. 0984D] to God and far more disposed than hitherto toward divine service. Know also that his son, together with him, swore concerning the aforesaid customs. Moreover, what was done there he publicly resolved to do again at Caen, in the presence of a larger gathering of persons, so that no room for doubt might remain to anyone. Furthermore, he released the bishops from the promise which they had made to him to preserve the customs, and promised that he would not exact it in the future. On the following day the aforesaid cardinals held there a great council with the archbishop, bishops, and clergy of Normandy; there they enacted and subscribed the following decrees, and firmly and inviolably enjoined them upon all.

## LETTER CCCLXXXIX. BERNARD, BISHOP OF PORTO, TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0985A]

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, BERNARD, bishop of Porto.

Since under Christ, our one head, we are mutually members, your belovedness ought not to doubt that we care for your affairs as our own, especially since in your cause our own cause is indeed at stake. Therefore, if it should sometimes happen that we do something which, as done, may perhaps displease you in some respect, that displeasure ought to yield to reason, so that you may bear less grievously what we arrange for ourselves for a short time; and this all the more willingly because [Col. 0985B] everything that seems even to oppose you in your business serves you wholly.

For when the lord pope writes to the king of England seemingly contrary to his own purpose, he does so in order that, if perhaps—as we do not believe—the king does not repent on this occasion, he may not even regard the sentence passed against him as unjust. Therefore we exhort your brotherhood in the Lord, as far as we can, that, as you have begun and have hitherto persevered praiseworthily, you may be both strong and patient, knowing that if he does not now correct himself, Mother Church will by no means longer restrain her hands, but will strike him all the more strongly because she has endured him with greater patience. For his malice has now raised itself so openly against the Church that no one can now be found who would not wish his wiles to be struck down [Col. 0985C]. Farewell always in the Lord; and may the spirit of counsel and fortitude always remain with us all. Amen.

## LETTER CCCXC. GRATIAN TO GAUFRED RIDEL AND OTHERS

GRATIAN, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church and notary of the lord pope, to GAUFRED, archdeacon of Canterbury, NIGEL OF SACKVILLE, and THOMAS son of Bernard: may they so pass through temporal goods that they do not lose eternal ones.

It ought not to have escaped your memory how, after receiving an oath from you, we caused you to be absolved in hope of the promised peace. Since the peace that had been hoped for [Col. 0985D] did not follow, we notified you through the venerable men, the archbishops of Rouen and Bordeaux, that unless peace had been restored by the then approaching feast of Saint Michael, you would by no means thereafter enjoy the benefit of the absolution granted to you, but would firmly observe, without deceit or evil contrivance, the sentence which the archbishop of Canterbury should pronounce against you.

Since, therefore, peace did not follow and the aforesaid archbishop of Canterbury publicly placed you under sentence of excommunication, we command you, by the force of the oath you gave, inviolably to observe that sentence until you deserve to be absolved. May God give you a heart to worship him and to do his will rather than that of man.

Vivian wrote similarly.

## LETTER CCCXCI. THE SAME TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0986A]

To his dearest and reverend father in Christ, THOMAS, by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury, most valiant and unconquered athlete of God: GRATIAN, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, greetings and, after the contest, glorious victory with the peace you desire.

I receive with every degree of gratitude and pleasure the fact that, as I gather from your letters and messengers, you hold an undoubting hope and confidence in my sincerity; and for this very reason I continue all the more devoted and faithful to your fatherhood. For the same motives that first induced me still hold me constant in my purpose of devotion and fidelity toward you and in the defence of your cause: namely, fear of God, love of what is right, and zeal and ardour [Col. 0986B] for ecclesiastical liberty. To these is added the worth and grace of your person, which now more urgently presses and incites me, with a kind of anxious spur, in that which I had previously approved, since the pursuit of virtue and the filial duty of love and care combine to the same end.

Therefore trust in me, as you do, and hope that this hope, God being favourable, will not disappoint you; nor can my fidelity or charity ever grow cold or lukewarm in your cause. I think, moreover, that the matter itself will confirm what I say, and in witness of this fact your enemies will agree with your friends.

Indeed, in this matter, had the man come against whom your concern forewarned my devotion, he would not have differed from the other satellites of the same wickedness [Col. 0986C] and forerunners of Antichrist. But since he did not come, my concern did not slacken in what remained to be done and what I judged expedient; nor did my daily urgency with the lord pope cease until, by the lord pope’s favour, I obtained the letters which, God willing, you will see with these. I believe—and, unless I am mistaken, you too will believe—that they will be effective for the matter and useful to the cause.

Act therefore confidently; and, so far as pertains to you, commend our cause to the Lord, who does not abandon those who hope in him and through whom all things work together for good to those who love him. For my part, whenever occasion requires, I shall not cease to perform the duty of a friend and a faithful man.

Furthermore, I would wish your discretion to amend the custom in your letters of coupling misery with exile. For, to speak boldly while preserving reverence [Col. 0986D], as I judge, those whom the Lord calls blessed ought not to be called miserable, according to the Gospel saying: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5). May the Lord grant you peace soon, and in the future the fellowship and glory of the blessed.

## LETTER CCCXCII. HUMBALD, BISHOP OF OSTIA, TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, the bishop of Ostia.

When your fatherhood’s letters were brought to us, we were suffering from such bodily infirmity that physicians despaired of our life. Yet, because we rightly sympathize and grieve with you in your persecutions and distresses, even in our own illness, we offered urgent and repeated prayers to the lord pope through certain of our brethren and household, that he might oppose so great an iniquity on the part of the archbishop of York and his accomplices, and put an end to their deceitfulness and malice [Col. 0987A].

But he, as one who must answer many persons, deferred attending so closely to this business of yours; and this, by God’s working from above, proved somewhat better for you. When he had sought counsel concerning these matters from his brother bishops and cardinals, more were found for you than against you. We believe it was the Lord’s doing that those who had been accustomed to oppose your interests spoke for you in this matter.

Through certain of our brethren the same lord pope sought our counsel; and in pure conscience we answered him through those same brethren that the aforesaid archbishop of York ought to be deposed and his accomplices excommunicated. From his letters you will be able to learn what he has decreed concerning this. Yet we ask your discretion to bear it with equanimity and patience. You are indeed pursuing the cause of God and of the Church; hence we both trust and hope that you will soon have peace.

Furthermore, know that we have sent word to the lord of Bourges to transmit to you seven marks of silver and forty-five marabots. If this has been done, it pleases us; otherwise, take care to inform us, so that we may bring it to completion [Col. 0987B].

## LETTER CCCXCIII. HYACINTH TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 0987C]

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, HYACINTH, cardinal.

There is no need to express in writing with how fervent an affection we have desired your peace, since, even while we are silent, you read in your mind how great is the love that binds us to you. Therefore, having heard and learned from the tenor of your letters that he in whose hand are the hearts of kings has inclined the mind of your prince to restore his favour to you, we rejoiced beyond what we can say, rendering thanks to him who has deigned to regard the humility of your steadfastness. We pray him to deign so to complete what he has begun that the honour [Col. 0987D] of the Church may thereby be increased and that whatever guilt the said prince has incurred through fault may be washed away by his ensuing satisfaction.

But if the body that corrupts does not allow him to bring his mind back to this point of rectitude, we counsel and admonish you in every way to strive to instruct him in a spirit of gentleness, so that he may take care to accomplish whatever is lacking for satisfaction; and, restored to his former love and returned to sound judgment, may firmly show you the favour due to you and may answer, according to your wish, for the malice of your enemies. For we think this is the path your discretion ought to follow: that the man’s impetuosity may be restrained and the perversity of your enemies destroyed; lest, if you should wish again to take the path of severity when his mind is not yet firmly established in what it ought to be, he might easily relapse into what it ought not to be, and thus the latter error would be worse than the former. May the power of the Almighty avert this [Col. 0988A].

We have been diligent in advancing your requests, and the lord pope has willingly done for us what he could. Inform us frequently of your situation, so that, desiring to respond to your wish as to that of a most dear brother, we may be in accord with you.

## LETTER CCCXCIV. JOHN OF NAPLES TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

To his most reverend and dearly beloved brother in Christ, THOMAS, by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury, his dearest friend JOHN, by the same grace priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul: every greeting [Col. 0988B] and peace, and joy in perpetual peace.

Various letters of your graciousness have been delivered to us from different periods of your exile and our own vicissitudes. From their combined import we have understood that your mind, assaulted by the pretences of rivals wholly ignorant of the secrets of our heart and the pledges of our speech, has been strongly stirred against us. Indeed, this calumny has grown so powerful as to move you not merely to suspect us but even to condemn us.

We do not wonder that your mind could be moved by detractions and false reports; but we do wonder that your faith, confirmed by countless proofs and services of our love, should have wavered even slightly. For before we had become established at Rome, the image of the Church of Canterbury was already impressed, as though in wax, and engraved within us; we have preserved it indelibly and have resolved to preserve it as long as we live against every accidental assault [Col. 0988C].

Certainly, if in the cause which you have against the king of England we have said anything by way of dispensation or temporarily moderated our language, God is witness that we did it in order to soften an angry man and his angry mind, and thus, as if with a gentle hand, draw him to peace. It is assuredly to our gentle counsels, not to ecclesiastical severity, that the very favour which he offers is to be attributed.

Moreover, priestly gravity and honour require that one pursue with steps of humility, patience, and moderation the peace of so great a prince. Although that peace has not been offered fully in accordance with either your desire or ours, we ask and counsel you in the Lord, with a clear conscience, not to reject it in any way, but to receive it with such gentleness and affection that by your sweetness you ought to soften him toward what remains. A weak beginning is accustomed to be attended by better fortune. And princes, especially at this time, ought rather to be soothed than provoked [Col. 0988D].

## LETTER CCCXV. THE SAME TO KING HENRY

To the most illustrious lord HENRY, by God’s grace king of England, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou: JOHN OF NAPLES, unworthy priest-cardinal, greetings, and may you always obtain the successes you desire.

[Col. 0989A] It greatly pleases us, and in every way we consider it welcome and acceptable, that you have more readily enlisted our efforts to carry out your will. Although even without an admonition from you, whenever an opportunity presents itself, we are always eager and take particular pains, as far as lies in our power, to accomplish and promote whatever we know will be useful to you or conducive to your honour, and more earnestly to repel and drive far away whatever is contrary; yet when we are urged by the letters of your greatness, we gird ourselves all the more strongly and prepare ourselves more carefully to fulfil your request, both because your own admonition and urging are highly pleasing to us and because it is our wish and desire to devote all that we can, in every way, to the determination of your will.

Accordingly, we honourably and gladly received at the Roman Church your distinguished envoys—the abbot of Saint Augustine, the archdeacon of Salisbury, Master Simon de Carcere, and Master Henry—together with the letters which your excellence sent us through them [Col. 0989B]. We attentively and carefully considered your wishes and the matters you communicated, and we devoted earnest effort and exact diligence to securing the lord pope’s execution of your first request, or at least of the second.

But when all our effort, every exertion, and every ingenious endeavour failed fruitlessly, and could obtain nothing of the things he sought in accordance with the terms of your request, it seemed good to us that our efforts should turn to another remedy. We therefore asked, and, although with much urgency, nevertheless obtained from the lord pope such letters as were believed to restrain and trample down the rash presumption and indiscreet audacity of the archbishop of Canterbury, and by which it was recognized that, given the circumstances of the time, some satisfaction had been afforded you.

Your aforesaid envoys, who, as industrious and upright men most faithful to you, had shown the greatest zeal in carrying out your command, knew for certain that they could obtain none of your requests in any way. At our counsel, exhortation, and almost compulsion, they accepted those letters [Col. 0989D] which the lord pope sends you through them. Although they greatly feared and dreaded accepting them, because they had no command from you concerning this, they nevertheless yielded to our admonition, having been induced and compelled by us, as we have said; for we clearly knew that it was in no way expedient, at this time, for them to leave behind such letters.

We therefore, who love your honour with a pure heart and mind and desire, to the extent of our ability, to comply with your will in all things, praise and advise you to accept and receive what the lord pope presently grants you and to regard it favourably. Know, and in no way doubt, that, if you trust our counsel which we disclose to you through your aforesaid envoys, that archbishop of Canterbury, seeing himself deprived of all help and knowing with certainty that he can no longer return by any means to govern the Church of Canterbury, will himself voluntarily resign and humbly request provision for himself in another church where he may live [Col. 0990A].

## LETTER CCCXCVI. OTTO, CARDINAL-DEACON OF SAINT NICHOLAS IN THE TULLIAN PRISON, TO POPE ALEXANDER ON BEHALF OF GILBERT, BISHOP OF LONDON

Our venerable brother the bishop of London, etc. See under Pope Alexander III, years 1159–1181.

## LETTER CCCXCVII. THE SAME TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, OTTO, cardinal.

[Col. 0990B] We inform you that the lord pope, the whole curia, and we ourselves are well by God’s grace. Letters recently arrived at the curia from Genoa. They say that Guy of Crema has been received at Pisa. The archbishop has departed, the clergy have fled, and all the people despise Guy himself. The lord pope had sent to Genoa for galleys; and the Genoese themselves are faithful and devoted to the lord pope and curia. But because they think and fear that the emperor has made great agreements and promises with the Pisans for the reception of Guy of Crema, they still hesitate.

Therefore, what we confess to you alone is what we gather from the letters: if the cities of Lombardy form a confederacy against the emperor, they will provide galleys and other services [Col. 0990C]; but otherwise they appear likely to hold back. Whether such a confederacy will come about, we shall hear soon.

The archbishop-elect of Mainz, who recently departed from the lord pope and curia, expelled from his territory an envoy of Guy who came to him, threatening that, should he or any other envoy of the schismatics come to him again, he would have his eyes torn out. He openly proclaims the name of the lord pope. The emperor knows this and is greatly distressed. It is regarded as nearly certain in the country that the aforesaid archbishop-elect of Mainz will come to the feet of the lord pope. The archbishops of Trier and Salzburg, and nearly all the remaining princes—as they say, both secular and ecclesiastical—agree entirely with the archbishop-elect of Mainz, except the emperor, the archbishop of Cologne, and the duke of Saxony [Col. 0990D].

The archbishop of Magdeburg recently returned from Jerusalem. Captured by the Saracens, he vowed that, if he were freed, he would openly adhere to the lord pope. And he does so openly.

## LETTER CCCXCVIII. THE SAME TO THE SAME

To his beloved father and dearest brother THOMAS, by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury: OTTO, by the same grace cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See, greetings.

We notify your belovedness, dearest one, that, proceeding by command of the lord pope through treacherous and exceedingly dangerous places, we arrived safely at Venice under the Lord’s guidance, while our enemies lay everywhere in ambush. By the Lord’s working, their snares were broken and we were delivered.

From Venice we proceeded, not secretly but openly, with great joy and much comfort from our friends, through Mantua and Verona; through our homeland, Brescia, where we stayed for a considerable time; through Bergamo, Milan, near Novara, Vercelli, and near Turin; passing on to Saint Michael of the Clusa. From there we came safe and unharmed through Provence to Saint-Gilles, intending to proceed thence to Montpellier [Col. 0991A].

As the lord W. . . ., your friend, is about to depart for other regions—as we believe, according to what you know—having been sent by the lord pope, we send you our clerk, bearer of this letter. Concerning the matters which he tells you on our behalf, believe him firmly as you would ourselves; and whatever you wish to communicate to us, report it through him as certainly as if you yourself did so [Col. 0991B].

## LETTER CCCXCIX. PETER, CARDINAL-DEACON, TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

PETER, cardinal-deacon, to the archbishop of Canterbury.

We do not believe your prudent discretion to be unaware that the church of Blessed Mary, called the church of the Saxons, situated in Rome, was, by the provident consideration of the Roman pontiffs, spiritually assigned for the reception of English people visiting the thresholds of the Apostles, so that after varied and diverse hardships they might find and receive there, as in their own home, the comforts [Col. 0991C] of consolation and the provisions of charity.

Because of our sins, this church has come to such poverty that scarcely a few clerics and almost no laypeople are found there for the service of that church and the comfort of pilgrims. Moved by compassion for its poverty and distress, our lord Alexander, the supreme pontiff, granted that church letters of exhortation directed to England; you will be able to see their tenor. Since we recognize your uprightness to be ready and benevolent in matters known to concern the observance of religion and piety, we beseech your brotherhood in the Lord, in whom we have great confidence, graciously to receive Nicholas, bearer of this letter and canon of the aforesaid church [Col. 0991D], and, in accordance with the form of the lord pope’s letters, to deign, for reverence toward the Mother of God and in regard for our prayers, to grant him your own letters in support of those letters. Farewell in the Lord.

## LETTER CCCC. THE SAME TO THE SAME

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, PETER, priest-cardinal.

We recently replied to your concern through Gunter, your faithful messenger, in the way that appeared better and more salutary to us. But now that we have seen the letters of your holiness, although your consolation still appears to rest in words alone, we nevertheless approve the way of humility upon which you have entered and commend your counsel’s purpose: namely, that in your cause [Col. 0992A] you proceed with all gentleness and patience, so that by this means, with the Lord’s help, the man’s savagery may be softened and his mind led to better things. For it is very difficult to take everything away at once from stubborn minds, and

> No one can restore what nature refuses to restore.

Furthermore, know that it is our purpose to advance your cause—indeed God’s cause—as far as we can, and, with his help, to stand manfully beside you in Christ’s battle-line. Know also that, after your letters had been read in the hearing of the brethren, the lord pope, by common counsel, sends you his answer.

## LETTER CCCCI. THEODWIN TO THE SAME

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, THEODWIN [Col. 0992B], cardinal.

Although we have greatly doubted the report of your peace which we heard, considering the malice of those who stand beside the king and who are accustomed both to speak with the tongue and to ensnare the upright in heart, we nevertheless trust in the Lord that, when their wicked counsel has been made foolish and their malice laid bare, our expectation—which has hitherto waited patiently—will, with the Lord’s favour, obtain an abundance of peace sooner than hoped.

We have laboured effectively, as you wished, to bring to completion the matters for which you sent to the curia; and behold, by God’s grace, you are now able to see with your own eyes what we report.

## LETTER CCCCII

[Col. 0992C] To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, THEODWIN, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Vitalis.

Having learned and accepted as true that, through the preceding grace of him who reconciled mortals to those above, peace has been fully restored between you and the lord king of England, we exulted with inexpressible joy and gladness. From our inmost hearts we gave thanks to him who showed mercy to you and granted a result attended by rejoicing, offering him likewise continual prayers that he who has deigned to restore it may preserve it unviolated and increase it, as is fitting, forever.

Although it seems more appropriate and fitting that we should be taught and admonished by you, nevertheless, presuming upon our sincere affection, we put on another’s arms and attempt to offer some counsel to your fatherhood [Col. 0992D]. We therefore ask and earnestly urge that you exercise mercy, not judgment, toward those who have sinned against you; that you open, not vengeance, but a fountain of pardon to the guilty and to your persecutors. Thus, by word and deed showing yourself before men to be an imitator of Christ, your holiness may be recognized as doing, as is fitting, what you teach, and may deservedly be commended by all.

For by this your adversaries will be shamed in their hearts, while your friends will greatly glory in countenance and spirit. Rejoicing with your charity in every way over these and your other successes, we have gladly brought about both the fulfilment of your earlier petitions and the acceptance by your generosity of a gift of our affection. Through the bearer of this letter we send you a green mantle, which he himself chose among other silk cloths [Col. 0993A]. And, placing whatever we have at the disposal of your prudence, we stand always ready to do for you whatever may be acceptable to your brotherhood.

(See also the two letters addressed to Albert and Theodwin.)

## LETTER CCCCIII. WILLIAM OF PAVIA TO ALEXANDER

To the lord pope, WILLIAM of Pavia.

It is expedient, most blessed Father, etc. See among the miscellaneous letters to Alexander III.

## LETTER CCCCIV. THE SAME WILLIAM AND OTTO TO THE SAME

To the most blessed father and lord, by God’s grace supreme [Col. 0993B] pontiff, WILLIAM and OTTO, by the same grace cardinals: greetings and services of submission, as devoted as they are due.

Having come into the land of the most illustrious king of the English, etc. See the same place.

## LETTER CCCCV. THE SAME WILLIAM TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

We have conceived so ardent a zeal of sincere love toward your person that we have immovably resolved to take up all your affairs as our own, to cherish them, and with the most diligent endeavour to advance them in every way toward your honour, preferring to be found in some degree sluggish or negligent in our own concerns rather than in yours.

Therefore we received the letters of your excellence with very glad hand; carefully considering their contents [Col. 0993C], we endeavoured to apply effective care so that your wishes might attain a fitting result. Furthermore, we ask your fatherhood in friendly consideration that, having complete confidence in us, you may most securely lay upon our diligence whatever may please your discretion; for in matters which we recognize to accord with your honour and advancement, we shall always take the greatest care to apply ourselves and cooperate.

## LETTER CCCCVI. THE SAME TO THE SAME

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, WILLIAM of Pavia.

[Col. 0993D] Although, owing to changed circumstances, lest the Roman Church, suffering from schism, should incur graver losses, we may appear, in some persons’ opinion, to have turned aside toward various policies concerning you, he who searches hearts knows that love for you has continually remained in our breast. As we recall having often informed your vigilance, we took care, as far as possible, to avoid the suspicion of the lord king of England, so that in time we might intervene more effectively as mediators of friendship between you and him and preserve the devotion of so great a prince toward the Apostolic See.

Now, having been sent with our venerable brother Otto, cardinal-deacon, into his land to settle the disputes between you and him as we judge most expedient for God’s Church, we earnestly exhort and advise your vigilance that, so far as lies with you, you avoid matters which tend to generate causes of greater discord and strive more diligently to pursue matters which may contribute to concord [Col. 0994A]. For our part, as divine grace allows, without respect of persons, we shall endeavour to cooperate both for peace and for your advancement, leaving no effort unmade which, as the circumstances of affairs show with the Lord’s help, we may devote to the honour of God and his Church.

## LETTER CCCCVII. THE SAME WILLIAM AND OTTO TO THE SAME

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, WILLIAM and OTTO, cardinals.

[Col. 0994B] We graciously received your messenger and carefully examined the letters. Giving credit, therefore, to the messenger and letters, and carefully considering the copies of the lord pope’s letters, so far as we could determine through deliberation of our counsel, these measures do not now appear capable of being usefully attempted, since no hope of correction or amendment appears possible from them.

For the goods and property of the clerical brethren who are with you are being held by royal command, as, we believe, you know well; and the king’s mind, heart, and will are so turned away from you and from them that he cannot endure a word of reconciliation from anyone. Therefore, as we recently informed you through our messengers, it seems expedient for the present to defer these matters until God himself opens a path to peace in some manner, or, if none can be found, until the lord pope orders, after fuller deliberation, what ought to be decided or done in the aforesaid business.

For, in our view, with a short hoe and slight digging we might prepare a great fissure and a deep pit; from this it is safer to abstain, at least until it reaches the lord pope’s knowledge [Col. 0994C].

## LETTER CCCCVIII. THE SAME TO THE SAME

To the venerable and most beloved brother THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, the cardinals, greetings.

The king has learned what answer you gave concerning concord and also concerning the cause, should he wish to proceed against you. Already sufficiently angered, as he said, by your preceding actions—and more than sufficiently stirred—he has now been moved to fuller and more vehement indignation, unequivocally accusing the loftiness of your heart and the lord pope’s injury toward himself.

Moreover, when the bishops and abbots of the kingdom of England heard that you were unwilling to negotiate anything with them or to submit yourself to our judgment, they read before us, in our presence, the lord pope’s letters in which he says that he commanded you not to place the kingdom of England under interdict [Col. 0994D]. They also asked us whether, by accepting a legation from either or both of us in England, they could be defended from your burdens.

When we replied that we had no authority whatever over the affairs of the kingdom of England, they immediately appealed there and then to the lord pope, both for themselves and for the whole kingdom; placing themselves and the kingdom under the protection of the lord pope and of us, and setting the day at the feast of Saint Martin. Therefore we direct your belovedness, and command you on behalf both of the lord pope and ourselves, that, deferring to the aforesaid appeal and observing also the prohibition which the lord pope testifies that he has made to you, you undertake no interdict and no excommunication in the kingdom of England until the Apostolic Presence has been approached and it is learned what pleases the lord pope and the Roman Church concerning these matters.

The bishops and abbots themselves are also sending their own messengers to you, who will notify you of the appeal made in our presence and of the appointed day [Col. 0995B].

## LETTER CCCCIX. THE SAME TO GILBERT OF LONDON

To the lord bishop of London, WILLIAM of Pavia, cardinal.

The regard of that affection which a welcome association long ago contracted between us through friendly intercourse continually encourages and moves our intention diligently to pursue everything consonant with your honour. With God’s favour, our purpose in this matter cannot change: we shall always bestow upon your affairs the care which we would wish applied to our own, and would almost prefer to be found negligent even in our own concerns.

Moved, therefore, by consideration of this love [Col. 0995C], we are bound, when expedient, to commend to your discretion those whom we know to be faithful and devoted to you, lest perhaps those who work faithfully should, through silence or ignorance, be deprived of the reward of their service. We know, then, that Master D., an outstanding man whose many branches of learning commend him, has come to the curia on your business. He has argued in your affairs with such steadfastness and foresight, and served you so faithfully, that, even if his father’s interests had been at issue, he could not have been more loyal.

Since the knowledge, integrity, and learning of the aforesaid master have abundantly won approval and favour in the sight of the supreme pontiff and the whole Roman Church, and especially before ourselves, we, who embrace your brotherhood with special affection, venture through this exchange of letters to urge and advise you to treat the said D. with the honour due to so prudent a man, and always to promote his advancement and interests in such a way that, devoted already, he may become still more devoted to you. Thus we shall deservedly have reason to commend your discernment, since you have chosen so useful a person, who can assist in many necessities [Col. 0995D].

But if, as frequently happens, anyone’s envy should seek to act as a stepmother toward him and tear him with its envious tooth, let not your sagacity give it any credence, for we have found him most faithful to you.

## LETTER CCCCX. THE SAME TO THE SAME

[Col. 0996A]

WILLIAM of Pavia, cardinal, to GILBERT, bishop of London.

The bond of friendship by which we are bound to you and to the most illustrious king of England, together with our unalterable purpose of serving and loving you, strongly urges us readily to assent to those things that seem consonant with his honour and yours. Therefore, so far as our means permitted, we have endeavoured with diligent concern to advance the matters which you communicated to us by letter. For just as, from the time we came to know the lord king, we laboured with watchful effort to ensure that the Roman Church might embrace and exalt him with special maternal affection, so, since these disturbances arose, we have taken every care to urge that forbearance should take precedence over severity, and that regard for royal dignity and his innumerable services should claim a wider place with apostolic mildness than diminished devotion and reverence perhaps subsequently withdrawn. Thus, through our labour and vigilant care, no act of vengeance or severity has yet been applied; nor, God forbid, will anything of the sort occur hereafter. With the Lord's help, we hope to bring this about until, by God's mercy, the way to full peace is opened and the former love between the Church and himself is wholly restored. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCCXI. OF THE SAME, AND OF OTTO, TO THE BISHOPS OF NORWICH AND CHICHESTER.

[Col. 0996C]

WILLIAM and OTTO, by the grace of God cardinals and legates of the Apostolic See, to their venerable and beloved brothers, the bishops of Norwich and Chichester.

By this present notice we command your discretion that, after receiving in your hands a promise from those persons whom the Archbishop of Canterbury has declared bound by the bonds of excommunication that they will abide by our command, you are to absolve them when you see these letters; and, security having thus been given, you are to impose upon each of them whatever seems fitting to you in moderation. Whichever of you first receives these letters shall endeavour, as occasion offers, to pursue and carry out this matter; and, once they have received your command, you shall signify that, after taking the oath, they have been absolved.

## LETTER CCCCXII. T., ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, TO GILBERT, BISHOP OF LONDON.

[Col. 0996D]

T., by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to his venerable brother GILBERT, formerly by God's grace bishop of Hereford and now by that same grace bishop of London, greeting.

Do not take it amiss, beloved brother in the Lord, that we have laid upon you a greater burden, that we have called you to the care of a greater Church, trusting that this has been beneficially provided by divine mercy. Your character, your known religious devotion, the wisdom bestowed from above, and the good work you performed in the Church of Hereford have earned for you the words: “Friend, go up higher; you have been faithful over a few things; deservedly you shall be set over many” (Matt. 25). We have not entrusted Peter's ship, as you write in humility, to a man unskilled and inexperienced in navigation, but to one who, long exercised on the river, ought now to steer that same vessel on the open sea.

The lighted lamp which was, as it were, hidden beneath a bushel has now been set upon a lampstand, that it may shine far and wide in the house of the Lord. To the Church of Canterbury, which is in the kingdom of the English as the head is in the body, that of London is more closely joined than all the rest. By God's ordering we have transferred you there, so that from nearby you may help us bear the burdens of your mother, the Church of Canterbury, to which you owe all that you can do.
