Moreover, since the lord pope has specially committed to you the care of the soul of our lord king, where is it more fitting for you to reside than in the royal city, so that, coming there more frequently on public business, he may often be instructed by your conversations and strengthened by your counsel?

Do not then fear to come where your worth calls you and the lord commands you; you will receive consolation from our support and assistance, such as is owed to a friend and fellow-worker. We believe, indeed, that this is a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, flowing from the source of divine disposition, not only so that the Church of Canterbury may rely more strongly in its affairs on so great an aid, but also so that our own deficiencies, which we perceive in many respects, may be supplied by your blessedness. Would that, if it had been possible, you had come to London on the previous Sunday, so that we might have received your arrival with fitting honour, since we were then present there. But now, because our affairs have drawn us away from that place, we have entrusted our duties to our archdeacon, with the lord Bishop of Rochester also joined to him, if he can be present. May your brotherhood prosper in Christ, most beloved brother.

## LETTER CCCCXIII. OF THEOBALD, AS IT SEEMS, TO . . . . . .

We have received the lord king's letters, in which he complains that William, abbot of his church of Lisleshula, has been badly treated by you. He asks that the case pending between you and the said abbot be brought by us to a canonical conclusion, and declares that, unless you are willing to comply, he will not permit you henceforth to hold anything belonging to the said church. We have persuaded the said abbot to renounce every appeal, provided that you are willing to renounce yours and submit to our judgment; and under this condition he has renounced both appeals already made and appeals yet to be made.

Accordingly, if you accept this condition, we appoint for you the Sunday on which *The mercy of the Lord* is sung. Then, with the Lord's help, we shall confirm what you have decreed against the abbot, if it appears just, and annul it if it is unjust. The merits of the case will become clearer to us, the parties will be able to obtain justice without vexation, and the practice of religion in the Church may be restored, if the truth is made known through the parties’ assertions. In this way you will be able to retain the king's favour, which is most necessary; you will wholly lose it if you seek by any wrongdoing to oppress his church. But if you are willing to appear on the day mentioned, on the stipulated condition, write back to us without delay, if you please; or write likewise if the condition displeases you. For it is unbecoming either that we should be deceived by friends or that we should deceive others.

## LETTER CCCCXIV. OF THE SAME TO KING HENRY.

T. of Canterbury to the king of the English.

Although we are pressed by our own private troubles, we are more grievously afflicted and more intensely tormented by public storms. In our own person the hand of the Lord has visited us; by the scourge of His mercy He has now somewhat raised us from a long and serious illness. Yet more grievous than every bodily sickness is the storm of discord in our soul which, by the Lord's permission, has torn the Church apart and, by setting kingdoms and principalities in collision, has stripped the people of God of security and peace.

This is our daily affliction, the most just sorrow of all good men, the bitterest groaning; and it is the more bitter because, in your absence, we are uncertain what we ought to hope and what to fear. Therefore we earnestly beseech your serenity to deem it worthy to inform us, who are anxious, about your situation. For if your affairs prosper, we hope in the Lord that the Church of God which is among us will prosper. For it stands in unity and, with the Lord's help, will never adhere to schismatics.

The Gallican Church, however, as trustworthy report has informed us, has received Alexander and withdrawn from Octavian. So far as human judgment is concerned, it seems to have adhered to the better and sounder party, since all agree that Alexander's person is more honourable, prudent, learned, and eloquent; and all who come from there proclaim his cause more upright and more just. Although we have not yet seen a messenger or writing from either of them, we nevertheless know that all our countrymen, if your consent is present, are more inclined to Alexander's side.

We have heard that the emperor is trying to draw you to Octavian's party. But far be it from you, amid so great a peril to the Church, to do anything for the love and honour of a man except what you believe will please the Lord. Nor is it fitting, if you please, for your majesty to set over the whole Church of your realm a man who, without election, as is publicly said, and without the grace of God, has dared to seize so great an honour through the favour of a single emperor. For nearly the whole Roman Church is on Alexander's side. It is incredible that the other party could prevail or win through a man lacking justice and opposed by the Lord. On the other hand, our frequent reading recalls that those whom the Gallican Church received and fostered prevailed in humble circumstances, while those introduced by the onrush of temptation had an unhappy end.

Thus in our own times Innocent prevailed against Peter, Calixtus against Burdinus, Urban against Wibert, and Paschal against three—Albert, Maginulf, and Theodoric—and many likewise in the days of the Fathers. Therefore may your graciousness provide for us, and may God incline your assent toward that party which rests upon the truth of justice and, Christ being favourable, will triumph. In so great a peril to the whole Church of the Lord, if it please you, you ought to use the counsel of your realm, and nothing prejudicial to it should be determined without the counsel of your clergy.

## LETTER CCCCXV. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME.

Greeting from Him who gives salvation to kings.

It is superfluous, I think, to recount in words with what devotion I have served you, since the manifest deeds of many years attest it for me, and the witness of my faith is in heaven, with the knower of my conscience on high. My flesh is worn away; my limbs are exhausted alike by age and labour; and a grave, prolonged illness announces that the end of my days is soon at hand.

I had hoped, before I died, to see your long-desired face and personally to commend to you, in the sight and with the witness of Him who had entrusted them to my care in your kingdom, those whom God had commended to me. But because I am called sooner to His judgment, before whose tribunal we shall all shortly stand, I address your serenity by letter, prostrate in heart at the royal feet, before God the judge of all who is present. I earnestly beg you to hear your faithful servant, whose devotion toward you has never grown cold, now at the point of death. Hear me, I beseech you, so that God may hear you in your last moments. Hear me for the house of the Lord and for His little ones, whom I leave deprived of human comfort, so that the Most High may protect your house and comfort your little ones and your children for ever.

I convey to you and to your seed a blessing from the Lord Jesus Christ; and you, if you please, send the consolation of your majesty to those whom I leave destitute. I commend to you the holy Church of Canterbury, from whose hand, through my ministry, you received the helm of the kingdom. If you please, protect it from the attack of wicked men; and strive to appoint in my place, I who, though unworthy, have hitherto ruled it as I could and knew how, by the Lord's ordering, such a shepherd as will not appear unworthy of so great a see—one in whom religion is pleasing and who is believed pleasing to the Most High through the merits of his virtues.

I am your faithful servant. I owe you counsel; and behold, before God and all His saints, I give you counsel. In this matter seek not what is yours, but what is God's. For I pledge this to you on His behalf: if you faithfully advance His cause, He too will advance yours most profitably. After many disturbances, with God's help, we restored peace in the Church of Canterbury, promoted religious observance, and set suitable guardians over the order, according to our conscience. May your graciousness forbid any of them to be changed through anyone's rashness before an archbishop is appointed, and restrain those who will contrive divisions and new schemes. For we too have prohibited this under anathema and excommunicated those who presume to alter the arrangement of the order which we made.

Furthermore, we commit to your protection our dependants, clerical and lay, whom we have had as servants of our service and often of yours. We ask you mercifully to preserve what we have bestowed upon them and not permit them to be troubled through anyone's opportunity. Let my most merciful lord hear one further word and gladden my departing soul. As God inspired me, I have ordered that the remainder of our movable goods, and those things which, owing to uncertainty of life and the duration of illness, had seemed to be retained for household use until my death, be distributed to the poor after my death; condemning under an anathema already pronounced those who commit fraud or who impede their distribution for the salvation of myself, yourself, and your children. If you please, ratify my disposition and confirm it by open letters sent to your officials. For no gold or silver remains, but only provisions and things whose loss would greatly harm the poor and bring no benefit to you. May your serenity flourish for ever.

## LETTER CCCCXVI. OF THE SAME TO . . . . . .

[Col. 1000B]

We are more grievously afflicted than we can tell you or others, and have not yet fully escaped. Yet we hope for a saving escape, because, with the Lord's help, we intend to make satisfaction to Him who scourges us, and by present correction to avert the eternal scourge. Nor are we more certain of pardon because we are more severely afflicted by the present punishment of the body. For the Lord chastens every son whom He receives. We are therefore ready to receive bitter things with a patient and cheerful mind from the hand of the Lord, from whom we have so often received sweet things for our use. Thus, whether we live or die, we are the Lord's.

For we desire nothing else in life, although we defer some intended measure until, regarding the lord king, we may use your counsel. Meanwhile, with the counsel of religious men, we shall make provision for our house and our soul; henceforth, with God's help, we shall do so more effectively. There is, moreover, something which we have conceived both through religious counsel and from our own spirit: before our death, we shall correct all evil customs which have arisen through us in the archbishopric in our time.

Accordingly, when we seemed to be at the point of death, we vowed among other things to the Lord that we would abolish the custom of “second aids” which our brother the archdeacon imposed upon churches, releasing and freeing the churches from it. Under anathema we have forbidden its further exaction by anyone. And lest this benefit of ours—or rather, this duty—should hereafter be weakened, we have confirmed this very matter by our written instrument.

If you too had seen our present distress, you would welcome whatever you saw done for our salvation; you would prefer our soul to be set free rather than acquire money and infinite riches from our sins and damnation. Therefore, at present we cannot heed you concerning the burden of this aid without violating our vow and imperilling our salvation. But if God grants us life and the health which we have not yet fully recovered, we hope that the Lord will still provide for you through our hand in such a way that you will not need aids of this sort, and will give thanks to the Lord for freeing His Church in your time from an evil custom. We therefore ask you to accept gratefully what we have done, because the whole world would profit us little if we lost our soul.

## LETTER CCCCXVII. OF THE SAME TO . . . . . .

In deciding, by command of the lord pope, the case pending between our beloved sons, the canons of Merton, and the monks of Messa, concerning possession of the place called Acchab. and B., and concerning the damages which the canons complained had been inflicted upon them, we condemned the monks in favour of the canons: to restore the aforesaid place and repair their damages. When the canons, preserving truth and using moderation, assessed the total at eighty marks, we intervened between the parties and reduced it to forty marks.

Therefore we command your brotherhood, and order you by the authority of the lord pope, to compel the aforesaid monks, all pretexts set aside, to restore to the said brothers the place already mentioned and the money aforesaid, lest anyone be able to accuse you of negligence in executing the apostolic mandate. The fact that, as they confessed to us, the monks delivered the aforesaid property to its advocate ought not to help them, since one who by fraud has ceased to possess is condemned as a possessor. They are therefore to restore the place immediately and pay the money before the approaching feast of All Saints. If the lord of the property opposes you on any pretext, do not delay diligently to restrain him by ecclesiastical severity.

## LETTER CCCCXVIII. OF THE SAME, AS IT SEEMS, TO . . . . . .

[Col. 1001C]

You have consulted us about a matter that is not doubtful and which especially ought to have been settled by wise men rather than deferred. For no deliberation is appropriate concerning shameful things; a delayed rejection of shamefulness presents a certain appearance of dishonourable consent. What indeed is more shameful than, despising the authority of the whole divine law, to burst shamelessly into the Holy of Holies and, driven by avarice, to claim, against right and justice, a hereditary right in ecclesiastical property—indeed, at the very altar?

Who but a profane person could patiently hear, much less request, something which the sacred canons so manifestly forbid and which the authority of both Testaments so expressly condemns? Look through the canons, for they are very extensive on this point: you will plainly see that the request of those who seek such things is disapproved, and that the consent of those who hear such persons must be punished most severely. No room has been left us for dissimulation, since at the Lateran council, at which both we and you, brother bishop, were present, we heard such vows condemned by a promulgated canon while Lord Innocent presided.

But perhaps royal authority presses you. It would do so rightly, unless you knew that the Lord must be preferred to man, unless a prince's religious devotion could be circumvented, unless experience had already taught you that some things have been extracted from him by deception. The sum of our counsel, therefore, is this: obey the law of the Lord and the sacred canons, in accordance with your profession. Whenever such pressures constrain you, judge it safer to fall into the hands of men than into the hands of the living God. Yet perhaps there is a reason why you have deserved to be troubled over successions of this kind: you are excessively inclined, in fraud of the canons, toward unlawful resignations and substitutions.

## LETTER CCCCXIX. TESTAMENT OF THEOBALD, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.

The laws grant their favour to the final wishes of the dying, and he himself provokes the Lord's anger as though inhuman who opposes their pious desires. It is indeed our will—and, with the Lord's help, it shall never be changed—that the remainder of our movable goods, which we considered ought to be retained until the end of our life because of household needs and the duration of our illness, should pass wholly to the uses of the poor, according as the Lord inspired us.

We have given this as an instruction to our venerable brother Walter, Bishop of Rochester; to our faithful servants Philip, our chancellor, Master R[adulf] of Lisieux, and John of Salisbury, whom we have appointed to distribute our alms. We have charged all our servants and faithful men, by the fidelity they owe us, to obey them and place all our goods at their disposal. We humbly entreat all friends of the clergy, for the mercy of almighty God, to offer them aid and counsel.

We have condemned by sentence of anathema all who commit fraud with respect to the aforesaid goods of the poor, or who hinder the execution of our disposition. The king's officials themselves, if they involve themselves in disturbing this disposition, are to know that they are deprived of the communion of the faithful; as sacrilegious persons and excommunicates, they are to abstain from entering all churches. To all helpers of our disposition we grant the blessing of the Lord and our own; we make them participants in the benefactions of the Church of Canterbury and grant them a remission of forty days from the penance imposed upon them.

Furthermore, in the name of almighty God and under anathema, we forbid any official of the lord king rashly to stretch out his hand toward goods set apart for the proper uses of the monks of the Church of Canterbury. Rather, they shall possess all their goods in the same integrity and freedom in which we caused them to be confirmed to them by privileges of the lord pope and ourselves.

Moreover, under the same anathema, we forbid any alienation of lands belonging to the archbishop, as well as the cutting down of woods and damage to forests, until a successor is appointed to us—except insofar as the Church's necessary use requires, or the lord king has commanded with his own mouth, or discreet mercy, with moderation, has granted relief to the need of poor people. Under the same threat we prohibit the clergy of our diocese from being oppressed by undue exactions and unjust vexations. We order that all the liberties and just customs which they possessed in the time of William, our predecessor of good memory, be observed for them.

## LETTER CCCCXX. OF THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF CANTERBURY TO POPE ALEXANDER.

To the lord pope, the prior of Canterbury and the convent.

[Col. 1003A] “We more confidently commend them to you,” etc. See among the letters of various persons to Pope Alexander III.

## LETTER CCCCXXI. OF ODO, PRIOR, AND THE CONVENT OF CANTERBURY TO POPE ALEXANDER.

To the lord pope, ODO, prior, and the convent of Canterbury.

“The calamities which our Church has now endured for a full decade,” etc. See in the same place.

## LETTER CCCCXXII. OF THE SAME, AS IT SEEMS, TO RICHARD, ARCHDEACON OF POITIERS.

To his venerable lord and friend RICHARD, Archdeacon of Poitiers, brother ODO, eternal salvation in Christ.

Although the lowliness of my poverty may seem unworthy of intimacy with so great a man, your prudent excellence, preferring spiritual riches to temporal ones, has deemed it worthy to ask that you be joined to me in fellowship through charity and the favour of prayers. I trust that you have not yet consigned this to oblivion. Therefore, since I am bound to you by the bond of charity according to the graciousness of your will, and acknowledge myself under obligation to you in the things of God, I ought to have no small confidence in writing to you. Nor do I think it too presumptuous, for the averting of danger from my church, to make supplication to you by letter.

Seeing, then, in the appeal of the bishops—to which we are compelled to consent by the king's justices—that an eternal danger and lasting disgrace threaten our Church, I am placed in great sorrow over this with our whole convent, and prostrate myself body and soul at the feet of your mercy. With loud cries and tears I offer you the evangelical words: “Lord, if you can do anything, help us” (Mark 9). Would that you might answer me as was answered there: “If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes” (ibid.). To this answer I immediately add: “I believe, Lord” (ibid.). Nor do I add: “Help my unbelief.” For I believe perfectly and know with complete certainty that, if you are willing, you can most easily free us from the imminent danger.

It seems to me, upon careful consideration, that this decree compelling us, contrary to justice and equity, to appeal against our archbishop did not proceed from the mouth of the lord king. For if it had been dictated by his own mouth, it would surely have proceeded in this order: first all bishops, then all abbots, afterward priors of every sort who possess any authority, and likewise all archdeacons and all deans would have been summoned to do this, since it concerns them to defend ecclesiastical rights and make appeals on their behalf. Finally, if necessary, cloistered monks—especially those lacking an abbot and a prior—would humbly have been asked to complete the appeal, not forcibly compelled, particularly since such affairs are known to concern them least of all.

But now, while many abbots have been passed over, likewise all priors of both monks and canons, men of great authority; while archdeacons and deans with most of their synods and chapters have also been left aside: why are mere cloistered monks, without abbot or prior, specially summoned before all others to this disturbance of our peace and so violently compelled to a course so unlawful for us, so dangerous, and certain always to be alleged against us, throughout all future ages, to our utmost disgrace? Why do I say “violently”? Rather, we are compelled to do this with such great and unavoidable danger that, if we try to avoid the danger of royal wrath which threatens us should we disobey him, by consenting to the appeal, we immediately incur a greater danger: that which threatens us from God in condemnation; from the lord pope and especially the archbishop, in excommunication or at least in the destruction of our order; from all future archbishops, in a perpetual occasion of hatred and oppression; and from the whole world, wherever this is heard, in the shame of everlasting disgrace.

O distress! O coercion dangerous on every side! Far be it, far be it from the piety and prudence of our lord king that he should have pronounced such a dangerous command against us, whom, deprived of every human consolation, he has taken into his own care. He who faithfully undertook to be to us in the place of archbishop and in the place of prior—and has hitherto mercifully done so. He is our sole patron on earth after God and His saints, and from him alone we hope for consolation, counsel, and aid.

I am certain that this decree did not proceed from our lord king against us, his sons, always and everywhere most faithful to him; rather, the cunning of the excommunicators has circumvented his justices, so that they may compel us, who are at the head of the kingdom, to make an appeal with them. By this they think the archbishop's cause will be greatly weakened and their own, conversely, very much strengthened. But whether any benefit can come to them from our appeal is doubtful. That from it the gravest danger threatens us from both God and men is entirely certain.

Nor can it be safe for us in relation to our lord king to do this, whether without his special command or an order from his own mouth, especially since we are wholly dependent on his counsel. I know that neither he nor his men has the slightest doubt about us such as would make it necessary to demand so dangerous a measure from us. Let your belovedness know, therefore, and let the prudence of your companions—that is, the king's justices—know with you, and let the whole land know through you, that we truly love our lord king above all men who are on earth, and maintain, and wish to maintain, his honour in all things and by every means, according to our capacity.

The witnesses to this truth are our prayers, which we offer to God day and night with affectionate charity for his salvation and that of his heirs, and for the well-being of his entire realm, more especially than for any other person. That we may always continue to do this peacefully, as we have hitherto done, if you are truly a friend of both our Church and the king—indeed, because you are—you ought, so far as you can, to provide for our escape from the imminent danger and induce your companions, the king's justices and friends, by every means likewise to provide for it.

Therefore, so that you may find Christ, whom we devoutly serve in His Church, not turned away from you in your greatest need, as you saw in a vision, but turned toward you, as you again saw, and favourable to you; and so that you may make blessed Dunstan and all the saints whose relics are kept in our Church not accusers against you before God but perpetual intercessors for you with God: behold, I, in the person of the whole convent, lie suppliant and humble at the feet of your mercy, beseeching with groans and tears the goodness implanted in you, that you may assist us in this dangerous necessity, who place very great confidence in your counsel and help. By the power and wisdom given to you by God, free us wholly from this distress in such a manner that, by avoiding the appeal, we do not incur the lord king's displeasure, and by making the appeal, do not become an object of everlasting disgrace to the whole world.

I believe in Christ and trust in your goodness that, in this our necessity, we shall find the proverb true in you: “A friend is proved in need.” Consider Christ Himself as supplicating you for this necessity of His Church, and all the saints whose relics are kept in it as seeking your protection for the place of their burial. Farewell, my lord and dearest friend. Know with certainty that, if you free us from the imminent danger, you will always have our whole Church bound to you in perpetual service of charity. May the Lord Jesus Christ help in the deliverance of His Church. Amen.

## LETTER CCCCXXIII. OF WILLIAM, PRIOR, AND THE CONVENT OF CHRIST CHURCH, CANTERBURY, TO ALL THE FAITHFUL OF CHRIST.

To all Christ's faithful who shall inspect these present letters, W., prior, and the humble convent of Christ Church, Canterbury: eternal salvation in the Lord.

It is fitting and honourable to believe that matters which contribute to devotion and honour for the glorious martyr Thomas, and which concern the salvation of the souls of the faithful, should be proclaimed in the hearing of all. Therefore let all and each know that Pope Honorius, in reverence for the said martyr, granted and confirmed indulgences, in the following form, to those who come within fifteen days of the feast of his translation: “Pope Honorius, etc., to his most beloved sons, the prior and convent of Christ Church, Canterbury, greeting, etc.” (See the letter of Honorius inserted earlier in its proper place.)

## LETTER CCCCXXIV. OF ROGER, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK, TO POPE ALEXANDER.

“If eloquence were available to me,” etc. See among the letters of various persons to Pope Alexander III, after his *Regesta*.

## LETTER CCCCXXV. OF THE SAME TO HUGH, BISHOP OF DURHAM, AND OTHERS.

[Col. 1006A]

ROGER, by the grace of God Archbishop of York and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother HUGH, by God's grace Bishop of Durham; to his beloved sons R., dean, and WILLIAM of Canterbury; to the whole chapter of York; and to all the canons of St Mary of Southwell and St Wilfrid of Ripon, to the abbots, priors, clergy, and all the people established throughout the province of York: greeting and grace.

Your belovedness is not unaware how much I have suffered in this time for the dignity of our Church, in which envy was allowed so much license against me [Col. 1006B] that scarcely any place was left for truth. It is customary for all the wicked, whenever they can find an opportunity, to brand with slanders those whom they envy and to wound the innocent with the poisoned darts of words. This was done by those who have long lain in wait for me. At first indeed they prepared the noose of suspension, by which the lord pope, following their false insinuations more than the order of law, bound me. Then, lest I might by any means be released, adding iniquity to iniquity, on the one hand they sought out, by manifold artifice, the writings of great men, as they had been prepared to do for many years past; on the other, they suborned a crowd of foreigners and persons who had never seen me, so that, lying about matters of which they knew nothing, they might by whatever means [Col. 1006C] burden my reputation before the supreme pontiff and the Roman curia.

I was absent; and the few men at the curia who acted on my behalf could scarcely withstand so great a multitude, hard pressed by such elaborate lies—especially since certain persons, religious only in outward dress, seeing those men prosper in their wickedness, ran with them. Casting aside the fear of God, they spoke much for the overthrow of the dignity of our Church, together with the prostitutes whom they had brought with them, lest any sex should be lacking from my persecution. All these, assembled together, resolved in their hearts to imitate the giants: from great men as though from certain stones, and from many lies, from counterfeit sighs and groans which for a time filled not only houses but streets with howling by day and night, they built a wall; and that same wall they plastered with feigned tears, as with some indissoluble bitumen, doing violence to nature, hoping in this way to close heaven and consign truth to perpetual imprisonment.

[Col. 1006D] Why say more? That spiritual Pharaoh of theirs, whose members they are, seemed to ride in such a cavalcade with a crown; while I, wretchedly assigned to the servitude of the basket, looked for human help, and there was none. For, my flesh consumed, my bone clung to my skin. Therefore I lifted my eyes to heaven and, in the anguish of my spirit, cried to the Lord; and through the interceding merits and prayers of you all, He heard me for His own honour. With the hammer of His innate goodness He shattered and reduced to nothing the aforesaid wall; the Babylonians fled; and He brought forth the truth which had been kept shut up [Col. 1007A]. Having wiped away its prison-filth, He commanded it to go freely forth in public.

As soon as it was restored to its liberty, it swiftly flew to me, and in the presence of Lord Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen, of those whom the bishop of Amiens had delegated in his place—men to whom my case had been entrusted by the lord pope—and also of the bishop of Évreux and many religious men, both abbots and priors, it stood at my right hand, clearer than light. When the aforesaid archbishop and the religious men sent by the lord of Amiens beheld its grave and radiant face, they rejoiced exceedingly with great joy; and, making no delay, according to the form prescribed to them by the lord pope, they immediately absolved me from the suspension under which I was held. All present blessed the Lord, who humbles the proud, catches the wise in their own craftiness, frees those who presume upon His mercy, and brings forth the bound in strength. To Him be glory now and through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

I shall come to you shortly, God willing, so that my joy in you may be fulfilled. I desire beyond expression to see you. May the blessing of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit descend upon you as you pray for us.

These things took place on the Monday after the Sunday on which “Rejoice” (*Gaudete*) is sung, on the feast-day of Saint Lucy, at Aumale.

## LETTER 426. FROM THE ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS TO POPE ALEXANDER

[Col. 1007C] To Pope ALEXANDER, from the archbishop of Reims.

“Venerable brother and friend of ours,” etc. See under Alexander III, years 1159–81.

## LETTER 427. FROM THE CANONS OF REIMS TO POPE ALEXANDER

To Pope ALEXANDER, from the canons of Reims.

“Father, scandals are gaining strength in our times,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER 428. FROM ROTROU OF ROUEN TO POPE ALEXANDER

“Summoned by our lord the king, when we had come to the court,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER 429. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME

[Col. 1007D] To Pope ALEXANDER, ROTROU, archbishop of Rouen: obedience and the fullness of reverence.

“The desire to behold the longed-for presence of your serenity, enduring in our heart,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER 430. FROM THE SAME TO CARDINAL HENRY OF PISA

ROTROU, archbishop of Rouen, to HENRY, cardinal priest.

On behalf of the lord king of England, we give every assurance that he has neither personally nor through envoys sworn an oath or made a promise to the emperor that he wishes to adhere to the schismatic and abandon the Church. Indeed, we are certain that in whatever arrangements concerning marriage were being negotiated, although the Germans laboured upon the matter for three days, he was never willing to concede anything unless loyalty in all things to the lord pope, the Church, and the king of France came first.

[Col. 1008A] The empress lady and we have instructed her by your letters to clear herself of this reproach as soon as possible. When we were at Rouen and the emperor’s envoys were there, we heard about them but did not see them. When they urgently sought to see the empress lady, she replied that she did not dare because of the bishops. Nor did they see her. Let no doubt be entertained before you that she has wavered in any way. On the contrary, girded with strength, she is greatly astonished by such reports. We sent to her the messenger whom you sent to us; he will report to you what he heard.

[Col. 1008B] After the lord king’s envoys have returned from the emperor, we shall not delay in informing you of the whole truth of the matter, carefully investigated. From the tenor of these statements you may discern their falsity, because the king does not possess fifty bishops whom he could produce. As for us, we could neither endure nor, so far as lies in us, look upon harm to the Church. Concerning these matters, you shall communicate to the lord pope whatever seems right to you.

## LETTER 431. FROM THE SAME TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, from ROTROU, archbishop of Rouen.

When we had in mind to labour devotedly on your behalf, the command and exhortation of the lord pope came to reinforce our desire. He instructed our lady the empress and us to employ diligent efforts to reconcile you with the lord king. Therefore she and we, as best we knew and were able, wrote to him, exhorting, counselling, and admonishing him on behalf of the lord pope and ourselves.

[Col. 1008C] But in the letter in which he replied, asserting that he had neither expelled you nor compelled you to leave, he complained of you as follows: “It is plainly known how wickedly he has acted against me and my kingdom; how pompous, rebellious, and seditious he has always been towards me; and how wickedly he has attempted to defame my name and good reputation and, so far as he could, diminish the dignities of my kingdom.” Consider whether you have a suitable defence on these matters, and reflect in what humility and affection you may present it to him.

## LETTER 432. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, from the archbishop of Rouen.

We know that your prudence is aware that obedience is better than sacrifices, and that unwillingness to submit is the sin of idolatry—especially towards him to whom all obedience is due in the present Church. The lord pope, who has the power to compel, prescribed to us and to our venerable brother, the bishop of Nevers, a definite form according to which we should absolve our venerable brother, the bishop of London. The command further provided that, if both of us could not be present, either one, when requested by him, should nevertheless absolve him.

[Col. 1009A] Accordingly, when requested, we absolved him on the day of Easter, according to the form of the mandate, enjoining upon you by the authority of the lord pope that this be kept secret by you, as will appear more clearly to your discretion from the rescript of the lord pope’s letters which we are sending you. Farewell.

## LETTER 433. FROM THE SAME TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF ENGLAND

ROTROU, by the grace of God archbishop of Rouen, to all bishops, abbots, clerics, and other faithful of Christ throughout England, beloved by him in the Lord: greeting, grace, and blessing.

[Col. 1009B] If, as the Apostle teaches, we accept the law of charity, we ought mutually both to rejoice in another’s prosperity and to sympathize with adversity. Therefore, as we have deeply sympathized with our venerable brother Gilbert, bishop of London, over the sentence pronounced against him in whatever manner by the lord of Canterbury, so now we rejoice with full gladness of heart at the kindness and grace granted him by the lord pope. Let your brotherhood know that we received instructions from the supreme pontiff to absolve him, by apostolic authority, from the aforementioned sentence, so that on account of it he may suffer absolutely no mark of infamy, nor any loss whatsoever of honour, dignity, or order.

[Col. 1009C] As we were commanded, we took care to fulfil this mandate in deed; and by this present testimony we commend to all of you, beloved by us in the Lord, our aforementioned brother, solemnly absolved by us through the authority of the supreme pontiff from the sentence pronounced against him. We wish you well in the Lord, dearest friends.

## LETTER 434. FROM THE SAME TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF LONDON

ROTROU, by the grace of God archbishop of Rouen, to his beloved brothers in Christ, the clergy and people of the diocese of London: greeting, grace, and blessing.

[Col. 1009D] We make known to you all that, by mandate of the lord pope, we have absolved our venerable brother Gilbert, your bishop, from the sentence of excommunication pronounced against him by the archbishop of Canterbury. We received from the pope’s mandate the provision that, because he had been excommunicated, he should suffer neither loss of honour nor office nor a mark of infamy. Therefore, by the authority of the lord pope, we command you not to hesitate to communicate with him as one absolved by the lord pope, rendering him the customary and due obedience and reverence. Farewell.

## LETTER 435. FROM THE SAME TO KING HENRY

To his reverend lord H., illustrious king of England, from ROTROU, archbishop of Rouen.

We could not obtain from the legates the formula of words which you left with us, because many and ambiguous qualifications were being put forward on both sides, both by you and by them. Yet it did not seem consistent either with your honour or advantage for them to depart abruptly and without hope of peace.

[Col. 1010A] Therefore, while very many matters were discussed between us, a formula was proposed which in no respect derogates from your dignity or honour and furnishes Canterbury with no future matter for litigation. The formula is this: that, for the love of God and of the lord pope, you should permit the archbishop to return to England and should cause him to have his archbishopric as fully as he possessed it before he departed, and likewise restore their possessions to those who departed with him or because of him. We approved the brevity and simplicity [Col. 1010B] of this formula because it seemed entangled in no contrivances or suspicions. Therefore we advise and commend that you should not hesitate to give your assent to it.

## LETTER 436. FROM THE ENGLISH CHURCH TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

To the venerable father and lord THOMAS, by the grace of God archbishop of Canterbury: from the bishops, his suffragans in the same Church, and persons established in various places throughout their dioceses, due submission and obedience.

Those things which, Father, were troubled by the unexpected novelty of the event at your distant departure, we hoped would, through your humility and prudence and with God’s grace assisting, be restored to the serenity of their former peace.

[Col. 1010C] It was indeed a comfort to us that, immediately after your departure, report spread everywhere that you, living alone beyond the sea, entertained no high designs; that you raised no plot against our lord the king or his kingdom; but that you bore with moderation the burden of poverty voluntarily undertaken, devoted yourself to reading and prayer, redeemed the loss of past time by fasts, vigils, and tears, and, occupied with spiritual pursuits, ascended toward the summit of perfection through blessed growth in virtues. We rejoiced that you were applying yourself to such pursuits for restoring the blessings of peace, from which there was hope that you might call down upon the heart of our lord the king such grace from above that, in royal mercy, he would remit his anger toward you and would no longer recall to mind the injuries inflicted at and through your departure.

[Col. 1010D] While these reports about you were heard, your friends and well-wishers had access to him, and he sometimes kindly endured their petitions seeking to win you favour. But now, from the reports of certain persons, we have learned, with anxious recollection, that you issued against him a threatening letter: one in which you omit a greeting; in which you offer neither counsel nor prayers to obtain favour; in which you neither think nor write anything as a friend; but in which, with many severe threats, you propose that an interdict or sentence of cutting off is soon to be pronounced against him. If what has been spoken so harshly is carried out with equal severity, we no longer hope that what has been disturbed will be restored to peace; rather, we fear that it will be inflamed into a certain everlasting and inexorable hatred.

[Col. 1011A] Holy prudence considers the end of matters, carefully ensuring that what it wisely begins it also concludes with a good end. Let your discretion therefore consider, if it please you, whither this tends, and whether such measures can obtain the end which it desires. For our part, because of these actions we have fallen from great hope; and we who once conceived hope of obtaining peace are now driven from the very threshold of hope by a grave despair. And while battle is joined as though the sword had been drawn, there is certainly no place for pleading on your behalf. Therefore, in charity, we write counsel to you as a father: do not add labours to labours and injuries to injuries; but, setting threats aside, serve patience and humility; entrust your cause to the merciful clemency of God and the grace of your lord; and thus heap and pile coals of fire upon many heads.

[Col. 1011B] In this way charity would be kindled; and perhaps mercy alone, by the Lord’s inspiration and the persuasion of good counsel, would achieve what threats could not. It was good to be gloriously praised for voluntary poverty rather than publicly marked by all for ingratitude toward a benefactor.

It is deeply impressed on everyone’s minds how kindly our lord the king treated you; to what glory he raised you from exile; and with how generous a spirit he received you into familiar favour, submitting all the places of his dominion—from the northern Ocean as far as the Pyrenees—so completely to your power that in those regions public opinion regarded as blessed only those who could please your eyes.

[Col. 1011C] And lest worldly instability should shake your glory, he wished to root you immovably in the things of God. Though his mother dissuaded him, the kingdom protested, and the Church of God, so far as it could, sighed and groaned, he nevertheless strove by every means to raise you to the dignity over which you preside, hoping thereafter to reign happily and to enjoy the greatest security through your help and counsel. If, then, he receives the axe from which he hoped for security, what account of you will be on everyone’s lips? What recollection of hitherto unheard-of requital? Spare, therefore, if you please, your reputation; spare also your glory; and strive by humility to conquer your lord and son, and by charity.

If our warnings cannot move you to this, at least love and loyalty to the supreme pontiff and the holy Roman Church ought to incline you.

[Col. 1011D] You ought readily to be persuaded not to undertake anything that would increase the labours of your mother, already long afflicted, or that would augment the grief of one who laments the disobedience of many by the loss of those who obey. For what if—God forbid!—through your exasperation and action our lord the king, whom peoples and kingdoms follow by the Lord’s bounty, should withdraw from the lord pope, and thereafter choose to follow one who perhaps denies him assistance against you? What entreaties, what gifts, how many and how great promises solicit him to do this! Yet up to now he has stood firm upon the rock, and has victoriously trampled underfoot with lofty mind all that the world can offer. One thing alone causes us fear: that anger of mind by itself may overthrow one whom offered riches and everything precious in human glory could not bend.

[Col. 1012A] If this should happen through you, you will be able to give yourselves wholly to lamentations, and thereafter will have no possible reason to withhold from your eyes a fountain of tears. Recall therefore, if it please your highness, a course of action which, if it proceeds, will harm in every way the lord pope, the holy Roman Church, and—if you please to notice—you yourselves. But those who entertain lofty designs in your circle perhaps do not permit you to go forward by this route. They urge you to test what you are in relation to our lord the king and to exercise over all that is his the power which you possess. That power is indeed to be feared by one who sins and dreaded by one unwilling to make satisfaction. Yet we do not say that the lord king has never sinned; rather, we confidently say and proclaim that he is always ready to make satisfaction to the Lord.

[Col. 1012B] The king, established by the Lord, provides in every way for the peace of his subjects. To preserve it for the churches and peoples entrusted to him, he wishes and requires that the dignities due to kings before him and rendered to him be rendered. If any dispute has arisen between him and you concerning this, then, when approached and admonished by paternal grace from the supreme pontiff through our venerable brothers, the bishops of London and Hereford, he did not set his mouth against heaven. Rather, concerning every matter in which either the Church or any ecclesiastical person alleged injury, he replied humbly and gently that he did not seek a foreign tribunal but would submit to the judgment of the Church of his realm. This he is prepared to fulfil in deeds as well. He considers it sweet service, when he is admonished to correct anything in which he offends against God. He is ready not only to make satisfaction but also, if law requires it, to give adequate satisfaction in this matter.

[Col. 1012C] Therefore, by what right, law, or canon will you burden with an interdict—or, God forbid, cut down with the evangelical axe—one who wishes to make amends and to make satisfaction; who, in matters belonging to the Church, withdraws himself not even in the least from the Church’s judgment; and who bows his neck beneath Christ’s yoke? It is praiseworthy to be guided prudently by judgment, not by an onrush of iron. Therefore this is the united petition of us all: do not continue to slaughter and destroy by hasty counsel, but strive with fatherly grace to provide for the sheep committed to you, so that they may have life, peace, and security.

[Col. 1012D] What has recently been done to our brother, the lord bishop of Salisbury, and his dean also moves us all: against them, as some think, you improperly inflicted the penalty of suspension or condemnation before any dispute concerning the alleged fault had arisen, following, it seems, the heat of anger rather than the path of justice. This is a new order of judgments, hitherto, as we hoped, unknown to laws and canons: first to condemn, and only afterwards to investigate guilt. To prevent you from attempting and extending this practice against our lord the king and his kingdom, against us and the churches and parishes entrusted to us, to the harm of the lord pope and the disgrace and detriment of the holy Roman Church, and to no small increase of our own confusion, we oppose to you the remedy of appeal.

[Col. 1013A] And we who long ago appealed to the lord pope in person, with a living voice, against the fear of such burdens in the face of the Church now appeal again to him in writing. We designate the day of the Ascension of the Lord as the term of appeal, earnestly entreating, with all the devotion in our power, that you adopt a sounder counsel, spare your and our labours and expenses, and strive to put your cause in such a position that it may obtain a remedy. We wish you well in the Lord, Father.

## LETTER 439. FROM THE CLERGY OF NORMANDY TO THE SAME

[Col. 1013C]

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER, the bishops and clergy of Normandy: greeting and obedience.

## LETTER 440. FROM CERTAIN CLERICS TO KING HENRY

To their dearest lord HENRY, illustrious king of England, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou: R. . . . . ., abbot of Wallatia; REGINALD, archdeacon of Salisbury; R. . . . . ., archdeacon of Lisieux; RICHARD BARRE; and Master HENRY, greeting and faithful service in all things and everywhere.

[Col. 1013D] Let your Majesty know that, since Richard Barre had gone before us and, with much danger and hardship, had reached the court of the lord pope before us, we four, with two bishops, the dean of Évreux, and Master Henry, came with much difficulty as far as Siena. There we were detained for several days. For Count Macharius so blockaded the roads on every side that no exit was open to anyone. Since we four, together with the bishops, who greatly desired to depart, were unable to do so, placed in the utmost anguish of mind, we left secretly and stealthily at midnight by common counsel. Thus, through steep mountain paths and places almost impassable, under great fear and danger, we finally came to Tusculum.

[Col. 1014A] There we found Richard Barre, properly concerned for your honour and labouring prudently and urgently for your advantage, yet much grieved and distressed because neither the lord pope had received him nor had others treated him kindly and humanely. When we arrived, the lord pope would admit us neither to see him, nor to kiss him, nor to kiss his foot. Indeed, scarcely did most of the cardinals deign even to receive us with a word. Long troubled in the bitterness of our spirits and anxious distress, we earnestly begged in every way those whom we knew to love you more faithfully that, through their intervention, the lord pope might somehow grant us an audience. At their urging, the lord abbot of Wallatia and R. . . . . ., archdeacon of Lisieux, who were held less suspect, were received.

[Col. 1014B] When they introduced in your name, as on behalf of a most devoted son of the Roman Church, their greeting on your behalf, the entire curia cried out, “Wait, wait!” as though it were abhorrent to the lord pope to hear your name. Thus they came away from the curia and returned late to the lord pope, setting forth to him, by our common counsel, what had been enjoined upon us by your Majesty. They also recounted in order each benefice which you had conferred upon the archbishop of Canterbury and each offence and unwelcome act that he had committed against your dignity. They did all this first privately and afterwards before the lord pope and all the cardinals, with Alexander of Wales and Gunter of Flanders, clerics of Canterbury, arguing against them.

[Col. 1014C] As Thursday before Easter approached, on which by Roman Church custom the lord pope is accustomed publicly to absolve or publicly to excommunicate, we were certain that they had long deliberated, being as though disposed to do so, about imposing a burden upon you and your kingdom. We therefore consulted those whom we knew to be more faithful to your Majesty—namely the lord bishop of Porto, Lord Hyacinth, the lord bishop of Pavia, the lord bishop of Tusculum, Lord Peter of Mursa; Lord John of Naples was absent—earnestly and urgently entreating them to disclose to us the lord pope’s mind and what he intended to decide concerning you.

[Col. 1014D] When they brought back nothing but what was adverse and dishonourable to your highness, we perceived from their sobbing report, and that of Brother Franco, your faithful servant, that on that day the lord pope had irrevocably resolved, by common counsel of the brethren, to pronounce a sentence of interdict specifically against you and against all your lands on both this side and the other side of the sea, and to confirm the sentence which had been pronounced against them. Thus placed in the tightest straits, we attempted by every means, through the cardinals, those of our companions who had access to him, and his household, to make him desist from this purpose, or at least defer it until the arrival of your bishops.

Since this could not be accomplished in any way, we, as was fitting and as we owe you, being neither able nor bound to endure the disgrace to your person and the burden upon all your land, at last summoned our companions before certain cardinals and found a good and secure course for your safety and honour, useful to all your land and necessary for the bishops.

[Col. 1015A] By it we averted from you, your land, and your bishops the disgrace and danger which threatened; and for this deliverance exposed ourselves to the whole danger, believing and firmly hoping that the entire affair would proceed as we believe you wish, and as we believe you ought to wish. For, terrified by fear and with the intervention of those cardinals, we informed the lord pope that we had received instructions from you to swear in his presence that you would abide by his mandate, and that you would swear this in your own person. Therefore, on that same Thursday, about the ninth hour, the envoys of both yourself and the bishops were summoned; and in general consistory we—namely the abbot of Wallatia and the archdeacon of Salisbury, on behalf of the archdeacon of Lisieux [the printed syntax is uncertain], together with Master Henry and Richard Barre—swore that you would abide by the pope’s mandate and would swear this at his command.

[Col. 1015B] The envoys of the archbishop of York and the bishops of London and Salisbury likewise swore that their lords would abide by his command and would swear this. On that same day, however, he excommunicated generally the killers of the archbishop of Canterbury, all who had given them counsel, aid, or assent, and all who knowingly received or sheltered them in their land. The lord bishops of Worcester and Évreux, Robert of Neubourg of Évreux, and Master Henry were soon to arrive; we left them exceedingly anxious and troubled because, to carry out your affair according to their wish, they could not come. It was their counsel and ours that we should somehow precede them, so that we might prevent the disgrace and evil which our adversaries were preparing for us. For we were certain that a burden upon you was being prepared at the curia, and we feared the custom of that day.

[Col. 1015C] Of the envoys whom you sent to the lord emperor, we have heard nothing further. From what you sent me confidentially through Reginald, in the presence of William son of Hamo and afterwards the abbot of Wallace, we have conceived good hope that it will be done. May your highness thrive and flourish for a long time. Take courage in the Lord, and let your heart rejoice, because the present cloud will be followed by fair weather to your glory. We arrived at the curia on the Saturday before Palm Sunday, and the bearer of this letter left us on Easter Day.

## LETTER 441. FROM THE ENGLISH CHURCH TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

The English Church to the archbishop of Canterbury: greeting and due charity.

We know that it has not escaped your prudence that, already in the preceding year, we appealed to the lord pope and informed you of the same by letters sent to you. If you are unwilling to conceal them, you know that the grounds of this appeal are entirely just. For it is not lawful that one who offers himself to law, submitting himself and his cause in all things to the divine laws, should be excommunicated.

[Col. 1016A] Yet against our lord the king, who both sought and awaited from the supreme pontiff judges for his cause, you proposed with severity—if you please to consider it—a sentence of excommunication and the imposition of an interdict upon his kingdom, not rightly moderated. If the affair had proceeded in that way, we do not doubt that great loss would by now have resulted to our lord pope and the holy Roman Church. Therefore, lest through our silence and a certain undiscerning connivance we should permit Christ’s garment to be torn and His seamless tunic wickedly rent by your act, we appealed to the lord pope and preserved the fidelity due to him by appealing to him.

[Col. 1016B] The prosecution of this appeal would indeed not have been delayed, had not apostolic clemency turned toward us eyes of compassion. Sharing in fatherly affection the burden of ourselves and of you, and mercifully sparing our labours and expenses, as he himself testifies in writing, he sent to us from his side wise and honourable men, learned in law and most proven in equity, that they might examine this case fully and, assuming plenitude of authority, bring it to an end and impose a conclusion upon labours so long prolonged. We received letters of the lord pope concerning this, by which we are enjoined by apostolic authority to attend upon them, set forth before them the grounds of our appeal, obey their sentence, and omit no respect due in all things to judicial authority.

[Col. 1016C] We therefore took care to present ourselves before them together with our lord the king, alike desiring and requesting that all matters in dispute between our lord the king and you, and likewise those concerning us, should be done openly and settled by their definitive judgment according to the form of the apostolic mandate. It is therefore clear that those who are known to have presented themselves to their judges in order to undergo judgment have not evaded judgment. But what else is it to have deliberately contrived that those who came for peace should not perform the office of peace, than to prolong the disturbance of the Church and perhaps to resist with excessive vehemence that Spirit who says, “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9)?

[Col. 1016D] Since we have hastened to the judges by mandate and, behold, have no one to hear us, lest the evils hitherto avoided by the remedy of appeal overtake us, lest you exercise less canonically against us the power which you ought to have received for the edification of the Church and not its destruction—since we observe that your prudence does not keep the statutes of the Fathers: that, if you have any complaint against subjects, you allow them neither place nor time for defence; that you suspend immediately and do not summon; that you treat as notorious matters which are neither known nor supported by truth; that in your mandates you impose heavy burdens upon those to whom you write—to oppose your judgments, which are suspect to us, and all your mandates that bring any burden upon our lord the king and his kingdom, upon us also and the churches and parishes committed to us, we appeal to him whose judgment cannot be declined, namely the lord pope. We appoint the day of the death of blessed Martin as the term of appeal.

## LETTER 442. FROM WALTER, BISHOP OF ALBANO, TO GILBERT

[Col. 1017A]

WALTER, by the grace of God bishop of Albano and vicar of the lord pope, to his venerable and beloved brother in Christ G., by the same grace bishop of London, and to his beloved sons in the Lord, the chapter of the Hundred of Rochford: greeting and the fullness of all joys.

Peter, a subdeacon and bearer of this letter, came before the clemency of the apostolic see and, before the lord pope and us, recounted in a humble and tearful confession that, at the instigation of the enemy of humankind, he had killed a certain subdeacon. Therefore, by command of the supreme pontiff, we absolved him [Col. 1017B] from the bond of excommunication by which he was held, imposing upon him the following penance: for fifteen years, he is to fast on Wednesday on Lenten food and on Friday on bread and water; he may redeem Monday, if he wishes, by reading the Psalter or feeding a poor person; he is to observe the Lent before the Nativity of the Lord as the greater Lent, besides prayers, almsgiving, and other works of piety to which he is to attend diligently.

And because God does not judge twice concerning the same matter, although the said Peter committed the crime not while a subdeacon but while an acolyte, he may henceforth serve God and the Church. Nevertheless, through the dispensation and kindness of the most holy Roman see, our lord granted him permission to retain his ecclesiastical benefice in full. He commands your discretion to permit him, now absolved [Col. 1017C], to remain in peace and possess freely and quietly the ecclesiastical benefice which he has hitherto held, and never thereafter to harass him in this matter for any reason.

## LETTER 443. FROM WILLIAM, BISHOP OF AUXERRE, TO POPE ALEXANDER
To Pope ALEXANDER, WILLIAM, bishop of Auxerre.

“If one member suffers,” etc. See under Alexander III, years 1159–81.

### LETTER 444. FROM THE ARCHDEACON OF BANGOR TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 1017D] With what exultation of mind, with what joy of heart, our Church is deprived, being bereft of the presence of so loving a Father, we can neither set down with the pen nor express in words. For in you mercy so relaxed all things that justice left nothing unpunished; and although all suffer loss through your exile, we nevertheless are afflicted, beyond all others, by a greater misfortune. For when present, you cherished us with a fatherly affection of mind, and, when absent, you frustrated the snares laid by enemies against us. May God abundantly reward you for this, since from our weakness the means of making a worthy return have been removed.

Unless distance of place separated us from the delight of your presence, you would perceive more clearly the affection of our heart toward you—both through our offering you our own persons and through offering you, as to the Lord, our substance. As for your having deigned to entrust the governance of the churches to us unworthy men, we call God to witness that we have employed every diligence in our power and obeyed all your commands; and this we shall continue to do. Whatever seems fit to your solicitude for governing the Church, communicate it to us in your letters.

### LETTER 445. FROM THE ARCHDEACON OF BOURGES TO THE SAME

To his most beloved Father and spiritual lord T., by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury, V. . . , his archdeacon of Bourges: all that he is and all that he can do.

I have received letters from your Highness, stating [Col. 1018B] that you wonder why I have given you no information through myself concerning the arrival of the cardinals. Had it not been so sudden that I could not have known it beforehand, with what readiness and delight I would have informed you, He knows who searches hearts and reins.

But I, solicitous for you as a friend ought to be, although hindered by another journey, met them near Ralph’s castle. With diligent inquiry, both separately and together, I asked what authority they had received in their instructions for you or against you. Finally, as I inferred from the report of one of them and as I learned with my own eyes from the letters of both legations, absolutely nothing was permitted them against you, but rather in your favour.

Moreover, taking occasion from this, I began to urge them by every means [Col. 1018C] to take care lest they devise anything against the lord king of France, or against his kingdom, or even against you. I reminded them how grievously the lord king had taken the absolution of that John of Oxford. When, sent by the king of England together with Reginald the archdeacon, I happened to meet him at the entrance of the court, I first refused him the kiss he offered, publicly asking whether he was excommunicated. But what wonder if he blushed when he was turned into laughter?

At last, as the legates were departing, I received from them the assurance that, even if they had received authority against you—which God forbid—they would show a ready spirit and a devoted will to stand by you, insofar as this might lawfully be done. Henceforth, communicate to me through the bearer of this letter whatever you please; I am prepared to obey in all things and through all things.

### LETTER 449. OF ROBERT [ARCHDEACON OF OXFORD], AFTERWARDS BISHOP OF HEREFORD

[Col. 1019A]

R., archdeacon of Oxford, afterwards bishop of Hereford, to GILBERT, bishop of London.

My state of mind cannot be tranquil when I recall, in continual meditation, the disturbance of your tranquillity. Yet I receive no small consolation in this: as my mind diligently searches, no guilt deserving the present cause of tribulation occurs to me in your prior conduct. If this is so, the virtue of fortitude ought to shine in you all the more brightly, because your conscience—conscious of its own uprightness—bears you a more abundant testimony of innocence before the most just Judge.

Therefore, if [Col. 1019B] through the tribulation of this world your outward person is being destroyed, your inward person ought to be renewed day by day: as formerly in prosperity for moderation, so now in adversity for the testing of patience. For it is written: “Tribulation produces patience; patience, testing; and testing, hope” (Romans 5). Therefore I have great hope that, through the merits of your innocence and humble patience together, God will deliver you unto glory and honour from the hands of those persecuting you—He who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4).

Accordingly, with unceasing prayers I strive to implore almighty God that no stain of creeping indignation may ever cloud the eye of your customary discernment, lest—God forbid—you incur through a new offence of obstinacy an offence which you have not yet had in the purity of your conscience. It is good to be humbled, so that we may be exalted more gloriously. Humility is good: it invites the favour of the heavenly Judge and frustrates the counsels of the proud.

Joseph was humbled in prison, in fetters; yet afterwards, when the word of the Lord had kindled him, he was set over all the land of Egypt and was adored by the brothers who had sold his blood. David was humbled by a prophetic rebuke and afterwards, pleasing God, was restored to the grace of the prophetic Spirit. Mary also was humbled at the oracle of the heavenly annunciation, and deserved, by the power of the Holy Spirit, to be overshadowed for the conception of the Most High. Christ too humbled himself; [Col. 1019D] therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name above every name.

If, then, someone has announced the sentence pronounced against you, it must be treated with circumspect deliberation, lest you either comply with it in a dishonourable way or—what might perhaps appear possible—proudly and dangerously despise it. I say this not because I have supposed that your wisdom, sufficiently instructed in every distinction of the canons concerning these questions, could be taught by my insignificance in any taint of presumption. But I cannot conceal the affection I have for your honour. I offer this, certainly, in proportion to my smallness: procure swift remedies while the disease is still fresh, lest, once chronic, it require a more difficult cure.

For [Col. 1020A] it must be feared lest what has been done be fortified by the force of a greater authority. Yet to fear even this would certainly be full of impiety, not to say sacrilege. For who would dare to think that the foundation of the ecclesiastical rock has been so overthrown that apostolic authority may break not only the rule of apostolic canons, but may also, by a change born of human presumption, so to speak profane that evangelical order consecrated by the ordinance of the Lord’s own mouth? For the Lord himself says: “A servant is not greater than his lord, nor an apostle greater than him who sent him” (John 13).

Thus no reasoning can persuade me that by apostolic authority even the least member of Christ’s body—much less an orthodox bishop—not warned, not regularly summoned, unheard, undefended, in no respect obstinate, and liable to no accusation of notorious crime, may lawfully be cut off from Christ’s own body. May almighty God strengthen your heart with the spirit of his wisdom, and fortify your actions with the spirit of counsel and fortitude, so that you may resist the assaults of present temptations as prudently as bravely. I, certainly, however small a portion of your creation I may be, shall be ready, if you command, to expend not only my resources but myself for your honour. May my lord prosper in Christ.

### LETTER 456. FROM WILLIAM OF NORWICH TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, WILLIAM, bishop of Norwich.

In accordance with the terms of your Holiness’s command, we have absolved the clerics from the land of Count Hugh who, after the pope’s interdict in his territory, presumed to celebrate divine offices. We received from them an oath that they would abide by your order, and forbade them to celebrate divine offices. Among their number are the bearers of this letter, the priests Gilbert and Baldwin. We send them suspended to the feet of your Holiness, with the testimony of our letter, because, coming to us in misery, they obtained this from us, hoping that your mercy would come before rather than await judgment. Fare well always.

### LETTER 459. FROM PETER OF PAVIA TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, PETER, bishop of Pavia: greeting and every good.

The Wise Man speaks thus: “Cold water to a thirsty soul, and good news from a far country” (Proverbs 25). Your gracious condescension has enabled me to experience how true that saying is. For by the blessing and greeting which you sent me from a far country, as a sign of your exceptional affection, you have indeed greatly refreshed my soul, which has thirsted for you ever since the day when I deserved to know and see you and to be received [Col. 1021D] among the intimacies of your friendship.

To such gracious condescension my humility returns, if not the thanks it ought, at least the thanks it can. I pray also that He, for whose love you both love and honour me, though unworthy, with such affection, may render you grace on my behalf. Henceforth, reverend Father, with filial boldness I beg you as a father, and counsel you as a friend: do not fail in the tribulations which have found you in abundance, especially since this is the way by which one goes to God.

For, according to the Apostle, since all things work together for good to those who love God, Christ’s soldier is tested in this worldly arena through prosperity and adversity, by patience, like gold in a furnace. Finally, just as for the elect tribulation produces patience, patience testing, and testing hope—which neither is put to shame nor puts to shame when supported by love—so conversely for the reprobate tribulation produces impatience, impatience faintheartedness, faintheartedness sadness, and sadness destroys, when through it the mind is swallowed up in despair.

Therefore act manfully; let your heart be strengthened. Let no one’s persuasion—God forbid—lead you to suppose that you ought to yield. Rather, do what you do and hold what you hold, so that from the supreme shepherd you may receive the full reward for the flock entrusted to you. This I counsel you as faithfully as I do amicably. Would that I could persuade myself of it also. This is wholesome for us and worthy of imitation by those committed to us: that by acting rightly, enduring whatever God wills and for as long as he wills, and cleaving to his footsteps, we may honour our ministry.

Because you commend yourself so earnestly to the prayers [Col. 1022B] of my lowliness, I am ashamed when I measure my own merits, but I embrace your devotion when I consider it. Whatever love and service I can render for you before God and human beings, know that it is yours on every day. And would that a place and time might present themselves when I may openly prove how purely I love you, not so much in word and speech as in deed and truth. Farewell.

### LETTER 460. FROM MAURICE OF PARIS TO POPE ALEXANDER

To the most holy Father and lord ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff and universal pope, MAURICE, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Paris: the fullness of obedience, service, and devotion.

[Col. 1022C] Let your Highness know, most serene Father, that recently negotiations took place near Paris for restoring peace between the king of England and the lord of Canterbury, etc. See under Alexander III, years 1159–81.

### LETTER 461. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME

To Pope ALEXANDER, MAURICE, bishop of Paris.

License to sin both begets and nourishes offences; and people rush on to greater crimes while they sin in the security of impunity. That bishop of London lay hidden for some time, etc. See there.

### LETTER 462. FROM JOHN OF POITIERS TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 1022D] To his most reverend lord and father, most blessed THOMAS, by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury, his JOHN, by the same grace humble priest of the Church of Poitiers: greeting and the strength of holy perseverance.

After receiving your letters, my lord, I scarcely allowed myself even a single day to prepare for the journey; indeed, after reading those letters, even the delay of one hour was hateful to me. They contained nothing but an earnest entreaty that I should render my service in a matter so necessary that, unless it were obtained, your conscience would not, as you declare, be free from scruple.

I confess, my lord, that those little letters drew tears from me. Their so earnest entreaty, made under such an imprecation, seemed to imply—I know not what—some doubt about a friend’s fidelity. Yet, with my lord’s leave, I would rather that you should be found a little distrustful, in accordance with the meaning of our name, than that I should be found less devoted.

And although, as you commanded, in undertaking this journey I disregarded the talk of my Poitevins, I nevertheless wished, without impairing the faithful conduct of the business, to avoid their frivolity. Therefore I publicly announced that I would meet at Tours the bishop of Évreux, Richard de Humet the constable, William son of Hamo, and the other officials of the king, who were to assemble there at the same time to negotiate concerning peace between the counts of Auvergne.

For I had to test the reliability of their counsel because of the unheard-of harshness of the new commands [Col. 1023B] which our One-Eyed Man—whose mind’s eye God has wholly blinded—and Simon de Turnebu, constable of Thouars, had brought from the king’s side. A few days after the feast of the Apostles’ Nativity, they had come to Poitiers and had drawn me aside alone, as though they held secret instructions for me; yet they brought with them Henry Panetarius, who, if necessary, was to be a witness that the mission entrusted to them had been faithfully carried out.

Though they pressed hard for me to bring with me even one person—whether an abbot, since I had several with me there, or any person of my Church, or at least a canon—this was not granted, because they had received commands to be delivered to me alone and not to those others. Under a strict threat, therefore, they prohibited me from assuming anything pertaining to the king’s dignity.

When I answered that I would willingly obey this command, they finally came to particulars. They prohibited me from summoning any of my parishioners into court, upon the complaints of widows, orphans, or clerics, concerning any immovable property, until the king’s officials, or those of the lords to whose fief the disputed property belonged, had failed to do them justice. Next, they forbade me to hear anyone upon an accusation of usury. Further, they forbade me to pronounce a sentence of anathema against any baron without consulting them—indeed, until they themselves should bring him before me for justice in those matters in which they ought to do so.

These were almost the matters in which I was said to act against royal dignity: above all, concerning clerics, whose estates, when they had devolved to those men under whatever title, I was said irreverently to protect from payment of base and personal dues. A penalty was also attached to all these matters if I should henceforth usurp them. For although, as they said, harsher commands had been imposed concerning my own person, they nevertheless spared me even at their own risk and extended to others the punishment laid upon themselves: namely, if anyone came in response to my summons to answer the aforesaid privileged persons, all that person’s goods would be confiscated, and he himself would be committed to public prison because he had answered before us.

In an accusation of usurers, the same penalty would be imposed both upon the accuser [Col. 1024A] who came to us and upon the accused who answered before us. If I pronounced a sentence of excommunication, without consulting them, either against these persons because they refused to answer before us, or against any others holding directly from the king, they were to know that it would not displease the king if those excommunicated laid hands upon my person, ravaged my goods, or attacked the persons or goods of my clerics who, at my command, pronounced such sentences or observed sentences already pronounced.

To this I answered them respectfully and humbly that I must refer all these matters, although I had heard them alone, to the conscience of my Church: for these were the liberties of that Church, which I had used hitherto and from which I was now forbidden to benefit. If I renounced them all without consulting the Church, nothing would be accomplished except what might recoil to the danger of my life.

But when, after communicating with our church, they learned that I would nevertheless persist in asserting our liberty, they first publicly proclaimed their edicts before many barons of Poitou and then before our citizens. Thus, as I said above, I received an occasion to go to Tours and to explore the counsel of the king’s other officials. I added that, if I could not obtain from them a definite form of reliable counsel, it would be useful to investigate the matter at Sens through the pope’s secretary.

Under cover of this consultation, when I arrived at Tours, I found that the aforesaid royal officials had already, having settled their plan to proceed into Auvergne, departed that day for the castle called Luchia.
