I pursued them without interruption as far as that castle; there I found William son of Hamo and Hugh de Cleers. The others had set out before dawn for Ralph’s castle. Since I found among them almost no counsel concerning the business of my Church, I nevertheless rejoiced that I had an opportunity to meet Hugh de Cleers himself regarding the letters you were sending him.

When I noticed that his clerk G. was not present, I added that I had received instructions from you that, if he were absent, I should take his place in reading the letters, in communicating them after they had been read, and also in writing back to you if he wished to reply. Since he did not have time for what he wished to write in reply, he obtained from me permission faithfully to receive in his own hand the letter which you were sending to his G. He promised on his faith to keep the letter which I had read to him until he wrote a reply to it, and that no eye but that of the said G. would inspect it.

And he, as far as appears to me, sympathizes with the injuries inflicted upon God’s Church—if perhaps not wholly from regard for God, yet, I believe, from regard for his lord’s affection. For, so far as I can perceive, he fears lest his lord be struck by God, whom he seems to offend in the things he does.

I, however, pursued the lord of Évreux and those travelling ahead with him only by letter, continued upon my intended journey, and from the same castle—that is, from Luchia—sent the bearer of this letter back to you. I also sent a courier ahead, by whom I invite the abbot of Pontigny to meet me at the curia, so that he may cooperate with us in your affair along with the abbots of Clairvaux and Fossanova of his order, should we happen to find them at the curia.

When these matters have been completed, as God permits, we shall take care to send you a messenger, through whom we shall strive to report to you whatever concerns either you or us and seems worthy of your knowledge. Henceforth I beseech your fatherhood on behalf of your clerk, my friend Thurstan de Burins: let him be permitted by your favour to come and see me even once. If he is necessary for your service, we shall send him back to you immediately. Fare well.

### LETTER 463. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME

To his most reverend lord and most holy Father THOMAS, by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury, his JOHN, humble priest of the Church of Poitiers: greeting and the spirit of fortitude.

Diligence in sending the blessing of your letters would have forestalled my delay, had not a lingering illness, as the bearer of this letter told us, detained him. Thus I owe it to the benefit of this sickness that I can excuse my silence to you—or rather, that my negligence has plainly not been detected.

But, to speak more truly, and, with due reverence for your Majesty, more freely and openly: neither of us appears rightly excusable, while we fear I know not what things that ought not to be feared, and veil our negligence under the name of caution, as though snares were spread for those going from you to us, or conversely. The necessity of that friendship, by which mutual affection of charity bound us without interruption to this day, from the first years of our early youth through every envy directed at our lot or condition, admits no excuses of this kind.

Now, however, distance of place or inequality of dignities will seem to have somewhat obscured the title of our former affection if we spare the labours of the couriers who travel between us; if each does not make his concern fully known to the other, so that we may seem to have removed every injury caused by local separation. Therefore, I beseech you, most serene lord, let this pretext of excuse cease henceforth; and let us grant to little sheets of writing what has been denied to speech. Let us express by letters what we cannot express in words.

Let us not be ungrateful to the inventors of letters. Anyone who, without an evident necessity, fails to make use of their benefit will seem to have diminished something from their merit. Nor should it be overlooked that, by God’s grace, none of our messengers has yet been able to complain of the wrong of being intercepted. But suppose—even though God forbid—that someone should meanwhile be detected: who could rightly be indignant if we lament to one another the injuries done to God’s Church and to ourselves? Who will forbid those beaten and wronged to weep? Shall our tears flow down our cheeks with impunity?

Finally, even if we were entirely silent and exchanged nothing by speech or writing, it is alleged that both we do everything by your counsel and you by ours. This is true if the same spirit of counsel inspires us both, so that we do not endure with equanimity the attacks which, in punishment for our sins, we see inflicted upon ourselves and the Church of God. For if we are God’s ministers, we certainly conduct these matters by a common—that is, divine—counsel: we do not look with dry eyes upon those destroying the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts; we pursue, at least with tears, the ruin of the house of Israel.

Although we have not opposed them with the perseverance which we certainly ought to have displayed; although we have not yet resisted unto blood; although, because of the difficulties of the times and the division of our mother, the holy Roman Church, we have overlooked much: nevertheless, by God’s grace no one can say that we have yet yielded to their threats or consented to their impious counsels. Rather, when opportunity presents itself, we shall be able freely to intervene in order to annul those things which were wrongly done and which can be annulled.

For I continually give thanks to God because, as I know with complete certainty both from the faithful report of others and now from the reliable testimony of your letter, you have not promised absolutely to observe those detestable and profane customs which have been promulgated in our days under the pretext of innovation, as their innovator boasts; nor, like the others, have you strengthened them by the sanction of your written act.

But you need not fear anything concerning the granting of the English legation if any faith can be placed in apostolic words. For he redeems by grievous penance that concession, whatever it was, which he had made to the archbishop of York. Nor should my lord take it ill that I refrain from more frequent visits to the lord pope and the curia. Deliberately, so far as I can, I avoid the slanders of our Poitevins. Whenever I went there, they never ceased to write to the king that I was plotting many things at the curia to disparage him and injure his enactments.

I therefore thought it more prudent to entrust both your affairs and mine to discreet and religious persons, and to employ their services in this matter. This I had done a few days before receiving your letters, at the time when I sent my pagan kinsman to you. For, having found an opportunity through the venerable man and incomparably holy lord abbot of Pontigny, who had come into our parts both from affection for us and to visit the abbeys which he has in our diocese, I entrusted to his care the safer conveyance to the lord pope of many matters concerning both you and me—especially concerning the question of the legation and of Saint Augustine.

For through our common friend, Lord Henry of Pisa, I had learned more fully how the letters concerning the legation had been returned to the lord pope amid insults mixed with indignation, and how, at the request of certain cardinals, stricter letters commanding you to bless the abbot of Saint Augustine had been sent, as if to appease the king’s anger.

Although the aforesaid abbot, through his prudence, religious standing, and the services he frequently renders them, has much influence at the curia, yet, if you command it and think it more useful for yourself, I fear neither the tongues of those who slander you nor the displeasure of him before whom they slander you. I do not so seek either to avoid bodily labour or to spare expense that, at the command of your instruction, I would fail to go up to them in person—counting no labour difficult in which I can serve the interests of my mother, the holy Church of Canterbury.

Nor, as it seems to me, is there reason for you to complain excessively about the lord pope’s urgent command concerning blessing the abbot of Saint Augustine, especially since, as I have heard, it was added that, if you should continue to refrain from blessing him, the pope himself would bless him if he came to him. Thus either freedom to depart will be open to you for the pursuit of your right; or, if it is so manifestly denied, whatever is done under such manifest coercion may, when the time is favourable, be treated as undone.

I advise your Holiness to enter into a closer friendship with the aforesaid abbot of Pontigny, whether in person, if you come into the regions of Gaul under pretext of your cause, or by your letters, if you are not granted leave to depart. Both I and our common friend, namely Isaac, abbot of Stella, have properly arranged that that most holy community of Pontigny may continually remember you in its prayers. You will also find that same house ready, if necessary, to serve even your temporal interests; for, by the skill and holiness of its aforesaid abbot, it has more influence than all the abbeys of the Cistercian order. And there, speaking as though to trustworthy ears, I have chosen a place of exile for myself when I can no longer endure the harassment of our tormentor.

As for your writing that I should entrust your business to no one except the supreme pontiff and our Pisan, you should, unless I am mistaken, also have added Cardinal Master Albert of Saint Lawrence. I consider him a servant of your advancement, not so much for regard to your person as to your cause, because he both declares and recognizes that you have undertaken not your own cause but the Church’s.

Nevertheless, unless I receive a new command from you, I shall not for the present transgress the limits prescribed to me. I would have written to you concerning Octavian’s wretched death and Guy of Crema’s execrable substitution, except that I know that our men who remain at the curia know all these matters more fully, and through them they ought to be made known to you more reliably. News of this kind comes down to us only from them and through them.

My household situation, which by God’s grace you command me to describe to you, has undergone no change since the departure of our pagan kinsman, through whom I instructed that everything be communicated to you orally. For our One-Eyed Man, who has returned to us in fullness of power but not fullness of light, has not yet promulgated his edicts. He has only summoned the forces of Aquitaine, so that they may meet the king of France with a strong hand if he persists in proceeding into Auvergne, as he intended.

Nevertheless, the lord of Évreux and Richard de Humez have been sent to the king to negotiate peace, as I believe you know. What they have accomplished had not yet reached us. When we learn the rest and find a trustworthy messenger, we shall not delay in reporting it to you. I beg you, however, not to delay in writing back, through that boy whom my often-mentioned pagan kinsman is shortly to send to me, everything that you judge necessary for me to know. May my lord prosper.

I kept the bearer of this letter with me for only one night, so that the speed of his return might excuse the delay in his arrival. Yet, as he states, illness excuses him; and lest he could suggest anything else to you, on the feast of Saint Alban his soul departed. I fear, my lord, that this sheet will bring you more weariness in reading than it has brought me in writing. Yet one who must redeem through its length all the negligence of the time gone by deserves pardon.

Still, I set an end to it with this conclusion: when you have opportunity, remember your most devoted servant, our common friend Master John of Salisbury. Recall often that he is the first to suffer the punishment of exile for this reason: he was believed to serve usefully and faithfully the needs of your Church and your own interests. Fare well again and always; remember us in your prayers.

### LETTER 464. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME

To the venerable lord and most holy Father THOMAS, by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury, his own and his men’s own, [JOHN, bishop of Poitiers]: greeting and the spirit of consolation.

Stirred by the renown of the fame that ran before you and by the proclamation of your name, I hastened to the court before I had seen your messenger; but before I myself could reach it, all things had already become known to everyone, and the whole land was full of the Lord’s glory, and every hearer extolled the fact that one had been found to speak wisdom before the princes of the earth. Although the see of your patriarchate shines forth with the eminent nobility of its own dignity, yet through the grace of God much honour has accrued to it by your merit, so that what seemed customary among the bishops of that place is now believed, through you, to have been perpetuated within it. And indeed now with so much greater glory, as the princes of that age bore themselves more modestly, and your predecessors were thought less subject to their princes; especially since our most holy mother, the Roman Church, at that time suffered no division of her integrity. He, therefore, who gave you courage to begin will also give you steadfastness in persevering. He will also grant success in perseverance in a good work: either that which we desire, or certainly one more fruitful.

For, as regards human help, there is nothing which you should expect from the court in anything that ought to offend the king. For although both we and the messenger sent from your side laboured for many days concerning the petitions we put forward, we scarcely obtained one point. And even that is concluded so timorously that nothing is committed to writing, but reliance is placed only on an answer given by word of mouth. Yet Lord Henry of Pisa continued to affirm that he would work to exact the profession of the lord of London. I fear this will be in vain, since I had alleged everything that seemed capable of being proposed to me for obtaining it.

First, I argued that his translation appeared to have released him from every obligation. For he could not be received as bishop of this Church unless he ceased to be bishop of another Church. But if he has ceased to be a bishop, he has also ceased to be bound to the Church of Canterbury. Moreover, what if he had moved into another province? Would he not then make his profession to his own metropolitan? It is manifest that translation releases him from the profession formerly made. We also did not conceal the reason why it might be expedient even for the Roman Church that this be done: namely, because at the recently held assembly he had conducted himself as though he seemed free in relation to it. We also alleged the common custom: if anyone receives a new fief from the same lord, he is compelled to render homage anew, as from a new cause.

To all this I received the answer that a profession once made so binds the person that he cannot be released by any change of his status until he passes under another jurisdiction; nor can it be required of you on any ground, unless perhaps it were the custom of your Church that the profession had been made to the person alone of the archbishop who consecrated him, and not canonically to that archbishop and his successors. If this were so, then you could indeed lawfully demand it, not by reason of his person, but of yours.

As for the rest, concerning the blessing of the abbot of Saint Augustine, you expect comfort in vain. Therefore, dearest Father and lord, whatever you do, do it solely with a view to preserving the liberties of God and of that Church over which, by God’s authorship, you preside; and expect from Him alone both consolation in this labour and recompense. I, as many tell me, expect not merely a similar but a harsher sentence. Would that I might become a companion or forerunner of your exile. Nor indeed will it be inglorious for us, who have often misused many worldly prosperities for vanities and the delights of this age, not to fear, if necessary, to endure adversities together for a heavenly recompense.

Yet our Pisan is working to secure provision for me in a safer place. And he affirms that he has informed you of this through the abbot of La Aumône. [Col. 1030A] I am going to Pontigny, that I may commend both your purpose and ours to the devotion of that religious community. For divine aid must be implored where human aid seems wanting. We have caused you to be commended to the prayers of the men of Clairvaux through the pope himself. May my lord fare well.

## LETTER 465. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME.

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, JOHN, bishop of Poitiers, greeting and patience in adversity.

Devoutly receiving the letters of your Paternity, which Brother Simon most recently brought us, we derived much consolation from them. We regarded them also as a kind of remedy for the things announced to us contrary to our desire. We received your letters of consolation, moreover, in a fitting place—namely, at Le Mans, in the presence of the lord of that see. He too, a Catholic man sympathizing with the tribulation of the holy Church, comforted his mind, greatly distressed by the sinister reports, from those same letters.

For we may conceive hope from this: if what is now reported is true, that emperor, being occupied with many matters, will be less free to exercise his tyranny against the Church. Yet we wonder that your letters did not state what was done at the conference which the lord king of the French held at Auxerre during the Octave of the Apostles. It seems advisable to us that you should accept the benefices said to have been offered you by that same king of the French and by Count Henry, so that you may endure your exile more patiently until the Lord prepares your return to your own possessions.

The aforesaid lord king would also more secretly and securely entrust his counsels to your discretion if, through some benefice, he hoped you to be more bound and beholden to him. He would likewise be much more attentive to provide for you in the receipt of revenues whenever a bishopric or archbishopric fell vacant, if he had conferred something from his own lordship for your use, so that what was his own might thus return to him. You must, so far as the present state of affairs permits us to judge, make provision for your circumstances by whatever means you can, so that, to the confusion of your enemies, you may appear ready for however great a patience in this exile.

Therefore, as we have repeatedly earnestly advised your discretion, we still intend to persuade you to lighten yourselves of those things you can do without, having regard to the evil of the time, which by no means promises you an easy or speedy return to your possessions. Your prudence should know that no one will count it shameful for you, in adapting yourselves to the present condition, and in accommodating yourselves to the religious house which supports you, to be willing to be content with a moderate and necessary number both of horses and of attendants.

We wish you to know that you can expect neither help nor counsel from the queen, especially since she has entrusted all her counsel to Ralph de Faye, who persecutes you no less than usual. And every day many presumptions arise which seem able to establish that the disgrace of which we previously spoke approaches the truth.

Further, of the rumours reported to the queen by those travelling from the king out of England, who seem to magnify his side, we can communicate these to you: namely, that the lord king has now met the Welsh for a second time, and, as they boast, attacked and routed them, killing an innumerable multitude of them. They say, however, that the king lost few of his own men. We send you a copy of the letter which the king sent to his mother. You will also receive, through the bearer of this letter, the writing which Master Hugh, clerk of Richard of Ilchester, sent to you.

What was done at the conference concerning Salisbury we do not know, except that the lord king squeezed the bishops whom he had summoned there and immediately dismissed them, retaining their households with him. If we learn anything else expedient for your knowledge, we shall take care to make it known to you. Do you also deign to return the favour to us. Farewell.

## LETTER 466. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME.

To his lord and reverend Father THOMAS, by God’s grace venerable archbishop of Canterbury, his own J., by the same grace humble priest of the Church of Poitiers, greeting and continual success in the Lord.

[Col. 1031C] On the very day of the Purification of Blessed Mary, on which I received your letters, I spoke with John Cumin and Ralph of Tamworth, who had entered Tours on the preceding day, returning directly from the court of the lord pope. Since I wished to discover many things from them both concerning their position and concerning their business, I could obtain certain knowledge through them only on a few points, as though they believed that by concealing everything from me they were rendering service to their lord. Nevertheless, I extorted from them, even against their will, a few things; I learned others from the dean of Saint Maurice, in whose lodging they were staying. I learned still others through a certain clerk of Saintes, who had accompanied them for some time.

That clerk told me that the lord of Pavia, having been urged by the many and most pressing requests of the king of England and obtained by the lord pope’s like urgency and insistence, is without doubt coming as legate into all the land of the aforesaid king. It is believed that he comes with the fullness of authority, to investigate, judge, plant, and uproot; especially to decide powerfully and pronounce irrefragably, with every obstacle of appeal removed, between the king or others and you concerning all your complaints. Thus the decree requiring your restoration would not be able to help you much, especially the provision that you should possess for as long a time as you endured deprivation before the principal case was instituted. For the full authority of the aforesaid legate would, it is said, prejudice every exception and every decree.

Lord Otto, cardinal deacon of the Tullian Prison, is also said to be joined to him. And would that he were! For the malignity of one star, if it does not extinguish it, is nevertheless tempered and mitigated by another, more favourable and benevolent star joined to it. These two, indeed, left the city on the Kalends of January, hastening toward our regions.

But that report which you signified to me, brought to you by one of your clerks returning from the court—that John of Oxford had been absolved under such a condition, and that he had renounced those customs before the lord pope, whether by the king’s command or otherwise—I cannot easily be persuaded to believe. This, however, is said: that the person of John himself has been removed from your power, as regards being bound by excommunication.

For, as John Cumin and Ralph of Tamworth, who have now returned, report, John of Oxford won greater grace and favour in the eyes of the lord pope because he suggested to him that peace between the king and you could be restored if there were someone to negotiate it faithfully; and he promised to devote every effort to this. Hence the aforesaid John and Ralph call and proclaim that John of Oxford a traitor to the king, because he promised to accomplish what the king considers impossible, in order that he might advance better in his own affairs. Thus these two, John and Ralph, disparage John of Oxford in all his actions.

They also say—as I learned from the dean of Saint Maurice, who faithfully elicited all this from them—that they are bringing to the king all the letters which you sent to the lord pope against the king, or which others sent on your behalf, together with all your petitions. Among them they are greatly astonished to have found letters of the lord of Bourges, of whom the king suspected nothing of the sort. They say also that they possess letters written against the king on your behalf by certain bishops from the king’s land—indeed, even by certain persons from the king’s household. But who the bishops or the persons of the king’s household were, they refused for any reason to reveal, except to the king himself.

John Cumin boasted that he had reproached the lord pope because you had sent him letters against the king. And so that he could not deny it, he said that the opening of the letter was: “More than enough, reverend lord, have I endured.” Its subsequent content, he said, was that you were to pronounce sentence against the person of the king. He said that he had obtained these letters at Viterbo, where one of your messengers carrying them is said to have been apprehended. But it is more likely that he had them in the chancery.

From John and Ralph themselves I learned that other persons excommunicated by you had been sent to receive absolution in certain regions of your jurisdiction; but who they were I could not learn through them. It is believed that John of Oxford has gone to England in order, with the advice of those thirsting for your blood, to prepare, instruct, and bring forward witnesses and accusers against you. While you have time, I advise you to meet their harsh and dreadful machinations by whatever means you can. For they are ready to attempt great and numerous things against you: to accuse your innocence of grave crimes.

Yet he received no consolation and conceived no confidence from the king’s promises. When physicians ask him the cause and occasion of his illness, he answers that if any medicine can take away the resentment and indignation of his mind, then—and not otherwise—he can be cured. Moreover, those who have now returned from the court threaten you greatly because in the letters which you sent to the lord pope, and which they now carry back to the king, you called the king a malicious tyrant and repeatedly described his malice. Fare well, and may the spirit of counsel be with you. Our master of the schools writes to you concerning the extent to which I have preserved his reputation.

## LETTER 467. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME.

[Col. 1033B]

To the most reverend Father and lord THOMAS, by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury, his own JOHN, by the same grace humble priest of the Church of Poitiers, greeting and the spirit of counsel.

I confess, most serene Father and lord, that it exceeds my powers to give counsel in so arduous a matter. Yet because I know that you have referred everything to the counsel of our littleness out of affection rather than because you presume that we can prescribe a certain course in so uncertain a matter, I shall say what I think.

First, in those matters concerning which the lord pope writes to advise you, he is acting more for his own cause than for yours. For although his cause is the cause of us all, yet at first sight he is dealing with this: that, at whatever loss to the liberties of your Church for which you are exiled, he may meanwhile retain the king in an appearance of fidelity and even simulated obedience toward himself. Although I seem to myself certain that it would have been greatly advantageous both to him and to the whole Church subject to him had he, from the outset, after canonical warnings, proceeded against the king according to the paths of justice.

But, leaving aside those matters which could not by any means be persuaded to the lord pope or to our lords the cardinals, let us deal with those which we can. As regards security for going, staying, and, if necessary, returning, we believe it should suffice if the three persons whom you mention in your letters receive you under their protection. Yet I should wish the brothers of the Temple to be added to them, if possible; for the king is now said to depend greatly upon their advice, as if he were discussing some secret matter with them. Yet I judge that he says and does everything deceitfully, just as we signified to you in other letters that he had acted through those same brothers in your affair, which was being negotiated through them.

If our messengers reported the truth, the clerks of the lord of Rouen—Daniel, namely, and his brother Master T.—had not yet, upon the return of our own men, received the security for your return which they desired. Indeed, the aforesaid Daniel, because he pressed more strongly for the firmness of that security, received harsh words from the king.

But if the empress and the lord of Rouen summon you to their conference, you should go confidently, but, as it seems to me, attended not by few but by very few, so that you may express the appearance of an exile by that very scantiness. For that small number will move all men more to compassion than if you dragged after you a hundred of your fellow-exiles. Who could see without deep grief him who was once the king’s chancellor, and now established at the summit of such dignity, who in either estate moved with such splendour, surrounded by so many ranks, reduced for the liberty of his Church to the utmost poverty, so that he can scarcely bring even two or three religious men after him?

Moreover, the Churches established along the way will be able to provide for you without burden when you go and return; you will turn aside to them not merely to avoid expenses but, more especially, for the sake of prayers. I could allege many things concerning this, but I hasten to the rest.

So far as I can judge, those who are negotiating your peace speak only at the outset of this: that you may be able to return to your Church in security and peace. No one addresses the manner and form of your return. Where, I ask, and when will these matters be discussed? After you have returned to England? There, of course, neither the empress nor the count of Flanders can be present; perhaps the archbishop of Rouen alone will come to pursue the matter. You know how everyone there speaks only what they think will please the king. Certainly I fear that, under whatever pretext of justice, you would have to go into exile again, and that the latter things would become worse than the former, while all bear witness against you, both in the court of the lord pope and before the king of France, in speech and writing.

Therefore let no one persuade you to attempt return unless under a certain and thoroughly settled form, unless you are willing to commit all that concerns you to the king’s discretion—a course which I do not dare recommend to you. But if these matters must be arranged before your return, by whose diligence and mental exertion can the minds of all be brought into one agreement while he acts in England and you live as an exile in Burgundy? The course of a year would not suffice for such negotiation. I do not see how these things can be properly discussed unless some necessity draws him into the regions on this side of the sea, or you come down toward the narrower sea, that is, toward Flanders.

But, to come at last to the very form of peace, whether it be negotiated by yourselves or through intermediaries: of the articles which you proposed to us, neither all nor none seem to us fit to be pressed. First, I think the fief of W. de Ros should for the present be passed over in silence—not because you could not easily prevail in a possessory action where you contended on equal terms, but because in a proprietary action you would have cause for fear; and one seems to sue deceitfully who seeks what he must immediately restore. Certainly, dispossession effected without judgment promises you restitution. But the author of the grant—or, to speak more truly, of the sale—will not rightly defend the claim of ownership.

The claim relating to the lands of H. de Essex should likewise be passed over for a time by dissimulation, although the king acts more manifestly unjustly against you in that matter. But this injury concerns your royal rights more than the diminution of ecclesiastical liberty, in defence of which you are now exiled.

Yet you can by no means conceal this: that from the very beginning you must demand back what has been taken from you, and still more insistently what has been violently taken from persons, especially ecclesiastics, who are exiles with you, both on this side of the sea and beyond it. Their innocence is known to all and has greatly justified your cause. In this article I think that nothing should be yielded, even to the evil of the times. To this category also belongs the money which, after your departure, he extorted from your sureties. Among them he is said to have burdened the lord of Salisbury so heavily that today not even one ox raises the estate of the Church of Salisbury. You did not mention this article in your letters.

Nor should this be omitted: that it be conceded that the Church of Canterbury shall remain in the state of its liberties in which you received it. Although this clause presents an appearance of honour before men more than it grants you any advantage, and under a show of justice does not finally cut off but continually introduces a cause of litigation.

In sum, I shall say what I think. If these and other matters which seem to require discussion begin to be negotiated between you, I cannot understand how such a diversity—indeed, certainly such an opposition—of minds and claims can be brought into a single agreement. One path of peace, both the shortest and most honourable for you and for the king, would seem to me to be this: that you should abide by the arbitration of a few specified persons, of whom those on your side should not be from his kingdom or power. Otherwise, unless it be by the finger of God, I cannot measure the outcome of difficulties so many and so manifold.

Under the pretext of such peace, you could at once return honourably and await the arbitrators’ decision in your Church. I seem to see many advantages in this return, even if the affair did not obtain its desired result. Among other things, he would be ashamed to expel again your fellow-exiles whom he had once admitted, even if he excluded you for whatever just cause. For, as those who seem able to speak from knowledge of his mind assert, he is more ashamed of their removal than of yours. For you, he claims, went out voluntarily; they were expelled unwillingly, against their will, and without examination of the case.

Moreover, perhaps that affliction has now given him understanding: this peaceful return, which would not be dishonourable to him, would prepare and produce favour for you in his eyes. For he is said often to complain that he lacks every sure and firm counsel and that, exceedingly troubled by what happened to him in Wales, he is now thinking of appointing his son as successor. When I was lately coming to Tours, Hugh of Sainte-Maure told me many things in private on this point. I have entrusted them, along with many other matters, to be whispered into your ears alone by the bearer of this letter: partly because I do not entirely trust those reports; partly because the length of a letter and the multiplicity of business prevented us from writing everything. Would that you would send us messengers of this kind! For they can speak to you without suspicion, and there is no need to doubt their fidelity. Fare well.

If you go to the conference in Normandy, take Master John of Salisbury with you, if possible: both because he is a man of good faith and profound counsel; because he is highly esteemed among religious and good men; and because both the empress and the lord of Rouen wish him well and think well of him. Fare well again and always. Greet your fellow-exiles in our name; remember us in your prayers.

## LETTER 468. OF THE SAME TO GILBERT OF LONDON.

[Col. 1036B] To the venerable lord and friend G., by God’s grace bishop of London, J., by the same grace humble priest of the Church of Poitiers, greeting and the joy of the heavenly homeland.

I greatly rejoice, and thank you, that I have been admitted into a further degree of your sincere favour. The actual outcome of events has indeed taught this to me while present, and does not allow me to doubt it while absent. For neither is the great honour bestowed by you upon me while I still lived in my native land hidden from others, nor can I forget it. But after, by divine disposal, I became an inhabitant of an unknown city, the bearer of this letter, our nephew, also received the clearest proofs of your affection.

For his sake the petitions submitted to you were received with such ready kindness that in no respect is he repulsed to his loss or I to my embarrassment. Therefore, that your benefits may be crowned by the fulfilment of our wishes, we ask that, when opportunity is given, he may obtain not only through the offering of prayers permission to devote himself to the reading of the divine page, but also that, for this purpose, he may deserve to hear your paternal admonition. And, just as I especially assign him to this, that he may adhere diligently to your service and labour with whole devotion, acting in his measure on our behalf, so, as a reward for his labour and faithful devotion, may he experience and rejoice in being a participant in the charity you have shown us. Farewell.

## LETTER 469. OF RICHARD, ARCHDEACON OF POITIERS.

Of the archdeacon of Poitiers.

[Col. 1036D] Who the first messengers of the king were, who the second, what both these and those requested, and how they departed from the court, I shall set forth as briefly as I can.

The first sent were John Cumin and Master David, to seek absolution and relaxation for the bishops. But John Cumin came first to the court and, before David arrived, remained there for nearly fifteen days. Only after much insistence, and after first making a promise of five hundred marks, was he heard, with the clerks of the archbishop of York and the messenger of Durham standing with him and arguing at length in excuse of the bishops. I believe that they would have brought back absolution had not the report of the archbishop’s death intervened, which darkened everything. For the lord pope was so disturbed that for almost eight days even his own men could scarcely have an audience with him. It was generally forbidden that Englishmen should have access to him, and all their business was suspended.

The second messengers were the bishops of Worcester and Évreux, the abbot of Waverley, the archdeacons of Salisbury and Lisieux, Lord Robert of Neubourg, Richard Barre, Master Henry Pinchun, and a certain Templar. They were sent to excuse the king, asserting that the archbishop of Canterbury had been killed neither by his command nor by his will. Yet it was not denied that he had given cause for his own death, nor that he had said something from which those killers took an occasion for killing him.

But these second messengers also did not come to the court together, were not admitted by the lord pope, and could not appear before him. Then, at the prayer of certain cardinals, the abbot and the archdeacon of Lisieux were received. As Thursday, the Thursday immediately before Easter, approached, it was generally said at court that the lord pope would pronounce on that day a sentence of excommunication against the king and kingdom. Terrified by fear, the messengers, through the intercession of certain cardinals, informed the lord pope that they had received commands from the lord king to swear in his presence that the king would abide by his order, and that he would swear this in person.

On that Thursday, at about the ninth hour, both the king’s messengers and the bishops’ messengers were summoned; and in a general consistory the king’s messengers—namely, the abbot of Waverley, the two aforesaid archdeacons, Henry, and Richard Barre—swore that the king would abide by the judgment of the lord pope and would swear this at his command. The messengers of the archbishop of York and of the bishops of London and Salisbury likewise swore that their lords would abide by his command and would swear this.

On the same day, however, he excommunicated generally the killers of the archbishop of Canterbury and all who had given counsel, aid, or consent, and all who received or sheltered them in their land. After Easter the bishops of Worcester and Évreux and Robert of Neubourg came; whether that oath was exacted from them I do not know, but I know that they did not swear it. After they had remained at court for fifteen days or more, they were summoned to hear their response. For they agreed with the others both in excusing the king and in accusation, according to what has been said.

When it was believed that they would receive a favourable decision, the lord pope confirmed the sentence of interdict which the lord of Sens had pronounced upon the king’s lands on this side of the sea, and the sentence of excommunication and suspension pronounced against the bishops of England. He further commanded that the king refrain from entering a church, and added that he would send his legates to the king to see and ascertain his humility.

Then, after much insistence by the messengers, the intervention of certain cardinals, and, it is also said, a great sum of money, this was obtained: the lord pope writes to the archbishop of Bourges that, if within a month after the arrival of the messengers in Normandy he has not heard that the legates have crossed the Alps, then he is to absolve the bishops of London and Salisbury from excommunication, after they have first sworn that they will abide by the command of the lord pope, as will the others who remain suspended. Thus the messengers of the lord king withdrew from the court and report nothing else. But when they are to come, or who they are, we do not yet believe has become known even to the cardinals.

But now, I think, you need not fear an interdict in England if the king is willing to obey the legates. The lord pope writes to him and invites him to humility. Yet it was scarcely obtained that he should write to him.

## LETTER 470. JOCELIN OF SALISBURY TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY.

[Col. 1038B] To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, JOCELIN, bishop of Salisbury.

A certain monk came to us from your side, as he asserted, and by his report informed us that your eminence most severely censured us concerning John of Oxford, a clerk and faithful servant of our lord king, admitted to the deanery of Salisbury. We received him as canonically elected by the common vote and unanimous assent of our chapter, and confirmed him according to God and according to the custom of the Church. In doing so, we considered that from this very act a greater firmness of the nascent affection between the lord pope and our lord king would result; while nevertheless having regard to your advantage, so that through this a readier way might be opened to your holiness for winning the favour of our lord king. We were no less earnest and solicitous for the restoration of your peace than for the peace of the Church of Salisbury and the preservation of its liberty.

But because the aforesaid monk pronounced against us an unheard-of sentence of suspension from every priestly and episcopal office, lest we, being innocent, should be oppressed by so grave a burden—absent, not summoned, undefended, not confessing, and not convicted—we appealed to the Apostolic See. And as then in speech, so now in writing in your presence we appeal, submitting both our persons and our whole Church to the protection of blessed Peter and of the lord pope.

Let your holiness know that we are moved with no small astonishment, and so are all who hear of this matter, that by so sudden an impulse and such a severe judgment—not, I say, by a hasty will—a father should have rushed against a son innocent, undeserving, not contumacious, neither summoned three times nor twice, indeed not even once; absent, undefended, not confessing, and not convicted, as stated above; and should have condemned him. Thus your prudence seems to have overlooked that saying of Gregory:

> “Often, in loosing and binding his subjects, a pastor follows the impulse of his own will, not the merits of their causes; and thus he deprives himself of the very power of binding and loosing, when he exercises it for his own will rather than for the conduct of his subjects, when he is moved toward any neighbour by hatred or favour.”

It ought to have been considered that pastors must loose or bind their subjects with great moderation. Worthy of remembrance was that saying of Augustine:

> “You have begun to treat your brother as a publican; you bind him on earth, but see that you bind him justly. For unjust bonds are broken by justice. You know that he who calls the just unjust, or the unjust just, is detestable.”

May the Lord avert from my Father and lord any assumption of the Pharisees’ arrogance, so that he should either condemn the innocent or think to absolve the guilty. Your holiness has read that lepers were commanded to show themselves to the priests, and that, if they had leprosy, they were then to be declared unclean by the priest. Knowledge of the offences had first to be obtained; the variety of sins had to be heard; then came binding or loosing.

For, as Gregory says, no one is to be judged precipitately or out of order—that is, without warning and conviction—while Pope Sixtus says: “Let none of the pontiffs ever presume to judge uncertain matters; and, even though they are true, matters are nevertheless not to be believed unless they are proved by certain indications, unless they are manifestly established, unless they are made public in judicial order.”

Finally, venerable Father, lest we be compelled to pursue the appeal we have made, we most devoutly beseech your holiness, with such humility as we can and ought to show, that for our sake, moved by paternal compassion, you may mercifully relax the severity of the sentence pronounced against us, against John, dean of Salisbury, and against our Church; and that whatever you perceive needs correction in us you may correct, according to place and time, according to the statutes of the Fathers and the form of the canons, with due reverence.

[Col. 1039C] Meanwhile, venerable Father, there is one matter by which we are greatly troubled, and which ought no less to touch you: that from you—a man of such authority, a person of such maturity, so great a father and pastor—there should have proceeded so facile a statement as that we should forswear or renounce our lord and pope, or any other prelate of ours. Far be it that the Lord should so abandon and confound us! We call God and Truth, who is God, to witness that this statement neither proceeded from our mouth nor was purposed in our heart, nor have we done or exacted anything contrary to the Church of God, or anything that ought in any respect to offend our lord the pope or our prelates. Therefore we call as witnesses the bishops of Chichester, Exeter, [Col. 1039D] and Lincoln, who were present in all that we said and did, when, by God’s grace, the king’s indignation was remitted toward us and our church. May your fatherhood, dear to us, prosper and flourish!

## LETTER CCCCLXXI. FROM THE SAME TO GILBERT

To his venerable lord and dearest Father G., by God’s grace bishop of London, JOCELIN, humble servant of the Church of Salisbury, greeting, and a small gift—himself.

The evangelical father rejoices when the son who had gone into a far country is restored to him. By God’s grace, we too rejoiced at the return of the evangelical son who was lost and has been found. We met him with tambourine and chorus as far as the [Col. 1040A] doors. We killed for him the fatted calf and prepared choice poultry; would that your fasts also might be refreshed by them. By God’s grace, our messengers, hastening to our lord the king, bring us favourable news. Upon their return or their instructions depend both our expectation and our lord king’s answer as to what he has decided that we should do. We therefore choose to remain at Le Mans until some other royal command draws us away—perhaps to Angers, since that city is not far from the route by which the lord king will return. But if we went down to Argentan, perhaps a longer road would remain for us, and the cupbearer, instead of the very pure wine in which we abound, would pour us more sparingly a cloudier beer, hated by gentlemen. This too is the counsel of the lord of Chichester, who [Col. 1040B] judges it less prudent to exchange a certain lodging for an uncertain one, and to marry Liber Bacchus to the handmaid, daughter of a straw.

May your affection, most dear to us, prosper.

## LETTER CCCCLXXII. FROM THE CHAPTER OF SALISBURY TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

To THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, the chapter of Salisbury.

It has reached us that your discretion has pronounced upon our bishop a sentence involving no slight burden, and that you have proposed to pronounce a still heavier one upon our dean. Since, therefore, we regard the burden laid upon our prelates as our own, immediately upon hearing this we appealed to the Roman see, and in [Col. 1040C] your presence we appeal, submitting ourselves and our church to the protection of blessed Peter and the lord pope. May your fatherhood prosper and flourish.

## LETTER CCCCLXXIII. FROM MATTHEW OF TROYES TO POPE ALEXANDER

To Pope ALEXANDER, MATTHEW, bishop of Troyes.

“I deal more confidently with my lord,” etc. See among the various letters to Alexander III, after his *Regesta*.

## LETTER CCCCLXXIV. FROM ROGER OF WORCESTER TO THE CHAPTER OF CANTERBURY

HENRY, bishop of Worcester, to the chapter of Canterbury.

I briefly set forth for your affection what has been done among us. For our people, fearing the interdict reported in [Col. 1040D] our regions, after deliberation and after summoning our bishops and convening an assembly, asked each individually whether they wished to include their persons and the churches committed to them in that appeal which our bishops had formerly made at the beginning of Lent, namely for the term of the Purification, and which they had proposed, by common counsel, to renew on the octave of Pentecost.

When the bishop of Durham was asked, as he sat first, he replied that he had not participated in that appeal, nor had he heard any admonitory mandate concerning it, either in writing or orally; that he would deliberate with his metropolitan on the matter, and would prudently do whatever was lawful, without prejudice to the order of God and his own order. By such evasion he gained the favour of his hearers and a delay.

[Col. 1041A] Thereafter, when the bishop of Exeter was asked what he thought of it, he replied that his fellow bishops had hastened too readily into that appeal without consulting him; that it was impossible both to rely upon that appeal and to avoid association with excommunicated persons; and that danger threatened if the supreme pontiff’s sentence should confirm that interdict—a risk to which he was unwilling on any ground to expose himself. Nevertheless, if the Church of God judged it expedient, and royal favour granted him leave to pursue it, so that he could immediately leave the kingdom, he would make a new appeal from a burden not imposed but feared, although special relief against every appeal might be obtained. But if this were made known to him and the sentence of his pastor struck him, he would receive it obediently.

At these words the bishop of London ridiculed his piety, [Col. 1041B] and thereafter the bishop of Exeter was outside the synagogue.

The lord bishop of Winchester was summoned through his representatives to answer at Northampton the question put to his fellow bishops. The lord bishop of Winchester therefore wrote back as follows:

“The divine law prescribes that one who has appealed to a higher judge cannot appeal to a lower. Moreover, whoever appeals necessarily binds himself to pursue the appeal. Hence, because I am summoned by the Lord through illness and old age, I do not consider myself fit to make a secular and forensic appeal. Therefore I wish your affection to understand that I beg you to spare me from being thrust into those straits of appeal where I ought to fear the dart of a curse.”

Although his hearers accused this form of reply of evasion, the lord of Winchester preferred to incur men’s displeasure rather than offend God’s law. He made this plain when he published the notice of excommunication communicated to him, and thereafter more carefully avoided association with excommunicated persons.

[Col. 1041C] We are further informed that Reginald, archdeacon of Wiltshire, obtained reconciliation for his father, and that the lord pope was wholly ignorant of the sentence pronounced. Hence it is also alleged that, with apostolic blessing, he may delegate to the bishops of London and Salisbury the hearing of a certain case; and the rescript is dated after the day on which the sentence was pronounced. On this point malicious persons quibble that the lord pope considers those excommunicated persons [Col. 1041D] absolved.

Concerning all these matters which I have endeavoured to write to your affection, when in your schools you have, in the manner of advocates, drawn out themes from them, and after the fashion of rhetoric or law have imitated Quintilian or Papinian in argument and allegation, report back to us the merits of the cases that spring from your anvil and hammers, as a longed-for antidote. You will later receive things more pleasing, and such as should greatly nourish your hope and raise your confidence, so that by them you may have assurance that you have conquered the world.

## LETTER CCCCLXXV. FROM HENRY OF WINCHESTER TO THE PRIOR AND CONVENT OF ST MARY’S, WORCESTER

HENRY, by God’s grace bishop of Winchester and legate of the apostolic see, to the prior and convent of the Church of St Mary of Worcester, greeting.

[Col. 1042A] We are greatly surprised that you have not yet paid St Peter’s penny from the church and parish of your church, although we have now received it from all the bishops by the term agreed with them. We therefore command and, by apostolic authority, order you that, upon seeing these letters, you send the same penny of blessed Peter to Winchester within fifteen days; otherwise we forbid the celebration of divine office in your church or parish, except for viaticum and baptism. For, since your bishop and archbishop are absent, we have no one but you to whom we can write concerning this matter. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCCLXXVI. FROM THE CARTHUSIAN BROTHERS TO KING HENRY

[Col. 1042B]

To the most excellent and most valiant king of the English, to be embraced in the bowels of Christ, the brethren of the Charterhouse: may he be poor in spirit, and so reign in the present age that he may be crowned in the age to come!

When holy Job sat like a king amid the host surrounding him, he was nevertheless a comforter of mourners. The King of kings and Lord of lords has opened His hand and in many ways enlarged the reins of your kingdom. You must therefore always keep before your eyes that terrible threat of Holy Scripture: “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments, and a stronger punishment awaits the stronger” (Wisdom 6). And the saying of the Psalmist: “Terrible is He, and terrible to him who takes away the spirit of princes; terrible among the kings of the earth” (Psalm 75).

[Col. 1042C] It has been proclaimed from East to West that you grievously afflict the churches of your kingdom and exact from them certain unheard-of and unusual demands—demands which, even if earlier kings had desired them, they ought not to have sought. It may indeed be that in your time, since God has bestowed much wisdom upon you, such great oppression can somehow be endured; but perhaps after your death there will reign men who will devour the Church with their whole mouth, and, hardened like Pharaoh, will say: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exodus 5).

Spare, we beseech you, spare your dignity; spare your nobility; spare your lineage; spare also your famous [Col. 1042D] name. You who are so richly endowed and powerful, do not leave to future generations a model of oppression. Look with a merciful eye upon the grief and distress of holy Church, which is trampled down almost everywhere; and labour unceasingly and tirelessly to cherish and protect her with royal consolation.

## LETTER CCCCLXXVII. FROM A. OF THE CERTESIAN HOUSE TO POPE ALEXANDER

To his venerable and dearest Father and lord ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff and universal pope, brother A., unworthy minister of the Certesian house, reverence of sincere affection and due obedience with all the faithful.

“To your majesty, dearest Father and lord,” etc. See under Alexander III, years 1159–81.

## LETTER CCCCLXXVIII. FROM H., ABBOT OF CLUNY, TO GILBERT

[Col. 1043A]

To the venerable lord and Father, Lord G., by God’s grace bishop of London, brother H., humble abbot of Cluny, greeting in the Lord and whatever service and love he is able to offer.

We have seen your letters, full of sweetness and affection. They raise our humility with such great praises that, before so great a light of commendation, the eyes of our weak heart are more likely to grow dim and hide themselves than to be able to endure with unblinking gaze so great a radiance. For our conscience recognizes nothing of the kind in us. But perhaps you chose to act thus by a higher design: by commending us undeservedly, you offer us the spur of shame, so that, hearing what we ought to be, [Col. 1043B] we may strive to appear before God as we are said to be.

In all these things the sincerity of your feeling toward us is made known to us; for surely, unless you loved us very greatly, you could not so sincerely and truthfully, though undeservedly, declare such things concerning us. For the rest, although divine favour has called you to a lofty pinnacle of honour, we nevertheless presume that you are one of the special sons of the Church of Cluny. Therefore, since we believe that you do not in any way blush at the name of the mother who begot you in the Lord through the Gospel, we ask that you attend diligently to her affairs, both with the lord king of England and with the other leading men of the kingdom.

Our venerable brother, Lord Arn[old], bearer of this letter, a man—as we believe—religious and energetic, will communicate more fully to your reverence the remaining matters to be said. We wish him to be earnestly commended to your care. Have compassion upon your mother; do not close the bowels of mercy against her. For many causes she has long been worn down by such great hardships that she can scarcely now breathe. We have done concerning brother Robert Broi what you asked.

## LETTER CCCCLXXIX. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME

To his venerable and dearest brother, Master G., by God’s grace bishop of London, lofty in the word of glory, brother H., humble abbot of Cluny, greeting and sincere love.

Since the religious devotion, wisdom, and eloquence with which [Col. 1043D] your person is adorned are an honour to the Church of God, they are nonetheless a special glory to the church which begot you in Christ and nursed you at her breasts. Blessed, I say, is the Church of Cluny, which deserved to have such a son: a flower of teachers, a mirror of religion, and an ornament of the present age. In him nature, with God’s grace preceding and following, has so completed everything worthy of praise that it has left scarcely anything worthy of blame. Of him it is doubtful whether he prefers to be adorned with virtues rather than cleansed of vices. In him knowledge of many arts was the destruction, not the accumulation, of vices. He so transformed the worldly philosopher into a philosopher of the true Christ that he retained the latter’s truth without casting aside the former’s shrewdness. He so left the mastership of the schools that he devotedly learned the discipleship of Christ’s unlearned ones.

[Col. 1044A] It was not necessity but charity alone that drew him to Christ; not misery but an intention of perfection alone that withdrew him from the world. For him manifold knowledge increased humility, and humility added constancy. He showed that he had it in his will to love only honourable things, to hate idle things, and to fear shameful things. For him it was an injury to honour not to be affected by injuries; labour was rest for the sake of justice; rest was to live in labour for the sake of truth. Having become a monk, he retained from the cleric nothing for himself beyond his order; having been appointed abbot, he did not abandon the works of a monk; raised to the high pontificate, he remained the same man as before. As many ranks were added, so many virtues followed. Through the manifold care imposed upon him, he increased rather than diminished his virtues. He preserved the monk in action; in his solicitude he lost nothing of the abbot; in observance of God’s commandments he honoured and exalted the bishop.

[Col. 1044B] This is the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes. The whole Gallican Church knows these things, and almost the whole Latin Church, and they praise the Church of Cluny in such a son. Cluny knows this too and therefore greatly rejoices in the Lord.

You have heard, dearest brother, that we had inclined to Octavian’s side, and your heart was troubled. But let not your heart be troubled, for we have never adhered to him. We have not yielded even in the least, either to the emperor’s prayers and promises, threats and blandishments. Nor would we attend his council held at Pavia, even for love of the empire.

We are on the frontier of kingdom [and] empire. Germany, Hungary, Russia, Lorraine, Burgundy, the province beyond the Saône, the greater part of Italy, and the province of Lyons obey Lord O. with the emperor. The emperor threatens to take from us everything we possess within his empire unless we consent to him. The count of Mâcon, who has sworn fealty to the emperor and in whose power we are, holds his drawn sword above our necks. The archbishop of Lyons with his suffragans prepares to hurl his anathema upon our heads. The lord cardinals who are in the kingdom promise us their curse, not their blessing. The kings of France and England threaten to drive out everything belonging to us situated in their kingdoms unless we obey Lord Pope A.

[Col. 1044D] The body of the Church of Cluny consists of two integral parts. One is in the empire; the other is in the kingdoms. If we lose either, woe to us: we are hemmed in on every side, as Susanna was. We trust to be delivered by a divine miracle, as she was. The almighty right hand is not powerless to save us. If He has decreed to free us, we shall immediately be saved. We are still in the middle, and have resolved to proceed by the royal road.

You therefore, who are our father by age, brother by love, son by grace, do not forget us, who are joined to you in all charity. Do not forget your mother, who, although she has now given you birth in Christ, nevertheless still bears you in her womb: she rejoices with you, grieves with you, and counts all your prosperity and adversity as her own.

[Col. 1045A] Certain other matters which a letter does not speak, the bearer of this letter—our monk and yours—will convey to you in our stead, concerning himself and concerning the Church of Lenton. Since, as we have heard, you are its special defender and helper in its causes, we earnestly ask your affection that, as you have begun, you may graciously watch over its love and protection for the cause of God and of the Church of Cluny.

## LETTER CCCCLXXX. FROM PHILIP, ABBOT OF L’AUMÔNE, TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

To the reverend Father and lord in Christ THOMAS, by God’s grace venerable archbishop of Canterbury, brother PHILIP of L’Aumône and brother L. of the Court of God, greeting and the affection of sincere love.

Our own interests are not diminished by that which profitably [Col. 1045B] increases the resources of friends. For friendship has this special quality: whatever is possessed by its adherents is a sweet and pleasant possession to it. With an enlarged heart and ready affection you received Master Girard kindly into the bosom of your favour. He repaid in return what he could: he was found a faithful friend; he became a valiant champion of your justice, a distinguished advocate, a prudent defender of your cause, and an outstanding herald of your deeds. He spared neither himself nor his own people in order to benefit you, and so wholly devoted himself to your interests and rendered grace for grace that he proposed to himself nothing joyful except what might serve your honour and name.

If the torrent of iniquity has swallowed up his faithful service to you before its great fruit was realized, he is no less worthy of your embrace because he could not accomplish what he wished; for, as far as he could, he did not cease to be useful. Now therefore, if through the support of great merits he has been able to find peace in the sight of that Prince, he ought not to be estranged from the sight of your heart; rather, as we believe, he ought to flourish in your mind with favour, if he has received favour from Him with whom he can more intimately and faithfully enter into fellowship for your honour and peace. For whoever is a friend loves at all times, and a sure friendship is excluded by no force and no necessity.

We therefore ask your charity, dear to us in Christ, and advise you with kindly persuasion that no harsh necessity of any kind be imposed upon your faithful servant. For, as Ovid says:

[Col. 1045D] “A gentle breeze nourishes the flame; a stronger wind extinguishes it.”

And eternal Wisdom, which reaches mightily from end to end, disposes all things sweetly and orders us with great reverence. May your sincerity always fare well in the Lord.

## LETTER CCCCLXXXI. FROM HENRY II, KING OF ENGLAND, TO THE BISHOPS OF ENGLAND

King HENRY of England sent these letters to each of the bishops of England.

You know how wickedly Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, has acted against me and my kingdom, and how wickedly he departed. Therefore I command you that his clerks who were with him after his flight, and the other clerks who have disparaged my honour and the honour of the kingdom, are to receive nothing from the revenues [Col. 1046A] which they held in your bishopric except through me, nor are they to have any help or counsel from you.

Witness Richard de Lucy, at Marlborough.

## LETTER CCCCLXXXII. FROM THE SAME TO THE SHERIFFS

King HENRY of England sent these letters to each sheriff of England, at the beginning of the persecution of Saint Thomas.

I command you that, if any cleric or layman within your bailiwick appeals to the Roman court, you are to arrest him and keep him securely until you receive my will; and you are to seize into my hand all revenues and possessions of the archbishop’s clerks, as Ranulf de Broc and my other officers shall tell you. You are to place under sureties the fathers and mothers, brothers and sisters, grandsons and granddaughters of all clerks who are with the archbishop, together with their chattels, until you receive my will concerning this; and when summoned, bring this writ with you.

## LETTER CCCCLXXXIII. FROM THE SAME TO REGINALD OF COLOGNE

HENRY, king of England, to REGINALD, schismatic of Cologne.

For a long time I have desired to have a just occasion for withdrawing from Pope Alexander and his faithless cardinals, who presume to support against me my traitor Thomas, formerly archbishop of Canterbury. Therefore, with the counsel of all my barons and the consent of the clergy, I shall send distinguished men [Col. 1046C] from my kingdom to Rome—namely, the archbishop of York, the bishop of London, the archdeacon of Poitiers, John of Oxford, and Richard de Lucy—who shall publicly and openly set forth and declare, on behalf of me, my entire kingdom, and all the other lands which I hold, to Pope Alexander and his cardinals that they must no longer support my traitor, but release me from him in such a manner that I may, with the counsel of the clergy, appoint another in the Church of Canterbury. They shall also declare that whatever Thomas has done they are to annul. They will further demand that the pope publicly cause an oath to be sworn before them that he and his successors will preserve for ever, so far as lies with them, unimpaired and inviolate for me and all my successors the royal customs of my grandfather Henry.

[Col. 1046D] But if they should perhaps choose to oppose any of my requests, neither I, nor my barons, nor my clergy will show them any further obedience; indeed, we shall openly attack him and all his people. And whoever is found in my land and wishes thereafter to adhere to him shall be expelled. Therefore we ask you, as a most dear friend, to send Brother Ernold, or Brother Ralph the Hospitaller, speedily to me, all obstacle removed, so that on behalf of the emperor and yourself he may provide my aforesaid messengers with guidance, going and returning through the emperor’s land.

Having seen these letters, the man of Cologne consulted the emperor as to what should be answered to the king of England. The emperor replied that the king of England’s wishes should be granted, [Col. 1047A] because the more solemnly these things were done, if Pope Alexander consented, the greater would be his confusion. And perhaps, secretly, through another Templar or Hospitaller, or someone else against whom no precaution could be taken, the king of England might obtain the same thing for his money. Brother Ralph the Hospitaller was therefore sent to the king of England, and provided guidance through the emperor’s territory to the messengers whom the king intended to send to the curia.

## LETTER CCCCLXXXIV. FROM THE SAME TO A CERTAIN CARDINAL

The king of England to a certain cardinal, or to a body of cardinals.

Concerning what the lord pope has signified to you—namely, that we had turned our mind and heart away from the love and devotion of the Roman Church—we reply first that your prudence knows most fully with what sincere affection we have always loved the Roman Church and the person of the lord pope, and how much we have done and endured for him. For, to pass over the rest in silence, when there was controversy concerning his reception, we received him not unwillingly, but drew and compelled others, though unwilling, to receive him. Nor have we withdrawn our heart from the fullness of love; but he, who, as is clear to you, has from former times proved excessively troublesome to us, as the execution of his acts has made plain in very many instances, now especially does not cease to defame our person in word, deed, [Col. 1047C] and writing—which above all wounds the minds of princes—when in his writing and speech he calls us a persecutor and oppressor of the Church.

But let the lord pope consider how fatherly his conduct toward us has been. He has signified to us that the highest caution and solicitude of princes ought to be to preserve their reputation uninjured; yet he does not appear to bear a fatherly affection toward us when in deed and word he so greatly disparages our reputation. We wish your whole body to know that whatever honour, exaltation, and power we possess—our kingdom also, and all else committed to our governance—we know and confess have been bestowed upon us, each and all, by the Lord and our Creator. To Him alone we offer not such acts of thanksgiving as we owe, for we are unequal to that, but such as we can. And would that the lord [Col. 1047D] pope prayed the Lord for us, that we might be able and know how to render to our Lord and Creator the devotion and reverence due to Him, and might be able to serve and love Him in at least a third part of the measure we owe Him!

Certainly, although we cannot love and venerate Him as much as we are bound to do, we nevertheless have the disposition and devotion to serve Him in every particular, obey Him in all things, and submit to Him in everything. We willingly desire and seek to persevere in the entirety of the lord pope’s favour and love, provided that he maintains toward us and our kingdom the same honour and preservation of honour and dignity which holy and upright Roman pontiffs showed to our noble and powerful predecessors.

Nevertheless, concerning the appeals which he alleges [Col. 1048A] that we have forbidden, and his assertion that we have prohibited anyone from our kingdom from visiting the Roman curia, we do not wish your prudence to be unaware that we have in no way impeded either appeals or visits, provided that they are made in the manner, for the reason, and in the order in which they were customarily made in the times of our illustrious predecessors, according to the customs and dignities of our kingdom, and as the oldest and wisest men of our realm, both clerical and lay, remember and recount.

As for his accusation that we have entered into a confederacy with excommunicated persons, we do not think that in this we have offended God or acted contrary to reason, because, as we received from the mouth of the lord pope, he had never regarded the lord Frederick, emperor of the Romans, as excommunicated; nor afterward have we learned by anyone’s report that he was excommunicated. Indeed, although we have given our daughter in marriage to the emperor’s son, we believe that we have not sinned in the slightest, but do not doubt that this was lawful for us. For, to take examples from like cases, we remember that the same was permitted to the most excellent and powerful King Henry, our grandfather, who joined his daughter in marriage to Henry, Roman emperor of blessed memory. We too, following the precedent received from our predecessors and after taking counsel with prudent and discreet men of our kingdom, permitted a marriage to be contracted between the emperor’s son and our daughter.

Moreover, as to his writing to us that we should restore the archbishop of Canterbury—whom he alleges that we [Col. 1048C] expelled from our kingdom—to the position from which he departed, and return him to his see: we know most clearly that it is plainly known to your whole body that we never expelled him or compelled him to leave our kingdom. Rather, prompted by his own fickleness and perversity more than by any reason inducing him to do so, he took flight, intending and proposing maliciously to act against us and maliciously to disparage us and our reputation—something which, as is clear to all, we had in no way deserved.

But if that archbishop, just as he fled by his own choice, wishes voluntarily to return in the same way, and does toward us what he ought to do toward his lord and prince, we shall do for him what we ought, according to the counsel of clerics and laymen, both of our kingdom and of overseas lands. Yet we do not judge that he should be recalled by us, since we did not compel him to leave our kingdom.

[Col. 1048D] Therefore, if you ascertain that we have sinned or transgressed in any respect, we shall willingly do whatever we ought according to the counsel of our clergy and barons, and according to the customs, dignities, and exalted standing of our kingdom. But if anyone attempts to impede or diminish the rights, customs, and dignities of our kingdom, we shall regard him as a public enemy and an open enemy of our name, honour, and kingdom; and, as long as life remains to us, we shall by no means endure a diminution of the dignities and customs of our kingdom which our illustrious predecessors possessed and maintained in the times of holy Roman [Col. 1049A] pontiffs.

Finally, concerning the command conveyed to us through you that we should not burden, or allow to be burdened, the churches or ecclesiastical persons of our kingdom and land: God and our clear conscience are witnesses that, to this present day, this has neither been done nor permitted by us.

## LETTER CCCCLXXXV. FROM THE SAME TO THE ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX

HENRY, king of England, to the abbot of Cîteaux.

When Lord William of Pavia and you came to our presence at Rouen, we complained to you that certain monks of your order—whom hitherto in our land, contrary to the will and assent of nearly all our barons and men, we had received and supported with every honour and reverence, [Col. 1049B] and promoted—were conveying to us certain messages from our adversaries full of bitterness, and certain seeds of discord and incentives to wrath and hatred, which should in no way be uttered by any worthy man. Your affection therefore promised us that you would correct this and restrain your monks from bearing such messages.

But after that promise, your abbot of Criscampo brought us a certain writing from Thomas, who had been our chancellor, on his behalf, and read it aloud; in it he reproached us for injury to the faith and appeared to accuse us of schism. The tenor of that writing also contained words of indignation and pride that disparaged our honour [Col. 1049C] and person. Therefore, in commanding you, we earnestly ask you not to fail to redress our injury by suitable correction, and to preserve both our honour and that of your order. Know that if you do not correct your monks’ excesses, we shall no longer be able to refrain from seeking a remedy for our injuries.

Witness Jocelin de Baille, at Caen.

## LETTER CCCCLXXXVI. FROM THE SAME TO WILLIAM OF SENS

HENRY, king of England, to WILLIAM, bishop of Sens.

I received honourably, as was fitting, the religious and venerable men of the Cistercian order whom you sent to me; I heard them attentively and considered them carefully. I kindly received the message which they conveyed on your behalf, namely—as they told me that you had received it by mandate of the lord pope—that you should speak with me concerning the restoration of peace between me and the archbishop of Canterbury. It therefore pleases me that you should speak with me on this matter. For the case in dispute between us has become known to you in large measure, as you heard in person when discussion of it was held between us in the presence of the lord king of France. He was the cause of discord; from him the cause of concord ought to proceed. He inflicted the wound; he should labour to heal it.

Through him the disease has grown strong; in him lies the possibility that, health having been restored, the disease may be removed. I neither initiated nor carried out the cause of evil. Therefore indicate in what place each of us is to remain until we can come together. I trust, moreover, in the integrity and constancy of your loyalty, that you will incline your favour toward the truth of this cause. I therefore receive it with greater affection, so that your discretion may consider more diligently my will and equity in this matter.

Furthermore, I direct to you my complaint concerning the fact that my lord, the king of France, recently, exceeding what is just, injured me in what was mine. Through your mediation and that of Count Theobald, your brother, setting aside the counsel of my own men, I recently, for the sake of peace and on a matter which my predecessors never did, wholly submitted myself to the will of the lord king of France, yielding to your counsel. Yet you cannot, I think, be unaware how recently he injured me.
