I complain to you, therefore, so that the transgression which he presumed to commit to the prejudice of the peace established between us [Col. 1050B] may displease you, and that you may endeavour to bring him to just satisfaction, since the deed itself was done at his instigation.

## LETTER CCCCLXXXVII. FROM THE SAME TO THE SAME

HENRY, king of England, to WILLIAM, archbishop of Sens.

Coming to me on the matter in dispute between myself and the Archbishop of Canterbury, the envoys of the lord pope, although they bore proposals harsh and contrary to all my honour, I received honourably out of reverence for the lord pope and the devotion due to the holy Roman Church; and I heard them with the kindness fitting to the occasion, very modestly accepting the lord pope’s command which they conveyed, although I felt myself aggrieved in the case of my own men, whom they held excommunicated—a sentence against them having been extraordinarily and precipitately pronounced more from emotional impulse and agitation of mind than from the weighed equity of reason or the counsel of deliberation. [Col. 1050C] When discussion on this point had continued for some time, I asked that those whom they had thus bound should be absolved. They promised, however, to absolve them if the same persons gave them sworn security that, once absolved, they would obey their decision. Moved more vehemently by this, I swore that they should by no means give such an oath; but that, if the envoys wished, I would arrange security for them—from laymen by a pledge of faith, from clerics by a promise upon their word of truth—so that they might deserve absolution. But they declared this to be foreign to custom and contrary to the terms laid upon them; [Col. 1050D] and said that they wished to have your advice in this matter—you who are both an archbishop and legate of the Apostolic See—so that, if they acted on your advice, it would suffice as their excuse should they ever be accused of transgression on this account. Therefore they send to you, and I too send and ask that, having regard to my honour and advantage, you apply your counsel to this matter. I trust firmly in you, whom I embrace as my chief friend with most abundant devotion, that in this and my other affairs you will show abundant favour, watchful diligence, and the most steadfast loyalty. I should count it a great fulfilment of my desire if I could speak with you; but the pressure of other business prevents this at present. I therefore ask that [Col. 1051A] you send me one of your people, through whom your wishes may become more fully known to me, and mine likewise made known to you.

## LETTER CCCC LXXXVIII. OF KING HENRY TO POPE ALEXANDER.

To the venerable Father and supreme pontiff ALEXANDER, HENRY, king of England, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou: greeting and due veneration.

“If, Father, you seek proof of my devotion toward your Holiness,” etc. See among the various letters to Alexander III, after his Registers.

## LETTER CCCC LXXXIX. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME.

[Col. 1051B] The lord king to the lord pope.

“The Roman Church knows from the long course of time,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER CCCC XC. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME.

To Pope ALEXANDER, HENRY, king of England.

“We have sent bishops as our envoys to the feet of your fatherhood,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER CCCC XCI. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME.

To Pope ALEXANDER, HENRY, king of England: the service due from utter submission.

“Your serenity is sufficiently aware,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER CCCC XCII. OF THE SAME TO GILBERT.

[Col. 1051C] H., by the grace of God king of England, to his dearest father G., bishop of London: greeting and affection.

Since I have learned by experience that you have always loved my person with a special grace of sincere affection, I know without doubt that you wish to be assured of my condition and safety, and to rejoice in my successes. I therefore send to you my dearest and familiar friend, the bishop of Bath, through whom I safely communicate my secrets to you, and moreover my wishes and the benefits that, with God’s help, have befallen me since I departed from England. Therefore give credence to what he shall tell you on my behalf; and hold dear, love, and show honour to this most beloved bishop and my familiar friend, who is always ready and [Col. 1051D] devoted in assisting with the dispatch of my affairs. I also earnestly and devoutly request the concern of your fatherhood, in which I place no small confidence: apply the utmost effort and diligence to my affairs, and strive, insofar as you can, to provide for the peace and defence of my realm. Witnessed by H., bishop of Bayeux, at Chivill’.

## LETTER CCCC XCIII. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME.

HENRY, king of England, to GILBERT, bishop of London.

I have heard of the injury which that traitor and adversary of mine, Thomas, has inflicted upon you and upon other persons of my realm. I bear it no less grievously with regard to [Col. 1052A] your person than if he had spewed forth his venom against my own person. Therefore know for certain that I shall make every effort, through the lord pope, through the king of the French, and through all my friends, to ensure that henceforth he cannot harm us or our realm. I therefore wish and advise that in the meantime you should not be troubled in mind in any way; rather, consider resolutely whether it is more expedient for you and for me that you come to me in Normandy, or remain in England. I entrust this whole matter to your own decision, being certain that, if you come to me and wish to go to Rome, I shall honourably and sufficiently furnish from my own resources everything necessary for the journey. Witnessed by G. . . . , clerk, at Saint-Macaire in Gascony.

## LETTER CCCC XCIV. OF THE SAME TO THE CISTERCIAN ABBOTS.

[Col. 1052B]

HENRY, king of England and duke of Normandy and Aquitaine and count of Anjou, to the venerable men, the abbot of Cîteaux and all abbots of the Cistercian order who assemble at the chapter of Cîteaux: greeting and the affection of sincere love.

Trusting more fully in your sincerity and religious devotion, and relying upon them more confidently, I devoutly beseech and humbly ask your whole community that you remember me, my heirs, and my faithful men; so that through your prayers divine mercy may be more favourably inclined towards me, and that you strive to render its compassion propitious to us, so that [Col. 1052C] it may guide us in firm and lasting peace and preserve my realm and the other lands subject to me.

Moreover, I wish you to know that I took pains honourably to receive the lord pope’s envoys, the venerable men Gratian, the lord pope’s notary, and Master Vivian, advocate of the Holy Roman Church, whom he sent to me concerning the business of the Archbishop of Canterbury; and to hear, as was fitting, with devotion the petition submitted to me through them. With the advice of several archbishops, bishops, and abbots, I endeavoured, with the consent of the aforesaid envoys, to give that petition a kind and adequate answer, as the following will show you. Thus I may seem to have shown every reverence to the lord pope in this affair, although from the beginning of this case I had always asked to stand by the law and to submit to whatever judgment the law should establish between us; [Col. 1052D] and had often requested that persons be sent from the lord pope’s side who, having more fully examined this cause, might conclude it by an equitable settlement.

The Archbishop of Canterbury, as report has spread even to the remotest parts of our dominions, left England without my permission or knowledge; and after his departure he sought to have me regarded among religious men as notably cruel, stirring up against me the wishes of princes and clerics and the hatred of foreign peoples. Nevertheless, at the request, for the reverence, and for the love of the lord pope—although it was most grievous to me, strongly opposed to my will, and appeared most burdensome—I grant that he return to England and hold his archbishopric with the same integrity [Col. 1053A] in which he held it when he left it; and likewise that his followers have what is theirs. Let him and his followers have peace, for the honour of God and of myself, the dignities of my realm being preserved.

What has been done in the present matter, and with what solemnity and in whose presence, the venerable brethren of yours who were present will report to you more carefully and fully than can be understood from this brief letter: Brother Geoffrey of Auxerre, the abbot of Mortemer, the abbot of Beaulieu, and the abbot of Rievaulx. Give them the credence that is fitting. I desire, however, that your whole community be dissuaded henceforth from too readily believing anyone who may seek, to my injury, to spread and persuade you of sinister allegations concerning me. Moreover, I offer abundant thanks to your affection because, at my request, you sent Brother Geoffrey [Col. 1053B] to me. And now I again earnestly ask that you send him back to me as quickly as possible. For I understand that his discernment and prudence are necessary to me, that he may be present with me and that his familiar companionship may be near me for some time. Witnessed by G., archdeacon, at Rurum.

## LETTER CCCC XCV. OF THE SAME TO ROTROU OF ROUEN.

The king of England to ROTROU, archbishop of Rouen.

By the advice of you and of my other faithful barons, I communicated by envoys and letters to the lord pope the arrangement undertaken for restoring peace between myself and the Archbishop of Canterbury. As he informed me in his letters, he received it with abundant thanksgiving in the form [Col. 1053C] in which it proceeded from your counsel and had been communicated to him on your behalf; and he commands, urges, begs, and earnestly counsels me to carry it out through your mediation and that of the bishop of Nevers. Therefore, through your mediation, I shall fully and willingly fulfil it, in no way departing from the arrangement proposed by your advice. Witnessed by Richard de Luci, at Westminster.

## LETTER CCCC XCVI. OF THE SAME, CONCERNING PEACE RESTORED TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.

For the love of God and of the lord pope, and for the welfare of myself and my heirs, I remit my anger and offence to the Archbishop of Canterbury and to his followers who are in exile with him and on his behalf; I remit to him all previous complaints, if I had any against him; and [Col. 1053D] I grant him and his followers true peace and firm security from myself and my people. I restore to him the Church of Canterbury in the full extent in which he held it when he was made archbishop, together with all possessions which the Church and he himself had and held, to hold and possess as freely and honourably as he and his predecessors held and possessed them most freely and honourably. I likewise restore to him, with the honour of my realm preserved, all churches and prebends belonging to the archbishopric which began to be vacant after the Archbishop of Canterbury left the realm, so that he may dispose of them as of his own, as he pleases.

## LETTER CCCC XCVII. OF THE SAME TO HIS SON.

HENRY, king of England, to his son the king: greeting.

[Col. 1054A] Know that Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, has made peace with me according to my will. I therefore command that he and all his people have peace; and that you cause the archbishop himself, and all his followers who departed England on his account, to have their possessions well, peacefully, and honourably, as they had them three months before the archbishop left England. Cause the best and oldest knights of the honour of Saltwood to appear before you, and have them declare upon oath what there is held from the fee of the archbishopric of Canterbury; and whatever shall be acknowledged to belong to his fee, cause it to be possessed by the archbishop himself. Witnessed by Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen, at Chinon.

## LETTER CCCC XCVIII. OF THE SAME TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY.

[Col. 1054B]

To THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, HENRY, king of England.

Know that I could not come to meet you at Rouen on the date which we had previously agreed between ourselves, because my friends in France informed me that the king of the French was preparing to go into Auvergne against my men and to do harm to them and to my land. The men of Auvergne themselves likewise informed me of this, asking me to assist them. Accordingly, I could not come to you at Rouen on the date we fixed between ourselves. But I send you John, dean of Salisbury, my familiar clerk, who will go with you into England; [Col. 1054C] through him I inform Henry, my son the king of the English, that you are to have all your possessions well, peacefully, and honourably, and that he is to make amends if anything has been done inadequately in matters pertaining to you. And since many reports are brought to me and to my son concerning the delay you are making—reports which perhaps are not true—it would, I think, be expedient for you not to defer your journey to England any longer. Witnessed by the king himself at Loches.

## LETTER CCCC XCIX. OF THE EMPRESS MATILDA TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY.

To THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, MATILDA, empress.

The lord pope has commanded me, and imposed it upon me for the remission of my sins, to concern myself with restoring peace and [Col. 1054D] concord between my son the king and you, and to endeavour to reconcile you to him. You also asked this of me, as you know. Therefore, with greater earnestness, I have taken care to undertake and pursue this matter both for the honour of God and for the honour of holy Church.

But it seems very grievous to the king, his barons, and his council that, after he loved and honoured you, made you lord of his whole realm and all his lands, and at last raised you to the greatest honour that you held in all his land, he should henceforth be able safely to trust you—especially since they maintain that, so far as you were able, you disturbed his entire realm against him and left nothing undone in your efforts to disinherit him by every means in your power. Therefore I send [Col. 1055A] to you our faithful and familiar friend Laurence, archdeacon, so that through him I may learn your will on all these matters, what disposition you have towards my son, and how you will intend to conduct yourself if it happens that he is willing fully to grant my petition and entreaty on your behalf. I also tell you one thing truthfully: unless by great humility and the clearest moderation, you will not be able to recover the king’s favour. Inform me by your own messenger and letters what you intend to do in this matter.

## LETTER D. OF OWAIN OF WALES TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY.

To the most religious THOMAS, by God’s grace Archbishop of the holy Church of Canterbury [Col. 1055B], his spiritual father: O., king of the Welsh, his spiritual son in the Lord, due and willing obedience in Christ.

The ears of your discernment, venerable Father, have heard how great were the losses to its rights suffered by our Church after the death of our bishop Maurice. Greatly struck by fear, we tremble lest, since the necessity of bearing the care and solicitude of this Church rests upon us, God may impute these matters to our negligence. You also know how greatly the king of England hates us without deserving cause, so that he does what he can to diminish our honour in both ecclesiastical and secular affairs; and in this we feel the harmful absence of your exile. But since you are not in a position to provide for our need in this affair, we earnestly [Col. 1055C] beseech your clemency that, since we can no longer remain thus situated, you grant us leave to ordain our bishop elsewhere, on this condition: that he render obedience to the holy Church of Canterbury and to you as if he had been consecrated by the laying on of your hands.

You ought properly to satisfy our request, for it is not any right that compels us to submit to you, but our will; and it shall always remain unshaken unless there remains in you something that prevents its continuance. If, should this happen, you regard us as suspect with respect to obedience, we shall give whatever security you wish. And as our archdeacon David follows all your commands, so shall we all do. But know this one thing: we can no longer remain so situated. Therefore [Col. 1055D] communicate your will in these matters to me by your letters.

## LETTER DI. OF AN ANONYMOUS WRITER TO POPE ALEXANDER.

“I was about to communicate certain matters to your magnificence with tranquillity of mind,” etc. See under Alexander III, years 1159–81.

## LETTER DII. OF LOUIS TO THE SAME.

To Pope ALEXANDER, LOUIS, king of France.

“On behalf of the Archbishop of Canterbury,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER DIII. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME.

To ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, LOUIS, [Col. 1056A] by the same grace king of the French: greeting and due reverence.

“A son departs from the law of human compassion,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER DIV. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME.

Of LOUIS, king of France, to Pope ALEXANDER.

“You may recall,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER DV. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME.

To Pope ALEXANDER, LOUIS, king of France.

“We firmly hold and recall,” etc. See the same place.

## LETTER DVI. OF THE SAME TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY.

[Col. 1056B] To THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, LOUIS, king of France.

Long ago we offered your Holiness a residence with us. We now offer you the same from a generous heart. To receive this would give us great joy. You do not receive messengers from us frequently because we are still waiting; and we should wish to hear other news and other reports by which it would be most pleasing to us to gladden you. But matters are not yet according to our desire. Farewell.

## LETTER DVII. OF THE SAME TO EMPEROR MANUEL.

To MANUEL, by God’s grace illustrious and glorious emperor of the Romans, ever augustus, his venerable brother and [Col. 1056C] dearest friend, LOUIS, by the same grace king of the French: greeting, and faithful and blessed adherence to Him who bestows kingdoms and transfers empires.

The honour which you showed us, pilgrims in the Lord, when we were among you will, with God’s help, never fade from our memory. Although seas and the spaces of intervening kingdoms separate us, no power shall dislodge from us the affection owed to your merits. Thus we rejoice in your prosperity as in our own, and we desire that what befalls your enemies should befall ours; if God gives opportunity, we are ready in the Lord to fulfil your will and extend your glory. In order that you may be more fully informed of our condition and we of yours, [Col. 1056D] we have instructed the bearer of this letter, Theobald, venerable prior of the Church of Crépy, to approach your imperial majesty and carry to the throne of your highness matters which we judged should be entrusted to his fidelity rather than committed to writing.

He is a man learned in letters, distinguished by holiness of life, of renowned name, and especially familiar to us. Therefore, above the others who were deemed perfect in his order, he was chosen to administer the needs of the Church of Cluny, which from ancient days has not only been the head of the monasteries of our realm but has possessed, above all others in the whole Latin world, the glory of monastic religion. We therefore implore your imperial clemency to receive so great a man fittingly, diligently hear the words we have placed in his mouth, [Col. 1057A] mercifully grant his requests, and give heed to the needs of the Church.

## LETTER DVIII. OF THE SAME TO WILLIAM, KING OF SICILY.

LOUIS, by God’s grace king of France, to WILLIAM, illustrious king of the Sicilians, his venerable brother and dearest friend: greeting, and continual adherence to Him who gives salvation to kings.

The honour which your magnificent grandfather showed us when we were pilgrims in God’s service; the generosity he displayed towards us and our fellow pilgrims; and the manifold comfort which he devoutly bestowed upon the weary and labouring cannot depart from our memory, but [Col. 1057B] continually kindle our hearts. Would that the devotion we bear towards you might shine forth in the performance of service, and that the effect of our deserving might offer manifest testimony to our desire to earn your favour. For it would be more welcome now, if divine providence opened the opportunity, to repay service to you than it was then to receive it from your forebears. And it will be like a great gift if you decide to command something that would provide our desire with an occasion of service.

Although the extent of intervening lands separates us and prevents reciprocal services, it cannot exclude from our heart its most ardent affection: we rejoice in your prosperity as in our own, and whenever we hear of adversity, we bear it as our own. Therefore, whatever we believe serves your honour and glory, we confidently ask and sincerely urge in charity, just as we are ready to receive your requests and likewise to follow expedient counsel. The nobleman Stephen, whom you have exalted with the honour of your intimacy, is our flesh and blood and is connected by name or kinship with the most illustrious nobles of the realm of the French. Your prudence remembers all the more surely [Col. 1057C] how he was cast down and expelled to the disgrace of his family and nation, because by your presence you more clearly learned what was done against him through the treachery of those who plotted against him.

We therefore earnestly ask your nobility to take care promptly to restore him, for the glory of your name and the consolation of the realm of the French, to the full possession of affection, intimacy, honour, and dignity. For this reason, and for others which we did not judge suitable to entrust to writing, we have confidently sent to your excellency the bearer of this letter, Theobald, venerable prior of the Church of Crépy. We ask that you give him credit in what he tells you on our behalf, as you would give it to us. He is a man full of faith, reverend by the title of holiness, distinguished in learning, and especially familiar, dear, and acceptable to us and to the realm of the French. He is administering the needs of the noble Church of Cluny in the East; we ask your highness graciously to hear him more favourably and to further him more effectively in these matters. May the King of kings and Lord of lords advance and preserve your glory for His own honour through long ages.

## LETTER DIX. OF A. . . . ., QUEEN OF THE FRENCH, TO POPE ALEXANDER.

[Col. 1058A]

To the most holy lord and dearest Father ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, his humble and devoted daughter A. . . . ., queen of the French: greeting, and devoted service with sincerity of heart.

“I shall speak to you as to a father and lord,” etc. See under Alexander III, years 1159–81.

## LETTER DX. OF EMPEROR FREDERICK TO KING HENRY.

FREDERICK, by God’s grace Roman emperor and ever augustus, to his dearest friend H., illustrious king of the English: greeting and the indissoluble affection of intimate love.

[Col. 1058B] Since Christ entrusted His Church, which He redeemed by His precious blood, as one and indivisible, to be governed by blessed Peter with a singular and special privilege above the other apostles, it seems certain that there ought to be one pontiff in the Roman Church, who is the vicar of the one God and Peter, and governor of the one universal Church. Therefore, ought not we, who cherish unity and are all one body of the Church, to grieve that, with that seamless tunic—the unity of the Church—torn apart, we seem to have two apostolic pontiffs in the Roman Church?

For when Pope Adrian died on the Kalends of September, the cardinals, who seemed to be immovable pillars upon which the holy and catholic Church rested, [Col. 1058C] seeking not the things of God but their own interests and dividing the unity of the Church, elected two pontiffs. Because of so great and destructive a loss to the Church, the whole Italian Church was thrown into turmoil; and the dissensions of schism, arising in the head, would already have flowed down into the lower members and stained the whole body of the Church, had we not, by the counsel and assistance of religious men guided by the Spirit of God, opposed the rigour of justice to such shameless wickedness.

Therefore, lest the universal Church be endangered amid so great a crisis of discord, the Roman Empire, which divine clemency has provided as a remedy for so destructive a disease, ought diligently to provide for the salvation of all and carefully forestall the future, lest such great evils prevail in the Church of God. Having assembled all bishops, Italian and German alike, together with the other princes and religious men who seemed to have zeal for God and the Church, [Col. 1058D] we carefully investigated what ought to be done. From the decrees of the Roman pontiffs and the ordinances of the Church we truly learned that, once a schism had arisen in the Roman Church through the election of two apostolic pontiffs, we ought to summon both and decide the dispute according to the judgment and counsel of orthodox men.

Therefore, by the counsel of all present—namely, the bishops and the other princes—we proclaimed a solemn court and a general assembly of all ecclesiastical men, to be held at Pavia on the octave of Epiphany. To it we summoned both those who call themselves [Col. 1059A] Roman pontiffs, and all the bishops of our empire. Certainly, since you are one of the principal members of the Church, and since without your counsel and help a matter so arduous and necessary neither ought nor can attain a salutary result, if it were possible, your exalted person too ought to labour for the restoration of the Church’s unity. But because necessary affairs prevent this long-desired wish of ours, we desire to entreat your affection as best we can: send to us, from the venerable college of bishops of your realm, abbots, and other orthodox men by whose wisdom and religious devotion the English Church excels, as many as you can, and cause them to attend the aforesaid sacred assembly. Thus, by the salutary counsel of them and the other [Col. 1059B] ecclesiastical men, the unity of the Roman Church may be restored, through God who makes both one; and the state of the churches, no longer battered by any storm of dissension, may in our times remain safe in its tranquillity. Meanwhile, however, do not incline your assent to either side of the aforesaid division, nor

[lacuna]

accept [them] as at all reasonable.

## LETTER DXI. OF THE SAME TO ALL PEOPLES.

FREDERICK, by God’s grace Roman emperor and ever augustus, to all peoples whom the empire of our clemency governs.

[Col. 1059C] We believe that it has long been known how a disagreement concerning the apostolic office, once arising among the cardinals of the Roman Church, has spread with pestilential force into kings and kingdoms. We do not doubt that it has already been heard even in the remotest parts of the world how great labours both we and our invincible princes have undergone in our own person, at Pavia, Milan, Laon, and in different parts of the empire, in order to restore it to the desirable good of peace after the catholic election and confirmation of Pope Victor of blessed memory; and how great resources we have expended from zeal for justice.

Finally, when the most blessed Pope Victor was happily received into the joys of paradise, and the lord Paschal, a most Christian man, had been canonically installed in his place by the bishops and cardinals of the gracious Apostolic See, in the presence of the bishops and religious men of Lombardy and Tuscany, the prefect of the illustrious city of Rome, and many Roman nobles, [Col. 1059D] we likewise solemnly received the lord Paschal himself, by the judgment and counsel of the Church and the princes of the empire, as pope and catholic father, and intend always to venerate him with due honour.

Accordingly, the obstinate perfidy of the schismatics, openly attributing the death of the just man to their own success, has again so worked to alter the minds of certain of our faithful men by its Siren-like blandishments that, unless new remedies were promptly applied to new diseases, no small part of our people seemed likely to be led astray through confidence in our leniency. Therefore, more ardently inflamed with zeal for restoring the beauty [Col. 1060A] of God’s house, when we had found the king of the French unyielding, despite many admonitions from us—he who, without any fault on our part, together with Roland, the public enemy of our empire, and Roland’s followers, is openly attempting to strip us of our imperial honour—we summoned all princes of the empire to a general court at Wicheburch on holy Pentecost.

When their very numerous assembly was there solemnly in session, we deemed it proper to strengthen decisively and magnificently the condition of God’s Church and the cause of the lord Pope Paschal. Therefore, after devoutly invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit and thoroughly taking counsel with all present, in order utterly to remove all ambiguity on our side, we ourselves publicly swore with our own hand upon the relics of the saints that we would never receive as pope Roland the schismatic, nor any successor whom his party should elect; nor would we ever give assent to anyone’s receiving him. Nor would we ever restore our favour to any of his supporters unless he were converted from the error of his way to the unity of the Church. But we shall always support and advance the lord Pope Paschal, and render him obedience, honour, and reverence as Catholic father and universal pontiff; and, so long as life is granted, we shall never depart from him or his party.

Moreover, we shall never permit elect persons who have received, or shall hereafter receive, consecration under him or his successor whom his party elects to be deprived, because of their obedience to him, of their honour or orders. [Col. 1060C] We shall never seek release from this oath, nor accept it if offered. Further, our successor in the empire, whom all the princes elect, shall always protect and uphold under the same oath this honour of God’s Church and empire, and this our party.

Likewise, all archbishops and bishops, and the forty elect persons who were present, each with his own hand beneath his stole, took and publicly confirmed the same oath upon the holy Gospels of God. No less did all the secular princes—the duke of Saxony, Margrave Albert the Elder of Bavaria, Conrad, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Louis the Landgrave, and all the rest—swear the same thing upon the relics of the saints. Then the Holy Spirit suddenly made the minds of all so completely of one will that, on the Ember Saturday, all the elect persons most devoutly received sacred orders to the praise of God and the honour of the empire. It was also firmly decreed by us and all that any remaining persons to be ordained should do likewise in the first four Ember seasons; otherwise, without any delay, they should be deprived of the honour of the dignity to which they had been elected.

And the honourable envoys of our illustrious friend Henry, glorious king of the English, sent to us by him, publicly swore to us upon the relics of the saints, in the presence of our whole court and on behalf of the king of England, that the king himself, together with his whole realm, [Col. 1061A] would faithfully stand on our side; and would always uphold with us the lord Paschal whom we uphold. Henceforth he would in no way involve himself in supporting Roland the schismatic. Since the justice which the enemies of God’s Church and of ourselves have avoided, either out of pride or from distrust of their cause, has always found us ready to uphold it, we have at last been driven by their manifest obstinacy to unprecedented oaths. Let every person and every order beware of communion with the schismatics. For their frenzy, though it may until now have seemed in some measure pardonable, will hereafter be wholly unforgivable.

Moreover, for the complete strengthening of this affair, by the decree of the whole council of Würzburg, we most firmly command that if anyone, at the command [Col. 1061B] of his bishop, does not take the above-written oath, then, if he is a clerk or monk, he shall be deprived of ecclesiastical honour and benefice; if a layman, whatever allods and benefices he possesses shall be wholly taken from him, by our authority, by his judge or lord.

Given at Wicheburch, on the Kalends of July.

## LETTER DXII. OF THE SAME TO THE ABBOT OF STABLAUN.

FREDERICK, emperor, to the abbot of Stavelot.

As your affection knows, we assembled splendidly, together with all the princes, secular as well as ecclesiastical, at the court of Würzburg which we had summoned for Pentecost. There, among other matters concerning the holy [Col. 1061C] Church, we deliberated especially upon the affair of Pope Paschal, which was held doubtful in many hearts; and, with the counsel of all—the princes, namely, and all the clergy and laity present—we happily and magnificently strengthened it. Having invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, we established and confirmed Lord Pope Paschal and his honour in this manner: we publicly swore with our own hand upon the relics of the saints that henceforth we would by no means receive the schismatic Roland as pope. And if he should die, we shall likewise never receive his successor, whom the opposing party may appoint.

But Pope Paschal, henceforth, we shall acknowledge and uphold, with obedience, honour, and reverence, as the [Col. 1061D] universal and Catholic Father; and we shall never depart from him or from his party so long as he and we live. If, however, it should happen that we depart this life, our successor, whom all the princes shall appoint, shall always defend and uphold this honour of the Empire and this our party under the same oath. All our archbishops, bishops, and elect bishops who were present, forty in number, likewise took this oath, each with his own hand upon the holy Gospels of God beneath his stole, and publicly confirmed it. And, to remove all doubt on our side, all the elect bishops—first the elect of Cologne, then the rest—received holy orders with all devotion on the Ember Saturday [Col. 1062A] at Würzburg, for the praise and honour of the Empire. Likewise all the secular princes—the duke of Saxony, the elder Margrave Albert, the Count Palatine of the Rhine, the Landgrave, and all the others—publicly swore upon the relics of the saints.

The honourable envoys of the king of England, our friend, sent to us by him, swore at Würzburg, in the presence of our whole court, upon the relics of the saints, on behalf of the king of England and his barons, that the king of England himself, with all his realm, would faithfully stand on our side; that he too would uphold Lord Pope Paschal, whom we uphold, and would maintain our party; and that henceforth he would no further concern himself with Roland the schismatic or his party.

Therefore, [Col. 1062B] trusting in your affection and fidelity and placing the fullest confidence in you, we command you, earnestly admonishing and enjoining you, publicly to swear and observe with all the faithful of your church the aforesaid oath which we swore with our own hand before the princes, and which the princes themselves swore and confirmed. Further, on every Sunday and feast day, in the public Mass, as has been decreed and ordained by us and the princes, you shall order a public prayer for Lord Pope Paschal to be recited expressly and continually, within and without.

It has also been decreed and ordained that all these oaths shall be completed by everyone within six weeks. If any monk, cleric, or [Col. 1062C] layman in our Empire should oppose this confirmation and our decree in any manner, you may be certain that he has been judged and condemned as a public enemy of the Empire, without any hope of restoration, and deprived of every office, honour, and benefice. We sent you letters of summons; and because, in view of your prudence, you would have been most necessary to us, we deeply regret that our letters did not reach you. Meanwhile, you shall await our presence in your region. When we are nearer there, we shall fully supply whatever justice may be lacking.

## LETTER DXIII. THE KING OF SICILY TO THE KING OF ENGLAND

[Col. 1062D]

The king of Sicily to the king of England.

Upon receiving the letters of your most special affection, we learned something which we cannot utter without the greatest amazement: namely, that, forgetting the order of humanity and casting off the law of nature, a son has risen against his parent, the child against his begetter. The inward parts have been stirred to civil war; the heart has rushed to arms; and—an unheard-of wonder in our age—the flesh has cooled into blood, and blood seeks to shed itself. Since the advantages of place do not permit the assistance of your power to restrain the onset of so great a frenzy, we embrace your person and honour with that affection of charity which distances of place do not confine; [Col. 1063A] we compassionately share your sorrow, take your persecution grievously, and reckon it as our own.

Yet we trust and hope in the Lord, by whose judgment the judgments of kings are brought to their end, that He will no longer permit your son to be tempted beyond what is fitting. He who became obedient unto death will inspire in him the light of filial obedience, through which he will remember that he is your flesh and blood; abandoning the errors of hostility, he will acknowledge himself a son, return to his father, repair nature’s injury, and the former order will preserve the bonds of due affection. Farewell, and rejoice in the Lord.

## LETTER DXVI. PHILIP, COUNT OF FLANDERS, TO POPE ALEXANDER

[Col. 1063B]

PHILIP, Count of Flanders, to Pope ALEXANDER.

I offer many thanks to Your Holiness, etc. See among the letters of various persons to Pope Alexander III, after his Registers.

## LETTER DXV. RANULF OF TOURS, BISHOP, TO GILBERT

RANULF of Tours, wholly and always his, to the Lord Bishop of London: may you abound in the bowels of mercy.

Although voluntary benefits require no inducements, the impulse of charity toward you prompts me to make this pious request. J. [Col. 1063C], son of A., your former master, your steward, your guardian—shall I call him yours or ours? Yet, to confess more truly, I shall call him both yours and ours—has come to the door of your mercy. He has come who, in order that he may come to you, ought not merely to be invited, but drawn. He has come, I say, led not by choice, not corrupted by pleasure, but driven by the force of necessity. For he is burdened beyond measure by narrow means, the load of his father’s debts, the scarcity of friends, the number of brothers and sisters, and the remaining burden of his kindred.

May there remain in Your Holiness’s mind the weight of Master Adam’s cares for you, his generous provision of sustenance, his diligence in teaching, and the special goodwill he bestowed. Who today governs his own children more prudently, brings them up more generously, instructs them more attentively, or loves them more warmly? Indeed, that affection almost exceeded all measure: [Col. 1063D] he loved you not merely exceptionally, but uniquely. Far be it from a bishop’s compassion to overlook such numerous and such great merits of so great a master, and not to have pity on the children of him who once adopted you as a son.

May God therefore give you the Angel of Great Counsel, so that you may receive the bearer of this letter with the honour that befits him, refresh him with the compassion in which you abound, and advance him by the authority in which you excel. But if Your Holiness is inclined rather toward his brothers, who have little—indeed, nothing—except through him, I confess before God that it is more praiseworthy and salutary to look upon needy persons such as these than to feed certain people who seek food from house to house. Since the kindness of your religious profession strives to extend itself everywhere to all, it ought especially to assist [Col. 1064A] those who seem to have some claim upon your goods: those who do not know how to dig and are ashamed to beg, and for whom, if the small heavenly assistance available to them is withdrawn, no support for life remains.

I do not presume to teach your wisdom, but exhort your charity, for your honour and salvation. Finally, your grace pledged itself to receive, support, and advance one of Master Adam’s dependants. Since this has not yet been fulfilled, the order of reason declares that it must be paid, and mercy commands that it be performed. In these matters and in all things may God fill your heart with the spirit of counsel, fortitude, and piety. Farewell always in the Lord.

## LETTER DXVI

[Col. 1064B]

You acted sufficiently cautiously and wisely in announcing your appeal. But the lord king had made more prudent provision in this matter for you and others by his favour, when immediately afterwards he came to an agreement with the king of France concerning a compact made between them under pledge of faith: that neither of them should retain in his own land an invader of the other, nor receive or support any aggressor who refused to abide by the judgment of his lord’s court. For he charged that the war of the Archbishop of Canterbury was most grievous and wholly disorderly.

Thus the matter finally came to this: the archbishop was asked whether he preferred to leave France or to moderate his excommunications and, moreover, absolve all those whom he had excommunicated. Furthermore, the Bishop of Sées and the Archdeacon of Canterbury have now gone to France as messengers concerning letters [the source wording is uncertain], for the great benefit, unity, and peace of the English Church. Likewise Reginald, Archdeacon of Salisbury, is returning, having completed all the lord king’s business to the satisfaction of himself and his followers. He brings with him two clerics belonging to the household of the lord pope: namely Gratian, subdeacon, nephew of Pope Eugenius and master of the notaries; and Vivian, advocate of the Roman court. For what purpose or in what manner we do not yet know; but we hope all will be well, as we have learned from certain persons what you will shortly hear.

## LETTER DXVII. … BISHOP TO GILBERT

[Col. 1064D]

To the Lord Bishop of London, present and future salvation.

As a certain eminent master of eloquence teaches, he is ungrateful who denies that he has received a benefit; more ungrateful is he who conceals it; and most ungrateful of all is he who has forgotten it. Therefore, lest the distinguished brightness of your reputation appear blackened by the coal of this or that sort of ingratitude, may Master Adam’s heavy cares for you, the depth of his teaching, the abundance of his support, and finally his ardent—indeed blazing—charity touch your memory. May your mind retain how great was the care, with what embrace, and by what special privilege the diligent vigilance of your teacher, steward, and guardian adopted you not only above his household but above all [Col. 1065A] mortals; and how his spirit, if I may say so, rested in your spirit.

In consideration, therefore, of such and still greater merits, and through the intervention of my prayers, may your grace regard J., the bearer of this letter, with that benevolent attention which befits your holiness and answers to paternal care, so that the son may experience in benefit what the father earned by labour. For when his father paid nature’s debt, he left his son burdened with debt, hindered by the number of his brothers, constrained by narrow means, and entangled in certain other bonds. It befits your most beloved religious profession, which even anticipates the merits of others, to consider the needs of this most devoted servant of yours and to open to the son the bosom of your exalted mercy. May Your Holiness [Col. 1065B], most dear, flourish in the Lord.

## LETTER DXVIII. R. … TO THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

R. …, his own to his own, servant to his lord, to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury: whatever in life is more pleasant and more conducive to salvation.

I consider that I have not written to you more often without fault. I have indeed sinned, but mercy knows how to spare one who confesses. For hitherto I have been less diligent in those matters known to belong to the care of your administration. The administration and solicitude of our whole Church rest upon you. To you all things have been entrusted; you are permitted to establish everything by your counsel or alter it by your judgment, advance good things to better, and recall what is perverse from confusion into [Col. 1065C] order.

The holy mother Church of Canterbury rejoices that she has entrusted herself and her possessions to your direction, having with unanimous will set you over herself as father, shepherd, and leader, through ordered care, solicitude, and consideration. For the inward and outward care of all things laid upon you summons you to watchfulness. It is a great honour, a heavy burden, and one unbearable to anyone unless supported by divine mercy. Much solicitude and very great labour, if I am not mistaken, rest upon you. Human presumption therefore presumes vainly in these matters, where divine mercy accomplishes everything.

Accordingly, great diligence is needed, and the heavy burden must be lightened by the participation of many. What one person can do less fully must be borne [Col. 1065D] by many. But such a distribution requires discerning and energetic men: men who know how prudently to administer outward matters and vigilantly to preside over inward things, armed with zeal for God according to knowledge; men who, preferring common interests to private, seek not their own things but those of Jesus Christ, and know wisely, desire humbly, and are able usefully to undertake the care assigned to them; men who do not serve flesh or blood, but know especially how to provide for those of the household of faith; who do not disperse the Church’s resources to enrich their relatives; who do not cast the children’s bread to dogs, diminishing the household while fattening outsiders; whom neither the blemish of excessive stinginess taints nor prodigal extravagance disgraces; who make no provision for the flesh in its desires, but strive to serve the spirit; whom neither gluttony over food nor drowsiness caused by wine [Col. 1066A] weighs down; to whom the melody of hymns or psalms is more delightful than wandering by day or sleeping by night; who have more at heart the care of souls than bodies; who desire the embraces of beautiful Rachel and yet do not refuse to endure Leah for her fruitfulness; who thirst ardently for Mary’s contemplation and do not neglect the solicitude of labouring Martha; who, by alternation, wisely apply themselves now to inward and now to outward matters, so that all other things may be added to them, and, seeking first the kingdom of God, prefer spiritual things to carnal and divine things to human.

For a bishop ought to have ministers such as these, to whom he may safely distribute those duties which, because of his concern for other churches also committed to him, he himself is less able to bear in addition [Col. 1066B] to his burdens. For this, I think, is sound counsel: counsel which commends an honourable and discerning man. Perhaps another will grow angry with me and say:

“Why do you proceed to teach Minerva, or set Apollo’s fingers to the lyre?

What business have you with princes, you scarcely fit even for common people?

Hardly worthy of earth, what do you do above the stars?”

They praise me for refraining from these things; I should wisely consider my lot and, conscious of my profession, blush to speak. They urge me to stop my mouth because I am a monk: for, as they say, we are dead men, and we who have renounced the world have absolutely nothing to do with the care of outward things. Let it be as they say. But, I ask, let them give me someone who can live in the world without worldly things. For there are [Col. 1066C] those in the world but not of the world, who use the world as though not using it and seek only to please God in all things. If anyone—God forbid—disguises himself while living otherwise, let him see to it himself; it is no concern of mine. Yet would that my conscience may not accuse me.

If there is anyone so glorious as to speak against me with unbridled brow, as though he did not know what he says, is not service owed? But what service greater, better, more useful, or more honourable can be rendered than preserving the indissoluble bond of friendship? To omit other considerations, should I make light of the danger of my lord and bishop? Is not that in which he is endangered also a danger to me? What ship escaped shipwreck when its pilot was [Col. 1066D] wrecked? Or who would dare deny that even the greatest may sometimes be helped by the least? We have often seen and heard it happen.

Moses, appointed by the Lord judge of the people of Israel, used Jethro’s counsel in all things. David refreshed an Amalekite youth whom he found exhausted on the journey, and, with him as guide, overtook and slew those Amalekites who had carried away his captive wives and plunder. Daniel also in Babylon undertook judgment against the elder judges who seemed to govern the people, and destroyed them with fitting punishment. Why, then, do my less discerning critics take offence? Is it not permitted here also in the Church of Christ, in which the Father of heaven and earth reveals to little ones what has been hidden from the wise? Who would not receive the spirit of divine counsel in brotherly [Col. 1067A] charity, when it is lawful even to learn from an enemy?

I neither doubt nor fail to recognize the prudent man appointed to so great a rule; yet no man is ever read to have possessed too much counsel or such foresight in administering affairs so great. He is sufficient unto himself; but I wish my affection to be known to him. I desire to merit his favour. For it pleases me if anything from me flows into his service. It is not a friendship newly formed yesterday or the day before yesterday, but one which took its origin almost from the beginning of his life and which, through time, I judge has been maintained and more richly increased by merits succeeding one another. It is pleasant and exceedingly gratifying to me that I have obtained such a man as friend, if I have deserved to preserve him as such.

If I have erred in anything, [Col. 1067B] I beg that it be attributed to ignorance, not malice. Yet I know that my former affection still remains, and that habitual practice persists by disposition, although its effect may have been less in outward manifestation. Would that it might endure and remain inviolate to the end, without limit to its increase. I do love, indeed I love; and, if I love too little, I pray that I may love more strongly. Yet this remains fixed with me: none of your sons can love you more abundantly, more joyfully, or more sweetly than I do. Though my affection can benefit you little, it is nevertheless less than I would wish; but may the mercy of almighty God make up what is imperfect in me.

I have exceeded the proper length of a letter in writing, [Col. 1067C] because it is too little for me to speak with you, as far as the page allows, with paper rather than with my tongue. Yet may kindly patience pardon me if I add this one thing: do not be unduly frightened, nor disturbed by flatteries. Let the flatterer perceive that you are a lover of truth, and let the tongue of the sycophant fall silent in your presence. Let the condition of your steadfastness stand upright; let it know neither bending nor breaking. Perhaps the world will be troubled, but the Lord has power to calm and cast down the rising storm. The hearts of kings are in the Lord’s hand; the merciful and just Lord uses them either in mercy or in judgment. Stand therefore in the faith; act manfully; be strengthened in the Lord; let all your deeds be done in charity; and may the God of peace and love be, and remain, with you. Amen.

## LETTER DXIX

[Col. 1067D]

Having firm confidence in the favour of your nobility, whenever need requires we confidently commend to you our friends, especially those whom we know to be faithful and devoted to the lord pope and to the whole Church of God. We do so, beyond doubt, [Col. 1068A] considering that you ought to incline toward our party as much as your support with us could achieve. Therefore we earnestly commend to your serenity our venerable brother, the Bishop of London, whom we have certainly found faithful to the Roman pontiff and the Church. With most earnest affection we entreat you to receive kindly his messengers coming to the court, and to endeavour amicably to cooperate in, and effectively advance, the requests which they bring on behalf of the said bishop.

If, however, any adverse report concerning the aforesaid bishop has been conveyed at the court of the lord pope—a charge from which we believe him free—let your skill take care so to erase it that the aforementioned messengers may be heard more favourably [Col. 1068B] by the supreme pontiff and favour may be shown in these matters to the one who sends them. Farewell.

## LETTER DXX

Master Otto, Bishop of Tusculum, and Lord Albert, cardinal priest, are said to be coming; and if the lord king is willing to abide by the lord’s command, they are believed then to be coming to England. Lord Hyacinth has crossed into Spain, where he is to discharge the office of legate. The Abbot of Clairvaux was at Piacenza on the first Sunday after the Ascension of the Lord, intending to cross over to the lord pope; he will present to the pope and court a plan for peace, just as the emperor and king of France have reached agreement.

[Col. 1068C]

Our messengers obtained passage near Rome by giving the senators twenty pounds, and the same messengers were at Bologna on their return on the first Sunday after the Ascension. The Bishop of Worcester, however, and Reginald the archdeacon did not dare entrust themselves to the senators’ good faith. Robert of Neubourg crossed into Sicily to visit the king and his relatives.

Furthermore, you should know that the lord king destroyed all the castles of Widomar of Léon in Brittany, except three which the lord king holds in his own hand. The open country was granted to Widomar. What Widomar occupied from the fiefs of his neighbours he shall restore, or on this matter he shall stand trial before the king; what he occupied from the fiefs of his own men he shall restore, or shall render them full justice in his own court, if the lord king commands it by his writ. The Archbishop of Bourges has lately departed from human affairs; in his place, by consent of clergy and people, was appointed the Bishop of Meaux, namely Lord Stephen, brother of Adam, formerly chamberlain of the king of France.

# THE COMPLETE EXTANT WORKS OF HERBERT OF BOSHAM, SECRETARY OF ST THOMAS OF CANTERBURY

Now first edited by J. A. GILES, LL.D., priest of the Church of England and lately Fellow of Corpus Christi College, Oxford. (Oxford and London, 1845, octavo, 2 volumes.)

[Col. 1069]

## DEDICATORY EPISTLE

To his most friendly brother James NORRIS, Doctor of Sacred Theology, President of Corpus Christi College, and to his other most friendly men and good brothers, the Fellows and pupils of the same college, John ALLEN GILES, their brother and former colleague: greetings, and may you enjoy the best success in good letters.

While I was long travelling in regions beyond the sea and had wandered through almost the whole West, your brotherhood cannot doubt how much joy it gave me finally to find an old copy of Herbert of Bosham in the Library of Arras. For this Herbert, the inseparable companion for so many years of St Thomas the Archbishop, described in a style considered at that time excessive and ranging beyond due bounds what he himself had seen and in which he himself had played a great part. Yet, by Hercules, no one can fail to regret that works which five hundred years ago utterly overcame our fathers’ diligence by the excessive labour of copying should, after the discovery of the noble art of printing, remain longer hidden in manuscript codices.

But a certain disgraceful librarian—his name has perished, though his memory still lives—had sacrilegiously torn out every tenth folio of that Arras book, which, so far as I knew, I had believed to be the only surviving copy, in order to make profit by selling its parchment for a few pennies. Consequently, throughout the book there are very many gaps, grievously to be deplored, which interrupt the reader’s study. Warned thus that the remaining portion might suffer a similar fate, I had the entire codex transcribed and now make it public in these volumes.

Yet not all of these gaps appear in my books. This resulted from divine Providence, which smiled upon me in this matter, not from any care of my own. For in the library of your brotherhood—indeed, of our brotherhood—there still survives a codex containing this golden work, except only the first three books. I had once indeed conceived a suspicion concerning it; but because the codices preserved in our college suffered from such confusion that books being sought could scarcely be found with any diligence, I had never seen that codex; nor, had I seen it, could I readily have recognized it, because it bears no author’s name and, mutilated and incomplete, does not even retain its beginning.

Since this is so, my brothers, I lay at your feet this first edition of Herbert of Bosham’s little work on the Life of St Thomas of Canterbury, mindful of that time when, among you, entangled in no worldly affairs and freed from every temporal care, I strove with pure and simple mind to seek the truth, approach the sources themselves, and drink deeply from them abundant draughts of divine learning.

I pray and earnestly beseech your brotherhood that my Herbert, supported by your favour and patronage, may come forth into the light; and that I may be allowed to commend him to you in the same words with which Horace commended his friend Septimius to Nero:

> Enrol him among your own company, and believe him brave and good.

The Kalends of December, 1845.

J. A. G.

[Col. 1069]

## J. A. GILES’S PREFACE TO VOLUME I, CONTAINING THE LIFE OF ST THOMAS

Since St Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, has deservedly obtained the distinction of having many contemporaneous writers of his life, he has certainly acquired none whom one receives with greater pleasure—indeed, I might say love—than this Herbert of Bosham. For he is celebrated among us for this reason alone: that he clung to his prelate in the closest bonds of friendship, so that no memory whatever of a certain Herbert would survive today had he not committed himself to posterity together with the name of that most holy prelate.

We learn from his own writings and those of others that he was English by birth, born at Bosham—or, as it is commonly called, Bosham in Sussex—which was formerly a lordship assigned to the see of Canterbury and afterward passed in turn into various hands: those, namely, of the earls of Kent, William Marshal, and the Berkeley family. Tall in stature and handsome in appearance, he stood out so greatly among all others that he seemed to savour rather of knighthood than priesthood; endowed with singular force of character and a vast abundance of physical strength, he seemed born, as events proved, for the undertakings which, with dangers threatening on every side, required the boldest men.

He embraced Thomas’s cause while Thomas still held no office except that of chancellor. He was present as witness at his consecration and subsequently accompanied him to the Council of Clarendon. He adhered so completely to him at the famous court held at Northampton Castle that, when the prelate fled by night—that night which became, as it were, the shameless source of all tumults and tyranny—he too fled during that same night, returning to Canterbury. There, as he had been ordered, he gathered together the greatest quantity he could of money, of gold and silver vessels, and of all kinds of furnishings; then, quickly crossing the sea, he reached Saint-Omer, where after seven or eight days he was to receive his lord.

Ordered from there to fleece certain envoys whom Henry had sent to Pope Alexander, he not long afterward confronted the king himself for a conference. There, when Henry repeatedly declared and promised that he would restore favour to each and all if only they abandoned the archbishop’s party, our Herbert yielded nothing at all, except that he displayed himself more freely and courageously—perhaps more insolently. Thereafter he is said to have performed many deeds to which his fidelity was entrusted in proportion to the dangers to which he committed himself. For the king’s utterly certain anger threatened him, without any favourable chance intervening, so savage that he gouged out the eyes of every conquered enemy and cruelly cut off other parts of the body.

Nevertheless, Thomas, with Herbert as companion, regained his Canterbury. Yet Herbert was not to see with his own eyes Thomas so soon and so miserably struck down, because he had left the city—indeed England itself—on the day before that most wicked day, having been sent to the French. From this, admittedly and from the opposite perspective, one may doubt whether, had that headstrong and bold man been present, he would have inspired such fear in the murderers that they could not have committed their crime, or whether he himself, though unwilling and resisting, would rather have become the cause of an even worse and more terrible slaughter.

After Thomas’s death we read little more concerning Herbert, except that, fourteen years after the murder, in order to satisfy his friends, he undertook to recount the life of this great man, whom he had followed for so many years that he placed all his affections in this one man and, as it were, made him “the object of his idolatrous worship.”

The work is arranged in seven books and contains a brief account of the bishop’s life. It is followed by another work, or book of *Melos*, whose subject consists of many comparisons, according to the author’s inclination, between Christ’s life and Thomas’s. Third, and last, comes another history: namely, of events after the archbishop’s death. So far as this goes. If you inquire what works belong to the same author, see the preface to volume II, where all the other items lacking here receive their own fairly appropriate explanation.

[Note: [Col. 1071] We have appended to the preface of volume I that which Dr Giles prefaced to volume II. EDITORS.]

And now what remains but to show by what arduous route I have nearly reached the conclusion of the entire undertaking, in order to print this book of such value? A Life of Thomas precedes the letters published by Wolf of Brussels, in which there are indeed ample fragments extracted both from our author and from various others. When I sought the sources of these passages throughout the collections of all Britain—if not Herbert’s own autograph, then some copies, or even one copy, of his books—I tried in vain. I had already begun to despair and to visit the libraries of every people, in which one might perhaps see the sole copy of an English work, while that England of ours did not even know that such a work existed.

Then, by God’s favour, I arrived at Arras, which claims first place among the peoples of French Flanders. There, among no few works of great importance, I found a most beautiful manuscript codex of Herbert of Bosham—but alas, almost a quarter of it had been torn away. “And who,” you will ask, “committed this sacrilege?” A librarian, truly most greedy and no less foolish, tore the work apart to obtain or sell the parchment.

On my return to England, the Reverend H. O. Coxe informed me that, while cataloguing the manuscripts of Corpus Christi College, he had encountered a copy of Herbert. They had known previously that it survived, but until then did not know where it lay hidden. What more need be said? That copy was of the greatest assistance to me in printing these works. For it contains the last four books, missing from the Arras manuscript; consequently the entire work has been brought almost to completeness, except for a few omitted folios, which admittedly pertain to the text of the earlier books but, it appears, only moderately to the matter itself.

If another codex, third in order and very nearly complete, should join this work now restored by us to something like its original form, its gaps would permit every missing passage in this book also to find and fill its own vacant place with the greatest ease.

Peace, then, to the shades of Herbert of Bosham! Peace to his soul! And if he was ever allowed to dwell upon these thoughts during the final years of his life, let him now be comforted and rejoice. For behold: this work—his own work—which he tearfully entreated should not be scattered, is being restored, established, and, I hope, shall live for ever.

[Col. 1071]

## PREFACE TO VOLUME II, CONTAINING THE SHORTER WORKS AND LETTERS OF HERBERT OF BOSHAM

In the very distinguished work which Bosham wrote on the Life of St Thomas, he more than once intimates that he is reluctantly bidding farewell to the work to which he had attached himself. This is nowhere clearer than when, after narrating the archbishop’s murder, material was already failing him as he wrote. To make good that deficiency, however, he added certain “consonances,” as he calls them, in which he presents the holy archbishop as a soldier in spiritual warfare and Christ as the commander.

There follows the book of *Melos*, or melodies: a mere and ill-arranged medley which, though separately considered seems scarcely worthy of publication, nevertheless contains some matters not unworthy of notice, especially where the author presents himself in conversation with Henry II. From the narrative of events after Becket’s murder, some light is shed upon Herbert’s life when he was already an old man. After his master’s death, he appears to have lived in England. The claim of some that Herbert wore the purple of the cardinals arose solely from the text of the *Catalogue of Learned Men*, extraordinarily corrupted in Wolf’s edition.

The book of *Melos* is followed by a homily delivered on the feast day of St Thomas, and by the Constitutions of Clarendon, which, as Bosham says in the prologue to the book of *Melos*, he copied from “that fatal written instrument which was first the cause of our exile and afterward of martyrdom.”

This memorial, raised by Herbert in remembrance of his beloved master, consists of these four parts. It contains very much that illuminates the history of England in this age and deserves, not without reason, to be numbered among the more important writings spared by time.

There also survives an unpublished work of Bosham, namely a Commentary on the Psalms, preserved in the Bodleian Library. We give its preface.

The work that follows is comparable to Herbert’s outstanding study of the Life of St Thomas; yet, surprisingly, writers who have treated the same matters scarcely mention it: namely, the collection of letters which Herbert wrote in the person of his master, while he served as his secretary. He seems to have assembled these letters in old age, as he reviewed past events in his memory and provided for posterity—events in which he himself, when young, had played a considerable part. The manuscript of these letters is preserved in the library of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge; apart from certain letters already published, they now come to light from that manuscript.

These are the writings of Herbert thus far discovered.

There are added several hitherto unpublished letters of Alan, abbot of Tewkesbury, supplied by a manuscript in the library of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge.

Oxford, December 1845.

[Col. 1073]

# LIFE OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP AND MARTYR, BY HERBERT OF BOSEHAM

## LETTER TO BALDWIN, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, AND TO HIS CATHOLIC SUCCESSORS

[Col. 1073A] To the most blessed BALDWIN, chief bishop of the holy Church of Canterbury, and to all his successors to be canonically appointed: HERBERT OF BOSEHAM, the least of the servants of your holiness, greeting in the Lord and the reverence due to fathers.

I have written a history of the life and deeds of our glorious new martyr, blessed Thomas, your predecessor—not, indeed, with that splendour of style or that solemnity of expression which the dignity of the subject demands, but according to what was granted from above. “Great subjects,” as someone says, “do not endure small talents.” Yet, lest the very famous deeds of so great a man should, through the so frequent and unbroken succession of times and generations, either be obscured by age or erased by forgetfulness, knowingly and deliberately I set my shoulders beneath a burden beyond my strength. This was especially incumbent upon me still surviving, since nearly all my companions and brethren who, with me, saw the man’s passion have been taken from the world and now sleep in Christ. Therefore I put my hand to the task, preferring, should necessity require it, to be accused of rashness rather than delay or negligence.

Yet before your fatherhood, I do not doubt, filial devotion will excuse me, who desire by the service of my pen to restore to you an exemplar withdrawn from the world: an exemplar truly incorruptible, according to which you ought to live, according to which you ought to govern, and in which you ought daily to read. For this exemplary man gave an example especially to you, that, as he himself did, you also might do likewise. Therefore throughout this history I have portrayed the man as an exemplar—not to be wondered at in miracles, but to be imitated in works. For miracles were given for unbelievers; since others have seen and written of them, throughout this whole historical book I am silent about them and pass them by, pursuing only those signs in the exemplary man’s deeds which were given to believers for wonder and imitation.

And especially to you, called by God and, if you dare—though I think you stand in awe—about to enter the contest, undertake the charge, and fill the chair of so great an athlete: may the Almighty grant you to receive the zeal of him whose ministry you have received; the strength of him whose dispensation has been entrusted to you; and his care in all things, whose chair you fill. Therefore I pray and desire that your little sheep, long straying through the trackless and pathless wastes of the desert, may be borne upon your shoulders back to the Lord’s flock. [Col. 1074A]

## Argument of the Martyr’s History

We divide this history of the glorious martyr Thomas into seven volumes.

I. The first volume touches briefly and cursorily, as in passing, on the place of the man’s birth, the names of his parents, and the first years of his life.

II. The second volume treats more fully of the man’s youth and the works of his youth; of his coming into the service of the great Father Theobald, then chief bishop of Canterbury; of his promotion to be archdeacon of Canterbury and the reason for that promotion; and afterwards how he was transferred by the chief bishop, as it were from the Church, to the court—namely, to the office of chancellor in the court of the illustrious King Henry II. There it is also shown what kind of man he was and how great he was at court. [Col. 1074B]

III. The third volume relates how, after the death of the aforesaid Father, he returned from court to his mother Church, promoted from archdeacon of Canterbury to chief bishop of Canterbury. It shows how, as the eminence of that see is accustomed to require, he at once endeavoured to fulfil the office of chief bishop, both before God and men, in a manner worthy of its greatness; why, with no great delay, so many and such great troubles, straits, oppressions, and persecutions arose against him; what was the cause of all these evils; and how, through malice, a profane discord was contrived to arise between so great a king and so great a chief bishop—men whose bonds of affection had previously been great, indeed greatest, as the world saw—and envied. [Col. 1074C]

IV. The fourth volume describes the flight into exile of the chief bishop, now thus pressed, distressed, and afflicted, avoiding the heat of persecution lest something worse should happen; and it describes not only the evils but also the advantages of exile, together with its duration and place.

V. The fifth volume records at last the reconciliation between him and the king, the manner and cause of that reconciliation, his return from exile to his homeland, and afterwards the renewed wrath of the king against him—instigated by not one but many malicious persons—and the cause of its renewal.

VI. The sixth volume, after the persecution of exile, adds the struggle of martyrdom, describing its manner and the martyr’s constancy and courage. [Col. 1075A]

VII. The seventh volume contains a catalogue of Thomas’s learned associates, mentioned throughout the history; it also discusses why this history must not be mutilated. At the end, the author commends himself to the prayers of those reading this history: “And whom,” etc.

When the history is finished, he immediately appends to it a little book, because almost its entire material depends upon the history, entitling it *Melorum* (“Of Melodies”) after its subject matter. For that little book, in the manner of a lyre, resounds with three harmonies, forming, as it were, three melodies. What those harmonies are from which the three melodies are formed, the prologue prefixed to the book explains.

[Col. 1076A] When the book of melodies, with its three melodies, has been completed, he adds one further homily of his on the martyr, beginning: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has gloriously magnified [himself].” At the very end of all is placed that fatal writing, drawn up in the form of a charter, which first dissolved the great and dear bonds between so great a king and so great a chief bishop, as the world saw and envied: the cause first of the chief bishop’s exile and finally of his martyrdom. And since some of the seven volumes which we have distinguished are longer, we have prefixed to each volume its own separate chapters, so that what is sought may more easily be found.

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST VOLUME BEGIN

[Col. 1075]

1. On the ecclesiastical custom by which the lives of holy Fathers are written, and why.
2–3. On the Lord’s abundant mercy toward Thomas; here it touches upon his birthplace and the names of his parents, and touches upon the man’s childhood and adolescence; it also briefly reports a vision of the man while still a boy, and that a disciple should write nothing as testimony concerning his master which he has not himself seen.

The chapters of the first volume end.

# THE FIRST VOLUME OF THE HISTORY BEGINS: ON THE LIFE AND DEEDS OF BLESSED THOMAS, MARTYR AND BISHOP OF CANTERBURY

## 1. ON THE ECCLESIASTICAL CUSTOM BY WHICH THE LIVES OF HOLY FATHERS ARE WRITTEN, AND WHY

[Col. 1075B]

It is an ecclesiastical custom to record the illustrious lives of holy Fathers and to set down in lasting written memorials, as is fitting, those immortal works which they performed while still in mortal flesh. Thus, by a certain remedy of the pen, those for whom the world was not worthy are restored to the world. And so we who still live, who remain engaged in the struggle of this present life, may be encouraged by their voice to run the race and may await victory with assured hope.

This is the saying in the song of love, of the Beloved to the beloved, of the Bride to the Bridegroom, of the Church to Christ: “All fruits, new and old,” she says, “are kept by the Bride for the Bridegroom,” when the Church stores in the memorial treasury of books the fruits of good works, plucked now from ancient and now from modern Fathers, like trees both life-giving and fruitful. From there the works of exemplary Fathers and the exemplars of their works are daily and gladly distributed to Christ’s poor, for the glory and praise of Christ, as a daily refreshment and for instruction in Christian conduct. [Col. 1075C]

Therefore, brothers, now not only cutting branches from the trees with the Hebrew children for Christ’s praise and glory, but recalling not merely the teachings of holy Fathers but their deeds also, let us run on the two twin feet of charity to a certain new tree, bearing for us new fruit, new fruits. And, according to the Bride’s promise, let us keep new fruits for the Bridegroom together with the old. For among the other trees of God’s paradise, both life-giving and fruitful, there is one from which in these days we gather new fruit more abundantly.

And there stands among the other princes of God’s Church, who have preceded and gone before us—after whose backs we still sing according to the Psalmist—one, I say, singular and distinguished, to whom in our days there was none like, contending for the law of his God. This man now stands among the princes who have gone before, joined to those who sing; and though his face is not recognised, his wound identifies him. For the martyr stands dancing and triumphing, his whole head torn open. And lest any of you should still doubt who he is whom we depict in the colour of such circumlocutory speech, let us lift up our eyes, raise our ears, and recognise this prince, our patron and father, by name: his name is Thomas. This is surely that Thomas who was once bishop of the people of Canterbury, but is now primate not of a city but of the world. Or rather, now standing beside the Ruler of the whole earth, he will judge not only the city but also the city and the world. [Col. 1076B–C]

## 2. ON THE LORD’S MERCY TOWARD THOMAS

O ineffable depths of divine mercy toward you, Thomas! O incomprehensible secrets of the divine counsel! For we saw you, Thomas, a human being liable to suffering like ourselves, bearing our burden with us and sharing our weakness. We saw you, I say, born in London, bodily begotten by a certain Gilbert as father and Matilda as mother. And behold how your lot is now among the companions, and how you are numbered among the children of God. Behold how these now come from afar! Behold, those from north and sea, and these from the southern land: at the tomb of one still asleep, they who are wounded invoke merits, seek patronage, and worship wounds—as though they breathed and scattered everywhere some life-giving fragrance of wondrous sweetness. [Col. 1076D–1077A]

This is indeed the work of him who raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dunghill, that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory.

## 3. ON THE MAN’S CHILDHOOD AND ADOLESCENCE

But since, with his aid, I have undertaken briefly to describe this man’s deeds, I pass over for the present the years of his childhood and adolescence, intending to report only those things concerning this man as testimony which I myself saw and heard—matters concerning which alone testimony is true.
