Thus may the Evangelist’s saying be applied in some fashion even to me, though unworthy in life and inept in writing: “This is the disciple who bears witness concerning these things, and who saw and wrote these things” (John 21). [Col. 1077B]

Yet I now pass over those ages of his childhood and adolescence, except that I have received from others who knew him intimately that he spent those years with the good simplicity and purity becoming to that age. There is, however, one thing which I learned from his own report and have taken care to insert here. While he was still a boy, when he had been seized for some time by a fever, and as it grew worse, a burning sweat gradually broke out from within over his whole little body, a certain lady appeared to him: tall in stature, gentle in face, and beautiful in appearance. She stood beside him as he lay in bed; having comforted the boy with a promise of recovery, she placed two golden keys in his hands, saying: “Thomas, these are the keys of Paradise, whose custody you shall yet have.” Having said this, she disappeared. [Col. 1078A–B]

## CHAPTERS OF THE SECOND VOLUME

[Col. 1077]

1. That, having become a young man, he grew in age and in favour among men, but not so much with the Lord.
2. On his continence in youth.
3. On the secular men whom he served in the first years of his adulthood.
4. On Theobald, chief bishop of Canterbury, into whose service he transferred himself.
5. On the favour which he obtained in the eyes of his lord, and the cause of that favour.
6. On his promotion to the archdeaconry of Canterbury and the reason for the promotion.
7. That, once made a deacon, he did not immediately set his shoulders to deacons’ burdens.
8. How, having been transferred to the court of the illustrious King Henry II, he was made chancellor.
9. How for a time he put off the cleric and put on the chancellor.
10. By what gifts of grace he quickly obtained the king’s favour above all others.
11. What kind of man and how great he was in the office of chancellor, and concerning certain vigorous works of his in that office, which he indicates in passing but does not set forth in detail.
12. How his fellow courtiers, seeing his great favour and glory, began suddenly but secretly to envy him.

# SECOND VOLUME

[Col. 1077C] 1. Therefore, when this man had passed the years of his childhood and adolescence, as he grew in age he also grew in ability and favour with men, but not to the same degree with the Lord. To see why I say this, let us recall a twofold grace. For grace among human beings is twofold.

There is a certain civic grace: urban, kind, sweet, sociable, inviting others to love its possessor; by it a person pleases the world more but God less, since it is still devoid of goodness—a certain worldly kindness without goodness. Therefore this civic and urban grace, lacking goodness as its companion, is worldly, deceptive, and vain. Yet in it one may more readily observe the vanity of the world alone than any baseness of deed or any wickedness. Nevertheless, though deceptive and vain, this grace is from God. This grace of the world is like a more striking beauty of the flesh: indeed from God, although the grace itself is deceptive and vain. As the Wise Man says: “Grace is deceptive and beauty is vain” (Proverbs 31:30; cited here as Proverbs 36). Yet this grace, when goodness is joined to such kindness, makes that kindness most excellent.

There is another grace, worldly indeed but belonging only to heaven, which seems greatly opposed to the grace just described. In the former there is kindness alone without goodness; in this, goodness alone without kindness. For this grace is sadder, stricter, more severe; unlike the former, it is not all things to all people, but only to itself and to God. By it a person pleases God more but the world less; such a person is always sadder and more austere, inviting neither worldly people nor even those with whom he is constantly joined in fellowship by any sweetness of his own, but rather seeming always to threaten them with a furrowed brow. This grace is spiritual, holy, and good, but less suitable and pleasant for companionship. Those endowed with it are certainly good, but not so much kindly—a quality produced by that former grace, namely civic and urban grace. [Col. 1077D–1078C]

Accordingly, it is especially desirable to possess this twofold grace, particularly for those who are in the world and dwell among worldly people: that, if they are good, they may also be kind. Those endowed with both graces are citizens of Jerusalem; yet they are especially fitted to administer the affairs of both cities—Jerusalem, that is, and Babylon. Thus Joseph, endowed with this twofold grace, though a citizen of Jerusalem, wisely and efficiently administered Egyptian affairs in Egypt, pleasing to God and human beings. Likewise Daniel administered Babylonian affairs in Babylon. And this master himself, excelling in this twofold grace, became all things to all people.

To show us that these graces are to be joined in us and for us, the Master, after listing fifteen works of the flesh, places kindness immediately after goodness among the twelve fruits of the Spirit. Goodness then becomes not only good but pleasant, if it has kindness as its companion—that civic and urban grace with which we began. Our Thomas excelled in this grace in the first years of his youth, though still lacking the goodness which the Master himself places among the fruits of the Spirit. But our God, being kind and good, afterwards gave him a remarkable goodness, unexpected by the world, and increased his kindness with goodness, so that he might advance in favour both with men and with the Lord. [Col. 1078D–1079A]

For the Lord, good and kind, is accustomed to look especially upon a person’s kindness—not only that kindness which has goodness as its companion, but also that which, as we said, exists even without goodness. He is accustomed, I say, to look upon such kindness, adding goodness to it as and when he wills. For the Spirit blows not only where he wills, but when he wills; and those who come last are made equal to those who came before.

Thus, from early youth he followed youthful pursuits. Removing his hand from the rod, he fled from the learning which he had acquired in the schools while still young, like Ephraim feeding on winds and pursuing a shadow. Thus he gave attention to courtly trifles, to wandering and empty pursuits—those things which are usually sweet and familiar to that age, according to the poet’s words:

> He delights in horses and dogs and in the grass of the sunny field.

And that he might excel over others, he always sought more elegant adornment than the rest. Yet the Master forbids buffoonery irrelevant to the matter at hand, and the Wise Man warns that one should never glory in one’s dress, since the more ambitious it is, the less it is free from suspicion. It does not make one thought upright even if perhaps all such outward arrangement sometimes depends not on desire but on virtue. But this man, following the spirit of popular acclaim which he sought as a youth, neither cared for the Master’s command nor followed the Wise Man’s counsel. [Col. 1079B–C]

## 2. ON THOMAS’S CONTINENCE WHEN A YOUNG MAN

Yet this is beyond all doubt concerning him: amid the ardour of that age and the worldly luxury in which he lived, though he eagerly embraced honourable pleasures, he was always a most ardent lover of chastity. In this he was already like one of the saints of whom it is written that, though proud and vain, he was nevertheless considered chaste in body. Moreover, he always detested lying lips and a slanderous tongue.

For the merciful God often, indeed very often, justly abandons his predestined ones in one respect because of certain stains of fault, while never ceasing to stand by them in another respect through certain gifts of grace. Thus, in abandoning them, he permits them to fall, so that when delivered they may be more indebted to grace; but in standing by them he does not permit those who fall to plunge into the depths, lest, if the sinner should reach that point, he should come to contempt, with the pit of repentance pressing upon him and closing over his mouth. The prophet, I think, observing this—that in one and the same person there may be, on this side, some stains of fault, and on that, certain gifts of grace—said that the Lord partly rains upon one and the same city, but partly leaves it dry and without rain.

Indeed, since human steps are prone to slipping, a great sign of hope is nevertheless given in a person if we see someone occasionally slip through certain sinful delights, yet be held back from falling into the depths by certain aids of grace, when the Lord puts forth his hand and raises him up when cast down. Such was our Thomas: although, while still a youth and less cautious, he seemed infected by vainglory through the poison of virtues, he was nevertheless not wholly deprived of every grace of virtue. As we have said, he was a lover of chastity, a champion of truth, and also always cultivated with the highest devotion the fidelity owed to earthly lords. [Col. 1079C–1080A]

## 3. ON THE SECULAR MEN WHOM HE SERVED

In the first years of his adulthood he served for some time earthly lords—noble men indeed, but secular men. Through faithfulness, prudence, and diligent devotion in service, he advanced quickly, as much as could be expected at his age and as those professing our office can advance among such people. But where the profession is different, the way of life is usually different. [Col. 1080A–B]

## 4. ON THE CHIEF BISHOP THEOBALD, TO WHOM HE TRANSFERRED HIMSELF

Therefore our Thomas, seeing that one profession was contrary to the other and thus one manner of life contrary to the other, considered transferring himself from the courts of secular men to some great ecclesiastical man. Thus, with the Lord inspiring and cooperating and confirming his purpose, he transferred himself into the service of Father Theobald of venerable and holy memory, then chief bishop of Canterbury.

## 5. ON THE FAVOUR HE OBTAINED IN SERVICE

Accordingly, after he had for several years of youth rendered to the bishop a service increasingly pleasing because increasingly faithful and devoted, he soon obtained great favour and intimacy in his lord’s eyes. Above all the many capable attendants who served there, he enjoyed increasingly frequent and confidential conversation with him and benefited from his counsel. [Col. 1080B–C]

## 6. HOW HE WAS MADE ARCHDEACON

Therefore, seeing certain new shoots of virtue then springing from this new tree of ours, the bishop resolved to plant this planting of the Lord among the fruits of the valleys in the Bridegroom’s garden. Thus, inspired by God, Bishop Theobald ordained Thomas—whom he had first, according to canonical form, ordained to the other lower orders and afterwards as a deacon—also as archdeacon of his Church, within that holy and humble community of monks. He ordained him, I say, without hesitation concerning the future fruit promised by the shoots of virtue, although those tender shoots, because they were still sprouting, were often buffeted by the pestilential breath of worldly glory, which strove to corrupt them. [Col. 1080C–D]

Yet he did not hesitate for this reason, but rather, taught by God in this, he observed that, besides the other gifts of grace which we have already enumerated, although as a young man Thomas had in other respects gone too far with a certain youthful lightness toward worldly pomp, he always restrained himself with tight reins by the bridle of continence, against the nature of that age and beyond his strength—something remarkable at that age and imitable by few. Therefore those youthful excesses, committed with bodily integrity and continence unimpaired, seemed attributable more to nature than fault, more to age than error, even in the judgement of the wise and of those experienced in the idiom of that age. The pleasant vanities of youth were also excused by certain other initial gifts of virtue in the young man, besides that grace of the flesh, as we have said; because of these gifts there was the surest hope of his future completion. [Col. 1080D–1081A]

Indeed, at the beginning of youth, vices coupled with virtues, as often happens, usually drive out virtues—unless chastity, the shield of the flesh, protects the cause of the virtues. But then indeed the ranks of virtues are safe, if defended by the protection of this shield. I say “safe” in the sense in which anything can be safe at so slippery an age and amid so many snares of this present way and life. The fall of a certain great and illustrious man bears witness to these words. But why do I say “great and illustrious”? Rather, one of the greatest and most illustrious of the outstanding prophets: David, I think. Though from early age he shone with many gifts of grace, because while still young he lacked the aforesaid shield of the flesh, he lay defeated by lust through a woman in the flesh; and at the same time, through sedition, he cast down a just man in the flesh. [Col. 1081A–B]

For this young David had many gifts of grace, but still lacked the one gift of continence with which our Thomas was endowed. Young David was like that prophetic city of which we touched above: partly rained upon by the Lord, partly left dry and without rain. But because in youth he lacked this one gift of continence, he was stripped bare of the other gifts of grace that he possessed by incontinence, the enemy of this virtue.

For such a city, then, for such a young man, who on the one side—as it were at the right hand—has certain gifts of grace, but on the other side—as it were at the left—has the desires of youth that wage war against them in order to despoil them, there is great security against the loss of the gifts of grace and virtues which he possesses in part if chastity, the grace of the flesh, is the helper and guardian of virtues. For this most faithful guardian is like an intact vessel for storing spiritual perfumes. What indeed is pure bodily chastity for the Lord except a certain soundness of a splendid and precious vessel, in which the charisms of spiritual gifts are stored as treasures of virtues, like precious perfumes of Bridegroom and Bride? [Col. 1081C–D]

Hence the Master says: “This is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication; that each one of you may know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honour” (1 Thessalonians 4), “not in passions of desire, like the gentiles who do not know God.” Likewise this same chastity is the strong helper and faithful guardian for preserving these perfumes and treasures of virtues, lest they be taken by thieves or robbers on the road. For it is accustomed, strongly and steadfastly, to drive out vices and render to virtues a free, quiet, and peaceful dwelling; and, with the door closed while vices still knock, it constantly opposes and beats back those that knock. These vices, being somewhat less shameless at the doors especially of the young, quickly knock again even before they have been knocked away. But the cautious gatekeeper of the house, the virtue of continence of which we have spoken—strong and ready—at once repels those who knock so frequently, importunately, and shamelessly. [Col. 1081D–1082A]

Thus it is if vices joined to virtues have been held back in a young person. To state it briefly: so great is the strength and security of this virtue in a young person that, concerning a young man who possesses it for the Lord’s sake, I almost dare say: “You have chastity: do whatever you wish.” For an old man given to lust, the opposite is wholly true.

We do not here call “virtues” those by which one lives rightly, but certain gifts of grace given even to a just person while vices are still retained: by these he is often called, stirred, and drawn, though still as if asleep, so that he may be fully awakened. For one who has vices together with virtues does not sleep deeply, but dozes, as one who frequently nods his head and, as sleep draws near, is overcome. At one moment he is drawn back from earthly and carnal desires by the hands of virtues, as it were from the right; at another he is rolled over by the weight of vices that lie in wait, as it were from the left—alternately nodding his head, and soon, unless he were drawn back by the hands of virtues which he possesses, indeed unless the Lord, putting forth his hand, drew him more strongly, he would after dozing sleep too deeply, as if lethargic. [Col. 1082A–B]

Accordingly, this aforesaid young king David, first touched by the Lord through certain graces of virtue and later fully awakened, says: “I will not give sleep to my eyes nor slumber to my eyelids” (Psalm 132 [131]). Behold, he who had first fallen asleep as an adulterer in the foulness of adulterous flesh, and while thus asleep had seditiously cast down a just man, now neither dozes nor sleeps. The king who guards Israel, with the Lord putting forth his hand upon the virtues which he had previously possessed and drawing him, though still asleep, more strongly, had already removed far away both slumber and sleep.

Thus many people, drawn first by certain gifts of grace previously bestowed on them, are afterwards fully awakened, run vigorously, arrive after their course, and at last gloriously win the prize, according to the Bride’s words to the Bridegroom: “Draw me after you, and we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song of Songs 1). And the Bridegroom himself says: “No one can come to me unless my Father draws him” (John 6). So too our Thomas, a chaste young man, another Joseph, first drawn through chastity and other gifts of grace, afterwards ran in the fragrance of virtues, until, as we now see, he no longer ran merely in the fragrance of virtues but attained the Lord of virtues himself, the King of glory. [Col. 1082B–D]

## 7. WHAT HE WAS LIKE AS ARCHDEACON

But having received the diaconal order, as we have said, and not yet running but still being drawn, let us see how he came to run in the fragrance of virtues, and then, once his course was ended, how he attained without end the prize of that course. For, once made a deacon, he did not immediately set his shoulders beneath deacons’ burdens; instead, from then on he devoted himself all the more to the works of frivolity and of this world, despising every moderation especially appropriate to men of sacred order. So much was this so that, soon after receiving his order, he adopted not merely the courtly magnificence of other fellow courtiers, but even the splendours of the royal court itself; and when he entered the court he shone above his fellow courtiers in every magnificence. How this happened must nevertheless be briefly set out here. [Col. 1082D–1083A]

## 8. HOW HE WAS TRANSFERRED AND MADE CHANCELLOR

When the illustrious king of the English, Henry II, began his reign—whose dominion extended not only over lands on this side of the sea, but beyond the kingdom also over lands across the sea, from the Northern Ocean to the Pyrenees—the aforesaid chief bishop Theobald, of happy memory, who had anointed him king, soon arranged that our Thomas, still young and a newly made archdeacon, should enter the court of the new king, likewise still young, and take up a courtly office in that court.

For the bishop had observed the young man, whose character and ability he had already tested amid varied events: vigorous in action, trustworthy in counsel, assured in uncertainties, great-souled in adversities, magnificent in display, generous in giving, ready at commands, diligent in service, and, finally, provident and circumspect in every work. He therefore judged, not without reason, that such a man would be worthy of the court and welcome to it, hoping likewise that through this man’s service and works the grace of peace and the bond of unity between kingdom and priesthood would henceforth be stronger. Accordingly, through the action and provision of Bishop Theobald, Thomas entered the court and, the king granting it, received in the court a courtly office, now commonly called the chancellorship: certainly an honourable office in the royal household, but an exceedingly burdensome one, as those experienced in that office know well. [Col. 1083A–C]

## 9. HOW FOR A TIME HE PUT OFF THE CLERIC

Therefore this deacon of ours, having entered the court and been assigned to the office of chancellor, put off the deacon for a time and put on the chancellor. O how great and admirable was the discerning ability established in our young man at his entrance into the court! O singular office of discernment in virtues and works! For discernment is the charioteer of virtues, the concealer of works from the eyes of intentions, and indeed the seasoning of wisdom and knowledge. By it, what is done is often concealed no less wisely than knowingly; what is not done is thought to be done, and what is done is thought not to be done. Under its instruction, it very often happens that charity acts against charity, law against law, and piety against piety.

Thus that outstanding teacher of the gentiles, reared in the Synagogue and advocate of the Jews, according to the discernment given to him, out of charity desired, against charity, to be accursed from Christ for his brethren; against law, for the sake of law, he purified himself and shaved his head in the Temple; and against piety, for the sake of piety, he circumcised the already adolescent Timothy. David likewise pretended to be mad in order to escape; Judith pretended to be a prostitute in order to save Jerusalem. Likewise our deacon—whom, if not our words, then the examples of so many deeds excuse—entered the court and immediately laid aside the deacon for a time, industriously obeying the time rather than reason, and vanity rather than truth, as though he daily heard that passage of apostolic praise cry out to his fellow courtiers: “I have become foolish; you compelled me” (2 Corinthians 12). [Col. 1083C–1084A]

I do not say this, however, as though silks, half-silks, and other ambitious, distinguished, and splendid displays were unfitting for royal chancellors among their fellow courtiers—for those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses. I say it because, unless there had been a reason, it would have been fitting neither that a deacon should be a courtier nor that courtly display should belong to a deacon. But in our deacon there was the reason already stated: that he should enter the court. And by a wonderful dispensation of divine judgement, when later he was removed from the world for a brief time through martyrdom, he was to benefit both priesthood and kingdom—not so much removed as alive in this flesh, as is seen today. [Col. 1084A–B]

## 10. BY WHAT GIFTS OF GRACE HE OBTAINED THE KING’S FAVOUR
Thomas, therefore, now having as it were laid aside the levitical office, acted as chancellor, bore the chancellor’s burden in every respect vigorously, and carried out its work diligently. In accordance with the opinion and desire of the often-mentioned pontiff, the king—wise and shrewd beyond his years—daily found in him, besides other gifts of favour, fidelity and discernment in counsel; foresight and fearlessness in difficulties; and strength and greatness of soul in adversity. Such hardships and uncertainties, indeed, always attend great power. Though its holder’s life is short, its cares are [Col. 1084C] deathless and innumerable; and ambiguous and adverse events in human affairs, as though sitting in ambush and laying snares for great fortune, arise suddenly and unexpectedly every day. Hence, against uncertainties and hardships—which occur so frequently, especially in high estate—there is daily need of courageous counsel, as if to break snares and evade traps. As someone has said: “In doubts and hardships, every courageous counsel will prove best.” The industrious king experienced this strength, discernment, and fidelity of counsel in him day by day.

### 11. HOW GREAT HE WAS IN THE CHANCERY

When the king saw such magnificence joined to prudence in his chancellor, the chancellor’s favour with the king increased daily. To put it briefly: in a short time, as he surpassed all others in magnificence, so he rose above all in the king’s favour. So much so that, in everyone’s judgment, all who had held first place before him became last. And rightly so. For I could scarcely enumerate here all his vigorous achievements in the chancery: how, for example, and with what energy he recovered for his lord the king from the king of the Franks, through marriage—without iron, sword, lance, or battle, in complete amity and peace between the kings—five exceedingly well-fortified strongholds situated on the frontier of France and Normandy, though they had long been recognized as belonging by right to his lord the king: namely, the most strongly fortified castle of Gisors and four others. And, more remarkable still, how boldly and vigorously he remained confidently beyond Gascony, in the region of Toulouse, [Col. 1085A] with a small military force, while his lord the king at that time postponed, for reasons of his own, the siege of Toulouse—a city which, he maintained, ought by every right to be subject to him. It is ever believed to be defended by the patronage of blessed Exuperius.

But when the king thus deferred the siege of the city and returned with his great army, the chancellor was left behind in that rebellious land to hold the fortifications which the king had captured there. How he held them, how vigorously he acquired others by force of arms, and many other vigorous deeds of his and of the chancery which the world knows, I pass over here. To return, then, omitting these matters, to his magnificence: he certainly exceeded the obligation of the office he had undertaken—an office whose burden, as those who have experienced it know, is great. Yet he himself was generous beyond obligation: lavish toward all, he appeared magnificent beyond all and before all; great in heart, great in body, and great in his establishment. Nothing about him was small; nothing was other than magnificent. If he ever had leisure, he was now sporting with the citizens of heaven, practising hawking, now exercising the hunt by mastering the beasts of earth.

Drawn by this, as people of that kind commonly are, companies of knights now flocked to him; young and noble offspring of the nobly born surrounded him on every side; sons of magnates, like young olive plants around his table. Here and there swarms of attendants multiplied. And because, as we have said, a certain prudent caution had caused him temporarily to lay aside the clerical character, [Col. 1085C] there were clergy in his household, but separately. You might see the entire household made bright by him as by the morning star, while the rest shone about him like stars. At last, when he had attained so high a degree of favour with the king amid such greatness, the king, as though entrusting to him the whole administration of affairs, made him guardian and father of his son Henry, heir of all his dominions: so that he might regard as his son by grace the one whom the king himself had begotten by nature. Such, then, was the chancellor’s favour with the king.

### 12. CONCERNING THE ENVY OF COURTIERS

But as the man’s favour and glory grew, the worm of courtly envy, conceived from these things, grew in the court: it crawled through the court, though still hidden.

For this worm is chiefly nurtured and grows in courts among courtiers, continually creeping through courts yet secretly, hiding serpent-fashion. It stings and corrodes even those clothed in silk and purple, drinking from gems; and it does so the more secretly because it pierces more deeply within. Though those at the summit may perhaps not themselves sting, they are nevertheless stung by those beneath them, as by a serpent trodden underfoot. Whoever fears this courtly serpent’s venom, whoever flees its poison, must therefore leave the court. For even if it does not itself sting him, he is stung and infected by another; and this is more dangerous because the more hidden it is, the less one knows who has inflicted the sting. Thus in courts especially one does not know from whom to guard oneself, in accordance with the Psalm: “If my enemy had cursed me, I would indeed have endured it; and if he who hated me had spoken great things against me, perhaps I would have hidden myself from him” (Ps. 54). But in court whom can one avoid, or from whom can one hide oneself? For all are friends and all are enemies; all applaud and all sting; all exalt and all disparage; they kiss in public and betray in sec[ret . . .

*(One leaf is missing here from the Arras manuscript, containing the end of Book II and the beginning of Book III, or pages 23 and 24 of our edition.)*

[Col. 1086B] . . . [lacuna] . . . they came, and concerning the council which the king convenes, at which the king asks the archbishop and his fellow bishops that degraded clerics be punished also bodily; and concerning the cause and controversy which is debated face to face between the king and the archbishop on this point, the one arguing for the peace of the people, the other for the liberty of the clergy; and concerning the observance of the royal customs exacted by the king; and how the archbishop and all the fellow bishops then answered together unanimously that they would observe them, saving their order; and how the king was offended by this addition.

19. Concerning the fortifications which the king demands back from the archbishop [Col. 1086C]; concerning the bishops who deserted their archbishop and adhered to the king; and how the archbishop, afterwards persuaded by many persons, promised that he would alter that addition, namely “saving their order.”

20. Concerning the council convened at that royal residence called Clarendon, where the archbishop and fellow bishops altered the aforesaid addition of the word; and concerning the customs called royal, to the observance of which the archbishop and bishops thereupon bound themselves by oath, as there set forth.

21. Concerning the reflection on the road of the archbishop returning from this council; what he answered when addressed; how the words of a disciple afforded some consolation to the archbishop; how he suspended himself from the office of the altar for about forty days, until he had obtained from the apostolic man both the grace of consolation and absolution; concerning his attempted flight twice over, without success; how he returned to the king and how he was received by him; concerning his pontifical acts while he had not yet been allowed to flee; concerning the summoning of the archbishop to a case at that royal castle called Northampton; concerning his suffering and struggle there; and finally concerning his flight and the reason for it.

## BOOK THREE BEGINS

[Col. 1085]

[Col. 1085D] 1. Such being the situation, while our Thomas in the royal court shone far beyond all others in the highest princely favour and glory, and now conducted affairs as though he bore their whole weight, the frequently named father Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury—a man illustrious for every holiness and religious virtue, who had been our Thomas’s chariot and charioteer—after ruling the Church of Canterbury vigorously and wisely for twenty-two years, now old and full of days, entered the decreed way of all flesh.

When this immediately became known to the king and courtiers, all at once suspected it; some murmured it, others declared it: that the chancellor would become successor to the deceased archbishop. The people themselves proclaimed the same. But the king entirely concealed his purpose, except that the archbishopric—as bishoprics and vacant abbeys commonly are—was entrusted to the chancellor’s care and custody. The chancellor, who already, as though from certain omens and conjectures, surmised the king’s will, nevertheless, like the king, dissimulated and silently considered the matter.

At that time the king was abroad beyond the sea, outside his kingdom, and the chancellor was with him. Because of frequent Welsh incursions and certain other affairs of the realm, the king resolved to send the chancellor to England. Since the reasons were many and weighty, he entrusted this embassy to the chancellor, finding none of his own men so fit for important business. When the chancellor, having already assumed the form and business of an embassy for several days, was at the very point of departure and entered the court at that Norman castle called Falaise—intending, after merely greeting the king, immediately to set out—the king summoned him aside and imparted a secret:

“You do not yet,” he said, “fully know the purpose of your embassy.” And he added: “It is my will that you become archbishop of Canterbury.”

The chancellor, displaying with a smile certain ridiculous garments which he was then wearing, and as it were thrusting them before the king’s eyes, said: “What a religious man, what a holy man, you desire to appoint to so holy a see and over so celebrated and holy a community of monks! Know most certainly that, if by the Lord’s ordering this should happen, you will very quickly turn away from me your affection and favour—so great as it is now between us—and change it into the bitterest hatred. For I know that you will require certain things, and that already you presume many things even in ecclesiastical matters which I could not endure with a calm mind. Then, once occasion has been found, the envious will intervene; when favour has been extinguished, they will stir up perpetual hatred between us.”

O wonderful magnificence of a man thus threatening his lord, while it was still in that lord’s power, despite the threat, to confer or remove the honour! O sincere purity of soul: neither courting honour nor yet rejecting it, but, along with the honour, immediately preparing his shoulders to bear honour’s burden for honour’s sake! Immediately, I say, at the first hearing of that honour, as one who knew from experience exactly how much burden that honour carries with it.

How great and certain a presage this saying was of a good shepherd who would benefit the Church! He himself testified, before that moment of his separation from the king, that neither he, by himself or through another, had ever spoken even a single word beforehand to the king about it, nor the king to him. Yet the king was not moved at all by this seemingly affectionate threat of his chancellor, but persisted in his intention. At once, in the chancellor’s presence, he earnestly and diligently charged the eminent and capable men accompanying the chancellor’s embassy to England to communicate this his wish and desire [Col. 1088A] concerning the chancellor’s promotion to the sacred community of the metropolitan church and to the clergy of his realm.

Turning his words particularly to one distinguished man among the envoys—Richard, surnamed de Luci—he said: “Richard, if I lay dead in a coffin, would you not strive that my firstborn, Henry, be raised to the kingship?”

“Yes, lord,” he replied, “to the extent of my power.”

And the king said to him: “With equal effort I desire you to promote the chancellor to the see of Canterbury.”

In this matter, assuredly, as in the earlier magnificence of the chancellor and his unambitious purity of mind, so too we may clearly see the constancy of the king’s favour and the glory of princely magnificence. For this very reason, I think—and the outcome of events soon proved it—he was more ardent for his chancellor’s promotion because he had heard him speak so magnificently, and because he judged him to be less ambitious. But above all, and beyond everything else, it is pleasant here to behold how truly the hearts of kings are in God’s hand, and how nothing can resist the dispositions of the Most High.

I learned this passage of the history from the pontiff himself, who in later exile often recalled it because the end of his words, as though they were a prophecy, had then been fulfilled. Therefore, the more readily because it is itself true and because I was taught it by the pontiff himself, I have taken care to insert this passage into this history—especially because from it one may observe the magnificence of the virtues of both the king and the chancellor, each in his own way. And so the king dismissed his chancellor on these terms; a few days later he landed in England.

### 2. HOW THE CHANCELLOR WAS ELECTED

Soon after the chancellor’s arrival, the king’s will and request concerning his promotion were declared to that holy and devout community of the holy Church of Canterbury, with certain bishops summoned. Immediately, as usually happens, varying opinions of different people were expressed—especially in that sacred community of monks, to whom the matter chiefly belonged. Some maintained that it was good for this to be done; others, on the contrary, that it was bad.

The former invoked the king’s favour, arguing that through so favoured a mediator between kingdom and priesthood, the Church would thereafter enjoy a peace both secure and prosperous. The latter, conversely, objected that this royal favour would not help but would greatly harm the Church precisely for that reason: since the officials of the emperor—especially all courtiers—would range more freely over the Church’s goods when a pontiff was chosen not from the Church but from the court. Moreover, they argued that it would be utterly discordant and contrary to every divine law to set over sheep as shepherd a man committed rather to the military belt than to clerical office, a pursuer of dogs and a keeper of birds; especially over so holy a monastic community and so great and numerous a flock of the Lord, spread throughout all England. Certainly, they thought, he was to be regarded not as a shepherd but as a destroyer and devourer of the entire flock, moved by courtly greed and a certain wolfish voracity, scattering everything for the breath of popular applause and displaying it with courtly ostentation.

[Col. 1089A] O how many did suspicion overthrow in this affair and hold their minds captive in vanity! They saw the man’s outward vanity, distrusting the future truth which they did not yet see. O divine judgments, terrible though they are in counsels concerning the children of men, yet no less delightful! O rash judgments of human beings, which, even when they seem plausible, nevertheless deceive! Thus worldly people judged a worldly man according to the judgment of the world; but concerning this worldly man there came about something very different, better, and more delightful—not according to the world’s rash judgment, but according to God’s delightful judgment.

Thus that king and prophet says: “Cut off my reproach which I have feared, because your judgments are delightful” (Ps. 118). Truly delightful are God’s judgments, contrary to the world’s expectation and every worldly suspicion: drawing honey from the rock, oil from the hardest stone, and raising up children to Abraham from these stones [also taking away and cutting off the reproach of his servant]. “Cut off,” he says, “my reproach which I have feared.” For who would believe—unless suspicion were cut away by God himself? Who, hearing the assertion, would give it credence: that a pursuer of dogs, as they called him, and a keeper of birds would become so good and faithful a shepherd of sheep?

Yet what could be not only better but more delightful in this event, and among God’s works more worthy of God? It was more worthy of God precisely because more merciful, and because God was more wonderful in it. For amid such great power, although all things are ineffably admirable, nothing is so worthy of astonishment and admiration as that there should be such great mercy in such great power. Therefore the Wise Man warns us not to praise a person before death—and likewise not to blame one before death. For who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and leave behind a blessing? Therefore the Master says: “Do not judge before the time” (John 5).

Thus, with every present suspicion cut away and controversy abandoned, Thomas, archdeacon of that same Church, was elected archbishop of London in that royal and splendid monastery called Westminster, by the common consent and unanimous agreement of the provincial bishops and the community of the holy Church of Canterbury, with the divine dispensation—to which all things render service—being served also in this by the king’s wish. He was elected, I say, after having held the office of chancellor at court for five years, and being about forty-four years of age. Immediately he was presented, by command of the king his father, to the king’s son Henry, still a boy and heir to the kingdom—the chancellor having received him, as we have said, through the exceptional favour of the king, almost as son and foster-child, while acting in this matter in his father’s place.

Royal assent joining the Church’s election, and royal authority releasing him from every bond of the court, he was restored free to the English Church; and in that freedom he was received by the Church, as is customary, with the greatest joy in hymns and spiritual songs.

### 3. HOW THE ELECTED MAN RETURNED TO HIMSELF

Our Thomas, therefore, no longer chancellor of the court but elected of the Church and released from all bonds of the court, immediately, like a man waking from a heavy sleep, reflected in his heart upon what he had long been and what he ought henceforth to become. For a time at court, as though lethargic, he had seemed to suffer forgetfulness of himself. But now, returning to his heart, he reflected with his heart. From that meditation his heart grew warm, and gradually a fire began to burn, by which the new man, thought extinguished, began to be warmed and restored, though not yet to raise his head.

Yet this new man, as we have already said, had been concealed rather than suppressed by the garment of the old man, through a certain prudent caution; except that this concealment was almost a suppression. But now, in the very newness of his transformation, the new man immediately desired to be uncovered and would not allow himself to remain oppressed any longer. Though our elect was born at London and elected there, shortly after his election he set out for the metropolitan city of Canterbury, with a large and distinguished company, to receive the grace of consecration.

While travelling—not turning aside into a field, but on the road itself—he summoned only the disciple who wrote these things and said secretly to him that in a vision the same night he had seen a certain venerable person standing before him and giving him ten talents. The disciple did not then perceive its interpretation and hesitated over the meaning of the dream. But soon afterwards, when the disposition of the Most High regarding the man had been fulfilled—something not then expected—the evangelical servant who, having received five talents by lot, gained another five beyond his allotment by trading, resolved the meaning most openly, without any hesitation or enigma.

Still more privately, addressing the same disciple while they were yet on the road, he immediately added: “This I desire, this I command you henceforth: tell me confidently and in secret what men say that I am, even if they say that I labour under some fault. I command you, I say, to tell me this freely, confidently, and secretly. For henceforth many things will be said of me which will not be said to me, just as many things are commonly said among the people about others, especially the rich, while few—or none at all—are said to them themselves. Likewise point out any excess, if you yourself see and judge that I go too far.” And at the end of his speech he added: “For four eyes see more carefully and clearly than two.”

[Col. 1090D] I believe that at that time he gave the same command, perhaps—unless I am mistaken—to others also, and at other times to persons holier and more discerning than I, though I was by no means such a person.

O prudence of the man! O episcopal model, already present in one not yet a bishop—certainly to be admired and imitated by everyone, but especially by bishops! O prophetic man! O seeing, keen-sighted creature of the Seer! So that in the night of this crooked and winding path and life he might by no means stumble, he was already fitting eyes to himself both before and behind. He was already indeed the fellow shepherd and disciple of that fellow shepherd who, giving a model to his fellow shepherds and disciples, said: “Whom do people say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16).

He gave this model, I say, so that those who are the light of the world, appointed as a light to the nations, should by no means disdain but should frequently and diligently inquire from their own people concerning the people’s opinion of them. Thus, without their knowing it, either the foul and black cloud of detraction might not obscure the rays of their light, or some adverse blast of sinister rumour might not scatter them abroad. Otherwise—God forbid!—from the light of the world, the lamp of the word, and the temple’s candlestick there would issue smoke rather than illumination. To prevent this, that shepherd of shepherds seeks the opinion of his own people concerning himself; and in this inquiry he notes also that many adverse things are said about us which are not said to us.

Hence it often happens in human affairs, lamentably, that even one conscious of no fault may nevertheless, perhaps because of some appearance of evil, be held infamous among the people, while he remains wholly unaware of the adverse things said of him. Such a person has eyes before him but lacks them behind; he attends neither to what is said of him through himself, because he cannot, nor through another, because he neglects or despises it, but only to what is said to him.

### 4. HOW MAGNIFICENTLY HE WAS CONSECRATED

But our elect, though not yet bishop, was already putting on the episcopal pattern; scarcely even elected, he at once chose those upon whom he might impose this concern for what was, as it were, his own personal visitation. We therefore left London, where the election had occurred, and came to Canterbury, where, as the metropolitan city, the consecration of the metropolitan was to be celebrated according to custom and the rule of the canons. Almost the entire kingdom had gathered for this consecration, out of reverence for the one to be consecrated. The clergy came from duty; the nobles and great men of the realm came to offer favour and service of honour both to the king, to whom the matter so greatly pleased, and to the elect, who had come forth from the court.

Accordingly, during that sacramental season, in those days of wonderful and wonder-working anointing, on the Saturday of the week of Pentecost—time and order agreeing, as the sacraments soon made clear—the elected archdeacon of the Church was ordained priest, to be consecrated bishop on the following Sunday. But once the priest had been ordained, the bishops immediately debated which provincial bishop ought to have the leading role in the consecration. Since the episcopal see of London, to which this was recognized as belonging, was then vacant, the bishop of Winchester, who exercises in the province the office of the absent or deceased bishop of London, asserted that the matter belonged to him in every way. The bishop of Rochester, on the contrary, maintained that it belonged to himself and not another, because from the foundation of his church and by a special and peculiar right he is the archbishop’s chaplain.

At length, for certain reasons which I omit to insert here, while preserving in this respect the right of the Church of Rochester, the consecration of the archbishop was entrusted, with the Rochester bishop’s consent, to the venerable Henry, bishop of Winchester, a man as distinguished in nobility as in holiness. On the following Sunday, the octave of Pentecost, it was completed with extraordinary festivity and magnificence, as befitted so great a future bishop. At his consecration there were present, besides an almost innumerable multitude of the nobles and great men of the realm—among whom that distinguished boy Henry, son and heir of the king, was prominent—fourteen fellow-provincial bishops, with the archbishop himself, I think, who consecrated him, making fifteen. Such was the consecration of our elect as archbishop, he then being about forty-four years old, as we have said above.

Envoys were immediately sent to Alexander III, pontiff of the Roman see of happy memory. Because of the schism then in the Roman Church, he had newly arrived at Montpellier and remained there for some time. The envoys were devout, learned, and honourable men. They urgently and forcefully sought the distinguished metropolitan insignia called the pallium, as was fitting; and because those who asked were well received, and especially because the person for whose use it was requested was favourably regarded, they obtained the pallium from the Apostolic See more quickly and easily. Shortly afterwards they returned joyfully and successfully with the pallium. Thus our Thomas, receiving the pallium with the deepest devotion, was made archbishop from bishop.

### 5. WHY THE DISCIPLE FEARS TO DESCRIBE THE CONSECRATED MAN’S VIRTUES

Up to this point I have portrayed, however inadequately, the image of the earthly man, the man of this age, directing his course through worldly prosperity as a little boat across calm waters. It remains now to portray the image of the heavenly man, the man of God, Christ’s bishop, passing through this world’s prosperity and adversity. This is no longer to guide a little boat by a breeze over the sea’s level surface; it is rather to lower the sail, raise the topsail, slacken the ropes, descend into the deep sea, and steer a merchant vessel through so many rocks and reefs, through the Syrtes and the dogs of Scylla.

For our Thomas, no longer an officer of the court but bishop of the Church, has gone down to the sea in ships, to work in great waters. Therefore I, an old man, possessing no pen save one thin and bloodless, considering the novelty and greatness of my subject, now stand and hesitate at the threshold with my frail pen, greatly uncertain how, as an ugly and unskilled painter, I can worthily portray in no longer a worldly man the image of the earthly, but in so new and great a bishop of Christ the features of the heavenly image; and how, in writing, I can bring that merchant ship, so richly laden with so many precious goods, through so many dangers of the sea to the harbour of salvation, toward which it always sailed.

Let those for whom it is easy undertake it; for me, I confess, it is difficult. He who is of the earth speaks of the earth and can fashion an earthly image in an earthly manner, since the maker resembles the thing made: as is the earthly man, so also are the earthly. But he who is of the earth is earthly—indeed, who is earth and soon to return to earth—how can he worthily expound the image of any heavenly being? For as is the heavenly one, so are the heavenly. Therefore the heavenly image requires a heavenly painter, not an earthly one, not one of clay.

There is also this added burden: it is not enough now to portray merely any heavenly image. Rather, as the novelty, dignity, and magnitude of the subject henceforth require, the new and super-heavenly episcopal form of this bishop of Christ must either be conceived and discerned by some inward and diligent vision, and then set before, or portrayed for, the human race to behold until the end of the ages—or else must be left altogether in silence.

Moses himself, so great in life and knowledge, was taken apart from the people to the summit of the mountain. There he beheld, in the pattern shown him, the form of the tabernacle to be made, with its vessels of ministry, the form of its ministers, and the rite and order of ministering. To him the Lord said: “See the pattern.” And among the other things, and, I think, above all the rest, the form of the priest of the law and of those ministering to him was shown in the pattern. But behold: this bishop is more than a legal priest. That one was legal; this one evangelical.

Yet I, wretched sinner, more an ugly than a faithful painter, though we have undertaken to describe his form, have not been led apart from the people to a mountain summit with Moses, nor with Joshua even to any mountain slope. I dwell in the valley of tears, amid my people, like them in guilt and punishment. Therefore, as I, an old man, am about to approach the new man, my mind is stunned by the novelty of the matter; my pen, which until now, thin and empty, had portrayed a worldly man passing through empty things, is exhausted by its greatness; and, as though struck back by the extraordinary brightness of the subject’s splendour, it is dazzled and almost blinded by its dignity.

Nevertheless, aided by such vision as I possess, and humble rather than conceited, instructed through heavenly grace by the Maker and Fashioner of men, as he is accustomed to instruct such persons, I shall in whatever fashion I am granted portray with a transformed pen the heavenly image and episcopal form in Christ’s bishop for the men of my time and all ages to come to behold and admire, and especially for bishops to imitate. Yet he ought rather to have been painted with stibium than described with a pen. Still, I shall describe him; I shall describe him, I say, aided by such vision as I possess.

For if one must boast—indeed, because one must and it is fitting now—I too have had a pattern shown to me, not indeed on a mountain but in this valley of tears. For I saw him, and I followed and attended upon the bishop through the whole period, until the day of his final departure, amid many and varied trials. And, since it is now fitting to boast, throughout all that time I was honoured by the favour of his intimacy in many ways, so that in this respect I believe no one was second to me.

Thus, I think, by a certain secret disposition of the Most High, since nearly all the others who saw with me and served with the bishop have now been taken from the world, this task is reserved for me, almost the only one still left: that according to the pattern which I observed more attentively and intimately than many others, though they too served the bishop, I should expound to the people of the present and future age the heavenly image of this heavenly man. This is especially so since, as I write, the fourteenth year has now passed since this man departed from the world—undoubtedly, I think, by the ordering of the Most High, without whose counsel not even a leaf falls from a tree, and because I delayed writing for years.

And this has happened well. For now, with the Lord as teacher, I can transmit in writing to future ages concerning this man not only what I saw of his life in this flesh, but also what happened after his death and through his death, precious and triumphant as it was. But let us return to the course of this historical song which we have begun.

### 6. HOW, HAVING PUT OFF THE OLD MAN, HE PUT ON THE NEW

Our Thomas, therefore, no longer an officer of the court, no longer merely elected by the Church, but now consecrated to the Church, immediately—beyond all expectation—laid aside the chancellorship. Living as a bishop, filled in the mighty force of the Spirit suddenly coming from heaven, with which he was then anointed in those days of anointing, he so thoroughly shook, cast off, and expelled the whole old man that no trace of the old state now appeared.

Thus the new man, whom above we said had been covered rather than crushed by the garb of the old man for a time, now uncovered and receiving greater strength in the Spirit given in anointing, immediately displayed himself wholly and vigorously girded himself for works—especially those which then befitted a new bishop. Therefore the bishop, no longer drawn along but anointed with sacred unction, ran swiftly: not as before, when the new man was still covered and he merely breathed in the fragrance of virtues, but now swift in strong and vigorous performance of virtues; no longer merely smelling virtues, but powerfully practising them.

And he who, while still elect, had reflected with his heart as though deliberating, now consecrated and anointed in that sacred unction as the Lord’s anointed, received from the Spirit of anointing the counsel by which he should leave the court in body and heart alike, lay aside purple, and take up haircloth. Thus he immediately cast off purple as the garment of the old man; in body as in mind he left the court, left purple, and put on haircloth—the new garb of the new man, a new vestment, unfamiliar to courtiers and foreign to the court.

Behold our Thomas, another Elijah in spirit and power, clothed in camel’s hair! Behold another virgin chosen by the Lord, who, having left behind the linen cloth, clothed himself in haircloth over his naked body and fled the men of blood, enemies of Christ’s cross; a new recruit, he follows in haircloth the banner of the new king. He is now a new recruit of that new king whose voice in the Psalm declares: “But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in haircloth” (Ps. 34); and again: “I made haircloth my garment, and I became a byword to them” (Ps. 68).

O Thomas—Thomas now no longer Thomas, and yet truly Thomas! No longer Thomas clad in whole silk or purple, but another Thomas, who, though his entire body, so delicate and so tender, had been reared amid the wealth of Croesus, the riches of Darius, and the pleasures of Sardanapalus, is now wrapped in a sackcloth garment, thereby afflicting an already frail body with this harshness. O how great, and in every way worthy of wonder, is the change wrought in you, Thomas, by the right hand of the Most High! You who were brought up in the palace amid imperial riches and delights, and who among the courtiers seemed to outshine the whole palace, as much by exceptional favor as by distinguished attire, are now wholly enveloped in the hair of a foul and shaggy animal, [Col. 1095A] taking sackcloth for footwear, haircloth for silk, and ashes for fine garments! But what of it? Truly, you are now a new recruit of the new king, for whom the old things have passed away and behold, all things have become new. For there is a new king, a new law, a new flock, a new garment, and he himself is new. Behold, all is now new: Christ is the new king; the love of Christ the new law; Christ’s Church the new flock; haircloth the new garment; and he himself the new recruit of Christ.

Accordingly, these too are new among the beginnings of our recruit’s service: the arms with which he was outwardly to fight against the beasts. In this military array, at that sacramental season of Pentecost, when he was consecrated and, an apostolic man among the apostles, clothed with power from on high, he is clothed. This was the first counsel, and among the beginnings, in those days of anointing: a counsel given from heaven to the Lord’s anointed, while the anointing itself taught him [Col. 1095B] as mistress; and this was the beginning of his works.

But those who put their hand to arduous tasks, though fervent in spirit at the outset, commonly grow gradually lukewarm day by day as time advances, as though wearied by their course or excessively burdened beneath a load, until at last forgetfulness—ever hostile to the duty of the holy office they have undertaken—comes upon them, and through the seductive enticements of the flesh, the daily pleasures of this life, and its various occupations, utterly extinguishes at the end the spirit that was so fervent at the beginning. By a certain shameful and ugly change, spirits once so fervent are at the end converted, as it were, into bodies—or rather corpses—insensible and lifeless; or, with that unhappy woman, their human form abolished, they are as though transubstantiated into a statue, like that corpse-like [Col. 1095C] or foolish—or, to use a new word, “statue-formed”—soul which, according to the prophet, first nourished in saffron later embraces dung. Of such persons the Master says: “Are you so foolish that, having begun in the Spirit, you are now being perfected in the flesh?” (Gal. 3).

Thomas, that watchful creature, carefully observing this and diligently guarding against it, immediately upon becoming a priest surrounded both shoulders—the shoulders proper to priests—with a certain badge of sacred rank called a stole or *orarium*, and wore it daily and continually in the sight of all. This accords with what the Lord commanded in the Law concerning the sign of the ten words of the Law: having this *orarium* as though continually hanging before his eyes and bound as a sign upon his hand. Thus this evangelical *orarium* served in this evangelical priest as a pattern corresponding to the legal fringes which, at the Lord’s own command, [Col. 1095D] were introduced. The Lord commanded that such fringes be made on the corners of the garments of the children of Israel, so that, when they saw them, they might remember the commandments of the Lord and not follow their own thoughts and eyes, which commit fornication through diverse things. Something similar, after the legal fringes, is found in this evangelical *orarium*: by it this evangelical priest might continually recall the evangelical yoke which he had now undertaken. By encompassing both shoulders with this *orarium*, a badge, I think, received from heaven as a sign, he visibly prophesied that, just as he had received good things from the hand of the Lord, so he would endure evil things for the Lord. This was the meaning of its encircling both shoulders: good things on one side, evil things on the other.

He wore it continually also for another worthy [Col. 1096A] reason: that he might always be more composed for the more solemn performance of the sacrament of confirmation, for which at all times he was readier and more devout than for other things. Therefore we recognize in the bishop two things which he wears as badges of the Lord: haircloth and the *orarium*. The first badge, that of haircloth, is the sign of Christ’s soldier; the other, the badge of the *orarium*, is the sign of Christ’s priest, as though still about to pray much for the people and for the holy city. First, when anointed, he recognized himself as Christ’s soldier; but by that which encircles him secondly, as Christ’s priest. Thus adorned, the bishop went forth daily in public, except that the haircloth, in keeping with the meaning of its name and the truth of the religious observance to be maintained, was very carefully concealed, known to no one except someone without whom such a thing [Col. 1096B] could not be managed. And he never thereafter laid aside this badge of his novitiate throughout the whole period, until he had completed the triumph of his glorious contest.

But the other thing, which we have called the *orarium* and which he wore in public, he immediately laid aside when driven into exile, because it did not become an exile to wear it in foreign provinces. For this reason, and rightly, he was stripped of that priestly badge: driven out as a true exile, and thus in some sense also as one deprived of priesthood.

These, then, were the badges of our new bishop. But in his remaining daily and ordinary attire, throughout the first year he was, in his customary manner, splendid and neat; afterward, however, especially in dress, he followed the clergy’s moderation, so that, as someone says, there was neither studied [Col. 1096C] shabbiness nor affected luxury. His outer garments were closed, dark, and long to the feet; his furs were not costly, but lambskin. Thus some, because of the resemblance of his clothing, supposed him to be what is commonly called a regular canon, although he was a canon only in devotion—which is common to all truly faithful persons—and by no means by profession.

The bishop’s garments, indeed, the more cheaply they were bought, the more often, as was customary, they were replaced; so that by this very means Christ naked—or rather Christ himself in the naked person—might more frequently be clothed in the very garments in which the Lord’s anointed himself was clothed. And this example of Christ, received from this great bishop of Christ, ought especially to be observed by all bishops who are Christs of the Lord: that Christ be clothed in their naked one in that which they themselves wear. Neither they nor those others should be clothed in these same things while Christ, the Lord’s Christ, is left alone and naked—he who entrusted to them the milk, wool, and fleeces of his sheep. [Col. 1096D]

For bishops especially ought to have recourse to the exemplary deed of that man, not yet even a bishop, who, having nothing besides the cloak with which he was clothed, divided it with a naked poor man. Accordingly, on the following night he heard Jesus say in a loud voice to the surrounding crowd of Englishmen: “Martin, still a catechumen, has covered me with this garment.” Let the bishop therefore consider what he does, if this man did so even while still a catechumen. Let the bishop, I say, consider what he does among so many changes of clothing, with garments now worn threadbare, when this catechumen, with the one cloak [Col. 1097A] that he possessed, both covered himself and the poor man—or rather, as Christ testifies, Christ himself in the poor man. For this was not like that narrow cloak in the prophet under the condition of the Old Law, but under the law of grace in the Gospel it was that most ample cloak of charity which fills heaven and earth, covering both Martin and him who covers.

But, leaving aside this cloak of Martin—or rather of Christ—now common to them both, let us return to the new attire of our new bishop, Christ’s new recruit; his bodily and visible bodily attire was as we have described it.

Yet there was another new attire of the new recruit, far different and far more splendid: not bodily and visible, but spiritual and invisible; certainly stronger in proportion as it was more inward and inaccessible. [Col. 1097B] Of it the Master, the tribune of the heavenly army, says: “Put on the armor of God” (Eph. 5): “the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, the sword of the Spirit, your feet shod.” Behold the new armor of the Lord’s new soldier, in which the breastplate of righteousness, as it held first place in this soldier of the Lord, is also placed first by the Master. Yet this breastplate must still be put away, to be assumed in its proper time: “For everything there is a time: a time of love and a time of hatred; a time of war and a time of peace” (Eccl. 3). It is therefore kept laid aside for now.

## 7. ON THE BISHOP’S FIRST, BODILY TABLE: THE NEW COMMANDMENT

Meanwhile, let us look at the new things surrounding the [Col. 1097C] new bishop. After the bishop’s dress, which we have briefly set down beforehand, let us approach the bishop’s table, considering his life as we considered his attire. For no one’s life is faithfully described if what he lived upon, or how he himself lived, is omitted; especially since this new table of the new bishop was so episcopal, so rich, so splendid—filled, surely, more with works of piety than with a variety of bodily delicacies, though these too were present in the fullest abundance. To this table, then, all are invited, but especially you bishops. Indeed, your new fellow-brother, the bishop himself, invites you all to approach, as is fitting and most just. For at this table reclines that great householder, the shepherd of shepherds and Master; first [Col. 1097D] at its head, and after him, in order and with him, his twelve.

At this new table the new bishop, as the Lord’s new steward, lays aside his garments, girds himself, and ministers to the Lord reclining with his own. Standing before the reclining Lord in his haircloth, ministering to his new king in his *orarium*, he is in these badges of the new steward both the new soldier of Christ the new king and Christ’s priest. This is the new commandment which he, now new, instituted. Every day, after the *synaxis* had been chanted—which he was accustomed to chant soon after cockcrow, in the deep night—thirteen brethren were immediately and secretly brought into some chamber. There he laid aside his garments, girded himself, and ministered to those reclining [giving four silver coins to each.] [Col. 1098A] He performed this commandment nightly, more stealthily than an actual thief; and not without reason he feared that, if he did it in daylight, the poison of empty glory, which infects virtues through the sight of men, might corrupt it—the poison by which, as we noted above, he seemed, while still young, to have been almost incurably infected. Therefore, the more secretly it was done, the more safely it was done. [lacuna] (On this gap, see below, col. 354.)

*(One leaf is missing from the Arras manuscript.)*

…just as there is little or no condemnation for the former, who, having been plausibly led—or, to speak more harshly, deceived—confess for their salvation not only the power but also the operation of that power, though it may perhaps not in fact obtain. For, in the first place, one who does not believe in a benefit bestowed suffers the burning torment of ingratitude for benefits not believed. [Col. 1098B] In the second case, to believe as a benefit something not bestowed, but thought to have been bestowed, is a certain sweet and grateful obligation. Even if some punishment perhaps awaits such persons because they believe what is false, nevertheless, as I now judge, there will not thereby be for them an eternal punishment in death. Rather, perhaps their devotion will be rewarded: they have piously and devoutly believed that the Lord mercifully did something for their salvation, even if he did not do it.

But let no one object to me here that saying of the Master: “If Christ has not risen, our preaching is empty and your faith also is empty” (1 Cor. 15). Let no one, I say, object to me now with that saying of the Master. For there the discourse properly concerns the apostles; and so he immediately adds: “We are found to be false witnesses of God, because we have borne testimony against God that he raised Jesus Christ, whom he did not raise if the dead do not rise” (ibid.). [Col. 1098C] The Master may be seen to speak not only of the apostles, but also of those persons and on their behalf: those who honor and exalt the Lord by flattering falsehoods, as though God could be soothed and caressed like a man. Against this, one of the doctors says that it would be a dreadful thing to say anything false about God, even if it seemed to contribute to his praise, because perhaps falsehood is praised in God with a crime no less, but greater, than truth is censured.

Behold the doctor’s words: “Therefore neither I nor God have anything to do now with flatterers of this kind, just as they themselves have nothing to do with God.” This is what I say, wholly different from them—indeed [Col. 1098D] altogether opposed to them—what I think, what I judge: namely, that if anyone piously, devoutly, and on probable grounds believed for his salvation that Christ had risen, then even if he had not risen, there would be little or no condemnation for one who so believed concerning Christ Jesus. But perhaps someone will object to me from what has been said: What then if the Church, from the Scriptures and from many probable signs, wonders, and miracles, believed that the Lord had now mercifully become incarnate for its salvation, and yet had not yet become incarnate? In the same way the erring Synagogue believes that the Messiah has not yet come but is still to come; it nevertheless denies that the Lord is to come in the flesh, maintaining that the coming Messiah will be a mere human being. Thus there is now nothing in common between us and those [Col. 1099A] who have faith neither in the present nor even in the future incarnation. What then if the Church believed the Lord to have been incarnate in this way, and yet he had not yet become incarnate?

Many people certainly think—and perhaps not irrationally—that if the Church so believed, the Church would by no means be condemnable on account of this faith, provided that faith in the remaining articles of faith, and especially in the one and triune God, remained whole. Conversely, Cornelius too was by no means condemnable even if he did not believe Christ incarnate—although, before he believed this, Christ had already become incarnate. Indeed, before he believed Christ already incarnate to be incarnate, the angel said to him: “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God.” And it was said earlier of him that he was [Col. 1099B] devout and feared God.

But having touched on this alone, and since this is not now the place for a discourse prolonged over it, let me return to what precedes. Whatever may be the case, without assertion on our part, concerning the aforesaid faith in the incarnation, this at least is evident: even if the sacramental conversion of bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ did not occur, although the Catholic Church believes it all with certain faith, this offering in pure bread and wine, according to the order of Melchizedek, would nevertheless in itself be, as I express it, a pure, clear, simple, sincere, and devout offering of our mother the Catholic Church. It would be purer and more sincere than the slaughtered flesh and bloody impurities of a thousand fat bulls, goats, or rams. This evangelical [Col. 1099C] offering of the Church is indeed purer and simpler than that of the Synagogue. And, as may be seen, that offering under the state of the Law was not so pious an offering of priests as a certain dreadful and inhuman slaughter of beasts by butchers, morning and evening every day. There daily so many sheep, so many oxen, so many bulls, so many goats, so many lambs, so many calves, so many wethers were slaughtered. From this slaughter neither the simplicity of the dove nor the chastity of the turtledove was protected.

But this evangelical sacrifice of ours, this sacrifice of our mother the Church for us, is, as it appears, solely a sacrifice of praise: not of torn flesh, not of entrails pulled out, not of stinking intestines, not of smoke, not of dung; in no respect, as it appears, the sacrifice of an unjust and sinful man. [Col. 1099D] In accordance with what the Lord says in the hymn-like song: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. 49). And afterward, distinguishing this evangelical sacrifice of ours from that legal one, he adds: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (ibid.); and at the end of the song: “A sacrifice of praise will honor me” (ibid.). Therefore this sacrifice of praise, the more honorable, more sincere, more health-giving, more peaceable, and, as a sacrifice of righteousness, the more acceptable it is to the Lord, the more the destroying angel at the hour of sacrifice makes subtle, sharp, and frequent assaults. If he can thus prevail without a defender, without delay and without any mercy, he strikes faith itself—the first-born among the virtues, triumphing here while reason is oppressed—and, if he can, extinguishes it forever. [Col. 1100A]

But let no one suppose—let no one suspect—that I have written anything here from disbelief or even slight hesitation concerning this most glorious and salutary sacrament of all our salvation. Once, however, when I began to think of it as though hesitating, on the following night the host seemed to me to turn and move about in the chalice, now this way, now that, as though in continual and exceedingly swift motion. When I secretly reported this on the next day to my lord the archbishop, along with the manner in which I had thought beforehand as though in doubt, the archbishop immediately answered that the motion of the host in the chalice indicated the wavering which had first begun in my mind. Accordingly, through the Lord’s grace, I stand ever firmer in faith in this sacrament and henceforth more devout. [Col. 1100B] But let us return to the aforesaid evil assaults of the evil angel.

If, perhaps, he finds faith adult, so robust and solid that he is unable, I do not say to destroy it, but even to prick it in the slightest degree with any stings of unbelief, he makes assaults of another kind—the kind that we experience daily, if only free from those which we have mentioned and from the stings of unbelief. He turns therefore to other things, he who has a thousand names and a thousand arts of harming, so that he may at least soften a heart firm and solid in faith, which he cannot pierce with stings of unbelief. He sends wandering and empty, unstable and fluid thoughts into the heart, as is said of him: “And supper having taken place, when the devil had already put it into Judas’s heart to betray him” (John 13). Behold, this sending—or insertion—[Col. 1100C] first plainly expressed by the prophet, then by the evangelist himself, who, reclining upon the very breast of wisdom, had drawn from it. For what else is a sending into the heart than an insertion? “He had put,” he says, “into the heart.” But that the Lord, teacher of humility and Lord of majesty, may be betrayed, mocked, scourged, spat upon, made an object of gain, made a spectacle, and finally crucified by tongues and hands—such harsh insertions, or by harsh insertions, the spirit of error daily works in the children of unbelief, the Lord himself, as the prophet has already testified, making these insertions through his evil angels according to the deserts of the lost. [Col. 1100D]

But these insertions, of which the same spirit of error now works daily, occur not only in the children of unbelief but also in the devout children of the Church, even in the Church’s first-born, that is, in the Lord’s anointed, Christ’s priests. They occur especially where these priests perform the office of priesthood and celebrate the rite of sacrifice. At that hour above all, he inserts these wandering and empty, unstable and fluid, ebbing and flowing thoughts; like decaying flies, they instantly ruin the fragrance of so sweet-smelling a sacrifice. They rush in especially in swarms at the hour of sacrifice, unless they are at once driven back by the faithful and watchful doorkeeper of the sanctuary—that is, devotion—and by the ready fan of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, in order that our priest, our new bishop, for whom this whole discourse is composed, might forestall and avert all these insertions—[Col. 1101A] both those which pierce and those which soften the heart—he was accustomed always to consume the immaculate Lamb, reverently indeed, yet also swiftly out of reverence for the command of the Law. Through the whole of this table of the Lord, festive in mystical and priestly attire, he was swift in eating and, as we said above, exceedingly brief in praying; yet he did everything devoutly and solemnly, though quickly for the reasons stated. Indeed, he was more devout precisely because he was swifter.

For the Lord speaks only in the whisper of a gentle breeze to Elijah, when he has come forth from his cave and stands at the entrance of his cave: he speaks only in passing.
