For only through a mirror and in an enigma, as though in the whisper of a gentle breeze, does the Lord speak to those who come forth from the clay-built houses of their bodies, [Col. 1101B] and, having come out, stand at the entrance of this clayey cave of theirs, desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ, already asking that their souls may die. To such persons alone, and yet only in passing, does the Lord speak. Theophanies frequently occur to them, but they are always brief and disappear with utmost speed; the splendors of the saints and God’s rejoicings are revealed in their hearts. These repeatedly refresh and illumine, even if they do not fully restore, the soul that sighs toward heavenly things with pious desire.

But the hour here is short and the delay slight while Elijah stands at the entrance of his clayey cave, until he has utterly gone out from that cave of clay. For the Wise Man says: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation burdens the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9). [Col. 1101C] And truly, in these theophanies the hour is brief and the delay slight. Hence, in the song of holy love, the Bride so often, so diligently, so devotedly seeks her Bridegroom with so many sighs. Seeking and sighing, now she finds, now she loses; now he flies away, now withdraws; now she knocks at the door, now holds him, now he slips away, now returns; now, called, he is silent, now, calling, he speaks. Thus the Bride compares her Bridegroom to a roe or a young hart leaping upon mountains and skipping over hills. The Bride herself, having frequently experienced this, teaches us through this parable of hers that those works and sacraments should be performed the more swiftly insofar as they must be performed the more devoutly.

For this reason our new priest, our new bishop, [Col. 1101D] celebrated the sacrament of the altar, of which we have now spoken for some time, the more swiftly because he most earnestly desired to perform and complete it more devoutly. By the example of so great a priest, many priests are therefore reproved: those who, in order to be regarded as devout—or perhaps because they are devout—delay and prolong this sacrament of the altar, though it is completed in very few words, and prolong this special kind of prayer, which is brief and ought to be extremely brief, if not in the Mass of the catechumens, at least in the Mass of the sacraments. I, who am present, hear, and ought to attend, meanwhile mount upon the empty and swift vehicle of my thoughts, flying from East to West; and along the way I build roads, streets, fortifications, and cities, [Col. 1102A] with neither my own money nor anyone else’s spent, and without any expense or labor. At times, as the spirit’s impulse carries me, I meanwhile arrange many wars without shedding any blood, or devise other trifling and idle things. Speaking for myself, I thus go, come, act, and contrive. And so, I think, do some hearers of Mass and others.

And is it surprising if that man, still human and like ourselves—our priest, I mean—who is about to offer for us the common sacrifice of our salvation, preparing himself for Mass or even in Mass itself, sometimes does not feel this within himself? Or if he does not feel it, should he not at least, as our priest, sympathize and condescend to us, so that, in accordance with the Master’s boast concerning the bishop, we may have a priest [Col. 1102B] who can have compassion upon our infirmities? Therefore I say that in a priest who lingers so at Mass, as the priest now under discussion does, there is either manifest hypocrisy or unwitting religious devotion.

But so that these priests may henceforth sympathize with us, and so that all you priests invited beforehand to the table may do so as well—you who have already reclined with the new priest, our new bishop—know that you too ought to prepare like things. For he gave you an example, that as he did, you should likewise do. After the reclining at the spiritual tables, according to the order laid down above and our promise above, we would now proceed to the bodily table, if it were not that the time for reclining has not yet come, especially for a bishop whom so many, so varied, secular and ecclesiastical occupations and cases summon; and it is still only about the sixth [Col. 1102C] hour of the day.

## 9. WHAT HE WAS LIKE IN THE COURTROOM

Once the celebration of Mass has been completed, the bishop leaves the church and immediately enters the courtroom, sitting to judge—as though ascending from seat to seat, from chair to tribunal. And as formerly to the table, so now to this courtroom he summons all his brethren, and especially his fellow-provincial bishops, that they may sit beside him and determine the law with him. For now he sits in judgment. Since this is the place to speak of the formation of judgments and the acceptance of gifts, which commonly pervert judgments, we must first consider what the person of the new judge, our new bishop, was like in these matters.

First of all, this new [Col. 1102D] judge, our new bishop, kept his hands clear, especially of suspect gifts, so that from those whom he knew to have cases he accepted not even an obol, nor anything of value—unless perhaps some food or drink was offered which he could not properly refuse. Since the subject of accepting gifts has presented itself, let us range more freely in praise of our new judge’s splendid and civic-minded conduct, and see what he was like in accepting gifts.

He was always accustomed to refuse gifts from those whom he believed needed to receive rather than give. Indeed, he was always most accustomed and most ready to give to such persons, especially among them to those ashamed to ask. From those too, whom he had offended on some account, he accepted only rarely, if ever, [Col. 1103A] even though they were wealthy; like the Lord, he despised Cain and his gifts, looking upon Abel’s gifts because of Abel, not upon Abel because of the gifts. But from others he received with much thanksgiving: those whom he knew to be his friends, to give cheerfully, and not to suffer loss after the gift. He was properly taught that in both giving and receiving gifts, particularly for a great man, much cautious discernment is necessary.

Thus also that moral censor among the Gentiles says: “See to whom you give.” This is paternal advice, and applies to the giver. But for the receiver the Wise Man says: “A gift from a fool will not benefit you” (Ecclus. 20), as though the former moral censor instructs the giver and this Wise Man the receiver. Thus, as the former moral censor instructs the giver and the Wise Man the receiver, [Col. 1103B] the former says to the giver, “See to whom you give,” and the latter says to the receiver, “See from whom you receive,” in accordance also with the Lord’s words: “I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks” (Ps. 49). For, as the same Wise Man testifies, “The Most High does not approve the gifts of the wicked” (Ecclus. 34); Scripture is everywhere read to show that he has always rejected them.

I say this as testimony because this new judge of ours, as far as I who wrote these things know—or even anyone more familiar with him, as I believe, should such a person be more favored than I—never accepted anything from anyone who himself made a request, while he still exercised his ecclesiastical authority freely and peaceably. Thus he interpreted by his actual conduct, with a certain and evident exposition for us, that saying of the [Col. 1103C] prophet which has been variously interpreted by different people. For one of the prophets, reproaching the greed of rulers, says: “The prince demands,” and immediately afterward adds: “And the judge is for repayment” (Mic. 7). He sets this down as the one, primary, and self-evident vice of the greedy ruler, saying: “The prince demands.” For what is a demand by a prince made known to a subject, except a kind of violent exaction from the subject, or a harsh extortion as though from an unwilling person? Then, heightening the charge, he adds the second vice of a ruler now both greedy and deceitful: “And the judge,” he says, “is for repayment.” It is as though the prophet, rebuking the ruler’s greed, said that if perhaps [Col. 1103D] the demanding ruler is not heard and does not obtain from his subject what he desires, either immediately, or—so that the fraud may be more covertly concealed—in the course of time, whether personally or through another, he brings some suit against the subject from whom he has suffered refusal, concerning the requested thing or any other matter whatsoever, treating him as an importunate holder of the thing requested. Thus he gains by some sort of sentence what he could not previously obtain by favor when making his demand. And so, the ruler who had first demanded but not obtained becomes afterward himself the judge, obtaining by calumny the thing demanded; and in this way himself renders it to himself through a calumnious judgment—or compels the person to render it to the ruler through such a judgment, after that person had refused freely to grant what was demanded to the demander.

[Col. 1104A] It is therefore a great vice of greed in a ruler even merely to ask something of a subject, even though he be free from the other vice which the prophet adds: namely, plotting nothing against the person who refuses after being denied the thing requested. For a ruler’s asking something from a subject, even if no other evil follows, differs little or not at all from shameful and burdensome exaction or unwilling extortion. The vineyard of Naboth, and afterward that of Ahab, confirms our interpretation of the prophet’s saying. Ahab, the ruler, demanded Naboth’s vineyard: behold the first vice of a greedy ruler. But after suffering refusal, he himself, through Jezebel the ruling woman, became “judge for repayment”: behold the second vice, far worse than the first. Read the sacred history at that place, and you will immediately [Col. 1104B] see clearly that this is so.

Our new judge, our new ecclesiastical ruler, likewise now confirms this interpretation by his own new practice, but contrariwise: he always avoided both extorting and asking, as though neither differed from exaction. For, as I frequently heard from his own testimony, he was especially embarrassed whenever, for any—even very pressing—reason, as sometimes happens, he had to ask for another’s property, even if he hoped to be heard devoutly and readily. He received with difficulty and asked with much greater difficulty, mindful of the Lord’s saying: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” Thus this new judge of ours kept his hands [Col. 1104C] clear of gifts, so that, together with all Israel’s holy prophet and most just judge, he too could gloriously and with equal freedom ask his subjects whether he had taken anyone’s ox or donkey, calumniated anyone, oppressed anyone, or accepted a gift from anyone’s hand; and together with the Master, the just judge of the Gentiles and outstanding teacher, he could boast that he had coveted no one’s silver, gold, or clothing.

At the very beginning our new judge, instructed by his mistress, the anointing—since, as we showed above, he too was anointed in those days of anointing when the rulers of the churches were anointed judges who despised the world—was especially taught that gifts blind the eyes of the wise and bend the force of authority. [Col. 1104D] This agrees with the saying of the Wise Man: “For hospitality-gifts and presents blind the eyes of judges, and, like a mute thing in their mouth, turn aside their reproofs” (Ecclus. 20). Nor should we omit here the further saying: “Fire will devour the tents of those who willingly accept gifts.” Behold how incorrupt, indeed how incorruptible, this new judge of ours was in himself.

He also cast greed, the deadly corruption of judges and a kind of fatal poison of judgments, far away from himself and his household, shook it off, and avoided it so thoroughly that he entirely expelled it from his house. Idolatry in a temple; greed in a bishop’s house. Accordingly, this new judge of ours now privately and individually, now publicly and collectively, most strictly forbade all his people [Col. 1105A] not only to exact anything, but even to accept what was offered by litigants; nor were they to make others’ vexations into their own spoils. I do not recall whether salaries were allowed only to advocates; but I know that everyone else was altogether forbidden to accept anything.

Accordingly, at that time it happened that one of the abbots entered the court and, having business there, offered several gold coins now to one person, now to another, among those able to influence judgments. But when all refused, the abbot completed his business, took back his gold, and as he departed said: “I have found a court more than golden: it not only does not go after gold, but throws gold away, despises gold, and tramples gold underfoot.” Such was the abbot’s glorious proclamation concerning the bishop’s household.

The bishop so yielded, through love of justice, compassion for those with business there, and hatred of greed, that in this house nothing was done for a price but everything freely. Nothing is accepted here by the keeper of the seal, nothing [Col. 1105B] by the signer, nothing by the notary. Nothing is sold here, nothing bought, nothing put up for sale: neither wax, nor sheets of parchment, nor the seal. For whose image or inscription is this upon the seal, that it should be sold or marketed? It is not Caesar’s, but the bishop’s. Truly, this house of our new judge, our new bishop, was not a house of trade, but the house of a true and just judge, the house of a holy bishop, and truly a house of prayer.

Of this holy pontiff and righteous judge, these three things above all and before all ought certainly to be characteristic: to love the holiness of continence, to cultivate justice, and to trample money underfoot. Hence among us neither the image of the pontiff nor the instrument of justice—the seal—was sold, nor was any profit made from it. But whether such profit is lawful in a pontiff’s household, let this consideration be yours, holy Fathers and fellow bishops who sit beside our new metropolitan; decide it yourselves. Perhaps this should be counted rather among voluntary gifts than among dues, rather among offerings than exactions, of which we have discussed some above. One thing I know for certain: even if it is lawful to acquire money thus, it is not expedient—especially in a pontiff’s household. Therefore, unless I am mistaken, it is far better and more glorious for a pontiff to provide the instrument of justice, the seal, free of charge, and to give to the poor his own likeness impressed upon wax or upon the seal—for he is still bound, on their behalf, to expend even himself. [Col. 1105D]

Thus, when every filthy trace of avarice had been expelled from the pontiff’s house, there was no one obedient to money; justice alone reigned in the pontiff’s house. This is that new breastplate of justice of the Lord Christ, the new anointed one, of which we spoke above: it immediately blunts within itself all the darts of covetousness that are driven against it and repels them from itself. Yet its strength will be revealed as greater in its own time, when the contest will be fought no longer with darts but with spears and swords. For the present, however, such a breastplate suffices.

Because of this singular and fervent zeal for justice, among the Spirit’s many gifts he was also abundantly granted this: that he might possess a spirit for judging between man and man. This came to him not from the instruction of a human master, but rather from the teaching anointing—just as that one was anointed above his fellows: “To him who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound” (Matt. 13). [Col. 1106A]

He exercised ecclesiastical jurisdiction most justly and sincerely, without any respect of persons and without any intervention of money, with as his assessors that company of learned men whom we commended above. Thus you could truly see as great a judge in the tribunal as you had lately seen a priest at the altar. Therefore you fellow-provincials who have been summoned to sit as assessors, you now observe, I think, your metropolitan’s learning in judicial matters; you grasp his method, and you see already how great is his zeal for justice and his contempt for money. Would that emulation might seize you also, so that you may obtain zeal like his, whose ministry you have obtained in likeness.

Having lingered for a while over all these matters, and having duly completed both the sittings at God’s tables and the hearings of secular cases, at about the ninth hour the pontiff rose from the tribunal, immediately entered the chamber, and prepared himself to recline for bodily nourishment. Pontiffs too ought to be invited to this table, as to the others, were it not that its refreshment appears to be merely animal and bodily rather than spiritual. Yet it is fitting and advantageous that they should be invited here also, since I hope that, from what they have heard and seen, they will come more willingly.

Let them therefore be invited, and, if they please, let them come, so that, as they know of their brother . . . .

[Col. 1106C]

*(One leaf is missing.)*

. . . surpassed [or: rivalled] the richness of the table. Hence, while reclining, he himself was always accustomed very frequently to cast his eyes over all the tables, so that he might seem less attentive even to his own dish. In this too he showed himself to be the many-eyed creature: not conspicuously, but in a restrained manner, with cultivated courtesy—not with the air of a wanderer or a man bewildered, but watchfully moving his eyes throughout the whole place, in order to see the order of those reclining and to render honour to whom honour was due.

And if among so many persons the one who ought to have presided happened to occupy the lowest place, he then compensated him with a more honourable place by frequent gifts from his own cup and dishes. At the same time he observed and noted how each person who presided over the service performed according to his rank and office; if anyone perhaps did so wrongly, he was sharply rebuked by the archbishop himself, on the spot and at the proper time, for negligence. Yet the ministers of this new master of the household, having experienced his daily practice at table, each became more diligent in the service assigned to him.

For over all who reclined at table, over each individual, and over the stewards and servants themselves, he spread his eyes so carefully and watchfully that you would say these were eyes assigned solely to the civil and domestic oversight of the bodily table. If one of his learned men happened to be absent, or because of some circumstance had changed his place and reclined in a lower position, this provident and courteous new master of our household immediately noticed it. [Col. 1107A] Just as King Saul, though otherwise unaware, was in this respect taught courtesy when, seated at table, he noticed David’s empty place: “Why has the son of Jesse not come to eat, neither yesterday nor today?” (1 Sam. 20). In the same way our master of the household immediately noticed this concerning his own men, and was accustomed to inquire after the absent person.

By sending and returning gifts to one whose place had been changed, he did not cease to show him honour, so that he himself might seem to be the first to have made himself last at table. Or if anyone else whom he wished to honour had withdrawn perhaps into the chamber or to some corner of the hall, either to yield place to others or because there was no room for him in the dining-room, he noticed this too very quickly. He honoured that person, as though he were continually looking through the intervening walls among all those reclining, by frequent visits of dishes.

Thus, with those eyes which nature had made large and very bright, he seemed to penetrate, illuminate, and gladden the whole banquet. But these eyes—the same eyes which, as we said above, had poured forth streams of tears—now shed nothing. For this is one table and that another: that the table of God, this the table of the world; there the food of spirits is set forth, here bodily feasts. To introduce tears among these would be as unseasonable as it would be uncivil. Therefore those eyes shed nothing here now.

This dining-room too has nothing in common with that secret nocturnal *mandatum* [service or injunction], in which, as we showed above, the pontiff, clad in haircloth, served poor men reclining at table. Great indeed is the distance between this abundance and that lowliness. [Col. 1107B]

[Col. 1107C]

But to what end is this? What is the purpose of this magnificent display and this almost imperial description of the table? This table appears to be Caesar’s rather than a pontiff’s. There seems to be no connection whatever between such a table and the table of Christ who was poor. This display has nothing in common with those ears of grain which the disciples plucked, rubbed in their hands, and ate; nor with those Gospel meals where there were only fish and barley, or where there was a piece of fish and a honeycomb. Christ also, after rising from the dead, asks only for something to eat: not *leopham* [an uncertain animal-name], not a boar, not a goat, not a kid, not a doe, not a stag, not pheasants, not poultry—but simply food. What he asks, it seems, is what he desires.

Yet the table we have begun to describe appears to be Augustus’s rather than Christ’s—or rather, Christ the Lord’s. But whoever you are who think thus, stop here. Go no further; do not judge. Rather, see, admire, and imitate, if you can, the many-eyed creature and the person of many faces. See the disciple made, after the pattern of his Master, all things to all: rejoicing with those who rejoice, weeping with those who weep, rendering to the world what belongs to the world and to God what belongs to God; now holy with the holy, now perverse with the perverse; now a Gentile with the Gentile, now a Jew with the Jew; now a servant with servants, now free with the free; now joyful with the joyful, now weak with the weak.

For according to that saying of the Wise Man, uttered as though from a watchtower over the world: “All things have their time: a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance, a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing” (Eccl. 3). “All things,” he says, “have their time”; and this especially belongs to a pontiff: that he obey the time, accommodate the time, and conform himself to the time. [Col. 1108A] Otherwise he will not be a creature with many eyes or a person with many faces. Otherwise he will not have favour with the Lord and with men—something especially required of a pontiff, who can neither devote himself to God alone at the expense of the world nor abandon the world for the Lord’s sake, but must please God and please the world.

“Please all men in all things,” says the Master, so that, deservedly, it may be written of the Pontiff of pontiffs, who is the pattern and glory of pontiffs: “He advanced in wisdom and grace before God and men” (Luke 2). So too this new pontiff of ours, beloved by God and by men, is wholly God’s and wholly the world’s, never his own—except that thereby he is all the more wholly his own. Such indeed ought a pontiff to be: never his own, never living for himself, but knowing that he was born for God and for his country, not for himself; the father of all, cherishing all and protecting them beneath the shadow of his wings.

Thus, I say, this creature of many eyes and person of many faces, made all things to all men, now serves poor people at table in haircloth, now serves the faithful at the altar in a liturgical stole; now, clothed in the breastplate of justice, sets an end to lawsuits at the tribunal; now, with temperance, rejoices together with those feasting at the banquet.

## 11. ON THE PONTIFF’S SOBRIETY

[Col. 1108C]

But with what temperance he did so—a matter not yet mentioned—must now be stated, so that, as we have already learned concerning his dress, we may likewise learn, amid this great abundance of the table, among so many diners and such delights of food, about his own diet, as we promised above. Truly, amid so many and such delicacies he savoured in no respect of Sardanapalus, but only of a bishop. He was not observably greedy for anything, nor did he abandon himself to any food whatever. As that wise and polished man says: “Do not be greedy at every feast, and do not give yourself up to every food” (Ecclus. 37).

In such abundance, therefore, not even a slight excess arising from greed for any dish could be observed in him. Since he was sober in all things, he gave the virtue of sobriety colour, as it were, by adding a certain courtesy to it: sober not only religiously in relation to God, but also courteously in relation to the world. Hence, as in other things, so particularly in this virtue of sobriety—almost the table’s own virtue—he pleased both God and men. For although abstinence is always sobriety’s companion, at table he customarily concealed that abstinence with a certain courteous dissimulation for the sake of those reclining with him, so that he seemed, just as he rejoiced with those rejoicing, to feast with those feasting.

At one time he concealed it by frequent gifts of dishes sent here and there; at another, by introducing a conversation from the Scriptures with his learned men, who reclined at his right hand—not tedious, but measured for the occasion. [Col. 1109A] At this table no flute-players are heard, no trumpeters, no lyre, no pipe, no cithara-player, no singer accompanied by the flute—things which the Lord reproaches through one of the prophets to a people given over to luxury: “Timbrel and lyre and cithara are at your feasts” (Isa. 5).

At this table, besides a clean, splendid, overflowing abundance of dishes, there are no incitements to gluttony, wantonness, or any luxury whatsoever. But when the other instruments and stimulants had been removed, the instrument of the Holy Spirit alone, the sacred reading—as we have already said above—sounded from the beginning to the end of the meal in a pleasant alternation, broken up suitably according to the time. Thus abstinence, sobriety’s companion, was lightened now by frequent gifts of dishes to one person, now to another, and now by an intervening discussion of Scripture. But above all he veiled all abstinence with a serene countenance and cheerful face, and thereby made the whole meal pleasant. Yet this abstinence itself was pleasing to God and burdensome to no one; as we said, covered with a courteous dissimulation for the sake of those reclining with him, it could scarcely even have been noticed. [Col. 1109B]

Let us hear more explicitly, then, the manner of his abstinence and the things he was accustomed to use. Sobriety requires three things: what, when, and how much we take—nothing forbidden, nothing before its time, nothing beyond measure. Hence Adam, who first ate what was forbidden, was immediately expelled; Jonathan, who ate before the appointed time, was cursed; but Israel, which ate beyond measure, was immediately punished: “Their food was still in their mouths, and the wrath of God rose against them.”

But the pontiff, chief of this dining-room, excelled in the virtue of sobriety and stood far apart from these. Here, since there was no need, no question was raised concerning time and measure. Let us hear only what he himself was accustomed to use, lest in this point—which might easily seem so to excessively rigorous and undiscerning religious persons—he should seem in any respect, even slightly, to have stained the splendid, beautiful, and pure virtue of sobriety which we proclaim in him.

Many and varied things were offered and set before him; yet from among the great number he retained only a few for his own use and eating. Nevertheless, among the things offered, those which he used were the more delicate and more costly—things which, although not forbidden, might appear alien to the perfection of sobriety and to the perfectly sober person, especially to those excessively rigorous persons we have mentioned. They might taunt this Christ of the Lord, as those still unformed disciples taunted Christ, crying: “Why this waste? It could have been sold and given to the poor.”

Accordingly, when one such rigorist once, while at table, remarked upon the pontiff with something like a smile, the pontiff, moved somewhat by zeal, answered him: “Certainly, brother, unless I am mistaken, you consume your bean with greater greed than I consume the pheasant set before me.” At that time this bird lay on a dish before the bishop. The brother had lived among us for some time and, because he had not been accustomed to such things, sought no delicacies; yet he was truly a greedy eater of coarser foods. [Col. 1110A]

The pontiff’s answer was good and prudent, both in view of the brother’s habit and in view of the truth. For, as the orthodox Fathers, physicians of souls, teach, it makes no difference what or how much anyone takes, provided that he serves necessity and health, not pleasure. Thus the first parent of all was driven out of paradise not for eating venison or goat’s flesh, but for tasting the forbidden fruit. Esau lost his birthright not for poultry, but for a meal of cheap lentils. David, fearing to drink water he had greatly desired, poured it out upon the ground; Elijah ate the meat brought to him morning and evening.

Thus it makes no difference what is taken for health, or how much for necessity; only desire, which always lies in ambush against the virtue of sobriety, must be banished. Desire is never satisfied by what suffices for necessity. “Human nature,” says someone, “is content with little.” Therefore it makes no difference what or how much is taken, provided it serves health or necessity alone, and not desire. And the Master says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 14). [Col. 1110B]

Since this chief of our dining-room could not manage coarser foods—being altogether unaccustomed to them—he partook of delicate foods, certainly, but very sparingly and soberly. As he himself said somewhere of himself, his beast of burden, reared in delicacies from childhood, was not fed on barley. This agrees with the saying of the Wise Man: “He who rears his servant in delicacies from childhood will later find him obstinate” (Prov. 29).

Indeed, it is altogether undiscerning and contrary to the truth of religion if a soul nourished amid saffron is compelled to embrace coarse things, and the beast of burden is shut off from its accustomed fodder. Otherwise, if it is kept from it for long, it will quickly fail on the road and be near death when its accustomed fare has been removed and new things are offered. It is no different from giving barley to one who finds only wheat palatable, or vetch instead of beans, or lentils instead of oats. This too is like giving a stone in place of bread, or offering a scorpion in place of a fish.

Such conduct is altogether irrational. But the Master, discussing the discipline of the body, says among other things: “Your reasonable service” (Rom. 12). “Reasonable,” that is, the chastisement of your body and mortification of the flesh should be undertaken with discernment. Even if the spirit is willing, nevertheless, in accordance with the common Greek proverb, “Nothing in excess,” one must, under the guidance of discernment—the charioteer of all virtues and moderator of works—make allowance for the weakness of the flesh and not altogether deny what is customary. [Col. 1110D] Otherwise, if fodder is withdrawn from a weakened beast, it may collapse under its burden before it carries the burden, and fail before it runs.

The wise Lord seeks a reasonable service: if there is zeal, let there be knowledge in that service also, and let knowledge moderate the heat of zeal. Therefore the Master, as if transformed from apostle into physician, forbids water to the disciple who punished his body without moderation and allows him to drink a little wine because of his stomach and his frequent infirmities. What was true in that disciple was likewise true in this fellow disciple of the Master, the chief of the present dining-room.

For a similar reason, because his stomach was always by nature very cold, drinking water in excess harmed him. Therefore, following the admonition of the Master and physician to the disciple, this fellow disciple rarely, indeed never, drank water unmixed, but used wine alone—taken moderately and with sobriety. This sobriety was beyond praise and admirable, and worthy of imitation by every priest, but especially by pontiffs. For before the meal, at the meal, and after the meal, he was always so even that one could not have discerned from face or speech whether he was thirsty or had been drinking. [Col. 1111A]

Further—and this approaches miracle and gives joy—as some of his religious intimates knew more secretly from his private confession, he experienced scarcely any more rebellion of the flesh when fed than when fasting, nor after wine than before it. Truly, it was a miraculous and singular privilege of grace: amid wines and feasts, and while the flesh’s desire had not yet been worn out by more advanced age, to live in so great and angelic a purity that, not to speak of action or consent, the flesh rarely—and more often not at all—stirred rebellion against the spirit.

We have now heard concerning the chief of our present dining-room how magnificent he was in that room; how immense at this table; how learnedly watchful; how courtly in his cultivation; how magnificently he reclined; how graciously he distributed; and how civilly sober in relation to the world and religiously sober in relation to God. Truly he was great and immeasurable at each table: great at God’s table and great at the world’s table; at the altar a most devout priest, in the dining-room a most provident master of the household, and—if we add the third, intermediate sphere set out above—at the tribunal a most equitable judge.

But now that all that belonged to the table has been splendidly and festively completed, it is time to rise from table. When the hymn has been sung, the pontiff leaves with his learned men and enters the chamber. [Col. 1111C]

To state once for all what need be stated only once: whenever in this history you frequently hear that the archbishop did this or that with his learned men, understand that this is said because, in matters to be done—whether those concerning the Lord or those concerning the world—no outsider was admitted, except his learned men alone and perhaps other counsellors such as the stewards. Even a visiting cleric was scarcely admitted to the archbishop’s own table among these learned men, but reclined honourably and properly apart at one of the tables, and was then visited by the archbishop with frequent table-gifts.

No one, I say, was admitted among the learned men at the meal unless perhaps he was someone whom the archbishop, calling by name, had resolved to honour greatly—always on the merit of holy conduct or learning rather than rank or office. This was done principally so that, at the table where the archbishop himself reclined among his learned men, no word might accidentally slip out—as often happens at such times—especially before an outsider, which it would have been better to leave unsaid. Thus, by honouring his own men at table, he took care both for himself and for them.

And, to add this for the sake of the matters mentioned, it was an ancient practice of his predecessors—and, following the Fathers, he himself had adopted it—not to retain in his household a cleric, especially one participating in counsels, whom he knew to be bound to kings by homage or an oath of fealty. [Col. 1112A] The reason for this, as I learned from the archbishop himself, was an old custom of his holy predecessors: from ancient times, excessively worldly dissension had often arisen between kings and archbishops. A cleric of the archbishop’s household and family bound to the king, as we have said, was in time of disagreement placed, as it were, between hammer and anvil—either faithless to the king or to the archbishop, or at least suspect. Thus, obedient and bound as he was, even if innocent, he could not easily avoid suffering loss to his reputation from one side or the other; often he also suffered an enormous loss of property.

Recognizing this, those holy Fathers, who were always, as it were, on the move and girded for action, provided in this matter both for themselves and for others, according to the saying of Wisdom that no one can serve two masters. But let us return to the order of the history. When the table-hymn had ended, then, as we have said, the pontiff rose from table with his learned men and entered the chamber, where he was either engaged in discussion of the Scriptures or in deliberations about business. This was his daily practice, unless perhaps he allowed himself a short sleep for the time being. But you invited pontiffs who sat at the table should know that you too ought to make like preparations. [Col. 1112C]

## 12. WHAT HE WAS LIKE IN CONFERRING ORDERS

But it is necessary that you, especially you fellow-provincials, return at the appointed and suitable time—and briefly—to your new metropolitan. For at the imminent solemn fast of the seventh month he intended to ordain and appoint ministers at God’s table. You too are needed for this: either by teaching, to provide a model of the sort of ministers the new pontiff should ordain and appoint at God’s table, or by learning, to receive an example from your metropolitan.

And indeed it happened as he had intended. After his own consecration, which, as we said above, had been celebrated so festively and splendidly in the octave of Pentecost, he celebrated ordinations at the following Ember fast of the seventh month. He did so all the sooner because the metropolitan see had already been vacant for some time. And truly—to confess the truth, the whole truth—above all things and more than anything else, he was exceedingly fearful and anxious in this particular pastoral duty.

For he had read the Master’s saying to the disciple: “Lay hands suddenly on no man, neither be partaker of other men’s sins.” At this passage, like a dreadful thunderclap—and especially as one of the sons of thunder he was to fear thunder—he was shaken with all his heart and body. He especially feared what is added at the end of that dreadful saying: “Neither,” it says, “be partaker of other men’s sins” (1 Tim. 5). Hence, in a certain exhortatory sermon which he himself then preached to those to be ordained, he interpreted this saying among other things—not offering an innovation, nor differing from the ancient orthodox interpretation.

For the instruction of many, by the Lord’s grant, I have taken care to insert here the very words of his interpretation, which he then addressed to those being ordained:

> “I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, do not permit my hands to be laid hastily upon you, except upon those who have resolved to minister worthily in the Church of God according to the rank of their office, lest I become a participant in other men’s sins, since I feel myself already too heavily burdened by the multitude of my own. For it is more certain than certain that one who knowingly, or without much testing, ordains an unworthy man gravely offends God, even if the man ordained later reforms. But if the ordained man does not reform, the ordainer stains himself with the sins of the ordained man, especially those which the ordained man commits after the day of his ordination.
>
> “But the Apostle commands Timothy: ‘Lay hands suddenly on no man, neither be partaker of other men’s sins’ [ibid.]. Therefore, brothers, on behalf of almighty God and of ourselves, we forbid any of you to allow the yoke of the Lord to be placed upon him by us if he considers himself insufficient. Let him rather remain in the good until he gains strength for what is better.”

These are his own words, among others, in that sermon to those being ordained. See from them whether he was not terrified, trembling, and anxious. Moreover, he was an exceedingly exact investigator in examining candidates for ordination. First, as ecclesiastical institution requires, he asked whether the candidate was worthy in life; second, whether he was adorned with learning appropriate, however, to the grade which he sought; third, whether he possessed a church benefice suitable to his life, learning, and the grade which he sought—lest after promotion they should wander about as vagrants or hirelings and regard holy orders not as religious service but rather as gain and display. [Col. 1113C]

These three requirements were indeed drawn not merely from a canon but rather from the pattern of Christ himself, the supreme priest. All the ministers ordained in this way serve at the table of his altar. For Christ first began both to do and to teach, and he possessed a purse for the use of himself, his followers, and the poor. Behold these three: life, learning, and benefice. You hear and see Christ’s purse; understand the benefice of Christ in the Church. Not canonry upon canonry, church upon church, benefice upon benefice—as though this were a heap of mammon—but a suitable ecclesiastical benefice, so that it may be Christ’s purse: not superabundant, but sufficient.

Such, and only such, is Christ’s purse, the wealth of the apostles: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6). Thus these three things—life, learning, and benefice—our pontiff, the new ordainer, sought in Christ’s ministers during the first ordinations which he celebrated, following the pattern of that great pontiff Christ. But he investigated them so severely that he scarcely entrusted this investigation to anyone but himself, so greatly did he fear, as he had himself just said, becoming a participant in others’ sins—or erecting idols in God’s temple instead of ministers of the temple, or, like a deceitful money-changer of the supreme King, debasing the coinage.

For to mark men contemptible in life and learning with the character of royal ministry is truly to adulterate the coin of the supreme King entrusted to pontiffs. It is to stamp the king’s seal not upon gold or silver but, in their place, upon tin, bronze, or lead. Such counterfeiters of the great King deserve disinheritance and the gallows. [Col. 1114A]

What then shall be said of those who, without great necessity in the Church, compel their clerics—who have not yet been tested for the canonically prescribed period in the orders they have already received—to proceed immediately to higher orders and force unwilling men to rise? Such persons, it seems, either desire to dominate the clergy or render themselves suspect of shameful exaction. For taking money in order that an ordination may proceed, or in order that it may be withheld, is an equal crime and is classed under the sin of simony. But more on this elsewhere.

You pontiffs summoned above who have come to these ordinations, observe whether this is not the canonical form of ordination in the new ordainer. I know, and do not doubt, that it will be judged canonical. It is moreover advantageous for the Church that, if you have not previously supplied this model to this new ordainer, you should henceforth at least preserve this model received from your new metropolitan. For the excess of ordainers in this matter is very frequent and enormous. It is more dangerous because, as one apostolic man among the teachers says, a person once ordained cannot be judged; and therefore he must be examined beforehand with all the greater care because after ordination he cannot be judged. [Col. 1114C]

But one thing, not without reason, deeply troubled our new archbishop, our new ordainer. He saw, both in his own province and in others—alas, all too commonly in these days—that few are called by God like Aaron, while almost everyone ascends to the summit of the episcopate solely through the favour of kings or men. Preference is given not to merit of life or learning, but to nobility of blood, money, favour, and above all service to princes or the applause of the world.

This is surely that evil which the wise king saw under the sun, as though it went forth by error from the ruler’s presence: namely, a fool set in lofty dignity, while the rich sit below; slaves riding on horses, and princes walking on the ground like slaves. Of this the same wise king says elsewhere: “Like one who throws a stone into a heap of mercury is one who gives honour to a fool” (Prov. 26).

Concerning this matter Jeroboam, successor of that wise king, though illegitimate and the first of schismatic kings—who first usurped both a kingdom for himself and a priesthood—is repeatedly rebuked by the prophets at the beginnings of his schismatic reign because he set up, over the people, idols for the people to worship, made shrines on the high places, and made priests from the lowest of the people. Thus that schismatic king, by usurping the priesthood, set up over the people idols for them to worship, and afterward made priests from the lowest of the people to minister to the idols. [Col. 1115A]

But because all these things happened to them as a figure of ourselves and were written for our sake, how many of our kings, after that shadow of things to come, have usurped the priesthood and still usurp it daily! Read our histories, read the books of the times, read the annals, and you will scarcely find among kings one who has not taken something from what was under anathema, who has not usurped something of the priesthood, who has not put his hand to the ark, carried something off from the temple, drunk from the temple vessels, or handled the temple’s vessels—just as though kingship did not suffice them unless they involved themselves also in the priesthood.

But, leaving these ancient examples and returning to newer ones and to our own concern: what was formerly the complaint concerning that first schismatic king is now the new complaint of our own time. For those kings who now set up idols over the people, producing as supposedly new things likenesses of those ancient errors, and who, like their predecessors, make priests from the lowest of the people to serve the idols—what are they doing? Are not foolish and ignorant pontiffs, set here and there over the people in the Church at the wish and nod of kings, Jeroboam’s idols in Dan and Bethel? As one of the prophets says: “O shepherd, and idol!” (Zech. 11).

And those priests from the lowest of the people who minister to these idols—what are they but the men now subject to these pontiffs and performing priestly functions: men of the lowest life? Such pontiffs and kings make such priests alike. Not indeed by laying hands on them themselves, but by setting over them men who will make such persons, who will readily lay hands on such persons. They make such men, I say, like themselves who make them: like false gods and the images of the nations, these are the lesser gods and those the greater. [Col. 1115C]

O how the usurpation of priestly office by kings and those set on high must be avoided, since it is ambitious and profane! It must be avoided, I say, lest they destroy their Abiah with the ambitious Jeroboam; lest they be divided with the rash Uzzah; and lest they be struck with leprosy upon the forehead with the presumptuous Uzziah. By “forehead” I mean that which, in the priest, the gold plate adorns and covers; which the impression of the letter *tau* protects from slayers in the prophet; and which the blow of the sling-stone shattered to destroy the insolent and challenging Philistine.

I pass over now that immense prophetic “burden of the wilderness of the sea”: namely, the destruction of the Babylonian empire, solely because, after other things had first been carried away, the princes of Babylon presumed to drink from the temple vessels and touch them irreverently. Yet the king or prince is not attacked in the present discourse if, like the holy King David and prophet, he loves the beauty of God’s house, desires it, works for it, and strives that, for the adornment of God’s house and to bear the fabric of the Church, hewn and strong columns may stand in that house; and that such men as may be found, after diligent seeking, should be taken from the clergy to govern peoples. [Col. 1115D]

For the men whom Holy Scripture commends, appoints, ordains, and especially assigns to so holy an office do not thrust themselves forward. Truly such men—and they alone—are worthy; all others are altogether unworthy men for our office. Especially unworthy are those who, rich from the goods of the Church and laboriously following military camps night and day only that they may grow still greater, seek ecclesiastical and especially pontifical honours as benefices. But if you object that no such column as Scripture describes and seeks is now found in the clergy—because, as was predicted long ago and is now fulfilled, our age is so poor in men—I answer: Would that the better men from the clergy were chosen, with all the more religious care because they had been all the more diligently sought! For, as we have said, such men do not push themselves toward honours; rather, they hide themselves from the world’s tribulation and contradiction in schools, in cloisters, or, more often, in mountains, caves, and hollows of the earth.

But to return from our digression to the point for which we digressed: today we certainly see many men ascend to the highest episcopal rank solely through the favour of kings—would that it were without offence to the King of kings, or, since not without offence, would that it were not without pardon. Yet, to say what I now think about this: in such cases the fault of metropolitans, rather than of princes, seems the graver; and the complaint against metropolitans is correspondingly sharper, by as much as willing differs from doing, or intention from action. For princes merely will it; but metropolitans both will and do it, since they first ratify the election of such men and afterwards lay hands upon them. Even their own book of scrutinies, which they call their *Ordinary*, most openly condemns this sacrilegious audacity by exposing it.

If, therefore, our new ordainer, our new archbishop, shrinks back when he sees this, it is no wonder. For to reject men first presented to him, so as first to ratify and confirm their election—such as it is—and finally, what is still greater, to lay his hand upon them and consecrate them, seems altogether unjust, since before the face of the Church they have neither been convicted nor confessed of a crime or other offence rendering them less fit, nor is any crime notorious that would prevent their consecration. Conversely, it is exceedingly dangerous to admit such a man, because his previous life does not accord with the pastoral office; or, if perhaps it does accord, it has nevertheless appeared to no one’s judgment to have done so. Yet by divine law and the testimony of all, that man alone ought to be chosen as the worthier whose manner of life appears the holier.

But, to leave aside for the moment conduct and life—for God sees these better than man, by how much more inwardly he sees them—what is immediately evident is that learning is by no means sufficient. I mean the learning of the man to be consecrated, or of the elect who is to be consecrated: a man who has spent his entire life amid the vanities and idleness of the world, not yet a disciple, yet seeking to be a master of the Scriptures—not in schools, as some merely discretionary teacher, but truly an established teacher in churches.

Our new archbishop was therefore constrained by these considerations: as we have shown, it was dangerous to admit such men, and yet it seemed unjust to reject them. Above all, the archbishop was constrained because the Master wrote this, among other things, to his disciple; and the apostolic man—indeed, rather, the great Apostle—wrote, as though to one of his own metropolitans:

> “For this reason I left you in Crete, that you might set right what remained to be corrected, and appoint presbyters in every city as I directed you.” [Col. 1117A]

He immediately adds what sort of men he directed should be appointed:

> “If anyone is without reproach,”

and the rest that the apostolic sequence sets forth one by one in that holy catalogue of episcopal virtues. In accordance with the interpretation of the holy orthodox fathers, he here understands bishops by the name “presbyters”: the name of an office under the name of an age.

Thus our new archbishop, the new ordainer, was constrained especially by these saving admonitions of the Master. For such a man—and he alone—is truly and fully worthy: the man whom the Master, himself a beautiful painter, beautifully portrays by this description. Yet, to speak still in human terms, given the sluggishness and lukewarmness of our age: even if the man to be consecrated is not altogether such a one, he must nevertheless shine conspicuously in some of the gifts of grace in this episcopal catalogue, and the consecrator himself must perceive this. Otherwise he assuredly consecrates unworthily and to his own judgment, unless he who consecrates has, through certain evidences, a well-grounded assurance particularly concerning the virtues of the man to be consecrated. If conscience protests, he shares in another’s sins when he lays hands too hastily upon him.

Thus, through the Master, as herald of divine law, two edicts of the heavenly Emperor were proclaimed together. The first decreed:

> “Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV);

and the second:

> “Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others” (I Tim. V).

Yet in this very matter there is dangerous dispensation if, after the better man has been neglected, an inferior is preferred, according to the prophet’s saying:

> “Cursed is the deceitful man who has a male in his flock and, making a vow, sacrifices a weak thing to the Lord” (Mal. I). [Col. 1117C]

And so, in the case of great priests, there is a great danger, and one scarcely avoidable. Lesser priests are less dangerously dealt with, because they may more freely be examined in life and learning, deferred, rejected, expelled, or removed. But who dares, or can, flee from or drive away men such as these, so great and so powerful, by as much the more dangerous as they are greater and more unworthy? Whoever attempted this anew would be considered either superstitious or rash. Such men have now long prevailed and multiplied beyond number.

Our new pontiff was therefore not without reason constrained by these considerations; and, so constrained, he was at first the sharpest accuser of himself, because, as he accused himself, he was like the men we have described: a vain and proud man, assumed from the court to the Church against every rule of law, as shamefully and monstrously as his elevation was irregular. When one of his learned advisers then brought forward by way of example many men raised from court, and many others from the secular world, to pastoral eminence; and said that many simple, uneducated men, ignorant of the Scriptures, had nevertheless fulfilled the pastoral charge holily and vigorously, and that grace had abounded most where sin had abounded—he immediately addressed these words specifically to that learned man who had spoken:

> “Brother, these things which you recall are indeed miracles of God’s mercy and are by no means to be made a precedent. Otherwise, in accordance with the examples you adduce, let men everywhere and without distinction be chosen in the Church: the just and the wicked alike, the clean and the unclean alike, the unlearned together with the learned. Let us see whether God is still powerful and whether there is strength in the Most High. Let us disregard ecclesiastical judgment and commit everything to a divine miracle, since the Most High can raise children to Abraham from these stones—and, as you indicate by your examples, has often done so.”

And in conclusion he said:

> “One thing I have resolved most firmly: if, with my conscience protesting, it should so happen by the Lord’s ordering, I will neither confirm the election offered to me of the appointed bishop nor consecrate the elect. Therefore I humbly invoke the Most High, that the merciful and compassionate Lord himself may daily increase, strengthen, and confirm this purpose and desire of mine, which I do not doubt to be just.”

The following parts of this history will plainly and shortly show that our new archbishop—an ordainer of priests, as we have already indicated, so strict, and, as is clear from what has been said, a consecrator of bishops so fearful—was heard by the Lord.

## 13. WHY HE LINGERS OVER DESCRIBING THE PONTIFF’S DEEDS

So far, as it has been granted us, we have pursued the question how great this Thomas of ours was at court, and how great he began to be in the Church immediately after attaining episcopal rank; how vigorously he first began to serve Henry, the illustrious king of the English, and how gloriously thereafter Christ, the supreme King of the English. At court he rendered to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and in the Church to God the things that are God’s.

But in recounting these episcopal deeds, as I did not conceal above what I feared, so here again I cannot avoid repeating it because I fear detractors. In describing these deeds of the pontiff, I may perhaps seem excessively slow, a wearisome repeater of words in praising the deeds themselves; I may seem to attend more to theological edification than to a historical exposition of the man’s acts, and thus to savour too much of the theologian and too little of the historian. Yet whoever notes this should at least not judge us thus before observing that we explain not only the pontiff’s deeds, but also the causes of those deeds—as we remember having already said above—as though we were setting forth not merely the actions but also the mind of the doer, which I received in this way from the doer himself.

Accordingly, I pursue the causes of his actions all the more carefully because I received them thus from the author himself; and, in pursuing the causes of the actions, I linger longer in describing the actions themselves. Let us run through each of the deeds already described, and it will plainly appear that this is so. Let us run, I say, through each: first, to the hair-shirt of the new recruit; to the stole of the new priest; to the steward’s secret command issued by night; to that yearling lamb solemnly and hastily eaten at the altar; to the judge unbendingly just upon the tribunal; to the householder at table, so civilly and religiously sober; to the master in the school, so strict an examiner of his pupils.

Let us run through each of these, and you will see clearly the cause of all of them—a cause which I either learned from him personally or received through myself beyond doubt—and for that reason inserted into this history not too briefly. [Col. 1119A] Therefore, because we have included both the deeds of so great a pontiff and the causes of those deeds, so ample and so worthy, I could not, as will appear below, compress them into an irksome brevity; but neither did I dare to obscure and constrict things so clear and striking by a laboured brevity.

Since, therefore, after describing the pontiff’s deeds we immediately set down the causes of those deeds, it is plain that the resulting edification is more fruitful, the instruction more complete; and hence the fabric of a more extended discourse had necessarily to be woven with the threads of many words. For this same reason, perhaps exceeding the proper rule of history, I savour more of the theologian. For the power of God’s works cannot, and ought not, be explained apart from theology, apart from the word of God.

If, then, I have exceeded the limit in this, the force of the deeds compelled me. And if there is anyone who will excuse the excess, so be it; if not, it will increase the merit and yield a more abundant fruit of edification.

Indeed, for acting rightly it is greatly necessary that one who performs divine works understand the cause and power of his works. The prophet too seeks understanding for the purpose of acting, so that he may know not only what he ought to do, but also why he does it when he does it:

> “Give me understanding, and I shall search out your law and keep it” (Ps. CXVIII).

See how, before practice, he asks for the theory of holy actions, so that, just as physicians work for bodily health according to their understanding of the body’s health, so he may work for the health of the spirit according to the understanding supplied by prior theory.

For holy action, the more fully it is understood, edifies more fruitfully, gives life more powerfully, and is either performed or deferred more safely according to the occasion. A work without knowledge is a body without a soul, earth without water, or a cloud dry for lack of rain. Thus charity possessed together with knowledge surpasses every other charity. This is what the Master desires his disciples to know, writing to them:

> “To know the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge” (Eph. III).

For whatever good is loved, it is loved with more feeling the more perfectly it is known. And if it is perhaps lost through the force of some temptation, the person who has the spirit of knowledge receives it again more easily, by as much as he grieves more fruitfully over its loss and understands more perfectly the manner and path by which to return to it. As that wise king says:

> “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow.”

For he who has knowledge grieves more sharply in repentance for a lost good of virtue. What vinegar is to taste, oil to fire, wood to a funeral pyre, and scammony (*diagridium*) to medicine, knowledge is to repentance.

Otherwise, what the Master entreats will not be “reasonable service,” because the reason for service is unknown. For just as it is better to do the Lord’s command than merely to know it, so it is prior to know it than to do it. To act while being ignorant of what one does is neither perfect knowledge nor perfect obedience; ignorance detracts from obedience and makes it less devout. Hence one of the prophets says:

> “And you, Israel, do not be ignorant.”

And the Master says:

> “Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of God is” (Eph. V). [Col. 1120A]

When you perform that will and know the reason for performing it, then you will be filled with all the fullness of God which the Master desires for his disciples.

But to return to the earlier point: in these new works of virtue of the new pontiff, we have shown, together with the works themselves, their causes and power. Therefore we have been more prolix in recounting them; yet this prolixity contributes alike to edification and to praise. For all who deign to read these things, however roughly written and in whatever hand copied, out of devotion to and remembrance of so great a pontiff, will recount not only his works but also the power and greatness of his works.

## 14. CONCERNING THE ESTATES WHICH HE CLAIMED FROM LAYMEN

Having, as far as granted to me, dealt with those matters by which the pontiff so gloriously ordered his life, we must proceed with the pontiff to other things. For he who until now had sailed in the harbour of the Church begins to enter the sea of the world and to handle secular matters. This is very often necessary for a pontiff, but never pleasant to a wise pontiff.

He now began disputes with certain magnates of the realm, men great and powerful, concerning estates of his church, claiming back some because of the incapacity or negligence of his predecessors, and recovering others without litigation where the injustice seemed manifest. Such were those estates which in the vernacular are called *firmae feodales* [feudal farms or farms held at fixed rent]. At the very beginning of his pontificate, the archbishop recovered all these, as belonging to his own table, into his personal lordship, having excluded those called *firmarii* [farmers or lessees], without seeking any judgment from a fiscal court. [Col. 1120C]

When asked why he did this, he answered that he would in no way litigate concerning things known to belong to his lordship, even if they had been unjustly alienated under whatever title. Thus he ordered and held those estates at his will, until, driven into exile and outlawed for the sake of justice, he lost both these and other possessions—a matter which what follows will relate more fully.

Moreover, he pressed most insistently his claim to the fief called that of William de Ros, a fief, unless I am mistaken, of seven knights, which had immediately been confiscated upon the death of Archbishop Father Theobald. But after merely raising the question concerning this fief, the archbishop halted here, awaiting the return of the king, who was then outside the realm. Yet because other matters arose, he did not raise the matter of this fief either then or at the king’s imminent return, but deferred it.

There was also a severe dispute at that time between the archbishop and the noble Earl de Clare, because the archbishop required homage to be rendered to him concerning that castle called Tonbridge and all the territory belonging to the castle, especially all that lay within the league surrounding the castle, commonly called the *banleuga*, or, more Latinely, the *bannum leugae* [the jurisdictional league]. The earl offered homage, but refused to specify that it was for the matter which the archbishop claimed.

Further, he claimed the custody of Rochester Tower, asserting it to be his right from his Church, and producing upon this point a public instrument: namely, the charter of William, of blessed memory, formerly the illustrious king of the English, who had vigorously acquired the kingdom in armed warfare by the strength of his hand. [Col. 1121A]

When these and similar claims had been raised, with some estates recovered and others demanded, disputes, lawsuits, and many adversaries immediately arose for the pontiff. Yet they were more hidden because they revered and feared the exceptional favour of the king which, as we have shown above, the pontiff still possessed, and consequently feared the pontiff’s displeasure not a little.

Nevertheless, some of those who felt themselves injured or feared injury approached the king while he was still abroad, complaining that some had suffered and others would suffer injustice from the pontiff unless royal clemency laid a hand to justice. Seeking to shake, even somewhat, the king’s steadfast favour toward the pontiff, they added that the king’s excessive favour was giving the pontiff horns with which to overstep the bounds. But the king, who loved him in deed and truth, was moved by none of this and turned his ear away from such people. Since he was on the point of crossing the sea, he deferred the complainants until his arrival in England.

And behold: shortly afterwards, the king, whose arrival had been repeatedly announced beforehand, as was fitting and customary, was reported to have landed at the southern port called Southampton. He landed in the first year of the pontiff’s consecration, if I am not mistaken, soon after the feast days of the Saviour’s Nativity.

The archbishop at once came to meet him, together with that excellent boy, Henry, the king’s son and heir to the kingdom, whom we have often named already; for, as the king approached by sea, he had been awaiting his arrival nearby for several days. And behold, when the pontiff entered the king’s lodging together with the king’s son, there was great joy and exultation throughout the court among the king and all who came to meet him. King and pontiff rushed into mutual kisses and embraces, each anticipating the other in honour—indeed, striving to outdo one another. It appeared that the king poured himself out little for his son, but wholly for the pontiff, and expanded into every kind of joy toward him, seeing now for the first time as a pontiff his former Thomas of the court. Above all else, he was expanded in joy because he had already privately and reliably learned so many and such great things about the holiness of this pontiff taken from his court, as we described above.

The pontiff, accommodating the king after the weariness and discomfort of the sea, withdrew soon after their mutual greeting and the joy they had celebrated together, and repaired to lodging nearby. The following morning, meeting together, they travelled in company; throughout the journey, the two alone, all others having been removed, conversed familiarly and privately and delighted one another. When they had been thus engaged for several days, the pontiff withdrew from the king in the highest favour, together with his aforesaid fosterling, the king’s son. The complainants mentioned above, seeing and hearing these things, hid themselves and suppressed their complaints.

## 15. CONCERNING HIS JOURNEY TO THE COUNCIL OF TOURS

And behold: shortly afterwards, Pope Alexander III, of happy memory—there was then a schism in the Roman Church—summoned a council throughout the whole Catholic Church. Our archbishop, great in all things, prepared himself most magnificently to cross the sea. Having approached the king, whom he loved as his lord and as more than a man, he restored his fosterling to his royal father. After spending several days with the king in sweet and familiar conversation and taking leave of him, he awaited a favourable wind at his own manor in Kent, called Romney, situated above the sea.

When, after a few days, the wind was granted, he put to sea and landed safely in Flanders, at the port called Gravesend, with a great and magnificent retinue. Immediately upon the shore itself, Philip, the noble count of Flanders and Vermandois, met him; and on the following day the magnates and nobles of that land did so too, showing him every honour, vying in offering both their own resources and whatever they could provide.

Then, travelling through Normandy and Maine, he was received throughout the dominions of the illustrious king of the English—in cities, castles, and villages—with such honour as though the king himself were being received. Approaching Tours, he entered the city on the third day, if I am not mistaken, before the council was to be held.

At news of the arrival of the Archbishop of Canterbury, the whole city was immediately stirred, and everyone went out to meet him: not only citizens and natives, but also the ecclesiastical persons who had almost all already gathered for the council, including archbishops and bishops from diverse nations. And, what must not be passed over in silence, contrary to the custom of the Roman Church, all the cardinals—the lord fathers and governors of the Church—came out to meet him long before he entered the city, except only two who remained sitting beside the lord pope, so that he might not be without attendants in so great an assembly. [Col. 1122C]

The crowd following him was so great that, as the archbishop entered the pope’s palace, the pope himself, as though compelled by necessity lest he be pressed upon, left the chamber in which he was and entered the palace. As though impelled by a spirit of prophecy, the pope—who scarcely rises for anyone—came, as it were, to meet the archbishop and already, as if in encounter, showed him reverence.

This entire reception, as it seems, was honourable and prophetic: in Christ, a kind of second feast of the Lord’s *Hypapante* [Meeting], as though foretelling things to come. We see this fulfilled today, when people now come to him from the whole world of churches, from East and West, through many difficulties, and adore him rather than merely meet him.

The lord pope then received the archbishop most graciously; and all the more graciously because he had long desired to see him and had already heard many good things about him. Seeming to feel compassion for him because of his journey, he dismissed him quickly, saying:

> “Go, brother, rest; rest is necessary after labour.”

And so we withdrew then and took lodging in the king’s castle near the papal palace.

On the next day you could see crowds immediately streaming to this lodging. For those who had assembled, both those who had heard and those who now saw the pontiff’s magnificence, came to him day after day: ecclesiastical persons from diverse kingdoms, seeking and offering favour and friendship. Moreover, the nobles and powerful men of the land repeatedly came and went to us; especially those exercising royal jurisdiction, knowing that the pontiff stood in the highest favour with the king, they were constant around us, either ready to serve or actually serving.

And, greater still than the rest, the Roman Church honoured our archbishop above the others, as though he were the firstborn among the many who had assembled, with something like the honour and reverence due to a firstborn. After the council had been held for several days, the apostolic man renewed certain privileges of his Church at our archbishop’s request and dismissed him with the kiss of peace, his blessing, and his favour. [Col. 1123B] With sea and air favourable, he soon returned joyfully to England, now in the second year of his consecration; and the king received him, as custom and duty required, like a son receiving a father, amid every expression of joy.

[lacuna]

> [Here there occurs in the Arras manuscript a gap of one leaf, whose beginning and end may apparently be supplied from the *Quadrilogus* as follows:
>
> [lacuna]
>
> **Concerning the consecration of the bishops of Worcester and Hereford.**
>
> In those days two episcopal sees in the province stood vacant: Worcester, because the bishop of the former see had now died; and Hereford, because its bishop had been transferred from Hereford to the see of London. [Col. 1123C] The man transferred was Gilbert Foliot, as he was called by his proper name and surname.]

[lacuna] let another be clothed; or let one poor man be stripped, so that another may be clothed naked. For according to Scripture, a man’s own riches are the redemption of his soul. For they went forth weeping, casting not another’s seed but their own seed. Accordingly, we also read that the Lord must be honoured from your own just labours. Otherwise, according to the Wise Man:

> “He who offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor—what else does he do but slay a son before his father’s eyes?” (Ecclus. XXXIV)

Moreover, throughout the whole time during which occupied churches remain vacant, work perishes, labour perishes, pastoral care and pastoral office utterly perish; and so the safety of the whole flock is endangered. If a monastery is thus occupied, discipline perishes in the monastery without a father; instruction perishes without a teacher; strict restraint perishes without a bridle; discipline perishes without a rod; obedience perishes without a prelate. Thus, as though emancipated into a harmful freedom, destructive laxity reigns in the cloisters. Those who had formerly served the monastic rule holily and strictly become free from the observances of that same rule.

And indeed a grave complaint lies on this account especially against archbishops, to whose provision and care the whole provincial Church has been entrusted. Through their neglect, kings often turn into tyrants—kings whom, alas, the archbishops themselves flatter, soothe, and caress, although they ought rather to command them as fathers command sons. Thus the Master says to one of his metropolitans:

> “Reprove with all authority” (Tit. II). [Col. 1124A]

But, to say nothing now of fear, negligence, or perhaps imprudence in masters, among these masters and fathers are some who are held back from corrections of this kind by mere mildness—lest I now call it laxity. They truly display less freedom for justice than they ought, because they fear to embitter the sweetness of friendship. Thus Adam sinned with his wife, and Eli with his profane sons. In this they harm both themselves and those whom they love, sometimes amid great slaughter of peoples, because, lest they offend friendship, they do not freely expose error and do not sternly rebuke, with the authority they hold, what ought to be reproved.

And thus, while they spare one man in this way, many fall. Such men, who flatter thus, connive thus, and suspend correction, are not to be compared with loving fathers or careful shepherds, but rather—as one of the doctors says—with thieves, who scatter fodder to mislead animals they should turn away, rather than threaten the wandering with a whip in order to call them back. This was well understood by that wise man who long ago said that quarrelling enemies are often more useful than friends afraid to rebuke. For enemies, in quarrelling, often disclose our crimes which we believed hidden, and we are thereby more ashamed. Friends, however, in keeping silence, foster us more in our sins: the farther they allow us to run according to our will, without the bridle of correction, in trackless ground while believing ourselves to be on the way.

At times, in this trackless ground, a way appears right to us whose end nevertheless leads to death; at other times we knowingly and deliberately take a crooked path, yet do not suppose that it leads so near and directly to a precipice. Hence, just as according to the prophecy, “the work of righteousness is silence” (Isa. XXXII), so according to the same prophet that very silence of righteousness is sometimes a precipice:

> “Woe is me, because I kept silent” (Isa. VI). [Col. 1124C]

Here the prophet pronounces woe upon himself and fears woe, especially because he did not sternly and freely rebuke King Ahab with the authority proper to him; for which reason he also accuses himself of having acquired unclean lips.

Our new archbishop, therefore, returning to himself and recalling and considering all these things, recognizing that it belonged to his office, now asked, now entreated, now admonished the king, whom he loved as more than a man, to permit the sees long vacant to be filled. He even reproved him as a friend, rebuking him for holding them vacant for so long and not keeping silent about the evils arising thence, both temporal and spiritual—particularly because of those two episcopal chairs which, as we have said, were then already vacant.

## 16. CONCERNING THE TWO MEN CHOSEN AS BISHOPS

At last, yielding to the archbishop’s repeated urgency, the king consented to bishops being appointed. Thus bishops were elected to the two aforementioned sees, men certainly conspicuous in every holiness. To the first see mentioned, Worcester, there was elected a certain Roger, young in years but old in character and gravity: a magnate, son of the great Robert, formerly Count of Gloucester, whose virtue still more notably surpassed the nobility of his blood. [Col. 1125A]

Oh, if it were now permitted to me, and if the rule of the history I have undertaken allowed it, to extol this man as he deserves with worthy praises for his virtues!
