Surely he would illuminate this whole history of the martyr like the morning star in the heavenly firmament; or he would shine and blaze beyond the rest in these shadows of our present life like some most burning carbuncle. Whenever I recall him to mind, I portray for myself another Simon, son of Onias, the high priest:

> “In his life he supported the house, and in his days strengthened the temple”;

like a shining rainbow amid clouds; like lilies by flowing waters; like a rose-flower in spring days; like incense burning in fire; like a solid vessel of gold—a precious vessel, a sanctified vessel, honourable and truly useful in the house of the Lord.

But the purpose of my present subject protests. Though my pen would dig among the pleasant meadows of his virtues, no stream, not even a little rivulet, may now be led forth, nor may I portray the lovely and beautiful variety of the flowers of his graces: how great a lily of purity he was; what a rose of modesty; what a violet of heavenly conduct; what music of delightful companionship; and, above all, what a pillar of justice and what an unbreakable diamond of constancy for the defence of others.

Having touched on these matters only thus, since this is not the place to linger over them, this man—young in age, but mature in character and virtues—was, by the common vote of all whom it concerned, the first whom our new archbishop consecrated Bishop of Worcester. Thereafter, both in prosperity and adversity, he always obeyed him, even to losses, outlawry, and many dangers. He judged it shameful if the commander were in the camp while the soldier remained at home, as though among women’s spindles or girls’ work-baskets, enjoying the comforts of baths and ointments. But because what follows in the present history compels us, let us pass over this matter for now.

Let us come to the other, Robert by name, surnamed de Melun, a renowned master in the schools of secular and sacred letters, and far more renowned still in life than in learning. The great priest of whom we spoke just before had formerly been his pupil in the schools. This great doctor, great both in life and learning, shone like a great luminary throughout the whole world of churches, sending out from himself a multitude of learned disciples like diverse rays of his light across the world.

He was the second, and also the last, whom our new archbishop consecrated Bishop of Hereford, with the unanimous assent of the entire body of clergy and people. And so, in the consecration of these two bishops, conspicuous in every holiness—as the world knows—and apart from whom our new consecrator consecrated no others, the purpose which, as we testified above in this history, he had formed remained firm; and his desire was fulfilled by the Most High. As we have shown, he had resolved and had petitioned the Most High that, during his archiepiscopate, he would lay hands for consecration upon no one, especially against his conscience, except a worthy man. [Col. 1126A]

Shortly afterwards, the archbishop summoned most of the bishops of his province and magnificently dedicated the noble and royal monastery of Reading. There Henry, of blessed memory, formerly king of the English and grandfather of Henry II, our present illustrious king, rests gloriously in a mausoleum; Henry was himself its founder. This was done with the king’s will and presence.

In the same year, at London in the distinguished and royal monastery called Westminster, he raised from the dust of the earth the body of the glorious and truly holy King Edward, like a most bright and precious vessel of perfect continence. On account of the many remarkable merits of his royal life, he solemnly and exaltedly placed it there in the Church among the bodies of the saints, again with the king’s will and presence.

As we said before, the illustrious king and the holy pontiff were one heart and one soul in God. Kingdom and priesthood came together in the highest peace and tranquillity, through the working of the God of peace and love.

But alas—and truly, sorrow! Nothing among human things is lasting; nothing endures. According to the saying of the Wise Man, which experience itself most fully confirms:

> “All things have their time, and all things under heaven pass through their appointed periods: a time for weeping and a time for laughing; a time for love and a time for hate; a time for war and a time for peace: all things have their time” (Eccl. III). [Col. 1126C]

Great indeed were the names, and dear the bonds, of so great a king and so great a pontiff. Truly, it would be difficult to find in another kingdom of the world at once so great a king and so great a pontiff, and such concord between such men. It was a great concord, but of brief duration. For in a short time discord, the extreme opposite of concord, took possession; and this great and firm bond of concord, so necessary for strengthening the unity of kingdom and priesthood, was miserably and unhappily dissolved by none other than the enemy of all peace and love.

But why do I call it a bond? For in the dying hearts of mortals—as we experience daily in ourselves—amid so many vain thoughts, so many cares and causes, so many occupations, divided, torn, rent, and shattered within themselves, hearts are so open to the goads of double-tongued men and whisperers and to the stings of suspicions that, as the event now proves, no firm bond of friendship with another seems possible at all. There may indeed be some such connection, like a clay-built or wall-like, ruinous joining, ready at once to dissolve at the first slight flood of waters or the first brief blast of the north wind. For how shall such a bond henceforth remain among others, when the bond of friendship between so great a king and so great an archbishop has, against all the world’s expectation, been so suddenly and unexpectedly dissolved? And who henceforth will not fear that one who is ever so much another’s friend may become his enemy? Among lovers of one another, however great their affection, if they remember King Henry and Archbishop Thomas, whose future hostile disagreement will not at least for some time be feared or suspected?

Truly, even if anywhere—though this itself is rare—love is secure, yet nowhere and never is it secure at court, especially amid so many flatterers, so many envious men among double-tongued speakers, so many whisperers, and so many suspicions. Rather, among mortals and most especially at court, it is always faithless, unstable, and uncertain, apparently subjected to vanity with the rest of creation. And especially among the powerful, who are like glass vessels of affection: if something strikes them slightly, they are slightly damaged; if offended slightly, they are broken. Among the powerful affection is delicate and tender: from a small cause it is wounded and soon expires.

O miserable and pitiable condition of human affairs among mortals, among all things and above all others! Today my spirit delights in the sweetness of love; tomorrow it dwells in the bitterness of hatred. Today you are to me as my own heart; tomorrow as an ulcer or a mortal wound: truly, human life upon earth is a trial.

O how unbelievable, and truly grievous, was this fierce, swift, utterly dreadful, and harsh transformation of so great a friendship between king and archbishop into such great enmities, as what follows will soon show! As this transformation is certainly incredible, so its marvel is also exceedingly sad. O friendship, once such, now so dead! Yet how much mourning and sorrow you brought upon kingdom and priesthood; how much, while you still survived, you surrounded them with rejoicing and gladness!

For, to anticipate here—and because the occasion somewhat demands it, to set forth in advance what should more fully be said later in its place—O how many and how great were the evils that befell both kingdom and priesthood from this disagreement between king and bishop! For, to pass over other things which perhaps have already happened to the realm without our knowledge, from which and from other evils yet to come may the Almighty deign to keep the kingdom safe and unharmed: certainly, as the following account will make clear, from this discord was hastened the premature anointing as king of that noble boy whom we have often named, Henry, son of our King Henry and heir of the kingdom; and afterward there followed twice a grave and wicked rebellion between the father king and the son king. And finally, unless I am mistaken, because of the son king’s sin of rebellion against his father, there came his death, too swift and too untimely. This was indeed an evil properly belonging to the kingdom arising from this discord.

From it likewise arose many evils and perils in the priesthood. First came the miserable and pitiable desolation of the whole clergy throughout the kingdom at the hands of the enemies of the Church; the wretched oppression of that clergy, left without a defender; and the abandonment for years of vacant churches while the archbishop wandered in exile. More grievous still were the effects upon the salvation of all, since every use of the sacraments then ceased, because in vacant churches every care of pastoral office failed.

Thus that famous desert of Egypt, once blooming with Christ’s flowers through its multitude of monks in cells, enclosed like swarms of honey-making bees in their hives; indeed, all Egypt, once flourishing in religion, like a paradise of every fruit and a storehouse full of the Holy Spirit—yet is said at last, through lack of shepherds, to have returned to paganism, while wolves raged in the absence of dogs.

And to add yet another evil to those already listed from that aforesaid discord: from this hostile disagreement, detestable to all later ages, there finally proceeded the death of the archbishop himself. Although the whole world of churches celebrates it—precious in itself and, as we now see, fruitful for the whole Church—it nevertheless resulted in the disgrace and ruin of many great persons. See how great and detestable an evil in the priesthood arose from this discord, which, like some deadly and harmful plague, drew after it through kingdom and priesthood a very long and tangled train of evils.

But let us who were present and saw and heard these things—and those still living who neither heard nor saw them, and especially those who shall come after us—read here the cause of the dissension. What we shall now relate was indeed the beginning of the discord, but not yet its end.

## 17. ON THE BEGINNING OF THE DISSENSION BETWEEN THE KING AND THE ARCHBISHOP

It happened that certain workers of the devil, clerics in name only but belonging to Satan’s lot, having been accused of crimes and arrested, were kept in chains—men of the sort who frequently commit monstrous offenses and violate the peace in the kingdom. Among them was a priest notorious for homicide and accused by the relatives of the deceased. [Col. 1128C]

By privilege of his order, this man, having been arrested, was sent to the diocesan bishop of Salisbury; the king’s officials and the deceased man’s relatives, who brought the accusation, urgently pressed the bishop to administer justice. But since the priest steadfastly denied the charge, and could not be convicted of the homicide by his accusers, canonical purgation was prescribed for the accused—especially since public repute supported the accusers and they themselves plausibly charged him. But when he failed in the purgation, the bishop sent to the archbishop for legal advice and in order to proceed more safely in carrying out the penalty.

The archbishop, having been consulted, directed in reply that the man be deprived of every ecclesiastical benefice, deposed, and permanently confined in a monastery to perform perpetual penance of the strictest life. This penalty was imposed because he had failed in the purgation adjudged by sentence, such failure being equivalent to conviction.

Indeed, clerics accused of crimes and convicted, caught in the act, or publicly infamous, or failing in an imposed purgation, were punished throughout the province—without any mutilation or disfigurement of limbs—by this kind of spiritual penalty alone and without any corporal punishment, in accordance with the archbishop’s decree, strengthened by the ancient enactments of authoritative canons. Yet the penalty was made harsher or milder according to the nature of the offense, the rank and order of the offender, and the manner and cause of the wrongdoing.

Nor should it be omitted that at about the same time a certain Philip, surnamed de Brois, a canon in the episcopal see of Lincoln, had insulted the king’s justices—commonly called the justices itinerant in the land—with certain disgraceful abuses. [Col. 1129A] On this account the king appeared enraged, not merely against him, but rather against the whole clergy of the realm. For if anything shameful or monstrous is committed by some members of a profession, it is customary for blame to be transferred at once to the whole profession. Yet such a judgment is truly as hasty and unconsidered as anger or envy: as though, if a blemish were found in one small part of a body, the entire body were immediately judged spattered with the filth of birthmarks.

It is certain that the cleric had sinned seriously in those insults and reproaches. But when the complaint was brought to the archbishop, the cleric was summoned and punished beyond the measure of his offense, so that the king’s indignation might thereby more readily be calmed. Public scourging was imposed upon the cleric, and he himself was suspended, for a number of years which I do not remember, from every ecclesiastical benefice he held in the realm. Yet even thus the angry king’s wish was not fully satisfied.

This is that fourth thing which the Wise Man enumerates: until the fire of anger is utterly extinguished, it never says, “Enough.” Since this did not satisfy the king, he seemed rather to demand some corporal punishment for the guilty cleric; but he feared to say so openly, having already perceived that the archbishop’s firmness could not be bent to it. Thus the king was pressed, and the bishop was pressed as well. [Col. 1129C]

For the king, zealous for the peace of his people, just as the archbishop was zealous for the liberty of his clergy, heard, saw, and received from many reports and complaints that by such punishments of these clerics—or rather, these branded demons—their crimes were not restrained, but were daily becoming worse throughout the kingdom. He therefore solemnly summoned to London, at Westminster, the archbishop, the bishops of the province, and the rest of the clergy of the realm.

## 18. HOW THE KING ARGUES FOR THE PEACE OF HIS PEOPLE

The king, after setting out the reason for the summons, immediately demanded insistently that clerics caught in, or deemed convicted of, such monstrous offenses should be handed over to his executioners, deprived of the Church’s protection. He added that they would be readier to harm unless, after spiritual punishment, they were subjected to corporal punishment; that they cared little for loss of order, since they did not hesitate, despite the consideration of their order, to commit such enormous acts; and that they were worse in crime precisely insofar as they were more worthy than others of the privilege of their order. Therefore, when found guilty, they ought to be restrained by severer punishments.

Trusting the counsel of certain persons who displayed expertise in both laws, the king most urgently demanded that such men, removed at once from the clergy, be handed over to the court; for, he maintained, not only human law but the canonical authority of divine law itself had ordained this. Thus in the canon one often finds concerning such men: “Let him be handed over to the court.” Those who argued for the king—deliberately unlearned, as it seemed, through favor for the royal cause—claimed that such persons should not be sent into exile or to a monastery, but, as the canons ordained, should instead be handed over to the court, thereafter to be servants of the court, to serve the court permanently, or to be punished by whatever other penalty the court might adjudge. [Col. 1130A]

They said that this is what it means to be “handed over to the court”: to be left to the secular judge to be punished by him. Thus the canon aptly continues: “And let him receive what he has wickedly done.” Whatever might be said about a monastery, they maintained firmly that exile was by no means the judgment of the priest but of Caesar: the one whose land it is has authority to make a man an exile, to banish, deport, or expel him; just as the one whose church it is has authority to excommunicate, suspend, and exclude from the altar. The latter belongs to the bishop, whose church it is; the former to Caesar, whose land it is.

I insert this point concerning exile because the archbishop had already compelled a certain priest, degraded for an offense, to abjure the land; and this was among the things that had provoked the king. [Col. 1130B] They further added that under the holy law given through Moses, transgressors were corporally punished according to the nature of their offense, without any exception for rank or order: they rendered life for life, eye for eye, and in other matters always received like retaliation. Priest and people alike, according to God’s justice, were subject to punishment for their offenses; no privilege of order or dignity was then granted to protect them. Indeed, those of higher order or preeminence, if they transgressed, received harsher judgment and more severe punishment.

They said that it was now a strange novelty of law, and truly a new kind of sanctity, if crimes by which the peace of kingdoms is disturbed, the justice of kings violated, and all holiness at last profaned, could protect themselves by privileges.

## How the Archbishop Argues in Reply for the Liberty of His Clergy

But shortly afterward, the archbishop, having weighed the matter with his fellow provincial bishops and with the learned men aforesaid, answered the king thus:

“My lord king, the most holy Church, mother of all, both kings and priests, has two kings, two laws, two jurisdictions, and two modes of coercion. The two kings are Christ, the heavenly king, and the earthly king; the two laws, human and divine; the two jurisdictions, priestly and legal; the two coercions, spiritual and corporal. ‘Behold, here are two swords.’ ‘It is enough,’ says the Lord [Luke 22]. Neither is superfluous; these two suffice.

“Men of this profession, called clerics, by reason of their order and office properly have Christ alone as king. They are assigned a certain distinctive mark placed upon the head, as though thereby separated from the nations of the Gentiles and especially and peculiarly taken up for the Lord’s work. Therefore, by privilege of order and office, they are not subject to earthly kings but are set over them, since they establish kings; from them the king receives the belt of knighthood and authority over the material sword. Accordingly, the king has no jurisdiction over these men by reason, I mean, of their profession and order; rather, they are themselves judges of kings.

“For though these men of our office are weak, contemptible, and unarmed in worldly terms, nevertheless, as a great king and prophet foretold concerning them, they ‘bind the kings of the nations in fetters, and the nobles of the world in iron shackles.’ Therefore they are ruled not under secular kings but under their own king, the King of Heaven, and by their own law; and, if transgressors, they are punished by their own law, which has its own proper coercion. [Col. 1131A]

“The law of which we now speak is not that public and common law which belongs to all who live devoutly in Christ. It is rather, together with—not apart from—that law, a certain private and proper law, promulgated for this particular profession: I mean for clerics. These are enactments of the holy Fathers issued specifically for us, which reward those who act well even in the present Church and condemn those who act otherwise. And just as their proper king is heavenly, their law spiritual, and their jurisdiction exercised in spiritual matters, so likewise their coercion within God’s peculiar portion is spiritual, separate in itself and distinct from secular coercion. For this reason it involves neither mutilation of limbs nor any disfigurement of the body. It is spiritual.

“Indeed, the privilege of order goes so far as to exclude branding with a hot iron, a penalty which even secular law generally condemns among men, lest the image of God be disfigured in God’s name.

“In these our enactments provision has also been made for the majesty and clemency of kings. For it is very shameful and improper that royal clemency should see something cruel and abominable: that hands consecrated to God, which shortly before formed at the altar the image of the Crucified King, Savior of the world, should now, bound behind the back, portray a public thief; and that a head anointed with the sacred chrism should hang from a shameful gallows with a noose around its neck—a head before whose feet royal majesty lately bowed, seeking grace and pardon. [Col. 1131C]

“The archbishop further maintained that it did not become either royal magnificence or royal clemency that hands from which the king himself had just received the gift of divine grace and heavenly blessing should immediately receive from him an ignominious punishment, placed beneath the executioner’s axe or otherwise mutilated in a deformed and monstrous fashion.

“And the archbishop speaking to the king added: ‘Likewise, my lord king, I say this concerning those clerics who are in sacred orders and are assistants to the priests of the Most High at the altar. By the ministry of such assistants, the kings of the earth obtain the blessing of the heavenly King. Yet if one who belonged to us has been deposed and handed over to the court, and thereafter, for a new cause, endures these things and undergoes corporal punishment as the secular judge directs, we do not deny that this would be fair and fitting; nor does the future coercion or punishment of such a man concern us at all. For he has been handed over to the royal court and subjected to secular jurisdiction, to serve the court permanently.

“‘This is what the canon means by “to be handed over to the court,” as this single expression is clearly understood from the histories. But after he has thus been handed over, we have nothing to do with him, now a servant of that court. Therefore, if any punishment is thereafter imposed, it will no longer be a punishment of one of ours, as of a member of the clergy, but a punishment of one of yours, as a member of the people. [Col. 1132A]

“‘As for your further assertion that the power to make our men exiles belongs not to us but to you, since the land is yours and not ours, and that this penalty would be civil rather than ecclesiastical, we answer briefly that we act in the place of Him who is above all kings, to whom belong the earth and its fullness. Moreover, as the sacred canons enact, by the authority of that King whose land it is and whose embassy we exercise upon earth, we sometimes sentence our convicted men to exile and proscription of their goods, according to their manner of sinning and the nature of their offense. The penalties of that King, whose power is infinite, are not limited.

“‘Except that we are not permitted even to take part in a judgment of blood. That belongs to you, who bear the other sword—the sword of iron, not the sword of the word, which is ours—as that iron sword is yours. “Behold, here are these two swords” [Luke 22], under which every coercive power is exercised: not, God forbid, as mutually rebellious, but helping one another, so that what one cannot accomplish, the other, as its helper, may perform and supply. Hence He says, “It is enough” [ibid.].

“‘And not only our own men, but also your secular subjects, whether noble or lowly, who are subject to your own royal jurisdiction—when, prevented by God’s grace, they repent of offenses committed in this world—we compel by authority of the supreme King to leave the land of their birth, to abandon those places in which they have easier cause and opportunity for sinning, and to go abroad. [Col. 1132C] Very often we send them, for a temporary or perpetual pilgrimage, to Jerusalem, to the Temple or the Hospital, or to other religious and distant places of stricter life. Thus, by the supreme King’s command, we in a manner banish or deport them, always according to the nature of their offenses and for the salvation of those repenting of their crimes.

“‘But if, as you say, our men are more inclined and ready to commit crimes because spiritual punishment is not followed by corporal punishment, perhaps this is so in some cases. Yet even in such persons, so far as is lawful and possible for us, we restrain not the mind—which belongs to God alone—but the hand from crimes, assigning the condemned man, when we see it expedient, to a monastery or another strict place under the closest custody; and we proceed no further.

“‘For our penalties, and likewise yours, are limited: to proceed beyond their limits is transgression. And if we fall short, our own king will supply what is imperfect in our punishments of His people—He who says, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” [Heb. 10]. [Col. 1132D]

“‘As for the priests and Levites of the Old Testament, who, when they transgressed the commandments of the law, were corporally punished: for the present we say nothing about them. Under the new law there is a new discipline. And because here there is a new law, a new king, and a new judgment is reformed, there are new penalties, and likewise new sacraments, sacrifices, works, and burdens. For the old things have passed away; and behold, all things have become new: a new king, a new law, a new flock, new sacraments, new sacrifices, new works, new burdens; and thus new coercions and new penalties.’ [Col. 1133A]

Thus far we have heard the king and the archbishop, who argued in this manner: the one for the peace of his people, the other for the liberty of his clergy—or rather, they were already pulling a contentious rope. At that time the archbishop’s brother bishops stood unanimously and firmly with him, so that they appeared like an ordered battle-line of camps which could not be penetrated. “This is the disciple who bears testimony concerning these things, and heard and wrote them” [John 21]. He wrote them, I say, and although not the same words in every respect, still the force and substance of the arguments are those here written.

O king and bishop, each of whom God’s zeal seized! One is zealous for the peace of his people; the other for the liberty of his clergy. O what a bishop among the clergy, to be embraced with what devotion by the clergy: for the liberty of the clergy he lost the favor of so great a king and set aside glory! For now the dispute is great; now the dissension is evident. With what devotion, then, should he be honored by the clergy, who, with joy set before him, endured the cross for the clergy, despising shame, choosing rather to be afflicted for God’s clergy than to possess the delights of royal majesty!

Yet this was not, on behalf of the clergy, anything beyond the beginning and first cause of the disagreement. What follows will disclose greater matters and fuller material for dissension. And O what a king among the people; how greatly ought the people to rejoice in him, and how devoutly and faithfully serve him with trembling, who immediately turned away for his people’s peace from a bishop so beloved and so faithful to him—a bishop for whom, as we have shown above, he himself had once so earnestly preferred the episcopal office! [Col. 1133C]

O zeal of king and zeal of bishop! O zeal and zeal—how harsh, how tearful, that the spirit of knowledge did not unite these men in their zeal; but the spirit of dizziness and error, which always divides, mingled itself between them! It is more certain than certain that each had zeal for God, the one for the people and the other for the clergy. But which of them had zeal with knowledge is for the Lord of knowledge, not for man, who is quickly deceived, to determine in the end when He reveals judgment.

Nevertheless, at the conclusion of his response written above, the archbishop most devoutly begged royal clemency not, under Christ the new King and under Christ’s new law, to introduce through the kingdom a new coercion against the ordinances of the holy Fathers within the Lord’s new and peculiar portion. [Col. 1133D]

He pleaded this humbly both for himself and for the stability of the kingdom, pleading it repeatedly; he frequently added that he neither ought nor could endure it. But the king was unmoved; indeed, he appeared all the more stirred because he saw the archbishop and his fellow bishops, as he judged, unanimous and steadfast against him. He immediately asked whether they would observe his royal customs.

The archbishop, after first taking counsel with his brethren, answered that he and his brethren would observe them, saving their order (*salvo ordine*). The bishops, questioned one by one by the king, gave the same answer in turn, each separately—except that in this music only one voice was discordant. One bishop, hearing that the king was more angered by this unanimous answer, changed the wording without consulting the archbishop and his fellow bishops; and indeed, I think, with a good intention, namely to calm the king’s mind. He said that they would observe the royal customs “in good faith” (*bona fide*). This was Hilary, bishop of Chichester, of good memory.

Yet the king was not softened, but spurned him with certain insulting reproaches. Turning to the archbishop and his fellow bishops, when he had heard them all speak in one and the same voice, he said that a battle-line had been drawn up against him, and that the phrase contained a trick and poison—namely, “saving their order.” Therefore he asked and repeatedly demanded that they promise absolutely and without qualification to observe his royal customs. [Col. 1134B]

The archbishop answered that they had sworn him fealty—namely life, limb, and earthly honor—saving their order; that royal customs were included in earthly honor; and that they would by no means bind themselves to their observance in another form than that in which they had previously sworn. He added that throughout the whole world of churches this form of oath had been established by the holy Fathers not only for bishops but also for lesser clerics, and was now common and customary. It was therefore unsafe to depart from it, especially since, as he argued, the privilege of the clergy is not silent in that qualification.

Thus he further said that men of this profession, when they swear fealty to temporal powers, by not omitting their order thereby declare themselves, by privilege of order, superior to those very persons to whom they bind themselves by oath—though they remain answerable to them for temporal matters or other just causes, for which they are obliged to render fealty under oath. Such was the archbishop’s response.

But the day was already far spent, indeed near the twilight between day and night. The king, vexed throughout the day, suddenly left the court in great anger and indignation, without taking leave of the bishops. The bishops too, vexed throughout the day, departed and withdrew to their lodgings. As they left, the bishop mentioned above was sharply rebuked by the archbishop because, without consulting either him or his fellow bishops, he had presumed to alter the common wording of them all.

## 19. ON THE FORTRESSES WHICH THE KING DEMANDS BACK FROM THE ARCHBISHOP, AND ON THE BISHOPS’ DESERTION OF HIM

[Col. 1134D]

On the next day, the king demanded back and received the fortresses and honors which the archbishop had held in custody from the king since the time of his chancellorship. Without greeting the bishops or being greeted by them—indeed, without their knowledge—he left London secretly and before dawn. This was a clear sign of great anger and indignation.

Some of the bishops, seeing this and terrified, immediately followed the king, obeying in everything the king’s will—as they had previously stood with their archbishop, as we said above, but now apart from his consent and knowledge. Whether this was right, let all those who are dead now have God, their living judge; let Him see and judge. For it accords neither with my measure nor with my lowliness to say anything unfavorable about such great men of our office. I know one thing: there is grave danger in false brethren. It began from the beginning and will not cease until the end of the age.

Other dangers may indeed come to rest; this one never does. Amid the temptations and struggles of this present life it continually exercises those who are called saints according to God’s purpose. For what the furnace is to gold, the flail to grain, and the file to iron, that is a false brother to a just man: by him he is, as it were, filed away until he reaches the sharp edge of truth. As one of the doctors says: “There can be no Abel whom the malice of Cain does not exercise.”

## How the Bishops Deserted the Archbishop

[Col. 1135B] Accordingly, after the rest had been winnowed and shaken away like chaff from grain, we alone remained; we sat alone, with only a few bishops now with us, while the others withdrew from us day by day. Even these few who were with us did so secretly, out of fear.

For many days we sat thus alone, nevertheless hoping for and daily awaiting the king’s favor, until the blaze of royal indignation should cool as that indignation subsided, and the king, once his anger had been calmed, should consider the cause of his indignation with wisdom and clemency and return to himself. Meanwhile, many great men, seeing this and grieving for it, traveled repeatedly between us and the king and urged the archbishop in many ways toward the king’s favor. At one time they set before him their former intimacy; at another, the honors lavishly bestowed or the benefits conferred; on one side, how great a good peace was, and on the other, how great an evil dissension. [Col. 1135C]

They further argued how foolish it would be, on account of contention over one little word, to incur the reproach of ingratitude for so many benefits; to lose the favor of one who had loved him so much and was so beloved; and to nourish the dissension that was the root of so many and such great evils—all because of contention over one word that offended the king. For the entire question then was that the archbishop, in the undertaking to observe royal customs which the king demanded from him, should either suppress or alter the phrase which, as said above, had offended the king: “saving their order” (*salvo ordine*).

More than all others, the bishop mentioned above—who, without consulting the archbishop and fellow bishops, had altered this phrase on his own authority—used every means he knew, and urged the archbishop to change it. He was certainly a man of great spirit and powerful speech. Thus these men urged, and those men urged; but above all pressed upon the archbishop the love which he bore toward the king. For true love, as the Master teaches, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

At length the archbishop was persuaded, but above all by the pressure of love. At the noble royal castle called Oxford he approached the king and promised to alter the phrase that gave the king offense. The king, now somewhat calmed, showed the archbishop a more serene countenance, though not yet his usual one.

The king said, however, that he wished the undertaking to observe royal customs to be given in the following form: before the bishops and magnates of the realm, publicly and in their hearing. [Col. 1136A] There also came certain long-standing enemies of the archbishop, clever in doing evil. They secretly advised the king that, as soon as the undertaking concerning the royal customs had been made, he should require them to be specified.

The king, persuaded by them, added that he wished the royal customs to be recited by the magnates and elders of the realm who knew them, lest thereafter, as he said, there should arise a schism between kingdom and priesthood, either by clergy usurping what belonged to the king or by the king usurping what belonged to the clergy. The bishops and magnates then present attested that this was good. The proposal seemed good on its surface, but was in truth utterly bad, and the tinder of a perpetual schism between king and archbishop. Those wise men in doing evil knew this thoroughly, offering gall for honey and poison for counsel.

## On Those Wise in Doing Evil

Such are ordinarily the counsels of those who, according to the prophet, are wise in order to do evil. For, according to the same prophet, Babylon is a golden cup: so that the person who sees the gold may not fear the poison, which is not ordinarily given except smeared with honey. These men, therefore, wise to do evil, bore honey in their mouths; but in truth, like the brothers of scorpions, they bore gall in their hearts and a sting in their tail, so as to shoot at the innocent in secret. The outcome will make this clearer at the end of events.

And indeed, in offering gall for honey, they offered the bitterness of dissension for the sweetness of peace. For all kingdoms, as everyone knows, have good customs which the Church approves, and other bad customs which the Church tolerates. Although, if perhaps compelled to make these explicit, she does not yield her authority and assent to them, she nevertheless tolerates them. For, as the legal expert says, “Things made explicit are harmful.” And as the Wise Man says, “He who presses the breast hard draws forth blood” [Prov. 30]. [Col. 1136C]

These viperish counselors sought to ensure that the Church would indiscriminately grant authority to good customs and to others once they had been specified; otherwise, there would be a perpetual schism between kingdom and priesthood.

O rashness of envy, ever striking at what is highest! O cunning of Satan, ever persecuting what is holy! Truly envy, Satan’s advocate, is the foster-child of schism, the mother of contention, and the inextinguishable fuel of detraction: sorrowful at prosperity, rejoicing in adversity; disturbed by peace, calmed by disturbance; made pleasant by sadness, lifted by depression, delighted by pain, and always fed by another’s misfortune. This envy, now joined with Satan’s cunning, has begun under the shadowed appearance of peace to sow the worst tares of perpetual schism between kingdom and priesthood.

## 20. ON THE SUMMONING OF THE ARCHBISHOP AT CLARENDON
The king, however, seeming zealous for peace between kingdom and priesthood, but insufficiently foreseeing the consequence both for himself and for his archbishop, and detecting no disguise of malice in the matter, immediately summoned the whole realm, its bishops and magnates, to a certain noble and splendid royal manor which takes its name from the place, Clarendon. Within a few days all assembled [Col. 1137A]. There, in the sight of all—and first before all others—the archbishop bound himself in the aforesaid form: namely, that he would observe the royal customs in good faith, omitting the phrase “saving the order”; and, adding as it were a sworn guarantee, he affirmed upon his word of truth that he would do so. All the bishops likewise bound themselves individually in the same form.

Although, by the persuasions and counsels of many great persons, he had scarcely been induced to enter into this obligation—which he had previously promised at the aforementioned castle, Oxford—the principal reason which induced him was brotherly and compassionate love. For he was moved with fraternal compassion for certain of his fellow bishops, fearing more for them than for himself: namely, for the noble men of glorious memory, Henry, then bishop of Winchester, [Col. 1137B] and Jocelin, then bishop of Salisbury. Unless this were done, they seemed threatened either by some snare, or by something worse, both because of old hostility and because, in the present affair concerning the Church, they were held suspect.

Such, then, was the general obligation of the archbishop and bishops to observe the royal customs—or, as they styled them, ancestral customs. Immediately after this obligation had been made in that form, certain magnates of the realm, who ought to have known them, set forth a recognition of the royal customs; and they were recited publicly and expressly. But when many had already been stated and, as it seemed, many more still remained to be stated, the archbishop intervened. He said that he was neither among the older men of the realm, so as to know the ancient customs of kings, [Col. 1137C] nor had he long been archbishop; therefore he did not know these matters. Moreover, since the day was already declining, so great a business should be deferred until the morrow.

The proposal pleased them; they withdrew to their lodgings and returned the next day for the same purpose. The royal customs omitted on the previous day were recognized and set forth, and were reduced to writing in the form of a charter, being designated “royal customs.” Yet many of them, as many maintained, were by no means royal customs, but rather—as we have already begun to say—the poison vomited forth by rivalry and envy, conceived through hatred of the archbishop in order to enslave the Church. The king himself did not know that wicked men intended by this cunning to sow between him and his archbishop the tares of dissension [Col. 1137D]. For the king, still young, knew the ancient customs of the realm only from others’ reports; nor did his newly appointed archbishop know them otherwise.

### On the Customs Demanded

That we may insert some of those customs—or liberties or dignities—which they called royal and which were then proposed to us, the first was this, in the words of the fatal charter of decree itself:

> “I. Concerning the advowson and presentation of churches: if a dispute arises between laymen, or between laymen and clerics, or between clerics, it shall be heard and determined in the court of the lord king.”

At once the archbishop replied that this plainly drew clerics before secular courts and converted ecclesiastical jurisdiction into secular jurisdiction. For the advowson of churches is joined to and dependent upon spiritual right, by which the person commonly called the representative of the Church obtains spiritual care and the governance of souls. Therefore, whoever has jurisdiction over the principal right also has jurisdiction over its accessory, since the one depends on the other and they are mutually connected and joined. Otherwise, if that which by the pernicious invention of certain persons is called the right of advowson is merely a secular and hereditary right, let it be sold, bought, and even brought, like other secular rights, to trial by single combat. Thus the archbishop argued in two ways against this fatal invention: first, because clerics were being drawn before a judge who was not theirs; second, because this controversy belonged not to the jurisdiction of a secular judge, but rather of an ecclesiastical judge [Col. 1138A–B].

To this fatal decree another, still more profane—though third, not immediately following, in the charter—was attached. Its words and enactment were as follows:

> “Clerics charged or accused concerning any matter, when summoned by the king’s justice, shall come into his court to answer there concerning that which the king’s court judges should be answered there, and in the ecclesiastical court concerning that which it judges should be answered there; so that the king’s justice shall send into the court of holy Church to see by what procedure the matter is there handled. And if a cleric is convicted or confesses, the Church ought not thereafter to protect him.”

When this so-called custom had been reduced to writing, the archbishop immediately perceived [Col. 1138C], and understood more certainly, that the poison of serpentine hostility was directed against him through this provision as well as the preceding one. He at once declared that the very words of the entire fatal charter were as full of malice as they were of tasteless elegance, and plainly subverted clerical liberty. He added:

> “Behold: according to this fatal canon, clerics are drawn before secular judgment in both criminal and civil cases. Christ is judged anew before Pilate the governor. And, to heap up still further penal servitude, contrary to the Lord’s command in the prophet, clerics will be judged twice for the same matter and their affliction will rise twofold. If this is so, the condition of clerics will henceforth surpass in wretchedness that of all criminals.”

The following decree of the fatal charter was:

> [Col. 1138D] “Archbishops, bishops, and persons of the realm may not leave the realm without the permission of the lord king. And if they leave, then, if it pleases the king, they shall give assurance that neither in going nor in staying abroad will they seek evil or harm to the king or kingdom.”

The archbishop objected that this proclamation would put an end to pilgrimages and vows concerning holy places, and would even nullify obedience. Above all, it would make the glorious realm a prison for persons of the realm, and thus their condition worse than that of private persons. What if one of those persons has vowed to go abroad, or is drawn overseas by some other just and honourable cause? What if, as sometimes happens, a quarrel has arisen between apostolic men and kings of England: the former summons him to a council or to attend to other necessities of the Church, while the latter forbids him? Must he not obey the former rather than the latter—the vicar of Christ rather than an earthly king? Certainly he must: one must obey God rather than man.

But, if ecclesiastical persons were bound to kings in this way, both a vow and obedience would, according to the form of this obligation, depend upon the kings’ will. Therefore the archbishop added in reply:

> “It is fitting and proper that any person of the realm who intends to leave the kingdom for a reason should first depart with the king’s permission; but to bind oneself by a sworn guarantee not to leave without permission is irreligious and improper.”

The seventh decree of the charter then followed [Col. 1139B]:

> “No one who holds of the king in chief, nor any of his household servants, shall be excommunicated; nor shall the lands of any of them be placed under interdict, unless the king, if he is in the land, has first been summoned, or his justice, if he is outside the realm, in order that he may do right concerning him. Thus what belongs to the royal court shall be determined there, and that which pertains to the ecclesiastical court shall be sent to that court, to be heard there.”

By this decree of the charter, the archbishop maintained, the Church was plainly deprived of its authority; and priests, chosen leaders and princes as it were of the army of the Lord of Hosts, were deprived of the belt of their service. They had received from the supreme Prince of all, who takes away the spirit of princes, the sword and the free power of binding and loosing even kings and princes. Thus the king and prophet himself says: “To bind their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron shackles” (Psalm 149). The leaders of the Christian warfare—priests, whose office it is to distinguish holy from profane, unclean from clean, and by whose judgment a leper is separated—would, I say, be deprived of their authority [Col. 1139C].

The eighth decree of the charter immediately followed:

> “Concerning appeals: if they arise, they ought to proceed from the archdeacon [Col. 1139D] to the bishop, and from him to the archbishop. If the archbishop fails to render justice, recourse must finally be had to the king, so that by his command the controversy may be determined in the archbishop’s court; and no appeal may proceed further without the king’s assent.”

At first sight the archbishop opposed this with head held high, declaring that, by consenting to such a decree, archbishops would manifestly be guilty of perjury, since, on receiving the pallium, they expressly swore among other things concerning appeals to be referred to the Roman pontiff. He added that here the refuge of all the oppressed was grievously and disastrously removed, since they were forbidden freely to have recourse to the Roman Church as the mother of all.

[Col. 1140A] Among many other provisions, the twelfth decree of the charter was then introduced:

> “When an archbishopric, bishopric, abbey, or priory of the king’s domain falls vacant, it shall be in his hand, and he shall receive all its rents and revenues as demesne revenues.”

To this the archbishop replied briefly that the possessions of the poor should by no means be applied to the treasury. This practice, perhaps, was contrary to royal clemency and magnificence, since even as another’s riches they could by no means be the redemption of a prince’s soul. Even if it had sometimes been done so in the days of those who went before us, it ought not therefore to be handed down as an hereditary sacrilege. The Church must always cry out, always resist, and resist as far as it can; and, if it endures what cannot be corrected, it must nevertheless never consent [Col. 1140B].

The same irregular canon continues:

> “And when it comes to providing for a church, the lord king ought to summon the more important persons of the Church, and the election shall take place in the king’s chapel.”

The archbishop, a vigorous defender of canonical election, having first consulted his learned advisers, immediately answered here as in the other matters. He said that this was a new canon, introducing from itself a new form of election wholly different from and opposed to the ancient and established institutions of apostolic decrees. Without the authority of an apostolic man—or rather of the whole universal Church—he could not grant authority or assent to a novelty so singular and a singularity so new, especially in the establishment of such important ecclesiastical persons in the island Church entrusted to him, even if this arrangement were greatly advantageous to the Church [Col. 1140C].

For this would be, as it were, to create a particular schism in the Church according to one’s own opinion and spirit, thus departing from the general and long-established decrees of the holy Fathers. He added that this new form of election in England, like a spark in the heart of the sea, might easily produce from itself a great conflagration throughout the world of Churches. For if the king of England had devised this form of election in his kingdom according to his own wish and pleasure, why should not other kings, on hearing of it, do the same in their own kingdoms?

He further added [Col. 1140D] that this new canon gravely impaired the liberty and honour of canonical election. Unless the most urgent necessity intervened, a bishop should be chosen in the place where he was to be consecrated, not in the prince’s presence, although with the prince’s principal concurrence and assent. For who would not fear the presence of a prince? Who would not be terrified? Who would name freely anyone except the person whom the prince desired and demanded? The holy Fathers, foreseeing this piously and wisely, decreed that the election of bishops should neither be conducted nor confirmed in a court, hall, chamber, chapel, oratory, or other place belonging to princes.

He further maintained that it was wholly unfitting for ecclesiastical princes—persons so eminent and distinguished, entrusted with the governance of so many peoples, the care of so many souls, and the oversight of so many Churches—to be elected or confirmed in such places, especially places assigned to the service of whatever laymen or even kings [Col. 1141A]. To objections, he immediately replied that, even if this had been done in the kingdom of England since the time of certain earlier kings, it had been tyrannically usurped rather than legitimately established.

Finally he added remarks on the various forms of elections, concerning which ecclesiastical histories throughout both Testaments instruct us. From them it is clear that, in the primitive Church, Catholic secular rulers sometimes took part in ecclesiastical elections and affairs. Yet according to the progress of the faith and changing circumstances concerning the Church, various dispensations of the holy Fathers concerning the forms of election are found. One arrangement is found in the beginnings of the Church’s birth; another now, when, according to the prophet’s oracle, she has been set “in the pride of the ages.” Therefore it was in no way safe to depart without the Church’s authority from that form of election which the universal Church had now adopted, approved, and observed [Col. 1141B].

And this was the answer made to the archbishop:

From these disastrous enactments which we have set forth, fabricated by enemies of the Church out of hatred for the archbishop and for the oppression of ecclesiastical liberty, anyone may immediately see how manifest and just was the cause of our archbishop’s first exile and at last [Col. 1141C] of his martyrdom. I have neither heard nor read of any martyr whose cause was more just or plain; let anyone who can teach otherwise do so. Yet many other provisions, similar in form and enactment, still remained inserted in that fatal charter of decree.

But it is not my task, not within my capacity, not within my littleness, to extend myself to royal or ecclesiastical customs, dignities, or liberties. Those dignities are nothing to my littleness; nor is it within my competence or learning to approve or condemn them. That consideration belongs rather to kings and bishops. I testify here only to what I have heard and seen.

One thing I know: these provisions which we have already stated, and some others like them—numbering, unless I am mistaken, about sixteen distinct articles—inserted in the aforesaid charter, already supplied ample material for dissension between king and archbishop [Col. 1141D]. By the Lord’s favour, we shall append at the end of this historical volume the entire charter of decree, copied from the original, so that every reader of this martyr’s history may see clearly, even beyond what has already been set out, how bright, plain, and manifest was the cause of the archbishop’s first exile and afterwards his martyrdom.

The Lord, judge of all, wonderfully indeed but most justly ordained that those provisions which had been introduced through hatred of him, and to which he seemed in some manner to have consented while accusing himself, should later be abolished through that very man in his own blood—thus “blotting out the bond of the decree which was against us, which was contrary to us,” and openly triumphing over principalities and powers in himself [Col. 1142A]. For, to pass over other matters, the king himself, recognizing this and returning at the end with all heart and body to his archbishop, renounced the present charter of decree under discussion, rejected it, and cast aside all its force and authority. This is plainly taught by the book which I entitled *Melorum* and appended to this history.

If you object that many of those unjust statutes are still observed throughout the realm, I reply briefly and with certainty that the king, as we have said, renounced them, and that Christ’s bride, the Church, triumphed victoriously in the blood of Christ’s martyr. Whether the king, repentant and renouncing them, persevered: God knows; God grant it; let the king himself see to it. If, as you object, certain customs of that fatal charter retain force, and, like harmful offshoots from a noxious stock, some bastard shoots grow wickedly after the harmful branches have been cut off, it must still be hoped that, at the urging of the successors of the martyred archbishop, through royal clemency, as they frequently and devoutly remember the martyr and the cause of his martyrdom, what remains incomplete will be supplied, and the yoke of ecclesiastical servitude will wholly rot away from before the face of the Church [Col. 1142B].

Or if, by the disposition of the Most High, the archbishops who succeed this martyr do not have in these days of their flesh such material for the exercise and proving of their virtue—but we are anticipating; this is not yet the place for the matters now touched upon—let us return to the question presently at issue: the full cause and material of dissension now set forth, and, unless I am mistaken, from these points alone, apart from other things which we here pass over, most just in the judgment of the whole Church. The apostolic man, primate of the whole Church, confirmed and justified it by his authority which presides over all, as what follows will show.

Let us return, I say, to the full cause of dissension. The material of dissension was now evident and extensive: soon, the cause of exile; later, of martyrdom.

O inveterate wickedness of rivals! O profane novelty of laws, all too effective for evil! You severed so irreparably a king and a bishop so great, united by a bond of charity so necessary and so worthy of praise [Col. 1142D]. Prophetic and eternal woe be upon those who framed these new laws! They are indeed inventions of diabolical rivalry. O rivalry, which has its dwelling in the hut of men of vile and contemptible life, yet seeks the thrones of kings and the chairs of teachers! Truly it has been said, and is only too true:

> Envy seeks the heights; the winds buffet the loftiest places.

And the saying of the Wise Man agrees with it: “The lizard supports itself with its hands and dwells in the houses of kings” (Proverbs 30). O how cruel, hard, and inhuman is this rivalry, dissolving bonds of love so sweet, so dear, and so illustrious to the world—bonds of such great affection and such great sweetness! It stands directly opposed to charity and, as we remember having said above, and as grief now compels us to repeat, it is always disturbed by peace, estranged by concord, wasted by safety, tormented by happiness, sorrowful at success, cheerful at pain, weeping with those who rejoice and rejoicing with those who weep [Col. 1143A].

But, setting aside these enemies of peace, these workers of Satan, let us return and carry out what we proposed.

When, as we have said, the customs had been set forth in writing and reduced to and published in the form of a charter, the king demanded that the archbishop and his fellow bishops append their seals for greater security and confirmation. The archbishop, although greatly moved and distressed, nevertheless concealed his feelings, not wishing then to provoke the king. Prudently, he did not refuse outright, but said that the matter must still be deferred. Although he added that they were ready to do it, the greatness of the business nevertheless called for at least a brief delay, since, according to the Wise Man, nothing serious should be done without counsel; and after some deliberation, he and the other bishops ought to be consulted more suitably on the matter [Col. 1143B].

He nevertheless received the document containing the said customs, deliberately and prudently, so that he might have his cause with him in writing. The archbishop of York received another copy of the document; the king himself retained the third, to be laid up in the royal archives. Thus we left the court and set out for the city of Winchester.

### 21. On the Archbishop’s Sorrow and Lament

But the archbishop seemed beyond measure troubled and grieved on the way [Col. 1143C]. Contrary to his custom, he spoke to none of his followers while travelling, nor did anyone speak to him. He summoned no one; no one approached him. He rode alone and apart along the road, meditating alone on the road.

We, his travelling companions, soon noticed this, speaking together and grieving with him, and beginning to suspect somewhat what it meant. At length the disciple who wrote these things ventured to approach him:

> “Lord,” he said, “why, contrary to your custom, has your countenance so fallen? You show neither the face which you showed yesterday and the day before, nor, as is customary on the road, do you have counsel or conversation with these men.”

The archbishop replied:

> “It is no wonder. For I now seem to see that, because my sins require it, the English Church must be enslaved through me—a Church which my predecessors governed so wisely amid so many and such great dangers, known to the world; for which they fought so bravely among its enemies and triumphed so powerfully. She who was before me a mistress now seems destined to be enslaved through wretched me. Would that I had been consumed so that no eye might see me! The Church is indeed deservedly to suffer this through me and in my time, since I was taken to this office not, like my predecessors, from the Church but from the court. I was taken not from a cloister, from any place of religion, or from the school of the Saviour, but rather from Caesar’s retinue: proud and vain, changed from a shepherd of birds into a shepherd of sheep; once a patron of actors and a follower of dogs, now pastor of so many souls. Some men, I know not who, set me as a keeper in vineyards, though I did not keep my own but neglected it. Certainly my former life was far from the salvation of the Church; and now these are my works. Therefore I clearly see that I am now deserted by God and worthy of being cast out from the holy see in which I have been placed.”

As grief thus pressed him, “streams of waters ran down from his eyes,” so that amid uninterrupted tears and frequent bursts of sobbing he was compelled rather to break off his speech than to finish it.

[lacuna: “This from the *Quadrilogus*, a gap of one folio.”]

[Col. 1144A] “…at the last, on the last day, he will not fear an evil report.” The compassionate disciple then, restraining his tears and sobs as best he could, addressed his master:

> “Lord, it is written that ‘all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to his purpose.’ Indeed, even if they stray and turn aside from the unbent and winding road of this life, and run in a trackless place rather than on the road, that very trackless place becomes for them, as it were, a short cut to the way of salvation and to the true homeland, precisely because they have strayed; for their leader and ruler, God, wonderfully directs them. Thus God, wonderful in his saints, leads them in a wonderful way—so wonderful that the trackless place itself becomes for them a way to salvation, a way to their homeland [Col. 1144B].

> “Therefore take courage, my lord. If you have fallen, you will rise stronger, the Lord putting forth his hand; if you have fallen through another’s prompting, you will rise more cautious; but if by your own impulse, you will rise more humble. Thus Peter, chief of the apostles and model for pastors, who presumed that he would die before he denied his master, first denied him at the voice of a maidservant, and afterwards, when brought before kings and governors, never again yielded: made wiser and humbler from presumption, more faithful from apostasy, more steadfast from denial.

> “Thus the almighty Spirit of wisdom knows how to bring good out of evils: as though a violet from dryness, a thorn from a rose, honey from a rock, and oil from the hardest stone. Henceforth, then, you must labour with the utmost effort so that what happened in the chief of the apostles and exemplar of pastors may likewise happen in you. If you have stumbled in word like Peter, do not stumble in deed like Peter. To observe good royal customs is good and just. But if, as you say, other customs are new inventions of your rivals, devised from hatred of you to the injury of the Church, it is well known what must be done concerning them. Surely, as is credible, the king himself would not demand them if he recognized that they were new and introduced by rivals [Col. 1144C–D]. For profane novelties of laws must be avoided, and against their inventors the prophet—indeed the Lord himself through his prophet—pronounces woe: ‘Woe to those who make new laws’ (Isaiah 10). The clemency of Christian kings does not customarily introduce such new and evil laws for Christ’s honour, or enforce them when introduced; rather, it abolishes them. Thus the Church’s liberty has grown; thus the clergy’s honour.

> “But let me add something concerning another matter which you have so tearfully lamented: I mean your former life. Know one thing with certainty: your former life does not accord with the office which you now hold, as you yourself acknowledge. Those delights and riches of Augustus do not belong with this pastoral burden. Therefore, unless I am mistaken, God will show you how great things you must suffer for him, since you were taken not from the Church but from the court, and yet presumed to ascend to this see and rank [Col. 1145A].

> “Therefore, what alone remains is this: if, as you say, you have fallen shamefully, rise strongly and fittingly. Shake yourself, if you are a son of those who shake themselves—indeed, because you are. Act manfully and let your heart be strengthened, lest sorrow swallow you up; rather, let righteousness raise you. Act manfully, I say, and be strong; henceforth be cautious, brave, and steadfast. Know certainly that the Lord will be with you as a mighty helper, as he is recorded to have been with David, king and prophet, though formerly an adulterer and betrayer; with him whom we have mentioned, the chief of the apostles, formerly an apostate; with that holy and apostolic sinner; and finally with that outstanding teacher of the Gentiles, formerly the foremost persecutor of the Church. You too, as it then seemed and was so said, were once Saul. If now you wish to be Paul, when the scales have been wiped from your eyes, your Jesus will show you openly in deed how great things you must suffer for his name.”

At these words, some consolation seemed to be poured into the sorrow described above. For he looked more to the love and faith of the exhorter than to the force of his words. Then suddenly it was reported that the bishop at whose persuasion and prompting, as we said above, the phrase “saving the order” had been suppressed, was following us. The archbishop turned to the disciple who had just been speaking with him and said: “Let him follow, and let Satan go behind me.”

### How the Archbishop Was Absolved by the Apostolic Man

[Col. 1145C]

A few days later, because he carried a conscience seared by what had happened, the archbishop sent with great haste to the Roman pontiff, whose office it is “to heal the broken in heart and bind up their wounds.” So far as one absent could do by writings, he disclosed his wound and sought medicine. During this time—about forty days—he kept himself from the altar, until, when the messenger returned from the pontiff, he obtained through an apostolic letter the grace of absolution concerning the matters for which he accused himself. The messenger returned so quickly because the supreme pontiff was then staying at the noble and royal city of Sens in Gaul on account of the schism.

Besides the benefit of absolution, he received much consolation through apostolic letters [Col. 1145D], in which the pope with fatherly affection exhorted him both to bear the pastoral burden bravely and cheerfully, and zealously to undertake pastoral works. The archbishop received this apostolic command as though it were a sacrifice sent to him from heaven, with every joy, being a man of most fervent spirit. His spirit was now fully refreshed, as it were by two breasts of a mother: on one side, the grace of apostolic absolution; on the other, the exhorting apostolic letter.

But because, as we have said, the lord pope was near, and because the most salutary practice of confession is neither customarily nor properly performed through writings, and because he also saw that, for the reasons mentioned above, he would scarcely bear fruit among his own people, he resolved to visit the supreme pontiff in person. Unknown even to his own men, except two or three whom he took with him, he attempted to cross secretly by night [Col. 1146A]. For if he had wished to depart openly, an exit would not have been available.

Among the aforementioned customs was this also: that no bishop or person of the realm should leave the land without permission of the king or his justices. Therefore the archbishop attempted to depart secretly. Twice he embarked upon the sea, but each time he embarked he was driven back, as though God through his own elements opposed him in this undertaking. For as all things have their time, so there is a time to confront and a time to flee; but the time for this flight had not yet come.

Though undertaken secretly, it was quickly spread throughout the land that the archbishop had attempted to cross the sea. The people were astonished, the magnates wondered, the bishops were troubled, and the king was deeply disturbed—chiefly, it was believed, because the archbishop had presumed so quickly and suddenly to act against his own statutes [Col. 1146B].

The archbishop, understanding that God did not approve what he had attempted, and hearing and knowing with certainty that the king had been provoked by it, was grieved; for he loved the king so much that he could not be cheerful and happy while the king was angry. He hurried to the king at the royal manor called Woodstock. The king received the archbishop who came to him with honour, though not with the honour he had formerly shown, and pretended not to have heard the news. Yet neither the archbishop nor those with him thought that he truly concealed it. He did conceal it, that is, except that, as if joking, he reproached the archbishop for wishing to leave his land, as though the land could not contain both of them together.

But the archbishop, who had known the king over a long period and in exceptional familiarity, now perceived that the king’s heart had drawn away from him; this was also already proclaimed in court. Therefore, after quickly taking leave of the king, and understanding clearly that the one to whom sea and winds obey had forbidden him to leave the land, he considered within himself, and expressed privately to his followers, that henceforward he must either yield shamefully or struggle bravely. Supported by apostolic authority and exhortation, and fervent in spirit as he was, the son of those who shake themselves immediately shook himself [Col. 1146C].

With the prophet’s hoe, he plucked up, destroyed, scattered, and rooted out whatever he found badly planted in the Lord’s garden. His hand did not rest; his eye spared nothing. Whatever was crooked, rough, or distorted he cast down, no longer with the prophet’s hoe but with the Gospel axe. He observed good royal and ecclesiastical customs; but other customs introduced to the injury of the Church and the dishonour of the clergy he cut off as bastard shoots, lest they put down deep roots. As from a very rough and thorny forest, so he strove, to the extent of his ability, to remove and drive out wholly from his people whatever was harsh, disordered, unseemly, or obstructive, that he might make crooked things straight and rough places into smooth ways [Col. 1146D].

But alas: great works, yet little delay. For now adversaries are stirred up against him on the right and on the left [Col. 1147A], so that what was prophesied concerning the Head might be applied to this member of that Head: that he was set for the fall and rising again of many, and for a sign that would be contradicted. Daily slanderers run to the king, accusing him of not observing the royal customs which he had sworn to observe. On the other hand, complainants knock at the doors, lamenting that, trusting excessively in royal favour, he had disinherited them.

But above all the courtly rivals prick and incite the king, now openly reproaching the archbishop’s ingratitude for so many and such great benefits. That venomous serpent, which, as we said near the beginning of this work, had crept secretly through the court and its corners, now openly raises its head. This is indeed, as the Wise Man says, “the third tongue, which has disturbed and scattered many from nation to nation.” These three groups—the slanderers, the complainants, and the courtly rivals—were: the first like gnats, the second like bees, the third like scorpions. All now stung the man and continually incited the king, so that the saying concerning the Head also fitted this member of the Head: “They surrounded me like bees,” he says, “and they blazed like fire among thorns” (Psalm 118) [Col. 1147B].

All these came together, pricking the archbishop and inciting the king against his archbishop. It is therefore no wonder if, under so many incitements, as under so many stings, the king’s heart was pierced and boiled over into flame of anger and indignation. From these straws collected every day, the king was kindled more and more; his anger, still restrained within, increased daily and at last burst forth. “If you blow upon it,” says Wisdom, “it will blaze like fire” (Ecclesiasticus 24). At the insistence of the complainants, the archbishop was first summoned to answer a charge, concerning certain estates, as they said, taken from them.

### On the Summoning of the Archbishop at Northampton

Because at the first summons he did not appear in person, although he sent a representative, he was summoned a second time. Besides the date, the place too was appointed: that noble and royal castle called Northampton. The time was, unless I am mistaken, October, Thursday, the sixth day before the feast of the blessed Pope and Martyr Callixtus. By royal proclamation all the bishops and magnates of the realm were most strictly summoned to this day and place [Col. 1147C].

[Col. 1147D] But the ship which has hitherto stood upon the shore must now be drawn out into the deep. For we who have sailed thus far in harbour must henceforth set sail upon the great and wide sea, and our ship must be steered among the dogs of Scylla and Charybdis, among the Syrtes and many other dangerous gulfs of the sea. O gulfs of the sea! O perils of the age! All Thy heights and Thy waves have passed over us. For He spoke, and the storm-wind stood forth, and its waves were lifted up.

### On the business of the first day, on which he came to the council

Summoned, as we have said, to a cause—indeed rather to a contest—the Lord’s champion appeared at the appointed time and place determined above. And first the aforesaid complainants, like bees, surrounded the Lord’s anointed, Christ’s bishop. And most fiercely [Col. 1148A] civil actions were brought against him, like so many stinging darts. And when it was learned that, as we have already said, he had not appeared in person at the king’s first summons—although, as he alleged in reply, he had sent an adequate representative—nevertheless, by the judgment of all, both magnates and bishops, all his movable goods were immediately confiscated, unless perhaps the royal clemency might choose to mitigate the judgment. That is, as it is commonly said in the country, he was adjudged to be “at the king’s mercy” as regards all his movable property.

But when he heard that he had thus been judged, he said: “What kind of sentence this is, what kind of judgment, is plain to every jurist, whether learned in written or customary law. I need say nothing against it; while I am silent, ages yet to come will not be silent.”

This was indeed a new [Col. 1148B] form of judicial proceeding, perhaps in accordance with the new canons recently promulgated at Clarendon. Yet, passing over the judgment, he protested that it had been unheard of from the beginning of time for a man of Canterbury to be judged in the court of the kings of England on any cause whatsoever, both because of the dignity of the Church and because of the authority of the person: namely, because the Archbishop of Canterbury is the spiritual parent of the king and of all who are in the realm; and for this reason kings and magnates of the realm had always shown deference to their archbishop.

Yet he complained far more of his brethren, his suffragan fellow-bishops, than of the judgment or of the magnates judging him. He called this a new form and a new order of judicial proceedings: that the archbishop should be judged by his suffragans, a father by his sons. He added that it would be a lesser [Col. 1148C] evil to mock at a father’s exposed private parts than to judge the person of the father himself. For, as he said, the bond of profession and obedience is so close and binding—rather, it joins and unites those who have made profession to their superior as members to a head—that, although they may be subject to kings in temporal matters, they neither can nor ought, even in a civil case, to judge their superiors concerning temporal matters, especially when forbidden to do so. Such is the power of obedience that they are bound not only to forsake temporal things, but even to give up themselves for its sake.

Above all, he protested against the bishops because they had pronounced such a sentence. Yet it deserved not even the name of sentence, but was rather a mere fabrication of hatred. Therefore he feared that these proceedings might create a prejudice against the liberty of his successors and ought not to be drawn into precedent in future times. Indeed, as he stated more privately, he would immediately have bound the bishops who thus judged their archbishop—or rather, who so raged with their tongues against their archbishop—under a sentence of suspension, had not Christ’s athlete been preparing himself for a still greater conflict. And this sentence, pronounced against the archbishop on Thursday, was the first business of the council.

### On the business of the second day

On the following day the king himself demanded from the archbishop the money which, as he maintained, the latter had received from him as a loan when he was chancellor: namely, five hundred pounds of silver. Hearing this, the archbishop was immediately [Col. 1149A] as though struck dumb and said that it was uncivil, especially in royal magnificence, to demand back gifts. “I do not deny,” he said, “that in my time as chancellor I received the money which, as I now hear, you demand back; but it was not lent to me, it was given. And, if it pleased you, it would be more fitting now to recall to mind what manner of service I rendered you in that office than, out of the indignation which, as I perceive, has been conceived against me, to take vengeance upon me now in this way because of what passed between us then.”

But the king paid no attention to his words and called for judgment; and those aforesaid men, ready to judge—our bishops as well as the magnates—adjudged that the money demanded should be paid, because the archbishop had acknowledged receiving it, although under the title of a gift, which at that time he could not prove. When the money had been [Col. 1149B] adjudged to him, the king demanded security.
