But the archbishop replied that he possessed in the realm property worth much more than the sum adjudged, and that, if it were the king’s pleasure, it was neither fitting that he should give other security nor that the king should require it.

But it was objected that he did not have so much even in movable goods, because on the preceding day all his movable property had been confiscated by judgment. They therefore pressed him and demanded security; and there it was said most sharply to his face that he must either provide it or remain—an intimation that he faced bodily arrest. But some, seeing that the king was now openly opposed to him, seeing the archbishop abandoned, beginning to suffer not help but rather shipwreck even at the hands of his suffragans—seeing this, I say, and moved by it—some voluntarily [Col. 1149C] offered themselves and stood surety for him. There were five sureties, each for one hundred pounds. And this money, thus exacted from the archbishop on Friday, was the second business of the council.

### On the business of the third day

On the morrow, namely Saturday, the Sabbath day did not dawn for us as a Sabbath, but as a day of labour and affliction, since the king himself, as we have said, had set himself openly against us. On this Sabbath day, therefore, the king demanded accounts from the archbishop concerning everything which, by the king’s command, he had held in custody during his chancellorship: I mean bishoprics and abbeys then vacant, as well as many great baronies and honours, the custody of all of which the chancellor had then held. Of all these, the king said, accounts had neither hitherto been demanded nor rendered. And the total to be rendered in accounts was assessed at about thirty thousand marks.

In the palace, all the others who had come to the council, hearing this, were now astonished. Here and there they began to mutter that only the archbishop’s arrest remained. Others suspected even graver things, and this was commonly spoken of. But the archbishop, who, as we have said above, had begun at this castle to descend upon the sea and to attempt the perilous gulfs of the worldly sea, was suddenly and unexpectedly disturbed by this demand for accounts: he was shaken like a drunken man, and all his wisdom was swallowed up. Of such men the Psalmist says: “They were troubled, they reeled like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up” [Col. 1150A] (Psalm 106 [107]). Yet, after summoning the bishops and much deliberation over what should be answered or done in this matter, Henry of holy memory, then bishop of Winchester—who favoured the archbishop, though secretly for fear—at last recalled that, when the archbishop, then archdeacon of Canterbury and the king’s chancellor, was elected, he had been released from all the bonds of the English Church’s court. We too remember having said this above when the archbishop’s election was under discussion.

The other bishops could not deny testimony so manifest; and at length all the bishops together bore witness to this statement before the king and council. Thus they were dismissed about the evening of Saturday. Yet we had not thereby been dismissed in peace because of this statement; nevertheless, this accounting demanded of the archbishop on Saturday was the third business of the council.

On the morrow, namely Sunday, we rested because of the day, summoned and expected for the contest on the second feria, commonly called Monday. But that day, even in the night belonging to that day, the archbishop was struck with a most severe illness called iliac passion. Yet the king and the magnates of the realm who were gathered in the court, considering this a pretence rather than a real illness, sent men to the archbishop to investigate what it meant. To them the archbishop said: “Today, as you yourselves see, I am prevented by God from coming to court through serious illness. But know assuredly that, with the Lord’s favour, tomorrow I shall present myself to the court, [Col. 1150C] unless otherwise ordained, to be carried in a litter.”

But it was otherwise ordained from above; and, by the Lord’s favour, it happened as Christ’s athlete desired: when night came, he recovered fully.

### On the business of the last day

On the morrow, namely the third feria, commonly called Tuesday—which truly dawned for us as a day of Mars—he entered the court not as an invalid borne in a litter, but like the tower in Jerusalem set directly against Damascus. Yet before he entered the court, very early in the morning the bishops came together to him, astonished and terrified. For a report had already spread throughout the palace and here and there through the council, though not yet openly, that on that day [Col. 1150D] only arrest, or something worse, threatened the archbishop. This same thing had also been secretly insinuated to the archbishop by certain courtiers who still loved him for the benefices and honours long ago bestowed upon them.

Therefore the bishops, not openly because of the enormity of the matter, but under the guise of suggestion, artfully advised that the archbishop should in all things submit himself to the king’s will and judgment, even concerning the archbishopric itself, if perhaps even thus the king’s anger and indignation might be appeased. They added that, unless this were done, he would immediately hear in court the accusation of perjury laid against him and would be judged as a traitor, because he did not preserve the earthly honour, embraced in an oath of fealty, due to his earthly lord: that is, because he did not observe the king’s customs, which he had bound himself by a new obligation of oath specially to observe. Some said this, others affirmed it; it profited little to incur the king’s indignation and to be archbishop. This was disturbance rather than peace for realm and priesthood, great loss and no benefit. Indeed, the bishopric itself was more truly a gallows than a bishopric. And in this counsel the bishops assembled together against the Lord and against His Christ.

Behold, now not only the aforesaid gnats, bees, and scorpions, but fat bulls also surrounded Christ’s athlete, so that the saying concerning the passion of the Head might be applied to this member of that Head now enduring: “Many calves have surrounded me; fat bulls have besieged me” [Col. 1151B] (Psalm 21 [22]). Such bishops were the fat bulls; the many calves were their followers. The counsel of them all was one: that he should submit himself wholly to the king’s judgment.

By these daily assaults, by the pressure of each successive day, they strove to make him bend his knees and yield, so that, pressed—indeed oppressed—he might submit to earthly power the shoulders which he had already placed beneath the pastoral burden. But the pillar of the Church, like one cut off and strong, once indeed shaken, as we have said above, but now thereby made more immovable, rooted in charity and founded upon the firm rock, standing firmly upon the rock, firm while the enemy drove against him, strong against falling—this chief pillar, as it were the prince among the pillars, namely among the bishops—perceiving now from the insinuations of his brethren their purpose and counsel, addressed them thus:

### The archbishop’s address to the bishops

“Brethren,” he said, “as you now see, the world rages against me, the enemy rises up; but what I lament with tears, because it is more detestable than all else, is that the sons of my mother fight against me. Though I remain silent, ages yet to come will recount how you abandoned me alone in the contest; how, in two successive days, you have already twice judged me, your archbishop and father, sinful man though I am—becoming nails in my eye and a spear in my side, you who ought to have risen with me against evildoers and stood together [Col. 1151D] with me.

“Moreover, from what you say I infer that you are prepared to judge me before a secular court not only in a civil but also in a criminal case. But in virtue of obedience, and at the peril of your order, I forbid all of you together henceforth to take part in a judgment in which my person is judged. And, lest you do so, I appeal to our mother, the Roman Church, the refuge of all the oppressed. And if, as rumour now circulates among the people, this is done and laymen lay hands upon me, we likewise command you in virtue of obedience to exercise, as is fitting, ecclesiastical censure on behalf of your father and archbishop.

“But know this one thing: though the world rage, though the enemy rise up, though the body tremble—for the flesh is weak—yet, with the Lord’s favour, I shall neither yield shamefully nor abandon outrageously the flock entrusted to me.”

When he had said this briefly, one of the bishops immediately appealed against the archbishop’s command—namely, that if laymen laid hands on him after judgment, the bishops should not delay to exercise ecclesiastical censure. This was Gilbert, bishop of London. After the archbishop’s words, the bishops departed, hastening to the court, except two who came later out of the archbishop’s chamber, where the bishops had assembled, and secretly comforted and encouraged the archbishop: Henry, bishop of Winchester, already often mentioned and of holy memory, who, as we have related above, had consecrated the archbishop and therefore had greater compassion for him in affliction; and Jocelin, bishop of Salisbury. Yet these too were secret supporters because of fear.

But the archbishop, as if now about to proceed to his final contest in the court—where he was expected alone because the contest was against him alone—prepared himself for the arena. After the bishops departed he quickly entered the church and himself celebrated the Mass of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, in the manner and spirit of a regular canon. The Introit of the Mass was: “For princes sat and spoke against me.” And on that day, although it was not a feast day, he celebrated this Mass in the pallium, except that it was the feast of the blessed Pope and martyr Callixtus. [The king’s attendants, who happened to be present there, silently observed this, and it seemed to them that the act itself portended something.]

[Col. 1152C] O how great was the celebrant’s devotion in this Mass, how great the compunction of his heart and the agitation of his whole outward and inward person! How many and how great were the sighs amid the streams of waters which his eyes poured forth, so that while praying he was often compelled to bring the collect to an end where there was no end, scarcely returning and returning again to what he had begun. At last the Mass was with difficulty finished, because of the abundance of tears and frequent eruptions of sobbing. Immediately he put off the countenance which he had worn in the Mass—the countenance, that is, of humility—and assumed the countenance of a man, the countenance of a lion, most like those prophetic—or rather evangelical—living creatures described by the prophet, among whose other faces were the face of a man and the face [Col. 1152D] of a lion.

Indeed, adorned in those mystical and priestly vestments, and even in the pallium in which he had there celebrated Mass, he would have proceeded to the court, had not certain Knights Templar, great men and men of religion, whom he had long had as close associates, prevented him. For he said that he wished the court to see and understand whom it had already judged twice, and whom it was still prepared to condemn. Yet at their urging he put off the sacred attire of which we have spoken.

Nevertheless, because many important persons already believed and feared that arrest, or something worse, threatened him that day—and because this had been privately suggested even to him by certain courtiers—he himself, but secretly, carried with him the viaticum of ecclesiastical communion, namely the Eucharist. But now made bolder and more confident, our evangelical lion hastened to the court as though toward prey. The bishops and magnates had already assembled there, awaiting the archbishop’s arrival and the end of the matter.

As the archbishop entered the hall, he immediately received the cross from the cross-bearer walking before him and himself carried it openly before the eyes of all, like the Lord’s standard-bearer in the Lord’s battle, raising the Lord’s banner; thus fulfilling the Lord’s saying not only spiritually but also figuratively: “If anyone wishes to be My disciple, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow Me” [Col. 1153A] (Matthew 16). Truly it was a mystical act, a presage of his future cross.

All who saw it were astonished; the bishops were distressed; the magnates were indignant. The king, who was apart in the upper chamber, on hearing of it was as though beside himself. One bishop immediately met the archbishop as he entered the hall; seeing this, he became as if stunned and at once tried to tear the cross from the archbishop’s hands, but could not. This was Master Robert of Melun, whom the archbishop had ordained priest and consecrated bishop of Hereford. Another bishop, who had likewise met him on the other side of the cross, rebuked and reviled him: “If the king draws his sword, as you have now drawn yours, what hope can there afterwards be of peace being restored between you? But, you who have always been foolish, your folly will show itself today against you.”

Behold the insult, lest the disciple, now on the cross, should in this respect be deprived of the title of his Master hanging upon the cross. This was the aforesaid Gilbert, bishop of London. But the disciple, following on the cross the Master who, when reviled, did not revile in return, disregarded the insult. Carrying the cross, he proceeded until he entered an inner house from the hall; there, seated among the bishops, he held the cross in his hands.

O what a spectacle: to behold Thomas, formerly so splendid in the court, amid so many changes of magnificent foreign garments, now in haircloth and with the cross! Formerly, wherever he went through the hall, surrounded by a circle of so many and such distinguished persons that scarcely anyone but the greatest magnates could approach him; now so solitary and alone that scarcely anyone wished [Col. 1153D] to come near him, all withdrawing from him. Thus the Master’s words might be applied to the disciple: “You have removed far from me friend and neighbour, and my acquaintances because of misery” (Psalm 87 [88]). And the prophet’s words: “He shall sit solitary and keep silence, because he has raised himself above himself” (Lamentations 3).

Truly in this spectacle was God’s judgment, terrible indeed yet pleasing: to behold Thomas carrying the cross in that court in which he had once abounded in so many delights and riches and displayed every form of vanity; now, by God’s just judgment, beginning to pay the penalty of abasement where he had still in the world taken the material of so great exaltation. And true indeed was that saying of the Wise Man: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclesiasticus 2).

Immediately, when all the bishops and magnates had been summoned by the herald’s voice, the king made a grave and great complaint: that the archbishop had entered the court in this manner to the disgrace of the king and the kingdom, not like a king but like a traitor, making himself thus notorious for treason; that such a thing had been unheard of from the beginning of time in the court of any king professing Christianity. All who bore witness to the king’s words said that he had always been vain and proud; that this disgrace fell not upon the king alone but upon the entire realm and upon all of them; and that it had deservedly happened to the king, who had made such a man second to himself in the realm, to whom all were subject and none equal.

Thus everyone openly and on all sides cried out that he was a traitor, as though he had no longer preserved the earthly honour he had sworn to preserve for his lord and king, from whom he had received so many and such great things, but had rather by this act branded both king and realm with the enduring stain of treason. Therefore punishment should be inflicted upon him as the king’s perjurer and traitor. The clamour about this grew stronger; and those hearing it throughout the hall were shaken with trembling and horror. Indeed, when some came down from the upper chamber in which the king was with his followers into the lower house where we were, the archbishop and all of us in the house raised our hands and fortified ourselves with the sign of the cross. No one addressed the archbishop, nor did he address anyone except the disciple who wrote these things, who sat at the feet of the one holding the cross.

Once certain courtiers, who appeared to hold the office of doorkeepers in the hall, came down in a great rush from the often-mentioned upper chamber, carrying rods [Col. 1154C] and staffs. With threatening faces and outstretched fingers they looked toward the archbishop and the disciple seated at his feet. As all in the house signed themselves with the sign of the cross, the archbishop, bowing his head to the disciple seated at his feet, said: “I fear now for you; yet do not be afraid, for you will still share in my crown.”

Immediately the disciple replied: “You need not fear, nor I. For you have raised that noble and triumphant banner, holy and terrible to every power, by which many have conquered many wars. And among others, the exemplary battles of Constantine the Great, of holy and divine memory, teach and confirm these our words. In that most glorious banner of the cross, not only earthly but also aerial powers were vanquished and despoiled, the world through it and in it, and hell likewise, being subdued.”

And the disciple speaking added: “Remember that once you were the unconquerable standard-bearer of the king of England; but if now, as standard-bearer of the King of angels, you are conquered, it will be most shameful.”

While master and disciple were thus speaking privately into each other’s ear, the bishops, having received the king’s permission, separated from the magnates and entered into consultation by themselves. The situation was straitened indeed: either the bishops would incur the king’s indignation, or together with the magnates they would condemn their own archbishop in the royal court upon a criminal charge. This they did not dare to do because it would be too manifest a violation of the holy canons.

[Col. 1155A] For those who are wise to do evil do not always put their hands to every sort of wickedness, but only to those evils which can be concealed by fabricated and artfully contrived deceit. Of such men the Psalm says: “They told how they might hide snares; they said, ‘Who shall see them?’” (Psalm 63 [64]). Such is the way of the adulterous woman who, according to the Wise Man’s saying, eats, wipes her mouth, and says: “I have done no evil.” Otherwise they would not be wise in doing evil if wickedness could be detected plainly and without any evasion. Therefore, in this difficult position the bishops turned over and over what should be done and how this necessity might be escaped.

At last, by the common counsel of all, this was contrived: that they should appeal their archbishop to the Roman See on the charge of perjury, and bind themselves to the king by a pledge of good faith, promising to use all work and effort within their power to secure the deposition of their archbishop, on condition that the king, of his good pleasure, would release them from the judgment now hanging over the archbishop. Thus, binding themselves to the king and expressly appealing the archbishop to a hearing before Rome on the charge, they included under the appeal their persons, their churches, and their office. Then, by the king’s good pleasure separated from the magnates, after the appeal had been made, each took his seat in his proper order beside the archbishop.

Now terror and horror seized everyone more than before. For while the king, the bishops having withdrawn, sat in judgment with the princes, it was considered absolutely certain that arrest—or something harsher—immediately threatened the archbishop. From that point the princes and all the greater men of the realm opened their mouths like a ravening and roaring lion and, as was afterwards reported to us, judged the archbishop perjured and traitorous. Yet what precisely was judged we could only conjecture rather than know, as will shortly appear.

Therefore, when sentence was to be pronounced, the king remaining with a few while all who were in the upper chamber came down to the lower house where we were, they stood to pronounce it before the archbishop. As they came down, the archbishop wished to rise; but the disciple who sat at the foot of the cross quietly suggested that it was wholly unfitting for a father to rise before sons at such a moment, especially while he held in his own hands the banner of so great a king. The archbishop agreed. He did not rise before those standing before him, and no sign of faint-heartedness or cowardly trembling could be detected in him by gesture, word, or action.

Then the noble Robert, earl of Leicester, most honoured among the honourable, in whose mouth the speech had been placed, began to speak. First he recalled into what intimate royal favour the archbishop had been received; how many and great things he had received from the king’s hand; and how he now appeared forgetful and ungrateful for all these things, returning evil for good, hatred and disgrace for favour and glory. Since this earl, a great and noble man, had always loved the archbishop purely and sincerely from the time of his chancellorship, though now secretly for fear, he spoke sadly and compassionately, as could plainly be observed, prolonging his words because he feared to pronounce sentence.

When the archbishop quickly noticed this, interrupting the earl’s words, he forbade all who stood before him, in virtue of obedience and under the Christian faith they professed, as a father forbids sons, to pronounce such a judgment by which his person should be judged. Yet the earl, though unwillingly as could be seen, proceeded nonetheless, though slowly and reluctantly, to pronounce the judgment. But when he reached the point at which he would touch the archbishop with the guilt of perjury, wishing, as could be seen, to pronounce him perjured and perhaps, as was conjectured, a traitor also, the archbishop immediately perceived this and, without waiting for the judgment, rose up, protesting that it was not for them to judge their archbishop on a criminal charge. Therefore we do not know for certain what was adjudged.

But immediately some of those who had stood to deliver judgment reproached and cried out that he was leaving the court as a perjurer and traitor. Turning toward those reproaching him and looking upon them with a fierce expression, he answered that, were the priestly order no impediment and were it lawful for him, he would defend himself against them from the accusation of perjury and treason by martial arms. And so we departed from the council. “This is the disciple who bears witness of these things, and saw them, and wrote them” (John 21). In that moment he alone followed outside the inner house the archbishop, bearing his cross, until we entered the hall. And that day we became a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men.

But when we had left the court and were already on horseback, the archbishop could scarcely govern his horse, carry the cross, and give a blessing to those asking for it, so great was the multitude of people seeking his blessing. For, as though a presage of things to come, when he came out of the court carrying the cross, crowds of people prostrated themselves through the lanes and streets, adoring him and asking his blessing.

When we arrived at our lodging, namely the conventual monastery of religious monks, the church of Saint Andrew, tables were immediately laid and, as usual, there was a great and splendid provision. But immediately many of our household—especially knights and noble youths—asked leave to depart because of fear of the king, and, having received permission, left us in great anxiety and bitterness. We now experienced among our own the Wise Man’s saying: “There is a friend who is a companion at table, and he does not remain in the day of necessity.” Yet these were excusable, because they were laymen and feared, not without reason, the king’s indignation.

But among those deserting us were some men of our own office—I mean clerics—who were less excusable and more culpable. As soon as they foresaw the cloud of future times between king and archbishop, like swallow-men, through fear of the coming winter, they gradually flew away from us. Truly they were swallow-like and reed-like, yielding immediately at the first blast of wind: truly children of the breeze, friends of fortune, following and seeking only plunder [Col. 1157A] and their own interests. But I shall not proceed further now to expose their shame; it is enough to have touched on it, especially since they afterwards, seeing the outcome of events, humbly confessed that they had erred and grievously repented of having thus abandoned their shepherd and father.

It was nevertheless fitting to mention this, so that hereafter men of our office, following their shepherd and father, may not look back or abandon him in distress. For according to the Wise Man’s saying: “At all times he who is a friend loves, and a brother is proved in distress” (Psal. XVII). Therefore, leaving aside those who went out from us but were not of us, let us continue the order of events. Let this alone be inserted for the glory of so great an archbishop: when these withdrew and those departed, that man, firmly supported by the constancy of virtues—the pillar upon which the whole structure of virtues rests, without which it could not stand even for a moment but would collapse utterly—disregarded all things with strength of spirit.

For a great soul is accustomed to regard as slight whatever happens in a time of prosperity or adversity, considering, as someone has said, that neither prosperity is lasting nor misery persistent. Therefore, because it was evening when we withdrew from the court, after the evening office had ended the archbishop immediately reclined at table with those whom he then had. During the meal there was a reading from the *Tripartite Ecclesiastical History* concerning the persecution of Bishop Liberius. When we heard inserted there the Gospel saying, “If they persecute you in [Col. 1157C] this city, flee into another” (Matthew 10), the archbishop looked at the disciple who wrote these things, already, as I conjectured—and as the outcome soon proved—conceiving in his mind an evangelical flight.

After the hymn had been sung, the archbishop rose from table and immediately summoned Roger, then bishop of Worcester, and Master Robert of Melun, then bishop of Hereford, whom he had ordained priests and consecrated bishops—for he consecrated no others before or after these two—and likewise the bishop of Rochester, his own chaplain. He sent them to the king, requesting a safe departure from his land. But those sent soon returned and reported that the king had replied that he would defer this counsel until the following day.

### On the archbishop’s undertaken flight

Meanwhile, persons privy to royal secrets secretly informed and advised the archbishop to make provision both for the king and for himself. Therefore, that same night, a little before cockcrow, the archbishop secretly began his intended flight on only four horses. Very few knew of it: only the disciple who wrote these things, his chaplains, and his chamberlains, without whose knowledge it could not have been done. He instructed the disciple to set out that same night for Canterbury.

And because at that time the accounts of revenues and the general payment of the whole archbishopric were being made, he ordered me to scrape together whatever I could and hurry overseas, namely to the very famous castle of Saint-Omer [Col. 1158A] in Flanders, and there await his arrival with certainty in the noble monastery of Saint Bertin, conspicuous for every form of religious observance. He declared that, with the Lord’s favour, he would come there without delay, unless arrest or death itself prevented him.

He added something which I have taken care to insert here: he asked me to look after a certain book of his, lest it perish among his other possessions, which, as it seemed, were to be plundered after his flight. From this may be observed how great was his contempt for possessions when duty demanded it: amid the vast, various, and splendid equipment which he left behind, he remembered only a single little book. Thus the archbishop departed, leaving behind him the disciple, lamenting and crying after him.

That same night, certain of our companions, unaware of this flight, slept apart in one chamber. One of them, as he afterwards related to me and others, distinctly heard in a dream the sound of a voice singing those two verses of the psalmist: “Our soul has escaped like a sparrow from the snare of hunters; the snare has been broken, and we have been delivered” [Col. 1158B] (Psalm 123 [124]).

And on this Tuesday began the fourth business of the council: the ruinous dissension of so great a king and so great an archbishop; the profane division of head and members, that is, metropolitan and suffragans; and finally the disturbance of the whole realm and priesthood, and the beginning of our exile, which was to endure for six full years until martyrdom.

Alas, accursed day! Alas, malign council! Alas, an act of day and council to be detested throughout all ages to come, by which the bonds so dear between so great a king and so great a pontiff [Col. 1158C] were so irreparably broken, the king and the archbishop thereafter never to see one another again in the kingdom. How many misfortunes for kingdom and priesthood followed from these deeds! Therefore I testify to what I saw, heard, and myself experienced: how profane, pestilential, and fatal it is to sow discord or schism between royal power and priesthood—unless, perhaps, a most manifest cause of justice calls forth priestly zeal.

For a schism or scandal arising between kings and priests for God’s truth is not so much a schism or scandal as a support of ecclesiastical peace and liberty. Yet many priests, to whom authority has been given, pass over such matters under the cover of a shadowed religion: they keep silent and conceal them [Col. 1158D] while the liberty of the clergy is endangered before their very eyes, unwilling, as they say and persuade themselves, to stir up a schism between kingdom and priesthood for the sake of ecclesiastical peace. Some of them, however, more truly conceal what they see because they consider the labour and suffering involved should they undertake these things—especially those excellent dissemblers, who endure everything for Caesar’s sake, whose promotion to higher rank Caesar has either readily granted or sometimes himself procured beyond what was lawful.

But this Thomas of ours, though, as we have previously shown, he was taken from the king’s service, endowed with such great royal favour, and promoted because the king so wished and procured it, nevertheless, when the time and cause came, forgot what lay behind and stretched himself toward what lay ahead. For the honour of the clergy [Col. 1159A] and the ecclesiastical liberty which he had undertaken to defend, he set himself against the king—whom he loved above man, and who was no less beloved by him then. He did not, like that ancient priest in the Gospel, or like the Levite, a minister of earthly things, pass by; he did not pass over the matter; he did not dissemble. Yet from this schism and dissension there followed many evils, not to be recounted here, for both kingdom and priesthood.

He himself, as a man provident in all things, had foretold this before these evils occurred; but, as he added, justice when endangered must not on that account be abandoned or even concealed. Great loss commonly follows or accompanies those who undertake arduous and great deeds. Yet when virtue itself is undertaken, and [Col. 1160A] virtue itself is thus finally tested, it is rendered more perfect and more commendable. “For,” says the Master, “virtue is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12). What and how great were the misfortunes that this dissension brought, on both sides, upon kingdom and priesthood, the subsequent course of this history will in part disclose. We recall that we have also touched upon them above in the text of this work. Whoever desires fuller knowledge should read our letters, written by us in our exile or sent to us or on our behalf. From all these materials has been compiled one great body of correspondence, to which recourse must be had. Since many matters are contained in the letters, we omit them from the following narrative for brevity’s sake.

## The Chapters of the Fourth Volume Begin

[Col. 1159]

1. How Thomas fled after laying aside the orarium, and how his flight was evangelical; with discussion of the twofold flight of pastors, bodily and spiritual.

2. What was done at court on the following day when the archbishop’s flight became known.

3. A description of Thomas’s route, as an example of humility.

4. How, when he arrived late and reclined at table, he was recognized by his host in the breaking of bread.

5. Why, after arriving overseas, he continued to conceal himself.

6. At what place the disciple who wrote these things rejoined his lord and master, the archbishop, now overseas; and of their mutual conversation.

7. How the king’s envoys, sent against the archbishop to the apostolic lord, arrived; likewise of the archbishop’s envoys to the apostolic lord; and how both parties passed through Louis, king of the French.

8. How the king’s envoys and the archbishop’s were received by the apostolic lord, and what was asked and done there.

9. How those sent by the king returned to England, and how the archbishop, arriving in France, was received by the king of the French.

10. How the archbishop, coming to Sens, was received by the apostolic lord; how, in the presence of him and the cardinals, the archbishop set forth the cause of all his troubles; likewise how he confessed his lapse; of the fatal written undertaking there produced and read, and rejected by the apostolic lord; and how we withdrew from the curia that day.

11. How the archbishop was accused by the cardinals of having risen against the king during a time of schism, and what he answered to the objections.

12. How the archbishop came as a pilgrim to a certain Cistercian monastery called Pontigny; how he was received there; and what spiritual pursuits he undertook there.

13. Of the expulsion and banishment of the archbishop’s relatives and of his followers who had accompanied him into exile; of the archbishop’s grief for the expelled; of the consoling discourse by which his learned fellow-exiles comforted him; of his reply; and how, by the Lord’s dispensation and mercy, provision was made for the multitude of our exiles.

14. How, with his exile made more burdensome by the multitude of exiles, the archbishop began to live more austerely; how, because of excessive mortification of the flesh, his health was soon gravely impaired; how he was visited and reproved by the disciple who wrote these things; and how, promptly corrected, he moderated his abstinence and devoted himself wholly with his companions to the Scriptures.

15. How, in the second year of his pilgrimage, zeal for justice seized the archbishop, as he addressed his followers in a deliberative speech concerning it.

16. How the king was approached the first time, and how the second.

17. How the archbishop, seeing that the king was not corrected, was constrained to act according to his commands; of the threatening edict which he publicly issued against the king; of the place where it was pronounced; and how it quickly reached the king.

18. That the king sent appellants to the archbishop, and that the appeal was complied with.

19. How both king and archbishop sent to the apostolic see; how the king drove the archbishop from Pontigny; and how the archbishop and his learned companions, brought into straits, deliberated together what ought to be done.

20. How the archbishop, intending to leave Pontigny, sent to Louis, king of the French; how and in what place the king received the archbishop for pilgrimage; and of his dream when departing from Pontigny.

21. How much humanity and kindness the French showed to the archbishop and his companions.

22. How the aforesaid Roman pilgrims of the archbishop returned; of the arrival of the cardinals to restore peace between king and archbishop; of the archbishop’s dream; and how, after an appeal had been lodged by certain persons of the realm, the cardinals returned with peace unmade.

23. How thereafter the archbishop, refusing to yield to the appeal, delivered many courtiers to anathema—at the entreaty of his learned companions leaving the king’s person alone and still untouched.

24. How the king, stirred on hearing that the appeal had not been accepted but that his own men had instead been excommunicated, sent to the apostolic lord, and the archbishop likewise.

25. How the Roman pontiff was pressed by the opposing envoys of king and archbishop, and how, under pressure, he appointed now these and now those as mediators of peace between king and archbishop.

26. How the king of the French, one of the mediators, summoned us to one of the conferences between himself and the king of England; how there, before the kings’ eyes, the archbishop was urged, assailed, and pressed to submit himself to the king’s will—provided only that this were added, namely, “saving the honour of God”; and how from the conference he withdrew, henceforth rejected, abandoned, and subjected to many insults. [Col. 1161]

27. How the archbishop, appearing with his companions to be grievously afflicted, strengthened them on the road; and how, after a few days, what the world had counted as disgrace to him at the earlier conference of kings turned to his glory.

28. How the archbishop sent a third time to the Roman pontiff; how the pontiff was again pressed for peace with the archbishop; and of envoys sent late from the side of the Roman pontiff on behalf of peace.

29. How, at another conference of kings, the archbishop’s peace hinged upon the kiss of peace alone; how he was approached and reproved by his own followers for thus abandoning peace over the kiss of peace alone; how he was encouraged to make peace while disregarding the kiss of peace; and of the archbishop’s being mocked.

30. How the archbishop sent a fourth time to the Roman pontiff; of the coronation of Henry, the king’s still-boy son; of our Roman pilgrims; and how the apostolic lord, moved against the bishops who had taken part in the coronation against the archbishop, sent the archbishop letters suspending them, and even anathematizing some of them; and how the king was thus pressed toward peace by an urgent apostolic command.

## The Fourth Volume Begins

[Col. 1161]

### 1. On Thomas’s Flight, and That It Was Evangelical

[Col. 1161A]

Thomas therefore laid aside the orarium, which, as we have shown above, he customarily wore openly and continually upon his shoulders in remembrance of the perpetual priestly yoke he had assumed. By this very act he seemed already to indicate that amid such great oppression he could no longer freely exercise the priesthood. Thus Thomas fled after laying aside the orarium, carrying on the road nothing with him but that distinctive insignia of metropolitans called the pallium and his seal: neither bag, nor bread, nor money in his belt, but clothed only in a hair-shirt over his naked body, he followed Jesus.

He followed, I say, Jesus, who first fled but later met danger fearlessly. For Jesus, shepherd of shepherds, fled in order to give his followers a model of flight suited to the time. Paul, master after the Master of masters, also fled. And if we seek still earlier fugitives: Jacob fled, Moses fled, Elijah too fled—indeed all who fulfilled the Lord’s command concerning flight: “If they persecute you,” he says, “in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 10).

Thomas therefore fled to fulfill the Lord’s command, taking thought in his flight both for the king, whom he loved so greatly, and for himself: for the king, that he might avoid the heat of royal indignation; for himself, that he might keep his hands innocent. “For the wrath of a king,” says the Wise Man, “is a messenger of death, and a wise man will appease it” (Prov. 16). Thus no apologetic discourse need be woven concerning this flight, for it was not the flight of a hireling but of a shepherd who seemed to be personally sought.

He fled also because, had he remained and set himself in opposition, he would have produced more fruit for death than for life, adding sorrow to sorrow. So too Apollos, the disciple of the Master—whom he had ordained bishop of the Corinthians—left by flight those over whom he had recently been set, because he could not calm them. Though earnestly asked by the Master to return to them, he was then unwilling, fearing that he would bear no fruit among men hardened against him. Concerning him the Master said to them: “As to brother Apollos, I make known to you that I earnestly asked him to come to you; and indeed it was not his will to come now” (1 Cor. 16).

Likewise, for a similar cause, many other good pastors have repeatedly either left the flock entrusted to them altogether without a shepherd, or have been transferred from one flock to another, where they might exercise a more useful care. No defence, therefore, is needed for this flight. Rather, the flight of those provincial bishops who remained is inexcusable.

### On Spiritual Flight, in Which Not the Shepherd but the Hireling Flees

[Col. 1162A]

And certainly those who remained fled. For who can deny that they fled when, abandoning their archbishop, the commander of their warfare, on the day of battle they crossed over to the opposing side? They truly fled like the sons of Ephraim, who, bending and shooting the bow—that is, preparing and promising aid before the battle—turned back on the day of battle. Though remaining in body and embracing the things of the flesh, they fled in mind, hiding beneath the bushel of fear the weapons of their warfare and the lamp of truth, when they ought to have mounted up against the rulers and powers of this world and stood in battle for the house of Israel on the day of the Lord.

Otherwise Christ’s soldier bears the sword in vain; indeed, as we have said, he hides his sword beneath the bushel of fear and flees—if not in body, yet in spirit. For this flight is one not of body but of spirit, always inexcusable; terror of the world or love of it produces it in hirelings. They chant and read daily in churches gleaming with gold and among gilded altars, yet they flee. Daily they splendidly feast and drink amid swarms of attendants, among gold and jewels, yet they flee. They sleep securely beneath their own fig tree and vine, yet they flee; for by fleeing thus they obtain the favour of princes and worldly glory.

Woe to our generation—I speak of the ministers of the altar—for this leaven, for this flight! There is now no one who sets himself in opposition, no one who mounts up against the adversary. [Col. 1162C] They join psalms to psalms, prayers to prayers, and masses to masses, and hear them every day with sufficient regularity. They open their hands generously to the poor and needy. But these things are common to all Christians; Jews and pagans indeed do them. The principle implied in the episcopal name, however, soars far above the common life of private persons. For the name of bishops itself declares what is required of them in the power of their action.

Their duty is continually to rebuke, reproach, and insist in season and out of season; to resist against the day; to oppose earthly powers. This is the steep ascent and this the proper burden of the pastoral office. This is the principle implied in the bishop’s name, the summit of bishops, the privilege of so eminent a rank in the Church, by which those who are above us, who preside over us, ought to surpass private persons and soar above us. [Col. 1163A] In fasts, vigils, giving, distributing, prayers, and all other works of piety or religion, they share with those beneath them, since these are not proper to bishops but common to all Christians.

But alas—how many such men are there? Even if they do these things, which ought not to be omitted, in these days they hide the weapons of their warfare. While they crave earthly advantages, pursue honours, or seek higher things through the spirit of ambition, they refuse to oppose evil, lest they lose what they love or fail to attain that toward which they strive. Thus the Church of the present age is plainly struck by the Lord’s threat through the prophet: “I will take away from Judah and Jerusalem the mighty man and the man of strength” (Isa. 3).

Another prophet likewise lamented this in his *Lamentations*, speaking in the person of the synagogue. He lamented not the loss of the temple’s walls or stones, but the scarcity of men: “He has taken away all my mighty men from me” (Lam. 1). Long ago foretold, it is now most fully accomplished today in Judah and Jerusalem: few are mighty, few strong. All turn their backs; all flee. By fleeing they obtain those very things which Thomas, by fleeing, despised. Their flight indeed perished before Thomas in flight, so that, fleeing, he might truly chant along the road the clause of the Psalmic verse: “Flight has perished from me, and there is none who seeks my soul” (Ps. 121).

For, seeing that there is a time for everything, a time to flee and a time to meet danger, he fled first but later met it; as the end of this work [Col. 1163C] and the end of the man will show. Therefore this flight of Thomas is commendable, and great was the faith of this fugitive: he thought nothing of the morrow and carried with him on the road nothing but faith in the Crucified One and poverty, though, as has been sufficiently shown above, he had been reared amid imperial luxuries.

Thus Thomas, an exile, was driven through the whole island of Britain, encircled by the Ocean, from which escape was difficult—especially since all things were suspect to one fleeing as a public enemy everywhere. But let us suspend our pen briefly concerning the fugitive’s route and departure, intending first to relate what counsel the princes and bishops adopted on the next day, Wednesday, when his flight was known, against the Lord and against His Christ.

### 2. What Was Done at Court When the Archbishop’s Flight Became Known

[Col. 1163D]

When morning came and the flight was known, bishops and princes assembled together. The king, troubled, asked what should be done. Their common counsel was that the senior bishops—especially those who, as we have said above, had bound themselves to the king—should go to the Roman pontiff, intending to accuse their archbishop of disturbing the peace of kingdom and priesthood and of the guilt of perjury. Meanwhile, all his possessions were to remain at peace until they should report what judgment the Roman pontiff had given.

Accordingly, by the king’s edict it was immediately proclaimed by a herald that no one should molest the archbishop’s men or possessions, or take anything from him, but that all his property should enjoy peace. These wise men gave such counsel to do evil, so that they might more conveniently justify their own case and suppress the archbishop’s: although he had rashly and dishonourably provoked the king, recklessly disturbed the peace of kingdom and priesthood, and foolishly and indiscreetly abandoned his church by fleeing at night, yet after all this he would undeservedly enjoy the benefit of royal peace through royal clemency.

Thus the bishops with the rich secretly prepared a snare for the fugitive. Roger, then archbishop of York; Gilbert, then bishop of London; Roger, bishop of Worcester; Hilary, then bishop of Chichester; and Bartholomew, bishop of Exeter, immediately set out. [Col. 1164A] Besides these, certain courtiers and other honourable and eminent men were sent with them from the king’s own side as witnesses. Through them the king informed, by letters of complaint, Louis, then king of the French of pious memory, and Philip, the noble count of Flanders, that Thomas, formerly archbishop of Canterbury—for so the document was phrased—had fled his kingdom as a traitor, and asked that they not receive him in their lands. They therefore departed; but before other matters, let us recall the route of the fleeing Thomas, as an example of humility.

### 3. On the Route of the Fleeing Thomas

As we have said, fleeing secretly by night, with a brother of the Order of Sempringham as his guide, he made toward the north, toward that noble city called Lincoln. He knowingly and deliberately took a trackless way rather than a road, in order more cautiously to escape pursuers sent after him and avoid their ambushes. That night he came to a village called Graham, about twenty-five miles from Northampton. After allowing himself a little sleep there, he set out the following day and came to Lincoln, another approximately twenty-five miles, lodging in the city in the house of a certain fuller.

There he entered the water flowing through the city and, by water, came about forty miles to a solitary place situated amid the waters, called the Hermitage, belonging to that holy congregation of nuns of Sempringham. Because of the solitude of the place and the difficulty of access, [Col. 1164D] since it stood amid the waters, he lay concealed there more safely for three days, recovering strength for the journey still remaining.

One day, as the brother who attended him saw him sitting alone at table and eating the dishes set before him, he was pierced with grief and could not restrain his tears. He immediately left, lest the tears he had shed disturb the man of God during the sacred meal.

From the Hermitage he came ten miles to St Botolph’s; and from there he traveled by water to a place called Haverol, likewise belonging to the aforesaid congregation of nuns. Thereafter he travelled only by night, fearing discovery. He was now heading eastward toward Kent, where his face was better known to the people of the land. He therefore travelled by night and hid by day, completing the journey in eight nights, until he reached in Kent a village on the sea called Estrei, where he intended to cross the sea.

There he was all the more cautious in proportion as he was safer, because that village belonged directly to the revenues of the sacred community of his metropolitan see, and was only eight miles from Canterbury. The light destined for the world lay hidden in this village until the feast of All Souls, for eight days. On All Souls’ Day, which was Tuesday—the fifteenth day from that Tuesday, the day when he had fought with beasts at Northampton—he entered the sea shortly before dawn in a small boat, without any conveyance. Around evening he landed on a part of the coast called by the local people Oie in Boulogne, one league from the port called Graveninges.

The man of God went on foot as far as he could—but he could go only a little way. For, after entering the small sea-vessel, he had, as we have said, been severely exhausted by the frequent and deep tossings of the sea. After a short distance, therefore, he lay down on the ground, unable to proceed, and said to the brothers with him: “I will not leave this place unless you carry me or seek transport for me.” They procured a beast for one silver coin; it had not a bridle, but only a rope around its neck. They put their garments upon its back and set him upon it.

O sight—to behold Thomas, once borne in chariots and on horses, now seated upon a beast that had only a rope around its neck instead of a bridle, and the rags of poor brothers and lay brethren upon its back instead of a saddle! [Col. 1165C] O Thomas, what a great reversal of circumstances has come over you! Where now are your many horses, your many horsemen, your rich and splendid trappings? Behold, all these things are now reduced to one beast and one rope; and even the beast and rope are not yours, but another’s. As you passed away, your things passed away too: your old things passed away, and all things became new.

Truly God is wonderful in His saints: He leads them by a wonderful way, makes them glad through tribulation, gives them room through pressure, proves them through temptation; by destroying He builds, by striking He heals, by killing He gives life. This was especially clear among other examples in Thomas our own. Thus, seated upon the beast, he came to the aforesaid port of Graveninges.

On Tuesday, therefore, which was All Souls’ Day, commonly called *dies Martis*, and which, as we have already said, was the fifteenth from the day when he had been in the danger described above at Northampton, he arrived overseas. I do not know by what presage of events—if it was rather a presage than an event—he began his flight on a Tuesday, arrived overseas on a Tuesday, left the coast on a Tuesday, returned and arrived in England again on a Tuesday, and finally fell by the sword on a Tuesday, only one month having elapsed from the day of his return and arrival. Thus the day of Mars became also the day of the martyr; on it, as if by some presage of things to come, he was three or four times so prepared for martyrdom. On Tuesday, then, All Souls’ Day, [Col. 1166A] he arrived overseas, and in the evening came to Graveninges.

### 4. How Thomas, Fleeing, Was Recognized by His Host in the Breaking of Bread

When, late in the day, he reclined at table with the three brothers who were his travelling companions, he was recognized by his host in the breaking of bread. Yet at table no more deference was paid to him than to the others—indeed, less, since he did not occupy the first place at table but the last. Throughout this journey, moreover, he was changed both in dress and in name. His fellow-brothers travelling with him called him Brother Christian, taking the name Christian as his own so that he might not be recognized.

But this observant host noticed that, unlike the other diners, he had a distinctive manner of eating and a special tenderness in distributing food. From the little placed before him on the table, he divided and gave portions to the children and to each of the others in the house.

### On the Archbishop’s Physical Appearance

Furthermore, as further evidence confirming the recognition he had already conceived, the host examined the whole man’s bearing and movement: his remarkable height, broad forehead and grave expression, long face, handsome shape of his long hands, and the proportionate, almost exquisitely extended joints of those hands. Seeing a man so wholly unlike the others in his manner of eating, bodily appearance, and bearing, he at once thought that he had received some great man into his house. He strongly suspected him to be the archbishop of Canterbury, [Col. 1166C] because rumour had by then spread thickly throughout the surrounding country that the archbishop of Canterbury had secretly left Northampton in this way and had either already landed in those parts or would land there soon.

The host immediately called his serving-woman aside and quietly told her that the man he had received as a guest was the archbishop of Canterbury. Unable to restrain herself, she had scarcely heard the words when she hurried to the table; after a brief look she at once returned smiling. “Certainly,” she said, “good man, it is he.” The woman therefore became at once more attentive in serving: she ran about and hurried, now setting nuts before Brother Christian, now apples, now a little cheese.

Brother Christian, suspecting from certain signs that he had already been discovered, would rather have been without the things which the woman was affectionately setting before him; yet he concealed his concern.

When supper had ended, the host came nearer with a new brightness of face. Brother Christian wished to place him beside himself on the seat, but the host firmly refused and sat on the ground at his feet. Shortly afterwards he said: “Lord, I give thanks to God that I was worthy for you to enter beneath my roof.” Brother Christian immediately replied: “Who, then, am I? Am I not a certain poor brother, and called Christian?” The host said: “Certainly—whatever you may be called, I know that you are a great man and the archbishop of Canterbury.”

Since Brother Christian could not disentangle himself from his host by any covering of words, and had to do one of two things—either confess the truth about himself firmly or deny it falsely—he confessed that he was indeed the man and did not deny it. Yet, so that the host might not betray him, he won him over with gentle words and took him along with himself the next day. Behold how long were the perils of the man of God, who was in danger even when already in harbour.

### 5. Why He Continued to Conceal Himself Even Now That He Was Overseas

For the king had already spread abroad by letter and word among Philip, the noble count of Flanders, his brother, and among his powerful friends in that land, that Thomas, formerly archbishop of Canterbury—for so the written formulation ran—had fled his realm as a traitor. As far-reaching as the king’s hand was, so far-reaching were the perils for one fleeing that royal hand; hence all things were full of suspicion and there was no safety.

Another reason why he feared to reveal himself in those regions was that Matthew, brother of Philip count of Flanders and then count of Boulogne, had, through the agency of the lord king of England, contracted a profane marriage, detestable to all ages to come, with a certain abbess, daughter of Stephen, formerly king of England. The archbishop, then the king’s chancellor, had opposed this because of the enormity of the deed and protested as far as he could. Therefore the count of Boulogne had thereafter hated him with a settled hatred. This was indeed so; and therefore he feared, nor was it without reason that he did not wish to disclose himself in those regions.

Because the next day’s journey was long, the road difficult, and he feared ambushes, he set out at earliest dawn the next day. From Graveninges the man of God went on foot the whole day, over a very muddy and slippery road, especially in winter weather. Toward night he came to a monastery of the holy Cistercian order, called in that country Clairmarais, having covered, by the local reckoning, twelve leagues that day. This monastery lies near the noble castle mentioned above, Saint-Omer.

### 6. On the Place Where the Disciple Rejoined His Master

At this monastery the disciple who wrote these things had arrived four or five days earlier, as we said above, in obedience to the command imposed upon him, and was awaiting his lord’s arrival at the noble abbey of Saint-Bertin, outstanding in every holiness. Therefore, as soon as news of his lord’s arrival was received, I came that very night. I rejoiced indeed at seeing my lord, but also deeply sympathized when I heard him himself recount the difficulties and perils of his journey: how he travelled by night and hid by day; how he went on foot; and how, having put on the short tunic in which I then saw him, he changed both his clothing and his name, being called Christian by his travelling companions as if it were his proper name, as we have mentioned above.

How unusual was the severity of his fare amid such labour! He was like another chosen vessel tested by perils on the road, perils at sea, perils from the nations, perils among false brethren, labour, hardship, vigils, hunger and thirst, fastings, cold, a short tunic, and a hair-shirt. I who wrote these things, hearing and seeing this, was shaken and convulsed in all heart and body. Yet even in that sorrow all that was within me brought forth praise and thanksgiving for the ordinances of the Most High, whose way it is to humble while He raises, and to raise while He humbles.

Great indeed was the praise and thanksgiving due to the Most High for the heaven-sent constancy and equanimity of this sufferer, who repeated as he spoke with me that saying of patience: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not receive evil things?” (Job 2:10). I immediately thought of the saying of the Wise Man, who truly declares that “Whatever happens to the righteous man will not grieve him” (Prov. 12).

After this, when he in turn asked concerning my own departure and how I had been able to fulfil the command which, as I said above, he had laid upon me at the moment of his departure from Northampton, I told him. I related that I had brought with me certain silver vessels belonging to him and only one hundred marks from his revenues, which I had scarcely been able to rescue from the land as though from a fire. [Col. 1168B] I added how, immediately when his departure became known, the evil counsel of the wise had caused a royal edict to be proclaimed that all his goods should remain at peace; and how what they had devised for his harm had turned to good. Iniquity had lied to itself, while the Most High disposed all things with him and always resisted iniquity. Otherwise, unless the royal edict had been proclaimed, I should have left the country utterly empty—if indeed I should have escaped at all—while both we and all our people were exposed to plunder and spoliation.

When the archbishop heard that this had happened, he gave thanks to God, who makes the wise of the world foolish and catches them in their own craftiness. Forgetting completely what had gone before, he was strengthened, as it seemed, thinking nothing of tomorrow, although the said hundred marks alone, a few silver vessels alone, and everything else constituted the travelling provision for our longer pilgrimage, which was to last more than six years.

### 7. How the Archbishop Arrived While His Opponents Were Shipwrecked

That same night on which the archbishop crossed, the aforesaid king’s envoys entered the sea with much great equipment. A storm suddenly arose, and they scarcely landed after much hardship and danger, whereas for the archbishop and his companions the sea in their small boat had been utterly calm. The brothers who were in the boat with the archbishop testified to this, as did others from the opposing side who crossed in ships.

Truly it was the work of Him to whom winds and sea are obedient, who, when He wills, [stirs] the sea, and when He wills calms the sound of the waves. This was closely like the seventh plague of the Egyptians in the catalogue of the Egyptian plagues: when Moses stretched his rod toward heaven, the Lord gave thunder and lightning flashing over the earth, raining hail upon the earth, and hail and mingled [matter: the Latin is defective] were borne together. Yet in the land of Goshen alone, where the children of Israel were, no hail fell. Likewise, in the ninth plague of those same Egyptians, terrible darkness came over the whole land of Egypt; but wherever the children of Israel lived there was light. For that same most mighty God of Israel, then and now, thus distinguishes in both reward and punishment the righteous from the wicked, and the God-fearing from the despiser.

[Col. 1169A] Therefore, on the same night as the archbishop, the said envoys of the king entered the sea; and on the same day as the archbishop they came to the castle of Saint-Omer. And because it was widely known in the land that the Archbishop of Canterbury intended to come to that monastery of Clairmarais, to which he had now arrived, on that same night, after the night office had been sung, he entered a large and spacious lake upon which that monastery is situated, and came by boat to a certain secluded place, surrounded by waters, called by the inhabitants Eldeminster, formerly the hermitage of the blessed and glorious confessor Bertin. For he feared that, if he remained in that monastery until the next day, he might perhaps be disclosed the following day, through information given by certain persons, to the natives, and especially to the king’s envoys, who [Col. 1169B] might perhaps turn aside to see him; and, seeing him in such a state, he might become a reproach to the prosperous and an object of contempt to the proud, who would readily mock him because he had foolishly and rashly fallen from such former prosperity into such present misery. Therefore, that same night he withdrew himself and lay hidden in the said hermitage for three days. On the fourth day, at the request of Godescalc, then abbot of blessed memory, and of the community of that place, he came to the abbey of Saint Bertin, like a ray of the true sun now slowly rising upon the world and revealing itself, after days of cloud and gloom had been somewhat cleared.

### How the king’s envoys, and afterwards the archbishop’s envoys, came to the King of the Franks, and how they were received

But, leaving the archbishop still at the aforesaid monastery of Saint Bertin near Saint-Omer, [Col. 1169C] let us first pursue the journey and actions of the envoys. They departed from Saint-Omer on the day after their arrival and, on the third or fourth day, made their way to Louis, then King of the Franks, of pious memory, whom they found at the royal castle called Compiègne. Having greeted the king, they presented letters in the name of the King of England, similar in form to those which, as we said above, had been sent to the Count of Flanders: namely, that Thomas, formerly Archbishop of Canterbury, had fled his kingdom as a traitor; and therefore the king begged him, as his lord, not to receive Thomas in his land.

But when, at the opening of the letter, he heard, “Thomas, formerly archbishop,” zeal immediately seized the king, as a most devoted son of the Church, [Col. 1169D] and he was greatly moved by the expression. For an insolent word gives rise to offence; and, as the Wise Man says, “He who restrains his words is learned and prudent” (Prov. 17). The king at once asked again and again who had deposed him, and added: “Certainly, as the King of England is a king, so am I a king; nevertheless, I would not be able to depose even the least of the clerics of my kingdom.” Thus those who had been sent could neither give a prudent answer to the king’s question nor carry back an answer to their petition as they wished.

But the disciple who wrote these things, and a certain other man from the archbishop’s company—prudent and learned men—by the archbishop’s counsel and command followed the envoys’ tracks daily, without their knowing it; yet those whom we followed were always one day ahead of us. This was indeed done by counsel and contrivance, so that we might more cautiously and certainly discover their words and schemes against us. When we came to that Christian King of the Franks, from whom the envoys had departed on the preceding day, as soon as we could obtain access, we devoutly and humbly greeted him in the archbishop’s name. From the time of the chancellorship he had regarded the archbishop as energetic and held him dear because of the man’s magnificence, integrity, and ability. Since we had previously been unknown to him, he repeatedly asked, in his usual manner, whether we were of the archbishop’s household and retinue. Once he learned this, he immediately received us with a kiss and heard us kindly.

When, [Col. 1170B] according to the command of our lord the archbishop, we had laid before him our tearful history—our labours and dangers—the inmost compassion of royal clemency was deeply stirred. Thereupon he deigned to tell us how and in what terms the king had written to him against the archbishop, and what reply he himself had made. He added: “The lord King of England ought indeed, had it pleased him, before treating so great a friend of his, the archbishop, and so great a person, so harshly and cruelly, to have remembered that verse: ‘Be angry, and do not sin’ (Ps. 4).”

The aforesaid man who was with me, our companion on the road and envoy, promptly replied in a playful manner: “My lord, perhaps he would have remembered that verse if he had heard it as frequently as we did at that canonical hour.” [Col. 1170C] And the king smiled.

On the following day, before we departed, after taking counsel with the men who were with him, he granted, in response to the archbishop’s request made through us, peace and security to the archbishop within his kingdom. He added that it belonged to the ancient dignity of the crown of the kings of the Franks that exiles—and especially ecclesiastical persons—should enjoy the peace and security of kings and kingdoms, and be defended from the violence of persecutors. Yet it was a delightful and wonderful thing to our monks that, against the King of England, Duke of the Normans and Aquitanians, and Count of the Angevins—against, I say, so great a power, and against envoys so numerous and great and honourable, pleading, as we have shown above, by word and writing—we two men only, contemptible and obscure, [Col. 1170D] obtained royal peace and security so swiftly and easily. They ascribed the whole matter to Him in whose hand are the hearts of kings, and who inclines them wherever He wills. Here also one may briefly consider how great are the merits of the saints, by whose power even the hearts of imperfect earthly authorities are bent to their desires. This is attested by the examples of many Fathers, which need not be enumerated here. But in this case, among others, as we have plainly seen in the book of experience, it was due to the innocence of the holy Archbishop Thomas, now an exile, and the justice of his cause. But more of this elsewhere; let us continue the course of the history we have begun.

## 8. HOW THE ARCHBISHOP’S ENVOYS CAME TO THE APOSTOLIC LORD, AND HOW THEY WERE RECEIVED

[Col. 1171A]

Therefore, rejoicing in the gift of royal peace and security, that Christian king dismissed us in peace, with gladness and joy. But we did not immediately return to the archbishop or report anything of this to him, because we hoped soon to return. Instead, as we had been charged, we hastened to the lord pope, and came to Sens, where the envoys had arrived one day before us. That same day in the evening, having gained access to the lord pope, we greeted him in the archbishop’s name as father and lord, with the devotion and humility that were fitting. We said that we were only two men who had escaped from the heat of the house of Rechab and had come to the feet of his holiness [Col. 1171B] to announce that his son Joseph still lived, but did not rule in the land of Egypt; rather, oppressed by the Egyptians, he had almost been destroyed.

Accordingly, while he listened willingly and with a fatherly sympathy, we recounted the oppressions, distresses, and griefs of his son the archbishop: dangers in that contest at Northampton, dangers among false brethren, dangers in flight, dangers on the road, dangers at sea and dangers in the harbour itself; labour, want, and hardship; and the change of dress and name undertaken to evade snares. Hearing these things, the father of the sheep’s fathers was moved in the depths of fatherly compassion for his son. Unable to conceal his paternal feeling, he wept; and, thus pierced with sorrow, addressed these words to us who were speaking: “Your lord,” he said, “is still alive in the flesh, as you say; yet even while living in the flesh, he now more fully claims for himself the privilege of martyrdom.” Since it was already very late and we were wearied from the journey, he gave us his blessing and apostolic consolation, and sent us quickly to our lodging, to return on the following day.

### What the king’s envoys alleged against the archbishop before the apostolic lord

On the following day the lord pope entered consistory with his venerable brethren the cardinals, who were then almost all present at the curia, and heard the envoys. First, dutifully greeting the lord pope in the king’s name, they set forth the cause [Col. 1171D] of their coming. First they charged their archbishop with having disturbed the peace of kingdom and priesthood, as an enemy of peace; with having carried the cross with his own hands in the king’s court; with having celebrated the Mass of blessed Stephen the Protomartyr; and, finally, with having entered upon a secret flight, most foolishly and disgracefully abandoning his church. They alleged that he had done all this to the king’s dishonour and contempt, and to that of the whole English Church, above all of his own province.

But those among them who were thought more eloquent and polished in speech—especially Master Gilbert Foliot of London and Master Hilary, bishop of Chichester—were confused while speaking, and in several words lost both the sequence of their speech and even the proper pronunciation of their accents, [Col. 1172A] in accordance with the saying of the Wise Man: “Because of a similar slip of the tongue, they fall as though upon a pavement” (Ecclus. 20). All this was then ascribed, and truly ought to be ascribed, to the work and power of Him who opens the mouths of the dumb and makes foolish the tongues of the eloquent.

The apostolic lord, who had learned both the cause of the disagreement between king and archbishop and the truth of what had occurred, not only from our faithful but secret account but from that of many others, gave no credence to the accusers. Rather, in public consistory he urged the bishops to deal more sparingly with their archbishop. Seeing this, the envoys strongly and urgently demanded in the king’s name that he send the archbishop back to England, together with a legate from his side, who, with appeal set aside, should hear the case there between king and archbishop and either reconcile them or conclude the case by judgment. There, they added, the truth of the events could be discovered more truly and conveniently.

But the Roman pontiff, neither granting nor refusing this request as yet, earnestly urged them to await the archbishop’s arrival at the curia, then to press their accusations in his presence, or, if alleging nothing against him, to make their request. He added that nothing ought to be determined against him in his absence, nor ought they to be heard in the manner they sought. But they refused to wait, because, as they said, they did not dare remain at the curia beyond the term fixed for them by the king. Repeatedly and urgently they demanded the fulfilment of the king’s stated request.

[Col. 1172C] The Roman pontiff was thus pressed hard. He saw the king’s youth and extensive dominion, and that harsh and terrible schism then afflicting God’s Church. He feared that, if the king suffered a refusal, especially when his request had been made by envoys so great and honourable, there would be a greater rupture in the Church; and this was what the envoys themselves, especially the laymen, threatened. On the other hand, he feared to send the archbishop back by his own authority to the island in which he was now treated as a public enemy, and from which, with such difficulty and through so many dangers, he had already emerged as though the Lord Himself had led him out. For in that way the archbishop’s innocence and the cause of justice might be crushed; he might thereby provoke God’s judgment against himself, and scandal would arise throughout the Church. Perhaps it was also for this reason that he feared to send him back to the island. For to contend in an island against the king of islands is like a man bound in prison fighting against the master and lord of the prison.

[Col. 1172D] Therefore the apostolic lord was constrained, especially because many of his brother cardinals—chiefly those accustomed to seek the favour of princes and magnates—judged that the king’s request ought to be granted, while others opposed it. Yet, after weighing the counsel at last and receiving from above the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Father of fathers could not dissemble. He decreed that the king’s stated request, conceived for the burden and oppression of the archbishop, was not to be fulfilled unless they would await the archbishop’s arrival at the curia; otherwise nothing was to be done against him in his absence.

But they, refusing to wait and frustrated in wish and cause, returned to England not with the apostolic blessing but rather, as it is truer to believe, with a father’s curse: cursed in themselves and in their offspring, because they did not cover their father’s shameful parts but, on the contrary, did not fear brazenly to uncover them. They hurried all the more because they feared a secret report that some knights of the land, favouring the archbishop and hating them, had prepared ambushes for their baggage on the road, baggage in which a considerable quantity of silver was expected. Thus they hastily and suddenly left France, fleeing many there who stood quite ready to despoil them because, as we have said, they favoured the archbishop.

[Col. 1173A] For, in a wonderful and incredible manner, as soon as the archbishop’s case became known throughout the whole world of churches, the Lord gave him the grace and favour of all, while stirring up against his opponents, conversely, the hatred of all. This was surely done by Him “whom a people whom He did not know served, and whom they obeyed at the hearing of the ear.” For it is scarcely possible that one who pleases the Author of all, and to whom the Author of all is pleasing, should not please everyone. Thus it is written of one of the saints: “Whomever God had suffused with grace was loved by all.” So much so that even persecutors of the Christian name, though they killed Christians by diverse and exquisite punishments, nevertheless commended them for the virtues which they observed. But more fully on this elsewhere; let us continue the course of the history we have begun.

## 9. HOW THE KING’S ENVOYS RETURNED TO ENGLAND, AND HOW THE ARCHBISHOP WAS RECEIVED BY THE KING OF THE FRANKS

[Col. 1173C] Thus, without waiting for the archbishop at the curia, the envoys returned to England, their enterprise unsuccessful and their purpose and desire frustrated. But the archbishop, whom we left above still in Flanders, at Saint-Omer in the renowned and religious abbey of Saint Bertin, remained there only a few days because of the plots in the land which, as we said above, he feared. By night he left Flanders, but with horses and the company of many men. For Milo, then bishop of Thérouanne, of good memory, and the above-named abbot of Saint Bertin, accompanied him for the security of the journey, led him out of the land, and brought him to that illustrious city of Gaul, Soissons.

By the Lord’s providence, the King of the Franks came there on the day after the archbishop’s arrival. [Col. 1173D] That Christian king, whom among the other ornaments of virtue the royal eminence adorned with the distinction of perfect humility, as soon as he heard that the Archbishop of Canterbury was in the city, came down to his lodging.
