He forestalled him in greeting and received him with every eagerness and joy: out of royal clemency, sympathizing with his distress and labour; out of royal magnificence, granting peace and security; and out of royal generosity, urging him to accept from the treasury whatever expenditure was necessary for as long as he remained an exile. Thus many now said: “The Lord gave; the Lord took away. The Lord took from the Archbishop of Canterbury the King of England; the Lord gave him the King of the Franks.”

Indeed, as we said above, the king had already granted peace and security to the archbishop through his envoys. Yet the king was seen by the archbishop first in this aforesaid city, before the envoys of peace had returned to the archbishop; for they had immediately, as we said above, followed on the heels of the English envoys, who had hastened to the lord pope at Sens against the archbishop. Seeing the king’s heart thus disposed toward him, the archbishop returned devout thanks to God and to the king, above all pursuing with heart and mouth the fullest thanksgiving to Him in whose hand are the hearts of kings.

It should also be remembered here that the archbishop already had, from that point onward, travelling provisions for himself and his companions for the long remaining route of his pilgrimage—[lacuna] given, as we said above—yet he refused to accept the expenses [Col. 1174B] so magnificently and liberally offered by the king himself on his word, since he had always been more ready to give than to receive, according to the Lord’s accustomed saying that it is more blessed to give than to receive. Still, the archbishop did not refuse altogether what the king offered. Thanking the king, he said that it was not yet time to receive, nor did necessity yet press him. Thus the lord king and the archbishop remained for some days in the city; then the archbishop departed from the king in great favour and hurried from Soissons to the lord pope. The king immediately entrusted to him members of his own household, to provide him with necessities on the journey and to guide him.

## 10. HOW THE ARCHBISHOP WAS RECEIVED BY THE APOSTOLIC LORD, AND CONCERNING THE CAUSE OF HIS EXILE

[Col. 1174C]

Thus we came to the lord pope at Sens. He received the arriving archbishop with fatherly kindness, sympathizing as a father with his manifold affliction and his journey so dangerous and hard. After a few days, the archbishop and his advisers resolved to lay before the lord pope and the cardinals the whole cause of the disagreement in England between the king and himself, and of his departure from the land. For the lord pope had not yet asked this of him, perhaps waiting for the archbishop, as a prudent man, to do so unasked. This course pleased the archbishop. For although the origin and cause of the whole evil had previously been communicated through his own envoys, and reported piecemeal by others travelling hither and thither, [Col. 1174D] it nevertheless seemed wiser that he himself should set forth the merits of his cause, recount the truth of what had occurred, and himself erase the stains which the aforesaid English envoys had attempted to impress upon him.

Accordingly, a few days after our arrival at the curia, in the presence of the lord pope and venerable cardinal bishops—not publicly in consistory, but more privately in a chamber—he narrated the whole sequence of events and the cause of his departure in a pleasing and concise brevity. Pleasing, I say, because his eloquence was restrained and elegant, and his tongue never gave offence. In regard to the granting of those customs which, as we said above, had been fabricated and put into writing at Clarendon, he plainly confessed and did not deny how he had fallen; and he stated by what means he had been led into that fall, matters which we have shown above when dealing with them. Then and there that fatal document, drawn up in the form of a charter, of which we have sufficiently spoken above, was brought forth and unfolded. Until now neither pope nor cardinals had heard the document itself, though they had heard of it. Therefore all its contents were immediately read aloud in the hearing of the lord pope and cardinals: namely, the sixteen customs.

[Col. 1175A] Although perhaps this would be the place for it, I have not wished to insert that document here in the course of this historical little book, both because of the excessive coarseness and impropriety of its language, and to avoid the length of this historical book now in hand. Yet that document contains the cause of our exile and martyrdom; indeed, God favouring, when this historical little book has been completed, it shall be written at its end. And whoever wishes to transcribe this historical little book should always transcribe that document at the end as well; and it should be read by those who do not know it but desire to know the cause of the exile and martyrdom of the most glorious martyr Thomas.

After all that was contained in the document had been read, with some passages read and reread, and every point carefully and attentively heard and understood, the lord pope was most sharply stirred and at once burned with indignation against the archbishop. He rebuked and harshly reproached him because, by assenting to those things which, as the pope said, were not customs [Col. 1175C] but tyrannical usurpations, both he and the bishops who were with him had renounced their priesthood and enslaved God’s Church. He added that it would have been far better to endure every danger than to consent to such overthrowings of God’s law. He recalled the holy history of the seven Maccabean brothers, wonderful indeed to all but imitable by few. He reproached him that they, though they were not evangelical priests or even priests under the Law but Jewish young laymen, suffered diverse and exquisite punishments with ready and devoted minds, not even for the evangelical law but for their ancestral law—for the law concerning swine.

He added: “Nevertheless, among these abominations which have here been read in our presence and heard from you, there are no good things, but some are tolerable. The Church can in some fashion tolerate these; but the greater part of them have been condemned by ancient and authoritative councils, since they are directly contrary to sacred enactments.” It is not necessary for us now to distinguish which things are these and which those, since this is clear even to those who have but slight knowledge of the sacred canons.

Nevertheless, the apostolic lord, in the hearing of the cardinals and in our presence, immediately rejected the aforesaid customs with brief but extreme indignation, just as the archbishop had done, and judged them henceforth to be condemned by the Church on account of these same causes. At last he turned to the archbishop and said: “Nevertheless, brother, although the transgression of you and your brother bishops has been great and monstrous, we must deal with you more gently. For though, as you yourself confess, you fell, you attempted to rise at once after your fall, and because of that fall have already endured many grievous and harsh things. As soon as you had fallen, while you were still in England, you sought and obtained from our clemency, through our letters, the benefit of absolution. And as though this were not enough, because confession is not customarily made through an envoy or in writing, now at last, confessing your fall devoutly and humbly, you have approached the apostolic see through much labour and varied dangers. Therefore it is fitting, and we grant it to you, that in your adversities you should feel the consolation and grace of our clemency more fully and affectionately than other ecclesiastical persons, inasmuch as you have abandoned greater things and endured graver ones for the liberty of the Church and for faith in and devotion to us.”

Thus the apostolic lord first rebuked the archbishop with fatherly severity, and then restored him with the sweetness of maternal consolation; and so he dismissed him. Having received this apostolic consolation, we returned joyfully to our lodging.

## 11. HOW HE WAS REBUKED BY THE CARDINALS FOR HAVING RAISED HIMSELF AGAINST THE KING IN A TIME OF SCHISM

But on the following day, the archbishop was rebuked, with a certain kindly and friendly sharpness, by some cardinals and by many other great and learned men of the curia, powerful in the Scriptures—for the curia was accustomed to abound and flourish in such men—as though by his familiar friends and supporters. [Col. 1176C] They said that in those very evil days, namely in the time of schism and amid the ruins of the Church, he had raised himself against his prince, against so great a power. One should rather yield to the time and endure, they said, since then was the hour and power of darkness; indeed, Peter was commanded not to wield his sword, but to put it back.

Further, they added, tares sown by the enemy among the wheat were not then to be gathered by the Gospel servants, lest in rooting them out they should uproot the wheat together with them; thus, according to the command of the householder, both are allowed to grow together until the time. This is also the counsel of the Teacher himself, who, because of the evil of the days, advises that time be redeemed: “Redeeming the time,” he says, “because the days are evil” (Eph. 5). Likewise the prophet: “Therefore the prudent man shall keep silence in that time, because it is an evil time” (Prov. 11).

They further added that the strong columns of the Church, in order to support the fabric of the Church more enduringly and firmly, are sometimes, by the hand of discretion, transformed for a time as it were into frail and slender reeds. For such reeds it is better to bend and yield for a while to the violent blast of the storm than to be broken by resisting beyond their strength. This the Teacher too, according to the wisdom given him, both taught and did. For though he preached the abolition of the old law, he himself nevertheless yielded to the time and fulfilled in himself the law whose abolition he taught: cutting his hair according to the law and being purified according to the law, entering the Temple and offering sacrifices, and even circumcising Timothy. Finally, although he was teacher of the Gentiles, advocate of the Jews, and the greatest among the great teachers of God, since he had learned the Gospel neither from man nor through man, yet after all these things he submitted himself to earthly authority by appealing to Caesar. Thus in all these acts he judged that, when the time so requires, one must yield to time and redeem time for the time.

### How the archbishop answered the cardinals’ objections

Having heard these things, the archbishop—who, being prudent, expected such objections to be made against him at the curia by its great and wise men, and who had already considered the matter with his own advisers and arranged his words for judgment—promptly answered according to the wisdom and grace given to him:

“Brothers,” he said, “I do not deny that, as you men so learned and instructed say, one must yield to time for the sake of the time, and endure much for the sake of the time. I acknowledge, I say, that in this hour and power of darkness—when there is so great an emperor, Frederick, and so great an antipope, Octavian, such distinguished schismatics—I acknowledge that Peter’s sword ought not to be wielded, but, as you say, put back, even against Catholic princes who have not departed from the Church but have remained within it, though they sin greatly; lest perhaps a worse division arise in God’s Church, especially because the evil of division always seeks to acquire more partners.

[Col. 1177C] For the evil of a time may be so great that nothing remains to the Church but groaning and sorrow, and a cry to the Lord; then the severity of ecclesiastical discipline sleeps, and the Church will obtain salvation solely through the prophetic *tau*. This is the evil time: when no hope remains for the correction of evildoers, but vengeance belongs to God alone, as the Lord Himself says: ‘Vengeance is mine’ (Heb. 10). You remember what was said above through the prophet: ‘Therefore the prudent man shall keep silence in that time, because it is an evil time’ (Prov. 11). Then indeed, according to the counsel of the Wise Man, room must be given to the vengeance of the Most High.

“But there is another time: when hope remains for the correction of the wicked. Then indeed one must wait, endure, and pray for those whom one endures. Otherwise, as it is said through the Wise Man, ‘Woe to those who have lost endurance’ (Ecclus. 2). The first is a dark time, and then is the hour and power of darkness; then, according to the Lord’s word, Peter’s sword must be put back. The second is, as it were, a cloudy time, and then Peter’s sword must be suspended, to be resumed in due time. According to these times Scripture speaks variously of ecclesiastical vengeance, or of Peter’s evangelical sword: now of wielding it, now of putting it back, and at other times of suspending and resuming it according to the time.

“You, brothers, know these things much better than I, since in so great a school of the teacher of the whole Church you daily learn or teach them. Yet we say these things in your hearing, not that a disciple may teach his masters, [Col. 1178A] but lest you suspect that I still ask or desire that this sword be drawn against my prince and lord, the King of England, even though he has acted more harshly against me. First one must endure and seek royal clemency with patient expectation, according to the counsel of the Wise Man: ‘My son, complete your works in gentleness, and you shall be loved beyond human glory’ (Ecclus. 3). For tranquillity sometimes accomplishes what violence cannot; whence also that saying of the pagan poet:

> … Quiet power accomplishes  
> What violent power cannot.

And one of the doctors says: ‘Humanity often bends those whom neither strength nor reason could overcome.’

“Therefore, not as you charge, do I fail to comply; rather, I comply, and gladly comply, with the time. I do not anticipate the time, but endure and am ready to endure, until, by the Lord’s favour, pardon follows upon the anger of my lord the king. So much so that, if I saw a sword drawn against him, I would place myself in its way and meet it, though it were drawn against me, to turn it upon myself. For first is the time of endurance; afterwards the time of mercy and justice, so that we may sing to the Lord of mercy and judgment.

“Nevertheless, as we have already touched upon, lest I dare say anything contrary to apostolic decrees or prejudicial to truth, it is neither without distinction nor altogether true that in evil days or in a time of schism ecclesiastical vengeance ought not to be exercised, or Peter’s sword drawn, against princes or against those who have a multitude of associates. For in a time of schism princes of peoples who have not departed from the Church but have remained within it may so dreadfully and harshly shake the sides of their mother Church by disturbing her peace, and shake out her entrails, that she would cast them away from herself as abortions and they would become as heathens and tax collectors.

“Thus the Teacher, while the new Church was still a tender planting, draws the evangelical sword not only against those who shake her sides and pour out her entrails—such as those who oppress ecclesiastical persons and disturb her peace—but also against those who disfigure the Church’s face with diverse stains of crimes: ‘If one called a brother is a fornicator, or covetous, or a worshipper of idols, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a one do not even eat’ (1 Cor. 5). And elsewhere: ‘If anyone does not obey our word by this letter, mark that man and do not associate with him, that he may be ashamed’ (2 Thess. 3).

[Col. 1178D] “Behold: while the Church was still tender and new, when she was still little in the cradle of her birth and already every hand was against her, the Teacher nevertheless confidently and fearlessly wielded the sword, in order that he might present to the Bridegroom a glorious bride, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor any such thing, but holy and without blemish. If, then, the Teacher of the Gentiles dared to do this in the tender and newly planted Church, there is much less reason for fear now, when, according to the prophet’s oracle, the Church has been set in the pride of all ages.

“Elsewhere too the Teacher rebukes the disciples whom he had appointed prelates at the beginnings of the rising Church: ‘You endure it,’ he says, ‘if anyone brings you into slavery, if anyone devours you, if anyone takes from you, if anyone strikes you in the face’ (2 Cor. 11). Behold the Teacher’s rebuke of disciples whom he had made prelates over the still new Church, because they endured ecclesiastical slavery. If such slavery was by no means to be endured then, when, as we have said, she herself was still little and every hand was against her, much less is it to be endured now.

“For even if there is now a schism, as has happened more frequently in the Roman Church, nevertheless those considered schismatics profess the Christian faith. They wound the Church indeed, but do not destroy her; by the Lord’s mercy they will shortly return to obedience to the Roman Church. And if ecclesiastical examples do not suffice, let us take examples even from the heathen. Among them one of the pagan poets commends another pagan in verse because, under a harsh prince and in evil times, he dared to be good—that is, free—addressing the man whom he commends in these words:

> You deserve praise because, under a harsh prince,
In evil times you dared to be good. “Good,” he says, that is, free—thus specifying the general term “good.” And indeed, unless the Church freely and fearlessly wields the sword against violators of ecclesiastical peace, the ecclesiastical judge bears the sword for no purpose.

Moreover, this ecclesiastical peace is disturbed not only by schismatics and heretics, but often also by tyrants who are sons of the Church. As we noted above [Col. 1179C], shaking the sides of their mother, they cast out her entrails; they oppress and expel ecclesiastical persons, enact new laws, and take away the liberty of the clergy, which is the Church’s beauty and strength. Thus they enslave the Church, set amid the pride of the ages, so that priest and people are alike.

Against such persons, therefore, even in a time of schism or heresy, ecclesiastical censure must be exercised and Peter’s sword must be drawn, just as against schismatics and heretics. Otherwise the vicar of Christ, Peter’s successor, bears this sword without cause, as we have said: like one inactive and fearful in wartime, he does not draw it but hides it, and the Church’s strength is not perfected in adversity but weakened. This is what the king and prophet lamented: “My strength has been weakened in my poverty” (Ps. 30 [Vulgate]). [Col. 1179D] But, conversely, the Master glories in his strength amid weakness: “When I am weak,” he says, “then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12). And elsewhere he says to his disciple: “Remember that the Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead according to my Gospel, for which I labour even unto bonds, as an evildoer; but the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2).

So too, following the Master’s example, the Church should glory in its strength amid its weakness. Thus the word of God—the sword of the Spirit—is not to be bound; rather, amid bonds it is then wielded more gloriously. The Church has no reason to hesitate or fear, for, as one of the distinguished doctors says: “It is peculiarly characteristic of her that she understands when she is reproved, conquers when she is wounded, and prevails when she is forsaken.” And, as another of the doctors says [Col. 1180A], she “rejoices in adversity, is enlarged by distress, raised up by sorrow, nourished by tears, watered by blood, made fruitful by deaths; she always knows how to triumph while pressed down by the calamities of the world, and grows precisely where the world declines.”

For she is an ark which, the more violently it is battered by the waves of the world, rises the higher. Therefore, brethren, as you have intimated to me in a certain suggestion of words, there is no reason, even in this time of schism, for the Church to fear, or to fear for the Church, so as to prevent the vicar of Christ, Peter’s successor, from wielding Peter’s sword against violators of ecclesiastical peace. I say: the Church need not fear, nor fear for the Church.

For, to introduce the surest and unshakable testimony, according to the word of Truth Himself in the Gospel, this Church is that house [Col. 1180B] of the wise man built upon solid rock, and therefore need not fear the assaults of winds or floods. For she is raised upon the rock, secure upon the rock, standing firm upon the rock—safe from the enemy and strong against a fall. And if the rock still does not suffice: “He has set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18 [Vulgate]): the Church is founded in Christ, the sun of righteousness. Hence also the Master says: “A foundation has been laid which no one can change, which is Christ Jesus.”

Let us therefore stand together, brethren—we who have not gone backward—and let not our strength be weakened in this poverty, this diminution of ours, this time of schism. But when the time requires, let us be not servants of worldly fear but ministers of justice. For it is written: “Justice and peace have kissed” (Ps. 84 [Vulgate]). They have kissed well, he says: that is, they are allied and harmonious. For justice begets peace, nourishes it, and protects it from violation. Therefore these two, like mother and daughter, nurse and foster-child, or guardian and ward, delight as it were in mutual kisses and cherish one another in continual embraces. So closely allied and concordant are they that neither exists without the other. Hence one of the illustrious doctors of the Church says of their alliance and harmony: “These two love one another, so that whoever does justice finds peace—and not otherwise.”

Therefore in evil days, at a time of schism or heresy, or when tyrants inflict violence upon the Church and disturb its peace, the weapons of justice must not be laid aside. Rather, provided that I dare nothing contrary to apostolic ordinances or prejudicial to truth, I judge—according alike to the Master’s teaching and the exhortations of the saints—that ministers of justice should freely and fearlessly wield the weapons of justice without distinction against all violators of ecclesiastical peace, so that on the day of the Lord’s wars the banners of justice may advance to rescue peace held captive. [Col. 1180D]

For, as the common saying goes, arms bring peace. Justice is depicted armed, but peace crowned with laurel and unarmed, because she conquers through justice, her champion. In a time when peace is violated or held captive, it is most shameful and improper if justice hides herself; for unless justice promptly aided peace either already captive or about to be captured, justice would betray peace’s kiss with peace. For justice and peace have kissed.

And certainly, brethren, to speak the truth without sparing you: by adding to those many evasions which you just now intimated in your address that the strong pillars of the Church ought, for the time being, to be transformed even into fragile, slender reeds, you truly give horns to sinners by so much dissembling, and kings become tyrants. The foremost sons of the Church become the foremost enemies of the Church, freely raging against their mother the Church while the severity of ecclesiastical discipline lies torpid. Thus the sword of unbelievers without is more tolerable than the rebellion of sons within; and with that holy king one must lament: “Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter” (Isa. 38). [Col. 1181A]

For the first bitterness is bitter suffering from enemies; the second is more bitter, enduring it from those near to us; but the third is most bitter, being attacked by one’s sons. This is as though one’s own entrails were turned into ulcers. Therefore the Wise Man says: “If you have sons, instruct them, and bend them from their childhood” (Ecclus. 7).

But, brethren, to speak to you in foolishness—for you compel me—you seek, as I see, to turn into blame against me that which, unless I am mistaken, is to be counted to me for the highest and immortal glory. For behold: when the ark of sanctification was tilting, I put forth my hand and set my shoulders beneath it, according to the obligation and ability of my office, amid the ruins of the Church, raising up its ruins insofar as I could; and I was almost buried amid its ruins, lest the Church herself should be buried.

And if one must boast—as indeed one must, since it is now also expedient—then amid the schisms of the Roman Church, with the world as it were collapsing, my fathers and predecessors, the archbishops of Canterbury, were accustomed always to stand unbending, their necks held high, like the strongest and most steadfast pillars of God’s house. Yet, to tell you one thing—though timidly, and I hope not rashly—although you at present collapse under the scandal of so grave a schism, for whatever cause, I nevertheless shall not collapse amid the ruins of your world, as it were, while the Lord puts His hand beneath me. You, as our lords and fathers, shall do what seems good in your eyes. I, your unworthy fellow-bishop under the supreme Shepherd, and fellow-servant of the same Lord, successor—though unworthy—of so many of my fathers, will reverence their footsteps. Though I cannot attain to them, I desire at least in some measure to follow them. [Col. 1181D]

Thus, as you now see—and as I know has happened by the Lord’s ordering—I must repay, not to you but to Him, the talents entrusted to me with interest. I, I say, now endure the cross for the Church for the joy set before me, despising shame; and, whether the world will or will not, approves or disapproves, I shall endure it, ready for scourges until the hand of the justly judging Lord, now stretched out over me, chooses to withdraw.

Indeed, I am prepared for scourges even to this extent, and choose rather to suffer affliction for the Church of God than to have the passing pleasure of sin and of the royal court. For clergy, people, and world know how great I was at court, and what glory would have attended me on my elevation from court to the Church, if I obeyed in all things the will of my lord the king. Then indeed I would have been adorned with the robe of a double glory, both priestly and royal. But, to confess the truth, it now matters very little to me that I should be judged in this matter by any human day; at present, let the testimony of my conscience alone be my glory. And if you are willing to consider that passage, wisely and piously written, which the lord pope yesterday condemned in your public hearing, your obedience is no small cause of our present disturbance. [Col. 1182A]

“But as for your tacit reproach that, according to the Master’s counsel, I ought to have redeemed the time: I cannot sufficiently marvel at your prudence. For I judge that I have redeemed the time according to the Master’s counsel. And if the interpretation of the saints concerning that saying of the Master is, as it is, general and necessary, and also true, then I do not merely judge but know with complete certainty that I have redeemed this time.

“For the Master does not there teach redemption of time where the loss of ecclesiastical liberty is at stake. Hence, as we said above—and it is necessary to repeat it here—the disciple rebukes those whom he had appointed over the still rough and newly founded Church for tolerating servitude: ‘You endure it,’ he says, ‘if someone reduces you to slavery, if someone devours you, if someone takes from you, if someone strikes you in the face’ (2 Cor. 11). Behold: the Master who elsewhere exhorts us to redeem the time when the days are evil does not at all understand redemption of time where, with servitude introduced, the honour of ecclesiastical liberty is lost. There, rather than redemption of time, there is loss of time and the shameful abasement of the Church. [Col. 1182C]

“For according to the explanation of the saints, what is it to redeem the time according to the Master’s counsel? Certainly—not to introduce anything here of my own, for this teaching is not mine but the saints’—many advise that time should be redeemed, but few know how; fewer still do or undertake what they know. According to the Master’s counsel and the saints’ interpretation, then, what is redeeming the time? It is giving and receiving temporal things: giving and receiving time—that is, an opportunity to serve God and to devote oneself to divine things. Temporal things—worldly and earthly occupations and concerns—turn us away from this. Therefore, to obtain time, temporal things must be given up for time; and thus we redeem time.

“Hence the Master of masters says in the Gospel, from which this saying of the Master seems to have taken its origin: ‘If anyone wishes to contend with you in court and take your tunic, let him have your cloak also’ (Matt. 5). As though He said: Do not, because of temporal losses, temporal anxieties, or lawsuits, lose the peace and quiet of your heart, so that you have no time to devote yourself to your God. Otherwise you redeem not the time according to the Master’s counsel, but lose it.

“This worn and ancient proverb of the pagans also agrees with this evangelical teaching: ‘The plague demands a coin; give it two, and let it be gone.’ Consider then, brethren, if you please, and observe whether I have not done this, whether I have not redeemed the time—I who gave temporal things for time; who abandoned the wealth and honour of the Church of Canterbury, which shines pre-eminent among the churches of the western world, together with the favour and glory of my lord [Col. 1183A] the king, for the liberty and peace of myself and of the clergy entrusted to me. By the Lord’s favour, I shall yet receive grace for grace and glory for glory, both for myself and for the Church. Among other reasons, I left the land by flight especially because at that time I could not have borne fruit there.

“This is also how that Apollos, the Master’s disciple, whom he had ordained bishop of the Corinthians, deserted them by fleeing, because he could not have pacified them. Thus, though earnestly asked by the Master, he was unwilling then to return to them, fearing that because of their incorrigibility he would bear no fruit. Of him the Master says to the disciples: ‘I make known to you concerning our brother Apollos how earnestly I urged him to come to you with the brethren; and it was certainly not his will to come at that time’ (1 Cor. 16).

“Thus many other good shepherds, for a similar reason, either wholly abandoned a flock once entrusted to them, or were transferred from one flock to another where they might more usefully expend the care of their pastoral office. Therefore I think it unnecessary to weave an apology either for their flight or for mine—especially since I withdrew myself not only because their correction was desperate, but also lest, by remaining, I should promote death more than life. [Col. 1183B]

“For had I remained in the land and opposed myself amid such a blaze of royal anger, I would easily have added sorrow to sorrow with great loss to ecclesiastical liberty. For, according to the Wise Man’s saying: ‘As the roaring of a lion, so is the anger of a king’ (Prov. 20). Anger has no mercy; and who can endure the onset of aroused fury? Therefore yielding at that time was the more prudent course. Otherwise a man who knowingly and deliberately meets a roaring lion, or strives against the swiftest rush of a torrent, might seem like not a governor of souls but rather a madman and rash fool. The Wise Man expressly forbids this: ‘Do not resist the face of a powerful man, and do not strive against the force of a river’ (Ecclus. 4).

“I followed this advice and yielded. For the heart of the prince—which, as the world knows, was once so much in my hands—has now, through my sins requiring it, become so hardened against me that, as I said, I withdrew by flight. Yet my flight does not strengthen by authority the servitude recently imposed upon the English Church; rather, with the Lord’s favour and the putting forth of His hand, it will finally and completely cast off that yoke all the more forcefully. Indeed, as appears from what has been said, unless I am mistaken, this servitude has been shaken more by my flight than it would have been had I then rashly resisted; by fleeing I thus opposed it.

“I do not say this, nor did I flee in this manner, because I wish to offer my successors an example of flight—unless perhaps it should be expedient and an urgent necessity of circumstances require it. I say it because Canterbury, when it contends against its prince, though gloriously when it has cause, nevertheless always contends dangerously. For it is as when a metropolitan in an island opposes an island king: as though a prisoner, held in chains and in the dark recesses of a prison, were to challenge his jailer. Almost all my predecessors experienced this danger. [Col. 1184A] For this has always been the hard and perilous struggle of all true archbishops of Canterbury: either that they oppose their king within the island, or, if flight is more expedient, that after beginning their flight they leave the island through many snares and straits of ambush.

“And I shall set before you one example: my immediate predecessor, my father and lord of blessed memory, Archbishop Theobald. I was his inseparable companion both in many other dangers and distresses and in the action which I shall now recall. It happened, as it often does, that a quarrel arose between the apostolic man Eugenius of holy memory and Stephen, then king of the English. The king forbade the archbishop and the persons of the realm, contrary to the apostolic command, to cross the sea to the Council of Reims, then being convened. Yet the archbishop, striving by every means to obey, secretly departed by night, in extreme danger; with two or three companions scarcely acquainted with the sea, he entrusted himself to the waves and winds of the ocean in a small and frail boat. Thus, as though without sailor or oar, he reached Reims.

“When he appeared at the council, the apostolic man had already learned the peril of his journey, and immediately said publicly before the whole council: ‘This is our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Canterbury; and he crossed the ocean to come to us more by swimming than by rowing.’ Thus my father fled at that time for a cause, as I do now. Otherwise, when there is cause, if an Archbishop of Canterbury does neither of these things, he degenerates from his fathers and will be not legitimate but illegitimate; for such a one perhaps stands outside the discipline in which all his fathers have shared.” [Col. 1184C]

When he had said these things, some listeners praised the archbishop’s zeal in leaving the land as necessary; others, not at all persuaded by what they had heard, repeated their earlier accusation, saying that it would have been better to remain in the land and endure at such a time. But the lord pope rebuked only this, as we said above: that, for whatever reason, he had consented to the aforesaid customs. Since we have so great a supporter of our departure, let us set aside for the moment those who objected and continue the course of the history we have begun.

## 12. HOW THE ARCHBISHOP CHOSE PONTIGNY FOR HIS PILGRIMAGE

When we had already spent some days at the curia, [Col. 1184D] the archbishop deliberated with his companions and considered some religious place to which we might withdraw more conveniently and honourably await the divinely provided outcome of our pilgrimage. Since it seemed more expedient for us who were conducting the Church’s cause to retire to one of the monasteries, out of regard for religious life, we chose before all others to live as exiles in a monastery of that holy Cistercian order. We chose it both because of the order’s outstanding religious observance and because of its great quiet and peace: the professed members of that order are removed from the world in body as well as heart.

Among the other monasteries of the order we selected one situated in Burgundy, named Pontigny. The religious observance of that monastery was regarded as distinguished and excellent. It was near the aforesaid city of Sens, where the lord pope was then staying because of the schism, being only twelve leagues distant; moreover, the monastery’s resources were extensive and abundant, and it had great charity in giving. [Col. 1185A]

Accordingly, at our request the apostolic man summoned the abbot of the place and the leading brethren. When the abbot and brothers learned more certainly, both from the lord pope’s account and from the widespread renown which they had previously heard, the archbishop’s uprightness and courage, and especially the cause of the Church which he was pursuing, they immediately gave most devout thanks to the Lord, by whose inspiration His champion had selected such a place as a kind of training-ground for his struggle.

Thus, after we had spent about three weeks at the curia from the time of our arrival, we received apostolic permission and blessing and came to Pontigny. The whole convent received us with such eagerness and joy as though we were a sacrifice sent from heaven. Showing us every kindness, they readily and voluntarily granted us, beyond the rule of the order, the eating of meat and certain other concessions. The order’s generosity and humanity toward us proved greater than can now be described. On the third or fourth day after our arrival, the archbishop entered the chapter house and commended to God and to their prayers the cause of the Church which he was pursuing. Then, our little bundles having been arranged and neighboring but separate lodgings assigned to us within the monastic enclosure, all of us whose duty it was immediately began diligently to devote ourselves to reading the sacred writings. [Col. 1185C]

After the many troubles of the archbishop which we have described above, he, as though emerging from dense and cloudy weather, immediately began to turn his whole mind toward the serenity and tranquillity of divine light, giving himself wholly to reading, prayer, and meditation. This was the life which, from the beginning of his promotion to the archbishopric—and even during his time as chancellor, as I received it from himself—he had preferred amid the vanities of the world, knowing that, as the Wise Man says, “Wisdom is written in leisure,” and likewise is learned and taught in leisure.

That monastery was therefore for us like a training-ground of contest, in which we were exercised, and likewise a school of virtues in which we were instructed for battle, so that every day we said to the Lord: “It is good for us that you have humbled us, that we might learn your ordinances.”

## CONCERNING THOSE EXPELLED FROM ENGLAND AND PROSCRIBED ON ACCOUNT OF THE ARCHBISHOP

But while we were thus being instructed and exercised in great quiet and leisure, after some days there came from England a bearer of harsh news. He announced that, upon the arrival in England of the aforesaid envoys from the lord pope, because, as we have shown above, they had returned disappointed of their purpose and with their petition unfulfilled, all the movable and immovable goods of the archbishop and his companions were confiscated by the king’s edict. It was as though another messenger brought Job news: “Behold, the Sabeans, rushing in, have taken everything” (Job 1).

Yet we endured even this joyfully, accepting the plundering of our goods with joy and crying out with that brave athlete: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done.” [Col. 1186A] But the man who had come added what caused us much greater suffering, since we sympathized with the sufferers: namely, that the whole kindred of the archbishop, all who had been his household servants, and all who had received from him any service of patronage, had all been expelled and proscribed and compelled to abjure the land. This was also contained in their oath: that they would not halt anywhere on the road, but would present themselves before the archbishop wherever he might be found, so that the archbishop’s anger might be further intensified and grow with grief.

The same and equal fury also raged against the kindred of those who had followed the archbishop out of the land. Thus both groups—the kindred of the archbishop and the kindred of his followers—were expelled and proscribed. All abjured the land of their birth, unless perhaps some could ransom themselves by payment of a large sum of money. But this was granted to very few. Therefore, in consequence of this edict, a great multitude, their goods all confiscated, left the land in great poverty and distress: men and women, youths and maidens, old people with younger ones, male and female servants, little children even in cradles, and infants still hanging at their mothers’ breasts. No regard was shown to sex, no deference to age, no consideration to rank; as though another messenger brought Job news again: “Behold, a wind from the wilderness shook the house, and it fell and crushed your children” (ibid.). [Col. 1186B]

A certain courtly retainer was set over all these confiscations and this punitive enforcement solely out of hatred for the archbishop. He had long hated the archbishop, and was chosen to carry out this work of malice precisely in order that the archbishop might be further embittered; it was confidently expected that he would pass over not one iota of the penal commands. This was Ranulf, surnamed de Broc, who is believed to have added something of his own beyond the command, adding sorrow to sorrow. For malice, though it sometimes has little power, always has many attempts; when an opportunity is granted and powers for evil are allowed by a superior, it always extends itself without measure and exceeds the limits set for wrongdoing.

[Col. 1186D] This malice indeed extended itself even to something unheard of, the more impious because the more profane. Since the Church was daily offering prayer for its archbishop, now a pilgrim, a public edict prohibited it from being done thereafter throughout the land. Thus we were barred from so common and universal an aid of the Church, like public enemies forbidden water and fire. Yet the broad command of the loving and compassionate Lord extends even to heretics, Jews, pagans, and even to those who crucified Christ.

But while the father was in exile and, as it were, now in danger, the mouths even of his children were closed, lest they aid their endangered father. Thus one must fear—unless I am mistaken, and if the true and just God so ordains—that at some time it may come to pass that the measure in which they measured for us may be measured back to those who measured it for us: sons may rise against father and father against sons; two may be divided against three and three against two; and out of division may finally come destruction. [Col. 1187A]

O malice—how living, powerful, penetrating you are! You wound man, the very image of God, not merely by piercing but rather by perforating him, and so dry up from man, as from a natural fountain of compassion, every sweetness of humanity that even to a father is denied by his sons what they themselves owe to those who persecute and slander them. For man is man by nature, and humane by nature; indeed, to speak more plainly and not rhetorically but properly, man himself has mercy and compassion implanted as certain primordial seeds of his nature from his very origin. These are, as it were, privileges of the divine nature which the Most High reserved to Himself alone from the beginning.

Yet the same wise, uniquely pious and merciful Creator of all adorned and beautified His image with them in the creation of man—except that, alas, through disobedience the stains of faults were quickly laid over it through the wrath of the avenging and justly judging Lord. But when that blackened image is restored by the hand of the merciful Creator, the ancient enemy is nowhere more driven and put to flight from this image of God than when he sees it adorned and beautified with compassion and mercy, as with most precious colours. Immediately, as though struck back by the dark and dreadful brilliance of the image, that power of darkness is driven away, flees, and fears to approach. [Col. 1187C]

But in this deed—detestable to all ages—malice, having most wicked anger as its counsellor, has taken captive in man the nature of man against nature itself, so that man, if indeed he is still man, here surpasses the savagery of every beast. For, to repeat in lament what must be lamented in repetition and repeated in lament: what is more inhuman than this act? Or, to speak still more plainly, what in man is more inhuman, what more dishonourable?

Here miserable mothers are driven out and proscribed with their little children still hanging at their breasts. Here, on the other hand, the common aid owed to all is taken away even from the father himself by his children; and the mouths of children praying to God for their endangered father are stopped. Turn and turn again the whole course of history; read and see whether in any persecution or proscription since the beginning of the world such a deed has been heard of.

## CONCERNING THE EXHORTATORY ADDRESS WITH WHICH THE ARCHBISHOP’S LEARNED COMPANIONS ADDRESSED HIM

When the archbishop first heard, and later saw, these events, he became anxious and sorrowful, and no longer showed the countenance which he had worn yesterday and the day before. Perceiving this, the learned companions of the archbishop’s pilgrimage approached him with an address at once exhortatory and consolatory:

“My lord,” they said, “why, on hearing this new report from England, has your face fallen so, and your countenance changed so completely? If it please you, bear with us now addressing you for a little while. For yours and ours—the cause of us who have followed you—is common; our punishment is common; our struggle is common; and, with the Lord’s favour, our victory and crown will be common.” [Col. 1188A]

“This newly added punishment of those expelled and proscribed, common to you and us—if it is a punishment—is medicinal. We say ‘if it is a punishment’ because, as it seems to us, it ought rather to be called a medicine than a punishment: a biting poultice, as it were, laid by the heavenly physician upon the wounds of our sins. Let us not therefore, through impatience, repel from ourselves the hand of the physician who heals us, nor grow weary because we are rebuked by a father, if the father adds scourges upon the backs of his sons. Let us not, I say, grow weary or weep because of the scourges, but let each of us sing with the penitent and scourged Prophet: ‘For I am ready for scourges’ (Ps. 37 [Vulgate]), if perhaps even thus the Lord, avenger of all injuries and all wrongs, may punish all our contrivances.

“For this reason God is said through the same Prophet to have been favourable to Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, because He punished all their contrivances: ‘O God, you were favourable to them, and avenging all their contrivances’ (Ps. 98 [Vulgate]). Unpunished wickedness is great wrath of God. Hence the Prophet, first prosperous and then scourged, says afterwards: ‘Do not envy the man who prospers in his way’ (Ps. 36 [Vulgate]), because, as the Lord says through another prophet, such a man is like a beast for slaughter, fattened to be led to sacrifice. [Col. 1188C]

“The prophet asks the Lord, as the Lord answers the prophet: ‘Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why do all who transgress and act unjustly fare well?’ (Jer. 12). The Lord replies: ‘Gather them like a flock for sacrifice, and consecrate them for the day of slaughter’ (ibid.). It is as if He said to the prophet: Proclaim and foretell by the prophetic spirit that they are to be gathered like a flock for sacrifice.

“And indeed, such great prosperity in this life, without any obstacle and without any scourge, is God’s mercy; yet such mercy of God surely surpasses all God’s wrath. For this mercy, according to one of the prophets, is ‘like a morning cloud and like dew passing away in the morning, like foam upon the surface of water, or like dust seized by a whirlwind from the threshing-floor, and like smoke from a chimney’ (Hos. 13). Therefore the Lord is more angry with the sinful Synagogue to which He shows mercy in this manner: ‘My zeal has departed from you; I will no longer be angry with you.’ And elsewhere, through another prophet: ‘I dismissed them according to the desires of their heart; they shall walk in their contrivances’ (Ps. 80 [Vulgate]).

“Behold the prosperity of this age, behold the prosperity of this life: it flows through the streets like amurca, the watery sediment left when oil has been pressed in the winepress and afterwards stored in cellars. And you, my lord—to speak, however, without offence to the Lord, for we are speaking God’s words—you indeed were for some time amurca flowing through the streets, with everything succeeding for you at will and according to desire, without any obstacle. But it now seems that He who turned water into wine wishes to turn the amurca into oil. If, therefore, you desire to be oil, you must endure the pressure of the winepress until you flow from the press into the storehouse. [Col. 1189A]

“Yet we are greatly troubled by the anxiety and sorrow which you show upon hearing this new report of so atrocious a deed. For we hoped that in this wilderness into which we have followed you, you would show yourself to us as a second Moses, and that under such a leader we might confidently undertake the Lord’s wars. But if you have not yet shown yourself such, you must show yourself so now, when a multitude is beginning to follow you into the wilderness.

“Therefore do not waste away in grief; do not fail in labour; do not grow faint in fear; do not let impatience dissolve you; do not let anxiety distract you; do not let cares disembowel you. Rather, in the multitude you must conduct yourself without disturbance, and amid cares as though without care, encouraging your followers in this wilderness by example and strengthening them by word. Thus, while the wicked are proud, the poor who follow you may be kindled, on the one hand by the fire of the heavenly word applied to them, and on the other hand stirred by the wind of pride or arrogance. [Col. 1189B]

“Let them be kindled, I say, like gold in a furnace, that, being tested, they may be purified; and like iron in fire, that in every respect they may be kindled to love. This wind of arrogance, which is now so contrary to us and drives out and scatters from the heart of the sea the poor multitude of expelled and proscribed people from their native island—this wind, I say, of pride and arrogance—you yourself sowed when you still lived in the world among the sons of pride. It is therefore just that you now reap the whirlwind. For from such seed comes such fruit, as one of the prophets says concerning Israel, schismatic through excessive arrogance: ‘They shall sow the wind and reap the whirlwind’ (Hos. 8).

“But even if this recent deed in England, done for our oppression, is a whirlwind of pride and arrogance, driving out and scattering the poor multitude from the heart of the sea, nevertheless this whirlwind cannot and ought not drive out us who have followed you, the Lord strengthening and guiding us. Whether it can drive out you, whom we have followed, you must see to; it can and ought neither to drive out us. Rather, this whirlwind calms us more than it disturbs us. We count it a favourable breeze, by which we may sail better and more conveniently toward harbour. For He who so marvellously orders this says, as the Psalmist says: ‘Though the swellings of the sea are wonderful, the Lord is wonderful on high’ (Ps. 92 [Vulgate]); and likewise: ‘He makes the whirlwind calm and the storm a breeze’ (Ps. 106 [Vulgate]). [Col. 1189D]

“And truly, even if we do not yet perceive it, we shall soon perceive that this new whirlwind will be made calm for us and this storm a favourable breeze, as the Lord works so wonderfully. This may readily be clear even to persons of little understanding. For now, through this deed, our pilgrimage is first ennobled, our weakness is strengthened, power to endure is given, the Church’s cause is made secure, and the favour of the world will incline toward us against the prince of this world: so greatly will the world detest the atrocity of this deed.”

But, to be silent for the moment about this: before long our eyes shall see it, and so too our heart shall rejoice. For now, as we have already begun to say, our pilgrimage is ennobled [Col. 1190A], and henceforth the cause of the Church which we have undertaken is secure on account of this. For, beyond all others of every age, sex, and condition, we have deserved to have so many innocents—little children, I mean, still hanging upon their mothers’ breasts—as companions of our pilgrimage, now joined to us and, together with us, new advocates before the Judge of all for the Church’s cause. Their crying, surely, sounds more pleasingly and persuasively in the ears of the Lord of Hosts than all the force and brilliance of lawyers’ pleadings.

There remains for us, therefore, from this deed only joy and exultation: namely, because before the Terrible One and before Him who takes away the spirit of princes, such numerous and such great protectors have accrued to us. Hence, if we have faith, there must be no hesitation [Col. 1190B] that, although we contend laboriously—for lawsuits are laborious, especially against an adversary so powerful and so harsh—the outcome of our cause will thereby be much happier.

“You, therefore, lord, on behalf of our expelled and proscribed people, who, as we have already shown, come to us in so necessary a manner, lay aside every anxiety and every sadness; wait for the Lord, act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened. For here, among the trees of the woods, among these rocks and these solitary monks, in this solitude, as in a kind of arena for our contest, we must either yield with disgrace or fight with glory. And as for our being forbidden the common suffrage of the Church: if the God of our heart is with us, then the hearts of His people are with us also—and all the more their hearts insofar as their mouths are thus closed. Certainly, when vocal prayer is thus forbidden, [Col. 1190C] the prayer of the heart, as though doubled, will now cry out more intensely, entreat more devoutly, knock more confidently, and be heard more readily by the Most High.”

### The archpriest’s reply to his learned companions

The archpriest, attentively hearing these words of his companions, after a brief silence, answered them thus, weeping and contrite:

“Blessed be the Lord, who by your learning teaches my hands for battle, and has made my arms a brazen bow by giving me companions in my contest so tireless, learned, and valiant. For I now see that you are much stronger than I in the struggle—you who call me your lord and leader. Therefore I pursue with devout thanksgiving Him whose gift it is that I have such and so great helpers, whom it is safer for me to follow [Col. 1190D] than for them to follow me.

“For I, brothers, as you say, was *amurca*—the bitter lees of oil: for a long time I ran through the broad and spacious ways of this life, as the vain and pleasurable things of this life succeeded one another at my whim and desire. Thus, abandoned to my own desires, like an untamed and unbridled man I ran, poured myself out, and wandered through the byways of the world; I erred where there was no road, and not on the road. Therefore, in this great crisis now impending, it is unsafe for you to follow me in this solitude. But I shall follow you, as men learned and practised in the things of God, as my guides and rulers, wherever you go.

“Thus from this day, from this hour, I entrust to your hands the cause of the Church—which, as you say, and as is true, is common to me and to you—to be fostered by your counsels and protected by your strength [Col. 1191A]. And, stirred by your example and strengthened by your words, I shall now follow you, as I have said; and, with the Lord’s favour, as He thus makes my steps broad beneath me even to the end, you shall not fail one such as I in following. Indeed, as you say, I was *amurca*; but I now desire, if perhaps the Lord should deign thus wonderfully to act, to be changed into oil. Therefore, aided henceforth by the strength of your counsel and assistance, I have resolved to endure more bravely and more vigorously the pressure of the winepress, if perhaps even thus the Father of mercies, the Lord of powers, may choose to draw me out of the pit of misery and the mire of dregs.

“Yet, my brothers, so valiant and so necessary fellow-workers of Christ in the present struggle, if I am moved, grieved, and pierced with sorrow by what has now happened, it is no wonder. For behold, to begin with you who have followed me: you have received nothing from me as yet, and already you have lost everything because of me. Because of me, I say—while I repay you evil for good, proscription and exile for service—you have been expelled and proscribed with me and for me. Nor are you and your possessions alone affected; your own people, your whole kindred, have likewise been expelled and proscribed—not on their own account in any respect, but because of me and you; indeed, altogether because of me. Thus that old parable and complaint of the old Law, though dead, seems as though newly revived to be capable once more of becoming a proverb: ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge’ (Ezek. XVIII) [Col. 1191B].

“For I alone sinned; I alone fell; I alone ought to have borne the Lord’s wrath. For, to say nothing of the rest, what has this flock of little ones, still sucking their mothers’ breasts, done? What have they deserved? Especially those who are not of my own kin; yet both these and the others, expelled and proscribed because of me, now experience because of me the dangers of the sea and the hardships of the roads—although they do not yet possess understanding, indeed neither speech nor understanding, since some of them are still journeying in their mothers’ wombs before they are known: strangers and outcasts before they are born.

“And those of you who followed me are indeed your own kindred. As for my own kindred, expelled and proscribed, I should endure this with all meekness and patience, although I am conscious of none of those notorious crimes for which human law commands this to be done. I could nevertheless patiently bear it concerning my own family; but how can I disguise compassion and grief for yours? [Col. 1191C]

“Yet your speech—rather, God’s speech, whose instruments you were above—being living and effectual, has produced no little power in me. Greatly strengthened and consoled by it, I can say that, according to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have made my soul glad. For from what I have heard I now plainly know that, in following me, you follow God more than a man; eternity more than time; and the cause of justice more than the plunder of temporal things. Indeed, now expelled, proscribed, and despoiled, you and yours receive the seizure of your goods with joy. From this I perceive most clearly that you follow, in God’s manner, a cause rather than booty, [Col. 1192A] and that, because the cause is common, as you say, you accept the punishment together as common.

“I see this and rejoice greatly because of you. I rejoice, I say, because I see you, together with the adornment of knowledge, strengthened also by the virtue of patience. For I see that your patience humbles your knowledge, so that it willingly subjects itself to the burden of poverty; while knowledge instructs patience, so that under such a burden it may rejoice from the heart. And patience, when it has knowledge as its companion, is accustomed always to rejoice in adversity; just as knowledge, when it has patience as its companion, is accustomed always bravely to endure adversity.

“Accordingly, in the knowledge and patience given you, you have wisely taught above that in this newly imposed punishment of our expelled and proscribed people we ought only to rejoice and exult, showing [Col. 1192B] that because wickedness has abounded, grace will abound still more (Rom. V). And by this very fact the favour of the world will be more inclined to sympathize with and assist us. It commonly happens that every excess of wickedness, precisely because it is excessive, harms most of all its own authors and supporters. For excessive wickedness is a crooked bow: it does not shoot its arrows far off, but bends them back upon itself, so that the excess in the limits of punishment is turned into an increase of grace for those against whom the excess has been committed.

“Thus moderation, restraint, and measure are necessary everywhere, and especially in punishments. Yet anger and envy—most pernicious counsellors of the mighty, as we now see and feel—are always accustomed to exceed all bounds. Hence Scripture says: ‘The anger of man does not work the righteousness of God’ (James I). Therefore the Christian emperor Theodosius, as you know much better than I, after humbly completing public penance publicly and patiently, enacted laws for the future that sentences pronounced by rulers concerning punishment should be delayed by their executors until the thirtieth day, so that room for mercy—or, if the matter required it, for repentance—might not be lost [Col. 1192C].

“Thus, although by natural law it is permissible to repel force by force, even pagan rulers decreed that this must be done with moderation. They said that it was permitted, but with the moderation of blameless self-defence; and that other penalties, as they ruled, should always be softened rather than intensified. Hence it is clear that even among pagan rulers mercy exalted itself above judgment, according to that well-known proverb among the Greeks: ‘Nothing in excess.’

“But, brothers, we now feel that, solely out of hatred for us, sheer cruelty has been laid over mercy and judgment through anger and envy. Thus even the innocent are brought under accusation, and those in whom the prince of this world has nothing are nevertheless proscribed by the ruler of the world, through the anger and envy of the mighty—those worst of counsellors, as we have said. Therefore, above all and before all others, I grieve for my lord, my king, whom I loved as my heart and as my soul, and from whose love neither tribulation, distress, nor persecution can even now separate me.

“He [Col. 1193A] alone is the one whom I lament, whom I mourn; for him I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. My enemies—his own king’s friends, I mean, false friends and true enemies—make this king, so Christian and so illustrious, become a tyrant; and with a kind of Herodian impiety they counsel and compel him to rage against little children, because at present they can do no more against me myself.

“Who, then, together with the Prophet, will now give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep? I shall weep, I say, not for myself, not for you, not for our expelled and proscribed people, not for loss of property, not for the desolation of churches; but I shall weep for so great a lord, so illustrious a king, who at the suggestion of wicked men has introduced into his kingdom a new punishment, so disgraceful to himself, newly devised [Col. 1193B], in order, beyond other things, to inflict new grief upon us and make the afflicted still more bitterly distressed—a punishment all the harsher because it is more general, because it extends even to the innocent, because no sex has been spared, no age respected, no rank considered.

“Saving the honour of our lord, saving the honour of Christ’s anointed, our king: eternal woe be upon those through whom this was done, through whom this new punishment was introduced and this new scandal came. Let their way be darkness and slipperiness, they who prescribed to innocent persons, pregnant women, and nursing mothers, unknown lands, untried seas, roads so difficult and so perilous. Thus, in accordance with the Lord’s lamentation, ‘Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days,’ whose flight has occurred in winter—so that the severity raging beyond measure [Col. 1193C], unconsidered besides toward persons so pitiable and infirm, is increased by the harshness of the season.

“When they are judged, let them go forth condemned, they who judged so without mercy. Let judgment without mercy be upon those who, in judging, showed no mercy. But let this be granted: this was surely the work of those who slandered me, who were my enemies at court. Then they crept secretly through fear; now they openly raise their heads and vomit out their poison. Nevertheless, as the common saying has it, and truly: he who increases his own pain avenges it badly. These men, as you taught above, have not increased our grief in this deed, as they hope, but rather their own. For, to say nothing at present of the wrath of God, which has already come upon them, they have certainly added perpetual disgrace for themselves to the grief and anger which they bear toward us in this matter [Col. 1193D]. For, so that a succeeding generation may know so atrocious a deed, the children who shall be born and arise will recount it to their children.

“Surely those wicked men, who in this deed did not offer counsel but rather poured out poison as counsel, ought first to have considered that the life of all powers, and especially royal powers, is always brief; but after life itself there follows either the immortal life of glorious reputation or the incurable wounds of injured fame. Therefore nothing is so fitting or so necessary to royal power as the spirit of counsel and knowledge, by which he who presides over all may observe measure above all and in all things: not transgressing, not exceeding, not stretching himself beyond himself, however great he may be.

“Therefore, above all, it is necessary that he who is the staff of the untamed, the nail of the obstinate, the hammer of the proud, and the conqueror of every hostile people—that is, the king, who ought to belong wholly to himself and wholly to all—must first and above all hold his anger in his own hands and always be able to say: ‘My anger is always in my hands.’ Thus, if he is angry—for it is not within even a king’s power not to be angry—he nevertheless does not sin. Otherwise, if in anger he sins, anger has slipped from his hands; it is no longer in his hands, but he himself is rather in the hand of anger: conquered by anger, not victor over himself or over anger [Col. 1194A].

“Consequently, from the excessively violent onset of anger, when the spirit of knowledge and counsel which is given from Him has been blown away, measure perishes; and the offspring born from measure as from a mother—justice, by which the throne is established, and clemency, by which it is adorned—fall together. By these two things kings obtain through this life the immortal life of blessed and pleasing fame. Thus, removed from the world by death, by a certain benefit of immortal fame they are restored to the world; and even after death they live holy and happily in the Church present here, if while still living in the flesh they observed measure in ruling, maintaining justice and mercy.

“Therefore that king alone is read to be blessed who ‘has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly.’ But if he has walked there, deprived of the spirit of knowledge and counsel, he is no longer king of peoples but rather dregs; no longer the Lord’s anointed, but an idol of the anointed—an anointed idol—is established as ruler of peoples; or, in the saying of the wise king [Col. 1194C], he is like a stone in a heap of mercury.

“But let them cast out, drive away, proscribe, prick, erase, incite, and rage: it is a time for endurance. We shall be patient and ready for the lash. Meanwhile, we shall return good for evil, love for hatred, prayer for cursing, as true disciples of that Master who said: ‘In return for my love, they opposed me; but I gave myself to prayer.’”

When these things had been said, and when we had mutually exchanged this exhortatory discourse, we were thus cheered and made more courageous; and we withdrew to our small dwellings, allotted to us, as mentioned above, within the enclosure of the monastery. Every day a new multitude of exiles flocked to us, except that many, absolved by apostolic authority from the oath previously mentioned [Col. 1194D], remained in Flanders—especially those who, because of the weakness of age or sex and the great harshness of the weather at that time, could not proceed to the archpriest, as they had sworn, without grave loss to themselves.

The rest came to us daily in groups, crying out and lamenting that they had been expelled from their native soil into unknown nations, deprived of their goods, and separated from friends and relatives. Thus daily, poor and needy, knocking at the gate of the Most High’s mercy, they moved the archpriest. For he could not fail to be moved; nor ought he not to have been shaken in all the inward parts of compassion at the plaintive cries of those expelled on his account. He was moved indeed, but like some precious spice, which the more it is stirred, the more [Col. 1195A] it gives forth fragrance; or like a grain of mustard, which, when someone grinds it more vigorously, exerts its force more strongly; and like a true silver trumpet, which the more vigorously it is struck, the more fully it is stretched and shaped.

He also suddenly seemed wholly to have melted into the purest oil under the winepress’s pressure, his face so gladdened with oil that he was always of a spirit so even, so composed, so uplifted, that in all his distress one could scarcely perceive that he felt any distress. As the prophet proclaims concerning the head: “Never sad nor troubled, but always cheerful, always joyful—joyful in mind, joyful in countenance, always joyful and even” (Isa. IV). For the wise man says: “The wise man remains as the sun, but the fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. XXVII).

Thus this man remained at all times [Col. 1195B] the same in adversity as in prosperity, and in prosperity as in adversity; him neither the sun by day nor the moon by night scorched. In this he fittingly fulfilled the apostolic command: “Count it all joy, brothers, when you fall into various temptations” (James I). And the Master says to the disciples: “Rejoice always” (Phil. IV). For, as the Master teaches other disciples: “The sorrow of the world works death” (II Cor. VII). The saying of the Wise Man agrees with this: “Do not give sorrow to your soul, for sorrow has killed many” (Ecclus. XXX).

And the wise king says: “All the days of the poor are evil, but a secure mind is like a continual feast” (Prov. XV). But the mind of this director of our contest [Col. 1195C] was as though at a continual feast, in unceasing joy. Hence I learned with the fullest certainty from him himself, as though from a certain book of experience, that the Master’s saying is wholly true: namely, that joy, no less than charity, is a fruit of the Spirit. “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy” (Gal. V). Therefore the wicked, who do not have the Spirit, lack this fruit of the Spirit not only according to the Master but also according to the Prophet. “There is no rejoicing for the wicked,” as the Lord says through the Prophet. But it is enough here to have touched upon this only for the praise and glory of so great an archpriest; preserving the order of the history, we must return to our little ones and the other expelled and proscribed persons.

Accordingly, apostolic men and the powers of lands, nations, and kingdoms, hearing of our expelled and proscribed people [Col. 1195D], were at first hearing immediately astonished and utterly condemned the deed; all who pitied the archpriest and so great and such a multitude of exiles with all the inward parts of compassion did so. Thus the archpriest soon saw fulfilled what he had earlier heard promised by his companions: that, by God’s wonderful ordering of this event, the world’s favour was turned toward us against the prince of the world.

Therefore, because the archpriest could not carry so great a multitude with him, he dispatched them, with their petitions, through different provinces, various nations, and even different kingdoms: some to ecclesiastical persons, others to the powerful of the earth. And all who were sent were graciously received by those to whom they were sent, both because of their hatred for such great wickedness and because of favour toward the sender. Thus, in this reception, even “the people whom he had not known served him” [Col. 1196A]: so great was now his favour among the people, and their pity for the expelled.

And what then? All having thus been driven out, the Lord soon provided that there should be no needy person among them, and that many should live more happily in exile than in their homeland. Therefore it was a happy exile—truly happy: happy because of the cause of justice; happy because of the world’s favour; happy because of the great courage and constancy of the exiles; happy also, distinguished by the title of innocence, the glory of virginity, the grace of widowhood, and conjugal honour. Through such a truly happy exile, and one so happy, they were being led only toward their homeland.

## 14. How the archpriest began to live more austerely

Yet although, by God’s mercy, provision had thus been made for our expelled people [Col. 1196B], the archpriest, observing that our exile was made heavier and our punishment harsher by so great a multitude of expelled and proscribed persons, resolved at the same time to increase the strictness of his penance. Besides the hair shirt which he wore continually and the frequent secret disciplines which he received while being scourged, he himself also began to live more strictly than usual.

One day he privately instructed one of the brothers, who was accustomed to serve him at table, that among his other, richer foods, which he had been accustomed to use, he should carefully—so that no one might notice—set before him daily the common food of the community, which alone he had resolved to use. To make this more cautiously and secretly possible, a table was set daily for him alone apart from us. Thus for several days he ate only dry and tasteless dishes, according to the regular institution of the Cistercian Order [Col. 1196C]. Yet, as we remember having written above, when we spoke of his physical table and manner of living, he had been reared in luxury from his earliest age, and for that reason could not endure coarser fare.

Nevertheless, because, as we have said, the punishment of his pilgrimage had been increased by the multitude of expelled and proscribed persons, his penance was increased among other things by greater strictness in living. But after mortifying himself in this way for some time and living so strictly contrary to his custom, after several days he was laid low by a severe illness.

The disciple who wrote these things, when, according to his daily habit, he came at morning time for sacred reading, in order, as had been enjoined upon him [Col. 1196D], to confer with the archpriest on the sacred writings, and as he customarily did each day either to learn from him or teach him, found, with grief, that this had occurred. Immediately coming nearer, I asked what could be the cause of so sudden an illness. But he, as I soon noticed, declined to reveal the cause and turned the conversation elsewhere. Yet I began to press him, opportunely and importunately, as far as I dared. At last, yielding to the importunity of my insistence, he disclosed the cause to me, but only on condition that I keep it secret. He did not assert it, however, but said that he suspected the illness had happened to him because of that more austere and unfamiliar abstinence.

### The disciple’s exhortation to the archpriest

And I immediately said to him: “Lord, if it please you, listen for a little while [Col. 1197A]. This temptation seems not human but rather diabolical. He whom the devil cannot overthrow through gluttony, he seeks to overthrow through excessive or unfamiliar abstinence. Against this the Master, not ignorant of that crafty enemy’s wiles, when speaking of the chastisement of bodies and mortification of the flesh, says: ‘I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God’ (Rom. XII). And he adds: ‘Your reasonable service’ (ibid.). It is as though he said: in this chastisement of bodies discernment must be employed. Therefore, ‘reasonable’: that is, with discernment, so that there may be nothing beyond or below the measure. ‘Reasonable’: so that the body’s natural capacity, not the abstainer’s will, may be assessed. ‘Reasonable’ [Col. 1197B]: so that both age and condition may be considered, and suitable provisions adapted to each person.

“If, therefore, lord, you desire that your service in chastising the body be reasonable, reason must accompany your service in abstaining and govern your will; the impulse of your will, which seems too violently intent upon good, must not carry you away. As the Wise Man says: ‘Do not be too righteous’ (Eccl. VII); and again: ‘Do not be wiser than is fitting’ (ibid.). Therefore, just as you must be neither too righteous nor too wise, so likewise do not be too abstinent. For through the few things which he expresses, the Wise Man enables us to understand many things which he does not express. As is said, a wise man becomes known through few words.

“Let us therefore desire nothing to excess, for, as someone says, ‘Everything excessive turns into vice.’ Hence, just as, according to the Wise Man, ‘there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness,’ so there is an abstinent person who perishes through abstinence (Eccl. IX). In abstaining, one must consider the weakness of the flesh, the capacity of nature, and the practice of long habit. For it happens very often that the spirit is willing but the flesh weak, nature powerless, and habit rebellious. Therefore a moderated strictness must then make allowance for these things. For, as the Wise Man says: ‘He who has reared his servant in luxury from childhood will afterwards find him stubborn’ (Prov. XXIX) [Col. 1197C].

“But you are the one who has done this: you have always reared your body from childhood in luxury; now, because you withdraw these things from it, you find it rebellious toward you. Therefore, since such is God’s will, let it please you henceforth that, because you cannot bear harsher fare, you use food suitable to you.
