“And so that my teaching may not be mine, hear, if you please, what one of the doctors says concerning these matters, speaking thus about bodily foods: ‘In all such matters, not the use of things but lust is at fault.’ For it can happen that a wise man uses the most costly food without any fault at all, while a foolish man burns with the foulest flame of gluttony even for the cheapest food. And anyone would more soundly prefer to eat fish after the Lord’s manner than lentils like Esau, or barley after the manner of beasts of burden. For most beasts are not more continent than we merely because they use cheaper foods. In such matters, what we do must be approved or disapproved not from the nature of the things we use, but from the reason for using or desiring them, and from the manner [Col. 1198A]. Behold, lord, my teaching is not mine, but rather the teaching of the orthodox.”

From these few words the archpriest immediately understood what he ought to do, according to the Wise Man’s saying: “Give an occasion to a wise man, and he will be wiser” (Prov. IX). Thus, by the Lord’s favour, soon restored to health, he always and in all things thereafter used food suitable to himself, accompanied by a sobriety remarkable indeed and beyond measure admirable, which we briefly showed above when speaking of his physical table.

Having inserted this concerning the holy and devout bishop’s ready spirit and weak flesh, for the edification of readers, let us henceforth continue the order of the history we had begun.

As we began to say, our expelled and proscribed people having thus been comforted by the Lord’s mercy, we lay hidden from the world in the solitude of Pontigny, among rocks and solitary monks, now withdrawn from the age. The freer because more peaceful, and the more fruitful because more secluded, we devoted our whole minds to spiritual matters. Above all, the archpriest was carried by a remarkable zeal for learning. Like a great luminary in the firmament of heaven, he clung constantly to Holy Scripture, giving diligent attention to apostolic institutions, but especially to theology. For this was the time which, as we said above, he had always longed for: a time when he might at last repair the loss of days wasted long ago, and when he, chosen to govern souls, might acquire for himself, if late, some knowledge of how to govern them [Col. 1198B].

He was such a lover of the Scriptures that, after the canonical hours, sacred books scarcely left his hands throughout the day—especially those two holy books, the Psalter and the Epistles, as though two spiritual eyes, the mystical and the moral. By one of these, as he said, he was perfectly taught ethics; by the other, especially contemplation. Through this love and study of the Scriptures he advanced so greatly in a short time that, in difficult and knotty passages of Scripture, he often understood even beyond those who taught him. Such, then, was our dwelling at Pontigny.

## 15. How, in the second year of his pilgrimage, the archpriest was seized by zeal for justice

In the second year of our pilgrimage [Col. 1198D], the bishop saw that the hearts of our enemies were hardened; that despite such outrages against us there were no signs of repentance in them, but rather that they continued to add sin to sin in what they could no longer accomplish by hand, pursuing us, though far away and dwelling in solitude, with slanderous tongues. Seeing this, the bishop began to think within himself and meditate in his heart; and in this meditation a fire burned. It was surely a fire not of spite but of love. For he saw his own children, though turned into enemies, daily going to destruction and rushing toward a precipice. And because he was a father, he could no longer conceal the matter. For though they had already withdrawn filial devotion, it was not consistent with episcopal perfection for him to withdraw paternal affection from them.

Therefore his heart grew hot within him for his perishing children [Col. 1199A], and in this meditation his fire burned—not with zeal for vengeance, but with zeal for justice for the sake of his children and with a father’s affection of compassion. Thus, as a father has compassion on his children, he too desired to have compassion on them: that is, to visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with stripes.

Accordingly, he was seized, on the one hand by a burning zeal for justice against the obstinate, which is especially fitting for priests; and on the other by an intense affection of compassion for erring children, which is especially proper to fathers. Thus he who had hitherto kept silence, who had hitherto endured in all patience, seeing and observing his patience trampled under pride and abuse, was now no longer patient, no longer sleeping; but rising and shaking himself, like a true son of those who have been shaken out [Col. 1199B], he immediately began to deliberate with his companions concerning what must be done. He was suddenly stirred and moved by the Lord’s threatening word in the prophet to the prophet: “And you, son of man, I have made you a watchman to the house of Israel” (Ezek. XXXIII). “But if you have not spoken so that the wicked may guard himself from his evil way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but I shall require his blood at your hand.”

He therefore addressed us, his companions in the struggle, first with a kind of deliberative discourse:

### The archpriest’s deliberative address to his companions
“Men and brethren,” he said, “fellow-workers with me for Christ in the cause of the Church, you know and understand—indeed, far better than I—that everything has its season: a time for endurance and a time for resistance, a time for mercy and a time for judgment. ‘When I shall have received the time,’ He says, ‘I will judge justices’ (Psalm 74 [75]). And the Master says to the disciples: ‘Serving the time.’ But we have served the time until now; we have endured until now; until now we have carried on our backs the sinners who build upon the Church, being patient toward all. Yet they, prolonging their iniquity, abuse our kindness and patience in the present day; and, heaping sins upon sins, they store up for themselves wrath, not mercy. For the Lord says through the prophet concerning one hardened and unrepentant, who continues still to add sin to sin: ‘Shall I not oppose him for three and four impieties?’ Therefore, brethren, [Col. 1199D] take counsel; consider what we must do henceforward. For because we have been silent until now, shall we always be silent thus? ‘Woe is me,’ says the prophet, ‘because I have kept silence’ (Isa. VI). Shall we therefore, terrified by the prophet, nevertheless remain silent in this way? And shall we, who have slept until now in this wilderness, among these rocks and these monks, not add to our conduct that we rise?

“It is indeed good and pleasant for us to be here: to sleep thus, and to enjoy the sweet embraces of long-desired Rachel. This is indeed good and delightful. Yet, lest I presently bring anything prejudicial to sounder counsel, it certainly seems to me that from now on the necessary business of the Bride calls us to work, and the obligation of our office presses us—that is, the pastoral care which we have undertaken. For behold, [Col. 1200A] foxes are laying waste the vineyards, and wolves do not cease openly to ravage the sheepfolds. And amid all these things there are none among the transgressors who return to their hearts—who perhaps would return if struck. Otherwise, unless the shepherd drives off the wolves, he bears the staff in vain; unless the judge restrains transgressors, he bears the sword in vain; and unless the priest casts out the unworthy, he has received the keys of the Church in vain.

“And now, brethren, I speak these things especially to you because the atrocity of the deed committed against us—in the case, I mean, of our followers who have been expelled and proscribed as enemies of justice—hastens the work. For it is customary that weakness or negligence be tolerated longer in a righteous man than raging malice. Therefore, in fulfillment of the obligation of our office, it now seems to me that henceforth we must work, not sleep, [Col. 1200B] so that with the Bride we may catch the foxes that lay waste the vineyards, and with the Beloved rise from the bed, go out into the field, lodge in the villages, and labor in the vineyards. As the Bride says: ‘Come, my Beloved; let us go out into the field, let us lodge in the villages, let us rise early to the vineyards’ (Song of Songs VII). For the Bride’s work or works perish and avail nothing unless the Beloved brings aid.

“Therefore, beloved, if this seems right to you, let us rise, go out, and work with the prophet’s hoe, uprooting, destroying, and scattering what is harmful, lest through our sloth or negligence these things grow and advance so far as to cover the entire garden of the Lord, and we be condemned by the Lord of the garden as idle or negligent gardeners [Col. 1200C] for sloth or negligence. Let us therefore do as the Lord of the garden commanded one of the gardeners to whose charge He had entrusted His garden: ‘Behold, this day I have appointed thee over nations and kingdoms, that thou mayest pluck up, destroy, ruin, scatter, build, and plant’ (Jer. I).

“But you, brethren, as men trained in the Scriptures and in the examples of many Fathers, know far better than I what is to be done in these and such matters. Yet, as my conscience dictates, I tell you what I think. Nevertheless, to add still more to what has already been said, this also seems to me among other considerations: if we wish to be imitators of Him whose disciples we are, then, after the pattern of the evangelical Samaritan—the true guardian and healer—we ought first to pour oil upon the wounds of sinners for their healing, and wine afterwards, if this should afterwards prove necessary. Therefore let the sweetest oil of gentleness, which is especially accustomed to heal the wounds of the powerful, first be poured in. And first of all let our lord the king be approached in every gentleness and humility, in case even thus the royal clemency—now sated with anger and indignation at our misfortunes—may look upon us in our humility.”

When the archbishop had proposed this course, it pleased us; all of us alike commended both the proposal and the counsel.

## 16. HOW THE KING WAS FIRST TO BE APPROACHED

Accordingly, one of the abbots of the Cistercian Order was sent, belonging to the monastery of Pontigny by a special bond of subjection. This abbot was named Urban, and was truly urbane: Urban in name, urbane in fact, urbane in speech. For he alone was such a man as was fit to undertake such an embassy. He was therefore sent; and he carried with him to the lord king, in the archbishop’s name, most courteous letters containing supplication alone, and no rebuke, or only the slightest. For the archbishop had sought words useful, gracious, and peaceable, and had composed exceedingly gentle expressions by which even thus the king’s heart might be softened.

But after some days the man who had been sent returned to us, bringing back in exchange for our gracious, gentle, and peaceable words nothing but bitterness, harshness, and greater disturbance, the king’s heart having thus been hardened against us.

### How He Was Approached a Second Time

Nevertheless, the archbishop did not cease to approach the king a second time through the same man. On this occasion he instructed the envoy to say orally things not as agreeable as before, but more severe; and he sent letters containing some measure of sternness. In them the archbishop rebuked the king, yet still in mercy and in a spirit of gentleness. But when the messenger returned shortly afterward, he again reported that there was still neither voice nor understanding.

On hearing this, and now perceiving with certainty that he would make no progress by this path of mercy and gentleness, the archbishop, in a spirit of judgment and burning zeal—for he was fervent in spirit—composed for the third time words that were harsh and stern. He no longer rebuked the king mercifully, as before, but sharply reproved him; and, as then befitted the occasion, he reproached the bishop with all authority, as a disciple of the true Samaritan, first pouring in oil and then wine. And, like the true evangelical creature prefigured in the prophet, having the face of a man in front and the face of a lion, he followed therein the Master Himself: “If anyone,” says the Master, “is overtaken in any fault, you who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. VI). And elsewhere, instructing His disciple concerning the episcopal office itself: “The servant of the Lord,” He says, “must not quarrel, but be gentle, correcting with meekness those who resist the truth” (II Tim. II). Behold the spirit of gentleness and meekness. Yet the same Teacher says elsewhere to the disciple: “For this cause rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith” (Tit. I). Behold gentleness and meekness; behold also [Col. 1201D] sharp rebuke. This is the Samaritan’s oil and wine; these are the evangelical faces in the prophet—the face of a man and the face of a lion.

And indeed such is ecclesiastical discipline and the order of ecclesiastical law: when a swelling of pride does not respond to soothing applications, it must be cut away with the iron. Therefore this doctor of the Church—our archbishop, I mean—proceeded by this path and in this order.

To carry out this now sterner message, a man of approved religious life was chosen, distinguished by exceptional religious devotion and fervor, rag-clad and poor, practising barefoot walking at all times. Hence he was surnamed “the Barefooted”; his proper name was Gerard. He was certainly a man who continually held death in desire and life in patience, whose chief and constant concern had been to recall the discordant to peace. He alone, therefore, was fit to undertake [Col. 1202A] this embassy. For in such men there is usually great freedom both to speak God’s words boldly and to perform mighty deeds, since the Spirit of the Lord is in them. He was therefore sent; besides the letters which he carried, the archbishop placed his own words in his mouth. Another religious man was sent with him. These envoys acted boldly indeed, but made no progress here either. Rather, while delivering harsh things, they brought back harsh things in return for harshness—indeed, matters far harsher than before.

## 17. HOW THE ARCHBISHOP WAS HARD PRESSED WHILE THE KING REMAINED UNCORRECTED

The archbishop, hearing this, began to be anxious and sorrowful, seeing that the king’s heart had been softened toward him neither in one way nor the other. The Christian king Louis and many princes of the lands had repeatedly and earnestly endeavoured to soften it and restore peace and favor between king and archbishop. But neither those great men nor the archbishop’s own envoys, now carrying bland messages, now sterner ones, had been able to succeed. Rather, “the pride of those who hate us” continually rose.

Troubled within himself, the archbishop began to cry more earnestly to the Lord, to pray more frequently, to eat more sparingly, and continually to mourn for the king, seeing him so insensible to all these things. Beholding such disturbance in the Church and the king’s mind thus hardened, he was pressed between two alternatives: on the one hand desiring release from his pastoral care and office; on the other, remaining for the cause of the Church, whose defense he had undertaken. After much inward agitation [Col. 1202C] he finally assembled his learned advisers upon this matter.

As soon as the abandonment of the bishopric was scarcely mentioned, they were scandalized at first hearing, crying out that he was failing before he had even begun to run, and falling in the Lord’s battle-line before he had fought. Like men trained in sacred matters, they distinguished the many causes for which a bishop may at times be permitted to transfer from one see to another, or even, in many cases, to abandon it altogether. But, as they testified, no such cause existed here. On the contrary, this would be ruinous and detestable to all future ages: as if a helmsman, dismayed and terrified amid the whirlwinds of a storm, should abandon a laden ship amid the waves; or as if a foolish commander setting out to fight, upon seeing the enemy’s squadrons, should at once be terrified and flee merely to save himself, thereby losing the battle-line of the camp which had resolved to stand courageously with him.

Therefore all our learned men steadfastly and salutarily exhorted him that this was by no means the time for flight, but for meeting the enemy—especially when the Church’s salvation alone was sought by the Church’s enemies, the honor of the clergy was being dishonored, and liberty attacked. And because the archbishop deeply mourned that the king, though thus approached, remained uncorrected, their counsel was that he should still endure, and by the example of his prolonged suffering attempt to soften the king’s heart, which he had not yet been able to change by exhortation. For nothing is so accustomed to change the heart of an angry man and turn it toward love as enduring and suffering for a long time according to the angry man’s desire.

Persuaded by the vigorous and salutary exhortation of his learned advisers, [Col. 1203A] the archbishop thought no more of abandoning his pastoral charge, but rather of exercising it henceforth more strongly and manfully than before. Drawing breath and taking courage, thinking now neither of flight, leisure, nor rest, but solely of care and battle, he resolved inwardly, after all this, to threaten the king with the pastoral staff, since he had not felt the lighter chastisement of the rod.

He considered and resolved this within himself, revealing it to none of his learned advisers and not bringing it into counsel. He did this cautiously and prudently, sparing them in this matter, lest those who had already incurred the king’s great anger by following him should perhaps be drawn into a greater and lasting hatred if they gave such counsel against the king—counsel which might perhaps be contrary to the king’s will, though serviceable to his interest.

Thus he thought within himself, without discussing or deliberating with his companions about it, that he should strike his king and son with the staff of more severe chastisement, as we have said, since he had until then been insensible to the touch of the rod, in the hope that, struck by the staff, he might even thus return from his deviation. Yet he was greatly doubtful and uncertain what ought to be done. For, as we have said, he did not wish, for the reason stated, to submit this matter to conference with his followers or to seek their counsel. Deliberating with himself alone, he was for some time inwardly tossed to and fro, standing and hesitating.

For he had read in the Law: “Thou shalt not curse the ruler of thy people” (Acts XXIII); and also the words of the sinful king: “Against thee only have I sinned” (Psalm 50 [51]). And the king truly sins against God alone. For, as one of the doctors and rulers of the Church teaches concerning that passage: “If one of the people errs, he sins both against God and against the king; but the king has no man to judge his deeds.” He had read these things in the Law and in the Psalmist, and many other things which learned and experienced rulers of the Church had laid down concerning them. One of them says: “Reproof by many cannot be salutary unless he is rebuked who has not a multitude as his associate.” Likewise: “When any one of the brethren has committed such a sin as to deserve anathema, let this be done where there is no danger of schism.” He had indeed read these things and others of a similar kind.

But in the Roman Church, as we have already said above, there was then a harsh schism: the emperor Frederick, so mighty an emperor, and Octavian, so high-born a man and then antipope, had separated from the Church and caused schism. Thus it did not seem without grave reason that there might be cause for an even greater and harsher schism if the king of the English—young in age and ruling so widely and magnificently in regions both on this side and beyond the sea—were separated from the Church by the drawn sword of the word. For fear that the young and powerful king, stirred by this, might readily pass to the party of the Church’s enemies. Above all, the archbishop feared that the authority of the Apostolic See, because of this more serious peril of schism which, as we have said, could easily arise, might invalidate entirely whatever he should decree without its counsel or concurrence. Such considerations and others like them urged him to put back his sword and not strike with his staff.

On the other hand, contrary considerations spoke against these and impelled him no longer to withhold the sword from blood, but to strike with the staff. For just as he had heard in the Law what we have set forth above—namely, “Thou shalt not curse the ruler of thy people”—so too he had read in the Law that both rulers of the Synagogue and others were, according to the gravity of their offense, reckoned unclean and put outside the Synagogue. This was by no means cursing a ruler, which the Law forbids; rather, such excommunication was a disciplinary restraint. And just as then, so now, to anathematize a ruler is not to curse the ruler, as the Law forbids, but to restrain him disciplinarily as a son of the Church; and, like one wounded by robbers, to cut him medicinally under the Samaritan’s care, so that the wound which does not respond to soothing treatment may be cut away with iron.

He had also read in the prophet: “Woe is me because I have kept silence” (Isa. VI). The prophet pronounces woe upon himself because he did not rebuke King Ahab with the authority which he ought, nor restrain him according to the power given him. For when, as we have stated above, the adulterous and homicidal king said to God, “Against thee only have I sinned” (Psalm 50 [51]), he did not mean that correction of kings was thereby taken from the prophets and priests of the Synagogue. For the prophet immediately rebuked the king for his sin. Rather, he said, “Against thee only,” speaking to God, because priests and prophets then acted in the place of the Lord. They were as it were the Lord Himself, whose vicars they were; and therefore, when they punished a man, it was God alone who inflicted that punishment through their ministry. And just as then, so now, if the Church or priest punishes a king, God alone is nevertheless said to punish. For He punishes who acts in the Lord’s place on earth, and who upon earth is given to the people as God. As the Lord says to Moses: “Behold, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. VII). And it is very common to find priests called gods in Scripture.

Thus he had read in the Law and the prophet, and likewise in the various passages of Scripture concerning the rebuking of kings. And, lest we proceed merely by divine laws and not also by the examples of orthodox Fathers and discerning rulers of the Church, he had heard and read that Ambrose, that ruler of the Church so learned, discerning, and illustrious a doctor, excommunicated the great emperor Theodosius and entirely excluded him from entering the Church. And, not to seek examples from afar, he had heard of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, of blessed memory, who, as a kind of storehouse of the Scriptures, poured forth in modern times a great light of learning for pastors and furnished in himself an admirable model. He had heard, I say, that Ivo excommunicated King Philip of the Franks and wholly barred him from the Church.

The archbishop had therefore read and heard both these things and those. He was consequently pressed by arguments on either side: above all, he feared that if he remained silent, woe would be his; but if he spoke, there was danger of discord. He did not indeed greatly fear the objections introduced above, because he understood the Scriptures; but he feared especially the danger of dissension. Yet, turning these things over in his heart, he at last considered that his king, his son, and his lord—whom through long and familiar intercourse he knew more truly and intimately—would be a son not of dissension but of peace; and that, however exasperated he might be by the threatened word, he would nevertheless not tear open the womb of his mother, the Church, so as to cast himself out. Thus considering, he firmly resolved in his heart to strike him with the pastoral staff, in the hope that, having deviated and transgressed the path of justice, he might even thus return.

Yet he feared, as we have said above, that his own Roman Church, which presides by supreme authority, might wholly nullify every work of justice that he had done. He indeed feared this; nevertheless, whatever the Roman Church might do as mother and mistress, he judged it better to fulfill the obligation of his office than, by his own silence and dissimulation, to leave wickedness unpunished and foster transgression. He judged—and not without reason—that the blood of the wicked would not then be required at his hand, even if a higher power should intervene and alter the work of justice which he had performed.

Therefore, persuaded by conscience—or rather, as I learned from him himself, compelled by it—he held most firmly in his heart the ecclesiastical correction of the king of which we have spoken. Otherwise it seemed to him that the evangelical shepherd had received his staff in vain, the ecclesiastical judge his sword in vain, and the priest of the Lord the keys of the Church in vain, unless, just as he possessed authority, he also possessed the power to admit to the Church and to exclude from it those whom he ought.

And because he judged that what he had resolved to do should be done not under a roof or secretly, but publicly and solemnly—as both our cause and the wrongdoing of the opposing party were public and now known throughout the whole world of churches—he proceeded to a celebrated place at a celebrated time, namely Vézelay, when that church’s festival day was at hand, more solemn than its other observances: the feast-day of blessed Mary Magdalene, in whose honor the church there was founded, and whose body gloriously rests there. Therefore, many peoples from different kingdoms gather for the feast-day. At such a solemn and festive time we came to so celebrated a place, one day’s journey distant from our dwelling at the monastery of Pontigny.

We came and arrived on the day before the feast. We who followed him did not know the reason for his coming; for he had not told us, because of the reason stated above, and we believed that he had come solely for the festival. On the following day, the feast itself, at the request of the abbot and convent, he celebrated the public Mass. When the Gospel had ended, he mounted the pulpit and delivered an elegant and fruitful sermon to the people. Then, in the hearing of the people, he set forth the cause of the dissension between himself and the king; how harshly and cruelly he and his followers had been treated; and how the king had been approached so often and had not shown mercy, but had been hardened all the more. He commended the cause of the Church, himself, and his followers to their prayers.

Then immediately, while all listened and were astonished, deeply moved in a remarkable manner, in a tearful voice and with most intense feeling of compassion, he pronounced by name a threatening decree against Henry, king of the English. We, indeed, his companions in the struggle, hearing this unexpectedly, were immediately amazed because he had done it without consulting us. As he himself soon afterward told us, he knowingly and deliberately concealed it from us, excusing his having acted without our counsel on the ground already stated.

This action, heard by the ears of the many and diverse nations gathered for the feast-day, was at once spread throughout the lands and swiftly reached the king’s ears. Therefore the king—and all who were with him—was stirred and disturbed, not without reason, to a degree beyond what it is now time to say or write.

## 18. CONCERNING THE KING’S APPEAL TO THE ROMAN PONTIFF

[Col. 1206B]

Accordingly a multitude assembled, and their minds were thrown into confusion when they had learned this with certainty. The Church of the English assembled in the regions on this side of the sea, and the Church of the Normans assembled beyond the sea, deliberating most earnestly among themselves what was to be done. They took the greatest care to ensure that the sentence against the king, whose threatening stage had now been issued, should not proceed to completion, nor that any burden of ecclesiastical coercion should fall upon the kingdom, the persons of the realm, or its churches.

They were already dismayed and terrified, not only because of what they had heard concerning the king, but also because the archbishop had suspended Jocelin, bishop of Salisbury, for manifest disobedience: namely, because, contrary to the prohibition of the lord pope and of the archbishop, he had conferred the deanery of Salisbury church, in accordance with the king’s will, upon one of the court clerks, without consulting certain canons of that church who were then travelling with him and who, together with their other fellow-canons, had the right to elect their dean. He had also bound that same court clerk in the bond of anathema because of certain compacts and obligations which he had contracted with the schismatics in Germany. Yet he was said to have made these compacts and obligations when sent by the king and at the king’s command.

Therefore the persons of the realm, fearing consequences for themselves and trying to forestall the burdens that might befall them, anxiously deliberated most carefully what was to be done.

“For your own affair is at stake when the wall next door is burning,” says one writer. They found no more advantageous remedy for themselves than to have recourse to appeals. This pleased the king—God, indeed, acting justly, to the mockery and derision of the new legislator and of the new laws which, as we showed above, had been devised and reduced to writing at that royal residence called Clarendon. For though those laws had forbidden appeals to the Roman Church, it now became necessary to resort to them for the defense of king and kingdom.

The persons of the realm, because they were farther away, appealed in writing on behalf of the king, the kingdom, themselves, and their churches. Through learned envoys, they sent to the archbishop at our wilderness of Pontigny a written instrument of appeal, drawn up in that form. Since the king was then outside the kingdom and beyond the sea, the king himself sent on his behalf great and venerable persons of the Norman Church: Rotherot, then archbishop of Rouen, of pious memory; Ernulf, then bishop of Lisieux; and with them several other eminent and learned men. When these arrived at Pontigny, however, they did not find us. For the archbishop, forewarned by one of his household who was then at the king’s court concerning the intended envoys, withdrew himself.

The said envoys therefore came to Pontigny on our account, but did not find us and immediately departed. First, however, in accordance with legal form, they made their appeal at Pontigny, where we seemed to have a kind of domicile; yet they did not, as civil law teaches, write it upon the doors, but appealed orally. We withdrew not because we were ignorant of the law—for we knew perfectly well that appeals can be made by reason of domicile, even against persons absent or withdrawing themselves—but because we wished to avoid conversation with the envoys when they arrived.

And just as these appeals were lodged, so certain unlawful and sacrilegious oaths were exacted throughout the whole kingdom for the kingdom’s defense: in cities, castles, villages, and every county of the realm, from all persons fifteen years old and above who could swear. They swore either to detain, if they could, the envoys or letters of the lord pope and likewise those of the archbishop, or to report them to those who could do this. How sacrilegious and profane this oath was, even the bleary-eyed and barbers can see. As it is said: “For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and refusal to comply is as the crime of idolatry” (I Sam. XV). But, passing over this deed as sacrilegious—a pollution rather than a defense of the realm—let us return to our appellants.

### How the Archbishop and His Followers Deliberated Whether the Appeal Was to Be Respected

We, returning to Pontigny soon after the departure of these appellants, immediately began to deliberate what ought to be done: namely, whether such an appeal ought to be respected. Most of us maintained that it should be respected, adducing many arguments in proof, as men learned and trained in law, both from divine and human law. Others of our number opposed this and contended that it should by no means be respected, supporting their position, conversely, with strong and varied arguments.

Especially, as they prudently maintained, such an unjust appeal should not be respected because it was devised not as a remedy for the oppressed, but as a palliative for prolonging the wickedness of oppressors—men whose hands were manifestly filled with the spoils of all the Church and whose right hands were full of plunder. Therefore the archbishop’s learned advisers, holding divergent opinions about the appeal, debated before him; and he, as was his custom, intervened between the parties, frequently questioning and challenging now one side, now the other, on points of law.

I would have inserted into this history the arguments then advanced on both sides concerning the appeal, had they allowed themselves to be confined within a brief compass without inconvenience. Especially since, as in many other matters, we omit them in this little book because much on these questions is contained in a certain collection of letters, of which we shall speak presently. There was then debate and argument on both sides. Yet the archbishop, though perhaps he could lawfully have proceeded in ecclesiastical severity against such manifest evildoers, whose evildoing was now accused by the very stones in the walls and beams in the houses, nevertheless still paused, following the counsel of the Wise Man: “He who is patient is governed by much prudence” (Prov. XIV).

He therefore paused and did not proceed, judging it better to defer the matter for a time until he had consulted the Roman Church about it. Above all, as we have already said, he feared that whatever he decreed without consulting her, especially at such a time, she might wholly invalidate. To the aforementioned instrument of appeal, sent to him in the name of the persons of the realm, he returned an elegant and sufficiently responsive letter, conceived in his own thought and written in his own style. In it he set forth, among other things, what seemed to him concerning appeals that had been made, whether justly or unjustly.

We pass over these matters here in this historical book for brevity, because they are contained in that letter, as we have said above. That letter exists among his other letters, whether written by himself or by some of his learned followers at his command and in his name. For a large collection of letters has been compiled from those written by us or for us during our exile—a collection which we promised above to mention here. It is, I say, a collection containing many letters, which the venerable Alan, prior of the holy Church of Canterbury, laboriously and diligently arranged according to the order of the history. In them are contained very many matters concerning the laborious history of our exile. Therefore, because these things are written more carefully in those letters, we have omitted much from this little book for the sake of brevity, especially since that book of letters is already possessed by many persons and churches.

But anyone who wishes to know sufficiently the archbishop’s words and deeds in exile, his endeavors and actions, his pastoral struggles and labors, should have recourse to that collection, so that after this historical little book he may read that book of letters as well. Although in many of its letters the formal refinements of diction are absent, it is sufficiently suitable for its subject matter. With its assistance, in order to weave together the history more easily, let us henceforth pursue more briefly the order of history which we have begun.

## 19. HOW THE ARCHBISHOP AND THE KING SENT ENVOYS TO THE APOSTOLIC MAN

Thus, after the appeal had been entered and ecclesiastical discipline suspended, envoys were prepared and sent to the Apostolic See. The king sent envoys; the persons of the realm also sent them; and the archbishop sent them as well. But there was a great difference between these envoys. The former travelled laden with silver and gold; ours were unencumbered and empty-handed, scarcely carrying provisions for the journey. At the curia, the former either gave, or most certainly promised, masses of gold and silver to this person and that; ours offered only bare words to apostolic clemency.

Yet this was not our first mission to the Roman Church. Previously we had sent some of our learned men to the Apostolic See, through whom we had already obtained from the apostolic man a legation of the Apostolic See over England. This was prudently done by us, so that any ecclesiastical sentence subsequently pronounced by the archbishop upon the kingdom or persons of the realm might have firmer and more authoritative force. Accordingly, when the archbishop at Vézelay, as we showed above, issued the threatening decree against the king, he was already legate of the Apostolic See, although he was prevented from entering the limits of his legation.

But let us return to our pilgrims to Rome.

### How the Archbishop Was Removed from Pontigny

Before saying more of these matters, however, let us first insert this: shortly after the aforementioned feast-day of blessed Mary Magdalene, when these envoys had departed for the Apostolic See, the lord king of the English sent certain letters to the general Cistercian chapter, which, according to custom, was celebrated the following September on the feast-day of the Holy Cross. He stated that they had received and were keeping with them one of his enemies, namely Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury. He therefore commanded that, if they held dear anything which they possessed in his land either on this side or beyond the sea, they should no longer keep him with them.

When the three days had elapsed during which the chapter is customarily celebrated, they set out for us at Pontigny: Gilbert, the abbot of Cîteaux, bishop of Pavia and formerly a monk of that Order; and certain abbots of the Order with him. They came in haste and announced to the archbishop in the chapter’s name that they had received such letters and such a command from the king. Yet they then addressed the archbishop:

“Lord, because of such a command, the chapter neither drives you from itself, expels you, nor dismisses you; but it makes this known to you and to your prudent counsel, so that after such a command you may see and consider what must be done. For the entire chapter knows most certainly—and we who have now come here all know together—that you love our Order so greatly that you will provide for its freedom from harm, lest on your account it suffer any diminution or loss, either in spiritual or temporal matters.”

The archbishop and his advisers, experienced in many matters and well trained by numerous trials, inferred the dispositions of those who had sent the message and of those who bore it, and immediately perceived what must be done. Accordingly, after consulting with his own people, the archbishop at once replied that he would on no account allow the Order to incur, on his account, any injury or even the slightest loss—an Order which had shown such great humanity both to himself and to his companions in so severe a strait. [Col. 1210A] He added that, wherever he might turn aside and wherever he might lay his head, he would remove himself from them with all speed. “The Lord,” he said, “if it please Him, will provide for me and for my fellow-exiles—He who feeds the birds of heaven and clothes the lilies.”

Thus the archbishop spoke briefly. But many others, especially the abbot and our brethren of Pontigny, who, as we have shown above, had received us so joyfully and devoutly, and who were present and heard what had been said concerning the archbishop and his companions, were moved to tears in the depths of their compassion and went weeping home. For, that we may bear witness to what we saw and heard: although Garin of Galardim, of holy memory, was then abbot of the place, and although the brethren were unwilling and resisted as far as they could, this decision concerning our departure was made. Upon hearing this reply of the archbishop, the holy Abbot of Cîteaux and those with him departed on the following day.

### On the archbishop’s deliberative address to his companions

The archbishop, having taken counsel with his companions, promptly decided what should be done; and, addressing his chief followers, he spoke thus:

“Brothers, you who are advocates with me before the Lord in the cause of the Church, see how Satan seeks to sift us like wheat—driving out, proscribing, casting down, and forcing away us and our people, that he may overcome us and make us yield. When the world persecuted us, we fled, expelled and outlawed, to this solitude; we turned aside to those dead to the world, hoping that at least in this solitude, among those dead to the world, we might be hidden from the disturbance of men and from the contradiction of tongues. But behold, [Col. 1210C] the prince of this world has great power here also: he persecutes us even here, casts us out from here, and will no longer allow us to dwell here as pilgrims.

“What then shall we do, brethren and men? Where shall we go? Where shall we turn aside? For the solitudes are forbidden to us; even among those dead to the world, a place is now denied us. We have no building or dwelling, no gold, no silver, no money, no possession whatever. We are far removed from friends and kinsmen; scarcely is there anyone who dares even to sympathize with us, much less receive or aid us. Who, indeed, would dare this? What church, what religious order, what monastery would receive us—when we have been driven out from such a distinguished and approved Order, which at the beginning of our pilgrimage we so greatly preferred and chose above all others? [Col. 1210D]

“Certainly, both because, setting aside others, we chose to live here as pilgrims, and because of fear of the world and threats of worldly power, there is no one to receive us: no church, no ecclesiastical person, no religious order, not even any solitude; much less any secular person. Yet to turn aside to such people, if any should perhaps exist, would be neither religious nor honorable for us—both because of the cause which we pursue and because of the religious life which we have observed from the beginning until now.

“Yet, brothers, I do not say this as though, contrary to the prohibition of the good householder, I were so anxious about tomorrow. For I hope that He who saw on the mountain—the Lord Himself—will look with the eyes of His customary mercy upon us, who have abandoned the world and are now abandoned both by the world and even by those who have abandoned the world. [Col. 1211A] I hope, I say, and most certainly hope, that in this strait the merciful and compassionate Lord will open His hand most abundantly to our distress and poverty and fill us with blessing.

“Yet the way by which the Lord intends to lead us from this solitude and provide for us once led forth has not yet been revealed to me. And this I now greatly desire, lest, after the announcement of our departure has been made, we remain here any longer. For that would be shameful and unbecoming for us. Let the Lord therefore provide for us now; apart from Him we have no other refuge.”

### On the disciple’s reply

The disciple who wrote these things, hearing among the rest these plaintive words of his lord the archbishop, immediately spoke out before the others:

“My lord,” he said, [Col. 1211B] “remember, if you please, that the lord king of the French, in the city of Soissons, offered himself to you most magnificently and generously, namely, as ready to provide most amply from his treasury for you and yours in whatever city, town, or other place within his dominions you might choose. You only deferred acceptance then until this should become necessary; you did not reject it altogether.”

“I remember,” said the archbishop. Then, addressing the speaker directly: “But now, brother,” he said, “it seems to me that you seek again the courtly accoutrements and urban delights which this present time requires us to abandon, we who are held in the bonds of the Gospel. It would be better, far more religious, and more honorable at this time for us to turn aside to some church [Col. 1211C] or solitude than to a court or city, where, in proportion as we were more humble, we might more confidently await in silence the salvation of God and the outcome of our pilgrimage foreseen by the Lord.”

But others of his learned advisers who were present at the consultation, hearing this, affirmed that such a course was indeed more religious, honorable, and humble; but, they said, this was by no means now within our choice or power, since we must turn aside not where we should wish, but where we are able. Thus we must follow the comic saying: “They went where they could; where they could not, they did not go.”

Accordingly, the common counsel of all his companions was that he should make a virtue of necessity; since he could no longer go to the solitudes forbidden to him, he should turn aside to a court or city, if he could do even that. They added:

“My lord, in a court or city one may, by grace, lead a solitary life and devote oneself to God; just as, conversely, one may in solitude overflow with courtly luxuries. The ancient and familiar history of the Israelites proves what we say: at their request they ate and were exceedingly filled; but while their food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God rose against them. This occurred in the wilderness. Conversely, we read that those chaste and wise youths, Joseph and Daniel—one in Egypt and the other in Babylon—administered royal revenues, yet lived in the greatest continence. Although already citizens of Jerusalem, they nevertheless then administered Egyptian and Babylonian affairs, amid so great a multitude without disturbance, [Col. 1212A] moving about and, as it were, remaining in solitude.

“Therefore that king, mighty in battle and strong of hand, though always in the battle-line, always in conflict, always amid a multitude, yet glories that he remained in solitude with the wings of the dove which he desired: ‘Behold,’ he says, ‘I fled far away and remained in solitude’ (Psalm 54). It is especially the characteristic of those who govern to move without disturbance amid crowds and to remain always in solitude among many people: always belonging to others, rarely to themselves—except that, when they belong to others for God’s sake, then they belong to themselves more truly.

“Thus the Teacher, though free from all, made Himself the servant of all: to those under the law, as under the law; to those without the law, as without the law; a Jew to Jews, a gentile to gentiles, weak to the weak, all things to all, that He might thus save all [Col. 1212B] (1 Corinthians 9). Therefore, holy Father, although we do not seek a city—rather, having been expelled from solitude, whether willing or unwilling, we must now enter a city—we shall be able, by the Lord’s working, to live in the city as though dwelling in solitude.

“If anyone wishes to resort to Latin, Greek, and barbarian histories in proof of this, he will find a great cloud of witnesses; for God accepts neither outward garb nor places, but only the merits of one’s life. Indeed, to return again to our own examples: our Lot, who was pure within the unclean city, became unclean upon the mountain. And, to bring forward greater instances: the first man fell from paradise, and the first angel from heaven; while our Job stood upon a dunghill.”

## 20. HOW THE ARCHBISHOP, LEAVING PONTIGNY, WAS RECEIVED AT SENS BY THE KING OF THE FRENCH AS A PILGRIM

[Col. 1212C]

Persuaded by these considerations, the archbishop did not delay sending the disciple who wrote these things to that Christian and glorious king of the French, Louis, whose memory is in eternal blessing, in order that he might report everything to the king concerning our departure from Pontigny and its cause. When the king heard it, he was greatly astonished. Since he was on the road when these matters were reported to him, he immediately summoned his companions on the journey and himself related the whole affair to them.

Then, with everyone listening, he said: “O religious life! O religious life, where are you? Behold: those whom we believed dead to the world fear the world’s threats, and for perishable and passing things—which they profess to have despised for God’s sake—they now turn back from the work of God which they had begun, driving from themselves the cause of God and an exile for God’s cause.” [Col. 1212D]

Turning then to the man who had been sent, the king said: “Greet your lord the archbishop, and confidently tell him in my name that, although the world and even those who seem dead to the world abandon him, I will not abandon him. Whatever the king of the English—though he is my liegeman—may undertake or carry out against him, I shall nevertheless receive one who suffers for God and for justice. Let him inform us whether he would prefer to turn aside to a city, a castle, or another place in our dominions, and he will find it ready.”

[Col. 1213A] Soon, therefore, the man who had been sent returned and brought this message to the archbishop in the king’s name.

Above the other royal places, we chose for the completion of the remainder of our pilgrimage that famous royal city of Sens. It was only twelve French leagues from our solitude of Pontigny, which we had begun to inhabit, as we remember having said above. We chose that city, I say, on the advice of its inhabitants because, as they testified—and as we ourselves discovered by direct experience—it had many advantages: it was well supplied with grain, wine, and oil; encircled by woods; adorned with meadows; springs bubbled up, streams flowed, and finally the serenity of autumn displayed its abundance in every respect. That land was indeed like the land which is reported to have devoured its inhabitants. [Col. 1213B]

But above all else, and more than anything else, the customs of the citizens drew us to the city. More than the city’s described advantages or the fertility of its fields, I say, we were attracted by the cultivated generosity of character among its clergy and people. For among both clergy and people of the city, as we had already experienced, there were generous, liberal, lavish men, especially honoring strangers and residents; affable and sociable men, sharing what was theirs and giving readily. For this reason above all we chose to complete the remainder of our pilgrimage among such people.

Near the city, at about a stadium’s distance, is a noble royal abbey where rests the body of the glorious virgin and mother, Saint Columba. There is a monastery dedicated in her honor, [Col. 1213C] so conveniently situated that it can easily enjoy the city’s advantages and avoid its tumults. The archbishop and his companions decided to turn aside there, both because of the religious character of the place and because the city’s disturbances could more easily be avoided. As soon as this became known to the aforesaid most Christian king, it pleased him.

Thus, after two years of our pilgrimage at Pontigny had been completed, we departed from Pontigny. On the day of our departure you might have seen the brethren sorrowing and lamenting, running after the archbishop, hurrying to and fro, pressing forward, greeting and returning greetings, asking again and again for his blessing, and again and again desiring to see and speak with him as he departed. At times they cried aloud: “Father, why do you leave us? To whom do you leave us desolate?” [Col. 1213D]

Seeing this, I recalled those most true words of the righteous man: “Those who fear you shall see me and rejoice” (Psalm 118). These brethren, therefore, fearing thus, ran to and fro in such a manner and strove so to outstrip one another that they might see him a little longer and rejoice. Neither the abbot’s command nor the regular hour could call them back, as they accompanied the archbishop and his companions far and long beyond the monastery gate. So eagerly did each strive, without any order, to surpass another and seize before him the last greeting and final blessing. Yet how devout, indeed, how ordered was this irregular and disordered rushing and excess, to which the force of extraordinary love impelled them! In this peace and love of the brethren, therefore, we departed from Pontigny.

### On the archbishop’s dream when leaving Pontigny

But on the day of our departure, as we travelled, the archbishop—who on the road was ordinarily the most eloquent and delightful of companions—began, contrary to his custom, to be exceedingly sad and sorrowful. He spoke with none of his companions on the journey, nor did any of them speak with him. We, his travelling companions, supposed that he grieved because he had left brethren who loved him so greatly and were so greatly beloved. Our abbot of Pontigny, then our companion on the road, a learned man of approved religious life, saw this and sympathized. He approached more closely and privately asked why the archbishop’s countenance had fallen so. He asked this again and again [Col. 1214B] until the archbishop disclosed the cause in response to his friendly persistence.

“Lord Abbot,” he said, “it is no wonder that my troubled mind has thus cast down my face. Yet, although you are my familiar friend, I shall not disclose the reason unless you promise to keep it secret as long as I live.”

The abbot immediately pledged that he would do so. The archbishop continued:

“Lord Abbot, this night I saw a dream, and the visions of my head troubled me. For by a revelation of God, unless I am mistaken, I have received knowledge that I shall pass from this world through a harsh death, though I hope a precious one. This night it seemed to me that, in a church—though I do not know which church—I was contending against the lord king of the English before the tribunal of the lord pope and the cardinals for the cause of the Church. [Col. 1214C] The lord pope favored my side, but the cardinals opposed me on the king’s behalf. Then suddenly four knights came upon me; immediately they dragged me away from the tribunal and, in that same church, flayed the crown of my head, where my tonsure is situated, so that I seemed to myself so distressed that I was about to fail.

“Because of this revelation—for I know that this is a revelation, not an empty dream—I am thus troubled and grieved. I am not grieved because of the revelation, for which rather I give such thanks as I can to the Most High, who has deigned to reveal to my littleness the manner of my departure from this world. But I grieve especially for those who followed me and endured so many and such great things for my sake. For I know most certainly that, when I am struck down, they will be scattered like sheep [Col. 1214D] without a shepherd.”

A few days later he similarly related this same vision in secret to another abbot of the Cistercian Order, likewise his friend and familiar, upon the same condition—that he should reveal it to no one until he saw the vision’s outcome. This abbot was called the abbot of Lucent Valley (de Valle Lucente). He told the vision to these two abbots so that, when he was removed from this world in the very manner of which the revelation had forewarned him, the word of the revelation might stand in the mouth of two witnesses.

As he told the same abbots, he did not wish to reveal it to any of his own people, lest he should make the companions of his suffering still more sorrowful. And indeed, as he foresaw and foretold, so he departed from the world in the manner which the following order of the history will explain. In this he was like one of the saints who likewise received a revelation concerning the end of his present course: at night he saw himself wholly burned by fire; afterward he was indeed burned by fire and, passing through fire, was brought into refreshment. This was, unless I am mistaken, blessed Polycarp. The said abbots kept silent at all times concerning the archbishop’s vision which had been related to them, until the end itself confirmed it at the close of our narrative. But having inserted this concerning the vision, let us return henceforth to the order of the history.

## 21. HOW THE ARCHBISHOP WAS RECEIVED AT SENS BY THE FRENCH

Having departed from Pontigny, we came to Sens. We were received with every joy and eagerness by Hugh, then archbishop of Sens, of pious memory, [Col. 1215B] and by the clergy and people of the city; and from the treasury we received most ample provision for our necessities.

Whenever the king came to the city, as was his custom everywhere, he would first go to church and then immediately, unless detained by some more important matter, hasten to visit the archbishop. At that time he enjoyed the archbishop’s abundant speech and weighty counsel, as of a man practised and experienced in royal affairs. But what need is there to say more? Now received by the French and living from the king’s own table, we were among them not as exiles but as citizens, not as strangers but as natives. More honor was bestowed upon us by the magnates and princes of the land than even upon their own noble and high-born inhabitants. Thus our earlier distresses were forgotten, [Col. 1215C] and the former things that had passed away were no longer remembered.

### In praise of the French

Therefore, just as ancient history records that Gaul always abounded in men most courageous and eloquent, so we now add to that ancient testimony of new history that it is exceedingly rich in men most generous and honorable, who especially show themselves such toward strangers and the oppressed. What we have seen, heard, and ourselves experienced, this we testify concerning the French; hence France has rightly from ancient times been called “sweet France.”

Sweet indeed because of the fruits of its land, which are most excellent; sweet also because of its climate, which is most mild there; but more truly sweet because of the free, gracious, and pleasant manners of its inhabitants, and their delightful companionship. Even if it may perhaps have been called sweet for some other reason, we nevertheless now proclaim it sweet for the reason by which we experienced its sweetness: so much so that, though we were distressed and afflicted pilgrims, we did not remember our troubles because of its sweetness. [Col. 1215D]

For our own nation had made us drink the cup of sorrow, the cup of bitterness; but this nation, receiving us as we came, made us drunk with the cup of its sweetness, so that because of the sweetness offered to us we no longer remembered our earlier bitterness and misfortunes. Sweet, therefore, is France, and truly sweet: sweet, I say, as we have already said, and love compels us still to repeat it—sweet. Truly sweet because of the excellence of its fruits and the mildness of its climate; but truly sweet, and sweeter still, because of the exceptional humanity of the nation and the ingrained kindness of the princes of the land. Sweetest of all because of the heaven-given gentleness bestowed upon the kings of that land.

For such great gentleness amid such great power is a gift properly bestowed from above. The kings of the French, as ancient deeds record, have always been warlike men, but scarcely ever—or never—tyrants. Sweet, sweeter, and sweetest, therefore, is France. Since we tasted of its sweetness—indeed, since we were wholly intoxicated by it—we who are now drunk from it cannot, when the time calls for it, refrain from pouring it forth in praise. Yet I would have poured forth more fully concerning its sweetness in praise and glory of that nation, had not the time now come, and the history required, that we resume the sequence of the narrative interrupted above. [Col. 1216B] We must therefore return to our envoys sent to Rome.

## 22. ON THE RETURN OF THE ARCHBISHOP’S ENVOYS TO ROME AND THE ARRIVAL OF THE CARDINALS FOR PEACE

For we had not spent many days at Sens when, behold, our Roman envoys returned. They announced that the lord pope would shortly send cardinals from his side to negotiate and, as far as possible, restore peace between the king and the archbishop. In the meantime, all matters were to remain suspended, and no act of ecclesiastical discipline was to be carried out. The apostolic man himself conveyed this instruction and counsel to the archbishop through our returning envoys in letters bearing his seal.

We therefore waited many days for the arrival of the cardinals. At length they came to Sens, and first came to us, [Col. 1216C] rather than to the king, because the course of their journey brought them so. Those who had been sent were well fitted to reconcile peace, being men of great spirit and great eloquence. One was called William of Pavia, the other Otto; both were priest-cardinals.

These men, coming first to us, explained the purpose of their arrival. It pleased us, and we consented devoutly, that, for God’s honor and with the Church’s liberty preserved, they should arrange a settlement between the lord king and ourselves. They then proceeded to the king in Normandy—for the king was then overseas, outside the kingdom—and remained with him no short time, neither returning to us nor reporting anything.

For, as was said—and as the subsequent outcome proved—the king sought only to prolong the time, having no wish whatever for our peace, though he pretended to wish it. Nevertheless, lest they appear to have come in vain, the cardinals repeatedly pressed the king about peace. They treated diligently and attentively of peace, sought peace, but found no way of peace. Finally, lest they appear to have come in vain and done nothing, they summoned us to a conference. The conference between us and them took place on the frontier of France and Normandy, between the two castles of Trie and Gisors.

### On the archbishop’s second dream

On the night immediately before the conference, the archbishop had a dream, as he himself related to us in the morning when we were going to the conference. He saw that poison was being offered to him in a golden cup. And so it came to pass.

For one of the cardinals, the aforementioned William of Pavia, a man of elegant speech and persuasive words, offered us pleasant and flattering language of peace. On the surface his words appeared good and peaceful; yet, if anyone examined them inwardly, they detracted considerably from ecclesiastical peace and liberty. As we heard and considered those words in the light of the night vision previously related to us, we immediately grasped the meaning. [Col. 1217B] Nearly every proposal concerning peace made by the cardinals was therefore suspect to us. We feared to be caught by words which were soft and honeyed, yet nevertheless were darts.

To state here briefly and in summary matters there spoken at greater length: the chief counsel of the cardinals, toward which they strove by every means, was that, without any express settlement between the king and the archbishop concerning the customs which, as we have said above, had been put into writing, and in opposition to which we were living as pilgrims, the archbishop should return to his church—if even this could be obtained from the king on such terms.

For they said that an express declaration would be harmful and would obstruct the progress of peace. As they added, it would be shameful and unbecoming for the king openly and expressly to renounce customs which had been acknowledged, by the older and greater men of the kingdom, by the bishops themselves, and even by ourselves, to belong to royal dignity and pertain to his crown. [Col. 1217C]

“But if,” they said, “the king grants you peace without any mention of whether these customs are to be retained or abolished, they are thereby understood to be annulled and abolished—especially since such a severe dispute has arisen between you and the king concerning them, and they constitute the entire matter of this dissension. Hence, if the king grants you peace, while you do not grant these customs and do not bind yourselves to retain them, they will thereby be understood to be annulled, and you to have prevailed in the case. For the king will thereby be understood to have consented to their abolition, though not expressly but tacitly.”

They added examples: thus, they said, if a bishop promotes someone to sacred orders, even though no express statement be made, there is nevertheless a tacit consent to continence. To prove this point, as men skilled both in divine and human law, [Col. 1217D] they introduced many other examples according to the manner in which each law speaks of consent as sometimes expressed and sometimes tacit and unexpressed.

We, on the other hand, demanded an express abolition of the customs and the formal annulment of that written instrument concerning which we have spoken sufficiently above. Otherwise, neither our peace nor the peace of the Church would be secure unless the first and principal cause of all disturbance and dissension, like the root of every evil, were eradicated. This was particularly necessary because, as we have shown above, the archbishop had been circumvented and deceived into giving his assent to those customs.

If, therefore, he reached an agreement with the king without any mention of the customs, either specific or general, he would seem to treat his former assent regarding the customs as valid and to confirm what had been wrongly done, according to the rule of civil law: “Ratification relates back and confirms the acts which have been done.” [Col. 1218A]

We further argued that the same reasoning which they advanced against the king on our behalf would rather support the king against us—namely, reasoning concerning tacit and unexpressed consent. Silence, we said, would not abolish those evil customs, but would rather bind the archbishop all the more to observe them. At one time he had wrongly and unlawfully bound himself to them; but through apostolic absolution, vehement opposition, and grievous exile, that unlawful obligation had been utterly broken and dissolved.

Therefore, if in the restoration of ecclesiastical peace there were such silence—and silence from a person obliged to oppose—so that no mention at all was made, either specifically or generally, of annulling those customs, manifest consent would seem to be present, and the former unlawful obligation, already expired, would revive. Many canons speak to this case. One says: “He who does not oppose when he can is proved to consent; nor is he free from the stain of hidden consent who ceases to oppose an open crime.” [Col. 1218B] Many other canons and examples to this effect were then introduced; but for brevity’s sake we omit them here, especially since they are very familiar even to persons possessing only modest legal experience.

Moreover, we most insistently demanded restitution of goods taken from us—or rather, from the Church—both movable and immovable, repeatedly invoking the rule of divine law: sin is not remitted unless what has been taken is restored. [Col. 1218C] We certainly demanded greater things, and things which we knew with certainty could not be obtained from the king through the cardinals, because some court officials—our friends, though secretly so—had privately forewarned us; and we discovered that they had not obtained from the king even what they offered us.

For the king had already determined with certainty and even publicly sworn that the archbishop should not return to his church while he himself reigned. Yet the cardinals, one of whom favored the king in every respect, proposed to us terms of peace of whatever sort, so that by some means they might excuse the king, as though peace failed to be made through no fault of his; and, as we have already said, lest they themselves appear to have come in vain and accomplished nothing.

Accordingly, peace remaining unmade—indeed, with all hope of peace through them thereafter absent—we departed from them in this manner; they immediately returned to the king. [Col. 1218D]

Meanwhile, in Maine, in the city of Le Mans, certain persons of the kingdom had already assembled. Seeing that peace could by no means be effected through the cardinals, they renewed in the cardinals’ hearing their appeals to the Apostolic See on behalf of the king, the kingdom, their own persons, and their churches. After some time, the cardinals, greatly honored by the king and laden with lavish gifts, returned to the Roman Church, our peace and the Church’s peace having remained unmade.

[Col. 1219A] We immediately began to inquire whether this second appeal ought to be respected. Although the law speaks without distinction and says that, once an appeal has been lodged, whether received or not, nothing is to be altered, lest prejudice be done to the judicial determination—and although under each law it belongs to the person to whom the appeal has been made to determine the appeal—our learned advisers did not teach this indiscriminately and without distinction. Rather, like men trained in these matters, they taught wisely and learnedly, advancing many arguments to show how the law speaking thus concerning appeal should be understood. We omit what they then advanced, for brevity’s sake, especially since such matters are familiar to learned men.

We therefore judged that the appeal in question was not to be complied with by an inferior judge, since it had manifestly been made in order to evade justice and to oppress the oppressed. Nevertheless, all of us urged, advised, and counselled our lord the archbishop that the person of the king alone should still remain untouched. [Col. 1219B]

## 23. HOW THE ARCHBISHOP ANATHEMATIZED MANY OF THE COURTIERS

Therefore the archbishop, knowing from the prophet that cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood and he who does the work of God negligently, girded himself for action. First, he most strictly summoned certain clerics among the courtiers who, by reason of their order or ecclesiastical benefice, were bound to him and obliged to render obedience, [Col. 1219C] requiring them not to postpone or delay coming to him. To some, by virtue of obedience and under peril to their order and benefice, he gave certain commands; but the former did not come, and the latter did not obey.

Therefore, without yielding to the appeal, the archbishop struck them with the sword of God’s word and publicly bound them with the bond of anathema. As the canons prescribe, insofar as the malice of the times permitted, he sent out his formal notices and declared them anathematized.

This was done concerning court clerics. Likewise he acted against court laymen, and for various causes: some because they were invaders; some as violent detainers of ecclesiastical property; some because, during his pilgrimage, they had received estates of the Church of Canterbury, not from him but from the king. In short, he struck with anathema all who had accepted, by the king’s authority, the custody of the lands and possessions of the archbishopric of Canterbury or of those who were accompanying him in exile. [Col. 1219D]

Nor did he act only against these and those: he also anathematized some of the bishops themselves because of their manifest disobedience, and especially because they had become promoters of the whole dissension between the king and himself and did not cease day by day to foster it. Among those thus anathematized was Gilbert Foliot, bishop of London. Those from the court who were anathematized were among the king’s more intimate friends and advisers.

Accordingly, nearly all those in the royal court were now either expressly excommunicated by name or, at least, excommunicated through participation with named excommunicates, whom they could neither avoid nor were permitted to avoid. Thus there was scarcely anyone in the king’s chapel who could offer the king at Mass the sacramental kiss of peace [Col. 1220A] who was not excommunicated either by name or by participation. These, therefore, were excommunicated, and those as well. For the archbishop could no longer endure it and would no longer do so. He did not cease, did not spare—neither these nor those.

He did not endure it, I say; he did not spare them, even though the apostolic man, by his authority which presides over all, had already absolved some whom the archbishop had bound: namely, the aforesaid bishop of Salisbury and that court cleric whom we mentioned above as having unlawfully entered into association with schismatics in Germany against the peace of the Church and against the apostolic man.

## 24. HOW, FOR A SECOND TIME, THE KING AND THE ARCHBISHOP SEND TO THE APOSTOLIC MAN
Hearing that the king was stirred and troubled, and that everything was going adversely for his party [Col. 1220B]—namely, since no deference was paid to the courtiers for the king’s sake, nor to the appeal for the Apostolic See’s sake—they send and send back messengers to the apostolic lord with all speed. Messengers run, hasten, hurry—messenger after messenger, and then again further messengers—to report these matters to the apostolic lord. We too send messengers. But since we had neither gold nor silver, we sent ourselves again, as before, only bare, grim words written in ink. They, however, sent gold and silver in abundance, and much more, and more numerous things than before.

Yet our pious king of France, whose court we were now, as it were, members of—for we ate at his table—sent devout petitions in his sacred letters to the apostolic lord and to his familiar lords, the cardinals, sending and sending back, commanding and repeating his command on our behalf [Col. 1220C]: that whoever touched us touched the apple of his eye. Above all, he commanded and begged that the apostolic lord should not absolve those whom so venerable and holy an archbishop had so justly bound, nor render void the works of justice which he had performed against the enemies of the Church. The bishops and princes of the land likewise petitioned the Roman pontiff and the venerable cardinals, with every devotion and affection, urging the same thing.

Thus, both by our own people and by our adversaries, the thresholds of the Apostles were worn down day by day. Both sides ran about, hastened, hurried. Men died on the way, on both sides alike; but others succeeded them and multiplied among both parties. For, to speak of our own side: from the multitude of our fellow-exiles we had an ample supply of messengers [Col. 1220D]. Thus, as we have sufficiently shown above, by the dispensation of the Most High, he who—without knowing it—had assisted our cause greatly in this as in other respects, by expelling us had joined so great a multitude of fellow-exiles to us. He furnished us with the counsel of men so learned and prudent, and prepared, even against himself, messengers so faithful on our behalf.

But what then? You might indeed have seen the poor archbishop and his ragged, wretched fellow-exiles striving vigorously, in varied and powerful fashion, against citizens, against kings, against men clothed in purple and rich men. Hence, as I then learned in some measure, there is no reason why a vigorous and learned man, though poor in silver or gold, should be compared with silver or gold. For such a man is beyond comparison; hence the Wise Man says of wisdom: “All good things came to me together with her” [Col. 1221A] (Wisdom 7). He does not say this of power or riches: rather, “Woe to the land whose king is a child!” (Ecclesiastes 10). And the Psalmist says: “The rich have lacked and suffered hunger” (Psalm 13). Therefore the wise man preferred wisdom to these things, and these things were added to him.

Such a man, as we have said—and it does not weary us to repeat it—is beyond comparison: always abounding, always rejoicing, never needy or sorrowful. “As having nothing,” he says, “and yet possessing all things; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Corinthians 6). In accordance with this, one of the philosophers said that each man’s soul is his own fortune. And one of the orthodox said: “A man whose spirit is great never has a small estate.” Hence also the Wise Man: “The plans of the strong are always for abundance” (Proverbs 21). Such a man is always fighting, always triumphing [Col. 1221B], never overcome or failing. As that master and contest-giver says: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12). And the Wise Man says: “Have you seen a man swift in his work? He shall stand before kings and shall not stand before the obscure” (Proverbs 22).

Such was this Thomas of ours: great-souled and strong, always abounding, always in battle, always bearing the palm—one of that catalogue of the strong and holy, who could be killed but could not be bent. This will be shown more fully at the end of this history. Meanwhile let this be added here: it is no wonder that this Thomas of ours is proclaimed great here, since he was always great—great at court, great in the Church, great when a citizen in England, great when an exile in France; but incomparably great, and greater than great, greatest today [Col. 1221C]. Though now enclosed in a small tomb, he has taken wings at dawn and, flying from us upon the wings of the winds, draws the whole world after him. But what follows will teach this more clearly. Meanwhile let us return to the course of the history. Thus, as we began to say, very many and opposing embassies were made to the apostolic lord.

## 25. HOW THE ROMAN PONTIFF WAS CONSTRAINED BY THE OPPOSING MESSENGERS OF THE KING AND THE ARCHBISHOP

The Roman pontiff was therefore under pressure. On the one hand, the cause of justice which we upheld pressed him not to invalidate what we had done, but rather, himself seized by apostolic zeal, to rise with us against evildoers [Col. 1221D]; so too did the favour of the world, which was with us, and the earnest desires and petitions on our behalf of our pious king Louis and his people. On the other hand stood against this the contrary requests of the king of England—still young, as we said above, yet so powerful—and of his party.
