The apostolic lord also considered that our archbishop was a man swift in his work and, as he himself saw and had already learned from others, could henceforth neither be recalled nor be willing to desist from the work of justice: that is, from wielding his sword and striking down and slaughtering those whom he had hitherto borne for so long and so patiently in their atrocious conduct. The apostolic lord therefore considered the archbishop’s zeal so inflamed and his adversaries’ obstinacy so hard. Hence [Col. 1222A] it seemed shameful, irreligious, and perhaps damnable for him to suspend from his office an archbishop inflamed with priestly zeal for such a just cause, or to invalidate the works of justice performed by him. From this there would arise a great and grave scandal to the whole Church, and he would incur no small indignation from the king and kingdom of France.

Therefore, since only one course seemed to remain, the Roman pontiff judged it necessary still to labour for the friendly restoration of peace between the king and the archbishop. He repeatedly and very frequently sent his sacred letters to the lord king of France, commanding, admonishing, and requesting the king to interpose himself as mediator of our peace. He also sent now to these men, now to those—especially to those believed to be more willingly and favourably heard by the lord king of England [Col. 1222B], and by whose work and industry it was hoped that the cause of peace might be advanced more effectively and successfully. He sent also to religious men, men of peace, whose diligent work and effective grace are customarily devoted to restoring peace and reconciling those at variance.

Thus the Roman pontiff sent and sent back, commanded and repeated his commands. Most of those apostolic writings still survive, collected into that body of letters mentioned above; whoever wishes to read and know these things may turn to it.

## 26. CONCERNING A CONFERENCE OF KINGS, AT WHICH OUR PEACE DEPENDED UPON THIS ADDITION: “SAVING GOD’S HONOUR”

The lord king of France, seeing the lord pope so concerned for our peace, acted diligently and attentively as a son of peace and one obedient to the apostolic lord [Col. 1222C]. Accordingly, he invited us to many of the conferences between himself and the lord king of England, acting there as mediator of our peace. Among them was one conference which I ought not to pass over in silence, to the praise and glory of so great an archbishop.

It happened that the Poitevins and Bretons, owing to certain disputes, took up arms against the lord king of England; and, that they might rebel more strongly and securely, they allied themselves with the illustrious king of France, who at that time was likewise at enmity with the king of England. But after many days a conference was arranged, and peace was restored among them all, until finally they came to us, who, likewise seeking peace, attended the conference [Col. 1222D].

Many and eminent ecclesiastical persons and many other great men gathered, all acting as mediators between the king and the archbishop. The king had already told certain of these mediators privately—those whom he suspected of favouring the archbishop more, and whom the archbishop regarded as his closest friends—that he wished to take the cross and depart for Jerusalem, provided only that peace first be made, with his honour preserved, between himself and his archbishop. He added that, in the present conference before the king of France and others, he sought from this peace only honour, at least in words.

After a lengthy discussion of our peace in the assembly of all the mediators, apart nevertheless from the kings, those whom we have mentioned as more intimate with the archbishop than the rest—and to whom the king had thus insinuated his statement about the cross and our peace [Col. 1223A]—drew the archbishop apart from that common circle of mediators. More secretly they put before him the king’s words which they had received from the king in private. Yet they did not report them in the king’s name, but truthfully affirmed that they had received this from the king.

Their principal counsel was this, and they laboured with all their strength to obtain it: that the archbishop should submit himself wholly to the king’s mercy and will regarding the entire dispute and the property taken both from himself and his followers. This was, as people commonly say, to place himself, concerning the whole complaint between them, “in the mercy of the king,” and to do so absolutely, without any addition. Indeed, at the urgent request and advice of mediators pressing him to this, the archbishop had already agreed in the hearing of all the mediators that he would do so, but with this addition: “saving God’s honour.” Yet those mediators who were more intimate with the archbishop—faithful men experienced in counsel, in whom the archbishop had confidence as in himself—strove to remove that addition, “saving God’s honour,” because, as they said, the king would be offended by those words.

They therefore urged him with the utmost exertion and earnestness to submit himself absolutely, in the whole controversy, to the king’s will and judgment; thus, before all men, he would give the king glory and honour, satisfy the king, and suffice for him; and the king in return would restore to him his full favour and peace. This wording resembled the earlier addition concerning the observance of royal customs, while we were still in England [Col. 1223B]. For the archbishop had said that he would observe the royal customs, “saving,” that is, “his own order”; we did not pass this over above in this historical little book. That addition, therefore, resembles this one: there, “saving his order”; here, “saving God’s honour.”

By the same persuasions and arguments through which the mediators of peace in England had then attempted to remove the addition “saving his order,” these men now in France attempted to remove the similar addition “saving God’s honour.” And indeed, the archbishop would have expressed again here that first addition concerning his order, had it not been that, as we showed above, the king was then offended by that addition—just as he would now be offended by this one, “saving God’s honour,” as will shortly be said.

But what happened? At last he was so persuaded, drawn, pressed, and impelled that he appeared persuaded [Col. 1223C]. When, finally, he spoke briefly and privately with his learned advisers, as time and opportunity then permitted, and laid before them individually the things he had received secretly from those mediators who were his closest friends, all their wisdom was swallowed up. For they saw on the one hand the good of peace and the king’s most desirable favour, but on the other hand it seemed that it might be shameful, irreligious, and dishonouring to the Church if the archbishop, in an ecclesiastical cause, submitted himself to the will and judgment of a lay person in such a way that no mention was made of the liberty of the Church or of God’s honour—especially since God’s honour had been mentioned and the question had already been raised.

Yet for the good of the Church and of ourselves, which they most confidently hoped and affirmed would follow [Col. 1224A], the mediators urgently advised this and sought it with every insistence—above all the faithful and religious men among them, who were most experienced in counsel and most intimate friends of the archbishop. Therefore all our learned men hesitated and feared to give advice, lest peace be impeded through them, or lest the cause of the Church which they were pursuing be endangered through them. Thus, in this predicament, all were silent; all counsel failed among our learned men, and their wisdom became useless, as though wisdom were no longer to be found in Teman.

I say that wisdom and counsel failed among our learned men, except that some murmured that in such a case it was by no means safe to suppress or pass over God’s honour, or ecclesiastical liberty, in order to acquire earthly favour [Col. 1224B]. This, they said, would be nothing else than putting a lamp under a bushel, as was likewise shown above in this little book, when the similar addition, “saving his order,” was removed in England for the supposed good of peace. Thus in this narrow strait wisdom and counsel failed.

Therefore, what seemed our only remaining course in so tight a crisis was to cry out to the Lord, beseeching him to give us the spirit of counsel and knowledge. But while we suspended our counsel and hesitated about what was to be done, the archbishop was so persuaded, drawn, and impelled by the mediators of peace—many and great men, especially the religious men and others among them who were the archbishop’s closest and most familiar friends—that, as we said above, he was thought persuaded.

[Col. 1224C] Thus, when he was already being led by the mediators of peace and others gathered about him to the kings—for the two kings were still together, awaiting the outcome of our peace—the disciple who wrote these things managed, though with difficulty amid so many and such great persons, to insert himself. Briefly and as quickly as possible, for he could do no otherwise, he whispered in the archbishop’s ear:

“Lord,” he said, “see how cautiously you walk. I tell you one thing most certainly, speaking from conscience: if in this settlement with the king you leave unspoken that addition, namely ‘saving God’s honour’—especially since the entire present effort is to have this silenced for the sake of the king’s favour—just as you suppressed in England the words ‘saving your order,’ when the observance of royal customs was then being discussed, your sorrow will now be renewed as it was then [Col. 1224D], because you have become mute and kept silent concerning good things. You will continually remember in grief that verse of the Psalm: ‘I was dumb and humbled, and kept silence even from good things; and my sorrow was renewed’ (Psalm 38). And your sorrow will be renewed even more, because, having then been struck for similar silence, you have still not received instruction.”

Hardly had these words been spoken, and the archbishop only looked at me, unable to reply—so great was the throng pressing upon him and seeking to speak with him—when he was led before the kings. Knowing that humility above all things usually softens hardened hearts, and that it is more pleasing than other virtues even to proud and exalted men, so much so that pride itself submits to be conquered by it [Col. 1225A], the archbishop, knowing this, immediately at the beginning threw himself at the king’s feet.

With him did so, in honour of the king, the venerable and universally praiseworthy William, son of the great and illustrious Count Theobald of blessed memory, then archbishop of Sens. Hugh, of holy memory, whom we named above in this history and who was alive at our first arrival at Sens, had by then died. But the king, scarcely had the archbishop fallen at his feet, immediately took hold of him and raised him up.

Raised up and standing before the kings, the archbishop humbly and devoutly began to appeal to the king’s clemency on behalf of the English Church entrusted, as he said, to him though unworthy and a sinner. As is the custom of the righteous, he accused himself at the beginning of his speech, attributing solely to his own deserts the great disturbance of the Church and its harsh affliction [Col. 1225B]. At the end of his speech he added:

“Therefore, my lord, with respect to the whole cause now pending between you and me, I submit myself to your clemency and judgment in the presence of our lord the king of France, the bishops and princes, and the others standing here.”

But he immediately added what neither the king, nor the mediators of peace, nor anyone else—not even his own advisers—expected him to add: namely, “saving God’s honour.” As has been sufficiently said above, the mediators of peace had been working to prevent him from adding such words, which would offend the king and thus hinder peace. Therefore they believed that the archbishop had been persuaded not to add words which, by causing offence, might impede peace [Col. 1225C].

And this is indeed what happened. On hearing such an addition, the king was immediately greatly offended and became furious with the archbishop. He assailed him with many insults, reproached him with much, heaped very many reproaches upon him, and accused and rebuked him as proud, arrogant, forgetful, and ungrateful for the royal generosity bestowed upon him.

Because the archbishop’s character, as we said near the beginning of this history, had from early youth been so upright and honourable that even liars and detractors, because of the integrity of his reputation, feared to make false accusations against him, the king expressly alleged against him only this charge: that when he was still chancellor, he had received acts of homage and oaths of fealty from his men, both on this side of the sea and beyond it [Col. 1225D], everywhere, from great and small alike, as the king claimed for the purpose of disinheriting his lord and king, who had bestowed so much upon him, and making himself lord of all. Hence also, as the king added reproachfully, while he was chancellor he made himself so magnificent and lavish.

The archbishop, however, heard these things with complete patience and, so far as could be seen, was neither disturbed nor disconcerted. He at once answered his reproacher. It was indeed a word full of humility and modesty, so measured in answering that he appeared neither harsh nor yielding. After the other things which he had first said briefly, he immediately added in answer to the king’s accusation concerning the chancellorship:

“My lord,” he said, “what in anger you now reproach me with concerning my conduct as chancellor, you appear to be seeking in anger to turn into a fault for me—though it is something by which I ought to have earned your perpetual favour. It is neither fitting nor necessary that I should now call to mind, in praise of myself, what I did in your service at that time and the loyalty I then kept toward you [Col. 1226A]. For our lord the king of France, who is here, knows it; those standing by know it; the world knows it; and my deeds bear witness what manner of man I showed myself, while I was still at court, in that courtly office, for your profit and honour. It would be disgraceful and improper to recall reproachfully the benefits of service rendered—benefits which the world saw and knows to have been bestowed.”

But the king, no longer enduring this, quickly snatched the words from his mouth, turned to the lord king of France, and said:

“My lord, observe, if you please, how foolishly and proudly this man has abandoned his church. Neither I nor anyone else expelled him from my kingdom; rather, of his own accord, by night, he undertook a secret flight when no one was expelling him. Yet now he persuades you that he is acting for the Church’s cause and suffering for justice, and by this he deceives many great men [Col. 1226B]. For I have always wished and allowed, and still wish and allow, that he should hold and govern the Church over which he presides in all that liberty in which any one of his holy predecessors held and governed it more fully and freely.”

The king of France, apparently somewhat moved against the archbishop and favouring the king because he had mentioned his holy predecessors, said briefly to the archbishop:

“My lord archbishop, do you seek to be more than a saint?”

This word, spoken by the king of France as if insulting the archbishop, greatly pleased the king and his party. For it was always their aim and effort, before everyone and especially before the king of France, to justify their own cause and lower ours, thereby alienating from us the heart of that king who, by the Lord’s gift, in our great distress was our entire and secure refuge [Col. 1226C].

But the archbishop, not visibly disturbed or moved in any respect even by the kings now appearing hostile to him, answered the kings immediately with the same composed and even spirit as before. He said that he was indeed willing and eager to receive the Church entrusted to him in those liberties in which his holy predecessors had governed it; but that he refused to accept other, new customs introduced to the detriment of ecclesiastical liberty, and would reject and condemn them as contrary to the ordinances of the holy Fathers.

When the archbishop began to excuse himself concerning the flight which the king had reproached as a rash and clandestine nighttime departure, and wished to allege that its cause had been just, the many and great men who had acted as mediators of peace, as we said above, immediately drew the archbishop apart from the kings’ hearing. They wisely perceived from these and other words exchanged between the king and the archbishop that not peace but rather greater discord would at once arise. Drawing him aside [Col. 1226D], some advised, others advised; they summoned and recalled, pressed and urged, all crying out:

“Give glory to the king. Let the words that offend the king be suppressed and kept silent; submit yourself absolutely to the king’s will and judgment, especially because this is now the most favourable time for peace: the lord king and the chief men of France are present, and all are now at peace except you and your people.”

Many and great persons urged the archbishop to do this, as we have said: secular princes and bishops, Frenchmen, Englishmen, Normans, Bretons, and Poitevins; even certain religious men who had come to the conference especially for us, and by command of the apostolic lord, as mediators of our peace, in the hope of a better and more secure restoration of our peace [Col. 1227A]. All alike asked, advised, and urged only this: that he should remove or leave unspoken that tiny phrase of submission, namely, “saving God’s honour,” and so immediately obtain, for himself and his followers, peace with honour and glory before kings and princes.

You might indeed have seen the archbishop standing like a victim, and all the others standing round like executioners armed not with iron but with tongues, seeking to extinguish God’s honour, though they thought even in this that they were rendering service to God. But shortly afterward all who had accused him openly and everywhere would acknowledge that they themselves had been outwitted and deceived, as what follows will show. Meanwhile let us continue what we began.

Thus the archbishop stood—truly stood—like a most firm tower set upright and facing Damascus [Col. 1227B]. Pressed by so many and such great men, he was not overthrown. Continually, now to these, now to those, he declared that he would do as they advised: “saving God’s honour.” For he said that it was in no way fitting that a priest and bishop should otherwise submit himself to the judgment of an earthly man, especially in a case concerning ecclesiastical liberty and most of all when the issue had been raised concerning this very phrase. It was indeed a great thing, and should be enough, if this were done—even more than justice required—unless the good of ecclesiastical peace supplied the reason for doing it.

And indeed, according to the Psalmist, “The righteous man washes his hands in the blood of the sinner” (Psalm 57). And, as the saying of the Wise Man testifies, when the pestilent man is scourged, the wise man becomes wiser; just as people commonly say that “one who has been scalded fears water” [Col. 1227C]. For in England the king had been offended, as we showed above in this history, by a phrase similar to this one, namely “saving his order.” At the advice of certain persons, the archbishop had kept silent about it, hoping thus to recover the king’s favour. Yet afterward he gained no favour from the king by this; rather, by becoming mute concerning good things, his sorrow was increased and renewed far more than before. Therefore he now feared what had then occurred.

Accordingly he stood immovable among so many and such great men pressing and urging him—like a house built upon firm rock, like an unmoving city set upon a mountain, like an iron pillar and a bronze wall over the land—singing, in heart, mouth, and deed, as it seemed in the midst of armies, to kings, princes, and bishops: “O God, who hast girded me with strength for battle, and hast made my arms like a bow of bronze” [Col. 1227D] (Psalm 22). Certainly not forgetting then that lawgiver’s command: “Do not follow a multitude to do evil, nor in judgment assent to the opinion of the many so as to depart from the truth” (Exodus 23). In accordance with this, one of the philosophers likewise said: “One ought rather to choose what the few choose.”

Seeing him thus unmoved and inflexible, the mediators of peace all immediately withdrew from him, and he remained alone. Alone, I say, he who alone had borne the pressure of the winepress: he had borne it bravely and trodden it victoriously. Thus, as we have said, the mediators of peace withdrew from him, leaving the athlete of the Most High alone in the field as though in an arena—for the conference was held on a level stretch of open ground [Col. 1228A]—and immediately reported to the kings the man’s obstinacy, interpreting the greatness of his constancy as obstinacy.

The kings then departed in great haste on horseback—for night had already ended the conference—without greeting the archbishop and without being greeted by him. Indeed, the king of England, even as he withdrew, did not cease from abuse, though not to the archbishop’s face; among other insults he said that that day he had taken vengeance upon his traitor. Likewise, the courtiers and those who had acted as mediators of peace uttered many reproaches against the archbishop as they withdrew, even to his face: namely, that he had always been proud, arrogant, wise in his own eyes, always a follower of his own will and judgment. They declared it a great evil, an enormous loss and danger to the Church, that he had ever been made governor of the Church, and that the Church, already partly destroyed through him, would soon be utterly destroyed [Col. 1228B].

But the archbishop set a guard upon his mouth while sinners thus stood against him. He seemed to ponder and say to the Lord that verse of the Psalmist: “You are my protector and my refuge, for you have delivered me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word” (Psalm 90); and this: “O Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Psalm 119). Thus, toward those reproaching and insulting him, he became like one who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth—except that he answered one man, who reproached him with the destruction of the Church, humbly and gently.

This man was one of the bishops, John by name, an Englishman by nation, then bishop of Poitiers, a man very intimate with, dear to, and esteemed by him through long companionship and association. The archbishop answered him thus:

“Brother, beware lest the Church of God be destroyed through you; through me, by the Lord’s favour, it shall not be destroyed” [Col. 1228C].

This alone he answered to him: a word of modesty and gentleness, amid a conference full of insults and reproaches. As we have said above, he so moderated all his speech that he could neither be charged with arrogance nor mocked for weakness, in accordance with the Psalmist’s boast that he had waited for the One who saved him from faintness of spirit and tempest (Psalm 54). For our archbishop likewise waited at this conference, and that One saved him in this way. And though, as we showed above, he was harshly rebuked by the king, he did not contend with the king, following the Psalmist’s counsel: “Do not contend against him who prospers in his way, against the man who carries out what he devises.” Likewise the Wise Man says: “Do not litigate with a powerful man, lest perhaps you fall into his hands.”

When abused by others, he did not return abuse: truly a disciple of him who, “when he was reviled, did not revile in return; when he suffered, did not threaten” [Col. 1228D].

Good God, how much your warrior suffered in that conference for this honour of yours! How greatly he was afflicted; with what reproaches he was treated; by what wrongs he was assailed! Yet he always spoke your honour before kings and was not ashamed. For although he was made a wonder to many, you were his strong helper. Therefore, though drawn, pressed, and urged, he was not overthrown, not conquered, did not yield; but, as the outcome of events will soon prove and what follows will show, he triumphed gloriously even in the judgment of all his enemies.

Why indeed should the Lord’s soldier not triumph, clothed as he was with the Lord’s armour? In that conference, as though in an amphitheatre, he set against the darts of words the breastplate of justice; against lances of tongues, the shield of patience; and against promises of earthly prosperity, the helmet of eternal salvation. With that vigorous warrior-king he sang: “Though camps rise up against me, my heart shall not fear; though battle rise up against me, in this will I hope” (Psalm 26) [Col. 1229A].

Thus he departed from the conference rejoicing—truly, rejoicing exceedingly—that he had been deemed worthy to suffer reproach for God’s honour. He went rejoicing, I say; his followers also went, though not rejoicing as he did, but somewhat sad and anxious because the word of our peace had not proceeded even in the form advised by all. Few among us did not dislike the fact that, despite the counsel of so many and such great men, that phrase, “saving God’s honour,” had not been suppressed or at least altered.

### Concerning the Disciple’s Words to His Master upon Their Departure

Nevertheless, as soon as he could gain access upon their departure, the disciple who wrote these things said to his lord and master:

“My lord, supreme thanks must be given by you and yours to the Almighty, in whose hand are death and life, who today so moderated and guided your tongue that neither arrogant nor weak words proceeded from your mouth. Amid the great tumult of this day, when so many and such great persons rushed upon you, when you were assailed with so many insults and wrongs [Col. 1229B], the Lord, the guardian, saved and preserved you from faintness of spirit and tempest. He guided your tongue—placed in wetness and so easily prone to slip—as though along the very middle of a royal road, so that in your answer neither faintheartedness could be discerned nor arrogance noted.

“And indeed, the world shall yet see eye to eye that the Most High will honour you before the world. In so tight a crisis you did not suppress, not even in words, the honour of the Most High for the world’s sake; rather, you confessed it so bravely and steadfastly. And according to his promise, he whom you have confessed will confess and honour you, as he promises those who honour him: ‘Whoever honours me, I will honour’ (John 5) [Col. 1230A].”

Thus we departed from the conference now in France, as earlier in England at Northampton, as we have sufficiently shown above in this historical little book, made a reproach to the prosperous and an object of contempt to the proud.

And we, departing thus, followed the lord king of France, whose lodgings had been prepared in the castle called Montmirail, situated on the border of the Chartres country and Maine; on that border the conference between the kings had been held that day, as they are accustomed sometimes to confer there. We too were lodged in that castle together with the king himself, who always abundantly supplied us with provisions through his court servants. Thus we arrived at our lodging before the king, though it was already late, at nightfall, since the business of the conference—many and great matters, and above all the question of our peace—had so occupied the whole day in discussion that it was prolonged almost until night. The king, however, who arrived later, did not turn aside, as he had been accustomed to do at other conferences, to see the archbishop at his lodging. From this we immediately inferred that his heart was not toward us as it had been yesterday and the day before.

Nevertheless, the archbishop showed himself cheerful and pleasant, as was his habit; no change of countenance betraying any disturbance on this account could be detected in him. Here one may observe the man’s great steadfastness, the unconquerable fortitude of his spirit: although the world had now turned against him, he showed no sign whatever, even a slight one, of being troubled or anxious because of it. Indeed, had he had only care and foresight for himself, this would not have been so striking or admirable; but, as has been sufficiently shown above, he had a large following of his fellow-exiles. Among them were many who did not know their right hand from their left; all of them depended upon his care and foresight as upon the breasts of their mother. Yet, though the world had now become hostile to him, he appeared disturbed in nothing and anxious about nothing. But truly, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “The righteous is as confident as a lion” (Prov. 28); even though the whole world be opposed and hostile to him, the whole world is nevertheless riches to him even then.

In accordance with this, the master-athlete whom the world persecuted, and who persecuted the world, said to some whom he had begotten in the faith: “All things are yours, whether life or death, things present or things to come.” Thus all things belong to the righteous man; whether the world wills it or not, the whole world is riches to him, even if the whole world opposes and resists him. Indeed, it is the more his own the more it opposes him, and the more obedient the more adversarial it is. For the world, though unaware of it, nevertheless forges an eternal crown for the righteous man, as it were between hammer and anvil—between the punitive evils which it inflicts and the virtue of patience which endures them. Therefore a hostile and offended world serves the righteous man more than one that is appeased; and it serves him better when it rebels in this way than when it obeys. As we experience daily, grief occupies the furthest bounds of joy; whence, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “Nothing that happens to him makes the righteous man sad” (Prov. 12).

For, lifted up from the earth, he draws all things to himself. The world’s prosperity and adversity alike serve in his campaign. Its darkness is as its light to him—except that, as we have briefly taught here for the occasion, the world’s adversities serve the righteous more. Our Thomas, therefore, lifted up from the earth, to whom earthly things now meant nothing, drew all things to himself; and hence, though the world had now turned against him, he became neither sadder nor more anxious, but remained unchanged.

## 27. HOW THE ARCHBISHOP ENCOURAGED HIS FOLLOWERS ON THE ROAD

On the following day, while the king, fatigued by the conference of the preceding day, was still resting, we left the castle early in the morning and came to Chartres, hastening toward Sens. While travelling, the archbishop, having perceived that many among his learned followers were displeased because the proposal for our peace had not proceeded as the mediators had advised on the preceding day, addressed them as follows:

> “Brothers, and fellow-soldiers of Christ with me: yesterday we were in military service; yesterday in combat; yesterday in the wrestling-ground, made a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men. And now the world mocks and derides us, because, like presumptuous fools, we have thus deferred the peace of the Church and our own peace. Indeed, it believes and proclaims that peace has henceforth been taken away from us rather than delayed.
>
> “But, brothers, as you know me better, according to the precept of the law, as men who know the law, one must not yield to the judgment of the multitude. This is particularly evident, for example, in truth and poverty, which are always friends to one another: few are their friends. On the other hand, the world is always a friend to vanity and riches; and, in the judgment of almost everyone, vanity is preferred to truth and riches to poverty. For even if some perhaps prefer truth and poverty to these in words, they deny them in deeds, following riches and vanities instead.
>
> “But because we have now chosen truth and poverty beforehand for the sake of justice, and belong to that small company of friends who embrace truth and poverty more dearly, let us not yield to the multitude, nor believe the world any more than the world believes us. For precisely because the world now mocks and derides us, our cause, in which the world does not share, must be judged more precious and purer by us: illuminated all the more by the light of truth, which few follow. It is like ‘the light shining in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it’ (John 1), and like ‘a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed’ (Song 4). Sealed, I say, and singular is our fountain, in which no stranger shares.
>
> “Let us now see and consider whether our cause has not, since yesterday, become purer, more just, clearer, and more evident. Before, indeed, we were pleading the cause of the Church, asserting ecclesiastical liberty and protesting that our adversaries tyrannically strive to lay upon her neck a yoke of slavery, which she will shake off when it pleases the Lord and in the manner that pleases the Lord. Now, beyond the Church’s cause, we have expressly undertaken to plead God’s own cause also: his honour we neither keep silent about for worldly wisdom, counsel, fear, or favour, nor, with the Lord’s help, shall we keep silent about it. Thus cause has been added to cause: the cause of God to the cause of the Church, the cause of the Bridegroom to the cause of the Bride, the cause of the Head to the cause of the body.
>
> “And so now, for the first time, the cause which we have undertaken to defend is whole: namely, the cause of God and the Church, of Bridegroom and Bride, of Head and body. Let us therefore see to it that henceforth we are, even more fully and more abundantly than before, vigorous, steadfast, and whole-hearted warriors—as the cause is whole, so may we be whole. By ‘whole,’ I mean that we must not separate or be divided, but stand together; and likewise whole, so that the crashing onset of the world may not break our battle-line—hitherto strong though few in number, but, as the Lord henceforth increases our strength, stronger still, since his own cause has now been added to it—whether fear should break it or favour soften it.
>
> “For these are the world’s two mighty arrows; but they are blunted and rebound, and will not pierce us, nor harm us even a little, if, as we have begun, we stand bravely in battle-array and put on the breastplate of righteousness, which we set against these arrows of the world. And behold, we have put it on and are protected by it on every side. For we now possess the weapons of righteousness at the right hand and at the left: the just cause of God and of the Church; the just cause of the King who reigns in heaven, and the just cause of the Queen still militant and a pilgrim upon earth. Therefore things go well with us, since help will come to us both from heaven and from earth. For the Church will pray, and the Lord will hear, whose cause of honour we have now undertaken to defend together with that of her liberty.
>
> “And behold, because the world sees and marvels that our small number and poverty still resist so great a power, with king now allied to king, it proclaims our folly all the more. And now, with the kings thus allied, they say of us: ‘Poor wretches! Where will they go? Where will they turn aside? Where will they flee? Do they not know that such great kings have exceedingly long hands? If they were driven from Pontigny at the king’s command, will they not now, when kings are friends and allies, be more quickly driven from the kingdom—indeed, even from the world?’
>
> “I know that you too hear the world speaking freely about us in this manner. And indeed, what is more grievous than all else, we have all now perceived that, because of this alliance, the favour and kindness of our lord the king of France toward us, though not yet altogether exhausted, have nevertheless been diminished. But what then? Certainly, whether the world wills it or not, whether it slanders, accuses, beseeches, or reproves; even if camps rise up against us and the battle of the world, with the Lord’s help we shall stand together. We shall not turn back; we shall not yield.
>
> “Rather, we must now act more strongly and more courageously, since our cause is now more just and the world more fiercely opposed to us, so that, seeing the constancy of our small number and poverty, the world may at last draw from it matter for praise on our behalf, where now it finds material for slander. For if God is for us, who is against us? (Rom. 8.) He destroys the wisdom of the wise and makes the wise men of the world foolish; and often, indeed very often, turns to the highest good what the world judges worst, and draws to the merit of virtue what that world assigns as the wages of sin and the penalty of condemnation.
>
> “Thus the Master teaches that the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For what the world, according to its own wisdom, judges evil or conducive to evil, God himself, by the event itself, judges to have been good for the world, and turns to good what the whole world judged conducive to evil. Thus it is with good things and bad things, and with things leading to good and things leading to evil: the world judges both sorts, and God judges them too. But God plays, and the world is played with, when the outcome proves other than, and directly contrary to, what it had judged.
>
> “Countless examples prove these words of ours. Among them is the famous example of Joseph: his brothers sold him so that they might not worship him, and later, because they had sold him, they worshipped him; and the wisdom of the world deceived itself. Likewise the Jews crucified Christ lest they lose their place and nation; yet afterward, because they crucified him, they lost both; and again the wisdom of the world deceived itself. Many examples of this kind are at hand, and many more arise daily—the world being thus mocked, and God thus playing in human affairs.
>
> “As one of the poets says:
>
> > Divine power plays amid human affairs.
>
> “But you, as men trained both in the Scriptures and in examples of deeds, know these matters better than I. Yet I have introduced them now so that, taking comfort in the present moment, you may know with complete certainty one thing which I now proclaim to you: the word by which we did not suppress God’s honour in the presence of kings through silence will shortly be turned by the world itself to our honour and glory, though the world now turns it to our disgrace and to the injury of ourselves and our cause. The world itself will furnish us from this the increase of virtue, from which it now derives such fuel for slander against us. For, as is its way, it will thus become contrary to itself, being so mocked by divine power, which is accustomed to play with you. Therefore, my brothers and fellow-workers with Christ, be comforted by these words.”

Having heard these things, all became more at peace in mind. Those among us who, as we said above, had been somewhat disheartened because the proposal for our peace had not proceeded according to the mediators’ advice, received from them no small consolation. For we all knew our lord archbishop to be a man exceedingly capable, trained in many things and experienced in much, and one to whom the events he had foretold had very often come to pass.

Accordingly, as we left the aforesaid castle called Montmirail and came by day to Chartres, many people, who according to popular custom had come out to see us pass, asked who it was that was going by. When they learned that this was the Archbishop of Canterbury, and who he was, they immediately pointed him out to others who did not know him, signalling and saying to one another, though in undertones: “Look: that is the archbishop who, at yesterday’s conference, refused to deny God for kings, or to keep silent about God’s honour.”

For they had already heard this among other reports through the widely circulated news of the conference. The archbishop, overhearing these words, was moved and touched by them, and looked at the disciple who wrote this, who was then near him. Later too, as we travelled through France, many among the people declared the same things about the archbishop. At the very departure from the conference, some who had counselled otherwise came to their senses and, moved by repentance, extolled in praises and proclamations the man’s constancy and the cause of justice, condemning themselves and all others who had urged the contrary. But the subsequent course of the history will shortly explain these things more fully and better.

Leaving Chartres, we came as quickly as we could to Sens, by a journey of two days. On returning to Sens we sat there for some days in solitude, kept silence, and awaited salvation from God alone. Our chief mediator on earth for our peace, our lord the king of France, and most of the others who, as we have said, had intervened for our peace at the command of the apostolic man, had now all abandoned the effort, since everyone had despaired of our peace. They said that we were by no means sons of peace, nor did we consider what belonged to peace, but that through ourselves we would rather prevent it from being made. Thus we sat for a time; we endured, kept silence, and waited. “Waiting, I waited,” and the Lord inclined toward us.

## HOW THAT WHICH THE WORLD HAD CONSIDERED A DISGRACE BECAME GLORY FOR THE ARCHBISHOP

For behold, after several days had passed, it became generally known throughout the land that the peace between the king of England and the Poitevins and Bretons—which had been made and confirmed at the aforesaid conference in the presence of, and through, the king of France—and other agreements also confirmed between the kings, had been outrageously and cruelly violated by the king of England, contrary to agreement and faith. Nothing done there now remained undone; no obligations or agreements had been observed. Some people who had been reconciled were despoiled of their possessions; others were expelled and proscribed; and some were captured, thrown into prison, and put in chains. Among those captured was a certain nobleman of Poitou, Robert of Sillé.

When the king of France heard this, receiving through their own messengers a most trustworthy account of what had been done, he was troubled beyond measure. He lamented that he himself had betrayed those nobles whom he had thus reconciled, and that their blood would be required from no hand other than his own. And in lamenting he repeatedly said: “How prudent, how discerning, how provident was that Archbishop of Canterbury, who opposed all of us so steadfastly and resisted everyone so courageously, lest he make the peace which all advised and desired! Certainly we ought to have sought and followed his counsel at the conference, for he knows that king’s character and mind.”

The whole land now declared likewise that the Canterbury archbishop was a great, provident, and discerning man, without an equal in the land: he had stood so bravely, steadfastly, and courageously against so many and such powerful opponents; he alone escaped where all the others, apart from him, were caught and deceived. Above all, those who had acted as mediators at the conference concerning our peace extolled us—some of whom, as we said above, had mediated by apostolic command. One of them confessed in his own words to the disciple who wrote this: “Certainly, I would rather have had my foot cut off than that your lord archbishop had made at the conference the peace which I and all the others advised.”

There was there a brother of Grandmont, the worthy Bernard of Corillet, a religious man experienced and prudent in affairs. He and another man with him, namely the then prior of Mont-Dieu, of the Carthusian order, a man of renowned religious life and learning, were at that time mediating by apostolic command between the king and the archbishop.

After these events had occurred, the king came to Sens a few days later. Visiting the archbishop as he had formerly been accustomed to do, he immediately, at the beginning of their conversation, commended and extolled the archbishop and his followers in a remarkable manner. Thereafter the king and archbishop were much more intimate and friendly than before. The whole land also, increasingly commending us, gave us greater honour and reverence day by day. Thus the archbishop’s saying was speedily fulfilled: as he had foretold, as shown above, when departing from the conference, what was then being turned to our disgrace would shortly be turned to our glory.

The disciple who wrote this often recalled with the archbishop the truth of that saying in which the Lord himself, righteous and true, declares: “Whoever honours me, I will honour him” (John 5). This was the saying which the disciple had recalled to his master above in that difficult situation, namely at their departure from the conference. It was indeed a recompense of honour on earth for the honour shown to God at the conference; yet it was only a small beginning of that honour, whose incomparably greater and happier consummation was reserved for the man’s future consummation, as the conclusion of the history will show. Meanwhile, however, this honour granted in return was some consolation amid the present affliction.

When therefore the archbishop and his followers saw that the king’s heart had thus returned toward them, they gave highest and devout thanks to God, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, as the supreme helper of the poor in times of tribulation. The archbishop, seeing that the time was now favourable, asked the king—who had already become our mediator in response to apostolic entreaties—to write to the apostolic man that our peace had not been accomplished, and to state what had occurred and how matters stood. He asked the same of bishops and princes, especially those who had been present at the conference, both themselves and those who had been mediators of our peace by apostolic command. The king agreed and wrote; these wrote and those wrote; and now, more warmly, keenly, and urgently than ever before, they pressed upon the ears of apostolic clemency against the opposing party. Whoever wishes to know the matter more fully should consult the frequently mentioned collection of letters.

## 28. HOW THE KING AND THE ARCHBISHOP SENT A THIRD TIME TO THE APOSTOLIC MAN, AND CONCERNING THOSE SENT FROM HIS SIDE FOR THE PEACE

[Col. 1236A]

Thus, while the king wrote, these wrote, and those wrote, and the writings, prayers, and messages of all were received by the apostolic man—pressing so warmly, keenly, and urgently at the door of apostolic mercy and justice, and stirring the bowels of apostolic compassion—the Roman pontiff was again placed under no small, indeed much greater, pressure than before. On the one hand he saw that peace could not be achieved through mediators; on the other, as we have sufficiently shown above, during so terrible and harsh a schism it was dangerous to exercise severity of ecclesiastical discipline upon one who had a multitude of allies. Yet the grave and enormous offence committed against us, and the cause of justice which we were pursuing, demanded it.

The apostolic man certainly judged that cause much more favourably, both through the letters and through messengers, after hearing what had taken place at the aforesaid conference of kings. He was especially distressed by such great and urgent advocates, who pressed him keenly on our behalf; and it would have caused no small scandal to them, and likewise to the whole Church, unless peace were henceforth restored to the archbishop, his followers, and the Church entrusted to him, whether through justice or through an amicable settlement.

Therefore the apostolic man, thus constrained and seeing these things, resolved once more, in accordance with the form of the canons, to cite the king, warning, exhorting, advising, and commanding him to cease troubling and disturbing the Church, and to restore their peace to the archbishop and his followers. He did not send cardinals from his side, as he had done before, but certain other learned and capable men of his court, his special agents, to execute the apostolic mandate. One of them was named Gratian, of blessed memory, nephew of the late Pope Eugenius; the other was a legal advocate at the curia named Vivian.

They arrived quickly and without difficulty. Unlike the cardinals, they brought with them neither so much baggage, nor so much finery, nor so many little packhorses burdened with bundles. Immediately, before even seeing us, they went to the king. Again and again they addressed him concerning the Church’s peace and our own, according to the apostolic mandate entrusted to them: now warning and exhorting with every gentleness, now rebuking and reproving more severely. One of the legates in particular did not flatter, defer to, or spare him; rather, with the authority of his apostolic embassy, he rebuked and reproved the king with every command, standing before his face. This was Gratian, more lively, sharper, and more urgent than Vivian, his companion in the embassy—truly Gratian both in name and in deed. In every way he laboured to restore to us the king’s favour and the Church’s peace; and through this mediation he acquired much favour before God and men.

Moreover, lest he place any stain upon the apostolic embassy entrusted to him, he accepted from the king neither gold nor silver—by which the king especially customarily corrupts hearts, and through which even the prudent are most often overthrown—nor any offered appearance of a gift. Instead, he trampled silver as mud and rejected gold and everything else. For he had resolved, in a holy and religious spirit, to accept nothing unless perhaps the peace for which he had come had been restored. Thus he coveted nothing and accepted nothing.

Yet, according to the testimony of the Lawgiver himself, gifts blind the eyes of the wise. This man, however, thinking holy, religious, and prudently upon what follows, feared to accept them; for the Lawgiver immediately adds: “And they bend the force of authority.” This is well and precisely said. For, according to one doctor’s interpretation, if he accepted something from the person whom he had come to rebuke, he would bend the authority of his teaching. One cannot rebuke insistently a person from whom one receives, especially when that person is ready to give in order to humble his superior.

Accordingly, he accepted nothing, lest the vigour of the apostolic embassy grow slack because of this. In this he followed the Master, who abstained even from lawful things lest, by accepting them, the authority of his Gospel embassy in rebuking, reproving, and restraining should be nullified or at least weakened. Hence he himself says: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial. All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any” [1 Cor. 6]. As if to say: “I do not wish to receive, because I do not wish to be subject; because I do not wish to make a servant of my freedom.”

For everyone who receives, especially one who exercises the office of teacher, is in some sense inferior to the giver and, by a certain lowest kind of contract, bound to his giver. Thus afterwards he does not possess the freedom in rebuking, reproving, and punishing which he had before: that freedom is not indeed annulled, but is violated and partly weakened. Therefore the Lawgiver rightly, having first said, “Gifts blind the eyes” (Deut. 16), immediately and carefully added, “and they bend the force of authority.” Gifts do not, as we have said, annul authority; but by weakening it, they lower and bend the persistence in rebuking and the power of restraint, which is the force of authority.

Thus, just as according to the Lord’s proverb, “It is always more blessed to give than to receive,” so it is always more glorious and magnificent. For it belongs to lords and to those who seek lordship to give; it belongs to subjects and inferiors to receive. The person who receives thereby shows himself inferior. Hence the Master said above that it was lawful for him to receive, but nevertheless: “I do not receive, because I will not place myself under anyone’s power” (1 Cor. 6). How great, how free, and how truly Christ’s legate was this man, accepting nothing and rejecting all things, lest by weakening his authority or violating his freedom he should, in any respect of obligation, be inferior to the one whom he had to correct. Hence, as he himself writes: “But we have not used this power, but endure all things, lest we give any offence to the Gospel of Christ” (1 Cor. 9). And he added that it was better for him to die than for anyone to deprive him of his glory.

[Col. 1238A] Likewise this Gratian, our legate—of whom, for his praise and that others may imitate him, we have digressed somewhat—rejected everything, lest he give offence to the apostolic embassy. He judged it preferable thus to reject all things and return empty to the Apostolic See than to let anyone deprive him of his glory. His glory was increased all the more because, though Roman, he did not go after gold. Would that all legates of the Apostolic See were like him: freely rebuking, reproving, and restraining; placing themselves under no one’s power; seeking nothing; accepting nothing; even rejecting gifts offered—unless only after the person rebuked and reproved had perhaps thus turned to a better course. Then they might look upon Abel and his gifts, but turn away from Cain and his gifts, and abhor offerings from the wicked; for, according to the testimony of the Scriptures, the Most High does not approve such gifts but abominates and rejects them. Nor ought those who on earth act in the place of the Most High and hold his office to approve such gifts; rather, they ought to reject and spurn them as abominable. This our legate did praiseworthily.

At length he and his said companion in the embassy, having repeatedly conferred with the king concerning peace, came to us and reported that, in every point of the business for which they had come, they had found the king evasive, double-dealing, tortuous, and dissembling concerning the matter at issue. He always sought through certain indirect courses, evasions, and carefully devised artifices to delay the business of peace for which they had come, while making every effort to justify his own side and depress ours. Gratian especially did not conceal, keep silent about, or hide this from us.

Therefore, now fully perceiving that peace could not be achieved through them, or perhaps through any other mediators, without compromising the honour of God and the Church, he was no longer detained by verbal evasions, enticed by promises, or laden down with gold or silver. He returned promptly and without delay to the Roman Church and to the apostolic man. He returned, I say, as a faithful legate, reporting fully and completely to the apostolic man what he had seen and heard. He returned quickly and expeditiously; while the other, who had been his companion in the journey and embassy, still remained with us on this side of the Alps. For, infected, as was said, by the poison of our western island and stuffed with our silver, he could not return nearly so quickly or readily.

When the king saw Gratian returning in this manner as a faithful legate, not seeking his own interests and weighing displeasure and favour in the matter for which he had come in an equal balance, he began to deliberate what should be done. Not without reason, he thought that Gratian, returning thus to the lord pope, would discredit his cause and justify ours. He also thought that the king of France, moved by the violation of the aforesaid peace of the nobles allied with him, would press the lord pope more strongly against him on our account. He therefore endeavoured by whatever art he could to calm the troubled king and either remove altogether or suspend the ecclesiastical censure which he now feared.

While considering these things, he first resolved to appease the king by some appearance of humility, knowing that a gentle and mild man is easily overcome by humility, which is pleasing even to the proud. He said that he would make a pilgrimage to the glorious martyr Dionysius, apostle of the French, and that he would thus see his new lord, the king’s son, whom he had never seen before. This was the desired boy, given by God beyond everyone’s hope to the king after many years of his reign—indeed, to the whole people—the only son of his father, Philip by name. He later succeeded his father in the kingdom and now reigns; may he reign happily and powerfully through years and ages.

## 29. HOW THE KING OF ENGLAND CAME INTO FRANCE, AND HOW THE ARCHBISHOP’S PEACE WAS THEN HELD UP BECAUSE THE KISS OF PEACE WAS REFUSED

[Col. 1239B]

Accordingly, a few days later the said king, as if unexpectedly and without warning, entered France and sought no conference with the king; for he knew that the troubled king would avoid it. But, under the guise of a pilgrim, he came to the glorious martyr Dionysius, apostle of the French, confidently hoping that, when the king heard of his arrival in the country, he would immediately come to meet him. He also hoped that the Archbishop of Canterbury would hasten to him and, as he had always been accustomed, beg for peace. For, as we learned with certainty, he had now repented that at the last-described conference he had not listened to us concerning peace, even in the aforesaid form and addition, namely, “saving the honour of God.”

And indeed, just as the king had anticipated, so it happened. The lord king of France himself came to meet him, and we too turned aside and went to that place between Paris and Saint-Denis which is commonly called Saint-Martyrdom: namely, to a chapel at the foot of the hill called Montmartre, or, as others call it, the Mount of the Martyr. That chapel, they say, was called Saint-Martyrdom because the aforesaid glorious martyr Dionysius had been beheaded there. We accordingly turned aside to that place of Saint-Martyrdom, to the chapel.

The kings, who had already met and had encountered the desired boy named above, brought outside Paris to meet them, had arrived before us and were awaiting our coming on a level expanse outside the chapel. When someone urged the archbishop to hurry, saying that the kings were now waiting only for him, he answered that it did not become a priest to walk except with dignity. Thus we were at Saint-Martyrdom, while the kings were outside.

The other legate of the Apostolic See, who, as we said above, remained behind when Gratian returned, seeing that the opportunity for action had now arisen, began urgently to press the lord king of England through the lord king of France, through other great men, and through himself, for our peace—the purpose for which he had come. He did so all the more urgently because, now that his companion and fellow-mediator in peace had returned, he alone remained, desiring, if perhaps the Lord should grant it, that peace might be made through him as mediator, to his greater glory. For in human affairs glory is greater in proportion as it is more singular, if in great and vigorous deeds one has neither an equal nor a partner.

The gentle king of France, together with the princes and bishops present, diligently and earnestly intervened, carrying out with the greatest care their part in the work of peace. Accordingly, like solicitous mediators, they went and came, arrived and returned, again and again between the king and the archbishop. But what followed? After many objections made on both sides, after many persuasions privately and publicly, when the day had now largely passed, everything had been smoothed over and brought to the calm of peace.

All evil customs—though not expressly, but in general terms, namely those by which the Church would be enslaved—were renounced by the king; and liberties for the Church’s honour and the clergy’s dignity were, as it appeared, graciously accepted by him. Yet no explicit statement concerning either of these matters was made on either side. For, as everyone maintained, explicit terms would have done harm, as likely to disturb completely the calm of a peace already arranged. And of that added phrase, “saving the honour of God,” over which there had been such contention and struggle at the preceding conference, there was here no recollection or mention. Nor was there need. For what was now being negotiated was not that the archbishop should subject himself, in an ecclesiastical cause or otherwise, to the king’s will and judgment.

The king said only that the archbishop should enter the land—from which, however, the king said he had not expelled him—and should there perform what belonged to an archbishop; and that in customs and other matters he should render due regard to the king as his king, and should not, under pretext of the Church, usurp things that belonged not to the Church but to the king; while the king, conversely, would not usurp what belonged not to the king but to the Church.

## CONCERNING RESTITUTION OF WHAT HAD BEEN TAKEN, REQUESTED FROM THE KING
The archbishop, however, spoke most urgently among other matters to the lord king of the Franks and the other mediators of peace concerning the property taken from himself and his followers. He repeatedly set forth that rule of divine law, in language common to learned and unlearned alike: a sin is not forgiven unless what has been taken is restored. He added that it in no way befitted royal magnificence to convert the goods of the poor or confiscated property of the Church to its own use, or to distribute gifts out of another’s property. That, he said, would be as if someone uncovered one altar in order to cover another [Col. 1240D], or crucified Paul in order to redeem Peter. He reckoned the money taken from himself and his adherents at thirty thousand marks.

But to this the lord king of the Franks and the others alike replied that it was neither honourable nor fitting for a peace so necessary and so desired by both kingdom and priesthood to be obstructed for money, especially between so great a king and so great an archbishop. While urging this, they recalled the former friendship between them and did not pass over in silence the mutual services and benefits bestowed on either side. Moreover, they added that it would by no means be the act of a just and pious shepherd, when all matters had now been smoothed out and the liberty of the Church restored, for him to reject his Church—his bride—when she was offered to him, and to remain an exile on account of a financial claim. Rather, he ought gladly to receive his bride [Col. 1241A], though stripped, torn, and violently rent, in both arms of affection; and, as her spiritual bridegroom, to render to one who asked what belonged to a spiritual bride.

Nevertheless, the mediators said that they would willingly and diligently confer with the king on this matter. When the king had been approached, he replied that, once the total amount of the losses had been made known and established through the archbishop’s representatives, he was prepared, upon the advice of prudent and religious men, to make restitution. Since the archbishop had raised the question of both immovable and movable property, the king added that he would likewise discuss the immovable property in due course.

### On the guarantee of peace requested from the king

Thus, after many and varied engulfing storms, when we seemed, and all hoped, to have been led almost to the very entrance of harbour [Col. 1241B], the archbishop, through the mediators, requested from the king a guarantee for the peace offered. He added, however, that in this respect he suspected nothing sinister of the king; rather, because of the great enmities that had preceded, the king’s men were not without reason to be suspected—especially unless some form of guarantee intervened, which would be an evident sign of restored peace and renewed favour.

Indeed, as a prudent man, he had many days before consulted the apostolic man—that is, the pope—about what he ought to do and what guarantee of peace should be required, if after so many hostilities he were reconciled to the king and allowed to enter the realm and return to his Church. The apostolic man replied to this consultation that it was by no means fitting for a priest, in such a cause and at such a juncture, to demand from his king a guarantee by surety, pledge, or even oath. Accordingly, it was not the apostolic man’s counsel that the archbishop should demand any of these.

The apostolic man further maintained that the cause which he was pursuing was the cause of justice, the cause of the Church; and that, if peace were made, it would likewise be the peace of the Church and of justice. For such peace, whether achieved or unachieved, it was precious and safe to die—and safer precisely insofar as it was more precious. Therefore the Roman pontiff answered that none of the aforesaid guarantees ought to be demanded by a priest in that circumstance and cause. Such guarantees should rather be demanded by worldly and secular persons than by ecclesiastical persons—by priests and bishops, that is—who, if they have the cause of justice, find life a loss and death a gain. [Col. 1241D]

The apostolic man therefore wrote to the archbishop that, if by the Lord’s favour peace should be granted between him and the king, he should be content with the kiss of peace alone, without exacting any other secular guarantee. This alone—the kiss of peace—ought to suffice a priest pursuing the cause of justice; nor was it fitting that he should accept another guarantee unless it were freely offered, not demanded.

The archbishop, therefore, having received this advice, when at last all matters had been completed toward peace with much difficulty and labour, requested at the conclusion of everything, in accordance with the apostolic man’s counsel, that guarantee alone as the sign of peace and favour between himself and the king: namely, the kiss of peace. He said that, after so many hostilities and under the hand of so powerful a king, he was content with this alone. When this had been conveyed to the king through the lord king of the Franks [Col. 1242A] and the other mediators, the king replied that he would gladly do it, except that in anger he had publicly sworn that he would never give the archbishop the kiss of peace, even if in the course of time he should restore peace and favour to him. He said that he now refused the kiss for no other reason than because he had so sworn—not because he retained any anger or resentment in his heart.

When the lord king of the Franks and most of the mediators heard this, they immediately suspected that beneath the honeyed words previously spoken, poison had secretly been administered to them. They at once returned to the archbishop, who was awaiting their return in the aforesaid chapel called Martyrdom, and reported the king’s answer. Being cautious men [Col. 1242B], to whom by now everything was suspect, they neither advised nor dissuaded him in either direction, but merely reported the king’s plain and bare reply.

The archbishop, most cautious among cautious men, and a man of much experience, at his first hearing fell at once into the same suspicion as the others. From the guarded and veiled words which he then spoke, it could already be seen that he foresaw what was to come. He did not defer his reply for consultation, but immediately and decisively answered that he would not at present make peace with the king unless, according to the apostolic man’s counsel, the kiss were given as the sign of peace.

This firm reply, together with the night which was now approaching, broke off the conference. The kings still had a long journey ahead, to Mantua, which lies twelve leagues by land from Paris, where lodging had been prepared for them. [Col. 1242C]

The king of the English, exhausted by the whole day and still having a night journey before him, repeatedly cursed the archbishop as he travelled, recalling and rehearsing on the road the labours, vexations, and annoyances he had already endured because of him. At the kings’ departure, we immediately returned to the house of the Templars, called the Temple, near and outside Paris, where we had been lodged.

At the very departure from the chapel called Martyrdom, in which, as we have said, our peace had been discussed that day, one of us approached the archbishop and said: “Today the peace of the Church was negotiated in Martyrdom; and I believe that the Church will obtain peace only through your martyrdom.” The archbishop, turning briefly to the speaker, replied: “Would that she might be set free even by my blood!” [Col. 1242D]

### The address of the archbishop’s learned companions to him

That same night, after the nocturns had been sung, most of our learned companions assembled and addressed the archbishop as follows:

“Lord, attend to us. It is necessary both for the Church of God and for us who have followed you that we consider how we may walk cautiously, understanding what is the good and acceptable will of God, and that we may not be carried away by impulse but governed by judgment. Behold: this is now the sixth year of our pilgrimage. During all this time we have attended many conferences of kings and princes, always, whenever opportunity was given, seeking peace and pursuing it [Col. 1243A].

“Yet we have not obtained it, nor have we yet advanced; nevertheless, by the Lord’s favour, we have not injured our cause even in the least. By the spirit of counsel given to us from above, we carry it back sound and whole amid so many trials and snares, amid so many instigators and overthrowers. And what consoles us in all things is that truth and justice have been inseparable companions of our poverty and pilgrimage. Indeed, our cause, like the rising light, has shone more and more brightly upon the world each day. It has been made conspicuous even by the testimony of our enemies, and in the recent conference which preceded yesterday’s, as you wisely taught your followers by way of consolation, it was glorified by God; so that it is now justified not only by its own children, but also by strangers, who exist only to extinguish the light of our truth.

“Thus God has dealt magnificently with us until now. He has caught the world in its own craftiness, making the world itself, whether it wished it or not, daily bring to light the cause of the Church which we pursue. Likewise, he has made us conspicuous to the world, and, as conspicuous, dear and acceptable to it for the present; so that neither we who followed you nor those expelled on our account have lacked anything. [Col. 1243B]

“But let us carefully examine and consider what was said and done in yesterday’s conference: at what point the peace of the Church and our peace came to a standstill, and for what reason it did not proceed. As it appears to us, yesterday all matters between us and the king were brought into agreement, all was made plain, except that peace stopped at the kiss of peace alone not being given. The sole obstacle to a peace which had progressed so well up to that point was this kiss not given.

“Therefore it is plainly evident that the one thing which obstructed the peace of the Church and our own peace is now the sole cause of our exile. Thus, whereas formerly we endured exile solely for the plainest cause of justice, we now remain exiles solely because a kiss has been refused. For no customs, good or bad, nor the honour of God, whether tacit or expressly stated, is now the cause of our exile; for since yesterday everything has been smoothed out and rough places have been turned into level paths. Therefore this alone now causes our exile, which alone obstructed our peace: the denied kiss of peace. [Col. 1243C]

“If, then, a priest should either abandon or refuse his Church solely because a kiss has been denied—though otherwise he would return to her—and suffer persecutions and exiles for this reason alone, you may judge; it does not seem so to us. Especially since the absence of the priest endangers many people in common.

“And behold, Lord: in this sixth year, as we have said, of our pilgrimage, many episcopal sees within your archbishopric have meanwhile stood vacant under your care; many dioceses have been deprived of their pastors. In consequence, pastoral care perishes, pastoral labour perishes, pastoral work and office perish. There are none to teach; none to celebrate the sacraments in God’s Church. Indeed, according to the prophet’s lamentation, that flock of the Lord, finding no pasture, goes away without strength before the face of its pursuer, like a flock without a shepherd, sheep wandering in pathless country and not upon the way. There is no one to terrify the wolves or drive them from the sheepfold; rather, in the lack of pastors, court retainers become guardians of churches. [Col. 1244A] The endowments of churches, established for the relief of the poor, are diverted into the royal treasury.

“Thus from your absence there comes to the Church a great injury in spiritual and temporal matters, an enormous loss and a common peril. Up to this point, certainly, the cause of your absence and exile was most just. But now, amid this common danger and general crisis, neither absence nor the cause of exile can be just or excusable; rather, it will truly be blameworthy, and more blameworthy than blameworthy. This is especially so because the personal persecution on whose account you fled has now ceased: the king publicly offers you your Church in complete security and peace, whatever he may himself be devising or secretly attempting.

“Therefore the preceding personal persecution now ceases; as we have already shown, a general persecution has succeeded it. In that persecution the good shepherd is bound not to absent himself or flee, but rather to come forth in opposition, to set himself in the way, to cast himself even among drawn and naked swords, and, if necessary, so to lay down his life for his sheep. Thus for a priestly man there is a time to flee and a time to meet the danger: a time to flee when his person is sought, according to the Lord’s saying: ‘If they persecute you in one city, flee into another’ (Matt. 10); but a time to meet it when the Church is endangered, of which Scripture says: ‘He meets it like a lion; he despises fear and does not yield to swords’ (Job 39). [Col. 1244B]

“So the Master first fled through a basket, but afterward went forth to meet danger. When the prophet foretold his departure to him, saying, ‘The man whose belt this is must thus be bound’ (Acts 21), he at once answered: ‘I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem; nor do I make my life more precious than myself’ (ibid.).

“Indeed, the Master of masters, Shepherd of shepherds, pattern and example, first fled into Egypt while yet an infant and tender child; but afterward, as an adult, strong and vigorous, he went forth to meet danger. Thus he who first said to his followers, as though still tender and at their mother’s milk, ‘If they persecute you in one city, flee into another’ (Matt. 10), afterward taught his now strengthened followers by deed as well as word that they should go forth to meet it: ‘Behold,’ he says, ‘I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves: go’ (ibid.). They, therefore, going out into the world and blown upon by the mighty Spirit, rushing upon their enemies, sought not a kiss [Col. 1244D] but a sword.

“Therefore, Lord, if you seek to imitate the zeal of those whose ministry you have received, and the courage of those whose stewardship has been entrusted to you, go and do likewise. Do not pant after a kiss of earthly dust, easily scattered by a single breath; nor fear the sword. Rather, do not reject your Church—not beneath a kiss, but beneath a sword—if need be, though stripped and despoiled, though violently torn and plucked away; but receive her with marital zeal, due affection, and devotion.

“Let not the snares of deceivers, which perhaps are now laid for you, hold you back; let threats not recall you, fear of swords not soften you, nor even the final danger of death delay you. Return, therefore, and we with you; and by the same confidence with which you dared while absent, dare now while present, so that with the prophet’s hoe you may courageously and manfully root up, overthrow, destroy, and scatter what has now grown up wickedly in the garden of the Lord during your absence. [Col. 1245A]

“Yet what we have said above about the grounds for fear and the dangers which might attend our entering the realm, we do not say because we suspect anything evil from so great and illustrious a king as ours. So great a power, so manifest and glorious to the world, could not conceal any lurking-place of so great a deception or plot. From such exalted rank the hiding-place of such deceitful pretence is far removed. Hence it is scarcely credible that he is plotting anything, especially against you, his superior priest in God and for God, or against us, an unarmed race of men—especially after he himself has publicly granted peace and security.

“Therefore, Lord, there is no reason why you should henceforth delay or defer your return to your Church, if this may be accomplished. Let us return promptly, confidently, and without any scruple of conscience in the form of peace offered, pursuing with the highest thanksgiving and praise him in whose strength we return. For the king publicly swore before many bishops and princes of the realm that, while he reigned, you would never return. Yet now he himself offers peace, pledges security, condemns evil customs, and approves good ones. This indeed is the Lord’s doing, whose weakness is stronger even than kings. That he might appear to the world as the only strong one, he chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong. [Col. 1245B]

“And, not to return to examples already past, you see, Lord, at present this little flock of yours—namely, us who have followed you, whom you called by God’s calling to follow you—not noble, not powerful, but the ignoble and contemptible things of the world. Yet, that he alone may be proclaimed victor, God conquers through these under your leadership and direction, so that with the utmost devotion to the Victor we ought to sing an Alleluia of return.

“For we may immediately be considered almost as having returned, when peace is publicly granted us and return permitted by so great a king, by so great a power which had formerly sworn the contrary. Even if it depended upon us not to return, we have nonetheless already conquered in our cause—or rather Christ conquers, Christ reigns, Christ rules.” [Col. 1245C]

### The archbishop’s answer to his followers

The archbishop carefully and attentively heard these persuasive words of his followers and promptly replied. Addressing them, he said:
