“You have spoken as learned men, to whom wisdom and the knowledge of holy things have been granted together with the spirit of counsel. I would answer each point, were it not that I approve all of them. But know this one thing: I should not have refused the peace thus offered by the king, except that I followed the advice of the apostolic man. Otherwise peace would not have stopped because the kiss was denied.

“But because matters have now advanced so far that peace is offered us simply, without condition or obligation of any kind, though it cannot be conformed to the counsel of the lord pope, who advised that the kiss of peace be requested for the firmness of peace, it seems to me at present—I do not know whether it does to you also—that a report should be sent to the pope himself. From his singular primacy, as all members depend upon the head, the whole Church depends. Let all that has occurred be reported to him: how far our cause and that of the Church has advanced, and at what boundaries it stands. [Col. 1246A]

“This is especially necessary now that we are in a narrow place, by no means in safety: peace has thus been granted, but its sign has been denied. Yet because that sign has been denied, as you have encouraged me in your prudent speech, I shall neither reject the Church peacefully offered to me nor despise, as you say, the salvation of souls in peril. Rather, before the cause of justice which we pursue, so manifest to God and the world, is disfigured, I shall, with God as author, be ready, as you advise, to go even to prison and death before yielding. Otherwise our labour is vain and ridiculous if hereafter we give a stain to our glory. And this is our glory: the truth of our cause. Truth, I say, and justice, as I remember that you have just said above, have hitherto been inseparable companions of our poverty.

“Therefore, if it seems good to you, it appears necessary and more prudent before all else to send to the apostolic man, lest whatever happens we should seem to have despised his counsel; and so that by his authority and with his approval, if perhaps the Lord so provides and permits, we may return and re-enter the realm, having first received apostolic permission, blessing, and absolution, prepared to suffer for the Church whatever the Lord decrees that we shall suffer there. Thus the Lord will guard our entrance better and more safely.” [Col. 1246B]

Such was the archbishop’s address to us. We, who had spoken before, hearing him speak so strongly and steadfastly of his own death for the cause of justice and the Church, and seeing him, as it seemed, utterly without need of persuasion and most ready, if necessary, to die for justice before yielding, were greatly moved and filled with compassion. Most of us burst into silent tears, which we wished but could not restrain; and we commended both his speech and his plan of sending to the lord pope. [Col. 1246C]

### 30. How the archbishop sent for the fifth time to the Roman pontiff

Accordingly, we came from Paris to Sens with all haste; and after a few days the messengers were ready. When they were now on the point of departure, the report was widely spread through the realm that a crown had been placed upon the boy Henry, the eldest son of the king of the English, who, as we noted above in this history, had been the foster-child of our lord the archbishop. Roger, then archbishop of York, had anointed him in the church of Blessed Peter in London, at Westminster, while suffragans of the Church of Canterbury stood by and performed the ministry.

For soon after the aforesaid conference, in which the kiss of peace was refused us, the king crossed the sea; and, in hatred of the archbishop and to injure the dignity of the Church of Canterbury, he caused his son, whom we have mentioned, to be anointed king by an alien metropolitan in an alien province. This was an injury to the person of the Church of Canterbury, to whose dignity and right the coronation of the kings of the English has from ancient times been known to belong. [Col. 1247A]

On hearing this, the archbishop at first could scarcely believe it. For, as a prudent man to whom everything concerning his adversaries was suspect, he had obtained letters from the Roman pontiff, sent before the coronation to the archbishop of York and to the other bishops of England. By apostolic authority and under obedience they were forbidden to place the crown upon the king’s son, to the prejudice of the archbishop of Canterbury, who was in exile for justice’s sake. Some bishops received these letters before the coronation; others, forewarned by command, refused to receive them. Therefore all who performed episcopal ministry at the consecration acted contrary to the apostolic prohibition.

But let us pause briefly to consider how profane was this anointing, how odious and hostile this consecration—if indeed it ought rather to be called an execration than a consecration—deprived of apostolic blessing, indeed performed in transgression against the apostolic man. It arose wholly from hatred, anger, and indignation: hatred of the spiritual father, while the spiritual mother mourned, devised by the carnal father. All here is profane; all is truly outside the sanctuary, alien and estranged: an alien province, an alien consecrator, and the boy consecrated king, himself alien, more suited still for play than for ruling peoples; and the king-father who procured the consecration, alienated and estranged from his spiritual father and mother. [Col. 1247B]

The mournful events which resulted from this consecration, detestable to all future ages, prove our words. First, by the authority of the apostolic man, there followed a general suspension of him who consecrated and of the bishops who took part, because, as we have said, his prohibition had preceded the act and had been contemptuously disregarded. Certain bishops were also bound by the chain of anathema for this and other causes.

Then this anointing furnished—not, I say, the full cause—but nevertheless a considerable and more immediate occasion for the precious death of our lord the archbishop. The subsequent course of the history will make this clearer and fuller. Third, in the course of time, this anointing occasioned a harsh and wicked rebellion between the king-father and the king-son; and finally the swift and all-too-early death, in miserable rebellion against his father, of that distinguished boy when he had become an adolescent, arising from that premature anointing. [Col. 1247C]

Behold what abominable and execrable evils came from this consecration: the suspension, anathematization, and killing of priests; rebellion once and again between father and son; and, in the end, the death in adolescence of that distinguished boy thus consecrated—a death detestable to the present age and to all future ages. Therefore one must lament, cry out, and exclaim:

“O your death, Henry—O death! How dreadful, how cruel, how bitter your memory, you who cut down such and so great a glory of the world while it was still only beginning! How thoughtless, how inhuman you were, you who with one brief blast of your violence blew away so certain, as it was thought, a hope of the world while its fruit was still in so brilliant a flower! May he who is the death of death be your death, so that through you he may pass to life—he who was hoped to live not for himself, but for the world.”

Indeed, I have already frequently inserted this distinguished boy into this history, here and elsewhere, as a lily beautifying the whole garden, almost as if set in an open plain, so that the history itself may be brighter and more beautiful by this grafting. [Col. 1248A]

But I cannot pass over in silence here the death of this boy, spiritually, and without doubt, foreshown to our lord the archbishop. While we were in exile at Sens in Gaul, at the monastery of the blessed virgin Columba, our lord the archbishop one night, after nocturns had been sung, retired to his bed to rest. But, as the disciple who wrote these things learned from his own mouth, the cares and thoughts which commonly crowd in then prevented him from yielding to sleep.

Among other thoughts, one occurred to him concerning the lord king of the English: his greatness, prosperity in sons, wealth, and extensive power. As he reflected at length on these, and especially on his sons—most particularly on his eldest son Henry, whom he loved above the others—and on one of the other sons, he said that on the next day he did not know for certain which of the others he had then been thinking of: whether Richard, who after Henry’s death became the king’s heir and count of Poitou, or Geoffrey, now count of Brittany. As he thus considered the king-father and his sons, he desired to know what would become of them and what the dispositions of the Most High concerning them would be. [Col. 1248B]

As he thought for some time in this desire, he began, while thinking, as it were to doze; and behold, a voice came to him, expressing itself in a hexameter verse. The verse was:

> One fate bore off two; another bore off the father—but grievously.

Behold the verse. Let no one suppose that it was composed by chance by one half asleep, when he could not have composed it even while fully awake; for he had not touched the art of versification even slightly, not even in the course of elementary study. But this I know: on the following day he reported the verse he had heard to the disciple who wrote these things, and added mournfully: “Alas! Our Henry dies before his father or his brothers.” [Col. 1248C]

The archbishop spoke thus to the disciple who wrote these things. And truly, in Henry’s death—alas, and how grievous—the archbishop proved an altogether true prophet by the outcome of his prophecy. Likewise, in Geoffrey’s death, while I was still writing this history, the archbishop’s prophecy was fulfilled: after Henry’s death, Geoffrey died, five or six years before his father, as Henry had done. And what adds to the miracle and commends the prophecy still more is this: “One death bore off two”—truly one death, because the same kind of death befell both brothers, who were killed by dysentery and, as those present testified, were taken away well and holily.

Finally, in accordance with the order of the prophecy, four or five years after Geoffrey’s death, the father himself died. The manner of his death, though I am silent, the Church knows and the world proclaims. I shall therefore not continue now to recount the manner of his death. It is enough to have touched upon it here solely that the man of God may be proved a true prophet by the fulfilment of his prediction. [Col. 1249A]

Certainly, I would have inserted here more concerning the vigorous deeds of this Henry of ours, though he was of tender age, and concerning the manner of his departure from life, had not the law of the history which I have undertaken to write stood in the way. Therefore, having greeted the boy snatched away on the journey and returned to his homeland, let us who are still on the road return to the course of the history which we began.

The archbishop, then, when he at last certainly knew that the coronation had been performed in this manner, informed the Roman pontiff, both orally and in writing, through our messengers, whom we have said above were on the point of setting out for Rome. When these reports were first heard, he reported how far our peace had advanced and at what point it had halted, together with the coronation thus carried out. He most humbly and tearfully besought the pope that, even now, he might shake himself, a son of those who had been shaken, and especially take notice of the false brethren who, to the injury of their father—who endured exile and proscription for their sakes—and of their mother, the Church of Canterbury, had now shown themselves manifest transgressors even of the apostolic command. Thus the messengers departed. [Col. 1249B]

When the apostolic man heard everything that had been done and how it had been done, he was greatly angered against both the king and the bishops. He felt a paternal compassion for the archbishop and his followers, far greater than before. Therefore, when our envoys returned—whom, out of compassion for us, he would not keep long, so that we oppressed people might sooner receive the remedy of apostolic consolation—he, like a merciful father grieving with us, administered through apostolic letters things sweet to us but exceedingly bitter to others.

For he wrote to Rotherot, then archbishop of Rouen, and Bernard, then bishop of Nevers, ordering and commanding them under obedience to approach the king of the English most strictly concerning our peace. He added that, if the king persisted in obstinacy and still refused peace, his entire land, both overseas and on this side of the sea, should be placed under interdict: every church office to cease, except the baptism of infants and penances for the dying.

He sent letters of suspension to the archbishop of York and all the bishops who had taken part in the consecration, sternly reproaching, rebuking, and accusing them in writing of shamefully and monstrously having sold their birthright for a vile dish of lentils. He anathematized certain bishops both because they had taken part in the coronation and for certain other causes. [Col. 1250A]

These letters of suspension and anathema were sent and delivered to us through our envoys, to be used by us in their proper place and time. Whoever wishes to know and read these and the other apostolic letters sent to us or on our behalf should turn to the collection of letters which, as I remember, I have mentioned above in this history. Since they are inserted there, we pass over them briefly here, although the occasion for speaking of them has arisen in the course of this history.

In a consolatory letter addressed to the archbishop, the apostolic man praised with congratulation the archbishop’s courage and steadfastness, especially because, if it could not be otherwise, he was ready to return to the realm without a guarantee and without the kiss of peace, like a sheep in the midst of wolves, mindful of the saying in which the Most High speaks to his own: “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves” (Matt. 10). Therefore, just as he received an apostolic blessing, so he then deserved to obtain written absolution from the apostolic man, whatever might happen to him when he entered the realm.

We therefore gratefully received these apostolic writings, whether directed to our adversaries on our behalf or to ourselves, singing of the mercy and judgment of the Lord. [Col. 1250B]

First, the said archbishop of Rouen and bishop of Nevers, in obedience to the apostolic command, repeatedly approached the king concerning our peace. They declared that, unless peace intervened, ecclesiastical censure would shortly fall upon both him and his land, as the apostolic man had commanded. They added that neither threats, flatteries, nor any evasions or shifts of words could remove or suspend this censure, except peace alone being granted; for the apostolic man’s resolve was now firmly fixed. They further declared that they did not dare in any way to let the time fixed by the Roman pontiff pass without carrying out the coercive measure entrusted to them, unless peace intervened. [Col. 1250C]

## The chapters of the fifth volume begin

[Col. 1249]

1. On peace restored between the king and the archbishop.  
2. On the messengers sent by the archbishop to the king, and why.  
3. On the archbishop’s first approach to the king after the peace, and why.  
4. On the archbishop’s second approach to the king after the peace, and why.  
5. On the preparation for our return to our homeland; on what was done in England through messengers before our return; on what we heard at the very point, as it were, of returning; and on the words of the disciple who wrote these things to the archbishop, and the archbishop’s reply.  
6. On the archbishop’s embarking upon the sea, how he landed, and how he was received by the people of the land.  
7. On events at the beginning of the archbishop’s entry into the realm.  
8. On the bishops again stirring up the king against the archbishop, and the reason.  
9. On the archbishop’s words and deeds on the day of the Nativity of the Lord.  
10. On the departure of the disciple who wrote these things from the archbishop, and the reason for his departure.  
11. On the king’s renewed wrath against the archbishop, and on those executioner-knights who came.

## Fifth Volume

[Col. 1251]

[Col. 1251A] 1. Therefore, seeing that matters had reached so critical a point, the king most certainly promised peace. Accordingly, being summoned to a conference of the kings which was imminent, we departed. When, however, the third conference of the kings had ended, and that Christian king of the French was already leaving, our peace was immediately discussed, and indeed through powerful mediators, to whom the lord king of France, on his departure, had entrusted us to negotiate our peace; for he himself could not, or would not, be present then. But why prolong the matter? There our peace was restored. The kiss of peace, which had previously been sought but refused at another conference, as we have said, was neither sought by the archbishop now nor offered or refused by the king. For no mention of the kiss was made there: publicly, before the bishops and princes who were present, the king granted peace and security to the archbishop and [Col. 1251B] his men. With respect to customary rights, and to possessions taken away, whether movable or immovable, and to other matters, the same form of peace was now observed and granted which we set out above at another conference of the kings, where our peace had then failed solely because the kiss of peace was refused. But now the strong athlete of Christ, desirous of peace and not afraid of death, did not demand the kiss of peace, lest peace perhaps be impeded even in that way. Knowing and deliberately accepting such peace as he received, he was truly overcome by love of peace, his fear of death having been driven out by that love, which is stronger than death.

The peace was made on the feast of blessed Mary Magdalene, near the place where the conference of the two kings had been held the previous day: namely, on the border of the territories of Chartres and Le Mans, between two castles, one called Viefui and [Col. 1251C] the other Fréteval. It was made there in a most pleasant meadow, which, as we learned much later, is called by the inhabitants from ancient times the Meadow of Traitors. And our peace was as follows.

The king and the archbishop, alone together, turned aside on horseback into an open plain and spoke privately. Among other matters, the archbishop begged the king to allow him, without giving offence to the king, to punish by ecclesiastical censure the injury which the bishops, his suffragans, together with the archbishop of York, had inflicted upon him and upon the Church at the coronation of Henry his son. The king consented. Giving thanks for this concession, the archbishop immediately dismounted before all eyes and humbly bowed himself at the king’s feet. When the archbishop remounted, [Col. 1251D] the king placed and held the mounting-stirrup for him, while all who stood around watched and marvelled, though they did not know the reason until the archbishop, upon departing, related it more privately to his own people. Then one might see the thoughts of many hearts revealed, especially among the courtiers: some rejoiced, while others were sad and disconcerted—the men who had earlier spewed out the poison of sedition and discord. Others, neither sad nor disconcerted, suspected pretence in these events and thought that, at the final rupture of the peace, mourning and sorrow would prevail. In this they were by no means mistaken, as the following course of the history will show.

## 2. CONCERNING HIS MESSENGERS SENT TO THE KING

Thus the king and the archbishop, apparently made friends on that day, parted from one another amicably. A few days later our messengers were sent to England with the king’s letters, by which the king instructed his officials—those whom they call the king’s justices in the land—concerning the peace that had been made, commanding them to restore the archbishop and his men to their possessions in complete peace and security.

We, meanwhile, returning to Sens in France, the city of our exile, prepared to return home. But before entering England himself, the archbishop decided to send ahead other messengers, senior men and more capable, to investigate cautiously through public report who stood for us and who against us, whether anyone was secretly plotting against us, and what method of restoring our confiscated possessions the king had ordered. The archbishop had determined upon this course chiefly because the lord king had pledged to restore certain estates held of the Church of Canterbury: namely, the fief of a nobleman called William de Ros, and a castle near Canterbury called Saltwood, which a certain Henry, a great man surnamed from eastern Saxony—or, as it is commonly called, Essex—had held from the archbishop before a certain judicial combat in which he had been defeated. Besides these, there was the custody of Rochester Tower, which the archbishop had already [Col. 1252C] protested most firmly and vehemently, again and again, belonged to him by right of his church.

These, then, were the matters specified here which, among others, the archbishop demanded most urgently and insistently, and which the king had promised to restore to him when he returned to Normandy. Our lord therefore sent for this purpose Master John of Salisbury, of holy memory, afterwards bishop of Chartres, together with the disciple who wrote this account. He instructed us also to proceed to England for the stated purpose if the king should fulfil the promised restoration; otherwise, not to do so, but to return promptly to him.

Setting out accordingly, we found the king in Normandy. But because an attack of tertian fever had come upon him, we remained at court longer than we expected. When [Col. 1252D] the king had recovered, we approached him in the archbishop’s name concerning the promised restoration of the aforesaid properties. As was his custom, he postponed, postponed again, and postponed yet again. At last, however, in response to our insistence, he dismissed us, directing his words especially to Master John, who was speaking and making the archbishop’s claim in his name:

“O John,” he said, “I will by no means surrender the castle to you until I first see you conduct yourselves toward me differently from the way you have conducted yourselves hitherto.”

Thus dismissed, and clearly understanding that we could make no progress then, we left the matter unfinished. We did not proceed to England, as we had been instructed, but returned to our lord in France. On hearing this, the archbishop was greatly disturbed, detesting the vain and ever-deceptive promises of the man.

## 3. CONCERNING HIS FIRST APPROACH TO THE KING AFTER THE PEACE

When we learned that a conference between the king and Count Theobald of Blois, a nobleman, would shortly take place, we went to the conference. But on the day before it, the archbishop went from Tours to the king. The conference had been arranged near Tours, on the boundary of the territories of Chartres and Tours. Hearing of the archbishop’s arrival, the king sent some courtiers to meet him; finally, he himself went out [Col. 1253B] of the city and met him.

But when they came together, the king’s eyes—or rather, as could be observed, his countenance—were not directed toward him. This was so marked that, that night in our lodging, neither the king nor any of his men looked at us. Indeed, early the next morning the king had Mass for the dead celebrated in his chapel, suspecting, as they said, that if the archbishop attended another Mass, he might offer him the kiss of peace during Mass; and to refuse it there would not be the act of a Christian, but plainly of an enemy of Christ. As soon as Mass had been celebrated, the king left the city and hurried to the conference. The archbishop followed as well, though more slowly, and caught up with the king before the conference. As they travelled, they reproached each other: each in turn threw in the other’s face benefits formerly conferred and services rendered.

When they had reached the conference, after much of the day had passed, and all matters for which the king and the count had come to the conference had been settled—the archbishop also acting diligently with others as an effective mediator between them—the archbishop at last pressed the king sharply and insistently concerning the promised but unfulfilled restoration of the aforementioned possessions. Yet he frequently reproached, indirectly, the man’s familiar instability in speech and habitual deceit in promises.

Then indeed one could see priestly zeal in the pontiff: true zeal, which, in the very newness of the peace, demanded so manfully and steadfastly the rights of his church from so great a prince, even though unwilling, in whose hand lay both our peace and our lack of peace—indeed, our life and death. Truly he was vehement with the spirit of justice, and in the priest the zeal of God’s house burned. But what followed? At the intervention of the aforementioned count and other nobles, the king again most certainly promised restoration of the often-mentioned properties. Yet the king wished him to return first to his church before the restoration, saying that he desired first to see what sort of man he would show himself to the kingdom. This was the end of the conference.

## 4. CONCERNING HIS SECOND APPROACH TO THE KING

A few days later, the archbishop set out to visit the king, who had then come to the castle called Montcalve, near Blois. He did so not to demand or reclaim anything, but merely to see the king and, if possible, to restore their former familiarity [Col. 1254A] and friendship, so far as the Lord might permit. The king received him as he came with excessive honour, as was fitting, and, as appeared, with great gladness and affection.

While they conversed familiarly and pleasantly, the king said among other things:

“Why is it that you do not do my will? Surely I would place everything in your hands.”

Some days later the archbishop reported these words of the king to the disciple who wrote this account, adding: “When the king spoke to me thus, I immediately remembered that saying in the Gospel: ‘All these things I will give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me’ [Matthew 4].”

I have often taken care to insert these and similar matters about this man into this history, so that, just as we showed shortly before how the priest’s zeal might be perceived, it may now likewise be heard that the affection of the priest was pure from every stain of greed. Not even the poison of imperial riches could corrupt him, though he had long endured poverty. Let no one suppose that these and similar passages are inserted contrary to the rule of brevity, superfluously and without profit. For I remember that I have inserted few, if any, things up to this point that do not pertain—though it may not be expressly stated—either to the edification of one’s neighbour or to the praise of the man. If to both, so much the better.

## 5. CONCERNING HIS PREPARATION TO RETURN TO HIS COUNTRY

The next day, having taken leave of the king, we left that castle and returned to Sens, the city of our exile. We made haste, as soon as we could, poor [Col. 1254C] and exiled though we still were, to prepare our journey home. I do not call us poor because the archbishop and his companions returned in meagre circumstances. Rather, he returned in great and splendid array, with, I think, more than one hundred mounted men. I mention this here so that he may be proved great everywhere and in every condition. And indeed he was always and everywhere great: great in the palace, great in the priesthood, great at court, great in the Church, great in exile, great in returning from exile, but greatest in the completion of his exile. Yet let us wait a little longer concerning this, for the man’s end, and the conclusion of this history, will declare it better.

Having greeted and taken leave of the lord king of France and the princes of that land, who, when the world had abandoned us, had received us so kindly and magnificently, we came on our homeward journey into the territory of Boulogne, to the harbour called Wissant. Before boarding the ships, the archbishop sent ahead letters of apostolic authority which, as we said above, concerned the general suspension of bishops throughout England and the anathema pronounced against certain persons. He sent these letters swiftly to be delivered to the bishops throughout England before his arrival.

Some of them were found in that very harbour intending to cross the sea, perhaps suspecting what unexpectedly happened to them at once: namely Roger, archbishop of York, who was suspended in that harbour; and Gilbert surnamed Foliot, bishop of London, and Jocelin, bishop of Salisbury, who likewise received letters of their anathema in that harbour. The mandate was immediately obeyed: the former acknowledged himself suspended by apostolic authority, and the others acknowledged themselves anathematized. While we, after sending these letters ahead, waited for a calmer wind, this was reported to us. When the archbishop heard it, he rejoiced with great joy, the righteous man being glad because he had already seen the vengeance he desired.

One day the archbishop went out, accompanied by his men and by many others, to inspect the ships in which we were to cross. And behold, we saw a ship, already near land, sailing from England into our harbour. When it had quickly put in, we asked the sailors for news and what people in England were saying about the archbishop’s return. They answered that it would be very welcome and acceptable to the whole land.

But one of them, who seemed to me to be the steersman, drew me, the writer of this account, aside more privately.

“Wretches,” he said, “what are you seeking? What are you doing? Where are you hastening? Certainly to your deaths. Thus those who know say for certain, and all in the country suspect the same. Look: many knights are in the harbour where you seek to land, as is said, so that as soon as the archbishop and his men arrive, they may lay hands upon them. For the country has been stirred up and embittered against you, especially the king’s followers, because at your first arrival in the land you moved and disturbed it by anathematizing and suspending the bishops of the land. Above all, as religious and wise men say, during this Advent of the Lord which is now upon us, an Advent so fruitful, welcome, and acceptable to the world, your arrival in the land should likewise have been one of tranquillity and peace. But you, on the contrary, have disturbed everything by yours.”

Having heard this, I thanked the informant. What he told me, moreover, others were already murmuring thickly among themselves.

A little later, calling the archbishop aside from the crowd, I said to him privately: “The steersman of the ship which has just arrived spoke to me thus and thus.” While the lord archbishop and I were discussing these things, one of our companions intruded: Gunter, a man of good memory, simple and fearing God. When he heard what we were discussing, he immediately said, unasked, that it would be better and more prudent to withdraw for the present, until the storm and disturbance in the country occasioned by the bishops’ suspension had subsided, so that we might return more acceptably and safely. He added: “If the country is already so stirred, what will happen when the king hears?” And he advised against returning to England then.

### The response of the disciple consulted by his master

Soon afterward the archbishop addressed the disciple who wrote this account, who had related what he had heard from the steersman:

“And what do you say?” he asked.

The disciple replied: “Lord, the matter is critical. The magnitude of this decision exceeds the measure of my smallness; and the advice is all the more uncertain because your learned advisers are now absent—some still in France, others sent ahead by you into England. Nevertheless, if you command and permit it, I shall say what I think.

“First, it seems to me that if we return to Flanders or to the land of our exile, it will turn to our shame and disgrace; we shall become a burden where until now we have been an honour. This is especially so now that apostolic leave, blessing, and absolution have been received for our entry and return to our country; that the land of our exile has been saluted; and that peace has publicly been granted and accepted. Thus we must either retreat disgracefully or proceed boldly and act courageously. Otherwise people will surely say: ‘Look, the archbishop of Canterbury who first fled from Northampton now flees a second time before fighting, though he had so steadfastly affirmed that he would stand so firmly and act so manfully for the Church!’ We shall be among those fearful sons who, having aimed and drawn the bow, turned back in the day of battle.

“One thing remains: if there is deceit in this peace of ours—as is indeed suspicious, and as many assert—then the danger is surely grave and unavoidable. For when force and deceit work together, malice can accomplish its designs by power, once power is malicious and malice powerful. Nothing can oppose or resist such a plague. Malice suggests; its allied and cooperating power carries out the suggestion. Earlier we were somehow able to escape the raging lion; but now it is exceedingly difficult to avoid the dragon’s deceit. Every power is more to be feared when it deceives than when it rages. Thus it is proclaimed as a great thing concerning the Saviour: ‘Thou shalt tread upon the lion and the dragon’ [Psalm 9]: the lion’s force, that is, and the dragon’s deceit. This will be the final persecution of the Church in the last days, than which none so grievous has preceded: a persecution composed of force and fraud.

“O then how happy, how glorious the completion of our exile would be, if this final persecution—in which the righteous will be tested at the end of the ages—should begin with us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. How happy, lord, would exile be if, after exile, it were granted from above that you should become not only a martyr, but the firstfruits of the martyrs of the last days. In this above all humbly acknowledge the title of your crucified Lord and King’s death: perhaps you will die by betrayal, just as he, betrayed, died for the Church.

“In this the Shepherd of shepherds gave an example to pastors: if they cannot avoid hidden enemies, they must endure them, even though they see that danger to life will come to them through those enemies. Yet between a cruel and hypocritical prince, who is both lion and dragon, and a good shepherd, the condition is always dangerous indeed, but victorious. Whether that prince rages or deceives, the good shepherd must always be ready to lay down his life for his sheep. Although he may perhaps protect himself from the violent man, there is no way for him to protect himself from the dragon—that is, from the hypocrite. As the common saying has it, no one can protect himself from betrayal, since peace itself is more effective for betraying.

“Therefore, my lord, as it appears to my limited understanding, there must now be no second flight, as formerly from Northampton, nor even any withdrawal, which is in effect flight. Withdrawal, I say, or flight would not now be fitting, as it was at first, nor excusable. For seven seasons have now changed over you. Behold: six years have already passed, and this is the seventh year of our wandering, the seventh of our exile. Throughout all this time sinners have built iniquity upon your back, prolonging their wrongdoing; yet, though they did not know it, throughout this time they have fashioned for you an incorruptible crown. Since this is the seventh year, the year of rest, the file is no longer needed: the crown is ready. No chisel is needed, with skin given for skin. No knife or cutting-tool is needed, when the stone has been cut for so long and has now been shaped and carved. No fiery furnace is needed for gold already tested in the furnace, in which the bones of the old man have dried up like a firebrand. Indeed, the old man in you seems utterly weakened, or rather wholly extinguished.

“For a man thus tested, what remains to hesitate over? What is there to fear or dread? Rather, what is there that he should not undertake, that he cannot accomplish, that he should not dare? You now see your land; enter your church with confidence, following, if need be, him who gave his body to those who struck him and his cheeks to those who plucked them. Let us enter, I say, confidently and powerfully, and we shall be gods to those who now seem to terrify us. Let us enter, lest perhaps it be reproached against us hereafter, when this opportunity has been given us from above: ‘When you could, you would not; when you wish to, you will not be able.’ Indeed, to Moses, so great a friend of God, it was said: ‘You shall see the promised land, but shall not enter it.’ Let us beware, then, lest you—far inferior to Moses—be struck by a similar or perhaps greater punishment, if you do not enter the land which it has nevertheless now been granted you to see.”

After this the archbishop said briefly: “Your speech seems faithful, but hard; and who will fulfil it?” Then, addressing specifically the man who had spoken first and had advised against proceeding to England, naming him directly, he said: “Certainly, Gunter, I see the land; and, with the Lord’s favour, I shall enter the land, though I know most certainly that suffering awaits me there.”

When he said this, I remembered the Lord’s saying to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling-block to me, because you do not savour the things that are of God, but those that are of men” [Matthew 16]. After this, at the dusk of night, we returned to our lodgings.

## 6. CONCERNING HIS ENTRY UPON THE SEA

A little later, after two or three days had passed—on the second or third day after the feast of blessed Andrew the Apostle, during Advent—we embarked by night. With a favourable wind, and because of the suspicion of ambushes which, as we heard, were already being prepared for us, we landed safely, not in the inlet of the sea at Canterbury as was expected, but in another inlet called Sandwich. This was the safer because the men dwelling along that inlet had the archbishop as their own lord, as being of the Church of Canterbury’s own fief.

On the archbishop’s ship, as it approached the shore, the banner [Col. 1258A] of the cross was raised. The archbishops of Canterbury, as primates of all England, customarily have it borne before them. When this sign was raised, by which the archbishop’s ship could be distinguished from the others, one could at once see the crowd of poor people gathered to meet him: some girded up so as to run ahead and receive their arriving father and seize his blessing first; others humbly prostrating themselves upon the ground; some crying aloud and others weeping for joy; all shouting, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, father of orphans and judge of widows!” Such were the poor.

## 7. CONCERNING WHAT HAPPENED AT THE BEGINNING OF HIS ENTRY INTO THE LAND

But the knights, who, as we said above, had expected us to land in the other inlet, hurried to us with all speed. Scarcely had they greeted the archbishop when they boldly asked why, at his first arrival in the land—which ought to have been one of tranquillity and peace—he had immediately, before even entering it, suspended and excommunicated the king’s bishops. They added threats that, as soon as the king learned of it, there would be no small disturbance; indeed, the kingdom and priesthood had already been disturbed by it.

The archbishop replied gently that the king would not be offended by this; that he had done nothing in it against either king or kingdom; but that it had been done, without injury to king or kingdom, with the king’s own permission, so that the injury which the bishops had inflicted upon him and his church at the coronation of the king’s son might not go unpunished, and so that so great a usurpation might not thereafter become a precedent. When they heard the king praised as the author of the act, they spoke more moderately. Nevertheless, they urgently requested that he absolve the bishops who had been excommunicated or suspended. The archbishop deferred this for counsel until he should come to Canterbury on the following day; and the knights then departed.

The next day, the archbishop set out for Canterbury from the inlet at which he had landed, about six miles from Canterbury. As we have already touched upon above, he was received by the poor of the land as gratefully and triumphantly as though he were a sacrifice sent from heaven, or an angel of God himself. But why do I say “triumphantly”? Rather, if it is fitting to speak in such terms of the poor, Christ’s poor displayed the Christ of the Lord as more laureate in triumph than merely honoured in ovation. Wherever the archbishop passed, crowds of poor people—little and great, old men with the young—came to meet him in throngs. Some prostrated themselves in the road; others took off their garments and spread them along the road; and they repeatedly cried out: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!”

The parish priests also, with their parishioners, came out in ordered procession with crosses to meet him as he passed, greeting their father and asking his blessing. Again and again they interspersed that often-repeated cry: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” Indeed, had you seen it, you would have said that the Lord was approaching his Passion a second time; that, with his Passion imminent, a welcome prepared for the Lord was being offered through children, nursing infants, and poor people; and that he who had once died at Jerusalem for the salvation of the whole world was coming again to die for the English Church at Canterbury.

Although the journey was short, he could scarcely reach Canterbury that day amid all the crowds meeting and pressing upon him. There, amid the ringing of bells, organs, hymns, and spiritual songs, he was received by Christ’s poor—his children, that is, his sacred community—with the devotion and reverence owed to their father.

Oh, what a countenance one might then have seen on the man as he first entered the church! Some who saw it observed and marvelled: like a heart on fire, his face too appeared aflame—truly a face made joyful with oil, pleasing to all and gracious to all. And, to add something further, I think that the outward face of the body shone from the inward abundance of the heart; indeed, the flame of brightness in his heart was so great that it could not contain itself without breaking forth. I think that this great grace of countenance, suddenly suffused and made lovely with a rosy hue at his entrance into the church of the Saviour—the very Saviour’s church in which his martyrdom was soon to be fulfilled—was as it were an omen of a heavenly oracle.

The disciple who wrote this account, seeing it with his own eyes, marvelling at what he saw and recording it in wonder, immediately remembered Moses. Moses’ glory of countenance, however, was made void and extinguished at the waters of contradiction; therefore he did not deserve to enter the promised country, but died outside it in exile. This man did not: after many contests, he finally conquered and obtained his country, and shortly afterwards in that very Jerusalem received the unfading crown of his palm. Therefore the glory of his countenance was not made void, nor was its flame of brightness extinguished. Rather, it was tested, not extinguished, at the waters of contradiction—burning and shining always amid peoples roaring and gnashing against him, as the ensuing outcome of events, by the Lord’s gift, will clearly and profitably show.

Standing in his episcopal seat, the archbishop received each of the brethren with the kiss of peace, while many on every side wept aloud and tears burst forth and flowed. As he stood there, the disciple who wrote this account approached him and said:

“Lord, we need no longer care at what hour you depart from this world, since today the bride of Christ, the Church, has conquered in you—indeed, Christ conquers, Christ reigns, Christ rules.”

He made no answer, but only looked at the man who said this to him. When all the ceremonies of that day had been performed in the church splendidly and solemnly, the archbishop withdrew to his palace and spent the whole day in joy and solemnity.

The next day the aforementioned knights returned to seek an answer to their request of the day before. Clerics came with them, sent in the name of their lords, the three previously named bishops, who were still waiting in the aforesaid inlet, and requesting absolution for their bishops. The archbishop replied that the three bishops and [Col. 1260A] the other bishops had been anathematized or suspended by the authority of the lord pope: some had been anathematized, others suspended; and that it did not belong to him to loose men bound by so great a judge, unless perhaps through himself.

When the clerics and knights pressed him most urgently, he took counsel and at last replied that, trusting in the clemency of the lord pope, for the good of peace he would in this particular case exercise what belonged to the lord pope, provided canonical security were given that they would submit to the judgment of the Church concerning the matters for which they had been excommunicated or suspended. Otherwise, he answered clearly and absolutely, he would by no means do this. Hearing this, both groups went away indignantly, speaking many proud and insulting words as they departed. Among them one, whom I remember having mentioned above in this history, named Ranulf de Broc, became especially arrogant in speech. But the archbishop, a man exceedingly patient, became among them like one who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth.

The clerics whom we said had been sent by the three bishops returned and reported to their lords what they had received from the archbishop concerning their request. As was said, two of the anathematized bishops, namely those of London and Salisbury, would have given the security required by the archbishop, had not the third, the archbishop of York, prevented it. Truly it is written: “A third tongue stirs up many.”

## 8. CONCERNING THE BISHOPS AGAIN INCITING THE KING AGAINST THE ARCHBISHOP

That third man so stirred the other two that they immediately crossed the sea to approach the king. They found him in Normandy, near the city called Bayeux, at a royal residence called Bur. This was a few days before Christmas. Having greeted the king, they immediately prostrated themselves at his feet, jointly appealing to his royal clemency and justice on behalf of the kingdom, the priesthood, and themselves, maintaining that he owed clemency to the injured and justice to the injurer.

Thus, in bitter and inflammatory speech, they immediately related how rashly, recklessly, and proudly the archbishop of Canterbury had disturbed kingdom and priesthood at the beginning of his arrival, abusing the peace granted to him and his men by the king’s mercy. They added that the whole English Church was in mourning, all bishops throughout England having been suspended, while they themselves had been both excommunicated [Col. 1260D] and suspended. They further represented all this humiliation as inflicted upon them for a cause so royal, so splendid, so necessary, and so honourable: namely, because they had crowned his firstborn son heir of the kingdom.

By these and similar, indeed greater, arguments, put forward day after day by themselves and their accomplices, they thus incited the king against the archbishop. But I pass over for the moment how and how greatly the king was stirred—rather, into what and how great rage and madness he was driven by their incitements. The subsequent course of the history will show it in its place. Meanwhile, let the pen of the history turn back to our archbishop, and let us set forth how he conducted himself in England after his arrival.

Thus, as we have said, having come to Canterbury, after a few days he sent to that distinguished boy Henry, the king’s son, then king crowned by the bishops now suspended. He sent Richard, then prior of St Martin’s at Canterbury, of good memory—and would that he had been good!—a man sufficiently eloquent and capable, who afterwards succeeded our lord in the metropolitan see. Coming to the king, he courteously greeted him in the archbishop’s name and announced the archbishop’s arrival in the land. He excused him, as instructed, concerning the bishops’ suspension, explaining that it had been done with the permission of the king’s father; and he added that the archbishop was preparing shortly to come to him as his lord.

But that boy king seemed unwilling to accept either messenger or message. Yet, as we learned for certain, this was not the boy’s own wish; rather, he did not dare act otherwise because of the king his father and because of the courtiers who were his tutors, to whose care the king had entrusted his son. They feared the father more than the son. Thus our messenger was not kindly received by either group at court, since they did not dare act otherwise because of the king his father.

Our messenger soon returned to us. Being, as we said, unwelcome to the boy king, he brought us no definite answer; but from his arrival at court he brought us a report of the court’s hauteur, bearing, and haughtiness. The archbishop, however, as a man of constancy, nonetheless prepared for the journey. He wished first, as he had determined, to see his foster-child, the boy king whom he had not yet seen; afterwards, he wished to make a circuit of the province from which he had been absent so long, hastening and longing to travel everywhere, in order to uproot and eradicate what had grown crookedly and disorderly in the Lord’s garden during his absence.

Accordingly, a few days after leaving Canterbury, we came to London with a large company. Some knights were with us, because, as was said, proud men had hidden a snare for us on the road. As we approached the city, the whole city was moved with joy, and all its citizens who came out to meet the archbishop received him with great joy and exultation.

The next day, as we were preparing to proceed, behold: in the morning came messengers of the younger king, forbidding the archbishop in the king’s name to proceed and ordering him to return to his church. But no one should suppose that this proceeded from the younger king’s own mind; rather, it came from the counsel of the courtiers in whose custody he was, who thought that in this way they would render service to the king his father. The archbishop, however, being fervent in spirit, immediately replied that he would by no means return because of this prohibition—except that the very solemn feast-day, namely Christmas, was then pressing, and he did not wish to be absent from his church on that day. Thus he did not proceed, but returned to Canterbury.

Accordingly, hearing this, his enemies raised their heads so that he might not proceed, and began to threaten his very life. Above all, that brood of vipers called de Broc provoked him with shameful and disgraceful insults. Among them was one of that accursed stock, a cleric, as they said, named Robert de Broc. [Col. 1262A] To disgrace and insult the archbishop, he mutilated a certain beast of burden which was carrying some necessities for our kitchen and which he happened to meet on the road. This mutilated animal was then led before the archbishop. By these and similar outrages that household daily embittered us, believing that it rendered an especially welcome service to the king-father, with whom we had made peace, by heaping contempt and injuries upon us.

But what can one say? The exile was indeed happy, but the peace which followed was more unhappy, because in peace our bitterness was most bitter. What, then, was the Lord’s champion to do? Where was he to go? To what was he to turn? To yield was shameful; to contend was dangerous. Bees surrounded him; fat bulls besieged him; the ocean enclosed him in the heart of the sea. [Col. 1262B] Yet, to confess the truth, that valiant champion of the Lord, recognizing himself as the ram of the Lord’s flock, thought not of flight but of battle, now understanding that he would have to fight not men but beasts, since his sheep had thus been turned into wolves.

## 9. OF HIS ACTS ON CHRISTMAS DAY

On Christmas Day—which, if I am not mistaken, was about the twenty-seventh day since our arrival in England—the archbishop mounted the pulpit and preached to the people. Among other things, at the end of the sermon he foretold that the time of his departure was at hand and that he would shortly leave them. Indeed, as he foretold his own passing, tears flowed forth more freely than words. At the same time the hearts of his hearers were [Col. 1262C] moved and broken beyond measure, so that throughout the whole church you could see and hear wailing and tears pouring forth, while they murmured among themselves: “Father, why do you leave us so soon? To whom do you leave us desolate?” For these were not wolves but sheep, who thus recognized their shepherd’s voice and grieved when they heard that their shepherd would shortly depart this world, though they did not know when, where, or how this would occur.

At last, after he had delivered a long discourse to the people, both for their edification and concerning his own departure, he was no longer weeping or shedding tears. Rather, as could be heard and seen, after his earlier tears he became so fierce, so indignant, so ardent, so bold, that he now attacked by name and expressly the stiff-necked and filthy men of the land. [Col. 1262D] No longer, as it seemed, was he at peace with those who hated peace: he did not sheathe his sword among his enemies, but drew it forth boldly and confidently. In a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning, he struck with anathema many of the courtiers most intimate with the king-father, and especially that exasperating household of which we spoke above. Among others, he consigned by name to perpetual anathema the aforesaid Ralph de Broc and that Robert mentioned above, who, as we have said, had mutilated the beast of burden in contempt of the archbishop.

Certainly, if you had seen these things, you would immediately have said that you had heard and seen face to face that prophetic creature which had the face of a man and the face of a lion. When these things had been done, throughout the whole following day the archbishop [Col. 1263A] showed himself devout at the table of God and afterwards, at the worldly table, cheerful in his accustomed manner. Indeed, on that day, which was both Friday and Christmas Day, he ate meat as he did at other times, judging it more religious on such a day to partake of it than to abstain.

## 10. OF THE DISCIPLE’S DEPARTURE FROM HIM

Now through certain courtiers and other friends of his, though secretly, he was frequently and secretly informed that men of faction and violent purpose were plotting his death. Thus many gave him warning, and many advised him to take precautions and forestall the snares laid for him. The archbishop, therefore, clearly seeing with the eyes of faith the land stirred up against him, and from the secret reports of many of his friends and household, [Col. 1263B] as we have just mentioned, now believing that snares were being prepared for his death, summoned in private, on the day after Christmas—the day, that is, of blessed Stephen the protomartyr—the disciple who wrote these things:

“I have now resolved,” he said, “to send you to our lord the king of the Franks, to our venerable brother the archbishop of Sens, and to the other princes of the land, so that you may tell them what you hear and see concerning our peace: namely, how there is for us ‘peace, peace,’ and yet there is no peace, but disturbance.”

At once the disciple, unable to restrain his tears, replied: “Holy Father, why have you resolved this? Why do you act thus? For I know, and am certain, that henceforth I shall not see you in this flesh. I had intended to stand faithfully with you; yet, as it seems to me, you seek to deprive me of the fruit of your consummation. I, who have remained with you thus far in your trials, shall not, as I now see, be a companion of your glory, though I was a companion of your punishment.”

The archbishop, now bursting into tears, answered: “Not so, my son, not so. You will not be deprived of the fruit, if you fulfil your father’s command and follow his counsel. Yet what you say and mourn is true: in truth, from now on you will not see me in this flesh. Nevertheless, I wish you to depart, especially because the king regards you as more suspect than the rest in the cause of the Church.”

Therefore, on the third day of Christmas, namely the feast of blessed John the Evangelist, in the darkness of night because ambushes on the road were feared, amid great lamentation [Col. 1263D] and flowing tears, having again and again received leave and a fatherly blessing, I departed from my father. As he himself foretold, I neither saw him thereafter in this flesh nor shall see him. Therefore, as I bring this history to its end, I pray with all my heart, soul, and strength that I may be worthy to see in eternity him whom I shall henceforth not see in time, and to share in his crown, since I was his companion in battle.

Thus far I have related, more faithfully and steadfastly, in this little historical work, for the edification of God’s Church, concerning so great a pillar of the Church, not what I received from others but what I myself saw and heard, for present and future ages. But because henceforth I must report not what I saw myself, but what I have received from others, so that this history of the holy man may be completed, my fingers are beginning somewhat [Col. 1264A] to grow stiff, and the pen is set down more slowly and more tremulously—more tremulously because one relates with greater hesitation things heard or seen by others rather than by oneself. Yet we must believe without doubt many holy men who heard and saw, from whom we too received these things, lest perhaps the Lord reproach us for our unbelief, as he reproached the unbelief and hardness of heart of those who did not believe those who had seen him risen from the dead.

## 11. OF THE KING’S RENEWED WRATH AND THE ARRIVAL OF THE EXECUTIONERS

Therefore, to return, as I promised, to what I left unfinished above: the king, as we have said, was incited by the three excommunicated bishops and kindled into a fury detestable to all future ages, like an oven heated by those who bake. [Col. 1264B] Unable any longer to contain the flame, he openly complained before all, especially before those of his court whom he had brought up and upon whom he had bestowed many honours and goods, of the archbishop as of an enemy. Often and again, inflamed with anger and breaking out into a baleful cry, he cursed all whom he had nurtured and who, through favour and the bestowal of benefits, were indebted to him, because they did not avenge him upon one priest who so troubled him and his kingdom and sought to strip him of his dignities and disinherit him.

As he repeated this over and over in his fury, four knights of his household chamber heard the words he spoke and conceived, from what they had heard, the intention—now quite certain that they would render the king a most welcome service if they killed the archbishop. Thus they conspired to murder the archbishop. I have taken care to insert their names here in this history, that they may be held in everlasting curse: Hugh de Morville, Reginald son of Urse, William de Tracy, and the fourth, Richard Brito. [Col. 1264C] These knights were royal courtiers and chamberlains; though in the end they proved degenerate, they were nevertheless men of noble birth, eminent in honours and great among the powerful. These four conspirators immediately set out for England.

During the journey of these four, something almost new—indeed miraculous—occurred. In winter, amid such frequent changes of weather and sea, and through the differing locations of the harbours, they did not all enter the sea together from the same harbour but from separate ones. Yet all landed on the same day, and on that same day—indeed, almost at the same hour—they gathered at the place they had appointed: namely, that castle called Saltwood, mentioned above, six miles from Canterbury. This was a property of the fee of the Church of Canterbury which, as we noted above, the king had promised to restore to the archbishop. Thus, as may be seen, the Lord, whom winds and sea obey, hastened on his priest—or rather, his priest as a victim pleasing to himself. [Col. 1264D]

All that night they deliberated in that castle about the murder of the archbishop. On the following day, the fourth day of Christmas, namely the feast of the Holy Innocents, they came to Canterbury with their accomplices, carrying with them nothing but their military weapons and unheard-of madness. Others came with swords and clubs, though all this was still concealed, lest perhaps the Lord’s anointed should flee and hide himself from them. Yet he, as we have said above and as the event itself will shortly prove, thought more of battle than of flight.

First, then, the four knights came haughtily toward evening to the archbishop in the chamber where he was sitting. Without greeting him either in their own name or in the king’s—for salvation was far from them, while death and ruin were near—they proudly assailed him, asking whether he would absolve the king’s suspended and excommunicated bishops. When he gently replied that, being bound by the authority of the lord pope, they could neither be absolved by his authority nor ought to be, they gnashed at him in a furious spirit and at once left him. [Col. 1266A] Immediately they gathered a band near the garden, now clothing themselves in their diabolical armour.

But since the subject now begins to swell, the style itself must henceforth change, so that the glory of the man’s approaching consummation may be written not in gloomy letters but, as it were, in certain rosy threads melting into golden shapes of syllables, and in some choice solemnity of expression. For deeds performed by a man above man are to be spoken not in the tongues of men but rather of angels; and such are the deeds henceforth to be described. Let us therefore first see and consider what was done, and afterwards judge whether it is not so.

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE SIXTH BOOK BEGIN

[Col. 1265]

1. Of the armed knights, who with their assembled band burst into the palace; of the Lord’s champion’s entrance into the church; and of the executioners’ words.  
2. Of the Lord’s champion’s encounter with the executioners, and what he did in addressing them.  
3. Of the excuse with which the disciple who wrote these things excuses himself, should he seem perhaps overlong in describing so great a champion’s contest.  
4. Of the manner of the martyr and of the martyrdom; here he also relates an incident concerning a certain cleric who placed his arm between the descending sword and the champion’s head.  
5. Of the champion’s authoritative prohibition, under anathema, that the executioners should harm none of his people; and of the praise of so great and glorious a martyrdom.  
6. Of the disciple’s renewed excuse, should he seem too prolix in describing the martyrdom’s struggle.  
7. Of how the disciple, though willing, nevertheless against his will approaches the task of describing the martyrdom’s final end.  
8. Of the man’s final consummation and of the number of the executioner-knights with their band.  
9. Of the man’s admirable virtue of patience and the unheard-of enormity of the crime.  
10. Of the pontiff’s spoils and garments, which the knights divided among themselves, and of the man’s hair-shirts, which they found and threw aside; yet some of them beat their breasts and silently said to themselves: “Truly this man was righteous.”  
11. Of how, within fifteen days after his consummation, the martyrdom became known in the holy land of Jerusalem, and of the manner in which it became known.  
12. He briefly touches upon the correspondence between the death of Christ and that of the Lord’s anointed, promising that this correspondence will be heard more fully and attentively at the end of this historical song.  
13. He continues the account of what was done after the martyrdom.  
14. Of the form and condition of the now lifeless body after the martyrdom had been consummated.  
15. Of events on the day after the martyrdom, while the body was still unburied; how, according to monastic custom, when they removed the outer garments in order to wash the body, they found the whole body beneath covered with hair-shirts; and of the burial, its manner and place, and in what year from the Incarnation of the Lord and from the year of his life it occurred.

# SIXTH BOOK

[Col. 1265]

[Col. 1265B] The armed knights, then, with their band assembled, began to burst in through the palace windows in a mass, with swords and clubs; some of our household had already shut the doors in fear. Those who were sitting in the chamber with the archbishop, hearing the commotion and crashing outside and now realizing what it meant, were understandably terrified. They urged the archbishop to take refuge in a holier and safer place, namely the church. Although he refused again and again, as one unafraid of death, they scarcely at last compelled him to proceed to the church. Even at this crisis the expression of his face was not changed in the least; so completely did no trace of fear appear either in his face or in his bearing.

When he had gone a little way and did not see the cross which was accustomed to be carried before him, he summoned the bearer of the cross and stopped, waiting for the cross to go before him—truly, I think, not forgetful of his Lord, who hastened with the cross to the cross.

[Col. 1266B] But when he entered the church, all his men scattered at once in fear: these fled and those fled, hiding from him in the crypts of the church and beneath the altars. Thus this member of the Head could have cried out and lamented: “I am poured out like water, and all my bones are scattered” (Psalm 21); and: “You have put friend and neighbour far from me, and my acquaintances from misery” (Psalm 87). For he alone was to tread the winepress, so that in that strait glory might be given not to another but to him alone. For if glory were given to another also, the glory of the one alone would be diminished. Therefore, by God’s providence, it was thus singularly ordered for the glory of his champion until he had passed through.

Yet one of his men, after he had entered the church, immediately shut and bolted the doors of the church. The executioner-knights, however, with their band, armed with swords and clubs, followed the archbishop on foot; and as they came to the doors of the church, they thundered terribly and noisily that the doors be quickly opened to them. [Col. 1266C]

Since this was delayed for a little while, they began preparing iron engines to break down the doors and burst in. [Col. 1267A] Hearing at once the crash and shouting at the church doors, the soon-to-be victim of Christ, the Lord’s anointed, ordered that they be opened immediately, adding that it was wholly unfitting for a church to be turned into a fortress. When the doors were opened, the executioners immediately rushed in. One shouted: “Where is that deceiver?” But the Lord’s anointed gave no answer. Then another shouted: “Where is the archbishop?” And the Lord’s anointed said: “I am he. What do you want?” He thundered: “That you may die; you shall by no means live.” And he replied: “And I am ready to lay down my life for my God and for the liberty of the Church.”

## 2. OF THE LORD’S CHAMPION’S ENCOUNTER

But what is remarkable to tell: this most strong champion of the Lord, [Col. 1267B] uniquely great and splendidly singular, had, before those executioners entered the church, been making his way toward the choir, which is reached by steps, and had already climbed seven or eight steps. Yet as soon as he saw swords drawn in the church, he hurried to meet them. Neither the announcement of his cruel death, nor the deadly word, nor the sword drawn to kill him, could deter him from going to meet them.

What adds still greater wonder and astonishment is that, rebuking the combatants with full authority because they had entered their mother the Church so disorderly and profanely, he at once seized by the hand one of them whom he had first approached and shook him so violently through his coat of mail that he nearly threw him to the pavement. [Col. 1267C] This was William de Tracy, as he himself afterwards confessed.

O how admirable was this burning zeal of the priest, so ardently jealous for the house of God: alone and unarmed, he went to meet so many men, so frenzied and already armed for his death, so boldly, confidently, readily, promptly, fearlessly, and prepared; and, imitating his Saviour, who drove men from the Temple, he did not fear to drive them from the Temple of his Saviour. I say that he followed his Saviour and commander in this matter, except that this vigorous soldier of the supreme commander attempted to drive out not money-changers and sellers of doves, but the very swordsmen then raging to kill him. He appeared to fear nothing and to tremble at nothing.

Thus, even in this moment and circumstance, his encounter is surely admirable, his rebuke admirable, and his attempted expulsion admirable; for he did not fear further to provoke men already so fiercely inflamed for his death. [Col. 1267D] He did not seek favour, beg pardon, or request delay; but, burning with priestly zeal and love of justice, he provoked rather than soothed the anger of those he had exasperated.

O the mighty hand of a bold champion! O the man’s courage! O the martyr’s constancy! O the purity of his soul! The same man stands commandingly among the executioners: priest and victim. He stands there, while they surround him with drawn swords. In their midst the priest performs the priest’s office—not flattering the executioners, not humbling himself, but, as we have said, reproving and rebuking them with full authority.

[Col. 1268A] Behold our Samson, fearless to meet them; behold our Paul, ready to rebuke; behold our Lord’s anointed, strong to expel. His bone, formed in secret, is now no longer hidden, even though his substance was in the lower parts of the earth. But why do I speak of his substance in the lower parts of the earth? Rather, now his flesh’s substance is in the heights of heaven—not as flesh any longer, but as though transformed into heaven by a certain wondrous change. For what flesh does not shrink from death? What flesh does not fear a drawn sword raised over it? Or strikes and despises a swordsman prepared for its death? O man who is not man; O flesh that is not flesh. O flesh of Adam; O flesh of Thomas.

Thomas, among swords, in the dung-heap, is stronger than Adam among fruit-bearing trees in paradise, [Col. 1268B] because, except for certain garments of death soon to be put off, he has laid aside all that he had inherited as old from the first Adam; and now all belongs to him from the second Adam. O Adam and Adam! O sons of the first Adam; O sons of the second, who after the first mortal birth from the first Adam have now been born a second time, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh, but from the second Adam.

Accordingly, from this second father they receive, as noble sons who have not degenerated, not the weak and infirm properties of the flesh but the strong gifts of the Spirit from above; spiritually begotten, they acquire from this father constancy, courage, and the other virtues of the mind. Hence, though they are struck by swords, they do not yield to swords but despise them. [Col. 1268C] Of them it is said: “They can be killed, but they cannot be bent.” Indeed, when these men are killed, they are the death of death, as conquerors of death. And to speak by way of example: “Where now, O death, is your sting? Where is your victory?” (1 Corinthians 15.) You who conquered Adam in his paradise are today conquered by Thomas in your dung-heap. You who oppressed Adam in his garments, today Thomas, stripping off your garments from himself, has crushed you in your own garments—he who, still clothed in your garments, does not tremble to reproach and mock you.

O that I knew—but I do not know—what hidden bone the Lord makes, or by what inward strength he so fortifies his own. In a time of peace this bone is hidden, this strength hidden; but it is not hidden in the hour when manifest temptation breaks in. Would that I had tasted, as truly solid food, of this hidden bone. I would gladly belch it forth for others. Yet because I have not tasted it, I know that I am not yet the Lord’s dog. But our Thomas, who has tasted this bone—or rather, who, like a true dog of the Lord, abundantly nourished by it, now belches it forth to us—no longer puts away or hides his bone. [Col. 1268D] As that mighty king and prophet says: “My bone, which you made in secret, was not hidden” (Psalm 138). Likewise, the bone of our Thomas, formed in secret, is now not hidden. He is no longer flesh of flesh, but bone of bones in the army of the Lord Sabaoth, strongest among the strong.

Thus he who once fled with the child Jesus now meets him when he is grown: now he goes out, now he reveals himself. And, as we have said—and I do not tire of repeating it in praise of our man of bone—he thrusts himself amid the swords, as though wholly bone, not fearing but despising their blows. His bone, hitherto almost hidden, is now not hidden on the boundary between death and life. He knows and most keenly recalls that this passing death, the death of the flesh, this brief death, is the death of death and the gate of life. To conclude all briefly rather than enumerate each thing: so great, as those who saw said, was this man’s contempt for death and security in battle that, while still fighting, he could seem already to be conquering; and while already conquering, still to be fighting. [Col. 1269A]

## 3. THE DISCIPLE’S EXCUSE FOR BEING OVERLONG IN DESCRIBING THE CONTEST

Let no one wonder, and let no one censure, if I seem perhaps too prolix [Col. 1269B] in describing the single combat of our David. That ancient single combat of the unarmed son of Jesse, still small, against Goliath was indeed wondrous. But this single combat of the new man, the son of the new law and the new king, is incomparably more wondrous. For he, neither persuaded, compelled, nor sent, but advancing to the contest alone and unarmed, in the ardour of his own spirit and with unheard-of courage, by will alone—forgetful of the flesh and, as it seemed, no longer recognizing himself as a man among the sons of Adam—was not afraid of death but eager for it. He thrust himself amid the swords and struck Goliath, as befitted such a champion, not with an iron sword but with the sword of speech, not with a sling-stone but with his tongue. Who ever heard of a sword in his lips? This is most marvellous even to the hearing of the ear.

Let no one, therefore, censure, and let the reader not grow weary, if I seem excessive in describing so singular and unheard-of a contest, which offers the world a spectacle, the Church an example, and the angels joy. [Col. 1269C] Let no one mock or disparage me if, contrary to the rule of writers, I often turn and return to the same matter, or if, according to the poet’s teaching, I do not hasten at once into the midst of events. For as the emotions of minds vary, so too vary the voices by which they express themselves: love has sweet tones, fear fearful ones, joy cheerful ones, while grief and compassion have groaning voices—voices which they repeat again and again, not according to the rule of writers but after the manner of mourners. No law of writing has been laid down for one who mourns. Therefore it is no wonder that those who suffer and grieve in writing do not follow the rules of writing. For as music at a funeral is an untimely tale, so there is absolutely no correspondence between writing and mourning.

Though I rejoice with my lord—whom I followed in my youth, to whom I ministered in the bonds of the Gospel, with whom I stood and ran, as God knows, and whom, even if not very wisely, I nevertheless obeyed faithfully—I cannot but sympathize and grieve for him as he contends and now exposes his head and body to the swords of uncircumcised and unclean men. Or rather, I do not merely grieve with him: I alone grieve; for he does not seem to have grieved. Thus I alone grieve while writing these things, and while grieving I alone write, especially since the burden and task of this writing [Col. 1270A] rest uniquely and particularly upon me.

For behold: this is now the fifteenth year since the events which are now written occurred, and almost all my brothers, once companions in the Passion, who with me heard and saw, have been taken from human affairs and sleep in Christ. They have passed on, while I remain in danger, left amid fires and waves. Thus the task and labour of writing about so great a man—my lord and foster-father—what I saw or heard, have been reserved particularly for me, who still survive. Otherwise, if I were silent, my mouth would condemn me as ignorant, lazy, fearful, or envious, and my silence would bring upon me that prophetic woe: “Woe is me, because I have kept silent” (Isaiah 6).

Yet because remembrance of my father’s contest is sweet to me, I approach the end unwillingly. For while I still describe him fighting, the pleasing service of the pen portrays before my eyes, as it were face to face, the person of the combatant, and he is still a little while with me. But when he has triumphed and mounts his fiery chariot, the disciple is left naked without his master’s cloak; if he seeks his master, he does not know where he is, for he does not know whither he should come or whither he should go. [Col. 1270B] The first Elijah was carried up into paradise; the second descended into hell; but this third, when he is carried away, will at once fly upon the wings of the winds and fly away from us. He will fly away, I say, to a country foreign and far off to us who still dwell in exile. He will fly away, I say, to the place which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the human heart (1 Corinthians 2).

[Col. 1270C] It is therefore no wonder if I am unwilling to be torn away from my father and master while he still fights; yet I must now be torn away, because he will be taken from me. For, pierced and shaken through all my inmost being, I must say it: the end comes, the end comes.
