Thus there is no more by which I can draw out in words this brief but mighty battle, this swift but glorious palm, and the unfading crown of the triumphant champion.

## 4. OF THE MARTYRDOM AND THE MANNER OF THE MARTYRDOM

Therefore, as we have just said, as soon as this champion of Christ, our man of bone, seized and shook so violently the executioner-knight whom we named above, the latter raised his sword and, with anger increasing his strength, vigorously attempted to strike the Lord’s anointed upon the head. But the blow had not yet fallen with its full force upon him, because a certain cleric, who had come near to see the pontiff and followed him closely in order to witness the end, [Col. 1270D] placed his arm between the descending sword and the pontiff’s head. He exposed the arm of his own flesh in order thus to fit to the pontiff a shield of protection, a defence of safety.

He was like that young man who left behind the linen cloth because he followed the Lord, but he differed far from him because he did not flee; indeed, more strongly, confidently, and boldly, he exposed himself and first received the first share in the sacrifice already begun. May his memory be blessed. I insert his name here: he was called Edward, surnamed Grim, and was a native of that castle in England called Cantebrige.

This cleric, grievously struck, began to bear the weight of the blow. But when, feeling himself struck, he could not bear its weight, he immediately withdrew his arm, and the remaining force of the blow fell upon the pontiff’s head. The sacred blood now began to flow down his face. The priest of the Most High, sensing that the sacrifice of himself to the Most High had now begun, at once cast aside the cap which he was accustomed to wear upon his head. Raising his eyes to heaven, bending his knee, and joining his hands before him in the posture of prayer, the priest in the temple before the altar offered himself to God as a living sacrifice—truly a living sacrifice, holy, spotless, and pleasing to God. [Col. 1271A]

He stretched out his neck and exposed his head, commending himself and the cause of the Church to God, to blessed Mary the Mother of God, to the holy patrons of the Church of Canterbury, [Col. 1271B] and to blessed Denis, apostle of the Franks. Thus, by God’s inspiration, the cause of the Church was especially commended among the martyrs to him whom the archbishop himself was now to resemble through a similar martyrdom in the Church, being stripped of his scalp in punishment, as Denis too had been. Having exposed himself, he immediately commended to these patrons the cause of the Church which he had championed, and prayed for his own people.

## 5. OF THE CHAMPION’S AUTHORITATIVE PROHIBITION

But why do I say that he prayed? Rather, although he had begun even to wallow in his own blood amid the hands of the executioners, he still exercised the authority of the priestly office over his executioners. In the name of almighty God and under anathema, he authoritatively forbade them to touch or harm any of his people. [Col. 1271C] Truly, I think, he remembered his Lord’s saying during the Passion: “If you seek me, let these go their way” (John 18). Except that here it is not so much a prayer as a command and restraint. Nor did he so much pray that they should spare them as anathematize them if they did not spare them.

And who can pass over, conceal, or remain silent about this thing—marvellous to tell and hear, but more marvellous in the deed itself—unless he is perhaps envious or ignorant? Who can be silent concerning this word? Who can suppress here the praise of so great a priest? Blood already flows from the wounded man, and yet amid the hands of those who strike him the authority of the priestly office does not yield even a little. Rather, amid swords, he does not, like a coward or a fearful man, put away his sword, but draws it boldly and manfully. “Behold, here are two swords” (Luke 22): amid iron swords is the sword of the word.

In this great extremity, in this hour of darkness, this our champion readily and confidently draws Peter’s sword, and thereby, as was fitting for a priest, protects his own. He could indeed have defended both himself and his own with the iron sword, but he had read that Peter, in the Lord’s Passion, was rebuked by the Lord for drawing the iron sword in his defence and cutting off the servant’s ear. Hence, when the ear was restored to the shame of him who had cut it off, Peter himself was commanded to put his sword back into its sheath, and the Lord added that terrible saying: “All who take the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matthew 26). [Col. 1271D]

The Lord used neither sword in his Passion: not the iron sword, thereby showing the Church that this is not fitting for churchmen—although it ought to serve at their will and command, not in their own hand but in another’s, when they see that this is expedient. [Col. 1272A] Nor, though he himself was the Word, did he use the sword of the word, thereby instructing the Church that those who are outside are not to be judged by the Church. As the disciple of this master of masters says: “For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Is it not those within whom you judge?” (1 Corinthians 5).

Therefore our Thomas, now in this contest wiser than Peter then was, yet taught through Peter by the Lord and most especially instructed by that master who was a combatant, the guardian of the nations, that the weapons of priests are not carnal but spiritual, and that those whom priests judge are those within, not those without—he scorns the first sword. He boldly draws and manfully strikes with the only sword that belongs to Peter and to himself as Peter’s successor against that profane band, which was within only in name, not in divine reality; only in number, not in merit. [Col. 1272B] In a marvellous and astonishing way, with this sword he defends not himself but only his people, exposing himself for them; nor does he strike back with this sword if they strike him, but only if they strike his people.

O merciful shepherd, truly merciful, who, as soon as he was struck, remembered no one but his sheep who were about to be scattered! O outstanding fount of blood and mercy, newly arisen in the house of David, who amid the hands of executioners, from which blood burst forth, did not cease to flow forth in an outpouring of mercy as in a flow of blood, [Col. 1272C] proving himself both shepherd of the sheep and father of orphans. O ineffable depths of mercy! O rich and marrow-filled burnt offering! Defending his own, not defending himself, but exposing himself undefended—at once priest and victim—he sacrifices himself in the temple before the altar, for himself and for his own: a sacrifice, I say, of I know not what life-giving fragrance of wondrous sweetness before God and the world.

You therefore, holy Father, most merciful shepherd, great priest of the Most High, most bold champion of Christ: in defending your own, you proved yourself father and shepherd. In sacrificing yourself for your own, you followed the pattern and expressed the image of the high priest of all. In exposing yourself, you even fulfilled evangelical perfection beyond measure. “If anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also” (Matthew 5). But you, struck upon the head, immediately exposed your whole [Col. 1272D] head, your body, and your entire self.

O how great, how unheard-of in your regard, Thomas, was the dispensation of divine mercy, by which you showed yourself such to your own people, and yourself such for their sake. Already struck to the shedding of blood, you do not strike back for yourself with the sword entrusted to you, but only for your own; lest, if you seemed less evangelical by avenging a personal injury, or if you ignored the plight of your own, you should appear not a shepherd but rather a hireling. O evangelical perfection! O man perfect in the evangelical manner—though we have not seen men more than perfect—where, amid such bitterness, there is so overflowing an abundance of such sweetness, so fervent, so unyielding, so rigorously joined to priestly zeal, as though the hottest wine were mixed with the sweetest oil! Truly [Col. 1273A] mercy and truth have met one another in this arena, in this contest. For this Thomas of ours, now indeed in the agony of the body, but, as it seems, in an ecstasy of mind, with his departure from the world now imminent, almost forgetful of himself, accepts punishment for his own, spares himself, and suspends the sword, so that, he alone being exposed, his people might be kept unharmed. His own, I say: those who had bravely followed him and faithfully obeyed him in their troubles, their oppressions, and their various temptations, through the hardships and roughnesses of exile.

O how delightful a memory, how sweet a recollection, of so great and so overflowing an abundance of sweetness. “They shall utter forth the memory of the abundance of thy sweetness” (Ps. 144 [CXLIV]). But who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep? (Jer. 9). I shall weep not for myself, still journeying and in peril amid fires and waves; not for my brethren, once bearers with me of the pastoral burden and companions in suffering, now taken from the world; but because I cannot utter forth that abundance of sweetness—hardly even, in a feeble belching, do I utter what I received from others. For how could I utter what I have not tasted? For, as I mentioned above, since, by the will and command of my lord and father, I was sent away the day before he entered the contest, I was not present; I did not see; I was not worthy to take part.

But wretchedly was I deprived, lest I should see the strength of my father and master in so great a struggle, his such steadfast firmness, such and so sweet an outpouring from the bowels of compassion, by which, exposing himself, he fought for his own. O if it had been granted me from above to be present, had I at least followed from afar, so that I might see the end! He also later appeared to me in a dream and said in the vision that he had wished me to be present then. And I said to him: “Lord, since I am a sinful man, I should indeed have perished had I been killed.” And he said: “No, because you would have been baptized in my blood.” Therefore, whenever I remember this vision, I am ashamed and pierced in my misery, and streams of water flow down from my eyes, because I who endured through the temptations was not worthy to be present at the end, like a rejected and reprobate son, at my father’s consummation. O had I been present, from the fullness of one so virtuous, so sweet, and so fruitful in his struggle, I would utter more fully and fruitfully for others that which I now, with bloodless and faltering pen, can scarcely distil through a slender vein!

### 6. CONCERNING THE DISCIPLE’S RENEWED EXCUSE.

[Col. 1273D]

But perhaps by now I seem, contrary to my promise, too prolix in describing my father as he contended. Yet whoever thinks so should reflect how great was the courage in this contest, the constancy in resistance, the authority in contradiction, the compassion in suffering with others, and finally such a model in every respect of the whole Christian warfare, that these things demand not the cursory, swift passage of a racing pen, but rather a fuller treatment of each point by a diligent pen lingering over its task.

Moreover, as I have already said above—and I cannot refrain from repeating it—I come unwillingly to the end; unwillingly, grieving and groaning, I recall the end. For it is more pleasant and fruitful for me to behold Thomas contending [Col. 1274A] than to recount him reigning. Thomas’s contest, though it is not of the world, is nevertheless still in the world and is with me, and I see it. But Thomas’s kingdom as victor, just as it is not of the world, is neither in the world nor with me, and I do not see it. Yet in the contest Thomas stands as though still among us, unconquered; fighting with arms outstretched, he summons us all to battle and teaches our hands for war. But in the kingdom, seated on a throne with hands now at rest, he no longer summons us to battle, but rather grants patronage to those who fight.

Yet in what manner, or on whose behalf, or how he gives that patronage, we do not know, we do not see, nor yet understand; nor do I think we can know before we see. But what then? Whether I will or not, though weeping and lamenting, though I watch the ascending father with my eyes fixed upward after him, alas! I must be torn away and believe him to reign, whom I described as contending by eyewitness faith. And I too, being a Christian, will do what a certain sacrificing pagan did: while he was sacrificing, he heard that his son had been slain in battle and immediately laid aside his crown; but when he immediately heard that his son had acted bravely in battle, he at once put back upon his head the crown he had sought out.

Why then do I delay? Why do I hesitate? Why do I defer the most glorious triumph of the athlete of the Lord, standing and fighting in the battle-line so gloriously and so vigorously? Why do I prolong so joyful a dance? Why, I say, do I delay? Why do I draw out at greater length the hope and salvation of the people, the liberty and glory of the clergy—indeed the patronage of the whole Church—and the father and, finally, the future [Col. 1274C] judge of the whole world? Let faith conquer; let affection triumph; and let us not so much suffer with him in his suffering as rejoice with him in his reign.

And yet we cannot but suffer with him and grieve for him. We, I say, and especially men of our office—the clergy, I mean—certainly cannot or ought not fail to grieve for him, who suffered such harsh, dreadful, and shameful things, first in exile and now in martyrdom, among the hands of such wicked, criminal, and sacrilegious men, not for himself but solely for the liberty of the clergy.

### 7. THAT THE DISCIPLE RELUCTANTLY DESCRIBES THE END OF THE MARTYRDOM.

What then? I shall open my mouth and draw breath, so that, willing though against my will, I may henceforth describe the end of the contest and the final outcome of the contender [Col. 1274D]; and at the end of him who is without end I shall make an end, where nevertheless there is no end. After the triumph of the contestant, now in glory, I shall henceforth be silent, speaking nothing thereafter of his kingdom, which “eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2), and which therefore lies beyond both word and pen. For that matter of eternity and unfailing brightness dulls every sound of temporal and mortal speech, stays the pen, and absorbs even the propriety of expressions, since it is a matter alike unheard, unseen, and unthought.

Therefore, passing silently over that which exceeds every manner of writing and speaking, the end of the consummate man is now to be described—an end which, by the excessive brightness of itself and the dignity of its subject, reflects back and obscures the pen of my little talent [Col. 1275A]. To this end indeed I approach the more gladly and ardently, though I know not by what emotion delayed, because at the end of the athlete’s contest the praise of the contender does not end, but is increased more and more, and ineffably more. And I hasten even more willingly to this end, because this end, though it is not the end of all consummation—that being reserved for the consummation of the Head alone—is nevertheless the end of a wondrous consummation: blood poured out here. In that blood then lay hidden, as medicine in a rose and balsam in bark—there lay hidden, I say, in the blood then, but is now manifest—the salvation of the people, the glory of the whole clergy, the patronage of the churches throughout the world, and his own unfading crown. That crown the swordsmen themselves fashioned: striking with iron upon the crown of his head and flesh as upon an anvil, they made a crown for a crown.

Therefore I ought no longer unwillingly to hasten to the end of so great a consummation. Thus, drying my tears and drawing breath, I shall now open my mouth at the end of the history concerning the end of the man. And may the Lord open my lips, that to the Lord’s glory I may worthily proclaim, at the end, the praise of His glorious new martyr, so that, according to that ancient saying, all praise may be sung to him at the end. For a precious end possesses a great privilege of praise: so much so that, even if someone is worthy of praise before death, the wise man nevertheless warns that no one should be praised before death. And so, if perhaps it were granted from above, we ought henceforth to expand still further [Col. 1275C] in praise of so precious an end, since, according to the wise man, a man’s precious end claims for itself the privilege of all praise. What I prayed above, then, I pray again now: may the Lord open my lips, that my mouth may worthily proclaim, to His glory, the praise of His glorious new martyr.

### 8. CONCERNING THE MAN’S FINAL CONSUMMATION.

Therefore, as we have said above, with neck outstretched, head exposed, hands joined as in prayer, and knees bent, the executioners—what I can scarcely say without an overflowing fountain of tears amid sobs and sighs breaking forth so frequently—the executioners, I say, strike and strike again from either side; they strike and strike again until they separate the crown of the head from the head. Thus the Christ of the Lord, the Lord’s anointed, was sacrificed there where he had been anointed: the sword of slaughter succeeding and displacing the sacred oil of anointing.

For while that holy body was untouched and unharmed in all other respects, that unheard-of sacrilege was committed upon the one part of his body in which the privilege of priesthood and high priesthood was pre-eminent. Thus he was scalped and uncrowned by the executioners. And indeed not from behind: rather, he who until the end had always stretched himself forward, the perpetual champion of what is right, now dying fell face forward, his body straight upon the pavement of the church. And this is the end of the man’s consummation.

The soldiers did these things, four men with their cohort, in this passion of the Christ of the Lord, as also in the passion of Christ himself; and, scarcely having gone out of the church with their profane cohort, they wondered whether he had died already. One of the cohort returned [Col. 1276A] and came nearer. To report with complete certainty that he was dead—though he was already dead—he pierced him with the point of his sword, drew out the brain of the holy head, and poured it upon the pavement of the church. As was said, this was Robert de Broc, of that aforementioned brood of vipers.

Behold this Robert, another Longinus—except that surely the former Longinus is justified in comparison with this one. That pagan opened Christ’s side with a spear, and blood came forth; but this Christian drove a sword into the head of the Christ of the Lord, drew out the brain, and poured it upon the pavement of the church, exposing it as vile mud or dust to be trampled underfoot. In the savagery of his crime he far surpassed even those who did not break Christ’s legs after they had seen that he was dead.

### 9. CONCERNING THE POWER OF THE MAN’S PATIENCE.

[Col. 1276B]

“O all ye that pass by the way, attend and see whether there hath been any sorrow like unto this sorrow,” whether from the beginning of the rising Church, or even from the first origin of the world. I stand here and hesitate; I cannot go farther. Sobs and sighs break forth more readily than words. The mind is stunned, the eye weeps, the hand trembles, the pen sticks fast; and I still stand here and hesitate, exceedingly uncertain by what kind of language I can express so great a power of patient endurance in death in the flesh, and, on the other hand, so great an enormity of wickedness perpetrated among Christians.

To the one belongs a commendation for the ages, as ineffable and incapable of inscription. To the others belongs everlasting profanation, likewise incapable of expression in words or description by the pen. [Col. 1276C] For, to speak first of the great power of the patient man in this scalping, this uncrowning, this so harsh and dreadful shearing of the head, in which the skull-cap with the crown of anointing was separated from the head: remarkable and scarcely credible though it is, no murmur was heard, no complaint.

Other martyrs, indeed, if decapitated at once and without murmuring, are remarkable—but not so remarkable. Yet this man of ours, in so harsh a shearing of the head, “as a sheep before her shearers,” did not open his mouth. And rightly and truly “shearers”: for what was this shearing of the head but the harsh and dreadful shearing away of a crown, in which the skull-cap with the crown of anointing was separated from the head? Truly, as a sheep before one who shears and strikes it; and truly as a sheep not led to slaughter, but leading itself to slaughter. “For he was offered because he willed it.”

#### Concerning the Broken Sword.

And while the swordsmen struck and struck again from either side, hastening the man’s death, the sword of one of the swordsmen broke upon the skull-cap of his head. It breaks indeed and is broken: the sword is broken, and breaks the outer bone; but against the inner bone, which, as we said above, was fashioned by the Lord in secret and was unbreakable, the sword is broken—yet Thomas’s spirit is not broken.

O bone and bone: bone from the first Adam, bone from the second. The bone of the first Adam is bone of bones and flesh of flesh; but in the second, it is indeed bone of bones, yet not flesh of flesh but spirit of spirit, strength from strength, firmness from constancy, joy from patience, death from charity. O bone of our bony athlete [Col. 1277A], now neither hidden nor concealed, truly fashioned by the Lord! Though wrapped in a certain thin and tender skin, the tunic of death, it is stronger, firmer, and harder than iron: in this arena it broke iron while itself remained unharmed.

#### Concerning the Arrangement of the Slain Body at the Very Moment of Martyrdom.

And further, in a matter pertaining not only to virtue but also to adornment, and as it were to a certain privileged glory of martyrdom, our patron here adorned the martyrdom prepared for him by a fitting outward arrangement of the limbs of the outer man, as though judging it unbecoming to die for Christ unless he also died becomingly for Christ. For until all was consummated and the offering begun was completed, he remained so motionless, so uniform, and—as calmly as he did so—equally poised, with bent knees and joined hands, as we have said; he continually stretched out his neck and exposed his head, so that the very arrangement of his body prayed to the Lord and at the same time invited the swordsmen to strike.

Against the force of the blows coming upon him he opposed nothing, interposed nothing; from his limbs he withdrew none, drew or pulled back none. He did not unclasp his joined hands; he did not turn or bend his head this way or that, so as to avoid receiving the force of the strokes upon his head. As we have said, the outward arrangement of his body was so motionless, so uniform, so even, that it invited the swordsmen to strike. O this unheard-of ordering, under so great a constraint, of the limbs of the outer man, by which he prayed to the Lord of heaven and simultaneously invited the swordsmen [Col. 1277C] to strike!

Truly wonderful and admirable was the constant courage and courageous constancy of the inner man, which so arranged the acts and limbs of the outer man that, even as he was dying, he fell not from behind, as we said above, but upon his face; and, prostrate in the manner of one praying upon the pavement of the church, the champion of rightness cast himself down with his body straight, maintaining even in the fall of death a fitting arrangement of the whole outer man. Behold how great, how unheard-of, how astounding was the power of patience in his inner man in his martyrdom; a power which the whole so fitting, so adorned arrangement of the outer man both adorned and revealed. It is a virtue admirable to every age yet to come, with its own beauty, but imitable by few; whether by anyone, I do not know. This virtue is the more admirable because, though it occurred in our time, it is not of our time or of its lukewarmness, in which people love themselves and seek only what is their own.

#### Concerning the Enormity of the Sacrilege.

But the more admirable and glorious the virtue of the sufferer, the more detestable and shameful is the deed of the sacrilegious men. Whoever considers and examines this work of sacrilege will find it surpasses every frenzy of Diocletian, Herod, Maximinus, or other enemies of Christ; every profanation of Antiochus, every faithlessness of Julian, and every cruelty of Herod—those others being justified by comparison with this sacrilegious deed. For they raged against adversaries of their faith, or against men whom they already regarded, or suspected would become, enemies [Col. 1278A]. But here it was far otherwise—far otherwise, I say, if one weighs the faith, profession, peace granted, rank, place, and time of these sacrilegious men.

For if faith is in question, they were accounted Christians; if profession, they were subject as sons to a father; if peace, peace had been publicly granted and put in writing; if rank, he was a priest and chief of priests; if place, it was the Church of the Saviour, mother of the other churches in the kingdom; and the sword of slaughter was driven into the very vessel of sacred anointing; if time, it was the Nativity of the Saviour. Behold how many titles, so noble, so new, and unheard-of in these times, illuminate the triumph of the martyrdom of our new martyr, so precious and so glorious, while on the other hand, by increasing its guilt, they profane the crime of the sacrilegious deed.

For these sacrilegious men, utterly forgetful of both their faith and profession, showed no respect for the covenant of peace that had been granted, for so high a rank, for so holy a place, or for the privilege of so celebrated a time. They were incomparably more savage than those who crucified Christ outside Jerusalem, in a place called Calvary, lest the place be defiled, as it were, by him. But these men, caring nothing whether the place might be defiled, purified, or sanctified, scalped the Christ of the Lord in Jerusalem itself, making from the Church of the Saviour, in that most holy city and mother of all churches on earth, a place of Calvary: sons more than bloodthirsty, scalping their mother’s spouse and their father in the very womb of their mother.

If these and the other circumstances set forth above are weighed, who has ever heard such a thing, or who has seen its like? Pass by and see; enter in and consider deeply whether such a deed has been done. For who has heard? Who has ever seen? Who has done such a thing: that in a place of consecration, in the very place of the anointing with sacred and holy chrism, Christians and sons should drive in the sword of slaughter; that there, and nowhere else, the brain of one already dead should be scattered with blood and shattered bones upon the pavement of so holy a place—while the other circumstances enumerated above increase the treachery of so great a crime, the wickedness of so unheard-of a sacrilege?

Surely the heavens are appalled at this. And what must be greatly feared by all is that at some time the whole earth may be utterly laid waste, upon which this crime was perpetrated so wickedly, so that it too may drink from this cup of suffering, although it neither shared in nor knew of the crime; just as in the Flood many perished who had not committed the sin, and in the Sodomite fire of the five cities many were burned who had not been corrupted. David numbered, and the sword raged against the people; Achan sinned, and the people fell; the sons of Eli ate, and Israel’s teeth were set on edge. Such are the fearful judgments of the Lord upon the children of men; and there are many examples concerning these things, which it would be lengthy and unsuitable at this time to recount.

But would that I were not a man possessing the spirit, and that I now uttered falsehood instead. For I neither pray for, desire, nor willingly prophesy evil to my nation. Rather, far be it, Lord, far be it in the day of Your wrath. Restrain the sword, and in the spirit of judgment make distinction; distinguish Your scourge, lest the righteous be trampled down with the wicked. Let Your people, the English nation, which so devoutly venerates the aforesaid martyrdom of Your new victorious martyr, not see the sword, not feel the blow, not bear the scourge; but let it rather be free from punishment, as it is free from guilt.

But if it unlawfully bound itself by unlawful oaths against its father and patron, or acted otherwise wrongly, as we mentioned above in this little historical book when the harshness of our exile was described, this was force, not consent. Therefore let those alone feel the arm of Your vengeance, Lord—those alone who committed the wickedness of so unheard-of a sacrilege, or who consented to those committing it. Yet even for them, though they have borne away and taken from me my lord, I who write these things pray and desire that the Lord may rebuke them in judgment, not in His wrath, and that in rebuking them He may convert rather than crush them; yet in such a way that the whole world, profaned by their most wicked act and as if stained by a certain incest, may wash its hands in their blood.

Nevertheless, the little book concerning those converted or crushed, which we have immediately appended to this history under the title *Concerning the Affair of the Melorum*, will instruct us at its end. For it belongs to the present place and time; and, as the order of history requires, we have now begun first to emphasize the guilt of this sacrilege, and afterwards to describe the punishment that followed from it. For punishment is the trace of sin, indicating that sin preceded it. Therefore we must first deal with the sin, and afterwards with punishment as its consequence; and this is necessary so that astonishment may seize all who read or hear, grief the sacrilegious men themselves, and fear may be instilled into every age yet to come, lest they attempt such things thereafter.

Accordingly, as we have briefly touched on, in comparison with these sacrilegious men the crimes of all wicked men who have been or are outside [the Church] are justified. There is no comparison of guilt with guilt, nor of the punishment due with punishment; there is, I say, no relation, no equality, no comparison at all. For one is the guilt and another the punishment of citizens who betray their city; another that of enemies who rage outside it.

One of the executioner-soldiers, repentant for what he had done, secretly revealed in confession to his diocesan bishop that, when they had first hastened with eager spirit and almost a kind of sudden exultation to kill the holy man, immediately after the crime was committed, as they withdrew, it seemed to each of them, in their now shaking and trembling steps, that the earth was opening and ready to swallow them alive. The bishop to whom this confession was made was Bartholomew, bishop of Exeter, of blessed memory; the executioner-soldier who confessed was the aforementioned William de Tracy. But now let us return to the begun sequence of the Passion, and to the still further disordered presumption of the sacrilegious men raging on.

### 10. CONCERNING THE SPOILS AND GARMENTS WHICH THEY DIVIDED AMONG THEMSELVES.

[Col. 1280A]

Immediately after this athlete of ours, the patron of the Church and father of the clergy, had thus passed from the world to the Father, those sacrilegious men ran to the spoil, broke open chests, boxes, coffers, packs, and baskets, and divided among themselves the garments of the Christ of the Lord. The soldiers did these things in such a way that what was said of Christ might fittingly be applied to this Christ of the Lord: “They divided my garments among themselves” (John 19).

And when among other things they found two hair-shirts, which that athlete of Christ had customarily worn over his naked body as a kind of imitation garment, they did not divide them among themselves, nor did they cast lots to determine whose they should be; rather, they threw them away as worthless and of no use to themselves. Yet they were now greatly dismayed and astonished that they saw so great and evident a sign of hidden religious devotion. Hence many of the cohort immediately, like that centurion in the Gospel, though quietly for fear, said to one another: “Truly this man was righteous” (Luke 23). And thus, beating their breasts, they returned.

Such was the end of our patron, the Christ of the Lord. Concerning this end, near the conclusion of this little historical book, I ought neither to pass over nor remain silent regarding a certain truly prophetic vision, as miraculous as it is certain. Throughout this whole history there are innumerable prophetic revelations concerning this man and signs given for unbelievers, by all of which his holiness is proved to the world, and especially to the incredulous. These things which others saw and wrote I shall pass over throughout this little book; but I shall insert here this single truly prophetic revelation which follows, both because of the extraordinary certainty of the events and because of the authority of the narrator—for the narrator’s authority is accustomed greatly to increase belief—and especially for our edification, for the sake of which we have written all that is written throughout this history concerning the man. The certainty of this vision was heard by us and came to us in the following manner.

### 11. CONCERNING THE MARTYRDOM LEARNED OF IN JERUSALEM WITHIN FIFTEEN DAYS.

The Patriarch of Jerusalem—Heraclius by name, as is known, one of the nobler pillars of the Church and still alive, not inferior in holiness of life—because of the frequent and intolerable hostile incursions of the pagans into that Holy Land, set out for regions on this side of the Alps and at last came to England, seeking assistance from the king and the military forces of the kingdom. When there was frequent discussion before him and others about blessed Thomas, his manner of life, his most holy life, and his most glorious end, he affirmed among other things with the greatest certainty that in Jerusalem, within fifteen days of the martyr’s martyrdom, the end of the martyr had been most certainly learned, and that it had been publicized throughout that whole kingdom. And, as he related, it became known in this way.

[Col. 1281A] There is in that land a monastery, one of whose brethren, from early life distinguished both by great purity and by a most holy manner of life, suffered a mortal illness on the very day on which blessed Thomas suffered. When he was already almost drawing his last breath, the father of the monastery came to the brother whom, because of his pre-eminent holiness, he loved above the others and with whom he had formed a greater bond of affection and intimacy. He therefore grieved more deeply for the sick man.

Seeing him labouring already at the point of death, he begged him fatherly and with tears that, when he had departed from the world, he should, if the Lord permitted it, make known to him the state in which he found himself—the man whom he had loved so greatly in life and by whom he had been so greatly loved. The brother consented; he died; and within a few days, according to his promise, he returned joyfully to the father of the monastery and announced that he saw God and that the reward of eternal salvation had already been given to him.

“To make you know this with complete certainty and without hesitation,” he said, “know that soon after I departed from the body and was borne away by angels, I saw the Lord. Soon afterwards, I say, there came a certain great and surpassing man with a procession ineffably wonderful, followed, surrounded on both sides, and led by a multitude of angels beyond all numbering; by a praiseworthy company of patriarchs and prophets; by the glorious choir of apostles; and by an innumerable host of holy martyrs, purple-clad, and confessors clad in white.

“He stood before the Lord as a martyr, his whole head torn open, with blood, as it seemed, slowly dripping through the fissures of the wounds. The Lord said to him: ‘Thomas, thus it is fitting for you to enter into the court of your Lord.’ And He added: ‘As much glory as I gave to Peter, no less will I give to you.’ Then the Lord immediately took a golden crown of wondrous size and placed it upon his mangled and torn head.”

And the dead brother who spoke added: “Know therefore with complete certainty that this great Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, has been killed in these days and has thus departed to the Lord. Meanwhile, mark carefully these words spoken to you; observe the times. For after a short interval, through the reliable report of many travellers, these things will be proved true. And through the accomplished end of the glorious martyr, now prophesied to you by me, you are henceforth not to doubt concerning my salvation—especially since you will soon receive from others, as I now prophesy to you, confirmation that it has thus been accomplished.” Having said these things, the brother who had spoken truly and truly prophetically immediately disappeared.

And indeed it was truly prophetic, and all this was prophetic; even the place itself was prophetic, the Holy Spirit signifying through the place that the glory of the new martyr, proclaimed so quickly in so holy and celebrated a place, was to be preached with the greatest speed throughout the four quarters of the world, so that the sound of one triumphing so gloriously might go forth into all the earth. For the palm of the soldier who had departed from the world was immediately proclaimed in the midst of the earth, where the Lord had wrought salvation, so that from there, as if from the navel of the world, the name of his glory might swiftly spread to all surrounding nations. “In the navel,” I say, according to what the Lord says through the prophet of Jerusalem: “I have set her in the midst of the nations, and lands round about her” (Ezek. 5).

The father of the monastery, receiving no small consolation concerning the brother’s death after this revelation had been made to him, went rejoicing without delay to the venerable patriarch already mentioned and disclosed everything in order, as the patriarch himself recounted to us with his own mouth.

Hence it is pleasing to consider how uniquely great, how magnificently singular, is he whose glory that brother, now made a fellow-citizen of the angels, first proclaimed to earthly people: first to the Holy Land, before the other parts of the world [Col. 1282B]. There the Christ of the Lord, truly a follower of Christ, was first proclaimed after his death, where Christ himself was first proclaimed after death. And just as Christ’s death was immediately made known to the world through the sun, so the death of the Christ of the Lord is immediately made known to the world at the Lord’s command, not through another sun but through a fellow-citizen of the angels. For the setting of Christ, the true sun, is proclaimed to the world through the darkening of the temporal sun; but the death of the Christ of the Lord through the eternal salvation granted, and the eternal brightness bestowed, upon his eternal fellow-citizen.

### 12. CONCERNING THE CORRESPONDENCE OF THE DEATH OF CHRIST AND OF THE CHRIST OF THE LORD.

O death of Christ, O death of the Christ of the Lord! This is the copy; that, the exemplar. And indeed it is so, if anyone attends and considers what great correspondence, what marvellous harmony, what concordant and sweet melody there is between the punishment of Christ and the punishment of the Christ of the Lord, offering and offering, passion and passion, death and death. It is a concordant melody, sweet to hear, though grievous to answer. For this is that song in the prophet, “for the King” (*Melech*), of the choir responding and following Christ, who leads the chant. The melody of this choir and its leader is indeed harmonious and the song exceedingly sweet—yet sweet with a certain bitterness because of compassion, unless all things are immediately sweetened by the delight of the fruit of the palm obtained.

But at the end of this little historical book this concordant melody and this song, both sweet and pleasant, will be heard more fully, more attentively, and more fittingly. For a song of this subject remains still to be added; the matter itself has not yet been completely woven together. Meanwhile, let us accompany to the tomb with the fitting offices of humanity the holy body of our patron and father, now returned to his homeland: that holy body which remains from us and with us, the spoils of his death which he left us when ascending, as a precious legacy.

### 13. CONCERNING EVENTS AFTER THE MARTYRDOM.

It should briefly be mentioned that, as soon as the city heard the previously unheard-of news of that so wicked and profane deed, the whole city was dismayed [Col. 1283A], stunned, and shaken. They beat their breasts and struck their hands upon their knees and hand against hand in astonishment and grief. Seeking and lamenting their father and patron, they ran immediately to the church.

But, leaving aside the rich, the poor alone hastened to the soldier of the supreme Emperor, thus slain; for while he still served as a soldier, he had been the support of the poor, father of orphans, helper of the fatherless, judge of widows, and comforter of the sorrowful. Such a class of people—and certainly such alone, while the rich shrank away in fear and hid themselves—such people, I say, and they alone, run, hurry, and hasten. All hurry; each hastens to outstrip the other, wailing, lamenting, and crying aloud, asking where their father and patron had gone.

Let us look back to Christ’s Passion and see whether in this Passion of the Christ of the Lord it was not so as in the Passion of Christ himself; whether in the suffering of the soldier it was not as in the suffering of the Emperor. There were fishermen there, women there—only the poor, the others likewise hidden through fear. Here we need not linger, nor compare and match the sufferings of Head and member more than necessary. For readers who know both, it suffices merely to have touched on them here.

Therefore, leaving the rest aside, let us return to our poor, who ran—as Christ’s poor then ran to Christ’s tomb—to the pavement of the church, upon which that holy body still lay, lifeless and not yet placed in the tomb. [Col. 1283C] The poor, running and outrunning one another, immediately worshipped it devoutly and kissed the hands and feet with the greatest reverence. Some dipped little cloths (*pitacia*), others towels (*mapulae*), in that sacred fountain of blood which flowed abundantly over the pavement of the church, already prophesying, as if by a certain foreknowledge of future events, both the devotion and reverence to be shown to the new martyr and the extension of his glory throughout the world in a short time.

At length, about nightfall—for it was evening when that work of darkness was done—the skull-cap, together with the crown of unction, which hung from the head like a disk and still adhered slightly to the forehead by a little skin, was, as best it could be, set firm again and fitted to the head. And as it lay upon the pavement, with the body neither yet unclothed [Col. 1283D] nor washed—as is especially the monastic custom in burying the dead—that holy body was borne on shoulders into the monks’ choir before the high altar.

## 14. ON THE APPEARANCE OF THE BODY, NOW LIFELESS

Throughout that whole night, after the great outpouring of blood which had already flowed across the church pavement, blood slowly dripped through the fissures of the wounds, though the head had been set firm again. Hence there was a miracle, wonderful and great to tell, a great miracle of the Lord’s power, worthy of grateful amazement: after so bitter a slaughter, after such hard blows of swords, when the skull-cap together with the crown of unction was separated from the head, after so great an outpouring of blood, and finally after such thick drops of blood throughout the entire night—after all [Col. 1284A] this—the face was not paler, not thinner; denser wrinkles did not furrow the brow; the circles of the eyes were not more contracted; the eyes were not more sunken; [nor did fluid run from mouth or nostrils]; the neck was not more wasted, the shoulder not more drooping, the finger not stiffer, nor the skin looser. In short, no wasting or depletion could be detected in any part of the body; the lifelike arrangement of the dead body itself demonstrated that this final lifelessness of the holy man had not been a depletion.

And indeed it was fitting that he who, in dying, had preserved for the Lord so seemly and beautiful an arrangement of his body as we have described—an arrangement which not even black death as it threatened could disfigure—it was fitting, I say, that the Lord should repay him with its like when dead, since he could no longer do so himself. And He did repay him. For this grace which we have described—this appearance more fit to be painted in antimony than described in the dark letters of a pen—this, I say, was the grace and beauty of the lifeless body, thus battered and shorn in the head. Certainly it was more like a dead man sleeping peacefully, so that some even hesitated whether he had yet died. This, I say, was the grace; this the beauty of the whole body; this the vitality of the face; this its pleasantness; this its cheerfulness, of one made glad—indeed, now made fat—with oil. This was, as we recall having said above, the glory of his countenance, begun when he returned from exile at his first entrance into his church, and now completed at his departure as he returned home: a glory which no violent breath of death could blow away, but which rather transformed him from glory into glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.

But what more? Most certainly, and more clearly than light itself, that beautiful and pleasant disposition of his body was at once the herald, preacher, and messenger of his eternal joy: so that what the aforesaid brother, a fellow-citizen of the angels, had beheld spiritually in a vision, might here be demonstrated bodily in the present, eye to eye; and thus, at the beginning, as it were, of his departure, the testimony of his glory might stand in the mouth of two witnesses. The holy man’s body therefore lay throughout that night upon a bier before the church’s high altar—he who nevertheless had now entered unto the altar of God, unto God who had made glad his sorrow. The body lay there still neither washed nor unclothed.

## 15. HOW THE HOLY MAN’S BODY WAS BORNE TO THE TOMB

[Col. 1284D] On the following day the vipers returned—of that oft-mentioned brood of vipers—and spewing their venom from their forked tongues, thundered terribly that the body of that deceiver should still be above ground. They added that, unless it were most swiftly removed from human sight and hidden under the earth, it should be dragged through the whole city by horses or hung upon a gallows. They also forbade that the deceiver’s body be laid among the sarcophagi of the holy bishops.

Some of the monastic brethren, immediately astonished and terrified by this dreadful and sacrilegious threat, hastened to take the body from the bier on which it lay. First they began to remove his garments and afterward, as is especially monastic custom, [Col. 1285A] to wash the body. But when they removed his outer garments, which he wore before human eyes, they found all things within to be different, in accordance with the saying of the Wise Man: “Let your forehead conform to the people, but let all things within be different.” And this indeed they found in him. For immediately underneath they found a certain black sleeveless tunic, but without a hood; they at once understood it to be a monastic cowl. When this was removed, they found the whole body closely covered with hair-cloth: hair-cloth upon the shoulder, hair-cloth upon the arm, hair-cloth upon the back, hair-cloth upon the shins—the man, as it were, sewn all over his body in hair-cloth.

This was Joseph’s long robe, this his garment reaching to the ankles. As we recall having said near the beginning of this history, he put it on as soon as he was promoted to the priesthood and did not take it off until the consummation of his martyrdom. The brethren, in whose hands that holy body lay, saw this beyond their expectation—indeed beyond the world’s estimation—and with great rejoicing, or rather with a certain exultation of mind, immediately summoned the other brethren. Since many among them had, like worldly people, doubted the man’s sanctity, now, seeing this, they were terribly astonished, beneficially broken in spirit, and immovably confirmed. And, as though they had seen an earthquake—indeed, an earthquake in his flesh, so delicate and frail, so violently shaken, or rather transformed—as though they had seen this, I say, evangelical earthquake, they immediately joined that centurion in crying aloud: “Truly this was the Son of God!” (Matt. XXVIII.)

Therefore, after the body had been unclothed and washed, they at once took Thomas’s body and clothed it in other garments, as is customary in burying bishops. In the church crypt was a new tomb, hewn from rock, apparently prepared for this very purpose long beforehand, in which no one had yet been laid. And, because of fear, hiding it as it were in the church crypt, they placed Thomas’s body in this new tomb hewn from rock, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1171, in about the fifty-third year of his life.

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE SEVENTH VOLUME BEGIN

[Col. 1285]

1. On the catalogue of Thomas’s learned companions.  
2. On why this history of the martyr is not to be mutilated.  
3. On the petition by which he commends himself to the merits and prayers of readers of this history.

# SEVENTH VOLUME

## I. ON THE CATALOGUE OF THOMAS’S LEARNED COMPANIONS

[Col. 1285C]

And since frequent mention has been made in this history of the learned companions of Thomas, now our lord and glorious new martyr, I have thought it commendable to set down their names at the end of this history, that their names may be in everlasting blessing. In so great a tempest, amid so many whirlpools of the sea, they had been fellow-helpers of the ship of their father, who nevertheless laboured to steer it through danger. I mean their names as illustrious men.

1. First, then, and above all these learned men, the most learned of all was Thomas himself. As he was more learned, so too was he more distinguished: rosy and ruddy, washing his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of grapes. After the likeness of his Emperor, he trod the winepress alone and ascended to heaven from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah.

2. Among Thomas’s learned companions, the most learned was a certain illustrious man, a Lombard by nation and name, native of the renowned city of Piacenza. Long hanging upon the two breasts of his mother-bride, he was at last weaned from milk and removed from the breasts, and became great in wisdom and knowledge. In the time when he was free for quiet and leisure, this disciple taught the master in exile the canons. At the feet of this teacher sat daily the disciple who wrote these things. He was always our inseparable companion, until at last, because of his outstanding merits, he was called from exile to the Roman Church, made cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, and finally promoted by the Roman pontiff to be archbishop of Benevento.

3. After him was John, surnamed of Salisbury, English by nation. Having a name suited to the thing, by God’s grace he had joined to himself in the head of the Bride two eyes—the word of wisdom and the word of knowledge—given him abundantly through the Spirit. He remained steadfastly and manfully with our new martyr in his trials to the end. Because of glorious merits—not his own, as he considered them, but rather those of our new martyr—soon after our lord’s martyrdom he was summoned by God’s calling from his native land and promoted to be bishop of Chartres, in the province of Sens, where he had earlier been exiled with us.

4. After him came Robert, surnamed Foliot, English by nation, then archdeacon of Oxford: a person of many aspects, rich in graces and virtues. If you considered his life and deeds, you would judge him another Laban, a father-in-law in respect of the two sisters joined to him in marriage. Yet he did not follow his father when he went forth from the land and became a pilgrim, save after obtaining his father’s permission and blessing. Later, on account of his distinguished merits, he was promoted to be bishop of Hereford.

[Col. 1287A] 5. After him came Reginald, English by nation, but Lombard in upbringing and surname: prudent and industrious beyond his age, spirited and effective in action. Having stood bravely with us outside his native land for some time, he soon became the cause of our sorrow, because of the reason for which he immediately transferred himself from our struggle and poverty to the court, in order that, serving there, he might fight more strongly for the prince against us. Yet, at the death of our lord—precious and triumphant as it was—by the saving grace of the Most High he turned back and returned to a former lord and father. Later, his industry and worth earning it, he was taken from the court to the Church and promoted to be bishop of Bath.

[Col. 1287B] 6. After him, famous in name and reputation, came Gerard by his personal name, surnamed Puella, English by nation. After long draughts of the turbid waters of the Sior, he at last drank for himself the purest waters from the springs of Siloam. Before our leader and father went into exile, he was the first to promote this man to the clerical order and the first to confer on him an ecclesiastical benefice. Though he had run with us throughout the day, at last, toward evening, slackening in the race and seeking a little rest, he turned aside from us. Yet after our lord’s passing from this world, the merits of his good, gentle, honourable conduct and learning secured his promotion to be bishop of Coventry.

7. After him came Hugh, surnamed de Nunant, a Norman by nation, then archdeacon of Lisieux: discerning in counsel for his youthful years, provident in action, and energetic in execution. But before our pilgrimage had ended, he was reconciled to the prince and returned with our father’s permission. Having for years been found faithful and energetic by the prince—whether through the court or the Church I do not know; but I know this: after Gerard of happy memory, of whom we have just spoken, had entered upon the way decreed for all flesh—he was promoted to that same episcopal see.

8. After him came Gilbert, surnamed de Glanville, English by nation, possessing a pattern of good and honourable conduct, conforming himself in character to the good men among whom he lived, and attaining commendable learning in both laws. Once he had joined himself to us, he did not afterward abandon us. Yet he was the last of all to be called. Nevertheless, by the disposition of the Most High, he who had been last in calling became nearest to our father in rank: for, as I write these things, he has been elected bishop of Rochester.

9. And now, to enumerate from our fellowship not bishops but other private persons—yet great and industrious men—after him came Ralph, surnamed de Serra, [English by nation, a mild, gentle, and companionable man]. Though not a bishop, he fulfilled the office of bishop through holiness of life and fullness of learning. Although he had not tasted the sour grape, his teeth were set on edge: for, though he was neither of the household nor of the archbishop’s household, he was driven out and proscribed, his parents now being fitter for the grave than exile. Later, because of the man’s distinguished merits, he was promoted at Reims to be dean of the metropolitan church.

10. Next was Jordan, or, as others call him, Gordian, surnamed de Melbourne, English by nation, then archdeacon of Chichester and afterward dean of that church. He had acquired no ordinary learning for his age and for the time he had devoted to letters; but because he had bought a farm, he excused himself and did not follow his pilgrim father.

11. After him came Matthew, English by nation, and of Chichester by both origin and surname: a young man sharp in intellect, upright and industrious. Though he had already made suitable progress in learning, he was drawn back from letters by the bonds of secular courts and worldly business; as I write this, he is dean of Chichester. Since he was not called at all, he did not follow his pilgrim father.

12. After him came Gervase, likewise of Chichester both by nation and surname, a young man then certainly commendable alike in conduct and in knowledge of letters. Yet he too, since he was not called, did not leave his native land.

13. After him came John, surnamed of Tilbury, English by nation, a man possessing much mind and much eloquence. Like a learned and swift scribe, whenever necessary he promptly brought forth new and old things from the treasure of his heart. But he is excused for not following his father as he departed into a foreign land, since his body was already heavy and he was advanced in years.

14. After him came Philip, surnamed de Caune, English by nation, a gentle and simple man. He had already greatly exhausted the strength of body and mind in the study of human law, and he followed his pilgrim father. But though he had borne his shoulders beneath the burden for some time, he was in no way sufficient to carry the burden of poverty for so long; he saw that rest was good and returned home, though only after receiving his father’s leave and blessing.

15. After him came Hervé, surnamed of London, whence he was also native. Borrowing vessels of gold and silver from the Egyptians, he desired in the desert to be filled with manna. But, sent by our father to the apostolic man, he was overtaken by death on the way.

16. After him came Gunter, surnamed of Winchester, whence he too was native: a simple and upright man, God-fearing and without complaint. What he lacked in learning was supplied to him more suitably from above in life. Small in stature like Zacchaeus, he climbed a sycamore tree that he might at least thus see Jesus passing by. He remained faithfully and steadfastly with his master in trials unto the end.

17. After him came Alexander, called Cuelin in his native tongue, Welsh by nation and surname. He was educated in letters, pleasant in speech, and abundant in pleasant words. Yet not all his virtue was in his speech; rather, neither tongue nor hand failed him. With our father and for our father, now voluntarily, now at command, and now sent on missions, he often worked carefully, bravely, and steadfastly amid many dangers; and, what is most precious in that nation, as he acted, so he always and everywhere kept faith with his lord.

18. There were also two others: one called Rothland, the other Hariald, Lombards by nation, men industrious indeed and highly capable in letters. Our father, already in exile, summoned them to himself. In view of their learning and prudence, though he possessed little, he shared his poverty with them, granting each year of his exile ten marks to the first named, and one hundred silver shillings to the other.

19. There remains one more from this fellowship of our blessed martyr-lord, very dear and acceptable to our lord. I set him apart, as singularly great and magnificently distinguished, and also because he was among the last in calling. His personal name was Humbert; he was a Lombard by nation, native of that illustrious city called Milan, a man exceedingly powerful in deed and speech. As he advanced from virtue to virtue, and likewise through ecclesiastical grades, while we were still in exile he first became archdeacon of Bourges. Then called by our lord, he became, as it were, one of us in our fellowship. Later, because of his distinguished merits, he was promoted to be archbishop of Milan, the city from which he had sprung. In the first or second year after that promotion he turned into the father and patron of all; raised from archbishop to the supreme pontiff of the Roman see, he is today ruler of the whole Church, Urban III in fact as well as name.

20. From this catalogue, therefore, of so prudent and valiant a fellowship, we may judge how great-souled, magnificent, and generous was this our glorious martyr-lord, who, though stripped of all things and proscribed for the cause of God and the Church, acquired for himself such and so great defenders.

21. There were nevertheless several others among these whom I do not name here, though learned and energetic, who nonetheless kept faith with their lord and courageously and manfully completed with him the course of the struggle to its appointed goal. Among them, by the Lord’s gift, was the writer of these things, as though one untimely born and the least disciple among the learned: Herbert by personal name, English by nation, and, in nation and surname, of Bosham.

22. And lest I pass over that man of such celebrated report, whom I recall having touched upon above in this history in his proper place—the cleric, namely, wounded in the arm during the martyr’s struggle—his personal name was Edward, his surname Grim, English by nation. I set him here separately from the others because, although he came from the province, he was not of the archbishop’s own household; rather, he had happened to come to see his archbishop, newly returned from exile. For this reason I do not place him in the catalogue of the archbishop’s learned companions in this history. Yet, now removed from human affairs, he has, as we may hope, been placed by the Most High in the heavenly catalogue of His saints.

23. Of those whom I have placed in this catalogue of learned companions, as I have indicated above in listing each one, some remained with us—bold, strong, energetic, steadfast friends of poverty—bearing the weight of battle; a few fell away. In this too the soldier was conformed to his Emperor. For, not to mention others now, not every one whom the Emperor Himself chose for apostles remained; and, to conclude now the catalogue of all our learned companions, they number twenty in all.

24. Let no one wonder, and let no one censure, if among the others in this catalogue of learned companions I have enumerated some who did not follow their father in pilgrimage. Such persons might seem rather to be reckoned among those friends who share the table but do not remain in the day of necessity. Or I may have named some who followed their pilgrim father, yet returned before the labour of the pilgrimage was completed. Such persons may nevertheless seem like that frail and easily deceived woman who, looking back, was turned into a pillar; or like him who set his hand to the plough and likewise looked back, thereby making himself unfit for the kingdom. Yet if I have listed among the other learned men both these and those, let no one wonder or censure this. Rather, let our whole Catholic mother know that those who did not follow their pilgrim father, and those who followed and returned, almost all returned after first receiving paternal permission and blessing; and all these were released by their father with paternal compassion. Besides, we all know one further thing, and the world sees it thus. Hence no apologetic speech on their behalf is now necessary: those who did not follow, and those who followed but did not remain, if they acted in any way against their father, if they gave offence in any manner, were beneficially converted; and, with the whole inward being of their hearts and in the utmost devotion of their minds, whatever they had done before, they humbled themselves before their father at and after his death, so precious and triumphant, and returned to him with the deepest love.

You therefore, holy father and glorious martyr, who first in the arena were a most valiant athlete together with your Emperor, but now upon the throne are a most glorious victor; who through your death conquered both death itself and him who held dominion of death over you: preserve those who remained with you in your trials, that those who were companions in suffering may deserve to become companions in consolation. Preserve, Lord, all whom the Lord gave you in His name, remembering Him who, having loved His own, loved them unto the end. Preserve also all who faithfully obeyed or followed you and returned, or who did not turn away from you because, by paternal permission, they did not follow you. And to me, your disciple—such as I am, now your historiographer—wandering through the trackless and pathless places of the wilderness, seeking you, deign to impart some small share of your double spirit. Not that I, a little sinful man, arrogate to myself anything belonging to the most eminent prophet Elisha; but because you are Elijah, as the spirit and power showed to the world, and, lest anything be lacking, even the very dress showed. Therefore cast down to me, your little one, as you ascend on high, something of what I was accustomed to minister to you in the bonds of the Gospel, or of the thread of your prophetic woof, lest I perish naked amid the cold of this wilderness.

For it is not to be believed that, although you have now mounted your fiery chariot, the burning heats of the Holy Spirit—the eternal, inaccessible brightness and love—have absorbed you so utterly in that abyss of joys that you forget your children still wandering and in peril. Rather, you are now, as is credible, more ready and more powerful to aid them, inasmuch as, drunk from that unfailing fountain of eternal mercy, your primacy has been further confirmed through your triumphant death. But lest anyone claim as private property what is the common benefit and joy of the whole Church, may the people find, as they hope, salvation in your blood, glorious martyr; the clergy, liberty; and the whole world of churches, protection. Thus, as there is peace for you, so may there be peace in your blood for your former fellow-workers, peace for your pilgrims, peace for your Church, and peace for the whole world of churches. And may the liberty which the clergy, though not yet wholly, have already obtained in part through your blood, become complete: liberty for which, in a new and unheard-of manner, you chose to offer yourself, strong in constancy and constant in strength.

## II. HE BEGS THAT NO ONE MUTILATE THIS HISTORY OF THE MARTYR

Near the end of this history, I ask, desire, and, insofar as I dare, even forbid in the martyr’s own name, that no reader at any time mutilate or abbreviate this history of the martyr, even if it should perhaps seem too long to someone. I call it too long, because I myself confess it to be lengthy; yet I could not avoid it, nor was I permitted to do so without offending many and great persons, to whom I was indebted for this historical work. They urgently demanded of me a description not only of the deeds of so great a man, but also of the causes of his deeds and the power of edification inherent in them. All this, enlarged by such wide magnificence of deeds and virtues, could not be compressed into the troublesome brevity of words. Hence come the frequent digressions which we have made throughout the history, wandering aside for the sake of edification.

If anyone perhaps censures this as contrary to the law of history, let him please forgive it, remembering that it was done not out of my verbosity but in accordance with the wishes of friends. Yet, if anyone has properly examined the forms of histories, this is not contrary to the law of history—indeed, it is more truly in accordance with that law. But of this elsewhere. Nevertheless, even if this historical book has thus grown beyond the law of history, I ask and desire that no one mutilate or abbreviate it, unless perhaps he wishes enviously to diminish the force of so great a man’s deeds or to lower his glory. Let him not mutilate it, I say, except perhaps by selecting something which he judges worthy to be read publicly in church, especially on the festive day of the martyr’s birth into heaven. If he knows better, let him correct it: this indeed is pleasing. But this I ask: let him not mutilate it.

I say this because of the many who, coining their own work as though new from another’s old work, often cut away as superfluous what is more necessary, or retain as more necessary the very things that are superfluous. They often corrupt what they find in the original by interpreting and mutilating it according to their own judgment; nor do they follow the author’s mind in the author’s own words, but bend those words to their own purposes. Such mutilators resemble incautious pruners of trees and vines when cutting back luxuriant branches and shoots: they often cut away what is more fruitful and more necessary while supposing that they have cut away dried or bastard growth as superfluous. Therefore, whoever you are, if you know how to compose a historical book or another work, compose your own; do not make a new work of yours, without labour, out of my old work which I have laboured over. Or if you do not know how to compose your own, how is it that, by correcting mine and cutting away from it what seems to you superfluous—and may perhaps be more necessary—you seek to make my work your own? If you can, come to me, that I may correct myself; but if not, leave mine untouched and compose your own new work. I say this one thing—which I wish I had said without offending mutilators: a mutilated historical book, or any other mutilated book, will never be wholly trustworthy to me, nor I to it. Even if it please me, it is always suspect to me, and I shall never give it full credit.

## III. HE COMMENDS HIMSELF TO THE PRAYERS OF THOSE READING THIS HISTORY

At the very end of this little historical work, I ask and beseech that whoever may desire, during this pilgrimage of mine or when it has ended, to hear this historical song of the martyr, may deign, in consideration of fraternal unity, to share with me—such as I am, the historiographer—by the aid of prayers and merits, and always remember one left behind. Amen.

[Col. 1291] (Only five sheets, or ten pages, are missing from this entire little book. In two or three places a few passages taken from the *Quadrilogus* have been inserted and enclosed in brackets. See more concerning this in the second *Quadrilogus*, *Life of St Thomas*, above.)

# HERBERT OF BOSHAM’S BOOK OF MELODIES

## THE PROLOGUE OF THE BOOK OF MELODIES BEGINS

[Col. 1293A] The history of the holy man having been completed, like a song set before it, we immediately add, as is the custom of cithara-players, three harmonies in praise of the martyr, from which three melodies are formed. The first harmony concerns the likeness or concord of the visible struggle of the martyr-soldier with the visible struggle of Christ the Emperor; from this the first melody is formed. The second harmony concerns the concord of the visible palm of victory of the soldier with the visible palm of victory of the Emperor; from this the second melody is formed. The third harmony concerns the concord of the invisible palm of victory of the soldier with the invisible palm of victory [Col. 1294A] of the Emperor; from this the third melody is formed. Therefore we have entitled this little book, sounding like a cithara with these harmonies, the *Book of Melodies*. It contains certain matters concerning events after the martyrdom. Since nearly its whole subject matter depends upon the preceding history of the martyr, we attach this *Book of Melodies* immediately to the historical book. When this little *Book of Melodies* is finished, I add in this volume one homily on the day of the martyr’s heavenly birth. At the end of the volume is appended that fatal writing, drawn up in the form of a bond, which was first the cause of our exile and afterward of the martyrdom.

## CHAPTERS OF THE BOOK OF MELODIES

[Col. 1293]

1. On the harmony of the visible struggle of the soldier with the visible struggle of the Emperor: behold the first melody.  
2. On the harmony of the visible palm of victory of the soldier with the visible palm of victory of the Emperor: behold the second melody.  
3. On the harmony of the invisible palm of victory of the soldier with the invisible palm of victory of the Emperor: behold the third melody.

The chapters of the *Book of Melodies* are complete.

[Col. 1293B] When the little *Book of Melodies*, with its three melodies, has been completed, he adds his one homily on the martyr, which begins thus: “Let us sing to the Lord.” At the very end of all is appended that fatal writing, composed in the form of a bond, which, as the world saw and begrudged, was first the cause of the archbishop’s exile and finally of his martyrdom.

# THIS FIRST MELODY CONCERNS THE VISIBLE AND CORRESPONDING STRUGGLE OF THE SOLDIER WITH THE LIKE STRUGGLE OF THE EMPEROR

## THE BOOK OF MELODIES BEGINS

When this history of the holy man’s life and deeds has been completed, like a song set forth concerning so great an athlete of Christ, now after whatever song this occasion requires, it is time that henceforth, after so difficult a struggle and so glorious a victory, we should move each hand in his praise, strike each set of strings, and touch David’s cithara, both humble and strong of hand. Thus, in accordance with the promise made above in this historical song, we may sound forth in a brief melody—though on the grave strings of the cithara, yet sweetly—the harmonious, consonant, and concordant relation between the soldier’s struggle and the Emperor’s struggle: contest to contest, toil to toil, sweat to sweat, punishment to punishment, encounter to encounter, offering to offering, hearing to hearing, passion to passion, and death to death.

Let no one suppose that I wish or attempt to make equal the toils and contests of the Emperor and the soldier, or the glory of their palms of victory on either side. I wish only to compare the soldier’s struggle to the Emperor’s: the soldier followed his Emperor so diligently, bravely, manfully, and immediately, though not indeed as an equal follower, but as one following after; and he sang in such accord, responding in the choir while Christ the Emperor Himself led the chant.

Let none of the hearers of this melody expect it to sound anything concerning the inward and invisible struggle. Yet every soldier, the Emperor alone excepted, is assailed by a twofold struggle. His struggle alone was outward, not within Himself: in Him alone the flesh never lusted against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh. But at present I have nothing to do with that struggle by which the soldier was assailed only as man, while the Emperor, God and man, never was. Therefore I now pass over that inward struggle between spirit and flesh, especially because I have proposed merely to demonstrate the conformity of the soldier’s struggle to the Emperor’s: the visible and outward only to the outward and visible, not the inward struggle with a struggle which the Emperor, of course, lacked.

And indeed, at the beginning of this first melody, let us strike, as it were, the first strings of this Davidic cithara and go back further, so that the melody of this harmony may be sweeter and more pleasing, though longer.

## FIRST NOTE OF THE FIRST MELODY

The Emperor, then, immediately at the first beginnings of His birth according to the flesh, when He began to appear to the world and had descended to overcome the powers of the world and hell—immediately, I say—fled, lay hidden, and concealed Himself, made an exile and banished person together with His father and mother. The soldier likewise, as soon as he entered upon the Emperor’s military service, as though newly born because made new from old, immediately fled, concealed himself, and lay hidden, likewise an exile and banished person, together with all his kindred. Let us now recall this passage from the preceding historical song.

## 2. NOTE

The Emperor returned in the seventh year to His native land and His kingdom, His hostile king now dead. The soldier likewise returned in the seventh year, when the pursuing king was, as was believed, beneficially overthrown and crushed.

## 3. NOTE

The Emperor, returned from exile in the seventh year, for twenty-six years present and not fleeing, fought bravely and manfully in His native land, in the kingdom of His almighty Father. The soldier likewise, returned from exile in the seventh year, renewed the Emperor’s battles strenuously, bravely, and fiercely in his native land, in his ecclesiastical principality, for twenty-six days—let a day be given to the soldier as a year to the Emperor. For twenty-six days only, I say, because no more was permitted, nor did the Emperor will more. The Emperor gave the day for a year to this other fellow-soldier, a prophetic man.

## 4. NOTE

[Col. 1295C]

As the Emperor approached Jerusalem, His passion drawing near, a vast throng of poor people came to meet Him in a great procession, singing to Him the prophetic blessing. Likewise they came to meet the soldier as he approached Canterbury, his passion now imminent. Let us recall this passage from the preceding historical song.

## 5. NOTE

The Emperor, as His passion drew near, entered the Temple and began to cast out those buying and selling. The soldier likewise, as his own passion drew near, entered the church and attempted to cast out the gladiators and trainers of gladiators.

## 6. NOTE

[Col. 1295D] The Emperor, the master, was betrayed to death by a fellow-soldier, a disciple. The soldier likewise was betrayed—not indeed by one but by many: betrayal sacrilegious there and here alike, Jews then killing their pontiff and Christians now killing theirs.

## 7. NOTE

The chief priests pronounced the Emperor’s and Priest’s judgment of death; and likewise did the chief priests pronounce that of the soldier and priest—indeed, more truly, the priestly chiefs. Let us recall here also these passages from the preceding historical song.

## 8. NOTE
The Emperor, when the time was now drawing near for him to pass from the world to the Father, went forward boldly and offered himself freely; and I do not think it has escaped notice how boldly, [Col. 1296A] how freely, the soldier too immediately followed here in the very footsteps of this his Emperor, as was said a little before.

**9. NOTE.**

The Emperor restrained the sword of iron; and the soldier likewise despised it, although, as occasion and the duty of his warfare required, he wielded and exercised another sword, the sword of the word.

**10. NOTE.**

The Emperor prayed for his fellow-soldiers; and likewise did the soldier, even while reproving the whole realm, and defending his own men, although not with the sword with which he had been girded by the Emperor himself.
