**11. NOTE.**

The Emperor, surrendering himself, was taken; and immediately [Col. 1296B] his own soldiers were scattered. Likewise the soldier, when he surrendered himself.

**12. NOTE.**

When the Emperor was struck down, his soldiers, previously scattered, returned to their own homes; likewise the soldier’s followers, when the soldier was struck down, exchanged the crown of flesh for the unfading crown of the spirit.

**13. NOTE.**

Before the one who sheared him, the Emperor was silent as a sheep; and likewise the soldier before the one who sheared him and even cut the crown of his head from his head. And certainly this was a harsh shearing.

**14. NOTE.**

The Emperor was crowned with a crown of thorns; but for [Col. 1296C] a crown a crown is given—for the crown of thorns, a crown of glory. The soldier’s crown indeed is taken away; but for a crown a crown is restored—for the crown of flesh, the unfading crown of the spirit.

**15. NOTE.**

As the Emperor went to the cross, he carried his own cross; and likewise the soldier, when he approached that of his Emperor.

**16. NOTE.**

When his fellow-soldiers had scattered from him, the Emperor trod the winepress alone; likewise the soldier scattered his own followers.

**17. NOTE.**

After the Emperor’s death, his fellow-soldiers were, through the chief priests, made outsiders from the synagogue; likewise, [Col. 1296D] after the soldier’s death, his followers were put outside the communion with which even our chief priests still scarcely dare to communicate. I who write these things bear witness to this note, because I myself see and feel it: the other companions of my suffering having already been taken from the world, I have been left like an orphan without father or brethren.

**18. NOTE.**

The Emperor’s death, like the setting of the true sun, is immediately proclaimed to the world by this temporal sun; and the soldier’s death, like the joy of angels, is immediately announced to the world by a fellow-citizen of the angels.

**19. NOTE.**

The Emperor is crucified by four soldiers; and likewise the soldier is scalped by four.

**20. NOTE.**

[Col. 1297A]

After the Emperor had died, his four soldiers divided his garments into four portions; and likewise those of the soldier.

**21. NOTE.**

The Emperor’s tunic was undivided because it was seamless; likewise the soldier’s cilicia (hair-shirts), because they were cheap and useless.

**22. NOTE.**

The Emperor is crucified near Jerusalem, at the place of Calvary; and the soldier is scalped in Jerusalem itself, in the holy church of his Saviour.

**23. NOTE.**

After the Emperor’s burial, the poor—and the poor alone—immediately come to his tomb; likewise, while the soldier still lay unburied, they ran to the pavement [Col. 1297B] where he lay, while the pavement still served him as a tomb.

**24. NOTE.**

After the Emperor’s burial, there were still wealthy persons who remained concealed through fear; likewise after the soldier too had been killed and still lay unburied.

**25. NOTE.**

After the Emperor’s death, on seeing the earthquake and the other things that happened, men immediately believed him to be the Son of God and proclaimed that he had truly been righteous. Likewise, once the dead soldier’s body had been stripped, unbelievers immediately proclaimed him to have been both the Son of God and truly righteous.

**26. NOTE.**

The Emperor’s body is placed in a new tomb, hewn from rock; [Col. 1297C] likewise the soldier’s, in a hewn rock, in a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid.

**27. NOTE.**

After his death the Emperor is called “deceiver,” not gloriously inglorious but ingloriously glorious; and the soldier likewise is glorified in the same manner after death by his executioners, being called “deceiver” even after death, just as the Emperor was by his crucifiers. They added concerning the soldier’s body that, unless it were hidden beneath the earth as swiftly as possible from human sight, it should immediately either be torn apart by horses or hung from a gibbet.

Let us recall, near the end of this historical song, this almost final pericope; and, so that at the close of the melody we may return, as it were, from Ω to [Col. 1297D] Α—from the end, that is, to the beginning—let us remember that this Emperor whom the soldier follows is Α as he is also Ω. Therefore, to return to Α: at the very time when the Emperor was born and the soldier reborn—or rather, as the Emperor was born, for then the martyr is truly born and then, as it were, first comes into being, when he reaches that which is true being, which alone is being, apart from which there is no being that is—these are the true birthdays of martyrs which mother Church observes: namely, the birthdays on which they attain the truly stable and eternal joys of eternity. Then, as though they had not existed before, they first begin to be, when they have thus arrived at that which is true being. Therefore, when the Emperor and the soldier were born—the one in flesh, the other in spirit.

**28. NOTE.**

[Col. 1298A]

The Emperor indeed was born in the fullness of time. Likewise the soldier, then—not only in the fullness of time, but also of eternity. And, to state more expressly what was, unless I am mistaken, an oracle and a kind of foretelling of future things: even the soldier’s birth in the flesh was near the Emperor’s birthday according to the flesh.

**29. NOTE.**

The Emperor, therefore, was born twice: once before the ages, God from God; and in the fullness of time, man from a human being. Thus also the soldier, in that same fullness of time, was first born in flesh and afterwards in spirit: a twofold birth was granted him by his Emperor in this fullness of time. Likewise the Emperor himself was twice born, as [Col. 1298B] we have already said: once before the ages, from the Father without a mother; afterwards, at the end of the ages, when the fullness of time had come, born from a mother without a father—the Emperor himself, without companion or example, claiming this privilege for himself in each birth.

And, as we have already touched upon, the soldier likewise had a twofold birth, and this on the Emperor’s birthday festivals. For the soldier, like the other sons of Adam, had his first, bodily birth from a fleshly father and mother; but the second was truly without father and without a fleshly mother—I mean, not without a spiritual mother. Yet this twofold birth of the soldier occurred on the Emperor’s birthday days, these two births and two birthday days of the soldier, as it were, enclosing on either side and equally flanking the Emperor’s birth according to the flesh, and as it were his central birthday.

For on the feast of the blessed apostle Thomas this soldier was born at night and named Thomas after Thomas. Thus, five days before the Emperor’s birthday according to the flesh, the soldier was born in flesh; and five days afterwards he was born again, but in spirit. Behold how the soldier’s twofold birth, as it were, stands equally about and bounds the Emperor’s birthday itself, his birth according to the flesh. It was as though in the very time of his birth—or rather of his births, which, like those of the Emperor, are twofold—and from that time, the Emperor’s fellow-soldier, who was to be exceedingly conformed to him and display a most similar following, was foreshown. And so that Thomas [Col. 1298D] the godfather may be joined with Thomas the godson, these two Thomases—the godfather and the godson, or rather the son now fully grown—these two, I say, are, as it were, heavenly sentinels appointed for the nativity of the Lord and of the Lord born in flesh.

Their days, so celebrated and solemn as the birthdays of each, surround the day of the Lord’s Nativity before and after with such equality that their Emperor, Jesus Christ, seems to stand directly and equally between these two fellow-soldiers of his. And what is still novel, and no less delightful to hear: if one may accept as certain the repeated testimony of many, just as the time of the Lord’s Nativity is, as it were, equally bounded by Thomas and Thomas, so also the place of the Lord’s Passion—Jerusalem, which is said by those who have tested it to stand equally distant, as from a centre, from Thomas in India and Thomas in England. And if this is so in this world, how much more, in that kingdom, is Christ Jesus the Emperor common with, indeed more united with, indeed one with Thomas and Thomas.

Since no one doubts that the things arranged by the Most High in this visible world are figures, or as it were shadows and oracles, of those things which are enacted in the invisible and principal world of archetypes under unfailing and true light and immutable truth. There all things which were made through him are life in him. But of these matters elsewhere. Let us return to the melodies to be sounded by those set over the harp.

[Col. 1299B] **HERE THE FIRST MELODY ENDS; HEREAFTER THE DAVIDIC HARP IS TUNED TO THE SECOND.**

Behold: having set forth the theme of the historical song, we have now, as promised, heard thus far upon the harp of the humble king, mighty of hand, the soldier’s conflict answered to the Emperor’s conflict—how harmonious, how consonant, how mutually responsive is the melody! Behold what a song, nowhere unmusical, nowhere discordant: a kind of alternating song of the Emperor’s conflict and the soldier’s conflict. I mean the Emperor’s, who goes before and leads the song, and the soldier’s, who follows his Emperor—not indeed as an equal successor, yet following in his tracks and answering in harmony to the leader of the choir. For this is that song of the prophet, “For Melech, to be answered.” [Col. 1299C]

But this entire melody is mournful, and the whole song is as it were hoarse and bitter, since it is sung upon the lower strings of the harp. For according to the rule of musical art, this harp has both low and high strings: the low strings sound as it were hoarse and thick, but the high ones ring. The low strings sound when the human things of the Emperor and the soldier are declared: from these come grief and sorrow—manifold punishment, frequent and laborious struggle in many battles, and finally death itself. Behold the hoarse and heavy sound; and of these things is the mournful melody on this harp.

But the high strings of this harp ring when the divine things of the Emperor and the soldier are proclaimed: from these come joy, dancing, and jubilation; the palm of victory and the crown of the palm; incorruption itself and immortality. Behold the clear and pure sound, and the melody concerning these things is most delightful upon this harp.

We have indeed performed one melody upon this harp, as the king, the skilled harpist, instructed us to play it: a sad and mournful melody, sounding only upon the low strings of the harp, concerning the Emperor’s and the soldier’s so varied and manifold suffering, their so frequent and difficult conflicts, and finally the Emperor’s and the soldier’s so hard and terrible death. This melody is mournful and grave. For, leaving aside many other hard, grievous, and shameful things, what is heavier than the Emperor’s cross? What more disgraceful? And likewise, what is harsher or more profane than such a scalping of the soldier? Yet the mournful melody concerning these things is bearable. For although compassion is due for what has been heard, nevertheless rejoicing is due to the hearer, because [Col. 1300A] later, according to the rule of musical art, after the low harp strings that sound below in the modulation of this mournful melody, the music rises, and upon the high strings of the harp there follows a melody certainly most sweet and joyful.

Thus the harp which, as we have heard, has thus far sounded for mourning, is afterwards turned into jubilation. Hence the voice of the master harpist, the true king David himself, playing upon this harp: “Behold,” he says, “we go up to Jerusalem; and the Son of Man shall be delivered to the chief priests and scribes, and they shall condemn him to death, and shall deliver him to the Gentiles to be mocked, scourged, and crucified” (Mark 10). Behold, a sorrowful melody upon this harp of David, while David himself strikes and plays it thus upon the lower strings. But that which was now sounding for mourning is immediately changed to joy: “And on the third day,” he says, “he shall rise again” (ibid.).

Likewise the disciple-harpist, playing upon this harp and following the Master: immediately after he had played the melody of pain and mourning upon the lower and deeper strings of the harp, he bent the plectrum, touched the upper strings—which are the sweeter because they are higher—and, sounding a melody of another mode upon the harp, sang pleasantly and as it were with dancing: “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2). Behold: after so sorrowful a melody, how sweet, how joyful, how full of gladness and dancing is the other melody, of another mode, which is immediately joined to the glory and unheard-of praise of the crucified Emperor! After the cross, and through the cross, he is exalted so highly, and receives a name—the name that is above every name—so that through such a shameful punishment he should possess by grace what he possessed by nature. To him, as it were the monarch of all, by the merit of that very punishment, as follows in the melody of the disciple-harpist just mentioned, every knee in the three ages or three worlds is bent: namely, of angels, human beings, and demons. And every believing tongue confesses that after such disgrace of the cross, he is in the coequal and coeternal glory of the omnipotent Father.

The notes of this melody, corresponding to those concerning the Emperor, must likewise be sounded upon this harp for the glory and praise of the soldier, though not upon strings of the harp so lofty or so high-pitched. [Col. 1300D] For behold, just as the Emperor receives, after the cross, the greatest name throughout all regions of the world, so too does the soldier receive it after his scalping. To him reverence is without doubt rendered by the heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings, and victory is acclaimed. Every tongue likewise confesses that after so harsh and dreadful a cutting away of his head, he is in the glory of God the Father, in the glory of his Emperor. Therefore now, from East and West and from the ends of the earth, people come to adore the wounds of the one still sleeping in the tomb, invoke his protection, and beg his aid.

Therefore we must wait here a little, so that meanwhile our harp, which formerly sounded a sad and mournful, though harmonious and consonant, melody upon its lower and heavier strings concerning the punishment and struggle, the sweat of the Emperor and the sweat of the soldier, and death, [Col. 1301A] may henceforth be played upon the upper and higher strings. As though the plectrum had been bent back, may it perform a melody of another kind, sounding sweeter because it sounds higher. Thus, as we promised above, after the punishment and battle, after the sweat and contests, after the Emperor’s death and the soldier’s death, the visible palm of victory of the soldier’s death may subsequently be compared with, though not made equal to, the visible palm of victory of the Emperor’s death. Such, as promised, will be the notes of the succeeding melody on these matters, which we shall henceforth play upon David’s harp as the king, the master harpist, shall teach us.

Yet this melody is to be played neither, as before, upon the low strings, nor upon the highest strings of the harp, but only upon the middle ones. For upon the middle strings we shall sound more intelligibly and safely.

But I now forewarn and fortify the hearers of one of these melodies, on account of what follows: just as the earlier melody of our harp sounded in advance concerning the visible struggle in this flesh of the Emperor and the soldier, so the whole following melody will sound concerning the visible palm of victory in the Emperor’s death and the soldier’s death. For the Emperor’s palm of victory in death, like the soldier’s, is twofold. One is obtained beneath the sun upon earth and is shown in part to us who still serve in the flesh; by it we are invited to something similar. This we call the visible palm. The other palm, which is above the sun and exceeds every sense, whose glory only those who already triumph see [Col. 1301C] and feel, we call the invisible palm of the Emperor and the soldier.

In order, therefore, to distinguish with the greatest clarity between these two palms, visible and invisible, for the explanation of what follows: by the Emperor’s visible palm of death we mean whatever he achieved triumphantly beneath the sun, in flesh and through flesh—whether seen bodily by human beings or not. Nevertheless, all this must be reckoned as belonging to the Emperor’s visible palm of death, because it was done beneath the sun, in flesh, through flesh, and for flesh. What I say concerning this visible palm of the Emperor, I say likewise concerning the soldier: whatever he himself achieved triumphantly beneath the sun—or rather, whatever the Emperor similarly achieved on his account—belongs to the visible palm of the soldier’s death.

But that marvellous and inconceivable glory of the Emperor, above every sun and above every [Col. 1301D] sense, in the heaven of heavens, obtained through obedience unto death, belongs to the invisible palm of the Emperor’s death. And what I say concerning the invisible palm of the Emperor’s death, I say likewise concerning the soldier, who, as the Emperor obtained glory through death, likewise obtained glory through the death of his Emperor.

But first, after the first melody concerning their visible and similar conflict, a melody concerning the visible palm of the soldier’s death in relation to the visible palm of the Emperor’s death shall next sound upon our Davidic harp, as order requires.

Indeed, consequence and order would require that after this second melody concerning the visible and similar palm of the soldier’s death in relation to the Emperor’s death, a third melody should be composed concerning their invisible and similar palm of death. Thus, at the end, after the deep and low strings of the harp, on which the first melody has now been formed in some manner, and after the middle strings of this our harp, on which the second melody will now be formed as the king, master harpist, teaches, the third melody would sound upon the higher and subtler harp strings. This, indeed, consequence and order would require—if anyone had learned so thoroughly the supercelestial music as to compose this melody on David’s harp according to the consonance and harmonious accord of the melody itself. But, unless I am mistaken, no one beneath the sun has done so.

For this melody concerns those secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak. Whether even an angel knows how to compose it, I do not know. For the melody is so sweet, so delightful, so subtle, that it surpasses all understanding. Nevertheless, if our true King David, the master harpist himself, should deign to instruct me even a little, as he will, when the time comes I shall attempt to move my hands, set my fingers in place, raise the pegs, twist the plectrum, and thus, with such powers as knowledge has given me, endeavour somehow to strike the harp so as to sound and compose this melody—at least like the man who, even if he does not sing sweetly to others, sings sweetly to himself. I shall attempt, I say, somehow to compose it, especially because, as we have already said, the logic of the order just described requires it.

But first, as our harp has now been tuned according to the order set out, we shall sound this second melody on the middle strings of the harp according to the measure [Col. 1302C] of our knowledge: singing before all else how great was the glory of the visible palm in the Emperor’s victorious death, and immediately likewise how great it was in the soldier, who, though not following his Emperor as an equal successor, nevertheless followed immediately in his footsteps and worshipped him.

## HERE BEGINS THE SECOND MELODY, WHOSE FIRST NOTE IS THIS.

First of all, the visible palm of the Emperor’s death was the death of death: “I will be thy death, O death” (Hosea 13). Likewise, the visible palm of the soldier’s death was the awakening, through the soldier’s triumphant death, of the devotion of a world now as it were dead and sluggish, and of faith as it were already dead. Even his enemies are judges in this matter.

**2. NOTE.**

[Col. 1302D]

The visible palm of the Emperor’s death is the salvation of the world. Likewise, that of the soldier is the salvation of the Church. On this matter, as I have already said, I cannot, for joy, refrain from repeating that even his enemies are judges.

**3. NOTE.**

The visible palm of the Emperor’s death is the resurrection of those dead in flesh and spirit. Likewise that of the soldier, for those dead both in flesh and in spirit. For he too, what is unheard of in our days, visibly raised bodily dead persons through the triumph of his death.

**4. NOTE.**

In his victorious blood, the visible palm of the Emperor’s death brought forth from the pit in which there was no water the bound, those bound by punishment in strength. Likewise [Col. 1303A] the soldier, in his victorious blood, brought forth those bound by guilt. But let us hear how this is so: the note of this melody must be sung more slowly.

For it was from a pit, not of water but of misery, and from the mire of dregs, that this victorious blood of the Emperor and the soldier brought forth the bound. For not since the discovery of Stephen the protomartyr have things so certain, so gloriously full of illustrious faith, so glorious and so miraculous, been done for the praise and glory of this our latest new martyr. All these things indeed serve to strengthen the Church’s faith, move sinners to repentance, and awaken the devotion of the faithful; so that, by the triumphant blood of the martyr, when the bonds of sins are broken, the bound may be brought forth in strength—likewise those who provoke him, who dwell in graves.

And truly many things have been done, and miraculously. Whoever desires to know them should read the book of signs published on these matters—the book of signs, I say, published concerning them, flourishing as it were with the flowers of recent miracles, distinguished by mighty works and prodigies.

Almighty God! What an abundance of gifts of healing, what workings of powers, are the signs of so victorious a death—indeed, an ocular demonstration of the martyr’s triumph. And these things have been written only in part. For if all that has happened throughout the world of the Churches were written down individually, according to the disciple’s testimony concerning the Master, I suppose that not even the world itself could contain the books that would be written.

## 5. CONCERNING THE REPENTANCE OF THE SACRILEGIOUS SOLDIERS.

Nevertheless, among the other visible virtues of this victorious death’s visible palm—great indeed and worthy of wonder—there is one that I consider more earnestly, contemplate more attentively, and embrace more devoutly. It is one, I say, exceptionally full of a pity marvellous, wondrous, and unheard of above the rest. Jubilantly, I ought not to be silent concerning it; and yet I am unable to express it adequately.

For, although this martyr in his victorious blood brought forth those bound by the devil, as we have already shown, there remains a thing full of a mercy exceeding all that can be said or conceived: the power of his shed blood reached and washed even those who shed it, the perpetrators of so unheard-of a sacrilege. The power of the blood washed them, I say—apparently washed them from blood, being washed by the very blood with which they had previously been so deeply stained.

And in this shed blood, the soldier’s shed blood was like [Col. 1303D] the Emperor’s shed blood. For, as some have handed down, the Emperor’s shed blood reached, washed, and cleansed from guilt the soldiers who crucified him. Concerning one of them, those who hand down this tradition give more certain testimony: the one who opened Christ’s side, from which blood and water immediately flowed. When his eyes had almost become dim, the blood flowing from the Emperor’s side chanced to touch his eyes, and he immediately saw clearly. They say that he was named Longinus.

But preferring what is certain to what is uncertain, in what we now set forth we see most certainly that the visible palm of the soldier’s death was assimilated to, though not equalled with, the visible palm of the Emperor’s death. For in his victorious death the Emperor stripped the principalities and powers, displaying them boldly and triumphing over them openly in himself. Likewise did the soldier in the victory of his death. For, to say nothing now of the faith and devotion of the world awakened through the martyr’s triumphant death, of which we have spoken above, he especially stripped the principalities and powers of darkness in his own murderers—powers which held them—displaying them boldly and dragging them from afar. He drew them from the region of unlikeness, to which they had already gone far away, to that solitude of repentance in which the penitent king desired to dwell, and where, fleeing the region of unlikeness, he remained far off: “Behold,” he says, “I fled far away and remained in the wilderness” (Psalm 54).

The soldier too, like the Emperor, triumphed openly over these powers in himself—in himself, because it was not in another but in his own blood. And this too was public, as with the Emperor: so public that, although these sacrilegious murderers had been great and noble in the world, lords of many possessions, and were in that age of life which is more vigorous and slippery than the rest, yet soon after committing the sacrilege they abandoned everything, went to Jerusalem, and performed public penance. Behold how, in these men, the principalities and powers of darkness were boldly displayed and openly triumphed over.

## 6. CONCERNING THEIR DEATH.

And, beyond doubt, this also happened miraculously. Although, as we said, they were energetic and worthy soldiers, trained and proven in the art of warfare, and in the more robust period of life, nevertheless all who departed this life within three years after committing [Col. 1304C] the sacrilege died, as is believed and as those who were present testify, in true and fruitful repentance. Because of horror at the deed and the enormity of the crime, which throughout their lives and at the moment of death they continually saw as it were hanging before their eyes and weighed upon them, they were always as though stunned, stupefied, torn apart, and convulsed in body and heart. They continually, especially at the moment of death, begged forgiveness and invoked the patronage of him whom they had so sacrilegiously wronged, above all among the advocates of sinners.

O how holy, how true, and how full of exceptional mercy is that teaching of the great and true Master: namely, that “all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to his purpose.” So greatly does even progress into worse things help them toward salvation, and even deviation itself in some way lead them to the way; the deeper they fall, the more vigorously they rise again through great exertion in virtues, stand more manfully, and afterwards ascend more highly. For such persons, under the wondrous ordering of the Most High, the very enormity of their guilt—which surpasses and exceeds that of other sinners all the more because it is more abominable—is turned into a greater increase of their crown.

We are now speaking of such persons, not of ordinary sinners: namely, of those who surpass other sinners by some enormity of crime and rise above the rest by the horror, as it were, of a singular sin. Such were these four sacrilegious soldiers, concerning whom the whole present discourse is concerned. Of such sinners, I say, not of ordinary ones, is our present speech, so that in such persons the power of the Almighty may be displayed more gloriously, embraced more devoutly, and preached more wonderfully.

For though God is wonderful in all his saints, he is certainly much more wonderful in sinners of this sort, insofar as it is more powerful and merciful to break the strong bonds of such sinners. While people who commit the daily and customary sins of humankind—sinners like other sinners, even though they perpetrate grave and great wrongs—nevertheless overlook them, pass over them, pay them no heed, do not return to themselves, do not awaken themselves, as committing deeds which other people commit also: they neither abhor others nor are abhorred by others. Rather, because they are sinners like sinners, they are all the more allied with sinners.

[Col. 1305B] But when perhaps, under the instigation of the enemy of the human race, such people surpass the other sinners whom they had formerly resembled by an excess that is new and unheard of, as though exceeding the broad, common, and customary rule of sinning, they become abominable even to sinners who had formerly been like themselves. Thus the profane novelty of an unheard-of sin, through the abhorrence and horror of the crime, brings terror and grief alike upon these new and profane sinners. Hence it often happens that they return to themselves, and through the horror and shame of their new crime set even their former life before their eyes. In the sins which they had committed before, when they resembled other sinners—sins which, as we said, they had formerly overlooked—they recognize that they have grievously offended.

Thus blood touches blood, according to the prophet; and God, the Lord rich in powers, works in such utterly sinful persons as powerfully as he does wonderfully, so that blood touches blood and, in a new manner, as though by a savage pity or pious savagery, blood wipes away blood. So, in his marvellous grace and great power, the Most High—who alone is wonderful because he alone performs wonders—casts out sin through sin, as though Satan’s kingdom were divided against itself, Satan driving out Satan. In this way, and in no other more especially, the power of darkness is defeated and mocked by the power of light: when that robber of the nations appears to have gained for himself all the spoil, then he loses it all.

But let no one surmise or mutter that, conversely, the power of light is sometimes similarly defeated and mocked by the power of darkness; let no one object that even the stronger soldiers among the Lord’s ranks, rooted and grounded in charity, are often, through the cunning power—or rather the powerful cunning—of the opposing power, as it were violently carried off captive from the army of the Lord of Hosts, and that thus the power of light, overcome in them, passes into the service of the opposing power. Let no one, I say, think or object this, as though the reverse analogy could hold. For it cannot hold: here there is an altogether different rationale, establishing a different judgment. But of this elsewhere.

Meanwhile, let us return, with harp strings and plectrum as it were bent back, to our sacrilegious men, concerning whom for some time now I know not how many notes of our melody have sounded upon our harp. The subject just touched upon—the conflict between the power of light and the power of darkness—demands another melody, perhaps sharper and longer than this one. Therefore, God willing—and may God will it—let us now return to these men reconciled to God, whose pilgrimage to Jerusalem, public penance, and swift death were as we have sung thus far.

Yet one of them, delaying day after day through the counsels of certain wicked persons, and not undertaking the journey to Jerusalem as soon as the others did, hoped to perform his penance in the regions on this side of the sea. When he had fallen gravely ill in the kingdom of the Sicilian king, near the celebrated city called Cosenza, even before his death the limbs of his body began at once to rot. The very flesh covering his sinews [Col. 1306B] and bones was, through decay, torn in pieces and convulsed by the sick man himself and thrown into the middle of the courtyard, leaving the sinews and bones exposed. Above all, the flesh of his arms and hands, scarcely clinging to the bones and sinews and seeming to desire separation, was easily, as it appeared, and without difficulty, thrown away by that accursed executioner, the soldier—yet would that he were truly penitent!—as it thus seemed to dissolve of itself. The flesh itself, as one might see, seemed to groan, to be indignant and ashamed that, after so great a crime perpetrated by the hand of a human being and through the service of his arms, it should thereafter remain in the composition of a human body.

Yet that wretched man, while living he thus tore, ripped, and mutilated himself and threw away his own flesh, unceasingly implored, with the greatest contrition, groans, and unutterable sighs, the pardon, aid, and patronage of the pious and glorious new martyr. This was William de Tracy, already named above in this history. Thus the Lord God of vengeance most justly avenged upon him the blood of his soldier crying out to him, especially because, as we said above in this little book, William had dared first to provoke the others and, before them, to brandish his sword against the head of Christ the Lord, unafraid to strike so profanely and impiously. Therefore, by the most just judgment of the Almighty, it happened that the hand which had wielded the sword—and the arm together with it—rotted, contrary to nature’s law, while he was still alive. The bishop of the city just mentioned, William’s confessor during this illness, reported this most certainly.

And to return to the other aforesaid accomplices in sacrilege, with whom we began: the deaths of all these men, wondrous because certainly miraculous, and of whatever others were of this kind, occurred within so short an interval—three years, as we have already said—that not one of them remained alive. As is believed, the mercy of the Most High perhaps intended what he willed; yet his justice struck them all down swiftly, as a terror and as a miraculous vengeance for his soldier. Thus these men of blood, although penitent as we have described, nevertheless, according to the word of the Lord, did not live out half their days.

Therefore, concerning them a twofold refrain must be sung in the middle of this melody upon the middle strings: [Col. 1307A] these men of blood were broken in their conversion and converted in their brokenness—broken in heart and broken in body.

O God, the Lord of vengeance! O Lord, no less the Father of mercies! Who knows how to number your wrath in awe of you? Or again, who can measure your mercy in proportion to your goodness? You so turn people back that you may break them, and so break them that you may turn them back, preserving for mercy and truth alike, as though with an equal balance, what belongs to each. And behold: through the wounds of your martyr you poured out the bowels of your compassion upon those who wounded him. And again, because of the wounds of your martyr, you crushed those same wounded men by the wrath of your indignation. This is the double refrain to be sung upon our lyre. These, indeed, are the two little notes now to be sounded together in the melody of this lyre.

[Col. 1307B] A grateful and assured melody concerning your mercy and your truth, O Lord: the deep strings of our lyre now alternate with the sweet ones in a mingled sound. The deep strings resound because of the truth of justice sung to you; the high and sweet strings because of the kindness of your mercy. Hence, in those turned in heart toward you, there is your holy compassion; but there, in those same persons broken in body by you, there is your just indignation: so that in this melody we may sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment.

We have already spoken of the powers of darkness and principalities, through the visible triumph over death of the soldier, as also through that of the triumphant Emperor; and our melody has for some time been prolonged here by fuller notes concerning him. [Col. 1307C] Yet let us still sing somewhat more expressly in this same melody, passing from the soldier’s visible triumph over death to the Emperor’s visible triumph over death.

### 7th Note

The visible triumph over death of the Emperor, assuredly, defeated aerial and earthly powers and overthrew laws and ordinances. Likewise the visible triumph over death of the soldier overcame aerial powers, as we have already shown, and earthly powers too, as we shall now show.

For behold: kings of the world and princes come from every region of the whole world of churches, either in person or, if they themselves cannot do so because they are occupied with the cares of their realms, through their envoys. They visit him wounded and buried; they venerate his wounds; they offer gifts; they implore aid; and [Col. 1307D] they hope for protection, firmly trusting that through the open wounds of the martyr the bowels of divine compassion are poured out upon them, the gate of salvation is opened, and the hand of almighty protection is not closed.

And, to pass over for the moment the body of the wounded man, the wounds of the slain man, and also the aforesaid hair-cloths which covered the whole body of the athlete-soldier: the world certainly knows and now sees that kings and queens of the world rejoice first in their silks and cloths of pure silk, in their foreign garments, their violet wrappings, and their patterned fabrics; likewise princes, and all courtiers arrayed in purple and clothed with gold, receive with the utmost devotion any small piece, perhaps, of the man’s girdle-cloths stained a little with his blood or even his sweat, or anything that may in whatever way have touched his body, if they can acquire it for themselves. [Col. 1308A] To obtain such things, altars are erected in gold, shrines are fashioned from precious stones; indeed, broad and spacious monasteries are founded, and many richly endowed and abundantly furnished churches are established throughout the whole world of churches.

For I have neither heard nor read—and I do not think that anyone has—that among the entire army of the Lord Sabaoth any combatant has, after his triumph in this world, attained throughout the whole world so great and so swift a glory. Let another teach us if he has heard or read otherwise concerning these matters. So swiftly—indeed, so exceedingly swiftly—was the glory of the new martyr made manifest to the world that, from the next-to-last island of the world in the western ocean, it was speedily proclaimed, by this fellow-citizen of the angels flying, as we have taught in the history, to the centre of our inhabited earth, or, as they say, to the navel of the whole world: thus at once flying upon the wings of the winds.

And truly, as his glory was great and swift: Thomas, only the day before yesterday, was a man like us, subject to suffering; and behold, today, by a wondrous change wrought by the right hand of God, the world venerates the wounds of the wounded man still sleeping in his tomb, and even glories in the fragments of girdle-cloth which in any way touched the body of the slain man.

Truly, Almighty God, moved by that unheard-of cruelty and the horror of the sacrilegious deed, and overcome by ineffable compassion for the soldier who endured so bravely and so humbly, both crushed those men so suddenly and exalted this man so swiftly. Nor could the merciful and just Lord any longer either conceal or restrain his wrath, nor his mercies within that wrath. [Col. 1308C] For in that cruelty toward a human being, exceeding all cruelty toward human beings, swift vengeance was hastened; and, conversely, in that unheard-of patience in a human being, swift glory of triumph was hastened.

O good Emperor Jesus, how wonderful you are in the army of your saints who fight for you; yet more wonderful still in your own sufferings and those of your people, which you endured in this military contest—unless it is because you endured the whole in yourself and in your people, and still endure it daily, for this one purpose: to sanctify your saints. You sanctify them so greatly that your saints are sanctified not only through your sufferings and those of your people—which are likewise yours—but even the punishment itself is holy: death itself, which kills the saint, is holy and precious.

Holy and precious indeed is death itself, though it is also the penalty of sin and sin’s wages. [Col. 1308D] “For the wages of sin is death” (Rom. 6), says the Master. But when the Emperor works wondrously and powerfully in his fellow-soldiers, this wage of sin becomes the weapons of his soldiers—“not carnal, but mighty through God.” What was imposed upon the human race as a punishment because of sin becomes for them the merit of triumph. The punishment for guilt becomes for them the gate of righteousness. And this indeed is the gate of the Lord.

“For with the Lord are the issues of death,” and the righteous enter through the same gate, since it is the gate of righteousness through which the righteous enter into glory. “Open to me the gates of righteousness,” he says, “and, entering through them, I will give thanks to the Lord” (Ps. 117 [118]). And he adds: “This,” he says, “is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (ibid.).

But you, most merciful Emperor—in whose majesty such mercy is all the more praiseworthy because it is joined to such power—what shall I say concerning punishment, concerning the death either of your people or of yourself, made holy and sanctifying through you? For you, together with your people, sanctify even places, times, and the very instruments of evils, to the glory of your own. [Col. 1309A] And, to add yet more: whatever has touched a saint, or has been about a saint—whether a garment or anything else—is regarded as sanctified.

The healing of the woman recalled here proves this by her touch of the Lord’s hem. For the touch of the Emperor’s hem healed a sick woman even before his departure from the world. Likewise, after the soldier’s departure from the world, many sick men and women were healed by touching pieces of his girdle-cloths. And what above all else both produces joy and works a miracle with delight: even the passing shadow of the passing saintly body sanctifies. The truth of this saying is visibly demonstrated, eye to eye, by Peter’s passing shadow overshadowing the sick.

But more concerning such sanctifying things and the causes of sanctification elsewhere. Let us return to the earthly powers visibly overcome through the soldier’s visible triumph over death, desiring to complete the note of this melody which we began concerning them—namely, by showing more fully, expressly, and by name in certain earthly powers the very thing we began to show.

For among the other powers of the world there are two great and illustrious powers, that is, two great and renowned kings, who are here to be named expressly.

### CONCERNING THE MOST CHRISTIAN KING OF THE FRANKS JOURNEYING ABROAD TO THE MARTYR

[Col. 1309C]

First among the rest, and more devout than the rest, was Louis, that most Christian king of the Franks, of blessed memory, often and repeatedly named, as is fitting, in this history. By the frequent insertion of the name of one so holy, illustrious, and beloved by both God and the world, I judge the whole history to be more sacred; and I do not doubt that it will be more brightly adorned and more pleasing even in ages to come.

As we sufficiently showed above in the historical booklet—though we cannot sufficiently display the mercy and immortal glory of so great a king—this king, unique among kings, when the world had not cast us out, already wandering, exiled, fugitive, and as though having no place in the world, [Col. 1309D] alone, moved by royal mercy, received us with imperial magnificence and generosity.

Then, after the martyr’s departure from the world, when the world soon proclaimed the martyr’s victory because of the signs of powers and wonders that occurred, that devout king was moved by it. At once—an unheard-of thing, that kings of the Franks should cross seas except perhaps to fight foreign nations or enemies of the faith—this most powerful king, drawn and overcome solely by the love of piety, left his realm, entrusted himself to winds and waves, and entered the island situated in the heart of the sea. He did this for one reason only: that he might venerate, wounded and still sleeping in his tomb, the man whom he had received and entertained as an exile. And, venerating him, he offered gifts befitting so great a king: namely wine and gold—an golden chalice, that is, and one hundred measures of wine each year in perpetuity, to celebrate the martyr’s feast-day with rejoicing. Thus that devout king, whether in his life or in his death, paid the blessed martyr, as it were, an annual tribute for himself and for his kingdom.

[Col. 1310A] Such an offering indeed befitted such a king: wine, I mean, together with a golden chalice. And truly, unless I am mistaken, this offering was mystical, even if the king himself who offered it perhaps did not know the mystery. Truly, it was a mystery to offer wine and gold to him who, for the truth of righteousness, received the cup of salvation. And the birthday in the flesh of the Emperor is here matched by the spiritual birthday of the soldier-martyr.

### 8th Note

[Col. 1310B] For when the Emperor was newly born in the flesh, gold, incense, and myrrh were offered in mystery by kings. Likewise, when the soldier was now truly born in the spirit, mystical gifts were offered by royal power.

### 9th–14th Notes

Gifts are offered to the Emperor to declare the birthday of his flesh; and likewise to the soldier to illuminate the birthday of his spirit.

O great works of the Lord! O works exquisitely wrought beyond searching in all his wills! Who would have believed what we now behold: so great a king leaving his kingdom, crossing seas, venerating the wounds of the slain son of parents I know not how humble, offering gifts, and so humbly and devoutly seeking protection for himself and his kingdom? Truly, “there is none like you among the gods, O Lord; there is none according to your works,” you who alone are wonderful, who alone do wonders. [Col. 1310C] Hence you rightly claim in the prophet the name “Wonderful” as especially your own: “And his name shall be called Wonderful” (Isa. 9). You humble the lofty tree and exalt the lowly tree; you dry up the green tree and make the dry tree flourish. You, O Lord, have spoken and do so.

### CONCERNING THE ILLUSTRIOUS KING OF THE ENGLISH, TRIUMPHED OVER THROUGH THE MARTYR

But what now? Shall not the next note of our melody sound upon our lyre concerning another renowned and immense power of the world, overcome in the victorious blood of the martyr? For that former power of the world, of which we sang in the immediately preceding note of the melody, is proclaimed not so much conquered as voluntarily humbled. But this power, of which the note of this melody will now sound, has plainly been conquered through the soldier’s visible triumph over death: for the glory of the almighty Emperor and the renown of his fellow-soldier the martyr, and, by God’s favour, for the unfading crown of that power itself now conquered.

That power, so renowned in the world, must not remain longer obscured by my silence: it is a power so great and so mighty, publicly overcome as fruitfully as gloriously. It is Henry, illustrious king of the English, grandson of that great Henry who was formerly king of the English. [Col. 1311A] Both the present age and all ages to come would perpetually celebrate him, proclaiming him in the British world a king as it were unique and singular, incomparable with all who preceded him—had he not, by some judgment of God, with most evil anger as counsellor and wicked men as instigators, been judged to have cast a stain upon this great glory of his through that profane deed committed against the martyr.

For this Henry—the foundation of his people, the stability of the nation, the support of the weak, protector of the poor, staff against the proud, hammer of tyrants, king of peace, and pillar of justice—was made by the Most High to increase like the dust of the earth, to exalt his seed as the stars, and to make them inherit from sea to sea. As the world knows and still attests, this singular soldier and martyr of the exalted Emperor, while he still served in the flesh in the flowering years of his youth, had acquired such favour in the king’s intimate affection, as we have sufficiently shown above in the historical booklet, [Col. 1311B] that in the courtly office of chancellor he seemed to reign jointly with the Augustus as a co-Augustus. Thus between the two there was, as it were, one kingdom, because there was one heart and one soul.

But, to pass briefly over matters now which have been set forth more fully in the history: with many courtiers and others, and especially men of our order—that is, clerics and bishops—thus egging him on at the instigation of the enemy of this mutual love and peace, of all peace and love, that bond of unity which had seemed indissoluble was broken. The king, so loving and so beloved, was inflamed against one so dear and beloved to him, as though a furnace had been heated by those who bake, so that, badly advised by wicked men, he could not contain within himself the heat of his spirit. Rather, publicly before the aforesaid soldiers, his executioners, and other courtiers, in the violent onset of his anger, he thundered such hard and harsh words against one so beloved and dear to him that the soldiers who heard them, shaken by what they heard, removed him by death and killed him, believing that by this they had performed an acceptable service for the king.

When the news reached the king, however, as those who were present attest, no heart can conceive, no tongue utter, no mouth express how immediately he was stupefied and stunned at the horror of the deed—how disturbed, how shaken and convulsed in all his inmost entrails, [Col. 1311C] as though tearing and rending himself apart. He was so stupefied and stunned that those who saw him more privately and intimately feared greatly lest he turn to madness or be otherwise swallowed up by grief.

Among others who then stood more intimately by the king, Henry, the venerable bishop of Bayeux, a man distinguished by every sanctity, reported this to me who wrote these things:

### THAT THE DISCIPLE WHO WROTE THESE THINGS OMITS NOTHING THROUGHOUT THE HISTORY EITHER FROM FEAR OR FROM FAVOUR

And, that I may say this once here by way of insertion, and may have said it once for all—especially since I now speak of the king of my own people—God and his martyr, whom I desire to serve with this pen, are my witnesses: in the entire history of the martyr, written as it was granted from above, there is nothing which, as is the custom of very many, I have timidly abbreviated, suppressed through fear, softened through favour, or smoothed with flattery.

For it is shameful, dangerous, and exceedingly dishonourable, especially for a disciple of a martyr-master, either to suppress the proclamations of truth owed to the martyr or to sew together for his enemies elaborate blandishments of flattery with which to cover their cruelty. It is shameful, I say, and dishonourable for a disciple of the martyr to sew together such things, especially in the history woven concerning him, where, once all fear, deceitful flattery, and empty favour have been banished, only the testimonies of truth should be contained—just as he himself is a martyr for truth.

But let us return to our king. Certainly, neither through favour—although he is my king and lord—nor through a fabricated testimony on behalf of my lord and master the martyr, do I knowingly and deliberately, throughout this history of the martyr, utter a falsehood against my conscience or conceal the truth through fear. [Col. 1312A] To do so would be to place the lamp beneath a bushel; and indeed, when I began to undertake the history of the martyr, I did not propose to set this lamp of truth beneath a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it might give light to all who are in the house of the Church.

Yet we must return again to our king, whose immortal reputation indeed requires that these matters should be written by the martyr’s disciple. Otherwise perhaps in later ages he might be judged to have directly commanded the death and not to have done penance for it. For in the human race the poisoned tongues of detractors quickly pour out much venom from any seedbed of evil through the whole body and infect it all.

But the king, as what follows will show, humbly repented concerning that in which he accused himself of having transgressed, and did so with a devotion beyond all belief. He did not repent, as the king himself deigned to confess to me, the martyr’s disciple who wrote these things, because he had directly ordered the martyr’s death—far be that from so great a power in the world and one so renowned—but because, although not through him, this death had nevertheless occurred for him and in his favour.

For I, the disciple who wrote these things, once having found a fitting opportunity of place and time, drew courage from zeal for justice and ventured to charge the lord king privately, between ourselves alone, that the death of my lord had been for him and through him. [Col. 1312B] He, without being seen to be disturbed in any respect, replied with complete calm, and, to use his own words: “‘For you,’” he said, “‘I sorrowfully concede; but ‘through you’ I boldly deny.” Thus spoke the king to me. God alone and he himself know.

If he transgressed only in this way—and may God will that it be no more!—it was still too much, alas, and grievous that it should have been so. Yet the king who deigned to speak with me on this matter added that this death had in some sense also been through him, because in his anger he had spoken such harsh and dreadful words before his courtiers and soldiers of his chamber as gave those men occasion for swift death. So great a power thus accused himself before my smallness; he did not excuse himself.

But let us for now leave this matter, praying first with all the deepest affections of our heart that, if perhaps he ordered this to be done—as is far from such a king and not credible—God may forgive him. But if without an order he somehow gave occasion for it, may God inspire him to a fruitful repentance. We shall henceforth pursue the performance of that repentance, concerning which we have already begun to speak, according to our promise above.

[Col. 1313A] And as we touched upon above, as soon as the report of so deadly a deed reached the king, he was afflicted with great affliction. In that most renowned town of Normandy called Argentan, where he first received the news, he sat mourning for forty days. Throughout that entire penitential number of days he made a lament far more bitter than the mourning for the dead. He ate the food of mourners; he did not mount a horse; no case of litigants, no deliberation concerning affairs to be conducted, no complaint of petitioners was admitted to him; no concern was laid before him for governing so many lands. In his grief he set all things aside.

For he sat alone, always groaning and grieving over what had happened, often and again repeating: “Alas, alas, that it happened thus!”

### CONCERNING THE ANGER OF KINGS

O how pestilential an evil is the anger of kings—hostile both to kings themselves and to the entire people—when it does not restrain itself but immediately bursts out into rage! Even if the king himself, having returned to himself, wishes to check its violent onset once aroused, it nevertheless often flies, as it were swiftly, through the far-reaching hands of kings, and is irrevocable even when the king has already repented and wishes it recalled.

For many people—and almost all in the world, whether lawfully or unlawfully—seek the favour and fear the displeasure of kings, who are as it were a kind of earthly gods. Indeed, among these are many who, even when not commanded, immediately hasten to obey when they infer the king’s pleasure from even a slight sign of suspicion, whether it concerns good or evil; and each tries to anticipate another in obedience. At times, though not commanded, they commit more atrocious deeds as though commanded, believing that in these matters they will render a pleasing service.

A very close example is at hand: such were our sacrilegious murderers, who, interpreting the king’s angry words so rashly, hastily, presumptuously, and perversely, brought upon the name of so great and world-renowned a power a stain, so ruinous a scandal, and so great a cause for sorrow.

### HE RETURNS TO THE ANGER OF KINGS

[Col. 1313D]

O how necessary it is to beware, and to act cautiously—above all for kings—that especially when they are angry, for it is not possible that they should never be angry, and they are angered more often because they are placed higher, they should then, I say, hold themselves in check and restrain themselves. Being heads of nations and rulers of peoples, they must especially govern themselves, lest one who is lord of all become a slave of anger and yet reign over all.

For this is, according to the Wise Man, one of the three things by which the earth is shaken; and he places it first as, so to speak, the worst among the three: “By three things the earth is moved: by a slave when he becomes king, by a fool when he is filled with food, and by a hateful woman when she is taken in marriage” (Prov. [Col. 1314A] 30). “By a slave,” he says, “when he becomes king”—this is one among the three, and he puts it first; and first because, as we have said, it is the worst, as though holding before all others the primacy of oppression among nations: “By a slave,” he says, “when he becomes king.”

Certainly, by a slave; but by “slave” I mean here one enslaved not so much to the soil as to anger. For there is no concern to be had about that earthly or native servitude to the soil, whether one rules or serves. “Were you called as a slave?” says the Master. “Do not be concerned about it” (1 Cor. 7).

Therefore kings above all must take the greatest care that, especially when they are angry—for it is not in kings’ power not to become angry—then, I say, especially when they are angry, they should so be angry that they do not sin. Hence one of the kings says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4); as though to say: although even kings cannot avoid anger, yet they are permitted to be angry only in such a way that sin does not follow upon anger—that is, so that the heat, generated and born from the penalty of death, does not go outward in flame and does not burst forth in fury.

[Col. 1314B] Rather, as soon as the flame of his indignation has gone forth, let a king reckon that his whole kingdom has been set ablaze. This is what we have already touched upon, and it is not superfluous to repeat it here: the teaching of the gentle king, so often and repeatedly experienced in the force of anger: “Be angry,” he says, “and do not sin.” It is as though he says: do not become slaves of anger, and thus also slaves of sin, by sinning after anger. For if a king sins after anger, he will reign as a slave of anger and sin. Through such a king who is a slave the earth is shaken, as the Wise Man teaches; and we daily see and suffer this.

And truly it is written, as daily experience itself teaches, that “according to the timber of the forest, so does the fire blaze; and according to the strength of a man, so will his anger be; and according to his wealth, he will exalt his anger.”

O how many evils came through the anger of our king, while the poisoned tongues of the envious gave their stings, as is plain throughout the whole history, both upon the kingdom and upon the priesthood! For thus, as it is most truly written, “the anger of man does not work the righteousness of God” (Jas. 1). But may the merciful and compassionate Lord turn away his wrath from the anger of this king his servant, and forgive every excess of his anger.

### CONCERNING ENVOYS SENT BY THE KING TO THE ROMAN CHURCH AFTER THE MARTYRDOM

[Col. 1314D]

This, indeed, was the provision for salvation made by the repentant king. The king, sitting alone and mourning during the entire forty days as we have shown, immediately upon first hearing of the sacrilege sent eminent and able men to Alexander III, Roman pontiff, seeking counsel from him, as from the supreme protector of the Church and father of all, as to what should be done; and, as is credible, humbly confessing wherein he had transgressed.

But because confession is not customarily, nor ought to be, made through writing or through representatives, and because the living voice of the confessor has the more power in proportion as it increases devotion, the apostolic man sent from his side two cardinals: Master Theodinus, cardinal bishop of Porto, of pious memory, and Albert, still surviving, chancellor of the holy Roman Church—men certainly endowed with every holiness of religious life [Col. 1315A] and learning. They were to absolve canonically the bishops of the realm, who had been excommunicated or suspended for the reasons previously set out in this history, and to provide for the salvation of the king who made petition.

Thus they were sent for the consolation of the king and of the whole Church. At their coming the bishops obtained absolution, which they had not deserved, through the mercy of the apostolic man and of those sent by him. The king, confessing devoutly and humbly before the Church that he had transgressed in the matter of the martyr’s death, was corrected; and he swore that thereafter, within three years, he would take the cross and set out for Jerusalem, unless he were prevented by the lord pope or his Catholic successors.

Indeed, the king’s repentance was then so devout and humble that the cardinals who saw it bore witness, with marginal notes, to the truth of that verse in the psalmist: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble; he touches the mountains and they smoke” (Ps. 103 [104]).

### CONCERNING THE FIRST DISSENSION WHICH AROSE BETWEEN THE FATHER-KING AND THE SON-KING

But after a short time had elapsed—about the fourth or, I think, the fifth year after the martyrdom and this repentance of the king—a profane rebellion and exceedingly civil war arose between the father-king and his son the king. As we have shown above in the history, the son had been anointed king by the bishops of the realm, at his father’s wish, to the injury of his metropolitan, then in exile. So great was the revolt that almost all the father-king’s own subjects and even foreigners—the king of the Franks, joining in alliance with the son-king in his great power—rose against him. The king’s lands, kingdoms, nations, and peoples, both his own, as we have said, and those of others, took up arms against the father-king alone.

### CONCERNING THE KING’S FIRST PILGRIMAGE TO THE MARTYR AND THE CAUSE OF THE PILGRIMAGE

[Col. 1315C]

What then was the father-king to do? Whither was he to turn? To whom was he to go? Nowhere was faith secure—indeed, there was none, for it had perished. “Without were fightings, within were fears.” Therefore, when human help failed, the only course remaining was that the king should turn solely to divine counsel and aid.

For, hearing daily and firmly believing, while the world now attested and proclaimed with wonder, of the mighty works, signs, and wonders occurring at Canterbury through the martyr, and, as I hope, not forgetful of the former mutual favour between himself and the martyr, he was all the more confident because he rejoiced and hoped that he had done penance for his transgression against the martyr. He departed from Normandy, where at that time almost the entire heat of the raging rebellion was concentrated. He left Normandy, I say, leaving it, like his other transmarine dominions and lordships, as it were wholly in the hand of God alone who protects, and of his martyr. Immediately, armed against his enemies only with the hope of divine protection, he crossed the sea and, setting aside every pretext and delay, came to Canterbury.

### HOW THE KING ENTERED CANTERBURY AS A PILGRIM

[Col. 1316A]

With unbelievable humility and devotion, as soon as he saw the city and the metropolitan church where the martyr rests, he emptied himself. So great a power immediately assumed the form of the poorest servant, barefoot and with his whole body stripped, except that he wore a single coarse tunic over his nakedness. Thus barefoot and naked, publicly by day and in the sight of all, he entered the city. Through the muddy lanes and streets of the city he walked humbly, like one of the meanest common people.

Behold another David: just as the first David left the city barefoot when pursued by his greatly beloved son, another Absalom, because of his sin, so this second David entered it. And thus, with sighs and groans—he at whose presence so many peoples and nations trembled, himself now fearful and trembling—he approached the martyr’s tomb.

[Col. 1316B] There he spent the whole day of his arrival and the following night fasting and wakeful before the martyr. I think—and indeed do not doubt—that as he poured out groaning and devout prayers before the martyr, whom he had loved so greatly and by whom he had been so greatly loved, he commended himself, with all the affection of his heart in such dire need, to the martyr’s merits, prayers, and protection. The outcome of events will soon demonstrate this.

There also, before the martyr’s tomb, as though before the martyr himself, with that holy and venerable gathering of brethren assembled, he received from each of the brethren one stroke of the disciplinary rod: a kind of new and, I think, hitherto unheard-of second apostolic forty—indeed, a royal forty.

### THAT THE KING RENOUNCED THOSE EVIL CUSTOMS WHICH HAD CAUSED THE EXILE AND MARTYRDOM

[Col. 1316C]

Those customs set down in writing which had been the whole matter of dissension between the martyr and himself, and later the cause of the confessor’s exile and finally of the martyr’s death, the king, now truly repentant and justified, renounced as evil and unjust. Thus, in devotion to the martyr, through the power of the martyrdom he blotted out the bond of the decree which stood against us—that is, against the clergy. Enough has been said concerning this above in the history.

He decreed that only the good customs were henceforth to be observed. Yet some of those customs thus renounced and condemned by the Church are still observed throughout the kingdom. If the king sees this with knowledge and approval, may God forbid it. Such was the king’s first pilgrimage to the martyr and his humiliation before him.

Therefore to you, O Lord, I now turn my face; to you I lift my eyes, that my lips may pour forth a hymn. For I am now so full that I can no longer contain myself from proclaiming your praises and recounting your wonders. For behold: in this you have done even more with Paul than with Saul. He was greater than Saul inasmuch as so great a king possessed more power both to do good and to do evil. And behold how, as though forgetting the whole height of his royal majesty, he humbled himself.

[Col. 1317A] And what is more—indeed, what with delight makes this mighty work a miracle, what illuminates and gladdens this profound judgment of God—the great king turns and returns thus to the man before whom he humbles himself, though, as we described above in the history, he had so humbled that man in the world that neither he nor his people had, as it were, any place among humankind in the world. Yet by a truly wondrous reversal wrought by the right hand of God, the king, so powerful, now laying aside every royal insignia, barefoot, with bare soles, wholly stripped except for a single coarse tunic over his nakedness, comes in abasement to venerate the man whom a little earlier he had stripped and proscribed with his companions, and, so far as he could, condemned to perpetual exile.

He now devoutly seeks the aid of the one whose merits he humbly invokes and whose protection he earnestly requests—the one for whom prayer to God had a little earlier been forbidden in the Church. The king also, now moving like an infant upon hands and feet, repeatedly kisses some little stone placed upon Thomas’s tomb, though a little earlier he had utterly denied him, mouth to mouth, a kiss.

How marvellous is so great a change of affairs in our own age! Truly, Lord, how marvellous—terrible and profound, yet no less joyful—are your judgments! You are indeed almighty over all your works. However greatly a man may be able and strive, yet you will prevail. And whatever the deceitful and vain thought of man, making its plans, may falsely promise itself, your wondrous magnificence, Lord, turns it all to the contrary, so that your eternal will may be done. What we have seen, what we have heard, what we had not hoped for, this we now attest and write. Thanks be to you, Almighty One, because, with my father and lord and my brethren, fellow-bearers of the same burden, now removed from human affairs and resting in Christ, I, almost the sole survivor, have deserved not only to see the end of our exile and the glory of martyrdom, but also to transmit it in writing to ages yet to come. Therefore I shall praise the Lord in my life; I shall sing praise to my God while I exist. Therefore I shall devoutly repeat these deeds of the Lord, which I recall with joy. O Lord, how great you are, how glorious in power, and whom no one can overcome! Rather, as the triumphant woman proclaims, through you mountains shall be moved from their foundations along with the waters, and rocks shall melt like wax before your face. For those who fear you shall be great before you in all things.

And behold: as it was proclaimed then, so we now see it fulfilled, that our proclamation may be joined to that proclamation. Behold the king’s heart, of which it is truly written that it is in the hand of God. Behold, I say, the heart of the king, so stubbornly hardened, embittered, and exalted a little before: how it has now been softened, sweetened, and humbled. Truly, a mountain moved from its foundation—and this amid the waters of many peoples flowing round and streaming toward the martyr’s tomb throughout the day. This mountain of ours also, this king of ours, is more moveable than others. Whenever he returns from overseas into the kingdom, immediately, before turning elsewhere, before other affairs of the realm, he visits the burial-place of his martyr—now his friend and lord—with his own waters likewise stirred.

For many peoples and nations whom he rules, and especially his own courtiers above the other nations of the world, visit more frequently the tomb of the martyr as their particular father and patron—whether more devoutly, I do not know; God knows, but this I know. Therefore, blessing, let us praise the Lord for this pilgrimage of our king, for so devout a conversion, so welcome a return, and so gloriously abject a humiliation. Let us praise him, I say, blessing him because the heart of the son has been turned toward the father and the heart of the father toward the son; because the beloved has returned to the beloved; because the exalted man has been humbled before the Most High. Therefore let us sound again and again to the Lord, in the melody of this our lyre, a hymn; let us sound a new hymn to our God. A new hymn, I say, for this first pilgrimage of our king, for a new conversion, for so joyful a return, so unexpected a humiliation, and so new, so glorious, and so complete a triumph through martyrdom.

Its glory is common both to him who has been vanquished and to him who triumphs; but which of them has the greater glory, I do not know. One thing I know: it is more fruitful for the one vanquished. For the triumphant martyr, I see that it is glory alone; but for the vanquished king, I see indeed that it is glory, and one may hope that it is also unto a crown: that he may pass from crown to crown, from the corruptible crown of an earthly kingdom to the unfading crown of the heavenly kingdom—provided only that he perseveres in what he has begun. To sing a new hymn, indeed, concerning this new glory both of the vanquished and of the triumphant is good and joyful. It is so good and joyful because this triumph is so ample and complete, because it is shared alike by both—the triumphant martyr and the vanquished king—and because it brings glory to the triumphant martyr and, for the vanquished king, both glory and favour before the Lord and men. Even over his own enemies, because he has been vanquished, he will immediately be triumphant, as will soon be shown when this pilgrimage is ended.

## Here he repeats that, in pursuing this history, he will maintain truth, setting aside every favour of flattery and every fear.

Let no one suppose or suspect that, under some veil of flattery, for the favour or advantage of my king—because he is king of my people, as we have said above and do not shrink from repeating here—or in elaborate praise of the martyr, because he is and was my father and lord, I sometimes loosen the reins of my tongue beyond the bounds of truth. For many still survive who themselves can testify to so great a glory of the triumphant one, to so great a glory and favour of power vanquished in this way—as we have described—through its humiliation: they saw it, since they were present at it.

For throughout the entire history of the martyr, God knows—as I have already once testified and now testify again—I neither mutilate the body of truth through fear of any man, nor exaggerate against truth for the favour of a man, nor pervert it with truth-deceiving flattery in order to please a man, nor insert or omit anything for the breath of popular applause. But let us return once more to our glorious power—now certainly more glorious, indeed almost now glorious for the first time, because it has been so gloriously vanquished—that the begun course of so glorious and devout a pilgrimage may be completed. In this melody of ours, its little note is no longer a mere note but rather a sustained strain, sounding more sweetly and at greater length: let us festively and solemnly sing the Alleluia of return, celebrating the common glory of this famous victory, of both victor and vanquished; the return, I say, of the new pilgrim to the new fellow-citizen of angels, of son to father and father to son, and of beloved to beloved. Yet let us linger a little longer over this great and distinguished pilgrim of ours; and then we must not pass over in silence what happened soon afterward through the humility and devotion of this pilgrimage.

## How the King, Returning from His Pilgrimage, Left Canterbury

Accordingly, when all had been completed in such humility and devotion as we have described, the king—now truly a king and so devout a pilgrim—on the following day, after Mass of the martyr had been celebrated before the martyr’s tomb, departed with feet still stained as when he had humbly come before the martyr, without even having refreshed himself, in great hope of the martyr’s patronage soon to be granted him.

## Concerning the Enemies Whom the King Soon Vanquished through the Martyr after His Pilgrimage

And what is remarkable to tell, and must not be passed over in silence for the commendation of the martyr’s glory and the king’s penitential devotion: hope did not put the king to shame. For on that very day—as the world knows, and as the king himself deigned to confess to me, the disciple who wrote these things—on that day, I say, on which he had heard Mass of the martyr before the martyr’s tomb in deep humility and devotion, and after affectionately greeting the martyr had departed, as though graciously dismissed by the martyr—it was Saturday—on that same day, I say, at the same hour of the day at which he had attended Mass, unceasingly invoking the martyr’s patronage, the prince of the Scots was captured.

This was indeed a great prince, then the greatest, or among the greatest, of the king’s many great enemies. He was intercepted by certain soldiers—a few men of middling rank—who were then among the few still loyal to the king; and, as if no sword had been drawn or wound inflicted, he was captured without battle and without blow. As I learned, having somehow wandered a little apart from the great army which he had gathered, he was thus delivered up by some chance occurrence, though I know not what, through the will of the Most High, in whose power all things are placed.

But why recount each detail? After the king’s most humble and devout pilgrimage described above, little by little and before long, his faithful men both on this side of the sea and beyond it—yet unfaithful precisely in being rebels—fell, sinners themselves, into the net which they had spread for their lord, their king. Truly sinners, since they did not keep faith with their lord and king. But when the others saw the Lord’s hand so suddenly and powerfully with the king, all were silent; and thus, beyond the world’s expectation and hope, as unexpectedly and suddenly as it had come about, “the whole earth was silent before him” (Mal. XI, 52). And his kingdom came to be in peace, the Lord extending his hand thus against the wrath of his enemies.

And so, as we briefly touched upon above concerning the day, when the king prayed and was heard against his enemies, it was truly Sabbath: a Sabbath of time, foreshadowing for the king the near approach of tranquillity and peace, so that from the Sabbath he might hope for Sabbath—from the Sabbath of time, the Sabbath of rest. As the Lord promises Israel through the prophet: “Month after month, Sabbath after Sabbath, it shall be” (Isa. LXVI). Thus a sabbatical rest remains for the king so humbled. The king attributed this success over his enemies and this peace, so great and so complete—and all the more miraculous because so swift, when every mind had been so firmly set against him—entirely to the Lord and to his glorious holy martyr, to whom it most certainly ought to be attributed.

## Concerning a Dream Prophetically Shown to the Martyr While Still in Exile, as a Prophecy, as It Were, of This Rebellion and Peace

That which befell the martyr, still an exile, concerning this rebellion of which we have spoken and the peace that followed the rebellion so swiftly, is most plainly proved by a certain prophetic dream, truly prophetic. My lord himself, while then in exile, recounted the dream to me, the disciple who wrote these things, in his own words as follows:

> “I was looking in the vision of the night” (Dan. VII). “And behold, I was shut up upon a very high mountain, while the lord king was below in the lowest place. And behold, suddenly all the birds of heaven gathered against the king, attacking him swiftly and suddenly with their claws and beaks and with the force of their wings, like a violent whirlwind.
