There were birds of every kind there, especially those which live by plunder: eagles, griffins, sea-eagles, vultures; kites, hawks, gulls, herons. But why go through them one by one? Every kind of bird, each according to its kind, seemed to me to be there attacking the king.
>
> “His garments being swiftly torn into little pieces by the claws and beaks of the birds, the king was soon scarcely covered by the thin appearance of a shirt alone, and was, as it were, already naked and exposed to the birds. And no longer able to endure the onslaught—like a violent whirlwind—of so many flying and attacking with beaks and claws, he was driven this way and that. And he gradually withdrew and drew back as far as he could, so as to lessen, if not wholly avoid, the force of the attack.
>
> “Behind the king, who did not look back—for so hemmed in, he could not look back—was a most hideous and very deep precipice, unforeseen by the king because it was behind him. When the king, withdrawing in this way and avoiding as far as he could the violence of his attackers, had approached it, one of the king’s most intimate courtiers, in whom the king trusted as in another self, since the king had distinguished him among the foremost of the realm with honours and wealth—this man, I say, more grim than grim, though more than inhuman—joined the birds in helping them. He violently attempted to strip from the king the shirt by which alone he was scarcely clothed over his nakedness, and along with the birds’ assault he himself began to drive the king over the precipice.
>
> “But as the king was about to fall, the depths of my most tender compassion were stirred for him, as I sat upon the lofty mountain and beheld these things. Remembering the former mutual favour and friendship between the king and me, although he had now offended me, I could not restrain my pity even in this offence. Rather, as it seemed to me, I descended with such speed from the summit of the very high mountain on which I sat, as in the twinkling of an eye; for the danger now so imminent, and great compassion, as though giving me wings and urging me to swift assistance, impelled me. Thus I stood beside the king, as it were in a moment. And at once a long and very sharp sword, placed there I know not by what chance, flashed in my hand. With it I seemed suddenly and instantaneously to scatter and disperse all those birds of heaven; and I immediately clothed the freed king gloriously and fittingly in his royal insignia, severely rebuking that courtier who, as we have said, had joined the birds in helping them, and adding that the king had not deserved this from him.”

My lord, as we have said, while in exile related this dream to me, who have now written it, in his own living voice, and also disclosed the courtier’s name. This courtier might furnish a proverbial saying when anyone, having accomplices, acts wickedly against loyalty to his lord: it might proverbially be said of him, “This man too joined the birds in helping them.” Nevertheless, though I omit none of the other matters belonging to this vision, I refrain from naming this courtier in this history, lest the name of one who is no longer alive, having entered upon the decreed way of all flesh, become more hateful to present and future ages; and also lest his descendants, who did not deserve it, be branded with any stain even of suspected treason and confounded by the reproach of their father’s crime.

Indeed, when he had recounted the dream, my lord, still speaking briefly to me and almost interpreting the dream, added that he would yet assist the king in some strait. By this very brief interpretation he indicated that the dream was truly prophetic. And when I, who now write, had later recounted this vision, once occasion and time permitted, to the lord king after the rebellion had ended, as we have said, and such peace had been granted from above, the king himself immediately interpreted it as concerning that rebellion and the most happy, glorious, peaceful, and truly miraculous outcome of that rebellion, by which the truth of this vision was most plainly to be fulfilled.

On the occasion of this related vision, the king, who deigned to speak to me concerning this, added what I have not passed over above:

> “And on the same day,” he said, “namely Saturday, at the same hour of the day at which, while devoutly hearing Mass before the martyr, I invoked the martyr’s patronage, the prince of the Scots—one of my greatest enemies, indeed among the greatest—was captured by certain soldiers of mine, few in number and men of fairly middling station; so precisely were marked both the day and the hour of his capture.”

Thus the king himself first instructed me and proclaimed to me the miracle by the day and the hour of the event. I have inserted it into this little book of melodies all the more devoutly because it is so certain. And I have done so all the more joyfully because in this episode of the history I had Augustus himself as master and as the most certain narrator of the event, and as witness and proclaimer of the miracle. For by God’s wondrous power, he who had once been Saul became for us Paul: by God’s mighty transformation he was now a preacher, though formerly so great a persecutor of him whose preacher he had become. Therefore this episode of the history is made more illustrious than the rest because it was published to the martyr’s glory by Augustus himself—once so great a persecutor, but now a master and preacher.

Nevertheless, when the king repeatedly and insistently asked the proper name of the courtier who, as stated above, had joined the birds in helping them, seeking to have him identified by name, I steadfastly refused to name him, for the reasons already given.

Let us therefore return to what came before and examine each point: see whether this great power has not been gloriously vanquished—vanquished precisely in being humbled, and humbled precisely in being vanquished. How good is the martyr’s triumph which humbles in this way; and how good the king’s humiliation which thus triumphs over his enemies! May God daily increase, perfect, and preserve this penitential humility in our king, that he may persevere in it to the end.

## That Perseverance in Penitence Is Rare and Difficult for Kings

Yet in this fleeting life, full of snares, temptations, and turnings away, it is exceedingly difficult for all flesh—but especially for kings—to remain thus in penitential humility. This is especially difficult for kings, surely, who, distracted by so many cares of lands, occupied by so many causes, entangled in so many affairs, can scarcely remain motionless in one thought or any purpose, their minds thus divided and torn apart. For they are oppressed by the cares of all mortals, pressed by their causes, and harassed by their complaints. A king is like a chariot of the human race: he is at once its charioteer and its javelin. He carries all, rules all, presses all; he is at once fear and spur to all. He raises all, leads all, and drives all. “He who boasts,” it says, “drives oxen with a goad” (Eccli. XXXVIII).

Besides these cares, occupations, and entanglements which tear, divide, and turn aside the mind, worldly glory exalts it. Amid the wealth of so many Croesuses and the delights of Sardanapalus, in kings’ bedchambers, upon hyacinth-coloured, purple, and richly woven beds, the seductive pleasure of the flesh is sweetly nurtured—a pleasure which not even cares can escape or put to flight. Behold care; behold glory; behold seduction: these three things do not allow high station to stand without danger. Behold burden, honour, and the stain of honour: the seduction of the flesh, as we have said, which lies in ambush beside the glory of honour, in order to cast it into that stain, to defile it as by some pestilential breath, or to contaminate and disfigure it as by vile mud. Thus high places are never without danger: by their very excessive height they always threaten a fall. Broken, as it were, within themselves by that very excessive height, they do not stand long; and the higher they fall from, the more heavily they fall.

Hence, to use examples from our sacred history: the kings of Israel, thirty-six in number if I am not mistaken, were all evil. Likewise the twenty-one kings of Judah, if I am not mistaken, all committed sin, as Scripture testifies, except David, Hezekiah, and Josiah. For, as it immediately adds there, “the powerful kings of Judah forsook the law and despised the fear of God.” This is wholly certain: among so many and such great kings, both these and those, some either never began, or, if they began, did not persevere. Perseverance in repentance is indeed so rare and so difficult among kings. Of them, not to speak of perseverance, even repentance once begun is rare; and when it does occur, its continuance is itself rare and brief.

Therefore we must pray more earnestly for our king, in whose hand lie both the life and the peace of so many nations and so many great peoples, that he may stand firm in the good in which we have so often lately described him, grow daily stronger by advancing toward better things, and at last—as befits so glorious a power—be consummated in a glorious end.

## Here He Briefly Repeats the Notes of the Preceding Melody in Order to Add Further Matter

And because the melody concerning our king, so gloriously vanquished, has sounded in our lyre not now as a mere little note but as an extended strain—drawn out the longer because it is sweeter and more delightful—let us resume the harmony, so consonant and concordant, between the visible palm of the emperor’s triumphant death and the visible palm of the soldier’s triumphant death, which we have interrupted for a while. I call it interrupted, unless indeed what has been inserted was not an interruption at all, but rather an ornament added to that harmony already begun.

Therefore, to add still more: so that the begun melody of the harmony between the visible palm of the emperor’s triumphant death and the visible palm of the soldier’s triumphant death may be heard more fully and concordantly, let us sound again those notes which we previously sounded at greater length while striking our lyre. And thus, the sweeter the better, and the briefer the more suitable for distinguishing and singing again the notes of the melody, let us sound them once more almost in one breath and as under one pause, in a more concise brevity. Thus this brevity may be compact, just as, in order to renew and restore the hearing, melody is joined continuously to melody and harmony to harmony, with nothing intervening and without any interval. Therefore we must begin again more deeply from the beginning.

## The First Note Repeated

The visible palm of the emperor’s death was the death of death, as we sang before; likewise, as we have shown, was the palm of the soldier’s death.

The visible palm of the emperor’s death raised the dead; likewise did the palm of the soldier’s death, as we have taught.

The visible palm of the emperor’s death is the salvation of the world; likewise the soldier’s is the salvation of the Church, as we daily experience and see, and as has already been said above.

The visible palm of the emperor’s death brought forth captives from hell; likewise did that of the soldier’s death, and we have proved this.

The visible palm of the emperor’s death saved his soldiers who crucified him, as many believe; likewise the soldier’s death saved his soldiers—his executioners—as all who saw it testify, and as we have stated above.

The visible palm of the emperor’s death stripped principalities and powers; likewise did that of the soldier’s death, as we have shown before.

The visible palm of the emperor’s death triumphed over principalities and powers in himself; likewise did that of the soldier’s death, as we have not passed over above.

The visible palm of the emperor’s death confidently led his own people through principalities and powers thus vanquished; likewise did that of the soldier’s death, as has been taught before.

The visible palm of the emperor’s death erased the bond written in the decree which stood against us and was contrary to us; likewise the soldier’s death erased the bond which was contrary to us—that is, to the clergy—as we have stated above.

The visible palm of the emperor’s death, removing that written bond of the decree from the midst, fastened it to the cross; likewise the soldier’s death fastened it to his head, so that it might be removed when his whole head had been exposed and wholly torn apart.

The visible palm of the emperor’s death defeated both aerial and earthly powers; likewise did that of the soldier’s death defeat aerial and earthly powers. I do not think it has escaped notice that this was most clearly demonstrated quite recently by eyewitness evidence.

The visible palm of the emperor’s death quickly drew all things to himself; likewise the soldier’s death most swiftly converted the world to himself. We have not passed this over among the other matters.

The visible palm of the emperor’s death is that all power was given to him in heaven and on earth; likewise great power given to the soldier shines forth both here and there. This alone, previously unmentioned, we add here.

## Here He Adds a Comparison between the Banner of the Cross and the Banner of the Vessel, Carried by the Soldier’s Pilgrims as the Cross Is Carried by the Emperor’s Pilgrims

To these notes of the emperor and soldier’s melody which we have already heard, we shall now add certain new ones, so that, weariness removed and the hearer refreshed, the hearing may be renewed.

Therefore the banner of the emperor’s visible palm of triumphant death is the cross, which is also the sign and image of his life in the flesh. Likewise the banner of the soldier’s triumphant death is the vessel of water and blood, which is also at once the sign and image of his life in this flesh. In this, as it were, final note of this melody, which our lyre must now strike, we must hear more sweetly and attentively how and in what manner this is so.

## First, Concerning the Mystery of the Cross Which the Emperor’s Pilgrims Carry Openly

First, then, we must sing how the emperor’s banner of the cross is an image and sign of his life in the flesh, insofar as our emperor himself, our precentor, supplies me with voice and the sense of the voice. And may this same emperor, as Lord of virtues and of all knowledge, now unlock for us, with the keys of his own cross, the mystery set forth by that cross. Then we must sing in response concerning the banner of the vessel of water and blood: how, in the likeness of the emperor, it is an image and sign of the soldier’s life in this flesh, and the banner of his triumphant death, insofar as this same emperor, the Word of God, supplies the voice and words.

Therefore, that we may first hear how the banner of the Lord’s cross is the sign and image of the emperor’s life, behold: the cross has four dimensions. It is broad and long, high and deep. The emperor’s life in the flesh had these four dimensions; it was, as it were, a square life: widest in charity, longest in perseverance, highest in contemplation, and deepest in fear or reverence of God. For in his life the emperor revered God above all. Hence the master teaches that he was heard because of his reverence, speaking thus of him: “Who, in the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears to him who could save him from death, was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. V).

Behold the emperor’s life in the likeness of the cross, having four dimensions: this life, as it were, square or fourfold. Thus the four dimensions of the cross are most plainly present in the life of the crucified emperor. Hence, if I am not mistaken, the banner of the cross is rightly called, and expressively is, an image and sign of the emperor’s life. Likewise this same banner of the cross—or the same cross as banner—signifies the emperor’s triumphant death in the flesh. For a life such as we have described, resembling the cross in four dimensions, as it were square or fourfold, is without doubt followed by a triumphant death. Thus plainly one and the same cross is the image and sign of the emperor’s life in the flesh, and the banner of his triumphant death.

And to add further: what the cross was to Christ the emperor, this same thing it is to his Christian fellow-soldiers: first, the image and sign of their life in this flesh, having four dimensions; and afterward, the banner of their triumphant death. This triumphant death always follows a life which has the four dimensions of the cross. These are the four spiritual dimensions of the Lord’s cross in the spiritual life of the Christian fellow-soldier of Christ the emperor, to which the Master exhorts his disciples: “Rooted and founded in charity, that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth” (Eph. III).

Certainly, if one of these dimensions is missing in the life of Christ’s fellow-soldier, his death will no longer be triumphant. To indicate this triumph, the triumphant banner of the cross precedes the bodies of the faithful dead, so that the opposing powers, vanquished through a life resembling the cross—like a square life, as it were through the sign of the cross—may immediately flee when they see the triumphant banner of the cross. In accordance with the words: “Behold the cross of the Lord; flee, hostile powers.” Thus the cross, which had first been the sign of Christ’s fellow-soldiers’ life, is afterward raised in death as the banner, as it were, of death itself triumphant, showing that triumphant death has followed the life of the Christian of which the cross had earlier been the sign.

## He Begins Mystically to Adapt the Soldier’s Sign to the Emperor’s Sign

What we have proposed concerning the sign or banner of the cross, both in the emperor and in any fellow-soldier of the emperor, is now clear, if I am not mistaken. It remains, according to our promise, to show how, in the likeness of the emperor, [concerning this vessel elsewhere] the vessel of water and blood is the image and sign of the soldier’s life, and likewise the banner of his triumphant death. We shall now teach concerning the soldier’s vessel and the soldier what we have taught above concerning the emperor and the emperor’s cross.

But first, lest anyone doubt what this vessel of water and blood is, I shall name it once before and now again—the vessel concerning which we must henceforth sing as in the final note of this melody. It is indeed that vessel by which the world, without any sermon having been preached, no assembly gathered, nor even a little conventicle convened, with no edict proclaimed and under no compulsion of any command, but solely, beyond doubt, by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, as though marked itself unanimously and collectively for the martyr’s glory and as a sign of its pilgrimage. This is the portable lead vessel by which the pilgrims of the blessed martyr especially mark themselves. It contains water and blood: water sanctified through contact with the blood, by the blood.

This vessel, I say, is not an empty human invention, neither from a human being nor through a human being; rather, as those who see inwardly judge more truly, it has been commended to humankind by the Spirit of truth alone, not of vanity. As we see, all alike, unanimously inspired, carry this portable vessel, by which they attest by a visible sign that they are devoutly bound to the glorious martyr and are his particular servant-pilgrims. This, therefore, is the vessel of pilgrimage—the vessel of water and blood which we mentioned above in passing, and of which our discourse will henceforth be woven—so that we may fit this vessel, the sign of the soldier’s life and banner of his death, to the soldier, just as we fitted the sign and banner of the cross above to the emperor.

Would that the emperor might now also deign to open it for us with the keys of his cross, to the praise and glory of his soldier and martyr, so that in this exposition of the vessel the sign and banner of his soldier may accord and harmonize with the sign and banner of the emperor. I shall therefore speak concerning this vessel—not, indeed, the vessel of a foolish shepherd, but truly of a good one. I shall say what I think; and I trust in the Lord that, revealing from his own riches to me his servant, far more and better than I can from myself, he will reveal as much as pleases him.

## Concerning the Mystery of the Vessel Carried by the Martyr’s Pilgrims

See then and observe that in the sign of this vessel there are three things, just as we distinguished four in the sign of the cross. But in this sign there are three: lead, water, and blood, because the water is sanctified in the blood through the blood’s touch. These three are three mystical things: in the lead, heaviness; in the water, purity; and in the blood, the power and pattern of death through martyrdom. Thus in the lead oldness is expressed; in the water, newness; and in the blood, the courage of martyrdom. Behold the old and heavy man; behold the new and pure man; behold the strong and valiant martyr.

These are, as is plainly clear from what precedes in the history, the three stages of a man’s life, that is, three ways in which he lives in this bodily life. The first manner of life, as the first old man, is in the court; the second manner of life, as the second new man, is in the Church; the third manner of life, now as the third strong man, is in the arena. The strength of this third man began not only then, in that brief time described above when he exposed his soul, but rather from the time when he was ready to expose it. Behold the three stages of the man’s life.

Among these, the old life, heavy and leaden, comes first and outweighs the rest. For first, as the Master says, “not that which is spiritual, but that which is animal; afterward that which is spiritual” (I Cor. XV). And truly afterward comes what is spiritual. For immediately there follows the spiritual man, the new man: life cleansed by water, stripped of oldness, renewed and unencumbered, the leaden burden of wickedness having been laid aside. That wickedness is deservedly read in the prophet as sitting upon a talent of lead. Then, as the new man gradually advances day by day, he passes into the perfect man, attaining the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, now of full age and perfect strength—like Christ the emperor and any Christian soldier—so that in the battle-line of Christ the emperor he may resist even unto blood, should this, as sometimes happens, be required.

These, therefore, are the three stages of the man’s life, ascending through them in order and by degrees, as it were from virtue to virtue and from life to life. From what has already been said, it is plainly clear, if I am not mistaken, that the portable vessel of pilgrimage, which is now the whole subject of our discourse, is a most evident image and sign of them. You need only look in this vessel at the three things: lead, water, and blood. Therefore, although this vessel is through these three things the image and sign of the soldier’s threefold life, it is nonetheless, in the manner of the cross, the banner of the soldier’s triumphant death. The outer engraving of this banner-like vessel openly proclaims that triumphant death to the world. It bears the inscription: “The dead rise; lepers are cleansed” (Luke VII), so that every person may daily read, behold, invoke, and praise in it so great a defender of ecclesiastical liberty.

And further, that the resemblance between the emperor’s banner and the soldier’s banner may be shown more plainly, and that this little note of the present melody may thereby be sweeter and more harmonious to the ear: this vessel is to Christ’s soldier—that is, to his Christian tent-companions and fellow-soldiers—a sign of their threefold life, as we distinguished above, and thereafter a banner of their triumphant death. This threefold life, indeed, just as we said above concerning the fourfold or [Col. 1328B] quadripartite life when we treated of the mystery of the cross, is followed by triumphant death; so that what we now see in Christ’s soldier, Christ’s fellow-soldiers may hope for and desire for themselves.

For beyond doubt triumphant death follows this threefold life: so that without this threefold life, just as we showed above concerning the fourfold character of the cross, none of the emperor’s soldiers can die with rejoicing or triumph. For behold: first there is the leaden life, the burdensome and heavy life, without which not even an infant of one day can exist. Indeed, one begins from this life alone. And if one dies in it without having been washed in our waters, one dies not as a victor but rather as conquered, yielding to the hostile side. Thus, after our lead, how necessary is our water! But once washed and cleansed by the water, one must with every vigilance [Col. 1328C] look about oneself, lest, walking in the night, one stumble, fall, and in falling be defiled by the mud beneath one’s feet. Thus it is necessary and fitting to stand bravely in the battle-line of one’s emperor: neither falling nor yielding, but resisting even unto blood, should such necessity arise.

Behold, after our lead and our water, third comes our blood. Thus the banner-like sign contained in our vessel includes these three necessary things for all soldierly tent-companions who seek the palm at the end after battle: namely lead, water, and blood. And let no one complain if I call even our lead necessary to us. For it is all the more glorious—and indeed better and more advantageous—if our lead is changed into silver; or if, once it has been wholly [Col. 1328D] purified, pure tested silver alone shines forth, fit to be placed in the treasury of the great king. These three things, then, are necessary to us: lead as well as water and blood. Yet the latter two would certainly have had no use had we been wholly without lead. But now these three remain to us; and lead fittingly stands among the three, since silver is cleansed only through lead.

Among these things, if anyone, in the likeness of our new martyr, proceeds cautiously and virtuously in due order and by degrees, so as to pass from life to life, he will most certainly regain the triumphant vessel of our soldier, which he himself possesses as the sign of his threefold life; and he himself will possess that same vessel as the spiritual banner of his triumphant death. Thus, when he has victoriously departed from the world, [Col. 1329A] for his lead, which he used well; for his water, in which he was cleanly washed; and for his blood, by which he was tested in battle, he may receive from God and from men in reality and in the very event itself praise corresponding to that which the soldier’s triumphant vessel proclaims figuratively.

We have now heard in part, as it seemed to me, the great conformity of sign to sign and banner to banner: of the emperor’s cross, its sign and banner, to the sign and banner of the soldier’s vessel.

## IT SHOWS THAT THE SOLDIER’S SIGN AND BANNER, LIKE THE EMPEROR’S, ARE MYSTICAL

Let no one judge within himself, or think, that these things enacted in the soldier’s death and after his death—and written by us as the Lord of knowledge deigns to reveal them according to his merits—things which the Church venerates so solemnly [Col. 1329B] and the world so universally reveres, happened by chance, were devised by human imagination, or have been set down vainly and frivolously by our pen. Rather, let him whose mind is blind enough to judge or think so come, invited by the prophet, and see the works of the Lord, the wonders which he has set upon the earth. Let him neither judge nor think thus, nor murmur secretly, but sing clearly and openly in the ways of the Lord, confessing how great is his glory; let him give thanks to the Lord and make known among the peoples his works.

For, according to the testimony of the Wise Man, nothing is made without cause, even though the world may not know the mystery of what has been done. For, as Wisdom herself says, “Man shall not discover the work which God has done from the beginning even to the end” (Eccles. III). Yet let those invited by the prophet come here [Col. 1329C] and see that in what occurred at and after the soldier’s triumphant death there was neither accidental chance nor the empty invention of vain children of men, but rather that will and counsel without which not even a leaf falls from a tree.

If, therefore, without this counsel no leaf falls from a tree, can anything be done without it in Christ’s body? Otherwise Christ himself, who is the counsel of the Most High, would take care for the leaves of trees but neglect the care of the members of his own body. Therefore one must most certainly believe that, just as nothing was done in the passion of Christ the head without a cause of mystery, so neither in his whole body—while it endures triumphant death as he himself did—is anything done without some cause of mystery. Yet among the members of this [Col. 1329D] body, as is fitting and just, there is more in some and less in others. Thus Christ entire—namely the head together with the members—is wholly mystical, although we, vain and foolish children of men, do not know the mystery.

Therefore, to return to my subject: among the other matters I attend especially to those things which occurred in and after the death of our soldier, so triumphant a death as the whole world of churches embraces with such gratitude, devotion, and piety. I do so the more diligently because I most certainly believe that for so great an athlete and a man so triumphant, whether in death or after death, not even one iota happened without some cause of mystery, though hidden. I hold of the soldier what I hold of the emperor. Of the emperor’s conduct in the world—which I judge wholly mystical, though I now pass it over—and especially [Col. 1330A] of whatever was done in his passion, resurrection, or ascension, whether by himself as man or by another at any time or place: I know indeed that it was done, but I also believe that it signifies something yet to be done. For these deeds are, as it were, pregnant, like a body which has within it a spirit that gives life.

Everything here is both wondrous and a mystery, indeed a wondrous mystery: so much so that even the places and times are mystical. For the emperor himself is not merely a man wholly mystical, but he is also the Word and the mystery of his Father and of every creature. For if he is counsel, he is also mystery.

I attend the more gladly and laboriously to those things which occurred in the soldier’s death or after his death, because I know that the mystery I seek lies hidden in them: like one digging for treasure, who [Col. 1330B] digs there most gladly and with all his strength where he knows with certainty that treasure is concealed. And since it matters little to me that this work concerning my lord the new martyr should be judged by a man or by a human day, in this work I seek as patron only him whom, inflamed with an unbearable ardor of mind, I had as the teacher of this work; and I appoint him likewise, either in person or through those wiser than I among his own, as my corrector. But let us return to bring our begun little note concerning the emperor’s and soldier’s signs and banners to a more harmonious conclusion.

Thus, as we have sung beforehand, there are three things in the soldier’s triumphant vessel. These are the three that bear witness to the soldier on earth: lead, water, [Col. 1330C] and blood. Thus there are three for the soldier, as there are three for the emperor.

## 15. LITTLE NOTE

For the emperor there are three who bear witness on earth: spirit, blood, and water. Likewise for the soldier there are three: lead, blood, and water. And truly these are the emperor’s three witnesses on earth. In the very banner-sign of the cross, while he himself still hung upon the cross, these were his three witnesses. For from the pierced side of him still hanging upon his cross, blood and water immediately came forth; but before this, crying with a loud voice and with great power yielding up the spirit, he said: “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII).

Behold: on earth, and on the very gibbet of the cross, while the emperor himself still hung upon it, these three wondrous witnesses—[Col. 1330D] spirit, water, and blood. And among the other witnesses, and above the others—whose testimony nevertheless was one harmonious and concordant testimony—the spirit, I say, uttered loudly, powerfully yielded up, delivered, and commended into his Father’s hands, testifies above all how the emperor Christ is truth.

But here the case of the soldier is very different from that of the emperor. Hence this melody, hitherto so harmonious and concordant between emperor and soldier, seems to differ most greatly in this one little note. For the soldier’s first witness, namely lead, testifies that the emperor’s soldier here was vanity; whereas, on the contrary, the emperor’s first witness, namely the spirit, testifies on behalf of the emperor that he is truth. These testimonies are far different—indeed wholly opposed. [Col. 1331A] As far as east is from west, truth from vanity, God from man, emperor Christ from the Christian soldier.

Yet truth cast out vanity, and thus the emperor freed his soldier. Freed in this way, and possessing the testimony of cleansing water, and besides this obtaining through the yet more certain and evident testimony of blood, he won by judgment the glory of his emperor. For “in the mouth of two”—not to say three, although there are three here, save that, as we have shown, the first among the three does not agree with the other two—“in the mouth,” I say, “of two every word of judgment stands.”

But let us add further material, that sign may be shown more conformed to sign and banner to banner, and that the little note of our melody concerning these signs and banners may sound all the more sweetly because more harmoniously. [Col. 1331B] The emperor’s banner is displayed openly to the world, not in a corner or under a roof. And pilgrims to Jerusalem wear the sign of the cross either before them upon the breast or attached to the shoulder; either is fitting.

## WHY THE CROSS IS WORN UPON THE BREAST

It is worn on the breast so that whoever has the faculty of the breast—that is, of the heart—may continually recall the memory of the Lord’s passion. Let him also attentively consider the emperor’s life, having four dimensions, of which the cross is both a sign and the outcome of his triumphant death, of which it is likewise the banner; so that he may conform himself to the life having four dimensions and may hope from it, after it, for a like triumphant death.

## WHY THE CROSS IS ATTACHED TO THE SHOULDER

That the sign of the cross is also attached to the shoulder is fitting, and its reason is evident. For according to [Col. 1331C] the prophet, “His dominion has been made upon his shoulder” (Isa. IX): that is, when the emperor himself was led to the place of his passion, he bore upon his own shoulders his cross, by triumphing on which he acquired dominion. Everyone who seeks to conform himself to the emperor’s passion and share his honor ought to place his shoulders beneath the burden of the cross. For, as the Master teaches, “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (II Tim. II). Thus the sign of the cross is at times attached to the shoulder, both as an example of what was done and because of its mystery.

## WHY THE SIGN OF THE CROSS IS ALWAYS BORNE ERECT BEFORE THE FACE OF THE ROMAN PONTIFF, AND LIKEWISE OF METROPOLITANS

[Col. 1331D] At times this sign is raised openly before the face, not upon the breast or shoulder. The Roman pontiff too, as an emperor—since he acts on earth in the emperor’s stead—always has it raised before him wherever he goes, as the banner of his imperial majesty. Likewise some rulers of certain churches, namely metropolitans, as the emperor’s fellow-soldiers and tent-companions, always have it borne erect before their faces. These chief rulers of churches thus raise that sign, which is the sign of the emperor’s life and likewise the banner of his triumphant death.

All this is chiefly so that those who possess among others, as it were by the inheritance of firstborn sons, the primacy of the emperor who has departed from the world, and who act in his stead on earth—these persons, I say, especially—may live as their father the emperor lived; and as he fought while still in the flesh, may themselves fight, so that afterward they too may triumph as he did.

[Col. 1332A] And this sign and banner of the emperor’s cross our soldier, while he still exercised on earth the office of his emperor and fought battles, as we showed above in the history, raised at Northampton when about to fight the beasts. He raised this sign against the opposing forces, against principalities and powers, triumphing then in this banner of his emperor. Thus that ancient utterance of the prophets concerning the emperor was likewise fulfilled in the soldier after the emperor: the imperial dominion was made upon the soldier’s shoulder as well. For then the soldier, as I repeat here what has been related above in the history, visibly bore in his own person the cross of Christ, as Christ himself did. In this way the dominion of the cross became common to emperor and soldier: [Col. 1332B] the soldier then triumphing over principalities and powers in it just as the emperor had triumphed.

Therefore, to insert this briefly here, I do not believe that I am mistaken even in this: because the soldier on earth, with great trust in the emperor, raised in his battle the emperor’s banner of the cross for protection, the emperor now grants on earth to the soldier a banner like his own—namely the banner of the vessel described above, like, as we have shown, the banner of the cross—and all this as praise of the soldier.

But to return to what went before: this sign of the cross, whether borne upon the shoulder, upon the breast, or before the face, [Col. 1332C] is always set openly before the outward eyes of humankind, so that a person may continually contemplate with the inward eyes of the mind and imitate the fourfold life of which it is the sign, and the triumphant death of which it is likewise the banner.

## WHY THE SOLDIER’S BANNER-VESSEL, LIKE THE EMPEROR’S BANNER, IS BORNE OPENLY AND UPON THE BREAST

We now see why and how the emperor’s sign and banner of the cross are always displayed openly to the world. Similarly, the sign and banner of the soldier’s vessel are always presented openly to the world: not hidden in a corner, under a roof, or behind the bearer, but borne before him, in his face, upon his breast. There is such a harmony of sign with sign and banner with banner that, using almost the same language, we can [Col. 1332D] say of the soldier’s sign and banner what we have already said concerning the emperor’s sign and banner: the soldier’s sign and banner, as we said of the emperor’s, are borne upon the breast so that whoever has the faculty of the breast may continually recall the memory of the soldier’s passion.

Let him also wisely examine and first consider the soldier’s threefold life which we distinguished above, of which the banner-vessel is the sign, and then the outcome of his triumphant death, of which the same vessel is the banner. Thus whoever is a watchful imitator of this threefold life of the soldier may await from it, after it, a like triumphant death. The Lord seems to command this concerning these two signs and banners of emperor and soldier, just as he says concerning the words of the law itself: “Put these my words in your hearts and in your [Col. 1333A] souls; bind them as a sign upon your hands and place them between your eyes. When you sit in your house, walk on the way, lie down, and rise, you shall write them upon the doorposts and gates of your house” (Deut. XI).

Likewise elsewhere in the law, and for the same reason, the Lord commanded fringes to be made at the corners of garments, with bands of hyacinth-blue set in them; when the children of Israel saw these, they would remember the commandments of the Lord. Hence the Pharisees, more zealous than others for the law, wrote the Decalogue on phylacteries, so that they might always have it hanging, as it were, before their eyes. But let us return to our signs and banners.

Behold the harmony of the emperor’s and soldier’s signs, as though in a single battle. Behold the joining of their banners, as though in one palm of victory. Hence in many churches [Col. 1333B] this conjunction may often be seen: namely the vessel with the cross and around the cross; and likewise the cross of the crucified emperor joined with the vessel of the soldier, beheaded for the emperor. Thus mystery works through the emperor and his soldier in their signs and banners, though by means of those who do not know what they are doing.

O, when I see in church the signs and banners thus joined, how great a brightness of joy immediately enters me through all my windows from that sight alone! When I see, I say, the sign and banner of this soldier, my lord, triumphant above others who have served in the army of the Lord of Hosts, thus joined with those familiar signs of the emperor. And indeed this conjunction in the Church of their signs and banners shows, as though undivided, the present conformity of their union in their homeland—or rather, what is truer because more explicit, their unity: emperor and soldier, who lived in conformity in this life, [Col. 1333C] and now triumph in conformity in death.

For the things below indicate to us what is done invisibly above in this valley of tears. As that heavenly and truly eminent theologian said, how beautifully divine and heavenly things are made manifest even through dissimilar symbols. And they are truly made manifest, although few come and see the works of the Lord, the wonders which he has placed upon the earth.

O how often, while this soldier, my lord, was still serving in the flesh, I foretold to him face to face the things that would happen to him which I now see fulfilled in him—provided, as I used to add, [Col. 1333D] that he would fight the battles of his emperor bravely, manfully, and steadfastly! O how often did I not cease, having found place and time, to set before the eyes of his mind as well the sign and banner of the emperor’s cross—which, according to the custom of that metropolitan church, was always raised before him and which he saw so continually with bodily eyes! I, the disciple instructing the master, explained what this sign and banner of the cross was, and why it was such; and why it was borne erect before his face, both on the road and in church, not behind him, not upon his shoulder or breast, but, greater still, always before his face. God knows that I always urged him insistently to recall especially by the virtue of his deeds the sign and banner of his emperor, which thus, as it were opportunely and importunately, presented itself to him throughout the day amid his business, cares, lawsuits, [Col. 1334A] and counsels.

O how often, when encouraging the man toward brave deeds, I promised him glory—though not so great a glory as I now see, indeed as the world itself sees and displays, and as even “the stone cries out from the wall”! Hence, to confess the truth, beneath the sun I have no joy greater than this, nor even one so great. Through so great a father and patron I have no slight confidence before the Most High; through him and for him my joy grows daily. Thus, in proportion to the multitude of my former sorrows, manifold consolations now gladden my soul. For as the man’s glory grows day by day, he increases my joy day by day. Though taken from the world, he consoles and gladdens [Col. 1334B] my soul—left orphaned, together with my brethren once companions in suffering—so that in this wretched pilgrimage I may daily sing how great is his glory.

Yet, to repeat what was said a little earlier: when we said that I, a sinful little man, encouraged this most swift and ready athlete of Christ toward brave deeds while he was still contending among us, no one should think that I said this because such a swift and vigorous runner in the course of this present way and life had great need to be pressed onward by the spurs of words, or even stirred to run. From the time that the spirit first began in him, it was always most fervent. He needed no spurs of words to urge him in his running, just as balsam needs no ointments to soothe it, the sun no torches [Col. 1334C] to assist it, or an eagle no adjustment of its wings for the prey it has seen and desires. Nevertheless, I sometimes spoke, like a talkative woman spinning in the house; but he acted. Yet let us return to our signs.

## IT BRIEFLY REVIEWS WHAT HAS BEEN SAID AT GREATER LENGTH ABOUT THE CONFORMITY OF THE SIGNS, ADDING SOME NEW POINTS

And since the final little notes of our present melody concerning signs and banners, now extended at such length, call for an end, let us do now what we remember having done above with other little notes of this melody of another kind: lest, as the common saying goes, even pleasant songs become wearisome. That is, let us henceforth sound briefly, continuously, and in order, without delay and without the pause which is customary in the psaltery but not at all in the lyre—for this would be against the rules of musical art—the little notes concerning the conformity of the emperor’s and soldier’s banner-signs which for that reason [Col. 1334D] we have sounded scatteredly, confusedly, and with insufficient order upon our lyre.

Thus, the shorter they are, the more pleasing; and the more distinct, the clearer and more harmonious will the melody of these little notes concerning banner-signs appear to the ear. And, once the hearer’s ear has been refreshed, let us add some new little notes concerning these banners to those which we have already set forth, as we remember having likewise done above in other little notes of this present melody. Let us therefore recapitulate briefly from the beginning.

## 14. LITTLE NOTE

[Col. 1335A]

The emperor’s banner, therefore—the first and chief of all banners—is both a sign and a banner. Likewise the soldier’s banner is both a sign and a banner of a similar thing. This has been shown at length, and I now pass it over.

### THIS IS, AS IT WERE, PART OF THE PRECEDING LITTLE NOTE

The emperor’s first banner is the sign of the cross. Likewise the soldier’s other banner is the vessel of blood. And in this I hear no discord with what was said before: there, the cross; here, blood.

## 15. LITTLE NOTE

In the emperor’s banner of his cross there are three things which bear witness on earth: spirit, blood, and water. Likewise, in the banner of the soldier’s vessel there are three: [Col. 1335B] lead, blood, and water. This too has been shown before.

## 16. LITTLE NOTE

The emperor’s banner of the cross was discovered through the revelation of the Holy Spirit. Likewise, the banner of the soldier’s vessel was discovered through the inspiration of the same Spirit. This we have stated above concerning the soldier’s vessel; and it is established and publicly known concerning the emperor’s banner of the cross, discovered by the Empress Helena, just as this vessel was discovered by the universal mother, the Church.

## 17. LITTLE NOTE

The emperor’s banner of the cross is placed by his pilgrim servants either before the breast or attached to the shoulder. Likewise, the soldier’s banner of the vessel is placed by his servants before the breast. We have above also made clear its mystical meaning.

## 18. LITTLE NOTE

[Col. 1335C]

The emperor’s banner of the cross is always openly displayed to the world for mystical edification. Likewise, the soldier’s other banner is openly displayed for a similar mystery. This too we have now explained.

## 19. LITTLE NOTE

The emperor’s banner of the cross is set in church above the altar in the more elevated place. Likewise, the banner of the soldier’s vessel is now placed beside, now beneath, the banner of the emperor’s cross, so that the visible similarity of the emperor’s and soldier’s battle and palm of victory may be shown to us through these banners, mystically, as I think, thus visibly joined.

## 20. LITTLE NOTE

Through the emperor’s banner of the cross come the grace of healings [Col. 1335D] and the working of miracles. Likewise through the banner of the soldier’s vessel. Read the book of the soldier’s signs published concerning these matters, which we mentioned above, and you will plainly see that this is so. This has not been said before; we add it here as something new.

## 21. LITTLE NOTE

The emperor’s banner of the cross protects those who bear it. Likewise the banner of the soldier’s vessel: so much so that the nation called the Welsh, though inexorable and most cruel toward its enemies, nevertheless shows respect even to the enemies who bear this banner-vessel. We omitted this earlier; we add it here again as something new, almost the last of all additions. And let the final little note of this present melody now be briefly concluded.

## 22. LITTLE NOTE

[Col. 1336A]

Certainly the emperor’s banner of the cross is borne abroad, but toward the emperor’s martyrdom. Likewise, the banner of the soldier’s vessel is borne abroad, but away from the soldier’s martyrdom, just as the former is borne toward the emperor’s martyrdom. In this little note the emperor and soldier may seem to differ slightly; yet this is certainly not without cause, though to explain it now would be beside the point. Both are signs of pilgrimage: the former of pilgrimage to Jerusalem, where the emperor is buried; the latter of pilgrimage to Canterbury, where the soldier is buried.

## IT BRIEFLY RECAPITULATES WHAT PRECEDES, IN ORDER TO PASS TO OTHER MATTERS

We have sufficiently, I think, sounded on our lyre, somewhat slowly and attentively, how great is the consonance between the emperor’s and the soldier’s signs and [Col. 1336B] banners, and how harmonious their accord. From this one must most clearly infer how great was the agreement between emperor and soldier in this military life, and how great their conformity in triumphant death.

Having carried this out, according to the slowness of my understanding and as was granted from above, I hope that by the strength of the emperor himself—though with my own unworthy hands—as we prayed above, the keys of his sign-bearing and banner-bearing cross have opened to us the vessel of his soldier’s glory, previously closed: the vessel which is at once the soldier’s sign and banner. And, as permitted, we have poured out something from this vessel and offered it to others. We have offered, I say, something new, though small, from this vessel—something which, whether [Col. 1336C] others had tasted it or not I do not know, but which I myself, who offered it, had not previously tasted. For this is a new instruction from the emperor himself, who opens for us the sealed and closed vessel of his soldier by the keys of his own cross. Thus, through the emperor’s sign and banner, another sign and banner consonant and harmonious with it may be made known to the world: namely that of the soldier.

For before this, the world did not ponder what it bore in this triumphant vessel, which it bears as the sign of pilgrimage to the glory of the martyr. Daily it bore the mystery openly before its eyes upon its breast, and yet did not know what it bore. For, first and most weightily among other matters, it bore lead and did not weigh the lead. Likewise it bore [Col. 1336D] water, weighty with the lead and in the lead, but pondered neither the lead nor the water. It bore them, I say, but did not ponder them, believing the lead to be nothing but lead and the water nothing but water. Did not someone, returning at some time to himself and to the sign that he bore, think within himself: Why do I bear lead, which is heavier, rather than a pebble, which is lighter? Likewise, why do I bear water rather than wine or cider, which would be more convenient for travelers on the way?

Thus the world bore those two things but did not ponder them. But what of something concerning this vessel which has nearly slipped from memory: something which happened most truly and most miraculously, and which proves most plainly the mystery of the vessel of which we have now spoken for some time?

## CONCERNING THE BOXES FORMERLY BORNE

[Col. 1337A]

For it is commonly and unquestionably reported that, at the beginning of the new pilgrim martyr’s pilgrimage, certain empty boxes were carried as the sign of pilgrimage. However firmly sealed, they could not contain the water said to be sanctified by the martyr’s blood. Indeed, the more it was poured in, the more they emptied themselves drop by drop. Therefore, when that vessel was thus miraculously rejected, this other vessel succeeded it. Many who saw the boxes thus rejected bear witness to what we say. And certain boxes thus rejected may still be seen hanging above the martyr’s tomb as a sign of the miracle.

Therefore, as seems likely, for the greater commendation of this pilgrim vessel now borne, and for the more effective [Col. 1337B] confirmation of its mystery, the former vessels were first miraculously rejected by the Holy Spirit in so evident a manner. Yet no one knows who first made this vessel or first bore it, except that, as seems likely, the Holy Spirit inspired it: not one person alone, but all together, suddenly, throughout the whole world of churches, all bearing this similar object as the sign of their pilgrimage. In it are lead and water, and these, as we have already explained, are mystical. Would that henceforth the world might weigh them in the mind as wisely and equitably as it bears them devoutly upon the breast! For each is mystical: both the lead and the water, and the water no less than the lead.

I say nothing of the third of the three, namely blood: [Col. 1337C] perhaps among other matters the world alone considers this and interprets it mystically, because the sign of martyrdom is so evident to everyone in blood. But the mystery in the other two is more hidden. Yet those two too, as has now been shown—and I think no one now doubts it—are mystical, just as the third is. For why should the third be mystical if the first and second are not? Or why should the third not be mystical if the first and second are?

But, as the Lord of knowledge, author and teacher alike of mystery in spoken words, writings, and deeds, has so ordered it, the sign of blood was placed third after the two signs of lead and water, I think, so that by this more evident sign among the three, entering into the sanctuary of God as by a door, we might be invited to seek the more hidden mystery of the first and [Col. 1337D] second.

For there are certain things in sayings, writings, deeds, visions, and dreams which are at times all prophetic. In all these, I say, there are sometimes things in which the mystical meaning at once presents itself, as it were, before the face even of one who gives little attention. By entering through these as through certain doors of mysteries, we are invited toward other things more hidden; and from these things thus made plain, hope and, as it were, a beginning of entry into other and more difficult matters are more readily given. But there are certainly other things in which mystery lies hidden the more subtly because it is deeper. Therefore a keener eye is required the subtler it is, and a more laborious hand, as it were, the deeper it is, to dig it out and draw it forth.

For in the depths of prophetic things, [Col. 1338A] mystery must be extracted just as gold is excavated from certain veins of the earth. There are some veins in which gold, even upon the very surface, offers itself at once to an unskilled seeker, immediately and without any difficulty. But there are others in which, after the earth has been repeatedly overturned with much labor and sweat and dug more deeply, gold hides itself as it were within the innermost bowels of the earth even from the diligent and experienced miner. Thus it often happens that, though they dig laboriously, they do not extract the gold hidden there, for it is too deep. So too the patriarchs themselves could not always find the water which they sought while thirstily digging wells, because the water, like the gold, was often too deep.

And what is similar in water and gold [Col. 1338B] is similar also in prophetic mystery. For this is that prophetic water which first reaches the ankles of one passing along the way, then the knees, afterward the loins, and at last swells into a torrent which the traveler on the way cannot pass through. For this is not the privilege of the road but of the homeland: that one may no longer be merely a passer through it, but, having passed through, may drink deeply of the torrent of divine will and be satisfied with the fullness of eternal knowledge.

And what is similar in the waters of the temple is also similar in the places of the temple. Thus in prophetic matters some things are open even to the common people; these are like the places around the temple belonging to the populace, namely the common courts of the temple. Other matters are more inward, as though open only to [Col. 1338C] Levites and priests; others are innermost, like the Holy of Holies, into which only the sole and supreme priest is allowed to enter.

Let us first return, then, to the tabernacle of Moses; second, contemplate the temple of Solomon; and third, recall enigmatically that other temple of Ezekiel—shadowy with so many miracles, already hidden in obscurity. By briefly and summarily touching for the present these buildings, so lofty, glorious, spacious, and mystical, I shall make for us a broad entrance into what remains to be said. And Ezekiel alone will confirm what we have already touched upon concerning the characteristics of mysteries, although, if we knock, he may perhaps repel us from entering when we come to the inner gate of his temple, through which the prince alone enters and departs. At [Col. 1338D] the threshold of that gate we may perhaps worship with the people of the land, but we cannot enter.

But where am I tending? I may now seem, having entered through some doorway of the sanctuary of God or court of the temple, either unwilling or unable to come out; and in truth I depart unwillingly, yet not as though unable to depart, but—as is said of a child—both unwilling and willing, and indeed more truly unwilling. Yet the desire and purpose alike compel me to depart, in order to sound the third melody concerning the unseen yet most certainly known invisible and similar palm of glory of emperor and soldier. Once I have begun that melody, striking the lyre, it will immediately be necessary for me, if the inner temple door is opened by the prince’s favor and by the prince himself, to enter again into the sanctuary of God. And if the first prince draw me after himself, [Col. 1339A] I must proceed so far that, though I do not enter the Holy of Holies—for I would not dare this, nor am I worthy; it is the privilege of the sole and supreme priest only once a year—yet I must at least through some crevice between those inner holy places and the outer holy places, which my guide the Lord may deign to show me, look somewhat faintly upon what is done within.

## THE SECOND MELODY ENDS HERE, AND THE LYRE IS TUNED FOR THE THIRD

## [THE THIRD MELODY.]

In the first place, then, let us briefly recall and touch upon what has preceded, so that, after those preliminaries, we may be judged to have approached this third melody [Col. 1339B] in due order by our hearers. For after the historical song about the martyr, set first and before all else—Christ being the precentor, supplying voice and words as it pleased him—after that historical song, I say, upon the Davidic harp, playing it as I believe we have been taught by that harpist himself, we have already performed two melodies upon it.

In the first melody, namely, which concerned the visible and corresponding combat of the soldier with the combat of the emperor, if I am not mistaken, and if we now recall it, a consonance was heard so clear, great, and manifest. In the second melody, however, which concerned the visible and similar palm of the soldier’s triumphant death corresponding to the visible palm of the emperor’s triumphant death, a consonance was likewise heard [Col. 1339C]—and I think it was no less, though I do not know whether it was greater. Yet one thing I know: this consonance sounded most sweetly in this melody, if the hands of a craftsman better instructed in heavenly music, with longer and subtler fingers, had struck the harp.

But let the hearer forgive me if his hearing is offended. For according to my instruction and learning, when my hands—though their fingers are coarser and less fitted to praise and glorify the visible and corresponding combat of emperor and soldier, and their visible and similar palm—have struck the harp, it may nevertheless appear, however it has been played, how great, pleasing, and delightful is the consonance of visible combat with visible combat, and of visible palm with visible palm: what a harmonious melody, what concordant harmony [Col. 1339D]—certainly the sweeter, the more concordant it is.

O how human, how kind, how companionable, how merciful is this emperor, who thus makes his soldiers like himself both in his combat and in his palm! He makes them like, I say, not equal. For a brook is not equal to its spring, a drop to the sea, an atom to a mountain, nor a lamp to the sun; indeed, to put it more expressly, a little human soldier cannot be made equal to a giant of twofold nature. Whatever likeness there can be is not equality. Yet this likeness itself is wonderful.

O how great, I now believe, is the exceedingly sweet harmony—like a most consonant harmony—between emperor and soldier, after so great a correspondence in their present visible combat and visible palm, within their invisible glory. I should no longer call it likeness [Col. 1340A] or correspondence, but rather, as it were, an undivided unity, both of grace and of nature. That unity, indeed, is now made firm in the homeland: on this side, by the bond of love so vehement that we have never experienced it amid the multiplicity and distraction of this life; on that side, by the everlasting security of the peace which surpasses all understanding.

And indeed, just as two melodies have been set before us concerning the corresponding likeness and similar correspondence of the emperor’s and soldier’s earthly and visible combat, and likewise of their earthly and visible palm, so now henceforth this entire third melody will sound forth concerning the unity between emperor and soldier—more wonderful beyond comparison than all else—or concerning those things which prove and signify that unity. For if, in this earthly life, so manifold, diverse, and divided [Col. 1340B] by adversities, there was such correspondence between emperor and soldier in this earthly combat and earthly palm, what will there be between emperor and soldier in that kingdom of love and peace—indeed, which is nothing but peace and love—except unity?

And if there is between them here such correspondence, where there is nothing but distracting vanity, what will there be between them there, where there is nothing but consolidating truth? Most certainly, there will be no unity in the homeland between the emperor and any of his soldiers unless correspondence between them has gone before on the way. There is no union there of head and members unless first there has been here a likeness and conjunction of way and life. For the soldier ought to walk as the emperor walked.

First, therefore, it is evident and consequent—and I am bound by the preceding promise—that after the earthly and visible combat of the soldier, conformed to the likewise earthly and visible combat of the emperor, as after the first melody; and after the earthly and visible palm of the soldier’s triumphant death, likewise conformed to the earthly and visible palm of the emperor, as after the second melody; there should now, next and consequently, be formed here as a third melody a consonance to be heard between the palm of the soldier’s suprasolar and invisible triumphant death and the likewise suprasolar and invisible palm of the emperor’s triumphant death [Col. 1340C]. Yet the consonance of this third melody is indeed marvellous and unheard by mortal ears, so uniform—indeed, so united—that, more than it renders consonance, it resounds with unity. This third melody will be the last concerning that unity: truly, a melody destined to resound with unity rather than consonance. For it comes after sweats and labours, after pressures and distresses, after persecutions and contradictions, after combats and palms: now the bridegroom is upon the bed, and the beloved is in his embrace. Thus this melody concerns the glory of the emperor’s and soldier’s suprasolar and invisible palm—as it were, a particular wedding song of bridegroom and bride [Col. 1340D].

But now my mind is astonished, my hand trembles, my finger grows stiff—indeed, as I feel, now far coarser and more rigid than before—for modulating and forming this third melody. Before its performance, indeed, as soon as I meditate upon it and remember and observe what our harp is now to perform [Col. 1341A], astonishment immediately seizes me. And when I raise the eyes of my mind toward that suprasolar and invisible palm, and toward the undivided unity in it, whereby the bride is now joined to the bridegroom on the bed in his embrace—when, I say, I raise them toward these things—enigmatic phantoms of shadowy things immediately present themselves to my mind’s eyes and in turn darken them with dense gloom. Like one who, according to the prophet, gropes as a blind man at the wall of a house. I do not know by what way I may proceed to the inner bridal chamber of emperor and soldier, now resting together.

And this is what I remember having already testified in the history when I described the single combat of the soldier who was still fighting: namely, that I was unwillingly torn away from the combatant, because after the combatant’s triumph I should thereafter become silent about him, once he was in glory [Col. 1341B], saying no more of that kingdom which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which has not arisen in the human heart (1 Cor. 2). Yet whatever I may say—whether on the way or in the homeland, in death or in life, in combat or in palm—I am unwillingly torn away from so great a lord and foster-father.

Nor is this surprising, since I have been left alone like an orphan, even while my lord and father triumphs so gloriously in the world over the world—as the world itself sees and proclaims it—and yet the world scarcely dares still to communicate with me, although through my father and lord the world has already been thus conquered. Therefore it is not surprising that, just as earlier I was unwillingly torn away from his visible combat and palm, which I at least prolonged in speech as best I could [Col. 1341C], so now I am much more unwillingly torn away, left thus alone, from the invisible glory of his invisible palm.

Yet concerning that glory, so victorious, I speak all the more fearfully and dangerously; I raise a proclamation, indulge my mind, set down my pen, move my hand, fit my finger, and shall form a melody, though the glory of this palm is more invisible to me—as being suprasolar—than visible to anyone. What, then, shall I say of this invisible glory, I a sinful little man, soon to be scattered by one light and brief breath into fine dust? Indeed, it is still foreign even to patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and all who are still pilgrims. One of them says: “No eye, O God, has seen apart from you what you have prepared for those who wait for you” (Isa. 64).

Nevertheless, he himself may now strengthen more powerfully the inner powers of my mind, so that I may more keenly and subtly form this third melody: he may enable me, with the little plectrum of my talent upon our harp, to turn the higher pegs for tuning the strings, to move my hands, to fit my fingers for striking the harp [Col. 1341D], in proportion as his dominion has now been more greatly confirmed. Certainly, the sequence of the order would require it, and it would be most fitting, if someone had learned after the first melody of the visible combat of emperor and soldier, and after the second melody of their visible palm, to sound forth as a third melody the glory of their invisible and suprasolar palm. By means of such a melody the history of this little book—by which the world, though unworthy, would be more fully restored—would indeed be restored more fully.

But this melody requires to be performed upon the sharper and subtler strings of the harp, entirely beyond the reach of the dull senses of an earthly and carnal spirit [Col. 1342A]. Otherwise all is unmelodious, all discordant; nothing harmonious, nothing pleasing to the ear—not even to the ear of the one who strikes the harp. Yet this is according to that old proverb: “Even he who does not sing sweetly should sing sweetly to himself.”

But my fingers, as I have already confessed above and confess here again, are certainly far too coarse and rigid, too dull and swollen, for these strings of the harp, so sharp and subtle—though they alone must be struck if this melody is to sound sweetly and harmoniously on the harp. These are the fingers of an earthly and carnal man; indeed, of a man made of earth and from earth—rather, of earth itself, soon to return to vile and putrid mud, not even worthy to be trodden underfoot [Col. 1342B]. Yet if this melody is to be formed on the harp worthily and fittingly, the finger of no one but God alone must be awaited.

For the Spirit of wisdom, as he is manifold, is himself alone simple, keen, subtle, and mobile—more mobile than all mobile things—so that he reaches mightily from end to end and disposes all things sweetly. Therefore his finger alone is fitted for forming this melody. And so he alone, who is such a Spirit and thus disposes all things sweetly, knows how to play this melody sweetly upon the harp; and he alone can sweetly teach those who play it, provided that they have a spirit like his: simple, keen, subtle, and mobile.

Yet I, following like a slow-stepping tortoise, looking up from this deep valley of tears in order to comprehend the glory of my Lord, the sun, whether I wish it or not, whether I can or cannot, shall pursue both with mind and pen, as it is given from above. With whatever hands and fingers I have, I shall strike both strings of the harp and form the melody. For love urges me, as I touched upon above. But because this subject of glory is so vast and entire that it dazzles, by the excessive brightness of its suprasolar and invisible radiance, all the illustrious minds that have been before us or are now among us [Col. 1342C], I shall nevertheless speak a little about it, aided by my lord who is already in it, and shall do what infants do, since here I am an infant. I shall do, I say, what infants do when attempting to speak: they cut off or halve words rather than form them.

And so I too shall form the melody, as one giving a sound without understanding: rejoicing, and yet not knowing the jubilation. That jubilation is claimed for itself not by the pilgrim upon the way, but by the blessed people alone in the homeland. As the voice of that instructed harpist, who experienced it, says upon the harp: “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. 88 [89]) [Col. 1342D].

## He excuses his prolixity of speech

That I delay, draw out, prolong, draw myself back, defer, and excuse myself in beginning this melody—let no one censure it; let no one wonder. For it is neither blameworthy nor surprising if a beast fears to touch a mountain, if a common man fears to enter the Holy of Holies, or if an animal of leaden heaviness fears to enter the torrent of swelling waters [Col. 1343A]. Not even the prophet himself, the figured image of the Saviour, could cross that torrent: first he was led through water up to the ankles, then to the knees, finally to the loins; but when he had reached this torrent of waters at a deeper point, he could not pass through, because, as he himself testifies, the deep waters of the torrent had swollen and could not be forded.

Nevertheless, because I am bound by my promise, and lest I fear this torrent too rashly, though I cannot ford it—for no one can—I shall nevertheless enter it: not, indeed, as a prophet more daring, but, as I do not doubt, more foolhardy. Unless, if I begin to sink through having too little faith and too much presumption, I immediately cry to the emperor and triumphant soldier that I may not perish. For although presumptuous and rash, I take this danger upon myself in order to proclaim the palm of their glory. Therefore, although my presumption may be blamed, I hope that before them devotion will come to my aid and excuse me [Col. 1343B].

Therefore, that I may now discharge the debt of my devotion promised above: after the two melodies, already formed as instructed from above, concerning the corresponding correspondence or conforming likeness of the visible combat of emperor and soldier, and likewise their visible palm, this third melody is now to be formed concerning not so much their correspondence or likeness as their, as it were, indivisible and everlasting unity. Thus after the historical song there will be three melodies in praise and glory of emperor and soldier.

The first melody concerned the similar combat of emperor and soldier; the second, their similar palm, but earthly and visible; this third, however, will likewise concern the emperor and soldier—not, I shall no longer say, a similar glory of the palm, but, as it were, one and the same glory of the palm—yet suprasolar and invisible. The first melody, concerning the visible combat of emperor and soldier, was for mourning because of compassion; the second, concerning their visible palm, was for joy because of victory; but this third melody, concerning the invisible glory of the invisible palm of emperor and soldier, as a particular wedding song of bridegroom and bride, will be for jubilation because of the vehemence of love, which we cannot keep silent about and yet are unable to express [Col. 1343C].

## Here begins the third melody, but not yet upon the higher strings of the harp

[Col. 1343D]

### Note

First, then, in order to demonstrate the fullness of the corresponding glory of emperor and soldier, after the signs and banners of emperor and soldier, we must not be silent about their crowns.

## That the soldier’s crown, like the emperor’s, is twofold

The emperor’s crown is twofold; similarly, the soldier’s is twofold. The soldier’s crown is twofold because his victory is twofold. Let us wait a little until we have heard this. But first the crowns of the emperor must be proclaimed.

## On the first crown of the emperor.—First note of the third melody

[Col. 1344A]

The emperor was born from eternity, crowned from eternity, and appointed heir of all things from eternity. This eternal crown of the emperor is that one majesty, eternal power, and eternal glory which he possesses with the Father and from the Father. This is the emperor’s first crown: as it is without end, so also—what is an even more enfolded mystery of faith—it is without beginning.

This indeed is a wonder above every wonder; but let us give heed humbly and devoutly, because faith comes by hearing. This crown of which we now speak is the first and eternal crown of the emperor who is God, not the crown of the man. It is, I say, the crown not of the emperor as man, but of the emperor as God, before every creature and before man was created [Col. 1344B].

## On the second crown of the emperor.—Second note

Yet this first crown of his, with which his Father Adonai crowned him before the ages, he, as it were, laid aside for humanity at the end of the ages, and assumed another, incomparably lower crown—as one putting off a fine shoe and putting on sackcloth. Hence he himself says: “You have torn my sackcloth” (Ps. 29 [30]).

If he had appeared to the world in that first and eternal crown proper to himself, and in his own fine shoe, he would no longer, I think, have been recognised as king, but rather as emperor of angels—indeed, more than of archangels; or rather, he would not have been recognised at all, for not even the whole world could have borne him thus. What person, what flesh, what living creature, what corruptible being could even approach, much less dwell with, that consuming fire, those everlasting burnings?

Therefore our emperor, descending to us, assumed among us and from us such a crown and put on such a fine shoe as was suitable for the Jews, for whose sake he then came to us especially—though in truth it was more sackcloth than a fine shoe [Col. 1344C]. Otherwise, unless by a judgment incomprehensible to us he had put on such a fine shoe, his sackcloth would not have been torn and he himself would not have been girded about with gladness. But lest I linger too long upon these things, hastening onward under the preceding promise of love, I must now speak more explicitly, though briefly, of this second crown of the emperor.

Just as the emperor, his Father’s only-begotten and first-born, possessed from eternity from his Father the first crown of his eternal Godhead, so in time he assumed from his mother, the Virgin, the crown of our humanity. This crown, indeed, is that diadem in which the wise king proclaimed that this emperor was crowned by his mother: “Go forth, daughters of Zion,” he says, “and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him” (Song 3).

And behold, here is Solomon—indeed, more than Solomon. And behold the crown of Solomon, by which his mother is praised as having crowned him rather than clothed him. For in this flesh of our humanity and humility we see him now triumphing over earthly and aerial powers. By the merit of obedience, whereby he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross, the Father exalted this crown of his Son; indeed, his flesh blossomed anew [Col. 1345A], and thus, death having been conquered, he triumphed over his enemies.

And so this crown, tested on the cross as in a furnace through the fire of suffering, and purged of every rust of oldness, shone wholly resplendent, because the whole man blossomed anew. It appears, as it were, in a dye of blood: sackcloth pressed and trodden down, and transformed into a fine shoe. Hence the prophet says: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? This one, beautiful in his robe, advancing in the multitude of his strength” (Isa. 63).

Even in this crown from his mother he is so glorious, beautiful, and strong that he whom we recently saw made lower than angels, we now see worshipped by angels, exalted above angels and above every creature. Hence the Master says: “We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than angels, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death” (Heb. 2) [Col. 1345B].
