Behold the emperor’s twofold crown: the first, with which his Father crowned him, is the crown of omnipotence; the second, with which his mother crowned him rather than clothed him, is the crown of glory, sackcloth having thus been transformed into a fine shoe. For behold, he whom we saw wrapped in sackcloth, in whom his face seemed hidden and despised—so that we did not esteem him—behold, I say, this great emperor bearing a twofold crown, like a giant of twofold substance and two-formed nature: according to his first and eternal nature, in which he has a Father and not a mother, bearing the crown of omnipotence; according to his other nature, in which he has a mother and not a Father, bearing the crown of glory.

I am now silent about the third crown of our emperor: namely, that crown of thorns with which, after his Father and mother, his stepmother the Synagogue crowned him. I am silent about it because it has now, as it were, been swallowed up by the emperor’s other two crowns. It was neither a crown of power nor of glory, but of disgrace; yet by it he gained the glorious palm of that second crown which he received from his mother. In the first crown of our emperor is incomprehensible majesty; in the second, admirable glory; as in the third there had been contemptible humility, in which he had neither form nor beauty. For this was not a crown of beauty, but rather of dishonour. Hence, now that the emperor has been so exalted, that crown means nothing to the emperor, just as it means nothing to those who then thus crowned their emperor, now ours [Col. 1345D].

## On the twofold crown of the soldier

Behold, we have now heard that the emperor’s crown is twofold. The soldier’s likewise is twofold: surely twofold because his victory is twofold. Let us recall the preceding historical song about the soldier; for I do not think this has escaped us, unless perhaps the whole song has already so quickly escaped our memory. Let us recall, I say, what was sung above, and now touch upon this twofold victory of the soldier.

For above it was sufficiently sung and sung again how great was the endurance of the sufferer in exile, and again how great was the constancy of the combatant in martyrdom. Thus this soldier first conquered through exile, and this is the palm of the confessor [Col. 1346A]; secondly, through martyrdom, and this is the palm of the martyr. Therefore a crown is due to this palm and to that one: one to the confessor and priest, the other to the new martyr and soldier. And I already know that these have been rendered by the swift rewarder and just debtor.

Thus, above the common golden crown of confessors, there is also the little crown of martyrs, fashioned according to the exemplary pattern given in the law by the supreme artificer of all things and the giver of that crown. It is lofty through a manifold and distinct variety of gifts [the printed wording here is uncertain: “in terra silis”], and especially through the four expressly expressed and impressed principal virtues, as though through the four fingers of the Holy Spirit, its maker. It is called an *aureola*, “little golden crown,” not because the crown is small or diminished, but rather because the perfect, to whom alone it is to be given, are few.

This twofold crown of the triumphant soldier is, if I am not mistaken, that crown of wonderful magnitude which, as we inserted above in the history, the brother of Jerusalem, after becoming a fellow-citizen with angels through death, saw the Lord himself place upon the martyr’s torn and mangled head. Let us recall this preceding passage of the history.

Behold Thomas, whom we saw as a passible man, like ourselves, bearing our burden with us and sharing our weakness: how great a victor he is now, wearing a twofold crown—one as confessor, another as martyr—so that what is fitting for the soldier may also correspond to the emperor. And just as above we passed over the emperor’s third crown, so now we pass over the soldier’s third crown [Col. 1346B].

By the soldier’s third crown I mean the crown which was cut away from his head in the contest of martyrdom, yet through which the soldier acquired by the palm of martyrdom the two crowns that we have shown. Thus, through the corruptible and weak crown of his flesh, he obtained a double crown, just as the emperor, in his humanity, obtained it through his contemptible and mocking crown of thorns. Nevertheless, just as above we passed over that mocking crown of the emperor, so now we pass over this weak crown of the soldier. For that crown now means nothing to the triumphant soldier, since, being perishable, it has been turned into the corruption of flesh, not of spirit [Col. 1346C].

O how great a triumphant soldier he is: in all other things, and even in his crowns, he follows in a corresponding and similar way his emperor, the giant of twofold substance and two-formed nature! Just as his emperor bears a twofold substance, so he bears a double person: one of a confessor, the other of a martyr.

But what we have sounded by striking our harp, now that this third melody has begun—concerning the crowns of emperor and soldier and the correspondence of their invisible palm—has resounded more concerning the correspondence of their invisible palm than concerning their proposed and promised unity in that invisible palm. Yet it was not to be passed over here, concerning this correspondence in the homeland between emperor and soldier in their invisible palm, just as many other matters concerning the correspondence of their visible combat and visible palm upon the way were set forth before us.

For such evident and admirable correspondence between emperor and soldier, both upon the way and, as we have now shown concerning their crowns, in the homeland, both foreshadows and proves a great and ineffable unity between them in the homeland [Col. 1347A]. Indeed, the things expressly set forth concerning emperor and soldier commend and prove to us the unity of the whole head and body.

For what I say and expressly teach concerning the soldier’s correspondence to his emperor upon the way, as concerning one member of the head to the head, is likewise true—although it may not be expressly written—of each member of this head: in every individual member there is a great and most fitting correspondence with its own head, and a corresponding grace of each member toward its head, which is not that of another, according to the varied gifts of grace descending from the head to the members.

Accordingly, the bridegroom, who is the head of the bride’s body, promises: “We will make for you golden ornaments, variegated with silver” (Song 1). And elsewhere the same speaker says: “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken for? If she is a wall, let us build bulwarks upon it; if she is a door, let us fasten it with cedar boards” (Song 8) [Col. 1347B].

Therefore, although it may not be expressly written as it is now concerning emperor and soldier, there has nonetheless gone before upon the way a great correspondence of the individual members of the body with their head. Otherwise there would be no consequent union of head and body, nor one that was fitting or harmonious.

Therefore, after we have expressly been taught about the correspondence of emperor and soldier—not only in their visible combat and visible palm upon the way, but also in their invisible palm, in their crowns, in the homeland—we are now to speak of their unity, which already exists in the homeland. This is much greater, keener, subtler, and more difficult, since henceforth this third melody is to be formed upon the higher and sharper strings of the harp.

And first we shall begin to sound in our harp, in part, the general unity in the homeland of the whole head and body—Christ the bridegroom and the Church the bride [Col. 1347C]. For this is an exceedingly sweet, harmonious, and concordant melody in this respect, in which it is most fitting that nothing discordant or unmelodious be heard, since it concerns not so much correspondence as unity itself.

But in the final melody we shall return to emperor and soldier, while for the present we begin from the general kind. For what we now sound on our harp concerning the unity of head and body is precisely what must be hoped for and expected at the end of all things in the whole head and body, for emperor and soldier. Except that certain members of the body, the nearer they are to the head, are also more worthy and more closely joined to it, as though one with the head. Thus the Master teaches that star differs from star in glory, and the Master of masters teaches that many dwelling places are prepared in his Father’s house [Col. 1347D].

## Here the third melody first begins to be formed upon the higher strings of the harp.—Third note

Therefore, intending henceforth to form more subtly and keenly this third melody, already begun in the crowns of emperor and soldier, concerning their unity in the homeland through their invisible palm, as the subtle and keen Spirit of wisdom may deign to teach, we must first distinguish three kinds of vanities, or three unities [Col. 1348A]. Thus it may plainly appear which of the three unities is that unity between emperor and soldier which their great correspondence upon the way, so carefully shown as we have taught, proves.

For above we proceeded by this argument: if there was such correspondence between emperor and soldier upon the way, where there is such variety, diversity, adversity, distraction, and tearing apart, what will there be in that homeland of unity and peace—indeed, which is nothing but peace and unity—except some wonderful and admirable unity? Behold, this is how we proceeded by argument, until at last we have now arrived from correspondence at unity. Therefore we distinguish here three vanities—or unities—that we may explain what is that unity which emperor and soldier now possess in the homeland, and which such great correspondence between them earlier proved upon the way [Col. 1348B].

## He distinguishes three unities.—Fourth note

There are, then, as we have now begun to distinguish, three unities.

The first unity is the unity of nature alone; the second, of grace alone; the third is unity both of nature and of grace. The first unity, of nature alone, is in God among the Three. The second, of grace alone, is in God between the Lord and the man singularly assumed into unity of person, not of nature. The third, both of nature and grace, is between the Lord as bridegroom and the Church as bride.

Behold these three unities, and these three are in God, who is the first, highest, and principal unity. Thus these three unities are in that first, highest, and principal unity. The first is the unity of three persons: this is the one we called unity of nature alone. The second is the unity of two natures: this is the one we called unity of grace alone. The third is the unity of all spirits—of all, I say, who from the beginning have been foreknown and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. This is the unity we called unity both of nature and grace [Col. 1348C].

And though the role of grace is evident, I call it a unity also of nature because our first and principal unity, God himself, the one true God of all, though from eternity he belonged solely to his own nature, in time became of our nature by incomprehensible grace, uniting humanity to himself. Thus we are united to him now not only through grace but also through nature.

This is the unity of nature and grace between humanity alone and God, not between God and angel. For, as the Master says, “He nowhere takes hold of angels.” Nor do I mean the unity between God and the assumed man, which is of grace alone; rather, I mean that which is between God and humanity—between bridegroom and bride, Christ and Church, and now between emperor and the triumphant soldier. This is our principal intention, and for its sake we here introduce the others [Col. 1348D].

For this unity of ours is special and proper: not angelic but human. We, who still wander in the body of this death, await it through patience; and the triumphant soldier and emperor are now in it. The first kind of unity, that of nature alone, is among the Three—indeed, it is the Three and three—and is incomprehensible and ineffable. Yet, for the sake of our third unity, which is of nature and grace, we must speak a little of it. Likewise afterwards we must speak of the second, which is of grace alone, for the sake of this same third unity. For this third unity of ours, which is of nature and grace, is, as it were, composed from those two: the first is of nature alone; the other, of grace alone.

Therefore we must speak first of the first unity, especially since this third unity, like the second, is in the first unity, which is first and principal. Indeed, these three unities are, as it were, that one first and principal unity, as what follows will teach; and that first unity is the highest and first cause of both the second unity and the third [Col. 1349A].

## Here he first treats of the first and principal unity

Therefore, as we are to speak of this first and principal unity, we must now touch the first and higher strings of our harp [Col. 1349B]. First we must entreat that first and principal unity that, as I—whatever sort of little harpist I may be—am about to strike the harp for it and concerning it, it may unveil my eyes, so that I may know how to sound forth something concerning it whereby it may be made manifest to us what it is, and afterward, according to the capacity of our analogy, what it is in itself.

Thus, as that master-harpist also prayed, may he unveil our eyes so that we may behold the wonders of the law of this principal unity. He says “eyes,” not “eye,” for these eyes are many. There is the eye of the body; there is the eye of the heart, or reason; and there is also the eye of contemplation.

The eye of the body is open and sees clearly; the eye of the heart is weak and bleary; the eye of contemplation is clouded and dim-sighted. With the first eye a human being sees what is outside himself; with the second, what is within himself; with the third, what is above himself. With the first eye one sees bodies and what belongs to bodies through outward appearance; with the second eye one sees spirits and what belongs to spirits through experience; with the third one sees the first and principal unity, but in an image, through the dark likeness of an enigma [Col. 1349C].

The first, bodily eye draws a person onto the way and awakens the eye of the heart, as though sleeping. The second, the eye of the heart, guides the traveller now on the way and shows the road. The third, the eye of contemplation, now beholds and greets the homeland from afar. Let us see how.

## The first manifestation of the first and principal unity through the first, bodily eye and through the second, rational eye, in the first exemplar of nature.—Fifth note

[Col. 1349D]

With a human being bodily beholding the world and the things in the world, and seeing that neither the world nor anything in it is uncreated and unmade—as man himself, who excels among creatures, has been made—the eye of his heart or reason is at once awakened, so that through the creature bodily seen he may immediately conceive that it has some Creator whom he does not see. And thus, running in meditation through the various kinds of creatures—now visible, now invisible, now lowest, now intermediate, now highest—as though upon a ladder distinguished by various intervening steps, he strives by investigating the Creator to ascend. And at last, under the guidance of the rational eye, he finds one Creator of all things: namely, our first [Col. 1350A] and principal unity, the first and highest cause of all that exists, the eye of the heart having thus been awakened by the eye of the body and directing the ascents of the investigator.

And this is the first manifestation of our first and principal unity: its first knowledge, namely, through its creatures. Hence the Master says: “What is known of God is manifest in them; for God has manifested it to them” (Rom. 1). Therefore this eye of the heart, though weak and bleary, is nevertheless sufficient, so far as this manifestation is concerned, under its own guidance. Thus, as the Master teaches, those are without excuse who held down the truth of God in unrighteousness. For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God. The first manifestation, therefore, of our first unity is through works. And no one [Col. 1350B] who has these two eyes can deny this. For this can now, as it were, be seen eye to eye: the eye of the body having awakened the eye of the heart, and guiding us, still pilgrims, along this straight path of understanding.

But I shall for the present pass quickly over this first manifestation, since it has been investigated and discovered with very frequent and strenuous inquiry not only by Catholic theologians, whose contemplation is more exalted, but also by the philosophers of the Gentiles, who followed the exemplars of nature alone and not those of grace. They too have left us outstanding monuments of their genius on this subject and transmitted them for posterity to read. In these writings they pursued with the greatest diligence whatever truth they could discern more subtly [Col. 1350C] and deeply, by the keener eye of human reason, in the first exemplar of nature of which we have spoken, concerning the living and true God.

For in this matter God did not make the wisdom of this world foolish, nor destroy the wisdom of the wise, nor reject the prudence of the prudent. Rather, he made it foolish, rejected it, and destroyed it because, while they gazed too intently with the eye of human reason upon their sole exemplar of nature, they supposed that by it alone they could obtain complete wisdom; and, besides this wisdom which is as it were visible and worldly, they imagined that God possessed no hidden wisdom. Therefore, judging the visible exemplar of nature sufficient for wisdom, and supposing that there was no other exemplar for this purpose beyond it—the exemplar of grace of which we have already spoken—they despised that other as base and lowly.

And [Col. 1350D] lest anyone be uncertain what these exemplars are, one of which I call the exemplar of nature and the other the exemplar of grace: just as we previously distinguished three eyes, so we shall distinguish three exemplars for the three eyes continually to behold. The first of these three is the exemplar of nature; the second, the exemplar of grace; the third, the exemplar of life. Elsewhere in sacred discourse this third is called by Wisdom itself the book of life.

By the first, the exemplar of nature, I mean the world and the works of creation that are in the world. By the second, of grace, I mean the sacred writings and the more secret mysteries, hidden in them from the ages, of human restoration and divine knowledge. For I am not now speaking of the sacred writings according to that part of them which a little child grasps, but according to [Col. 1351A] that which even one fully trained and perfected in the law of God understands. Of this the Master says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect; yet not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing; but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the wisdom hidden away, which none of the rulers of this age knew” (1 Cor. 2). Indeed, the rulers of this age despised it as base and lowly—namely, the philosophers of the Gentiles, who appeared, through their pre-eminence in learning and reputation, to rule over the rest.

By the third exemplar, that of life, I mean the book of eternal predestination. In it are written from eternity those who are called saints according to purpose: all who before the ages were foreknown to be made conformable to the image of his Son—the Word, namely, who was in the beginning with the Father—the art [Col. 1351B] and wisdom, as it were, of almighty God; and those things which are with him and in him, the incomprehensible things of his divine wisdom.

In the first exemplar, then, which is here called that of nature, two eyes chiefly behold. First, the eye which we set above as the first, the eye of the body; and second, the eye of reason. But the bodily eye sees visible things alone, whereas the eye of reason reads through visible things and sees in the creature the invisible Creator. But in the other two exemplars, one of which we called that of grace and the other that of life, that third eye alone, which we called the eye of contemplation, gazes; for the things written in these exemplars are far too remote from the eye of reason, and still much farther from the eye of the body.

For the things in these two [Col. 1351C] exemplars are known to God. In them faith in invisible things alone—not visible creation, not reason—assists this third eye of contemplation. Therefore that first manifestation of the first and principal unity through works, which is read and seen in the first exemplar of nature, though first and philosophical, and though carefully and keenly examined by both eyes, is nevertheless an exceedingly alien and feeble manifestation in comparison with those things so invisible and incomprehensible that are written in the remaining two exemplars. It is no more comparable to them than the pupil of the eye or the flame of a lamp is to the brightness of the sun illuminating the world.

And especially in comparison with what is written in the third exemplar, called the book of life, this first manifestation of the first unity through creatures is [Col. 1351D] exceedingly feeble. For from these created forms and likenesses, and from sensible natures, it is shown more what this first unity of ours is not than what it is. For it is neither said to be that thing, nor according to that thing; rather, it is wholly above and altogether outside that by which it is demonstrated.

Hence, since it is itself uncircumscribable and indescribable, if some knowledge of it is to be gained, it must in some manner be described more by what it is not than by what it is. So that, in order to know what it is, it may for the present suffice us to know what it is not. Let everything that it has made be removed from it, so that even thus it may be known to be that alone which it did not make: an altogether different, altogether other, superessential essence.

For, to give one example out of many for the sake of [Col. 1352A] understanding: when it is said of this uncreated unity that “it is,” and likewise of any created thing that “it is,” the same word seems to say either the same thing, or at least something similar or common, of the uncreated and the created. But in truth the statement is altogether divergent, and the manner of predication on either side altogether unconnected and discordant—something that is scarcely apparent even to theologians. The predication is truly no less discordant between these than between such other statements as: “A boar is wild; a human being is just.”

So great is the distance in being between the creating unity, for which being is nothing other than being life, and the creature, for which being is nothing other than being corruptible. Therefore the superessential essence of this uncreated unity has not entered into the human heart. For it is neither [Col. 1352B] among, nor according to, the things that the human heart can understand or think. And consequently it is apprehended neither by the eye of the body nor by the eye of the heart, which sees nothing except things it knows or according to things it knows.

Therefore, speaking now, as it is given me by that first and principal unity itself, I have first proposed to demonstrate this alone concerning it: that it is. And I propose this through the first eye of the body, awakening the second eye of reason. For “the fool has said in his heart, There is no God” (Ps. 13). And this especially serves our purpose: so that, once it has been shown beforehand that it exists, it may consequently be demonstrated that neither in it nor with it is there any contrariety or opposition, nor likewise diversity or multiplicity, but unity alone. As one of the Masters [Col. 1352C] says: “With whom there is no change nor shadow of turning” (Jas. 1). He did not say merely that there is none in him, but that there is none even with him.

This too, if it has not slipped from memory, pertains to the purpose: for, according to our earlier promise, after having demonstrated in many ways above the conformity of emperor and soldier on the way, we are henceforth obliged to demonstrate their unity in the homeland. Yet this cannot be explained in few words. Therefore, if I become rather lengthy in composing this third melody, let the hearer not blame me but indulge me, because such weighty matters—and matters without which the purpose cannot be accomplished—cannot be set forth briefly.

For this very reason I distinguished the three unities above: first, as seemed fitting [Col. 1352D], now speaking of the first and principal unity and wishing to show through the things made by it that it exists—a point which can be made manifest and pertains to the purpose. Yet although it can be manifested in this way by the eye of the heart, demonstrating it to us through the first revelation of its creation, we must nevertheless afterwards attempt still further to open this same eye of our heart, though, as we have said, it is bleary and weak, so that the power and strength of its sight may be enlarged further for seeing and making known to us something more concerning this first unity of ours.

## FIRST MANIFESTATION OF THE FIRST UNITY

Concerning the first manifestation of our first unity, which is brought forth through created things, we first lay down this: although the kinds of creatures are various, there is nevertheless no [Col. 1353A] created thing whatsoever that does not, by manifesting, prove, and by proving, manifest this creating unity. As rays reveal the sun, so individual creatures reveal their Creator.

Nor do I think that anything has been created, or can be created, which does not draw from its Creator, just as it has its substance from him, so also some likeness to him. I mean some likeness, although hidden from us, by which every creature agrees with its Creator in some respect. For just as everything made cannot possibly be equal to him by whom it was made, so it cannot possibly be wholly unlike him by whom it was made: the thing made necessarily contracts some likeness to its maker, just as fruit must always draw some flavor from its root.

For if, according to the testimony of Scripture, all things God [Col. 1353B] had made were very good (Gen. 1), there is nothing in the universe which, just as it has its being from the highest good, does not also derive a participation in goodness, and thereby a likeness and resemblance. From this participation in goodness it follows that nothing whatsoever has been created which cannot do something and be useful for something. Nor do I think that anything can be created which cannot be useful for something; so great is the goodness of the Creator.

Since, therefore, there is nothing which does not derive a participation in goodness from the highest good, it follows at once that there is nothing which does not have some likeness and resemblance to the highest good. By this resemblance of participation, the uncreated and highest good can in some measure be understood and known through the created and lowest good in every creature.

Therefore there is nothing created, neither above heaven [Col. 1353C] nor beneath heaven, that does not in some measure manifest this its creating unity; so that, according to the prophet, its confession is over heaven and earth. For not only fire, air, water, earth, camels, elephants, leopards, bears, and lions confess and prove it together with all the host of heaven; but also flies, gnats, mosquitoes, and beetles. In the words of that eminent theologian drawn from philosophy: “How beautifully divine and heavenly things are manifested even through dissimilar symbols.”

Considering all these things, both the lowest and the highest, as though with one voice confessing and bearing witness to their Creator, the prophet cries out in wonder to the Creator of all: “Wonderful are thy testimonies; therefore [Col. 1353D] my soul has searched them out!” (Ps. 118). Accordingly, in his hymn-like song he summons to the praise of their Creator even the smallest things and those held in contempt: “Beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds” (Ps. 148).

Thus not only do the heavens declare the glory of God, but work clearly and manifestly utters to work, like day to day, that Word through which all things were made. The fullness of created things proclaims in all fullness this one Word, which speaks once, as though each individual creature were a certain word. Thus the whole world is, as it were, a bodily and visible Gospel of that Word through which all things in the world were made; all created things joyfully and variously announce their Maker well. And indeed they announce him variously: from the permanence of creatures [Col. 1354A] he is declared eternal; from their magnitude, mighty and immeasurable; from their strength, powerful; from their splendor, luminous; and from their beauty, beautiful.

Hence the Master-prophet says that the invisible things of God are perceived through the things made; and our prophet, contemplating all these things, says: “Thou hast made me glad, O Lord, in thy workmanship” (Ps. 91). From what we have set forth, therefore, it is entirely clear that through created things we are taught, the eye of reason thus demonstrating not only that our first and principal unity exists, but also in some degree what it is.

## SECOND MANIFESTATION THROUGH THE CREATOR’S GOVERNANCE  
### Note 6

But, as we stated above, let this same eye of our reason be extended [Col. 1354B] still further for seeing more. For it can be demonstrated not only from creation, but also from the governance of created things, that this unity of ours exists and, in some measure, what it is. Thus, just as the things made show the invisible things of God through their creation, so the same things show God’s power through their governance. Therefore the Master immediately adds: “His eternal power also,” teaching that, just as God’s invisible things are perceived through the things made, so likewise his power—and true power—is perceived through those same things.

For this is the wondrous power of God: that, just as he created the things made once, so after they have been made he governs them without ceasing. Therefore, from creation, which comes first, and from governance, which comes afterward, the divinity—which the Master places third—is manifested. And it is much more manifest from governance [Col. 1354C] than from creation. For we hold creation by faith alone, except insofar as faith in this matter receives some assistance from the eye of reason. Thus the Master says: “By faith we understand that the ages were framed by the word of God, so that visible things came to be from invisible things” (Heb. 11). We hold creation, therefore, by faith; but we daily perceive and bodily see, by the actual experience of things, the governance of the world.

For behold: there remains a certain solemn and appointed order of all worldly things. The year passes through months, the month through weeks, the week through days and nights; and by the same alternations the established law of the revolutions of sun and moon returns. Thus, for all the days of the earth, seedtime and harvest return, as the Lord said to Noah: [Col. 1354D] “All the days of the earth, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, night and day, shall not cease” (Gen. 8). Likewise, there is the daily, certain ebb and flow of the ocean. We behold and experience all these things every day.

But why enumerate each thing? The immutable law once established for all things, whether living or devoid of life, endures; and governance is suited and appropriate to the kind and variety of each thing. Thus, just as nothing is without a cause, so nothing is without a law of governance, nor is anything without order. But from whom comes this governance, or who is he who orders and governs in this way? For it is impossible that anything should govern itself or be governed by itself.

To give an example from the more worthy of creatures, endowed beyond others with rational judgment, I mean the human being: [Col. 1355A] not even the human being is under a governance held in his own hand. To pass over other matters, conception occurs without his own knowledge, and in conception there is guilt; afterwards comes birth, and in being born, punishment; then life continually in toil, and at last death by necessity. Surely a human being would govern himself otherwise if his own governance were entrusted to himself.

I am not now speaking of that self-governance of a person in which, because of sin, God often abandons a person and he walks in his own inventions; nor of that in which, while human beings serve in the captivity of this present life, the unjust daily prevail against the just and devour those more righteous than themselves, so that, in the complaint of one of the prophets, human beings are made like the fish of the sea and like creeping things having no ruler. I do not speak, I say, either of this or of that governance of the human being, but of another kind, by which each created thing maintains, according to the law imposed upon it by nature, the fixed order that we have touched upon.

For these former kinds are two—or rather three—governances [Col. 1355B] of the human being: the first ones arise from guilt, God justly permitting it; but the governance of which I now speak belongs to nature, God being its author from the beginning through his goodness. If, then, the first and highest cause of this natural governance in all things is sought, it is necessary finally to have recourse to some principle which both contains and governs this whole mass of the world. This is our first and principal unity, which we now seek to manifest through the governance of created things. Thus, as it was formerly made plain from the creation of the world [Col. 1355C], so now, secondly, from its governance, it clearly appears that this first unity of ours exists.

Its strength in governing is shown by the sustaining of so great a mass; its wisdom, by its ordering; its justice, by the frequent disturbances that occur among worldly things; and its mercy, by their continual restoration. By these as most splendid titles the unceasing power of the governor is made illustrious; and from them, just as before from creation, so now also from governance, there shines forth not only that it exists, but also in some measure what it is.

### Note 7

But perhaps the foolish adversary of our unity, who says in his heart, “There is no God” (Ps. 13), will mock at all that we have set forth, and at the arguments by which we seem to bind him as with more compelling [Col. 1355D] chains, asserting that there is neither God nor any creature. For he will assert that the things we bodily see are not created, but rather, as the Prince of the Apostles touches upon the error of such great folly by inserting it in his teaching, that “all things continue as they were from the beginning.” Thus he will hold that there is neither Creator nor anything created; or perhaps he may grant that some things have been made, but deny that anything has been created.

This was also handed down by certain more eminent philosophers among the Gentiles. Yet they did not, with the fool, say that God does not exist; rather, they said that there is one God, but maintained that he is by no means a creator, but an artificer, and that the world was made by God from matter coeternal with God, but was not created—since to create is to make something out of nothing. The fool, however, says that there is not even a God.

## THIRD MANIFESTATION OF THE FIRST UNITY THROUGH THE EYE OF REASON ALONE

[Col. 1356A]

First, then, I ask this man whether there is any first and highest cause of this sensible world, which he contends has endured thus from the beginning, or none. Perhaps he will say that there is no cause of its existence, because it is eternal and exists from itself, not from another. Leaving other matters aside for the moment, I shall ask whether the things living in it, namely, living creatures, have life from themselves or from the world itself.

I do not think that anyone would be so extremely foolish as to say that they have it from themselves. Therefore the things which live in the world must have life from the world itself, since it could not be said that they have it from elsewhere, if the world itself exists not from elsewhere but from itself. Likewise, rational beings, which have judgment of reason and freedom [Col. 1356B] of will, must have these from the world itself, since they do not have them from themselves.

Therefore, if this sensible world is eternal and exists from itself and not from another, and gives life and, together with life, judgment of reason and freedom of will, then according to the fool it irrefutably has the nature of God. Thus the fool who imagines this in his heart, though unknowingly denying God in his heart, makes the world itself God by attributing to it the nature of divinity.

Since he denies that it has this nature, it remains that, although he says the world is eternal, he must assign it some cause—and an eternal cause, since the world itself, of which it is the cause, is eternal. Since, therefore, this cause of the world is eternal and is its first and highest cause, I ask whether this cause [Col. 1356C] is life itself, or participates in life, or is utterly without life.

But who is so foolish as to say that it is utterly without life, when so many things in the world have life from it and, together with life, judgment of reason and freedom of will? Furthermore, nothing without life is better or so good as that which is life or has life, because nothing without life can enjoy blessedness, and therefore nothing without life can be blessed. But this first and highest cause of the world, of which I am now speaking, must be both more powerful and better than everything possessing life, since this sensible world and everything living in it proceed from it.

Therefore, if this cause does not lack life—as it necessarily does not—it follows that this cause, so magnificent, is either life itself or a participant in life. But if it participates in life, there [Col. 1356D] will be some cause of that participation. For nothing participates in any good whose cause is not greater, fuller, and higher than it, and from which what it participates descends. But then this would not be the first and highest cause, as has been granted, but there would be another cause still greater and higher. Thus the inquiry would extend to infinity, until some cause were found in which life was not participated but was rather the fountain of life itself.

It remains, therefore, that our first cause and the cause of the sensible world, since it can neither lack life nor participate in life, is, as has been shown, life itself. And no one is so foolish as to deny that life is blessed, and blessed not from another but from itself. Therefore even the fool who says in his heart that there is no God must confess that this is God.

### Note 8. FOURTH MANIFESTATION OF THE FIRST UNITY

[Col. 1357A]

Furthermore, since this sensible world is always in motion, and there is nothing in it that does not fall under some kind of motion, our fool may be asked from whom comes all this motion. For philosophers long ago demonstrated in many ways, even apodeictically, that motion neither is nor can be except from something immovable. Indeed, they have shown that in everything moving in a circle the center always remains immovable. Therefore, according to the most certain demonstration of the philosophers, all motion of this sensible world must proceed from something immovable.

One of our theologians agrees with this when speaking of the spirit of wisdom: “It is,” he says, “an intelligent spirit, secure, stable, subtle, mobile, and comprehending all [Col. 1357B] spirits”; and immediately adds: “For wisdom is more mobile than all mobile things.” Behold: he who first called the spirit of wisdom stable afterwards calls it mobile, and even more mobile than all mobile things. I judge this to have been said chiefly because this spirit of wisdom, which comprehends all spirits, is the first and highest cause of every act and every motion, as is written elsewhere: “Remaining unmoved, it gives all things motion.”

Thus this immeasurable spirit, which comprehends all spirits and from which comes every motion of all moving heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings, is like an immovable center, more immovable than everything that appears immovable.

### Note 9. FIFTH MANIFESTATION

[Col. 1357C]

Furthermore, even if there were, as the fool asserts, no knowledge or foreknowledge of future things from eternity, yet true knowable things concerning the future would exist, and thus they could then be known and foreknown. I ask the fool, therefore, in what this power of knowing or foreknowing future things would reside. For this power then existed, and it was necessary that it should reside in something. I ask, then, in what it resided, and what that thing was which could know or foreknow future things.

### Note 10. SIXTH MANIFESTATION

I now pass over many arguments, both philosophical and theological, incomparably greater than those I have introduced, alike in brilliance and sharpness of thought, because of my own slowness of understanding. I pass them over because they belong more to others than to us, though they are customarily adduced, and can effectively be adduced, to manifest our first and principal [Col. 1357D] unity: namely, the one principle without a principle.

Among other arguments, by them the opponents of this one principle are submerged in the abyss of infinity. For they argue as follows: either there is some principle without a principle, or there is none. But no principle is without a [Col. 1358A] principle; therefore there was no first thing before which another was not earlier. Thus there will be an infinity, without a beginning and therefore eternal, of things or causes mutually preceding and following one another.

And so from the foregoing we now, as it were, hold two things: the infinity of preceding and succeeding causes, and its eternity. Thus with infinity we have eternity, and with eternity we now have infinity; and so we have some principle without a principle, because we have eternity. Moreover, we have an infinity of things preceding and succeeding one another. This must seem absurd and impossible to everyone who gives even a little attention.

And although many such arguments can be brought forward in these matters, the human mind is never satisfied and does not rest until it finds one principle of all things without a principle. It is as though this were implanted in it by nature: that it first ceases and rests when, by reasoning, it has found him who is both its own end and that of all things, and their principle.

### Note 11. SEVENTH MANIFESTATION

But why does this eye of our reason wander so far and so widely through the ethereal and airy regions, through heavenly and earthly things? What we seek is within ourselves; in ourselves above all else is that through which this first [Col. 1358B] unity of ours can be manifested to us—both that it exists and, to some extent, what it is. It is in us, I say, who above other things have been made in its image and likeness. Hence this knowledge is more familiar to us from ourselves and within ourselves.

Let us therefore turn the eye of our reason back upon ourselves. For behold, our rational mind possesses judgment of reason for discerning, freedom of will for choosing, and the treasure-house of memory for storing. We see and experience in ourselves, by the eye of our reason, what we are now saying. And likewise we see that these things belonging to us are not from ourselves but from another. For “what hast thou that thou didst not receive?” Consider your body and the things of the body; consider also your spirit and the things of the spirit. Both reason itself and most certain experience teach you that in either of these natures you have nothing which you did not receive.

You see plainly, therefore, that you have received these things; see next from whom you received them. Perhaps you will say: from the parents who begot [Col. 1358C] you. But from whom did they receive them? Truly, you will plunge into the abyss of infinity unless you find some first and highest principle, from which you received these things—though through many stages and descents—as from the first, highest, and principal cause.

Yet I ask further from whom you received all these things which you have and which you are known to have received. For I do not approve your first answer, by which you say that you received your whole self from your parents. For although you received flesh from the progenitors of your flesh, did you receive your [Col. 1358D] soul from them likewise? But let it be granted that you received the soul also; I say this because many great authorities taught that the soul descends by propagation.

Did you receive from them also the things in the soul—namely, judgment of reason, freedom of will, and the treasure-house of memory—which often flourish more vigorously in children than in their parents? But let it be granted that you received these too from them, together with the soul and the soul’s natural powers or capacities. But what of gratuitous gifts? If gifts of nature come from parents of the flesh, do gifts of grace likewise?

Did an unbelieving, fornicating, gluttonous father, defiled by the filth of every vice, confer upon his devout son the grace of faith, the purity of continence, the measure of sobriety, and, finally, the virtue of all uprightness and [Col. 1359A] holiness? Yet it is certain that the devout son of an iniquitous father possesses these things. Therefore, to leave aside gifts of nature, tell me, O fool: from whom does the devout son of an iniquitous man receive these gifts of grace? Certainly not from his parents, because they are wicked; nor from his own nature, which is from the mass of iniquity, this fruit being from an apostate root—namely, from wicked parents, grandparents, great-grandparents, and, if you wish, from wicked ancestors still farther back.

Here, then, I stand and press the fool to teach me whence such great gifts of grace come to this man. And because he is ashamed to confess it, I shall declare it: certainly from him “from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends, from the Father of lights.”

### Note 12. EIGHTH MANIFESTATION

[Col. 1359B]

And, to open our eye of reason still further, so that against the fool we may demonstrate other proofs necessary and helpful to our purpose, I ask the fool whether there is anything so powerful that nothing is more powerful than it. If he does not grant this, there will then be an infinity of powerful beings and powers. For if, although there are many powers, nothing is so powerful that there is not yet something more powerful, then there will be an infinity of powerful beings mutually preceding and succeeding one another, such that there will be no first and no last.

Since this is manifestly foolish, it remains that there is something so powerful that nothing is more powerful than it. And since nothing is more powerful than it, I immediately ask whether anything can be more powerful than it. If he grants that something can be more powerful than that than which nothing is now more powerful, I at once infer that there is some cause so strong and powerful that it can bring this about. Thus there is some cause so powerful and strong that it can make something more powerful than that than which nothing is now more powerful.

Therefore this cause itself is stronger, more effective, and more powerful than that of which you say that nothing is [Col. 1359C] now more powerful. For if the cause is powerful enough to make something still more powerful than that than which nothing is now more powerful, then beyond doubt it is itself more powerful than that than which you say that nothing is now more powerful. Thus, by your own concession, that thing of yours which you said is now such that nothing is more powerful than it will have above it something more powerful: namely, a cause so powerful that it can make something more powerful than that powerful thing of yours, than which you said nothing is now more [Col. 1359D] powerful. And thus that powerful thing of yours will not be as powerful as you said.

It remains, therefore, that if there is something than which nothing is more powerful—which is necessary, since otherwise there would follow an infinity of powerful beings mutually preceding and succeeding one another, as has already been shown—then it follows that this same thing is also such that nothing can be more powerful than it, according to the course of reasoning just demonstrated. Once it is granted, therefore, that there is something than which nothing is more powerful, it follows at once that there is something than which nothing can be more powerful. For that powerful thing than which nothing can be more powerful could not exist except through that which already exists and is already powerful, and than which nothing is more powerful.

Since, then, there is something than which nothing is more powerful, [Col. 1360A] and nothing can be more powerful than it, I add yet a third point and ask whether there can be anything else as powerful as that than which nothing is more powerful and than which nothing can be more powerful. If he grants this, it will at once consequently appear that nothing can be as powerful as that than which nothing is more powerful and than which nothing can be more powerful; and that this very thing is omnipotent. For these three converge: namely, that nothing is more powerful than it; that nothing can be more powerful; and, thirdly, that nothing can be equally powerful. But if he does not grant it, but asserts that something else can be as powerful as that than which nothing is more powerful and than which nothing can be more powerful, then, conversely, it will follow that there is, above that than which, as he has already granted, nothing is more powerful and [Col. 1360B] nothing can be more powerful, a cause so powerful and so strong that it can produce another power equal to that power than which nothing can be more powerful. For a cause which can produce another power equal to that power than which now nothing is more powerful and cannot be more powerful, is more powerful than that power; for, if another power were equal to it, it would be greater and more powerful. Therefore that same cause is now superior to and more powerful than this power, concerning which it has nevertheless already been granted that nothing is more powerful than it or can be. Hence it is now clear that, once it has been shown that there is something than which nothing is more powerful, and that nothing can be more powerful than it, it will consequently follow that nothing can be equally powerful.

For from the first point, namely [Col. 1360C] that there is something than which nothing is more powerful—which was demonstrated above—it follows immediately and necessarily, as we have shown beforehand, that this same thing is that than which nothing can be more powerful. And from this second point, namely that there is something than which nothing can be more powerful, this third necessarily follows immediately: namely, that this same thing is so powerful that nothing can be equally powerful. The course of reasoning is the same in these matters: as it is between the first and second points, so afterwards it is between the second and third. Since, therefore, these three coincide in one thing—namely, that there is something than which nothing is more powerful; that it itself is that than which nothing can be more powerful; and further, that this same thing is that than which nothing can be equally powerful—it follows that this same thing is omnipotent, powerful over [Col. 1360D] all things; and thus, whether he will or no, the fool must admit that God exists.

## Briefly Recapitulating What Has Preceded, He Next Shows How the First Unity Is Manifested through the Third Eye, That of Contemplation. Note 13.

From what has preceded, then, it has already been shown to some extent, both through the first eye of the body, which awakens the eye of reason, and through the second eye, reason alone, that our first and principal unity exists. This has indeed been shown in many ways: first through the creation of things, secondly through their governance, and variously through other matters introduced here and there. It remains now—and the previously laid-out order so requires, if this too is granted from above—that after those two eyes of body and heart, which direct the progress of our mind in that first pattern of nature [Col. 1361A] which, as we recalled above, is the world and the things in the world, and through which we have read thus far, thereby making it somewhat manifest that our first unity exists, we should next show, through the third eye of contemplation, what it is and how it is.

For neither the eye of the body nor that of the heart suffices for this; only the eye called that of contemplation is necessary. Hence, after the first pattern, that of nature—the world and the things in the world—we must proceed to the second pattern, that of grace, which we said above consists in the sacred utterances and in the mysteries of divine knowledge contained in them. Finally, we must proceed to the third pattern, which we likewise named above: the pattern of life, and the incomprehensible things of the divine majesty contained in it. It is chiefly in these two patterns that the third eye, [Col. 1361B] called the eye of contemplation, beholds.

Of this eye of contemplation the Bridegroom says to the Bride: “You have captured my heart with one of your eyes.” “With one,” he says, “of the eyes that are in your heart you have captured me.” For each eye—the eye of the heart and the eye of contemplation alike—is in the heart. But one alone is called the eye of the heart or of reason; the other, though it too is in the heart, is not called the eye of the heart but of contemplation. By it the Bridegroom is captured by the Bride; by it the incomprehensible is held, the infinite comprehended, and the inaccessible attained. Hence this is pre-eminently called the eye of contemplation. For here, as the sun to a cloud, the very form of faith is joined to a shadow, while reason alone stands, as it were, astonished and stunned before so great [Col. 1361C] a vision, its entire office in this respect being abolished.

## He Teaches That There Is a Twofold Mode of Manifestation through the Third Eye, That of Contemplation. Note 14.

Nevertheless, according to the two patterns which we have distinguished, this holy manifestation has a twofold mode. The eye of contemplation, of which we speak, beholds by each: one is instruction through the sacred utterances, and this belongs to the second pattern, that of grace; the other is inspiration through the Spirit’s invisible illumination, and this belongs to the third pattern, that of life. For by these two modes one contemplates our first unity: either as instructed or as inspired.

Yet the sacred utterances contain much which the eye of reason alone suffices to apprehend, as being more open; and in these is the first part of theology, which may be called worldly. They also contain matters more secret and more hidden, in apprehending which the eye of reason immediately fails. Thus our Prophet says: “My eyes have failed for thy word” (Ps. CXVIII). In these is the second part of theology, which may be called supercelestial or mystical. For these, therefore, the sharper eye of contemplation is now necessary to us. Though it is one, it contemplates in two ways: either by mystical instruction in the Scriptures or by inward inspiration.

I say that it contemplates not only that our first and principal unity exists—for the revelation given by the preceding eye suffices for that—but, in accordance with the capacity of mortal human nature, also what it is and how it is. Concerning the first mode of manifestation, that through instruction, our Prophet says: “The unfolding of thy words gives light” (ibid.). The second mode of holy manifestation is in obedience to the commandments, when the commandments are not merely known but performed. Of this mode of manifestation our Prophet likewise says: “From thy commandments I have understood” (ibid.). For he did not say that he understood the commandments, but that he understood *from* the commandments—that is, from keeping them. Accordingly the Wise Man says: “You have desired wisdom: keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to you” (Ecclus. I).

The first mode of manifestation, through instruction in the Scriptures, is from God but mediately, because it is through human beings—namely, through mystical theologians, who have ministered to us both the Scriptures and mystical instruction in the Scriptures. Some of them, the greater ones, were taught the sacred utterances immediately by the very Spirit of wisdom. Hence they too were called *theodidacti*, “God-taught”; one of them boasts that he received the Gospel not from a human being nor through a human being, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ. The second mode of manifestation, through inward inspiration, is always immediately from God himself, not from a human being nor through a human being. Hence this mode of holy manifestation is far worthier, far more exalted, and keener, by as much as truth differs from figure, brightness from shadow, and the body itself from an image.

For sacred Scripture is, as it were, a figure of truth, a shadow of light, and a mirror of a reflected [Col. 1362C] image. Through parables, figures, and riddles in the mystical utterances of Scripture, truth is reflected to us as in certain images in a mirror. Hence, as an image in a mirror, God is in sacred utterance; and the sacred utterances themselves are called imaginary Scriptures, in which there is reflected to us something like an image of truth rather than truth itself. Therefore, for us who live in the shadow of faith and pass through an image, this mode of manifestation through imaginary Scriptures is far more familiar, since it is common to good persons and evil alike; whereas the other, which occurs through inspiration, belongs only to the good, not to the evil.

## First, Concerning the Mode of Manifestation That Occurs through Scripture. Note 15.

[Col. 1362D]

Therefore, in order that we may take our beginning in the Scriptures, and even in the Lord’s commandments themselves, for this mode of manifestation which occurs through the Scriptures—may the Lord, the sanctuary itself of this manifestation, grant us understanding—Scripture says: “Hear, for the Lord thy God is one God” (Deut. VI). Behold: the beginning of the heavenly commandments starts from one, points to one, and commends one to us. “Hear,” it says, “the Lord thy God is one God.”

And truly he is one—the one whom the patriarch, father of all believers, seeing three, worshipped as one. And this too is one: that One concerning whom another, from the Father yet one with the Father, says: “I and the Father are one” (John X). In this One, although there are three, there is not a ternary, because there is no number. For whenever we use numerable names, it does not immediately follow that there is number there. Thus we count unities themselves and forms, which nevertheless cannot be subjects because they are forms. Similarly, we count names, true or false propositions, and many things of this kind, although number is not in them.

Therefore, to ascend from these lowest things to higher things: when we speak of God and say three persons, what is understood is not a ternary but a Trinity, and solitude is removed. “Trinity” is as though one were to say “the unity of three.” “Three” or “of three” is said only for the sake of distinction, not on account of number. Hence one of the orthodox says: “This is truly that which is one, in which there is no number, nothing else in it besides that which it is.” For it cannot become a subject, since it is form; and forms cannot be subjects.

Concerning this form the Master says: “Who, being in the form of God” (Phil. II). Therefore there is nothing in this form which is not itself. Nothing is added to it, nothing removed from it, because nothing happens to it accidentally. Hence those personal properties by which the three persons are distinguished from one another do not, contrary to the foolish doctrine of certain persons, accrue to the divine *ousia*; rather, they inhere in it. For this reason our Catholic mother worships, as unity in the essence and equality in the majesty, so also property in the persons. Accordingly, in that special kind of prayer called the Mass, she solemnly sings: “That in the confession of the true and eternal Godhead, property may be adored in the persons, unity in the essence, and equality in the majesty.”

Property, then, is worshipped in the persons—not any property common to the three persons, for then it would no longer be property but commonality—but the proper and indivisible property of each individual person. Thus the meaning is: in the confession of the true and eternal Godhead, property is worshipped in the persons, that is, the proper property in each of the persons. Although some of the orthodox interpret the entire statement thus: “Property in the persons, unity in the essence, and equality in majesty are worshipped”—that is, the persons are distinct, the essence one, and the majesty equal.

But to return to our subject: in this supremely excellent essence, everything that it has is in it; nothing is added, [Col. 1363D] nothing absent; everything which it is, it itself is. Hence, when we speak of it by participial names, these must be understood rather substantively and essentially, even if something is said participially. Things said of it participially immediately signify that it is the complete nature of those things which are said of it. Thus, according to that rule of the logicians, predicates are such as their subjects permit them to be.

Therefore, when we speak of so great a matter, the force of all our words is immediately swallowed up by the profundity of the subject, and their proper significance is exhausted. To say once what it is is to have said under one word everything that it is. Its truth is its eternity; its eternity, its goodness; its goodness, its immutability; and this is its wisdom, and this its [Col. 1364A] essence. Likewise, whichever of these you name, each will in turn be the other—indeed, neither one nor another, but the simplest and indivisible unity, without otherness. So completely is this the case that there is no plurality, diversity, or multiplicity either within it or likewise alongside it.

Hence one of the teachers wisely says: “With whom there is no change nor shadow of turning” (Jas. I). He did not say “in whom,” but that even “with him” it is not; thus he makes most clear that it is much less in him, since it cannot even be beside him. Hence at the end of the ages, when all things have been brought back to this our first and principal unity, and all the members formerly scattered have then been united to the Head and Christ made whole, there will then be absolutely no opposition or diversity even beside [Col. 1364B] him, but that unity of nature and grace which we numbered above as the third, indivisible and indissoluble for eternity. What follows will show this better and more fittingly in its proper place.

It is clear, then, from what has preceded that when God is called powerful, wise, good, and the like, this is a repetition of the same thing, not a numbering of different things. It is as if one were to say of one and the same weapon: “This weapon is a sword, this is a blade, this is an edge”; or of one person: “This man is Simon, this is Peter, this is Cephas.” Yet that eternal and omnipotent nature is called by many names because of the various effects it visibly displays in things, and the powers of those effects: as it is called powerful because of the greatness of the works which we behold; merciful because of the works of mercy which it bestows upon us; and similarly in other respects.

Thus the sun is said to be hotter in summer and less hot in winter, although in itself it is neither more intense nor less intense in heat, but is so described because of its varied effects which we see and feel according to the variation of the seasons. Similarly, one person, or any one thing, is often designated by two or three names for various causes, although it is only one person. But every comparison of earthly things with God is exceedingly inadequate and dissimilar. Nevertheless, for the sake of speaking about ineffable things—so that we may in some fashion say what we cannot say in any fashion—the weakness of our understanding compels us to have recourse to visible and familiar things, so that, veiled in figures and similitudes known to us, the inaccessible light of truth may enlighten us. Weak eyes behold the sun’s light more freely when it is covered by a cloud, which they could not look upon in its brilliance.

God, therefore, is spoken of in many ways. Accordingly, one of the theosophers describes, among other things, the Spirit of wisdom as manifold and yet the same simple Spirit; likewise the same author describes that same Spirit of wisdom as moving and yet stable, as we have recalled that we explained above. The Spirit of wisdom is called manifold both because it receives many names and because it distributes many gifts, and especially because it is said to possess many things in itself—for example, eternity, goodness, power, wisdom, and many others of this kind. Yet it is described as the same simple Spirit, because, although it is said to possess many things in itself, it has nothing other than what it is itself.

For in God essence is not one thing, so that he exists, and power another, by which he is able; nor is wisdom another, by which he is wise. Rather, his essence is whatever belongs to him, and everything belonging to him is God. Therefore it truly and necessarily follows that God is the simplest essence, since there is nothing belonging to him which is not himself: he participates in nothing. Behold how lofty, how hidden, and how incomprehensible to the eye of human reason are the mysteries of divine knowledge in the pattern of grace! To behold them in whatever measure, the third eye—the eye of contemplation alone—is necessary.

Behold upon what sharp and subtle strings of our harp you move your hand, while I strike the harp amid all the harmony of sacred utterances. For nothing of my own is heard here, but only the sound and meaning of thy utterances, O Lord, whom I have understood from thy commandments, and of thine orthodox teachers: all of whom, undoubtedly, unanimously and harmoniously sing, according to the understanding of sacred utterances given to them, concerning the wholly simple unity of the Creator and Governor of all things, what we have hitherto echoed concerning it upon our harp.

Yet I, a sinful little man, though I move my hand, strike the harp, and hear the sound, have become to myself, who speak these things, like a barbarian—like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal, producing sound without understanding. For the corruptible body weighs down the mind and constricts the understanding. I utter words of holy faith and of the saints, by which we are taught not only that our first and principal unity exists, but also what it is and how it is. But the understanding hidden in these holy and profound words of sound faith is far removed from me, like a hungry person carrying on the road bread unbroken in its crust, a kernel in its shell, and marrow in a bone.

O glorious Unity, I call thee thyself as witness: I believe—indeed, if I, still a pilgrim on the way, dared to go beyond faith, I know—these things are not lacking to thee. I know, I say, that thou art power living in itself, which is nowhere absent and never fails; eternity which neither began nor ends; [Col. 1365D] truth which can neither be deceived nor deceive; wisdom which neither seeks nor diminishes. I know thee to be good without quality, great without quantity, presiding without position, and ruling and containing all things without motion. I know likewise that thou art before all things as their beginning, above all things as their summit, within all things as their remedy, beneath all things as their foundation, outside all things as having no fellowship, and after all things as the last, in accordance with thy sacred utterance concerning thyself: “I am Alpha and Omega; I am the first and I am the last” (Apoc. XX).

Hence I know thee to be Trinity without ternarity; incommunicable without singleness; incomparable without weight; and inestimable without measure. Yet thou alone, without number, weight, and measure, dost order all things in number, weight, and [Col. 1366A] measure. According to thy Scriptures I know thee thus, and I know these things concerning thee: nevertheless, there is nothing belonging to thee which is not thou thyself. Thou art superessential essence and the simplest essence, without rank, without difference, without diversity, without number, participating in nothing and subject to none. These things, I say, by the holy instruction of thy Scriptures, I know thee to be; these things I know concerning thee.

But in this long pilgrimage of mine, I am much as if torn apart and unstitched. Even though I know from thy Scriptures that thou art these things, I understand little or nothing of how or in what way thou art them. Rather, this one thing alone—O my Lady and Creator—how thou art this first, principal, and most simple unity: my eyes fail for this word which is thine and concerns thee. Thus thy knowledge, from thee, has become marvellous above me.

But, my Lady and Creator, Unity most sweet and most radiant to me, grant to thy boy, whatever kind of harpist he may be, so to hear upon this thy harp the sound of thy voice concerning thee that thou mayest also grant him some meaning or understanding. Then this melody will be better, more pleasing—indeed truly sweetest—to me, who now strike the harp as thou thyself deignest to speak concerning thyself and through thyself; and, if it should please thee that my mother the Church also hear it at some time, it will be a melody more welcome and sweeter to her hearing.

Indeed, to attain this desire of mine, the sacred utterances themselves teach me, speaking somewhere to me thus: “Son, thou hast desired wisdom: keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to thee” (Ecclus. I). Thus this manifestation of our first and principal unity will come not through bare and naked knowledge of the Scriptures alone, concerning which we have already introduced some matters, but rather through obedience to the commandments.

But since it seems to me that I must now proceed from pattern to pattern, from the pattern of grace to the pattern of life, I must in passing repeat what is like the first. For it is evident, unless I am mistaken, and most clear from the matters we have introduced, that through the pattern of grace we are instructed, to some extent according to the capacity of the human condition, not only that our first and principal unity exists, but also what it is and how it is; and that to apprehend the mysteries of divine teaching contained in this pattern of grace, neither the eye of the body nor even that of reason suffices, but only the gaze of the eye of contemplation. Now, therefore, we must proceed from the second pattern, that of grace, to the third pattern, that of life, in which, as we said beforehand, our third eye—the eye of contemplation alone—beholds, just as it does in the pattern of grace.

## Manifestation of the First and Principal Unity through the Third Eye, That of Contemplation, in the Third Pattern, That of Life. Note 16.

The pattern of life, as we have recalled that we said above, is the book of eternal predestination. In it are written all who are predestined to life. Of it Truth itself says: “Rejoice, because your names are written in the book of life.” And our Prophet says: “In thy book all shall be written; days shall be formed, and none among them” (Ps. CXXXVIII). He says that they “shall be written,” though they were written before the ages; for they appear, as it were, to be written for the first time when they begin to act. Then their days are formed, when, ascending little by little from virtue to virtue, as from brightness to brightness, they are fully enlightened by the Sun of righteousness; and, brought out of corrupted human darkness, are made the light of the world—transformed into days, though formerly they were children of darkness, children of men, human beings, flesh from flesh.

Hence it fittingly follows: “and none among them.” For those written in the book of life and whose days are thus formed ought now rather to be called gods or days than human beings, in accordance with the saying of this same Prophet: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. LXXXI); “but you shall die like all others.” Therefore, in this pattern [Col. 1367B] of life, all who are written in it, all who are foreordained to life, read attentively when they continually devote themselves to the works of their salvation; and they study in it when they labor to understand what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.

Thus, in this third pattern, by the third eye of contemplation, our first and principal unity is manifested to the righteous through inward inspiration, just as it is shown to those instructed in the preceding pattern of grace through instruction understood by the same eye of contemplation. But in the earlier pattern of grace this manifestation occurs, as it were, through bare and naked knowledge of the commandments; while in this pattern of life the same manifestation occurs through obedience to the commandments inspired from above. Thus, as we have set forth above and repeat here, is the fatherly counsel of the Wise Man: “Thou hast desired wisdom: keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to thee” (Ecclus. I). “Keep,” he says, “the commandments.” For this other knowledge is far holier, worthier, and more familiar through obedience itself than through knowledge of the sacred law; without such obedience, knowledge is, as it were, foreign and remote.

Hence those who know from afar and are themselves known from afar are said to know thus: “He knows the lofty from afar”; they are lofty indeed by knowledge, though remote by disobedience. Therefore they know from afar like strangers, not as fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household. So foreign is this knowledge without the obedience of the commandments that the sacred utterances themselves, through which they know, testify that they do not know, according to the saying of one of the teachers: “He who says that he knows him and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John II); and: “Everyone who sins has neither seen him nor known him” (1 John III); and: “He who does not love does not know God.” Yet the sacred utterances frequently and plainly testify that knowledge of God may be possessed without keeping the commandments and without love of God.

Hence a distinction must be made between the two kinds of knowledge of God concerning which Scripture speaks so differently and, seemingly, in opposition. For as leaves differ from fruit, so these two knowledges of God differ. In that knowledge of God which belongs to the pattern of grace through knowledge of the Scriptures, there are sayings of wisdom; but in this knowledge which belongs to the pattern of life through obedience to the commandments, there are the deeds themselves. The former is for adornment, but the latter for fruit. Therefore the former does not suffice for itself without the latter, but the latter suffices for itself without the former.

Thus many have lived truly and holily in solitudes, possessing no books but only charity, by which they fulfilled the commandments of the law; and so the more inwardly, the more intimately they possessed the knowledge of God. Thus Truth itself says in the Gospel: “He who loves me shall be loved by my Father, and I will love him and will manifest myself to him” (John XIV). For no manifestation of the truth of the Church is so perceptive or so effective as inward love of God himself, arising from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned and rooted faith. To love him is like a ray of heavenly fire rising from the lover’s heart to that supreme object which alone is truly to be loved; it unites with that which it loves, and this surely does not occur without a certain delightful manifestation. Thus the Beloved says above: “I will manifest myself to him.”

Nor should this be understood of the future manifestation for which we wait, any more than the preceding statement about love should be understood of the future. This manifestation is present because it is brought about through inwardly bestowed love. Hence we said that obedience to the commandments occurs through inward inspiration; and this manifestation belongs only to the good, and to all of them, yet to each according as God has apportioned the measure of faith. The former manifestation through instruction in the Scriptures, however, is common to good and evil persons.

But this manifestation of our first unity is perfect when knowledge is joined to action. Then, for the manifestation of this unity, the two patterns concur: the pattern of grace and the pattern of life, while the eye of contemplation guides the mind’s steps from each direction. From the pattern of grace comes knowledge; from the pattern of life, righteous action. Then there will be an intellectual manifestation of our first unity. For then you understand for the first time, because then you first read in yourself what you know more in your heart than in a book, your knowledge then first passing into understanding. Otherwise, if you read in me and not in yourself, you will not have read in yourself, and thus there will be no understanding: “The fear of the Lord is understanding.”

Hence the saints so devoutly desire and so frequently ask that understanding may be granted to them in the sacred utterances. Thus our Prophet says in the Psalm: “Give me understanding, and I shall search thy law and keep it with my whole heart” (Ps. CXVIII). As though he said: “When understanding has been given me, I shall obtain these two things: knowledge of the law and observance of the commandments.” And elsewhere: “Give me understanding, and I shall live” (Ps. LXXIII). If understanding consisted in knowledge alone, life would not thereby result.
