Thus understanding encompasses both manifestations of our first unity: that which comes through knowledge from the second pattern, that of grace, and the other which comes through righteous action from the third pattern, that of life.

Thus the manifestations of our first and principal unity, which we have pursued from the beginning to this point, are three: the first is, as it were, bodily, from created things, through the first eye of the body awakening the second eye of reason; the second is spiritual, from principles implanted by nature in the rational mind, through the second eye, reason alone; and the third is an intellectual manifestation for knowing, when knowledge and action are joined. But if knowledge alone is present, the manifestation will no longer occur through understanding, but through bare instruction in the Scriptures alone. If action alone is present, likewise the manifestation will no longer occur through understanding, but through inward inspiration alone.

## He Touches Briefly upon and Passes Over That Kind of Manifestation Called Theophany.

[Col. 1369B]

I now pass over that kind of manifestation which is pre-eminently called *theophany*. For it does not belong to all good persons, but only to the perfect, and indeed to few even among them. Therefore I, unhappy as I am, dwelling in a house of clay, cannot bring forth for others that sweetness of so excellent a manifestation which I have not tasted myself.

Yet, instructed about this kind of manifestation by others, I have received these reports of a soul wholly detached from earthly things and so inflamed with desire for eternal things that it almost fails from itself, and that frequent and unexpected visitations come upon it. Such is that perfect soul which, burning with the Psalms that concern charity, complains thus: “As the hart longs for fountains of water, so my soul longs for thee, O God. My soul has thirsted for God, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI). And in another Psalm it sings likewise: “How beloved are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII).

These divine apparitions called theophanies, as I have learned, belong to such persons, and to such alone. They often refresh the soul anxious with so vehement a desire, and illuminate it even for an hour so that, by a wonderful, secret, and singular manner, even what is unknown of God becomes manifest in it. Yet although this is a frequent grace for such persons as we have described, it remains only a little while. Thus in the Song of Love the Bride is introduced as seeking her Bridegroom with such anxious and unceasing care: now she rises by night to seek her Bridegroom, now circles the city, now goes, now returns, now asks about him, now seeks him. He, however, now presents himself, now withdraws; now meets her, now leaps, now passes over; now is held, now slips away; now returns, now speaks.

What are these searches, questions, conversations, encounters, leaps, movements to and fro, flights away, returns, and so many escapes between Bridegroom and Bride, but certain sweet and delightful signs of sweet and pleasant love, which the perfect soul described above experiences delightfully in itself each day? This is according to the Bridegroom’s own testimony in one place that his delights are with the children of men. And indeed in a wonderful manner—but I speak as one inexperienced and unable to express it—the Bride delights in these manifestations when they are present, but is greatly afflicted when they depart and do not return as she desires.

Nevertheless, however great the privilege of divine manifestation granted to any blessed soul on this way, the brightness of so great a manifestation will be revealed much more sublimely, fully, delightfully, and therefore more blessedly in the homeland of light, in that infinite abyss of light. For manifestations of this kind must be understood as always occurring in this life through some signs or similitudes, and therefore mediately; whereas that homeland of light claims for itself the manifestation of God which occurs immediately alone.

Hence the Master, caught up to the third heaven, who might seem to have comprehended, says: “Brethren, I reckon that I have comprehended” (Phil. III). He immediately adds what that is which he has not comprehended: “But one thing”; as though he said: that which I do not reckon that I have comprehended is that which is one—namely, this first and principal unity of ours, which is called one in a singular and pre-eminent sense.

I seem now to have carried out what I proposed from the beginning concerning our first and principal unity. First, by means of the eye of the body, which awakens the eye of the heart or reason, it was shown that it exists; and because this was shown through visible things made, it may be called the visible or bodily manifestation of the first unity. [Col. 1370C] Secondly, by the eye of reason alone, it was likewise demonstrated in many and various ways that it exists; and because it was shown from visible moral arguments gathered from various quarters, this may be called the spiritual manifestation of the first unity. Having therefore first shown concerning the first unity that it exists, we subsequently showed, through the third eye of contemplation, insofar as it was granted us, what it is and how it is; and this in two ways. First, through the instruction of the Scriptures, by which we are taught concerning the first and principal unity not only that it is, but also what it is and how it is; and we called this manifestation of our first and principal unity common to the good and the bad. Secondly, through inward inspiration and manifestation—this belonging only to the good, and then more fully, when the holy operation is joined to knowledge of the Scriptures; for then, we said, knowledge passes into understanding. Hence, as we said before, this may be called the intellectual manifestation. We further said of inward inspiration that there are certain pre-eminent manifestations of the first and principal unity which, as they are singularly and pre-eminently called theophanies, rightly belong to that third kind of manifestation already called intellectual. Thus there will be three manifestations of our first and principal unity: its first manifestation, visible or bodily; its second, spiritual; and its third, natural.

Yet although this principal unity has thus been manifested by us in many ways [Col. 1371A] because of the narrowness of our understanding, I confess the truth: in some manner it has become more incomprehensible to my knowledge. I have now experienced in myself that saying of our prophet: when a man approaches the deep heart, God is exalted all the more above man. Yet God tolerates what man says faithfully and humbly concerning God, so that the man speaking thus of God may delight in his God; and, by the grace of faith, the merciful God accepts as though true the figures of speech by which man speaks of the truth, although God himself, truth and unity, is above and beyond everything that is said.

Yet although this unity of ours, so glorious and so principal—the worker of all virtues, faith, hope, salvation, and the strength of all—is so great as to be incomprehensible, I have introduced small matters in relation to its manifestation, so great [Col. 1371B] and holy; perhaps some will criticize me because I have introduced these matters here through it. But if they please, let them kindly forgive me, for I do not think that I have gone too far. For the things introduced by us concerning this first and principal unity do not wander from, nor oppose, but rather assist and will assist my purpose. I, a sinful little man, have introduced them concerning it and for its sake, speaking timidly indeed, yet neither against the faith—far be it!—nor irrelevantly, on account of those two unities which we distinguished above after it; and especially on account of that third unity of emperor and soldier, because of which, compelled by the third, I dared to approach this first unity and the second.

Therefore, amid so many, so great, and so varied temptations, snares, and distracting cares of this way and life, while dwelling as an inhabitant and pilgrim, I have nevertheless dared to presume to speak, though I fear I may speak rashly, yet catholically, concerning the first and principal unity. [Col. 1371C] Thus, making here an end of that which is infinite, I beg forgiveness from that unity itself if I have exceeded the measure. And, being about to speak of the remaining two unities, I commend myself to that supremely glorious, principally glorious, eternal unity—my faith, my salvation, and my entire hope. Having greeted and now adored it, may it, if it please, lead and teach its child through unknown paths, as one about to pass henceforth from sanctuary to sanctuary, indeed as from the incomprehensibly immense palace of the creative and imperial unity itself to the bridegroom’s and bride’s chamber.

For concerning the two remaining unities, our little musical piece will henceforth be shaped as we are taught from above. For the present we shall make no sound upon our lyre concerning the Trinity of this first and principal unity: first, because just as unity is commended on almost every page of the Old Testament, so the Trinity of unity is proclaimed in almost every syllable of the New Testament; and also because the veil of faith is far more deeply enfolded in the Trinity of unity than in unity itself. But above all, I insert nothing here concerning the Trinity of unity, from which I am certainly torn unwillingly away, because my present purpose in no way requires this subject; nor may I excuse myself even through the greatness of the matter. If I have inserted some small thing as though disputing concerning unity [Col. 1372A]—which someone perhaps will criticize as irrelevant to my purpose—let him know certainly, before criticizing, that I have spoken at greater length about it, and disputed both for and against it, chiefly so that I myself, its particular disputant and examiner, might confess here not error—far be it!—but my ignorance concerning it and in relation to it. For although I know that unity exists, and to some extent what it is, yet exceedingly little has been granted me to know concerning it or about it.

For faith, like an exceedingly folded veil, wraps, enfolds, and covers all: both concerning the unity commended in the Old Testament and concerning the Trinity of unity proclaimed in the New Law. [Col. 1372B] By its benefit I certainly believe all things, but see nothing except perhaps in a mirror and in an enigma. Yet this vision is not claimed by me or by those like me, but perhaps only by those rooted and founded in charity; faith, as we have said, covering all and enfolding all. This is why I above lamented, prolonged, and delayed the matter thus: fearing and trembling to enter the sanctuary of God, which the veil of faith wholly enfolds, hides, and covers from us. For this tabernacle of faith around which we stand watch while we still serve in the wilderness is shaded by so many symbolic representations—covered altogether, namely, by so many rams’ skins, so many violet-blue coverings, so many sacks of haircloth, and so many curtains.

But now, as it seems, forgetful of our military service, as though the tabernacle were insufficient for those serving, I appear to presume to ascend into the prophet’s heavenly temple, where the fellow-citizens of the saints already are; [Col. 1372C] a temple in which there are so many gates, so many courts, lesser courts, treasuries, vestibules, houses, buildings, upper rooms, doors, little doors, ways, streets, paths, places, sanctuaries, and chambers. When I recall this, I immediately remember the Savior himself in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John 14). Yet at the end of his prophetic book the prophet calls it no longer a house, nor even a temple, but a city; and, speaking of the name of the city from that day, he there gives it a changed name, most plainly indicating to us that all was spoken mystically by him. [Col. 1372D]

And therefore, because the places and dwelling-places of this temple—or rather, city—which we distinguished above are so various, entrance is dangerous. Whoever enters may, even if—far be it!—he does not err from the way of faith, nevertheless easily err by proceeding too far and investigating the secret things of the sanctuary. Therefore, since I earlier dared to enter the unsearchable sanctuary of the first and principal unity, it is safer for me now to draw back, lest by proceeding further I advance more rashly inward. Yet I must immediately turn from sanctuary to sanctuary, indeed as from the palace to one of the palace’s chambers: that is, from unity to unity; from the unity of nature alone, which is in the triune God among the Three, to the unity of grace alone, which exists only between the Word and the flesh, between God and man. Concerning the cause and origin of this unity, the seventeenth little section of this, our third musical piece, will now be formed. For this second unity of grace alone is not eternal as that first and principal unity is; rather, it was made by that first and principal unity of nature alone, at the end of the ages in the fullness of time, between itself and the first and principal unity and our humanity. Therefore our lyre shall sound, as granted from above, first concerning its cause and origin.

## HERE BEGINS THE THIRD MUSICAL PIECE, ON THE UNITY OF GRACE ALONE; AND FIRST, ON ITS CAUSE. LITTLE SECTION 17.

When, in paradise, man was violently separated and torn away by the tempter from the first and principal unity, as by sedition and tyranny, immediately man himself was divided within himself: divided, I say, torn apart, scattered, and rebellious against himself, as though split from one into two. For he was divided from that which is truly one—indeed, as we have already heard in the preceding musical piece, from that which is true, simple, eternal, and undivided unity; which alone truly is. And that which is divided from it indeed has being, but being such as being is: that is, a multiple being, as though it had not one being but many beings differing and opposing one another—through the various and conflicting afflictions of its spirit, through varied, vain, incessant, and importunate thoughts, [Col. 1373C] through the manifold and contrary dispositions of its body, and through the frequent and continual changes of times and places. Thus man was ever more manifoldly and miserably scattered, torn apart, and convulsed.

Accordingly, man represented in himself no longer the image of God, in which he had been created, but rather the poetically invented likeness of some monstrous Proteus, so devoid of unity and so changeable. Indeed—alas!—he was so pressed down, oppressed, and divided that he often neither remembered himself nor knew himself. But why say “often”? For even now it belongs to very few to know themselves: perhaps they recollect in heart, but by no means in deed, what they were, what they are, and what they will be. Thus, when one was asked briefly and at one time what he had been, what he was, and what he would be, he is recorded to have answered each question elegantly and briefly: “Worthless seed, a vessel of excrement, and food for worms.”

In this schism of man, therefore, scarcely anyone knew himself, or returned to his proper unity within himself. For man was thus scattered and divided, and a schism had arisen—not only between God and man, but also within man himself, man against himself. Indeed, to put it thus, he had now become a schismatic against himself: as soon as he divided himself from unity, a harsh and dreadful schism arose between his own soul and his own flesh, each desiring what the other did not; and moreover both soul and flesh were wholly contrary within themselves. [Col. 1374A] Thus the whole life of man was schism within man: a strange and unheard-of schism, when man had become contrary not only to God but also to himself, and burdensome to himself, according to that lamenting, grieving, and complaining man: “Why have you set me as contrary to you, and I have become burdensome to myself?” (Job 7). Likewise the prophet laments: “My heart has forsaken me” (Psalm 39); and again: “My soul is filled with illusions.”

Nor is it surprising that this should befall the man who so rashly, foolishly, and presumptuously divided himself from the first and principal unity. For it is more certain than certainty and clearer than light—though those who have experienced it know it more familiarly and fully—that no heart is truly joyful, truly at rest, or peaceful; indeed, none is wholly un-torn, undivided, contrary to itself, and schismatic, unless it is joined to this our first and principal unity. So natural is it to the human heart to be with this unity of nature, in whose image it was naturally made. Hence one who had fully experienced this and returned from schism says, “God of my heart” (Psalm 72); and again, “It is good for me to cling to God” (ibid.). This is that sole and unique one beneath the sun in which it is good and pleasant to dwell and to which it is good to cling.

But unhappy, foolish, and miserable man, made schismatic and thus divided from the first and principal unity, was immediately expelled from the Church triumphant, from the congregation of the righteous, and from the fellowship of angels; and so he was joined to the party of that ancient schismatic Lucifer, [Col. 1374C] who had already troubled the Church triumphant and brought about a great schism in the ruin of many, as an inseparable and indivisible companion of schism.

O how unhappy, unfortunate, and vile a schism: first born in heaven between God and angel, then reborn in paradise between God and man! First expelled from heaven, then from paradise, it has now descended at last into this dung-heap, often and repeatedly disturbing this Church militant—the Church triumphant which it tore apart and troubled from the beginning. It often stirs up and disturbs the domestic household of any private family, even where only two or three are gathered; so that, when peace has been disturbed, not according to Christ’s Gospel but according to the dissension sent by Lucifer, two are divided against three and three against two. So dear to Lucifer are schism and dissension.

O how accursed, profane, and viperous is this offspring, whose mother is ambition and whose father is Lucifer, and whose worst sister among the works of the flesh is heresy! Alas, alas: what was wretched man to do? Where was he to turn? How was he to return to unity? The first and principal schism was between the first and principal unity itself and him; and from this followed division between him and angel, and also between him and the whole creation made for his sake—all because of the unity that created all things, from which he had so foolishly, rashly, and presumptuously divided himself. [Col. 1375A] And, stranger still, this schism was so harsh and dreadful that man became schismatic within himself, seemingly irrevocable and irreconcilable, made contrary to himself and burdensome to himself.

How then could he return or be restored? Who would dare or be able to summon back to unity one so divided from unity? For the first and principal unity itself, the one and highest God, had expelled him because of schism from the fellowship of the righteous and from the Church triumphant. The angel would not associate with the one expelled for schism. Lucifer hindered reconciliation, lest his fellow-schismatic—whom he had already enticed into his own retinue—should be reconciled. Nor did man himself seek reconciliation; rather, day by day he became ever more wild, rejoicing throughout his life in Lucifer’s service, until at last the final outcome of joy seized him as grief.

So too, when wretched mankind had multiplied and was still daily increasing on the earth, for many ages it ran through the pathless wilderness and wastelands of this world, always feeding on winds and pursuing a shadow, proclaiming itself blessed in the desires of its own soul. Until, according to the prophet, this miserable race, which throughout its life had sown wind, would reap the whirlwind. Thus too, according to the saying of the wise man, lightning precedes hail and favor precedes shame; likewise the heart was exalted before ruin, but after exaltation came man’s irrevocable fall. For all those of the human race who, after this fleeting and shadowy life—without mercy for age, without distinction of sex, and without regard to condition—were hurled without mercy, protection, remedy, or aid into the insatiable abyss of death, [Col. 1375C] entered into the offspring of the fellow-schismatic spirits, the apostate angels, where life without end is in toil and darkness. Thus miserable humankind was daily trampled down to the glory of that notable schismatic Lucifer, in accordance with his desire and command. And this could appear to redound both to the misery of created and seduced man, and to the injury and disgrace of the creative unity itself; for that seditious schismatic had first unjustly and deceitfully withdrawn its creature from it, and then cruelly and tyrannically trampled it down at will and according to his desire, as though for the creator’s dishonor and contempt.

## ON THE UNITY THAT PITIES MAN’S OPPRESSION AND CONSIDERS THE MEANS OF HIS DELIVERANCE. LITTLE SECTION 18.

[Col. 1375D]

Therefore that first, principal, and omnipotent unity—the natural and true fountain of mercy, indeed truly the eternally overflowing and unfailing stream of compassion, which flows not sluggishly but abundantly and without ceasing over all its works—seeing its poor creature thus oppressed and miserable, considered the means of deliverance. Yet in this deliberation of the compassionate unity, mercy and truth seemed to meet each other, according to the royal prophet’s saying: “Mercy and truth have met each other” (Psalm 84). Mercy indeed pleaded for man thus condemned; but truth met the mercy that knocked, standing in the way lest it should be heard, because man, though justly condemned, had not stood in truth, when nothing existed in him that could draw him back from the way of truth.

## ON THE JUDGMENT PRONOUNCED FOR MAN’S DELIVERANCE.

But immediately, as though a third party, justice intervened for the peace and reconciliation of man, as mercy’s helper. It no longer pleaded, but plainly showed that man must be taken away by every right from such a possessor. Thus justice—whose nature is wisdom, and which has begotten wisdom—immediately, before all else, as man’s chief advocate for peace in this case, proves that the possessor would be wholly unjust, since he had so deceitfully and seditiously entrapped man and withdrawn his servant from the common Lord of both. [Col. 1376B] Therefore justice establishes that the man whom he had claimed for himself through iniquity could by every right be taken away from him, and that man ought one day to be restored to his Lord, even though, as an ignorant and unsuspecting servant, he had allowed himself to be entrapped.

And, lest I prolong a matter so evident concerning justice: mercy, which had been pleading, now fulfills the office of advocate for peace; but I, insofar as is permitted me as justice, declare decisively and pronounce this judgment: when the servant has been taken away from his unjust possessor, he is to return free and absolved by judgment to his former Lord. And because justice and truth are always friends, truth assented to the judgment, and mercy, which had previously pleaded, rejoiced in obtaining it. Therefore, by the judgment of justice, once the enmities between God and man had been wholly removed, justice and peace kissed one another. Thus, when the sentence on behalf of man had been delivered, these four came together: mercy and truth, which had first met one another; and justice and peace, which had kissed one another.

Yet when the matter had thus been declared, that omnipotent and eternal justice which had pronounced the judgment immediately considered how and at what time the sentence thus issued might most fittingly be carried out and brought into effect. For even after the judgment had been pronounced, the servant fled from his true Lord; mercy’s presence supplied for his absence in the judgment, and he was by no means admitted into the Church from which he had been expelled for schism. Lucifer still opposed peace and reconciliation, except that he was wholly ignorant of the sentence thus pronounced, [Col. 1376D] and especially of the execution of the sentence and the manner of that execution, of which we shall now speak. For if, as the Master teaches, he had known, he would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

Justice, I say, considered the execution of the pronounced sentence and the manner of execution. For although it was possible for the Omnipotent One to take by power the servant justly condemned and expelled from the fellowship of the righteous for schism from his violent and unjust possessor, this did not please justice—though it could likewise have been done powerfully and unjustly. Therefore that true and highest justice considered how, and by what way, the sentence which it had pronounced for the servant’s peace might be put into execution more justly, effectively, fruitfully for the servant, and to the greater confusion of the violent possessor.

## HERE HE BRIEFLY TOUCHES UPON THE MANNER OF EXECUTING THE PRONOUNCED SENTENCE, AND AFTERWARD UPON THE EXECUTOR HIMSELF.

[Col. 1377A]

Seeing, then, in that wonderful and incomprehensible treasury of its wisdom and knowledge, that nothing was so just, so effective, or so fitting—and that nothing could bring such future confusion upon the tyrant—it ordained and disposed this: that the fugitive, schismatic servant should be recalled through unity to unity. Thus, at the end of the ages, it established a certain new unity, unheard of and unknown from the ages, indeed most reverently to be admired and wondered at by the ages of all ages. And this occurred fittingly and in order, at the end of the ages, when the fullness of time had come.

First, the law of nature was given, but it was powerless and ineffectual for man’s peace. For, since the law of nature has three parts, it was ineffective for man’s peace in every respect. The knowledge of God the Creator, which is the first part of the natural law, was not sufficient; nor was a life rightly ordered according to the knowledge of God, which is the second part of the natural law. Thus even those who lived according to God’s will nevertheless descended to the lower world. Nor was it sufficient, by a good life, to furnish others with an example of right living, which is the third part of the natural law. [Col. 1377C] Therefore no part of the natural law, nor even the whole of it, was sufficient for man’s peace: neither the first, which may be called *theosebia*—the worship of one God; nor the second, which may be called ethics, because it orders life by good morals; nor the third, which may be called doctrinal, because it provides an example for teaching the worship of God through good works.

And just as the law of nature was powerless and insufficient, so also was the law of the letter, given through Moses, which entered afterward. Indeed, this law of deeds, or of the letter, not only did not reconcile God and man, but disturbed them even more; or rather, as the Master teaches, it resulted in increasing transgression and making sin, beyond measure, sinful. Therefore, after the law of nature and then the law of the letter had run their course through many ages, both being unable to reconcile God and man, at the end of time a third law succeeded those other two: the law of mercy alone, after the first law of nature and the second law of the letter. This law was introduced by that new and unheard-of unity of grace alone, of which and for which our whole discourse is concerned, according to the Master’s words: “But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son” (Galatians 4).

Behold the fullness of time: namely, the time of full reconciliation between God and man, granted and ordained beforehand by God. And rightly it is called the time of fullness: the time of abundant peace between Lord and man. In this completed time of fullness, that promise made long before was fulfilled: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace.” And truly, according to both the desire and the prophecy of our prophet, in his days an abundance of peace arose between God and man. [Col. 1378A] For who has ever heard such a thing? Who has seen its like? “Who has believed our report?” Or to whom has this deed of the almighty and compassionate justice judging for man’s peace truly been revealed?

For behold the new thing which that eternal and highest justice, our first and principal unity, has made; behold, I say, the new thing it has made upon the earth. Do you wish to hear something new—something newly unheard of, indeed incomparably more marvelous than every power, sign, and wonder? That true and highest justice, that first and principal eternal unity, united to itself man, who was so hostile, so turned away, so fugitive, and schismatic; and it united him to itself so that it became he. Truly, no sweeter or more closely allied peace between God and man could be imagined than that God should become man.

O how wonderful—and truly wonderful, indeed truly more than wonderful—is this unity of the first and eternal unity with fugitive and schismatic man! It is not a unity of nature, [Col. 1378B] but of grace alone, ineffably incomprehensible: light in a vessel of clay, the Word in flesh, God in man and man God. Thus the order of nature was reversed so that the course of grace might have a freer way. Therefore, rejecting the old song, “Such as is the earthly man, such also are the earthly,” let us sing the new song, a song wonderful because of its goodness, to the Wonderful One: “Such as is the heavenly man, such also are the earthly; as is heaven, so is earth,” because heaven itself is also earth: the Word is flesh.

And truly it is a new and wondrous song. For contrary to the dogmas of some who are incapable of so great a unity, the Word is not in the flesh by virtue, power, adoption, or indwelling; but—what is stupendous because of its overwhelming wonder and to be embraced because of its incomprehensible condescension—the Word is in the flesh in such a way that the Word truly, fully, and perfectly became flesh. The same one is eternal God and temporal man, greater than himself and less than himself, his own lord and his own servant—while preserving, nevertheless, the dogmas concerning these words of the orthodox Fathers and holy councils. For remaining what he was, he became what he was not: the same one both lord and servant. This is indeed entrusted to faith alone. Faith is aided by no likeness among created things, for every comparison fails and is impossible in making this unity manifest. Here faith alone rules, and reason, with all its power, wholly yields.

## ON THOSE WHO SAY THAT GOD BECAME MAN BY HABIT.

Many in our time, attempting by the notion of habit to loosen that humble, and therefore all the more gratuitous, bond of so great a unity between God and the assumed man—as though they were trying to loosen the sandal-strap of divinity shod with our mortal flesh—preach that God is man solely by habit. The Master says of him that he was “found in habit as a man.” These men do not teach that God is man essentially, but only by habit, not in essence, according to the Master. For it seems absurd to them, and wholly contrary to truth, to confess that for God to be man is for God to be, since for God being is nothing other than seeing, knowing, being able, being blessed, being eternal, and being God. Likewise, they reject anything new: namely, confessing that God is man and believing in the state of the New Law something which the fathers of the Old Law did not believe, nor even Abraham himself, the father of all believers. [Col. 1379A] Those who teach that God became man by habit alone and not by essence raise these and similar objections against those who affirm dogmatically that God is man essentially; and the matters stated above seem necessarily to follow from the latter’s assertion.

## ON THOSE WHO SAY THAT GOD BECAME MAN IN ESSENCE.

Conversely, those who maintain that God is man essentially consider that the former, who preach that God is man by the notion of habit, diminish most foolishly and with scant reverence the grace of so great a unity between God and man, loosen its bond, and most presumptuously derogate from this miraculous work of the Most High—so admirably singular and singularly admirable. They regard them as plainly opposed to the promise of the great preacher and messenger who addressed the Virgin: “That holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). [Col. 1379B]

And they add that this is the sacrament, admirable and hidden from all ages and generations, before which every introduced comparison immediately recoils, proves discordant, and is powerless. This, I say, is that eternal God, Creator and Lord of all things, who, remaining what he was, became something temporal, passible, and created—something which he himself had not been before—without any change in himself or even any shadow of change.

Yet for the present I neither approve nor disapprove assertions of this sort, since the faith of the Incarnation is the same among these and among those, though investigators of so great a mystery, perhaps more rash and curious than necessary, are variously moved by reasons concerning faith and faith itself. Therefore, setting these matters aside, let us return to the proposed mystery of so ineffable, incomprehensible, and incomparable a unity. The Jew mocks the bond of this great unity and the grace of this wondrous, new, and glorious unity; the pagan does not believe it; nor does the philosopher grasp it. Here too the Christian is endangered, who errs by wrongly understanding the Scriptures, or follows one who errs, and thereby thinks wrongly concerning this sacrament of the grace of truth and unity, even if he deviates only slightly. Such a person, perhaps because of the foundation, will attain salvation; yet he will be saved as through fire—like perhaps those mentioned a little earlier. [Col. 1379D]

Therefore it is safest not to depart either from the faith itself or from the words of faith found in the treatises of the orthodox Fathers or in the decrees of holy councils. For these men, now affirming and now refuting, have used fitting words of faith sufficiently, fully, and appropriately. To depart from them is dangerous, lest under some finely wrought novelty of language we follow an old error or produce a new one. For what is not perilous when guilt arises here not only from a guilty mind but also from the tongue, and when not only the meaning but also the expression is liable to accusation? One thing I certainly venture to say: doctrine will not be entirely holy and sound unless it is also delivered to believers in the holy and authoritative words of the saints. For faith belongs to the faithful; so too, the knowledge [Col. 1380A] by which they are instructed in faith is not the knowledge of these or those persons, but solely the knowledge of the saints, now fully ministered to us through the words of the saints.

But to return to what was said before, and to that new work by which we proclaim the eternal God to be a temporal, true, and perfect man: behold that new and unheard-of execution of the sentence for man’s peace, forethought by the highest and eternal justice before all ages. Behold the new executor, admirable in reality and in name. This name, indeed, he claims as his own from the reality, according to the prophet: “And his name shall be called Wonderful” (Isaiah 9). Truly, the executor of the judgment pronounced for man is new and wonderful: God-man, man-God.

For, to speak boldly now—may the Lord not turn away in displeasure, for the astonishment and trembling which have seized me at the newness of this deed compel me—I think I see that in the so incomprehensible and immense power of the works of the Most High, and in the so hidden and profound treasuries of his wisdom and knowledge, nothing could be found which would be so effective for recalling the fugitive servant, so fitting for retaining the servant once recovered, so just for triumphing over that tyrant, or so suited to confounding the conquered one throughout all ages. How this is so, anyone even moderately practiced in the sacred writings will quickly see, if he looks with a simple and pure eye. Yet I touch on these matters only now and do not pursue them, for it would not belong to the present work to pursue them all: each would demand its own volumes.

Therefore, putting these aside, let us return to that unity by which the first and principal unity united schismatic man to itself, and concerning which our whole lyre now resounds in this part of the present musical piece. When I say “schismatic man united,” I say it because the nature of schismatic man was united to the first unity: in that man who was specially and personally united, with every schism silenced in the union itself and with no further rebellion of spirit and flesh in him. [Col. 1380C] Thus, the unity of his spirit and flesh, once lost by man in paradise, was now partly restored in this privileged man. And this occurred through the principal and first unity itself, which united to itself in this manner the wholly new man, the old man having been put off but not yet extinguished.

## IN THE ASSUMED MAN HE DISTINGUISHES TWO UNITIES.

[Col. 1380D]

Thus, in the man so united there is a twofold unity. One is between the principal Unity itself and the man thus united to it: a unity not of nature, but rather contrary to nature—indeed, more truly, above nature—of grace alone. The other unity is, in the man thus united, between the spirit and flesh of the man united in this way: neither spirit being opposed to flesh, nor flesh lusting against spirit—the condition proper to man before sin. This is the unity of new glory in the new man. For I am not now speaking of that natural union of spirit and flesh in the assumed man, common by shared nature to other human beings as well, but of the freely bestowed, now full and perfect peace without any schism or rebellion between the assumed flesh [Col. 1381A] and the spirit.

Therefore, in this man assumed from our race, as a privilege of our race, peace between God and man has been restored and, as it were, committed to writing. The parchment of this book is a sheep’s dead skin: that is, flesh assumed from us, inscribed in human blood as though in a holocaust, and in bones and sinews as though with a pen; containing within itself, without schism, contradiction, or any rebellion, the peace of man. This peace of man was written in the book and also in the very head of the book.

Hence our prophet, speaking in the person of the fugitive servant who has returned, says: “In the head of the book it is written of me, that I should do thy will, O God.” This book is the assumed man. For he is the book of humankind, instructing man by the example of his deeds and the teaching [Col. 1381B] of truth; every word and action of Christ is a lesson. But the head of the book is God. Therefore it is written not only in the book but in the book’s head, “of me,” says the universal man. He says “written,” that is, established and fixed, as what is committed to writing; and he immediately adds what is written—that is, established and fixed—concerning him: “that I should do thy will, O God.” This is as though he said: It is there written and immutably decreed concerning me that peace should be made between me and thee, O God; and this will surely occur when I have done thy will. It is as though he said: “that peace should be made between me and thee, O God.” Thus “that I should do thy will, O God,” is the same thing. That will of God the blessed man whom God chose and assumed firmly and inviolably performed, as he himself says of himself: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 5). And so the man performed God’s will in himself and afterwards, increased and multiplied beyond number, through himself.

Therefore the peace of man is manifold and multiple, written in this head of the book, in the book of life and the book of wisdom: the peace of man with God, peace with the angel, peace with the neighbor, and peace with himself. Behold once more the abundant peace which, according to the prophecy and longing of our prophet, arose in the days of the Desired One, and was confirmed in our new man, God, as by a new, glorious, and eminent privilege: through this mediator of God and men, between God and man, with every contradiction, rebellion, and schism removed far away—or rather now extinguished—except [Col. 1381D] that which remained between man alone and Lucifer alone, by whom man had formerly been seduced, his fellow-schismatic. Thus man’s peace, manifold and multiple, is written in the head of the book, in the book of life, in the book of wisdom.

## ON THE MANNER OF EXECUTING THE PRONOUNCED SENTENCE THROUGH THE UNITY OF GRACE ALONE

And since we now have the executor of the pronounced sentence, wonderful both in reality and in name, let us hear more attentively here about the manner of its execution, which was mentioned briefly above: namely, how he recalled the fugitive servant to his master; how he reconciled the schismatic; how, after driving out the schism, he restored peace and gave back the homeland. You, therefore, O man, hear and attend, in astonishment at such excessive condescension, to the marvels of this manner of execution, so that you may return to unity. Hear, I say, what prophecy and Gospel—the two truest witnesses—jointly testify concerning this manner.

Wonderful indeed, truly wonderful, and new is this manner of execution: by it not only did the one become many, but even the first and principal Unity itself became, as it were, wretched and miserably dispersed, torn apart, and convulsed into multiplicity; personally uniting to itself the form of a servant—a wretched and despised servant, having neither comeliness nor beauty. For, according to the prophet, this servant had neither appearance nor esteem; he was despised among men and the last of them, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity; he was as one hidden and not accounted; bearing our sicknesses and carrying our pains; like a leper, struck by God and humbled. Upon him was the discipline of our peace, and healing by his bruises; he was offered for every iniquity, like a sheep of his own will; he was led to slaughter, like a lamb before its shearer; taken away from distress and judgment; of unutterable generation; cut off from the earth; struck down because of wickedness; giving the ungodly for his burial and the rich for his death—he in whose hand was no iniquity, nor deceit in his mouth; counted among criminals and praying for transgressors.

The same one is prophetically, now for me a lion, now a worm, now a boar, now a sheep, now a bull, now a goat, now a stag, now a fawn, now a she-goat, now a kid, now a lamb, now a calf, now a sparrow, now a heron, now a turtledove, now an eagle, now a serpent, now a dove, now a rock, now a vine, now a lily of the valleys, [Col. 1382C] now a flower of the field, now an olive, now a palm, now a rose, now myrrh, now a candlestick, now a lamp, now water, now dry land, now a mountain, now a fountain, now an arrow, now a sword, now bread, now a fish, now fire, now ointment, now wood, now wine, now oil, now gold, now heaven, now day, now sun, now a foundation, now a temple, now a pillar, now a crown, now a lord, now the son of a handmaid.

And so that the Gospel may set forth the prophecy by confirming it, as a column set upon its base: this first and principal Unity, as prophecy had already foretold, truly united to itself the form of a servant, a passible and mortal servant, enduring the weariness of ten months in the womb, while professing itself the beginning of all things.

## THESE THINGS PERTAIN TO THE INCARNATION

[Col. 1382D] The same one is both the son of a workman and of a wage-earning woman, and the splendor of glory and image of the substance of God the Father.

The same one is now wrapped in a stable for beasts, now worshiped by kings at the indication of the stars.

The same one is now subject to his parents, now commanding even winds and sea.

The same one is now fasting for forty days and forty nights, now a drinker and glutton, a companion at table of tax collectors and prostitutes.

The same one is now tempted by the devil, now surrounded by the service of angels.

The same one is now taken up by the devil, now sending legions of demons into the abyss.

The same one is now having nowhere to lay his head, now possessing all that belongs to the Father.

[Col. 1383A] The same one is now asking for drinks drawn from the well, now perpetually giving streams of living water to the thirsty.

The same one is now crossing the waters in a fragile boat, now treading those same waters with dry foot.

The same one is now unable to do anything of himself, now himself doing all that the Father does.

The same one is now declaring that he cannot give seats to two disciples, now granting twelve the authority to judge upon twelve thrones.

The same one is now hungry, now satisfying thousands of people from a few loaves.

The same one is now thirsty, now changing water into wine.

The same one is now profaning the Sabbath, now teaching the way of God in truth.

[Col. 1383B] The same one is now truthful, now a deceiver.

The same one now does not know the day of judgment, now announces with absolute certainty the signs of the coming judgment.

## THESE THINGS PERTAIN TO THE PASSION

The same one is now healing an ear, now pierced by a lance.

The same one is now fearing death, now mocking death.

The same one is now seized by fear of death, now leading captives back.

The same one is now counted among criminals in death, now victor over death.

The same one is now hanging on the cross, now moving all things upon that same cross.

The same one is now complaining upon the cross that he has been forsaken, [Col. 1383C] now opening Paradise of delight upon that same cross to the thief.

The same one is now veiling the power of the sun’s brightness in darkness upon the cross, now illuminating the dark places of hell with flashing light.

The same one is now the raiser of the dead, now the curse of the cross.

## THESE THINGS PERTAIN TO THE BURIAL

The same one is now buried in a tomb, now opening the graves of the dead.

The same one is now lying in the sepulchre, pressed beneath a stone, now proclaimed as risen from the dead, free among the dead.

## THESE THINGS PERTAIN TO THE RESURRECTION

The same one is now presenting himself as tangible to his own amid their hands, now suddenly vanishing.

[Col. 1383D] The same one is now knocking at the door, now unexpectedly standing among his own although the doors are shut.

## THIS PERTAINS TO THE ASCENSION

The same one is now refreshing himself with his own, with fish and a honeycomb, as though possessing an animate body; now raised from them as though ethereal, ascending above the stars.

Behold how great the dispersion, tearing apart, multiplicity, division, humiliation, confusion, and disgrace of the principal and eternal Unity itself in man, for the sake of recalling schismatic man to unity. Heaven is astonished; earth marvels; the angel inquires; the Jew takes offence; the Gentile does not believe; the philosopher investigates what this work is, why it is, and what sort of manner of executing the pronounced sentence for man this may be.

[Col. 1384A] O glorious, blessed, and principal Unity! O good God, O great emperor Christ Jesus: how marvelous—indeed, in accordance with the proper meaning of thy name, how wondrous—thou art in the sufferings of this way and life! Thou art yet far more wondrous than in thy saints, except that these sufferings of thine exist solely to sanctify thy saints; and thy sufferings are true, as they are to be revered, venerated, and admired.

For it seemed as though thy glory could not be given to thine without battle, and thy suffering as though the suffering and battle of soldiers were not enough to obtain the palm unless, upon the very field, the emperor himself fought and sweated for his own. Nor could schismatic man otherwise be recalled to unity and shake off the yoke of tyrannical slavery, unless the principal Unity itself, emptied out, mediated in the form of a servant through the unity of grace alone.

For this is the great spectacle and wonder in our eyes; lest they see it, the eyes of the synagogue are veiled, the hearts of the Gentiles are made brutish, and the understanding of every philosopher is dulled. The bride alone—to whom the bridegroom, as a sign of privileged love, gave a name from his own name, so that from Christ she is called Christian—recognizes her bridegroom, the emperor, fighting in the field for her.

But, if I may insert something here concerning this unity of grace alone and this most marvelous manner of execution—and would that it were not my own thought; this I fear—yet when I sometimes consider, with wonder beyond wonder, this manner of reconciliation between God and man and how man was thus freed and delivered [Col. 1384C] from the hand of those stronger than he, my conscience immediately suggests to me that something still remains very hidden from us concerning the power of light and the power of darkness. Between these powers man is placed as though a disputed possession in the field of this way and life, and a kind of single combat is renewed between the prince of heaven and the prince of this world. One claims man as his prey, and the other claims him; one gains him, and the other gains him; one protects him, the other snatches him away. Thus even as many little ones of the human race as would have been taken by the prince of this world would not have escaped, unless the prince of heaven himself had paid and suffered for them.

But why do I speak of little ones? Indeed, the entire human race, just and unjust alike, was captive under the power of darkness, freed neither by its virtues nor by virtuous works, except through the suffering and battle of the power of light itself. Yet I know and have read what our orthodox writers have written about these matters. Their statements are true; but whether they have spoken fully of them, God knows—they must see to that themselves. For my part, I do not think so; yet I most certainly believe that they have spoken truly, but by no means fully or perfectly, on these subjects. Nor do I suppose that they comprehended them, so hidden are these things.

Especially since the full reason for them is heard neither in the song of the Old nor in that of the New instrument; all the fathers of both Old and New Testament cry out together with the Master: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?” (Romans 11).

O if it were granted us from above to know that mighty force of God’s secret love for man! O if it were granted [Col. 1385A] us to understand what that love was, stronger than death, which so overcame even the invincible conqueror of death himself; which so emptied the Almighty, made eternity temporal, weakened power, bound the unconquerable, wounded the impassible, and finally killed the immortal!

O love, love, how strong thou art, and how mighty even among human beings, not only in the God-man! I call thee mighty and strong where thou art truly love, and love alone: proceeding from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. But such love belongs to God alone and to very few human beings—and even in them, only from God. Yet this love is so much more sincere, pure, and strong in the Creator than in the creature, since nothing can disturb that fountain of love, because he is God—except that he himself, from the excessive vehemence and overflowing abundance of love, seems, as if by some flood, to have stirred up himself, the fountain of love. Love so compelled him that he willed not merely to be eternal God, but also temporal man: man with human beings for man’s sake, enduring for man so many weaknesses, indignities, injuries, temptations, pressures, distresses, difficulties, and finally the very shame of the cross.

The first and principal Unity, united to man, suffered these things for our sake, in order that, by inviting man to love itself through the various forms of its sufferings endured for man, it might draw him after itself and recall him to that third unity of nature and grace of which we principally intend to speak and for whose sake we have inserted discussion of the other two.

## NOTE 21 OF THE THIRD MELODY

## HERE ENDS THE THIRD MELODY ON THE UNITY OF GRACE ALONE; HENCEFORTH IT WILL ALSO RESOUND ON THE UNITY OF NATURE AND GRACE

It remains, therefore—and our purpose and promise so require—that from this point our Davidic harp should sound concerning that third unity. For this third melody has first proceeded concerning the unity of nature alone; second, concerning the unity of grace alone; third, it will henceforth concern the unity of nature and grace.

Yet let this first be stated. When the discourse had proceeded concerning the unity of nature alone, I was scarcely able, within the Holy of Holies, as through a narrow chink and with, as it were, divided sight, to discern the mercy-seat over the ark [Col. 1385D], being overshadowed. Then, when the discourse concerned the unity of grace alone, I looked somewhat upon the surface of the ark of sanctification within those same holy places, as through a chink slightly less narrow. But now, thirdly, when discourse is proposed concerning the unity of nature and grace, within that same Holy of Holies I see somewhat more freely the Cherubim standing on either side around the mercy-seat. Now that schism has been stilled and peace restored between God and man, they have become our fellow-citizens and members of the household, and allow us, so far as is permitted, freer access to them.

This is the same thing that, though in other words, I remember saying above when I first spoke of the first and principal, omnipotent Unity that contains all things, and then descended to the unity of grace alone which exists between God and man: I passed, as it were, from an incomprehensibly immense palace to the bridal chamber of bridegroom and bride. But this chamber was exceedingly narrow, since within it were only the Word of the Father and the one and only soul of the Word with assumed flesh.

But now that this third melody of ours is to be formed and completed by treating henceforth of the third unity, that of nature and grace, we must turn aside to the larger bridal chamber of bridegroom and bride. For in it the bride, now of full maturity, is in the embrace of the bridegroom: a queen in her gold-wrought garment, surrounded by the varied host of men and angels. Accordingly, from this point the following portions of our melody will be formed concerning this unity of nature and grace, so that, as we promised above, it may be plainly shown what kind of unity this is: not a unity of nature alone nor a unity of grace alone, but, as we have joined the terms, a unity of nature and grace. I do not doubt that even the slow will readily understand this from what has been set forth.

For, as previously shown, that first and principal Unity of nature alone deigned to become a sharer in our nature. Thus we and it are now of one common nature. Therefore, when we are united to it, having been made conformed to the image of the Son of God—which occurs only through his grace—we who had first been united to it by nature, through the nature assumed from us, are afterwards united to it by grace bestowed upon us by it. Thus, as is now most evident, this third unity of ours with that first and principal Unity will be [Col. 1386C] not only a unity of nature but also of grace. This is the third kind, or third unity, for whose sake we introduced the other two and which we principally proposed to discuss.

O how great, and how plainly manifested to all—angels and human beings alike—is this grace and glory of man! He who was once so wretched, so oppressed, so hardened in schism, is united with the supercelestial spirits of angels by grace alone; but to the Creator of the angelic spirits—indeed, of all spirits—he is united not only now by grace but also by nature.

O happy and desired schism, after which schismatic man had to be recalled to so glorious a unity! O how discriminating is the mercy of omnipotent Unity, and how foolish the malice of seditious Lucifer! For while the Lord wisely ordered all things, that which Lucifer had devised for man’s irreparable ruin resulted in man’s unlooked-for glory. Thus iniquity, as it is accustomed to do, lied to itself—indeed, it lied to God, to the angel, to man, and even to itself. It plainly lied to itself, while God, wise, mighty, and just, always detects the snares of iniquity and malice, scatters their nets, evades their traps, and frustrates their devices. He so often turns every thought and cunning plan of iniquity and malice to the contrary that our prophet, who had often experienced this very thing, rightly says: “Iniquity lied to itself.”

We too see this daily in our ordinary affairs; but it is most evident in this work so singularly glorious, so gloriously singular, and so illustrious. For after man had first been driven out by iniquity, because of schism, from the assembly of the just, the fellowship of angels, and the triumphant Church, justice turned the work of iniquity to the contrary: man is now crowned with glory and honor all the more above every order of angels.

For our God—and truly ours—nowhere, as the Master teaches, takes hold of angels, but takes hold of the seed of Abraham as fugitive, because schismatic; and, as we have sufficiently shown above, personally united it to himself through grace alone, incomprehensible grace. But just as this third unity of nature and grace proceeded from the first unity of nature alone, so it proceeded also from this second unity of grace alone: the unity by which the Church is united to God both through the nature he assumed from her and through the grace that he bestowed upon her in overflowing measure.

Accordingly, just as the body is united to the head, so the individual members of the body are united to one another by this same unity of nature and grace, because of the same conformity of nature and participation in grace which they share. This third unity of nature and grace, therefore, is the unity of the whole universal Church, one part of which still serves as a soldier on earth, while another already triumphs in heaven.

Yet this unity of nature and grace, which we call common—or rather, as it were, one and the same—to both the Church militant and the Church triumphant, is, in the triumphant Church, incomprehensibly greater and therefore better and more delightful, because more blessed. For this unity of the Church militant, compared with what it itself is in the triumphant Church, is no longer a unity but rather what may be called a conjunction; or, if a unity, it is a torn and convulsed unity. Thus this is a kind of foreign and military unity, while that of the supercelestial Church is truly civic and triumphant.

## HERE THE THIRD MELODY FULLY RESOUNDS CONCERNING THE UNITY OF NATURE AND GRACE; IT FIRST DIVIDES IT INTO MILITARY AND TRIUMPHAL UNITY, AND FIRST TEACHES CONCERNING THE MILITARY. NOTE 22

This unity of nature and grace, then, is now as it were divided in two, although it is only one unity of the Church militant and triumphant. Just as charity and unity are one, yet this unity is as it were divided in two, because in triumph unity, like charity, is incomparably greater, better, and more delightful than in military service.

For the Church militant in this warfare, in which malice so abounds amid so many labors and sweats, such various and hostile dangers—where she has daily, as it were as a punishment, battle from the heart, the flesh, the world, and the enemy; amid so many impediments, so varied temptations, so many fiery rebellions of the flesh, and so many earthly desires of flesh and world—how can she be one when so divided, scattered, torn apart, and convulsed? And, to add the prophet’s words, how can she, “a poor woman tossed with tempest, without consolation,” stand in unity?

Yet because she tends toward unity in the homeland, she retains in the way such unity as she has; otherwise, as she knows, she would never reach that unity of the homeland. In the contest of this warfare, her unity is such and so great as her charity is: wounded charity, wounded and almost ruined unity; half-full charity, and half-full unity—they walk with equal steps. And if I add a third, I shall not exceed the truth: for as great as charity is, so great are unity and peace. The relation is reciprocal among these three. These three are equal, alike, and coeval.

And this military unity, although compared with triumphant unity it is in the present warfare like a kind of rupture, is nevertheless of marvelous strength and power, holding and containing the whole world of Churches through such varied ranks and orders. Of it our prophet says: “Set your hearts upon her strength” (Psalm 47): that is, upon our unity, the unity of the city of God of which the prophet there speaks. It is a strength which nothing conquers and no one tears apart; for it is the Lord’s seamless tunic.

For charity can do as much as charity is, from charity and with charity, and so can this unity of charity. For these two—unity and charity—are most friendly to one another; indeed, so are these three: peace, unity, and charity. How happy, good, and delightful, upon the way, is this still-pilgrim and subsolar Trinity: the Trinity of charity, unity, and peace. Each of them is in each; one is in all, and one is all things. How desirable, useful, and necessary is this subsolar Trinity upon the way, for the way, tending most straight toward that Trinity above the sun which is in the homeland, where there is eternal unity, eternal peace, and charity—as co-omnipotent and co-eternal: the Father, unity; the Son, peace; and the Holy Spirit, charity.

These are the three things which the Master prays and wishes for his disciples: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the charity of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be always with us all” (2 Corinthians 13). This grace of Jesus Christ, which he puts first, is peace, which is preeminently called grace. For peace is the end of every intention and work. And because he himself is properly, as the Master teaches, “our peace, who made both one.” The charity of God is the charity by which we love God and which comes only from God. The fellowship of the Holy Spirit is the communion made in us by charity or love, which is properly the Holy Spirit.

This communion or fellowship is unity, which charity held in common alone produces. Hence the Master speaks carefully of “the fellowship of the Holy Spirit.” Otherwise, unless charity is held in common, so that we love one another, there will not be fellowship or communion of the Holy Spirit, but rather a kind of individualism or solitude: this one loving and that one not loving. Thus in the one who loves and in the one who does not love, there will no longer be the unity produced by charity, but a singular and solitary charity. Therefore, desiring unity among brothers, the Master prays and wishes for them the fellowship of the Holy Spirit—that is, the communion of charity. Thus, in his prayerful words, he embraces our three things: peace, charity, and unity. Behold our military unity accompanied by charity and peace.

[Col. 1389A] Though sweet, good, and delightful, it is nevertheless always, while it serves here as a soldier, in anxiety and fear. The Master speaks of it thus, according to the likeness of the animate body: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; or if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it” (1 Corinthians 12). This is likewise daily and most fully experienced among the members of Christ’s spiritual body. Hence the Master himself, so sturdy and strong a member of this body, says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” (2 Corinthians 11). For a member of this spiritual body is more compassionate and more anxious the stronger and sturdier it is.

Otherwise, as the same Master teaches, there will be schism in the body if its members are not concerned for one another in the same way (1 Corinthians 12). Hence the unity of members in the body will not exist unless, so long as it serves here as a soldier, it remains in anxiety and fear.

And because we have inserted discussion of charity and peace on account of this third unity of nature and grace, in order that the measure of peace and unity might be shown in this subsolar Church according to the measure of charity, we must henceforth, leaving the other matters aside, treat this same unity more fully. And since we have already taught in part what this unity of nature and grace is like and how great it is in the Church militant, it remains to show what it is like and how great it is in the Church triumphant—more through the testimony of Scripture than through our own experience.

For the good and delight—indeed, the blessedness—of this unity surpasses all our understanding. Nevertheless, as it is granted from above, something must now be said concerning it, since it is that unity of the triumphant Church for whose sake all the preceding matters were introduced. For in this triumphant unity the soldier who has become a victor is with his triumphant emperor, to whose praise and glory our whole harp now resounds. Since their conformity both in battle and in victory on the way has been shown beforehand, so, according to our purpose and promise, their unity in the homeland must at last now be displayed.

## HE ALSO DIVIDES MILITARY UNITY INTO THE COMMON UNITY OF ALL THE JUST AND THE PRIVATE UNITY OF THE PERFECT; HE FIRST TEACHES CONCERNING THE COMMON. NOTE 23

Yet before we proceed, this must not be left unsaid: this military unity of our warfare is here among us as it were divided in two. One unity belongs commonly to all the emperor’s soldiers in the contest of the present life, established in faith, hope, and charity. Of it the Master says: “I beseech you, I, a prisoner in the Lord, that you walk worthily of the calling wherewith you are called, with all humility and meekness, with patience bearing one another in charity, eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, as you are called in one hope of your calling” (Ephesians 4). And the Master of masters says: “Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18:20). This is the common unity of all believers.

[Col. 1390A]

## ON THE PRIVATE MILITARY UNITY OF THE PERFECT, ETC.

There is another military unity—or rather, the same unity, but as it were another—more beautiful and perfect insofar as it more closely conforms to the triumphant and supercelestial unity of which we principally intend to speak in what follows. Of it our prophet says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together as one” (Psalm 132).

For there are certain soldiers of the emperor who sell all that they have, distribute all, abandon all, and renounce every ownership of visible things. They strip themselves so that, naked, they may run the way of this life the more safely because they carry nothing with them, and may fight the more freely because they are clothed only in the armor of God. Among these soldiers, once every possession has been removed, there is such unity that nothing is “mine” or “yours,” yet all is mine and all is yours.

For the life of these soldiers on the way is an image and exemplar of the supercelestial life of the victors in the homeland. This military unity is, insofar as is possible upon the way, an express likeness of that triumphant unity. Certainly this is the pattern of apostolic unity and of those first soldiers, of whom it is written: “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul; nor did anyone say that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them.”

Yet, as we have already said, we do not make two unities in the warfare of our present Church between emperor and soldiers, but one unity, though as it were divided in two: it is all the more adorned and made illustrious by certain illustrious soldiers because they, as nobler and more distinguished than the rest in the emperor’s battle-line, and magnificent and generous above the others, deem it unworthy to possess anything privately, but make all things common.

For the present I pass over that unity which exists among worldly people. It does not always have virtues as companions, but is a kind of secular and earthly unity, by which the wise of this world know how to govern their households well: maintaining a disciplined house, a quiet household, servants who fear and respect their master, ready for battle or quarrel. Such servants either yield to blows or, if incorrigible, are cast out of the house, like restless animals unyoked from a cart, lest they disturb the good and delight of their household’s unity.

So necessary is unity always and everywhere: whether it exists with virtues in God, and is then fruitful and best; or even without virtues among peaceful customs in the world, and is then likewise useful and pleasant. I have touched briefly upon this worldly unity only to recall that without unity there is nothing good or pleasant, either in God or in the world.

In that unity of illustrious soldiers, who deem it unworthy to possess anything privately but have all things in common, I would gladly and devoutly dwell, intending still to make many notes on it resound in our present melody upon the harp, were it not that this same unity of nature and grace—however beautiful, delightful, and perfect it may be in the present warfare—is incomparably greater, better, more delightful, and more perfect in the homeland. Therefore its own perfection and fullness compel me to hasten toward it.

For I remember having shown above that this unity of our pilgrimage is half-full. And because it is so imperfect here, nothing concerning it will here be taught fully, unless we proceed to other matters. For our principal intention has been entirely directed to this: that, because of which the preceding matters were introduced as though incidentally, something might be said by us—so far as the eternal and principal Unity, whose work this is, might deign to teach us—about the fullness of this third unity.

And indeed, unless our purpose and promise have perhaps slipped away because of the many intervening matters, our principal intention concerns this third, triumphant unity of nature and grace. For if, as we sufficiently showed above and set forth by argument, there was such great conformity between emperor and soldier in this way and life of such varied, diverse, manifold, invisible battle and invisible victory, how great will their unity be in the homeland?

Therefore we must henceforth approach this unity of the Church militant and triumphant, as from the outer sanctuary to the inner, and indeed as to the more inward bridal chamber of bridegroom and bride, in which, after sufferings and battles, sweat and labor, emperor and soldier rest together—so far as is permitted to pilgrims and strangers.

But before we set foot toward the bridal chamber, lest, knocking there irreverently or rashly, we suffer a shameful rebuff, let us address the chamber-maid of bridegroom and bride, the spokeswoman of all love, aware of all things, and somewhat familiar to us from our earliest years: named Prophecy. Let her be the guide of our way toward the chamber and its secret forerunner. Unless I am mistaken, since she has been my familiar and friend from early years, even if she cannot or does not dare grant us free entrance, she will nevertheless, leading us close behind her, permit us access as near as may be allowed.

### Concerning that triumphant unity of nature and grace, which is principally intended and is treated at length in the third melody, now sounding forth clearly and openly. Note 24.

And, that I may choose from the prophetic Scriptures a chamber-attendant more familiar to the bridegroom and bride, as the herald and confidante of all love, this is that chamber-attendant through whom the bridegroom—or rather, because of so great a unity, I know not whether bridegroom or bride—speaks thus: “He bound a mitre upon me as upon a bridegroom, and adorned me with ornaments as a bride” [Isa. 61:10]. Behold: that Splendor of glory and Image of the Father’s substance and Brightness of eternal life, the Heir of all things, who is the bridegroom, calls himself both bridegroom and bride because of the unity of pre-eminent and incomprehensible love. As a sign also of such unity and privileged love, he grants his bride a name from his own name: from Christ she is called Christian.

And this is so not only on the way, but also in the homeland, amid that multitude of a thousand thousands of angels—not angelic, indeed, but Christian—known and distinguished by this as by her own proper humanity, and united to her bridegroom, the supreme King’s Son, [Col. 1392A] distinct from the angels: united as in one flesh and one heart, and as in one name and one voice; all the spirits of the saints then being as it were one Holy Spirit, since all are united to him—truly, as well as ineffably and inconceivably, great Spirit—through the incomprehensibly pleasing, delightful, and unfailing unity of nature and grace. Then every spatial distance, every interval of time, every bodily obstacle, and even every schism of thought or action will have been removed far away.

By the first and principal unity, through this unity of nature and grace, there will then be between head and body, bridegroom and bride, Christ and Church, what from eternity exists by nature between Father and Son and Holy Spirit: grace bringing about what nature there brings about. Thus head and body, bride and bridegroom, Church and Christ will then be as one. That first and principal unity is so familiar and friendly to this unity of nature and grace, and desires it so greatly, that in order to join this unity to itself, it emptied itself through that second unity which we set forth above, the unity of grace alone, working this unity within itself and through itself.

Hence, unless I am mistaken, someone may perhaps now think this third unity of nature and grace between bridegroom and bride either worthier than, or at least equal to, that second unity of grace alone, by which “the Word was made flesh,” God in man and man God. He may think this, I say, because that unity exists for the sake of this one: namely, the unity of grace alone exists for the sake of this unity [Col. 1392C] of grace and nature. But who would dare define this? Who examine it? Who would dare prefer, or even equate, the unity of bridegroom and bride with the unity of the Word Most High, uniting and united to his flesh? Or conversely, if no one would dare prefer it, who would dare subordinate it?

For the union of Word and flesh exists for the sake of this unity of bridegroom and bride; and it is also established that the mystical and invisible flesh of the emperor—that is, the unity of the faithful—is far worthier and dearer to the emperor than that visible, weighty, bodily flesh of Christ which he took from the Virgin. And among the chief reasons for this, as it seems, is that for the sake of this mystical and invisible flesh he assumed that visible flesh and united it to himself. For its sake he exposed that flesh to reproaches, insults, scourges, spitting, [Col. 1392D] blows, and manifold misery and ignominy; throughout all thirty-three years he worked and labored for this invisible flesh and for its sake in his visible flesh. Such considerations may indeed lead one to prefer one unity to the other—or, since perhaps no one would dare prefer it, at least to equate unity with unity.

Yet let none of us, approaching this bridal chamber, where the bridegroom is upon the bed and the bride is in so great an embrace of unity—let none of us, I say, cry out, make a disturbance, or knock presumptuously. That friend and intimate of ours, the aforesaid chamber-attendant of bridegroom and bride, guide and forerunner of our way toward the chamber, commands us to stand here. Here she whispers that we should rest. “My secret,” she says, [Col. 1393A] “is for myself; my secret is for myself” [Isa. 24:16]. She adds this too, as if threatening: “He makes the searchers-out of secrets as though they were not, and makes the judges of the earth as vanity” [Isa. 40:23].

It is therefore good and fitting that each of us, as he makes his way toward the chamber, restrain his tongue, spare his words, and merely ponder within himself what he has wished and how he is moved by what has been said—if only according to what the principal unity, friend of both unities, has deemed worthy to reveal to him. Yet there is one thing I dare to say because I see it: between the uniting Word and the flesh united to it there is indeed a privileged, new, unheard-of, singular unity; but it may seem that, although that unity is more wonderful because of its singularity, this third unity is more fruitful because of its universality, by which all the members of the head are united to the head, so that Christ may be whole—the head together with the members.

But why do I distinguish in this way between these two unities, as though declaring the one more wonderful and the other possibly more fruitful? Unless I had that friend of mine as guide and forerunner on my way toward the chamber of bridegroom and bride, I could easily stray in a trackless place rather than on the way. For that prior unity of Word and flesh, the unity of grace alone, is truly not only more wonderful but, if one wishes to consider it, more fruitful as well. The whole fruit of this third unity of ours comes through and from it.

But, to answer here the preceding observations by which I might have seemed to wish to prefer this unity of nature and grace to that second unity of grace alone, or at least to equate it with it, I say now briefly and absolutely: although that second unity of Word and flesh was made for the sake of this third unity of bridegroom and bride, nevertheless, as it seems to me, that second unity is far worthier than this third. For the second was made for the sake of the third in such a way that the third itself was made through the second. Thus that second unity is both the cause and the agent of this third—indeed, its co-worker.
