The first and principal unity effected the second for the sake of the third, and afterwards that same first and principal unity effected the third through the second.

The case is otherwise, however, with the mystical body of Christ and the body which he drew from the Virgin, of both of which we touched above. Here a wholly different consideration revises the judgment. But of this elsewhere. Therefore, to return to the point: although I do not dare either to prefer or equate this our third unity with that unity of grace alone, nevertheless, for the dignity of this third unity of ours—to which, though I am now in the way of this mortal life so variously scattered, torn, and convulsed, I hope at least through death, incineration, and fire still to be joined—for the dignity of this third unity, I say, I dare one thing, and shall now allege one thing.

For it is certainly true, and let no one doubt it—for it will now be shown—that the second unity of Word and flesh is the bright, glorious, and most exquisite exemplar of this our third unity. Therefore, such as the unity is now between Word and flesh, such a unity between bridegroom and bride do we expect in that kingdom of unity and peace. The Holy Spirit signifies this to us through the Word of the Father, uniting to himself man, so that we may become like him, and that we too ought to hope for unity between beloved and beloved: Christ, I mean, and the Church.

And as I often meditate in my heart: he who foreknew all things from eternity created such a man that his nature was suitable for union with the Godhead, and such that the Godhead itself neither disdained nor shrank from it, but rather, as it were, desired to unite it to itself. I judge that no such worthy and unheard-of privilege of human nature was implanted in angelic nature or in any other nature whatsoever at its creation: namely, that the Godhead should desire to unite to itself the nature of any nature other than man alone. Whether it neither united, nor even could unite, another nature to itself, I presume neither to affirm nor deny. [Col. 1394B]

Leaving this aside, then, let us return to that glorious and express exemplar of our unity. We hope that there will be for us between bridegroom and bride such a unity of our nature and grace as we already see preceded it: the unity of grace alone between God alone and the sole, one, unique man Christ Jesus. Such, I say—yet not altogether such, but most expressly such. For who will believe our faith? Who will believe our change, so new and unheard-of? But why do I say “change”? Rather, transformation. Indeed, why should there even be mention here of change or transformation? It seems to be transubstantiation rather than any change or transformation: man then, as it were, transubstantiated into God, and human nature, as it were, into one nature of the Godhead.

Even the first motions of the mind will be swallowed up in this kind of transubstantiation; and the blessed soul, through the vehement spirit of love, will then be transubstantiated, as it were forever, into ardor because of such great grace and glory. I call it ardor because my friend and intimate, guide and forerunner of my way toward the chamber, suggested it to me thus while I was journeying. Speaking beforehand of the chamber, she had used this very word “ardor” in one place, asking who would be worthy to dwell in that chamber: “Which of you,” she says, “can dwell with devouring fire? Which of you can dwell with everlasting burnings?” [Isa. 33:14]. And she immediately adds the answer: “He who walks in righteousness and speaks truth; who casts away avarice born of oppression, and shakes his hands free [Col. 1394D] from every gift” [Isa. 33:15]. Behold, then: a righteous man with God; a man with devouring fire; a man with everlasting ardor. For elsewhere also it is read that “our God is a consuming fire” [Deut. 4:24].

God here is indeed a consuming fire on the way, and the same God is perfecting in the homeland. On the way, this fire, our God, tests and examines his own in many ways; in the homeland he glorifies and illumines them variously and in manifold ways. Therefore our God is a consuming fire on the way, testing and examining his own so that no trace of old rust may be found in them, and so that they may at last be transferred to the kingdom: just as, when oil has been most purely strained, no dregs remain and it is thus carried into the storehouse; and when silver has been purified sevenfold, no slag remains and it is thus transferred into the treasury; and similarly, when grain has been thoroughly winnowed, the chaff flies away and it is thus stored in the granary.

These and other examples may aid the point we have proposed; but none suffices. For silver, however thoroughly purified, might again be corrupted by slag, just as most purely strained oil might be corrupted by dregs. But once this corruptible has put on incorruption and this mortal immortality, it will thereafter be unable either to die or to be corrupted. Thus, for fully showing this, an example created under the sun, though helpful, is insufficient. That above-the-sun, bright, glorious, incorruptible exemplar alone is adequate—indeed, more than adequately sufficient—for explaining this third unity of bridegroom and bride: namely, the unity of God assuming and humanity assumed.

For that assumed man, while still on the way clothed in our mortal, corruptible skin amid all the vain and deceptive things of this way and life—something which is astonishing to say and a great merit of faith and virtue—neither sinned nor could sin even in a passing thought of anything vain or idle. And surely it is a great merit of faith for us to believe this: that a man of our nature could not even sin on the way, whereas, as we experience in ourselves, it is impossible for us, though similarly human, scarcely to pass even a moment without sin. What wonder, therefore, if, after death has been swallowed up in victory, and we have put on in the homeland a new, immortal, incorruptible form, freed from all vanity and, after incineration and fire, made drunk from the sole pure fountain of truth—what wonder, I say, if thereafter we neither sin nor are even able to sin?

And yet this very thing is wondrous and miraculous, for the miraculous power of God does this in the example. But the form of the exemplar is much more wonderful—so much more wonderful that, compared with it, even this does not seem wonderful. Thus the form of the exemplar is the truest and fullest certainty of the example. Yet this is more wonderful in the example than in the exemplar: although the soul here has experienced so many desires, temptations, allurements, idle thoughts, and vanities—or rather, although throughout all the days of its flesh it has been not merely exposed to these but worn down by them—there it will neither sin in these things, nor wish to sin, nor even be capable of sinning.

For, according to the teaching of this friend and intimate guide of ours, who knows the inner chamber, when a new heaven and a new earth have been created, “the former things shall no longer be remembered, nor shall they rise upon the heart” [Isa. 65:17], while the bridegroom rejoices over his bride forever. And the spirit of man will thus stand forever, though a man, whether he wishes or not, can scarcely stand here without sin even for a moment. Hence, if anyone examines diligently, he will immediately understand that through grace the unity of nature and grace in man is rather a certain transubstantiation than a transfiguration or transformation in the homeland: man then, as it were, converted into some nature of the Godhead. So that then that saying first finds fulfillment which was foretold by the Prophet: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” [Ps. 81:6]. [Col. 1396A]

And indeed the Master, who was caught up to the third heaven, to whom, as the heavenly bridegroom’s and bride’s paranymph, many things of the inner chamber were shown, and who, admitted even to the chamber’s innermost places, heard secret words which it is not lawful for a man to utter—he, I say, did not remain silent in many places of his Gospel about this unity of our nature and grace. But among other things, this is one passage I distinguish and prefer, because it is more relevant to our purpose: “When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all” [1 Cor. 15:28].

Because of the slowness of my understanding, I used unwillingly to think doubtfully and hesitantly about this subjection, say little, and write nothing. And especially now I ought to write or say nothing about it, since the present subject is not subjection but unity. Therefore I hold to the Master’s final words of the verse that concern our purpose: “that God may be all in all.” I hold to them, indeed, because I do not hesitate that the Master commends in these few words this third unity of our nature and grace, which is the whole subject of the present discourse: “God,” he says, “all in all.” Thus, according to the Master, God is all, and God is in all.

Let us note the Master’s word—he who, admitted to the inner chamber, heard even mysteries which it is not lawful for a man to utter [2 Cor. 12:4]. Therefore this word of the chamber, which it has been lawful for us human beings to speak, must now be noted; and it must be noted all the more attentively because we know that he spoke thus as the paranymph of the chamber. Let us weigh and note the word, so that the bond of our unity may perhaps become more evident even through some enigma; yet I regard this as the indissoluble bond of this unity, and as a word intelligible even to my slowness, unless perhaps this too, if it has been granted from above, is to be seen speculatively and enigmatically: “God,” he says, “all in all.”

Therefore, through this unity of yours, ineffably devised, according to the Master’s teaching, all things then will be as it were one nature, as it were one spirit, one God—then, for the first time, as a whole, when the members now scattered piecemeal along the way have finally been joined to the head in the homeland. This will be so for all who now, in this pilgrimage, tend toward the unity of the homeland: in unity then—indeed, as a certain simple, true, first, and principal unity—everything then. Yet the Master does not say “that God may be as it were all,” but, without “as it were,” says, “God all.” [Col. 1396D]

The Master, caught up to the third heaven and acquainted with the more secret things of the chamber, seems, I say, to teach that from the uncreated Spirit and the created spirits—which nevertheless were eternally in God’s eternal mind—there will then be a certain full, perfect, consummated unity, with all the spirits of the blessed as though transubstantiated, and with our two unities, the second and third, brought back into that first and principal unity. Perhaps this is why the bridegroom says: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” [John 3:13]; and again: “I am the first and I am the last” [Rev. 1:17], Alpha then returned to Omega, and Omega to Alpha, all things, namely, as we have already begun to say, that now hold to and tend toward the first unity being brought back to it.

But let us hear how they are brought back. For I neither think nor believe—far be it—that this is according to essence, but according to an emphasis incomprehensible and ineffable to us. Thus, just as there is a Trinity of three persons and yet one first and principal unity of those same persons, so there may be a trinity of our three unities, and yet one first and principal unity of those same unities. Yet I do not dare say that their unity is according to essence, but according to a certain privileged emphasis incomprehensible to us.

Nevertheless, the Master seems to teach, not emphatically but substantively, that God is all, as though all things then in God are in the homeland by inherence which now are in him on the way by adhesion. Inherence is, as it were, the privilege of the homeland in which its citizens rejoice happily, just as adhesion is the good of the way by which pilgrims walk more steadily lest they fail on the way. Thus our Prophet says: “But for me, still a pilgrim, it is good to adhere to God” [Ps. 72:28].

Yet I believe the Master spoke of “God all” to signify the ineffable and incomprehensible unity of bridegroom and bride. For all Scripture together with the Master proclaims a unity so great, glorious, and excellent that Scripture neither wishes nor is able to be read with understanding, or understood when read, unless this unity is read and understood in it. Thus bridegroom and bride, as they are now one flesh, are likewise one voice even while still in the field and not yet in bed; so much so that in the frequent places of Scripture it is often and repeatedly ambiguous whether he or she is speaking. By these sacred utterances the Holy Spirit even now signifies to us the privilege of that great and most excellent future unity between bridegroom and bride, toward which we now tend. Nor is it necessary now, in order to prove this unity between bridegroom and bride in one voice, to add examples from Scripture; the immense and numerous forest of Scriptures abounds copiously with them. [Col. 1397D]

Unless I am mistaken, we now see in part the great, friendly, and incomprehensible unity between bridegroom and bride in the chamber, which the aforementioned guide and forerunner of our way first suggested to us while we were journeying; and which afterwards the Master disclosed, as much as pleased him and perhaps as much as was permitted him, all the more surely and faithfully because in his empyrean rapture he had entered the innermost places of the chamber. Although in his manner he revealed much in few words, from them not only this melody of ours might be formed, but many bright volumes also might be subtly and elegantly composed, as from splendid, almost pregnant and weighty material.

And since this third melody of unity—or rather, of unities—which is now being composed last after the others concerning our third unity, desires an end; and since I am weary from plucking this lyre for a while with whatever fingers I have upon its sharper and subtler strings, let me conclude the melody more quickly and briefly repeat this in a more harmonious form from what has preceded. Just as there is a Trinity of three persons and yet unity, so there is, in its own manner, a trinity of our unities and yet a first and principal unity of the three. For, as we recall having taught above, trinity is nothing else than unity of three. Therefore there is a trinity of three unities because there is one first and principal unity of the three.

Indeed, these three unities are this one first and principal unity. In the assumed man it operated through grace alone; hence it was called the unity of grace alone. But in the union of bridegroom and bride it operates through nature and grace; hence this same unity is called the unity [Col. 1398B] of nature and grace. And this is what the Master teaches when he says, “God all.” For if God is all, nothing will remain that is not God; and so our two unities are God, because they are the one first and principal unity, and thus God.

Consider likewise the assumed man: God, because here too God is man and man is God. This is the second unity of grace alone, and it is God, living thus by grace alone. Likewise, in the body united to the head there is God, because here too whole Christ—the head together with the body—is full and perfect God. This is our third unity of nature and grace. And this too, if one considers it, is likewise the first and principal unity: God thus uniting by nature and grace. For it is not that which is united, but only that which truly and properly unites, that is this unity.

Yet perhaps, as in the former unity of grace alone, so also in this unity of nature and grace there is a certain created unity—or, more truly, union. But whether there is there a created unity or union matters now neither to me nor to it. This, however, I say according to the Scriptures, faithfully and confidently: at the end of all things, when judgment has been completed, whole Christ, head together with body, will be full and perfect God—according to the faithful witness in heaven, the moon then forever perfect. No one will deny that the head together with the body is God, and then full and perfect God, unless perhaps he wishes, like one dreaming, to assert that the head alone is God and refuses to admit that Christ whole—head together with body—is true and perfect God.

But we must neither hesitate nor delay over these matters: not that the body of the head is God, but that Christ whole, head with body, is full and none other than true and perfect God, then as it were through victorious unity, with every schism and with all diversity and difference—the perpetual consequences of schism—swallowed up, and thus also in number. For the head of this body itself says: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” [John 3:13].

Therefore, just as we now worship one God made man—which the second unity of grace alone effects—so likewise, when the form of this world has passed away and judgment has been accomplished, that same God will be praised without end, clothed as it were in his destined garment, his glorious Church, which he presented to himself without spot or wrinkle. This our third unity [Col. 1399A] of nature and grace effects for our Lord: as he is now made man, so then he will be not only made man but gloriously clothed, when the queen shall stand at his right hand and he will then be surrounded by the variety of humans and angels, yet more strongly and firmly united by this unity.

Man is united to God more strongly and firmly by this unity than an angel is united to God, whether now or then; for between God and angel there is unity of grace only, not of nature. But between God and man there is unity both of nature and grace—certainly, unless I am mistaken, sweeter, more welcome, and firmer between God and man in the homeland, because man has arrived there only with great difficulty through so many labors and pains in this way, through such varied temptations, through so many and such great tribulations and struggles, and finally through death and confinement.

### Here he first inserts a discussion of a certain name of the bridegroom, which serves to commend this third unity, but especially on the way.

But let us return to our Christ, full, perfect, and whole. He is not yet full while he is still with us and for our sake amid persecution and labor. Thus the intimate forerunner of my way toward the chamber informed me, while I journeyed, concerning the bridegroom’s name, secretly instilling that the bridegroom, though unseen, accompanied us secretly with us on the way. “Do you know,” she said, “the name of the bridegroom to whose chamber I am leading you? His name,” she said, “is called Emmanuel” [Matt. 1:23].

And I immediately answered her: “I thank you, my lady and friend. Now that the name has first been disclosed, I perceive; now I know. For this one is truly and properly our Emmanuel: not yet continually with his bride in the chamber, but daily still with us in the field, and truly with us now on this way which we walk. This one is indeed truly our Emmanuel—truly God with us; God and with us, God truly with us: with us in our flesh and in our heart; with us in persecution; with us also in labor; with us in distress; with us in pressure; with us in punishment; with us in battle; with us in temptation; with us in pilgrimage; with us on the way; with us in the homeland; with us in death; with us in consummation; with us according to our desire; with us according to his promise.

Therefore you, my lady, my intimate and [Col. 1399D] friend, rightly and properly called him this. For, as we have said, he acts thus with us and promised to do so as a consolation in our miserable pilgrimage: ‘Behold, I am with you unto the consummation of the age’ [Matt. 28:20]. For daily and continually he fulfills in his body—which we are, which is the Church—those things still lacking of his sufferings. And this is the work of our third unity, which thus unites our Emmanuel to us on the way, laboring with us in this manner until the consummation of the age. Therefore before that consummation of the age Christ is at every time imperfect and not whole. Likewise, when all labor has finally ended in the consummation, he will then be in full and most blessed rest.

### Secondly he inserts a discussion of the bride’s name, which likewise serves to commend this third unity, but especially in the homeland.

[Col. 1400A]

After, as we have set forth, the bride’s name had been explained [as the source reads] for the commendation of this unity of ours according to our intention, I immediately asked my guide also about the bride’s name, hoping that this too would advance my purpose. And she at once replied: “You see,” she said, “that this name of my lady and bride which you seek is very relevant to what you intend.” Yet the bride’s name which you now seek is new: the bridegroom’s own mouth named it and bestowed it upon her as a signal of the privileged mutual love—“My will in her.”

And I immediately said to my inward guide: “Truly, my guide and sweet friend, how new and unheard-of this name is!” Truly it is a new name, and it is altogether credible that the bridegroom’s own mouth named it and that the bride was thus called by the bridegroom. Truly it is a new name; and I know not what name of new love—wonderful, astonishing, most desirable, privileged love—derived from the name of God, good God, merciful and compassionate God. She who formerly both in reality and in name was deserted and forsaken is now called by God himself, by the Lord himself and bridegroom, by his own proper name, because of the privilege of unheard-of love: “My will in her.”

The very new name indicates that what the Lord’s own mouth named is a reality; and I judge that not a single iota, nor even half an iota, of that name is empty. Nothing in it is superfluous, nothing void of mystery, nothing lacking the privilege of love. I feel each of its letters as though ignited by love itself. Therefore my guide, the most intimate chamber-attendant of bridegroom and bride, rightly says both that it is new and that the Lord’s own mouth named it, since it most expressly indicates the bridegroom, outwardly by the number of its words and inwardly by the meanings of the same words.

Leaving aside other things that might be said, I shall now say only what concerns me: above all, I note that in this one name of the bride are several names, and these several names are one name; the name is, as it were, threefold and yet one. Such a name is surely fitting for that bride who is bride of the one and triune God. And not only, as we recall having said above concerning the name “Christian,” is Christ alone indicated as the bride’s name; but in this new name her bridegroom, namely God, is designated more fully as one and three.

First, he who speaks says to the Father: “My will in her.” Behold, the Son is the Father’s will—unless perhaps we have forgotten that word of the Gospel: “This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased” [Matt. 17:5]. Then, in the words “in her,” love is expressed—the love that is in the very marrow of the heart. Behold the Holy Spirit. It is noteworthy that he does not say “My will from her” or “through her,” but “in her,” so that love itself may be named more expressly with all its force. Thus in this new name of the bride, named by the bridegroom’s own mouth, the whole, full, true, and eternal bridegroom of the bride is declared: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. And just as the bridegroom is threefold, so in this new name he is declared to be one; for here three names are one new name of the bride. [Col. 1401A]

### That the first name of the bridegroom commends this third unity, but on the way; whereas the second name of the bride likewise commends it, but in the homeland.

We now have two names of bridegroom and bride commending this our third unity of nature and grace. First, the bride’s name, which is Emmanuel [as the source reads], commends this unity to us on the way; but the bride’s name commends the same unity to us in the homeland. Thus the bride, having her bridegroom as her inseparable companion on the way—as the first name indicates—may run more easily toward the unity in the homeland expressed by the second name. For that name of the bridegroom, Emmanuel, is the name of the way; but the bride’s name, “My will in her,” is the name of the homeland. The bride’s name thus indicates what kind of bridegroom she has with her on the way, so that she may run more strongly toward the homeland and God may invite her. The first name of the bridegroom is, as it were, in the field and in battle, because, as we have said, it is the name of the way; but the second name of the bride is, as it were, in the chamber and on the bed, because it is the name of the homeland.

### Concerning the second name of the bridegroom, which he does not have on the way but in the homeland, and how greatly it accords with the bride’s name of the homeland.

Yet just as the bridegroom has a name of the way, so he also has a name of the homeland. This accords wonderfully with the bride’s new name of the homeland. When I sought it, the Master, paranymph of the bridegroom and bride, suggested it to me now upon this way toward the chamber—not as something new, but as already named above and now to be repeated because it is fitting. It is that which the Master taught us above: “God all in all” [1 Cor. 15:28]. God, namely, is all in all; this is, as it were, one name of the bridegroom in the homeland, just as “My will in her” is the bride’s name there.

Let us therefore lift our eyes, raise our ears, and with our whole heart consider these two names of bridegroom and bride in the homeland: how fitting, harmonious, and concordant they are. Even their outward composition—the composition of only three words—is how concordant; and the same word, “in,” is placed between them, as it were a preposition of love. Here and there these names, unfamiliar and unimagined by us, expressed in love and as it were inflamed and ignited by love, wholly commend to us this incomprehensible unity of our nature and grace.

One name so harmonizes with the other that each entails the other. For if God is all in all, it follows that God’s will—and God’s will alone—is in her: she is rightly called by God himself, by his proper name, “My will in her.” If a will other than God’s will alone were in her, God would no longer be all in all. Therefore, if God’s will alone is in her, nothing in her is her own; rather, everything in her is God, and thus God is all in all. And conversely, as has now been shown, if God is all in all and . . . [A few words are missing.]

[Col. 1402A]

### Thirtieth note of the third melody, and also the last.

[lacuna] [Here, as happened by mischance, the C.C.C. manuscript ends, with two or even more folios lost from the end of the book. At the same place the Arras manuscript is also imperfect; consequently a gap, though a very short one, occurs here.] [lacuna] …ra [fragmentary] are more splendid and beautiful the nearer and more closely joined they are to the head of the body. For member differs from member in beauty, as star from star in brightness, and soldier from soldier at an emperor’s banquet. And likewise, in the kingdom of unity, spirit differs from spirit in unity. O how great a unity I now see, by certain faith, in that kingdom of unity between the emperor and his soldier—those whose life here was so torn, so divided, so disjointed, yet in conduct, work, suffering, battle, and victory I had previously seen so great a conformity.

[Col. 1402B] Therefore let us cry out, knocking; and crying out again, let us knock at the emperor and his triumphant soldier; wailing and crying after them, in the hope that they may, even thus, show us pilgrims and those in danger amid so many temptations and changes of this journey and life, amid so many goads of the flesh, thorns of vices, and stings of tribulations—us who are torn and scattered from that unity in which they now are—the way here, and draw us after themselves to it; so that, as the whole history of the martyr has been fulfilled, we may run in the fragrance of their virtues. Let us run, I say, until we are brought to that unity of bridegroom and bride, emperor and soldier, in which, just as we shall not be dissolved bodily, so neither shall we thereafter be torn or scattered spiritually by schisms of deeds or even of thoughts.

[Col. 1402C] And since the triumphant soldier is now with his emperor in victory, brought through conformity to his emperor upon the way to the most glorious unity of that emperor in the homeland, where the bridegroom is now in the bed and the beloved in his embrace, let the third and final melody of the threefold unity now be brought to its end here. For to the praise and glory alike of emperor and soldier, upon David’s harp, we have already fashioned, in some fashion, three melodies. The first melody was of the visible and conforming battle of emperor and soldier, and that melody was for lamentation. The second melody was of the visible and conforming victory of emperor and soldier, and that melody was for joy. But this third and final melody is of the invisible and conforming victory of emperor and soldier. And this melody is for jubilation. Its entire

[Col. 1402D] subject concerns those things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart. Accordingly, this melody fittingly ends here, brought to the glorious end of the triumphant emperor and soldier, where there is an end without end.

This third melody is indeed rather long, because with hands too fleshy and heavy for playing the harp, and fingers less fitted to make the higher and sharper strings of the harp resound upon a subject so worthy of melody, it has been shaped—if not gracefully—yet somehow, even if awkwardly; its form showing the unskilled skill of the harpist’s melody.

It is also longer, to confess the truth, because I am torn away most unwillingly from my lord—whether upon the way or in the homeland, whether in battle or in victory, whether in the field or in the bed.

[Col. 1403A] Yet now I must be torn away. For I am still in danger and a pilgrim. My lord having been taken from me, I have been left so utterly alone in this pilgrimage—without companion, comfort, or help—that the British world, in which I stayed for some time while writing this history of the martyr, scarcely wishes, I do not know whether it deigns or dares, to share fellowship with me. And this is especially my complaint concerning the bishops of my land. Perhaps, because of our king’s first anger against me, they are still frightened and either do not deign, or fear, to communicate with me. Or perhaps, again, they count it an injury to themselves that I rendered to my father and lord—their predecessor—through so many labours, so many difficulties, losses, and dangers, service as devoted, as the world knows, and as faithful as I did.

And, what is most strange, they daily venerate the dead relics of the body of my father and lord, who, as they report, was likewise their father and patron, a body dead and descending into corruption; but they despise his living relics. A remarkable devotion indeed—

[Col. 1403B] whether fruitful, God knows; let them see to it. It would certainly seem worthier and more devout that, over the wounds of their dead patron’s body, they should pour out the bowels of their compassion upon his relics that are still living.

Nevertheless, concerning the two successors of my lord in the metropolitan see whom I saw while I was still writing the history of the martyr, I now raise no question and make no complaint. To them alone, as the spouses of my mother, the holy Church of Canterbury,

[Col. 1404A] I owe reverence, not the raising of any question or complaint. They themselves know what is fitting, and let them see what they have done. To confess the truth, this contempt of me—whether from these or those persons, or from the judgment of men—I count as very small. For it is my glory if, with my lord and master taken from me and ascending his fiery chariot, I, his disciple still a pilgrim, fulfil in myself what is lacking of his sufferings, singing with the Prophet: “I am little and despised; I have not forgotten thy statutes” (Ps. 118). And likewise: “Redeem me from the slanders of men, that I may keep thy commandments” (ibid.). For after my lord’s departure from this world, appearing to me soon afterward in a vision, he enjoined on me a continual remembrance of this verse as an antidote against the poisoned tongues of slanderers. He added also that this verse excelled among the psalmist’s verses. Therefore I pray, and pray again, that the Lord may redeem me from the slanders of men, that I may keep his commandments.

[Col. 1404B] HERE ENDS THE THIRD MELODY.

The three melodies upon David’s harp, according to our promise, for the praise and glory of emperor and soldier, having now been completed as we were instructed from above, there follows, likewise according to our earlier promise, our humble homily for the anniversary day of the martyr, which begins thus: “Let us sing to the Lord.”

[Col. 1403]

HOMILY OF HERBERT OF BOSEHAM, DISCIPLE AND HISTORIAN OF THE MARTYR, ON THE ANNIVERSARY DAY OF THE MARTYR.

[Col. 1403C] “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified: horse and rider he cast into the sea” (Exod. 15).

We know, brethren, we all know that this song is a song of the Hebrews: indeed, the song of those who passed through fire and water. Yet, just as the synagogue of the Hebrews then, so now the Church of the Hebrews claims—or rather borrows—this song for herself, saying, “Let us sing to the Lord.” For we, who are true Israelites and are called God’s Church, like our Hebrew brethren who have already gone before us on the way and preceded us into the homeland, have passed through fire and water. But where the children are saved, the enemies perish; riders and horses are submerged. This is the cause and subject of the song. Therefore let us too sing to the Lord.

But first

[Col. 1403D] it must be observed that there are three kinds of songs among the children of Israel. And this, I say, must first be observed, so that it may clearly appear whether, by saying “Let us sing to the Lord,” the Church today invites us to each of them or especially to one of the three. Thus the children of Israel have a threefold song. The first song is a song of sorrow; the second, of praise;

[Col. 1404C] the third, of jubilation. The first is sung in Egypt; the second in the wilderness; the third in the kingdom. The first song belongs to the oldness of sin; the second to the newness of life; the third to the overflowing of joy. The first is, as it were, without hope in the misery of this world; the second is in the consolation of hope; the third in the vision of reality. Those of the first sing with groaning and hold their hands raised in supplication for pardon; those of the second sing while labouring and hold their hands outstretched, watchful for battle; those of the third sing in triumph and hold their hands at rest, already secure in victory.

The first song belongs to those returning to themselves and preparing themselves for the race: they constantly utter lamentation and “woe.” The second belongs to those now running: in their mouths is constantly “a new song, a hymn to our God.” But the third

[Col. 1404D] song belongs to those who have arrived. Yet the tongue, still subject to death, does not express the sounds of this song, because at the unveiling of spiritual joys the human voice grows hoarse; for the eternal joys of angels are not like these transitory festivals of human beings. These are the things which eye has not seen, because they are hidden; nor ear heard, because they are in most tranquil peace; nor have they

[Col. 1405A] entered into the human heart, because they are incomprehensible. The first song invokes God and asks forgiveness; the second propitiates God and seeks help; but the third delights God and displays joy. For this is the supercelestial song, the admirable song, the song of proclamation which cannot be expressed and cannot be kept silent. This song is the Song of Songs, the nuptial song, when the bride is now in the bed and the bridegroom in her embrace.

But perhaps, brethren, some of you are now noting that the children of Israel are not read to have sung to the Lord in Egypt, but rather to have cried to the Lord. Yet that cry was a song in the ears of the Lord of Hosts. Nor shall I call it merely a song: rather, it was also a sacrifice.

[Col. 1405B] For what is it but a sacrifice where there is such affliction of flesh and contrition of heart? For even without affliction of flesh God does not despise a heart alone that is contrite and humbled: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.”

We have now distinguished, brethren, three songs of the children of Israel. But concerning the first, which we said was a song of sorrow and was sung in Egypt, it must be observed that it has a threefold cause and subject: namely, that famous and well-known threefold oppression of that threefold slavery under Pharaoh among the Egyptians—mud, brick, and straw. And those Hebrew brethren of ours were then oppressed bodily; but we now, their fellow brethren and fellow servants, are oppressed by the same yoke, though spiritually—by the spiritual yoke of spiritual slavery.

[Col. 1405C] It is certainly now so much heavier and more burdensome, because in them there was then only a figure of slavery, whereas in us there is now the fulfilment of the slavery signified. And this notwithstanding the destruction alike of the power of slavery, the yoke of slavery, and the taskmaster of so many slaveries.

For the sake of this peace, brethren, which is consummated in the salvation of the children and the vengeance upon their enemies, there is praise; and this peace is the subject of the second song, which we have repeatedly called the song of praise. Therefore, for this peace, the entire Church militant especially invites us by these words to this song of praise, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he cast into the sea.” She invites us, I say, and does so in particular through an athlete of Christ singular in our days, an anointed one of the Lord: first indeed fighting manfully,

[Col. 1405D] but in our days triumphing happily. Or rather, this athlete of Christ, this anointed one of the Lord, himself summons the whole Church of Christ at this time to this song of praise by his example and confirms her in praise by his triumph.

And lest anyone be in doubt as to who this man is, whom I thus touch upon but do not yet name, attend, brethren; raise your hands, lift up your eyes, prick up your ears, and recognize by his name as your own leader this athlete of Christ, this anointed one of the Lord. This athlete of Christ, this anointed one of the Lord, is surely the glorious new martyr of Christ, Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury and now, without contradiction, primate of all England. He stands in our midst—would that we also knew him. And indeed he is recognizable, because if his face does not distinguish him,

[Col. 1406A] his wound does. For the martyr stands for us and among us, dancing and triumphing, his whole head torn open. The martyr stands, I say, stronger amid the strokes of swords in exile than Adam amid the apples of delight in paradise. The martyr stands, I say, among swordsmen, fearless and unconquered. The martyr stands, I say, praying and supplicating, not for himself but for us, for those entrusted to him.

O precious, O conspicuous sacrifice—more conspicuous the rarer it is—where the same person is both sacrifice and priest, thereby bearing the title of his Lord, prince of martyrs. It adds to the spectacle that he was sacrificed where he had been consecrated; and further, that, in the body of so holy a saint—otherwise wholly untouched—upon its very summit, the crown of the head, the very place of pontifical anointing,

[Col. 1406B] he attained the martyr’s palm with the punishment of a wound—losing a crown but receiving a crown: a crown for a crown; in place of the corruptible crown of flesh, the unfading crown of spirit. Indeed, immediately, if I am not mistaken, he received for one simple crown a double crown, namely a golden crown and a martyr’s aureole.

O sacrifice truly bringing salvation, offered for the salvation of the Church at the Savior’s nativity, and in the Savior’s Church. And offered not between temple and altar, nor in the corners or recesses of the church as though fleeing the executioners, but between the horns of the church’s altar, presenting himself before the altar of the blessed abbot Benedict. Thus God wondrously ordained it for his martyr’s glory, so that both the time and place of the sacrifice should be marked most expressly, not only by the grace

[Col. 1406C] of salvation and blessing but also by the very names of salvation and blessing, like splendid and chosen titles. For here is the Savior’s Church; here is the Savior’s nativity feast; and, lest anything be wanting to the sacrifice, here is the altar of blessed Benedict. Thus, just as the places and times are full of salvation and blessing, so too by the names of places and times they express salvation and blessing.

O if we saw—and if it were granted us to see—the bishop, the true living sacrifice, standing in these places and at these times among executioners surrounding him with hands armed with iron, we should surely say that Phinehas was standing here in zeal, and Moses, a man of God in all meekness, there. For he stands like Phinehas, his pontificate now drawing near its end, by no means forgetful that he is bishop; with all authority he rebukes the very swordsmen amid the swords by pontifical authority,

[Col. 1406D] not defending himself with the priestly sword but exposing both his own people and himself for his people, under perpetual anathema most sternly and imperiously forbidding them to harm or touch any of his own. He also stands as another Moses, praying for the people and for the whole holy city; the martyr stands, I say, like another Moses, praying and supplicating—praying and supplicating as shepherd and special leader and patron of the English Church. For her sake, “with the joy set before him,” he endured the cross, despising shame, choosing rather to be afflicted for his brethren than to enjoy the pleasure of temporary sin. In this too he certainly showed himself to us as another Moses.

For although he was a companion at court to the Augusti—indeed, as it were co-emperor with the emperor—

[Col. 1407A] immediately and unexpectedly, as soon as he was called by God, he stripped off purple and put on sackcloth. Thus, like a new recruit of Christ, he girded himself for the spiritual contest, to fight with beasts. Against them, as the world knows, he fought so manfully that today, as the whole world of churches celebrates, he triumphs so mightily.

For who ever heard such a thing? Who saw its like? Or to whom was this deed revealed? Some martyr has prayed for his persecutors, offering himself. But who at the same time drew his sword—not for himself, but defending his own people so sternly and imperiously amid swords? Truly, in this new martyr of ours this is new and unheard of. Therefore this triumph, so singular, so new, so splendid, summons the whole world of churches to a new and unheard-of heralding song of praise: “Let us sing,” he says, “to the Lord.”

Yet though at this triumphant time praise is owed especially to the victor, by his example we are stirred not only to this song but also to the other songs which we have already distinguished; and would that we might be aided by his merits. I mean the songs which he himself, leaving us an example, first sang and completed with a blessed end; and they were set out above in order that we might apply them to him here. The first song, which we arranged above, was a song of sorrow: he sang this in exile. The second was of praise: he sang this in martyrdom.

[Col. 1407B] For then the persecutor was conquered by the very means through which he might seem to have conquered. The third song, we said, was one of jubilation: this is that splendid and notable song which he now sings in the kingdom. The first song was grievous, the second strong, but the third is now sweet—indeed sweeter than every delight.

And these three songs, which he himself, as is surely credible, fulfilled first in himself, are indicated by the emblems of his triumph which pilgrims coming to him from the whole world of churches bear upon their breasts: namely, lead, blood, and water—water, that is, reddened with blood. For it must not be believed that it happened apart from the providence of divine counsel, without which not even a leaf falls from a tree, that persons of every nation and tongue should in one manner and with one heart, as though they had issued a common decree among themselves, bring forth the new triumphal banners of the new martyr.

[Col. 1407C] I think this is a mystery rather than an accident; and would that I could speak a mystery to you. Yet I shall say what I think—would that it is what the Lord has revealed. Lead is the old human being; this is the subject of the song of sorrow. Blood is that of the martyr; this is the subject of the song of praise. Nor do I understand martyrdom only when he laid down his life, but from the moment he exposed himself, indeed from the moment he was ready for martyrdom. Water is “the stream of the river which makes glad the city of God,” and this is the subject of the third song, the song of jubilation.

These signs or banners are borne openly upon the breast, not on the forehead, shoulder, back, or side, so that we may always have before our eyes his threefold life, like the threefold way of our Hebrew, according to the wisdom and grace granted us by God; and so that we may wonder and, insofar as it is granted us from above, imitate.

For his way and life have been set before the world in these last days both for admiration

[Col. 1408A] and imitation. For he who is wonderful in his other saints was admirable in this saint of his, leading him on a way not only wonderful but admirable. See whether it is not admirable. For in these last days, in this time of our lethargy and lukewarmness—when what was predicted long ago is now fulfilled, that iniquity should abound and human beings should be lovers of themselves—the departure and undertaking of this Hebrew are admirable.

Let us consider his departure. His departure was from purple to sackcloth, from sackcloth to exile, from exile to martyrdom, from martyrdom to the kingdom. But his undertaking was no less admirable. For he girded himself for Christ against the man at whose command he himself had stood second—indeed, almost first—in the realm, and by whose cooperation he had attained primacy in the clergy.

[Col. 1408B] Yet when called by Christ, he rose against that man for Christ, understanding by faith that nothing is to be preferred to God. Behold, in brief, the undertaking and departure of our Hebrew. His undertaking was strong; but his departure, his ways—although admirable and hard—were nevertheless beautiful. “How beautiful are thy steps in sandals, O daughter of the prince.”

These three ways of our Hebrew, these three songs upon the ways, are visibly represented, as I conjecture, by the three things which we have begun to distinguish: lead, blood, and water. For lead, as we have begun to say, is the old human being laid aside in exile; blood is the new priest sacrificed in the temple; and water is the fountain of life and torrent of delight in heaven.

And these indeed are the three ways of our Hebrew and the songs upon those ways—except that he no longer sings the third as a Hebrew upon the way, but now as a fellow-citizen of angels in the homeland.

[Col. 1408C] Yet the songs of the Egyptians, which it is not without cause fitting to touch upon at present, are greatly discordant with the Hebrew songs of which we have so often spoken, being arranged and composed as their antithesis. For these Egyptian songs begin with a voice of exaltation, in accordance with their leader and chief singer: “I will set my throne from the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). They then descend to a voice of pleasure, encouraging one another and singing: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (1 Cor. 15). But they end with a voice of confusion, repeating at the end, with shame and disgrace: “What did pride profit us, and what did boasting of riches bring us? All things have passed away like a shadow.”

[Col. 1408D] Behold, these are the three voices from which Egyptian songs are composed in the devil’s music. The first began in heaven; the second in paradise; the third in hell. But it is enough to have touched on these songs only for this reason: our present leader and sweetest chief singer, whom we have said above completed three songs with a blessed end, interrupted these Egyptian melodies composed in the devil’s music by a marvellous power and God’s merciful will.

For he himself too was for some time among the Egyptians so favoured by the emperor that he was even condemned throughout the whole land of Egypt; yet in this he differed greatly from Joseph, because he did not yet recognize his brethren labouring in the Egyptians’ prison-house.

[Col. 1409A] Hence he did not grieve over Joseph’s ruin; rather, he was chief over the overseers of the works. At his ordering and nod, all things were done in Egypt. Then among the Egyptians, conforming himself to the Egyptian songs after the Egyptian manner, he had begun in the devil’s music from a voice of exaltation and frequently gave himself over to the song of pleasure, which savoured of pots of meat, garlic, and melons.

But when, through the Lord’s mercy, he at length heard and took heed of that third voice of confusion which follows, he immediately interrupted the devilish melody. And, what is wonderful to say and incredible to hear, except that we, brethren, who now speak to you testify to what we have seen:

[Col. 1409B] as soon as he was called and enlightened by God, so that at a touch of the eye he recognized his brethren and saw that it was time to fight for them—as soon, I say, and unexpectedly, as we have already said, and as must be repeated more often because the act was so new and rare—he went out, stripped off courtly purple, and put on sackcloth.

O right hand of the Lord, working such power and converting so proud a sinner, as though making a rod again from a dragon and changing water once more into wine! O right hand of the Lord, working power, inspiring humility in one who was proud, as though drawing honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone! O power of the Lord, raising from this stone a child of Abraham!

Brethren, I marvel more at Thomas’s conversion than at Thomas’s creation. Thomas was created,

[Col. 1409C] like all human beings. Why then do I speak of Thomas’s creation? For Thomas’s conversion is more astonishing and more worthy of wonder—indeed, far more so than the creation of the entire world. How much stronger is the work of grace than that of nature! For in the creation of the world there was the power of nature creating nature: he spoke, and it was done. But here there is the power of grace—not merely changing nature, I would say, but in a certain sense transubstantiating it—saying: “Live: you are no longer yourself.” “I live,” says the Teacher, “yet no longer I” (Gal. 2).

And these words—the discourse of grace—were in and toward this man of whom we now speak living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword; for it so shook and shook out the old human being in him, and finally cut it down piece by piece and bit by bit,

[Col. 1409D] that, with the old one slain, a certain new human being, “created according to God,” might live again out of the old. Thus, flesh denying itself becomes not flesh but spirit; the human being becomes not a human being, no longer as it were from earth, but from heaven. Therefore, having forgotten and rejected that worn-out song of oldness, “Such as is the earthly one, such also are the earthly” (1 Cor. 15), let us on this solemn, triumphant day, mindful of so marvellous and holy a conversion, sing a new song: a song of mercy, a song of grace, a heralding song: “Such as are the heavenly, such also are the earthly.”

For was it of flesh, was it of a human being, to leave behind joys of the Augusti proposed to him—indeed, now already possessed—and to endure for his brethren the cross of the condemned, despising shame? Was this, I ask, the work of a human being of this

[Col. 1410A] age, or of this age itself? Certainly it was neither of this age nor of modern lukewarmness. Nevertheless this Thomas of ours, allotted a spirit belonging neither to our time nor to its lukewarmness, in vehement spirit broke all the bonds of the enticements both of the world and of the flesh. He preferred to endure the cross and be afflicted for the people of God entrusted to him rather than enjoy the pleasure of temporary sin. Thus, as we have already said—and it is not unwelcome to repeat it here—he showed himself to us as another Moses, save that here he is greater than Moses.

For Moses left behind the joys of court proposed to him; but this man left behind joys already possessed, withdrawing and fleeing, and remaining in solitude with David. There, following the Prophet’s counsel, sitting so as to persevere and keeping silence so as to learn, he raised himself above himself. For in this solitude, as in a school of virtue owing to him,

[Col. 1410B] he diligently exercised himself in divine things. And among other works of divine devotion, he especially meditated upon the law of the Lord, learning there the sacred Scriptures, which he had not learned while he was still living a secular life among the Egyptians. He learned, indeed, not so much from a human teacher as from an anointing that taught him, often giving thanks as he recalled and acted upon that verse: “It is good for me, Lord, that thou hast humbled me, that I may learn thy statutes” (Ps. 118).

He exercised himself in this and in other works of divine devotion; and others also exercised him—though they should rather be called strangers than others. “Alien children,” I say, “have lied to him”; “alien children have grown old and have limped from thy paths” (Ps. 17). They limped, I say, desiring in part to serve Mammon,

[Col. 1410C] although, according to the saying of Truth, no one can serve God and Mammon. But these alien children, limping and divided, assailed with marvellous and incredible attacks the man seated in solitude, daily breaking his silence and disturbing his quiet as he sat in solitude and awaited the salvation of God in silence.

Their attacks upon him were indeed marvellous and incredible. Who could adequately express how greatly he was harassed by them, what insults he suffered, what injuries provoked him? O good Jesus, how much he suffered for thy name from alien children, from wicked brethren; how much he endured from those very persons for whom and on whose behalf he laboured and did good! Even when they could not inflict harsher things themselves,

[Col. 1410D] they made incursions through evil angels, stirring up the world that he might be driven from the world—he who had undertaken and endured the pastoral burden for their sake.

Certainly, brethren, I myself who now speak would scarcely believe it if another told me, unless I had been in the company of his disciples and fellow exiles and had myself experienced, at least in part, what I am saying. Therefore, because I was then a companion in his suffering, I am now a witness of those same sufferings and may not be excluded from bearing witness. For what we saw, what we heard, and what we ourselves in part felt, this we testify.

And those alien children, those wicked brethren, were indeed such as I have said. Yet he was peaceable with those who hated peace, persevering nevertheless in season and out of season. For God, who according to the Prophet girded him with strength, also fashioned his arms

[Col. 1411A] like a bronze bow.

And this is the first song of sorrow, which, converted to the Lord, he sang to the Lord in exile in Christ’s music, as the antithesis of that Egyptian song which, as we said above, he had been accustomed to sing among the Egyptians. That song began in the devil’s music with a voice of exaltation; but this song begins in Christ’s music, with the low sound of sorrow, with a voice of humility. For thus the Master also instructs his disciples in this music: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11). And at the beginning of his preaching, as it were the first air in the song of his music: “Do penance,” he says, “for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 4).

Thus, according to this pattern, the Hebrew songs were arranged and composed by the Master:

[Col. 1411B] they begin first with the song of sorrow, with a humble voice, and then gradually proceed to higher things: namely, to songs of exultation and praise, and finally, at the summit, there is the highest and sharpest voice, jubilation. Thus the first songs set before the Hebrews begin with groaning indeed, but end in praise. Consider one, for the rest are similar. “O Lord,” he says, “rebuke me not in thy fury” (Ps. 6), and the rest. Then, after several intervening passages which are groans in this music, we gradually advance toward a sweeter sound, a gentler and loftier voice: “Depart from me, all ye that work iniquity, for the Lord hath heard the voice of my weeping” (ibid.).

So also in the remaining Hebrew songs, namely in the penitential psalms first proposed to the Hebrews for singing: in all of them, the beginning is from tears, but the end is in joy. And these Hebrew songs are thus the reverse of the Egyptian songs, which begin, as we said above, with the highest and sharpest voice but end in a most discordant and lowest voice. For “the heart is exalted before ruin.”

This Hebrew, therefore—our leader and chief singer—while he was still a Hebrew, passing through fire and water, began in Christ’s music from the song of sorrow and, through the various and manifold modes of this melody called sorrow, namely through various and manifold temptations, was gradually led to a loftier song: namely, the second song of praise, which we have so often named. To this he invites us on this triumphal day, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord.”

[Col. 1411D] And immediately he adds the cause of the song: “For he has been gloriously magnified.” And at once he appends the cause of this so glorious magnificence: “Because he cast horse and rider into the sea.” Hence we must first pause and consider that he says not simply “magnified” or “great,” but “gloriously magnified.” For just as the Lord is magnified mightily, so too he is magnified in many ways by his works. Sometimes he is magnified through works of power, as in the creation of the world; sometimes through works of mercy, as in the restoration of the created world; sometimes through works of justice, as in rewarding the good and condemning the wicked; sometimes he is magnified miraculously, when he works certain things through the movement of wrath or grace, overturning the order of nature.

[Col. 1412A] In these and in many other ways he is variously and manifoldly magnified. Therefore on this triumphal day of the martyr the Church fittingly gives thanks, saying: “He delivered me from my strongest enemies and from those who hated me, when they had become too strong for me” (Ps. 17).

Yet the Church had long ago experienced this very thing in herself, and now, from the new triumph of her new martyr, she offers new thanksgivings. For the Church has always been accustomed to grow by the very means through which the world knows how to make her fail. By what empties the one, the other is tested; where the one falls, the other triumphs. For, dug by wounds and pruned by martyrdoms, she spreads the more, like the vineyard of the heavenly farmer; and, beaten by the lashes of tribulations, she is extended the more, like the trumpet of the heavenly craftsman. And, struck by the persecutions of tyrants as by the swelling of the sea,

[Col. 1412B] she is lifted higher, like the ark of heavenly refuge.

These are what, according to the Psalmist, the rulers of churches see: “the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep” (Ps. 106). Hence elsewhere in the Psalm: “The swellings of the sea are wonderful; wonderful is the Lord on high” (Ps. 92). And, to add something from the Gospel: this our mother the Church is the fruit of that evangelical grain which, unless it had fallen into the earth and died, would have remained by itself alone. Such is the grain, and such its fruit. Leaving aside other examples, let us see whether this is not now fulfilled in the new fruit of this Gospel grain, namely in our new martyr. In him we now see fully accomplished what was set forth concerning the Church’s strength. Living Thomas belonged to England alone; but now, slain,

[Col. 1412C] he belongs to all nations. Thomas was known in England, but now his name is great throughout the world. For the Lord, who “stretches out the heavens like a skin,” has now, in a reversal, stretched out the wounded and lifeless skin of his slain soldier like the heavens, drawing it out to such vast breadth. In accordance with this, after her preceding thanksgiving for her own deliverance, our mother Church adds: “And he brought me out into a broad place; he saved me because he willed me” (Ps. 17).

Therefore let the rulers of churches rise to this song of the Church concerning her own deliverance, so that, consoled by most certain hope, they may immediately rejoice that they are delivered by the very fact that they see their strongest enemies strengthened against them. And let them not despair of the strength bestowed from above upon the Church herself. Let them look also upon Thomas, once their fellow brother and a ruler of the Church, that in him they may see

[Col. 1412D] the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep. Let them see in him, I say, the works of the Lord and his wonders—he who, in the deep sea of this world, guided the little boat of Peter entrusted to him so strongly and so prudently amid so great a storm, among so many rocks and such perilous whirlpools of the sea. Indeed, he guided it so bravely and manfully that, in what had been unheard of from the beginning of the age, at last he voluntarily exposed himself in the very midst of the storm, and the little boat entrusted to him tossed and sped onward in his own blood—so that it might sail, as it were flying, more safely and swiftly from the storm of the sea of this world toward the homeland.

[Col. 1413A] And therefore Thou, O Lord, who today hast been so gloriously magnified, at the so glorious departure from Egypt of Thy martyr, the leader and patron of Thy Church, according to the greatness of Thy arm, when horse and rider were cast into the sea: as Thou didst then save and deliver the synagogue of the Hebrews, so now ever save and deliver Thy Church of Thy faithful; that, by Thee, she may always be saved and free, delivered from the yoke of slavery and the oppression of the persecutor; her own special leader and patron continually helping her—Thy glorious martyr Thomas, who, to deliver her, laid down his life, and who with Thee in glory shall come to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire. Amen.

[Col. 1414A] HERE ENDS THE HOMILY ON THE MARTYR.

But this song of praise is immediately followed by a song altogether different and of another kind: a song of sorrow, a song of tribulation and distress—namely, that fatal and celebrated written instrument of the decree, so frequently mentioned throughout the martyr’s history, containing sixteen articles.

In accordance with our promise above, we append it here at the end of all things, so that ages to come may read it and may learn from it how just and how manifest was the cause of our glorious new martyr’s first exile and afterward his martyrdom. The first of these articles is this: Concerning advocations, etc.

[Col. 1413]

## THE CAUSE OF THE EXILE AND MARTYRDOM OF BLESSED THOMAS, MARTYR AND ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

### THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH UNDER POPE ALEXANDER III CONDEMNED THIS FIRST ARTICLE

[Col. 1413B]

If a dispute arises concerning the advowson and presentation of churches between laymen, or between clerics and laymen, or between clerics, it shall be heard and determined in the court of the lord king.

### IT TOLERATED THE SECOND ARTICLE

Churches held of the king’s fee cannot be granted in perpetuity without his assent and permission.

### IT TOLERATED THIS ARTICLE

Clerics arrested and accused of any matter, when summoned by the king’s justice, shall come into his court and there answer concerning that of which the king’s court judges that answer should there be made, and in the ecclesiastical court concerning that of which it judges that answer should there be made; [Col. 1413C] provided that the king’s justice shall send into the court of Holy Church to see by what procedure the case is there handled. And if the cleric is convicted or confesses, thereafter the Church ought not to protect him.

### NOTE 4. IT CONDEMNED THIS ARTICLE

Archbishops, bishops, and persons of the realm may not leave the kingdom without the king’s permission; and, if they leave, should it please the king, they shall give assurance that neither in going nor in remaining abroad will they seek evil or harm to the king or kingdom.

### NOTE 5. IT CONDEMNED THIS ARTICLE

Excommunicated persons ought not to give a pledge for remaining, nor take an oath, but only give a pledge and surety to stand by the judgment of the Church, so that they may be absolved.

### NOTE 6. IT TOLERATED THIS ARTICLE

[Col. 1413D]

Laymen ought not to be accused except by definite and lawful accusers and witnesses in the presence of the archbishop or bishop, provided that the archdeacon does not lose [Col. 1414B] his right, nor anything which he ought thence to receive. And if those who are accused are such that no one is willing or dares to accuse them, the sheriff, when required to do so, shall cause twelve lawful men of the neighbourhood or township to swear before the bishop that they will disclose the truth concerning the matter according to their conscience.

### NOTE 7. IT CONDEMNED THIS ARTICLE

No one who holds directly of the king, nor any of his household officers, shall be excommunicated; nor shall the lands of any of them be placed under interdict, unless the king, if he is in the land, is first summoned, or his justiciar, if he is outside the realm, so that he may do right concerning him. Thus what belongs to the royal court shall there be determined, and what pertains to [Col. 1414C] the ecclesiastical court shall be sent to that court to be determined there.

### NOTE 8. IT CONDEMNED THIS ARTICLE

Concerning appeals, should they arise, they must proceed from the archdeacon to the bishop, and from the bishop to the archbishop; and if the archbishop fails to render justice, recourse must finally be had to the king, so that by his command the controversy may be determined in the archbishop’s court, and it must not proceed further without the king’s assent.

### NOTE 9. IT CONDEMNED THIS ARTICLE

If a dispute arises between a cleric and a layman, or conversely, concerning any tenement which the cleric wishes to claim as alms-land, but the layman as a lay fee, the customary inquest of twelve lawful men, held before the king’s chief justiciar, shall determine whether the tenement belongs to alms-land or to a lay fee. And if it is found to belong to alms-land, [Col. 1415A] the plea shall be in the ecclesiastical court. But if it belongs to a lay fee, the plea shall be in the king’s court, unless both parties claim under the same bishop or baron from that fee. But if each claims that fee under the same bishop or baron, the plea shall be in his court; provided that, by reason of the inquest having been made, he who was first seised shall not lose seisin until the plea has been judicially decided.

### NOTE 10. IT CONDEMNED THIS ARTICLE

Whoever belongs to a city, castle, borough, or royal demesne manor, if summoned by an archdeacon or bishop for an offence for which he ought to answer them, and refuses to comply with their citations, may indeed be put under interdict; [Col. 1415B] but he must not be excommunicated before the king’s chief officer of that place has been summoned, so that he may compel him to make satisfaction. And if the king’s officer fails in this matter, he shall be at the king’s mercy; and thereafter the bishop may restrain the accused person by ecclesiastical justice.

### NOTE 11. IT TOLERATED THIS ARTICLE

Archbishops, bishops, and all persons of the realm who hold directly of the king shall hold their possessions from the king as a barony, and shall answer thence to the king’s justices and officers, and shall observe and perform all royal rights and customs. And, like the other barons, they ought to attend the judgments of the king’s court with the barons, until judgment reaches mutilation of limbs or [Col. 1415C] death.

### NOTE 12. IT CONDEMNED THIS ARTICLE

When an archbishopric, bishopric, abbey, or priory of the king’s lordship falls vacant, it shall be in his hand, and he shall receive from it all revenues and proceeds as from demesne. And when the time comes to take counsel for the Church, the lord king must summon the more important persons of the Church, and election shall be held in his chapel, with the king’s assent and by the counsel of those persons of the realm whom he has summoned for this purpose. And there [Col. 1416A] the person elected shall do homage and fealty to the lord king, as to his liege lord, for his life, limbs, and earthly honour, saving his ecclesiastical order, before he is consecrated.

### NOTE 13. IT TOLERATED THIS ARTICLE

If any magnate of the realm refuses to render justice to an archbishop, bishop, or archdeacon concerning himself or his men, the king must do justice. And if perhaps anyone refuses the lord king his due right, archbishops and bishops [and archdeacons] must do justice upon him, so that he makes satisfaction to the king.

### NOTE 14. IT TOLERATED THIS ARTICLE

The Church or cemetery shall not withhold, against the king’s justice, the chattels of those who are under the king’s forfeiture; for they belong to the king, whether found in churches or [Col. 1416B] outside them.

### NOTE 15. IT CONDEMNED THIS ARTICLE

Pleas concerning debts owed upon a pledge of faith, or without a pledge of faith, shall be in the king’s court.

### NOTE 16. IT TOLERATED THIS ARTICLE

The sons of rustics must not be ordained without the assent of the lord from whose land they are known to have been born.

I would immediately have appended to each of these condemned articles the individual grounds for its condemnation, were they not instantly obvious at first hearing to anyone possessing even slight knowledge of the sacred canons.

A record of the aforesaid customs and royal dignities was made by the archbishops, bishops, earls, barons, and the nobler and [Col. 1416C] elder men of the realm, at Clarendon, on the fourth day before the Purification of Saint Mary the Virgin, when the lord Henry, son of the king, was present there with his father.] [lacuna]

These final words, enclosed in brackets, I have added from the *Quadrilogus*: for the manuscript of Arras is defective after the words “archbishops and bishops.” But the manuscript of the College of Corpus Christi does not even carry the book of Melorum to its end; it is mutilated and torn at the end as at the beginning.

[Col. 1415]

## LETTERS OF HERBERT OF BOSEHAM WRITTEN IN THE PERSON OF ST THOMAS OF CANTERBURY AND OF OTHERS

### FIRST LETTER [TO . . .]

[Col. 1415D]

[The beginning is missing, one or more leaves having been lost from the manuscript of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge.] [lacuna] [dis]cernment, most serene counsellor. Stripping, therefore, from this letter that formal rhetorical ornament, I have presumed to present myself to the eyes of your glory in this slight form of plain speech, especially since the matters reported, as I hope, will delight your hearing. For since the Lord has granted you abundant knowledge and experience of secular, and especially divine, histories of both Laws, [Col. 1417A] I am certain that you will embrace the truth of Gospel history more devoutly when you hear it, because the Gospel itself excels all other branches of scriptural learning.

Yet I recall—but doubt whether it has escaped your illustrious memory—that, when I travelled with you this year, I discussed with you somewhat, though briefly and in broken fashion, as commonly happens on a journey, the subject which I had undertaken: namely, Anna, who is said to have had three husbands, and the name Salome used by Mark. And because I judged that the meaning I was advancing then sufficiently pleased you, from that time I sought out and read commentators on Holy Scripture, especially those to whom the truth of the matters placed before them ought to have become more fully clear; and, so that the doubtful matter might be made plain, I gathered and selected testimonies from various quarters, as this present [Col. 1417B] letter shows.

Moreover, our beloved companion Master John of Salisbury, whom, I think, you know, brought a certain little paper on behalf of a brother, Master William of London—a man, as you know, learned and, as is believed, religious, who is a monk at Saint-Denis. It was entitled “Claudius on Matthew,” and stated that this Claudius, following Origen’s conjecture, held that she whom Matthew calls the mother of the sons of Zebedee is called by Mark Salome as her proper name. The said brother had sent me the paper after a laborious search through expositors, because, knowing that he possessed some ability in letters, I had pressed him this year concerning the name Salome.

For when, as I questioned him diligently, he maintained the tale current among our people that Salome was Anna’s third husband, I repeatedly asked, as is customary, upon what authority of Scripture he defended this. And lest, amid verbal disputation, he should appeal to Jerome’s letter against Helvidius, as others commonly do, I quickly blocked that path, affirming from thorough experience that throughout that whole letter there is no mention either of Anna or of any husband of Anna, nor is the name Salome found there at all. Rather, Jerome seems in that letter not to establish but to remove this assertion concerning Anna’s three husbands. For he says that Mary, who is written to be the mother of James the Less, was the wife of Alphaeus and the sister of Mary the mother of the Lord; John the Evangelist surnames this Mary “Mary of Cleophas,” [Col. 1417D] giving her that name, he says, from her father, or from the family lineage, or for some other reason.

Likewise Bede, perceiving where the old ox—that is, Jerome—fears to plant his foot more deeply, follows hesitantly but walks with a measured step. In his explanations of the Evangelists he says that this Mary, wife of Alphaeus, was surnamed Mary of Cleophas by John either because Alphaeus himself was also called Cleophas, or because, after Alphaeus had died following the birth of James, Mary herself married Cleophas. See how Bede, following Jerome, ventures to assert nothing, though he offers conjectures concerning the surname Cleophas different from Jerome’s. And the second opinion which he adds is found to be greatly opposed to the assertion concerning those three husbands of Anna. For Cleophas, whom they assert to have been Anna’s husband and Mary’s father, is, according to Bede’s conjecture, thought to be the husband of that same Mary.

Hence, if the assertion of the opponents is true, I cannot but wonder how such great teachers, such investigators of histories, who laboured so greatly to expound the Evangelists, could have been ignorant of Gospel history which modern men know—or rather, how they could have committed to enduring monuments of voluminous writings opinions so absurdly discordant with the truth of history. I could scarcely believe that we, animal and carnal people, had learned, especially concerning Gospel history, what had escaped those foremost and earliest teachers of the Church—who, indeed, wrote more than we are even capable of reading.

Let us therefore dismiss these defenders of Anna’s three marriages as followers of the ravings of certain apocryphal books. Let us consider more carefully that the aforesaid teachers, Jerome and Bede, do not assert that Mary of Cleophas was so surnamed after her father; rather, being uncertain and sparing in style, they were reluctant to confine an uncertain matter within the limits of a definite conclusion. I am therefore greatly astonished whence such shameless error arose, that slander should be devised against the balanced teaching of so great a man—I mean Jerome—in order to assert an uncertain matter, and that falsely invoked ecclesiastical authority should make Spanish trifles into authoritative truths.

Yet I think that this error has been especially prevalent in these days through the occasion of my master, Peter of Paris, bishop of blessed memory. When, in his exposition on the Epistle to the Galatians, at the passage, “But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord’s brother” (Gal. 1), he set forth the familiar history of Annula [so written], who had three husbands, he separately marked the name of Jerome in the margin in red ink. But if Jerome had woven that history of Anna with the same threads of words in his letter against Helvidius—although, as we have said and know from experience, Jerome does not give to that story the authority of testimony in a single point—would Master Peter therefore be liable to the charge of misrepresenting Scripture and so be the cause of error and fault? I shall not concede it. For the present I prefer to blame a careless hand and the ignorance of a copyist rather than charge so great a teacher with falsehood or error.

But he who is excused on this point will be excused on another: namely, that at the aforesaid passage in Galatians he recounts that famous history of Anna, apparently following no authority of Scripture, not in the slow and hesitant manner of uncertain speech but firmly and rapidly, without any scruple of hesitation. Indeed, even if he followed the ravings of apocryphal writings, it is not easy to discover where they report it thus; for even in that apocryphal work entitled *On the Infancy of the Saviour*, there is no mention of Anna’s three husbands except Joachim alone.
