Yet for this reason I do not presently dare to impute rashness or ignorance to that aforesaid doctor, who in modern times had no equal in ecclesiastical learning; nor do I presume to accuse him of anything. Let no one therefore think that I am so immoderate in praise of my teachers that I wish to follow their faults, utterly abolish ignorance, or defend those who err. But I know that it is very dangerous, and not easily pardoned, to judge another man’s servant, much less one’s own master—especially since he read so much and with such diligence, whereas we Epicurean animals, Pelusiotes, and dormice stiff with lethargy scarcely run through such things perfunctorily, indeed have not even seen many of them.

Let the authority of so great a teacher, therefore, be removed from our present discussion. If he were alive, I have no doubt that he would defend his writings much more vigorously against his opponents with diverse and powerful scriptural testimonies, the weapons of his warfare. Yet at present it is unknown what authority he followed in the aforementioned account. His authority having thus been set aside—I neither wholly excuse him here nor, as I have said, presume rashly to accuse him—let us prefer things certain to things uncertain, and defend, not by slippery argument but by firm scriptural testimonies, that the name Salome used by Mark is the name of a woman there, not of a man.

Let that greatest and most ancient interpreter of Scripture come forward first—I mean Origen. As is well known from the testimony of history, more than one hundred and fifty years before Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and the other interpreters of Holy Scripture, he laboured day and night in expounding the divine laws; and, first without an example and alone without a companion, he taught as much as he could of those writings. Would that we accepted him as Catholic in doctrine as we admire him as a faithful interpreter.

Let him, I say, come first. He ought all the more to have known the truth of Gospel history and the companions of the Lord’s life in the flesh, because he was nearer to the first times of the Church’s birth. Let us therefore first set out the Evangelist’s words:

> “Now,” says Matthew, “there were women there looking on from afar, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him; among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee” (Matt. 27).

Here are the Evangelist’s words. Origen, in his commentary upon him, expounds among other things as follows:

> “But if it is necessary to conjecture and state also the name of the mother of the sons of Zebedee, I say that she herself was called Salome, meaning ‘peaceful.’ I have conjectured this because I saw that in Matthew and Mark three principal women are named, concerning whom the present discussion is being held. The present Evangelist expressly identifies two of them, Mary Magdalene and Mary of James; but he calls the third the mother of the sons of Zebedee. In Mark, however, that third woman is called Salome.”

And below:

> “Observe this too: that above, these two Marys and the mother of the sons of Zebedee, whom we take to be Salome, were looking from afar at the wonders occurring in the Passion and at his body hanging upon the wood.”

We have heard Origen. Claudius agrees with him in his exposition of the same passage of the same Evangelist. After quoting the Evangelist’s words set above, he says:

> “Great ambiguity frequently arises concerning these women, as at this place, where Matthew says that the mother [Col. 1420A] of the sons of Zebedee was with the other two. Mark recalls that she was Salome. Nor is it surprising, since each of them, though they name three, implies that there were more who had followed him from Galilee and were looking on from afar; among these were the three whom Matthew mentions and Mark likewise names, unless Mark sets Salome, as though another woman, in place of the mother of the sons of Zebedee. For it could be that she was the woman whom Mark named third among the many. It does not matter to the truth which women, whether the same ones together or separately, each Evangelist named from among them all. Origen nevertheless conjectures that Salome was the mother of the sons of Zebedee, who is called their mother.”

And shortly afterward the same Claudius says:

> “Hence it is permissible to conjecture and say that the name of the mother of the sons of Zebedee is that she herself is the one whom Mark calls Salome. For without doubt each Evangelist designated by name the principal women among the others; and perhaps she is called Salome because Salome means ‘peaceful.’ Therefore, since the other two were women of great merit, I reasonably conjecture that this third woman too is the mother of the sons of Zebedee, who is also called Salome as the third woman in Mark.”

John Chrysostom likewise, in a homily on the Lord’s Passion upon Matthew, maintained more strongly and expressly than the others, in language not slippery but straightforward, that the name Salome used by Mark was the proper name of the mother of the sons of Zebedee. I have not inserted his words in this letter because, while writing it, I could not find them at Sens.

Likewise, in the martyrology read in the Church of God throughout the yearly cycle, under the chapter inscribed “the eleventh day before the Kalends of November,” it is written:

> “At Hadrianople in Thrace, the birthday of the holy martyrs Philip the bishop, Eusebius, Hermes,”

and below:

> “Likewise, of Saint Salome, who in the Gospel is recorded as solicitous at the Lord’s burial.”

From all this it is clearer than light that, by the name Salome which Mark uses, the woman whom Matthew calls the mother of the sons of Zebedee is designated by Mark as it were by her own proper name. We are likewise plainly taught from another source that Salome is a woman’s name. Jerome, in the book of Hebrew names, says that Salome means “peaceful”; and in Josephus’s *Antiquities* Herod’s daughter is everywhere called Salome, as one called by that name of her own.

But when, as I have said, I was at Saint-Denis and questioned the aforesaid Master William of London—not immoderately, indeed, but diligently and persistently—about the name Salome so often mentioned, another brother arrived, also named Master William. Formerly he was a physician by profession, but now, as we hope, he bears not only the habit but the disposition of a monk. When he noticed the cause of the dispute, he asked to be heard and said that he had spent some time among Syrians. There, he said, is a church dedicated in honour of the Three Marys, held by the Syrians in the highest devotion. He added that, according to the tradition of the people of that land which he had received, one was Mary Magdalene; the second, Mary the mother of James and Joseph; and the third, the mother of the sons of Zebedee, who among the Syrians too is called Mary. Then, directing his speech specifically to me, he said:

> “This same woman could also, as you plausibly argue upon the testimonies of the ancients, have been called Salome.”

“Granted,” I said, “I shall not draw a contentious rope on this point, provided that it is established that the name Salome is used by Mark in identifying a woman.”

On this point, I say, I shall not be contentious. For I have learned that it is Scripture’s practice to call the same person by diverse names, although this occurs much more rarely with women. Nevertheless, I derive from this a probable conjecture that the Gospel woman of whom I have spoken so much was called not only Salome but also Mary. For many churches have long been accustomed, through every annual cycle, at dawn on the Lord’s Resurrection, to present, for the increase of devotion, a reverent dramatic representation of the Three Marys zealously and devoutly seeking the Lord in the tomb with spices. And who these Three Marys are will, I think, be more truly indicated if one is called Mary Magdalene, another Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the third Mary, also Salome, mother of the sons of Zebedee. But, as I have said, I shall not be contentious on this point; let it only be established that Salome was a woman’s name in Mark.

Yet the following, read concerning these women in a certain Easter homily which I saw entitled as Gregory’s, might for a while move us away from this assertion—not opinion:

> “Mary Magdalene,” says the Evangelist Mark, “and Mary of James bought spices, that they might come and anoint Jesus” (Mark 16:1), etc. The Gospel reading, says Gregory, commends the devotion of the holy women; and below: “Mary Magdalene is Lazarus’s sister, who anointed the Lord with ointment” (John 11:2). “Mary, mother of James, is the mother of James the Less and Joseph, and the sister of the Lord’s mother. Mary Salome was so called after her husband or her grandfather. For they relate that she had two husbands, namely Cleophas and Saloma; and they also hold that she is the woman elsewhere called Mary of Cleophas.”

These are the words of the homily which I read ascribed to Gregory, although it is beyond doubt not his, but rather belongs among apocryphal writings. Yet, if it were Gregory’s, or that of any ecclesiastical writer, even so it would not support the defenders of Anna’s three marriages, but would rather oppose them. For it reports an opinion according to which Cleophas—whom the supporters of this new history make Anna’s husband and Mary’s father—is considered the husband of Mary herself.

I perceive, my lord most dear to me in Christ, that while I hastily despoiled the Scriptures here and there to the extent of my ability, so that the truth might shine out ever more richly adorned by whatever testimonies they supplied, I have suddenly been borne forward by the rush of speech as by an unbridled horse and have exceeded the bounds of an ordinary letter, so that I seem to have spared neither the character of a letter nor your many occupations. But let my lord consider that, being a dead dog and a single flea, I have entered upon a new course of dispute against the great and modern defenders of a new history—or rather, an inveterate fable newly advanced. Hence it was necessary to pursue each point more carefully and overthrow falsehood not by slippery argument but by the clear and irrefragable testimonies of the ancients.

At the end of this discourse I add that I would now and often write to you about these matters which so frequently trouble me in the Scriptures, were I not afraid of causing annoyance rather than rendering service amid the great and manifold affairs which rarely are, or can be, absent from you. For I owe you all that little which I am: indeed, your magnificent and renowned generosity has mitigated the pressure upon me and mine in exile, a pressure which we still endure so justly. As is well known, no one who has sought refuge with you has departed disappointed. For this reason especially I can scarcely restrain my pen from repeatedly recording that you have surpassed not only modern princes but also many notable men in this office, in your love of learning and in your attainment of its summit.

Moreover, if Pythagoras were alive, because of this especial love and because of the other endowments, if we consider them, of a nature well ordered, he would proclaim that the spirit of Constantine the Great, of divine memory, had descended upon you. But I shall not now continue further to enumerate the gifts of our gratitude. It is enough that I have touched upon what all men know—especially lest I seem to have undertaken this discourse not for the subject proposed but rather to list the catalogue of your benefits.

At its close I pray this: if perhaps the messengers of the lord king of the English, in the presence of your highness, attempt to prejudice the reputation of the lord of Canterbury or of my own insignificance by derogatory speech, let not your prudence give them credence. For although we suffer penalties according to our deserts, and are placed in darkness like the dead of old, yet those who drink wine daily sing against us; and they persecute everywhere with their tongues me especially, an exiled and obscure man, whom they cannot presently reach with their hands. They charge me with having spoken, last year, I know not what words at Angers to the lord king of England in pride and mockery; what those words were, however, I believe I faithfully reported to you—unless your prudence now no longer recalls it.

But let it be so. I shall implore David’s meekness and shall not fear Shimei’s reproach. By this very means the wounds of my sins will rather be healed; and meanwhile, setting a guard upon my mouth, I shall break forth into the necessary cry for mercy:

> “Have mercy on me, O Lord, have mercy on me, for I am filled with contempt; I am made a reproach to the prosperous and contempt to the proud” (Psalm 122).

## LETTER II. A LETTER OF HERBERT WRITTEN IN THE PERSON OF THOMAS, EXILED ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, TO POPE ALEXANDER, AGAINST GILBERT, BISHOP OF LONDON, ALREADY EXCOMMUNICATED

To his father and lord most beloved in Christ, ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: THOMAS, wretched exile of the Church of Canterbury, his due obedience with every devotion.

That I so often and with such plaintive cries force myself upon the presence of so great a majesty is not caused by irreverence, but by the pressure which even now compels my speech to run, not slowly, but—as is its wont—mournfully; and now all the more mournfully because I am more gravely endangered by an evil that is domestic and internal. For behold: the sentence of an anathema, believed to be wholly just, pronounced against our brother—and would that he were truly a brother!—the bishop of London, which our other brother bishops of the province, having heard the tenor of our letters, approved as truly just, he alone despises. Alone, wholly given over to anger and dispute, he conducts everything by contention; his fury is, as is now said, according to the likeness of the serpent, like that of the deaf asp which stops its ears lest it hear the voice of the wise charmer.

And what I yet more tearfully lament, because it is more detestable than all else, is that in this spirit of fury and impatience he breaks the bonds of profession and obedience, shakes the sides of his mother, and casts himself out. Among other things, indeed, in order to invalidate the sentence passed against him, having convened for this purpose all the clergy of the city, with many also standing by and listening, he publicly declared that neither by reason of his own person nor by reason of the Church now entrusted to him was he bound to the metropolitan Church or to the person of the metropolitan by any bond of profession or obedience. He asserts that he is not bound in respect of his person because his person was transferred without his making a new profession or rendering new obedience. And from this he has indeed inclined to this—would that his dregs had thereby been emptied!—that “the Church to which he was transferred likewise wholly frees him, because it too, from ancient times, as he relates, from the age of the pagans, was free from every subjection to the Church of Canterbury.” Therefore he publicly contended that by right he ought to become archprimate, and did not blush most brazenly to claim the archprimacy for himself.

These things, moreover, were done not in a corner, but, as I have said, with the whole clergy of the city convened for this very purpose and many of the people also standing by and listening. Thus, as the world has long cried out, his deeds now openly testify. For the iniquity of his works has at length come forth as though from fatness; it could no longer be concealed, since anger and impatience had made use of the worst advisers. To the accumulation of evils is added the fact that he supposes this most detestable severing and these execrable words of manifest disobedience will heal beneath the shelter of your wings. When he learned that I might freely exercise my priestly office, he immediately fled—not, as he says, to some refuge from appeal, but to an appeal for refuge—though he had not yet been burdened in any respect, but intended to burden [me], unless perhaps he considered it a burden to himself if he could not, after casting me back into the former chains, strip me of the arms of my warfare.

Indeed, though burdened in no respect, by appealing he burdened [us] greatly. By that very act he turned the air of ecclesiastical peace—peace which even its enemies, and those long despairing of it, believed [was at hand]—into storm, and by the wind of his pride raised still higher waves that had been somewhat calmed. Let your consideration, therefore, gracious Father and just Judge, awaken itself. Let it awaken itself to the abuse of so unjust an appeal, lest at the invocation of your great and most holy name obedience should be extinguished, as if beneath the shadow of your wings, and iniquity nourished. Rather, let the son of those cast out shake himself; let your compassion be moved, and let your indignation be moved: for you owe the one to the injured, the other to the injurer, lest under so great a power either the mercy of clemency or the rectitude of zeal be endangered. For no one will be innocent if he either punishes him who ought to be spared, or spares him who ought to have been punished.

Accordingly, most merciful Father, let the censure of justice move you on the one side and the fellow-feeling of mercy on the other, so that in the vicar of Christ and the Christ of the Lord justice and peace may kiss each other. “For these two love each other,” says a certain writer, “so that he who does justice may find peace, and not otherwise.” Let, therefore, the pressure upon me and mine, the cause of that pressure, and above all the shipwreck of the little vessel in which, by your command, I put out into the deep to cast the nets for a catch, move you. You yourselves entrusted this vessel to my governance; yet without your strength I am altogether unable to steer it with my own hands, especially amid such storms of sedition and dissension.

Let your compassion also consider by how many waves this little vessel has been tossed since those ancient times of our fathers: often battered indeed, but never broken; rather, it always gave forth its free voice from among the rocks, not as broken but as sound. For the Church of Canterbury, now seen under such great pressure, has not, I say, withdrawn from obedience to the Apostolic See, over which you now preside by God’s mercy toward His Church; nor, though situated in the heart of the sea, has it even in the least wavered through fear of, or favour toward, any earthly powers. Therefore, for her—so devoted to your apostolic office down to these days and entrusted to me by yourselves—I and the companions of my suffering, prostrate with all the strength of our hearts and on our knees, implore that, though her children and her ruler are endangered, she herself may at least be preserved whole in her former condition and rank by the strength of your singular primacy.

At the end of this letter we report that near its completion we received news that very many are greatly disturbed because Reginald, archdeacon of Salisbury, the messenger of the lord king of the English, returning from you and passing through the city of our exile, spoke, as is said, many things in arrogance and abuse. Among other things, speaking of himself, he added that, even if he himself were not archbishop of Canterbury, he would nevertheless absolve those of the archbishop of Canterbury bound by anathema, and would wholly release the invaders of the possessions of the Church of Canterbury from every restitution of things taken away, both movable and immovable. As evidence of his word he pointed, as though with a finger, to certain merchants whom he had brought with him, declaring that he would pay them money in your name.

To some, something; but to me, nothing. Nor am I ashamed or shaken by these words: whether the world wills it or not, I shall do nothing, so far as I am able, for glory, and, by the Lord’s mercy, nothing to the shame or injury of the Church. Nor, with my assent, shall Belshazzar ever turn to his wanton use the possessions or vessels of the temple, fashioned at the cost of Christ’s blood and dedicated to the poor for the service of Christ Himself. Rather, with your help and command, O vicar of Christ and Christ of the Lord, I am ready to devote to this cause the remainder of my calamitous and exiled life.

## LETTER III. HERBERT’S LETTER, IN THE PERSON OF THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, AGAINST THE SAME MAN

To the most reverend Father and lord ALEXANDER, by the grace of God supreme pontiff: THOMAS, humble minister of the afflicted Church of Canterbury and wretched exile, greeting and every obedience with the utmost devotion.

Since I, poor and sorrowful, have very frequently and importunately knocked with plaintive cries at the royal court of so great a majesty, amid all the pressing and often urgent perils of my present struggle, now, being more gravely pressed, we have recourse more urgently to the accustomed help. Therefore, putting shame aside and in some fashion not weighing that majesty, I thrust myself naked and deprived of all human help before the eyes of so great a majesty. Or rather, in this poor and slight sheet of parchment, all of us who are children of exile and migration cast ourselves at the feet of so great a compassion, knocking at that royal clemency with a certain right hand of our tears and with the misery, now long-standing, of our life, so that our wretched prayer may enter the doors of your mercy.

Especially now, when that alien, at last revealed, despising my smallness by the bulk of his own body, challenges all Israel to single combat, so that, by taking upon himself the whole sum of the war and weight of the entire battle, all Philistia may be granted victory, and he, above all others, the glory of victory. But what do I mean? I mean Goliath. Would that he had shown himself only Goliath; rather, he is more dangerous. For, as the world cries out and his deeds testify, he instructs the son against the father by every counsel in his power, so that he is to us Ahithophel in secret and Goliath in the open. Let your discernment consider for a moment whether his own deeds do not bear witness to what is said concerning him.

**First accusation.** First, in England at Northampton, when I was in such danger that I strictly commanded both him and our other brother bishops and fellow bishops to cease divine offices if violent hands were laid upon my own person—as many then rightly foresaw—this man immediately appealed, in the hearing of many of our fellow bishops who were present then, and also of certain clerics, as though he were burdened if chains were not laid upon me. Let your consideration, if it please you, judge how unjust this appeal was and how great a presumption it creates against the appellant.

**Second accusation.** Further, at Sens, in the presence of your sublimity, I do not think you have forgotten how greatly he sharpened his tongue against my smallness, and with how many reproaches and insults he would have torn his own father, now exiled and absent, had your compassion not restrained him. By that fact alone he deserved to be called a slanderer, because he dared to uncover his father’s shame.

**Third accusation.** Further, when I was hastening from Sens, from my vexations and straits, to the bosom of your clemency, he returned at the same time to his country with the others, without waiting for the oft-mentioned brother—and would that he were truly a brother!—and, more than all the others, before receiving any royal command on this matter, plundered [the Church] and caused all the Church’s goods to be confiscated.

**Fourth accusation.** Further, no fabricated or contrived fraud will be able, or in the eyes of so great a majesty dare, to hide the fact that knowingly and deliberately, before his own excommunication, he communicated with persons excommunicated by me. Moreover, he has dissolved the bond of anathema in which he is now bound—as I am most certainly persuaded—by entering the church and even attending the solemnities of Mass.

**Fifth accusation.** It is universally known how he suppressed the sacred letters of your excellency and despised the commands of my smallness.

**Sixth accusation.** How often, and for what causes, he has appealed over these same articles of dispute, even uneducated people and common folk chatter in lanes and squares. They hope that, at the invocation of your holy name, as though under the protection of your wings, the iniquity and injustice of those persecuting us might grow strong.

**Seventh accusation.** Finally, while he was employing this customary device—not a refuge, but a flight for refuge—which I judge far inferior to all heavenly things, he did not secretly but before the people attempt to ascend his father’s bed, and did not blush publicly to contend that he was metropolitan by right. He further added that, having inclined from one thing to another, becoming a Londoner from Hereford, he was bound to the metropolitan of Canterbury by no bond of profession or obedience, because these things had not been required at his transfer. Yet I recall that I have elsewhere written more fully to your charity on these matters.

Therefore the Church of Canterbury herself, unable any longer to bear the many snares of this seductive art, crushed his head, though he had so often lain in wait for her heel. But I do not now proceed to assail his other offences; it is enough to have touched upon them. Passing over many things, I recall only those which stones and marble cry aloud. Nor do I think that many of these things have escaped you through the reports of many persons coming to you. In all these matters he went out armed before the people into the field, to wage the wars of the Philistines. Yet Goliath was in the field; in the chamber he was Ahithophel. So much so that, when the messengers of the lord king were lately returning from your Holiness—namely Richard Barre and the archdeacon Ralph—he, together with that archdevil Geoffrey Ridel, by the efforts of his counsel, broke off the word of peace which was then being diligently and dutifully negotiated.

In hope of that settlement, I with my fellow exiles, with the king’s knowledge and by the will of the Pope, had already proceeded as far as Pontoise, intending to hold a conference at Mont Calv with our venerable brother the lord archbishop of Rouen, and then, according to the outcome of the conference, to proceed to the king, who had arranged to come nearer for this purpose. But at that point, as the aforesaid royal messengers were arriving, the whole arrangement was frustrated by the counsel of Ahithophel, as I have faithfully learned from Hushai; perhaps he received from the messengers some assurance of increasing my humiliation and restoring his own hopes.

But let it be so: “The Lord is my helper” (Ps. 117); “I will not fear what flesh may do to me” (Ps. 55). I also most certainly hope that, with you as leader and ruler, my storm will become calm air, and the tempest bursting forth will come upon the head of the wicked. Therefore I, as the least and today the most wretched of them all, together with all who are companions in this suffering, prostrate at the knees of your Holiness and with hands outstretched, supplicate and offer such prayers as we dare to so great a majesty: “Scatter, O Lord, the counsel of Ahithophel, and strike the head from the house of the wicked.” And since you perform David’s office in this respect, let your work prove it: by your singular skill and strength let another Goliath be cast down and lose the head which, as we have shown above, he turns to so many arts and deceits. For you alone are judged fit in the host for so great a contest.

Then indeed you will triumph to the testimony of ten thousand maidens singing. For when the pestilent man perishes, others will wash their hands in the sinner’s blood, according to what one of the saints says: “It is better that very many be freed by the condemnation of a few than that more should be endangered by their absolution.” Otherwise mercy is certainly unjust. Therefore let not Elijah’s zeal and Phinehas’s sword fall from the hands of your heart; and see with what zeal he deserves to be met who has acted thus: who shut his father in prison, stripped him, and still holds him in chains; and, what I lament more tearfully because it is more detestable than the rest, who coveted his father’s bride for himself. Nor was this done in a chamber: rather, as we have said above, he publicly attempted to violate his father’s bed, declaring, with the people and clergy of his city hearing, that by right he ought to hold the metropolitan see and was bound to Canterbury by no bond of profession or obedience.

Whether one who has acted so maliciously and spoken so proudly has deserved absolution or condemnation, let the consideration of your singular primacy decide. And if perhaps he has obtained, according to ecclesiastical custom, absolution from anathema, whether authority ought in this very matter to be reserved for my smallness, which he has so contumaciously despised—or rather for his mother Church, whose bonds of profession and obedience he has publicly and so shamelessly broken—let your consideration likewise decide. And, lest I seem to speak to so great a majesty recklessly rather than timidly: for all who are grievously oppressed, this hope would not be incongruous, and the way to the Church’s peace would certainly become easier if he returned as he comes. Otherwise, know—and I am sure—that, as has often happened, our wound will be healed with disgrace. For they will say: “Peace, peace,” and there is no peace (Ezek. 13).

I have said these things so confidently because humility and approach to peace will arise from fear of justice alone, and peace can be secured only by justice, according to that eminent teacher and ruler: “These two love each other,” etc., etc., etc. [lacuna]

Perhaps I shall seem excessive in assailing the person of the bishop of London, and to have written things so harsh and bitter from hatred rather than judgment. But He is my witness, to whom every will speaks, and who knows how I now desire him in the bowels of Christ Jesus, even amid my chains; though he has acted toward me not as a son, I have not withdrawn from him, God knows, the affection of a father. Rather, amid my chains I desire more and more that we may have walked worthily of the calling in which we were called, with all humility and gentleness, bearing one another’s burdens.

I perceive that in such length of discourse I have now exceeded every epistolary brevity. Therefore I fear that I have offended the hearing of so great a majesty, occupied with the other great and manifold concerns of this mortal life. But I hope that he who sympathizes with my afflictions with affection so fatherly, indeed so motherly, will readily grant pardon for this excess of words, especially since what is enlarged by feelings and pains could not be compressed into a brief discourse. Moreover, I had already written other shorter letters, which I send to your Holiness besides these, when suddenly a courier entered and announced the departure of the bishop of London for the Curia and many other matters contained here. Therefore, as such great news came upon us, it was necessary to write new things and, after the end of the former letters, to begin the present one. May the Spirit of counsel and knowledge teach you concerning all things, Father most dear to me.

## LETTER IV. HERBERT’S LETTER, IN THE PERSON OF STEPHEN, BISHOP OF MEAUX, TO POPE ALEXANDER FOR THOMAS, EXILED ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

Although, holy Father, the care of all the Churches has been entrusted to you by reason of the excellence of your singular primacy, yet the children of that Church especially deserve consolation and protection from you who do not fear to go up against [their opponents] and freely resist earthly powers lest they usurp what belongs to the Church. Therefore I, the least of bishops, prostrate at your knees for our venerable brother, your son Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury—a man, as is believed, beloved by God and faithful to our mother the holy Roman Church—offer such prayers as I can and dare to so great a majesty. For the sake of your name and the Church’s protection, as the world of Churches knows, he has suffered such grave things; and beyond everyone’s expectation, though he had been brought up in palaces and was the companion and fellow student of emperors, he despised the prince’s favour and all the glory of his house, undertook alone pastoral labours, and for that reason trod the winepress alone—unless because wrath was poured out, according to the prophet’s lament: “Upon the child outside and upon the council of young men together. A man with his wife was driven out, and old men full of days; their houses passed to others, and their fields and wives alike” (Jer. 6).

Look, then, most loving Father, upon your children, who with him have been so cruelly and inhumanely proscribed and expelled. Look, good Shepherd, upon the sheep of your pasture. Holy Judge, drive out and scatter those who scatter your inheritance, lest so great a power bear the sword without cause—especially now when Malchus has stretched out his hand against Christ and Belshazzar against the vessels of the temple. And because you are Christ’s vicar, let your action prove it: raise your hands against the pride of those who malign the Holy One. Rebuke the beasts of the reeds; break kings in the day of your wrath and judge among the nations, so that, as you are the Father of mercies, you may also be the Lord of vengeance, the just and strong Judge, terrible and taking away the spirit of princes, terrible among the kings of the earth, that, as we know you to be Christ’s vicar, you may fulfil Christ’s ministry.

Therefore I pray, and pray again: let the vicar of Christ, the Christ of the Lord, no longer overlook Christ’s injury. Yet that worn-out and commonplace saying is written to us, which flesh and blood have revealed to our wise men: “Wait,” they say, “wait again; it is not the time for vengeance but for endurance, in so great a multitude of the Church’s enemies.” I pray, Father, endure a little, and bear with me as I speak to so great a majesty, not rashly but timidly: this is indeed wondrous—rather monstrous—wisdom, that the sword of the priesthood should then be borne without cause because Christ has many adversaries; as if it were safer for Christ’s athletes, frightened by the multitude of opponents, temporarily to yield, bend their knees, relax their hands, and turn the sword back into its sheath.

O blind wisdom of the world, exceedingly grovelling and gross, weakening all the strength of faith, stifling the censure of judgment, and setting the lamp of justice under a bushel. For such people the prophet says: “Open, Lord, their eyes, that they may see, because there are more with us” (4 Kings 6). I do not deny, however, that one must often yield to circumstances; sometimes certain things must be overlooked, and many things endured; some matters must be administered by dispensation. Yet this can be done well only if justice is preserved. But, to pass over an exile so dreadful and unheard of in the times of Christian princes, where, by the blow against one man, so many and such great persons are punished: how can justice be preserved when Christ is led bound a second time before the governor, Peter is deprived of the office of his apostolate, the Church of the English is, as is now universally known, stripped of office, clerics are everywhere dragged before secular courts, and priests dare not exercise the power of binding and loosing?

Come then, man of God: put on strength, you who hold their inheritance. Shake yourself, son of those cast out, that you may be the rod of the disciplined, the staff of the untaught, the hammer of the proud, and the relief of the oppressed. And since I have begun, I will speak to my lord, though I am dust and ashes. Let not your strength be weakened in tribulation; otherwise there is danger that one spark, which arose in the west in the heart of the sea, unless it is quickly extinguished, may lay waste the whole world of Churches. May the Angel of Great Counsel be with you.

## LETTER V. HERBERT THE EXILE TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS, ALREADY SET OUT FOR ROME

By what vehicles can my smallness now present itself before your sublimity? Rather, in the written form of a letter, all of us who are children of migration cast ourselves at the feet of your compassion, knocking at that royal court of your clemency, so that our prayer may enter the door of your mercy. If you do not hear the cry of our voice, hear at least the cry of our blood; for our blood cries to you, now more strongly because we are tested more dangerously.

For the proud have now hidden a snare for us in the guise of a stranger. He—yes, he—came to us in the guise of a stranger. He came as a stranger, but did not remain hidden as a stranger for long. Pretending to devise thoughts of peace—our peace—he was graciously admitted, himself also speaking words of peace. Thus, seeing so fair an appearance, the eyes of many were held fast, confidently awaiting peace. But at last they complained that their eyes had been plundered by the bird-catching tricks of his words. For when all already hoped for the end and completion of the whole affair, our stranger had turned aside from the straight way through certain winding paths well known to him, and that devout man was found to have devised not thoughts of peace but rather of affliction. For whereas he first offered peace, afterwards he refused the kiss of peace.

When this was heard, those standing by were perplexed, the mediators hesitated, the people were astonished, all wondered, and the hopes of everyone were frustrated. Some cried out that he was the destroyer not merely of ecclesiastical order but of all human custom, or rather that he offended against the very law of nature, which is known to have taught human beings the sign of love and peace, so that the sign of concord might appear especially in that member from which quarrels and disputes are accustomed to arise. Others testified that this openly disclosed the form of a seduction hidden in the heart, and even exceeded diabolical presumption: for a man did not deign to share with a man what the Lord had shown to man; and He Himself, in the sign of reconciliation and peace, “kissed me with the kiss of His mouth.”

But, to speak more secretly to my lord, silently considering the matter, I judge that the kiss of peace was denied us not without cause, indeed by divine ordering: namely, because his peace, which we seek, and our justice, which we foster, cannot agree—his kingdom and our priesthood. For elsewhere we read of the kiss of peace and justice: “Justice,” he says, “and peace have kissed” (Ps. 84). Yet would that, as the prophet wishes for himself, I were a man without the Spirit and spoke falsehood.

Further, the written petition of the lord of Canterbury, containing the terms of our peace and composed with sufficient moderation and discretion in the judgment of prudent men, was offered to him and read. At first he seemed to accept it; but afterwards, as is the man’s manner, using I know not what softening phrases, he altered the meaning of the written petition, so that, according to his customary faithlessness, while doing nothing he seemed to have done everything. Thus we departed frustrated, carrying away nothing but our distress.

Therefore, man of God, prepare yourself—the staff of the proud, hammer of tyrants, and relief of the oppressed—that you may inherit the zeal as well as the ministry of those whose ministry you have inherited, and may show yourself to us as another Mattathias against the sacrileges of Antiochus. With your fiery utterance, diligently take care to stir the cold hearts of the Israelites, lest they be extinguished by the blasts of lepers. For what now remains is this: our eyes are upon you; indeed, the whole English Church, whose milk you still sucked as a little child, sighs toward you and awaits peaceful sacrifices, especially now that you yourself have entered into the holy places.

Fearing this, our aforesaid stranger was thrown into strange alarm. From fear of your departure alone he feigned humility and even pretended to be a pilgrim, by deception and a certain cunning, as we have said. In this pilgrimage, having taken advantage of your absence, he seems already to have swallowed up the rivers of Gaul in large part; so much so that Jordan itself is said to have flowed into his mouth. By this art he attempts, unless I am mistaken, to swallow us also. Your prudence knows what I mean. It is therefore necessary that the healing power of your counsel quickly come to meet [the danger], lest he swallow not merely the portion of land which he seeks and now appears to hold in certain hope, but the whole land—which God forbid.

At the end of this discourse, I and the companions of my suffering, prostrate on our knees, entreat your discernment that, with your consent or assent, we may never be compelled by superior authority to remit injuries inflicted upon the patrimony purchased by Christ’s blood and upon the widow’s dowry. For this would introduce a ruinous precedent and would contaminate us ourselves with wrongful consent; it would also justify one guilty of manifest sacrilege, especially since the rule of divine law is that sin is not remitted unless what has been taken away is restored; and again, that true repentance is not practised but rather feigned so long as the thing taken remains with the thief or robber, unless perhaps he is excused by constraining poverty.

Further, let it be your care and consideration that our excommunicated persons should not be absolved except after giving the security prescribed by ecclesiastical custom, lest what has once or twice been done otherwise may turn to the Church’s injury. Therefore we would greatly welcome an explicit command from the Roman pontiff on this matter. We have lately heard that certain men will bear witness in the Curia, by their writings, against us and in disparagement of us for the person of the bishop of London. One of them, it is said, is a cismarine bishop in Normandy; yet whether he is a bishop, though he has grown old among bishops, is unknown. Indeed, what is truer: if anyone thinks seriously of Christ, we shall profess him not merely no bishop but not even truly a Christian—unless words, not works, make a Christian.

His whole strength is in his mouth: a golden tongue and an iron heart. His epistolary composition, which we lately saw, laboriously but most viperously devised against us, falsely represents a hideous idol with excessive brightness; or rather, it is a real idol, because what it has fashioned is false and there is no spirit in it. This is the man who spoke peace with us in his mouth and now secretly lays snares; therefore he is the more dangerous, of whom the prophet says: “Their tongue is a wounding arrow; it has spoken deceit” (Jer. 9).

But I do not now proceed further to assail this man’s disgrace; it is enough to have touched upon it, especially since I know and do not doubt that, though I am silent, from the circumstances of the persons already mentioned the man himself with all his characteristics has immediately come to your mind. Yet we hope that these men, and those like them who oppose us without cause, will, by the Lord’s gift, return ashamed when your majesty is present. Among them, too, certain persons are said to have been fined, so that they may oppose us rather than you, dreaming with their lord that you will seek some embassy in their transmarine land.

But paying little attention to their dreams, together with the whole Church we also, hiding among monks and rocks, pray in our distress that you may come—come with rejoicing, with us accompanying you—by whose gift it comes to pass that He has visited His people through the ministry of so great a pontiff; that you may serve as ambassador for the children of captivity; that you may reconcile our hearts to the justice of our forefathers and make known the desires of the wretched. May the Angel of Great Counsel be with us, who may fit us for every good work, so that you may understand what is right and always fulfil it in deed.

## LETTER VI. HERBERT THE EXILE TO THE SAME MAN AGAINST THE BISHOP OF LONDON, NOW SETTING OUT FOR ROME

To the most reverend Father and lord, his most beloved in Christ, W., by the grace of God archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See: his own HERBERT, now wretched and exiled, offers such little as he can now offer.

Although the authority of him to whom I write might command silence, charity has broken silence; for charity is strong as death and often does not know how to weigh majesty, as that pagan poet also says:

> Majesty and love neither agree well nor dwell in one seat.

Therefore I would set this whole humble sheet aflame with the fire of charity, were I not chilled by the pressure of urgent cares and compelled by pressing necessity to turn my pen to other matters. For behold, that great dragon, the ancient serpent, wounded by the sword of the word of God, is at last compelled to emerge from the pit of his slippery error. Yet we know that he proceeds from evil to evil, so that he who formerly attacked by deceit will now become the manifest accuser of his brothers and put on weapons of slander far heavier than weapons of war.

Therefore, as soon as the cry of the oppressed—whether in wilderness or city, whether travellers or those settled in one place—reaches the ears of your clemency, your compassion must come to their aid, that with the weapons of your warfare you may shatter the fighting vessels of iniquity. For thus the assembly of the hypocrite will be barren, when your fire has devoured the tents of those who gladly receive gifts. Yet those blasts of lepers, hostile to this holy fire, are always suspect to me; my lord sees what this speech means.

But that I may say to your sublimity, not recklessly but timidly, what might benefit the business: if perhaps we find a traveller, it is expedient that one of yours be sent back together with ours; otherwise, unless those rulers of ours fear your countenance, we fear that we may be swallowed by the dragon and that they will fill their belly from our tenderness. Unless I am mistaken, your prudence knows even now what I mean by prophetic words.

But lest I delay the hearing of your Holiness longer with the words of my foolishness, I add at the end of this discourse how greatly the whole Church celebrates your charity beyond measure for the mercies shown to the lord of Canterbury, especially in this our journey; and I hear and rejoice that peace restored to us by your labours, with the Lord’s favour—or even justice, if it precedes peace—is already numbered in the catalogue of your mercies.

One thing, however, I cannot conceal: certain lying messengers of the king of the English, returning from the Curia, have filled the whole land with windy words, disseminating to anyone whatever they chose concerning the cause of your journey and the secret particulars of the business, even hissing them into unwilling listeners’ ears. Richard Barre was the chief prophet. One thing I know: if you entrusted your counsels to them, they are traitors; but if you did not, they are liars. Yet some of your people, too ready to believe, have been stirred by this wind. Very many, indeed, to speak the truth to my lord without sparing him, complain more justly that they have deserved no consolation at all during so long an absence of yours, through your own messengers or letters; and in this I dare say their complaint is altogether just.

Still, these failings will easily obtain pardon if the desolation of your absence is compensated by the swift joy of your presence. May that great guide of your journey grant this to us—the God of our salvation—who, as He acts, will make your journey prosperous.

## LETTER VII. HERBERT THE EXILE TO THE SAME MAN FOR THE SAME CAUSE
By what eloquence of words, or by what praises of speech, can we find means worthily to extol the many and great acts of mercy which you have shown us from the beginning of our sufferings? Yet now especially, when a fuller occasion for mercy presented itself, all the bowels of your compassion have been opened for healing our wounds. All, from the least to the greatest, have recognized and proclaim you an apostolic man, who has borne our burden [Col. 1433D] with such charity. Hence, by God’s granting mercy, there shall be a reward for your work and hope for your latter end. And we—not merely your fellow-brethren and friends, but I and the companions of my suffering—have become the footstool of your feet.

But while your servants are still in peril, it is necessary, my lord, that you stretch out the hands of your aid, especially to him who strengthened the hands of the worst men at home, and has now at last turned again to his course; and, like a horse, rushes headlong to battle, perhaps taking advantage of David’s absence so that he may freely reproach Israel, when there is none able or daring to thwart his onset. This is the Londoner, who has now begun to make a journey of falsehood. Therefore, fearing the violence of the lion, whose dragon-like snares we have long experienced, we flee beneath the covering of your wings [Col. 1434A], so that, should we perhaps find you at the lodging-place, you may employ Davidic prudence and strength, lest his assault prevail as he advances to battle against Israel. Rather, let the reproach of the whole people be turned back upon the enemy. May the Spirit of counsel and knowledge be with you, and, for the sake of our children less fitted for this contest, teach our hands for battle and our fingers for war.

## LETTER VIII. THIS LETTER, IN THE PERSON OF THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, TO ALL THE CLERGY AND LAITY OF ALL ENGLAND, ABSOLVES THEM FROM THE OATH WHICH THEY HAD MADE AGAINST THE LORD POPE AND HIMSELF—NAMELY, THAT THEY WOULD NEITHER RECEIVE THEIR MESSENGER NOR THEIR LETTERS, AND WOULD BETRAY THOSE WHO DID RECEIVE THEM.

[Col. 1434B] “Know, most beloved, that out of much tribulation,” etc. It is printed among the letters of St Thomas as no. 78.

## LETTER IX. A LETTER OF HERBERT, IN THE PERSON OF THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, TO ALL THE BISHOPS AND ABBOTS OF ENGLAND, WARNING THEM NOT TO BELIEVE THE FALSE REPORTS OF THE MESSENGERS OF THE KING OF ENGLAND, WHICH THEY WERE SPREADING ABOUT HIM EVERYWHERE; AND NOT TO GIVE THE KING NEW OATHS OR ANY OTHER NEW OBLIGATION.

THOMAS, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother H., bishop of Winchester, and to all his fellow-brethren and fellow-bishops, to abbots also established throughout the province, and likewise to his venerable brother HUGH, bishop of Durham [Col. 1434C]: act manfully and be strengthened in the Lord.

I give thanks to my Lord whom I now serve. See among the letters of St Thomas, letter 79.

## LETTER X. THIS LETTER, IN THE PERSON OF THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, TO ROGER, BISHOP OF WORCESTER.

THOMAS, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to his venerable brother ROGER, bishop of Worcester: may he bring to a better end what he has well begun.

We remember that we have often written to your charity what we think of your crossing of the sea, and we rejoice greatly at your obedience. But because we believe stricter times and cruel punishment by our enemies to be imminent, we again repeat our command, firmly enjoining and commanding you by virtue of obedience not under any circumstances to attempt to cross the sea until you have received the command of our lord the pope and of ourselves concerning the affairs of the Church. By the same virtue of obedience we command that you never, through anyone’s fear or favour, give assent contrary to the dignity of your mother Church of Canterbury, for the crowning of the lord king’s son. Rather, should you learn that so great a liberty of the Church is endangered or even shaken, oppose it manfully, as befits so great a son.

And because I know that the messengers of the lord king, lately returned from the curia, have broad tongues and have scattered much into the wind, we have taken care to send to you the man whom I do not doubt will faithfully report the truth of the events [Col. 1435A], which he knows exceedingly well, since he himself left the curia later, so that our consolations may also gladden your soul. Moreover, we desire you to be warned that you should take care to send a copy of the letter which we are directing to you to our fellow-brethren and fellow-bishops, namely the lord of Winchester and the lord of Exeter, consoling and exhorting them also by your own letter, that they may stand with us together, stoutly fighting the battles of the Lord; and especially that they, as the rams of the Lord’s flock, may set themselves in opposition if they are summoned to meet concerning the crowning of the king’s son while our authority is excluded. May the Angel of Great Counsel and our blessing be with you, my dearest son.

## LETTER XI. A LETTER OF HERBERT, IN THE PERSON OF THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, TO ROBERT, PROVOST OF SAINT-OMER.

[Col. 1435B]

THOMAS, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to his beloved and loving friend R., provost of Saint-Omer: may he so pass through temporal goods that he does not lose eternal ones.

We know and hold, by the testimony of events themselves, that neither the great inequality of the times nor any hazard of our fortune has cooled the ardour of that charity; and we render devout thanks to the giver of all charity, by whose gift it has come about that, among so many friends of prosperity, he has preserved for me even one friend in adversity. Therefore, if amid so great a revolution of time I have written little to you [Col. 1435C], this must in no way be attributed to forgetfulness or indolence. For I suspended my intended message because, concerning that matter which our messenger sent to you conveyed, I was daily awaiting your reply. We still desire and affectionately request that you expedite it.

But what you inserted in your letter—namely, that you had received reports concerning our affair not in accordance with your heart—what you intended to signify by this is by no means entirely clear to me. For through the mercy of Him who cannot even in His anger restrain His mercies, all things are proceeding prosperously for us, given the condition of affairs and the state of the times. For the healing wisdom of God so moderates our adversities that it causes us to endure patiently and with an even mind those things through which the gate of heaven is promised to be opened; so that what is the medicine of God is reckoned the wound of the world, and what is the scourge of the persecutor becomes the comfort of the sufferer.

But while I turned over and over what the covering of that aforementioned expression might contain, I suspected that perhaps you were troubled because of certain letters obtained from the Roman pontiff, by which the lord king of England, the persons of the realm, and the kingdom seem to be exempted from our pontifical jurisdiction. Yet your prudence ought to consider that such a mandate may soon expire. Thus we ourselves have not at present been moved against the lord pope in any respect, nor do we complain of an injury. But whether the world will or will not, against the world we shall, God granting, contend in the great contest [Col. 1436A], pursuing onward the palm of the heavenly calling. But enough of this.

Moreover, to speak with the confidence of affection, I cannot sufficiently wonder that, in the conduct of these kings, you do not diligently consider the glory of your lord—my most beloved in Christ—and your own. For you know that every counsel is to be rejected which an ill repute accompanies or follows; and indeed the world is already sounding this report against us, and it appears no new attestation of their conduct. Therefore we exhort you in the Lord, as one beloved more dearly than the beloved, to see how carefully you walk. Do not show yourself so favourably disposed to one that you suffer injury to the glory of your name and the other hates you forever; rather, let both be bound by a consideration being brought to bear. A word to the wise [Col. 1436B] is sufficient.

For the cause of the Church and our own, we still ask, having often asked, that you apply diligent and prompt care, as you know to be expedient, as one to whom, after God, we owe the little that we now know and whatever we may ever be able to do. May your affection for us, my dearest friend in Christ, flourish and remain strong.

## LETTER XII. A LETTER OF HERBERT TO NICHOLAS, PRIOR OF THE INFIRMARY OF MONT-ROUEN.

To his beloved in Christ, N., man of God: H., companion of THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, now a wretched yet distinguished exile, offers such small service as he can.

I received your charitable letter, in which, if I recall rightly, you urged me to bring it about by whatever means I could that the man of Canterbury should not abandon his ardour once begun. But balsam needs no ointments, nor the sun torches to assist it; nor is it necessary to spur breathless runners in their course. I see Christ’s athlete fighting bravely, stronger than any exhorter of his; he does not need the goads of words in the course of the contest. I see, I say, the one true athlete of Christ in our days, taught by Him, anointed from Him, sold with Him, fleeing as He fled, yet glorious in Him; against whom his friends and neighbours drew near, the nations raged, kings stood by and princes assembled—made in every respect an imitator of Him who inherited the promises through faith and patience.

Therefore, set against the world in the theatre of this world, made a spectacle [Col. 1436D] both to angels and to human beings, he lawfully fights the great contest and presses onward towards the palm of the heavenly calling. To reach it through perseverance, he needs not my exhortation as a sinful man, but rather the strength of the prayer of your flock, weak in body yet stronger in spirit, and of your own prayer. I would have written much, had I not learned from the brevity of your letter of your daily necessities. Therefore, not forgetful of your care amid many concerns, and taking from yourself a model not indeed of writing but of living, I have answered a few things with a few words—yet writing more to you than you wrote, returning with interest what I received.

But know this for certain, my dearest friend, part of my soul and another Nicholas: amid the shipwreck of my present exile [Col. 1437A], I want you to return with interest what you now receive; and since, as I think, you carry a great thing in your breast, let me not find you inferior in speech. May Christ’s poor man fare well in the Lord.

## LETTER XIII. A LETTER OF HERBERT TO PRIOR WIBERT OF THE CHURCH OF CANTERBURY AND TO THE WHOLE CONVENT.

To his beloved in Christ, the prior of Holy Trinity and the remaining brothers of that place devoted to God: H., companion of THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, now a wretched yet distinguished exile—fight with tears and prayer.

When I took up the pen to write the work of this present page, my mind immediately hesitated, my hand trembled, and, as grief returned, my eyes filled with tears [Col. 1437B], deeply sympathizing with your desolation. To you now applies that mournful song of the Bride: “They struck me and wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took away my cloak” (Song of Songs 5). The cloak of your honour has indeed been taken away, and you have put on confusion and mourning. You mourn Jonah swallowed up and Joseph sold; nor can you bear with an even mind the miseries of your father and the wrongs done to your mother.

But now weapons of consolation must be taken up against grief, so that your hope may achieve victory. Therefore, amid the beginnings of the world’s birth, let us see Abel in the field, Noah in the flood, Job on the dung-heap, Daniel in the pit; and, since it would take too long to run through each generation of the righteous—of whom indeed there are as many scourged as there are righteous—let us look more closely and attentively upon the labours, insults, and injuries of our Saviour. This father of ours, though altogether unworthy, would govern His city if he refused the martial labours and contests of service under his Emperor. We therefore take our example from a man and our help from the Mighty One, going forth with Him outside the camp and bearing His reproach.

This also contributes to consolation: it is peculiar to you that your fathers pass through such miseries and sufferings and are tested by the fire of tribulation, not emptied. Therefore I shall now add consolation upon consolation for you; and, to speak something confidently, I dare adapt that utterance to you: “We passed through fire and water, and were brought out into refreshment” (Psalm 65). Jonah, though swallowed, has now been brought forth from the beast’s belly [Col. 1437D]; and Joseph, sold by his brothers, surely lives and rules. Yet they showed his father the blood-stained many-coloured tunic, saying that a most savage beast had devoured him.

For those who had been sent to bring various accusations against our Joseph attempted to do so, calling him a criminal man, a disturber of the peace of the kingdom and Church. But all were caught in their own craftiness, and their words were not believed. One of them, who is an abstainer, when he thirsted for innocent blood and still attempted in many ways to harm the person of the lord of Canterbury, was commanded by the supreme Father of fathers to proceed more sparingly. When his long-prepared speech was cut short by so brief an intervention, he moved forward not as before with running speed, but with the pace of a tortoise in speaking, scarcely uttering three words together—not speaking, but stammering. Another, who is especially accustomed to glory in the words of human wisdom, immediately after he had spoken had neither voice nor understanding, speaking as though he did not know the letters taught to children or the first combinations of words. Hence very many were astonished and wondered, ascribing it all to Him who makes the tongues of the prudent eloquent and makes the eloquent foolish.

I shall name no one, for I suppose that from what has already been said you will very easily understand even what has not been said. I would write further things about further persons, had not a detailed account of each exceeded the limits of a letter and the work of a single night’s composition. Therefore, to preserve brevity and state everything at once and in summary: as we saw and as we heard, those who sought our lives return with shame and confusion [Col. 1438B]; and those from whom, as we have said, God took away their voice, so that they could scarcely be heard, were not heard. Therefore be comforted, be comforted by these words; do not hesitate in anything, but know certainly that the great God of the Hebrews, who brought your Joseph out of prison, will shortly make him great in the land.

Meanwhile, act manfully and let your heart be strengthened for your most holy city and its guardian. Fight with tears and psalms, remembering that at Hezekiah’s tears one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians were destroyed by a single angel in one night. Joseph likewise sang praises to the Lord, and the Lord conquered for him who praised. Moses fought against Amalek not by the sword but by prayer. Therefore now keep watch and pray all the more urgently as you see your mother herself more grievously afflicted—indeed by her own household and children. Above all, provide for the poor shepherd of Jesus Christ, I mean your own father, who, as every tongue testifies, is a disciple of that great prophet: he left his house, abandoned his inheritance, set aside the favour of princes for the love of justice, despised threats, and at last did not shrink from the hardships of exile and the burdens of poverty, but rather embraced them devoutly. He did not hesitate to place his shoulders beneath the burdens of men and endure pastoral labours, though until these times he had been reared in royal houses and was the son of so many and such great delights, as the world proclaims. Now [Col. 1438D], however, he has nowhere to lay his head, except that in him the foreign princes and nations to whom we have been driven in exile believe that they honour not a man but God.

It befits the renown of your holiness to take care of him in every way and above all others, providing for him continually day and night in spiritual matters, and in temporal matters frequently and even beyond the measure of your means, with every cheerfulness. May your prayers prosper.

## LETTER XIV. A LETTER OF THE BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF CANTERBURY AND OF OTHER PERSONS ESTABLISHED IN VARIOUS PLACES THROUGHOUT THE SAME PROVINCE, SENT TO THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, WHILE HE WAS STILL LIVING IN EXILE AT PONTIGNY; IT ALSO CONTAINS THEIR APPEAL.

[Col. 1439A]

“To the venerable father and lord,” etc.

“What things, Father, at a distance,” etc. [It is the same as letter 436 among the Letters of Gilbert Foliot.]

## LETTER XV. A LETTER OF HERBERT TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF CANTERBURY AND TO THE OTHER PERSONS ESTABLISHED IN VARIOUS PLACES THROUGHOUT THAT PROVINCE, COMPOSED IN THE PERSON OF THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, AND CONTAINING A REPLY TO THE APPELLATE MEMORIAL OF THOSE SAME BISHOPS.

THOMAS, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, to his beloved brothers in Christ, the sons of the same Church, his fellow-bishops, and the other ministers of God’s churches established throughout the province [Col. 1439B]: may you understand what is right and provide for the last things.

“I waited and waited day after day to see whether any of my friends and acquaintances would take thought for me, a man of no account and as one appointed to death, hoping that I should receive from you at least, brothers, some consolation, even late, in this great contest of sufferings. And behold, while I was dwelling in the wilderness of Pontigny, your writings were at last brought to me; they seemed to express both affection and complaint: affection, because—to pass over longer matters briefly—you wrote that after my departure it was a comfort to me that public report declared that I thought nothing lofty,” etc. [lacuna] [Col. 1439C]

“But, to return to the appeal made by you: from what has already been said it ought to be clear to you, if not from my mouth, then at least from your conscience bearing witness for me, how unjust this appeal is. Moreover, as you yourselves write, you appealed long ago in the face of the Church concerning the same matter, should you find yourselves involved in another. But the time for pursuing that appeal—which is granted only for the most urgent reason—has now almost expired. For it is two years; wherefore, since you have not pursued the appeal within so long a period, which was allowed only for an exceedingly urgent cause, this old appeal now renewed affords no remedy to the appellants, especially since you had access to the judge,” etc. [lacuna]

[Let these excerpts from the lengthy letter suffice; for it is nothing but a rhetorical little treatise fashioned by our good Herbert. The letter which Saint Thomas actually sent to the bishops of England has already been published among the Letters of St Thomas as no. 75.]

## LETTER XVI. A LETTER OF LOMBARD, IN THE PERSON OF THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, REPLYING TO THE WRITTEN APPEAL OF THE BISHOPS OF ENGLAND.

I have received and carefully examined the letter of your brotherhood, in which I am greatly disturbed by the assertion that I have wronged my lord the king, and have troubled him and his kingdom. I am not conscious, indeed, of having inflicted wrongs; but I know that I have endured grievous wrongs, and I greatly lament that this has been spread abroad through kings and kingdoms [Col. 1440A]. For no one is said to commit an injury unless he has an intention to injure—unless someone wishes less prudently to construe as an injury the fact that I did not yield or consent to the serpentine suggestions and deceitful persuasions by which I was cunningly induced to renounce the administration of the Church of Canterbury, which I neither ought nor could do.

For just as the ordinances of the Fathers reject those who rashly and shamelessly seek lordship and hurry prematurely to a place of governance, and the edicts of princes punish them most severely, so the same sanctions forbid one called by the Lord and advanced by canonical election to refuse the burden undertaken. Accordingly, if I did not yield, I obeyed the law; I injured no one. For in the judgment of no good person will he be said to have committed an injury who is plainly seen, in the act for which he is accused, to have obeyed the commands of the canons.

Nor do I think that in my departure, or because of it, I injured anyone. I departed, indeed, and followed our teacher, the founder of the Christian religion, whose every action ought to be an instruction for our life and a pattern for our conduct; I also followed His disciples, our teachers. Persecuted by the brothers and children of my mother, I fled. I fled, I say, led by no fickleness of mind, but compelled by that fear which would have fallen upon even the most steadfast person: certain men, by whose counsel it was clear that such things were being done, said openly to my face that there would be no small cause for rejoicing if I could remain not yet archbishop, but Thomas. Seeking to avoid the rage of those raging against me [Col. 1440C] and the disposition of my lord the king—more instilled than innate—I departed. Thus my flight had a reasonable, just, and most urgent cause.

Therefore my flight was not that of a cowardly, fearful, pliant, frivolous, and inconstant man, as Assur slandered without cause, but of a steadfast and prudent man—although not steadfast and prudent [the text appears corrupt or incomplete]. If the circumstances of the entire affair and the things which were probably feared are carefully examined and considered more attentively—for one prudently fears what can easily occur—it will be clearer than light that much provision was made for the reputation of my lord the king. Let him who is wise understand; and you are prudent, so that you easily understand what I say.

And indeed after my departure—or, more truthfully, my expulsion—I sought solitude. I set before myself the table which the Lord prepared in our sight against those who afflict us; I devoted myself to prayer and applied myself to reading, to see whether I might somehow repair the time that had been lost and, in the days in which I had seen and done evils, see and do good. While I persistently did these things in silence and humility, hoping for the redemption of the Church of Canterbury and her children, it was announced to Job that his house had collapsed and that his children had died crushed in its fall. So too it was announced to me that the goods of the Church of Canterbury and of the poor had been seized and occupied, and that monks and clerics were being harassed more cruelly than before. Yet I remained silent, sympathizing with those who suffered, groaning for those who transgressed, while my eyes brought forth most abundant streams of tears [Col. 1441A], because they did not keep Thy law, O Lord.

I still waited, receiving some hope and consolation as the Lord’s rod and staff comforted me; but those who persecuted their mother added still further sin, dragging clerics of every rank everywhere before secular courts. If any wished to plead the exemption of the forum or desired to have recourse to the remedy of appeal, they were torn by interrogations and subjected to refined tortures, as though they had plotted against the prince’s life; ecclesiastical judges too, as is said, at times decreeing this. When these things happened, I was no longer permitted to keep silence, lest I should one day be forced to break forth into that complaint: “Woe is me, because I held my peace and was silent from good things” (Isaiah 6); “therefore my sorrow was renewed” (Psalm 38).

Accordingly I wrote to my lord the king, offering counsel in all humility, that he might restrain those committing such monstrous offences. I suggested and advised; but, woe is me, I did not persuade. I issued a warning; but he did not accept it. I declared to him in a threat that it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God; but he rejected it. In these letters I did not omit the offices of greeting, but with all devotion I desired that he might prosper in the ways of the Lord.

In all this there was nothing hostile, nothing undevoted—indeed, nothing at all except what I, as a faithful servant to my lord and a father to a son, enjoined, with this purpose and desired end: that he might be recalled from those ways in which he is known to stray. Why, then, you have fallen away from hope of reconciliation between my lord and me, if indeed you had conceived such hope, I do not understand. Nor do I understand on what ground one may be said to join battle with drawn sword where such sincere devotion of a faithful man toward his lord is heard [Col. 1441C].

Indeed, he ought rather from my silence to have inferred that I was his rival, the enemy of his life, and a despiser of my office, if—God forbid!—he rejected altogether the excellent and well-tested counsel of his faithful servant and contemned his pastor. But if I faithfully admonished my lord as I ought; if, in consideration of the benefits bestowed and in accordance with the duty of the office laid upon me, I set before him that he must fear divine judgment, there is now no reason for him to be angry with me rather than to thank me.

I shall direct all my efforts to this; I shall add labours to labours; I shall spend even myself, if need be, so that my lord may be reformed to better things. Thus admonition towards good, correction so that one may be recalled from evil, and rebuke for obstinacy win for me glory and renown in Christ, and at the same time protect me from the shameful mark of ingratitude. Even if I could, why would anyone vainly fear that they might incur the axe and disturbance of the kingdom, when they do not permit the state of Christ’s Church—through which kings reign happily and in peace—to be deformed, but strive to reform it for the better, insisting in season and out of season [Col. 1441D]?

Therefore I shall beseech, argue with, and rebuke my lord severely, yet also mercifully, so that I may thereby win him more fully in Christ and become more pleasing to him.

These things I repay to my lord, who has raised me to higher rank, [Col. 1442A] for benefits bestowed and dignity granted to me: I repay them for his correction, not for his humiliation. I would by no means repay them unless I desired to embrace him in the compassion of Christ. For a father corrects the son whom he loves; and, in the words of the Wise Man: “Better are the wounds of one who loves than the deceitful kisses of one who hates” (Prov. XXVII). Eli the priest, because he did not correct his sons, deserved suddenly to perish. If, guilty of ingratitude, I could hate my lord, I would be altogether silent about these matters; I would anoint his head with the oil of the sinner. I would not destroy the wall which he built, but would merely whitewash it.

Thus my sincere devotion toward him and the stewardship entrusted to me produce two effects: the one, that I do not wish him to depart from the ways of the Lord; the other, that, when he does depart, I sometimes exercise toward him the severity of a judge. You urge [Col. 1442B] patience upon me, brothers, that through it I may obtain what, as you say, cannot be obtained by a strong hand. It is indeed written that a man’s teaching is recognized through patience. Yet, in the judgment of Holy Scripture, to be silent and not to rebuke the transgressions of offenders, whatever rank they hold, is by no means patience, but culpable negligence. For one who ceases to oppose an openly manifest crime is not free from the taint of secret complicity; an error not resisted is approved; truth, when it is not defended, is crushed. We must fear—so it seems to many—that this patience may terribly bring upon us the office of the heavenly judge.

But the arguments which you advance as stronger reasons for persuading me that patience should be punished rather than accepted, as most people suppose, [Col. 1442C] redound, if you consider carefully, to the confusion of my lord the king and indeed to an indelible stain upon him in the judgment of serious and mature men. Can this be the voice of royal majesty: that he may apostatize, depart from the law of God, violate and profane it, and join himself to the sacrilegious assemblies of schismatics and heretics—unless his monstrous wrongdoing and wholly irreligious excess are patiently tolerated? Those very persons whom, as schismatics and heretics, he utterly abjured when he received Pope Alexander as father and lord no less devoutly than willingly—must he, who ought to pursue them by his decrees and subdue them by the most severe edicts, now enter their profane fellowship, if he is devoutly warned and justly corrected?

See [Col. 1442D] what you have inferred at length from a few things. It would have been wiser for these matters to remain unspoken rather than published in writing, read, and detrimentally twisted into a conjecture concerning the matter. Far be it that such intentions and threats should have been conceived in the mind of my illustrious lord the king, a discerning and provident prince, to whom kingdoms obey and thousands of peoples render service, and to whom it has been divinely granted to triumph most victoriously over his enemies! Far be it, I say, that he should have conceived these designs and threats! It is nearly heresy, brothers, to put forward such allegations. Do not, I beg you, do not, to the injury of the reputation of our lord the king and under the pretext of a fear which ought not to arise in an upright man, contrive or attempt anything against religion and against the holy Roman Church, our mother. “The net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures.”

Would that others among us were as free from suspicion of contrivances [Col. 1443A] of this kind as religion requires—and I desire—that you should be innocent of the charge of apostasy and the like. But if the fear conceived is just, if there has been a lapse—especially on the part of our lord the king, which may God in His most merciful kindness avert—then come forward as friends, but friends of Christ; as judges, but following in the footsteps of Moses: not soothing the offender, but frightening him with divine judgment if he refuses to repent. For to soothe him is to kill, not to heal, souls. To rebuke and reprove is to heal.
