This is my work; this is my glory; this is the reputation in Christ which I desire: that I may rebuke and reprove my lord, so that I may be able to cure and heal him and call him back from a purpose less than just.

His mother, the Church of Canterbury, is ready, [Col. 1443B] with arms outstretched, to receive into her bosom and cherish as a dearest son one who not merely gives satisfaction but even wishes to give satisfaction; and I, within her, shall henceforth be found most ready to follow all his wishes in Christ, according to my knowledge and ability. But, as my sins deserve, I have received no report from anyone that he has either offered satisfaction or wished to make it. For a man is by no means said to provide security or to wish to give satisfaction when he offers to furnish these things at his own discretion. Certainly, providing security is to lords what giving satisfaction is. A man is said to give satisfaction to one whose rightful desire he fulfills.

Therefore, one who offers to provide security and give satisfaction according to the judgment of persons whom every law wholly restrains from judging him in a case against one providing security—or whom an intervening legally established ground of challenge for the time suspends from the office of judging—offers security and satisfaction unlawfully, [Col. 1443C] and does so because he desires neither to provide security nor to give satisfaction. For whenever security has been furnished or satisfaction made unlawfully, it is not deemed furnished or made; for the term *satisdatio* (“giving security”) belongs not only to fact but also to law.

You, indeed, being sons of the Church of Canterbury and of ourselves, are not permitted by the decrees of the holy Fathers and the ordinances of councils to be my judges. These expressly forbid prelates to be submitted to the deliberations of inferiors, and decree that, when complaints against bishops arise, recourse must be had to the examination of a superior judge. Therefore, since you have presumed, contrary to canonical order and to the reverence owed to a father, to judge me—a pastor, though a sinner, a prelate, though unworthy—you have also made yourselves suspect, even if you were otherwise lawful judges, by the very grave cause at issue. Every reason and every law make you as remote from judgment as they allow you to be excluded from arbitration.

From these facts, I do not doubt that it will be clear to attentive observers that he has not merely been unwilling to give satisfaction, [Col. 1443D] but has treated it with contempt—especially since day by day he has raised his hands against his mother, the Church of Canterbury. Moreover, all laws have decreed that one who despises the provision of security and satisfaction, though frequently and repeatedly warned and long awaited, and who does not obey, is to be condemned as contumacious. Hence our Lord, the most just Lawgiver, commands that one who, after being admonished three times, does not obey the priest and the Church be treated as a heathen and a publican. The Roman pontiffs have judged this to be firmly observed as a commandment of God. They have also decreed that a prince cited by three letters, or by one final edict serving for all, who does not appear in person, is to be condemned.

To threaten one who could by every law be condemned is not to be carried away by impulse, but to be guided by merciful reason. Therefore, if it proceeds, the condemnation—not merely the threat—of one who despises providing security and giving satisfaction, supported as it is by every law, will stand most firmly. Yet you see holy things given to dogs, pearls cast before swine, and the stones of the sanctuary scattered at the heads of the streets; and you are angry with me even over a threat, [Col. 1443D] and, what is far less, over an admonition.

Brothers, do not be deceived: God is not mocked. His rebuke is directed both at me and at you when He says: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. LVI); and likewise that of the prophet: “Your prophets saw for you false and foolish things, and did not disclose your iniquity to you” (Lam. II). Although this is said concerning subjects, it is turned into a rebuke of prelates. Let us therefore put silence away. Let us declare their crimes to those who offend, lest we incur divine judgment and fall into the punishment of eternal Gehenna. For priests have been appointed judges over nations and kingdoms, that they may root up and destroy, ruin and scatter, and annul unjust laws, in order that they may build and plant and introduce more equitable laws.

For “the lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth” (Mal. II), [Col. 1444C] not the priests themselves from the mouth of the prince. The peoples of the lands and Christian princes are to seek the law from the priest. It belongs to them to obey ecclesiastical ordinances, not to impose unjust laws upon priests and ministers of God. The most pious emperor Justinian did not differ from this view when he said: “Our laws do not disdain to imitate the sacred canons.” Woe to those who enact unjust laws (Isa. X), overturning God’s judgments by their unrighteous judgments. Woe to their followers and imitators.

The Lord has given us a law, a holy and spotless law that converts souls: I speak of the law of the Gospel, the ordinances of the apostles, and the decrees of the Roman pontiff. Since He has conferred upon them the power of binding and loosing over kings and princes as well as all peoples, He has also granted them authority to make laws by which all might be bound. We know without hesitation that the Roman Church possesses this authority. Whoever establishes ordinances contrary to its institutions is most justly restrained, not merely as contumacious but, if the canonical writings are believed, as a heretic.

Accordingly, lest my silence be presumed to imply consent, and guilt arise from consent, I have anathematized the customs which you call ancestral customs, as contrary to the enactments of the holy Roman Church, our mother, together with their authors, observers, and defenders. [Col. 1444D] I commanded you, and command you now by my authority, to regard them as anathematized; otherwise you too must fear lest the Lord, girded with strength, seize shield and arms and rise terribly in aid of His law, and destroy all alike who establish, observe, and defend a law contrary to Him.

[Col. 1445A] But I judge that the lawful customs of the realm should be observed and embraced with every devotion; whether the hostile man wishes it or not, I shall observe them reverently. I have carried out two judgments according to the customary course, observing the path of canons and laws. You seek to stone me for both; and before you knew how or for what reasons I had done these things, you attacked me for a sentence allegedly unjustly pronounced and for a perverse judgment. Yet I believe that, by God’s most just judgment, matters have gone against you: you have fallen into the snare which you prepared for me. For although, as you state in your letter, you did not know how and to what extent I had acted, and said that I ought first to ascertain the matter and then pronounce sentence upon a matter thus ascertained, [Col. 1445B] you nevertheless condemned me for what was most justly done, and thereby condemned yourselves.

For against our brother, the Bishop of Salisbury, because contrary to the command of the lord pope and to our prohibition issued under pain of excommunication, he promoted John of Oxford—already excommunicated by the law itself—to be dean, when the canons rather decree that he should be deposed, I reasonably pronounced a sentence of suspension. His disobedience had first become known to me through his own confession, not only after judgment. At present we do not pursue his offence, lest we be compelled to increase his punishment.

But John of Oxford, for a crime most publicly known—a crime which, if he wished to deny it, he would not dare deny when the evidence of the deed committed and the wrongdoing still flagrantly continuing convicts him—I declared excommunicated and anathematized. For it is known and notorious how he was a minister of the bond of iniquity and the chain of impiety, and how, by his agency, assistance, and counsel, the schism which had almost been lulled to sleep was most manifestly stirred up again. From this it is proved that he is no less a heretic than a schismatic. For, by a most just interpretation, those are shown to be heretics who are discovered, even on slight evidence, to have departed from the path of Catholic religion or from the unity of the Roman Church.

But no slight evidence is involved: it is the strongest proof of the crime of heresy committed in the presence of the king of the Germans and before the peoples. [Col. 1445C] The documents of iniquity, containing the bond tied by John’s ministry, were circulated almost throughout the whole world. Nor does a lord’s command excuse him from this crime, since not even servants are pardoned when they render obedience to their masters in matters involving the atrocity of crime. John therefore committed a sacrilegious offence which no penitence can erase while lasting infamy attends him. For he fell into condemned heresy and schism; he was excommunicated for participation in, and association with, the condemned; and thus he is bound by the sentence of the Roman pontiff. It is not clear to me that anyone apart from the Roman pontiff—or without his mandate—can absolve him from that bond.

For the canons have decided that whoever has once stained himself with the contagion of error or schism already condemned is bound by the prince’s sentence of condemnation. Against such a man, [Col. 1446A] not newly promulgated enactments but those already issued against the originator are to be applied: that is, the judge is not to condemn him as though he had not been condemned, but is to pronounce him condemned. Therefore, when the laws declare a man condemned and excommunicated by the nature of his offence, and also decree that he must be deposed, why are you astonishingly angry if I have declared him excommunicated and dared to command that he be avoided as anathematized? You should rather be justly angry with me for silence, though you seem scandalized in me by my observance of the canons.

Beware of John’s leaven, lest—God forbid!—you be defiled through sharing in him. None of us ought to communicate with him, even if, as you slanderously allege, I had excommunicated him in a rash heat of mind. If we may observe the venerable councils, it is plainly ordained that no one should communicate with a person whom even an angry bishop, quickly and harshly provoked, has excommunicated before it is lawfully examined and fully ascertained whether he deserved excommunication. Therefore, much more must you abstain from John, since I have commanded you by lawful authority to avoid him as anathematized.

For, as canonical decree establishes, no one knowingly communicates with an excommunicated person without danger to his own order. Whoever carefully considers these things will see that our brother the Bishop of Salisbury was justly suspended for a time, that John of Oxford was anathematized, [Col. 1446B] and that this was not unreasonably declared.

Therefore, if you put forward the obstacle of an appeal so that I may not, as justice dictates and law commands, proceed against the aforesaid persons—or against you or perhaps your subjects—when they resist insolently and commit public and persistent offences, you yourselves must consider whether an appeal issued in order to prevent judicial force from being exercised against the disobedient and publicly offending ought to be admitted. Certainly, it seems utterly unjust that the artifices of cunning law and a contrived appeal should exclude the punishment of offenders and thereby introduce liberty to offend.

But if by appealing you mean, in the customary manner and under the best law, that I should not unjustly condemn you—as some of our people think that I have rebuked those men unjustly, though a wise man is convinced that the contrary is true—then the appeal has its proper force, and I am ready to hear it. Far be it from me to presume to decree anything against you in contempt of the ordinances of the Fathers. Yet I cannot sufficiently wonder that you have appealed in order that I should not proceed against [Col. 1446D] our lord the king, as the highest justice demands. The due reverence for an appeal publicly made by me has been altogether scorned; it is most manifestly known that he has despoiled me, driven away those to whom I had entrusted the administration of the possessions of the Church of Canterbury and of the poor, taken from my clerics their churches contrary to every law and right, and proscribed old men with younger men, nursing mothers with their infants—not only to us, but, would that it were not so, to almost the whole world.

You do not fail to know, brothers, that he who does not cease to offend against a law is unworthy of its benefit, especially a law whose observance he has despised to another’s loss. For equity approved by the law of nations requires equal laws in comparable cases. No one ought indeed to be angry at suffering in his own person what he judged equitable in another’s. Therefore my lord the king must first observe, and not trample underfoot, ecclesiastical rights; he must cease from injury to the Church of Canterbury, to me, and to mine, if he wishes justly to obtain the remedy of appeal which he invokes—or, if he does not invoke it himself, wishes it to be invoked for him by others.

An appeal made to prevent correction of those who have usurped the goods of churches and of the poor, and consume their usurpations as they please, is unknown to law and to those skilled in law. For the mercy of laws and canons has conferred the benefit of appeal as a remedy not upon invaders of ecclesiastical property and oppressors of others, [Col. 1447B] but upon the oppressed and unjustly burdened. By what law does one who overturns the laws of appeal appeal? By what canon does one who sets his own perverse institutions above canonical ordinances invoke the aid of the canons? By what law does one who makes unjust laws for overthrowing the Church of God and oppressing its ministers seek the remedy of laws? Brothers, what you write—and what I myself repeatedly consider with concern and anxiety—distresses me so greatly that I can scarcely discern fully what is most advantageous for me and for the Church of Canterbury.

## LETTER XVII. LETTER OF THOMAS, EXILED ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, IN REPLY TO THE APPEAL MADE IN WRITING BY THE BISHOPS OF ENGLAND, AND TO CERTAIN OTHER CHARGES BROUGHT AGAINST HIM BY THEM.

THOMAS, by the grace of God, etc.

[Col. 1447C] “The letter of your brotherhood, however, etc.” [See the Letters of St Thomas below, no. 75.]

## LETTER XVIII. LETTER OF HERBERT, AN EXILE, TO WILLIAM, ELECT OF CHARTRES.

When, therefore, I took up the pen to weave with the threads of words the bright and many-coloured garment of epistolary discourse, and thereby to perform the office of mutual charity, suddenly my hand fell, my fingers grew numb, and the pen itself, as though conscious of a grieving mind, became covered with rust. It rebuked and dissuaded me from seeking the formal graces of diction and the charms of words. For I am compelled daily to drink bitter things: when, my dearest friend, can I offer you sweet things?

For Scripture says that music in mourning is an untimely tale; [Col. 1447D] “my harp has been turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of those who weep.” For, not to mention the remaining multitude of exiles, who are punished and compelled to go into exile by the wholly unjust blow dealt by one man—where no sex is spared and no regard is paid to age—the wrath and fury of the king of the English have been confirmed against me more than against others. He has now made me settled in my exile, and while he rules the kingdom has deprived me of all hope of return.

But blessed be the Lord, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who comforts us in all our tribulation. For by this very fact I pronounce myself blessed in accordance with the Gospel saying, since I suffer persecution and am a companion of one who suffers for righteousness. I remember also that every tyrant is the hammer of the heavenly Craftsman and is allowed to do evil only for a short time. Moreover, in this tribulation the Lord has given me help, a sure refuge for my hope: for you alone after God are my refuge from the tribulation which surrounds me. But I pass over these matters quickly and briefly, lest, placed in adversity, I should seem to have sought your help rather than you, in return for our former affection.

Know also, my beloved in Christ, that the judgment about the Romans which we once expressed when we were comforted by mutual and private conversations is true: they “put light for darkness and darkness for light”; their right hand is filled with gifts, and they deem gain godliness; seeking only what is their own, not the things of Jesus Christ—and would that they sought only their own, if only hand and heart restrained themselves from what belongs to others! Brothers, truly, in the prophet’s words, Ephraim is like a dove without a heart; rams that find no pasture have gone away without strength before the face of their pursuer: enough has been said to the wise.

Yet, that I may speak somewhat more openly, those who make themselves the supreme leaders of Christian warfare do not dare at all to go up against the enemy or set themselves as a wall for the house of God. They have already turned their backs and placed the lamp of justice under a bushel, fearing that king of the English more than the Lord of angels. And indeed, unless the narrow limits of time and the restraint proper to the pen prevented me, I would now bring forward so much against them that I would exceed not merely the brief measure but every measure of a letter. Nevertheless, while discussing their inadequacy—or rather their complete malice—I am compelled to end where there is no end.

## LETTER XIX. LETTER OF HERBERT, NOW AN EXILE, TO GREGORY, ABBOT OF MALMESBURY.

[Col. 1448C]

To his beloved abbot of Malmesbury in Christ, his own H., now wretched and exiled, wishes joy with those who rejoice and weeping with those who weep.

That even now a late but long-desired opportunity has enabled me to send you a letter of your charity is all joy to me. The bearer of this letter asked that I give written requests to some of my friends in England. I quickly consented and took up the pen; but when it had scarcely been prepared and the tip of the first letter formed, my hand immediately trembled and my mind hesitated, discouraging me from writing, since there is scarcely one friend in adversity while there are so many in prosperity; and, as that eminent saying at Canterbury has it, “friends, neighbours, and acquaintances have been put far from us because of misery.”

For I know that public report has already conveyed to your ears what has happened in these days: namely, how many and how great reproaches our Canterbury father has endured for righteousness, and I am a companion of his sufferings. Yet, “as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Jesus Christ our consolation also abounds.” Kings and kingdoms sympathize with us; and, I do not doubt, the fellow citizens of that heavenly city also sympathize, since many of them have passed through the same sufferings and miseries. For their voice is in the Psalm: “We passed through fire and water” (Ps. LXV).

Many of these have passed through them: those who, while they still served in the tabernacle of the flesh, ruled the same city of the Saviour—the holy Church of Canterbury, I mean—prudently amid dangers, fought bravely against enemies, and triumphed mightily. And, that what we say may be taught more certainly by examples, among the very many who are “from the land of Egypt” and who governed the aforesaid city amid the dangers of this present life—to recount all their catalogue in succession would exceed the brevity of a letter—it is enough for the moment to call forward three: Dunstan, Ælfheah, and Anselm, whose memory is blessed and whose names are written in the book of life.

Let us therefore join our own endurance of the same sufferings and miseries, in which we still live for a time, [Col. 1449B] with those in which they also lived while still in the flesh. There is no doubt amid how many and how great dangers they ruled this Church, which is the house of God, and for which they resisted even unto blood. Let us lift up our eyes and look upon the three watchmen named above. If the face is not distinguishable, at least the wound is. In the midst stands one whom we know: rosy and ruddy beyond the beloved. A martyr stands, rejoicing and triumphing, with his whole body torn. Unless I am mistaken, this is Ælfheah, whose wounds your words attest, so that in his body there still remain the raw scars of wounds, the sprinkling of blood, and the bruising of blows. He bears the mark of his Emperor and presents to the Father of all what he endured for the city entrusted to him; he is in this very respect an image of his Saviour and a follower of the Crucified One.

And I think that, when the day of the Lord comes, Christ’s fellow-soldiers of this kind will appear with Christ in such bodily form. Then they will see Him whom they pierced: that rosy company of martyrs, the wounded head with the members, the Emperor with His own, that household of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.

But let us now pass over that companion multitude of sheep destined for slaughter. Ælfheah is on our lips: he stood firmer amid the blows of stones in exile than Adam among the trees of delight in Paradise; he was stronger among stones than Adam among fruits. Adam, once he had smelled the scent of the fruit, immediately fell and was overcome. But Ælfheah stood immovable among the stones. How often, I suppose, amid the stones did he pray for those who executed him, that in this also he might show himself to us another Stephen! How often, struck down by the blows or bending his knees, did he beat upon heaven with prayers so pious and so devout! Nor do I doubt that he pierced heaven with prayers sprinkled indeed with blood and tears, praying and repeatedly crying: “Holy Father, I pray not for the world, but for those whom Thou hast given me, for Thy holy city which Thou hast entrusted to me, though unworthy!”

It is beyond doubt that, in the shipwreck of this present life, Dunstan and Anselm likewise prayed the same among their papers. Though they did not drink the cup wholly with Ælfheah, they drank its same most bitter drops. Each of them, having been proscribed, was compelled twice to go into exile; with great difficulty they left the land set in the heart of the sea; and often, when the agitation of princes pressed upon them, they entrusted themselves to an uncertain vessel. [Col. 1450A] They endured the injuries of the sea for righteousness, carrying nothing with them.

I would now devote myself wholly to their praises, were it not that I have no new things to tell one who is ignorant of none of them, and that so great a subject does not permit itself to be confined within the narrowness of a letter. Therefore, that I may comply with the custom of a letter and spare the ears of its readers, I shall add only something concerning the aforesaid watchmen, since I am unwillingly torn from their remembrance amid present distresses.

For we see especially these three watchmen stationed in the holy church of the supreme Trinity, as in the city of the great King, and we hope that they protect it by day and by night—that is, in their life and in their death. Nor ought we to suppose them so inhuman that they should be contemptuous in death of that of which they were rulers and leaders in life. Indeed, it is more credible that they protect it all the more powerfully in death, because their authority has been more fully confirmed after death. For who could doubt that the very Church which, while still strangers and amid dangers, they governed so prudently, for which they fought so bravely among enemies and triumphed over enemies so mightily, they would now, made citizens and members of God’s household, abandon so cruelly or pass by so ungratefully? For her, as good watchmen, they often spent the night in prayer, pouring forth prayers so frequent and devout, often bedewed with secret tears and interrupted with cries of grief—more luminous because more hidden, and purer because more secret.

Finally, their tombs among us are glorious: their bodies are held in honour and their spirits in majesty. I ask, then: will they no longer have pity on us? They remember that they themselves passed through the same sufferings and miseries, and that they entrusted their cause and see to our Canterbury Church. What then? They themselves passed through fire and water, while we sin amid flames and waves; and will they not at least stretch out a hand to their children in danger?

It is not so. All is well with you, city of the Saviour, city of the great King! O our mother, the Church of Canterbury: help shall come to you from heaven and from earth. Those who guard you neither slumber nor sleep. Your guardians are holy angels; your watchmen are the spirits and souls of the righteous. They have come forth from your womb—the very ones from whom you ask help. Your watchmen also are the holy community of the Church of Canterbury and all the sacred congregations in the church of the English, who persist day and night in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, and who frequently spend the night in tears and prayers for the defence of our house—indeed, the house of the Saviour.

Placing our hope in these, we have a celebrated consolation amid evils and are not swallowed up by sorrow. Rather, to confess the truth, my soul rejoices and exults. It certainly rejoices and exults because we have help in our homeland and help on the way; we possess weapons on the right and on the left. “We rejoice,” he says, “and exult, because that heavenly court has among us those who care for us, who protect us by their merits, instruct us by their examples, and strengthen us by their miracles. We rejoice because our angels [Col. 1451A] have gone up to their fellow citizens, to act as ambassadors for the children of captivity, to reconcile to us the hearts of the blessed, and to make known to them the prayers of the wretched.”

Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who through the ministry of so many bishops has visited His people; and now that they have been received into our holy city, they do not cease to console the captive city.

## LETTER XX. LETTER OF HERBERT TO POPE ALEXANDER, WRITTEN IN THE PERSON OF THOMAS, EXILED ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.

To his lord and father A., supreme pontiff by the grace of God, his son T., called bishop of Canterbury, wishes an abundance of strength of spirit.

I count it all joy, beloved Father, that I have been found worthy to share in your tribulations, [Col. 1451B] hoping that, as I have been a companion in suffering, so I shall also be a companion in consolation. For I trust, with Christ Jesus working with us, and I bring back a good hope with us: that, under his leadership, we shall attain the prize—he who set us running—and, at his command under your governance, shall reach the harbour—he who stirred up the storm-wind. For he spoke, and the storm-wind arose, and its waves were lifted up. “They go up to the heavens” (Psalm 106 [Vulgate]). But what then? “Afterwards they go down again into the depths” (ibid.); for they are the waves of the sea. And behold: those who troubled the breeze of ecclesiastical peace have themselves been troubled, and have reeled like a drunken man, and all their wisdom has been swallowed up (ibid.). “He has poured out contempt upon princes, and they have wandered where there is no path, and not in the way.”

For, as the report is widespread and has been conveyed to me in writing, that distinguished [Col. 1451C] schismatic who seeks sole primacy in the world, though many companions in error, has been wonderfully dismayed in spirit. He complains that he has been deceived by the king of the English, whom he calls an unjust and deceitful man, because the king did not stand by him in good faith—especially since he had arranged that, without excuse, eight days after the feast of Saint Michael, the king would come to his conference and cause sixty bishops to swear allegiance to that antipope, Guy of Cremona. But now he alleges as an excuse the war which he has in Wales—the very excuse he had removed. Hence, as they say, the treaty of friendship, known to have been made in Christ’s death, will be entirely dissolved. For scale has been joined to scale, but the breath of life shall not pass [Col. 1451D] between them. For the Lord is he who frustrates the counsels of nations and rejects the designs of princes.

Moreover, letters asserted very confidently that the archbishops of Trier, Magdeburg, and Salzburg, with certain of their suffragans; the son of King Conrad; the Duke of the East, his uncle; Duke Berthold of Zähringen; Duke Welf; Frederick, brother of the lord of Mainz; and very many other supporters, have sworn to make a new emperor unless this man complies with their will concerning the cause of the Church and the liberty of Germany.

Furthermore, that other man, who persecutes my lowliness—or rather, in me, your exalted person—with such stubborn purpose and such grievous assault, is clothed only in confusion and shame, because, despite the abundance of his strength, he cannot prevail against an unarmed, bare-armed [Col. 1452A] and rag-clad people. He is burdened besides by the many failures of his own men, and no less by daily expenses; for among a rude and impoverished people he can find no spoil except the heads of enemies. Thus the encounter is perilous, where the ransom of the body is nothing but the soul; and anxiety is great where every day is awaited together with daily deaths and expenditures.

Three days ago our venerable brother, the archbishop of Rouen, came as envoy to that most Christian king of the Franks, Louis. Urging him privately, by earnest admonition, repeated entreaty, and much persuasion, to make an alliance with the king of the English, he received a public answer, all who were then present having been summoned. The king said that the king of the English [Col. 1452B] was sufficiently bound to him; and he added that henceforth he would never enter into a new treaty of friendship with him unless he first renounced in full whatever he had sworn to the emperor. The king thus mocked the man before all as though the matter were already accomplished, and branded him as readily given to perjury. But the archbishop of Rouen replied that the king of the English had sworn nothing to the emperor against the king of the Franks or the crown of his realm; and so he departed. The king of the Franks himself communicated all this to me.

I have also been informed that the aforesaid brother of Rouen has received letters from the king of England, saying that the king wishes me to return to England, provided that I am willing to submit myself, concerning the accusations he will bring against me, to the judgement of the bishops of the land and of others whom he will summon. Moreover, concerning the customs—indeed, those subversions—which he has reduced to writing, he considers, as he asserts, none of them unjust or contrary to the law of God. Yet if any should prove so, he will commit the matter to examination by certain of our brother bishops, whom he has already selected and named: namely, the archbishop of York, the bishop of London, the bishop of Worcester, the bishop of Hereford; with, from across the sea, the archbishop of Rouen and the bishop of Bayeux added to them. He utterly denies that appeals to you have been forbidden; and, as I have been told, he has already sent those royal letters, together with his own, to your Holiness through the archbishop of Rouen. For certainly this is presumed to have been done with the king’s knowledge and approval.

I have also received word that our brother of London has likewise sent certain letters to Your Blessedness, [Col. 1452D] teaching that, as he says, the king did not at all compel me to leave the land, and that he now rather desires my return, provided that I submit to judgement concerning the charges, as already stated, which he intends to bring against me. Finally, in those letters he also begs that the land not be placed under an interdict.

And therefore now, holy Father, let your discernment be watchful. Every one of these words is a net, “which is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures.” For what is it that, among the aforesaid bishops, he seeks as examiners of unjust laws those who were their authors? Moreover, this is not an inquiry for lesser judges, who have no authority or interpretation regarding ecclesiastical matters; while dispensation has been entrusted to only a few. But in these matters there is your singular judgement. And when he denies that appeals have been prohibited, his tongue indeed speaks in favour of justice, but his hand is very much against it. No one would dare, under the protection of an appeal, to confess in that land the name of your supreme primacy. All alike are dragged before the court, people as well as priest; and Christ is still judged by Pilate.

As to what he states concerning my return, subject to the aforesaid condition: “his eyes look upon the poor man, but he lies in wait like a lion in his den.” He lies in wait indeed to seize the poor man while he draws him in. Therefore let the wisdom of my father keep watch over these snares laid for me, and consider how violent and deceitful is my persecution—where force and fraud are matched, where malice has power for its companion. Hence, knowingly and prudently, I fear being put in fetters, caught in snares, and falling into the pit. I fear to cast myself a second time into the flame. Once I passed through fire and water; a second time it will now be necessary for me, for an uncertain or no advantage, to expose myself to certain dangers—especially since at that assembly I would by no means be allowed to speak the truth with impunity. For the aforesaid truth and obedience to the Apostolic See have already brought upon me such severity that the sons of Ephraim—who bent the bow with me but turned back without me on the day of battle—accuse me of having incurred perjury and diminished the royal majesty. Yet it is quite shameless for a woman remaining at home to reproach a soldier fighting in battle.

As to the lord king’s assertion that he did not compel me to depart, I hope there is no need now, as though anew, to establish the causes [Col. 1453C] of my departure, to plead the grounds of my fears, and to write an apology for my flight. For I do not think, gracious Father, that it has escaped your memory how many and how great perils I endured in the deep, from the time when, at your command, I put out into the deep to let down the nets for a catch: in the shipwreck of my life, so grievous that, leaving my garment behind, I scarcely escaped naked; and finally, after very many labours, I was brought to the bosom of your mercy as to the harbour of my desire. Even if I were silent, the world cries out. Perhaps, as I recall these matters and speak of what the world knows, your merciful fatherhood also compassionates me.

Though I had been reared in the palace as companion and fellow student of emperors, I alone nevertheless undertook the shepherd’s labours; alone I attempted resistance; alone I strove to repel wrongs done to Christ; alone I confessed my father’s name on earth; and therefore I trod the winepress alone. Moreover, I would return on no terms to a people who seek my life, unless immunity for my person had first been guaranteed and full restitution made to me and to those despoiled for my sake of what had been taken from them.

For, I beg, let your discernment recall how great were the losses suffered by the English Church in the time of this king through the expulsions of bishops: first, the expulsion of John, bishop of Worcester, of holy memory; afterwards, that of my venerable brother, your son Henry, bishop of Winchester, who lost more than three thousand marks without any restitution. Thus, even to this day, the ease of pardon provides security for wrongdoing.

But let them do against my lowliness, together with the lord king, whatever God permits them to desire and accomplish: let them imprison, exclude, proscribe. I, certainly, by the grace of God inspiring and pursuing me, have resolved to suffer for the law of my God; nor, through any fear compelling me or any favour offered by them, shall I ever consent in the guilt of those whose companion in punishment I do not wish to be. I have also resolved that it is better to die in exile than to furnish this precedent for plundering the dowry of the widow and the patrimony of the Crucified One.

But you henceforth, holy Father, remember that you are a father, whose office it is always to have mercy and to spare. Do not regard my scourging, for I am a very sinful man. But if the hand of the Lord has touched me and is still stretched out over me, allow me alone to drink the cup of my misery to the dregs. Look upon your sons, who have been so cruelly and inhumanly [Col. 1454B] proscribed and driven out with me without cause. Although they are blessedly miserable, since it is clear that they have not deserved what they endure, their tribulation nevertheless increases my misery. Look therefore, good shepherd, upon the sheep of your pasture. It is yours to seek the sheep wandering and scattered through the mists and pathless places of the wilderness and to bring them back to pasture.

Because you are Christ’s vicar, let the deed prove it. Raise your hand against the arrogances of those who deal wickedly against the sanctuary. Rebuke the beasts of the reeds; scatter the nations that desire wars; break kings in the day of your wrath and judge among the nations. Thus, as you are the Father of mercies, be also the Lord of avengings: a just and mighty judge, terrible, taking away the spirit of princes, terrible among the kings of the earth; so that, as we know you to be Christ’s vicar, you may fulfil Christ’s [Col. 1454C] ministry.

I pray, therefore, and pray again: Vicar of Christ, anointed of the Lord, no longer overlook the wrong done to Christ. But that worn and commonplace saying is now suspicious to me, which flesh and blood have revealed to our wise men: “Wait, wait again” (Isaiah 28); “it is not the time for vengeance but for endurance,” they say, “with so great a multitude of enemies of the Church.” Father, I pray, bear with me a little and endure my speaking these things to so great a majesty, not so much rashly as fearfully. Surely this is strange—indeed monstrous—wisdom: that the sword of the priesthood should then be borne without cause because Christ has many adversaries; as though it were safer, terrified by the multitude of opponents, for Christ’s athletes temporarily to yield, bend the knee, relax their hands, and return the sword to its [Col. 1454D] sheath.

O blind wisdom of the world, all too sluggish and gross, weakening every strength of faith, choking the censure of judgement, and setting the lamp of justice under a bushel! For them the prophet says: “Open, Lord, their eyes, that they may see that those with us are more numerous” (4 Kings 6). I do not deny, however, that one must often yield to the times; that sometimes certain matters must be overlooked and many endured; and that some require dispensation—but this can be done rightly only if justice is preserved.

But, to pass over this exile so dreadful and unheard of in the times of Christian princes, where by striking one man they punish so many and so great persons, and the many other enormities committed in the English Church: how can justice be preserved where Christ is for a second time led bound before the governor, [Col. 1455A] and where Peter is deprived of the office of his apostolate? Clerics everywhere are dragged before secular tribunals; priests do not dare freely exercise the power of binding and loosing.

Come then, man of God: put on the strength of those whose inheritance you hold. Shake yourself, son of those who have been shaken; gird your sword upon your thigh. Dislodge and scatter those who scatter your inheritance, lest so great a power bear the sword without cause—especially now, when Malchus has stretched out his hand against Christ and Belshazzar against the vessels of the temple. For I trust in the Lord that, when he sees the sword coming upon the land as the trumpet sounds, that enemy will turn to flight: he who boasts that, because we have not come up against him, we have turned our backs and cut off the tongues of bulls, as his prophet Merlin, among other things, long ago prophesied concerning him, as he boasts: “And he shall cut off the tongues of bulls.”

Yet now, solely from fear and fear of offending your majesty, he humbles himself with a certain deceit and cunning. For it is characteristic of cunning and deceitful men to feign humility when fear is the cause, or when they wish to obtain something. Of such men Scripture says: “There is one who humbles himself wickedly, and his inward parts are full of deceit” (Ecclesiasticus 19). Therefore, prince of the Christian soldiery, awake. No longer keep your sword sheathed, but draw it—especially since another sword threatens him: not, I mean, the sword of the word, but of iron—so that each sword may thus serve the Church. For “he has provoked thee, O Lord, because he said in his heart, ‘He will not require it’” (Psalm 9); or rather, more truly, “He will not dare,” he says, “to require it.”

But arise, O Lord, in your anger (Psalm 7), and repay abundantly those who act proudly; and, because of my blood, do not any longer overlook the murmur of the whole earth against you. Or if you do not hear the murmur of the earth, hear the cry of blood. For my blood has cried to you from the earth. Act therefore: avenge the blood of your servants—not, I say, of one, but of many. Remember that your day is short; therefore work while it is day, while you are on the way, while you are still in battle. Do not delay vengeance, for it is the time of justice. Do not put away the sword, for it is the time of war. Do not cast aside the hoe, for it is the time of pruning, so that, as a son of the prophets, you may do a prophet’s work: uproot, destroy, scatter, build, and plant, [Col. 1455D] lest otherwise my blood be required of your hands by the judge of all.

I foretell these things to you, and foretell them again, knocking at the door of justice, lest perhaps, if you depart from this light to your kingdom, the heavenly host reproach you because you abandoned your son in the deep, crying to you in such grievous shipwreck, and did not lend a hand to one endangered for your sake. There too the supreme judge of all will ask you why you did not lay down your life for me, who, following his example, have already once laid down mine for you—while he laid down his for me and for you. There too that supreme judge of all will ask why you concealed your justice and truth, or even allowed them for a time to be trampled underfoot, as though he who is both justice and truth were unable to withstand the first and grievous assaults of his adversaries unless he himself were first trampled down.

Unless I am mistaken, there will then be no place for dissimulation in a cause clearly judged by truth, where Truth itself is judge. Dispensation or dissimulation may indeed be useful in other matters, if justice is not violated; otherwise it contains much fear, little strength of faith, and none at all [Col. 1456A] of fortitude. Hence someone says: “Recognize his voice, for it is of your parents.” The word of God is not bound. He would not dispense; he would not dissemble, until he had escaped the confines of prison, until he was released from the chain. Rather, with all boldness he acted in bonds—not merely so that he might not be endangered, but so that justice might not even be delayed.

O how blessed were those times of the apostles, when they did not walk clothed in purple, mitres, or gold; did not glitter with jewels, blossom in silks, or wear crowns of feathers; were not loaded with gold or silver, surrounded by a circle of mitred attendants, or attended by a train of servants. Then, without a veil, they considered themselves naked in this respect: that human beings are born for labour, not honour; for misery, not glory.

Remember, holy Father, this most holy lineage of yours which was from the beginning. Consider the deeds—the deeds of Adrian, Anastasius, and Eugenius, but above all of Peter and Paul, and of the others in their catalogue—from whom all your so noble posterity has sprung. Amid gold-woven fabrics and silks, recognize yourself as the son of the shaken and heir of fishermen. I think that, if these your forefathers were still living with me in the flesh, [Col. 1456C] they would help and lend a hand to their shipwrecked son. Nor have I said these things because I do not hope that you will act likewise, you who claim so noble a lineage through constancy of spirit, strength of faith, and the illustrious inheritance of your conduct. I indeed hope, and do not doubt, that, with you as leader and ruler, the little vessel entrusted to me will be brought into the harbour of my desire, and my storm will be changed into a breeze.

## LETTER XXI. LETTER OF HERBERT, IN EXILE, TO HENRY, BISHOP OF BAYEUX, ON THE OCCASION OF HIS RECENT PROMOTION; IN WHICH LETTER SOME MATTERS ARE TAKEN FROM THE TREATISE OF BERNARD OF CLAIRVAUX COMPOSED AT THE REQUEST OF POPE EUGENIUS.

While writing this—or rather, before I wrote it—I immediately stopped and hesitated; and though I had taken up pen and tablets, [Col. 1456D] before I had written any marks of the present discourse, I hung up my instruments, greatly uncertain in what manner of speech I should now address my lord. For, on the one hand, the brilliant and glorious change of your title, and on the other, the hard and harsh lot of my exile, commanded different and opposite modes of writing . . . [lacuna]

[The exhortations which follow, down to the end of the letter, having no bearing upon the history of Saint Thomas and being worth not a single penny otherwise, I omit.] [lacuna]

## LETTER XXII. LETTER OF B., ABBOT OF SAINT-CRISPIN AT SOISSONS, TO HERBERT.

To his dearest and heart-beloved friend, Master H., [Col. 1457A] Brother B., humble servant of the holy martyrs Crispin and Crispinian of the church, wishes him to choose the way of truth.

“I waited and waited” for the appointed time of your promise, and received nothing. If perhaps, through a failing memory, either the promise or the appointed time of the promise has slipped from your mind, know assuredly that neither has perished from mine. You promised that you would send me, or yourself bring to me, by the fixed date, your synodal addresses and sermons to the people. The date has passed; the promise still languishes below the past date. Allow, therefore, the promise which is shut up with you to come forth from you within its appointed time and to enter to me, to whom it is due, lest you seem further to transgress against truth.

If knowingly or unknowingly you have strayed from the way of truth, [Col. 1457B] you may still return to it. Therefore choose the way of truth without delay, while it is permitted and while you desire it; and do not make wholly void what has proceeded from your lips. And if I grieve that for a time I have been disappointed in my expectation, you may safely entrust to the bearer of this letter that which, once I have received and read it, will entirely expel from my mind the pain of disappointment.

Therefore hasten, excellent master, dearest to me among masters, to satisfy my wishes and prayers, so that you may never seek an occasion to send our bearer back to us empty-handed. Do not delay in offering, on our behalf, your most dutiful greetings to the most excellent and beloved lord archbishop of Canterbury, in whose service I am ready to expend everything of mine, body and soul together. May you fare well—not according to your merit, but as I desire. For merit would take health away from you; but our desire for your welfare will confer it, through Jesus Christ. And I pray that, on his return, the bearer of this letter may make me desire it more ardently by saying: “Master Herbert, your faithful and most truthful friend, sends this to you.” Farewell again. I place myself under your care; and farewell a third time. For you know that a threefold cord is not easily broken. Beware lest you disclose to others what this present little page contains.

## LETTER XXIII. LETTER OF HERBERT, IN EXILE, TO B., ABBOT OF GREAT SAINT-CRISPIN AT SOISSONS.

To the dearest lord and honoured in Christ, B., [Col. 1457D] abbot: H. wishes him salvation in the Lord.

Your gracious letter, when read, gave me pleasure on one side and inspired fear on the other: it accuses me on the one hand, while on the other it flatters me. For, as your letter sounds, you judge that I am rightly to be rebuked as forgetful of my promise; but immediately, as if by the counsel of charity, you grant me indulgence, inviting me to fulfil what was promised. You also seem to accuse me of inconsistency because I did not come at the promised time. But you ought to have remembered that a person’s way is not in his own power, nor is it for a man to walk and direct his steps—especially as I am a man placed under authority, to whom, if it is said, “Go,” I go and obey my lords.

But when I was with you, I hoped that I should return shortly and promised as I believed. Since, therefore, I did not come, did I act inconsistently, so that with me there should be both “yes” and “no”? I judge that, in Your Blessedness’s opinion, not only one who speaks truth, but also one who speaks what is false while believing it true, is free from lying; otherwise the Apostle too must be accused because he did not come to the Corinthians according to his promise. Yet true friendship ought not conceal what it feels. Thus I have accepted your rebuke, thereby showing that you wish to draw me, even unwilling, to come and see you.

I still hope, however, that when I set out for Flanders I shall pass through your place, without delay. Meanwhile receive the pledge of my promise: namely, a few little papers—or only a few—which I send through this bearer, and which you have graciously asked to have prepared by me. Like one who seems, in the city, to have feigned disgust and been sated with costly banquets, you desire the fare of our bread and rustic vegetables; fare by which my poor life is now sustained in the solitude of Pontigny, lest it fail on the way.

Receive these, therefore, not as refreshment for yourself but rather for the crowd reclining at table. Yet if you find in them any fragments that may perhaps seek to revive your spirit, let thanks be returned not to me but to the master of the household, from whose fullness the things distributed have been received. I would have written much more, but a sudden and unexpected departure pressed me, so that I had scarcely time to write even one little night-work. Therefore, if these little letters are scant and unadorned, contrary to the wish of one who loves you, do not be surprised. You know yourself that what is done too hastily or with a distracted mind is not done altogether well. Moreover, remember how few of your books are being repaid to you in these writings, whereas you yourself are wholly occupied with books.

Now above all, I beg that you pour out earnest prayers to the Lord, that the lord of Canterbury and those who share his tribulation may obtain victory in this contest. At the same time I earnestly ask that all the brothers with you be greeted in my name, and that you affectionately urge them to remember our tribulation in their prayers.

## LETTER XXIV. LETTER OF HERBERT TO POPE ALEXANDER, IN THE PERSON OF HENRY, COUNT OF TROYES.

To A., the one and supreme Roman pontiff by the grace of God, his son H., count palatine of Troyes, wishes him to understand what is true [Col. 1458D] and provide for the last things.

Both filial love has urged me to strike at the ears of your clemency in the present circumstances, and a certain general necessity of the Church has compelled me. For the glory of your name, which until these days shone admirably throughout the whole world, has now become a mockery and derision to those around us, and has been turned by many into reproach. For behold, your enemies have made a noise, and those who hate you have lifted up their head: I mean the envoys of the king of the English. Returning from the curia, to the disgrace of the magnificent and wholly praiseworthy archbishop of Canterbury—or rather, to the oppression of holy Church—they boast and spread abroad everywhere that all their petitions have been granted: namely, that you have accepted those notorious customs, or rather [Col. 1459A] subversions of the Church of God, on account of which the lord of Canterbury is known to be in exile; that he is exempt from all episcopal jurisdiction; and that you have honoured the king of the English himself, who by his laws dissolves the privileges of the clergy, with such a privilege that he is exempt from all episcopal jurisdiction—made, above other kings, your special son, though above others he has deserved your wrath and indignation.

They also add that you have suspended all authority of the lord of Canterbury until you send from your side certain cardinals, I know not whom, who, having full jurisdiction, may settle the case pending between the aforesaid archbishop and the king of the English. Among them, too, that most notorious schismatic—whose name, although I do not mention it, is well known because of the enormous perjury committed to diminish your supreme primacy—is raised above the rest in proportion as he has been exalted still higher. For, as he boasts, scarcely had he been absolved when he was immediately restored by your own hand, through a gold ring, to the deanery; and afterwards, what increases the astonishment above all else, you received him, together with his king, as a special son, subject, as he boasts, to no episcopal jurisdiction.

On hearing these things, holy Father, the earth has been moved and shaken. Our king himself is amazed; princes wonder; peoples are angry; and priests are confounded. Yet all sympathize and grieve, both because of the overthrow of the Church which they fear and because of the present desolation of a man beloved by God and men. Though he had been reared in royal houses [Col. 1459C] and enjoyed, as the world knows, such worldly glory and favour, he nevertheless did not refuse to submit his shoulders to the burdens of men, and with high resolve to trample underfoot all the precious things of the world for Christ’s justice.

I too, who both loved and love no small part of your honour and glory, have been greatly saddened and troubled; yet I remain uncertain and doubtful whether, as those talkative men disseminate, the strong rod and glorious staff have been broken, and whether the land from which bread sprang has been so suddenly overthrown by fire. I do not yet wholly assent to what I have heard. Therefore, holy Father, do not despise the counsel of prudence and fidelity offered by your son. Spare your glory; spare your reputation; spare the Church of God; spare Christ’s athlete. Following the example of that illustrious predecessor of yours, be stronger and more powerful in proportion as he is weaker. Arise therefore, Lord, in your anger, and destroy the loud-speaking tongues, so that the labour of their lips may cover them. Otherwise know assuredly—and the time is near—that the princes of the earth will devise an evil plan against your people and plot against your chosen ones.

## LETTER XXV. LETTER OF HERBERT TO POPE A., IN THE PERSON OF MATTHEW, PRECENTOR OF SENS.

To A., the one and supreme pontiff by God’s grace of the holy Apostolic See, his son M., least member of the Church of Sens, wishes in all things submission and fidelity.

Since I have begun once, I shall speak to my lord, though I am dust and ashes. Zealous love on the one hand has prompted this, [Col. 1460A] and pressing necessity on the other compels it. For behold, the sound of a report has come and the earth has been moved; the heart of the king and the hearts of princes have failed; priests are astounded and all hands have been weakened. For it is a widespread report, on every tongue, that amid so many enemies of the Church you turn your hands against your own vitals: that the one unique athlete of Christ in our day has been handed over to Christ’s enemies—your son, I mean, the archbishop of Canterbury. For the glory of your name, as the whole world of Churches proclaims, he spurned the favour of princes, endured shame and reproach, and finally left his home and abandoned his inheritance.

The scandal of these evils is increased because that notorious schismatic, John of Oxford—released by your authority, which rules over all—has so readily obtained restoration to the deanery of Salisbury, as though that public perjury of schism which, as the world knows and cries out, he perpetrated so outrageously in Germany had been accounted to him as righteousness. By its occasion he stirred up that distinguished schismatic who seeks sole primacy in the world, though many companions in error, to the abasement of your glory.

Moreover this John and the other envoys of the king of the English, returning from the curia, have opened their mouths and boast that they have obtained everything against our archbishop of Canterbury—or, to interpret it more truly, for the oppression of God’s Church. In this they, being men of many words, have given many grounds for others to disparage your holy name. And hence confusion covers the whole face of the Church. Fear and trembling have come upon us, because, upon hearing this, the mighty gods of the earth have been greatly lifted up, waiting day by day so that, if the aforesaid athlete of Christ should fail in the stadium, they may receive the prize by humbling your people and intruding themselves into the inheritance of your fathers.

Since, therefore, I have begun once, I shall speak to my lord, though I am dust and ashes. Let not your strength grow weak in tribulation; rather, Lord, cast down and divide their tongues, so that all the earth may know that they have spoken iniquity against the righteous in pride and derision. Let your hand be upon the son of your right hand, and let lying lips be silenced. Otherwise the present turmoil is now so great that I trembled to set it in writing [Col. 1460D] and yet, as one devoted to you and faithful to your Holiness, I ought not wholly to have kept silent. May God grant you, supreme Father, according to your heart, and confirm all your counsel.

## LETTER XXVI. LETTER OF HERBERT TO RAYMOND, CARDINAL DEACON OF THE ROMAN CHURCH, IN THE PERSON OF T., ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.

To his venerable father and dearest brother in Christ, Master Raymond, by God’s grace cardinal deacon of the Roman Church of Saint Mary the Unviolated, T., humble, wretched, and now exiled minister of the Church of Canterbury, sends what little he can now offer.

I, who am compelled daily to drink bitter things, cannot offer sweet things to you, holy Father and brother most dear to me in Christ. Rather, it is the act of a superstitious man to seek glory for himself from the elegance of a carefully polished style amid groans and the filth of tears. And, dear to me in Christ, this is why I have not now wished to boast of the power of my lips: I scarcely remain standing amid present miseries. I have not wished, I say, to exalt myself through eloquence, since the Most High has placed me in darkness, as one dead to the world, because of my sins.

I come, therefore, to you not in the learned words of human wisdom but in the word of the cross, which indeed is foolishness to those who perish; but to those who are saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God. For we are those who preach Christ crucified. “Who, for the joy set before him,” etc. [lacuna] For we have heard the report, and the enemies of the Church sent to the curia boast everywhere that your princes have despised us—or rather, have delivered us into the hand of our enemies—etc. [lacuna] I pray that, concerning our present tribulation and the cause of the Church, you intercede, by prayers and written exhortations sent forth, as you know best, with the Roman pontiff and your fellow brothers, etc. [lacuna]

## LETTER XXVII. LETTER OF HERBERT TO LOUIS, THE MOST CHRISTIAN KING OF THE FRANKS, IN THE PERSON OF T., ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.

To L., most Christian and illustrious king of the Franks, T., humble and wretched minister of the Church of Canterbury, now an illustrious exile, wishes an unfading crown of life.

Glory to God in the highest, who in these days has established so strong and hewn a pillar in his house, and who, amid the dark storms of his shipwrecked Church, has made a great light in the firmament of heaven, etc. [lacuna] among other things, because you remember us in exile in the solitude of Pontigny, etc. [lacuna]

## LETTER XXVIII. LETTER OF HERBERT TO WALDEMAR, KING OF THE DANES, IN THE PERSON OF THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.

To the noble and illustrious Waldemar, by God’s grace king of the Danes, T., by the same grace archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, wishes him so to enjoy temporal goods that he may deserve eternal ones.

From the reports of others we have learned that your glory has been informed how great are the evils which the King of the English has inflicted upon us and ours since God called us to the dignity of the pontificate [Col. 1461D]—by anger and harshness wholly unworthy of a king, employing the worst advisers. Nor does he yet cease to persecute us; but blessed be God, for he has not as much power to harm as he has eagerness to do so. Yet He in whose hand are the hearts of kings has turned Louis, the Christian King of the Franks, and the princes and magnates of his realm, so that they show us every honour and the highest reverence. But since the greatness of your name and the royal justice with which the King of kings has adorned you have become known to us by widespread report, we wish that, by our own command, our persecution may likewise become known to your Excellence, so that we may find greater favour in your eyes. And if [Col. 1462A] God perhaps so decrees, strengthened by the protection of your counsel and assistance against our enemies, may we deserve to become sharers in your prosperity and peace in Christ, for whose glory we now endure reproaches and every offence. For, though I say nothing, the world knows well enough how faithfully and magnificently we served the aforesaid King of the English before our promotion, while we were still engaged in worldly service. Therefore, illustrious King, we beg your Excellence to make your good pleasure known to us; and graciously to lend the ears of your mercy to the matters which we have not written here but make known through our venerable brother, and to give them full credence as though spoken by ourselves. May He who gives salvation to kings preserve and exalt you.

## LETTER XXIX. HERBERT’S LETTER TO WILLIAM, ABBOT OF VEZELAY, SEEKING ADVICE CONCERNING CERTAIN APPREHENDED HERETICS COMMONLY CALLED DAGENEIS OR DEONAS

[Col. 1462B]

We have gratefully received the letter of your charity. Now concerning the matters on which you seek advice: would that there were as much discernment available for giving kindly counsel to a dearest brother as there is charity! Your pious kindness has referred to us what is to be done with those heretics called *Deonas* among you, who have been apprehended and even publicly convicted. Consulting divine law, we have not been able to find any penalty expressly laid down in written law for heretics of this kind. For these offspring of the hostile power [Col. 1462C] have lately sprung up: among angels they rend Christ to pieces, and they infect, by hidden corruption, those whom they can; for theirs is a business that walks in darkness. Yet, because the body of this whole head, though it has different faces, does not differ in its hind parts, but, with the consuming fire which all alike drag by their tails, burns the harvests of foreigners: therefore, where their vanity is one, their punishment will not differ. For a common fellowship inseparably joins like guilt to like punishment. Accordingly, by legal consequence, since an ordinary and canonical penalty has been promulgated against others, a like rigour of law must be applied against these as well.

Pope Liberius, speaking without distinction concerning the penalty of heretics, says: “Those who act against the peace of the Church, etc.: if they possess rank or a military belt, let them be stripped of these; but if they are private persons—if indeed they are nobles, let them suffer confiscation of their property; but if they are of low condition, [Col. 1462D] let them not only be beaten bodily, but be punished with perpetual exile.” There are also many other legal bonds by which such frenzied beasts are restrained, lest they harm land and sea, lest they slip away, being checked by losses of property and exiles. But it is exceedingly difficult to hold a slippery dragon on a hook so that it cannot escape.

Therefore these men concerning whom you have inquired, angular puffers-away of truth, troubling with their hissing and stings the peace of the very body, perhaps expose—or have already exposed—the rest of the body to cutting and injury for the sake of protecting the head alone, through confiscation of property. They reckon this no loss; indeed, because of it they rejoice, if not with apostolic joy, at least after the manner of the apostles [Col. 1463A], in that part alone of themselves which is free from danger, namely that which contains within it their venomous tongues. By what bonds, then, are they to be bound? How are these serpents to be crushed, lest by their pestilential breath they infect the temperate air of our faith? What does the law provide? They are naked and cannot be stripped; moreover, the Church has no prison of exile. Rather, this whole world is the prison of Christ’s body, still in exile; the islands of exile belong to Augustus, not to the Crucified One. Further, if we sought the sentence of the old law, the question would have no legal difficulty: for they fall by the edge of the sword. Likewise, if Roman law be added, the matter would be readily settled, for the final penalty follows.

But we, who have cast away the old things because new ones have come, and who have a new King and a new law, are forbidden to gather the tares [Col. 1463B] lest we root up the wheat with them. Against these new serpents we shall direct certain new stings of law. For those who dispense the sacraments of the death of the gentle and meek Lord may not exercise judgment of blood, nor may they inflict, or command to be inflicted, mutilations of limbs upon any persons—especially since the spiritual punishment of the new law, of which we are ministers, has succeeded the bodily penalty of the old law. Except that a certain slight bodily restraint has been entrusted to us, so slight that it cannot be called vengeance for an offence but the discipline of a teacher: that is, correction of the body by beatings alone, with the infliction of bodily death or the mutilation of any limb excluded.

Therefore, since these men have nothing besides themselves, perhaps, upon which they can be punished, it remains that, as infamous persons, they be assigned to [Col. 1463C] public beatings. But because you allege that you possess secular jurisdiction in your town, I do not think you would overturn the order of law if you handed the aforementioned men over to your defender—not, I say, so that he may punish them bodily, but so that he may have them heard before himself and impose an end to the case consistent with his human laws. Yet above all, it seems to me more advisable that they be sent under suitable guard to the most clement prince, namely the most Christian King of the Franks, especially if they persist incorrigibly in their error. For he is by right the supreme and principal defender and guardian of the common law of all the churches of the realm, as I recall you do not deny.

And lest I seem to be advancing this from my own resources, let us hear [Col. 1463D] what Pope Pelagius wrote to Narses the patrician. “Do not hesitate,” he says, “to repress men of this kind by princely authority, because the Rules of the Fathers have specially established that, if any person of ecclesiastical office resists one to whom he is subject, or gathers people apart, or sets up another altar, or causes schism, he is to be excommunicated and condemned. And if he should also despise this and persist in making divisions and schisms, let him be suppressed by the public authorities.” Behold the words of our father Pelagius, of holy memory. Therefore, if ecclesiastical persons persisting incorrigibly in error ought to be suppressed by public powers, they ought certainly also to be deprived. May the Angel of great counsel be with you, that you may understand what is right and carry it out in deed.

## LETTER XXX. HERBERT’S LETTER TO BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF EXETER

[Col. 1464A]

To his beloved and loving master and father, the Bishop of Exeter: his own H., now wretched and exiled, sends the little that he is now able to send.

I who am daily compelled to drink bitter things cannot offer sweet things to you, holy Father. It is rather the part of a superstitious man, amid wailings and the filth of tears, to wish to gain glory for himself from an elaborate style of speech. Therefore, at present I have not wished to boast of the power of my lips, I who can scarcely stand amid my present miseries; I have not wished, I say, to exalt myself through eloquence, I whom the Most High has placed in darkness, like one dead to the world, because of my misdeeds. But, without the artificial colouring of eloquence, I set forth my mind to your Holiness in very few words [Col. 1464B].

Yet I hesitate and am uncertain; for, as the world cries out and events attest, the urn, that is, of our adverse lot has cast down all those who stood at our right hand. We look to the right and see, but recognize no one. Yet, not unmindful of former charity, which is not usually destroyed either by the old age of time or the slipperiness of fortune, I have been encouraged and confirmed.

The bearer of this letter is a worthy and discreet young man, very dear and acceptable both to my lord the archbishop and to me. Coming to us from England, he urged me to write on his behalf to some friend of mine in England. When I repeatedly told this insistent man that I had no friend in that land of forgetfulness, he nevertheless hoped otherwise [Col. 1464C]; at last, remembering you, he earnestly begged that I write to you for him. Taking pity on him, in the hope that God may someday take pity on us, I offer your Holiness such prayers as I presently dare and am able to make: that, out of regard for pity and at my intercession, you retain him in your service at least for a short time; or, if this in no way pleases you, that you commend him warmly and diligently to one of your friends. Your discernment will certainly recognize that he is a serviceable attendant and exceedingly fit for the service of some worthy man. Unless you provide for him, he will return to us; nor would he be burdensome to our poverty, except that he is drawn by the sweetness of his native soil. The bearer can fully inform you about what is being done around us. [Col. 1464D] For I judged it safer to communicate such matters secretly by word of mouth than to commit them to writing, which, whoever reads it, exposes whatever it contains openly to the eyes.

## LETTER XXXI. HERBERT’S LETTER TO BALDWIN, ARCHDEACON OF EXETER

To his beloved in Christ and, as I hope, loving fellow-idler, Master B., Archdeacon of Exeter: his own H., now wretched and exiled, sends the little that he is now able to send.

Dearest to me in Christ, I come to you not in loftiness of speech or in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the word of the cross, which indeed is foolishness to those who perish, but to those who are being saved—[Col. 1465A] that is, to us—it is the power of God. For we are those who preach Christ crucified; who, for the joy set before us, endure the cross, despising shame; who prefer to be afflicted with the people of God rather than to enjoy the pleasure of temporal sin. Hence an unadorned discourse, without any elegance or ceremonial turns of phrase, reveals the hard lot of its writer. For it is quite unfitting, amid the belchings and sobs of weeping, to frolic in festive rhetorical clauses and ornamental divisions of speech.

But amid the abundant riches of your secular and sacred learning, receive in this slender guise your friend coming from afar: truly a man of sorrows, who has neither beauty nor comeliness. Yet I write these things not to grieve you, but lest, in these days of cloud and darkness, the shadow of forgetfulness [Col. 1465B] cover me. For we have become like a lost vessel and have been given over to oblivion, like dead men out of mind.

## LETTER XXXII. HERBERT’S LETTER TO POPE ALEXANDER, IN THE PERSON OF A., BISHOP OF SENLIS

To ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, A., called Bishop of Senlis, sends greeting in Christ and due obedience to his father.

Although, holy Father, the care of all Churches has been entrusted to you, the children of that Church especially deserve consolation and the help of your protection from you when they do not fear to go up against opposition and freely resist earthly powers, lest they usurp what belongs to the Church. Therefore [Col. 1465C] I, the least of bishops, for your son and our brother T., Archbishop of Canterbury—a man, as is known, religious and faithful to our mother the holy Roman Church—offer to your Holiness as many entreaties as I dare and am able, etc., etc., etc. [lacuna]

[The remainder of this letter I find expressed in Letters 24 and 25, not in the same words but to the same effect.]

## LETTER XXXIII. HERBERT’S LETTER, IN THE PERSON OF WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS, TO POPE ALEXANDER AGAINST THE MURDERERS OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY AND MARTYR

While writing these things—indeed, even before [writing them]—etc.

[See the Letters of St Thomas.]

## LETTER XXXIV. HERBERT, IN EXILE AFTER THE MARTYRDOM OF SAINT THOMAS, TO POPE ALEXANDER, COMPLAINING THAT, WHILE HIS LORD WAS IN GLORY AND HIS COMPANIONS IN PEACE, HE ALONE REMAINED IN THE STRUGGLE

[Col. 1465D]

That my littleness intrudes itself upon the eyes of so great a Majesty no less boldly than irreverently, I beg you, Father, do not attribute to presumption, because oppression drives me to it. Shame indeed protests, and reverence protests; but sorrow prevails. Its force often neither waits for judgment, nor restrains itself by counsel, nor is checked by shame, nor submits to reason. Suffering this force, therefore, Lord, I cry out to you.

For behold, that Robert, a hunter before the Lord, who hunted his own father to death and was fattened by his blood, [Col. 1466A] still spreads his net to gather even the remnant of his slain father and incorporate it into himself. Those who bore so courageously—as the world knows—the burdens in exile of that mighty athlete, first an exile and now a martyr, he now seeks to kill in spirit, perhaps later to kill in flesh. For those unwilling to be considered enemies he compels to take oaths—whether lawful oaths, you will judge. The form of the oath is this: “For I swear to the lord King of the English, both father and son, that I shall keep his peace; that he shall suffer no loss of his royal rights through me; and that I shall not depart from his land without his permission, nor send letters beyond the sea.” And, to omit the rest, even the slowest understand what he wishes to comprehend under the name of royal rights [Col. 1466B] in this oath.

He has already compelled many of our people to take such an oath: namely Master John of Salisbury, Lord Gunther, and others. But if those who have so sworn appear in any respect to have transgressed against your Highness, they surely have no slight excuse for their sin, being enclosed amid the most cruel hands and in the heart of the sea. Yet the judgment concerning my own littleness would certainly be very different if—God forbid!—led by my own choice I should undertake to swear in this way. Especially since, on the day immediately before the martyr’s death, when we dared suspect nothing so dreadful, I left the land, at the will and command of the martyr of God himself, together with our beloved companion Master Alexander. And thus the Lord, whose eyes always look upon [Col. 1466C] faithfulness, favouring me, preserved me by his grace uncontaminated by this affair, and did not allow the glory of my exile to be stained by the blot of disgrace.

But why do I name the glory of exile, I who was not worthy to see the palm of martyrdom? Rather, he trod the winepress alone, and among the peoples there was none with him. Hence, as often as I set his exile before the eyes of my mind, so often I lament my own exile. I fear, indeed, that I laboured with that mighty athlete in his trials in vain; I do not say that I persevered, since I was denied the privilege of being present at the consummation. Thus I now suffer a double burning of tribulation: I mourn that I departed; I mourn that he died.

Yet in my departure I see that the Lord mercifully provided for my weakness, because amid so great a terror of evils I might perhaps have fled and hidden myself from him. [Col. 1466D] But not even thus do I receive consolation; rather I groan like one without help. For behold: leaning on the staff of my weakness, I ran as best I could; with that strong Issachar I bore burdens according to my strength; and with another Jerubbaal I repelled, as it was granted me, the common perils of Israel. But one swifter and stronger went before and has already seized the prize. I, however, now gradually fail in the race, deprived as I am of the staff of my weakness. I groan beneath the burden when his shoulders have been withdrawn—he who bore everything wholly, and who was everything to me.

Holy Father, I beg that so great a Majesty not be angered if I set forth my affliction a little before it. I am ashamed of the presumption [Col. 1467A] by which I seem to aspire to lofty things and perhaps to dare more than is fitting. I dare, indeed, mindful of mercy and forgetful of majesty. Moreover, the force of grief draws out my spirit, and against my will extracts in turn now threads of words, now of tears. For the fire and flame which burns my sad breast within and feeds upon my innermost parts must necessarily come forth.
