It must indeed come forth before the eyes of so merciful a father, who, knowing how unjust my grief is, may judge my lament more humanely and console it more sweetly. Perhaps he will remember his son, my lord, and will be greatly moved to pity me—especially now, when that true martyr of Christ triumphs so gloriously after the struggle, while in me they still afflict him himself, etc., etc.

Therefore, most merciful Father, I beg—by letters and by tears—and I entreat so great a [Col. 1467B] Majesty, not so much rashly as timidly, not to disdain to tell me what is permitted or expedient for my littleness, lest, if I should perhaps remain in exile longer, this be imputed rather to error than prudence, and rather to pride than justice, etc. You must also, if it please you, write to the Lord of Sens concerning this very matter, adding thanksgivings; for the inward compassion of his charity has been opened to me through the wounds of your son, etc. [lacuna]

In accordance with which, to one of the brothers of Pontigny, as is confidently believed a monk both in feeling and habit, he appeared clothed in red and carrying his cross; and when asked how he was, he replied: “Tell my brothers that I have conquered the world,” and then showed him the scars of his wounds, etc.

[There follow a few matters concerning the miraculous power [Col. 1467C] of St Thomas, of no use.]

## LETTER XXXV. HERBERT, IN EXILE AFTER THE MARTYRDOM OF SAINT THOMAS, TO JOHN OF SALISBURY

Whenever even a small sheet bearing your letters reaches me, it is to me in this time of tribulation like a cloud in time of drought. For amid the heat of this present oppression, your correspondence affords me great refreshment: there I behold you, absent in body but most present in spirit, etc., etc., etc. Nor, as you write, should my absence be attributed to my own will, as the archdeacon of Canterbury asserts, so that henceforth I ought no longer to be regarded as an exile. [Col. 1467D] His assertion, certainly, does not arise, I think, from the slander of ill will, but, as I know with complete certainty, from ignorance of the truth. For the cause of my exile is just; and even if it had not been just in itself, it has been justified by the supervening command of a higher authority. I write this briefly, not setting forth everything so much as showing from a little how much I leave unsaid. For I judge this still expedient, especially since a wise man infers much from a few things.

## LETTER XXXVI. HERBERT, AFTER THE MARTYRDOM OF SAINT THOMAS, TO A CERTAIN COMPANION OF HIS, GUNTHER

Glory to God in the highest: by his unspeakable gift your incredible sorrow has been turned into the joy of the whole world, so that even the authors of persecution [Col. 1468A] share in our consolation. For the Lord has opened his hand and filled every living creature with abundance, drawing and attracting all persons by the sweet and life-giving fragrance of one wounded and sleeping in the tomb. Hence we now experience visibly and immediately the truth of that saying: “What is foolish in God is wiser than men,” and “Every man has become foolish through knowledge.” But it is unnecessary to dwell on these things, which you more faithfully—and, etc., etc. [lacuna]

## LETTER XXXVII. LETTER IN THE PERSON OF WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP [OF SENS], TO THE ABBOT OF VEZELAY

WILLIAM, by the grace of God Archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother G., Abbot of Vezelay, and to his beloved sons, the convent of the same place: greeting and the glory [Col. 1468B] which the Lord will give.

We who have placed tender shoulders beneath the burdens of men can provide more fittingly for the pastoral burden in no way better than by establishing in the Church such persons as may shine in learning and honourable conduct, and whose virtues may seem to contribute more to that Church than they themselves have grown through the benefit conferred. For then, beyond doubt, the house of the Lord is adorned, when in its ordering zeal for God according to knowledge is kindled by him who presides: when not flesh, blood, or that notorious threefold acceptance of gifts, nor nobility of birth, but personal merits are weighed.

Accordingly, with the Lord’s inspiration, considering the case of the person alone [Col. 1468C] and commending the learning and life of your beloved son and our brother, Lord G., prior of Vilmustir, we have decreed that he be set over, as abbot and father, the monastery of Saint Columba the Elder—God, as we believe, revealing this, and the unanimous wishes of all the brothers of that place concurring. And that we may be bound by this petition, so holy and so consonant with the rule and form of the sacred canons, we ask and exhort you, lord abbot, in the Lord, to send him to us with all speed, released and free from every bond of profession and obedience by which he is bound to you. Thus, with the son emancipated and transformed into the father of many peoples, he may inherit the blessing by the right of the firstborn. Thus he will give glory to his father and heap grace upon grace for his fellow brothers.

## LETTER XXXVIII. HERBERT, IN EXILE AFTER THE MARTYRDOM OF SAINT THOMAS, TO JOHN, BISHOP OF POITIERS

[Col. 1468D]

We all know what we have all seen: that true charity is not abandoned in adversity. The truth of this saying has been visibly and tangibly proved in you. Recalling this frequently amid my adversities, I often wished still to restrain my pen, but I was unable to do so any longer. Thus, in some manner against my own will and protest, it has traced these gloomy paths of ink and the renowned furrows of the present little letter. For I feared to intrude upon you amid your many occupations. Yet charity persuaded me to break silence now, while the necessity of my present [Col. 1469A] weakness compelled me. For I think you pity me now with so much greater affection as he for whom I still suffer is loved more. And my wound is the more cruel. To see q., etc., etc., etc. [lacuna] That mighty athlete, etc. [lacuna] appeared to me in a vision and strengthened me, with a consolation more complete than can be expressed. Many other things also are frequently reported; if you too knew them, they would afford both joy and wonder, etc. [lacuna] Even men who are friendly to me send repeated messages, write, and advise that I return. Foolishly, they add, I behave as an exile when the king’s peace and the ashes of my homeland are offered to me [lacuna].

If you please, let your living spoken exhortation make the lord cardinals [Col. 1469B], whom I hope are very kindly disposed toward me, still more kindly disposed.

A certain servant, a native of Kent, recently came to us. He had lived for some time in my lord’s household: truly a man of sin, a dwelling-place of every lie and deceit. This year he has travelled throughout all France and scattered everywhere a substantial portion of the blood of our glorious martyr, as well as a cap in which our man suffered, claiming to possess them, wishing thereby to gain people’s favour and money for himself. The bearer of this letter will tell you his name, if he should come to you, for he said that he intended to do so. Receive such a man as he is; and because I know you to be very kindly disposed toward our people, I wish you to be forewarned and to beware of his leaven. If you please, warn the lord cardinals also about this. For I know [Col. 1469C] that he will approach them with a purse full of falsehoods.

## LETTER XXXIX. HERBERT, IN EXILE AFTER THE MARTYRDOM OF SAINT THOMAS, TO THE TWO CARDINALS ALBERT AND THEODWIN, SENT TO HEAL THE WOUND OF SO GREAT A CHURCH, WHEN THE KING OF THE ENGLISH HAD GONE TO IRELAND, REMOVING HIMSELF, AS WAS SAID

First I write what, hiding day and night in my little chamber [Col. 1469D], I pray and desire more abundantly: namely, that the Church may derive great and lasting benefit from the long duration of its expectation of you. Yet, as it appears, he does not desire this—the man who is said to have fled to the ends of the world from the face of the Church, thus wishing, as the result still shows, to frustrate your holy purpose and prolong the oppression of the suffering Church. I do not know, however, whether, fleeing God’s face in this way, he has wholly escaped God’s hand, for he is said there to be subject to various and repeated distresses, etc. [lacuna]

People chatter in streets and squares that your kinsmen proceed deceitfully with you and weave many plots behind your back, seeking, with rivalry and envy alike, utterly to extinguish the Church’s cause which you have undertaken to foster, so that the business may perish in your hands, etc. [lacuna] Therefore, as they say, in order to make you more hateful in these regions and more contemptible in the territories of your legation, that northern Satan was released by the forces of his counsel [Col. 1470A]. Consequently, the horns of all the Church’s enemies have certainly been greatly exalted, and especially in the case of that one-horned man of ours every fear of penance has, I do not doubt, vanished. For who would fear to be held in chains or bound when that man has been loosed from chains? This, certainly, is why the heart of our holy king, as he secretly testified to me, has utterly failed him, as he says, toward the Roman pontiff. This is why priests are astonished, princes dismayed, and all hands are weakened. And this is certainly why you are less loved among us and, I think, less feared in the regions of your legation. Yet by what means and through whom this was done, I think that you, holy Fathers, know far more truly in your prudence than I. But one thing I know, and do not wish to conceal from you.

A certain man, recently returning from the curia [Col. 1470B], formerly familiar to me, of good reputation and also learned, told me among other things that he had received from that very notorious sacrilegious parricide, William de Tracy—who, it is said, set out for the lord pope this year, ostensibly for the sake of penance—the most secret words of an embassy, intended only for the lord King of England. I, anxious to investigate these matters, turned and returned many secrets in my mind, as is the custom of those who probe mysteries. At last I inferred that the message conveyed to that detestable king was that under no circumstances should he comply with your commands to the detriment of his honour or even his disposition; it was represented that the lord pope and all the cardinals were highly favourable to the king, beyond what could be believed. As a token, it was added [Col. 1470C] that in a town of Normandy called Argentan, in the royal residence, the king had placed a cap upon his head. The man who spoke with me also added that this instruction had come from some of our brothers, who, as many now loudly proclaim, did not wish the Church’s cause, as we have already mentioned, to prosper in your hands. That notorious sacrilegious man further exerted himself as much as he could to excuse the king concerning that infamous deed committed at his command. Hence many think he was deliberately sent and suborned to come to the curia.

Therefore see, holy and discerning Fathers, see how cautiously you walk, understanding that the time is most evil: for every brother, supplanting, will supplant his brother, and every friend will proceed deceitfully. For [Col. 1470D] from the least to the greatest all pursue greed, and from prophet to priest all practise deceit. Thus they heal the wound of the Church to its shame, making alive souls that do not live and putting to death souls that do not die. But I, placed in darkness like one dead to the world and fulfilling in myself what is lacking of the sufferings of my lord Christ’s martyr, at the close of my letter pray and desire that you may abound in the spirit of counsel and knowledge in all things, and that, when you have received an opportunity, you will remember my distress. I want your prudence to know that I have recently heard a report from the lord by whose command I am bound, so that I cannot return even if I wish it; and the same was recently enjoined upon my beloved companion Gunther, who has returned, that he should communicate it to your Holiness.

## LETTER XL. PETITION OF HERBERT, IN EXILE AFTER THE MARTYRDOM OF HIS LORD SAINT THOMAS, TO POPE ALEXANDER, REQUESTING THAT THE FEAST OF THAT HOLY MARTYR BE ORDERED TO BE CELEBRATED THROUGHOUT THE WHOLE WORLD OF THE CHURCHES; PROVING THAT MARTYRDOM SHOULD BY NO MEANS BE HELD TO REQUIRE CANONIZATION BY THE ROMAN PONTIFF, BUT THAT GLORY SHOULD AT ONCE FOLLOW THE MARTYR’S PALM, WITHOUT AWAITING ANY COMMAND

[Col. 1471A]

I, Herbert, servant of your Holiness and prisoner of Jesus Christ, throw myself at the feet of so great a Majesty with all the knees of my mind, praying, etc. [lacuna]

Especially since certain persons who have already returned from your side have given varied testimony to your good pleasure concerning me. Other matters, not inserted in this present writing, which I judged necessary to communicate to your Holiness through the Lord-elect of Meaux, all the more conveniently because more secretly, etc., etc. [lacuna]

## LETTER XLI. POPE ALEXANDER’S CONSOLATORY LETTER TO HERBERT, IN EXILE AFTER THE MARTYRDOM OF HIS LORD SAINT THOMAS

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Master HERBERT: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the letter of your devotion with fatherly kindness; and, understanding the anxieties and distresses, troubles and oppressions, which you bear with equanimity, we sympathize with you in sincere affection of heart as with a devout and special son of the Church, and gladly impart whatever [Col. 1471C] consolation of welcome comfort we can. Indeed, we regard as welcome and acceptable the fact that you clung with so steadfast a spirit to Thomas, of holy memory, formerly Archbishop of Canterbury, that you refused to abandon him in the exile of his persecution, and that you now steadfastly observe his memory in word and deed. We duly commend the constancy of your devotion in this matter with worthy praises in the Lord. We hold the firm purpose and will to love you, as an honourable and learned man, with a closer charity, and to consider with watchful care and concern your advancement and benefit.

Therefore, being exceedingly watchful and concerned for your condition, we have firmly commanded our beloved sons Albert, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and Theodwin, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Vitalis, legates of the Apostolic See [Col. 1471D], to obtain for you and the other clerics and laymen of the aforesaid archbishop the favour and peace of the King of the English, and to have us restored to the land and enabled to remain there safely. But if, in accordance with our desire, they cannot prevail with the aforesaid king and secure for you his peace and favour, it will be for you to tell us how we may attend more suitably to your provision and in what way we may honourably and beneficially provide for you. For we desire gladly to attend to your needs and, as to a special and devoted son of the Church, will, with the Lord’s help, take care effectively to provide for you in whatever is fitting for us and we judge expedient. Therefore take strength in the Lord, and place your hope and trust [Col. 1472A] in him, who does not abandon those who hope in him, but after the storm makes calm and grants an outcome with temptation.

Given at Tusculum, 8 Kalends of July [24 June].

## LETTER XLII. HERBERT, IN EXILE AFTER THE MARTYRDOM OF SAINT THOMAS, TO HUGH, BISHOP OF DURHAM

To his venerable father and most beloved lord in Christ, H., by God’s grace Bishop of Durham: his own Herbert, still a wretched exile, sends the little that he is now able to send.

Learning that the bearer of this letter was to travel as far as you, I judged it necessary to bring the memory of my littleness before your Excellence by this slight message of a little letter, lest the word of forgetfulness cover me in these days of cloud and darkness, placed in obscurity [Col. 1472B] like one dead to the world and fulfilling in myself what is lacking of the sufferings of the glorious martyr of Christ. This is especially so since I know that you, more than others, have grieved for our so prolonged affliction; and we are still certain that, just as you rejoice in the glory of our martyr, so you sympathize with his bonds. For he is still bound—truly bound—since the Church has not yet escaped the yoke of bondage even through the blood shed for her, nor has obtained any reward of redeemed liberty.

How, then, may she now rightly and boldly proclaim the glory of her new redeemer amid oppressions and sighs, singing hymns and weeping at once? The seats remain empty which the fathers [Col. 1472C] preceding us, translated from the world, have left vacant, while Belshazzar misuses all the vessels of the temple. In my own case also—I who speak, or rather, a member of this body—the more pitiably because apparently the more innocently afflicted and still proscribed, if we weigh the testimony of Scripture and the affection of a loving Father, etc., etc.

## LETTER XLIII. LETTER OF THE CARDINALS SENT FROM THE POPE’S SIDE TO THE KING OF ENGLAND, CONTAINING THE TERMS OF PEACE CONCLUDED BETWEEN THE CHURCH AND HIM AFTER THE DEATH OF SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY AND MARTYR

To HENRY, by God’s grace illustrious King of the English, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou: ALBERT, by divine favour cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and THEODWIN, [Col. 1472D] cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Vitalis, legates of the Apostolic See, greeting in him who gives salvation to kings.

Lest there be doubt, etc.

[This letter is printed among the Letters of Gilbert Foliot, no. 385; but it has appended at its end these few words which follow.]

You certainly swore this before a multitude of persons, out of reverence for the divine majesty. Your son also swore, excepting that which particularly concerned your own person. And you both swore that, from Lord Pope Alexander and his Catholic successors [lacuna].

[After the half-word *cath*, at the bottom of the page, a leaf appears to have been lost; for what follows, and forms the end of the letter, does not at all cohere with the foregoing [Col. 1473A].] [lacuna] that you would be willing to furnish us as quickly as possible; for by it you could undoubtedly free us from the repeated anxieties of our adversity. Witness myself at Tours, on the twenty-third day of July.

## LETTER XLIV. A REPLY TO THE SAME PERSON

To his lord, from his own man. My lowliness received Your Highness’s letter with the devotion due to it. On examining and reading it, my soul was made glad by its receipt, but was immediately troubled by what I had read. For you write that you cannot but wonder that, “in our persecutions, you have not received letters of our consolation,” after you last wrote to me, “which might soften the severity of our fortune.” Thus I saw it written [Col. 1473B], read it, and read it again. And precisely on that account I was more and more disturbed within myself, suspecting and fearing that no letters at all sent in the name of my lowliness had reached Your Blessedness—especially since in neither Your Condescension’s earlier nor later letters had you made any mention of receiving mine. This is indeed necessary because of the negligence of letter-carriers, who readily undertake the duty of delivery, but with the same frivolity, turning their heel, make light of it.

I know—I certainly know—that I have anticipated every letter of Your Condescension with a letter in return, unless perhaps a messenger’s carelessness intervened; and that, as was right, I greeted you before I had yet been greeted. And I wrote to Your Holiness in this form and in these words:

> To his lord, from his own man. While writing this—or rather, before I began to write—I immediately stopped and hesitated, very uncertain by what manner of address I should speak to your fatherhood. But if I knew the condition of your inner man, neither would the mind of one hesitating be tossed about, nor would the pen of one writing go astray.

And so forth, as is contained in that same letter. If such a letter has come into Your Holiness’s hands, I rejoice. But if not, this must be ascribed not to my delay or negligence, but to the fault of the messenger; and I call to account for suppression—or rather, for suffocation—of it the messenger of my most dear treasure, devoted to your service, Geoffrey by name. And what we touched upon above concerning the omission of any mention of letters sent across long distances by land and sea requires henceforth correction more than rebuke, because of the carelessness of messengers [Col. 1473D].

So much, then, on these matters. And now I must reply to Your Blessedness’s letter. In it there is an expression which I particularly noticed while reading, at which I particularly paused and hesitated. For I found inserted in it both the word “persecution” and “the severity of your fortune,” etc., etc. [lacuna] [Col. 1474A] [lacuna] as though Your Fatherhood’s letter were instilling into my ear, I know not how, a certain sweet whisper:

> Write nothing back to me; nevertheless, come yourself.

For this I give thanks, and again give thanks, to Your Highness, prostrate at your knees. And indeed, now that I have completed the small work on the Psalms translated by Father Jerome from the Hebrew truth—a work over which I have laboured for years—I hope, God willing, to see you and to enjoy, even in passing, that conversation with you for which I so long.

## LETTER XLV. WILLIAM OF ELY TO HERBERT

WILLIAM, by God’s grace bishop of Ely, legate of the Apostolic See, and chancellor of the lord king, to his most beloved master H. DE BOSEHAM: greetings, and may he not lack remembrance of an absent friend.

[Col. 1474B] We received with a rejoicing heart the most welcome words of your consolation. They restored in us a stronger spirit amid your adversities, in proportion as we learned that you had overcome the misfortunes of temporal fortune more courageously. For who could have offered us such sweet consolation in so great a tempest of circumstance except one who knew the measure and outcome of that same circumstance? Thus the sweetness of your letter makes our mind cheerful, gives hope of recovery, and in great part moderates the matter for sorrow and sadness—that which has oppressed us, not through our deserts but through the envy of malicious men alone. For this we return to your affection such thanks as we can and are able.

Moreover, with God’s favour, we believe that he is soon to come whom we await, whom we desire, whose coming will bring us and all our friends joy in full measure—indeed, in the fullest measure. For his sake we count our endurance of such great and grievous sufferings more as glory than as loss [Col. 1474C]. Nor does your conscience weigh upon you, which we know to be sound, except only because such inhumanity, such excessive persecution and cruelty, committed against the lord king and ourselves, are so slow to reach their deserved end.

Further, you should know that we have earnestly desired that your discretion should complete the small work on the Psalms translated by Father Jerome from the Hebrew truth, so that nothing further might hinder us from enjoying your presence and the conversations we desire [Col. 1474D].

## LETTER XLVI. HERNULF, BISHOP OF LUXEUIL, TO THOMAS, EXILED ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

“Great [is] to me,” etc. It is found as no. 34 among the letters of Arnulf of Luxeuil, shortly to be published.

[Col. 1475]

# GLOSS ON THE PSALTER

[The gloss on the first part appears to have perished.]

# GLOSS ON THE SECOND AND THIRD PARTS OF THE PSALTER

## HERBERT’S PREFACE TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

[Col. 1475A]

Although the Book of Psalms is one book and not several, we have nevertheless divided it into two volumes—not, indeed, contrary to custom, but not without reason. We did the same also with the book of letters: though it too is only one book, we divided it into two, doing with books what is customarily done with burdens. For individual portions are more convenient and suitable for containing and handling than if everything were pressed together in a single volume. Moreover, such a partial division of books can at once and often be more useful for the reading of several persons [Col. 1476A].

Therefore, most blessed bishop, receive these four divisions together, but read them separately. And if your scribes set their hands to copying them, careful attention must be paid to placing the concordances and detached notes properly in their respective places, lest—as often happens—the work should be more difficult to correct than to copy through the incompetence or negligence of scribes, especially since the corrupter of a new work is none other than the brother of its destroyer.

[ALAN OF TEWKESBURY.]

[Col. 1475]

# LETTERS OF ALAN, PRIOR OF CANTERBURY AND AFTERWARDS ABBOT OF TEWKESBURY

## LETTER I. TO PHILIP, KING OF FRANCE

[Col. 1475B]

To PHILIP, by God’s grace illustrious king of the Franks: may increase of age bring increase of glory and grace before the Most High.

We neither ought nor wish ever, at any time, to be unmindful of Louis of pious memory, your father and our benefactor. Rather, as we are bound, it is our prayer and desire that we may in some measure repay his benefactions and honour, which he showed to the blessed martyr Thomas during his exile and, after his glorious victory, in person at Canterbury. Thus, as far as is now permitted, we pursue his soul with devout prayers, so that he who, while alive [Col. 1475C], fully earned this from the Church of Canterbury may now perceive the devotion of that martyr and his people to benefit him—he who proved so devoted to that martyr and his people in their tribulations and distresses.

In this matter too we are bound to Your Excellency: we are to be no less concerned for your salvation than for his. Clearly, he left to us, as to many others, your magnificence as heir to the advancement not only of his crown and kingdom but also of faith and devotion; so that [Col. 1476B], as he went before in a spirit of gentleness, directing those subject to him into the way of peace and tranquillity, so Your Serenity may follow his footsteps, adding what he himself also added: namely, that it pertains pre-eminently, by hereditary right, to the crown of royal dignity that all who are afflicted, and especially those exiled for righteousness’ sake, should find their highest refuge in him.

In this we too have conceived undoubted hope: if such necessity should nevertheless come upon us, we ought also, in our lowly station, to find with your clemency what our elders are said to have obtained in the same or a similar case. But when it pleases Your Royal Highness to make us more certain concerning these matters, then at last we shall be more firmly prepared to bring forward, more keenly and more strongly, that which some men threaten [Col. 1476C]. If, moreover, a reply from Your Sublimity concerning your favour in these matters should return to us, we believe and desire that it would bring us great—indeed the greatest—consolation amid the very distresses by which we are pressed.

## LETTER II. TO THE PRIOR OF WINCHESTER

ALAN, prior of Christ Church, Canterbury, to the prior of Winchester: the salvation which he wishes for himself.

[Col. 1477A] The affection of our mutual fellowship, by which long ago we were joined to one another in poverty itself, though tolerable poverty, certainly teaches us how we ought to live amid the very delights of this world and abundance of possessions. For, if one examines it more fully, one can plainly see how that lack of material resources then gave us knowledge of temporal abundance: we believed its possessors very happy, but now, when vanity has been stripped away and shaken off, they are plainly found empty and void.

What do you think, my friend, if you compare those former scholarly hardships with the anxieties we now endure? Will you call that bitterness more bitter than this honey which, in the heat and burning of these days’ tribulation, we now draw from thorns and briars? Then the day’s own evil was in some degree sufficient for the day [Col. 1477B]; but now the accumulation of miseries which arises from prosperity itself so increases its bitterness that life itself at times becomes wearisome. Thus, choked by anxiety and care, we bring upon ourselves in every way the loss of salvation, at the cost of time which cannot be recovered. Nor is there anything in which consolation is found without a graver danger. Wherever you turn, an obstacle to salvation meets you.

Having found these things in myself, anxiety of mind does not allow the movement of my thoughts to be secure until the day shall breathe upon us which the Lord will give for the consolation of us both, so that we may truly say of ourselves: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). I measure your tribulation by my own. Therefore I have undertaken thus far to speak to you as to myself, out of heartfelt affection, having no small wish and desire for fuller knowledge of the condition of the lord bishop and of yourself. For if anything moves in your conscience such that your friend ought to be moved on your behalf, you may entrust it to me as safely as to yourself, since my soul seeks your advancement altogether as it seeks my own. May my friend prosper and live in Christ.

## LETTER III. TO ARCHBISHOP BALDWIN

To the reverend father and lord B., by God’s grace archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all England, A., prior, and the convent of Christ Church, Canterbury: due and devout reverence in the Lord.

[Col. 1477D] We rejoice with you exceedingly in the Lord, whose mercy has stirred the royal excellency to become more ready to do what it knows is pleasing to your will. Therefore, if it please you, the opportunity offered should be used, lest, if the opportunity now at hand is neglected, repentance be too late if what may now readily and presently be accomplished cannot be done at another time.

The Church of Rochester, then, if it came to its senses, would surely acknowledge wherein it has offended. It remains for your discretion to apply its hand, so that what has been presumed to the detriment of the Church of Canterbury may be restored to its former condition of due honour. By ancient custom, the election of the Church of Rochester is customarily held in the chapter of the Church of Canterbury; and there the person elected customarily receives both spiritualities and temporalities from the hand of his archbishop, and consequently swears fealty. This was fully observed until the time of Waleran; and what was done otherwise in his case, when he returned from Normandy, where he had also been consecrated, was reformed for the better.

As a sign of this dignity, upon the death of its pastor the Church of Rochester must carry the pastoral staff to the Church of Canterbury and lay it upon Christ’s altar. This staff, however, having been secretly buried with Walter, formerly bishop of Rochester of good memory, and afterwards removed from there by the hand of Richard of pious memory, then archbishop, the monks of Rochester buried again with Bishop Waleran [Col. 1478B]. We therefore earnestly ask Your Fatherhood that Your Discretion may give attention to these and other matters, and restore what has been presumed, so that the whole body of sheep committed to you may, together with us, both ought and be able to glorify God in your works.

We add this concerning the bishop-elect of Llandaff: since he is the first to be consecrated by you, it would be pleasing and acceptable to us if his consecration could be celebrated in that see itself. But where necessity itself calls for a dispensation, it will be for your discretion to provide for it.

Further, concerning the translation of the blessed martyr Thomas and the date for it, something more definite ought to be determined, so that all nations desiring it may be informed how and when they may be able to come to the glory of that solemnity [Col. 1478C]. Since we are assailed from every direction and harassed by many distresses, and hope to have our principal refuge in your fatherhood, we shall, God granting, send our prior to your kindness as soon as possible. We earnestly entreat you to incline a more favourable ear to the matters which he shall present to you on his own behalf and ours.

Certainly, if in these times we are compelled by any persons to be humiliated under your authority, those who are accustomed to interpret even good things maliciously will be given a clearer opportunity to insult us. Moreover, unless he who has heaped insults on our head finds resistance, he will not cease from injuring the members [Col. 1478D]. He does you little honour who despises us, unless perhaps someone believes that even in this he is rendering you service. And undoubtedly, as we believe, it will contribute greatly to your reverence and honour if it appears from manifest signs that an injury inflicted upon the sons is wholly displeasing to their father. Farewell.

## LETTER IV. TO KING HENRY

To HENRY, king of the English, ALAN, prior of Christ Church, Canterbury: greetings.

How greatly the whole world desires with us that the body of the blessed martyr Thomas be placed in a more worthy place with due honour is known even to barbarian nations [Col. 1479A]. The untimely death of our former father Richard delayed this for a time, though we had long found your will more ready for this purpose. Now, however, by God’s grace, those things are prepared which the undertaking itself appeared chiefly to require—provided that it may accord with your good pleasure for so great a matter to be completed in the following year, about the middle of May.

[Note: [Col. 1479D] In the margin of manuscript C.C.C. is written: “The following year was 1182; but he was not translated until the year of the Lord 1208, by Stephen Langton.” In James’s transcript of the same manuscript, [Bodl. James 17, p. 134], this note occurs: “This year,” says the marginal note, “was 1182; but he was not translated until the year of the Lord 1208, by Stephen Langton.” But concerning his feast Gerald says as follows in the *Life of Baldwin*, to whom the same prior and convent also write concerning Thomas’s translation:

> When, at the first feast of Blessed Thomas publicly celebrated at Canterbury—two years, that is, having already elapsed after his martyrdom, at which feast, God granting, I myself was present—many barons of the kingdom had gathered there in pious devotion, the archbishop, after they had entered the chamber following their meal, complained in the common hearing of the officials and servants of the public authority, who had lately injured him and his people, more than usual, contrary to the dignity of his Church. He said and swore that he would in no way endure this; extending his hand also to his head, he confirmed by oath that he would expose it to swords before he endured it. But Hugh de Lacy, a noble and high-spirited man who had arrived with the others, answered: “There is no need, O archbishop, for you to put forward either your head or even your foot for this. You can safely defend your right and exercise ecclesiastical justice. God has done so much for the holy martyr, your predecessor, that the king would not find in all his land even a single ruffian who, even if he wished it, would dare raise his hand against you. The war is over. Maintain, if you wish, what the martyr won.”]

For many things must be prepared for its execution. It is also expedient that the time of this feast be announced in such a way to those who live farther away that they may more suitably arrive for it, as they desire. May it therefore please Your Serenity to make your will known to our lord and father Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury, and to us. For we await this: that by your counsel and aid our desire—or rather, the desire of all Christians—may in this respect be fulfilled [Col. 1479B]. Farewell.

## LETTER V. TO BENEDICT, ABBOT OF BURGH

To BENEDICT, abbot of Burgh, ALAN, prior of Christ Church, Canterbury: greetings.

Although he who presides, having been taken from among men, is appointed by the Lord for the correction of those subject to him, nevertheless, while he corrects the errors of others, he must look to himself, since he too is surrounded by weakness. And when it becomes known to him that he too is weak with the rest, he is thereby certainly admonished to sympathize with the weakness of others, learning by the teaching of punishment itself, in his own wounds, how he ought to treat those of others [Col. 1479C].

Therefore, divine providence did not wish anyone to be found free from weakness, so that no one might boast in what is more weak when set above the weak. Rather, he who is weighed down by his own burden should, humbled in himself, endeavour with more ardent affection humbly to bear the burdens of those subject to him; so that no one might boast that one who is himself weaker is set over the weak; and, when he sees another erring, remember that he himself has at some time erred.

A sheep of your flock erred and, wandering in the wilderness of solitude, had perished; but it has been found and is returning to the fold. Open the door to it, if you please, lest it err further and its error be imputed to him who refused to receive it when it returned from error. It does not excuse itself, but confesses that it has erred; it promises amendment and asks, not for judgment, but for mercy. Grant pardon and restore the afflicted man. Perhaps he fell in order to rise stronger [Col. 1480A], and he who trusted in himself beyond what was proper is being taught humility, lest he wander further. Thus, he who became unruly and unbridled will submit his hand to correction and become teachable, so that your pastoral care may rightly rejoice at his salvation, whose destruction it could and ought formerly to have lamented.

We have thought fit to write this to you, together with the earnest request and petition of our brethren, who certainly desire your honour, so that the tenor of this letter may make more fully known the affection by which, and the purpose for which, we are moved in this matter. And, if we remember rightly, we learned from your goodness’s teaching that the transgression and departure of the bearer of this letter had been wholly displeasing to your mercy. Farewell.

## LETTER VI. TO ROBERT DE HARDRES

[Col. 1480B]

ALAN, prior of Christ Church, Canterbury, to ROBERT de Hardres: greetings, and may he look to his future.

Divine grace has raised both you and me so far, and we have now reached such an age that, if we are wise, we ought henceforth to render fuller thanksgivings to him who has deigned to advance us both beyond what anyone of our lineage has dared to hope. Therefore we are bound to take more earnest care lest, marked by the stain of ingratitude, we should appear even to wish in any degree to assail our mother. At her breasts we grew up, and under the extremity of disgrace and deepest poverty we received such great consolation that we are preferred above so many and such great men—not by our merit, but through God’s grace—men whose birth, life, and conduct, if you consider them, would make us unworthy even to untie the strap of their sandal [Col. 1480C].

If, then, warned by him who gave an abundant end to covetousness, we do not impose an end upon it, we must certainly fear lest, our faults demanding it, we be permitted to wander so far that it may be said:

> Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity.  
> *(Ps. 51)*

And:

> Though he was in honour, he did not understand; therefore he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them.  
> *(Ps. 48)*

Remember moreover that when you die, you will not take all things with you, nor will your glory descend with you. Our life is brief and like a point. Therefore, if we lose what remains, may God avert it, who will restore to us on that day the losses both of age and of time [Col. 1481A]?

Furthermore, even if the complaint you put forward rested upon truth, and if you could recently prove that a right properly belonging to you was at issue here, you would sooner choose—if I gave you faithful counsel—to suspend such a complaint for a time than to trouble so many saints to whom you are bound by faith and devotion. But now, merely on the pretext of the roll of Winchester, you seek to bring our ancient possession back under your claim. In this, without doubt, so far as lies in you, you utterly overthrow the established order of the English Church by a destructive example. For if all rights of that antiquity are to be restored to their former condition in accordance with that roll, the charters and privileges of the whole English Church must necessarily be disturbed from their stability.

Indeed, if neither devotion to the saints nor love for our convent moves you [Col. 1481B], at least let this occur to you: do not let me be held suspect on account of your friendship with me, as though you were doing, with my consent, what you have begun. Be certain of this: while the vital breath endures in my body, so far as lies in me, my mother shall not lose even a foot’s breadth of all those possessions which I found at the time when the administration I now bear was entrusted to me—especially where she can defend and protect herself by right. And since until now I have preserved her rights whole and uninjured, I shall press vigorously lest, with you as author, my mother suffer diminution in any part of herself. Farewell.

## LETTER VII. TO BENEDICT, ABBOT OF BURGH

[Col. 1481C] To BENEDICT, abbot of Burgh, ALAN, prior of Christ Church, Canterbury: greetings, and may he know himself.

As Your Discretion knows more fully, it is one thing to correct and another to crush. Certainly, one who squeezes too hard sometimes draws blood itself; nor does he take good counsel for himself who multiplies losses through vehemence or obstinacy. Yet we do not say this because we wish to foster anyone’s error, but lest immoderate punishment should—or could—drive him for whom you are bound, by the obligation of nature and office, to provide, into the final reckoning of despair or error.

The Lord indeed chastens the one whom he loves; but does he hand over to death or assign to error the one whom he chastens? Certainly, one who receives a father’s blows ought not to be deprived of a mother’s breasts. And although our own flesh presents us with continual warfare [Col. 1481D], can you therefore cast it away? On the contrary, you are bound to provide it even with necessities. Thus, he who cannot achieve such a victory over himself ought not to be excessively troubled by another’s transgression. For he has in himself an example of how he ought to act toward his neighbour.

Moreover, although your brother has acted rather rashly up to now, he ought in some degree to have earned your favour in this: that he applied himself more diligently to study and discipline amid the straitness of his household, lest, together with losses of property, he should incur losses of time. He has not, then, squandered all his substance with harlots, since he has retained for himself not merely another part, but a much better part. But if you allow your brother to roam about and arrange loans at interest [Col. 1482A], then when it finally becomes necessary to provide for him, both his loss of goods will increase and his loss of time will not diminish. Indeed, without your authority he will be unable to pledge his income to anyone, because no one will lend him anything; and if he did so, he would be forced to beg again.

Allow yourself, therefore, if you please, to be defeated even once, so that your brother himself, since he is now of age, may be bound by your more abundant grace to conquer himself. The person addressed, and the friend by whom this is said, will be sufficiently clear to one who understands. Farewell.

## LETTER VIII. TO THE SAME PERSON

To BENEDICT, abbot of Burgh, ALAN, prior of Christ Church, Canterbury: greetings, and may he know himself.

[Col. 1482B] We have not thought fit to desist from what we began, although Your Belovedness’s severity, which appears to many less kindly than it should be, has thus far resisted our desire—and would that it had not resisted your honour. Certainly, where gentle discretion has persuaded this, severity must for a time be greatly relaxed, for the protection not only of conscience but also of reputation; lest, if we cast aside care for our own household, for whom we are surely bound to provide by natural obligation, we seem to have put off humanity and, so far as lies in us, annulled the force of nature’s laws. As for those who have no care for their own people, especially those of their household, you neither can nor ought to be ignorant of the Apostle’s judgment.

We wrote these things before, but have been so completely unheard that we have not deserved even to receive a reply; and for shame we should rather desist [Col. 1482C]. But undoubtedly affection conquered shame itself—the affection by which we are bound to stand by you and yours against every fortune, lest it seem to have been through us that the honour due to Your Fatherhood did not everywhere remain whole.

Indeed, your brother and ours in Christ, Richard, afflicts his soul in grief and distress and receives no even slight consolation within himself. He confesses his error, promises correction, and submits himself and his own affairs to your will. You desire him to become a monk; he agrees, provided only that there be no dispute over the place. He chooses the Church of Canterbury as the place of his dwelling and rest; so far as concerns us, entrance lies open. It remains, therefore, since this is expedient [Col. 1482D], that the lord archbishop’s assent be sought through you. If you please, bring together your household and friends in our church, that they may solicit us concerning this as though we were ignorant of it; and we shall do our part so that the matter may take effect.

Let the bearer of this letter also return before our synod with letters containing your will, so that through you we and your friends may be instructed how the matter ought to proceed. Nevertheless, if it seems good to you, it would be expedient for these things to be done through a suitable messenger sent on your behalf—or, what we desire more, through your own person, if it pleases you to come down to us for this purpose or to visit the lord archbishop. We believe that this too, if it could be done, would be beneficially advantageous to both you and us. With what affection and purpose we do these things [Col. 1483A], he who searches hearts himself knows. May Your Fatherhood, most dearly beloved by me, prosper in Christ.

## LETTER IX. JOHN, PRIOR OF ST SWITHUN’S, WINCHESTER, TO ALAN

To the lord and most dear friend in Christ, the venerable ALAN, prior of Canterbury, JOHN, called prior of the Church of St Swithun, Winchester, his own man: greetings in him who is the salvation of all.

At your letter of consolation, my spirit revived, and, drawing from it a double remedy, I returned thanks to your affection. From its unquestioned sincerity there flowed for me two lessons, in humility and patience. By your favour you have provided one for my protection and the other for the adornment of virtue: one warned me to shun proud Moab [Col. 1483B]; the other to put on stricken Job.

In my judgment, the chief possession of humility is the remembrance of former poverty. Even amid delights, it sings praise to their giver, whose providence is as praiseworthy as it is wonderful. For nothing makes the abundance of present things so ungrateful as failure to recognize one’s own condition and forgetfulness of the past. Meanwhile, nothing so strengthens the mind amid the storms of this life as embracing patience, which I should not without reason call the offspring of humility. And the offspring is no less good than its excellent mother.

You have therefore summoned your friend to the consideration of these virtues; you have roused one who was sluggish, more disturbed than concerned by our common shipwreck [Col. 1483C]. Whatever turmoil had settled upon my mind, whatever precipice of despair had threatened, the breeze of your consolation has so utterly driven it away that the day seemed to have breathed upon me and the shadow to have declined. What is more serene than the sincerity of words? What more effective than the consolation of a beloved lord? What more pleasant for one placed in the winepress of adversities than the promise of eternity as a shortcut through sorrow?

Thus “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed” in those saints “who are called according to the purpose,” as the Apostle says (Rom. 8). Therefore we must in no way murmur if the Lord cuts or burns, because whether we die or live, we are the Lord’s, through whom all things work together for our good. Only let faith not sleep and endurance not fail [Col. 1483D]. Let the memory of the saints flourish in your hearts. By their examples, indeed, the flesh with its desires and the world with its enticements are trodden underfoot. In short, whatever is brought against us is crushed.

And if there are those who disturb your Sabbath, it is nevertheless impossible that they should drive it away; and this has indeed been providently arranged, so that matter for struggle may never be lacking to those for whom the crown remains when they conquer. Let us therefore stand together in the Lord, keeping mutual love and patiently bearing the evil of these days. Let days pass, and days; years, and years:

> [Lacuna] God will give these also an end.

Certainly, what is an honour to me is a burden; yet I do not think it should be cast aside, since a man doing evil is said to be better than a woman sitting at home and spinning, and since we read that the faithful servant is to be set over much after being faithful in little [Col. 1484A]. Therefore, showing obedience to superiors and service to inferiors, and having peace with all, let us strive together, dearest lord, to keep the Sabbath of the heart; to drive away gnats coming from every quarter with the whip of discernment; and, if you please, to strengthen one another with frequent consolations of banquets.

My lord of Winchester, greeted by you through me, returns your greeting through me as to his most beloved friend. You should know that, by God’s action, he has improved and been strengthened in respect of both the health of soul and body; and that he is possessed by the utmost desire to visit the memorial of your blessed martyr Thomas. Farewell always in the Lord.

## LETTER X. ALAN TO THE ASS OF BURGH

[Col. 1484B]

To that ASS of St Peter of Burgh, from one like himself in the contest: greetings in the three razors—that is, patience, discernment, and charity—by which not only superfluities, but also all impending adversities, must be shaved away and uprooted.

O blessed Ass, if indeed beneath Peter’s garment—that is, purity of mind and performance of deed—you bear Christ in your body unto the disgrace of the cross, there, under the banner of faith, Nero’s savagery can harm you little. Let the malice of the envious rise for a time, to be sure, and let the storm of perversity swell more highly. Peter’s little boat is shaken, but even the gates of hell do not prevail against it; much less Nero’s audacity, even if Herod’s cunning should be renewed along with it [Col. 1484C].

It is clear, then, that Judas the traitor and Pilate the judge have been appointed even down to these times, and Nero too as heir of malice; so that Christ is now again demanded to be crucified, while those guilty of sedition and murder may be released. That Simon:
. . . . . still teaches magical arts under Nero. There are also those who follow his teaching; yet Peter has not timidly abandoned the she-ass of the synagogue or the colt of the Gentiles, but, with his own, presses on more vigorously, lest under the sword the liberty of the Spirit poured out in our hearts should perish.

Therefore, that as you run more nimbly in the race you may more swiftly and surely attain both your goal and the prize, with the razor of patience shave away utterly the unconsidered heats of the mind; hang in the rod of right direction under examination, and weigh carefully [Col. 1484D] what the rigour of law prescribes, what equity counsels, and what iniquity induces. Untie and break apart the bundles of ungodliness, so that justice itself may advance by means of you on a smoother road; and by its exceedingly sharp edge you may shave away whatever rust of conscience has adhered within, or whatever may occur without that needs examining amid uncertainties. But, wherever with a more fervent affection of charity you find hatred or envy, zeal and contention, immediately pull it out and cast it far away: so that you may be found ready for burdens of wheat, should the Lord ever have need of the ass; so that, when you have been led out of the bonds and fortress of tribulation in which you are held, binding your soul, the yoked she-ass, to the vine, and its colt, your untamed flesh, to the vineyard, you may wash your robe with Christ in wine, [Col. 1485A] and your cloak in the blood of grapes.

To you, therefore, as an ass, belong burden and rod: so that, if you grow slack beneath the burden, the rod of threatening may rouse you. Do not emulate the ass’s sluggishness, but its gentleness; for that Gentle One sits only upon the gentle. O how light is the yoke and sweet the burden which unloads the one who bears it, lifts up the one pressed down, and changes and turns sorrow into joy which no one shall take away! Willingly therefore endure, for a time, the senseless people to whom the power of darkness has been permitted, for the purification of those who will receive the inheritance of the children of God; so that they may walk about in a circle without rest, until the righteous man rejoices when he sees vengeance and washes his hands in the blood of sinners.

Come, good ass: be strengthened and be stout-hearted, and do not make fear your support, lest [Col. 1485B] you fear the face of those who exult in most evil things, whose joy is like mist and who descend to hell as swiftly as a point. A senseless man will not know, and a fool will not understand these things. Yet when sinners have sprung up and appeared like grass, so that they may perish for ever and ever, then at last the heart of the righteous will pour forth a good word: “Surely there is fruit for the righteous; surely there is a God judging them upon earth.” Meanwhile, it is fitting to await the salvation of God in silence and to walk simply in the paths of righteousness, because a man who enters upon two ways will have no rest. Therefore cast your care upon the Lord, and he will nourish you; nor, when you fall, will you be dashed down, while he himself places his hand beneath you. Do not therefore be weighed down by the burden laid upon you while you walk in [Col. 1485C] the straight path, because the Lord will not for ever permit the righteous to be shaken.

Therefore shave away the biting cares of mortals, together with their mother, ambition or avarice; do not give place to moth or rust in the chest of your conscience; and fear little lest thieves break in or steal the deposit of the crown laid up for you, because evil shall not approach you when the Most High is your refuge. Say these things to yourself and exhort yourself to them in Christ Jesus, with him as author and witness you shall possess your soul in patience. Amen.

Finally, you should believe that this exhortation concerns not so much instruction as the consolation of us both, since, by sharing with a single friend the inward distresses of mind which I suffer concerning the lot of us both, I may [Col. 1485D] more safely give them utterance at least in part; lest, if this bitterness swells further while my throat suppresses it, those with whom my belly is joined should be burst apart. Therefore I, your singular friend—as I believe you are mine—have spoken singularly to you, my singular friend, lest I seem to invent several friends out of the one true friend, scarcely found among so many thousands, according to the practice of the flattering tongue, which is accustomed to address to any one person whose favour it wishes to attract not singular but plural speech. Farewell!

## LETTER XI. TO JOHN, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS

To JOHN, by God’s grace Archbishop of Lyons, ALAN, prior of the Church of Canterbury, greeting.

[Col. 1486A] Among the children whom she has reared and exalted and who still survive, the holy Church of Canterbury, mother of the Britains, counts and regards the Archbishop of Lyons as pre-eminent. In her straits and disturbances, by which she is continually compelled to be afflicted, she has so often experienced this son’s faithfulness, devotion, and effective diligence that henceforth she is assured that so great a son cannot be forgetful of the sweetness which he long drew from his mother’s breasts, among which he also grew from the cradle.

Far be it, far be it from the faith and devotion of so great a foster-child—who has so often exposed himself to certain dangers in defence of his mother—that anyone should even suspect him of wishing to take the side of those who disturb the maternal womb from which they themselves have come forth, especially where a very slight occasion counsels an act [Col. 1486B] which, even if in some fashion it were lawful, is nevertheless less expedient, and is altogether unbecoming.

For although he in whose hands the highest affairs rest may, as it were lawfully, by the authority which he possesses, under a title still unknown and in some measure foreign to the form of the canons, not merely assign but rather transfer the benefice of the Church of Canterbury to a bishop of another province who is less needy, let the gracious discretion of a son consider whether it is expedient, to his mother’s confusion, to disturb the church of Eynsford from its due condition—a church unjustly taken away for so long and finally recovered through justice not without much labour and distress. Certainly, your mother did not apply that church to the pleasures of monks, but in pious affection assigned it to the uses of the poor.

[Col. 1486C] If, therefore, in the overthrow of Christ’s poor, whom she herself undertook to feed, the mother should happen to be more bitterly troubled by the son’s wrongdoing—may God avert it—what sort of fruit can arise from the root of such a tree? The prudent devotion of a son will judge more quickly if it chooses to consider this: the sole reason proposed for stripping Christ’s poor is that the very powerful son, passing over his mother, may, should that occur which can scarcely happen once in an age, possess a dwelling of his own where perhaps he will lay down his head apart from his mother for no more than one night. And certainly your pious mother has not yet emancipated your affection so far.

Nor does your reverence either wish or ought to refuse her whom it holds exceedingly dear and welcome admission into the more ready embraces of its mother’s breast, since it is her prayer and desire to see [Col. 1486D] that day on which, enjoying your presence and counsel, she may breathe somewhat from the distresses by which she is constrained. It is indeed no less necessary to consider what accords with your reputation, since what a man of such authority leaves as an example to posterity ought by right to acquire force for like cases.

But whether it be fitting for the Archbishop of Lyons, son and foster-child of the Church of Canterbury, to inflict such injury either upon his mother or upon Christ’s poor and sick for the acquisition of so slight a benefice and under such a title or intention, let the prudence of your holiness see and provide; for it concerns you to preserve unimpaired both your conscience before God and your reputation among men. Clearly, [Col. 1487A] we neither are ignorant of this nor fail fully to acknowledge that, through your merits and those of your people, we stand indebted to you. And although the question now under discussion between us has sunk into an abyss, we are nonetheless bound to assist those to whom you too are bound, whether by the debt of nature or by the favour of service.

Accordingly, that we may correspond in some measure both to your affection and to your work, we propose, as you please, to give yearly from our treasury one hundred shillings to one of your people, until we can otherwise provide for him in something of equal or greater value. Let us know, however, what you would wish done concerning this.

## LETTER XII. TO THE SAME PERSON

To JOHN, Archbishop of Lyons, A., prior of the Church of Canterbury, greeting.

[Col. 1487B] If the reverence of your holiness is most dear to me, this is because I act toward one to whom I am bound as a debtor; for, owing to the holiness and grace which are in you in common with the rest, and especially to that considerable generosity which I found in you when needy and a stranger, I am bound, to the extent of my power, to render to your honour service that is due and devoted. I am the more anxious in this matter if any opportunity could be given by which I might, in some degree, correspond to your kindness in accordance with the affection I bear.

But if this seems not to have been done in regard to the church of Eynsford, may your fatherhood forgive its son, if you please—provided, however, that in this respect I ought by right to be charged with negligence. For I am one and alone among many [Col. 1487C] whose will is various and diverse, as is their judgment, especially where that which they intend seems to rest upon law and reason. I speak to one who understands what it is to serve the habits of many. What grounds they advance for holding that what is claimed from them through you ought not to be done may more easily be considered after inspecting the tenor of our convent’s letters.

But if your prudence accepts the counsel of my littleness, I say with the sounder conscience that it is safer and more honourable either to come peacefully to an agreement with our convent in the manner communicated to you, or in another and more acceptable manner if one can be found, than to create scandal among the people and grieve your mother more than is supposed. Moreover, if the words of the lord king of England are to be believed, during his lifetime he will not permit [Col. 1487D] the Archbishop of Lyons to possess the church of Eynsford in any way. Let your discretion therefore provide, if you please, how the matter itself may more fully and better reach its proper end; and, so far as lies in me, there shall be no withdrawal from carrying it out. Farewell.

## LETTER XIII. TO MASTER G., CARDINAL

To Master G., cardinal, A., prior of Christ Church, Canterbury, greeting.

[Col. 1488A] We have greatly grieved, and grieve exceedingly, that in the tribulations and distresses by which we are pressed your affection, which we have been accustomed to find so useful and necessary in the Roman curia, is so far removed. And though distance of place separates us from one another, the affection of our hearts, by which we indivisibly cleave to your reverence, can in no way be separated from you.

Certainly, for your nephew in our parts we have done what we could, being the more anxious because in his case there has not been greater progress, as we desired. For, apart even from the affection by which we are bound to you, he himself has deserved in his own right, and daily deserves, that whoever sees his life and conduct should watch more affectionately over his advancement. May it therefore please [Col. 1488B] your fatherhood to look upon him with a more merciful eye, so that he may run more freely in the course in which he struggles and may come with a more eager spirit to advancement in the discipline to which he is devoted. So far as it lies in us and opportunity is afforded, we shall devote more ready care to his needs.

## LETTER XIV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

To the lord Archbishop of Canterbury, his own A., greeting.

We have learned that it has pleased your fatherhood that a man be appointed to the office of cellarer upon whom the votes of all of us converge together. Accordingly, as we are bound to do, we offer ample and heartfelt thanksgivings to your kindness for this. May it therefore please your graciousness to know that our common petition is that Brother Honorius, whom you surely know for the present from his manner of life, should undertake upon himself the weight of this office. [Col. 1488C] We have had some experience of his prudence, faithfulness, and compassion toward his brethren, and we hope not a little from his goodwill in respect of that office.

And although at present you cannot dispense with his service without inconvenience, experience has taught us that your prudence prefers to provide for public rather than private advantage. Therefore we request him more confidently, adding, however, that if in this matter we are in any degree troublesome concerning the appointment of one who ought to succeed him, it shall be done according to your will, as you please. We have therefore thought fit to send the bearer of this letter, our beloved brother in Christ R., the almoner, [Col. 1488D] on this business, so that by his presence, under the witness of our letter, he may obtain from you what your attention has been more earnestly inclined to seek jointly for the common benefit. Farewell.

Thus far I have given everything contained in the manuscript of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, comprising eighteen pages. Whether this manuscript once contained more leaves, containing other letters of Alan, is difficult to say.

[Col. 1487]

## TABLE OF THE LETTERS OF GILBERT FOLIOT, ARRANGED ACCORDING TO THEIR INITIAL LETTER

The letters contained in this volume under Gilbert’s name are partly Gilbert’s own, and partly other letters relating to the same history, namely either to Gilbert himself or to St Thomas. But a reader who wishes correctly to learn about the matters described in these letters must consult the letters of St Thomas, Arnulf of Lisieux, and John of Salisbury. Moreover, the source and foundation of this edition of Gilbert Foliot is that outstanding manuscript kept in the Bodleian Library under the shelfmark *e Mus. 249*, which contains about 440 letters. All of these are included either in this edition or in the other volumes mentioned above. This has been done because regard has been had to the author in the individual collections, not to the manuscript. We have thought it necessary to remind the reader of this repeatedly, lest our editions should be judged in some manner incomplete.

The table which follows explains the order of the letters.

The appended letters identify the manuscripts, and the numbers indicate the order of the letters occurring in those manuscripts. Fuller information concerning the manuscripts themselves is found in the table to the letters of St Thomas.

The first number, with no preceding letter, indicates the order in our edition.

A1, A2: Bodleian MS [Douce 287], divided into two parts. B: second Bodleian MS [509]. C1, C2, C3, C4: third Bodleian MS [937]. D: fourth Bodleian MS, donated by Cave [e Mus. 249]. E: letters of St Thomas edited by Lupus. F: letters of John of Salisbury, Paris edition. G: Lambeth manuscript. H: Paris MS [5320]. I: second Paris MS [5372]. K: third Paris MS [8562], letters of John of Salisbury. L: fourth Paris MS [8625], of the same John of Salisbury. M: British Museum, Cotton MS Claudius B. II. N: letters of Arnulf in the collection of St John Baptist’s, Oxford. O: Wharton’s *Anglia Sacra*. P: Cotton MS Vespasian E IV. Q: Bouquet, *Histoire de France*. R: Lambeth no. 577. S: Bodleian 603. T: Stapleton, *Three Thomases*. U: Arundel 27. V: Corpus Christi College, Cambridge MS. W: Trinity College, Cambridge MS, in five volumes. X: Bodleian MS 868. Y: Arundel 219. Z: Royal MS 2 D XXXII. # SECOND TABLE OF THE LETTERS OF ST THOMAS, ARRANGED ACCORDING TO LUPUS’S EDITION, WHICH IS DIVIDED INTO FIVE BOOKS

The first number indicates the order of the letters in Lupus’s edition; the second, our order. Where the letters A, GF, and JS are inserted, the letters of Arnulf, Gilbert Foliot, and John of Salisbury respectively must be understood. But because we have not yet published the letters of this John, it was altogether impossible to insert numbers. An asterisk indicates that a document is not correctly termed a letter and has therefore been placed among the historical documents in another book which we are publishing, *On the Life of St Thomas*.

# TABLE OF THE LETTERS OF ST THOMAS OF CANTERBURY, ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY BY INITIAL LETTER

Lupus’s edition of the letters of St Thomas of Canterbury, published at Brussels in 1682 in two quarto volumes, contains altogether 536 letters, among which about 110 have Arnulf of Lisieux and John of Salisbury as their authors. We have now entirely separated these from the letters of St Thomas: Arnulf’s, because we recently published all his works in volume 35 of this edition of the English Fathers of the Church; John of Salisbury’s, because, God willing, we shall shortly publish all his extant works as well.

About 426 remain, which we publish either in these volumes containing the letters of St Thomas or in those containing the letters of Gilbert Foliot. For we judged it better to divide these documents into two parts, because the Bodleian Library possesses letters so numerous and so substantial that they bear Gilbert Foliot’s name, and it seemed preferable to assign these a separate place and publish them in an edition of their own. For the same reason, whereas Lupus’s edition contains 426 letters apart from those of Arnulf and John of Salisbury, we shall now make public in this edition up to a thousand (!) letters, the greater part previously unpublished. How this has come about, and what resources we have used, will become clear to the reader from inspection of the following table.

A number without a prefixed letter indicates the sequence of letters observed in our edition.

A indicates manuscript 287 in the Douce Collection, preserved in the Bodleian Library. This book is divided into two parts. The first contains the *Life of St Thomas* by William fitzStephen and John of Salisbury, with a few letters interspersed—six or seven, perhaps no more—which we have indicated by smaller numbers followed by the letter (1). The second part (2) of the manuscript contains about ninety-three letters, more than thirty of which, hitherto unpublished, now appear for the first time either in these volumes or among the letters of Gilbert Foliot. This manuscript was written about the year 1200.

B indicates Bodleian manuscript 509, written about A.D. 1200. It contains eighty letters, together with other material not concerning the letters of St Thomas.

C indicates Bodleian manuscript 937, no more recent than the preceding manuscripts, a book of the greatest value; for it is almost an index for correctly arranging in relation to one another Alan’s little book on the *Life of St Thomas* and John of Salisbury’s treatise on the same subject. It contains about 600 letters, distributed in four parts; accordingly we have appended the figures 1, 2, 3, and 4, so that the reader may know in which part of the volume each letter is to be sought.

D indicates Bodleian manuscript e Mus. 249, which contains more than 400 letters. We publish not many of these in the present volumes, but shall publish by far the greater part in the other volumes mentioned above, which contain the letters of Gilbert Foliot.

E indicates Lupus’s edition, divided into five books. F indicates the letters of John of Salisbury, published at Paris in 1611. G indicates the Lambeth manuscript, of the thirteenth–fourteenth century, containing about 350 letters. H indicates Paris manuscript no. 5320. I indicates Paris manuscript no. 5372, which contains about 270 letters inserted into a *Life of St Thomas* by Roger of Crowland. K indicates Paris manuscript no. 8562, containing letters of John of Salisbury. L indicates Paris manuscript no. 8625, likewise containing letters of John of Salisbury. These two manuscripts contain the same letters as are included in the printed editions, and preserve the same order; but where one ends the other begins, and thus together they make up the same total number of letters. We shall see this more clearly hereafter, when we come to publish John of Salisbury. For the present, we have extracted very few letters from these manuscripts.

M indicates a magnificent manuscript, of inestimable value, preserved in the British Museum under the shelfmark Cotton Claudius B. II. This manuscript contains about 500 letters, divided into five books. Its arrangement is for the most part that of Lupus, with a few letters added; we have extracted all of these [Col. 1500] and now publish them. We have not supplied the numbers of many letters in this manuscript, because our edition, already supported by the aid of so many manuscripts, did not seem greatly to require the assistance of further books.

Q: Bouquet, *Histoire de France*. W: manuscript of Trinity College, Cambridge, in five volumes. X: Bodleian manuscript 868. AA: Vespasian F. XIII. EE: Galba A. III. FF: Galba A. IV.

# CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER OF THE LETTERS OF ST THOMAS, GILBERT FOLIOT, AND OTHERS

**Note.** Very many letters cannot possibly be arranged in chronological order. Most also have no connection whatever with the history of St Thomas. Nor may one boast that, in arranging even those letters which truly were written concerning St Thomas, the goal has always been attained; for this remains altogether difficult even after Baronius, Bouquet, and Froude. **GF** indicates the volumes containing Gilbert Foliot’s letters.

## HERBERT OF BOSEHAM, PRIVATE SECRETARY TO ST. THOMAS

Dedicatory epistle. 1068. Preface by J. A. Giles. 1069.

Epistle to Baldwin, Archbishop of Canterbury, and to his Catholic successors. 1073.
