# BOOK OF MELORUM
Prologue. 1293. FIRST MELODY.—On the visible and corresponding combat of the soldier with the similar combat of the emperor. 1293. SECOND MELODY.—On the concordance of the soldier’s visible palm of victory with the emperor’s visible palm of victory. 1302.—On the repentance of the sacrilegious soldiers. 1303.—On their death. 1304.—On the most Christian king of the Franks setting out abroad to visit the martyr. 1309.—On the illustrious king of the English being victorious through the martyr. 1310.—On the wrath of kings. 1313.—On the envoys sent by the king to the Roman Church after the martyrdom. 1314.—On the first dissension arising between the king the father and the king the son. 1315.—On the king’s first pilgrimage to the martyr, and the reason for that pilgrimage. 1315.—How the pilgrim king entered Canterbury. 1315.—That the king renounced those evil customs which had caused the exile and martyrdom. 1316.—Here he repeats that, throughout this history, he pursues truth, setting aside every favor of flattery and every fear. 1318.—How the king, returning from his pilgrimage, left Canterbury. 1319.—On the enemies whom the king swiftly defeated through the martyr after his pilgrimage. 1319.—On a dream prophetically shown to the martyr while still in exile, as a prophecy, as it were, of this rebellion and of peace. 1320.—That penitential perseverance is rare and difficult for kings. 1322.—Here he briefly repeats notes upon the preceding melody, in order to add further material. 1323. [Col. 1525]—Here he inserts an addition concerning the banner of the cross and the banner of the vessel, which are borne by the pilgrims of the soldier, just as that of the cross is borne by the pilgrims of the emperor. 1324.—First, on the mystery of the cross which the emperor’s pilgrims openly bear. 1325.—He begins mystically to adapt the sign of the soldier to the sign of the emperor. 1326.—On the mystery of the vessel borne by the martyr’s pilgrims. 1327.—He shows that the soldier’s sign and banner are mystical, just as are the emperor’s. 1329.—Why the cross is worn upon the breast. 1331.—Why the cross is fastened upon the shoulder. 1331.—Why the sign of the cross is always carried upright before the face of the Roman pontiff and likewise of metropolitan bishops. 1331. Why the soldier’s banner-bearing vessel, like the emperor’s banner, is openly borne upon the breast. 1332.—He briefly runs through what has been said at greater length concerning the correspondence of the signs, adding certain new points. 1334.—He briefly recapitulates what has preceded, intending to pass on to other matters. 1336.—On the pyxes formerly carried. 1337.—He tunes the lyre for the third melody. 1339.—He excuses the lengthiness of his words. 1342.

THIRD MELODY.—On the concordance of the soldier’s invisible palm of victory with the emperor’s invisible palm of victory. 1343.—That the soldier, like the emperor, has a double crown. 1343.—On the emperor’s first crown. 1344.—On the emperor’s second crown. 1344.—On the soldier’s twofold crown. 1345.—Here, first, the third melody begins to be formed upon the strings of the heart’s lyre set forth above. 1347.—He distinguishes three unities. 1348.—Here he first treats of the first and principal unity. 1349.—The first manifestation of the first and principal unity. 1349.—The second manifestation, through the governance of the Creator. 1354.—The third manifestation, through the eye of reason alone. 1356.—The fourth manifestation of the first unity. 1357.—The fifth and sixth manifestations. 1357.—The seventh manifestation. 1358.—The eighth manifestation. 1359.—How the first unity is manifested through the third eye, that of contemplation. 1360.—That there are two modes of manifestation through the third eye, that of contemplation. 1361.—First, on the mode of manifestation that occurs through Scripture. 1362.—The manifestation of the first and principal unity through the third eye, that of contemplation, in the third exemplar of life. 1366.—On that kind of manifestation called *Theophany*. 1369.—On the unity of grace alone, and first on its cause. 1373.—On the unity which has compassion upon humankind’s oppression and considers a means of deliverance. 1375.—On the judgment pronounced for humanity’s deliverance. 1376.—On the manner in which the pronounced judgment was executed, and on the executor himself. 1377.—On those who say that God became man in appearance (*habitu*). 1378.—On those who say that God became man in essence. 1379.—He distinguishes two unities in the assumed man. 1380.—On the manner in which the pronounced judgment was executed through the unity of grace alone. 1381.—Here the third melody ends, concerning the unity of grace alone; thereafter it will also sound forth concerning the unity of nature and grace. 1385.—Here the third melody clearly sounds forth concerning the unity of grace and nature; he first divides it into the militant and the triumphant unity, and first teaches concerning the militant. 1387.—He divides the militant unity into that common to all the righteous and that proper to the perfect, and first teaches concerning the common unity. 1389.—He fully treats, in the third melody now sounding clearly and openly concerning it, of that triumphant unity of nature and grace which is his principal subject. 1391.—Here he first inserts something concerning one name of the bridegroom, which serves to commend this third unity, but especially on the way. 1399.—On the name of the bride, which likewise serves to commend this third unity, but especially in the homeland. 1400. [Col. 1526]—That the bridegroom’s first name commends this third unity, but on the way; whereas the bride’s second name likewise commends it, but in the homeland. 1401.—On the bridegroom’s second name, which he does not have on the way but in the homeland, and how greatly this accords with the bride’s name in the homeland. 1401.

HOMILY on the feast of Saint Thomas. 1403. The cause of the exile and martyrdom of blessed Thomas of Canterbury. 1413.
